\section[{Source 14: Scope, contributions, and relation to the sources}]{Source 14. Scope, contributions, and relation to the sources}\label{gsr:fm:14:sec:d1}
\srcnote{14}{Section 1}
\partsource{\textbf{Added in the third write, 6~October 2026. Delivered title block.} ``Additive combinatorics / Sharp Extremal Refinements in Gowers's Szemer\'edi Framework / Secondary cube asymptotics, arrangement stability, and polynomial supersaturation / Prepared for Vladimir Reshetnikov / Research report prepared by ChatGPT / 6 October 2026''; \emph{the PDF author field reads ``ChatGPT, prepared for Vladimir Reshetnikov''}. Archive \file{gowers\_extremal\_refinements.zip} (arrival \texttt{d179062cc}), manuscript \file{gowers\_extremal\_refinements.tex} (2,767 lines, 37 pages), pin \texttt{9ea383e9b} (its \file{source\_manifest.json}). Printed below: the abstract, the title page's statement of principal conclusions and its closing note, and Section~1; Sections~2, 3, 6, 7 and Appendix~A are in Part~III, 4--5 in Part~II, 8--9 and Appendix~B in Part~V. Its macro \texttt{\textbackslash leanfile} is kept; its \texttt{\textbackslash repo} (unused) is dropped.}
\begin{partabstract}{14}
We study three local extremal problems suggested by Gowers's proof of
Szemer\'edi's theorem and its accompanying formalization.  First, for a
real mean-zero function $f$ on a finite abelian group of order coprime
to six, with $u=\|f\|_{U^3}$, we prove the uniform upper expansion
\[
 \|\delta+f\|_{U^3}^8
 \le \delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4
 +(9/4)^{1/3}\delta^{8/3}u^{16/3}
 +O(\delta^{7/3}u^{17/3}).
\]
The secondary coefficient is attained asymptotically by a precisely
tuned two-harmonic weight, and near attainment forces the same
amplitude, phase alignment, and Fourier concentration.  Additional
order-five resonances change the next extremal exponent from $16/3$
to $6$ on groups of exponent five.

Second, if a set of size $m$ supports at least $(1-\varepsilon)m^3$
respected pairs of congruent coordinate cubes, with
$0\le\varepsilon\le1/100$, it is within
$\tfrac12(1-\sqrt{1-4\varepsilon})m$ points of a unique product of
subgroup cosets.  An infinite family attains this error envelope.
We classify equality in the single-section collision bound, the
arrangement moment inequality, and their combination.  Geometric
defects give an explicit stronger denominator in higher arrangement
counts.

Third, for $k=2m\ge4$, characteristic $p>k$, and polynomial color
coordinates of degrees at most $D_\ell\le k$, put
$B=\sum_\ell\lceil D_\ell/2\rceil^2$.  The exact minimum number of
ordered nontrivial symmetrically colored $k$-term progressions on
$\mathbb F_q^d$ is
$q^d(q^{\max(d-B,0)}-1)$.  Equality forces a linear space of
directions at every center, and the first supercritical prime-field
dimension has a sharp gap.  Classical minimum-support theorems and
norm constructions are explicitly credited.  The conclusions refine
local components and solve specified finite extremal questions;
they do not supply a new global quantitative Szemer\'edi bound.
\end{partabstract}
\begin{quote}\small
\noindent\textbf{Three principal conclusions.}
The optimal secondary coefficient in the centered three-cube problem is
$(9/4)^{1/3}$; near-maximal congruent-cube collisions force a unique
nearby product of subgroup cosets with error
$(1-\sqrt{1-4\varepsilon})/2$; and the exact number of unavoidable
symmetric arithmetic progressions is determined for polynomial
colorings with specified low coordinate degrees.

\smallskip
\noindent Based on the supplied Gowers paper and the accompanying Lean development,
inspected at repository commit
\texttt{9ea383e9b28d885a936d5d681cd5584fffd2cb29}.
The report includes complete written proofs, exact finite certificates,
reproducible diagnostics, a source-to-theorem map, and a research agenda.
The results have not been externally peer reviewed or newly certified
by the Lean kernel; bibliographic priority is not asserted.
\end{quote}
\label{gsr:fm:14:sec:scope}

Gowers's proof \cite{gowers} makes repeated use of a productive
principle: a configuration count is controlled by a norm or moment,
and a sufficiently large value eventually yields algebraic structure.
The coarse estimate is often enough to finish the density-increment
argument.  This leaves several worthwhile local questions.  What is
the correct first or second term of an extremal count?  Which examples
attain a moment inequality?  How much structure survives near
equality?  Can an existence obstruction be upgraded to an exact
counting theorem?

This report gives three connected answers.  Its scope is the
precisely stated extremal models below.  Every main claim comes with
a written proof, including the finite-field support lemmas used in
the coloring application.  The supporting computations check
delicate finite identities and small equality cases; the general
claims rest on the proofs.

\subsection{What is strengthened}

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Three-cube counts.}
Gowers's Lemma~3.10 bounds the normalized number of $d$-cubes by
$(\delta+u)^{2^d}$, where $u$ is the normalized uniformity norm of
the balanced function.  Centering removes the apparent first-order
error when $d=3$.  Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:14:thm:secondary-exact} goes further:
it determines the optimal coefficient of the next fractional power
after the sharp quartic term.  Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:14:thm:secondary-rigidity}
identifies the associated extremizing Fourier geometry.

\item \textbf{Collision and arrangement counts.}
The moment step behind Lemmas~12.3 and~14.7 can retain the
cross-section profile $S=\sum_r|B_r|^3$.  Theorems
\ref{gsr:en:14:thm:energy-sharp-stability} and
\ref{gsr:en:14:thm:collision-sharp-stability} identify what almost saturating
that profile means.  Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:14:thm:joint-geometric-equality}
classifies simultaneous equality in the geometric and spectral
steps.  Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:14:eq:geometry-enhanced-lifting} improves the
moment denominator whenever a geometric defect is known.

\item \textbf{A related finite-field coloring question.}
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:14:thm:coloring-exact-supersaturation} determines an exact
minimum in a restricted but natural polynomial-coordinate model.
It strengthens an existence threshold to pointwise and global
supersaturation, with equality geometry and an arithmetic gap.
The symmetry condition is defined explicitly; it differs from the
monochromatic condition in Gowers's Corollary~8.3.
\end{enumerate}

An earlier project note \cite{comp14four} established the sharp
quartic cube coefficient $6\sqrt2$, exhibited the fractional
$u^{16/3}$ correction, and obtained an upper secondary coefficient
$6$ against a lower example $(9/4)^{1/3}$.  A separate project report
\cite{comp14ten} established the polynomial-coloring
dimension threshold.  The present report closes
the cube coefficient gap and determines the full minimum count
above the coloring threshold.  All prerequisites from those
unpublished reports that are needed here are reproved, so the proofs
can be read independently.

\subsection{Classical ingredients and limits of the comparison}

The real, centered comparison
$\|f\|_{U^3}^8\ge2\|f\|_{U^2}^8$ leads to a single Fourier pair
at leading order.  Our secondary problem measures a small violation
of that equality structure.  It is different from comparing a
Gowers norm to an $L^p$ or $L^\infty$ norm and classifying values
near their maximum; the latter is treated in depth by Eisner and
Tao \cite{eisnertao}.  We use elementary finite Fourier analysis
for the particular comparison needed here.

Near-maximal additive energy and proximity to a coset are classical.
For example, Proposition~1.1 in Sanders's survey
\cite{sanders} displays a conclusion with square-root loss in
the normalized energy defect.  The elementary disjoint-defect
count below yields the explicit envelope
$\tau(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon+\varepsilon^2+2\varepsilon^3+\cdots$
in a specified small-defect range, and then forces coordinate
splitting for cube collisions.  This is a comparison with that
displayed proposition, not a claim that no linear stability estimate
has appeared elsewhere.  Karam \cite{karam} discusses related
coset-approximation questions under different distributional
small-doubling hypotheses; those assumptions should not be
identified with ours.

Warning's second theorem \cite{warning,asgarli} supplies a
lower bound for a nonempty finite-field zero set from the sum of
degrees.  The equality case used here follows from the classical
minimum-weight Reed--Muller theorem, for which Leducq
\cite{leducq} gives a modern proof.  Odd norm layers already
occur in the symmetric-coloring construction of Shi and Dong
\cite{shidong}.  Our counting and rigidity conclusions combine
these ingredients after an exact reduction to odd Taylor
coefficients.  The ingredients themselves are not new results of
this report.

The local results must also be distinguished from an improvement
of the final density bound for long progressions.  For context,
Leng, Sah, and Sawhney \cite{lssbounds} obtained, for every
$k\ge5$, a bound of the form
\[
 r_k(N)\ll_k N\exp\bigl(-(\log\log N)^{c_k}\bigr),
 \qquad c_k>0,
\]
where $r_k(N)$ is the largest size of a subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$
with no nontrivial $k$-term arithmetic progression.  No new bound
for $r_k(N)$ is derived here.  The research questions at the end
identify which additional bridges would be needed to turn the
local gains into a global improvement.

\subsection{Conventions that matter}

There are two different kinds of cube in this report.
A three-dimensional \emph{additive cube} in one abelian group has
parameters $(x,h_1,h_2,h_3)\in G^4$ and eight vertices
$x+\omega_1h_1+\omega_2h_2+\omega_3h_3$.  Its normalized weighted
count is $Q_3(W)$.  An \emph{axis-parallel coordinate cube} in
$G_1\times\cdots\times G_k$ has a base $x$ and a vector of
coordinate sidelengths $h$; its vertices choose either $x_i$
or $x_i+h_i$ in each coordinate.  Congruent pairs of these cubes
are counted by $Q_\phi(A)$.  The distinction prevents a mistaken
identification of their parameter spaces or normalizations.

All averages $\mathbb E$ are uniform probability averages.
Fourier transforms in the cube section are normalized by $|G|^{-1}$.
The arrangement section explicitly uses an unnormalized transform,
with the compensating $|R\times K|^{-1}$ in its moment formula.
All combinatorial counts are counts of ordered parameter tuples.
Zero sidelengths and repeated cube vertices are included.
Nontrivial arithmetic progressions in the coloring section have
nonzero direction, and their points are distinct under $p>k$.

The constant in $O_\delta(\cdot)$ may depend on a fixed density
$\delta$.  An unadorned $O(\cdot)$ in the normalized cube proof
has an absolute constant, independent of both the group and the
function.  The restrictions on order or characteristic are part
of each statement and are not silently omitted in applications.

\subsection{An explicit translation back to Lemma 3.10}
\label{gsr:fm:14:sec:uniformity-translation}

Let $A\subset\mathbb Z_N$, let $\delta=|A|/N>0$, assume
$\gcd(N,6)=1$, and write $f=1_A-\delta$.  In the normalization
of the paper and the inspected Lean statement, degree-two
$\alpha$-uniformity means
$\|f\|_{U^3}^8\le\alpha$.  Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:14:thm:secondary-exact}
therefore gives, whenever $\alpha^{1/8}\le c\delta$,
\begin{align}
 \#\{\text{three-cubes in }A\}
 \le N^4\Bigl(&\delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4\alpha^{1/2}
       +(9/4)^{1/3}\delta^{8/3}\alpha^{2/3}\notag\\
       &+C\delta^{7/3}\alpha^{17/24}\Bigr).
 \label{gsr:fm:14:eq:alpha-improved-cube}
\end{align}
The passage from the actual norm to its budget uses monotonicity
of the positive powers in the upper bound.  At fixed positive
density, the error begins at $\alpha^{1/2}$, whereas expanding
the bound in Lemma~3.10 begins at $\alpha^{1/8}$.  The sharper
statement uses the additional mean-zero, real-valued, and
coprime-order structure specified above.  Its optimal secondary
constant is meaningful asymptotically; it is not a claim that
the displayed truncated expression without its remainder is a
finite-parameter bound.

\section[{Source 15: Results, scope, and the source discrepancy}]{Source 15. Results, scope, and the source discrepancy}\label{gsr:fm:15:sec:d1}\label{gsr:fm:15:sec:intro}
\srcnote{15}{Section 1}
\partsource{\textbf{Added in the fourth write, 6~October 2026. Delivered title block.} ``Collision-Sensitive Amplification of Respected Arrangements / Sharp refinements of Gowers's Lemma 14.7, coupled product-property bounds, and Cartesian stability / Research manuscript prepared for Vladimir Reshetnikov / 6 October 2026''; the PDF author field reads ``Research manuscript prepared for Vladimir Reshetnikov'' and the running head ``Research manuscript''. Archive \file{collision\_sensitive\_arrangements.zip} (arrival \texttt{212999d4b}), manuscript \file{collision\_sensitive\_arrangements.tex} (1,752 lines, 27 pages), pin \texttt{9ea383e9b} (its \file{provenance.json}, shipped as \file{data/15-collision-amplification-provenance.json}). Printed below: the abstract and Section~1; Sections~2--12 form a chapter of Part~II (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:collision}), Sections~13--15 and Appendices~A--B are in Part~V.}
\begin{partabstract}{15}
We retain the exact collision count that is discarded in the second-moment
estimate of Gowers's arrangement-amplification argument. If $R_d$ counts
ordered respected $d$-arrangements and $C=R_1$, then
$R_d C^{d-2}\ge R_2^{d-1}$ for every integer $d\ge2$.
The collision count satisfies the sharper geometric bound
$C\le\sum_x |B_x|^3$, giving sharp density-sensitive versions of Lemma 14.7.
More substantially, retaining the same parameter in the preceding
product-property step gives $a_2\ge\gamma^{8\cdot2^k}\chi^4$ and hence
$a_d\ge\gamma^{8(d-1)2^k}\chi^{3d-2}$, in normalized notation.
For eight-arrangements this yields
$\beta^{22\cdot4^k}\gamma^{44k4^k+56\cdot2^k}$, strengthening the
repository's corrected product-property bound. We also characterize equality
in the cubic collision bound and prove an explicit dimension-free stability
result: a set with at least $(1-\varepsilon)|A|^3$ parallel axis-cube pairs is
within $18\varepsilon|A|$ points of a Cartesian coset when
$\varepsilon\le1/100$. Further results include spectral stability,
side-vector refinements, weighted extensions, sharp examples, and an
integration plan for the supplied Lean development. All new assertions are
proved in ordinary mathematics; finite tests are supplied separately.
No improvement to a final Szemer\'edi bound, independently checked Lean
formalization, or literature-priority claim is made.
\end{partabstract}

Gowers's Section 14 converts a supply of respected pairs of
parallelepipeds into a supply of longer respected arrangements. The relevant
analytic step is a moment interpolation, while its quantitative input comes
from a weighted simultaneous-additivity property. These two steps share a
natural intermediate parameter. Eliminating it independently in each step
loses information. This manuscript instead keeps that parameter until the
steps have been combined.

The source comparison uses the paper \cite{gowers} and the supplied ProveIt
files at commit \shorthash\ \cite{repo15,repo15defs,repo15moments,repo15product}.
The finite cyclic notation in the paper is generalized here to arbitrary
finite abelian coordinate groups and an arbitrary finite abelian value group.
Every count is ordered and allows repeated vertices. These conventions are
essential to the exact identities.

\subsection{Three levels of improvement}
Write $R_d$ for the respected $d$-arrangement count, $C=R_1$ for the
collision count, and $B_x$ for a horizontal fibre. The first improvement is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:15:eq:introexact}
 R_8\ge \frac{R_2^7}{C^6}
 \ge \frac{R_2^7}{\bigl(\sum_x |B_x|^3\bigr)^6}.
\end{equation}
The first inequality is the exact form of the interpolation already underlying
the paper; the second retains the geometry of the domain instead of replacing
it by the entire ambient space. The constant is sharp.

The second improvement couples this interpolation to the preceding
product-property argument. For horizontal ambient size $M$, vertical size $n$,
and density $\beta=|B|/(Mn)$, set
\[
 a_d=\frac{R_d}{M^{2d+1}n^{2d-1}},\qquad
 \chi=\frac{C}{M^3n}.
\]
Under the product property with parameter $\gamma$, we prove
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:15:eq:introcoupled}
 a_d\ge\gamma^{8(d-1)2^k}\chi^{3d-2}
 \ge
 \beta^{(3d-2)4^k}
 \gamma^{(6d-4)k4^k+8(d-1)2^k}.
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:15:eq:intro8}
 \boxed{a_8\ge
 \beta^{22\cdot4^k}\gamma^{44k4^k+56\cdot2^k}.}
\end{equation}
Section~\ref{gsr:en:15:sec:product} supplies the complete proof, including the
configuration-count input. No inverse theorem or unproved catalogue
statement is assumed in that proof.

The third improvement is structural. For $A\subseteq G_1\times\cdots\times G_k$,
let $Q(A)$ be the number of pairs of contained axis cubes with the same side
vector. We prove
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:15:eq:introstability}
 Q(A)\ge(1-\varepsilon)|A|^3,
 \quad 0\le\varepsilon\le\frac1{100}
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 |A\symdiff(c+H_1\times\cdots\times H_k)|\le18\varepsilon|A|.
\end{equation}
The constant does not depend on the number or sizes of the coordinate groups.
The linear order in $\varepsilon$ cannot be improved uniformly to
$o(\varepsilon)$. This answers the specific near-extremal Cartesian inverse
question formulated by the left-hand side of \eqref{gsr:fm:15:eq:introstability}.
It is a near-maximal-energy theorem, not a sparse inverse theorem.

\subsection{The printed and corrected product-property exponents}
A source-fidelity issue materially changes the comparison. The printed
Corollary 14.6 uses $k4^{k+1}$ as the exponent of $\gamma$.
The supplied definition file explicitly records that its proof only gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:15:eq:correctedgamma}
 E_k=2k4^{k+1}+8\cdot2^k,
\end{equation}
and adopts the safe weakening $3k4^{k+1}$ for $k\ge1$ and
$0<\gamma\le1$. Its Lemma 14.8 therefore has exponent
$21k4^{k+1}$, rather than the printed $7k4^{k+1}$
\cite{repo15defs,repo15product}. We reproduce the unweakened exponent
\eqref{gsr:fm:15:eq:correctedgamma} below and use the corrected statement as the
benchmark. The discrepancy was already documented in the repository; it is
not a discovery claimed by this manuscript.

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{Formal status understated (checked at HEAD \texttt{0b4890a1c}, unchanged since the pin).} The unweakened exponent \eqref{gsr:fm:15:eq:correctedgamma} is not only documented: it is the conclusion of the private, kernel-checked lemma \file{cor146_direct_lower} (\file{Proofs14Arrangements.lean}, line~759), which proves $\beta^{4^{k+1}}\gamma^{2k4^{k+1}+8\cdot2^k}N^{5k+3}\le R_2$ from the fourth-moment bound of \file{cor146_average_fourth_moment}. The public \file{corollary_14_6_holds} (line~838) obtains it and only then weakens it to $3k4^{k+1}$ through the private \file{cor146_gamma_exponent_le} (line~817). So the corrected exponent $2k4^{k+1}+8\cdot2^k$ is a proof-level fact of the formal development; the public statement \file{corollary_14_6} (\file{Sections14\_15.lean}, line~266) has the weakened $3k4^{k+1}$, and \file{lemma_14_8} (line~292) the resulting $21k4^{k+1}$.
\end{writenote}


Consequently, \eqref{gsr:fm:15:eq:intro8} strengthens the \emph{corrected, supported}
product-property bound. It must not be described as proving the smaller
unsupported printed $\gamma$ exponent. Lemma 14.7 itself has no such
exponent issue, and its refinement \eqref{gsr:fm:15:eq:introexact} is unconditional.

\subsection{What is, and is not, claimed}
The proofs below establish the displayed finite theorems. The Fourier
identities, interpolation mechanism, and configuration induction are
established ingredients, not new methods. The contribution developed here is
the parameter-retaining combination, its sharp density refinements, and the
explicit quantitative Cartesian analysis. A targeted literature check does
not establish priority over all existing work on additive energy,
near-extremizers, or product-space inequalities.

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{Credit and novelty within this report.} The pin \texttt{9ea383e9b} (13:35 on 6~October 2026) predates the placement of sources~01--14 in this directory, so this source could see neither source~04 nor source~14; its results are independent. In this report, however, two of the three contributions named above are not new. The density-sensitive interpolation \eqref{gsr:fm:15:eq:introexact} with the cubic cap and the balanced factor is source~04's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:04:mom:arrangements}, displays (A5)--(A11). The ``explicit quantitative Cartesian analysis'' is superseded by source~14's Section~\ref{gsr:en:14:sec:d4}: under the same hypothesis $Q(A)\ge(1-\varepsilon)|A|^3$, $\varepsilon\le1/100$, source~14's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:14:thm:collision-sharp-stability} gives a unique closest product coset at distance at most $\tau(\varepsilon)|A|$, $\tau(\varepsilon)=(1-\sqrt{1-4\varepsilon})/2\le1.0102\,\varepsilon$, in place of $18\varepsilon|A|$ (note after Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:15:thm:stability}). New in this report: the collision-parametrized product step and the coupled bounds (Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:15:thm:PPcollision} and~\ref{gsr:en:15:thm:coupled}), the automatic weak parameter (Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:15:lem:weakPP}), the band and profile results (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:15:cor:band}, Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:15:prop:profile}, Example~\ref{gsr:en:15:ex:diagonal}) and the vertex weights (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:15:thm:weighted}). The sentence ``This answers the specific near-extremal Cartesian inverse question'' above refers to the source's own formulation; source~14 answers it with the sharp constant.
\end{writenote}


These are local improvements within an older proof architecture. For
comparison, Leng, Sah, and Sawhney prove for $\ell\ge5$ the global estimate
$r_\ell(N)\ll N\exp(- (\log\log N)^{c_\ell})$ \cite{lssbounds}.
We do not propagate the present changes through every later extraction,
recurrence, and density-increment step, and claim no improvement to that or
any other final Szemer\'edi estimate.

\section[{Source 16: Scope, source comparison, and principal results}]{Source 16. Scope, source comparison, and principal results}\label{gsr:fm:16:sec:d1}\label{gsr:fm:16:sec:intro}
\srcnote{16}{Section 1}
\partsource{\textbf{Added in the fourth write, 6~October 2026. Delivered title block.} ``Local Phase Removal Without Carry Patterns / and further quantitative refinements of Gowers' proof of Szemer\'edi's theorem / Research report prepared for Vladimir Reshetnikov / 6 October 2026''; the same in the PDF author field. Archive \file{Gowers\_Localization\_and\_Quantitative\_Refinements.zip} (arrival \texttt{99f28708e}), manuscript \file{Gowers\_Localization\_and\_Quantitative\_Refinements.tex} (2,127 lines, 30 pages), pin \texttt{dca9f0638} (its delivery README and Section~1). Printed below: the abstract and Section~1; Sections~2--5 form a chapter of Part~IV (Section~\ref{gsr:fp:sec:windows}), Sections~6--7 are in Part~I, Section~8 in Part~III, Sections~9--12 and Appendix~A in Part~V. Its macros \texttt{\textbackslash conj} and \texttt{\textbackslash BB} are renamed \texttt{\textbackslash conjsixteen} and \texttt{\textbackslash BBsixteen} (the report's own have other meanings); its equation numbers are delivered as explicit tags $(k.j)$ and are kept, so they print as delivered.}
\begin{partabstract}{16}
We give three families of local refinements of the arguments in Gowers'
2001 proof of Szemer\'edi's theorem. The principal result replaces the
carry-pattern decomposition in Proposition~17.7 by a finite family of
sliding interval windows. The resulting relative
uniformity factor is
\[
 \alpha\left(\frac{4}{3(k+2)}\right)^{k+2},
\]
in place of the displayed factor \(2^{-2(k+1)^3}\alpha\). We retain an
exact partition and the required minimum cell length, and give an
explicit upper cell length \(3km\). A more precise finite formula admits
a width optimization whose fixed-dimension limiting coefficient is
\((2/(k+2))^{k+2}\). A local-scale obstruction proves that the leading
logarithmic loss \(k\log k\) is optimal. We also give a version that preserves the
original smaller cell scale, replacing a squared carry-count loss by
an active-pattern count times a global count.

Second, we construct exact partitions on which affine frequencies are
small after multiplication by each cell's own step. An elementary
certificate theorem, combined with a precisely cited simultaneous
quadratic recurrence theorem, yields every balanced exponent
\(\gamma<((q+1)(42q+1))^{-1}\). A matching problem is formulated through a
rigorous obstruction \(\gamma\le(3q+1)^{-1}\), leaving a substantial
and explicit gap. Third, we compute the fourth-order coefficient of
centered cubes in every dimension and the fifth-order coefficient over
odd-order groups, including the first additional \(3\)-torsion term in
dimension four. The resulting error exponent $4/2^d$ is proved optimal
even for genuine sets of exact density $1/3$ in odd cyclic groups.

All new assertions are supplied with proofs. Exact combinatorial and
rational computations, and a separate numerical localization check,
are included for reproducibility. The modern recurrence estimate is an
external input. Historical priority of the formulations developed here
is not asserted, and the results do not establish a new global
Szemer\'edi bound or a Lean formalization of these refinements.
\end{partabstract}

The target is a collection of concrete, verifiable improvements to local
arguments in \cite{gowers}, rather than a claim that the full
quantitative Szemer\'edi problem has been settled. The distinction matters:
a substantial improvement at one stage may be numerically dominated by a
different stage, or may change a scale that must be transported through
the induction.

The source repository was inspected at commit
\[
\texttt{dca9f06383ccdfc2ed208ccb7c9882214fdb09ac}.
\]
We used its paper transcription, its Section~17 and Section~13 Lean
interfaces, its formalization status, and its existing local-refinements
article \cite{repo16}. The existing research already covers numerous
three-dimensional cube estimates, density-selection inequalities,
Freiman restrictions, and carry-pattern counts. The present work
concentrates on a different localization argument, direct control of
moving frequencies on their own steps, and coefficients for cubes of
arbitrary dimension.

\subsection{A strengthened local phase-removal theorem}

Let \(N\) be prime, let \(f:\Z/N\Z\to\C\) be bounded in modulus by one, and
let
\[
 P=\prod_{i=1}^k(r_i+d[-h,h]),\qquad m=2h+1,\qquad m^2\le N,
\]
where \(d\ne0\). For a \(k\)-tuple \(a\), write
\[
 \Delta(f;a)(s)=\prod_{\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^k}
       \conjsixteen^{|\epsilon|}f(s-\epsilon\cdot a),
 \qquad
 \widehat u(r)=\sum_s u(s)e_N(-rs),
 \quad e_N(t)=e^{2\pi it/N}.
\]
A polynomial is called \emph{multi-affine} if its degree in each variable
is at most one. This includes the affine lower-degree terms that occur
after translating a multilinear expression.

\begin{theorem}[Main phase-removal consequence]\label{gsr:fm:16:thm:mainphase}
Suppose \(k\ge1\), \(\alpha>0\), and \(\sigma\) is the restriction to
\(P\) of a multi-affine polynomial over \(\F_N\). If
\[
 \sum_{a\in P}\abs{\widehat{\Delta(f;a)}(\sigma(a))}^2
       \ge \alpha N^2m^k,
 \tag{1.1}\label{gsr:fm:16:eq:introinput}
\]
then there are a polynomial \(\phi\in\F_N[X]\) of degree at most \(k+1\),
an integer \(l\ge1\), and a partition \(\mathcal Q\) of \(\Z/N\Z\) into
proper modular arithmetic progressions, all of cardinality \(l\) or
\(l+1\), such that
\[
 l\ge\frac{m}{3k}
 \quad\hbox{and}\quad
 \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{Q\in\mathcal Q}
          \Cube_{k+1}(\ind_Q f e_N(-\phi))}
      {\displaystyle|\mathcal Q|(l+1)^{k+2}}
       >\alpha\left(\frac{4}{3(k+2)}\right)^{k+2}.
 \tag{1.2}\label{gsr:fm:16:eq:introoutput}
\]
Here
\(\Cube_j(u)=N^{j+1}\norm{u}_{U^j}^{2^j}\)
is the unnormalized \(j\)-cube form.
When \(m>3k\), the construction gives the stronger lower bound
\(l\ge m/3\), and \(l+1\le3km\).
\end{theorem}

The proof occupies Sections~\ref{gsr:fp:16:sec:polarization}--\ref{gsr:fp:16:sec:windows}.
It changes the geometry of the intermediate cells. Gowers' proof
uses relatively short cells and counts all the ways a cube can cross
their boundaries; we average windows that contain the entire cube and count their
coverage multiplicity exactly.
The upper size \(3km\) is therefore part of the result and part of any
downstream accounting.

The quantity in \eqref{gsr:fm:16:eq:introoutput} is precisely the relevant
partition-uniformity quotient with upper size \(l+1\). Thus the strict
inequality states failure of uniformity at the displayed factor.
The comparison with Proposition~17.7 of \cite{gowers} is at this
explicit normalization, rather than at an unstated choice of cell size.

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:16:thm:mainphase} strengthens a statement that is already formal} (checked at HEAD \texttt{0b4890a1c}; the source does not say so). Proposition~17.7 is \file{proposition_17_7} (\file{Sections17\_18.lean}, line~140) with the exact companion \file{proposition_17_7_holds} (\file{Proofs17LocalizedPhaseRemoval.lean}, line~2900, proved since \texttt{e336d1b3a}, 24~August 2026, and present at the pin). Its hypotheses are those of the theorem here: $N$ prime, $0<\alpha$, $0<k$, $m$ odd with $m\le\sqrt N$, a box of width $m$ with nonzero common difference, a multilinear $\sigma$, and $\alpha N^2m^k$ at most the sum of the squared Fourier coefficients (with \texttt{cubeDifference} and \texttt{fourier} the conventions here). Its conclusion is a polynomial phase of degree at most $k+1$ and a partition into proper modular progressions of lengths $l$ or $l+1$ with $m/(3k)\le l$ on which \file{UniformOnPartition} (line~132), normalized by $(l+1)^{k+2}$, fails at $2^{-2(k+1)^3}\alpha$; that is exactly \eqref{gsr:fm:16:eq:introoutput} with a smaller constant. Since $c_k=(4/(3(k+2)))^{k+2}>2^{-2(k+1)^3}$ for every $k\ge1$ (proof at the write: $\log_2(3(k+2)/4)<k+2$, so $\log_2(1/c_k)<(k+2)^2\le2(k+1)^3$), the theorem implies the formal statement, with a far better constant ($29.07$ against $1{,}458$ lost bits at $k=8$; Section~\ref{gsr:fp:sec:windows}). It is a drop-in strengthening of a proved statement; it is not formalized. The output bound $l+1\le3km$ is information the formal statement does not ask for. Under the printed reading of the cell size as ``at most $m$'' (source~04's), these cells are too long; the formal statement and source~06 use the $(l+1)$ normalization, as Section~18 does. No formal declaration consumes \file{proposition_17_7} (\file{theorem_18_1} is open).
\end{writenote}


\subsection{Direct control of the step}

For affine frequencies \(A_i n+B_i\in\R/\Z\), we construct a partition
of \(\{0,\ldots,R-1\}\) into progressions \(Q\) satisfying
\[
 \norm{(A_i n+B_i)d_Q}_{\T}\le\delta_i\qquad(n\in Q),
 \tag{1.3}\label{gsr:fm:16:eq:ownstepintro}
\]
where \(d_Q\) is the actual positive integer step of \(Q\).
The elementary theorem is driven by a checkable simultaneous quadratic
recurrence certificate. Combining it with \cite[Theorem~1.1]{lau}
gives, for every fixed \(q\),
\[
 |Q|\in[\lceil R^\gamma\rceil,2\lceil R^\gamma\rceil-1],
 \qquad
 \delta_i=R^{-\gamma},
 \qquad
 0<\gamma<\frac1{(q+1)(42q+1)},
 \tag{1.4}\label{gsr:fm:16:eq:introexponent}
\]
for all sufficiently large \(R\), uniformly in the coefficients.
The threshold is not numerically explicit, because the cited recurrence
theorem does not provide a numerical threshold. The certificate version
has no such hidden existence condition.

A probabilistic obstruction proves that a universal full-partition
statement with the same balanced powers must have
\(\gamma\le1/(3q+1)\). This produces a well-defined optimization problem
rather than an unsupported optimality claim.

\subsection{Arbitrary-dimensional cube coefficients}

For \(d\ge2\) and real centered \(f\) on a finite abelian group, let
\[
 \mathcal Q_d(\delta+t f)=
 \E_{x,h_1,\ldots,h_d}\prod_{\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^d}
                  (\delta+t f(x+\epsilon\cdot h)).
\]
The first three nonconstant coefficients vanish. The fourth coefficient
is determined by
\[
 P_d=\frac{6^d-2\cdot4^d+2^d}{8},
 \qquad
 T_d=\frac{8^d-3\cdot6^d+3\cdot4^d-2^d}{24}.
 \tag{1.5}\label{gsr:fm:16:eq:introPT}
\]
It equals \(\delta^{2^d-4}(P_d Q(f)+T_d Q_2(f))\), where
\(Q(f)=\norm f_{U^2}^4\) and \(Q_2\) is its nontrivial order-two
Fourier contribution. Section~\ref{gsr:cc:16:sec:cubes} proves this statement and
a fifth-order formula with a further order-three term over odd-order
groups.

The claims in this article have three different dependencies.

Result & Dependence & Quantitative status\\

\srcnote{17}{Section 1}
\partsource{\textbf{Added in the fourth write, 6~October 2026. Delivered title block.} ``Polynomial-loss restriction in Gowers's Szemer\'edi argument / Fej\'er filters, density-sensitive moments, and finite-field systems / Research note prepared for the ProveIt project / 6 October 2026''; the same in the PDF author field; running head ``Polynomial-loss restriction / Gowers's Section 9 and beyond''. \begin{partabstract}{17}
We give a quantitative replacement for the random-restriction step in
Section 9 of Gowers's 2001 proof of Szemer\'edi's theorem.  A single
normalized Fej\'er kernel replaces a long product of low-degree cosine
filters.  For a balanced relation with $m=2r\ge4$ variables, the method
retains at least
\[
 \frac{\alpha^m\eta^{m-1}}{2(m+2)^m}\,|B|^{m-1}
\]
relations on a subset where at least a $1-\eta$ proportion are respected.
The hypotheses include an explicit polynomial ambient-size threshold.
For $m=16$, this replaces the exponent $2^{19}$ in the printed Lemma 9.3
by exponents $16$ in $\alpha$ and $15$ in $\eta$.
The result also allows fractional initial weights and vector-valued maps
in sufficiently large characteristic.  Keeping the exact second Fourier
moment improves the input to Corollary 9.4 from
$\gamma^7\beta^6$ to $\gamma^7$.
A separate random-linear-map construction works in fixed characteristic
and treats arbitrary translation-invariant systems of linear relations;
its bounds depend on the rank of the relations broken by the map.
Finally, a moment inequality identifies a limitation of the scalar
filter-certificate method, not a limitation of all possible restrictions.
All assertions specific to this note are proved below, and a reproducible
finite-audit script is supplied.
\end{partabstract}
\statusbox{\textbf{Scope and verification.}
This is an unrefereed research manuscript giving local quantitative
refinements, not a claimed improvement to the global bounds for
Szemer\'edi's theorem.  Bibliographic priority for the refinements has not
been established.  The proofs are written out, but have not been
independently refereed or compiled in Lean.  The finite computations
reported in Section~\ref{gsr:fz:17:sec:checks} are checks, not substitutes for the
proofs.}


\subsection{Where the improvement occurs}
The target is Gowers's restriction of a partially additive map to a domain
on which almost every relevant additive relation is respected.  In the
notation of his Lemma 9.3, a set $B\subseteq\Z_N$ has size $\beta N$,
and at least $\alpha\beta^{15}N^{15}$ additive sixteen-tuples are respected
by a map $\phi$.  The printed conclusion retains
$(\alpha\eta/4)^{2^{19}}\beta^{15}N^{15}$ additive sixteen-tuples while
making their respected proportion at least $1-\eta$
\cite[Section 9, pp.~515--518]{gowers}.
We work in the prime cyclic setting used in that argument and then state
precisely which extensions are valid.

There are two independent losses to address.  The first is the extremely
small distinguishing advantage of a degree-one cosine filter on a
sixteen-variable relation.  The second is the replacement of $|B|$ by
$N$ in a second-moment estimate before interpolation.  The former loss is
removed by a higher-degree filter; the latter by keeping the actual
mass throughout the calculation.

The resulting prime-cyclic statement is the following.  Its full weighted
version, and its proof, appear in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:17:thm:main}.

\begin{theorem}[Prime-cyclic restriction, headline form]\label{gsr:fm:17:thm:headline}
Let $m=2r\ge4$, let $N$ be prime, let $B\subseteq\F_N$ have size
$\beta N>0$, and let $\phi:B\to\F_N$.  Suppose that $0<\alpha,\eta\le1$
and that at least $\alpha|B|^{m-1}$ ordered tuples satisfy both
\[
 x_1+\cdots+x_r=x_{r+1}+\cdots+x_m,
 \qquad
 \phi(x_1)+\cdots+\phi(x_r)=\phi(x_{r+1})+\cdots+\phi(x_m).
\]
Set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:17:eq:headlineL}
 L=\ceil{\frac{m+1}{\alpha\eta}}.
\end{equation}
If
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:17:eq:headlineN}
 N\ge 2L^m(2L-1)^{m-1}\beta^{-(m-1)},
\end{equation}
there is a subset $B'\subseteq B$ on which at least a $1-\eta$ proportion
of the additive $m$-tuples are respected and which contains at least
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:17:eq:headlinecount}
 \frac{|B|^{m-1}}{2\eta L^m}
 \ \ge\ \frac{\alpha^m\eta^{m-1}}{2(m+2)^m}\,|B|^{m-1}
\end{equation}
additive $m$-tuples.  In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:17:eq:headlinesize}
 |B'|\ge
 \left(\frac{\alpha^m\eta^{m-1}}{2(m+2)^m}\right)^{1/(m-1)}|B|.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

The characteristic condition needed later is automatic here: the right
side of \eqref{gsr:fm:17:eq:headlineN} is larger than $2L-2$.
A simpler, larger sufficient threshold is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:17:eq:simplifiedN}
 N\ge 2^m(m+2)^{2m-1}
       (\alpha\eta)^{-(2m-1)}\beta^{-(m-1)}.
\end{equation}
Thus the phrase ``sufficiently large'' has an explicit polynomial meaning
for each fixed number of variables.

\subsection{The order-eight consequence}
Putting $m=16$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:17:eq:16main}
 T_{16}(B')\ge
 \frac{\alpha^{16}\eta^{15}}{2\cdot18^{16}}\,
 \beta^{15}N^{15}.
\end{equation}
Here and below $T_m$ counts all ordered additive $m$-tuples, including
repetitions; the proof does not silently discard them from the final
conclusion.  The comparison is with the printed local restriction bound,
not with the current global quantitative theory.

The density-sensitive moment calculation proves that if the number of
respected additive quadruples is at least $\gamma|B|^3$, then the number
of respected additive sixteen-tuples is at least $\gamma^7|B|^{15}$.
Consequently \eqref{gsr:fm:17:eq:16main} can be applied with $\alpha=\gamma^7$:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:17:eq:cor94headline}
 T_{16}(B')\ge
 \frac{\gamma^{112}\eta^{15}}{2\cdot18^{16}}\,\beta^{15}N^{15}.
\end{equation}
No extra factor $\beta^{96}$ is introduced by the interpolation input.
The corresponding convenient sufficient threshold is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:17:eq:cor94threshold}
 N\ge 2^{16}18^{31}\gamma^{-217}\eta^{-31}\beta^{-15}.
\end{equation}

\subsection{What is, and is not, being claimed}
The Fej\'er kernel, Fourier orthogonality, interpolation of moments, and
random linear maps are standard tools.  The contribution here is the
specific restriction estimate, its complete exceptional-set accounting,
the weighted and vector-valued extension, the rank-sensitive system
version, and the identification of the corresponding proof-method
limitation.  The note does not claim that these tools themselves are new.

The high-dimensional fixed-characteristic results in
Section~\ref{gsr:en:17:sec:systems} are different from the prime-cyclic theorem.
One cannot apply a high-dimensional rank argument to the one-dimensional
space $\F_N$ when there are many variables.  Conversely, one cannot use
a high-degree trigonometric filter in small characteristic without
checking Fourier aliasing.

For perspective, Leng, Sah, and Sawhney prove the global bound
$r_k(N)\ll N\exp(- (\log\log N)^{c_k})$ for $k\ge5$, by a different
combination of inverse theorems and density increments
\cite{lssbounds,lssinverse}.  No assertion in this note improves that
bound.  Gowers also explicitly presents Section 9 as a preparatory
special case for more complicated later configurations
\cite[p.~515]{gowers}; improving it alone does not propagate automatically
through the final induction.

Printed below: the abstract, its keywords and Section~1; Section~2 is in Part~II (with source~19, Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:sections1516}), Section~3 in Part~III, Sections~4--5 in Part~I, Sections~6--9 and Appendix~A in Part~V. \begin{partabstract}{18}
We develop three explicit refinements of the local machinery in Gowers'
\emph{A new proof of Szemer\'edi's theorem}. First, for the full definition of
degeneracy in Section~15, we determine the sharp first-order density of
degenerate $d$-arrangements. For fixed $k\ge1$, $d\ge2$ and primes $p\to\infty$,
this density is $(k+C_d)/p+O_{k,d}(p^{-2})$, where
$C_d=\tfrac12(T_{2d}-2\binom{2d}{d}+1)$ and $T_n$ is a central trinomial
coefficient. In particular $C_8=2\,585\,444$. The proof uses paired horizontal
and vertical moment equations and gives explicit finite bounds and a direct
improvement of the ambient-size hypothesis in Lemma~15.5.
Second, we compute the complete fourth- and fifth-order expansion of real
cube moments in every dimension, over every finite abelian group. The
formula identifies all corrections from characters of orders two and three,
and yields a sharp fourth-order leading bound, including sharpness for
indicator sets. Third, we give an elementary transfer from simultaneous
monomial recurrence to partitions on which several polynomial phases have
small oscillation. Existing recurrence theorems yield a polynomial dependence
on the number of phases in place of the exponential dependence displayed
in Lemma~5.9; a shared-leading-coefficient quadratic family admits a stronger
source-internal specialization. An independent volume argument proves a
necessary exponent frontier for every polynomial degree. Complete proofs,
exact finite checks, a source-level Lean integration plan, and further
research questions are included. These are local mathematical results; the
report does not claim a new global Szemer\'edi bound or priority over the
entire literature.
\end{partabstract}
\begin{quote}\small
\noindent\textbf{Keywords.} Gowers norms; Boolean cube circuits; additive
arrangements; polynomial recurrence; finite-field rank; Szemer\'edi's theorem.
\end{quote}
\label{gsr:fm:18:sec:overview}

The aim is to improve particular statements in Gowers' proof while retaining
enough information to say exactly what has been gained. The three parts of
this report address different losses: the treatment of exceptional
arrangements in Section~15, the triangle inequality for cube counts in
Section~3, and the repeated refinement of polynomial partitions in
Section~5. Each produces a theorem with a full proof, and each has a
different consequence for the surrounding argument.

Throughout, references such as ``Lemma~15.4'' refer to Gowers'
paper~\cite{gowers}, not to the numbering of the present article. The
repository supplied with the research request contains both a reconstructed
\LaTeX\ source and a substantial Lean development~\cite{repo18}. We read
the relevant source files and compared the formulations with the published
paper. The reconstructed source includes corrections and explicit
hypotheses absent from some printed statements; these are relevant when a
local improvement is substituted into a later lemma.

\subsection{A sharp asymptotic for degenerate arrangements}

A $d$-arrangement in $\F_p^{k+1}$ consists of $2d$ labelled $k$-cubes with
common side vector, whose last coordinates satisfy an additive relation.
It has
\[
 D=(2d+1)k+2d-1
\]
free scalar parameters. There is a universal alternating dependence among
its vertices. Degeneracy means that some other ternary dependence annihilates
every coordinate monomial in the definition. Gowers' Lemma~15.4 bounds the
number of degenerate arrangements by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:18:eq:old-degeneracy-overview}
 k\,3^{2d\,2^k}p^{D-1}.
\end{equation}
The full definition, rather than the weaker list of tests mentioned after
the lemma, permits the following substantially more precise conclusion:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:18:eq:sharp-degeneracy-overview}
 \#\{\hbox{degenerate $d$-arrangements}\}
 =(k+C_d)p^{D-1}+O_{k,d}(p^{D-2}),
 \qquad
 C_d=\frac{T_{2d}-2\binom{2d}{d}+1}{2},
\end{equation}
where
\[
 T_n=[z^0](z^{-1}+1+z)^n.
\]
The coefficient $k+C_d$ is optimal. Its $k$ part counts zero-side
hyperplanes, and its $C_d$ part counts distinct additional relations among
the last coordinates. Every other kind of certificate contributes only at
second order or smaller. This separation is what the general polynomial
zero estimate in the original proof does not record.

For the $8$-arrangements used later in the proof, put
\[
 M=2^{k+4},\qquad E_k=2^{M+k+3},\qquad
 \lambda=(\alpha\eta/4)^{E_k}\beta^{15}.
\]
In the usual range $0<\alpha,\beta,\eta\le1$, a sufficient condition for
the degeneracy absorption in Lemma~15.5 is improved from
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:18:eq:threshold-comparison-overview}
 \lambda p\ge k3^M
 \quad\hbox{to}\quad
 p\ge17,\qquad \lambda p\ge k+2\,585\,445.
\end{equation}
The very large sampling exponent $E_k$ remains the same. Thus the report
improves a specific finite threshold, and identifies its asymptotically
correct first-order coefficient, without attributing a further consequence
to parts of the proof that have not been re-estimated.

\subsection{Exact cube coefficients in every dimension}

For a real function $g$ on a finite abelian group $G$, let
\[
 \mathcal C_\ell(g)=
 \E_{x,h_1,\ldots,h_\ell\in G}
 \prod_{v\in\{0,1\}^\ell}g(x+v\cdot h)
 =\norm{g}_{U^\ell}^{2^\ell}.
\]
We use $\ell$ here to avoid confusing cube dimension with the arrangement
parameter $d$. If $\E f=0$ and $m=2^\ell$, the first three nonconstant
coefficients in $\mathcal C_\ell(\delta+t f)$ vanish. The fourth coefficient
is an explicit combination of the ordinary Fourier fourth moment and its
restriction to characters of order two. The fifth is a combination of a
five-circuit Fourier correlation and an order-three correction. The four
counting constants are
\begin{align*}
 R_\ell&=\frac{6^\ell-2\cdot4^\ell+2^\ell}{8},&
 B_\ell&=\frac{2^\ell(2^\ell-1)(2^\ell-2)}{24},\\
 Q_\ell&=\frac{8^\ell-3\cdot6^\ell+3\cdot4^\ell-2^\ell}{6},&
 S_\ell&=\frac{10^\ell-4\cdot8^\ell+6\cdot6^\ell-4\cdot4^\ell+2^\ell}{24}.
\end{align*}
These formulas count the relevant four- and five-vertex configurations in
the Boolean cube. Smith normal form explains why only orders two and three
can enter at these orders. The result is valid for every finite abelian
group; excluding small torsion is a corollary, rather than a tacit
assumption in the proof.

For an indicator $\ind_A=\delta+f_A$ with
$\norm{f_A}_{U^\ell}\le\varepsilon$, the resulting estimate begins at
$B_\ell\delta^{m-4}\varepsilon^4$ instead of the linear term in
$(\delta+\varepsilon)^m$. For odd-order groups the fourth coefficient can
be bounded using $R_\ell$ instead. The all-group coefficient $B_\ell$ is
sharp, even along sequences of indicator sets with density tending to any
fixed $\delta\in(0,1)$. The proof first gives an exact order-two-character
example for real weights, and then transfers it to sets by independent
rounding with a quantified Gowers-norm error.

\subsection{Partitions and their quantitative limits}

The polynomial part keeps the near-prescribed lengths of Lemma~5.9:
every cell has length $v-1$ or $v$. It replaces repeated induction on the
number $q$ of phases by an induction on polynomial degree which treats all
$q$ leading coefficients together. A recurrence-radius function is the
only analytic input, so the elementary partition argument can be combined
with either the source's scalar estimate or later simultaneous recurrence
theorems~\cite{maynard,lau}.

For arbitrary quadratic phases, Lau's stated recurrence estimate gives
every strict exponent
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:18:eq:quad-rate-overview}
 a<\frac{1}{126q^2+129q+2}
\end{equation}
for lengths $v-1,v$ with $v\le r^a$ and containing-arc diameter at most
$r^{-2a}$, once $r$ is sufficiently large. The displayed quadratic case of
Gowers' lemma uses $a=1/(2\cdot2048^q)$. The new conclusion has an
unspecified coefficient-independent threshold inherited from the cited
recurrence theorem. Its numerical exponent should not be confused with a
small or fully numerical threshold for $r$.

For quadratics whose leading coefficients are bounded integer multiples of
one common frequency, the scalar estimate in Gowers' own Lemma~5.5 instead
gives every $a<1/(99q+98)$, with an explicit, though enormous, threshold.
Arbitrary lower coefficients are permitted in this specialization.

There is also a rigorous obstruction. If a universal degree-$k$, $q$-phase
partition theorem guaranteed all cell lengths $\gg r^a$ and all
oscillations $\ll r^{-b}$, with $b>0$, it would necessarily satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:18:eq:necessary-frontier-overview}
 \left(\frac{qk(k+1)}2+1\right)a+kqb\le1.
\end{equation}
For quadratics and $b=2a$, this says $a\le1/(7q+1)$. The sufficient
$q^{-2}$ rate and this $q^{-1}$ obstruction leave a substantive research
gap. No optimality assertion for the general quadratic partition exponent
is made.

\subsection{What is established, imported, and left open}

The rank arguments, coefficient counts, cube expansion, rounding
sharpness, recurrence-to-partition transfer, and polynomial obstruction
are proved in this article. Gowers--Cauchy--Schwarz, Fourier orthogonality,
Smith normal form, and the cited recurrence estimates are established
inputs. The familiar twenty circuits of the three-dimensional cube were
explicitly described in earlier literature, for example
Beerenwinkel--Pachter--Sturmfels~\cite{bps}; the low-dimensional
configuration itself is not presented as a discovery of this report.

The article extends the earlier local calculations to precise
all-dimensional statements and pursues the Section~15 and nonlinear
partition questions further. The statements can be assessed from their
proofs independently of a claim of historical priority. A targeted
literature check does not establish that no equivalent result appears
elsewhere.

Nor does a collection of local improvements establish a new best bound for
Szemer\'edi's theorem. For context, Leng--Sah--Sawhney proved, for each
$k\ge5$, a bound of the form
\[
 r_k(N)\ll_k N\exp\!\bigl(- (\log\log N)^{c_k}\bigr),
 \qquad c_k>0,
\]
using quantitative inverse theorems and a density-increment
strategy~\cite{lssbounds}. The results here have a different, explicitly
local purpose. Their value includes sharp information about exceptional
sets, exact spectral expansions, and more effective interchangeable
components for proofs and formalizations.

\subsection{Conventions}

Finite averages are normalized. A finite group has at least one element.
Characters are written additively in the dual group; $j\chi=0$ means that
the character's order divides $j$. A cube is a labelled affine map, so
coincident vertices are included in cube counts. In the arrangement part,
$d\ge2$ is the number of cubes on either side of the additive relation,
and $k\ge1$ is their horizontal dimension. In the partition part, $k$ is
polynomial degree and $q$ is the number of phases. These parameters are
reintroduced at the start of each part. Polynomial oscillation always means
the length of a containing circle arc, as in Gowers' diameter convention.

\srcnote{19}{Section 1}
\partsource{\textbf{Added in the fourth write, 6~October 2026. Delivered title page.} ``Research article / Additive combinatorics / Efficient Interpolation in Gowers' Szemer\'edi Framework / Exact sampling losses, shared refinements, and simultaneous polynomial recurrence / Prepared for Vladimir Reshetnikov / 6 October 2026''; \emph{the PDF author field reads ``ChatGPT, research report prepared for Vladimir Reshetnikov''}. Archive \file{gowers\_interpolation\_article.zip} (arrival \texttt{82bc38a30}), manuscript \file{gowers\_interpolation.tex} (2,505 lines, 32 pages), pin \texttt{dca9f0638} (its \file{provenance/source-audit.json}, shipped as \file{data/19-shared-interpolation-source-audit.json}). Printed below: the abstract, the closing statement of its title page and Section~1; Sections~2--5 and~8 are in Part~II (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:sections1516}), Section~6 in Part~I, Sections~7, 9 and~10 in Part~V. Its `question' environment (printed ``Research question'') is set in this report's `Research question' style; its macro \texttt{\textbackslash commit} (its own pin) is renamed \texttt{\textbackslash commitnineteen}; its \texttt{cleveref} references are written out as cleveref prints them.}
\begin{partabstract}{19}
We strengthen the interpolation mechanism in Section~16 of Gowers' proof
of Szemer\'edi's theorem and give a complementary refinement of its
polynomial phase partition lemma.  A common sample of
$\min\{n,\lceil qd/\sigma\rceil-1\}$ distinct columns recovers all but
$\sigma$ of the ambient mass in any family of partial rows containing
at most $q$ polynomial classes of degree at most $d-1$.  We determine
the exact finite minimax loss by a hypergeometric optimization and prove
its sharp sparse-sampling asymptotic.  For affine interpolation the
constant is $\varphi^3e^{-\varphi}=0.839962094657\ldots$, where
$\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2$.  Refining the sampled cross-sections once, before
forming their interpolants, replaces a quadratic number of structural
refinement steps by a linear number and reduces the list count to an
elementary symmetric polynomial in the slice list sizes.  The result
extends to arbitrary fixed degree in the final variable and includes a
proper-box synchronization argument.  Separately, Maynard's established
simultaneous recurrence theorem yields polynomial rather than
exponential dependence on the number of polynomial phases, for fixed
degree.  A self-contained volume obstruction gives a necessary
degree-sensitive frontier for any such partition theorem.  Full written
proofs, exact finite diagnostics, a source audit, and a research agenda
are supplied.  These are local refinements; neither a new global
Szemer\'edi bound nor a new Lean kernel certification is asserted.
\end{partabstract}
\begin{quote}\small
\noindent The source comparison is pinned to ProveIt commit\par
\noindent\commitnineteen.\par
\noindent The original 2001 publication and the repository's edited
transcription are distinguished throughout.  The article is a research
report; historical priority for its exact formulations is not claimed.
\end{quote}

The difficult part of the inverse machinery in Gowers' argument is not
merely finding many local affine pieces.  Those pieces must be related
across different fibres, and the resulting descriptions must remain
economical after repeated partitioning.  Section~16 uses sampled
cross-sections and interpolation to make that transition.  This is the
main target of the present article \cite{gowers,repo19paper}.

Two losses can be treated separately.  First, the sampling argument
discards small classes and then insists on a small failure probability
for every remaining class.  Averaging the \emph{mass} of failed classes
gives a better estimate.  Second, once interpolation candidates have
been formed, treating them as independent functions causes the same
sampled data to be refined repeatedly.  A common refinement of the
sampled cross-sections allows all interpolants to be formed afterward.

These changes are independent of the more difficult global inverse
theorem.  They give explicit local statements with transparent inputs,
and they also suggest exact extremal questions.  We solve the finite
sampling optimization for the specified interpolation recovery rule
and identify its sharp asymptotic constant.  A separate part of the
article uses modern recurrence theory to improve the dependence on the
number of phases in Lemma~5.9.

\subsection{The main conclusions at a glance}

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{\Alph*.}]
\item \textbf{Exact finite sampling loss.}  For an $n$-point column set,
at most $q$ disjoint classes per row, and interpolation order $d$, define
\[
 W_{n,r,d}(s)=\frac{s}{n\binom nr}
 \sum_{j=0}^{\min(d,s)-1}\binom{s}{j}\binom{n-s}{r-j}.
\]
The worst possible loss of the best common $r$-column sample is exactly
\[
 \mathcal M_{n,q,d}(r)=
 \max_{\substack{s_1,\ldots,s_q\in\Z_{\ge0}\\s_1+\cdots+s_q\le n}}
 \sum_{i=1}^{q} W_{n,r,d}(s_i).
\]
The loss is at most $\min\{1,qd/(r+1)\}$ and is zero for $r=n$.
The equality statement is a genuine finite minimax theorem for the
specified common-anchor recovery mechanism.

\item \textbf{Sharp asymptotic constant.}  For fixed $d$, as
$r\to\infty$, $r/n\to0$, and $q/r\to0$,
\[
 \mathcal M_{n,q,d}(r)\sim\frac{qC_d}{r},\qquad
 C_d=\max_{\lambda\ge0}
 \lambda e^{-\lambda}\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}\frac{\lambda^j}{j!}.
\]
In the affine case, $d=2$, this is
$C_2=\varphi^3e^{-\varphi}$.  The order $q/\sigma$ is therefore
optimal within this sampling model in the sparse-sampling limit.

\item \textbf{Shared interpolation refinement.}  If the $r$ sampled
cross-sections have list sizes $M_1,\ldots,M_r$ on a common partition,
then all degree-at-most-$d-1$ interpolants require at most
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^{\min(d,r)}e_j(M_1,\ldots,M_r)
\]
candidate graphs, where $e_j$ is the $j$th elementary symmetric
polynomial.  With a common list size $M$, the affine count is
$rM+\binom r2M^2$.  The partition is refined once per sampled
cross-section, rather than once for every interpolation pair.

\item \textbf{A degree-sensitive recurrence transfer.}  Let $q_j$ count
the phases whose degree is at least $j$, and let $\kappa_j$ be a valid
simultaneous recurrence constant of degree $j$, with $\kappa_1=1$.
Define $F_0=1$, $G_0=0$, and
\[
 F_j=(1+j\kappa_jq_j)F_{j-1},\qquad
 G_j=(1+j\kappa_jq_j)G_{j-1}+\kappa_jq_j.
\]
For $F_ka+G_kb<1$, every sufficiently long integer interval can be
partitioned into progressions of length at least $N^a$ on which all
phase diameters are at most $N^{-b}$.  Maynard's published theorem
supplies the constants; its recurrence assertion is an external input
\cite{maynard}.  For fixed degree, $F_k+G_k=O_k(q^k)$ when $q_j=q$.

\item \textbf{A necessary polynomial frontier.}  If the prescribed
phase degrees are $d_1,\ldots,d_q$, set
$D=\sum_i d_i$ and $S=\sum_i d_i(d_i+1)/2$.  A universal progression
partition with length exponent $a$ and diameter exponent $b$ must satisfy
\[
 (S+1)a+Db\le1.
\]
The proof uses finite differences and a volume estimate, not an
unproved Diophantine approximation conjecture.  For nonlinear phases
the gap between this obstruction and the sufficient frontier remains
open in the present approach.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{How the results differ from earlier project refinements}

This article concentrates on the conversion of fibrewise polynomial
descriptions into compatible descriptions in all variables, and on
simultaneous recurrence for several nonlinear phases.  It does not
repackage the project's earlier cube expansions, energy inequalities,
Bohr extension estimates, or sharp linear phase-density selection
results.  The relevant source targets are Lemmas~16.9--16.10 and the
nonlinear part of Lemma~5.9.  The original and edited source statements,
and the live Lean interfaces, are examined in section~\ref{gsr:fz:19:audit:section}.

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{What this ``does not repackage''.} At the pin the report directory held source~04's manuscript as \file{article.tex}; sources~05 and~13 (linear phase partitions) were not visible to this source. Within this report, Section~\ref{gsr:dt:19:sec:d6} meets source~18's Sections~4--5 (the same theorem, proved independently: note after Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:18:part:cor:quadratic-polynomial-q}) and extends source~13's linear results; Sections~\ref{gsr:en:19:sec:d2}--\ref{gsr:en:19:sec:d5} are new ground: no other source treats Section~16 of the paper.
\end{writenote}


\subsection{Novelty, attribution, and the scope of the conclusions}

The tools used here have substantial precedents.  Missing-mass
optimization and occupancy estimates are established subjects
\cite{missingmass,occupancy}.  Lagrange interpolation, finite averaging,
and common refinement of partitions are classical.  Maynard's
recurrence theorem is imported with attribution; the optional numerical
specialization from Lau is explicitly identified as a preprint input
\cite{maynard,lau}.

The contributions claimed here are the precise finite minimax
formulation, its interpolation-compatible endpoint, the sharp
asymptotic analysis for that model, the more economical lifting theorem,
and the proved recurrence transfer and obstruction.  These results
improve the specified local procedures.  A complete priority search
would be needed before claiming that every individual formulation is
new to the literature.  No well-known open global conjecture is claimed
to be resolved.

For perspective, substantially stronger global bounds than the 2001
estimate are already available.  Leng, Sah, and Sawhney prove, for each
$k\ge5$, a bound of the form
$r_k(N)\ll N\exp(- (\log\log N)^{c_k})$, where $c_k>0$ and $r_k(N)$
is the largest size of a $k$-term-progression-free subset of $[N]$
\cite{lssbounds}.  The local comparisons here do not improve that result.
More fundamentally, the explicit closing graph-budget comparison in
the supplied Section~16 proof requires repair; reducing a sampling
constant does not discharge it.

\begin{partabstract}{20}
\noindent
We refine the counting stage of Gowers's proof by retaining two functions
through the Cauchy--Schwarz argument. For surjective homomorphisms from a
finite abelian parameter group, the resulting bound is a product of two
directional Gowers seminorms and one ordinary $L^2$ norm. A sharp
finite-index comparison converts the directional norms to global norms,
with explicit constants that record torsion rather than hiding it behind
a prime-modulus hypothesis. A second-order telescoping identity then gives
quadratic, rather than linear, error in the balanced uniformity norm.
For a set of density $\delta$ and admissible $k$-term progressions,
\[
 \abs{\La_k(1_A)-\delta^k}
 \le B_k(\delta)\,\Useminorm{1_A-\delta}{k-1}^{\,2},
 \qquad B_k(\delta)\le \frac{\sqrt\delta}{(1-\delta)^2}.
\]
We give a sharper explicit formula for $B_k$, unequal-density versions,
and supersaturation consequences. An exact quadratic-phase construction,
followed by probabilistic rounding, proves that the exponent two cannot
be increased for three-term counts, even for indicator sets on growing
$\F_{29}$-vector spaces. The article includes proofs, limitations,
10,389 exact finite checks, a formalization plan, and twelve research
questions. The improvements are relative to specified local estimates;
worldwide priority and a new best global Szemer\'edi bound are not asserted.
\end{partabstract}
\begin{quote}\small
\noindent Research article and reproducibility package. The supplied proofs are
human-readable mathematical proofs; no new Lean kernel verification is claimed.
\end{quote}
\label{gsr:fm:20:sec:intro}

The target is the passage from uniformity to counting in Section~3 of
Gowers's paper \cite{gowers}. In normalized notation, its Theorem~3.2
controls a progression average by the $U^{k-1}$ norm of one function.
Corollary~3.3 expands balanced functions and obtains a counting estimate
with a factor $2^k$. Its hypotheses are asymmetric: the first two sets
need not be uniform. The ProveIt transcription makes the coefficient
invertibility conditions explicit \cite{repo20lean}.

The inspected research article in the repository already improves this
expansion by density-weighted, first-order telescoping \cite{repo20research}.
For a single set $A$ of density $\delta$, that argument gives
\begin{equation}
 \abs{\La_k(1_A)-\delta^k}
 \le S_{k-2}(\delta)u,
 \qquad
 u=\Useminorm{1_A-\delta}{k-1},\quad
 S_{k-2}(\delta)=\sum_{r=0}^{k-3}\delta^r.
 \label{gsr:fm:20:eq:old}
\end{equation}
The improvement developed here is not another reordering of this linear
estimate. We retain a second uniformity factor before estimating the
balanced expansion.

\subsection{A concrete statement to keep in view}

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group, $|G|=N$, and let
\[
 \La_k(a)=\E_{x,y\in G}\prod_{r=0}^{k-1}a(x+ry).
\]
Call the progression system \emph{admissible} when multiplication by every
integer $1,\ldots,k-1$ is an automorphism of $G$. In a cyclic group this
means $\gcd(N,(k-1)!)=1$, not necessarily that $N$ is prime.

For $0<\delta<1$, write $\sigma=\sqrt{\delta(1-\delta)}$ and define
\begin{align}
 R_m(\delta)
 &=\min\left\{\sqrt\delta,
       \sigma\frac{1-\delta^m}{1-\delta}\right\},\qquad m\ge1,
 \label{gsr:fm:20:eq:Rm-intro}\\
 B_k(\delta)
 &=\sum_{j=2}^{k-1}(j-1)\delta^{j-2}R_{k-j}(\delta).
 \label{gsr:fm:20:eq:B-intro}
\end{align}
We prove
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\quad
 \abs{\La_k(1_A)-\delta^k}\le B_k(\delta)u^2.
 \quad}
 \label{gsr:fm:20:eq:headline}
\end{equation}
The coefficient is explicit, and satisfies
\begin{equation}
 B_3(\delta)=\sqrt{\delta(1-\delta)},\qquad
 B_k(\delta)\le\frac{\sqrt\delta}{(1-\delta)^2}.
 \label{gsr:fm:20:eq:B-simple}
\end{equation}
For $0<\delta\le1/2$ there is the simpler exact expression
\begin{equation}
 B_k(\delta)
 =\sqrt\delta\sum_{r=0}^{k-4}(r+1)\delta^r
 +(k-2)\delta^{k-3}\sqrt{\delta(1-\delta)}.
 \label{gsr:fm:20:eq:B-small}
\end{equation}
An empty sum, here and below, is zero. The cases $\delta=0,1$ have zero
error and are treated separately.

The two estimates \eqref{gsr:fm:20:eq:old} and \eqref{gsr:fm:20:eq:headline} can be used
together by taking their minimum. The quadratic estimate is particularly
useful when $u$ is small. It requires uniformity at two marked positions
in each surviving term. Consequently it is a strengthening for the
symmetric counting problem, not a replacement of the asymmetric
Corollary~3.3 under unchanged hypotheses.

\subsection{What is proved, and what remains distinct}

The principal structural result is Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:20:thm:two}, for arbitrary
surjective homomorphisms of finite abelian groups. Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:20:thm:index}
determines the optimal constant in a directional-to-global norm
comparison for every fixed tuple of subgroups. Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:20:thm:count}
and Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:20:cor:symmetric} give the counting refinements.
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:20:thm:indicator-sharpness} establishes sharpness of the exponent
two for actual three-term counts on a specified family of groups.

These statements resolve several local questions posed by the argument:
linear dependence on the balanced norm is not intrinsic to symmetric
counting; torsion can be included quantitatively; the subgroup norm
conversion has an exact sharp constant; and, for three-term counts,
quadratic dependence cannot be replaced uniformly by any higher power.
The last assertion is about finite abelian groups in a growing-dimensional
family. We do not claim the corresponding sharpness construction here for
prime cyclic groups, or for $k\ge4$.

The underlying tools---Cauchy--Schwarz, Fourier orthogonality, and
quadratic Gauss sums---are classical. Directional Gowers norms have an
established theory, including the substantially deeper concatenation
results of Tao and Ziegler \cite{taoziegler}. Our comparison concerns
finite-index subgroups and needs no concatenation theorem. A targeted
source check does not establish worldwide priority for the exact
formulations below; they should be viewed as proved refinements relative
to the specified source estimates.

Nor does a sharper counting lemma by itself establish a new record for
$r_k(N)$. For perspective, Leng, Sah, and Sawhney prove
$r_k(N)\ll N\exp(- (\log\log N)^{c_k})$ for $k\ge5$, using
quasipolynomial inverse bounds and a density-increment strategy
\cite{lssbounds}. We make no global bound claim beyond the local implications
proved in Section~\ref{gsr:cc:20:sec:super}.

\begin{partabstract}{21}
Let $G$ be a nontrivial finite abelian group of exponent five, let $f:G\to\R$
have mean zero, and put $u=\|f\|_{U^3}$.  We prove, with absolute constants
$c,C>0$ and without a pointwise bound on $f$, that
\[
 \|\delta+f\|_{U^3}^8
 \le \delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4
      +\frac{2^{3/4}}3\delta^2u^6+Cu^8
 \qquad(\delta>0,\ u\le c\delta).
\]
The coefficient at $u^6$ is optimal even on a fixed five-point quotient.
This closes the characteristic-five coefficient gap in an earlier
project report, which established the exponent and a matching lower
candidate but only an unspecified upper constant.

The proof strengthens the treatment of the sixth- and seventh-degree
terms in the centered cube expansion.  A positive cubic convolution
statistic controls both terms, and its Fourier-tail estimate permits
their absorption against a retained norm deficit.  Four further
Fourier squares yield the sharp phase-dependent coefficient
\[
 \frac{2^{3/4}}3\,
 \frac{(\cos\theta)_+^2}{1+\cos^2\phi},\qquad
 \theta=2\arg\widehat f(\xi)-\arg\widehat f(2\xi),\quad
 \phi=3\arg\widehat f(\xi)+\arg\widehat f(2\xi),
\]
when $\{\pm\xi\}$ is a largest conjugate Fourier pair.
Near equality forces a second harmonic of size
$2^{1/4}u^2/(6\delta)$ and the phase condition
$e^{10i\arg\widehat f(\xi)}\to-1$.

On $G=\Z/5\Z$, an exact six-row Fourier formula and analytic
optimization determine the next term of the weighted supremum:
\[
 M_{\delta,5}(u)=\delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4
       +\frac{2^{3/4}}3\delta^2u^6+\frac{20}{9}u^8
       +O_\delta(u^{10}).
\]
We transfer sharpness to indicator sets in growing exponent-five groups,
give explicit finite profile inequalities, explain the interface with
Gowers's Lemmas~3.8--3.10 and the repository, and distinguish the
remaining higher-dimensional eighth-order problem from the questions
resolved here.
\end{partabstract}
\begin{quote}\small
\noindent\textbf{Principal result.} On every nontrivial finite abelian group
of exponent five, the sharp next coefficient after
$6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4$ in the centered three-cube problem is
$2^{3/4}\delta^2/3$, at order $u^6$.  The uniform error is $O(u^8)$.
On the five-point group the following coefficient is exactly $20/9$.

\smallskip
\noindent Based on the supplied Ramsey development in
\texttt{VladimirReshetnikov/ProveIt}, inspected at commit
\texttt{43306653afaaaaa0b58a7ca71e4067c245594867}.
Complete written proofs, exact finite formulas, computational checks,
and a further research agenda are included.  The report solves a
specified extremal question left open in an earlier project manuscript;
it does not assert bibliographic priority or a new global quantitative
Szemer\'edi bound.  The new proofs have not been certified by Lean.
\end{quote}
\label{gsr:fm:21:sec:introduction}

Gowers's proof of Szemer\'edi's theorem develops higher uniformity norms
to measure additive structure \cite{gowers}.  Lemma~3.10 bounds the
number of $d$-dimensional additive cubes in a set of density $\delta$ by
\[
       (\delta+\alpha^{1/2^d})^{2^d}N^{d+1},
\]
where $\alpha$ is the degree-$(d-1)$ uniformity parameter.  Its proof
uses the triangle inequality from Lemma~3.9, itself a consequence of
the cube Cauchy--Schwarz inequality in Lemma~3.8.  This is an effective
general estimate, but it does not exploit the real-valued, mean-zero
structure of the balanced function.

The Ramsey research collection in the supplied repository
\cite{repo21} already contains extensive local improvements.
In particular, the quartic leading term in the real, centered
three-cube problem and its Fourier concentration mechanism are prior
project results.  An additional manuscript, \emph{Sharp Extremal
Refinements in Gowers's Szemer\'edi Framework} \cite{prior21extremal},
determines a secondary $u^{16/3}$ term over suitable odd-order groups.
Its Section~3 shows that exponent five changes the next exponent to
$6$ and constructs the lower coefficient $2^{3/4}/3$, while explicitly
leaving the optimal upper coefficient unresolved.

The manuscript \emph{Sharp Extremal Refinements in Gowers's Szemer\'edi Framework} \cite{prior21extremal} is source~14; its Section~3 is Section~\ref{gsr:cc:14:sec:d3}, with the exponent six and the lower coefficient in Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:14:thm:exponent-five}. Source~23, written the same day from a pin three minutes later, proves the same theorem independently (its Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:23:five:main}); neither cites the other. In this report source~21 is the main source and source~23 a credited second route (Section~\ref{gsr:cc:sec:charfive}).
\end{writenote}

The present report develops that unresolved direction.  It does not
relabel the existing quartic estimate or the previous lower example as
new.  Instead, it proves a matching uniform upper coefficient, a sharp
phase envelope, a stronger error estimate, and an exact further term
on the smallest group.  Background inequalities are reproved because
their precise constants and equality defects are needed.

\subsection{Statements at a glance}

All averages in this report are probability averages.  For real $W$,
write
\[
 Q_3(W)=\E_{x,h_1,h_2,h_3\in G}
        \prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^3}W(x+\omega\cdot h)
        =\|W\|_{U^3}^8.
\]
The constants used repeatedly are
\begin{equation}
 C_5=\frac{2^{3/4}}3=0.5605976101\ldots,
 \qquad \beta_5=\frac{2^{1/4}}6=0.1982011858\ldots.
 \label{gsr:fm:21:eq:constants}
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform characteristic-five expansion]
\label{gsr:fm:21:thm:main}
There are absolute constants $c,C>0$ such that, for every nontrivial
finite abelian group $G$ of exponent five, every real mean-zero $f$,
and every $\delta>0$, putting $u=\|f\|_{U^3}$, one has
\begin{equation}
 Q_3(\delta+f)\le
 \delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4+C_5\delta^2u^6+Cu^8
 \quad\text{if }u\le c\delta.
 \label{gsr:fm:21:eq:main-upper}
\end{equation}
For every fixed $0<\delta<1$ and every fixed nontrivial such group,
$[0,1]$-valued weights of mean $\delta$ attain the displayed coefficients
through order $u^6$.  Both the constants in the upper bound and the
smallness condition are independent of the dimension of $G$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Second route, and a check.} Source~23's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:23:five:main} is the same statement, with the supremum over weights on every fixed group and over all such groups; its constants are cruder (its sextic tail term $84t^6\sqrt D$ against $42\sqrt3\,t^6D^{1/2}$ here), and its rigidity statement is equivalent to Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:21:thm:rigidity} (note there). The coefficient was re-derived at the write: $\sup_{b\ge0}\{-12\cdot2^{1/4}b^2+4\sqrt2\,b\}=(4\sqrt2)^2/(48\cdot2^{1/4})=2^{3/4}/3$, attained at $b=2^{1/4}/6=\beta_5$. The theorem answers source~14's Question~1, including its sub-question on the rank of the group: the bound is uniform, and the coefficient is attained on every fixed group (Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:21:cor:pullback}).
\end{writenote}

Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:21:thm:phase} refines $C_5$ to an explicit function of two
Fourier phases.  Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:21:thm:rigidity} gives necessary conditions
for asymptotic equality.  Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:21:thm:five-point-next} proves the
additional coefficient $20/9$ on $\Z/5\Z$, including a proof that the
formula describes the global maximum for small $u$.

\subsection{Scope and comparison with the literature}

The optimization problem is local in the uniformity norm.  It asks how
large the cube count of a small perturbation of a constant can be when
the norm of that perturbation is fixed.  Eisner and Tao
\cite{eisnertao} study a different extremizer problem: Gowers--Host--Kra
seminorms that are large under $L^\infty$ or critical $L^p$ constraints.
Hatami \cite{hatami} develops norm geometry and Hanner inequalities for
generalizations of Gowers norms.  These works provide appropriate
context for rigidity and convexity, but their constraints should not be
identified with the fixed-mean, small-centered-norm problem here.

The literature search did not establish bibliographic priority for
the new formulas.  Accordingly, ``sharp'' always means that the stated
inequality has matching examples in its specified mathematical class;
it does not mean that no related observation exists elsewhere.
The unresolved question settled here is explicitly the coefficient
question in the earlier project report.

No new bound for the largest progression-free subset of
$\{1,\ldots,N\}$ is obtained.  As a quantitative benchmark, Leng,
Sah, and Sawhney \cite{lssbounds} prove for each fixed $k\ge5$ a bound
$r_k(N)\ll_k N\exp(-(\log\log N)^{c_k})$ with $c_k>0$.
The present characteristic-five results concern a different local
step and do not propagate through a new global density-increment
argument.  In particular, a group of exponent five has no progression
with more than five distinct points; its cube geometry remains
meaningful independently of that restriction.

\subsection{What is counted}

A three-cube is an ordered parameter tuple $(x,h_1,h_2,h_3)\in G^4$.
Its vertices may coincide, and a sidelength may be zero.  Thus
$|G|^4Q_3(1_A)$ is an integer count of parameterized cubes, not a count
of unlabelled eight-point subsets.  This convention is the one relevant
to the uniformity norm and to Lemma~3.10.

Every nontrivial finite abelian group of exponent five is a finite
dimensional vector space over $\F_5$.  We use additive notation for
both $G$ and its character group $\widehat G$; a dual element $r$
is also the character $x\mapsto r(x)$ when it occurs in Fourier
inversion.  No coordinate basis is needed in the proofs.

\srcnote{22}{Section 1}
\partsource{\textbf{Added in the fifth write, 6~October 2026.
