\begin{partabstract}{33}
Gowers's proof of Szemer\'edi's theorem uses arrangements of vertical
edges whose horizontal coordinates obey one balanced additive relation.
We study the high-agreement inverse problem for these same arrangements
on a full product of finite abelian groups. The exact models are not just
biaffine maps: they are
$\phi(x,y)=a(x)+B(x,y)+\ell(y)$, with an arbitrary row function $a$, a
biadditive map $B$, and a homomorphism $\ell$.

For a test involving an even number $s\ge4$ of vertical differences,
write $\eps_s$ for its failure probability and $\dd$ for distance to this
model class. We give a self-contained, dimension-free decoder and prove
that, when $\eps_s\le 1/(240(s-1))$,
\[
 \dd\le\frac{1-\sqrt{1-8(s-1)\eps_s/s}}{4(s-1)}
 =\frac{\eps_s}{s}+\frac{2(s-1)}{s^2}\eps_s^2+O_s(\eps_s^3).
\]
Both displayed asymptotic coefficients are optimal uniformly over finite
abelian groups. The leading coefficient remains optimal even for
$G=H=K=\F_p$, with $p$ an odd prime tending to infinity.
For $s=4$ we prove the stronger local inequality
$\eps_4\ge4\dd-24\dd^2+32\dd^3$ for $\dd\le1/4$;
an explicit family attains this entire cubic.
For Gowers's eight-arrangements, $s=16$, the repair bound starts with
$\eps_{16}/16+15\eps_{16}^2/128$.
A further moment bound sharpens the high-density case of Gowers's
Lemma 12.3: $\theta N^8$ respected pairs imply at least
$\max\{\theta^7,4\theta-3\}N^{32}$ respected eight-arrangements.
We also retain a row-collision profile, treat erasures, give exact cyclic
counting and decoding algorithms, and report reproducible integer-arithmetic
checks. These are high-agreement full-domain results, not an improvement
to the general sparse restriction step or to the global bounds for
Szemer\'edi's theorem.
\end{partabstract}
\begin{quote}\small
\noindent\textbf{Status.} Self-contained research manuscript with proofs and
finite computational checks. Unrefereed; not Lean-verified. The mathematical
claims below are the claims proved in this manuscript, not a certification
of literature priority. No human authorship or independent referee review
is implied.
\end{quote}

\subsection{From many respected arrangements to a global model}

In Section 12 of \cite{gowers}, Gowers first obtains many respected
arrangements and then restricts the domain so that almost all arrangements
are respected. The subsequent structural argument finds bilinear pieces.
The present paper isolates a different endpoint question: when the domain
is already a full product and the respected fraction is close to one,
how many function values must be changed to obtain an exact model?

The distinction between a full and a sparse domain is essential. A full
product supplies independent vertical base points, uniform marginals,
and an exact derivative cocycle on every pair of increments. On a sparse
set these features need not survive conditioning. Our argument exploits
these full-domain properties rather than silently assuming them in the
sparse case.

Throughout, $G,H,K$ are finite abelian groups, written additively.
All probabilities are uniform on the finite sets specified, and all
auxiliary random choices are independent unless a relation is explicitly
imposed. We allow trivial groups. Let $s=2m\ge4$. A random test chooses
$h\in H$, $x_1,\dots,x_s\in G$ uniformly subject to
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:33:ras:eq:horizontal}
 x_1+\cdots+x_m=x_{m+1}+\cdots+x_s,
\end{equation}
and independently chooses $y_1,\dots,y_s\in H$. It accepts $\phi:G\times H\to K$
when the corresponding vertical differences satisfy the same relation:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:33:ras:eq:test}
 \sum_{i=1}^{m}D_h\phi(x_i,y_i)
 =\sum_{i=m+1}^{s}D_h\phi(x_i,y_i),
 \qquad D_h\phi(x,y)=\phi(x,y+h)-\phi(x,y).
\end{equation}
This is Gowers's $m$-arrangement, with $s=2m$ edge occurrences and
$2s=4m$ point occurrences. We count repetitions and the increment $h=0$.
Let $\eps_s(\phi)$ be its failure probability.

\begin{definition}[The exact vertical model class]\label{gsr:fm:33:ras:def:model}
Let $\Vthirtythree(G,H;K)$ consist of the functions
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:33:ras:eq:model}
 \psi(x,y)=a(x)+B(x,y)+\ell(y),
\end{equation}
where $a:G\to K$ is arbitrary, $B:G\times H\to K$ is additive in each
argument, and $\ell:H\to K$ is a homomorphism. Put
\[
 \dd(\phi)=\min_{\psi\in\Vthirtythree(G,H;K)}
    \Prob_{x,y}[\phi(x,y)\ne\psi(x,y)].
\]
\end{definition}
The class is a subgroup of the group of all functions. Its arbitrary
$a(x)$ is necessary: vertical differences cannot see an added function
of $x$. In particular, no test of the form \eqref{gsr:fm:33:ras:eq:test} alone can
force $a$ to be affine. Every model passes every test, since
$D_h\psi(x,y)=B(x,h)+\ell(h)$.

\subsection{Main theorems}

\begin{theorem}[Dimension-free high-agreement repair]\label{gsr:fm:33:ras:thm:main}
Let $s\ge4$ be even, and write $\eps=\eps_s(\phi)$. If
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:33:ras:eq:threshold}
 0\le\eps\le\frac{1}{240(s-1)},
\end{equation}
then some $\psi\in\Vthirtythree(G,H;K)$ differs from $\phi$ on at most
$R_s(\eps)|G||H|$ inputs, where
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:33:ras:eq:radical}
 R_s(u)=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-\frac{8(s-1)}s u}}{4(s-1)}.
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:33:ras:eq:main-expansion}
 \dd(\phi)\le\frac{\eps}{s}
       +\frac{2(s-1)}{s^2}\eps^2+O_s(\eps^3).
\end{equation}
The leading coefficient $1/s$ is optimal even on common odd prime cyclic
groups. With that leading coefficient fixed, the quadratic coefficient
$2(s-1)/s^2$ cannot be decreased uniformly over all finite abelian groups.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
\emph{In this report.} The first full-product repair theorem for Gowers's arrangements, with sharp first and second coefficients; it advances item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:arrange} (source~11's Question~7, source~14's Questions~5--6, source~15's Questions~2--3) on full or near-full products; the sparse case is open (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:endpoint}). At $s=16$: $1/16$ and $15/128$; the common-prime bracket of Research question~\ref{gsr:fz:33:ras:q:odd} is $23/512\le c_{16}^{\mathrm{prime}}\le15/128$ (checked at the write).
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Every order and every coefficient} (source~60, Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:arrangementpolynomial}): $\varepsilon_s\ge B_s(\delta)$ for $\delta\le1/4$ and every even $s\ge4$, with all interior equality cases, and every Taylor coefficient of the repair bound optimal in succession (its Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:60:arr:local}, \ref{gsr:en:60:arr:equality} and Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:60:arr:coefficients}).
\end{writenote}

The repair statement is proved in Section~\ref{gsr:en:33:ras:sec:sharp}; the two
optimality statements are proved in Section~\ref{gsr:en:33:ras:sec:examples}.
The numerical threshold in \eqref{gsr:fm:33:ras:eq:threshold} is a convenient explicit
one and is not claimed optimal.

\begin{theorem}[A sharp cubic and a higher-order local bound]\label{gsr:fm:33:ras:thm:local-main}
If $\dd=\dd(\phi)\le1/4$, then for every even $s\ge4$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:33:ras:eq:local-main}
 \eps_s(\phi)\ge F_s(\dd),\qquad
 F_s(v)=sv(1-2v)\big((1-2v)^{s-2}-(2v)^{s-2}\big).
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:33:ras:eq:cubic-main}
 \eps_4(\phi)\ge4\dd-24\dd^2+32\dd^3.
\end{equation}
For each odd $n\ge3$, equality in \eqref{gsr:fm:33:ras:eq:cubic-main} is attained
with $G=\Z_n$, $H=K=\Z_2$, and $\dd=1/(2n)$.
For $s>4$ we do not assert that the whole function $F_s$ is optimal.
\end{theorem}

\begin{corollary}[Gowers's eight-arrangements]\label{gsr:fm:33:ras:cor:eight}
Suppose a function $\phi:G\times H\to K$ respects at least a fraction
$1-\eps$ of its eight-arrangements and $\eps\le1/3600$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:33:ras:eq:eight}
 \dd(\phi)\le
 \frac{1-\sqrt{1-\frac{15}{2}\eps}}{60}
 =\frac{\eps}{16}+\frac{15}{128}\eps^2+O(\eps^3).
\end{equation}
For $G=H=K=\F_p$, the approximating function has the form
$a(x)+(bx+c)y$, where $b,c\in\F_p$ and $a$ is arbitrary.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Take $s=16$ in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:33:ras:thm:main}. A biadditive map
$\F_p\times\F_p\to\F_p$ is determined by its value at $(1,1)$, and a
homomorphism $\F_p\to\F_p$ by its value at $1$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Position relative to the source and existing refinements}

The primary source is Gowers's 2001 paper \cite{gowers}; the
repository's corrected transcription \cite{repo33} was used to check the
arrangement definition and the nearby lemma interfaces. Table~\ref{gsr:fm:33:ras:tab:crosswalk}
records the logical relationship rather than claiming that a theorem with
stronger hypotheses replaces its sparse counterpart.

The existing local-refinements report in the repository treats, among
other topics, density extraction, energy inequalities, moment amplification,
transport rigidity and cubical expansions \cite{repo33}. The elementary
majority correction used here belongs to the self-testing tradition of
Blum--Luby--Rubinfeld \cite{blr}; it is not presented as a new general
principle. Our specific target is a row-gauge arrangement code and its
quantitative defect-to-distance relation. The proof includes all required
self-correction estimates, so no theorem from an unrefereed repository
report is an unproved input.

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
\emph{Identifications within this report.} At this source's pin the ``existing local-refinements report'' \cite{repo33} was its second write (sources~01--10). The arrangement material it does not cite: source~14's equality theory for arrangement moments (Section~\ref{gsr:en:14:sec:d5}) and source~15's collision-sensitive amplification (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:collision}; its Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:15:lem:interpolation} is the moment interpolation behind Gowers's $\theta^7$). The high-agreement repair asked for by source~11's Question~7 and sources~14 and~15 (label repair near a product) is the subject here (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:arrange}).
\end{writenote}

For broader context, Gowers--Mili\'cevi\'c study Freiman
multi-homomorphisms on dense subsets of products of finite vector spaces
\cite{gowersmilicevic}. Their sparse-domain structure problem is substantially
more general in domain geometry and has different conclusions. Directional
uniformity norms also provide a related setting \cite{milicevicdirectional}.
Neither comparison constitutes a priority claim for the constants here.

There is no deduction here of a new upper bound for progression-free
sets. For example, the global estimates of Leng--Sah--Sawhney
\cite{lssbounds} require machinery and parameter propagation not supplied
by a full-domain high-agreement lemma alone. The proposed sparse extension
is left explicitly as a research question.

\begin{partabstract}{34}
We develop local refinements of the cube-counting and rigidity steps
in Gowers's proof of Szemer\'edi's theorem. Let $h(p)$ be the least
support of an affinely independent Boolean configuration admitting a
full-support characteristic-$p$ relation. We prove
$h(p)=D_{\mathrm{div}}(p)+1$, where $D_{\mathrm{div}}(p)$ is the
least order of a nonsingular binary matrix whose determinant is
divisible by $p$. This identifies the first dimension permitting
any $p$-primary Smith torsion, and gives
$h(7)=7$ and $h(11)=h(13)=h(17)=8$.

Retaining integral equivalence in Shitov's composition, we prove that
every positive integer up to
$\exp(\tfrac12N\log N-N\log\log N-4N)$ is the sole nonunit
Smith factor of a binary matrix of order $N$, eventually. The
published Alon--Vu construction is the only deep input. Consequently,
even exact cyclic quotients of order $m$ have optimal support
$(2+o(1))\log m/\log\log m$.
We also characterize universal nonnegativity of cyclic Fourier
moments: the relation coefficients must occur in opposite pairs.
The corresponding optimal support is
$(4+o(1))\log m/\log\log m$, so positivity doubles the leading
cost.

An exact fourth dual-function calculation, combined with positive
resonance terms, gives
$\|f\|_{U^2}^{4}\le(2/3)\|f\|_{U^4}^{4}$ for every real centered
function on every finite odd-order abelian group. A two-pair example
on $\Z/29\Z$ gives ratio $0.558729\ldots$, exceeding every
single-pair ratio. This improves the leading fourth-dimensional
cube coefficient to $200/3$. An appendix proves the sharp
nonuniform directional rigidity threshold
$[2+(2k-2)\kappa]^{-1}$. Full proofs, exact finite certificates,
source attribution, and a research and formalization program are
provided.
\end{partabstract}
\label{gsr:fm:34:sec:scope}

\noindent\textbf{Manuscript status.}
Complete mathematical arguments and exact finite certificates are
supplied, with internal proof review. External peer review and
Lean certification remain separate steps. Statements of improvement
refer to the sources identified below.

Gowers's Lemmas~3.8--3.10 supply a multilinear Cauchy--Schwarz
inequality, the triangle inequality for the uniformity norm, and an
upper bound on cube counts \cite{gowers}. These are natural places
to ask how centering, Fourier symmetry, and the arithmetic of the
ambient group improve a general-purpose norm estimate. The ProveIt
research collection already develops fourth- and fifth-order cube
expansions and explicitly asks for the first appearance of prime
torsion and the sharp higher-dimensional norm gaps \cite{repo34}.
We concentrate on those questions.

The repository was inspected at commit
\begin{center}\small\ttfamily
12da356730b12cb73c276a258aaadf3223e3662b.
\end{center}
The merged research article contains sources 01--10. Later numbered
ancillary files and incoming archives are distinct parts of the
audited material; they are not silently counted as chapters of that
merged article. In particular, the incoming report
\emph{Further Quantitative Refinements of Gowers's Szemer\'edi
Argument} already proves the stronger baseline
$c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le(8/35)^{1/4}$ \cite{repo34moments}.
The comparison in this report uses that bound, as well as the merged
article's earlier $2^{-1/2}$ bound.

\subsection{What is established here}

The structural parameter $h(p)$ is defined precisely in
Section~\ref{gsr:cc:34:sec:setup}; $\hc(m)$ imposes the stronger condition of
an exact cyclic quotient. Our principal conclusions are:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{An exact extremal reduction.}
For every prime $p$,
\[
 h(p)=\Ddiv(p)+1.
\]
The same value is the minimum number of Boolean vertices whose row
quotient has any $p$-torsion. The minimum ambient cube dimension is
$\Ddiv(p)$. The result resolves the apparent extra full-support
obstruction at the minimum dimension, while preserving that
obstruction for a general nonminimal matrix.

\item \textbf{Optimal asymptotic support.}
As $p$ tends to infinity through primes and $m$ through integers,
\[
 h(p)\sim\hc(p)\sim\frac{2\log p}{\log\log p},
 \qquad
 \hc(m)\sim\frac{2\log m}{\log\log m}.
\]
This closes the leading-order gap between the repository's Hadamard
lower bound and its linear upper bound $h(p)\le p+2$.

\item \textbf{An improved consecutive range with prescribed Smith form.}
For every sufficiently large $N$, each integer
\[
 1\le m\le
 \left\lfloor\exp\left(\frac N2\log N-N\log\log N-4N\right)
 \right\rfloor
\]
is realized by a binary matrix with Smith form
$\diag(1,\ldots,1,m)$. The construction follows Shitov's
architecture \cite{shitov}; the smaller secondary loss and the
cyclic Smith-form conclusion are proved with all rounding and
integral-equivalence details retained. A further parameter optimization allows any
linear-loss constant greater than
$2\log2+\tfrac12\log(3/(2\log2))+\tfrac12
=2.272283\ldots$ in place of $4$.

\item \textbf{Exact small cases and an elementary detector.}
We prove
\[
 h(7)=\hc(7)=7,\qquad
 h(p)=\hc(p)=8\quad(p=11,13,17).
\]
For every $m\ge2$, a separate elementary construction gives a
nonnegative Fourier moment on at most
$2\lceil\log_2m\rceil+2$ Boolean vertices.

\item \textbf{A strict norm improvement and a resolved extremizer question.}
If
\[
 c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}:=
 \sup_{\substack{G\text{ finite abelian, }|G|\text{ odd}\\
                       f:G\to\R,\ \E f=0,\ f\ne0}}
 \frac{\|f\|_{U^2}^{4}}{\|f\|_{U^d}^{4}},
\]
then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:34:eq:main-norm-interval}
 \frac{4804}{5465198316262956^{1/4}}
 \le c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le\frac{2}{3}.
\end{equation}
The lower endpoint is approximately $0.558729391$ and the upper
endpoint $0.666666667$. Every single inverse Fourier
pair has ratio at most $2/222^{1/4}\simeq0.518133595$, so it cannot
be extremal for this problem.

\item \textbf{A classification and a sharp cost of positivity.}
For an exact full-support cyclic quotient of any order $m$, its
moment is nonnegative for every real centered function precisely
when the quotient coordinates can be paired as $(a,-a)$.
The minimum such positive support satisfies
\[
 h_{\mathrm{pos}}(m)\sim\frac{4\log m}{\log\log m}.
\]
Thus universal positivity has asymptotically twice the support cost
of an unrestricted cyclic detector.

\item \textbf{A sharp nonuniform rigidity threshold.}
In the finite-fiber directional model of source~07, the optimal
universal strict threshold is
$[2+(2k-2)\kappa]^{-1}$ for Freiman order $k$ and fiber ratio
at most $\kappa$. Sharpness already holds with zero boundary loss.
\end{enumerate}

The determinant method is not presented as a new invention: Alon--Vu
provide the large inverse entry in a unimodular binary matrix
\cite{alonvu}, and Shitov supplies the composition strategy
\cite{shitov}. The moment method also precedes this report
\cite{repo34moments}. The contributions are the exact transfer,
the retained cyclic invariant and quantitative refinement, the
explicit certificates, and the new dual-function consequences.
Targeted primary-source searches did not locate these conclusions
in the same form. That search is not a certificate of historical
priority. Theorems are supported by their proofs, independently of
any priority claim.

The results refine local cube and rigidity estimates. A new bound
for the global extremal quantity $r_k(N)$ would require propagating
the changed estimates through a complete density-increment iteration.
That calculation remains a separate research task.

\begin{partabstract}{35}
We prove three quantitative refinements related to Gowers'
proof of Szemer\'edi's theorem, with the main emphasis on the
arrangement-selection step. For \(d\)-arrangements of \(k\)-cubes,
write \(m=2d\ge4\) and \(s=m2^k\). Weighting Fourier certificates
according to their actual probability, and imposing their necessary
degree balances before estimating their mass, gives the sufficient
field-size exponent
\[
 E_{k,m}=\max_{0\le t\le k}
 \frac{m\sum_{i=0}^t\binom{k}{i}-\binom{k}{t}}{t+1}.
\]
The retained-arrangement guarantee has powers
\(\alpha^s\eta^{s-1}\), as in the recent one-stage Fej\'er refinement,
while its convenient field-size exponent \(2s\) is replaced by
\(E_{k,m}\sim 2s/k\). For eight-arrangements and \(k=2\), the
comparison is \(128\) versus \(23\). The proof handles repeated
physical vertices and works over finite extension fields of
sufficient characteristic.

A second argument retains additional positive Fourier energy
configurations and proves
\(\norm{f}_{U^4}^{16}\ge5\norm{f}_{U^2}^{16}\)
for real mean-zero functions on finite abelian groups of odd order,
improving the strongest inspected \(U^4\) coefficient \(35/8\).
A third argument constructs polynomial phases for which every
sufficiently long flat progression has step divisible by an explicit
integer \(D\). For an allowed length set with numerical-semigroup
conductor \(C\), the exact eventual full-partition threshold is \(DC\).
This answers the inspected report's higher-degree divisibility question
and strengthens the corresponding necessary exponent for prescribed
lengths. Full proofs, exact finite checks, limitations, and a research
agenda are included. These results improve specified local statements;
they do not supply a new global bound for progression-free sets.
\end{partabstract}
\begin{quote}\small

No Lean verification, external refereeing, or established priority is claimed.
\end{quote}
\label{gsr:fm:35:sec:introduction}

Gowers' proof \cite{gowers} turns a failure of uniformity into
progressively more coherent algebraic structure and then into a density
increment. Its quantitative cost is distributed among several distinct
steps. A useful refinement must identify which step changes, preserve
the normalization needed by the next one, and state the new largeness
conditions explicitly. This article carries out that program for
arrangement selection and gives two additional, independently proved
results on the analytic and partition components.

The comparison is with the supplied ProveIt transcription and research
collection, fixed at commit \pinthirtyfive, together with earlier source archives
whose contents were already placed in that snapshot. In particular,
the comparison includes the current incoming Fej\'er, moment, and
higher-uniformity reports, not only the merged manuscript
\cite{repo35,repo35merged,repo35fejer,repo35moments,repo35higher}.
This matters: several seemingly natural improvements, including the
secondary three-cube constant, had already been obtained in those reports.

\subsection{The main advance: the mass of a relation stratum}

An arrangement consists of \(m=2d\) axis-parallel \(k\)-cubes with common
sides, lying on levels that satisfy one balanced relation. There are
\(s=m2^k\) labelled vertices. A map respects it when the corresponding
alternating sum of its values vanishes. The selection problem is to
retain many arrangements while making almost all retained arrangements
respected.

The original repeated cosine selection has a very large parameter
exponent. A recent repository report already replaces it by one
Fej\'er selection \cite{repo35fejer}. Its simple sufficient field-size
condition still pays for all short coefficient relations. We instead
make two distinctions. First, a coefficient array is sampled with a
product probability law whose largest atom is \(1/L\), where \(L\)
is the Fourier bandwidth. Second, after removing Boolean parity,
the array has a definite polynomial degree \(t\). A successful array
of that degree belongs to a linear subspace of dimension
\[
 D_t=m\sum_{i=0}^t\binom{k}{i}-\binom{k}{t},
\]
and each fixed array imposes at least \(t+1\) independent restrictions
in the relevant probability estimate, apart from a precisely controlled
degree-one diagonal. Combining these two facts yields a contribution
of order
\[
 L^{D_t}q^{-t-1}
\]
to the normalized error budget. The maximum of
\(D_t/(t+1)\), rather than the number of coefficient arrays, therefore
governs the sufficient exponent.

\begin{theorem}[Main selection consequence, informal notation]
\label{gsr:fm:35:thm:headline-selection}
Fix \(k\ge1\), \(d\ge2\), \(m=2d\), and a density \(0<\beta\le1\).
Suppose a map on a density-\(\beta\) subset of
\(\F_q^{k+1}\) respects at least a proportion \(\alpha\) of the
natural arrangement upper bound. Under the explicit field-size
and characteristic conditions of Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:35:sel:cor:explicit},
there is a subset with purity at least \(1/(1+\eta)\) and at least
\[
 \frac{\alpha^s\eta^{s-1}}{2(s+2)^s}
 \,\beta^{m-1}q^{(m+1)k+m-1}
\]
respected arrangements. For fixed \(k,m,\beta\), the field-size
condition is
\[
 q\ge C_{k,m,\beta}(\alpha\eta)^{-E_{k,m}},\qquad
 E_{k,m}=\max_{0\le t\le k}\frac{D_t}{t+1},
\]
together with a characteristic condition of order
\((\alpha\eta)^{-1}\). For prime fields the displayed sufficient
size condition below already enforces the characteristic condition.
\end{theorem}

The exact theorem, including a bandwidth that may be chosen freely,
is Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:35:sel:thm:exact}. The constant \(C_{k,m,\beta}\)
in the headline is not suppressed in the actual result.

\subsection{Two additional results}

The second result strengthens a real, centered norm comparison:
\[
 \norm{f}_{U^4}^{16}\ge5\norm{f}_{U^2}^{16}
 \qquad\text{for finite odd-order groups and }\E f=0.
\]
The new ingredient is a positive contribution from repeated-entry
additive configurations in the Fourier energy. It penalizes the third
harmonic that can otherwise reduce the fourth-order norm of a cosine.
The strongest inspected previous coefficient for this comparison is
\(35/8\), from \cite{repo35moments}. We distinguish this improvement at
\(U^4\) from higher-order bounds already available in that report.

The third result concerns simultaneous polynomial phases. Assigning
a different prime denominator to each degree makes flatness force
divisibility of the step, one degree at a time. If the phases have
degrees \(d_1,\ldots,d_\nu\), write
\[
 W=\sum_{i=1}^{\nu}\frac{d_i(d_i+1)}2.
\]
For minimum cell length \(L\) and oscillation tolerances \(\eps_i\),
the construction has
\[
 D\asymp_{d_1,\ldots,d_\nu}
 L^W\prod_{i=1}^{\nu}\eps_i^{-d_i}.
\]
Every good progression of length at least \(L\) has step divisible
by \(D\), regardless of where it starts. This converts the
numerical-semigroup conductor of the permitted cell lengths into an
exact partition threshold. It extends the linear construction of
\cite{repo35thresholds} and strengthens the polynomial endpoint
obstruction of \cite{repo35barrier}.

\begin{partabstract}{36}
Let $V=\Fp^n$, with $p$ odd, and let a multilinear frequency selector
$\sigma:V^k\to V^*$ be tested against the $k$-fold derivatives of a
$1$-bounded function $f$. We prove the dimension-independent sharp implication
\[
 \E_{\hh}\abs{\widehat{\partial_{\hh}f}(\sigma(\hh))}^{2}
 >1-(1-1/p)^k
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 (\hh,y)\longmapsto\sigma(\hh)(y)\text{ is fully symmetric}.
\]
The threshold is attained by nonsymmetric selectors in every dimension at
least two, even when the selector is symmetric in its first $k$ variables.
A stronger estimate averages $p^{-r}$ over the half-ranks of the alternating
bilinear slices and retains the amplitudes of the frozen derivatives.
The proof uses an explicit finite Heisenberg orthogonality inequality,
proved here by a short eigenspace-multiplicity argument; its equality and
stability structure are also derived. If $p>k+1$, symmetry yields a canonical
polynomial $P(x)=\sigma(x,\ldots,x)(x)/(k+1)!$ and an exact identity between
the tested energy and $\|f e_p(-P)\|_{U^{k+1}}^{2^{k+1}}$, with a pointwise
identity before averaging. This refines the global phase-extraction step
around Proposition 17.2 of Gowers's proof and extends it to vector spaces.
We give noisy-selector, dense-domain, coset, multiaffine, and prime-power
variants, together with explicit limitations in small characteristic.
The proposed contribution is a sharp local criterion, not a new global
Szemer\'edi bound or a general quantitative inverse theorem. The proofs
are self-contained; computational checks are supplementary. Priority has
not been established, and the manuscript is not proof-assistant verified.
\end{partabstract}

\subsection{A precise extremal problem}
Gowers's global phase-extraction argument in Section 17 of
\cite{gowers} starts with large Fourier coefficients of multiplicative
derivatives along a multilinear frequency pattern. Over a one-dimensional
prime field the relevant multilinear form is automatically symmetric.
Over a vector space that property is no longer automatic. This distinction
suggests an extremal question that can be answered exactly:
\begin{quote}
How much derivative-spectrum energy can a genuinely nonsymmetric
multilinear selector carry, uniformly in the dimension and in the bounded
function being differentiated?
\end{quote}
Here and throughout, ``nonsymmetric'' refers to all variables, including
the variable on which the selected frequency is evaluated. Symmetry merely
among the derivative directions is weaker.

Fix an odd prime $p$, an integer $k\geq1$, and $V=\Fp^n$. The dual $V^*$
consists of $\Fp$-linear functionals $V\to\Fp$. All averages are normalized.
Set $e_p(t)=\exp(2\pi i t/p)$ and use the conventions
\begin{align}
 \partial_h f(x)&=f(x+h)\overline{f(x)},\label{gsr:fm:36:ssc:eq:derivative}\\
 \widehat g(\xi)&=\E_{x\in V}g(x)e_p(-\xi(x)).\label{gsr:fm:36:ssc:eq:fourier}
\end{align}
Write $\partial_{\hh}=\partial_{h_1}\cdots\partial_{h_k}$. The derivatives
commute. A function is $1$-bounded when $|f(x)|\leq1$ for every $x$.

For a multilinear $\sigma:V^k\to V^*$ define
\begin{equation}
 \A_f(\sigma)=\E_{\hh\in V^k}
       \abs{\widehat{\partial_{\hh}f}(\sigma(\hh))}^{2},
 \qquad T(h_1,\ldots,h_k,y)=\sigma(h_1,\ldots,h_k)(y).
 \label{gsr:fm:36:ssc:eq:energy}
\end{equation}
Thus $T$ is a scalar $(k+1)$-linear form, and $0\leq\A_f(\sigma)\leq1$
for $1$-bounded $f$. Put
\begin{equation}
 \thresh=1-(1-1/p)^k.\label{gsr:fm:36:ssc:eq:threshold}
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp symmetry certification]\label{gsr:fm:36:ssc:thm:main}
Let $f:V\to\C$ be $1$-bounded and let $\sigma:V^k\to V^*$ be
multilinear. If $T$ is not fully symmetric, then
\begin{equation}
 \A_f(\sigma)\leq\thresh.\label{gsr:fm:36:ssc:eq:mainbound}
\end{equation}
Consequently $\A_f(\sigma)>\thresh$ forces full symmetry. For every
odd prime $p$, every $k\geq1$, and every $n\geq2$, equality in
\eqref{gsr:fm:36:ssc:eq:mainbound} is attained by a nonsymmetric $T$ and a
unit-modulus $f$. The selector in this example is symmetric in its
first $k$ variables.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 40--46]
\emph{Characteristic two and general groups} (sources~43 and~46, Section~\ref{gsr:fp:sec:binary}). Source~43's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:group-symmetry} proves the threshold $1-(1-1/p_*(G))^k$ on every noncyclic finite abelian group, $p_*(G)$ the least $p$ with a quotient $\F_p^2$, characteristic two included; for symmetric trilinear forms over $\F_2^n$ sources~43 and~46 determine the exact energy $2^{-r/2}$ and the integrable codimension $r/2$.
\end{writenote}

This theorem determines the supremum in the stated extremal problem; it
is not a claim to have settled a previously named conjecture. Its proof
will follow from a more informative rank-profile estimate. The basic
constant is useful in a large-characteristic regime:
\begin{equation}
 \thresh\leq\frac{k}{p},\qquad
 \thresh=\frac{k}{p}-\binom{k}{2}\frac1{p^2}+O_k(p^{-3}).
 \label{gsr:fm:36:ssc:eq:thresholdexpansion}
\end{equation}
In particular a fixed energy lower bound $a>0$ certifies symmetry whenever
$p>k/a$. This restriction matters: for fixed $p$ and very small energy the
criterion may say nothing.

\begin{theorem}[Canonical, lossless phase extraction]\label{gsr:fm:36:ssc:thm:extraction}
Suppose that $p>k+1$ and that $T$ is fully symmetric. Define
\begin{equation}
 P(x)=\frac{T(x,\ldots,x)}{(k+1)!},\qquad g(x)=f(x)e_p(-P(x)).
 \label{gsr:fm:36:ssc:eq:canonical}
\end{equation}
For every $\hh\in V^k$, not just on average,
\begin{equation}
 \abs{\widehat{\partial_{\hh}f}(\sigma(\hh))}
       =\abs{\E_x\partial_{\hh}g(x)}.
 \label{gsr:fm:36:ssc:eq:pointwise}
\end{equation}
Therefore
\begin{equation}
 \A_f(\sigma)=\norm{f e_p(-P)}_{U^{k+1}}^{2^{k+1}}.
 \label{gsr:fm:36:ssc:eq:lossless}
\end{equation}
In particular the conclusion holds if the energy exceeds $\thresh$.
For the identity itself neither an energy lower bound nor boundedness of
$f$ is needed.
\end{theorem}

The diagonal polynomial in this statement is elementary polarization,
not a new integration mechanism. The refinement is the explicit,
pointwise, equality-form interface together with a sharp test that
certifies its symmetry hypothesis in arbitrary dimension.

\subsection{What is, and is not, improved}
Proposition 17.2 in the corrected ProveIt transcription assumes
$k+1<N$ and concludes a polynomial of degree at most $k+1$
\cite{repo36}. We retain that indexing. In its global one-dimensional
setting, Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:36:ssc:thm:extraction} gives a particular polynomial
and equality, rather than selecting a phase through a mixed cube
inequality. Its scalar lower bound in the parameter $\alpha$ already
has coefficient one; we do not claim to improve that coefficient.
The genuinely additional quantitative statement is
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:36:ssc:thm:main} and its rank-profile refinement over vector spaces.

The finite Heisenberg representation theory behind the proof is standard;
see, for example, Gurevich--Hadani \cite{gurevichhadani}. The present manuscript
proves the needed finite-dimensional facts directly. Existing inverse
theorems also address much weaker correlations and much more general
intermediate forms. In particular, Tidor \cite{tidor} separates
symmetrization from integration in low characteristic. Our exact
criterion is for the derivative array of one function and does not
replace general mixed-function symmetrization.

The contemporary benchmark also includes Mili\'cevi\'c's September 2026
preprint \cite{milicevic}, whose stated high-characteristic inverse
theorem has quasipolynomial bounds. We do not derive a competing inverse
theorem here. Nor do we change an estimate for progression-free subsets
of $[N]$; for comparison, Leng--Sah--Sawhney \cite{lssbounds} prove, for
$\ell\geq5$, bounds of the form
$r_\ell(N)\ll N\exp(- (\log\log N)^{c_\ell})$.
These comparisons delimit the claim, rather than supply ingredients for
our proofs.

Source~38 reproves the same gap for odd order (its Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:38:lem:odd-twirl}). Its macros \texttt{\textbackslash T} (the circle $\R/2\pi\Z$), \texttt{\textbackslash Prob} (calligraphic $\mathcal P$, a set of measures), \texttt{\textbackslash code} (\texttt{\textbackslash nolinkurl}) and \texttt{\textbackslash pin} are renamed \texttt{\textbackslash Tthirtyseven}, \texttt{\textbackslash Probthirtyseven}, \texttt{\textbackslash codethirtyseven} and \texttt{\textbackslash pinthirtyseven}; its `question' environment (``Question'', numbered on its own counter within sections) is set in this report's `Question' style, and its Questions~11.1--11.10 keep their indices. \begin{partabstract}{37}
A missing interval forces a low Fourier coefficient. We solve an exact version
of this problem in the first nontrivial spectral window, including the complete
tradeoff between interval mass and a uniform bound on finitely many Fourier
moments. For a probability measure on the circle and
$\pi/(R+1)<a<2\pi/(R+1)$, the optimal lower bound for the largest of its first
$R$ Fourier coefficients, when the open arc $(-a,a)$ is empty, is
\[
 \rho_R(a)=\frac{1}{R-\cot(a/2)\tan((R+1)a/2)}.
\]
The proof gives a positive-coefficient polynomial certificate, a unique
$R+1$-point extremizer, exact noisy-gap extremizers, and stability estimates.
A finite-cyclic consequence replaces the frequency range $(N/M)^2$ in the
proof-supported version of Gowers's Lemma 5.2 by $\lfloor N/M\rfloor-1$, and
replaces the coefficient bound $tM/(4N)$ by $tM/(N-M)$. Using the same Weyl
input, a separate optimization of the Dirichlet denominator improves the
monomial-recurrence exponent in Lemma 5.5. All new assertions are proved in the
manuscript; the quantitative Weyl estimate is an explicitly identified input.
Numerical and symbolic regression checks, a repository integration plan, and
further research problems accompany the proofs.
\end{partabstract}
\begin{quote}\small
\noindent\textbf{Status and scope.}
This is an unrefereed mathematical research draft, not a Lean-verified result.
The exact formulas and refinements are developed and proved here, but their
historical priority is not established. Classical positive-polynomial and
truncated-moment machinery is credited explicitly. No improved global
Szemer\'edi bound or record Diophantine-approximation bound is claimed.

\smallskip
\noindent Intended integration: \codethirtyseven{Combinatorics/Ramsey/Research/GowersSzemeredi/}
\end{quote}

\subsection{A local bottleneck with an exact extremal formulation}
The target is the missing-interval step in Section 5 of Gowers's proof
\cite{gowers}. A positive measure supported away from zero must have a
nontrivial low Fourier moment. Gowers uses an interval convolution and a
Fourier tail estimate. The present approach constructs a genuinely
bandlimited polynomial with the required sign pattern. The resulting
improvement is not just a change in a tail constant: the frequency scale
changes from quadratic to linear in the inverse gap radius.

The natural optimization problem is more informative than the single lemma.
Given a gap radius $a$ and a cutoff $R$, how small can all of the first $R$
Fourier moments be? If those moments are merely small rather than forced by an
empty gap, how much mass must lie in the gap? We solve both questions exactly
when $\pi<(R+1)a<2\pi$. We also identify the equality measures, prove a
quantitative rigidity statement, and derive a recurrence consequence using
an independently adjustable Dirichlet scale.

\subsection{The precise baseline}
The repository version of Section 5 distinguishes a printed assertion from
what its proof supports \cite{repo37}. Its formal target for Lemma 5.2 uses
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:37:eq:old52}
 0<|r|_N\le \frac{N^2}{M^2},\qquad
 |\widehat{1_A}(r)|\ge \frac{|A|M}{4N},
\end{equation}
under the assumptions $0<M$, $M$ even, $2M\le N$, and
$A\cap[-M,M)=\varnothing$ in $\Z/N\Z$. Here the Fourier transform is
unnormalized and $|r|_N$ is the least absolute residue. The printed statement
has $1/2$ where the displayed proof gives $1/4$. We compare with the
proof-supported $1/4$ version. This does \emph{not} assert that the printed
$1/2$ inequality is false: the stronger theorem below implies it.

The source file \codethirtyseven{Proofs05PolynomialPartition.lean} already handles
colliding polynomial values with a multiplicity function. We retain that
correction and do not present it as a new contribution. Likewise, the
repository's squared threshold for square-root-length recurrence is respected;
we do not substitute an unrounded real square root into a theorem whose
hypothesis is an integer sample length.

The main inspected Section 5 files are pinned at
\begin{center}\small\pinthirtyseven.\end{center}
The research-directory README was also inspected for overlap. It describes
many earlier refinements of density extraction, cube counts, arrangement
selection, and related inverse steps. The present manuscript instead focuses
on the missing-interval extremal problem and its recurrence consequence. That
comparison is an overlap audit of the inspected material, not an assertion
that all unpublished work or all classical literature has been exhausted.

\subsection{What is proved, and what is imported}
The main exact theorem is Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:37:thm:main}. Its lower bound uses an
explicit trigonometric polynomial. Its attainment uses a finite-dimensional
moment criterion proved in Section~\ref{gsr:dt:37:sec:moments}; this is classical
positive-polynomial territory, closely related to the frequency-selective
Toeplitz decomposition of Yang and Xie \cite{yangxie}. The explicit extremal
formula, equality analysis, and application are the focus here, not a claim to
have invented the general moment criterion.

The recurrence argument imports the Weyl inequality in a precisely stated
form. It does not claim to improve that inequality. Work such as Baker's on
small fractional parts \cite{baker} and Maynard's on simultaneous polynomial
recurrence \cite{maynard} belongs to a stronger and broader
Diophantine-approximation literature. Our recurrence theorem is a transparent
improvement of the selected local argument, not a claim of a best-known
exponent. Propagating it through the polynomial partition and the later
Szemer\'edi induction is a further problem, not a completed consequence.

\section[{Source 38: Research question, main results, and provenance}]{Source 38. Research question, main results, and provenance}\label{gsr:fm:38:sec:d1}
\srcnote{38}{Section 1}
\partsource{\textbf{Added in the seventh write, 6~October 2026. Delivered title block.} ``Exact Quotient Reduction and Sharp Stability in Gowers' Ramsey Framework / Characteristic-five cube extremizers, odd-order rigidity, and six-term norm-extension defects / Prepared for Vladimir Reshetnikov / Mathematical development and verification with ChatGPT / 6 October 2026''; \emph{the PDF author field reads ``Mathematical research developed with ChatGPT for Vladimir Reshetnikov''}. Archive \file{gowers\_quotients\_rigidity.zip} (arrival \texttt{b103a65d4}), manuscript \file{gowers\_quotients\_rigidity.tex} (3,217 lines, 46 pages), pin \texttt{12da35673} (its \file{SOURCE\_LEDGER.json}, shipped as \file{data/38-quotients-SOURCE\_LEDGER.json}). Printed below: the abstract and Section~1; its four delivered \texttt{\textbackslash part} headings are printed, unnumbered, at the head of the sections they introduce: Part~I (Sections~2--5) is a chapter of Part~III (Section~\ref{gsr:cc:sec:quotient}), Part~II (Section~6) a chapter of Part~II (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:oddstability}), Part~III (Section~7) a chapter of Part~III (Section~\ref{gsr:cc:sec:sixterm}), Part~IV (Sections~8--10) is in Part~V. Its macro \texttt{\textbackslash Q} (the cube count, a calligraphic $\mathcal C_3$) is renamed \texttt{\textbackslash Qthirtyeight}, and its \texttt{\textbackslash ip} (no \texttt{\textbackslash left}/\texttt{\textbackslash right}) is set as source~31's \texttt{\textbackslash ipthirtyone}, which has the same definition; its figure path is renamed to the shipped file.}
\begin{partabstract}{38}
We resolve three local questions left open by the preceding Ramsey
research reports. First, on every nontrivial finite abelian group of
exponent five, the maximum three-cube count of a real perturbation of
a positive constant, at fixed centered $U^3$ norm $u$, reduces exactly
to a five-point quotient whenever $u/\delta\le10^{-5}$. Every maximizer
has this quotient form. The proof retains a coercive Fourier energy
defect and shows that the sixth- and seventh-degree errors are linear
in the norm lost under projection. This settles the formerly
undetermined dimension-uniform eighth-order coefficient at $20/9$.
We additionally obtain the tenth- and twelfth-order coefficients
$869/(216\,2^{3/4})$ and $65759/(5832\,2^{3/2})$, an even analytic
extremal profile, and quantitative control of the off-quotient remainder.
More generally, for every fixed odd exponent $m$, exact reduction to a
cyclic quotient holds when $u/\delta\le10^{-8}m^{-8}$.

Second, we determine the sharp odd-order local stability modulus for
the critical $U^3$--$L^2$ inequality through its first fractional term:
$\varepsilon/4+3\varepsilon^2/16+
(\sqrt2/64)\varepsilon^{5/2}+O(\varepsilon^3)$.
The fractional term is forced by order-three characters and disappears
when the group order is coprime to six. A finite Weyl-coset expansion
gives an explicit uniform error bound.

Third, for a layered linear--cubic--quintic norm coloring plus an
arbitrary function of independent coordinates, we calculate the exact
number of symmetric six-term progressions. Its excess above the basic
surjectivity count is governed by centered third and fifth differences
and a quadratic-character statistic. All three results have complete
proofs, sharpness or equality analysis, and reproducible checks.
They refine local parts of Gowers' framework; they do not produce a
new global bound in Szemer\'edi's theorem.
\end{partabstract}
\label{gsr:fm:38:sec:introduction}

The supplied Ramsey project contains both a reconstruction of
Gowers' proof of Szemer\'edi's theorem and a growing collection of
local refinements \cite{gowers,repo38,repo38collected}.
A useful next contribution must do more than repeat the existing
density-selection estimates or improve a constant already computed
in another report. We therefore start from three explicitly
unresolved questions: whether characteristic-five cube extremizers
depend only on a five-point quotient, what the optimal
odd-order stability coefficients are, and how higher norm layers
interact with independent additions to a coloring.

The first question has the strongest answer here. The ambient number
of variables disappears from the entire small-norm optimization
problem. The equality of maxima is exact, has a dimension-independent
numerical range, and includes a classification of all maximizing
functions by a quotient. The second result identifies a new
fractional-power correction rather than only improving a rough
integer-power bound. The third supplies an exact formula for the first
extension problem where two nonlinear norm layers interact.

\subsection{Three distinct extremal problems}

For a finite abelian group $G$, all spatial averages are normalized.
For real $W$ put
\[
 \Qthirtyeight(W)=\E_{x,h_1,h_2,h_3\in G}
       \prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^3}W(x+\omega\cdot h)
       =\|W\|_{U^3}^8.
\]
For a nontrivial $G$ and $\delta,u>0$, define
\[
 \mathcal M_{\delta,G}(u)
 =\max\{\Qthirtyeight(\delta+f): f:G\to\R,\ \E f=0,\
                                  \|f\|_{U^3}=u\}.
\]
The maximum exists because the norm sphere in this finite-dimensional
real space is compact.

\begin{theorem}[Main quotient and expansion theorem]
\label{gsr:fm:38:thm:main-quotient}
If $G$ is nontrivial and $5G=0$, then
\[
 \mathcal M_{\delta,G}(u)=\mathcal M_{\delta,\Z/5\Z}(u)
       \qquad(0<u\le10^{-5}\delta).
\]
Every maximizer factors through a nonzero homomorphism
$G\to\Z/5\Z$. As $u/\delta\to0$,
\begin{align}
 \mathcal M_{\delta,G}(u)
 ={}&\delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4
       +\frac{2^{3/4}}3\delta^2u^6+\frac{20}{9}u^8 \notag\\
    &+\frac{869}{216\,2^{3/4}}\frac{u^{10}}{\delta^2}
       +\frac{65759}{5832\,2^{3/2}}\frac{u^{12}}{\delta^4}
       +O\!\left(\frac{u^{14}}{\delta^6}\right).
 \label{gsr:fm:38:eq:main-cube-expansion}
\end{align}
The implicit constant is absolute and independent of $G$.
More generally, the extremal value is given near zero by a convergent
power series in $(u/\delta)^2$, multiplied by $\delta^8$.
For $0<\delta<1$, the same maximum is attainable with
$0\le\delta+f\le1$ if also
$4u\le\min\{\delta,1-\delta\}$.
\end{theorem}

The exact reduction is proved in Section~\ref{gsr:cc:38:sec:quotient};
the analytic calculation, including its phase optimization, is in
Section~\ref{gsr:cc:38:sec:five-profile}. The small numerical cutoff is an explicit sufficient certificate;
its optimal value remains to be determined. The convergent
series is asserted on a possibly smaller absolute neighborhood of
zero, as is appropriate for the implicit function theorem.

The quotient principle extends beyond exponent five. If $G$ has
fixed odd exponent $m\ge3$, then
\[
 \mathcal M_{\delta,G}(u)=\mathcal M_{\delta,\Z/m\Z}(u)
       \quad\text{for }0<u\le10^{-8}m^{-8}\delta.
\]
Every maximizing function factors through some cyclic quotient of order
dividing $m$. This broader result, proved after the five-point profile,
separates the arithmetic of a single cyclic group from the ambient
number of variables. The dependence of the sufficient cutoff on $m$
is not claimed optimal.

A separate problem concerns large uniformity norm relative to $L^2$.
Let $\Qcos(G)$ be the normalized quadratic phases on subgroup cosets,
as defined precisely in Part~II. For $\|v\|_2=1$, set
\[
 \kappa(v)=\|v\|_{U^3}^8,\qquad
 \mathcal F(v)=\max_{\psi\in\Qcos(G)}|\ipthirtyone v\psi|^2.
\]
Thus $\mathcal F$ is squared correlation, sometimes called fidelity.
Define the worst infidelity at deficit at most $\varepsilon$ by
\[
 \mathfrak S_{\rm odd}(\varepsilon)
 =\sup_{\substack{|G|\ {\rm odd}\\\|v\|_2=1\\
                         \kappa(v)\ge1-\varepsilon}}
                      (1-\mathcal F(v)).
\]

\begin{theorem}[Main odd-order stability theorem]
\label{gsr:fm:38:thm:main-odd}
Uniformly over finite abelian groups of odd order,
\[
 \mathfrak S_{\rm odd}(\varepsilon)
 =\frac{\varepsilon}{4}+\frac{3\varepsilon^2}{16}
       +\frac{\sqrt2}{64}\varepsilon^{5/2}
       +O(\varepsilon^3).
\]
For the supremum restricted to $\gcd(|G|,6)=1$, the corresponding formula is
\[
 \mathfrak S_{6'}(\varepsilon)
 =\frac{\varepsilon}{4}+\frac{3\varepsilon^2}{16}
       +O(\varepsilon^3).
\]
Both assertions are sharp through the displayed orders.
\end{theorem}

An explicit finite estimate and matching examples are proved in
Section~\ref{gsr:en:38:sec:odd-local}. Here the parameter measures proximity to
a \emph{maximal} norm under an $L^2$ constraint. It is unrelated to the
small centered norm in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:38:thm:main-quotient}.

The third result concerns a finite field $\F_q$ of characteristic
greater than five. Let $N_j:\F_{q^j}\to\F_q$ be the field norm and
let $R:\F_q^e\to\F_q$ be arbitrary. For
\[
 P(a,u,v,w)=a+N_3(u)+N_5(v)+R(w),
\]
we count all nonzero directions for which the six values at a
center plus $\pm h/2,\pm3h/2,\pm5h/2$ agree in opposite pairs.
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:38:thm:six-ap-defect} gives the exact count in terms of
third and fifth differences of $R$, with a quadratic-character
correction. Equality in the earlier surjectivity bound is classified
by additive quadraticity of $R$. These are symmetric color equalities;
the six colors need not all coincide.

\Needspace{17\baselineskip}
\subsection{What is added to the preceding reports}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}P{.25\textwidth}P{.36\textwidth}P{.33\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Question & Previously established & Addition in this article\\ \midrule
Characteristic-five cube profile
& Sharp $u^6$ coefficient; $20/9$ at order $u^8$ on $\Z/5\Z$ only
  \cite{repo38five,repo38thresholds}
& Exact quotient reduction, all ambient dimensions, $u^{10}$ and $u^{12}$
  coefficients, and a theorem for every fixed odd exponent\\
Odd-order critical-norm stability
& An envelope with coefficient $12$; its optimal odd-order second
  coefficient left open \cite{repo38rigidity}
& Sharp asymptotic coefficient $6$, the order-three fractional
  correction, and a uniform finite remainder\\
Independent additions to norm colorings
& Surjectivity for complete norm cores and an exact cubic-core defect
  \cite{repo38degrees}
& Exact six-term count for the cubic--quintic core, including the
  character correction and zero-defect classification\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The old five-point coefficient $20/9$ is not presented as newly
calculated here. The new conclusion is that it governs the unrestricted
dimension-uniform problem, because all exact maximizers reduce to
five points. The tenth- and twelfth-order coefficients and the exact quotient
theorems are additional results. Likewise, the norm-layer construction
itself is due to earlier work; our addition is its exact response to
an arbitrary independent extension.

\subsection{Literature and scope}

Gowers' Lemmas~3.8--3.10 supply cube Cauchy--Schwarz, the norm triangle
inequality, and an upper cube-count bound \cite{gowers}. Part~I
sharpens the last of these in a specified finite-field regime.
The underlying norm-geometric perspective is consistent with
Hatami's work on generalizations of Gowers norms \cite{hatami}.
For the critical $U^3$--$L^2$ problem, the classification of extremizers
and qualitative near-extremizers is established by Eisner--Tao
\cite[Theorem~1.4]{eisnertao}. Weyl operators and isotropic subgroups
also occur in stabilizer testing \cite{gnw}; our calculation determines
a particular sharp asymptotic modulus within that framework.

For symmetric progression colorings, Shi--Dong's layered norm method
is the relevant primary source \cite{shidong}. Their paper also explains
why the historical conjectures in Gowers' Section~4 cannot simply be
treated as unresolved in 2026. We use the construction as prior work
and study an exact extension question, without claiming a better
coloring exponent.

The present results do not improve the global size bound for
progression-free subsets of the integers. For orientation, the
Leng--Sah--Sawhney theorem gives, for fixed $k\ge5$,
\[
 r_k(N)\ll_k N\exp\bigl(-(\log\log N)^{c_k}\bigr),\qquad c_k>0
 \quad\cite{lssbounds}.
\]
A local sharp coefficient does not imply an improvement of this
theorem or of the complete historical density-increment argument.
In particular, an exponent-five group has no arithmetic progression
with more than five distinct points, although its cube norms remain
well defined.

The claims here are mathematical statements with proofs and finite
verification, developed with AI assistance. Independent checks in
this package are separate AI derivations and computations, not
external refereeing or Lean kernel certification. The source search
establishes the relation to the inspected reports and papers; it
does not establish exhaustive bibliographic priority.

\section[{Source 39: The local problem and the scope of the improvement}]{Source 39. The local problem and the scope of the improvement}\label{gsr:fm:39:sec:d1}
\srcnote{39}{Section 1}
\partsource{\textbf{Added in the seventh write, 6~October 2026. Delivered title block.} ``Optimal Shared-Anchor Interpolation and Labelled Slice Refinement in Gowers's Szemer\'edi Argument / Exact finite minimax bounds, sharp Poisson limits, and a replacement for the sampling step of Lemma 16.10 / Research manuscript prepared with ChatGPT for Vladimir Reshetnikov / 6 October 2026''; \emph{the PDF author field reads the same}. Archive \file{ramsey\_shared\_anchor\_interpolation.zip} (arrival \texttt{b103a65d4}), manuscript \file{article.tex} (2,164 lines, 31 pages), pin \texttt{869289aa3} (its \file{SOURCE\_AUDIT.md}, shipped as \file{39-shared-anchor-SOURCE\_AUDIT.md}). Printed below: the abstract, its keywords and Section~1; Sections~2--11 form a chapter of Part~II (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:sharedanchor}), Sections~12--15 and Appendices~A--B are in Part~V. Its macro \texttt{\textbackslash file} (typewriter type, detokenized) is set as this report's \texttt{\textbackslash filename}, which has the same definition, and its \texttt{\textbackslash pin} is renamed \texttt{\textbackslash pinthirtynine}; its `question' environment (``Research question'', on the shared counter) is set in this report's `Research question' style.}
\begin{partabstract}{39}
A local step in Gowers's proof of Szemer\'edi's theorem selects common column
coordinates from which affine functions on many different fibres can be
reconstructed. We replace size truncation followed by repeated sampling with
uniform sampling of a fixed-size subset, retaining targets that are themselves
sampled. For fibres partitioned into at most $q$ reconstruction classes and a
threshold of $t$ distinct anchors, we prove that $r$ shared anchors leave at most
$tq(m-r)/(m(r+1))$ of the ambient mass uncertified, where $m$ is the number of
columns. In particular, affine reconstruction has an $O(q/\sigma)$ anchor budget
at exceptional mass $\sigma$, without a minimum class size or a separate
long-column hypothesis.

We determine the exact finite minimax loss, prove that balanced class sizes
capped at the first one-class maximum attain it, and obtain an explicit
quadratic formula for the affine cap. Matching permutation-orbit examples
and an exact conditional-expectation algorithm are supplied. A uniform hypergeometric-to-Poisson
argument yields the complete asymptotic profile for $r\to\infty$ and $r/m\to0$.
For affine reconstruction in the low-loss regime, the sharp coefficient is
$\varphi^3e^{-\varphi}=0.8399620946\ldots$, where $\varphi$ is the golden ratio.
We also prove higher-degree and interpolation-space extensions, an additive
corruption bound, and a labelled slice-refinement theorem that avoids replacing
each individual slice list by the entire union list.

The results are local to the interpolation mechanism. Their finite minimax
optimality concerns the explicitly defined certification rule, not unrestricted
algebraic reconstruction. We compare the new bounds with the inspected
\repo\ development, including its existing sampled-or-anchored interface and
geometric synchronization. The separate closing-parameter obstruction in
Lemma 16.10 is not resolved. Complete mathematical proofs and reproducible
exact-arithmetic checks are supplied; no new Lean theorem is claimed to have
been kernel-checked, and priority has not been established.
\end{partabstract}
\begin{quote}\small
\noindent\textbf{Keywords.} Szemer\'edi's theorem; shared sampling; hypergeometric
occupancy; minimax bounds; interpolation; multilinear graph covers.
\end{quote}
\label{gsr:fm:39:sec:introduction}

\subsection{Why the interpolation step is worth isolating}
Gowers's argument \cite{gowers} passes through functions that are approximately
polynomial in several variables. In the step surrounding Lemma 16.10, a
function of a base variable $h$ and a final coordinate $x$ is covered, on each
vertical fibre, by a bounded number of affine graphs. One seeks a small set of
coordinates $a_1,\ldots,a_r$ that can serve as interpolation anchors for many
fibres simultaneously. The horizontal sections at those coordinates can then
be refined and lifted to multilinear candidates in $(h,x)$.

The important word is \emph{simultaneously}. Selecting two points separately in
each fibre does not give a bounded family of horizontal sections. Conversely,
requiring every fibre class to be hit by a common sample is unnecessarily
strong. The argument only needs to discard a small amount of total ambient
mass. That distinction makes a size-weighted sampling estimate more effective
than a worst-class failure estimate followed by a union bound.

The printed argument first removes small classes, then samples with
replacement. Its estimate for the chance of obtaining two distinct points
uses a two-hit expression that does not account for repeated draws of the same
point. The inspected \repo\ development already records this obstruction and
proves corrected distinct-anchor sampling statements
\cite{repo39distinct,repo39anchored}. The counterexample and its repair are not
new results of this article.

The repository also already handles short column sets by sampling all columns
and allowing a target to survive when its own column is sampled
\cite{repo39short}. Its later files perform a common slice refinement and
synchronize suitable rectangular products into proper common-step boxes
\cite{repo39recovered,repo39sync,repo39syncslice}. We use these facts to identify
precisely what is improved here: the \emph{mass-weighted shared sample}, its
\emph{exact extremal theory}, and the \emph{preservation of individual slice
lists}. We do not claim that direct sampling or synchronized interpolation is
new to the repository.

\subsection{The principal statements}
Write $J$ for an $m$-element set of columns. In row $h$, let $B_h\subseteq J$ be
the domain of interest, partitioned into at most $q$ classes. A target is
certified if it lies in the sample itself, or if its class contains $t$ distinct
sampled columns. For affine functions $t=2$; for polynomials of degree at most
$d$, take $t=d+1$.

The basic bound, proved in Section~\ref{gsr:en:39:sec:selection}, is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:39:eq:intro-bound}
 \min_{|R|=r}\frac{1}{m|H|}\sum_{h\in H}|B_h\setminus K_h(R)|
 \le \frac{tq(m-r)}{m(r+1)}.
\end{equation}
Here $K_h(R)$ is the certified set. The same statement holds for arbitrary
nonnegative row weights, with $q$ replaced by the weighted mean number of
classes. The minimum is over one set $R$ shared by every row.

The finite answer is more precise. Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:39:eq:intro-loss}
 \ell_{m,r,t}(s)=\frac{1}{m\binom mr}
 \sum_{j=0}^{\min(s,r,t-1)}(s-j)\binom sj\binom{m-s}{r-j}.
\end{equation}
Then the worst possible best-anchor loss is exactly
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:39:eq:intro-minimax}
 \cM_{m,q,r,t}=
 \max_{\substack{s_1,\ldots,s_q\in\N_0\\s_1+\cdots+s_q\le m}}
 \sum_{i=1}^q\ell_{m,r,t}(s_i).
\end{equation}
The upper bound is an averaging argument. For the reverse inequality we build a
family containing all coordinate permutations of an extremizing class profile;
every anchor set then has the same loss. Section~\ref{gsr:en:39:sec:finite-shape} goes
further: an optimal profile is balanced and capped at the first maximum of
$\ell$, and the affine cap has an explicit quadratic-radical formula. Thus the
finite minimax problem is solved without an optimization oracle.

Set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:39:eq:intro-F}
 F_t(x)=xe^{-x}\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}\frac{x^j}{j!},\qquad
 \lambda_t=\mathop{\rm argmax}_{x\ge0}F_t(x),\qquad
 \kappa_t=F_t(\lambda_t).
\end{equation}
For fixed $t$, as $r\to\infty$, $r/m\to0$, and $q/r$ remains bounded,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:39:eq:intro-asymptotic}
 \cM_{m,q,r,t}=
 \frac qr\left[F_t\!\left(\min\left\{\lambda_t,\frac rq\right\}\right)
 +o(1)\right].
\end{equation}
In particular, if also $q/r\to0$, then
$\cM_{m,q,r,t}\sim\kappa_t q/r$. For $t=2$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:39:eq:intro-golden}
 \lambda_2=\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2},\qquad
 \kappa_2=\varphi^3e^{-\varphi}.
\end{equation}
Thus the order $q/\sigma$ of the sufficient affine anchor budget is optimal for
this class-based certification mechanism in a sparse-sampling regime.

\subsection{What is, and is not, being optimized}
The minimax game fixes a recovery rule. It does not charge computation time,
and it does not allow extra algebraic information to certify a point that the
rule leaves uncertified. An interpolation routine might infer a polynomial
from other identities, notice that two labelled classes carry the same
polynomial, or exploit special geometric restrictions on the row family.
Those possibilities are deliberately outside the lower-bound model.

This distinction is particularly important in applying the results to
Gowers's proof: the extremizing permutation-orbit examples are arbitrary
families of class partitions. We do not show that they satisfy every other
hypothesis of the full inverse argument. Our sharpness assertion is a sharp
statement about a local reusable lemma, not a lower bound for Szemer\'edi
numbers or for the entire inverse theorem.

Occupancy and missing-mass optimization are established subjects. Berend and
Kontorovich study extremal expected missing mass \cite{missingmass};
low-frequency occupancy masses also occur in work on Good--Turing estimation
\cite{painsky}. We therefore make no claim to originate occupancy methods.
The package here connects a finite, without-replacement, partial-domain
occupancy problem to shared interpolation, proves its exact minimax
realization, and tracks the resulting labelled graph-cover parameters.
All arguments needed for our results are included below.

\section[{Source 40: The local problem and the contribution}]{Source 40. The local problem and the contribution}\label{gsr:fm:40:sec:d1}
\srcnote{40}{Section 1}
\partsource{\textbf{Added in the eighth write, 7~October 2026. Delivered title block.} ``One-stage Fej\'er selection for Gowers arrangements / Single-monomial relation isolation, polynomial parameter loss, and sharp exponents within a positive-Fourier selection class / Research note prepared for the ProveIt repository / October 6, 2026''; \emph{the PDF author field reads the same; no statement on AI assistance is made}. Archive \file{fejer-arrangement-selection.zip} (arrival \texttt{13f105f42}), manuscript \file{fejer-arrangement-selection.tex} (1,281 lines, 20 pages); \emph{no pin and no blob identifiers} (its bibliography records the repository paths and ``inspection date rather than \ldots\ a commit-pinned audit''). Printed below: the abstract and Section~1; Sections~2--9 form a chapter of Part~II (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:fejer}), Sections~10--12 are in Part~V. Its `question' environment (``Research question'', on the shared counter) is set in this report's `Research question' style. Source~35 builds on this source (its \texttt{PriorFejer}): that forward reference is now resolved.}
\begin{partabstract}{40}
Section 15 of Gowers' 2001 proof of Szemer\'edi's theorem uses repeated
cosine-based random selections to pass from many respected cubical
arrangements to a subset in which almost every arrangement is respected.
We give a self-contained alternative based on a single normalized Fej\'er
kernel. For ordered $d$-arrangements of $k$-cubes, put
$s=2d2^k$ and $M=(2d+1)k+2d-1$. If a map on a density-$\beta$ subset of
$\F_q^{k+1}$ respects at least $\alpha\beta^{2d-1}q^M$ arrangements,
then, under explicit characteristic and field-size conditions, there is a
subset containing at least
\[
 \frac{\alpha^s\eta^{s-1}}{3^{s-1}(s+1)^s}\,
 \beta^{2d-1}q^M
\]
arrangements, of which at least a proportion $1-\eta$ are respected.
For $d=8$, this replaces the exponent $s2^{s-1}$ in Gowers' Lemma 15.5 by
exponents $s$ and $s-1$ in the abundance and accuracy parameters. A single feature,
$F(y,r)=r\prod_i y_i$, is enough: we identify its universal relation
space and bound all unintended bounded-coefficient relations.
The proof treats repeated vertices explicitly. Further results include
vector-valued targets with dimension-free constants, an exact formula
for target-torsion losses, and an exponent obstruction for homogeneous
nonnegative-Fourier kernels, including independent repeated stages.
These are local refinements, not a claimed new bound for Szemer\'edi's
theorem. All main results are proved here; finite exact checks are supplied
as supplementary evidence, not as a formal verification or a claim of
established priority.
\end{partabstract}
\subsection{Why focus on the selection step?}
Gowers' paper \cite{gowers} develops several transitions from abundant
combinatorial configurations to increasingly coherent algebraic
structure. This note concerns one such transition in Section 15: a map
respects a positive proportion of certain cubical arrangements, and one
wants to find a subset where the proportion is close to one without
losing all the configurations. The repository contains an edited
transcription of this paper and a collection of local quantitative
refinements \cite{repo40}. We use the transcription's explicit largeness
hypothesis for Lemma 15.5, rather than silently suppressing it.

The local question is concrete:
\begin{quote}
Is the extremely large exponent produced by repeating the degree-one
cosine kernel intrinsic to this arrangement-selection problem?
\end{quote}
We answer this question negatively under an explicit, substantially
smaller field-size threshold. This is a question extracted from a proof
and its constants; we do not assert that it was previously advertised as
a named open problem.

There are two main changes. First, the full family of squarefree
coordinate monomials can be replaced by the single monomial consisting
of the product of all $k+1$ coordinates. The relevant requirement is not
linear independence over the whole finite field, which would be
impossible for so many scalar values. It is the absence of
\emph{short} unintended relations, and a polynomial zero-count controls
these. Second, a high-degree Fej\'er kernel has an arrangement survival
advantage proportional to its bandwidth, rather than an advantage
$1+2^{1-s}$ barely exceeding one. This makes one selection sufficient.

\subsection{Main explicit statement}
Definitions of arrangements and respect are given in Section~\ref{gsr:en:40:sec:arrangements}.
All arrangements are ordered and counted with their parameters; zero
sidelengths and repeated vertices are allowed in the counts.

\begin{theorem}[Explicit one-stage selection]\label{gsr:fm:40:thm:explicit}
Let $k,d\geq 1$, let $s=2d2^k$ and $M=(2d+1)k+2d-1$, and let
$0<\alpha,\beta,\eta\leq 1$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:40:eq:Lchoice}
 L=\left\lceil\frac{2(s+1)}{\alpha\eta}\right\rceil,
 \qquad
 \Gamma_s(\alpha,\eta)=
 \frac{\alpha^s\eta^{s-1}}{3^{s-1}(s+1)^s}.
\end{equation}
Let $q$ be a prime power of characteristic $p$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:40:eq:simplethreshold}
 p>2(L-1),\qquad
 q\geq (k+1)\beta^{-(2d-1)}
 \left(\frac{18(s+1)^2}{(\alpha\eta)^2}\right)^s.
\end{equation}
Suppose $B\subseteq\F_q^{k+1}$ has $|B|=\beta q^{k+1}$ and
$\phi:B\to\F_q$ respects at least
$\alpha\beta^{2d-1}q^M$ $d$-arrangements in $B$.
Then there is $B'\subseteq B$ containing at least
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:40:eq:mainmass}
 \Gamma_s(\alpha,\eta)\,\beta^{2d-1}q^M
\end{equation}
$d$-arrangements. In fact at least this many are respected, and the
proportion of all arrangements in $B'$ that are respected is at least
$1/(1+\eta)\geq 1-\eta$. Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:40:eq:densityout}
 \frac{|B'|}{q^{k+1}}
 \geq \beta\,\Gamma_s(\alpha,\eta)^{1/(2d-1)}.
\end{equation}
If $q=p$ is prime, the field-size inequality in
\eqref{gsr:fm:40:eq:simplethreshold} already implies its characteristic inequality.
\end{theorem}

The theorem is proved in Section~\ref{gsr:en:40:sec:selection}. The more flexible
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:40:thm:exact} uses the exact finite Fej\'er sum and a smaller
exceptional-set constant; \eqref{gsr:fm:40:eq:simplethreshold} is a convenient
closed-form sufficient condition, not an optimized one.

\subsection{Scope and relationship to existing work}
The basic probabilistic architecture comes from Gowers' Lemma 15.5.
The features, bandwidth, exceptional-set accounting, and one-stage
parameter choice are reworked here. The algebraic and analytic tools
are elementary, and the note supplies their proofs to make the
quantitative conclusions independently auditable.

A local improvement should not be confused with a new global estimate
for progression-free sets. For perspective, Leng, Sah, and Sawhney
\cite{lssbounds} prove, for each progression length $\ell\geq 5$, a bound
$r_\ell(N)\ll N\exp(- (\log\log N)^{c_\ell})$ using a different package
of inverse-theorem and density-increment inputs. Nothing here improves
or competes with that theorem. Propagating the present constants
through all later steps of Gowers' argument is a separate task.

The repository comparison is scoped to the Section 15 source and the
local-refinement index inspected for this note. A literature search is
not a proof of priority. The results below are presented as proved
refinements for review and integration, rather than as a certified
first discovery or a claimed solution of a major global open problem.

\section[{Source 41: The theorem and its scope}]{Source 41. The theorem and its scope}\label{gsr:fm:41:sec:d1}\label{gsr:fm:41:sec:main}
\srcnote{41}{Section 1}
\partsource{\textbf{Added in the eighth write, 7~October 2026. Delivered title block.} ``Threshold free polynomial density increments on cyclic groups / Report277 / Research report prepared for Vladimir / 6 October 2026''; \emph{the PDF author field reads ``Research report prepared for Vladimir''; no statement on AI assistance is made}. Archive \file{Report277\_Threshold\_Free\_All\_Degree\_Density\_Increments.zip} (arrival \texttt{a6eea2a19}), manuscript \file{article.tex} (1,022 lines, 21 pages), pin \texttt{c94998a5d} (its \file{SOURCES.md}, shipped as \file{41-all-degree-increments-SOURCES.md}). It is the third report of the series of sources~26 (Report275) and~32 (Report276), and its Sections~2 and~5 are source~32's Sections~2 and~4 word for word (note in Section~\ref{gsr:dt:41:sec:d2}). Printed below: the abstract and Section~1; Sections~2--7 form, with source~42, a chapter of Part~I (Section~\ref{gsr:dt:sec:alldegree}), Sections~8--9 are in Part~V. Its macro \texttt{\textbackslash norm} omits \texttt{\textbackslash left}/\texttt{\textbackslash right}, as source~26's did, and prints with this report's.}
\begin{partabstract}{41}
For every polynomial degree $k\ge1$ and every cyclic modulus, a disjoint comparable cover carrying total balanced polynomial correlation $\alpha N$ yields a proper progression of density at least $\delta+\alpha/3$ and length at least
\[
 \max\{1,(N/M)^{1/D_k}/8\},\qquad
 D_1=4,\quad D_k=\tfrac14(k!)^2 2^{(k+1)^2}+1\quad(k\ge2).
\]
There is no missing large-scale premise. We prove every analytic input, including a coefficient-uniform monomial recurrence estimate with explicit constants, the sharper quadratic base, a lossless recursive phase partition, and a subgroup-coset variance alternative over arbitrary cyclic groups. We also retain the exact recursive partition budget and sharper affine, quadratic, and cubic alternatives. For $k\ge2$, a compact bound gives length at least $\max\{1,2^{-(k+8)}(N/M)^{1/(12\mathcal P_k+1)}\}$, where $\mathcal P_k=k!2^{k(k+1)/2}$. The conclusion implies the entire pinned Corollary 5.8 interface in every degree. This is a written mathematical theorem, not a Lean verification, a global quantitative Ramsey or Szemer\'edi improvement, or a priority claim. The companion provides bounded exact diagnostics and reproducible packaging; finite samples do not prove recurrence for arbitrary real coefficients.
\end{partabstract}
For a real $t$, write $e(t)=\exp(2\pi i t)$ and
$\norm{t}=\min_{v\in\Z}|t-v|$. Let $G=\Z/N\Z$, where $N\ge2$ is an integer, and put $e_N(y)=e(\widetilde y/N)$ using any integer representative of $y\in G$.
A \emph{proper modular arithmetic progression} is a set
\[
 P=\{u+jd:0\le j<n\}\subseteq G
\]
whose displayed parameterization is injective. Its length is $n$. Modular wrapping is allowed; the step need not be a unit. A singleton is proper. The polynomials considered here are \emph{coefficient polynomials}
\[
 \phi(x)=\sum_{j=0}^k a_jx^j,\qquad a_j\in G.
\]
This includes lower-degree and constant polynomials. Over composite moduli it does not silently substitute an arbitrary finite-difference definition of polynomial.

Let $A\subseteq G$, $\delta=|A|/N$, and $f=\one_A-\delta$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:41:eq:KD}
 K_k=(k!)^2 2^{(k+1)^2},\qquad
 D_1=4,\qquad D_k=K_k/4+1\quad(k\ge2).
\end{equation}
These are positive integers. In particular $K_1=16$ and $K_2=2048$.

\begin{theorem}[All degree local cover increment]\label{gsr:fm:41:thm:main}
Let $k,M\ge1$ be integers. Let $P_1,\ldots,P_M$ be nonempty pairwise disjoint proper modular progressions such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:41:eq:cover}
 A\subseteq U:=\bigcup_{i=1}^M P_i,
 \qquad |P_i|\le2|P_j|\quad(1\le i,j\le M).
\end{equation}
Let each $\phi_i$ be a coefficient polynomial of degree at most $k$. Suppose $\alpha>0$ and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:41:eq:corr}
 \sum_{i=1}^M\left|\sum_{x\in P_i}f(x)e_N(-\phi_i(x))\right|
 \ge\alpha N.
\end{equation}
There is a nonempty proper modular progression $Q$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:41:eq:main}
 |Q|\ge\max\left\{1,\frac{(N/M)^{1/D_k}}8\right\},
 \qquad |A\cap Q|\ge(\delta+\alpha/3)|Q|.
\end{equation}
There is no lower bound on $\alpha$ or $N/M$, and no primality or least-prime-factor hypothesis. The conclusion does not require $Q\subseteq U$.
\end{theorem}

The construction has two regimes. If the correlation is small at the chosen integer target length, a second moment gives the requested density increment directly. Otherwise the correlation forces enough mass in the cover that every parent meets the explicit phase-partition threshold. Thus ``threshold free'' describes the final hypotheses, not the absence of internal quantitative estimates.

The proof is self-contained. Section~\ref{gsr:dt:41:sec:recurrence} establishes the quadratic base and explains the Fourier detection step in full. Section~\ref{gsr:dt:41:sec:generalrec} proves recurrence in every degree with an explicit ordered-divisor constant. Section~\ref{gsr:dt:41:sec:partition} constructs the partitions and verifies their all-degree budget. Sections~\ref{gsr:dt:41:sec:variance} and~\ref{gsr:dt:41:sec:assembly} prove the moment alternative and final assembly. Section~\ref{gsr:dt:41:sec:alternatives} preserves the actual recursive budget and sharper small-degree conclusions. Section~\ref{gsr:fz:41:sec:source} compares the exact pinned source interface and credits the classical mechanisms.

Throughout, $k$ is the polynomial degree. In repeated differencing the number of shifts is $s=k-1$, and the power on an exponential sum is $w=2^s$. These are separate from the density exponent $D_k$. The recurrence accuracy $R$ is an integer at least two; the progression target length is $L$, also an integer. Locally introduced $H,T$ are explicitly integer scales. All logarithms without a subscript are natural.
