\section[{Source 94: The local problem and the contribution}]{Source 94. The local problem and the contribution}\label{gsr:fm:94:sec:d1}\label{gsr:fm:94:st3:sec-intro}
\srcnote{94}{Section 1}
\partsource{\textbf{Added in the thirteenth write, 7~October 2026.} \textbf{Delivered title block.} ``Sharp Three-Term Progression Bounds with Torsion / Exact constants, spectral decomposition, and optimal stability exponents / Research contribution for the ProveIt project / 7 October 2026''; \emph{the PDF author field reads ``Research contribution for the ProveIt project''}; no statement on AI assistance. Archive \file{proveit\_sharp\_three\_term\_torsion.zip} (arrival \texttt{0049d075d}, 7~October 2026, 10:10), manuscript \file{article.tex} (1,405 lines, 20 pages), pin \texttt{0ef37201d} (09:26), with the transcription and the verifiers of sources~10 and~20 by blob; its \file{INTEGRATION.md} and \file{SOURCE\_AUDIT.md} are shipped with the prefix \file{94-three-term-torsion-}, its verifier and \file{Makefile} under \file{code/}, its records under \file{data/}. Printed below: the abstract, its keywords and Section~1; Sections~2--7 stand in the Part~III chapter on three-term counting with torsion (Section~\ref{gsr:cc:sec:threeterm}), which continues source~20's chapter; Sections~8--11 are in Part~V. Its st-prefixed macros are added unchanged and its st-prefixed environments (\texttt{stthm}, \texttt{stlem}, \texttt{stprop}, \texttt{stcor}, \texttt{stdef}, \texttt{stex}, \texttt{strem}) are set as the report's environments of the same printed names, on the shared counter as delivered. Its equations, numbered consecutively through the manuscript, are numbered within sections here.}
\begin{partabstract}{94}
Let $G,D$ be finite abelian groups and let $A,B:D\to G$ be arbitrary
homomorphisms. We determine, for every $1\le p\le\infty$, the exact constant
in the estimate of
$\stE_{x\in G,d\in D}f_0(x)f_1(x+Ad)f_2(x+Bd)$ by
$\stnorm{\widehat f_0}_{\ell^p}\stnorm{f_1}_{L^2}\stnorm{f_2}_{L^2}$.
At $p=4$ this gives a sharp $U^2$ generalization of the Fourier counting
step in Gowers' proof, with coefficient
\[
 \bigl([G:A(D)]\,[G:B(D)]\,[G:A(D)+B(D)]\bigr)^{1/4}.
\]
No invertibility, distinctness, or coprimality hypothesis is needed, and
subgroup indicators attain the coefficient. We then determine the full
nonzero singular spectrum of the associated Fourier operator and classify
all complex extremizers for $2<p<\infty$. A dimension-free stability theorem gives distance
at most $4\varepsilon^{1/4}$ in the marked Fourier $\ell^4$ norm and at most
$7\sqrt\varepsilon$ in each of the other $L^2$ norms, for a normalized
$(1-\varepsilon)$-extremizing triple and $\varepsilon\le1/64$.
Both powers of $\varepsilon$ are optimal. Ordinary three-term progressions
admit especially simple exact control seminorms and a quotient-corrected
three-set counting formula. The sharp-constant calculation is a concrete
specialization of finite-group H\"older--Brascamp--Lieb theory; the paper
supplies direct proofs, explicit structure and stability, and a reproducible
finite verification package. No new global bound in Szemer\'edi's theorem
is asserted.
\end{partabstract}
\begin{quote}\small\raggedright
\noindent\textbf{Keywords.} Gowers uniformity; three-term progressions; finite
abelian groups; torsion; sharp inequalities; near-extremizers.
\end{quote}

The Fourier proof of the three-term case of Szemer\'edi's theorem turns a
progression average into a trilinear Fourier sum. In Gowers' presentation,
Lemma~2.2 relates fourth Fourier moments to uniformity, and the proof of
Theorem~2.6 uses a Fourier counting estimate after reducing to a prime
cyclic ambient group \cite{gowers}. These are natural places to ask a
sharp local question: what survives on a general finite abelian group,
and precisely what does failure of invertibility cost?

There are three different issues. First, the coefficient in an inequality
may depend on torsion. Second, the best estimate for a \emph{fixed} marked
function can be much better than a cardinality-based coefficient. Third,
a coefficient alone does not explain equality or near-equality. This
article treats all three issues for the full two-increment system
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:94:st3:def-lambda}
 \stLa(f_0,f_1,f_2)
 =\stE_{x\in G,d\in D}f_0(x)f_1(x+Ad)f_2(x+Bd),
\end{equation}
where $A,B:D\to G$ are arbitrary homomorphisms between finite abelian
groups. The groups $D$ and $G$ need not be equal.

\subsection{Normalization and headline results}
All physical-space averages and $L^2$ norms use probability measure.
Fourier transforms are normalized, while Fourier $\ell^p$ norms use
\emph{counting} measure. Write
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:94:st3:physical-indices}
 u=[G:A(D)],\qquad v=[G:B(D)],\qquad
 \ell=[G:A(D)+B(D)],\qquad k=uv/\ell.
\end{equation}
The letter $\ell$ denotes a positive integer, not a norm exponent.

The exact coefficient $C_p$ in
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:94:st3:headline-p}
 |\stLa(f_0,f_1,f_2)|
 \le C_p\stnorm{\widehat f_0}_{\ell^p}
        \stnorm{f_1}_{L^2}\stnorm{f_2}_{L^2}
\end{equation}
is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:94:st3:headline-cp}
 C_p=
 \begin{cases}
 \ell^{\,1-1/p},&1\le p\le2,\\[2pt]
 (uv)^{1/2}k^{-1/p},&2\le p\le\infty.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
In particular, since $\stnorm{\widehat f}_{\ell^4}=\stnorm f_{U^2}$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:94:st3:headline-u2}
 |\stLa(f_0,f_1,f_2)|
 \le (uv\ell)^{1/4}\stnorm{f_0}_{U^2}
                         \stnorm{f_1}_{L^2}\stnorm{f_2}_{L^2}.
\end{equation}
Every coefficient in \eqref{gsr:fm:94:st3:headline-cp} is attained by indicator
functions of explicitly specified subgroups. Thus the general coefficient
cannot be lowered even by restricting the three inputs to $\{0,1\}$.

For the normalized $p=4$ problem, every triple with value at least
$(1-\varepsilon)(uv\ell)^{1/4}$, where $0\le\varepsilon\le1/64$, is close
to an exactly extremizing triple $(f_0^\star,f_1^\star,f_2^\star)$:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:94:st3:headline-stability}
 \begin{split}
 \stnorm{f_0-f_0^\star}_{U^2}&\le4\varepsilon^{1/4},\\
 \stnorm{f_1-f_1^\star}_{L^2},\quad
 \stnorm{f_2-f_2^\star}_{L^2}&\le7\sqrt\varepsilon.
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
The normalization here is
$\stnorm{f_0}_{U^2}=\stnorm{f_1}_{L^2}=\stnorm{f_2}_{L^2}=1$.
The powers $1/4$ and $1/2$ cannot be replaced by larger powers uniformly,
already on the fixed group $\stZ/5\stZ$.

\subsection{What is, and is not, being claimed}
The sharp-constant part fits within Christ's theorem identifying
finite-group H\"older--Brascamp--Lieb constants by subgroup optimization
\cite{christhbl}. We do not present the general sharp-constant principle
as new. The corresponding HBL datum is the finite subgroup
$\Omega=\{(\beta,\gamma)\in\Gamma^2:a\beta+b\gamma=0\}$
with maps $(\beta,\gamma)\mapsto-\beta-\gamma$, $\beta$, and $\gamma$,
and exponents $(1/p,1/2,1/2)$. We explicitly evaluate this family, prove it
without invoking that general theorem, and derive its full spectral
structure, all complex equality cases for $2<p<\infty$, and the quantitative
stability theorem \eqref{gsr:fm:94:st3:headline-stability}.

The repository already contains torsion-sensitive mixed-norm estimates
and directional refinements \cite{srcten,srctwenty}. In
particular, the ordinary endpoint coefficient $|G[2]|^{1/4}$ is not a new
claim here. The substantive extension is the treatment of \emph{all}
increment homomorphisms together with a complete operator-level and
near-equality analysis. A targeted source review has not established
literature priority for these particular structural and stability
formulations; they should be reviewed as proved research claims, not as
an assertion of priority based on an exhaustive search.

No asymptotic estimate for $r_j(N)$ is improved in this article. A sharp
three-term estimate does not by itself improve the higher-degree inverse
theorems or the density-increment iteration. The further questions in
Section~\ref{gsr:fz:94:st3:sec-questions} distinguish those additional tasks from
results actually proved here.

\begin{partabstract}{95}
The phase-removal step in Gowers's argument naturally leads to a simultaneous
question: how much codimension is needed to integrate two multilinear phase
models on the same subspace? For symmetric Boolean cubics, the obstruction is
an alternating bilinear form. We combine the classical normal form of an
alternating pencil with a finite-test Pfaffian argument to determine the
optimal answer from three derivative-spectrum energy bounds.
If the energies of $T_0,T_1,T_0+T_1$ are at least $2^{-K_0},2^{-K_1},2^{-K_+}$,
respectively, then both $T_0,T_1$ integrate on a subspace of codimension at most
\[
 \min\left\{K_0+K_1,K_0+K_+,K_1+K_+,
 \left\lfloor\frac{K_0+K_1+K_+}{2}\right\rfloor\right\}.
\]
Every nonnegative integral budget triple has an extremizer, even with one
common test function. In particular, the common-budget coefficient improves
from $2$ to the optimal $3/2$.
For an arbitrary finite set of rational directions in an alternating pencil,
we prove the exact unequal-budget frontier and characterize all realizable
rank profiles when the ambient dimension is unrestricted.
An integral rank defect measures departure from a direct sum of scalar
symplectic planes: deletion of at most that many dimensions produces this
normal form, with sharp coefficient one. A six-dimensional example shows
why the maximum rank over the base field cannot replace generic rank.
The algebraic conclusions extend to symmetric $(p+1)$-linear forms over
$\F_p$. The single-cubic energy theorem, nonclassical integration, and pencil
classification are credited inputs, not claimed discoveries. All subsequent
inferences are proved. This is a local research contribution, not a new
end-to-end bound for Szemer\'edi's theorem.
\end{partabstract}
\begin{quote}\small
\noindent\textbf{Status.} Unrefereed mathematical manuscript. Exact finite checks
are supplied; no new Lean verification or exhaustive publication-priority
claim is made. The repository comparison is pinned and recorded in
section~\ref{gsr:fz:95:spi:sec:provenance}.
\end{quote}

\subsection{From one phase model to two}
Gowers's Section~17 converts structured derivative Fourier coefficients into
polynomial phase removal \cite{gowers}. The corrected ProveIt interface
records the degree as $k+1$ and states the factorial-invertibility assumptions
explicitly \cite{repo95lean}. Small characteristic changes this algebraic
step: a symmetric multilinear form need not be the highest derivative of a
polynomial, even when polynomials take values in $\Tcirc$. One must test the
additional repeated-variable identities of nonclassical integration
\cite{tidor}.

For a symmetric trilinear form $T:V^3\to\Ftwo$, with $V=\Ftwo^n$, the complete
obstruction is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:95:spi:eq:omega}
 \Omega_T(a,b)=T(a,a,b)+T(a,b,b).
\end{equation}
It is alternating and bilinear. The preceding Boolean-phase manuscript in
this project establishes, for one tensor, that the least integration
codimension and the negative logarithm of the largest selected energy both
equal $\rk\Omega_T/2$ \cite{srcfortythree}. We reproduce the needed argument
in section~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:sec:scalar}, with attribution.

The genuinely simultaneous problem is different. Given $T_0$ and $T_1$, we
require one subspace $W$ on which \emph{both} restrictions integrate. Taking
separately optimal subspaces and intersecting them loses the sum of their
codimensions. Testing the third tensor $T_+=T_0+T_1$ should detect compatibility,
but it does not make the two obstructions identical. The objective here is to
compute the precise universal improvement, including all integer effects and
all unequal parameter regimes.

\subsection{Definitions for the main theorem}
Use normalized counting measure. Set $e(t)=\exp(2\pi i t)$ and
\[
 \partial_h f(x)=f(x+h)\overline{f(x)},\qquad
 \widehat g(\xi)=\E_x g(x)(-1)^{\xi(x)}\quad (\xi\in V^*).
\]
For symmetric $T$ define the selected derivative energy
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:95:spi:eq:energy}
 \en_T(f)=\E_{a,b\in V}
 \abs{\widehat{\partial_a\partial_b f}\bigl(T(a,b,\cdot)\bigr)}^2.
\end{equation}
The functions are complex-valued and $1$-bounded unless stated otherwise.
The energy is real, nonnegative, and at most one.

A nonclassical polynomial of degree at most $d$ is a function $P:V\to\Tcirc$
whose $(d+1)$-fold additive derivatives vanish. The assertion that $P$
integrates $T$ means
\[
 \Delta_a\Delta_b\Delta_cP(x)=T(a,b,c)/2
 \quad\text{for all }a,b,c,x,
 \qquad\Delta_hP(x)=P(x+h)-P(x).
\]
We write
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:95:spi:eq:joint-codim}
 c(T_0,T_1)=\min\{\codim W:T_0|_{W^3},T_1|_{W^3}
                   \text{ both have such primitives}\}.
\end{equation}
This is an algebraic quantity; it does not require the primitives to correlate
with a specified function.

\begin{theorem}[Optimal three-test integration budget]\label{gsr:fm:95:spi:thm:main}
Let $K_0,K_1,K_+$ be nonnegative integers. Suppose
\[
 \en_{T_i}(f_i)\ge 2^{-K_i}\quad(i=0,1,+),\qquad T_+=T_0+T_1.
\]
The three functions may be different or identical. Put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:95:spi:eq:three-budget}
 B(K_0,K_1,K_+)=\min\left\{
 K_0+K_1,K_0+K_+,K_1+K_+,
 \left\lfloor\frac{K_0+K_1+K_+}{2}\right\rfloor\right\}.
\end{equation}
Then
\[
 c(T_0,T_1)\le\min\{\lfloor n/2\rfloor,B(K_0,K_1,K_+)\}.
\]
For every budget triple the bound $B$ is attained on a space of dimension
$2B$, by explicit symmetric cubics and the common function $f_0=f_1=f_+=1$.
With a fixed dimension $n$, the displayed dimension-capped bound is also
attainable after removing blocks and adjoining inactive coordinates.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Identifications} (Section~\ref{gsr:fp:sec:pencils}). $c(T_0,T_1)$ is source~92's common codimension $\kappa(\mathcal T)$ for the family $\{T_0,T_1\}$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:92:thm:family}), which this source computes exactly (its Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:joint-exact}); source~92's lower bound by the largest rank in the span (Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:92:prop:familybounds}) is not sharp even for pencils. This also answers source~89's question on optimizing a higher-degree defect pencil when the defect span is two-dimensional. Neither source~89 nor source~92 is cited: both were unplaced archives at this source's pin \texttt{c9a9f2662}. Checked at the write: the closed form $B$ equals the budget frontier for all triples at most~$6$, and $\lfloor3K/2\rfloor$, $2K$ (\file{verify14.py}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{corollary}[The sharp common-budget coefficient]\label{gsr:fm:95:spi:cor:common}
If all three energies are at least $\delta>0$, let
$K=\lfloor\log_2(1/\delta)\rfloor$. Then
\[
 c(T_0,T_1)\le\left\lfloor\frac{3K}{2}\right\rfloor.
\]
The coefficient $3/2$ and the displayed integral bound are optimal. Testing
only $T_0,T_1$ instead gives the sharp bound $2K$ in unrestricted dimension.
\end{corollary}

We prove theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:95:spi:thm:main} in section~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:sec:joint}. The additional half-budget is
not a technical inefficiency: the extremizers in section~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:sec:examples} rule out
replacing $3/2$ by $1$ even though each of the three individual models repairs
at cost at most $K$.

\subsection{The algebraic results behind the improvement}
For alternating forms $A_0,A_1$ over a field $k$, call
\[
 A(s,t)=sA_0+tA_1
\]
an alternating pencil. The pair need not be linearly independent. Its
\emph{generic half-rank} is
\[
 r=\tfrac12\rk_{k(z)}(A_0+zA_1).
\]
For a rational projective direction $a=[s:t]\in\Prob^1(k)$, put
$r_a=\rk A(s,t)/2$. The rank does not depend on the representative.

For a finite set $S$ of $m\ge2$ distinct directions, the principal conclusions
are as follows; their proofs occupy sections~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:sec:pencils}, \ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:sec:budgets} and \ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:sec:stability}.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The largest common isotropic dimension is $n-r$. This is a consequence
of the classical alternating-pencil normal form, not a new classification
of pencils.
\item The finite-test rank budget is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:95:spi:eq:rank-loss-intro}
 \sum_{a\in S}(r-r_a)\le r.
\end{equation}
Consequently, if $r_a\le K_a$, the optimal universal upper bound on $r$ is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:95:spi:eq:budget-intro}
 B_S(K)=\min_{\substack{I\subseteq S\\ |I|\ge2}}
       \left\lfloor\frac{\sum_{a\in I}K_a}{|I|-1}\right\rfloor.
\end{equation}
\item The defect
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:95:spi:eq:defect-intro}
 D_S=\sum_{a\in S}r_a-(m-1)r
\end{equation}
is nonnegative. It vanishes precisely for pencils which, apart from a
common radical, split as two-dimensional blocks $L(s,t)J$ with the zero of
each $L$ in $S$. Here $J=\J$.
Deleting at most $D_S$ dimensions produces such a pencil; the coefficient
one is sharp.
\end{enumerate}

The equal-budget specialization over $\F_q$, using all $q+1$ directions,
is $r\le\lfloor(q+1)K/q\rfloor$. The Boolean coefficient $3/2$ is its
smallest-field instance. The general finite-test statement also describes
what can be gained from only some tested combinations.

\subsection{What is and is not being claimed}
The questions answered here concern exact simultaneous integration and the
information carried by a finite rank profile. They are natural continuations
of the inspected phase-integration work; we do not assert that they were
previously advertised open problems in the literature. The new package
consists of the sharp finite-test frontier, rank-profile realization,
rank-defect restriction theorem, and their simultaneous phase consequences.
Several ingredients are elementary once the right classical normal form is
used. Publication priority for these formulations is not established.

The finite-field theorem is not a literal replacement for the cyclic-group
statement of Proposition~17.2 in the repository. In particular it does not
supply the missing quantitative localization or density iteration needed for
a better global Szemer\'edi bound. These interfaces are separated explicitly
in section~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:sec:interface}.

\section[{Source 96: Research setting and principal contributions}]{Source 96. Research setting and principal contributions}\label{gsr:fm:96:sec:d1}
\srcnote{96}{Section 1}
\partsource{\textbf{Added in the fourteenth write, 7~October 2026.} \textbf{Delivered title block.} ``Sharper Local Stability and Uniformity Bounds in Gowers's Szemer\'edi Argument / Prepared with ChatGPT for Vladimir Reshetnikov / 7 October 2026''; the PDF author field agrees. \begin{partabstract}{96}
We prove three complementary refinements of the local analytic and
algebraic machinery surrounding Gowers's proof of Szemer\'edi's theorem.
First, for maps into a finite abelian group of odd order, the affine
four-point rejection probability obeys the cubic bound
$4t-10t^2+6t^3$ throughout its entire positive range $0\le t\le2/3$,
where $t$ is disagreement with any specified affine map. A new remainder
couples variation among the error labels with the additive-energy deficit
of their support, and gives a complete equality classification below
$2/3$. Second, for odd targets we improve the quadratic arrangement
repair bound and construct a stronger common-prime obstruction, narrowing
both endpoints of its second-order coefficient interval. We also remove
the nonvanishing erasure term from an existing high-agreement arrangement
decoder. The observed disagreement tends to
zero with the conditional test defect, at the optimal square-root order
for arbitrary row densities and at linear order when rows have a positive
density lower bound. Third, for every centered real function on every
finite abelian group of odd order, we prove
$\norm f_{U^4}^{16}\ge(843/100)\norm f_{U^2}^{16}$, improving the
coefficient $29/4$ recorded in the inspected research collection.
The proof combines Fourier-pair mass profiles, a mean-sensitive
third-order inequality, and phase-sensitive dual certificates.
All new arguments, boundary conditions, exact finite certificates,
and proposed further questions are supplied. These are local refinements;
we do not derive a new record bound for the global Szemer\'edi problem.
\end{partabstract}

\label{gsr:fm:96:sec:introduction}

Gowers's 2001 proof \cite{gowers} turns a counting problem for arithmetic
progressions into a sequence of statements about uniformity norms,
approximate homomorphisms, respected arrangements, and density increments.
Each of these interfaces has its own quantitative losses. Improving an
interface is useful only when its hypotheses, normalization, and output
are preserved explicitly.

The present investigation began with the supplied
\href{https://github.com/VladimirReshetnikov/ProveIt/tree/main/Combinatorics/Ramsey}{Ramsey directory}
and fixed the repository snapshot \repocommitninetysix. The large combined report
\cite{repo96} contains sources 01--46 in its mathematical body and records
later source artifacts through 59. We inspected that body, its status
and attribution notes, and the newer relevant supplements before choosing
the results below. Source numbers in this article refer to that existing
collection; no new intake number is reserved.

\subsection{What is added}

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{A full positive-range affine defect theorem.}
Let $f:G\to K$, where $G$ is finite abelian and $K$ has odd order.
If $f$ differs from a specified affine map on a fraction $t$ of its
domain, then its four-point rejection probability is at least
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:96:eq:intro-cubic}
 \Psi(t)=4t-10t^2+6t^3=2t(1-t)(2-3t).
\end{equation}
The substantive range is $0\le t\le2/3$. The new proof also controls
two structural defects and classifies equality. It extends the
$t<4/9$ odd-target range and the $t<1/2$ range without three-torsion
recorded in source 59 \cite{srcfiftynine}.

\item \textbf{A narrower arrangement-repair coefficient interval.}
For an even number $s\ge4$ of vertical edges and an odd-order target,
the rejection probability $\epsilon_s$ and nearest-model distance $d$
satisfy
\[
 \epsilon_s\ge sd-\frac{s(3s-2)}2d^2.
\]
Together with a new half-interval construction over common prime groups,
this gives
\[
 \frac{s-1}{s^2}\le c_s^{\mathrm{prime}}
 \le\frac{3s-2}{2s^2}.
\]
For Gowers's eight-arrangements, $s=16$, the interval becomes
$[15/256,23/256]$, improving both endpoints of source 33's interval
$[23/512,15/128]$. The coefficient is defined precisely in
Section~\ref{gsr:en:96:sec:arrangement-repair}.

\item \textbf{An erasure-sensitive arrangement decoder.}
Write $\tau$ for the erased fraction, $\lambda$ for the probability that
an arrangement is fully observed, $\eta$ for its rejection probability
conditional on being observed, and $d$ for observed disagreement,
normalized by the ambient product size. Under an explicit
high-agreement hypothesis inherited from source 33, put
$\theta=\lambda\eta$ and $T=\theta/(s b)$, where $b\ge79/80$.
We prove
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:96:eq:intro-erasure}
 d\le \frac{T+\sqrt{T^2+4(1-|K|^{-1})\tau T}}2.
\end{equation}
This vanishes with $\eta$ even when erasures remain. We construct
examples proving that its square-root order and its leading coefficient
in a specified joint limit cannot be improved. A lower bound $\beta$
on nonempty row densities gives the stronger linear estimate $d\le T/\beta$.

\item \textbf{A stronger fourth-uniformity comparison.}
For a centered real function on a finite abelian group of odd order,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:96:eq:intro-norm}
 \norm f_{U^4}^{16}\ge\NormFactor\norm f_{U^2}^{16},
 \qquad
 \norm f_{U^2}^4\le\NormUpper\norm f_{U^d}^4\quad(d\ge4).
\end{equation}
The first coefficient improves $29/4$ from source 49
\cite{srcfortynine}. The new argument retains the distribution of
opposite Fourier-pair masses in a prior scalar certificate and treats
the phase of order-five characters jointly in the dual estimate.
\end{enumerate}

These results change a validity range, narrow a second-order interval,
remove a qualitative obstruction in an earlier bound, and improve a
uniform numerical constant. They do not resolve the optimal global
progression bound.

\subsection{Relation to the literature}

The affine test belongs to the homomorphism-testing tradition of Blum,
Luby and Rubinfeld and Ben-Or, Coppersmith, Luby and Rubinfeld
\cite{blr,bclr}. Those correction theorems and the existing report's
local cubic are prior work. Our contribution in the affine part is the
coupled remainder and the resulting extension of the cubic to its whole
positive range. The erasure argument uses the full-product theorem of
source 33 as an explicit input; it does not rebrand that theorem as new.

The norm arguments use Gowers--Cauchy--Schwarz and elementary Fourier
identities from the original framework. Eisner and Tao \cite{eisnertao}
study extremizers and near-extremizers for Gowers--Host--Kra seminorms
under other constraints. The quotient here compares $U^4$ with $U^2$
under both realness and centering, so it requires its own estimates.
The relevant previous repository arguments are sources 28, 29, 34,
45 and 49; their roles are distinguished in the proofs below.

For the global benchmark, Leng, Sah and Sawhney \cite{lssbounds} prove, for
each $k\ge5$, a bound of the form
\[
 r_k(N)\ll_k N\exp\bigl(- (\log\log N)^{c_k}\bigr),\qquad c_k>0.
\]
Their proof explains why quantitative local and global inverse theorems
cannot simply be substituted for one another: the strength of the
correlation, the structural object, and the density-increment mechanism
all matter. Our local refinements have not been propagated through a
complete argument establishing a stronger global estimate.

\subsection{Status and scope}

\toprule
Item & Status in this article\\
\midrule
Affine cubic and structural remainder & Proved over every finite abelian
domain and every finite abelian odd-order target.\\
Odd-target arrangement repair & Improved quadratic upper bound and
common-prime lower construction, with a narrower coefficient interval.\\
Erasure modulus & Proved from the explicitly stated full-product decoder;
the thin-row obstruction proves the claimed optimal orders.\\
Fourth-uniformity factor $843/100$ & Proved over all finite abelian groups of
odd order, with exact rational certificates.\\
Equality and optimality & Complete for the affine cubic below $2/3$;
asymptotic in the stated erasure regimes; not claimed for the norm factor.\\
Computation & Exact finite checks and reproducible certificate generation;
these supplement the proofs and are not Lean formalizations.\\
Publication priority & No exhaustive priority certification is claimed.
All identified earlier components are credited.\\

\end{center}

\begin{partabstract}{97}
The preceding ProveIt manuscripts determine the largest selected derivative
Fourier energy of a nonintegrable symmetric Boolean tensor, but leave its
maximizing functions and their phase stability open. For every degree $d\ge4$
and every Boolean dimension, we classify all maximizing functions for the
canonical tensor $C_d^{u,v}$. They are exactly
$\e(P+\theta |u|)$, where $P$ is a circle-valued polynomial of degree at most
$d-1$ and $\theta$ is arbitrary. Thus a genuine continuous, and potentially
nonpolynomial, phase direction survives at the endpoint.

Writing $\delta=1-(d+1)/2^d-\En_{C_d}(f)$ and $D$ for the squared normalized
$L^2$ distance to this explicitly described family, we prove, uniformly in
ambient dimension,
\[
 D\le \left(\frac{2}{2^d-2d-2}+O_d(\sqrt\delta)\right)\delta
 \qquad(\delta\downarrow0).
\]
The leading coefficient is optimal. The proof combines exact relative
polynomial gluing, a bounded-index relative testing theorem, and an explicit
Fourier diagonalization of the endpoint Hessian. A finite-product remainder
estimate handles bounded complex functions without assuming pointwise-small
phase errors. The published near-extremizer theorem of Eisner and Tao supplies
the qualitative entry step; the local radius and remainder constant are
explicit. We also give the topology of the extremizer family, exact truth-table
certificates, and reproducible integer and cyclotomic checks. No improved global
Szemer\'edi bound is inferred from this local extremal result.
\end{partabstract}
\begin{quote}\small
\noindent\textbf{Status.} AI-assisted research manuscript. The new statements
are proved below using explicitly identified existing inputs. The work has not
been independently refereed or checked in a proof assistant. External publication
priority is not established.
\end{quote}
\label{gsr:fm:97:sec:choice}

\subsection{What the two repositories contribute}
The two repositories in the request contain materially different kinds of
mathematical evidence. The inspected \gitpath{VladimirReshetnikov/math} snapshot
is \gitpath{adc7f1241b42e322a6451854ab7e4b4c146bf78a}; its README explicitly
warns that verification status varies across the manuscripts. Its progression
family, \emph{Quasipolynomial Bounds for Arithmetic Progressions}, reports that
for each fixed $k\ge3$ there are positive constants with
\begin{equation}
 r_k(N)\le C_k N\exp\bigl(-c_k(\log N)^{\epsilon_k}\bigr).
 \label{gsr:fm:97:eq:reported-ap}
\end{equation}
Its introduction describes triangular polynomial cells with a descending
precision dependency: a newly created precision at one weight depends on
higher-weight precisions, rather than feeding back into itself. This is a
promising architecture for quantitative iteration. However, the associated
\gitpath{lean/docs/159.md} identifies the formal comparator as the
reciprocal-sum consequence and explicitly excludes the quantitative bound from
that comparator's statement. Equation~\eqref{gsr:fm:97:eq:reported-ap} is therefore
recorded here as a claim of the inspected preprint, not as a theorem verified
in the present work or used in any proof below~\cite{repo97math,oaiprogressions}.

The neighboring van der Waerden family reports the lower bound
$W_r(k)>k^{c k\lfloor\log_2 r\rfloor}$ for all sufficiently large $k$, uniformly
in $r\ge2$~\cite{repo97math}. This is another potentially major quantitative
development, but neither its argument nor the progression paper is needed
for the present results. The review was targeted at selecting a tractable,
substantial continuation, not an audit of every manuscript in either repository.

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{The repository named here.} \file{VladimirReshetnikov/math} at \texttt{adc7f124} is Vladimir's fork of \file{openai/math}, identical to the upstream at that commit (confirmed by Vladimir at the fourteenth write); the other sources of this report cite \file{openai/math} at the same commit (\cite{oaimath}). The quantitative claims recorded here are claims of that external release, used in no proof.
\end{writenote}

The inspected ProveIt snapshot is
\gitpath{52faf9fcdc7214af5c3a130c6c3bd6d50bbdacae}. Its Ramsey research README
places the Boolean obstruction papers in the phase-integration part of
Gowers's framework, and distinguishes unrefereed research sources from
proof-assistant developments~\cite{repo97}. Three recent developments are
particularly relevant:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),itemsep=3pt]
\item the canonical obstruction energy in every degree, including arbitrary
inactive coordinates, in \emph{Exact Boolean Obstruction Energies}~\cite{srcfortyseven};
\item the all-degree nonintegrability threshold and classification of endpoint
\emph{tensors} in \emph{Sharp Boolean Phase Integration in Every Degree}~\cite{srcsixtyfive};
\item second-order stability at the ordinary polynomial-phase endpoint of
Gowers norms, using a finite cube-product expansion rather than a
pointwise-small phase assumption~\cite{srcfiftyfive}.
\end{enumerate}
The third item provides methodological context, not the twisted-energy
classification sought here. Its extremizers are polynomial phases; the
extremizers below include an extra continuous direction that is not generally
a polynomial phase. We rederive the local estimates required in this new setting.

\subsection{The precise project question answered}
Research Question~3 of~\cite{srcsixtyfive}, entitled \emph{Maximizing functions and phase
stability}, asks for all functions at the canonical endpoint and a distance
estimate independent of the ambient dimension. The preceding paper~\cite{srcfortyseven}
also leaves the function part of its endpoint question unresolved. We answer
both parts for every $d\ge4$, including the sharp leading stability coefficient.
The all-degree value and endpoint tensor classification are \emph{not} claimed
as new here.

The new mechanism has three distinct parts. First, equality in a positive
fraction of slices imposes polynomiality of derivatives in the inactive
subspace. An exact coefficient argument glues these constraints, rather than
assuming that the optimizing function ignores inactive coordinates. Second,
a continuous optimization on four phase values identifies the remaining free
direction. Third, a relative testing argument supplies a dimension-independent
entry into that family, after which its transverse spectrum gives sharp stability.

\subsection{Relation to established literature}
Nonclassical circle-valued polynomials, and the need for a repetition condition
when integrating symmetric tensors in small characteristic, are established
background; see Tidor's Definition~3.1 and Proposition~3.5~\cite{tidor}.
The qualitative near-maximal Gowers-norm theorem used in Section~\ref{gsr:fp:97:sec:relative-test}
is Eisner--Tao, Theorem~1.1~\cite{eisnertao}. The present results concern a supplied
homogeneous symmetric frequency tensor on a full Boolean group. They do not
construct such a tensor from a merely positive Gowers norm, localize the
argument to progression cells, or remove the other losses in a Szemer\'edi
iteration. This distinction is essential when comparing the results with
Gowers's Section~17~\cite{gowers} and with~\eqref{gsr:fm:97:eq:reported-ap}.

\section[{Source 98: Definitions, main results, and research status}]{Source 98. Definitions, main results, and research status}\label{gsr:fm:98:sec:d1}
\srcnote{98}{Section 1}
\partsource{\textbf{Added in the fourteenth write, 7~October 2026.} \textbf{Delivered title block.} ``Sharp Third-Energy Rigidity and Higher-Energy Fingerprints of Index-Two Defects / Research report prepared for Vladimir Reshetnikov / OpenAI-assisted mathematical development for the ProveIt collection / 7 October 2026''; \emph{the PDF author field reads ``OpenAI-assisted research report prepared for Vladimir Reshetnikov''}. It is the \file{third\_energy} half of the archive \file{ProveIt\_Spectral\_Transfer\_and\_Third\_Energy\_2026-10-07.zip} (arrival \texttt{98f4b3b67}, 7~October 2026, 11:32); the archive's other paper, \file{spectral\_transfer}, concerns an external square-difference manuscript and was placed separately by \texttt{d294770a7} in \file{Combinatorics/Ramsey/Research/SquareDifferences/spectral-list-mixing/}, which retired the archive. Manuscript \file{third\_energy.tex} (946 lines, 13 pages), pin \texttt{fe7165a3c} (10:58), naming also \texttt{579f95dfe} (Report~288's arrival), \texttt{487859db5} and \texttt{bbde2b873}; the shared \file{SOURCE\_REVIEW.txt} is shipped as \file{98-third-energy-SOURCE\_REVIEW.txt}, its certificate generator and verifier under \file{code/}, the certificate under \file{data/}. Printed below: the abstract, its keywords and Section~1 (definitions and main results); Sections~2--9 form the Part~II chapter on third-energy rigidity (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:thirdenergy}), which closes the hereditary block of sources~75--85; Sections~10--11 are in Part~V. \emph{It credits Report~288 (source~76)}; its sum-of-squares equality criterion $e*e=o*o$ is source~77's fixed-weight criterion and its $J_2=5/8$ is the conditional bound of sources~76 and~78, neither cited in its \TeX{} (its \file{SOURCE\_REVIEW.txt} names Report~290). \emph{Its threshold $5/8$ is for the energy of order $m=3$}, not the quadruple ratio ($m=2$) of sources~76, 80 and~85.}
\begin{partabstract}{98}
For a full-domain map between arbitrary abelian groups, take the infimum,
over finitely supported nonnegative weights, of the fraction of additive
\(2m\)-tuples whose equality of sums is respected by the map. We prove that
the third-energy infimum is greater than \(5/8\) if and only if the map is
affine. The threshold is sharp, and finite indicator weights suffice for
the rigidity implication. Integer parity has infimum exactly \(5/8\),
although every individual finite-weight ratio is strictly larger.

The proof combines an explicit four-point calculation, an exact finite
certificate for cyclic groups of orders three, four and five, a
torsion-aware Jensen reduction, and a Fourier sum of squares for an
index-two family. We give the reduction that makes the finite certificate
valid for arbitrary, including infinite, target groups. Further exact
results hold at every energy order: a nonzero order-two index-two defect
has infimum \(1/2+2^{-m}\); a defect of order greater than \(m/2\) has
infimum \(2^{1-2m}\binom{2m}{m}\); and the sharp conditional bound for
maps affine on every cyclic coset is \(1/2+2^{1-2m}\). Fourth energy
therefore distinguishes order-two defects from all other nonzero
index-two defects, while second and third energy do not.
\end{partabstract}
\begin{quote}\small
\noindent\textbf{Keywords.} Hereditary additive energy; additive six-tuples;
functional equations; affine rigidity; index-two defects; Fourier inequalities.
\end{quote}

Let \(G,H\) be arbitrary abelian groups, written additively, and let
\(a:G\to H\) be defined on the whole group. A weight is a function
\(w:G\to[0,\infty)\) of finite nonempty support. For an integer
\(m\ge2\), put
\begin{align}
 E_m(w)
 &=\sum_{x_1+\cdots+x_m=y_1+\cdots+y_m}
       \prod_{i=1}^m w(x_i)w(y_i)
   =\|w^{*m}\|_2^2,\label{gsr:fm:98:he:def-ordinary}\\
 E_{m,a}(w)
 &=\sum_{\substack{x_1+\cdots+x_m=y_1+\cdots+y_m\\
              a(x_1)+\cdots+a(x_m)=a(y_1)+\cdots+a(y_m)}}
       \prod_{i=1}^m w(x_i)w(y_i),\label{gsr:fm:98:he:def-lifted}\\
 r_m(a)&=\inf_{0\ne w\ge0,\ |\operatorname{supp}w|<\infty}
                  \frac{E_{m,a}(w)}{E_m(w)},\qquad
 r_{m,\mathrm{ind}}(a)=\inf_{\varnothing\ne A\subseteq G,\ |A|<\infty}
                  \frac{E_{m,a}(\mathbf1_A)}{E_m(\mathbf1_A)}.
 \label{gsr:fm:98:he:def-infima}
\end{align}
All tuples are ordered and repetitions are allowed. Thus third energy
counts additive six-tuples, with three entries on each side of an equality
of sums. The denominator is
positive. A map is affine if \(a(x)=\beta+\phi(x)\) for a homomorphism
\(\phi:G\to H\). Affine maps have both infima equal to one.

\begin{theorem}[Sharp third-energy rigidity]\label{gsr:fm:98:he:main}
For every full-domain map \(a:G\to H\) between arbitrary abelian groups,
the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item \(a\) is affine;
 \item \(r_3(a)>5/8\);
 \item \(r_{3,\mathrm{ind}}(a)>5/8\).
\end{enumerate}
The constant \(5/8\) is sharp already for \(G=H=\mathbb Z\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Which $5/8$} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:thirdenergy}). This threshold concerns the energy of order $m=3$. The $5/8$ of source~76's conditional theorem (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:76:thm:conditional}) and of source~85's $\eta_4$ is the quadruple ratio, $m=2$ (one extremal object, thirteenth write), and source~80's is the fixed-target maximum at $N=4$, also $m=2$. Checked at the write: $Q_{m,d}$ gives $r_3=5/8$ for every defect order (\file{verify14.py}). The finite lemma of Section~\ref{gsr:en:98:sec:d6} is computer-assisted; its certificate reran exactly.
\end{writenote}

The condition on indicator weights requires a uniform positive margin
above \(5/8\). On an infinite group, requiring each individual finite
test to be strictly larger than \(5/8\) does not suffice. We prove this
using an exact interval formula and a strict equality obstruction.

The arbitrary-group second-energy threshold \(3/4\) and the local Jensen
structure used below were established in ProveIt Report~288~\cite{srcseventysix}. The present
article extends that route to third and higher energies. The reviewed
ProveIt snapshot~\cite{repo98} is
\begin{center}\small
\texttt{fe7165a3cda1f9182b2a258cf13431a906c4b0c5}.
\end{center}
All new
algebraic and analytic steps are proved here. The small cyclic lemma in
Section~\ref{gsr:en:98:he:small} is computer-assisted: its proof reduces an
infinite family of possible targets and characteristics to an explicit
finite integer computation, performed by the supplied short Python
checker. It is not a bounded-target numerical search. No claim of
publication priority, complete classification of all third-energy
endpoint maps, or proof-assistant certification is made.

Here is the family that explains the sharp threshold. Let \(K\le G\)
have index two, choose \(t\notin K\), let \(\psi:K\to H\) be a
homomorphism, and set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:98:he:index-two}
 a(k)=\beta+\psi(k),\qquad
 a(t+k)=\beta+u+\psi(k)\quad(k\in K),\qquad
 \eta=2u-\psi(2t).
\end{equation}
There is no assumption that \(\psi\) extends to \(G\), and no division
by two in \(H\) is used. The map is affine exactly when \(\eta=0\).

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
\begin{theorem}[Exact higher-energy values in the index-two family]
\label{gsr:fm:98:he:fingerprints}
Suppose \(\eta\ne0\) in \eqref{gsr:fm:98:he:index-two}, and write
\(d=\operatorname{ord}(\eta)\in\{2,3,\ldots,\infty\}\).
\begin{enumerate}
 \item If \(d=2\), then for every \(m\ge2\),
 \[
 r_m(a)=r_{m,\mathrm{ind}}(a)=\frac12+2^{-m}.
 \]
 \item If \(d>m/2\), including \(d=\infty\), then
 \[
 r_m(a)=r_{m,\mathrm{ind}}(a)
       =2^{1-2m}\binom{2m}{m}.
 \]
\end{enumerate}
In particular every nonzero defect has \(r_3=5/8\). At order four,
\[
 r_4(a)=
 \begin{cases}
 9/16,&d=2,\\
 35/64,&d\ge3\text{ or }d=\infty.
 \end{cases}
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp conditional bound at every order]\label{gsr:fm:98:he:jensen-main}
Suppose \(a\) is affine on every coset of every cyclic subgroup but is
not globally affine. Then, for every \(m\ge2\),
\[
 r_m(a)\le r_{m,\mathrm{ind}}(a)\le
 J_m:=\frac12+2^{1-2m}.
\]
The bound is sharp for the map
\(q(s,t)=st:\mathbb F_2^2\to\mathbb F_2\).
In particular the conditional third-energy bound is \(17/32\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Every order of source~76's conditional bound.} At $m=2$, $J_2=5/8$ is source~76's sharp conditional bound and source~78's $(P)$-branch bound (the latter not cited in this source's \TeX); checked at the write: on $\F_2^2$ with $a=st$ the indicator minimum is exactly $J_m$ for $m=2,\ldots,5$.
\end{writenote}

We first establish exact energy identities and limiting weights, then
prove the cyclic and Jensen reductions that complete
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:98:he:main}.

\begin{partabstract}{99}
For a Bohr set defined by $r$ characters, how large can its one-step boundary be relative to the angular size of the step? We construct examples in every sufficiently large prime cyclic group for which the normalized boundary ratio approaches $(2^r-1)/2$. More precisely, for each $r\ge2$ and $\eps>0$ there are fixed, distinct positive integer frequencies $a_0,\ldots,a_{r-1}$ and a fixed radius $0<\rho<1/4$ such that, for all sufficiently large primes $p$, the set
\[
 B_p=\{x\in\Z/p\Z:\normT{a_jx/p}\le\rho\text{ for all }j\}
\]
has exactly $2^r-1$ cyclic runs and satisfies
\[
 \frac{|B_p\setminus(B_p+1)|}{\eta_p|B_p|}
 > (1-\eps)\frac{2^r-1}{2},
 \qquad \eta_p=\frac{\max_j a_j}{\rho p}\longrightarrow0.
\]
The defining frequencies can be arbitrarily close in relative size, and every defining inequality is individually essential. An exact circle model gives the component intervals, their total measure, a radius interval on which the component count persists, and finite-prime error bounds. We also prove a total-variation tradeoff: approximating the sharp Bohr probability measure and making the approximation translation-stable cannot both have polynomial rank cost at the step scale. The construction strengthens the exponential lower obstruction in the inspected ProveIt fixed-radius package and answers the prime-order polynomial-bound question negatively. It supplies an obstruction relevant to Gowers-style localization and to the smooth/padded-cell interfaces in OpenAI's progression manuscript; it does not establish or refute an all-length quantitative Szemer\'edi theorem.
\end{partabstract}
\begin{quote}\small
\noindent\textbf{Status.} The results below have complete ordinary mathematical proofs and accompanying exact-arithmetic regression checks. This is an unrefereed AI-assisted manuscript, not a Lean-verified development. The source comparison is targeted, not an exhaustive literature or repository priority search.
\end{quote}

\subsection{What was reviewed}
The intersection selected here is quantitative additive combinatorics, specifically the geometry of the structured sets on which density increments are localized. Two snapshots were used:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule
Repository & Pinned commit \\
\midrule
\texttt{openai/math} & \texttt{adc7f1241b42e} \\
\texttt{VladimirReshetnikov/ProveIt} & \texttt{bbde2b873b2d} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The full commit identifiers and inspected paths are in the accompanying \texttt{SOURCE\_AUDIT.md}. The review covered catalogue-level descriptions and a smaller set of proof interfaces, rather than every manuscript in either repository.

The OpenAI catalogue reports 722 manuscripts in 372 families and explicitly distinguishes verification stages \cite{oaimath}. Among the closely related families, number 159 claims quasipolynomial bounds for progression-free sets, number 160 concerns superexponential van der Waerden lower bounds, and number 161 concerns a counterexample to Sidorenko's conjecture. The first family is the most direct match to ProveIt's Gowers program. We inspected the introduction and the polynomial-cell/increment setup of its manuscript \cite{oaiprogressions}. Its headline claim is that, for every fixed $k\ge3$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:99:eq:oai-claim}
 r_k(N)\le C_kN\exp\bigl[-c_k(\log N)^{\eps_k}\bigr].
\end{equation}
Here and throughout this review, a statement that a repository manuscript \emph{claims} a theorem is not an assertion that this work independently verified that theorem. None of our proofs assumes \eqref{gsr:fm:99:eq:oai-claim}.

At the pinned ProveIt checkpoint, the repository reports 113 exact companions among 120 numbered Gowers statements, with seven still open; its reported audit covers 755 reachable modules and 4,836 public theorems \cite{repo99status}. Particularly relevant is an existing bridge between the repositories: the qualitative Szemer\'edi theorem and the Freiman/Balog--Szemer\'edi companions use vendored OpenAI Lean material. The qualitative closure is explicitly a hypergraph-regularity/removal route, not a completion of Gowers's quantitative proof. This is also not a formalization claim for \eqref{gsr:fm:99:eq:oai-claim}. We did not rerun the full repository build.

\subsection{The common interface: boundary control}
Gowers's argument uses Bohr neighborhoods and their behavior under small translations \cite[Lemma 10.10]{gowers}. A separate ProveIt research package, referred to here as the \emph{fixed-radius package}, sharpens this local interface by escape-tube counting \cite{srcthirty}. In its notation, translated boundary points create disjoint tubes inside a slightly enlarged Bohr set. Its recorded estimate, restated and proved in Section~\ref{gsr:en:99:sec:upper}, has exponential rank cost $3^r-1$ in the infinitesimal-step limit.

The OpenAI progression manuscript instead uses strict and enlarged polynomial-cell indicators, with certificates of the form
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:99:eq:certificate}
 \E fB^- > a\E B^+,
 \qquad 0\le f\le1,
 \qquad B^-\le B^+,
\end{equation}
and discusses smooth cutoffs and averaging over translated boxes \cite[polynomial-cell setup]{oaiprogressions}. Its precision bookkeeping is triangular: new precision at one weight is controlled by higher-weight precisions, not by repeatedly raising the current precision to a power. Ordinary linear Bohr constraints are a basic special case of such modular cell geometry, but sharp and smoothed indicators are different objects.

The local question is therefore substantive: can prime order, or the near-parallel nature of the defining frequencies, make an arbitrary \emph{fixed-radius sharp} Bohr set polynomially stable in its number of defining characters? An affirmative answer could simplify localization interfaces. We give a negative answer, together with an exact quantitative obstruction.

\subsection{Comparison with the inspected fixed-radius construction}
The earlier fixed-radius package constructs, at rank $2s+1$, examples with normalized boundary ratio tending to $3^s/2$. Its model has a long one-dimensional part and a $3^s$-point exceptional fiber; it also gives composite-cyclic examples by the Chinese remainder theorem \cite{srcthirty}. This is exponential with rank base $\sqrt3$. The construction below achieves $(2^r-1)/2$ with $r$ individually essential defining characters, and it works in \emph{every sufficiently large prime cyclic group}. Thus the rank base in this targeted comparison increases from $\sqrt3$ to $2$.

This comparison is not a claim that every exponential phenomenon for Bohr sets is new. Irregular radii and the need for regularization or smoothing are classical; Green explains both the difficulties and the Bourgain/Tao remedies \cite[Sections 3--4]{greenregularity}. Our specific contribution is the explicit prime-cyclic, near-parallel, irredundant construction and its exact boundary, mass, robustness and approximation formulas. Literature priority for that complete statement remains to be assessed independently.

\begin{partabstract}{100}
\noindent
For every fixed $k\ge3$ and $0<\delta<1$, we construct indicator sets of density tending to $\delta$ for which the discrepancy of the $k$-term arithmetic-progression count is asymptotic to a nonzero constant times the square of the balanced $U^{k-1}$ norm. The construction works on growing powers of a fixed prime field and on every sufficiently large prime cyclic group. Either sign of the discrepancy is possible. It follows that a quadratic counting-error bound cannot be replaced by $o(u^2)$, even in the prime cyclic setting.

The construction applies a centered sine to a normalized sum of independent coordinate observables. Progression triples contribute at order $n^{-1/2}$. Cube moments are controlled by partitions of the cube vertices into four-element affine circuits and yield Gowers norms of order $n^{-1/4}$. We prove a general first-dependent-subset partition formula by an analytic cumulant expansion with exact centering. A bounded-frequency, signed-radix transfer preserves the needed torus averages on prime cyclic groups; probabilistic rounding and a cardinality correction produce actual sets.

These results resolve the longer-progression and prime-cyclic sharpness questions left open in the inspected ProveIt counting manuscript. They do not give a new bound for the largest progression-free subset of an interval and do not depend on accepting the recent all-length quasipolynomial bound claimed in the OpenAI mathematics collection. The package includes full proofs, 8,916 exact finite checks, high-precision characteristic-function tests, and a formalization roadmap.
\end{partabstract}

\subsection{A precise question at the intersection of the repositories}
For a finite abelian group $G$, use normalized counting measure and write
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:100:eq:Lambda}
 \La_k(f)=\E_{x,y\in G}\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}f(x+jy).
\end{equation}
If $A\subseteq G$ has density $\delta_A$, the random-density benchmark is $\delta_A^k$. The present problem is not merely whether small uniformity forces
$\La_k(\ind_A)-\delta_A^k\to0$, but the best possible \emph{power of the uniformity norm} in that implication.

The ProveIt manuscript \emph{Quadratic Counting Errors and Sharp Directional Bounds in Gowers's Szemer\'edi Argument}, incorporated as source 20 of the local-quantitative-refinements report, proves a quadratic estimate
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:100:eq:source20}
 \abs{\La_k(\ind_A)-\delta_A^k}
 \le B_k(\delta_A)\Unorm{\ind_A-\delta_A}{k-1}^{2}
\end{equation}
under coefficient-invertibility assumptions. Its sharpness example treats three-term progressions on powers of $\F_{29}$; it explicitly does not claim sharpness for $k\ge4$ or for prime cyclic groups \cite{srctwenty,repo100research}. Those two omissions define the concrete research target here. More explicitly, its research questions titled \emph{Optimal exponent for longer symmetric counts} and \emph{Prime-cyclic sharpness} ask for exactly these extensions. The latter requires preserving the count excess relative to the square of the norm, not merely preserving positivity. Theorems~\ref{gsr:cc:100:thm:prime} and \ref{gsr:cc:100:thm:field} answer those questions; the separate question about the optimal density coefficient remains open.

The related OpenAI manuscript \emph{Quasipolynomial Bounds for Arithmetic Progressions} studies the larger density-increment program in which progression counting is an essential interface \cite{oaiprogressions}. Understanding whether one can improve the power in \eqref{gsr:fm:100:eq:source20} is relevant to that program: a genuinely sharp local obstruction rules out one tempting route to a better global argument. It does not rule out improvements in structure extraction, localization, iteration, or the coefficient in \eqref{gsr:fm:100:eq:source20}.

\subsection{What was reviewed, and what the source claims establish}
The review is focused rather than a certification of the hundreds of manuscripts in the two repositories. The OpenAI repository snapshot is commit
\texttt{adc7f1241b42e322a6451854ab7e4b4c146bf78a}, dated 6 October 2026. The ProveIt snapshot is
\texttt{fe7165a3cda1f9182b2a258cf13431a906c4b0c5}, dated 7 October 2026. Exact paths, selected blob hashes, and the depth of inspection are recorded in \texttt{sources.json}.

The OpenAI README lists 722 manuscripts in 372 result families and warns that results are at different verification stages \cite{oaimath}. Family 159 claims, for every fixed $k\ge3$, a bound
\[
 r_k(N)\le C_kN\exp\{-c_k(\log N)^{\eps_k}\},
\]
with positive constants depending on $k$. Its introduction explains a density-increment architecture with triangular polynomial cells and descending dimension/precision budgets. Its selected Lean comparator, as described in \texttt{lean/docs/159.md}, concerns the reciprocal-sum consequence, not the quantitative inequality itself \cite{oaiprogressions,oaiscope}. These are source claims and scope statements; this article does not independently audit the full global proof.

The adjacent catalogue family on superexponential lower bounds for van der Waerden numbers is another direct Ramsey connection. Its advertised lower bound has the shape
$W_r(k)>k^{c k\lfloor\log_2 r\rfloor}$ in its stated range \cite{oaivdw}. We inspected this as a catalogue-level alternative, not as a proof on which the present article relies.

ProveIt's 7 October formalization checkpoint reports 113 exact companion proofs and seven open statements in a 120-statement catalogue. It also reports a qualitative Szemer\'edi theorem obtained through a vendored ordered-hypergraph argument, rather than Gowers's quantitative route, and explicitly disclaims a new general all-length bound \cite{repo100status}. We did not rerun that repository-wide Lean audit. The local-refinements README likewise states that placement in its Research directory conveys no formal status \cite{repo100research}.

Against this background, the deliverable here is an unconditional, self-contained \emph{sharpness theorem for the counting interface}. Its dependence on the repositories is motivational and comparative, not a reliance on an unverified deep theorem.

\subsection{Relation to the general counting literature}
Gowers's uniformity norms and repeated Cauchy--Schwarz estimates provide the basic language \cite{gowers}. The true-complexity program asks which \emph{order} of Gowers norm controls a system of linear forms \cite{gowerswolf}; polynomial quantitative control by iterated Cauchy--Schwarz is developed in Manners's work \cite{manners}. Our question is different: with the norm order fixed, what is the largest possible \emph{power} in a symmetric, balanced counting bound?

The analytic tools below---finite Fourier expansions, cumulants, and independent rounding---are classical. The contribution is their precise combination into an all-length saturation construction, an explicit circuit-partition leading coefficient, and a prime-cyclic transfer preserving both the discrepancy and its controlling norm. A targeted source review does not establish exhaustive priority for every formulation in this manuscript.

\begin{partabstract}{101}
For a finite nonempty subset $A$ of an abelian group, let $\Ck_k(A)$ count all additive $k$-cubes, including degenerate cubes, and put $\eps_k=1-\Ck_k(A)/|A|^{k+1}$. We give explicit local bounds for the relative symmetric-difference distance $\delta$ from $A$ to its nearest finite subgroup coset. The central auxiliary result is the sharp inequality
\[
\Ck_k(H\cup D)\le |H|^{k+1}+(2^{k+1}-2)|H||D|^k+|D|^{k+1},
\]
where $H$ is a finite subgroup and $D$ is disjoint from $H$. We classify its equality cases. This yields a dimension-dependent local stability theory: for $k=2$ the sharp profile is $\delta-\delta^2$; for $k=3$ it is $4\delta-10\delta^2+6\delta^3$; for every fixed $k\ge4$, on an explicit neighborhood of zero it is
\[
1-(1-\delta)^{k+1}-(2^{k+1}-2)(1-\delta)\delta^k-\delta^{k+1}.
\]
The equality cases change from deleting a subcoset to adjoining an outside subcoset. At dimension three and above, elementary two-group quotients determine exact equality. For odd-order groups we additionally obtain the sharp cubic-order lower bound $4\delta-10\delta^2+8\delta^3-O(\delta^4)$ in dimension three. All proofs are elementary and uniform in the ambient group. Exact algebraic checks, finite tests, source-audit records, and integration instructions accompany the manuscript.
\end{partabstract}

The standard coset-stability mechanism is not claimed as new. Priority for the sharp boundary inequality, its equality classification, and the resulting exact local profiles remains unverified. The available repository access did not provide a readable, independently assessable review of the latest contents during drafting. Any successfully retrieved repository metadata are therefore recorded as an inventory, not certified as ``breakthrough results.'' No improvement to the quantitative bounds in Szemer\'edi's theorem is claimed.

\subsection{Why this problem belongs to the Ramsey--Gowers program}
The Gowers uniformity norms encode additive cubes and are central to quantitative approaches to arithmetic progressions. Here we study a different, but related, regime: a set whose cube count is close to the largest value allowed by its cardinality. The qualitative fact that such sets resemble cosets belongs to the established near-extremizer program; see the contextual references \cite{gowers,eisnertao}. Our question is quantitative and geometric:
\begin{quote}
What is the exact local deficit forced by a prescribed small distance from a subgroup coset, and which perturbations attain it?
\end{quote}
It is essential to distinguish this question from a density-increment theorem. A large Gowers norm relative to a small density need not be close to the cardinality maximum considered here. Consequently, the results below do not by themselves sharpen a Szemer\'edi bound.

The supplied repositories \cite{oaimath,repo101} motivate seeking a self-contained, checkable theorem package rather than assuming that an unverified manuscript title establishes a new result. The selected direction is the Ramsey/Gowers side of the ProveIt program. A verified intersection with a specific current theorem in \texttt{openai/math} is not asserted. Appendix~\ref{gsr:fz:101:sec:audit} records the narrower source-review status.

\subsection{Cube counts and distance}
Throughout, $G$ is an abelian group written additively, and every set being counted is finite. Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:101:eq:cubedef}
\Ck_k(A)=\#\{(x,h_1,\ldots,h_k)\in G^{k+1}:x+\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^k\omega_i h_i\in A\ \text{for every }\omega\in\{0,1\}^k\}.
\end{equation}
Degenerate cubes are included. For $n=|A|>0$, put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:101:eq:deficit}
\eps_k(A)=1-\frac{\Ck_k(A)}{n^{k+1}}.
\end{equation}
The $k+1$ values at $0,e_1,\ldots,e_k$ determine a cube, so $0\le\eps_k\le1$. Write $E(A)=\Ck_2(A)$.

For a finite coset $C=a+H$, set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:101:eq:rs}
R=C\setminus A,\quad D=A\setminus C,\quad r=|R|,\quad s=|D|,\quad m=|A\cap C|,\quad h=|H|.
\end{equation}
Thus $n=m+s$, $h=m+r$, and
\[
\delta_C=\frac{|A\symd C|}{n}=\frac{r+s}{n},\qquad x=\frac rn,\quad y=\frac sn,\quad x+y=\delta_C.
\]
The denominator is $|A|$, not $|H|$ and not the size of the ambient group. Let $\delta(A)$ be the minimum of $\delta_C$ over finite cosets. A minimum exists: the possible finite symmetric-difference sizes are nonnegative integers, and singleton cosets are available.

If $G$ is finite of size $N$ and $\alpha=n/N$, then
\[
\frac{\|\1_A\|_{U^k(G)}^{2^k}}{\alpha^{k+1}}=1-\eps_k(A).
\]
Our deficit is a deficit of the \emph{powered} norm ratio. Replacing it by a deficit of the norm itself changes the numerical coefficients.

\subsection{Main theorem package}
\begin{theorem}[Exact local profiles]\label{gsr:fm:101:thm:main}
Let $A\ne\varnothing$ be finite in an abelian group.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=*]
\item If $\eps_2(A)<1/60$, there is a unique nearest finite coset $C$, its relative distance $\delta$ is less than $1/50$, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:101:eq:main2}
\eps_2(A)\ge\delta-\delta^2,\qquad
\delta\le\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4\eps_2(A)}}2.
\end{equation}
Apart from $A=C$, equality holds exactly when $A=C\setminus L$ for a coset $L$ of a subgroup of $H$.
\item If $\eps_3(A)<1/60$, the same uniqueness conclusion holds and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:101:eq:main3}
\eps_3(A)\ge P_3(\delta):=4\delta-10\delta^2+6\delta^3.
\end{equation}
Apart from $A=C$, equality holds exactly when $A=C\setminus L$, where $L$ is a coset of $K\le H$ and $H/K$ is an elementary abelian two-group.
\item Fix $k\ge4$, and define
\begin{align}\label{gsr:fm:101:eq:thresholds}
q&=k+1,\quad M=2^k,\quad a_k=M-2q,\\
S_k&=\binom q2+\binom M2,\qquad
\eta_k=\min\left\{\frac1q,\frac{a_k}{6S_k}\right\},\qquad
\delta_k=\frac{\eta_k}{1+\eta_k}.
\end{align}
If
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:101:eq:epsilonthreshold}
\eps_k(A)<\min\left\{\frac1{60},\frac{\eta_k}{(1+\eta_k)^2}\right\},
\end{equation}
then $A$ has a unique nearest finite coset and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:101:eq:mainhigher}
\eps_k(A)\ge P_k(\delta):=1-(1-\delta)^{k+1}-(2^{k+1}-2)(1-\delta)\delta^k-\delta^{k+1}.
\end{equation}
Apart from $A=C$, equality holds exactly when, after translating $C$ to $H$,
\[
A=H\cup(b+K),\qquad K\le H,\quad b\notin H,\quad 2H\subseteq K,\quad 2b\in K.
\]
\end{enumerate}
Each profile has equality examples with positive distances tending to zero. Thus its local Taylor coefficients cannot be improved successively. This does not assert that every real value of $\delta$ is feasible as an equality distance.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Part~(i) is not new to this report} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:cubestability}): source~14 proved it for $\varepsilon\le1/100$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:14:thm:energy-sharp-stability}), source~45 for $\varepsilon<1/9$ with the same equality cases (Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:45:co:envelope}, \ref{gsr:en:45:co:equality}), and source~68 on the optimal range $\varepsilon\le1/4$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:coset}). This source could read neither repository and cites none of them. Parts~(ii) and~(iii) are new. Its odd-order Conjecture~\ref{gsr:fz:101:conj:oddexact} is proved by sources~103 and~104.
\end{writenote}

For $k=4$, one may take $\eta_4=1/130$, $\delta_4=1/131$, and the sufficient deficit threshold $130/17161$. The exact profile is
\[
P_4(\delta)=5\delta-10\delta^2+10\delta^3-35\delta^4+30\delta^5.
\]
The general thresholds are deliberately conservative. In dimension four, Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:101:cor:k4threshold} below improves the sufficient deficit threshold to $1/60$. Optimizing the largest local neighborhoods remains a separate problem.

\begin{theorem}[Sharp boundary inequality]\label{gsr:fm:101:thm:boundaryintro}
Let $H$ be a finite subgroup, $D$ a finite set disjoint from $H$, $h=|H|$, and $s=|D|$. For every $k\ge1$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:101:eq:boundary}
\Ck_k(H\cup D)\le h^{k+1}+c_khs^k+s^{k+1},\qquad c_k=2^{k+1}-2.
\end{equation}
For $s>0$ and $k=2$, equality is equivalent to $D=b+K$ with $K\le H$, $b\notin H$, and $2b\in H$. For $k\ge3$, equality is equivalent to the stronger conditions $2H\subseteq K$ and $2b\in K$.
\end{theorem}

The proof of the boundary theorem uses only cube recursion, a convexity inequality, and the elementary characterization of maximal cube counts. It is the principal reusable lemma in this manuscript.

\begin{partabstract}{102}
For a map on a finite vector space, we study the minimum number of affine subspaces in a partition on which the map is constant. This exact localization problem distinguishes a joint construction from successive or product localization. Over an odd finite field, we prove that the split quadratic form $Q(x,y,z)=x\cdot y$ of rank $2r$, with any number of inactive coordinates, has exact partition cost $q^{r+1}-q+1$, and derive an exact defect identity.

The principal result concerns two independent rank-one quadratic forms. Writing $C=\{(x,y)\in\Fq^2:xy=0\}$, we prove $\Psf(C^2)=4q-3$, whereas $\Psf(C)^2=q^2$. For $q\ge5$, exactly two partitions attain $4q-3$: cyclic families of $4(q-1)$ lines together with the origin. Consequently the map $(x_1,y_1,x_2,y_2)\mapsto(x_1y_1,x_2y_2)$ has exact cost $q^4-2q^3+2q^2+2q-2$, strictly below the product of the two scalar costs. We classify all its optimal partitions, giving exactly $2^{2(q-1)^2+1}$ choices in fixed coordinates.

For arbitrarily many independent rank-one phases, we obtain an exact binomial reduction to joint zero fibers. If $\rho(q)$ is the regularized zero-fiber cost, the regularized full-map cost is exactly $(q-1)^2+\rho(q)$, and $2-1/q\le\rho(q)\le\sqrt{4q-3}$. We also establish defect identities, pullback invariance, a general quadratic bottleneck-dimension theorem, and the equivalence between field-valued and additive-character localization on field-linear affine cells. These results require none of the recent global conjecture claims in the motivating repositories.
\end{partabstract}
\begin{quote}\small
\noindent\textbf{Status.} This is a research manuscript with complete mathematical arguments and finite computational corroboration, not a peer-reviewed or Lean-verified paper. The exact two-phase optimization and rigidity are proposed contributions; historical priority has not been established exhaustively. No new integer Szemer\'edi bound is claimed.
\end{quote}

\subsection{The optimization problem}
Suppose several quadratic phases must be constant on every cell of an affine partition. A straightforward construction localizes each phase separately and takes products or common refinements. Does optimal scalar localization determine the optimal joint cost? Even for two completely independent quadratic forms, the answer is no.

For a nonempty subset $X$ of a finite-dimensional $\Fq$-vector space, let $\Psf(X)$ denote the minimum number of nonempty affine subspaces whose disjoint union is $X$. For a map $f:V\to Y$, let $\Asf(f)$ denote the minimum number of affine cells partitioning $V$ on each of which $f$ is constant. Points are permitted as cells. All affine subspaces in this article are over the full field $\Fq$, not merely its prime subfield. We assume throughout that $q$ is an odd prime power, except where a proof is explicitly stated for all $q>2$.

Set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:102:eq:cross}
 C=\{(x,y)\in\Fq^2:xy=0\},\qquad
 \Psi_m(x_1,y_1,\ldots,x_m,y_m)=(x_1y_1,\ldots,x_my_m).
\end{equation}
The geometry responsible for nonmultiplicativity is concentrated in $C^2$. The nonzero fibers of $xy$ contain no affine lines, whereas the zero fiber is a union of two lines. Joint localization can exploit the intersections among four coordinate planes without using any of the planes as a cell.

\begin{theorem}[Principal conclusions]\label{gsr:fm:102:thm:main}
For every odd prime power $q\ge3$,
\begin{align}
 \Psf(C)&=q, & \Psf(C^2)&=4q-3,\label{gsr:fm:102:eq:mainzero}\\
 \Asf(\Psi_1)&=q^2-q+1, &
 \Asf(\Psi_2)&=q^4-2q^3+2q^2+2q-2.\label{gsr:fm:102:eq:mainfull}
\end{align}
For $q\ge5$ the following stronger statements hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item Exactly two unordered affine partitions of $C^2$ are optimal. Each consists of the singleton origin and $4(q-1)$ coordinate-parallel lines arranged cyclically among the four coordinate planes.
\item Exactly $2^{2(q-1)^2+1}$ unordered affine partitions of $\Fq^4$ are optimal for $\Psi_2$.
\item Every optimal partition for $\Psi_2$ contains only points and lines, even though its zero fiber contains affine planes. Every partition containing a plane has at least $\Asf(\Psi_1)^2$ cells.
\end{enumerate}
In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:102:eq:maingap}
 \Asf(\Psi_1)^2-\Asf(\Psi_2)=(q-1)(q-3)>0
 \qquad(q\ge5).
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

The proof of the exact minimum is in Section~\ref{gsr:dt:102:sec:cross}; the rigidity and enumeration require the extra incidence argument in Sections~\ref{gsr:dt:102:sec:rigidity} and~\ref{gsr:dt:102:sec:full}. Thus the result is more than an upper-bound construction or a numerical counterexample to multiplicativity. It determines the optimum and all equality cases for an infinite family of finite fields.

There is a useful generalization of the full-map formula. Put $P_m=\Psf(C^m)$ and $P_0=1$. Section~\ref{gsr:dt:102:sec:tensor} proves the exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:102:eq:mainbinomial}
 \Asf(\Psi_m)=\sum_{k=0}^m\binom{m}{k}(q-1)^{2(m-k)}P_k.
\end{equation}
It follows that the difficult part of this entire rank-one family is the geometry of its joint zero fibers. If
\[
 \rho(q)=\lim_{m\to\infty}P_m^{1/m},
\]
then the limit exists and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:102:eq:mainrates}
 2-\frac1q\le\rho(q)\le\sqrt{4q-3},\qquad
 \lim_{m\to\infty}\Asf(\Psi_m)^{1/m}=(q-1)^2+\rho(q).
\end{equation}
The exact value of $\rho(q)$ is not determined here.

\subsection{What the scalar theory contributes}
For $Q(x,y,z)=x\cdot y$, with $x,y\in\Fq^r$ and $z\in\Fq^s$, we prove
\[
 \Asf(Q)=q^{r+1}-q+1.
\]
Every scalar optimizer contains one largest possible flat. In contrast, every two-phase optimizer above avoids its largest possible flats. This contrast isolates a concrete obstruction to a greedy localization rule: selecting a largest admissible cell need not minimize the eventual number of cells.

The scalar theorem also supplies exact error accounting. For a partition $\mathcal P$ of such a split form, let $t\in\{0,1\}$ count the cells of dimension $r+s$ and put $d=r+s-1$. Then
\[
 |\mathcal P|-\Asf(Q)
 =(q-1)(1-t)+\sum_{\substack{L\in\mathcal P\\\dim L<d}}
       \bigl(1-q^{\dim L-d}\bigr).
\]
This identity, rather than an unspecified stability constant, quantifies every possible loss.

\subsection{Scope and intended significance}
The contribution is an exact finite-geometric optimization and classification, with consequences for simultaneous quadratic phase partitions and their asymptotic complexity. The problem is introduced and resolved here in the stated two-phase setting; we do not identify it as a previously advertised famous open problem. Nor do we claim that a four-variable construction alone improves an integer density-increment theorem. The connections to that research program are the choice of optimization target, the sharp failure of independent localization, and the explicit higher-family questions opened by~\eqref{gsr:fm:102:eq:mainbinomial}.

\begin{partabstract}{103}
We prove an exact local stability inequality for additive three-dimensional cubes in odd-order abelian groups. If a nonempty finite set $A$ is at relative symmetric-difference distance $\delta\le 1/50$ from a coset of a finite odd-order subgroup, then its normalized cube deficit is at least
$4\delta-10\delta^2+8\delta^3$. Equality occurs precisely for deletion of one subgroup coset, subject to the stated small-distance condition. This removes the fourth-order loss in the earlier manuscript \emph{Sharp local stability for additive cubes} and proves its explicitly stated odd-order conjecture in a quantitative neighborhood.

The main result is an identity, valid for every finite abelian group and every hole function $f:H\to[0,1]$, decomposing the complement cube count into an explicit polynomial, a fourth-moment parity correction, the additive-energy defect of $f$, and a nonnegative remainder. A 256-pattern Boolean certificate controls the complete fifth-through-eighth-order inclusion--exclusion tail; its energy coefficient $35$ is universally optimal, even over odd cyclic groups. We derive a weighted subgroup-boundary inequality, a global weighted near-extremizer theorem, an exact inverse profile, and a quantitative two-level coset rigidity statement. All arguments are self-contained. The accompanying standard-library Python verifier checks the finite certificate, 21,518 subsets of 18 groups, 12 independently evaluated rational-weight examples, and the polynomial identities.
\end{partabstract}
