The prior conjecture is identified explicitly; historical novelty of the stronger identities is provisional pending broader literature and expert review. No improvement to global Szemer\'edi bounds is claimed.
\end{quote}

\subsection{What was reviewed, and what is actually used}
The motivating intersection of the two requested repositories is quantitative higher-order additive structure. The \texttt{openai/math} collection contains a September 23, 2026 preprint entitled \emph{Quasipolynomial Bounds for Arithmetic Progressions}; its source announces strong arithmetic-progression conclusions and develops weighted polynomial-cell bookkeeping \cite{oaimath,oaiprogressions}. The repository itself warns that checking status varies across entries. We treat those global conclusions as claims of that source, not as established hypotheses of the present paper.

The ProveIt Ramsey collection combines research manuscripts with formalization status reports \cite{repo103,repo103status}. The reviewed status text distinguishes finite weighted cube identities, energy-maximality stability and conditional interfaces from an ungated multiscale progression argument. This distinction matters: a finite cube lemma can be proved and useful without completing a global density-increment architecture. The present paper makes no inference from a conditional wrapper to a source-free Szemer\'edi theorem.

The concrete starting point is the earlier manuscript \emph{Sharp local stability for additive cubes: Exact energy bounds, a sharp subgroup-boundary inequality, and the deletion--addition transition} \cite{srconehundredone}. Its odd-order analysis obtains a cubic expression with an additional $-35\delta^4$ error and explicitly proposes, in the source label \texttt{conj:oddexact}, the loss-free inequality
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:103:eq:target}
\eps_3(A)\ge 4\delta-10\delta^2+8\delta^3
\end{equation}
for sufficiently small distance to a nearest odd-order subgroup coset. That manuscript was accessible in the user's Library. A corresponding research-directory name was returned by a repository directory listing, but direct retrieval of that subdirectory failed; we therefore do not pretend that the Library artifact has been independently matched to a particular repository commit. Appendix~\ref{gsr:fz:103:app:sources} records this provenance limitation.

We chose this problem because its obstruction is concrete: the old argument discarded too much information in the high-order inclusion--exclusion tail. The missing information is precisely the additive energy of the deleted set. Retaining it closes the conjecture rather than merely improving an error constant.

\subsection{Relation to the general near-extremizer literature}
The general fact that near-maximal Gowers seminorms force polynomial or subgroup structure is not new. Eisner and Tao study near-extremizers under $L^\infty$ and critical $L^p$ constraints, with polynomial phases possibly localized to subgroups \cite{eisnertao}. General $U^3$ inverse theory is also a major established subject \cite{greentaoUthree}. Our question is different and more specific: with $0\le a\le1$, mass fixed, and unnormalized cube count compared with the fourth power of that mass, what is the exact local deficit as a function of distance from an indicator of a subgroup coset?

The contribution here is not the qualitative slogan ``near-extremizers resemble cosets.'' It is the explicit identity of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:103:thm:identity}, its parity term, the exact cubic local profile, and the resulting quantitative rigidity and weighted extension. These statements are proved without invoking an inverse theorem.

\subsection{Statement of the principal local result}
For a finitely supported function $a:G\to[0,1]$ on an abelian group, put
\begin{align}
 n&=\sum_x a(x),\\
 \CkS_3(a)&=\sum_{x,t_1,t_2,t_3\in G}
       \prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^3}a(x+\omega\cdot t),\\
 \eps_3(a)&=1-\frac{\CkS_3(a)}{n^4}\qquad(n>0).
\end{align}
All cubes, including degenerate ones, are counted. For a set $A$, write $\CkS_3(A)=\CkS_3(\one_A)$ and $\eps_3(A)=\eps_3(\one_A)$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:103:eq:Pdelta}
 P(u)=4u-10u^2+8u^3.
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Exact local weighted profile]\label{gsr:fm:103:thm:main}
Let $G$ be abelian, let $a:G\to[0,1]$ have finite support and positive mass $n$, and let $C=x_0+H$ be a coset of a finite subgroup of odd order. If
\[
 \delta=\frac{\norm{a-\one_C}_1}{n}\le\frac1{50},
\]
then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:103:eq:main}
 \eps_3(a)\ge P(\delta).
\end{equation}
For $\delta>0$, equality holds if and only if
\[
 a=\one_{C\setminus L}
\]
for a coset $L$ of a subgroup $K\le H$ lying in $C$. For $\delta=0$, equality means simply $a=\one_C$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Source~101's Conjecture~\ref{gsr:fz:101:conj:oddexact}} (delivered as Conjecture~12.1) is proved here, the first proof; source~104 proves it again independently for sets (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:cubestability}). Checked at the write: $\Z/51\Z$ minus a point attains $P(1/50)=2377/31250$ ($C_3=5{,}774{,}600$).
\end{writenote}

The coset $C$ in this statement need not initially be declared nearest. A coset this close is automatically the unique closest finite subgroup coset; see Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:103:lem:unique}. Consequently Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:103:thm:main} proves the precise local conjecture described above. The function version is genuinely stronger than the set version: the equality conclusion forces an extremal $[0,1]$ function to be Boolean.

\begin{theorem}[Global weighted near-extremizers]\label{gsr:fm:103:thm:globalintro}
Let $G$ be a finite abelian group of odd order and let $a:G\to[0,1]$ have mass $n>0$. If $\eps=\eps_3(a)<1/2000$, there is a unique nearest subgroup coset $C$ and
\[
 \frac{\norm{a-\one_C}_1}{n}\le35\eps<\frac1{50}.
\]
Writing the left-hand side as $\delta$, one has $\eps\ge P(\delta)$, with the equality cases of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:103:thm:main}.
\end{theorem}

The constants $1/50$, $1/2000$, and $35$ in the rounding estimate are convenient explicit constants, not asserted optimal. In contrast, the local polynomial is exact on an infinite sequence of admissible distances, and the coefficient $35$ in the tail-energy inequality of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:103:thm:35} is optimal.

\begin{partabstract}{104}
Let $\cC_k(A)$ count the labelled additive $k$-cubes in a finite set $A$, including degeneracies, and let $\eps_k(A)=1-\cC_k(A)/|A|^{k+1}$. We prove the optimal comparison
$\eps_2\le\eps_k\le(2^k-k-1)\eps_2$ in every abelian group. Retaining the full-cube term in a fourth-order inclusion--exclusion expansion then gives an exact odd-order complement identity with nonnegative occupancy remainders. It yields the local bound
\[
\eps_3(A)\ge4\delta-10\delta^2+8\delta^3,
\]
where $\delta\le1/50$ is the relative distance to an odd-order coset, with equality exactly for subcoset deletions. This proves the odd-order conjecture stated in the earlier \emph{Sharp local stability for additive cubes} manuscript and removes its fourth-order error.

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]

Its proof is an independent second route, printed after source~103's (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:cubestability}); ``removes its fourth-order error'' is correct, but no longer first.
\end{writenote}

Independently, when $G/H$ has no nonzero two-torsion and $s/h$ lies in an explicit interval, we prove
\[
\cC_k(H\cup D)\le h^{k+1}+2khs^k+s^{k+1},
\qquad h=|H|,\ s=|D|,\ D\cap H=\varnothing.
\]
The coefficient $2k$ is sharp; equality and near-equality force $D$ to be an outside subcoset. For each $k\ge4$ this gives the sharp local odd-order profile
$1-(1-\delta)^{k+1}-2k(1-\delta)\delta^k-\delta^{k+1}$.
The proofs include explicit stability remainders, a quantitative nested-coset theorem, and torsion and size obstructions. Exact finite verification scripts and a source audit accompany the article.
\end{partabstract}

\subsection{What was reviewed, and what is used}
The starting point is the additive-cube interface common to Gowers's proof of Szemer\'edi's theorem \cite{gowers}, the near-extremizer theory of Eisner and Tao \cite{eisnertao}, the progression manuscripts in \texttt{openai/math}, and the local-refinement program in ProveIt. This article concerns the cardinality-extremal regime, not a general inverse theorem at small density.

The September 23, 2026 manuscript \emph{Quasipolynomial Bounds for Arithmetic Progressions} in \texttt{openai/math} states, for every fixed $k\ge3$, a bound of the form
\[
 r_k(N)\le C_kN\exp\{-c_k(\log N)^{\varepsilon_k}\}.
\]
Its introduction derives the divergent-reciprocal-sum consequence, and its normalized cube-comparison section discusses conditional image-measure and lattice-mask issues \cite{oaiprogressions}. These statements and the selected comparison section were inspected; the complete large proof was not independently rechecked. They motivate attention to normalization and cube interfaces, but are not premises of any theorem here.

The October 7 ProveIt integration record carefully separates partial formal verification from the remaining quantitative conclusion. Commit \texttt{97ce7d847a} reports a compiled closure of 106 modules for the first 100 pinned upstream entries, with an axiom audit of 2,928 public OAI theorems, while explicitly leaving \texttt{Results.Conclusions} unverified \cite{repo104port}. These are repository-reported checks, not checks rerun in this work. The local-refinement README and the source-101 formalization plan likewise distinguish written research from a checked Lean development \cite{repo104,repo104plan}.

Our direct mathematical predecessor is \emph{Sharp local stability for additive cubes} \cite{srconehundredone}. It proves an unrestricted boundary coefficient $2^{k+1}-2$, exact unrestricted local profiles, and an odd-order cubic estimate with a $35\delta^4$ loss. Its Conjecture 12.1 asks whether that loss can be removed. Its subsequent questions ask for an odd-order boundary constant and quantitative boundary stability. The present article addresses those concrete questions, rather than treating a repository title as a certificate of a breakthrough.

\subsection{Normalization and notation}\label{gsr:fm:104:ocb:sec:notation}
All groups are abelian and written additively. Sets being counted are finite. For $k\ge1$ define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:104:ocb:eq:cubes}
\cC_k(A)=\#\left\{(x,t_1,\ldots,t_k):
 x+\sum_{i=1}^k\omega_it_i\in A\quad
 \text{for every }\omega\in\{0,1\}^k\right\}.
\end{equation}
The ambient group need not be finite: the $k+1$ values at $0,e_1,\ldots,e_k$ determine all parameters. Thus the count is finite and at most $|A|^{k+1}$. Degenerate cubes are included throughout. Put
\[
 E(A)=\cC_2(A),\qquad \de(A)=|A|^3-E(A),\qquad
 \eps_k(A)=1-\frac{\cC_k(A)}{|A|^{k+1}}\quad(A\ne\varnothing).
\]
In a finite ambient group of order $N$, with density $\alpha=|A|/N$, our normalization is
\[
 1-\eps_k(A)=\frac{\|\1_A\|_{U^k(G)}^{2^k}}{\alpha^{k+1}}.
\]
It is the deficit of the powered, density-normalized norm, not the deficit of the norm itself.

For a finite coset $C=a+H$, write
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:104:ocb:eq:parameters}
 R=C\setminus A,\quad D=A\setminus C,\quad
 r=|R|,\quad s=|D|,\quad h=|H|,\quad m=h-r,\quad n=|A|=m+s.
\end{equation}
After translating by $-a$, we view $R$ as a subset of $H$. Set
\[
 x=\frac rn,\qquad y=\frac sn,\qquad
 \delta_C=\frac{|A\symd C|}{n}=x+y,\qquad
 \delta(A)=\min_C\delta_C.
\]
The minimum exists because singleton cosets are allowed and the unnormalized errors are nonnegative integers. The denominator is always $n$, not $h$.

\subsection{Main results}
The first theorem solves the earlier odd-order cubic question, with a quantitative remainder.
\begin{theorem}[Exact odd-order cubic stability]\label{gsr:fm:104:ocb:thm:cubic-main}
Let $A\ne\varnothing$ be finite in an abelian group, and let $C=a+H$ be a finite coset of odd order. If $\delta=\delta_C\le1/50$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:104:ocb:eq:cubic-main}
\eps_3(A)\ge \po_3(\delta)+\frac72\delta\frac{s}{n}
       +\frac{(12h-140r)\de(R)}{n^4},
\qquad \po_3(u)=4u-10u^2+8u^3.
\end{equation}
In particular $\eps_3(A)\ge\po_3(\delta)$. For $\delta>0$, equality in this last inequality holds exactly when $A=C\setminus L$, where $L$ is a coset of a subgroup of $H$.

If $G$ is finite of odd order and $\eps_3(A)<1/60$, there is a unique nearest coset, its distance is less than $1/50$, and the same conclusions apply to $\delta(A)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Second route} to source~103's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:103:thm:main}; source~103's remainder is stronger ($12h-35r$ on $r<12h/35$), this source's rigidity constants sharper (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:104:ocb:thm:cubic-rigidity}).
\end{writenote}

The second theorem distinguishes torsion in the quotient from torsion in $H$ itself. Write $Q[2]=\{q\in Q:2q=0\}$.
\begin{theorem}[Sharp boundary without quotient two-torsion]\label{gsr:fm:104:ocb:thm:boundary-main}
Let $H\le G$ be finite, let $D\subseteq G\setminus H$ be finite and nonempty, and put $h=|H|$, $s=|D|$. Suppose $(G/H)[2]=\{0\}$. For $k\ge2$ define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:104:ocb:eq:alpha}
 \beta_k=2\bigl((3/2)^k-1\bigr),\qquad
 \alpha_k=\frac{2(k-1)}{\beta_k-1}
          =\frac{2(k-1)}{2(3/2)^k-3}.
\end{equation}
If $s/h\le\alpha_k$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:104:ocb:eq:boundary-main}
 \cC_k(H\cup D)\le h^{k+1}+2khs^k+s^{k+1}.
\end{equation}
The coefficient $2k$ cannot be decreased, even as $s/h\to0$ through finite odd-order examples. If $s/h<\alpha_k$, equality holds exactly when $D=b+K$ for a subgroup $K\le H$ and $b\notin H$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Answers source~101's questions on the boundary inequality locally} (its Section~\ref{gsr:fz:101:sec:d12}, delivered Questions~12.3 and~12.4): under $(G/H)[2]=0$ and $s/h\le\alpha_k$; checked at the write: $\alpha_2,\ldots,\alpha_5=4/3,16/15,16/19,128/195$.
\end{writenote}

The first few sufficient ratios are
\[
 \alpha_2=\frac43,\quad \alpha_3=\frac{16}{15},\quad
 \alpha_4=\frac{16}{19},\quad \alpha_5=\frac{128}{195}.
\]
These radii are not claimed to be optimal. Section~\ref{gsr:en:104:ocb:sec:boundary} proves stronger bounds measuring the dispersion and energy deficit of $D$, and derives an explicit inverse theorem.

For higher dimensions the local extremizers add rather than remove an outside subcoset.
\begin{theorem}[Higher-dimensional odd-order profile]\label{gsr:fm:104:ocb:thm:higher-main}
Fix $k\ge4$. There is an explicit $\rho_k>0$, given in \eqref{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:rho}, such that the following holds. Let $A$ be finite and nonempty, let $C=a+H$ be a finite coset with $(G/H)[2]=\{0\}$, and suppose $\delta=\delta_C\le\rho_k$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:104:ocb:eq:higher-main}
 \eps_k(A)\ge\po_k(\delta)+\frac{2^k-2(k+1)}2(1-\delta)^k\frac rn,
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:104:ocb:eq:oddprofile}
 \po_k(u)=1-(1-u)^{k+1}-2k(1-u)u^k-u^{k+1}.
\end{equation}
For $\delta>0$, equality in $\eps_k(A)\ge\po_k(\delta)$ holds exactly when, after translating $C$ to $H$, one has $A=H\cup(b+K)$ with $K\le H$ and $b\notin H$.

For $k=4$, one may use $\rho_4=1/50$. In a finite odd-order group, the assumption $\eps_4(A)<1/60$ therefore implies the sharp nearest-coset bound
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:104:ocb:eq:four-profile}
 \eps_4(A)\ge5\delta-10\delta^2+10\delta^3-13\delta^4+8\delta^5.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\subsection{Logical dependence and novelty relative to the predecessor}
The universal cube recursion, elementary coset rounding, unrestricted boundary estimate, and higher-dimensional hole estimate are reused from the earlier framework and reproved here. The new route to the odd cubic profile is the combination of an optimal energy comparison with a full occupancy correction. The new boundary argument retains quotient-fiber information and uses the absence of order-two quotient elements to improve cross-intersection capacity. The resulting explicit remainders supply quantitative inverse theorems rather than equality classifications alone.

The two torsion hypotheses are deliberately different. The cubic complement theorem needs $|H|$ odd and allows arbitrary torsion outside $H$. The boundary theorem needs $(G/H)[2]=\{0\}$ and allows even-order $H$. In a finite odd-order ambient group both conditions hold. No theorem below asserts that near-maximal cube counts are typical in a density-increment argument, or that these bounds improve a global Szemer\'edi estimate.

\begin{partabstract}{105}
For the symmetric quartic tensor
\(T_0(h_1,h_2,h_3,h_4)=\sum_j y_j\prod_{k\ne j}x_k\) on
\(\F_3^2\), we prove that the maximum of its twisted fourth-cube energy
on the complex unit polydisc is exactly \(11/27\). This resolves
Conjecture~11.4 of the project manuscript \emph{Finite-cover polarization
and optimal repair of multilinear phase obstructions}, whose previous
certified upper bound was \(1099/2187\).

The proof changes from nine point phases to twelve affine-line phases,
subject to four product constraints. The resulting eight-variable
Laurent polynomial has a positive semidefinite Hermitian Gram
representation of order 241 over \(\Q(\exp(2\pi i/3))\). Its coefficient
identity, kernel and positivity are verified by a supplied
standard-library Python program using integer arithmetic only. No
numerical optimizer is in the verification chain.

We classify every extremizer explicitly as a nonclassical cubic phase
times a prescribed quartic correction times an arbitrary unimodular
function of one of four linear coordinates. The extremizer set consists
of 2916 disjoint three-dimensional tori in the original nine-point phase
torus. The certificate also gives a quantitative stability inequality in
monomial coordinates. Finally, for every dimension, a symmetric quartic
tensor with nonzero alternating transfer defect has energy at most
\(11/27\). Consequently an energy strictly exceeding \(11/27\) forces
exact nonclassical integration. This last constant is sharp. The result
concerns an already symmetric quartic tensor; it is not a new complete
inverse theorem or a claimed improvement of an integer progression bound.
\end{partabstract}
\begin{quote}\small
\noindent\textbf{Verification status.}
The finite certificates in this article have been executed successfully.
The proof is computer-assisted, not Lean-verified or independently
refereed. The electronic matrix data are an essential part of the proof
and are included with the article source and verifier.
\end{quote}

\subsection{A focused review of the two repositories}

The \texttt{openai/math} catalogue inspected on 7 October 2026 includes a
September~23 manuscript, \emph{Quasipolynomial Bounds for Arithmetic
Progressions} \cite{oaiprogressions}. Its main statement asserts, for every fixed
\(k\ge3\), a bound of the form
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:105:eq:oai-claim}
 r_k(N)\le C_kN\exp\bigl(-c_k(\log N)^{\varepsilon_k}\bigr),
 \qquad C_k,c_k,\varepsilon_k>0.
\end{equation}
The introduction describes an iteration on triangular polynomial cells,
with descending control of the dimensions and precisions of inherited
constraints. It explicitly separates finding structured correlations
from returning a density increment to a previously constructed cell.
This is relevant here as a research direction: exact algebraic structure
and the losses incurred in using it are different problems. We report
\eqref{gsr:fm:105:eq:oai-claim} as the repository manuscript's assertion, not as a
result independently verified by this article. None of our proofs assumes it.

The adjacent catalogue entries on superexponential van der Waerden
numbers and fixed off-diagonal Ramsey numbers similarly concern global
quantitative extremal problems \cite{oaimath}. They suggest several
possible directions, but do not supply a verified replacement for a
local low-characteristic phase argument. The present work selects that
local issue rather than extrapolating a new global theorem from a
catalogue description.

The inspected ProveIt research compilation,
\emph{Local Quantitative Refinements of Gowers's Proof of Szemer\'edi's
Theorem}, has dated additions through 7 October 2026. Its themes include
density transfer, phase-flat partitions, restriction and arrangement
energies, and the phase-extraction interface in Section~17 of Gowers's
proof. Its README distinguishes written research arguments from formal
status \cite{repo105}. We preserve this distinction. The current article
adds a separate research package; it does not change a Lean ledger or
claim to discharge a named Lean declaration.

For comparison with established work, Leng, Sah and Sawhney's 2024
preprint gives, for fixed \(k\ge5\), a saving of the form
\(\exp[-(\log\log N)^{c_k}]\) \cite{lssbounds}. That expression is not the same
as the \(\log N\) saving asserted in \eqref{gsr:fm:105:eq:oai-claim}. Our sharp
constant is a finite-field obstruction threshold, not another bound for
\(r_k(N)\), so neither comparison is a claim of improving the same theorem.

\subsection{The precise predecessor and the missing endpoint}

A separate project-associated manuscript, \emph{Finite-cover
polarization and optimal repair of multilinear phase obstructions}
\cite{srcninetytwo}, proves an integrating-cover construction, lossless subgroup
comparison, and reduction of extremal phase energy to a canonical
low-characteristic obstruction. Its ternary quartic computation gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:105:eq:oldinterval}
 \frac{11}{27}\le m_{3,1}\le\frac{1099}{2187}.
\end{equation}
Its Conjecture~11.4 proposes equality at the lower endpoint. Question~14.1
asks for a positivity certificate, and Question~14.4 asks about stability.
This manuscript was retrieved from the user's project materials rather
than assigned an unverified path in the public repository. The provenance
file accompanying this article records that distinction.

The gap in \eqref{gsr:fm:105:eq:oldinterval} is not a matter of rounding. Its upper
bound takes absolute values of all coefficients of an exactly enumerated
Laurent polynomial. It discards compatibility among monomial phases.
The new ingredient is a positive semidefinite identity that retains those
compatibilities. The sharp inequality, the complete equality
classification and the explicit monomial-coordinate stability bound are
the proposed contributions of this article. The general integration
criterion for nonclassical symmetric forms is already due to Tidor
\cite{tidor}; we do not claim it as a new result.

\subsection{Scope of the novelty and proof dependencies}

Resolving the specifically identified project conjecture is an exact,
checkable assertion. A broader priority claim would require further
literature review. The proof below is written so that it does not depend
on the correctness of any unreviewed global claim in either repository.
The general analytic input is the standard Gowers--Cauchy--Schwarz
inequality and the norm property of \(U^4\). The algebraic integration
criterion is recalled with a direct proof in characteristic three.
All new finite coefficient and matrix assertions are accompanied by
complete exact checks.

\srcnote{106}{Section 1}
\partsource{\textbf{Added in the fourteenth write, 7~October 2026.} \textbf{Delivered title block.} ``Torus Defects and Sharp Affine Partition Laws / Products of coordinate crosses, asymptotic rigidity, and simultaneous quadratic localization / AI-assisted research manuscript / Prepared for the ProveIt project / October 7, 2026''; the PDF author field reads ``AI-assisted research manuscript for the ProveIt project''. Archive \file{torus\_defect\_affine\_partitions.zip} (arrival \texttt{d96a456d2}, 7~October 2026, 15:39), manuscript \file{article.tex} (1,035 lines, 23 pages), pin \texttt{6896b6297} (13:48), with the blob \texttt{04e7ed74} of \file{Proofs05QuadraticFamily.lean}; it read source~102's manuscript from a private copy (912 lines, the delivered \file{article.tex}). Its \file{INTEGRATION.md} is shipped as \file{106-torus-defect-INTEGRATION.md}, its verifier and \file{Makefile} under \file{code/}, its records, source manifest, theorem status and build report under \file{data/}. Its \texttt{\textbackslash F} ($\mathbb F_q$), \texttt{\textbackslash PP} and \texttt{\textbackslash T} ($\mathcal T$) are set as the report's \texttt{\textbackslash Fq} and as \texttt{\textbackslash Psf}, \texttt{\textbackslash Tcal}; its \texttt{\textbackslash stirling} is added. \emph{It credits source~102} for $\Psf(C^2)=4q-3$, the binomial reduction and the existence of $\rho$, and extends them from odd $q$ to every $q>2$; it answers source~102's Question~13.2 at the large-field scale ($\rho(q)\sim2\sqrt q$) and brackets its Question~13.1 (Section~\ref{gsr:dt:sec:affinecells}). Its $q$ is the order of the field, as in source~102.}
\begin{partabstract}{106}
Let $C_{s,q}$ be the union of the $s$ coordinate lines in $\mathbb F_q^s$, and let $P_{s,m}(q)$ be the minimum number of affine subspaces in a partition of $C_{s,q}^m$. For every fixed $s\ge2$ and $m\ge1$, write $m=rs+\ell$ with $0\le\ell<s$. We prove
\[
 P_{s,m}(q)=s^{m-1}(s-\ell)q^{m-r}
              +O_{s,m}(q^{m-r-1})
 \qquad(q\longrightarrow\infty).
\]
The result holds through all prime powers $q>2$. In particular, for the singular quadratic fiber $C_{2,q}=\{(x,y):xy=0\}$, the answer is
$P_{2,m}(q)\sim4^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}q^{\lceil m/2\rceil}$.
This determines both the exponent and the leading coefficient in the higher-product problem left open by the preceding quadratic-localization manuscript.

The proof gives an exact nonnegative defect identity combining the total number of points with the number of points having every block nonzero. It yields finite rational lower bounds, an optimal two-moment linear-programming relaxation, and quantitative geometric stability. In an optimal partition, all but $O_{s,m}(1/q)$ of the points lie in torus-saturating flats of dimensions $r$ and $r+1$; their point-mass proportions tend to $1-\ell/s$ and $\ell/s$. We classify and enumerate these flats. Matching constructions attain the asymptotic lower bounds.

For the regularized cost $\rho_s(q)=\lim_{m\to\infty}P_{s,m}(q)^{1/m}$ we prove explicit bounds implying
$\rho_s(q)=s q^{1-1/s}(1+O_s(\log q/q))$. Thus $\rho_2(q)\sim2\sqrt q$, replacing a previously constant-order lower bound by the sharp large-field scale. Exact finite-field optimization remains distinct: we prove
$4q^2-5q+2\le P_{2,3}(q)\le4q^2-3q$, but do not assert equality at either endpoint.
\end{partabstract}
\begin{quote}\small
\noindent\textbf{Status and scope.} Complete mathematical arguments and exact finite checks are supplied. The proposed contributions are new relative to the preceding project manuscript; exhaustive historical priority has not been established. This is not a peer-reviewed or Lean-verified paper. No global conjecture claim in the motivating repositories is assumed, and no new integer Szemer\'edi bound is claimed.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Why count affine cells?}
A simultaneous localization problem asks for a partition on which several structured functions are constant, or nearly constant. Applying a scalar localization theorem repeatedly is a natural construction, but it does not establish that independent localization has optimal cost. Even completely independent quadratic phases can have joint singular fibers whose optimal affine partitions are not products of scalar optimizers.

The preceding project manuscript, \emph{Sharp Affine Localization for Quadratic Phases}~\cite{srconehundredtwo}, resolved the two-block example. For
\[
 C_{2,q}=\{(x,y)\in\Fq^2:xy=0\},
\]
it established $\Psf(C_{2,q})=q$ and $\Psf(C_{2,q}^2)=4q-3$, where $\Psf$ denotes the minimum number of cells in an affine partition. For $q>3$, this is a strict improvement over $q^2$. Products of those constructions gave
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:106:eq:old-pairing}
 P_{2,m}(q)\le (4q-3)^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}q^{m\bmod2}.
\end{equation}
The same manuscript explicitly left open a matching exponent lower bound for $m\ge3$, the exact three-block cost, and the regularized rate. Its only general rate lower bound was $2-1/q$~\cite[Sections 9 and 13]{srconehundredtwo}.

The decisive additional statistic is the mass of the full-support stratum. A $d$-dimensional affine cell has $q^d$ points, but at most $(q-1)^d$ of them can avoid every coordinate hyperplane of a containing orthant. These two capacities are close, but their mismatch determines the leading partition cost. Retaining the mismatch rather than using only the largest possible cell is the main mechanism of this paper.

\subsection{The sharp all-arm law}
For $s\ge2$, let $e_1,\ldots,e_s$ denote the standard basis of $\Fq^s$ and put
\[
 C_{s,q}=\bigcup_{i=1}^s\Fq e_i,
 \qquad
 P_{s,m}(q)=\Psf(C_{s,q}^m),\qquad P_{s,0}(q)=1.
\]
The cells are affine over the \emph{whole field} $\Fq$, and they must be pairwise disjoint. Covers and partitions over a proper subfield are different problems.

\begin{theorem}[Sharp fixed-product asymptotics]\label{gsr:fm:106:thm:main-intro}
Fix integers $s\ge2$ and $m\ge1$. Write $m=rs+\ell$ with $0\le\ell<s$. As $q$ tends to infinity through prime powers greater than two,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:106:eq:main}
 \boxed{P_{s,m}(q)=s^{m-1}(s-\ell)q^{m-r}
                     +O_{s,m}(q^{m-r-1}).}
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:106:eq:main-two}
 P_{2,m}(q)=4^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}q^{\lceil m/2\rceil}
                       +O_m(q^{\lceil m/2\rceil-1}).
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
A proof appears in Section~\ref{gsr:dt:106:sec:asymptotic}. The leading coefficient is part of the conclusion: a result only of the form $q^{\lceil m/2\rceil+o(1)}$ would not identify the efficiency of the existing pairing construction.

\begin{theorem}[Regularized asymptotics]\label{gsr:fm:106:thm:rate-intro}
For every $s\ge2$ and prime power $q>2$, the limit
\[
 \rho_s(q)=\lim_{m\to\infty}P_{s,m}(q)^{1/m}
          =\inf_{m\ge1}P_{s,m}(q)^{1/m}
\]
exists. For fixed $s$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fm:106:eq:rate-intro}
 \boxed{\rho_s(q)=s q^{1-1/s}
                   \left(1+O_s\!\left(\frac{\log q}{q}\right)\right).}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Source~102's Question~13.2 at the large-field scale}: $\rho(q)=\rho_2(q)\sim2\sqrt q$, so source~102's upper bound $\sqrt{4q-3}$ is asymptotically sharp (its lower bound was $2-1/q$). Checked at the write: at $q=10^6+3$ the lower bound $Dq^{-\Lambda}$ and $\sqrt{4q-3}$ are within $2\cdot10^{-6}$ of $2\sqrt q$, relatively.
\end{writenote}
This is a statement about a different order of limits from Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:106:thm:main-intro}. In Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:106:thm:main-intro}, $m$ is fixed first. Here $m$ tends to infinity first, with $q$ fixed. The proof in Section~\ref{gsr:dt:106:sec:rates} does not interchange those limits.

The structural conclusion is also quantitative. For fixed $s,m$ and an optimal partition, almost all points belong to two adjacent cell dimensions, and almost all cells in point-mass terms have a very special coordinate description. Section~\ref{gsr:dt:106:sec:stability} states the precise bounds. This is a local geometric statement, not an unproved assertion that every optimizer equals a product construction.

\section[{The finite weighted phase problem\srctag{01}}]{The finite weighted phase problem}\label{gsr:dt:01:sec:d2}\label{gsr:dt:01:sec:phase}
\srcnote{01}{Section 2}

\subsection{Conventions}
Let $(\Omega,\mu)$ be a finite probability space with positive atom weights.
Let $h:\Omega\to[0,1]$, and put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:01:eq:basic}
 \delta=\E h\in(0,1),\quad b=1-\delta,\quad f=h-\delta,
 \quad M_\delta=2\delta b.
\end{equation}
A partition $\mathcal P=(P_j)$ consists of nonempty cells. Set
\[
 w_j=\mu(P_j),\qquad q_j=\E(h\mid P_j).
\]
Then $\sum_jw_j=1$ and $\sum_jw_jq_j=\delta$.
Every assertion for this model includes ordinary subsets of a finite set,
by taking uniform weights and $h=\one_A$.

A unit-modulus function $\psi$ is \emph{short-arc on a cell} if there is a
real $\gamma_j$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:01:eq:arc}
 \psi(x)\in\{\exp(i(\gamma_j+t)):-\theta\le t\le\theta\}
 \quad(x\in P_j),\qquad 0\le\theta<\pi/2.
\end{equation}
Write $s=\sin\theta\in[0,1)$. Arc centers may differ between cells.
We assume
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:01:eq:eta}
 |\E f\psi|\ge\eta\ge0.
\end{equation}
The elementary chord inequality
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:01:eq:abslinear}
 |u-\delta|\le\delta+(1-2\delta)u\qquad(0\le u\le1)
\end{equation}
gives $\E|f|\le M_\delta$, and hence $\eta\le M_\delta$.
Equality holds in the first inequality for indicator functions.

\subsection{A cancellation-sensitive preliminary bound}

\begin{lemma}[Cancellation and phase diameter]\label{gsr:dt:01:lem:cancellation}
Let $f$ be any real function on a finite probability space, and suppose
$|\psi|\le1$ and the diameter of $\psi(P_j)$ is at most $2s$, where
$0\le s\le1$. If
\[
 M=\E|f|,\qquad D=\sum_j\abs{\E(f\one_{P_j})},
\]
then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:01:eq:cancellation}
 |\E f\psi|\le sM+(1-s)D.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
In one cell let $A$ and $B$ be the positive and negative masses of $f$,
measured with the original probability weights. Choose the corresponding phase
averages $u,v$ (arbitrarily within the phase hull if a mass is zero). They
belong to the convex hull of the cell's phase values, so
$|u|,|v|\le1$ and $|u-v|\le2s$. If $A\ge B$, then
\[
 |Au-Bv|=|(A-B)u+B(u-v)|\le A-B+2sB.
\]
This equals $s(A+B)+(1-s)|A-B|$. Interchanging the two signs proves the
same estimate when $B>A$. Sum over cells and apply the triangle inequality.
\end{proof}

For indicators, the coefficient $M$ in~\eqref{gsr:dt:01:eq:cancellation} is
$2\delta(1-\delta)$, not the cruder bound $1$. Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:01:eq:Dfrometa}
 D\ge \frac{\eta-2\delta(1-\delta)s}{1-s}
\end{equation}
whenever the right-hand side is positive. The next calculation retains
more information than $D$ alone.

\subsection{The exact one-cell envelope}
Define, for $0\le q\le1$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:01:eq:Phi}
 \ph(q)=\sqrt{(q-\delta)^2+4\delta bq(1-q)s^2}.
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}[Sharp cell bound]\label{gsr:dt:01:lem:cell}
Under~\eqref{gsr:dt:01:eq:arc},
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:01:eq:cell}
 \abs{\E((h-\delta)\psi\mid P_j)}\le\ph(q_j).
\end{equation}
For each $q\in[0,1]$, equality can be realized on a finite weighted cell
with mean $q$ and an indicator $h$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
First suppose $h$ is an indicator. Relative to the cell probability
measure, the positive mass is $A=bq$ and the negative mass is
$B=\delta(1-q)$. Let $U,V$ be the phase averages on the occupied and
unoccupied portions. Taking independent samples of their phase values,
\[
 |AU-BV|\le\max_{|u|,|v|\le\theta}
             |Ae^{iu}-Be^{iv}|.
\]
The omitted common rotation has modulus one. Since $|u-v|\le2\theta<\pi$,
\[
 |Ae^{iu}-Be^{iv}|^2
  =(A-B)^2+4AB\sin^2\frac{u-v}{2}
  \le(A-B)^2+4ABs^2.
\]
Here $A-B=q-\delta$, giving~\eqref{gsr:dt:01:eq:cell}. Place all occupied mass at
one endpoint of the arc and all unoccupied mass at the other to attain
it. Cases $q=0,1$ use only one phase value.

For general $h$, replace an atom of weight $w$ and value $h(x)$ by an
occupied atom of weight $wh(x)$ and an unoccupied atom of weight
$w(1-h(x))$, with the same phase. Delete zero-weight atoms. This preserves
both the cell mean and the correlation, so the indicator argument applies.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Convexity and the endpoint chord]\label{gsr:dt:01:lem:convex}
The function $\ph$ is convex on $[0,1]$, with
$\ph(0)=\delta$ and $\ph(1)=b$. Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:01:eq:strictchord}
 \ph(q)<\delta+(1-2\delta)q\quad(0<q<1,
 \ 0\le s<1).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $s=0$, this is the convex function $|q-\delta|$.
For $0<s<1$, differentiation gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:01:eq:curvature}
 \ph''(q)=\frac{4\delta^2b^2s^2(1-s^2)}{\ph(q)^3}>0.
\end{equation}
For completeness, if $G=\ph^2$ then
$(\sqrt G)''=(2GG''-(G')^2)/(4G^{3/2})$, and the numerator divided by
four is $4\delta^2b^2s^2(1-s^2)$.
The endpoint values are immediate. Finally, the square of the right-hand
side of~\eqref{gsr:dt:01:eq:strictchord}, minus $\ph(q)^2$, is
$4\delta bq(1-q)(1-s^2)>0$. The chord is positive, so taking square
roots proves the strict inequality.
\end{proof}
\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026]
\emph{One bound, two parametrizations.} Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:01:lem:cell} and source~02's Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:02:thm:localphase} are the same bound. In a cell with positive mass $A=bq$ and negative mass $B=\delta(1-q)$ (cell-normalized), source~02's signed and absolute masses are $F=A-B=q-\delta$ and $L=A+B$, and its bound $C^2\le(1-\rho^2)F^2+\rho^2L^2=F^2+4\rho^2AB$ is $\ph(q)^2$ with $\rho=s$. The arc conventions agree: an arc of half-angle $\theta$ has chordal diameter $2\sin\theta$, so source~02's $\rho$ (half the chordal diameter) is this $s=\sin\theta$. Both proofs sample the phases of the positive and the negative mass independently; source~02's statement is for arbitrary real $f$, and this one reduces bounded weights to indicators by splitting atoms. The linear consequence, Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:01:lem:cancellation}, is source~02's \eqref{gsr:dt:02:eq:linearphase} and Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:02:cor:freezing}, proved here directly and there from the quadratic bound. Credited to both sources. Source~05's Proposition~\ref{gsr:dt:05:prop:transfer} (a disk centre inside the arc) and source~03's Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:03:selection:phase} (arbitrary unit constants) are different, complex-valued transfer estimates.
\end{writenote}

\section[{A sharp density-tail theorem\srctag{01}}]{A sharp density-tail theorem}\label{gsr:dt:01:sec:d3}\label{gsr:dt:01:sec:tail}
\srcnote{01}{Section 3}

Fix a target density $a\in[\delta,1)$. Define
\begin{align}
 u_a&=\frac{\ph(a)-\delta}{a},\label{gsr:dt:01:eq:u}\\
 \BB(a)&=\delta+\delta u_a,\label{gsr:dt:01:eq:B}\\
 \GG(a)&=1-2\delta-u_a
       =\frac{M_\delta-\BB(a)}{\delta}>0.\label{gsr:dt:01:eq:Gamma}
\end{align}
Positivity in~\eqref{gsr:dt:01:eq:Gamma} follows from~\eqref{gsr:dt:01:eq:strictchord}.
The quantity $\BB(a)$ is the largest correlation permitted by these
constraints if every cell density is at most $a$.

\begin{theorem}[Sharp excess and density-tail transfer]\label{gsr:dt:01:thm:tail}
Under the hypotheses of Section~\ref{gsr:dt:01:sec:phase}, put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:01:eq:lambda}
 \lambda_*(\delta,s,a,\eta)
  =\frac{\pos{\eta-\BB(a)}}{\GG(a)}
  =\frac{\delta\pos{\eta-\BB(a)}}{M_\delta-\BB(a)}.
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:01:eq:tail}
 \sum_{q_j>a}w_j
 \ \ge\ \sum_jw_j\frac{\pos{q_j-a}}{1-a}
 \ \ge\ \lambda_*(\delta,s,a,\eta).
\end{equation}
For every $\eta\in[0,M_\delta]$, the last bound and the corresponding
lower bound on the mass of cells with $q_j>a$ are optimal among all finite
weighted spaces and phases satisfying the stated constraints.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Convexity bounds $\ph$ by the chord joining $0$ to $a$ on the first
interval, and by the chord joining $a$ to $1$ on the second. Written as
one formula, this is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:01:eq:brokenchord}
 \ph(q)\le\delta+u_aq+
       \GG(a)\frac{\pos{q-a}}{1-a}.
\end{equation}
To check the second chord, its slope minus $u_a$ is
\[
 \frac{b-\ph(a)}{1-a}-u_a
 =\frac{b-\delta-u_a}{1-a}
 =\frac{\GG(a)}{1-a}.
\]
Lemmas~\ref{gsr:dt:01:lem:cell} and~\ref{gsr:dt:01:lem:convex}, the triangle inequality, and
$\sum_jw_jq_j=\delta$ now give
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:01:eq:mainchord}
 \eta\le\sum_jw_j\ph(q_j)
 \le\BB(a)+\GG(a)\sum_jw_j\frac{\pos{q_j-a}}{1-a}.
\end{equation}
Rearrange and use $0\le(q-a)_+/(1-a)\le\one_{q>a}$.

For sharpness, first take $\eta\ge\BB(a)$ and write
$\lambda=(\eta-\BB(a))/\GG(a)$. Since $\eta\le M_\delta$, we have
$0\le\lambda\le\delta$. Give cells of densities $1,a,0$ respective weights
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:01:eq:extremalweights}
 w_1=\lambda,\qquad
 w_a=\frac{\delta-\lambda}{a},\qquad
 w_0=1-\lambda-\frac{\delta-\lambda}{a}.
\end{equation}
They are nonnegative, sum to one, and have weighted mean $\delta$.
Use the equality construction of Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:01:lem:cell} in each cell, and
rotate the arcs independently so that all cell correlations point along
the positive real axis. The resulting correlation is
\[
 w_0\delta+w_a\ph(a)+w_1b=\BB(a)+\GG(a)\lambda=\eta.
\]
Only the density-$1$ cells exceed $a$, and their normalized excess is also
$\lambda$. Thus both bounds in~\eqref{gsr:dt:01:eq:tail} are equalities.

For $0\le\eta\le\BB(a)$, use the $\lambda=0$ configuration. If
$\BB(a)>0$, take two disjoint copies with opposite global phase rotations
and relative weights $(1+\eta/\BB(a))/2$ and
$(1-\eta/\BB(a))/2$. They still have mean $\delta$, no cell exceeds $a$,
and their total correlation is $\eta$. If $\BB(a)=0$, only $\eta=0$
arises in this case. Zero-weight cells are omitted throughout.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The scope of sharpness]\label{gsr:dt:01:rem:sharpnessscope}
The extremizers allow arbitrary real atom weights and independent choices
of arc centers. With rational weights they can be converted to ordinary
finite sets by replacing an atom with equally weighted copies. General
weights can be approximated by rational ones. This is not a proof that the
same extremizers occur for a fixed character on $\Z/N\Z$, a fixed
progression partition, or a prescribed list of cell sizes. Such arithmetic
constraints may permit further improvements.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Exceptional cells cost occupied mass}
A usual exceptional-set estimate pays for the whole exceptional set.
Here its occupied mass is the relevant quantity.

\begin{theorem}[Occupied-mass robust transfer]\label{gsr:dt:01:thm:exception}
Let $E\subseteq\Omega$, and partition $\Omega\setminus E$ into nonempty
regular cells $P_j$. Impose the short-arc condition only on regular cells,
and set
\[
 \beta_E=\E(h\one_E).
\]
Retain the global mean $\delta$ and correlation lower bound $\eta$.
For $\delta\le a<1$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:01:eq:exception}
 \sum_{\substack{j\text{ regular}\\q_j>a}}w_j
 \ge\sum_{j\text{ regular}}w_j\frac{\pos{q_j-a}}{1-a}
 \ge\max\{0,\lambda_*(\delta,s,a,\eta)-\beta_E\}.
\end{equation}
Here $w_j=\mu(P_j)$ uses the original measure, not the measure conditioned
on the regular set.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Write $\varepsilon=\mu(E)$. On regular cells use~\eqref{gsr:dt:01:eq:brokenchord};
their total weight and occupied mass are $1-\varepsilon$ and
$\delta-\beta_E$. On $E$, use~\eqref{gsr:dt:01:eq:abslinear}. Thus
\begin{align*}
 \eta
 &\le\delta(1-\varepsilon)+u_a(\delta-\beta_E)
   +\GG(a)\sum_{j\text{ regular}}w_j\frac{\pos{q_j-a}}{1-a}
   +\delta\varepsilon+(1-2\delta)\beta_E\\
 &=\BB(a)+\GG(a)\left(\beta_E+
       \sum_{j\text{ regular}}w_j\frac{\pos{q_j-a}}{1-a}\right).
\end{align*}
Rearranging proves the result, including the case $\eta\le\BB(a)$.
\end{proof}

The estimate is especially useful when the excluded cells have little of
$A$, even if their total length is not particularly small. An exceptional
set consisting of unoccupied points has $\beta_E=0$: it incurs no loss
in this formula. There is no contradiction with global cancellation,
since the density and constant term were never renormalized after deletion.
\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 06--10]
\emph{Exceptional mass in three models.} Source~06's Proposition~\ref{gsr:dt:06:den:defect} (extraction from a cell variation after a set of mass $\rho$ is discarded, or with a signed mean of size at most $\varepsilon$) and source~10's Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:10:thm:exception} (correlation transfer with an exceptional set of mass $\varepsilon<\delta$, under $s>2(1-\delta)\varepsilon$) also allow an exceptional set. The theorem above charges only the occupied mass $\beta_E\le\mu(E)$; the other two charge the total exceptional mass. The three statements have different hypotheses and conclusions, and none is claimed to imply another.
\end{writenote}

\begin{corollary}[A large good cell]\label{gsr:dt:01:cor:largecell}
For a uniform space of $N$ points with $m$ regular cells, let
$\rho=\max\{0,\lambda_* -\beta_E\}$. If $\rho>0$, some regular cell has
\[
 q_j>a,\qquad |P_j|\ge\frac{\rho N}{m}.
\]
If all regular cells have size at least $L$, that cell also has size at
least $L$. If instead all have size at most $U$, there are at least
$\rho N/U$ good cells.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Their union has at least $\rho N$ points by Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:01:thm:exception}.
Pigeonhole over at most $m$ cells for the first assertion; divide their
total size by the upper size bound for the last.
\end{proof}

\section[{The optimal forced maximum and its tradeoff\srctag{01}}]{The optimal forced maximum and its tradeoff}\label{gsr:dt:01:sec:d4}\label{gsr:dt:01:sec:maximum}
\srcnote{01}{Section 4}

The density-tail theorem contains a closed-form answer to a simpler
question: how large must at least one cell density be?

\begin{theorem}[Optimal maximum density from a short-arc correlation]
\label{gsr:dt:01:thm:maximum}
Assume there are no exceptional points, and put
$\kappa=\eta/M_\delta$. If $0\le s<\kappa\le1$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:01:eq:amax}
 \max_jq_j\ge a_*=
 \frac{\delta(\kappa-s^2)}
      {\kappa(1-b\kappa)-\delta s^2}.
\end{equation}
Equivalently, the forced increment is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:01:eq:tmax}
 t_*=a_*-\delta=
 \frac{\delta b(\kappa^2-s^2)}
      {\kappa(1-b\kappa)-\delta s^2}.
\end{equation}
These bounds are sharp in the finite weighted model. If $\kappa\le s$,
no positive density increment is forced by this information alone.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The function $\BB(a)$ is continuous and strictly increasing for
$\delta\le a\le1$, after defining its endpoint value at $1$ by continuity.
Indeed, its nonconstant part is the secant slope
$(\ph(a)-\ph(0))/a$. Strict convexity proves the assertion for $s>0$;
for $s=0$ and $a\ge\delta$ it follows directly from
$\BB(a)=2\delta(a-\delta)/a$. Its endpoint values are
\[
 \BB(\delta)=M_\delta s,\qquad \BB(1)=M_\delta.
\]
If all $q_j\le a$, the first chord gives $\eta\le\BB(a)$.
Thus the unique solution of $\BB(a_*)=M_\delta\kappa$ is a lower bound
on $\max_jq_j$, including the endpoint $a_*=1$ when $\kappa=1$.

The equation for $a_*$ is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:01:eq:root}
 \ph(a_*)=\delta+a_*(2b\kappa-1).
\end{equation}
Squaring, cancelling the common constant term, and removing the positive
factor $a_*$ gives a linear equation in $a_*$. It yields~\eqref{gsr:dt:01:eq:amax}.
There is no extraneous square-root branch. To see this explicitly, let
\[
 D_0=\kappa(1-b\kappa)-\delta s^2.
\]
Since $s<\kappa$,
$D_0>\kappa(1-b\kappa)-\delta\kappa^2=\kappa(1-\kappa)\ge0$.
Also
\[
 D_0-\delta(\kappa-s^2)=b\kappa(1-\kappa)\ge0,
\]
so $a_*\le1$, and~\eqref{gsr:dt:01:eq:tmax} shows $a_*>\delta$.
The right side of~\eqref{gsr:dt:01:eq:root}, after substitution, equals
\[
 \frac{\delta b\bigl(\kappa^2+(1-2\kappa)s^2\bigr)}{D_0}>0.
\]
For $\kappa\le1/2$ positivity is immediate; for $\kappa>1/2$, use
$s^2<\kappa^2$ and $1-2\kappa<0$, with the case $\kappa=1$
giving $1-s^2>0$. Hence the squared solution satisfies the original
root equation.

Sharpness uses densities $0$ and $a_*$ with weights
$1-\delta/a_*$ and $\delta/a_*$ and the aligned equality phases from
Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:01:lem:cell}. Their correlation is $\BB(a_*)=\eta$.
Finally, if $\kappa\le s$, cells all of density $\delta$ can have
correlation $M_\delta s$; opposite rotated copies reduce it to any
$\eta\le M_\delta s$ without changing any cell density.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Solving for the allowed arc width}
At $s=0$, the optimal increment is
\[
 t_0=\frac{\delta b\kappa}{1-b\kappa}.
\]
For $0<\kappa<1$ and a requested increment $0<t\le t_0$, solving
$t_*(s)=t$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:01:eq:pareto}
 s_{\max}^2(t)=
 \frac{\kappa\bigl[\delta b\kappa-t(1-b\kappa)\bigr]}
      {\delta(b-t)}.
\end{equation}
Here $t_0<b$, so the denominator is positive. The right side decreases
from $\kappa^2$ to $0$ as $t$ increases from $0$ to $t_0$.
For $0\le s\le s_{\max}(t)$ the forced increment is at least $t$.
This follows either from~\eqref{gsr:dt:01:eq:tmax}, or from monotonicity of
$\ph$ in $s$, which makes a fixed correlation easier to obtain when
the allowed arc is wider. At $\kappa=1$, maximal correlation instead
forces a density-$1$ cell for every $s<1$; formula~\eqref{gsr:dt:01:eq:pareto}
need not be used at its removable endpoint.

The tradeoff has a practical interpretation. A wider allowed arc permits
longer phase-flat progressions, but weakens the density increase. Formula
\eqref{gsr:dt:01:eq:pareto} separates this exact probabilistic tradeoff from the
Diophantine approximation that constructs the progressions.

\section[{Partition discrepancy and finite convex optimization\srctag{01}}]{Partition discrepancy and finite convex optimization}\label{gsr:dt:01:sec:d5}\label{gsr:dt:01:sec:lp}
\srcnote{01}{Section 5}

\subsection{A sharp transfer using only cell discrepancy}
For a partition define its normalized balanced discrepancy by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:01:eq:discrepancy}
 D=\sum_jw_j|q_j-\delta|.
\end{equation}
The equality $\sum_jw_j(q_j-\delta)=0$ implies
$D=2\sum_jw_j(q_j-\delta)_+$, and convexity gives $D\le M_\delta$.

\begin{theorem}[Discrepancy-to-density tail]\label{gsr:dt:01:thm:L1}
Let $0\le t<1-\delta$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:01:eq:L1tail}
 \sum_{q_j>\delta+t}w_j\ge
 \max\left\{0,
 \frac{D(\delta+t)-2\delta t}
      {2\delta(1-\delta-t)}\right\}.
\end{equation}
The lower bound is sharp among all finite weighted partitions of mean
$\delta$ and discrepancy $D$. In addition,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:01:eq:L1max}
 \max_jq_j\ge\delta+\frac{\delta D}{2\delta-D}.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Choose a phase constant on each cell, equal to $1$ or $-1$ according to
the sign of $q_j-\delta$. Then its global correlation is exactly $D$.
Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:01:thm:tail} with $s=0$, $\eta=D$, and $a=\delta+t$.
In this case
\[
 \BB(a)=\frac{2\delta t}{\delta+t},\qquad
 \GG(a)=\frac{2\delta(1-\delta-t)}{\delta+t},
\]
which gives~\eqref{gsr:dt:01:eq:L1tail}. The three-density equality construction
in~\eqref{gsr:dt:01:eq:extremalweights} has exactly this discrepancy, proving
sharpness. For~\eqref{gsr:dt:01:eq:L1max}, use Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:01:thm:maximum} with
$s=0$ and $\kappa=D/M_\delta$; the case $D=0$ is just the mean bound.
The denominator is positive because $D\le2\delta(1-\delta)<2\delta$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 11--14]
Source~13's Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:13:thm:selection} is a seventh independent proof of the sharp one-sided bound, in source~02's form $R_p(t)=Q_{a,b}(p,t)$, with discarded mass and a signed drift (note there).
\end{writenote}

Suppose a uniform $N$-point space has a partition into $m$ cells and a
lower bound on its \emph{average} cell size, $\overline L=N/m$.
Let the positive right-hand side of~\eqref{gsr:dt:01:eq:L1tail} be $\Lambda$.
Then some cell simultaneously has density greater than $\delta+t$ and
size at least $\Lambda\overline L$. This is a direct local output for
any supplied partition; it neither replaces an average by a minimum nor
assumes that the good cell is among the largest cells in advance.
\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026]
\emph{The sharp one-sided bound, in four sources.} The bound \eqref{gsr:dt:01:eq:L1tail} is the case $a=\delta$, $b=1-\delta$ of a sharp one-sided mass bound that four of the five sources prove independently, each in its own form: source~02's Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:02:thm:tail} (cell means in $[-a,b]$, with the nonzero-mean extension \eqref{gsr:dt:02:eq:nonzero}), source~03's Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:03:selection:sharp} (a random variable in $[-a,b]$, with the bound \eqref{gsr:dt:03:selection:max} on its essential supremum), and source~05's Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:05:lem:capacity} ($a=\delta$, $b=1-\delta$, with the non-strict event $g\ge t$, which makes its bound weaker, and a popularity corollary). The identification (checked at the write): the discrepancy is twice the positive mass, so with $T=D/2$, $a=\delta$ and $b=1-\delta$,
\[
 \frac{(a+t)T-at}{a(b-t)}=\frac{D(\delta+t)-2\delta t}{2\delta(1-\delta-t)},\qquad \frac{aT}{a-T}=\frac{\delta D}{2\delta-D},
\]
which are \eqref{gsr:dt:01:eq:L1tail} and \eqref{gsr:dt:01:eq:L1max}. The proof above is a genuinely different route, the case $s=0$ of the broken-chord envelope of Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:01:thm:tail}; sources~02, 03 and~05 count the negative support directly. All four statements and proofs are kept. Only source~01 proves a tail bound that is sharp for a positive arc parameter $s>0$ (Theorems~\ref{gsr:dt:01:thm:tail}, \ref{gsr:dt:01:thm:exception} and~\ref{gsr:dt:01:thm:maximum}); source~02's Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:02:thm:transfer}, source~03's Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:03:phase:increment} and source~05's Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:05:thm:density} first remove the phase and then apply the $s=0$ bound.
\end{writenote}
\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 06--10]
\emph{Two more sources prove the same bound.} Source~06's Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:06:den:sharp} states it in mass form: for cell averages in $[-a,b]$ with total mass $W$, positive and negative integrals $P_\pm$ and threshold $\eta$, the cells above $\eta$ have mass at least $S=(P_+-\eta(W-P_-/a))/(b-\eta)$. With $W=1$ and $P_+=P_-=T$ (mean zero) this is $((a+\eta)T-a\eta)/(a(b-\eta))$, source~02's bound at $t=\eta$; source~06 keeps a nonzero signed mean (its \eqref{gsr:dt:06:den:drift-bound}) and adds the exact optimum for a fixed number of cells (note after Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:02:cor:515}). Source~10's Proposition~\ref{gsr:dt:10:prop:tail} is the case $a=\delta$, $b=1-\delta$: with $T=S_{\mathcal P}/2$ and $t=\tau-\delta$, the bound $((\delta+t)T-\delta t)/(\delta(1-\delta-t))$ equals its $(\tau S_{\mathcal P}-2\delta(\tau-\delta))/(2\delta(1-\tau))$; and its \eqref{gsr:dt:10:eq:cap-lower} is the forced maximum $aT/(a-T)=\delta S_{\mathcal P}/(2\delta-S_{\mathcal P})$, i.e.\ \eqref{gsr:dt:01:eq:L1max} with $D=S_{\mathcal P}$ (identifications checked at the second write). Source~10's variance form \eqref{gsr:dt:10:eq:variance-cap} is not in the other sources. The bound is therefore proved independently in six sources (01, 02, 03, 05, 06, 10); all six statements and proofs are kept.
\end{writenote}

\subsection{A master reduction for additional moment information}
The preceding broken-chord argument is a small exact linear program.
The same mechanism handles more density statistics without repeated
pigeonholing.

\begin{theorem}[Finite-knot extremal reduction]\label{gsr:dt:01:thm:knots}
Let $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_m=1$, let $F:[0,1]\to\R$ be convex, and let
$g_1,\ldots,g_r$ be continuous functions affine on each interval
$[t_i,t_{i+1}]$. Fix feasible values of $\E g_\ell(Q)$ for a finitely
supported random variable $Q\in[0,1]$. The maximum possible $\E F(Q)$
is attained by a distribution supported on $\{t_0,\ldots,t_m\}$.
It is therefore the value of a finite linear program. An optimizer may
be chosen with at most the rank of the equality-constraint matrix
(including total mass) many positive weights.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $q\in[t_i,t_{i+1}]$, write
$q=(1-\lambda)t_i+\lambda t_{i+1}$. Replace its probability mass by
masses in the proportions $1-\lambda$ and $\lambda$ at the two endpoints.
Every prescribed $g_\ell$-moment is unchanged, since $g_\ell$ is affine
on this interval. The objective does not decrease, by convexity of $F$.
Do this for every atom. The resulting optimization has finitely many
nonnegative weights, one mass equation, and the given linear moment
equations. Its feasible set is a closed subset of the probability simplex,
so an optimum exists.

If an optimum has more positive weights than the equality matrix rank,
there is a nonzero vector supported on those weights in the kernel of
that matrix. Move in one of its two directions without decreasing the
objective, until a weight first becomes zero. The mass equation ensures
that the kernel vector has both signs, so such a move is possible.
Iterate to reach the claimed support size.
\end{proof}

Suitable moments include the mean, $|Q-\delta|$, and the stop-loss
quantities $(Q-a_i)_+$, provided their breakpoints are included among the
knots. The discontinuous function $\one_{Q>a_i}$ is not among the
permitted continuous moments; its lower bound is obtained afterward from
$(Q-a_i)_+/(1-a_i)\le\one_{Q>a_i}$. This distinction matters at equality.

\subsection{Several phases on one common partition}

\begin{corollary}[A simultaneous-phase score]\label{gsr:dt:01:cor:multiphase}
Suppose phases $\psi_1,\ldots,\psi_d$ are short-arc on the same partition,
with half-angles $\theta_i$ and $s_i=\sin\theta_i<1$. For weights
$\omega_i\ge0$ with $\sum_i\omega_i=1$, put
\[
 F(q)=\sum_i\omega_i\Phi_{\delta,s_i}(q),\qquad
 \eta=\sum_i\omega_i\abs{\E(h-\delta)\psi_i}.
\]
Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:01:thm:tail} and its occupied-mass version hold with $\ph$
replaced by $F$ in the definitions of $u_a$, $B$, and $\Gamma$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The cell bound and the triangle inequality give $\eta\le\sum_jw_jF(q_j)$.
The function $F$ is convex, has endpoint values $\delta,b$, and lies
strictly below their chord in the interior. The proofs of
Theorems~\ref{gsr:dt:01:thm:tail} and~\ref{gsr:dt:01:thm:exception} use exactly these facts.
\end{proof}

This is an interface, not an unconditional gain over choosing the largest
Fourier coefficient. Requiring one partition to control many phases has
its own dimension cost. Additional relations between phases could also
rule out the independent equality constructions used for the scalar
weighted model.

\section[{Integer-exact simultaneous progression partitions\srctag{01}}]{Integer-exact simultaneous progression partitions}\label{gsr:dt:01:sec:d6}\label{gsr:dt:01:sec:AP}
\srcnote{01}{Section 6}

We now construct short-arc cells without asymptotic rounding conventions.
An arithmetic progression here has the form
$\{a,a+q,\ldots,a+(\ell-1)q\}$ with positive integer $q$ and $\ell\ge1$.
All its terms are required to lie in $[N]_0$; no modular wrapping is used.

\begin{theorem}[Anisotropic phase-flat partition]\label{gsr:dt:01:thm:partition}
Let $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_d\in\R$, $d\ge1$, and let
$0<r_i\le1/2$. Choose an integer $L\ge2$ and set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:01:eq:Q}
 Q_i=\ceil{\frac{2(L-1)}{r_i}},\qquad T=\prod_{i=1}^dQ_i.
\end{equation}
If $N\ge LT$, there is a partition of $[N]_0$ into arithmetic
progressions, all with the same positive step $q\le T$, such that every
cell has length between $L$ and $2L-1$ and, on every cell, each
$e(\xi_i n)$ lies in an arc of length at most $r_i$ turns.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Partition $[0,1)^d$ into $T$ half-open boxes with side lengths $1/Q_i$.
Among the $T+1$ points
\[
 (\{j\xi_1\},\ldots,\{j\xi_d\}),\qquad 0\le j\le T,
\]
two belong to the same box. Subtracting their indices gives an integer
$1\le q\le T$ and integers $p_i$ with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:01:eq:Dirichlet}
 q\xi_i=p_i+\varepsilon_i,\qquad |\varepsilon_i|<1/Q_i.
\end{equation}
Partition $[N]_0$ first into residue classes modulo $q$. Each class has
at least $\lfloor N/q\rfloor\ge L$ elements. If a class has $n=vL+w$
elements, where $v\ge1$ and $0\le w<L$, divide its ordered list into
$v-1$ consecutive blocks of length $L$ and one final block of length
$L+w$. Thus every block has length in $[L,2L-1]$ and retains step $q$.

On a block of length $\ell$, a real lift of the $i$th phase has successive
differences $\varepsilon_i$. Its total span in turns is at most
\[
 (\ell-1)|\varepsilon_i|
 \le\frac{2L-2}{Q_i}\le r_i.
\]
Projection of this real interval to the circle gives the required arc.
Every point belongs to exactly one block, proving the partition assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 11--14]
Source~13's Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:13:thm:flexible} and Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:13:cor:flexscale} are the same partition, proved independently; source~13 adds complete partitions with prescribed lengths $v-1$ or $v$ (its Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:13:thm:exactlengths}) and an obstruction with independent tolerances (its Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:13:thm:obstruction}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{corollary}[A convenient explicit length]\label{gsr:dt:01:cor:partitionlength}
For every positive integer $N$ and the same frequencies and widths, one
may take
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:01:eq:Lexplicit}
 L=\max\left\{1,
 \floor{\left(\frac{N\prod_i r_i}{2^d}\right)^{1/(d+1)}}\right\}
\end{equation}
and obtain cell lengths between $L$ and $2L-1$ with the stated arc widths.
When $L=1$, use the singleton partition with step $1$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For $L\ge2$, the definition of $Q_i$ gives
\[
 Q_i\le\frac{2(L-1)}{r_i}+1\le\frac{2L}{r_i}.
\]
Consequently $L\prod_iQ_i\le2^dL^{d+1}/\prod_i r_i\le N$ by
\eqref{gsr:dt:01:eq:Lexplicit}. Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:01:thm:partition}. Singletons
satisfy the remaining case directly.
\end{proof}

The exact condition $N\ge L\prod_i\lceil2(L-1)/r_i\rceil$ can sometimes
permit a larger $L$ than~\eqref{gsr:dt:01:eq:Lexplicit}. It is monotone in $L$ and
can be checked by integer arithmetic once the widths have certified
rational lower bounds. The proof requires no optimal Diophantine
approximation algorithm: the pigeonhole construction suffices.
\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026]
Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:01:thm:partition} with Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:01:cor:partitionlength} and source~05's Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:05:thm:multi} are the same construction, a rectangular pigeonhole followed by residue-class blocking into lengths $[L,2L-1]$, with the same box counts $\lceil2(L-1)/r_i\rceil$ and the same explicit length; credited to both. The hypotheses differ slightly: here the widths satisfy $r_i\le1/2$ and the theorem takes $L\ge2$ (the corollary adds singletons), while source~05 allows widths $\varepsilon_i\le1$ and treats $L=1$ inside the theorem. The one-phase case is also source~05's Proposition~\ref{gsr:dt:05:prop:flexible} and, with a chordal error in place of an arc width, source~03's Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:03:phase:flatten}.
\end{writenote}

\section[{A strengthened Fourier density-increment lemma\srctag{01}}]{A strengthened Fourier density-increment lemma}\label{gsr:dt:01:sec:d7}\label{gsr:dt:01:sec:fourier}
\srcnote{01}{Section 7}
\begin{theorem}[An explicit replacement for Corollary 2.5]\label{gsr:dt:01:thm:fourier}
Let $N\ge1$, $h:[N]_0\to[0,1]$, and
$\delta=N^{-1}\sum_nh(n)\in(0,1)$. Suppose
\[
 \left|\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}(h(n)-\delta)e(\xi n)\right|\ge\eta>0
\]
for some real $\xi$. Put $b=1-\delta$ and
$\kappa=\eta/(2\delta b)$. There exists a proper arithmetic progression
$P\subseteq[N]_0$ such that
\begin{align}
 |P|&\ge L:=\max\left\{1,
 \floor{\sqrt{\frac{N}{2\pi}\arcsin\frac{\eta}{4\delta b}}}
 \right\},\label{gsr:dt:01:eq:finalL}\\
 \frac1{|P|}\sum_{n\in P}h(n)
 &\ge\delta+\frac{3\delta b\kappa}{4-(4-3\delta)\kappa}
 \ge\delta+\frac{3\eta}{8}.\label{gsr:dt:01:eq:finalincrement}
\end{align}
The progression can be chosen from a partition whose cell lengths all lie
between $L$ and $2L-1$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
As in~\eqref{gsr:dt:01:eq:abslinear}, $0<\kappa\le1$. Set
\[
 \theta=\arcsin(\kappa/2),\quad s=\sin\theta=\kappa/2,
 \quad r=\theta/\pi.
\]
Then $0<r\le1/6$. Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:01:cor:partitionlength}, with one
frequency, supplies the claimed partition and length. Each arc of length
$r$ turns has half-angle $\pi r=\theta$, so Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:01:thm:maximum}
applies, also for the singleton partition. Substituting $s=\kappa/2$
into~\eqref{gsr:dt:01:eq:tmax} gives
\[
 t_*=
 \frac{\delta b(3\kappa^2/4)}
      {\kappa(1-b\kappa)-\delta\kappa^2/4}
 =\frac{3\delta b\kappa}{4-(4-3\delta)\kappa}.
\]
The denominator is positive and at most $4$. Since
$\eta=2\delta b\kappa$, this is at least $3\eta/8$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Nonzero cyclic Fourier coefficients, any modulus]
\label{gsr:dt:01:cor:cyclic}
Let $N\ge2$, $A\subseteq\Z/N\Z$ have density $0<\delta<1$, and let
$r\not\equiv0\pmod N$. Use the unnormalized transform
\[
 \widehat{\one_A}(r)=\sum_{x\in\Z/N\Z}\one_A(x)e(-rx/N).
\]
If $|\widehat{\one_A}(r)|\ge\eta N>0$, the set of standard representatives
of $A$ has the density-increment conclusion of Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:01:thm:fourier}
on some ambient progression $P\subseteq[N]_0$. Primality of $N$ is unnecessary.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The geometric sum $\sum_{x=0}^{N-1}e(-rx/N)$ vanishes for any nonzero
residue $r$, whether or not $r$ is a unit. Thus the Fourier coefficient
of $\one_A-\delta$ is the same as that of $\one_A$ at $r$.
Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:01:thm:fourier} with $h=\one_A$ and $\xi=-r/N$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A simpler asymptotic comparison with all rounding exposed}
Since $\arcsin u\ge u$ for $0\le u\le1$, if
$N\eta\ge32\pi\delta(1-\delta)$ then the square root in
\eqref{gsr:dt:01:eq:finalL} is at least $2$, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:01:eq:roughL}
 L\ge\sqrt{\frac{N\eta}{32\pi\delta(1-\delta)}}.
\end{equation}
Here we used only $\lfloor x\rfloor\ge x/2$ for $x\ge2$.
Compared with the printed lower bound
$L_{\mathrm{old}}=\sqrt{\eta^3N/(128\pi)}$, this yields
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:01:eq:ratio}
 \frac{L}{L_{\mathrm{old}}}\ge
       \frac{2}{\eta\sqrt{\delta(1-\delta)}}
\end{equation}
in that parameter range. This is a comparison of two valid local
conclusions, not a global extremal-set estimate.

The repository's proof of that corollary already obtains the stronger pair $\sqrt{\eta N/(128\pi)}$ and $\eta/4$ before weakening it (inside the proof of the private lemma \file{cor25_large_scale}, \file{Proofs02DensityIncrement.lean}, line~375 at HEAD, lines~446--509; the lemma's own statement is already the weakened pair, and it assumes $4\pi\le\alpha N$) \textup{(corrected after the independent check of 6~October 2026; the first wording read ``(the private lemma \file{cor25_large_scale}, \ldots)'')}; sources~03 and~05 say so (Remark~\ref{gsr:dt:03:rem:repo} and Section~\ref{gsr:dt:05:sec:d3}, Subsection ``Comparison with the actual repository baseline'').  \frac{3\delta b\kappa}{4-(4-3\delta)\kappa}\cdot\frac{4-2b\kappa}{2\delta b\kappa}

Source~10's Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:10:thm:frontier} is a one-parameter family: for $0<\gamma<1$, length $L_\gamma=\max\{1,\lfloor\sqrt{N\lambda_\gamma/(2\pi)}\rfloor\}$ with $\lambda_\gamma=\arcsin((1-\gamma)\kappa)$, and increment $D_\gamma=\delta\gamma\eta/(2\delta-\gamma\eta)=\gamma\delta b\kappa/(1-\gamma b\kappa)$, in the notation $b=1-\delta$, $\kappa=\eta/(2\delta b)\in(0,1]$ used above. \emph{Claim.} Writing $I$ for the increment in \eqref{gsr:dt:01:eq:finalincrement}, $I\ge D_\gamma$ if and only if $\gamma(4-\kappa)\le3$, and $I\ge\frac32D_\gamma$ if and only if $\gamma(4-(2-\delta)\kappa)\le2$. \emph{Proof.} Both denominators are positive ($4-(4-3\delta)\kappa\ge3\delta\kappa>0$ and $1-\gamma b\kappa>0$), so $I\ge cD_\gamma$ is equivalent to $3(1-\gamma b\kappa)\ge c\gamma(4-(4-3\delta)\kappa)$. For $c=1$ this is $3-4\gamma+\gamma\kappa(4-3\delta-3b)\ge0$, and $4-3\delta-3b=1$. For $c=3/2$ it is $2-4\gamma+\gamma\kappa(4-3\delta-2b)\ge0$, and $4-3\delta-2b=2-\delta$. So the intake's ``at least $3/2$'' comparison holds for source~10 at its stated choice $\gamma=1/2$ and for every $\gamma\le1/2$, not along the whole frontier. As $\gamma\to1$, $D_\gamma\to\delta\eta/(2\delta-\eta)$, the limit described in part~(2) for sources~03 and~05.
