\section[{Real phase removal and a joint extremal theorem\srctag{13}}]{Real phase removal and a joint extremal theorem}\label{gsr:dt:13:sec:d5}\label{gsr:dt:13:sec:phase}
\srcnote{13}{Section 5}

The real-valuedness assumption in Lemma 5.14 permits a stronger estimate than a direct triangle-inequality subtraction. Let $z:X\to\C$ satisfy $|z|=1$. For one cell, use unnormalized integrals and put
\[
 c=\left|\int_Pfz\,d\mu\right|,\qquad
 d=\left|\int_Pf\,d\mu\right|,\qquad
 v=\int_P|f|\,d\mu.
\]

\begin{theorem}[An exact cell envelope]\label{gsr:dt:13:thm:phasecell}
If $f$ is real and the phase values on $P$ have chord diameter at most $2s$, where $0\le s\le1$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:13:eq:phasecell}
 c^2\le(1-s^2)d^2+s^2v^2.
\end{equation}
For every permissible pair of positive and negative masses, equality can be attained.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $u_+$ and $u_-$ be the positive and negative integrals of $f$ on $P$. Then $d=|u_+-u_-|$ and $v=u_++u_-$. For any pair of phase values, the chord condition gives $\Re(z_x\overline{z_y})\ge1-2s^2$. Expanding the squared correlation, bounding the two same-sign terms by $u_+^2$ and $u_-^2$, and using this lower bound on the subtracted cross term gives
\[
 c^2\le u_+^2+u_-^2-2u_+u_-(1-2s^2)
 =d^2+4s^2u_+u_-.
\]
This is \eqref{gsr:dt:13:eq:phasecell}. Equality holds if all positive mass has one unit phase and all negative mass another unit phase at chord distance $2s$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The optimal affine aggregate envelope]\label{gsr:dt:13:cor:phaseaggregate}
If every cell has chord diameter at most $2s$, define
\[
 C=\sum_j\left|\int_{P_j}fz\,d\mu\right|,
 \qquad V=\int_X|f|\,d\mu.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:13:eq:phaseaggregate}
 C\le sV+(1-s)D.
\end{equation}
For $s<1$, this gives $D\ge\max\{0,(C-sV)/(1-s)\}$. The coefficients in \eqref{gsr:dt:13:eq:phaseaggregate} are optimal using only these data.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For $0\le d\le v$, the square of $sv+(1-s)d$ exceeds $(1-s^2)d^2+s^2v^2$ by $2s(1-s)d(v-d)\ge0$. Apply theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:13:thm:phasecell} and sum. Sign-pure cells attain $d=v,c=v$; sign-balanced cells at the two phase endpoints attain $d=0,c=sv$. Mixtures attain every point on the asserted affine envelope. The signs of sign-pure cells can be paired if zero mean is also required.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 11--14]
\emph{Credit.} Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:13:thm:phasecell} is the one-cell envelope of source~01's Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:01:lem:cell} and source~02's Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:02:thm:localphase}, and this corollary is source~01's linear law (Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:01:lem:cancellation}) and source~02's Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:02:cor:freezing}; the complex two-atom example below plays the role of source~02's complex counterexample. Proved independently here; printed in this source's form.
\end{writenote}

For a balanced set, $V=2\delta(1-\delta)$ exactly. For general mean-zero $f\in[-a,b]$, $V\le2ab/(a+b)$. Thus a fixed target $D\ge\vartheta\alpha$ from $C\ge\alpha$, $0<\vartheta<1$, is ensured by the single global choice
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:13:eq:phasetolerance}
 s\le\frac{\alpha(1-\vartheta)}{V-\vartheta\alpha}.
\end{equation}
Here $V\ge C\ge\alpha$, so the denominator is positive. For $\vartheta=1/2$, the condition is $s\le\alpha/(2V-\alpha)$.

This separation is useful in Lemma 5.14. First construct a refinement with a globally chosen phase tolerance; then apply \eqref{gsr:dt:13:eq:phaseaggregate}. A cell-count constant obtained by applying a polynomial partition theorem separately to local correlations $\alpha_j$ is not automatically uniform as $\alpha_j\to0$. A global tolerance, or a global cutoff with its discarded correlation charged explicitly, prevents that hidden dependency. The repository's full-partition proof is a relevant insertion point \cite{repo13lean}.

The real hypothesis is essential. With two equal-weight atoms, take phases $e^{i\theta},e^{-i\theta}$ and function values $e^{-i\theta},e^{i\theta}$, $0<\theta<\pi/2$. Then $C=V=1$, $D=\cos\theta$, and $s=\sin\theta$, so the right side of \eqref{gsr:dt:13:eq:phaseaggregate} is strictly less than $1$. The result applies to real phase-removal and balanced-set steps, rather than to an arbitrary complex-valued input.

\subsection{Solving phase geometry and density selection together}

Composing corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:13:cor:phaseaggregate} with theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:13:thm:selection} is valid, but can lose information: an extremizer for the first bound need not be an extremizer for the second. The following theorem optimizes both constraints at once.

For $-a\le x\le b$, define
\begin{align}
 v(x)&=\frac{2ab+(b-a)x}{a+b},\label{gsr:dt:13:eq:vx}\\
 h_s(x)&=\sqrt{(1-s^2)x^2+s^2v(x)^2}.\label{gsr:dt:13:eq:hx}
\end{align}
For $0\le t<b$ and $0\le s<1$, put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:13:eq:HK}
 H_s(t)=\frac{a(t+h_s(t))}{a+t},\qquad
 K_s(t)=\frac{(a+b)(v(t)-h_s(t))}{a+t}.
\end{equation}
The number $K_s(t)$ is strictly positive: $v(t)>t\ge0$ for $t<b$, and $s<1$.

\begin{theorem}[Sharp joint phase, density, and exceptional-mass frontier]\label{gsr:dt:13:thm:joint}
Let $-a\le f\le b$, $\E f=0$, and let $C$ be the aggregate cell correlation above. Suppose phase chord diameter is at most $2s$ on every nonexceptional cell, where $0\le s<1$. Let $e$ be exceptional mass, and $q_t$ the mass of nonexceptional cells with average greater than $t$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:13:eq:jointupper}
 C\le H_s(t)+K_s(t)(e+q_t).
\end{equation}
In particular, if $C\ge\alpha$ and $e\le e_0$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:13:eq:jointlower}
 q_t\ge\max\left\{0,
 \frac{\alpha-H_s(t)}{K_s(t)}-e_0\right\}.
\end{equation}
This is the exact lower frontier for high-average mass in the finite weighted problem with the stated information.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 11--14]
\emph{Credit.} This joint frontier is the content of source~01's Theorems~\ref{gsr:dt:01:thm:tail}, \ref{gsr:dt:01:thm:exception} and~\ref{gsr:dt:01:thm:maximum} (the short-arc density tail with exceptional mass and the optimal forced maximum); the intake found $(H_s,K_s)$ equal to source~01's $(B_{\delta,s},\Gamma_{\delta,s})$ numerically. Source~01 charges exceptions by occupied mass, which is stronger for indicators; ``exact'' here refers to the mass budget stated.
\end{writenote}
\begin{proof}
The chord joining $(-a,a)$ and $(b,b)$ majorizes absolute value, so $|f|\le v(f)$ pointwise. Therefore a cell of average $x$ has conditional absolute integral at most $v(x)$. By theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:13:thm:phasecell}, a nonexceptional cell has conditional correlation at most $h_s(x)$.

The function $h_s$ is convex, being the Euclidean norm of the affine vector $(\sqrt{1-s^2}\,x,sv(x))$. Let $\ell_t$ be the line through $(-a,a)$ and $(t,h_s(t))$. Convexity gives $h_s(x)\le\ell_t(x)$ on $[-a,t]$. The affine function $v(x)-\ell_t(x)$ vanishes at $-a$, has nonnegative slope, and at $b$ equals $K_s(t)$. Thus every exceptional or high-average cell has conditional correlation at most
\[
 v(x)\le\ell_t(x)+K_s(t),
\]
whereas every other cell has conditional correlation at most $\ell_t(x)$. Average these inequalities. Since $\E f=0$, the affine terms sum to $\ell_t(0)=H_s(t)$, proving \eqref{gsr:dt:13:eq:jointupper} and \eqref{gsr:dt:13:eq:jointlower}.

For sharpness, put $A_0=a+b$ and choose $0\le u\le a/A_0$. Use three cell types with masses and averages
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}ccc@{}}
\toprule
Type & Mass & Average\\
\midrule
High & $u$ & $b$\\
Threshold & $(a-A_0u)/(a+t)$ & $t$\\
Negative & $(t+(b-t)u)/(a+t)$ & $-a$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The masses sum to $1$ and the mean is zero. On the threshold cell, take values $b$ and $-a$ in proportions $(a+t)/A_0$ and $(b-t)/A_0$, and assign them unit phases at chord distance $2s$. Its conditional correlation is exactly $h_s(t)$. Give the other two cells constant phases. Direct substitution yields
\[
 C=H_s(t)+K_s(t)u.
\]
Any mass $e\le u$ of the high cell may be split off as exceptional, leaving $q_t=u-e$. The identity
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:13:eq:HKendpoint}
 H_s(t)+\frac{a}{a+b}K_s(t)=\frac{2ab}{a+b}
\end{equation}
shows that these constructions cover every $\alpha$ between $H_s(t)$ and the maximal possible correlation $2ab/(a+b)$. If $\alpha\le H_s(t)$, take $u=0$; if the exceptional budget covers the required $u$, declare the whole high cell exceptional. In either case the zero lower bound is attainable. This proves the full sharpness statement.
\end{proof}

The extremizers use only the endpoint values $-a,b$. For $a=\delta$, $b=1-\delta$, those are exactly the values of a balanced indicator. Finite weighted realizations are exact, and uniform finite realizations approximate arbitrary real weights. However, an additional requirement that the phase be one fixed low-degree polynomial can restrict the extremizers; the theorem does not assert optimality under that extra structure.

\subsection{An exact maximum-average guarantee}

With no exceptional cells, $H_s$ is continuous and strictly increasing on $[0,b]$, with
\[
 H_s(0)=s\frac{2ab}{a+b},\qquad
 H_s(b)=\frac{2ab}{a+b}.
\]
For $0<s<1$, strict convexity of $h_s$ makes the secant slopes from $(-a,a)$ strictly increase. For $s=0$, the formula is $H_0(t)=2at/(a+t)$, which is strictly increasing directly. Thus, whenever
\[
 s\frac{2ab}{a+b}<\alpha\le\frac{2ab}{a+b},
\]
the exact least possible maximum cell average is the unique $t_*\in(0,b]$ satisfying $H_s(t_*)=\alpha$. A two-cell construction with averages $-a,t_*$ attains it. When a partition already guarantees a minimum cell length, this gives a density increment with no division by the cell count.

For example, $\delta=0.2$, $\alpha=0.04$, and $s=0.1$ give $V=0.32$. Separate affine phase removal and selection guarantee a maximum average of $0.00454545\ldots$; the joint theorem gives $0.00814479\ldots$. At $t=0.005$, it forces high-average mass at least $0.00228653\ldots$, whereas the separate composition gives no positive bound. These are evaluations of explicit formulas, rather than empirical estimates of an unknown extremum.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.92\textwidth]{figures/13-simultaneous-recurrence-density_frontier.pdf}
\caption{Guaranteed high-average mass at $a=0.2$, $b=0.8$, $\alpha=0.04$, $s=0.1$, with no exceptional cells. The joint frontier retains information lost by applying two sharp inequalities separately. The dotted vertical line marks the example $t=0.005$.}
\label{gsr:dt:13:fig:density}
\end{figure}

\section[{A density-sensitive Fourier increment\srctag{13}}]{A density-sensitive Fourier increment}\label{gsr:dt:13:sec:d6}\label{gsr:dt:13:sec:fourierincrement}
\srcnote{13}{Section 6}

The partition and selection results combine into an explicit finite corollary. It improves the actual strengthened conclusion already visible in the corrected proof of Corollary 2.5, rather than merely restating that correction.

\begin{theorem}[Fourier correlation yields a longer dense progression]\label{gsr:dt:13:thm:fourierincrement}
Let $A\subset\Z/N\Z$, $\delta=|A|/N$, and suppose some nonzero frequency $r$ satisfies
\[
 \left|\sum_{x\in A}e(-rx/N)\right|\ge\alpha N>0.
\]
There is a proper integer progression $P\subset\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:13:eq:fourierlength}
 |P|\ge\sqrt{\frac{\alpha N}{32\pi\delta(1-\delta)}}
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:13:eq:fourierdensity}
 \frac{|A\cap P|}{|P|}
 \ge\delta+
 \frac{\alpha}{4-\alpha(2-\delta)/(\delta(1-\delta))}
 \ge\delta+\frac\alpha4.
\end{equation}
The intersection uses the standard representative of each residue. No primality or additional size hypothesis is needed.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Set $a=\delta$, $b=1-\delta$. The nontrivial character sums to zero on the group, so its sum on $A$ is the negative of its sum on the complement. Hence
\[
 0<\alpha\le\min(a,b)\le2ab,
 \qquad 0<a,b<1.
\]
Put $\rho_0=\alpha/(4ab)\le1/2$ and $\varepsilon=\arcsin(\rho_0)/\pi\le1/6$. Apply corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:13:cor:flexscale} for one phase to $rx/N$ on $I_N$. Every cell has length at least
\[
 L=\max\{1,\lfloor\sqrt{\varepsilon N/2}\rfloor\}
\]
and phase chord diameter at most $2\rho_0$. For $f=\ind_A-a$, one has $\E f=0$ and $V=2ab$. The aggregate cell correlation is at least $\alpha$, by the triangle inequality. Therefore corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:13:cor:phaseaggregate} gives
\[
 D\ge\frac{\alpha-2ab\rho_0}{1-\rho_0}
 =\frac{\alpha}{2(1-\rho_0)}.
\]
Let $p_0=\alpha/[4(1-\rho_0)]$. Then $p_0\le ab<a$, and corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:13:cor:discard} gives a cell with average at least
\[
 \frac{ap_0}{a-p_0}
 =\frac{\alpha}{4-\alpha(1+b)/(ab)}.
\]
The denominator is positive, since $\alpha\le2ab$ gives a lower bound $2a>0$. This increment is at most $b$ and at least $\alpha/4$, so it is compatible with all finite and singleton cases.

Finally, $\max\{1,\lfloor x\rfloor\}\ge x/2$ for every $x\ge0$, and $\arcsin\rho_0\ge\rho_0$. Thus
\[
 L\ge\frac12\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon N}{2}}
 \ge\sqrt{\frac{\alpha N}{32\pi ab}}.
\]
Every cell in the partition has this length, proving both conclusions for the selected cell.
\end{proof}

The repository's Corollary 2.5 statement gives length $(\alpha^3N/(128\pi))^{1/2}$ and increment $\alpha/8$. Its corrected proof already obtains length $(\alpha N/(128\pi))^{1/2}$ and increment $\alpha/4$ \cite{repo13paper}. The additional length gain in theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:13:thm:fourierincrement}, relative to that stronger proof output, is
\[
 \frac{2}{\sqrt{\delta(1-\delta)}}.
\]
It comes from retaining the exact absolute mass of the balanced function, the real phase envelope, and the finite simultaneous-partition construction. A sharper increment is available by solving $H_{\rho_0}(t)=\alpha$ from theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:13:thm:joint}; \eqref{gsr:dt:13:eq:fourierdensity} has the advantage of a simple closed form.

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 11--14]
\emph{Comparison with source~01 (proved at the third write).} Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:13:thm:fourierincrement} is dominated by source~01's Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:01:thm:fourier} at the same length. Its partition has every cell of length $L=\max\{1,\lfloor\sqrt{N\arcsin(\rho_0)/(2\pi)}\rfloor\}$ with $\rho_0=\alpha/(4\delta(1-\delta))$, which is the length \eqref{gsr:dt:01:eq:finalL} of source~01 (whose $\eta$ is this $\alpha$). Put $b=1-\delta$ and $\kappa=\alpha/(2\delta b)\in(0,1]$. Since $2-\delta=1+b$, the increment \eqref{gsr:dt:13:eq:fourierdensity} is $\alpha/(4-2\kappa(1+b))=\delta b\kappa/(2-(2-\delta)\kappa)$, and source~01's is $I=3\delta b\kappa/(4-(4-3\delta)\kappa)$. Both denominators are positive (they are at least $\delta\kappa$ and $3\delta\kappa$), and
\[
 \frac{I}{\delta b\kappa/(2-(2-\delta)\kappa)}=\frac{3(2-(2-\delta)\kappa)}{4-(4-3\delta)\kappa}=1+\frac{2(1-\kappa)}{4-(4-3\delta)\kappa},
\]
because $3(2-(2-\delta)\kappa)-(4-(4-3\delta)\kappa)=2-2\kappa$. So source~01's increment is at least this one, with equality only at $\kappa=1$, and the ratio is at most $3/2$ (the denominator is at least $4-4\kappa$). (Exact rational check of the identity at the write: 200,000 random $(\delta,\kappa)$, ratios between $1$ and $1.499997$.) The ``sharper increment'' by solving $H_{\rho_0}(t)=\alpha$ is the route of source~01's optimal forced maximum (Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:01:thm:maximum}). The length lower bound \eqref{gsr:dt:13:eq:fourierlength} is a factor $\sqrt2$ below source~05's $\sqrt{\alpha N/(16\pi\delta(1-\delta))}$; the integer length is the same as source~01's. So the abstract's and Section~\ref{gsr:fm:13:sec:d1}'s presentation of this theorem as a gain is a gain over the formal Corollary~2.5 only; within this report it is a second route, printed in its own form.
\end{writenote}

\section[{Direct partitions for affine frequencies and their own steps\srctag{16}}]{Direct partitions for affine frequencies and their own steps}\label{gsr:dt:16:sec:d6}
\srcnote{16}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:dt:16:sec:ownstep}

\subsection{The finite certificate theorem}

Let \([R]_0=\{0,\ldots,R-1\}\), and let \(\norm{\cdot}_{\T}\) denote
distance to the nearest integer. All integer progressions in this
section have positive steps and are contained in \([R]_0\).

\begin{lemma}[Two elementary tools]\label{gsr:dt:16:lem:twotools}
An interval with at least \(L\ge1\) integer points can be partitioned
into consecutive intervals with lengths in \([L,2L-1]\).
Also, for \(\beta_i\in\T\) and positive integers \(J_i\), there is
\(1\le t\le\prod_iJ_i\) with
\[
                   \norm{t\beta_i}_{\T}\le J_i^{-1}
                   \quad\hbox{for every }i.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For the first statement, write the length as \(uL+r\),
\(u\ge1\), \(0\le r<L\), and use \(u-1\) blocks of length \(L\)
and one of length \(L+r\).
For the second, place the \(\prod J_i+1\) points \(j\beta\),
\(0\le j\le\prod J_i\), in \(\prod J_i\) half-open rectangular
boxes of side lengths \(1/J_i\). Two share a box; subtract their
indices.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Certificate for an exact step-controlled partition]
\label{gsr:dt:16:thm:certificate}
Let \(q\ge1\), \(L\ge2\), \(A_i,B_i\in\T\), and
\(0<\delta_i\le1/2\). Put
\[
 J_i=\left\lceil\frac2{\delta_i}\right\rceil,\quad
 T=\prod_{i=1}^qJ_i,\quad M_0=LT,\quad
 \varepsilon_i=\frac{\delta_i}{4LT^2}.
 \tag{6.1}\label{gsr:dt:16:eq:certificateparams}
\]
Suppose an integer \(s\) satisfies
\[
 1\le s\le\left\lfloor\frac R{LT}\right\rfloor,
 \qquad
       \norm{A_i s^2}_{\T}\le\varepsilon_i
       \quad(1\le i\le q).
 \tag{6.2}\label{gsr:dt:16:eq:certificate}
\]
Then \([R]_0\) has an exact partition into progressions \(Q\), with
\[
 L\le |Q|\le2L-1,
 \qquad
       \norm{(A_i n+B_i)d_Q}_{\T}\le\delta_i
       \quad(n\in Q,\ 1\le i\le q).
 \tag{6.3}\label{gsr:dt:16:eq:certificateout}
\]
No primality, irrationality, or genericity hypothesis is imposed on
the coefficients.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Split \([R]_0\) into residue classes modulo \(s\). Every class
has at least \(\lfloor R/s\rfloor\ge LT\) points.
In each class, partition its ordered index interval into blocks
\[
        P=\{x+s j:0\le j<m'\},
                \qquad LT\le m'\le2LT-1,
\]
using Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:16:lem:twotools}. On one such block put
\(\beta_i=(A_i x+B_i)s\). The rectangular Dirichlet argument gives
\(1\le t\le T\) with
\(\norm{t\beta_i}_{\T}\le\delta_i/2\).

Split \([m']_0\) into residue classes modulo \(t\).
Each has at least \(\lfloor m'/t\rfloor\ge L\) points, so it can
again be divided into blocks of lengths in \([L,2L-1]\).
Their images in the original interval have actual step \(d_Q=st\).
For every \(n=x+sj\) in the intermediate block,
\[
           (A_i n+B_i)st
              =t\beta_i+j t(A_i s^2)\quad\hbox{in }\T.
\]
Since \(j<2LT\) and \(t\le T\),
\[
 \norm{(A_i n+B_i)st}_{\T}
 \le\frac{\delta_i}{2}
       +(2LT)T\frac{\delta_i}{4LT^2}
 \le\delta_i.
\]
All splits use disjoint residue classes or consecutive blocks.
They therefore preserve exact coverage and disjointness, and each
final cell has the required length.
\end{proof}

The distinction from quadratic flattening is concrete: at the second
recurrence step the tolerance is \(\delta_i\), rather than a tolerance
divided by the final cell length. The first recurrence controls the
variation of the affine frequency along that step.

\subsection{The external recurrence theorem and the finite threshold}

We use the following precise consequence of
\cite[Theorem~1.1]{lau}. Its proof is external to this article.

\begin{proposition}[Cited simultaneous quadratic recurrence]\label{gsr:dt:16:prop:lau}
For every \(C>21\) and \(q\ge1\), there is a constant \(X_0(C,q)\)
such that the following holds. If \(0<\eta_i\le1/100\),
\(X>X_0(C,q)\), and
\[
                 \prod_i\eta_i^{-1}\le X^{1/C},
 \tag{6.4}\label{gsr:dt:16:eq:lauinput}
\]
then, for arbitrary \(A_i\in\T\), there is an integer \(1\le s<X\)
such that \(\norm{A_i s^2}_{\T}\le\eta_i\) for every \(i\).
\end{proposition}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{External input.} The cited preprint is not reproved here and its threshold $X_0(C,q)$ is not numerical (the source says so). The intake fetched it: its Theorem~1.1 gives $c_2=10.5+9m/(2m)^M+\varepsilon$, so $C>21$ at degree two is accurate; arXiv lists the author as Cheuk Fung Lau. Sources~18 and~19 use the same input in Part~I (Sections~\ref{gsr:dt:18:sec:d4} and~\ref{gsr:dt:19:sec:d6}).
\end{writenote}

To verify the specialization, Lau's theorem has degree \(d\) and
constant
\(c_2=10.5+9q/(2q)^{\mathcal M}+\epsilon\), with adjustable
\(\mathcal M,\epsilon\) subject to his stated lower bound.
For \(d=2\), first make \(2c_2<C\).
His requirement
\(\prod\eta_i^{-1}\le X^{1/(2c_2)}\)
then follows from the stronger \eqref{gsr:dt:16:eq:lauinput}.
The choices are fixed in terms of \(C,q\) and absorbed in \(X_0\).
Maynard's published result \cite{maynard} supplies a corresponding
input with a degree-dependent constant and suffices for the
\(q^{-2}\) nature of the conclusion below. The numerical limiting
constant \(42\) uses Lau's stated theorem.

\begin{corollary}[Finite sufficient condition]\label{gsr:dt:16:cor:finitecriterion}
In Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:16:thm:certificate}, set
\(\Delta=\prod_i\delta_i\) and \(Q_0=\lfloor R/(LT)\rfloor\).
For any \(C>21\), it is sufficient that
\[
 Q_0>X_0(C,q),\qquad
 Q_0\ge(4LT^2)^{Cq}\Delta^{-C}.
 \tag{6.5}\label{gsr:dt:16:eq:finitelau}
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The parameters \(\varepsilon_i\) in \eqref{gsr:dt:16:eq:certificateparams}
are at most \(1/100\), and
\[
               \prod_i\varepsilon_i^{-1}
                         =(4LT^2)^q\Delta^{-1}.
\]
Apply Proposition~\ref{gsr:dt:16:prop:lau} with \(X=Q_0\).
Its integer \(s<Q_0\) is an admissible certificate.
\end{proof}

The explicit certificate can be searched for and verified at a
particular finite size. The sufficient existence condition
\eqref{gsr:dt:16:eq:finitelau} contains the nonnumerical constant \(X_0\);
these are different kinds of information.

\subsection{The anisotropic exponent region}

\begin{theorem}[Power-law partition region]\label{gsr:dt:16:thm:frontier}
Fix \(q\ge1\), \(C>21\), and positive \(a,b_1,\ldots,b_q\).
If
\[
 (Cq+1)a+\bigl(C(2q+1)+1\bigr)\sum_{i=1}^qb_i<1,
 \tag{6.6}\label{gsr:dt:16:eq:frontier}
\]
then for all sufficiently large \(R\), uniformly in all \(A_i,B_i\),
there is a partition satisfying \eqref{gsr:dt:16:eq:certificateout} with
\[
                      L=\lceil R^a\rceil,\qquad
                      \delta_i=R^{-b_i}.
\]
In particular, every
\[
                  0<\gamma<\frac1{(q+1)(42q+1)}
 \tag{6.7}\label{gsr:dt:16:eq:balanced}
\]
is valid with \(a=b_1=\cdots=b_q=\gamma\).
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For large \(R\),
\(J_i\le3/\delta_i\), hence
\(T\le3^qR^{\sum b_i}\).
The exponent of \(R\) in the size requirement obtained from
\eqref{gsr:dt:16:eq:finitelau} is
\[
 a+\sum b_i+Cq\left(a+2\sum b_i\right)+C\sum b_i,
\]
which equals the left side of \eqref{gsr:dt:16:eq:frontier}.
The strict inequality absorbs the fixed constants, ceiling and floor
effects, and \(X_0(C,q)\).

If all exponents equal \(\gamma\), the displayed expression is
\((q+1)(2Cq+1)\gamma\).
For any \(\gamma\) as in \eqref{gsr:dt:16:eq:balanced}, choose \(C>21\)
sufficiently close to \(21\), and apply the first assertion.
\end{proof}

For comparison, the reciprocal limiting denominators are
\(86,255,508,845\) at \(q=1,2,3,4\).
Gowers' Lemma~13.5 has length exponent \(2^{-12q}\) and accuracy
exponent \(2^{-11q}\), together with a factor \(1/2\) in length
\cite{gowers}. The theorem above improves both powers for any
fixed \(q\), once its uniform threshold is met; it does not assert
the limiting exponent with an absolute constant-one threshold.

\subsection{Transport to cyclic groups}

\begin{corollary}[Composite moduli are allowed in the local transfer]
\label{gsr:dt:16:cor:modtransport}
Let \(P=\{h_0+d_0n:0\le n<R\}\subseteq\Z/N\Z\) be properly
parameterized, and let \(a_i h+b_i\) be affine frequencies.
Set
\[
 A_i=\frac{a_i d_0^2}{N}\pmod1,\qquad
 B_i=\frac{(a_i h_0+b_i)d_0}{N}\pmod1.
 \tag{6.8}\label{gsr:dt:16:eq:cycliccoeff}
\]
A partition supplied by Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:16:thm:certificate} transports to a
proper partition of \(P\), and its ambient steps satisfy
\[
             \abs{(a_i h+b_i)d_Q}_N\le\delta_iN.
 \tag{6.9}\label{gsr:dt:16:eq:modownstep}
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
A cell with index step \(st\) has ambient step \(d_Q=d_0st\).
For \(h=h_0+d_0n\),
\[
       \frac{(a_i h+b_i)d_Q}{N}
                    =(A_i n+B_i)st\pmod1.
\]
This proves the bound. Every output index cell is contained in the
injective parameter domain of \(P\), so properness is preserved.
The formula requires no inverse of \(d_0\), \(2\), or \(4\), and
therefore remains valid for arbitrary \(N\).
\end{proof}

\subsection{Weighted extraction for the Section 13 interface}

\begin{lemma}[Selecting a weighted cell]\label{gsr:dt:16:lem:weighted}
Suppose \(0\le w(n)\le U_0\) and
\(\sum_{n\in[R]_0}w(n)\ge\mu U_0R\).
Every exact partition has a cell \(Q\) with
\(\sum_{n\in Q}w(n)\ge\mu U_0|Q|\).
For \(0\le\tau<\mu\le1\), this cell has at least
\[
                    \frac{\mu-\tau}{1-\tau}|Q|
 \tag{6.10}\label{gsr:dt:16:eq:weighted}
\]
points at which \(w(n)\ge\tau U_0\).
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The first statement follows by summing the contrary strict
inequalities over the cells. If the high-value fraction is \(v\),
the average on \(Q\) is at most \(v+(1-v)\tau\), in units of \(U_0\).
Solving \(\mu\le v+(1-v)\tau\) proves \eqref{gsr:dt:16:eq:weighted}.
Two-valued weights at \(U_0\) and arbitrarily below \(\tau U_0\)
show sharpness of the bounded-variable factor.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]

\[
 w(h)=C(h)\ind_{\{h\in H,\ G(h)\ge(1-2\eta)C(h)\}}.
\]
The source input is
\(\sum_{h\in P}w(h)\ge\alpha^{32}N^{31}|P|/8\);
the pointwise cap is \(N^{31}\).
Applying the preceding partition and weighted lemma with
\(\mu=\alpha^{32}/8\), \(\tau=\alpha^{32}/16\), gives a cell \(Q\)
having at least
\[
              \frac{\alpha^{32}}{16-\alpha^{32}}|Q|
                      \ge\frac{\alpha^{32}}{16}|Q|
 \tag{6.11}\label{gsr:dt:16:eq:weighted13}
\]

\subsection{Effective slope dimension}

The recurrence certificate only concerns \(A_i\), not \(B_i\).
If only \(r\) of the \(A_i\) are nonzero in \(\T\), then
Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:16:cor:finitecriterion} can use
\[
 Q_0\ge (4LT^2)^{Cr}
                  \left(\prod_{A_i\ne0}\delta_i\right)^{-C},
 \qquad Q_0>X_0(C,r).
 \tag{6.12}\label{gsr:dt:16:eq:effectivedim}
\]
The rectangular step \(t\) must still handle all \(q\) intercepts.

\begin{corollary}[Fewer varying slopes]\label{gsr:dt:16:cor:fewslopes}
With \(r\ge1\) varying slopes, the sufficient power region becomes
\[
 (Cr+1)a+(2Cr+1)\sum_i b_i+
                 C\sum_{A_i\ne0}b_i<1.
 \tag{6.13}\label{gsr:dt:16:eq:dimfrontier}
\]
Every balanced exponent
\(\gamma<((q+1)(42r+1))^{-1}\) follows.
If \(r=0\), the certificate \(s=1\) works whenever \(R\ge LT\).
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply the recurrence theorem only to the nonzero slopes and repeat
the exponent calculation in Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:16:thm:frontier}.
At equal powers the total coefficient is
\((q+1)(2Cr+1)\). For \(r=0\), all quadratic errors are zero.
\end{proof}

More generally, if the \(A_i\) are integer combinations of \(r\)
torus elements with row sums of absolute coefficients bounded by a
fixed \(H\), a simultaneous certificate for those \(r\) elements at
accuracy \(\min_i\varepsilon_i/H\) implies all the required
certificates. At equal accuracies a fixed \(H\) changes thresholds,
but does not change the balanced power in
Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:16:cor:fewslopes}. A height bound is essential for a
uniform quantitative formulation.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{An obstruction and a precise remaining partition problem\srctag{16}}]{An obstruction and a precise remaining partition problem}\label{gsr:dt:16:sec:d7}
\srcnote{16}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:dt:16:sec:obstruction}

\begin{theorem}[Endpoint-cell obstruction]\label{gsr:dt:16:thm:obstruction}
Let \(q\ge1\), \(2\le L\le R\), and \(0<\delta_i<1/4\), and set
\(\Delta=\prod_i\delta_i\).
If
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{R-1}{L-1}\right\rfloor
       \frac{4^q\Delta^2}{(L-1)^q}<1,
 \tag{7.1}\label{gsr:dt:16:eq:obstruct}
\]
then there are coefficients \(A_i,B_i\in\T\) for which no progression
contained in \([R]_0\), containing \(0\), and of length at least \(L\),
satisfies \eqref{gsr:fm:16:eq:ownstepintro}.
Consequently no full partition into such progressions exists.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Choose all \(A_i,B_i\) independently with Haar distribution.
A progression containing \(0\) in \([R]_0\) begins at zero when
listed in increasing order, so its step \(d\) satisfies
\(1\le d\le\lfloor(R-1)/(L-1)\rfloor\).
For this step put
\[
                    u_i=A_i d^2,\qquad v_i=B_i d.
\]
The \(2q\) variables remain independent and Haar distributed, since
multiplication by a positive integer preserves Haar measure.
The first \(L\) points can satisfy the required inequalities only if
\[
                 \norm{v_i+j u_i}_{\T}\le\delta_i
                   \qquad(0\le j<L).
 \tag{7.2}\label{gsr:dt:16:eq:torusline}
\]

For a single pair \((u,v)\), the exact measure of
\eqref{gsr:dt:16:eq:torusline} is \(4\delta^2/(L-1)\).
Indeed choose the unique representatives \(v_j\in[-\delta,\delta]\).
All adjacent differences represent \(u\) and lie in
\([-2\delta,2\delta]\), an interval of length less than one.
They therefore coincide as real numbers. The sequence is a real
arithmetic progression between its endpoints \(v_0,v_{L-1}\).
Conversely every pair of endpoints in \([-\delta,\delta]\) defines
such a sequence, and the map to \((u,v)\) has absolute Jacobian
\(1/(L-1)\). Its image has no multiplicity modulo \(\Z^2\).
The measure is \((2\delta)^2/(L-1)\).

Independence over \(i\) gives probability
\(4^q\Delta^2/(L-1)^q\) for each fixed step.
The union bound and \eqref{gsr:dt:16:eq:obstruct} leave positive probability
that no candidate step works.
A full partition would have a cell containing \(0\), proving the
last assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Necessary power region]\label{gsr:dt:16:cor:necessary}
For positive \(a,b_1,\ldots,b_q\), a coefficient-uniform full-partition theorem with
\(L\asymp R^a\) and \(\delta_i\asymp R^{-b_i}\) can hold only if
\[
                       (q+1)a+2\sum_i b_i\le1.
 \tag{7.3}\label{gsr:dt:16:eq:necessary}
\]
In the balanced case this requires \(\gamma\le1/(3q+1)\).
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The left side of \eqref{gsr:dt:16:eq:obstruct} is, up to fixed factors, at most
\(R^{1-(q+1)a-2\sum b_i}\).
It tends to zero if the claimed necessary inequality fails.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{Relation to the other partition results.} This is the own-step, affine-frequency analogue of source~13's frontier $(q+1)a+qb=1$ for linear phases and diameters (Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:13:cor:frontier}), by the same random-slope union bound as source~13's Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:13:thm:obstruction} and source~05's Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:05:thm:minimax}; here $q$ counts affine frequencies (source~13's $q$), not a common difference. Sources~18 and~19 prove the polynomial-phase analogues $(qk(k+1)/2+1)a+kqb\le1$ and $(S+1)a+Db\le1$ (Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:18:part:cor:necessary-polynomial-partition-exponents}, Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:19:poly:obstruction}) for partitions controlling diameters, a different problem with the same recurrence input.
\end{writenote}

The obstruction can be realized with rational coefficients.
For a strict instance of \eqref{gsr:dt:16:eq:obstruct}, the acceptable
coefficients for any fixed step form a closed set, and their finite
union does not fill the torus. Its complement is nonempty and open,
so it contains a rational tuple with common denominator \(N>2(R-1)\).
The interval \([R]_0\) then embeds properly into \(\Z/N\Z\).
Moreover every modular progression contained in this interval lifts to
an integer progression, up to reversal: adjacent lifted differences
lie in an interval of length less than \(N\), so their common residue
forces them to coincide as integers. This shows that the obstruction is also relevant to finite cyclic
models.

There remains a gap between the sufficient region
\eqref{gsr:dt:16:eq:frontier} and the necessary region \eqref{gsr:dt:16:eq:necessary}.
In particular, the balanced bounds are of orders \(q^{-2}\) and
\(q^{-1}\). The obstruction is for a \emph{full partition}; it does
not upper-bound every possible weighted extraction of one
progression. That distinction is useful when deciding which
improvement would have the greatest effect in Section~13.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Simultaneous polynomial partitions by descent in degree\srctag{18}}]{Simultaneous polynomial partitions by descent in degree}\label{gsr:dt:18:sec:d4}
\srcnote{18}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:dt:18:part:sec:simultaneous-partitions}

Lemma~5.9 of \cite{gowers} handles several polynomial phases by
successively refining for one polynomial at a time.  This produces an
exponential dependence on the number of phases in the reciprocal
partition exponent.  We give a different organization of the argument:
all leading coefficients are treated simultaneously, and induction is
performed on the degree.  The resulting combinatorial transfer is
elementary.  Its analytic input is a simultaneous monomial recurrence
bound, which we state explicitly rather than incorporate silently into
the proof.

There are two distinct conclusions.  First, established simultaneous
recurrence estimates yield partition exponents with polynomial dependence
on the number of phases.  Second, an independent volume argument proves
a necessary restriction on every universal partition theorem of this
kind.  The latter argument explains a remaining gap: for quadratics our
general sufficient exponents have order $q^{-2}$, whereas the obstruction
only rules out exponents larger than a constant times $q^{-1}$.

\subsection{Arc diameter and the modular interpretation}

Throughout this section, $\Tcirc=\R/\Z$, and
$\|x\|_{\Tcirc}=\min_{m\in\Z}|x-m|$.  For a nonempty finite set
$S\subset\Tcirc$, define
\[
 \operatorname{adiam}(S)
 =\inf\{\ell\in[0,1]:S\subset a+[0,\ell]\pmod1
                         \text{ for some }a\in\Tcirc\}.
\]
This is the length of a shortest containing arc.  It is stronger than
merely bounding all pairwise geodesic distances.  For a polynomial
$F\in\R[X]$ and a finite set $P\subset\Z$, put
\[
 \operatorname{osc}_{P}(F)
 =\operatorname{adiam}\{F(x)\pmod1:x\in P\}.
\]
If two functions have images in arcs of lengths $\eta_1$ and $\eta_2$,
then their pointwise sum has image in an arc of length at most
$\eta_1+\eta_2$ whenever this sum is at most one.  We shall repeatedly
use this elementary consequence of addition of real intervals.

For a modular polynomial
$\phi(X)=\sum_j a_jX^j\in(\Z/N\Z)[X]$, choose integer representatives
of its coefficients and put $F(X)=\sum_j(a_j/N)X^j$.  Then
\[
 \operatorname{osc}_{P}(F)
   =\frac1N\operatorname{diam}\bigl(\phi(P)\bigr),
 \label{gsr:dt:18:part:eq:modular-arc-identity}\tag{*}
\]
where the diameter on the right is Gowers' containing-arc diameter.
Indeed a shortest arc containing a finite subset of the grid
$N^{-1}\Z/\Z$ may be chosen with endpoints in that grid.  Thus every
statement below applies directly to the modular polynomials in the
repository.  No primality assumption is used.  On the integer parameter
interval there is no restriction relating its length to $N$; when that
interval itself is regarded as a subset of $\Z/N\Z$, we retain
$r\leq N$ so that its points remain distinct.

\subsection{A recurrence input with an explicit interface}

Fix an integer $q\geq1$.  For each $j\geq2$, suppose that an
integer-valued function $\mathcal R_{j,q}:(0,1]\to\Z_{\geq1}$ has the
following property:
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 &\text{for every }\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_q\in\Tcirc
   \text{ there exists }1\leq p\leq\mathcal R_{j,q}(\eta)\\
 &\hspace{32mm}\text{such that }
       \max_{1\leq i\leq q}\|\alpha_i p^j\|_{\Tcirc}\leq\eta.
 \end{split}
 \label{gsr:dt:18:part:eq:monomial-recurrence-interface}
\end{equation}
The function $\mathcal R_{j,q}$ is a recurrence radius.  It may come
from any proved recurrence theorem.  This formulation separates the
analytic problem of producing a common step from the combinatorial
problem of turning that step into a partition covering every point.

We shall prescribe the two possible final cell lengths.  The elementary
integer fact that makes this possible deserves to be stated explicitly.

\begin{lemma}[Two integer subdivision rules]
\label{gsr:dt:18:part:lem:integer-subdivision}
Let $v\geq2$ and put
\[
 g(v)=\max\{1,(v-1)(v-2)\}.
\]
Every integer $n\geq g(v)$ is a sum of positive integers each equal
to $v-1$ or $v$.  Also, for every integer $U\geq1$, every integer
$n\geq U$ is a sum of integers in $[U,2U-1]$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For the first assertion put $d=v-1$ and write $n=ad+b$ with
$0\leq b<d$.  If $d\geq2$, the hypothesis gives
$a\geq d-1\geq b$, and
\[
 n=(a-b)d+b(d+1).
\]
The case $d=1$ is immediate.  For the second assertion write
$n=aU+b$, where $a\geq1$ and $0\leq b<U$; use $a-1$ summands
equal to $U$ and one summand equal to $U+b$.
\end{proof}

Define integer thresholds recursively, for $v\geq2$ and
$0<\varepsilon\leq1$, by
\begin{align}
 \mathcal P_{1,q}(v,\varepsilon)
   &=g(v)\left\lceil\frac{v-1}{\varepsilon}\right\rceil^q,
       \label{gsr:dt:18:part:eq:partition-threshold-base}\\
 U&=\mathcal P_{j-1,q}(v,\varepsilon/2),\qquad
 T=\mathcal R_{j,q}\!\left(
             \frac{\varepsilon}{2^{j+1}U^j}\right),
       \notag\\
 \mathcal P_{j,q}(v,\varepsilon)&=UT \qquad(j\geq2).
       \label{gsr:dt:18:part:eq:partition-threshold-recursion}
\end{align}
All quantities that count steps or lengths are integers.  In particular,
there is no unmentioned rounding loss in this recursion.

\begin{theorem}[Simultaneous recurrence-to-partition transfer]
\label{gsr:dt:18:part:thm:degree-descent-transfer}
Assume \eqref{gsr:dt:18:part:eq:monomial-recurrence-interface} for
$j=2,\ldots,k$.  Let $F_1,\ldots,F_q\in\R[X]$ have degree at
most $k$.  If an interval $I$ consists of
\[
 r\geq\mathcal P_{k,q}(v,\varepsilon)
\]
consecutive integers, then $I$ has a partition into nonempty arithmetic
progressions $P$ satisfying
\[
 |P|\in\{v-1,v\},\qquad
 \operatorname{osc}_{P}(F_i)\leq\varepsilon
      \quad(1\leq i\leq q).
\]
The number of cells is determined by the construction; it is not
prescribed in advance.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{Relation to the other partition results.} With one linear phase per degree this is source~13's prescribed-length theorem: in degree one the exponent recursion gives source~13's $1/(3q+2)$ (Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:13:cor:linear59}). Source~19's Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:19:poly:partition} proves the same transfer independently, with degree profiles and flexible lengths (note after Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:18:part:cor:quadratic-polynomial-q}). The formal \file{lemma_5_9} (\file{Section05.lean}, line~261; exact companion \file{lemma_5_9_holds}, \file{Proofs05FullPartition.lean}, line~98) has the exponent $1/(2K^q)$ with $K=(k!)^22^{(k+1)^2}$; the improvement here is not formalized.
\end{writenote}

For $v=1$, the analogous conclusion follows from the singleton
partition, so the restriction $v\geq2$ omits only a trivial case.

\begin{proof}
We induct on the degree.  For degree one, constants can be discarded.
Write $F_i(x)=\alpha_i x+\beta_i$ and put
$Q=\lceil(v-1)/\varepsilon\rceil$.  Place the $Q^q+1$ points
\[
 0,\ \alpha,\ 2\alpha,\ldots,Q^q\alpha\quad\text{in }\Tcirc^q,
 \qquad\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_q),
\]
in $Q^q$ half-open boxes of side $1/Q$.  Two points lie in the same
box, so their index difference gives an integer $1\leq p\leq Q^q$
with $\|p\alpha_i\|_{\Tcirc}\leq1/Q$ for every $i$.

Split $I$ into residue chains modulo $p$.  Each chain has length at
least $\lfloor r/p\rfloor\geq g(v)$.  By
Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:18:part:lem:integer-subdivision}, each chain can be subdivided into
consecutive blocks of lengths $v-1$ or $v$.  On any such block the
$i$th phase admits a real lift with range length at most
$(v-1)\|p\alpha_i\|_{\Tcirc}\leq\varepsilon$.  This proves the
base case, including the containing-arc conclusion.

Suppose the theorem has been proved through degree $j-1$.  Write
\[
 F_i(x)=\alpha_i x^j+\text{terms of degree at most }j-1.
\]
With $U,T$ as in \eqref{gsr:dt:18:part:eq:partition-threshold-recursion}, choose
$p\leq T$ using \eqref{gsr:dt:18:part:eq:monomial-recurrence-interface}.  Since
$r\geq UT$, every residue chain modulo $p$ has length at least
$U$.  Subdivide these chains into blocks of lengths in $[U,2U-1]$.

On one block write $x=b+pt$, where $0\leq t<n$ and
$U\leq n<2U$.  Expansion gives
\[
 F_i(b+pt)=\alpha_i p^j t^j+G_i(t),
 \qquad \deg G_i\leq j-1.
\]
Choose a representative $c_i\in\R$ of $\alpha_i p^j\pmod1$
with
\[
 |c_i|\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{2^{j+1}U^j}.
\]
The real numbers $c_i t^j$, $0\leq t<n$, lie in an interval of
length at most
\[
 (2U)^j|c_i|\leq\varepsilon/2.
\]
Apply the induction hypothesis simultaneously to
$G_1,\ldots,G_q$ on $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, with error
$\varepsilon/2$.  Its length condition holds because
$n\geq U=\mathcal P_{j-1,q}(v,\varepsilon/2)$.
Pull the resulting subprogressions back by $t\mapsto b+pt$.
Their lengths are $v-1$ or $v$.  On each one, the lower-degree part
lies in an arc of length $\varepsilon/2$, and the leading part in
an arc of length $\varepsilon/2$.  Their sum lies in an arc of
length $\varepsilon$.  Performing this construction on all blocks
gives a disjoint partition of the original interval.
\end{proof}

The necessity of descending through the lower coefficients is real.
A return $\|\alpha_i p^j\|_{\Tcirc}\ll1$ controls the coefficient
of $t^j$ in $F_i(b+pt)$, but the translated lower coefficients
contain the possibly large integer $b$.  They do not become small
merely because the leading coefficient does.  The proof treats them
as a new simultaneous lower-degree problem.

\subsection{Power laws and their constants}

Suppose the recurrence radii satisfy
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal R_{j,q}(\eta)\leq C_j\eta^{-s_j}
       \quad(0<\eta\leq1),
 \qquad C_j\geq1,\quad s_j>0.
 \label{gsr:dt:18:part:eq:powerlaw-recurrence-radius}
\end{equation}
Dependence of $C_j$ and $s_j$ on $q$ is allowed.  Define
\begin{align}
 A_1&=q+2, & B_1&=q, & D_1&=2^q,\notag\\
 A_j&=(1+js_j)A_{j-1},
 &B_j&=(1+js_j)B_{j-1}+s_j,
 \label{gsr:dt:18:part:eq:partition-exponent-recursion}\\
 D_j&=C_j\,
   2^{(j+1)s_j+B_{j-1}(1+js_j)}
   D_{j-1}^{1+js_j}.
 &&&\notag
\end{align}

\begin{proposition}[A quantitative exponent region]
\label{gsr:dt:18:part:prop:partition-powerlaws}
Under \eqref{gsr:dt:18:part:eq:powerlaw-recurrence-radius},
\[
 \mathcal P_{k,q}(v,\varepsilon)
       \leq D_k v^{A_k}\varepsilon^{-B_k}.
\]
Consequently, for every $a,b>0$ with
\begin{equation}
 A_k a+B_k b<1,
 \label{gsr:dt:18:part:eq:partition-sufficient-region}
\end{equation}
all sufficiently large intervals of length $r$ have the partition in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:18:part:thm:degree-descent-transfer} with error $r^{-b}$,
for every integer $2\leq v\leq r^a$.  Once the constants $C_j$
are known, the sufficient threshold
$r\geq D_k^{1/(1-A_k a-B_k b)}$ is explicit.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The inequalities $g(v)\leq v^2$ and
$\lceil(v-1)/\varepsilon\rceil\leq2v/\varepsilon$ prove
the base case.  Assuming the asserted bound in degree $j-1$, we have
\[
 U\leq D_{j-1}2^{B_{j-1}}
          v^{A_{j-1}}\varepsilon^{-B_{j-1}}.
\]
The defining recursion and \eqref{gsr:dt:18:part:eq:powerlaw-recurrence-radius} give
\[
 \mathcal P_{j,q}(v,\varepsilon)
 \leq C_j 2^{(j+1)s_j}U^{1+js_j}\varepsilon^{-s_j}.
\]
Substitution proves precisely
\eqref{gsr:dt:18:part:eq:partition-exponent-recursion}.  Finally,
$D_k v^{A_k}r^{B_k b}\leq D_k r^{A_k a+B_k b}\leq r$
under the displayed threshold.
\end{proof}

The exponents can also be written without recursion:
\begin{align}
 A_k&=(q+2)\prod_{j=2}^k(1+js_j),
       \label{gsr:dt:18:part:eq:partition-exponent-product-A}\\
 B_k&=q\prod_{j=2}^k(1+js_j)
       +\sum_{i=2}^k s_i\prod_{j=i+1}^k(1+js_j).
       \label{gsr:dt:18:part:eq:partition-exponent-product-B}
\end{align}
An empty product is one.  On the boundary of
\eqref{gsr:dt:18:part:eq:partition-sufficient-region}, one may retain the explicit
prefactor
\[
 v\leq D_k^{-1/A_k}r^{(1-B_k b)/A_k}.
\]
Thus the strict inequality in the simpler asymptotic statement is
accounting for constants, not concealing an additional loss of a power.

The ratio in Gowers' Lemma~5.9 is $b=2a$.  Put $E_k=A_k+2B_k$.
Then
\begin{equation}
 E_1=3q+2,\qquad
 E_j=(1+js_j)E_{j-1}+2s_j.
 \label{gsr:dt:18:part:eq:partition-E-recursion}
\end{equation}
Every $a<1/E_k$ is therefore a valid prescribed-length exponent at
that error ratio.

There is a useful distinction between prescribed adjacent lengths and
lengths allowed to vary over a factor of two.  If the desired final
lengths are any integers in $[v,2v-1]$, the degree-one threshold can
instead be taken to be
\[
 v\left\lceil\frac{2v}{\varepsilon}\right\rceil^q.
\]
Use the same Dirichlet step and the second subdivision rule in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:18:part:lem:integer-subdivision}.  The rest of the induction is
unchanged.  In this variant $A_1=q+1$ and $B_1=q$; one may take
$D_1=4^q$.  The additional factor of $v$ in the adjacent-length
threshold is the cost of the elementary integer representation used
to force those two particular lengths.

\subsection{Consequences of modern simultaneous recurrence}

Maynard's published theorem \cite{maynard} gives, for fixed degree
$j$, a constant $c_j>0$ such that for any $q$ real polynomials
$h_i$ of degree at most $j$ with $h_i(0)=0$, there is
$1\leq p<T$ with
\[
 \max_i\|h_i(p)\|_{\Tcirc}
       \ll_{j,q}T^{-c_j/q}.
\]
Apply this to $h_i(X)=\alpha_iX^j$ and invert the error bound.
After allowing for an initial threshold and integer rounding, it gives
\eqref{gsr:dt:18:part:eq:powerlaw-recurrence-radius} with $s_j=q/c_j$.
Equations~\eqref{gsr:dt:18:part:eq:partition-exponent-product-A}--
\eqref{gsr:dt:18:part:eq:partition-exponent-product-B} therefore give
\[
 A_k,B_k,E_k=O_k(q^k)
\]
for each fixed degree.  This conclusion uses an established analytic
input; the contribution proved above is its exact partition transfer.

The preprint \cite{lau}, Corollary~1.2, gives a more explicit
degree dependence.  For every fixed $\kappa>10.5$, its bound permits
\begin{equation}
 s_j=\kappa qj(j-1),\qquad j\geq2.
 \label{gsr:dt:18:part:eq:Lau-recurrence-exponents}
\end{equation}
The implied constants are uniform over the polynomial coefficients,
but depend on $j,q,\kappa$; they are not supplied here as numerical
finite-size constants.  We use this result as an imported preprint
theorem and do not claim a new proof of it.  Substitution yields
\begin{align*}
 A_j&=\bigl(1+\kappa qj^2(j-1)\bigr)A_{j-1},\\
 B_j&=\bigl(1+\kappa qj^2(j-1)\bigr)B_{j-1}
                          +\kappa qj(j-1).
\end{align*}
For example,
\[
 E_k=3\kappa^{k-1}(k!)^2(k-1)!\,q^k
                  +O_{k,\kappa}(q^{k-1}).
\]

\begin{corollary}[Simultaneous quadratic partitions]
\label{gsr:dt:18:part:cor:quadratic-polynomial-q}
Let $q\geq1$ and
\[
 0<a<\frac1{126q^2+129q+2}.
\]
For all sufficiently large $r$, every family of $q$ real quadratic
polynomials on an interval of $r$ integers admits, for every integer
$2\leq v\leq r^a$, a partition into progressions of lengths
$v-1$ or $v$ on which all containing-arc oscillations are at most
$r^{-2a}$.  The threshold is uniform over the coefficients.
The same conclusion holds for $q$ modular quadratic polynomials,
with diameters at most $Nr^{-2a}$, for every $N\geq r$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
For degree two, \eqref{gsr:dt:18:part:eq:Lau-recurrence-exponents} gives
$s_2=2\kappa q$, and hence
\begin{align*}
 A_2&=(q+2)(1+4\kappa q),\\
 B_2&=q(1+4\kappa q)+2\kappa q,\\
 E_2&=12\kappa q^2+(3+12\kappa)q+2.
\end{align*}
The strict hypothesis allows $\kappa>10.5$ sufficiently close to
$10.5$ that $aE_2<1$.  Apply
Proposition~\ref{gsr:dt:18:part:prop:partition-powerlaws} with $b=2a$, and then
use the modular interpretation.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{Source~13's Question~3 is answered} by this corollary and Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:18:part:cor:shared-quadratic-coefficient} (for quadratics, exponents polynomial in the number of phases; for a shared leading coefficient, linear in $q$, from the source's own scalar Lemma~5.5), and independently by source~19's Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:19:poly:partition} with Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:19:poly:target} (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:I:higher}). Both rest on Maynard's published theorem; the numbers rest on Lau's preprint. \emph{Two routes compared} (checked at the write): at the same recurrence constant this corollary's prescribed-length exponent is strictly better than source~19's, because source~19 squares the length only at the end (its Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:19:poly:rounding}) while this proof pays $v^2$ once at the base: with $\kappa=11$ the reciprocal exponents at $q=1$ are $269$ here and $314$ in source~19 ($2(F_2+G_2)$, source~19's Table~\ref{gsr:dt:19:poly:q-table}). Source~19's is more general (mixed degree profiles). Source~16's Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:16:thm:frontier} is a different problem (own steps, affine frequencies) with the same input.
\end{writenote}

Taking the convenient value $\kappa=11$ gives the slightly weaker
denominator $132q^2+135q+2$ without a limiting choice of $\kappa$.
In contrast, the degree-two value of Gowers' constant is
$K=(2!)^2 2^9=2048$, so the displayed exponent in Lemma~5.9 is
$1/(2\cdot2048^q)$ at the same ratio of diameter and length powers.
The corollary improves this local dependence from exponential to
polynomial in $q$.  It does not, by itself, improve the paper's final
bound for Szemer\'edi's theorem: the other multilinear partition and
inverse-theorem losses must also be propagated before such a claim
would be justified.

\subsection{A special case requiring only scalar recurrence}

The transfer can exploit a smaller number of independent leading
frequencies even when the lower coefficients are unrestricted.  Here
is a concrete quadratic example.

\begin{corollary}[A shared leading coefficient]
\label{gsr:dt:18:part:cor:shared-quadratic-coefficient}
Suppose a scalar recurrence estimate has the following form: for every
$\alpha\in\Tcirc$ and integer $T\geq T_0$, where
$T_0\in\Z_{\geq1}$, there is $1\leq p\leq T$
with $\|\alpha p^2\|_{\Tcirc}\leq T^{-1/s}$, where $s>0$.
Let
\[
 F_i(X)=h_i\alpha X^2+b_iX+c_i\pmod1,
 \qquad h_i\in\Z,\quad |h_i|\leq H,
\]
where $H\geq1$ and the lower coefficients are arbitrary.  Put
\[
 U=g(v)\left\lceil\frac{2(v-1)}{\varepsilon}\right\rceil^q,
 \qquad
 T=\max\left\{T_0,
       \left\lceil\left(\frac{8HU^2}{\varepsilon}\right)^s
                  \right\rceil\right\}.
\]
Every integer interval of length at least $UT$ has the partition of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:18:part:thm:degree-descent-transfer}.  For fixed $H,T_0,s,q$,
every exponent
\[
 a<\frac1{(1+2s)(3q+2)+2s}
\]
works asymptotically with $v\leq r^a$ and error $r^{-2a}$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The chosen $T$ ensures
$\|h_i\alpha p^2\|_{\Tcirc}\leq HT^{-1/s}
\leq\varepsilon/(8U^2)$ for every $i$.  The quadratic step of
the transfer now applies.  Its recurrence-radius exponent is $s$,
independent of $q$, whereas the lower linear step still has $q$
slopes.  Equation~\eqref{gsr:dt:18:part:eq:partition-E-recursion} gives the stated
denominator.
\end{proof}

The ordinary degree-two recurrence exponent in the supplied version
of Gowers' Lemma~5.5 is $1/16$.  Taking that lemma with the explicit repaired threshold
$T_0=2^{2^{320}}$ gives $s=16$ and denominator $99q+98$ in this
special case.  In particular the finite threshold in
Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:18:part:cor:shared-quadratic-coefficient} is
$U\max\{2^{2^{320}},\lceil(8HU^2/\varepsilon)^{16}\rceil\}$,
with $U$ as displayed there.  Thus a linear reciprocal dependence on $q$ is already
available from scalar recurrence when the leading coefficient is
shared; no modern simultaneous recurrence theorem is needed for
that consequence.  Bounded integer combinations of $s_0$ leading
frequencies similarly replace the recurrence dimension $q$ by $s_0$
at the quadratic step, while retaining all $q$ lower slopes.

For completeness, the modular scalar recurrence extends to an arbitrary
real $\alpha$ at the same fixed integer $T$ by approximating $\alpha$
with rational coefficients whose denominators tend to infinity.
The finitely many possible values $1\leq p\leq T$ include one occurring
on an infinite subsequence, and continuity then gives the asserted
torus recurrence.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A volume obstruction to polynomial partition exponents\srctag{18}}]{A volume obstruction to polynomial partition exponents}\label{gsr:dt:18:sec:d5}
\srcnote{18}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:dt:18:part:sec:polynomial-partition-obstruction}

The preceding sufficient exponents need not be optimal.  We now prove
an obstruction that applies to every universal theorem, regardless
of the construction used to obtain its partition.  Its proof is
elementary and independent of all imported recurrence estimates.

\subsection{Lifting a polynomial from a short arc}

\begin{lemma}[Finite-difference rigidity]
\label{gsr:dt:18:part:lem:short-arc-rigidity}
Let $F\in\R[X]$ have degree at most $k$, let $F(0)=0$, and let
$n\geq k$.  Suppose
\[
 \|F(t)\|_{\Tcirc}\leq\varepsilon
       \quad(0\leq t\leq n),\qquad
 0<\varepsilon<2^{-k-1}.
\]
Let $y_t\in[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]$ be the unique lift of
$F(t)\pmod1$.  Then
\[
 y_t=\sum_{j=1}^k b_j\binom tj\quad(0\leq t\leq n),
 \qquad b_j=\Delta^j y_0,
\]
where $\Delta y_t=y_{t+1}-y_t$.  Moreover
$|b_j|\leq2^j\varepsilon<1/2$, and $b_j$ is the canonical lift
of the $j$th binomial coefficient of $F$ modulo one.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The $k$th finite differences of the real lifts all lie in
$[-2^k\varepsilon,2^k\varepsilon]\subset(-1/2,1/2)$.
Modulo one, each equals the same $k$th finite difference of the
polynomial $F$.  Uniqueness of a representative in this interval
therefore makes these real finite differences equal.  The Newton
formula for a finite sequence with constant $k$th differences gives
the displayed polynomial representation.  The formula
\[
 \Delta^j y_0
   =\sum_{t=0}^j(-1)^{j-t}\binom jt y_t
\]
gives $|b_j|\leq2^j\varepsilon$.  Reduction modulo one identifies
$b_j$ with the corresponding binomial coefficient of $F$, and the
strict bound $|b_j|<1/2$ makes the lift canonical.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[A binomial evaluation determinant]
\label{gsr:dt:18:part:lem:binomial-evaluation-determinant}
For positive integers $k,m$, put $H=k(k+1)/2$.  Then
\[
 \det\left[\binom{im}{j}\right]_{1\leq i,j\leq k}=m^H.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The polynomial $\binom Xj$ has degree $j$, leading coefficient
$1/j!$, and vanishes at zero for $j\geq1$.  The Vandermonde
determinant at $0,m,2m,\ldots,km$ therefore gives
\[
 \det\left[\binom{im}{j}\right]
  =\frac{\displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^k im
                \prod_{1\leq i<\ell\leq k}(\ell-i)m}
          {\displaystyle\prod_{j=1}^k j!}
  =m^{k(k+1)/2}.
\]
The integer factors in the numerator cancel the factorials in the
denominator.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The probability of a flat progression}

Choose independent Haar-uniform coefficients
$\alpha_{i,j}\in\Tcirc$, $1\leq i\leq q$, $1\leq j\leq k$,
and interpret
\[
 F_i(X)=\sum_{j=1}^k\alpha_{i,j}X^j\pmod1
\]
as random polynomial phases.  Any real representatives define the
same values at integers.

\begin{theorem}[A fixed-progression volume bound]
\label{gsr:dt:18:part:thm:polynomial-flatness-volume}
Let $k,q\geq1$, $n\geq k$, and
$0<\varepsilon<2^{-k-1}$.  Put
\[
 H=\frac{k(k+1)}2,\qquad m=\left\lfloor\frac nk\right\rfloor.
\]
For every positive integer $p$,
\begin{equation}
 \Pr\!\left[
   \operatorname{osc}_{\{0,p,\ldots,np\}}(F_i)
      \leq\varepsilon\text{ for all }i
      \right]
 \leq\left(\frac{(2\varepsilon)^k}{m^H}\right)^q.
 \label{gsr:dt:18:part:eq:flat-progression-probability}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
It suffices to treat a single polynomial.  Express its values in
the binomial basis:
\[
 F(pt)=\sum_{j=1}^k c_j\binom tj\pmod1.
\]
The transformation from the monomial coefficients
$(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_k)$ to $(c_1,\ldots,c_k)$ is an
integer triangular endomorphism of $\Tcirc^k$ with diagonal entries
$j!p^j$.  Its determinant is nonzero, so the endomorphism is
surjective and sends Haar measure to Haar measure.  In particular,
the vector $c=(c_1,\ldots,c_k)$ is uniform on $\Tcirc^k$.

On the event under consideration, $F(0)=0$ and all values are
within geodesic distance $\varepsilon$ of zero.  Apply
Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:18:part:lem:short-arc-rigidity} to $t\mapsto F(pt)$.
There are canonical representatives $b_j\in(-1/2,1/2)$ of $c_j$
such that the lifted values are
\[
 y_t=\sum_{j=1}^k b_j\binom tj,
 \qquad |y_t|\leq\varepsilon.
\]
Evaluate at $t=m,2m,\ldots,km$, all of which are at most $n$.
By Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:18:part:lem:binomial-evaluation-determinant}, the linear
map from $b$ to these $k$ values has determinant $m^H$.
The conditions that all those values lie in
$[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]$ define a parallelotope of volume
$(2\varepsilon)^k/m^H$.  Intersecting it with the fundamental
cube cannot increase the volume.  There is no sum over different
integer lifts: the rigidity lemma has already made the representative
$b$ unique.  This proves the one-polynomial estimate, and independence
of the $q$ coefficient vectors gives
\eqref{gsr:dt:18:part:eq:flat-progression-probability}.
\end{proof}

The powers in this fixed-progression estimate are sharp up to
constants depending on $k$.  For one polynomial, the sufficient
restrictions on its canonical binomial coefficients
\[
 |c_j|\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{2k\binom nj},
       \qquad 1\leq j\leq k,
\]
ensure that all lifted values lie in
$[-\varepsilon/2,\varepsilon/2]$, and hence that their containing
arc has length at most $\varepsilon$.  The Haar measure of this
rectangle is
\[
 \prod_{j=1}^k\frac{\varepsilon}{k\binom nj}
 \geq\frac{\prod_{j=1}^k j!}{k^k}
                \varepsilon^k n^{-H}.
\]
On the other hand, $m\geq n/(2k)$ in
\eqref{gsr:dt:18:part:eq:flat-progression-probability}.  Thus the one-polynomial
probability is
\[
 \Theta_k\!\left(\varepsilon^k n^{-k(k+1)/2}\right)
\]
throughout the stated small-arc range.  Sharpness of this probability
scale does not establish a matching universal partition theorem:
one still has to cover every point by disjoint progressions, and
the flatness events for different progressions are dependent.

\subsection{Counterexamples to excessive universal exponents}

\begin{theorem}[An explicit obstruction]
\label{gsr:dt:18:part:thm:polynomial-partition-obstruction}
Let $k,q,n,\varepsilon$ satisfy the hypotheses of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:18:part:thm:polynomial-flatness-volume}, let $r\geq n+1$,
and retain $H=k(k+1)/2$.  If
\begin{equation}
 \left\lfloor\frac{r-1}{n}\right\rfloor
 \left(\frac{(2\varepsilon)^k}
             {\lfloor n/k\rfloor^H}\right)^q<1,
 \label{gsr:dt:18:part:eq:exact-polynomial-partition-obstruction}
\end{equation}
then there are $q$ polynomial phases of degree at most $k$ for
which $\{0,\ldots,r-1\}$ has no partition into arithmetic
progressions all of length at least $n+1$ and having all $q$
oscillations at most $\varepsilon$.  These counterexamples may
also be realized by modular polynomials with a sufficiently large
common modulus $N\geq r$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Any arithmetic progression in $\{0,\ldots,r-1\}$ containing
zero can be enumerated as $0,p,2p,\ldots$ with positive step.
If it has length at least $n+1$ and all $q$ oscillations at most
$\varepsilon$, its first $n+1$ points have the same property,
and $p\leq\lfloor(r-1)/n\rfloor$.  The union bound and
Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:18:part:thm:polynomial-flatness-volume} show that the
probability of any such progression is less than one.  There is
therefore a coefficient vector for which zero belongs to no such
progression.  The cell containing zero rules out the asserted
partition.

For the modular assertion, there are only finitely many candidate
steps.  Each good-progression event is closed in the coefficient
torus: it asks that a finite collection of continuously varying
points fit into a closed arc of prescribed length.  One may make the
arc's starting point an auxiliary circle variable and project the
resulting closed subset of a compact space.  Consequently
the nonempty complement just constructed is open.  Approximate
one of its points by rational coefficient vectors with a common
denominator $N\geq r$ sufficiently large.  The strict failure
for every candidate step persists.  Multiplication by $N$ then
gives polynomials over $\Z/N\Z$.
\end{proof}

Using $\lfloor n/k\rfloor\geq n/(2k)$, a simpler sufficient
condition for the same obstruction is
\begin{equation}
 r\left[2^k(2k)^{k(k+1)/2}\varepsilon^k\right]^q
       <n^{qk(k+1)/2+1}.
 \label{gsr:dt:18:part:eq:simple-polynomial-partition-obstruction}
\end{equation}

\begin{corollary}[A necessary exponent region]
\label{gsr:dt:18:part:cor:necessary-polynomial-partition-exponents}
Suppose $a,b,c,C>0$, and suppose a universal assertion states that
for every sufficiently large $r$ and every $q$ polynomial phases
of degree at most $k$, an interval of $r$ integers has a partition
whose cells all have length at least $cr^a$ and all $q$
oscillations at most $Cr^{-b}$.  Then necessarily
\begin{equation}
 \left(\frac{qk(k+1)}2+1\right)a+kqb\leq1.
 \label{gsr:dt:18:part:eq:necessary-polynomial-partition-region}
\end{equation}
The same necessary condition holds if the universal assertion is
restricted to modular polynomials and is uniform over $N\geq r$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
If \eqref{gsr:dt:18:part:eq:necessary-polynomial-partition-region} fails, choose
an integer $n$ comparable to $r^a$ and just below the guaranteed
minimum cell length, and put $\varepsilon=Cr^{-b}$.  For large
$r$ the small-arc hypothesis holds, while the ratio of the left
side of \eqref{gsr:dt:18:part:eq:simple-polynomial-partition-obstruction} to
its right side tends to zero.  The preceding theorem contradicts
the universal assertion.  If the proposed minimum length already
exceeds $r$, the assertion is impossible directly.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{Credit.} At $k=1$ this is source~13's frontier $(q+1)a+qb\le1$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:13:thm:obstruction}, Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:13:cor:frontier}) and source~05's minimax order (Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:05:thm:minimax}). Source~19's Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:19:poly:obstruction} is the same obstruction for arbitrary degree profiles, $(S+1)a+Db\le1$; at uniform degree $k$ it is this one. Source~16's Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:16:cor:necessary} is the own-step analogue.

For $k=1$, the necessary region is
$(q+1)a+qb\leq1$, agreeing with the flexible linear partition
region.  For quadratics it is
\[
 (3q+1)a+2qb\leq1.
\]
At the ratio $b=2a$ this becomes $a\leq1/(7q+1)$.
More generally, that ratio gives
\[
 a\leq\frac1{qk(k+5)/2+1}.
\]
These are universal obstructions, not constructions.  In particular,
the quadratic sufficient denominator
$126q^2+129q+2$ and the necessary denominator $7q+1$ should not
be presented as matching bounds.  Closing their dimensional gap,
while also distinguishing flexible cell lengths from prescribed
adjacent lengths, is a concrete further research problem.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Simultaneous polynomial phase partitions\srctag{19}}]{Simultaneous polynomial phase partitions}\label{gsr:dt:19:sec:d6}
\srcnote{19}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:dt:19:poly:section}

Lemma~5.9 of Gowers' paper obtains simultaneous control of $q$ polynomial
phases by refining a partition once for each phase. Its exponent therefore
contains $K^{-q}$, where $K=(k!)^2 2^{(k+1)^2}$ for degree at most $k$.
The repository repairs the statement to prescribe a target cell length,
with an emergent number of cells \cite{gowers,repo19paper}.
Here we replace refinement by phase with refinement by degree. At a given
degree, all leading coefficients are made small simultaneously.
The resulting exponent has polynomial dependence on $q$ for fixed $k$.

The substantial recurrence input is an established theorem of Maynard;
the contribution proved here is its transfer to complete partitions,
including the degree profile, rounding, and error budgets. We also prove
a separate obstruction by random coefficients. That obstruction shows
that the sufficient bounds below still leave a substantial gap.

\subsection{The recurrence input and its precise status}

Write $\|t\|_{\R/\Z}$ for distance to the nearest integer. We use the
following published result.

\begin{theorem}[Maynard, Theorem~1.1 \cite{maynard}]
\label{gsr:dt:19:poly:maynard}
For every positive integer $j$ there is a constant $\kappa_j>2$, independent
of the number $m$ of polynomials, and for every $m$ a constant
$U_{j,m}>2$, with the following property. Let
$f_1,\ldots,f_m\in\R[X]$ have degree at most $j$ and vanish at zero.
If $0<\varepsilon_i\leq 1/100$,
\[
 \left(\prod_{i=1}^m\varepsilon_i\right)^{-1}
 \leq x^{1/\kappa_j},\qquad x>U_{j,m},
\]
then some integer $1\leq h<x$ satisfies
$\|f_i(h)\|_{\R/\Z}\leq\varepsilon_i$ for every $i$.
\end{theorem}

The theorem is uniform in every polynomial coefficient. Maynard does not
give numerical values for the constants needed here. In particular, his
discussion that a certain numerical degree dependence would probably
suffice is not a proved numerical choice. We keep the published constants
symbolic in the principal result.

For degree one we improve the input to $\kappa_1=1$ using simultaneous
Dirichlet approximation. More generally, all subsequent arguments work
with any valid recurrence constants. Lau's preprint gives an optional
numerical specialization, discussed separately below; it is not needed
for the conclusion about polynomial dependence on the number of phases.

\begin{lemma}[Power-scale recurrence]
\label{gsr:dt:19:poly:recurrence}
Set $\kappa_1=1$, and for $j\geq2$ take the constants in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:19:poly:maynard}. If $e,s>0$ and $\kappa_jme<s$, then for all
sufficiently large $r$, uniformly for $\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_m\in\R$,
there is an integer $1\leq h\leq r^s$ with
\[
 \|\eta_i h^j\|_{\R/\Z}\leq r^{-e}
 \qquad(1\leq i\leq m).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For $j\geq2$, apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:19:poly:maynard} with $x=r^s$,
$f_i(X)=\eta_iX^j$, and $\varepsilon_i=r^{-e}$.
Its product condition follows from $\kappa_jme<s$, and the other conditions
hold once $r^e\geq100$ and $r^s>U_{j,m}$.
For $j=1$, partition the unit $m$-cube into $Q^m$ equal subcubes and
apply the pigeonhole principle to the $Q^m+1$ points
$n(\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_m)\bmod1$, $0\leq n\leq Q^m$.
With $Q=\lceil r^e\rceil$, the difference of two points in one subcube
gives $h\leq Q^m\leq2^m r^{me}$ and errors at most $1/Q\leq r^{-e}$.
The bound $h\leq r^s$ follows once
$r\geq2^{m/(s-me)}$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A theorem sensitive to the degree profile}

For a finite subset $S\subset\R/\Z$, let $\operatorname{ad}(S)$ be the
least length of a real interval whose projection contains $S$, allowing
the upper bound~$1$. This circular arc diameter is monotone under
restriction and satisfies
\[
 \operatorname{ad}(S+T)
 \leq\operatorname{ad}(S)+\operatorname{ad}(T).
\]
We apply it to polynomial values modulo one.

Let $q_1\geq\cdots\geq q_k\geq0$ be integers. The interpretation is
that at most $q_j$ of the phases have degree at least $j$.
Define
\begin{align}
 F_0&=1,&G_0&=0,\notag\\
 F_j&=(1+j\kappa_jq_j)F_{j-1},&
 G_j&=(1+j\kappa_jq_j)G_{j-1}+\kappa_jq_j.
 \label{gsr:dt:19:poly:budget}
\end{align}
Thus
\begin{align}
 F_k&=\prod_{j=1}^k(1+j\kappa_jq_j),\label{gsr:dt:19:poly:F}\\
 G_k&=\sum_{j=1}^k \kappa_jq_j
       \prod_{\ell=j+1}^k(1+\ell \kappa_\ell q_\ell).
 \label{gsr:dt:19:poly:G}
\end{align}

\begin{theorem}[Complete polynomial phase partitions]
\label{gsr:dt:19:poly:partition}
Let $a,b>0$ satisfy
\begin{equation}
 F_ka+G_kb<1.
 \label{gsr:dt:19:poly:frontier}
\end{equation}
There is a threshold $R$, depending only on the displayed parameters
and the recurrence constants, with the following property. For every
integer $r\geq R$ and every family of real polynomials of degree at most
$k$ with the stated degree profile, the interval
$[0,r)\cap\Z$ has a partition into nonempty ordinary arithmetic
progressions $P$ such that
\[
 |P|\geq r^a,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{ad}(\phi_i(P)\bmod1)\leq r^{-b}
 \quad\hbox{for every phase $i$ and every cell $P$.}
\]
The threshold is independent of the coefficients and constant terms.
Different cells may have different common differences.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
We induct on the maximal degree. For degree zero the phases are constant
and the whole interval is a valid cell, since $a<1$.
At a positive degree $k$, discard an empty top degree if $q_k=0$.
Otherwise put $m=q_k$. The strict inequality
\eqref{gsr:dt:19:poly:frontier} is
\[
 (1+k\kappa_km)(F_{k-1}a+G_{k-1}b)+\kappa_kmb<1.
\]
We can therefore choose $b'>b$, followed by $\tau$ and $s$, so that
\begin{equation}
 F_{k-1}a+G_{k-1}b'<\tau,
 \qquad
 \kappa_km(k\tau+b')<s<1-\tau.
 \label{gsr:dt:19:poly:choices}
\end{equation}
These choices depend only on the theorem's parameters.

Write $\eta_i$ for the leading coefficient of each degree-$k$ phase,
padding by zero coefficients if fewer than $m$ phases have that degree.
Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:19:poly:recurrence} with $e=k\tau+b'$. We obtain
$1\leq h\leq r^s$ and integers $z_i$ with
\begin{equation}
 \eta_i h^k=z_i+\delta_i,
 \qquad |\delta_i|\leq r^{-(k\tau+b')}.
 \label{gsr:dt:19:poly:top}
\end{equation}

Partition the original interval into residue chains modulo $h$.
Every chain has at least $\lfloor r/h\rfloor\geq r^{1-s}-1$ points.
Put $L=\lceil r^\tau\rceil$. Since $s+\tau<1$, each chain has at least
$L$ points once $r$ is large enough. Split a chain into consecutive blocks
of $L$ points and merge any final remainder with the last full block.
This produces subprogressions $Q$ with lengths $w$ satisfying
\begin{equation}
 L\leq w<2L\leq4r^\tau.
 \label{gsr:dt:19:poly:blocks}
\end{equation}
The blocks cover all points; no exceptional set is discarded.

On $Q=\{x,x+h,\ldots,x+(w-1)h\}$, subtract the actual leading term
$\eta_i h^k t^k$ from the polynomial $\phi_i(x+ht)$.
The remainder $\psi_i(t)$ has degree at most $k-1$, and
\begin{equation}
 \phi_i(x+ht)\equiv\delta_i t^k+\psi_i(t)\pmod1
 \qquad(0\leq t<w),
 \label{gsr:dt:19:poly:lower}
\end{equation}
because $z_it^k$ is integer. For a phase of degree less than $k$, use
$\delta_i=0$ and simply reparameterize that phase.
The coefficients of $\psi_i$ can depend on the starting point $x$;
uniformity of the induction hypothesis permits this dependence.

At each lower degree $j<k$, the number of resulting phases of degree at
least $j$ is at most the original $q_j$. Indeed, affine reparameterization
does not increase degree, and a degree-$k$ phase has only been lowered
to degree at most $k-1$. Thus the lower profile is
$q_1,\ldots,q_{k-1}$, including the phases that have just lost their
top degree.

Apply the induction hypothesis on $[0,w)$ with exponents
$a/\tau$ and $b'/\tau$. Their admissibility follows from
\eqref{gsr:dt:19:poly:choices}. The resulting cells have at least
$w^{a/\tau}\geq r^a$ points, and each lower phase has arc diameter at
most $w^{-b'/\tau}\leq r^{-b'}$. On the same cell, the first term of
\eqref{gsr:dt:19:poly:lower} has arc diameter at most its real range, namely
\[
 |\delta_i|(w-1)^k\leq4^k r^{-b'}.
\]
Subadditivity gives a total bound of $(1+4^k)r^{-b'}$, which is at most
$r^{-b}$ once $r\geq(1+4^k)^{1/(b'-b)}$.
Affine images of the child cells are ordinary arithmetic progressions,
and all these images partition the original interval.
\end{proof}

Two features of the proof matter. First, one cannot simply approximate
all coefficients at the origin and assume that those approximations
remain useful on every residue class: translation creates additional
lower coefficients. Formula~\eqref{gsr:dt:19:poly:lower} handles those coefficients
by a new, uniform lower-degree problem. Second, refinement runs through
the degrees, rather than through the individual phases. When $q_j=q$,
$F_k+G_k$ is a polynomial in $q$ of degree $k$.

\paragraph{An explicit recursive threshold in the imported constants.}
The proof supplies a threshold rather than merely a coefficient-dependent
``sufficiently large'' condition. For a particular choice
$b',\tau,s$ in \eqref{gsr:dt:19:poly:choices}, put $e=k\tau+b'$ and define
\[
 H_{k,m}(e,s)=
 \begin{cases}
  2^{m/(s-me)},&k=1,\\[2pt]
  \max\{100^{1/e},(U_{k,m}+1)^{1/s}\},&k\geq2.
 \end{cases}
\]
Starting with $R_0=2$, it suffices at degree $k$ to choose an integer
threshold at least
\begin{equation}
 \max\left\{
 2,\ H_{k,m}(e,s),\
 4^{1/(1-s-\tau)},\
 (1+4^k)^{1/(b'-b)},\
 R_{k-1}(a/\tau,b'/\tau)^{1/\tau}
 \right\}.
 \label{gsr:dt:19:poly:threshold}
\end{equation}
The lower-degree profile is understood in the last term.
The third term guarantees enough points in every residue chain for
\eqref{gsr:dt:19:poly:blocks}, and the last term makes every child application
legal. This expression is recursive and explicit in the imported
$U_{j,m}$. It is not a numerical global threshold unless those external
constants are themselves supplied numerically.

\subsection{Prescribed target lengths and a numerical illustration}

\begin{lemma}[The final rounding step]
\label{gsr:dt:19:poly:rounding}
If an arithmetic progression has $n\geq u^2$ points, with $u\geq1$
integer, it can be partitioned into consecutive subprogressions of
length $u$ or $u+1$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write $n=tu+v$, $0\leq v<u$. Then $t\geq u>v$.
Use $v$ blocks of size $u+1$ and $t-v$ blocks of size $u$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A replacement for the target-length form of Lemma~5.9]
\label{gsr:dt:19:poly:target}
Under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:19:poly:partition}, every integer
target $v\geq2$ with $(v-1)^2\leq r^a$ is attainable by a further
partition into cells of length $v-1$ or $v$, with the same phase-diameter
bound. The target $v=1$ is attained by singletons.
In particular, for
\begin{equation}
 0<\theta<\frac{1}{2(F_k+G_k)},
 \label{gsr:dt:19:poly:theta}
\end{equation}
all sufficiently large $r$ admit every target $v\leq r^\theta$, with
diameters at most $r^{-2\theta}$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Use Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:19:poly:rounding} with $u=v-1$ inside each cell.
Taking $a=b=2\theta$ in Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:19:poly:partition} gives the final
assertion. Restriction to subsets does not increase diameter.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{Second route.} Source~18's Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:18:part:cor:quadratic-polynomial-q} proves the prescribed-length quadratic statement with the better exponent $1/(126q^2+129q+2)$ at the same input (note there); this corollary's degree profiles are more general. The formal \file{lemma_5_9} (\file{Section05.lean}, line~261; exact companion \file{lemma_5_9_holds}) has $\theta=1/(2K^q)$; not formalized.
\end{writenote}

For comparison, the repository's Lemma~5.9 has
$\theta=1/(2K^q)$ in this same ratio between length and diameter
exponents \cite{repo19paper}. For fixed $k$, the denominator in
\eqref{gsr:dt:19:poly:theta} is $O_k(q^k)$ rather than exponential in $q$.
With the symbolic constants from Maynard this proves an improvement for
all sufficiently large $q$; it does not justify an uncomputed numerical
comparison at every small $q$.

\paragraph{A numerical specialization from Lau's preprint.}
Lau's Theorem~1.1 permits recurrence constants
$\kappa_j=c_2j(j-1)$ for $j\geq2$, where
$c_2=10.5+9m/(2m)^M+\varepsilon$, with the stated conditions on
$M$ and $\varepsilon$ \cite{lau}. Choose $M=5$ and
$\varepsilon=1/10$. These meet those conditions and give
\[
 c_2\leq10.5+\frac9{32}+\frac1{10}
 =10.88125<11.
\]
We may consequently use the weaker, convenient constants
$\kappa_j=11j(j-1)$, with an unspecified finite threshold.
All numerical illustrations in the remainder of this subsection import
that preprint statement. The published Maynard theorem alone supplies
the symbolic version above.

For $m$ nonconstant phases, of which $s$ are quadratic and the remaining
$m-s$ are linear, the degree profile is $(q_1,q_2)=(m,s)$.
Since $\kappa_2=22$, formulas \eqref{gsr:dt:19:poly:F}--\eqref{gsr:dt:19:poly:G} give
\begin{equation}
 F_2=(m+1)(44s+1),\qquad
 G_2=m(44s+1)+22s.
 \label{gsr:dt:19:poly:quadratic-profile}
\end{equation}
The case $s=0$ reduces to the linear result. Table~\ref{gsr:dt:19:poly:profile-table}
