The theorem applies directly to modular phases by dividing polynomial
coefficients by the modulus. It requires neither a prime modulus nor
$r\leq N$ as an analytic statement on integer inputs. Using it inside a
later part of the repository proof still requires checking every local
width, threshold, and progression convention. These local improvements
by themselves establish no new global bound for Szemer\'edi's theorem.

\subsection{An obstruction from random polynomial coefficients}

The sufficient frontier has degree-$k$ polynomial dependence on the
number of degree-$k$ phases. A necessary condition has only linear
dependence. The following elementary argument identifies that gap.

\begin{lemma}[A polynomial phase small on one progression]
\label{gsr:dt:19:poly:probability}
Let $d\geq1$, $L\geq d+1$, and $0<\varepsilon<2^{-d-1}$.
Choose $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d$ independently and uniformly in
$[0,1)$, and put $P(X)=\sum_{j=1}^d\alpha_jX^j$.
For every positive integer $h$,
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb P\left(
 \|P(ht)\|_{\R/\Z}\leq\varepsilon\
 \text{for every }0\leq t<L\right)
 \leq(2\varepsilon)^d
 \left\lfloor\frac{L-1}{d}\right\rfloor^{-d(d+1)/2}.
 \label{gsr:dt:19:poly:probability-bound}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write $F(t)=P(ht)$. On the event in question, choose the unique centered
representative $y_t\in[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]$ with
$F(t)-y_t=m_t\in\Z$. Uniqueness holds because $\varepsilon<1/2$,
and $y_0=0$.
Since $F$ has degree at most $d$, every defined $(d+1)$st difference
satisfies
\[
 \Delta^{d+1}m_t=-\Delta^{d+1}y_t\in\Z,
 \qquad
 |\Delta^{d+1}y_t|\leq2^{d+1}\varepsilon<1.
\]
Thus $\Delta^{d+1}m_t=0$. The finite integer sequence $m_t$ is the
restriction of the integer-valued polynomial
\[
 \sum_{j=0}^d\Delta^j m_0\binom tj.
\]
For $L=d+1$ the same assertion follows directly by Newton interpolation;
for larger $L$ the vanishing differences propagate that interpolation.
Consequently
\begin{equation}
 y_t=\sum_{j=1}^d c_j\binom tj,
 \qquad c_j=\Delta^j y_0,
 \qquad |c_j|\leq2^j\varepsilon<\tfrac12.
 \label{gsr:dt:19:poly:newton-lift}
\end{equation}

Now consider the torus vector
\[
 \beta_j=\Delta^j F(0)\pmod1,
 \qquad1\leq j\leq d.
\]
The linear map from $(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d)$ to
$(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_d)$ is an integer triangular matrix with
diagonal entries $j!h^j$ and nonzero determinant. It is therefore a
surjective endomorphism of $(\R/\Z)^d$ and preserves normalized Haar
measure. For example, this follows by integrating characters: every
nonzero character pulls back to a nonzero character because the transpose
matrix is injective over $\Z^d$. Hence $\beta$ is uniform on the torus.

The determinant of this map need not be $1$, and by itself does not
justify a Euclidean volume estimate for a chosen lift. The required extra
fact is \eqref{gsr:dt:19:poly:newton-lift}: every $c_j$ lies in
$(-1/2,1/2)$ and is congruent to $\beta_j$ modulo one. Thus $c$ is
the unique representative of $\beta$ in that fundamental cube.
The probability of the event is bounded by the Euclidean volume of its
permissible $c$-vectors in the cube, whose normalized volume is one.

Put $u=\lfloor(L-1)/d\rfloor$. The values
$y_u,y_{2u},\ldots,y_{du}$ belong to $[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]$.
The matrix taking $c$ to these values is
$B_{ij}=\binom{iu}{j}$, $1\leq i,j\leq d$. Because its columns are
polynomials of degrees $1,\ldots,d$, with zero constant terms and
leading coefficients $1/j!$, the Vandermonde determinant gives
\begin{align*}
 \det B
 &=\frac{\displaystyle
       \prod_{i=1}^d(iu)
       \prod_{1\leq i<\ell\leq d}(\ell u-iu)}
       {\displaystyle\prod_{j=1}^d j!}\\
 &=u^{d(d+1)/2}.
\end{align*}
The inverse image of the cube $[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]^d$ under
$B$ has volume $(2\varepsilon)^d/\det B$. It contains all permissible
$c$-vectors, proving \eqref{gsr:dt:19:poly:probability-bound}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[A necessary exponent inequality]
\label{gsr:dt:19:poly:obstruction}
Fix positive degrees $d_1,\ldots,d_q$, and set
\[
 D=\sum_{i=1}^q d_i,\qquad
 S=\sum_{i=1}^q\frac{d_i(d_i+1)}2.
\]
If $a,b>0$ satisfy
\begin{equation}
 (S+1)a+Db>1,
 \label{gsr:dt:19:poly:necessary}
\end{equation}
then for all sufficiently large $r$ there are polynomials of these
degrees for which no partition of $[0,r)\cap\Z$ into arithmetic
progressions can have both $|P|\geq r^a$ and
$\operatorname{ad}(\phi_i(P)\bmod1)\leq r^{-b}$ for every $i,P$.
The phases can be chosen with rational coefficients, and can also be
realized modulo a sufficiently large prime.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If $a>1$, the length requirement is already impossible. Assume
$0<a\leq1$, put $L=\lceil r^a\rceil$, and set
$\varepsilon=r^{-b}$. Independently choose all nonconstant coefficients
of each polynomial uniformly modulo one, with constant term zero.
For large $r$ the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:19:poly:probability} hold for
every $d_i$, and
$\lfloor(L-1)/d_i\rfloor\geq L/(4d_i)$.

Consider one progression
$\{0,h,\ldots,(L-1)h\}$ contained in $[0,r)$.
If its phase arc diameter is at most $\varepsilon$, then every phase
value has circular distance at most $\varepsilon$ from the value at
zero, which is zero. Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:19:poly:probability}, independently for
the $q$ phases, bounds the probability of this event by
\[
 K\varepsilon^D L^{-S},\qquad
 K=\prod_{i=1}^q
 \left[2^{d_i}(4d_i)^{d_i(d_i+1)/2}\right].
\]
There are at most $(r-1)/(L-1)\leq2r/L$ admissible positive $h$.
A union bound therefore bounds the probability that any such progression
has all the required small diameters by
\begin{equation}
 2Kr\varepsilon^D L^{-S-1}.
 \label{gsr:dt:19:poly:union}
\end{equation}
This tends to zero under \eqref{gsr:dt:19:poly:necessary}. Thus some tuple of
polynomials has no such progression through zero.

Every complete partition into progressions of lengths at least $L$ has
a cell containing zero. Orient its common difference positively.
Since the ambient interval contains no negative points, this cell starts
at zero; its first $L$ points give one of the forbidden progressions.
This is a contradiction.

For fixed $r,L$, only finitely many progressions through zero must be
excluded. The arc diameter of a fixed finite set of polynomial values
is continuous in the coefficients. Failure of a weak diameter condition
is therefore open, and the tuple just obtained has a neighborhood
consisting of counterexamples. This neighborhood contains rational
coefficient tuples of the prescribed degrees. A common denominator
realizes them as normalized modular polynomials. Alternatively, take
a sufficiently large prime $p\geq\max\{r,d_1+1,\ldots,d_q+1\}$ and
approximate every coefficient by a multiple of $1/p$ within that
neighborhood. The resulting phases are normalized polynomials modulo
$p$ and retain the obstruction.
\end{proof}

\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 34--39]
For the prescribed lengths $L$ or $L+1$ (every target), source~35 adds the numerical-semigroup conductor and obtains $(W+2)a+\sum_id_ib_i\le1$, $W=S$ (quadratics at $b=2a$: $1/(7\nu+2)$), by explicit phases forcing $D\mid h$ (its Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:35:po:cor:exponents} and the note there); the obstruction here, for flexible lengths, is unchanged.
\end{writenote}

In degree-profile notation,
\[
 D=\sum_{j=1}^k q_j,\qquad S=\sum_{j=1}^k jq_j.
\]
Thus a necessary condition for any uniform theorem of this kind is
\begin{equation}
 \left(1+\sum_{j=1}^k jq_j\right)a
 +\left(\sum_{j=1}^kq_j\right)b\leq1.
 \label{gsr:dt:19:poly:profile-obstruction}
\end{equation}
For $q$ linear phases this is $(q+1)a+qb\leq1$, matching the strict
sufficient region supplied by Dirichlet approximation. For $q$ phases of
degree $k$, it becomes
\[
 \left(1+\frac{qk(k+1)}2\right)a+qkb\leq1.
\]
We establish no matching nonlinear partition theorem. In particular,
the exponent denominator $O_k(q^k)$ from the recurrence transfer remains
larger than the $O_k(q)$ obstruction scale.

\subsection{Finite diagnostics and a concrete obstruction}

The accompanying exact-arithmetic script checks the determinant identity
in Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:19:poly:probability} for degrees $1$ through $8$ and five
spacings, for a total of $40$ cases. It also exhaustively checks all
$101^2$ quadratic coefficient pairs modulo $101$, at each of the two
spacings $1$ and $7$, on five-point progressions with
$\varepsilon=1/9<1/8$. At both spacings it finds $61$ centered-small
events and $45$ events with arc diameter at most $1/9$; every centered
event has the asserted Newton lift and vanishing third differences.
The finite coefficient-to-Newton map is bijective in these tests because
$101$ is coprime to its determinant. These checks are diagnostics of the
proof's bookkeeping; an atomic finite grid is not substituted for the
continuous Haar-volume argument.

For a concrete example, consider
\[
 \phi(x)=\frac{690x+294x^2}{1009}\pmod1,
 \qquad x\in[0,80)\cap\Z.
\]
The $11$ candidate eight-point progressions starting at zero have common
differences $1,\ldots,11$. Exact enumeration gives minimum circular arc
diameter $523/1009$, which exceeds $1/9$. Therefore no partition of
$[0,80)$ into arithmetic progressions of at least eight points has phase
arc diameter at most $1/9$ on every cell. This finite witness illustrates
the endpoint-cell mechanism used in Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:19:poly:obstruction}; the
asymptotic obstruction itself is proved by \eqref{gsr:dt:19:poly:union}.

\subsection{Questions left by the partition results}

\begin{enumerate}
\item Can the dependence on $q$ in the degree-$k$ sufficient frontier be
reduced from order $q^k$ to order $q$, or even by one power of $q$?
Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:19:poly:obstruction} leaves room for such a gain.
\item Is the boundary \eqref{gsr:dt:19:poly:profile-obstruction} achievable for
nonlinear phases? It is sharp for linear phases, but the present work
provides neither sharpness nor a counterexample in higher degree.
\item Can simultaneous recurrence be made sufficiently explicit in both
degree and dimension to support numerical thresholds throughout the
repository's density-increment argument?
\item Can prescribed target lengths be obtained without the squaring
loss in Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:19:poly:rounding}, while covering every point?
\item Can bounded-height rational dependencies among leading
coefficients replace $q_j$ by a smaller effective dimension in the
recurrence step?
\end{enumerate}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The partition problem and its arithmetic parameter\srctag{23}}]{The partition problem and its arithmetic parameter}\label{gsr:dt:23:sec:d2}
\srcnote{23}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:dt:23:sec:phase-model}

Write $I_R=\{0,1,\ldots,R-1\}$ and $\T=\R/\Z$.  A progression in
$I_R$ is an ordinary integer progression
\[
 P=\{a,a+d,\ldots,a+(\ell-1)d\}\subset I_R,
 \qquad d\ge1.
\]
Its length is its cardinality $\ell$.  All partitions below are disjoint
and cover their indicated domain exactly, unless an exceptional set is
explicitly allowed.  Distinct cells may have different common differences.

For a finite subset $X\subset\T$, let $\operatorname{adiam}(X)$ be the
length of the shortest closed circular arc containing $X$.  For example,
$\operatorname{adiam}\{0,1/3,2/3\}=2/3$, although the largest pairwise
circular distance is $1/3$.  This is the normalized version of Gowers's
definition immediately before Lemma~2.3: the smallest $s$ for which a set
in $\Z/N\Z$ lies in $\{a,a+1,\ldots,a+s\}$ \cite{gowers}.
This distinction will matter in the lower bound.

Fix $q\ge1$ and affine phases
\[
 \phi_i(n)=\alpha_i n+\beta_i\pmod1,\qquad 1\le i\le q.
\]
Let $\mathcal S\subset\N$ be a finite set of allowed lengths, and write
\[
 L=\min\mathcal S\ge2,\qquad H=\max\mathcal S.
\]
The additive semigroup generated by these lengths is
\[
 \langle\mathcal S\rangle
 =\left\{\sum_{s\in\mathcal S}n_s s:n_s\in\Z_{\ge0}\right\}.
\]
If $\gcd(\mathcal S)=1$, its \emph{conductor} $C=C(\mathcal S)$ is the
least integer such that every integer at least $C$ belongs to this
semigroup.  Consequently $C-1\notin\langle\mathcal S\rangle$.
Our assumption $L\ge2$ implies $C\ge L$.

For completeness, finiteness of the conductor needs no deep theorem.
The residues modulo $L$ attained by the semigroup form a subgroup of
$\Z/L\Z$: any additive subsemigroup of a finite group is a subgroup,
since repeated addition supplies inverses.  The gcd assumption makes this
subgroup the whole group. Choose a nonnegative representable integer in
each residue class. Every sufficiently large integer is one of these
representatives plus a nonnegative multiple of $L$.

\begin{definition}[Universal eventual threshold]
\label{gsr:dt:23:def:threshold}
For $\boldsymbol\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_q)$ with
$0<\varepsilon_i<1/2$, define $T_{\mathcal S}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)$
to be the least positive integer $R_0$ such that for every $R\ge R_0$ and
every choice of the $q$ affine phases, $I_R$ has a partition into
progressions $P$ satisfying
\[
 |P|\in\mathcal S,\qquad
 \operatorname{adiam}(\phi_i(P))\le\varepsilon_i
 \quad(1\le i\le q).
\]
\end{definition}

The word ``eventual'' makes the quantifiers explicit.  Particular values
of $R$ below the threshold can still be easy; for example, a useful
divisibility relation may make an exact tiling possible.  The threshold
requires one guarantee valid at \emph{every} later interval length.  The
upper bound below will prove that it is finite.  If
$\gcd(\mathcal S)>1$, such an eventual threshold cannot be finite:
infinitely many total cardinalities are not sums of allowed lengths,
even for constant phases.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{An explicit theorem with matching upper and lower scales\srctag{23}}]{An explicit theorem with matching upper and lower scales}\label{gsr:dt:23:sec:d3}
\srcnote{23}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:dt:23:sec:phase-theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Semigroup bounds for simultaneous phase partitions]
\label{gsr:dt:23:thm:semigroup}
Let $\mathcal S,L,H,C,q$ be as above, with $\gcd(\mathcal S)=1$.
For $0<\varepsilon_i<1/2$, put
\[
 B=\left\lceil\frac{(H-1)^q}{\varepsilon_1\cdots\varepsilon_q}\right\rceil-1,
 \qquad
 M_i=\left\lceil\frac{L-1}{\varepsilon_i}\right\rceil-1.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\quad
 C\prod_{i=1}^qM_i
 \ \le\ T_{\mathcal S}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)
 \ \le\ CB .\quad}
 \label{gsr:dt:23:eq:semigroup-bounds}
\end{equation}
The upper construction uses one common difference for every cell.  The
lower bound holds even when the difference is chosen separately for each
cell.  The lower examples can also be realized by affine maps on a prime
cyclic group, restricted to a proper interval.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Credit.} For $\mathcal S=\{v-1,v\}$ the conductor is $(v-1)(v-2)$, so the upper bound with one common difference is source~13's Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:13:thm:exactlengths} (the source reproduces it with attribution, Section~\ref{gsr:dt:23:sec:d5}); the matching lower bound, valid for cell-dependent differences, is new in this report.
\end{writenote}

The proof separates approximation of the phases from exact tiling of
the resulting residue chains.  The upper construction is the familiar
Dirichlet argument, with the conductor recording the exact tiling
requirement.  The lower construction makes that requirement unavoidable.

\subsection{Simultaneous approximation with unequal tolerances}

We first record a slightly sharper finite form of the usual rectangular
pigeonhole estimate.  Its only additional ingredient is translation
invariance of volume on the finite-dimensional torus.

\begin{lemma}[Torus packing estimate]
\label{gsr:dt:23:lem:torus-packing}
For $\alpha_i\in\T$ and $0<\Delta_i<1/2$, there is an integer
\[
 1\le d\le\left\lceil(\Delta_1\cdots\Delta_q)^{-1}\right\rceil-1
 \quad\text{with}\quad \|d\alpha_i\|_{\T}\le\Delta_i
 \quad\text{for all }i.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $K=\ceil{(\prod_i\Delta_i)^{-1}}$ and place a closed rectangular
box of coordinate side lengths $\Delta_i$ at each of the $K$ orbit
points $n\boldsymbol\alpha$, $0\le n<K$.  Intersection of two boxes
implies all the required coordinate inequalities for their index
difference.  If there is no such pair, the finitely many compact boxes
are disjoint with positive separation.  Enlarge every side by a
sufficiently small positive amount so that they remain disjoint and all
side lengths stay below one.  Their total volume is then strictly
greater than $K\prod_i\Delta_i\ge1$, impossible in a torus of volume
one.  Thus two boxes intersect, and their difference is at most $K-1$.
\end{proof}

The weak inequality in the conclusion handles the exact-volume boundary.
For a completely discrete construction one can instead use the following
slightly less sharp integer bound.

\begin{lemma}[Rectangular pigeonhole principle]
\label{gsr:dt:23:lem:dirichlet}
Given $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_q\in\T$ and positive integers
$Q_1,\ldots,Q_q$, there is an integer
\[
 1\le d\le Q_1\cdots Q_q
 \quad\text{such that}\quad
 \|d\alpha_i\|_{\T}<Q_i^{-1}\quad\text{for every }i.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Partition $[0,1)^q$ into $Q_1\cdots Q_q$ half-open rectangular boxes,
with side lengths $Q_i^{-1}$ in coordinate $i$.  Among the
$1+Q_1\cdots Q_q$ points
$n(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_q)$, $0\le n\le Q_1\cdots Q_q$, two lie
in the same box.  Their positive index difference is the required $d$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of the upper bound in Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:23:thm:semigroup}]
Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:23:lem:torus-packing} with
$\Delta_i=\varepsilon_i/(H-1)$ to obtain $d\le B$. If
$R\ge CB$, each residue class modulo $d$ meets $I_R$ in a
chain with at least $\floor{R/d}\ge C$ elements.  Every chain length is
therefore a sum of elements of $\mathcal S$. Cut the chain consecutively
into blocks having those lengths.

Choose the centered representative $\theta_i$ of $d\alpha_i$.
On any resulting cell of length $\ell\le H$, its phase has a real lift
with successive differences $\theta_i$, and hence span
\[
 (\ell-1)|\theta_i|\le\frac{\ell-1}{H-1}\varepsilon_i
 \le\varepsilon_i.
\]
Reduction modulo one gives the required containing arc.  The residue
chains partition $I_R$, and cutting each chain preserves exact coverage.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Flatness forces a small step}

\begin{lemma}[Rigidity inside a short arc]
\label{gsr:dt:23:lem:arc-rigidity}
Suppose $\ell\ge2$ and
$c,c+\theta,\ldots,c+(\ell-1)\theta\in\T$ lie in an arc of length
$\varepsilon<1/2$.  Then
\[
 \|\theta\|_{\T}\le\frac{\varepsilon}{\ell-1}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Lift every point to one real interval of length $\varepsilon$ containing
the arc.  Each consecutive lifted difference belongs to
$[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]$ and is congruent to $\theta$ modulo one.
Two such differences differ by an integer of absolute value at most
$2\varepsilon<1$, so they are equal.  Call their common value $t$.
The first and last lifts differ by $(\ell-1)t$, proving
$(\ell-1)|t|\le\varepsilon$.  Since $|t|<1/2$, it is the centered
representative of $\theta$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[An alternative diameter convention]
If diameter means largest pairwise circular distance, the lemma remains
true for $\varepsilon<1/3$.  Indeed, a set of that pairwise diameter lies
in an arc of the same length: after placing one point at zero, the largest
positive and negative centered representatives cannot have sum greater
than $\varepsilon$, since their sum is at most $2\varepsilon<1-\varepsilon$.
At $\varepsilon=1/3$, the three equally spaced points give a counterexample.
We use arc diameter throughout, so this extra restriction is unnecessary.
\end{remark}

\subsection{A mixed-radix obstruction}

\begin{proof}[Proof of the lower bound in Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:23:thm:semigroup}]
The integers $M_i$ are at least two and satisfy
\[
 \frac1{M_i}>\frac{\varepsilon_i}{L-1}.
\]
Set $D_0=1$, $D_i=M_1\cdots M_i$, and $D=D_q$.  Take
\begin{equation}
 \alpha_i=\frac1{D_i}\pmod1,
 \qquad R=DC-1.
 \label{gsr:dt:23:eq:radix-phases}
\end{equation}
Suppose an allowed flat progression has common difference $d$.
If $D\nmid d$, choose the least $i$ with $D_i\nmid d$.
Then $D_{i-1}\mid d$, and the nonzero residue of $d/D_{i-1}$ modulo
$M_i$ gives
\[
 \left\|\frac d{D_i}\right\|_{\T}
 \ge\frac1{M_i}>\frac{\varepsilon_i}{L-1}.
\]
This contradicts Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:23:lem:arc-rigidity}, because the cell has
at least $L$ points.  Thus every allowed cell has $D\mid d$ and lies in
one residue class modulo $D$.

The last residue class, $D-1$ modulo $D$, has exactly $C-1$ points in
$I_R$; the other classes have $C$ points.  A partition would express
$C-1$ as a sum of allowed cell lengths, contradicting the defining gap
of the conductor.  We have exhibited a bad interval of length $DC-1$,
so the eventual threshold is at least $DC$.
\end{proof}

The use of several phases is essential to the full product in the lower
bound.  The first phase checks divisibility by $M_1$; the next checks the
next digit, and so on.  This forces the same residue obstruction on every
cell without assuming a common difference in the proposed partition.

\subsection{Prime cyclic realization}

\begin{proposition}[Robustness of the obstruction]
\label{gsr:dt:23:prop:prime}
Let $R,D_i,M_i$ be those in \eqref{gsr:dt:23:eq:radix-phases}, and put
\[
 \gamma=\min_i\left(\frac1{M_i}-\frac{\varepsilon_i}{L-1}\right)>0.
\]
For any prime $p$ with
\begin{equation}
 p\ge R,\qquad
 p>\frac{R-1}{2(L-1)\gamma},
 \label{gsr:dt:23:eq:prime-size}
\end{equation}
choose integers $a_i$ nearest to $p/D_i$.  The affine maps
$x\mapsto a_i x$ on $\Z/p\Z$, restricted to $I_R$, admit no partition
as in Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:23:thm:semigroup}, with normalized diameters
$\varepsilon_i$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
An ordinary progression in $I_R$ of length at least $L$ has
$d\le(R-1)/(L-1)$.  Also
$|a_i/p-1/D_i|\le1/(2p)$.  If $D\nmid d$, its first failing digit
therefore satisfies
\[
 \left\|\frac{da_i}{p}\right\|_{\T}
 \ge\left\|\frac d{D_i}\right\|_{\T}-\frac d{2p}
 >\frac1{M_i}-\gamma
 \ge\frac{\varepsilon_i}{L-1}.
\]
Rigidity again forces $D\mid d$, and the same cardinality contradiction
finishes the proof.  Arbitrarily large primes exist, so the required prime
can always be chosen.
\end{proof}

This statement concerns an ordinary interval inside a prime cyclic group.
It does not identify the interval length with the ambient prime.  That
is exactly the $r\le N$ interval setting of Lemma~5.9.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Sharp asymptotics and the permitted range of cell sizes\srctag{23}}]{Sharp asymptotics and the permitted range of cell sizes}\label{gsr:dt:23:sec:d4}
\srcnote{23}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:dt:23:sec:phase-asymptotics}

\subsection{Two consecutive lengths}

The semigroup generated by $L$ and $L+1$ has conductor $L(L-1)$.
One elementary proof is to write $n=kL+r$, $0\le r<L$:
if $k\ge L-1$, then
\[
 n=(k-r)L+r(L+1).
\]
On the other hand, $L(L-1)-1$ is not representable, as is also immediate
from the residue $L-1$ modulo $L$.

\begin{corollary}[Sharp threshold for nearly equal cells]
\label{gsr:dt:23:cor:consecutive}
For $\mathcal S=\{L,L+1\}$,
\begin{align}
 L(L-1)\prod_{i=1}^q
 \left(\left\lceil\frac{L-1}{\varepsilon_i}\right\rceil-1\right)
 &\le T_{\{L,L+1\}}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon),
 \label{gsr:dt:23:eq:consecutive-lower}\\
 T_{\{L,L+1\}}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)
 &\le L(L-1)\left(
 \left\lceil\frac{L^q}{\varepsilon_1\cdots\varepsilon_q}\right\rceil-1
 \right).
 \label{gsr:dt:23:eq:consecutive-upper}
\end{align}
For fixed $q$, as $L\to\infty$,
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 T_{\{L,L+1\}}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)
 =\left(1+O_q(L^{-1})\right)
 \frac{L^{q+2}}{\varepsilon_1\cdots\varepsilon_q}.}
 \label{gsr:dt:23:eq:sharp-leading}
\end{equation}
The error estimate is uniform over all $0<\varepsilon_i<1/2$, including
tolerances tending to zero with $L$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The finite inequalities are Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:23:thm:semigroup}.  Uniformly in
the indicated tolerances,
\[
 \left\lceil\frac{L-1}{\varepsilon_i}\right\rceil-1
 =\frac L{\varepsilon_i}\bigl(1+O(L^{-1})\bigr),
 \quad
 \left\lceil\frac{L^q}{\prod_i\varepsilon_i}\right\rceil-1
 =\frac{L^q}{\prod_i\varepsilon_i}\bigl(1+O(L^{-1})\bigr).
\]
The conductor is $L^2(1+O(L^{-1}))$.
Multiplication and squeezing prove the assertion.
\end{proof}

This gives the leading constant one, not just matching exponents.  It
also settles the question whether a clever choice of different
progression differences can remove the quadratic tiling cost in the
worst case.  The lower construction allows all such choices and still
forces them into residue classes of a forbidden cardinality.

\subsection{Arbitrary narrow sets of lengths}

\begin{corollary}[Narrow length sets]
\label{gsr:dt:23:cor:narrow}
For fixed $q$, let $\mathcal S$ vary with $L=\min\mathcal S\to\infty$,
$\gcd(\mathcal S)=1$, and $H/L\to1$.  Then, uniformly for
$0<\varepsilon_i<1/2$,
\[
 T_{\mathcal S}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)
 \sim\frac{C(\mathcal S)L^q}{\varepsilon_1\cdots\varepsilon_q}.
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Divide \eqref{gsr:dt:23:eq:semigroup-bounds} by
$C L^q/(\prod_i\varepsilon_i)$.  A lower bound for the ratio is
\[
 \left(1-\frac{3}{2L}\right)^q,
\]
and an upper bound is
\[
 \left(1+\frac{H-L-1}{L}\right)^q.
\]
Both tend to one.  These displayed bounds also give a
version with growing $q$: it is enough that
$q(H-L+1)/L\to0$.
\end{proof}

The conductor can depend strongly on which lengths are allowed, even
when their minimum and maximum are close.  For example, for the two
coprime lengths $L$ and $L+s$, their conductor is
$(L-1)(L+s-1)$; if every intermediate length is allowed, the next
proposition gives a conductor of order $L^2/s$.  Exact tiling therefore
detects more than just the width of the allowed range.

\subsection{An interval of permitted lengths}

The following classical conductor computation is a consecutive-integer
case of the Frobenius problem for arithmetic progressions
\cite{roberts}.  We give the full argument because it directly determines
the partition scale.

\begin{proposition}[Conductor of a consecutive interval]
\label{gsr:dt:23:prop:interval-conductor}
For $1\le w\le L-1$,
\begin{equation}
 C(\{L,L+1,\ldots,L+w\})
 =L\left\lceil\frac{L-1}{w}\right\rceil.
 \label{gsr:dt:23:eq:interval-conductor}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Sums of exactly $k$ permitted lengths fill every integer in
$[kL,k(L+w)]$: distribute any excess between zero and $kw$ among $k$
slots, each with capacity $w$.  The $k$th and $(k+1)$st intervals touch
or overlap exactly when $kw\ge L-1$.  Put
$k_0=\ceil{(L-1)/w}$.  All intervals from $k_0$ onward join to cover
$[k_0L,\infty)$.  Meanwhile $k_0L-1$ lies above the end of the
$(k_0-1)$st interval and below the start of the $k_0$th.  Earlier
intervals have still smaller endpoints.  It is the last gap.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The cost of reducing length variation]
\label{gsr:dt:23:cor:spread}
For fixed $q$ and $1\le w\le L-1$,
\begin{equation}
 T_{\{L,\ldots,L+w\}}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)
 \asymp_q\frac{L^{q+2}}{w\,\varepsilon_1\cdots\varepsilon_q}.
 \label{gsr:dt:23:eq:spread-order}
\end{equation}
If $w=o(L)$ as $L\to\infty$, then the sharper statement is
\begin{equation}
 T_{\{L,\ldots,L+w\}}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)
 \sim\frac{L^{q+2}}{w\,\varepsilon_1\cdots\varepsilon_q}.
 \label{gsr:dt:23:eq:spread-leading}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Use \eqref{gsr:dt:23:eq:interval-conductor} in Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:23:thm:semigroup}.
Here $L\le H<2L$, and the conductor is comparable to $L^2/w$.
If $w=o(L)$, its ceiling has relative error $O(w/L)$ and $H/L\to1$,
so Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:23:cor:narrow} gives the leading constant.
\end{proof}

For equal tolerances $\varepsilon$, a logarithmic parametrization
$L=X^a$, $\varepsilon=X^{-b}$, and $w=X^c$ gives the scale
\[
 T\asymp X^{(q+2)a+qb-c},\qquad 0\le c\le a,
\]
up to integer rounding and fixed factors.  Thus the sharp scaling boundary
is $(q+2)a+qb-c=1$.  Consecutive lengths have $c=0$; a range of
lengths comparable with $L$ has $c=a$.  The latter recovers the boundary
$(q+1)a+qb=1$ for flexible cell sizes.  This is a statement about the
threshold as its input parameters vary; it does not assert failure at
every individual length below that threshold.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\caption{Dependence on the allowed lengths, for fixed $q$.  The symbol
$\sim$ includes leading constant one; $\asymp_q$ allows constants
depending on $q$. All tolerances lie in $(0,1/2)$.}
\label{gsr:dt:23:tab:length-spread}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
Allowed lengths & Conductor & Eventual threshold\\
\midrule
$\{L,L+1\}$ & $L(L-1)$ & $\displaystyle\sim L^{q+2}/\prod_i\varepsilon_i$\\[5pt]
$\{L,\ldots,L+w\}$, $w=o(L)$
& $L\ceil{(L-1)/w}$
& $\displaystyle\sim L^{q+2}/(w\prod_i\varepsilon_i)$\\[5pt]
$\{L,\ldots,2L-1\}$ & $L$
& $\displaystyle\asymp_q L^{q+1}/\prod_i\varepsilon_i$\\[5pt]
$\gcd(\mathcal S)>1$ & No finite conductor & No finite exact threshold\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Consequences for Lemma 5.9 and exact finite witnesses\srctag{23}}]{Consequences for Lemma 5.9 and exact finite witnesses}\label{gsr:dt:23:sec:d5}
\srcnote{23}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:dt:23:sec:lemma59}

\subsection{Which previously sufficient exponent is now optimal?}

In Gowers's degree-one specialization, $K=16$; the simultaneous lemma
has target lengths $v-1,v$ with
$v\le R^{1/(2\cdot16^q)}$ and diameter
$R^{-1/16^q}$.  The repository has repaired the printed exact cell-count
wording to this prescribed-length interface \cite{repo23source}.

The earlier report \emph{Sharp Local Refinements in Gowers' Szemer\'edi
Framework}, Theorem~3.8, already gave the upper bound
\[
 R\ge(v-1)(v-2)\prod_i
 \left\lceil\frac{v-1}{\varepsilon_i}\right\rceil,
\]
and its Corollary~3.9 gave the exponent $a_q=1/(3q+2)$ with phase
diameter $R^{-2a_q}$ \cite{prior23linear}.  This upper result is not
claimed as new here.  Its Question~11.1 asked whether the extra tiling
cost was intrinsic.  Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:23:thm:semigroup} answers that question
in the affirmative.

It is important to compare equal normalizations.  If target length is
$R^a$ and diameter is $R^{-b}$, the prescribed-length boundary is
\begin{equation}
 (q+2)a+qb=1.
 \label{gsr:dt:23:eq:prescribed-frontier}
\end{equation}
Under Gowers's relation $b=2a$, this gives $a=1/(3q+2)$.
Under the different relation $b=a$, it gives $a=1/(2q+2)$.
Those are two slices of the same result, not competing improvements.

\begin{proposition}[Optimality for the all-targets interface]
\label{gsr:dt:23:prop:frontier}
Fix $q\ge1$, $a>0$, $b\ge0$ and $0<c<1/2$.  Suppose
$(q+2)a+qb>1$.  There are arbitrarily large $R$, $q$ affine phases,
and an integer $v\le R^a$ such that no partition into cells of lengths
$v-1,v$ has all phase diameters at most $cR^{-b}$.
The differences may be chosen separately on different cells.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Choose $t>0$ with
\[
 a(qt+2)>1,
 \qquad t(1-qb)<1+2b.
\]
Such $t$ exists.  If $qb\ge1$, the second inequality is automatic.  If
$qb<1$, the available interval for $t$ is nonempty precisely because
$a(q+2)>1-qb$.

Let $L\to\infty$, $M=\floor{L^t}$, $D=M^q$, and
$R=D(L^2-L-1)$.  Set $v=L+1$ and $\alpha_i=M^{-i}$.
Since $R\sim L^{qt+2}$, the first inequality gives $v\le R^a$
eventually.  Moreover,
\[
 \frac{M cR^{-b}}{L-1}
 \sim cL^{t(1-qb)-1-2b}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Thus $1/M>cR^{-b}/(L-1)$ eventually.  The same mixed-radix argument
forces every admissible step to be divisible by $D$.  Each residue has
$L^2-L-1$ elements, the last gap of $\langle L,L+1\rangle$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Answers source~13's Question~1} (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:I:conductor}). The prescribed-length region $(q+2)a+qb\le1$ of source~13's Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:13:cor:linear59} cannot be enlarged, even with cell-dependent differences, so at Gowers's $b=2a$ its exponent $1/(3q+2)$ is optimal; the flexible frontier $(q+1)a+qb=1$ needs an exceptional set or flexible lengths. The existence of $t$ in the proof was re-derived at the write: for $qb<1$ the two conditions say $(1/a-2)/q<t<(1+2b)/(1-qb)$, an interval that is nonempty exactly when $(q+2)a+qb>1$.
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 34--39]
Source~35's Section~\ref{gsr:dt:35:sec:d7} extends the construction to polynomial phases of every degree, with exact thresholds $D\,C(\mathcal S)$; at degree one its frontier is this one (its Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:35:po:cor:exponents}).
\end{writenote}

Constants and ceilings at the boundary itself are governed by the finite
inequalities, not by this strict-exponent statement.  In particular the
proposition establishes impossibility of any larger universal exponent;
it does not prescribe an endpoint constant for a formula with exact
powers and no rounding slack.

\subsection{A small explicit obstruction}

Take two phases, permitted lengths $4,5$, and tolerance $1/4$ for each.
The construction gives
\[
 M_1=M_2=11,\quad D_1=11,\quad D=121,\quad C=12,
 \quad R=121\cdot11=1331.
\]
The phases are $n/11$ and $n/121$.  Flatness of a cell of length at
least four requires each step phase to have distance at most $1/12$.
If $11\nmid d$, the first phase has distance at least $1/11$.
If $11\mid d$ but $121\nmid d$, the second does.  Therefore every cell
stays in a residue class modulo $121$.  Every residue class has eleven
points, while eleven is not $4u+5v$ for nonnegative integers $u,v$.

For a prime-field witness, take permitted lengths $3,4$, tolerance $1/4$,
$D=49$, and $R=245$.  In $\Z/3433\Z$ use slopes $490$ and $70$.
For $1\le d\le122$, the simultaneous necessary small-step inequalities
allow only $d=49,98$.  Both preserve the residues modulo $49$, each of
which contains five points.  Five is not a sum of threes and fours.
The accompanying script checks this claim with integer arithmetic,
including primality and every candidate difference.

\subsection{Why an exact prescribed number of cells is different}

An exact number of nearly equal cells cannot be substituted silently for
the allowed-length formulation.  Here is a direct explanation of the
repair already present in the repository.

Let $R=4t+2$ and request exactly $m=R/2=2t+1$ nonempty cells with lengths
differing by at most one.  Their mean length is two, so every cell must
have exactly two points.  Choose a prime $p>2R$ and the phase
$\alpha=(p-1)/(2p)$.  Points of opposite parity in $I_R$ have phase
distance greater than $1/4$: for an odd difference $s$, the distance is
$1/2-|s|/(2p)>1/4$.  A flat cell of diameter at most $1/4$ is therefore
parity-homogeneous.  Each parity class has the odd cardinality $2t+1$,
so it cannot be partitioned into pairs.  This remains a counterexample
at arbitrarily large $R$.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Partial coverage and the exact cost of exceptions\srctag{23}}]{Partial coverage and the exact cost of exceptions}\label{gsr:dt:23:sec:d6}
\srcnote{23}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:dt:23:sec:partial}

The obstruction above is strong for exact partitions.  Its behavior under
deletion is different, and can also be computed exactly.  This matters
when a later argument only requires that most of the original points be
retained.

For any finite allowed-length set $\mathcal S$, without a gcd assumption,
define
\[
 A_{\mathcal S}(n)=\max\{s\le n:s\in\langle\mathcal S\rangle\},
 \qquad g_{\mathcal S}(n)=n-A_{\mathcal S}(n).
\]
The maximum exists because zero is representable.

\begin{theorem}[Exact packing for the rigid phase examples]
\label{gsr:dt:23:thm:packing}
Choose radices $M_i$ with $1/M_i>\varepsilon_i/(L-1)$ and phases
$\alpha_i=1/D_i$ as before.  For every $R=Dt+r$, $0\le r<D$, the
smallest number of uncovered points in a disjoint collection of flat
progressions with lengths in $\mathcal S$ is exactly
\begin{equation}
 (D-r)g_{\mathcal S}(t)+r g_{\mathcal S}(t+1).
 \label{gsr:dt:23:eq:packing}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Every flat cell lies in a residue class modulo $D$.  The residue chains
have lengths $t$ or $t+1$, with multiplicities $D-r$ and $r$.  A disjoint
collection covers a representable number of points in each chain, so its
uncovered count is at least the right side.

Conversely, cover the first $A_{\mathcal S}(n)$ points of each chain of
length $n$ by consecutive blocks whose lengths express that number in
$\langle\mathcal S\rangle$.  All blocks have step $D$, on which all
phases are exactly constant.  This attains the lower bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Exact threshold of the constructed phase vector]
\label{gsr:dt:23:cor:fixed-vector}
For the mixed-radix phases in Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:23:thm:packing}, if
$\gcd(\mathcal S)=1$, the eventual exact-partition threshold is exactly
$DC(\mathcal S)$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
At $R=DC-1$ the last residue chain has the gap cardinality $C-1$.
At every $R\ge DC$, all residue-chain cardinalities are at least $C$,
and hence representable. Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:23:thm:packing} then gives zero
uncovered points.
\end{proof}

For $\mathcal S=\{L,L+1\}$, the last gap
$F=L^2-L-1$ has $g_{\mathcal S}(F)=1$, because
$F-1=(L-2)(L+1)$.  Thus the exact-partition obstruction at $R=DF$
disappears after deleting exactly $D$ points, a fraction $1/F$.
The conductor obstruction alone therefore cannot exclude an almost
partition with exceptional proportion appreciably larger than $L^{-2}$.

\begin{proposition}[A general almost-partition into one exact length]
\label{gsr:dt:23:prop:almost-upper}
Given $L\ge2$, arbitrary affine phases and positive tolerances, put
\[
 Q=\prod_{i=1}^q\left\lceil\frac{L-1}{\varepsilon_i}\right\rceil.
\]
There is a disjoint collection of flat progressions of length exactly $L$
covering all but at most $(L-1)Q$ points of $I_R$.  In particular, an
exceptional proportion at most $\eta>0$ is guaranteed when
\[
 R\ge\frac{(L-1)Q}{\eta}.
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Choose $d\le Q$ by Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:23:lem:dirichlet}.  Cut each residue chain
into blocks of length $L$, discarding a remainder of at most $L-1$.
There are at most $d$ nonempty chains, and each block is flat by the same
phase-span estimate as before.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Sharp scale when a small exceptional set is allowed]
\label{gsr:dt:23:cor:partial-asymptotic}
Let $T_{L,\eta}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)$ be the least eventual threshold
for covering at least $(1-\eta)R$ points by disjoint flat progressions of
length exactly $L$.  For fixed $q$, as $L\to\infty$ and
$\eta\to0^+$,
\begin{equation}
 T_{L,\eta}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)
 \sim\frac{L^{q+1}}{\eta\,\varepsilon_1\cdots\varepsilon_q},
 \label{gsr:dt:23:eq:partial-asymptotic}
\end{equation}
uniformly for $0<\varepsilon_i<1/2$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The upper bound follows from Proposition~\ref{gsr:dt:23:prop:almost-upper} and
the uniform ceiling estimates used earlier.  For the lower bound take
the mixed-radix phases with
$M_i=\ceil{(L-1)/\varepsilon_i}-1$ and $D=\prod_iM_i$.
Choose $t=kL-1$ to be the largest integer of that form strictly smaller
than $(L-1)/\eta$.  For sufficiently small $\eta$, it is positive and
\[
 t=\frac{L-1}{\eta}+O(L),\qquad
 \frac{L-1}{t}>\eta.
\]
At $R=Dt$, Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:23:thm:packing} with $\mathcal S=\{L\}$ gives
uncovered fraction $(L-1)/t$, strictly greater than $\eta$.
Consequently $T_{L,\eta}>Dt$.  Now
\[
 Dt=\bigl(1+O_q(L^{-1})+O(\eta)\bigr)
 \frac{L^{q+1}}{\eta\prod_i\varepsilon_i},
\]
which squeezes the threshold to the asserted asymptotic.
\end{proof}

The exact-cover scale and the almost-cover scale coincide at the level
of powers when $\eta$ is of order $L^{-1}$.  This comparison uses a
universal bound over all phases.  The particular last-gap example is
easier to repair, as the exact formula \eqref{gsr:dt:23:eq:packing} demonstrates.

\subsection{Constructive use and computational complexity}

The upper theorem is constructive at the finite combinatorial level.
For rational phases and tolerances, enumerate
$d=1,\ldots,B$, where
$B=\ceil{(H-1)^q/(\prod_i\varepsilon_i)}-1$, testing
$\|d\alpha_i\|_{\T}\le\varepsilon_i/(H-1)$ for every $i$.
All comparisons can be made exactly.  Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:23:lem:torus-packing}
guarantees a successful difference in this range, so the stated sharp
threshold leaves every residue chain at least $C$ points long.
Then compute one representation in
$\langle\mathcal S\rangle$ for each of the two possible residue-chain
lengths.  Dynamic programming up to the largest chain length suffices;
for an interval of allowed lengths, the explicit distribution of excess
in Proposition~\ref{gsr:dt:23:prop:interval-conductor} gives a simpler construction.
Cutting and listing all cells takes time linear in the output size.

This elementary implementation is not presented as an optimal algorithm
for simultaneous Diophantine approximation.  It exposes the exact
certificates needed by a checker: one integer difference, its phase
increments, the chain cardinalities, and representations of those
cardinalities as sums of permitted lengths.

\section{Corollary~5.8 without a scale threshold: degrees one and two \wtag}\label{gsr:dt:sec:cor58}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the fifth write, 6~October 2026.}}\par
This chapter is about Gowers's Corollary~5.8, the local density increment that turns correlations with polynomial phases on a cover by progressions into a progression of higher density. Source~02's Section~\ref{gsr:dt:02:sec:d8} gives a replacement interface and declines to restate the corollary itself (``assertions about the length \ldots\ must be supplied by an actual partition theorem''); the formal statement \file{corollary_5_8} (\file{Section05.lean}, line~242, at HEAD \texttt{2dfe46f44}) is open, and of the corollary itself the repository proves only the scale-qualified repair \file{corollary_5_8_with_scale_holds} (\file{Proofs05FullPartition.lean}, line~94). It also proves, since \texttt{1c1371304}, the refinement step with cell-dependent phases, \file{variable_polynomial_phase_refinement} (\file{Proofs05VariablePhaseRefinement.lean}, line~13: common degree, coefficients varying between cells, half the correlation kept); that is an ingredient, not the density increment. The next four sections are source~26's Sections~2--4 and Appendix~A, which prove the degree-one case with no scale hypothesis on every cyclic group. The chapter is planned for more sources: source~32 (Report276, placed by \texttt{c5513046e}, write pending), the degree-two sibling of source~26 with the same pin and format, belongs directly after it, and its placement records it as proving the degree-two case; sources~41 (Report277) and~42 (Report278), placed by \texttt{2dfe46f44} while this write was in progress, follow it, and their placement records 41 as a written proof of the whole statement in every degree with no scale premise, extending source~32, and 42 as replacing source~26's cube-root length cap by a square root. Those are for the writes that add them. Source~26's introduction is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:26:sec:d1}; its source comparison, questions and companion are in Part~V (Sections~\ref{gsr:fz:26:sec:d5}--\ref{gsr:fz:26:sec:d6}). Its notation is in the table at the head of this Part.

\emph{What is proved, in one paragraph.} Let $A\subseteq\Z/N\Z$ be covered by disjoint proper modular progressions of shortest length $r$, with affine phases whose summed correlations with $\one_A-\delta$ are at least $\alpha N$. Then some proper progression has density at least $\delta+\alpha/3$ and length at least $\min\{(r(1-\delta)/(128\mu))^{1/3},(N/8)^{1/3}\}$, where $\mu$ is the normalized balanced mass of the cover (Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:26:thm:cube}), and some progression inside a parent has density $\delta+c\alpha$ and length $\sqrt{(1-2c)\alpha r/(8\pi\mu)}$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:26:thm:sqrt}); for two-comparable parents this gives $\max\{(N/M)^{1/3}/8,\sqrt{\alpha(N/M)/(96\pi(1-\delta))}\}$ (Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:26:cor:comparable}). The two regimes are a second-moment increment over all steps, with the nonproper steps removed, when $\alpha$ is small (Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:26:lem:variance}), and phase-flat refinement with positive-cell extraction when it is large (Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:26:lem:transfer}). Appendix~A converts proper modular boxes into an almost-cover by ordinary integer boxes with one common step (Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:26:thm:box}), and shows that exact long ordinary partitions of arbitrary proper modular parents are impossible. The source credits the cube-root scale and the mechanisms to Gowers, Zhao and Lewko, and claims no higher-degree result.

\emph{Relation to the formal statements} (checked at HEAD \texttt{2dfe46f44}). With $k=1$, \file{PolynomialOn} (\file{Definitions.lean}, line~222) is exactly an affine map and \file{polynomialPartitionConstant}~$1=16$ (\file{Section05.lean}, line~45), so the degree-one instance of \file{corollary_5_8} asks for gain $\alpha/16$ at length $(N/M)^{1/16}/8$; Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:26:cor:comparable} implies it on paper, and that instance holds trivially when $N/M\le2^{48}$ (note in Section~\ref{gsr:fm:26:sec:d1}). The ledger is unchanged: the formal statement quantifies over every degree. A formalization candidate, not formalized. Appendix~A bears on the caveat of \file{FORMALIZATION\_STATUS.txt} that proper boxes may wrap in integer representatives; it gives an almost-cover, not the exact-partition and base-loss interface of Section~16 (the source says so), and sits beside source~23's Section~\ref{gsr:en:23:sec:d8} and source~19's Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:19:lift:source-corollary}.

\section[{Definitions and the two main bounds\srctag{26}}]{Definitions and the two main bounds}\label{gsr:dt:26:sec:d2}\label{gsr:dt:26:sec:main}
\srcnote{26}{Section 2}

Let $N\ge2$ be an integer and write $G=\Z/N\Z$. For a residue $y$ define
\[
 e_N(y)=\exp(2\pi i\widetilde y/N),
\]
where $\widetilde y$ is any integer representative. A \emph{proper modular progression} of length $n\ge1$ is a set
\[
 P=\{u+jd:0\le j<n\}\subseteq G
\]
with this parameterization injective. The step $d$ need not be a unit. Singletons are allowed. In particular, ``proper'' does not mean that standard integer representatives form a nonwrapping progression.

Let $A\subseteq G$, let $\delta=|A|/N$, and let $f=\one_A-\delta$. Suppose $P_1,\ldots,P_M$ are nonempty pairwise disjoint proper progressions, $M\ge1$, and
\[
 A\subseteq U:=\bigcup_{i=1}^{M}P_i.
\]
For each $i$ let $\phi_i(x)=a_ix+b_i$ be an affine map $G\to G$. Our correlation hypothesis is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:26:eq:corr}
 \sum_{i=1}^{M}\left|\sum_{x\in P_i}f(x)e_N(-\phi_i(x))\right|\ge\alpha N,
 \qquad \alpha>0.
\end{equation}
Define the cover parameters
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:26:eq:params}
 \tau=\frac{|U|}{N},\qquad r=\min_i|P_i|,\qquad
 \mu=\frac1N\sum_{x\in U}|f(x)|.
\end{equation}
The hypotheses force $0<\delta<1$, and direct counting gives
\begin{align}
 \mu&=\delta(1+\tau-2\delta),\label{gsr:dt:26:eq:mu}\\
 0<\alpha&\le\mu\le2\delta(1-\delta),\qquad
 \mu\ge\delta(1-\delta),\qquad \delta\le\tau\le1,\label{gsr:dt:26:eq:basic}\\
 \sum_{x\in U}f(x)&=\delta N(1-\tau)\ge0.\label{gsr:dt:26:eq:sign}
\end{align}
For example, \eqref{gsr:dt:26:eq:mu} follows by separating the $\delta N$ points of $A$, where $|f|=1-\delta$, from the $(\tau-\delta)N$ other points of $U$, where $|f|=\delta$. The first inequality in \eqref{gsr:dt:26:eq:basic} follows from \eqref{gsr:dt:26:eq:corr} and the triangle inequality. If $\delta$ were zero or one, every correlation would vanish.

\begin{theorem}[Threshold free cube root bound]\label{gsr:dt:26:thm:cube}
Under the hypotheses above, there is a proper modular progression $Q$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:26:eq:cube}
 |Q|\ge\min\left\{\left(\frac{r(1-\delta)}{128\mu}\right)^{1/3},(N/8)^{1/3}\right\},
 \qquad \dens_Q(A):=\frac{|A\cap Q|}{|Q|}\ge\delta+\frac\alpha3.
\end{equation}
No scale threshold or lower bound on $\alpha$ is imposed, and no primality assumption is needed. The progression $Q$ need not lie in $U$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 40--46]
Source~42's Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:42:thm:affine} replaces the modulus cap $(N/8)^{1/3}$ by $\sqrt{N/2}$, never smaller; the term $(r(1-\delta)/(128\mu))^{1/3}$ is unchanged (note there).
\end{writenote}

\begin{theorem}[Correlation dependent square root bound]\label{gsr:dt:26:thm:sqrt}
Under the same hypotheses, for every real $c$ with $0<c<1/2$ there is a proper modular progression $Q$, contained in one of the parents $P_i$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:26:eq:sqrt}
 |Q|\ge\sqrt{\frac{(1-2c)\alpha r}{8\pi\mu}},
 \qquad \dens_Q(A)\ge\delta+c\alpha.
\end{equation}
This result has no separate modulus-dependent cap. In particular, $c=1/3$ gives length at least $\sqrt{\alpha r/(24\pi\mu)}$ and gain $\alpha/3$.
\end{theorem}

The two conclusions can be combined at gain $\alpha/3$: select the progression supplied by the theorem with the larger length guarantee. This gives the maximum of the two right-hand sides, but parent containment is assured only when the square-root conclusion is selected. The square-root estimate depends on $\alpha$; it is not an $\alpha$-independent replacement of the cube-root estimate.

\begin{corollary}[Intrinsic cover and comparable parents]\label{gsr:dt:26:cor:comparable}
The cube-root guarantee in Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:26:thm:cube} is at least
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:26:eq:intrinsic}
 \left(\frac{r}{256\tau}\right)^{1/3}.
\end{equation}
If, in addition, $|P_i|\le B|P_j|$ for all $i,j$, where $B\ge1$, put $t=N/M$. There are progressions with gain $\alpha/3$ and respective length guarantees
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:26:eq:B}
 \left(\frac{t}{256B}\right)^{1/3},
 \qquad \sqrt{\frac{\alpha t}{48\pi B(1-\delta)}}.
\end{equation}
For $B=2$ and every $N\ge2$, their maximum is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:26:eq:prime}
 \max\left\{\frac{(N/M)^{1/3}}8,
             \sqrt{\frac{\alpha(N/M)}{96\pi(1-\delta)}}\right\}.
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
By \eqref{gsr:dt:26:eq:basic}, $\mu\le2\tau(1-\delta)$, while $r\le|U|=\tau N$. Thus $r/(256\tau)\le N/256\le N/8$, proving \eqref{gsr:dt:26:eq:intrinsic}. The same mass bound gives the square-root guarantee $\sqrt{\alpha r/(48\pi\tau(1-\delta))}$. Comparability gives $|U|\le BMr$, hence $r/\tau\ge N/(BM)=t/B$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{It implies the degree-one instance of \file{corollary_5_8}} (checked at the write). The formal hypotheses at $k=1$ are those of Section~\ref{gsr:dt:26:sec:main} with $B=2$: \file{PolynomialOn}~$1$ (\file{Definitions.lean}, line~222) is an affine map $c_0+c_1x$, \file{ModAP.IsProper} is injective parameterization, the parents are disjoint and two-comparable, and the correlation uses \file{balanced} and \file{exponential}, that is $\one_A-\delta$ and $e_N$. The parents are nonempty (one empty parent would make all of them empty, and then $A=\emptyset$, contradicting $\alpha>0$), so $M\le N$ and $(N/M)^{1/3}/8\ge(N/M)^{1/16}/8$; and $\delta+\alpha/3\ge\delta+\alpha/16$. So \eqref{gsr:dt:26:eq:prime} gives the formal conclusion with room to spare, for every modulus $N\ge2$ (and $N=1$ is vacuous, Section~\ref{gsr:fz:26:sec:d5}). Not formalized.
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
