\section[{Two elementary mechanisms\srctag{26}}]{Two elementary mechanisms}\label{gsr:dt:26:sec:d3}\label{gsr:dt:26:sec:mechanisms}
\srcnote{26}{Section 3}

\subsection{Moments and the removal of nonproper directions}

\begin{lemma}[Proper progression increment over every cyclic modulus]\label{gsr:dt:26:lem:variance}
Let $0<\delta<1$, and let $L\ge2$ be an integer with $N\ge L^3$. Some proper $L$-term modular progression has $A$-density at least
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:26:eq:momentgain}
 \delta+\frac{1-\delta}{2L}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose $a,d$ independently and uniformly from all of $G$, including $d=0$, and put
\[
 X(a,d)=\frac1L\sum_{j=0}^{L-1}\one_A(a+jd).
\]
Here repeated positions are counted with their index multiplicity. For every fixed $d$, averaging over $a$ gives $\E_aX=\delta$.

For distinct indices $j,k$, put $H=(k-j)G$, a subgroup of $G$. Under the bijective change of variables $x=a+jd$, the pair $(x,d)$ is still uniform on $G^2$, and $(k-j)d$ is uniform on $H$. Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:26:eq:cosets}
 \E[\one_A(a+jd)\one_A(a+kd)]
 =\sum_{C\in G/H}\frac{|H|}{N}
       \left(\frac{|A\cap C|}{|H|}\right)^2
 \ge\delta^2.
\end{equation}
Indeed the densities in the cosets have weighted mean $\delta$, and their weighted squared deviations from that mean are nonnegative. Thus every off-diagonal covariance is nonnegative. The $L$ diagonal terms give
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:26:eq:allvar}
 \Var_{a,d}X\ge\frac{\delta(1-\delta)}L.
\end{equation}

Let $D_{\rm bad}$ be the directions for which the displayed progression is not proper. Properness depends only on $d$. Such a direction satisfies $hd=0$ for some integer $1\le h<L$, and conversely this condition produces a repetition. The kernel of multiplication by $h$ on $G$ has $\gcd(h,N)\le h$ elements. To see the equality, write $h=g h'$, $N=gN'$ with $g=\gcd(h,N)$ and $\gcd(h',N')=1$; the condition $N\mid hd$ is equivalent to $N'\mid d$, leaving exactly $g$ residues. The union bound now yields
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:26:eq:bad}
 b:=\frac{|D_{\rm bad}|}{N}
 \le\frac1N\sum_{h=1}^{L-1}h
 =\frac{L(L-1)}{2N}<\frac1{2L}<1.
\end{equation}

Let $h_*=\max(X(a,d)-\delta)$ over proper directions. Such directions exist, since $d=1$ is proper when $L\le N$. For a proper direction, $0\le X\le\delta+h_*$ and $\E_aX=\delta$, so
\[
 \Var_aX\le\delta h_*.
\]
For a bad direction, $0\le X\le1$ instead gives $\Var_aX\le\delta(1-\delta)$. Since the conditional means are all $\delta$, the total variance is exactly the average of the conditional variances. Combining with \eqref{gsr:dt:26:eq:allvar} gives
\[
 \frac{\delta(1-\delta)}L
 \le\Var_{a,d}X
 \le(1-b)\delta h_*+b\delta(1-\delta).
\]
It follows that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:26:eq:badgain}
 h_*\ge(1-\delta)\frac{1/L-b}{1-b}
 \ge\frac{1-\delta}{2L}.
\end{equation}
For the last inequality, \eqref{gsr:dt:26:eq:bad} gives $1/L-b\ge1/(2L)$ and $1-b\le1$. On proper directions $X$ is the actual set density, proving the lemma.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 40--46]
\emph{Two later facts} (sources~41 and~42; checked at HEAD \texttt{6d4942222}). The lemma is repeated verbatim as source~32's Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:32:lem:variance} and source~41's Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:41:lem:variance}, and is formalized as \file{exists_proper_progression_density_increment} (\file{Proofs05VarianceIncrement.lean}, line~89). Source~42 proves the same gain under $N\ge2(L-1)^2+1$ (Corollary~\ref{gsr:fm:42:cor:scale}), with an arithmetic refinement and a sharp constant.
\end{writenote}

\begin{remark}[The exact prime and short index identity]\label{gsr:dt:26:rem:exactvariance}
A useful exact diagnostic uses $a$ uniform on $G$ and $d$ uniform on its nonzero residues. Write $\spf(N)$ for the least prime divisor of $N$. If $1\le L\le\spf(N)$, every nonzero index difference $j-k$ is a unit. Every progression is then proper, and for $j\ne k$ the map
\[
 (a,d)\longmapsto(a+jd,a+kd)
\]
is a bijection onto the ordered distinct residue pairs: its inverse is $d=(j-k)^{-1}(x-y)$, $a=x-jd$. Expanding $X^2$ therefore gives
\begin{align*}
 \E X^2&=\frac\delta L+\frac{L-1}{L}\frac{\delta(\delta N-1)}{N-1},\\
 \Var X&=\frac{\delta(1-\delta)(N-L)}{L(N-1)}.
\end{align*}
This equality is not valid without the index restriction. For example, $N=4$, $L=3$, $A=\{0,2\}$ gives actual variance $11/108$, whereas the displayed formula would give $1/36$. The all-direction lower bound \eqref{gsr:dt:26:eq:allvar}, followed by removal of bad directions, is what removes any prime-factor restriction from the main result. Sampling only unit steps would not justify the same pair-uniformity argument over a composite modulus.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Phase flat residue cells with exact rounding}

\begin{lemma}[Elementary circle gap]\label{gsr:dt:26:lem:dirichlet}
For a real number $\theta$ and an integer $R\ge1$, there exist integers $q,v$ with
\[
 1\le q\le R,\qquad |q\theta-v|\le\frac1{R+1}.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If two of $0,\theta,\ldots,R\theta$ agree modulo one, their index difference gives the assertion with zero error. Otherwise these $R+1$ points are distinct on the circle. Their cyclic gaps sum to one, so a gap has length at most $1/(R+1)$. The index difference of its endpoints has absolute value between one and $R$; taking its positive absolute value changes at most the sign of the error. The wraparound gap is treated the same way modulo an integer.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Balanced chunks]\label{gsr:dt:26:lem:chunks}
If integers $n,L$ satisfy $n\ge L\ge1$, a chain of $n$ points can be partitioned consecutively into chunks with cardinalities in $[L,2L-1]$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Write $n=hL+b$ with integers $h\ge1$ and $0\le b<L$. Use $h-1$ chunks of size $L$ and one chunk of size $L+b$. There is no discarded tail, including when $b=0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Phase flat refinement]\label{gsr:dt:26:lem:flat}
Let $P=\{u+jd:0\le j<n\}$ be a proper progression, let $\phi(x)=ax+b$ be affine, and let $1\le L\le n$ be an integer. There is a disjoint partition of $P$ into proper progressions $C$ with
\[
 L\le|C|\le2L-1,
\]
and unit complex numbers $z_C$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:26:eq:flat}
 |e_N(-\phi(x))-z_C|\le\frac{2\pi L^2}{n}
 \quad(x\in C).
\end{equation}
This holds over every cyclic modulus.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose a real representative $\theta$ of $ad/N$ and put $R=\lfloor n/L\rfloor\ge1$. Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:26:lem:dirichlet} supplies $1\le q\le R$ and
\[
 q\theta=v+\varepsilon,\qquad v\in\Z,
 \qquad |\varepsilon|\le\frac1{R+1}.
\]
Partition $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ into residue classes modulo $q$, in increasing order in each class. Each chain has at least $\lfloor n/q\rfloor\ge L$ points. Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:26:lem:chunks} to every chain and take the images in $P$. They are disjoint and proper because the entire parent parameterization is injective.

For one resulting cell write $C=\{x_0+jqd:0\le j<m\}$, where $L\le m\le2L-1$, and define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:26:eq:midpoint}
 z_C=e_N(-\phi(x_0))\exp\left(-2\pi i\varepsilon\frac{m-1}{2}\right).
\end{equation}
For integer $j$, the integer part $vj$ disappears, so
\[
 e_N(-\phi(x_0+jqd))
 =e_N(-\phi(x_0))\exp(-2\pi i\varepsilon j).
\]
The chord--arc inequality $|e^{iu}-e^{iv}|\le|u-v|$ now gives
\begin{align*}
 |e_N(-\phi(x_0+jqd))-z_C|
 &\le2\pi|\varepsilon|\left|j-\frac{m-1}{2}\right|\\
 &\le\frac{2\pi(L-1)}{R+1}
 <\frac{2\pi L^2}{n}.
\end{align*}
Here $R+1>n/L$; for $L=1$ the left side is zero. The weak bound \eqref{gsr:dt:26:eq:flat} follows.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The midpoint must use the reduced increment]\label{gsr:dt:26:rem:midpoint}
The midpoint in \eqref{gsr:dt:26:eq:midpoint} is formed after writing $q\theta=v+\varepsilon$. Replacing $\varepsilon$ by the unreduced $q\theta$ multiplies it by $\exp(-\pi i v(m-1))$, which can be $-1$. For an exact regression, take $N=6$, $\phi(x)=3x$, and the proper two-point parent $P=\{0,2\}$ of step $2$, with target $L=2$. Using the integer lifts gives $\theta=3\cdot2/6=1$, $R=1$, $q=1$, $v=1$ and $\varepsilon=0$. Both endpoint phases and the reduced midpoint equal $+1$. The unreduced midpoint is $\exp(-\pi i)=-1$, at distance $2$ from both endpoints, although the reduced-lift radius is zero. Thus unreduced midpoint wording would be false even for a phase constant on the entire parent.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Turning correlation into positive balanced mass}

\begin{lemma}[Refinement transfer]\label{gsr:dt:26:lem:transfer}
Under the hypotheses of Section~\ref{gsr:dt:26:sec:main}, let $1\le L\le r$ be an integer. There is a partition of $U$ into parent-contained proper progression cells, each of cardinality in $[L,2L-1]$, such that, with $F_C=\sum_{x\in C}f(x)$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:26:eq:transfer}
 \sum_C|F_C|\ge\alpha N-E,
 \qquad E=\frac{2\pi L^2\mu N}{r}.
\end{equation}
If $E\le(1-2c)\alpha N$ for $0<c<1/2$, one of these cells has density at least $\delta+c\alpha$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:26:lem:flat} separately to each parent. For that parent, subtract the constant phase $z_C$ on each child and use the triangle inequality. Summing gives
\[
 \sum_i\left|\sum_{P_i}f(x)e_N(-\phi_i(x))\right|
 \le\sum_C|F_C|+\frac{2\pi L^2}{r}\sum_{U}|f(x)|.
\]
This proves \eqref{gsr:dt:26:eq:transfer}. The $F_C$ are real and \eqref{gsr:dt:26:eq:sign} gives $\sum_CF_C\ge0$. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:26:eq:positive}
 \sum_{F_C>0}F_C
 =\frac12\left(\sum_C|F_C|+\sum_CF_C\right)
 \ge\frac{\alpha N-E}{2}.
\end{equation}
If $E\le(1-2c)\alpha N$, the right side is at least $c\alpha N>0$. The positive cells together have at most $N$ points, so at least one satisfies $F_C/|C|\ge c\alpha$.
\end{proof}

Only $A\subseteq U$ was assumed. In general $\sum_U f$ is nonnegative rather than zero; the identity \eqref{gsr:dt:26:eq:sign} is exactly what is needed in \eqref{gsr:dt:26:eq:positive}.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Proofs of the main theorems\srctag{26}}]{Proofs of the main theorems}\label{gsr:dt:26:sec:d4}\label{gsr:dt:26:sec:proofs}
\srcnote{26}{Section 4}

\subsection{The cube root bound}
\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:26:thm:cube}]
Put
\[
 H=\frac{r(1-\delta)}{\mu},\qquad
 x=\min\{(H/128)^{1/3},(N/8)^{1/3}\},\qquad L=\lceil x\rceil.
\]
The integer $L\ge1$ satisfies $L\ge x$. If $L=1$, take a singleton in $A$. Its density is one, which exceeds $\delta+\alpha/3$ since $\alpha\le2\delta(1-\delta)$ and $0<\delta<1$.

Assume $L\ge2$. Then $x>1$, and therefore
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:26:eq:Hlarge}
 L=\lceil x\rceil<2x,\qquad H>16L^3,\qquad N>L^3.
\end{equation}
The last two inequalities follow from the respective upper bounds defining $x$. Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:26:lem:variance} is therefore applicable.

If
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:26:eq:smallalpha}
 \alpha\le\frac{3(1-\delta)}{2L},
\end{equation}
that lemma supplies a proper progression of length exactly $L$ and density at least $\delta+\alpha/3$. This settles the small-correlation range without refining any parent.

Otherwise $\alpha>3(1-\delta)/(2L)$. Since $\alpha\le\mu$, \eqref{gsr:dt:26:eq:Hlarge} gives
\[
 r=\frac{H\mu}{1-\delta}
 >16L^3\frac{3}{2L}=24L^2>L.
\]
Refinement is therefore legal. Its error in Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:26:lem:transfer} satisfies
\begin{align*}
 E&=\frac{2\pi L^2\mu N}{r}
   =\frac{2\pi L^2(1-\delta)N}{H}\\
  &<\frac{\pi(1-\delta)N}{8L}
   <\frac{(1-\delta)N}{2L}
   <\frac{\alpha N}{3},
\end{align*}
using $\pi<4$. Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:26:lem:transfer}, or its strict version from \eqref{gsr:dt:26:eq:positive}, yields a parent-contained cell of length at least $L$ with density exceeding $\delta+\alpha/3$. This completes both cases.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[A complementary short index refinement]\label{gsr:dt:26:rem:rough}
The exact identity in Remark~\ref{gsr:dt:26:rem:exactvariance} also retains the bound
\[
 |Q|\ge\min\left\{\spf(N),
        \left(\frac{r(1-\delta)}{128\mu}\right)^{1/3}\right\},
 \qquad\dens_Q(A)\ge\delta+\alpha/3.
\]
Here is the rounding and range check. Put $H=r(1-\delta)/\mu$, $x_0=(H/128)^{1/3}$ and $L=\min\{\spf(N),\lceil x_0\rceil\}$. The singleton case is as before. Otherwise $L<2x_0$, hence $H>16L^3$. Also $H\le r/\delta\le N^2$, since $\mu\ge\delta(1-\delta)$ and the nonempty $A$ has $\delta\ge1/N$. Therefore $N>2L$. For nonzero-step sampling the exact identity and $\Var X\le\delta\max(X-\delta)$ give gain at least $(1-\delta)/(2L)$. The two cases of the preceding proof now apply unchanged. For prime $N$ the least-prime-factor cap never binds, so this gives the uncapped exact-mass cube root. This complementary bound may be stronger than Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:26:thm:cube} for sparse sets with prime or rough modulus; the all-modulus theorem is not claimed to dominate it pointwise.
\end{remark}

The exact-mass form exposes the mechanism particularly directly: the large-$\alpha$ condition itself forces $r>24L^2$. For the comparable-parent formulation one can instead track
\[
 r\ge\frac{\tau t}{B},\qquad
 \mu\le2\delta(1-\delta),\qquad \delta\le\tau.
\]
Then the freezing error is at most
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:26:eq:cancellation}
 \frac{4\pi BL^2\delta(1-\delta)N}{\tau t}
 \le\frac{4\pi BL^2(1-\delta)N}{t}.
\end{equation}
This is the $\delta/\tau$ cancellation. It explains why sparse covers do not introduce an unaccounted inverse-density scale assumption.

\subsection{The square root bound}
\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:26:thm:sqrt}]
Set
\[
 R=\sqrt{\frac{(1-2c)\alpha r}{2\pi\mu}},\qquad
 L=\max\{1,\lfloor R\rfloor\}.
\]
If $L=1$, then $R<2$ and a singleton in $A$ has length greater than $R/2$, the required right side of \eqref{gsr:dt:26:eq:sqrt}. It lies in a parent because $A\subseteq U$. Its density is at least $\delta+c\alpha$: indeed
\[
 c\alpha<\alpha/2\le\delta(1-\delta)<1-\delta.
\]

Suppose $L\ge2$. Since $\alpha\le\mu$ and $0<1-2c<1$,
\[
 R^2\le\frac{(1-2c)r}{2\pi}<r.
\]
Thus $r>R^2\ge L^2\ge L$, and Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:26:lem:transfer} applies. Moreover
\[
 E=\frac{2\pi L^2\mu N}{r}
 \le\frac{2\pi R^2\mu N}{r}=(1-2c)\alpha N.
\]
The selected cell has density at least $\delta+c\alpha$. Finally, $R\ge2$ implies $L=\lfloor R\rfloor\ge R/2$, proving the length bound with the stated constant. No moment estimate or primality assumption was used.
\end{proof}

For two-comparable parents, the simplified square-root bound in \eqref{gsr:dt:26:eq:prime} is at least as large as the simplified cube-root bound precisely when
\[
 \frac{\alpha}{1-\delta}\ge\frac{3\pi}{2}\,t^{-1/3}.
\]
This comparison concerns the two convenient lower bounds, not the optimal length obtainable from the hypotheses. The exact-mass bounds can be stronger.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Common step integer box rectification\srctag{26}}]{Common step integer box rectification}\label{gsr:dt:26:sec:dA}\label{gsr:dt:26:app:boxes}
\srcnote{26}{Appendix A}

The width of a nonempty box is its smallest axis cardinality. A common modular step across the axes of one proper box can be converted into a common positive integer step on a large retained product. Loss is measured in the ambient product. No density-increment property of an arbitrary retained subset is inferred merely from its size.

\begin{theorem}[Ordinary box almost cover]\label{gsr:dt:26:thm:box}
Let $N\ge1$, $D\ge1$, and
\[
 P=P_1\times\cdots\times P_D\subseteq(\Z/N\Z)^D,
 \qquad P_i=\{a_i+jd:0\le j<n_i\},
\]
where every axis parameterization is injective and $m=\min_i n_i\ge1$. For $0<\eta\le1$, set the integer
\[
 L=1+\left\lfloor\frac{\eta\sqrt m}{3D}\right\rfloor.
\]
There is $G\subseteq P$ with $|P\setminus G|\le\eta|P|$ and a disjoint partition of $G$ into boxes whose axes, in standard representatives $0,\ldots,N-1$, are ordinary arithmetic progressions. Every axis has cardinality in $[L,2L-1]$, and all axes of all output boxes use one positive integer difference $\Delta$. In particular the width is at least $L>\eta\sqrt m/(3D)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $L=1$, use singleton boxes and $\Delta=1$. Suppose $L\ge2$. Then $m\ge2$, and $Q=\lfloor\sqrt m\rfloor$ satisfies $1\le Q<m$. Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:26:lem:dirichlet}, applied to $d/N$, gives $1\le q\le Q$ whose centered residue $b$ for $qd$ has $|b|\le N/(Q+1)$. It is nonzero: otherwise indices $0$ and $q<m\le n_i$ would have the same parent image. Put $\Delta=|b|>0$.

Partition every parent index interval into its $q$ residue chains. If $b<0$, reverse every chain, so that all traversals have modular increment $+\Delta$. Consecutive standard representatives then differ by either $\Delta$ or $\Delta-N$. Cut at every decrease of standard representatives. Each resulting run is an ordinary progression of positive difference $\Delta$.

For a chain of $h$ points with initial representative $z\in[0,N-1]$, the number of cuts is exactly
\[
 W=\left\lfloor\frac{z+(h-1)\Delta}{N}\right\rfloor
 <\frac{(h-1)\Delta}{N}+1.
\]
Summing the number $W+1$ of runs over all $q$ chains on axis $i$ gives a run count $R_i$ satisfying
\[
 R_i\le\frac{n_i}{Q+1}+2q\le\frac{n_i}{Q+1}+2Q.
\]
Delete the runs of cardinality less than $L$. Their total cardinality $D_i$ is at most $(L-1)R_i$, and therefore
\begin{align*}
 \frac{D_i}{n_i}
 &\le(L-1)\left(\frac1{Q+1}+\frac{2Q}{n_i}\right)\\
 &\le\frac{3(L-1)}{\sqrt m}\le\frac\eta D.
\end{align*}
Here $Q+1>\sqrt m$, $Q\le\sqrt m$, and $n_i\ge m$. Split each surviving run by Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:26:lem:chunks}, without further loss. Let $G_i$ be the union of the surviving chunks and $G=\prod_iG_i$. Products of chunks partition $G$ disjointly, retain the same $\Delta$, and satisfy
\[
 \frac{|P\setminus G|}{|P|}
 =1-\prod_i\left(1-\frac{D_i}{n_i}\right)
 \le\sum_i\frac{D_i}{n_i}\le\eta.
\]
The product inequality follows by repeated use of $(1-u)(1-v)\ge1-u-v$ for $u,v\in[0,1]$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Relation to the Section~16 material.} The boxes here are proper modular boxes made into ordinary integer boxes on most of their mass; source~23's Section~\ref{gsr:en:23:sec:d8} works with proper modular boxes throughout and lists integer-representative fidelity among its non-claims, and source~19's Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:19:lift:source-corollary} needs an inherited-coordinate hypothesis. As the source says in Section~\ref{gsr:dt:26:app:scope}, this almost-cover does not give the exact-partition and base-loss interface of the formal Section~16 statements, so it bears on, and does not discharge, the caveat of \file{FORMALIZATION\_STATUS.txt} that proper boxes may wrap in integer representatives.
\end{writenote}

The proof handles composite moduli and nonunit original steps. If the common step is zero, proper nonempty axes have length one, so the singleton branch applies. It also handles $N=1$. Although the weak estimate at $\eta=1$ permits zero retention, the construction has nonempty retention: in the nonsingleton branch the bound $1/(Q+1)+2Q/n_i<3/\sqrt m$ is strict.

\begin{corollary}[Anisotropic budget]\label{gsr:dt:26:cor:boxbudget}
For integers $1\le Q<m$ and $L\ge1$, the same conclusion with axis lengths in $[L,2L-1]$ holds whenever
\[
 (L-1)\sum_{i=1}^{D}\left(\frac1{Q+1}+\frac{2Q}{n_i}\right)\le\eta.
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Repeat the proof, sum its individual deletion bounds, and use the product inequality. For $L=1$ the singleton partition suffices.
\end{proof}
The integer hypotheses are essential: cardinality intervals need not contain an integer for an arbitrary real $L$. For numerical optimization of the budget, write $S=\sum_i1/n_i$. The real function $D/(Q+1)+2SQ$ has its stationary point at $\sqrt{D/(2S)}-1$. Clamping this to $[1,m-1]$ and checking neighboring integers and endpoints gives the discrete optimum by convexity.

\subsection{What this gives for the source geometry}\label{gsr:dt:26:app:scope}

Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:26:thm:box} separately to a disjoint family of proper modular boxes of width at least $w$. The union of the retained products loses at most $\eta$ of the ambient product mass; each output box has width greater than $\eta\sqrt w/(3D)$. The positive integer step is common within each original box's descendants. It can differ across original boxes. Existing identities expressing agreement with a fixed affine or multilinear function remain valid upon restriction. A numerical condition involving the old modular step is not automatically unchanged when the new step is $\pm qd$.

There is a concrete obstruction to demanding long exact ordinary partitions from arbitrary proper modular parents. For any integer $m\ge3$, take
\[
 N=4m+1,\qquad P=\{4m\}\cup\{1,3,\ldots,2m-3\}.
\]
This is a proper $m$-term modular progression of step $2$, starting at $4m$. An ordinary progression contained in $P$ and containing $4m$ has at most two terms. Otherwise its last three terms $a,b,4m$ would satisfy $a\ge1$ and $b=(a+4m)/2>2m$, whereas every other member of $P$ is at most $2m-3$. Thus every exact ordinary-progression partition has a cell of size at most two, even as $m$ grows and even if cells may use different steps. Removing the single outlier leaves an ordinary $(m-1)$-term progression, so this example establishes an obstruction to exact long partitions, not optimality of the square-root almost-cover bound. It concerns arbitrary modular input and does not refute a source theorem with stronger integer-geometric input.

This does not replace the current source-faithful Section 16 interface~\cite{repo26status}. First, that interface requests an exact partition of the whole parent, whereas the theorem partitions only a retained subset. Adding singleton boxes covers the remainder but destroys a nontrivial uniform width bound. Second, the source's exceptional loss is on a base $Q$ in a product $Q\times I$, whereas our loss is on product points. Deleting $Q\times\{y_0\}$ has product proportion $1/|I|$ but leaves no full original fiber untouched. Small product loss alone therefore does not control the base points whose full fibers survive. These two requirements need a separate construction or an explicitly changed interface followed through downstream uses. In a Section 16 product with $k$ base axes and one last axis, the total dimension here is $D=k+1$, so the denominator is $3(k+1)$.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{An explicit quadratic recurrence estimate\srctag{32}}]{An explicit quadratic recurrence estimate}\label{gsr:dt:32:sec:d2}\label{gsr:dt:32:sec:recurrence}
\srcnote{32}{Section 2}

We give the exponential-sum argument in full, including the denominator and tail bounds. All logarithms are natural.

\begin{lemma}[Circle approximation]\label{gsr:dt:32:lem:dirichlet}
For a real $\beta$ and an integer $D\ge1$, there are integers $a,q$ with
\[
 1\le q\le D,\qquad \gcd(a,q)=1,
 \qquad \left|\beta-\frac aq\right|\le\frac1{qD}.
\]
There is also, without the coprimality requirement, an integer $1\le q\le D$ such that $\norm{q\beta}\le1/(D+1)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Consider $0,\beta,\ldots,D\beta$ on the unit circle. If two coincide, their index difference gives distance zero. Otherwise some circular gap between neighboring points is at most $1/(D+1)$. The absolute difference of their indices gives $1\le q_0\le D$ and an integer $a_0$ with $|q_0\beta-a_0|\le1/(D+1)$. This also covers a gap crossing zero. Reduce $a_0/q_0$ to $a/q$. Then $q\le q_0\le D$ and
\[
 \left|\beta-\frac aq\right|
 \le\frac1{q_0(D+1)}\le\frac1{qD}.
\]
The unreduced pair supplies the second assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Quadratic exponential sum]\label{gsr:dt:32:lem:weyl}
Let $T\ge2$ be an integer, let $\omega\in\R$, and put $\beta=2\omega$. If
\[
 \gcd(a,q)=1,\qquad 1\le q\le T,\qquad
 |\beta-a/q|\le1/(qT),
\]
then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:32:eq:weyl}
 \left|\sum_{n=1}^T e(\omega n^2)\right|^2
 \le\frac{8T^2}{q}+32T\log(2T).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The case $q=1$ follows from the trivial bound $T^2$. Suppose $q\ge2$ and put $b=\lfloor q/2\rfloor\ge q/3$. Split $\{1,\ldots,T-1\}$ into consecutive blocks of at most $b$ terms. Their number is at most $T/b+1\le4T/q$.

For distinct indices $u,v$ in the same block, $0<|u-v|<q/2$. Coprimality and $q\le T$ give
\[
 \norm{\beta(u-v)}
 \ge\norm{a(u-v)/q}-\frac{|u-v|}{qT}
 \ge\frac1q-\frac1{2T}\ge\frac1{2q}.
\]
Thus the points $\beta u$ belonging to one block have pairwise circle distance at least $1/(2q)$. Order their distances from zero as $d_1\le\cdots\le d_m$. An arc of length $2d$ contains at most $4qd+1$ such points, so
\[
 d_j\ge\frac{j-1}{4q}.
\]
Interpreting $1/0$ as infinity, it follows that
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{u\text{ in block}}\min\left(T,\frac1{2\norm{\beta u}}\right)
 &\le T+\sum_{j=2}^m\frac{2q}{j-1}\\
 &\le T+2q(1+\log q).
\end{align*}
The last step uses $\sum_{j=1}^{s}1/j\le1+\log s$ for $s\ge1$; the empty sum causes no problem. Summing over blocks gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:32:eq:spacing}
 \sum_{u=1}^{T-1}\min\left(T,\frac1{2\norm{\beta u}}\right)
 \le\frac{4T^2}{q}+8T(1+\log q).
\end{equation}

For a geometric sum, $|1-e(t)|=2|\sin(\pi t)|\ge4\norm{t}$, and consequently
\[
 \left|\sum_{n=1}^K e(nt)\right|
 \le\min\left(K,\frac1{2\norm{t}}\right).
\]
Expanding the squared quadratic sum and grouping pairs by their difference $u$ now yields
\begin{align*}
 \left|\sum_{n=1}^T e(\omega n^2)\right|^2
 &\le T+2\sum_{u=1}^{T-1}
        \left|\sum_{n=1}^{T-u}e(2\omega un)\right|\\
 &\le\frac{8T^2}{q}+17T+16T\log T\\
 &\le\frac{8T^2}{q}+32T\log(2T).
\end{align*}
Here the constant phase $e(\omega u^2)$ has modulus one. The last inequality holds for $T\ge2$, since $17\le32\log2+16\log T$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Uniform quadratic recurrence]\label{gsr:dt:32:lem:recurrence}
For every real $\theta$ and every integer $R\ge2$, there is an integer $p$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:32:eq:recurrence}
 1\le p\le2^{10}R^5,\qquad \norm{\theta p^2}<1/R.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Set $T=2^{10}R^5$ and $H=4R^2$. Suppose for a contradiction that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:32:eq:nohit}
 \norm{\theta n^2}\ge1/R\qquad(1\le n\le T).
\end{equation}
On $\R/\Z$ consider the continuous triangle function
\[
 F(x)=\max\{1-R\norm{x},0\}.
\]
Its Fourier coefficients are
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:32:eq:fourier}
 c_0=1/R,\qquad
 c_h=R\left(\frac{\sin(\pi h/R)}{\pi h}\right)^2\ge0
 \quad(h\ne0).
\end{equation}
For example, $F$ is $R$ times the circle convolution of the indicator of $[-1/(2R),1/(2R)]$ with itself. Integrating that indicator against $e(-hx)$ and squaring gives \eqref{gsr:dt:32:eq:fourier}. Also $c_h\le R/(\pi^2h^2)$, so the Fourier series is absolutely and uniformly convergent.

For completeness, this series indeed equals $F$. The Fej\'er kernel of order $J$ is
\[
 K_J(x)=\frac1{J+1}\left|\sum_{v=0}^J e(vx)\right|^2.
\]
It is nonnegative, its integral is one by termwise integration, and away from zero it is bounded by $1/((J+1)\sin^2(\pi x))$. Consequently convolution with $K_J$ converges uniformly to any continuous periodic function: uniform continuity controls the near-zero integral, and the displayed bound controls the complement. Applied to $F$, these convolutions are also the Fej\'er averages of its absolutely convergent Fourier series, whose limit is the series itself. Hence $F(x)=\sum_h c_he(hx)$, and at zero
\[
 \sum_{h\in\Z}c_h=F(0)=1.
\]
The high-frequency tail satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:32:eq:tail}
 \sum_{|h|>H}c_h
 \le\frac{2R}{\pi^2}\sum_{h>H}h^{-2}
 \le\frac{2R}{\pi^2H}<\frac1{2R}.
\end{equation}

Write $S_h=\sum_{n=1}^T e(h\theta n^2)$. Assumption \eqref{gsr:dt:32:eq:nohit} says that $F(\theta n^2)=0$ for all $n$ in the sum. Interchanging a finite sum and the absolutely convergent Fourier series gives
\[
 0=\frac TR+\sum_{h\ne0}c_hS_h.
\]
Using $|S_h|\le T$ and \eqref{gsr:dt:32:eq:tail}, we obtain
\[
 \left|\sum_{0<|h|\le H}c_hS_h\right|>\frac{T}{2R}.
\]
Since the coefficients in this sum have total at most one and $S_{-h}=\overline{S_h}$, some integer $1\le h\le H$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:32:eq:largeS}
 |S_h|>T/(2R).
\end{equation}

Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:32:lem:dirichlet} with denominator budget $T$ to $\beta=2h\theta$. For the resulting relatively prime $a,q$, Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:32:lem:weyl} and \eqref{gsr:dt:32:eq:largeS} give
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:32:eq:qbound}
 \frac1{4R^2}<\frac8q+\frac{32\log(2T)}T.
\end{equation}
For $R\ge2$, one has $\log R\le R/2$: the difference $R/2-\log R$ is positive at two and nondecreasing thereafter. Therefore
\[
 \log(2T)=11\log2+5\log R<8R.
\]
Indeed $11\log2<11\le11R/2$. Since
\[
 T=1024R^5\ge4096R^3>256R^2\log(2T),
\]
the second term on the right of \eqref{gsr:dt:32:eq:qbound} is less than $1/(8R^2)$. It follows that $q<64R^2$.

Set $p=2hq$. Then
\[
 1\le p<512R^4<T,
 \qquad \norm{\beta q}\le1/T,
\]
and the exact identity $\theta p^2=p(\beta q)$ gives
\[
 \norm{\theta p^2}\le p\norm{\beta q}
 \le\frac pT<\frac1{2R}<\frac1R.
\]
This contradicts \eqref{gsr:dt:32:eq:nohit}, since this integer $p$ lies in its excluded interval. The contradiction proves \eqref{gsr:dt:32:eq:recurrence}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
\emph{Evidence, not part of the proof.} The intake's search over all $\theta=a/q$ with $q\le4R^2$ and 300 random $\theta$ for each $R=2,\ldots,12$ found the least admissible $p$ at most $53$, far below $2^{10}R^5$: the bound is valid and very loose.
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 40--46]
Source~41 repeats this section verbatim (Section~\ref{gsr:dt:41:sec:d2}) and extends the recurrence to every degree, $p\le2^{A_k}R^{B_k}$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:41:thm:generalrec}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{remark}\label{gsr:dt:32:rem:conditional}
The bound $p<512R^4$ in the last paragraph is obtained \emph{under the contradiction hypothesis} \eqref{gsr:dt:32:eq:nohit}. That hypothesis was used to force the large Fourier coefficient. It does not establish an unconditional $R^4$ recurrence theorem. The bound carried into every subsequent argument is $2^{10}R^5$.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Lossless phase partitions\srctag{32}}]{Lossless phase partitions}\label{gsr:dt:32:sec:d3}\label{gsr:dt:32:sec:partition}
\srcnote{32}{Section 3}

The partitions below keep every point. A basic rounding fact is useful: a chain of length $s\ge L$ can be partitioned into chunks of lengths from $L$ through $2L-1$. Write $s=hL+b$ with $h\ge1$ and $0\le b<L$, use $h-1$ chunks of length $L$, and a last chunk of length $L+b$.

\begin{lemma}[Affine refinement]\label{gsr:dt:32:lem:affine}
Let $m,L$ be integers with $1\le L\le m$, and let $\ell,c\in\R$. The index interval $\{0,\ldots,m-1\}$ has a partition into arithmetic progressions $C$ of lengths $L\le|C|\le2L-1$ and complex units $z_C$ for which
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:32:eq:affine}
 |e(-(\ell j+c))-z_C|\le\frac{2\pi L^2}{m}\qquad(j\in C).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Put $D=\lfloor m/L\rfloor\ge1$. By the circle part of Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:32:lem:dirichlet}, choose $1\le q\le D$ with $\norm{q\ell}\le1/(D+1)$. Split the interval into its residue chains modulo $q$. Every chain has at least $\lfloor m/q\rfloor\ge L$ points. Apply the chunking rule above to each chain.

Write $q\ell=v+\epsilon$, where $v\in\Z$ and $|\epsilon|\le1/(D+1)$. For a chunk $j=j_0+tq$, $0\le t<s$, set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:32:eq:midpoint}
 z_C=e(-(\ell j_0+c))e(-\epsilon(s-1)/2).
\end{equation}
The integer $vt$ does not affect the exponential. The chord--arc inequality gives
\begin{align*}
 |e(-(\ell j+c))-z_C|
 &\le2\pi|\epsilon|\left|t-\frac{s-1}{2}\right|\\
 &\le\pi|\epsilon|(s-1)
 \le\frac{2\pi(L-1)}{D+1}
 <\frac{2\pi L^2}{m}
\end{align*}
when $L>1$, using $D+1>m/L$. When $L=1$, every chunk is a singleton and the error is zero. This proves the stated weak bound in all cases.
\end{proof}

The reduction before taking the midpoint in \eqref{gsr:dt:32:eq:midpoint} matters. If $q\ell=1$ and $s=2$, both sampled phase values agree, while the midpoint obtained from the unreduced increment contributes $e(-1/2)=-1$. The reduced increment is zero and its midpoint has the correct phase. Integer shifts are harmless at integer parameters but need not be harmless at half-integer midpoints.

\begin{lemma}[Quadratic refinement]\label{gsr:dt:32:lem:quadratic}
Let $L\ge2$ and $n\ge2^{116}L^{38}$ be integers. Let $P=\{u+jd:0\le j<n\}$ be a proper modular progression in $G$ and let $\phi(x)=ax^2+bx+c$. There is a partition of $P$ into proper modular subprogressions $C$ and complex units $z_C$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:32:eq:quadratic}
 L\le|C|\le2L-1,
 \qquad |e_N(-\phi(x))-z_C|<\frac1{4L}\quad(x\in C).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose integer representatives $u,d,a,b,c$. Define the real polynomial
\[
 p_0(j)=\theta j^2+\beta j+\gamma,
 \quad
 \theta=\frac{ad^2}{N},\quad
 \beta=\frac{2aud+bd}{N},\quad
 \gamma=\frac{au^2+bu+c}{N}.
\]
Then $e_N(-\phi(u+jd))=e(-p_0(j))$ for every integer $j$. The identity remains true when $u+jd$ wraps modulo $N$: replacing an integer representative changes the normalized polynomial value by an integer. No division inside $G$ is involved, and neither $d$ nor $2$ needs to be a unit.

Set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:32:eq:budgets}
 H=64L^3=2^6L^3,\quad
 R=256LH^2=2^{20}L^7,\quad
 T=2^{10}R^5=2^{110}L^{35}.
\end{equation}
Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:32:lem:recurrence} supplies $1\le p\le T$ with $\norm{\theta p^2}<1/R$. Since $n\ge TH$, each residue chain modulo $p$ in the parent index interval has at least $\lfloor n/p\rfloor\ge H$ points. Chunk each chain into pieces of lengths $H$ through $2H-1$.

On one piece $j=j_0+pt$, $0\le t<m$, $H\le m\le2H-1$, expansion gives
\[
 p_0(j_0+pt)=\theta p^2t^2+\ell t+c_0,
 \quad \ell=2\theta j_0p+\beta p,
 \quad c_0=p_0(j_0).
\]
Choose $v\in\Z$ so that $\epsilon=\theta p^2-v$ has $|\epsilon|<1/R$. Subtracting $vt^2$ leaves the exponential unchanged at integer $t$. Since $t<2H$, the curvature error satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:32:eq:curvature}
 |e(-p_0(j_0+pt))-e(-(\ell t+c_0))|
 \le2\pi|\epsilon|t^2
 <\frac{8\pi H^2}{R}=\frac{\pi}{32L}.
\end{equation}
Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:32:lem:affine} to the affine phase on this $t$-interval with target length $L$. Its extra error is at most
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:32:eq:affbudget}
 \frac{2\pi L^2}{m}\le\frac{2\pi L^2}{H}=\frac{\pi}{32L}.
\end{equation}
Combining \eqref{gsr:dt:32:eq:curvature} and \eqref{gsr:dt:32:eq:affbudget} gives error less than $\pi/(16L)<1/(4L)$.

Each final cell has a parameterization $t=t_0+qs$ within a first-stage piece, hence $j=j_0+pt_0+pqs$ in the original interval. Its image in $G$ is a modular progression. The parent index map is injective, so its restriction to each final cell is injective and preserves cardinality. Distinct cells stay disjoint, and all parent indices are retained. Finally,
\[
 TH=2^{116}L^{38},
\]
which is exactly the hypothesis.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A second moment over every cyclic modulus\srctag{32}}]{A second moment over every cyclic modulus}\label{gsr:dt:32:sec:d4}\label{gsr:dt:32:sec:variance}
\srcnote{32}{Section 4}

Over a prime modulus, pairs of distinct progression positions often have a particularly simple distribution. Over an arbitrary cyclic modulus their distribution is instead controlled by additive subgroup cosets. The resulting inequality is enough here.

\begin{lemma}[Proper progression from variance]\label{gsr:dt:32:lem:variance}
Let $0<\delta<1$, let $L\ge2$ be an integer, and suppose $N\ge L^3$. There is a proper $L$-term modular progression $Q$ with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:32:eq:variancegain}
 \dens_Q(A):=\frac{|A\cap Q|}{|Q|}
 \ge\delta+\frac{1-\delta}{2L}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose $a,d$ independently and uniformly in $G$, including $d=0$, and put
\[
 X(a,d)=\frac1L\sum_{j=0}^{L-1}\one_A(a+jd).
\]
Repeated positions are counted with their index multiplicity. For every fixed $d$, averaging over $a$ gives $\E_a X=\delta$.

For distinct $j,k$, let $H=(k-j)G$. The change of variables $(a,d)\mapsto(x,d)=(a+jd,d)$ is a bijection of $G^2$. The element $(k-j)d$ is uniform in $H$, independently of $x$. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:32:eq:coset}
 \E[\one_A(a+jd)\one_A(a+kd)]
 =\sum_{C\in G/H}\frac{|H|}{N}
       \left(\frac{|A\cap C|}{|H|}\right)^2\ge\delta^2.
\end{equation}
Indeed the coset densities have weighted mean $\delta$, and their weighted squared deviations from that mean sum to a nonnegative number. Thus all off-diagonal covariances are nonnegative, and the $L$ diagonal terms yield
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:32:eq:varlower}
 \Var_{a,d}X\ge\frac{\delta(1-\delta)}L.
\end{equation}

A direction $d$ is bad precisely when the $L$-term parameterization is not injective. This means $hd=0$ for some $1\le h<L$. The kernel of multiplication by $h$ on $G$ has $\gcd(h,N)\le h$ elements: if $g=\gcd(h,N)$, then $N\mid hd$ is equivalent to $N/g\mid d$. Hence the proportion $\eta$ of bad directions obeys
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:32:eq:bad}
 \eta\le\frac1N\sum_{h=1}^{L-1}h
 =\frac{L(L-1)}{2N}<\frac1{2L}.
\end{equation}
At least one proper direction exists, since $d=1$ works for $L\le N$.

Let $h_*$ be the largest value of $X(a,d)-\delta$ over proper directions and all $a$. For a proper direction, $0\le X\le\delta+h_*$ implies $X^2\le(\delta+h_*)X$, and so $\Var_aX\le\delta h_*$. For any bad direction, $0\le X\le1$ similarly gives $\Var_aX\le\delta(1-\delta)$. Since every conditional mean is $\delta$, averaging these variances and using \eqref{gsr:dt:32:eq:varlower} gives
\[
 \frac{\delta(1-\delta)}L
 \le(1-\eta)\delta h_*+\eta\delta(1-\delta).
\]
Dividing by $\delta>0$ and rearranging,
\[
 h_*\ge(1-\delta)\frac{1/L-\eta}{1-\eta}
 \ge\frac{1-\delta}{2L},
\]
where \eqref{gsr:dt:32:eq:bad} and $1-\eta\le1$ justify the last step. A maximizing proper progression proves the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
Source~26's Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:26:lem:variance} is the same second-moment argument over every cyclic modulus (the sibling reports share this section); source~42's placement records a version needing only $N\ge2(L-1)^2+1$ (for its write).
\end{writenote}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Assembly and every scale\srctag{32}}]{Assembly and every scale}\label{gsr:dt:32:sec:d5}\label{gsr:dt:32:sec:assembly}
\srcnote{32}{Section 5}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:32:thm:main}]
Let
\[
 b=1-\delta,\quad \tau=|U|/N,\quad
 r=\min_i|P_i|,\quad S=N/M,\quad
 \mu=\frac1N\sum_{x\in U}|f(x)|.
\]
Because the parents are nonempty and disjoint, $M\le N$ and $S\ge1$. The cover hypothesis implies $\delta\le\tau\le1$. Separating the $\delta N$ points of $A$ from the $(\tau-\delta)N$ other points of $U$, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:32:eq:mass}
 \mu=\delta(1+\tau-2\delta),\qquad
 0<\alpha\le\mu\le2\delta b\le2\tau b\le2b.
\end{equation}
Here $\alpha\le\mu$ follows from the correlation and the triangle inequality. The positive correlation also rules out $\delta=0$ and $\delta=1$, so $0<\delta<1$, $b>0$, and $A$ is nonempty. Comparability gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:32:eq:parent}
 \tau N=\sum_i|P_i|\le2Mr,
 \qquad r\ge\frac{\tau S}{2}.
\end{equation}

Set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:32:eq:rounding}
 x=\frac{S^{1/39}}{17},\qquad L=\lceil x\rceil.
\end{equation}
If $L=1$, choose a singleton in $A$. It has length at least $x$ and density one. By \eqref{gsr:dt:32:eq:mass}, $\alpha/3\le2\delta b/3<b$, so its density is strictly greater than $\delta+\alpha/3$.

Now suppose $L\ge2$. Then $x>1$ and $L<x+1<2x$, so
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:32:eq:Sscale}
 S>(17L/2)^{39}>L^3,
 \qquad N\ge S>L^3.
\end{equation}
If $\alpha\le3b/(2L)$, Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:32:lem:variance} gives a proper progression of length $L$ with density at least
\[
 \delta+\frac{b}{2L}\ge\delta+\frac\alpha3.
\]
Its length is at least $x$, as required.

It remains to consider $\alpha>3b/(2L)$. Since $\alpha\le2\tau b$, this implies $\tau>3/(4L)$. Equations \eqref{gsr:dt:32:eq:parent} and \eqref{gsr:dt:32:eq:Sscale} give
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:32:eq:rscale}
 r>\frac{3S}{8L}
 >\frac{3\cdot17^{39}}{2^{42}}L^{38}
 >2^{116}L^{38}.
\end{equation}
The last numerical inequality follows entirely with integers. Bernoulli's inequality gives
\[
 17^{39}=2^{156}(1+1/16)^{39}
 \ge2^{156}(1+39/16)=\frac{55}{16}2^{156},
\]
and $3\cdot55/16>4$, hence $3\cdot17^{39}>2^{158}$.

Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:32:lem:quadratic} to every parent at this common target length $L$. For each resulting cell $C$, let $i(C)$ denote its parent, let $z_C$ be its approximating unit, and set $F_C=\sum_{x\in C}f(x)\in\R$. The total phase error is
\begin{align}
 E&:=\sum_C\sum_{x\in C}|f(x)|
       |e_N(-\phi_{i(C)}(x))-z_C|\notag\\
  &<\frac{\mu N}{4L}
   \le\frac{bN}{2L}<\frac{\alpha N}{3}.
 \label{gsr:dt:32:eq:error}
\end{align}
For each parent, replacing its phase on each cell by $z_C$ and then applying the triangle inequality bounds its correlation by the sum of its $|F_C|$ plus its phase error. Summing over the parents and using \eqref{gsr:fm:32:eq:corr} yields
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:32:eq:absF}
 \sum_C|F_C|\ge\alpha N-E>2\alpha N/3.
\end{equation}
The signed total has a favorable sign, because $A\subseteq U$:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:32:eq:signedF}
 \sum_C F_C=|A|-\delta|U|=\delta(N-|U|)\ge0.
\end{equation}
The sum of the positive $F_C$ is half the sum of \eqref{gsr:dt:32:eq:absF} and \eqref{gsr:dt:32:eq:signedF}, and is therefore greater than $\alpha N/3$. These positive cells together have at most $N$ points. If each had $F_C/|C|\le\alpha/3$, their positive total would be at most $\alpha N/3$, a contradiction. Thus some cell $Q$ satisfies
\[
 \frac{|A\cap Q|}{|Q|}=\delta+\frac{F_Q}{|Q|}
 >\delta+\frac\alpha3.
\]
This cell is proper and has length at least $L\ge x$. In all branches the progression is nonempty, which also proves the maximum with one in \eqref{gsr:fm:32:eq:main}.
\end{proof}

The large-correlation branch finds its progression inside a parent. The variance branch searches all modular directions in $G$, so the theorem as a whole does not promise parent containment. The word ``threshold free'' refers to the theorem's hypotheses; the internal phase-partition lemma has its explicit threshold, and the preceding dichotomy supplies it exactly where needed.

\section{Source~37's chapter: missing intervals at Lemmas~5.2 and~5.5 \wtag}\label{gsr:dt:sec:missing}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the seventh write, 6~October 2026.}}\par
The next ten sections are source~37's Sections~2--9 and Appendices~A--B, on the missing-interval step of Gowers's Section~5: a set, or a measure, that avoids an arc around zero must have a large low Fourier coefficient. \emph{Logically the chapter belongs before the partition material of Section~5} (Lemma~5.2 precedes the polynomial recurrence of Lemma~5.5 and the partitions of Corollary~5.6); it is printed here, at the end of Part~I, because no number printed earlier may move. No earlier source of this report treats Lemma~5.2. Source~37's introduction is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:37:sec:d1}; its verification, questions and source audit are in Part~V.

\emph{What is proved, in one paragraph.} For $\pi<(R+1)a<2\pi$ the least possible value of $\max_{1\le r\le R}|\widehat\mu(r)|$ over probability measures on the circle avoiding the open arc of radius $a$ is $\rho_R(a)=1/(R-\cot(a/2)\tan((R+1)a/2))$, attained by a unique measure with $R+1$ atoms, all of whose first $R$ coefficients equal $-\rho_R(a)$; with coefficients at most $\varepsilon$ the least mass of the arc is $\max\{0,(\rho-\varepsilon)/(1+\rho)\}$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:37:thm:main}), with an explicit polynomial certificate (Section~\ref{gsr:dt:37:sec:d3}), a moment criterion (Section~\ref{gsr:dt:37:sec:d4}), the critical radius (Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:37:thm:critical}) and stability (Theorems~\ref{gsr:dt:37:thm:criticalstable}, \ref{gsr:dt:37:thm:stable}). The universal consequence (Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:37:thm:universal}) gives a replacement for Lemma~5.2 on $\Z/N\Z$ with frequency at most $\lfloor N/M\rfloor-1$ (not $(N/M)^2$) and coefficient $|A|M/(N-M)$ (not $|A|M/(4N)$), for arbitrary nonnegative weights and without the parity of $M$ (Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:37:cor:cyclic}); with the explicit Weyl input recorded in the formal \file{lemma_5_3} it gives the recurrence exponent $b_k=(1-1/(4k))/(2^{k-1}+1)$ ($7/24$ at $k=2$, against Lemma~5.5's $1/16$; Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:37:cor:explicitrec}) and a short-step version (Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:37:cor:short}). The general moment criterion is classical (Yang and Xie are credited); the Weyl inequality is imported.
