\section[{The exact gap--moment theorem\srctag{37}}]{The exact gap--moment theorem}\label{gsr:dt:37:sec:d2}\label{gsr:dt:37:sec:main}
\srcnote{37}{Section 2}

\subsection{Conventions}
Let $\Tthirtyseven=\R/(2\pi\Z)$, with angular distance $|\theta|_\circ$ from zero.
Write
\[
 I_a=\{\theta\in\Tthirtyseven:|\theta|_\circ<a\},\qquad
 K_a=\Tthirtyseven\setminus I_a,\qquad 0<a\le\pi.
\]
The arc is \emph{open}; its endpoints belong to $K_a$. All measures are Borel
probability measures unless a different total mass is specified; $\Probthirtyseven(K_a)$
denotes the probability measures supported on $K_a$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:momentnotation}
 \widehat\mu(r)=\int_\Tthirtyseven e^{-ir\theta}\,d\mu(\theta),\qquad
 E_R(\mu)=\max_{1\le r\le R}|\widehat\mu(r)|.
\end{equation}
No absolute continuity, distinctness of sample points, rationality of angles,
or primality of an underlying modulus is assumed.

For an integer $R\ge1$, set $m=R+1$. In the \emph{strict first window}
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:window}
 \frac{\pi}{m}<a<\frac{2\pi}{m},
\end{equation}
put
\begin{align}
 S_R(a)&=m-\cot(a/2)\tan(ma/2),\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:S}\\
 d_R(a)&=S_R(a)^{-1},\qquad
 \rho_R(a)=\frac{d_R(a)}{1-d_R(a)}
 =\frac{1}{R-\cot(a/2)\tan(ma/2)}.\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:rho}
\end{align}
Since $\tan(ma/2)<0$, one has $S_R(a)>m$ and
$0<\rho_R(a)<1/R$.

\begin{theorem}[Exact first-window tradeoff]\label{gsr:dt:37:thm:main}
Suppose \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:window} holds, and abbreviate $d=d_R(a)$ and
$\rho=\rho_R(a)$.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2em]
\item For every probability measure $\mu$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:mainmass}
 \mu(I_a)\ge d-(1-d)E_R(\mu).
\end{equation}
If $\mu(I_a)=0$, then for some $1\le r\le R$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:onesided}
 \Rea\widehat\mu(r)\le-\rho.
\end{equation}
\item There is a unique probability measure $\mu_{R,a}$ supported on $K_a$
with $E_R(\mu_{R,a})=\rho$. It satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:equalmoments}
 \widehat\mu_{R,a}(r)=-\rho\qquad(1\le r\le R),
\end{equation}
and has exactly $R+1$ support points with strictly positive masses.
Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:minimax}
 \inf_{\mu\in\Probthirtyseven(K_a)}E_R(\mu)
 =\inf_{\mu\in\Probthirtyseven(K_a)}\max_{1\le r\le R}
       \bigl(-\Rea\widehat\mu(r)\bigr)=\rho.
\end{equation}
\item For every $\varepsilon\ge0$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:exactmass}
 \inf_{E_R(\mu)\le\varepsilon}\mu(I_a)
 =\max\left\{0,\frac{\rho-\varepsilon}{1+\rho}\right\}.
\end{equation}
For $0\le\varepsilon\le\rho$, the unique minimizing measure is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:mix}
 \mu_{\varepsilon}
 =s\delta_0+(1-s)\mu_{R,a},\qquad
 s=\frac{\rho-\varepsilon}{1+\rho}.
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Unequal budgets} (source~67, Section~\ref{gsr:dt:sec:unequalbudgets}): when the $R$ coefficient budgets differ, the least mass is $-1/((1-\cos a)\,\mathbf e^TL(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)^{-1}\mathbf e)$ on an explicit neighbourhood of every interior point of this theorem's equal-budget branch, and this theorem's certificate stays optimal exactly on a polytope of local dimension $\lfloor R/2\rfloor+1$ (its Theorems~\ref{gsr:dt:67:fourier:matrix}--\ref{gsr:dt:67:fourier:polytope}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 82--94]
\emph{Beyond the first window} (sources~90 and~93, Section~\ref{gsr:dt:sec:phifour}): the formula of this theorem persists past $a=2\pi/(R+1)$ up to an explicit $a_R$, with $a_R-2\pi/(R+1)=8\pi/R^3+O(R^{-4})$, and not beyond (source~90's Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:90:thm:continuation}); at the other end a final band $\pi-a\le2\pi/(R+1)$ is explicit at every cutoff (source~93's Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:93:new:allR}); and at $R=4$ the whole profile is known (two independent proofs).
\end{writenote}

The equality case is part of the assertion: the bound is not simply the best
one obtained from a chosen family of test polynomials. It is optimal over all
probability measures. The proof occupies Sections~\ref{gsr:dt:37:sec:certificate}--
\ref{gsr:dt:37:sec:attainment}. Endpoint values and the critical geometry are treated
separately in Section~\ref{gsr:dt:37:sec:endpoints}.

\subsection{Description of the extremizer}
The support has an explicit algebraic description. Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:w}
 w_j=\frac{1-\cos\bigl((j-(R-1)/2)a\bigr)/\cos(ma/2)}{S_R(a)},
 \qquad 0\le j\le R-1,
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:P}
 P_{R,a}(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{R-1}w_jz^j.
\end{equation}
Then $\supp\mu_{R,a}$ consists of $-a$, $a$, and the arguments of the
$R-1$ zeros of $P_{R,a}$. All of those zeros are simple and lie on the unit
circle strictly inside the complementary arc. These root facts are proved,
not assumed from numerics. The masses are the unique solution of
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:weightsystem}
 \sum_{j=1}^{R+1}u_j=1,\qquad
 \sum_{j=1}^{R+1}u_je^{-ir\theta_j}=-\rho
 \quad(1\le r\le R).
\end{equation}
The matrix of this system is Vandermonde and hence nonsingular. The proof
also establishes $u_j>0$ and reflection symmetry. Thus root finding followed
by a small linear solve gives a numerical realization of the exact measure.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A positive-coefficient polynomial certificate\srctag{37}}]{A positive-coefficient polynomial certificate}\label{gsr:dt:37:sec:d3}\label{gsr:dt:37:sec:certificate}
\srcnote{37}{Section 3}

\subsection{A path recurrence}
Let $T_R$ be the $R\times R$ real symmetric matrix with $1/2$ on each adjacent
off-diagonal and zero elsewhere. Write $c=\cos a$, $S=S_R(a)$, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:lambda}
 \lambda=\frac{1-c}{S}=(1-c)d.
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}[The coefficient vector]\label{gsr:dt:37:lem:w}
The vector in \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:w} has positive entries, is symmetric under
$j\mapsto R-1-j$, and satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:recw}
 \sum_{j=0}^{R-1}w_j=1,\qquad
 (T_R-cI)w=\lambda\one.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
In the first window $\cos(ma/2)<0$. Moreover,
$|(j-(R-1)/2)a|<ma/2<\pi$, so its cosine is strictly larger than
$\cos(ma/2)$. Dividing by the negative denominator proves $w_j>0$.
Symmetry is immediate. The finite cosine sum gives
\[
 \sum_{j=0}^{R-1}\cos\bigl((j-(R-1)/2)a\bigr)
 =\frac{\sin(Ra/2)}{\sin(a/2)}.
\]
Since $R=m-1$,
\[
 \frac{\sin(Ra/2)}{\sin(a/2)\cos(ma/2)}
 =\cot(a/2)\tan(ma/2)-1.
\]
The sum of the numerators in \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:w} is therefore $S$.
For the recurrence, extend the displayed formula to $j=-1,R$; it gives
$w_{-1}=w_R=0$. The cosine addition formula then yields
\[
 \frac{w_{j-1}+w_{j+1}}2-cw_j=\frac{1-c}{S}=\lambda
 \qquad(0\le j\le R-1).
\]
This includes both boundary coordinates of the path matrix.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The crucial sign computation}
Define a real even trigonometric polynomial of degree $R$ by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:Q}
 Q(\theta)=(\cos\theta-c)|P_{R,a}(e^{i\theta})|^2
 =q_0+2\sum_{k=1}^Rq_k\cos(k\theta).
\end{equation}
The sign of $Q$ is already correct for detecting the gap. The useful extra
fact is positivity of \emph{every} nonconstant Fourier coefficient.

\begin{lemma}[Exact Fourier coefficients]\label{gsr:dt:37:lem:q}
One has $q_0=\lambda$ and, for $1\le k\le R$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:qpositive}
 q_k=\lambda\sum_{j=0}^{R-k-1}w_j
        +\frac12w_{R-k}w_{R-1}>0.
\end{equation}
An empty sum is zero. In particular $q_R=w_0w_{R-1}/2>0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Extend $w_j$ by zero outside $0\le j<R$ and put
$A_k=\sum_jw_jw_{j+k}$, so $A_{-k}=A_k$. Multiplication in
\eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:Q} gives
\[
 q_k=\frac12(A_{k-1}+A_{k+1})-cA_k
 =\sum_{j=0}^{R-1}w_j
       \left(\frac{w_{j+k-1}+w_{j+k+1}}2-cw_{j+k}\right).
\]
For $k=0$, every bracket equals $\lambda$, so $q_0=\lambda$.
For $1\le k\le R$, the brackets with $0\le j<R-k$ equal $\lambda$;
the bracket at $j=R-k$ equals $w_{R-1}/2$; all later brackets vanish.
This proves \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:qpositive}. Positivity follows from
Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:37:lem:w} and $\lambda>0$.
\end{proof}

Normalize by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:F}
 F(\theta)=\frac{Q(\theta)}{1-c}
 =d+2\sum_{k=1}^Rf_k\cos(k\theta),\qquad f_k=\frac{q_k}{1-c}.
\end{equation}
Because $P(1)=1$, we have $F(0)=1$. Thus
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:coefsum}
 f_k>0,\qquad 2\sum_{k=1}^Rf_k=1-d.
\end{equation}
On $K_a$, $F\le0$. On the whole circle, positivity of the Fourier
coefficients gives $F(\theta)\le F(0)=1$. Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:minorant}
 F\le\one_{I_a}.
\end{equation}
The value at either endpoint is zero, so the open-arc convention causes no
error.

\begin{proposition}[Mass and one-sided spectral inequalities]\label{gsr:dt:37:prop:lower}
For any probability measure $\mu$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:anisotropic}
 \mu(I_a)\ge d+2\sum_{k=1}^Rf_k\Rea\widehat\mu(k).
\end{equation}
In particular \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:mainmass} holds. If $\mu(I_a)=0$, at least one
$\Rea\widehat\mu(k)$ is at most $-\rho$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Integrate \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:minorant}. Each real part is at least $-E_R(\mu)$;
\eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:coefsum} gives \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:mainmass}. If all real parts were strictly
greater than $-\rho$, then the integral of $F$ would be strictly greater than
$d-(1-d)\rho=0$, contradicting $F\le0$ on the support.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Unequal moment information]
The unsimplified inequality \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:anisotropic} is useful when frequencies
have different error bounds. From $|\widehat\mu(k)|\le\varepsilon_k$ it gives
$\mu(I_a)\ge d-2\sum f_k\varepsilon_k$. We do not claim that this last
anisotropic bound is optimal for an arbitrary vector of caps. Exact
optimality is proved here for equal caps.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A supported trigonometric moment criterion\srctag{37}}]{A supported trigonometric moment criterion}\label{gsr:dt:37:sec:d4}\label{gsr:dt:37:sec:moments}
\srcnote{37}{Section 4}

Attainment requires more than a dual certificate. We give the relevant
finite-dimensional moment result and its proof, so that the construction of
the extremal measure does not rest on an unexplained semidefinite program.
This criterion is classical in substance; compare \cite{yangxie}.

\subsection{Positive trigonometric polynomials on one arc}

\begin{lemma}[Arc positivity representation]\label{gsr:dt:37:lem:arcpos}
Let $0<a<\pi$, $c=\cos a$, and let $H$ be a real-valued trigonometric
polynomial of degree at most $R$. If $H\ge0$ on $K_a$, then there are complex
polynomials $A,B$ with $\deg A\le R$ and $\deg B\le R-1$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:arcSOS}
 H(\theta)=|A(e^{i\theta})|^2
           +(c-\cos\theta)|B(e^{i\theta})|^2.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Set $t=\cot(\theta/2)$ and $b=\cot(a/2)>0$. The closed arc $K_a$ maps to
$[-b,b]$. Because $e^{i\theta}=(t+i)/(t-i)$,
\[
 p(t)=(1+t^2)^R H(\theta(t))
\]
is a real polynomial of degree at most $2R$, nonnegative on $[-b,b]$.
The elementary interval factorization proved in
Appendix~\ref{gsr:dt:37:app:factorization} gives
\[
 p(t)=U(t)^2+(b^2-t^2)V(t)^2,
 \qquad \deg U\le R,\quad \deg V\le R-1.
\]
Now $U(t)/(t-i)^R$ and $V(t)/(t-i)^{R-1}$ are polynomials in
$z=(t+i)/(t-i)$ of the indicated degrees. Also
\[
 \frac{b^2-t^2}{1+t^2}=\frac{c-\cos\theta}{1-c}.
\]
Divide the factorization by $(1+t^2)^R$ and absorb the positive factor
$(1-c)^{-1/2}$ into the second polynomial. The identity extends to $\theta=0$
by continuity.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[One-arc moment criterion]\label{gsr:dt:37:thm:moment}
Let complex numbers $h_{-R},\ldots,h_R$ satisfy
$h_0=1$ and $h_{-j}=\overline{h_j}$. They are the moments
$h_j=\widehat\mu(j)$ of a probability measure supported on $K_a$ if and only if
both matrices
\begin{align}
 M&=(h_{j-k})_{0\le j,k\le R},\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:M}\\
 L&=\left(c h_{j-k}-\frac{h_{j-k+1}+h_{j-k-1}}2\right)_{0\le j,k<R}
 \label{gsr:dt:37:eq:L}
\end{align}
are positive semidefinite.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Necessity follows by integrating respectively
$|A(e^{i\theta})|^2$ and $(c-\cos\theta)|B(e^{i\theta})|^2$ against $\mu$.
For sufficiency, let $\mathcal L$ be the real-linear functional on real
trigonometric polynomials of degree at most $R$ determined by these moments.
Its value on a constant is that constant. The two matrix inequalities imply
that it is nonnegative on both terms in \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:arcSOS}, and hence on every
such polynomial nonnegative on $K_a$.

Consider the compact curve
\[
 v(\theta)=(\cos\theta,-\sin\theta,\ldots,
                    \cos R\theta,-\sin R\theta)\in\R^{2R},\quad \theta\in K_a.
\]
Its convex hull is compact: by the finite-dimensional Carath\'eodory argument,
every convex combination can be reduced to at most $2R+1$ points by removing
an affine dependence; compactness then follows from the compactness of the
parameter spaces for those combinations. If the vector
$(\Rea h_1,\Im h_1,\ldots,\Rea h_R,\Im h_R)$ lay outside this hull, a strict
separating affine functional would give a real trigonometric polynomial $H$
nonnegative on $K_a$ but with $\mathcal L(H)<0$. This is impossible. A convex
combination representing that vector gives the desired probability measure.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The needed spectral inequality}

\begin{lemma}[Zero-sum path bound]\label{gsr:dt:37:lem:path}
For $v\in\C^R$ with $\sum_jv_j=0$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:path}
 v^*T_Rv\le \cos\left(\frac{2\pi}{R+1}\right)\|v\|_2^2.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Append one zero coordinate to obtain a vector $y\in\C^{R+1}$ of mean zero.
Let $C_m$ act on cyclic coordinates by
$(C_my)_j=(y_{j-1}+y_{j+1})/2$. Then $y^*C_my=v^*T_Rv$, since every term
involving the appended coordinate is zero. The cyclic Fourier vectors have
eigenvalues $\cos(2\pi\ell/m)$, $0\le\ell<m$. The mean-zero condition removes
$\ell=0$, so the largest remaining eigenvalue is $\cos(2\pi/m)$.
This proves the inequality. For $R=1$ the only zero-sum vector is zero,
and the same conclusion holds.
\end{proof}

The use of the second cyclic eigenvalue is essential. On the full path
space the largest eigenvalue is $\cos(\pi/m)$, which exceeds $\cos a$ in the
first window. The rank-one correction below removes precisely that bad
one-dimensional direction.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Attainment, support, and equality\srctag{37}}]{Attainment, support, and equality}\label{gsr:dt:37:sec:d5}\label{gsr:dt:37:sec:attainment}
\srcnote{37}{Section 5}

\subsection{Constructing the negative equimoment measure}
We prescribe
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:hprescribe}
 h_0=1,\qquad h_j=-\rho\quad(1\le |j|\le R).
\end{equation}
For these moments the Toeplitz matrix is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:Mexplicit}
 M=(1+\rho)I_m-\rho J_m,
\end{equation}
where $J_m=\one\one^*$. Its eigenvalues are $1+\rho$ on $\one^\perp$ and
$1-R\rho$ on $\one$. Both are positive in the strict first window.

The localizing matrix has the explicit form
\begin{align}
 L&=(1+\rho)(cI_R-T_R)+\rho(1-c)J_R\notag\\
  &=(1+\rho)\bigl(cI_R-T_R+\lambda J_R\bigr),\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:Lexplicit}
\end{align}
since $\lambda=(1-c)\rho/(1+\rho)$.

\begin{lemma}[The rank-one correction is positive]\label{gsr:dt:37:lem:rankone}
The matrix $K=cI_R-T_R+\lambda J_R$ is positive semidefinite, has kernel
$\C w$, and has rank $R-1$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Equation~\eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:recw} and $\sum w_j=1$ give $Kw=0$. Every
$x\in\C^R$ can be written uniquely as
\[
 x=u+\left(\sum_jx_j\right)w,\qquad \sum_ju_j=0.
\]
Since $K$ is Hermitian and $Kw=0$,
\[
 x^*Kx=u^*Ku=u^*(cI_R-T_R)u.
\]
The first-window upper inequality gives
$c>\cos(2\pi/m)$, because $0<a<2\pi/m\le\pi$.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:37:lem:path} shows that the last quadratic form is positive for every
nonzero $u$. This proves positivity, the stated kernel, and the rank.
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:37:thm:moment} now produces a probability measure $\mu$ on $K_a$
with the prescribed moments. This establishes attainment of the lower bound,
but there is considerably more structure.

\subsection{Why all roots lie on the circle}

\begin{proposition}[Support and uniqueness]\label{gsr:dt:37:prop:uniqueness}
The prescribed measure exists uniquely. It has the support and positive
weights described in \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:P}--\eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:weightsystem}. In particular,
$P_{R,a}$ has $R-1$ distinct unit-circle zeros in the relative interior of
$K_a$, and neither endpoint is a zero.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For any representing measure on $K_a$,
\[
 \int(c-\cos\theta)|P_{R,a}(e^{i\theta})|^2\,d\mu
 =w^*Lw=0.
\]
The integrand is nonnegative. Thus the support is contained in the two
endpoints and the unit-circle zeros of $P_{R,a}$. Since $P$ has degree
$R-1$ and nonzero leading coefficient, there are at most $R+1$ distinct
possible support points.

On the other hand $M$ in \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:Mexplicit} is positive definite and has
rank $R+1$. A measure supported at $s$ points has a moment matrix that is a
sum of $s$ rank-one matrices and therefore has rank at most $s$. Hence at
least $R+1$ support points are necessary. Every inequality is therefore an
equality: both endpoints occur; all $R-1$ roots occur, are distinct, lie on
the unit circle, and are not endpoints; and every mass is positive.

For this fixed support, the equations for $h_0,\ldots,h_R$ form a square
Vandermonde system in the distinct numbers $e^{-i\theta_j}$. Its determinant
is nonzero, so the weights are unique. The support was determined by $P$,
so the measure is unique. Reflecting the measure changes each moment to its
complex conjugate and preserves the support; the moments are real, so
uniqueness also proves reflection symmetry.
\end{proof}

This argument is also a proof of the root-location assertion. Numerical
root plots are not being used as a substitute for a unit-circle theorem.

\subsection{Equality in the minimax and noisy problems}
If $\mu\in\Probthirtyseven(K_a)$ and $E_R(\mu)=\rho$, the inequalities in
Proposition~\ref{gsr:dt:37:prop:lower} are all equalities. Since every $f_k>0$ and
$\Rea\widehat\mu(k)\ge-\rho$, each real part is $-\rho$. Together with
$|\widehat\mu(k)|\le\rho$, this forces $\widehat\mu(k)=-\rho$.
Proposition~\ref{gsr:dt:37:prop:uniqueness} proves the uniqueness claimed in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:37:thm:main}(ii). The same argument proves the one-sided minimax
identity.

For $0\le\varepsilon\le\rho$, the measure in \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:mix} has
\[
 \widehat\mu_\varepsilon(k)=s-(1-s)\rho=-\varepsilon,
 \qquad \mu_\varepsilon(I_a)=s.
\]
It therefore attains the lower bound in \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:mainmass}. If
$\varepsilon\ge\rho$, $\mu_{R,a}$ gives gap mass zero. This proves the value
in \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:exactmass}.

For completeness, suppose $0\le\varepsilon\le\rho$ and equality is attained.
Every nonnegative term in
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:slack}
 \mu(I_a)-\bigl[d-(1-d)\varepsilon\bigr]
 =\int(\one_{I_a}-F)\,d\mu
       +2\sum_{k=1}^Rf_k\bigl(\Rea\widehat\mu(k)+\varepsilon\bigr)
\end{equation}
must vanish. Thus all moments equal $-\varepsilon$. Inside $I_a$, equality
$F=1$ is possible only at zero: the positive coefficient $f_1$ already
forces $\cos\theta=1$. Outside, equality $F=0$ occurs precisely at the
$R+1$ support points from Proposition~\ref{gsr:dt:37:prop:uniqueness}. Consequently
any equality measure is supported on the fixed $R+2$-point set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:Z}
 Z=\{0\}\cup\supp\mu_{R,a}.
\end{equation}
The matrix with columns $e^{-ik\theta_j}$, $-R\le k\le R$, has full column
rank: multiplying each column by $e^{-iR\theta_j}$ turns it into a
Vandermonde matrix with powers $0,\ldots,2R$, and
$R+2\le2R+1$. Thus the moments determine the weights uniquely. The measure
\eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:mix} is that unique measure. This completes the proof of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:37:thm:main}.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Endpoints and the first spectral transition\srctag{37}}]{Endpoints and the first spectral transition}\label{gsr:dt:37:sec:d6}\label{gsr:dt:37:sec:endpoints}
\srcnote{37}{Section 6}

\subsection{Zero moments and the critical gap}

\begin{theorem}[The critical radius]\label{gsr:dt:37:thm:critical}
Let $m=R+1$ and $\beta=\pi/m$.
For $0<a\le\beta$ there exists $\mu\in\Probthirtyseven(K_a)$ with $E_R(\mu)=0$.
At $a=\beta$ that measure is unique: it is the uniform measure on
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:oddgrid}
 Z_m=\left\{\frac{(2j+1)\pi}{m}:0\le j<m\right\}\pmod{2\pi}.
\end{equation}
For $a>\beta$, no probability measure on $K_a$ can have all of its first
$R$ moments zero.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The uniform measure on $Z_m$ has its first $m-1$ moments zero by summing a
geometric progression, and its nearest points to zero have angular distance
$\beta$. This proves existence for $a\le\beta$.

For uniqueness at $\beta$, define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:Pcritical}
 P_0(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{m-2}\sin((j+1)\beta)z^j.
\end{equation}
The sine vector is a path eigenvector with eigenvalue $\cos\beta$. Therefore
$Q_0(\theta)=(\cos\theta-\cos\beta)|P_0(e^{i\theta})|^2$ has constant
Fourier coefficient zero. The calculation in Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:37:lem:q}, with
$\lambda=0$ and without normalizing the vector, also shows that all its
nonconstant Fourier coefficients are positive.
The finite recurrence gives the polynomial identity
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:criticalidentity}
 (1-2\cos\beta\,z+z^2)P_0(z)=\sin\beta\,(1+z^m).
\end{equation}
On $K_\beta$, the zeros of $Q_0$ are exactly $Z_m$: the two roots
$e^{\pm i\beta}$ of the denominator in \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:criticalidentity} are the
endpoints, and the other $m-2$ roots of $1+z^m$ are the zeros of $P_0$.

If the first $R$ moments vanish, then $\int Q_0\,d\mu=0$.
Since $Q_0\le0$ on $K_\beta$, the support lies in $Z_m$. The Vandermonde
moment equations uniquely give the uniform weights. Finally, if $a>\beta$
and $\mu\in\Probthirtyseven(K_a)$ had these zero moments, it would also be a measure
on $K_\beta$ and hence this uniform measure. But that measure charges the
points $\pm\beta$ inside $I_a$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The other endpoint}
At $a=2\pi/m$, define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:uppermeasure}
 \nu_m=\frac1{m-1}\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}\delta_{2\pi j/m}.
\end{equation}
Its first $R=m-1$ moments all equal $-1/R$. The polynomial coefficients
constructed above have finite limits at this endpoint, so
\eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:mainmass} remains valid with $d=1/m$ and $\rho=1/R$.
The measure \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:uppermeasure} attains the gap bound, and its mixture
with $\delta_0$ attains the noisy-gap value for $0\le\varepsilon\le1/R$.
For $m=2$, this says simply that the open arc $I_\pi$ is the circle with the antipode removed, so the only
measure supported on its complement is $\delta_\pi$.

There is also uniqueness for the endpoint \emph{empty-gap} optimizer.
Equality forces all first $R$ moments to be $-1/R$. Its Toeplitz matrix
annihilates $\one$, hence
\[
 \int\left|1+e^{i\theta}+\cdots+e^{iR\theta}\right|^2d\mu=0.
\]
The support is therefore among the $m$th roots of unity other than $1$.
The moment equations give exactly \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:uppermeasure}.

We use the endpoint constants only by continuous extension or by these
explicit measures. The strict-window root-simplicity and stability
statements are not automatically extended to endpoints.

\subsection{An asymptotically exact frequency--amplitude frontier}
Write the normalized gap radius as $\delta=a/(2\pi)$. If $\delta\to0$
and the integer cutoff satisfies $R\delta\to\tau\in(1/2,1)$, then eventually
we are in the first window. Directly from \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:rho},
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:frontier}
 \frac{\rho_R(2\pi\delta)}{\delta}
 \longrightarrow
 \mathcal C(\tau):=
 \frac{1}{\tau-\pi^{-1}\tan(\pi\tau)}.
\end{equation}
Indeed, $\delta R\to\tau$, $\delta\cot(\pi\delta)\to1/\pi$, and
$(R+1)\delta\to\tau$. This limit is optimal because each finite-parameter
value comes with an attaining measure.

The denominator in \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:frontier} decreases from $+\infty$ to $1$ as
$\tau$ increases from $1/2$ to $1$; its derivative is
$-\tan^2(\pi\tau)$. Thus $\mathcal C$ increases from zero to one.
The exact tradeoff distinguishes two questions that a single big-$O$ lemma
conflates: detecting \emph{any} nonzero coefficient requires about half the
inverse gap radius, whereas forcing an asymptotic coefficient of size
$\delta$ requires a cutoff approaching the full inverse radius within this
window.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A linear-frequency replacement for Lemma 5.2\srctag{37}}]{A linear-frequency replacement for Lemma 5.2}\label{gsr:dt:37:sec:d7}\label{gsr:dt:37:sec:cyclic}
\srcnote{37}{Section 7}

\subsection{A simple bound without a trigonometric denominator}
We now use normalized coordinates $x\in\R/\Z$, with
$\widehat\mu(r)=\int e^{-2\pi irx}\,d\mu(x)$.

\begin{theorem}[Universal small-arc inequality]\label{gsr:dt:37:thm:universal}
Let $0<\delta\le1/2$ and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:Rdelta}
 R=\lfloor\delta^{-1}\rfloor-1.
\end{equation}
Then every probability measure satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:universal}
 \mu\{x:\fracnorm{x}<\delta\}
 \ge \delta-(1-\delta)\max_{1\le r\le R}|\widehat\mu(r)|.
\end{equation}
If the open arc on the left is empty, there is $1\le r\le R$ with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:universalnegative}
 \Rea\widehat\mu(r)\le-\frac{\delta}{1-\delta}.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
First let $\delta<1/2$, and write $\delta^{-1}=m+s$ with
$m=\lfloor\delta^{-1}\rfloor\ge2$ and $0\le s<1$. Then $R=m-1$ and
$\pi<m(2\pi\delta)\le2\pi$, so the first-window theorem or its upper
endpoint applies. As $m\pi\delta=\pi-s\pi\delta$,
\[
 \rho_R(2\pi\delta)
 =\frac{1}{m-1+\cot(\pi\delta)\tan(s\pi\delta)}.
\]
Convexity of $\tan$ on $[0,\pi/2)$ gives
$\tan(sx)\le s\tan x$ for $0\le s\le1$. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:rholower}
 \rho_R(2\pi\delta)\ge\frac1{m-1+s}
 =\frac{\delta}{1-\delta},\qquad d_R(2\pi\delta)\ge\delta.
\end{equation}
In \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:mainmass}, replacing $d$ by the smaller number $\delta$ weakens
the right side, since $d-(1-d)E$ is increasing in $d$ for $E\ge0$.
This proves \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:universal}; the one-sided statement follows from
\eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:onesided} and \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:rholower}. At $\delta=1/2$, use the endpoint
$R=1,a=\pi$, or the certificate $(1+\cos\theta)/2$ directly.
\end{proof}

Translation is harmless. For an arc centered at $x_0$, replace
$\widehat\mu(r)$ in the one-sided conclusion by
$e^{2\pi irx_0}\widehat\mu(r)$. The modulus conclusion is unchanged.

\subsection{Finite cyclic groups, arbitrary weights, and collisions}

\begin{corollary}[Weighted finite-cyclic missing interval]\label{gsr:dt:37:cor:cyclic}
Let $N,M$ be integers with $N\ge2$, $1\le M\le N/2$, and let $w:\Z/N\Z\to[0,\infty)$ have
positive total mass $W=\sum_xw(x)$. Suppose $w(x)=0$ whenever the least
absolute residue of $x$ is strictly less than $M$. Then there is an integer
$r$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:new52}
 1\le r\le\left\lfloor\frac NM\right\rfloor-1<N,
 \qquad
 -\Rea\widehat w(r)\ge\frac{M}{N-M}W,
\end{equation}
where
$\widehat w(r)=\sum_{x\in\Z/N\Z}w(x)e^{-2\pi irx/N}$.
The residue class of $r$ is nonzero and has least absolute residue at most
the displayed upper bound.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:37:thm:universal} to the probability measure that assigns
mass $w(x)/W$ to $x/N$ in $\R/\Z$, with $\delta=M/N$.
Since $M\ge1$, the cutoff is at most $N-1$, so no zero residue is selected.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 34--39]
\emph{It implies the formal conclusion} (proved at the write). Under the hypotheses of \file{lemma_5_2} ($1<N$, $0<M$, $2M\le N$; the parity of $M$ is not needed), $A\cap[-M,M)=\varnothing$ implies that $w=1_A$ vanishes where the least absolute residue is below $M$. The corollary gives $1\le r\le\lfloor N/M\rfloor-1<N$, so $r\ne0$ in $\Z/N\Z$ and $|r|_N\le r\le N/M-1\le(N/M)^2$; and $|\widehat{1_A}(r)|\ge-\Rea\widehat{1_A}(r)\ge|A|M/(N-M)\ge|A|M/(4N)$, since $N-M\le4N$. The sign convention of the exponential does not affect the modulus. So the conclusion of \file{lemma_5_2} follows, with frequency linear in $N/M$ and coefficient larger by the factor $4N/(N-M)\in(4,8]$. The formal statement is already exact; its status does not change. The intake checked the corollary exhaustively on $\Z/N\Z$ for $N\le14$, every $M\le N/2$ and every nonempty $A$ avoiding the open gap: $21{,}781$ cases, no failure, $171$ equalities. Formalization candidate (the source's lower-bound track), claimed by nobody: the explicit vector $w$, its path recurrence and the coefficient identity of Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:37:lem:q}.
\end{writenote}

For an indicator function $w=1_A$, this gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:setreplacement}
 |\widehat{1_A}(r)|\ge\frac{|A|M}{N-M}.
\end{equation}
The original exclusion $A\cap[-M,M)=\varnothing$ implies the open-gap
exclusion used here. Thus the corollary applies under the hypotheses of the
repository's Lemma 5.2 and additionally removes the parity assumption on
$M$. If $A$ is empty, the coefficient lower bound is zero and a nonzero
frequency exists because $N>1$; the positive-mass proof is unnecessary.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.29\textwidth}p{0.29\textwidth}p{0.29\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Quantity & Proof-supported Lemma 5.2 & Present corollary\\
\midrule
Frequency bound & $(N/M)^2$ & $\lfloor N/M\rfloor-1$\\[3pt]
Coefficient bound & $|A|M/(4N)$ & $|A|M/(N-M)$\\[3pt]
Coefficient direction & Absolute value & A negative real part\\[3pt]
Input & A subset & Any nonnegative weights\\[3pt]
Gap assumption & Half-open interval; $M$ even & Open interval; no parity condition\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The gain in the coefficient relative to the proof-supported version is
$4N/(N-M)$, approaching $4$ for a small gap. The frequency range is linear,
rather than quadratic, in $N/M$. The weighted formulation includes empirical
measures of polynomial values, with all repetitions counted. Again, the
repository already repairs the multiplicity issue; the new part is the
bound, not the observation that repeated values must be counted.

\subsection{Sharpness and endpoint discipline}
For $\delta=1/m$, the measure uniformly supported at
$j/m$, $1\le j<m$, has no mass in the \emph{open} arc of radius $\delta$ and
has $\widehat\mu(r)=-1/(m-1)$ for $1\le r\le m-1$. Thus the coefficient
$\delta/(1-\delta)$ in \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:universalnegative} is exactly sharp for
these radii. When $m\mid N$, this is an indicator example on $\Z/N\Z$ after
normalization.

This extremizer charges both endpoints. It therefore need not satisfy the
original \emph{half-open} exclusion, which deletes one of them. The exact
sharpness assertion is for the open-gap theorem, not for every stronger
finite-grid hypothesis. This distinction matters when comparing constants
at a fixed small modulus.

The linear order of the cutoff cannot be improved to $o(\delta^{-1})$ in a
uniform missing-arc lemma with a positive conclusion. The critical grid
in Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:37:thm:critical} has a gap radius $1/(2m)$ in normalized
coordinates and its first $m-1$ moments vanish. Taking $m\to\infty$ proves
the obstruction. The sharper coefficient-versus-cutoff information is
\eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:frontier}; it is not captured by this order-of-magnitude example.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Stability and near extremizers\srctag{37}}]{Stability and near extremizers}\label{gsr:dt:37:sec:d8}\label{gsr:dt:37:sec:stability}
\srcnote{37}{Section 8}

\subsection{A dimension-independent geometric estimate at the threshold}
The critical grid has a useful stability property even though the optimal
empty-gap coefficient is zero there.

\begin{theorem}[Critical geometric stability]\label{gsr:dt:37:thm:criticalstable}
Let $m=R+1$, $\beta=\pi/m$, and let $Z_m$ be the odd grid in
\eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:oddgrid}. If $\mu\in\Probthirtyseven(K_\beta)$ and $E_R(\mu)\le\varepsilon$,
then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:criticalstable}
 \int\dist(\theta,Z_m)^2\,d\mu(\theta)
 \le \frac{\pi^2}{m^2}\cot^2\left(\frac{\pi}{2m}\right)\varepsilon
 \le4\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
Distance is angular geodesic distance on $\Tthirtyseven$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Use $P_0,Q_0$ from the proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:37:thm:critical}, and set
$D=-Q_0\ge0$ on $K_\beta$. Since the constant Fourier coefficient of $Q_0$
is zero and its other coefficients are positive,
\[
 \int D\,d\mu\le Q_0(0)\varepsilon.
\]
The sine sum equals $\cot(\beta/2)$, so
\[
 Q_0(0)=(1-\cos\beta)\cot^2(\beta/2)=1+\cos\beta.
\]
Away from the endpoints, \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:criticalidentity} gives
\[
 D(\theta)=\frac{\sin^2\beta\,\cos^2(m\theta/2)}
                         {\cos\beta-\cos\theta}
 \ge(1-\cos\beta)\cos^2(m\theta/2).
\]
The inequality extends to the endpoints by continuity. Consequently
\[
 \int\cos^2(m\theta/2)\,d\mu
 \le\cot^2(\beta/2)\varepsilon.
\]
If $u=\dist(\theta,Z_m)$, then $0\le u\le\pi/m$ and
$\cos^2(m\theta/2)=\sin^2(mu/2)\ge m^2u^2/\pi^2$.
This proves the first inequality in \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:criticalstable}. The second
follows from $x\cot x\le1$ for $0<x\le\pi/4$.
\end{proof}

The conclusion concerns concentration near the grid, not closeness to the
\emph{uniformly weighted} grid in a dimension-independent transport metric.
Redistributing the masses among the grid points is a separate issue. At
$\varepsilon=0$, the moment equations do force uniform weights, as already
proved.

\subsection{Quantitative rigidity throughout the strict window}
For fixed strict-window parameters, the full extremizer is stable. We give
an effective finite-dimensional bound rather than hide the dependence on
$R$ and $a$ in an unspecified compactness argument.

Let $Z=\{\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_n\}$ be the contact set in \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:Z},
where $n=R+2$. Let
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:V}
 V=(e^{-ik\theta_j})_{-R\le k\le R,\,1\le j\le n},\qquad
 \sigma=\sigma_{\min}(V)>0.
\end{equation}
With $F$ from \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:F}, define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:kappa}
 h(\theta)=\one_{I_a}(\theta)-F(\theta),\qquad
 \kappa=\inf_{\theta\notin Z}
               \frac{h(\theta)}{\dist(\theta,Z)^2}.
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}\label{gsr:dt:37:lem:kappa}
For fixed $R,a$ in the strict window, $\kappa>0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The zero set of $h$ is precisely $Z$. Near zero, $h=1-F$ has positive
quadratic term $\sum_{k=1}^Rk^2f_k\,\theta^2$. At every interior point of
$K_a$ in $Z$, the corresponding root of $P$ is simple and
$c-\cos\theta>0$, so $h=-F$ has a positive quadratic zero. At either
endpoint, $P$ is nonzero and $\sin a>0$, so $h$ grows linearly on the
outside; on the inside its limit is $1$. These observations give a positive
lower bound for the ratio in neighborhoods of all contact points. Away
from those neighborhoods the function is continuous and positive on a
compact set. This proves the claim despite the one-sided jumps at the
endpoints.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Stability of the exact mass tradeoff]\label{gsr:dt:37:thm:stable}
Fix $0\le\varepsilon\le\rho_R(a)$ and let $\mu_\varepsilon$ be the exact
extremizer in \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:mix}. Suppose $E_R(\mu)\le\varepsilon$ and set
\[
 \Delta=\mu(I_a)-\frac{\rho_R(a)-\varepsilon}{1+\rho_R(a)}\ge0,
 \qquad t=\sqrt{\Delta/\kappa}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:stableW}
 W_1(\mu,\mu_\varepsilon)
 \le t+\frac{\pi\sqrt{R+2}}{2\sigma}
       \left[2\sum_{k=1}^R
          \left(kt+\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon\Delta}{f_k}}\right)^2
       \right]^{1/2}.
\end{equation}
In particular the distance is $O_{R,a,\varepsilon}(\sqrt\Delta)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By the exact slack decomposition \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:slack},
$\int h\,d\mu\le\Delta$, whence
$\int\dist(\theta,Z)^2d\mu\le\Delta/\kappa$.
Push each point to a nearest point of $Z$, with a fixed rule for ties, and
call the resulting measure $\nu$. Cauchy--Schwarz gives
$W_1(\mu,\nu)\le t$.

For $z=\widehat\mu(k)$, the disk constraint $|z|\le\varepsilon$ gives
\[
 |z+\varepsilon|^2
 \le2\varepsilon(\Rea z+\varepsilon)
 \le\frac{\varepsilon\Delta}{f_k},
\]
where the last inequality follows again from \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:slack}.
The function $e^{-ik\theta}$ is $k$-Lipschitz in angular distance, hence
\[
 |\widehat\nu(k)-\widehat\mu_\varepsilon(k)|
 \le kt+\sqrt{\varepsilon\Delta/f_k}.
\]
Both measures have total mass one, and negative moments are conjugates of
positive ones. If $u,u^*$ are their weight vectors on $Z$, then
\[
 \|V(u-u^*)\|_2^2
 \le2\sum_{k=1}^R(kt+\sqrt{\varepsilon\Delta/f_k})^2.
\]
Use $\|u-u^*\|_2\le\sigma^{-1}\|V(u-u^*)\|_2$ and
$\TV(\nu,\mu_\varepsilon)\le\sqrt{R+2}\|u-u^*\|_2/2$.
Since the diameter of the circle is $\pi$,
$W_1(\nu,\mu_\varepsilon)\le\pi\TV(\nu,\mu_\varepsilon)$.
The triangle inequality completes the proof.
\end{proof}

The coefficients $f_k$, the nodes, and the Vandermonde matrix are explicit.
The constant $\kappa$ is a one-variable positive minimum with explicitly
controlled local behavior. The estimate is therefore suitable for certified
parameter-specific bounds. We do not assert uniform control of $\kappa$ or
$\sigma$ as the cutoff grows or as the endpoints of the window are approached.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A stronger monomial-recurrence deduction\srctag{37}}]{A stronger monomial-recurrence deduction}\label{gsr:dt:37:sec:d9}\label{gsr:dt:37:sec:recurrence}
\srcnote{37}{Section 9}

The sharp spectral lemma can be used without its full extremal formula.
The simple conclusion \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:universalnegative} is enough. A second
improvement is to choose the Dirichlet denominator scale according to the
size of the detected Weyl sum, rather than fixing it at the sample length.

\subsection{The external exponential-sum input}
Write $\ee{x}=e^{2\pi ix}$ and
\[
 S_k(\alpha;T)=\sum_{n=1}^T\ee{\alpha n^k}.
\]
For fixed integers $k\ge2$, $T\ge1$, and real parameters $D\ge1$, $B\ge1$, consider the hypothesis
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:Winput}
 \frac{|S_k(\beta;T)|}{T}
 \le B\left(q^{-1}+T^{-1}+qT^{-k}\right)^{1/D}
\end{equation}
for all $\beta\in\R$ and all coprime integers $u,q$ with $q>0$ and
$|\beta-u/q|\le q^{-2}$. It is important that the hypothesis permits any
positive denominator; no restriction $q\le T$ is imposed.

\begin{theorem}[A recurrence conversion with optimized denominator]\label{gsr:dt:37:thm:master}
Assume \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:Winput}. If $0<\delta\le1/2$ and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:mastercondition}
 T\delta^{D+1}\ge16B^D,
\end{equation}
then every $\alpha\in\R$ admits an integer $1\le p\le T$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:masterresult}
 \fracnorm{\alpha p^k}<\delta.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Suppose the conclusion fails. The probability measure
\[
 \mu=\frac1T\sum_{n=1}^T\delta_{\alpha n^k\bmod1}
\]
has no mass in the open arc of radius $\delta$. This is an empirical
measure, not a set of distinct values; repetitions are counted.
Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:37:thm:universal} provides
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:largesum}
 1\le r\le\lfloor\delta^{-1}\rfloor-1<\delta^{-1},\qquad
 \frac{|S_k(r\alpha;T)|}{T}\ge\frac{\delta}{1-\delta}\ge\delta.
\end{equation}
Put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:sQ}
 s=(\delta/B)^D,\qquad Q=\left\lfloor\frac{T^ks}{4}\right\rfloor.
\end{equation}
The assumption says $T\delta s\ge16$, and therefore $Ts\ge32$.
Since $k\ge2$, the expression inside the floor is at least $2$, so
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:Qround}
 \frac{T^ks}{8}\le Q\le\frac{T^ks}{4},\qquad Q\ge1.
\end{equation}

Dirichlet approximation gives coprime $u,q$, $1\le q\le Q$, with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:Dirichlet}
 |r\alpha-u/q|\le\frac1{qQ}\le\frac1{q^2}.
\end{equation}
For clarity, this version follows by placing the $Q+1$ fractional parts of
$0,\beta,\ldots,Q\beta$ in $Q$ equal intervals and subtracting two in the
same interval; reducing the resulting fraction only improves the displayed
bound with its reduced denominator.

Apply \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:Winput} to $r\alpha$. By \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:largesum},
\[
 s\le q^{-1}+T^{-1}+qT^{-k}.
\]
We have $qT^{-k}\le s/4$, and
$T^{-1}\le\delta s/16\le s/16$. Thus $q^{-1}>s/2$, and in particular
$q\le2/s$. Set $p=rq$. It is a positive integer, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:pbound}
 p<\frac2{\delta s}=\frac{2B^D}{\delta^{D+1}}\le\frac T8.
\end{equation}
Multiplying \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:Dirichlet} by $p^k/r$ shows that $\alpha p^k$ lies
within $p^{k-1}/Q$ of the integer $u r^{k-1}q^{k-1}$. Hence
\[
 \fracnorm{\alpha p^k}
 \le\frac{p^{k-1}}Q
 \le\frac8{Ts}
 \le\frac\delta2<\delta.
\]
This contradicts the assumed absence of recurrence and proves the theorem.
\end{proof}

The use of $Q\asymp T^ks$ is legitimate because the rational approximation
still meets the $q^{-2}$ condition in the Weyl input. It is precisely the
smallness of the term $qT^{-k}$ that allows this larger search scale.

\subsection{Power-law consequences}

\begin{corollary}[General power-law Weyl input]\label{gsr:dt:37:cor:powerrec}
Suppose \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:Winput} holds for all integers $T\ge T_0$ with
$B=CT^\eta$, where $C\ge1$ and $0\le\eta<1/D$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:Ab}
 A=(16C^D)^{1/(D+1)},\qquad b=\frac{1-D\eta}{D+1}.
\end{equation}
Then for every $T\ge T_0$ and every $\alpha\in\R$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:powerrec}
 \min_{1\le p\le T}\fracnorm{\alpha p^k}\le A T^{-b}.
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Set $\delta=AT^{-b}$. If $\delta\ge1/2$, the bound is trivial. Otherwise
\[
 T\delta^{D+1}=16C^DT^{D\eta}=16B^D,
\]
and Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:37:thm:master} applies.
\end{proof}

For the classical all-$\eta$ Weyl inequality, $D=2^{k-1}$. Choosing
$\eta>0$ arbitrarily small gives the transparent local consequence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:epsrec}
 \min_{1\le p\le T}\fracnorm{\alpha p^k}
 \ll_{k,\epsilon}T^{-1/(2^{k-1}+1)+\epsilon}
 \qquad(\epsilon>0).
\end{equation}
The point here is the deduction and its explicit dependence on the Weyl
input. No claim is made that \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:epsrec} is a new record.

\subsection{Using the explicit input recorded in ProveIt}
The explicit version of the Weyl input in the inspected Section 5 source
and its companion \codethirtyseven{lemma_5_3_holds} has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:repoW}
 D=2^{k-1},\qquad C=1000,\qquad
 \eta=\frac1{k2^{k+1}}=\frac1{4kD},\qquad
 T_0=2^{\,2^{40k^3}}.
\end{equation}
We use this statement as an external input; its proof is not reproduced
here, and the Lean project was not built during preparation of this
manuscript. The displayed companion was inspected in
\codethirtyseven{Proofs05Weyl.lean} at the pinned revision \cite{repo37}.

\begin{corollary}[Explicit refinement of the monomial recurrence step]
\label{gsr:dt:37:cor:explicitrec}
For $k\ge2$, let
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:explicitAb}
 A_k=(16\cdot1000^{2^{k-1}})^{1/(2^{k-1}+1)},\qquad
 b_k=\frac{1-1/(4k)}{2^{k-1}+1}.
\end{equation}
Using the input \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:repoW}, for every integer
$T\ge2^{2^{40k^3}}$ and every $\alpha\in\R$ there is $1\le p\le T$ with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:explicitrec}
 \fracnorm{\alpha p^k}\le A_kT^{-b_k}.
\end{equation}
For an integer $N\ge2$ and $a\in\Z/N\Z$, the corresponding least-residue bound is
$|p^ka|_N\le A_kT^{-b_k}N$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Substitute \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:repoW} into Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:37:cor:powerrec}.
For the finite-cyclic assertion take $\alpha$ to be any integer
representative of $a$ divided by $N$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 34--39]
\emph{It implies the formal bound of Lemma~5.5} (proved at the write). The input \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:repoW} is the second conjunct of \file{lemma_5_3} exactly: the constant $1000$, the exponent $1/(k2^{k+1})$, any $q>0$ coprime to $a$ with $|\alpha-a/q|\le q^{-2}$, \file{weylSum} summing over $1\le s\le t$, and $t\ge$ \file{weylThreshold}~$k=2^{2^{40k^3}}$. For such $t$, $A_kt^{-b_k}\le t^{-a_k}$ because $A_k<16\cdot1000$ while $t^{b_k-a_k}\ge2^{2^{40k^3}(b_k-a_k)}$ is far larger; so the corollary gives the conclusion of \file{lemma_5_5} (with $p\le t$, $|p^ka|_N\le t^{-a_k}N$). The comparison is with one local step at its chosen Weyl parameters, as the source says; source~32's explicit quadratic recurrence $p\le2^{10}R^5$ (Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:32:lem:recurrence}, every scale, small constants) and the Lau- and Maynard-based recurrences of sources~13, 16, 18 and~19 are other regimes. Formalization candidate, claimed by nobody: Dirichlet at scale $\lfloor T^ks/4\rfloor$ with Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:37:thm:universal}.
\end{writenote}

The recurrence exponent in the selected Lemma 5.5 is
$a_k=1/(k2^{k+1})=1/(4kD)$. The new exponent is larger by the factor
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:exponentratio}
 \frac{b_k}{a_k}=\frac{(4k-1)2^{k-1}}{2^{k-1}+1}.
\end{equation}
The improvement comes with the explicitly displayed multiplicative
constant $A_k$; it is not a constant-free comparison for every small $T$.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}cccc@{}}
\toprule
Degree $k$ & Selected exponent $a_k$ & Exponent $b_k$ here & $b_k/a_k$\\
\midrule
2 & $1/16$ & $7/24$ & $14/3$\\[3pt]
3 & $1/48$ & $11/60$ & $44/5$\\[3pt]
4 & $1/128$ & $5/48$ & $40/3$\\[3pt]
5 & $1/320$ & $19/340$ & $304/17$\\[3pt]
6 & $1/768$ & $23/792$ & $736/33$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

This is a comparison against a particular local step, with exactly its
chosen Weyl parameters. It is not a comparison against the strongest
available bounds for fractional parts of monomials or general polynomials.

\subsection{The square-root-length interface}
The degree induction in a polynomial partition needs a short step as well
as a small leading coefficient. Integer rounding can be kept explicit.

\begin{corollary}[Short-step recurrence]\label{gsr:dt:37:cor:short}
Under the hypotheses of Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:37:cor:powerrec}, let $U\ge4$ be an
integer with $\lfloor\sqrt U\rfloor\ge T_0$. There is a positive integer
$p$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:short}
 p^2\le U,\qquad
 \fracnorm{\alpha p^k}\le2^bA\,U^{-b/2}.
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:powerrec} with $T=\lfloor\sqrt U\rfloor$.
Then $p\le T\le\sqrt U$, while $T\ge\sqrt U/2$ because $U\ge4$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 34--39]
The hypothesis $\lfloor\sqrt U\rfloor\ge T_0$ is the rounding-safe form of the squared threshold of the formal \file{lemma_5_5_square_root_auxiliary} (\file{Section05.lean}, line~192: \file{weylThreshold}~$k^2\le t$, $p^2\le t$), as the source says in Section~\ref{gsr:fm:37:sec:d1}.
\end{writenote}

For \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:repoW}, this gives exponent $b_k/2$, rather than silently
claiming exponent $b_k$ at a square-root sample length. Since $b_k/2>a_k$
for every $k\ge2$, it also recovers the original auxiliary target
$U^{-a_k}$ whenever, in addition,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:absorb}
 U\ge(2^{b_k}A_k)^{1/(b_k/2-a_k)}.
\end{equation}
The explicit square-root threshold and the constant-absorption threshold
must both be propagated in any replacement proof of a partition lemma.

\subsection{Where the improvement stops in this manuscript}
The conclusions above concern \emph{monomial} recurrence. A bound for
$\alpha p^k$ does not by itself make the lower coefficients of an arbitrary
polynomial small. The partition induction must still control those terms,
its target lengths, and the losses from refinement. The existing source
also records corrections to exact-cell formulations. None of those issues
is bypassed by an improved leading-coefficient estimate.

Likewise, a better local recurrence exponent is not an improved global
Szemer\'edi bound until every later parameter has been recomputed. The
present work establishes the spectral and recurrence substitutions, gives
the precise short-step interface, and leaves that global propagation as a
separate research task.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The real interval factorization used above\srctag{37}}]{The real interval factorization used above}\label{gsr:dt:37:sec:dA}\label{gsr:dt:37:app:factorization}
\srcnote{37}{Appendix A}

We include the elementary factorization argument behind
Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:37:lem:arcpos}. This avoids treating supported moment existence as a
black box.

\begin{lemma}[Real spectral factorization]\label{gsr:dt:37:lem:realFR}
If a real even trigonometric polynomial $q(\phi)$ of degree at most $n$ is
nonnegative for all $\phi$, then
\[
 q(\phi)=|D(e^{i\phi})|^2
\]
for a polynomial $D$ of degree at most $n$ with real coefficients.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The zero polynomial is immediate. Otherwise, let $d\le n$ be the actual
trigonometric degree and write $q(\phi)=\sum_{j=-d}^dc_jz^j$ on
$z=e^{i\phi}$. Since $q$ is real and even, $c_j=c_{-j}\in\R$.
Thus $H(z)=z^dq(\phi)$ is a real reciprocal polynomial of degree $2d$,
with nonzero constant term. Its zeros off the unit circle occur with their
reciprocals and conjugates. A zero on the unit circle has even multiplicity:
otherwise the real analytic nonnegative function $q(\phi)$ would change
sign at that zero. The local change of variable $z=e^{i\phi}$ has nonzero
derivative, so the multiplicities agree.

Select from each reciprocal pair off the unit circle the zeros inside the
circle, respecting conjugate pairs, and select half of each unit-circle
multiplicity, again respecting conjugation. The resulting monic factor
$D_0$ has degree $d$ and real coefficients. Its reciprocal polynomial
$D_0^*(z)=z^dD_0(1/z)$ supplies the complementary zeros. Hence
$H(z)=cD_0(z)D_0^*(z)$ for a real constant $c$.
On the unit circle, $z^{-d}D_0(z)D_0^*(z)=|D_0(z)|^2$.
At a point where $q$ is positive this shows $c>0$. Taking
$D=\sqrt c\,D_0$ proves the assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Interval factorization]\label{gsr:dt:37:lem:ML}
If $p$ is a real polynomial of degree at most $2R$ and is nonnegative on
$[-b,b]$, where $b>0$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:37:eq:ML}
 p(t)=U(t)^2+(b^2-t^2)V(t)^2
\end{equation}
for real polynomials with $\deg U\le R$ and $\deg V\le R-1$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:37:lem:realFR} to $q(\phi)=p(b\cos\phi)$, which has degree at
most $2R$. Let $D(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{2R}d_jz^j$ be the resulting real factor,
with zeros added to the coefficient list if its degree is smaller.
The Laurent polynomial $e^{-iR\phi}D(e^{i\phi})$ has frequencies between
$-R$ and $R$. Its real part is a real polynomial $A(\cos\phi)$ of degree
at most $R$, because each $\cos(j\phi)$ is such a polynomial. Its imaginary
part is $\sin\phi\,B(\cos\phi)$ with $\deg B\le R-1$, because
$\sin(j\phi)/\sin\phi$ is a polynomial of degree $|j|-1$ for nonzero
integer $j$. Therefore
\[
 p(b\cos\phi)=A(\cos\phi)^2+
                  (1-\cos^2\phi)B(\cos\phi)^2.
\]
Set $U(t)=A(t/b)$ and $V(t)=B(t/b)/b$. This proves \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:ML} on the
whole interval and hence as a polynomial identity on $\R$.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Low-dimensional examples\srctag{37}}]{Low-dimensional examples}\label{gsr:dt:37:sec:dB}\label{gsr:dt:37:app:examples}
\srcnote{37}{Appendix B}

\subsection{One retained frequency}
For $R=1$, the first window is $\pi/2<a<\pi$. Let $c=\cos a<0$.
Then
\[
 P(z)=1,\qquad \rho=-c,\qquad d=\frac{-c}{1-c},\qquad
 F(\theta)=\frac{\cos\theta-c}{1-c}.
\]
The unique empty-gap extremizer is
$(\delta_{-a}+\delta_a)/2$. For $0\le\varepsilon\le-c$, the exact
minimum gap mass is $(-c-\varepsilon)/(1-c)$, attained by adding that mass
at zero and rescaling the two endpoint atoms. This example checks the sign,
normalization, and open-endpoint conventions directly.

\subsection{Two retained frequencies}
For $R=2$, the first window is $\pi/3<a<2\pi/3$, so
$-1/2<c=\cos a<1/2$. Symmetry gives
\begin{align*}
 P(z)&=\frac{1+z}{2},&
 F(\theta)&=\frac{(\cos\theta-c)(1+\cos\theta)}{2(1-c)},\\
 \rho&=\frac{1-2c}{3-2c},&
 d&=\frac{1-2c}{4(1-c)}.
\end{align*}
The support is $\{-a,a,\pi\}$. The mass at each endpoint is
\[
 u=\frac{1}{(3-2c)(1+c)},
\]
and the mass at $\pi$ is
\[
 v=1-2u=\frac{(1-c)(1+2c)}{(3-2c)(1+c)}.
\]
All masses are positive in the strict window. The two required identities
are
\[
 2uc-v=-\rho,\qquad 2u(2c^2-1)+v=-\rho.
\]
They are included as exact symbolic checks in \codethirtyseven{verify.py}.
At $a=\pi/2$, the three masses are equal, $\rho=1/3$, and $d=1/4$.
Thus zero first and second moments force at least $1/4$ of the mass into
the open arc $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$, with equality at the uniform measure on the
fourth roots of unity. This is a concrete instance of the general noisy-gap
extremizer at $\varepsilon=0$.

\subsection{Practical recovery of an extremizer}
For a strict-window pair $(R,a)$, the following steps implement the exact
mathematical construction numerically.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em]
\item Compute $S,d,\rho$ and the coefficients $w_j$ from
\eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:S}--\eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:w}.
\item Find the $R-1$ roots of $P(z)$ and combine their arguments with
$-a,a$. The proof guarantees distinct unit-circle roots on the allowed arc.
\item Solve \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:weightsystem}, or its overdetermined version using
frequencies $-R,\ldots,R$. Check positivity and moment residuals.
\item For a chosen $\varepsilon\le\rho$, add the atom at zero with mass
$(\rho-\varepsilon)/(1+\rho)$ and rescale the other masses.
\end{enumerate}
Near a window endpoint, direct trigonometric evaluation can lose relative
accuracy. A production implementation should use stable limiting formulas
or higher precision, and certified interval arithmetic for a machine-checkable
numerical artifact. The included double-precision script is a regression
suite, not that certification layer.
