\section{Source~35's Part~3: polynomial divisibility and prescribed lengths \wtag}\label{gsr:dt:sec:polydiv}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the seventh write, 6~October 2026.}}\par
The next section is source~35's Section~7, its delivered Part~3, on partitions of an interval into progressions of prescribed lengths on which several polynomial phases are nearly constant (Gowers's Lemma~5.9). \emph{Logically it follows source~23's chapter} (Sections~\ref{gsr:dt:23:sec:d2}--\ref{gsr:dt:23:sec:d6}, the linear mixed-radix construction and the numerical-semigroup thresholds) \emph{and source~19's polynomial obstruction} (Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:19:poly:obstruction}); it is printed here because no number printed earlier may move. Source~35's introduction is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:35:sec:d1}; its Parts~1 and~2 are in Parts~II and~III.

\emph{What is proved.} Assigning a different prime denominator to each degree, explicit phases with degrees $d_1,\ldots,d_\nu$ force every flat progression of length at least $L$ to have step divisible by an explicit $D\asymp L^W\prod_i\varepsilon_i^{-d_i}$, $W=\sum_id_i(d_i+1)/2$, whatever its starting point (Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:35:po:thm:divisibility}); the exact full-partition threshold for a set of lengths with conductor $C(\mathcal S)$ is then $D\,C(\mathcal S)$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:35:po:thm:thresholds}); for the lengths $L$ or $L+1$, every target, the necessary frontier is $(W+2)a+\sum_id_ib_i\le1$ (Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:35:po:cor:exponents}), that is $1/(7\nu+2)$ for quadratics at $b=2a$ and source~23's sharp $1/(3\nu+2)$ in degree one. This is the higher-degree analogue of source~23's construction (its Question~6, item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:I:polygap}); the matching sufficient theorem in degree at least two is open. The flexible-length obstruction of source~19 is unchanged (note after the corollary).

\emph{Relation to the formal statements} (checked at HEAD \texttt{89c1cbc38}). \file{lemma_5_9} (\file{Section05.lean}, line~261) has the exact companion \file{lemma_5_9_holds} (\file{Proofs05FullPartition.lean}, line~98). The results here are obstructions, lower bounds on what any prescribed-length theorem can give; nothing is formalized.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Polynomial divisibility and prescribed progression lengths\srctag{35}}]{Polynomial divisibility and prescribed progression lengths}\label{gsr:dt:35:sec:d7}
\srcnote{35}{Section 7}
\gsrsrcpartof{35}{Polynomial phase partitions and exact obstructions}
\label{gsr:dt:35:po:sec}

The loss caused by prescribing progression lengths is already understood
for linear phases in the preceding report \cite{repo35thresholds}.  Its
construction forces every sufficiently long flat progression to have a
common divisor in its step, after which a numerical-semigroup obstruction
prevents an exact partition.  The higher-degree version was left as a
research question.  We resolve that construction problem here.  Distinct
prime denominators at successive polynomial degrees force successive
divisibility conditions; their product has the weighted-degree scale
suggested by the earlier volume argument \cite{repo35barrier}.

The resulting obstruction has two consequences.  It excludes long flat
progressions at \emph{every} initial point, whereas the volume argument
only needed to exclude a cell through one endpoint.  For prescribed
lengths, the period is multiplied by the conductor of the allowed
lengths.  This strengthens the necessary exponent region for that
interface of Gowers' Lemma~5.9 \cite{gowers}.  The construction does
not provide a matching upper bound for general polynomial phases of
degree at least two.

\subsection{A small-arc estimate with an explicit constant}

Write $\T=\R/\mathbb Z$.  The arc diameter of a finite subset of $\T$
is the length of its shortest containing closed circular arc.  A proper
integer progression has the form
\[
 P=\{a,a+h,\ldots,a+(\ell-1)h\},\qquad h\in\mathbb Z_{>0}.
\]
All progressions in this section are understood in this sense, including
when the phases themselves take values in a cyclic group.

\begin{lemma}[Leading coefficient of a phase in a short arc]
\label{gsr:dt:35:po:lem:lift}
Let $j\geq1$, $L\geq j+1$, and $0<\eps<2^{-j}$.  Suppose a real
polynomial $P(t)$ of degree at most $j$, with coefficient $\alpha_j$ of
$t^j$, satisfies
\[
 \operatorname{diam}_{\rm arc}
   \{P(0),\ldots,P(L-1)\}\leq\eps
 \quad\text{in }\T.
\]
With $H_j=\lfloor(L-1)/j\rfloor$, one has
\begin{equation}
 \|j!\alpha_j\|_{\T}
 \leq \frac{2^{j-1}\eps}{H_j^j}.
 \label{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:leading}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Choose real lifts $u_n$ of $P(n)$ in one interval of length $\eps$.
Every available $(j+1)$st forward difference of this sequence is an
integer, because the corresponding difference of $P$ is zero.  The
positive and negative binomial weights each sum to $2^j$.  Consequently
\[
 |\Delta^{j+1}u_n|\leq2^j\eps<1,
\]
so all these differences vanish.  Newton interpolation therefore gives
a real polynomial $Q$ of degree at most $j$ with $Q(n)=u_n$ throughout
the given interval.  If $L=j+1$, ordinary interpolation gives the same
conclusion directly, without a difference condition.

Let $\beta_j$ be the coefficient of $t^j$ in $Q$.  Since $u_n-P(n)$
is integral,
\[
 j!\beta_j=\Delta_1^j Q(0)
 \equiv \Delta_1^j P(0)=j!\alpha_j\pmod1.
\]
The points $0,H_j,\ldots,jH_j$ all lie in $[0,L-1]$.  Taking a
difference with this larger step gives
\[
 |H_j^j j!\beta_j|
 =|\Delta_{H_j}^jQ(0)|
 \leq2^{j-1}\eps.
\]
The last inequality again uses the positive and negative binomial
weights, whose sums are now $2^{j-1}$.  Dividing by $H_j^j$ and using
the congruence proves \eqref{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:leading}.
\end{proof}

This is a concrete polynomial smoothness estimate.  Such estimates are
part of the broader quantitative theory of polynomial orbits
\cite{greentaoorbits}; the elementary proof above is all that is needed
here.  The strict small-arc hypothesis is what permits the modular
differences to be lifted without an integer ambiguity.

\subsection{One prime denominator at each degree}

To avoid confusing the number of phases with the field size in the
preceding sections, write $\nu$ for the number of phases.  Fix positive
degrees $d_1,\ldots,d_\nu$, and put
\begin{equation}
 d_* =\max_i d_i,\qquad
 J=\sum_{i=1}^{\nu}d_i,\qquad
 W=\sum_{i=1}^{\nu}\frac{d_i(d_i+1)}2.
 \label{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:degrees}
\end{equation}
Thus $J$ counts the nonconstant coefficients and $W$ is their total
degree weight.

\begin{theorem}[Exact divisibility of all sufficiently long flat cells]
\label{gsr:dt:35:po:thm:divisibility}
Let $L\geq d_*+1$ and $0<\eps_i<2^{-d_i}$.  For every pair
$(i,j)$ with $1\leq i\leq\nu$ and $1\leq j\leq d_i$, choose a
prime $p_{ij}>j$.  Assume all these primes are distinct and
\begin{equation}
 p_{ij}\,2^{j-1}\eps_i
 <\left\lfloor\frac{L-1}{j}\right\rfloor^{j}.
 \label{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:prime-condition}
\end{equation}
Define
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_i(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{d_i}\frac{x^j}{p_{ij}}\pmod1,
 \qquad
 D=\prod_{i=1}^{\nu}\prod_{j=1}^{d_i}p_{ij}.
 \label{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:phases}
\end{equation}
For every integer progression $P$ of length at least $L$ and positive
step $h$, the following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\operatorname{diam}_{\rm arc}\Phi_i(P)\leq\eps_i$ for every $i$;
\item $D$ divides $h$.
\end{enumerate}
In the second case every $\Phi_i$ is constant on $P$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Assume the diameter bounds and retain the first $L$ points of $P$.
Fix $i$.  We prove $p_{ij}\mid h$ by descending induction on $j$.
Suppose this has been proved for every larger degree $t$.  Then
\[
 \frac{(a+nh)^t-a^t}{p_{it}}\in\mathbb Z
 \qquad(n\in\mathbb Z),
\]
because $p_{it}\mid h$.  Thus each term of degree greater than $j$
is constant modulo one along the progression.  Subtracting these
constants leaves a degree-$j$ polynomial in $n$ whose leading
coefficient is $h^j/p_{ij}$ and whose arc diameter is still at most
$\eps_i$.

Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:35:po:lem:lift}, applicable since
$\eps_i<2^{-d_i}\leq2^{-j}$, gives
\[
 \left\|\frac{j!h^j}{p_{ij}}\right\|_{\T}
 \leq\frac{2^{j-1}\eps_i}{\lfloor(L-1)/j\rfloor^j}
 <\frac1{p_{ij}}.
\]
If $p_{ij}\nmid h$, then $p_{ij}>j$ makes $j!h^j$ nonzero modulo
$p_{ij}$.  Its distance, divided by $p_{ij}$, from the nearest integer
is at least $1/p_{ij}$, a contradiction.  This proves $p_{ij}\mid h$
and completes the descending induction.  Repeating it for every phase
and using the distinctness of the primes proves $D\mid h$.

Conversely, if $D\mid h$, then for every term in
\eqref{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:phases} the difference $(a+nh)^j-a^j$ is divisible by
its denominator.  Every phase is therefore constant on $P$.
\end{proof}

The order of the induction matters.  A lower-degree coefficient of
$\Phi_i(a+nh)$ generally contains contributions from all higher
degrees.  Once a higher denominator divides $h$, its \emph{entire}
term becomes constant modulo one along the progression, so those
contributions disappear before the next degree is examined.

\begin{lemma}[Choosing distinct denominators]
\label{gsr:dt:35:po:lem:primes}
Set
\begin{equation}
 X_{ij}=\frac{\lfloor(L-1)/j\rfloor^j}{2^{j-1}\eps_i}.
 \label{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:X}
\end{equation}
If $X_{ij}/2^J>\max(d_*,2)$ for every pair $(i,j)$, primes satisfying
Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:35:po:thm:divisibility} can be chosen so that
\begin{equation}
 2^{-J^2}\prod_{i,j}X_{ij}<D<\prod_{i,j}X_{ij}.
 \label{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:Dfinite}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For a fixed $X=X_{ij}$, the $J$ disjoint intervals
\[
 (X/2^{u+1},X/2^u),\qquad 0\leq u<J,
\]
each contain a prime by Bertrand's postulate.  Its usual integer
form suffices: for a real lower endpoint $y>2$, apply it to
$\lfloor y\rfloor$; the resulting prime lies strictly between $y$
and $2y$.  All these primes exceed $d_*$.  Choose the pairs $(i,j)$
in any order.  At most $J-1$ primes have previously been used, so one
of the $J$ candidates is new.  It lies between $X_{ij}/2^J$ and
$X_{ij}$ and therefore satisfies \eqref{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:prime-condition}.
Multiplying the $J$ resulting inequalities proves
\eqref{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:Dfinite}.
\end{proof}

In particular, for a fixed degree list and sufficiently large $L$, this
choice is available uniformly for all tolerances in the stipulated
range.  An explicit lower constant is useful.  If $L\geq2d_*+2$, then
$\lfloor(L-1)/j\rfloor\geq L/(2j)$, and
\begin{equation}
 D>c_{\mathbf d}\,L^W\prod_{i=1}^{\nu}\eps_i^{-d_i},
 \qquad
 c_{\mathbf d}
 =2^{-J^2-\sum_i d_i^2}
   \prod_{i=1}^{\nu}\prod_{j=1}^{d_i}j^{-j}.
 \label{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:Dscale}
\end{equation}
Here and below the explicit hypothesis in Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:35:po:lem:primes}
is retained whenever a finite bound is used.  The corresponding upper
bound $D<L^W\prod_i\eps_i^{-d_i}$ follows immediately from
\eqref{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:Dfinite}.  No optimality is claimed for the constants in
\eqref{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:Dscale}.

\subsection{Exact partition thresholds and exceptional sets}

Let $\mathcal S$ be a nonempty finite set of permitted positive
lengths, with $\min\mathcal S=L$.  Write
\[
 \langle\mathcal S\rangle
 =\left\{\sum_{u\in\mathcal S}n_u u:
             n_u\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\right\}.
\]
If $\gcd(\mathcal S)=1$, its conductor $C(\mathcal S)$ is the least
integer $C$ for which every integer $n\geq C$ belongs to this
semigroup.  In particular $C-1\notin\langle\mathcal S\rangle$.
We use the term \emph{good} for progressions satisfying all the
diameter bounds in Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:35:po:thm:divisibility}.

\begin{theorem}[Exact thresholds for the constructed phases]
\label{gsr:dt:35:po:thm:thresholds}
For the phases in Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:35:po:thm:divisibility}:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The least length of an integer interval containing a good
progression of length $L$ is exactly $D(L-1)+1$.  This is independent
of the initial point of the interval.
\item If $\gcd(\mathcal S)=1$, the least integer $R_0$ such that every
interval of every length $R\geq R_0$ has a complete partition into
good progressions of lengths in $\mathcal S$ is exactly
\begin{equation}
 R_0=D\,C(\mathcal S).
 \label{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:exact-threshold}
\end{equation}
The statement permits different cells to have different steps.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Every good progression of length at least $L$ has step at least $D$.
Its integer span is therefore at least $D(L-1)$.  Conversely, a
progression of length $L$ and step $D$ is good and can start at the
first point of any interval with at least $D(L-1)+1$ points.

For the second assertion, every good cell lies in one residue class
modulo $D$.  An interval of length $DC-1$ has $D-1$ residue classes
with $C$ points and one with $C-1$ points.  A partition would express
the size of the latter class as a sum of lengths in $\mathcal S$,
contradicting the definition of the conductor.

If $R\geq DC$, every residue class in an interval of length $R$ has
at least $C$ points.  Express its size as a sum of permitted lengths
and split that residue chain into consecutive blocks of those sizes.
Every block has step $D$ and is good.  Doing this for all residue
classes gives the required complete partition.
\end{proof}

The same argument gives the full packing profile, including sizes
below the conductor.  Define
\begin{equation}
 s_{\mathcal S}(n)
 =\max\bigl(\langle\mathcal S\rangle\cap[0,n]\bigr),
 \qquad g_{\mathcal S}(n)=n-s_{\mathcal S}(n).
 \label{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:gaps}
\end{equation}
The maximum exists because zero is allowed in the semigroup.

\begin{proposition}[Exact uncovered mass]
\label{gsr:dt:35:po:prop:packing}
Write $R=aD+b$ with $0\leq b<D$.  The minimum number of uncovered
points in a packing of an interval of length $R$ by disjoint good
progressions with lengths in $\mathcal S$ is
\begin{equation}
 (D-b)g_{\mathcal S}(a)+b g_{\mathcal S}(a+1).
 \label{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:packing}
\end{equation}
This remains valid without the assumption $\gcd(\mathcal S)=1$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
There are $D-b$ residue classes of size $a$ and $b$ of size $a+1$.
All cells remain within individual classes.  The number of covered
points in a class of size $n$ is a semigroup element at most $n$, and
is therefore at most $s_{\mathcal S}(n)$.  This proves the lower bound
on uncovered points.  To attain it, use a semigroup representation of
$s_{\mathcal S}(n)$ and take consecutive blocks of the corresponding
lengths in that residue chain.  All have step $D$ and are good.
\end{proof}

Thus the exceptional-set issue is also explicit for these examples.
If $\gcd(\mathcal S)>1$, arbitrarily large residue-class sizes fail
the divisibility condition for membership in the semigroup, and no
finite full-partition threshold exists for these phases.

\subsection{Consequences for universal polynomial partition bounds}

Let $\mathcal T_{\mathcal S,\mathbf d}(\boldsymbol\eps)$ denote the
least threshold after which \emph{every} family of $\nu$ real
polynomial phases of degrees at most $d_i$ admits the prescribed
partition on every integer interval.  Allow the value $+\infty$ if
there is no such threshold.  Theorems~\ref{gsr:dt:35:po:thm:divisibility} and
\ref{gsr:dt:35:po:thm:thresholds} give the unconditional lower bound
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal T_{\mathcal S,\mathbf d}(\boldsymbol\eps)
 \geq D C(\mathcal S)
 >c_{\mathbf d} C(\mathcal S)
       L^W\prod_i\eps_i^{-d_i}.
 \label{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:universal-lower}
\end{equation}
This combines two distinct constraints: polynomial flatness forces
the step divisor $D$, and exact coverage forces the conductor.

For two consecutive permitted lengths, the elementary Frobenius
calculation gives
\begin{equation}
 C(\{L,L+1\})=L(L-1).
 \label{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:consecutive-conductor}
\end{equation}
Indeed, write $n=aL+b$, $0\leq b<L$.  If $n\geq L(L-1)$, then
$a\geq L-1\geq b$ and
$n=(a-b)L+b(L+1)$.  On the other hand, a representation
$L(L-1)-1=uL+v(L+1)$ would force $v\equiv L-1\pmod L$, and hence
$v(L+1)\geq(L-1)(L+1)>L(L-1)-1$.

Consequently \eqref{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:universal-lower} has order at least
\begin{equation}
 L^{W+2}\prod_i\eps_i^{-d_i}
 \quad\text{for }\mathcal S=\{L,L+1\}.
 \label{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:prescribed-scale}
\end{equation}
For equal degrees $d_i=k$ and equal tolerances $\eps_i=\eps$, this is
\[
 L^{\nu k(k+1)/2+2}\eps^{-k\nu}.
\]

\begin{corollary}[Necessary exponents for prescribed lengths]
\label{gsr:dt:35:po:cor:exponents}
Fix $c>0$ and $C_i>0$.  Suppose a universal assertion supplies, for
every sufficiently large integer $R$ and every integer target $L$ with
$2\leq L\leq cR^a$, a complete
partition into lengths $L$ or $L+1$, for arbitrary phases of degrees
at most $d_i$, with diameters at most $C_iR^{-b_i}$.  Assume $a>0$
and $b_i\geq0$; if $b_i=0$, require $C_i<2^{-d_i}$.
Then necessarily
\begin{equation}
 (W+2)a+\sum_i d_i b_i\leq1.
 \label{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:heterogeneous-frontier}
\end{equation}
For equal degrees and tolerances, this becomes
\begin{equation}
 \left(\frac{\nu k(k+1)}2+2\right)a+k\nu b\leq1.
 \label{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:frontier}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Fix a large target $L$ and let
$R_L=\lceil(L/c)^{1/a}\rceil$, increased by a fixed amount if
needed to enter the asserted large-$R$ range.  Put
$\eps_i=C_iR_L^{-b_i}$.  The universal assertion, applied to this
same target for every $R\geq R_L$, gives a partition with tolerance
at most $\eps_i$, since $b_i\geq0$.  Hence
\[
 \mathcal T_{\{L,L+1\},\mathbf d}(\boldsymbol\eps)\leq R_L.
\]
For large $L$ the small-arc conditions hold.  Combining this upper
bound with \eqref{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:universal-lower} and
\eqref{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:consecutive-conductor} gives, up to fixed positive
constants,
\[
 L^{1/a}\ \geq\ L^{W+2+\sum_i d_i b_i/a}.
\]
Letting $L$ tend to infinity proves
\eqref{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:heterogeneous-frontier}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 34--39]
\emph{In this report} (checked at the write). The corollary concerns partitions into the prescribed lengths $L$ or $L+1$ for every target $L$, the quantifier of Gowers's Lemma~5.9. Source~19's Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:19:poly:obstruction} ($(S+1)a+Db\le1$; at $b=2a$ for quadratics $1/(7\nu+1)$) is an obstruction for partitions with flexible lengths at least $r^a$, which implies one for prescribed lengths; the conductor contributes one more power of $L$ here, giving $(W+2)a+\sum_id_ib_i\le1$, $W=S$ (at $b=2a$: $a\le1/(\nu k(k+5)/2+2)$, which is $1/(7\nu+2)$ for quadratics and source~23's sharp $1/(3\nu+2)$ for $k=1$, Proposition~\ref{gsr:dt:23:prop:frontier}). The flexible-length obstruction of source~19 is unchanged. With Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:35:po:thm:divisibility} this answers the construction half of source~23's Question~6 (a higher-degree analogue of its mixed-radix construction; item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:I:polygap}); the matching necessity, that is a sufficient theorem in degree at least two, is open (Research question~\ref{gsr:fz:35:rq:quadratic-upper}). The intake checked the conductor formula for $L\le14$ and, by brute force over 1,162, 10,680, 14,220 and 80,968 progressions for the degrees $1$, $2$, $2$, $3$ (prime lists $(7)$, $(3,5)$, $(5,3)$, $(5,7,11)$), that flat progressions are exactly those with $D\mid h$.
\end{writenote}

The quantifier over all target lengths is the one relevant to the
prescribed-length conclusion of Gowers' Lemma~5.9.  Its role in the
proof is essential: a fixed target remains admissible as $R$ increases.
An assertion restricted to the single target $L=\lfloor cR^a\rfloor$
has different quantifiers and is not covered by this corollary.
Only the failure at $DC-1$ enters the threshold lower bound; the exact
gap profile \eqref{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:packing} allows other smaller interval lengths
to behave differently.  Replacing $L,L+1$
by $v-1,v$ only changes the target variable by one.  At the ratio
$b=2a$ used there, \eqref{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:frontier} yields
\begin{equation}
 a\leq\frac1{\nu k(k+5)/2+2}.
 \label{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:two-to-one}
\end{equation}
For quadratics the bound is $1/(7\nu+2)$, strengthening the earlier
$1/(7\nu+1)$ obstruction \cite{repo35barrier}.  At degree
one it recovers the already sharp $1/(3\nu+2)$ threshold from
\cite{repo35thresholds}.  For $k\geq2$, \eqref{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:two-to-one}
is a necessary bound; this article does not assert that it is attainable.

There is a continuous range of intermediate constraints.  For
$1\leq w\leq L-1$, the conductor is
\begin{equation}
 C(\{L,L+1,\ldots,L+w\})
 =L\left\lceil\frac{L-1}{w}\right\rceil.
 \label{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:width-conductor}
\end{equation}
To verify it, sums of exactly $u$ permitted lengths fill the interval
$[uL,u(L+w)]$.  Consecutive such intervals first meet when
$uw\geq L-1$; the integer immediately preceding that first joined
interval is the last gap.  Substitution in
\eqref{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:universal-lower} gives the scale
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal T_{\{L,\ldots,L+w\},\mathbf d}(\boldsymbol\eps)
 \geq c'_{\mathbf d}\frac{L^{W+2}}{w}
                       \prod_i\eps_i^{-d_i}
 \label{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:width-scale}
\end{equation}
for a fixed positive constant $c'_{\mathbf d}$.  When $w$ is
comparable to $L$, the extra tiling factor has order $L$; for a
fixed-width range, it has order $L^2$.

Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:35:po:thm:thresholds}(1) also gives a lower bound of order
$L^{W+1}\prod_i\eps_i^{-d_i}$ for the universal problem of finding
\emph{one} good progression of length $L$.  This has the same powers
as the earlier endpoint obstruction, but is realized here by explicit
rational coefficients and excludes every initial point.

\subsection{Cyclic moduli, an exact example, and finite checks}

The phases in \eqref{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:phases} are genuine polynomial maps on
$\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ whenever $D\mid N$: their coefficients in
that group are $N/p_{ij}$.  For the bad interval of length
$R=DC-1$, take $N=DC=R+1$.  Thus the construction fits the
interval-within-a-cyclic-group interface with an ambient modulus only
one larger than the interval.  This exact modulus is generally composite.

\begin{proposition}[Transfer of the obstruction to prime moduli]
\label{gsr:dt:35:po:prop:prime-transfer}
Fix $R$ and construct an obstruction above with tolerances $2\eps_i$,
where $2\eps_i<2^{-d_i}$.  Choose a prime $N>2R$ large enough that
\begin{equation}
 N\geq\max_i\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{d_i}(R-1)^j}{\eps_i}.
 \label{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:prime-size}
\end{equation}
For each coefficient $1/p_{ij}$ choose an integer $a_{ij}$ nearest
to $N/p_{ij}$.  Then the polynomial phases
\[
 \widetilde\Phi_i(x)=\sum_j\frac{a_{ij}}N x^j\pmod1
\]
retain the obstruction at the smaller tolerances $\eps_i$ on
$\{0,\ldots,R-1\}$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
At every point in this interval, the difference of the two real
polynomials has absolute value at most
\[
 \frac1{2N}\sum_{j=1}^{d_i}(R-1)^j\leq\frac{\eps_i}{2}.
\]
If the values of $\widetilde\Phi_i$ on a progression lie in an arc
of length $\eps_i$, expanding that arc by $\eps_i/2$ at both ends
contains the corresponding values of $\Phi_i$.  They therefore have
diameter at most $2\eps_i$.  Such a progression must have step
divisible by $D$.  A prohibited partition would consequently give
the same impossible residue-class tiling as before.
\end{proof}

The extra condition $N>2R$ also covers proper modular progressions
whose carriers lie in this short integer interval.  Consecutive integer
representatives differ by numbers in $[-(R-1),R-1]$ that are congruent
modulo $N$.  Since this range has width less than $N$, those differences
are equal.  The progression therefore has an ordinary integer lift,
with positive difference after reversal if necessary.

The prime modulus in \eqref{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:prime-size} may be much larger
than $R$.  A restriction to prime ambient moduli comparable with the
interval length is a different problem and is not resolved by this
approximation argument.

For a small exact example, let $L=3$, $\eps=1/16$, and
\begin{equation}
 \Phi(x)=\frac{x}{31}+\frac{x^2}{7}\pmod1.
 \label{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:example}
\end{equation}
The prime conditions are $31/16<2$ and $7/8<1$, so every
$1/16$-flat progression of length at least three has step divisible
by $D=217$.  If the permitted lengths are three and four, their
conductor is six.  An interval of length $1301=217\cdot6-1$ has
one residue class with five points; five is not a sum of threes and
fours.  At length $1302$, every class has six points and splits into
two triples of step $217$.  Over $\mathbb Z/1302\mathbb Z$, the
same phase is represented by
\[
 x\longmapsto42x+186x^2.
\]
An integer arc diameter at most $\lfloor1302/16\rfloor=81$ is
therefore insufficient for the prohibited partition.

The accompanying standard-library checker exhaustively tests all
starting residues and all step residues for three examples.  It computes
arc diameters with integer residues, without floating-point arithmetic.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{rrrrrr}
\hline
Degree & $L$ & Tolerance & $D$ & Pairs tested & Good pairs\\
\hline
2 & 3 & $1/16$ & 217 & 47,089 & 217\\
2 & 4 & $1/16$ & 301 & 90,601 & 301\\
3 & 4 & $1/64$ & 385 & 148,225 & 385\\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
In each row the good pairs are exactly the zero step modulo $D$, with
arbitrary starting residue.  The program also checks the semigroup
obstructions and a prime-modulus approximation of
\eqref{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:example}.  These finite checks support the exact examples;
the proofs establish the general assertions.

\subsection{What remains to determine}

The construction answers the higher-degree divisibility question in
\cite{repo35thresholds} and strengthens the prescribed-length
obstruction from \cite{repo35barrier}.  Further targets include:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item Can general quadratic phases attain a prescribed-length upper
bound at the scale $L^{3\nu+2}\eps^{-2\nu}$, up to constants or
subpower factors?
\item Can the leading constants be improved by replacing
Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:35:po:lem:lift} with the exact discrete minimax bound on a
polynomial's leading coefficient, and by optimizing the denominator
construction?
\item Does the same obstruction scale hold for prime ambient moduli
restricted by $N\asymp R$?
\item Must nearly extremal obstructions exhibit a comparable hierarchy
of rational coefficients, in a suitable quantified metric?
\item Can the exact gap profile \eqref{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:packing} improve a
density-increment argument that permits a controlled exceptional set?
\end{enumerate}

\section{Sources~41 and~42: Corollary~5.8 in every degree, and the quadratic variance scale \wtag}\label{gsr:dt:sec:alldegree}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the eighth write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next twelve sections are source~41's Sections~2--7 and source~42's Sections~2--7. \emph{Logically they close the chapter of sources~26 and~32} (Section~\ref{gsr:dt:sec:cor58}, Corollary~5.8 without a scale threshold in degrees one and two), after source~32's Section~5; they are printed here, at the end of Part~I, because no number printed earlier may move. Sources~41 (Report277) and~42 (Report278) continue the series of sources~26 (Report275) and~32 (Report276). Their introductions are Sections~\ref{gsr:fm:41:sec:d1} and~\ref{gsr:fm:42:sec:d1}; their source comparisons and questions are in Part~V.

\emph{What source~41 proves, in one paragraph.} Let $A\subseteq\Z/N\Z$ be covered by pairwise disjoint, two-comparable proper modular progressions $P_1,\ldots,P_M$, with coefficient polynomials of degree at most $k$ whose summed correlations with $\one_A-\delta$ are at least $\alpha N$. Then some proper progression $Q$ has $|A\cap Q|\ge(\delta+\alpha/3)|Q|$ and $|Q|\ge\max\{1,(N/M)^{1/D_k}/8\}$, $D_1=4$, $D_k=(k!)^22^{(k+1)^2}/4+1$, with no lower bound on $\alpha$ or $N/M$ and no primality hypothesis (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:41:thm:main}). The ingredients: tent-function Fourier detection and Weyl differencing with an explicit ordered-divisor constant give $p\le2^{A_k}R^{B_k}$ with $\norm{\theta p^k}<1/R$ for every real $\theta$ and every integer $R\ge2$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:41:thm:generalrec}); a recursive localization keeps every point and partitions any interval of length at least $2^{c_k}L^{e_k}$ into progressions of lengths $L$ to $2L-1$ on which the phase varies by less than $1/(4L)$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:41:thm:localization}), with $c_k+e_k\le K_k/4$ (Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:41:lem:Kbudget}); the subgroup-coset variance lemma (Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:41:lem:variance}) handles small $\alpha$, and large $\alpha$ forces long parents (Section~\ref{gsr:dt:41:sec:d6}). Section~\ref{gsr:dt:41:sec:d7} keeps the exact budgets, a compact bound $2^{-(k+8)}(N/M)^{1/(12\mathcal P_k+1)}$ with limiting constants, and the sharper bounds in degrees one, two and three: the first two are source~26's Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:26:cor:comparable} and source~32's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:32:thm:main}, the third, $\max\{1,(N/M)^{1/4096}/8\}$, is new. The two-regime method is that of sources~26 and~32; source~41 runs it in every degree. The constants are deliberately weak; the main bound is nontrivial only for $N/M>8^{D_k}$ ($4{,}096$ for $k=1$, $8^{513}$ for $k=2$), the variance branch may leave the cover, and no rectification is claimed.

\emph{What source~42 proves.} With $m$ the largest divisor of $N$ below $L$ and $q=N/m$, every $A\subseteq\Z/N\Z$ of density $0<\delta<1$ has a proper $L$-term progression of density at least $\delta+\frac{1-\delta}L\frac{\max\{q-L,0\}}{q-1}$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:42:thm:main}), by sampling the step as a difference of independent samples from an interval of admissible steps; so the gain $(1-\delta)/(2L)$ of the variance lemma of sources~26, 32 and~41 holds already for $N\ge2(L-1)^2+1$ in place of $N\ge L^3$, and the coefficient $1-1/C$ under $N\ge CL^2$ is best possible uniformly in the density, with equality on the prime-quotient sets $p\Z/p(L-1)\Z$ (Corollary~\ref{gsr:fm:42:cor:scale}, Theorems~\ref{gsr:dt:42:thm:sharp}, \ref{gsr:dt:42:thm:constant}); a sliding-window argument gives gain greater than $\delta(1-\delta)/(2L)$ for $N>L(L-1)$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:42:thm:endpoint}); in source~26's affine exact-mass bound the modulus cap $(N/8)^{1/3}$ becomes $\sqrt{N/2}$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:42:thm:affine}). Source~42 does not change source~41's all-degree exponents (it says so), and its Proposition~\ref{gsr:dt:42:prop:packing} is the Kolountzakis--R\'ev\'esz bound.

\section[{An explicit quadratic recurrence estimate\srctag{41}}]{An explicit quadratic recurrence estimate}\label{gsr:dt:41:sec:d2}\label{gsr:dt:41:sec:recurrence}
\srcnote{41}{Section 2}

We give the exponential-sum argument in full, including the denominator and tail bounds. All logarithms are natural.

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 40--46]
\emph{This section is source~32's Section~2, character for character} (Section~\ref{gsr:dt:32:sec:d2}; a line diff of the two delivered sections finds no difference): Lemmas~\ref{gsr:dt:41:lem:dirichlet}, \ref{gsr:dt:41:lem:weyl}, \ref{gsr:dt:41:lem:recurrence} and Remark~\ref{gsr:dt:41:rem:conditional} are source~32's Lemmas~\ref{gsr:dt:32:lem:dirichlet}, \ref{gsr:dt:32:lem:weyl}, \ref{gsr:dt:32:lem:recurrence} and Remark~\ref{gsr:dt:32:rem:conditional}. It is printed again because source~41's later sections cite these labels; the reader of source~32's chapter may skip it.
\end{writenote}

\begin{lemma}[Circle approximation]\label{gsr:dt:41:lem:dirichlet}
For a real $\beta$ and an integer $D\ge1$, there are integers $a,q$ with
\[
 1\le q\le D,\qquad \gcd(a,q)=1,
 \qquad \left|\beta-\frac aq\right|\le\frac1{qD}.
\]
There is also, without the coprimality requirement, an integer $1\le q\le D$ such that $\norm{q\beta}\le1/(D+1)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Consider $0,\beta,\ldots,D\beta$ on the unit circle. If two coincide, their index difference gives distance zero. Otherwise some circular gap between neighboring points is at most $1/(D+1)$. The absolute difference of their indices gives $1\le q_0\le D$ and an integer $a_0$ with $|q_0\beta-a_0|\le1/(D+1)$. This also covers a gap crossing zero. Reduce $a_0/q_0$ to $a/q$. Then $q\le q_0\le D$ and
\[
 \left|\beta-\frac aq\right|
 \le\frac1{q_0(D+1)}\le\frac1{qD}.
\]
The unreduced pair supplies the second assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Quadratic exponential sum]\label{gsr:dt:41:lem:weyl}
Let $T\ge2$ be an integer, let $\omega\in\R$, and put $\beta=2\omega$. If
\[
 \gcd(a,q)=1,\qquad 1\le q\le T,\qquad
 |\beta-a/q|\le1/(qT),
\]
then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:weyl}
 \left|\sum_{n=1}^T e(\omega n^2)\right|^2
 \le\frac{8T^2}{q}+32T\log(2T).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The case $q=1$ follows from the trivial bound $T^2$. Suppose $q\ge2$ and put $b=\lfloor q/2\rfloor\ge q/3$. Split $\{1,\ldots,T-1\}$ into consecutive blocks of at most $b$ terms. Their number is at most $T/b+1\le4T/q$.

For distinct indices $u,v$ in the same block, $0<|u-v|<q/2$. Coprimality and $q\le T$ give
\[
 \norm{\beta(u-v)}
 \ge\norm{a(u-v)/q}-\frac{|u-v|}{qT}
 \ge\frac1q-\frac1{2T}\ge\frac1{2q}.
\]
Thus the points $\beta u$ belonging to one block have pairwise circle distance at least $1/(2q)$. Order their distances from zero as $d_1\le\cdots\le d_m$. An arc of length $2d$ contains at most $4qd+1$ such points, so
\[
 d_j\ge\frac{j-1}{4q}.
\]
Interpreting $1/0$ as infinity, it follows that
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{u\text{ in block}}\min\left(T,\frac1{2\norm{\beta u}}\right)
 &\le T+\sum_{j=2}^m\frac{2q}{j-1}\\
 &\le T+2q(1+\log q).
\end{align*}
The last step uses $\sum_{j=1}^{s}1/j\le1+\log s$ for $s\ge1$; the empty sum causes no problem. Summing over blocks gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:spacing}
 \sum_{u=1}^{T-1}\min\left(T,\frac1{2\norm{\beta u}}\right)
 \le\frac{4T^2}{q}+8T(1+\log q).
\end{equation}

For a geometric sum, $|1-e(t)|=2|\sin(\pi t)|\ge4\norm{t}$, and consequently
\[
 \left|\sum_{n=1}^K e(nt)\right|
 \le\min\left(K,\frac1{2\norm{t}}\right).
\]
Expanding the squared quadratic sum and grouping pairs by their difference $u$ now yields
\begin{align*}
 \left|\sum_{n=1}^T e(\omega n^2)\right|^2
 &\le T+2\sum_{u=1}^{T-1}
        \left|\sum_{n=1}^{T-u}e(2\omega un)\right|\\
 &\le\frac{8T^2}{q}+17T+16T\log T\\
 &\le\frac{8T^2}{q}+32T\log(2T).
\end{align*}
Here the constant phase $e(\omega u^2)$ has modulus one. The last inequality holds for $T\ge2$, since $17\le32\log2+16\log T$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Uniform quadratic recurrence]\label{gsr:dt:41:lem:recurrence}
For every real $\theta$ and every integer $R\ge2$, there is an integer $p$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:recurrence}
 1\le p\le2^{10}R^5,\qquad \norm{\theta p^2}<1/R.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Set $T=2^{10}R^5$ and $H=4R^2$. Suppose for a contradiction that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:nohit}
 \norm{\theta n^2}\ge1/R\qquad(1\le n\le T).
\end{equation}
On $\R/\Z$ consider the continuous triangle function
\[
 F(x)=\max\{1-R\norm{x},0\}.
\]
Its Fourier coefficients are
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:fourier}
 c_0=1/R,\qquad
 c_h=R\left(\frac{\sin(\pi h/R)}{\pi h}\right)^2\ge0
 \quad(h\ne0).
\end{equation}
For example, $F$ is $R$ times the circle convolution of the indicator of $[-1/(2R),1/(2R)]$ with itself. Integrating that indicator against $e(-hx)$ and squaring gives \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:fourier}. Also $c_h\le R/(\pi^2h^2)$, so the Fourier series is absolutely and uniformly convergent.

For completeness, this series indeed equals $F$. The Fej\'er kernel of order $J$ is
\[
 K_J(x)=\frac1{J+1}\left|\sum_{v=0}^J e(vx)\right|^2.
\]
It is nonnegative, its integral is one by termwise integration, and away from zero it is bounded by $1/((J+1)\sin^2(\pi x))$. Consequently convolution with $K_J$ converges uniformly to any continuous periodic function: uniform continuity controls the near-zero integral, and the displayed bound controls the complement. Applied to $F$, these convolutions are also the Fej\'er averages of its absolutely convergent Fourier series, whose limit is the series itself. Hence $F(x)=\sum_h c_he(hx)$, and at zero
\[
 \sum_{h\in\Z}c_h=F(0)=1.
\]
The high-frequency tail satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:tail}
 \sum_{|h|>H}c_h
 \le\frac{2R}{\pi^2}\sum_{h>H}h^{-2}
 \le\frac{2R}{\pi^2H}<\frac1{2R}.
\end{equation}

Write $S_h=\sum_{n=1}^T e(h\theta n^2)$. Assumption \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:nohit} says that $F(\theta n^2)=0$ for all $n$ in the sum. Interchanging a finite sum and the absolutely convergent Fourier series gives
\[
 0=\frac TR+\sum_{h\ne0}c_hS_h.
\]
Using $|S_h|\le T$ and \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:tail}, we obtain
\[
 \left|\sum_{0<|h|\le H}c_hS_h\right|>\frac{T}{2R}.
\]
Since the coefficients in this sum have total at most one and $S_{-h}=\overline{S_h}$, some integer $1\le h\le H$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:largeS}
 |S_h|>T/(2R).
\end{equation}

Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:41:lem:dirichlet} with denominator budget $T$ to $\beta=2h\theta$. For the resulting relatively prime $a,q$, Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:41:lem:weyl} and \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:largeS} give
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:qbound}
 \frac1{4R^2}<\frac8q+\frac{32\log(2T)}T.
\end{equation}
For $R\ge2$, one has $\log R\le R/2$: the difference $R/2-\log R$ is positive at two and nondecreasing thereafter. Therefore
\[
 \log(2T)=11\log2+5\log R<8R.
\]
Indeed $11\log2<11\le11R/2$. Since
\[
 T=1024R^5\ge4096R^3>256R^2\log(2T),
\]
the second term on the right of \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:qbound} is less than $1/(8R^2)$. It follows that $q<64R^2$.

Set $p=2hq$. Then
\[
 1\le p<512R^4<T,
 \qquad \norm{\beta q}\le1/T,
\]
and the exact identity $\theta p^2=p(\beta q)$ gives
\[
 \norm{\theta p^2}\le p\norm{\beta q}
 \le\frac pT<\frac1{2R}<\frac1R.
\]
This contradicts \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:nohit}, since this integer $p$ lies in its excluded interval. The contradiction proves \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:recurrence}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}\label{gsr:dt:41:rem:conditional}
The bound $p<512R^4$ in the last paragraph is obtained \emph{under the contradiction hypothesis} \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:nohit}. That hypothesis was used to force the large Fourier coefficient. It does not establish an unconditional $R^4$ recurrence theorem. The bound carried into every subsequent argument is $2^{10}R^5$.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Explicit recurrence in every degree\srctag{41}}]{Explicit recurrence in every degree}\label{gsr:dt:41:sec:d3}\label{gsr:dt:41:sec:generalrec}
\srcnote{41}{Section 3}
The argument is classical repeated differencing with deliberately generous constants. The point of the calculations is uniformity down to the smallest permitted scales, not a sharp recurrence exponent.

\begin{lemma}[An explicit ordered divisor estimate]\label{gsr:dt:41:lem:divisor}
Let $d_s(m)$ count ordered $s$-tuples of positive integers with product $m$. For all integers $s,m\ge1$,
\[
 d_s(m)\le 2^{3s^{2s+2}}m^{1/(2s)}.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For a prime power $\ell^a$, unique factorization gives
$d_s(\ell^a)=\binom{a+s-1}{s-1}$. This counts weak compositions of $a$ into $s$ parts. Each composition is realized by a word of length $a$ over an $s$-letter alphabet, and words realizing different compositions are disjoint. Hence this binomial coefficient is at most $s^a$. If $\ell\ge s^{2s}$, it is at most $\ell^{a/(2s)}$.

For the remaining primes use $\binom{a+s-1}{s-1}\le(a+1)^s$. Write $a=2s^2b+t$ with $0\le t<2s^2$. Since $b+1\le2^b$ for every integer $b\ge0$,
\begin{align*}
 (a+1)^s&\le(2s^2)^s(b+1)^s
 \le(2s^2)^s2^{sb}\\
 &\le(2s^2)^s2^{a/(2s)}
 \le2^{3s^2}\ell^{a/(2s)}.
\end{align*}
The final constant uses $s+2s\log_2s\le3s^2$. There are at most $s^{2s}$ primes below $s^{2s}$. Multiplying the prime-power estimates therefore costs at most
$2^{3s^2s^{2s}}=2^{3s^{2s+2}}$. For $m=1$ the empty product is one. For $s=1$ the small-prime range is empty, so that endpoint is included.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Tracked repeated differencing]\label{gsr:dt:41:lem:generalweyl}
Let $k\ge2$, $s=k-1$, $w=2^s$, and $C=2^{3s^{2s+2}}$. Let $P$ be a real polynomial of degree at most $k$, with coefficient $\omega$ at $x^k$, and let $T\ge2$ be an integer. Set $\beta=k!\omega$. If coprime integers $a,q$ satisfy
\[
 1\le q\le T^s,\qquad |\beta-a/q|\le1/(qT^s),
\]
then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:generalweyl}
 \left|\frac1T\sum_{n=1}^T e(P(n))\right|^w
 \le \frac{s2^{w-2}}T
      +\frac{C2^{w+1}T^{1/2}}q
      +\frac{C2^{w+2}(1+\log q)}{T^{1/2}}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Put $S_P=\sum_{n=1}^T e(P(n))$ and $\Delta_hP(n)=P(n+h)-P(n)$. Repeated correlation expansion and Cauchy--Schwarz give, for $1\le j\le s$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:differencing}
 |S_P|^{2^j}\le(2T)^{2^j-j-1}
 \sum_{|h_1|,\ldots,|h_j|<T}
 \left|\sum_{n\in I_{\boldsymbol h}}
 e(\Delta_{h_j}\cdots\Delta_{h_1}P(n))\right|.
\end{equation}
Here $I_{\boldsymbol h}$ is the intersection of the original interval with the translates that keep every required shifted argument inside it; it is an integer interval, possibly empty, of length at most $T$. At $j=1$ the bound is the expansion of $|S_P|^2$ followed by the triangle inequality. To pass from $j$ to $j+1$, square the right side and use Cauchy--Schwarz over at most $(2T)^j$ shift tuples. Expand the square of each inner interval sum by correlations and take absolute values. The new prefactor exponent is
\[
 2(2^j-j-1)+j=2^{j+1}-j-2,
\]
which proves \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:differencing}. Padding any shorter shift ranges to $|h|<T$ adds only nonnegative quantities.

At $j=s$, a tuple with a zero shift has identically zero phase. At most $s(2T)^{s-1}$ tuples have a zero coordinate. Bounding each inner sum by $T$ and dividing by $T^w$ gives their contribution $s2^{w-2}/T$.

For nonzero shifts the phase is linear, with linear coefficient
$\beta h_1\cdots h_s$. This follows by differencing the leading monomial $k-1$ times; the lower terms contribute only to the constant term. The geometric-sum bound used in Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:41:lem:weyl} applies to any interval of length at most $T$. Replacing shifts by their absolute values costs at most $2^s$ sign choices. For each positive product $m$, there are at most $d_s(m)$ positive tuples, and $m\le T^s$. Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:41:lem:divisor} gives $d_s(m)\le CT^{1/2}$. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:productsum}
 |S_P/T|^w\le\frac{s2^{w-2}}T+
 C2^{w-1}T^{-k+1/2}
 \sum_{m=1}^{T^s}\min\left(T,\frac1{2\norm{\beta m}}\right).
\end{equation}
A zero distance in this minimum is interpreted as the value $T$. The displayed normalization is the product of $(2T)^{w-s-1}/T^w$, the $2^s$ sign choices, and $CT^{1/2}$; thus it contains no suppressed shift factor.

For $q\ge2$, divide $\{1,\ldots,T^s\}$ into consecutive blocks of length at most $\lfloor q/2\rfloor$. Since $\lfloor q/2\rfloor\ge q/3$ and $q\le T^s$, at most $4T^s/q$ blocks suffice. In one block a nonzero index difference has $|u|<q/2$, so
\[
 \norm{\beta u}\ge\frac1q-\frac{|u|}{qT^s}\ge\frac1{2q}.
\]
The points in that block are $1/(2q)$-separated on the circle. Ordering their distances from zero as $d_1\le\cdots\le d_b$, the interval $[-d_j,d_j]$ must accommodate $j$ separated points, whence $d_j\ge(j-1)/(4q)$. Each block contributes at most
$T+2q(1+\log q)$ to the sum in \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:productsum}, by the harmonic-sum estimate; an empty harmonic sum is zero. Hence
\[
 \sum_{m=1}^{T^s}\min\left(T,\frac1{2\norm{\beta m}}\right)
 \le\frac{4T^{s+1}}q+8T^s(1+\log q).
\]
For $q=1$ this follows already from the trivial bound $T^{s+1}$. Substitution into \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:productsum} proves \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:generalweyl}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Threshold free monomial recurrence]\label{gsr:dt:41:thm:generalrec}
For every integer $k\ge2$, define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:recconstants}
 \begin{split}
 s&=k-1,\quad w=2^s,\quad \gamma=3s^{2s+2},\\
 B_k&=2w+8=2^k+8,\qquad A_k=16(w+\gamma+k^2).
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
For every real $\theta$ and every integer $R\ge2$, there is an integer $p$ with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:generalrec}
 1\le p\le2^{A_k}R^{B_k},\qquad \norm{\theta p^k}<1/R.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Set $T=2^{A_k}R^{B_k}$, an integer, and suppose that no $1\le n\le T$ has $\norm{\theta n^k}<1/R$. The tent-function proof of Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:41:lem:recurrence} uses only the sampled real numbers, not the fact that their exponent is two. Applying exactly its Fourier coefficients \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:fourier}, inversion argument, and tail estimate \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:tail} to $\theta n^k$, some $1\le h\le4R^2$ has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:largedeg}
 \left|\sum_{n=1}^T e(h\theta n^k)\right|>T/(2R).
\end{equation}
The samples are counted with multiplicity; no distinctness of their images is assumed.

Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:41:lem:dirichlet} with denominator budget $T^s$ to $\beta=k!h\theta$, and then apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:41:lem:generalweyl}. Its left side exceeds
$W=2^{-w}R^{-w}$. We now show that the first and third right-side terms of \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:generalweyl} have sum less than $W/2$.

Write $A=A_k$, $B=B_k$, and $C=2^\gamma$ in the following estimates. The first term divided by $W$ is
\[
 s2^{2w-2-A}R^{-w-8}<1/4,
\]
since $s\le2^{k^2}$ and $A\ge k^2+2w$. For the third term, $q\le T^s$, $\log R\le R$, and $R\ge2$ give
\[
 1+\log q\le1+s\log T\le s(A+B+1)R.
\]
Its ratio to $W$ is consequently at most
\[
 2^{\gamma+2w+2-A/2}s(A+B+1)R^{-3}
 \le2^{\gamma+2w-1-A/2}s(A+B+1).
\]
Here $A\ge64$, $B+1\le A$, and $s\le A/2$, so
$s(A+B+1)\le A^2\le2^{A/4}$. The last inequality holds at $A=64$ and continues for larger $A$: the derivative of $(A/4)\log2-2\log A$ is positive there. Thus the ratio is at most
\[
 2^{\gamma+2w-1-A/4}
 =2^{-3\gamma-2w-4k^2-1}<1/4.
\]
All these comparisons include $k=2,R=2$.

The middle term of \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:generalweyl} must therefore exceed $W/2$, yielding
\[
 q<C2^{2w+2}T^{1/2}R^w.
\]
Set $p=k!hq$. This is a positive integer and
\[
 p<V T^{1/2}R^{w+2},\qquad V=k!C2^{2w+4}.
\]
Since $k!\le2^{k^2}$,
\[
 \log_2 V\le k^2+\gamma+2w+4\le A/2;
\]
the slack in the second inequality is $6w+7\gamma+7k^2-4>0$.
Using $B/2=w+4$, we obtain
\[
 p<2^{A/2}T^{1/2}R^{w+2}=T/R^2<T.
\]
The rational approximation gives $\norm{\beta q}\le T^{-s}$. The exact real identity $\beta q=\theta p$ and multiplication by the integer $p^s$ imply
\[
 \norm{\theta p^k}\le p^s\norm{\beta q}
 \le(p/T)^s<R^{-2s}<1/R.
\]
This contradicts the assumed exclusion for $1\le p\le T$, proving the theorem.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The conditional witness is not a stronger recurrence theorem]\label{gsr:dt:41:rem:genconditional}
The integer with $p<T/R^2$ was manufactured after assuming that the whole interval $1\le n\le T$ contains no recurrence. That assumption supplied \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:largedeg}. The unconditional conclusion is \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:generalrec}, with budget $T$; the internal comparison cannot simply be promoted to a smaller global budget. Likewise, the quadratic argument carries the unconditional $2^{10}R^5$ bound, not its conditional $R^4$ witness.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[A sharper cubic constant]\label{gsr:dt:41:cor:cubicrec}
For every real $\theta$ and every integer $R\ge2$, some integer $1\le p\le2^{128}R^{16}$ satisfies $\norm{\theta p^3}<1/R$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For $s=2$, $d_2(m)\le2^{12}m^{1/4}$. Indeed $d_2(\ell^a)=a+1$. For primes $\ell\ge16$, $a+1\le2^a\le\ell^{a/4}$. For each of the six primes $2,3,5,7,11,13$, write $a=4b+t$ with $0\le t<4$; then $a+1\le4(b+1)\le4\cdot2^b\le4\ell^{a/4}$. Their constants multiply to $4^6$.

Weaken this to $C=2^{16}$ and reuse the proof of Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:41:lem:generalweyl}, which at $k=3$ gives
\[
 |S_P/T|^4\le8/T+32CT^{1/2}/q+
 64C(1+\log q)/T^{1/2}.
\]
Take $T=2^{128}R^{16}$ and $W=1/(16R^4)$. Under the exclusion hypothesis, Fourier detection supplies $1\le h\le4R^2$. Apply the displayed estimate to $P(n)=h\theta n^3$, so $\beta=6h\theta$; its left side is greater than $W$, and Dirichlet gives $q\le T^2$. The first term divided by $W$ is $2^{-121}R^{-12}<1/4$. Moreover
\[
 1+\log q\le1+2\log T\le1+256+32R\le161R,
\]
since $257\le129R$ for $R\ge2$. The third term divided by $W$ is at most $2^{-38}161/R^3<1/4$. Therefore
\[
 q<1024CT^{1/2}R^4,\qquad
 p=6hq<24576CT^{1/2}R^6<2^{31}T^{1/2}R^6<T/R^2.
\]
The last comparison is $2^{95}R^{14}<2^{128}R^{14}$. The approximation and the same integer identity give
\[
 \norm{\theta p^3}\le(p/T)^2<R^{-4}<1/R.
\]
The first comparison is weak, as warranted by Dirichlet approximation; the next ones are strict. This is the desired contradiction. The general formula gives $A_3=3280$, $B_3=16$, so the sharper constant is an alternative to that general specialization.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Lossless phase partitions\srctag{41}}]{Lossless phase partitions}\label{gsr:dt:41:sec:d4}\label{gsr:dt:41:sec:partition}
\srcnote{41}{Section 4}

The partitions below keep every point. A basic rounding fact is useful: a chain of length $s\ge L$ can be partitioned into chunks of lengths from $L$ through $2L-1$. Write $s=hL+b$ with $h\ge1$ and $0\le b<L$, use $h-1$ chunks of length $L$, and a last chunk of length $L+b$.

\begin{lemma}[Affine refinement]\label{gsr:dt:41:lem:affine}
Let $m,L$ be integers with $1\le L\le m$, and let $\ell,c\in\R$. The index interval $\{0,\ldots,m-1\}$ has a partition into arithmetic progressions $C$ of lengths $L\le|C|\le2L-1$ and complex units $z_C$ for which
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:affine}
 |e(-(\ell j+c))-z_C|\le\frac{2\pi L^2}{m}\qquad(j\in C).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Put $D=\lfloor m/L\rfloor\ge1$. By the circle part of Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:41:lem:dirichlet}, choose $1\le q\le D$ with $\norm{q\ell}\le1/(D+1)$. Split the interval into its residue chains modulo $q$. Every chain has at least $\lfloor m/q\rfloor\ge L$ points. Apply the chunking rule above to each chain.

Write $q\ell=v+\epsilon$, where $v\in\Z$ and $|\epsilon|\le1/(D+1)$. For a chunk $j=j_0+tq$, $0\le t<s$, set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:midpoint}
 z_C=e(-(\ell j_0+c))e(-\epsilon(s-1)/2).
\end{equation}
The integer $vt$ does not affect the exponential. The chord--arc inequality gives
\begin{align*}
 |e(-(\ell j+c))-z_C|
 &\le2\pi|\epsilon|\left|t-\frac{s-1}{2}\right|\\
 &\le\pi|\epsilon|(s-1)
 \le\frac{2\pi(L-1)}{D+1}
 <\frac{2\pi L^2}{m}
\end{align*}
when $L>1$, using $D+1>m/L$. When $L=1$, every chunk is a singleton and the error is zero. This proves the stated weak bound in all cases.
\end{proof}

The reduction before taking the midpoint in \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:midpoint} matters. If $q\ell=1$ and $s=2$, both sampled phase values agree, while the midpoint obtained from the unreduced increment contributes $e(-1/2)=-1$. The reduced increment is zero and its midpoint has the correct phase. Integer shifts are harmless at integer parameters but need not be harmless at half-integer midpoints.


\begin{lemma}[Quadratic refinement for real coefficients]\label{gsr:dt:41:lem:quadratic}
Let $n,L$ be integers with $L\ge2$ and $n\ge2^{116}L^{38}$. For every real polynomial $p_0$ of degree at most two on $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ there is a partition into integer arithmetic progressions $C$, with units $z_C$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:quadratic}
 L\le|C|\le2L-1,\qquad |e(-p_0(j))-z_C|<1/(4L)\quad(j\in C).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Write $p_0(j)=\theta j^2+\beta j+\gamma_0$ with real coefficients, and set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:budgets}
 H=64L^3=2^6L^3,\quad R=256LH^2=2^{20}L^7,
 \quad T=2^{10}R^5=2^{110}L^{35}.
\end{equation}
All are integers, and $R\ge2$. Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:41:lem:recurrence} supplies $1\le p\le T$ with $\norm{\theta p^2}<1/R$. Since $n\ge TH\ge pH$, each residue chain modulo $p$ in the index interval has at least $H$ terms. Chunk each into lengths $H$ through $2H-1$ by the rule above.

On a piece $j=j_0+pt$, $0\le t<m$, where $H\le m\le2H-1$, expansion gives
\[
 p_0(j_0+pt)=\theta p^2t^2+\ell t+c_0,
 \quad \ell=2\theta j_0p+\beta p,\quad c_0=p_0(j_0).
\]
Choose $v\in\Z$ with $\epsilon=\theta p^2-v$ and $|\epsilon|<1/R$. Subtracting $vt^2$ leaves the exponential unchanged at integer $t$. The chord--arc inequality gives
\[
 |e(-p_0(j_0+pt))-e(-(\ell t+c_0))|
 \le2\pi|\epsilon|t^2<8\pi H^2/R=\pi/(32L).
\]
Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:41:lem:affine} to the remaining affine phase at target $L$. Its error is at most $2\pi L^2/m\le2\pi L^2/H=\pi/(32L)$. Their sum is less than $\pi/(16L)<1/(4L)$. Each final cell $t=t_0+qv$ gives an arithmetic progression $j=j_0+pt_0+pqv$ in the original interval. These cells remain disjoint and retain every index. Finally $TH=2^{116}L^{38}$, as required.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Recursive polynomial localization]\label{gsr:dt:41:thm:localization}
Set $c_2=116$, $e_2=38$. For each integer $k\ge3$, use $A_k,B_k$ from \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:recconstants} and define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:recursivebudget}
 \begin{split}
 m_k&=kB_k+1,\\
 e_k&=B_k+m_ke_{k-1},\\
 c_k&=A_k+(k+7)B_k+m_k(c_{k-1}+e_{k-1}),\\
 F_k(L)&=2^{c_k}L^{e_k}.
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
Also set $F_2(L)=2^{116}L^{38}$. For integers $n,L$ with $L\ge2$ and $n\ge F_k(L)$, every real polynomial $p_0$ of degree at most $k$ on $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ has a partition into arithmetic progressions $C$, with units $z_C$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:Pk}
 L\le|C|\le2L-1,\qquad |e(-p_0(j))-z_C|<1/(4L)\quad(j\in C).
\end{equation}
For degree at most one, $n\ge64L^3$ is sufficient.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The degree-two assertion is Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:41:lem:quadratic}. For degree one, Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:41:lem:affine} gives error at most $2\pi L^2/n\le\pi/(32L)<1/(4L)$.

Suppose $k\ge3$ and the assertion holds at degree $k-1$. Set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:localscales}
 H=F_{k-1}(2L)=2^{c_{k-1}+e_{k-1}}L^{e_{k-1}},
 \quad R=2^{k+7}LH^k,
 \quad T=2^{A_k}R^{B_k}.
\end{equation}
Every scale is an integer and $R\ge2$. The definitions give the exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:THidentity}
 TH=2^{A_k+(k+7)B_k}L^{B_k}H^{kB_k+1}
    =2^{c_k}L^{e_k}=F_k(L).
\end{equation}
Let $\theta$ be the coefficient of $x^k$ in $p_0$. Then Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:41:thm:generalrec} supplies $1\le p\le T$ with $\norm{\theta p^k}<1/R$. This coefficient is zero when the degree is below $k$. Split the index interval into residue chains modulo $p$. Each has at least $H$ terms since $n\ge TH\ge pH$. The chunking rule splits each chain into pieces of lengths $H$ through $2H-1$.

On one such piece write $j=j_0+pt$, $0\le t<m$, with $H\le m\le2H-1$. For some real polynomial $\psi$ of degree at most $k-1$ and integer $v$,
\[
 p_0(j_0+pt)=vt^k+\epsilon t^k+\psi(t),\qquad |\epsilon|<1/R.
\]
The coefficient at $t^k$ before reduction is exactly $\theta p^k$. At integer $t$ the term $vt^k$ disappears from the exponential, so
\[
 |e(-p_0(j_0+pt))-e(-\psi(t))|
 \le2\pi|\epsilon|t^k
 <\frac{2\pi(2H)^k}{R}=\frac\pi{64L}.
\]
Apply the induction hypothesis to $\psi$ at target length $2L$. This is legal because $m\ge H=F_{k-1}(2L)$. Its cells have lengths $2L$ through $4L-1$, with constant-unit error less than $1/(8L)$. Split each such cell again by the chunking rule into lengths $L$ through $2L-1$. Restrict its same unit to the smaller cells; this does not increase the error. The combined error is
\[
 <\frac\pi{64L}+\frac1{8L}<\frac3{16L}<\frac1{4L}.
\]
Every stage partitions its input exactly and composes arithmetic parameterizations, so all final cells are arithmetic progressions and every original index occurs once.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The uniform source budget]\label{gsr:dt:41:lem:Kbudget}
For all integers $k\ge2$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:Kbudget}
 c_k+e_k\le K_k/4.
\end{equation}
Consequently the sufficient condition $n\ge(2L)^{K_k/4}$ implies \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:Pk} for integer $L\ge2$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $U_k=c_k+e_k$. The base is $U_2=154\le2048/4$. For $k\ge3$, \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:recursivebudget} gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:Urec}
 U_k=A_k+(k+8)B_k+m_k(c_{k-1}+2e_{k-1})
 \le A_k+(k+8)B_k+2m_kU_{k-1}.
\end{equation}
We bound the three terms separately. First $k-1\le2^{k/2}$ for $k\ge2$. Check $k=2,3,4$ directly; thereafter the induction follows from $k/(k-1)\le4/3<\sqrt2$. Thus $(k-1)^{2k}\le2^{k^2}$; also $2^{k-1}+k^2\le2^{k^2}$ for $k\ge3$, since each summand is at most $2^{k^2-1}$. Therefore
\[
 A_k\le64\cdot2^{k^2},\qquad
 \frac{A_k}{K_k}\le\frac{64}{(k!)^2 2^{2k+1}}
 \le\frac{64}{36\cdot128}=\frac1{72}<\frac1{64}.
\]
Second, $B_k\le2^{k+1}$ and $k+8\le4k$ for $k\ge3$. Since $k!\ge k$ and $(k+1)^2\ge k+9$,
\[
 (k+8)B_k\le k2^{k+3}\le K_k/64.
\]
Third, $m_k\le k2^{k+2}$ and
\[
 K_k/K_{k-1}=k^2 2^{2k+1},\qquad
 \frac{m_k}{K_k/K_{k-1}}\le\frac1{k2^{k-1}}\le\frac1{12}.
\]
By the induction hypothesis,
$2m_kU_{k-1}\le m_kK_{k-1}/2\le K_k/24$. Substituting into \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:Urec} yields
\[
 U_k\le\left(\frac1{64}+\frac1{64}+\frac1{24}\right)K_k
 =\frac7{96}K_k<K_k/4.
\]
This is an induction for every integer $k$, with no finite range or asymptotic cutoff left unchecked. Finally
\[
 F_k(L)=2^{c_k}L^{e_k}\le(2L)^{c_k+e_k}\le(2L)^{K_k/4},
\]
which proves the sufficient condition.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 40--46]

\paragraph{Passage to modular parents.}
If $P=\{u+jd:0\le j<n\}$ is proper and $\phi(x)=\sum_{v=0}^k a_vx^v$ over $G$, choose integer representatives $\widetilde a_v,\widetilde u,\widetilde d$ and set
\[
 p_0(j)=\frac1N\sum_{v=0}^k\widetilde a_v
                    (\widetilde u+j\widetilde d)^v.
\]
This is a real coefficient polynomial of degree at most $k$ and
$e_N(-\phi(u+jd))=e(-p_0(j))$ for every integer $j$. Integer representatives may change the normalized value by an integer, leaving the phase unchanged even through modular wrapping. The real-variable localization therefore applies. Each index cell maps to a modular progression, and injectivity of the parent map restricts to injectivity on the cell. Cardinalities and disjointness are preserved. No division in $G$ and no invertibility of $d$ or $k!$ is used.

\paragraph{Two cubic budgets.}
The general recursion has $A_3=3280$, $B_3=16$, $m_3=49$, hence
$(c_3,e_3)=(10986,1878)$. Replacing only its cubic recurrence input by Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:41:cor:cubicrec} gives instead
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:sharpbudget}
 c_3'=128+10\cdot16+49(116+38)=7834,
 \qquad e_3'=16+49\cdot38=1878.
\end{equation}
The same localization proof gives $n\ge2^{7834}L^{1878}$. The all-degree induction above uses the unmodified constants; the sharper cubic option does not alter that proof.

\section[{A second moment over every cyclic modulus\srctag{41}}]{A second moment over every cyclic modulus}\label{gsr:dt:41:sec:d5}\label{gsr:dt:41:sec:variance}
\srcnote{41}{Section 5}

Over a prime modulus, pairs of distinct progression positions often have a particularly simple distribution. Over an arbitrary cyclic modulus their distribution is instead controlled by additive subgroup cosets. The resulting inequality is enough here.

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 40--46]
\emph{This section is source~32's Section~4, character for character} (Section~\ref{gsr:dt:32:sec:d4}); Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:41:lem:variance} is source~32's Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:32:lem:variance} and source~26's Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:26:lem:variance}. \emph{Formalized since the seventh write} (checked at HEAD \texttt{6d4942222}): \file{exists_proper_progression_density_increment} (\file{Proofs05VarianceIncrement.lean}, line~89) proves exactly this statement for $A\subseteq\Z/N\Z$, $2\le L$, $L^3\le N$, $0<\delta<1$, a proper progression of length $L$ with density at least $\delta+(1-\delta)/(2L)$; its docstring credits Report277. The ingredients are \file{cyclic_progression_second_moment_lower} (\file{Proofs05ProgressionMoments.lean}, line~74) and \file{badProgressionDirections_card_le} (\file{Proofs05ProperDirections.lean}, line~14). Source~42 proves the same gain under $N\ge2(L-1)^2+1$ (Corollary~\ref{gsr:fm:42:cor:scale}); that version is not formalized.
\end{writenote}

\begin{lemma}[Proper progression from variance]\label{gsr:dt:41:lem:variance}
Let $0<\delta<1$, let $L\ge2$ be an integer, and suppose $N\ge L^3$. There is a proper $L$-term modular progression $Q$ with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:variancegain}
 \dens_Q(A):=\frac{|A\cap Q|}{|Q|}
 \ge\delta+\frac{1-\delta}{2L}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose $a,d$ independently and uniformly in $G$, including $d=0$, and put
\[
 X(a,d)=\frac1L\sum_{j=0}^{L-1}\one_A(a+jd).
\]
Repeated positions are counted with their index multiplicity. For every fixed $d$, averaging over $a$ gives $\E_a X=\delta$.

For distinct $j,k$, let $H=(k-j)G$. The change of variables $(a,d)\mapsto(x,d)=(a+jd,d)$ is a bijection of $G^2$. The element $(k-j)d$ is uniform in $H$, independently of $x$. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:coset}
 \E[\one_A(a+jd)\one_A(a+kd)]
 =\sum_{C\in G/H}\frac{|H|}{N}
       \left(\frac{|A\cap C|}{|H|}\right)^2\ge\delta^2.
\end{equation}
Indeed the coset densities have weighted mean $\delta$, and their weighted squared deviations from that mean sum to a nonnegative number. Thus all off-diagonal covariances are nonnegative, and the $L$ diagonal terms yield
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:varlower}
 \Var_{a,d}X\ge\frac{\delta(1-\delta)}L.
\end{equation}

A direction $d$ is bad precisely when the $L$-term parameterization is not injective. This means $hd=0$ for some $1\le h<L$. The kernel of multiplication by $h$ on $G$ has $\gcd(h,N)\le h$ elements: if $g=\gcd(h,N)$, then $N\mid hd$ is equivalent to $N/g\mid d$. Hence the proportion $\eta$ of bad directions obeys
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:bad}
 \eta\le\frac1N\sum_{h=1}^{L-1}h
 =\frac{L(L-1)}{2N}<\frac1{2L}.
\end{equation}
At least one proper direction exists, since $d=1$ works for $L\le N$.

Let $h_*$ be the largest value of $X(a,d)-\delta$ over proper directions and all $a$. For a proper direction, $0\le X\le\delta+h_*$ implies $X^2\le(\delta+h_*)X$, and so $\Var_aX\le\delta h_*$. For any bad direction, $0\le X\le1$ similarly gives $\Var_aX\le\delta(1-\delta)$. Since every conditional mean is $\delta$, averaging these variances and using \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:varlower} gives
\[
 \frac{\delta(1-\delta)}L
 \le(1-\eta)\delta h_*+\eta\delta(1-\delta).
\]
Dividing by $\delta>0$ and rearranging,
\[
 h_*\ge(1-\delta)\frac{1/L-\eta}{1-\eta}
 \ge\frac{1-\delta}{2L},
\]
where \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:bad} and $1-\eta\le1$ justify the last step. A maximizing proper progression proves the claim.
\end{proof}

\section[{Assembly at every scale\srctag{41}}]{Assembly at every scale}\label{gsr:dt:41:sec:d6}\label{gsr:dt:41:sec:assembly}
\srcnote{41}{Section 6}
We first collect the cover algebra, since the same quantities will also govern the sharper alternatives.
Put
\[
 b=1-\delta,\quad \tau=|U|/N,\quad r=\min_i|P_i|,
 \quad S=N/M,\quad \mu=\frac1N\sum_{x\in U}|f(x)|.
\]
Nonempty disjointness gives $M\le N$ and $S\ge1$; coverage gives $\delta\le\tau\le1$. Counting points of $A$ and $U\setminus A$ separately gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:mass}
 \mu=\delta(1+\tau-2\delta),\qquad
 0<\alpha\le\mu\le2\delta b\le2\tau b\le2b.
\end{equation}
Here the correlation and triangle inequality imply $\alpha\le\mu$, which rules out $\delta=0,1$. Thus $0<\delta<1$, $b>0$, and $A$ is nonempty. Comparability yields
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:parent}
 \tau N=\sum_i|P_i|\le2Mr,
 \qquad r\ge\tau S/2.
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}[From a full phase partition to a positive cell]\label{gsr:dt:41:lem:transfer}
Suppose the parents are partitioned into proper cells $C$, with units $z_C$. Let $i(C)$ be the parent of $C$, put $F_C=\sum_{x\in C}f(x)\in\R$, and define
\[
 E=\sum_C\sum_{x\in C}|f(x)|
          |e_N(-\phi_{i(C)}(x))-z_C|.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:transfer}
 \sum_C|F_C|\ge\alpha N-E,\qquad
 \sum_C F_C=\delta(N-|U|)\ge0.
\end{equation}
If $E\le\alpha N/3$, some cell has density at least $\delta+\alpha/3$. If the error inequality is strict, so is the resulting density inequality.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For each parent, replace the phase by $z_C$ on each cell, bound the replacement error, and apply the triangle inequality. Since $|z_C|=1$, summing gives the first inequality in \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:transfer}. Every point of $U$ occurs exactly once, and $A\subseteq U$, so the signed sum is $|A|-\delta|U|=\delta(N-|U|)$.
The positive $F_C$ sum to
\[
 \frac12\left(\sum_C|F_C|+\sum_CF_C\right)
 \ge\frac{\alpha N-E}{2}\ge\frac{\alpha N}{3}.
\]
These cells have total cardinality at most $N$. Their weighted average discrepancy is therefore at least $\alpha/3$, and some cell has at least that discrepancy. The same calculation preserves strictness. Coverage gives a nonnegative signed total, not necessarily zero.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:41:thm:main}]
Set $x=S^{1/D_k}/8$ and $L=\lceil x\rceil$. If $L=1$, take a singleton in $A$. Its length is at least $x$, and its density is one, strictly larger than $\delta+\alpha/3$, since \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:mass} gives $\alpha/3\le2\delta b/3<b$.

Suppose $L\ge2$. Then $x>1$ and $L<x+1<2x$, whence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:Sscale}
 S>(4L)^{D_k}>L^3,\qquad N\ge S>L^3.
\end{equation}
If $\alpha\le3b/(2L)$, Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:41:lem:variance} supplies a proper $L$-term progression of density at least $\delta+b/(2L)\ge\delta+\alpha/3$. Its length is at least $x$.

Otherwise $\alpha>3b/(2L)$. Together with \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:mass} and \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:parent}, this implies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:highbranch}
 \tau>3/(4L),\qquad r>3S/(8L).
\end{equation}
For $k=1$, $D_1=4$, so \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:Sscale} gives $r>96L^3>64L^3$. For $k\ge2$, put $t=K_k/4$, so $D_k=t+1$; then
\[
 r>\frac38\frac{(4L)^{t+1}}L
   =\frac32\,4^tL^t>(2L)^t.
\]
Thus every parent meets the affine or all-degree localization threshold. Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:41:thm:localization} and Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:41:lem:Kbudget}, with the modular passage established there, at the same target length $L$. The total phase error satisfies
\[
 E<\frac{\mu N}{4L}\le\frac{bN}{2L}<\frac{\alpha N}{3}.
\]
Strictness in the first comparison follows from the strict pointwise error and $\mu>0$. Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:41:lem:transfer} supplies a proper cell of density greater than $\delta+\alpha/3$ and length at least $L\ge x$. Every branch gives a nonempty progression, which proves the maximum with one in \eqref{gsr:fm:41:eq:main}.
\end{proof}

The high-correlation branch finds $Q$ inside a parent. The variance branch searches all directions in the whole group. Requiring parent containment in the final theorem would add a conclusion not established by that branch.
