\section[{Exact budgets and sharper alternatives\srctag{41}}]{Exact budgets and sharper alternatives}\label{gsr:dt:41:sec:d7}\label{gsr:dt:41:sec:alternatives}
\srcnote{41}{Section 7}
The uniform $K_k$ comparison is useful for matching the source interface. It intentionally loses information. Neither its degree-one nor its degree-two specialization replaces the stronger small-degree bounds below.

\begin{corollary}[The actual recursive budget]\label{gsr:dt:41:cor:exactbudget}
Under the cover and correlation hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:41:thm:main}, suppose that degree at most $k$ phases have a valid partition threshold $n\ge2^cL^e$ for integer $L\ge2$, giving cells of lengths $L$ through $2L-1$ and phase error less than $1/(4L)$. Here $c\ge0$, $e\ge2$ are fixed real numbers. Put
\[
 R_0=\left(\frac{3S}{8\cdot2^c}\right)^{1/(e+1)},
 \qquad L_0=\max\{1,\lfloor R_0\rfloor\}.
\]
There is a proper progression $Q$ with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:exactlength}
 |Q|\ge L_0\ge\max\{1,R_0/2\},\qquad
 |A\cap Q|\ge(\delta+\alpha/3)|Q|.
\end{equation}
Available choices are $(c,e)=(6,3)$ for degree one, $(116,38)$ for degree two, $(c_k,e_k)$ from \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:recursivebudget} for every $k\ge3$, and $(7834,1878)$ for the sharper cubic alternative.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
If $L_0=1$, a singleton in $A$ works as before. Otherwise $L_0\le R_0$, and
\[
 S\ge\frac{8\cdot2^c}{3}L_0^{e+1}\ge L_0^3,
 \qquad N\ge S.
\]
If $\alpha\le3b/(2L_0)$, apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:41:lem:variance}. Otherwise \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:highbranch}, with $L=L_0$, gives
\[
 r>3S/(8L_0)\ge2^cL_0^e.
\]
Every parent therefore meets the stipulated partition threshold, and its total phase error is less than $\mu N/(4L_0)\le bN/(2L_0)<\alpha N/3$. Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:41:lem:transfer} finishes this branch. If $R_0<2$, the last lower bound in \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:exactlength} is one; if $R_0\ge2$, then $\lfloor R_0\rfloor\ge R_0/2$. This includes all floor boundaries without an unproved real-root rounding step.
\end{proof}

For fixed $k$, the actual power of $S$ in this corollary is $1/(e_k+1)$, accompanied by its explicit constant. In particular the sharper cubic budget gives a power $1/1879$ with a substantial fixed prefactor. One should compare the complete guarantees, including the singleton floor and constants, rather than compare exponents alone.


\begin{corollary}[A compact bound for the degree dependence]\label{gsr:dt:41:cor:compact}
For $k\ge2$, put $\mathcal P_k=k!\,2^{k(k+1)/2}$. The unmodified recursive budgets in \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:recursivebudget} satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:compactbudget}
 e_k<12\mathcal P_k,\qquad c_k<(k+7)e_k,
 \qquad c_k+e_k<12(k+8)\mathcal P_k.
\end{equation}
Consequently, for integers $n,L\ge2$, the condition $n\ge(2^{k+7}L)^{12\mathcal P_k}$ suffices for the degree-$k$ localization at target $L$. Under Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:41:thm:main}'s hypotheses, a proper progression has gain $\alpha/3$ and length at least
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:compactlength}
 \max\left\{1,2^{-(k+8)}S^{1/(12\mathcal P_k+1)}\right\}.
\end{equation}
Here $\mathcal P_k=2^{-(k+1)/2}\sqrt{K_k}$. This is a bound on the growth of the proved sufficient budget, not an optimality statement. The calligraphic symbol distinguishes this numerical quantity from a parent progression $P_i$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Let $\Pi_2=1$ and $\Pi_k=\prod_{j=3}^k m_j$. Dividing the $e_k$ recurrence by $\Pi_k$ gives
\[
 E_k:=\frac{e_k}{\Pi_k}=38+\sum_{j=3}^k\frac{B_j}{\Pi_j}.
\]
The $m_j$ increase, $m_3=49$, $m_4=97$, and $B_j/m_j<1/j$. Let $E_\infty=38+\sum_{j=3}^{\infty}B_j/\Pi_j$; the following comparison proves convergence. Since $\Pi_{j-1}\ge49\cdot97^{j-4}$ for $j\ge4$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:Ebound}
 E_k\le E_\infty<38+\frac{16}{49}
   +\frac1{4\cdot49}\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}97^{-t}
 =38+\frac{16}{49}+\frac{97}{18816}<\frac{115}{3}.
\end{equation}
The final comparison uses $97/18816<1/147$.

Set $d_j=(8+1/j)/2^j$ and $q_k=\Pi_k/\mathcal P_k$. Then
\[
 q_k=\frac1{16}\prod_{j=3}^k(1+d_j),\qquad
 q_7=\frac{18772640957}{64424509440}<\frac7{24}.
\]
The last strict comparison is $18772640957<18790481920$. Also
$\sum_{j=8}^{\infty}d_j\le(8+1/8)\sum_{j=8}^{\infty}2^{-j}=65/1024$.
For nonnegative $x_i$ of sum at most $t<1$, expanding a finite product and bounding each elementary symmetric sum by $t^r$ gives $\prod_i(1+x_i)\le\sum_{r\ge0}t^r=1/(1-t)$. This bounds the increasing finite products and proves convergence here. Write $q_\infty=\lim_{k\to\infty}q_k$. Consequently, including $k<7$ by monotonicity,
\[
 q_k\le q_\infty<\frac{7/24}{1-65/1024}=\frac{896}{2877},
 \qquad
 \frac{e_k}{\mathcal P_k}<\frac{896}{2877}\frac{115}{3}
   =\frac{103040}{8631}<12.
\]

For the coefficient bound let $J_k=(k+7)e_k-c_k$. Direct substitution into \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:recursivebudget} yields
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:deficit}
 J_2=226,\quad J_k=m_kJ_{k-1}-A_k,
 \qquad \frac{J_k}{\Pi_k}=226-\sum_{j=3}^k a_j,
 \quad a_j=\frac{A_j}{\Pi_j}.
\end{equation}
We show that the infinite sum is less than $226$. For $j\ge9$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:tailratio}
 a_{j+1}/a_j<1/8.
\end{equation}
Indeed, compare the three positive summands $2^{j-1}$, $3(j-1)^{2j}$, and $j^2$ defining $A_j/16$, and divide their respective next-term ratios by $m_{j+1}$. The first ratio is $2/m_{j+1}<1/8$. The third is $((j+1)/j)^2/m_{j+1}<2/m_{j+1}<1/8$. The middle is
\[
 \frac{j^2(1+1/(j-1))^{2j}}{m_{j+1}}.
\]
For $n\ge1$, the binomial expansion gives
$(1+1/n)^n\le\sum_{r=0}^n1/r!<3$; here $r!\ge2^{r-1}$ for $r\ge2$, with strictness in the finite sum. Therefore, for $j\ge9$,
\[
 (1+1/(j-1))^{2j}<9(j/(j-1))^2
 \le9(9/8)^2<12.
\]
Since $m_{j+1}\ge(j+1)2^{j+1}$, the middle ratio is less than
$12j/2^{j+1}\le108/1024=27/256<1/8$. The sequence $j/2^{j+1}$ is nonincreasing for $j\ge1$. Each positive summand has the required ratio, proving \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:tailratio} for their sum.

For the finite calculation, the following integers $z_j$ satisfy the exact certificates
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:certificates}
 z_j\Pi_j\le100000A_j<(z_j+1)\Pi_j.
\end{equation}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{c|rrrrrrrr}
$j$&3&4&5&6&7&8&9&10\\\hline
$z_j$&6693877&6633957&5268450&2832889&954144&191498&22175&1450
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Each certificate is integer substitution into the displayed formulas for $A_j$ and $\Pi_j$. They are also reproduced by the exact companion. Summing the upper bounds through $j=9$, and retaining the $j=10$ bound for the tail, gives
\[
 \sum_{j=3}^9a_j<\frac{22596997}{100000}<\frac{22597}{100},
 \qquad a_{10}<\frac{1451}{100000}<\frac3{200}.
\]
Thus \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:tailratio} implies
\[
 \sum_{j=3}^{\infty}a_j
 <\frac{22597}{100}+\frac87\frac3{200}
 =226-\frac9{700}<226.
\]
Equation~\eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:deficit} now gives $J_k>0$ for every $k\ge2$. This proves \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:compactbudget} with no unverified degree range.

The partition conclusion follows from
$2^{c_k}L^{e_k}<(2^{k+7}L)^{12\mathcal P_k}$. Apply Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:41:cor:exactbudget} with integer exponents $C=12(k+7)\mathcal P_k$ and $E=12\mathcal P_k$. Its real-valued length term is $R_0/2$, and the exact identity
\[
 \frac{R_0}{2}
 =2^{-(k+8)}\bigl(3\cdot2^{k+4}S\bigr)^{1/(12\mathcal P_k+1)}
 \ge2^{-(k+8)}S^{1/(12\mathcal P_k+1)}
\]
proves \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:compactlength}. Finally, the comparison with $K_k$ is direct algebra from their definitions.
\end{proof}


\begin{corollary}[Exact limiting constants]\label{gsr:dt:41:cor:limits}
Retain $\Pi_k,q_k,E_k,a_j$ from the proof of Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:41:cor:compact}, and define
\[
 \Theta_\infty=226-\sum_{j=3}^{\infty}a_j,
 \qquad \lambda=q_\infty E_\infty,
 \qquad \gamma_*=7-\Theta_\infty/E_\infty.
\]
These are constants defined by convergent series and a convergent product, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:limitconstants}
 11<\lambda<12,\qquad
 7-\frac1{1900}<\gamma_*<7-\frac{27}{80500}<7.
\end{equation}
As $k\to\infty$ through integers,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:asymptotics}
 \frac{e_k}{\mathcal P_k}=\lambda+O(2^{-k}),\qquad
 \frac{c_k}{e_k}-k\longrightarrow\gamma_* ,\qquad
 \frac{c_k}{\mathcal P_k}
 =\lambda(k+\gamma_*)+O(k2^{-k}).
\end{equation}
In particular $c_k/\mathcal P_k-\lambda k\to\lambda\gamma_*$. The constants and error terms describe this proved construction, not the optimal density-increment problem.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The previous proof gives $\Theta_\infty>9/700$. The lower integer certificates \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:certificates}, summed through $j=10$, give
\[
 \sum_{j=3}^{10}a_j\ge\frac{22598440}{100000}>
 \frac{11299}{50}=226-\frac1{50},
\]
so $\Theta_\infty<1/50$. Since $38\le E_\infty<115/3$, the bounds on $\gamma_*$ follow. Also $\lambda<12$, while $\lambda>38q_7>11$, the latter a direct integer comparison using the displayed value of $q_7$.

Here are explicit rational errors, which also justify the rates in \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:asymptotics}. For $k\ge4$ put
\[
 s_k=\frac{8+1/(k+1)}{2^k},\qquad
 t_k=\frac{m_{k+1}}{(k+1)(m_{k+1}-1)\Pi_k}.
\]
Then $s_k<1$. The same product estimate as before and the tail identity for $E_k$ give
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:limittails}
 0<E_\infty-E_k<t_k,\qquad
 q_k<q_\infty\le\frac{q_k}{1-s_k}.
\end{equation}
Indeed $\sum_{j>k}d_j\le s_k$, and for $j\ge k+1$ one has
$B_j/m_j<1/j\le1/(k+1)$ and
$\Pi_{j-1}\ge\Pi_k m_{k+1}^{j-k-1}$; summing the resulting geometric series gives $t_k$. In particular, splitting the difference $q_\infty E_\infty-q_kE_k$ yields
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:eerror}
 0<\lambda-\frac{e_k}{\mathcal P_k}
 <12s_k+q_kt_k
 =12s_k+\frac{m_{k+1}}{(k+1)(m_{k+1}-1)\mathcal P_k}.
\end{equation}
We used $q_\infty-q_k\le s_kq_\infty$ and $q_\infty E_\infty<12$.

For $k\ge9$, put $h_k=(8/7)a_{k+1}$,
$\Theta_k=226-\sum_{j=3}^k a_j$, and $g_k=c_k/e_k-k$. Equation~\eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:deficit} gives $g_k=7-\Theta_k/E_k$. The geometric tail \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:tailratio} implies $0<\Theta_k-\Theta_\infty<h_k$, so
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:gerror}
 \begin{split}
 0<\gamma_*-g_k
 &=\frac{\Theta_k-\Theta_\infty}{E_k}
   +\frac{\Theta_\infty(E_\infty-E_k)}{E_kE_\infty}\\
 &<\frac{h_k}{38}+\frac{t_k}{50\cdot38^2}.
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
Finally $c_k/\mathcal P_k=(e_k/\mathcal P_k)(k+g_k)$, and hence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:cerror}
 \begin{split}
 0<\lambda(k+\gamma_*)-\frac{c_k}{\mathcal P_k}
 <(k+7)(12s_k+q_kt_k)
 +12\left(\frac{h_k}{38}+\frac{t_k}{50\cdot38^2}\right).
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
Now $s_k=O(2^{-k})$, $q_kt_k=O(1/(k\mathcal P_k))$, $\Pi_k\ge49^{k-2}$, and \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:tailratio} gives $h_k=O(8^{-k})$. These explicit bounds prove all limits and rates claimed; no decimal approximation of an infinite sum is needed.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Retained affine bounds]\label{gsr:dt:41:cor:affinebetter}
When the phases have degree at most one, the same gain $\alpha/3$ is available with each of the length guarantees
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:affinereal}
 \min\left\{\left(\frac{rb}{128\mu}\right)^{1/3},(N/8)^{1/3}\right\},
 \qquad \sqrt{\frac{\alpha r}{24\pi\mu}}.
\end{equation}
The second progression can be chosen inside one parent. For the two-comparable cover in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:41:thm:main}, one may consequently choose a progression of length at least
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:affinebetter}
 \max\left\{1,\frac{S^{1/3}}8,
                  \sqrt{\frac{\alpha S}{96\pi b}}\right\}.
\end{equation}
Parent containment is assured for the square-root alternative, not for an arbitrary selection attaining the maximum.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For any integer $1\le L\le r$, apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:41:lem:affine} to each real pullback phase. The resulting error in Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:41:lem:transfer} is at most
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:affineerror}
 E\le2\pi L^2\mu N/r.
\end{equation}
For the cube-root guarantee, put $H_*=rb/\mu$, choose
$x=\min\{(H_*/128)^{1/3},(N/8)^{1/3}\}$ and $L=\lceil x\rceil$. A singleton handles $L=1$. Otherwise $L<2x$, hence $H_*>16L^3$ and $N>L^3$. If $\alpha\le3b/(2L)$, use the variance lemma. In the other branch, $\mu\ge\alpha>3b/(2L)$ gives $r=H_*\mu/b>24L^2>L$, so affine refinement is legal, and
\[
 E\le\frac{2\pi L^2bN}{H_*}
 <\frac{\pi bN}{8L}<\frac{bN}{2L}<\frac{\alpha N}{3}.
\]
Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:41:lem:transfer} proves the first bound in \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:affinereal}.

For the square-root guarantee, put $Y=\sqrt{\alpha r/(6\pi\mu)}$ and $L=\max\{1,\lfloor Y\rfloor\}$. If $L=1$, then $Y<2$, and a singleton in $A$ lies in a parent and has length at least $Y/2$. Otherwise $Y^2\le r/(6\pi)<r$, so $L\le r$, and \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:affineerror} gives $E\le\alpha N/3$. The selected cell is parent-contained and has length $L\ge Y/2=\sqrt{\alpha r/(24\pi\mu)}$.

Finally $\mu\le2\tau b$, $r\le\tau N$, and $r/\tau\ge S/2$. The cube-root minimum in \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:affinereal} is at least $(r/(256\tau))^{1/3}$: this is no larger than either entry of that minimum, since $r/(256\tau)\le N/256\le N/8$. It is at least $S^{1/3}/8$. The square-root bound is at least $\sqrt{\alpha r/(48\pi\tau b)}\ge\sqrt{\alpha S/(96\pi b)}$. A singleton supplies the remaining one in the maximum. Selecting a theorem with the largest applicable length guarantee proves \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:affinebetter}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 40--46]
This is source~26's Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:26:cor:comparable} with its proof (Theorems~\ref{gsr:dt:26:thm:cube} and~\ref{gsr:dt:26:thm:sqrt}); source~42's Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:42:thm:affine} replaces the cap $(N/8)^{1/3}$ of the first bound by $\sqrt{N/2}$.
\end{writenote}

\begin{corollary}[Retained quadratic and cubic bounds]\label{gsr:dt:41:cor:smallbetter}
For degree at most two, one may replace the length in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:41:thm:main} by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:quadbetter}
 \max\{1,S^{1/39}/17\}.
\end{equation}
For degree at most three, one may replace it by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:41:eq:cubicbetter}
 \max\{1,S^{1/4096}/8\}.
\end{equation}
Both conclusions retain the density gain $\alpha/3$ over every cyclic modulus.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For degree two, set $x=S^{1/39}/17$ and $L=\lceil x\rceil$. The singleton branch is unchanged. If $L\ge2$, then $S>(17L/2)^{39}>L^3$, so the variance branch is valid. In the high-correlation branch,
\[
 r>\frac{3S}{8L}>\frac{3\cdot17^{39}}{2^{42}}L^{38}
 >2^{116}L^{38}.
\]
The last inequality is $3\cdot17^{39}>2^{158}$. To verify it entirely with integers, Bernoulli's inequality gives
$17^{39}=2^{156}(1+1/16)^{39}\ge(55/16)2^{156}$, and $3\cdot55/16>4$. The quadratic partition and transfer lemmas now apply.

For degree three, set $x=S^{1/4096}/8$ and $L=\lceil x\rceil$. In the nonsingleton case $S>(4L)^{4096}>L^3$. In the high-correlation branch,
\[
 r>\frac{3S}{8L}>3\cdot2^{8189}L^{4095}
   >2^{7834}L^{1878}.
\]
Use the sharper cubic budget \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:sharpbudget}. The same variance and transfer arguments complete the proof.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 40--46]
The quadratic bound \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:quadbetter} is source~32's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:32:thm:main}; the cubic bound \eqref{gsr:dt:41:eq:cubicbetter} is new here and answers source~32's degree-three question (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:I:cor58}).
\end{writenote}

The quadratic guarantee also satisfies, for every $S\ge1$,
\[
 \max\{1,S^{1/39}/17\}\ge S^{1/64}/8.
\]
If the right side is at most one this is immediate. Otherwise $S>8^{64}$ and
$S^{1/39-1/64}>8^{25/39}>\sqrt8>17/8$; the last comparison is $512>289$ after squaring. This illustrates why constants and small scales matter. For any fixed input one may select the largest among the applicable exact-budget, uniform, and small-degree guarantees. The uniform all-degree theorem is not asserted to dominate those earlier bounds pointwise.

\section[{The covariance square and the range inequality\srctag{42}}]{The covariance square and the range inequality}\label{gsr:dt:42:sec:d2}\label{gsr:dt:42:sec:moment}
\srcnote{42}{Section 2}
We first work in an arbitrary finite abelian group $G$. For a probability mass function $\mu$ on $G$, let $s,t$ be independent samples with law $\mu$, let $a$ be independent and uniform on $G$, and put $d=s-t$.

\begin{lemma}[Covariance square]\label{gsr:dt:42:lem:square}
For every real-valued function $f$ on $G$ and every integer $h$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:42:eq:square}
 \E_{a,s,t} f(a)f(a+h(s-t))
 =\E_z\left(\sum_{s\in G}\mu(s)f(z+hs)\right)^2\ge0.
\end{equation}
No invertibility assumption on the map $x\mapsto hx$ is needed.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For each fixed $s,t$, substitute $a=z+ht$. This is a translation of the uniformly sampled group element, so the left side becomes
\[
 \E_z\sum_{s,t\in G}\mu(s)\mu(t)f(z+ht)f(z+hs).
\]
Independence factors the double sum into the square in \eqref{gsr:dt:42:eq:square}. The change of variable only uses translation, never division by $h$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Variance and maximum]\label{gsr:dt:42:lem:range}
If a nonnegative random variable $Y$ satisfies $Y\le M$ and $\E Y=\delta>0$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:42:eq:range}
 \Var(Y)\le\delta(M-\delta).
\end{equation}
Equality holds if and only if $Y\in\{0,M\}$ almost surely.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The pointwise inequality $Y^2\le MY$ gives
$\Var(Y)=\E Y^2-\delta^2\le M\delta-\delta^2$.
Equality is equivalent to $Y(M-Y)=0$ almost surely.
\end{proof}
This is the lower-endpoint-zero case of the classical variance bound of Bhatia and Davis~\cite{bhatiadavis}. The square identity is likewise a classical autocorrelation-positivity calculation. Neither ingredient is asserted to be new.

\begin{theorem}[Admissible difference support]\label{gsr:dt:42:thm:group}
Let $G$ be finite abelian and $L\ge2$. Suppose $B\subseteq G$, $|B|=S\ge2$, and every nonzero element of $B-B$ has additive order at least $L$. Let $g:G\to[0,1]$ have mean $\delta>0$ and variance
$\sigma^2=\E(g-\delta)^2$. There is a proper $L$-term progression $P$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:42:eq:function}
 \frac1L\sum_{x\in P}g(x)-\delta
 \ge \frac{\sigma^2}{\delta}
       \max\left\{\frac{S-L}{L(S-1)},0\right\}.
\end{equation}
For $g=\one_A$, this becomes the increment
$(1-\delta)\max\{S-L,0\}/(L(S-1))$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Choose $s,t$ uniformly from $B$ and $a$ uniformly from $G$, independently, and define
\[
 X=\frac1L\sum_{j=0}^{L-1}g(a+j(s-t)),\qquad f=g-\delta.
\]
For every fixed $s,t$, translation invariance gives $\E_aX=\delta$. Expanding the variance yields
\[
 \Var(X)=\frac1{L^2}\sum_{j,k=0}^{L-1}
 \E_{a,s,t} f(a+j(s-t))f(a+k(s-t)).
\]
Each of the $L$ diagonal terms is $\sigma^2$. For $j\ne k$, translating $a$ and applying Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:42:lem:square} with $h=k-j$ makes the term a nonnegative square. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:42:eq:varlower}
 \Var(X)\ge\frac{\sigma^2}{L}.
\end{equation}

The event $d=0$ is precisely $s=t$ and has probability $\eta=1/S$. On this event, $X=g(a)$ and the conditional variance is $\sigma^2$. On the event $d\ne0$, every sampled progression is proper by the assumption on $B-B$. Both conditional means are $\delta$, since each fixed step has that translation average. Consequently the law of total variance gives the exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:42:eq:totalvariance}
 \Var(X)=\eta\sigma^2+(1-\eta)\Var(X\mid d\ne0).
\end{equation}
Let $M$ be the maximum of the window averages of $g$ over all translates and all nonzero steps in $B-B$. These windows are proper. The maximum exists: distinct points of $B$ supply a nonzero step, and the group is finite. Conditionally on $d\ne0$, one has $0\le X\le M$. Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:42:lem:range} therefore gives
\[
 \Var(X\mid d\ne0)\le\delta(M-\delta).
\]
Combining this with \eqref{gsr:dt:42:eq:varlower} and \eqref{gsr:dt:42:eq:totalvariance}, then dividing by $\delta(1-\eta)>0$, gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:42:eq:eta}
 M-\delta\ge\frac{\sigma^2}{\delta}
                 \frac{1/L-\eta}{1-\eta}
 =\frac{\sigma^2}{\delta}\frac{S-L}{L(S-1)}.
\end{equation}
Finally, averaging over translates of any nonzero step in $B-B$ gives $M\ge\delta$, which replaces a negative right side by zero. For an indicator, $\sigma^2=\delta(1-\delta)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Nonuniform sampling]\label{gsr:dt:42:rem:nonuniform}
The same proof applies when $s,t$ have any common probability distribution supported on an admissible $B$ and at least two points have positive mass. The collision probability becomes
\[
 \eta=\sum_{x\in B}\mu(x)^2<1,
\]
and \eqref{gsr:dt:42:eq:eta} remains valid. The scalar factor
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:42:eq:decreasing}
 F_L(\eta):=\frac{1/L-\eta}{1-\eta},\qquad
 F_L'(\eta)=-\frac{L-1}{L(1-\eta)^2}<0
\end{equation}
is strictly decreasing on $[0,1)$. Minimizing collisions therefore optimizes this particular variance calculation.
\end{remark}
The bounded-function statement records the correct variance dependence. Replacing $\sigma^2/\delta$ by $1-\delta$ for an arbitrary $[0,1]$-valued function would be invalid: a constant function has no positive increment. The case $\sigma^2=0$ in \eqref{gsr:dt:42:eq:function} correctly gives zero.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Exact support optimization and integer scales\srctag{42}}]{Exact support optimization and integer scales}\label{gsr:dt:42:sec:d3}\label{gsr:dt:42:sec:support}
\srcnote{42}{Section 3}
Return to $G=\Z/N\Z$ and the integers $m,q$ in \eqref{gsr:fm:42:eq:mq}.
\begin{lemma}[Largest admissible support]\label{gsr:dt:42:lem:support}
The interval of residues
\[
 B=\{0,1,\ldots,q-1\}\subseteq\Z/N\Z
\]
has no nonzero difference of additive order below $L$. Every subset with this property has at most $q$ elements. Moreover, $q-1$ is the largest integer $D<N$ for which all steps $1,\ldots,D$ are proper for length $L$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A nonzero difference of two displayed elements has an integer representative $d$ with $0<|d|<q$. If its additive order $h$ were below $L$, then $h\mid N$ and $h\le m$. The relation $hd=0$ modulo $N$ says that $d$ is a nonzero multiple of $N/h$, whence
\[
 |d|\ge\frac Nh\ge\frac Nm=q,
\]
a contradiction.

For the upper bound, let $K$ be the unique subgroup of order $m$. It has $q$ cosets. Two distinct points in the same coset have nonzero difference in $K$, whose order divides $m<L$. An admissible support can therefore meet each coset in at most one point, and has size at most $q$. The displayed interval attains $q$.

The preceding argument certifies all positive steps smaller than $q$. The residue represented by $q$ has additive order $m<L$. If $q=N$, the same statement means that $N$ is the zero residue; in either case the largest permissible $D<N$ is $q-1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:42:thm:main}]
Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:42:thm:group} with $S=q$ and the support in Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:42:lem:support}. The nonzero sampled differences have representatives of absolute value less than $q$. If $q\le L$, use the translation-average bound $M_L(A)\ge\delta$.
\end{proof}

For any iid distribution supported on an admissible $B$, Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
 \eta=\sum_{x\in B}\mu(x)^2\ge\frac1{|B|}\ge\frac1q.
\]
Equality holds for the uniform distribution on the displayed interval. By \eqref{gsr:dt:42:eq:decreasing}, this optimizes the support-and-collision form of the argument for every pair $(N,L)$. This is a statement about the specified method. It does not assert that \eqref{gsr:fm:42:eq:main} is the exact optimum over all sets of every fixed density for each individual pair $(N,L)$.

\subsection{The geometric triangular law}
A useful factorization-free construction takes $B=\{0,\ldots,D\}$ with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:42:eq:properD}
 D\ge1,\qquad (L-1)D<N.
\end{equation}
For $0<|d|\le D$ and $1\le h\le L-1$, one then has $0<|hd|<N$. Thus $hd$ is not zero modulo $N$, and every nonzero supported step is proper. The integer step before reduction modulo $N$ has the triangular law
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:42:eq:triangular}
 \Pr(s-t=u)=\frac{D+1-|u|}{(D+1)^2},\qquad -D\le u\le D.
\end{equation}
If distinct representatives give the same residue, their masses are added. Since $D<N$, the zero residue comes only from $s=t$, with mass $1/(D+1)$. Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:42:thm:group} yields
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:42:eq:generalD}
 H_L(A)\ge\frac{1-\delta}{L}\left(1-\frac{L-1}{D}\right).
\end{equation}
The right side increases with $D$, so the largest integer permitted by \eqref{gsr:dt:42:eq:properD} is
\[
 D_*:=\left\lfloor\frac{N-1}{L-1}\right\rfloor.
\]
This gives \eqref{gsr:fm:42:eq:geometric} after taking the maximum with zero.

The arithmetic theorem never weakens the geometric one. Indeed $m\le L-1$ gives $N\le q(L-1)$, and hence
\[
 \frac{N-1}{L-1}<q,\qquad D_*\le q-1.
\]
It can be strictly stronger. For prime $N$, the arithmetic half-gain holds as soon as $N\ge2L-1$, well beyond the length range certified by the size-only quadratic condition.

\subsection{Exact thresholds and rounding}
For a requested coefficient $0<c<1$ in the increment $c(1-\delta)/L$, the geometric calculation certifies it exactly when
\[
 D_*\ge\left\lceil\frac{L-1}{1-c}\right\rceil.
\]
Equivalently, the sufficient size condition is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:42:eq:generalc}
 N\ge (L-1)\left\lceil\frac{L-1}{1-c}\right\rceil+1.
\end{equation}
This is an exact equivalence for this size-only certificate, not a necessary condition for every possible density-increment argument.

\begin{proof}[Proof of Corollary~\ref{gsr:fm:42:cor:scale} except sharpness]
Strict positivity of \eqref{gsr:dt:42:eq:generalD} is equivalent to $D_*\ge L$, which holds exactly when $N\ge L(L-1)+1$. Taking $c=1/2$ in \eqref{gsr:dt:42:eq:generalc} gives $N\ge2(L-1)^2+1$. For $N\ge CL^2$ with $C>1$, the admissible budget satisfies
\[
 D_*\ge\left\lfloor\frac NL\right\rfloor
       \ge\lfloor CL\rfloor\ge CL-1\ge C(L-1).
\]
For the first inequality, write $D_0=\lfloor N/L\rfloor$. Then $D_0\ge1$ and $(L-1)D_0\le N-D_0<N$, so $D_0$ is permitted by \eqref{gsr:dt:42:eq:properD}. The displayed chain implies
$1-(L-1)/D_*\ge1-1/C$, as required.
\end{proof}

For fixed $N$, the largest length certified by the size-only half-gain condition is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:42:eq:lengthcap}
 1+\left\lfloor\sqrt{\frac{N-1}{2}}\right\rfloor.
\end{equation}
The qualification ``size-only'' is essential: the arithmetic parameter $q$ can certify a larger length. Formula~\eqref{gsr:dt:42:eq:lengthcap} describes the certificate $N\ge2(L-1)^2+1$, not the absolute largest length for which all subsets must exhibit that gain.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Positive definite weights and the classical packing bound\srctag{42}}]{Positive definite weights and the classical packing bound}\label{gsr:dt:42:sec:d4}\label{gsr:dt:42:sec:weights}
\srcnote{42}{Section 4}
The collision optimum extends beyond iid probability differences. We state the normalization explicitly to avoid factors of $N$.
For a probability mass function $w:G\to[0,1]$, set
\[
 W(\chi)=\sum_{d\in G}w(d)\overline{\chi(d)},\qquad \chi\in\widehat G.
\]
Here $\widehat G$ is the character group, and $W$ is an unnormalized Fourier transform. We call $w$ \emph{positive definite} when every $W(\chi)$ is real and nonnegative. The finite Fourier equivalence with the usual positive-semidefinite definition is classical; we only need the displayed condition.

\begin{proposition}[Optimal zero-step mass]\label{gsr:dt:42:prop:packing}
Suppose $G=\Z/N\Z$, $N\ge L\ge2$, and $w$ is a probability mass function such that
\[
 W(\chi)\ge0\quad(\chi\in\widehat G),\qquad
 w(d)=0\quad\text{if }d\ne0\text{ and }\ord(d)<L.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:42:eq:packing}
 w(0)\ge\frac1q.
\end{equation}
Equality is attained by the law of $s-t$ for independent uniform $s,t\in\{0,\ldots,q-1\}$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Let $K\le G$ be the subgroup of order $m$, and let
$K^\perp=\{\chi:\chi(k)=1\text{ for all }k\in K\}$.
Every nonzero $k\in K$ has order below $L$, so $\sum_{k\in K}w(k)=w(0)$.
Fourier inversion and character orthogonality give
\begin{align*}
 w(0)&=\sum_{k\in K}\frac1N\sum_{\chi\in\widehat G}W(\chi)\chi(k)\\
     &=\frac mN\sum_{\chi\in K^\perp}W(\chi)
      \ge\frac mN W(1)=\frac mN=\frac1q.
\end{align*}
For completeness, inversion follows from
$\sum_{\chi\in\widehat G}\chi(k-d)=N\one_{k=d}$, and the subgroup sum is $m$ for $\chi\in K^\perp$ and zero otherwise: a nontrivial character on $K$ makes that sum invariant under multiplication by a scalar different from $1$. The trivial character has $W(1)=\sum_d w(d)=1$.

For attainment, let $\mu$ be uniform on $\{0,\ldots,q-1\}$ and set
$w(d)=\sum_x\mu(x)\mu(x-d)$. This law has total mass $1$ and
\[
 W(\chi)=\left|\sum_x\mu(x)\overline{\chi(x)}\right|^2\ge0,
 \qquad w(0)=\sum_x\mu(x)^2=\frac1q.
\]
Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:42:lem:support} verifies the proper nonzero support condition.
\end{proof}

This proposition is a direct specialization of the classical finite-group Tur\'an packing theorem of Kolountzakis and R\'ev\'esz~\cite[Theorem 2]{kolountzakisrevesz}. In their notation take
\[
 \Omega=\{0\}\cup\{d:\ord(d)\ge L\},\qquad \Lambda=K.
\]
Then $(\Lambda-\Lambda)\cap\Omega=\{0\}$, and their bound reads
$\sum_G w\le (N/m)w(0)=qw(0)$. The short proof above is finite-group Poisson summation. The report claims neither this extremal principle nor the positivity principle as new.

\subsection{Exactly what is optimized}
For a real function $f$ use the normalized transform
\[
 \widehat f(\chi)=\frac1N\sum_{a\in G}f(a)\overline{\chi(a)}.
\]
For an integer $h$ write $(h\chi)(d)=\chi(hd)$. Fourier expansion and the uniform average over $a$ give
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:42:eq:weightedcov}
 \E_a\sum_d w(d)f(a)f(a+hd)
   =\sum_{\chi\in\widehat G}|\widehat f(\chi)|^2 W(h\chi)\ge0.
\end{equation}
Indeed the $a$-average pairs inverse characters, and the remaining character factor is $\overline{\chi(hd)}$. This remains a character when multiplication by $h$ is not invertible.

For $f=\one_A-\delta$, the same progression-variance expansion as in Section~\ref{gsr:dt:42:sec:moment} gives $\Var(X)\ge\delta(1-\delta)/L$. With $\eta=w(0)<1$, removing the zero step and applying the range inequality yields
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:42:eq:weightedgain}
 H_L(A)\ge(1-\delta)\frac{1/L-\eta}{1-\eta}.
\end{equation}
By Proposition~\ref{gsr:dt:42:prop:packing} and \eqref{gsr:dt:42:eq:decreasing}, the largest right side obtained by this exact covariance-positivity, zero-step-removal, and range-bound calculation is attained at $\eta=1/q$. It is the untruncated arithmetic expression in \eqref{gsr:fm:42:eq:main}. The point mass at zero is allowed in Proposition~\ref{gsr:dt:42:prop:packing}, but has $\eta=1$ and cannot be used in this conditional calculation.

Thus method optimality holds in the entire class of nonnegative probability weights with nonnegative Fourier transform and proper nonzero support. This does not rule out stronger arguments using additional information about $A$, sharper off-diagonal covariances, or more than its mean and range. For a bounded function $g$, the same discussion replaces $1-\delta$ by $\sigma^2/\delta$.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Exact extremizers and the optimal uniform constant\srctag{42}}]{Exact extremizers and the optimal uniform constant}\label{gsr:dt:42:sec:d5}\label{gsr:dt:42:sec:sharp}
\srcnote{42}{Section 5}
We now prove all optimality claims about the density increment itself.
\begin{theorem}[Prime-quotient equality]\label{gsr:dt:42:thm:sharp}
Let $p$ be prime, let $2\le L\le p$, and put
\[
 N=p(L-1),\qquad A=\{x\in\Z/N\Z:x\equiv0\pmod p\}.
\]
Then $\delta=1/p$, $m(N,L)=L-1$, $q(N,L)=p$, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:42:eq:sharp}
 M_L(A)=\frac1L,\qquad
 H_L(A)=\frac{p-L}{Lp}
       =\frac{1-\delta}{L}\frac{p-L}{p-1}.
\end{equation}
Hence the arithmetic theorem is attained exactly throughout this family.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The set consists of $L-1$ multiples of $p$ modulo $N$, so it has density $1/p$. The integer $L-1$ divides $N$ and is the largest possible integer below $L$, giving $m=L-1$.

If $p\mid d$, the additive order of $d$ modulo $N$ divides $L-1$. Such a step cannot be proper for length $L$. For every proper step, therefore, $d$ is nonzero modulo $p$. Since $p$ is prime and $L\le p$, the first $L$ residues
\[
 a,\ a+d,\ \ldots,\ a+(L-1)d\pmod p
\]
are distinct. At most one is zero, so every proper progression meets $A$ in at most one point. Conversely, $P(0,1;L)$ is proper because $N\ge L$, and contains precisely one point of $A$. Thus $M_L(A)=1/L$ and \eqref{gsr:dt:42:eq:sharp} follows.
\end{proof}

For $L<p$, equality can also be seen inside the proof. Use $B=\{0,\ldots,p-1\}$. For every nonzero difference of indices $h$ with $|h|<L\le p$, multiplication by $h$ permutes residues modulo $p$. The local average of $\one_A-1/p$ in the covariance square is therefore zero. Every nonzero sampled window has average $0$ or $1/L$, giving equality in the range bound. The endpoint $L=p$ has zero increment; all proper progressions then meet $A$ exactly once.

\begin{corollary}[Sharp positivity threshold and failure at coefficient one]\label{gsr:dt:42:cor:obstructions}
For infinitely many $L$, at $N=L(L-1)$ there is a nonempty proper subset with no positive density increment on any proper $L$-term progression. No condition $N\ge cL^\gamma$ with fixed $c>0$ and $\gamma<2$ can guarantee such a positive increment uniformly. Further, the condition $N\ge L^2$ does not guarantee $H_L(A)\ge c(1-\delta)/L$ for any absolute $c>0$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Take $L=p$ in Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:42:thm:sharp}. Then $N=p(p-1)$ and $H_L(A)=0$. As primes tend to infinity, $p(p-1)/(p^\gamma)\to\infty$ for every $\gamma<2$, proving the second assertion.

For the last assertion take primes $p\ge5$ and $L=p-2$. Then
\[
 N=p(p-3)=L^2+L-2>L^2,
 \qquad \frac{LH_L(A)}{1-\delta}=\frac2{p-1}\longrightarrow0.
\]
An absolute positive coefficient is therefore impossible even with the strict inequality $N>L^2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Optimal quadratic size--gain tradeoff]\label{gsr:dt:42:thm:constant}
Fix a real number $C>1$. The largest real $c$ for which
\[
 N\ge CL^2,\quad N\ge L\ge2,\quad 0<|A|<N
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 H_L(A)\ge c\frac{1-|A|/N}{L}
\]
holds for every such $N,L,A$ is exactly $c=1-1/C$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Corollary~\ref{gsr:fm:42:cor:scale} proves that $c=1-1/C$ works. To rule out every larger value while satisfying the exact nonasymptotic size hypothesis, let $p$ tend to infinity through primes and set
\[
 L=\left\lfloor\frac pC\right\rfloor-2,\qquad N=p(L-1).
\]
Eventually $L\ge2$, and $L\le p$. Moreover $p\ge C(L+2)$, so
\[
 N\ge C(L+2)(L-1)=C(L^2+L-2)\ge CL^2.
\]
Use the sets of Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:42:thm:sharp}. Since $L/p\to1/C$,
\[
 \frac{LH_L(A)}{1-\delta}=\frac{p-L}{p-1}\longrightarrow1-\frac1C.
\]
Any proposed coefficient larger than this limit fails for all sufficiently large members of the sequence. Only the infinitude of primes is used, not a prime-gap estimate.
\end{proof}

The theorem optimizes a bound over \emph{all} nontrivial densities. Its extremizers satisfy $\delta=1/p\to0$. Nothing in this argument identifies the best coefficient when $\delta$ is held fixed or bounded below. In particular, the phrase ``sharp quadratic scale'' refers to the explicit arithmetic equalities and the stated uniform size--gain tradeoff, not to a complete extremal classification.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A density sensitive gain at the quadratic endpoint\srctag{42}}]{A density sensitive gain at the quadratic endpoint}\label{gsr:dt:42:sec:d6}\label{gsr:dt:42:sec:endpoint}
\srcnote{42}{Section 6}
The uniform coefficient in Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:42:thm:constant} tends to zero as $C$ decreases to $1$. That conclusion is driven by sparse examples. A different elementary argument gives a positive coefficient at the endpoint when density is kept away from zero and one.

\begin{theorem}[Sliding-window endpoint bound]\label{gsr:dt:42:thm:endpoint}
Let $L\ge2$, $N>L(L-1)$, and $0<\delta=|A|/N<1$. Define the proportion of short-order directions by
\[
 \beta=\frac1N\sum_{\substack{h\mid N\\h<L}}\varphi(h),
\]
where $\varphi$ is Euler's totient function. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:42:eq:endpoint}
 H_L(A)\ge\frac{\delta(1-\delta)}{L(1+\beta)+\delta}
          >\frac{\delta(1-\delta)}{2L}.
\end{equation}
In particular, if $0<\varepsilon\le1/2$ and $\varepsilon\le\delta\le1-\varepsilon$, the density gain exceeds $\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)/(2L)$. No optimality is claimed for this coefficient.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $\mathcal P=\{d\in G:\ord(d)\ge L\}$ be the proper directions. Set
\[
 T_d(a)=\sum_{j=0}^{L-1}\one_A(a+jd),\qquad
 M=\max_{a,\,d\in\mathcal P}T_d(a),\qquad \eta=M-\delta L=L H_L(A).
\]
Averaging over $a$ for any proper direction gives $\eta\ge0$. For each $d\in\mathcal P$, the deficits $D_d(a)=M-T_d(a)$ are nonnegative and have mean $\eta$. The sliding identity is
\[
 T_d(a+d)-T_d(a)=\one_A(a+Ld)-\one_A(a).
\]
Consequently
\[
 |\one_A(a+Ld)-\one_A(a)|
   =|D_d(a+d)-D_d(a)|\le D_d(a+d)+D_d(a).
\]
Define $F(x)=|A\mathbin{\triangle}(A+Lx)|/(2N)$ for every $x\in G$.
After averaging over $a$, the preceding inequality becomes
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:42:eq:sliding}
 F(d)\le\eta\qquad(d\in\mathcal P).
\end{equation}

A cyclic group has $\varphi(h)$ elements of order $h$ when $h\mid N$ and none otherwise. Indeed such elements correspond to generators of its unique subgroup of order $h$. Thus
\[
 |G\setminus\mathcal P|=\sum_{\substack{h\mid N\\h<L}}\varphi(h)
 \le\sum_{h=1}^{L-1}h=\frac{L(L-1)}2<\frac N2.
\]
Hence $|\mathcal P|>N/2$ and $\mathcal P-\mathcal P=G$: for every $x$, the sets $\mathcal P$ and $x+\mathcal P$ intersect. Translation invariance and the triangle inequality for symmetric difference give $F(x+y)\le F(x)+F(y)$ and $F(-x)=F(x)$. Writing $x=d_1-d_2$ with $d_1,d_2\in\mathcal P$, \eqref{gsr:dt:42:eq:sliding} therefore gives $F(x)\le2\eta$ for every $x\in G$. Averaging the better bound on $\mathcal P$ and this bound on its complement yields
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:42:eq:Faverage}
 \E_x F(x)\le(1-\beta)\eta+2\beta\eta=(1+\beta)\eta.
\end{equation}

Put $g=\gcd(N,L)$ and $K=LG=gG$, so $|K|=N/g\ge N/L>L-1$. The integer $|K|$ is therefore at least $L$. Let $p_C=|A\cap C|/|K|$ for each coset $C$ of $K$, and average equally over these cosets. Then $\E_Cp_C=\delta$. The variable $Lx$, for uniform $x\in G$, is uniform on $K$; averaging the symmetric difference within each coset gives the exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:42:eq:cosetvariance}
 \E_x F(x)=\E_C p_C(1-p_C).
\end{equation}
For example, the averaged normalized number of ordered pairs with the first point in $A\cap C$ and the second in $C\setminus A$ is $p_C(1-p_C)$; the symmetric difference counts both orientations and its denominator contains the factor $2$.

The step $g$ has order $|K|\ge L$, so it is proper. Averaging its $L$-window counts over starting points in any coset $C$ gives $Lp_C\le M$. It follows that
\[
 p_C\le\delta+\frac\eta L,\qquad
 \E_Cp_C(1-p_C)=\delta-\E_Cp_C^2
 \ge\delta(1-\delta)-\frac{\delta\eta}{L}.
\]
Combining this with \eqref{gsr:dt:42:eq:Faverage}--\eqref{gsr:dt:42:eq:cosetvariance} gives
\[
 \eta\left(1+\beta+\frac\delta L\right)\ge\delta(1-\delta).
\]
Since $\beta<1/2$ and $\delta/L<1/2$, the factor in parentheses is strictly below $2$. Division by $L$ proves \eqref{gsr:dt:42:eq:endpoint}; the stated density-range corollary follows from $\delta(1-\delta)\ge\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)$.
\end{proof}

The proof only needs $|\mathcal P|>N/2$ and $N/\gcd(N,L)\ge L$; the displayed size condition is a convenient sufficient condition for both. Unlike the positive-definite calculation, this argument uses the maximum of all windows to force approximate invariance under $L$-multiple shifts. Its factor $\delta$ makes it compatible with the vanishing-density equality examples in Section~\ref{gsr:dt:42:sec:sharp}.

\begin{proposition}[Dense examples at the strict boundary]\label{gsr:dt:42:prop:denseboundary}
Let $p$ be prime, let $L=p$ and $N=p(p-1)$, and let $A$ be the inverse image of any $k$-element subset of $\Z/p\Z$, $0<k<p$. Then every proper $L$-term progression has density exactly $\delta=k/p$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
A step divisible by $p$ has order at most $p-1$ and is not proper. Every proper step is nonzero modulo $p$, so its $p$ projected points visit every residue modulo $p$ exactly once. Exactly $k$ points belong to the prescribed inverse image.
\end{proof}
Choosing $k=\lfloor\delta_0p\rfloor$ for any fixed $0<\delta_0<1$ gives densities tending to $\delta_0$ and no positive gain at $N=L(L-1)$. Thus the strict universal positivity threshold is sharp even for densities confined to a fixed interval away from zero and one. This does not prove sharpness of the quantitative constant in Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:42:thm:endpoint}.

The cyclic size condition cannot simply be extended to all finite abelian groups by replacing $N$ with group cardinality. For a fixed prime $p\ge3$, take
$G=(\Z/(p-1)\Z)^s\times\Z/p\Z$ and let $A$ be the inverse image of a nonempty proper subset of the last factor. A direction with zero last coordinate has order dividing $p-1$; every proper $p$-term progression therefore projects bijectively onto the last factor and has exactly the global density. The group size tends to infinity with $s$, without a positive increment. The admissible-support hypothesis of Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:42:thm:group} remains essential.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A sparse affine cover consequence\srctag{42}}]{A sparse affine cover consequence}\label{gsr:dt:42:sec:d7}\label{gsr:dt:42:sec:affine}
\srcnote{42}{Section 7}
We give a self-contained application in which the new scale changes a concrete part of a density-increment conclusion. Write $e(t)=\exp(2\pi it)$, and $e_N(y)=e(\widetilde y/N)$ for any integer representative of $y\in\Z/N\Z$.

\begin{theorem}[Affine exact-mass bound]\label{gsr:dt:42:thm:affine}
Let $N\ge2$ and let $A\subseteq\Z/N\Z$ have density $\delta$. Put $f=\one_A-\delta$. Let $M\ge1$ and let $P_1,\ldots,P_M$ be nonempty pairwise disjoint proper modular progressions with
$A\subseteq U:=\bigcup_iP_i$. Let $\phi_i(x)=a_ix+b_i$ be affine maps with coefficients in $\Z/N\Z$, and suppose $\alpha>0$ and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:42:eq:affcorr}
 \sum_{i=1}^M\left|\sum_{x\in P_i}f(x)e_N(-\phi_i(x))\right|\ge\alpha N.
\end{equation}
Set
\[
 r=\min_i|P_i|,\qquad
 \mu=\frac1N\sum_{x\in U}|f(x)|,\qquad b=1-\delta.
\]
Then some proper modular progression $Q$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:42:eq:affine}
 |Q|\ge\max\left\{1,\min\left\{
 \left(\frac{rb}{128\mu}\right)^{1/3},\sqrt{\frac N2}\right\}\right\},
 \qquad \dens_Q(A)\ge\delta+\frac\alpha3.
\end{equation}
No comparability assumption on parent lengths is required. The overall conclusion does not assert $Q\subseteq U$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 40--46]
\emph{Against source~26} (checked at the write). Source~26's Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:26:thm:cube} gives length $\min\{(r(1-\delta)/(128\mu))^{1/3},(N/8)^{1/3}\}$; here the first term is the same and only the modulus cap $(N/8)^{1/3}$, which comes from the sufficient condition $N\ge L^3$ of the variance step, becomes $\sqrt{N/2}$. Since $\sqrt{N/2}/(N/8)^{1/3}=\sqrt2\,N^{1/6}>1$, the new bound is never smaller, and it is larger exactly when the cap binds, that is when $r>16\mu N/(1-\delta)$ (sparse sets; hence the section title). So ``26's affine cap $(N/8)^{1/3}$ becomes $\sqrt{N/2}$'' is the precise reading of the placement's ``square-root cap''; the cube-root dependence on $r$ is not changed. This answers the first of source~26's questions (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:I:cor58}).
\end{writenote}

The corresponding exact-mass statement of Report275~\cite{repo42affine}, retained in Report277, has the modulus cap $(N/8)^{1/3}$ instead of $\sqrt{N/2}$. The first term in \eqref{gsr:dt:42:eq:affine} and its gain are unchanged. Thus this consequence improves the independent variance cap, without changing a uniform comparable-cover exponent or any polynomial phase exponent.

\subsection{Mass identities and affine refinement}
Let $\tau=|U|/N$. The correlation hypothesis implies $0<\delta<1$; otherwise $f=0$. Counting $A$ and $U\setminus A$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:42:eq:mass}
 0<\alpha\le\mu=\delta(1+\tau-2\delta)\le2\delta b,
 \qquad \sum_{x\in U}f(x)=\delta N(1-\tau)\ge0.
\end{equation}
The first inequality also uses the triangle inequality and $\tau\le1$. In particular, all quantities in \eqref{gsr:dt:42:eq:affine} are well-defined and positive.

\begin{lemma}[Affine cells]\label{gsr:dt:42:lem:affinecells}
For an integer $1\le L\le r$, the parents admit a partition into proper progression cells $C$ with
$L\le|C|\le2L-1$. Each cell has a unit complex number $z_C$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:42:eq:error}
 E:=\sum_C\sum_{x\in C}|f(x)|
       |e_N(-\phi_{i(C)}(x))-z_C|
 \le\frac{2\pi L^2\mu N}{r}.
\end{equation}
If $E\le\alpha N/3$, one of the cells has density at least $\delta+\alpha/3$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Write a parent as $u+jd$, $0\le j<n$, with injective parameterization. Its affine phase is a constant multiple of $e(-j\theta)$ for a real representative $\theta$ of $a_id/N$. Put $R=\lfloor n/L\rfloor\ge1$. Among the $R+1$ points
$0,\theta,\ldots,R\theta$ on the circle, some circular gap has length at most $1/(R+1)$. Subtract the corresponding two indices and change sign if necessary. This produces integers $1\le p\le R$ and $v$ with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:42:eq:circle}
 p\theta=v+\varepsilon,\qquad |\varepsilon|\le\frac1{R+1}.
\end{equation}
Coincident points give $\varepsilon=0$; the circular gap crossing zero is included. This is the elementary circle pigeonhole estimate.

Partition the parameter interval into increasing residue chains modulo $p$. Each chain has at least $\lfloor n/p\rfloor\ge L$ elements. A chain of length $T=kL+s$, $0\le s<L$, splits into $k-1$ chunks of length $L$ and one of length $L+s$. Each chunk maps to a proper modular progression because the full parent parameterization is injective.

On a chunk of length $\ell$, write its phase as a constant multiple of $e(-j\varepsilon)$, $0\le j<\ell$, using \eqref{gsr:dt:42:eq:circle}. Choose $z_C$ to be the phase at the real midpoint $(\ell-1)/2$ of this \emph{reduced} phase. The elementary chord--arc bound $|e(t)-e(u)|\le2\pi|t-u|$ gives
\[
 |e_N(-\phi_i(x))-z_C|
 \le2\pi|\varepsilon|\left|j-\frac{\ell-1}2\right|
 \le\frac{2\pi(L-1)}{R+1}
 <\frac{2\pi L^2}{n}
\]
when $L\ge2$. For $L=1$, the cells are singletons and the error is zero. The reduction of the integer $v$ before evaluating the midpoint is important: a half-integral midpoint must not inadvertently retain an integer phase increment. Summing the pointwise estimate over parents, using $n\ge r$, proves \eqref{gsr:dt:42:eq:error}.

Put $F_C=\sum_{x\in C}f(x)$. Replacing the phases by $z_C$ and using the triangle inequality gives
\[
 \sum_C|F_C|\ge\alpha N-E.
\]
Also $\sum_CF_C=\sum_Uf\ge0$ by \eqref{gsr:dt:42:eq:mass}. Thus
\[
 \sum_{F_C>0}F_C
 =\frac12\left(\sum_C|F_C|+\sum_CF_C\right)
 \ge\frac{\alpha N-E}{2}.
\]
If $E\le\alpha N/3$, the positive cells carry balanced mass at least $\alpha N/3$ and occupy at most $N$ points. At least one consequently satisfies $F_C/|C|\ge\alpha/3$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The two branches with exact ceiling control}
\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:42:thm:affine}]
Set
\[
 H=\frac{rb}{\mu},\qquad
 x=\min\{(H/128)^{1/3},\sqrt{N/2}\},\qquad L=\lceil x\rceil.
\]
If $L=1$, choose a singleton in $A$. This has the requested length, and
$\alpha/3\le2\delta b/3<b$ by \eqref{gsr:dt:42:eq:mass}, so its density $1$ exceeds $\delta+\alpha/3$.

Suppose $L\ge2$. Then $x>1$, $L<2x$, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:42:eq:Hbound}
 H\ge128x^3>16L^3.
\end{equation}
Independently, the definition of $L$ gives
\[
 L-1<x\le\sqrt{N/2},\qquad 2(L-1)^2<N.
\]
Both $N$ and $2(L-1)^2$ are integers, hence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:42:eq:ceilvar}
 N\ge2(L-1)^2+1.
\end{equation}
In particular $N\ge L$, and the quadratic half-gain corollary applies.

If $\alpha\le3b/(2L)$, Corollary~\ref{gsr:fm:42:cor:scale} yields a proper progression of length $L$ with density at least
$\delta+b/(2L)\ge\delta+\alpha/3$.
Since $L\ge x$ and $L\ge1$, this proves \eqref{gsr:dt:42:eq:affine} in the low-correlation branch.

Otherwise $\alpha>3b/(2L)$. By \eqref{gsr:dt:42:eq:mass} and \eqref{gsr:dt:42:eq:Hbound},
\[
 r=\frac{H\mu}{b}>\frac{16L^3\mu}{b}>24L^2>L.
\]
Thus Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:42:lem:affinecells} is applicable. Its error satisfies
\[
 E\le\frac{2\pi L^2\mu N}{r}
   =\frac{2\pi L^2bN}{H}
   <\frac{\pi bN}{8L}
   <\frac{bN}{2L}
   <\frac{\alpha N}{3},
\]
where $\pi<4$ was used. The lemma supplies a proper cell of length at least $L$ with the required density. This proves the high-correlation branch and the theorem.
\end{proof}

The high-correlation cell is contained in a parent. The low-correlation progression comes from the variance theorem and need not lie in $U$. For that reason the theorem as a whole carries no containment assertion. Nor does properness imply that the progression is nonwrapping when represented in an ordinary integer interval.

\section{Source~67's Section~2: unequal Fourier budgets at Lemmas~5.2 and~5.5 \wtag}\label{gsr:dt:sec:unequalbudgets}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the eleventh write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next section is source~67's Section~2. \emph{Logically it continues source~37's chapter} on the missing-interval step of Gowers's Section~5 (Section~\ref{gsr:dt:sec:missing}); it is printed here, at the end of Part~I, because no number printed earlier may move. Source~67's introduction is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:67:sec:d1}; its other sections are in Parts~II, III and~V.

\emph{What is proved.} Source~37 found the least mass of the open arc $I_a$ for a probability measure on the circle whose first $R$ Fourier coefficients are bounded by one common budget $e\le\rho$, namely $(\rho-e)/(1+\rho)$ in the window $\pi/(R+1)<a<2\pi/(R+1)$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:37:thm:main}). With unequal budgets $|\widehat\mu(j)|\le\varepsilon_j$ the least mass is $V_{R,a}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)=-1/((1-\cos a)\,\mathbf e^TL(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)^{-1}\mathbf e)$ under finitely checkable strict hypotheses on the localizing matrix $L$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:67:fourier:matrix}), which hold on an open neighbourhood of every interior point $e\mathbf e$, $0<e<\rho$, of the equal-budget branch (Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:67:fourier:local}). Source~37's certificate stays optimal exactly on an explicit polytope of local dimension $\lfloor R/2\rfloor+1$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:67:fourier:polytope}); at every strict-certificate point the Hessian of the value has rank $\lfloor(R-1)/2\rfloor$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:67:fourier:hessian}), so for $R\ge3$ unequal budgets usually need a moving certificate, with an exact rational example at $R=3$, $a=\pi/3$ (Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:67:fourier:example}); on aligned grids the elementary approximation improves to order $N^{-2}$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:67:fourier:grid}). The supported Toeplitz moment criterion is Yang and Xie's, as for source~37, and is credited.

\emph{Relation to the formal statements} (checked at HEAD \texttt{fb9602e55}). \file{lemma_5_2} (\file{Section05.lean}, line~141) has the exact companion \file{lemma_5_2_holds} (\file{Proofs05MissingInterval.lean}, line~220); source~67's formula concerns the extremal problem behind it, not a different statement, and is not formalized.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Exact Fourier-gap profiles with unequal budgets\srctag{67}}]{Exact Fourier-gap profiles with unequal budgets}\label{gsr:dt:67:sec:d2}
\srcnote{67}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:dt:67:fourier:section}

The missing-interval step in Gowers' Lemma~5.2 converts a gap in the support
of a measure into a large Fourier coefficient. Source~37 of the repository
obtained the exact answer when the first several coefficients have a common
bound. Its Question~4 asks for unequal bounds and for the region on which
the old certificate remains optimal. We give a matrix formula on an open
neighbourhood of every interior equal-budget point, a finite certificate
valid beyond those neighbourhoods, and an exact description of the old
certificate's entire optimality region. These statements concern genuine
optima over measures, rather than the output of a discretized optimization.

\subsection{The extremal problem and its moment matrices}

Write $\mathbb T=\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)$, and, for $0<a<\pi$, put
\[
 I_a=\{\theta:|\theta|_\circ<a\},\qquad
 K_a=\mathbb T\setminus I_a,\qquad c=\cos a.
\]
The excluded arc is open. Its endpoints are allowed in $K_a$.
For an integer $R\ge1$ and a vector
$\boldsymbol\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_R)\ge0$, use
$\widehat\mu(j)=\int e^{-ij\theta}\,d\mu(\theta)$ and define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:67:fourier:value}
 V_{R,a}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)
 =\inf\left\{\mu(I_a):\mu\text{ a probability measure on }\mathbb T,
       \ |\widehat\mu(j)|\le\varepsilon_j\ (1\le j\le R)\right\}.
\end{equation}
Reflection followed by averaging preserves arc mass and does not increase
any Fourier modulus, so a symmetric minimizer may be sought. The uniqueness
conclusions below nevertheless apply to all probability measures.
Minimizers exist: probability measures on the compact circle form a weakly
compact space, the moment constraints are closed, and the mass of the open
set $I_a$ is lower semicontinuous by the Portmanteau theorem.

Set $h_0=1$ and $h_j=h_{-j}=-\varepsilon_j$ for $1\le j\le R$.
The following real symmetric matrices depend affinely on the budgets:
\begin{align}
 M(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)&=(h_{j-k})_{0\le j,k\le R},\label{gsr:dt:67:fourier:M}\\
 L(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)&=
 \left(c h_{j-k}-\frac{h_{j-k+1}+h_{j-k-1}}2\right)_{0\le j,k<R}.
 \label{gsr:dt:67:fourier:L}
\end{align}
Let $\mathbf e$ denote the all-ones vector in $\mathbb R^R$ and
$Z=\mathbf e^\perp$. We say that $L$ is positive on $Z$ when
$v^TLv>0$ for every nonzero $v\in Z$; for $R=1$ this condition is vacuous.

We use a standard supported moment theorem, in the normalization needed here.
The matrix criterion is classical; see Yang and Xie~\cite{yangxie}.

\begin{lemma}[Moment criterion for the complementary arc]\label{gsr:dt:67:fourier:moment}
Given $g_{-R},\ldots,g_R$ with $g_{-j}=\overline{g_j}$ and $g_0>0$,
there is a positive measure of mass $g_0$ supported on $K_a$ with moments
$g_j$ if and only if
\[
 (g_{j-k})_{0\le j,k\le R}\succeq0,
 \qquad
 \left(cg_{j-k}-\frac{g_{j-k+1}+g_{j-k-1}}2\right)_{0\le j,k<R}
 \succeq0.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Necessity follows by integrating $|A(e^{i\theta})|^2$ and
$(c-\cos\theta)|B(e^{i\theta})|^2$. For sufficiency, the interval
factorization for nonnegative real polynomials gives the following
one-arc representation: every real trigonometric polynomial $H$ of degree
at most $R$ which is nonnegative on $K_a$ has the form
\[
 H(\theta)=|A(e^{i\theta})|^2+
             (c-\cos\theta)|B(e^{i\theta})|^2,
 \quad \deg A\le R,\quad \deg B\le R-1.
\]
Indeed, $t=\cot(\theta/2)$ maps $K_a$ to
$[-b,b]$, $b=\cot(a/2)$. Multiply $H$ by $(1+t^2)^R$ and apply the
real interval factorization
$p(t)=U(t)^2+(b^2-t^2)W(t)^2$, with degrees at most $R$ and $R-1$.
Dividing back and using
$(b^2-t^2)/(1+t^2)=(c-\cos\theta)/(1-c)$ proves the representation.
This is the usual Markov--Luk\'acs factorization; the one-arc criterion
can equivalently be imported directly from~\cite{yangxie}.

The prescribed moments define a real linear functional on degree-$R$
trigonometric polynomials. The two matrix inequalities and the
representation make it nonnegative on every polynomial nonnegative on
$K_a$. If the normalized moment vector were outside the convex hull of
$\theta\mapsto(\cos\theta,-\sin\theta,\ldots,\cos R\theta,-\sin R\theta)$
for $\theta\in K_a$, strict separation would contradict that positivity.
The convex hull is compact by finite-dimensional Carath\'eodory, so this
argument supplies a positive representing measure.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A finite matrix certificate for the exact answer}

\begin{theorem}[Exact unequal-budget formula]\label{gsr:dt:67:fourier:matrix}
Suppose the following conditions hold:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $L=L(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)$ is positive on $Z$, is invertible,
      and $\beta=\mathbf e^TL^{-1}\mathbf e<0$.
\item For
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:67:fourier:sw}
 s=-\frac{1}{(1-c)\beta},\qquad
 w=\frac{L^{-1}\mathbf e}{\beta},\qquad
 P_w(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{R-1}w_jz^j,
\end{equation}
one has $0<s<1$ and $M(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)-sJ_{R+1}\succ0$.
\item In the expansion
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:67:fourier:F}
 F_w(\theta)=\frac{(\cos\theta-c)|P_w(e^{i\theta})|^2}{1-c}
       =f_0+2\sum_{j=1}^R f_j\cos(j\theta),
\end{equation}
every $f_j$ with $1\le j\le R$ is strictly positive.
\end{enumerate}
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:67:fourier:answer}
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 V_{R,a}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)
 =-\frac{1}{(1-\cos a)\,
      \mathbf e^TL(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)^{-1}\mathbf e}.}
\end{equation}
There is a unique minimizing measure. It has an atom of mass $s$ at $0$,
exactly $R+1$ further atoms in $K_a$, and moments
$\widehat\mu(j)=-\varepsilon_j$ for $1\le j\le R$.
The other atoms are $-a$, $a$, and the arguments of the $R-1$ zeros of
$P_w$; those zeros are simple, are on the unit circle, and are different
from the endpoints. All $R+2$ masses are strictly positive.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Put $\kappa=\beta^{-1}=-(1-c)s$. Then
$\mathbf e^Tw=1$ and $Lw=\kappa\mathbf e$. Thus
\[
 K=L+s(1-c)J_R=L-\kappa J_R
\]
annihilates $w$. Every $x$ decomposes uniquely as
$x=u+(\mathbf e^Tx)w$, with $u\in Z$, and
$x^TKx=u^TLu$. Consequently $K\succeq0$ has kernel $\mathbb Rw$
and rank $R-1$.

Subtracting an atom of mass $s$ at zero from the prescribed moments changes
$M$ to $M-sJ_{R+1}$ and $L$ to $L+s(1-c)J_R$. The former is positive
definite and the latter positive semidefinite. Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:67:fourier:moment}
therefore gives a positive measure $\sigma$ of mass $1-s$ on $K_a$
with moments $h_j-s$. Adding $s\delta_0$ gives a feasible measure $\mu$.

Since $P_w(1)=1$, $F_w(0)=1$. Its positive nonconstant Fourier coefficients
give $F_w(\theta)\le1$ everywhere, with equality only at $0$. Also
$F_w\le0$ on $K_a$, so $F_w\le\mathbf1_{I_a}$. For any feasible measure
$\nu$,
\[
 \nu(I_a)\ge f_0+2\sum_{j=1}^R f_j\Re\widehat\nu(j)
        \ge f_0-2\sum_{j=1}^R f_j\varepsilon_j
        =-\frac{w^TLw}{1-c}=s.
\]
For the constructed measure, the localizing quadratic form at $w$ vanishes:
\[
 \int_{K_a}(c-\cos\theta)|P_w(e^{i\theta})|^2\,d\sigma(\theta)=0.
\]
Hence its support consists only of endpoints and unit-circle zeros of
$P_w$. The coefficient $f_R>0$ implies $w_0w_{R-1}>0$, so $P_w$ has
degree exactly $R-1$. At most $R+1$ such contact points are possible.
On the other hand, the positive definite matrix $M-sJ_{R+1}$ has rank
$R+1$, and a measure on fewer points cannot have this rank. There are
therefore exactly $R+1$ contact points, each with positive mass. This
also proves all the root assertions without a numerical root assumption.

Equality for any feasible $\nu$ forces every moment to be
$-\varepsilon_j$, because each $f_j>0$, and forces support on the same
$R+2$ contact points, including $0$. The moments of orders $-R,\ldots,R$
determine weights on this support: the corresponding Vandermonde matrix
has full column rank since $R+2\le2R+1$. Thus $\nu=\mu$.
\end{proof}

All tests in this theorem involve matrices of order at most $R+1$ and
the coefficients of one polynomial. They are sufficient conditions,
not an assertion that one rational branch describes every budget vector.
At a boundary, a mass, coefficient, or eigenvalue can vanish and the
contact pattern can change.

\subsection{An open region around every interior equal-budget point}

For the rest of this subsection suppose
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:67:fourier:window}
 \frac{\pi}{R+1}<a<\frac{2\pi}{R+1},
 \qquad 0<a<\pi.
\end{equation}
Write $m=R+1$ and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:67:fourier:rho}
 S=m-\cot(a/2)\tan(ma/2),\qquad
 d=S^{-1},\qquad \rho=\frac{d}{1-d}.
\end{equation}
The equal-budget result of source~37 is
$V_{R,a}(e\mathbf e)=(\rho-e)/(1+\rho)$ for $0\le e\le\rho$.
We recall enough of its certificate to verify the hypotheses of our
extension rather than treating their persistence as an assumption.

\begin{lemma}[The equal-budget certificate]\label{gsr:dt:67:fourier:baseline}
Let $T_R$ have $1/2$ in the two adjacent off-diagonals and zero elsewhere.
The vector
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:67:fourier:w0}
 w_j^0=\frac{1-\cos((j-(R-1)/2)a)/\cos(ma/2)}{S},
 \qquad 0\le j<R,
\end{equation}
has positive entries, has sum one, and satisfies
\[
 (T_R-cI)w^0=(1-c)d\mathbf e.
\]
The polynomial $F_{w^0}$ has constant coefficient $d$ and all its other
Fourier coefficients are positive. Also
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:67:fourier:path}
 v^TT_Rv\le\cos(2\pi/m)\|v\|_2^2\qquad(v\in Z).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
In the strict window $\cos(ma/2)<0$. The cosine in each numerator is
larger than that denominator, which proves positivity. Summing a finite
cosine progression gives the normalization, and the cosine recurrence,
extended by $w_{-1}^0=w_R^0=0$, gives the displayed linear equation.
Let $A_k=\sum_jw_j^0w_{j+k}^0$, with zero extension. The coefficient
$q_k$ of $e^{ik\theta}$ in $(\cos\theta-c)|P_{w^0}|^2$ is
\[
 q_0=(1-c)d,\qquad
 q_k=(1-c)d\sum_{j=0}^{R-k-1}w_j^0
       +\frac12w_{R-k}^0w_{R-1}^0>0\quad(1\le k\le R).
\]
Division by $1-c$ proves the coefficient assertion. For
\eqref{gsr:dt:67:fourier:path}, append a zero to $v$ and use the Fourier eigenvalues
$\cos(2\pi\ell/m)$ of the cyclic nearest-neighbour matrix. The appended
vector still has sum zero, so its constant Fourier mode is absent.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Unequal-budget neighbourhoods]\label{gsr:dt:67:fourier:local}
For every $R,a$ satisfying \eqref{gsr:dt:67:fourier:window} and every
$e\in(0,\rho)$, there is an open neighbourhood $\mathcal U$ of
$e\mathbf e$ in $\mathbb R^R$ on which all the hypotheses of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:67:fourier:matrix} hold. In particular the exact optimum is a
real analytic rational function of the budgets on $\mathcal U$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
At equal budgets,
\[
 L=(1+e)(cI-T_R)+e(1-c)J_R.
\]
On $Z$ this is positive definite by \eqref{gsr:dt:67:fourier:path} and
$c>\cos(2\pi/m)$. The vector $w^0$ satisfies
\[
 Lw^0=(1-c)\bigl(e-(1+e)d\bigr)\mathbf e
      =-(1-c)\frac{\rho-e}{1+\rho}\mathbf e.
\]
This scalar is negative, so $L$ is invertible and $\beta<0$.
With $s=(\rho-e)/(1+\rho)$,
\[
 M-sJ_m=(1+e)I_m-(e+s)J_m.
\]
Its constant-mode eigenvalue is
$(1+e)(1-md)>0$ since $d<1/m$, and its other eigenvalues are $1+e$.
The coefficient condition follows from Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:67:fourier:baseline}.
All these inequalities are strict and persist in a sufficiently small
neighbourhood; budgets there can also be kept positive.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The exact region for the old certificate}

Fix the equal-budget certificate $F_0=F_{w^0}$, and let
\[
 Z_0=\{0,-a,a\}\cup\{\arg z:P_{w^0}(z)=0\}.
\]
It has $R+2$ points. Write $F_0=d+2\sum f_j^0\cos(j\theta)$.

\begin{theorem}[Complete fixed-certificate optimality region]
\label{gsr:dt:67:fourier:polytope}
For an arbitrary nonnegative budget vector, the lower bound
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:67:fourier:oldbound}
 V_{R,a}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)
 \ge d-2\sum_{j=1}^R f_j^0\varepsilon_j
\end{equation}
is an equality if and only if the finite system
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:67:fourier:polytope-system}
 p_z\ge0,\quad \sum_{z\in Z_0}p_z=1,\quad
 \sum_{z\in Z_0}p_ze^{-ijz}=-\varepsilon_j\quad(1\le j\le R)
\end{equation}
is feasible. Its solution, when it exists, is unique. Thus the exact
optimality region is a computable polytope intersected with the
nonnegative budget orthant. Near an interior equal-budget point its
dimension is $\lfloor R/2\rfloor+1$ and its codimension is
$\lfloor(R-1)/2\rfloor$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The certificate proves \eqref{gsr:dt:67:fourier:oldbound}. If equality holds, each
positive coefficient forces the corresponding moment to be
$-\varepsilon_j$ and the measure to be supported on the contact set
$Z_0$. Conversely a measure in \eqref{gsr:dt:67:fourier:polytope-system} has
exactly the certificate's integral as its arc mass, because
$F_0=\mathbf1_{I_a}$ on $Z_0$. Uniqueness follows from the same
Vandermonde argument as before. Reflection consequently fixes the measure.

There are $\lfloor R/2\rfloor+2$ reflection orbits in $Z_0$:
zero, endpoint pairs and interior conjugate pairs, with an additional
point at $\pi$ when $R$ is even. This count follows because
$P_{w^0}$ is palindromic, has simple
unit-circle roots, and satisfies $P_{w^0}(1)=1$: odd degree forces a root
at $-1$, whereas an even-degree palindromic polynomial cannot have a
simple root at $-1$. Thus the symmetric probability weights have
dimension $\lfloor R/2\rfloor+1$, and the moment map is injective on
them. At an interior equal-budget point all weights and budgets are
positive, so no inequality reduces this local dimension.
\end{proof}

In particular, for $R\ge3$ the old certificate is generically not optimal
after an unequal perturbation. A linear weighted estimate is therefore
insufficient even arbitrarily close to equal budgets. The next theorem
quantifies its loss.

\subsection{Curvature and the precise loss of a frozen certificate}

Let $\Pi_Z$ be orthogonal projection onto $Z$. At a point satisfying
Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:67:fourier:matrix}, let $A_Z$ denote the positive definite
operator $\Pi_ZL|_Z$. For a budget direction $v\in\mathbb R^R$, write
$H_v=\frac{d}{dt}L(\boldsymbol\varepsilon+tv)|_{t=0}$.

\begin{theorem}[Exact first and second variations]\label{gsr:dt:67:fourier:hessian}
On every open region of positive budgets satisfying the strict
matrix certificate,
\begin{align}
 DV[v]&=-\frac{w^TH_vw}{1-c}
          =-2\sum_{j=1}^R f_jv_j,\label{gsr:dt:67:fourier:gradient}\\
 D^2V[v,v]&=\frac{2}{1-c}
    (\Pi_ZH_vw)^TA_Z^{-1}(\Pi_ZH_vw)\ge0.
 \label{gsr:dt:67:fourier:hessian-formula}
\end{align}
At every strict-certificate point the Hessian has rank exactly
$\lfloor(R-1)/2\rfloor$. At an interior equal-budget point its kernel
is the tangent space of the fixed-certificate polytope in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:67:fourier:polytope}.
At a zero budget, the same formulas describe the analytic extension
of the rational branch, or its feasible one-sided restrictions.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The scalar $\kappa=-(1-c)V$ is the minimum of $u^TLu$ under
$\mathbf e^Tu=1$. The constrained quadratic is strictly convex on its
affine domain, and its unique minimizer is $w$. Differentiation gives
$\kappa'=w^TH_vw$. Differentiating the stationarity equation on $Z$
gives $w'=-A_Z^{-1}\Pi_ZH_vw$. Consequently
$\kappa''=-2(\Pi_ZH_vw)^TA_Z^{-1}(\Pi_ZH_vw)$, proving the formulas.

Both $L$ and $H_v$ commute with reversal of coordinates, and $w$ is
reversal-invariant. Hence $\Pi_ZH_vw$ belongs to the symmetric subspace
of $Z$, which has dimension $\lfloor(R-1)/2\rfloor$.
This image has full dimension. Indeed, if a symmetric $u\in Z$ is
orthogonal to every $H_vw$, all nonconstant Fourier coefficients of
\[
 (c-\cos\theta)\Re\bigl(P_u(e^{i\theta})
                          \overline{P_w(e^{i\theta})}\bigr)
\]
vanish. The polynomial is constant and vanishes at $\theta=a$, so is
identically zero. Symmetry of the coefficient vectors makes the product
inside the real part real on the circle after cancellation of their
common phase. Since $P_w$ is not identically zero, $P_u=0$, hence $u=0$.
This proves the rank assertion.

Finally $\Pi_ZH_vw^0=0$ is precisely the condition that $w^0$ remain
stationary for the entire affine family $L+ tH_v$. Along such a direction
the same certificate and its positive representing weights persist
locally. The dimensions in Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:67:fourier:polytope} agree, proving
the asserted identification of the kernel.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A rational example with a strict improvement}

For $R=3$, put
\[
 \ell_0=c+\varepsilon_1,\quad
 \ell_1=-c\varepsilon_1-(1-\varepsilon_2)/2,\quad
 \ell_2=-c\varepsilon_2+(\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_3)/2,
 \quad A=6\ell_0-8\ell_1+2\ell_2.
\]
The normalized symmetric minimizer has the form $(x,1-2x,x)$, where
$x=2(\ell_0-\ell_1)/A$. Whenever the strict certificate applies,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:67:fourier:R3}
 V_{3,a}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)
 =\frac{4(\ell_0-\ell_1)^2/A-\ell_0}{1-c}.
\end{equation}
This follows by minimizing
$\ell_0-4(\ell_0-\ell_1)x+Ax^2$.

\begin{corollary}[An explicit unequal third-frequency budget]
\label{gsr:dt:67:fourier:example}
Let $a=\pi/3$ and
$\boldsymbol\varepsilon=(1/12,1/12,1/12+t)$, with $|t|\le1/100$.
Then
\begin{align}
 V_{3,\pi/3}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)
 &=\frac{338}{3(91+12t)}-\frac76\notag\\
 &=\frac1{14}-\frac{8t}{49}
       +\frac{96t^2}{49(91+12t)}.
 \label{gsr:dt:67:fourier:example-value}
\end{align}
The fixed equal-budget certificate gives only the first two terms.
The displayed positive rational remainder is its exact loss.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Here $w=(x,1-2x,x)$ with $x=26/(91+12t)$, and
\eqref{gsr:dt:67:fourier:R3} gives the formula. At $t=0$ the restriction of $L$
to $Z$ is bounded below by $13/24$, while the perturbation of $L$ has
operator norm $|t|/2$. The matrix $M-sJ_4$ has smallest eigenvalue
$13/28$ at zero. Its perturbation has norm at most
$|t|+4|s(t)-s(0)|<2|t|$, because $|s'(t)|<1/5$ on the specified interval.
It stays positive. The value $s(t)$ is between $0$ and $1$.
Finally $0<x<2/5$, and the three nonconstant coefficients before
division by $1-c$ are
\[
 \frac{3x^2+(1-2x)^2}{2}-x(1-2x),\qquad
 x(1-\tfrac52x),\qquad \tfrac12x^2.
\]
They are all positive. The restriction of $L$ to $Z$ is positive and
its constrained minimum is negative, which also verifies invertibility
and $\beta<0$. Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:67:fourier:matrix} applies.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]

\subsection{A quadratic finite-grid approximation}

The second question in source~37 asks how much is lost when contact atoms
must lie on a cyclic grid. The following theorem separates the endpoint
displacement from the interior rounding error, and proves the proposed
second-order upper approximation. It does not claim a complete exact
solution of every finite grid problem.

\begin{theorem}[Aligned-endpoint grid bound]\label{gsr:dt:67:fourier:grid}
Fix $R,a$ in the strict window \eqref{gsr:dt:67:fourier:window}. On the angular grid
$2\pi\mathbb Z/N$, let $a_N$ be its smallest nonnegative allowed angle
of size at least $a$, for the symmetric open exclusion $I_a$.
Suppose $a_N<2\pi/(R+1)$, and let $\rho_R$ denote \eqref{gsr:dt:67:fourier:rho}.
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:67:fourier:grid-bound}
 0\le \inf_{\substack{\mu\text{ on }2\pi\mathbb Z/N\\\mu(I_a)=0}}
       \max_{1\le j\le R}|\widehat\mu(j)|-\rho_R(a_N)
 \le \frac{\pi^2R^2}{2N^2}.
\end{equation}
Uniformly for $a$ in a compact subinterval of the strict window,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:67:fourier:grid-firstorder}
 \inf_{\substack{\mu\text{ on }2\pi\mathbb Z/N\\\mu(I_a)=0}}
       \max_{1\le j\le R}|\widehat\mu(j)|
 =\rho_R(a)+\rho_R'(a)(a_N-a)+O_{R,a}(N^{-2}).
\end{equation}
In particular, when the endpoints align, the excess is $O_R(N^{-2})$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The allowed grid is contained in $K_{a_N}$, so the continuous optimum
$\rho_R(a_N)$ is a lower bound. Take its extremal measure. Its endpoint
atoms are already on the grid. Replace each other atom, of mass $u$ at
angle $\theta$, by the convex combination of its two adjacent grid
angles with mean $\theta$. Both neighbours are in the allowed
complementary arc, using an unwrapped interval from $a_N$ to $2\pi-a_N$.

For a twice differentiable vector-valued function $g$ on an interval
$[b,b+h]$, its linear interpolant at $\theta$ differs from $g(\theta)$
by at most $\frac12\sup\|g''\|(\theta-b)(b+h-\theta)$.
Apply this to $g(\theta)=e^{-ij\theta}$ and $h=2\pi/N$.
Each Fourier moment changes by at most $j^2h^2/8$ after summing the
atom masses. This proves \eqref{gsr:dt:67:fourier:grid-bound}; Taylor expansion of
the explicit analytic function $\rho_R$ gives
\eqref{gsr:dt:67:fourier:grid-firstorder}.
\end{proof}

For a half-open excluded interval, the two first allowed endpoints need
not be symmetric. Formula~\eqref{gsr:dt:67:fourier:grid-bound} specifically uses
the symmetric open convention. The same interpolation proof gives the
quadratic rounding bound whenever the two endpoints of the chosen
continuous comparison arc belong to the allowed grid; a shifted,
possibly narrower comparison arc must be chosen first. No endpoint is
silently moved into an excluded half-open boundary.

The practical implication for Lemma~5.2 is that unequal spectral
information can be retained through a sharp finite-dimensional
optimization, and discretization need not incur a first-order interior
loss. Propagating the resulting constants through polynomial recurrence
and a full Szemer\'edi iteration is a separate calculation.
