\section[{An exact family of later ranges for every Fourier cutoff\srctag{93}}]{An exact family of later ranges for every Fourier cutoff}\label{gsr:dt:93:sec:d2}
\srcnote{93}{Section 2}

Let $\mathbb T=\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)$,
$I_a=\{\theta:|\theta|_\circ<a\}$, and $K_a=\mathbb T\setminus I_a$.
The interval is open, so its endpoints are allowed. Define
\[
 E_R(\mu)=\max_{1\le j\le R}|\widehat\mu(j)|,
 \qquad \widehat\mu(j)=\int e^{-ij\theta}\,d\mu(\theta),
 \qquad \Phi_R(a)=\min_{\operatorname{supp}\mu\subseteq K_a}E_R(\mu).
\]
All measures are Borel probability measures. The minimum exists by weak
compactness. Reflection averaging shows that the problem may be solved
using probability measures on $[-1,\cos a]$ and their Chebyshev moments.
The uniqueness arguments below also treat measures which are not initially
assumed reflection symmetric.

\begin{theorem}[A complete final band, at every cutoff]\label{gsr:dt:93:new:allR}
Let $R\ge2$, put $b=\pi-a$, and write $z=\cos b$.
If $0\le b\le\pi/(R+1)$, then
\[
 \Phi_R(a)=z,
 \qquad \mu_* = \frac12(\delta_{\pi-b}+\delta_{\pi+b}).
\]
Coincident atoms are combined when $b=0$.

If
\[
 \frac{\pi}{R+1}\le b\le\frac{2\pi}{R+1},
\]
choose an integer $r\in\{1,\ldots,R\}$ minimizing $\cos(rb)$ and put
\[
 w=\cos(rb),\quad D=2-z-w,\quad
 p=\frac2D,\quad \rho=\frac{z-w}{D}.
\]
Then
\[
 \Phi_R(a)=\rho,\qquad
 \mu_* =\frac p2(\delta_{\pi-b}+\delta_{\pi+b})+(1-p)\delta_\pi.
\]
The extremizer is unique, including transition points. One may always
choose
\[
 r=\min\left\{R,\left\lfloor\frac\pi b+\frac12\right\rfloor\right\},
\]
which is at least two. If two choices minimize the cosine, they give
the same formula and the same measure.
\end{theorem}

This determines $\Phi_R$ throughout
$a\ge(R-1)\pi/(R+1)$. The earlier ``last two exact ranges'' theorem
of \cite{extremallimits} is the part with $r=R$, together with the pure endpoint range. The new
statement contains every change of the active frequency within this
larger band. Its additional transition values are
$b=2\pi/(2r+1)$, when they lie in the displayed band.

\begin{proof}
In the first range, every allowed angle satisfies $-\cos\theta\ge z$,
so $E_R(\mu)\ge-\operatorname{Re}\widehat\mu(1)\ge z$.
The asserted measure has moments $(-1)^j\cos(jb)$, whose absolute
values are at most $z$ because $b\le jb\le\pi-b$. Equality forces
support on the two endpoints and equal masses, so uniqueness follows.

For the second range, $jb\in[b,2\pi-b]$ for $1\le j\le R$.
Consequently
\[
 w\le\cos(jb)\le z\qquad(1\le j\le R).
\]
On this interval, minimizing the cosine is the same as minimizing
$|jb-\pi|$. This proves the stated nearest-integer rule, including
the truncation at $R$. For this rule $\pi-b\le rb\le\pi+b$, whence
$w\le-z$ and $0<p\le1$. Also $0<rb<2\pi$. The moments of the proposed
measure are
\[
 \widehat\mu_*(j)=(-1)^j(1-p+p\cos(jb)).
\]
The affine expression in parentheses maps $w$ to $-\rho$ and $z$ to
$\rho$, proving $E_R(\mu_*)=\rho$.

For completeness, the matching dual proof is elementary. Put
\[
 u=\frac{1-w}{D},\qquad 1-u=\frac{1-z}{D},\qquad
 L(\theta)=-u\cos\theta+(-1)^{r+1}(1-u)\cos(r\theta).
\]
The nonconstant coefficient absolute sum is one, so
$\int L\,d\mu\le E_R(\mu)$. On the allowed arc write
$\theta=\pi\pm t$, $0\le t\le b$, and $y=\cos t$. Set
\[
 F_r(t)=\left(\frac{\sin(rt/2)}{\sin(t/2)}\right)^2,
 \quad F_r(0)=r^2.
\]
The identity $1-T_r(\cos t)=(1-\cos t)F_r(t)$ gives
\[
 L(\theta)-\rho
 =(1-u)(1-y)(F_r(t)-F_r(b)).
\]
The function $F_r$ is strictly decreasing on $[0,2\pi/r]$:
for $x=t/2$ the logarithmic derivative of
$\sin(rx)/\sin x$ is $r\cot(rx)-\cot x<0$, because
$s\cot s$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,\pi)$.
Our choice gives $rb<2\pi$, so $L\ge\rho$ on the entire allowed arc,
with equality exactly at $t=0,b$.

Any extremizer must therefore be supported on
$\{\pi-b,\pi,\pi+b\}$. Equality in the two positively weighted
moment bounds forces its first moment to be real and equal to
$-\rho$. Its imaginary part makes the endpoint weights equal; its
real part fixes their total mass as $p$. This proves uniqueness.
At the lower endpoint of the band $p=1$; the argument remains valid.
At the upper endpoint for $R=2$, $\rho=0$, and the unique measure is
the uniform measure on three equally spaced points. No strict positivity
of $\rho$ was used in the uniqueness argument.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The complete four-frequency problem\srctag{93}}]{The complete four-frequency problem}\label{gsr:dt:93:sec:d3}
\srcnote{93}{Section 3}

Set
\[
 c_- = \cos(3\pi/5)=\frac{1-\sqrt5}{4},\qquad
 c_0 = \cos(2\pi/5)=\frac{\sqrt5-1}{4},
\]
and let $c_*$ be the unique root in $(0,1/5)$ of
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:93:new:transitionpoly}
 A(c)=12c^4+6c^3-11c^2-5c+1=0.
\end{equation}
Numerically,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 c_*&=0.1537156928586777\ldots,\\
 a_*:=\arccos c_*&=1.4164687598172978\ldots\\
       &=0.4508760097203392\ldots\,\pi.
\end{aligned}
\]
Existence and uniqueness follow from $A(0)>0>A(1/5)$ and
$A'(c)<0$ on $[0,1/3]$: indeed
$48c^3+18c^2\le48/27+2<5$ there.

For $c\in[c_-,c_*]$, define
\[
 D(x)=(1-x)(2x+1),\qquad
 h(x)=\frac{x^2(4x^2-3)}{D(x)},
\]
and let $v=v(c)$ be the unique number in $[-1,-\sqrt3/2]$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:93:new:nodeeq}
 h(v)=h(c).
\end{equation}
The letter $v$ here denotes a cosine value, not an angle. An equivalent
cubic equation, with no rational denominators, is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:93:new:nodecubic}
 4D(c)v^3+4cD(c)v^2+(c+1)(4c^2-3)v+c(4c^2-3)=0.
\end{equation}
This follows by factoring $v-c$ from
$v^2(4v^2-3)D(c)-c^2(4c^2-3)D(v)$; its unique root in the
specified interval is the one intended. Define
\[
 G(c)=\frac{1+2cv(c)}{1-2c-2v(c)}.
\]

\begin{theorem}[Every radius for four moments]\label{gsr:dt:93:new:Phi4}
For $0\le a\le\pi$, with $c=\cos a$, one has
\[
\Phi_4(a)=
\begin{cases}
0,&0\le a\le\pi/5,\\[2pt]
\displaystyle\frac{1+2c-4c^2}{3+10c-12c^2},
  &\pi/5\le a\le2\pi/5,\\[7pt]
\displaystyle\frac{1-2c^2}{3+2c-4c^2},
  &2\pi/5\le a\le a_*,\\[7pt]
G(c),&a_*\le a\le3\pi/5,\\[2pt]
\displaystyle\frac{2c(c-1)}{2c^2-2c+1},
  &3\pi/5\le a\le5\pi/7,\\[7pt]
\displaystyle\frac{-c-T_4(c)}{2+c-T_4(c)},
  &5\pi/7\le a\le4\pi/5,\\[7pt]
-c,&4\pi/5\le a\le\pi,
\end{cases}
\qquad T_4(c)=8c^4-8c^2+1.
\]
All adjacent formulas agree at their common endpoints. For every
$a\ge\pi/5$ the extremizer is unique. The transition $a_*$ is specified by \eqref{gsr:dt:93:new:transitionpoly}.
Its ratio with $\pi$ is irrational, as proved in
Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:93:new:irrational-transition}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 82--94]
\emph{Proved independently by source~90} (Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:90:thm:four}), with the same pin and without either citing the other; the formulas agree, and source~90's radical for $c_*$ has the quartic \eqref{gsr:dt:93:new:transitionpoly} as minimal polynomial (checked at the write). A linear program on a $20001$-point grid reproduces $\Phi_4(\pi/2)=(\sqrt3-1)/2$ and the second and third branches (corroboration).
\end{writenote}

\subsection{The new central branch: construction and all feasibility checks}

\begin{lemma}[The unique interior contact]\label{gsr:dt:93:new:node}
The definition \eqref{gsr:dt:93:new:nodeeq} is valid for every
$c\in[c_-,c_*]$. Its endpoint values include
\[
 v(c_-)=-1,\qquad v(0)=-\sqrt3/2,
 \qquad v(c_*)=-\frac{1+c_*}{1+2c_*}.
\]
Moreover, $v(c)>-1$ for $c>c_-$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For $y\in[\sqrt3/2,1]$,
\[
 -h(-y)=\frac{y^2}{y+1}\,\frac{4y^2-3}{2y-1}.
\]
Both factors are nonnegative and strictly increasing. For the second
factor, the derivative numerator is $8y^2-8y+6>0$. Thus $h$ is
strictly increasing on $[-1,-\sqrt3/2]$, with endpoint values
$-1/2$ and zero.

For $c\in[c_-,c_*]$, $D(c)>0$, $c^2<3/4$, so $h(c)\le0$.
The other inequality $h(c)\ge-1/2$ is equivalent to
\[
 2c^2(4c^2-3)+D(c)
 =(c+1)(2c-1)(4c^2-2c-1)\ge0.
\]
This is true since $c\in[c_-,c_*]\subset[c_-,1/2]$.
Equality occurs only at $c=c_-$. Existence, uniqueness, and the
first two displayed values follow.

For $0\le c\le c_*$ put $v_3(c)=-(1+c)/(1+2c)$.
Since $A(1/6)<0$, one has $c_*<1/6$, and hence
$-1\le v_3(c)\le-7/8<-\sqrt3/2$. Direct factorization gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:93:new:transitionidentity}
 h(c)-h(v_3(c))
 =\frac{(2c^2+2c+1)A(c)}{(1-c)(1+2c)^2(2+3c)}.
\end{equation}
At $c=c_*$ the right side vanishes, proving the final endpoint identity.
More generally it is nonnegative on $[0,c_*]$, so
$v(c)\ge v_3(c)$ on that interval.
\end{proof}

Fix $c\in[c_-,c_*]$, abbreviate $v=v(c)$, and put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:93:new:centralweights}
 p=\frac{-D(v)}{D(c)-D(v)},\qquad
 \nu_*=p\delta_c+(1-p)\delta_v.
\end{equation}
The two masses are strictly positive: $D(c)>0>D(v)$.
By construction,
\[
 \mathbb E_{\nu_*}D(x)=0,\qquad
 \mathbb E_{\nu_*}x^2(4x^2-3)=0.
\]
Since $D=T_1-T_2$ and
$T_4+T_1=D+2x^2(4x^2-3)$, its cosine moments satisfy
\[
 m_1=m_2=-\rho,\qquad m_4=\rho,
 \qquad \rho=-\mathbb E x=\frac{1+2cv}{1-2c-2v}=G(c)>0.
\]
The formula for $\rho$ follows either by substitution or from
$\mathbb E x^2=(1-\rho)/2$ and
$x^2=(c+v)x-cv$ on the support.

The remaining inequality $|m_3|\le\rho$ requires proof. Set
$s=v+c<0$, $t=vc$, and $B=1-2s>0$. A two-point moment calculation gives
\begin{align}
 m_3+\rho&=\frac{4(1-v)(1-c)(1+v+c+2vc)}{B},\label{gsr:dt:93:new:m3lower}\\
 m_3-\rho&=\frac{2J}{B},\qquad
 J=(1+2t)^2-2s(s+t).\label{gsr:dt:93:new:m3upper}
\end{align}
Equation \eqref{gsr:dt:93:new:nodecubic}, equivalently
\[
 4s^3+4ts^2-8t^2s-8ts-4t^2-3s-3t=0,
\]
also gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:93:new:Jidentity}
 J=-\frac{s+3t+4t^2}{2s}.
\end{equation}

For the lower bound in \eqref{gsr:dt:93:new:m3lower}, if $c\le0$ then
\[
 1+v+c+2vc=(1+v)+c(1+2v)\ge0.
\]
If $c\ge0$, the same expression is nonnegative precisely when
$v\ge-(1+c)/(1+2c)$, which was proved in
\eqref{gsr:dt:93:new:transitionidentity}. Equality in this lower moment bound
occurs exactly at $c=c_*$.

For the upper bound, it suffices by \eqref{gsr:dt:93:new:Jidentity} to prove
$s+3t+4t^2\le0$. When $c\ge0$, one has $s<0$ and
$-1/5<t\le0$, so $t(3+4t)\le0$. When $c\le0$, write
$u=-v\in[\sqrt3/2,1]$ and $z=-c\in[0,(\sqrt5-1)/4]$.
Then the expression in question is
\[
 4u^2z^2+3uz-u-z.
\]
As a function of $u\in[0,1]$ this is convex. Its endpoint values
are $-z\le0$ and $4z^2+2z-1\le0$, so it is nonpositive
throughout. In the present parameter range equality occurs only when
$u=1$, $z=(\sqrt5-1)/4$, namely $c=c_-$. Therefore
\[
 -\rho<m_3<\rho\qquad(c_-<c<c_*),
\]
with $m_3=-\rho$ at $c_*$ and $m_3=\rho$ at $c_-$.
This proves all primal constraints, rather than only the active ones.

\subsection{The central quartic certificate}

Define the monic polynomial
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:93:new:centraldual}
 Q(x)=(x-v)^2(x-c)(x+2v+c).
\end{equation}
Because $v+c<0$, the fourth root $-2v-c$ is strictly larger than
$c$. Consequently $Q(x)\ge0$ for every $x\in[-1,c]$, with zeros
exactly $v,c$ on that interval. Put
$H=3v^2+2vc+c^2=2v^2+(v+c)^2$. Its Chebyshev expansion is
\[
 Q(x)=q_0+q_1T_1(x)+q_2T_2(x)+q_4T_4(x),
\]
where
\begin{align*}
 q_0&=\frac38-\frac H2-v^2c(2v+c),\\
 q_1&=2v(v+c)^2<0,\\
 q_2&=\frac{1-H}{2}<0,\\
 q_4&=\frac18>0.
\end{align*}
There is no third Chebyshev term. The sign of $q_2$ follows from
$H\ge2v^2\ge3/2$. Let
\[
 K=-q_1-q_2+q_4=-2v(v+c)^2+\frac H2-\frac38>0.
\]
Integrating $Q$ against \eqref{gsr:dt:93:new:centralweights} gives
$q_0+K\rho=0$. Hence
\[
 L(\theta)=\frac{q_1\cos\theta+q_2\cos(2\theta)+q_4\cos(4\theta)}K
          =\rho+\frac{Q(\cos\theta)}K\ge\rho
\]
on $K_a$, while its nonconstant coefficient absolute sum is one.
For every allowed measure $\mu$,
$E_4(\mu)\ge\int L\,d\mu\ge\rho$. The symmetric lift of
\eqref{gsr:dt:93:new:centralweights} attains equality. This proves the new
central formula, with a certificate valid on the entire allowed arc.

For uniqueness, equality forces support at the cosine values $c,v$
and forces moments one, two, and four to be real and equal to
$-\rho,-\rho,\rho$, respectively. If $v>-1$, the imaginary parts
of moments one and two make the two masses in each conjugate pair
equal: the determinant is a nonzero multiple of
$\sin(\arccos c)\sin(\arccos v)(v-c)$. If $v=-1$, only the
pair above $c$ remains, and the first imaginary moment suffices.
The first real moment fixes its total mass. Thus the extremizer is
unique among all measures, not merely the even ones.

\subsection{Self-contained certificates for the earlier branches}

The following two certificates reprove the already known low-degree
branches. They are included to make the complete classification
checkable without importing an unprinted moment calculation. The first
is the $R=4$ case of source~37's first-window theorem \cite{srcthirtyseven};
the second is the cutoff-three first branch of \cite{extremallimits}. The new conclusions
begin with the fourth-moment feasibility intervals and the central
quartic certificate above.

\begin{lemma}[The known first branch for cutoff four]\label{gsr:dt:93:new:first4}
Let
\[
 c_0=\frac{\sqrt5-1}{4}\le c\le
 c_1=\frac{\sqrt5+1}{4},\qquad
 v=-\frac1{4c},\quad B_4=3+10c-12c^2,
 \quad \rho=\frac{1+2c-4c^2}{B_4}.
\]
Then $\Phi_4(\arccos c)=\rho$, with a unique optimizer. Its cosine
measure is $w_{-1}\delta_{-1}+w_v\delta_v+w_c\delta_c$, where
\begin{align*}
 w_{-1}&=\frac{(1-c)(4c+1)(4c^2+2c-1)}
 {B_4(4c-1)(c+1)},\\
 w_v&=\frac{128c^4(1-c)}{B_4(4c-1)(4c^2+1)},\\
 w_c&=\frac{2(4c+1)}{B_4(c+1)(4c^2+1)}.
\end{align*}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
All denominators are positive: $c>1/4$ and
$4c^2\le2c+1$ imply $B_4\ge4c>0$. Every numerator is nonnegative,
and only $w_{-1}$ can vanish, at $c=c_0$. Substitution gives
\[
 w_{-1}+w_v+w_c=1,\qquad
 \sum_{x\in\{-1,v,c\}}w_xT_j(x)=-\rho
 \quad(1\le j\le4).
\]
These identities can also be obtained by solving the first two moment
equations with the three-point support. The raw moment numerators used
in the Lagrange solution are
\[
 \mathbb E(x-v)(x-c)=\frac14+\rho(v+c-1/2),
\]
\[
 \mathbb E(x+1)(x-c)=\frac12-c-\rho(3/2-c),\qquad
 \mathbb E(x+1)(x-v)=\frac12-v-\rho(3/2-v).
\]
Division by the corresponding Lagrange denominators gives the displayed
weights. The support relation and $v=-1/(4c)$ then give the third and
fourth moments, or they can be checked directly from the displayed formulas.

For the lower bound take
\[
 Q_4(x)=(x+1)(c-x)(x-v)^2\ge0\qquad(-1\le x\le c).
\]
In its Chebyshev expansion, the nonconstant coefficients are
\begin{align*}
 q_4&=-1/8,\\
 q_3&=(c-1+2v)/4,\\
 q_2&=((c-1)(1-2v)-v^2)/2,\\
 q_1&=(c-1)(3/4+v^2)+v(3/2-2c)
      =\frac{12c^3-4c^2-5c-1}{16c^2}.
\end{align*}
They are all strictly negative. The first three signs are immediate.
For $q_1$, the numerator $g(c)$ has derivative
$36(c-1/2)(c+5/18)$, so its maximum on $[c_0,c_1]$ is at an endpoint.
Using the quadratic equations for those endpoints gives
$g(c_0)=3c_0-7/2<0$ and $g(c_1)=-c_1-1/2<0$.

Put $K=-\sum_{j=1}^4q_j>0$. The constructed measure has
$\int Q_4=0$ and all four moments $-\rho$, whence $q_0+K\rho=0$.
Thus $K^{-1}\sum q_jT_j\ge\rho$ on $[-1,c]$ and its coefficient
absolute sum is one. This gives the matching lower bound. Equality
forces support on the three displayed cosine nodes and all first four
complex moments to be real and equal to $-\rho$. Imaginary moments
one and two force reflection symmetry on the two nonreal pairs; total
mass and the first two real moments uniquely determine the weights.
The same argument works when $w_{-1}=0$ or $\rho=0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The known first branch for cutoff three]\label{gsr:dt:93:new:first3}
For $0\le c\le1/\sqrt2$, set
\[
 v=-\frac{c+1}{2c+1},\qquad
 \rho=\frac{1-2c^2}{3+2c-4c^2},\qquad
 p=\frac{-\rho-v}{c-v}.
\]
Then $\Phi_3(\arccos c)=\rho$, and its unique cosine optimizer is
$p\delta_c+(1-p)\delta_v$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Here $-1\le v\le-1/\sqrt2$, $0\le\rho\le1/3$, and $0<p<1$.
Direct substitution, or the two-point support recurrence, gives
\[
 \mathbb E x=-\rho,\qquad
 \mathbb E x^2=(1-\rho)/2,\qquad \mathbb E x^3=-\rho.
\]
Thus the first three cosine moments are $-\rho$. The certificate
\[
 Q_3(x)=(c-x)(x-v)^2=q_0+q_1T_1(x)+q_2T_2(x)+q_3T_3(x)
\]
has
\[
 q_0=(c+2v)/2+cv^2,\quad q_1=-3/4-2cv-v^2,\quad
 q_2=(c+2v)/2,\quad q_3=-1/4.
\]
All nonconstant coefficients are strictly negative: $q_2,q_3<0$,
while $-2cv\le1$ and $v^2\ge1/2$ give $q_1\le-1/4$.
Let $K=-(q_1+q_2+q_3)>0$. Since $Q_3$ vanishes on the proposed support,
$q_0+K\rho=0$, so its normalized nonconstant part is at least
$\rho$ on the entire allowed interval and has coefficient absolute sum one.
This proves the sharp lower bound. Equality forces the two cosine nodes
and real first and second moments; the same determinant argument used
for the central branch proves uniqueness, also when $v=-1$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The two inheritance intervals and completion}

The previously proved cutoff-three first formula is
\[
 F_3(c)=\frac{1-2c^2}{3+2c-4c^2},\qquad
 v_3(c)=-\frac{c+1}{2c+1},
\]
with the two-point cosine measure having first three moments
$-F_3(c)$. In the range relevant here, $c_*\le c\le c_0$, its
fourth moment obeys the exact identities
\begin{align}
 m_4-F_3(c)&=
 \frac{2A(c)}{(2c+1)(3+2c-4c^2)},\label{gsr:dt:93:new:inheritupper}\\
 m_4+F_3(c)&=
 \frac{2(c-1)(3c+2)(4c^2+2c-1)}
 {(2c+1)(3+2c-4c^2)}.\label{gsr:dt:93:new:inheritlower}
\end{align}
The denominators are positive. The first numerator is nonpositive
because $A$ decreases on $[0,1/3]$ and vanishes at $c_*$. The second
is nonnegative because $c\le c_0$ and $c<1$. Thus the cutoff-three
extremizer is feasible for four moments in precisely the displayed
inheritance range, and
\[
 \Phi_4(a)=\Phi_3(a)=F_3(c)
 \quad(2\pi/5\le a\le a_*).
\]
The lower bound follows from $E_4\ge E_3$; uniqueness is inherited.
For $c<c_*$ close to $c_*$, the same measure violates $m_4\le F_3(c)$,
so this is a real active-constraint transition, not an artificial
subdivision of one formula.

The entire range $a\ge3\pi/5$ follows from Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:93:new:allR}
with $R=4$. Specifically, for
\[
 2\pi/7\le b\le2\pi/5
\]
the minimizing index is $r=3$ (at the upper endpoint $r=2$ ties),
which gives $2c(c-1)/(2c^2-2c+1)$. For
\[
 \pi/5\le b\le2\pi/7
\]
it is $r=4$, giving $(-c-T_4(c))/(2+c-T_4(c))$.
The remaining pure endpoint interval is $0\le b\le\pi/5$.

For $\pi/5\le a\le2\pi/5$, the source-37 first-window formula
simplifies to
\[
 \frac{1}{4-\cot(a/2)\tan(5a/2)}
 =\frac{1+2c-4c^2}{3+10c-12c^2},
\]
with the continuous endpoint values understood. Its critical endpoint
$a=\pi/5$ is the unique uniform measure on
$\{(2j+1)\pi/5:0\le j<5\}$; the same measure gives zero moments
for every smaller radius.

Agreement at $a_*$ follows from the identity for $v(c_*)$ in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:93:new:node}; both sides use the same two cosine nodes and
the same first two moments. At $a=3\pi/5$, $v=-1$, and the central
measure has $m_1=m_2=-\rho$, $m_3=m_4=\rho$; it is exactly the
three-atom endpoint measure in Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:93:new:allR}. At
$a=5\pi/7$, the minimizing cosine values for $r=3,4$ coincide.
At $a=4\pi/5$, $p=1$. Finally, at $a=2\pi/5$, both earlier
formulas equal $1/4$ and have the uniform measure on the four
nonidentity fifth roots. These observations prove all endpoint
agreements and complete Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:93:new:Phi4}.

\subsection{An explicit central value}

At $a=\pi/2$ one has $c=0$, $v=-\sqrt3/2$, and
\[
 \Phi_4(\pi/2)=\frac{\sqrt3-1}{2}.
\]
The unique cosine measure is
\[
 \frac1{\sqrt3}\delta_0+
 \left(1-\frac1{\sqrt3}\right)\delta_{-\sqrt3/2}.
\]
On the circle this means equal weights within the pairs
$\{\pi/2,3\pi/2\}$ and $\{5\pi/6,7\pi/6\}$.
Its moments are $(-\rho,-\rho,0,\rho)$, and a monic certificate is
\[
 Q(x)=x^4-\frac94x^2-\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}x,
 \qquad K=\frac{3(\sqrt3+1)}4.
\]
This strictly improves the three-frequency detector $\Phi_3(\pi/2)=1/3$.


\subsection{The arithmetic nature of the new transition}

% Self-contained corollary for integration after the cutoff-four theorem.
\begin{corollary}[An irrational angular transition]\label{gsr:dt:93:new:irrational-transition}
Let $c_*$ be the root in $(0,1/5)$ of
$12c^4+6c^3-11c^2-5c+1=0$, and let $a_* = \arccos c_*$.
Then $a_*/\pi$ is irrational.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The number $y_*=2c_*$ is a root of the primitive integer polynomial
\[
 P(y)=3y^4+3y^3-11y^2-10y+4,
\]
since $P(2c)=4(12c^4+6c^3-11c^2-5c+1)$.
Modulo five, multiplication by the inverse of the leading coefficient
gives the monic polynomial
\[
 f(y)=y^4+y^3+3y^2+3\in\mathbb F_5[y].
\]
It has no root in $\mathbb F_5$, as the complete evaluation table is
\[
 \begin{array}{c|ccccc}
 y&0&1&2&3&4\\\hline
 f(y)&3&3&4&3&1
 \end{array}.
\]
It also has no factorization into two monic quadratics. Indeed, a
factorization
\[
 f(y)=(y^2+\alpha y+\beta)(y^2+\gamma y+\delta)
\]
would require
\[
 \beta\delta=3,\quad \alpha+\gamma=1,\quad
 \alpha\delta+\beta\gamma=0,\quad
 \alpha\gamma+\beta+\delta=3.
\]
All calculations in this paragraph are in $\mathbb F_5$. The first
three equations give exactly the following possibilities:
\[
 \begin{array}{cc|cc|c}
 \beta&\delta&\alpha&\gamma&\alpha\gamma+\beta+\delta\\\hline
 1&3&2&4&2\\
 2&4&4&2&4\\
 3&1&4&2&2\\
 4&2&2&4&4
 \end{array}.
\]
None satisfies the fourth equation. A reducible quartic over a field
has a linear factor or is a product of two quadratics, so $f$ is
irreducible. Reduction modulo five and Gauss's lemma show that $P$ is
irreducible over $\mathbb Q$.

Consequently the monic minimal polynomial of $y_*$ is $P(y)/3$.
It does not have integer coefficients, so $y_*$ is not an algebraic
integer. Here the standard integral form of Gauss's lemma suffices:
a primitive irreducible integer polynomial which divides a monic
integer polynomial must have leading coefficient $1$ or $-1$.

If $a_*/\pi=m/n$ were rational, with $n\ge1$, put
$\zeta=e^{ia_*}$. Then $\zeta^{2n}=1$ and
$y_* = \zeta+\zeta^{-1}$. To see directly that this is an algebraic
integer, define
\[
 S_0(Y)=2,\quad S_1(Y)=Y,\quad
 S_{j+1}(Y)=Y S_j(Y)-S_{j-1}(Y).
\]
For $j\ge1$, $S_j$ is monic with integer coefficients, and induction
gives $S_j(\zeta+\zeta^{-1})=\zeta^j+\zeta^{-j}$.
Thus the monic integer polynomial $S_{2n}(Y)-2$ vanishes at $y_*$,
contradicting the preceding paragraph. Hence $a_*/\pi$ is irrational.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Exact cyclic-grid corrections in the new branch\srctag{93}}]{Exact cyclic-grid corrections in the new branch}\label{gsr:dt:93:sec:d4}
\srcnote{93}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:dt:93:grid:section}

The continuous extremizer also determines an exact discrete answer. The
previous manuscripts \cite{extremallimits,srcsixtyseven} established a uniform quadratic error after rounding
the forbidden radius. Here we compute the error itself on the interior
of the new four-frequency branch, including its leading coefficient and
an arithmetic subsequence on which it is identically zero.

\subsection{A finite certificate with three cosine nodes}

Let $c$ belong to the open central branch of the four-frequency theorem,
and let $b=b(c):=v(c)$ be its interior cosine node, using the $v(c)$ of the preceding section. Write $\rho=\Phi_4(\arccos c)$
and let $w_b$ be the mass of the continuous cosine measure at $b$.
Thus $-1<b\le-\sqrt3/2$, $b<c$, and the continuous measure has
$m_1=m_2=-\rho$, $m_4=\rho$, with $|m_3|<\rho$.
Set
\[
 \mathsf D(x)=T_2(x)-T_1(x)=2x^2-x-1,\qquad
 \mathsf E(x)=T_4(x)+T_1(x)=8x^4-8x^2+x+1,
\]
and
\[
 F_c(x)=\mathsf E(x)-\frac{\mathsf E(c)}{\mathsf D(c)}\mathsf D(x).
\]
The contact equation is $F_c(b)=0$.

Let $\mathcal X$ be a finite subset of $[-1,c]$ containing $c$, and
let $u<v$ be consecutive points of $\mathcal X$ with $u<b<v$ and
$u,v<-1/2$. Put
\begin{align*}
 s&=u+v,&p&=uv,&q&=c(s+c),\\
 A_2&=p-s^2-q,&
 q_1&=s(p+q),&q_2&=(1+A_2)/2,\\
 q_0&=3/8+A_2/2-pq,&
 K&=-q_1-q_2+1/8,&\rho_{\mathcal X}&=-q_0/K.
\end{align*}
These are coefficients in the exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:93:grid:polynomial}
 Q_{\mathcal X}(x):=(x-u)(x-v)(x-c)(x+s+c)
 =q_0+q_1T_1(x)+q_2T_2(x)+\tfrac18T_4(x).
\end{equation}
In particular the third Chebyshev coefficient is exactly zero.

Define unnormalized positive weights
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:93:grid:weights}
 \eta_u=-F_c(v),\qquad \eta_v=F_c(u),\qquad
 \eta_c=-\frac{\eta_u\mathsf D(u)+\eta_v\mathsf D(v)}{\mathsf D(c)},
\end{equation}
and divide them by $Z=\eta_u+\eta_v+\eta_c$ to obtain $\nu_{\mathcal X}$.

\begin{theorem}[Exact finite-node certificate]\label{gsr:dt:93:grid:certificate}
Assume in addition that
\[
 s+2c<0,\qquad q_1<0,\quad q_2<0,\quad \rho_{\mathcal X}>0,
 \qquad \left|\int T_3\,d\nu_{\mathcal X}\right|\le\rho_{\mathcal X}.
\]
Then the minimum of $\max_{1\le j\le4}|\int T_j\,d\nu|$ over
probability measures supported on $\mathcal X$ is exactly
$\rho_{\mathcal X}$. The measure $\nu_{\mathcal X}$ attains it.
For the cosine image of a symmetric angular grid, its symmetric angular
lift is an optimizer of the original complex-Fourier problem.
Moreover, the exact error is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:93:grid:exact-error}
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 \rho_{\mathcal X}-\rho
 =\frac{w_b(b-u)(v-b)(b-c)(b+s+c)}{K}.}
\end{equation}
If $b$ itself is an allowed node, the discrete and continuous optima agree.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
First, the weights in \eqref{gsr:dt:93:grid:weights} are positive. Indeed $\mathsf D(c)<0$
and $\mathsf D(x)>0$ for $-1\le x<-1/2$. Direct differentiation gives
\[
 \left(\frac{\mathsf E(x)}{\mathsf D(x)}\right)'
 =\frac{2x(16x^4-12x^3-16x^2+3x+6)}{\mathsf D(x)^2}<0
 \quad(-1\le x<-1/2).
\]
To check the sign without numerical estimates, put $y=-x\in(1/2,1]$.
The polynomial in parentheses becomes
$16y^2(y^2-1)+3y(4y^2-1)+6\ge-4+0+6>0$.
As $F_c(x)=\mathsf D(x)(\mathsf E(x)/\mathsf D(x)-\mathsf E(c)/\mathsf D(c))$ and $F_c(b)=0$,
we have $F_c(u)>0>F_c(v)$. The assertion follows.

The weights give $\int\mathsf D\,d\nu_{\mathcal X}=0$ and
$\int F_c\,d\nu_{\mathcal X}=0$, hence also $\int\mathsf E\,d\nu_{\mathcal X}=0$.
Consequently its moments have the form $m_1=m_2=-r$, $m_4=r$.
Since its support consists of zeros of $Q_{\mathcal X}$,
\eqref{gsr:dt:93:grid:polynomial} gives $q_0+Kr=0$. Thus $r=\rho_{\mathcal X}$,
and the remaining moment hypothesis proves primal feasibility.

For every $x\in\mathcal X$, consecutive-node adjacency implies
$(x-u)(x-v)\ge0$. Also $x-c\le0$ and
$x+s+c\le s+2c<0$. Therefore $Q_{\mathcal X}(x)\ge0$.
The nonconstant coefficients of
\[
 P_{\mathcal X}(x)=
 \frac{q_1T_1(x)+q_2T_2(x)+\tfrac18T_4(x)}{K}
\]
have absolute sum one and $P_{\mathcal X}\ge\rho_{\mathcal X}$ on the
grid. Integration proves that every admissible measure has at least one
moment of modulus at least $\rho_{\mathcal X}$. This is the matching
dual certificate. Symmetrizing an angular measure cannot increase any
Fourier modulus, and its cosine image has these Chebyshev moments.

Finally integrate $Q_{\mathcal X}$ against the continuous two-node
measure. Its active moments give
\[
 \int Q_{\mathcal X}\,d\nu=q_0+K\rho
 =K(\rho-\rho_{\mathcal X}),
\]
while its support gives $\int Q_{\mathcal X}\,d\nu=w_bQ_{\mathcal X}(b)$.
These two identities prove \eqref{gsr:dt:93:grid:exact-error}. If $b$ is allowed,
the continuous optimizer is already feasible on the grid, and the two
optima agree by inclusion of admissible classes.
\end{proof}

The polynomial is allowed to be negative between $u$ and $v$: those
points are absent from the discrete support. This precise change from a
double contact to two adjacent simple contacts accounts for the strict
improvement in the discrete lower bound.

\subsection{The leading correction and the required radius rounding}

Let $\Phi_{4,N}(a)$ denote the same minimax problem restricted to
$\{2\pi j/N:0\le j<N\}$. Set
\[
 a_N=\frac{2\pi}{N}\left\lceil\frac{Na}{2\pi}\right\rceil,
 \qquad c_N=\cos a_N,
 \qquad \mathcal X_N=\{\cos(2\pi j/N):\cos(2\pi j/N)\le c_N\}.
\]
In the ranges used here $a_N<\pi$, so the admissible grid is nonempty.
It depends on $a$ only through $a_N$.

\begin{theorem}[Exact and asymptotic cyclic-grid correction]
\label{gsr:dt:93:grid:asymptotic}
Let $J$ be a compact subinterval of the open central branch in the cosine
parameter. For all sufficiently large $N$, uniformly when $c_N\in J$,
Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:93:grid:certificate} applies to the two grid nodes surrounding
$b_N=b(c_N)$, unless $b_N$ is itself a grid node, when the error is zero.
Thus it gives an exact formula for $\Phi_{4,N}(a)$.

For $c\in J$, let
\begin{align*}
 K(c)&=-2b(b+c)^2-\tfrac12(1-3b^2-2bc-c^2)+\tfrac18,\\
 \mathcal R(c)&=\frac{w_b(b-c)(3b+c)}{K(c)},\qquad b=b(c),\\
 \vartheta_N&=\left\{\frac{N\arccos b_N}{2\pi}\right\},
\end{align*}
where braces denote fractional part. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:93:grid:leading}
 \Phi_{4,N}(a)-\Phi_4(a_N)
 =\mathcal R(c_N)(1-b_N^2)\frac{4\pi^2}{N^2}
       \vartheta_N(1-\vartheta_N)+O_J(N^{-3}).
\end{equation}
Every coefficient displayed in the leading term is explicit and positive,
apart from the possible zero factor $\vartheta_N(1-\vartheta_N)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
On $J$, the continuous contact is a simple root of $F_c$ and remains a
positive distance from $-1$, $-1/2$, and $c$. The coefficients of its dual
certificate have strict signs and its third moment has strict slack.
The adjacent grid nodes tend uniformly to $b(c)$. The weights in
\eqref{gsr:dt:93:grid:weights} consequently tend to the two-node measure: their
combined mass at $u,v$ tends to $w_b$, while their mass at $c$ tends to
$1-w_b$. All certificate inequalities therefore persist uniformly on
$J$ for large $N$.

Put $h=2\pi/N$ and $\theta=\arccos b_N$. For the adjacent angular nodes,
Taylor's theorem for cosine gives
\[
 (b_N-u)(v-b_N)
 =(1-b_N^2)h^2\vartheta_N(1-\vartheta_N)+O_J(h^3).
\]
Also $s=2b_N+O(h)$, $K=K(c_N)+O_J(h)$, and the denominators are uniformly
positive. Substitution in the exact identity \eqref{gsr:dt:93:grid:exact-error}
proves \eqref{gsr:dt:93:grid:leading}. The same expression remains valid at exact
grid contact because its leading term and exact error are both zero.
\end{proof}

Comparing with $\Phi_4(a)$ instead of $\Phi_4(a_N)$ generally introduces
an $N^{-1}$ term from the endpoint. Formula~\eqref{gsr:dt:93:grid:leading} isolates
the distinct displacement of the interior contact. Its oscillating
fractional-part factor also explains why a single limit for
$N^2(\Phi_{4,N}-\Phi_4)$ need not exist.

\subsection{An exact arithmetic example at a half-circle gap}

\begin{theorem}[Exact half-circle formula and residue classes]
\label{gsr:dt:93:grid:half-circle}
Suppose $4\mid N$ and $N\ge8$. If $12\mid N$, then
\[
 \Phi_{4,N}(\pi/2)=\frac{\sqrt3-1}{2}.
\]
Otherwise let $u<v$ be the adjacent cosine-grid nodes surrounding
$b=-\sqrt3/2$. Put $s=u+v$, $p=uv$, and
\[
 T=\frac{4s^2-4p-3}{8}.
\]
Then the exact value is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:93:grid:half-exact}
 \Phi_{4,N}(\pi/2)=\frac{T}{T-sp}.
\end{equation}
For the other two residue classes,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:93:grid:half-asymptotic}
 \Phi_{4,N}(\pi/2)
 =\frac{\sqrt3-1}{2}
  +\frac{2\pi^2(2\sqrt3-3)}{9N^2}+O(N^{-3})
 \qquad(N\equiv4,8\pmod{12}).
\end{equation}
In each case the minimizing angular measure is unique and symmetric.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Here $c=0$, $b=-\sqrt3/2$, and $\arccos b=5\pi/6$. If $12\mid N$,
both continuous contact angles are on the grid. Otherwise $u<v<0$ and
$u,v\in[-1,-1/\sqrt2]$. To see the latter bound, write $N=4n$.
The angular node immediately below $5\pi/6$ is at least $3\pi/4$:
this is direct for $n=2,3$, and follows from
$\lfloor5n/3\rfloor\ge3n/2$ for $n\ge4$.

The certificate coefficients have $q_1=sp<0$ and
$q_2=(1-u^2-uv-v^2)/2<0$. Also $q_0=-T<0$ and $K=T-sp>0$.
For every $x\in[-1,-1/\sqrt2]\cup\{0\}$,
\[
 T_3(x)-x=4x(x^2-1)\ge0,\qquad
 T_3(x)+x=2x(2x^2-1)\le0.
\]
Therefore any measure on the three contact nodes has
$m_1\le m_3\le-m_1$. This verifies the otherwise unused third-moment
constraint, so Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:93:grid:certificate} proves
\eqref{gsr:dt:93:grid:half-exact} for every stated $N$.

At $c=0$ the continuous interior mass is
$w_b=1-1/\sqrt3$, and direct substitution gives
\[
 \mathcal R(0)=2\sqrt3-3,\qquad 1-b^2=1/4.
\]
When $N\equiv4,8\pmod{12}$, the fractional part of $5N/12$ is
$2/3$ or $1/3$. Formula~\eqref{gsr:dt:93:grid:leading} gives
\eqref{gsr:dt:93:grid:half-asymptotic}.

For uniqueness, equality in the dual bound confines the cosine support
to $\{u,v,0\}$ and forces $m_1=m_2=-\rho_N$, $m_4=\rho_N$.
The equations defining the positive weights have a unique normalized
solution. For a possibly nonsymmetric angular optimizer, equality in
each active complex modulus forces its imaginary moments at frequencies
$1,2,4$ to vanish. On two distinct interior negative cosine nodes, the
frequency-$2$ and frequency-$4$ equations are independent, since
$\sin4\theta=2\sin2\theta\cos2\theta$ and their $\cos2\theta$ values
are distinct. They force the mass imbalances at both nodes to be zero;
the frequency-$1$ equation then does the same at $\pi/2$.
If a node is $-1$, it is the single antipodal point and has no imbalance.
If the continuous node is already on the grid, only that node and zero
are needed, and frequencies $2$ and $1$ give the same conclusion.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Consequences for missing intervals and weighted detection\srctag{93}}]{Consequences for missing intervals and weighted detection}\label{gsr:dt:93:sec:d5}
\srcnote{93}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:dt:93:sec:missing-app}

\begin{proposition}[A direct refinement in the missing-interval interface]
Let $A\subset\Z/N\Z$ be nonempty and suppose its angular image avoids
the open arc $(-a,a)$. Then, for every $R\ge2$,
\[
 \max_{1\le r\le R}
 \left|\sum_{x\in A}e^{-2\pi i rx/N}\right|
 \ge |A|\,\Phi_R(a).
\]
The stronger finite-grid value $\Phi_{R,N}(a)$ may replace $\Phi_R(a)$.
The same assertion holds for nonnegative weights supported outside the
arc, with $|A|$ replaced by their total mass.
Taking $R<N$ ensures that all these frequencies are nonzero in $\Z/N\Z$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Divide the counting measure of the angular image, or the weighted
measure, by its total mass. It is feasible in the defining extremal
problem. Its $r$th Fourier coefficient is the displayed sum divided
by that mass. The finite-grid problem restricts the feasible measures
further and therefore has a value at least $\Phi_R(a)$.
\end{proof}

For example, if $4\mid N$, $N\ge8$, and $A$ avoids the interval
$[-N/4,N/4)$ in the usual signed representatives, then
\[
 \max_{1\le r\le4}
 \left|\sum_{x\in A}e^{-2\pi i rx/N}\right|
 \ge\frac{\sqrt3-1}{2}|A|.
\]
Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:93:grid:half-circle} gives the exact weighted constant when the
excluded interval is open, $(-N/4,N/4)$, so both endpoints are allowed.
That grid constant is also a valid lower bound under the stronger
half-open exclusion used in this example. When the evenness hypothesis in Gowers' original
Lemma~5.2 is also satisfied, its direct specialization at $M=N/4$
gives $|A|/16$ with a frequency cutoff $16$. Thus this fixed-radius
specialization improves both the guaranteed amplitude and the cutoff.
It makes no assertion about retaining those same constants for a
vanishingly short missing interval \cite{gowers}.

The exactness of $\Phi_R$ is exactness among probability measures.
Uniform measures on sets of a prescribed density form a smaller class.
An optimal atomic weighted measure need not be the uniform measure of
a set on a particular grid. The displayed set inequalities hold
without that realizability assumption, but they do not classify the
sharp density-constrained indicator problem.

\begin{figure}[tbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/93-spectral-uniformity-fourier_profiles.pdf}
\caption{The exact four-frequency profile and the earlier
three-frequency profile. The shaded region is the new central branch,
$a_*<a<3\pi/5$. The second panel resolves the departure from the inherited
three-frequency optimizer at $a_*$. Curves are evaluations of the
proved formulas, not numerical optimizations.}
\label{gsr:dt:93:fig:profiles}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[tbp]

\includegraphics[width=0.94\textwidth]{figures/93-spectral-uniformity-grid_correction.pdf}
\caption{The scaled half-circle grid correction for $4\mid N$.
For $12\mid N$ it vanishes exactly. For $N\equiv4,8\pmod{12}$ it
converges to $2\pi^2(2\sqrt3-3)/9$. The displayed points have $20\le N\le512$ and evaluate the
exact trigonometric formula; the equality and limiting coefficient are
proved in Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:93:grid:half-circle}.}
\label{gsr:dt:93:fig:grid}
\end{figure}

\section[{The complete four-frequency missing-arc frontier\srctag{90}}]{The complete four-frequency missing-arc frontier}\label{gsr:dt:90:sec:d2}
\srcnote{90}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:dt:90:sec:frontiers}

Gowers' Lemma~5.2 uses a missing interval to detect a Fourier coefficient
\cite{gowers}. The exact first-window weighted extremum, with all the
relevant moments equal and negative, was determined in source~37 of the
preceding project reports \cite{srcthirtyseven}. Later work determined the whole
cutoff-three frontier and the last two ranges for every cutoff
\cite{extremallimits}; a separate report determined a local matrix formula
for unequal Fourier budgets in the first-window setting \cite{srcsixtyseven}.
The unresolved middle ranges already require a new extremizer at cutoff
four. We determine that extremizer, both of its junctions, and the complete
frontier. Section~\ref{gsr:dt:90:sec:continuation} then identifies the first
continuation interval for every cutoff.

Let $\T=\R/(2\pi\Z)$, let
$K_a=\{\theta:|\theta|_\circ\ge a\}$, and define
\[
 \Phi_R(a)=\inf_{\mu\in\mathcal P(K_a)}
       \max_{1\le j\le R}|\widehat\mu(j)|,
 \qquad \widehat\mu(j)=\int e^{-ij\theta}\,d\mu(\theta).
\]
The excluded arc is open and its endpoints are allowed. For $x\in[-1,1]$
write $\sigma_x$ for the probability measure equally supported at the two
angles with cosine $x$, with coincident atoms combined at $x=\pm1$.
Then $\widehat\sigma_x(j)=T_j(x)$, where $T_j$ is the Chebyshev polynomial.

Put
\[
 c_+=\frac{\sqrt5-1}{4},\qquad c_-=\frac{1-\sqrt5}{4},\qquad
 P(c)=-1+5c+11c^2-6c^3-12c^4.
\]
Let $c_*$ be the unique zero of $P$ in $(0,1/6)$ and let $a_*=\arccos c_*$.
Numerically $c_*=0.1537156928586777\ldots$ and
$a_*/\pi=0.4508760097203392\ldots$; these decimals play no role in the proof.
For $c\in[c_-,c_*]$ let $v(c)$ be the unique root in
$[-1,-\sqrt3/2]$ of
\begin{align}\label{gsr:dt:90:eq:F}
 F(c,v)={}&4(1-c)(1+2c)v^3+4c(1-c)(1+2c)v^2\\
 &+(1+c)(4c^2-3)v+c(4c^2-3).
\end{align}
The existence and uniqueness assertion is part of the theorem below.
Set
\[
 \rho_*(c)=\frac{1+2cv(c)}{1-2c-2v(c)}.
\]

\begin{theorem}[All radii for cutoff four]\label{gsr:dt:90:thm:four}
With $c=\cos a$, $b=\pi-a$, $z=\cos b=-c$, and $w=\cos(4b)$,
\[
\Phi_4(a)=
\begin{cases}
0,&0<a\le\pi/5,\\[2pt]
\dfrac{1+2c-4c^2}{3+10c-12c^2},&\pi/5\le a\le2\pi/5,\\[7pt]
\dfrac{1-2c^2}{3+2c-4c^2},&2\pi/5\le a\le a_*,\\[7pt]
\rho_*(c),&a_*\le a\le3\pi/5,\\[4pt]
\dfrac{2c(c-1)}{2c^2-2c+1},&3\pi/5\le a\le5\pi/7,\\[7pt]
\dfrac{z-w}{2-z-w},&5\pi/7\le a\le4\pi/5,\\[7pt]
-c,&4\pi/5\le a\le\pi.
\end{cases}
\]
Adjacent formulas agree at their common endpoints. For every
$a\in[\pi/5,\pi]$ the extremizing probability measure is unique, even among
measures not assumed reflection invariant.

On the new algebraic branch it is
\[
 \mu_a=p\sigma_c+(1-p)\sigma_v,
 \qquad p=\frac{-\rho_*(c)-v}{c-v},\qquad v=v(c),
\]
and its active moments are
\[
 \widehat\mu_a(1)=\widehat\mu_a(2)=-\rho_*(c),\qquad
 \widehat\mu_a(4)=\rho_*(c).
\]
The third moment lies strictly between these two bounds for
$a_*<a<3\pi/5$. At $a=a_*$ it is $-\rho_*(c)$ and at $a=3\pi/5$ it is
$+\rho_*(c)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 82--94]
\emph{Proved independently by source~93} (Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:93:new:Phi4}), which arrived ten minutes later with the same pin and does not cite this source; the two seven-branch formulas agree (the sixth branch is source~93's $(-c-T_4(c))/(2+c-T_4(c))$ with $z=-c$, $w=T_4(c)$), and the junction radical of Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:90:cor:transitionradicals} has source~93's quartic as minimal polynomial (checked at the write). \emph{This answers source~37's Question~\ref{gsr:fz:37:q:windows} for $R=4$.} Uniqueness without assuming symmetry is this source's.
\end{writenote}

\subsection{The elementary certificate principle}\label{gsr:dt:90:subsec:certificate}
If
\[
 Q(x)=q_0+\sum_{j=1}^R q_jT_j(x)\ge0\quad(-1\le x\le c),
 \qquad A=\sum_{j=1}^R|q_j|>0,
\]
then every admissible probability measure satisfies
\[
 E_R(\mu)\ge -q_0/A.
\]
Indeed $\int Q(\cos\theta)d\mu\ge0$, whereas
$\sum q_j\operatorname{Re}\widehat\mu(j)\le A E_R(\mu)$.
If a proposed measure is supported on the zeros of $Q$, and its moments
satisfy $\widehat\mu(j)=\rho\operatorname{sgn}(q_j)$ whenever $q_j\ne0$,
with $|\widehat\mu(j)|\le\rho$ at every remaining frequency, it attains
$\rho=-q_0/A$. Equality forces support in the zero set and forces all
nonzero-coefficient moments to have the stated real values. This principle
also applies to measures without reflection symmetry.

\subsection{The new algebraic branch}
We first prove the difficult part of the theorem. All subsequent intervals
are elementary continuations of lower-cutoff certificates.

\begin{lemma}[The branch root]\label{gsr:dt:90:lem:branchroot}
For each $c\in[c_-,c_*]$ the equation $F(c,v)=0$ has exactly one root
$v\in[-1,-\sqrt3/2]$. The root is continuous in $c$, is $-1$ only at $c=c_-$,
and is $-\sqrt3/2$ only at $c=0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
First $c_-\in(-1/3,0)$ and $c_*\in(0,1/6)$. Writing $r=\sqrt3/2$,
direct substitution gives
\[
 F(c,-1)=(1-2c)(4c^2-2c-1)\le0,
 \qquad
 F(c,-r)=c^2\bigl(3+2r-2c(1+2r)\bigr)\ge0.
\]
The first equality can occur in the stated interval only at $c=c_-$,
and the second only at $c=0$.
Let $A_c=4(1-c)(1+2c)$. Then
\[
 F_v(c,v)=A_c(3v^2+2cv)+(1+c)(4c^2-3).
\]
For $-1/3\le c\le0$, $A_c\ge16/9$, $2cv\ge0$,
$3v^2\ge9/4$, and $(1+c)(4c^2-3)\ge-3$; thus $F_v\ge1$.
For $0\le c\le1/6$, $A_c\ge4$, $3v^2+2cv\ge9/4-1/3=23/12$,
and $(1+c)(4c^2-3)\ge-7/2$; thus $F_v\ge25/6>0$.
The intermediate value theorem and strict monotonicity prove existence
and uniqueness. Continuity follows from the implicit function theorem,
or from compactness and uniqueness of the root.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The branch measure and its moments]\label{gsr:dt:90:lem:branchmoments}
For $c\in[c_-,c_*]$, $v=v(c)$, $D=1-2c-2v$, and
$\rho=(1+2cv)/D$, put $p=(-\rho-v)/(c-v)$.
Then $0<p<1$, $\rho>0$, and
$\mu=p\sigma_c+(1-p)\sigma_v$ satisfies
\[
 \widehat\mu(1)=\widehat\mu(2)=-\rho,
 \qquad \widehat\mu(4)=\rho,
 \qquad -\rho\le\widehat\mu(3)\le\rho.
\]
Both inequalities for the third moment are strict in the interior of the
branch. The lower equality occurs precisely at $c=c_*$ and the upper
precisely at $c=c_-$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
We have $c>-1/2$, $v<-1/2$, $c<1/6$, and $-1\le v\le-\sqrt3/2$.
Therefore $D>0$ and $1+2cv>0$. The exact identities
\[
 -\rho-v=\frac{(2v+1)(v-1)}D>0,
 \qquad
 c+\rho=\frac{(1-c)(2c+1)}D>0
\]
prove $0<p<1$.
Write $s=c+v$ and $t=cv$. Since the cosine random variable $X$ has its
values in $\{c,v\}$,
\[
 \E X=-\rho,\qquad
 \E X^2=s\E X-t=\frac{1-\rho}{2}.
\]
This proves the first two Fourier moments. Its higher raw moments obey
$\E X^{j+2}=s\E X^{j+1}-t\E X^j$. In particular
\[
 \widehat\mu(4)-\rho=-\frac{2}{D}\mathcal F(s,t),
 \quad
 \mathcal F(s,t)=(s+t)(4s^2-4t-3)-4st(1+2t).
\]
Expanding $\mathcal F(c+v,cv)$ gives exactly $F(c,v)$ above. Thus the fourth
moment is $\rho$.

For the third moment the same recurrence gives
\begin{align*}
 \widehat\mu(3)+\rho
 &=\frac{4(1-c)(1-v)}D\bigl((1+2c)v+c+1\bigr),\\
 \widehat\mu(3)-\rho
 &=\frac{2}{D}\bigl((1+2t)^2-2s^2-2st\bigr).
\end{align*}
For $c\le0$, the last factor in the first line is at least $-c$, since
$v\ge-1$. At $c=0$ it is strictly positive because $v>-1$. For $c\ge0$
let $v_0=-(c+1)/(1+2c)$, which belongs to $[-1,-\sqrt3/2]$ when
$0\le c\le c_*$: it increases from $-1$, and
$v_0(c_*)<v_0(1/6)=-7/8<-\sqrt3/2$. Direct substitution gives
\[
 F(c,v_0)=\frac{P(c)}{(1+2c)^2}.
\]
The polynomial $P$ increases strictly on $[0,1/6]$, since
$P'(c)=5+22c-18c^2-48c^3>0$ there, and $P(0)<0<P(1/6)$.
Consequently $P(c)\le0$ precisely when $c\le c_*$ in this interval.
By the branch-root monotonicity, $v\ge v_0$, with equality only at $c=c_*$.
This proves the asserted lower third-moment inequality.

To prove the upper inequality, suppose first that equality holds and set
$B=(1+2t)^2-2s^2-2st$. Combining $B=0$ with $\mathcal F(s,t)=0$ yields
\[
 s=-t(4t+3),\qquad
 (4t+1)(4t^2+2t-1)=0.
\]
The division by $1+2t$ used in obtaining the second identity is legitimate
because $\rho>0$. More explicitly, substitute
$2s^2=(1+2t)^2-2st$ into $\mathcal F$ to obtain
$\mathcal F=-s-4t^2-3t$, and then substitute $s=-t(4t+3)$ into $B$.
On the branch $-1/6<t<1/3$. Thus the only possible root is
$t=(\sqrt5-1)/4$. The two roots of $X^2-sX+t$ must then be
$-1$ and $(1-\sqrt5)/4$. Their ranges force $c=c_-$ and $v=-1$.
At $c=0$, $v=-\sqrt3/2$ and $\widehat\mu(3)=0<\rho$.
Continuity and the absence of any other equality point prove
$\widehat\mu(3)<\rho$ throughout $(c_-,c_*]$.
\end{proof}



\begin{lemma}[Quartic certificate and uniqueness]\label{gsr:dt:90:lem:quarticcertificate}
For the branch measure above, put $w=-c-2v$ and
\[
 Q(x)=(c-x)(w-x)(x-v)^2.
\]
Then $Q\ge0$ on $[-1,c]$, and its only zeros in that interval are $c,v$.
In the Chebyshev basis its coefficients are
\begin{align*}
 q_4&=\frac18,&q_3&=0,&
 q_2&=\frac{1-c^2-2cv-3v^2}{2},\\
 q_1&=2v(c+v)^2,&
 q_0&=\frac38-\frac{c^2+2cv+3v^2}{2}-c(c+2v)v^2.
\end{align*}
Here $q_1,q_2<0$, $q_4>0$. With $A=-q_1-q_2+q_4$,
$-q_0/A=\rho$. The branch measure is the unique minimizer of $E_4$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Since $w\ge\sqrt3-1/6>1$, the factorization proves positivity and the zero
set. Expansion gives the displayed coefficients. The first is strictly
negative because $v<0$ and $c+v<0$. If $c\le0$, then
$c^2+2cv+3v^2\ge9/4>1$; if $c\ge0$, it is at least
$-1/3+9/4=23/12>1$. Thus $q_2<0$.
The constructed measure is supported on the zeros and has the sign-matching
moments $(-\rho,-\rho,\rho)$ at frequencies $(1,2,4)$. Integrating $Q$
therefore gives $q_0+A\rho=0$, and the certificate principle proves
optimality.

For an arbitrary extremizer, equality forces support at the angles with
cosines $c,v$, and forces moments one and two to be real and equal to
$-\rho$. In the interior, the imaginary equations for moments one and two
force each pair of conjugate angles to have equal weights: their
coefficient determinant is
$2\sin(\arccos c)\sin(\arccos v)(v-c)\ne0$.
The real first moment then fixes $p$. At the endpoint $v=-1$, the atom at
$\pi$ is real already and the first imaginary equation suffices.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A self-contained first-window calculation for cutoff four}
Although the general first-window theorem is prior work, its cutoff-four
specialization has an especially short algebraic proof. Suppose
\[
 c_+\le c\le\frac{1+\sqrt5}{4},\qquad v=-\frac1{4c},\qquad s=c+v,
 \qquad \rho=\frac{1-2s}{5-6s}.
\]
Then $-1/2\le s\le1/2$, and the expression for $\rho$ simplifies to
$(1+2c-4c^2)/(3+10c-12c^2)$. Define the three cosine masses
\begin{align*}
 p_c&=\frac{4v(v-1)}{(5-6s)(c-v)(c+1)},\\
 p_v&=\frac{4c(c-1)}{(5-6s)(v-c)(v+1)},\\
 p_{-1}&=\frac{(3-4s)(1+2s)}{4(5-6s)(c+1)(v+1)}.
\end{align*}
These are positive except that $p_{-1}=0$ at $s=-1/2$. They sum to one,
and the measure $p_c\sigma_c+p_v\sigma_v+p_{-1}\delta_\pi$ has its first
four Fourier moments all equal to $-\rho$. One direct verification starts
from the raw moments $\E X=-\rho$, $\E X^2=(1-\rho)/2$ and uses
$\E[(X-c)(X-v)(X+1)]=\E[X(X-c)(X-v)(X+1)]=0$; the equalities
$cv=-1/4$ and $\rho=(1-2s)/(5-6s)$ yield the required third and fourth
moments.

The dual certificate is
\[
 Q(x)=(c-x)(x+1)(x-v)^2.
\]
All four nonconstant Chebyshev coefficients are strictly negative. Indeed
\begin{align*}
 q_4&=-1/8,&q_3&=(2v+c-1)/4,\\
 q_2&=((c-1)(1-2v)-v^2)/2,&
 q_1&=(12c^3-4c^2-5c-1)/(16c^2).
\end{align*}
For the last sign use $4c^2\le2c+1$, which gives
$12c^3-4c^2-5c-1\le2c^2-2c-1<0$.
The first-window assertion and uniqueness now follow from the certificate
principle and the same imaginary-moment argument. All four nonconstant
coefficients remain strictly negative at both endpoints, including the
zero-value endpoint $a=\pi/5$. The imaginary parts of moments one and two
fix reflection symmetry; total mass and the first two real moments fix
the three cosine masses. At $a=\pi/5$, this
measure is the uniform measure on the five rotated fifth roots of unity.
It has its first four moments zero and remains admissible for every smaller
$a$, proving the zero branch as well.

\subsection{Continuation of the three-frequency first branch}
The prior cutoff-three first-branch extremizer~\cite{extremallimits}, for $0\le c\le1/\sqrt2$,
has cosine nodes
\[
 c,\qquad v_0=-\frac{c+1}{2c+1},\qquad
 \rho_3=\frac{1-2c^2}{3+2c-4c^2},\qquad
 p=\frac{-\rho_3-v_0}{c-v_0}.
\]
Its first three moments are $-\rho_3$. The elementary certificate
$(c-x)(x-v_0)^2$ proves its optimality for cutoff three.
For its fourth moment, put $A=1+2c$ and $D=3+2c-4c^2$. Direct algebra gives
\begin{align*}
 \widehat\mu(4)-\rho_3&=-\frac{2P(c)}{AD},\\
 \widehat\mu(4)+\rho_3&=
 \frac{2(c-1)(3c+2)(4c^2+2c-1)}{AD}.
\end{align*}
For $c_*\le c\le c_+$ these quantities have signs $\le0$ and $\ge0$,
respectively. To check the first, $P$ is increasing on $[0,c_+]$:
for example $c_+<1/3$ gives
$P'(c)\ge5-18/9-48/27=11/9>0$. The second follows from
$4c^2+2c-1\le0$ and $c<1$.
Thus the cutoff-three extremizer remains feasible for cutoff four exactly
through the stated continuation interval. It is unique there because it
is already the unique cutoff-three extremizer. At $c=c_*$, the lower
third-moment equality and the fourth-moment equality identify it with the
new branch measure.

\subsection{The remaining three-point and two-point branches}
For completeness, the elementary two-moment mechanism used in the prior
last-window theorem~\cite{extremallimits} is recalled here. Write $b=\pi-a$, $z=\cos b$, and
$w_k=\cos(kb)$. Whenever
\[
 \frac\pi{k+1}\le b\le\frac{2\pi}{2k-1},
\]
the measure
\[
 \nu_{k,b}=\frac p2(\delta_{\pi-b}+\delta_{\pi+b})+(1-p)\delta_\pi,
 \quad p=\frac2{2-z-w_k},\quad \rho=\frac{z-w_k}{2-z-w_k}
\]
is the unique cutoff-$k$ minimizer. Its moments are
$(-1)^j(1-p+p\cos(jb))$.
A dual polynomial is
\[
 L(\theta)=-u\cos\theta+(-1)^{k+1}(1-u)\cos(k\theta),
 \qquad u=\frac{1-w_k}{2-z-w_k}.
\]
For $0\le t\le b$ and $y=\cos t$, its gap from $\rho$ factors as
\[
 L-\rho=(1-u)(1-y)\left[
 \left(\frac{\sin(kt/2)}{\sin(t/2)}\right)^2-
 \left(\frac{\sin(kb/2)}{\sin(b/2)}\right)^2\right]\ge0.
\]
The sine quotient decreases strictly on $(0,2\pi/k)$ because
$x\cot x$ decreases on $(0,\pi)$. The only zeros are the endpoints and
the center, and all moments have absolute value at most $\rho$ because
$w_k\le\cos(jb)\le z$ for $1\le j\le k$. This proves the stated
three-point mechanism, including uniqueness. If $0\le b\le\pi/(k+1)$,
the endpoint measure alone gives the unique optimum $z$ by the first
moment lower bound.

Apply this mechanism first with $k=3$ and
$2\pi/7\le b\le2\pi/5$. Its fourth moment also lies in $[-\rho,\rho]$:
\[
 \cos(4b)\ge\cos(3b),\qquad \cos(4b)\le\cos b,
\]
as follows from
\begin{align*}
 \cos(4b)-\cos(3b)&=-2\sin(7b/2)\sin(b/2)\ge0,\\
 \cos b-\cos(4b)&=2\sin(5b/2)\sin(3b/2)\ge0.
\end{align*}
This proves the branch $3\pi/5\le a\le5\pi/7$, with
$\rho=2c(c-1)/(2c^2-2c+1)$. The fourth moment is $+\rho$ at its left
endpoint and $-\rho$ at its right endpoint.
Next apply the same mechanism with $k=4$ and
$\pi/5\le b\le2\pi/7$ to obtain the next branch. Finally the endpoint
measure gives $\Phi_4(a)=-c$ for $0\le b\le\pi/5$.
Uniqueness in every branch follows from the indicated prior-cutoff or
new-cutoff certificate, and the endpoint measures agree by uniqueness.

\subsection{Useful exact values and interpretation}
The algebraic branch passes through a simple radical value:
\[
 v(0)=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2},\quad
 \Phi_4(\pi/2)=\frac{\sqrt3-1}{2},\quad
 p(\pi/2)=\frac1{\sqrt3}.
\]
At $a=3\pi/5$ one has $\Phi_4(a)=1/\sqrt5$, with total endpoint mass
$4/5$ and central mass $1/5$. The support has five points for
$\pi/5<a<2\pi/5$, four for $2\pi/5\le a<3\pi/5$, three for
$3\pi/5\le a<4\pi/5$, and two for $4\pi/5\le a<\pi$.
At $a=\pi$ the two points coalesce to one.
The vanishing masses and active constraints distinguish all
the transition mechanisms.
The nontrivial new information is the algebraic four-atom branch and its
exact junctions with adjacent lower-cutoff branches. The preexisting
first-window and last-window formulas do not cover this branch. All
claims concern arbitrary nonnegative probability weights and the stated
open missing arc; they do not identify exact extrema for a fixed
unweighted finite subset.
