\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The exact first continuation for every frequency cutoff\srctag{90}}]{The exact first continuation for every frequency cutoff}\label{gsr:dt:90:sec:d3}
\srcnote{90}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:dt:90:sec:continuation}

The four-frequency transition is one member of an explicit family. In the
known first window, all Fourier constraints are active with the same
negative real value. At its far endpoint, the extremizer loses one atom.
For a further interval, the new highest frequency becomes inactive and the
extremizer is exactly the one for the preceding cutoff. The next theorem
determines that entire interval and proves that it cannot be extended.

\subsection{The prior first-window input}
The previously established first-window theorem~\cite{srcthirtyseven} gives the
following facts. For an integer $k\ge1$ and
$\pi/(k+1)<a<2\pi/(k+1)$, put
\[
 S_k(a)=k+1-\cot(a/2)\tan((k+1)a/2),\qquad
 \rho_k(a)=\frac1{S_k(a)-1}.
\]
Then $\Phi_k(a)=\rho_k(a)$, and there is a unique minimizing measure
$\mu_{k,a}$. It is even, has exactly $k+1$ support points, and
\[
 \widehat\mu_{k,a}(j)=-\rho_k(a)\qquad(1\le j\le k).
\]
Define
\[
 P_{k,a}(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}w_jz^j,
 \qquad
 w_j=\frac{1-\cos((j-(k-1)/2)a)/\cos((k+1)a/2)}{S_k(a)}.
\]
The coefficients are real, strictly positive, symmetric, and sum to one.
The support of $\mu_{k,a}$ consists of the angles $\pm a$ and the arguments
of the zeros of $P_{k,a}$. In particular,
\[
 (z^2-2\cos(a)z+1)P_{k,a}(z)
\]
vanishes at every support point $z=e^{i\theta}$.
These are imported results, not novelty claims in this article. The
continuation theorem below uses only these exact algebraic facts.

\begin{theorem}[The maximal first continuation]
\label{gsr:dt:90:thm:continuation}
Let $R\ge3$, and define
\[
 \xi_R=\frac{\sqrt{(R-1)(R+7)}-R-1}{2}\in(0,1),
 \qquad
 X_R(a)=-\cot(a/2)\tan(Ra/2).
\]
There is a unique
\[
 a_R\in\left(\frac{2\pi}{R+1},\frac{2\pi}{R}\right)
 \quad\text{such that}\quad X_R(a_R)=\xi_R.
\]
For every $a$ in the closed interval
$[2\pi/(R+1),a_R]$,
\begin{equation}
\label{gsr:dt:90:eq:continuationprofile}
 \Phi_R(a)=\Phi_{R-1}(a)
          =\frac1{R-1+X_R(a)}.
\end{equation}
The unique extremizer is the prior first-window measure $\mu_{R-1,a}$.
Its first $R-1$ moments are all $-\rho$, where
$\rho=1/(R-1+X_R(a))$, and its last moment is
\begin{equation}
\label{gsr:dt:90:eq:nextmoment}
 \widehat\mu_{R-1,a}(R)
 =\frac{R-1-RX_R(a)-X_R(a)^2}
        {(R-1+X_R(a))(1+X_R(a))}.
\end{equation}
At $a=2\pi/(R+1)$ the last moment equals $-\rho$; at $a=a_R$ it equals
$+\rho$; in between it lies strictly between these values.
The continuation is maximal in the precise sense that
\[
 \Phi_R(a)>\Phi_{R-1}(a)
 \qquad\left(a_R<a<\frac{2\pi}{R}\right).
\]
At its final point the exact value is
\begin{equation}
\label{gsr:dt:90:eq:transitionheight}
 \Phi_R(a_R)=\frac2{R-3+\sqrt{(R-1)(R+7)}}.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Put $t=a/2$. On
$2\pi/(R+1)\le a<2\pi/R$, both $\cot t$ and $-\tan(Rt)$ are positive
and strictly decreasing (with the latter approaching zero). Thus
$X=X_R(a)$ decreases strictly from $1$ to $0$. The polynomial
$x^2+(R+1)x-(R-2)$ has its unique positive root $\xi_R$, which lies
strictly between zero and one because its values at those endpoints
are $-(R-2)$ and $4$. This proves existence and uniqueness of $a_R$.

The entire interval under consideration lies strictly inside the first
window for cutoff $k=R-1$, so the imported theorem applies without any
endpoint interpretation. Abbreviate $S=R+X$, $\rho=(S-1)^{-1}$, and
$c=\cos a$. The annihilating polynomial
\[
 Z(z)=(z^2-2cz+1)P_{R-1,a}(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{R}z_jz^j
\]
has $z_0=z_R=w_0$ and $Z(1)=2(1-c)$. Integrating it against the even measure
$\mu_{R-1,a}$, whose lower moments are all $-\rho$, gives
\[
 0=w_0+w_0\widehat\mu_{R-1,a}(R)
       -\rho\bigl(2(1-c)-2w_0\bigr).
\]
The explicit first-window endpoint coefficient is
\[
 w_0=-\frac{2\sin((R-1)t)\sin t}{S\cos(Rt)}.
\]
Consequently
\[
 \frac{1-c}{w_0}
 =-\frac{S\cos(Rt)\sin t}{\sin((R-1)t)}
 =\frac{S}{1+X}.
\]
For the last identity use
\[
 \sin((R-1)t)=\sin(Rt)\cos t-\cos(Rt)\sin t,\qquad
 X=-\frac{\sin(Rt)\cos t}{\cos(Rt)\sin t}.
\]
Substitution yields
\[
 \widehat\mu_{R-1,a}(R)
 =-1+\frac{2\rho(R-1)}{1+X},
\]
which is equivalent to~\eqref{gsr:dt:90:eq:nextmoment}.

Two useful exact differences are
\begin{align}
 \widehat\mu_{R-1,a}(R)+\rho
 &=\frac{(R+X)(1-X)}{(R-1+X)(1+X)},
 \label{gsr:dt:90:eq:continuationlowerslack}\\
 \widehat\mu_{R-1,a}(R)-\rho
 &=\frac{R-2-(R+1)X-X^2}{(R-1+X)(1+X)}.
 \label{gsr:dt:90:eq:continuationupperslack}
\end{align}
The first is nonnegative for $0\le X\le1$. The second is nonpositive
exactly when $X\ge\xi_R$. Thus the prior minimizer remains feasible for
cutoff $R$ exactly on the claimed continuation interval. Since
$\Phi_R\ge\Phi_{R-1}$, this proves~\eqref{gsr:dt:90:eq:continuationprofile}. Uniqueness
follows from the uniqueness for cutoff $R-1$.

For $a_R<a<2\pi/R$, equation~\eqref{gsr:dt:90:eq:continuationupperslack} is positive.
If $\Phi_R(a)=\Phi_{R-1}(a)$, a minimizing measure for cutoff $R$ would
also minimize cutoff $R-1$ and hence would equal $\mu_{R-1,a}$. But its
$R$th moment exceeds that common bound. This is impossible. The infimum
for cutoff $R$ is attained because the allowed arc is compact and the
finitely many Fourier moments are weakly continuous.
Finally substituting $X=\xi_R$ gives~\eqref{gsr:dt:90:eq:transitionheight}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The intrinsic positivity obstruction at the transition}

The transition value is independent of the arc in a second, precise
sense. It is the largest possible value in the signed moment pattern
that becomes active at the transition. This explains why preserving all
those equalities cannot extend the preceding phase.

\begin{theorem}[Sharp signed-moment ceiling]\label{gsr:dt:90:thm:signedmoment}
Let $R\ge3$, and set
\[
 \kappa_R=\frac2{R-3+\sqrt{(R-1)(R+7)}}.
\]
There is a probability measure on $\T$ satisfying
\[
 \widehat\mu(j)=-\rho\quad(1\le j<R),\qquad
 \widehat\mu(R)=\rho
\]
if and only if $0\le\rho\le\kappa_R$, where $\rho$ is restricted to be
nonnegative. At $\rho=\kappa_R$ that probability measure is unique and
equals $\mu_{R-1,a_R}$ from Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:90:thm:continuation}.
Its support is exactly the $R$ distinct roots on the unit circle of
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:90:eq:ceilingannihilator}
 H_R(z)=1+z^R+
 \frac{1+\kappa_R}{\kappa_R(R-1)}\sum_{j=1}^{R-1}z^j
 =1+z^R+\frac2{1+\xi_R}\sum_{j=1}^{R-1}z^j.
\end{equation}
Here ``support'' refers to the associated points $z=e^{i\theta}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The $(R+1)\times(R+1)$ moment matrix
$M=(\widehat\mu(i-j))_{0\le i,j\le R}$ is positive semidefinite:
its quadratic form is the integral of the squared absolute value of a
polynomial in $e^{i\theta}$. Under the stated prescription all diagonal
entries are one, every off-diagonal entry is $-\rho$ except for the two
corner entries, which are $+\rho$.
Restrict $M$ to the orthonormal vectors
\[
 \frac{e_0+e_R}{\sqrt2},\qquad
 \frac{e_1+\cdots+e_{R-1}}{\sqrt{R-1}}.
\]
The resulting matrix is
\[
 \begin{pmatrix}
 1+\rho&-\rho\sqrt{2(R-1)}\\
 -\rho\sqrt{2(R-1)}&1-(R-2)\rho
 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its determinant must be nonnegative, giving
\[
 1-(R-3)\rho-(3R-4)\rho^2\ge0.
\]
The positive root is exactly $\kappa_R$. This proves necessity using only
positivity of the moment matrix.

The measure from Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:90:thm:continuation} at $a=a_R$ realizes the
prescription with $\rho=\kappa_R$. Mixing it with normalized Haar measure
in proportions $\rho/\kappa_R$ and $1-\rho/\kappa_R$ realizes every
$0\le\rho\le\kappa_R$, proving sufficiency.

At equality the coefficient vector with entries
$u=\kappa_R(R-1)/(1+\kappa_R)$ at the two endpoints and one at all interior
positions lies in the kernel of $M$. Thus
\[
 \int\left|u(1+e^{iR\theta})+
               \sum_{j=1}^{R-1}e^{ij\theta}\right|^2d\mu(\theta)=0,
\]
which forces support on the zeros of $H_R$. The known extremizer
$\mu_{R-1,a_R}$ has exactly $R$ distinct support points by the imported
first-window theorem; all are zeros of this degree-$R$ polynomial.
They are therefore its entire zero set, and all zeros are simple and on
the unit circle. Any other equality measure must use the same possible
support. Its moments of orders $0,1,\ldots,R-1$ then fix its weights by an
invertible Vandermonde matrix. This proves uniqueness without assuming
reflection symmetry or any missing-arc hypothesis.
Finally, the defining equation for $\xi_R$ gives
$(1+\xi_R)(R+\xi_R)=2(R-1)$, which proves the second expression
in~\eqref{gsr:dt:90:eq:ceilingannihilator}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Width and height of the continuation interval]
\label{gsr:dt:90:cor:continuationwidth}
As $R\to\infty$,
\[
 a_R-\frac{2\pi}{R+1}=\frac{8\pi}{R^3}+O(R^{-4}),
 \qquad
 \Phi_R(a_R)=\frac1R+\frac4{R^3}+O(R^{-4}).
\]
The implied constants are absolute.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Let $\delta_R=1-\xi_R$. Its defining quadratic gives
\[
 \delta_R^2-(R+3)\delta_R+4=0,
 \qquad
 \delta_R=\frac8{R+3+\sqrt{(R+3)^2-16}}
          =\frac4R+O(R^{-2}).
\]
Uniformly for $2\pi/(R+1)\le a\le2\pi/R$, put $t=a/2$ and
$u=\pi-Rt$. Then $t=\pi/R+O(R^{-2})$, $0\le u=O(R^{-1})$, and
$X_R(a)=\tan u/\tan t$. Differentiation yields
\[
 X_R'(a)=-\frac R2\frac{\sec^2u}{\tan t}
          -\frac12\frac{\tan u\,\sec^2t}{\tan^2t}
        =-\frac{R^2}{2\pi}(1+O(R^{-1})).
\]
The mean value theorem between $2\pi/(R+1)$ and $a_R$ proves the width.
For the height use
$\Phi_R(a_R)=1/(R-\delta_R)=1/R+\delta_R/R^2+O(R^{-5})$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Radicals at the four-frequency junction]
\label{gsr:dt:90:cor:transitionradicals}
The breakpoint $a_*$ in the complete cutoff-four theorem satisfies
\[
 c_*=
 \frac{\sqrt{25-4\sqrt{33}}-1}{\sqrt{33}-3},
 \qquad
 \Phi_4(a_*)=\frac{\sqrt{33}-1}{16}.
\]
For $R=3$, the continuation endpoint is $a_3=3\pi/5$, recovering the
previously determined cutoff-three transition.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For $R=4$, $X_4(a)=2c(1+c)/(1-2c^2)$ on the relevant interval.
The transition equation is $X_4(a)^2+5X_4(a)-2=0$. Multiplying by
$(1-2c^2)^2$ gives $2P(c)=0$, so the root is the previously defined $c_*$.
Solving the quadratic in $c$ after substituting
$\xi_4=(\sqrt{33}-5)/2$ gives the displayed radical. Equation
\eqref{gsr:dt:90:eq:transitionheight} gives the value.
For $R=3$, substitution $a=3\pi/5$ gives
$X_3(a)=\sqrt5-2=\xi_3$; the endpoint uniqueness proves the assertion.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{What is resolved.}
Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:90:thm:four} determines every interval for cutoff four, including
all the extremizing measures and transition points.
Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:90:thm:continuation} determines the exact next-moment formula,
the full first continuation interval, its maximality, and its asymptotic
width and height for every cutoff. Its first-window input is explicitly
attributed to \cite{srcthirtyseven}. The subsequent middle intervals for
$R\ge5$ remain to be determined.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Exact finite-grid correction on the algebraic branch\srctag{90}}]{Exact finite-grid correction on the algebraic branch}\label{gsr:dt:90:sec:d4}
\srcnote{90}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:dt:90:sec:grid}

The continuous extremizer need not lie on a finite cyclic group. An
estimate of order \(N^{-2}\), after rounding the excluded arc to the
grid, was obtained in the preceding project reports
\cite{extremallimits,srcsixtyseven}. We now identify the correction exactly on
the new algebraic branch. The proof replaces a double root of the
continuous certificate by two adjacent grid points. It also explains
why the leading correction oscillates with the group order.

\subsection{A certificate for an arbitrary finite cosine grid}

Throughout this section \(a_*<a<3\pi/5\),
\(c=\cos a\), \(v=v(c)\), \(\rho=\rho_*(c)\), and
\[
 p=\frac{-\rho-v}{c-v},\qquad
 \mu_*=p\sigma_c+(1-p)\sigma_v.
\]
Thus \(v>-1\), and the third moment of \(\mu_*\) is strictly inside
the interval \((-\rho,\rho)\). The notation \(\sigma_x\) denotes the
even probability measure with cosine coordinate \(x\).

Let \(X\subset[-1,c]\) be finite, contain \(c\), and have adjacent
points \(r<s<-1/2\) with \(r\le v\le s<c\). Adjacency means
\(X\cap(r,s)=\varnothing\). Put
\begin{align}
 w&=-c-r-s, \label{gsr:dt:90:eq:gridw}\\
 q_1&=(r+s)(c+r)(c+s),\nonumber\\
 q_2&=\frac{1-c^2-c(r+s)-r^2-rs-s^2}{2},\nonumber\\
 q_0&=-c(c+r+s)rs+q_2-\frac18,\nonumber\\
 A&=-q_1-q_2+\frac18,\qquad R(c;r,s)=-\frac{q_0}{A}.
 \label{gsr:dt:90:eq:gridrho}
\end{align}
For \(g(x)=2x^2-x-1\) and \(h(x)=8x^4-8x^2+1+x\), define
\[
 J_c(x)=h(x)g(c)-g(x)h(c).
 \tag{G1}\label{gsr:dt:90:eq:J}
\]
When \(J_c(r)\) and \(J_c(s)\) have opposite signs, allowing one to be
zero but requiring \(J_c(s)-J_c(r)\ne0\), set
\begin{align}
 \theta&=\frac{J_c(s)}{J_c(s)-J_c(r)},&
 G&=\theta g(r)+(1-\theta)g(s),\nonumber\\
 p_X&=\frac{G}{G-g(c)},&
 \nu_X&=p_X\sigma_c+
       (1-p_X)\bigl(\theta\sigma_r+(1-\theta)\sigma_s\bigr).
 \label{gsr:dt:90:eq:gridmeasure}
\end{align}

\begin{theorem}[Exact adjacent-node formula]\label{gsr:dt:90:thm:gridexact}
Suppose \(w>c\), \(q_1,q_2<0\), \(0\le\theta\le1\), \(G>0\), and
the measure in \eqref{gsr:dt:90:eq:gridmeasure} satisfies
\[
 R(c;r,s)>0,\qquad
 |\widehat{\nu_X}(3)|\le R(c;r,s).
 \tag{G2}\label{gsr:dt:90:eq:gridtests}
\]
Then
\[
 \min_{\substack{\mu\text{ a probability measure}\\
                  \cos(\supp\mu)\subset X}}
       \max_{1\le j\le4}|\widehat\mu(j)|
       =R(c;r,s).
 \tag{G3}\label{gsr:dt:90:eq:gridexact}
\]
The measure \(\nu_X\) attains the minimum. If
\(-1<r<s<c<1\), it is the unique minimizer, without a symmetry
assumption.

For \(c\) in any compact subinterval of \((c_-,c_*)\), all the
hypotheses hold whenever \(r\le v(c)\le s\) are sufficiently close
to \(v(c)\), uniformly in \(c\). In particular, this is an
unconditional eventual formula for the ordinary cyclic grids.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The polynomial
\[
 Q_X(x)=(c-x)(w-x)(x-r)(x-s)
\]
is nonnegative on \(X\): the first two factors are nonnegative, and
the last two have a negative product only between the adjacent
nodes. Its expansion is
\[
 Q_X(x)=q_0+q_1T_1(x)+q_2T_2(x)+\frac18T_4(x).
 \tag{G4}\label{gsr:dt:90:eq:gridQ}
\]
The choice of \(w\) cancels the cubic term, hence the coefficient of
\(T_3\). The certificate principle gives the lower bound
\(-q_0/A\).

Since \(g(c)<0<G\), the number \(p_X\) lies strictly between zero
and one. By construction,
\[
 \int g\,d\nu_X=0,\qquad \int J_c\,d\nu_X=0.
\]
As \(g(c)\ne0\), the second identity and the first imply
\(\int h\,d\nu_X=0\). Consequently, for
\(\rho_X=-\int x\,d\nu_X\),
\[
 \widehat{\nu_X}(1)=\widehat{\nu_X}(2)=-\rho_X,
 \qquad \widehat{\nu_X}(4)=\rho_X.
\]
Integrating \eqref{gsr:dt:90:eq:gridQ} over its zero set gives
\(q_0+A\rho_X=0\). Assumption \eqref{gsr:dt:90:eq:gridtests} proves that the
remaining moment is feasible and establishes \eqref{gsr:dt:90:eq:gridexact}.

For uniqueness, equality in the certificate restricts support to
the cosine coordinates \(c,r,s\) and makes moments \(1,2,4\)
real, with the displayed values. The equations consisting of total
mass and the two identities \(\int g=\int h=0\) determine the
three cosine masses uniquely. To see nonsingularity, eliminate the
mass at \(c\); the remaining relation involves the two nonzero
numbers \(J_c(r),J_c(s)\), or their endpoint limits. Equivalently,
the determinant of this system is nonzero because
\[
 g(c)\ne0,\qquad
 \frac{J_c(r)}{g(r)}\ne\frac{J_c(s)}{g(s)}.
\]
This last inequality holds under the sign and positivity
hypotheses, including a zero at one endpoint.
For the differences between masses at conjugate angles, the
imaginary equations for \(1,2,4\), after dividing each column by
its positive sine, have determinant
\[
 -16(r-c)(s-c)(r-s)(c+r+s)\ne0.
\]
Here \(c+r+s=-w\ne0\), since \(r+s<-1\) and \(c<1/6\).
Thus each conjugate pair has equal masses.

It remains to justify the eventual assertions. Direct expansion
gives
\[
 J_c(x)=-2(x-c)F(c,x).
 \tag{G5}\label{gsr:dt:90:eq:Jfactor}
\]
By the root lemma, \(F_v(c,v)>0\); hence \(J_c\) has a simple zero
at \(v\), changes sign there, and has no other zero in a fixed
small neighbourhood, uniformly on compact parameter intervals.
Both \(g(r)\) and \(g(s)\) are positive there. The formulas in
\eqref{gsr:dt:90:eq:gridmeasure} then give a probability measure converging
to \(\mu_*\) as \(r,s\to v\), even if the ratio of the two distances
to \(v\) has no limit: their combined mass converges to \(1-p\).
The strict coefficient signs, \(w>1\), positivity of \(\rho\),
and the strict third-moment margin persist. Compactness makes the
neighbourhood uniform.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Fully explicit finite certification]
Conditions \eqref{gsr:dt:90:eq:gridtests}, the signs in
\eqref{gsr:dt:90:eq:gridrho}, and the masses in \eqref{gsr:dt:90:eq:gridmeasure} are
finite algebraic tests. Thus the exact formula can be certified at
any specified modulus; the eventual assertion does not require
guessing how large that modulus must be. When a neighbouring node
equals \(v\), one of the two split masses is zero and the
continuous extremizer itself is feasible.
\end{remark}

\subsection{The exact gap and its oscillatory asymptotic}

\begin{theorem}[An exact discretization identity]\label{gsr:dt:90:thm:gridgap}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:90:thm:gridexact},
\[
 R(c;r,s)-\rho
 =\frac{(1-p)(c-v)(w-v)}{A}\,(v-r)(s-v).
 \tag{G6}\label{gsr:dt:90:eq:gridgap}
\]
In the eventual range this is positive unless \(v\) is a grid node.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Integrate \(Q_X\) against the continuous optimizer. Its cosine mass
at \(c\) contributes zero, while its other mass gives
\[
 q_0+A\rho
 =(1-p)(c-v)(w-v)(v-r)(v-s).
\]
Rearranging proves the identity. Every factor other than the final
two distances is strictly positive in the stated range.
\end{proof}

For the grid \(\{2\pi j/N:0\le j<N\}\), let
\[
 \Phi_{4,N}(a)=
 \min_{\substack{\mu\text{ a probability measure on the grid}\\
                 \supp\mu\subset K_a}}E_4(\mu).
\]
If the admissible grid is empty, the minimum is not defined; all
the asymptotic statements below concern sufficiently large \(N\).
Set
\[
 h_N=\frac{2\pi}{N},\qquad
 a_N=h_N\left\lceil\frac{a}{h_N}\right\rceil,\qquad
 c_N=\cos a_N,\qquad \beta_N=\arccos v(c_N).
\]
The first rounding is essential: the allowed cosine grid has
largest coordinate \(c_N\), so the appropriate continuous
comparison is at \(a_N\).

Define
\[
 A_0(c)=-2v(c)(c+v(c))^2
       -\frac{1-c^2-2cv(c)-3v(c)^2}{2}+\frac18,
\]
and
\[
 C(c)=
 \frac{(1-p)(c-v)(-c-3v)}{A_0(c)}(1-v^2)>0.
 \tag{G7}\label{gsr:dt:90:eq:amplitude}
\]
Here \(p,v\) are evaluated at \(c\).

\begin{corollary}[The leading grid correction]\label{gsr:dt:90:cor:gridasymptotic}
For \(a\) in a compact subinterval of \((a_*,3\pi/5)\), uniformly
as \(N\to\infty\),
\[
 \Phi_{4,N}(a)
 =\Phi_4(a_N)+
 C(c_N)h_N^2\,
 \left\{\frac{\beta_N}{h_N}\right\}
 \left(1-\left\{\frac{\beta_N}{h_N}\right\}\right)
 +O(h_N^3).
 \tag{G8}\label{gsr:dt:90:eq:gridasymptotic}
\]
Braces denote fractional part. Thus the second-order coefficient
depends on the position of the interior contact point inside its
grid cell.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Take \(j=\lfloor\beta_N/h_N\rfloor\),
\(s=\cos(jh_N)\), and \(r=\cos((j+1)h_N)\).
These are adjacent cosine nodes for all sufficiently large \(N\).
Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:90:thm:gridexact} applies uniformly. With
\(t=\{\beta_N/h_N\}\), Taylor expansion gives
\[
 (v-r)(s-v)=(1-v^2)h_N^2t(1-t)+O(h_N^3),
\]
uniformly for \(0\le t\le1\). The other factor in
\eqref{gsr:dt:90:eq:gridgap} differs from its value at \(r=s=v\) by
\(O(h_N)\). The formula follows. It also holds when a distance is
zero, in which case the exact correction vanishes.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A closed formula for every aligned semicircle grid}

At \(a=\pi/2\) the continuous data simplify to
\[
 c=0,\quad v=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2},\quad
 \beta=\frac{5\pi}{6},\quad
 \rho_0=\frac{\sqrt3-1}{2},\quad
 p=\frac1{\sqrt3},\quad
 C(0)=\frac{2\sqrt3-3}{4}.
 \tag{G9}\label{gsr:dt:90:eq:semicircledata}
\]
This gives an exact finite formula, without an unspecified
large-modulus threshold.

\begin{theorem}[All aligned semicircle moduli]\label{gsr:dt:90:thm:semicircleexact}
Let \(4\mid N\), \(N\ge8\), and set
\[
 j=\left\lfloor\frac{5N}{12}\right\rfloor,\qquad
 r=\cos\frac{2\pi(j+1)}N,\qquad s=\cos\frac{2\pi j}N.
\]
Then
\[
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 \Phi_{4,N}(\pi/2)=
 \frac{4(r^2+rs+s^2)-3}
      {4(r^2+rs+s^2)-3-8rs(r+s)}.}
 \tag{G10}\label{gsr:dt:90:eq:semicircleexact}
\]
If \(12\mid N\), this is exactly \(\rho_0\). If
\(N\equiv4\) or \(8\pmod{12}\), it is strictly greater and
\[
 \Phi_{4,N}(\pi/2)
 =\rho_0+\frac{2\pi^2(2\sqrt3-3)}{9N^2}+O(N^{-3}).
 \tag{G11}\label{gsr:dt:90:eq:semicircleresidue}
\]
For the exceptional modulus \(N=4\), the value is \(1\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For these moduli,
\[
 -1\le r\le-\sqrt3/2\le s\le-1/\sqrt2.
\]
In particular, \(q_1=rs(r+s)<0\), \(q_2<0\), and \(w=-r-s>0\).
For \(c=0\),
\[
 J_0(x)=2x^2(3-4x^2).
\]
Thus \(J_0(r)\le0\le J_0(s)\), and the weights
\eqref{gsr:dt:90:eq:gridmeasure} are nonnegative, with \(G>0\).
They satisfy the required three active-moment equations.
The numerator of \eqref{gsr:dt:90:eq:semicircleexact} is positive, as is its
denominator. It remains only to check the third moment.

Put \(u=rs\), \(t=r+s\), \(B=4(t^2-u)-3\), and
\(D=B-8ut>0\). On the three support points \(0,r,s\),
\(x^3=tx^2-ux\). Therefore, writing \(m_3\) for the third moment,
\begin{align*}
 D(m_3-\rho_X)&=2(4t^2-8u^2-10u-3),\\
 D(m_3+\rho_X)&=4(4t^2-4u^2-7u-3).
\end{align*}
Let \(R=-r\in[\sqrt3/2,1]\) and
\(S=-s\in[1/\sqrt2,\sqrt3/2]\).
The expression in the first parentheses becomes
\[
 4R^2-3+(4-8R^2)S^2-2RS.
\]
It decreases with \(S\), and at \(S=1/\sqrt2\) it is
\(-1-\sqrt2R<0\).
The second parentheses is
\[
 4R^2+4S^2+RS-4R^2S^2-3>0,
\]
because \(4R^2+4S^2-4R^2S^2\ge7/2\).
Hence the third moment is strictly between the two bounds.
The polynomial certificate and the constructed measure prove
\eqref{gsr:dt:90:eq:semicircleexact}, also when \(r=-1\).

When \(12\mid N\), \(s=v\), so \eqref{gsr:dt:90:eq:gridgap} vanishes.
In the other two aligned residue classes,
\(\{5N/12\}\) equals \(2/3\) or \(1/3\); substituting
\eqref{gsr:dt:90:eq:semicircledata} into \eqref{gsr:dt:90:eq:gridasymptotic} gives
\eqref{gsr:dt:90:eq:semicircleresidue}. Finally every point of the four-point
grid has fourth Fourier phase equal to one.
\end{proof}

\begin{figure}[!htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.94\textwidth]{figures/90-fourier-directional-semicircle_grid.pdf}
\caption{Exact aligned-semicircle grid corrections, multiplied by $N^2$. The residue class $N\equiv0\pmod{12}$ has zero correction. The other two aligned classes approach $2\pi^2(2\sqrt3-3)/9$ from their exact finite values. Formula~\eqref{gsr:dt:90:eq:semicircleexact}, rather than a numerical optimization, determines every plotted point.}
\label{gsr:dt:90:fig:semicircle}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Twelve residue classes and expansions to every order}

The radius-rounding term can also be retained explicitly when
\(4\nmid N\). Put
\[
 \kappa_N=\left\lceil\frac N4\right\rceil-\frac N4,\qquad
 t_N=\left\{\frac{5N}{12}\right\},\qquad h=\frac{2\pi}{N}.
\]
These numbers depend only on \(N\bmod12\).

\begin{theorem}[The full semicircle expansion]\label{gsr:dt:90:thm:semicircleallorders}
As \(N\to\infty\),
\begin{align}
 \Phi_{4,N}(\pi/2)
 ={}&\rho_0+\rho_0\kappa_Nh \nonumber\\
 &+\left[
 \left(-\frac52+\frac{7\sqrt3}{6}\right)\kappa_N^2+
 \frac{2\sqrt3-3}{4}\,t_N(1-t_N)
 \right]h^2+O(h^3).
 \label{gsr:dt:90:eq:semicircleallorders}
\end{align}
For each fixed residue class modulo twelve, the value is, for all
sufficiently large \(N\) in that class, an analytic function of
\(h=2\pi/N\). Its Taylor series is a convergent expansion near
\(h=0\); every coefficient belongs to \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt3)\).
An exact generating expression for that series is
\[
 R\left(-\sin(\kappa_Nh);\
    \cos\bigl(5\pi/6+(1-t_N)h\bigr),\
    \cos\bigl(5\pi/6-t_Nh\bigr)\right).
 \tag{G12}\label{gsr:dt:90:eq:residuegenerator}
\]
For the residue class \(N\equiv0\pmod{12}\), it is the constant
\(\rho_0\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The implicit root is analytic near \(c=0\), since \(F_v(0,v)>0\).
Differentiating \(F(c,v(c))=0\) and the formula for \(\rho_*(c)\)
gives
\[
 v'(0)=0,\quad v''(0)=-1-\frac{\sqrt3}{3},\qquad
 \rho_*'(0)=-\rho_0,\quad
 \rho_*''(0)=-5+\frac{7\sqrt3}{3}.
\]
These identities follow by two polynomial differentiations and
substitution of \(v(0)=-\sqrt3/2\).
Since \(a_N=\pi/2+\kappa_Nh\), they give the first three terms of
\(\Phi_4(a_N)\). They also give
\(\beta_N=5\pi/6+O(h^2)\).

If \(t_N\ne0\), this perturbation is too small to cross either
endpoint of the fixed grid cell containing \(5\pi/6\), for
sufficiently small \(h\) in the specified residue class. If
\(t_N=0\), then \(12\mid N\), \(\kappa_N=0\), and the contact point
lies on the grid exactly. Thus the adjacent nodes are precisely
those in \eqref{gsr:dt:90:eq:residuegenerator}. Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:90:thm:gridexact}
proves this exact expression. Its denominator has a nonzero limit,
so it is analytic at zero. Sines and cosines at \(5\pi/6\), together
with the rational values of \(\kappa_N,t_N\), show that its
coefficients lie in \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt3)\).
Finally \eqref{gsr:dt:90:eq:gridasymptotic} and the displayed derivatives
give \eqref{gsr:dt:90:eq:semicircleallorders}.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Quantitative stability of the four-atom extremizer\srctag{90}}]{Quantitative stability of the four-atom extremizer}\label{gsr:dt:90:sec:d5}
\srcnote{90}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:dt:90:sec:stability}

The certificate gives more information than the optimum. A measure
whose first four coefficients are almost as small as possible must
concentrate near the contact points. On the algebraic branch this
has an explicit square-root modulus, and the exponent is optimal.
The statement below uses the cosine coordinate so that it applies
to arbitrary measures without first discarding their even part.

For probability measures on a compact metric space, write \(W_1\)
for the infimum, over all couplings, of the expected distance. No
transport theorem is needed below: every bound is supplied by an
explicit coupling or by a function which changes by at most the
distance between its arguments.

Fix \(a_*<a<3\pi/5\). Use the notation \(c,v,p,\rho\) from
Section~\ref{gsr:dt:90:sec:grid}, and put
\[
 d=c-v,\qquad w_0=-c-2v,\qquad A_0=A_0(c),\qquad
 b_1=\frac{-2v(c+v)^2}{A_0}>0,
\]
\[
 K=\frac{(w_0-c)(c-v)}{2A_0}>0,\qquad
 \nu_*=p\delta_c+(1-p)\delta_v.
 \tag{S1}\label{gsr:dt:90:eq:stabilityconstants}
\]
Here \(\nu_*\) is the cosine pushforward of the unique optimizer.

\begin{theorem}[Explicit stability]\label{gsr:dt:90:thm:stability}
Let \(\mu\) be supported on \(K_a\), with
\(E_4(\mu)\le\rho+\varepsilon\), \(\varepsilon\ge0\), and let
\(\nu\) be its pushforward by \(x=\cos\theta\). Then
\begin{align}
 \int \operatorname{dist}(x,\{c,v\})^2\,d\nu(x)
 &\le\frac{\varepsilon}{K}, \label{gsr:dt:90:eq:stabilitycost}\\
 W_1(\nu,\nu_*)
 &\le2\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon}{K}}+\frac{\varepsilon}{b_1}.
 \label{gsr:dt:90:eq:stabilitytransport}
\end{align}
For reflection-invariant \(\mu\), with circular distance on
\(\mathbb T\), one also has
\[
 W_1(\mu,\mu_*)\le
 \frac{\pi}{2\min\{\sin a,\cos(\beta/2)\}}
 \left(2\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon}{K}}+
             \frac{\varepsilon}{b_1}\right),
 \qquad \beta=\arccos v.
 \tag{S2}\label{gsr:dt:90:eq:stabilitycircle}
\]
The exponent \(1/2\) cannot be increased, even for even measures
and a single fixed interior radius.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write the normalized certificate as
\[
 \frac{Q(x)}{A_0}
 =-\rho-b_1T_1(x)-b_2T_2(x)+b_4T_4(x),
 \qquad b_1,b_2,b_4>0,\quad b_1+b_2+b_4=1.
\]
Since each real Fourier moment has absolute value at most
\(\rho+\varepsilon\),
\[
 0\le\int\frac{Q}{A_0}\,d\nu\le\varepsilon.
 \tag{S3}\label{gsr:dt:90:eq:certificateexcess}
\]
For \(x\le(c+v)/2\), one has \(c-x\ge d/2\). For
\((c+v)/2\le x\le c\), one has \(x-v\ge d/2\) and
\(c-x\le d/2\). These two cases prove
\[
 (c-x)(x-v)^2\ge
 \frac d2\operatorname{dist}(x,\{c,v\})^2
 \qquad(-1\le x\le c).
\]
As \(w_0-x\ge w_0-c\), this and
\eqref{gsr:dt:90:eq:certificateexcess} give \eqref{gsr:dt:90:eq:stabilitycost}.

There is also a useful bound on the first moment. For
\(j=1,2,4\), let \(\sigma_1=\sigma_2=-1\), \(\sigma_4=1\), and
\[
 \Delta_j=(\rho+\varepsilon)
          -\sigma_j\operatorname{Re}\widehat\mu(j)\ge0.
\]
The nonnegative integral in \eqref{gsr:dt:90:eq:certificateexcess} implies
\(\sum b_j\Delta_j\le\varepsilon\). In particular,
\[
 \left|\int x\,d\nu+\rho\right|\le\varepsilon/b_1.
 \tag{S4}\label{gsr:dt:90:eq:firstmomentstable}
\]

Project \(x\) to a nearest point of \(\{c,v\}\), choosing either
at the midpoint, and call the resulting measure
\(\widetilde\nu=p'\delta_c+(1-p')\delta_v\). The projection
coupling and Cauchy--Schwarz give
\[
 W_1(\nu,\widetilde\nu)\le\sqrt{\varepsilon/K}.
\]
The difference of the means of \(\widetilde\nu\) and \(\nu_*\)
is \((p'-p)d\). By \eqref{gsr:dt:90:eq:firstmomentstable} and the projection
bound,
\[
 |p'-p|d\le\varepsilon/b_1+\sqrt{\varepsilon/K}.
\]
Move the excess mass between \(c\) and \(v\); this costs exactly
\(|p'-p|d\), proving \eqref{gsr:dt:90:eq:stabilitytransport}.

For the circular assertion, lift this particular coupling to
matching signs of the angles. Every intermediate transport has
one endpoint at \(a\) or \(\beta\). For
\(\theta\in[a,\pi]\), \(\phi\in\{a,\beta\}\),
\[
 |\cos\theta-\cos\phi|
 =2\sin\frac{\theta+\phi}{2}
       \left|\sin\frac{\theta-\phi}{2}\right|
 \ge\frac{2m}{\pi}|\theta-\phi|,
 \quad m=\min\{\sin a,\cos(\beta/2)\}>0.
\]
This proves \eqref{gsr:dt:90:eq:stabilitycircle}.

Finally, for sufficiently small \(t>0\), replace
\(\sigma_v=(\delta_\beta+\delta_{-\beta})/2\) by
\[
 \frac14\bigl(
 \delta_{\beta-t}+\delta_{\beta+t}+
 \delta_{-\beta-t}+\delta_{-\beta+t}\bigr),
\]
leaving the mass \(p\sigma_c\) unchanged. The resulting even
measure \(\mu_t\) is still admissible, and its \(j\)th moment is
\[
 p\cos(ja)+(1-p)\cos(j\beta)\cos(jt).
\]
Thus \(E_4(\mu_t)\le\rho+8(1-p)t^2\). Its circular
\(W_1\)-distance from \(\mu_*\) is exactly \((1-p)t\):
the direct coupling gives this cost, and distance to the four
original support points gives the matching lower bound.
For its cosine pushforward \(\nu_t\), the same nearest-support
argument gives
\[
 W_1(\nu_t,\nu_*)=(1-p)\sin\beta\,\sin t
\]
for sufficiently small \(t\). Thus the same obstruction applies
to the cosine-coordinate bound.
Consequently no uniform estimate with a power greater than
\(1/2\) can hold as the deficit tends to zero.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The role of the symmetry assumption]
The cosine-coordinate bounds hold for every admissible measure.
They control the masses and locations of the two conjugate pairs.
The angular bound is stated for even measures because their
orientation is fixed by those masses. The exact optimizer itself
is unique among all measures by Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:90:thm:four}; a
quantitative bound on unequal masses within conjugate pairs can
also be obtained from the imaginary parts of the first two active
moments. This additional estimate is not used in any theorem here.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{How to use the results in a quantitative argument\srctag{90}}]{How to use the results in a quantitative argument}\label{gsr:dt:90:sec:d7}
\srcnote{90}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:dt:90:sec:integration}

\subsection{A weighted replacement at the missing-interval interface}

The normalization relating the circle problem to a cyclic Fourier
transform is elementary but should be made explicit.

\begin{corollary}[Four-frequency detection with an exact weighted constant]
\label{gsr:dt:90:cor:detection}
Let \(w_x\ge0\), \(x\in C_N\), have positive total mass
\(M_w=\sum_xw_x\). Suppose its angular support, after a rotation,
is contained in \(K_a\). Then
\[
 \max_{1\le j\le4}
 \left|\sum_{x\in C_N}w_xe^{-2\pi ijx/N}\right|
 \ge M_w\Phi_4(a).
\]
If the removed arc is centered at a grid point, the constant may
be replaced by \(\Phi_{4,N}(a)\). Whenever
Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:90:thm:gridexact} applies, its adjacent-node expression
is the exact best constant over all such nonnegative grid weights.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Divide the weights by \(M_w\) and regard them as a probability
measure on the angular grid. Translation of the arc center
multiplies its \(j\)th Fourier coefficient by a unit complex number
and does not change its modulus. The definition of \(\Phi_4\)
gives the first inequality; the finite-grid definition gives
the second. The attaining measures constructed above prove
the stated sharpness over nonnegative grid weights.
\end{proof}

For an unweighted set \(A\), take \(w_x=\mathbf1_A(x)\) and
\(M_w=|A|\). The lower bound still applies, but fixed-cardinality
sharpness need not follow: the extremal masses generally need not
be equal rational multiples of \(1/|A|\).
Likewise, if the original missing interval uses a half-open
convention, it implies exclusion of the corresponding open
interval, so the bound applies; equality may be lost if one
of the two extremal boundary points is additionally forbidden.

For a missing open semicircle, only four frequencies are needed
for the exact universal guarantee
\[
 \frac{\sqrt3-1}{2}M_w=0.3660254037\ldots\,M_w.
\]
The extremizer is supported at
\[
 \theta=\pm\pi/2,\quad \pm5\pi/6,
\]
with masses \(1/(2\sqrt3)\) at each boundary point and
\((1-1/\sqrt3)/2\) at each interior contact point.
The cutoff-three guarantee at this radius is \(M_w/3\)
\cite{extremallimits}; thus the extra frequency gives an exact
strict improvement. The quotient of the two guarantees is
\(3(\sqrt3-1)/2\).

The cutoff-four guarantee vanishes for \(a\le\pi/5\).
Consequently a proof in which the excluded interval becomes
arbitrarily narrow must also allow the frequency cutoff to grow.
The general continuation theorem identifies one precise additional
range of that growing-cutoff problem. It does not solve all
subsequent phases for \(R\ge5\).

\subsection{Finite-grid losses can be separated exactly}

There are two distinct sources of finite-grid loss.
The largest allowed cosine is \(\cos a_N\), where
\(a_N=(2\pi/N)\lceil aN/(2\pi)\rceil\). Rounding the boundary
from \(a\) to \(a_N\) typically creates a first-order change in
the optimum. Splitting the interior contact point between
adjacent grid nodes creates the second-order change in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:90:thm:gridgap}.

This distinction matters when reporting an \(N^{-2}\) estimate.
The comparison at that order is with \(\Phi_4(a_N)\), not
automatically with \(\Phi_4(a)\). At the semicircle radius and
\(4\mid N\), the boundary rounding disappears, leaving exactly
the arithmetic oscillation described by
Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:90:thm:semicircleexact}. In particular,
\[
 \Phi_{4,N}(\pi/2)=\Phi_4(\pi/2)
 \quad\text{for }12\mid N,
\]
whereas in each of the other two aligned residue classes the
first nonzero correction has the positive coefficient
\(2\pi^2(2\sqrt3-3)/9\).
One therefore cannot replace this oscillation by a single
strictly positive lower error term valid for every modulus.

For an explicit finite instance, the certificate procedure is:
round the boundary, bracket the continuous interior contact
point by adjacent cosine nodes, compute the three masses, and
verify the coefficient signs and the one unused Fourier
constraint. If those finite tests pass, the resulting value
is exact; an optimization solver is not part of the proof.
Close to a phase junction, the uniform interior theorem no
longer supplies an automatic threshold, so the finite tests
should be retained.

\subsection{Directional information and graph energy}

The cycle theorem has a direct conditional interpretation.
If \(d_1(f)\le\eta\), then
\[
 E(\Gamma_f)\ge
 N^3\left(1-\frac{N+1}{6}\eta\right).
\]
For a nontrivial positive conclusion, \(\eta\) must be of order
\(1/N\) or smaller. This is the natural scale: the equality maps
have \(d_1=2(N-1)/N^2\), while their average defect approaches
\(1/3\).
The factor cannot be replaced by an absolute constant uniformly
in \(N\), even for cyclic prime targets varying with \(N\).

The theorem applies to a map defined on the entire cycle.
Gowers' graph arguments also encounter functions defined only
on a subset. Extending a partial map arbitrarily does not
preserve the useful derivative statistics: windows may leave
the domain, and different extensions may introduce unrelated
collisions. A sparse-domain version needs its own hypotheses
and proof. This is a substantive next problem, not a suppressed
technical step.

The graph-energy lower bound is also distinct from a conclusion
about distance to an affine map. The explicit map
\(f:C_N\to\Z\), \(f(j)=j\) on the standard representatives,
has average defect below \(1/3\) and is far from every affine
map. Thus any use of an affine-recovery lemma must retain
that lemma's target assumptions and admissible defect range.

\subsection{Requirements for a global improvement}

To turn one of these local improvements into a new quantitative
Szemer\'edi theorem, one would have to identify an occurrence
of the corresponding hypotheses inside the full proof, carry
the improved constants through all subsequent selections and
partitions, and compare the resulting final bound with an
explicit baseline. In particular, frequency growth, domain
density, progression length, and the losses in inverse and
structure theorems cannot be treated as fixed constants when
they vary during the iteration.

The present results settle exact optimization questions at
these interfaces. They supply better inputs where their
hypotheses occur, and classify the examples that prevent
further improvement by the same local formulation. We have
not carried out the global propagation, so no change in a
global exponent or tower height is asserted.

\section{Sources~102 and~106: exact affine cells for quadratic phases over finite fields \wtag}\label{gsr:dt:sec:affinecells}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the fourteenth write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next nineteen sections are source~102's Sections~2--10 and source~106's Sections~2--10 and Appendix~A. They study a finite-field model of the simultaneous quadratic localization behind Gowers's Lemma~13.5: over $\Fq$, the least number $\Asf(\Psi)$ of affine cells (points allowed) on which a family of quadratic phases is \emph{exactly} constant, and the zero-fibre costs $P_m=\Psf(C^m)$ of the products of the coordinate cross $C=\{xy=0\}$. \emph{Logically they continue Part~I's simultaneous-partition sequence}, sources~13, 16, 18, 19, 23 and~35, and in particular source~16's precise remaining partition problem (Section~\ref{gsr:dt:16:sec:d7}); they are printed here because no number printed earlier may move. The introductions are Sections~\ref{gsr:fm:102:sec:d1} and~\ref{gsr:fm:106:sec:d1}. \emph{A notational warning for the whole chapter}: $q$ is the order of the field, while in sources~13--19 and in the Lean family $q$ is the number of phases (sources~102 and~106 call that number $m$ and~$j$).

\emph{Source~102} proves $\Psf(C)=q$ and $\Psf(C^2)=4q-3$, with exactly two optimal partitions of $C^2$ (two cyclic families of $4(q-1)$ lines and the origin) for odd $q\ge5$; $\Asf(\Psi_1)=q^2-q+1$ and $\Asf(\Psi_2)=q^4-2q^3+2q^2+2q-2$, strictly below the product $\Asf(\Psi_1)^2$ by $(q-1)(q-3)$, with exactly $2^{2(q-1)^2+1}$ optimizers; the binomial singular-fibre reduction $\Asf(\Psi_m)=\sum_k\binom mk(q-1)^{2(m-k)}P_k$; $2-1/q\le\rho(q)\le\sqrt{4q-3}$ for $\rho(q)=\lim P_m^{1/m}$; the scalar split forms of rank $2r$ cost $q^{r+1}-q+1$, with an exact defect identity, and every scalar quadratic has an explicit bottleneck dimension (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:102:thm:main} and Sections~\ref{gsr:dt:102:sec:d4}--\ref{gsr:dt:102:sec:d10}). \emph{Source~106} generalizes the cross to $s$ arms and the field to every $q>2$: torus capacity $|A\cap(\Fq^\times)^m|\le(q-1)^{\dim A}$ with equality exactly for diagonal-coordinate flats (counted by Stirling numbers), an exact torus/dimension defect identity, the two-moment linear-programming optimum, $P_{s,m}(q)=s^{m-1}(s-\ell)q^{m-r}+O(q^{m-r-1})$ for $m=rs+\ell$, asymptotic rigidity, and $\rho_s(q)=sq^{1-1/s}(1+O(\log q/q))$ (Theorems~\ref{gsr:fm:106:thm:main-intro}, \ref{gsr:fm:106:thm:rate-intro}).

\emph{What source~106 does to source~102.} It answers source~102's Question~13.2 at the large-field scale: $\rho(q)=\rho_2(q)\sim2\sqrt q$, so source~102's upper bound $\sqrt{4q-3}$ is asymptotically sharp (its lower bound was $2-1/q$); it brackets Question~13.1, $4q^2-5q+2\le P_{2,3}(q)\le4q^2-3q$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:106:thm:three}); and it re-proves, with credit, $\Psf(C^2)=4q-3$ and the binomial reduction, for every $q>2$, so \emph{for even $q$ as well} (orthant containment and the hyperbola lemma need only $q>2$). Source~102's classification of the two optimal partitions is for odd $q\ge5$ and is not extended by source~106. \emph{Checked at the write} (\file{verify14.py}, exact-cover searches written for this write): $\Psf(C)=q$ with two optimal partitions and $\Psf(C^2)=4q-3$ for $q=3,4,5$, with exactly two optimal partitions at $q=4$ and $q=5$ and $30$ at $q=3$; so the rigidity of source~102 also holds at $q=4$, which neither source claims; source~106's finite lower bound equals $4q-3$ at $m=2$ and $4q^2-5q+2$ at $m=3$ for all $59$ prime powers $3\le q<200$; the closed forms of $\Asf(\Psi_1)$, $\Asf(\Psi_2)$ and the gap $(q-1)(q-3)$; the rate bounds approach $2\sqrt q$ (at $q=10^6+3$ both are within $2\cdot10^{-6}$ of it).

\emph{The Lean interface} (HEAD \texttt{a0c3e9b67}). Both sources read the Lean family behind Gowers's Lemma~13.5: \file{quadratic_family_phase_localization} (\file{Proofs05QuadraticFamily}:34), with the budget \file{quadraticFamilyBudget} (\file{Proofs05QuadraticFamily}:9) and \file{quadraticFamilyBudget_bound} (\file{Proofs05QuadraticFamily}:20), which feeds \file{lemma_13_5_prime} (\file{Proofs13FiniteRecurrence}:9) and the exact companion \file{lemma_13_5_holds} (\file{Proofs13FiniteRecurrence}:19); the one-phase case is \file{corollary_5_8_degree_two} (\file{Proofs05QuadraticLocalization}:87). \section[{Repository review and mathematical provenance\srctag{102}}]{Repository review and mathematical provenance}\label{gsr:dt:102:sec:d2}\label{gsr:dt:102:sec:review}
\srcnote{102}{Section 2}

\subsection{The reviewed snapshots}
The review was conducted on October 7, 2026. To avoid conflating changing branches, this manuscript records fixed source revisions:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ll}
\toprule
Repository & Reviewed commit prefix\\
\midrule
\texttt{openai/math} & \texttt{adc7f1241b42}\\
\texttt{VladimirReshetnikov/ProveIt} & \texttt{3f61aea0a351}\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Full hashes and selected blob identifiers are in the companion \texttt{source\_manifest.json}. The mathematical proofs below use no global theorem from either snapshot as an assumption.

The \texttt{openai/math} catalog at the reviewed revision advertises several recent results directly adjacent to additive combinatorics: family 159 claims all-length bounds
\[
 r_k(N)\le C_kN\exp\bigl[-c_k(\log N)^{\varepsilon_k}\bigr]
\]
and the reciprocal-sum consequence; family 160 claims superexponential van der Waerden lower bounds; family 161 claims a counterexample to Sidorenko's conjecture\cite{oaimath}. These are descriptions of repository claims, not independent certifications by this article. The selected family-159 introduction was read directly\cite{oaiprogressions}. Its discussion separates obtaining structured correlation from controlling the cost of preserving and localizing that structure through later increments. That distinction motivated the present local optimization problem.

On the ProveIt side, the reviewed October 7 commit reports a five-term sufficient threshold
\[
 N\ge 2^{\,2^{\delta^{-2^{73}}}},\qquad 0<\delta\le\tfrac12,
\]
with an audit of 766 modules and 4,887 public Gowers theorem declarations using the stated standard Lean axioms. Its message explicitly leaves the original all-length objective incomplete\cite{repo102checkpoint}. These are repository-reported checks, not builds rerun for this manuscript.

More immediately relevant is the actual source file \texttt{Proofs05QuadraticFamily.lean}\cite{repo102family}. It defines
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:102:eq:repobudget}
 B(0,U)=U,\qquad B(j+1,U)=(2B(j,U))^{1024},\qquad
 4B(j,U)\le(4U)^{1024^j}.
\end{equation}
Under a proper modular-progression length hypothesis, its theorem produces a partition into proper progressions of length at least $U$, with each quadratic phase within $1/(4U)$ of a cellwise unit complex number. The proof iterates a one-phase localization. Reading this construction suggested asking what a genuinely joint partition can gain in a model where optimality is accessible.

\subsection{A crucial distinction between the models}
Equation~\eqref{gsr:dt:102:eq:repobudget} controls a \emph{minimum progression length} under a near-constancy requirement. Our invariant controls the \emph{number of affine cells} under exact constancy. The optimal partitions in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:102:thm:main} contain singleton cells. Consequently they cannot simply be substituted into the ProveIt theorem while retaining its length guarantee. This is a mathematical limitation of the transfer, not a formalization detail.

Likewise, simultaneous quadratic localization itself is not a new strategy. Henriot's treatment of quadratic harmonics contains a simultaneous linearization theorem based on the Schmidt--Green--Tao recurrence estimate\cite[Propositions 9.1--9.2]{henriot}. Croot, Lyall, and Rice give an elementary approach to simultaneous polynomial recurrence\cite{crootlyallrice}. The proposed new content here is the exact affine partition invariant and its two-phase equality classification, not the general idea of localizing several phases together.

Affine partitions of whole vector spaces have an established literature. Bamberg, Filmus, Ihringer, and Kurz study affine vector space partitions, including minimum sizes and structural classification\cite{bfik}. Our partitions are constrained by polynomial fibers, and the decisive set $C^2$ is a union of intersecting coordinate planes rather than a whole affine space. The literature search found this neighboring framework and the recurrence literature; it was not an exhaustive priority search for every special union of subspaces. Accordingly the article distinguishes a proved statement from a verified claim of historical novelty.

\subsection{Dependency boundary}
The proofs use finite affine geometry, elementary counting, polarization, and a short quadratic decomposition argument supplied in Section~\ref{gsr:dt:102:sec:general}. The computer checks are corroboration, not premises. In particular the results remain valid independently of the truth, interpretation, or eventual review of the much stronger catalog claims motivating the investigation.

\section[{Definitions, invariance, and quadratic phases\srctag{102}}]{Definitions, invariance, and quadratic phases}\label{gsr:dt:102:sec:d3}\label{gsr:dt:102:sec:prelim}
\srcnote{102}{Section 3}

\begin{definition}[Affine partition invariants]
A cell is a nonempty affine subspace $a+U$ over $\Fq$. An affine partition of $X$ is a finite family of pairwise disjoint cells with union $X$. Define $\Psf(\varnothing)=0$, and let $\Psf(X)$ be the minimum size of such a partition when $X\ne\varnothing$. For any map $f:V\to Y$, let $\Asf(f)$ be the minimum size of an affine partition of $V$ such that $f$ is constant on each cell. Partitions are unordered families of subsets, not lists or parameterizations.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Fiber additivity]\label{gsr:dt:102:lem:fibers}
For every map on a finite vector space,
\[
 \Asf(f)=\sum_{y\in f(V)}\Psf(f^{-1}(y)).
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Every constant cell is contained in one fiber, so restricting a partition to the cells in each fiber gives the lower bound. Conversely, combine optimal partitions of the disjoint fibers. The minima exist because singleton partitions always exist and the domain is finite.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Pullbacks and products]\label{gsr:dt:102:lem:invariance}
Let $\pi:W\to V$ be a surjective linear map.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $\Psf(\pi^{-1}(X))=\Psf(X)$ for every $X\subseteq V$.
\item $\Asf(f\circ\pi)=\Asf(f)$.
\item $\Psf(X\times Y)\le\Psf(X)\Psf(Y)$, and
$\Asf((f,g))\le\Asf(f)\Asf(g)$ for independent domains.
\end{enumerate}
Affine changes of domain coordinates and bijective relabelings of outputs preserve the corresponding invariants.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The inverse image of a nonempty affine cell under a surjective linear map is a nonempty affine cell. Pulling back a partition proves the upper bound in (i). Choose a linear section $\sigma:V\to W$ of $\pi$. Intersect a partition of $\pi^{-1}(X)$ with $\sigma(V)$ and discard empty intersections. Transport by $\sigma^{-1}$ to obtain a partition of $X$ with no more cells. This proves (i). The same argument, or fiber additivity, proves (ii). Cartesian products of cells prove (iii). The final assertions follow by transporting partitions in both directions.
\end{proof}

Thus inactive coordinates do not change the cost. In particular all exact examples below occur as pullbacks in arbitrarily large ambient vector spaces. This invariance concerns the minimum cost; it need not preserve the number or the detailed geometry of all optimizers.

\begin{lemma}[Polarization criterion]\label{gsr:dt:102:lem:polar}
Let $Q$ be a homogeneous quadratic form over a field of odd characteristic and
\[
 B(u,v)=Q(u+v)-Q(u)-Q(v).
\]
For $P=Q+\ell+c$, the restriction of $P$ to $a+U$ is constant if and only if
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:102:eq:polarcrit}
 Q|_U=0,\qquad B(a,u)+\ell(u)=0\quad(u\in U).
\end{equation}
Equivalently the first condition says that $U$ is totally isotropic for $B$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $u\in U$ and $t\in\Fq$,
\[
 P(a+tu)-P(a)=t^2Q(u)+t\bigl(B(a,u)+\ell(u)\bigr).
\]
If this is zero for all $t$, substituting $t=1,-1$ gives both coefficients zero, since 2 is invertible. Conversely those conditions make the expression zero at $t=1$. Finally $B(u,u)=2Q(u)$, and polarization identifies the vanishing of $Q|_U$ with total isotropy.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Exact phase localization]\label{gsr:dt:102:prop:phase}
Let $q=p^e$ be odd, and let $\psi:\Fq\to\mathbb C^\times$ be a nontrivial additive character. For a quadratic polynomial $P$ and an $\Fq$-affine cell $a+U$, the phase $\psi\circ P$ is constant on the cell if and only if $P$ is constant there. Hence the affine partition costs of a tuple of quadratic polynomials and of their componentwise phases are identical.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Only the forward implication needs proof. If the phase is constant, the fourfold ratio of its values at $a+u+v,a+u,a+v,a$ gives
\[
 \psi(B(u,v))=1\qquad(u,v\in U).
\]
Replacing $u$ by $tu$ gives $\psi(tB(u,v))=1$ for all $t\in\Fq$. If $B(u,v)\ne0$, multiplication by it is a bijection of $\Fq$, forcing $\psi$ to be trivial. Thus $B(U,U)=0$, and $Q|_U=0$ because the characteristic is odd. The remaining variation is the linear function $B(a,u)+\ell(u)$. Testing its multiples $tu$ in the same way forces it to vanish. Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:102:lem:polar}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Extension fields and error tolerances]\label{gsr:dt:102:rem:tolerance}
An additive character is generally not injective when $e>1$. The proof works because the directions are closed under \emph{all} field scalars; one cannot replace this hypothesis silently by prime-subfield affinity. Every value of $\psi$ is a $p$th root of unity. Distinct values are separated by at least $2\sin(\pi/p)$. Therefore a cellwise phase diameter strictly below this quantity forces exact constancy. A uniform distance strictly below $\sin(\pi/p)$ from one complex number is another sufficient condition. These observations do not supply a localization theorem at a tolerance independent of $p$.
\end{remark}

\section[{Sharp scalar localization and an exact defect identity\srctag{102}}]{Sharp scalar localization and an exact defect identity}\label{gsr:dt:102:sec:d4}\label{gsr:dt:102:sec:scalar}
\srcnote{102}{Section 4}

Fix integers $r\ge1$ and $s\ge0$, and consider
\[
 V=\Fq^r\times\Fq^r\times\Fq^s,
 \qquad Q(x,y,z)=x\cdot y.
\]
Its polar radical is $R=\{(0,0,z):z\in\Fq^s\}$.

\begin{lemma}[Largest constant flats]\label{gsr:dt:102:lem:scalarflats}
Every constant affine flat for $Q$ has dimension at most $r+s$. Every flat of dimension $r+s$ is a linear subspace, contains $R$, and lies in the zero fiber. Consequently a disjoint constant partition contains at most one such flat.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Write a flat as $a+U$. By Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:102:lem:polar}, $U$ is totally isotropic. Its image $\overline U$ in $V/R$ is totally isotropic for a nondegenerate bilinear form on a $2r$-dimensional space. Since $\overline U\subseteq\overline U^\perp$, nondegeneracy gives $\dim\overline U\le r$. Thus $\dim U\le r+s$.

If equality holds, $R\subseteq U$ and $\dim\overline U=r$, so $\overline U=\overline U^\perp$. Lifting gives $U=U^\perp$. Constancy also requires $a\in U^\perp$, hence $a\in U$ and $a+U=U$. Such a cell contains the origin, so two of them cannot be disjoint.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact scalar cost and equality dimensions]\label{gsr:dt:102:thm:scalar}
For the split quadratic form above,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:102:eq:scalarcost}
 \Asf(Q)=q^{r+1}-q+1.
\end{equation}
Every optimal partition consists of exactly one cell of dimension $r+s$ and $q^{r+1}-q$ cells of dimension $r+s-1$. Its zero fiber has optimal cost $q^r$, and each nonzero fiber has optimal cost $q^r-1$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Put $d=r+s-1$. If a partition has no $(d+1)$-cell, its cells have at most $q^d$ points, so it has at least $q^{2r+s-d}=q^{r+1}$ cells. If it has one such cell, every other cell has at most $q^d$ points, so the number of cells is at least
\[
 1+\frac{q^{2r+s}-q^{r+s}}{q^{r+s-1}}
 =q^{r+1}-q+1.
\]
To attain this, use the cell $x=0$ with $y,z$ unrestricted. For each $x\ne0$ and each $a\in\Fq$, use
\[
 \{x\}\times\{y:x\cdot y=a\}\times\Fq^s.
\]
The linear functional $y\mapsto x\cdot y$ is surjective, so each of these cells has dimension $r+s-1$. They are disjoint and cover the complement of $x=0$. Equality in the point count forces every smaller cell of any optimizer to have this same dimension.

For the fiber costs, direct counting gives
\[
 |Q^{-1}(0)|=q^{r+s}+(q^r-1)q^{r+s-1},\qquad
 |Q^{-1}(a)|=(q^r-1)q^{r+s-1}\quad(a\ne0).
\]
The nonzero fibers have no $(r+s)$-cell, so their costs are at least $q^r-1$. For the zero fiber, a partition with a largest cell requires at least $1+(q^r-1)=q^r$ cells; one without a largest cell requires at least $q^r+q-1$. The displayed construction realizes the asserted costs in every fiber.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact scalar defect]\label{gsr:dt:102:thm:scalardefect}
Let $\mathcal P$ be any constant affine partition for $Q$, put $d=r+s-1$, and let $t\in\{0,1\}$ count its cells of dimension $d+1$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:102:eq:scalardefect}
 |\mathcal P|-\bigl(q^{r+1}-q+1\bigr)
 =(q-1)(1-t)+\sum_{\substack{L\in\mathcal P\\\dim L<d}}
       \bigl(1-q^{\dim L-d}\bigr).
\end{equation}
If the deficit on the left is $E$, then there are at most $qE/(q-1)$ cells of dimension less than $d$, containing altogether at most $q^dE/(q-1)$ points. If $E<q-1$, a largest cell must occur.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Divide the identity $\sum_{L\in\mathcal P}|L|=q^{2r+s}$ by $q^d$. The largest cells contribute $tq$, dimension-$d$ cells contribute 1 each, and smaller cells contribute $q^{\dim L-d}$. Thus
\[
 q^{r+1}=|\mathcal P|+t(q-1)
       -\sum_{\dim L<d}(1-q^{\dim L-d}),
\]
which rearranges to~\eqref{gsr:dt:102:eq:scalardefect}. For $\dim L<d$, each summand is at least $(q-1)/q$. Also
\[
 q^{\dim L}\le\frac{q^d}{q-1}\bigl(1-q^{\dim L-d}\bigr),
\]
since $q^{\dim L-d}\le1/q$. Summation proves the two bounds. The final assertion follows from the first term in~\eqref{gsr:dt:102:eq:scalardefect}.
\end{proof}

When $d\ge1$, splitting one dimension-$d$ cell of an optimal partition into its $q$ parallel codimension-one subcells gives $E=q-1$ and attains both quantitative bounds. If $d=0$, there are no smaller nonempty cells, and the summation is empty.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The cross-square optimum\srctag{102}}]{The cross-square optimum}\label{gsr:dt:102:sec:d5}\label{gsr:dt:102:sec:cross}
\srcnote{102}{Section 5}

Let
\[
 L_0=\{(t,0):t\in\Fq\},\qquad L_1=\{(0,t):t\in\Fq\},
 \qquad C=L_0\cup L_1.
\]
Write $0$ for the zero vector in any of these spaces. For $i,j\in\{0,1\}$ set
\[
 P_{ij}=L_i\times L_j\subseteq C^2.
\]
These four coordinate planes meet along coordinate axes, and all contain the origin of $\Fq^4$.

\begin{lemma}[Orthant containment]\label{gsr:dt:102:lem:orthant}
For every finite field with $q>2$, every affine subspace contained in $C^m$ is contained in a coordinate $m$-plane
\[
 L_{i_1}\times\cdots\times L_{i_m},\qquad i_j\in\{0,1\}.
\]
In particular a cell in $C^2$ has dimension at most two. A two-dimensional cell is one of the four $P_{ij}$, and a partition of $C^2$ has at most one such cell.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
On a cell $A$ of dimension $d$, the coordinate functions $x_j,y_j$ are affine-linear and satisfy $x_jy_j=0$ everywhere. If neither is identically zero, each of its zero sets is either empty or a proper affine hyperplane with $q^{d-1}$ points. For $d\ge1$, the union of two such sets has at most $2q^{d-1}<q^d$ points, a contradiction. If $d=0$, one coordinate is zero at the unique point. Thus for each block one coordinate is identically zero. Choosing the corresponding axis proves containment. A dimension-two affine subspace in a coordinate plane is the entire plane; any two of these contain the origin.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[A single cross]\label{gsr:dt:102:lem:singlecross}
For $q>2$, $\Psf(C)=q$, and there are exactly two optimal partitions: choose one full axis and use the $q-1$ nonzero points of the other axis as singleton cells.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Orthant containment says that a line in $C$ must be one of its two axes. The axes intersect, so at most one can occur in a partition. If one occurs, all other points are singletons, giving $q$ cells. If none occurs, the cost is $2q-1>q$. This also proves the equality classification.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The lower bound when a plane is selected}
The next bound explains why taking a largest cell is suboptimal for the joint problem.

\begin{lemma}[Plane penalty]\label{gsr:dt:102:lem:planepenalty}
Any affine partition of $C^2$ containing a plane has at least $q^2$ cells. The bound is attained.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
By axis symmetries take the selected plane to be $W=P_{00}$. Let
\[
 T=((L_1\sm\{0\})\times\{0\})
     \cup(\{0\}\times(L_1\sm\{0\})).
\]
Thus $|T|=2(q-1)$ and $T\subset C^2\sm W$.

Every line $D\subset C^2$ disjoint from $W$ meets $T$. Indeed, by orthant containment it is in some $P_{ij}$. It cannot be in $P_{00}$. In $P_{01}$, it must avoid the first coordinate axis, so it is parallel to that axis at a nonzero second coordinate; it meets $\{0\}\times(L_1\sm\{0\})$. The argument for $P_{10}$ is symmetric. In $P_{11}$, the line avoids the origin. Any affine line in a coordinate plane meets at least one coordinate axis, and that intersection is nonzero, so it belongs to $T$.

Disjoint lines meet $T$ in disjoint nonempty sets. Hence the number $\ell$ of line cells outside $W$ is at most $2(q-1)$. All remaining cells are points. Since $|C^2|=(2q-1)^2$, the total number of cells is
\begin{align*}
 1+\bigl((2q-1)^2-q^2\bigr)-(q-1)\ell
 &\ge1+\bigl((2q-1)^2-q^2\bigr)-2(q-1)^2\\
 &=q^2.
\end{align*}
Taking the product of two optimal cross partitions realizes this bound. It consists of one plane, $2(q-1)$ lines, and $(q-1)^2$ points.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The lower bound without planes}
\begin{lemma}[No-plane bound]\label{gsr:dt:102:lem:noplanebound}
An affine partition of $C^2$ without planes has at least $4q-3$ cells. Equality holds precisely when it has one singleton and $4(q-1)$ lines.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Write $s$ for its number of singleton cells and $\ell$ for its number of lines. Then
\[
 s+q\ell=(2q-1)^2.
\]
Reducing modulo $q$ gives $s\equiv1\pmod q$, hence $s\ge1$. Thus
\[
 s+\ell=\frac{(2q-1)^2+(q-1)s}{q}\ge4q-3.
\]
Equality is equivalent to $s=1$, which forces $\ell=4(q-1)$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The cyclic construction}
For an element $a\in L_i\sm\{0\}$, the notation $\{a\}\times L_j$ means a line with its first block fixed; similarly $L_i\times\{b\}$ fixes its second block.

\begin{proposition}[Two cyclic partitions]\label{gsr:dt:102:prop:cycles}
The following family partitions $C^2$:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:102:eq:cycle}
 \{\{(0,0)\}\}
 \ \cup\!\bigcup_{i=j}\{\{a\}\times L_j:a\in L_i\sm\{0\}\}
 \ \cup\!\bigcup_{i\ne j}\{L_i\times\{b\}:b\in L_j\sm\{0\}\}.
\end{equation}
It has one singleton and $4(q-1)$ lines. Reversing fixed-first and fixed-second in every $P_{ij}$ gives a second such partition.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
A point with both blocks nonzero belongs to a unique $P_{ij}$ and is covered by the unique displayed line with its prescribed fixed coordinate. In a point with first block nonzero and second block zero, the first block determines $i$; exactly the plane $P_{ii}$ supplies its line. In a point with first block zero and second block nonzero, the second block determines $j$; exactly the plane with $i\ne j$ supplies its line. The origin belongs only to its singleton cell. These observations prove both coverage and disjointness. The reversed construction has the same properties.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact cross-square cost]\label{gsr:dt:102:thm:crosssquare}
For $q>2$, $\Psf(C^2)=4q-3$. A partition containing a plane is optimal only when $q=3$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The two lower bounds give $\Psf(C^2)\ge\min(q^2,4q-3)$. For $q\ge3$,
\[
 q^2-(4q-3)=(q-1)(q-3)\ge0.
\]
The cyclic construction attains $4q-3$. The final assertion follows from strict inequality when $q>3$ and the product construction when $q=3$.
\end{proof}

\section[{Rigidity: exactly two zero-fiber optimizers\srctag{102}}]{Rigidity: exactly two zero-fiber optimizers}\label{gsr:dt:102:sec:d6}\label{gsr:dt:102:sec:rigidity}
\srcnote{102}{Section 6}

Define the coordinate skeleton
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:102:eq:skeleton}
 S=(C\times\{0\})\cup(\{0\}\times C),\qquad |S|=4q-3.
\end{equation}
For each plane $P_{ij}$ its complement of the two coordinate axes will be called its \emph{torus}; it has $(q-1)^2$ points. This term refers only to that set of points.

\begin{lemma}[Skeleton intersections]\label{gsr:dt:102:lem:skeleton}
Every line $D\subset C^2$ meets $S$. More precisely, its intersection size is one of $1,2,q$:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item a coordinate-axis line has $q$ skeleton points;
\item a coordinate-parallel line not through the origin has one;
\item a line with both coordinates varying has one if it passes through the origin, and two otherwise.
\end{enumerate}
The latter lines are contained in a unique $P_{ij}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Work in a containing coordinate plane and parameterize a line as $(a+tu,b+tv)$. If one of $u,v$ is zero, the line is an axis or is parallel to an axis at a nonzero coordinate. If both are nonzero, each coordinate vanishes at one parameter; the two parameters agree exactly when the line passes through the origin. A line with a point in the torus determines its two axes uniquely.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Zero-fiber rigidity]\label{gsr:dt:102:thm:rigidity}
For every field with $q>3$, the two cyclic partitions in Proposition~\ref{gsr:dt:102:prop:cycles} are the only optimal affine partitions of $C^2$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $\mathcal P$ be optimal. Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:102:lem:planepenalty} excludes planes. By Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:102:lem:noplanebound}, $\mathcal P$ consists of $4(q-1)$ lines and one singleton $\{z\}$. Since every line meets $S$ and the intersections are disjoint,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:102:eq:skeletonexcess}
 \sum_{D\text{ a line cell}}(|D\cap S|-1)
 =1-\one_{z\in S}.
\end{equation}
We first show $z=0$.

Suppose $z\in S$ but $z\ne0$. Then every line has exactly one skeleton point. The cell containing the origin is a line $D$ with both coordinates varying, contained in a unique plane $P$. It cannot be a coordinate axis because that would give $q$ skeleton points. Every other line with one skeleton point, not through the origin, is coordinate-parallel.

Every coordinate-parallel line of $P$ at a nonzero fixed coordinate intersects $D$: along $D$, either coordinate ranges bijectively over the field. Hence none of those lines can occur in the partition. A line covering a torus point of $P$ must lie in $P$, so after $D$ there is no line available for the remaining
\[
 (q-1)^2-(q-1)=(q-1)(q-2)>0
\]
torus points. The only singleton lies in $S$, not in the torus. This is impossible.

Next suppose $z\notin S$. Equation~\eqref{gsr:dt:102:eq:skeletonexcess} says that exactly one line $E$ has two skeleton points and every other line has one; an axis line with excess $q-1>1$ cannot occur. Again the origin lies on a line $D$ with both coordinates varying in a unique plane $P$. Ordinary coordinate-parallel lines in $P$ intersect $D$ and are forbidden. The exceptional line $E$ can cover at most $q-2$ torus points of $P$: if it lies in $P$, its two skeleton points leave exactly $q-2$ torus points, and otherwise it covers none. At least
\[
 (q-1)^2-(q-1)-(q-2)=(q-2)^2>1
\]
torus points remain uncovered by lines. One singleton cannot cover them. This is again impossible. We conclude $z=0$.

Now all line cells avoid the origin and have exactly one skeleton point. Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:102:lem:skeleton} makes every one coordinate-parallel at a nonzero fixed coordinate. Within one $P_{ij}$, a line with first block fixed and a line with second block fixed intersect in the torus, so both orientations cannot occur. To cover all torus points of $P_{ij}$ requires all $q-1$ lines of exactly one orientation.

There are four remaining binary choices, one per plane. Along the shared nonzero first axis of $P_{i0}$ and $P_{i1}$, exactly one plane must use first-block-fixed lines. Along the shared nonzero second axis of $P_{0j}$ and $P_{1j}$, exactly one must use second-block-fixed lines. Thus each row and each column of the $2\times2$ array of orientations contains one choice of each type. There are precisely two such arrays: first block fixed on the diagonal and on the off-diagonal, respectively. These are the two cyclic partitions.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Checked at the write} (exact-cover search written for this write): exactly two optimal partitions of $C^2$ at $q=5$, and also at $q=4$, which this theorem (odd $q$) does not claim; $30$ at $q=3$, as the exception allows. Source~106 extends $\Psf(C^2)=4q-3$ to every $q>2$ but not this classification.
\end{writenote}

\begin{remark}[The field of order three]
At $q=3$, the numerical minimum is still $9$, but a product partition with one plane also attains it. The rigidity argument's strict inequalities are not available in the same form. This article does not classify all equality cases for $q=3$.
\end{remark}
