\section[{The full two-phase problem and all equality cases\srctag{102}}]{The full two-phase problem and all equality cases}\label{gsr:dt:102:sec:d7}\label{gsr:dt:102:sec:full}
\srcnote{102}{Section 7}

\begin{lemma}[Nonzero product fibers are affine-line-free]\label{gsr:dt:102:lem:hyperbola}
For $a\in\Fq^\times$ and $q>2$, the set
\[
 H_a=\{(x,y):xy=a\}
\]
contains no affine line. Consequently the image in this block of an affine cell contained in a fiber with nonzero product is a single point.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $(x+tu,y+tv)$ lay in $H_a$ for every $t$, the degree-two polynomial
\[
 (x+tu)(y+tv)-a=(xy-a)+t(xv+yu)+t^2uv
\]
would vanish on more than two field elements. Hence $uv=0$ and $xv+yu=0$. Since $xy=a\ne0$, both $x,y$ are nonzero, forcing $u=v=0$. This is not a line. The image of an affine subspace under a linear projection is affine; if it had positive dimension, it would contain a line.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Two-phase cost and enumeration]\label{gsr:dt:102:thm:fulltwo}
For $q>2$,
\begin{align}
 \Asf(\Psi_2)&=(q-1)^4+2q(q-1)^2+4q-3\label{gsr:dt:102:eq:fullfiberformula}\\
 &=q^4-2q^3+2q^2+2q-2.\nonumber
\end{align}
For $q>3$, every optimal partition has $2q^2-2$ lines and $(q-1)^3(q+1)+1$ singleton cells. There are exactly $2^{2(q-1)^2+1}$ optimal partitions in the fixed coordinate system.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Separate the domain according to which block products vanish. If both are nonzero, Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:102:lem:hyperbola} forces every constant cell to be a point. There are $(q-1)^4$ such points.

If only the first product vanishes, the second block is fixed on every affine constant cell. For each of the $(q-1)^2$ second-block points having nonzero product, the remaining slice is a copy of $C$. Each copy requires exactly $q$ cells. The symmetric case contributes the same number. If both products vanish, the domain is $C^2$, with cost $4q-3$. This proves~\eqref{gsr:dt:102:eq:fullfiberformula}, since the lower bounds for the separate pieces are attained independently.

For $q>3$, each of the $2(q-1)^2$ mixed slices has exactly two optimal partitions by Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:102:lem:singlecross}. The joint zero fiber has exactly two by Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:102:thm:rigidity}; all points in the nonzero--nonzero part are forced singletons. Choices in the disjoint slices are independent, giving $2^{2(q-1)^2+1}$.

The mixed slices contribute $2(q-1)^2$ lines and $2(q-1)^3$ singleton cells. The joint zero fiber contributes $4(q-1)$ lines and one singleton. Adding the forced nonzero--nonzero points gives the claimed cell counts.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Strict nonmultiplicativity and the largest-cell obstruction]\label{gsr:dt:102:cor:nonmulti}
For $q>3$,
\[
 \Asf(\Psi_2)<\Asf(\Psi_1)^2,
 \qquad \Asf(\Psi_1)^2-\Asf(\Psi_2)=(q-1)(q-3).
\]
Every constant affine partition for $\Psi_2$ containing a plane has at least $\Asf(\Psi_1)^2$ cells. The optimum among such plane-containing partitions is exactly $\Asf(\Psi_1)^2$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The scalar theorem at $r=1,s=0$ gives $\Asf(\Psi_1)=q^2-q+1$. Expanding its square and subtracting~\eqref{gsr:dt:102:eq:fullfiberformula} yields the difference. A plane cell cannot occur when either product is nonzero, by Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:102:lem:hyperbola} and the fact that $C$ contains no plane. It therefore occurs in $C^2$, where Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:102:lem:planepenalty} replaces the optimum $4q-3$ by the lower bound $q^2$. The other pieces retain their preceding lower bounds, giving exactly $\Asf(\Psi_1)^2$. A product of scalar optimal partitions attains it.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Where the saving occurs]
The entire difference $(q-1)(q-3)$ comes from the singular fiber $C^2$. On the other domain pieces, separate localization is already optimal. Also, for $\Psi_2$, no partition can have all cells of positive dimension: every point with both products nonzero is a forced singleton. Thus minimum cell dimension cannot detect the improvement in cell number. The two invariants answer different questions.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Near-optimal partitions: exact arithmetic and incidence defects\srctag{102}}]{Near-optimal partitions: exact arithmetic and incidence defects}\label{gsr:dt:102:sec:d8}\label{gsr:dt:102:sec:stability}
\srcnote{102}{Section 8}

\begin{proposition}[No-plane defect identities]\label{gsr:dt:102:prop:crossdefect}
Let a partition of $C^2$ have no planes, $s$ singleton cells, and $\ell$ line cells. There is an integer $k\ge0$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:102:eq:crossdefect}
 s=1+qk,\qquad \ell=4(q-1)-k,\qquad
 |\mathcal P|=4q-3+(q-1)k.
\end{equation}
Let $s_S$ count the singleton cells whose point is in the skeleton $S$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:102:eq:incidencedefect}
 \sum_{D\text{ a line cell}}(|D\cap S|-1)=1+k-s_S.
\end{equation}
In particular, at most $k+1$ line cells meet $S$ in two or more points.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The identity $s+q\ell=(2q-1)^2$ gives $s\equiv1\pmod q$, so write $s=1+qk$. Since $s\ge1$, $k\ge0$. Substitution gives all of~\eqref{gsr:dt:102:eq:crossdefect}. Disjointness and coverage of $S$ give
\[
 \sum_D|D\cap S|=|S|-s_S=4q-3-s_S.
\]
Subtracting the number $\ell=4q-4-k$ of lines proves~\eqref{gsr:dt:102:eq:incidencedefect}. Every line with at least two skeleton points contributes at least one to the nonnegative sum.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The plane threshold and the first gap]\label{gsr:dt:102:cor:firstgap}
A partition of $C^2$ with fewer than $q^2$ cells cannot contain a plane. For $q>3$, a partition whose deficit above $4q-3$ is less than $(q-1)(q-3)$ is therefore described by Proposition~\ref{gsr:dt:102:prop:crossdefect}.

Every affine partition of $C^2$ has size congruent to $1$ modulo $q-1$. Thus any nonoptimal partition has at least $4q-3+(q-1)$ cells; this next size is attained by splitting one line in a cyclic partition into $q$ points.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The threshold is Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:102:lem:planepenalty}. For congruence, every affine cell has $q^d\equiv1\pmod{q-1}$ points, while $|C^2|=(2q-1)^2\equiv1\pmod{q-1}$. The splitting construction increases the number of cells by $q-1$.
\end{proof}

For the full map, the decomposition in the proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:102:thm:fulltwo} is exact for every partition, not only optimizers. A mixed cross-slice has either its optimal $q$ cells or all $2q-1$ points. Hence if a partition for $\Psi_2$ has total deficit $E$, at most $E/(q-1)$ mixed slices can be nonoptimal. Its zero-fiber partition has the remaining deficit and satisfies the preceding dichotomy.

These results are deliberately stated as defect and incidence identities. They do not prove that every near-optimal partition is close to one cyclic partition in a global symmetric-difference or pointwise metric. Establishing such edit-distance stability requires an additional argument, particularly when exceptional lines cover points in several different torus regions.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Arbitrary families: a singular-fiber reduction and asymptotic costs\srctag{102}}]{Arbitrary families: a singular-fiber reduction and asymptotic costs}\label{gsr:dt:102:sec:d9}\label{gsr:dt:102:sec:tensor}
\srcnote{102}{Section 9}

Put $P_m=\Psf(C^m)$ for $m\ge1$, $P_0=1$, and $A_m=\Asf(\Psi_m)$. Let $b=(q-1)^2$.

\begin{theorem}[Exact singular-fiber reduction]\label{gsr:dt:102:thm:binomial}
For every $m\ge0$ and $q>2$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:102:eq:binomial}
 A_m=\sum_{k=0}^m\binom{m}{k}b^{m-k}P_k.
\end{equation}
Here $\Psi_0$ is the constant map on a one-point space, so $A_0=1$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
In any constant affine cell, fix the set $I$ of blocks with zero product. This set is well-defined since the entire output tuple is constant. For each block outside $I$, Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:102:lem:hyperbola} says that the block itself is a fixed point, not just a fixed product value. After those points are fixed, the remaining piece is a copy of $C^{|I|}$; every cell of any partition belongs to one such piece.

For $|I|=k$ there are $\binom{m}{k}$ choices of $I$, and each of the other $m-k$ blocks has $b$ possible points with both coordinates nonzero. Thus there are $\binom{m}{k}b^{m-k}$ disjoint pieces isomorphic to $C^k$, with no admissible cell joining two pieces. Each has exact partition cost $P_k$, and their optimizers may be chosen independently. Summing gives~\eqref{gsr:dt:102:eq:binomial}.
\end{proof}

The reduction is sharper than applying a common pairing of all input blocks before examining their fibers. It allows the zero blocks to be grouped differently in different fibers, while all nonzero blocks are simply fixed.

\begin{proposition}[Finite pairing bounds]\label{gsr:dt:102:prop:pairing}
For $m\ge0$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:102:eq:pairing}
 P_m\le(4q-3)^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}q^{m\bmod2},\qquad
 A_m\le A_2^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}A_1^{m\bmod2}.
\end{equation}
More sharply, writing $t=\sqrt{4q-3}$, one has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:102:eq:adaptivepairing}
 A_m\le\frac{1+q/t}{2}(b+t)^m+
             \frac{1-q/t}{2}(b-t)^m.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Take products of the exact one- and two-block partitions to obtain~\eqref{gsr:dt:102:eq:pairing}. Define $g_{2j}=t^{2j}$ and $g_{2j+1}=qt^{2j}$. The first bound says $P_k\le g_k$. Elementary algebra gives
\[
 g_k=\frac{1+q/t}{2}t^k+\frac{1-q/t}{2}(-t)^k.
\]
Insert this equality into the binomial upper bound from Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:102:thm:binomial}; the binomial theorem yields~\eqref{gsr:dt:102:eq:adaptivepairing}. Although the second coefficient is negative for $q>3$, the derivation starts with the positive termwise inequalities $P_k\le g_k$, so no order reversal is involved.
\end{proof}

For example, the adaptive upper bound at three blocks is
\[
 A_3\le b^3+3b^2q+3b(4q-3)+q(4q-3).
\]
It improves the simpler $A_2A_1$ bound by exactly
\[
 2b\bigl(q^2-(4q-3)\bigr)=2(q-1)^3(q-3)>0\qquad(q>3).
\]
This does not assert that either bound is optimal for three blocks.

\begin{theorem}[Regularized zero-fiber and full-map costs]\label{gsr:dt:102:thm:rates}
For each $q>2$, the limit
\[
 \rho(q)=\lim_{m\to\infty}P_m^{1/m}=\inf_{m\ge1}P_m^{1/m}
\]
exists and satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:102:eq:rhorange}
 2-\frac1q\le\rho(q)\le\sqrt{4q-3}.
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:102:eq:Arate}
 \lim_{m\to\infty}A_m^{1/m}=(q-1)^2+\rho(q).
\end{equation}
For $q>3$, this is strictly smaller than $A_1=q^2-q+1$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Product partitions give $P_{m+n}\le P_mP_n$. To see the limit directly, fix $k\ge1$ and write $m=ak+r$ with $0\le r<k$. Then
\[
 P_m\le P_k^aP_r.
\]
As $m\to\infty$ with $k$ fixed, the $m$th root of $P_r$ tends to one uniformly in the finitely many remainders. Hence $\limsup P_m^{1/m}\le P_k^{1/k}$. Taking the infimum over $k$ and comparing with the evident lower bound for $\liminf$ proves the existence and infimum characterization.

By Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:102:lem:orthant}, a cell in $C^m$ has at most $q^m$ points. Since $|C^m|=(2q-1)^m$, we have
\[
 P_m\ge\left(2-\frac1q\right)^m.
\]
The upper bound on $\rho$ follows from $P_2=4q-3$.

For~\eqref{gsr:dt:102:eq:Arate}, the infimum characterization gives $P_k\ge\rho^k$ for all $k\ge0$. Thus the binomial identity gives $A_m\ge(b+\rho)^m$. Conversely fix $\varepsilon>0$. The convergence $P_k^{1/k}\to\rho$ implies that there is a finite constant $M_\varepsilon\ge1$ such that
\[
 P_k\le M_\varepsilon(\rho+\varepsilon)^k\qquad(k\ge0).
\]
Then $A_m\le M_\varepsilon(b+\rho+\varepsilon)^m$. Take $m$th roots, let $m\to\infty$, and then let $\varepsilon\downarrow0$.

Finally $\sqrt{4q-3}<q$ when $q>3$, so $b+\rho\le b+\sqrt{4q-3}<b+q=A_1$.
\end{proof}

For fixed $m$ and $q\to\infty$, the zero-fiber construction has size
\[
 P_m=O_m(q^{\lceil m/2\rceil})\quad\text{as an upper bound},
\]
compared with the separate cost $q^m$. No matching exponent lower bound for $m\ge3$ is proved here. The point-count lower bound in Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:102:thm:rates} is much weaker in that regime. This gap is a principal research question, not a suppressed loss in an asserted exact formula.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{General quadratic bottleneck dimensions\srctag{102}}]{General quadratic bottleneck dimensions}\label{gsr:dt:102:sec:d10}\label{gsr:dt:102:sec:general}
\srcnote{102}{Section 10}

Cell count and minimum cell dimension are different invariants. This section supplies a complete answer for the latter for a scalar quadratic polynomial, and an additional exact count in the noncentral case.

\begin{definition}
For a polynomial $P:V\to\Fq$, define
\[
 \beta(P)=\max_{\mathcal P}\ \min_{L\in\mathcal P}\dim L,
\]
where $\mathcal P$ ranges over all constant affine partitions for $P$.
\end{definition}

Let $Q$ be the homogeneous degree-two part, $B$ its polar form, and $R=\rad(B)$ with dimension $s$. In odd characteristic $Q|_R=0$, since $2Q(v)=B(v,v)$. Let $w$ denote the Witt index of the nondegenerate quotient $V/R$, that is, the largest dimension of a totally isotropic subspace of that quotient.

\subsection{A decomposition argument}
For completeness, a nondegenerate quadratic space with a nonzero isotropic vector $u$ splits off a hyperbolic plane. Choose $v$ with $B(u,v)=1$ and replace $v$ by $v-Q(v)u$. The new vector remains paired to $u$ by 1 and is isotropic because
\[
 Q(v-Q(v)u)=Q(v)-Q(v)B(v,u)=0.
\]
On their span, the form is $xy$, and its polar form is nondegenerate. Split off its orthogonal complement and repeat. The remaining form is anisotropic. Together with the radical this yields coordinates
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:102:eq:wittcoords}
 Q(x,y,z,r)=x\cdot y+Q_{\mathrm{an}}(z),\qquad
 x,y\in\Fq^w,\quad r\in R.
\end{equation}
To obtain exactly the defined number $w$, begin with a maximal totally isotropic subspace $W$ and choose $u\in W\sm\{0\}$. With $H=\Span(u,v)$ as above, the map
\[
 W\longrightarrow W\cap H^\perp,\qquad z\longmapsto z-B(z,v)u
\]
has kernel $\Span(u)$ and image of dimension $w-1$. Any isotropic subspace of $H^\perp$ of dimension greater than $w-1$ could be enlarged by $u$, contradicting maximality of $w$ in the original space. Induction therefore splits off precisely $w$ hyperbolic planes, after which the remaining nondegenerate form is anisotropic. This also proves the decomposition used below without assuming a classification of anisotropic forms.

\begin{theorem}[Bottleneck dimension for any scalar quadratic]\label{gsr:dt:102:thm:bottleneck}
Let $P=Q+\ell+c$ on an $n$-dimensional vector space over an odd finite field, with radical dimension $s$ and quotient Witt index $w$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item If $\ell|_R=0$, then
\[
 \beta(P)=
 \begin{cases}
 s,&w=0,\\
 s+w-1,&w\ge1.
 \end{cases}
\]
\item If $\ell|_R\ne0$, then
\[
 \beta(P)=s+w-1,\qquad \Asf(P)=q^{n-s-w+1}.
\]
In (ii) a constant partition attaining this cost has every cell of dimension $s+w-1$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
First suppose $\ell|_R=0$. The image of the map $a\mapsto B(a,\cdot)$ consists exactly of the linear functionals vanishing on $R$, by nondegeneracy on $V/R$. Thus translating the variable removes $\ell$, up to a constant. Both invariants are translation-invariant, so it is enough to treat $Q$.

For $w=0$, Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:102:lem:polar} implies that every constant direction is contained in $R$. Cosets of $R$ form a constant partition, so $\beta(Q)=s$.

Now let $w\ge1$. In coordinates~\eqref{gsr:dt:102:eq:wittcoords}, fix $x$ and $z$. If $x=0$, allow all $y,r$; this is a constant cell of dimension $w+s$. If $x\ne0$, impose one value of $x\cdot y$ and allow all $r$, giving a cell of dimension $w+s-1$. These cells partition the whole space, proving the lower bound for $\beta$.

For the upper bound, a totally isotropic direction has dimension at most $s+w$. We show that every constant affine flat of this dimension in the zero fiber contains the origin. Write it as $a+U$. Maximal dimension implies $R\subseteq U$ and that its image $\overline U$ is a maximal-dimensional isotropic subspace in the nondegenerate quotient. Constancy gives $a\in U^\perp$. The quadratic form on $U^\perp/U$ is anisotropic: a nonzero isotropic vector there would enlarge $U$ to an isotropic subspace of dimension $s+w+1$. Since $Q(a)=0$, it follows that $a\in U$. Thus the flat is $U$ and contains zero.

The zero fiber is not contained in one dimension-$(s+w)$ isotropic subspace. For example, the two coordinate isotropic subspaces consisting of all $x,r$ and all $y,r$ in~\eqref{gsr:dt:102:eq:wittcoords} span a space of dimension $s+2w>s+w$. A partition all of whose cells had dimension $s+w$ could contain at most one cell in the zero fiber, and that one could not cover it. Hence some cell has dimension at most $s+w-1$.

For (ii), choose a decomposition $V=E\oplus R$, with $Q$ nondegenerate on $E$. Translate to eliminate the $E$-component of $\ell$, and choose a coordinate $t$ on $R$ with $\ell(r)=t$. Up to a constant, the polynomial is
\[
 P(e,t,r')=Q_E(e)+t,\qquad r'\in\Fq^{s-1}.
\]
For a constant affine flat with direction $U$, its image in $E$ is isotropic and has dimension at most $w$. Its kernel under that projection lies in $R\cap\ker\ell$, of dimension $s-1$. Hence $\dim U\le s+w-1$, proving both the bottleneck upper bound and the point-count lower bound $\Asf(P)\ge q^{n-s-w+1}$.

For an attaining partition, fix a maximal isotropic subspace $W\subset E$, partition $E$ into its cosets $a+W$, and for each coset and output value $h$ use
\[
 \{(a+u,\ h-Q_E(a+u),\ r'):u\in W,\ r'\in\Fq^{s-1}\}.
\]
Because $Q_E(a+u)=Q_E(a)+B(a,u)$ on $W$, this is an affine graph of dimension $w+s-1$. These graphs partition the domain and are constant for $P$. Their number is $q^{\dim E-w}q=q^{n-s-w+1}$, proving the assertions.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Degenerate and linear endpoints]
If $Q=0$ and $\ell=0$, then $s=n,w=0$ and the whole space is one cell, with $\beta(P)=n$. If $Q=0$ but $\ell\ne0$, case (ii) gives $q$ affine hyperplanes and $\beta(P)=n-1$, as expected. A zero-dimensional ambient space belongs only to case (i). Thus the theorem includes these endpoints without a separate nondegeneracy convention.
\end{remark}

\section[{Repository review, provenance, and boundaries\srctag{106}}]{Repository review, provenance, and boundaries}\label{gsr:dt:106:sec:d2}\label{gsr:dt:106:sec:review}
\srcnote{106}{Section 2}

\subsection{What was inspected}
The research was conducted on October 7, 2026. The source manifest records the following repository snapshots:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ll}
\toprule
Repository & Inspected head prefix\\
\midrule
\texttt{openai/math} & \texttt{adc7f1241b42}\\
\texttt{VladimirReshetnikov/ProveIt} & \texttt{6896b62972d4}\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Full hashes and selected source identifiers are recorded in \nolinkurl{source_manifest.json}. The preceding localization article~\cite{srconehundredtwo} was read from a separately supplied Library source snapshot; it is not silently attributed to a path that was not verified in the repository.

The OpenAI repository introduction describes a collection of 722 manuscripts in 372 families and explicitly distinguishes stages of verification~\cite{oaimath}. The targeted review concentrated on additive-combinatorial claims rather than attempting to certify that entire collection. The catalog describes family 159 as proving all-length quasipolynomial progression bounds and the divergent-reciprocal-sum consequence; family 160 as giving superexponential van der Waerden lower bounds; and family 161 as giving a counterexample to Sidorenko's conjecture~\cite{oaimath}. These are descriptions of \emph{repository claims}, not independent confirmations by the present article.

The introduction source of family 159 was read directly~\cite{oaiprogressions}. Its stated main estimate is
\[
 r_k(N)\le C_k N\exp\bigl(-c_k(\log N)^{\eps_k}\bigr)
 \qquad(k\ge3\text{ fixed}).
\]
Its discussion separates the detection of structured correlation from preserving and localizing that structure during density increments. That distinction suggests studying joint localization costs as mathematical invariants in their own right. The proofs below do not use the displayed progression estimate.

\subsection{A concrete ProveIt interface}
The inspected ProveIt module \texttt{Proofs05QuadraticFamily.lean} defines a successive-localization budget~\cite{repo106module}. Renaming its phase-count variable to $j$ to avoid confusion with our field order, the recurrence is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:budget}
 B(0,U)=U,\qquad B(j+1,U)=(2B(j,U))^{1024}.
\end{equation}
The module contains a theorem bounding $4B(j,U)$ by $(4U)^{1024^j}$, and a simultaneous quadratic-phase partition theorem that retains a minimum progression length $U$ and a phase tolerance $1/(4U)$. The source was inspected; its compiler and dependency chain were not rerun for this manuscript.

Our invariant has a different objective: the number of \emph{exact, field-linear affine cells}. In particular, minimizing this number can force singleton cells. Consequently, replacing the budget in~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:budget} by a power derived from~\eqref{gsr:fm:106:eq:main} would be unjustified. Any transfer to the integer development would require a separate theorem preserving cell lengths, ambient containment, and the necessary error budget.

\subsection{Prior work and contribution ledger}
Affine vector space partitions are an established finite-geometric subject. Bamberg, Filmus, Ihringer, and Kurz study minimum sizes, constructions, and small-parameter classifications of partitions of an entire affine space into proper affine subspaces~\cite{bfik}. Here the domain is a singular union of coordinate subspaces, not the entire affine space, and a torus stratum supplies an additional obstruction. This comparison indicates the relevant neighboring literature, but is not an exhaustive priority survey.

The two-block optimum, the binomial reduction for independent quadratic products, and the existence mechanism for the regularized limit were already present in~\cite{srconehundredtwo}. We reproduce the portions needed for self-contained arguments. The new conclusions relative to that manuscript are the sharp higher-product asymptotics, their extension to all $s$-arm crosses, the dimension and torus defect identity, the resulting asymptotic rigidity, and the sharp large-field scale of the regularized cost. The exact three-block value and the exact fixed-field regularized rate are left explicitly unresolved.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Geometry of crosses and their full-support strata\srctag{106}}]{Geometry of crosses and their full-support strata}\label{gsr:dt:106:sec:d3}\label{gsr:dt:106:sec:geometry}
\srcnote{106}{Section 3}

\begin{definition}[Affine partitions]
For a nonempty subset $Y$ of a finite-dimensional vector space over $\Fq$, an \emph{affine partition} is a finite family of nonempty affine subspaces whose union is $Y$ and which are pairwise disjoint as sets. Its cost is the number of cells. The minimum cost is denoted by $\Psf(Y)$. The singleton partition shows that the minimum exists.
\end{definition}
Products of partitions immediately give
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:submultiplicative}
 P_{s,m+n}(q)\le P_{s,m}(q)P_{s,n}(q).
\end{equation}
No reverse inequality is assumed.

Throughout, set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:notation}
 t=q-1,\qquad X=C_{s,q}^m,\qquad
 N=|X|=(1+st)^m,
\end{equation}
and let
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:torus}
 \Tcal=\{(v_1,\ldots,v_m)\in X:v_j\ne0\text{ for every }j\},
 \qquad M=|\Tcal|=(st)^m.
\end{equation}
A choice of one arm in each block defines a \emph{coordinate orthant}
\[
 W_{i_1,\ldots,i_m}=
 \Fq e_{i_1}\times\cdots\times\Fq e_{i_m}\cong\Fq^m.
\]
The term orthant refers to this algebraic subspace, not to an order or a positivity condition. The intersection $\Tcal\cap W$ identifies with $(\Fq^\times)^m$.

\begin{lemma}[Orthant containment]\label{gsr:dt:106:lem:orthant}
Suppose $q>2$. Every affine subspace $A\subseteq C_{s,q}^m$ lies in a coordinate orthant. In particular $\dim A\le m$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $d=\dim A$. Fix one block, and restrict its $s$ coordinate functions to $A$. The product of any two distinct coordinates vanishes at every point of $A$. If $d>0$ and neither of two affine coordinate functions is identically zero, each zero set has at most $q^{d-1}$ points. Their union cannot cover $A$, because $2q^{d-1}<q^d$. Hence at most one coordinate in this block is not identically zero. Choose that arm, or an arbitrary arm if the whole block vanishes. Make this choice independently in every block. For $d=0$, choose an arm containing each component of the unique point. The resulting orthant contains $A$.
\end{proof}

This proof does not require odd characteristic. It does require $q>2$: in $\mathbb F_2^2$ the two-point affine line $\{(1,0),(0,1)\}$ lies in the cross but in neither coordinate arm. The exclusion of $q=2$ is therefore structural.

\begin{lemma}[Partition congruence]\label{gsr:dt:106:lem:congruence}
Every affine partition $\calP$ of $X$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:congruence}
 |\calP|\equiv1\pmod{q-1}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Each cell has $q^d\equiv1\pmod{q-1}$ points. Sum its cardinality over the disjoint partition and use $N=(1+s(q-1))^m\equiv1\pmod{q-1}$.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Torus capacity, equality, and a quantitative gap\srctag{106}}]{Torus capacity, equality, and a quantitative gap}\label{gsr:dt:106:sec:d4}\label{gsr:dt:106:sec:capacity}
\srcnote{106}{Section 4}

\begin{lemma}[Torus capacity]\label{gsr:dt:106:lem:capacity}
For a $d$-dimensional affine subspace $A\subseteq\Fq^m$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:capacity}
 |A\cap(\Fq^\times)^m|\le t^d.
\end{equation}
Consequently, every affine cell $A\subseteq X$ satisfies $|A\cap\Tcal|\le t^{\dim A}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Write $A=a+U$, with $\dim U=d$. The restrictions of the ambient coordinate linear functionals span $U^*$. Select $d$ of them whose restrictions are independent. Their associated affine-coordinate map $A\to\Fq^d$ is an affine bijection. A point of $A\cap(\Fq^\times)^m$ must have all these selected coordinates nonzero. There are exactly $t^d$ possible tuples. The case $d=0$ says only that a point contributes at most one. Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:106:lem:orthant} for the final assertion.
\end{proof}

The upper bound is not restricted to coordinate-parallel flats. Diagonal relations such as $x_2=cx_1$ can attain it. The following classification is important both for stability and for avoiding a false axis-parallel reduction.

\begin{lemma}[Affine forms nonvanishing on a torus]\label{gsr:dt:106:lem:nonvanishing}
Assume $q>2$ and let
\[
 f(z_1,\ldots,z_d)=b+\sum_{i=1}^d a_i z_i.
\]
Then $f$ is nonzero at every point of $(\Fq^\times)^d$ if and only if it is a nonzero constant or a nonzero scalar multiple of a single coordinate $z_i$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Both listed forms are nonvanishing. If all $a_i=0$, the constant must be nonzero. If precisely one coefficient is nonzero, say $a_1$, then $b\ne0$ would give a zero at $z_1=-b/a_1\ne0$; therefore $b=0$. If at least two coefficients are nonzero, fix nonzero values of all other variables. The equation $a_1z_1+a_2z_2=c$ has $q-1$ solutions with $z_1,z_2\ne0$ when $c=0$, and $q-2$ such solutions when $c\ne0$. Both numbers are positive. This contradicts nonvanishing.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Torus-saturating and diagonal-coordinate flats]
A flat $A\subseteq X$ is \emph{torus-saturating} if $|A\cap\Tcal|=t^{\dim A}$. Inside an orthant, a \emph{diagonal-coordinate flat} has the following form: some coordinates are fixed nonzero constants, and the remaining coordinates are divided into nonempty blocks; within each block all coordinates are nonzero scalar multiples of one free parameter. Different blocks use independent parameters.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Equality classification and loss]\label{gsr:dt:106:thm:capacity-equality}
For $q>2$, a $d$-flat in $\Fq^m$ attains equality in~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:capacity} if and only if it is diagonal-coordinate. The same characterization applies inside the unique containing orthant of a torus-saturating cell of $X$.

For any nonsaturating $d$-flat, its capacity defect
\[
 \Delta(A)=t^d-|A\cap(\Fq^\times)^m|
\]
satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:gap}
 \Delta(A)\ge
 \begin{cases}
 1,&d=0\text{ or }1,\\
 (q-2)t^{d-2},&d\ge2.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
The same inequality holds for $\Delta(A)=t^d-|A\cap\Tcal|$ in $X$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Use the selected actual coordinate values $z_1,\ldots,z_d$ from Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:106:lem:capacity} as affine parameters. Every other coordinate is an affine-linear function of these parameters. Equality means that all of them are nonvanishing on $(\Fq^\times)^d$. Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:106:lem:nonvanishing} gives exactly the stated form. Conversely, such a form has precisely $t^d$ torus points.

A torus-saturating cell meets $\Tcal$, so each block determines its arm uniquely. Thus it has a unique containing orthant. For $d=0$ or $1$, failure of saturation gives an integral loss of at least one. For $d\ge2$, choose an ambient coordinate that fails the nonvanishing criterion in the parameterization. If it is identically zero, all $t^d$ parameter tuples fail. If it has exactly one nonzero linear coefficient and a nonzero constant, it vanishes on $t^{d-1}$ torus tuples. If it has at least two nonzero coefficients, fix the other $d-2$ nonzero parameters; the two-variable count in Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:106:lem:nonvanishing} gives at least $(q-2)t^{d-2}$ zeros. Every such zero removes a tuple from $A\cap(\Fq^\times)^m$. These estimates imply~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:gap}. Orthant containment gives the statement in $X$, including cells whose full-support intersection is empty.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Enumeration of efficient cell candidates]\label{gsr:dt:106:cor:enumeration}
Let $\stirling{a}{b}$ denote a Stirling number of the second kind. The number of torus-saturating $d$-flats in $\Fq^m$ is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:saturating-count}
 \stirling{m+1}{d+1}t^{m-d}.
\end{equation}
The number of torus-saturating $d$-flats in $C_{s,q}^m$ is $s^m$ times~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:saturating-count}.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Add one distinguished symbol to the $m$ coordinate positions and partition these $m+1$ objects into $d+1$ nonempty blocks. The block containing the distinguished symbol specifies the fixed coordinates, and is allowed to contain no coordinate position. The other $d$ blocks are the variable blocks. Normalize the coefficient of the least coordinate in each variable block to one. Every remaining coordinate has $t$ choices: a nonzero fixed value or a nonzero proportionality coefficient. There are $m-d$ such choices. This parameterization is unique. In $X$, a saturating flat has a unique orthant, with $s^m$ choices.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{An exact two-moment defect identity\srctag{106}}]{An exact two-moment defect identity}\label{gsr:dt:106:sec:d5}\label{gsr:dt:106:sec:defect}
\srcnote{106}{Section 5}

\subsection{The dimension weights}
For an integer $k\ge0$ and $d\ge0$, define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:G}
 G_k(d)=1+(q-2)q^{d-k}-t^{d+1-k}.
\end{equation}
All powers in this section are ordinary positive real or rational powers with integer exponents; negative exponents cause no ambiguity.

\begin{lemma}[Nonnegativity and quantitative separation]\label{gsr:dt:106:lem:G}
For $q>2$, $G_k(d)\ge0$, with equality exactly when $d=k$ or $d=k+1$. If $k\ge1$ and $d\le k-1$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:G-low}
 G_k(d)\ge\frac{q-2}{q}.
\end{equation}
If $d\ge k+2$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:G-high}
 G_k(d)\ge t(q-2)q^{d-k-2}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Set $n=d-k$ and $g(n)=1+(q-2)q^n-t^{n+1}$. Direct calculation gives $g(0)=g(1)=0$ and
\[
 g(n+1)-g(n)=(q-2)t(q^n-t^n).
\]
This difference is negative for $n<0$ and positive for $n>0$. Hence $g$ is strictly decreasing toward zero on the negative integers, vanishes at zero and one, and is strictly increasing afterward. Moreover $g(-1)=(q-2)/q$, proving~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:G-low}.

For $n\ge2$, divide by $q^n$ and observe
\[
 \frac{g(n)}{q^n}=q^{-n}+(q-2)-t(t/q)^n.
\]
The difference of this expression at $n+1$ and $n$ is
\[
 \frac{t}{q}\bigl((t/q)^n-q^{-n}\bigr)\ge0.
\]
Since $g(2)=t(q-2)$, multiplication by $q^n$ proves~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:G-high}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact torus-defect identity]\label{gsr:dt:106:thm:defect}
For $k\ge0$, put
\begin{align}
 B_k&=t^{1-k}M-(q-2)q^{-k}N\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:B}\\
 &=s^m t^{m+1-k}-\frac{q-2}{q^k}(1+st)^m.\nonumber
\end{align}
Every affine partition $\calP$ of $X$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:defect-identity}
 \boxed{|\calP|-B_k
  =\sum_{A\in\calP}G_k(\dim A)
     +t^{1-k}\sum_{A\in\calP}\bigl(t^{\dim A}-|A\cap\Tcal|\bigr).}
\end{equation}
All summands on the right are nonnegative.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $d_A=\dim A$, the summand associated with $A$ expands to
\[
 1+(q-2)q^{d_A-k}-t^{1-k}|A\cap\Tcal|.
\]
Sum over the partition. Disjointness and coverage give
$\sum_Aq^{d_A}=N$ and $\sum_A|A\cap\Tcal|=M$, yielding the left side. Nonnegativity follows from Lemmas~\ref{gsr:dt:106:lem:capacity} and~\ref{gsr:dt:106:lem:G}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Finite lower bounds and equality constraints]\label{gsr:dt:106:cor:lower}
For $m\ge1$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:finite-lower}
 P_{s,m}(q)\ge
 1+t\left\lceil\frac{\max_{0\le k\le m-1}B_k-1}{t}\right\rceil.
\end{equation}
If a partition attains $|\calP|=B_k$ before integer rounding, then all its cells have dimensions $k$ or $k+1$ and are torus-saturating. Conversely, those two properties imply equality.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The identity gives $|\calP|\ge B_k$ for every $k$. Round up to the next integer congruent to one modulo $t$, using Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:106:lem:congruence}. Equality before rounding is equivalent to every nonnegative summand in~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:defect-identity} vanishing.
\end{proof}

This is an exact accounting formula, not merely an inequality with an unspecified stability constant. It separates two possible inefficiencies: using the wrong cell dimensions and using too little full-support mass at a given dimension.

\subsection{Optimality within the two-moment relaxation}\label{gsr:dt:106:subsec:LP}
The preceding family of lower bounds is the best one available from these two numerical capacities alone, before integrality and incidence constraints are imposed.

\begin{theorem}[Exact relaxed optimum]\label{gsr:dt:106:thm:LP}
Consider the finite linear program in real variables $n_0,\ldots,n_m\ge0$:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:LP}
 \text{minimize }\sum_{d=0}^m n_d,
 \qquad
 \sum_{d=0}^m q^d n_d=N,
 \qquad
 \sum_{d=0}^m t^d n_d\ge M.
\end{equation}
Its optimum is $\max_{0\le k\le m-1}B_k$. More explicitly, set
\[
 a=\frac{t}{q},\qquad R=\frac MN,
 \qquad \eta=\frac{\log R}{\log a}\in(0,m),\qquad k=\lfloor\eta\rfloor.
\]
An optimum uses only dimensions $k$ and $k+1$. Its point masses are
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:LP-mixture}
 \lambda_k=\frac{R-a^{k+1}}{a^k-a^{k+1}},\qquad
 \lambda_{k+1}=1-\lambda_k,
 \qquad n_d=N\lambda_dq^{-d}.
\end{equation}
When $\eta$ is an integer, the optimum has all point mass at dimension $\eta$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Put $\lambda_d=q^dn_d/N$. Then $\sum_d\lambda_d=1$, and the constraints and normalized objective become
\[
 \sum_d\lambda_da^d\ge R,
 \qquad
 \frac1N\sum_dn_d=\sum_d\lambda_dq^{-d}.
\]
The points $(a^d,q^{-d})$ lie on the strictly convex increasing curve $y=x^p$, where
\[
 p=\frac{\log q}{\log(q/t)}>1.
\]
The lower boundary of their convex hull is the polygonal chain joining adjacent points in increasing order of $x$. It is increasing and convex. Indeed, the slopes of successive chords of a strictly convex function are increasing, so no chord between nonadjacent points lies below that chain. Therefore the minimum with first-coordinate average at least $R$ occurs at average exactly $R$, on the chord containing $R$.

The ratio $st/(1+st)$ lies strictly between $a$ and one because $s>1$. Hence $a^m<R<1$, proving $0<\eta<m$. The chord is between dimensions $k$ and $k+1$, and~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:LP-mixture} gives its unique masses except for the harmless repeated description at a vertex. All torus capacity is used, and $G_k$ vanishes at both dimensions, so the algebra underlying~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:defect-identity} gives objective $B_k$. Every $B_j$ is a valid lower bound for~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:LP}; thus this value equals their maximum.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What relaxed optimality does not prove]
The numbers $n_d$ in~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:LP} need not be integers, and the program does not encode which flats intersect. Even an integral relaxed solution need not be realizable by a partition. Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:106:thm:LP} identifies the exact strength of the two-moment method; it is not an assertion of exact finite-field optimality.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Matching constructions for products of crosses\srctag{106}}]{Matching constructions for products of crosses}\label{gsr:dt:106:sec:d6}\label{gsr:dt:106:sec:construction}
\srcnote{106}{Section 6}

The lower bounds must be paired with actual disjoint constructions. A single matching between two support levels supplies the necessary block partitions.

\begin{lemma}[A support-level matching]\label{gsr:dt:106:lem:matching}
Let $1\le h\le s$. There is an injection from the words in $\{0,1,\ldots,s\}^h$ having exactly one zero into the words in $\{1,\ldots,s\}^h$, such that each word maps to an extension obtained by replacing its zero by a nonzero symbol.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Form a bipartite graph with the one-zero words on the left and the all-nonzero words on the right, joined when extension is possible. Every left vertex has degree $s$ and every right vertex has degree $h$. For any subset $F$ of left vertices, counting its incident edges gives
\[
 s|F|\le h|\Gamma(F)|.
\]
Since $h\le s$, this implies $|\Gamma(F)|\ge|F|$.

For completeness, take a maximum matching. If a left vertex were unmatched, follow alternating paths from it. No reachable right vertex can be unmatched, since that would produce an augmenting path. The reachable left set has one more vertex than the reachable right set, while its entire neighborhood is reachable. This contradicts the displayed inequality. Thus a matching saturates the left side.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Explicit block upper bound]\label{gsr:dt:106:thm:block}
For $1\le h\le s$, there is an affine partition of $C_{s,q}^h$ having
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:U}
 U_{s,h}(q)=(1+st)^h-hs^{h-1}t^h
\end{equation}
cells, all of dimension zero or one. Put $U_{s,0}(q)=1$. For $m=rs+\ell$, $0\le\ell<s$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:upper}
 P_{s,m}(q)\le U_{s,s}(q)^r U_{s,\ell}(q).
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For a point of $C_{s,q}^h$, its \emph{support word} records zero in a zero block and the arm index in a nonzero block. A word with $j$ nonzero entries specifies a stratum of $t^j$ points.

Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:106:lem:matching}. For a matched pair $(f,w)$, let $z$ be the zero position of $f$. Fix arbitrary nonzero values on the $h-1$ arms specified by $f$ and let the $z$th block vary over the whole arm specified by $w_z$. This gives one affine line for each of $t^{h-1}$ fixed-value choices. The lines partition exactly the union of the two strata indexed by $f$ and $w$: at parameter zero they cover the first stratum, and at nonzero parameter they cover the second. They are disjoint because their fixed coordinates differ. Distinct matched pairs have disjoint support words, so their line families are also disjoint.

Leave every point of every other support stratum as a singleton. There are $hs^{h-1}$ matched pairs. Replacing the singleton partition of one pair of strata, which has $t^{h-1}+t^h=qt^{h-1}$ points, by $t^{h-1}$ lines saves $t^h$ cells. Subtracting this saving from $(1+st)^h$ proves~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:U}. Finally take products of $r$ blocks of size $s$ and one block of size $\ell$.
\end{proof}

For $h=s$, the matching is perfect on both sides. All points with support $s$ or $s-1$ are grouped into lines; only support at most $s-2$ remains in singleton cells. For $h<s$, some full-support strata remain singletons. This distinction is exactly responsible for the remainder $\ell$ in the leading coefficient of the main theorem.

\begin{corollary}[One arm-family block and the two-cross product]\label{gsr:dt:106:cor:small-exact}
For $s\ge2$ and $q>2$,
\[
 P_{s,1}(q)=1+(s-1)(q-1).
\]
For $s=2$,
\[
 U_{2,1}(q)=q,\qquad U_{2,2}(q)=4q-3,
 \qquad P_{2,2}(q)=4q-3.
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
At $m=1$, the lower bound $B_0$ is exactly $1+(s-1)t$, matching the construction. For $s=m=2$, the choice $k=1$ gives
\[
 B_1=4q-5+\frac2q.
\]
The number $4q-3$ is congruent to one modulo $q-1$, and its excess above $B_1$ is $2(q-1)/q$, strictly between zero and $q-1$. Congruence rounding therefore gives the same value as the construction.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Even fields included.} Source~102 proved $P_{2,2}(q)=\Psf(C^2)=4q-3$ for odd $q$; here it holds for every $q>2$. Checked at the write by exact search at $q=3,4,5$; at $q=4$ there are exactly two optimal partitions, as for odd $q\ge5$ (source~102's Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:102:thm:rigidity}); neither source claims the case $q=4$.
\end{writenote}

The preceding corollary provides a new short lower-bound proof of the known two-cross optimum~\cite{srconehundredtwo}. It is included as a check on normalization, not counted as a new exact value.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Sharp leading asymptotics and finite three-block bounds\srctag{106}}]{Sharp leading asymptotics and finite three-block bounds}\label{gsr:dt:106:sec:d7}\label{gsr:dt:106:sec:asymptotic}
\srcnote{106}{Section 7}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:106:thm:main-intro}]
Write $m=rs+\ell$, with $0\le\ell<s$, and select $k=r$ in~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:B}. For fixed $s,m$, the elementary expansions
\[
 t^{m+1-r}=q^{m+1-r}
       \left(1-\frac{m+1-r}{q}+O_{s,m}(q^{-2})\right)
\]
and
\[
 (1+st)^m=s^m q^m
       \left(1-\frac{m(s-1)}{sq}+O_{s,m}(q^{-2})\right)
\]
yield
\begin{align*}
 B_r
 &=s^m\left(1+r-\frac ms\right)q^{m-r}
                    +O_{s,m}(q^{m-r-1})\\
 &=s^{m-1}(s-\ell)q^{m-r}
                    +O_{s,m}(q^{m-r-1}).
\end{align*}
The terms of order $q^{m+1-r}$ cancel. This cancellation is why retaining the difference between $q^d$ and $t^d$ matters.

For the upper bound, formula~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:U} gives
\[
 U_{s,s}(q)=s^s q^{s-1}+O_s(q^{s-2}).
\]
If $1\le\ell<s$, then
\[
 U_{s,\ell}(q)=s^{\ell-1}(s-\ell)q^\ell
                              +O_s(q^{\ell-1}).
\]
For $\ell=0$, the remainder factor is one. Substitute these estimates into~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:upper}. If $\ell>0$, the leading coefficient is
\[
 (s^s)^r s^{\ell-1}(s-\ell)=s^{m-1}(s-\ell),
\]
and the exponent is $r(s-1)+\ell=m-r$. If $\ell=0$, the coefficient is $s^{rs}=s^m$, which is again $s^{m-1}(s-\ell)$. Thus the upper and lower bounds agree to the stated leading order. Taking $s=2$ gives~\eqref{gsr:fm:106:eq:main-two}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Examples and interpretation}
For two arms, the first few leading terms are
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ccl}
\toprule
Number of blocks $m$ & Leading cost & Explicit product upper bound\\
\midrule
1 & $q$ & $q$\\
2 & $4q$ & $4q-3$\\
3 & $4q^2$ & $q(4q-3)$\\
4 & $16q^2$ & $(4q-3)^2$\\
5 & $16q^3$ & $q(4q-3)^2$\\
6 & $64q^3$ & $(4q-3)^3$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The table does not assert that the product upper bounds are exact beyond the first two rows. Rather, it proves that any improvement in a fixed higher product can only alter lower-order terms.

For three arms, the first three costs have leading terms $2q$, $3q^2$, and $27q^2$. At six blocks the leading term is $729q^4$. Grouping $s$ coordinates at a time is asymptotically optimal for an $s$-arm cross, whereas grouping only pairs would miss this general pattern.

\begin{theorem}[The first unresolved exact value, sharply bracketed]\label{gsr:dt:106:thm:three}
For every prime power $q>2$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:three}
 \boxed{4q^2-5q+2\le P_{2,3}(q)\le4q^2-3q.}
\end{equation}
A partition of $C_{2,q}^3$ containing a three-dimensional cell has at least
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:three-plane}
 5q^2-8q+4
\end{equation}
cells. Therefore, for $q\ge5$, no optimal partition contains a three-dimensional cell.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $s=2,m=3,k=1$, direct expansion gives
\[
 B_1=4q^2-6q+5-\frac2q.
\]
The integer $4q^2-5q+2$ is congruent to one modulo $t$, and its excess above $B_1$ is
\[
 q-3+\frac2q=\frac{(q-1)(q-2)}q\in(0,t).
\]
Thus Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:106:lem:congruence} gives the lower bound. A product of one single-cross partition and one two-cross partition gives the upper bound.

If a three-dimensional cell occurs, its dimension contribution in~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:defect-identity} is
\[
 G_1(3)=(q-1)(q-2).
\]
Discard the other nonnegative contributions. Rounding $B_1+G_1(3)$ to the next allowed congruence class gives~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:three-plane}; again the rounding difference is $t(q-2)/q$. Finally,
\[
 (5q^2-8q+4)-(4q^2-3q)=(q-1)(q-4)>0
 \qquad(q\ge5).
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Source~102's Question~13.1 narrowed} (Section~\ref{gsr:dt:sec:affinecells}). Checked at the write: the lower bound equals $4q^2-5q+2$ for all $59$ prime powers $3\le q<200$. The intake's search at $q=3$ found no partition of $C^3$ with at most $26$ cells but did not finish, so $P_{2,3}(3)\in[23,27]$ stays open.
\end{writenote}

For illustration, the rigorous intervals from~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:three} are $[23,27]$ at $q=3$, $[46,52]$ at $q=4$, $[77,85]$ at $q=5$, and $[163,175]$ at $q=7$. No exact optimizer is inferred from these intervals or from numerical search.

\section[{Quantitative defect bounds and asymptotic rigidity\srctag{106}}]{Quantitative defect bounds and asymptotic rigidity}\label{gsr:dt:106:sec:d8}\label{gsr:dt:106:sec:stability}
\srcnote{106}{Section 8}

\subsection{Exact finite estimates}
Fix an affine partition $\calP$ and $k\ge0$, and write
\[
 E=|\calP|-B_k\ge0.
\]
For a collection of cells, its \emph{point mass} means the cardinality of their disjoint union, not the number of cells in that collection.

\begin{theorem}[Quantitative dimension and geometry control]\label{gsr:dt:106:thm:finite-stability}
If $k\ge1$, the number of cells with dimension at most $k-1$ is at most $qE/(q-2)$, and their total point mass is at most
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:low-mass}
 \frac{q^k}{q-2}E.
\end{equation}
The total point mass in cells of dimension at least $k+2$ is at most
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:high-mass}
 \frac{q^{k+2}}{(q-1)(q-2)}E.
\end{equation}
For every $k\ge0$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:total-torus-defect}
 \sum_{A\in\calP}\bigl(t^{\dim A}-|A\cap\Tcal|\bigr)
 \le t^{k-1}E.
\end{equation}
If $m\ge2$, the total point mass in nonsaturating cells is at most
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:bad-mass}
 \frac{q^m t^{k-m+1}}{q-2}E.
\end{equation}
The low-dimensional collection is empty when $k=0$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Every low-dimensional cell contributes at least $(q-2)/q$ to the first sum in~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:defect-identity}, by Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:106:lem:G}. This proves the bound on their number. Each has at most $q^{k-1}$ points, giving~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:low-mass}. For a cell of dimension $d\ge k+2$, inequality~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:G-high} rearranges to
\[
 q^d\le\frac{q^{k+2}}{t(q-2)}G_k(d).
\]
Sum to obtain~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:high-mass}. The second nonnegative sum in the identity directly gives~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:total-torus-defect}.

For the geometry estimate, set
\[
 \gamma_m(q)=\frac{(q-2)t^{m-2}}{q^m}.
\]
A nonsaturating cell of dimension $d\ge2$ satisfies, by~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:gap},
\[
 \frac{\Delta(A)}{|A|}
 \ge\frac{q-2}{q^2}\left(\frac tq\right)^{d-2}
 \ge\gamma_m(q),
\]
since $d\le m$. For $d=0,1$, the lower bound $\Delta(A)\ge1$ also gives the same conclusion, because $\gamma_m(q)\le1/q$. Thus the point mass of all nonsaturating cells is at most
$\gamma_m(q)^{-1}\sum_A\Delta(A)$. Apply~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:total-torus-defect} and simplify.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The structure of optimal and near-optimal partitions}

\begin{theorem}[Asymptotic rigidity and dimension proportions]\label{gsr:dt:106:thm:rigidity}
Fix $s\ge2$ and $m\ge2$, write $m=rs+\ell$ with $0\le\ell<s$, and let $\calP_q$ be an optimal affine partition of $C_{s,q}^m$. Then all but an $O_{s,m}(1/q)$ fraction of the points lie in torus-saturating cells of dimension $r$ or $r+1$. In particular these cells are diagonal-coordinate flats in unique orthants.

If $\lambda_d(q)$ is the fraction of points whose cell has dimension $d$, then
\begin{align}
 \lambda_r(q)&=1-\frac\ell s+O_{s,m}(q^{-1}),\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:mix-r}\\
 \lambda_{r+1}(q)&=\frac\ell s+O_{s,m}(q^{-1}).\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:mix-r1}
\end{align}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
We prove a stronger near-optimal version at the same time. If $0\le\eps\le1$ and
\[
 |\calP_q|\le P_{s,m}(q)+\eps q^{m-r},
\]
then the exceptional fraction and both error terms are $O_{s,m}(\eps+1/q)$, uniformly in $\eps$.
The lower-bound expansion and the construction in the proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:106:thm:main-intro} imply, with $k=r$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:E-asymptotic}
 E=|\calP_q|-B_r
 \le \eps q^{m-r}+O_{s,m}(q^{m-r-1}).
\end{equation}
For optimal partitions take $\eps=0$. Since $N\asymp_{s,m}q^m$, the high-dimensional point-mass bound~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:high-mass} divided by $N$ is $O_{s,m}(\eps+1/q)$. If $r\ge1$, the corresponding low-dimensional fraction is even $O_{s,m}(\eps/q+q^{-2})$, by~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:low-mass}. If $r=0$, there are no such cells. Formula~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:bad-mass} gives a nonsaturating fraction $O_{s,m}(\eps+1/q)$. This proves the geometric assertion.

It remains to identify the proportions, rather than just the two possible dimensions. Put $a=t/q$, and let
\[
 \overline d=\sum_{d=0}^m d\lambda_d(q)
\]
be the point-weighted mean cell dimension. Exact counting gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:moment-difference}
 0\le\sum_{d=0}^m\lambda_d(q)a^d-\frac MN
   =\frac1N\sum_{A\in\calP_q}\Delta(A)
   \le O_{s,m}\!\left(\frac\eps q+\frac1{q^2}\right),
\end{equation}
using~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:total-torus-defect} and~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:E-asymptotic}. Uniformly for $0\le d\le m$,
\[
 a^d=1-\frac dq+O_m(q^{-2}),
 \qquad
 \frac MN=\left(\frac{st}{1+st}\right)^m
         =1-\frac{m}{sq}+O_{s,m}(q^{-2}).
\]
Insert these expansions in~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:moment-difference}; it follows that
\[
 \overline d=\frac ms+O_{s,m}(\eps+q^{-1}).
\]
The mass outside dimensions $r,r+1$ is already $O_{s,m}(\eps+1/q)$, and $m$ is fixed. Therefore
\[
 \lambda_r+\lambda_{r+1}=1+O_{s,m}(\eps+q^{-1}),
 \quad
 r\lambda_r+(r+1)\lambda_{r+1}
    =r+\frac\ell s+O_{s,m}(\eps+q^{-1}).
\]
Solving these two equations gives~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:mix-r}--\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:mix-r1} and their near-optimal variants.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The one-block endpoint]
For $m=1$, the exact optimizer selects one full arm and makes every nonzero point of the other arms a singleton. The proportions tend to $1/s$ in dimension one and $1-1/s$ in dimension zero, consistent with the formulas. Every cell is torus-saturating. Thus the conclusion extends to this endpoint directly, without invoking the $m\ge2$ gap normalization.
\end{remark}

For two arms and an even number $m=2r$ of blocks, almost every point of an optimal partition lies in a torus-saturating $r$-flat. For an odd number $m=2r+1$, asymptotically half the points lie in dimension $r$ and half in dimension $r+1$. This distinguishes point-weighted geometry from the number of cells: in the odd case the smaller cells dominate the leading cell count even though each dimension receives half of the points.

\begin{remark}[Local rigidity versus global edit distance]
The theorem classifies almost all cells in point-mass terms. It does not identify how their orthants and proportionality blocks fit together globally, and it does not show closeness to one chosen Hall-matching or product partition. Such a global edit-distance theorem would require an additional compatibility argument. Allowing diagonal-coordinate cells is essential; the torus bound does not force every efficient cell to be coordinate-parallel.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Regularized partition costs and the second order of limits\srctag{106}}]{Regularized partition costs and the second order of limits}\label{gsr:dt:106:sec:d9}\label{gsr:dt:106:sec:rates}
\srcnote{106}{Section 9}

\begin{lemma}[Existence of the regularized rate]\label{gsr:dt:106:lem:rate-exists}
For fixed $s,q$, the limit
\[
 \rho_s(q)=\lim_{m\to\infty}P_{s,m}(q)^{1/m}
\]
exists and equals the infimum of these roots over $m\ge1$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Fix $h\ge1$ and write $m=ah+b$ with $0\le b<h$. Product partitions give
\[
 P_{s,m}(q)\le P_{s,h}(q)^a P_{s,b}(q).
\]
Taking $m$th roots and then a limsup yields
$\limsup_m P_{s,m}(q)^{1/m}\le P_{s,h}(q)^{1/h}$; the finitely many remainder factors have roots tending to one. Take the infimum over $h$ and compare with the immediate lower bound on the liminf.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Explicit uniform-in-product rate bounds]\label{gsr:dt:106:thm:rate-bounds}
Let $D=1+s(q-1)$ and define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:lambda-rate}
 \Lambda_s(q)=\frac{\log\bigl(D/(s(q-1))\bigr)}
                    {\log\bigl(q/(q-1)\bigr)}.
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:rate-bounds}
 \boxed{Dq^{-\Lambda_s(q)}\le\rho_s(q)
       \le\bigl(D^s-s^s(q-1)^s\bigr)^{1/s}.}
\end{equation}
The lower bound arises from the finite inequality
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:Jensen-finite}
 P_{s,m}(q)\ge\bigl(Dq^{-\Lambda_s(q)}\bigr)^m
 \qquad(m\ge1).
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Given a partition, let $n_d$ be the number of its $d$-dimensional cells and $\lambda_d=q^dn_d/N$ its point-mass distribution. Put $a=(q-1)/q$ and $p=\log q/\log(q/(q-1))>1$. Torus capacity gives $\sum_d\lambda_da^d\ge M/N$. By convexity of $x\mapsto x^p$,
\begin{align*}
 \frac{|\calP|}{N}
 &=\sum_d\lambda_dq^{-d}
   =\sum_d\lambda_d(a^d)^p\\
 &\ge\left(\sum_d\lambda_da^d\right)^p
 \ge\left(\frac MN\right)^p.
\end{align*}
Substitute $N=D^m$ and $M=(s(q-1))^m$. The resulting base is
\[
 D\left(\frac{s(q-1)}D\right)^p
       =Dq^{-\Lambda_s(q)},
\]
proving~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:Jensen-finite}. Take roots and the limit. The upper bound is $\rho_s(q)\le P_{s,s}(q)^{1/s}\le U_{s,s}(q)^{1/s}$, by the block construction.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:106:thm:rate-intro}]
Existence is Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:106:lem:rate-exists}. For fixed $s$, expansions of the logarithms in~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:lambda-rate} give
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:lambda-expansion}
 \Lambda_s(q)=\frac1s+\frac{s-1}{2s^2q}+O_s(q^{-2}).
\end{equation}
For clarity, the numerator is
\[
 \log\left(1+\frac1{s(q-1)}\right)
 =\frac1{sq}+\left(\frac1s-\frac1{2s^2}\right)\frac1{q^2}
            +O_s(q^{-3}),
\]
and the denominator is $q^{-1}+\tfrac12q^{-2}+O(q^{-3})$; division yields~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:lambda-expansion}. Since $D=sq-(s-1)$, the lower endpoint in~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:rate-bounds} is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:lower-rate-expansion}
 s q^{1-1/s}\left[
 1-\frac{s-1}{sq}-\frac{s-1}{2s^2}\frac{\log q}{q}
    +O_s\!\left(\frac{(\log q)^2}{q^2}\right)\right].
\end{equation}
The upper endpoint, using~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:U}, is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:upper-rate-expansion}
 s q^{1-1/s}\left[
 1-\frac{(s-1)(2s-1)}{2s^2q}+O_s(q^{-2})\right].
\end{equation}
Indeed, $D^s-(s(q-1))^s$ has leading term $s^s q^{s-1}$ and relative next coefficient $-(s-1)(2s-1)/(2s)$. Taking the $s$th root gives~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:upper-rate-expansion}. The two bounds prove~\eqref{gsr:fm:106:eq:rate-intro}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The quadratic two-arm case}
For $s=2$, the explicit interval becomes
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:rho-two}
 (2q-1)q^{-\frac{\log((2q-1)/(2q-2))}{\log(q/(q-1))}}
 \le\rho_2(q)\le\sqrt{4q-3}.
\end{equation}
Its large-field consequences are
\[
 \rho_2(q)=2\sqrt q
  \left(1+O\!\left(\frac{\log q}{q}\right)\right)
\]
and, more explicitly, a lower endpoint
\[
 2\sqrt q\left[1-\frac1{2q}-\frac{\log q}{8q}
              +O\!\left(\frac{(\log q)^2}{q^2}\right)\right],
\]
versus the upper endpoint $2\sqrt q(1-3/(8q)+O(q^{-2}))$.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{rrrr}
\toprule
$q$ & Old volume lower bound & New lower endpoint & Upper endpoint\\
\midrule
3 & 1.666667 & 2.731437 & 3.000000\\
5 & 1.800000 & 3.848589 & 4.123106\\
7 & 1.857143 & 4.732890 & 5.000000\\
11 & 1.909091 & 6.153479 & 6.403124\\
101 & 1.990099 & 19.885771 & 20.024984\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The decimal entries are rounded evaluations of exact formulas, not certified directional decimal bounds. The inequalities themselves are~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:rho-two}. The old lower bound was $(2q-1)/q$, obtained by dividing total points by the largest cell size~\cite{srconehundredtwo}.

\begin{remark}[No limit interchange]
The error constant in~\eqref{gsr:fm:106:eq:main} depends on $m$, so the fixed-$m$ theorem alone does not establish the regularized result. The Jensen inequality~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:Jensen-finite} is valid for every $m$ with the same exponential base, and supplies the missing uniform control. Conversely, the regularized result by itself would not determine the parity-sensitive leading coefficient in~\eqref{gsr:fm:106:eq:main-two}. Indeed, the Jensen bound alone gives the fixed-$m$ power $q^{m(1-1/s)}$. When $\ell>0$, this is smaller than the sharp power $q^{m-\lfloor m/s\rfloor}$ by a factor $q^{\ell/s}$. The discrete adjacent-dimension bound is essential for recovering that fixed-product threshold.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Consequences for simultaneous quadratic localization\srctag{106}}]{Consequences for simultaneous quadratic localization}\label{gsr:dt:106:sec:d10}\label{gsr:dt:106:sec:quadratic}
\srcnote{106}{Section 10}

Let
\[
 \Psi_m:\Fq^{2m}\longrightarrow\Fq^m,
 \qquad
 \Psi_m(x_1,y_1,\ldots,x_m,y_m)
      =(x_1y_1,\ldots,x_my_m),
\]
and let $A_m(q)$ be the minimum number of affine cells in a partition of the whole domain on which $\Psi_m$ is constant. Set $A_0(q)=1$ and $b=(q-1)^2$.

\begin{lemma}[Nonzero product fibers contain no affine lines]\label{gsr:dt:106:lem:hyperbola}
For $q>2$ and $c\ne0$, the set $\{(x,y):xy=c\}$ contains no affine line. Therefore the projection to a block with nonzero output of any constant affine cell for $\Psi_m$ is one fixed point.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $(x+au,y+av)$ were in the fiber for every $a\in\Fq$, then
\[
 (xy-c)+a(xv+yu)+a^2uv
\]
would vanish at more than two field elements. All its coefficients are zero. Thus $xy=c\ne0$, $uv=0$, and $xv+yu=0$. If $u=0$, then $xv=0$ forces $v=0$; if $v=0$, then $yu=0$ forces $u=0$. No nonconstant line is possible. A positive-dimensional affine image under a projection would contain a line, so the projection of a cell must be a point.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact singular-fiber reduction]\label{gsr:dt:106:thm:binomial}
For $q>2$ and every $m\ge0$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:binomial}
 A_m(q)=\sum_{j=0}^m\binom mj b^{m-j}P_{2,j}(q).
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:full-rate}
 \lim_{m\to\infty}A_m(q)^{1/m}=(q-1)^2+\rho_2(q).
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For a constant affine cell, the set $I$ of blocks whose output is zero is fixed. By Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:106:lem:hyperbola}, every block outside $I$ is a fixed point with both coordinates nonzero, with $b$ possibilities per block. After those points are specified, the remaining domain piece is a copy of $C_{2,q}^{|I|}$. Every admissible cell belongs to exactly one such piece, and no cell joins two pieces. For $|I|=j$, there are $\binom mj b^{m-j}$ pieces, each with optimal partition cost $P_{2,j}(q)$. Their optimal partitions can be chosen independently. This proves~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:binomial}.

Put $\rho=\rho_2(q)$. The infimum characterization of the rate gives $P_{2,j}(q)\ge\rho^j$ for every $j$, so~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:binomial} implies $A_m(q)\ge(b+\rho)^m$. Given $\delta>0$, convergence of the roots gives a finite constant $K_\delta$ such that
\[
 P_{2,j}(q)\le K_\delta(\rho+\delta)^j
 \qquad(j\ge0).
\]
Then $A_m(q)\le K_\delta(b+\rho+\delta)^m$. Take $m$th roots and limits, and let $\delta$ decrease to zero.
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:106:thm:binomial} is the reduction established in~\cite{srconehundredtwo}; its proof is reproduced to state exactly which new input enters the consequence below.

\begin{corollary}[Sharp singular correction to the full localization rate]\label{gsr:dt:106:cor:full-rate}
As $q$ tends to infinity through prime powers greater than two,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:dt:106:eq:quadratic-correction}
 \boxed{\lim_{m\to\infty}A_m(q)^{1/m}
       =(q-1)^2+2\sqrt q
            +O\!\left(\frac{\log q}{\sqrt q}\right).}
\end{equation}
At fixed $q$, adding $(q-1)^2$ to the two endpoints in~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:rho-two} gives explicit lower and upper bounds on this rate.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Combine~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:full-rate} with Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:106:thm:rate-intro} at $s=2$.
\end{proof}

The correction $\rho_2(q)$ is the exact contribution of optimizing joint zero fibers after all nonzero blocks have been fixed. It is not visible in the leading $q^2$ scale of the full-map rate. Isolating that singular correction is more informative than merely giving a relative $1+o(1)$ estimate for the whole rate.

There is a fundamental boundary to the application. Points for which every product is nonzero are forced singleton cells by Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:106:lem:hyperbola}. Thus a theorem about minimizing the total cell count cannot by itself guarantee a positive minimum cell dimension, let alone a long arithmetic progression in the integer setting. The interface issue identified in Section~\ref{gsr:dt:106:sec:review} remains a genuine research problem.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Expanded two-arm lower bounds\srctag{106}}]{Expanded two-arm lower bounds}\label{gsr:dt:106:sec:dA}\label{gsr:dt:106:app:expansions}
\srcnote{106}{Appendix A}
The following unrounded expressions are obtained from~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:B}. They can be strengthened by the congruence rounding in~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:finite-lower}, or by maximizing over a different $k$ for particular parameters.
\begin{align*}
 B_1\big|_{s=2,m=2}&=4q-5+\frac2q,\\
 B_1\big|_{s=2,m=3}&=4q^2-6q+5-\frac2q,\\
 B_2\big|_{s=2,m=4}&=16q^2-40q+40-\frac{17}q+\frac2{q^2},\\
 B_2\big|_{s=2,m=5}&=16q^3-48q^2+72q-58+\frac{21}q-\frac2{q^2},\\
 B_3\big|_{s=2,m=6}&=64q^3-240q^2+384q-316
                      +\frac{132}q-\frac{25}{q^2}+\frac2{q^3}.
\end{align*}
For example, at $m=4$ the product construction is
\[
 (4q-3)^2=16q^2-24q+9.
\]
The gap between this value and the displayed lower bound is of order $q$, whereas the leading cost is of order $q^2$. This is an explicit instance of the general one-power error term.

\section[{Normalization and finite Fourier identities\srctag{02}}]{Normalization and finite Fourier identities}\label{gsr:en:02:sec:d2}
\srcnote{02}{Section 2}
Let $G$ be a finite abelian group of order $N\geq1$, written additively, and let $\widehat G$ be its character group, written multiplicatively. Thus $(h,\chi)+(k,\psi)$ in $G\times\widehat G$ means $(h+k,\chi\psi)$. All averages over $G$ are normalized; sums over $\widehat G$ are not:
\[
 \E_x a(x)=\frac1N\sum_{x\in G}a(x),\qquad
 \widehat a(\chi)=\E_xa(x)\overline{\chi(x)}.
\]
Fourier orthogonality gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:02:eq:parseval}
 \E_x|a(x)|^2=\sum_{\chi\in\widehat G}|\widehat a(\chi)|^2.
\end{equation}
For normalized convolution $(a*b)(s)=\E_h a(s-h)b(h)$, we have $\widehat{a*b}=\widehat a\,\widehat b$. These facts follow by expanding the sums and using $\E_x\chi(x)=0$ for a nontrivial character and $1$ for the trivial character.

Define
\[
 \Delta_hf(x)=f(x)\overline{f(x-h)},\qquad m(f)=\E_x|f(x)|^2,
\]
and define the eighth power of the normalized $U^3$ norm by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:02:eq:u3spectral}
 \U(f)=\E_h\sum_{\chi\in\widehat G}
              |\widehat{\Delta_hf}(\chi)|^4.
\end{equation}
It also equals the usual cube average
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:02:eq:u3cube}
 \E_{x,a,b,c}\prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^3}
  \mathcal C^{|\omega|} f(x+\omega_1a+\omega_2b+\omega_3c),
\end{equation}
where $\mathcal C$ denotes complex conjugation. One proof first expands the fourth Fourier moment in~\eqref{gsr:en:02:eq:u3spectral}; character orthogonality leaves the additive quadruple constraint, which is parameterized by three variables. The remaining derivative variable gives~\eqref{gsr:en:02:eq:u3cube}, after changes of signs in the increment variables. In particular $\U(f)$ is nonnegative.

For $f,g:G\to\C$, write
\[
 A_{f,g}(h,\chi)=\E_x f(x)\overline{g(x-h)}\overline{\chi(x)}.
\]
This is just a Fourier transform of a mixed derivative, not an additional assumption about $f$ or $g$.

\begin{definition}[Weighted correlation and energy]
For any $w:G\times\widehat G\to[0,\infty)$, define
\begin{align}
 \calT_w(f,g)&=\E_h\sum_\chi w(h,\chi)|A_{f,g}(h,\chi)|^2,
       \label{gsr:en:02:eq:Tdef}\\
 \calE(w)&=\frac1{N^3}
 \sum_{\substack{h_1+h_2=h_3+h_4\\
                 \chi_1\chi_2=\chi_3\chi_4}}
           \prod_{j=1}^4w(h_j,\chi_j). \label{gsr:en:02:eq:Edef}
\end{align}
\end{definition}
The factor $N^{-3}$ in~\eqref{gsr:en:02:eq:Edef} is deliberate: it normalizes the energy of a full additive graph to $1$. It is not the uniform-probability normalization on the group of order $N^2$. If $w=\one_\Gamma$, then $N^3\calE(w)$ is the ordinary ordered additive-quadruple count of $\Gamma$.

\section[{A sharp weighted extension of Proposition 6.1\srctag{02}}]{A sharp weighted extension of Proposition 6.1}\label{gsr:en:02:sec:d3}
\srcnote{02}{Section 3}

\begin{theorem}[Mixed energy-sensitive inverse step]\label{gsr:en:02:thm:main}
For every finite abelian group $G$, every $f,g:G\to\C$, and every nonnegative weight $w:G\times\widehat G\to[0,\infty)$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:02:eq:main}
 \boxed{\quad
 \calT_w(f,g)^4\leq
 \min\{m(f)^4\U(g),\ m(g)^4\U(f)\}\,\calE(w).
 \quad}
\end{equation}
There is no pointwise boundedness assumption on $f,g$, and no graph or bounded-fiber assumption on $w$. The coefficient $1$ cannot be decreased.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 11--14]
Source~11's chapter (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:affine}) starts from the output of Proposition~6.1 in the range $\alpha^4>8/9$ and recovers an affine map (its Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:11:cor:prop61}); it is complementary to this theorem, which strengthens the energy lower bound itself.
\end{writenote}

\subsection{Three exact identities}
For $u\in G$ define
\[
 F_u(s)=f(s)\overline{f(s-u)},\qquad
 D_u(s)=g(s)\overline{g(s-u)},\qquad
 V_u(h)=\sum_\chi w(h,\chi)\chi(u),
\]
and put $K_u=D_u*V_u$. Use the normalized inner product
\[
 \ip{F}{K}=\E_{u,s}F_u(s)\overline{K_u(s)}.
\]
Then
\begin{align}
 \calT_w(f,g)&=\ip{F}{K}, \label{gsr:en:02:eq:identity1}\\
 R:=\E_{u,s}|K_u(s)|^2
   &=\E_u\sum_\psi|\widehat D_u(\psi)|^2
                         |\widehat V_u(\psi)|^2, \label{gsr:en:02:eq:identity2}\\
 \E_u\sum_\psi|\widehat V_u(\psi)|^4&=\calE(w). \label{gsr:en:02:eq:identity3}
\end{align}
For~\eqref{gsr:en:02:eq:identity1}, expand the square in~\eqref{gsr:en:02:eq:Tdef}, set the second spatial variable equal to $s-u$, and obtain
\[
 \E_{u,s} f(s)\overline{f(s-u)}
 \E_h \overline{g(s-h)}g(s-u-h)
                  \sum_\chi w(h,\chi)\overline{\chi(u)}.
\]
This is exactly $\ip{F}{K}$. Nonnegativity of $w$ also makes the original expression visibly real and nonnegative. Identity~\eqref{gsr:en:02:eq:identity2} is Parseval and the convolution identity.

For~\eqref{gsr:en:02:eq:identity3}, expand
\[
 \widehat V_u(\psi)=\frac1N\sum_{h,\chi}
                  w(h,\chi)\chi(u)\overline{\psi(h)}.
\]
The fourth power contributes $N^{-4}$. Summing over $\psi$ contributes $N$ and imposes $h_1+h_2=h_3+h_4$. Averaging over $u$ imposes $\chi_1\chi_2=\chi_3\chi_4$ without another factor. The remaining normalization is $N^{-3}$, proving the identity.

\subsection{Proof of the theorem}
The first exact norm is
\[
 \|F\|_2^2=\E_{u,s}|f(s)|^2|f(s-u)|^2=m(f)^2.
\]
Cauchy--Schwarz applied to~\eqref{gsr:en:02:eq:identity1} therefore gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:02:eq:CS1}
 \calT_w(f,g)^2\leq m(f)^2R.
\end{equation}
Applying Cauchy--Schwarz to~\eqref{gsr:en:02:eq:identity2}, this time on the measure space with average in $u$ and counting measure in $\psi$, gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:02:eq:CS2}
 R^2\leq
 \left(\E_u\sum_\psi|\widehat D_u(\psi)|^4\right)
 \left(\E_u\sum_\psi|\widehat V_u(\psi)|^4\right)
 =\U(g)\calE(w).
\end{equation}
Squaring~\eqref{gsr:en:02:eq:CS1} and using~\eqref{gsr:en:02:eq:CS2} proves the first bound in~\eqref{gsr:en:02:eq:main}.

For the other bound, let $w^\vee(h,\chi)=w(-h,\chi^{-1})$. Directly changing variables in the mixed Fourier coefficient gives
\[
 |A_{f,g}(h,\chi)|=|A_{g,f}(-h,\chi^{-1})|.
\]
Consequently $\calT_w(f,g)=\calT_{w^\vee}(g,f)$. Inversion is an automorphism of the abelian group $G\times\widehat G$, so $\calE(w^\vee)=\calE(w)$. Apply the first bound with $f$ and $g$ exchanged. Equality examples establishing the final assertion are given in Section~\ref{gsr:en:02:sec:sharp}. \qed

\begin{corollary}[Graph version]\label{gsr:en:02:cor:graph}
Let $B\subseteq G$, $\phi:B\to\widehat G$, and $\Gamma=\{(h,\phi(h)):h\in B\}$. If
\[
 T=\E_h\one_B(h)|\widehat{\Delta_hf}(\phi(h))|^2>0,
\]
then, writing $E(\Gamma)$ for the unnormalized additive energy,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:02:eq:graphbound}
 \frac{E(\Gamma)}{N^3}\geq\frac{T^4}{m(f)^4\U(f)}.
\end{equation}
In particular, the hypothesis~\eqref{gsr:fm:02:eq:old61} implies
\[
 E(\Gamma)\geq\frac{\alpha^4}{m(f)^4\U(f)}N^3.
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Take $g=f$ and $w=\one_\Gamma$. The unnormalized Fourier coefficient is $N$ times our normalized coefficient, so the statistic in~\eqref{gsr:fm:02:eq:old61}, divided by $N^3$, is precisely $T$. Positive $T$ makes the denominator nonzero by Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:02:thm:main}.
\end{proof}
