\section[{Graph energy, derivatives, and the exact endpoint\srctag{11}}]{Graph energy, derivatives, and the exact endpoint}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:d2}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:basics}
\srcnote{11}{Section 2}

\begin{lemma}[Derivative collision identity]\label{gsr:en:11:lem:derivative}
Put $\Delta_h f(x)=f(x+h)-f(x)$ and
\[
 r_h(w)=|\{x\in G:\Delta_hf(x)=w\}|.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:derivative}
\Energy(f)=\sum_{h\in G}\sum_{w\in W}r_h(w)^2.
\end{equation}
Moreover, adding or subtracting an affine map from $f$ does not change
$\Energy(f)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Pairs $x,y$ with $\Delta_h f(x)=\Delta_h f(y)$ correspond bijectively to
respected quadruples $(x+h,y,x,y+h)$. Conversely, from any respected
quadruple one recovers $h=x_1-x_3=x_4-x_2$, $x=x_3$, and $y=x_2$.
For an affine map $\ell(x)=L(x)+b$, the derivative $\Delta_h\ell(x)=L(h)$
is independent of $x$. Subtracting it just permutes the labels of each
histogram $r_h$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Full energy]\label{gsr:en:11:lem:full}
One has $\Energy(f)\le N^3$, with equality if and only if $f$ is affine.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For each $h$, the nonnegative integers $r_h(w)$ sum to $N$, so their
squares sum to at most $N^2$. Equality holds precisely when the derivative
is constant. If all derivatives are constant, let their values be $L(h)$.
The identity
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:cocycle}
\Delta_{h+k}f(x)=\Delta_hf(x+k)+\Delta_kf(x)
\end{equation}
implies $L(h+k)=L(h)+L(k)$. Also $f(x)=L(x)+f(0)$.
The converse is immediate.
\end{proof}

In the derivative-imbalance normalization used in \cite{ffwc}, if
$M=|W|$, the corresponding quantity is
\[
 NB_f=\Energy(f)-N^2-(N-1)N^2/M.
\]
The ambiguity statistic is
\[
 \sum_{h\ne0}\sum_w\binom{r_h(w)}2
   =\frac{\Energy(f)-2N^2+N}{2}.
\]
These formulas allow the results here to be translated into those
normalizations without confusing componentwise Fourier nonlinearity with
the distance from a vector-valued map to a single affine map.

\subsection{A basic fact about error supports}
For a subset $S\subseteq G$ let
\[
 E(S)=\#\{(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)\in S^4:x_1+x_2=x_3+x_4\}.
\]
This is set energy, as distinct from the graph energy $\Energy(f)$.

\begin{lemma}[Maximum set energy and its equality case]\label{gsr:en:11:lem:setcoset}
If $|S|=s$, then $E(S)\le s^3$. If $S\ne\varnothing$, equality holds if
and only if $S$ is a coset of a subgroup of $G$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Write $c_h=|S\cap(S-h)|$. Then
$E(S)=\sum_hc_h^2$ and $\sum_hc_h=s^2$. Since $0\le c_h\le s$,
$E(S)\le s\sum_hc_h=s^3$. Equality forces each $c_h$ to be either $0$ or
$s$. Let $T=\{h:S+h=S\}$, a subgroup. Fix $a\in S$. For every $x\in S$,
$c_{x-a}>0$, so $x-a\in T$. Thus $S\subseteq a+T$, while
$a+T\subseteq S$ follows from translation invariance. A subgroup coset
plainly attains equality.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Exact counting for a one-valued error\srctag{11}}]{Exact counting for a one-valued error}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:d3}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:onecolor}
\srcnote{11}{Section 3}

Let $S\subseteq G$, $|S|=s$, and $b\ne0$ in $W$. Consider
$g=b\one_S$. Every additive quadruple has four positions, with signs
$+,+,-,-$. Let $J$ denote the set of positions whose coordinates belong
to $S$.

Any choice of three coordinates uniquely determines the fourth, and any
choice of two coordinates has exactly $N$ completions. This remains true
when coordinates coincide or $G$ has torsion. Consequently, fixing three
specified positions in $S$ gives $s^3$ quadruples, fixing two gives $s^2N$,
and fixing one gives $sN^2$.

\begin{lemma}[Support-pattern counts]\label{gsr:en:11:lem:patterns}
The numbers of additive quadruples with exactly one, exactly three, or
exactly two same-side positions in $S$ are, respectively,
\begin{align}
 Q_1&=4sN^2-12s^2N+12s^3-4E(S),\label{gsr:en:11:eq:Q1}\\
 Q_3&=4s^3-4E(S),\label{gsr:en:11:eq:Q3}\\
 Q_{2,\mathrm{same}}&=2s^2N-4s^3+2E(S).\label{gsr:en:11:eq:Q2}
\end{align}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For one prescribed position in $S$ and the remaining three outside $S$,
inclusion--exclusion gives
$sN^2-3s^2N+3s^3-E(S)$; sum over the four positions.
For a prescribed triple of positions in $S$ and the remaining position
outside, the answer is $s^3-E(S)$; again there are four choices.
The two same-side pairs are $\{1,2\}$ and $\{3,4\}$. For either pair,
requiring the other two positions to lie outside $S$ gives
$s^2N-2s^3+E(S)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Exact one-valued defect]\label{gsr:en:11:prop:onecolor}
If $2b\ne0$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:oneodd}
 N^3-\Energy(b\one_S)=4sN^2-10s^2N+12s^3-6E(S).
\end{equation}
If $2b=0$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:onetwo}
 N^3-\Energy(b\one_S)=4sN^2-12s^2N+16s^3-8E(S).
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
When $2b\ne0$, the rejected support patterns have exactly one position,
exactly three positions, or exactly two positions on the same side.
Patterns with two opposite-side positions have equal contributions on
both sides, and patterns with zero or four positions also pass.
Thus the defect is $Q_1+Q_3+Q_{2,\mathrm{same}}$.

When $2b=0$, the same-side two-position patterns pass as well. The rejected
patterns are exactly those with an odd number of positions in $S$, giving
$Q_1+Q_3$.
\end{proof}

Write $t=s/N$ and $e_S=E(S)/N^3$. The two formulas become
\begin{align}
\defect(b\one_S)&=\Psi_0(t)+6(t^3-e_S),&&2b\ne0,\label{gsr:en:11:eq:oneoddnorm}\\
\defect(b\one_S)&=\Psi_1(t)+8(t^3-e_S),&&2b=0.\label{gsr:en:11:eq:onetwonorm}
\end{align}
The set-energy gap is therefore visible without any asymptotic notation.

\begin{example}[One corrupted point]\label{gsr:en:11:ex:spike}
Take $S=\{x_0\}$. Then $E(S)=1$, and
\[
 \Energy(b\one_{\{x_0\}})=
 \begin{cases}
 N^3-4N^2+10N-6,&2b\ne0,\\
 N^3-4N^2+12N-8,&2b=0.
 \end{cases}
\]
For $h\ne0$, the derivative histogram has entries $N-2,1,1$ in the first
case and $N-2,2$ in the second. This gives an independent check of the
counting formulas. The distinction depends on the target, not merely on
the parity of the domain size.
\end{example}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Replacing many error values by one: odd targets\srctag{11}}]{Replacing many error values by one: odd targets}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:d4}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:odd}
\srcnote{11}{Section 4}

Subtract an affine map and suppose now that $g$ is zero outside $S$ and
nonzero on $S$. For $b\ne0$ put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:colorstats}
 c_b=|\{x:g(x)=b\}|,\qquad
 M=\sum_{b\ne0}c_b^2,\qquad
 A=s^2-M,\qquad C=\sum_{b\ne0}c_bc_{-b}.
\end{equation}
The quantity $A$ counts ordered pairs of errors with different nonzero
values. It is zero exactly when all errors have one value.

\begin{lemma}[Two elementary color inequalities]\label{gsr:en:11:lem:color}
Let $T=s^3-\sum_{b\ne0}c_b^3$, the number of ordered non-monochromatic
triples of error positions. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:Tbound}
 T\le\frac32sA.
\end{equation}
For every target $W$, $C\le M$. If $W$ has no nonzero element of order two,
one also has $C\le A$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A non-monochromatic triple has at least two unequal pairs among its three
pairs of positions. Counting unequal pairs together with the third entry
gives $3sA$, which proves \eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:Tbound}.
The inequality $C\le M$ follows from
\[
 M-C=\frac12\sum_{b\ne0}(c_b-c_{-b})^2\ge0.
\]
When $b\ne-b$ for every nonzero $b$, the ordered pairs counted by $C$ form
a subset of the unequal-value ordered pairs counted by $A$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Odd-target error-value comparison]\label{gsr:en:11:prop:oddmono}
Suppose that $W$ has no nonzero element of order two. Choose any $b_0\ne0$
and put $g_0=b_0\one_S$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:oddmono}
 \Energy(g_0)-\Energy(g)\ge2(N-7s)A.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Separate additive quadruples according to the exact number of positions
in $S$. With zero positions, both maps pass; with one position, both fail;
with four positions, $g_0$ always passes and therefore cannot lose.
Only the cases with two or three positions need attention.

For two opposite-side positions, $g_0$ passes, whereas $g$ passes exactly
when the two nonzero values agree. There are four opposite-side pairs.
For one fixed pair and one of its $A$ unequal-value assignments, the
remaining coordinates have $N$ possible completions. For either remaining coordinate, at most $s$ completions put that
coordinate in $S$, since it varies bijectively with the free parameter. Thus at least
$N-2s$ completions have exactly these two errors. The total gain is at
least $4(N-2s)A$.

For two same-side positions, $g_0$ fails. The map $g$ can pass only when
the values are negatives of one another. Ignoring the restriction on the
other positions gives an upper bound $2NC$ for this loss, because there
are two same-side pairs.

For exactly three error positions, $g_0$ fails. If all three nonzero
values of $g$ are equal, $g$ fails as well: the signed sum is that value
or its negative. Therefore a gain for $g$ requires a non-monochromatic
triple. There are four triples of positions, and dropping the restriction
on the fourth position bounds this loss by $4T$.

Combining the three estimates and applying Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:11:lem:color},
\[
\begin{split}
 \Energy(g_0)-\Energy(g)
 &\ge4(N-2s)A-2NC-4T\\
 &\ge4(N-2s)A-2NA-6sA\\
 &=2(N-7s)A.
\end{split}
\]
Repeated coordinates create no missing cases: the fixed-position
parametrizations count them with their proper multiplicities.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Odd-target deficit decomposition]\label{gsr:en:11:thm:oddmaster}
Let $W$ have no nonzero element of order two, let $g=f-\ell$ for an affine
$\ell$, and use the notation above. Put
$a=A/N^2$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:oddmaster}
 \defect(f)\ge\Psi_0(t)+6(t^3-e_S)+2(1-7t)a.
\end{equation}
In particular, if $0<t<1/7$, the lower bound $\Psi_0(t)$ holds, and equality
is equivalent to $S$ being a subgroup coset and $g$ having one nonzero value.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Affine invariance, Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:11:prop:onecolor}, and
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:11:prop:oddmono} give \eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:oddmaster}.
If $t<1/7$, both remainder terms are nonnegative. Equality forces
$A=0$ and $E(S)=s^3$, giving the description by
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:11:lem:setcoset}. Conversely, that description attains equality
by \eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:oneoddnorm}.
\end{proof}

The comparison inequality is stronger than merely proving a cubic upper
bound for graph energy. It gives two independently meaningful certificates
of failure to be extremal: the support may have insufficient additive
energy, and the errors may use too many different values.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Targets with two-torsion, including mixed targets\srctag{11}}]{Targets with two-torsion, including mixed targets}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:d5}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:two}
\srcnote{11}{Section 5}

It is not necessary for the target to have characteristic two. In this
section $W$ may, for example, be $\Z/6\Z$; the hypothesis is only that it
contains a nonzero involution $b_0$. Keep $M,A,C$ as in
\eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:colorstats}, and put
\[
 J=M-C\ge0.
\]
The extra statistic $J$ measures the asymmetry between the multiplicities
of $b$ and $-b$.

\begin{proposition}[Error-value comparison with an involution]\label{gsr:en:11:prop:twomono}
If $s<N/3$ and $g_0=b_0\one_S$, with $2b_0=0$ and $b_0\ne0$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:twomono}
 \Energy(g_0)-\Energy(g)
 \ge6(N-3s)A+2(N-2s)J.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For exactly two errors, $g_0$ always passes. For an opposite-side pair,
$g$ fails on $A$ ordered assignments; for a same-side pair it fails on
$s^2-C=A+J$ assignments. Requiring the other two positions to be outside
$S$ leaves at least $N-2s$ completions for each assignment. Hence the
two-error gain is at least
\[
 (N-2s)\bigl(4A+2(A+J)\bigr).
\]
For exactly three errors, the loss is bounded by $4T\le6sA$ just as
before. With zero, one, or four errors, $g_0$ cannot lose. Subtraction
proves the assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Two-torsion deficit decomposition]\label{gsr:en:11:thm:twomaster}
Under these hypotheses, with $a=A/N^2$ and $j=J/N^2$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:twomaster}
 \defect(f)\ge\Psi_1(t)+8(t^3-e_S)
       +6(1-3t)a+2(1-2t)j.
\end{equation}
If $0<t<1/3$, equality with $\Psi_1(t)$ holds precisely when the error is
one involution-valued constant on a subgroup coset.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Combine \eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:onetwonorm} and \eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:twomono}.
At equality all three remainder terms vanish. The condition $A=0$ says
that exactly one nonzero value $b$ occurs. In this case $J=0$ is equivalent
to $b=-b$. The support condition again follows from
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:11:lem:setcoset}. The converse follows from the exact counting
formula.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why an odd-target assertion cannot simply ignore torsion]
For a one-point error into a target containing an involution,
Example~\ref{gsr:en:11:ex:spike} exceeds the odd-target extremal energy by $2N-2$.
The odd-target cubic is therefore false in this setting, not just
nonoptimal. The distinction has been incorporated at the level of the
hypotheses rather than hidden in a proof convention.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Quantitative information about near-extremizers\srctag{11}}]{Quantitative information about near-extremizers}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:d6}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:near}
\srcnote{11}{Section 6}

The preceding theorems also describe how an almost extremizer can fail to
be an exact extremizer. This does not require any compactness argument.

\begin{corollary}[Two separate defects in the odd case]\label{gsr:en:11:cor:nearodd}
Assume $0<t<1/7$ and
$\defect(f)\le\Psi_0(t)+\eta$. Then
\begin{align}
 t^3-e_S&\le\eta/6,\label{gsr:en:11:eq:nearsupport}\\
 \frac{A}{N^2}&\le\frac{\eta}{2(1-7t)}.\label{gsr:en:11:eq:nearcolor}
\end{align}
There is a nonzero value $b$ such that the proportion of domain points
with nonzero error different from $b$ is at most
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:minority}
 \frac{\eta}{2t(1-7t)}.
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The first two claims follow by dropping the other nonnegative term in
\eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:oddmaster}. If $m=\max_b c_b$ and $u=s-m$, then
$M\le sm$, so $A=s^2-M\ge su$. Divide by $N^2$ and use
\eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:nearcolor}.
\end{proof}

For a target with an involution, \eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:twomaster} similarly gives
\[
 t^3-e_S\le\eta/8,\qquad
 \frac A{N^2}\le\frac{\eta}{6(1-3t)},\qquad
 \frac J{N^2}\le\frac{\eta}{2(1-2t)}.
\]
The minority-value estimate follows by dividing the second inequality by
$t$. The third inequality is additional information not present in the
odd-target case.

These estimates do not by themselves state that $S$ is close in symmetric
difference to a subgroup coset. They reduce that remaining stability issue
to a precise high-energy question about $S$, with
$E(S)/s^3\ge1-\eta/(6t^3)$ in the odd case. That normalization matters:
an additive error small compared with one need not be small compared with
$t^3$. A full relative stability statement would have to retain this
scale.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Removing the assumption of proximity to an affine map\srctag{11}}]{Removing the assumption of proximity to an affine map}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:d7}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:correction}
\srcnote{11}{Section 7}

We now prove a correction lemma rather than taking it as a black box.
The method is classical; its role here is to enter the range where the
sharp cubics apply.

\begin{lemma}[Elementary correction of a nearly additive map]\label{gsr:en:11:lem:blr}
Let $F:G\to W$ and suppose
\[
 \Prb_{x,y}\bigl(F(x+y)\ne F(x)+F(y)\bigr)=\rho<1/6.
\]
Then there is a homomorphism $L:G\to W$ with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:coarse}
 \Prb_x(F(x)\ne L(x))\le\frac{\rho}{1-2\rho}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Fix $h\in G$ and consider the random value
$Z_h(y)=F(h+y)-F(y)$. For independent uniform $y,z$, both equations
\[
 F(h+y)+F(z)=F(h+y+z),\qquad
 F(y)+F(h+z)=F(h+y+z)
\]
hold except with probability at most $2\rho$. Each tested pair is uniformly
distributed on $G^2$, even for fixed $h$. When both equations hold,
$Z_h(y)=Z_h(z)$. Hence the collision probability of $Z_h$ is at least
$1-2\rho$.

For any probability distribution $(p_w)$, $\sum_wp_w^2\le\max_wp_w$.
Thus $Z_h$ has a unique modal value $L(h)$ of probability at least
$1-2\rho>1/2$. For fixed $h,k$, the three identities
\[
 Z_{h+k}(x)=L(h+k),\quad Z_h(x+k)=L(h),\quad Z_k(x)=L(k)
\]
hold simultaneously for some $x$, since their total failure probability
is at most $6\rho<1$. The exact derivative identity
$Z_{h+k}(x)=Z_h(x+k)+Z_k(x)$ then proves additivity of $L$.

If $F(h)\ne L(h)$, at least a proportion $1-2\rho$ of the values $Z_h(y)$
differ from $F(h)$. Averaging this observation over $h$ gives
\[
 \rho=\Prb_{h,y}(Z_h(y)\ne F(h))
 \ge(1-2\rho)\Prb_h(F(h)\ne L(h)),
\]
which proves \eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:coarse}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 11--14]
\emph{Credit and comparison.} The majority step $\sum_wp_w^2\le\max_wp_w$ used here is the coarsest of three collision-to-mode bounds in this report: source~07's Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:07:prop:collision} and source~12's sharp Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:12:lem:majority}, whose mode bound $1-\chi(\eta)$, $\chi(\eta)=(1-\sqrt{1-2\eta})/2\le\eta$, is optimal. Inserting source~12's lemma into this proof (with $\eta=2\rho$) would give disagreement at most $\rho/(1-\chi(2\rho))$ in \eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:coarse}; the consequence for the cutoff $34$ of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:11:thm:maingap} is recorded as a marked question, item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:smallgroups}, because neither source writes it.
\end{writenote}

\begin{lemma}[Passing from graph energy to the correction test]\label{gsr:en:11:lem:anchor}
There is an anchor $a\in G$ such that
$F_a(x)=f(a+x)-f(a)$ fails the test in Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:11:lem:blr} with
probability at most $\defect(f)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The average over $a,x,y$ of the acceptance condition is the probability
of
\[
 f(a+x)+f(a+y)=f(a)+f(a+x+y).
\]
The parametrization
$(a,x,y)\mapsto(a+x,a+y,a,a+x+y)$ is a bijection onto the ordered additive
quadruples. Its acceptance probability is exactly $1-\defect(f)$.
One anchor is at least as good as the average.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:11:thm:mainstability}]
Write $\defect=\defect(f)$. Applying Lemmas~\ref{gsr:en:11:lem:anchor} and
\ref{gsr:en:11:lem:blr} gives an affine map with disagreement proportion at most
\[
 \frac{\defect}{1-2\defect}<\frac17
 \qquad(\defect<1/9).
\]
In original coordinates this map is
$x\mapsto L(x-a)+f(a)$. The closest affine map has disagreement proportion
$d(f)<1/7$ as well, so Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:11:thm:mainlocal} gives
$\defect\ge\Psi_\kappa(d(f))$. Monotonicity on $[0,1/7]$ yields
\eqref{gsr:fm:11:eq:mainstability}.

Two distinct affine maps agree either nowhere or on a coset of the kernel
of a nonzero homomorphism. Such a coset has size at most $N/2$.
Their mutual Hamming distance is therefore at least $N/2$.
Two affine maps each at distance less than $N/7$ from $f$ cannot be
distinct. This proves uniqueness. Finally, equality in the inverse
inequality is equality in the corresponding local profile, whose equality
cases have already been classified.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A deterministic reconstruction algorithm}
The proof gives an explicit, though not optimized, algorithm for a finite
input table. Count the failed tests for each anchor $a$, select an anchor
with failure at most the average, and compute the modal derivative value
$L(h)$ for every $h$. Output $L(x-a)+f(a)$ and count its disagreements with
$f$. With group operations available by tables, straightforward enumeration
uses $O(N^3)$ elementary operations for the anchor search and $O(N^2)$
for the histograms, with sparse counters for target values. These operation
counts describe this implementation, not a claim of optimal complexity.
The cubic gives a certificate stronger than the preliminary
$\defect/(1-2\defect)$ estimate.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Exact inversion and sharp recovery constants\srctag{11}}]{Exact inversion and sharp recovery constants}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:d8}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:inverse}
\srcnote{11}{Section 8}

The odd-target cubic factors as
\[
 \Psi_0(t)=4t(1-t)(1-3t/2).
\]
The analytic inverse at zero therefore has a particularly explicit series.

\begin{proposition}[All-orders odd-target inverse]\label{gsr:en:11:prop:inverse}
For sufficiently small $u$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:lagrange}
 D_0(u)=\sum_{n\ge1} a_nu^n,
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:an}
 a_n=\frac{1}{n4^n}
 \sum_{j=0}^{n-1}
 \binom{n+j-1}{j}\binom{2n-j-2}{n-1-j}
 \left(\frac32\right)^{n-1-j}.
\end{equation}
In particular all the coefficients are positive, and the first eight are
\[
\begin{gathered}
\frac14,\quad\frac5{32},\quad\frac{11}{64},\quad\frac{475}{2048},\\
\frac{1427}{4096},\quad\frac{36645}{65536},\quad
\frac{123051}{131072},\quad\frac{13661175}{8388608}.
\end{gathered}
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The inverse equation is
\[
 t=u\,\frac{1}{4(1-t)(1-3t/2)}.
\]
The formal Lagrange coefficient identity gives
\[
 a_n=\frac1{n4^n}[z^{n-1}](1-z)^{-n}(1-3z/2)^{-n}.
\]
Expanding the two binomial series gives \eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:an}.
Since $\Psi_0'(0)=4$, the analytic inverse function theorem identifies the
formal expansion with a convergent inverse in a neighborhood of zero.
The exact rational substitution check through degree eight is included in
the verification script.
\end{proof}

No radius of convergence is needed for the quantitative theorem:
$D_0$ is defined there by the unique root in $[0,1/7]$. For numerical use,
bisection on that interval gives a certified value without relying on a
truncated asymptotic series. The beginning of the other branch is
\[
 D_1(u)=\frac u4+\frac{3u^2}{16}+\frac{u^3}{4}+O(u^4).
\]

\begin{proposition}[Sharpness along vanishing-density families]\label{gsr:en:11:prop:sharpinverse}
For either target type there are finite examples with $d(f)\to0$ and
\[
 d(f)=D_\kappa(\defect(f)).
\]
Consequently, no coefficient in the full small-$u$ expansion can be
decreased while keeping all preceding coefficients unchanged and an
error of smaller order, uniformly over finite groups.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Take a one-point error in cyclic groups of increasing order, or a coset
error of increasing index, using an involution when required. Let the
error density be $t$. Once $t<1/4$, the zero affine map is uniquely closest:
any other affine map differs from it on at least half the domain and
therefore differs from the error map on more than $tN$ points.
The exact defect is $\Psi_\kappa(t)$. For sufficiently large index this
defect is below $1/9$, and equality in the inverse follows. Comparison
along this sequence proves the coefficient assertion.
\end{proof}

\section[{The largest non-affine energy in arbitrary large finite groups\srctag{11}}]{The largest non-affine energy in arbitrary large finite groups}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:d9}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:global}
\srcnote{11}{Section 9}

We first prove the unrestricted-group part of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:11:thm:maingap}.
The key additional ingredient is merely the discreteness of Hamming
distance.

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:11:thm:maingap} for $N\ge34$]
For $N\ge34$,
\[
 \Psi_\kappa(1/N)\le\Psi_0(1/34)
 =\frac{4290}{39304}<\frac19.
\]
Suppose a non-affine $f$ had graph energy larger than the right-hand side
of \eqref{gsr:fm:11:eq:globalmax}. Its defect would be smaller than
$\Psi_\kappa(1/N)$. Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:11:thm:mainstability} would imply
$d(f)<1/N$, impossible for a non-affine function on an $N$-point set.

At equality the same theorem gives $d(f)\le1/N$. Non-affinity forces
$d(f)=1/N$, and the equality description of the small-error theorem gives
a one-point modification, of the required target order.
Conversely, such a modification has exactly the asserted energy by
Example~\ref{gsr:en:11:ex:spike}. It is non-affine because two distinct affine maps
cannot differ on only one point when $N\ge34$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Exact affine certification threshold]\label{gsr:en:11:cor:certificate}
For $N\ge34$, if
\[
 \Energy(f)>N^3-4N^2+(10+2\kappa)N-(6+2\kappa),
\]
then $f$ is affine. The strict inequality cannot be weakened.
\end{corollary}

This assertion is a complete extremal statement for this finite problem,
not just a stability estimate with an unspecified constant. It is also
uniform in the structures and cardinalities of the target groups, except
for the stated two-torsion distinction. The cutoff $34$ is a convenient
consequence of the correction radius, not a demonstrated optimal cutoff.

\begin{writeremarkc}[The cutoff cannot simply be dropped; added at the third write, 6~October 2026]\label{gsr:en:11:rem:cutoff}
For general finite abelian groups the formula \eqref{gsr:fm:11:eq:globalmax} can fail for $N<34$ (it holds for some such $N$ and fails for others); the smallest failure found has $N=4$. Take $G=\Z/12\Z$, $W=\Z/2\Z$ (so $\kappa=1$), and $f(x)=1$ if $x\bmod4\in\{0,1\}$, $f(x)=0$ otherwise. Then $f$ is not affine and
\[
 \Energy(f)=1296>1288=N^3-4N^2+12N-8\qquad(N=12).
\]
\emph{Proof.} Write $f=g\circ\pi$ with $\pi:\Z/12\Z\to\Z/4\Z$ the reduction and $g=\one_{\{0,1\}}$ on $\Z/4\Z$. Every additive quadruple of $\Z/12\Z$ maps to one of $\Z/4\Z$, and over each quadruple of $\Z/4\Z$ there are exactly $3^3=27$ (the lifts of $x_1,x_2,x_3$ are free and $x_4$ is then determined, and lies over the right point); whether $f$ respects a quadruple depends only on its image. Hence $\Energy(f)=27\,\Energy(g)$. By Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:11:lem:derivative}, $\Energy(g)=\sum_h\sum_wr_h(w)^2$: the derivatives in directions $0$ and $2$ are constant ($\Delta_2g\equiv1$), contributing $16$ each, and those in directions $1$ and $3$ take each value twice, contributing $8$ each; so $\Energy(g)=48$ and $\Energy(f)=1296$. The derivative $\Delta_1f$ takes both values ($\Delta_1f(0)=0$, $\Delta_1f(1)=1$), so $f$ is not affine by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:11:lem:full}. \emph{Exhaustive check at the write} (all maps, exact integers): the largest non-affine energies of maps $\Z/n\Z\to\Z/m\Z$ against the value of \eqref{gsr:fm:11:eq:globalmax} are $48$ against $40$ for $\Z/4\to\Z/2$, $85$ against $77$ for $\Z/5\to\Z/2$, $231$ against $223$ for $\Z/7\to\Z/2$, $162$ against $126$ for $\Z/6\to\Z/3$, $513$ against $489$ for $\Z/9\to\Z/3$ and $1296$ against $1288$ for $\Z/12\to\Z/2$, while the formula holds for $\Z/10$, $\Z/14$, $\Z/15$ and $\Z/16\to\Z/2$ (the intake found the same table, dossier \texttt{dossier116\_GOWERS}). This does not contradict the theorem, which assumes $N\ge34$, or its vector-space part ($\Z/12\Z$ and $\Z/4\Z$ are not vector spaces over a prime field). It shows that the cutoff cannot be removed for general groups and that its exact value is open (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:smallgroups}).
\end{writeremarkc}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{All finite vector-space sizes: a second proof\srctag{11}}]{All finite vector-space sizes: a second proof}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:d10}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:vector}
\srcnote{11}{Section 10}

Let $V=\F_p^n$, $W=\F_p^m$, and $N=p^n$. Assume throughout this section
that $f$ is non-affine. The proof has no high-energy correction hypothesis. It explains exactly where
prime-field structure helps with the small cardinalities.

\subsection{Constant-derivative directions and quotienting}
Define
\[
 H=\{h\in V:\Delta_hf\text{ is constant on }V\}.
\]
By \eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:cocycle}, $H$ is a subspace, and the constant derivative
values form a linear map $\lambda:H\to W$. Extend $\lambda$ to a linear
map $L:V\to W$ by extending a basis of $H$ to a basis of $V$.
The map $f-L$ is constant on each coset of $H$, so it factors through
$\bar f:V/H\to W$.

\begin{lemma}[Energy under quotienting]\label{gsr:en:11:lem:quotient}
Let $q=|V/H|$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:quotient}
 \frac{\Energy(f)}{N^3}=\frac{\Energy(\bar f)}{q^3}.
\end{equation}
The map $\bar f$ has no constant derivative in a nonzero direction.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Every additive quadruple in the quotient lifts to exactly $|H|^3$
additive quadruples in $V$, and respect for the function is unchanged
under this lift and subtraction of $L$. A nonzero constant-derivative
direction in the quotient would lift to a direction in $H$, a
contradiction.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The odd-characteristic histogram bound}
\begin{lemma}\label{gsr:en:11:lem:oddhist}
Let $p$ be odd, $q$ a positive power of $p$, and let a nonconstant
$q$-term list in $\F_p^m$ have sum zero. Its value multiplicities satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:oddhist}
 \sum_w r(w)^2\le(q-2)^2+2.
\end{equation}
Equality holds precisely when the three nonzero multiplicities are
$q-2,1,1$; the values are of the form $a,a+b,a-b$ with $b\ne0$.
For $q=3$ these three multiplicities are all one.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A multiplicity $q-1$ would give $(q-1)a+b=0$. Since $qa=0$, this forces
$b=a$, contradicting nonconstancy. If a value has multiplicity $q-2$,
the remaining two entries cannot be equal: equality to $b$ would give
$2(b-a)=0$. Thus they are distinct, and their sum must be $2a$.
This gives the asserted equality configuration.

If the maximum multiplicity is at most $q-3$ and $q\ge7$, convexity
(or transferring units from smaller counts to larger counts) bounds the
sum of squares by $(q-3)^2+3^2$, which is strictly less than
$(q-2)^2+2$. For $q=5$, a cap of two gives at most $2^2+2^2+1^2=9<11$.
For $q=3$, a nonconstant zero-sum list must have three distinct entries,
which is exactly the asserted configuration.
\end{proof}

For each derivative of $\bar f$, the sum of its values is zero, since
translation permutes the domain. Applying the lemma in every nonzero
direction and using the constant zero derivative in direction zero gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:quotoddgap}
 \defect(f)\ge\Psi_0(1/q).
\end{equation}
For real $q\ge4$, the function
$\Psi_0(1/q)=4/q-10/q^2+6/q^3$ is strictly decreasing; its derivative has
numerator $-4q^2+20q-18<0$ there. The only additional comparison needed
among powers of an odd prime is
$\Psi_0(1/3)>\Psi_0(1/9)$.
Thus if $q<N$, the inequality in \eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:quotoddgap} is strictly stronger
than $\defect(f)\ge\Psi_0(1/N)$.
This proves the odd-characteristic bound and shows that equality requires
$H=\{0\}$ and equality in every nonzero-direction histogram.

\subsection{Equality for odd characteristic}
Assume first that $N\ge7$. For each nonzero $h$, let $L(h)$ be the unique
modal derivative value, attained $N-2$ times, and put $L(0)=0$.
For any $h,k$, the three modal identities in
\eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:cocycle} exclude at most six choices of $x$. Since $N>6$, there
is a choice where all hold. Hence $L(h+k)=L(h)+L(k)$, and $L$ is linear.

Put $g=f-L$. For every $h\ne0$, exactly $N-2$ values of $x$ satisfy
$g(x+h)=g(x)$. If $t_w=|g^{-1}(w)|$, summing these equality counts gives
\[
 \sum_wt_w^2=N+(N-1)(N-2)=(N-1)^2+1.
\]
For a nonconstant map on $N$ points, the largest sum of squared fiber
sizes is $(N-1)^2+1$, and equality forces the fiber sizes $N-1,1$.
Indeed, among partitions of $N$ into at least two positive parts, moving
mass to the largest part increases the sum of squares until these two
parts remain. Thus $g$ is constant except at one point.

If $N=5$, take a generator and write its derivative values as
$a,a,a+b,a-b$, with $b\ne0$. After subtracting the linear map $x\mapsto ax$,
the derivative is zero except for one $b$ and one $-b$. Going around the
five-cycle, the function has two values on complementary cyclic intervals.
If either interval is a singleton, the required conclusion follows.
Otherwise their sizes are two and three; the step-two derivative then has
multiplicities $1,2,2$, whose squared sum is $9<11$, contradicting equality.

If $N=3$, subtract the affine map interpolating any two of the three
points. A non-affine map then differs at exactly the remaining point.
This completes the equality proof for every odd characteristic.

\subsection{Characteristic two}
If $p=2$, each derivative obeys
$\Delta_hf(x+h)=\Delta_hf(x)$, so for $h\ne0$ every histogram multiplicity
is even. On a quotient of size $q$, a nonconstant histogram therefore has
squared sum at most $(q-2)^2+4$, attained by multiplicities $q-2,2$.
A non-affine map cannot have quotient size two, since every map from
$\F_2$ to $W$ is affine. Thus $q\ge4$, and
\[
 \defect(f)\ge\Psi_1(1/q).
\]
The function $\Psi_1(1/q)$ is decreasing for real $q\ge8$, and
$\Psi_1(1/4)>\Psi_1(1/8)$. Hence it is strictly decreasing along the powers
of two that arise here. Equality at the $N$-point bound again forces
$H=\{0\}$ and extremal histograms in every nonzero direction.

For $N\ge8$, the modal values have exactly two exceptions, so the same
six-exception argument makes them a linear map. The fiber-square argument
then gives a one-point modification. For $N=4$, interpolate a linear-affine
map through $0,e_1,e_2$ and subtract it. Only the point $e_1+e_2$ remains,
so every non-affine map has the required form. This proves the remaining
part of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:11:thm:maingap}.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Partial domains and the interface with Proposition 6.1\srctag{11}}]{Partial domains and the interface with Proposition 6.1}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:d11}\label{gsr:en:11:sec:partial}
\srcnote{11}{Section 11}

Gowers's frequency-selection map is naturally defined on a subset rather
than the entire group. The full-energy normalization, not a normalization
by the subset size, gives a clean extension.

\begin{theorem}[Canonical affine recovery from a partial graph]\label{gsr:en:11:thm:partial}
Let $B\subseteq G$, $\phi:B\to W$, and let $\Gamma_B$ be its graph.
Suppose
\[
 E(\Gamma_B)\ge(1-\defect)N^3,\qquad 0\le\defect<1/9.
\]
There is a unique affine map $\ell:G\to W$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:partialerr}
 |\{x\in B:\phi(x)\ne\ell(x)\}|\le D_\kappa(\defect)N.
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:11:eq:holes}
 |G\setminus B|/N\le1-(1-\defect)^{1/3}.
\end{equation}
The same affine map is recovered by applying the full-domain theorem to
any completion of $\phi$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Set $\beta=|B|/N$. A graph with $|B|$ points has energy at most $|B|^3$,
so $\beta^3\ge1-\defect$, proving \eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:holes}.
Extend $\phi$ arbitrarily to $f:G\to W$. Every respected quadruple of the
partial graph is also a respected quadruple of the full graph, so
$\defect(f)\le\defect$. Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:11:thm:mainstability} and monotonicity of
$D_\kappa$ give an affine map satisfying \eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:partialerr}.

If two affine maps satisfy this inequality, their agreement set has size
at least $(\beta-2D_\kappa(\defect))N$. Here $D_\kappa(\defect)<1/7$,
while $\beta>(8/9)$, unless $\defect=0$, when the conclusion is immediate.
Thus
\[
 \beta-2D_\kappa(\defect)>\frac89-\frac27=\frac{38}{63}>\frac12.
\]
Distinct affine maps cannot agree on more than half the domain. This proves
uniqueness and independence from the completion.
\end{proof}

The error in \eqref{gsr:en:11:eq:partialerr} is normalized by $N$, not by $|B|$.
The statement requires a graph energy close to $N^3$. It does not assert
that an arbitrary sparse partial homomorphism with energy close to
$|B|^3$ extends to an affine map on the ambient group.

\begin{corollary}[A high-correlation refinement of the Section 6 output]\label{gsr:en:11:cor:prop61}
Let $N$ be an odd prime, $F:\Z/N\Z\to\mathbb C$ satisfy $|F|\le1$,
and let $\phi:B\to\Z/N\Z$ for $B\subseteq\Z/N\Z$. Use the unnormalized
Fourier transform $\widehat u(r)=\sum_xu(x)\exp(-2\pi i rx/N)$ and put
$\partial_hF(x)=F(x)\overline{F(x-h)}$. Suppose $\alpha>0$ and
\[
 \sum_{h\in B}|\widehat{\partial_hF}(\phi(h))|^2\ge\alpha N^3,
 \qquad \alpha^4>8/9.
\]
Then the frequency-selection map $\phi$ agrees on $B$ with a unique
affine map, except on at most
\[
 D_0(1-\alpha^4)N
\]
points. Also $|B|\ge\alpha^{4/3}N$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Proposition 6.1 gives at least $\alpha^4N^3$ respected quadruples, and the
graph identity in Lemma 6.2 converts this to the hypothesis of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:11:thm:partial}. The target $\Z/N\Z$ has no nonzero involution.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
Source~31's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:31:thm:graph} treats selected graphs on every finite abelian group, partial graphs included and with no amplitude bound: graph errors at most $\varepsilon$ and quadratic infidelity at most $(1-\sqrt{1-2\varepsilon})/2$ for score $1-\varepsilon$, $\varepsilon\le1/400$, both separately sharp.
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 54--59]
Source~59 lowers the condition $\alpha^4>8/9$ to $\alpha^4>7/9$ for targets without involutions (its Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:59:cor:affine-partial-two-ninths} and the paragraph after it).
\end{writenote}

The approximation error begins
\[
 \left(\frac{1-\alpha^4}{4}
 +\frac5{32}(1-\alpha^4)^2
 +\frac{11}{64}(1-\alpha^4)^3+O((1-\alpha^4)^4)\right)N.
\]
This corollary genuinely strengthens the structural information obtained
from that proposition in its high-correlation range. It does not improve
the exponent four in the original energy lower bound. In the usual
small-$\alpha$ inverse-theorem regime, its hypothesis is unavailable; this
is the precise reason it does not automatically improve the global
Szemer\'edi bound.

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 11--14]
\emph{Scope (intake observation, checked at the write).} The hypothesis that $N$ is an odd prime is not needed for the argument. The formal \file{proposition_6_1} (\file{Sections06\_07.lean}, line~37; exact companion \file{proposition_6_1_holds}, \file{Proofs05\_10.lean}, line~505, at HEAD \texttt{e1db00e99}) assumes only $N\ge1$, $0<\alpha$, $|F|\le1$ and the displayed Fourier hypothesis with the unnormalized transform and the same derivative $F(x)\overline{F(x-h)}$, and concludes at least $\alpha^4N^3$ respected quadruples; the graph identity of Lemma~6.2 and Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:11:thm:partial} hold for every finite abelian group. So the corollary holds for every odd $N$ as stated, and for even $N$ with $D_1$ in place of $D_0$ (then $\Z/N\Z$ contains the involution $N/2$). \section{Source~12's chapter: Freiman extension and Bohr radii in Section~10 \wtag}\label{gsr:en:sec:bohr}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the third write, 6~October 2026.}}\par
The next nine sections are source~12, a manuscript on the second half of Gowers's Section~10, Lemmas~10.10--10.14: extending a Freiman homomorphism from a dense subset of a Bohr set to a smaller Bohr set, choosing the Bohr radii, and the local model of Theorem~10.13. \emph{Logically the chapter continues source~07's chapter} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:transport}), which treats Lemma~10.9, the step just before: together they cover Section~10 from Lemma~10.6 to Corollary~10.14, and they share no statement. It is printed here, at the end of Part~II, because no number printed earlier may move. Its notation follows the Section~10 table at the head of this Part. Its introduction is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:12:sec:d1}; its formalization interfaces, checks, questions and parameter ledger are in Part~V (Sections~\ref{gsr:fz:12:sec:d10}--\ref{gsr:fz:12:sec:dB}). Its Appendix~A, the fixed-domain repair of the extraction input, is printed at the end of this chapter, beside the theorem that uses it.

\emph{What is proved, in one paragraph.} If $S\subseteq B$ misses at most a fraction $\varepsilon$ of $B$ and every shift in $C$ loses at most a fraction $\kappa$ of $B$, a Freiman homomorphism on $S$ induces one on $C$ whenever $3\varepsilon+2\kappa<1$, and every rational boundary point has a counterexample (Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:sharp-extension}, \ref{gsr:en:12:thm:sharpness}); the collision-to-mode bound $1-\chi(\eta)$ is sharp (Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:12:lem:majority}); a finite pigeonhole among $m$ radii selects an ambient radius with overlap $4^{-d/m}$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:radius}); a fourth-moment estimate enlarges the initial radius from $2^{-148}\alpha^{18}/\pi$ to $2^{-74}\alpha^9/\pi$ with the same spectrum (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:smoothing}); and Theorem~10.13 holds on a Bohr set of radius at least $\alpha^{19}/(3\pi2^{149})$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:main}, Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:12:cor:fixed-spectrum}). The component-extraction input (Lemmas~10.3--10.9) is borrowed, with its hypotheses stated (Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:12:lem:component-input}); sharpness is universal over groups, not for prime cyclic groups with the same target (the source's non-claims).

\section[{Translation loss and intersections along a tree\srctag{12}}]{Translation loss and intersections along a tree}\label{gsr:en:12:sec:d2}
\srcnote{12}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:en:12:sec:boundary}

Throughout the algebraic parts, $G$ and $H$ are abelian groups written additively. The ambient group $G$ need not be finite, but $B\subseteq G$ is finite and nonempty. For $t\in G$, $B-t=\{x:x+t\in B\}$. All missing densities are measured relative to $|B|$, not $|G|$.

\begin{definition}
A function $\phi:S\to H$ is a \emph{Freiman homomorphism of order two} if
\[
 a+b=c+d,\quad a,b,c,d\in S
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \phi(a)+\phi(b)=\phi(c)+\phi(d).
\]
Repeated elements are permitted. A Freiman homomorphism of order $r$ preserves all equalities between sums of $r$ elements of its domain.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Elementary properties of translation loss]
\label{gsr:en:12:lem:boundary-properties}
For every $u,v\in G$,
\[
 b_B(0)=0,\quad b_B(-u)=b_B(u),\quad
 0\le b_B(u)\le1,\quad b_B(u+v)\le b_B(u)+b_B(v).
\]
Also $|B\mathbin\triangle(B-u)|=2b_B(u)|B|$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Finite translates have equal cardinality, so each one-sided difference has half the cardinality of the symmetric difference. Translation gives symmetry. For subadditivity, use
\[
 B\setminus(B-u-v)\subseteq
 [B\setminus(B-u)]\cup[(B-u)\setminus(B-u-v)]
\]
and count. The other claims follow directly from the definition.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Intersection bound along a tree]
\label{gsr:en:12:lem:tree}
Let $t_0,\dots,t_m\in G$, and let $T$ be a tree on the labels $0,\dots,m$. Suppose $S_i\subseteq B$ and $|B\setminus S_i|\le\eps_i|B|$. Then
\begin{equation}
 \left|\bigcap_{i=0}^m(S_i-t_i)\right|
 \ge\left(1-\sum_{i=0}^m\eps_i
              -\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E(T)}b_B(t_i-t_j)\right)|B|.
 \label{gsr:en:12:eq:tree}
\end{equation}
The right side may be negative; its useful content is when it is positive.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Root the tree at 0 and add its vertices in an order in which each parent precedes its children. Before adding a child $j$ with parent $i$, the current intersection of ambient translates is contained in $B-t_i$. Imposing membership in $B-t_j$ therefore removes at most
\[
 |(B-t_i)\setminus(B-t_j)|=b_B(t_j-t_i)|B|
\]
points. Starting with a translate of $B$ proves the bound with all $S_i=B$. Replacing $B-t_i$ by $S_i-t_i$ removes at most $\eps_i|B|$ further points. Summing these losses proves \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:tree}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
Source~30's Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:30:lem:tree} is this lemma (with losses counted in points), proved again without citation.
\end{writenote}

This formulation records the geometry of the configuration. One pays for the edges of a spanning tree, and can choose the tree of least total translation loss. It avoids charging every displacement independently from a single base point.

\begin{corollary}[Two and three translated copies]
\label{gsr:en:12:cor:triangle}
If $S\subseteq B$ and $|S|\ge(1-\eps)|B|$, then
\begin{align}
 |S\cap(S-t)|&\ge(1-2\eps-b_B(t))|B|,\label{gsr:en:12:eq:pair}\\
 |S\cap(S-c)\cap(S-c-d)|
 &\ge(1-3\eps-b_B(c)-b_B(d))|B|.\label{gsr:en:12:eq:triangle}
\end{align}
In the second inequality, $b_B(c)+b_B(d)$ can be replaced by
\[
 \tau_B(c,d)=\min\{b_B(c)+b_B(d),\ b_B(c)+b_B(c+d),\ b_B(d)+b_B(c+d)\}.
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply lemma~\ref{gsr:en:12:lem:tree} to the vertices $0,t$ or $0,c,c+d$. The three possible trees on the latter vertices give the stated minimum.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A sharp theorem for induced Freiman homomorphisms\srctag{12}}]{A sharp theorem for induced Freiman homomorphisms}\label{gsr:en:12:sec:d3}
\srcnote{12}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:en:12:sec:exact}

\begin{lemma}[The canonical difference map]
\label{gsr:en:12:lem:difference}
If $S\ne\varnothing$ and $\phi:S\to H$ is a Freiman homomorphism, there is a unique map $D:S-S\to H$ satisfying
\[
 D(y-x)=\phi(y)-\phi(x)\qquad(x,y\in S).
\]
It obeys $D(0)=0$ and $D(-t)=-D(t)$. If $x,x+c,x+c+d\in S$, then
\begin{equation}
                       D(c)+D(d)=D(c+d).\label{gsr:en:12:eq:triangle-add}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $y-x=v-u$, then $y+u=v+x$, so the Freiman property gives $\phi(y)-\phi(x)=\phi(v)-\phi(u)$. This proves well-definedness and uniqueness. Swapping the ordered pair gives oddness. The three-point identity follows by telescoping the two successive increments.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp density--overlap extension]
\label{gsr:en:12:thm:sharp-extension}
Let $S\subseteq B$ with $|S|\ge(1-\eps)|B|$, and let $C\subseteq G$ be symmetric with $0\in C$. Suppose
\[
 b_B(c)\le\kappa\quad(c\in C),\qquad 3\eps+2\kappa<1.
\]
Then, for every Freiman homomorphism $\phi:S\to H$:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $C+C\subseteq S-S$;
\item its canonical difference map satisfies $D(c)+D(d)=D(c+d)$ for every $c,d\in C$;
\item $D|_C$ is a Freiman homomorphism of order two and $D(0)=0$.
\end{enumerate}
More precisely, every ordered pair $c,d\in C$ has at least $(1-3\eps-2\kappa)|B|$ witnesses $x$ with $x,x+c,x+c+d\in S$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The witness count is \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:triangle}. It is positive, so for each $c,d$ a witness exists. Its endpoints show that $c+d\in S-S$, and lemma~\ref{gsr:en:12:lem:difference} gives (ii). If $c_1+c_2=c_3+c_4$, with all $c_i\in C$, both sums of $D$-values equal the same well-defined value $D(c_1+c_2)$. This proves (iii).
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
Source~30's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:30:thm:extension} needs $4\varepsilon+3\kappa<1$ at order two, which implies the condition here; with source~30's fixed-radius estimate this theorem gives the larger fixed radius of the note after its Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:30:cor:extension-only}.
\end{writenote}

Only losses for shifts in $C$ are required. Imposing the same loss bound on $C+C$ would unnecessarily shrink the eventual Bohr radius. The proof also explains why one does not need to find one base point supporting two entire decompositions of a sum: the canonical difference at their common endpoint makes two separate triangles sufficient.

\begin{theorem}[Sharpness on the whole boundary]
\label{gsr:en:12:thm:sharpness}
Every rational pair $(\eps,\kappa)$ with $0\le\eps\le1/3$, $0\le\kappa\le1/2$, and $3\eps+2\kappa=1$ occurs in a finite example satisfying the size and overlap hypotheses of theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:sharp-extension} but not its conclusion.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $K$ be a finite abelian group of size $m$, choose $T\subseteq K$ of size $t$, $0\le t\le m$, and put
\[
 G=\Z/3\Z\times K,\quad
 S=\{0,1\}\times K,\quad
 B=S\cup(\{2\}\times T),\quad
 C=\Z/3\Z\times\{0\}.
\]
Define $\phi:S\to\Z$ by $\phi(a,k)=a$ using the representatives $a=0,1$. This is a Freiman homomorphism: the sum of two first coordinates is one of $0,1,2$, and equality modulo 3 of such sums is equality as integers.

We have $|B|=2m+t$, $|S|=2m$, and, for either nonzero $c\in C$, $|B\cap(B-c)|=m+2t$. Therefore
\[
 \eps=\frac{t}{2m+t},\qquad
 \kappa=\frac{m-t}{2m+t},\qquad
 3\eps+2\kappa=1.
\]
Writing $e=(1,0)$, the induced values are $D(e)=1$, $D(2e)=-1$, and $D(0)=0$. But $e+e=2e+0$, whereas $1+1\ne-1+0$. Thus $D|_C$ is not a Freiman homomorphism. Finally, every rational $\eps\in[0,1/3]$ is obtained by taking $t/m=2\eps/(1-\eps)$ and clearing denominators.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Scope of sharpness]
This is a sharp universal statement over abelian ambient and target groups. It does not assert an optimal threshold when both groups are the same prime cyclic group. The example uses a target in which three times a nonzero value need not vanish. Symmetric ambient examples are also available by using the two slices $\{-1,1\}\times K$ and a symmetric subset of the zero slice, with the corresponding integer-valued map.
\end{remark}

\begin{figure}[ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=.76\textwidth]{figures/12-bohr-extension-extension_frontier.pdf}
\caption{The universal sufficient region is below the line $3\eps+2\kappa=1$. The construction in theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:sharpness} supplies counterexamples densely along the boundary. The diagram records an exact theorem, not an empirical fit.}
\label{gsr:en:12:fig:frontier}
\end{figure}

\begin{corollary}[Global extension above two thirds]
\label{gsr:en:12:cor:global}
If $G$ is finite, $|S|>2|G|/3$, and $\phi:S\to H$ is a Freiman homomorphism, then there are a unique homomorphism $D:G\to H$ and a unique $h_0\in H$ such that
\[
                         \phi(x)=h_0+D(x)\quad(x\in S).
\]
The constant $2/3$ cannot be reduced uniformly over $G,H$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Take $B=C=G$ and $\kappa=0$. The canonical difference map is additive on all of $G$. Fix $x_0\in S$ and put $h_0=\phi(x_0)-D(x_0)$. The difference identity gives the formula for all $x\in S$. Since $S-S=G$, any affine extension has this same difference map and then the same constant. Set $t=m$ in theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:sharpness} for the endpoint obstruction.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Higher-order local extension]
\label{gsr:en:12:thm:higher}
Let $r\ge2$ be an integer. Under the same set hypotheses, replace the numerical condition by $3\eps+r\kappa<1$. Then $rC\subseteq S-S$, and the canonical difference map satisfies
\[
 D(c_1+\cdots+c_j)=D(c_1)+\cdots+D(c_j)
 \quad(1\le j\le r,\ c_i\in C).
\]
In particular, $D|_C$ is a Freiman homomorphism of order $r$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Subadditivity gives $b_B(t)\le r\kappa$ for $t\in rC$. The pair bound is positive since $1-2\eps-r\kappa>0$, so $rC\subseteq S-S$. For a partial sum $u=c_1+\cdots+c_{j-1}$, the triangle loss is at most $b_B(u)+b_B(c_j)\le j\kappa$. Thus \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:triangle-add} applies and proves the identity inductively. Two equal sums of $r$ elements have the same canonical difference value. We make no optimality claim for this higher-order numerical condition.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Correction from concentrated directional increments\srctag{12}}]{Correction from concentrated directional increments}\label{gsr:en:12:sec:d4}
\srcnote{12}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:en:12:sec:robust}

The exact Freiman hypothesis can be weakened in a way that separates algebraic errors from missing points. This is useful for local repair, although a global average over all additive quadruples does not by itself give the uniform directional hypothesis below.

For any function $\phi:S\to H$ and any $t\in S-S$, let
\[
 E_t=\{x\in S:x+t\in S\},\qquad
 p_t(h)=\frac{|\{x\in E_t:\phi(x+t)-\phi(x)=h\}|}{|E_t|}.
\]
These distributions have finite support even when $H$ is infinite. Their collision probabilities are
\[
 Q_t=\sum_{h\in H}p_t(h)^2.
\]
Equivalently, $Q_t$ is the fraction of ordered pairs of $t$-edges with the same increment label.

\begin{lemma}[Sharp collision-to-majority bound]
\label{gsr:en:12:lem:majority}
For $0\le\eta<1/2$ define
\[
                  \chi(\eta)=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-2\eta}}2.
\]
If a finite probability distribution $p$ has $\sum p_i^2\ge1-\eta$, its largest atom is unique and has mass at least $1-\chi(\eta)$. This bound is sharp.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $a=\max p_i$. Since $\sum p_i^2\le a$, we have $a\ge1-\eta>1/2$. Also
\[
 \sum p_i^2\le a^2+(1-a)^2.
\]
Solving $a^2+(1-a)^2\ge1-\eta$ on the interval $a>1/2$ gives the asserted lower bound. A two-atom distribution with masses $1-\chi(\eta)$ and $\chi(\eta)$ attains equality.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 11--14]
\emph{Credit.} This is the sharpest of the report's collision-to-mode bounds: source~07's Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:07:prop:collision} and source~11's Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:11:lem:blr} (which uses $\sum p_i^2\le\max p_i$, mode at least $1-\eta$) are weaker, since $\chi(\eta)\le\eta$. Source~14's envelope $\tau(\varepsilon)=(1-\sqrt{1-4\varepsilon})/2$ is the same function, $\tau(\varepsilon)=\chi(2\varepsilon)$, in a different problem.
\end{writenote}

\begin{theorem}[Directional repair]
\label{gsr:en:12:thm:repair}
Let $S\subseteq B$, $C=-C$, $0\in C$, $|S|\ge(1-\eps)|B|$, and $b_B(c)\le\kappa$ for $c\in C$. Suppose
\begin{equation}
                         3\eps+2\kappa+3\chi(\eta)<1,
 \qquad 0\le\eta<1/2.\label{gsr:en:12:eq:robust-budget}
\end{equation}
Assume $Q_t\ge1-\eta$ for every $t\in C+C$. Then the majority increment $D(t)$ is well defined on $C+C$, and
\[
              D(c)+D(d)=D(c+d)\qquad(c,d\in C).
\]
Consequently $D|_C$ is an exact Freiman homomorphism, $D(0)=0$, and at least $1-\chi(\eta)$ of the $t$-edges carry label $D(t)$ for every $t\in C+C$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The strict budget first implies $3\eps+2\kappa<1$, so the geometric triangle bound shows $C+C\subseteq S-S$ without any algebraic assumption on $\phi$. Thus the distributions in the hypothesis exist. By lemma~\ref{gsr:en:12:lem:majority}, each majority label is unique and at most $\chi(\eta)|E_t|$ of its edges are bad.

Fix $c,d\in C$ and put $s=c+d$. There are at least $(1-3\eps-2\kappa)|B|$ points $x$ with $x,x+c,x+s\in S$. Among these witnesses, at most $\chi(\eta)|E_c|$ have a bad first edge, at most $\chi(\eta)|E_d|$ have a bad second edge (translate its starting point by $c$), and at most $\chi(\eta)|E_s|$ have a bad direct edge. Each $|E_t|\le|B|$, so \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:robust-budget} leaves a witness with all three edges good. Telescoping its actual $\phi$-increments proves the additive identity. The remaining conclusions follow as in theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:sharp-extension}; the zero increment is identically zero.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The exact nonuniform budget]
For a fixed triangle, one may instead require
\[
 1-3\eps-\tau_B(c,d)
 >\frac{\chi(\eta_c)|E_c|+\chi(\eta_d)|E_d|+
              \chi(\eta_{c+d})|E_{c+d}|}{|B|},
\]
where $Q_t\ge1-\eta_t$ and each $\eta_t<1/2$. This follows from precisely the same witness count. The three equal error allowances in \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:robust-budget} are a convenient uniform specialization, not an asserted optimal repair threshold.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[Global affine repair]
\label{gsr:en:12:cor:global-repair}
Take $B=C=G$ finite, $|S|\ge(1-\eps)|G|$, and assume $3\eps+3\chi(\eta)<1$ and $Q_t\ge1-\eta$ for every $t\in G$. Then the majority increments give a homomorphism $D:G\to H$, and some $h_0\in H$ satisfies
\[
 |\{x\in S:\phi(x)=h_0+D(x)\}|
 \ge [1-\chi(\chi(\eta))]|S|.
\]
In particular the weaker, simpler proportion $1-\chi(\eta)$ also holds.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The repair theorem makes $D$ additive everywhere. Put $F(x)=\phi(x)-D(x)$ on $S$. Every ordered pair $(x,y)\in S^2$ appears in exactly one direction $t=y-x$. It has $F(y)\ne F(x)$ exactly when its directional edge is bad. Hence
\[
 |\{(x,y)\in S^2:F(x)\ne F(y)\}|
 \le \chi(\eta)\sum_t|E_t|=\chi(\eta)|S|^2.
\]
The distribution of $F$ therefore has collision probability at least $1-\chi(\eta)$. A second application of lemma~\ref{gsr:en:12:lem:majority} gives the result.
\end{proof}

The error parameter is conditional on a direction. Replacing this by the assertion that a $1-\eta$ fraction of all additive quadruples is respected is a different problem: directions with few representations can have large conditional error. The component-extraction stage of Gowers's proof is designed to cope with this difficulty. Our repair theorem does not silently remove that stage.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A finite selection argument for Bohr radii\srctag{12}}]{A finite selection argument for Bohr radii}\label{gsr:en:12:sec:d5}
\srcnote{12}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:en:12:sec:bohr}

Let $G$ now be a finite abelian group of order $N$, and identify characters with homomorphisms $\gamma:G\to\T=\R/\Z$. Write $\|u\|_\T$ for distance to the nearest integer. For a finite set $\Gamma$ of $d$ characters and $r>0$, set
\[
 \Bohr(\Gamma,r)=\{x\in G:\|\gamma(x)\|_\T\le r
                                      \text{ for every }\gamma\in\Gamma\}.
\]
These are closed Bohr sets, matching the weak inequalities in the repository. The case $\Gamma=\varnothing$ gives $G$ and reduces to the global extension theorem; below $d\ge1$.

\begin{lemma}[Elementary size and doubling bounds]
\label{gsr:en:12:lem:bohr-cover}
For $0<r\le1/2$,
\begin{align}
 |\Bohr(\Gamma,r)|&\ge \frac{N}{\lceil1/r\rceil^d}
                    \ge (r/2)^dN,\label{gsr:en:12:eq:bohr-size}\\
 |\Bohr(\Gamma,r)|&\le4^d|\Bohr(\Gamma,r/2)|.\label{gsr:en:12:eq:bohr-double}
\end{align}
Also $\Bohr(\Gamma,r)+\Bohr(\Gamma,s)\subseteq\Bohr(\Gamma,r+s)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Map $x$ to its $d$ character values in $\T^d$. Divide each circle into $\lceil1/r\rceil$ half-open intervals of equal length at most $r$. Some product cell has at least $N/\lceil1/r\rceil^d$ preimages. Subtract a fixed preimage from all others in that cell; the differences belong to $\Bohr(\Gamma,r)$. The weaker bound follows from $\lceil1/r\rceil\le2/r$.

For \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:bohr-double}, represent all character values of $\Bohr(\Gamma,r)$ in $[-r,r]$. Partition this cube into $4^d$ cells of side length $r/2$, assigning boundary points consistently. In each occupied cell choose one preimage. Subtraction from that preimage injects the cell's preimages into $\Bohr(\Gamma,r/2)$. Sum over the cells. The final assertion is the triangle inequality on $\T$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[One-scale radius selection]
\label{gsr:en:12:thm:radius}
Let $0<\rho\le1/2$ and let $m\ge1$ be an integer. Put $s=\rho/(2m)$. There is
\[
 r\in\left\{\frac\rho2+js:1\le j\le m\right\}\subseteq(\rho/2,\rho]
\]
such that, for $B=\Bohr(\Gamma,r)$,
\begin{equation}
 |B\cap(B-c)|\ge4^{-d/m}|B|
                 \qquad(c\in\Bohr(\Gamma,s)).\label{gsr:en:12:eq:one-scale}
\end{equation}
More generally, replace $4^d$ by the actual ratio
\[
             R=\frac{|\Bohr(\Gamma,\rho)|}{|\Bohr(\Gamma,\rho/2)|}
\]
and replace $4^{-d/m}$ by $R^{-1/m}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Set $r_j=\rho/2+js$, $0\le j\le m$, and $a_j=|\Bohr(\Gamma,r_j)|$. The product of $a_{j-1}/a_j$ is $a_0/a_m=R^{-1}\ge4^{-d}$. Therefore some ratio is at least $R^{-1/m}\ge4^{-d/m}$. Choose that $j$ and $r=r_j$. If $x\in\Bohr(\Gamma,r-s)$ and $c\in\Bohr(\Gamma,s)$, both $x$ and $x+c$ belong to $B$. Thus the inner set is contained in $B\cap(B-c)$, proving the assertion.
\end{proof}

This proves the needed overlap at one scale with a finite pigeonhole argument. It does not assert that $B$ is regular at every smaller relative change of radius in the standard sense. Full regularity is available from the classical theory \cite{greentaoUthree}, but is unnecessary here.

\begin{corollary}[A replacement for Corollary 10.11]
\label{gsr:en:12:cor:bohr-extension}
Given $\Gamma$, $d\ge1$, and $0<\rho\le1/2$, there exists $r\in(\rho/2,\rho]$ such that every $S\subseteq B=\Bohr(\Gamma,r)$ with $|S|\ge7|B|/8$ and every Freiman homomorphism $\phi:S\to H$ induce a Freiman homomorphism on
\[
                         C=\Bohr(\Gamma,\rho/(8d)).
\]
In fact $C+C\subseteq S-S$ and the induced difference map is additive on pairs from $C$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Take $m=4d$ in theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:radius}. Then $\kappa=1-1/\sqrt2$ is admissible, and
\[
 3\cdot\frac18+2\left(1-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)
                  =\frac{19}{8}-\sqrt2<1.
\]
Apply theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:sharp-extension}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 11--14]
\emph{Scope.} As the remark ``Why the order of selection matters'' in Section~\ref{gsr:en:12:sec:bohr} and the caption of Table~\ref{gsr:fm:12:tab:overview} say, the ambient radius $r$ is \emph{selected} in $(\rho/2,\rho]$ before the dense subset is chosen. So this corollary is an alternative to Corollary~10.11 with a changed quantifier order, not a replacement for it at a prescribed radius; the abstract's word ``replaces'' (Section~\ref{gsr:fm:12:sec:d1}) should be read this way. \emph{Observation (intake, checked at the write):} the hypotheses $C=-C$ and $0\in C$ of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:sharp-extension} are not used by its proof: for $c,d\in C$ the witness count gives $x,x+c,x+c+d\in S$, hence $c,d,c+d\in S-S$, and the conclusions follow; $D(0)=0$ holds since $S\ne\varnothing$.
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
At a prescribed radius $\rho\le1/4$ source~30 gives $\rho/(8(3^r-1))$ with the same margins (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:30:cor:margin}; $r$ here is $d$), and shows that a fixed-radius estimate must depend exponentially on the rank (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:30:cor:exponential}); this corollary's $\rho/(8d)$ uses the selected radius.
\end{writenote}

\begin{corollary}[General density and extension order]
\label{gsr:en:12:cor:bohr-general}
Let $0\le\eps<1/3$ and $q\ge2$. If the integer $m$ satisfies
\[
                         3\eps+q(1-4^{-d/m})<1,
\]
the selected radius in theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:radius} makes every Freiman homomorphism on a $(1-\eps)$-dense subset of $B$ induce a Freiman homomorphism of order $q$ on $\Bohr(\Gamma,\rho/(2m))$. In particular, one can take any integer
\[
 m>\frac{d\log4}{-\log\left(1-(1-3\eps)/q\right)}.
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Use theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:higher} with $\kappa=1-4^{-d/m}$. Rearranging the strict inequality gives the displayed sufficient choice.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why the order of selection matters]
The radius $r$ depends only on $\Gamma,\rho,m$, not on the later subset or map. This is exactly the quantifier order required in the application. If a dense subset of $\Bohr(\Gamma,\rho)$ has already been fixed, shrinking the ambient radius can concentrate all its missing points in the smaller set. Its relative density need not survive. We therefore select $r$ before invoking component extraction.
\end{remark}

\begin{example}[Why a factor of the rank is natural]
In $G=(\Z/L\Z)^d$, take the $d$ coordinate characters and $\rho<1/4$. For large $L$, the Bohr set is a product of intervals of length about $2\rho L$. A shift whose every coordinate is about $sL$ has overlap ratio tending to
\[
                           \left(1-\frac{s}{2\rho}\right)^d.
\]
Keeping this uniformly above a fixed positive constant requires $s=O(\rho/d)$. Thus the inverse-rank scale in the overlap method is necessary for this family; the example does not assert optimality of the constants 6 or 8.
\end{example}

\section[{Fourier smoothing with the full fourth moment\srctag{12}}]{Fourier smoothing with the full fourth moment}\label{gsr:en:12:sec:d6}
\srcnote{12}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:en:12:sec:fourier}

We use unnormalized Fourier transforms and convolutions in this section:
\[
 \widehat g(\gamma)=\sum_{x\in G}g(x)e^{-2\pi i\gamma(x)},\qquad
 (f*g)(x)=\sum_{y\in G}f(y)g(x-y).
\]
Thus $g(x)=N^{-1}\sum_\gamma\widehat g(\gamma)e^{2\pi i\gamma(x)}$ and $\sum_\gamma|\widehat g(\gamma)|^2=N\sum_x|g(x)|^2$.

\begin{theorem}[Fourth-moment smoothing]
\label{gsr:en:12:thm:smoothing}
Let $0\le g(x)\le M$ and $\sum_xg(x)=\alpha MN$, where $M>0$ and $0<\alpha\le1$. Put
\[
 L=\alpha^3M^4N^3,\quad
 h=g*\widetilde g*g*\widetilde g,\quad
 \widetilde g(x)=g(-x),
\]
and, for $\lambda>0$, let
\[
 \Gamma=\{\gamma:|\widehat g(\gamma)|\ge\lambda MN\},\qquad d=|\Gamma|.
\]
Then, for every $\rho>0$,
\begin{align}
 d&\le\frac{\alpha}{\lambda^2},\label{gsr:en:12:eq:rank}\\
 \sum_\gamma|\widehat g(\gamma)|^4&\le LN,\label{gsr:en:12:eq:fourth}\\
 \sup_x|h(x+t)-h(x)|
 &\le\left(2\pi\rho+\frac{2\lambda^2}{\alpha^2}\right)L
       \quad(t\in\Bohr(\Gamma,\rho)).\label{gsr:en:12:eq:smooth}
\end{align}
More precisely, if $\xi=(LN)^{-1}\sum_\gamma|\widehat g(\gamma)|^4$, then $\alpha\le\xi\le1$ and $2\pi\rho$ in \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:smooth} can be replaced by $2\pi\rho\xi$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Parseval and $g^2\le Mg$ give
\[
 \sum_\gamma|\widehat g(\gamma)|^2
       =N\sum_xg(x)^2\le\alpha M^2N^2.
\]
Each element of $\Gamma$ contributes at least $\lambda^2M^2N^2$, proving \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:rank}. Since $|\widehat g(\gamma)|\le\alpha MN$,
\[
 \sum_\gamma|\widehat g(\gamma)|^4
 \le(\alpha MN)^2\sum_\gamma|\widehat g(\gamma)|^2
 \le\alpha^3M^4N^4=LN.
\]
The zero-frequency term alone is $\alpha^4M^4N^4=\alpha LN$, proving the lower bound for $\xi$.

The convolution identity is $\widehat h(\gamma)=|\widehat g(\gamma)|^4$. On $\Gamma$, membership of $t$ in the Bohr set gives
\[
 |e^{2\pi i\gamma(t)}-1|\le2\pi\rho.
\]
On the complement, use the bound 2 and
\[
 \sum_{\gamma\notin\Gamma}|\widehat g(\gamma)|^4
 \le\lambda^2M^2N^2\sum_\gamma|\widehat g(\gamma)|^2
 \le\alpha\lambda^2M^4N^4.
\]
Fourier inversion, with its factor $1/N$, now yields
\[
 |h(x+t)-h(x)|
 \le2\pi\rho\xi L+2\alpha\lambda^2M^4N^3
 =\left(2\pi\rho\xi+\frac{2\lambda^2}{\alpha^2}\right)L.
\]
This proves all the claims.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The precise improvement over the original estimate}

The original large-spectrum estimate bounds the sum of fourth powers on $\Gamma$ by $d(\alpha MN)^4$, and then bounds $d$ by $\alpha/\lambda^2$. The available moment estimate \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:fourth} is stronger by a factor $\alpha^2/\lambda^2$. To achieve the same total translation error $4\alpha\lambda^2M^4N^3$, one may therefore replace
\[
 \rho_{\rm old}=\frac{\lambda^4}{\pi\alpha^4}
 \quad\hbox{by}\quad
 \rho_{\rm new}=\frac{\lambda^2}{\pi\alpha^2}.
\]
With $\lambda=2^{-37}\alpha^{11/2}$, this is the change
\begin{equation}
 \frac{2^{-148}\alpha^{18}}\pi
 \quad\longrightarrow\quad
 \frac{2^{-74}\alpha^9}\pi.
 \label{gsr:en:12:eq:initial-gain}
\end{equation}
No character has been added or removed from $\Gamma$. The gain comes entirely from a better estimate of the same Fourier expression.

\begin{proposition}[Optimal allocation within the moment bounds]
\label{gsr:en:12:prop:allocation}
Fix a desired relative translation error $0<\sigma\le1$, with the spectrum and rank defined as in theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:smoothing}, and use only the bounds \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:rank} and \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:smooth}. Among positive choices of $\lambda,\rho$ satisfying
\[
                     2\pi\rho+2\lambda^2/\alpha^2\le\sigma,
\]
the lower bound for $\rho/d$ obtained by substituting $d\le\alpha/\lambda^2$ is maximized at
\[
 \lambda^2=\frac{\sigma\alpha^2}{4},\qquad
 \rho=\frac{\sigma}{4\pi}.
\]
Its maximum is $\sigma^2\alpha/(16\pi)$. After the $3d$ radius-selection step, the resulting guaranteed inner radius is $\sigma^2\alpha/(96\pi)$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Write $\lambda^2=q\sigma\alpha^2$, $0<q<1/2$. Saturating the error budget gives $\rho=\sigma(1-2q)/(2\pi)$, so
\[
 \frac\rho d\ge\frac{\rho\lambda^2}{\alpha}
        =\frac{q(1-2q)\sigma^2\alpha}{2\pi}.
\]
The quadratic $q(1-2q)=1/8-2(q-1/4)^2$ is maximized at $q=1/4$. Divide by 6 for the selected inner radius.
\end{proof}

This is an optimization of the guaranteed expression furnished by these estimates. It does not claim optimality of the actual radius for each input function. If the measured fourth moment is smaller, the factor $\xi$ yields the further admissible choice $\rho=\sigma/(4\pi\xi)$, provided it is within the range used for radius selection.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Synchronizing a local model across fibres\srctag{12}}]{Synchronizing a local model across fibres}\label{gsr:en:12:sec:d7}
\srcnote{12}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:en:12:sec:synchronization}

The extension theorem concerns a map on a set of directions. Gowers's argument also requires it to agree with differences between elements of another, possibly multivalued, domain. The next lemma makes this second use of overlap explicit.

Let $\Omega$ be a finite set with an index map $r:\Omega\to G$ and a value map $F:\Omega\to H$. Write $\Omega_a=r^{-1}(a)$ for its fibres. Let $S\subseteq B\subseteq G$, $|S|=a|B|$, and let $\psi:S\to H$ be a Freiman homomorphism with canonical difference map $D$.

\begin{lemma}[Common-fibre synchronization]
\label{gsr:en:12:lem:sync}
Let $W_1\subseteq\Omega$. Suppose that for each $w\in W_1$ there is a set $T_w\subseteq S$ with $|T_w|\ge(1-q)|S|$, and for each $d\in T_w$ the fibre $\Omega_{r(w)+d}$ is nonempty and
\[
 |\{z\in\Omega_{r(w)+d}:F(z)-F(w)=\psi(d)\}|
                  \ge(1-\theta)|\Omega_{r(w)+d}|.
\]
For $w_1,w_2\in W_1$, if $c=r(w_1)-r(w_2)$ satisfies $b_B(c)\le\kappa$ and
\begin{equation}
              2(1-q)a>1+\kappa,\qquad 2\theta<1,
 \label{gsr:en:12:eq:sync-budget}
\end{equation}
then $c\in S-S$ and
\[
                         F(w_1)-F(w_2)=D(c).
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Both $T_{w_1}\subseteq B$ and $T_{w_2}-c\subseteq B-c$. The two-set form of lemma~\ref{gsr:en:12:lem:tree}, or direct subtraction of their complements, gives
\[
 |T_{w_1}\cap(T_{w_2}-c)|
 \ge[2(1-q)a-1-\kappa]|B|>0.
\]
Choose $d$ in this intersection, so $d\in T_{w_1}$ and $d+c\in T_{w_2}$. Their fibres coincide because
\[
                    r(w_1)+d=r(w_2)+(d+c).
\]
This common fibre is nonempty. The two subsets on which the required value equations hold have combined missing fraction at most $2\theta<1$, so they contain a common $z$. Subtracting the two equations gives
\[
 F(w_1)-F(w_2)=\psi(d+c)-\psi(d)=D(c).
\]
The same choice of $d$ also establishes $c\in S-S$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
Source~30's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:30:thm:compatibility} is this lemma, with the same condition $2(1-\sigma)a_0>1+\kappa$, proved again without citation.
\end{writenote}

If $a\ge1-\eps$, the convenient sufficient condition is $2(1-q)(1-\eps)>1+\kappa$. This retains the actual relative density and improves the coarse overlap bookkeeping used in the source's Lemma 10.12.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A strengthened version of the Section 10 local-model theorem\srctag{12}}]{A strengthened version of the Section 10 local-model theorem}\label{gsr:en:12:sec:d8}
\srcnote{12}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:en:12:sec:main}

We now specialize to $G=\Z/N\Z$, $N\ge2$. Primality is unnecessary until the later scalar-linearity corollary. A \emph{multifunction domain} is a finite set $X$ with an index map $r:X\to G$, or equivalently a partition $X=\bigsqcup_{s\in G}X_s$. A function $\phi:X\to G$ is a $(1-\eta)$-homomorphism of order $j$ if at least a $1-\eta$ fraction of all ordered tuples
\[
 (x_1,\dots,x_{2j})\in X^{2j},\qquad
 \sum_{i=1}^{j}r(x_i)=\sum_{i=j+1}^{2j}r(x_i),
\]
also satisfy the analogous equality of their $\phi$-values. The denominator counts all such tuples, including repeated elements.

\subsection{The established component-extraction input}

Fix, for the remainder of this section,
\begin{equation}
 \eta=2^{-43},\qquad \theta=10\eta^{1/5},\qquad q=\sqrt\theta.
 \label{gsr:en:12:eq:eta}
\end{equation}
One has
\begin{equation}
                   \theta<1/36,\qquad q<1/6.
 \label{gsr:en:12:eq:theta-small}
\end{equation}
Indeed, $\theta<1/36$ is equivalent to $360^5<2^{43}$, an integer inequality.

\begin{lemma}[Gowers's component input, with explicit hypotheses]
\label{gsr:en:12:lem:component-input}
Let $\Omega=\bigsqcup_{s\in G}\Omega_s$, with $|\Omega|=\alpha LN$, $|\Omega_s|\le L$, where $L$ is a positive integer and $0<\alpha\le1$. Let $F:\Omega\to G$ be a $(1-\eta)$-homomorphism of order two. Suppose $B=-B$ is nonempty and
\[
           \big||\Omega_{s+b}|-|\Omega_s|\big|\le\sigma L
                           \quad(s\in G,\ b\in B).
\]
Let $\varrho>0$ satisfy
\begin{align}
 \varrho&\le\min\{\alpha/192,\alpha^2/32\},\label{gsr:en:12:eq:component-rho}\\
 0<\sigma&\le\min\{\eta\alpha^2,
               \eta\varrho^4\alpha/384,
               \eta\varrho\alpha^2/16\},\qquad
 \sigma<\alpha^2/16.\label{gsr:en:12:eq:component-sigma}
\end{align}
Then there exist $W_1\subseteq W\subseteq\Omega$, $S\subseteq B$, and a Freiman homomorphism $\psi:S\to G$, such that
\begin{align}
 |W|&\ge\varrho^2\alpha^2 LN/16,\label{gsr:en:12:eq:W-bound}\\
 |W_1|&\ge(1-q)|W|,\qquad |S|\ge(1-\theta)|B|,\label{gsr:en:12:eq:W1-bound}
\end{align}
and the hypotheses about the sets $T_w$ and the good fibre fractions in lemma~\ref{gsr:en:12:lem:sync} hold with this $W_1$, $S$, $q$, and $\theta$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}[Source and deduction]
This is the required output of Gowers's Lemmas 10.3--10.9, in the corrected form recorded in \cite{repo12section10,repo12extraction}. Lemma 10.3 selects an anchor under $\sigma\le\eta\alpha^2$. Lemma 10.5 selects a fibre-saturated component $W$ under \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:component-rho} and $\sigma\le\eta\varrho^4\alpha/384$, with \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:W-bound} and fibre sizes at least $\alpha^2L/16$ on $W$. Lemma 10.6 supplies $S$ and the nested $1-\theta$ difference model under the remaining extraction bound. Lemma 10.7 reverses the two outer counting quantifiers, losing $q=\sqrt\theta$ and defining $W_1$. Lemmas 10.8--10.9 give the exact Freiman property using $6q<1$ and $W\ne\varnothing$.

The fibre sizes needed in lemma~\ref{gsr:en:12:lem:sync} are positive: for $w\in W$ and $d\in S\subseteq B$,
\[
 |\Omega_{r(w)+d}|\ge|\Omega_{r(w)}|-\sigma L
                 \ge(\alpha^2/16-\sigma)L>0.
\]
This last point is a necessary hypothesis of the synchronization argument, not a consequence of a proportionate statement on a possibly empty fibre.

The printed proof of Lemma 10.6 has an ambiguity involving a set depending on the direction and a later exchange of quantifiers. The corrected proof used here works on a fixed product of a low-error set with $B$ and chooses each direction's value from an anchor-fibre mode. Appendix~\ref{gsr:en:12:sec:repair-audit} records the count behind this repair. No Bohr-specific property of $B$ is used in this component input.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The parameterized theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Local model with a polynomial radius]
\label{gsr:en:12:thm:main}
Let $X=\bigsqcup_{s\in\Z/N\Z}X_s$ be finite, $M\ge1$ an integer, $|X_s|\le M$, and $|X|=\alpha MN$ with $0<\alpha\le1$. Suppose $\phi:X\to\Z/N\Z$ is a $(1-2^{-43})$-homomorphism of order eight. Choose $\varrho,\sigma$ satisfying \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:component-rho}--\eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:component-sigma}, let $\lambda>0$, and put
\begin{equation}
 \lambda^2=\frac{\sigma\alpha^2}{4},\qquad
 \rho=\frac\sigma{4\pi},\qquad
 \Gamma=\{\gamma:|\widehat g(\gamma)|\ge\lambda MN\},
 \quad g(s)=|X_s|.
 \label{gsr:en:12:eq:main-parameters}
\end{equation}
Then $1\le d=|\Gamma|\le4/(\sigma\alpha)$. On
\begin{equation}
 C=\Bohr(\Gamma,\zeta),\qquad
 \zeta=\frac{\sigma}{24\pi d}
           \ge\frac{\sigma^2\alpha}{96\pi},
 \label{gsr:en:12:eq:new-zeta}
\end{equation}
there is a Freiman homomorphism $\psi_1:C\to\Z/N\Z$ with $\psi_1(0)=0$, and there is $Y\subseteq X$ with
\begin{equation}
               |Y|\ge\frac{(1-q)\varrho^2\alpha}{16}|X|,
 \label{gsr:en:12:eq:Y-exact}
\end{equation}
such that, whenever $y,z\in Y$ and $r(y)-r(z)\in C$,
\begin{equation}
           \phi(y)-\phi(z)=\psi_1(r(y)-r(z)).
 \label{gsr:en:12:eq:local-model}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
We give the full parameter propagation.

\textbf{1. The fourfold domain.}
Let $\Omega=X^4$, with
\[
 r_\Omega(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)=r(x_1)+r(x_2)-r(x_3)-r(x_4)
\]
and the identical signed expression defining $F$ from $\phi$. Set
\[
                     L=M|X|^3=\alpha^3M^4N^3.
\]
Each fibre of $\Omega$ has at most $M|X|^3=L$ elements: after choosing three entries, the index of the fourth is determined, and at most $M$ elements have that index. Moreover
\begin{equation}
                 |\Omega|=|X|^4=\alpha LN.\label{gsr:en:12:eq:omega-density}
\end{equation}
An additive quadruple in $\Omega$ expands, after a permutation of its 16 entries, into an equality between two sums of eight indices in $X$. This is a bijective rearrangement of all tested tuples, and the same rearrangement applies to values. Thus $F$ is a $(1-\eta)$-homomorphism of order two.

\textbf{2. Fourier control and nonempty spectrum.}
The fibre-count function of $\Omega$ is $h=g*\widetilde g*g*\widetilde g$. By theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:smoothing} and \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:main-parameters}, it is $(\Bohr(\Gamma,\rho),\sigma L)$-invariant. The rank bound is $d\le4/(\sigma\alpha)$. The parameter conditions imply $\sigma<1$, hence $\lambda<\alpha$, so the zero character belongs to $\Gamma$ and $d\ge1$. They also imply $0<\rho<1/2$.

\textbf{3. Choose the ambient Bohr set before extraction.}
Apply theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:radius} with $m=3d$. It provides $r_0\in(\rho/2,\rho]$ such that $B=\Bohr(\Gamma,r_0)$ satisfies
\[
 b_B(c)\le\kappa:=1-4^{-1/3}<3/8
                    \quad(c\in C=\Bohr(\Gamma,\rho/(6d))).
\]
Since $B\subseteq\Bohr(\Gamma,\rho)$, the already established invariance holds on $B$. Now, and only now, apply lemma~\ref{gsr:en:12:lem:component-input} to obtain fresh $W,W_1,S,\psi$. The character set is unchanged.

\textbf{4. Extend the directional model.}
The actual missing density of $S$ is at most $\theta<1/36$. Therefore
\[
 3\theta+2\kappa<\frac1{12}+\frac34=\frac56<1.
\]
By theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:sharp-extension}, the canonical difference map of $\psi$ induces a Freiman homomorphism $\psi_1$ on $C$, with zero value at zero.

\textbf{5. Synchronize values on the selected component.}
For the parameters of lemma~\ref{gsr:en:12:lem:sync}, $a\ge1-\theta>35/36$, $1-q>5/6$, and $1+\kappa<11/8$. Thus
\[
 2(1-q)a>2\cdot\frac56\cdot\frac{35}{36}
            =\frac{175}{108}>\frac{11}{8}>1+\kappa,
\]
and $2\theta<1$. The synchronization lemma gives
\[
 F(w_1)-F(w_2)=\psi_1(r_\Omega(w_1)-r_\Omega(w_2))
\]
for $w_1,w_2\in W_1$ with index difference in $C$.

\textbf{6. Retain the full slice count.}
By \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:W-bound}--\eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:omega-density},
\[
 |W_1|\ge(1-q)\frac{\varrho^2\alpha^2LN}{16}
          =\frac{(1-q)\varrho^2\alpha}{16}|X|^4.
\]
Average over the last three coordinates. Some $(x_2,x_3,x_4)\in X^3$ leaves at least the fraction in \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:Y-exact} of $X$ in the fibre
\[
 Y=\{y\in X:(y,x_2,x_3,x_4)\in W_1\}.
\]
On this slice, differences of indices and of values are exactly $r(y)-r(z)$ and $\phi(y)-\phi(z)$, proving \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:local-model}. Finally, the bound on $d$ gives \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:new-zeta}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
Source~28's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:28:thm:main} replaces the component selection by logarithmic windows: retained fraction $\alpha p(\alpha)/20$, $O(\alpha^{-3})$ original-domain frequencies, radius $\Omega(\alpha^5)$, input defect $2^{-21}$ (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:section10}); it credits this theorem's $\alpha^5$ retention, extension and smoothing.
