\subsection{Keeping exactly the original large spectrum}

\begin{corollary}[Explicit sparse-density specialization]
\label{gsr:en:12:cor:fixed-spectrum}
Under the hypotheses on $X,\phi$ in theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:main}, suppose $0<\alpha\le1/6$. Keep Gowers's threshold
\[
 \lambda=2^{-37}\alpha^{11/2},\qquad
 \Gamma=\{\gamma:|\widehat g(\gamma)|\ge\lambda MN\}.
\]
Then $d=|\Gamma|\le2^{74}\alpha^{-10}$, and one can take
\begin{equation}
 C=\Bohr\left(\Gamma,\frac{2^{-74}\alpha^9}{6\pi d}\right),
 \qquad |Y|\ge\frac{\alpha^5}{20000}|X|.
 \label{gsr:en:12:eq:fixed-spectrum}
\end{equation}
The local model identity \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:local-model} holds on $C$, whose radius is at least $\alpha^{19}/(3\pi2^{149})$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Choose $\varrho=\alpha^2/32$ and $\sigma=2^{-72}\alpha^9$. The bound $\varrho\le\alpha/192$ is exactly $\alpha\le1/6$. The most restrictive smallness comparison is
\[
 \sigma=2^{-72}\alpha^9
 \le\frac{2^{-70}}3\alpha^9
       =\frac{\eta\varrho^4\alpha}{384}.
\]
The other conditions in \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:component-sigma} follow directly from $\alpha\le1$; for example $\sigma\le\eta\varrho\alpha^2/16$ reduces to $\alpha^5\le2^{20}$. Then \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:main-parameters} gives exactly the displayed $\lambda$. Also
\[
 \frac{(1-q)\varrho^2\alpha}{16}
 >\frac{5\alpha^5}{98304}\ge\frac{\alpha^5}{20000}.
\]
Substitute the rank bound into the radius and simplify.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 11--14]
\emph{Against the formal statement} (HEAD \texttt{e1db00e99}). \file{theorem_10_13} (\file{Section10.lean}, line~473; exact companion \file{theorem_10_13_holds}, \file{Proofs10Main.lean}, line~1292) concludes $|Y|\ge\alpha^6|X|/20000$ on the Bohr set of radius \texttt{section10Zeta}, under $0<\alpha\le1/6$. The fraction $\alpha^5/20000$ here is below the $5\alpha^5/98304$ that the formal proof already establishes internally (note in Section~\ref{gsr:fm:12:sec:d1}), so the improvement in the retained fraction is a proof-level fact of the development, not new; the polynomial radius is new. Not formalized.
\end{writenote}

\subsection{An all-density schedule and a moment-sensitive version}

\begin{corollary}[All densities]
\label{gsr:en:12:cor:all-density}
For every $0<\alpha\le1$, the choices
\begin{equation}
 \varrho=\min\{\alpha/192,\alpha^2/32\},\qquad
 \sigma=\frac{2^{-43}\alpha\varrho^4}{384}
 \label{gsr:en:12:eq:all-density}
\end{equation}
satisfy the conditions of theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:main}. Thus its explicit radius and retained-fraction conclusions hold without the restriction $\alpha\le1/6$. \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 11--14]} This schedule is Gowers's own printed choice (transcription \file{sz-thm-gowers-proof.tex}, line~2201: $\rho=\min\{\alpha/192,\alpha^2/32\}$, $\sigma=\eta\rho^4\alpha/384$); it is new relative to the formal statement, which assumes $\alpha\le1/6$.

On the branch $\alpha\le1/6$, these choices give
\[
 \sigma=\frac{2^{-70}}3\alpha^9,\quad
 \lambda^2=\frac{2^{-72}}3\alpha^{11},\quad
 d\le3\cdot2^{72}\alpha^{-10},\quad
 \zeta\ge\frac{2^{-145}}{27\pi}\alpha^{19}.
\]
This last constant is $16/9$ times the radius lower bound in corollary~\ref{gsr:en:12:cor:fixed-spectrum}, but uses a slightly different spectral threshold.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The only remaining comparisons are $\varrho^4\le384\alpha$, $\varrho^3\le24\alpha$, and $\eta\varrho^4<24\alpha$. They follow from $\varrho\le\alpha/192$, $0<\alpha\le1$, and $\eta<1$. These inequalities give the three conditions on $\sigma$ and fibre positivity. The sparse-branch formulas follow by substituting $\varrho=\alpha^2/32$ and simplifying powers of 2 and 3.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Using the measured fourth moment]
\label{gsr:en:12:cor:measured-moment}
In theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:main}, let $\xi=(LN)^{-1}\sum|\widehat g|^4$. If $\rho_*:=\sigma/(4\pi\xi)\le1/2$, the same spectrum and retained fraction work on the larger Bohr set of radius
\[
                \zeta_* =\frac{\sigma}{24\pi\xi d}
                          \ge\frac{\sigma^2\alpha}{96\pi\xi}.
\]
For the schedule \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:all-density}, the required bound on $\rho_*$ is automatic.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Use the precise version of \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:smooth}. Nothing after the smoothing step changes. For the final assertion, $\xi\ge\alpha$ gives $\rho_*\le\eta\varrho^4/(1536\pi)<1/2$.
\end{proof}

\section[{Consequences and the size of the improvement\srctag{12}}]{Consequences and the size of the improvement}\label{gsr:en:12:sec:d9}
\srcnote{12}{Section 9}
\label{gsr:en:12:sec:consequences}

\subsection{The volume cost changes from quadratic to linear in the rank}

Let $k=\lceil2^{74}\alpha^{-10}\rceil$ and compare the explicit rank-based radius
\[
 \zeta_{\rm old}=2^{-155k}\alpha^{18k}/k
 \quad\hbox{with}\quad
 \zeta_{\rm new}=\frac{\alpha^{19}}{3\pi2^{149}}.
\]
The latter is a guaranteed smaller radius inside the actual set in corollary~\ref{gsr:en:12:cor:fixed-spectrum}; hence the local model also holds on $\Bohr(\Gamma,\zeta_{\rm new})$. The size bound \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:bohr-size} gives
\begin{align*}
 |\Bohr(\Gamma,\zeta_{\rm old})|
 &\ge 2^{-E_{\rm old}}N,\\
 E_{\rm old}
 &=k\bigl[1+155k+18k\log_2(1/\alpha)+\log_2 k\bigr],\\
 |\Bohr(\Gamma,\zeta_{\rm new})|
 &\ge 2^{-E_{\rm new}}N,\\
 E_{\rm new}
 &=k\bigl[150+\log_2(3\pi)+19\log_2(1/\alpha)\bigr].
\end{align*}
Here using $k$ rather than the actual $d$ only weakens a lower bound because the base is below one. Thus the certified logarithmic volume cost changes from
\[
 O\bigl(k^2[1+\log(1/\alpha)]\bigr)
 \quad\hbox{to}\quad
 O\bigl(k[1+\log(1/\alpha)]\bigr).
\]
The large rank itself remains. This is a substantial improvement at this stage of the proof, but the resulting numerical constants are still enormous.

\begin{example}[Density $\alpha=1/8$]
Then $k=2^{104}$. The old negative base-two logarithm of the radius is
\[
                  \log_2(1/\zeta_{\rm old})=209\cdot2^{104}+104.
\]
The new guaranteed radius has
\[
                  \log_2(1/\zeta_{\rm new})
                   =206+\log_2(3\pi)\approx209.2365.
\]
The retained fraction improves by a factor of 8 relative to the corrected $\alpha^6/20000$ statement. \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 11--14]} Relative to what the formal proof already establishes ($5\alpha^5/98304$, note in Section~\ref{gsr:fm:12:sec:d1}) there is no gain in the fraction; the gain is in the radius. These are parameter comparisons; they do not assert that a set of feasible computational size meets the full theorem's worst-case volume bound.
\end{example}

\subsection{Long progressions of locally linear directions}

\begin{corollary}[Scalar linearity along short Bohr progressions]
\label{gsr:en:12:cor:linearity}
Let $N=p$ be prime, and suppose $Y,\psi_1,C=\Bohr(\Gamma,\zeta)$ satisfy theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:main}. If $m\ge1$, $0\ne h\in\Bohr(\Gamma,\zeta/m)$, and $m<p$, then there is $a\in\Z/p\Z$ such that
\[
 \phi(y)-\phi(z)=a(r(y)-r(z))
\]
whenever $y,z\in Y$ and $r(y)-r(z)\in\{jh:-m\le j\le m\}$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
All $jh$, $|j|\le m$, belong to $C$ by the triangle inequality. Since $\psi_1$ is a Freiman homomorphism and $\psi_1(0)=0$, the relations
\[
                      jh+h=(j+1)h+0
\]
give $\psi_1(jh)=j\psi_1(h)$ by induction for nonnegative $j$, and oddness gives the negative values. Take $a=\psi_1(h)/h$, which is legitimate since $h\ne0$ in the prime field. Then use \eqref{gsr:en:12:eq:local-model}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[An explicit supply of nonzero directions]
\label{gsr:en:12:cor:progression-size}
If $0<\zeta\le1/2$ and $\zeta p^{1/d}\ge4$, put
\[
                     m=\left\lfloor\zeta p^{1/d}/4\right\rfloor.
\]
Then $\Bohr(\Gamma,\zeta/m)$ contains a nonzero $h$, and the progression $P=\{jh:-m\le j\le m\}\subseteq C$ is proper. A single scalar governs all index differences of pairs from $Y$ which belong to $P$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
We have $m\ge1$ and
\[
 |\Bohr(\Gamma,\zeta/m)|
       \ge\left(\frac{\zeta}{2m}\right)^dp\ge2^d>1.
\]
The elementary size bound remains valid if $\zeta/m=1/2$. Also $m\le p/8$, since $d\ge1$ and $\zeta\le1/2$. Thus $2m<p$, so the distinct integers $-m,\ldots,m$ give distinct multiples of a nonzero element in $\Z/p\Z$. Apply corollary~\ref{gsr:en:12:cor:linearity}.
\end{proof}

This supplies the direct analogue of Gowers's Corollary 10.14 with the larger radius. It does not assert that $Y$ itself contains a progression of this length; it asserts that differences in the displayed progression are governed by one scalar.

\subsection{What does not yet follow}

The later proof still requires compatible multilinear structure, partitions with controlled widths, recurrence thresholds, and an iteration which pays for the density lost when changing cyclic models. The current repository records unresolved obligations in Sections 13, 16, and 18 \cite{repo12status}. \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 11--14] Incomplete list:} the ledger at the pin also had open statements in Sections~1, 5, 7 and~8, and at HEAD \texttt{e1db00e99} the 20 open statements are \file{theorem_1_2}, \file{theorem_1_3}, \file{corollary_5_8}, \file{theorem_7_1}, \file{theorem_7_2}, \file{theorem_8_2}, \file{corollary_8_3}, \file{lemma_13_5}--\file{lemma_13_7}, \file{lemma_13_9}, \file{corollary_13_10}, \file{theorem_13_12}, \file{theorem_16_2}, \file{lemma_16_4}, \file{lemma_16_10}, \file{corollary_16_11}, \file{theorem_18_1}, \file{theorem_18_2} and \file{corollary_18_7}. A local radius improvement cannot be substituted into every later theorem without checking these dependencies.

In particular, the theorem established here is a complete replacement of the Section 10 local-model output under its stated assumptions. It does not prove a better final $r_\ell(N)$ bound. Determining how much of the local gain survives the entire argument is one of the proposed research projects below.

\section[{The fixed-domain repair in the Section 10 extraction input\srctag{12}}]{The fixed-domain repair in the Section 10 extraction input}\label{gsr:en:12:sec:dA}
\srcnote{12}{Appendix A}
\label{gsr:en:12:sec:repair-audit}

This appendix explains the specific quantifier issue checked when using lemma~\ref{gsr:en:12:lem:component-input}. It is not a reproof of every component-selection lemma. The construction below is the one present in the exact companion proof of Lemma 10.6 in \texttt{Proofs10Extraction.lean} \cite{repo12extraction}.

Let $t=\eta^{1/5}$, so $0<t<1/10$ for the value of $\eta$ used here. Let $x$ be the anchor selected by Lemma 10.3, and let $W$ be the component selected by Lemma 10.5. For two domain points $x,w$, let $b(x,w)$ count pairs $(y,z)$ with
\[
 r(y)-r(x)=r(z)-r(w)\in B,
\]
and let $e(x,w)$ count those pairs for which
\[
                    F(y)-F(x)\ne F(z)-F(w).
\]
Write $\epsilon(x,w)=e(x,w)/b(x,w)$ when the denominator is positive. The hypotheses below ensure that it is positive for $w\in W$.

Define the \emph{fixed} low-error set
\[
 \mathcal L=\{w\in W:\epsilon(x,w)\le300t^4\}.
\]
The regular-component estimate gives $|\mathcal L|\ge(1-5t)|W|$. For $w\in\mathcal L$ and $d\in B$, set
\[
 A_d=\Omega_{r(x)+d},\qquad
 C_{w,d}=\Omega_{r(w)+d},\qquad
 P_w(d)=|A_d|\,|C_{w,d}|.
\]
The anchor and component fibre bounds, together with pointwise invariance and the inherited bound on $\varrho$, imply that all these fibres are nonempty and that
\[
                          P_w(d)\le4P_w(d')\quad(d,d'\in B).
\]
For example, it suffices that each translated fibre size lies between $3/4$ and $5/4$ of its unshifted size; the product ratio is then at most $(5/3)^2<4$. The parameter schedule of theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:main} is stronger than this requirement.

Disintegrating over the \emph{fixed set of directions} $B$ gives exact identities
\[
 b(x,w)=\sum_{d\in B}P_w(d),\qquad
 e(x,w)=\sum_{d\in B}\#\{\text{disagreeing pairs in }A_d\times C_{w,d}\}.
\]
Let $p=\min_{d\in B}P_w(d)>0$. Then
\[
 e(x,w)\le300t^4b(x,w)\le1200t^4|B|p.
\]
If more than $35t^2|B|$ directions each had more than a $35t^2$ fraction of disagreeing pairs, the last count would exceed
\[
                        35^2t^4|B|p=1225t^4|B|p,
\]
a contradiction. Thus, for each $w\in\mathcal L$, at most a $35t^2$ fraction of directions are bad.

Now double-count the bad pairs in $\mathcal L\times B$. At most a $7t$ fraction of directions can have more than a $5t$ fraction of $\mathcal L$ bad, since $(7t)(5t)=35t^2$. Retain the remaining set $S$ of directions. It has size at least $(1-7t)|B|$, hence at least $(1-10t)|B|$. For each retained direction, the good points of $\mathcal L$ comprise at least
\[
                    (1-5t)|\mathcal L|\ge(1-5t)^2|W|
                                            \ge(1-10t)|W|.
\]

For each $d\in S$, choose $\psi(d)$ to be the mode of $F(y)-F(x)$ on the anchor fibre $A_d$. This choice depends on $d$ but is independent of $w$. For any good pair $(w,d)$, pair agreement at least $1-35t^2$ forces that mode to occupy at least a $1-35t^2$ fraction of $A_d$. Every product of a point in the mode class with an incorrectly labelled point of $C_{w,d}$ is a disagreeing pair. Hence the incorrectly labelled fraction of $C_{w,d}$ is at most
\[
                  \frac{35t^2}{1-35t^2}\le10t.
\]
This proves the nested $1-10t$ conclusion on the fixed $W$.

The proof never exchanges quantifiers over a set of the form $W\cap(W-d)$ treated as if it were independent of $d$. Its invariance input is pointwise for each $d\in B$, which is why choosing the smaller ambient Bohr radius before component extraction is legitimate. The later exact Freiman step, Lemma 10.9, likewise uses a fixed $W$ and the strict bound $6\sqrt\theta<1$.

\section[{Sharp stability of the cross-section collision bound\srctag{14}}]{Sharp stability of the cross-section collision bound}\label{gsr:en:14:sec:d4}
\srcnote{14}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:en:14:sec:collision-stability}

The arrangement argument in Sections~12 and~14 of Gowers's proof passes
through a second moment that counts pairs of congruent cubes in the same
cross-section.  A useful profile bound is
\[
 R_1\leq \sum_r |B_r|^3.
\]
The numerical inequality conceals a strong geometric restriction: a
cross-section can nearly attain its cubic upper bound only when it is
nearly a product of subgroup cosets.  We prove a dimension-independent
stability statement, classify exact equality including the labeling,
and explain the resulting extra information in the arrangement moment
inequalities.  The group-theoretic ingredient is the classical
three-halves difference-set lemma, for which we include the short proof.
Our sharpness assertion concerns an infinite family of exact equality
examples and the leading asymptotic constant; we do not assert that
every real value of the error parameter is attained by a finite set.

\subsection{Cube collisions and two elementary upper bounds}

Let $G_1,\ldots,G_k$ be finite abelian groups, where $k\geq1$, and put
$G=\prod_{i=1}^kG_i$.  Write $e_i:G\to G$ for the coordinate projection
followed by the coordinate inclusion: $e_i(x)$ has coordinate $x_i$ in
position $i$ and zero elsewhere.  If $x,h\in G$, the axis-parallel cube
with base $x$ and sidelengths $h$ has vertices
\[
 x+\omega\cdot h=(x_i+\omega_i h_i)_{i=1}^k,
 \qquad \omega\in\{0,1\}^k.
\]
Zero sidelengths and repeated vertices are included throughout.

Let $A\subset G$, and let $\phi:A\to K$, where $K$ is an abelian group.
For a cube contained in $A$ define
\[
 D_h\phi(x)=\sum_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^k}
                 (-1)^{k-|\omega|}\phi(x+\omega\cdot h).
\]
Let $Q_\phi(A)$ count triples $(x,z,h)\in G^3$ for which both cubes
are contained in $A$ and $D_h\phi(x)=D_h\phi(z)$.  Let $Q(A)$ denote
the same count without the value condition.  With $m=|A|$, put
\[
 E(A)=\#\{(x,z,w)\in A^3:z+w-x\in A\}.
\]
The injective change of variables $(x,z,h)\mapsto(x,z,x+h)$ gives
\begin{equation}
 Q_\phi(A)\leq Q(A)\leq E(A)\leq m^3.       \label{gsr:en:14:eq:collision-chain}
\end{equation}
For every coordinate $i$, also define
\[
 C_i(A)=\#\{(x,w)\in A^2:x+e_i(w-x)\in A\}.
\]
The same change of variables shows that
\begin{equation}
 Q_\phi(A)\leq m C_i(A).                   \label{gsr:en:14:eq:collision-corners}
\end{equation}
Indeed, a failed corner condition for $(x,w)$ excludes every possible
choice of the second base $z$.

\subsection{A sharp near-maximal energy lemma}

We first prove a statement that applies to an arbitrary finite abelian
group, without a specified product structure.  Define
\[
 \tau(\varepsilon)=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4\varepsilon}}2
 =\varepsilon+\varepsilon^2+2\varepsilon^3+O(\varepsilon^4).
\]
Thus $\tau(\varepsilon)(1-\tau(\varepsilon))=\varepsilon$.

\begin{lemma}[The three-halves difference-set lemma]
\label{gsr:en:14:lem:three-halves}
If $B$ is a nonempty finite subset of an abelian group and
$|B-B|<3|B|/2$, then $B-B$ is a subgroup.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Put $b=|B|$ and $D=B-B$.  If $d=b_1-b_2\in D$, the two subsets
$B-b_1$ and $B-b_2$ of $D$ have intersection of size at least
$2b-|D|>b/2$.  Consequently
\[
 |B\cap(B+d)|>b/2\qquad(d\in D).
\]
For $d,e\in D$, the two subsets $B\cap(B+d)$ and
$B\cap(B+e)$ of $B$ intersect.  Hence $d-e\in B-B=D$.
The nonempty finite set $D$ is closed under differences and is a subgroup.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 11--14]
This is a classical fact of additive combinatorics (usually credited to Freiman); the source calls it classical and proves it, without a citation.
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
Source~15 proves the same lemma (its Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:15:lem:smalldifference}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{theorem}[Near-maximal energy, with the quadratic error envelope]
\label{gsr:en:14:thm:energy-sharp-stability}
Let $A$ be a nonempty subset of a finite abelian group, let $m=|A|$,
and let $0\leq\varepsilon\leq1/100$.  If
\[
 E(A)\geq(1-\varepsilon)m^3,
\]
then there is a coset $C=c+H$ of a subgroup such that
\begin{equation}
 |A\mathbin{\triangle}C|\leq\tau(\varepsilon)m.
                                                        \label{gsr:en:14:eq:sharp-distance}
\end{equation}
The coset satisfying this bound is unique, and is the unique coset
minimizing symmetric difference with $A$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write $r(d)=|A\cap(A+d)|$ and $\mathcal D=m^3-E(A)$.  The identities
\[
 \sum_d r(d)=m^2,
 \qquad E(A)=\sum_d r(d)^2
\]
give
\[
 \sum_{a_0,b\in A}(m-r(b-a_0))=\mathcal D.
\]
Choose $a_0\in A$ such that
\[
 \sum_{b\in A}(m-r(b-a_0))\leq\varepsilon m^2
\]
and define
\[
 B=\{b\in A:r(b-a_0)\geq9m/10\}.
\]
Then $|B|\geq(1-10\varepsilon)m\geq9m/10$.
The elementary overlap inequality
\[
 r(d-e)\geq r(d)+r(e)-m
\]
shows that $r(d)\geq4m/5$ for every $d\in B-B$.  Therefore
\[
 |B-B|\leq\frac{5m}{4}<\frac32|B|.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:14:lem:three-halves}, $H=B-B$ is a subgroup.  Choose
$b_0\in B$ and let $C=b_0+H$.  If
\[
 A_0=A\cap C,\quad a=|A_0|,\quad
 t=|A\setminus C|,\quad u=|C\setminus A|,\quad h=|H|,
\]
then
\begin{equation}
 a\geq9m/10,\qquad t\leq m/10,\qquad h\leq5m/4.
                                                        \label{gsr:en:14:eq:rough-coset}
\end{equation}

We now sharpen this rough approximation by counting disjoint families
of triples in $A^3$ whose alternating sum is outside $A$.  For every
$v\in C\setminus A$, and every middle entry $y\in A_0$, the number
of pairs $x,z\in A_0$ with $x-y+z=v$ is at least $2a-h$.
This follows by intersecting $A_0$ and $(v+y)-A_0$, two subsets of
the coset $C$, both of size $a$.  These triples contribute at least
$u a(2a-h)$ to $\mathcal D$.

Next consider triples with exactly one entry in $A\setminus C$.
There are three positions for that entry.  Fix one of its $t$ values
and one of the three positions.  The other two entries range over
$A_0^2$.  Their alternating sum is outside $C$.  For it to belong
to $A$, it must therefore belong to the $t$-element set
$A\setminus C$.  Fixing one of the two entries in $A_0$ and this
output determines the remaining entry, so at most $at$ of the
$a^2$ choices give an output in $A$.  At least $a(a-t)$ choices fail.
These three families are disjoint from one another and from the
all-inside family.  We obtain
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal D\geq u a(2a-h)+3t a(a-t).       \label{gsr:en:14:eq:exact-defect-lower}
\end{equation}

Using \eqref{gsr:en:14:eq:rough-coset}, the coefficients on the right are at least
\[
 a(2a-h)\geq\frac{99}{200}m^2,
 \qquad 3a(a-t)\geq\frac{54}{25}m^2.
\]
In particular, if $\delta=(t+u)/m$ then
\[
 \delta\leq\frac{200}{99}\varepsilon<\frac13.
\]
Put $x=t/m$; thus $0\leq x\leq\delta$, $a/m=1-x$, and
$h/m=1+\delta-2x$.  Dividing \eqref{gsr:en:14:eq:exact-defect-lower} by $m^3$
and simplifying gives
\begin{align*}
 \frac{\mathcal D}{m^3}
 &\geq (1-x)\bigl[(\delta-x)(1-\delta)+3x(1-2x)\bigr]\\
 &=\delta(1-\delta)
   +x\bigl[2+\delta^2-(8+\delta)x+6x^2\bigr].
\end{align*}
For $0\leq x\leq\delta\leq1/3$, the bracket is nonnegative.
Indeed, its derivative in $x$ is $-(8+\delta)+12x<0$ on this
interval, and its value at $x=\delta$ is
$2(1-\delta)(1-3\delta)\geq0$.  Thus
\[
 \delta(1-\delta)\leq\frac{\mathcal D}{m^3}\leq\varepsilon.
\]
Since $\delta<1/3$, inversion of this increasing quadratic proves
\eqref{gsr:en:14:eq:sharp-distance}.

For uniqueness, suppose two cosets $C,C'$ satisfy
$|A\triangle C|,|A\triangle C'|\leq\tau m$, with
$\tau=\tau(\varepsilon)<1/5$.  Then
\[
 |C\cap C'|\geq(1-2\tau)m,
 \qquad |C|,|C'|\leq(1+\tau)m.
\]
Their intersection is consequently larger than half of each coset.
A nonempty intersection of cosets is a coset of the intersection of
their subgroups.  An index other than one is at least two, so the
two subgroups and then the two cosets must coincide.  Any closer
coset would also satisfy the displayed distance bound, proving the
last assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{writeremarkc}[Source~11's Question~3 in substance; added at the third write, 6~October 2026]\label{gsr:en:14:rem:composition}
Source~11's set energy $E(S)$ (Section~\ref{gsr:en:11:sec:d2}) is this $E(A)$: both count ordered $(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)\in A^4$ with $x_1+x_2=x_3+x_4$. Let $f:G\to W$, an affine $\ell$, $S=\{f\ne\ell\}$, $s=|S|=tN$ with $0<t<1/7$, $W$ without involutions, and suppose $\defect(f)\le\Psi_0(t)+\eta$ with $\theta:=\eta/(6t^3)\le1/100$. \emph{Then there are a unique subgroup coset $C=c+H$ of $G$ and a nonzero $b\in W$ such that}
\[
 |S\triangle C|\le\tau(\theta)\,s,\qquad
 |\{x:f(x)-\ell(x)\ne b\one_C(x)\}|\le\Bigl(\tau(\theta)+\frac{\eta}{2t^2(1-7t)}\Bigr)s .
\]
\emph{Proof.} Source~11's Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:11:cor:nearodd} gives $t^3-E(S)/N^3\le\eta/6$, that is $E(S)\ge(1-\theta)s^3$; Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:14:thm:energy-sharp-stability} (applied to the nonempty set $S$) gives the unique coset $C$ with $|S\triangle C|\le\tau(\theta)s$. Let $b$ be a most frequent nonzero value of $g=f-\ell$ on $S$ and $u$ the number of points of $S$ with another value; the proof of Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:11:cor:nearodd} gives $su\le A\le\eta N^2/(2(1-7t))$, so $u/s\le\eta/(2t^2(1-7t))$. The map $g-b\one_C$ is nonzero only on $S\triangle C$ and on those $u$ points of $S\cap C$. \emph{With an involution in $W$} the same argument, using source~11's bounds $t^3-e_S\le\eta/8$ and $A/N^2\le\eta/(6(1-3t))$ for $0<t<1/3$, gives $\theta=\eta/(8t^3)$ and $u/s\le\eta/(6t^2(1-3t))$. Both bounds are relative to $s$ and depend on $\eta/t^3$, the scale that source~11's Question~3 asks for; the coset part is sharp to first order by Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:14:prop:collision-sharpness} (with $\phi=0$, $Q_\phi=E$). Neither source writes this composition (the intake found it); not formalized. What remains of the question: the range $\theta>1/100$, and whether the value term can be improved.
\end{writeremarkc}

\subsection{The product structure is forced, independently of dimension}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp stability for cube collisions]
\label{gsr:en:14:thm:collision-sharp-stability}
Let $A\subset\prod_{i=1}^kG_i$ be nonempty, let $m=|A|$, and let
$\phi:A\to K$ be any function to an abelian group.  Suppose
\[
 Q_\phi(A)\geq(1-\varepsilon)m^3,
 \qquad 0\leq\varepsilon\leq1/100.
\]
Then there are subgroups $H_i\leq G_i$ and points $c_i\in G_i$ such
that the unique closest coset to $A$ is the coordinate product
\begin{equation}
 C=\prod_{i=1}^k(c_i+H_i),\qquad
 |A\triangle C|\leq\tau(\varepsilon)m.    \label{gsr:en:14:eq:product-stability}
\end{equation}
The statement holds also with $Q(A)$ in place of $Q_\phi(A)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By \eqref{gsr:en:14:eq:collision-chain}, Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:14:thm:energy-sharp-stability}
applies.  Use the subgroup $H$, coset $C=c+H$, and notation from
its proof.  We show that $e_iH\subset H$ for every $i$.

Suppose instead that $e_iH\not\subset H$.  The homomorphism
\[
 F_i:H\times H\longrightarrow G,
 \qquad F_i(y,w)=y+e_i(w-y),
\]
has image $H+e_iH$.  To verify this, its image contains $H$ by
taking $y=w$, and contains $e_iH$ by taking $y=0$; the reverse
inclusion is immediate.  The image has at least $2h$ elements,
so every nonempty fiber of $F_i$ has size at most $h/2$.
After translation by $c$, at most $mh/2$ pairs in $C^2$ have
their mixed corner in $A$.

At most $m^2-a^2$ pairs in $A^2$ fail to belong to $C^2$.
Consequently the rough bounds \eqref{gsr:en:14:eq:rough-coset} yield
\[
 C_i(A)\leq m^2-a^2+\frac{mh}{2}
 \leq\left(1-\frac{81}{100}+\frac58\right)m^2
 =\frac{163}{200}m^2.
\]
But \eqref{gsr:en:14:eq:collision-corners} gives
$C_i(A)\geq(1-\varepsilon)m^2\geq99m^2/100$, a contradiction.
Thus each coordinate component of an element of $H$ is again in $H$.
If $H_i$ is its projection into $G_i$, it follows that
$H=\prod_iH_i$.  The distance estimate and uniqueness were already
proved in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:14:thm:energy-sharp-stability}.
\end{proof}

With them the leading constant asked for by source~15's first question is $1$ (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:cosetrange}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 40--46]
Source~45's Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:45:col:stability} and~\ref{gsr:en:45:col:equality} extend the range to defect below $1/9$ and show that positive-defect equality forces one punctured coordinate.
\end{writenote}

For $G_i=\mathbb F_p$, every $H_i$ is either $\{0\}$ or $\mathbb F_p$.
The approximating set is therefore an affine coordinate subspace:
each coordinate is either fixed or completely free.  No primality
or torsion assumption was needed for the general result.

\begin{proposition}[Exact sharpness at infinitely many errors]
\label{gsr:en:14:prop:collision-sharpness}
For every prime $p\geq101$ and every $k\geq1$, let
\[
 A=(\mathbb F_p\setminus\{0\})\times\mathbb F_p^{k-1},
 \qquad \phi=0,
 \qquad \delta_p=\frac1{p-1},\quad
 \varepsilon_p=\delta_p(1-\delta_p).
\]
Then $\varepsilon_p\leq1/100$,
\[
 Q_\phi(A)=(1-\varepsilon_p)|A|^3,
 \qquad
 \min_{\text{coordinate cosets }C}
       \frac{|A\triangle C|}{|A|}
       =\delta_p=\tau(\varepsilon_p).
\]
Thus the envelope is attained at an infinite sequence of errors tending
to zero, and its leading coefficient one cannot be decreased.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Put $n=p-1$.  For $A_1=\mathbb F_p\setminus\{0\}$, the difference
multiplicity is $n$ at zero and $n-1$ at every nonzero element.
Therefore
\[
 E(A_1)=n^2+n(n-1)^2=n^3-n^2+n.
\]
In the remaining full coordinates, every choice of the two bases and
sidelength is valid.  Hence
\[
 Q_\phi(A)=E(A_1)p^{3(k-1)},
 \qquad |A|=np^{k-1},
\]
which proves the count.  The full space differs from $A$ in
$p^{k-1}=\delta_p|A|$ points.  Every proper coordinate coset has
at most $p^{k-1}$ points and hence differs from $A$ in at least
$(p-2)p^{k-1}>p^{k-1}$ points.  This proves the distance assertion.
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:14:thm:energy-sharp-stability} in fact shows that the full
space is the unique closest coset among all subgroup cosets.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Exact equality, including the labeling}

The value condition in $Q_\phi$ is sensitive only to the highest
interaction among the $k$ coordinates.  Lower interactions must be
retained when describing equality; declaring the entire labeling
multilinear would be false.

\begin{theorem}[Complete equality classification for one cross-section]
\label{gsr:en:14:thm:collision-equality}
For a nonempty $A\subset\prod_{i=1}^kG_i$, with $m=|A|$, one has
$Q_\phi(A)=m^3$ if and only if both of the following conditions hold.
\begin{enumerate}
 \item $A=\prod_i(c_i+H_i)$ for subgroups $H_i\leq G_i$.
 \item After translation, $f(x)=\phi(c+x)$ on $\prod_iH_i$ has the form
 \begin{equation}
 f(x)=M(x_1,\ldots,x_k)
          +\sum_{S\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,k\}}f_S(x_S),
                                                        \label{gsr:en:14:eq:top-additive}
 \end{equation}
 where $M$ is additive in each variable separately, and the functions
 $f_S:\prod_{i\in S}H_i\to K$ are arbitrary.  The empty-set term is
 a constant.
\end{enumerate}
The full interaction $M$ is uniquely determined by $f$ and the chosen
origin $c$, although the lower-term representation need not be unique.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:14:thm:collision-sharp-stability} with $\varepsilon=0$ proves
the first condition.  On this product coset, every triple of the two
bases and sidelengths is a valid cube pair.  Equality says precisely
that $D_h f(x)$ is independent of $x$ for each $h$.
Let
\[
 M(h)=D_hf(0)
    =\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,k\}}
             (-1)^{k-|S|}f(h_S,0_{S^c}).
\]
The finite-difference identity
\[
 \Delta^i_{u+v}g(x)
       =\Delta^i_u g(x)+\Delta^i_v g(x+e_i u)
\]
and the base-independence of the full mixed difference imply that
$M$ is additive in its $i$th variable, for every $i$.  Rearranging
the defining inclusion-exclusion formula for $M$ gives
\eqref{gsr:en:14:eq:top-additive} with functions of proper subsets of the
coordinates.  Conversely, the full mixed difference of every
proper-subset term is zero, while that of a separately additive
$M$ equals $M(h)$ and is independent of the base.  This proves
sufficiency and also identifies the unique full interaction.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
Source~15's Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:15:thm:exactCartesian} and~\ref{gsr:en:15:thm:exactlabels} prove the same classification independently, without the uniqueness of the top interaction.
\end{writenote}

When $k=1$, the conclusion is an affine homomorphism on a coset.
When some $H_i$ is the trivial subgroup, $D_hf$ vanishes identically,
so every labeling is allowed; this agrees with
\eqref{gsr:en:14:eq:top-additive}, because that coordinate is redundant.
For a full cross-section $\mathbb F_p^k$ with values in $\mathbb F_p$,
separate additivity gives
\[
 M(x)=a x_1\cdots x_k,
\]
but the lower-coordinate functions remain arbitrary.  For example,
$a xy+u(x)+v(y)$ is the complete form in dimension two.  Empty
cross-sections contribute zero and impose no condition.

\subsection{Consequences for a family of cross-sections}

Let $B\subset G\times R$, where $R$ is a finite abelian group, and
let $\phi:B\to K$.  Put $A_r=B_r$, $m_r=|A_r|$, and
\[
 S=\sum_r m_r^3,\qquad R_1=\sum_r Q_{\phi|_{A_r}}(A_r).
\]
Then $R_1=S$ holds exactly when every nonempty cross-section has the
product-coset geometry and labeling described in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:14:thm:collision-equality}.  The different cross-sections
may have different coordinate subgroups and different top interactions.

Suppose $S>0$ and $R_1\geq(1-\varepsilon)S$.  For $m_r>0$ define
\[
 \varepsilon_r=1-\frac{Q_{\phi|_{A_r}}(A_r)}{m_r^3}.
\]
Thus $\sum_r\varepsilon_rm_r^3\leq\varepsilon S$.
For any $0<\theta\leq1/100$, the cross-sections with
$\varepsilon_r\leq\theta$ have total cubic weight at least
$(1-\varepsilon/\theta)S$.  Each of them has a unique product
coset $C_r$ satisfying
\[
 |A_r\triangle C_r|\leq\tau(\varepsilon_r)m_r
                         \leq\tau(\theta)m_r.
\]
Moreover the edits on these cross-sections satisfy the weighted bound
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{\varepsilon_r\leq\theta}m_r^2|A_r\triangle C_r|
 \leq \frac{\varepsilon S}{1-\tau(\theta)}.
                                                        \label{gsr:en:14:eq:weighted-edits}
\end{equation}
Indeed $\tau(u)=u/(1-\tau(u))\leq u/(1-\tau(\theta))$ for
$0\leq u\leq\theta$.

There is also a useful contrapositive.  Let
\[
 d_r=\min_{\text{coordinate cosets }C}
           \frac{|A_r\triangle C|}{m_r},\qquad
 \rho_r=\min\{d_r,\tau(1/100)\}
\]
for nonempty cross-sections.  The stability theorem implies
\begin{equation}
 Q_{\phi|_{A_r}}(A_r)
 \leq m_r^3\bigl(1-\rho_r(1-\rho_r)\bigr).
                                                        \label{gsr:en:14:eq:geometric-defect}
\end{equation}
If the collision deficit is at most $1/100$, invert the stability
bound; otherwise the capped right-hand defect is at most $1/100$.
Consequently, with
\[
 \Xi=\sum_{r:m_r>0}m_r^3\rho_r(1-\rho_r),
\]
one has $R_1\leq S-\Xi$.  Retaining a lower bound for the distance
from product cosets therefore strengthens the denominator used by
the arrangement interpolation argument.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Equality and stability in arrangement moment interpolation\srctag{14}}]{Equality and stability in arrangement moment interpolation}\label{gsr:en:14:sec:d5}
\srcnote{14}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:en:14:sec:moment-rigidity}

We recall the exact representation in a form allowing different groups
for the cube coordinates, the cross-section index, and the label.
Assume now that $K$ is finite, and put $T=R\times K$.  For $h\in G$
define a nonnegative integer weight
\[
 a_h(r,v)=\#\{x\in G:x+\{0,1\}^k\cdot h\subset B_r,
                                \ D_h\phi(x,r)=v\}.
\]
Let $R_j$ count ordered lists of $2j$ congruent cubes for which the
sum of the first $j$ cross-section indices equals the sum of the last
$j$, and likewise for their mixed-difference labels.  Character
orthogonality gives
\begin{equation}
 R_j=\frac1{|T|}\sum_{h\in G}\sum_{\chi\in\widehat T}
                     |\widehat a_h(\chi)|^{2j},
 \qquad
 R_1=\sum_{h,r,v}a_h(r,v)^2.
                                                        \label{gsr:en:14:eq:arrangement-fourier}
\end{equation}
The Fourier transform here is unnormalized.  Replacing $D_h$ by
$(-1)^kD_h$, as in an alternative sign convention in the source,
does not change these counts.

\begin{theorem}[Complete equality criterion for the moment inequality]
\label{gsr:en:14:thm:moment-equality}
Suppose $R_2>0$ and $j\geq3$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 R_j\geq\frac{R_2^{j-1}}{R_1^{j-2}}.       \label{gsr:en:14:eq:moment-interpolation}
\end{equation}
Equality holds if and only if there is a common number $M>0$ with
the following property: for every $h$, either $a_h=0$, or there
are a subgroup $L_h\leq T$ and a point $z_h\in T$ such that
\begin{equation}
 a_h=\frac{M}{|L_h|}\,1_{z_h+L_h}.
                                                        \label{gsr:en:14:eq:moment-coset-weights}
\end{equation}
In particular, all active sidelengths have exactly the same total
number $M$ of cubes, whereas their support subgroups may differ.
The integer-valued nature of $a_h$ imposes the evident divisibility
condition in \eqref{gsr:en:14:eq:moment-coset-weights}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Set $X_{h,\chi}=|\widehat a_h(\chi)|^2$ and give this finite index
set the probability weights
\[
 \nu(h,\chi)=\frac{X_{h,\chi}}{|T|R_1}.
\]
The mean of $X$ under $\nu$ is $\mu=R_2/R_1>0$.  Jensen's
inequality for the strictly convex function $x\mapsto x^{j-1}$
gives \eqref{gsr:en:14:eq:moment-interpolation}; equality is equivalent to
every nonzero $X_{h,\chi}$ being the same positive number $\mu$.

For active $h$, the trivial character gives
$\sum_z a_h(z)=\sqrt\mu=M$, independently of $h$.  We claim that
a nonnegative weight $a$ of mass $M$ whose Fourier coefficients
all have modulus either zero or $M$ is a constant multiple of a
coset indicator.  Choose $z_0$ in its support and let $L$ be the
subgroup generated by all support differences.  Equality in the
triangle inequality says
\[
 |\widehat a(\chi)|=M
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \chi\hbox{ is constant on the support of }a
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \chi\in L^\perp.
\]
The assumed zero-or-$M$ alternative thus identifies the entire Fourier
transform with that of $(M/|L|)1_{z_0+L}$.  Fourier inversion proves
the claim.  This establishes necessity of
\eqref{gsr:en:14:eq:moment-coset-weights}.  Conversely, each such weight has
Fourier modulus $M$ on $L_h^\perp$ and zero elsewhere, proving
equality in \eqref{gsr:en:14:eq:moment-interpolation}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
Source~15's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:15:thm:amplification} is the same inequality and equality criterion in a division-free form.
\end{writenote}

For $j=2$ the moment inequality is an identity and has no rigidity
content.  This is why the strict assumption $j\geq3$ is necessary.


\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 11--14]
\emph{Credit.} Inequality \eqref{gsr:en:14:eq:moment-interpolation} with the profile $S$ is source~04's arrangement interpolation (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:04:mom:arrangements}, its (A5) and (A7)), and source~04's equality models (A13), (A14) are special cases of the classification here. This advances source~04's Question~7 (carrying the profile) without answering it (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:profiles}).
\end{writenote}
\begin{corollary}[Equality in the profile bound for higher arrangements]
\label{gsr:en:14:cor:joint-equality}
If $R_2>0$ and $j\geq3$, then
\[
 R_j\geq\frac{R_2^{j-1}}{S^{j-2}}.
\]
Equality holds exactly when both the cross-section classification
of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:14:thm:collision-equality} and the common-mass coset
condition of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:14:thm:moment-equality} hold.  More generally,
\begin{equation}
 R_j\geq\frac{R_2^{j-1}}{(S-\Xi)^{j-2}}.
                                                        \label{gsr:en:14:eq:geometry-enhanced-lifting}
\end{equation}
The denominator is positive whenever $R_2>0$, because
$R_1\leq S-\Xi$ and $R_1>0$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[A defect computable from cross-section cardinalities]
\label{gsr:en:14:cor:cardinality-profile-defect}
Suppose the cube coordinates form $\mathbb F_p^k$.  For
$1\leq m\leq p^k$ define
\[
 b_p(m)=\min\left\{\tau(1/100),\
                    \min_{0\leq a\leq k}\frac{|m-p^a|}{m}\right\},
 \qquad
 S_{\rm card}=\sum_{r:m_r>0}
 m_r^3\bigl(1-b_p(m_r)(1-b_p(m_r))\bigr).
\]
Then
\[
 R_1\leq S_{\rm card}\leq S,
 \qquad
 R_j\geq\frac{R_2^{j-1}}{S_{\rm card}^{j-2}}
       \quad (R_2>0,\ j\geq3).
\]
Thus section sizes alone can give an explicit improvement over the cubic
profile denominator; no search over the geometry of a section is needed.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Every nonempty coordinate product coset in $\mathbb F_p^k$ has
cardinality $p^a$ for some $0\leq a\leq k$.  Since
$|A_r\triangle C|\geq\bigl||A_r|-|C|\bigr|$, we have
$b_p(m_r)\leq\rho_r$.  Both quantities lie in $[0,\tau(1/100)]$,
where $x(1-x)$ is increasing.  Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:14:eq:geometric-defect}
therefore gives the asserted bound for $R_1$ after summation.
Insert it into \eqref{gsr:en:14:eq:moment-interpolation} for the higher moments.
\end{proof}

The two criteria can in fact be combined into a direct description of
the original set and label, without keeping the auxiliary weights.

\begin{theorem}[Direct geometric classification of simultaneous equality]
\label{gsr:en:14:thm:joint-geometric-equality}
Suppose $R_2>0$ and $j\geq3$.  Equality
\[
 R_j=\frac{R_2^{j-1}}{S^{j-2}}
\]
holds if and only if there are subgroups $H_i\leq G_i$, a subgroup
$R'\leq R$, a point $r_0\in R$, and representatives $c_r\in G$
for $r\in r_0+R'$, with the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}
 \item The nonempty cross-sections are exactly those with
 $r\in r_0+R'$, and each is $B_r=c_r+H$, where $H=\prod_iH_i$.
 \item There is a separately additive map $M_0:H\to K$ and a map
 $T:R'\times H_1\times\cdots\times H_k\to K$ additive in all
 $k+1$ variables such that, for $x\in H$,
 \begin{equation}
 \phi(c_r+x,r)=M_0(x)+T(r-r_0,x)
                   +\sum_{U\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,k\}}f_{r,U}(x_U),
                                                        \label{gsr:en:14:eq:joint-geometric-label}
 \end{equation}
 where all the lower-coordinate functions $f_{r,U}$ are arbitrary.
\end{enumerate}
The representatives $c_r$ may vary arbitrarily with $r$.
Writing $m=|H|$ and $s=|R'|$, every such example satisfies
\begin{equation}
 R_t=m^{2t+1}s^{2t-1}\qquad(t\geq1).
                                                        \label{gsr:en:14:eq:joint-equality-counts}
\end{equation}
Thus equality at one moment $j\geq3$ implies equality at every
higher moment.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:14:cor:joint-equality}, each active cross-section is
$c_r+H_r$, where $H_r$ is a coordinate product subgroup, and its
full interaction is a separately additive map $M_r:H_r\to K$.
Let $m_r=|H_r|$.  A cube with sidelength $h$ belongs to this section
precisely when $h\in H_r$, and then it has $m_r$ possible bases and
the fixed label $M_r(h)$.  Hence
\[
 a_h(r,v)=m_r\,1_{h\in H_r}\,1_{v=M_r(h)}.
\]
At $h=0$, the total mass of $a_0$ is $\sum_r m_r$.  At any active
$h$, it is $\sum_{r:h\in H_r}m_r$.  The common-mass condition of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:14:thm:moment-equality} forces these two sums to coincide.
All summands are positive, so an element lying in any $H_r$ lies
in every $H_r$.  The subgroups $H_r$ are therefore all the same
coordinate product subgroup $H$.

Let $I$ be the set of active indices.  Since $M_r(0)=0$, the support
of $a_0$ is $I\times\{0\}$.  Its being a coset forces
$I=r_0+R'$ for a subgroup $R'\leq R$.  For each $h\in H$, the
support of $a_h$ is the graph
\[
 \{(r,M_r(h)):r\in r_0+R'\}.
\]
A graph over a subgroup coset is a subgroup coset in $R\times K$
exactly when its function is affine additive on that coset: translate
the graph by its point at $r_0$, then use closure under addition
and the uniqueness of the graph value.  Consequently
\[
 T(u,h)=M_{r_0+u}(h)-M_{r_0}(h)
\]
is additive in $u\in R'$.  For fixed $u$, it is a difference of
two separately additive functions of $h$, so it is separately
additive in the $k$ remaining variables as well.  Taking
$M_0=M_{r_0}$ and using Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:14:thm:collision-equality} gives
\eqref{gsr:en:14:eq:joint-geometric-label}.

Conversely, this description gives
$a_h=m1_{\Gamma_h}$ for $h\in H$ and $a_h=0$ otherwise, where
each $\Gamma_h$ is a coset graph of size $s$ and every active mass
is $ms$.  Both equality criteria hold.  More explicitly, there
are $m$ choices of $h$, $s^{2t-1}$ index tuples with equal half
sums, and $m^{2t}$ choices of cube bases.  The affine-additive
dependence of $M_r(h)$ on $r$ makes the label relation automatic.
This proves \eqref{gsr:en:14:eq:joint-equality-counts}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
Source~15's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:15:thm:joint} is the same normal form, proved independently.
\end{writenote}

This classification allows very nonrectangular sets $B$ as subsets of
$G\times R$: the section translations may vary freely.  If some
$H_i$ is trivial then $M_0$ and $T$ vanish, and every labeling of
each section is allowed.  Such degenerate configurations are a
necessary part of the exact arrangement count, rather than exceptions
that may be discarded.

For $j=8$, a known geometric defect supplies the explicit additional
factor $(1-\Xi/S)^{-6}$ relative to the cubic-profile moment bound.
This is a local strengthening of Lemma~14.7's moment step.  It does
not by itself change the final quantitative bound for Szemer\'edi's
theorem, because the later extraction and inductive losses must also
be tracked.

\subsection{A quantitative form of spectral flatness}

\begin{proposition}[Near equality concentrates the active Fourier mass]
\label{gsr:en:14:prop:moment-spectral-stability}
Let $R_2>0$, $j\geq3$, and suppose
\[
 R_j\leq(1+\eta)\frac{R_2^{j-1}}{R_1^{j-2}},\qquad\eta\geq0.
\]
With $X$, $\nu$, and $\mu$ as in the preceding proof,
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb E_\nu\left(\frac X\mu-1\right)^2
 =\frac{R_3R_1}{R_2^2}-1
 \leq (1+\eta)^{1/(j-2)}-1.
                                                        \label{gsr:en:14:eq:flat-variance}
\end{equation}
Thus, for every $s>0$,
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{|X/\mu-1|\geq s}\nu(h,\chi)
 \leq\frac{(1+\eta)^{1/(j-2)}-1}{s^2}.
                                                        \label{gsr:en:14:eq:flat-tail}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The identity in \eqref{gsr:en:14:eq:flat-variance} follows by expanding the
square.  Interpolating the moments of the nonnegative spectrum gives
\[
 R_j\geq\frac{R_3^{j-2}}{R_2^{j-3}}.
\]
For $j=3$ this is equality.  For $j>3$, it follows directly from
H\"older interpolation between the powers $2$, $3$, and $j$.
Combining this inequality with the hypothesis yields
\[
 \left(\frac{R_3R_1}{R_2^2}\right)^{j-2}\leq1+\eta.
\]
Chebyshev's inequality proves \eqref{gsr:en:14:eq:flat-tail}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
Source~15's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:15:thm:spectral} bounds the same variance by $\eta/(j-2)$, which this proposition improves; its Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:15:cor:band} and Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:15:prop:profile} add the size of the near-flat band and the side-vector profile.
\end{writenote}

This conclusion concerns the Fourier mass weighted by its contribution
to $R_1$.  It does not assert that the labeling is close to a separately
additive function, or that every active weight $a_h$ is close to a coset
indicator.  Those stronger inverse statements require additional work.

\section[{Axis cubes and collision measures\srctag{15}}]{Axis cubes and collision measures}\label{gsr:en:15:sec:d2}\label{gsr:en:15:sec:setup}
\srcnote{15}{Section 2}

Fix $k\ge1$, finite abelian groups $G_1,\ldots,G_k,T,V$, and write
\[
 X=\prod_{i=1}^kG_i,\qquad M=|X|,\quad n=|T|,\quad q=|V|.
\]
Let $B\subseteq X\times T$ and let $\phi:B\to V$ be a partial map.
For $y,h\in X$ and $\omega\in\{0,1\}^k$, the expression
$y+\omega h$ means $(y_i+\omega_i h_i)_{i=1}^k$.

\begin{definition}[Admissible cube and its value]
A triple $(y,h,x)\in X\times X\times T$ is admissible when
$(y+\omega h,x)\in B$ for every $\omega\in\{0,1\}^k$.
For an admissible triple put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:derivative}
 D_h\phi(y,x)=\sum_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^k}
 (-1)^{k-|\omega|}\phi(y+\omega h,x).
\end{equation}
This is an alternating sum in the abelian group $V$.
\end{definition}

The repository uses $(-1)^{|\omega|}$ instead. Its cube value differs by
the fixed sign $(-1)^k$. Both equality and additive-respect conditions are
unchanged. No extension of $\phi$ outside $B$ affects any count.

\begin{definition}[Respected arrangement]
For an integer $d\ge1$, a respected $d$-arrangement consists of a common
side vector $h\in X$ and $2d$ ordered admissible cubes
$(y_j,h,x_j)$ such that
\begin{align}
 \sum_{j=1}^{d}x_j&=\sum_{j=d+1}^{2d}x_j,\label{gsr:en:15:eq:verticalrelation}\\
 \sum_{j=1}^{d}D_h\phi(y_j,x_j)
 &=\sum_{j=d+1}^{2d}D_h\phi(y_j,x_j).\label{gsr:en:15:eq:valuerelation}
\end{align}
Let $R_d$ count these arrangements, and let $R_d(h)$ count those with
prescribed $h$.
\end{definition}

In the unrestricted domain, ignoring \eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:valuerelation}, there are
$M^{2d+1}n^{2d-1}$ arrangements: choose $h$, all $2d$ base points,
and all but one of the vertical coordinates. This explains the normalization
of $a_d$ used in Section~\ref{gsr:fm:15:sec:intro}. For $G_i=T=V=\Z/N\Z$,
$R_2$ and $R_8$ are exactly the counts relevant to Lemmas 14.7--14.8,
with ambient powers $N^{5k+3}$ and $N^{17k+15}$.

Define a nonnegative integer-valued measure on $T\times V$ by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:measure}
 m_h(x,v)=\#\{y\in X:(y,h,x)\text{ is admissible and }
 D_h\phi(y,x)=v\}.
\end{equation}
The collision count and its two useful decompositions are
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:collision}
 C=R_1=\sum_{h,x,v}m_h(x,v)^2
   =\sum_h C_h=\sum_x C_x,
\end{equation}
where $C_h=\sum_{x,v}m_h(x,v)^2$ and
$C_x=\sum_{h,v}m_h(x,v)^2$. The subscripts $h$ and $x$ distinguish
side-vector and vertical-fibre disintegrations.

For the fibre $B_x=\{y:(y,x)\in B\}$, put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:densities}
 b_x=|B_x|,\quad \beta_x=b_x/M,\quad
 \beta=\E_{x\in T}\beta_x,\quad
 \rho_3=\E_{x\in T}\beta_x^3,\quad
 \Gamma=\sum_x b_x^3=M^3n\rho_3.
\end{equation}
When $B$ is nonempty, $C>0$: the zero side vector already supplies
collisions. Empty domains are dealt with by the division-free statements.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Exact moment amplification\srctag{15}}]{Exact moment amplification}\label{gsr:en:15:sec:d3}\label{gsr:en:15:sec:moments}
\srcnote{15}{Section 3}

Let $\widehat T$ and $\widehat V$ denote the character groups, with
characters valued in the unit circle. All Fourier transforms below are
unnormalized.

\begin{lemma}[Moment--count identity]\label{gsr:en:15:lem:moment}
For
\[
 F_h(\alpha,\psi)=\sum_{x\in T,v\in V}m_h(x,v)\alpha(x)\psi(v),
 \qquad \alpha\in\widehat T,\ \psi\in\widehat V,
\]
and every integer $d\ge1$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:momentidentity}
 \sum_{h,\alpha,\psi}|F_h(\alpha,\psi)|^{2d}=nqR_d.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Expand $F_h^d\overline{F_h}^{\,d}$. For an ordered selection
$(x_1,v_1),\ldots,(x_{2d},v_{2d})$, its coefficient is
$\prod_jm_h(x_j,v_j)$, and its character factor is
\[
 \alpha\left(\sum_{j\le d}x_j-\sum_{j>d}x_j\right)
 \psi\left(\sum_{j\le d}v_j-\sum_{j>d}v_j\right).
\]
The sum over $\alpha,\psi$ is $nq$ precisely when both arguments are zero,
and is otherwise zero, by finite character orthogonality. The multiplicity
$\prod_jm_h(x_j,v_j)$ chooses exactly the corresponding admissible base
points. Summing over $h$ proves the identity. This also proves the identity
for general finite abelian value groups, without a prime-modulus assumption.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Finite moment interpolation]\label{gsr:en:15:lem:interpolation}
For finitely many nonnegative real numbers $t_i$ and an integer $d\ge2$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:interpolation}
 \left(\sum_i t_i^2\right)^{d-1}
 \le \left(\sum_i t_i\right)^{d-2}\sum_i t_i^d.
\end{equation}
If $d>2$ and $\sum_i t_i>0$, equality holds exactly when all positive $t_i$
are equal.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $S_1=\sum_i t_i$ is zero, all terms vanish. Otherwise give index $i$
probability $p_i=t_i/S_1$. Jensen's inequality for the convex function
$u\mapsto u^{d-1}$ gives
\[
 \sum_i p_it_i^{d-1}\ge\left(\sum_i p_it_i\right)^{d-1}.
\]
Multiplying by $S_1^{d-1}$ yields \eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:interpolation}. For $d>2$,
strict convexity says that equality holds precisely when $t_i$ is constant
on the support of $p$. For $d=2$, the inequality is an identity.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Collision-sensitive amplification]\label{gsr:en:15:thm:amplification}
For every integer $d\ge2$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:rawamp}
 \boxed{R_2^{d-1}\le C^{d-2}R_d.}
\end{equation}
If $C>0$, this is equivalently
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:normalizedamp}
 \boxed{a_d\ge\frac{a_2^{d-1}}{\chi^{d-2}}.}
\end{equation}
For $d>2$, equality holds exactly when the nonzero numbers
$|F_h(\alpha,\psi)|^2$, across all three indices, have a common value.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:15:lem:interpolation} to
$t_{h,\alpha,\psi}=|F_h(\alpha,\psi)|^2$. By
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:15:lem:moment}, the three sums in that inequality are
$nqR_2$, $nqC$, and $nqR_d$. The common factor $(nq)^{d-1}$ cancels.
The powers of $M$ and $n$ also cancel in the stated normalization.
The equality assertion is exactly the equality assertion of the
interpolation lemma. If $C=0$, every $m_h$ vanishes, so all counts vanish.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{Credit.} This is source~04's interpolation (A5) (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:04:mom:arrangements}) and source~14's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:14:thm:moment-equality}, with the same equality criterion (source~14 proves it through the same coset-weight description, this source's Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:15:lem:positiveflat}); proved independently here, in a division-free form that also allows $C=0$ and $d=2$. \emph{Formal status} (HEAD \texttt{0b4890a1c}): Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:15:lem:moment} for general $d$ is the private \file{cor147_moment_eq_count} (\file{Proofs14HigherArrangements.lean}, line~484); the interpolation exists only at $d=8$, in the private \file{cor147_interpolation} and \file{cor147_moment_interpolation} (lines~653 and~701, exponents $2,4,16$), inside the proof of \file{lemma_14_7_holds} (line~712). The theorem for general $d$ is not stated in Lean, and the ``interpolation infrastructure'' of Section~\ref{gsr:fz:15:sec:d13} is $d=8$ only.
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
For Gowers's Lemma~12.3 source~33 adds a linear branch: $\theta N^8$ respected parallelogram pairs give at least $\max\{\theta^7,4\theta-3\}N^{32}$ respected eight-arrangements (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:33:ras:cor:gowers-amplification}; the branch is active for $\theta>0.8045\ldots$), and a sharp repair theorem on full products (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:arrangements}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{remark}[Restriction of the side-vector family]
The same proof works with $h$ restricted to any fixed subset of $X$.
It also works with a fixed nonnegative weight on $h$, provided the same
weight is used in every moment and arrangement count. Excluding zero
side coordinates alone therefore does not destroy the moment identity.
Excluding arbitrary coincidences between different constituent cubes is
another matter: such exclusions need not factor through $m_h$.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The cubic fibre bound and sharp density improvements\srctag{15}}]{The cubic fibre bound and sharp density improvements}\label{gsr:en:15:sec:d4}\label{gsr:en:15:sec:cubic}
\srcnote{15}{Section 4}

For $A\subseteq X$, define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:Q}
 Q(A)=\#\{(h,y,z)\in X^3:
 y+\omega h,z+\omega h\in A\text{ for every }\omega\in\{0,1\}^k\}.
\end{equation}
No label condition appears in $Q$.

\begin{lemma}[Cubic domination]\label{gsr:en:15:lem:cubic}
For every $A\subseteq X$ and every labelled domain $B$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:cubic}
 Q(A)\le|A|^3,\qquad C_x\le Q(B_x)\le b_x^3,
 \qquad C\le\Gamma.
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:chain}
 0<\chi\le\rho_3\le\beta\le1
\end{equation}
for nonempty $B$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The map
\[
 (h,y,z)\longmapsto (y,y+h,z)
\]
injects the configurations counted by $Q(A)$ into $A^3$. Its inverse on its
image recovers $h$ as the second entry minus the first. Forgetting equality
of the mixed values gives $C_x\le Q(B_x)$. Sum over $x$.
Finally, $0\le\beta_x\le1$ implies $\beta_x^3\le\beta_x$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Density-sensitive version of Lemma 14.7]\label{gsr:en:15:cor:147}
In the cyclic setting $G_i=T=V=\Z/N\Z$, suppose
$R_2\ge\theta N^{5k+3}$ with $\theta>0$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:147improved}
 R_8\ge\theta^7\chi^{-6}N^{17k+15}
 \ge\theta^7\rho_3^{-6}N^{17k+15}
 \ge\theta^7\beta^{-6}N^{17k+15}.
\end{equation}
If, in addition, $\beta_x\le\kappa\beta$ for every $x$, where
$\kappa\ge1$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:147balanced}
 R_8\ge\kappa^{-12}\theta^7\beta^{-18}N^{17k+15}.
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Use Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:15:thm:amplification} with $d=8$ and
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:15:lem:cubic}. Under the fibre cap,
\[
 \rho_3=\E_x\beta_x^3
 \le (\kappa\beta)^2\E_x\beta_x=\kappa^2\beta^3.
\]
Substitute this upper bound into \eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:147improved}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{Credit.} Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:15:lem:cubic} and this corollary are source~04's (A6)--(A11) (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:04:mom:arrangements}): source~04's profile $\sigma$ is this $\rho_3$ and its $K$ is this $\kappa$; the cubic cap $C\le\sum_x b_x^3$ is source~04's (A9) and source~14's chain \eqref{gsr:en:14:eq:collision-chain}. Example~\ref{gsr:en:15:ex:sharp} below has source~04's (A13) and (A14) as its two faces $H=X$ and $J=T$.
\end{writenote}

For arbitrary $d$, the same argument gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:all-density}
 a_d\ge a_2^{d-1}\rho_3^{-(d-2)}
 \ge a_2^{d-1}\beta^{-(d-2)},
\end{equation}
and the fibre cap gives the factor
$\kappa^{-2(d-2)}\beta^{-3(d-2)}$.
The density of a fibre matters cubically, not merely through its contribution
to total mass.

\begin{example}[A sharp two-parameter family]\label{gsr:en:15:ex:sharp}
Let $H_i\le G_i$, put $H=\prod_iH_i$, let $J\le T$, and take
\[
 B=(c+H)\times(t+J),\qquad \phi=0.
\]
Writing $a=|H|/M$ and $b=|J|/n$, direct counting gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:sharp}
 \beta=ab,\quad \rho_3=\chi=a^3b,\quad
 a_d=a^{2d+1}b^{2d-1}.
\end{equation}
Indeed, an admissible side lies in $H$, every base lies in $c+H$, and
there are $|J|^{2d-1}$ vertical additive tuples in $t+J$.
Thus $R_d=|H|^{2d+1}|J|^{2d-1}$, and
\eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:normalizedamp} is equality for every $d$.
When $H=X$, the factor $\beta^{-(d-2)}$ in
\eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:all-density} is sharp. When $J=T$, all fibres have the same
density, and the balanced factor $\beta^{-3(d-2)}$ is sharp.
\end{example}

\begin{example}[Why balance cannot be silently assumed]\label{gsr:en:15:ex:balance}
Take $B=X\times J$, where $J<T$ is a subgroup, and $\phi=0$.
Then $\rho_3=\chi=\beta$, $a_2=\beta^3$, and $a_8=\beta^{15}$.
Replacing $\rho_3$ by $\beta^3$ without a fibre hypothesis would assert
$a_8\ge a_2^7/\beta^{18}=\beta^3$, which is false for $0<\beta<1$.
Jensen's inequality actually gives $\rho_3\ge\beta^3$, the opposite
of the upper bound needed in that argument.
\end{example}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Coupling the product property to the collision count\srctag{15}}]{Coupling the product property to the collision count}\label{gsr:en:15:sec:d5}\label{gsr:en:15:sec:product}
\srcnote{15}{Section 5}

This section proves \eqref{gsr:fm:15:eq:introcoupled}. The important point is that
$\chi$ enters the product-property lower bound with a positive fourth power
before it enters the interpolation denominator. It must be retained in both
places until these exponents have been combined.

\subsection{The generalized product property}
Let the $k+1$ coordinate groups of $X\times T$ be denoted by
$K_1,\ldots,K_{k+1}$, with $K_{k+1}=T$.

\begin{definition}[Product property]\label{gsr:en:15:def:PP}
The map $\phi:B\to V$ has $\PP_\gamma$ if the following holds for every
coordinate $j$, every integer $p\ge0$, every family of $p$ parallel
$j$-coordinate lines, every common subset $E\subseteq K_j$ on which
all these lines lie in $B$, and every function $w:E\to[0,\infty)$.
If $\psi_1,\ldots,\psi_p:E\to V$ are the corresponding restrictions of
$\phi$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:PP}
 \sum_{\substack{u_1+u_2=u_3+u_4\ \text{in }E\\
 \psi_i(u_1)+\psi_i(u_2)=\psi_i(u_3)+\psi_i(u_4)\ (1\le i\le p)}}
 \prod_{s=1}^4w(u_s)
 \ \ge\ \frac{\gamma^{8p}}{|K_j|}
 \left(\sum_{u\in E}w(u)\right)^4.
\end{equation}
Repeated lines are allowed. We assume $0<\gamma\le1$.
\end{definition}

For equal cyclic coordinate and value groups this is the repository's
\filename{HasProductProperty}, with its normalization unchanged
\cite{repo15defs}. Restriction to a coordinate fibre preserves the property:
every relevant family of lines is still a family of lines in the original
domain.

\begin{lemma}[An automatic weak parameter]\label{gsr:en:15:lem:weakPP}
Every $V$-valued partial map on a product of finite abelian groups has
$\PP_\gamma$ for $\gamma=q^{-1/8}$. A constant map has $\PP_1$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For a chosen family of $p$ restrictions, place mass $w(u)$ at
$(u,\psi_1(u),\ldots,\psi_p(u))\in K_j\times V^p$.
Call this nonnegative measure $\mu$. The left side of \eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:PP}
is $\sum_z(\mu*\mu)(z)^2$. Cauchy--Schwarz bounds it below by
\[
 \frac{(\sum_z(\mu*\mu)(z))^2}{|K_j|q^p}
 =\frac{(\sum_uw(u))^4}{|K_j|q^p}.
\]
This is \eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:PP} for the stated $\gamma$.
For constant restrictions the value conditions are automatic, so the same
argument on $K_j$ alone gives $\gamma=1$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The configuration input, with all exponents retained}
For a set $A\subseteq G_1\times\cdots\times G_j$, a configuration is
specified by $(y,h,t)$ and has vertices
\[
 y+\varepsilon h+\delta t,
 \qquad \varepsilon,\delta\in\{0,1\}^j.
\]
It is contained if all vertices lie in $A$. It is respected if each
coordinate parallelogram face satisfies the additive value identity:
with all other binary coordinates fixed, the values at positions
$00$ and $11$ sum to the values at positions $10$ and $01$.
Let $\mathcal F_j(A,\phi)$ be the number of contained respected
configurations.

\begin{lemma}[Configuration lower bound]\label{gsr:en:15:lem:configuration}
Suppose $A$ has density $\alpha$ in a product of $j$ finite abelian groups
of total size $L$, and the restricted map has $\PP_\gamma$.
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:configuration}
 \mathcal F_j(A,\phi)\ge
 \alpha^{4^j}\gamma^{2j4^j}L^3.
\end{equation}
The configuration count is at most the respected parallel cube-pair count
on that domain.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
We prove the lower bound by induction, including $j=0$. A product of zero
groups has one point; its density is zero or one, so
$\mathcal F_0=\alpha$ and the assertion holds.
For the induction step, write the ambient product as $Z\times K_j$,
where $|Z|=L_0$ and $|K_j|=s$. For each potential
$(j-1)$-configuration $\zeta$ in $Z$, let $E_\zeta$ be the set of
$u\in K_j$ at which $\zeta$ is contained and respected in the fibre $A_u$.
Apply the product property to the $4^{j-1}$ vertical restrictions through
its vertices, with weight $\one_{E_\zeta}$. The resulting additive
quadruples supply exactly the final-coordinate faces; membership in
$E_\zeta$ supplies all other faces. An additive quadruple is uniquely
parameterized by its base and two side increments. Hence
\[
 \mathcal F_j(A,\phi)\ge
 \frac{\gamma^{8\cdot4^{j-1}}}{s}
 \sum_\zeta |E_\zeta|^4.
\]
There are $L_0^3$ potential $\zeta$. Also
\[
 \sum_\zeta|E_\zeta|
 =\sum_{u\in K_j}\mathcal F_{j-1}(A_u,\phi_u)
 \ge L_0^3s\,\gamma^{e_{j-1}}\alpha^{4^{j-1}},
\]
where $e_{j-1}=2(j-1)4^{j-1}$; the last step uses the induction hypothesis
and Jensen in the fibre densities. A further Jensen application gives
\[
 \mathcal F_j\ge
 \alpha^{4^j}\gamma^{4e_{j-1}+8\cdot4^{j-1}}L_0^3s^3.
\]
Since $4e_{j-1}+8\cdot4^{j-1}=2j4^j$, this proves
\eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:configuration}.

For the final assertion, send $(y,h,t)$ to the two cubes with bases $y$
and $y+t$, both with side $h$. The map is injective. Their mixed values
are equal: move the base from $y$ to $y+t$ one coordinate at a time.
At coordinate $i$, the mixed-value change contains the face difference
$\Delta_{h_i}\Delta_{t_i}\phi$, which vanishes at every required vertex by
respect of the corresponding face. Every vertex used belongs to the
configuration. Thus the image is a respected cube pair.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Collision lower bound]\label{gsr:en:15:cor:collisionlower}
If $B\subseteq X\times T$ has density $\beta$ and $\phi$ has
$\PP_\gamma$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:collisionlower}
 \chi\ge\beta^{4^k}\gamma^{e_k},\qquad e_k=2k4^k.
\end{equation}
More precisely,
$\chi\ge\gamma^{e_k}\E_x\beta_x^{4^k}$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:15:lem:configuration} to every horizontal fibre, where the
product property is inherited. Its respected cube-pair count is $C_x$.
Sum and divide by $M^3n$. Jensen gives the displayed weaker form in $\beta$.
\end{proof}

The argument above recovers the configuration and cube-pair input of
Gowers's Lemma 14.4 and Corollary 14.5 in the present group notation.
It is included to make the subsequent coupled bound self-contained, not as
a claimed new configuration theorem.

\subsection{The collision-parametrized pair bound}
\begin{theorem}[Retaining the collision parameter]\label{gsr:en:15:thm:PPcollision}
Under $\PP_\gamma$, put $u_k=8\cdot2^k$. For every $h\in X$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:localPP}
 R_2(h)\ge\frac{\gamma^{u_k}C_h^4}{nM^4}.
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:globalPP}
 R_2\ge\frac{\gamma^{u_k}C^4}{nM^7},
 \qquad \boxed{a_2\ge\gamma^{u_k}\chi^4.}
\end{equation}
Only the product property in the vertical coordinate is needed here.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Fix $h$ and a reference base $y\in X$. For each $x\in T$, define
\[
 w_y(x)=
 \begin{cases}
 m_h(x,D_h\phi(y,x)),&(y,h,x)\text{ admissible},\\
 0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
This counts admissible cubes at level $x$ with the same side and mixed value
as the reference cube. Let $E_y$ be the set of levels where the reference
cube is admissible. Apply \eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:PP} to the $2^k$ vertical lines through
$y+\omega h$, the common domain $E_y$, and the nonnegative weight $w_y$.
It gives at least
\[
 \frac{\gamma^{u_k}}{n}\left(\sum_xw_y(x)\right)^4
\]
weighted additive quadruples of levels whose values are additive at every
vertex of the reference cube. Alternating over the vertices shows that
the reference mixed values also satisfy the additive relation.

For each of the four levels, choose a cube counted by $w_y$.
Its mixed value equals the corresponding reference mixed value, so the four
chosen cubes form a respected $2$-arrangement with side $h$.
For this fixed reference base $y$, the resulting choices inject into the
arrangements counted by $R_2(h)$: the levels and the four chosen bases
recover the choices. Therefore
\[
 R_2(h)\ge\frac{\gamma^{u_k}}{n}
       \left(\sum_xw_y(x)\right)^4
 \quad\text{for each }y.
\]
Average over all $M$ reference bases and apply Jensen. The exact identity
\[
 \sum_{y,x}w_y(x)=\sum_{x,v}m_h(x,v)^2=C_h
\]
then gives \eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:localPP}. Notice that the injection is asserted for a
\emph{fixed} reference base. Averaging, rather than claiming a global
injection without that base, accounts for the factor $M$.

Finally sum over the $M$ side vectors and use
$\sum_hC_h^4\ge C^4/M^3$. This proves \eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:globalPP} and its
normalized form.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{Formal status} (HEAD \texttt{0b4890a1c}). The ingredients are proof-level facts of the development: the first moment $\sum\theta=C$ is the right side of the private \file{cor146_pair_first_moment} (\file{Proofs14Arrangements.lean}, line~183), and the private \file{cor146_average_fourth_moment} takes the first-moment lower bound as a hypothesis; the $C$-parametrized form proved here is not stated in Lean. Not formalized; new as a stated theorem.

\begin{theorem}[Coupled amplification]\label{gsr:en:15:thm:coupled}
Suppose $\phi:B\to V$ has $\PP_\gamma$ and $B$ has density $\beta>0$.
For every integer $d\ge2$,
\begin{align}
 a_d&\ge\gamma^{u_k(d-1)}\chi^{3d-2},\label{gsr:en:15:eq:coupledchi}\\
 a_d&\ge\beta^{(3d-2)4^k}
 \gamma^{(6d-4)k4^k+8(d-1)2^k}.\label{gsr:en:15:eq:coupledbeta}
\end{align}
For $d=8$, this becomes \eqref{gsr:fm:15:eq:intro8}.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Since $C>0$, combine Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:15:thm:amplification}
and~\ref{gsr:en:15:thm:PPcollision} before estimating $\chi$:
\[
 a_d\ge\frac{a_2^{d-1}}{\chi^{d-2}}
 \ge\frac{(\gamma^{u_k}\chi^4)^{d-1}}{\chi^{d-2}}
 =\gamma^{u_k(d-1)}\chi^{3d-2}.
\]
The remaining power of $\chi$ is positive. We may now apply the
\emph{lower} bound \eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:collisionlower}. The exponent of $\gamma$ is
\[
 (3d-2)e_k+(d-1)u_k
 =(6d-4)k4^k+8(d-1)2^k,
\]
which proves \eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:coupledbeta}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[A direction-of-inequality trap]
It would be invalid to replace the denominator $\chi^{d-2}$ by a
\emph{lower} bound while independently replacing $a_2$ by a lower bound.
The argument succeeds because it first substitutes the functional inequality
$a_2\ge\gamma^{u_k}\chi^4$, leaving a positive power of the same $\chi$.
This is why the gain is larger than simply replacing the ambient
second-moment cap by a density cap.
\end{remark}

A finer, immediately available version of \eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:coupledbeta} replaces
$\beta^{(3d-2)4^k}$ by
$\bigl(\E_x\beta_x^{4^k}\bigr)^{3d-2}$.
The theorem does not claim that its exponents are optimal. The sharpness
examples in Section~\ref{gsr:en:15:sec:cubic} establish sharpness of the collision
interpolation and the cubic-density substitutions, not of every
product-property estimate used here.

\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:15:eq:unweakenedpairs}

 \gamma^{2k4^{k+1}+8\cdot2^k}.

 E_k\le3k4^{k+1}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 8\cdot2^k\le k4^{k+1},

which holds, with equality at $k=1$.
