Formal results written after that pin confirm source~19's audit points (the distinct-anchor counterexample, the failure of the same-dimension comparison) and prove a local affine lift with weaker constants (notes after Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:19:sampling:anchors} and Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:19:lift:source-corollary}); they are not source~19's statements. Nothing in these sections is formalized.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A sharp first-order count of degenerate arrangements\srctag{18}}]{A sharp first-order count of degenerate arrangements}\label{gsr:en:18:sec:d2}
\srcnote{18}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:en:18:deg:sec-main}

The purpose of this section is to refine Lemma~15.4 of
Gowers~\cite{gowers}.  We retain the full definition of degeneracy
given immediately before that lemma.  This qualification matters:
Gowers observes after his proof that several tests involving the last
coordinate can be discarded.  Those tests are exactly what produces
the additional saving proved below.  The result therefore applies to
the original definition, and to the random selection in Lemma~15.5,
which uses all the coordinate monomials.  It is not a corresponding
claim about the weaker definition mentioned in that remark.

For fixed cube dimension $k$ and arrangement order $d\geq2$, we determine
the leading coefficient in the proportion of degenerate arrangements:
\[
 \frac{k+C_d}{p}+O_{k,d}(p^{-2}),
 \qquad
 C_d=\frac{T_{2d}-2\binom{2d}{d}+1}{2},
 \qquad
 T_n=[z^0](z^{-1}+1+z)^n.
\]
The coefficient $k+C_d$ is sharp.  We also give a finite inequality,
so that the asymptotic statement can be used without an unspecified
error constant.  In the case $d=8$ relevant to Gowers's proof,
$C_8=2\,585\,444$.  Under the usual restrictions that the density and
error parameters lie in $(0,1]$, this replaces the factor
$k3^{2^{k+4}}$ in the size hypothesis of Lemma~15.5 by
$k+2\,585\,445$.  The random-selection exponent itself is unchanged.

These are refinements proved in this article.  We make no claim that
their precise formulation is absent from all previous literature.
The numbered source statements refer to Gowers's paper and, where
explicit hypotheses have been supplied, to the repository transcription
\cite{gowers,repo18}.

\subsection{Arrangements and their certificates}

Fix integers $k\geq1$ and $d\geq2$, and write
\[
 q=2d,\qquad
 s=(\underbrace{1,\ldots,1}_{d},
       \underbrace{-1,\ldots,-1}_{d})\in\F_p^q,
 \qquad H=\{r\in\F_p^q:s\cdot r=0\}.
\]
An arrangement is specified by
\[
 h\in\F_p^k,\qquad r\in H,\qquad
 y=(y^1,\ldots,y^q)\in(\F_p^k)^q,
\]
through the map
\begin{equation}
 \rho(\epsilon,j)=
 (y_1^j+\epsilon_1h_1,\ldots,y_k^j+\epsilon_kh_k,r_j),
 \qquad \epsilon\in\{0,1\}^k,
 \quad 1\leq j\leq q.
 \label{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-arrangement}
\end{equation}
Put
\[
 M=q2^k,\qquad D=(q+1)k+q-1.
\]
There are $p^D$ arrangements.  All probabilities in this section use
independent uniform choices of $h$, $r\in H$, and $y$.
Set
\[
 \pi(\epsilon)=(-1)^{\epsilon_1+\cdots+\epsilon_k},
 \qquad \eta_0(\epsilon,j)=s_j\pi(\epsilon).
\]

\begin{definition}[Certificate and degeneracy]
A \emph{certificate} is a function
$\eta:\{0,1\}^k\times\{1,\ldots,q\}\to\{-1,0,1\}\subset\F_p$.
It is \emph{successful} for $\rho$ if
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{\epsilon,j}\eta(\epsilon,j)
       \prod_{i\in A}\rho(\epsilon,j)_i=0
 \quad\text{for every } A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,k+1\}.
 \label{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-tests}
\end{equation}
The arrangement is \emph{degenerate} if a successful certificate lies
outside $\operatorname{span}_{\F_p}\{\eta_0\}$.
A certificate is \emph{pure parity} if it has the form
$\eta(\epsilon,j)=c_j\pi(\epsilon)$ for some $c\in\F_p^q$.
\end{definition}

The certificate $\eta_0$ is successful for every arrangement.
Indeed, summation against parity annihilates every proper horizontal
coordinate monomial.  The two remaining expressions are multiples of
$\sum_j s_j=0$ and $\sum_j s_jr_j=0$.
If one sidelength is zero, two vertices in a cube coincide.  Assigning
coefficients $1$ and $-1$ to those vertices, and zero elsewhere, gives
a successful certificate outside the span of $\eta_0$.  Consequently
every such arrangement is degenerate, and their proportion is exactly
\begin{equation}
 z_k(p)=1-(1-p^{-1})^k.
 \label{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-zero-sides}
\end{equation}

\subsection{The rank supplied by the first nonzero moment}

The next lemma is the main algebraic step.  It uses the equations with
the last coordinate to distinguish most cross-sections from the
exceptional diagonal $r_1=\cdots=r_q$.

\begin{lemma}[Rank of a nonparity certificate]
\label{gsr:en:18:deg:lem-rank}
Let $p$ be an odd prime, and fix nonzero sidelengths $h_1,\ldots,h_k$.
For a nonparity certificate, define its Boolean moments by
\[
 c_{j,S}=\sum_{\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^k}
             \eta(\epsilon,j)\prod_{i\in S}\epsilon_i.
\]
Let $m<k$ be the smallest cardinality of a set $S$ for which some
$c_{j,S}$ is nonzero.  Choose $B\subseteq[k]$ with $|B|=m$ and
$b=(c_{1,B},\ldots,c_{q,B})\ne0$, and put $t=k-m$.
Then the conditional probability that this certificate is successful
is at most
\begin{equation}
 \begin{cases}
 p^{-(t+1)},&b\notin\operatorname{span}\{s\},\\[2mm]
 (1-p^{-(q-2)})p^{-2t}+p^{-(q-2+t)},&
 b\in\operatorname{span}\{s\}.
 \end{cases}
 \label{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-rank-bound}
\end{equation}
In particular, every nonparity certificate has conditional success
probability at most
\begin{equation}
 Q_d(p)=p^{-2}+(p-1)p^{-2d}.
 \label{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-Q}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
First, $m$ exists and is less than $k$.  If $\epsilon_T$ denotes the
Boolean vector with support $T$, the moment transform is
\[
 c_{j,S}=\sum_{T\supseteq S}\eta(\epsilon_T,j),
 \qquad
 \eta(\epsilon_T,j)=
       \sum_{S\supseteq T}(-1)^{|S\setminus T|}c_{j,S}.
\]
Thus vanishing of every proper moment in a slice is equivalent to that
slice being a multiple of parity.  If it happened in every slice, the
certificate would be pure parity, contrary to the hypothesis.

For $A\subseteq[k]$, write $h_A=\prod_{i\in A}h_i$ and
\[
 P_{j,A}(y^j)=\sum_\epsilon\eta(\epsilon,j)
                  \prod_{i\in A}(y_i^j+\epsilon_i h_i).
\]
Expanding gives the exact identity
\begin{equation}
 P_{j,A}(y^j)=
 \sum_{S\subseteq A}h_Sc_{j,S}
                    \prod_{i\in A\setminus S}y_i^j.
 \label{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-moment-expansion}
\end{equation}
All moments of degree less than $m$ vanish.  Hence
$P_{j,B}=h_Bb_j$.  The tests indexed by $B$ and by
$B\cup\{k+1\}$ therefore imply
\begin{equation}
 \sum_j b_j=0,\qquad b\cdot r=0.
 \label{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-lowest-constraints}
\end{equation}

For each $i\notin B$, the polynomial $P_{j,B\cup\{i\}}$ is affine
in $y^j$.  Its coefficient of $y_i^j$ is $h_Bb_j$.
Fix an index $j_0$ with $b_{j_0}\ne0$.  In the equations
\[
 \sum_jP_{j,B\cup\{i\}}(y^j)=0,
 \qquad i\notin B,
\]
the columns indexed by $y_l^{j_0}$, $l\notin B$, form a diagonal
$t\times t$ matrix with nonzero diagonal $h_Bb_{j_0}$.
Here all other variables are held fixed, including the coordinates
whose indices lie in $B$.
Thus these equations have rank at least $t$ and admit at most
$p^{qk-t}$ choices of $y$, for every fixed $r$.

Suppose first that $b$ is not proportional to $s$.
If $\sum_jb_j\ne0$, there are no successful arrangements.
Otherwise $b\cdot r=0$ is an independent linear restriction on
$H=\ker(s\cdot{})$.  There are $p^{q-2}$ possible cross-sections,
and the preceding rank bound gives probability at most
$p^{-1}p^{-t}$.

Now suppose $b=cs$ with $c\ne0$.  Pair each of the preceding affine
equations with its vertical counterpart
\[
 \sum_jr_jP_{j,B\cup\{i\}}(y^j)=0.
\]
If $r_a\ne r_b$, the two columns $y_i^a,y_i^b$ in this pair form
the block
\[
 h_Bc
 \begin{pmatrix}
 s_a&s_b\\r_as_a&r_bs_b
 \end{pmatrix},
\]
whose determinant is nonzero.  Different indices $i\notin B$ give
diagonal blocks, since a variable $y_l^j$ with $l\notin B$ occurs in
$P_{j,B\cup\{i\}}$ only when $l=i$.  The paired equations therefore
have rank at least $2t$ whenever $r$ is not constant.
For constant $r$ the rank is still at least $t$.
There are $p$ constant cross-sections among $p^{q-1}$ members of $H$,
so averaging gives the second expression in
\eqref{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-rank-bound}.

Finally, the first expression is at most $p^{-2}$, since $t\geq1$.
The second decreases as $t$ increases; at $t=1$ it is
\[
 (1-p^{-(q-2)})p^{-2}+p^{-(q-1)}
 =p^{-2}+(p-1)p^{-q}.
\]
This is \eqref{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-Q}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Sharpness for an individual certificate]
\label{gsr:en:18:deg:prop-single-sharp}
For every $k\geq1$, $d\geq2$, and odd prime $p$, the bound
$Q_d(p)$ is attained by a nonparity certificate, conditional on any
fixed nonzero sidelengths.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Fix a coordinate $i$ and take
\[
 \eta(\epsilon,j)=s_j\pi(\epsilon)
                              \mathbf1_{\{\epsilon_i=0\}}.
\]
Parity summation in the remaining $k-1$ coordinates makes every test
automatic except
\[
 \sum_j s_jy_i^j=0,
 \qquad
 \sum_j s_jr_jy_i^j=0.
\]
The tests without $y_i^j$ reduce to $\sum_js_j=0$ and $s\cdot r=0$.
The displayed pair has rank two for nonconstant $r$ and rank one for
constant $r$.  Counting as in Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:18:deg:lem-rank} gives exactly
$Q_d(p)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
Re-derived independently by source~25 (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:25:thm:single}) and source~27 (Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:27:prop:perclass}, every characteristic), and reproved with credit by source~22 (Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:22:lem:rank}, degree one).
\end{writenote}

\begin{remark}
The restriction $d\geq2$ is essential for the saving $O(p^{-2})$.
If $d=1$, the constraint $r_1-r_2=0$ forces every cross-section to be
constant.  The certificate in Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:18:deg:prop-single-sharp}
then succeeds with probability $p^{-1}$.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Counting different certificate classes}

A direct union bound over all $3^M$ certificates counts many identical
tests.  Their most immediate equivalences can be removed exactly.

\begin{lemma}[Affine classes of ternary patterns]
\label{gsr:en:18:deg:lem-pattern-classes}
Let $p\geq5$, and let $e\in\{-1,1\}^n$.  Among ternary vectors outside
$\operatorname{span}\{e\}$, identify $u$ and $u'$ when
$u'=au+be$ for some $a\in\F_p^\times$ and $b\in\F_p$.
The number of equivalence classes is
\begin{equation}
 A_n=\frac{3^n-2^{n+1}+1}{2}.
 \label{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-An}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Dividing coordinatewise by $e$ reduces the equivalence to
$v'=av+b\mathbf1$.  Constant patterns are excluded.
A pattern taking exactly two values determines an unordered
nontrivial partition of the $n$ coordinates.  Conversely any two
patterns with that partition are affinely equivalent.  These give
$(2^n-2)/2$ classes.

For a pattern using all three values, an affine equivalence must
permute $\{-1,0,1\}$.  Summing these three values before and after
the affine map gives $3b=0$, so $b=0$ because $p\geq5$.
It follows that $a=1$ or $a=-1$.
There are $3^n-3\cdot2^n+3$ patterns using all three values, and
reflection pairs them without fixed points.  Adding their classes
to the two-value classes proves \eqref{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-An}.
\end{proof}

Since $\eta_0$ is always successful, certificates related by
\[
 \eta'=a\eta+b\eta_0,\qquad a\ne0,
\]
have precisely the same success locus.  The pure-parity subspace is
preserved by this equivalence.  After division by $\eta_0$, its
members are patterns constant on each of the $q$ cube slices.
There are therefore $A_q$ nontrivial pure-parity classes, and exactly
\begin{equation}
 J_{k,d}=A_{q2^k}-A_q
 \label{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-J}
\end{equation}
nonparity classes.  This count may still include impossible
certificates and further coincident success loci; it is a safe
coefficient for a union bound.

\subsection{The hyperplanes that determine the leading term}

\begin{lemma}[Pure-parity hyperplanes]
\label{gsr:en:18:deg:lem-parity-hyperplanes}
Let $p>2d$ be prime.  For nonzero sidelengths, a pure-parity certificate
$\eta(\epsilon,j)=c_j\pi(\epsilon)$ is successful exactly when
\[
 \sum_jc_j=0,\qquad c\cdot r=0.
\]
After excluding $c\in\operatorname{span}\{s\}$, the number of
distinct hyperplanes $c\cdot r=0$ in $H$ obtained this way is
\begin{equation}
 C_d=\frac{T_{2d}-2\binom{2d}{d}+1}{2},
 \qquad
 T_{2d}=\sum_{a=0}^d\binom{2d}{2a}\binom{2a}{a}.
 \label{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-Cd}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Parity kills every proper horizontal monomial.  Summing the full
horizontal monomial gives $(-1)^kh_1\cdots h_k\sum_jc_j$;
adding the last coordinate gives the same nonzero prefactor times
$\sum_jc_jr_j$.  This proves the characterization.

Write $q=2d$.  Because $p>q$, the equality $\sum_jc_j=0$ for
$c_j\in\{-1,0,1\}$ holds in the field if and only if it holds in
the integers.  There are $T_q$ such vectors: choose the $2a$ nonzero
coordinates and then choose which $a$ are positive.

Set $v_j=s_jc_j$.  The condition is now $\sum_js_jv_j=0$, and it
is preserved by $v\mapsto av+b\mathbf1$.
For a pattern taking two distinct values, let $I$ be the set of
coordinates taking one of them.  Admissibility is equivalent to
$\sum_{j\in I}s_j=0$.  There are
\[
 \sum_{a=0}^d\binom da^2=\binom{2d}{d}
\]
such subsets, including the empty and full sets.  Thus there are
$\bigl(\binom{2d}{d}-2\bigr)/2$ two-value classes.
The number of admissible ternary patterns using all three values is
\[
 T_{2d}-3\binom{2d}{d}+3.
\]
As in Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:18:deg:lem-pattern-classes}, their classes have size two.
Adding the two contributions proves \eqref{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-Cd}.

It remains to verify that this is a count of distinct hyperplanes,
not just of certificate classes.  Two nonzero linear functionals on
$H$ have the same kernel exactly when they are proportional.
The annihilator of $H$ in the ambient dual space is
$\operatorname{span}\{s\}$.  Hence $c$ and $c'$ define the same
hyperplane on $H$ exactly when $c'=ac+bs$ with $a\ne0$, the
equivalence already counted.
\end{proof}

For reference, the first few constants are
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{r|r|r|r}
$d$&$T_{2d}$&$\binom{2d}{d}$&$C_d$\\ \hline
2&19&6&4\\
3&141&20&51\\
4&1107&70&484\\
8&5\,196\,627&12\,870&2\,585\,444
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\begin{proposition}[Growth of the leading coefficient]
\label{gsr:en:18:deg:prop-Cd-growth}
Set $C_0=C_1=0$.  The ordinary generating function of the constants
in \eqref{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-Cd} is
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{d\geq0}C_dz^d
 ={}&\frac14\left(
       (1-2\sqrt z-3z)^{-1/2}
      +(1+2\sqrt z-3z)^{-1/2}\right)\\
 &-(1-4z)^{-1/2}+\frac{1}{2(1-z)}.
\end{align*}
The paired square-root expressions have only integer powers of $z$.
Moreover,
\[
 C_d\sim\frac{\sqrt3}{4\sqrt{2\pi d}}\,9^d
 \qquad(d\to\infty).
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The formula for $T_n$ in \eqref{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-Cd} gives
\[
 \sum_{n\geq0}T_nt^n
 =\frac{1}{1-t}\sum_{a\geq0}\binom{2a}{a}
                       \left(\frac{t}{1-t}\right)^{2a}
 =(1-2t-3t^2)^{-1/2}.
\]
Taking its even part and combining the three terms in
$C_d=(T_{2d}-2\binom{2d}{d}+1)/2$ proves the generating function.
For the asymptotic, the constant-term integral is
\[
 T_{2d}=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}
                           (1+2\cos\theta)^{2d}\,d\theta.
\]
The absolute value of the base is strictly less than $3$ away from
$\theta=0$, and near zero
\[
 \log\frac{1+2\cos\theta}{3}
                   =-\theta^2/3+O(\theta^4).
\]
The Gaussian scaling $\theta=u/\sqrt d$ therefore gives
$T_{2d}\sim\sqrt3\,9^d/(2\sqrt{2\pi d})$.
The central binomial term is $O(4^d)$ and is exponentially smaller.
Dividing by two proves the stated equivalent.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Finite bounds and the optimal leading coefficient}

\begin{theorem}[Degenerate-arrangement count]
\label{gsr:en:18:deg:thm-count}
Let $k\geq1$, $d\geq2$, and let $p>2d$ be prime.  Write
$\delta_{k,d}(p)$ for the proportion of degenerate $d$-arrangements
in $\F_p^{k+1}$, and define $z_k$, $J_{k,d}$, $Q_d$, and $C_d$ by
\eqref{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-zero-sides}, \eqref{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-J},
\eqref{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-Q}, and \eqref{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-Cd}.  Then
\begin{align}
 \delta_{k,d}(p)
 &\leq z_k(p)+(1-z_k(p))
                \left(\frac{C_d}{p}+J_{k,d}Q_d(p)\right)
 \label{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-finite-exact}\\
 &\leq\frac{k+C_d}{p}
       +J_{k,d}\bigl(p^{-2}+(p-1)p^{-2d}\bigr),
 \label{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-finite-simple}
\end{align}
whereas
\begin{equation}
 \delta_{k,d}(p)\geq
 \frac{k+C_d}{p}-\frac{\binom{k+C_d}{2}}{p^2}.
 \label{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-lower}
\end{equation}
Consequently, for fixed $k,d$ and primes $p\to\infty$,
\begin{equation}
 \delta_{k,d}(p)=\frac{k+C_d}{p}+O_{k,d}(p^{-2}).
 \label{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-asymptotic}
\end{equation}
Equivalently, the number of degenerate arrangements is
\[
 (k+C_d)p^{(2d+1)k+2d-2}
       +O_{k,d}\bigl(p^{(2d+1)k+2d-3}\bigr).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The event of a zero sidelength has probability $z_k(p)$ and consists
entirely of degenerate arrangements.  Conditional on nonzero sides,
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:18:deg:lem-parity-hyperplanes} and a union bound give at most
$C_d/p$ for pure-parity certificates.  Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:18:deg:lem-rank} gives
at most $Q_d(p)$ for each of the $J_{k,d}$ nonparity classes.
This proves \eqref{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-finite-exact}.
Using $z_k(p)\leq k/p$ and discarding the survival factor proves
\eqref{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-finite-simple}.

For the lower bound, consider the $k$ zero-side hyperplanes and the
$C_d$ pure-parity hyperplanes as subsets of the linear parameter
space
\[
 \F_p^k\times H\times\F_p^{qk}.
\]
They are distinct hyperplanes, each with probability $1/p$.
Two distinct ones have independent defining linear functionals, so
their intersection has probability $1/p^2$.
All these hyperplanes consist of degenerate arrangements, including
when sidelengths vanish.  The first two terms of inclusion-exclusion
therefore give \eqref{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-lower}.
Together, the upper and lower bounds prove
\eqref{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-asymptotic}, with an explicit error constant if desired.
\end{proof}

Gowers's bound has coefficient $k3^{2d2^k}$ in front of
$p^{(2d+1)k+2d-2}$.  Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:18:deg:thm-count} identifies the
optimal first-order coefficient as $k+C_d$.  The extra
$J_{k,d}p^{-2}$ term must be retained when using the theorem at a
finite prime.  Thus one should not simply replace the old coefficient
by $k+C_d$ in every finite-size inequality.  The next corollary shows
how to use the full bound in the intended application.

\subsection{An explicit replacement for the size condition in Lemma 15.5}

For a map $\phi$ defined on all the vertices of an arrangement, the
statement that it \emph{respects} the arrangement means
$\sum_{\epsilon,j}\eta_0(\epsilon,j)\phi(\rho(\epsilon,j))=0$.
Equivalently, the alternating sums of $\phi$ on the first $d$ cubes
add to the corresponding sum on the last $d$ cubes.

\begin{corollary}[Refined arrangement selection]
\label{gsr:en:18:deg:cor-selection}
Let $k\geq1$, let $0<\alpha,\beta,\eta\leq1$, and let $p\geq17$ be
prime.  Suppose that $B\subseteq\F_p^{k+1}$ has size
$\beta p^{k+1}$ and that $\phi:B\to\F_p$ respects at least
$\alpha\beta^{15}p^{17k+15}$ eight-arrangements in $B$.
Set
\[
 M=2^{k+4},\qquad
 E_k=2^{2^{k+4}+k+3},\qquad
 \lambda=(\alpha\eta/4)^{E_k}\beta^{15},
\]
and
\[
 a_k=k+2\,585\,444,\qquad
 J_k=A_{2^{k+4}}-A_{16},\qquad A_{16}=21\,457\,825.
\]
If
\begin{equation}
 z_k(p)+(1-z_k(p))
 \left(\frac{2\,585\,444}{p}
       +J_k\bigl(p^{-2}+(p-1)p^{-16}\bigr)\right)\leq\lambda,
 \label{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-selection-exact}
\end{equation}
then $B$ has a subset $B'$ containing at least
$\lambda p^{17k+15}$ eight-arrangements, of which a proportion at
least $1-\eta$ is respected by $\phi$.

An explicit sufficient condition for
\eqref{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-selection-exact} is
\begin{equation}
 p\geq
 \frac{a_k+\sqrt{a_k^2+(72/17)J_k\lambda}}{2\lambda}.
 \label{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-selection-quadratic}
\end{equation}
A simpler sufficient condition, using the stated parameter ranges, is
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\ \lambda p\geq k+2\,585\,445.\ }
 \label{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-selection-simple}
\end{equation}
In particular, \eqref{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-selection-simple} replaces the source
condition $\lambda p\geq k3^{2^{k+4}}$ without changing the
conclusion or the exponent $E_k$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
We first recall the part of Gowers's selection argument that does not
use a lower bound on $p$.  For a positive integer $R$, choose independent
uniform field elements $t_\ell$ and $u_{A,\ell}$ for
$1\leq\ell\leq R$ and $A\subseteq[k+1]$.  Given these choices,
retain each $x\in B$ independently with probability
\[
 \prod_{\ell=1}^R\frac12
 \left(1+\cos\frac{2\pi}{p}
 \left(t_\ell\phi(x)+
       \sum_{A\subseteq[k+1]}u_{A,\ell}\prod_{i\in A}x_i\right)
 \right).
\]
The field element inside the cosine may be represented by any integer
residue.  Expanding one factor as
$(2+\omega^v+\omega^{-v})/4$ and averaging the phase parameters shows
that an unrespected nondegenerate arrangement is retained with
probability $2^{-MR}$.  A respected arrangement is retained with
probability at least
\[
 2^{-MR}(1+2^{1-M})^R.
\]
For a nondegenerate arrangement the only surviving ternary
certificates are $0,\eta_0,-\eta_0$; its vertices are distinct,
since a repeated pair would give a two-point certificate.
For a respected degenerate
arrangement these same terms still contribute, and all further
surviving terms have nonnegative coefficients, so the inequality
remains valid.  If vertices repeat, the actual joint retention
probability is at least the product with vertex multiplicities,
since every individual retention factor lies in $[0,1]$.

Let $X$ count respected arrangements in the selected set, and let $Y$
count its unrespected nondegenerate arrangements.  There are at most
$\beta^{15}p^{17k+15}$ eight-arrangements in $B$: choose the first
fifteen base vertices in $B$, the sidelengths in $\F_p^k$, and the
last horizontal base point in $\F_p^k$; the last cross-section is
forced.  It follows that
\[
 \eta\E X-\E Y\geq
 2^{-MR}\beta^{15}p^{17k+15}
           \bigl(\alpha\eta(1+2^{1-M})^R-1\bigr).
\]
Choose
\[
 R=\left\lceil 2^{M-1}\log_2\frac{2}{\alpha\eta}\right\rceil.
\]
The inequality $1+x\geq2^x$ for $0\leq x\leq1$ gives
$\alpha\eta(1+2^{1-M})^R\geq2$.
Since $E_k=M2^{M-1}$, the choice of $R$ also gives
\[
 2^{-MR}\geq 2^{-M}(\alpha\eta/2)^{E_k}
           \geq 2(\alpha\eta/4)^{E_k};
\]
the final inequality is equivalent to $E_k\geq M+1$, which holds
here.  With $L=\lambda p^{17k+15}$, some realization therefore
satisfies $\eta X-Y\geq2L$.

By Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:18:deg:thm-count} and
\eqref{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-selection-exact}, the total number of degenerate
arrangements in the entire ambient space is at most $L$.
Thus the number $Z$ of unrespected degenerate arrangements in this
realization is at most $L$.  We obtain
\[
 Y+Z\leq\eta X-L\leq\eta X,
 \qquad X\geq L.
\]
The total number of arrangements is at least $X$, and its bad
proportion is at most $\eta X/(X+Y+Z)\leq\eta$.
This proves the conclusion.

For the quadratic criterion, $p\geq17$ gives
\[
 p^{-2}+(p-1)p^{-16}\leq p^{-2}+p^{-3}
                         \leq\frac{18}{17}p^{-2}.
\]
The left side of \eqref{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-selection-exact} is consequently at
most $a_k/p+(18/17)J_k/p^2$.  Solving the resulting quadratic
inequality gives \eqref{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-selection-quadratic}.

Finally, the parameter ranges imply $\lambda\leq4^{-E_k}$.
Since $J_k<3^M/2$ and $E_k\geq M$,
\[
 J_k\lambda\leq\frac12(3/4)^M\leq\frac12.
\]
If $\lambda p\geq a_k+1$, then
\[
 \frac{a_k}{p}+\frac{18J_k}{17p^2}
 \leq\lambda\left(
 \frac{a_k}{a_k+1}+
 \frac{(18/17)J_k\lambda}{(a_k+1)^2}\right)
 \leq\lambda.
\]
This proves \eqref{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-selection-simple}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What has and has not propagated]
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:18:deg:cor-selection} is a proved improvement of one
ambient-size requirement in the density-increasing selection.
It retains the same Riesz-product exponent, the same guaranteed
number of arrangements, and the same error proportion.
A final improved quantitative Szemer\'edi theorem would require
propagating all later requirements and verifying which one dominates.
That further conclusion is not asserted here.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Further questions suggested by the proof}

The next term in \eqref{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-asymptotic} is a concrete finite
problem.  Intersections of the $k+C_d$ leading hyperplanes contribute
at order $p^{-2}$, and Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:18:deg:prop-single-sharp} shows
that nonparity certificates also contribute on that scale.
Computing the exact coefficient requires accounting for coincident
and intersecting success loci, rather than merely counting
certificate classes.

A second direction is to preserve the full parameter $t=k-m$ in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:18:deg:lem-rank}.  A certificate whose first nonzero moment
has low degree imposes considerably more than two conditions.
Counting certificates according to this degree and according to
their moment vectors could reduce $J_{k,d}$ substantially in finite
bounds.

The pure-parity hyperplanes form a finite arrangement of balanced
subset-sum equations on $H$.  Determining its intersection lattice
would give an exact counting polynomial for the corresponding
nondegenerate cross-sections away from exceptional characteristics.
The proof of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:18:deg:lem-parity-hyperplanes} already supplies
its number of distinct hyperplanes.

For formalization, the natural first units are the Boolean moment
expansion, the diagonal minors in Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:18:deg:lem-rank}, and the
finite-field counts for kernels and constant cross-sections.
The affine-pattern enumeration and the two-term inclusion-exclusion
bound can then be developed separately.  No Lean verification of
these new statements is claimed in this article.

\section[{The finite common-sampling problem\srctag{19}}]{The finite common-sampling problem}\label{gsr:en:19:sec:d2}\label{gsr:en:19:sec:sampling}
\srcnote{19}{Section 2}

\subsection{Rows, classes, and the recovery rule}

Let $J$ be a finite set with $n=|J|\ge1$, and let $H$ be a nonempty
finite set of rows.  For each $h\in H$, let
\[
 C_1(h),\ldots,C_q(h)\subseteq J
\]
be pairwise disjoint; empty classes are allowed.  Their union may be a
proper subset of $J$.  This last point is essential in applications,
because the original function is defined only on a subset of the
ambient box.  All loss fractions below use the ambient normalization
$|H|n$, not the possibly much smaller size of that partial domain.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$.  A subset $R\subseteq J$ is the common set of
sampled columns, also called the \emph{anchor set}.  A class $C$ is
\emph{recovered} when
\begin{equation}
 |R\cap C|\ge\min(d,|C|).
 \label{gsr:en:19:eq:recovery}
\end{equation}
If $|C|\ge d$, this provides $d$ distinct interpolation nodes.  If
$0<|C|<d$, it says that every point of $C$ is sampled.  In that case
the interpolant of degree at most $|C|-1$ agrees with the function on
the entire class, which is all that the covering argument needs.

Define the normalized loss
\begin{equation}
 L_H(R)=\frac{1}{|H|n}
 \sum_{h\in H}\sum_{t=1}^{q}|C_t(h)|
 \ind_{\{|R\cap C_t(h)|<\min(d,|C_t(h)|)\}}.
 \label{gsr:en:19:eq:loss}
\end{equation}
Classes are discarded as whole classes.  Consequently, every retained
class still contains all of its chosen interpolation nodes.

\begin{remark}[What the extremal model measures]
The loss in \eqref{gsr:en:19:eq:loss} measures this specific recovery certificate.
A function might happen to be covered by some other polynomial even
when its assigned class fails \eqref{gsr:en:19:eq:recovery}.  Our lower bounds
do not rule out methods that exploit such additional coincidences,
use different anchors in different rows, or infer structure without
this interpolation certificate.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Exact finite expectation}

Use the convention $\binom ab=0$ if $b<0$ or $b>a$, and let a sum over
an empty index set equal zero.  For $0\le r\le n$ and $0\le s\le n$,
write
\begin{equation}
 P_{n,r,d}(s)=\frac{1}{\binom nr}
 \sum_{j=0}^{\min(d,s)-1}\binom{s}{j}\binom{n-s}{r-j},
 \qquad W_{n,r,d}(s)=\frac{s}{n}P_{n,r,d}(s).
 \label{gsr:en:19:eq:hypergeom}
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}[Exact expected loss]\label{gsr:en:19:sampling:expectation}
If $R$ is uniformly distributed among the $r$-element subsets of $J$,
then
\[
 \E_R L_H(R)=\frac{1}{|H|}
 \sum_{h\in H}\sum_{t=1}^{q}W_{n,r,d}(|C_t(h)|).
\]
The statement remains valid with any nonnegative row weights
$w_h$ summing to one, after replacing the row average by $\sum_hw_h$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For a fixed class of size $s$, the number of $r$-element samples having
exactly $j$ points in that class is
$\binom{s}{j}\binom{n-s}{r-j}$.  Division by the total number
$\binom nr$ gives the hypergeometric probability.  Sum over the
failure values $j<\min(d,s)$, multiply by the class mass $s/n$, and
use linearity of expectation.  No independence between different
rows or between different classes is required.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A uniform bound that retains class mass}

\begin{lemma}[Marked-sample estimate]\label{gsr:en:19:sampling:marked}
Let $X=|R\cap C|$, where $|C|=s$ and $R$ is a uniform $r$-element
subset of an $n$-point set.  If $d-1\le r<n$, then
\begin{equation}
 \frac{s}{n}\Pr(X<d)
 \le \frac{d(n-r)}{n(r+1)}+\frac{d-1}{n}
 =\frac{d}{r+1}-\frac{r-d+1}{n(r+1)}
 \le\frac{d}{r+1}.
 \label{gsr:en:19:eq:marked}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
First choose an $(r+1)$-element subset $U$ uniformly, and then mark one
of its elements $z$ uniformly.  The pair $(U\setminus\{z\},z)$ has
the same law as a uniform $r$-element sample followed by a uniform
element of its complement.  Put $Y=|U\cap C|$.  The event that the
marked point belongs to $C$ and that the unmarked sample contains
fewer than $d$ points of $C$ has probability
\[
 \E\left[\frac{s-X}{n-r}\ind_{\{X<d\}}\right]
 =\E\left[\frac{Y}{r+1}\ind_{\{1\le Y\le d\}}\right]
 \le\frac{d}{r+1}.
\]
Also $\E[X\ind_{\{X<d\}}]\le d-1$.  Adding the two contributions
to $s\Pr(X<d)=\E[(s-X)\ind_{\{X<d\}}]+
\E[X\ind_{\{X<d\}}]$ proves the first inequality.  The displayed
identity and the last inequality are elementary algebra, using
$r\ge d-1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Common anchors with controlled lost mass]
\label{gsr:en:19:sampling:anchors}
For every $0\le r\le n$, there is an $r$-element set $R\subseteq J$
such that
\begin{equation}
 L_H(R)\le\min\left\{1,\frac{qd}{r+1}\right\}.
 \label{gsr:en:19:eq:sample-bound}
\end{equation}
If $r=n$, the loss is zero.  In particular, for $0<\sigma<1$, the
choice
\begin{equation}
 r=\min\left\{n,\left\lceil\frac{qd}{\sigma}\right\rceil-1\right\}
 \label{gsr:en:19:eq:sample-r}
\end{equation}
guarantees $L_H(R)\le\sigma$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For $d-1\le r<n$, the failure event in \eqref{gsr:en:19:eq:recovery} is contained
in $\{X<d\}$.  Apply lemma~\ref{gsr:en:19:sampling:marked} to each class and sum.
The expectation is at most $qd/(r+1)$, so some sample attains that
bound.  The loss is always at most one because the classes in a row
are disjoint.  If $r<d-1$, then $qd/(r+1)\ge1$, so the trivial bound
suffices.  If $r=n$, every class is recovered.

For \eqref{gsr:en:19:eq:sample-r}, either all columns are chosen, or
$r+1=\lceil qd/\sigma\rceil\ge qd/\sigma$, which gives the stated
loss bound.  The sample size is a nonnegative integer; indeed it is
at least one unless the full population itself is empty, which was
excluded.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Weighted rows and nonuniform class counts]
\label{gsr:en:19:sampling:weighted}
If row $h$ has at most $q_h$ classes and weight $w_h\ge0$, with
$\sum_hw_h=1$, the same argument gives weighted loss at most
\[
 \min\left\{1,\frac{d}{r+1}\sum_h w_hq_h\right\}.
\]
The exact weighted expectation in lemma~\ref{gsr:en:19:sampling:expectation} may be
used instead when class sizes are known.
\end{corollary}

This estimate avoids the need to discard every small class before
sampling.  The contribution of a class that is difficult to hit is
automatically multiplied by its small mass.  For the affine step of
Lemma~16.10, it changes the sample scale from $q\sigma^{-2}$ to
$q\sigma^{-1}$.  Sampling without replacement also ensures that
different anchors are distinct, which is necessary for secant
interpolation over a field.

\section[{An exact minimax theorem and a deterministic algorithm\srctag{19}}]{An exact minimax theorem and a deterministic algorithm}\label{gsr:en:19:sec:d3}
\srcnote{19}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:en:19:sec:minimax}

\subsection{The finite extremal value}

\begin{definition}
For integers $n,q,d\ge1$ and $0\le r\le n$, define
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal M_{n,q,d}(r)=
 \max_{\substack{s_1,\ldots,s_q\in\Z_{\ge0}\\
                  s_1+\cdots+s_q\le n}}
 \sum_{i=1}^{q}W_{n,r,d}(s_i).
 \label{gsr:en:19:eq:minimax-definition}
\end{equation}
The feasible set is finite, so the maximum is attained.  A maximizing
vector records the sizes of the classes; it does not prescribe how
classes are arranged across different rows.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Exact common-anchor minimax value]
\label{gsr:en:19:sampling:minimax}
Let the supremum below range over every nonempty finite row set $H$
and every family of at most $q$ pairwise disjoint classes in each row.
Then
\begin{equation}
 \sup_{H,\,(C_t(h))}\;min_{\substack{R\subseteq J\\|R|=r}}L_H(R)
 =\mathcal M_{n,q,d}(r).
 \label{gsr:en:19:eq:exact-minimax}
\end{equation}
In fact, a finite family of rows attains the supremum, and in that
family every $r$-element anchor set has exactly the same loss.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For the upper bound, each row's class sizes form a feasible vector in
\eqref{gsr:en:19:eq:minimax-definition}.  The exact expectation in
lemma~\ref{gsr:en:19:sampling:expectation} is therefore at most
$\mathcal M_{n,q,d}(r)$.  At least one sample has loss no larger than
its expectation.

For the lower bound, take a maximizing vector $(s_1,\ldots,s_q)$ and
choose disjoint subsets $C_1^0,\ldots,C_q^0$ of $J$ having those sizes.
Use all permutations $\pi$ of $J$ as rows, with
$C_i(\pi)=\pi(C_i^0)$.  Fix any $r$-element anchor set $R$.  As $\pi$
ranges uniformly over all permutations, $|R\cap\pi(C_i^0)|$ has the
hypergeometric distribution with population size $n$, class size
$s_i$, and sample size $r$.  Consequently its average contribution
to the loss is exactly $W_{n,r,d}(s_i)$.  Summing over $i$ gives
$L_H(R)=\mathcal M_{n,q,d}(r)$ for every $R$.  Since this construction
uses only $n!$ rows, the supremum is attained by a finite family.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 34--39]
Source~39 re-derives this theorem for its own rule, which keeps sampled points (its Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:39:thm:minimax}), without citing this source, and solves the profile problem in closed form for that rule (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:39:thm:balanced}). For the rule here the closed form fails in $199$ of $2{,}835$ small cases (note there); the classification asked in source~19's Question~1 stays open for this rule (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:sampling}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{remark}[The importance of partial rows]
The optimization uses $\sum_i s_i\le n$.  If every row had to be
completely partitioned into exactly $q$ classes, the constraint would
be $\sum_i s_i=n$ and the answer would be a different optimization.
In particular, forcing a large leftover class can change the leading
constant when $q$ is fixed.  Partial domains in the Gowers application
make the inequality constraint the appropriate one here.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Exact evaluation by integer dynamic programming}

All terms in \eqref{gsr:en:19:eq:minimax-definition} have the same denominator
$n\binom nr$.  Put
\[
 u_s=s\sum_{j=0}^{\min(d,s)-1}
              \binom{s}{j}\binom{n-s}{r-j},\qquad 0\le s\le n,
\]
and define integers
\[
 V_0(b)=0,\qquad
 V_t(b)=\max_{0\le s\le b}\{u_s+V_{t-1}(b-s)\},
 \quad 0\le b\le n.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal M_{n,q,d}(r)=\frac{V_q(n)}{n\binom nr}.
 \label{gsr:en:19:eq:dp}
\end{equation}
The proof is induction on the number of allowed classes: choose the
size of the last class and allocate the remaining budget to the
preceding classes.  Storing an optimizing size at each stage also
recovers an extremal profile.  The number of arithmetic comparisons
is $O(qn^2)$, with $O(n)$ working memory if the profiles themselves
are not stored.  These operation counts do not count the bit length
of the binomial coefficients.

The zero loss in the last row is not an asymptotic statement.  Choosing
all columns recovers every class, including singleton classes.  The
general $qd/(r+1)$ estimate is deliberately uniform and need not be
sharp at the finite endpoint.

\subsection{Choosing the anchors deterministically}

The existence proof can be turned into a finite deterministic
algorithm whenever the class memberships are supplied.  Suppose
$A\subseteq J$ is the set of anchors already selected, $a=|A|\le r$,
and let $F(A)$ be the expected unnormalized final lost mass after
completing $A$ uniformly to an $r$-element subset.  For a class $C$,
put $s=|C|$ and $b_C=|A\cap C|$.  Its contribution to $F(A)$ is
\begin{equation}
 \frac{s}{\binom{n-a}{r-a}}
 \sum_{j=0}^{\min(d,s)-b_C-1}
 \binom{s-b_C}{j}\binom{n-a-s+b_C}{r-a-j},
 \label{gsr:en:19:eq:conditional}
\end{equation}
interpreted as zero when the upper limit is negative.  The full
$F(A)$ is the sum of these contributions over all rows and classes.

For $a<r$, the tower property for finite averages gives
\begin{equation}
 F(A)=\frac{1}{n-a}\sum_{x\in J\setminus A}F(A\cup\{x\}).
 \label{gsr:en:19:eq:greedy-average}
\end{equation}
Choose a column minimizing the right-hand summand, append it to $A$,
and repeat.  The conditional expectation never increases.  After
$r$ choices it equals the actual loss, proving a deterministic
version of the sampling theorem.  Formula \eqref{gsr:en:19:eq:conditional}
makes the algorithm exact, using rational arithmetic.

This is an algorithm for explicit finite class data.  It does not
turn the entire inverse theorem into an efficient algorithm: the
number of rows, the structural partition procedures, and the
polynomial lists may themselves be enormous.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Sharp asymptotics of the sampling loss\srctag{19}}]{Sharp asymptotics of the sampling loss}\label{gsr:en:19:sec:d4}\label{gsr:en:19:sec:poisson}
\srcnote{19}{Section 4}

The finite optimization has a clean limiting form when the sample
occupies a vanishing fraction of the columns.  The critical classes
then have size of order $n/r$, and a sample sees a bounded expected
number of their points.

\subsection{The occupancy constant}

For an integer $d\ge1$, set
\[
 S_{d-1}(\lambda)=\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}\frac{\lambda^j}{j!},\qquad
 f_d(\lambda)=\lambda e^{-\lambda}S_{d-1}(\lambda),\qquad
 C_d=\max_{\lambda\ge0}f_d(\lambda).
\]

\begin{lemma}[Unique maximizing mean]\label{gsr:en:19:sampling:constant}
There is a unique positive solution $\lambda_d$ of
\begin{equation}
 S_{d-1}(\lambda)=\frac{\lambda^d}{(d-1)!}.
 \label{gsr:en:19:eq:critical}
\end{equation}
The function $f_d$ increases up to $\lambda_d$ and decreases
afterward.  Thus $C_d=f_d(\lambda_d)$.  In particular,
\[
 \lambda_1=1,\quad C_1=e^{-1},\qquad
 \lambda_2=\varphi,\quad C_2=\varphi^3e^{-\varphi}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Differentiation gives
\[
 f_d'(\lambda)=e^{-\lambda}
 \left(S_{d-1}(\lambda)-\frac{\lambda^d}{(d-1)!}\right).
\]
For $\lambda>0$, the quotient
$S_{d-1}(\lambda)/\lambda^d=
\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}\lambda^{j-d}/j!$ is strictly decreasing from
$+\infty$ to zero.  This proves uniqueness and the sign change.
Also $f_d(0)=0$ and $f_d(\lambda)\to0$ at infinity, so the critical
point is the global maximum.  For $d=2$, the equation is
$1+\lambda=\lambda^2$, and $1+\varphi=\varphi^2$ gives the formula.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Uniform control of the hypergeometric tails}

\begin{lemma}[A finite exponential-moment bound]
\label{gsr:en:19:sampling:mgf}
If $X$ is hypergeometric with parameters $(n,s,r)$ and $t\ge0$, then
\begin{equation}
 \E e^{-tX}\le
 \left(1-\frac{s}{n}+\frac{s}{n}e^{-t}\right)^r
 \le\exp\left(-\frac{rs}{n}(1-e^{-t})\right).
 \label{gsr:en:19:eq:hg-mgf}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Assign weight $e^{-t}$ to each point in the class and weight one to
each other population point.  The expectation is the mean product
of $r$ distinct weights, namely the $r$th elementary symmetric
polynomial divided by $\binom nr$.  This mean is at most the $r$th
power of the arithmetic mean of the weights.

For completeness, the last assertion follows by averaging two
unequal coordinates while preserving their sum.  In the elementary
symmetric polynomial, terms containing neither coordinate stay
fixed, terms containing exactly one depend only on their sum, and
terms containing both are a nonnegative multiple of their product.
Replacing the two coordinates by their average cannot decrease the
polynomial.  Equivalently, on the compact set of nonnegative weights
with fixed sum a maximum is attained at equal coordinates; for
positive weights and $r\ge2$, any unequal pair would increase it.
The cases $r=0,1$ are immediate.  This proves the first inequality.
The second is $1-u\le e^{-u}$.
\end{proof}

Writing $\lambda=rs/n$ and taking $t=1$, Markov's inequality gives
\begin{equation}
 \lambda\Pr(X<d)
 \le\lambda\exp\bigl(d-1-(1-e^{-1})\lambda\bigr).
 \label{gsr:en:19:eq:tail-tight}
\end{equation}
This tends uniformly to zero as $\lambda\to\infty$.  It is the
tail estimate needed to pass from pointwise Poisson convergence to
a maximum over all class sizes.

\begin{lemma}[Uniform bounded-mean Poisson limit]
\label{gsr:en:19:sampling:poisson-limit}
Suppose $r\to\infty$ and $r/n\to0$.  Uniformly over integers $s$
for which $\lambda=rs/n$ lies in a fixed compact subinterval of
$(0,\infty)$, the hypergeometric probabilities satisfy
\[
 \Pr(X=j)=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^j}{j!}+o(1)
 \qquad(j\text{ fixed}).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
In the stated range, $s\asymp n/r\to\infty$, $s/n=O(1/r)$,
and $r/n\to0$.  For sufficiently large parameters, $n-s\ge r$,
and
\[
 \Pr(X=0)=\prod_{i=0}^{r-1}
 \left(1-\frac{s}{n-i}\right).
\]
The sum of the quantities $s/(n-i)$ is
$\lambda(1+O(r/n))$, while the sum of their squares is $O(1/r)$,
uniformly on the compact interval.  Taking logarithms therefore
gives $\Pr(X=0)=e^{-\lambda}+o(1)$.

For fixed $j$, division by the zero-count probability gives
\[
 \frac{\Pr(X=j)}{\Pr(X=0)}
 =\frac{(s)_j(r)_j}{j!\,(n-s-r+1)^{\overline j}}
 =\frac{\lambda^j}{j!}+o(1),
\]
where $(a)_j$ and $a^{\overline j}$ denote falling and rising
factorials.  This proves the assertion.  In particular, no hypothesis
$r^2/n\to0$ is required.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The sharp minimax asymptotic}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp sparse-sampling law]\label{gsr:en:19:sampling:asymptotic}
Fix $d\ge1$.  Along any sequence of integers $n,q,r$ with
\[
 r\longrightarrow\infty,\qquad r/n\longrightarrow0,
 \qquad q/r\longrightarrow0,
\]
one has
\begin{equation}
 \frac{r}{q}\mathcal M_{n,q,d}(r)\longrightarrow C_d.
 \label{gsr:en:19:eq:sharp-limit}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For a single class size $s$, put $\lambda=rs/n$.  Then
\[
 rW_{n,r,d}(s)
 =\lambda\Pr\{X<\min(d,s)\}.
\]
If $\lambda$ is small, this is at most $\lambda$.  On any compact
interval bounded away from zero, one has $s\to\infty$, so
$\min(d,s)=d$ eventually; lemma~\ref{gsr:en:19:sampling:poisson-limit} gives
uniform convergence to $f_d(\lambda)$.  For large $\lambda$, the
failure event is contained in $\{X<d\}$, and
\eqref{gsr:en:19:eq:tail-tight} controls the tail uniformly.  These three
observations imply
\[
 \max_{0\le s\le n}rW_{n,r,d}(s)\longrightarrow C_d.
\]
Since there are at most $q$ classes, this proves the upper bound
in \eqref{gsr:en:19:eq:sharp-limit}.

For the lower bound choose
$s=\lfloor\lambda_dn/r\rfloor$ and set all $q$ class sizes equal
to $s$.  The vector is feasible for all sufficiently large parameters,
because $qs/n\le\lambda_dq/r\to0$.  Also $rs/n\to\lambda_d$
since $r/n\to0$.  The single-class limit gives
$rW_{n,r,d}(s)\to C_d$, and hence
$\mathcal M_{n,q,d}(r)\ge qW_{n,r,d}(s)$ gives the matching lower
bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Sharp affine sampling constant]
\label{gsr:en:19:sampling:affine-constant}
Under the hypotheses of theorem~\ref{gsr:en:19:sampling:asymptotic}, the affine
recovery problem satisfies
\[
 \mathcal M_{n,q,2}(r)=
 \left(0.839962094657\ldots+o(1)\right)\frac qr.
\]
Thus, in a regime where the desired loss $\sigma\to0$ and
$n$ is sufficiently large relative to the required sample,
the sharp common-sample budget for this recovery mechanism is
$(C_2+o(1))q/\sigma$.  The unconditional finite budget
$\lceil2q/\sigma\rceil-1$ is a simpler uniform guarantee.
\end{corollary}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 34--39]
The same constant is source~39's Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:39:cor:golden}, derived independently; source~39 also gives the limit when $q/r$ stays bounded (its Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:39:thm:asymptotic}).
\end{writenote}

\caption{Left: the limiting one-class loss profiles and their unique

\subsection{What the asymptotic does not say}

The constant $C_d$ concerns partial rows and the sample-based recovery
rule \eqref{gsr:en:19:eq:recovery}.  It does not replace the finite formula when
$r$ is comparable to $n$, and it does not assert that an arbitrary
polynomial-cover construction requires that many anchors.  Nor does
it improve the structural complexity of a single sampled slice.
The next part of the article addresses how to combine the slices
once they have been chosen.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Recovering polynomial pieces from a common set of slices\srctag{19}}]{Recovering polynomial pieces from a common set of slices}\label{gsr:en:19:sec:d5}
\srcnote{19}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:en:19:lift:section}

The point of the next theorem is that all interpolants can be constructed
\emph{after one common refinement of the sampled slices}. Refining each
pair-generated slope and intercept separately, as in the displayed proof
of Gowers' Lemma~16.10, repeats work that the interpolation formula does
not require. The distinction affects both the number of refinement
steps and the final number of graph candidates.

We allow polynomial degrees to differ between coordinates. This also
makes clear that the argument is not special to affine functions. For a
field \(F\), a finite set \(U\subset F^k\), and a vector
\(\boldsymbol b=(b_1,\ldots,b_k)\) of nonnegative integers, write
\[
 \mathcal P_{\boldsymbol b}(U)
 =
 \left\{P|_U:\ P\in F[X_1,\ldots,X_k],\
                   \deg_{X_i}P\le b_i\ \text{for all }i\right\}.
\]
This is a vector space of functions, even when different polynomials
induce the same function on \(U\). Multiaffine functions correspond to
\(\boldsymbol b=(1,\ldots,1)\).

\subsection{The finite interpolation statement}

Let \(J=\{\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n\}\subset F\) consist of distinct field
elements, with \(n\ge1\), let \(H\) be finite and nonempty, and let \(A\subset H\times J\). Assume \(q,d\ge1\). Suppose
\(f:A\to F\). For each \(h\in H\), suppose the row domain
\(A_h=\{x:(h,x)\in A\}\) has a partition into at most \(q\) nonempty
classes \(C_{h,t}\), and that \(f(h,\cdot)\) agrees on each class with
a polynomial of degree less than \(d\), where \(d\ge1\).
There is no requirement that the row partitions or their polynomials
vary regularly with \(h\).

For a set of distinct anchors \(R\subset J\), call a row class \(C\)
\emph{certified} if
\[
 |R\cap C|\ge \min(d,|C|).
\]
If a class has at least \(d\) points, this condition gives \(d\)
interpolation nodes. If it has fewer points, the condition samples the
whole class; interpolating those finitely many values is then enough.

\begin{lemma}[Interpolation after a common slice cover]
\label{gsr:en:19:lift:algebra}
Let \(R=\{\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_r\}\subset J\), and let \(U\subset H\).
For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,r\}\), suppose functions
\[
 g_{i,1},\ldots,g_{i,M_i}:U\to F
\]
belong to a vector space \(V_U\) of functions on \(U\). Suppose also
that \(G\subset U\) has the following property: whenever \(h\in G\)
and \((h,\zeta_i)\in A\), one of these functions takes the value
\(f(h,\zeta_i)\) at \(h\).

Then the graph of \(f\), on the certified classes in rows \(G\),
is contained in a union of at most
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^{\min(d,r)}e_j(M_1,\ldots,M_r)
 \label{gsr:en:19:lift:elementary-symmetric-count}
 \tag{L1}
\]
graphs of functions in
\(V_U\otimes_F F[X]_{<d}\). Here \(e_j\) denotes the \(j\)-th
elementary symmetric polynomial. In particular, if \(M_i\le M\), the
number of candidates is at most
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^{\min(d,r)}\binom rj M^j.
 \label{gsr:en:19:lift:uniform-count}
 \tag{L2}
\]
If all classes being retained have at least \(d\) points, the single
term \(e_d(M_1,\ldots,M_r)\) suffices.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For a nonempty set \(S\subset\{1,\ldots,r\}\) of size at most \(d\),
and indices \(a_i\in\{1,\ldots,M_i\}\) for \(i\in S\), form
\[
 P_{S,\boldsymbol a}(h,x)
 =
 \sum_{i\in S}g_{i,a_i}(h)
       \prod_{v\in S\setminus\{i\}}
                  \frac{x-\zeta_v}{\zeta_i-\zeta_v}.
 \label{gsr:en:19:lift:lagrange}
 \tag{L3}
\]
All denominators are nonzero because the anchors are distinct.
The displayed function has degree at most \(|S|-1<d\) in \(x\), and
each of its coefficients, as a polynomial in \(x\), belongs to \(V_U\).
The number of choices with \(|S|=j\) is
\(\sum_{|S|=j}\prod_{i\in S}M_i=e_j(M_1,\ldots,M_r)\).

Fix \(h\in G\) and a certified class \(C\). If \(|C|\ge d\), choose
\(d\) of its anchors and let \(S\) be their index set. For each
\(i\in S\), choose a covering function whose value at \(h\) is
\(f(h,\zeta_i)\). The polynomial in~(L3), with \(h\) fixed, agrees
at \(d\) distinct points with the degree-\(<d\) polynomial supplied
for \(C\); their difference therefore vanishes identically.
Thus it agrees with \(f\) at every point of \(C\).

If \(|C|=s<d\), certification says that every point of \(C\) is an
anchor. Use all of them in \(S\), and choose the matching covering
functions. Formula~(L3) agrees with \(f\) at every point of \(C\)
by the interpolation identity itself. Its degree is at most \(s-1\).
It need not agree outside this finite class with the originally
supplied polynomial, and no such agreement is required.

Taking all \(S\) and all index choices proves the graph cover and
the counts.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
\label{gsr:en:19:lift:characteristic}
The lemma works over every field, including fields of small
characteristic. It uses distinct-node interpolation and not division
by factorials. If \(V_U=\mathcal P_{\boldsymbol b}(U)\), its candidates
have degree bounds \((b_1,\ldots,b_k,d-1)\).
\end{remark}

\subsection{A weighted local lifting theorem}

A local slice-cover hypothesis can be stated independently of any
particular regularity theorem. Let \(H\) have a finite nonnegative
measure \(\mu\), and let the allowed regions \(U\subset H\) have a
notion of width. Assume that an allowed region can be partitioned into
allowed subregions and that the relevant function spaces restrict
to subregions. The product measure on \(H\times J\) gives each column
counting measure, so its total mass is \(n\mu(H)\).

For each fixed \(x\in J\), assume the following slice-cover property.
For every real scale \(m\ge1\), on every allowed region \(U\) of width at least \(m\), and for every
\(0<\epsilon<1\), the partial function \(h\mapsto f(h,x)\) has:
\begin{itemize}
\item a partition of \(U\) into allowed subregions of width at least
\(m^{\mathfrak c(\epsilon)}\);
\item an exceptional subset of \(\mu\)-mass at most
\(\epsilon\mu(U)\);
\item on every subregion, a cover of its remaining graph by at most
\(\mathfrak q(\epsilon)\) functions in its prescribed vector space.
\end{itemize}
Here \(0<\mathfrak c(\epsilon)\le1\) and
\(\mathfrak q(\epsilon)\ge1\). The measure is part of the hypothesis:
a counting-measure regularity theorem is not being asserted to hold
for arbitrary weights automatically.

\begin{theorem}[Shared-slice lifting]
\label{gsr:en:19:lift:main}
Under the rowwise degree-\(<d\) hypothesis above, suppose that the
slice-cover property holds on an initial region \(H\) of width at
least \(m\ge1\). Let \(0<\sigma,\tau<1\), and set
\[
 r=\min\{n,\lceil qd/\sigma\rceil-1\},\qquad
 a=\mathfrak c(\tau/r),\qquad M=\mathfrak q(\tau/r).
 \label{gsr:en:19:lift:parameters}
 \tag{L4}
\]
There is a partition of \(H\) into regions of width at least
\[
 m^{a^r}
 \label{gsr:en:19:lift:width}
 \tag{L5}
\]
and an exceptional subset of \(H\times J\), of product mass at most
\[
 (\sigma+\tau)n\mu(H),
 \label{gsr:en:19:lift:error}
 \tag{L6}
\]
such that, on every product of a final region with \(J\), the
remaining graph of \(f\) is covered by at most
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^{\min(d,r)}\binom rj M^j
 \label{gsr:en:19:lift:graph-bound}
 \tag{L7}
\]
functions in the corresponding tensor space \(V_U\otimes_F
F[X]_{<d}\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The finite sampling estimate proved in the preceding section, with
row weight \(\mu(\{h\})\), supplies \(r\) distinct anchors such that
the union of uncertified classes has product mass at most
\(\sigma n\mu(H)\). For completeness, the required bound follows
from
\[
 |C|\,\Pr\{|R\cap C|<\min(d,|C|)\}
 \le \frac{dn}{r+1}\qquad(d-1\le r<n)
\]
and summation over the at most \(q\) classes per row. If \(r=n\),
every class is certified. The choice~(L4) therefore applies without
any lower bound on \(n\).

Fix such an anchor set \(R=\{\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_r\}\).
Refine first for the slice at \(\zeta_1\), using slice error
\(\tau/r\). In every resulting region refine for the slice at
\(\zeta_2\), with the same relative error, and continue through all
\(r\) slices. At each stage, the exceptional masses sum over a
partition of the initial region to at most
\((\tau/r)\mu(H)\). The union of the slice exceptions consequently
has mass at most \(\tau\mu(H)\). Its product with \(J\) has mass at
most \(\tau n\mu(H)\).

At the \(i\)-th stage the lower bound for width is raised to the
power \(a\). The final width is therefore at least \(m^{a^r}\).
Every earlier slice cover survives restriction to the final
regions. Thus all \(r\) sampled slices have covers on one common
partition, with at most \(M\) candidates for each slice.

Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:19:lift:algebra} separately on each final region.
Outside the slice exceptions it covers every certified class.
The uncertified classes and the products of the slice exceptions
with \(J\) together have mass at most~(L6), and the graph count is
exactly the upper bound~(L7).
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Different slice costs]
\label{gsr:en:19:lift:anisotropic}
The uniform allocation \(\tau/r\) is not essential. If the selected
slice \(i\) has controls
\(\mathfrak c_i(\epsilon)\) and \(\mathfrak q_i(\epsilon)\), choose
positive errors \(\epsilon_i\) with
\(\sum_i\epsilon_i\le\tau\). The same proof gives width exponent
\[
 \prod_{i=1}^r\mathfrak c_i(\epsilon_i)
\]
and graph count
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^{\min(d,r)}
 e_j\bigl(\mathfrak q_1(\epsilon_1),\ldots,
          \mathfrak q_r(\epsilon_r)\bigr).
\]
This retains information about heterogeneous slice complexity.
For \(\mathcal P_{\boldsymbol b}\), the independent degree bounds
in \(\boldsymbol b\) are preserved as well.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Why the refinement count is linear in the anchors]
\label{gsr:en:19:lift:linear-count}
The number of possible pairs of anchors is quadratic in \(r\),
but the number of slice functions that must be regularized is \(r\).
All pair interpolants are fixed linear combinations of functions
already present on the common partition. The quadratic quantity
belongs in the final candidate count, not in the number of
successive partition refinements.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Common differences of arithmetic-progression boxes}

The theorem gives Cartesian products of horizontal regions with the
column set. Gowers uses boxes whose coordinate progressions all have
one common difference. A final synchronization step supplies this
geometry with a single explicit factor, instead of paying a
geometric loss at every slice refinement.

We use integer arithmetic progressions embedded injectively in the
field and subprogressions in their inherited integer coordinates.
Thus, if a parent progression has common difference \(d_0\), a
subprogression used in a refinement has step \(t d_0\) with a positive
integer \(t\). The containment and length inequalities below are
integer inequalities before reduction in the field. This is the
no-wrap convention needed for the lemma; an arbitrary progression
description in a cyclic group without this convention does not
supply those inequalities.

\begin{lemma}[One final synchronization]
\label{gsr:en:19:lift:synchronization}
Let \(k\ge1\), and let \(P=T\times J\) be a \((k+1)\)-dimensional box of width \(m\),
where \(m\ge1\) is an integer and all coordinate progressions have
the same inherited integer step. Partition \(T\), if necessary,
into boxes whose coordinate lengths belong to
\(\{m,m+1,\ldots,2m-1\}\). Suppose each of these horizontal boxes
has been refined into horizontal boxes of width at least \(L\),
where \(1\le L\le m\), by subprogressions in the inherited
coordinates.

Then the corresponding Cartesian products with \(J\) admit a
partition into synchronized \((k+1)\)-boxes of width at least
\[
 \max\{1,L/4\}.
 \label{gsr:en:19:lift:synchronized-width}
 \tag{L8}
\]
Every function cover on a horizontal box times \(J\) remains valid
on its synchronized subboxes, with no increase in its graph count
and no additional exceptional points.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
A progression of length at least \(m\) can be partitioned into
consecutive blocks whose lengths are between \(m\) and \(2m-1\):
take blocks of length \(m\), and join a final shorter block to its
predecessor. This proves the asserted preliminary balancing.

If \(L<4\), singleton boxes give~(L8), so assume \(L\ge4\).
Let \(U\) be a final horizontal box inside a balanced horizontal
parent, and let \(t\) be the ratio of its common difference to that
of the parent. Since each side of \(U\) has at least
\(\lceil L\rceil\) points and the parent's side lengths are at most
\(2m-1\), containment gives
\[
 t(\lceil L\rceil-1)\le2m-2.
 \label{gsr:en:19:lift:step-bound}
 \tag{L9}
\]
Partition \(J\), in its inherited coordinates, into its nonempty
residue progressions of step \(t\). Since \(|J|\ge m\), each of
these progressions has length at least \(\lfloor m/t\rfloor\).
By~(L9),
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac mt\right\rfloor
 \ge
 \left\lfloor\frac{\lceil L\rceil-1}{2}\right\rfloor
 \ge \frac{\lceil L\rceil}{4}
 \ge \frac L4.
\]
Here the middle inequality holds for every integer
\(\lceil L\rceil\ge4\). The products of \(U\) with the residue
progressions have the common difference of \(U\), and all their
sides have at least \(L/4\) points. The products partition
\(U\times J\). They merely restrict previously constructed graph
covers, so neither candidate counts nor exceptional sets grow.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Shared-slice lifting on synchronized boxes]
\label{gsr:en:19:lift:synchronized-lift}
Suppose the slice-cover hypothesis holds for horizontal arithmetic
boxes and their inherited-coordinate refinements. On an initial
synchronized box \(T\times J\) of width \(m\), the conclusion of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:19:lift:main} holds with synchronized final boxes of width
at least
\[
 \max\{1,\tfrac14 m^{a^r}\},
 \label{gsr:en:19:lift:source-geometry}
 \tag{L10}
\]
the same exceptional proportion, and the same candidate count.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Balance \(T\) into horizontal boxes with side lengths in
\([m,2m-1]\), and choose the anchor set by averaging over all rows
of the original \(T\), with their original weights. Refine the
same sampled slices in each balanced box. The proof of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:19:lift:main} gives horizontal width
\(L=m^{a^r}\), with errors summing over the balanced partition.
Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:19:lift:synchronization} only after all \(r\)
horizontal refinements are finished.
\end{proof}

\subsection{An explicit replacement for the local step in Lemma 16.10}

We now substitute the parameters used in the pinned source into
the theorem. This is a local quantitative statement; it does not
presume that its output fits a separately prescribed inductive
control function.

At the start of Gowers' Lemma~16.10, put
\[
 s_0=\gamma^{-2}s(2^{-(k+2)}\theta,\gamma,k).
 \label{gsr:en:19:lift:source-s0}
 \tag{L11}
\]
The cross-section obtained by fixing the final variable is
\((\gamma,s_0)\)-multiply \(k\)-linear. Its horizontal slice controls
have the numerical bounds
\[
 \mathfrak c(\epsilon)
   =c(\epsilon/s_0,\gamma,k)^{s_0},
 \qquad
 \mathfrak q(\epsilon)
   =q(\epsilon/s_0,\gamma,k)^{s_0}.
 \label{gsr:en:19:lift:source-controls}
 \tag{L12}
\]
For the geometric conclusion below, assume in addition that these
controls are realized by the slice-cover property at every scale using
inherited integer-coordinate refinements. This is an explicit extra
geometric hypothesis, not a consequence asserted here of the live Lean
predicate for proper modular boxes.

Let \(S=T\times J\) be a nonempty proper inherited-coordinate box
from the preceding line-cover stage, with \(k\ge1\) and width at least
\(\ell\ge1\). Work over a field, or over a prime modulus. Put
\(A=B_1\cap E\cap S\), where \(E\) is the global good set supplied
by Lemma~16.9, and let the integer \(q_0\ge1\) bound the affine
graph count on each row of this restricted domain.
This is the quantity denoted \(q_\gamma\), and then \(q\), in the
pinned proof. Partition each row domain by assigning a point to
the first affine graph containing it; this gives the disjoint
classes required above.

\begin{corollary}[Local affine lift with shared refinement]
\label{gsr:en:19:lift:source-corollary}
Let \(0<\sigma,\tau<1\), set \(n=|J|\), and define
\[
 \begin{split}
 r&=\min\{n,\lceil2q_0/\sigma\rceil-1\},\\
 a&=c(\tau/(rs_0),\gamma,k)^{s_0},\\
 M&=q(\tau/(rs_0),\gamma,k)^{s_0}.
 \end{split}
 \label{gsr:en:19:lift:source-parameters}
 \tag{L13}
\]
Under the inherited-coordinate slice-cover hypothesis just stated,
after deleting at most \((\sigma+\tau)|S|\) additional ambient
points, the graph of the function restricted to \(A\) has a cover on synchronized boxes
of width at least
\[
 \max\left\{1,\frac14
   \ell^{\,c(\tau/(rs_0),\gamma,k)^{rs_0}}\right\}
 \label{gsr:en:19:lift:source-final-width}
 \tag{L14}
\]
by at most
\[
 r\,q(\tau/(rs_0),\gamma,k)^{s_0}
 +\binom r2q(\tau/(rs_0),\gamma,k)^{2s_0}
 \label{gsr:en:19:lift:source-final-count}
 \tag{L15}
\]
multiaffine graph candidates on each box.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Use degree parameter \(d=2\) in
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:19:lift:synchronized-lift}, with the controls~(L12).
The first term in~(L15) covers the certified singleton classes;
the second term covers classes having at least two points.
Every candidate is affine in the final variable and multiaffine
in the preceding \(k\) variables, hence multiaffine in all
\(k+1\) variables. The identity
\(a^r=c(\tau/(rs_0),\gamma,k)^{rs_0}\) gives~(L14).
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
Source~23's Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:23:glue:common-refinement} and~\ref{gsr:en:23:glue:affine-gluing} carry out the geometric part of this step without the inherited-coordinate hypothesis, with width $L_m^A\ge(m/3)^A$ in place of the formal $\sqrt{(m/8)^a}/4$, conditionally on the slice covers they assume; this advances this source's Question~6 (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:synchronization}). Not formalized.
\end{writenote}

Here a real number \(M\) is simply an upper bound for an integer
number of slice candidates. Using the polynomial expression in
\(M\) remains valid and does not require rounding it upwards.
The common-difference conclusion uses the additional
inherited-coordinate slice-refinement hypothesis. If only rectangular
products are required, Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:19:lift:main} supplies that conclusion
without the synchronization step.

For comparison, the displayed source proof uses
\[
 r_{\rm old}=\lceil q_0\sigma^{-2}\rceil,\qquad
 p_{\rm old}=4r_{\rm old}^{\,2}s_0
\]
and then applies a multiple-multilinearity cover with refinement
and graph exponents \(p_{\rm old}\). In~(L14), the corresponding
refinement count is \(rs_0\), of order \(q_0s_0/\sigma\).
In~(L15), the exponent on the slice graph bound is only \(2s_0\),
with the separate combinatorial factor \(\binom r2\).
Thus, up to explicit constants and finite rounding, the
refinement count changes from
\[
 O(q_0^2s_0\sigma^{-4})
 \quad\text{to}\quad
 O(q_0s_0\sigma^{-1}).
\]
This comparison retains \(q_0\) as an input parameter. It does not
hide its dependence on earlier parameters in Lemma~16.9.

The original exceptional set supplied by Lemma~16.9 is still
present. Its bound is global over the preceding partition; it need not
have small relative size in each individual box \(S\). Our theorem
only bounds the additional loss from the graph on \(A\). For a total error allowance \(\rho\), one may allocate
\(\rho/3\) to that initial step, \(\rho/3\) to sampling, and
\(\rho/3\) to the shared slice refinement. The separate deletion
of small row classes is unnecessary.

\begin{remark}[Limits of the source substitution]
\label{gsr:en:19:lift:no-global-claim}
The local cover~(L14)--(L15) is the proved output. To infer the
particular conclusion called \((\gamma,1)\)-multiple multilinearity
in the source, one would still have to compare this output with
its fixed functions \(c(\rho,\gamma,k+1)\) and
\(q(\rho,\gamma,k+1)\), uniformly in all outer parameters.
The pinned repository version explicitly flags the failure of
the displayed older closing comparison. The shared-refinement
theorem removes a major avoidable loss, but it does not by itself
establish that remaining comparison or a new bound for the
full Szemer\'edi theorem.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Potential formalization interface]
\label{gsr:en:19:lift:formalization}
The finite interpolation statement has a direct formalization
interface: a finite row partition; a finite anchor subset;
evaluation of partial row functions; the Lagrange interpolation
identity over a field; and an elementary symmetric count of
candidate tuples. The local-cover theorem adds finite
partitions, restricted graph covers, and a telescoping bound
for exceptional masses. It can be stated independently of the
source's large numerical control functions. This makes the
proved local output available for later, separately verified
closure calculations.
\end{remark}

\section[{Quantitative interpretation and worked comparisons\srctag{19}}]{Quantitative interpretation and worked comparisons}\label{gsr:en:19:sec:d8}
\srcnote{19}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:en:19:sec:comparisons}

\subsection{Two independent savings in the interpolation stage}

The sampling estimate and the shared refinement address different
parameters.  Let $q_0$ be the number of affine classes per row and
$s_0$ the structural iteration parameter of one sampled slice.
For a fixed sampling loss $\sigma$, the source construction uses
$r_{\mathrm{old}}=\lceil q_0\sigma^{-2}\rceil$ sampled coordinates.
Its subsequent iteration parameter is
$4r_{\mathrm{old}}^2s_0$.  The common-slice construction uses
\[
 r=\min\{|J|,\lceil2q_0/\sigma\rceil-1\}
\]
and a shared-refinement parameter $rs_0$.  The former improvement is
in the choice of the anchors; the latter is in how the anchored
information is combined.

For illustration, hold $q_0=10$ and $\sigma=1/10$, and suppose
$|J|\ge1000$.  The source sample count is $1000$, while the finite
guarantee here is $199$.  The structural iteration parameters are
then $4{,}000{,}000s_0$ and $199s_0$, respectively.  This comparison
does not require $s_0$ to be small.  The new affine list has at most
\[
 199M+19{,}701M^2
\]
candidates, where the slice list bound is evaluated at its actual
new error budget.  The figure $19{,}701$ is $\binom{199}{2}$.
This is a count of candidate functions, not a claim about runtime.

When $q_0$ and $\sigma$ themselves arise from previous stages, their
dependence must be substituted before making a global comparison.
Likewise, the new and old slice-list functions are evaluated at
different arguments.  The gain in the number of refinement steps
is explicit, but multiplying ratios of unrelated local bounds
would not establish a valid final density increment.

\subsection{General polynomial degree and a vector-valued extension}

For degree at most $D$ in the final coordinate, take $d=D+1$.
The sample count is of order $q(D+1)/\sigma$, and for a common slice
list size $M$ the final count is
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^{D+1}\binom rjM^j
\]
with out-of-range terms interpreted as zero.  For fixed $D$ this is
a polynomial in $rM$ of degree $D+1$.  A direct use of an abstract
closure lemma on every interpolation candidate would instead put
the number of candidates into the refinement iteration.  The
shared-slice theorem avoids that additional iteration.

The algebraic statement also extends to functions taking values in
an $F$-vector space $V$.  Define a polynomial with values in $V$ by
specifying its coefficient vectors.  Lagrange interpolation uses
only scalar multiplication and addition of these vectors, so the
proof of lemma~\ref{gsr:en:19:lift:algebra} is unchanged.  For a recovered large
class, the scalar Vandermonde matrix is invertible, and hence its
action on a vector of coefficients is invertible as well.  This
gives uniqueness of a vector-valued polynomial of degree less than
$d$ from $d$ distinct values.  For a smaller recovered class, direct
interpolation still gives agreement at every class point.

Over a commutative ring, the same argument is valid if every
denominator $\zeta_i-\zeta_j$ used in interpolation is a unit.
Distinctness alone is insufficient.  For example, modulo $8$ the
two polynomials $0$ and $2X$ agree at $X=0$ and $X=4$ but disagree
at $X=1$.  Thus an unrestricted composite-modulus version cannot
use a two-point uniqueness assertion.

\subsection{The gap in nonlinear partition exponents}

For $q$ quadratic phases, the optional Lau specialization gives
the sufficient flexible partition condition
\[
 (44q^2+45q+1)a+(44q^2+23q)b<1.
\]
The independently proved necessary condition is
\[
 (3q+1)a+2qb\le1.
\]
The difference between quadratic and linear dependence on $q$ is
substantial.  The recurrence transfer improves an exponential
dependence inherited from phase-by-phase refinement, but it does
not determine the optimal nonlinear frontier.

The obstruction already applies to the single cell containing the
left endpoint of the interval.  This is why the number of candidate
common differences is only of order $N/L$.  A proof that handles
only a positive fraction of the interval could evade this endpoint
argument by discarding the endpoint, and would be a different
partition problem.  Complete coverage is therefore a material
part of both the sufficient and necessary theorems.
