\section[{Notation and the exact moment--defect principle\srctag{24}}]{Notation and the exact moment--defect principle}\label{gsr:en:24:sec:d2}
\srcnote{24}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:en:24:sec:selector}

All sets used in counting arguments are finite. Unless explicitly
weighted, pairs and tuples are ordered, and diagonal entries are
included. Graphs below are symmetric incidence relations that may have
loops. Walks may repeat vertices. These conventions make the identities
exact; excluding repetitions would introduce avoidable error terms.

For finite subsets of an abelian group, write
\[
 r_A(d)=|\{(a,b)\in A^2:a-b=d\}|,
 \qquad E(A)=\sum_d r_A(d)^2.
\]
Equivalently, $E(A)$ counts the ordered solutions of $a+b=c+d$ in
$A^4$. If $m=|A|>0$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:energy-elementary}
 \sum_d r_A(d)=m^2,\qquad r_A(d)\le m,\qquad 0<E(A)\le m^3.
\end{equation}
For $k\ge1$, $kA$ denotes the $k$-fold sumset; $0A=\{0\}$.

\subsection{Weighted selection with the full codegree profile}

Let $(I,\mu)$ and $(V,\nu)$ be finite probability spaces, and let
$A_i\subseteq V$ for each $i\in I$. Define
\[
 c(i,j)=\nu(A_i\cap A_j).
\]
For a subset $K\subseteq I$ and $0<\beta\le1$, set
\[
 \bad_\beta(K)=
 \sum_{\substack{i,j\in K\\c(i,j)<\beta}}\mu(i)\mu(j).
\]
This is a weighted pair mass, not a conditional probability within $K$.

\begin{theorem}[Exact moment--defect selector]\label{gsr:en:24:thm:selector}
Fix an integer $t\ge1$ and $0<\eta<1$. Put
\begin{align}
 M_t&=\sum_{i,j}\mu(i)\mu(j)c(i,j)^t,\notag\\
 B_t&=\sum_{c(i,j)<\beta}\mu(i)\mu(j)c(i,j)^t,\notag\\
 \Delta&=M_t-\eta^{-1}B_t.\label{gsr:en:24:eq:Delta}
\end{align}
If $\Delta>0$, there is a set $K\subseteq I$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:selector-conclusion}
 \mu(K)^2-\eta^{-1}\bad_\beta(K)\ge\Delta.
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\[
 \mu(K)\ge\sqrt\Delta,
 \qquad \bad_\beta(K)<\eta\mu(K)^2.
\]
Moreover, $K$ may be chosen as the indices whose sets contain all the
points of one ordered $t$-sample from $V$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Sample $v_1,\ldots,v_t$ independently according to $\nu$, and put
$K=\{i:v_1,\ldots,v_t\in A_i\}$. For every ordered pair $(i,j)$,
\[
 \Pr(i,j\in K)=c(i,j)^t.
\]
Expanding the square of $\mu(K)$ and taking expectations gives
$\E\mu(K)^2=M_t$. The identical calculation restricted to bad pairs
 gives $\E\bad_\beta(K)=B_t$. Therefore
\[
 \E\bigl[\mu(K)^2-\eta^{-1}\bad_\beta(K)\bigr]=\Delta.
\]
At least one sample in the finite support has score at least its
expectation. The two consequences follow because the bad mass is
nonnegative and $\Delta$ is positive.
\end{proof}

The point is to retain $B_t$ as a \emph{truncated moment}. The often-used
estimates $M_t\ge u^t$ and $B_t\le\beta^t$, where
$u=\E_{i,j}c(i,j)$, discard the fact that the two terms come from the
same distribution. The cubic argument in the next section exploits
precisely this dependence.

\begin{corollary}[Higher-arity and heterogeneous versions]\label{gsr:en:24:cor:arity}
For an integer $r\ge1$, put
$c(i_1,\ldots,i_r)=\nu(A_{i_1}\cap\cdots\cap A_{i_r})$.
Replace the pair distribution in \eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:Delta} by $\mu^{\otimes r}$
and define the bad $r$-tuple mass analogously. Then $\Delta>0$ implies
that some $t$-sample core satisfies
\[
 \mu(K)^r-\eta^{-1}\bad(K)\ge\Delta,
 \qquad \mu(K)\ge\Delta^{1/r}.
\]
The identity remains valid if ``bad'' is specified by any fixed set of
index tuples, including tuple-dependent intersection thresholds.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Expand $\mu(K)^r$ as a sum over ordered $r$-tuples. The probability that
all their indices survive is $c(i_1,\ldots,i_r)^t$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The unweighted form}

When $|I|=n$ and $|V|=m$ carry uniform measure, a sample core has score
\[
 |K|^2-\eta^{-1}b_\beta(K),
 \quad
 b_\beta(K)=|\{(i,j)\in K^2:|A_i\cap A_j|<\beta m\}|.
\]
The expectation is $n^2\Delta$. Thus the normalization introduces
neither an extra density factor nor a loss from unordered pairs.
For later use, if the total number of incidences is $pmn$, then
Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:incidence-mean}
 \frac1{mn^2}\sum_{i,j}|A_i\cap A_j|
 =\frac1{mn^2}\sum_{v\in V}d(v)^2\ge p^2,
 \qquad d(v)=|\{i:v\in A_i\}|.
\end{equation}
There is no need to remove low-degree indices before applying this
inequality.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A three-sample strengthening of Lemma 7.4\srctag{24}}]{A three-sample strengthening of Lemma 7.4}\label{gsr:en:24:sec:d3}
\srcnote{24}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:en:24:sec:cubic}

\begin{theorem}[Cubic dense-intersection theorem]\label{gsr:en:24:thm:cubic}
Let $A_1,\ldots,A_n\subseteq V$, with $|V|=m>0$, $n>0$, and
$0<\delta\le1$. Suppose
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:gowers-hyp}
 \sum_{i,j=1}^n|A_i\cap A_j|\ge\delta^2mn^2.
\end{equation}
Then there is a set $K\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:cubic-size}
 |K|\ge\frac7{3\sqrt6}\,\delta^3n
\end{equation}
and at least $90\%$ of the ordered pairs in $K^2$ satisfy
\[
 |A_i\cap A_j|\ge\frac{\delta^2m}{2}.
\]
More strongly, if $b(K)$ is the number of pairs violating this
inequality, one can arrange
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:cubic-score}
 |K|^2-10b(K)\ge\frac{49}{54}\delta^6n^2.
\end{equation}
The set $K$ is the common incidence core of three points of $V$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Set $u=\delta^2$, and consider
\[
 h(s)=s^3-10s^3\one_{s<u/2}
 =\begin{cases}-9s^3,&0\le s<u/2,\\s^3,&s\ge u/2.\end{cases}
\]
We claim that, for every $s\ge0$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:cubic-line}
 h(s)\ge L(s):=\frac{49}{12}u^2s-\frac{343}{108}u^3.
\end{equation}
Put $b=7u/6$. If $s\ge u/2$, then
\[
 s^3-L(s)=(s-b)^2(s+2b)\ge0.
\]
For $0\le s\le u/2$, the function $-9s^3-L(s)$ is decreasing.
Its value at $u/2$ is $u^3/108>0$. This proves
\eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:cubic-line}, including the threshold where the definition of
$h$ jumps upwards. The parameter $b$ need not lie in $[0,1]$; the
factorization is valid for all nonnegative $s$.

For $c(i,j)=|A_i\cap A_j|/m$, hypothesis \eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:gowers-hyp} says
$\E_{i,j}c(i,j)\ge u$. Since $L$ has positive slope,
\[
 \E_{i,j}h(c(i,j))\ge L(u)
 =\left(\frac{49}{12}-\frac{343}{108}\right)u^3
 =\frac{49}{54}u^3.
\]
Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:24:thm:selector} with $t=3$, $\eta=1/10$, and
$\beta=u/2$. It yields \eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:cubic-score}, from which both
conclusions follow.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Second route.} This is source~03's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:03:drc:cubic-selection}: the same hypothesis, the same supporting line (tangent to $s^3$ at $7u/6$, value $u^3/108$ at $u/2$, hence $49/54$) and the same conclusion; proved independently (see the note in Section~\ref{gsr:fm:24:sec:d1}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{corollary}[Individual density hypothesis]
The same conclusion holds if $|A_i|\ge\delta m$ for every $i$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The total incidence count is at least $\delta mn$, so
\eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:incidence-mean} implies \eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:gowers-hyp}.
\end{proof}

The retained-size ratio relative to the source's lemma is
\[
 \frac{7\delta^3/(3\sqrt6)}{\delta^5/\sqrt2}
 =\frac7{3\sqrt3}\delta^{-2}>1.
\]
For instance, at $\delta=1/10$ the improvement factor in the stated
lower bound is approximately $134.7$. This numerical example is only
an illustration of an exact inequality, not evidence for it.

If $n=0$, choose $K=\varnothing$. If $m=0$ and $0<\delta\le1$,
choose all indices: every intersection meets the zero threshold and
$7\delta^3/(3\sqrt6)\le1$. Thus the theorem can be extended to the
zero-cardinality cases required by a fully general finite-set API.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The sharp scalar relaxation and a two-sample barrier\srctag{24}}]{The sharp scalar relaxation and a two-sample barrier}\label{gsr:en:24:sec:d4}
\srcnote{24}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:en:24:sec:scalar-sharp}

We now solve the scalar optimization problem behind the preceding
certificate. The distinction between a scalar distribution and a
realizable codegree matrix is important: the latter has additional
constraints, including positive semidefiniteness.

\subsection{An exact infimum for the score}

For $t\in\{2,3\}$, let $z_t>1$ be the unique solution of
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:root}
 (t-1)z_t^t-tz_t^{t-1}-9=0.
\end{equation}
The derivative of the left side is
$t(t-1)z^{t-2}(z-1)>0$ for $z>1$, and its value at $z=1$ is negative.
For both these values of $t$, the solution satisfies $z_t>2$.
Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:Ct}
 C_t=\frac{t z_t^{t-1}-9}{2^t}.
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp mean-only score]\label{gsr:en:24:thm:sharp-scalar}
Fix $t\in\{2,3\}$ and $0<u\le2/z_t$. Among all probability laws on
$[0,1]$ with mean exactly $u$, the infimum of
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:scalar-objective}
 \E\left[Z^t-10Z^t\one_{Z<u/2}\right]
\end{equation}
is $C_tu^t$. The same value is the infimum when the mean is required
only to be at least $u$.
For every $u>0$, without the restriction $u\le2/z_t$, the lower bound
$C_tu^t$ still holds for laws on $[0,1]$ of mean at least $u$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write $\beta=u/2$ and $b=z_t\beta$. Let
\[
 h_t(s)=s^t-10s^t\one_{s<\beta},
 \qquad \ell(s)=t b^{t-1}s-(t-1)b^t.
\]
The line $\ell$ is tangent to $s^t$ at $b$, and
\eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:root} gives
\[
 \ell(\beta)=-9\beta^t.
\]
For $s\ge\beta$, convexity of $s^t$ gives $h_t(s)\ge\ell(s)$.
For $0\le s\le\beta$, the difference $-9s^t-\ell(s)$ is decreasing
and vanishes at $\beta$, so is nonnegative. This proves the global
pointwise minorant, with the value at the threshold interpreted on
the lower branch only for the purpose of the comparison.
Consequently, if $\E Z\ge u$, then
\[
 \E h_t(Z)\ge\ell(u)
 =-9\beta^t+t b^{t-1}(u-\beta)=C_tu^t.
\]

For sharpness assume $b\le1$. Since $z_t>2$, we have
$\beta<u<b$. For each sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$, place
mass
\[
 q_\varepsilon=\frac{u-(\beta-\varepsilon)}{b-(\beta-\varepsilon)}
\]
at $b$, and the remaining mass at $\beta-\varepsilon$.
This law has mean exactly $u$. As $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, both
support points approach points of contact with the minorant, from
the correct side of the jump at $\beta$. The objective therefore
converges to $\ell(u)=C_tu^t$. The lower bound and the matching
sequence of laws prove the infimum statements.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Source~03's constants} (checked at the write). For $t=3$, \eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:root} is source~03's equation $2z^3-3z^2=9$ \eqref{gsr:en:03:drc:z-root}, and $C_3=(3z^2-9)/8$ equals source~03's $\kappa_*^2=(3z^2-z^3)/4$ because $z^3=(3z^2+9)/2$; so $\sqrt{C_3}=0.9537881585\ldots$ is source~03's \eqref{gsr:en:03:drc:optimized-constant}. For $t=2$, $z_2/2=(1+\sqrt{10})/2$ is source~03's $h$, and $C_2=(-7+2\sqrt{10})/4=2h-h^2$ is source~03's two-witness value. Source~03 states the optimality of its scalar argument and the two-witness barrier in prose; the exact infimum statement, for means exactly $u$ and at least $u$, and the range $u\le2/z_t$ are this source's.
\end{writenote}

\subsection{The improved cubic constant}

For $t=3$, the root and coefficient are
\[
 z_3=2.3293557629\ldots,
 \qquad C_3=\frac{3z_3^2-9}{8}=0.9097118514\ldots.
\]
Thus Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:24:thm:cubic} admits the slightly stronger conclusion
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:optimal-cubic}
 |K|\ge\sqrt{C_3}\,\delta^3n
 =0.9537881585\ldots\,\delta^3n.
\end{equation}
The rational certificate $49/54$ is only slightly weaker than $C_3$,
and avoids algebraic-root infrastructure in a formalization.
The coefficient $C_3$ cannot be increased using only the mean
constraint and this fixed scalar score, since
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:24:thm:sharp-scalar} supplies matching scalar laws for all
sufficiently small $u$.

\subsection{What exactly fails with two samples}

For $t=2$, equation \eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:root} gives $z_2=1+\sqrt{10}$, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:negative-two}
 C_2=\frac{-7+2\sqrt{10}}4=-0.1688611699\ldots<0.
\end{equation}
For $0<u\le2/(1+\sqrt{10})$, a mean constraint alone therefore
cannot force a positive expectation of the two-sample score
$|K|^2-10b(K)$ at threshold $u/2$. The near-extremizers in the proof
have two codegree levels, just below $u/2$ and near
$(1+\sqrt{10})u/2$.

This is a precise obstruction to one proposed proof strategy, not a
counterexample to a two-sample combinatorial theorem. A scalar
near-extremizer need not be the distribution of entries of a
codegree matrix. It is also not an obstruction to changing the
score, changing the sampling law, or lowering the threshold. Indeed,
the next section uses one sample successfully at a different
threshold.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{From a profile certificate to many four-step walks\srctag{24}}]{From a profile certificate to many four-step walks}\label{gsr:en:24:sec:d5}
\srcnote{24}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:en:24:sec:walks}

Let $A$ be a finite subset of an abelian group, with $m=|A|>0$.
Let $D$ be a finite symmetric set of possible edge differences, and
join $a,b\in A$ when $a-b\in D$. Write
\[
 N(a)=\{b\in A:a-b\in D\},\qquad
 c(a,a')=\frac{|N(a)\cap N(a')|}{m}.
\]
Apply the uniform version of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:24:thm:selector} to these
neighbourhoods. The following lemma records the full profile without
rounding it to a power of the original energy.

\begin{lemma}[Profile-to-difference-set certificate]\label{gsr:en:24:lem:profile-walk}
Suppose some core $K\subseteq A$ satisfies
\[
 |K|\ge\sqrt\Delta\,m,\qquad b_\beta(K)\le\eta|K|^2,
 \qquad \Delta>0,
\]
where a pair is bad when $c(a,a')<\beta$.
Choose $\eta<\lambda<1/2$, and put $r=1-\eta/\lambda$.
Then there is a nonempty $S\subseteq K$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:profile-size}
 |S|\ge r|K|\ge r\sqrt\Delta\,m
\end{equation}
and
\begin{align}
 \frac{|S-S|}{m}
 &\le \frac{(|D|/m)^4}{(1-2\lambda)\sqrt\Delta\,\beta^2},
 \label{gsr:en:24:eq:profile-abs}\\
 \frac{|S-S|}{|S|}
 &\le \frac{(|D|/m)^4}
 {(1-2\lambda)(1-\eta/\lambda)\Delta\beta^2}.
 \label{gsr:en:24:eq:profile-rel}
\end{align}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Remove from $K$ every vertex with more than $\lambda|K|$ bad partners
in $K$. Since the sum of these bad degrees is $b_\beta(K)$, at most
$(\eta/\lambda)|K|$ vertices are removed. This gives
\eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:profile-size}.

Fix $a,a'\in S$. At least $(1-2\lambda)|K|$ vertices $v\in K$ form
good pairs with both $a$ and $a'$. For every such $v$, there are at
least $\beta m$ choices of $b\in N(a)\cap N(v)$ and at least
$\beta m$ choices of $c\in N(v)\cap N(a')$. Thus there are at least
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:walk-lower}
 R=(1-2\lambda)|K|\beta^2m^2
\end{equation}
walks $a,b,v,c,a'$.
Each walk determines a tuple
\[
 (a-b,\ b-v,\ v-c,\ c-a')\in D^4
\]
whose sum is $a-a'$. For fixed endpoints, this map is injective:
the first three entries successively recover $b,v,c$.

For each $d\in S-S$, select one endpoint pair with difference $d$.
It contributes at least $R$ distinct elements of the sum fibre
$\{(d_1,d_2,d_3,d_4)\in D^4:d_1+d_2+d_3+d_4=d\}$.
Fibres for different $d$ are disjoint. Hence
\[
 |S-S|R\le |D|^4.
\]
Use $|K|\ge\sqrt\Delta m$ to obtain \eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:profile-abs}, and
also $|S|\ge r|K|$ to obtain \eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:profile-rel}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why repetitions do not cause a loss]
Nothing in the injection requires the vertices of a walk to be
 distinct. Likewise, the pair $a=a'$ is legitimate. All estimates are
therefore exact for small sets as well as asymptotically valid for
large ones.
\end{remark}

\subsection{The one-sample specialization}

A one-neighbourhood score followed by bad-degree pruning also appears,
with different parameters, in Reiher--Schoen, Lemma~2.1
\cite{reiherschoen}. This selection component is an adaptation of
established machinery, not a claim of a new sampling method.

Suppose the graph has ordered edge density
\[
 p=\frac1{m^2}\sum_{a\in A}|N(a)|>0.
\]
By \eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:incidence-mean}, the mean normalized codegree is at
least $p^2$. Use
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:one-parameters}
 t=1,\qquad \beta=p^2/16,\qquad \eta=1/8.
\end{equation}
Since $B_1\le\beta$, its profile score satisfies
\[
 \Delta=M_1-8B_1\ge p^2-8\beta=p^2/2.
\]
Choose $\lambda=1/4$ in Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:24:lem:profile-walk}. We obtain
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:core-size-simple}
 |K|\ge pm/\sqrt2,\qquad |S|\ge |K|/2\ge pm/(2\sqrt2).
\end{equation}
For each fixed endpoint pair in $S$, the number of walks is at least
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:simple-walk-number}
 \frac{|K|}{2}\left(\frac{p^2m}{16}\right)^2
 =\frac{|K|p^4m^2}{512}.
\end{equation}
The weaker codegree threshold makes one sample sufficient; there is
no contradiction with the two-sample obstruction at threshold $p^2/2$.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{An explicit energy-to-small-difference-set theorem\srctag{24}}]{An explicit energy-to-small-difference-set theorem}\label{gsr:en:24:sec:d6}
\srcnote{24}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:en:24:sec:bsg}

The key improvement in the energy reduction is not merely a more
favourable choice of constants in dependent random choice. It is the
retention of the \emph{same actual popular-edge mass} in two places:
the incidence density and the size of the popular difference set.
The resulting powers cancel in the four-walk count.

\begin{theorem}[Popular-mass form]\label{gsr:en:24:thm:bsg-profile}
Let $A$ be a nonempty finite subset of an abelian group, $m=|A|$, and
$\kappa=E(A)/m^3$. Choose $0<\tau<\kappa$, and define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:Dp}
 D=\{d:r_A(d)\ge\tau m\},\qquad
 p=\frac1{m^2}\sum_{d\in D}r_A(d).
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:popular-estimates}
 p\ge\frac{\kappa-\tau}{1-\tau},
 \qquad |D|\le\frac{p}{\tau}m.
\end{equation}
There is a nonempty $S\subseteq A$ with
\begin{align}
 |S|&\ge\frac{p}{2\sqrt2}m,\label{gsr:en:24:eq:bsg-profile-size}\\
 |S-S|&\le\frac{512\sqrt2}{p\tau^4}m,
 \label{gsr:en:24:eq:bsg-profile-abs}\\
 |S-S|&\le\frac{2048}{p^2\tau^4}|S|.
 \label{gsr:en:24:eq:bsg-profile-rel}
\end{align}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The difference function is symmetric, so $D=-D$. On $D$ we have
$r_A(d)^2\le mr_A(d)$, and outside $D$ we have
$r_A(d)^2\le\tau m r_A(d)$. Summing gives
\[
 \kappa m^3\le m\sum_{d\in D}r_A(d)
       +\tau m\sum_{d\notin D}r_A(d)
 =\bigl(p+\tau(1-p)\bigr)m^3.
\]
This proves the first estimate in \eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:popular-estimates}.
The second follows from
$\tau m|D|\le\sum_{d\in D}r_A(d)=pm^2$.

Construct the popular-difference graph. Its ordered edge density is
exactly $p$, not just a lower bound in terms of $\kappa$. Apply the
one-sample construction of Section~\ref{gsr:en:24:sec:walks}, obtaining $K,S$
as in \eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:core-size-simple}. The four-walk injection gives
\[
 |S-S|\le\frac{512|D|^4}{|K|p^4m^2}
 \le\frac{512m^2}{|K|\tau^4}
 \le\frac{512\sqrt2}{p\tau^4}m.
\]
For the relative estimate, divide the middle expression by
$|S|\ge|K|/2$, rather than by a separately rounded lower bound:
\[
 \frac{|S-S|}{|S|}
 \le\frac{1024m^2}{|K|^2\tau^4}
 \le\frac{2048}{p^2\tau^4}.
\]
This proves all assertions.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Dyadic constants]\label{gsr:en:24:cor:bsg-dyadic}
If $E(A)\ge\kappa m^3$ with $0<\kappa\le1$, there is a nonempty
$S\subseteq A$ satisfying, simultaneously,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:bsg-dyadic}
 \boxed{\quad
 |S|\ge2^{-3}\kappa m,\qquad
 |S-S|\le2^{15}\kappa^{-5}m,\qquad
 |S-S|\le2^{17}\kappa^{-6}|S|.
 \quad}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For equality in the energy hypothesis, set $\tau=\kappa/2$.
Then $p\ge\kappa/(2-\kappa)\ge\kappa/2$. The first two bounds follow
from
\[
 \frac{p}{2\sqrt2}\ge\frac{\kappa}{4\sqrt2}\ge2^{-3}\kappa,
 \quad
 \frac{512\sqrt2}{p\tau^4}
 \le2^{14}\sqrt2\,\kappa^{-5}\le2^{15}\kappa^{-5}.
\]
The relative estimate is
\[
 \frac{2048}{p^2\tau^4}
 \le 2^{11}\cdot 2^2\cdot2^4\kappa^{-6}
 =2^{17}\kappa^{-6}.
\]
If the assumed energy parameter is smaller than the actual normalized
energy, apply the equality case to the latter and then weaken each
bound using its monotonicity.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Against sources~03 and~10.} Source~03's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:03:drc:elementary-bsg} gives $(c/8,2^{19}c^{-9})$: the same retained size, a weaker difference bound. Source~10's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:10:thm:weighted-bsg} gives $(c/4,2^{10}c^{-5})$, hence relative doubling $2^{12}c^{-6}$ (the proof of its Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:10:cor:improved-order-eight}): better in all three conclusions. Reiher--Schoen's theorem is stronger than all three, as the source says.
\end{writenote}

\begin{remark}[A constant that must not be recomputed incorrectly]
Dividing the \emph{rounded} absolute difference bound by the
\emph{rounded} retained-size bound gives only
$2^{18}\kappa^{-6}$. The better factor $2^{17}$ comes from the direct
relative estimate in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:24:thm:bsg-profile}. The main exponent
ledger uses that direct estimate.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Why retaining \texorpdfstring{$p$}{p} matters}

The coarse bound $|D|\le m/\tau$ is true, but replacing the second
estimate in \eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:popular-estimates} by it loses the factor $p^4$
in $|D|^4$. That factor exactly cancels the $p^4$ coming from two
common-neighbour choices in \eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:simple-walk-number}. Keeping
only an energy lower bound for the edge count while discarding the
same count in the popular-set estimate would therefore produce a
substantially weaker power of $\kappa$.

Similarly, pruning the original graph to force a minimum degree is
unnecessary here. The mean codegree estimate follows directly from
all its incidences, and the only pruning occurs after a sample has
produced a core with few bad pairs. This is what permits the linear
retained fraction in \eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:bsg-dyadic}.

\subsection{Optimizing the popularity threshold}
\label{gsr:en:24:subsec:threshold}

The choice $\tau=\kappa/2$ makes the constants simple, but is not
optimal for every downstream objective. To optimize the absolute
bound in \eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:bsg-profile-abs} using only
$p\ge(\kappa-\tau)/(1-\tau)$, maximize
\[
 F(\tau)=\frac{\tau^4(\kappa-\tau)}{1-\tau}.
\]
For $0<\kappa<1$, the maximizing root in $(0,\kappa)$ is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:tau-absolute}
 \tau_{\rm abs}=
 \frac{5+3\kappa-\sqrt{25-34\kappa+9\kappa^2}}8.
\end{equation}
Indeed, logarithmic differentiation gives
$4/\tau-1/(\kappa-\tau)+1/(1-\tau)=0$, equivalently
\[
 4\tau^2-(5+3\kappa)\tau+4\kappa=0.
\]
The derivative changes sign from positive to negative at the smaller
root. In particular $\tau_{\rm abs}/\kappa\to4/5$ as
$\kappa\downarrow0$. At $\kappa=1$ the optimum is approached at the
endpoint, and there is no need to use this formula in the proof of
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:24:cor:bsg-dyadic}.

More importantly, the threshold that optimizes a final Freiman
restriction differs from the one that optimizes $|S-S|$ alone.
Section~\ref{gsr:en:24:subsec:downstream-opt} gives its exact equation.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The sumset-growth input, with a complete proof\srctag{24}}]{The sumset-growth input, with a complete proof}\label{gsr:en:24:sec:d7}
\srcnote{24}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:en:24:sec:plunnecke}

For self-containment, we record the classical Pl\"unnecke--Ruzsa bound
needed below. The short minimal-growth argument is due to
Petridis~\cite{petridis}; no novelty is claimed for this section.

\begin{lemma}[Minimal growth]\label{gsr:en:24:lem:min-growth}
Let $A,B$ be nonempty finite subsets of an abelian group. Choose a
nonempty $X\subseteq A$ minimizing $|X+B|/|X|$, and denote that
minimum by $K$. For every finite $T$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:min-growth}
 |X+B+T|\le K|X+T|.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The assertion is immediate for $T=\varnothing$. Otherwise order its
elements $t_1,\ldots,t_r$, and define
\[
 X_i=\{x\in X:x+t_i\notin\bigcup_{j<i}(X+t_j)\}.
\]
The translates $X_i+t_i$ partition $X+T$, so
$|X+T|=\sum_i|X_i|$. If $x\in X\setminus X_i$, then
$x+t_i=x'+t_j$ for some $x'\in X$ and $j<i$. Adding any $b\in B$
shows that $((X\setminus X_i)+B)+t_i$ is already contained in
$\bigcup_{j<i}(X+B+t_j)$. Thus the number of new points contributed
by $X+B+t_i$ is at most
\[
 |X+B|-|(X\setminus X_i)+B|
 \le K|X|-K|X\setminus X_i|=K|X_i|.
\]
The inequality follows from minimality, with the empty-set case
interpreted as $0\ge K\cdot0$. Summing over $i$ proves
\eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:min-growth}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Ruzsa's triangle inequality]\label{gsr:en:24:lem:ruzsa}
For finite subsets $U,V,W$ of an abelian group with $V\ne\varnothing$,
\[
 |U-W||V|\le|U-V||V-W|.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For each $d\in U-W$, choose a representation $d=u_d-w_d$.
The map
\[
 (d,v)\longmapsto(u_d-v,\,v-w_d)
\]
from $(U-W)\times V$ to $(U-V)\times(V-W)$ is injective: the sum of
the outputs recovers $d$, and then the first output recovers $v$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Pl\"unnecke--Ruzsa in the required form]\label{gsr:en:24:thm:pr}
If $|A+B|\le C|A|$ for nonempty finite sets $A,B$, then for all
nonnegative integers $r,s$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:PR}
 |rB-sB|\le C^{r+s}|A|.
\end{equation}
In particular, if $|\Gamma-\Gamma|\le C|\Gamma|$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:PR-graph}
 |r\Gamma-s\Gamma|\le C^{r+s}|\Gamma|.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Choose $X$ as in Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:24:lem:min-growth}; then $K\le C$.
Applying that lemma with $T=(j-1)B$ and inducting gives
$|X+jB|\le K^j|X|$ for every $j\ge0$.
Take $U=rB$, $V=-X$, and $W=sB$ in Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:24:lem:ruzsa}. Then
\[
 |rB-sB||X|\le|X+rB||X+sB|
 \le K^{r+s}|X|^2.
\]
Divide by $|X|$, and use $|X|\le|A|$ and $K\le C$.
For \eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:PR-graph}, apply \eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:PR} with $A=\Gamma$ and
$B=-\Gamma$, and interchange $r,s$ if necessary.
\end{proof}

All exponents in \eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:PR-graph} count the \emph{total} number
of summands, positive and negative. In particular,
$|2k\Gamma-2k\Gamma|$ is controlled by $C^{4k}|\Gamma|$, not by
$C^{2k}|\Gamma|$. The fibre argument below is designed to use a
smaller sumset, rather than to miscount this exponent.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Vertical-fibre compression and Freiman restrictions\srctag{24}}]{Vertical-fibre compression and Freiman restrictions}\label{gsr:en:24:sec:d8}
\srcnote{24}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:en:24:sec:fibre}

Let $G,H$ be abelian groups, $B\subset G$ finite and nonempty, and
$\phi:B\to H$. Its graph is
\[
 \Gamma=\{(x,\phi(x)):x\in B\}\subset G\times H.
\]
For an integer $k\ge1$, define the vertical defect fibre
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:defect}
 F_k=\{y\in H:(0,y)\in k\Gamma-k\Gamma\},\qquad Q_k=|F_k|.
\end{equation}
Then $0\in F_k$, $F_k=-F_k$, and $Q_k\ge1$.
The condition $F_k=\{0\}$ is equivalent to $\phi$ already being a
Freiman homomorphism of order $k$.

\subsection{Counting only the relevant obstruction}

\begin{lemma}[Compressed vertical-fibre estimate]\label{gsr:en:24:lem:fibre-count}
For every $k\ge1$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:fibre-count}
 Q_k|\Gamma|\le |(k+1)\Gamma-k\Gamma|.
\end{equation}
Consequently, if $|\Gamma-\Gamma|\le C|\Gamma|$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:Q-bound}
 Q_k\le C^{2k+1}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Use the map
\[
 F_k\times\Gamma\longrightarrow(k+1)\Gamma-k\Gamma,
 \qquad (y,(x,\phi(x)))\longmapsto(x,\phi(x)+y).
\]
Membership in the target follows from $(0,y)\in k\Gamma-k\Gamma$.
The first coordinate of the image determines $x$, hence determines
the graph point; its second coordinate then determines $y$.
Thus the map is injective. Equation \eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:Q-bound} follows from
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:24:thm:pr} with $r=k+1$ and $s=k$.
\end{proof}

The inspected repository proof of Lemma~7.5 uses a vertical fibre
and bounds it through $2k\Gamma-2k\Gamma$, resulting in $C^{4k}$;
its edited paper source explains why this repairs a larger-sumset
problem in the printed proof~\cite{repo24}. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:24:lem:fibre-count}
uses the graph property more directly. One added graph point already
makes the fibre injection work, so the total growth exponent becomes
$2k+1$.

\subsection{A prime-cyclic avoidance lemma with the exact symmetry gain}

\begin{lemma}[Avoiding a symmetric defect set]\label{gsr:en:24:lem:avoidance}
Let $p$ be prime, let $F\subseteq\F_p$ be symmetric with $0\in F$,
and let $Q=|F|>1$. For every integer $k\ge1$, there are a nonzero
$d\in\F_p$ and an integer $L\ge0$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:avoid-properties}
 jd\notin F\quad(0<|j|\le kL),
 \qquad \frac{L+1}{p}\ge\frac1{kQ}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:avoid-L}
 L=\floor{\frac{p-2}{k(Q-1)}}.
\end{equation}
For each integer $1\le j\le kL$ and $w\in F\setminus\{0\}$,
the equation $jd=w$ has exactly one solution $d\in\F_p^\times$.
Indeed, $j\le kL\le(p-2)/(Q-1)<p$, so $j$ is invertible modulo $p$.
There are at most $kL(Q-1)\le p-2$ forbidden nonzero scalars, whereas
$\F_p^\times$ has $p-1$ elements. Choose an allowed $d$.
Positive multiples in this range avoid $F\setminus\{0\}$ and cannot
be zero; negative multiples also avoid $F$ because $F=-F$.
This proves the first assertion, including the case $L=0$.

For the second, integer division gives
\[
 k(Q-1)(L+1)\ge p-1.
\]
Since $Q\le p$,
\[
 \frac{L+1}{p}\ge\frac{p-1}{pk(Q-1)}\ge\frac1{kQ}.
\]
The last comparison is exactly $Q(p-1)\ge p(Q-1)$.
\end{proof}

The use of symmetry avoids counting positive and negative multiples
as unrelated obstructions. Removing the zero element from the defect
set also matters at small primes. These elementary details improve
the constant in the extraction lemma, not just its power of $C$.

\begin{theorem}[Prime-codomain Freiman extraction]\label{gsr:en:24:thm:extraction}
Let $B$ be a nonempty finite subset of an abelian group and
$\phi:B\to\F_p$, with $p$ prime. For every $k\ge1$, there is
$B'\subseteq B$ such that $\phi|_{B'}$ is a Freiman homomorphism of
order $k$ and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:exact-fibre-extraction}
 |B'|\ge\frac{|B|}{kQ_k}.
\end{equation}
If the graph has $|\Gamma-\Gamma|\le C|\Gamma|$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:extraction}
 \boxed{\qquad |B'|\ge\frac{|B|}{kC^{2k+1}}.\qquad}
\end{equation}
When $Q_k=1$, one can take $B'=B$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The case $Q_k=1$ follows from the definition of the defect fibre.
Otherwise apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:24:lem:avoidance} to $F_k$, obtaining $d,L$.
Assign to each pair $(x,j)$ with $x\in B$, $0\le j\le L$, the colour
\[
 \phi(x)-jd\in\F_p.
\]
Some colour $a$ occurs at least $(L+1)|B|/p$ times. Since $L<p$ and
$d\ne0$, the same $x$ cannot contribute twice to one colour.
Hence
\[
 B'=\{x\in B:\phi(x)=a+j(x)d\text{ for some }0\le j(x)\le L\}
\]
has at least $(L+1)|B|/p\ge|B|/(kQ_k)$ elements; the index $j(x)$
is unique.

Suppose $x_1+\cdots+x_k=x'_1+\cdots+x'_k$ with all entries in $B'$.
The difference of the corresponding graph sums has the form
\[
 \left(0,Jd\right),\qquad
 J=\sum_{i=1}^k j(x_i)-\sum_{i=1}^k j(x'_i),\qquad |J|\le kL.
\]
Thus $Jd\in F_k$. By \eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:avoid-properties}, $J$ must be zero,
which says exactly that the two output sums agree.
Finally use $Q_k\le C^{2k+1}$ from Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:24:lem:fibre-count}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Second route.} This is source~10's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:10:thm:fibre-extraction} (the same set, $F_k=H_k$, the same injection into $(k+1)\Gamma-k\Gamma$ and the same avoidance length), whose prefactor $|B|/(k(h_k-1)+1)$ is at least $|B|/(kQ_k)$ (here $Q_k=h_k$); proved independently. The extension beyond prime cyclic domains is also in source~10's statement, which allows any abelian group.
\end{writenote}

\begin{remark}[Why the domain need not be prime cyclic]
Primality was used only to invert $j$ in the \emph{codomain}.
The domain was used only as an abelian group supporting equal sums
and an injective graph projection. The theorem therefore genuinely
extends the prime-cyclic-domain formulation in the source.
For $k=1$ every function already has the required property, so the
quantitative extraction bound is deliberately nonoptimal in that
trivial order.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Vector-space codomains in finite characteristic}

\begin{theorem}[Linear hashing of the defect fibre]\label{gsr:en:24:thm:hash}
Let $\phi:B\to\F_p^d$, where $p$ is prime, and let $Q_k$ be defined
by \eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:defect}. Put
\[
 r=\ceil{\log_p Q_k}.
\]
There is a subset $B'\subseteq B$ on which $\phi$ is a Freiman
homomorphism of order $k$ and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:hash-bound}
 |B'|\ge\frac{|B|}{p^r}\ge\frac{|B|}{pQ_k}.
\end{equation}
If $|\Gamma-\Gamma|\le C|\Gamma|$, it follows that
$|B'|\ge |B|/(pC^{2k+1})$.
For $Q_k=1$, take $r=0$ and $B'=B$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Assume $Q_k>1$. Choose a linear map
$T:\F_p^d\to\F_p^r$ uniformly at random. For each fixed nonzero
$y\in\F_p^d$, the image $T(y)$ is uniform, so
$\Pr(T(y)=0)=p^{-r}$. A union bound gives
\[
 \Pr\bigl(\ker T\cap(F_k\setminus\{0\})\ne\varnothing\bigr)
 \le(Q_k-1)p^{-r}<1.
\]
Choose $T$ for which $\ker T\cap F_k=\{0\}$. A fibre of $T\circ\phi$
has at least $|B|/p^r$ elements; let $B'$ be such a fibre.
If two $k$-term domain sums from $B'$ agree, their output difference
$y$ lies in $F_k$. Its image under $T$ is the difference between two
sums of $k$ copies of the same fibre value, hence zero. Therefore
$y=0$, proving the Freiman property.
Since $p^{\ceil{\log_p Q_k}}\le pQ_k$, the numerical bounds follow.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{New in this report, and a comparison proved at the write.} Against source~10's torsion-budget Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:10:thm:torsion-fibre-extraction} on $V=\F_p^d$, $n=p^d$: for every multiple $j$ of $p$, $V[j]=V$ and $jV=\{0\}$, so the summand $|V[j]|\,|F\cap jV|-1$ of its budget equals $n-1>n-2$; hence its budget fails as soon as $kL\ge p$, so $L\le\lfloor(p-1)/k\rfloor$ and its retention $(L+1)/n$ is at most $(\lfloor(p-1)/k\rfloor+1)p^{-d}$. For $k\ge2$ this is less than $p^{1-d}$, while the bound here is $p^{-\lceil\log_pQ_k\rceil}\ge p^{1-d}$ whenever $Q_k\le p^{d-1}$. So for $k\ge2$ and $Q_k\le p^{d-1}$ the bound here is strictly larger (the intake confirmed this numerically for $p\le11$, $d\in\{2,3\}$, $k\in\{2,3,8\}$). For $d=1$ source~10's prime-codomain bound is far better, as the remark below says, and in general neither dominates. Not formalized; the general finite abelian codomain remains open (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:groups}).
\end{writenote}

This theorem complements the prime-cyclic interval argument rather
than replacing it: for a large prime $p$ and a small order $k$,
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:24:thm:extraction} has a better prefactor. For a vector-space
codomain, the hashing bound is independent of its dimension.
For a completely general finite abelian codomain, no corresponding
uniform-characteristic assertion is being assumed.

\section[{Compiling energy bounds into coherent restrictions\srctag{24}}]{Compiling energy bounds into coherent restrictions}\label{gsr:en:24:sec:d9}
\srcnote{24}{Section 9}
\label{gsr:en:24:sec:compiler}

\begin{lemma}[Quantitative compiler]\label{gsr:en:24:lem:compiler}
Suppose a graph $\Gamma_0$ on a domain of size $m$ has a subgraph
$\Gamma_1$ on $B_1$ satisfying
\[
 |B_1|\ge a\gamma^u m,
 \qquad |\Gamma_1-\Gamma_1|\le b\gamma^{-v}|\Gamma_1|,
\]
where $a,b>0$. If the codomain is $\F_p$, then an order-$k$ Freiman
restriction exists with size at least
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:compiler}
 \frac{a}{k b^{2k+1}}\,
 \gamma^{u+v(2k+1)}m.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:24:thm:extraction} to $\Gamma_1$, then substitute the
two assumed bounds. A subset of a graph is still a graph, with
cardinality equal to that of its domain.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Proof of the headline theorem}

The graph
\[
 \Gamma_0=\{(x,\phi(x)):x\in B_0\}\subset G\times\F_p
\]
has $m$ points. Its additive energy is precisely the number of
respected quadruples, so is at least $\gamma m^3$.
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:24:cor:bsg-dyadic}, applied in the abelian product group,
provides a graph subset $\Gamma_1$ on a domain $B_1$ with
\[
 |B_1|\ge2^{-3}\gamma m,
 \qquad |\Gamma_1-\Gamma_1|
 \le2^{17}\gamma^{-6}|\Gamma_1|.
\]
Use Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:24:lem:compiler} with $a=2^{-3}$, $u=1$, $b=2^{17}$,
and $v=6$:
\begin{align*}
 |B|&\ge\frac{2^{-3}}{k(2^{17})^{2k+1}}
             \gamma^{1+6(2k+1)}m\\
 &=\frac{2^{-(34k+20)}}k\gamma^{12k+7}m.
\end{align*}
This proves Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:24:thm:headline}. For $k=8$, the power of
$\gamma$ is $1+6\cdot17=103$, and the power-of-two loss is
$3+17\cdot17+3=295$.

\subsection{Separating the two sources of improvement}

The following counterfactual calculations are useful for checking that
no improvement is counted twice. The source's energy reduction
retains $2^{-20}\gamma^{12}$ of the graph and has relative doubling
$2^{58}\gamma^{-36}$; its extraction loss at order eight is
$64C^{32}$~\cite{gowers,repo24}.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule
Energy reduction & Freiman extraction & Order-eight retained fraction\\
\midrule
Source & Source & $2^{-1882}\gamma^{1164}$\\[0.3em]
Source & Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:24:thm:extraction} & $2^{-1009}\gamma^{624}$\\[0.3em]
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:24:cor:bsg-dyadic} & Source & $2^{-553}\gamma^{193}$\\[0.3em]
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:24:cor:bsg-dyadic} & Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:24:thm:extraction}
 & $2^{-295}\gamma^{103}$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{The improvement in the energy exponent is genuinely
compositional: both the energy step and the fibre step contribute.}
\label{gsr:en:24:tab:compiler}
\end{table}

For example, using only the new extraction lemma gives
$12+36\cdot17=624$ and $20+58\cdot17+3=1009$.
Using only the new energy reduction gives
$1+6\cdot32=193$ and $3+17\cdot32+6=553$.
These equalities also make the provenance of the source's
$1164=12+36\cdot32$ transparent.

\subsection{An explicit corollary from a modern imported theorem}
\label{gsr:en:24:subsec:modern}

Theorem~1.2 of Reiher--Schoen~\cite{reiherschoen} states that for
$0<\varepsilon<1/2$, energy at least $\gamma m^3$ yields a subset
of size at least $(1-\varepsilon)\gamma^{1/2}m$ with relative
difference-set bound $2^{33}\varepsilon^{-9}\gamma^{-4}$.
This theorem is an \emph{external input} in the next corollary; its
proof is not reproduced here.

\begin{corollary}[Modern-input restriction bound]\label{gsr:en:24:cor:modern}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:24:thm:headline}, for every
$0<\varepsilon<1/2$ there is an order-$k$ Freiman restriction of size
at least
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:modern-bound}
 \frac{(1-\varepsilon)\varepsilon^{9(2k+1)}}
 {k\,2^{33(2k+1)}}\,
 \gamma^{8k+9/2}m.
\end{equation}
In particular, taking $k=8$ and $\varepsilon=1/4$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:modern-eight}
 |B|\ge3\cdot2^{-872}\gamma^{137/2}m.
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply the imported theorem to $\Gamma_0$ and use
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:24:lem:compiler} with
$a=1-\varepsilon$, $u=1/2$,
$b=2^{33}\varepsilon^{-9}$, and $v=4$.
For the displayed specialization,
$b=2^{51}$, $2k+1=17$, and
$(1-\varepsilon)/k=3/32$, giving
$3\cdot2^{-5-51\cdot17}=3\cdot2^{-872}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Second route.} This bound is identical to source~10's modern-input alternative (the paragraph after Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:10:cor:improved-order-eight}), from the same imported Reiher--Schoen theorem and the same fibre argument.
\end{writenote}

The smaller energy exponent in \eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:modern-eight} comes with a
larger explicit constant loss. Consequently it does not uniformly
dominate \eqref{gsr:fm:24:eq:headline-eight} for every $\gamma\in(0,1]$.
For fixed parameters one may take the larger of the two guaranteed
sizes. This comparison illustrates why optimizing only an exponent,
without its constants or the intended density regime, can mislead.

\subsection{Optimizing for the final restriction rather than a single step}
\label{gsr:en:24:subsec:downstream-opt}

Use the unrounded popular-mass estimates in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:24:thm:bsg-profile}. The resulting order-$k$ retained
fraction is at least
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:unrounded-compiler}
 \frac{p}{2\sqrt2\,k}
 \left(2^{11}p^{-2}\tau^{-4}\right)^{-(2k+1)}.
\end{equation}
Its parameter-dependent part is
$p^{4k+3}\tau^{8k+4}$. If the only information about $p$ is its
energy lower bound, set
\[
 a=4k+3,\qquad b=8k+4,
 \qquad H(\tau)=
 \left(\frac{\kappa-\tau}{1-\tau}\right)^a\tau^b.
\]
For $0<\kappa<1$, the unique maximizer in $(0,\kappa)$ is the
smaller root of
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:downstream-quadratic}
 b\tau^2-\bigl[b(1+\kappa)+a(1-\kappa)\bigr]\tau+b\kappa=0.
\end{equation}
Indeed, the logarithmic derivative vanishes exactly when
\[
 \frac b\tau-\frac a{\kappa-\tau}+\frac a{1-\tau}=0,
\]
and the quadratic changes from positive to negative across its
first root in the interval. As $\kappa\downarrow0$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:24:eq:optimal-threshold-asymptotic}
 \frac{\tau}{\kappa}\longrightarrow\frac{b}{a+b}
 =\frac{8k+4}{12k+7}.
\end{equation}
For order eight the limiting ratio is $68/103$, not $1/2$ and not
the $4/5$ that optimizes the absolute difference bound.
The clean dyadic theorem uses $\tau=\kappa/2$ to keep the statement
simple; \eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:unrounded-compiler} and
\eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:downstream-quadratic} supply an explicitly sharper
parameter-specific certificate.
