\section[{Arrangements, parity, and the degree of a certificate\srctag{22}}]{Arrangements, parity, and the degree of a certificate}\label{gsr:en:22:sec:d2}
\srcnote{22}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:en:22:sec:arrangements}

In Sections~\ref{gsr:en:22:sec:arrangements}--\ref{gsr:en:22:sec:finite}, let $k\ge1$,
$d\ge2$, $q=2d$, and let $p>4d$ be prime. Here $q$ is the number of
cubes, not a field cardinality. Later sections reuse $q$ for the customary
finite-field cardinality, after saying so explicitly.
Set
\[
 s=(\underbrace{1,\ldots,1}_{d},\underbrace{-1,\ldots,-1}_{d}),
 \qquad H=\{r\in\F_p^q:s\cdot r=0\}.
\]
An arrangement is parametrized by
\[
 h\in\F_p^k,\quad r\in H,\quad
 (y^1,\ldots,y^q)\in(\F_p^k)^q,
\]
and its labeled vertices are
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:22:eq:rho}
 \rho(\epsilon,j)=
 (y_1^j+\epsilon_1h_1,\ldots,y_k^j+\epsilon_kh_k,r_j),
 \quad \epsilon\in\{0,1\}^k,\quad j\in[q].
\end{equation}
There are $p^D$ parameterized arrangements, where $D=(q+1)k+q-1$.
All probabilities use the uniform measure on this parameter space.

\begin{definition}
A certificate is a function $\eta:\{0,1\}^k\times[q]\to\{-1,0,1\}$.
It succeeds when
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:22:eq:moment-tests}
 \sum_{\epsilon,j}\eta(\epsilon,j)
           \prod_{i\in A}\rho(\epsilon,j)_i=0
 \qquad\text{for every }A\subseteq[k+1].
\end{equation}
Write $\pi(\epsilon)=(-1)^{|\epsilon|}$ and
$\eta_0(\epsilon,j)=s_j\pi(\epsilon)$.
The arrangement is degenerate if a successful certificate is not in
$\spanof\{\eta_0\}$. Its degeneracy probability is denoted
$\delta_{k,d}(p)$.
\end{definition}

The universal certificate $\eta_0$ always succeeds: parity annihilates
proper horizontal monomials; the remaining two tests are proportional to
$\sum s_j=0$ and $s\cdot r=0$. A zero side identifies two labeled
vertices and gives another successful certificate. Thus the exact
probability of this first source of degeneracy is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:22:eq:zprob}
 z_k(p)=1-(1-p^{-1})^k.
\end{equation}
For the rest of this section fix nonzero sides.

\subsection{Removing the parity factor}

Normalize a certificate by
\[
 v_j(\epsilon)=\eta(\epsilon,j)/\eta_0(\epsilon,j)
             =s_j\pi(\epsilon)\eta(\epsilon,j).
\]
Each $v_j$ still takes values in $\{-1,0,1\}$. Let its unique multilinear
interpolation polynomial over $\F_p$ be
\[
 v_j(\epsilon)=\sum_{T\subseteq[k]} a_{j,T}\epsilon_T,
 \qquad \epsilon_T=\prod_{i\in T}\epsilon_i.
\]
Define the degree of $\eta$ to be $t=\max_j\deg v_j$, taking a nonzero
constant slice to have degree zero. The zero certificate is excluded
whenever an equivalence class is counted.

\begin{lemma}[Moment--degree duality]\label{gsr:en:22:lem:degree-duality}
Put $c_{j,S}=\sum_\epsilon\eta(\epsilon,j)\epsilon_S$.
If a nonzero certificate has degree $t$, then the smallest $|S|$ for
which some $c_{j,S}$ is nonzero is exactly $k-t$.
In particular, degree zero is precisely the pure-parity case.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Parity summation of a Boolean monomial is zero unless that monomial
uses all $k$ coordinates, when it is $(-1)^k$. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:22:eq:duality}
 c_{j,S}=s_j(-1)^k
      \sum_{T:T\cup S=[k]}a_{j,T}.
\end{equation}
If $|S|<k-t$, no set $T$ of size at most $t$ can occur in the sum.
Conversely, choose $a_{j,T}\ne0$ with $|T|=t$ and set $S=[k]\setminus T$.
The only possibly nonzero summand is $a_{j,T}$, proving equality.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The rank gained at a given degree}

The following lemma reproves and preserves the degree information in the
paired-moment argument of \cite{prior22degeneracy}.

\begin{lemma}[Degree-sensitive certificate probability]\label{gsr:en:22:lem:rank}
Let a nonparity certificate have degree $t\ge1$. Conditional on any
fixed nonzero sides, its probability of success is at most
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:22:eq:rank-bound}
 Q_t(p)=
 \begin{cases}
 p^{-2}+(p-1)p^{-q},&t=1,\\
 p^{-t-1},&2\le t\le k.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
The degree-one bound is attained by an individual certificate.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose $B\subseteq[k]$ of size $k-t$ with
$b=(c_{1,B},\ldots,c_{q,B})\ne0$. For $A\subseteq[k]$ define
\[
 P_{j,A}(y^j)=\sum_\epsilon\eta(\epsilon,j)
                   \prod_{i\in A}(y_i^j+\epsilon_i h_i).
\]
Expansion and the minimality of $|B|$ give
\[
 P_{j,A}=\sum_{S\subseteq A}h_Sc_{j,S}y^j_{A\setminus S},
 \qquad P_{j,B}=h_Bb_j.
\]
The tests for $B$ and $B\cup\{k+1\}$ force
$\sum_jb_j=0$ and $b\cdot r=0$.

For each $i\notin B$, the equation
$\sum_jP_{j,B\cup\{i\}}=0$ is affine in the horizontal variables.
Choose $j_0$ with $b_{j_0}\ne0$ and hold all variables other than
$y_i^{j_0}$, $i\notin B$, fixed. Their coefficient matrix is diagonal
with nonzero diagonal $h_Bb_{j_0}$. Thus these equations have rank $t$.
If $b$ is not proportional to $s$, then $b\cdot r=0$ is an independent
restriction on $H$, giving probability at most $p^{-1}p^{-t}$.
An inconsistent condition $\sum b_j\ne0$ only reduces the probability.

If $b=cs$ with $c\ne0$, pair each affine equation with its vertical
counterpart $\sum_jr_jP_{j,B\cup\{i\}}=0$. For $r_a\ne r_b$, the
columns indexed by $y_i^a,y_i^b$ have coefficient block
\[
 h_Bc\begin{pmatrix}s_a&s_b\\r_as_a&r_bs_b\end{pmatrix},
\]
with nonzero determinant. Distinct $i\notin B$ give disjoint diagonal
blocks, so the rank is at least $2t$ when $r$ is not constant. It remains
at least $t$ when $r$ is constant. There are $p$ constant vectors among
the $p^{q-1}$ vectors of $H$. The probability is therefore at most
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:22:eq:paired-rank}
 (1-p^{-(q-2)})p^{-2t}+p^{-(q-2+t)}.
\end{equation}
For $t=1$ this equals the first expression in \eqref{gsr:en:22:eq:rank-bound}.
For $t\ge2$, its ratio to $p^{-t-1}$ is at most
$p^{1-t}+p^{3-q}\le2/p<1$, since $q\ge4$.

Finally, fix an index $i$ and take
$\eta=s_j\pi(\epsilon)\ind_{\{\epsilon_i=0\}}$.
Only the equations $\sum_js_jy_i^j=0$ and
$\sum_js_jr_jy_i^j=0$ remain nonautomatic. Their ranks are exactly
two or one according as $r$ is nonconstant or constant. This realizes
the first line of \eqref{gsr:en:22:eq:rank-bound}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Equivalent certificates and cumulative counts}

Two certificates related by $\eta'=a\eta+b\eta_0$, $a\ne0$, have the
same success locus. In normalized form this is the affine change
$v'=av+b\mathbf1$. The count of these equivalence classes is elementary.

\begin{lemma}[Ternary affine classes]\label{gsr:en:22:lem:ternary-classes}
For $p\ge5$, nonconstant ternary patterns on $n$ positions have
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:22:eq:An}
 \Aclass_n=\frac{3^n-2^{n+1}+1}{2}
\end{equation}
classes under invertible affine changes of values.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Two-valued patterns correspond to unordered nontrivial bipartitions,
giving $(2^n-2)/2$ classes. A pattern using all three values can only
be affinely equivalent to itself or its negative: an affine permutation
of $\{-1,0,1\}$ has translation part zero, by summing the three values,
and multiplier $1$ or $-1$. Inclusion--exclusion counts
$3^n-3\cdot2^n+3$ three-valued patterns. Half this number, added to the
two-valued count, gives \eqref{gsr:en:22:eq:An}.
\end{proof}

Let $C_t$ be the actual number of nonconstant normalized certificate
classes of degree at most $t$; they need not succeed. Set
\[
 \Hball_t(k)=\sum_{j=0}^t\binom{k}{j}.
\]
A degree-at-most-$t$ multilinear polynomial is determined by its values
on the Boolean vectors of weight at most $t$. Indeed its coefficients
are recovered successively by Boolean interpolation. Restriction to
these vectors in every slice therefore injects affine classes. Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:22:eq:cumulative-ball}
 C_t\le\Aclass_{q\Hball_t(k)},\qquad C_0=\Aclass_q,
 \qquad C_k=\Aclass_{q2^k}.
\end{equation}
This inequality is valid over $\F_p$ directly; it does not require
identifying a finite-field degree with a real polynomial degree.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{An exact polynomial count for the first nonparity degree\srctag{22}}]{An exact polynomial count for the first nonparity degree}\label{gsr:en:22:sec:d3}
\srcnote{22}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:en:22:sec:affine}

\subsection{Affine maps with three allowed values}

\begin{lemma}[Affine ternary slices]\label{gsr:en:22:lem:affine-slices}
Over $\F_p$, $p\ge5$, an affine function on $\{0,1\}^k$ with values
in $\{-1,0,1\}$ is one of the following:
\begin{enumerate}
\item a constant;
\item a function with one slope $\pm1$ and one of two intercepts;
\item a function with one slope $\pm2$ and its unique intercept;
\item a function with two slopes, both in $\{-1,1\}$, and their
      unique admissible intercept.
\end{enumerate}
Hence the numbers of ternary and binary affine functions are respectively
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:22:eq:fk-bk}
 f_k=2k^2+4k+3,
 \qquad b_k=2k+2.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Fix an active slope $a$ and put $S=\{-1,0,1\}$.
The values on the remaining coordinates must lie in $S\cap(S-a)$.
This intersection is empty unless $a\in\{\pm1,\pm2\}$; it has two
elements for $a=\pm1$ and one for $a=\pm2$. An affine Boolean map
into a two-point set has at most one active coordinate: two active
slopes would force the four values $x,x+b,x+c,x+b+c$ into that set,
implying $b=c$ and $2b=0$. This is impossible in odd characteristic.
Thus at most two coordinates are active. The listed intercepts follow
by checking their two or four vertex values. Counting gives
$3+6k+4\binom{k}{2}=f_k$. A binary affine map is constant or a coordinate
or its complement, giving $b_k$.
\end{proof}

Applying the orbit argument of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:22:lem:ternary-classes} to all
$q$ slices gives the exact cumulative count
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:22:eq:Uone}
 C_1=\Uprof_1=\frac{f_k^q-2b_k^q+1}{2}.
\end{equation}
This already replaces a count exponential in $2^k$ by a polynomial in
$k$ of degree $2q$. The success equations impose further useful restrictions.

\subsection{Balancing the slopes}

Write a degree-one slice as $v_j=c_j+\sum_i a_{ij}\epsilon_i$.
Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:22:eq:duality}, applied with $S=[k]\setminus\{i\}$,
shows that success requires
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:22:eq:slope-balance}
 \sum_{j=1}^q s_j a_{ij}=0\qquad(1\le i\le k).
\end{equation}
The slopes have their integer representatives in $\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}$.
Since $p>2q=4d$, their sums in \eqref{gsr:en:22:eq:slope-balance} vanish over
the field exactly when the corresponding integer sums vanish.

Introduce independent Laurent variables $z_1,\ldots,z_k$ and set
$u_i=z_i+z_i^{-1}$. Define
\begin{align}
 F_k(z)&=3+\sum_{i=1}^k\bigl(2u_i+z_i^2+z_i^{-2}\bigr)
                  +\sum_{i<j}u_iu_j,\label{gsr:en:22:eq:Fpoly}\\
 B_k(z)&=2+\sum_{i=1}^ku_i.\label{gsr:en:22:eq:Bpoly}
\end{align}
The coefficient of $z^a$ in $F_k$ counts the allowed intercepts for
slope vector $a$. The corresponding statement for binary slices uses
$B_k$. Both Laurent polynomials are invariant under inversion of all
variables.

\begin{theorem}[Balanced degree-one certificate count]\label{gsr:en:22:thm:balanced-count}
For $p>4d$, the exact number of degree-one normalized certificate
classes satisfying all necessary slope balances is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:22:eq:Jbalanced}
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 \Bal_{k,d}=\frac{\CT F_k^{2d}-2\CT B_k^{2d}
                         -3^{2d}+2^{2d+1}}2.}
\end{equation}
The constant term is taken in all $k$ variables.
For fixed $d$, $\Bal_{k,d}$ is a polynomial in $k$ of degree exactly
$2d$, with leading coefficient
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:22:eq:Jleading}
 \lambda_d=2^{2d-1}(2d)![z^{2d}]
                 \frac{e^{-z/2}}{\sqrt{1-z}}>0.
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:22:eq:Jd2}
 \Bal_{k,2}=30k^4+204k^3+111k^2+114k.
\end{equation}
This counts potentially successful classes, not distinct geometric
success loci and not actual successful certificates in one arrangement.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The first $d$ and last $d$ slices contribute opposite slope sums.
Their balanced tuples are counted by
$\CT F_k(z)^dF_k(z^{-1})^d=\CT F_k(z)^{2d}$.
Similarly, the binary balanced tuples number $\CT B_k^{2d}$.
Slope balance is preserved by affine value changes, so the two-value
and three-value orbit argument gives
\[
 \frac{\CT F_k^{2d}-2\CT B_k^{2d}+1}{2}
\]
classes of degree at most one satisfying balance. Every pure-parity
class satisfies balance, and their number is $\Aclass_{2d}$.
Subtracting it proves \eqref{gsr:en:22:eq:Jbalanced}.

For polynomiality put $q=2d$. A constant-term monomial in $F_k^q$
contains each active variable in at least two slice factors: one
nonzero signed exponent cannot sum to zero. Each slice contains at
most two active variables. Thus at most $q$ variables are active.
Classify terms by their actual active set. For every $0\le j\le q$
the contribution is a constant, independent of $k$, times $\binom{k}{j}$.
Therefore $\CT F_k^q$ is a polynomial of degree at most $q$ in $k$.
The same argument gives degree at most $\lfloor q/2\rfloor$ for
$\CT B_k^q$.

In the top-degree contribution, each of the $q$ slices uses exactly
two different variables, with slopes $\pm1$, and each of the $q$
active variables occurs twice. Represent the slices by labeled
vertices and each active variable by an edge between its two slices.
The result is a loopless 2-regular multigraph; a two-vertex component
has a pair of parallel edges. Each edge has two balanced sign choices.
After assigning distinct variables to edges, a multigraph with edge
multiplicities $m_{ab}$ has weight $1/\prod m_{ab}!$.
The weighted exponential generating function for these graphs is
\[
 \exp\left(\sum_{j\ge2}\frac{z^j}{2j}\right)
             =\frac{e^{-z/2}}{\sqrt{1-z}}.
\]
For $j\ge3$ this uses the $(j-1)!/2$ undirected cycles; for $j=2$
the parallel pair has weight $1/2$, giving the same term $z^2/4$.
The leading coefficient of $\CT F_k^q$ is consequently
$2^q q![z^q]e^{-z/2}(1-z)^{-1/2}$. The binary correction has lower
degree. Dividing by two proves \eqref{gsr:en:22:eq:Jleading} and positivity.

For $q=4$, expansion gives
\begin{align*}
 \CT F_k^4&=60k^4+408k^3+246k^2+312k+81,\\
 \CT B_k^4&=12k^2+42k+16.
\end{align*}
Substitution in \eqref{gsr:en:22:eq:Jbalanced} gives \eqref{gsr:en:22:eq:Jd2}.
These expansions can be obtained by classifying active sets of size at
most four, or by the exact moment calculation below.
\end{proof}

\subsection{An efficient exact evaluation of the constant terms}

The displayed constant-term formula does not require expanding in $k$
Laurent variables. Set $S=\sum_i u_i$ and $T=\sum_i u_i^2$. Then
\[
 F_k=3-2k+2S+\frac{S^2+T}{2},\qquad B_k=2+S,
\]
and
\[
 \CT u_i^a=
 \begin{cases}\binom{a}{a/2},&a\text{ even},\\0,&a\text{ odd}.
 \end{cases}
\]
Independence of the Laurent variables yields the recurrence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:22:eq:moment-recurrence}
 M_{k+1}(a,b)=\sum_{i=0}^a\sum_{j=0}^b
  \binom ai\binom bj M_k(a-i,b-j)\mu_{i+2j},
\end{equation}
where $M_k(a,b)=\CT S^aT^b$, $\mu_r=\CT(z+z^{-1})^r$, and
$M_0(a,b)=\ind_{\{a=b=0\}}$. Only $a+2b\le2q$ is needed.
The script \file{code/verify_certificates.py} implements this recurrence
using integers and compares it with independent sparse Laurent convolution.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The finite exceptional-set bound and its quantitative use\srctag{22}}]{The finite exceptional-set bound and its quantitative use}\label{gsr:en:22:sec:d4}
\srcnote{22}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:en:22:sec:finite}

\subsection{The degree-zero hyperplanes}

For completeness, the earlier coefficient $C_d$ has the following exact
interpretation. A pure-parity certificate has
$\eta(\epsilon,j)=c_j\pi(\epsilon)$ with $c_j\in\{-1,0,1\}$.
For nonzero sides it succeeds exactly when
\[
 \sum_jc_j=0,\qquad c\cdot r=0.
\]
Excluding the universal direction $\spanof\{s\}$, these equations
give $C_d$ distinct hyperplanes on $H$.

Here is the count. There are $T_{2d}$ integer-balanced ternary vectors
$c$. Write $v_j=s_jc_j$. Two vectors define the same hyperplane on
$H$ exactly when $v'=av+b\mathbf1$. The admissible two-valued
patterns correspond to balanced subsets of the $d$ positive and $d$
negative positions, of which there are $\binom{2d}{d}$ including the
empty and full subsets. They contribute
$(\binom{2d}{d}-2)/2$ classes. The admissible three-valued patterns
number $T_{2d}-3\binom{2d}{d}+3$ and are paired by negation.
Adding gives \eqref{gsr:fm:22:eq:Cd-intro}. The assumption $p>2d$ prevents
integer balance from aliasing modulo $p$ and $p\ge5$ validates the
orbit count.

For reference $C_2=4$, $C_3=51$, $C_4=484$, and
$C_8=2\,585\,444$. Their union has probability at most $C_d/p$.
Any two distinct such hyperplanes intersect in codimension two in $H$.

\subsection{Summing the degree strata correctly}

Define an explicit cumulative profile by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:22:eq:Uprofile}
 \Uprof_0=\Aclass_q,\qquad
 \Uprof_1=\frac{f_k^q-2b_k^q+1}{2},\qquad
 \Uprof_t=\Aclass_{q\Hball_t(k)}\quad(2\le t\le k).
\end{equation}
For $k=1$ only the first two terms are used. This profile is increasing,
$C_t\le\Uprof_t$, and equality holds for $t=0,1,k$.

\begin{theorem}[Stratified finite degeneracy bound]\label{gsr:en:22:thm:filtration-bound}
Let $k\ge1$, $d\ge2$, and $p>4d$ be prime. Then
\begin{align}
 \delta_{k,d}(p)\le z_k(p)+(1-z_k(p))\bigg[
  \frac{C_d}{p}
  +\Bal_{k,d}\bigl(p^{-2}+(p-1)p^{-2d}\bigr)
  +\sum_{t=2}^k\frac{\Uprof_t-\Uprof_{t-1}}{p^{t+1}}
                                      \bigg].\label{gsr:en:22:eq:main-degeneracy}
\end{align}
The empty sum is zero. One may take the minimum of this expression and
one. Multiplication by $p^D$ gives the corresponding count of arrangements.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Condition on nonzero sides. The pure-parity classes contribute at most
$C_d/p$. Among degree-one classes, only the $\Bal_{k,d}$ balanced
ones can succeed, and Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:22:lem:rank} applies to each.
For degree $t\ge2$, that lemma gives an upper bound
\[
 \sum_{t=2}^k(C_t-C_{t-1})w_t,
 \qquad w_t=p^{-t-1}.
\]
For $k\ge2$, summation by parts rewrites this as
\[
 C_kw_k-C_1w_2+\sum_{t=2}^{k-1}C_t(w_t-w_{t+1}).
\]
The differences $w_t-w_{t+1}$ are positive, and $C_1=\Uprof_1$.
Replacing the other $C_t$ by their cumulative upper bounds and reversing
the summation by parts gives
$\sum_{t=2}^k(\Uprof_t-\Uprof_{t-1})w_t$.
The case $k=1$ has no such tail. Finally include the zero-side event
\eqref{gsr:en:22:eq:zprob}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Against source~18 and the formal statement} (checked at the write). With $q=2d$, the probability $Q_1(p)=p^{-2}+(p-1)p^{-2d}$ of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:22:lem:rank} is source~18's $Q_d(p)$, and the remark at the end of this section shows that the right side of \eqref{gsr:en:22:eq:main-degeneracy} is at most the bound obtained by charging $Q_1(p)$ to every nonparity class, which is source~18's finite bound \eqref{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-finite-exact}. That bound lies below the formal $k3^{2d2^k}/p$ of \file{lemma_15_4} for $d\ge2$ and $p>2d$ (note after Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:18:deg:thm-count}). So this theorem implies the formal bound for $d\ge2$ and primes $p>4d$; it is not formalized. It needs $p>4d$ where source~18 needs $p>2d$.
\end{writenote}

\begin{remark}[Why cumulative differences need this proof]
It is not asserted that $C_t-C_{t-1}\le\Uprof_t-\Uprof_{t-1}$ for
every $t$. Such an assertion would not follow from cumulative bounds.
The decreasing weights and exact endpoint at degree one are essential
to the valid aggregate comparison. Also, $\Bal_{k,d}$ replaces only the
degree-one term; its use does not silently subtract unbalanced classes
from the higher-degree profile.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[A smaller second-order upper coefficient]\label{gsr:en:22:cor:secondupper}
For fixed $k,d\ge1$ with $d\ge2$, as $p\to\infty$ through primes,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:22:eq:second-upper}
 \delta_{k,d}(p)
 \le\frac{k+C_d}{p}
 +\frac{\Bal_{k,d}-kC_d-\binom{k}{2}}{p^2}
 +O_{k,d}(p^{-3}).
\end{equation}
In particular the positive contribution to this upper coefficient from
nonparity certificates is polynomial of degree $2d$ in $k$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Expand $z_k=k/p-\binom{k}{2}/p^2+O_k(p^{-3})$.
The extra term $(p-1)p^{-2d}$ is $O_d(p^{-3})$ and every tail term
has order at most $p^{-3}$. Multiplication in
\eqref{gsr:en:22:eq:main-degeneracy} gives the result.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{An upper coefficient, now known exactly for $d=2$.} Source~27's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:27:thm:d2main} determines the second coefficient for $d=2$: $(k^2+21k-6)/2$, which is $8$ at $k=1$ and $20$ at $k=2$, against the upper coefficients $\Bal_{1,2}-4=455$ and $\Bal_{2,2}-8-1=2{,}775$ given here. As the text says, the class count alone cannot give the true coefficient.
\end{writenote}

The true second coefficient need not equal the coefficient in
\eqref{gsr:en:22:eq:second-upper}: hyperplane intersections and coincident
nonparity loci still matter. Retaining the zero-side and parity
hyperplanes gives the earlier lower estimate
\[
 \delta_{k,d}(p)\ge\frac{k+C_d}{p}
             -\frac{\binom{k+C_d}{2}}{p^2}.
\]
Together these bounds recover the sharp leading term while narrowing
the source of its next-order error.

\subsection{Examples and the size of the improvement}

Let $J^{\rm old}_{k,d}=\Aclass_{2d2^k}-\Aclass_{2d}$ be the earlier
count of all nonparity classes. The following table compares coefficients
that had previously been charged at the same $p^{-2}$ scale. The new
finite theorem also includes its explicitly displayed higher-degree tail.

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{rrr r r}
\toprule
$k$ & $d$ & $\Bal_{k,d}$ & $\log_{10}(\Uprof_1-\Uprof_0)$
 & $\log_{10}J^{\rm old}_{k,d}$\\
\midrule
1&2&459&3.477&3.477\\
2&2&2\,784&4.805&7.332\\
4&2&22\,968&6.528&30.235\\
8&2&235\,344&8.548&488.271\\
2&8&$1.68440\cdot10^{18}$&20.159&30.235\\
4&8&$4.58798\cdot10^{23}$&27.020&121.842\\
8&8&$3.27723\cdot10^{29}$&35.094&1953.988\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Rounded values in this table are explanatory only. Exact integers are
recorded in \file{data/certificate_verification.json}.

For example, for $k=d=2$, one has
\[
 C_d=4,\quad \Bal_{2,2}=2784,\quad
 \Uprof_1-\Uprof_0=63\,840,\quad
 \Uprof_2-\Uprof_1=21\,393\,960.
\]
Thus the conditional exceptional probability is bounded by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:22:eq:small-finite-example}
 \frac4p+2784\left(\frac1{p^2}+\frac{p-1}{p^4}\right)
             +\frac{21\,393\,960}{p^3}.
\end{equation}
One sees explicitly why a finite-size comparison must retain the tail:
the asymptotic gain can be much larger than the gain at moderate $p$.

\subsection{Explicit absorption thresholds}

For $0<\varepsilon\le1$ define
\begin{align}
 \mathcal P_{k,d}(\varepsilon)=\max\bigg\{&4d,
 \frac{(k+1)(k+C_d)}{\varepsilon},
 \left(\frac{2(k+1)\Bal_{k,d}}{\varepsilon}\right)^{1/2},\notag
 \\ &\max_{2\le t\le k}
 \left(\frac{(k+1)(\Uprof_t-\Uprof_{t-1})}
                  {\varepsilon}\right)^{1/(t+1)}\bigg\}.
 \label{gsr:en:22:eq:threshold}
\end{align}
Omit the inner maximum when $k=1$.

\begin{corollary}[Finite exceptional-set absorption]\label{gsr:en:22:cor:absorption}
Every prime $p>\mathcal P_{k,d}(\varepsilon)$ satisfies
$\delta_{k,d}(p)\le\varepsilon$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Use $z_k\le k/p$, $1-z_k\le1$, and
$p^{-2}+(p-1)p^{-2d}\le2p^{-2}$.
The resulting sum has $k+1$ nonnegative terms: one leading term,
one degree-one term, and $k-1$ higher-degree terms.
Each is at most $\varepsilon/(k+1)$ under \eqref{gsr:en:22:eq:threshold}.
\end{proof}

The equal allocation in \eqref{gsr:en:22:eq:threshold} is convenient, but it need
not be the smallest available sufficient condition. There is a second
explicit form retaining the optimal leading scale as
$\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Write $a=k+C_d$,
$J=\Bal_{k,d}$, and $\Delta_t=\Uprof_t-\Uprof_{t-1}$, and set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:22:eq:additive-threshold}
 \mathcal A_{k,d}(\varepsilon)=
 \frac{a}{\varepsilon}+\frac{J}{a}
 +\frac{J\varepsilon^{2d-3}}{a^{2d-2}}
 +\sum_{t=2}^k\frac{\Delta_t\varepsilon^{t-1}}{a^t}.
\end{equation}

\begin{corollary}[A threshold with the sharp leading scale]\label{gsr:en:22:cor:sharpscale}
If $p>4d$ is prime and $p\ge\mathcal A_{k,d}(\varepsilon)$, then
$\delta_{k,d}(p)\le\varepsilon$. For fixed $k,d$,
\[
 \mathcal A_{k,d}(\varepsilon)=
 \frac{k+C_d}{\varepsilon}
       +\frac{\Bal_{k,d}}{k+C_d}+O_{k,d}(\varepsilon).
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:22:thm:filtration-bound} gives
\[
 p\delta_{k,d}(p)\le a+\frac Jp+\frac J{p^{2d-2}}
                               +\sum_{t=2}^k\frac{\Delta_t}{p^t}.
\]
Since $p\ge a/\varepsilon$, replace $1/p$ on the right by
$\varepsilon/a$. The resulting right side is exactly
$\varepsilon\mathcal A_{k,d}(\varepsilon)$, at most
$\varepsilon p$. The asymptotic expansion follows from $d\ge2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{At Lemma~15.5 there is no gain at leading order} (checked at the write). There the scale is $\varepsilon=\lambda=(\alpha\eta/4)^{E_k}\beta^{15}$, astronomically small, so a threshold is judged by its leading term in $1/\lambda$. Source~18's Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:18:deg:cor-selection} asks for $\lambda p\ge k+2{,}585{,}445$, i.e.\ $p\ge(k+C_8+1)/\lambda$, or, by its quadratic form \eqref{gsr:en:18:deg:eq-selection-quadratic}, $p\ge(k+C_8)/\lambda+(18/17)J_k/(k+C_8)+o(1)$. The threshold $\mathcal A_{k,8}(\lambda)=(k+C_8)/\lambda+\Bal_{k,8}/(k+C_8)+O(\lambda)$ of this corollary has the same leading term; its lower-order term is smaller, because $\Bal_{k,8}$ is polynomial in $k$ while source~18's $J_k$ grows like $3^{2^{k+4}}$, but that term is negligible against $1/\lambda$. The equal-allocation threshold \eqref{gsr:en:22:eq:threshold} is worse: $\mathcal P_{k,8}(\lambda)\ge(k+1)(k+C_8)/\lambda$, larger by the factor $k+1$. So the sentence below that Lemma~15.4 ``can therefore be replaced, for that purpose, by the concrete condition $p>\mathcal P_{k,8}(\varepsilon)$'' is correct, and the replacement is weaker than source~18's at leading order; the text says only that the equal-budget threshold ``is not claimed to dominate every earlier optimized threshold''. The finite bound of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:22:thm:filtration-bound} at moderate $p$ is where this section improves on source~18.
\end{writenote}

Either sufficient condition may be used. More precisely, the complete
right side of \eqref{gsr:en:22:eq:main-degeneracy} is uniformly no larger than the
earlier bound that assigns $Q_1(p)$ to every nonparity class: all the
tail weights are at most $Q_1(p)$, their profile differences sum to
$\Uprof_k-\Uprof_1$, and $J\le\Uprof_1-\Uprof_0$.
The convenient equal-budget threshold \eqref{gsr:en:22:eq:threshold} by itself
is not claimed to dominate every earlier optimized threshold.

In Gowers' Lemma~15.5, and in the corrected transcription, the random
selection step produces a scale
\[
 \varepsilon=
 (\alpha\eta/4)^{\,2^{\,2^{k+4}+k+3}}\beta^{15},
 \qquad 0<\alpha,\eta,\beta\le1.
\]
The use of Lemma~15.4 at that step is to ensure that at most
$\varepsilon p^{17k+15}$ eight-arrangements are degenerate. It can
therefore be replaced, for that purpose, by the concrete condition
\[
 p>\mathcal P_{k,8}(\varepsilon).
\]
This changes only the exceptional-set absorption requirement. All other
hypotheses of the selection lemma remain in force. In particular it does
not establish the downstream partition and inverse-theorem estimates
needed to state a new bound for Szemer\'edi's theorem. The substantial
point is that high-degree certificate counts enter through roots of
orders $t+1$, instead of all being charged through a square root or a
single worst-case term.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The exceptional two-cube case: a signed-coordinate arrangement\srctag{22}}]{The exceptional two-cube case: a signed-coordinate arrangement}\label{gsr:en:22:sec:d5}
\srcnote{22}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:en:22:sec:d1-new}

The assumption $d\ge2$ in the codimension-two bound for nonparity
certificates cannot be discarded: when $d=1$, the vertical constraint is
$r_1=r_2$, so the vertical equations supply no independent information.
Nevertheless the first-order count can be determined exactly.

\begin{theorem}[Sharp first-order degeneracy for two cubes]\label{gsr:en:22:thm:twocube}
Let $k\ge1$ and let $p>\max\{3,2k+1\}$ be prime.  Define
\[
 L_k(p)=1-(1-p^{-1})^k\prod_{i=1}^k\left(1-\frac{2i+1}{p}\right),
 \qquad
 R_k=\frac12\left(3^{2^k}-(2k^2+4k+3)\right)^2.
\]
For the proportion $\delta_{k,1}(p)$ of degenerate $1$-arrangements,
\[
 L_k(p)\le\delta_{k,1}(p)
 \le L_k(p)+(1-p^{-1})^kR_kp^{-2}.
\]
Consequently
\[
 \delta_{k,1}(p)=\frac{k^2+3k}{p}+O_k(p^{-2}).
\]
For $k=1$ the error term in the finite inequality is zero, and hence
$\delta_{1,1}(p)=4p^{-1}-3p^{-2}$ for every prime $p\ge5$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The proportion of arrangements having a zero side is exactly
$1-(1-p^{-1})^k$, and every such arrangement is degenerate.  Condition
on nonzero sides, write $z_i^j=y_i^j/h_i$, and set
$t_i=z_i^1-z_i^2$.
The variables $t_1,\ldots,t_k$ are independent and uniform in
$\mathbb F_p$.  For a slice coefficient pattern
$\eta:\{0,1\}^k\to\{-1,0,1\}$, put
\[
 F_\eta(X)=\sum_{\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^k}
            \eta(\epsilon)\prod_{i=1}^k(X_i+\epsilon_i).
\]
The map $\eta\mapsto F_\eta$ is an invertible linear transformation:
in one coordinate its basis is $X,X+1$, and the general transform is
the tensor product of these invertible two-dimensional transforms.
Comparing coefficients of $X_{[k]\setminus A}$ shows that all the
horizontal moment equations are equivalent to
\[
 F_{\eta_1}(X+t)+F_{\eta_2}(X)=0.
 \tag{D1.1}
\]
The vertical equations duplicate them because $r_1=r_2$.

We first describe the solution set of (D1.1) for fixed patterns.
For any multiaffine polynomial $F$, let
\[
 D_u=\sum_i u_i\frac{\partial}{\partial X_i}.
\]
Since $\deg F\le k<p$, Taylor's identity gives
$F(X+u)=\exp(D_u)F(X)$.  On the space of polynomials of degree at most
$k$, the operator $D_u$ is nilpotent.  Therefore
\[
 \exp(D_u)-1
 =D_u\left(1+D_u/2!+\cdots+D_u^{k-1}/k!\right),
\]
and the parenthesized operator is invertible.  It follows that the
translation stabilizer of $F$ is the linear subspace
\[
 \operatorname{Stab}(F)
 =\{u:F(X+u)=F(X)\}
 =\{u:D_uF=0\}.
 \tag{D1.2}
\]
If (D1.1) has one solution, all its solutions form a coset of this
subspace.  Its codimension is
\[
 \dim_{\mathbb F_p}\operatorname{span}
       \{\partial_1F,\ldots,\partial_kF\}.
 \tag{D1.3}
\]

If the dimension in (D1.3) is one, write $\partial_iF=a_iG$ for a
nonzero polynomial $G$.  When $a_i\ne0$, multilinearity implies that
$G$ is independent of $X_i$.  When $a_i=0$, $F$ is independent of
$X_i$, and hence so is $G$.  Thus $G$ is constant and $F$ is affine.
In particular, every nonaffine $F$ has a stabilizer of codimension at
least two.  For each pair of nonaffine slice patterns, (D1.1) consequently
has at most $p^{k-2}$ solutions.

It remains to determine the hypersurfaces supplied by affine $F$.
Write $\pi(\epsilon)=(-1)^{\sum_i\epsilon_i}$ and
$\eta(\epsilon)=\pi(\epsilon)v(\epsilon)$.  The polynomial $F_\eta$
is affine if and only if the unique multilinear representation of
$v$ is affine: direct expansion gives
$F_\eta(X)=(-1)^k\sum_Ta_T\prod_{i\in T}(X_i+1)$ when
$v(\epsilon)=\sum_Ta_T\prod_{i\in T}\epsilon_i$, and substitution
$X_i\mapsto X_i+1$ preserves total degree.  More explicitly, if
\[
 v(\epsilon)=c+\sum_i b_i\epsilon_i,
\]
then
\[
 F_\eta(X)=(-1)^k
        \left(c+\sum_i b_i(X_i+1)\right).
 \tag{D1.4}
\]
For $p\ge5$, an affine Boolean function taking values only in
$\{-1,0,1\}$ has one of the following forms:
\begin{itemize}
\item a constant (three choices);
\item one nonzero slope $b_i=\pm1$, with two admissible intercepts;
\item one nonzero slope $b_i=\pm2$, with one admissible intercept;
\item two nonzero slopes $b_i,b_j\in\{-1,1\}$, with one admissible
      intercept.
\end{itemize}
Indeed, after fixing a nonzero slope $a$, the values on the other
coordinates must lie in
$S\cap(S-a)$, where $S=\{-1,0,1\}$.  This set has at most two
elements, and has two only when $a=\pm1$.  An affine Boolean function
with two values can depend on at most one coordinate in odd
characteristic: otherwise the four values
$x,x+b,x+c,x+b+c$, with $b,c\ne0$, force $b=c$ and $2b=0$.
The displayed list and its intercept counts follow.  Thus the number
of affine slice patterns is
\[
 f_k=3+6k+4\binom{k}{2}=2k^2+4k+3.
 \tag{D1.5}
\]

In (D1.1), replace $\eta_2$ by its negative, which is another allowed
pattern.  Formula (D1.4) shows that a successful pair must have the
same slopes $b_i$ and satisfy
$\sum_i b_it_i=c_2-c_1$.  Constant polynomials give only multiples
of the universal certificate.  The remaining cases give exactly
the following distinct affine hyperplanes:
\[
 t_i=0,1,-1\quad(1\le i\le k),\qquad
 t_i-t_j=0,\quad t_i+t_j=0\quad(i<j).
 \tag{D1.6}
\]
Each equation is realized by allowed patterns.  A vector outside all
these hyperplanes has nonzero coordinates, none equal to $\pm1$,
and its coordinates belong to distinct unordered sign pairs.
There are $p-3$ choices for $t_1$, $p-5$ for $t_2$, and in general
$p-(2i+1)$ for $t_i$.  Hence the number outside (D1.6) is exactly
\[
 \prod_{i=1}^k(p-2i-1).
 \tag{D1.7}
\]

There are $3^{2^k}-f_k$ nonaffine slice patterns.  Translation
preserves degree, so any successful pair involving a nonaffine slice
has two nonaffine slices.  Simultaneously negating both slices gives
the same solution set and has no fixed point on these pairs.
There are therefore at most $R_k$ such solution sets.  Applying the
codimension-two bound to each proves the asserted finite upper bound;
retaining only (D1.6) and the zero-side loci proves the lower bound.
Finally, the linear coefficient of the complement probability is
\[
 k+\sum_{i=1}^k(2i+1)=k^2+3k.
\]
For $k=1$ every polynomial $F_\eta$ is affine, so $R_1=0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Answers source~18's question on $d=1$ in its leading coefficient} (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:degeneracy}); source~18 set the case aside after its Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:18:deg:prop-single-sharp}. Source~27's Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:27:prop:d1} is the case $k=1$, proved independently. The intake computed $\delta_{k,1}(p)$ from the full definition and found it equal to $L_k(p)$ for $k=2$ at $p=7,11,13,17,19,23$ and for $k=3$ at $p=11,13$, beyond this source's checks; that is evidence for its question on exactness (Research question~\ref{gsr:fz:22:sec:d12}.2 here), not a proof.
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 47--53]
\emph{Sharpened by source~49} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:twocube}): rank-two certificates add no locus outside the signed-coordinate arrangement, so $0\le\delta_{k,1}(p)-L_k(p)\le(1-p^{-1})^kM_k^2/(2p^3)$ and the coefficient of $p^{-2}$ is $-k(3k^3+14k^2+15k-14)/6$ (its Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:49:deg:finite}); $\delta_{k,1}=L_k$ exactly for $k\le3$ at every odd prime (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:49:deg:exact12}, Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:49:deg:exact3}), which answers this source's exactness question for $k\le3$ (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:degenstructure}).
\end{writenote}

\paragraph{Connection with the balanced degree-one count.}
The Laurent-polynomial calculation has a particularly simple
$q=2$ specialization:
\[
 \operatorname{CT}F_k^2=2k^2+8k+9,
 \qquad \operatorname{CT}B_k^2=2k+4.
\]
Thus the number of balanced classes of degree at most one is
$(k+1)^2$.  Removing the one nonconstant degree-zero class gives
$k^2+2k=3k+2\binom{k}{2}$ classes of degree exactly one.
In the present two-cube setting these classes give precisely the
distinct hypersurfaces in (D1.6).  The $k$ zero-side hypersurfaces
account for the remaining $k$ in the coefficient $k^2+3k$.

\paragraph{Scope.}
The theorem determines the optimal leading coefficient for the
two-cube case omitted from the earlier $d\ge2$ argument.  It does
not assert that all higher-codimension degeneracy is contained in
(D1.6), and its explicit remainder is only a union bound.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Arrangements and their moment relations\srctag{25}}]{Arrangements and their moment relations}\label{gsr:en:25:sec:d2}
\srcnote{25}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:en:25:sec:arrangements}

Put $m=2d$ and
\[
 w=(\underbrace{1,\ldots,1}_{d},
       \underbrace{-1,\ldots,-1}_{d}),\qquad
 \W=w^\perp\subseteq\F_q^m.
\]
An arrangement is specified by
\[
 h=(h_1,\ldots,h_k)\in\F_q^k,\quad
 x=(x_{ji})_{1\le j\le m,\,1\le i\le k},\quad r\in\W,
\]
and its vertices are
\begin{equation}
 \rho(\eps,j)=(x_{j1}+\eps_1h_1,\ldots,
 x_{jk}+\eps_kh_k,r_j),\qquad \eps\in\{-1,1\}^k.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:vertices}
\end{equation}
The relation $r\in\W$ is $r_1+\cdots+r_d=r_{d+1}+\cdots+r_{2d}$.
There are $q^k q^{2dk}q^{2d-1}=q^D$ arrangements.
The usual vertices $y_{ji}+e_iH_i$, $e_i\in\{0,1\}$, are obtained by
$x_{ji}=y_{ji}+H_i/2$ and $h_i=H_i/2$.  This is a bijection of parameter
spaces, not an approximation or a restriction.

Write $[k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}$ and
$\pi(\eps)=\prod_{i=1}^k\eps_i$.  The distinguished coefficient pattern is
\begin{equation}
 \eta_0(\eps,j)=w_j\pi(\eps).
\end{equation}
The Boolean convention $(-1)^{\sum e_i}$ differs by the harmless global
factor $(-1)^k$.

For a ternary pattern
$\eta:\{-1,1\}^k\times[m]\to\{-1,0,1\}\subset\F_q$ define
\begin{align}
 M_A(\eta)&=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\sum_{\eps}
 \eta(\eps,j)\prod_{i\in A}(x_{ji}+\eps_i h_i),\\
 M_{A,r}(\eta)&=\sum_{j=1}^{m}r_j\sum_{\eps}
 \eta(\eps,j)\prod_{i\in A}(x_{ji}+\eps_i h_i),
 \qquad A\subseteq[k].
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:moments}
\end{align}
These are exactly all coordinate-monomial moments in $k+1$ variables.
In particular, $A=\varnothing$ is included.

\begin{definition}
An arrangement is \emph{degenerate} if some ternary $\eta$ outside the
one-dimensional space $\F_q\eta_0$ satisfies
$M_A(\eta)=M_{A,r}(\eta)=0$ for every $A\subseteq[k]$.
Such an $\eta$ is a witness.
A pattern is \emph{block-parity} if
$\eta(\eps,j)=a_j\pi(\eps)$ for every $j$.
\end{definition}

Orthogonality on the sign cube shows that the block moment of $\pi$ is
zero unless $A=[k]$, and is then $2^k\prod_i h_i$.
Thus $\eta_0$ annihilates all moments because both $\sum_j w_j=0$ and
$\sum_jw_jr_j=0$.  Since the values of $\eta_0$ are $\pm1$, its only
ternary scalar multiples are $0,\eta_0,-\eta_0$.

\begin{lemma}[Coincidences and zero sides]
\label{gsr:en:25:lem:collisions}
Every arrangement with a zero sidelength is degenerate.  Every
nondegenerate arrangement has distinct labelled vertices.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If two labelled vertices coincide, put coefficient $1$ at one and $-1$
at the other, and zero elsewhere.  Every monomial moment cancels.
This pattern cannot be a nonzero scalar multiple of $\eta_0$, whose
support consists of all $n\ge8$ labels.  If $h_i=0$, the vertices within
one block whose signs differ only at $i$ coincide, so the first assertion
is a special case of the second argument.
\end{proof}

A function $\phi:B\to\F_q$ \emph{respects} an arrangement in $B$ if
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{j,\eps}w_j\pi(\eps)\phi(\rho(\eps,j))=0.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:respected}
\end{equation}
We will need an elementary upper bound for the total number of
arrangements contained in an arbitrary set.

\begin{lemma}[Density cap]
\label{gsr:en:25:lem:densitycap}
If $B\subseteq\F_q^{k+1}$ has size $\beta q^{k+1}$, then it contains at
most $\beta^{2d-1}q^D$ labelled $d$-arrangements.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose $h$, the all-minus vertex of each of the first $2d-1$ blocks,
and the $k$ spatial coordinates of the all-minus vertex of the last
block.  The cross-section relation determines the remaining coordinate
of the last block.  These choices determine the entire arrangement.
For an arrangement in $B$, the first $2d-1$ selected vertices must be in
$B$.  There are at most
$q^k\cardtwentyfive B^{2d-1}q^k=\beta^{2d-1}q^D$ choices.  Ignoring the other
containment requirements only increases this upper bound.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Minimal Walsh layers give independent linear equations\srctag{25}}]{Minimal Walsh layers give independent linear equations}\label{gsr:en:25:sec:d3}
\srcnote{25}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:en:25:sec:walsh}

For $S\subseteq[k]$, let $\chi_S(\eps)=\prod_{i\in S}\eps_i$ and put
\begin{equation}
 c_{j,S}=2^{-k}\sum_\eps\eta(\eps,j)\chi_S(\eps).
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:walsh}
\end{equation}
Here $2^{-k}$ denotes inversion in the field.  Orthogonality gives
\begin{equation}
 \sum_\eps\chi_S(\eps)\chi_T(\eps)
 =\begin{cases}2^k&S=T,\\0&S\ne T,\end{cases}
 \qquad
 \eta(\eps,j)=\sum_{S\subseteq[k]}c_{j,S}\chi_S(\eps).
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:inversion}
\end{equation}
Indeed, a coordinate in $S\mathbin\triangle T$ makes the sum cancel in
pairs; otherwise every summand is one.  This proves inversion as well.

Use $h_S=\prod_{i\in S}h_i$ and
$x_{j,S}=\prod_{i\in S}x_{ji}$.  Expanding the product in a block moment
and applying \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:walsh} gives
\begin{equation}
 \sum_\eps\eta(\eps,j)\prod_{i\in A}(x_{ji}+\eps_i h_i)
 =2^k\sum_{S\subseteq A}c_{j,S}h_Sx_{j,A\setminus S}.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:expansion}
\end{equation}
This identity is valid for arbitrary field-valued patterns, not only
ternary ones.

\begin{lemma}[Minimal-layer linearization]
\label{gsr:en:25:lem:layer}
Suppose $h_i\ne0$ for every $i$.  For a nonzero pattern let
\[
 s=\min\{\cardtwentyfive S:c_{j,S}\ne0\text{ for some }j\}.
\]
If $s<k$, then the equations $M_A(\eta)=0$ with $\cardtwentyfive A=s+1$ include
$k-s$ independent affine-linear equations in the $2dk$ base coordinates.
For every fixed $r$, the probability over uniform $x$ that all moments
vanish is therefore at most $q^{-(k-s)}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
All coefficients of degree below $s$ vanish, so
\eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:expansion}, for $\cardtwentyfive A=s+1$, contains only terms linear in
$x$ and constant terms.  Choose $j_0,S_0$ with $\cardtwentyfive{S_0}=s$ and
$c_{j_0,S_0}\ne0$.  For each $i\notin S_0$, use the equation indexed by
$A_i=S_0\cup\{i\}$, and use $x_{j_0i}$ as its pivot variable.
The coefficient of this variable is
$2^kc_{j_0,S_0}h_{S_0}\ne0$.  If $i'\notin S_0$ and $i'\ne i$,
then $i'\notin A_i$, so $x_{j_0i'}$ does not occur in that equation.
The indicated square minor is diagonal and nonsingular.

After every other base coordinate has been fixed, these $k-s$ equations
determine the pivot coordinates uniquely.  They therefore have exactly
$q^{2dk-(k-s)}$ simultaneous solutions; imposing the remaining moment
equations can only reduce this number.  No polynomial zero-counting
estimate is needed.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Gowers's Lemma 15.3 is sharp for a single arbitrary multilinear polynomial:
a product of $k$ coordinates can vanish on approximately $k/q$ of the
space.  Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:25:lem:layer} does not contradict that fact.  It exploits
the simultaneous moment system, in which a lowest nonzero Walsh layer
provides specially chosen \emph{linear} equations.  It strengthens the
use of Lemma 15.3 inside the arrangement argument, not the original fibre
bound without extra hypotheses.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Non-parity witnesses have codimension at least two\srctag{25}}]{Non-parity witnesses have codimension at least two}\label{gsr:en:25:sec:d4}
\srcnote{25}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:en:25:sec:witnesses}

Fix nonzero $h$ and a ternary pattern that is not block-parity.  Its
minimal layer has $s\le k-1$.  If $s\le k-2$, Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:25:lem:layer}
already gives a $q^{-2}$ bound, uniformly in the cross-sections.  Only
$s=k-1$ needs a second argument.

In this remaining case write
\begin{equation}
 \eta(\eps,j)=a_j\pi(\eps)
       +\sum_{i=1}^k b_{ji}\pi(\eps)\eps_i,
 \qquad
 a_j=c_{j,[k]},\quad b_{ji}=c_{j,[k]\setminus\{i\}}.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:toplayers}
\end{equation}
At least one vector $b_i=(b_{1i},\ldots,b_{mi})$ is nonzero.  The
coefficients $a_j,b_{ji}$ are field elements; they need not be ternary.
The moments indexed by $[k]\setminus\{i\}$ imply
\begin{equation}
 \sum_jb_{ji}=0,\qquad b_i\cdot r=0\quad(1\le i\le k).
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:lowerconstraints}
\end{equation}
After division by $2^kh_{[k]}$, the two top moments become
\begin{align}
 \sum_{j,i}b_{ji}\frac{x_{ji}}{h_i}+\sum_ja_j&=0,
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:top1}\\
 \sum_{j,i}r_jb_{ji}\frac{x_{ji}}{h_i}+\sum_jr_ja_j&=0.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:top2}
\end{align}
These equations also display why keeping moments containing the final
coordinate is useful.

\begin{theorem}[Sharp single-witness bound]
\label{gsr:en:25:thm:single}
Let $d\ge2$, $k\ge1$, and let the field have odd characteristic.
For each fixed nonzero sidelength vector and each non-block-parity
ternary pattern, uniform $r\in\W$ and uniform $x$ satisfy all moment
equations with probability at most
\begin{equation}
 e_d(q)=q^{-2}+(q-1)q^{-2d}.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:single}
\end{equation}
This bound is attained, for every $k$, by
\begin{equation}
 \eta(\eps,j)=w_j\pi(\eps)\eps_{i_0}
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:sharpwitness}
\end{equation}
for any fixed $i_0\in[k]$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The case $s\le k-2$ follows from Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:25:lem:layer}.  Suppose $s=k-1$.
If a constant constraint in \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:lowerconstraints} fails, there are
no solutions.  Otherwise put
\[
 e=\dim\spanof(w,b_1,\ldots,b_k)-1.
\]
When $e\ge1$, the equations $b_i\cdot r=0$ cut out a subspace of
codimension $e$ in $\W$.  Their probability is $q^{-e}$.  For every
admissible $r$, equation \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:top1} is a nonconstant affine-linear
equation in $x$, of probability $q^{-1}$.  Thus the simultaneous
probability is at most $q^{-e-1}\le q^{-2}$.

When $e=0$, write $b_i=t_iw$, where some $t_i\ne0$.  The cross-section
constraints are automatic.  The coefficient rows of \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:top1}
and \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:top2} are linearly dependent exactly when all $r_j$ are
equal: for an $i$ with $t_i\ne0$, comparison of the coefficients of
$x_{ji}$ forces $r_j$ to be the same scalar for every $j$.  Outside that
one-dimensional diagonal subspace of $\W$, the two equations have
independent rows and hence exactly $q^{2dk-2}$ solutions for any right
hand sides.  On the diagonal they have at most $q^{2dk-1}$ solutions.
The diagonal occupies a proportion $q^{-(2d-2)}$ of $\W$.  Therefore the
probability is at most
\[
 (1-q^{-(2d-2)})q^{-2}+q^{-(2d-2)}q^{-1}
 =q^{-2}+(q-1)q^{-2d}.
\]

For \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:sharpwitness}, we have $a_j=0$, $b_{i_0}=w$, and $b_i=0$
for $i\ne i_0$.  All nontrivial conditions are exactly
\[
 \sum_jw_jx_{j i_0}=0,\qquad
 \sum_jw_jr_jx_{j i_0}=0.
\]
They have rank two off the diagonal and rank one on it, and they are
always consistent.  Thus equality holds in the displayed count.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Credit.} First printed as source~18's Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:18:deg:prop-single-sharp} (with the same witness up to the Boolean--sign convention); also source~22's Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:22:lem:rank} at degree one and source~27's Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:27:prop:perclass} (every characteristic).
\end{writenote}

\begin{example}[The restriction $d\ge2$ is necessary]
For $d=1$, the cross-section relation forces $r_1=r_2$.
The same witness \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:sharpwitness} gives just
$x_{1i_0}=x_{2i_0}$, a probability $q^{-1}$ event.  Consequently a
blanket codimension-two assertion for non-parity witnesses is false
for $d=1$.  This is a structural obstruction, not a weakness of the
proof.  The formula in \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:single} itself becomes $q^{-1}$ in
this case.
\end{example}

For the final count it is useful to exclude a set of cross-sections that
will already be counted as degenerate.

\begin{lemma}[Removing the diagonal exception]
\label{gsr:en:25:lem:regularwitness}
Let $\mathcal R\subseteq\W$ omit every constant vector.  Under the
hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:25:thm:single}, for each fixed non-parity pattern
and each fixed nonzero $h$,
\begin{equation}
 \Prob_{r\in\W,x}\bigl(r\in\mathcal R
 \text{ and all moments vanish}\bigr)\le q^{-2}.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:regularjoint}
\end{equation}
For the witness \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:sharpwitness}, equality holds with the right
side replaced by $(\cardtwentyfive{\mathcal R}/\cardtwentyfive\W)q^{-2}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $s\le k-2$ and for $e\ge1$, the corresponding bounds in the previous
proof were already $q^{-2}$.  For $e=0$, the only rank-one exception
was the diagonal, now excluded.  The final assertion follows from the
two independent homogeneous equations for the sharp witness.
\end{proof}

Notice the normalization: \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:regularjoint} is a \emph{joint}
probability with $r$ uniform in all of $\W$.  Conditioning $r$ to belong
to $\mathcal R$ requires division by $\cardtwentyfive{\mathcal R}/\cardtwentyfive\W$.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The cross-section hyperplanes and their exact number\srctag{25}}]{The cross-section hyperplanes and their exact number}\label{gsr:en:25:sec:d5}
\srcnote{25}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:en:25:sec:hyperplanes}

Suppose all sidelengths are nonzero and $\eta$ is block-parity,
$\eta(\eps,j)=a_j\pi(\eps)$.  Since the pattern is ternary, every
$a_j$ belongs to $\{-1,0,1\}$.  Its moment conditions reduce exactly to
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{j=1}^{m}a_j=0,\qquad a\cdot r=0.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:parityconditions}
\end{equation}
The first equality follows from the top spatial moment, and the second
from the top moment including the last coordinate.  All other moments
vanish identically.  The condition $p>2d$ makes the first equality
in the field equivalent to the integer equality: its integer sum has
absolute value at most $2d$.

Exclude $a=0,w,-w$, which give the distinguished scalar multiples.
Every remaining balanced ternary vector defines a hyperplane
\begin{equation}
 H_a=\{r\in\W:a\cdot r=0\}.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:crosshyperplane}
\end{equation}
Let $\Hh_d$ be the set of \emph{distinct} such hyperplanes.
Each contains the diagonal of constant cross-sections, since $\sum a_j=0$.

\begin{theorem}[Projective enumeration]
\label{gsr:en:25:thm:hyperplanes}
For $d\ge1$ and $p>\max(3,2d)$,
\[
 \cardtwentyfive{\Hh_d}=H_d
 =\frac{T_{2d}-2\binom{2d}{d}+1}{2}.
\]
For $d\ge2$, this family is nonempty.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Two nonzero restrictions $a|_\W$ and $a'|_\W$ have the same kernel
exactly when
\begin{equation}
 a'=\lambda a+\mu w,\qquad \lambda\ne0.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:equivalence}
\end{equation}
This is the elementary fact that two nonzero linear forms with the same
kernel are proportional, together with $\W^\perp=\F_qw$.
Set $z_j=w_ja_j$.  Then $z\in\{-1,0,1\}^{2d}$,
$\sum_jw_jz_j=0$, and \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:equivalence} becomes
\begin{equation}
 z'=\lambda z+\mu\ind.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:affineclasses}
\end{equation}
We must count nonconstant balanced ternary vectors modulo affine changes
of their values.

There are $T_{2d}$ balanced vectors: multiplying their coordinates by
$w_j$ bijects them with the integer-balanced vectors $a$ in
\eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:parityconditions}.  Exactly three are constant, and they
correspond to $a=0,w,-w$.

First suppose $z$ uses exactly two values $u<v$.  If $S$ is the set of
coordinates at the larger value, then
\[
 \sum_jw_jz_j=(v-u)\sum_{j\in S}w_j.
\]
It vanishes exactly when $S$ contains equally many coordinates from the
first and second halves.  The number of nonempty proper such subsets is
\begin{equation}
 B_d=\sum_{t=0}^d\binom dt^2-2=\binom{2d}{d}-2.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:balancedsubsets}
\end{equation}
The binomial identity follows by counting $d$-element subsets of two
disjoint $d$-element sets, according to the number chosen from the first.
There are three choices of a two-element value set, hence $3B_d$ vectors
of this type.  Each affine class consists of six vectors: three choices
of value set and the two choices of which part gets the larger value.
Thus there are $B_d/2$ two-value classes.

If $z$ uses all three values, an affine change preserving ternarity
must permute $\{-1,0,1\}$.  Summing the three images gives $3\mu=0$;
as $p>3$, we have $\mu=0$.  The image of $1$ now forces
$\lambda=1$ or $-1$.  Consequently every three-value class consists
exactly of $z$ and $-z$.  No invertible affine change can alter the
number of distinct values.  The three-value classes therefore number
$(T_{2d}-3-3B_d)/2$.  Adding the two contributions gives
\[
 \frac{B_d}{2}+\frac{T_{2d}-3-3B_d}{2}
 =\frac{T_{2d}-2\binom{2d}{d}+1}{2}.
\]
For $d\ge2$, for example $a=(1,-1,0,\ldots,0)$ is balanced and not a
multiple of $w$, so at least one hyperplane occurs.
\end{proof}

The intake counted the distinct kernels by rank tests and found $0$, $4$, $51$ for $d=1,2,3$ over $\F_{101}$, and $57$ for $d=3$ over $\F_5$, as Example~\ref{gsr:en:25:ex:smallchar} and source~27's Example~\ref{gsr:en:27:ex:char} say.
\end{writenote}

\subsection{An explicit canonical representative}
Eliminate the last cross-section coordinate using
$r_m=\sum_{i<m}w_ir_i$.  The restricted normal of $H_a$ is
\begin{equation}
 v(a)=(a_i+a_mw_i)_{i<m}.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:normal}
\end{equation}
Over the rationals one divides this nonzero integer vector by the gcd
of its entries and chooses its first nonzero entry positive.  Over a
prime field one divides by its first nonzero entry.  These are the two
independent representations used in the supplied enumeration check.
The closed formula does not rely on either computation.

\begin{example}[Why a large field cardinality is not enough]
\label{gsr:en:25:ex:smallchar}
For $d=3$ in characteristic $5$, the integer sums $\pm5$ also vanish in
the field.  They arise from five coefficients equal to $1$ and one zero,
or from their negatives.  There are twelve such vectors.  Each gives a
three-value $z=w\cdot a$, so the preceding affine classification groups
them only in opposite pairs; they cannot coincide with integer-balanced
classes.  There are therefore six extra hyperplanes:
\[
 \cardtwentyfive{\Hh_3(\F_5)}=57\ne51.
\]
The same phenomenon persists in every extension field of characteristic
$5$.  The hypothesis is on the characteristic, not merely on $q$.
\end{example}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The global count and the geometry of the exceptional set\srctag{25}}]{The global count and the geometry of the exceptional set}\label{gsr:en:25:sec:d6}
\srcnote{25}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:en:25:sec:global}

Let
\[
 \mathcal V_d=\bigcup_{H\in\Hh_d}H\subseteq\W,\qquad
 v_d(q)=\frac{\cardtwentyfive{\mathcal V_d}}{q^{2d-1}}.
\]
Call an arrangement \emph{base-exceptional} if some $h_i=0$ or if
$r\in\mathcal V_d$.  The word ``base'' here refers to the explicitly
classified exception set, not to the spatial base coordinates $x$.
The probability of this event is exactly
\begin{equation}
 b_{k,d}(q)=1-(1-q^{-1})^k(1-v_d(q)).
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:baseline}
\end{equation}
Every base-exceptional arrangement is degenerate.  For zero sides this
is Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:25:lem:collisions}; for the cross-section part, use the
corresponding block-parity witness, whose moment identities hold for all
spatial bases and all sidelengths.

\begin{theorem}[Residual count after all hypersurfaces are removed]
\label{gsr:en:25:thm:residual}
Under \eqref{gsr:fm:25:eq:parameters},
\begin{equation}
 b_{k,d}(q)+(1-b_{k,d}(q))q^{-2}
 \ \le\ \frac{Z_{k,d}(q)}{q^D}
 \ \le\ b_{k,d}(q)+(1-q^{-1})^kU_{k,d}q^{-2}.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:residual}
\end{equation}
In particular, the residual degeneracy outside the classified
hyperplanes is genuinely of order $q^{-2}$ for fixed $k,d$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Outside the base-exceptional set, all sides are nonzero and no
block-parity witness is available.  There are $3^n$ ternary patterns in
all, and precisely $3^{2d}$ block-parity patterns.  The remaining
patterns come in opposite pairs defining identical vanishing events.
Thus there are $U_{k,d}$ sign classes to consider.

The regular cross-section set $\W\setminus\mathcal V_d$ omits the
constant vectors, since $\Hh_d$ is nonempty and all its hyperplanes
contain them.  For each non-parity sign class,
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:25:lem:regularwitness} bounds the joint probability of vanishing
and regular cross-sections by $q^{-2}$ for every nonzero $h$.  Summing
these bounds and multiplying by $(1-q^{-1})^k$ proves the upper bound.
This is a union bound, so overlaps cause no problem.

For the lower bound fix one witness \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:sharpwitness}.  At every
nonzero $h$ and every regular $r$, its two equations have rank two and
have exactly probability $q^{-2}$ over $x$.  All these configurations
are degenerate and none is base-exceptional.  Their probability is
$(1-b_{k,d}(q))q^{-2}$, proving the lower bound.

Finally $v_d(q)\le H_d/q$, so $b_{k,d}(q)=O_{k,d}(q^{-1})$.
The extra term on the lower side is consequently
$q^{-2}+O_{k,d}(q^{-3})$, whereas the extra term on the upper side is
$O_{k,d}(q^{-2})$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of the counting part of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:25:thm:main}]
The base-exceptional set is the union of $L_{k,d}=k+H_d$ distinct linear
hyperplanes in the $D$-dimensional parameter space
$\F_q^k\times\F_q^{2dk}\times\W$.
Each hyperplane has probability $q^{-1}$, and each pair of distinct
hyperplanes has intersection probability $q^{-2}$.  The union bound
and the first two terms of inclusion--exclusion give
\begin{equation}
 \frac{L_{k,d}}q-\frac{\binom{L_{k,d}}2}{q^2}
 \le b_{k,d}(q)\le\frac{L_{k,d}}q.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:bonferroni}
\end{equation}
The lower estimate may be negative for small $q$, which does not affect
its validity.  Combine \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:bonferroni} with
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:25:thm:residual}, and discard $(1-q^{-1})^k\le1$ on the upper
side.  Multiplication by $q^D$ proves \eqref{gsr:fm:25:eq:mainbounds}; division by
$q^{D-1}$ proves \eqref{gsr:fm:25:eq:limit}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Codimension-one components over an infinite field}
The codimension assertion is stronger than a finite counting heuristic,
so we give its geometric justification.  Work over an algebraically
closed field $K$ of characteristic zero or greater than $2d$.  The
ambient space is affine $D$-space after eliminating $r_m$.
For each of the finitely many ternary patterns, its moment-vanishing
locus is a closed algebraic set.  The degeneracy locus is the finite
union of these sets, with the three distinguished patterns excluded.

The zero-side hyperplanes and parity hyperplanes lie in this locus.
On the open set $h_1\cdots h_k\ne0$, a non-parity witness with
minimal layer $s\le k-2$ has at least two independent affine equations
with a nonsingular pivot minor.  Its dimension is at most $D-2$.
For $s=k-1$ and $e\ge1$, the cross-section equations give codimension
at least one and \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:top1} gives another independent condition in
spatial variables.  For $e=0$, the generic cross-section fibre has two
independent spatial equations; the exceptional diagonal has codimension
$2d-2$ in $\W$ and still has one nonconstant spatial equation.  Its total
codimension is at least $2d-1\ge3$.

Thus every non-parity witness has codimension at least two away from
the zero-side hyperplanes.  Taking a finite union cannot create a new
codimension-one component.  Conversely, each of the listed distinct
hyperplanes is irreducible of codimension one and is already contained
in the degeneracy locus.  This proves the remaining assertion of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:25:thm:main} without deriving geometry from point counts.

\subsection{The first nontrivial example}
For $d=2$, on $r_1+r_2=r_3+r_4$ the four hyperplanes can be written
\begin{equation}
 r_1=r_2,\qquad r_3=r_4,\qquad r_1=r_3,\qquad r_1=r_4.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:d2planes}
\end{equation}
Other balanced ternary equations give one of these or the defining
relation.  The four hyperplanes share the diagonal line; in the
quotient by that line, they are four distinct lines in a two-dimensional
space.  Their union has size $4(q^2-q)+q=4q^2-3q$, so
\begin{equation}
 v_2(q)=\frac4q-\frac3{q^2},\qquad
 b_{k,2}(q)=1-(1-q^{-1})^k(1-4q^{-1}+3q^{-2}).
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:d2baseline}
\end{equation}
For example, $b_{1,2}(q)=5q^{-1}-7q^{-2}+3q^{-3}$.
This is an exact count of the classified hyperplanes, not an assertion
that all degeneracies have been counted exactly.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Explicit ambient-size savings\srctag{25}}]{Explicit ambient-size savings}\label{gsr:en:25:sec:d7}
\srcnote{25}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:en:25:sec:cutoff}

Suppose a later argument can tolerate at most a fraction $\tau>0$ of
ambient arrangements being degenerate.  Gowers's bound
\eqref{gsr:fm:25:eq:gowers} gives the sufficient condition
$q\ge k3^n/\tau$.  The refined count instead gives the following.

\begin{corollary}[Two-scale sufficient cutoff]
\label{gsr:en:25:cor:cutoff}
Subject to \eqref{gsr:fm:25:eq:parameters}, the condition
\begin{equation}
 q\ge \max\left\{\frac{2L_{k,d}}{\tau},
                   \sqrt{\frac{2U_{k,d}}{\tau}}\right\}
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:cutoff}
\end{equation}
implies $Z_{k,d}(q)\le\tau q^D$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The first requirement makes $L_{k,d}/q\le\tau/2$ and the second makes
$U_{k,d}/q^2\le\tau/2$.  Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:25:thm:main}.
\end{proof}

The large ternary count now enters only through its square root, while
the first-order contribution uses the much smaller exact coefficient.
For extremely small $\tau$, the first term in \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:cutoff} can
dominate; thus it would be inaccurate to describe the entire threshold
as always a square-root improvement.
