\centering
\begin{tabular}{rrrrr}
\toprule
$k$ & $n=2^{k+4}$ & $\log_{10}(k3^n/\tau)$ &
$\log_{10}$ of \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:cutoff} & controlling term\\
\midrule
1 & 32  & 21.268 & 12.714 & first-order\\
2 & 64  & 36.837 & 18.268 & second-order\\
3 & 128 & 67.549 & 33.536 & second-order\\
4 & 256 & 128.745 & 64.072 & second-order\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Illustrative sufficient thresholds for $d=8$ and
$\tau=10^{-6}$, before rounding to a permissible field cardinality.
These are comparisons of proven upper-bound criteria, not measured
minimal field sizes.  Values are rounded to three decimals.}
\label{gsr:en:25:tab:cutoffs}
\end{table}

The tolerated fraction $\tau$ in the actual Riesz-product application
can be far smaller than $10^{-6}$, and the resulting sufficient field-size
criterion far larger than this illustration.  The next section supplies
its precise value instead of silently treating
``sufficiently large'' as a parameter-free condition.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A finite-field random-selection theorem with exact parameters\srctag{25}}]{A finite-field random-selection theorem with exact parameters}\label{gsr:en:25:sec:d8}
\srcnote{25}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:en:25:sec:selection}

We now generalize the selection step to arbitrary $d\ge2$ and finite
fields satisfying \eqref{gsr:fm:25:eq:parameters}.  The construction is the
Riesz-product idea of Gowers \cite[Section 15]{gowers}; the proof below
keeps exact survival probabilities and handles repeated labels explicitly.

Set
\begin{equation}
 a_n=2^{-n},\qquad
 b_n=2^{-n}(1+2^{1-n}),\qquad
 R_n=b_n/a_n=1+2^{1-n}.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:survival}
\end{equation}
Let $0<\alpha,\beta,\eta\le1$.  Define the integer
\begin{equation}
 t=\min\{u\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}:R_n^u\ge4/(\alpha\eta)\}
 =\left\lceil\frac{\log(4/(\alpha\eta))}{\log R_n}\right\rceil,
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:t}
\end{equation}
and let
\begin{equation}
 \tau=\frac{\alpha\eta}{4}\,\beta^{2d-1}b_n^t.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:tau}
\end{equation}
For numerical implementation the minimum characterization avoids any
rounding ambiguity at an integer logarithmic boundary.

\begin{theorem}[Explicit arrangement purification]
\label{gsr:en:25:thm:selection}
Let $B\subseteq\F_q^{k+1}$ have size $\beta q^{k+1}$, and let
$\phi:B\to\F_q$ respect at least
$\alpha\beta^{2d-1}q^D$ arrangements in $B$.  Suppose
\eqref{gsr:fm:25:eq:parameters} holds and
\begin{equation}
 \frac{L_{k,d}}q+\frac{U_{k,d}}{q^2}\le\tau.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:selectioncondition}
\end{equation}
Then a subset $B'\subseteq B$ exists which contains at least
\begin{equation}
 \frac\alpha2\,\beta^{2d-1}b_n^t q^D
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:retained}
\end{equation}
respected arrangements, and the number of its non-respected arrangements
is at most $\eta$ times its number of respected arrangements.
In particular, the proportion respected is at least $1/(1+\eta)\ge1-\eta$.
Condition \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:cutoff} with \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:tau} is a sufficient explicit
condition for \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:selectioncondition}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Against source~18 and the formal statement} (checked at the write). Source~18's Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:18:deg:cor-selection} treats $d=8$ over prime fields with the retention $(\alpha\eta/4)^{E_k}\beta^{15}$ of \file{lemma_15_5} (\file{Sections14\_15.lean}, line~414; \file{arrangementSelectionExponent}, line~409, is $E_k=2^{2^{k+4}+k+3}$); this theorem treats every $d\ge2$ and every finite field of characteristic $p>2d$ and keeps the exact number $t$ of factors. At $d=8$, $n=2^{k+4}$ and $E_k=n2^{n-1}$, so \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:Kasymptotic} says $K_n/E_k\to\log2$: the power-form retention $b_n(\alpha\eta/4)^{K_n}$ improves the leading factor of the exponent, not its form, at the cost of the prefactor $(\alpha/2)b_n$. Numerically $K_n/E_k=0.69315$ already for $k=1,2,3$. Not formalized; \file{lemma_15_5_holds} (\file{Proofs15Restriction.lean}, line~3086) proves the formal statement.
\end{writenote}

\subsection{One Riesz factor}
Choose a nontrivial additive character $\psi:\F_q\to\mathbb C$.
For example, choose a nonzero $\F_p$-linear functional
$\ell:\F_q\to\F_p$ and take $\psi(z)=\exp(2\pi i\ell(z)/p)$,
where the exponential is independent of the integer representative of
$\ell(z)$.  For independent uniform $u$ and $s_A$ in $\F_q$, with
$A\subseteq[k+1]$, put
\begin{equation}
 P(z)=\frac{1+\Re\psi\bigl(u\phi(z)+
             \sum_{A\subseteq[k+1]}s_A z_A\bigr)}2,
 \qquad z_A=\prod_{i\in A}z_i.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:Rieszfactor}
\end{equation}
Thus $0\le P(z)\le1$.  The empty monomial is included.
The expansion of this factor is
\begin{equation}
 P(z)=\frac12+\frac14\psi\bigl(u\phi(z)+\sum_As_Az_A\bigr)
             +\frac14\psi\bigl(-u\phi(z)-\sum_As_Az_A\bigr).
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:Rieszexpansion}
\end{equation}
All coefficients are nonnegative.

Orthogonality says that $\E_s\psi(sc)$ is $1$ if $c=0$ and $0$
otherwise.  For $c\ne0$, multiplication by $c$ permutes the field, and
the average of a nontrivial character is zero: translating its sum by
an element on which it is not one multiplies the sum by a scalar different from one without changing it.  Applying this to every $s_A$, the surviving
terms in the product of \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:Rieszexpansion} over arrangement labels
are exactly the ternary patterns whose monomial moments vanish.
Averaging over $u$ additionally requires
$\sum_{j,\eps}\eta(\eps,j)\phi(\rho(\eps,j))=0$.

For a nondegenerate arrangement, the only possibilities are
$0,\eta_0,-\eta_0$.  The zero pattern contributes $2^{-n}$.
Each of the two nonzero patterns has full support and contributes
$4^{-n}$ precisely when $\phi$ respects the arrangement.  Hence
\begin{equation}
 \E\prod_{j,\eps}P(\rho(\eps,j))=
 \begin{cases}
 a_n,&\phi\text{ does not respect the arrangement},\\
 b_n,&\phi\text{ respects the arrangement}.
 \end{cases}
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:onefactor}
\end{equation}
For a degenerate but respected arrangement the expectation is at least
$b_n$: the same three terms still survive, and all additional surviving
terms have nonnegative coefficients.

\subsection{Several factors and repeated vertices}
Take $t$ independent choices of the parameters in
\eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:Rieszfactor}, giving factors $P_1,\ldots,P_t$.
Conditional on these choices, put each \emph{point} $z\in B$ in $B'$
independently with probability
\[
 p(z)=\prod_{\ell=1}^tP_\ell(z).
\]
A nondegenerate arrangement has distinct vertices by
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:25:lem:collisions}.  Its conditional survival probability is
therefore the product of $p(z)$ over its labels.  Independence between
the $t$ parameter choices and \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:onefactor} give survival
probability $a_n^t$ or $b_n^t$ according as the arrangement is not respected
or respected.

For a repeated-vertex arrangement the conditional survival probability
is a product over \emph{distinct} points.  Since all factors belong to
$[0,1]$, this is at least the product over all labelled occurrences.
The preceding nonnegative Fourier expansion therefore proves that every
respected arrangement, even a degenerate one, survives with probability
at least $b_n^t$.  It would be incorrect to assert equality of the two
products when labels collide.

\subsection{The positive-potential argument}
\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:25:thm:selection}]
Let $M=\beta^{2d-1}q^D$.  Let $X$ count respected arrangements in the
selected set and $Y$ count non-respected ones.  By the preceding survival
calculations, the hypothesis, and Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:25:lem:densitycap},
\begin{equation}
 \E X\ge\alpha M b_n^t,\qquad
 \E Y\le M a_n^t+Z_{k,d}(q).
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:expectations}
\end{equation}
For the second inequality, treat nondegenerate arrangements using their
exact probability $a_n^t$, and bound the total contribution of degenerate
arrangements by their ambient number.

By the definition of $t$, $a_n^t\le(\alpha\eta/4)b_n^t$.
By Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:25:thm:main}, \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:selectioncondition}, and
\eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:tau},
$Z_{k,d}(q)\le(\alpha\eta/4)M b_n^t$.  Consequently
\[
 \E\left(X-\eta^{-1}Y\right)
 \ge \alpha M b_n^t-\frac\alpha4M b_n^t-\frac\alpha4M b_n^t
 =\frac\alpha2M b_n^t.
\]
There is an outcome with
$X-\eta^{-1}Y\ge(\alpha/2)M b_n^t$.
For that outcome, $X$ is at least the right side of
\eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:retained}, and $Y\le\eta X$.
Thus $X/(X+Y)\ge1/(1+\eta)\ge1-\eta$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A power-form bound and the remaining loss}
Put
\begin{equation}
 K_n=\frac{\log(1/b_n)}{\log R_n}.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:K}
\end{equation}
Since $t<1+\log(4/(\alpha\eta))/\log R_n$ and $0<b_n<1$,
\begin{equation}
 b_n^t\ge b_n\left(\frac{\alpha\eta}{4}\right)^{K_n}.
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:powerretention}
\end{equation}
This gives a power-form lower bound for \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:retained} with no
unspecified constants.  Direct expansion of $\log(1+2^{1-n})$ gives
\begin{equation}
 K_n=(\log2)\,n2^{n-1}+O(n)\qquad(n\to\infty).
 \label{gsr:en:25:eq:Kasymptotic}
\end{equation}
For $d=8$, the exponent recorded in the repository for the original
coarse selection bound is
$2^{2^{k+4}+k+3}=n2^{n-1}$ \cite{repo25lean}.
Keeping the exact logarithm changes the leading numerical factor in
this local exponent, but not its exponential dependence on $n$.
The very small likelihood advantage $R_n-1=2^{1-n}$ remains the main
loss in this particular selection mechanism.

The theorem neither assumes an improved inverse theorem nor silently
imports a result about prime fields into a composite ring.  It is valid
over finite \emph{fields}; the additive character averages are taken over
that field, and the rank calculations are field calculations.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Labelled arrangements and their moment relations\srctag{27}}]{Labelled arrangements and their moment relations}\label{gsr:en:27:sec:d2}\label{gsr:en:27:sec:setup}
\srcnote{27}{Section 2}

\subsection{The parameter space}

Let $s=(s_1,\ldots,s_n)$ have its first $d$ coordinates equal to $1$ and
its last $d$ coordinates equal to $-1$. All signs are interpreted in the field
when the characteristic is two. Put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:U}
 U=\{u=(u_1,\ldots,u_n)\in\F_q^n:s\cdot u=0\}.
\end{equation}
It has dimension $n-1$ because $s\ne0$. A labelled arrangement consists of
\[
 h\in\F_q^k,\qquad x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\F_q^k,\qquad u\in U.
\]
Its labelled vertices, indexed by $\eps\in\{0,1\}^k$ and $1\le j\le n$,
are
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:vertex}
 v_{\eps,j}=
 (x_{j1}+\eps_1h_1,\ldots,x_{jk}+\eps_kh_k,u_j)\in\F_q^{k+1}.
\end{equation}
There are $q^kq^{nk}q^{n-1}=q^D$ parameter tuples, as asserted in
\eqref{gsr:fm:27:eq:dimensions}. All probabilities below refer to the uniform measure on
this parameter space. In particular the bases, side coordinates, and the
uniform cross section in $U$ are independent.

For a coefficient array $\eta=(\eta_{\eps,j})$ and a subset
$A\subseteq[k+1]$, define the squarefree moment
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:moment}
 M_A(\eta)=\sum_{j=1}^n\sum_{\eps\in\{0,1\}^k}
     \eta_{\eps,j}\prod_{i\in A}v_{\eps,j,i}.
\end{equation}
The empty product is $1$; thus $M_\varnothing(\eta)=\sum\eta_{\eps,j}$.

\subsection{The intrinsic relation and the alphabet}

Write
\[
 \pi(\eps)=(-1)^{|\eps|},\qquad e_{\eps,j}=\pi(\eps)s_j.
\]
For $A\subsetneq[k]$, the alternating cube sum of the associated monomial
vanishes. For $A=[k]$ it is $(-1)^k\prod_i h_i$, independent of the base.
The same statement with the final coordinate present acquires the factor
$u_j$. Since $\sum s_j=0$ and $\sum s_ju_j=0$, this proves
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:intrinsic}
 M_A(e)=0\qquad(A\subseteq[k+1])
\end{equation}
in every characteristic, including when some $h_i=0$.

Let $D_p\subseteq\F_p\subseteq\F_q$ be the image of $\{-1,0,1\}$. In
characteristic two this alphabet has two elements, not three.

\begin{definition}\label{gsr:en:27:def:degen}
An arrangement is \emph{degenerate} if there is an array
$\eta\in D_p^{\{0,1\}^k\times[n]}$ such that
\[
 \eta\notin\F_q e,
 \qquad M_A(\eta)=0\quad\hbox{for every }A\subseteq[k+1].
\]
The quantity $\Delta_{k,d}(q)$ is its degeneracy probability.
\end{definition}

This definition records relations among labelled vertices, so repeated
vertices can themselves generate degeneracy. It also excludes all field
multiples of the intrinsic relation, not only its two signed integer
representatives.

\begin{lemma}[Zero-side degeneracy]\label{gsr:en:27:lem:zeroside}
If $h_i=0$ for some $i$, then the arrangement is degenerate.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose two labels differing only in $\eps_i$, with the same $j$. Their
vertices coincide. The coefficient array with entries $1,-1$ on those labels
and $0$ elsewhere annihilates all moments. In characteristic two the two
nonzero entries are both $1$ and still give zero. Its support has size two,
whereas every nonzero multiple of $e$ has full support $m\ge8$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Quotienting coefficient arrays before using a union bound}

Suppose $\eta'=a\eta+be$ with $a\ne0$. By \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:intrinsic}, the two
arrays have precisely the same simultaneous moment-zero event. We therefore
identify them whenever both arrays are admissible. On dividing pointwise by
$e$, this is simply affine equivalence of profiles:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:affineq}
 t_{\eps,j}=\eta_{\eps,j}/e_{\eps,j},
 \qquad t'=at+b\one.
\end{equation}
Constant profiles correspond exactly to multiples of the intrinsic relation.

If $t,t'$ are nonconstant prime-field profiles and \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:affineq} holds
with $a,b\in\F_q$, then in fact $a,b\in\F_p$. Indeed, choose two coordinates
where $t$ differs; their differences determine $a$, and either coordinate
then determines $b$. Thus coefficient-class counts depend on the
characteristic $p$, not on the extension degree of $q$.

Only arrays with $M_\varnothing(\eta)=0$ can occur in the exceptional set.
The intrinsic signs have equally many positive and negative entries as
integer signs. Hence the counting problem is the following one: count
nonconstant ternary profiles on an even number of positions with a balanced
signed sum, modulo affine equivalence. We solve that problem in
Section~\ref{gsr:en:27:sec:classes}.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Boolean coefficient extraction and a rank lemma\srctag{27}}]{Boolean coefficient extraction and a rank lemma}\label{gsr:en:27:sec:d3}\label{gsr:en:27:sec:boolean}
\srcnote{27}{Section 3}

The original Walsh argument is naturally adapted to odd characteristic.
For the present purpose the Boolean zeta transform gives a simpler identity
with no division by two.

For $B\subseteq[k]$, define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:cB}
 c_{B,j}=\sum_{\eps\in\{0,1\}^k}
                    \eta_{\eps,j}\prod_{i\in B}\eps_i.
\end{equation}
For $A\subseteq[k]$, write
\[
 F_{A,j}(x_j,h)=\sum_{\eps}\eta_{\eps,j}
                       \prod_{i\in A}(x_{ji}+\eps_i h_i),
 \qquad h_B=\prod_{i\in B}h_i.
\]
Direct expansion gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:booleanexpansion}
 F_{A,j}=\sum_{B\subseteq A}h_B c_{B,j}
                                      \prod_{i\in A\setminus B}x_{ji}.
\end{equation}
The moments in \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:moment} can be written
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:pairedmoments}
 M_A(\eta)=\sum_jF_{A,j},\qquad
 M_{A\cup\{k+1\}}(\eta)=\sum_ju_jF_{A,j}.
\end{equation}
It is important that \emph{both} equations are available for every $A$.

\begin{lemma}[Parity detection]\label{gsr:en:27:lem:paritydetect}
For a fixed column $j$, all $c_{B,j}$ with $B\subsetneq[k]$ vanish if and
only if $\eta_{\eps,j}$ is a scalar multiple of $\pi(\eps)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If the support of a Boolean vertex is $E\subseteq[k]$, then
$c_{B,j}=\sum_{E\supseteq B}\eta_{E,j}$. Boolean M\"obius inversion gives
\[
 \eta_{E,j}=\sum_{B\supseteq E}(-1)^{|B\setminus E|}c_{B,j}.
\]
If only $c_{[k],j}$ can be nonzero, the right side is
$(-1)^{k-|E|}c_{[k],j}$, a scalar parity column. Conversely, a parity column
has zero sum over every proper upper interval. The inversion matrix has
integer diagonal entries $1$, so the argument is valid over every field.
\end{proof}

Call an array \emph{column-parity} if each of its columns is a scalar parity
column. An array that is not column-parity has a smallest integer $r<k$ for
which $c_A=(c_{A,1},\ldots,c_{A,n})\ne0$ for some $|A|=r$. Fix such an $A$
and set $c=c_A$. Equation \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:booleanexpansion} gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:lowest}
 F_{A,j}=h_Ac_j,
\end{equation}
and, for every $i\notin A$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:next}
 F_{A\cup\{i\},j}=h_Ac_jx_{ji}+b_{i,j}.
\end{equation}
Here $b_{i,j}$ can depend on $h$ and on the coordinates of $x_j$ indexed by
$A$, but not on \emph{any} of the variables $x_{1i},\ldots,x_{ni}$. It can
involve other degree-$r$ coefficients, so it must not be replaced by just
$h_{A\cup\{i\}}c_{A\cup\{i\},j}$.

\begin{lemma}[Two necessary equations]\label{gsr:en:27:lem:rank}
Assume all $h_i\ne0$. For a non-column-parity array and the above choice of
$c$, simultaneous vanishing of the moments implies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:constantconstraints}
 \sum_jc_j=0,\qquad c\cdot u=0,
\end{equation}
and two affine equations in $z=(x_{1i},\ldots,x_{ni})$ with coefficient rows
$c$ and $u\odot c=(u_jc_j)_j$, for each $i\notin A$.

If the $u_j$ are pairwise distinct and $\sum_jc_j=0$, these two rows have
rank two.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Apply \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:pairedmoments} first to \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:lowest}, and then to
\eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:next}; divide by the nonzero $h_A$. A nonzero $c$ of coordinate sum
zero has support of size at least two. If the rows were dependent, $u_j$
would have the same value on every index in that support, contrary to
pairwise distinctness.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[An all-characteristic per-direction bound]\label{gsr:en:27:prop:perclass}
For a fixed non-column-parity coefficient direction, conditional on all
$h_i\ne0$, its moment-zero probability is at most
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:perclass}
 q^{-2}+(q-1)q^{-n}.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Use the first nonzero coefficient vector $c$ above. If $\sum c_j\ne0$, the
probability is zero. If $c\notin\F_qs$, the equation $c\cdot u=0$ cuts a
codimension-one subspace of $U$, costing a factor $q^{-1}$. The first affine
base equation has a nonzero coefficient row and costs another $q^{-1}$.

If $c=\lambda s\ne0$, the cross-section equation is automatic. The two base
rows have rank two unless all the $u_j$ coincide. The diagonal line lies in
$U$ and has relative size $q^{-(n-2)}$. Off the diagonal the probability is
at most $q^{-2}$; on it the first equation alone gives at most $q^{-1}$.
Averaging gives
\[
 (1-q^{-(n-2)})q^{-2}+q^{-(n-2)}q^{-1}
       =q^{-2}+(q-1)q^{-n}.
\]
The other base variables may be fixed throughout, since the two equations
are affine in the remaining coordinate block.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Counting coefficient directions exactly\srctag{27}}]{Counting coefficient directions exactly}\label{gsr:en:27:sec:d4}\label{gsr:en:27:sec:classes}
\srcnote{27}{Section 4}

\subsection{Balanced profiles}

For even $\ell\ge2$, let $\Qc_\ell(p)$ count affine classes of nonconstant
profiles $t\in D_p^\ell$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:profilebalance}
 \sum_{i=1}^{\ell/2}t_i-
 \sum_{i=\ell/2+1}^{\ell}t_i=0\quad\hbox{in }\F_p.
\end{equation}
Let $\Uc_\ell(p)$ count affine classes of nonconstant profiles without the
balance condition. Define
\begin{align}
 \Tc_\ell(p)&=\sum_{a\equiv0\ (p)}[z^a](z^{-1}+1+z)^\ell,\label{gsr:en:27:eq:Tp}\\
 \Bc_\ell(p)&=\sum_{j\in\Z}\binom{\ell}{\ell/2+jp},\label{gsr:en:27:eq:Bp}
\end{align}
where binomial coefficients outside their ordinary range are zero.

\begin{theorem}[Affine ternary profile counts]\label{gsr:en:27:thm:profiles}
For $p\ge5$,
\begin{align}
 \Qc_\ell(p)&=\frac{\Tc_\ell(p)-2\Bc_\ell(p)+1}{2},\label{gsr:en:27:eq:Qp}\\
 \Uc_\ell(p)&=\frac{3^\ell-2^{\ell+1}+1}{2}.\label{gsr:en:27:eq:Up}
\end{align}
For $p=2$ or $3$,
\begin{align}
 \Qc_\ell(p)&=\frac{p^{\ell-2}-1}{p-1},\label{gsr:en:27:eq:Qsmall}\\
 \Uc_\ell(p)&=\frac{p^{\ell-1}-1}{p-1}.\label{gsr:en:27:eq:Usmall}
\end{align}
If $p>\ell$, then $\Tc_\ell(p)=\Tc_\ell$ and
$\Bc_\ell(p)=\binom\ell{\ell/2}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
First take $p\ge5$. Changing the signs of the last half of the coordinates is
a bijection of the ternary alphabet, so the number of balanced profiles is
$\Tc_\ell(p)$. The number of balanced binary profiles is $\Bc_\ell(p)$:
if $a,b$ positions are selected in the two halves, balance says
$a-b\equiv0\pmod p$, and Vandermonde's identity sums their number to
\eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:Bp}.

There are three constant ternary profiles. For each of the three unordered
pairs of distinct alphabet values, the number of profiles using exactly
that pair and satisfying balance is $\Bc_\ell(p)-2$. All two-valued
profiles are affinely equivalent to binary ones, and the only ambiguity of
the underlying nontrivial subset is complementation. They therefore give
$(\Bc_\ell(p)-2)/2$ classes.

The number of profiles using all three values is
$\Tc_\ell(p)-3-3(\Bc_\ell(p)-2)=\Tc_\ell(p)-3\Bc_\ell(p)+3$.
An affine bijection preserving $\{-1,0,1\}$ in characteristic at least five
is either the identity or negation. To see this, the image of $0$ must be
the midpoint of the images of $-1$ and $1$; the only alphabet element that
is the midpoint of the other two is $0$ when $p\ne3$. Thus these profiles
form classes of size two. Adding the two types gives \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:Qp}.
Removing balance replaces $\Tc_\ell(p)$ by $3^\ell$ and $\Bc_\ell(p)$ by
$2^\ell$, proving \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:Up}.

For $p=2,3$, the alphabet is the entire prime field. Balanced profiles form
an $(\ell-1)$-dimensional vector space containing the constant line.
Quotienting by that line gives dimension $\ell-2$; quotienting nonzero
vectors by nonzero scalar multiplication gives \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:Qsmall}. Without
balance the quotient dimension is $\ell-1$, giving \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:Usmall}.
The last assertion follows because the relevant integer sums have absolute
value at most $\ell$ (and the binary differences at most $\ell/2$).
\end{proof}

\subsection{The two counts needed for arrangements}

Set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:LRp}
 L_{d,p}=\Qc_n(p),\qquad
 R_{k,d,p}=\Qc_m(p)-\Uc_n(p).
\end{equation}
The first quantity will count cross-section hyperplanes. The second is the
number of non-column-parity coefficient directions satisfying the constant
moment condition.

Indeed a column-parity array has the form
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:columnparity}
 \eta_{\eps,j}=\pi(\eps)c_j,\qquad c_j\in D_p.
\end{equation}
Its empty moment vanishes automatically, since $k\ge1$. Dividing by $e$
gives an arbitrary profile $c_j/s_j$ on the $n$ columns, repeated along each
column. The resulting number of nonconstant affine classes is
$\Uc_n(p)$. All balanced arrays on $m$ positions give $\Qc_m(p)$ classes;
subtracting proves the interpretation of $R_{k,d,p}$. In particular it is a
nonnegative integer, even though many of these directions may never vanish
on a particular regular region.

For $p>m$, formulas \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:LRp} reduce exactly to
\eqref{gsr:fm:27:eq:Llarge} and \eqref{gsr:fm:27:eq:Rlarge}. For the two small characteristics they become
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:LRsmall}
 L_{d,p}=\frac{p^{n-2}-1}{p-1},\qquad
 R_{k,d,p}=\frac{p^{m-2}-p^{n-1}}{p-1}.
\end{equation}

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\caption{Some exact large-characteristic constants. Here $p>n2^k$.}
\label{gsr:en:27:tab:constants}
\begin{tabular}{rrrrr}
\toprule
$d$ & $k$ & $L_d$ & $S_{k,d}$ & $R_{k,d}$\\
\midrule
2&1&4&15&459\\
2&2&4&32&2\,585\,419\\
3&1&51&63&35\,670\\
3&2&51&128&13\,971\,463\,734\\
4&1&484&255&2\,582\,419\\
8&1&2\,585\,444&65\,535&79\,556\,623\,497\,667\\

\end{table}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{All first-order obstructions\srctag{27}}]{All first-order obstructions}\label{gsr:en:27:sec:d5}\label{gsr:en:27:sec:allchar}
\srcnote{27}{Section 5}

\subsection{The cross-section hyperplanes}

For a column-parity array \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:columnparity}, all its moments vanish
except possibly those indexed by $[k]$ and $[k+1]$. If all sides are
nonzero, these last two moments vanish exactly when
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:parityconditions}
 \sum_jc_j=0,\qquad c\cdot u=0.
\end{equation}
The excluded intrinsic arrays are precisely $c\in\F_qs$.

\begin{definition}\label{gsr:en:27:def:hyperplanes}
Let $\cH_{d,p}$ be the collection of distinct hyperplanes of $U$ of the form
\[
 H_c=\{u\in U:c\cdot u=0\},
 \qquad c\in D_p^n,\quad \sum_jc_j=0,\quad c\notin\F_qs.
\]
Define the regular cross-section set and its density by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:regular}
 U^\circ=U\setminus\bigcup_{H\in\cH_{d,p}}H,
 \qquad g_{d,p}(q)=\frac{|U^\circ|}{q^{n-1}}.
\end{equation}
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{gsr:en:27:lem:hyperplanecount}
The collection $\cH_{d,p}$ has exactly $L_{d,p}$ members. Every
$u\in U^\circ$ has pairwise distinct coordinates.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Two nonzero linear forms on $U$ have the same kernel if and only if they
are scalar multiples as forms on $U$. The annihilator of $U$ is the line
$\F_qs$, so $H_c=H_{c'}$ exactly when
$c'=ac+bs$ for some $a\ne0$. Dividing by $s$ turns this into affine
profile equivalence. The balance condition becomes a balanced signed sum,
so the class count is $\Qc_n(p)=L_{d,p}$.

If $u_i=u_j$ for distinct indices, choose $c$ supported on those two
coordinates with entries $1,-1$. It is balanced and not proportional to
$s$, because $n\ge4$ and $s$ has full support. Thus $u\in H_c$, contradicting
regularity.
\end{proof}

The diagonal translation direction $\one$ is contained in every member of
$\cH_{d,p}$, because $\sum c_j=0$. Thus this is essentially a hyperplane
arrangement in $U/\F_q\one$, of dimension $n-2$. No general theory of
hyperplane arrangements is required for the bounds below; the intersection
structure becomes relevant when higher coefficients are sought.

\subsection{The sharp first-order theorem in every characteristic}

\begin{theorem}\label{gsr:en:27:thm:allchar}
For $k\ge1,d\ge2$, over any finite field of characteristic $p$, put
$A_p=k+L_{d,p}$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:allcharbound}
 \frac{A_p}{q}-\frac{\binom{A_p}{2}}{q^2}
 \le\Delta_{k,d}(q)
 \le\frac{A_p}{q}
       +R_{k,d,p}\bigl(q^{-2}+(q-1)q^{-n}\bigr).
\end{equation}
In particular, for fixed $k,d,p$ and $q=p^a\to\infty$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:fixedcharasy}
 \Delta_{k,d}(q)=\frac{k+L_{d,p}}q+O_{k,d,p}(q^{-2}).
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
There are $k$ side hyperplanes $h_i=0$ and $L_{d,p}$ cross-section
hyperplanes. Every tuple on any of them is degenerate: use
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:27:lem:zeroside} or its defining column-parity relation. These hyperplanes
are distinct in the full parameter space. Every pair intersects in
codimension two. The first two terms of inclusion--exclusion therefore give
the lower bound.

For the upper bound, their union has measure at most $A_p/q$. Outside that
union, a degeneracy witness cannot be column-parity. There are
$R_{k,d,p}$ remaining coefficient directions, and
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:27:prop:perclass} bounds the moment-zero probability of each, conditional
on nonzero sides. Dropping the factor $(1-q^{-1})^k\le1$ gives the upper
bound. Since $n\ge4$, its remaining term is $O(q^{-2})$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Credit and a cross-answer.} For $p>m$ this is source~18's theorem with its lower bound. In small characteristic it gives the first-order count that source~25 asks for (its Question~4; item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:degeneracy}): $L_{d,p}$ by Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:27:thm:profiles}, for instance $L_{3,5}=57$, as in source~25's Example~\ref{gsr:en:25:ex:smallchar}. The classification of the additional components in characteristics two and three is not given.
\end{writenote}

This proves in a concrete counting sense that all order-$q^{-1}$
obstructions have been identified: the complement of their union contains
only $O(q^{D-2})$ degenerate tuples. The word ``first-order'' here refers to
this counting statement; no unproved assertion about geometric
irreducibility is being used.

\begin{example}[Characteristic dependence]\label{gsr:en:27:ex:char}
For $d=3$, the numbers $L_{3,p}$ are
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
 p&2&3&5& p>6\\\hline
 L_{3,p}&15&40&57&51.
\end{array}
\]
In characteristic five, ternary integer sums equal to $\pm5$
also become zero, increasing the count. Large field size alone does not
remove this effect: it persists in every extension of $\F_5$.
\end{example}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Second-order structure on the regular region\srctag{27}}]{Second-order structure on the regular region}\label{gsr:en:27:sec:d6}\label{gsr:en:27:sec:second}
\srcnote{27}{Section 6}

From now until the end of Section~\ref{gsr:en:27:sec:dtwo}, assume $p>m$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:G}
 G=(1-q^{-1})^k g_{d,p}(q).
\end{equation}
This is exactly the probability that all sides are nonzero and $u\in U^\circ$.
Its complement is entirely degenerate.

\subsection{Directions that are not second-order}

Fix a non-column-parity direction and let $r<k$ be its smallest nonzero
Boolean coefficient degree, as in Section~\ref{gsr:en:27:sec:boolean}. If some degree-$r$
vector $c_A$ is not proportional to $s$, then its event on the regular
region costs one cross-section equation and two base equations. More
precisely, $c_A\cdot u=0$ defines a codimension-one subspace in $U$; after
fixing such a regular $u$, Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:27:lem:rank} gives rank two in any coordinate
block outside $A$. Hence its probability on the regular region, conditional
only on nonzero sides, is at most $q^{-3}$.

Suppose instead that every nonzero degree-$r$ vector is proportional to $s$.
If $r\le k-2$, choose one such $A$ and two different indices $i,\ell\notin A$.
The paired moments for $A\cup\{i\}$ give two affine equations in the $i$th
base-coordinate block; those for $A\cup\{\ell\}$ give two in the $\ell$th
block. Their right sides depend only on the $A$-coordinates and $h$, not on
either other variable block. On regular $u$, each pair has rank two.
Together they have rank four and cost $q^{-4}$.

Thus the only remaining possibility for a direction contributing at the
second order is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:coreconditions}
 c_{B,j}=0\ (|B|\le k-2),\qquad
 c_{[k]\setminus\{i\},j}=\lambda_i s_j\ (1\le i\le k),
\end{equation}
with at least one $\lambda_i\ne0$.

\begin{definition}\label{gsr:en:27:def:core}
A non-column-parity direction satisfying \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:coreconditions} is called
a \emph{core direction}. This term is local to this article.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}\label{gsr:en:27:prop:noncore}
For every non-column-parity direction that is not a core direction, its
moment-zero event on the regular region, conditional on nonzero sides, has
probability at most $q^{-3}$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The two cases above exhaust the possibilities. The first gives $q^{-3}$.
The second gives at most $g_{d,p}(q)q^{-4}\le q^{-3}$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Classification of all core profiles}

\begin{lemma}[Affine Boolean form]\label{gsr:en:27:lem:affineboolean}
Condition \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:coreconditions} is equivalent to
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:affineboolean}
 \eta_{\eps,j}=e_{\eps,j}
          \left(t_j+\sum_{i=1}^k b_i\eps_i\right)
\end{equation}
for some $t_j,b_i\in\F_p$, with $b\ne0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Divide each column by its parity and by $s_j$. The Boolean coefficient
transform is invertible. Vanishing of the coefficients below degree $k-1$
means that the resulting Boolean function has degree at most one, and
proportionality of its degree-$k-1$ coefficients to $s_j$ says that the
linear coefficients are common to the columns.

For completeness this can also be checked directly: a constant term times
parity has no proper nonzero $c_B$; a term $\eps_i$ times parity has no
nonzero $c_B$ unless $B\supseteq[k]\setminus\{i\}$, and at that set its
coefficient is $(-1)^{k-1}$. These $k+1$ arrays are linearly independent.
Boolean inversion shows that they exhaust the solution space of the stated
vanishing conditions in each column. The common proportionality factors
then give common $b_i$.
\end{proof}

Every value in parentheses in \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:affineboolean} must belong to the
three-element alphabet. This severely restricts $b$.

\begin{lemma}[Width two]\label{gsr:en:27:lem:width}
If $p>m$ and a nonconstant affine Boolean function takes values in
$\{-1,0,1\}\subset\F_p$, its slopes have integer representatives $b_i$
with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:width}
 \sum_i|b_i|\le2.
\end{equation}
Consequently it has either one active coordinate, or two active coordinates
with unit slopes.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose the representative $t\in\{-1,0,1\}$ of the value at the zero vertex.
Each slope is a difference of two alphabet values, so has a representative
in $\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}$. At any vertex the integer affine sum differs from the
chosen representative of its field value by an integer of absolute value
at most $2k+2$. Since $p>m\ge4\cdot2^k>2k+2$, no nonzero multiple of $p$
can occur. Thus the ordinary integer affine function really takes all its
values in $[-1,1]$. Its range width is $\sum_i|b_i|$, proving the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The characteristic cutoff in the width argument]
The proof actually requires only $p>2k+2$ (and hence $p\ge5$), not $p>m$.
Accordingly the core count and the resolved bound remain valid in that
range with $L_{d,p},R_{k,d,p}$ in place of their clean large-characteristic
forms. The stronger assumption $p>m$ in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:27:thm:main} also removes modular
wraparound from the balanced coefficient-class counts.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[The core direction count]\label{gsr:en:27:thm:corecount}
There are exactly
\[
 S=S_{k,d}=k(2^n-1)+2\binom k2
\]
core directions. For fixed nonzero sides and regular $u$, every one of their
moment-zero events has probability exactly $q^{-2}$ in the base variables.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For one active coordinate $i$, divide by its slope and use translation of
the entire profile. A unit slope allows each column offset to be one of two
adjacent values. A nonconstant binary offset pattern gives one direction;
there are $2^n-2$ such patterns. The two constant patterns are equivalent
under translation and contribute one further direction. A slope of
absolute value two forces a constant offset and belongs to that same
constant-pattern direction after affine normalization. This gives $2^n-1$
directions for each $i$.

For two active coordinates $i,\ell$, their slopes have absolute value one.
After common scaling, their ratio is either $1$ or $-1$. The total width is
two, so every column offset is forced to the same value: $-1$ for slopes
$(1,1)$, or $0$ for slopes $(1,-1)$. These give two directions for every
unordered coordinate pair. Distinct slope ratios, coordinate supports, and
nonconstant offset patterns cannot be related by one common affine
transformation. This proves the count.

For a core profile, all moments except the two top ones vanish identically
on $U$. Expanding the top moment shows that the remaining conditions are
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:coreequations}
 \sum_j s_j\left(t_j+\sum_i b_i\frac{x_{ji}}{h_i}\right)=0,
 \qquad
 \sum_j s_ju_j\left(t_j+\sum_i b_i\frac{x_{ji}}{h_i}\right)=0.
\end{equation}
To check the expansion, each $\eps_i$ term contributes the factor
$1+x_{ji}/h_i$ after division by the common alternating top-cube factor.
The additional constant $\sum_i b_i$ disappears from both sums because
$\sum s_j=\sum s_ju_j=0$.

At least one $b_i$ is nonzero. In that coordinate block the coefficient rows
are nonzero multiples of $s$ and $s\odot u$. Since the $u_j$ are pairwise
distinct, these rows are independent. Therefore \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:coreequations} is
an affine rank-two system and has exactly a $q^{-2}$ fraction of solutions.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 40--46]
Source~44's Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:44:lem:width} removes the condition $p>2k+2$: the core directions are those of this theorem in every characteristic $p\ge5$, and the union of the core events is counted exactly (its Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:44:thm:oddproduct} and~\ref{gsr:en:44:thm:smallproduct}).
\end{writenote}

\subsection{Intersections of core events}

\begin{lemma}\label{gsr:en:27:lem:coreintersections}
Fix regular $u$ and nonzero sides. Distinct core directions with parallel
slope vectors have disjoint zero events. Core directions with nonparallel
slope vectors have intersection probability $q^{-4}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Only the one-coordinate families have more than one direction with a given
slope. Normalize both to slope $1$. If their zero events meet, subtracting
\eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:coreequations} gives
\[
 \sum_j s_j(t_j-t'_j)=0,
 \qquad \sum_j s_ju_j(t_j-t'_j)=0.
\]
The differences can be chosen in $\{-1,0,1\}$. For distinct directions the
vector $c_j=s_j(t_j-t'_j)$ is not proportional to $s$, since a constant
difference would make the profiles affinely equivalent. Thus $u$ belongs
to a forbidden hyperplane, a contradiction.

For nonparallel slopes $b,b'$, consider the two independent coordinate
functionals $b_i/h_i$ and $b'_i/h_i$, and the two independent column
functionals $s$ and $s\odot u$. The four tensor-product functionals are
linearly independent. They are exactly the coefficient rows of the four
affine equations defining the intersection, so that system is surjective
onto $\F_q^4$ and has fraction $q^{-4}$ of solutions.
\end{proof}

Put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:P}
 P_{k,d}=\binom{S_{k,d}}2-k\binom{2^n-1}2.
\end{equation}
This is the number of unordered pairs of nonparallel core directions.
Bonferroni's inequality and Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:27:lem:coreintersections} show that the
conditional probability of their union lies between
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:coreunion}
 \frac{S_{k,d}}{q^2}-\frac{P_{k,d}}{q^4}
 \quad\hbox{and}\quad \frac{S_{k,d}}{q^2}.
\end{equation}
There is no $q^{-3}$ loss from intersections of core events on this region.

\begin{theorem}[Hyperplane-resolved bound]\label{gsr:en:27:thm:resolved}
Let $p>m$ and use $G$ from \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:G}. Then
\begin{align}
 \Delta_{k,d}(q)&\ge
 1-G+G\left(\frac{S_{k,d}}{q^2}-\frac{P_{k,d}}{q^4}\right),\label{gsr:en:27:eq:resolvedlower}\\
 \Delta_{k,d}(q)&\le
 1-G+G\frac{S_{k,d}}{q^2}
 +(1-q^{-1})^k\frac{R_{k,d}-S_{k,d}}{q^3}.\label{gsr:en:27:eq:resolvedupper}
\end{align}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The complement of the regular region has measure $1-G$ and is entirely
degenerate. Apply \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:coreunion} on the regular region. For the upper
bound add the $R_{k,d}-S_{k,d}$ remaining directions, each bounded by
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:27:prop:noncore}. Their estimates were conditional on nonzero sides, so
the factor $(1-q^{-1})^k$ is retained.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:27:thm:main}]
The lower bound is the lower bound of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:27:thm:allchar}. For the upper
bound in \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:resolvedupper}, use $1-G\le(k+L_d)/q$, $G\le1$, and
$(1-q^{-1})^k\le1$. This proves \eqref{gsr:fm:27:eq:mainbounds}. Its lower and upper
bounds have the same $q^{-1}$ coefficient, proving sharpness.
\end{proof}

\section[{Two pairs of cross sections and the second coefficient\srctag{27}}]{Two pairs of cross sections and the second coefficient}\label{gsr:en:27:sec:d7}\label{gsr:en:27:sec:dtwo}
\srcnote{27}{Section 7}

For $d=2$, $s=(1,1,-1,-1)$. Subtract a common translation from $u$ and write
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:ab}
 u=(a,b,0,a+b).
\end{equation}
The quotient $U/\F_q\one$ is thus identified with the $(a,b)$-plane.

\begin{proposition}\label{gsr:en:27:prop:g2}
In odd characteristic,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:g2}
 g_{2,p}(q)=\frac{(q-1)(q-3)}{q^2}
          =1-\frac4q+\frac3{q^2}.
\end{equation}
In characteristic two,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:g2char2}
 g_{2,2}(q)=\frac{(q-1)(q-2)}{q^2}.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For odd characteristic, $L_{2,p}=4$ by Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:27:thm:profiles}. The four
hyperplanes are represented in the quotient by the distinct lines
\[
 a=0,\quad b=0,\quad a=b,\quad a=-b.
\]
They can all be obtained from pairwise cross-section equalities. Their
union contains $1+4(q-1)$ points. Its complement therefore has
$q^2-4q+3=(q-1)(q-3)$ points. In characteristic two the last two lines
coincide, and $L_{2,2}=3$; the same argument gives
$q^2-3q+2=(q-1)(q-2)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of the asymptotic assertion in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:27:thm:d2main}]
Under its large-characteristic assumption,
\[
 G=(1-q^{-1})^k(1-4q^{-1}+3q^{-2})
 =1-\frac{k+4}{q}
  +\frac{\binom k2+4k+3}{q^2}+O_k(q^{-3}).
\]
Here $S_{k,2}=k^2+14k$. Both sides of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:27:thm:resolved} therefore have
second coefficient
\[
 S_{k,2}-\binom k2-4k-3=\frac{k^2+21k-6}{2}.
\]
The residual upper term is $O_k(q^{-3})$ and the core-intersection lower
term is $O_k(q^{-4})$, proving \eqref{gsr:fm:27:eq:d2asy}.
\end{proof}

For $k=1$, all 15 core directions have parallel slopes, so their events
are pairwise disjoint on the regular region. Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:base15}
 1-G+\frac{15G}{q^2}
 =\frac5q+\frac8{q^2}-\frac{72}{q^3}
                     +\frac{105}{q^4}-\frac{45}{q^5}
\end{equation}
is an exact lower bound. The difference from the full degeneracy fraction
is between $0$ and $444(1-q^{-1})q^{-3}$. In particular the conventional
proofs already give
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:k1rough}
 \frac5q+\frac8{q^2}-\frac{72}{q^3}
 \le\Delta_{1,2}(q)
 \le\frac5q+\frac8{q^2}+\frac{372}{q^3}.
\end{equation}
The exact computation below determines the entire remaining expression.

\section[{Two extensions of the second-order theorem\srctag{27}}]{Two extensions of the second-order theorem}\label{gsr:en:27:sec:d8}\label{gsr:en:27:sec:extensions}
\srcnote{27}{Section 8}

\subsection{A hyperplane statistic determines the second coefficient}

Let $\mathcal L_2$ be the set of distinct codimension-two subspaces of $U$
that arise as intersections of two members of $\cH_{d,p}$. For
$F\in\mathcal L_2$, let $\nu_F$ be the number of members containing $F$, and
put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:b2}
 b_{2,d,p}=\sum_{F\in\mathcal L_2}(\nu_F-1).
\end{equation}
This is a finite invariant of the cross-section hyperplane arrangement over
$\F_p$.

\begin{lemma}\label{gsr:en:27:lem:hyperplane2}
For fixed $d,p$ and $q=p^a$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:gexpansion}
 g_{d,p}(q)=1-\frac{L_{d,p}}q+\frac{b_{2,d,p}}{q^2}
                            +O_{d,p}(q^{-3}).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Apply finite inclusion--exclusion to the hyperplanes. A nonempty
intersection of codimension $r$ has relative size $q^{-r}$. A
codimension-two flat $F$ contributes the alternating sum over subsets of
at least two of the $\nu_F$ hyperplanes containing it. Any two of these
hyperplanes already intersect in $F$. The resulting coefficient is
\[
 \sum_{j=2}^{\nu_F}(-1)^j\binom{\nu_F}{j}=\nu_F-1.
\]
All other terms have codimension at least three. Their number is finite and
depends only on the original prime-field arrangement. This proves the
expansion, and also shows that the exact complement density is a polynomial
in $q^{-1}$ for fixed $d,p$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The second coefficient for arbitrary $d$]\label{gsr:en:27:cor:general2}
Fix $k,d$ and a prime $p>m$. Along the extensions $q=p^a$,
\begin{align}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:generalsecond}
 \Delta_{k,d}(q)
 &=\frac{k+L_d}{q}\\[-1mm]
 &\quad+\frac{S_{k,d}-\binom k2-kL_d-b_{2,d,p}}{q^2}
       +O_{k,d,p}(q^{-3}).\notag
\end{align}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Substitute \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:gexpansion} in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:27:thm:resolved} and expand
$(1-q^{-1})^k$ to second order. The core union has no intersection loss
before order $q^{-4}$, and the remaining directions cost at most $q^{-3}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 40--46]
\emph{The statistic $b_{2,d,p}$ is now computed} (source~44, Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:gridcore}): it is characteristic-independent for $p>\max(2d,16)$ and given for every $d$ by a nine-point grid formula; $b_{2,8}=3{,}280{,}234{,}631{,}541$ (Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:44:thm:stability}, \ref{gsr:en:44:thm:grid}, \ref{gsr:en:44:thm:compact}).
\end{writenote}

This gives the second coefficient as a finite linear-algebra problem even
when a closed form for $b_{2,d,p}$ is unavailable. One must not silently
replace $b_{2,d,p}$ by a characteristic-independent number: ranks among
ternary normals may change in particular characteristics. For $d=2$ in odd
characteristic all four quotient lines meet at the origin, so $b_{2,2,p}=3$,
recovering \eqref{gsr:fm:27:eq:d2asy}. Hyperplane arrangements and their intersection
posets provide a natural language for further computations; a standard
background reference is Stanley's survey \cite{stanley}. The elementary
argument above is the only input needed here.

\subsection{An exact core count in characteristics two and three}

The width-two argument was needed because a large prime field contains many
values outside the allowed alphabet. In characteristic two or three, the
alphabet is the whole prime field. In these cases the core count is easier,
not harder.

\begin{theorem}[Small-characteristic cubic bounds]\label{gsr:en:27:thm:smallcore}
For $p\in\{2,3\}$, define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:smallS}
 \begin{aligned}
 B_{k,p}&=\frac{p^k-1}{p-1},\qquad S_{k,d,p}=p^{n-1}B_{k,p},\\
 P_{k,d,p}&=\binom{S_{k,d,p}}2-B_{k,p}\binom{p^{n-1}}2.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The bounds in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:27:thm:resolved} remain valid after replacing
$S_{k,d}$ by $S_{k,d,p}$, $P_{k,d}$ by $P_{k,d,p}$, and $R_{k,d}$ by
$R_{k,d,p}$.
In particular, for every extension $q=p^a$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:smallcubic}
 \Delta_{k,d}(q)\le\frac{k+L_{d,p}}q
       +\frac{S_{k,d,p}}{q^2}
       +\frac{R_{k,d,p}-S_{k,d,p}}{q^3}.
\end{equation}
The second-coefficient formula in \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:generalsecond} also holds with
these characteristic-dependent constants.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The Boolean form \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:affineboolean}, the rank argument of
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:27:prop:noncore}, and the core equations \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:coreequations} are valid
in every characteristic. In the present two cases all choices
$t\in\F_p^n$ and $0\ne b\in\F_p^k$ are admissible. Choose a projective
slope direction, of which there are $B_{k,p}$. After fixing a representative
of that direction, the offsets are identified exactly by common
translation; their quotient has $p^{n-1}$ elements. This proves the core
count.

The difference of two offsets is still alphabet-valued, since the alphabet
is $\F_p$. The proof of disjointness for parallel slopes in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:27:lem:coreintersections} therefore applies unchanged. Nonparallel
slopes again give four independent tensor-product rows. The same union
bounds prove the assertions.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}
For $d=2,k=1$, the second-order asymptotics in the two small characteristics
are
\[
 \Delta_{1,2}(2^a)=\frac4{2^a}+\frac3{2^{2a}}+O(2^{-3a}),
\]
\[
 \Delta_{1,2}(3^a)=\frac5{3^a}+\frac{20}{3^{2a}}+O(3^{-3a}).
\]
Indeed the hyperplane coefficients are $(L,b_2)=(3,2)$ and $(4,3)$,
respectively, and the core counts are $8$ and $27$. These differ from the
large-characteristic coefficient $8$ in \eqref{gsr:fm:27:eq:exactmain}; keeping track of
characteristic is mathematically necessary.
\end{example}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{An exact count for eight labelled vertices\srctag{27}}]{An exact count for eight labelled vertices}\label{gsr:en:27:sec:d9}\label{gsr:en:27:sec:exact}
\srcnote{27}{Section 9}

This section proves the exact assertion in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:27:thm:d2main}. Its only
computer-assisted component is a finite arrangement of rational affine lines,
specified below and in the accompanying certificate. The general theorems
of the preceding sections do not depend on it.

\subsection{Normalization on the regular region}

Take $k=1,d=2$ and characteristic $p\ge11$. On the regular region, $h\ne0$
and $u_2-u_3\ne0$. Independent affine changes in the first and final
coordinates preserve the span of the squarefree monomials and hence
preserve degeneracy. We may normalize
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:normalization}
 h=1,\qquad x_4=0,\qquad u=(r,1,0,r+1),\qquad
 r\notin\{0,1,-1\}.
\end{equation}
The remaining free variables are $x_1,x_2,x_3\in\F_q$.

For each fixed normalized tuple there are exactly
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:normalizationfactor}
 (q-1)\cdot q\cdot(q-1)\cdot q=q^2(q-1)^2
\end{equation}
original tuples: choose the nonzero side, the first-coordinate translation,
the nonzero cross-section scale, and the cross-section translation.
This count is independent of the normalized tuple.

In the order $(j,\eps)=(1,0),(1,1),\ldots,(4,1)$, put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:cbexact}
 c_j=\eta_{0,j}+\eta_{1,j},\qquad b_j=\eta_{1,j}.
\end{equation}
There are exactly $484$ balanced non-intrinsic coefficient classes, of
which $25$ are column-parity and $459$ are not. Of the latter, $15$ are core.
The first two moment constraints for a non-parity array are
\[
 \sum_jc_j=0,\qquad (c_1+c_4)r+(c_2+c_4)=0.
\]
The two remaining constraints are precisely
\begin{align}
 c_1x_1+c_2x_2+c_3x_3&=-\sum_jb_j,\label{gsr:en:27:eq:exactline1}\\
 c_1r x_1+c_2x_2&=-(b_1+b_4)r-b_2-b_4.\label{gsr:en:27:eq:exactline2}
\end{align}
For a regular ratio and an eligible non-parity class these two equations
have rank two, so they describe an affine line in $\F_q^3$.

A core class has $c\in\F_qs$ and is eligible for every regular $r$.
For any other class, at most one ratio can be eligible, unless the
cross-section equation is a nonzero constant and hence impossible. The
complete list of rational exceptional ratios is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:ratios}
 \mathcal E=\{-3,-2,-\tfrac12,-\tfrac13,
                  \tfrac13,\tfrac12,2,3\}.
\end{equation}
Outside this list there are only the $15$ disjoint core lines, containing
$15q$ normalized degenerate base triples.

\subsection{The finite line certificate}

To make the finite calculation unambiguous, the complete algorithm is as
follows. All operations in this paragraph take place over $\Q$.

\begin{enumerate}
\item Enumerate the $3^8$ vectors $\eta\in\{-1,0,1\}^8$ and retain those
with integer coordinate sum zero. Divide coordinatewise by
$e=(1,-1,1,-1,-1,1,-1,1)$ to obtain $t$.
\item Discard constant $t$. Canonicalize every other profile by subtracting
its first entry and dividing by its first nonzero resulting entry. Keep one
$\eta$ for every canonical profile. Exactly $484$ profiles remain.
\item Discard the $25$ column-parity profiles. For each of the remaining
$459$, calculate $c,b$ from \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:cbexact}. Those with
$c_1+c_4=c_2+c_4=0$ are the $15$ core profiles. For every other one, solve
$(c_1+c_4)r+c_2+c_4=0$ and discard impossible or nonregular ratios.
\item For every ratio in \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:ratios}, adjoin all $15$ core profiles to
its eligible profiles. Put the two augmented rows of
\eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:exactline1} and \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:exactline2} in reduced row-echelon form. Identical
row spaces represent the same affine line and are deduplicated.
\item For every pair of distinct lines, stack their augmented equations.
A consistent system of coefficient rank three yields one intersection
point. Deduplicate these points and record \emph{all} lines through each
point. If $\mu_P$ lines meet at $P$, the correction at that point is
$\mu_P-1$.
\end{enumerate}

The exact output is given in Table~\ref{gsr:en:27:tab:lines}. The JSON certificate records
every rational line equation, every intersection point, and its incident
line indices; it is not merely a list of the aggregate numbers.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\caption{The complete rational line enumeration for the exceptional ratios.
The last column is $I_r=\sum_P(\mu_P-1)$.}
\label{gsr:en:27:tab:lines}
\small
\begin{tabular}{r r r r r}
\toprule
$r$ & Additional eligible profiles & Distinct lines $N_r$
 & Intersection points & $I_r$\\
\midrule
$-3$&4&19&18&18\\
$-2$&24&39&32&44\\
$-1/2$&24&39&32&44\\
$-1/3$&4&19&18&18\\
