\begin{lemma}[Stability of the certificate]\label{gsr:en:27:lem:certificate}
For every prime $p\ge11$, reduction of the rational data in
Table~\ref{gsr:en:27:tab:lines} modulo $p$ preserves the distinct ratios, the distinct
lines, every pairwise intersection type, and all intersection-point
multiplicities. The same is true over every extension of $\F_p$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}[Proof by the supplied finite certificate]
The code reconstructs the full data directly from the $3^8$ coefficient
vectors. For every pair of lines it checks both the coefficient matrix and
the augmented matrix. In each matrix it chooses a nonzero maximal-rank
minor. This amounts to $7296$ exact matrix checks across the eight ratios.
It also checks all denominators of line and point coordinates, and for
every pair of distinct recorded intersection points chooses one nonzero
coordinate difference. Finally it checks the differences among all
exceptional ratios and $0,1,-1$.

The prime factors of the selected nonzero minors, nonzero differences, and
denominators are all contained in $\{2,3,5,7\}$. This is verified by exact
integer factorization in the supplied standard-library program. Therefore
none vanishes in characteristic at least $11$. All larger minors are zero
over $\Q$ and remain zero after reduction; the selected minors keep the
rank from dropping. Coefficient and augmented ranks together preserve
whether two lines are parallel, skew, or intersecting. The point-difference
checks keep distinct intersection points from merging.

No new point-line incidence can then appear: if a point from two lines lay
on a third line after reduction, that third line would have to meet one of
the first two. Rank preservation forces a rational intersection already to
exist, and the distinct-point checks force it to be the original common
point. This proves preservation of the complete incidence data. Ranks and
distinctness are unchanged by field extension.

There is also no loss of coefficient profiles in reducing this
certificate. For $p>8$ the balanced class count is $484$, exactly as over
$\Q$. Rational affine equivalences remain valid modulo $p$ (their
normalizing denominators divide $2$); the equal class counts therefore
exclude any new identifications. The coefficients $c_1+c_4,c_2+c_4$ have
absolute value at most $4$, so the classification of their linear equations
introduces no new exceptional ratios or discarded regular ratios for
$p\ge11$. The explicit ratio checks exclude collisions in the listed
ratios themselves.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Scope of the computer-assisted step]
The lemma is a finite, reproducible computation, not an appeal to a
numerical pattern. Its rational input space has $6561$ elements; every
elimination, determinant, incidence test, and factorization is exact. The
code is included so that the table and its exceptional-prime assertion can
be audited or formalized. It has not been checked by a proof assistant.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Counting the union and restoring the parameters}

Distinct affine lines in three-dimensional affine space meet in at most one
point. If their distinct intersection points are $P$, the size of their
union is exactly
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:lineunion}
 N_r q-\sum_P(\mu_P-1)=N_rq-I_r.
\end{equation}
This formula already accounts for multiple intersections; subtracting only
the number of intersecting pairs would be incorrect when three or more
lines concur.

There are $q-3$ regular ratios. For $p\ge11$ all eight exceptional ratios
are distinct and regular. Start with the $15q$ contribution at each regular
ratio, and then add the corrections from Table~\ref{gsr:en:27:tab:lines}. The total number
of normalized degenerate triples, summed over regular ratios, is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:Mexact}
 M(q)=15q(q-3)+112q-248=15q^2+67q-248.
\end{equation}
Since $G=(1-q^{-1})(1-4q^{-1}+3q^{-2})$, the full degeneracy proportion is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:restore}
 \Delta_{1,2}(q)=1-G+\frac{q^2(q-1)^2M(q)}{q^8}
               =1-G+\frac{(q-1)^2}{q^6}M(q).
\end{equation}
Expansion proves \eqref{gsr:fm:27:eq:exactmain}. Equivalently, the integer count is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:integerexact}
 5q^7+8q^6+40q^5-367q^4+563q^3-248q^2.
\end{equation}
This completes the proof of the exact part of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:27:thm:d2main}.

\subsection{An independent subset-sum test}

There is a different way to test degeneracy without using the line
classification. For each labelled vertex, form its column of squarefree
moments. Let $V_S$ be the sum of the columns indexed by a subset $S$ of the
$m$ labels. Every collision $V_S=V_T$ yields a ternary relation by taking the
difference of the two indicator vectors.

\begin{lemma}[Subset-sum criterion]\label{gsr:en:27:lem:subset}
In odd characteristic, an arrangement with $m$ labels is nondegenerate if
and only if its $2^m$ subset moment sums have exactly $2^m-1$ distinct values.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The positive and negative supports of $e$ give one unavoidable collision.
Conversely every ternary relation is a difference of two subset indicator
vectors. If all such relations are intrinsic, their nonzero coefficient
vectors can only be $e$ and $-e$: an intrinsic scalar multiple has all
coordinates nonzero, and an alphabet-valued one in odd characteristic has
scalar $1$ or $-1$. Full support means that the two subsets giving this
collision must be exactly the positive and negative supports of $e$, in
either order. Thus there is exactly one duplicated value and all other
subset sums are distinct. Any further collision supplies a non-intrinsic
relation.
\end{proof}

For the present eight-vertex case the four moment columns are
$(1,x,u,xu)$. The accompanying independent test enumerates every normalized
base triple for every regular ratio at $q=5,7,11,13,17,19$, calculates all
$256$ subset sums, and checks whether their number of distinct values is
less than $255$. Its results are in Table~\ref{gsr:en:27:tab:independent}.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\caption{Independent exhaustive checks, not using the line certificate.
The failed predictions at $5,7$ are intentional negative controls outside
the exact theorem's characteristic range.}
\label{gsr:en:27:tab:independent}
\begin{tabular}{r r r r c}
\toprule
$q$&Base triples examined&Observed $M(q)$&$15q^2+67q-248$&Match\\
\midrule
5&250&250&462&No\\
7&1\,372&900&956&No\\
11&10\,648&2\,304&2\,304&Yes\\
13&21\,970&3\,158&3\,158&Yes\\
17&68\,782&5\,226&5\,226&Yes\\
19&109\,744&6\,440&6\,440&Yes\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

These $212\,766$ exhaustive checks corroborate the formula but do not prove
its validity for untested fields. That validity comes from the exact
rational incidence calculation and Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:27:lem:certificate}, which also
cover all extension fields of the permitted characteristics.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Consequences for an exceptional-arrangement budget\srctag{27}}]{Consequences for an exceptional-arrangement budget}\label{gsr:en:27:sec:d10}\label{gsr:en:27:sec:budget}
\srcnote{27}{Section 10}

\subsection{Absolute and relative counting}

The benefit to Gowers's selection step is a smaller sufficient ambient
field size for making the number of exceptional arrangements negligible.
The printed application of Lemma 15.4 in the proof of Lemma 15.5 charges
its full ambient degeneracy bound against a positive expectation surplus
\cite[p.~565]{gowers}. The present estimates can be inserted wherever that
same absolute count is the only use of Lemma 15.4.

\begin{proposition}[Relative and weighted versions]\label{gsr:en:27:prop:relative}
Let $\mathcal A$ be any collection of arrangement tuples with
$|\mathcal A|\ge\rho q^D$, where $\rho>0$. The fraction of degenerate tuples
in $\mathcal A$ is at most $\Delta_{k,d}(q)/\rho$.

More generally, let $w$ be a nonnegative weight on ambient tuples with
$w\le W$ and $\sum w\ge\rho q^D$. Then the fraction of total weight on
degenerate tuples is at most
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:weighted}
 \frac{W\Delta_{k,d}(q)}{\rho}.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
There are $\Delta_{k,d}(q)q^D$ ambient degenerate tuples. Their contribution
in a subset is no larger, and their weighted contribution is at most $W$
times their number. Divide by the stated lower bound on total mass.
\end{proof}

Thus to guarantee an exceptional fraction at most $\eps$ inside a collection
of relative density at least $\rho$, it suffices to use the ambient budget
$\rho\eps$ in Corollary~\ref{gsr:fm:27:cor:budget}. In the weighted setting use
$\rho\eps/W$. This is an absolute-to-relative transfer, not an assertion
that the hyperplane events remain equidistributed within an arbitrary
structured subset.

\subsection{Quantitative comparison}

The original estimate \eqref{gsr:fm:27:eq:gowers} requires
$q\ge k3^m/\eps$ for an ambient error budget $\eps$. In the new estimate,
only the third term contains the full coefficient-direction inventory.
Since $R_{k,d}\le3^m/2$, that contribution is at most
\[
 \left(\frac{3^{m+1}}{2\eps}\right)^{1/3}
\]
as a sufficient field-size threshold. This statement does not approximate
$R_{k,d}$; it uses only a crude upper bound for it. In particular the
exponential dependence of that \emph{particular} threshold changes from
$3^m$ to at most a constant times $3^{m/3}$. The separate hyperplane threshold
can still dominate.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\caption{Sufficient real thresholds for $\eps=0.01$, rounded up in the last
column. A field with the required characteristic and size must still be
chosen. No assertion of primality is made for the displayed integers.}
\label{gsr:en:27:tab:thresholds}
\begin{tabular}{r r r r}
\toprule
$d$&$k$&Threshold from $k3^m/\eps$&Threshold from \eqref{gsr:fm:27:eq:threshold}\\
\midrule
2&1&656\,100&1\,500\\
2&2&8\,609\,344\,200&1\,800\\
3&1&53\,144\,100&15\,600\\
8&1&185\,302\,018\,885\,184\,100&775\,633\,500\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

For the $d=8$ arrangements used in the selection argument, the first-order
coefficient is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:d8}
 k+2\,585\,444,
\end{equation}
rather than $k3^{16\cdot2^k}$. The precise cubic remainder and the
characteristic requirement must accompany this coefficient in any finite
application; quoting the leading term alone would be insufficient.

\subsection{Limits of the conclusion}

A complete improved bound for Szemer\'edi's theorem would require rerunning
all subsequent parameter choices, preserving every hypothesis, and checking
whether another threshold dominates. This article has not done that.
Neither Table~\ref{gsr:en:27:tab:thresholds} nor \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:d8} is a claim about the best
known global density bound or about a final improvement to Gowers's
Theorem 18.2. The contribution is an explicit replacement for the local
exceptional count and a documented interface for carrying that replacement
further.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Boundary cases and safeguards\srctag{27}}]{Boundary cases and safeguards}\label{gsr:en:27:sec:d11}\label{gsr:en:27:sec:safeguards}
\srcnote{27}{Section 11}

\subsection{Why the hypothesis \texorpdfstring{$d\ge2$}{d >= 2} matters}

When $d=1$, $U$ is the diagonal line $u_1=u_2$. The two rows $s$ and
$s\odot u$ are always dependent. Therefore the rank-two gain underlying
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:27:prop:perclass} is not available.

\begin{proposition}[The endpoint $k=d=1$]\label{gsr:en:27:prop:d1}
In odd characteristic,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:27:eq:d1}
 \Delta_{1,1}(q)=\frac4q-\frac3{q^2}.
\end{equation}
In characteristic two it is $3/q-2/q^2$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
All final coordinates agree. The four first-coordinate labels are
$x_1,x_1+h,x_2,x_2+h$, and the intrinsic relation is
$(1,-1,-1,1)$. Up to affine profile equivalence, the non-intrinsic balanced
ternary relations yield exactly
\[
 h=0,\quad x_1-x_2=0,\quad x_1-x_2=h,\quad x_1-x_2=-h.
\]
For an explicit exhaustion argument, Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:27:thm:profiles} gives
$\Qc_4(p)=4$ for every odd characteristic. Balanced non-intrinsic witnesses
for the four displayed lines belong to four distinct classes, so these
exhaust all possibilities. They are four distinct central lines
in the $(h,x_1-x_2)$-plane and have union size $1+4(q-1)$. The common
translation and final coordinate cancel when taking the fraction. In
characteristic two the last two lines coincide; the same count uses three
lines.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Credit.} In odd characteristic this is source~22's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:22:thm:twocube} at $k=1$; source~22 proves the leading coefficient $(k^2+3k)/p$ for every $k$, which answers the leading-coefficient part of this source's question on the single-pair regime (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:degeneracy}).
\end{writenote}

The endpoint has leading coefficient four in odd characteristic, not the
one that a naive substitution $L_1=0$ into the main theorem would suggest.
This is a genuine change of rank behavior, not a removable technicality.

\subsection{All squarefree moments are required}

After Lemma 15.4, Gowers remarks that his proof uses only the full top
monomial among the monomials containing the last coordinate
\cite[p.~563]{gowers}. The present refinement is deliberately for the
\emph{original all-moments definition}, also encoded in the inspected
repository interface.

The paired constraints \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:pairedmoments} are indispensable here.
For example, when $k=1$, the relation with coefficient $1$ on $(1,0)$ and
$-1$ on $(2,0)$ automatically satisfies the constant moment. Its first and
mixed moments vanish when $x_1=x_2=0$, even if $u_1\ne u_2$. The omitted
final-coordinate moment would be $u_1-u_2$, which is nonzero. Thus removing
that moment changes the individual witness zero sets and defeats the
specific rank argument. No extension to that weakened definition is
claimed.

\subsection{Other distinctions that must be retained}

The field size $q$ and the characteristic $p$ play different roles. Counts
of prime-field coefficient directions can change with $p$ even when $q$ is
arbitrarily large. Modular scalar multiples of the intrinsic relation must
be removed before counting; integer signs alone are not enough. Labelled
parameter counts must not be divided by cube symmetries without analyzing
stabilizers. Finally, the cubic bounds are upper bounds on unions: they do
not assert that all non-core directions have distinct or nonempty
codimension-three loci.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Common base partitions and exact transport of affine fibres\srctag{23}}]{Common base partitions and exact transport of affine fibres}\label{gsr:en:23:sec:d8}
\srcnote{23}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:en:23:glue:sec}

The interpolation step of Lemma~16.10 has two distinct requirements.
Its sampled cross-sections need covers on one common base partition, and
each resulting base box must be extended to boxes in the full product.
The second requirement is substantive: the final axis of the original
product need not have the step of a refined base box.  We prove an
explicit construction which addresses both requirements.  A preliminary
localization from width $m$ to width at least $m/3$ is sufficient; after
that localization, transport preserves the complete width of every
refined base box.  There is no additional power loss at the transport
stage.  The final axes are allowed to be long, which is appropriate once
the fibre functions are already affine on the original final axis.

Throughout this section, $p$ is prime.  A proper progression of length
$n$ is
\[
 P(a,d,n)=\{a+jd:0\leq j<n\}\subseteq\F_p,
\]
with distinct displayed points.  A proper $k$-box is a Cartesian product
of $k$ such progressions with one common step; its width is the minimum
of the displayed lengths.  We assume $k\geq1$.  A multiaffine function
on a box means the restriction of a polynomial over $\F_p$ having degree
at most one in each variable.  This is the convention called
multilinearity in the relevant Section~16 interpolation statements.

\subsection{A sharp elementary localization bound}

\begin{lemma}[Balanced localization]
\label{gsr:en:23:glue:localization}
Let $m\geq4$ be an integer, and set
\[
 B_m=\floor{m/2}+1,
 \qquad L_m=\floor{(2B_m+1)/3}.
\]
Every integer interval of length $n\geq m$ has a partition into intervals
whose lengths lie in $[L_m,B_m]$.  Moreover, $L_m\geq m/3$ and
$L_m\geq2$.  Consequently every proper $k$-box of width at least $m$
has a partition into proper boxes of width at least $L_m$, all having
the original step and all axis lengths at most $B_m$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Put $B=B_m$ and $q=\ceil{n/B}$.  Partition the interval into $q$
consecutive intervals with lengths $\floor{n/q}$ and $\ceil{n/q}$.
Their maximum length is at most $B$.  Since $m\geq4$, we have $B<m$,
and hence $q\geq2$.  If $q=2$, their minimum length is at least
$\floor{m/2}=B-1\geq L_m$.  If $q\geq3$, then
\[
 \frac nq\geq\frac{(q-1)B+1}{q}
 =B-\frac{B-1}{q}\geq\frac{2B+1}{3},
\]
which again gives the required lower bound after taking floors.
If $m$ is even, $2B_m+1=m+3$, and if $m$ is odd,
$2B_m+1=m+2$; these identities show $L_m\geq m/3$ directly.
The inequality $L_m\geq2$ follows from $B_m\geq3$.
For a progression, apply the interval construction to its injective
index parametrization.  Apply this independently to the axes of a box
and take the Cartesian products of the resulting parts.  The index
partitions give exact coverage and disjointness, and each part inherits
properness and the original common step.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Against the formal localization} (checked at HEAD \texttt{2dfe46f44}). \file{Box.short_parent_partition} (\file{Proofs16ShortParents.lean}, line~23) localizes to width at least $m/8$, with axes of length at most half the modulus; the lemma here keeps $L_m\ge m/3$ with axes of length at most $\lfloor m/2\rfloor+1$. Not formalized.
\end{writenote}

\begin{remark}[Scope of the constant]
\label{gsr:en:23:glue:localization-sharp}
The asymptotic constant $1/3$ is optimal for localization by consecutive
index intervals subject to the cap $B_m$.  Indeed, an axis of length
$2B_m+1$ needs at least three parts of length at most $B_m$; one part
therefore has length at most $\floor{(2B_m+1)/3}=L_m$.
This is a sharp statement about this localization problem.  It is not
an optimality claim for every conceivable proof of Lemma~16.10.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Transport with no further width loss}

\begin{lemma}[Integer lift of a contained short progression]
\label{gsr:en:23:glue:integer-step}
Suppose $2(b-1)<p$.  A proper progression
$\{c+je:0\leq j<u\}$ of length $u\geq2$, contained in the residues
$\{0,\ldots,b-1\}$, has a nonzero integer step $a$ such that
\[
 a\equiv e\pmod p,
 \qquad |a|(u-1)\leq b-1.
\]
The natural representatives, in their displayed order, form an ordinary
integer progression of step $a$; $a$ may be negative.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $z_j\in\{0,\ldots,b-1\}$ represent $c+je$.  Every difference
$z_{j+1}-z_j$ lies in $[-(b-1),b-1]$ and represents $e$ modulo $p$.
This interval contains at most one representative of any residue,
because its length is less than $p$.  All these differences are
therefore one integer $a$.  Properness gives $a\ne0$, and the distance
between the two endpoints is $|a|(u-1)\leq b-1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Exact cylindrical transport]
\label{gsr:en:23:glue:transport}
Let $R$ be a proper $k$-box with common step $e$ and width at least
the integer $w\geq2$.  Suppose one axis of $R$ is contained in a proper
progression $U=P(c,d,b)$, where $d\ne0$, and suppose
\[
 2(b-1)<p.
\]
Let $J=P(z,d,n)$ be proper with $n\geq2(b-1)$.  Then $R\times J$
has a partition into proper $(k+1)$-boxes, each with base exactly $R$,
common step $e$, and width at least $w$.

More precisely, if the selected axis of $R$ has length $u$, the number
of parts can be taken to be an integer $t\geq1$ satisfying
\[
 t(u-1)\leq b-1.
\]
The final axes have lengths $\floor{n/t}$ or $\ceil{n/t}$, and thus
have length at least $w$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Pull the selected axis back by the affine bijection
$y\mapsto d^{-1}(y-c)$.  Its carrier lies in $\{0,\ldots,b-1\}$,
it remains proper, and its step is $d^{-1}e$.  By
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:23:glue:integer-step}, this step has a nonzero integer
representative $a$ with $|a|(u-1)\leq b-1$.  Set $t=|a|$.
Since $u\geq w\geq2$,
\[
 tw\leq tu\leq2t(u-1)\leq2(b-1)\leq n.
\]
Partition the index interval $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ of $J$ into its
$t$ residue classes modulo $t$.  Each class is an integer progression
of length $\floor{n/t}$ or $\ceil{n/t}$, at least $w$.
Use increasing order if $a>0$ and decreasing order if $a<0$.
After the map $j\mapsto z+dj$, every final progression has step
$da=e$ in $\F_p$.  It is proper because it is a subsequence of the
injective parametrization of $J$.  These progressions partition $J$.
Their products with $R$ are consequently disjoint proper boxes,
have the asserted width, and cover $R\times J$ exactly.
\end{proof}

The integer-step and transport lemmas also hold in $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$
for composite $N$, provided $d$ is a unit and $2(b-1)<N$.
Their proofs use no inverse of the child step.  Primality is used in
the subsequent interpolation theorem to invert distinct anchor
differences, and in the common-partition construction to obtain a unit
parent step from properness.

\begin{remark}[Why the length separation is real]
\label{gsr:en:23:glue:obstruction}
The factor two in the sufficient condition $n\geq2(b-1)$ cannot be
decreased uniformly when children of width two are permitted.
Let $b\geq3$, choose a prime $p>4b$, and take
\[
 U=\{0,\ldots,b-1\},\quad R=\{0,b-1\},\quad
 J=\{0,\ldots,2b-4\}.
\]
Here $|J|=2(b-1)-1$.  Any box of width at least two contained in
$R\times J$ has base $R$, and its common step must be $b-1$ or
$-(b-1)$.  The final coordinate $b-2$ has neither neighbor at one
of these steps in $J$.  Thus the point $(0,b-2)$ cannot belong to
such a box.  For example, $p=17$, $R=\{0,3\}$ and
$J=\{0,1,2,3,4\}$ already give an obstruction at $(0,2)$.
Taking the Cartesian product of a refined base with the original final
axis, without checking their steps, would overlook this obstruction.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Many slice covers on one base partition}

\begin{theorem}[Common base refinement with exact transport]
\label{gsr:en:23:glue:common-refinement}
Let $P=T\times J$ be a proper $(k+1)$-box of width at least an
integer $m\geq4$.  For $i=1,\ldots,r$, let
$f_i:D_i\to\F_p$ be a partial function with $D_i\subseteq T$.
Fix $a_i\in(0,1]$, $\varepsilon_i\geq0$, and positive integer
$Q_i$.  Assume the following cover statement for each $i$:
for every proper $k$-box $U\subseteq T$, there is a partition of $U$
into proper boxes of width at least $\operatorname{width}(U)^{a_i}$,
a set $G_{i,U}\subseteq U$ satisfying
\[
 |U\setminus G_{i,U}|\leq\varepsilon_i|U|,
\]
and, on each partition cell, at most $Q_i$ multiaffine functions covering
$f_i$ on $D_i\cap G_{i,U}$ in that cell.

Put
\[
 A=\prod_{i=1}^r a_i,
 \qquad \eta=\sum_{i=1}^r\varepsilon_i.
\]
Then there are a common proper-box partition $\mathcal R$ of $T$
and a set $G\subseteq T$ such that
\[
 |T\setminus G|\leq\eta|T|,
 \qquad \operatorname{width}(R)\geq L_m^A
 \geq(m/3)^A\quad(R\in\mathcal R).
\]
On each $R\in\mathcal R$, every $f_i$ is covered on $D_i\cap G\cap R$
by its own list of at most $Q_i$ multiaffine functions.
Furthermore, $P$ has a partition into proper $(k+1)$-boxes with these
bases and width at least $L_m^A$.  The product good set has
$|(T\setminus G)\times J|\leq\eta|P|$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
First use Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:23:glue:localization} to partition $T$ into proper
boxes $T_\alpha$ with widths at least $L_m$, original common step,
and all axis lengths at most $B_m$.  On each $T_\alpha$, apply the
cover assumption for $f_1$.  Apply that for $f_2$ to every resulting
cell, and continue through $f_r$.  This is a sequence of refinements,
not an intersection of independently chosen partitions.

At stage $i$, the current cells partition $T$, so the union of their
exceptional sets has size at most $\varepsilon_i|T|$.  Let $G$ be
the complement of the union of all these stage exceptions.  The union
bound gives the claimed loss.  Every final cell lies in a unique cell
at each earlier stage, so the earlier lists restrict to that final
cell without any increase of their lengths.  This proves simultaneous
coverage on $G$.  Successively raising the width lower bounds to the
powers $a_1,\ldots,a_r$ gives $L_m^A$.

It remains to extend the base cells.  The original common step $d$ is
nonzero because the input axes have length at least four.  Each final
base cell $R$ lies in one of the $T_\alpha$.  Choose an axis of that
parent, of length $b\leq B_m$, which contains the corresponding axis
of $R$.  Since $m\leq p$ and $p$ is odd,
\[
 2(b-1)\leq2\floor{m/2}\leq p-1,
 \qquad 2(b-1)\leq m\leq|J|.
\]
Also $L_m\geq2$ and $A>0$, so $L_m^A>1$; the integer width of $R$
is therefore at least two.  Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:23:glue:transport} with
$w=\ceil{L_m^A}$.  It partitions each $R\times J$ into genuine
common-step boxes without decreasing the desired width.  Different
$R$ have disjoint bases, so these partitions combine to partition $P$.
Finally the product cardinality identity gives
$|(T\setminus G)\times J|=|T\setminus G|\,|J|$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{A formalization candidate, not a formal result} (compared at HEAD \texttt{2dfe46f44}). The formal local lift \file{section16_local_affine_lift_sqrt} (\file{Proofs16LiftWidth.lean}, line~31) has output width $\sqrt{(m/8)^a}/4$; the formal tiling \file{box_product_tiling_of_contained_axis} (\file{Proofs16RelativeSteps.lean}, line~89) needs $v^2\le\operatorname{width}-1$ and produces final axes of length $v-1$ or $v$. The theorem here keeps width $L_m^A\ge(m/3)^A$ because it allows full residue chains as final axes, and it needs no inherited-coordinate hypothesis, which source~19's Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:19:lift:source-corollary} assumes. Whether the formal Section~16 interface (\file{Section16LineCover}, \file{Section16.lean}, line~691) accepts long final axes was not checked at the write; the source itself notes that long axes need not satisfy the Bohr budgets of Lemma~16.6 and argues that they are harmless at Lemma~16.10. No Lean statement of this theorem exists.
\end{writenote}

\subsection{Affine interpolation and endpoint retention}

\begin{theorem}[Geometric gluing of affine class covers]
\label{gsr:en:23:glue:affine-gluing}
Let $P=T\times J$ and $m\geq4$ be as above.  Let
$f:D\to\F_p$, where $D\subseteq P$, and let $E\subseteq P$ satisfy
$|P\setminus E|\leq\varepsilon_0|P|$.
For every $h\in T$, suppose the fibre
\[
 \{x\in J:(h,x)\in D\cap E\}
\]
is partitioned into at most $q$ classes $C_t(h)$, on each of which
$x\mapsto f(h,x)$ agrees with an affine function over $\F_p$.

Fix distinct anchors $x_1,\ldots,x_r\in J$.  Retain each complete
class having at least two anchors, and retain every sampled point in
each other class.  Let $D'$ denote the resulting subset of $D\cap E$,
and assume
\[
 |(D\cap E)\setminus D'|\leq\delta|P|.
\]
For the partial slice functions $f_i(h)=f(h,x_i)$, assume the cover
hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:23:glue:common-refinement}, with parameters
$a_i,\varepsilon_i,Q_i$.

Then there are a set $H\subseteq P$ and a partition of $P$ into proper
boxes of width at least $L_m^A\geq(m/3)^A$, where
$A=\prod_i a_i$, such that
\[
 |P\setminus H|\leq
 \left(\varepsilon_0+\delta+\sum_i\varepsilon_i\right)|P|,
\]
and on every partition cell the restriction of $f$ to $D\cap H$ is
covered by at most
\begin{equation}
 M=\sum_i Q_i+\sum_{i<j}Q_iQ_j
 \label{gsr:en:23:glue:candidate-count}
\end{equation}
multiaffine functions of all $k+1$ coordinates.
If $D'$ instead retains only the complete classes with two anchors,
the first sum in \eqref{gsr:en:23:glue:candidate-count} can be omitted.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Construct the common base partition, its simultaneous good set $G$,
and the full-box partition by Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:23:glue:common-refinement}.
On a base cell $R$, write its $i$th slice list as
$\nu_{i,1},\ldots,\nu_{i,Q_i}$, padding if necessary.
Include the functions $\nu_{i,u}(h)$, independent of $x$, and for
$i<j$ include all functions
\begin{equation}
 F_{i,j,u,v}(h,x)=
 \frac{(x-x_j)\nu_{i,u}(h)+(x_i-x)\nu_{j,v}(h)}{x_i-x_j}.
 \label{gsr:en:23:glue:interpolant}
\end{equation}
The denominator is nonzero, and hence invertible, because the anchors
are distinct and the modulus is prime.  Each displayed function is
multiaffine in the base variables and in $x$; the new variable only
multiplies polynomials that are independent of it.  The number of
candidates is exactly the upper bound in
\eqref{gsr:en:23:glue:candidate-count} before deleting any duplications.

Set
\[
 H=E\cap(G\times J)\setminus((D\cap E)\setminus D').
\]
The union bound gives the asserted ambient loss.  Consider
$(h,x)\in D\cap H$ in one of the full-box cells.  If $x=x_i$ is an
anchor, the slice coverage gives
$f(h,x)=\nu_{i,u}(h)$ for some $u$.
Otherwise $(h,x)$ belongs to a retained affine class with two anchors
$x_i,x_j$.  These two points lie in the domains of their slice
functions, and $h\in G$, so their values are
$\nu_{i,u}(h)$ and $\nu_{j,v}(h)$ for some $u,v$.  The affine function
on this class agrees with \eqref{gsr:en:23:glue:interpolant} at two distinct
points.  Subtracting the two affine functions shows their slopes and
intercepts agree, so they agree at $x$ as well.

The anchors need not lie in the final axis of the particular output
cell.  Both their slice covers and the affine identity refer to the
original class in $J$; restricting the candidate functions to a
smaller final axis does not change that identity.  This is why the
transport step imposes no new sampling or coverage loss.
\end{proof}

The following elementary sampling statement provides a completely
uniform way to supply $D'$.  It is included as a usable quantitative
input, without a claim of a new optimal sampling constant.

\begin{lemma}[Finite-population sampling with retained observations]
\label{gsr:en:23:glue:sampling}
Let $J$ have $n\geq1$ elements, and for every $h$ in a nonempty finite
set $T$ let
$C_1(h),\ldots,C_q(h)$ be disjoint subsets of $J$.
Choose a uniformly random $r$-element subset $S\subseteq J$, with
$0\leq r\leq n$.  Retain every sampled point and every complete class
meeting $S$ in at least two elements.  If $L(S)$ is the total number
of discarded points, summed over $h$, then
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\mathbb E L(S)}{|T|n}
 \leq\left(1-\frac rn\right)
 \min\left\{1,\frac{2q}{r+1}\right\}.
 \label{gsr:en:23:glue:finite-population}
\end{equation}
In particular, for $0<\delta\leq1$ there is one shared sample with
loss at most $\delta|T|n$ and
\[
 r=\min\{n,\ceil{2q/\delta}\}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The assertion is immediate for $r=n$, so suppose $r<n$.
Fix $h$ and then choose a uniform point $y$ outside the random sample.
Equivalently, choose a uniform $(r+1)$-element set $S^+$ and then a
uniform distinguished point $y\in S^+$, and put $S=S^+\setminus\{y\}$.
Write $K_t=|C_t(h)\cap S^+|$.  The point $y$ is discarded precisely
when it belongs to a class for which $K_t\leq2$.  Thus the expected
discarded mass in this fibre is
\[
 \frac{n-r}{r+1}
 \mathbb E\sum_t K_t\mathbf1_{\{K_t\leq2\}}.
\]
Disjointness gives $\sum_tK_t\leq r+1$, while there are at most $q$
terms and each surviving term is at most two.  The sum is at most
$\min\{r+1,2q\}$.  Sum over $h$ and divide by $|T|n$.
An outcome no worse than the average supplies the shared sample.
For the stated choice of $r$, either every point is sampled or
$2q/(r+1)\leq\delta$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Against source~19} (checked at the write). The add-one argument (choose $r+1$ points and mark one) is source~19's Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:19:sampling:marked}, and its Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:19:sampling:anchors} with interpolation order $d=2$ gives lost mass at most $\min\{1,2q/(r+1)\}$ with $r=\min\{n,\lceil2q/\sigma\rceil-1\}$ anchors; source~19 also has the exact minimax and the sharp constant (Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:19:sampling:minimax}, \ref{gsr:en:19:sampling:asymptotic}). The bound here has the extra factor $1-r/n$ because it counts a different loss: sampled points are retained as observations and paid for by the extra $\sum_iQ_i$ candidates of \eqref{gsr:en:23:glue:candidate-count}, while source~19 counts a sampled point of an unrecovered class as lost. Its stated sample size $\lceil2q/\delta\rceil$ is one more than its own inequality needs and than source~19's at the same loss. In this report source~19's theorems are the first print and the sharper results; this lemma is printed as delivered. The formal \file{section16_distinct_sampling_budget} (\file{Proofs16DistinctSampling.lean}, line~117) uses $r\ge6q/\sigma^2$.
\end{writenote}

In particular, short final axes require no separate pruning hypothesis:
when $r=n$, the retained observations recover even singleton classes.
The additional $\sum_i Q_i$ candidates in
\eqref{gsr:en:23:glue:candidate-count} pay for precisely these observations.
For the remaining geometric input scales $m\in\{1,2,3\}$, partition
the whole product into singleton boxes.  On each such box the value of
any partial function is covered by one constant function, with no loss
and width $1\geq(m/3)^A$.  Thus the common-partition mechanism has an
explicit small-scale branch as well as the case $m\geq4$ proved above.

\subsection{An explicit specialization to the Section 16 controls}

\begin{corollary}[Equal slice profiles]
\label{gsr:en:23:glue:profile}
Assume the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:23:glue:affine-gluing}, and suppose
there is at least one anchor ($r\ge1$) and every sampled slice has the
following common profile: an exceptional
fraction $\varepsilon$ permits a width exponent
\[
 a(\varepsilon)=\left(\frac{\gamma\varepsilon}{s}\right)^{D_k s},
 \qquad
 Q(\varepsilon)=a(\varepsilon)^{-1},
 \qquad D_k=2^{2^{k+8}},
\]
with $0<\gamma\leq1$ and $s\geq1$.  Here an integer list length is
bounded by the displayed real number $Q(\varepsilon)$.
Give the $r$ slices a total exceptional fraction $0<\eta\leq1$,
using $\varepsilon=\eta/r$ for each.  Then the final width is at least
\[
 L_m^{A_*}\geq(m/3)^{A_*},
 \qquad A_*=
 \left(\frac{\gamma\eta}{rs}\right)^{D_krs},
\]
and the number of candidates on each cell is at most
\[
 rQ_*+\binom r2Q_*^2,
 \qquad
 Q_*=\left(\frac{rs}{\gamma\eta}\right)^{D_ks}.
\]
The ambient loss is at most $\varepsilon_0+\delta+\eta$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Substitute the slice profile into Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:23:glue:affine-gluing}.
The product of the $r$ identical width exponents is $A_*$.
\end{proof}

There is also a profile uniform in the size of the final axis.  Assume
the displayed slice-cover profile is available for every possible anchor
in $J$, before choosing the sample.
Given the fibre-class bound $q\geq1$ and a loss budget $0<\delta\leq1$, put
$R_0=\ceil{2q/\delta}$.  Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:23:glue:sampling} uses
$r=\min\{|J|,R_0\}$ distinct anchors.  Give each actual slice the
budget $\eta/R_0$, so the total slice loss is at most $\eta$.
Then all final boxes have width at least
\[
 L_m^{A_0},\qquad
 A_0=\left(\frac{\gamma\eta}{R_0s}\right)^{D_kR_0s},
\]
and have at most
\[
 R_0Q_0+\binom{R_0}{2}Q_0^2,\qquad
 Q_0=\left(\frac{R_0s}{\gamma\eta}\right)^{D_ks}
\]
candidates.  Indeed the actual exponent is $a^r\geq a^{R_0}=A_0$
for $a=Q_0^{-1}\in(0,1]$, and the candidate count increases with the
number of slices.  This gives one bound for both $|J|\leq R_0$ and
$|J|>R_0$, without padding a short axis with nonexistent distinct
anchors.

For unequal parameters $s_i\ge1$, with a common $\gamma$ and $D_k$,
the analogous product of width exponents is maximized, subject to
$\sum_i\varepsilon_i=\eta$, by
\[
 \varepsilon_i=\eta\frac{s_i}{S},\qquad S=\sum_i s_i.
\]
Indeed its logarithm is
$D_k\sum_i s_i\log(\gamma\varepsilon_i/s_i)$, a strictly concave
function; its constrained critical point satisfies
$s_i/\varepsilon_i=S/\eta$.  The optimized exponent is
$(\gamma\eta/S)^{D_kS}$, with the exact heterogeneous candidate count
still given by \eqref{gsr:en:23:glue:candidate-count}.

\subsection{Integration boundary and further questions}

The conditional inputs above match the two types of data appearing in
the Lemma~16.10 argument: affine fibre lists from Lemma~16.9 and
multiply multilinear slice covers from the induction hypothesis.
The construction supplies an actual common base partition, all needed
step alignment, exact coverage of the resulting product partition,
and a small-final-axis sampling branch.  The comparison is specifically
with the proper-box formulation used at repository revision
\texttt{65f4e039fc4ad30a8f492e63abde2bcd0740d7c9}.

The existing modules \texttt{Proofs16Interpolation.lean} and
\texttt{Proofs16RelativeSteps.lean} already contain the two-anchor
algebra and related transport tools.  The latter's named product
tiling theorem imposes $v^2\leq\operatorname{width}(R)-1$ and produces
final lengths $v-1$ or $v$.  Our transport theorem has a different
purpose: it permits full residue progressions as final axes and thus
preserves the child width.  Those long axes would not automatically
satisfy the Bohr-linearity budgets needed earlier in Lemma~16.6.
They are legitimate here because the relevant functions have already
been shown affine on each original fibre class.  No new Lean
verification is asserted by the present ordinary mathematical proof.

These results also do not prove the displayed final parameter
comparison in the repository's Lemma~16.10.  The exponent $A_*$ still
depends on the number $r$ of sampled slices, which in turn depends on
the fibre-cover count and the requested loss.  Substituting these
dependencies and comparing them with the claimed
$c(\rho,\gamma,k+1)$ is a separate quantitative obligation.
Nor does a result for proper modular boxes by itself settle the
repository's separate question about nonwrapping progressions in
integer representatives.  The argument above explicitly uses modular
boxes and local affine index pullbacks.

\section{Sources~31 and~29: the Proposition~6.1 endpoint \wtag}\label{gsr:en:sec:endpoint}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the sixth write, 6~October 2026.}}\par
The next nine sections are about the endpoint of Gowers's Proposition~6.1: functions whose derivative spectrum is almost as concentrated as possible, and selectors of derivative frequencies that capture almost all of it. \emph{Logically the chapter continues source~02's Sections~\ref{gsr:en:02:sec:d3}--\ref{gsr:en:02:sec:d5} and source~11's chapter} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:affine}, with its Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:11:cor:prop61}); it is printed here, at the end of Part~II, because no number printed earlier may move. Sections~\ref{gsr:en:31:sec:d2}--\ref{gsr:en:31:sec:d5} and~\ref{gsr:en:31:sec:d9} are source~31, the main source; Sections~\ref{gsr:en:29:sec:d5}--\ref{gsr:en:29:sec:d8} are source~29's, written the same day from the same pin, a second route with cruder constants and with soft and mixed selectors. Neither cites the other. Their introductions are Sections~\ref{gsr:fm:31:sec:d1} and~\ref{gsr:fm:29:sec:d1}; source~31's Sections~6--8 form the next chapter. The notation is in the table at the head of this Part.

\emph{What is proved, in one paragraph.} For every finite abelian group and nonzero $f$, with $\kappa=\norm f_{U^3}^8/\norm f_2^8$ and $\delta=1-\kappa<1/120$, the best squared correlation $F$ with a normalized quadratic phase on a coset satisfies $1-F\le\Rsharp(\delta)=(1-\sqrt{(1+\sqrt{1-4\delta})/2})/2$, and this function is optimal, with equality on $\Z/2\Z$ (source~31's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:31:thm:sharp}; the preliminary bound $20\delta$ is Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:31:thm:coarse}, the quartic envelope Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:31:thm:envelope}). For a selected derivative graph of score $1-\varepsilon$, $\varepsilon\le1/400$, the graph errors are at most $\varepsilon$ and the infidelity at most $(1-\sqrt{1-2\varepsilon})/2$, both separately sharp (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:31:thm:graph}); a weight-defect inequality controls the weights in the $U^2$ and coset topology, and explicit examples show that near equality cannot control them in normalized $L^1$ without complexity assumptions (Section~\ref{gsr:en:31:sec:d9}). Source~29 proves the same endpoint with graph error $20\varepsilon$ and squared distance $22\varepsilon$ for $\varepsilon\le2^{-9}$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:29:jr:joint}), and extends it to soft selectors and to two functions (Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:29:jr:soft}, \ref{gsr:en:29:jr:mixed}); the linear order is sharp (Section~\ref{gsr:en:29:sec:d8}). The qualitative near-extremizer classification is Eisner and Tao's; both sources credit it.

\emph{Relation to the formal statements} (checked at HEAD \texttt{5d4718772}). \file{proposition_6_1} (\file{Sections06\_07.lean}, line~37) has the exact companion \file{proposition_6_1_holds} (\file{Proofs05\_10.lean}, line~505). No near-extremal stability statement is formal; nothing in this chapter is formalized.

\section[{Normalized derivatives and their phase space\srctag{31}}]{Normalized derivatives and their phase space}\label{gsr:en:31:sec:d2}
\srcnote{31}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:en:31:sec:spectrum}

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group, written additively, and let $N=|G|$.
Spatial averages are normalized. Fourier sums over the character group
$\widehat G$ use counting measure. We use the inner product
$\ipthirtyone{u}{v}=\E_xu(x)\overline{v(x)}$, linear in its first argument.
For $f\ne0$, set
\[
 m=\E_x|f(x)|^2,\qquad v=f/\sqrt m,
 \qquad \Delta_hf(x)=f(x)\overline{f(x-h)}.
\]
Write
\begin{align}
 A_f(h,\chi)&=\E_x\Delta_hf(x)\overline{\chi(x)},\label{gsr:en:31:eq:A}\\
 q_f(h,\chi)&=\frac{|A_f(h,\chi)|^2}{m^2},\label{gsr:en:31:eq:q}\\
 \kappa(f)&=\frac{\|f\|_{U^3}^8}{m^4}.
 \label{gsr:en:31:eq:kappa}
\end{align}
The $U^3$ norm uses the usual alternating-conjugation cube average.
Equivalently,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:U3Fourier}
 \|f\|_{U^3}^8=\E_h\sum_{\chi\in\widehat G}|A_f(h,\chi)|^4.
\end{equation}
This follows from the identity $\|g\|_{U^2}^4=\sum_\chi|\widehat g(\chi)|^4$
applied to each derivative. All these expressions include zero directions
and repeated cube vertices.

The phase space is the abelian group $V=G\times\widehat G$, of size $N^2$.
For $z=(h,\chi)$ define the unitary Weyl operator
\[
 W_z=M_\chi T_h,\qquad
 (M_\chi u)(x)=\chi(x)u(x),\quad (T_hu)(x)=u(x-h).
\]
Then $q_f(z)=|\ipthirtyone{v}{W_zv}|^2$. Multiplication of Weyl operators agrees
with addition in $V$ up to a scalar of modulus one. Their commutator is
the alternating bicharacter
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:commutator}
 B((h,\chi),(k,\psi))=\chi(k)\overline{\psi(h)}.
\end{equation}
Thus $W_zW_{z'}=B(z,z')W_{z'}W_z$. This convention fixes every sign used
below; changing all signs consistently leaves the squared coefficients
unchanged.

\begin{lemma}[Mass, critical norm, and self-duality]\label{gsr:en:31:lem:moyal}
For $q=q_f$ one has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:mass}
 0\le q(z)\le1,\qquad \sum_{z\in V}q(z)=N,
 \qquad \kappa=\frac1N\sum_{z\in V}q(z)^2\le1.
\end{equation}
Define the unitary symplectic Fourier transform on $V$ by
\[
 (\mathscr F a)(z)=\frac1N\sum_{y\in V}\overline{B(z,y)}a(y).
\]
Then $\mathscr Fq=q$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The pointwise bound is Cauchy--Schwarz. Parseval in $\chi$ gives
\[
 \sum_{h,\chi}|A_f(h,\chi)|^2
 =\sum_h\E_x|f(x)|^2|f(x-h)|^2=Nm^2.
\]
Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:U3Fourier} gives the third identity, and $q^2\le q$
gives the inequality. In particular this proves the finite critical
inequality $\|f\|_{U^3}\le\|f\|_2$ directly.

For self-duality one can expand the squared coefficient. At
$z=(a,\alpha)$, summation over $\chi$ forces the two base variables
to differ by $a$. With $m=1$ the remaining expression is
\[
 \frac1{N^2}\sum_{h,x}
 f(x)\overline{f(x-h)}\overline{f(x-a)}f(x-a-h)
 \overline{\alpha(h)}.
\]
Substitute $y=x-h$. The two sums separate into a quantity and its
conjugate, giving $|A_f(a,\alpha)|^2=q_f(a,\alpha)$.
Scaling handles general $m$. Character orthogonality proves unitarity
of $\mathscr F$; its kernel satisfies
$B(y,z)=\overline{B(z,y)}$, so it is also self-adjoint.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The weighted derivative-energy inequality}

For a nonnegative weight $w:V\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$ define
\begin{align}
 \Theta_w(f)&=\frac1N\sum_{z\in V}w(z)q_f(z),\label{gsr:en:31:eq:Theta}\\
 \Energythirtyone(w)&=\sum_{z_1+z_2=z_3+z_4}
 w(z_1)w(z_2)w(z_3)w(z_4),\label{gsr:en:31:eq:energy}\\
 \En(w)&=N^{-3}\Energythirtyone(w).
\end{align}
Notice that the energy is divided by $N^3$, not by $|V|^3=N^6$.
The distinction matters because the extremal subgroups of $V$ have size
$N$. When $0\le w\le1$, the score $\Theta_w$ lies in $[0,1]$.

\begin{proposition}[Weighted energy certificate]\label{gsr:en:31:prop:energy}
For every such $w$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:weighted-energy}
 \Theta_w(f)^4\le\kappa(f)\En(w).
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Self-duality and Parseval give
$\Theta_w=N^{-1}\sum_zq(z)\overline{(\mathscr Fw)(z)}$.
Apply Cauchy--Schwarz first with weights $q/N$, whose sum is one,
and then with counting measure:
\[
 \Theta_w^2\le\frac1N\sum_zq(z)|\mathscr Fw(z)|^2,
 \qquad
 \Theta_w^4\le
 \left(\frac1N\sum_zq(z)^2\right)
 \left(\frac1N\sum_z|\mathscr Fw(z)|^4\right).
\]
Fourier orthogonality on the group of size $N^2$ gives
$\sum_z|\mathscr Fw(z)|^4=N^{-2}\Energythirtyone(w)$.
The desired inequality follows.
\end{proof}

This is the single-function specialization of the weighted refinement of
Gowers' Proposition~6.1 in the existing project report \cite{repo31prior}.
We include a short phase-space proof to make the later extraction
independent of normalization conventions. The proposition itself is a
credited prerequisite, not an additional novelty claim.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
Quantity & This article & Unnormalized spatial Fourier sum\\\midrule
Derivative coefficient & $A_f(h,\chi)$ & $N A_f(h,\chi)$\\
Selected graph score & $m^2\Theta_{\ind_\Gamma}$ & $N^3m^2\Theta_{\ind_\Gamma}$\\
Additive graph energy & $\Energythirtyone(\ind_\Gamma)$ & Same ordered quadruple count\\
Critical ratio & $\kappa=\|f\|_{U^3}^8/m^4$ & Dimensionless\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
