\section[{Recovering an extremal subgroup without an exponent loss\srctag{31}}]{Recovering an extremal subgroup without an exponent loss}\label{gsr:en:31:sec:d3}
\srcnote{31}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:en:31:sec:subgroup}

\begin{definition}[Quadratic coset phases]
A unit phase $Q:K\to\T$ on a subgroup $K\le G$ is quadratic if all its
third multiplicative derivatives are one. Equivalently, each derivative
has the form $\Delta_hQ(x)=c_h\chi_h(x)$ with $\chi_h\in\widehat K$,
where $h\mapsto\chi_h$ is a symmetric homomorphism. A normalized
quadratic coset phase on $G$ is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:cosetphase}
 \psi(x)=\left(\frac N{|K|}\right)^{1/2}
 \ind_{x_0+K}(x)Q(x-x_0).
\end{equation}
Let $\Qcos(G)$ denote this collection, including arbitrary constant
unit phases. Its elements have $L^2$ norm one. Define the fidelity
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:fidelity}
 F(f)=\max_{\psi\in\Qcos(G)}|\ipthirtyone{f/\sqrt m}{\psi}|^2.
\end{equation}
\end{definition}

The maximum exists: apart from global phase, there are finitely many
subgroups, cosets, symmetric bicharacters, and quadratic refinements on a
finite group. We will also identify these phases as common eigenvectors
of maximal commuting Weyl families, which gives another finite description.

\subsection{Two elementary closure lemmas}

\begin{lemma}[Projective overlap]\label{gsr:en:31:lem:overlap}
If $q(z),q(z')\ge1-a$, with $0\le a\le1/2$, then
\[
 q(z-z')\ge(1-2a)^2\ge1-4a.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For unit vectors $u_1,u_2$ each having squared overlap at least $1-a$
with the same unit vector $v$, orthogonal decomposition along $v$ gives
\[
 |\ipthirtyone{u_1}{u_2}|\ge(1-a)-a=1-2a.
\]
Apply this to suitable scalar multiples of $W_zv$ and $W_{z'}v$.
Their overlap has squared modulus $q(z-z')$, because Weyl products
differ from the operator with the summed label only by a unit scalar.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Small difference set]\label{gsr:en:31:lem:small-difference}
If a finite nonempty subset $S$ of an abelian group satisfies
$|S-S|<3|S|/2$, then $S-S$ is a subgroup.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Put $D=S-S$. For $d=a-b\in D$, the sets $S-a$ and $S-b$ both lie
in $D$, so their intersection has size greater than $|S|/2$.
Consequently $|S\cap(S+d)|>|S|/2$. For $d,e\in D$, the subsets
of $S$ whose translates by $d$ and by $e$ remain in $S$ must
intersect. Thus $d-e\in D$. Since $D$ is nonempty and closed under
subtraction, it is a subgroup.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Averaging forces exact commutativity}

A subgroup $H\le V$ is called isotropic when $B(h,h')=1$ for all
$h,h'\in H$. The following argument is useful because its lower gap is
$1/2$, independent of the orders of the roots of unity that occur.

\begin{lemma}[Noncommuting subgroup gap]\label{gsr:en:31:lem:twirl}
If $H\le V$ is not isotropic, then for every unit vector $v$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:twirl-gap}
 \frac1{|H|}\sum_{h\in H}|\ipthirtyone{v}{W_hv}|^2\le\frac12.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $P$ be the rank-one orthogonal projection onto $v$, and put
\[
 \rho=\frac1{|H|}\sum_{h\in H}W_hPW_h^*.
\]
Conjugation is an honest group action even though the Weyl operators
themselves form a projective representation. Therefore $\rho$ commutes
with every $W_h$. It is positive, has trace one, and the averaging map
is an orthogonal projection for the Hilbert--Schmidt inner product.
In particular,
\[
 \frac1{|H|}\sum_h|\ipthirtyone{v}{W_hv}|^2
 =\tr(P\rho)=\tr(\rho^2).
\]
Choose $a,b\in H$ with $W_aW_b=\zeta W_bW_a$, where $\zeta\ne1$
has order $r\ge2$. Every eigenspace of $\rho$ is invariant under
both operators. Within a nonzero eigenspace, choose an eigenvector
of $W_a$. Its images under $1,W_b,\ldots,W_b^{r-1}$ have distinct
$W_a$ eigenvalues and are linearly independent. Hence every nonzero
eigenvalue of $\rho$ has multiplicity at least $r$, and is at most
$1/r$. It follows that $\tr(\rho^2)\le(1/r)\tr\rho\le1/2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 34--39]
Source~36's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:thm:bilinear} is the sharp, rank-sensitive form of this lemma over $\F_p^n$ (bound $p^{-r}$ averaged over half-ranks), and source~38 reproves the lemma for odd order (its Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:38:lem:odd-twirl}); neither source~36 nor this source cites the other.
\end{writenote}

\begin{lemma}[Maximal isotropic subgroups and coset phases]
\label{gsr:en:31:lem:classification}
If $H\le V$ is isotropic, then $|H|$ divides $N$. If $|H|=N$, its
common Weyl eigenspaces are one dimensional and their unit vectors are
quadratic coset phases. Conversely every quadratic coset phase has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:extremal-spectrum}
 q_\psi=\ind_H
\end{equation}
for an isotropic subgroup $H$ of size $N$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The operators $W_h$, $h\in H$, commute and are unitary, so they are
simultaneously diagonalizable. Choose a common eigenvector with
eigenvalues $\lambda_h$, and divide $W_h$ by $\lambda_h$.
The resulting operators $U_h$ form an honest representation of $H$:
the projective multiplication scalars cancel by evaluating them on the
chosen eigenvector. For $\gamma\in\widehat H$, the character projector
is
\[
 P_\gamma=\frac1{|H|}\sum_{h\in H}\overline{\gamma(h)}U_h.
\]
The trace of $W_h$ is zero for $h\ne0$: a nonzero translation has
no diagonal entries, and a nontrivial pure modulation has character
sum zero. Thus $\tr P_\gamma=N/|H|$. A projector has integer trace,
proving divisibility; when $|H|=N$, each projector has rank one.

For the structural description let $K$ be the projection of $H$ to
$G$, and let $D=\{\chi:(0,\chi)\in H\}$. Isotropy implies
$D\subseteq K^\perp$. When $|H|=N$, cardinalities give
$D=K^\perp$. The modulation eigenrelations force the support of
a common eigenvector into one coset $x_0+K$. The translation
eigenrelations for $K$ force every point of that coset into the
support and make the modulus constant there. Normalization gives
the amplitude in \eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:cosetphase}. The same eigenrelations say
that every derivative on $K$ is a scalar times a character. Their
commutativity supplies symmetry, and hence vanishing third
multiplicative derivatives.

Conversely take \eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:cosetphase}. For each $h\in K$, its
derivative character on $K$ has exactly $|K^\perp|$ extensions
to $G$. Together these extensions give a subgroup $H\le V$ of
size $|K||K^\perp|=N$. Its Weyl operators preserve the line through
$\psi$ and therefore commute on that line; their scalar
commutators are consequently one. Thus $H$ is isotropic and
$q_\psi=1$ on $H$. The mass identity \eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:mass} forces
$q_\psi=0$ elsewhere.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[A uniform preliminary stability bound]\label{gsr:en:31:thm:coarse}
If $\delta=1-\kappa(f)<1/120$, then there is an isotropic subgroup
$H\le V$ of size $N$, and a common eigenstate $\psi\in\Qcos(G)$,
such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:coarse-fidelity}
 |\ipthirtyone{v}{\psi}|^2\ge1-20\delta.
\end{equation}
One can take
$H=S-S$ with $S=\{z:q_f(z)\ge19/20\}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Since $\sum_zq(z)(1-q(z))=N\delta$, the $q$-mass outside $S$
is at most $20N\delta$. Therefore
\[
 |S|\ge\sum_{z\in S}q(z)\ge(1-20\delta)N.
\]
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:31:lem:overlap} gives $S-S\subseteq\{q\ge4/5\}$,
so $|S-S|\le5N/4$. The strict inequality $\delta<1/120$ makes
$5N/4<3|S|/2$. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:31:lem:small-difference} therefore makes
$H=S-S$ a subgroup. Every coefficient on $H$ is at least $4/5$;
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:31:lem:twirl} makes $H$ isotropic. Also
$|H|\ge|S|>5N/6>N/2$, so divisibility in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:31:lem:classification} gives $|H|=N$.

We have $0\in S$, hence $S\subseteq H$. Expand $v$ in the common
eigenbasis of $H$, and let the squared coefficients be $p_\gamma$.
Character orthogonality gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:Hmass}
 \frac1N\sum_{h\in H}q(h)=\sum_\gamma p_\gamma^2
 \ge1-20\delta.
\end{equation}
The $p_\gamma$ sum to one, so their maximum is at least their
sum of squares. A maximizing basis vector is the required $\psi$.
\end{proof}

The particular threshold $19/20$ is a convenient rational choice.
Optimizing it would slightly enlarge the preliminary range; the final
sharp modulus below comes from a different calculation and is not
limited by the coefficient $20$ as a local error constant.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The sharp local quartic envelope\srctag{31}}]{The sharp local quartic envelope}\label{gsr:en:31:sec:d4}
\srcnote{31}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:en:31:sec:sharp}

Fix a maximal isotropic subgroup $H$ and a common unit eigenvector
$\psi$. Assume $|\ipthirtyone{v}{\psi}|^2=F=1-t$, where $0\le t\le1/6$.
Index the common eigenbasis so that $\psi$ has label zero. Write its
coefficient probabilities as
\[
 p_0=F,\qquad r_\gamma=p_\gamma\ (\gamma\ne0),\qquad
 r_0=0,\qquad \sum_\gamma r_\gamma=t.
\]
The labels form the abelian group $\widehat H$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:tailstatistics}
 A=\sum_\gamma r_\gamma^2,\qquad
 B_0=\sum_\gamma r_\gamma r_{-\gamma},\qquad
 C_0=\sum_{a+b=c}r_ar_br_c.
\end{equation}
We distinguish $B_0$ from the symplectic bicharacter $B$.

\begin{lemma}[Tail estimates]\label{gsr:en:31:lem:tails}
These statistics satisfy
\[
 B_0\le A\le t^2,\qquad
 C_0\le\frac32t(t^2-A),\qquad
 \Energythirtyone(r)\le t^2A.
\]
If $H$ has odd order, then also $B_0\le t^2-A$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The first assertions are Cauchy--Schwarz and nonnegativity. In a relation
$a+b=c$ with $r_ar_br_c>0$, all three labels are nonzero; they cannot
all coincide. At least two of the three pairwise comparisons are
unequal. Summing this observation with weights gives
$2C_0\le3t(t^2-A)$. For the energy bound, Young's inequality gives
$\|r*r\|_2\le\|r\|_1\|r\|_2=t\sqrt A$; alternatively this follows
by applying Cauchy--Schwarz to each convolution sum and then summing.
Finally, in odd order every nonzero label differs from its negative,
so the terms defining $B_0$ occur among the off-diagonal terms
whose total is $t^2-A$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Outside coefficients]\label{gsr:en:31:lem:outside}
For $z\notin H$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:outside}
 q_f(z)\le4F t.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Maximality and nondegeneracy of the symplectic pairing imply
$H^\perp=H$. Therefore $W_z\psi$ and $W_z^*\psi$ are common
eigenvectors with labels different from that of $\psi$, and are
orthogonal to it. It follows that
$s=|\ipthirtyone{W_zv}{\psi}|^2\le t$.
Decompose $v$ and $W_zv$ along the line through $\psi$ and its
orthogonal complement. Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
 |\ipthirtyone{v}{W_zv}|\le\sqrt{Fs}+\sqrt{t(1-s)}.
\]
For $0\le s\le t\le F$ the right side is increasing in $s$.
Its maximum is $2\sqrt{Ft}$, proving the assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Quartic envelope and its deficit]\label{gsr:en:31:thm:envelope}
Under the preceding hypotheses,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:quartic}
 \kappa(f)\le\Phi(t):=(1-t)^4+14(1-t)^2t^2+t^4
 =1-4t+20t^2-32t^3+16t^4.
\end{equation}
More precisely, with $a(t)=6(1-t)^2-10(1-t)t+t^2$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:envelope-deficit}
 \Phi(t)-\kappa(f)
 \ge a(t)(t^2-A)+2(1-t)^2(A-B_0).
\end{equation}
For odd $|G|$ this implies the following bound, strictly smaller when $t>0$:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:odd-envelope}
 \kappa(f)\le(1-t)^4+12(1-t)^2t^2+t^4.
\end{equation}
The universal envelope \eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:quartic} is attained on $G=\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
On $H$ the Weyl coefficient is, up to a unit scalar, the Fourier
transform of $p$. Its fourth moment is the additive energy of $p$.
Classify an additive quadruple by the positions occupied by nonzero
labels. One nonzero position contributes nothing; two opposite-side
positions contribute $4F^2A$; two same-side positions contribute
$2F^2B_0$; three positions contribute $4FC_0$. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:Hfourth}
 \frac1N\sum_{h\in H}q(h)^2
 =F^4+4F^2A+2F^2B_0+4FC_0+\Energythirtyone(r).
\end{equation}
This identity counts positions, so repetitions are already included.
Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:Hmass} without its inequality says that the $q$-mass
outside $H$, divided by $N$, is $1-F^2-A$. Thus
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:31:lem:outside} bounds its fourth-moment contribution by
$4Ft(1-F^2-A)$. Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:31:lem:tails} to obtain
\begin{align*}
 \kappa
 &\le F^4+6Ft^3+4Ft(1-F^2)
       +a(t)A-2F^2(A-B_0).
\end{align*}
Replacing $A$ by $t^2$ in the first occurrence gives exactly
$F^4+14F^2t^2+t^4$. Since $a(t)>0$ for $t\le1/6$, this proves
\eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:quartic} and \eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:envelope-deficit}.

For odd order, put $x=t^2-A$. Then
$A-B_0\ge\max(0,t^2-2x)$. Also
\[
 a(t)-4F^2=2-14t+13t^2\ge1/36>0\quad(0\le t\le1/6).
\]
Minimizing $a(t)x+2F^2\max(0,t^2-2x)$ over $x\ge0$ gives
$2F^2t^2$. Subtract this from \eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:quartic} to obtain
\eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:odd-envelope}. The equality example is calculated below.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 34--39]
The optimal odd-order coefficients, which source~31 leaves open (its Research questions), are source~38's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:38:thm:odd-modulus}: $\varepsilon/4+3\varepsilon^2/16+(\sqrt2/64)\varepsilon^{5/2}+O(\varepsilon^3)$, the fractional term from characters of order three (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:sharpprofile}).
\end{writenote}

\subsection{Exact inversion and optimality}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp local critical-norm stability]\label{gsr:en:31:thm:sharp}
Let $G$ be any finite abelian group and $f\ne0$. If
$\delta=1-\kappa(f)<1/120$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:sharp-fidelity}
 1-F(f)\le\Rsharp(\delta)
 =\frac{1-\sqrt{(1+\sqrt{1-4\delta})/2}}{2}.
\end{equation}
Equivalently,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:sharp-distance}
 \min_{\psi\in\Qcos(G)}\|f/\sqrt m-\psi\|_2^2
 \le2\bigl(1-\sqrt{1-\Rsharp(\delta)}\bigr).
\end{equation}
For every $0\le\delta<1/120$, equality is possible in both formulas.
Thus the functions on their right sides are optimal uniformly over
finite abelian groups on this interval.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:31:thm:coarse} gives $F(f)\ge1-20\delta$.
Choose a maximizing coset phase in \eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:fidelity}, and its
maximal isotropic subgroup from Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:31:lem:classification}.
Then $t=1-F(f)<1/6$, so Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:31:thm:envelope} applies:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:P}
 \delta\ge P(t):=1-\Phi(t)
       =4t(1-t)(1-2t)^2.
\end{equation}
On $[0,1/6]$ one has $P(t)\ge(40/27)t$, so
$t\le27\delta/40<9/1600$. In particular $t$ lies in the
increasing branch of $P$, which extends to
$(2-\sqrt2)/4$.

Set $x=4t(1-t)$. Then $P(t)=x(1-x)$. Inverting first this
quadratic and then $x=4t(1-t)$ on the smaller branches gives
\eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:sharp-fidelity}. Optimizing the constant phase of $\psi$
gives the identity
$\min_\psi\|v-\psi\|_2^2=2(1-\sqrt{F(f)})$,
which proves \eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:sharp-distance}.

For equality, take $G=\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$ and, in the unit
point-mass basis for normalized $L^2$, let
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:qubit}
 v=\sqrt{1-t}\,e_0+\sqrt t\,e_1.
\end{equation}
The four squared Weyl coefficients are
\[
 1,\quad(1-2t)^2,\quad4t(1-t),\quad0.
\]
Their squared sum divided by two is $\Phi(t)$. The coset phases
on this group are the two point masses and, up to global phase,
$(e_0+\zeta e_1)/\sqrt2$ for $\zeta\in\{1,-1,i,-i\}$.
For $t<(2-\sqrt2)/4$, their greatest fidelity with \eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:qubit}
is $1-t$. Taking $t=\Rsharp(\delta)$ proves simultaneous equality.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
\emph{The strongest endpoint result in this report} (checked at the write with the intake's enumeration: on $\Z/p\Z$, $p\le13$, $764$ cases with $\delta<1/120$, $\max(1-F)/\Rsharp(\delta)=0.999997$). It supersedes source~29's constants for the same endpoint (note after its Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:29:jr:joint}) and answers source~02's question on near equality for the function in a sharp form (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:near}); the qualitative statement is Eisner and Tao's, as the source says.
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 54--59]
\emph{The second coefficient in every degree} (source~55, Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:phaseendpoint}): the squared distance on the right of \eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:sharp-distance} is $\delta/4+21\delta^2/64+O(\delta^3)$, and source~55's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:55:thm:main} gives, for $|f|\le1$ and phase polynomials of degree at most $d-1$, the coefficients $2^{1-d}$ and $(q^2-1)/(3q^2)$ on even-order groups ($21/64$ at $d=3$), $(3^d-1)/(2q^2)$ on odd-order groups, both sharp (note there). Source~55 does not cite this source.
\end{writenote}

The local expansion is explicit:
\begin{align}
 \Rsharp(\delta)
 &=\frac\delta4+\frac{5\delta^2}{16}
   +\frac{21\delta^3}{32}+\frac{429\delta^4}{256}
   +O(\delta^5),\label{gsr:en:31:eq:Rseries}\\
 2(1-\sqrt{1-\Rsharp(\delta)})
 &=\frac\delta4+\frac{21\delta^2}{64}
   +\frac{357\delta^3}{512}
   +\frac{29325\delta^4}{16384}+O(\delta^5).
 \label{gsr:en:31:eq:Dseries}
\end{align}
Thus the sharp first-order constant for squared $L^2$ distance is $1/4$.
The error variable is $1-\|f\|_{U^3}^8/\|f\|_2^8$, not
$1-\|f\|_{U^3}/\|f\|_2$; their first-order conversion differs by
a factor of eight.

\subsection{What near equality in the envelope forces}

The deficit formula supplies more than an extremal value. If $t>0$ and
$\Delta=\Phi(t)-\kappa$, then
\[
 \max_{\gamma\ne0}\frac{r_\gamma}{t}
 \ge\frac A{t^2}\ge1-\frac{\Delta}{a(t)t^2}.
\]
So a near-extremizer at a fixed small infidelity has almost all its
remaining mass in a single other common eigenvector. At exact equality,
$A=t^2$ and $B_0=A$ force that other label to have order two.
The outside-coefficient bound must also be saturated wherever the
outside coefficient is nonzero. Conversely, these conditions yield
the universal envelope: a single order-two tail label makes
$C_0=0$, $\Energythirtyone(r)=t^4$, and the saturated outside contribution
is $8F^2t^2$.

This describes the two-state mechanism behind sharpness and explains
the strict improvement in odd order. Formula~\eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:odd-envelope}
is only an upper envelope; determining the optimal odd-order second
coefficient remains an interesting separate problem.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Sharp stability of a selected derivative graph\srctag{31}}]{Sharp stability of a selected derivative graph}\label{gsr:en:31:sec:d5}
\srcnote{31}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:en:31:sec:graph}

Let $B\subseteq G$ and let $\phi:B\to\widehat G$. Its normalized
score is
\[
 T_\phi=\frac1N\sum_{h\in B}q_f(h,\phi(h)).
\]
For the full-domain case $B=G$, this is the square-correlation form
of the input used at Gowers' Proposition~6.1. Partial graphs are
allowed with the same ambient normalization.

\begin{theorem}[Phase error, graph error, and missing directions]
\label{gsr:en:31:thm:graph}
Suppose $T_\phi\ge1-\varepsilon$, where $0\le\varepsilon\le1/400$.
There is a unit quadratic phase $Q$ on all of $G$, with symmetric
derivative homomorphism $L:G\to\widehat G$, such that, with
\[
 t=1-|\ipthirtyone{v}{Q}|^2,\qquad
 z=1-|B|/N,\qquad
 \beta=N^{-1}|\{h\in B:\phi(h)\ne L(h)\}|,
\]
one has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:joint-graph}
 \varepsilon\ge
 2t(1-t)+z\bigl(1-4t(1-t)\bigr)
       +\beta\bigl(1-8t(1-t)\bigr).
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:graph-sharp}
 t\le\Gsharp(\varepsilon):=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-2\varepsilon}}2,
 \qquad z+\beta\le\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
The best phase is attained within the full-support quadratic phases,
and $L$ is the unique homomorphism having at most $\varepsilon N$
disagreements on $B$ when missing directions are also charged.
The two bounds in \eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:graph-sharp} are separately sharp.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Cauchy--Schwarz on the $N$ possible directions, putting zero on
missing ones, gives $\kappa\ge T_\phi^2\ge(1-\varepsilon)^2$.
Thus $\delta\le2\varepsilon-\varepsilon^2<1/120$.
Choose a maximizing coset phase $Q$ by Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:31:thm:sharp},
and let $H$ be its extremal subgroup. The preliminary estimate already
gives $t\le20\delta\le1/10$.

If the projection $K$ of $H$ into $G$ were proper, it would have
density at most $1/2$. For directions outside $K$, every selected
coefficient is outside $H$, so Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:31:lem:outside} gives
\[
 T_\phi\le\frac12+2t(1-t)\le\frac12+\frac15<1-\varepsilon.
\]
This contradiction forces $K=G$. Consequently $H$ is the graph of
a homomorphism $L:G\to\widehat G$, and isotropy makes it symmetric.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:31:lem:classification} makes $Q$ a full-support unit phase.

Put $u=t(1-t)$. On $H$ the coefficient amplitude is the Fourier
transform of the probability vector with atom $1-t$ at zero and
remaining mass $t$. Therefore $q(h,L(h))\ge(1-2t)^2=1-4u$.
Outside $H$ the coefficient is at most $4u$. The full correct-graph
score is $F^2+A\le F^2+t^2=1-2u$. Removing a direction loses at
least $1-4u$; replacing its label by a wrong one loses at least
$1-8u$. This proves \eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:joint-graph}.

Since $t\le1/10$, all these coefficients are positive. Dropping
the last two terms gives the infidelity bound. Also
\[
 z+\beta\le\frac{\varepsilon-2u}{1-8u}\le\varepsilon,
\]
the last step using $\varepsilon\le1/4$. Two distinct homomorphisms
agree on at most half of $G$; two candidates satisfying the stated
error bound would agree on more than half, proving uniqueness.

For phase sharpness take $G=\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$, a nontrivial
character $\chi$, $v=\sqrt{1-t}+\sqrt t\,\chi$, and the correct
trivial derivative graph. Its score is $(1-t)^2+t^2$, and the
best quadratic fidelity is $1-t$ for these small $t$.
For graph sharpness take $v=1$, and change the trivial label to a
nontrivial one on any prescribed set of directions, or omit those
directions. The score is exactly one minus the error fraction.
Rational error fractions are attained on finite groups, which
also establishes uniform sharpness by approximation.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
\emph{Against sources~11 and~29.} Source~11's Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:11:cor:prop61} treats selected graphs over an odd prime $N$ with $|F|\le1$, with error $D_0(1-\alpha^4)N$; the theorem here holds on every finite abelian group, with partial graphs and no amplitude bound. Source~29's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:29:jr:joint} has $20\varepsilon$ and $22\varepsilon$ where this theorem has $\varepsilon$ and $\varepsilon/2+O(\varepsilon^2)$ (note there).
\end{writenote}

The corresponding best squared-distance bound is
$2(1-\sqrt{1-\Gsharp(\varepsilon)})$.
Here $\Gsharp(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon/2+\varepsilon^2/4+
\varepsilon^3/4+O(\varepsilon^4)$.
No claim of joint optimality is made for the coefficient
$1-8t(1-t)$ in \eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:joint-graph}.

The theorem uses no bound on $\|f\|_\infty$ and no restriction on
torsion. On groups with two-torsion the phase must be interpreted
in the finite-difference sense: for example, the phase taking values
$1,i$ on $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$ is quadratic. Restricting quadratic
phases to expressions that divide by two inside the group would
incorrectly exclude such examples.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The correct stability statement for the weights\srctag{31}}]{The correct stability statement for the weights}\label{gsr:en:31:sec:d9}
\srcnote{31}{Section 9}
\label{gsr:en:31:sec:weights}

Near equality of a sharp inequality often suggests closeness to its
extremizers. Here the topology is decisive. Even with the input
function exactly extremal, the weight need not approach the
extremal ray in normalized $L^1$.

Fix $\psi\in\Qcos(G)$ and its maximal isotropic subgroup $H$.
Thus $|H|=N$ and $q_\psi=\ind_H$.
For $w:V\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$ put
\[
 v_H=w|_H,\qquad a=\E_{h\in H}v_H(h),\qquad
 w_{\rm out}=w\ind_{V\setminus H},\qquad
 D=\En(w)-a^4.
\]
For a nonzero coset $z\in V/H$, let
$a_z=N^{-1}\sum_{u\in z}w(u)$.
The notation $v_H$ here denotes a weight, not the normalized input
function $v=f/\sqrt m$ used earlier.

\begin{theorem}[Uniformity and coset-leakage defect]\label{gsr:en:31:thm:weightdefect}
For every nonnegative $w$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:weightdefect}
 D\ge\|v_H-a\|_{U^2(H)}^4
       +\En(w_{\rm out})+4a^2\sum_{z\ne0}a_z^2.
\end{equation}
If $a>0$, equality $D=0$ holds exactly for $w=a\ind_H$.
If $a>0$, $v_H-a$ has at most $R$ nonzero Fourier coefficients, and $w$
occupies at most $J$ nonzero cosets, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:weightL1}
 \frac1N\sum_{u\in V}|w(u)-a\ind_H(u)|
 \le R^{1/4}D^{1/4}+\frac{\sqrt J}{2a}D^{1/2}.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The additive quadruples wholly in $H$ contribute
\[
 \En(w\ind_H)=\sum_{\gamma\in\widehat H}|\widehat v_H(\gamma)|^4
 =a^4+\|v_H-a\|_{U^2(H)}^4.
\]
Those wholly outside contribute $\En(w_{\rm out})$.
Among the remaining nonnegative terms, retain quadruples with
exactly two outside positions, one on each side of the additive
equation. There are four choices of these positions. The two
outside elements must be in the same nonzero coset $z$.
Writing the weights in this coset as a function $w_z$ on $H$,
each choice contributes
\[
 \sum_\gamma|\widehat v_H(\gamma)|^2|\widehat w_z(\gamma)|^2
 \ge a^2a_z^2.
\]
This proves \eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:weightdefect}. If $D=0$ and $a>0$, every
outside mass vanishes and every nontrivial Fourier coefficient
of $v_H$ vanishes, giving the equality classification.

For \eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:weightL1}, Fourier Cauchy--Schwarz and Parseval give
\[
 \|v_H-a\|_1\le\|v_H-a\|_2
 \le R^{1/4}\|v_H-a\|_{U^2(H)}.
\]
For the outside term, Cauchy--Schwarz on the $J$ coset masses and
\eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:weightdefect} gives
$\sum_{z\ne0}a_z\le\sqrt J\,D^{1/2}/(2a)$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Oscillating weights on the exact graph}

\begin{proposition}[No uniform $L^1$ modulus for graph weights]
\label{gsr:en:31:prop:oscillation}
There is no function $\omega(s)\to0$ as $s\downarrow0$ such that
\[
 \En(w)\le(1+s)a^4
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \frac1{aN}\sum_{u\in V}|w(u)-a\ind_H(u)|\le\omega(s)
\]
for all finite abelian groups, even when $w$ is an indicator
supported on $H$ and the input function is the constant phase.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Let $G=\F_2^n\times\F_2^n$, $N=2^{2n}$, and
$b(x,y)=(-1)^{x\cdot y}$. Put $\alpha=N^{-1/2}$,
$H=G\times\{1\}$, and $w(h,\chi)=v_0(h)\ind_{\chi=1}$ with
$v_0=(1+b)/2$. Summing first over $y$ shows
\[
 \widehat b(u,v)=\alpha(-1)^{u\cdot v},\qquad \E b=\alpha.
\]
Thus $a=(1+\alpha)/2$, and exact Fourier calculation gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:bent-counterexample}
 \frac{\En(w)}{a^4}
 =1+\frac{N-1}{N^2(1+\alpha)^4}\longrightarrow1,
 \qquad
 \frac{\E|v_0-a|}{a}=1-\alpha\longrightarrow1.
\end{equation}
The displayed implication would contradict these limits.
\end{proof}

This example spreads its oscillation over many small Fourier
coefficients. Its $U^2$ discrepancy tends to zero, exactly as
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:31:thm:weightdefect} predicts, while its $L^1$ discrepancy
does not. The complexity factor $R^{1/4}$ cannot simply be omitted.

\subsection{Diffuse weight outside the extremal subgroup}

Fix $L>0$. Let $w$ be constant on the $N$ cosets of $H$, with
value one on $H$ and value $L/(N-1)$ on every other coset.
Then $a=1$, and the outside mass divided by $N$ is exactly $L$.
Fourier orthogonality on $V/H$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:diffuse-counterexample}
 \En(w)=\frac{(1+L)^4+(N-1)(1-L/(N-1))^4}{N}
 \longrightarrow1.
\end{equation}
For all sufficiently large $N$, these weights lie in $[0,1]$.
Even $L=N^c$, $0<c<1/4$, makes the defect tend to zero while
the normalized outside mass tends to infinity. This independently
shows why an $\ell^2$ coset profile does not control its $\ell^1$
mass without a bound on the number of occupied cosets.

\subsection{Transfer to a nearby input}

\begin{lemma}[Bounded-weight measurement transfer]\label{gsr:en:31:lem:transfer}
For unit vectors $v,\psi$ and $0\le w\le1$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:transfer}
 |\Theta_w(v)-\Theta_w(\psi)|
 \le\sqrt{1-|\ipthirtyone{v}{\psi}|^4}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The ambiguity arrays $A_v,A_\psi$ have norm one with respect to
normalized $h$ and counting $\chi$ measure, and
\[
 \frac1N\sum_{h,\chi}A_v(h,\chi)\overline{A_\psi(h,\chi)}
 =|\ipthirtyone{v}{\psi}|^2.
\]
Both assertions follow from Parseval and the bijection
$(h,x)\mapsto(x,x-h)$. The arrays of squared moduli, divided by
$N$, are probabilities. For any probabilities $p,q$,
\[
 \frac12\sum|p-q|\le
 \sqrt{1-\left(\sum\sqrt{pq}\right)^2},
\]
by Cauchy--Schwarz applied to
$|\sqrt p-\sqrt q|(\sqrt p+\sqrt q)$.
The triangle inequality bounds the sum of square roots below
by the modulus of the ambiguity-array inner product. Finally
a weight in $[0,1]$ changes its expectation by at most total
variation, proving the lemma.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Exact transfer to a coset phase]\label{gsr:en:31:prop:coset-transfer}
If $\psi\in\Qcos(G)$, let $H$ be its extremal subgroup and let
$p_\gamma$ be the coefficient probabilities of a unit vector $v$
in its common eigenbasis. Label $\psi$ by zero, put
$F=p_0=|\ipthirtyone{v}{\psi}|^2$, and set
$A=\sum_{\gamma\ne0}p_\gamma^2$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:exact-transfer}
 \sup_{0\le w\le1}|\Theta_w(v)-\Theta_w(\psi)|
 =1-\sum_\gamma p_\gamma^2=1-F^2-A\le1-F^2.
\end{equation}
There is no small-error hypothesis in this identity.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The supremum is the total variation distance between the
probabilities $q_v/N$ and $q_\psi/N$. On $H$ one has
$q_v\le1=q_\psi$, while outside $H$ one has $q_\psi=0$.
The mass identity therefore gives
\[
 \frac1{2N}\sum_{z\in V}|q_v(z)-\ind_H(z)|
 =\frac1N\sum_{z\notin H}q_v(z)
 =1-\frac1N\sum_{z\in H}q_v(z)
 =1-\sum_\gamma p_\gamma^2.
\]
Taking $w=\ind_H$ attains this absolute difference.
\end{proof}

For example, suppose $0\le w\le1$, $\delta<1/120$, $0\le\eta<1$, and
\[
 \Theta_w(v)^4\ge(1-\eta)\kappa(v)\En(w).
\]
Choose the coset phase supplied by Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:31:thm:sharp}.
Writing $F=|\ipthirtyone{v}{\psi}|^2$, $a=\Theta_w(\psi)$ and
$\eta_*=[(1-\eta)\kappa]^{-1}-1$, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:coupled-transfer}
 0\le\En(w)-a^4
 \le\eta_*+4(1-F^2-A)\le\eta_*+4(1-F^2).
\end{equation}
Indeed both scores lie in $[0,1]$, so their fourth powers differ
by at most four times their difference. Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:31:thm:weightdefect}
now supplies a coupled stability statement in the topology it
actually controls. Since $1-F\le\Rsharp(\delta)$, a convenient
bound depending only on the two input errors is
\[
 \En(w)-a^4
 \le\frac1{(1-\eta)(1-\delta)}-1
       +8\Rsharp(\delta)-4\Rsharp(\delta)^2.
\]
This is $\eta+3\delta+O(\eta^2+\eta\delta+\delta^2)$ as
both errors tend to zero. The exact transfer identity is sharp;
the subsequent bound for the coupled energy defect is not claimed optimal.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A joint endpoint rigidity theorem\srctag{29}}]{A joint endpoint rigidity theorem}\label{gsr:en:29:sec:d5}\label{gsr:en:29:gmsr:joint}
\srcnote{29}{Section 5}

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group, with normalized averaging on $G$ and
counting measure on its character group $\widehat G$. Put
\[
 A_f(h,\chi)=\mathbb E_x f(x)\overline{f(x-h)}\overline{\chi(x)},
 \qquad
 T_\phi(f)=\mathbb E_h |A_f(h,\phi(h))|^2,
\]
where $\phi:G\to\widehat G$ is arbitrary. A quadratic phase means a map
$Q:G\to\mathbb S^1$ all of whose third multiplicative derivatives are
identically one. Its derivative frequency map is the unique map
$\psi:G\to\widehat G$ for which
$\Delta_h Q=c_h\psi(h)$ with $|c_h|=1$.
This map exists: every first derivative of a quadratic phase has all
second derivatives equal to one, and every such unit phase is a
constant multiple of a character. The latter assertion follows by
evaluating its constant first derivatives at zero. Uniqueness follows
from character orthogonality. The derivative cocycle then shows that
$\psi$ is a homomorphism.

\begin{samepage}
\begin{theorem}[Explicit joint endpoint rigidity]\label{gsr:en:29:jr:joint}
Suppose $f:G\to\mathbb C$ has $m=\mathbb E|f|^2>0$, and
\[
 T_\phi(f)\geq(1-\varepsilon)m^2,
 \qquad 0\leq\varepsilon\leq 2^{-9}.
\]
There are a quadratic phase $Q$, its homomorphic derivative frequency map
$\psi:G\to\widehat G$, and $c\in\mathbb C$ with $|c|^2=m$ such that
\[
 \mathbb P_h[\phi(h)\ne\psi(h)]\leq20\varepsilon,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E_x|f(x)-cQ(x)|^2\leq22\varepsilon m.
\]
The proof also gives
\[
 T_\psi(f)\geq(1-21\varepsilon)m^2.
\]
Thus each displayed conclusion remains valid with the simpler common
constant $24$ where applicable. No restriction on the exponent, rank, or
order of $G$ is imposed, and there is no pointwise bound on $f$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
\emph{Constants superseded the same day by source~31} (checked at the write). With $v=f/\sqrt m$ the normalized score of source~31's Section~\ref{gsr:en:31:sec:d5} is $T_\phi(f)/m^2$, so its Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:31:thm:graph} applies under the hypothesis here on the larger range $\varepsilon\le1/400$: the graph error is at most $\varepsilon$ (here $20\varepsilon$), and the quadratic infidelity at most $(1-\sqrt{1-2\varepsilon})/2=\varepsilon/2+O(\varepsilon^2)$, so the squared distance $\E|f-cQ|^2/m$ is at most $2(1-\sqrt{1-\varepsilon/2+O(\varepsilon^2)})=\varepsilon/2+O(\varepsilon^2)$ (here $22\varepsilon$); both bounds of source~31 are separately sharp. The soft-selector, mixed and distance-equivalence results of Sections~\ref{gsr:en:29:sec:d6}--\ref{gsr:en:29:sec:d7} have no counterpart in source~31. Written from the same pin; neither source cites the other.
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 34--39]
The symmetry step of this section (``Forcing symmetry without dividing by two'', gap $1/2$) has a sharp-in-$p$ vector-space analogue in source~36's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:36:ssc:thm:main} at $k=1$; source~36 does not cite this source.
\end{writenote}
\end{samepage}

\subsection{Amplitude control and projection}

By scaling it suffices to prove the theorem when $m=1$. Parseval gives
\[
 \mathbb E_h\sum_\chi|A_f(h,\chi)|^2
 =\mathbb E_{h,x}|f(x)|^2|f(x-h)|^2=1.
\]
Also, for every $(h,\chi)$, Cauchy--Schwarz gives $|A_f(h,\chi)|\leq1$.
Put $a=|f|$. The triangle inequality, followed by the Fourier identity for
autocorrelations, implies
\begin{align*}
 T_\phi(f)
 &\leq\mathbb E_h\bigl(\mathbb E_xa(x)a(x-h)\bigr)^2\\
 &=\sum_\chi|\widehat a(\chi)|^4
 \leq (\mathbb E a)^2\sum_\chi|\widehat a(\chi)|^2
 =(\mathbb E a)^2.
\end{align*}
The penultimate step uses $a\geq0$, whence
$|\widehat a(\chi)|\leq\widehat a(1)=\mathbb E a$.
Consequently $(\mathbb E a)^2\geq1-\varepsilon$.

Define $q(x)=f(x)/a(x)$ when $a(x)>0$, and choose $q(x)=1$ when $a(x)=0$.
Thus $|q|=1$ and $f=aq$ everywhere. The exact derivative distance is
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb E_{h,x}|\Delta_hf(x)-\Delta_hq(x)|^2
 &=\mathbb E_{x,y}(a(x)a(y)-1)^2\\
 &=2-2(\mathbb E a)^2\leq2\varepsilon.
\end{align*}
In the Hilbert space of functions on $G_h\times G_x$, let $P_\phi$ be the
orthogonal projection which, separately in each $h$-fiber, retains only
the character $\phi(h)$. Then
\[
 \|(I-P_\phi)\Delta f\|_2^2=1-T_\phi(f)\leq\varepsilon.
\]
Both $\Delta f$ and $\Delta q$ have squared Hilbert norm one. Hence
\begin{align*}
 \eta:=1-T_\phi(q)
 &=\|(I-P_\phi)\Delta q\|_2^2\\
 &\leq\bigl(\sqrt\varepsilon+\sqrt{2\varepsilon}\bigr)^2
 =(3+2\sqrt2)\varepsilon<6\varepsilon
\end{align*}
unless $\varepsilon=0$, in which case $\eta=0$.
This use of the complementary projection is what avoids an unnecessary
square-root loss in the final stability rate.

\subsection{The derivative cocycle gives a homomorphism test}

For each $h$ put $a_h=A_q(h,\phi(h))$, and choose a unit scalar $c_h$ such
that $c_h=a_h/|a_h|$ when $a_h\ne0$ (any unit scalar otherwise). Set
$v_h(x)=c_h\phi(h)(x)$ and
\[
 d_h=\|\Delta_hq-v_h\|_2,
 \qquad d_h^2=2(1-|a_h|)\leq2(1-|a_h|^2).
\]
Thus $\mathbb E_h d_h^2\leq2\eta$. The exact cocycle identity is
\[
 \Delta_{h+k}q(x)=\Delta_hq(x)\Delta_kq(x-h).
\]
All factors here and in $v_h$ are unimodular. The triangle inequality
therefore gives
\[
 \|v_{h+k}-v_h\,v_k(\cdot-h)\|_2
 \leq d_{h+k}+d_h+d_k.
\]
If $\phi(h+k)\ne\phi(h)\phi(k)$, the two unit character multiples on
the left have different frequencies and are orthogonal, so their
distance is exactly $\sqrt2$. It follows that
\[
 \mathbf1_{\phi(h+k)\ne\phi(h)\phi(k)}
 \leq\frac12(d_{h+k}+d_h+d_k)^2
 \leq\frac32(d_{h+k}^2+d_h^2+d_k^2).
\]
Averaging proves
\[
 \delta:=\mathbb P_{h,k}[\phi(h+k)\ne\phi(h)\phi(k)]
 \leq9\eta\leq54\varepsilon.
\]

\subsection{A complete elementary repair lemma}

\begin{samepage}
\begin{lemma}[Majority repair]\label{gsr:en:29:jr:repair}
Let $G,H$ be finite abelian groups, written additively, and let
$\phi:G\to H$ satisfy
\[
 \mathbb P_{x,y}[\phi(x+y)\ne\phi(x)+\phi(y)]=\delta<1/6.
\]
There is a homomorphism $\psi:G\to H$ such that
\[
 \mathbb P_x[\phi(x)\ne\psi(x)]\leq\frac\delta{1-2\delta}.
\]
\end{lemma}
\end{samepage}
\begin{proof}
For fixed $x$ define $D_x(y)=\phi(x+y)-\phi(y)$. If both additive tests
on the pairs $(x+y,z-y)$ and $(y,z-y)$ hold, then $D_x(y)=D_x(z)$.
As $(y,z)$ ranges uniformly over $G^2$, each of these two ordered pairs
is uniform in $G^2$. Thus, for every fixed $x$,
\[
 \mathbb P_{y,z}[D_x(y)\ne D_x(z)]\leq2\delta.
\]
Writing $p_b=\mathbb P_y[D_x(y)=b]$, one has
$\sum_b p_b^2\geq1-2\delta$ and hence $\max_b p_b\geq1-2\delta>1/2$.
Let $\psi(x)$ be this unique majority value. For all $x,y$ we have the
identity
\[
 D_{x_1+x_2}(y)=D_{x_1}(x_2+y)+D_{x_2}(y).
\]
For fixed $x_1,x_2$, each of the three terms equals its majority value
except on a set of $y$ of measure at most $2\delta$. Since $6\delta<1$,
some $y$ realizes all three majority values, proving
$\psi(x_1+x_2)=\psi(x_1)+\psi(x_2)$.
If $\phi(x)\ne\psi(x)$, the original additive test at that $x$ fails
on every $y$ with $D_x(y)=\psi(x)$, a set of measure at least
$1-2\delta$. Averaging the original test therefore gives
$\delta\geq(1-2\delta)\mathbb P_x[\phi(x)\ne\psi(x)]$.
\end{proof}

Apply this lemma to $H=\widehat G$ in multiplicative notation.
Since $\varepsilon\leq1/512$, one has $\delta\leq54/512<1/6$, and
\[
 \theta:=\mathbb P_h[\phi(h)\ne\psi(h)]
 \leq\frac{54\varepsilon}{1-108\varepsilon}
 \leq69\varepsilon.
\]
The crude constant is improved using a standard ingredient of
homomorphism testing: every test with exactly one erroneous value must
fail. This observation is classical; see the homomorphism-testing work
of Blum--Luby--Rubinfeld and
Ben-Or--Coppersmith--Luby--Rubinfeld~\cite{blr,benor}.
We include the elementary counting argument to make the constants explicit.

Let $E_x=\mathbf1_{\phi(x)\ne\psi(x)}$. For uniformly independent
$h,k$, the three indicators $E_h,E_k,E_{h+k}$ are pairwise independent,
because each pair among $h,k,h+k$ is uniformly distributed on $G^2$.
If exactly one indicator is one, the homomorphism identity for $\psi$
shows that the test for $\phi$ fails. Inclusion--exclusion therefore gives
\begin{align*}
 \delta
 &\geq\mathbb P[E_h+E_k+E_{h+k}=1]\\
 &=3\theta-6\theta^2
   +3\mathbb P[E_h=E_k=E_{h+k}=1]
 \geq\theta(3-6\theta).
\end{align*}
Substituting the successive upper bounds on $\theta$ yields
\[
 \theta\leq\frac{54\varepsilon}{3-414\varepsilon}
 \leq25\varepsilon,
 \qquad
 \theta\leq\frac{54\varepsilon}{3-150\varepsilon}
 \leq20\varepsilon.
\]
All denominators are positive in the stated range. The numerical
inequalities follow respectively from
\[
 \frac{54}{1-108/512}<69,\qquad
 \frac{54}{3-414/512}<25,\qquad
 \frac{54}{3-150/512}<20.
\]
Since every coefficient of a unit phase has modulus at most one,
\[
 T_\psi(q)\geq T_\phi(q)-\theta
 \geq1-\eta-\theta\geq1-26\varepsilon.
\]

\subsection{Forcing symmetry without dividing by two}

For the repaired homomorphism put
$B(h,k)=\psi(h)(k)$; it is a bicharacter. Write
$\zeta=1-T_\psi(q)\leq26\varepsilon$.
For each $h$ put $u_h(x)=\Delta_hq(x)\overline{\psi(h)(x)}$.
This function is unimodular, its mean is $A_q(h,\psi(h))$, and
\[
 \Delta_k\Delta_hq(x)=B(h,k)\Delta_ku_h(x).
\]
Consequently the following identity, with its average over the entire
increment variable, is exact:
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb E_{k,x}|\Delta_k\Delta_hq(x)-B(h,k)|^2
 &=\mathbb E_{k,x}|\Delta_ku_h(x)-1|^2\\
 &=2-2\operatorname{Re}\mathbb E_{k,x}
                     u_h(x)\overline{u_h(x-k)}\\
 &=2-2|\mathbb E_xu_h(x)|^2.
\end{align*}
Averaging in $h$ gives $2\zeta$. Multiplicative derivatives commute,
so both $B(h,k)$ and $B(k,h)$ can be compared with the same function
$\Delta_k\Delta_hq=\Delta_h\Delta_kq$. The squared triangle inequality
therefore gives
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb E_{h,k}|B(h,k)-B(k,h)|^2
 &\leq2\mathbb E_{h,k,x}|B(h,k)-\Delta_k\Delta_hq(x)|^2\\
 &\quad+2\mathbb E_{h,k,x}|\Delta_h\Delta_kq(x)-B(k,h)|^2\\
 &\leq8\zeta\leq208\varepsilon<1.
\end{align*}
Retaining this averaged identity avoids the loss incurred by estimating
each derivative separately in norm.
If the bicharacter
$D(h,k)=B(h,k)\overline{B(k,h)}$ were nontrivial, its radical
\[
 R=\{h:D(h,k)=1\text{ for all }k\}
\]
would be a proper subgroup, so $|R|/|G|\leq1/2$.
Character orthogonality yields
\[
 \mathbb E_{h,k}D(h,k)=|R|/|G|,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E_{h,k}|B(h,k)-B(k,h)|^2
 =2(1-|R|/|G|)\geq1,
\]
contradiction. Hence $B$ is exactly symmetric.

\subsection{Explicit integration on every finite abelian group}

Write $G=\bigoplus_{i=1}^r(\mathbb Z/n_i\mathbb Z)e_i$, and put
$z_{ij}=B(e_i,e_j)$. Then $z_{ij}=z_{ji}$ and
$z_{ij}^{n_i}=z_{ij}^{n_j}=1$. Choose $u_i\in\mathbb S^1$ with
\[
 u_i^{n_i}=z_{ii}^{-n_i(n_i-1)/2}.
\]
For integer coordinates define
\[
 Q_0\left(\sum_i x_i e_i\right)
 =\prod_i u_i^{x_i}z_{ii}^{x_i(x_i-1)/2}
   \prod_{i<j}z_{ij}^{x_ix_j}.
\]
Increasing $x_i$ by $n_i$ changes the right side by
\[
 u_i^{n_i}z_{ii}^{n_ix_i+n_i(n_i-1)/2}
       \prod_{j\ne i}z_{ij}^{n_ix_j}=1,
\]
so the definition descends to $G$. Direct multiplication shows
\[
 Q_0(x+y)=Q_0(x)Q_0(y)B(x,y).
\]
Therefore
\[
 \Delta_hQ_0(x)=Q_0(h)B(h,h)^{-1}\psi(h)(x).
\]
This explicitly includes even-order groups. The roots $u_i$ may have
order larger than $n_i$, which is precisely why a classical polynomial
with denominator dividing the group exponent must not be imposed.

\subsection{The last Fourier concentration step}

The earlier graph comparison also applies directly to $f$, because
$|A_f(h,\chi)|\leq1$. Thus
\[
 T_\psi(f)\geq T_\phi(f)-\theta\geq1-21\varepsilon.
\]
Let $g=f\overline{Q_0}$. The derivative formula for $Q_0$ gives
\[
 T_\psi(f)
 =\mathbb E_h\left|\mathbb E_xg(x)\overline{g(x-h)}\right|^2
 =\sum_\chi|\widehat g(\chi)|^4.
\]
Parseval gives $\sum_\chi|\widehat g(\chi)|^2=1$. Setting
$p_\chi=|\widehat g(\chi)|^2$ therefore gives
$\max p_\chi\geq\sum p_\chi^2\geq1-21\varepsilon$.
Choose a maximizing $\chi_0$ and a unit scalar $c$ aligned with
$\widehat g(\chi_0)$. Set $Q=Q_0\chi_0$. Multiplication by a character
does not change the derivative frequency map $\psi$. Finally,
\[
 \mathbb E|f-cQ|^2
 =2-2|\widehat g(\chi_0)|
 \leq2\bigl(1-\sqrt{1-21\varepsilon}\bigr)
 \leq22\varepsilon.
\]
For the last inequality it suffices that
$\sqrt{1-21\varepsilon}\geq10/11$, which follows from
$\varepsilon\leq1/512$. Rescaling proves the theorem.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Soft selectors\srctag{29}}]{Soft selectors}\label{gsr:en:29:sec:d6}\label{gsr:en:29:gmsr:soft}
\srcnote{29}{Section 6}

Suppose $w:G\times\widehat G\to[0,\infty)$ satisfies
$\sum_\chi w(h,\chi)\leq1$ for every $h$, and put
\[
 T_w(f)=\mathbb E_h\sum_\chi w(h,\chi)|A_f(h,\chi)|^2.
\]
\begin{samepage}
\begin{theorem}[Joint stability for soft selectors]\label{gsr:en:29:jr:soft}
Suppose $m=\mathbb E|f|^2>0$ and
\[
 T_w(f)\geq(1-\varepsilon)m^2,
 \qquad 0\leq\varepsilon\leq2^{-9}.
\]
There are a unit quadratic phase $Q$, its derivative homomorphism
$\psi:G\to\widehat G$, and a scalar $c$ with $|c|^2=m$, such that
\[
 \mathbb E_x|f(x)-cQ(x)|^2\leq22\varepsilon m,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E_h[1-w(h,\psi(h))]\leq22\varepsilon.
\]
In particular, the common constant $24$ is valid for both errors.
\end{theorem}
\end{samepage}

\begin{proof}
Choose $\phi(h)$ maximizing $|A_f(h,\chi)|^2$. Then $T_\phi(f)\geq T_w(f)$.
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:29:jr:joint} yields $Q,\psi,c$ with the stated function error and
$T_\psi(f)\geq(1-21\varepsilon)m^2$. Since $w(h,\chi)\leq1$,
\begin{align*}
 T_w(f)
 &\leq m^2\mathbb E_h w(h,\psi(h))
       +\mathbb E_h\sum_{\chi\ne\psi(h)}|A_f(h,\chi)|^2\\
 &\leq m^2\mathbb E_h w(h,\psi(h))+21\varepsilon m^2.
\end{align*}
Consequently
\[
 \mathbb E_h[1-w(h,\psi(h))]\leq22\varepsilon,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E_x|f(x)-cQ(x)|^2\leq22\varepsilon m.
\]
\end{proof}
The first defect counts both omitted row mass and mass assigned to
incorrect frequencies. The substochastic row hypothesis is part of the
theorem. A classification of near equality in the unrestricted
relative-energy inequality remains a separate question.

\subsection{Two-sided comparison with distance to the joint model}

\begin{samepage}
\begin{corollary}[Joint distance equivalence]\label{gsr:en:29:jr:distance}
Assume $m=1$. For a unit quadratic phase $Q$ with derivative map $\psi_Q$
define
\[
 d_Q=\inf_{|c|=1}\mathbb E|f-cQ|^2
     =2-2|\langle f,Q\rangle|,
 \qquad
 s_Q=\mathbb E_h[1-w(h,\psi_Q(h))],
 \qquad D=\inf_Q(d_Q+s_Q).
\]
If $\varepsilon=1-T_w(f)\leq2^{-9}$, then
\[
 \frac\varepsilon2\leq D\leq44\varepsilon.
\]
The upper constant $48$ is a convenient simplification. The lower bound
holds for the full range $0\leq\varepsilon\leq1$.
\end{corollary}
\end{samepage}

\begin{proof}
Since $|A_f(h,\chi)|^2\leq1$,
\[
 T_w(f)\geq T_{\psi_Q}(f)-s_Q.
\]
Quadratic twisting and the fourth Fourier moment give
\[
 T_{\psi_Q}(f)\geq|\langle f,Q\rangle|^4
 =(1-d_Q/2)^4\geq1-2d_Q,
\]
where the last inequality is Bernoulli's inequality and uses
$0\leq d_Q\leq2$. Thus $\varepsilon\leq2d_Q+s_Q\leq2(d_Q+s_Q)$.
Taking the infimum gives the lower bound. The two error estimates of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:29:jr:soft} give the upper bound.
\end{proof}

\subsection{An explicit near-maximal \texorpdfstring{$U^3$}{U3} corollary}

\begin{samepage}
\begin{corollary}[Explicit near-maximal $U^3$ stability]\label{gsr:en:29:jr:u3}
If $|f|\leq1$ and $\|f\|_{U^3}^8\geq1-\varepsilon$, where
$0\leq\varepsilon\leq2^{-9}$, there are a unit quadratic phase $Q$
and a unit scalar $c$ such that
\[
 \mathbb E|f-cQ|^2\leq24\varepsilon.
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
Source~31's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:31:thm:sharp} gives the sharp profile without the bound $|f|\le1$: infidelity at most $(1-\sqrt{(1+\sqrt{1-4\delta})/2})/2=\delta/4+O(\delta^2)$ for $\delta=1-\kappa<1/120$, on every finite abelian group.
\end{writenote}
\end{samepage}

\begin{proof}
Put $U=\|f\|_{U^3}^8$ and $m=\mathbb E|f|^2\leq1$, and choose
$\phi(h)$ maximizing $|A_f(h,\chi)|^2$. The Fourier mass of each
derivative satisfies
\[
 \sum_\chi|A_f(h,\chi)|^2
 =\mathbb E_x|f(x)|^2|f(x-h)|^2\leq m.
\]
Consequently
\[
 U=\mathbb E_h\sum_\chi|A_f(h,\chi)|^4\leq mT_\phi(f),
 \qquad T_\phi(f)/m^2\geq U/m^3\geq1-\varepsilon.
\]
Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:29:jr:joint} to $f/\sqrt m$. The already proved inequalities
$U\leq mT_\phi(f)\leq m^3$ imply $m\geq1-\varepsilon$, and the selected phase $Q$ has
$|\langle f/\sqrt m,Q\rangle|\geq\sqrt{1-21\varepsilon}$.
After rotating $Q$, its squared distance to $f$ is at most
\begin{align*}
 m+1-2\sqrt m\sqrt{1-21\varepsilon}
 &=(1-\sqrt m)^2+2\sqrt m(1-\sqrt{1-21\varepsilon})\\
 &\leq\varepsilon^2+22\varepsilon\leq23\varepsilon.
\end{align*}
This implies the stated bound.
\end{proof}
The qualitative near-extremizer conclusion is established mathematics;
the displayed constant and error normalization make it explicit in the
present finite-group setting~\cite{eisnertao}.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Mixed endpoint rigidity and affine derivative selectors\srctag{29}}]{Mixed endpoint rigidity and affine derivative selectors}\label{gsr:en:29:sec:d7}\label{gsr:en:29:gmsr:mixed}
\srcnote{29}{Section 7}

For two functions define
\[
 A_{f,g}(h,\chi)=\mathbb E_x f(x)\overline{g(x-h)}\overline{\chi(x)},
 \qquad
 T_w(f,g)=\mathbb E_h\sum_\chi w(h,\chi)|A_{f,g}(h,\chi)|^2.
\]
Suppose $m_f=\mathbb E|f|^2>0$, $m_g=\mathbb E|g|^2>0$ and the
nonnegative selector satisfies $\sum_\chi w(h,\chi)\leq1$. Then
$T_w(f,g)\leq m_fm_g$ by global Parseval. A mixed endpoint generalization
identifies a common quadratic part and a possible relative linear twist.

\begin{samepage}
\begin{theorem}[Mixed joint endpoint]\label{gsr:en:29:jr:mixed}
If
\[
 T_w(f,g)\geq(1-\varepsilon)m_fm_g,
 \qquad 0\leq\varepsilon\leq2^{-12},
\]
there are a unit quadratic phase $Q$, its derivative homomorphism
$\psi:G\to\widehat G$, a character $\rho\in\widehat G$, and scalars
$c_f,c_g$ with $|c_f|^2=m_f$, $|c_g|^2=m_g$, such that
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb E|f-c_fQ|^2&\leq192\varepsilon m_f,\\
 \mathbb E|g-c_gQ\overline\rho|^2&\leq192\varepsilon m_g,\\
 \mathbb E_h[1-w(h,\rho\psi(h))]&\leq192\varepsilon.
\end{align*}
In particular, the recovered mixed selector is affine rather than
necessarily a homomorphism. The theorem is valid on every finite
abelian group without pointwise bounds on either function.
\end{theorem}
\end{samepage}

\begin{proof}
Normalize $m_f=m_g=1$. Since the total selector mass
$\mathbb E_h\sum_\chi w(h,\chi)$ is at most one, some pair
$(h_0,\chi_0)$ satisfies $|A_{f,g}(h_0,\chi_0)|^2\geq1-\varepsilon$.
Choose a unit scalar $c$ aligned with this coefficient. With
$(T_hu)(x)=u(x-h)$ and $(M_\chi u)(x)=\chi(x)u(x)$, put
\[
 g_0=\overline c\,T_{-h_0}M_{\chi_0}^{-1}f,
 \qquad
 g_0(y)=\overline c\,\overline{\chi_0(y+h_0)}f(y+h_0).
\]
The inverse modulation and translation are unitary, so
\[
 d_0:=\|g-g_0\|_2^2
 =\|f-cM_{\chi_0}T_{h_0}g\|_2^2
 =2-2|A_{f,g}(h_0,\chi_0)|
 \leq2\varepsilon.
\]
Both mixed coefficient arrays have total squared norm one in the
Hilbert space with averaging in $h$ and counting measure in $\chi$.
Parseval also gives their exact squared distance
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb E_h\sum_\chi|A_{f,g}(h,\chi)-A_{f,g_0}(h,\chi)|^2
 &=\mathbb E_{h,x}|f(x)|^2|g(x-h)-g_0(x-h)|^2\\
 &=d_0.
\end{align*}
Since each $w(h,\chi)\leq1$, multiplication by
$\sqrt{1-w(h,\chi)}$ is a contraction. Applying its triangle inequality
to the two coefficient arrays yields
\[
 1-T_w(f,g_0)
 \leq\bigl(\sqrt{1-T_w(f,g)}+\sqrt{d_0}\bigr)^2
 \leq6\varepsilon.
\]
This is again a complementary-projection argument, with a positive
contraction replacing an orthogonal projection.

Set
\[
 w_0(k,\xi)=w(k+h_0,\xi\chi_0).
\]
The rows of $w_0$ still have sum at most one. Direct substitution gives
\[
 A_{f,g_0}(h,\chi)
 =c\chi_0(h_0-h)A_f(h-h_0,\chi\chi_0^{-1}),
\]
and hence $T_{w_0}(f)=T_w(f,g_0)\geq1-6\varepsilon$.
Because $6\varepsilon\leq6\cdot2^{-12}<2^{-9}$, the soft self-endpoint
theorem applies with defect parameter $6\varepsilon$. Using its common
constant $24$, there are $Q,\psi,c_f$ satisfying
\[
 \|f-c_fQ\|_2^2\leq144\varepsilon,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E_k[1-w_0(k,\psi(k))]\leq144\varepsilon.
\]
Define $\rho=\chi_0\psi(h_0)^{-1}$. Replacing $k$ by $h-h_0$ gives
\[
 \psi(h-h_0)\chi_0=\rho\psi(h),
\]
so the last estimate is the claimed affine-selector conclusion, with
the stronger constant $144$.

It remains to identify the second phase. The unitary transform defining
$g_0$ carries $c_fQ$ to
\[
 \overline c\,c_f\overline{\chi_0(x+h_0)}Q(x+h_0).
\]
The derivative identity for $Q$ shows that $Q(x+h_0)/Q(x)$ is a unit
constant times $\psi(h_0)(x)$. Therefore the displayed phase is
$c_gQ(x)\overline{\rho(x)}$ for a unit scalar $c_g$.
The triangle inequality now gives
\[
 \|g-c_gQ\overline\rho\|_2^2
 \leq(\sqrt{d_0}+\|f-c_fQ\|_2)^2
 \leq(\sqrt2+\sqrt{144})^2\varepsilon
 <180\varepsilon<192\varepsilon.
\]
The first function error and selector error already have constant $144$,
so $192$ works for all three. Rescaling proves the stated form.
\end{proof}

At $\varepsilon=0$, this classifies exact mixed absolute endpoints:
both functions have a common quadratic phase, their ratio is a scalar
times a character, and every selector row has total mass one on the
corresponding affine derivative graph. This is an endpoint of the
substochastic selector problem, not a classification of equality in an
arbitrarily normalized weighted-energy inequality.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Sharpness of the error order\srctag{29}}]{Sharpness of the error order}\label{gsr:en:29:sec:d8}\label{gsr:en:29:gmsr:sharpness}
\srcnote{29}{Section 8}

On $G=\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$, let $\chi$ be its nontrivial character and
take $0<t<1/2$,
\[
 f=\sqrt{1-t}+\sqrt t\,\chi,\qquad \psi(h)=1.
\]
Then $\mathbb E|f|^2=1$ and
\[
 T_\psi(f)=(1-t)^2+t^2=1-\varepsilon,
 \qquad \varepsilon=2t(1-t).
\]
The function $f$ is strictly positive. Therefore its best squared
distance to any unit phase is attained by the constant phase one and is
\[
 \inf_{|Q|=1}\mathbb E|f-Q|^2
 =2-2\mathbb E f=2-2\sqrt{1-t}\sim\varepsilon/2.
\]
No $o(\varepsilon)$ replacement of the squared $L^2$ error is possible.
For the selector error, take $f=1$, a nontrivial character $\chi_0$, and
\[
 w(h,\chi)=(1-\varepsilon)\mathbf1_{\chi=1}
            +\varepsilon\mathbf1_{\chi=\chi_0}.
\]
Then $T_w(f)=1-\varepsilon$ and the correct-graph mass defect is exactly
$\varepsilon$. These show optimality of the linear order, not of the
numerical constant $24$.

\paragraph{Relation to established extremizer theory.}
Polynomial-phase near-extremizers of Gowers norms are studied by
Eisner--Tao~\cite{eisnertao}. The mixed array $A_{f,g}$ is a finite
short-time Fourier transform, whose exact minimum-support geometry is
classified by Nicola~\cite{nicola}. The statements here quantify joint
function and selector recovery under the specified substochastic row
hypothesis; the exact extremizer geometries are not asserted as new.

\section[{An elementary weighted energy extraction\srctag{31}}]{An elementary weighted energy extraction}\label{gsr:en:31:sec:d6}
\srcnote{31}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:en:31:sec:bsg}

The high-correlation theorem above recovers essentially all structure
when the score is close to one. We now turn to arbitrary positive
energy. Let $A$ be an abelian group, possibly infinite, and let
$w:A\to[0,1]$ have finite nonempty support. In this section all sums
and energies are unnormalized. Put
\[
 M=\sum_xw(x),\qquad r_w(d)=\sum_xw(x)w(x-d),\qquad
 \Energythirtyone(w)=\sum_dr_w(d)^2.
\]

\begin{theorem}[Elementary weighted BSG]\label{gsr:en:31:thm:bsg}
If $\Energythirtyone(w)\ge cM^3$ with $0<c\le1$, put $\rho=c/(2-c)$.
There is $S\subseteq\supp w$ such that
\begin{align}
 w(S)&\ge\frac{\rho M}{2\sqrt2},\label{gsr:en:31:eq:bsgmass}\\
 |S-S|&\le6912\sqrt2\,\rho^{-5}c^{-4}M.
 \label{gsr:en:31:eq:bsgdifference}
\end{align}
In particular $w(S)\ge cM/8$ and
$|S-S|\le2^{19}c^{-9}M$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $D=\{d:r_w(d)\ge cM/2\}$ and $J=\sum_{d\in D}r_w(d)$.
Since $r_w(d)\le M$ and $\sum_dr_w(d)=M^2$,
\[
 |D|\le2M/c,\qquad
 cM^3\le MJ+(cM/2)(M^2-J),
\]
so $J\ge\rho M^2$. Give $X=\supp w$ the probability measure
$\mu(x)=w(x)/M$, and join $x,y$ when $x-y\in D$. This is a
symmetric relation of weighted edge density at least $\rho$.
Write $N(x)$ for its neighborhood and
$t(x,z)=\mu(N(x)\cap N(z))$.

Call a pair bad when $t(x,z)<\rho^2/12$. Choose $y$ with law
$\mu$ and put $U=N(y)$, $u=\mu(U)$, and
\[
 b=(\mu\times\mu)\{(x,z)\in U^2:(x,z)\text{ is bad}\}.
\]
Double counting and Cauchy--Schwarz give
$\E u^2\ge\rho^2$, whereas $\E b\le\rho^2/12$.
Thus some realization has $u^2-6b\ge\rho^2/2$.
For this realization, $u\ge\rho/\sqrt2$ and $b\le u^2/6$.
Delete from $U$ the points whose bad partners in $U$ have
$\mu$-measure greater than $u/3$. The surviving set $S$ has
measure at least $u-3b/u\ge u/2$, proving \eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:bsgmass}.

For any $a,b\in S$, the common set of good partners has measure
at least $u/3$. For each such partner $z$, the choices
$x\in N(a)\cap N(z)$ and $y\in N(b)\cap N(z)$ each have measure
at least $\rho^2/12$. Consequently the triples $(z,x,y)$ have
total raw weight at least
\[
 \frac{u\rho^4}{432}M^3
 \ge\frac{\rho^5}{432\sqrt2}M^3.
\]
Each raw weight is at most one. The number of these triples is
therefore at least the displayed quantity. The map
\[
 (z,x,y)\longmapsto(a-x,z-x,z-y,b-y)\in D^4
\]
is injective for fixed $a,b$, and its labels determine
$a-b=d_1-d_2+d_3-d_4$. Choose one pair representing each member
of $S-S$; the corresponding label sets are disjoint. Hence
\[
 |S-S|\frac{\rho^5M^3}{432\sqrt2}\le|D|^4,
\]
which proves \eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:bsgdifference}. Finally $\rho\ge c/2$
gives the relaxed constants.
\end{proof}

The proof is a weighted version of the elementary dependent-random-choice
route in the earlier project report. Its purpose is a self-contained
quantitative interface, not an improvement over the strongest general
BSG theorem. Loops and repeated vertices are allowed throughout, so
there is no hidden lower bound on $M$ or on the ambient group size.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A weighted finite form of Gowers' Freiman restriction\srctag{31}}]{A weighted finite form of Gowers' Freiman restriction}\label{gsr:en:31:sec:d7}
\srcnote{31}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:en:31:sec:freiman}

For a map $\phi:B\to\F_p$, a Freiman homomorphism of order $k$
means that every equality between sums of $k$ elements of $B$,
with repetitions allowed, is preserved by $\phi$.
The source domain may be any abelian group.

\begin{theorem}[Restriction through the actual vertical defects]
\label{gsr:en:31:thm:freiman}
Let $p$ be prime, $B$ finite and nonempty, $\phi:B\to\F_p$, and
$\Gamma$ its graph. For $k\ge2$ put
\[
 V_k=\{y\in\F_p:(0,y)\in k\Gamma-k\Gamma\},\qquad q=|V_k|.
\]
For any nonnegative weights $a(x)$ on $B$, there is a subset $B'$
on which $\phi$ is a Freiman homomorphism of order $k$, with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:finite-freiman}
 \sum_{x\in B'}a(x)\ge
 \frac{1+\lfloor p/(kq)\rfloor}{p}\sum_{x\in B}a(x)
 \ge\frac1{kq}\sum_{x\in B}a(x).
\end{equation}
If $q=1$, the whole domain can be retained. If additionally
$|\Gamma-\Gamma|\le C|\Gamma|$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:freiman-C}
 \sum_{B'}a\ge\frac1{kC^{2k+1}}\sum_Ba.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The defect set is symmetric and contains zero. The case $q=1$ is
immediate. Otherwise put $L=\lfloor p/(kq)\rfloor$.
Then $kL\le p/q<p$. Call $d\in\F_p^\times$ bad if
$jd\in V_k\setminus\{0\}$ for some integer $1\le j\le kL$.
There are at most $kL(q-1)$ bad directions: for each pair $(j,y)$
there is a unique possible $d$, because $j$ is nonzero modulo $p$.
If $q<p$, this count is at most $p(q-1)/q<p-1$.
If $q=p$, then $L=0$ since $k\ge2$. In both cases there is a
good nonzero direction $d$.

The progression $P=\{0,d,\ldots,Ld\}$ has $L+1$ distinct points.
Average the weight of $\phi^{-1}(t+P)$ over $t\in\F_p$ and
choose a translate attaining at least the mean. For two $k$-tuples
from this inverse image having the same domain sum, the difference
of their image sums belongs to $V_k$ and equals $jd$ for an
integer $|j|\le kL$. Symmetry and goodness of $d$ force $j=0$.
This proves \eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:finite-freiman}. The case $p=2$ is included.

For the small-difference-set consequence, the map
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:vertical-injection}
 V_k\times\Gamma\longrightarrow(k+1)\Gamma-k\Gamma,
 \qquad(y,\gamma)\longmapsto\gamma+(0,y)
\end{equation}
is injective. The first coordinate determines $\gamma$, because
$\Gamma$ is a graph, and then the second determines $y$.
Pl\"unnecke--Ruzsa gives
\[
 q|\Gamma|\le|(k+1)\Gamma-k\Gamma|
 \le C^{2k+1}|\Gamma|.
\]
Insert this into \eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:finite-freiman}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
\emph{Second route to source~10} (checked at the write). Unweighted, this is source~10's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:10:thm:fibre-extraction}, with the same injection $V_k\times\Gamma\to(k+1)\Gamma-k\Gamma$ ($V_k=H_k$, $q=h_k$) and the same $C^{2k+1}$; source~31 credits Green and Tao and source~03, not source~10, which it could not see (note in Section~\ref{gsr:fm:31:sec:d1}). Source~10's proof uses the progression $\{0,d,\ldots,Ld\}$ with $L=\lfloor(p-2)/(k(h_k-1))\rfloor$, never shorter than the $\lfloor p/(kq)\rfloor$ here: if $kqL'\le p$ with $L'\ge1$, then $k(q-1)L'\le p-kL'\le p-2$. (The intake found it strictly longer in 5,001 of 96,663 cases $p<400$, $k\le8$.) New here: arbitrary nonnegative weights.
\end{writenote}

We use the standard form
$|rA-sA|\le C^{r+s}|A|$ under $|A-A|\le C|A|$.
For completeness, it follows from the minimal-growth lemma of
Petridis \cite{petridis}: choose nonempty $X\subseteq A$ minimizing
$|X-A|/|X|\le C$; that lemma gives $|X-jA|\le C^j|X|$.
Ruzsa's triangle inequality then gives
$|rA-sA|\le|X-rA||X-sA|/|X|\le C^{r+s}|A|$.
This standard theorem is the only imported additive-growth input
in the elementary restriction route.

\paragraph{The exact comparison.}
Gowers' Lemma~7.5, and its corrected repository statement, retain
$|B|/(8kC^{4k})$ in the unweighted case \cite{gowers,repo31}.
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:31:thm:freiman} increases this particular guarantee by
the factor $8C^{2k-1}$ and permits arbitrary nonnegative weights.
The smaller sumset in \eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:vertical-injection} is not a new
mechanism: Green--Tao use the order-eight instance
$\Gamma'+V_8\subseteq9\Gamma'-8\Gamma'$ \cite{greentaoUthree}.
The exact finite factor in \eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:finite-freiman} also records
the rounding and includes the singleton-progression regime.

\Needspace{10\baselineskip}
\subsection{Completing the weighted graph extraction}

\begin{theorem}[A prescribed weight on an exact Freiman graph]
\label{gsr:en:31:thm:weightedgraph}
Let $A$ be an abelian group, let $p$ be prime, and let
$w:A\times\F_p\to[0,1]$ have finite nonempty support, mass
$M$, and $\Energythirtyone(w)\ge cM^3$, where $0<c\le1$.
Suppose each first-coordinate
fiber of its support contains at most $K\ge1$ points. For every
$k\ge2$ there is an order-$k$ Freiman map $\phi:B\to\F_p$
whose graph lies in $\supp w$ and satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:weightedgraph}
 \sum_{x\in B}w(x,\phi(x))
 \ge\frac{c^{20k+11}}{k\,2^{42k+24}K^{2k+2}}M.
\end{equation}
For $k=8$ the fraction is $2^{-363}c^{171}K^{-18}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Use Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:31:thm:bsg} to obtain $S$. In each nonempty fiber
of $S$, retain a point of maximum original weight, forming a
graph $\Gamma_1$. Its weight and cardinality are at least
$\rho M/(2\sqrt2K)$. Its difference set is contained in $S-S$,
so
\[
 \frac{|\Gamma_1-\Gamma_1|}{|\Gamma_1|}
 \le27648K\rho^{-6}c^{-4}
 \le1769472Kc^{-10}<2^{21}Kc^{-10}.
\]
Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:31:thm:freiman} to $\Gamma_1$ with the original
weights and use $\rho/(2\sqrt2)\ge c/8$. The retained fraction is
at least
\[
 \frac c{8K}\cdot\frac1{k(2^{21}Kc^{-10})^{2k+1}},
\]
which is exactly \eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:weightedgraph}.
\end{proof}

The argument can retain the actual maximum-weight graph mass and the
actual defect count $q$ instead of replacing them by $K$ and
$C^{2k+1}$. The displayed theorem is a uniform statement suitable
for a quantitative dependency ledger, not a recommendation to
discard those measured improvements.

\subsection{Order-eight comparison, including the modern input}

For an unweighted graph with domain size $M$ and at least $cM^3$
additive quadruples, $K=1$. The historical Corollary~7.6 gives
$2^{-1882}c^{1164}M$. The elementary route just proved gives
$2^{-363}c^{171}M$.

Reiher--Schoen's theorem \cite[Theorem~1.2]{reiherschoen} gives a subset of
size at least $(1-\eta)\sqrt c\,M$ and difference ratio at most
$2^{33}\eta^{-9}c^{-4}$, for $0<\eta<1/2$.
Combining this published input with Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:31:thm:freiman}
gives the further valid bound
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:modern-restriction}
 \frac{(1-\eta)\eta^{18k+9}}{k\,2^{66k+33}}
 c^{8k+9/2}M.
\end{equation}
For $k=8$, $\eta=1/4$, this is $3\cdot2^{-872}c^{137/2}M$.

\begin{tabular}{@{}L{.36\linewidth}L{.30\linewidth}L{.28\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
Route & Retained domain & Status\\\midrule
Gowers Corollary~7.6 & $2^{-1882}c^{1164}M$ & Historical baseline\\
Elementary weighted route, $K=1$ & $2^{-363}c^{171}M$ & Proved here\\
Reiher--Schoen plus restriction & $3\cdot2^{-872}c^{137/2}M$
 & Derived corollary\\

\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The second and third rows are not uniformly ordered because their
constants differ. One may take their maximum, or optimize
\eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:modern-restriction} in $\eta$. These are local comparisons;
none has been propagated through every stage of Gowers' proof.

\emph{Against source~10} (checked at the write). \section[{Keeping the original derivative correlation\srctag{31}}]{Keeping the original derivative correlation}\label{gsr:en:31:sec:d8}
\srcnote{31}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:en:31:sec:weighted-spectrum}

Now let $G=\F_p$ and identify its characters with $\F_p$.
Continue to use the normalized coefficients $q=q_f\in[0,1]$.
Fix any candidate set $\Omega\subseteq\F_p^2$.
For $0<\tau\le1$ let
\[
 \Delta_\tau=\{(h,r)\in\Omega:q(h,r)\ge\tau\}
\]
be nonempty, and define its profile
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:profile}
 \mu=\frac1p\sum_{\Delta_\tau}q,
 \qquad\nu=\frac1p\sum_{\Delta_\tau}q^2,
 \qquad b=\max_{\Delta_\tau}q,
 \qquad K=\max_h|\{r:(h,r)\in\Delta_\tau\}|.
\end{equation}
These statistics retain more information than a threshold alone.
We have $0<\nu\le\mu\le1$ and $0<b\le1$.
For the unrestricted choice $\Omega=\F_p^2$, one has $b=1$
because $q(0,0)=1$; restricting the candidate set allows $b<1$.

\begin{theorem}[Correlation-preserving exact restriction]
\label{gsr:en:31:thm:spectral-extraction}
Put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:profile-c}
 c=\frac{\nu^4}{b\kappa\mu^3}.
\end{equation}
Then $0<c\le1$. For every $k\ge2$, there is an order-$k$
Freiman map $\phi:B\to\F_p$ with graph contained in
$\Delta_\tau$, for which
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:spectral-retention}
 \frac1p\sum_{h\in B}q_f(h,\phi(h))
 \ge\frac{c^{20k+11}}{k\,2^{42k+24}K^{2k+2}}\mu.
\end{equation}
In the original derivative normalization, both sides are multiplied
by $m^2$. Every selected Fourier coefficient has modulus at least
$m\sqrt\tau$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Take $w=b^{-1}q\ind_{\Delta_\tau}$. It lies in $[0,1]$,
has mass $M=p\mu/b$, and score $\Theta_w=\nu/b$.
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:31:prop:energy} yields
\[
 \Energythirtyone(w)\ge\frac{p^3\nu^4}{b^4\kappa}=cM^3.
\]
For any weight in $[0,1]$, one has
$r_w(d)\le M$ and $\sum_dr_w(d)=M^2$, so
$\Energythirtyone(w)\le M^3$. This proves $c\le1$; positivity is
immediate. Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:31:thm:weightedgraph}, and multiply
its weight conclusion by $b/p$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
\emph{Answers source~02's Subsection~11.1 in a prime-cyclic, bounded-fibre form} (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:structure}): a fixed fraction, explicit in $\mu,\nu,b,\kappa,K$, of the selected derivative correlation survives to an exact Freiman graph. Compatibility across slices is open (Research question in Section~\ref{gsr:fz:31:sec:d11}).
\end{writenote}

For arbitrary $f$ an available fiber cap is
\[
 K\le\left\lfloor\frac{R_f}{\tau}\right\rfloor,
 \qquad R_f=\max_h\frac{\E_x|f(x)|^2|f(x-h)|^2}{m^2}.
\]
If $|f|\le1$, then $R_f\le1/m$. In particular the theorem
does not silently assume that every fiber has total normalized
mass one; that assertion would fail for nonconstant amplitudes.

The information in $\kappa$ survives all the way to an exact Freiman
map. For instance, with the same $\mu,\nu,b,K$, a smaller $\kappa$
increases the certified relative energy $c$. This is a valid
profile comparison, not a claim that these statistics vary
independently for actual functions.

\paragraph{A threshold chosen from the norm.}
For $\Omega=\F_p^2$ and $\tau=\kappa/2$, the discarded fourth-moment contribution is at
most $\tau p^{-1}\sum q=\kappa/2$, so $\nu\ge\kappa/2$.
This gives a completely explicit positive-correlation application
for every nonzero $f$. The profile version is preferable because
the worst-case powers are large and actual spectra can be much
more concentrated. The theorem makes no claim that independently
selected graphs from different higher-order slices agree with one
another; such compatibility is required for further integration.

\section[{A square-root weighted mass theorem from Reiher--Schoen\srctag{31}}]{A square-root weighted mass theorem from Reiher--Schoen}\label{gsr:en:31:sec:dA}
\srcnote{31}{Appendix A}
\label{gsr:en:31:app:thickening}

This appendix records a stronger weighted mass conclusion available
from a published input. It is a derived corollary, not a claim that
weighted BSG or probabilistic thickening is new.

\begin{theorem}[Weighted square-root mass]\label{gsr:en:31:thm:sqrtmass}
Let $A$ be an abelian group and let $w:A\to[0,1]$ have finite
nonempty support, mass $M$, and $\Energythirtyone(w)\ge cM^3$, where
$0<c\le1$. For every $0<\epsilon<1$ there is
$S\subseteq\{x:w(x)\ge\epsilon c/16\}$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:sqrtmass}
 w(S)\ge(1-\epsilon)\sqrt c\,M,
 \qquad |S-S|\le2^{60}\epsilon^{-11}c^{-11/2}|S|.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
We first prove a parameterized version. Choose
$0<\eta<1/2$, $0<\theta<1$, and $0<\tau<c/4$; put $q=c-4\tau$.
Truncate to $v=w\ind_{w\ge\tau}$, and write
$M_v=\sum v$, $e=\Energythirtyone(v)$, and $n=|\supp v|$.
Telescoping the four factors of the energy gives
\[
 e\ge qM^3,\qquad n\le M/\tau,
 \qquad M_v\le M.
\]
Indeed, in a term containing one discarded factor, bound that
factor by $\tau$ and eliminate its coordinate from the additive
equation. The other three sums are at most $M$ each.

For integers $L\to\infty$, independently include each point
$(x,z)\in\supp v\times\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z$ in a random set
$A_L$ with probability $v(x)$. There are deterministic choices
along which
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:31:eq:liftlimits}
 |(A_L)_x|/L\to v(x),\quad |A_L|/L\to M_v,
 \quad\Energythirtyone(A_L)/L^3\to e.
\end{equation}
Here are explicit second-moment estimates establishing this step.
Each fiber size has variance at most $L$. For every base additive
quadruple, all but at most $6L^2$ of its $L^3$ lifted quadruples
have distinct lifted points. Thus
\[
 |\E\Energythirtyone(A_L)-L^3e|\le6n^3L^2.
\]
Two energy monomials have zero covariance unless they share a
lifted point. Choosing the shared positions and the five free
points bounds the number of such pairs by $16n^5L^5$.
Therefore $\operatorname{Var}(\Energythirtyone(A_L))\le16n^5L^5$.
Chebyshev and a finite union bound give \eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:liftlimits},
for example with normalized deviations $L^{-1/4}$.
Only coefficients $1$ and $-1$ were eliminated, so no torsion
restriction is used.

Apply Reiher--Schoen to $A_L$ with its actual
$K_L=|A_L|^3/\Energythirtyone(A_L)$. It gives $B_L\subseteq A_L$ with
\[
 |B_L|\ge(1-\eta)K_L^{-1/2}|A_L|,
 \qquad |B_L-B_L|\le2^{33}\eta^{-9}K_L^4|B_L|.
\]
Pass to a subsequence so that every fiber ratio
$|(B_L)_x|/L$ converges to $b(x)$. Then $0\le b\le v$, and,
with $r=\sum b$,
\[
 r\ge(1-\eta)\sqrt{e/M_v}\ge(1-\eta)\sqrt q\,M.
\]
The difference-set factors tend to a number
$D_0\le2^{33}\eta^{-9}q^{-4}$.

Put $t_0=\theta(1-\eta)\tau\sqrt q$ and
$S=\{x:b(x)\ge t_0\}$. The discarded $b$-mass is at most
$t_0n\le\theta r$. Hence
$w(S)\ge(1-\theta)r$ and $|S|\ge(1-\theta)r$.
For every $z\in S-S$, choose a representing pair of fibers.
The corresponding fiber of $B_L-B_L$ contains their difference
set, of size at least $(t_0-o(1))L$. Summing over distinct base
differences, dividing by $L$, and taking limits gives
$|S-S|\le D_0r/t_0$. Consequently
\begin{align*}
 w(S)&\ge(1-\eta)(1-\theta)\sqrt q\,M,\\
 \frac{|S-S|}{|S|}
 &\le\frac{2^{33}\eta^{-9}}
 {(1-\eta)\theta(1-\theta)\tau q^{9/2}}.
\end{align*}
Finally choose $\eta=\theta=\epsilon/4$ and
$\tau=\epsilon c/16$. The mass factor is
$(1-\epsilon/4)^{5/2}\sqrt c\ge(1-\epsilon)\sqrt c$.
The doubling factor is
\[
 2^{57}\epsilon^{-11}c^{-11/2}(1-\epsilon/4)^{-13/2}
 <2^{60}\epsilon^{-11}c^{-11/2},
\]
as required.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
This bears on source~10's Question~7 (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:energyprop}): it is the weighted form of the Reiher--Schoen retention that question asks to propagate; the propagation itself is not attempted here.
\end{writenote}

Reiher--Schoen's indicator examples already show that the square-root
order of the retained mass cannot in general be replaced by a larger
order with uniform small doubling. The numerical constant and the
doubling exponent in \eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:sqrtmass} are not claimed optimal.
The passage through large auxiliary cyclic groups is an existence
proof; it is not presented as an efficient extraction algorithm.
