\section[{Conventions and finite translation calculus\srctag{30}}]{Conventions and finite translation calculus}\label{gsr:en:30:sec:d2}
\srcnote{30}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:en:30:sec:definitions}

All groups in the mathematical proofs are written additively. The ambient
group $G$ is finite and abelian. The target group $H$ for partial maps may
be any abelian group. For $t\in\T$, let
\[
 \normt t=\min_{n\in\Z}|\widetilde t-n|,
\]
where $\widetilde t$ is any real lift. An additive character means a
homomorphism $\chi:G\to\T$; exponentiation by $2\pi i$ converts this to
the usual unit-circle convention.

\begin{definition}[Rectangular Bohr set]
For characters $\boldsymbol\chi=(\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_r)$ and positive
widths $\boldsymbol\rho=(\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_r)$, define
\[
 B(\boldsymbol\chi,\boldsymbol\rho)
 =\{x\in G:\normt{\chi_i(x)}\le\rho_i\ (1\le i\le r)\}.
\]
When the characters have been fixed, we abbreviate this to
$B(\boldsymbol\rho)$, and write $B(\rho)$ for equal widths. The number
$r$ counts the listed characters, not the algebraic rank of the dual group.
\end{definition}

Every such set contains zero and is symmetric. An empty list of characters
defines the whole group; a maximum over that empty list is defined to be zero. Repeated or zero characters are allowed in the
general theorem, although removing redundant constraints can improve the
numerical bound. Equalities on boundaries are included throughout.

\begin{definition}[Translation defect and exit sets]
For a nonempty subset $B\subseteq G$ and $d\in G$, set
\[
 b_B(d)=\defectthirty_B(d)=|B|-|B\cap(B+d)|,
\]
\[
 E_+(B,d)=\{x\in B:x+d\notin B\},\qquad
 E_-(B,d)=\{x\in B:x-d\notin B\}.
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Elementary identities]\label{gsr:en:30:lem:identities}
For every finite $B$ and $d$,
\[
 |E_+(B,d)|=|E_-(B,d)|=b_B(d)=b_B(-d),
 \qquad |B\mathbin\triangle(B+d)|=2b_B(d).
\]
Moreover, $b_B(d+e)\le b_B(d)+b_B(e)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Translation by $d$ bijects $B\cap(B-d)$ with $(B+d)\cap B$, so these
intersections have equal size. Subtracting each size from $|B|$ proves the
exit identities. Since $B$ and $B+d$ have equal size, the two one-sided
parts of their symmetric difference have equal size, giving its stated
cardinality. Finally,
\[
 B\mathbin\triangle(B+d+e)
 \subseteq (B\mathbin\triangle(B+d))
 \cup ((B+d)\mathbin\triangle(B+d+e)).
\]
Take cardinalities, use translation invariance, and divide by two.
\end{proof}

The estimates below are relative to $|B|$, not to $|G|$. This normalization
is essential: an estimate that first divides an ambient boundary count by
a very small Bohr density recreates the loss we seek to avoid.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The escape-tube inequality\srctag{30}}]{The escape-tube inequality}\label{gsr:en:30:sec:d3}
\srcnote{30}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:en:30:sec:tubes}

\subsection{The combinatorial mechanism}

\begin{lemma}[Two-sided escape packing]\label{gsr:en:30:lem:abstract-tube}
Let $B\subseteq G$, $d\in G$, and $m\ge1$ be an integer. Suppose
\begin{align*}
 x\in E_+(B,d)&\Longrightarrow x+jd\notin B\quad(1\le j\le2m),\\
 x\in E_-(B,d)&\Longrightarrow x-jd\notin B\quad(1\le j\le2m).
\end{align*}
If all the sets $E_+(B,d)+jd$ and $E_-(B,d)-jd$, $1\le j\le m$, lie
in a set $U$, then
\[
 2m\,b_B(d)\le |U\setminus B|.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
All the displayed translates avoid $B$ by hypothesis. We prove they are
pairwise disjoint. If
$x+jd=y+kd$ with $x,y\in E_+$ and $j>k$, then
$y=x+(j-k)d\in B$, contrary to non-return after the exit at $x$.
The negative-sign case is identical. If
$x+jd=y-kd$ with $x\in E_+$ and $y\in E_-$, then
$y=x+(j+k)d\in B$, and $2\le j+k\le2m$, again a contradiction.
Thus the $2m$ translates are disjoint. Each has cardinality $b_B(d)$ by
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:30:lem:identities}. Their union lies in $U\setminus B$.
\end{proof}

The use of both signs is important. A one-sided argument loses a factor
of two. The non-return statement is needed through $2m$, not merely
through $m$, because a collision between opposite tubes uses $j+k$.

\subsection{A boundary exit from a narrow Bohr strip cannot return quickly}

\begin{lemma}[Coordinate non-return]\label{gsr:en:30:lem:nonreturn}
Let $B=B(\boldsymbol\rho)$ with $0<\rho_i\le1/4$, and suppose
$\normt{\chi_i(d)}\le\rho_i/(2m)$ for every $i$. Then the non-return
hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:30:lem:abstract-tube} hold.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Take $x\in E_+(B,d)$ and choose a character witnessing $x+d\notin B$.
Write $\rho=\rho_i$. There are real representatives
\[
 a\in[-\rho,\rho],\qquad
 v\in[-\rho/(2m),\rho/(2m)]
\]
for $\chi_i(x)$ and $\chi_i(d)$. Since
$|a+v|\le3\rho/2\le3/8<1/2$, the failure at $x+d$ means
$|a+v|>\rho$ without any ambiguity from reduction modulo one.

Suppose first that $a+v>\rho$. Then $v>0$, and for $1\le j\le2m$,
\[
 \rho<a+jv\le\rho+2m|v|\le2\rho\le1/2.
\]
Therefore $\normt{\chi_i(x+jd)}>\rho$, so $x+jd\notin B$.
The case $a+v<-\rho$ is the same with signs reversed. Applying the
argument to $-d$ proves the assertion for $E_-$. The endpoint
$2\rho=1/2$ causes no problem, because $1/2>\rho$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Intrinsic fixed-radius escape inequality]\label{gsr:en:30:thm:intrinsic}
Let $G$ be a finite abelian group, $B=B(\boldsymbol\chi,
\boldsymbol\rho)$, and $0<\rho_i\le1/4$. Suppose $m\ge1$ is an integer
and $v_i=\normt{\chi_i(d)}\le\rho_i/(2m)$ for every $i$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:30:eq:intrinsic}
 2m\,b_B(d)
 \le |B(\boldsymbol\rho+m\boldsymbol v)|-|B|
 \le |B(3\boldsymbol\rho/2)|-|B|.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $x\in B$ and $1\le j\le m$, the triangle inequality on $\T$ gives
\[
 \normt{\chi_i(x\pm jd)}\le\rho_i+jv_i\le\rho_i+mv_i.
\]
Consequently every tube in Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:30:lem:abstract-tube} lies in
$B(\boldsymbol\rho+m\boldsymbol v)$. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:30:lem:nonreturn} supplies
non-return and hence the first inequality. The coordinatewise inequality
$\rho_i+mv_i\le3\rho_i/2$ gives the second.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Degenerate steps and torsion]
If $d$ belongs to the common kernel of the characters, then $B+d=B$ and
both exit sets are empty. No division by a step size is used in the proof.
Similarly, no lower bound for the order of $d$ is assumed: if an orbit is
too short to support a nonempty exit tube, the non-return argument forces
the relevant exit set to be empty. This is why the theorem does not need
prime modulus or invertible frequencies.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Packing the enlarged Bohr set\srctag{30}}]{Packing the enlarged Bohr set}\label{gsr:en:30:sec:d4}
\srcnote{30}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:en:30:sec:packing}

\begin{lemma}[Three-cell packing]\label{gsr:en:30:lem:packing}
If $0<\rho_i\le1/4$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:30:eq:packing}
 |B(3\boldsymbol\rho/2)|\le3^r|B(\boldsymbol\rho)|.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For each point of the enlarged Bohr set, choose the unique coordinate
representative in $[-3\rho_i/2,3\rho_i/2]\subset(-1/2,1/2)$.
Partition this interval into three disjoint intervals of diameter at most
$\rho_i$; assign the two internal endpoints consistently to one adjacent
interval. The coordinate partitions give at most $3^r$ cells.

Fix a nonempty cell and a point $y$ in it. If $x$ is another point in the
same cell, the chosen coordinate representatives differ by at most
$\rho_i$. Their difference represents $\chi_i(x-y)$, so $x-y\in B$.
The map $x\mapsto x-y$ is injective. Thus each cell has at most $|B|$
points, proving the bound. This argument counts points of $G$ itself;
it does not incorrectly discard multiplicities of the character map.
\end{proof}

This is a finite box-packing argument of the same general kind as the
standard Bohr doubling estimates; compare Green's Lemma 4.1
\cite{greenregularity}. The constants here correspond specifically to enlargement
by $3/2$ and cells of width $\rho_i$.

\begin{theorem}[Rank-explicit fixed-radius invariance]\label{gsr:en:30:thm:main}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:30:thm:intrinsic},
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:30:eq:main}
 |B\cap(B+d)|\ge
 \left(1-\frac{3^r-1}{2m}\right)|B|.
\end{equation}
More precisely, with
\[
 D_B=\frac{|B(3\boldsymbol\rho/2)|}{|B|},
\]
one may replace $3^r-1$ by $D_B-1$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Combine Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:30:thm:intrinsic} and Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:30:lem:packing}, then
use $|B\cap(B+d)|=|B|-b_B(d)$.
\end{proof}

If $D_B=1$, every shift satisfying the step hypothesis in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:30:thm:intrinsic} is an exact period of $B$. This conclusion
requires no logarithm or division by $D_B-1$.

\begin{corollary}[A floor-free relative-step estimate]\label{gsr:en:30:cor:floorfree}
Let $t=\max_i\normt{\chi_i(d)}/\rho_i$. If $0<t<1/2$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:30:eq:floorfree}
 \frac{b_B(d)}{|B|}
 \le\min\left\{1,\frac{D_B-1}{2\lfloor1/(2t)\rfloor}\right\}
 \le\min\left\{1,\frac{(D_B-1)t}{1-2t}\right\}.
\end{equation}
In particular, the last numerator can be replaced by $(3^r-1)t$.
For $t=0$, the defect is zero.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Set $m=\lfloor1/(2t)\rfloor\ge1$. Then $t\le1/(2m)$, so the main
theorem applies. The inequality $m\ge1/(2t)-1$ yields
$1/(2m)\le t/(1-2t)$, and the trivial bound is $b_B(d)\le|B|$.
If $t=0$, all the characters vanish on $d$ and $B+d=B$.
\end{proof}

The original estimate \eqref{gsr:fm:30:eq:old} has relative-step coefficient
$2^{r+1}r\rho^{1-r}$. The new small-step coefficient is at most $3^r-1$,
independent of the width. The comparison is asserted on the new theorem's
range $0<\rho\le1/4$, not on all the larger range allowed by the old
declaration. There is no hidden replacement of $\rho$ by a regular radius.

\subsection{Exact sharpness of the two constituent estimates}

\begin{proposition}[The factor $2m$ is sharp]\label{gsr:en:30:prop:tube-sharp}
For every positive even integer $a$ and integer $N>4a$, let
$G=\Z/N\Z$, $\chi(x)=x/N$, $\rho=a/N$, $d=1$, and $m=a/2$.
Then equality holds in the first and second inequalities of
\eqref{gsr:en:30:eq:intrinsic}.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The set $B$ is the interval $[-a,a]$ modulo $N$, of size $2a+1$.
Translation by one has defect one. Since $a$ is even, the enlarged set is
$[-3a/2,3a/2]$, of size $3a+1$. Thus
\[
 2m b_B(1)=a=(3a+1)-(2a+1).
\]
Also $\rho+m/N=3\rho/2$, so the direction-dependent enlargement is exactly
the $3/2$ enlargement.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The packing factor $3^r$ is sharp]\label{gsr:en:30:prop:packing-sharp}
For every $r\ge1$ there is a Bohr set with widths at most $1/4$ for which
$|B(3\boldsymbol\rho/2)|=3^r|B|$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Take $G=(\Z/p\Z)^r$ with $p\ge5$, coordinate characters, and
$\rho_i=3/(4p)$. Then $B=\{0\}$, whereas the enlarged set consists of
the coordinate choices $0,1,-1$, because its width is $9/(8p)$.
Its cardinality is $3^r$.
\end{proof}

The two sharpness assertions concern different inequalities. The packing
example has no nonzero qualifying coordinate step. It does \emph{not}
show that the combined coefficient $3^r-1$ in the translation estimate is
optimal. Confusing these two forms of sharpness would erase the main
remaining extremal problem.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Dense-domain extension of partial homomorphisms\srctag{30}}]{Dense-domain extension of partial homomorphisms}\label{gsr:en:30:sec:d5}
\srcnote{30}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:en:30:sec:extension}

\begin{definition}[Freiman homomorphism]
A map $\psi:A\to H$ is a Freiman homomorphism of order $k$ if every
relation $a_1+\cdots+a_k=b_1+\cdots+b_k$ with entries in $A$, allowing
repetition, implies
$\psi(a_1)+\cdots+\psi(a_k)=\psi(b_1)+\cdots+\psi(b_k)$.
\end{definition}

\subsection{A general finite-pattern intersection bound}

\begin{lemma}[Tree intersection budget]\label{gsr:en:30:lem:tree}
Let $A\subseteq B\subseteq G$, $|B|>0$, and let $v_1,\ldots,v_q\in G$
be positions indexed by the vertices of a tree $T$. Repeated positions
are permitted. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:30:eq:tree}
 \left|\bigcap_{j=1}^q(A+v_j)\right|
 \ge |B|-\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E(T)}b_B(v_i-v_j)-q|B\setminus A|.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Root the tree and adjoin vertices so that every new vertex has a previously
adjoined parent. The intersection initially has size $|B|$. Adjoining
$B+v_j$ can remove at most
\[
 |(B+v_i)\setminus(B+v_j)|=b_B(v_i-v_j)
\]
points, where $i$ is the parent, since the current intersection is already
a subset of $B+v_i$. Sum these losses. Finally, replacing each translate
of $B$ by the corresponding translate of $A$ removes at most
$|B\setminus A|$ points for each of the $q$ labels. This remains valid
when two positions coincide; then it merely overcounts a possible loss.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
This is source~12's Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:12:lem:tree} (there with $S_i$ in place of $A$ and normalized losses $b_B$; here $b_B$ counts points).
\end{writenote}

\subsection{Difference maps and higher-order relations}

\begin{theorem}[Dense-domain extension with an explicit budget]
\label{gsr:en:30:thm:extension}
Let $A\subseteq B\subseteq G$, $|B|>0$, and suppose
\[
 |B\setminus A|\le\eta|B|,\qquad
 b_B(d)\le\kappa|B|\quad(d\in C),
\]
where $\eta,\kappa\ge0$. Let $\psi:A\to H$ be a Freiman homomorphism
of order two. For an integer $k\ge2$, assume
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:30:eq:extension-budget}
 (2k-1)\kappa+2k\eta<1.
\end{equation}
Then $C\subseteq A-A$, and there is a uniquely induced map
$\psi_1:C\to H$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:30:eq:induced}
 \psi_1(x-y)=\psi(x)-\psi(y)
 \quad(x,y\in A,\ x-y\in C).
\end{equation}
This map is a Freiman homomorphism of order $k$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $d\in C$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:30:eq:pair-overlap}
 |A\cap(A+d)|\ge(1-\kappa-2\eta)|B|>0,
\end{equation}
because \eqref{gsr:en:30:eq:extension-budget} implies $\kappa+2\eta<1$.
Thus every $d$ is a difference of two elements of $A$.
If $x-y=x'-y'$, then $x+y'=x'+y$. The order-two hypothesis gives
$\psi(x)-\psi(y)=\psi(x')-\psi(y')$. This proves existence and uniqueness
of the induced difference map.

Now take $d_1,\ldots,d_k,e_1,\ldots,e_k\in C$ with equal total sums.
Form two paths from zero to their common sum: their successive edge labels
are $d_1,\ldots,d_k$ and $e_1,\ldots,e_k$. Regard the initial and final
vertices as shared, but keep all other path positions as distinct formal
labels even if their group values coincide. There are $2k$ vertex labels.
Removing one edge from the resulting formal cycle gives a tree with
$2k-1$ edges. Each edge displacement is a member of $C$ or its negative;
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:30:lem:identities} gives the same defect for both signs.

Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:30:lem:tree} to the negatives of these positions. The
intersection contains at least
\[
 [1-(2k-1)\kappa-2k\eta]|B|>0
\]
points. Choose $x$ in it. Then every vertex $x+v$ of both translated paths
lies in $A$. Along every edge, \eqref{gsr:en:30:eq:induced} identifies its image
increment with the corresponding value of $\psi_1$. Telescoping along
the two paths gives
\[
 \sum_{i=1}^k\psi_1(d_i)
 =\psi\left(x+\sum_i d_i\right)-\psi(x)
 =\sum_{i=1}^k\psi_1(e_i).
\]
This is the required order-$k$ relation.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
\emph{Against source~12} (checked at the write). In source~12's notation $\varepsilon$ is the missing fraction $\eta$ here and $\kappa$ the normalized loss. Its Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:sharp-extension} gives the order-two conclusion under $3\eta+2\kappa<1$, sharp on its whole boundary (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:sharpness}); the budget here at $k=2$ is $4\eta+3\kappa<1$, which implies it. For higher order compare source~12's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:higher}. The budget here is a weaker form of source~12's results, which source~30 does not cite.
\end{writenote}

For $k=2$, the budget is $3\kappa+4\eta<1$. This is exactly the
four-vertex mechanism in Gowers's proof of Corollary 10.11, with the
parameters left visible. We do not claim that this sufficient budget is
necessary. For example, extra structure of $A$ or of the map can make the
extension valid far beyond what a union bound certifies.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Larger Bohr neighborhoods in Corollary 10.11\srctag{30}}]{Larger Bohr neighborhoods in Corollary 10.11}\label{gsr:en:30:sec:d6}
\srcnote{30}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:en:30:sec:larger}

\begin{corollary}[Margin-preserving radius]\label{gsr:en:30:cor:margin}
Let $r\ge1$, $0<\rho\le1/4$, and $B=B(\boldsymbol\chi,\rho)$ in a
finite abelian group. Suppose $A\subseteq B$, $|A|\ge7|B|/8$, and
$\psi:A\to H$ is a Freiman homomorphism of order two. Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:30:eq:margin-radius}
 \zeta_{\mathrm{margin}}=\frac{\rho}{8(3^r-1)},\qquad
 C_{\mathrm{margin}}=B(\boldsymbol\chi,\zeta_{\mathrm{margin}}).
\end{equation}
Then $C_{\mathrm{margin}}\subseteq A-A$ and the induced difference map is
a Freiman homomorphism of order two on $C_{\mathrm{margin}}$.
Moreover, for every $d\in C_{\mathrm{margin}}$,
\[
 |B\cap(B+d)|\ge\frac78|B|,\qquad
 |A\cap(A+d)|\ge\frac58|B|.
\]
For each four-term relation on $C_{\mathrm{margin}}$, the four-vertex
construction has at least $|B|/8$ possible base points in $A$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Set $m=4(3^r-1)$, which is a positive integer. The shift radius in
\eqref{gsr:en:30:eq:margin-radius} is exactly $\rho/(2m)$.
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:30:thm:main} gives $\kappa=1/8$.
Use Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:30:thm:extension} with $k=2$ and $\eta=1/8$; its budget is
$3/8+4/8=7/8<1$. The pair and four-vertex lower bounds follow from the
same counting argument.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A larger extension-only radius]\label{gsr:en:30:cor:extension-only}
Under the hypotheses of Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:30:cor:margin}, the extension conclusion
also holds on
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:30:eq:extension-radius}
 C_{\mathrm{ext}}=B\left(\boldsymbol\chi,
 \zeta_{\mathrm{ext}}\right),\qquad
 \zeta_{\mathrm{ext}}=\frac{\rho}{6\cdot3^r-4}.
\end{equation}
For $c_r=3^r-1$, the four-vertex base-point count is at least
$|B|/(6c_r+2)$, and the pair overlap is greater than $7|B|/12$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Choose $m=3c_r+1$. Then
\[
 \kappa=\frac{c_r}{6c_r+2}<\frac16,
 \qquad 3\kappa+4\eta=\frac{3c_r}{6c_r+2}+\frac12<1.
\]
The residual four-vertex fraction is
$1-3\kappa-1/2=1/(6c_r+2)$.
The pair fraction is $3/4-\kappa>7/12$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
\emph{A larger fixed radius, by composition with source~12} (proved at the write). Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:30:thm:main} gives normalized losses $b_B(d)/|B|\le c_r/(2m)$ on the symmetric set $B(\boldsymbol\chi,\rho/(2m))\ni0$. Source~12's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:sharp-extension} with $\varepsilon=\eta=1/8$ needs $2\kappa<5/8$, that is $m>8c_r/5$. So the extension conclusion of this corollary holds on $B(\boldsymbol\chi,\rho/(2m))$ with $m=\lfloor8c_r/5\rfloor+1$, about $5\rho/(16c_r)$, against $\rho/(6\cdot3^r-4)=\rho/(2(3c_r+1))$ here: larger by the factor $(3c_r+1)/m$, which is $1.75$ at $r=1$, $1.92$ at $r=2$ and tends to $1.875$ (exact for $r\le10$). The radius is still fixed; the four-vertex base-point count is then $(1-3/8-2\kappa)|B|>0$.
\end{writenote}

The two radii serve different interfaces. The margin-preserving radius
can be used wherever the downstream proof explicitly consumes the
$5/8$ pair overlap. The extension-only radius requires recalculation of
that downstream budget; it must not be substituted while silently retaining
$5/8$.

\subsection{Quantitative gain over the corrected baseline}
Combining \eqref{gsr:fm:30:eq:oldradius} and \eqref{gsr:en:30:eq:margin-radius} gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:30:eq:gain}
 \frac{\zeta_{\mathrm{margin}}}{\zeta_{\mathrm{old}}}
 =\frac{2^{r+1}r}{3^r-1}\,\rho^{1-r}.
\end{equation}
This ratio is at least two for every $r\ge1$ and $0<\rho\le1/4$.
Indeed, $c_1=2$ and $c_{r+1}=3c_r+2\le4c_r$, so
$3^r-1\le2\cdot4^{r-1}$. Together with $\rho^{1-r}\ge4^{r-1}$, this gives
\[
 \frac{\zeta_{\mathrm{margin}}}{\zeta_{\mathrm{old}}}
 \ge 2^r r\ge2.
\]
The equality at $r=1$ is the radius comparison, not an assertion that the
radius itself is optimal. For $r>1$, the gain diverges as $\rho\to0$.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}rrrr@{}}
\toprule
$r$ & $\zeta_{\rm old}$ at $\rho=10^{-2}$ &
$\zeta_{\rm margin}$ & gain \\
\midrule
1 & $3.125\cdot10^{-4}$ & $6.250\cdot10^{-4}$ & $2$\\
2 & $7.813\cdot10^{-7}$ & $1.563\cdot10^{-4}$ & $200$\\
3 & $2.604\cdot10^{-9}$ & $4.808\cdot10^{-5}$ & $1.846\cdot10^4$\\
5 & $3.906\cdot10^{-14}$ & $5.165\cdot10^{-6}$ & $1.322\cdot10^8$\\
10 & $6.104\cdot10^{-26}$ & $2.117\cdot10^{-8}$ & $3.468\cdot10^{17}$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
These are rounded displays of rational numbers. The exact fractions and
comparison identities are included in the verification output. A large
radius ratio does not by itself imply a comparable improvement in a final
Szemer\'edi bound.

\subsection{Higher order and measured local growth}
The same calculation gives a useful family of choices. Suppose
$|A|\ge(1-\eta)|B|$, $\eta<1/(2k)$, and $k\ge2$. Any integer
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:30:eq:order-radius}
 m>\frac{(2k-1)(D_B-1)}{2(1-2k\eta)}
\end{equation}
makes the induced difference map an order-$k$ Freiman homomorphism on
$B(\boldsymbol\rho/(2m))$. One may replace $D_B-1$ by $3^r-1$.
For example, density $7/8$ and $k=3$ are covered by
$m=10(3^r-1)+1$. This illustrates a gain that is qualitatively different
from merely changing a constant: the same order-two map on a very dense
domain acquires higher-order relations on a sufficiently small neighborhood.

For measured local growth, a margin-preserving choice is
$m=\max\{1,\lceil4(D_B-1)\rceil\}$. Its radius is
$\rho/(2m)$; in the rectangular case all widths are divided by $2m$.
The ceiling and the maximum are needed to handle integral and degenerate
cases correctly.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A density-sensitive compatibility step for Lemma 10.12\srctag{30}}]{A density-sensitive compatibility step for Lemma 10.12}\label{gsr:en:30:sec:d7}
\srcnote{30}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:en:30:sec:compatibility}

We now isolate the finite-fibre argument that transfers an induced map
back to the multifunction domain. Keeping the actual size of $A$ in the
exception count improves a local numerical margin. This argument is
independent of how the map $\psi$ was obtained.

Let $X$ be a finite set with an index map $r_X:X\to G$, write
$X_g=\{z\in X:r_X(z)=g\}$, and let $\phi:X\to H$.
Let $W_1\subseteq X$, $A\subseteq B$, and $\psi:A\to H$.
Assume that for each $u\in W_1$ there is a set $A_u\subseteq A$ with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:30:eq:good-directions}
 |A_u|\ge(1-\sigma)|A|,
\end{equation}
and that, for each $a\in A_u$, the fibre $X_{r_X(u)+a}$ is nonempty and
at least a proportion $1-\theta$ of it satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:30:eq:local-values}
 \phi(z)-\phi(u)=\psi(a).
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Compatibility with exact direction-density budget]
\label{gsr:en:30:thm:compatibility}
Let $a_0=|A|/|B|$, $0\le\theta<1/2$, and $\sigma\ge0$.
Suppose \eqref{gsr:en:30:eq:good-directions}--\eqref{gsr:en:30:eq:local-values} hold, and
$\psi_1:C\to H$ is induced by $\psi$ as in \eqref{gsr:en:30:eq:induced}.
If $b_B(c)\le\kappa|B|$ for $c\in C$ and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:30:eq:compat-budget}
 2(1-\sigma)a_0>1+\kappa,
\end{equation}
then, for $u,v\in W_1$ with $c=r_X(u)-r_X(v)\in C$,
\[
 \phi(u)-\phi(v)=\psi_1(c).
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The set of directions $a$ with $a\in A$ and $a+c\in A$ has cardinality
at least
\[
 |B\cap(B-c)|-2|B\setminus A|
 \ge 2|A|-(1+\kappa)|B|.
\]
Requiring additionally $a\in A_u$ and $a+c\in A_v$ removes at most
$2\sigma|A|$ directions. The resulting count is positive by
\eqref{gsr:en:30:eq:compat-budget}; choose such an $a$.
The two target fibres coincide because
$r_X(u)+a=r_X(v)+(a+c)$, and they are nonempty by hypothesis.
The two good-value sets inside this common fibre each have relative size
at least $1-\theta$. Since $2\theta<1$, their intersection is nonempty.
Choose $z$ in the intersection. Then
\[
 \phi(z)-\phi(u)=\psi(a),\qquad
 \phi(z)-\phi(v)=\psi(a+c).
\]
Subtract and use the induced difference identity to obtain the result.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
The condition \eqref{gsr:en:30:eq:compat-budget} is that of source~12's Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:12:lem:sync}, $2(1-q)a>1+\kappa$ with $q=\sigma$ and $a=a_0$, proved by the same intersection. The $5/14$ of the corollary below improves the formal \file{lemma_10_12}'s $\sqrt\theta<5/16$ (\file{Section10.lean}, line~401, at HEAD \texttt{5d4718772}), as the text says.
\end{writenote}

\begin{corollary}[The $5/14$ margin]\label{gsr:en:30:cor:five-fourteen}
In the setting of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:30:thm:compatibility}, suppose
$|A|\ge7|B|/8$, $\kappa\le1/8$, and $\sigma=\sqrt\theta$ with
$0\le\theta$ and $\sqrt\theta<5/14$. Then the compatibility conclusion
holds. In particular it applies on $C_{\mathrm{margin}}$ from
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:30:cor:margin} whenever the stated fibre hypotheses hold.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The condition $\sqrt\theta<5/14$ implies $\theta<25/196<1/2$ and
\[
 2(1-\sqrt\theta)\frac78>2\left(1-\frac5{14}\right)\frac78
 =\frac98\ge1+\kappa.
\]
Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:30:thm:compatibility}.
\end{proof}

The repository's corrected Lemma 10.12 explicitly uses
$\sqrt\theta<5/16$, together with nonempty target fibres
\cite{repo30}. That budget comes from a $5|B|/8$ pair overlap and two
exception counts each bounded by $\sqrt\theta|B|$. The refined count
above retains $|A|$ until the end, giving $5/14$ instead. This does not
assert that $5/14$ is an optimal compatibility threshold. Nor does it
remove the nonempty-fibre condition: on an empty fibre a relative
``almost every'' statement can be vacuous.

For the larger extension-only radius, the bound
$\kappa<1/6$ gives the convenient sufficient condition
$\sqrt\theta\le1/3$ under the same nonempty-fibre assumptions. Indeed,
$2(1-1/3)(7/8)=7/6>1+\kappa$. Thus one may trade some compatibility
margin for a larger neighborhood, with the tradeoff recorded explicitly.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Further consequences without radius regularization\srctag{30}}]{Further consequences without radius regularization}\label{gsr:en:30:sec:d8}
\srcnote{30}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:en:30:sec:consequences}

\subsection{Uniform measures and bounded observables}
Let $\mu_B=\ind_B/|B|$ be the uniform probability mass function on $B$,
and let $\tau_d\mu_B(x)=\mu_B(x-d)$. With total variation defined as
one half of the counting $\ell^1$ distance,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:30:eq:TV}
 \TV(\mu_B,\tau_d\mu_B)=\frac{b_B(d)}{|B|}.
\end{equation}
This is immediate from Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:30:lem:identities}. Therefore the main
theorem gives
\[
 \|\tau_d\mu_B-\mu_B\|_1\le\frac{D_B-1}{m}.
\]
For an observable $0\le f\le1$, the difference between its expectations
under the two measures is at most $(D_B-1)/(2m)$. To see this without
invoking a general duality theorem, separate the positive and negative
parts of the signed measure: both have mass $b_B(d)/|B|$.
For complex $f$ with $|f|\le1$, the triangle inequality gives twice that
bound.

If convolution is defined by
$(f*\mu)(x)=\sum_y f(x-y)\mu(y)$, then
\[
 \|f*(\tau_d\mu_B-\mu_B)\|_\infty
 \le \|f\|_\infty\frac{D_B-1}{m}.
\]
No smoothed cutoff is introduced. These estimates can be useful when a
proof must retain exactly the original indicator of a Bohr set.

\subsection{Long orbit segments inside the original set}
For an integer $L\ge0$, define
\[
 B_{L,d}=\{x\in G:x+jd\in B\text{ for }-L\le j\le L\}.
\]
Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:30:lem:tree} to the path of $2L+1$ positions, with $A=B$:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:30:eq:orbitcore}
 |B_{L,d}|\ge |B|-2L\,b_B(d)
 \ge\left(1-\frac{L(D_B-1)}m\right)|B|.
\end{equation}
This counts base points of orbit segments. It does not claim the segment
has $2L+1$ distinct points; that requires a separate lower bound on the
order of $d$. The statement remains valid when the orbit repeats.

More generally, any finite pattern equipped with a tree of small
character-displacement edges has a large intersection of its translated
Bohr sets, with the sum of the intrinsic edge defects controlling the
loss. This is an interface for higher-order local identities; the tree
budget should be carried to the final application rather than replaced
prematurely by a worst-case cardinality factor.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Exponential-rank obstructions, including cyclic groups\srctag{30}}]{Exponential-rank obstructions, including cyclic groups}\label{gsr:en:30:sec:d9}
\srcnote{30}{Section 9}
\label{gsr:en:30:sec:obstruction}

The factor $3^r$ suggests asking whether a more careful argument could give
a polynomial in $r$ instead. We show that no universal polynomial-rank
translation bound is possible for arbitrary fixed input Bohr sets, even
when the ambient group is required to be cyclic. The meaning of
``fixed'' here is that the radius is not adjusted within an instance;
the group and radius may vary across a family of counterexamples.

\subsection{A simple product-group model}

\begin{proposition}[A line with a transverse spike]\label{gsr:en:30:prop:product-spike}
Fix $p\ge5$, $s\ge1$, and $L\ge2$, and put $q=Lp-1$.
On $G=\Z/q\Z\times(\Z/p\Z)^s$, use the $2s+1$ characters
\[
 \chi_0(x,\boldsymbol y)=x/q,\qquad
 \chi_i^{\pm}(x,\boldsymbol y)=y_i/p\pm x/q
 \quad(1\le i\le s)
\]
and common width $\rho=1/p$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:30:eq:spike}
 B=\bigl(I\times\{\boldsymbol0\}\bigr)
 \cup\bigl(\{0\}\times\{-1,0,1\}^s\bigr),
 \qquad I=[-(L-1),L-1]\pmod q.
\end{equation}
For $d=(1,\boldsymbol0)$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:30:eq:spike-size}
 |B|=2L-2+3^s,\qquad b_B(d)=3^s,\qquad
 \max_\chi\frac{\normt{\chi(d)}}\rho=\frac pq.
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\[
 \frac{b_B(d)/|B|}{p/q}\longrightarrow\frac{3^s}{2}
 \quad\text{as }L\to\infty.
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Choose a representative $t=x/q$ with $|t|\le\rho$, as forced by $\chi_0$.
If both $\normt{y_i/p+t}$ and $\normt{y_i/p-t}$ are at most $\rho$,
there are real lifts $u,v\in[-\rho,\rho]$ of these two elements.
Now $u-v$ represents $2t$. Since
$|u-v-2t|\le4\rho<1$, the integral difference must be zero. Thus
$u=z+t$ and $v=z-t$ for a lift $z$ of $y_i/p$, and
\[
 |z|+|t|=\max\{|z+t|,|z-t|\}\le\rho.
\]
In particular $z\in\{0,1/p,-1/p\}$. If $z\ne0$, the inequality forces
$t=0$. If all $z$ vanish, the only restriction is
$|x|\le\lfloor q/p\rfloor=L-1$. This proves \eqref{gsr:en:30:eq:spike}.
The nonzero transverse fibres of $B$ have only the point $x=0$; their
translates have only $x=1$. The axial fibre is an interval whose overlap
with its translate loses one point. Hence the defect is one per transverse
choice, namely $3^s$, and the size is as stated. Finally,
$q/p=L-1/p$, so the ratio tends to $3^s/2$.
\end{proof}

The finite products with $s>1$ are not cyclic. The following construction
removes that limitation rather than silently identifying a product with a
cyclic group when its factors are not coprime.

\subsection{An explicit Chinese-remainder realization}
For $s\ge1$ and integer $L\ge9$, define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:30:eq:crt-parameters}
 D=s!,\quad R_i=LiD+1,\quad
 P=\left(\prod_{i=1}^s R_i\right)^2,\quad
 P_i=P+iD,\quad q=LP-1.
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}[Arithmetic of the parameters]\label{gsr:en:30:lem:crt-arithmetic}
The integers $q,P_1,\ldots,P_s$ are pairwise coprime. Also
\[
 P\ge100,\qquad P>LsD,\qquad
 0<\frac1P-\frac1{P_i}<\frac1q.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Each $R_i$ is congruent to one modulo $D$, so $P\equiv1\pmod D$.
If a prime divides both $P_i$ and $P_j$ for $i<j$, it divides
$(j-i)D$. Every prime divisor of this number divides $D$: primes dividing
$j-i\le s-1$ are among the primes dividing $s!$. But $P_i\equiv1\pmod D$,
a contradiction. For $s=1$ this pairwise argument is vacuous.

A common divisor of $q$ and $P_i$ divides
$LP_i-q=LiD+1=R_i$. Since $R_i\mid P$,
\[
 \gcd(P_i,R_i)=\gcd(iD,R_i)=1.
\]
Thus $\gcd(q,P_i)=1$. The product defining $P$ contains
$R_s=LsD+1$, and its square is larger still, so $P>LsD$.
The smallest case gives $P\ge(L+1)^2\ge100$. Finally,
\[
 0<\frac1P-\frac1{P_i}=\frac{iD}{PP_i}
 \le\frac{sD}{P^2}<\frac1{LP}<\frac1q.
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Cyclic spiked Bohr sets]\label{gsr:en:30:thm:cyclic-spikes}
Use the group
\[
 G=\Z/q\Z\times\prod_{i=1}^s\Z/P_i\Z
\]
with the parameters \eqref{gsr:en:30:eq:crt-parameters}. It is cyclic of order
$N=q\prod_iP_i$. With characters
\[
 \chi_0(x,\boldsymbol y)=x/q,\qquad
 \chi_i^{\pm}(x,\boldsymbol y)=y_i/P_i\pm x/q
\]
and common width $\rho=1/P$, its Bohr set is exactly
\eqref{gsr:en:30:eq:spike}, with $\{-1,0,1\}$ now interpreted in each $\Z/P_i\Z$.
For $d=(1,\boldsymbol0)$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:30:eq:crt-ratio}
 |B|=2L-2+3^s,\quad b_B(d)=3^s,\quad
 t=\max_\chi\frac{\normt{\chi(d)}}\rho=\frac Pq,
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:30:eq:crt-limit}
 \frac{b_B(d)/|B|}{t}
 =\frac{3^s(L-1/P)}{2L-2+3^s}
 \longrightarrow\frac{3^s}{2}
 \quad(L\to\infty).
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Cyclicity follows from Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:30:lem:crt-arithmetic} and the Chinese
remainder theorem. The base character gives a lift $t_x=x/q$ with
$|t_x|\le1/P$. As in Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:30:prop:product-spike}, the two
constraints for a fixed $i$ imply the existence of a lift $z_i$ of
$y_i/P_i$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:30:eq:lift-spike}
 |z_i|+|t_x|\le1/P.
\end{equation}
The lift argument applies since $4/P<1$.
As $P_i/P=1+iD/P<2$, the only possible values are
$z_i=0,\pm1/P_i$. If any $z_i$ is nonzero, then
\[
 |t_x|\le1/P-1/P_i<1/q.
\]
But $t_x$ is an integer multiple of $1/q$, so $x=0$. Conversely, at
$x=0$ all $3^s$ transverse choices are allowed because $P_i>P$.
When all $z_i=0$, the remaining restriction is
$|x|\le\lfloor q/P\rfloor=L-1$. This proves the exact description.
The cardinality and defect follow by the same interval calculation as in
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:30:prop:product-spike}. All character values at $d$ have
norm $1/q$, giving $t=P/q$. Since $P\ge100$, the limit follows directly
from the displayed rational formula.
\end{proof}

The construction can be written entirely in $\Z/N\Z$. Under the map
$z\mapsto(z\bmod q,z\bmod P_1,\ldots,z\bmod P_s)$, the frequencies are
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:30:eq:explicit-frequencies}
 K=\left\{\frac Nq\right\}
 \cup\left\{\frac N{P_i}+\frac Nq,\
                 \frac N{P_i}-\frac Nq:1\le i\le s\right\}\pmod N.
\end{equation}
They are distinct: restrictions to the individual direct factors
separate different $i$, and restriction to the $q$-factor separates the
two signs, since $q>2$. The shift is the unique residue with
$d\equiv1\pmod q$ and $d\equiv0\pmod{P_i}$ for every $i$.
Thus no abstract existence of unspecified frequencies is needed.

\subsection{The precise obstruction to polynomial rank}

\begin{definition}[Small-step extremal coefficient]
Let $S_r(\eps)$ be the supremum of
\[
 \frac{b_B(d)}{t|B|},\qquad
 t=\max_i\frac{\normt{\chi_i(d)}}{\rho_i},
\]
over finite cyclic groups, Bohr sets with $r$ listed characters and
$0<\rho_i\le1/4$, and shifts with $0<t\le\eps$.
Set $\mathcal L_r=\lim_{\eps\downarrow0}S_r(\eps)$.
The limit exists as an extended real number by monotonicity.
\end{definition}

\begin{corollary}[Exponential dependence is necessary]\label{gsr:en:30:cor:exponential}
For every $r\ge1$, $\mathcal L_r\le3^r-1$. For $s\ge1$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:30:eq:extremal-bracket}
 \frac12\,3^s\le\mathcal L_{2s+1}\le3^{2s+1}-1.
\end{equation}
Consequently no coefficient bounded by a polynomial in $r$ can give a
universal linear relative-shift bound, even restricted to cyclic groups
and sufficiently small shifts.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:30:cor:floorfree} gives
$S_r(\eps)\le(3^r-1)/(1-2\eps)$ for $0<\eps<1/2$.
Take the limit. For the lower bound, the cyclic family in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:30:thm:cyclic-spikes} has $t=P/(LP-1)\to0$ and its normalized
ratio tends to $3^s/2$. Thus every sufficiently small-step supremum is
at least this limiting value. Exponential growth on the odd subsequence
already rules out any polynomial bound valid for all $r$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{The prime case and a larger base} (source~99, Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:primebohr}): in every large prime cyclic group, fixed frequencies and a fixed radius give $2^r-1$ runs and boundary ratio near $(2^r-1)/2$ for every $r\ge2$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:99:thm:main}), above $3^s/2$ at every odd rank $r=2s+1\ge3$; so $(2^r-1)/2\le c_r^{\mathrm{prime}}\le\mathcal L_r$, and $\mathcal L_1=1/2$ (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:99:cor:constants}). The base $2$ against $3$ is open.
\end{writenote}

These examples do not settle the prime-order case. They also do not settle
the optimal exponential base: the lower bound grows like $(\sqrt3)^r$,
whereas the upper bound grows like $3^r$. The local-growth formulation
of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:30:thm:intrinsic} remains preferable when more structure of
the individual Bohr set is available.
