\section[{Degree balances and the probability of a certificate\srctag{35}}]{Degree balances and the probability of a certificate}\label{gsr:en:35:sec:d3}
\srcnote{35}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:en:35:sel:sec:certificates}

\subsection{Product probability on a subspace}

The following elementary fact replaces a count of all available
Fourier coefficients by the mass that the selector assigns to them.

\begin{lemma}[Subspace mass under a product law]
\label{gsr:en:35:sel:lem:mass}
Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be independent random variables in \(\F_q\),
each with largest atom at most \(\mu\). If \(V\subseteq\F_q^n\)
is an affine subspace of dimension \(D\), then
\begin{equation}
 \Pr((X_1,\ldots,X_n)\in V)\le\mu^{n-D}.
 \label{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:mass}
\end{equation}
More generally, if the \(i\)th largest atom is at most \(\mu_i\)
and projection onto a coordinate set \(I\), \(|I|=D\), is injective
on \(V\), the right side can be replaced by
\(\prod_{i\notin I}\mu_i\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Choose \(D\) coordinates for which the coordinate projection on
the direction space has rank \(D\). Every choice of their values
has at most one completion in \(V\). Conditional on those values,
independence bounds the probability of that completion by the
product of the largest atoms of the other coordinates. Averaging
over the chosen coordinates proves both claims.
\end{proof}

The exponent in this general lemma cannot be increased for arbitrary
subspaces: a coordinate subspace fixing \(n-D\) coordinates at their
largest atoms attains it. This does not assert sharpness for the
particular arrangement subspaces below.

\subsection{The degree of a coefficient array}

Consider a field coefficient array
\(b=(b_{j,e})\in\F_q^{s}\). For each cube, interpolate the values
\(\pi(e)b_{j,e}\) by the unique multilinear polynomial
\begin{equation}
 V_j(u)=\sum_{T\subseteq[k]}A_{j,T}u_T,\qquad
 u_T=\prod_{i\in T}u_i.
 \label{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:interpolation}
\end{equation}
Here and below the empty product is one. For \(b\ne0\), its
parity-removed degree is
\[
 t(b)=\max\{|T|:A_{j,T}\ne0\text{ for some }j\}.
 \]
This definition is valid over every field: evaluation of multilinear
polynomials on the Boolean cube is invertible by triangular
interpolation.

For \(S\subseteq[k]\), define the Boolean moments
\[
 b^\flat_{j,S}=\sum_{e\in\{0,1\}^k}b_{j,e}e_S.
\]
Summing each coordinate of the Boolean cube separately gives
\begin{equation}
 b^\flat_{j,S}
 =(-1)^k\sum_{\substack{T\subseteq[k]\\T\cup S=[k]}}A_{j,T}.
 \label{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:moment-transform}
\end{equation}
In particular, for an array of degree \(t\),
\begin{align}
 b^\flat_{j,S}&=0 &&(|S|<k-t), \label{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:lower-zero}\\
 b^\flat_{j,S}&=(-1)^kA_{j,[k]\setminus S}
       &&(|S|=k-t). \label{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:first-moment}
\end{align}

For each \(A\subseteq[k+1]\), the associated feature relation is
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{j,e}b_{j,e}(v_{j,e})_A=0.
 \label{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:feature}
\end{equation}
There are \(2^{k+1}\) such relations, including \(A=\varnothing\).
The universal line
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal U=\{\lambda(\sigma_j\pi(e))_{j,e}:\lambda\in\F_q\}
 \label{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:universal}
\end{equation}
satisfies all of them for every arrangement. Indeed, the
alternating sum on a cube vanishes unless a squarefree horizontal
feature contains every horizontal coordinate. In that last case
the two remaining sums are multiples of \(\sum_j\sigma_j=0\)
and \(\sum_j\sigma_jz_j=0\).

In estimating nonuniversal certificates, restrict first to
arrangements with every \(h_i\ne0\). This restriction is justified
later because a zero side automatically makes
\eqref{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:respect} hold for every map.

\begin{lemma}[Necessary top-degree balances]
\label{gsr:en:35:sel:lem:balances}
For \(0\le t\le k\), let \(\mathcal V_t\) be the space of arrays
whose polynomials in \eqref{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:interpolation} have degree at
most \(t\), and which satisfy
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{j=1}^m A_{j,T}=0\qquad(|T|=t).
 \label{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:top-balance}
\end{equation}
Then \(\dim\mathcal V_t=D_t\). Every degree-\(t\) array satisfying
all feature relations on an arrangement with nonzero sides
belongs to \(\mathcal V_t\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
There are \(mc_t\) independent interpolation coefficients of
degree at most \(t\). For each of the \(\binom{k}{t}\) top
monomials, \eqref{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:top-balance} is one independent equation,
giving exactly the asserted dimension.

For a horizontal coordinate set \(A\subseteq[k]\), expansion at
the anchor gives
\begin{equation}
 \sum_e b_{j,e}(x_j+e\odot h)_A
 =\sum_{S\subseteq A}h_S b^\flat_{j,S}(x_j)_{A\setminus S}.
 \label{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:anchor-expand}
\end{equation}
Choose \(|A|=k-t\). All terms except \(S=A\) vanish by
\eqref{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:lower-zero}. The feature relation is therefore
\[
 0=h_A\sum_j b^\flat_{j,A}
   =(-1)^kh_A\sum_j A_{j,[k]\setminus A}.
 \]
Because \(h_A\ne0\), this is \eqref{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:top-balance}.
\end{proof}

The spaces \(\mathcal V_t\) need not be nested. We never subtract
their upper bounds to estimate a stratum. The coefficient arrays
are first partitioned by their exact degree, and each resulting
mass is bounded above by the mass of the appropriate
\(\mathcal V_t\).

\subsection{A rank estimate valid for arbitrary field coefficients}

The next estimate extends the degree-sensitive certificate argument
of \cite{repo35degree} from its small coefficient alphabet to arbitrary
field coefficients. That extension is essential for a Fej\'er
kernel of arbitrary bandwidth.

\begin{lemma}[Probability of a nonuniversal certificate]
\label{gsr:en:35:sel:lem:certificate}
Fix \(b\in\F_q^s\setminus\mathcal U\) of parity-removed degree \(t\).
For every fixed \(h\in(\F_q^\times)^k\), choose the anchors
uniformly in \((\F_q^k)^m\) and the levels uniformly in \(W\).
The probability that all feature relations
\eqref{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:feature} hold is at most \(Q_t(q)\).
Consequently the number of successful arrangements with nonzero
sides is at most \(q^M Q_t(q)\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
First let \(t=0\). Then \(b_{j,e}=a_j\pi(e)\) for some
nonzero vector \(a\). The full horizontal feature requires
\(\sum_j a_j=0\), and adjoining the level coordinate requires
\(a\cdot z=0\). If the first condition fails there are no successful
arrangements. Otherwise \(a\) is not a multiple of \(\sigma\),
since the universal line was excluded. The linear form
\(a\cdot z\) is therefore nonzero on \(W=\sigma^\perp\)
and vanishes on exactly a fraction \(q^{-1}\) of \(W\).
This proves the degree-zero bound.

Now suppose \(t\ge1\). Choose \(S_0\subseteq[k]\), of size
\(k-t\), for which
\[
 b^\flat=(b^\flat_{1,S_0},\ldots,b^\flat_{m,S_0})\ne0.
\]
Such a set exists by \eqref{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:first-moment}.
For brevity write \(b_j^\flat=b^\flat_{j,S_0}\).
The lowest horizontal and vertical feature relations give
\begin{equation}
 \sum_jb_j^\flat=0,\qquad
 \sum_jb_j^\flat z_j=0.
 \label{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:lowest-tests}
\end{equation}
For each \(i\notin S_0\), the feature with horizontal set
\(S_0\cup\{i\}\) gives an affine linear equation in the anchors.
Its terms involving \(x_{j,i}\) are
\[
 h_{S_0}\sum_jb_j^\flat x_{j,i}.
\]
All remaining anchor terms use coordinates \(x_{j,a}\) with
\(a\in S_0\); condition on those coordinates. In particular,
choosing one \(j_0\) with
\(b_{j_0}^\flat\ne0\) gives a diagonal nonsingular minor in
the \(t\) variables \(x_{j_0,i}\), \(i\notin S_0\).
For every choice of the other variables, at most a fraction
\(q^{-t}\) of the anchors can pass these tests.

If \(b^\flat\) is not proportional to \(\sigma\), the second
condition in \eqref{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:lowest-tests} independently holds
on a fraction \(q^{-1}\) of \(W\). Thus the success probability
is at most \(q^{-t-1}\).

Suppose instead \(b^\flat=c\sigma\), with \(c\ne0\).
When the level vector \(z\) is nonconstant, choose \(a,b\)
with \(z_a\ne z_b\). For each \(i\notin S_0\), use both the
horizontal test just described and the same test multiplied
by the level coordinate. On the variables \(x_{a,i},x_{b,i}\)
their coefficient matrix is
\[
 c h_{S_0}
 \begin{pmatrix}
 \sigma_a&\sigma_b\\
 z_a\sigma_a&z_b\sigma_b
 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its determinant is nonzero. The \(t\) blocks use disjoint
variables, so their combined rank is \(2t\).
For constant \(z\), the rank-\(t\) argument still applies.
The constant vectors form a one-dimensional subspace of
\(W\), which has dimension \(m-1\). The fraction of constant
level vectors is consequently \(q^{-(m-2)}\), and the total
probability is at most
\begin{equation}
 (1-q^{-(m-2)})q^{-2t}+q^{-(m-2+t)}.
 \label{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:diagonal-prob}
\end{equation}
At \(t=1\), this is exactly
\(q^{-2}+(q-1)q^{-m}=Q_1(q)\).
For \(t\ge2\), after division by \(q^{-t-1}\) it is at most
\(q^{1-t}+q^{3-m}\le2/q<1\), since \(p>2\).
This proves every stated probability. There are fewer than
\(q^k\) choices of nonzero \(h\), yielding the final counting
bound.
\end{proof}

The exception at degree one is thus geometrically explicit:
all levels coincide, and the extra vertical rank disappears.
Suppressing this event would incorrectly replace \(Q_1\) by
\(q^{-2}\). The exhaustive small-field check in
Section~\ref{gsr:fz:35:sec:verification} attains the stated \(Q_1\).

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The random restriction and its collision correction\srctag{35}}]{The random restriction and its collision correction}\label{gsr:en:35:sec:d4}
\srcnote{35}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:en:35:sel:sec:restriction}

\subsection{A finite positive Fourier selector}

For \(|z|=1\), use the normalized Fej\'er kernel
\begin{equation}
 K_L(z)=\left|\frac1L\sum_{a=0}^{L-1}z^a\right|^2
       =\sum_{n=-(L-1)}^{L-1}c_nz^n,\qquad
 c_n=\frac{L-|n|}{L^2}.
 \label{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:kernel}
\end{equation}
Thus \(0\le K_L\le1\), every \(c_n\ge0\),
\(\sum_n c_n=1\), and
\[
 \mu:=c_0=L^{-1}=\max_n c_n.
\]
Because \(p>2(L-1)\), the support integers \(n\) embed injectively
in \(\F_p\subseteq\F_q\). We regard \(c_n\) as a probability law
on that field subset.

Choose a nontrivial additive character \(\chi:\F_q\to\C\).
Let \(v\in\F_q\) and \(u_A\in\F_q\), for every
\(A\subseteq[k+1]\), be independent uniform variables. Conditional
on these seeds, include each \emph{distinct physical point}
\(y\in B\) independently with probability
\begin{equation}
 K_L\left(\chi\left(v\phi(y)+
                   \sum_{A\subseteq[k+1]}u_A y_A\right)\right).
 \label{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:retention}
\end{equation}
Call the resulting set \(B'\). The empty feature is included.
By orthogonality, its random coefficient makes the unconditional
inclusion probability of each physical point exactly \(\mu\).
All random choices here have finite support; no continuous phase
averaging is required.

For a fixed arrangement, first multiply the retention probabilities
over its \(s\) labels, whether or not some labels coincide.
Fourier expansion and averaging the seeds give
\begin{align}
 &\E_{\rm seeds}\prod_{j,e}
 K_L\left(\chi\left(v\phi(v_{j,e})
                 +\sum_Au_A(v_{j,e})_A\right)\right)
 \nonumber\\
 &\quad=
 \sum_{b\in\F_q^s}
 \left(\prod_{j,e}c_{b_{j,e}}\right)
 \mathbf1_{\{\text{all feature relations hold}\}}\,
 \mathbf1_{\{\sum_{j,e}b_{j,e}\phi(v_{j,e})=0\}}.
 \label{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:Fourier-expansion}
\end{align}
Coefficients outside the embedded support have weight zero.
Every summand is nonnegative. This positivity allows us to retain
a useful signal and bound each unwanted family separately.

\begin{lemma}[The universal Fourier signal]
\label{gsr:en:35:sel:lem:signal}
On a respected arrangement, the contribution of \(\mathcal U\)
to \eqref{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:Fourier-expansion} is
\begin{equation}
 S_s(L)=\sum_{n=-(L-1)}^{L-1}c_n^s
       =\mu^sR_s(L).
 \label{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:signal}
\end{equation}
On an unrespected arrangement its contribution is exactly \(\mu^s\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Every array in \(\mathcal U\) satisfies the feature relations.
An array from this line with positive weight must have the form
\(b_{j,e}=n\sigma_j\pi(e)\) with one integer
\(|n|<L\): this follows from the injectivity of the support
in the field and its symmetry. Its product weight is \(c_n^s\).
For a respected arrangement it satisfies the target relation
for every such \(n\). For an unrespected arrangement the target
relation is \(n\) times a nonzero element of \(\F_q\), so only
\(n=0\) can contribute. This proves both statements.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Why physical coincidences require a separate term}

If labels coincide, the survival probability of the arrangement
is the product over its \emph{distinct} points, whereas
\eqref{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:Fourier-expansion} used every label. Because each
factor lies in \([0,1]\), actual survival is at least the
labelled product. This is favorable for the respected count.
For the unrespected count it requires an upper correction.

\begin{lemma}[Coincident vertices of an unrespected arrangement]
\label{gsr:en:35:sel:lem:collisions}
An unrespected arrangement has all \(h_i\ne0\).
The total number of arrangement parameters with nonzero sides
and at least one coincident pair of vertex labels is at most
\begin{equation}
 C_{\rm coll}\,q^{M-k-1}.
 \label{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:collision-count}
\end{equation}
For any such arrangement in \(B\), its unconditional actual
survival probability is at most \(\mu\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If \(h_i=0\), pair the terms \(e\) and \(e+\mathbf e_i\) in
each cube of \eqref{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:respect}. Their physical vertices
are equal and their signs are opposite, so the arrangement is
respected by every map. This proves the first assertion.

With nonzero sides, distinct labels in the same cube are
different points. A coincidence between cubes \(j\ne\ell\)
requires
\begin{equation}
 z_j=z_\ell,\qquad x_\ell-x_j=\delta\odot h
       \quad\text{for some }\delta\in\{-1,0,1\}^k.
 \label{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:collision-locus}
\end{equation}
For a fixed unordered pair \(j,\ell\) and \(\delta\), these
are \(k+1\) independent linear conditions on the arrangement
parameter space. In particular the form \(z_j-z_\ell\) is
independent of \(\sigma\cdot z\), because \(m\ge4\) and
\(\sigma\) has nonzero coordinates outside \(j,\ell\).
The locus has exactly \(q^{M-k-1}\) parameters before the
nonzero-side restriction. There are \(\binom m2\,3^k\)
loci, so the union bound proves \eqref{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:collision-count}.

Survival implies that any one specified vertex survives.
That vertex has unconditional inclusion probability \(\mu\),
which proves the last assertion.
\end{proof}

Counting raw pairs of Boolean labels would introduce \(4^k\)
in this estimate. Grouping pairs that define the same
\(\delta\) produces \(3^k\). More importantly, the compensation
is \(\mu\) per possible collision, rather than one. The empty
feature is what gives this exact marginal probability.

\subsection{Completion of the selection proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:35:sel:thm:exact}]
Let \(X=G_\phi(B')\) and \(Y=T(B')-G_\phi(B')\).
For every respected arrangement, actual survival is at least
its labelled product. By the nonnegative Fourier expansion
and Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:35:sel:lem:signal},
\begin{equation}
 \E X\ge S_s(L)G_\phi(B)
       \ge\alpha\mu^sR_s(L)T_0.
 \label{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:EX}
\end{equation}

For unrespected arrangements, first bound the expected labelled
product. Their number is at most
\(T(B)-G_\phi(B)\le(1-\alpha)T_0\), and the universal line
contributes \(\mu^s\) to each.
For a nonuniversal array of exact degree \(t\), successful
nonzero-side arrangements are possible only if the array is
in \(\mathcal V_t\), by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:35:sel:lem:balances}.
The product-law mass of that space is at most
\(\mu^{s-D_t}\), by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:35:sel:lem:mass}.
Each fixed array succeeds on at most \(q^MQ_t(q)\)
arrangements by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:35:sel:lem:certificate}.
We may discard both membership in \(B\) and the target
relation when taking an upper bound. The total expected
labelled contribution of these arrays is therefore at most
\[
 q^M\sum_{t=0}^k\mu^{s-D_t}Q_t(q).
 \]
The universal line has already been removed, so the degree-zero
probability bound is being used only on its valid domain.

For arrangements with distinct labels, actual survival is
the labelled product. For the remaining unrespected arrangements,
add their actual survival probabilities as a compensation.
This may overcount their labelled products, which is harmless.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:35:sel:lem:collisions} bounds the compensation by
\(C_{\rm coll}\mu q^{M-k-1}\). Thus
\begin{align}
 \E Y
 \le{}&\mu^s(1-\alpha)T_0
 \nonumber\\
 &+q^M\left(
     \sum_{t=0}^k\mu^{s-D_t}Q_t(q)
       +C_{\rm coll}\mu q^{-k-1}\right).
 \label{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:EY}
\end{align}
Subtracting \eqref{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:EY} from \(\eta\) times
\eqref{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:EX}, and using \(q^M=\beta^{-(m-1)}T_0\),
gives
\[
 \E(\eta X-Y)\ge\mu^sT_0F_*.
\]
Some outcome consequently satisfies
\(\eta X-Y\ge\mu^sT_0F_*>0\). For that outcome,
\[
 X\ge\frac{\mu^sT_0F_*}{\eta},
 \qquad Y\le\eta X,
\]
proving the count and purity assertions. Finally the general
bound \(T(B')\le(|B'|/q^{k+1})^{m-1}q^M\), together with
the lower bound on \(X\), proves the density assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[A larger class of target groups]
\label{gsr:en:35:sel:rem:targets}
The same theorem holds for a map into \(\F_q^a\), for any
positive integer \(a\): use a random linear functional on the
target in the selector. More generally, it holds for a finite
abelian target \(H\) whenever multiplication by every integer
\(1\le n<L\) is injective on \(H\). For example, it suffices
that every prime divisor of \(|H|\) exceed \(L-1\).
Replace the phase in \eqref{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:retention} by
\[
 \psi(\phi(y))\,
 \chi\left(\sum_Au_Ay_A\right),
 \]
where \(\psi\) is a uniform character of \(H\), and apply
\(K_L\) to this unit complex number. Orthogonality on \(H\)
now enforces the target relation. The injectivity assumption
ensures that no nonzero integer on the universal line annihilates
the defect of an unrespected arrangement. Every other part of
the proof is unchanged. The field characteristic condition is
still required for the coefficient support used by the features.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The exponent, a fair comparison, and a downstream substitution\srctag{35}}]{The exponent, a fair comparison, and a downstream substitution}\label{gsr:en:35:sec:d5}
\srcnote{35}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:en:35:sel:sec:comparison}

\subsection{A weighted comparison without the full degree stratification}

To isolate the contribution of the degree calculation, one should
compare it with a weighted argument that uses the same feature
family but remembers only whether an array is pure parity.
This intermediate comparison is useful even though it is weaker
than the main theorem.

\begin{proposition}[A weighted unstratified bound]
\label{gsr:en:35:sel:prop:unstratified}
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:35:sel:thm:exact} remains valid if its budget is replaced by
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal K_{\rm un}(L,q)
 =L^{m-1}q^{-1}+2L^{s-1}q^{-2}
       +C_{\rm coll}L^{s-1}q^{-k-1}.
 \label{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:unstratified}
\end{equation}
For fixed \(k,m,\beta\), this yields the sufficient bandwidth
exponent \((s-1)/2\).
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The nonuniversal pure-parity arrays lie in the balanced
\((m-1)\)-dimensional space \(\mathcal V_0\), of mass at most
\(\mu^{s-m+1}\), and each has success probability at most \(q^{-1}\).
Every other successful array satisfies the empty-feature equation
\(\sum_{j,e}b_{j,e}=0\). This is a nonzero linear equation on
\(\F_q^s\), so all these arrays together have mass at most \(\mu\).
Their individual success probabilities are at most \(2q^{-2}\),
by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:35:sel:lem:certificate}. The collision correction is
unchanged. Normalizing these contributions by \(\mu^sq^M\)
gives \eqref{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:unstratified}.

For example, it is enough to impose
\begin{equation}
 q\ge\max\left\{
 4\beta^{-(m-1)}L^{m-1},
 \ 2\sqrt{(2+C_{\rm coll})\beta^{-(m-1)}}\,L^{(s-1)/2}
 \right\}.
 \label{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:unstratified-threshold}
\end{equation}
Then the first term of the budget is at most \(\beta^{m-1}/4\);
the other two together are at most the same amount, using
\(q^{-k-1}\le q^{-2}\). Since \(s=m2^k\ge2m\), the governing
power of \(L\) is \((s-1)/2\).
\end{proof}

Thus the advance is more than a substitution of a probability
weight for an unweighted union bound. Degree stratification
further reduces the exponent from \((s-1)/2\) to \(E_{k,m}\),
strictly so when \(k\ge2\). The unstratified proposition above
is itself a consequence of the full feature system and the
certificate estimates; it is not attributed to the earlier
one-monomial report.

\subsection{The exponent profile}

\begin{proposition}[Unimodality and asymptotic size]
\label{gsr:en:35:sel:prop:exponent}
Let
\[
 E_{k,m}=\max_{0\le t\le k}\frac{D_t}{t+1}.
\]
The sequence \(D_t/(t+1)\) is unimodal and has at most two
adjacent maximizing indices. It increases strictly whenever
\(t<k/2\). Moreover,
\begin{equation}
 E_{k,m}\le\frac{s-1}{2},
 \quad\text{strictly if }k\ge2,\qquad
 E_{k,m}\sim\frac{2s}{k}\quad(k\longrightarrow\infty)
 \label{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:asymptotic}
\end{equation}
for each fixed \(m\ge4\).
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Put \(b_t=\binom{k}{t}\), \(g_t=D_t/(t+1)\).
For \(0\le t<k\), the binomial recurrence gives the exact identity
\begin{equation}
 g_{t+1}-g_t
 =\frac{mb_t}{(t+1)(t+2)}
 \left(
 \frac{(m-1)k-(m-2)t+2}{m}-\frac{c_t}{b_t}
 \right).
 \label{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:difference}
\end{equation}
The first expression in parentheses decreases strictly with \(t\).
The second increases strictly, as is seen from
\[
 \frac{c_t}{b_t}
 =\sum_{j=0}^t
   \prod_{i=0}^{j-1}\frac{t-i}{k-t+i+1}.
\]
When \(t\) increases, each existing nonempty product increases
and a positive summand is added. Hence the sign in
\eqref{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:difference} changes at most once, from positive
to negative, and at most one difference can be zero.
If \(t<k/2\), then \(c_t/b_t\le t+1\), while
\[
 \frac{(m-1)k-(m-2)t+2}{m}-(t+1)
 =\frac{(m-1)(k-2t)-(m-2)}m\ge\frac1m.
\]
This proves the assertions about the profile.

For the elementary upper bound, the \(t=0\) term is
\(m-1<(s-1)/2\). For \(t\ge1\), use \(D_t\le s-1\)
and \(t+1\ge2\). If \(k\ge2\), the degree-one numerator
is strictly below \(s-1\), and the terms \(t\ge2\) have
denominator at least three, proving strictness.

For the asymptotic, let \(X\) be binomial with parameters
\(k,1/2\). Then
\[
 \frac{D_t}{s}
 =\Pr(X\le t)-\frac1m\Pr(X=t).
\]
Take \(t=\lceil k/2+k^{2/3}\rceil\). Chebyshev's inequality
shows that both \(1-\Pr(X\le t)\) and \(\Pr(X=t)\) tend to zero,
while \(k/(t+1)\to2\). Thus
\(\liminf kE_{k,m}/s\ge2\).

For the reverse inequality fix \(0<\delta<1/2\).
If \(t\ge(1/2-\delta)k\), then
\[
 \frac{kD_t}{s(t+1)}\le\frac1{1/2-\delta}.
\]
If \(\sqrt{k}\le t<(1/2-\delta)k\), Chebyshev gives
\(\Pr(X\le t)\le1/(4\delta^2k)\), so this same ratio is
at most \(1/(4\delta^2(t+1))\), which tends uniformly to zero.
For \(t<\sqrt{k}\),
\[
 c_t\le(\sqrt{k}+1)k^{\sqrt{k}},\qquad
 \frac{kD_t}{s(t+1)}\le \frac{kc_t}{2^k}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Hence the limsup is at most \(1/(1/2-\delta)\).
Letting \(\delta\) decrease to zero proves the asymptotic.
\end{proof}

The maximizing index can be found without comparing large rational
numbers: locate the first \(t\) for which the parenthesized
expression in \eqref{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:difference} is nonpositive.
Equality gives exactly two adjacent maximizers. If no such index
occurs before \(k\), the maximum is attained at \(t=k\).

\subsection{Eight-arrangements: explicit numbers}

In the interface of the original proof, \(d=8\), so \(m=16\),
\(s=2^{k+4}\), and \(M=17k+15\). The original
Lemma~15.5 \cite{repo35} uses
\[
 J=s2^{s-1}=2^{\,2^{k+4}+k+3}
\]
and a sufficient condition
\[
 (\alpha\eta/4)^J\beta^{15}q\ge k\,3^s.
\]
Its guaranteed retained count is
\((\alpha\eta/4)^J\beta^{15}q^{17k+15}\).
The recent one-stage Fej\'er report \cite{repo35fejer} already
replaces this count loss by
\[
 \frac{\alpha^s\eta^{s-1}}{3^{s-1}(s+1)^s}
       \beta^{15}q^{17k+15},
\]
under its explicit sufficient size condition
\[
 q\ge(k+1)\beta^{-15}
 \left(\frac{18(s+1)^2}{(\alpha\eta)^2}\right)^s
\]
and its separate characteristic condition. We retain the same
powers \(\alpha^s\eta^{s-1}\) and replace the field-size exponent
\(2s\) in that convenient condition by the following smaller values.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}rrrrrr@{}}
\toprule
\(k\)&\(s\)&Maximizing \(t\)&Earlier \(2s\)&
Weighted \((s-1)/2\)&Graded \(E_{k,16}\)\\
\midrule
1&32&1&64&\(31/2\)&\(31/2\)\\
2&64&1&128&\(63/2\)&\(23\)\\
3&128&2&256&\(127/2\)&\(109/3\)\\
4&256&3&512&\(255/2\)&\(59\)\\
5&512&3&1024&\(511/2\)&\(203/2\)\\
6&1024&4&2048&\(1023/2\)&\(897/5\)\\
7&2048&5&4096&\(2047/2\)&\(633/2\)\\
8&4096&5&8192&\(4095/2\)&\(1724/3\)\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Sufficient inverse-\(\alpha\eta\) exponents for
eight-arrangements, with \(k,m,\beta\) fixed. The weighted
column is Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:35:sel:prop:unstratified}, proved here.
Constants and density powers are given separately in the theorems.}
\label{gsr:en:35:sel:tab:exponents}
\end{table}

For \(k=2,m=16\), the exact dimensions are
\[
 (D_0,D_1,D_2)=(15,46,63),\qquad C_{\rm coll}=1080.
\]
Thus one may take \(L=\lceil65/(\alpha\eta)\rceil\) and require
\begin{equation}
 q\ge\max\left\{
 6\beta^{-15}L^{15},
 \ (12\beta^{-15}L^{46})^{1/2},
 \ (6486\beta^{-15}L^{63})^{1/3}
 \right\}.
 \label{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:k2}
\end{equation}
The corresponding respected count is at least
\[
 \frac{\alpha^{64}\eta^{63}}{2\cdot66^{64}}\,\beta^{15}q^{49},
\]
with purity at least \(1/(1+\eta)\).
In particular, the largest bandwidth power in
\eqref{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:k2} is \(23\), not \(128\). When the density
\(\beta\) also varies, the full maximum in \eqref{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:k2}
must be retained; the single exponent comparison does not
discard those density dependences.

\subsection{One explicit substitution into the original proof}

The preceding improvements can be passed through one adjacent
interface without redoing the entire inverse argument. The
arrangement-count input supplied by the product-property lemma
in the source transcription (Lemma~14.8) is
\begin{equation}
 G_\phi(B)\ge
 \beta^{7\cdot4^{k+1}}\gamma^{21k4^{k+1}}q^{17k+15}.
 \label{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:product-input}
\end{equation}
Here \(0<\beta,\gamma\le1\), and \(\beta\) is the density of
the relevant domain \(B\). We state the consequence conditionally
on this numerical input, so that no unstated variant of the
product-property definition is needed.

\begin{corollary}[A replacement at the Lemma 15.6 interface]
\label{gsr:en:35:sel:cor:downstream}
Suppose the eight-arrangement count \eqref{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:product-input}
holds, and put
\[
 A_k=7\cdot4^{k+1}-15,\qquad B_k=21k4^{k+1},\qquad s=2^{k+4}.
\]
Take
\[
 L=\left\lceil 2^{44}(s+1)\beta^{-A_k}\gamma^{-B_k}\right\rceil.
\]
If \eqref{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:explicit-q} holds with \(m=16\) and this
bandwidth, and \(p>2(L-1)\), there is a subset with purity
at least \(1-2^{-44}\) and at least
\begin{equation}
 \frac{2^{-44(s-1)-1}}{(s+2)^s}\,
 \beta^{sA_k+15}\gamma^{sB_k}q^{17k+15}
 \label{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:downstream-count}
\end{equation}
respected arrangements.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
In Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:35:sel:cor:explicit}, substitute
\(\alpha=\beta^{A_k}\gamma^{B_k}\) and \(\eta=2^{-44}\).
Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:product-input} is precisely the required
lower bound \(\alpha T_0\). Expanding the parameter powers in
\eqref{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:polynomial-count} gives
\eqref{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:downstream-count}.
\end{proof}

The input \eqref{gsr:en:35:sel:eq:product-input} has exactly the corrected exponents of the formal \file{lemma_14_8} (\file{Sections14\_15.lean}, line~292; companion \file{lemma_14_8_holds}, \file{Proofs14ProductToArrangements.lean}, line~18, at HEAD \texttt{89c1cbc38}): $\beta^{7\cdot4^{k+1}}\gamma^{21k4^{k+1}}N^{17k+15}$, the exponent $21k4^{k+1}$ in place of the printed $7k4^{k+1}$, as the formal \file{lemma_15_6} records.

Obtaining a global bound for \(r_\ell(N)\) would additionally

\section{Source~38's Part~II: sharp odd-order stability at the Proposition~6.1 endpoint \wtag}\label{gsr:en:sec:oddstability}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the seventh write, 6~October 2026.}}\par
The next section is source~38's Section~6, its delivered Part~II. \emph{Logically it continues source~31's chapter on the Proposition~6.1 endpoint} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:endpoint}), which gives the exact profile over all finite abelian groups and leaves the odd-order coefficients open; it is printed here because no number printed earlier may move. Source~38's introduction is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:38:sec:d1}.

\emph{What is proved.} For unit vectors $v$ on groups of odd order with $\norm v_{U^3}^8\ge1-\varepsilon$, the optimal distance $\mathfrak S_{\rm odd}(\varepsilon)$ from quadratic coset phases is $\varepsilon/4+3\varepsilon^2/16+(\sqrt2/64)\varepsilon^{5/2}+O(\varepsilon^3)$, uniformly in the group; the fractional term comes from characters of order three and disappears when $\gcd(|G|,6)=1$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:38:thm:odd-modulus}); through a uniform preliminary stability (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:38:thm:odd-coarse}, credited to source~31), an explicit local envelope (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:38:thm:odd-local-envelope}) and tangent rigidity at order-three characters. Over all groups source~31's profile has the second coefficient $5/16$, attained on $\Z/2\Z$ (note after the theorem). \section[{The sharp odd-order local stability coefficients\srctag{38}}]{The sharp odd-order local stability coefficients}\label{gsr:en:38:sec:d6}
\srcnote{38}{Section 6}
\gsrsrcpartof{38}{Sharp odd-order stability for the critical uniformity inequality}
\label{gsr:en:38:sec:odd-local}

The preceding project report proves an odd-order envelope with coefficient
$12$ in front of $(1-t)^2t^2$ and leaves its optimal local coefficient
open \cite{repo38rigidity}. We determine that coefficient and the next,
fractional-power term. The latter distinguishes groups with three-torsion
from groups whose order is coprime to six. The resulting statement is a
sharp asymptotic modulus, with an explicit finite remainder.

The classification of critical-norm extremizers and qualitative
near-extremizers is established by Eisner--Tao
\cite[Theorem~1.4]{eisnertao}. We begin with the finite argument and the
explicit preliminary estimate needed here, including their proofs. This
makes the quantitative conclusions independent of any unproved assertion
in a preceding report. The original Fourier-to-structure setting is
Gowers' Proposition~6.1 \cite{gowers}; the Weyl representation also
connects the calculation to stabilizer-state testing \cite{gnw}.

\subsection{Normalization and quadratic coset phases}

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group, $N=|G|$, and let
$\ipthirtyone uv=\E_xu(x)\overline{v(x)}$ be the inner product, linear in its
first argument. Write $\T=\{z\in\C:|z|=1\}$. A phase $Q:K\to\T$ on a subgroup $K\le G$ is
\emph{quadratic} if all its third multiplicative derivatives equal one.
Equivalently, for every $h\in K$,
\[
 Q(x)\overline{Q(x-h)}=c_h\chi_h(x),
 \qquad |c_h|=1,\quad \chi_h\in\widehat K.
\]
To see the equivalence, a unit phase with constant first differences is
a constant times a character; apply this observation to the first
derivatives of $Q$. A normalized quadratic coset phase is a function
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:38:eq:odd-coset-phase}
 \psi(x)=\sqrt{\frac N{|K|}}\,
       \ind_{x_0+K}(x)Q(x-x_0).
\end{equation}
Let $\Qcos(G)$ be this family, including arbitrary constant unit phases.
For $\|v\|_2=1$, put
\[
 \kappa(v)=\|v\|_{U^3}^8,
 \qquad
 \mathcal F(v)=\max_{\psi\in\Qcos(G)}|\ipthirtyone v\psi|^2.
\]
The maximum exists, as follows also from the finite eigenline
classification below. For a nonzero unnormalized function $f$, take
$v=f/\|f\|_2$; then
$\kappa(v)=\|f\|_{U^3}^8/\|f\|_2^8$.

The phase space $V=G\times\widehat G$ has size $N^2$. For
$z=(h,\chi)$ define
\[
 W_z=M_\chi T_h,\qquad
 (M_\chi u)(x)=\chi(x)u(x),\qquad T_hu(x)=u(x-h).
\]
These unitary operators multiply according to addition of their labels,
up to unit scalars. Their commutator is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:38:eq:odd-symplectic}
 W_zW_y=B(z,y)W_yW_z,\qquad
 B((h,\chi),(k,\eta))=\chi(k)\overline{\eta(h)}.
\end{equation}
The alternating bicharacter $B$ is nondegenerate, by character
separation on $G$ and on $\widehat G$.

For $\|v\|_2=1$ set $q_v(z)=|\ipthirtyone v{W_zv}|^2$. Fourier Parseval
and the derivative formula for the $U^3$ norm give
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:38:eq:odd-moyal}
 0\le q_v\le1,\qquad \sum_{z\in V}q_v(z)=N,\qquad
 \kappa(v)=\frac1N\sum_{z\in V}q_v(z)^2\le1.
\end{equation}
Indeed $\ipthirtyone v{W_{(h,\chi)}v}$ is the normalized Fourier coefficient
of $v(x)\overline{v(x-h)}$ at $\chi$. Its squared sum in $\chi$ is
$\E_x|v(x)|^2|v(x-h)|^2$; summing in $h$ gives $N$.
Its fourth-power sum in $\chi$ is the fourth power of the derivative's
$U^2$ norm, and averaging in $h$ gives $\kappa(v)$.
The inequality follows from $q_v^2\le q_v$ and proves the critical
$U^3$--$L^2$ bound with coefficient one.

\subsection{An explicit preliminary stability theorem}

We prove the following estimate on all finite abelian groups. The
constant and high-coefficient argument are credited to
\cite{repo38rigidity}; they serve here as a self-contained prerequisite.

\begin{theorem}[Uniform preliminary stability]
\label{gsr:en:38:thm:odd-coarse}
If $\|v\|_2=1$ and $\varepsilon=1-\kappa(v)<1/120$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:38:eq:odd-coarse}
 \mathcal F(v)\ge1-20\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
The bound is independent of the order and exponent of $G$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{lemma}[Projective overlap and additive closure]
\label{gsr:en:38:lem:odd-overlap-closure}
If $q_v(z),q_v(y)\ge1-a$ with $0\le a\le1/2$, then
\[
 q_v(z-y)\ge(1-2a)^2.
\]
If a nonempty finite subset $S$ of an abelian group satisfies
$|S-S|<3|S|/2$, then $S-S$ is a subgroup.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Decompose the unit vectors $W_zv,W_yv$ along $v$ and its orthogonal
complement. After adjusting their constant phases, their inner product
has absolute value at least $(1-a)-a=1-2a$. The projective Weyl
multiplication law identifies its squared modulus with $q_v(z-y)$.

For the second assertion put $D=S-S$. If $d=b-c\in D$, the sets
$S-b,S-c\subseteq D$ have intersection of size greater than $|S|/2$.
Equivalently more than half of $x\in S$ satisfy $x+d\in S$.
For any $d,e\in D$, the two corresponding subsets of $S$ intersect;
for an $x$ in their intersection, both $x+d,x+e$ belong to $S$.
Thus $d-e\in D$, so the nonempty set $D$ is closed under subtraction
and is a subgroup.
\end{proof}

Call a subgroup $H\le V$ \emph{isotropic} if $B(h,k)=1$ for all
$h,k\in H$.

\begin{lemma}[A gap for noncommuting subgroups]
\label{gsr:en:38:lem:odd-twirl}
If $H\le V$ is not isotropic, then every unit vector $v$ satisfies
\[
 \frac1{|H|}\sum_{h\in H}|\ipthirtyone v{W_hv}|^2\le\frac12.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For an operator $A$, average its conjugates:
\[
 \mathcal P(A)=\frac1{|H|}\sum_{h\in H}W_hAW_h^*.
\]
Conjugation removes the projective scalars, so $\mathcal P$ is the
orthogonal projection, for the Hilbert--Schmidt inner product, onto
the operators commuting with all $W_h$. Put $\rho=|v\rangle\langle v|$
and $\sigma=\mathcal P(\rho)$. This is a positive operator of trace one,
and
\[
 \frac1{|H|}\sum_{h\in H}|\ipthirtyone v{W_hv}|^2
   =\tr(\rho\sigma)=\tr(\sigma^2).
\]
Every eigenspace of $\sigma$ is invariant under all $W_h$. None can
be one-dimensional: a common eigenline would force every scalar
commutator in \eqref{gsr:en:38:eq:odd-symplectic} to equal one, contrary to the
hypothesis. Each positive eigenvalue therefore has multiplicity at
least two, and is at most $1/2$. Hence
$\tr(\sigma^2)\le\tfrac12\tr\sigma=1/2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 34--39]
This is source~31's Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:31:lem:twirl}, reproved for completeness; the preliminary stability around it is credited to source~31 by the source. Source~36's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:thm:bilinear} is its sharp rank-sensitive form over $\F_p^n$.
\end{writenote}

\begin{lemma}[Isotropic eigenspaces and quadratic coset phases]
\label{gsr:en:38:lem:odd-classification}
If $H\le V$ is isotropic, then $|H|$ divides $N$, and each common
character eigenspace of its normalized representation has dimension
$N/|H|$. In particular, if $|H|=N$, the common eigenvectors form an
orthonormal basis indexed by $\widehat H$, and each is a quadratic
coset phase. Conversely, every quadratic coset phase arises this way
for an isotropic subgroup of size $N$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The commuting unitary operators $W_h$ are simultaneously diagonalizable.
Choose a common eigenvector with eigenvalues $\lambda_h$ and put
$U_h=\lambda_h^{-1}W_h$. Evaluating the projective product on that
eigenvector shows that $U_hU_k=U_{h+k}$. For each
$\gamma\in\widehat H$ its character projector is
\[
 P_\gamma=\frac1{|H|}\sum_{h\in H}\overline{\gamma(h)}U_h.
\]
Every nonidentity Weyl operator has trace zero: a nonzero translation
has no diagonal entries, while a nontrivial pure modulation has
character sum zero. Thus $\tr P_\gamma=N/|H|$. This positive number
is an integer, proving the divisibility and dimension statements.

Assume now that $|H|=N$. Let $K$ be its projection into $G$ and let
$D=\{\chi:(0,\chi)\in H\}$. Isotropy gives $D\subseteq K^\perp$;
the equality $|H|=|K||D|=N$ forces $D=K^\perp$.
The modulation eigenrelations restrict the support of a common
eigenvector to one coset $x_0+K$. The translation eigenrelations for
$h\in K$ force that entire coset into the support, with constant
modulus. Normalization fixes the modulus to $\sqrt{N/|K|}$.
The same relations state that each derivative of its phase on $K$
is a constant times a character, which is precisely quadraticity.

Conversely consider \eqref{gsr:en:38:eq:odd-coset-phase}. For every $h\in K$
the derivative character on $K$ has $|K^\perp|$ extensions to $G$.
Each extension gives a Weyl operator preserving the line through
$\psi$. The labels of all line-preserving Weyl operators form a
subgroup, by the projective multiplication law, and its commutators
must be one since they act on a nonzero common eigenvector. No label
whose translation lies outside $K$ can preserve that line. Consequently
this isotropic subgroup has exactly $|K||K^\perp|=N$ elements.
The finite-group character-extension fact used here follows, for
example, by extending a character one cyclic generator at a time and
choosing a suitable root of its already specified value.

There are finitely many subgroups of $V$ and exactly $N$ eigenlines
for each isotropic subgroup of size $N$. The classification therefore
also proves that $\Qcos(G)$ is finite modulo constant unit phases,
and that the maximum defining $\mathcal F(v)$ is attained.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:38:thm:odd-coarse}]
Write $q=q_v$ and put $S=\{z:q(z)\ge19/20\}$. Equation
\eqref{gsr:en:38:eq:odd-moyal} gives
$\sum_zq(z)(1-q(z))=N\varepsilon$, so the $q$-mass outside $S$
is at most $20N\varepsilon$. Hence
\[
 |S|\ge\sum_{z\in S}q(z)\ge(1-20\varepsilon)N.
\]
The overlap lemma puts $S-S$ inside $\{q\ge4/5\}$, so
$|S-S|\le5N/4$. Since $\varepsilon<1/120$,
\[
 |S-S|\le5N/4<\tfrac32(1-20\varepsilon)N\le3|S|/2.
\]
Thus $H=S-S$ is a subgroup. Every coefficient there is at least
$4/5$, so Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:38:lem:odd-twirl} makes $H$ isotropic. Also
$|H|\ge|S|>5N/6>N/2$, and divisibility in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:38:lem:odd-classification} implies $|H|=N$.

Since $q(0)=1$, one has $0\in S$ and $S\subseteq H$. Expand $v$
in the common eigenbasis of $H$, with coefficient probabilities
$p_\gamma$. Character orthogonality gives
\[
 \sum_\gamma p_\gamma^2
 =\frac1N\sum_{h\in H}q(h)\ge1-20\varepsilon.
\]
The largest $p_\gamma$ is at least their sum of squares because their
sum is one. Its eigenvector is a quadratic coset phase, proving
\eqref{gsr:en:38:eq:odd-coarse}.
\end{proof}

At $\varepsilon=0$, the argument and the mass identity also recover
the exact extremizers: they are precisely the normalized quadratic
coset phases. The cutoff $1/120$ and preliminary coefficient $20$
are sufficient constants; their optimality is not asserted.

\subsection{The explicit odd-order local envelope}

\begin{theorem}[Explicit odd-order local envelope]
\label{gsr:en:38:thm:odd-local-envelope}
Suppose $|G|$ is odd and $\|v\|_2=1$. Let $\psi$ be any normalized quadratic coset phase
with $|\langle v,\psi\rangle|^2=1-t$, where $0\le t\le1/6$.
Set $F=1-t$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:38:eq:odd-local-envelope}
 \kappa(v)\le F^4+6F^2t^2
       +2\sqrt2 F^{3/2}t^{5/2}+104Ft^3+t^4.
\end{equation}
If $3\nmid |G|$, the term $2\sqrt2 F^{3/2}t^{5/2}$ may be omitted.
The constants $6$ and $2\sqrt2$, in that order of asymptotic comparison,
are optimal uniformly over odd-order groups. No optimality is claimed
for $104$.
\end{theorem}

Here ``in that order'' means that the coefficient of $F^2t^2$ is first
minimized; among envelopes with that coefficient equal to $6$, the
coefficient of $F^{3/2}t^{5/2}$ is then minimized. The theorem does not
assert an exact finite-$t$ optimum.

\subsection{A Weyl-coset expansion}

Choose the isotropic subgroup $H$ of size $N$ associated with $\psi$
by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:38:lem:odd-classification}, and normalize its representation
so that $\psi$ has character label zero. Its common eigenbasis is
indexed by $\Gamma=\widehat H$. Nondegeneracy of the commutator
pairing gives $|H^\perp|=N^2/|H|=N$, hence $H^\perp=H$.
The map sending a Weyl label to its commutator character on $H$
therefore identifies $V/H$ with $\Gamma$.
A Weyl operator from a coset with label $\gamma$ shifts eigenvector
labels by $\gamma$, up to unit scalar factors. This follows by
commuting that operator past each $U_h$. These facts hold for every
maximal isotropic subgroup; no change to a coordinate subgroup is
assumed.

Choose the global phase so that
\[
 v=\sqrt F\,\psi+\sqrt t\,w,\qquad
 \langle w,\psi\rangle=0,\qquad \|w\|_2=1.
\]
The case $t=0$ is immediate and is henceforth suppressed. Let
$s_\gamma$ be the coefficient probabilities of $w$ in the common
eigenbasis. Then $s_0=0$, $\sum s_\gamma=1$. Define
\[
 A=\sum_\gamma s_\gamma^2,\qquad
 B=\sum_\gamma s_\gamma s_{-\gamma},\qquad
 C=\sum_{\alpha+\beta=\gamma}s_\alpha s_\beta s_\gamma.
\]
Since $|\Gamma|$ is odd, its nonzero elements form disjoint pairs
$\{\gamma,-\gamma\}$. If $m_i$ are their total probabilities, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:38:eq:pair-collision}
 A+B=\sum_i m_i^2\le1,\qquad B\le\tfrac12.
\end{equation}
In particular $2A+4B\le3$.

For $z\notin H$ put
\[
 l_z=\langle\psi,W_zw\rangle+\langle w,W_z\psi\rangle,
 \qquad d_z=\langle w,W_zw\rangle.
\]
Write $\int_{V\setminus H} a=N^{-1}\sum_{z\notin H}a(z)$;
this is a finite measure, not necessarily a probability measure.

Here is an explicit formula for the coset coordinates, including the
phase factors. Write $w=\sum_\beta b_\beta\psi_\beta$, where
$U_h\psi_\beta=\beta(h)\psi_\beta$ and $b_0=0$.
Choose a representative $z_\gamma$ for a Weyl coset. There are unit
scalars $u_{\gamma,\beta}$ such that, after removing the same common
unit factor from all coefficients at $z_\gamma+h$, the ambiguity
coefficient of a vector with coordinates $c_\beta$ is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:38:eq:odd-coset-coordinates}
 \sum_{\beta\in\Gamma}
 c_{\beta+\gamma}\overline{c_\beta}\,
 u_{\gamma,\beta}\overline{\beta(h)}.
\end{equation}
This follows by first applying $U_h$ and then the label-shifting
operator $W_{z_\gamma}$. Thus, for $\gamma\ne0$, the linear term is
\[
 l_\gamma(h)=b_\gamma u_{\gamma,0}
       +\overline{b_{-\gamma}}u_{\gamma,-\gamma}\gamma(h).
\]
The same common factor multiplies $l$ and $d$, and cancels from every
product $|l|^4$, $|l|^2|d|^2$, and
$l^2\overline l\,\overline d$ used below. In particular the argument
does not require the projective scalar factors to vanish separately.

\begin{lemma}[The exact fourth-order coefficient]
\label{gsr:en:38:lem:odd-fourth}
One has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:38:eq:l-fourth}
 \int_{V\setminus H}|l|^4=2A+4B.
\end{equation}
Furthermore, with
\[
 K(w)=4\operatorname{Re}\int_{V\setminus H}l^2\overline l\,
                    \overline d,
\]
there exist real numbers $J(w),M(w)$ such that
\begin{align}
 \kappa(v)={}&F^4+6F^2t^2(A+B)
      +F^{3/2}t^{5/2}K(w)\notag\\
 &+Ft^3J(w)+F^{1/2}t^{7/2}M(w)+t^4\kappa(w),
 \label{gsr:en:38:eq:odd-exact-expansion}\\
 0\le J(w)&\le4+6\sqrt3,
 \qquad |M(w)|\le4\,3^{1/4},
 \qquad \kappa(w)\le1.\label{gsr:en:38:eq:odd-remainder-bounds}
\end{align}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
On $H$ the coefficient of $v$ is, up to a unit scalar,
$F+t\widehat s(h)$. Character orthogonality gives its fourth moment as
\[
 F^4+F^2t^2(4A+2B)+4Ft^3C+t^4\mathsf E(s),
\]
where $\mathsf E(s)=\sum_{a+b=c+d}s_as_bs_cs_d$. The term with one
nonzero label vanishes because $s_0=0$.

Consider a Weyl coset with nonzero shift label $\gamma$. Up to a common
unit scalar, the two summands of $l$ are two characters on $H$ with
coefficient magnitudes $\sqrt{s_\gamma}$ and
$\sqrt{s_{-\gamma}}$. The ratio character has label $\gamma$.
Both that character and its square are nontrivial since $\Gamma$ has
odd order. Therefore the fourth moment over this coset is
\[
 s_\gamma^2+s_{-\gamma}^2+4s_\gamma s_{-\gamma}.
\]
Summing over nonzero shift labels proves \eqref{gsr:en:38:eq:l-fourth}.

Outside $H$ the Weyl coefficient is
$\sqrt{Ft}\,l+td$. Expand its fourth power. Besides the fourth and
fifth-order terms already displayed, the coefficients are
\[
 J=4C+\int_{V\setminus H}
    \bigl(2|l|^2|d|^2+4(\operatorname{Re}(l\overline d))^2\bigr),
 \qquad
 M=4\operatorname{Re}\int_{V\setminus H}|d|^2l\overline d.
\]
The $t^4$ terms on and off $H$ add up to $t^4\kappa(w)$.
The fourth-order coefficients add to $6(A+B)$, proving the exact
identity. Since $C\le1$, $\|l\|_4\le3^{1/4}$, and
$\|d\|_4\le\kappa(w)^{1/4}\le1$, H\"older's inequality gives
\eqref{gsr:en:38:eq:odd-remainder-bounds}.
\end{proof}

For clarity, the critical estimate for $w$ in this proof does not require
an inverse theorem. For any vectors $u_1,u_2$, the mixed ambiguity
coefficient satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:38:eq:mixed-ambiguity}
 \left(\frac1N\sum_z|\langle u_1,W_zu_2\rangle|^4\right)^{1/4}
       \le\|u_1\|_2\|u_2\|_2.
\end{equation}
Indeed the maximum squared coefficient is at most
$\|u_1\|_2^2\|u_2\|_2^2$, and Weyl orthogonality gives total squared
mass $N\|u_1\|_2^2\|u_2\|_2^2$. Multiplying these two bounds proves
\eqref{gsr:en:38:eq:mixed-ambiguity}. Taking $u_1=u_2=w$ gives $\kappa(w)\le1$.

\subsection{The order-three resonance}

\begin{lemma}[A single opposite pair]
\label{gsr:en:38:lem:opposite-pair}
Let $w_0$ be supported on the two eigenvector labels
$\{\gamma,-\gamma\}$, with $\|w_0\|_2\le1$. Then
\[
 |K(w_0)|\le2\sqrt2.
\]
If $3\gamma\ne0$, then $K(w_0)=0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The linear coefficient $l(w_0)$ is supported on Weyl cosets with shift
labels $\pm\gamma$. The coefficient $d(w_0)$, away from $H$, is
supported on shift labels $\pm2\gamma$. These sets meet only if
$3\gamma=0$, proving the vanishing assertion.

In the remaining case choose the shift-$\gamma$ coset. Its linear
coefficient has the form $b+c\chi$, up to unit scalars, where
$|b|=u$, $|c|=v$, and $\chi$ is an order-three character. Its quadratic
coefficient has the form $d\chi^{-1}$, with $|d|=uv$. In the average
of $l^2\overline l\,\overline d$, precisely the powers $\chi^{-1}$
and $\chi^2$ can contribute after multiplication by $\chi$.
Their total absolute value is at most
$u^3v^2+u^2v^3$. The other shift coset has the same bound.
Consequently
\[
 |K(w_0)|\le8u^2v^2(u+v)\le2\sqrt2,
\]
using $u^2+v^2\le1$. Equality in the scalar bound occurs at
$u=v=1/\sqrt2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Stability of the fifth-order coefficient]
\label{gsr:en:38:lem:fifth-stability}
Put $D=1-A-B$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:38:eq:K-stability}
 K(w)\le K_*+20\,3^{3/4}\sqrt D,
 \qquad
 K_*=
 \begin{cases}2\sqrt2,&3\mid N,\\0,&3\nmid N.\end{cases}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:38:eq:pair-collision} implies that the greatest opposite-pair
mass is at least $1-D$. Let $w_0$ be the unnormalized orthogonal
projection of $w$ onto that pair. Then
$\|w-w_0\|_2\le\sqrt D$. The fourth-moment formula for $l$, by
homogeneity, gives
\[
 \|l(w)-l(w_0)\|_4\le3^{1/4}\sqrt D,
 \qquad \|l(w)\|_4,\|l(w_0)\|_4\le3^{1/4}.
\]
The mixed ambiguity estimate \eqref{gsr:en:38:eq:mixed-ambiguity} gives
\[
 \|d(w)-d(w_0)\|_4
 \le(\|w\|_2+\|w_0\|_2)\|w-w_0\|_2\le2\sqrt D.
\]
Expand the difference of $l^2\overline l\,\overline d$ at $w$ and
$w_0$, using three terms for the cubic factor and one for $d$. H\"older
gives
\[
 |K(w)-K(w_0)|
 \le4\bigl(3\,3^{3/4}+2\,3^{3/4}\bigr)\sqrt D
 =20\,3^{3/4}\sqrt D.
\]
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:38:lem:opposite-pair} concludes the proof. If $3\nmid N$,
no label has order three because $|\Gamma|=N$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:38:thm:odd-local-envelope}]
Insert \eqref{gsr:en:38:eq:K-stability} into the exact expansion and set
$L=20\,3^{3/4}$. Completing the square gives
\[
 -6F^2t^2D+L F^{3/2}t^{5/2}\sqrt D
 \le\frac{L^2}{24}Ft^3=50\sqrt3\,Ft^3.
\]
The remaining terms are at most
\[
 F^4+6F^2t^2+K_*F^{3/2}t^{5/2}
 +(4+56\sqrt3)Ft^3+4\,3^{1/4}F^{1/2}t^{7/2}+t^4.
\]
Since $t/F\le1/5$ for $t\le1/6$, the last two intermediate
remainder coefficients satisfy
\[
 4+56\sqrt3+4\,3^{1/4}\sqrt{t/F}
 \le4+56\sqrt3+\frac{4\,3^{1/4}}{\sqrt5}<104.
\]
This proves the explicit envelope. Sharpness of the two asymptotic
coefficients follows from the examples below.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Tangent rigidity at the optimal coefficients]
\label{gsr:en:38:cor:odd-tangent-rigidity}
Consider any sequence of unit vectors on finite abelian groups of odd
order, and choose a maximizing quadratic coset phase for each vector.
After adjusting its constant phase, write
\[
 v=\sqrt F\,\psi+\sqrt t\,w,\qquad
 F=\mathcal F(v)=1-t,\qquad t\downarrow0.
\]
If
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:38:eq:odd-tangent-assumption}
 \kappa(v)=F^4+6F^2t^2
       +2\sqrt2 F^{3/2}t^{5/2}+o(t^{5/2}),
\end{equation}
then, in the common eigenbasis associated with $\psi$, the tangent
$w$ concentrates in a pair $\{\gamma,-\gamma\}$ with $3\gamma=0$.
More precisely, these labels have order three for all sufficiently
late terms, the two coefficient moduli tend to $1/\sqrt2$, and the
orthogonal projection $w_0$ to that pair satisfies
\[
 1-A-B=o(\sqrt t),\qquad \|w-w_0\|_2=o(t^{1/4}).
\]
No classification of the two coefficient phases is asserted.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Put $D=1-A-B\ge0$ and $K_0=2\sqrt2$. Comparing
\eqref{gsr:en:38:eq:odd-tangent-assumption} with the exact expansion
\eqref{gsr:en:38:eq:odd-exact-expansion}, using its uniform remainder bounds,
gives
\[
 6\sqrt F\,\frac D{\sqrt t}
       =K(w)-K_0+o(1).
\]
The bound \eqref{gsr:en:38:eq:K-stability} implies that $K(w)$ is bounded,
so first $D=O(\sqrt t)$ and hence $D\to0$. It then gives
$K(w)\le K_0+o(1)$. Since the left side of the displayed identity
is nonnegative, both $D/\sqrt t\to0$ and $K(w)\to K_0$ follow.

Choose a pair of greatest mass and project to it as in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:38:lem:fifth-stability}. Then
$\|w-w_0\|_2^2\le D=o(\sqrt t)$, and the same Lipschitz estimate
gives $K(w_0)\to2\sqrt2$. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:38:lem:opposite-pair} forces
the pair label to have order three eventually. If its coefficient
moduli are $a,b$, then $a^2+b^2\to1$ and
\[
 K(w_0)\le8a^2b^2(a+b)\le2\sqrt2.
\]
The limiting upper bound can be attained only when
$a^2b^2\to1/4$: use $a+b\le\sqrt2$ and $a^2b^2\le1/4$.
Together with $a^2+b^2\to1$, this implies
$a,b\to1/\sqrt2$, as required.
\end{proof}

\subsection{An exact three-element sharpness family}

Let $e_j=\sqrt3\,\mathbf1_{\{j\}}$ be the normalized point-mass
basis on $\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z$. For $0\le t\le1/6$ put
\[
 v_t=\sqrt{1-t}\,e_0+\sqrt{t/2}\,(e_1+e_2).
\]
Then its best quadratic-coset fidelity is $\mathcal F(v_t)=1-t$. To verify this,
note that a quadratic coset phase is either a point mass or has full
support and constant modulus one. The latter's squared overlap is at
most $(\sqrt{1-t}+\sqrt{2t})^2/3$, which is smaller than $1-t$ on
this interval. (Squaring the equivalent positive inequality reduces
the assertion to $6t(1-t)<1$.)

The norm is exactly
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:38:eq:qutrit-exact}
 \kappa(v_t)=(1-t)^4+6(1-t)^2t^2
    +2\sqrt2(1-t)^{3/2}t^{5/2}
    +4(1-t)t^3+\tfrac12t^4.
\end{equation}
One direct verification expands the cube sum. Of the $3^4=81$ affine
maps $(x,h_1,h_2,h_3)$, the numbers with exactly $r$ zero cube vertices
are
\[
 \begin{array}{c|rrrrr}
 r&0&2&3&4&8\\\hline
 \text{number}&8&32&16&24&1.
 \end{array}
\]
The values at every nonzero vertex coincide and are real. Substituting
$a=\sqrt{1-t}$ and $b=\sqrt{t/2}$ gives
$a^8+24a^4b^4+16a^3b^5+32a^2b^6+8b^8$, which is
\eqref{gsr:en:38:eq:qutrit-exact}. Here is an elementary derivation of the count.
With no nonzero directions there are one map with $r=8$ and two with
$r=0$. With one nonzero direction there are six direction tuples; each
has two translates with $r=4$ and one with $r=0$. With two nonzero
directions there are twelve direction tuples; each has residue
multiplicities $4,2,2$ on the cube, hence one translate with $r=4$ and
two with $r=2$. With three nonzero directions there are eight tuples;
their residue multiplicities are $3,3,2$, hence two translates with
$r=3$ and one with $r=2$. Adding these contributions gives the table.
A short exhaustive verification script accompanies the article.

This proves that the coefficient $6$ cannot decrease, and that after
it is fixed the coefficient $2\sqrt2$ cannot decrease. It also
disproves the putative remainder-free envelope
$\kappa\le(1-t)^4+6(1-t)^2t^2+t^4$ on all odd-order groups.

For an example with $3\nmid N$, use $G=\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z$, now
with normalized point masses $e_j=\sqrt5\,\ind_{\{j\}}$, and put
$v_t=\sqrt{1-t}\,e_0+\sqrt t\,e_1$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:38:eq:two-state-exact}
 \mathcal F(v_t)=1-t,\qquad
 \kappa(v_t)=(1-t)^4+6(1-t)^2t^2+t^4.
\end{equation}
Indeed the zero-shift coset contributes
$F^4+4F^2t^2+t^4$, and the two nonzero shift cosets $\pm1$ each
contribute $F^2t^2$. Full-support phases have squared correlation at
most $2/5$, so the point mass is the maximizer for $t\le1/6$.

\begin{remark}[Finite comparison and the meaning of the coefficient]
The earlier envelope is $F^4+12F^2t^2+t^4$ on odd-order groups
\cite{repo38rigidity}. Our explicit upper bound is strictly smaller
for $0<t\le1/25$, because
\[
 2\sqrt2\sqrt{t/F}+104\,t/F
 \le\frac1{\sqrt3}+\frac{13}{3}<6.
\]
More significantly, its two successive asymptotic coefficients are
optimal. The exact three-element family shows why there is no
remainder-free replacement by the polynomial with coefficient $6$.
The next contribution is larger than any constant multiple of $t^3$
as $t\downarrow0$, and must be retained when three-torsion is allowed.
\end{remark}

\subsection{The optimal local modulus through its fractional term}

Define
\[
 \mathfrak S_{\rm odd}(\varepsilon)=\sup\{1-\mathcal F(v):\ |G|\text{ odd},\
                \|v\|_2=1,\ \kappa(v)\ge1-\varepsilon\},
\]
where the supremum ranges over all finite abelian groups as well as
all such functions. Define $\mathfrak S_{6'}$ by restricting to $\gcd(|G|,6)=1$.

\begin{theorem}[Sharp uniform asymptotic stability]
\label{gsr:en:38:thm:odd-modulus}
As $\varepsilon\downarrow0$,
\begin{align}
 \mathfrak S_{\rm odd}(\varepsilon)
 &=\frac\varepsilon4+\frac{3\varepsilon^2}{16}
       +\frac{\sqrt2}{64}\varepsilon^{5/2}+O(\varepsilon^3),
 \label{gsr:en:38:eq:odd-modulus}\\
 \mathfrak S_{6'}(\varepsilon)
 &=\frac\varepsilon4+\frac{3\varepsilon^2}{16}+O(\varepsilon^3).
 \label{gsr:en:38:eq:six-prime-modulus}
\end{align}
The implied constants are independent of group order and exponent.
For optimal squared distance to a normalized coset phase, replace these
right sides respectively by
\[
 \frac\varepsilon4+\frac{13\varepsilon^2}{64}
       +\frac{\sqrt2}{64}\varepsilon^{5/2}+O(\varepsilon^3),
 \qquad
 \frac\varepsilon4+\frac{13\varepsilon^2}{64}+O(\varepsilon^3).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:38:thm:odd-coarse} gives $1-\mathcal F(v)\le20\varepsilon$
when $\varepsilon<1/120$, on every finite abelian group. Thus
$t=1-\mathcal F(v)$ is at most $1/6$ and is $O(\varepsilon)$ uniformly. Apply
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:38:thm:odd-local-envelope} to a maximizing phase and expand:
\[
 \varepsilon\ge4t-12t^2-K_*t^{5/2}-O(t^3).
\]
First this gives $t\le\varepsilon/4+O(\varepsilon^2)$; inserting that estimate
back into the quadratic and fractional terms gives
\[
 t\le\frac\varepsilon4+\frac{3\varepsilon^2}{16}
           +\frac{K_*}{128}\varepsilon^{5/2}+O(\varepsilon^3).
\]
All constants are uniform because the explicit envelope and preliminary
bound are uniform. The exact family \eqref{gsr:en:38:eq:qutrit-exact} gives the
matching lower asymptotic expansion: its deficit is continuous and
strictly increasing for all sufficiently small $t$, with derivative
$4$ at zero, so every sufficiently small $\varepsilon$ is attained.
Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:38:eq:two-state-exact} gives the analogous lower bound
when $3\nmid N$.

Finally optimizing the constant phase of an extremizer gives
\[
 \min_{\psi\in\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{cos}}(G)}\|v-\psi\|_2^2
       =2(1-\sqrt{\mathcal F(v)})=t+\tfrac14t^2+O(t^3).
\]
This changes $3/16$ to $3/16+1/64=13/64$ and preserves the
$\varepsilon^{5/2}$ coefficient.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 34--39]
\emph{Answers source~31's odd-order question} (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:sharpprofile}; checked at the write). Over all finite abelian groups source~31's exact profile $(1-\sqrt{(1+\sqrt{1-4\varepsilon})/2})/2$ expands as $\varepsilon/4+5\varepsilon^2/16+O(\varepsilon^3)$, with equality on $\Z/2\Z$; on odd-order groups the second coefficient drops to $3/16$, and the term $(\sqrt2/64)\varepsilon^{5/2}$ comes from characters of order three, absent when $\gcd(|G|,6)=1$. The two profiles are compatible ($3/16<5/16$). The local envelope's constant $104$ is not claimed optimal.
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 54--59]
Source~55's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:55:thm:main} has the odd-order squared-distance coefficient $(3^d-1)/(2q^2)$ in every degree, $13/64$ at $d=3$ as here, for functions bounded by one, where no $\varepsilon^{5/2}$ term occurs: the fractional term above comes from $L^2$-normalized near point masses, which are not bounded by one (note after source~55's theorem). Source~55 does not cite this source.
\end{writenote}

\paragraph{Scope and remaining questions.}
The critical-norm classification and the preliminary stability estimate
are credited prerequisites, proved above for completeness. The new
conclusion is the uniform sharp odd-order expansion through
$\varepsilon^{5/2}$, together with an explicit finite-$t$ estimate.
It refines the local near-extremal regime of the derivative-Fourier
framework; no new global inverse theorem is asserted.

Is the exact odd-order local optimum attained by the three-element
family \eqref{gsr:en:38:eq:qutrit-exact} throughout some nonzero interval?
What is the sharp coefficient of $\varepsilon^3$ in
$\mathfrak S_{\rm odd}$ and $\mathfrak S_{6'}$? Does the latter
coefficient depend on five-torsion? A sharper remainder retaining the
opposite-pair deficit $1-\sum_i m_i^2$ could help distinguish these
possibilities.

\emph{What is proved, and what is new in this report.} Second routes (source~19's results, re-derived): the common $r$-subset sampler with an $O(q/\sigma)$ budget, the exact finite minimax as a maximum over class profiles attained by permutation orbits, the dynamic program, conditional-expectation selection, the sharp affine constant $\varphi^3e^{-\varphi}$ (Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:39:thm:selection}, \ref{gsr:en:39:thm:minimax}, \ref{gsr:en:39:thm:derandomization}, Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:39:cor:golden}). \section[{A finite model of shared-anchor certification\srctag{39}}]{A finite model of shared-anchor certification}\label{gsr:en:39:sec:d2}
\srcnote{39}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:en:39:sec:model}

\begin{definition}[Row families and ambient mass]\label{gsr:en:39:def:family}
Let $J$ be a finite set with $|J|=m\ge1$, and let $H$ be a finite row set.
Assign weights $w_h\ge0$ with $W=\sum_h w_h>0$. In each row choose pairwise
disjoint sets
\[
 C_{h,1},\ldots,C_{h,q_h}\subseteq J,
 \qquad B_h=\bigcup_{i=1}^{q_h}C_{h,i}.
\]
Empty classes are permitted. The weighted mean class count and domain density
are
\[
 \bar q=\frac1W\sum_h w_hq_h,\qquad
 \delta_B=\frac1{mW}\sum_h w_h|B_h|.
\]
All mass bounds in this article are normalized by the full ambient mass $mW$,
not by $\sum_h w_h|B_h|$.
\end{definition}

Allowing $B_h$ to be a proper subset of $J$ is essential. An intermediate
partial graph in the inverse argument need not meet every vertical line in
every column. It is also essential for the extremal profiles: in one of the
asymptotic regimes it is best to use only part of the column set.

\begin{definition}[Certification]\label{gsr:en:39:def:certification}
Fix an integer $t\ge1$ and a sample $R\subseteq J$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:certified}
 K_h(R)=(B_h\cap R)\ \cup\!
 \bigcup_{\substack{1\le i\le q_h\\|C_{h,i}\cap R|\ge t}} C_{h,i}.
\end{equation}
The normalized uncertified mass is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:D}
 D_{\cC}(R)=\frac1{mW}\sum_h w_h|B_h\setminus K_h(R)|.
\end{equation}
The ambient good set $E_R\subseteq H\times J$ is obtained by deleting just
these uncertified points. Thus all points outside the domain $B$ remain in
$E_R$, and all sampled domain points remain in $E_R$.
\end{definition}

For a class $C$ of size $s$ with $a=|C\cap R|$, the discarded count is precisely
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:class-discard}
 (s-a)\ind_{\{a<t\}}.
\end{equation}
There are two contributions to the definition, and neither should be dropped:
a class with enough anchors is retained entirely, while a class with too few
anchors still retains its sampled points.

\begin{remark}[Monotonicity]\label{gsr:en:39:rem:monotonicity}
If $R\subseteq R'$, then $K_h(R)\subseteq K_h(R')$ and
$D_{\cC}(R')\le D_{\cC}(R)$. Consequently, a result for at most $r$ anchors can
be padded to exactly $r\le m$ distinct anchors without increasing the loss.
The statements below use exact-size samples because their probability law and
extremal problem are especially clean.
\end{remark}

We use the convention $\binom ab=0$ when $a\ge0$ and $b\notin\{0,\ldots,a\}$.
A hypergeometric variable $\HG(m,s,u)$ counts the members of a fixed
$s$-element class in a uniformly chosen $u$-subset of an $m$-element set.
The case $r=m$ is treated explicitly whenever an $(r+1)$-subset appears.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A cutoff-free shared sampling theorem\srctag{39}}]{A cutoff-free shared sampling theorem}\label{gsr:en:39:sec:d3}
\srcnote{39}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:en:39:sec:selection}

\begin{lemma}[Exact one-class loss]\label{gsr:en:39:lem:marginal}
Let $R$ be a uniformly chosen $r$-subset of $J$, where $0\le r\le m$. A class
of size $s$ contributes expected normalized loss $\ell_{m,r,t}(s)$ from
\eqref{gsr:fm:39:eq:intro-loss}. If $r<m$ and $Z\sim\HG(m,s,r+1)$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:double-identity}
 \ell_{m,r,t}(s)=\frac{m-r}{m(r+1)}
 \E\bigl[Z\ind_{\{1\le Z\le t\}}\bigr].
\end{equation}
For $r=m$, this loss is zero.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The random variable $A=|C\cap R|$ has probability
$\binom sj\binom{m-s}{r-j}/\binom mr$ of equalling $j$.
Taking the expectation of \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:class-discard} and dividing by $m$ gives
\eqref{gsr:fm:39:eq:intro-loss}.

For the second formula, count ordered pairs $(R,x)$ such that $|R|=r$,
$x\in C\setminus R$, and $|C\cap R|<t$. The number of such pairs is
\[
 \sum_{|R|=r}|C\setminus R|\ind_{\{|C\cap R|<t\}}.
\]
Map a pair to $T=R\cup\{x\}$, an $(r+1)$-subset. Conversely, for fixed $T$,
a choice $x\in T\cap C$ gives a valid pair exactly when
$1\le |T\cap C|\le t$. Hence the same count is
\[
 \sum_{|T|=r+1}|T\cap C|\ind_{\{1\le |T\cap C|\le t\}}.
\]
Divide by $m\binom mr$ and use
$\binom m{r+1}/\binom mr=(m-r)/(r+1)$. When $r=m$, every domain point is
sampled, so no point is discarded.
\end{proof}

The shift from an $r$-sample to an $(r+1)$-sample is the central combinatorial
identity. It converts the size-weighted error into the expectation of a
variable bounded by $t$. No lower bound on $s$ is required.

\begin{theorem}[Shared-anchor selection]\label{gsr:en:39:thm:selection}
For every row family in Definition~\ref{gsr:en:39:def:family}, every $t\ge1$, and every
$0\le r\le m$, there is one set $R\subseteq J$ with $|R|=r$ such that
\begin{align}
 D_{\cC}(R)
 &\le \frac1W\sum_h w_h\sum_{i=1}^{q_h}
             \ell_{m,r,t}(|C_{h,i}|)\label{gsr:en:39:eq:profile-upper}\\
 &\le \min\left\{\delta_B,
       \frac{t\bar q(m-r)}{m(r+1)}\right\}.
       \label{gsr:en:39:eq:universal-upper}
\end{align}
In particular, if every row has at most $q$ classes, then
$D_{\cC}(R)\le tq/(r+1)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For a uniform $r$-subset, linearity of expectation and disjointness of the
classes give
\[
 \E_R D_{\cC}(R)=\frac1W\sum_h w_h\sum_i\ell_{m,r,t}(|C_{h,i}|).
\]
At least one sample has loss no greater than this average. Formula
\eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:double-identity} bounds each summand by
$t(m-r)/(m(r+1))$ when $r<m$; the endpoint $r=m$ is immediate. Also, the
loss is always at most $\delta_B$, so its expectation has this bound as well.
Finally, $\bar q\le q$ and $(m-r)/m\le1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[An explicit anchor budget]\label{gsr:en:39:cor:budget}
Let $0<\sigma<1$ and suppose every row has at most $q\ge1$ classes. The choice
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:simple-budget}
 r=\min\left\{m,\left\lceil\frac{tq}{\sigma}\right\rceil\right\}
\end{equation}
permits $D_{\cC}(R)\le\sigma$. A sufficient budget using the finite-population
correction is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:finite-budget}
 r\ge\left\lceil\frac{m(tq-\sigma)}{tq+\sigma m}\right\rceil,
 \qquad 0\le r\le m.
\end{equation}
The same formulas are valid with $q$ replaced by any upper bound on $\bar q$,
using a maximum with zero in \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:finite-budget} if its numerator is
negative.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
If \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:simple-budget} gives $r=m$, the loss is zero. Otherwise
$tq/(r+1)<\sigma$. For \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:finite-budget}, rearrange
$tq(m-r)\le\sigma m(r+1)$ to obtain
$m(tq-\sigma)\le r(tq+\sigma m)$, and apply
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:39:thm:selection}.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[Singletons are not an exception]\label{gsr:en:39:ex:singletons}
If $t\ge2$ and $C=\{x\}$, its class can never contain $t$ distinct anchors.
Nevertheless $x$ is certified when $x\in R$, and its exact expected loss is
\[
 \ell_{m,r,t}(1)=\frac{m-r}{m^2}.
\]
No false two-hit estimate is used. If every row consists of at most $q$
singletons, the total expected loss is at most $q(m-r)/m^2$, which can be much
smaller than the universal bound.
\end{example}

\begin{remark}[Why this improves the power of the error parameter]
A truncation proof discards classes of density below $\sigma/q$ and then
requires each surviving class to fail with probability at most $\sigma$.
That two-stage requirement can introduce an unnecessary second small
parameter. Here the loss of a class is multiplied by its own mass before any
estimate is made. The exact double count controls the \emph{sum of discarded
masses}, directly giving $q/r$ rather than a per-class accuracy demand.
\end{remark}

For affine interpolation, take $t=2$. The repository's corrected long-column
lemma requires $6q\le r\sigma^2$, together with a size condition, and loses at
most $2\sigma$ ambient mass \cite{repo39anchored}. Its short-column wrapper
removes the separate long-column hypothesis by sampling all columns when
needed \cite{repo39short}. Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:39:thm:selection} instead uses the one
uniform-subset procedure at all column lengths, gives loss $\sigma$ with
\eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:simple-budget}, and supplies the same sampled-or-anchored type of
output. This comparison concerns the actual stated budgets, not a claim that
all possible refinements of the older proof require a quadratic budget.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The exact finite minimax problem\srctag{39}}]{The exact finite minimax problem}\label{gsr:en:39:sec:d4}
\srcnote{39}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:en:39:sec:minimax}

\begin{definition}[Worst best-sample loss]\label{gsr:en:39:def:minimax}
For $m\ge1$, $q\ge1$, $0\le r\le m$, and $t\ge1$, let
\[
 \cM_{m,q,r,t}=\sup_{\cC}\ \min_{\substack{R\subseteq J\\|R|=r}}
 D_{\cC}(R),
\]
where $\cC$ ranges over all finite weighted row families with at most $q$
pairwise-disjoint classes in each row, on an $m$-element column set.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Exact finite minimax formula]\label{gsr:en:39:thm:minimax}
The supremum in Definition~\ref{gsr:en:39:def:minimax} is attained by a finite unweighted
family. Its value is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:minimax}
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 \cM_{m,q,r,t}=
 \max_{\substack{(s_1,\ldots,s_q)\in\N_0^q\\\sum_i s_i\le m}}
          \sum_{i=1}^q\ell_{m,r,t}(s_i).}
\end{equation}
An attaining family can be obtained by applying all permutations of $J$ to any
maximizing disjoint class profile.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let the maximum on the right be $A$. There are finitely many profiles, so it is
attained. Pad rows with empty classes to give exactly $q$ labels. In each row,
$\sum_i|C_{h,i}|\le m$, hence
$\sum_i\ell_{m,r,t}(|C_{h,i}|)\le A$. Averaging over rows and applying
\eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:profile-upper} gives an $r$-set with loss at most $A$. Thus
$\cM_{m,q,r,t}\le A$.

For the reverse inequality, choose a maximizing profile $(s_i)$ and disjoint
sets $C_1,\ldots,C_q\subseteq J$ of those sizes. Let the row set be the
symmetric group $\operatorname{Sym}(J)$, with equal weights. In row $\pi$, use
classes $\pi(C_1),\ldots,\pi(C_q)$. Fix any $r$-subset $R$. The loss in this row
is the loss of the original profile against $\pi^{-1}(R)$, divided by $m$.
As $\pi$ runs uniformly through the symmetric group, $\pi^{-1}(R)$ is uniform
among all $r$-subsets: each such subset occurs $r!(m-r)!$ times. Therefore the
average row loss for this fixed $R$ is
$\sum_i\ell_{m,r,t}(s_i)=A$.

This holds for every $R$, so even the best sample has loss $A$. The family is
finite and unweighted, proving both the lower bound and attainment. Equal
copies of a row may be removed by passing to the orbit of the labelled
partition, since orbit fibres have equal cardinality.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A finite criterion for any proposed universal bound]
\label{gsr:en:39:cor:criterion}
A number $a$ bounds the best shared-sample loss for every row family with the
parameters $(m,q,r,t)$ if and only if
\[
 \sum_{i=1}^q\ell_{m,r,t}(s_i)\le a
 \quad\hbox{for every integer profile with }\sum_i s_i\le m.
\]
Thus any improvement in a universal finite sampling constant can be checked
against a finite one-row profile optimization, even though the original
minimax problem permits arbitrarily many rows.
\end{corollary}

\subsection{Exact evaluation by dynamic programming}
For $0\le a\le q$ and $0\le b\le m$, let $V_a(b)$ be the best sum of losses
from $a$ classes using at most $b$ columns. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:dp}
 V_0(b)=0,\qquad
 V_a(b)=\max_{0\le s\le b}\bigl(V_{a-1}(b-s)+\ell_{m,r,t}(s)\bigr).
\end{equation}
The minimax value is $V_q(m)$. Storing a maximizing $s$ at each state recovers a
profile. Once the $m+1$ rational values of $\ell$ are available, the dynamic
program performs $O(qm^2)$ rational comparisons and additions. Memory is
$O(qm)$ with parent pointers, or $O(m)$ when only the value is needed. These are
arithmetic-operation counts; they do not bound the bit complexity of large
binomial coefficients by a constant.

\begin{example}[Exact small extremizers]\label{gsr:en:39:ex:orbit}
For $(m,q,r,t)=(6,2,2,2)$, the profile $(3,3)$ gives
$\cM=3/5$. The $20$ labelled partitions of a six-element set into two
three-element classes form a family for which all $15$ two-element anchor sets
have loss exactly $3/5$.

For $(7,2,3,2)$, the maximizing profile $(3,3)$ leaves one unused column and
gives $\cM=96/245$. Its $140$ labelled placements have this average loss against
every one of the $35$ three-element samples. These identities are also checked
by exhaustive rational enumeration in the supplied certificates.
\end{example}

\begin{proposition}[Boundary regimes]\label{gsr:en:39:prop:boundary}
For $q\ge1$, one has $\cM_{m,q,m,t}=0$. If $r<t$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:small-r}
 \cM_{m,q,r,t}=1-\frac rm.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The first assertion follows because every point is sampled. If $r<t$, no class
can have $t$ sampled points, so only sampled targets are retained. For a class
of size $s$, its expected discarded count is $s(1-r/m)$; hence
$\ell_{m,r,t}(s)=s(m-r)/m^2$. The profile maximum is obtained by using all $m$
columns, for example in a single class. This gives \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:small-r}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The scope of the extremal family]\label{gsr:en:39:rem:scope}
The symmetrization theorem is valid with no field structure on $J$. If a field
structure is subsequently added, the class family still need not exhibit the
horizontal regularity required elsewhere in Gowers's proof. Moreover, even if
a function is assigned to each class, a point left uncertified by this rule
might be algebraically recoverable in some other way. The theorem proves
minimax optimality of the rule in Definition~\ref{gsr:en:39:def:certification}, and no
stronger algorithmic lower bound.
\end{remark}
