\section[{A closed finite profile formula and the affine quadratic cap\srctag{39}}]{A closed finite profile formula and the affine quadratic cap}\label{gsr:en:39:sec:d5}
\srcnote{39}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:en:39:sec:finite-shape}

The profile optimization in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:39:thm:minimax} can in fact be solved
without dynamic programming. The key extra fact is that the one-class loss
is concave up to its first maximum and never increases afterwards. The
hypergeometric expression makes this shape accessible through exact finite
differences.

Write $\Delta u(s)=u(s+1)-u(s)$ and
$\Delta^2u(s)=u(s+2)-2u(s+1)+u(s)$. These expressions are only used when their
arguments lie between $0$ and $m$.

\begin{lemma}[Finite differences of a hypergeometric average]
\label{gsr:en:39:lem:hyp-differences}
Let $g$ be any function on $\{0,\ldots,n\}$ and let
$A_n(s)=\E[g(Z_s)]$ for $Z_s\sim\HG(m,s,n)$, with $0\le n\le m$.
For $n\ge1$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:hyp-first}
 \Delta A_n(s)=\frac nm\E[\Delta g(Y)],
 \qquad Y\sim\HG(m-1,s,n-1).
\end{equation}
For $n\ge2$ and $m\ge2$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:hyp-second}
 \Delta^2 A_n(s)=\frac{n(n-1)}{m(m-1)}\E[\Delta^2g(Y)],
 \qquad Y\sim\HG(m-2,s,n-2).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Couple the class of size $s$ with that of size $s+1$ by adding one distinguished
column. A uniform $n$-subset contains that column with probability $n/m$.
Conditional on containing it, its other $n-1$ columns are uniform in the
remaining population of size $m-1$, with $s$ successes. If the distinguished
column is absent, the class count does not change; if it is present, the
change in $g$ is $\Delta g(Y)$. This proves \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:hyp-first}.
Apply the same argument to the hypergeometric average on its right, with
population $m-1$, sample size $n-1$, and function $\Delta g$, to obtain
\eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:hyp-second}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Exact curvature and the one-class shape]\label{gsr:en:39:lem:finite-shape}
Fix $m,r,t$. The sequence $s\mapsto\ell_{m,r,t}(s)$ is nondecreasing up to
its first maximizing index $a=a_{m,r,t}$ and nonincreasing thereafter.
It is discretely concave on $\{0,\ldots,a\}$.

More explicitly, when $1\le t\le r<m$ and $0\le s\le m-2$, put
\[
 K_{m,r}=\frac{r(m-r)}{m^2(m-1)\binom{m-2}{r-1}}>0.
\]
Then
\begin{align}
 \Delta^2\ell_{m,r,t}(s)
 =K_{m,r}\biggl[&t\binom st\binom{m-s-2}{r-t-1}\notag\\
 &-(t+1)\binom{s}{t-1}\binom{m-s-2}{r-t}\biggr].
 \label{gsr:en:39:eq:finite-curvature}
\end{align}
For $r>t$ this factors as
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:curvature-sign}
 \Delta^2\ell_{m,r,t}(s)
 =\frac{K_{m,r}}{r-t}\binom{s}{t-1}\binom{m-s-2}{r-t-1}
 \bigl[(r+1)(s+2)-(t+1)(m+1)\bigr].
\end{equation}
For $r=t$ the second difference is nonpositive everywhere.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $r=m$, the sequence is identically zero. If $r<t$, then
$\ell(s)=s(m-r)/m^2$ by Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:39:prop:boundary}, so it is linear and
nondecreasing. These cases already give the claimed shape.

Suppose $1\le t\le r<m$. In \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:double-identity} set
$g(z)=z\ind_{\{z\le t\}}$ for $z\ge0$. Its second difference is zero except
at $z=t-1$ and $z=t$, where it equals $-(t+1)$ and $t$, respectively.
Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:39:lem:hyp-differences} with $n=r+1$, and multiply by the
prefactor $(m-r)/(m(r+1))$. The remaining hypergeometric variable has
population $m-2$, class size $s$, and sample size $r-1$. Writing its two
relevant probabilities with binomial coefficients yields
\eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:finite-curvature}.

If $r=t$, its first term is zero, proving global concavity. If $r>t$, use
\[
 t\binom st=(s-t+1)\binom{s}{t-1},\qquad
 \binom{m-s-2}{r-t}
 =\frac{m-s-r+t-1}{r-t}\binom{m-s-2}{r-t-1}.
\]
These identities remain valid at the boundary with the zero convention.
The bracket after factoring is
\[
 (s-t+1)(r-t)-(t+1)(m-s-r+t-1)
 =(r+1)(s+2)-(t+1)(m+1),
\]
which proves \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:curvature-sign}.

Consequently the finite-difference sequence
$d_s=\ell(s+1)-\ell(s)$ is first nonincreasing and then nondecreasing; in the
case $r=t$ it is simply nonincreasing. Also
$d_0=(m-r)/m^2>0$, while $\ell(m)=0$ and $\ell(m-1)\ge0$, so
$d_{m-1}\le0$. Every term on the final nondecreasing part is therefore
nonpositive. On the initial nonincreasing part, the differences can cross
from positive to nonpositive at most once. It follows that $\ell$ increases
to its first maximum and never increases after it. The differences before
that first maximum belong to the nonincreasing part, proving discrete
concavity up to $a$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Balanced-and-capped finite extremizers]
\label{gsr:en:39:thm:balanced}
Let $a=a_{m,r,t}$ be the least size maximizing $\ell_{m,r,t}$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:balance-parameters}
 B=\min\{m,qa\},\qquad
 v=\lfloor B/q\rfloor,\qquad u=\lceil B/q\rceil,\qquad
 \beta=B-qv.
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:balanced-formula}
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 \cM_{m,q,r,t}=(q-\beta)\ell_{m,r,t}(v)
                      +\beta\ell_{m,r,t}(u).}
\end{equation}
An extremizing profile has $q-\beta$ classes of size $v$ and $\beta$ classes
of size $u$. In particular, an extremizer exists with at most two positive
class sizes, and those sizes differ by at most one.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Start with any feasible profile. Replace every size greater than $a$ by $a$.
By Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:39:lem:finite-shape}, this does not decrease its objective and does
not increase its total size. All sizes now lie in $[0,a]$. Since $\ell$ is
nondecreasing there, add columns to classes until their total is
$B=\min\{m,qa\}$; this is feasible and does not decrease the objective.

If two sizes satisfy $y\ge x+2$, move one column from the larger to the
smaller. The objective changes by
\[
 \ell(x+1)-\ell(x)-\bigl(\ell(y)-\ell(y-1)\bigr)
 =\Delta\ell(x)-\Delta\ell(y-1)\ge0,
\]
using discrete concavity on $[0,a]$. Iterating this balancing operation
terminates, for example because the sum of squared sizes strictly decreases
at each nontrivial step. At termination the sizes differ by at most one and
sum to $B$, hence have the multiplicities in \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:balance-parameters}.
Their objective is \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:balanced-formula}. This profile is feasible, so
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:39:thm:minimax} proves equality.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 34--39]
\emph{Source~19's question, answered for this rule only} (checked at the write by exact rational arithmetic; the intake found the same counts). Source~19's Question~1 asks for the structure of the maximizers of its finite minimax (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:sampling}). For source~39's rule the formula \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:balanced-formula} agrees with an exact maximization over all class profiles in all $2{,}835$ cases $m\le18$, $0\le r\le m$, $t\le3$, $q\le5$. For source~19's rule it does not: with source~19's one-class loss $W_{m,r,t}(s)=(s/m)\Pr\{X<\min(t,s)\}$ in place of $\ell_{m,r,t}$, the balanced-and-capped value differs from the exact maximum in $199$ of the same $2{,}835$ cases; the first is $m=2$, $r=1$, $t=2$, $q=2$, where the formula gives $1/2$ and the exact value is $1$ (one class of size $2$, lost with its one sampled point; under source~39's rule the same profile loses $1/2$). Source~19's one-class loss is not concave up to its first maximum, which is what the proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:39:thm:balanced} uses. The rules also give different values, for example $0.3512$ (source~39) against $0.3944$ (source~19) at $m=20$, $q=2$, $r=4$, $t=2$. So the classification for source~19's rule stays open (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:sampling}).
\end{writenote}

When $\beta=0$, one has $u=v$, so formula \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:balanced-formula} never
requires evaluating $\ell$ outside its domain. When $r=m$, the first mode is
$a=0$, giving zero. When $r<t$, it is $a=m$, and the formula reproduces
$1-r/m$. Empty classes cause no problem when $q>m$.

This theorem solves the finite optimization, rather than merely reducing it
to a dynamic program. A scan of the $m+1$ one-class values determines $a$;
the remaining computation is a single balancing operation. The dynamic
program in Section~\ref{gsr:en:39:sec:minimax} is retained as an independent exact
verification method.

\begin{theorem}[An explicit quadratic cap for affine fibres]
\label{gsr:en:39:thm:affine-cap}
Let $t=2$. If $r=m$, then $a_{m,r,2}=0$; if $r<2$ and $r<m$, then
$a_{m,r,2}=m$. For $2\le r<m$, define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:affine-root}
 \zeta_{m,r}=
 \frac{B_{m,r}+\sqrt{B_{m,r}^2+
       4(r^2-1)(m-r)(m-r+1)}}{2(r^2-1)},
 \qquad B_{m,r}=(r-2)m+2r-1.
\end{equation}
Then the least maximizing class size is exactly
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:affine-cap}
 a_{m,r,2}=\lceil\zeta_{m,r}\rceil.
\end{equation}
Together with Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:39:thm:balanced}, this is a closed finite formula for
the affine minimax loss, requiring no search over profiles or class sizes.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The endpoint and $r<2$ cases have already been established. For $2\le r<m$,
apply \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:hyp-first} to \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:double-identity}. Since
$\Delta g(z)=1$ for $z=0,1$, $\Delta g(2)=-2$, and it is zero afterwards,
\[
 \Delta\ell_{m,r,2}(s)=\frac{m-r}{m^2}
 \bigl[\Prob(Z=0)+\Prob(Z=1)-2\Prob(Z=2)\bigr],
 \quad Z\sim\HG(m-1,s,r).
\]
Apart from positive factors, the bracket has numerator
\[
 \binom{m-1-s}{r}+s\binom{m-1-s}{r-1}
                 -s(s-1)\binom{m-1-s}{r-2}.
\]
For $0\le s\le m-r+1$, factor out the positive quantity
$\binom{m-1-s}{r-2}/(r(r-1))$. The remaining quadratic is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:affine-sign}
 -(r^2-1)s^2+B_{m,r}s+(m-r)(m-r+1).
\end{equation}
Its constant term is positive and its quadratic coefficient negative, so
it has one positive root, namely \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:affine-root}. At
$s=m-r+1\ge2$, the unfactored numerator is strictly negative: only its last
term is nonzero. Thus the positive root lies strictly between $0$ and
$m-r+1$.

The first difference is positive at integer $s<\zeta_{m,r}$ and nonpositive
at the first integer $s\ge\zeta_{m,r}$. By the unimodality already proved,
this first change determines the least maximum, giving
$a_{m,r,2}=\lceil\zeta_{m,r}\rceil$. If the root is an integer, the difference
there is zero and the first of the two equal maximizing values is precisely
that integer, so the ceiling formula still applies.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Exact implementation of the radical ceiling]
Let $A=r^2-1$, $B=B_{m,r}$, $C=(m-r)(m-r+1)$, and $D=B^2+4AC$.
Set $k=\lfloor(B+\lfloor\sqrt D\rfloor)/(2A)\rfloor$. This is
$\lfloor\zeta_{m,r}\rfloor$. The cap equals $k$ when $Ak^2-Bk-C=0$, and
otherwise equals $k+1$. Integer square root and this exact equality test avoid
floating-point decisions near an integer root. The supplied implementation
uses this procedure.
\end{remark}

\begin{example}[A genuinely finite improvement]\label{gsr:en:39:ex:finite-balanced}
For $(m,q,r,t)=(20,2,4,2)$, the affine root formula gives $a=7$. Since
$qa=14\le20$, the exact worst-case profile is $(7,7)$ and
\[
 \cM_{20,2,4,2}=\frac{1001}{2850}=0.351228\ldots.
\]
The simple universal bound is $16/25=0.64$. The improved value is not an
asymptotic estimate: every such row family has a four-anchor sample with loss
at most $1001/2850$, and a finite permutation-orbit family attains equality.
\end{example}

\section[{The Poisson profile and its exact optimization\srctag{39}}]{The Poisson profile and its exact optimization}\label{gsr:en:39:sec:d6}
\srcnote{39}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:en:39:sec:poisson}

The expression $F_t$ from \eqref{gsr:fm:39:eq:intro-F} has a direct interpretation:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:F-probability}
 F_t(x)=x\Prob\{\Pois(x)<t\}.
\end{equation}
It balances class mass against the probability that a class receives too few
anchors. This section solves the associated continuous optimization exactly;
Section~\ref{gsr:en:39:sec:asymptotic} justifies its use for the finite minimax problem.

\begin{lemma}[Unique maximum and the useful concavity interval]
\label{gsr:en:39:lem:shape}
For every $t\ge1$, the function $F_t$ has a unique positive maximizer
$\lambda_t$. It is characterized by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:lambda-root}
 \sum_{j=0}^{t-1}\frac{\lambda_t^j}{j!}
       =\frac{\lambda_t^t}{(t-1)!}.
\end{equation}
One has $0<\lambda_t\le t$, with strict inequality when $t>1$.
The function is strictly increasing before $\lambda_t$, strictly decreasing
after $\lambda_t$, and concave on $[0,\lambda_t]$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Put $P_{t-1}(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}x^j/j!$. Direct differentiation gives
\begin{align}
 F_t'(x)&=e^{-x}\left(P_{t-1}(x)-\frac{x^t}{(t-1)!}\right),
       \label{gsr:en:39:eq:Fprime}\\
 F_t''(x)&=\frac{e^{-x}x^{t-1}}{(t-1)!}(x-t-1).
       \label{gsr:en:39:eq:Fsecond}
\end{align}
For $x>0$, the equation $F_t'(x)=0$ becomes
\[
 \sum_{j=0}^{t-1}\frac{x^{j-t}}{j!}=\frac1{(t-1)!}.
\]
The left side is strictly decreasing from infinity to zero. This proves a
unique root and the claimed signs of the derivative.

At $x=t$, the terms $t^j/j!$ are nondecreasing for $0\le j\le t-1$, and each is
at most $t^{t-1}/(t-1)!$. Therefore
$P_{t-1}(t)\le t^t/(t-1)!$, strictly for $t>1$. Hence $\lambda_t\le t$,
strictly for $t>1$. Formula~\eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:Fsecond} now proves concavity on
$[0,\lambda_t]$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Poissonized subprobability optimization]\label{gsr:en:39:thm:poisson}
For real $r>0$, integer $q\ge1$, and integer $t\ge1$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:poisson-optimum}
 \max_{\substack{p_1,\ldots,p_q\ge0\\\sum_i p_i\le1}}
 \sum_{i=1}^q p_i\Prob\{\Pois(rp_i)<t\}
 =\frac qr F_t\!\left(\min\left\{\lambda_t,\frac rq\right\}\right).
\end{equation}
An optimizer has all $rp_i$ equal to $\min\{\lambda_t,r/q\}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Write $x_i=rp_i$. The optimization is $r^{-1}\max\sum_iF_t(x_i)$ subject to
$x_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i x_i\le r$. Any coordinate larger than $\lambda_t$ may be
replaced by $\lambda_t$, decreasing the resource consumption and increasing
the objective. We may therefore restrict to $x_i\in[0,\lambda_t]$.

By concavity and Jensen's inequality,
\[
 \sum_{i=1}^qF_t(x_i)\le qF_t\left(\frac1q\sum_i x_i\right).
\]
The average is at most both $\lambda_t$ and $r/q$. Since $F_t$ is increasing on
$[0,\lambda_t]$, this is at most
$qF_t(\min\{\lambda_t,r/q\})$. Equal coordinates at that value are feasible
and attain the bound.
\end{proof}

The inequality $\sum p_i\le1$, rather than equality, is part of the theorem.
If $r/q>\lambda_t$, the optimizer leaves mass $1-q\lambda_t/r$ unused. If the
classes were forced to partition all columns with no leftover domain, the
optimization would be different. The partial-graph application permits the
subprobability formulation naturally.

\begin{corollary}[The affine constant]\label{gsr:en:39:cor:golden}
For $t=2$,
\[
 \lambda_2=\varphi,\qquad
 \kappa_2=\varphi^3e^{-\varphi}=0.839962094657\ldots.
\]
For $t=1$, $\lambda_1=1$ and $\kappa_1=e^{-1}$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:lambda-root} is $1+x=x^2$ for $t=2$. Its positive root is
$\varphi$, and $F_2(\varphi)=\varphi(1+\varphi)e^{-\varphi}
=\varphi^3e^{-\varphi}$. The $t=1$ case is immediate.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 34--39]
This is source~19's Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:19:sampling:affine-constant} (the constant $0.839962094657$; source~19's Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:19:sampling:constant} gives the maximizing mean). In the regime $q/r\to0$ the two rules have the same limit, since the sampled points of a failed class carry vanishing mass.
\end{writenote}

\section[{Uniform asymptotics and a sharp sample-complexity law\srctag{39}}]{Uniform asymptotics and a sharp sample-complexity law}\label{gsr:en:39:sec:d7}
\srcnote{39}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:en:39:sec:asymptotic}

Pointwise Poisson convergence is not by itself enough to optimize over every
class-size profile. The maximizing sizes vary with $m$, $r$, and $q$, and a
profile may contain very large classes. We therefore prove a uniform marginal
estimate, including a tail bound, before interchanging the limit with the
profile maximum.

\begin{lemma}[An elementary product bound for sampling without replacement]
\label{gsr:en:39:lem:product}
Let $z_1,\ldots,z_m\ge0$ and let $R$ be a uniform $r$-subset of
$\{1,\ldots,m\}$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:product-bound}
 \E\prod_{i\in R}z_i\le\left(\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m z_i\right)^r.
\end{equation}
In particular, for $A\sim\HG(m,s,r)$ and $c>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:hypergeo-laplace}
 \E e^{-cA}\le\left(1-\frac sm(1-e^{-c})\right)^r
 \le \exp\left(-\frac{rs}{m}(1-e^{-c})\right).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The left side of \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:product-bound} is the normalized elementary
symmetric polynomial $e_r(z_1,\ldots,z_m)/\binom mr$. Holding all but two
coordinates $u,v$ fixed, this polynomial before normalization has the form
$A_0+(u+v)B_0+uvC_0$ with $A_0,B_0,C_0\ge0$. Replacing $u,v$ by their average
preserves their sum and increases their product, so does not decrease $e_r$.

Repeatedly average a largest and a smallest coordinate. The sum remains fixed
and the sum of squared deviations from the mean decreases by half the square
of the current spread. Thus the spread tends to zero, and the coordinates
converge to the common mean. By continuity, $e_r$ at the original vector is
at most $\binom mr$ times the $r$th power of the mean. The cases $r=0,1$ also
follow directly.

For \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:hypergeo-laplace}, set $z_i=e^{-c}$ on the class and $z_i=1$
outside it. Apply \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:product-bound} and $1-u\le e^{-u}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform one-class Poisson limit]\label{gsr:en:39:thm:uniform}
Fix $t\ge1$. Along any sequence of integer pairs $(m,r)$ with
$r\to\infty$ and $r/m\to0$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:uniform-limit}
 \sup_{0\le s\le m}
 \left|r\ell_{m,r,t}(s)-F_t\!\left(\frac{rs}{m}\right)\right|\longrightarrow0.
\end{equation}
The supremum is over integer class sizes.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Write $x=rs/m$ and $A\sim\HG(m,s,r)$. By the definition of $\ell$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:scaled-loss}
 r\ell_{m,r,t}(s)=
 x\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}\left(1-\frac js\right)\Prob(A=j)
\end{equation}
when $s>0$, with zero terms for impossible $j$. The $s=0$ case is zero.
The expression is nonnegative and at most $x\Prob(A<t)$.

First consider any sequence with $x\to x_0\in(0,\infty)$. Then $s\to\infty$,
$s/m\to0$, and eventually $s+r<m$. The zero-count probability satisfies
\begin{align*}
 \Prob(A=0)&=\prod_{i=0}^{r-1}\left(1-\frac{s}{m-i}\right),\\
 \log\Prob(A=0)&=-x+O\left(\frac{xr}{m}+\frac{x^2}{r}\right).
\end{align*}
Indeed, uniformly for $0\le i<r$, the quantity $s/(m-i)$ is $O(x/r)$; summing
its first-order terms gives $x+O(xr/m)$, and summing its squares gives
$O(x^2/r)$. For any fixed $j\ge0$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:hyp-ratio}
 \frac{\Prob(A=j)}{\Prob(A=0)}
 =\frac{\fall{s}{j}\fall{r}{j}}
 {j!\prod_{a=1}^{j}(m-s-r+a)}
 \longrightarrow\frac{x_0^j}{j!},
\end{equation}
where $\fall{s}{j}=s(s-1)\cdots(s-j+1)$. Consequently
$\Prob(A=j)\to e^{-x_0}x_0^j/j!$, and \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:scaled-loss} tends to
$F_t(x_0)$. If $x\to0$, both $r\ell$ and $F_t(x)$ lie between zero and $x$,
so the same conclusion holds.

These sequential statements imply uniform convergence on every bounded
interval of $x$. Otherwise one could choose a sequence of bounded $x$ at
which the error stays above a fixed positive number, pass to a convergent
subsequence, and contradict the preceding argument.

It remains to control unbounded $x$. Since $A<t$ means $A\le t-1$,
\[
 \Prob(A<t)\le e^{t-1}\E e^{-A}
 \le\exp\bigl(t-1-(1-e^{-1})x\bigr)
\]
by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:39:lem:product}. Thus, uniformly in $m,r,s$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:uniform-tail}
 0\le r\ell_{m,r,t}(s)
 \le x\exp\bigl(t-1-(1-e^{-1})x\bigr).
\end{equation}
The same bound holds for $F_t(x)$ by the Laplace transform of a Poisson
variable, or it follows directly from \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:F-probability}.
Both tails tend uniformly to zero as $x\to\infty$. Combining the compact
interval convergence with these tail estimates proves
\eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:uniform-limit}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Asymptotic minimax profile]\label{gsr:en:39:thm:asymptotic}
Fix $t\ge1$. Let $m,r,q$ vary with $r\to\infty$, $r/m\to0$, and $q\ge1$.
If $q/r$ stays bounded, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:asymptotic}
 \cM_{m,q,r,t}
 =\frac qr\left[
 F_t\!\left(\min\left\{\lambda_t,\frac rq\right\}\right)+o(1)\right].
\end{equation}
In particular, if $q/r\to0$, then $\cM_{m,q,r,t}\sim\kappa_tq/r$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $\varepsilon_{m,r}$ denote the supremum in \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:uniform-limit}.
It tends to zero. For any feasible finite profile $(s_i)$, put $x_i=rs_i/m$.
Then $\sum_i x_i\le r$, so Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:39:thm:minimax}, \ref{gsr:en:39:thm:poisson},
and \ref{gsr:en:39:thm:uniform} give
\[
 \cM_{m,q,r,t}
 \le\frac qr\left[
 F_t\!\left(\min\left\{\lambda_t,\frac rq\right\}\right)
 +\varepsilon_{m,r}\right].
\]
For a matching lower bound, set $x_* =\min\{\lambda_t,r/q\}$ and choose all
$q$ class sizes equal to $s_* =\lfloor mx_*/r\rfloor$. This is feasible since
$qs_*\le mq x_*/r\le m$. Also
$0\le x_*-rs_*/m<r/m\to0$. The function $F_t$ is uniformly continuous on
$[0,\lambda_t]$, so
\[
 \cM_{m,q,r,t}\ge q\ell_{m,r,t}(s_*)
 \ge\frac qr\bigl(F_t(x_*)-o(1)-\varepsilon_{m,r}\bigr).
\]
This proves \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:asymptotic}. If $q/r\to0$, then $x_* =\lambda_t$
eventually, and $\kappa_t>0$, giving the relative asymptotic.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 34--39]
Source~19's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:19:sampling:asymptotic} is the case $q/r\to0$; the regime $q/r$ bounded, where it is best to use only part of the column set, is new here and advances source~19's question on rates in the sharp law (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:sampling}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{corollary}[Two asymptotic regimes]\label{gsr:en:39:cor:phase}
Under the hypotheses above, if $q/r\to\theta\in(0,\infty)$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:phase}
 \cM_{m,q,r,t}\longrightarrow\Psi_t(\theta):=
 \begin{cases}
  \theta\kappa_t,&0<\theta\le1/\lambda_t,\\[3pt]
  \displaystyle e^{-1/\theta}\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}
                      \frac{\theta^{-j}}{j!},&\theta\ge1/\lambda_t.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
In the first regime, asymptotically extremal class sizes are
$s_i\sim\lambda_t m/r$ and need not exhaust the columns. In the second, they
are $s_i\sim m/q$ and asymptotically exhaust the column budget.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Substitute $r/q\to1/\theta$ in \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:asymptotic}. The profiles in the lower
bound proof have the stated sizes. At the transition the two expressions
coincide because $\kappa_t=F_t(\lambda_t)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Shape of the limiting loss curve]\label{gsr:en:39:prop:phase-shape}
Extend $\Psi_t$ by $\Psi_t(0)=0$. It is continuously differentiable, increasing,
and concave on $[0,\infty)$. It is linear on $[0,1/\lambda_t]$ and strictly
concave thereafter. Moreover, $\Psi_t(\theta)\to1$ as $\theta\to\infty$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
On the nonlinear branch, differentiation gives
\[
 \Psi_t'(\theta)=\frac{e^{-1/\theta}}{(t-1)!\,\theta^{t+1}}>0,
 \qquad
 \frac{\Psi_t''(\theta)}{\Psi_t'(\theta)}
 =\frac{1-(t+1)\theta}{\theta^2}<0.
\]
The last inequality holds because $\theta\ge1/\lambda_t\ge1/t$.
At $\theta=1/\lambda_t$, the right derivative is
$e^{-\lambda_t}\lambda_t^{t+1}/(t-1)!=\kappa_t$ by
\eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:lambda-root}; this equals the slope of the linear branch.
The limit at infinity follows from \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:phase}.
\end{proof}

The statement about $\theta\to\infty$ describes the explicitly defined curve
$\Psi_t$, not an additional uniform finite-parameter limit outside the stated
hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:39:thm:asymptotic}.

\begin{theorem}[Sharp sparse-sampling anchor budget]\label{gsr:en:39:thm:sharp-budget}
For $0<\sigma<1$, define the smallest worst-case sufficient sample size by
\[
 r_*(m,q,t,\sigma)=
 \min\{0\le r\le m:\cM_{m,q,r,t}\le\sigma\}.
\]
Fix $t$. Along sequences with $\sigma\to0$, $q\ge1$, and
$q/(\sigma m)\to0$, one has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:sharp-budget}
 r_*(m,q,t,\sigma)\sim\frac{\kappa_tq}{\sigma}.
\end{equation}
For affine certification the coefficient is
$\kappa_2=\varphi^3e^{-\varphi}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The minimum exists since sampling all $m$ columns gives zero loss.
Fix $0<\epsilon<\kappa_t$ and compare
\[
 r_- =\left\lfloor\frac{(\kappa_t-\epsilon)q}{\sigma}\right\rfloor,
 \qquad
 r_+ =\left\lceil\frac{(\kappa_t+\epsilon)q}{\sigma}\right\rceil.
\]
Both tend to infinity, both satisfy $r_\pm/m\to0$, and
$q/r_\pm\to0$. Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:39:thm:asymptotic} therefore gives
\[
 \frac{\cM_{m,q,r_-,t}}{\sigma}\longrightarrow
 \frac{\kappa_t}{\kappa_t-\epsilon}>1,
 \qquad
 \frac{\cM_{m,q,r_+,t}}{\sigma}\longrightarrow
 \frac{\kappa_t}{\kappa_t+\epsilon}<1.
\]
The best-sample loss is nonincreasing in $r$, by
Remark~\ref{gsr:en:39:rem:monotonicity}, and the same is true of its supremum.
Hence eventually $r_-<r_*\le r_+$. Divide by $q/\sigma$ and let
$\epsilon\downarrow0$.
\end{proof}

Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:sharp-budget} is a genuine optimality statement for a
sample-complexity problem. It does not say that the simple finite coefficient
$t$ in Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:39:cor:budget} is sharp, nor that the asymptotic coefficient
$\kappa_t$ can be substituted into that finite corollary without an error
term and additional scale assumptions.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Deterministic anchor selection by conditional expectation\srctag{39}}]{Deterministic anchor selection by conditional expectation}\label{gsr:en:39:sec:d8}
\srcnote{39}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:en:39:sec:algorithm}

The existence proof can be made constructive when the row classes are given
explicitly. There is no need to enumerate all $\binom mr$ possible final
samples.

Suppose $T\subseteq J$ is a partial sample of size $a\le r$. Complete it by a
uniform $(r-a)$-subset of $J\setminus T$. For a class $C$, write
\[
 b=|C\cap T|,\qquad c=|C\setminus T|,\qquad n=m-a,\qquad u=r-a.
\]
If $b\ge t$, its conditional expected discarded count is zero. Otherwise it is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:conditional-class}
 L_C(T)=\frac{1}{\binom nu}
 \sum_{j=0}^{t-b-1}(c-j)\binom cj\binom{n-c}{u-j},
\end{equation}
with zero terms outside the feasible range. Indeed, the additional hits have
law $\HG(n,c,u)$, and after $j$ such hits there are $c-j$ unsampled points in
the class.

Define the conditional potential
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:potential}
 \Phi(T)=\frac1{mW}\sum_h w_h\sum_i L_{C_{h,i}}(T).
\end{equation}
It is the expected final loss conditioned on $T$ being contained in the final
sample, with the remaining columns chosen uniformly.

\begin{lemma}[One-step potential identity]\label{gsr:en:39:lem:potential}
If $|T|<r$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:potential-step}
 \Phi(T)=\frac1{m-|T|}\sum_{x\in J\setminus T}\Phi(T\cup\{x\}).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose the next column uniformly from $J\setminus T$, then choose the rest
uniformly without replacement. This yields a uniform final $r$-subset
containing $T$. More explicitly, each particular completion of size $r-|T|$
can have any of its $r-|T|$ points selected first, and these choices give the
same total probability for every completion. The law of total expectation
now gives \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:potential-step}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact derandomization]\label{gsr:en:39:thm:derandomization}
Start with $T=\varnothing$. While $|T|<r$, add a column minimizing
$\Phi(T\cup\{x\})$ over $x\notin T$. The final sample $R$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:derandomization}
 D_{\cC}(R)=\Phi(R)\le\Phi(\varnothing)
 =\frac1W\sum_h w_h\sum_i\ell_{m,r,t}(|C_{h,i}|).
\end{equation}
For rational row weights, every comparison can be performed exactly with
rational arithmetic.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
A minimum of finitely many real numbers is at most their average, so
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:39:lem:potential} makes the potential nonincreasing at every step.
When $|T|=r$, there is no remaining randomness; formula
\eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:conditional-class} is the actual discarded count. At the initial
state it is the unconditional expectation from Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:39:lem:marginal}.
\end{proof}

The supplied implementation follows this algorithm with exact rational
arithmetic. Its main module is \filename{code/anchor_selection.py}; values have
Python's \filename{fractions.Fraction} type. It validates that classes within
a row are disjoint and that columns and parameters are in range. A
straightforward implementation evaluates at most $rm$ candidate extensions,
each using the supplied row classes. This is a finite algorithm for explicitly
represented data; it is not asserted to be an efficient implementation of the
entire inverse proof, where the class descriptions and the number of rows may
be extremely large.

For a fixed row family the derandomized loss can be much smaller than the
universal minimax value. The permutation-orbit construction is the limiting
case: the final loss is the same for every sample, so no deterministic choice
can improve on the average. This gives a useful exact test case for the
implementation.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Polynomial reconstruction, general interpolation spaces, and errors\srctag{39}}]{Polynomial reconstruction, general interpolation spaces, and errors}\label{gsr:en:39:sec:d9}
\srcnote{39}{Section 9}
\label{gsr:en:39:sec:interpolation}

\subsection{A polynomial graph-cover theorem}
Let $\F$ be any field, and now regard $J$ as an $m$-element subset of $\F$.
The distinctness of the elements of $J$ is the only hypothesis needed for the
Vandermonde denominators. Let $B\subseteq H\times J$ and let $f:B\to\F$.
Suppose each fibre $B_h$ has a partition into at most $q$ classes such that on
each class $f(h,\cdot)$ agrees with a polynomial of degree at most $t-1$.
The polynomials may depend on both the row and the class.

For $a\in J$, define the partial horizontal section
\[
 B_a=\{h:(h,a)\in B\},\qquad \psi_a(h)=f(h,a)\quad(h\in B_a).
\]
For a $t$-subset $S\subseteq J$ and $a\in S$, put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:Lagrange}
 L_{S,a}(x)=\prod_{b\in S\setminus\{a\}}\frac{x-b}{a-b}.
\end{equation}
These polynomials satisfy $L_{S,a}(b)=\ind_{\{a=b\}}$ for $b\in S$.

\begin{theorem}[Shared polynomial interpolants]\label{gsr:en:39:thm:polynomial}
There is an $r$-subset $R\subseteq J$ and an ambient good set $E_R$ with
weighted complement at most
\[
 \frac1W\sum_h w_h\sum_i\ell_{m,r,t}(|C_{h,i}|)
 \le\frac{tq(m-r)}{m(r+1)}
\]
(as a fraction of $mW$), such that every $(h,x)\in B\cap E_R$ lies on one of
the following partial graphs:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:single-graphs}
 (h,x)\longmapsto\psi_a(h)\quad(a\in R),
 \qquad\text{defined when }h\in B_a;
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:multi-graphs}
 I_S(h,x)=\sum_{a\in S}L_{S,a}(x)\psi_a(h)
 \quad\left(S\in\binom Rt\right),
 \qquad\text{defined when }h\in\bigcap_{a\in S}B_a.
\end{equation}
There are at most $r+\binom rt$ candidate expressions. Every anchor actually
used to certify a nonsampled target belongs to $B\cap E_R$ in the same row.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Choose the sample by Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:39:thm:selection} and use the good set from
Definition~\ref{gsr:en:39:def:certification}. If $x\in R$, then the single expression
with $a=x$ equals $f(h,x)$.

Otherwise, certification means that the class containing $x$ contains at least
$t$ elements of $R$. Choose any $t$ of them and call this set $S$. Let $P$ be
the polynomial of degree at most $t-1$ agreeing with $f(h,\cdot)$ on the class.
Lagrange interpolation gives
\[
 P(x)=\sum_{a\in S}L_{S,a}(x)P(a)
     =\sum_{a\in S}L_{S,a}(x)\psi_a(h)=I_S(h,x).
\]
For completeness, the interpolation formula follows because its right side
is a polynomial of degree at most $t-1$ agreeing with $P$ at the $t$ distinct
points of $S$; their difference has $t$ roots and degree at most $t-1$, and
hence is zero. The root bound follows by repeatedly factoring $X-a$ at each
root over a field.

The domain conditions hold because $S$ is contained in the same class. All
its points are sampled, and the definition of $E_R$ retains every sampled
domain point. The number of expressions is the number of singletons plus
the number of $t$-subsets of $R$.
\end{proof}

For $t=2$, the paired expression can be written without separating slope and
intercept:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:affine-interpolant}
 I_{\{a,b\}}(h,x)
 =\frac{x-b}{a-b}\psi_a(h)+\frac{a-x}{a-b}\psi_b(h).
\end{equation}
This is a linear combination of only two horizontal sections, with affine
coefficients in $x$. If each section is multilinear in the base coordinates,
the displayed function is multilinear in the base coordinates and $x$.
There is no need to first place all pairwise slopes and intercepts into a
larger common union and then refine that union.

\begin{remark}[Partial graphs and harmless spurious candidates]
The theorem is a cover theorem, not a uniqueness theorem. Different candidate
expressions may coincide, and many candidates need not agree with $f$ at a
given point. Only one correct expression is required for each retained
point. Later list-cover bounds count all candidates because removing spurious
ones is not needed for validity.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Unisolvent reconstruction spaces}

\begin{definition}[A unisolvent space]\label{gsr:en:39:def:unisolvent}
A $t$-dimensional linear subspace $\cW\subseteq\F^J$ is called
$t$-point unisolvent if, for every $S\in\binom Jt$, the evaluation map
$\cW\to\F^S$ is an isomorphism. We additionally require that the constant
function $1$ belong to $\cW$.
\end{definition}

The assumption about constants ensures that the direct single-anchor
expressions in \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:single-graphs} remain in the same reconstruction
space. If only the nonsampled targets were being considered, this extra
assumption would not be needed.

\begin{corollary}[Interpolation-space extension]\label{gsr:en:39:cor:unisolvent}
Replace polynomial class functions in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:39:thm:polynomial} by members
of a $t$-point unisolvent space $\cW$ containing constants. Then the same
sample, mass bounds, and candidate count hold, with the Lagrange functions
$L_{S,a}$ replaced by the unique elements of $\cW$ whose evaluations on $S$
are the standard coordinate vectors.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Invert the evaluation isomorphism on each $S$. If $P\in\cW$, its vector of
values on $S$ determines it, so $P=\sum_{a\in S}P(a)L_{S,a}$ in $\cW$.
The rest of the proof is exactly the certification and domain argument of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:39:thm:polynomial}. Constant functions handle sampled targets.
\end{proof}

The polynomial theorem itself remains valid when $m<t$; in that case no
$t$-subset of $J$ exists, and only direct sampled targets can be certified.
A $t$-dimensional subspace of $\F^J$ cannot exist when $m<t$, so the general
space formulation is only applicable when its hypotheses can actually hold.

\subsection{Additive robustness to corrupted domain points}

\begin{theorem}[Robust shared interpolation]\label{gsr:en:39:thm:robust}
Suppose $B^\circ\subseteq B\subseteq H\times J$ has weighted complement
within $B$ of normalized mass at most $\delta$:
\[
 \frac1{mW}\sum_h w_h|B_h\setminus B_h^\circ|\le\delta.
\]
Assume that $f$ restricted to each $B_h^\circ$ can be partitioned into at most
$q$ polynomial classes of degree at most $t-1$. Then there is a shared
$r$-subset $R$ and a family of the forms \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:single-graphs} and
\eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:multi-graphs}, using the \emph{actual} sections of $f$ on $B$, which
covers all but at most
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:robust}
 \delta+\frac{tq(m-r)}{m(r+1)}
\end{equation}
of the ambient mass in $B$. The exact class-profile bound may replace the
second term. No factor of $r$ multiplies $\delta$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:39:thm:selection} to the good classes inside $B^\circ$. The
points in $B^\circ$ that fail certification have at most the stated sampling
mass. Every certified nonsampled good point has $t$ anchors in its own good
class, where the actual values of $f$ agree with the class polynomial.
Consequently the candidate built from those actual sections is correct.
A good sampled point is covered directly.

Candidates using a corrupted anchor can be ignored for this correctness
argument: their presence only adds possible graphs. Discarding the corrupt
points themselves costs at most $\delta$, and discarding uncertified good
points costs at most the sampling term. The losses add.
\end{proof}

The theorem does not claim that the unknown good set or its class partition
can be discovered efficiently from corrupted data. It is an existence and
list-cover result. The conditional-expectation algorithm applies directly
when the good class descriptions are supplied.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Labelled slice covers and candidate counts\srctag{39}}]{Labelled slice covers and candidate counts}\label{gsr:en:39:sec:d10}
\srcnote{39}{Section 10}
\label{gsr:en:39:sec:labelled}

The sampling theorem controls how many horizontal sections are needed. A
second, separate issue is how the candidate lists for those sections are
carried through a common refinement. Replacing each individual slice list by
one large union list is safe but can be very wasteful.

Let the base $H$ have a partition into cells $U$. On each cell let
$\cV_U\subseteq\F^U$ be a linear space. Suppose that for each sampled anchor
$a\in R$ there is a list
\[
 \mu_{U,a,1},\ldots,\mu_{U,a,L_a}\in\cV_U
\]
covering the partial section $\psi_a$ at every good base point of its domain.
The list sizes may depend on $U$; uniform upper bounds are used below to avoid
clutter. The phrase ``covering'' means that at least one member equals
$\psi_a(h)$ at the point in question. No globally consistent branch is assumed.

\begin{theorem}[Labelled interpolation of slice lists]\label{gsr:en:39:thm:labelled}
Let $H_0\subseteq H$ be a common good base set for the slice lists above. On
$U\times J$, the points certified by Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:39:thm:polynomial} whose base
lies in $H_0$ are covered by at most
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:labelled-count}
 \sum_{a\in R}L_a+
 \sum_{\substack{S\subseteq R\\|S|=t}}\prod_{a\in S}L_a
\end{equation}
candidates in
\[
 \cV_U\otimes\Poly_{<t}(J):=
 \left\{\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}v_j(h)x^j:v_j\in\cV_U\right\}.
\]
For a common bound $L_a\le L$, the count is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:uniform-labelled}
 rL+\binom rt L^t.
\end{equation}
If the base exceptional set has weighted mass at most $\epsilon W$, the total
ambient exceptional mass is at most the sampling loss plus $\epsilon$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For each anchor $a$ and each list member, include the direct lift
$\mu_{U,a,j}(h)$, constant in $x$. For each $t$-subset $S\subseteq R$ and each
choice of a list index $j_a$ for every $a\in S$, include
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:labelled-candidate}
 \nu_{U,S,(j_a)}(h,x)
 =\sum_{a\in S}L_{S,a}(x)\mu_{U,a,j_a}(h).
\end{equation}
The direct lifts belong to the stated space because constants have degree
less than $t$. Expanding the coefficients $L_{S,a}(x)$ in powers of $x$ shows
that every function in \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:labelled-candidate} also belongs to that space,
using linearity of $\cV_U$.

If a certified point is directly sampled, select a correct member of that
anchor's list. Otherwise choose its $t$ valid anchors from the same class.
At its base point $h\in H_0$, each of those $t$ anchor sections has at least one
correct list member. Select these members individually. Formula
\eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:multi-graphs} shows that the resulting candidate is correct at the
target. A choice for other anchors is irrelevant.

The number of direct candidates is $\sum_aL_a$. For a fixed $S$, the number
of possible assignments is $\prod_{a\in S}L_a$, giving
\eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:labelled-count}. Removing a base set of weight $\epsilon W$ deletes
at most $m\epsilon W$ ambient mass, so the exceptional fractions add.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{The direct-anchor term is unnecessary} (source~67, Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:interpolationcost}): the $t$-anchor interpolants also cover the sampled points, so $E_t(L_1,\ldots,L_r)$ candidates suffice, exactly in this interface (its Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:67:interp:thm:anchor-upper} and~\ref{gsr:en:67:interp:thm:anchor-lower}); the affine case is formalized since \texttt{081abc4d3} (\file{Section16SampledOrAnchoredOn.compressed_multilinear_cover}, \file{Proofs16CompressedInterpolation.lean}, line~56, at HEAD \texttt{fb9602e55}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{corollary}[Affine and multilinear specialization]\label{gsr:en:39:cor:affine-list}
For affine fibres, the bound is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:affine-count}
 rL+\binom r2L^2.
\end{equation}
If $\cV_U$ consists of functions affine separately in every base coordinate,
all the lifted candidates are affine separately in every base coordinate and
in the final coordinate $x$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Set $t=2$ in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:39:thm:labelled}. Each coefficient in
\eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:affine-interpolant} is affine in $x$ and independent of the base
variables, while each list member is independent of $x$. The sum has degree
at most one in each variable separately.
\end{proof}

The mixed list count in \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:labelled-count} is the sum of the first and
$t$th elementary symmetric polynomials in the list sizes. This formulation is
useful when the horizontal sections have unequal complexity. The uniform
bound \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:uniform-labelled} is a convenient corollary, not the sharpest
piece of information furnished by the construction.

There is no claim that all these expressions are different. The count is an
upper bound on a concrete generated list, not a matching lower bound on the
number of distinct necessary graphs. Algebraic coincidences, zero
coefficients, repeated lists, or extra relations can reduce the number.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Hereditary refinement without loss of slice labels\srctag{39}}]{Hereditary refinement without loss of slice labels}\label{gsr:en:39:sec:d11}
\srcnote{39}{Section 11}
\label{gsr:en:39:sec:refinement}

A common refinement is only useful if it preserves the required geometric
scale. The next theorem states an explicit abstract hypothesis that is
sufficient. It does not assume that arbitrary intersections of progression
partitions retain large scale.

\begin{definition}[Hereditary single-slice refinement]\label{gsr:en:39:def:refinement}
Let a finite base set $H$ carry an additive nonnegative measure $\mu$ with
$\mu(H)>0$. Suppose there is a class of admissible nonempty cells, a scale
$\scale(U)\ge1$ for each such cell, and linear candidate spaces
$\cV_U\subseteq\F^U$. Assume restrictions of members of $\cV_U$ to an
admissible subcell $U'\subseteq U$ belong to $\cV_{U'}$.

Let $\psi_1,\ldots,\psi_r$ be partial functions on $H$. Assume that for each
$i$, every admissible $U$, and each error parameter $\tau$ under consideration,
there is a finite partition of $U$ into admissible cells $U'$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:single-refinement}
 \scale(U')\ge\scale(U)^{a(\tau)},\qquad 0<a(\tau)\le1,
\end{equation}
and an exceptional set in $U$ of measure at most $\tau\mu(U)$, outside which
$\psi_i$ on each $U'$ is covered by a list of at most $L(\tau)$ members of
$\cV_{U'}$. The same functions $a,L$ are valid for every $i$ and every cell
encountered in the refinement.
\end{definition}

If a concrete refinement lemma has additional lower-size hypotheses, those
hypotheses must hold at every stage where it is invoked. They are not removed
by Definition~\ref{gsr:en:39:def:refinement}. In an application, admissibility can encode
properness, coordinate restrictions, or inheritance from a specified parent
progression.

\begin{theorem}[Label-preserving common refinement]\label{gsr:en:39:thm:refinement}
Suppose $H$ itself is admissible, with scale $M$. Under
Definition~\ref{gsr:en:39:def:refinement}, choose errors $\tau_1,\ldots,\tau_r>0$.
There is a common admissible partition of $H$ and a common good base set such
that the total exceptional measure is at most
$\mu(H)\sum_i\tau_i$, every final cell has scale at least
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:common-scale}
 M^{\prod_{i=1}^r a(\tau_i)},
\end{equation}
and on each final cell, slice $i$ retains its \emph{own} list of at most
$L(\tau_i)$ candidates. It is not necessary to replace that list size by
$\prod_iL(\tau_i)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Refine the initial cell using the single-slice property for $\psi_1$ at error
$\tau_1$. Then refine every current cell using the property for $\psi_2$ at
error $\tau_2$, and continue. At each stage retain, by restriction, the lists
already attached to all earlier slices. Restriction closure ensures that these
remain valid candidates and does not increase their sizes.

At stage $i$, the new exceptional sets in the parent cells have total measure
at most $\tau_i\sum_U\mu(U)=\tau_i\mu(H)$ because the parent cells partition
$H$. The union of all stage exceptions therefore has measure at most
$\mu(H)\sum_i\tau_i$.

For scales, induction gives after stage $i$ the lower bound
$M^{\prod_{j=1}^i a(\tau_j)}$: if the parent scale is at least the previous
bound, then raising it to the positive power $a(\tau_i)$ preserves the
inequality. Once a slice acquires its list at its own stage, later stages only
restrict it. Thus its final list has at most $L(\tau_i)$ elements, as claimed.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Equal error allocation]\label{gsr:en:39:cor:equal-refinement}
For $\tau_i=\epsilon/r$, the common good set loses at most $\epsilon$ of the
base mass, the scale bound is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:equal-scale}
 M^{a(\epsilon/r)^r},
\end{equation}
and each slice list has size at most $L(\epsilon/r)$.
Combined with affine shared-anchor selection, the graph count per base cell is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:equal-list}
 rL(\epsilon/r)+\binom r2L(\epsilon/r)^2.
\end{equation}
The total ambient exceptional fraction is at most
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:two-errors}
 \frac{2q(m-r)}{m(r+1)}+\epsilon.
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:39:thm:refinement}, then
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:39:thm:labelled} and Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:39:thm:selection} with $t=2$.
All interpolation anchors lie in the same row as their target, so restricting
to a common good base point preserves all the required anchor lists.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Unequal slice costs and a parameter frontier}
If slice $i$ has its own functions $a_i(\tau_i)$ and $L_i(\tau_i)$, the same
proof gives scale $M^{\prod_i a_i(\tau_i)}$ and a labelled candidate bound
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:39:eq:heterogeneous}
 \sum_iL_i(\tau_i)+
 \sum_{|S|=t}\prod_{i\in S}L_i(\tau_i),
 \qquad \sum_i\tau_i\le\epsilon.
\end{equation}
This gives an explicit optimization problem for error allocation; equal
errors need not be optimal for heterogeneous slices. The theorem asserts the
whole feasible frontier \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:heterogeneous}. It does not solve an
unspecified optimization without information about the cost functions.

The asymmetric version can also use the exact profile loss
\eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:profile-upper} in place of the universal sampling term. Thus the
method retains three separate forms of information: the row class-size
profile, the number of anchors actually chosen, and the list cost of each
horizontal section. Collapsing all of them to a single worst-case parameter
is optional rather than built into the proof.

\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the seventh write, 6~October 2026.}}\par
The next section is source~34's Appendix~A. \emph{Logically it belongs in source~07's chapter on transport rigidity} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:transport}), after its Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:07:cor:freiman}; it is printed here because no number printed earlier may move. In source~07's finite-fibre directional model the sufficient threshold $1/(2[1+(k-1)\kappa])=1/(2+(2k-2)\kappa)$ is optimal for every Freiman order $k\ge2$ and every fibre ratio $\kappa\ge1$, already with zero boundary loss, so a boundary bound alone gives no further improvement (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:34:thm:rigidity-threshold}). \gsrnewfloats
\section[{The sharp nonuniform directional rigidity threshold\srctag{34}}]{The sharp nonuniform directional rigidity threshold}\label{gsr:en:34:sec:dA}
\srcnote{34}{Appendix A}
\label{gsr:en:34:app:rigidity}

This appendix supplies an independent local result for the inverse
part of the argument. Source~07 of the merged report proves a
sufficient nonuniform directional threshold and asks whether it is
sharp \cite{repo34}. The following construction settles that
question in the same finite-fiber model. The sharpness examples
have no boundary loss.

\subsection{The precise sampling model}

Let $G,H$ be finite abelian groups, let $S\subseteq G$ be nonempty,
and let $X_g$ be a finite nonempty fiber for $g\in S$. Write
\[
 R_g=|X_g|,\quad \Omega=\sum_{g\in S}R_g,
 \quad\mu(g)=R_g/\Omega,\qquad
 \frac{\max_gR_g}{\min_gR_g}\le\kappa.
\]
Let $\phi:\bigsqcup_{g\in S}X_g\to H$, let $D\subseteq G$,
and let $\psi:D\to H$. For a direction $d\in D$, draw
$g\sim\mu$ and $x$ uniformly from $X_g$. If $g+d\notin S$,
declare failure. Otherwise draw $y$ independently and uniformly
from $X_{g+d}$ and test
\[
 \phi(y)-\phi(x)=\psi(d).
\]
Let $\delta_d$ be its failure probability.
The map $\psi$ is a Freiman homomorphism of order $k$ if every
relation $d_1+\cdots+d_k=e_1+\cdots+e_k$ with directions in
$D$, repetitions allowed, implies equality of the corresponding
image sums.

\begin{theorem}[The exact universal strict threshold]
\label{gsr:en:34:thm:rigidity-threshold}
For every integer $k\ge2$ and every real $\kappa\ge1$, the
optimal universal strict threshold is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:34:eq:rigidity-threshold}
 \delta_{\mathrm{crit}}(k,\kappa)
 =\frac{1}{2+(2k-2)\kappa}.
\end{equation}
If every $\delta_d<\delta_{\mathrm{crit}}(k,\kappa)$, then
$\psi$ is a Freiman homomorphism of order $k$. No larger
universal strict threshold is valid. For rational $\kappa$, a
counterexample attains equality in \eqref{gsr:en:34:eq:rigidity-threshold}.
Sharpness holds with $S=G$, hence with zero exit probability in
every direction.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
We first recall the sufficient bound with its sampling weights.
Fix a relation $\sum_i d_i=\sum_i e_i$. Choose one common
initial fiber with index $g\sim\mu$. Follow the two paths of
partial sums. Where their indices are in $S$, choose uniform
fiber samples, using the same initial and terminal samples for
both paths and independent internal samples. Samples at distinct
path positions are drawn separately even if their fiber indices
coincide. Leaving $S$ is a failure.

Each first edge has its prescribed defect at most
$\delta:=\max_{d\in D}\delta_d$. For a later edge, its starting
index is $g+s$ for a fixed partial sum $s$. On indices for which
both $g$ and $g+s$ are in $S$,
\[
 \mu(g)\le\kappa\mu(g+s).
\]
Therefore the probability of failure at that edge, restricted to
paths that have not already left $S$, is at most $\kappa\delta$.
This includes the first exit at that edge. A union bound over the
two paths gives total failure probability at most
\[
 [2+(2k-2)\kappa]\delta<1.
\]
Some realization has every edge correct. Telescoping along its
two paths, with their common endpoints, proves the required image
relation. For an empty $D$ the assertion is immediate; otherwise
the maximum is attained because $G$ is finite.

For sharpness, fix an integer $m\ge2$ and positive integers
$a\le b$. Put $N=2km$ and $G=H=\Z/N\Z$, with $S=G$.
Partition the representatives $0\le r<N$ into $2k$ consecutive
blocks of length $m$. Give every point-index in blocks $0$ and
$2k-1$ a fiber of size $a$, and every other point-index a fiber
of size $b$. On the fiber indexed by $r$, let $\phi$ be constant
with value $\lfloor r/m\rfloor\in\Z/N\Z$. Take
\[
 D=\{m,-m\},\qquad \psi(m)=1,\qquad\psi(-m)=-1.
\]
Only the final block fails in direction $m$, and only the first
block fails in direction $-m$. Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:34:eq:rigidity-counterexample}
 \delta_m=\delta_{-m}
 =\frac{a}{2a+(2k-2)b}.
\end{equation}
There is no boundary failure. Yet the domain relation consisting
of $k$ copies of $m$ and $k$ copies of $-m$ is valid modulo
$N=2km$, whereas its image relation $k=-k$ fails because
$N>2k$. The map is not Freiman of order $k$.

For rational $\kappa$, take $b/a=\kappa$ to attain the stated
threshold. For arbitrary real $\kappa$, choose rational ratios
$b/a\le\kappa$ tending to $\kappa$. The defects in
\eqref{gsr:en:34:eq:rigidity-counterexample} tend to
\eqref{gsr:en:34:eq:rigidity-threshold} from above, so every larger proposed
universal strict threshold admits a counterexample.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}
At $k=2$, $\kappa=3$, take $m=2$, $a=1$, and $b=3$.
The group is $\Z/8\Z$, the fiber sizes by block are
$(1,3,3,1)$, and each block has two indices. Both directional
defects are $1/8$. The relation $2+2=(-2)+(-2)$ holds modulo
eight, but $1+1\ne(-1)+(-1)$. This realizes equality at the
threshold $1/(2+2\cdot3)$.
\end{example}

\begin{corollary}[A boundary bound alone gives no further improvement]
Within this model, adding an arbitrary upper bound on the exit
probabilities, including the bound zero, does not increase the
universal threshold in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:34:thm:rigidity-threshold}.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Every sharpness example in the theorem has $S=G$ and exit
probability zero.
\end{proof}

The sufficient threshold is credited to source~07; the matching
nonuniform example resolves its sharpness question. The examples
use composite cyclic groups. They do not determine the maximal
Freiman order available under Gowers's original prime-order and
nested-set hypotheses at Lemma~10.9. Those additional hypotheses
can carry information absent from this general model.

\section{Source~40's chapter: one-stage Fej\'er selection at Lemma~15.5 \wtag}\label{gsr:en:sec:fejer}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the eighth write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next eight sections are source~40's Sections~2--9, on the arrangement-selection step of Gowers's Lemma~15.5. \emph{Logically the chapter comes before source~35's degree-weighted selection} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:gradedselection}), which builds on it and cites it ahead of its placement, and after source~17's Fej\'er restriction (its Section~9) and the Section~15 material of sources~25 and~27; it is printed here because no number printed earlier may move. Source~40's introduction, with its explicit theorem, is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:40:sec:d1}; its checks and questions are in Part~V.

\emph{What is proved.} For ordered $d$-arrangements of $k$-cubes in a density-$\beta$ set $B\subseteq\F_q^{k+1}$, a single normalized Fej\'er kernel of bandwidth $L=\lceil2(s+1)/(\alpha\eta)\rceil$, $s=2d2^k$, applied to the single feature $F(y,r)=r\prod_iy_i$, retains at least $\alpha^s\eta^{s-1}\beta^{2d-1}q^M/(3^{s-1}(s+1)^s)$ arrangements, a proportion $1/(1+\eta)$ of them respected, as soon as $p>2(L-1)$ and $q\ge(k+1)\beta^{-(2d-1)}(18(s+1)^2/(\alpha\eta)^2)^s$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:40:thm:explicit}; the exact form is Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:40:thm:exact}). Gowers's repeated degree-one Riesz products lose the exponent $s2^{s-1}$; here the exponents are $s$ and $s-1$, and the sufficient field size is also smaller (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:40:cor:eight} at $d=8$). The feature has exactly the intended universal relation space (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:40:thm:universal}), and all other bounded-coefficient relations are counted by a zero-count with repeated vertices treated explicitly (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:40:thm:exceptional}). Vector-valued targets cost nothing, target torsion is computed exactly (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:40:cor:vector}, Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:40:prop:torsion}), and within homogeneous positive-Fourier kernels a gain $Q$ forces good survival at most $Q^{-(s-1)}$, attained by Fej\'er kernels (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:40:thm:barrier}, Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:40:prop:attain}). Source~35 improves the field-size exponent from $2s$ to $E_{k,m}\sim2s/k$ and the retention constant to $\alpha^s\eta^{s-1}/(2(s+2)^s)$ (note after Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:40:thm:exact}).

\emph{Relation to the formal statements} (checked at HEAD \texttt{6d4942222}). \file{lemma_15_5} (\file{Sections14\_15.lean}, line~414) has the exact companion \file{lemma_15_5_holds} (\file{Proofs15Restriction.lean}, line~3116), with an existential threshold. Whether Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:40:cor:eight} gives it with an explicit threshold depends on matching the formal count conventions, as for source~35 (marked question, item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:gradedselection}). Nothing in this chapter is formalized.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Arrangements, respect, and the counting normalization\srctag{40}}]{Arrangements, respect, and the counting normalization}\label{gsr:en:40:sec:d2}
\srcnote{40}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:en:40:sec:arrangements}
Throughout, $\F_q$ denotes a finite field. Write
$E_k=\{0,1\}^k$, $\pi(\eps)=(-1)^{|\eps|}$, and
\[
 \sigma_j=\begin{cases}1&1\leq j\leq d,\\-1&d<j\leq 2d.\end{cases}
\]
Products and sums occurring in coordinates are taken in $\F_q$.
The symbols $\pi$ and $\sigma$ also denote their images in that field.

\begin{definition}[Ordered $d$-arrangement]\label{gsr:en:40:def:arrangement}
An ordered $d$-arrangement is a choice of
\[
 h\in\F_q^k,\qquad x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(2d)}\in\F_q^k,
 \qquad r_1,\ldots,r_{2d}\in\F_q,
 \quad \sum_{j=1}^{2d}\sigma_jr_j=0.
\]
Its labeled vertices are
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:40:eq:vertices}
 v_{j,\eps}=(x^{(j)}+\eps\mathbin{\odot}h,r_j),
 \qquad 1\leq j\leq 2d,\quad \eps\in E_k,
\end{equation}
where $\odot$ denotes coordinatewise multiplication. It is an
arrangement in $B$ when every vertex belongs to $B$. Set
\[
 s=2d2^k,\qquad M=k+2dk+(2d-1)=(2d+1)k+2d-1,
 \qquad (\eta_0)_{j,\eps}=\sigma_j\pi(\eps).
\]
For $\phi:B\to\F_q$, its defect on the arrangement is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:40:eq:defect}
 \Delta_\phi(\rhoo)=
 \sum_{j,\eps}\sigma_j\pi(\eps)\phi(v_{j,\eps}).
\end{equation}
The arrangement is \emph{respected} when this defect is zero.
Let $T(B)$ be the number of all arrangements in $B$ and $G_\phi(B)$
the number of respected ones.
\end{definition}

There are exactly $q^M$ arrangements in the ambient space: the last
$r$ coordinate is uniquely determined by the first $2d-1$. Labeling is
important. We never divide by a cube symmetry group, and we do not
remove coincident configurations before forming $T(B)$.

\begin{lemma}[Density-sensitive total count]\label{gsr:en:40:lem:total}
For $B\subseteq\F_q^{k+1}$ of density $\beta$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:40:eq:total}
 T(B)\leq T_0:=\beta^{2d-1}q^M.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For fixed $h$ and $r$, let $C_h(r)$ be the number of anchors
$x\in\F_q^k$ for which the whole cube $(x+\eps\odot h,r)$ lies in
$B$. Necessarily
\[
 0\leq C_h(r)\leq q^k,
 \qquad \sum_{r\in\F_q}C_h(r)\leq |B|,
\]
since the anchor itself is a vertex. Once $r_1,\ldots,r_{2d-1}$
are fixed, $r_{2d}$ is determined. Hence the arrangement count at this
$h$ is at most
\[
 q^k\sum_{r_1,\ldots,r_{2d-1}}
       \prod_{j<2d}C_h(r_j)
 =q^k\left(\sum_r C_h(r)\right)^{2d-1}
 \leq q^k|B|^{2d-1}.
\]
Summing over the $q^k$ possible $h$ gives
$q^{2k}|B|^{2d-1}=\beta^{2d-1}q^M$, as claimed.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why this normalization is natural]
For $B=\F_q^{k+1}$ there is equality. More generally, if
$B=\F_q^k\times R$ for an additive subgroup $R\leq(\F_q,+)$,
then all the final $r$ coordinates determined by the constraint remain
in $R$, and there is again equality in \eqref{gsr:en:40:eq:total}. Thus the
factor $\beta^{2d-1}$ cannot be universally reduced for finite fields.
This observation concerns the total-count normalization, not optimality
of the later selection theorem.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A single monomial isolates the universal relation\srctag{40}}]{A single monomial isolates the universal relation}\label{gsr:en:40:sec:d3}
\srcnote{40}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:en:40:sec:feature}
Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:40:eq:feature}
 P(y)=\prod_{i=1}^k y_i,\qquad F(y,r)=rP(y).
\end{equation}
The next lemma strengthens the hypothesis in the cube-moment step
underlying Gowers' Corollary 15.2: constancy of the top monomial alone
is enough. No separate hypotheses for every squarefree submonomial
are needed.

\begin{lemma}[Top-monomial cube rigidity]\label{gsr:en:40:lem:cubemoment}
Let $K$ be any field, let each $h_i\in K$ be nonzero, and let
$\eta:E_k\to K$. The formal polynomial
\[
 U_\eta(x)=\sum_{\eps\in E_k}\eta_\eps
               \prod_{i=1}^k(x_i+\eps_i h_i)
\]
is constant in $x_1,\ldots,x_k$ if and only if
$\eta_\eps=c\pi(\eps)$ for some $c\in K$. In that case
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:40:eq:paritymoment}
 U_\eta(x)=c(-1)^k\prod_i h_i.
\end{equation}
The assertion is valid in every characteristic.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $A\subseteq[k]$, set
$M_A=\sum_{\eps}\eta_\eps\prod_{i\in A}\eps_i$.
Expansion gives
\[
 U_\eta(x)=\sum_{A\subseteq[k]}
    M_A\prod_{i\in A}h_i\prod_{i\notin A}x_i.
\]
The distinct $x$ monomials are linearly independent. Since the $h_i$
are nonzero, constancy is equivalent to $M_A=0$ for every proper $A$.
Writing $S=\supp(\eps)$, the moments are upper subset sums
$M_A=\sum_{S\supseteq A}\eta_S$. Finite inclusion--exclusion gives
\[
 \eta_S=\sum_{A\supseteq S}(-1)^{|A|-|S|}M_A.
\]
Indeed, after substituting for $M_A$, the coefficient of $\eta_T$ is
$\sum_{S\subseteq A\subseteq T}(-1)^{|A|-|S|}$, which is one for
$T=S$ and zero otherwise. Thus
$\eta_S=(-1)^{k-|S|}M_{[k]}=c(-1)^{|S|}$ with
$c=(-1)^k M_{[k]}$. The constant term is
$M_{[k]}\prod_i h_i$, giving \eqref{gsr:en:40:eq:paritymoment}.
The reverse implication follows from the same expansion, or from
$\prod_i(x_i-(x_i+h_i))=(-1)^k\prod_i h_i$.
\end{proof}

Eliminate $r_{2d}$ using the arrangement equation:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:40:eq:rlast}
 r_{2d}=\sum_{j<2d}\sigma_jr_j.
\end{equation}
The free parameters then form $K^M$.

\begin{theorem}[Universal relation space for one feature]
\label{gsr:en:40:thm:universal}
For coefficients $\eta=(\eta_{j,\eps})\in K^s$, the formal polynomial
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:40:eq:universalpoly}
 \mathcal P_\eta(h,x,r)
 =\sum_{j,\eps}\eta_{j,\eps}F(v_{j,\eps}),
\end{equation}
with \eqref{gsr:en:40:eq:rlast} substituted, is identically zero if and only if
$\eta\in K\eta_0$. If it is not zero, its total degree is at most
$k+1$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Put
\[
 U_j(x^{(j)},h)=
 \sum_{\eps}\eta_{j,\eps}P(x^{(j)}+\eps\odot h).
\]
After substitution, the polynomial in \eqref{gsr:en:40:eq:universalpoly} is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:40:eq:rcoeff}
 \sum_{j<2d}r_j\bigl(U_j+\sigma_jU_{2d}\bigr).
\end{equation}
Suppose it is identically zero. Specialize all $h_i$ to one. Each
coefficient $U_j+\sigma_jU_{2d}$ of the independent variable $r_j$
is zero. The two summands depend on disjoint anchor variables.
Consequently both are constant in their own anchor variables: this
follows, for example, by fixing the other anchor at zero and comparing
polynomial coefficients. As $j$ ranges over $1,\ldots,2d-1$, every
block is covered. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:40:lem:cubemoment} now gives
$\eta_{j,\eps}=c_j\pi(\eps)$ for each $j$.

For general $h$ the coefficient of $r_j$ is therefore
$(-1)^k(\prod_i h_i)(c_j+\sigma_jc_{2d})$. Its vanishing gives
$c_j=-\sigma_jc_{2d}$, so with $c=-c_{2d}$ we have
$c_j=c\sigma_j$ for all $j$, including $j=2d$.
Thus $\eta=c\eta_0$.

Conversely, if $\eta=c\eta_0$, the parity identity gives
\[
 \sum_{j,\eps}\eta_{j,\eps}F(v_{j,\eps})
 =c(-1)^k\left(\prod_i h_i\right)\sum_j\sigma_jr_j=0.
\]
Finally, each term is a product of $k+1$ linear coordinate expressions
in the free parameters, so its total degree is at most $k+1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Formal polynomial versus finite-field function]
The theorem is a polynomial identity statement over any field. It does
not identify every pointwise relation in a small finite field with a
formal identity. The passage to a large finite field is made through
a zero-count in the next section. This distinction avoids a hidden
small-characteristic assumption in the algebraic argument.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Bounded-coefficient exceptional arrangements\srctag{40}}]{Bounded-coefficient exceptional arrangements}\label{gsr:en:40:sec:d4}
\srcnote{40}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:en:40:sec:exceptional}
Let $H\geq 1$ and suppose $p>2H$. Thus distinct integers in
$[-H,H]$ have distinct images in $\F_q$.

\begin{definition}[$H$-regularity]
An arrangement is $H$-regular if every vector
$\eta\in\{-H,\ldots,H\}^s$ satisfying
\[
 \sum_{j,\eps}\eta_{j,\eps}F(v_{j,\eps})=0
\]
is $a\eta_0$ for some integer $a\in[-H,H]$.
All other arrangements are $H$-exceptional. Write $D_H$ for the number
of exceptional arrangements in the full ambient space.
\end{definition}

This definition uses one feature, not the larger feature family in the
source paper. Therefore it is a stronger regularity requirement.
All signed multiples $a\eta_0$ really are relations by
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:40:thm:universal}.

\begin{lemma}[Polynomial zero-count]\label{gsr:en:40:lem:zeros}
A nonzero polynomial of total degree at most $D$ in $m\geq1$ variables
over $\F_q$ has at most $Dq^{m-1}$ zeros in $\F_q^m$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The one-variable case is the usual root bound. Induct on $m$. Write
the polynomial as a polynomial of degree $t$ in the last variable,
with nonzero leading coefficient $A$ of degree at most $D-t$ in the
other variables. There are at most $(D-t)q^{m-2}$ choices where $A$
vanishes, and at most $t$ last-coordinate roots for every other choice.
Bounding the first group by $q$ roots each and the second by
$tq^{m-1}$ in total yields at most $Dq^{m-1}$ roots. The case of a
nonzero constant leading coefficient is included, and the bound is
harmless when it exceeds $q^m$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Single-feature exceptional count]\label{gsr:en:40:thm:exceptional}
Set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:40:eq:Cdef}
 C_{k,s,H}=\frac{k+1}{2}\bigl((2H+1)^s-(2H+1)\bigr).
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:40:eq:Dbound}
 D_H\leq C_{k,s,H}\,q^{M-1}
 \leq (k+1)(2H+1)^s q^{M-1}.
\end{equation}
Every $H$-regular arrangement has $s$ distinct physical vertices and,
in particular, has all sidelengths nonzero.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The bounded coefficient box contains $(2H+1)^s$ integer vectors.
Its intersection with the field line $\F_q\eta_0$ consists of exactly
$2H+1$ vectors: one coordinate with sign $+1$ determines the scalar,
and injectivity of reduction modulo $p$ on $[-H,H]$ determines every
other coordinate as the corresponding signed integer. These are just
the intended multiples.

For each remaining coefficient vector, Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:40:thm:universal}
gives a nonzero polynomial of degree at most $k+1$ in the $M$ free
parameters. Its zero set has size at most $(k+1)q^{M-1}$ by
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:40:lem:zeros}. The vectors $\eta$ and $-\eta$ have the same
zero set. None of the remaining vectors is zero, and their sign pairs
have size two, giving exactly
$((2H+1)^s-(2H+1))/2$ pairs. A union bound proves the first inequality
in \eqref{gsr:en:40:eq:Dbound}; the second only simplifies it.

If two labeled vertices $v_a,v_b$ coincide, the vector with entries
$1$ at $a$, $-1$ at $b$, and zero elsewhere is a bounded relation.
It is not a multiple of $\eta_0$: it is nonzero, while $s\geq4$ and
a nonzero multiple of $\eta_0$ has no zero coordinate. Such an
arrangement is exceptional. A zero sidelength forces precisely such
a repeated vertex, proving the final assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What the exceptional bound pays for]
The bound includes zero sidelengths, repeated vertices, and all other
bounded relations. No additional diagonal error is left to be inserted
later. It is deliberately a union bound, not a claim that the
corresponding algebraic hypersurfaces are disjoint or independent.
The price of increasing $H$ is explicit: roughly $(2H+1)^s/q$ of the
ambient parameter space may have to be discarded from the exact
survival calculation.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Fej\'er kernels and exact survival probabilities\srctag{40}}]{Fej\'er kernels and exact survival probabilities}\label{gsr:en:40:sec:d5}
\srcnote{40}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:en:40:sec:kernel}
\subsection{The normalized kernel}
For $L\geq2$ define a function on the unit circle by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:40:eq:kernel}
 K_L(z)=\left|\frac1L\sum_{n=0}^{L-1}z^n\right|^2
 =\sum_{a=-(L-1)}^{L-1}c_a z^a,
 \qquad c_a=\frac{L-|a|}{L^2}.
\end{equation}
The coefficient formula follows by counting pairs $(n,m)$ with
$n-m=a$. All coefficients are nonnegative, $c_{-a}=c_a$, and
$0\leq K_L(z)\leq1$ by the triangle inequality. Also $c_0=1/L$ and
$\sum_a c_a=K_L(1)=1$.

For an arrangement with $s$ vertices set
\begin{align}
 b_{s,L}&=c_0^s=L^{-s},\label{gsr:en:40:eq:b}\\
 a_{s,L}&=\sum_{a=-(L-1)}^{L-1}c_a^s
            =L^{-s}R_s(L),\label{gsr:en:40:eq:a}\\
 R_s(L)&=1+2\sum_{a=1}^{L-1}\left(1-\frac aL\right)^s
          =1+2L^{-s}\sum_{a=1}^{L-1}a^s.\label{gsr:en:40:eq:R}
\end{align}

\begin{lemma}[Finite gain bounds]\label{gsr:en:40:lem:R}
For integers $s\geq1$ and $L\geq2$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:40:eq:Rbounds}
 \frac{2L}{s+1}\leq R_s(L)\leq L.
\end{equation}
For fixed $s$, as $L\to\infty$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:40:eq:Rasym}
 \frac{R_s(L)}{L}\longrightarrow\frac{2}{s+1},
 \qquad
 a_{s,L}\sim\frac{2}{s+1}L^{1-s}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The trapezoidal sum for the convex function $f(x)=(1-x)^s$ on
$[0,1]$ lies above its integral. That sum is
$R_s(L)/(2L)$, whereas the integral is $1/(s+1)$.
For the upper bound, use $(1-a/L)^s\leq1-a/L$ in \eqref{gsr:en:40:eq:R}, giving
$R_s(L)\leq1+(L-1)=L$. Finally, the trapezoidal sums converge to the
integral by continuity; multiplying by the powers of $L$ in
\eqref{gsr:en:40:eq:a} gives \eqref{gsr:en:40:eq:Rasym}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The correlated random subset}
Choose a nontrivial additive character $\chi:\F_q\to\C$ with
$|\chi(x)|=1$. For example, if $q=p^m$, take
$\chi(x)=\exp(2\pi i\Tr_{\F_q/\F_p}(x)/p)$, interpreting the trace
as an integer modulo $p$. The elementary orthogonality relation is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:40:eq:orthog}
 \E_{u\in\F_q}\chi(uz)=\one_{z=0}.
\end{equation}
For $z\ne0$, multiplication by $z$ permutes the field and the sum of
a nontrivial character is zero: translating that sum by an element
where the character is not one multiplies it by a scalar
factor different from one while leaving it unchanged.

Choose $t,u\in\F_q$ uniformly and independently. Conditional on these
two seeds, select each physical point $v\in B$ independently with
probability
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:40:eq:prob}
 w_{t,u}(v)=K_L\bigl(\chi(t\phi(v)+uF(v))\bigr).
\end{equation}
Let $B'$ be the resulting random subset. Only two field-valued seeds
are used for the correlated part of the selection; the pointwise
Bernoulli choices are additional randomness.

\begin{lemma}[Exact labeled moment]\label{gsr:en:40:lem:moment}
For any labeled arrangement in $B$,
\begin{multline}\label{gsr:en:40:eq:labeledmoment}
 \E_{t,u}\prod_{j,\eps}w_{t,u}(v_{j,\eps})\\
 =\sum_{\eta\in[-(L-1),L-1]^s\cap\Z^s}
   \left(\prod_{j,\eps}c_{\eta_{j,\eps}}\right)
   \one_{\sum\eta_{j,\eps}F(v_{j,\eps})=0}
   \one_{\sum\eta_{j,\eps}\phi(v_{j,\eps})=0}.
\end{multline}
In particular, every summand is nonnegative.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Expand each factor using \eqref{gsr:en:40:eq:kernel}. Character multiplicativity
turns the product into
$\chi(u\sum\eta F+t\sum\eta\phi)$ times its coefficient.
Averaging independently over $u$ and $t$ applies \eqref{gsr:en:40:eq:orthog}
twice. All sums are finite, so their interchange needs no limiting
argument.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Good and bad survival]\label{gsr:en:40:prop:survival}
Assume $p>2(L-1)$ and write $H=L-1$.
Every respected arrangement, whether regular or exceptional, survives
in $B'$ with probability at least $a_{s,L}$.
Every $H$-regular nonrespected arrangement survives with probability
exactly $b_{s,L}$. Every $H$-regular respected arrangement survives
with probability exactly $a_{s,L}$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
First consider the labeled moment in \eqref{gsr:en:40:eq:labeledmoment}.
For a respected arrangement, all intended coefficient vectors
$\eta=a\eta_0$ contribute. They satisfy the feature equation by
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:40:thm:universal}, and their $\phi$ sum is
$a\Delta_\phi=0$. Since $c_{-a}=c_a$, their total contribution is
$\sum_a c_a^s=a_{s,L}$. All other contributions are nonnegative.

There is a distinction between the labeled moment and actual subset
survival when vertices repeat. Conditional on the seeds, actual
survival is the product of $w_{t,u}(v)$ over \emph{distinct} physical
vertices. As each weight lies in $[0,1]$, this product is at least the
product over all labeled occurrences. Averaging therefore preserves
the lower bound $a_{s,L}$, even for exceptional respected arrangements.

For an $H$-regular arrangement the vertices are distinct by
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:40:thm:exceptional}, so the labeled moment is exactly its
survival probability. Regularity allows only $\eta=a\eta_0$ in that
moment. If $\Delta_\phi\ne0$, the remaining equation is
$a\Delta_\phi=0$ in $\F_q$. The only $a\in[-H,H]$ satisfying it is
$a=0$, since $p>2H$. The sole contribution is then $c_0^s=b_{s,L}$.
If the defect is zero, all intended multiples contribute and the
sum is exactly $a_{s,L}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Two easily missed issues]
Nonnegativity of the Fourier coefficients is what permits us to retain
only the intended terms for a lower bound; it is not merely a convenient
normalization. Separately, conditional independence applies to physical
points, not to vertex labels. The repeated-vertex inequality above is
necessary before any first-moment estimate for the good arrangements
is justified.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The one-stage selection theorem\srctag{40}}]{The one-stage selection theorem}\label{gsr:en:40:sec:d6}
\srcnote{40}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:en:40:sec:selection}
\subsection{An abstract first-moment step}
The following elementary observation separates the probabilistic
selection argument from the specific choice of kernel.

\begin{lemma}[Score selection]\label{gsr:en:40:lem:score}
Suppose a family of configurations has at most $T_0$ members, at least
$\alpha T_0$ of them good. A random subset retains each good
configuration with probability at least $a>0$. Each nonexceptional bad
configuration is retained with probability at most $b$, and there are
at most $D$ exceptional bad configurations. If
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:40:eq:scorehyp}
 \alpha a-\frac{b+D/T_0}{\eta}>0,
\end{equation}
there is an outcome with at least
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:40:eq:scoremass}
 \left(\alpha a-\frac{b+D/T_0}{\eta}\right)T_0
\end{equation}
good configurations, in which the proportion of good configurations
is at least $1/(1+\eta)$. In particular, if $D\leq bT_0$ and
$a/b\geq4/(\alpha\eta)$, this lower bound is at least
$\alpha aT_0/2$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $X$ and $Y$ count the retained good and bad configurations. By
linearity of expectation, without any independence assumption between
configurations,
\[
 \E X\geq\alpha aT_0,\qquad \E Y\leq bT_0+D.
\]
Thus the real score $Z=X-Y/\eta$ has expectation at least
\eqref{gsr:en:40:eq:scoremass}. There is an outcome with $Z\geq\E Z$.
For it, $X\geq Z$ and $Y\leq\eta X$, so
$X/(X+Y)\geq1/(1+\eta)$. The denominator is positive by
\eqref{gsr:en:40:eq:scorehyp}. Under the final hypotheses,
$(b+D/T_0)/\eta\leq2b/\eta\leq\alpha a/2$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The exact finite-bandwidth form}
\begin{theorem}[Exact one-stage Fej\'er selection]\label{gsr:en:40:thm:exact}
Let $k,d\geq1$, $s=2d2^k$, and $M=(2d+1)k+2d-1$.
Let $B\subseteq\F_q^{k+1}$ have density $\beta>0$, and suppose
$\phi:B\to\F_q$ respects at least $\alpha T_0$ arrangements, where
$T_0=\beta^{2d-1}q^M$ and $0<\alpha,\eta\leq1$.
Choose an integer $L\geq2$ for which
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:40:eq:exacthyp}
 p>2(L-1),\qquad R_s(L)\geq\frac4{\alpha\eta},\qquad
 \beta^{2d-1}q\geq C_{k,s,L-1}L^s.
\end{equation}
There is $B'\subseteq B$ for which
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:40:eq:exactmass}
 G_\phi(B')\geq\frac\alpha2 L^{-s}R_s(L)T_0,
 \qquad
 \frac{G_\phi(B')}{T(B')}\geq\frac1{1+\eta}.
\end{equation}
More generally, for any $L$ satisfying only the characteristic
condition, the same construction gives a positive lower bound
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:40:eq:continuousmass}
 G_\phi(B')\geq
 \left(\alpha L^{-s}R_s(L)-\frac{L^{-s}}{\eta}
       -\frac{C_{k,s,L-1}}{\eta\beta^{2d-1}q}\right)T_0
\end{equation}
with the same good proportion whenever the displayed coefficient is
strictly positive.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Use the random subset in \eqref{gsr:en:40:eq:prob}. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:40:lem:total} bounds
the total family by $T_0$; Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:40:prop:survival} supplies
the good probability $a=L^{-s}R_s(L)$ and the nonexceptional bad
probability $b=L^{-s}$. The exceptional count is at most
$C_{k,s,L-1}q^{M-1}$ by Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:40:thm:exceptional}.
The last inequality in \eqref{gsr:en:40:eq:exacthyp} makes this at most $bT_0$,
and the middle inequality gives the gain needed in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:40:lem:score}. This proves \eqref{gsr:en:40:eq:exactmass}.
Using the full score lower bound instead gives
\eqref{gsr:en:40:eq:continuousmass}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:40:thm:explicit}]
Take $L$ from \eqref{gsr:fm:40:eq:Lchoice}. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:40:lem:R} gives
$R_s(L)\geq2L/(s+1)\geq4/(\alpha\eta)$.
As $\alpha\eta\leq1$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:40:eq:Lupper}
 L\leq\frac{2(s+1)}{\alpha\eta}+1
 \leq\frac{3(s+1)}{\alpha\eta}.
\end{equation}
Also
\begin{align*}
 C_{k,s,L-1}L^s
 &\leq(k+1)[L(2L-1)]^s\\
 &\leq(k+1)(2L^2)^s\\
 &\leq(k+1)
       \left(\frac{18(s+1)^2}{(\alpha\eta)^2}\right)^s.
\end{align*}
Thus the field-size hypothesis implies the last condition in
\eqref{gsr:en:40:eq:exacthyp}. Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:40:thm:exact} yields a subset with
\begin{align*}
 G_\phi(B')
 &\geq\frac\alpha2 L^{-s}R_s(L)T_0\\
 &\geq\frac\alpha{s+1}L^{1-s}T_0\\
 &\geq\frac\alpha{s+1}
       \left(\frac{\alpha\eta}{3(s+1)}\right)^{s-1}T_0
 =\Gamma_s(\alpha,\eta)T_0.
\end{align*}
Since $T(B')\geq G_\phi(B')$, this proves the arrangement lower
bound. The good proportion is at least $1/(1+\eta)$, which is at
least $1-\eta$ because their difference is $\eta^2/(1+\eta)$.

Write $\beta'=|B'|/q^{k+1}$. Applying Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:40:lem:total} to $B'$
gives
$\Gamma_s\beta^{2d-1}q^M\leq T(B')\leq(\beta')^{2d-1}q^M$.
Taking positive $(2d-1)$st roots proves \eqref{gsr:fm:40:eq:densityout}.

For prime $q=p$, put $X=(s+1)/(\alpha\eta)\geq5$.
The size bound implies $q\geq(18X^2)^s\geq6X\geq2L$ by
\eqref{gsr:en:40:eq:Lupper}, and hence $p>2(L-1)$.
\end{proof}
