\section[{Comparison with Gowers' Lemma 15.5\srctag{40}}]{Comparison with Gowers' Lemma 15.5}\label{gsr:en:40:sec:d7}
\srcnote{40}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:en:40:sec:comparison}
The source result concerns $d=8$, so
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:40:eq:Eold}
 s=2^{k+4},\qquad M=17k+15,\qquad
 E_k=2^{2^{k+4}+k+3}=s2^{s-1}.
\end{equation}
In the repository's edited statement \cite[Section 15]{repo40}, the
retained arrangement lower bound is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:40:eq:oldbound}
 \left(\frac{\alpha\eta}{4}\right)^{E_k}
   \beta^{15}N^{17k+15},
\end{equation}
with sufficient largeness condition
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:40:eq:oldthreshold}
 N\geq k3^s\beta^{-15}
       \left(\frac4{\alpha\eta}\right)^{E_k}.
\end{equation}
The transcription explicitly notes that the printed statement did not
quantify $\alpha$ and omitted a largeness condition used by its proof.
We compare against the corrected, meaningful form, not the
unqualified statement.

\begin{corollary}[Replacement for the eight-arrangement selection]
\label{gsr:en:40:cor:eight}
Under the setup of Gowers' Lemma 15.5, with $N$ prime and
$0<\alpha,\beta,\eta\leq1$, it is enough to assume
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:40:eq:newN8}
 N\geq(k+1)\beta^{-15}
       \left(\frac{18(s+1)^2}{(\alpha\eta)^2}\right)^s,
 \qquad s=2^{k+4}.
\end{equation}
There is $B'\subseteq B$ containing at least
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:40:eq:new8}
 \frac{\alpha^s\eta^{s-1}}{3^{s-1}(s+1)^s}
       \beta^{15}N^{17k+15}
\end{equation}
arrangements, with at least a proportion $1-\eta$ respected.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:40:thm:explicit} with $d=8$ and use the final
prime-field observation in its proof.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Both the loss and the sufficient field size improve}
For $s\geq32$ and $0<\alpha,\eta\leq1$, the lower bound
\eqref{gsr:en:40:eq:new8} is larger than \eqref{gsr:en:40:eq:oldbound}. To see this,
$E_k\geq s$ and $E_k\geq s-1$, so the ratio is bounded below by
\[
 \frac{4^{E_k}}{3^{s-1}(s+1)^s}>1.
\]
The last inequality follows, after taking $s$th roots, from
$4^{2^{s-1}}>3(s+1)$.

The sufficient threshold \eqref{gsr:en:40:eq:newN8} is also smaller than
\eqref{gsr:en:40:eq:oldthreshold}. With $\delta=\alpha\eta\leq1$, the ratio
of the old threshold to the new one is
\[
 \frac{k}{k+1}
 \frac{4^{E_k}}{[6(s+1)^2]^s}\,\delta^{-(E_k-2s)}.
\]
Here $E_k\geq2s$, $k/(k+1)\geq1/2$, and
$4^{2^{s-1}}>12(s+1)^2$ for $s\geq32$. These facts make the ratio
larger than one. Thus the result is not merely a better retained-mass
bound purchased by a worse ambient-size assumption.

\subsection{Why increasing bandwidth helps}
At $L=2$ the normalized Fej\'er kernel is the original probability
kernel $(1+\cos\theta)/2$, and
\[
 b_{s,2}=2^{-s},\qquad R_s(2)=1+2^{1-s}.
\]
With $r$ independent stages, regular good and bad survival probabilities
are $a_{s,2}^r$ and $b_{s,2}^r$; the ratio is $R_s(2)^r$.
Making it at least a prescribed $Q>1$ takes
\[
 r\geq\frac{\log Q}{\log(1+2^{1-s})}
       \sim 2^{s-1}\log Q
 \quad\text{as }s\to\infty.
\]
This explains the large exponent in the original route.
In contrast, $R_s(L)\geq2L/(s+1)$: a single stage with
$L$ proportional to $(s+1)Q$ produces the required ratio and has
$a_{s,L}$ of order $L^{1-s}$ for fixed $s$.

The trade-off has not disappeared. The higher kernel degree requires
excluding a larger bounded coefficient box. The exceptional count
pays for that box, and the explicit field-size hypothesis makes its
contribution no larger than the ordinary bad survival mass.

\subsection{Scale illustration}
For illustration only, set $\alpha=\eta=0.1$ and $\beta=1/2$.
The table reports the negative base-ten logarithm of the coefficient
multiplying $\beta^{15}N^{17k+15}$, and the base-ten logarithm of the
new sufficient prime-field threshold. These are formula evaluations,
not experiments constructing the selected subset.
\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}rrrrr@{}}
\toprule
$k$ & $s$ & Old $-\log_{10}$ loss & New $-\log_{10}$ loss
 & New $\log_{10}N$ threshold\\
\midrule
1 & 32 & $1.788\times10^{11}$ & 126.38 & 270.17\\
2 & 64 & $1.536\times10^{21}$ & 273.09 & 573.38\\
3 & 128 & $5.667\times10^{40}$ & 585.75 & 1218.10\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The improvement is enormous locally, while the new field thresholds
are still far beyond a practical exhaustive construction. The theorem
is a quantitative structural statement, not a claim of an efficient
large-instance algorithm.

\section[{Vector targets and exact torsion dependence\srctag{40}}]{Vector targets and exact torsion dependence}\label{gsr:en:40:sec:d8}
\srcnote{40}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:en:40:sec:targets}
\subsection{Dimension-free simultaneous selection}
\begin{corollary}[Vector-valued maps]\label{gsr:en:40:cor:vector}
Theorems~\ref{gsr:fm:40:thm:explicit} and \ref{gsr:en:40:thm:exact} hold, with unchanged
constants, for $\phi:B\to\F_q^m$ for every $m\geq1$, when respected
means that the vector defect is zero.
Consequently the same bounds hold for simultaneously respecting any
finite family of scalar maps, provided the hypothesis counts
arrangements simultaneously respected by all of them.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Choose $t\in\F_q^m$ uniformly and replace $t\phi(v)$ in
\eqref{gsr:en:40:eq:prob} by the dot product $t\cdot\phi(v)$.
Orthogonality now gives
$\E_t\chi(t\cdot z)=\one_{z=0}$ for $z\in\F_q^m$ by taking the
product of the coordinate identities. All remaining steps are
unchanged. A nonzero scalar $a\in\F_q$ cannot annihilate a nonzero
vector defect. The only dimension dependence is the number of field
coordinates in the random seed, not any counting constant.
\end{proof}

The hypothesis is essential: knowing that each map separately respects
many arrangements need not give a comparable intersection of their
good arrangement families. The corollary does not manufacture this
missing intersection.

\subsection{General finite abelian targets}
Let $A$ be a finite abelian group, written additively, and
$\phi:B\to A$. Define the defect by the same integer signed sum.
Choose a character $\psi$ of $A$ uniformly from its character group
$\widehat A$ and choose $u\in\F_q$ uniformly. Use the probability
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:40:eq:abelianprob}
 K_L\bigl(\psi(\phi(v))\chi(uF(v))\bigr).
\end{equation}
Character orthogonality on $A$ says
$\E_{\psi\in\widehat A}\psi(a)=\one_{a=0}$; it follows by writing
a finite abelian group as a product of cyclic groups and applying the
finite geometric sum on each factor.

\begin{proposition}[Defect-order survival formula]\label{gsr:en:40:prop:torsion}
Assume $p>2(L-1)$. For an $(L-1)$-regular arrangement whose defect
in $A$ has order $\nu$, its survival probability under
\eqref{gsr:en:40:eq:abelianprob} is exactly
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:40:eq:torsionmass}
 b_{s,L}R_{s,L}^{(\nu)},\qquad
 R_{s,L}^{(\nu)}
 =1+2\sum_{m=1}^{\lfloor(L-1)/\nu\rfloor}
                  \left(1-\frac{m\nu}{L}\right)^s.
\end{equation}
For a zero defect, take $\nu=1$, so the probability is $a_{s,L}$.
For a nonzero defect of order $\nu>L-1$, it is $b_{s,L}$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The feature orthogonality still restricts coefficient vectors to
$\eta=a\eta_0$. Target-character orthogonality then requires
$a\Delta_\phi=0$ in $A$, or equivalently $\nu\mid a$.
Summing $c_a^s$ over those multiples gives \eqref{gsr:en:40:eq:torsionmass}.
Regularity gives distinct vertices, just as before.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Targets without small torsion]\label{gsr:en:40:cor:notorsion}
The selection theorems hold for $\phi:B\to A$ with unchanged constants
provided $A$ has no nonzero element killed by any integer
$1\leq a\leq L-1$. In particular, it suffices that every prime divisor
of $|A|$ exceed $L-1$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Every nonzero defect then has order greater than $L-1$, so
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:40:prop:torsion} supplies exactly the bad probability
$b_{s,L}$. Good arrangements, including repeated ones, retain the
same lower bound by nonnegative coefficients. The score argument is
unchanged. The sufficient condition on prime divisors implies that
multiplication by each integer $1,\ldots,L-1$ is an automorphism of $A$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[A concrete small-torsion obstruction]
For fixed $s$ and $\nu\geq2$, Riemann sums in
\eqref{gsr:en:40:eq:torsionmass} show that
\[
 \frac{R_{s,L}^{(\nu)}}{R_s(L)}\longrightarrow\frac1\nu
 \qquad(L\to\infty).
\]
Thus the good-to-bad survival ratio against a defect of fixed order
$\nu$ tends only to $\nu$, rather than increasing without bound.
One cannot extend the one-stage high-bandwidth conclusion to arbitrary
small-torsion targets by reusing the same proof. This is an exact
obstruction for this kernel calculation, not a nonexistence theorem
for all selection methods.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A sharp exponent obstruction for positive Fourier kernels\srctag{40}}]{A sharp exponent obstruction for positive Fourier kernels}\label{gsr:en:40:sec:d9}
\srcnote{40}{Section 9}
\label{gsr:en:40:sec:barrier}
This section explains in which precise sense the powers $s$ and $s-1$
are natural. It does not claim a universal extremal theorem about
all subsets or all probabilistic constructions.

\begin{definition}[The homogeneous positive-Fourier class]
Let
\[
 W(e^{i\theta})=\sum_{a=-H}^H c_a e^{ia\theta}
\]
be a trigonometric polynomial with real coefficients
$c_{-a}=c_a\geq0$, with $c_0>0$, and $0\leq W\leq1$ on the unit
circle. For a single signed relation using every one of $s$ distinct
vertices, define the intended-relation good and bad probabilities by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:40:eq:generalab}
 a(W)=\sum_{a=-H}^H c_a^s,\qquad b(W)=c_0^s,
 \qquad R(W)=a(W)/b(W).
\end{equation}
These are the exact probabilities on regular configurations in the
same orthogonality calculation as above. The same kernel is used at
every vertex; this is the meaning of homogeneous here.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Gain--mass obstruction]\label{gsr:en:40:thm:barrier}
For every kernel in this class and every integer $s\geq2$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:40:eq:barrier}
 R(W)\leq\frac1{c_0},\qquad
 a(W)\leq b(W)^{(s-1)/s},\qquad
 a(W)\leq R(W)^{-(s-1)}.
\end{equation}
Consequently a required gain $R(W)\geq Q\geq1$ forces
$a(W)\leq Q^{-(s-1)}$.
The same conclusion holds for any finite sequence of independent
stages from this class: if their combined gain is at least $Q$, their
combined intended-relation good survival probability is at most
$Q^{-(s-1)}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Fourier inversion and $W\geq0$ imply
\[
 0\leq c_a
 \leq\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}W(e^{i\theta})\,d\theta=c_0.
\]
Also $\sum_a c_a=W(1)\leq1$. Hence
\[
 \sum_a c_a^s\leq c_0^{s-1}\sum_a c_a\leq c_0^{s-1}.
\]
Dividing by $c_0^s$ gives $R(W)\leq1/c_0$, while the same inequality
is $a(W)\leq b(W)^{(s-1)/s}$. Since
$c_0\leq1/R(W)$, it also gives the third inequality.
If $R(W)\geq Q$, this is at most $Q^{-(s-1)}$.

For independent stages $W_1,\ldots,W_r$, the regular good and bad
probabilities multiply, so the gains multiply as well. Apply the third
inequality to each stage and multiply:
\[
 \prod_i a(W_i)\leq
     \left(\prod_i R(W_i)\right)^{-(s-1)}.
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 40--46]
This barrier concerns the scalar first-moment certificate within the homogeneous positive-Fourier class. It advances source~04's and source~17's retention questions (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:retention}) and sits beside source~17's Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:17:prop:methodbarrier}, which settles the scalar certificate in another class; it is not a lower bound for every selection method, as source~40 says.
\end{writenote}

\begin{proposition}[Fej\'er kernels attain the exponent]
\label{gsr:en:40:prop:attain}
For fixed $s\geq2$ and any $Q\geq1$, there is a Fej\'er kernel with
$R_s(L)\geq Q$ and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:40:eq:attain}
 a_{s,L}\geq
 \frac{2^s}{(s+1)(s+3)^{s-1}}\,Q^{-(s-1)}.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Take $L=\lceil(s+1)Q/2\rceil\geq2$. Then
$R_s(L)\geq2L/(s+1)\geq Q$, and
$L\leq(s+3)Q/2$ because $Q\geq1$. Thus
\[
 a_{s,L}\geq\frac2{s+1}L^{1-s}
 \geq\frac{2^s}{(s+1)(s+3)^{s-1}}Q^{1-s}.
\]
\end{proof}

\subsection{Exactly what is optimal}
Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:40:thm:barrier} and Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:40:prop:attain} determine
the power $Q^{-(s-1)}$ in the gain--good-mass trade-off, up to constants
depending on $s$, within the stated class. A first-moment purity
certificate using only the lower bound $\alpha T_0$ for the initial
good mass and an upper bound $T_0$ for the total mass requires gain of
order $1/(\alpha\eta)$. In that certificate, the quantity
$\alpha a(W)$ therefore has natural scale
$\alpha^s\eta^{s-1}$, and the Fej\'er choice attains those powers.

This is not a lower bound on the actual number of good arrangements in
the best selected subset. It does not exclude improvements from
negative Fourier coefficients with a different positivity argument,
vertex-dependent kernels, adaptive correlated stages, additional
geometric information, higher-rank relation families, or a method
that avoids the coarse $T_0$ comparison altogether. It also does not
optimize the $s$-dependent constant or the field-size threshold.

The next nine sections are source~44's Sections~2--10, on the count of degenerate arrangements in Gowers's Lemma~15.4. \emph{Logically the chapter follows the degeneracy material of sources~18, 22, 25 and~27} (Sections~\ref{gsr:en:sec:sections1516} and~\ref{gsr:en:sec:degeneracy}): source~18 found the leading term, source~25 the codimension-one classification and source~27 the core directions for $p>2k+2$, the second coefficient for $d=2$ and the second coefficient for general $d$ up to one unknown statistic $b_{2,d,p}$; it is printed here because no number printed earlier may move. Source~44 calls sources~25 and~27 ``Baseline~A'' and ``Baseline~B'' (note in Section~\ref{gsr:fm:44:sec:d1}). Its introduction is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:44:sec:d1}; its verification, questions and reproduction appendix are in Part~V.

\emph{What is proved.} In every characteristic $p\ge5$ the core directions have width two, so the core count $k(2^{2d}-1)+2\binom k2$ holds without source~27's condition $p>2k+2$ (Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:44:lem:width}, Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:44:cor:corecount}); the union of all core events is counted exactly, by $\prod_{i<k}(1-(2^{2d}-1+2i)/q^2)$ for $p\ge5$ and $\prod_{i<k}(1-p^{2d-1+i}/q^2)$ for $p=2,3$ (Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:44:thm:oddproduct}, \ref{gsr:en:44:thm:smallproduct}), with an explicit non-core remainder of order $q^{-3}$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:44:thm:sandwich}); the second Whitney coefficient $b_{2,d}$ of the cross-section arrangement is characteristic-independent for $p>\max(2d,16)$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:44:thm:stability}) and is computed for every $d$ by a weighted double count over subsets of the nine-point grid $\Tfortyfour^2$, in $O(d^3)$ operations (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:44:thm:grid}), compressed by a finite rational certificate to eight lattice-walk energies (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:44:thm:compact}). At $d=8$, $b_{2,8}=3{,}280{,}234{,}631{,}541$, so the second coefficient of the degenerate count is $\binom k2-2{,}519{,}909k-3{,}280{,}234{,}631{,}541$ ($2^{16}-1-H_8=-2{,}519{,}909$, $H_8=2{,}585{,}444$, source~18's $C_8$; checked at the write). The deficit of $b_{2,d}$ from $\binom{H_d}2$ has order $49^d/d$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:44:thm:defectasy}). The intake reproduced $b_{2,d}=3$, $889$, $97{,}081$ for $d=2,3,4$ by brute force over hyperplane pairs ($3$ is source~27's $b_{2,2}$); $b_{2,8}$ rests on source~44's certificate, whose run was repeated at the write with identical output. This answers source~27's two questions (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:degeneracy}). The results are fixed-$k$ asymptotics; core avoidance is not full nondegeneracy.

\section[{Arrangements, coefficient directions, and the regular region\srctag{44}}]{Arrangements, coefficient directions, and the regular region}\label{gsr:en:44:sec:d2}
\srcnote{44}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:en:44:sec:setup}

Fix $d\ge2$, $k\ge1$, and a finite field $\F_q$ of characteristic $p$. Write
\begin{equation}
 m=2d,\qquad v=m2^k,\qquad D=(m+1)k+m-1,
 \qquad w=(\underbrace{1,\ldots,1}_{d},
           \underbrace{-1,\ldots,-1}_{d}).\label{gsr:en:44:eq:parameters}
\end{equation}
The signs are interpreted in the field, even when $p=2$. Since $w\ne0$,
\[
 W=\{r\in\F_q^m:w\cdot r=0\}
\]
has dimension $m-1$. A labelled arrangement consists of
$h\in\F_q^k$, $x=(x_{ji})\in\F_q^{m\times k}$, and $r\in W$, with vertices
\begin{equation}
 \rho(\epsilon,j)=(x_{j1}+\epsilon_1h_1,\ldots,
 x_{jk}+\epsilon_kh_k,r_j),
 \quad \epsilon\in\{0,1\}^k,\quad 1\le j\le m.
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:vertices}
\end{equation}
There are exactly $q^D$ parameter tuples. No distinctness of vertices is
assumed in this count.

Let $\mathcal A_p$ be the image of $\{-1,0,1\}$ in $\F_p$. For an array
$\eta\in\mathcal A_p^{\{0,1\}^k\times[m]}$ and $A\subseteq[k+1]$, define
\[
 M_A(\eta)=\sum_{j,\epsilon}\eta(\epsilon,j)
                   \prod_{i\in A}\rho(\epsilon,j)_i.
\]
The empty set is included. Put
\[
 e(\epsilon,j)=(-1)^{\epsilon_1+\cdots+\epsilon_k}w_j.
\]
The alternating cube identity, together with $\sum_jw_j=0$ and
$w\cdot r=0$, proves $M_A(e)=0$ for every $A$.

\begin{definition}
An arrangement is \emph{degenerate} if there exists such an $\eta$ outside
$\F_q e$ for which every $M_A(\eta)$ vanishes. Write
$\Delta_{k,d}(q)=Z_{k,d}(q)/q^D$.
Two admissible non-intrinsic arrays are in the same \emph{direction} if
$\eta'=a\eta+be$ for some $a\ne0$.
\end{definition}

Equivalent arrays have exactly the same moment-zero event. Dividing
pointwise by $e$ turns the equivalence into affine equivalence of profiles
$t'=at+b\one$. If nonconstant profiles take prime-field values, their
relating scalars $a,b$ lie in the prime field: two unequal coordinates
determine $a$, and either coordinate then determines $b$.

An array is \emph{column-parity} if
$\eta(\epsilon,j)=(-1)^{|\epsilon|}a_j$ for every $j$. When all $h_i$ are
nonzero, its moment equations are precisely
\begin{equation}
 \sum_j a_j=0,\qquad a\cdot r=0.\label{gsr:en:44:eq:parity}
\end{equation}
Here $a\in\mathcal A_p^m$, and $a$ must not be proportional to $w$.
Let $\cH_{d,p}$ be the distinct hyperplanes in $W$ so obtained, and set
\begin{equation}
 W^\circ=W\setminus\bigcup_{H\in\cH_{d,p}}H,
 \qquad g_{d,p}(q)=\frac{\cardtwentyfive{W^\circ}}{q^{m-1}},
 \qquad H_{d,p}=\cardtwentyfive{\cH_{d,p}}.\label{gsr:en:44:eq:regular}
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}\label{gsr:en:44:lem:regular}
Every arrangement with some $h_i=0$ is degenerate. If $r\in W^\circ$, its
coordinates are pairwise distinct. The complement of the region
$h_i\ne0$ for all $i$ and $r\in W^\circ$ is entirely degenerate.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A zero side gives two equal labelled vertices. Coefficients $1,-1$ at
these labels and zero elsewhere annihilate all moments, but cannot be a
nonzero multiple of the full-support array $e$. This works in
characteristic two as well. For distinct $u,t\in[m]$, the vector
$a=\mathbf e_u-\mathbf e_t$ is alphabet-valued, has sum zero, and is not
proportional to $w$, since $m\ge4$. Thus $r_u=r_t$ is one of the forbidden
hyperplanes. The final assertion follows from \eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:parity}.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A width theorem with no dimension-dependent characteristic cutoff\srctag{44}}]{A width theorem with no dimension-dependent characteristic cutoff}\label{gsr:en:44:sec:d3}
\srcnote{44}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:en:44:sec:width}

The core directions from \cite{repo44b} can be written as
\begin{equation}
 \eta(\epsilon,j)=e(\epsilon,j)
       \left(t_j+\sum_{i=1}^k b_i\epsilon_i\right),\qquad b\ne0,
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:coreprofile}
\end{equation}
with all displayed profile values in $\mathcal A_p$. In particular,
the slopes $b_i$ are common to the columns. The elementary lemma below
removes the earlier requirement $p>2k+2$.

\begin{lemma}[Characteristic-uniform width two]\label{gsr:en:44:lem:width}
Let $p\ge5$. A nonconstant affine Boolean function
$f(\epsilon)=t+\sum_i b_i\epsilon_i$ with values in $\mathcal A_p$ has at
most two nonzero slopes. With one active coordinate, the two endpoint
values are any two distinct alphabet elements. With two active coordinates,
the slopes are $\pm1$, and the offset is forced so that the three attained
values are $-1,0,1$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The value at zero and every single-coordinate difference belong to
$\F_p$, so all parameters are in that field. If $A$ is a nonempty proper
subset of $\F_p$ and $b\ne0$, then $A+b\ne A$: otherwise translation by
$b$ would make $A$ invariant under the whole additive group. Consequently
$\cardtwentyfive{A\cup(A+b)}\ge\cardtwentyfive A+1$. Adding active slopes successively grows
the attained-value set by at least one until it fills the field.
Three active slopes would therefore give at least four values, which is
impossible when $p\ge5$.

For two active slopes $b,c$, the four values are
$t,t+b,t+c,t+b+c$. A collision, with both slopes nonzero, forces
$b=c$ or $b=-c$. The resulting three values form an arithmetic progression.
If they are exactly the ternary alphabet, their middle value is zero:
their sum is three times that middle value, and $3\ne0$. The step is
therefore $1$ or $-1$. The one-coordinate case requires only that its two
endpoint values be distinct alphabet elements.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 40--46]
This removes the condition $p>2k+2$ of source~27's core classification (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:27:thm:corecount}), answering source~27's question on intermediate characteristics $5\le p\le2k+2$.
\end{writenote}

\begin{corollary}\label{gsr:en:44:cor:corecount}
For every $p\ge5$, every $d\ge2$, and every $k\ge1$, the number of core
directions is
\begin{equation}
 S_{k,d}=k(2^m-1)+2\binom{k}{2}.
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:corecount}
\end{equation}
Thus no new core families occur for $5\le p\le2k+2$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For a fixed single-coordinate slope direction, normalize a unit slope to
$1$. Each offset can be chosen in $\{-1,0\}$. The two constant offset
patterns are equivalent under common translation; all other binary
patterns remain distinct. This gives $2^m-1$ directions. A slope of
absolute value two forces constant offsets and yields the already counted
constant-offset direction after affine rescaling.

For two active coordinates, the normalized slope ratio is $1$ or $-1$.
The width lemma forces a common offset, which disappears modulo constant
translation. These give two directions for each coordinate pair. Distinct
supports or slope ratios cannot be related by a single affine change of
profile values.
\end{proof}

This answers the intermediate-characteristic question in
\cite{repo44b} without assuming that an integer lift of a long Boolean
sum has small absolute value. The translation argument works directly in
the prime field. Characteristics two and three are genuinely different:
the alphabet is then the entire prime field and allows arbitrarily many
active slopes.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Exact core-avoidance laws\srctag{44}}]{Exact core-avoidance laws}\label{gsr:en:44:sec:d4}
\srcnote{44}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:en:44:sec:core}

Fix nonzero sides and a regular cross-section vector $r$. Define the paired
linear map
\begin{equation}
 L_r(t)=\left(\sum_jw_jt_j,\ \sum_jw_jr_jt_j\right),
 \qquad Z_i=L_r\bigl((x_{ji}/h_i)_{j=1}^m\bigr)\in\F_q^2.
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:summary}
\end{equation}
Its two coefficient rows, $w$ and $w\odot r$, are independent because
$r$ is not constant. Thus $Z_1,\ldots,Z_k$ are independent uniform points
of $\F_q^2$ when the bases $x$ are uniform.

For a core profile \eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:coreprofile}, all but the two top moments
vanish automatically. Expansion of those top moments gives the equivalent
condition
\begin{equation}
 \sum_i b_i Z_i=-L_r(t).\label{gsr:en:44:eq:coreequation}
\end{equation}
Indeed each term $\epsilon_i$ contributes $1+x_{ji}/h_i$ after division by
the alternating top-cube factor. The extra common constant $\sum_i b_i$
vanishes under $L_r$, since $L_r(\one)=0$.

\subsection{Characteristics at least five: signed collisions}

Put $L=2^m-1$ and define the binary offset set
\begin{equation}
 \cC_r=\{L_r(u):u\in\{0,1\}^m\}\subseteq\F_q^2.
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:constellation}
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}\label{gsr:en:44:lem:constellation}
For $p\ge5$ and $r\in W^\circ$, the set $\cC_r$ has exactly $L$ elements,
contains zero, and is invariant under negation.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The all-zero and all-one vectors have the same image, namely zero. If two
binary vectors $u,u'$ have the same image, then
$a=w\odot(u-u')$ is ternary, has sum zero, and satisfies $a\cdot r=0$.
Regularity forces $a=\lambda w$, hence $u-u'=\lambda\one$.
Since a binary difference is $0,1$ or $-1$, a nonzero constant difference
occurs only for the all-one and all-zero pair. These are the only duplicate
images. Finally $L_r(\one-u)=-L_r(u)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact signed-collision product]\label{gsr:en:44:thm:oddproduct}
For every $p\ge5$, nonzero $h$, and regular $r$, the probability that no
core direction vanishes is
\begin{equation}
 F_{k,d,p}(q)=\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}
        \left(1-\frac{2^m-1+2i}{q^2}\right).
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:oddproduct}
\end{equation}
Equivalently, the exact number of such base matrices is
\begin{equation}
 q^{(m-2)k}\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}(q^2-L-2i).
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:oddcount}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The single-coordinate core events are exactly $Z_i\in\cC_r$ by
\eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:coreequation} and the proof of Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:44:cor:corecount}.
The two-coordinate events are $Z_i=Z_j$ or $Z_i=-Z_j$.
Outside $\cC_r$, negation has no fixed points, because $0\in\cC_r$ and
$p$ is odd. There are $(q^2-L)/2$ two-element sign orbits. Choose an
ordered list of $k$ distinct orbits and one of the two signs in each:
the number of possible paired tuples is
$\prod_{i<k}(q^2-L-2i)$. Each paired tuple has
$q^{(m-2)k}$ preimages under the independent rank-two maps in
\eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:summary}.
\end{proof}

If $k$ exceeds the number of available orbits, the product is zero: a zero
factor occurs before any negative factors. Thus the formula also covers
the saturation range. If there are no regular cross-sections, the
conditional statement is vacuous and the unconditional regular-region
count below is zero.

\subsection{Characteristics two and three: linear independence}

\begin{theorem}[Exact prime-field rank product]\label{gsr:en:44:thm:smallproduct}
Let $p\in\{2,3\}$ and $q=p^a$. For fixed nonzero sides and regular $r$,
\begin{equation}
 F_{k,d,p}(q)=\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}
       \left(1-\frac{p^{m-1+i}}{q^2}\right)
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:smallproduct}
\end{equation}
is the exact probability that no core direction vanishes. Moreover,
\begin{equation}
 g_{d,p}(q)=\prod_{j=0}^{m-3}\left(1-\frac{p^j}{q}\right).
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:smallg}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The allowed offsets form all of $\F_p^m$. Let
$C_r=L_r(\F_p^m)$, an $\F_p$-subspace of $\F_q^2$.
Its kernel consists exactly of the constant vectors. To see this,
$L_r(t)=0$ says that $c=w\odot t\in\F_p^m$ has sum zero and
$c\cdot r=0$. Since the alphabet is all of $\F_p$, regularity implies
$c\in\F_p w$, or $t\in\F_p\one$. Therefore
\[
 \dim_{\F_p}C_r=m-1.
\]
A core relation exists precisely when a nonzero vector
$b\in\F_p^k$ satisfies $\sum_i b_i Z_i\in C_r$. The images of the $Z_i$
in the quotient $\F_q^2/C_r$ must therefore be linearly independent.
This quotient has dimension $2a-m+1$. After $i$ independent images have
been chosen, the preimage of their span contains $p^{m-1+i}$ of the
$q^2$ possible next summaries. Multiplying the successive avoidance
probabilities proves \eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:smallproduct}.

For \eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:smallg}, put
\[
 E_0=\{c\in\F_p^m:\textstyle\sum_jc_j=0\}/\F_p w,
 \qquad \dim_{\F_p} E_0=m-2.
\]
A cross-section $r\in W$ induces the $\F_p$-linear map
$E_0\to\F_q$, $c\mapsto c\cdot r$. The map from $W$ onto the space of
all such linear maps is surjective and has kernel $\F_q\one$.
Indeed the annihilator of all coordinate-sum-zero vectors is the constant
line, and the dimensions over $\F_q$ then give surjectivity.
Regularity is exactly injectivity of the induced map on $E_0$.
The probability that $m-2$ uniform elements of $\F_q$ are
$\F_p$-linearly independent is the product in \eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:smallg}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Universal obstructions]\label{gsr:en:44:cor:thresholds}
In characteristics two and three, every arrangement is degenerate if
$a<m-2$ or $k>2a-m+1$. In characteristic at least five, every arrangement
is degenerate if $k>(q^2-2^m+1)/2$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Nondegeneracy requires nonzero sides, a regular cross-section, and core
avoidance. The required injections or distinct sign orbits cannot exist
beyond the displayed dimensions. If no regular cross-section exists, the
conclusion follows already from Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:44:lem:regular}.
\end{proof}

These are sufficient conditions for universal degeneracy, or equivalently
necessary conditions for the existence of a nondegenerate arrangement.
Their converses are not asserted.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{From exact core avoidance to the full degeneracy count\srctag{44}}]{From exact core avoidance to the full degeneracy count}\label{gsr:en:44:sec:d5}
\srcnote{44}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:en:44:sec:remainder}

The product formula is not, by itself, a formula for full nondegeneracy.
Other coefficient directions remain. This section retains the cubic
remainder from the earlier analysis \cite{repo44b}, proves the needed
rank statement, and substitutes the exact product in place of the earlier
pairwise estimate.

\subsection{The exact inventory of coefficient directions}
For even $\ell$, define
\begin{align}
 T_\ell(p)&=\sum_{a\equiv0\ (p)}[z^a](z^{-1}+1+z)^\ell,\\
 B_\ell(p)&=\sum_{j\in\Z}\binom{\ell}{\ell/2+jp}.
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:modularinventory}
\end{align}
A binomial coefficient is zero outside its usual range. Let $Q_\ell(p)$
count nonconstant affine classes of alphabet-valued profiles with balanced
signed coordinate sum, and let $U_\ell(p)$ count such classes without the
balance requirement. Then
\begin{align}
 Q_\ell(p)&=\frac{T_\ell(p)-2B_\ell(p)+1}{2},&
 U_\ell(p)&=\frac{3^\ell-2^{\ell+1}+1}{2}&& (p\ge5),\label{gsr:en:44:eq:inventorylarge}\\
 Q_\ell(p)&=\frac{p^{\ell-2}-1}{p-1},&
 U_\ell(p)&=\frac{p^{\ell-1}-1}{p-1}&& (p=2,3).\label{gsr:en:44:eq:inventorysmall}
\end{align}
Here the balanced signs have equally many $1$ and $-1$ entries.

For completeness, when $p\ge5$ there are $T_\ell(p)$ balanced ternary
profiles and $B_\ell(p)$ balanced binary profiles. There are three constant
ternary profiles. Profiles using exactly two values give
$(B_\ell(p)-2)/2$ affine classes, because the underlying subset is identified
with its complement. Profiles using all three values have only identity
and negation as affine alphabet symmetries; they give
$(T_\ell(p)-3B_\ell(p)+3)/2$ classes. Their sum is
\eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:inventorylarge}. Removing balance replaces these two profile
counts by $3^\ell$ and $2^\ell$. In characteristics two and three the
alphabet is the whole field. Quotient the vector space of profiles first
by the constant line and then projectivize; this proves
\eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:inventorysmall}.

Consequently the relevant inventory is
\begin{equation}
 H_{d,p}=Q_m(p),\qquad R_{k,d,p}=Q_v(p)-U_m(p),
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:HRinventory}
\end{equation}
where $R_{k,d,p}$ is the number of non-column-parity directions satisfying
the empty moment. Indeed column-parity profiles are arbitrary profiles on
$m$ columns and automatically have zero empty moment. The core inventory is
\begin{equation}
 S_{k,d,p}=\begin{cases}
 k(2^m-1)+k(k-1),&p\ge5,\\
 p^{m-1}(p^k-1)/(p-1),&p=2,3.
 \end{cases}\label{gsr:en:44:eq:allS}
\end{equation}
The second line follows by choosing a projective nonzero slope in
$\F_p^k$ and an offset modulo the constant line. In particular
$R_{k,d,p}-S_{k,d,p}$ is nonnegative: it counts the remaining directions.
The inventory formulae themselves are inherited from \cite{repo44b};
our improvement is that the large-characteristic core formula now holds
for every $p\ge5$.

\subsection{Why every remaining direction costs three powers of the field size}
For $A\subseteq[k]$ write
\[
 c_{A,j}=\sum_{\epsilon}\eta(\epsilon,j)\prod_{i\in A}\epsilon_i,
 \qquad h_A=\prod_{i\in A}h_i.
\]
The block moment satisfies the exact Boolean expansion
\begin{equation}
 F_{A,j}:=\sum_\epsilon\eta(\epsilon,j)
                 \prod_{i\in A}(x_{ji}+\epsilon_i h_i)
 =\sum_{B\subseteq A} h_Bc_{B,j}
                 \prod_{i\in A\setminus B}x_{ji}.
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:boolean}
\end{equation}
The two full moments associated with $A$ are
$\sum_jF_{A,j}$ and $\sum_jr_jF_{A,j}$. Boolean inversion, valid in every
characteristic, shows that column-parity is equivalent to the vanishing
of all vectors $c_A$ with $A\subsetneq[k]$.

\begin{lemma}[Non-core remainder]\label{gsr:en:44:lem:noncore}
For a fixed non-column-parity direction which is not core, conditional
on nonzero sides, the probability that its moments vanish and the
cross-section is regular is at most $q^{-3}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $s<k$ be the smallest degree for which some $c_A\ne0$, $|A|=s$.
The degree-$s$ moments force
\begin{equation}
 \sum_jc_{A,j}=0,\qquad c_A\cdot r=0.\label{gsr:en:44:eq:minconstraints}
\end{equation}
If the first condition fails there are no solutions. For each $i\notin A$,
\eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:boolean} at $A\cup\{i\}$ is affine in the coordinate block
$(x_{1i},\ldots,x_{mi})$, with coefficient vector $h_Ac_A$.
Its paired last-coordinate moment has coefficient vector
$h_A(r\odot c_A)$. A nonzero vector of sum zero has at least two nonzero
coordinates. Since regular $r$ has pairwise distinct entries, these two
rows have rank two.

If some minimal-degree $c_A$ is not proportional to $w$, its cross-section
constraint in \eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:minconstraints} has codimension one in $W$.
For each admissible regular $r$, the two base equations cost a further
factor $q^{-2}$. Their joint probability is at most $q^{-3}$.

Suppose instead that every minimal-degree vector is proportional to $w$.
If $s\le k-2$, choose $i,\ell\notin A$ distinct. The paired moments at
$A\cup\{i\}$ and $A\cup\{\ell\}$ give four independent equations: the
first pair has its rank-two rows in the $i$-coordinate block and the second
in the $\ell$-coordinate block. Their other terms depend only on the
$A$-coordinates and the sides. Fixing those coordinates therefore gives
probability at most $q^{-4}$, which is sufficient.

The remaining case has $s=k-1$ and every proper coefficient vector
proportional to $w$. Boolean inversion then says precisely
$\eta/e=t_j+\sum_i b_i\epsilon_i$ with common slopes and $b\ne0$.
This is a core direction, contrary to the hypothesis. These cases exhaust
the possibilities.
\end{proof}

The assertion about the other terms is important. In
\eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:boolean}, at $A\cup\{i\}$, every term involving $x_{ji}$ has
coefficient $c_B$ with $B\subseteq A$. Minimality leaves only $B=A$.
All other surviving terms use coordinates from $A$, not from another
block outside $A$. Thus the rank-four step does not assume independence
of unexamined right sides.

Let $F_{k,d,p}(q)$ be the product in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:44:thm:oddproduct} or
\ref{gsr:en:44:thm:smallproduct}, as appropriate, and put
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_{k,d,p}(q)=(1-q^{-1})^k g_{d,p}(q)F_{k,d,p}(q).
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:Phi}
\end{equation}
When there are no regular cross-sections set $\Phi=0$; this agrees with
the product expression because $g=0$.

\begin{theorem}[Exact principal part and explicit cubic remainder]
\label{gsr:en:44:thm:sandwich}
In every characteristic,
\begin{equation}
 0\le \Delta_{k,d}(q)-\bigl(1-\Phi_{k,d,p}(q)\bigr)
 \le (1-q^{-1})^k\frac{R_{k,d,p}-S_{k,d,p}}{q^3}.
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:sandwich}
\end{equation}
The quantity $\Phi$ is the exact probability of simultaneously avoiding
zero sides, all cross-section hyperplanes, and all core relations.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Every excluded zero side or cross-section is degenerate. On the remaining
region, all core events have the exact avoidance probability already
proved, independently of the particular regular $r$ and nonzero $h$.
This proves the interpretation of $\Phi$ and the lower inequality.
Every additional degeneracy has a non-core witness. Sum
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:44:lem:noncore} over the $R-S$ directions, then multiply by the
probability of nonzero sides. This proves the upper inequality.
\end{proof}

For example, the earlier $S/q^2$ upper bound for the core union discards
its exact intersections. The replacement is
$1-\prod_{i<k}(1-(2^m-1+2i)/q^2)$ in characteristics at least five.
The improvement is an exact finite identity, not a claim that the
non-core term is uniformly small when $k$ grows. A convenient inherited
coarse consequence remains
\begin{equation}
 \Delta_{k,d}(q)\le\frac{k+H_{d,p}}q
       +\frac{S_{k,d,p}}{q^2}
       +\frac{R_{k,d,p}-S_{k,d,p}}{q^3}.
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:coarse}
\end{equation}
The exact expression \eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:sandwich} is preferable whenever the
cross-section complement can itself be evaluated.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The second Whitney coefficient and a uniform characteristic cutoff\srctag{44}}]{The second Whitney coefficient and a uniform characteristic cutoff}\label{gsr:en:44:sec:d6}
\srcnote{44}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:en:44:sec:whitney}

Work first over $\Q$. The cross-section arrangement is defined by the
integer-balanced ternary vectors $a\in\Tfortyfour^m$, $\sum_ja_j=0$, modulo the
intrinsic line $\Q w$. Let $\mathcal L_2$ be its distinct codimension-two
flats in $W$, and let $\nu_F$ be the number of hyperplanes containing $F$.
Define
\begin{equation}
 b_{2,d}=\sum_{F\in\mathcal L_2}(\nu_F-1).
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:b2def}
\end{equation}
This is the second Whitney coefficient of the characteristic polynomial;
we will use only the finite inclusion--exclusion interpretation, not any
structural theorem about arrangements.

Put
\begin{equation}
 T_n=[z^0](z^{-1}+1+z)^n,
 \qquad H_d=\frac{T_m-2\binom{m}{d}+1}{2}.
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:H}
\end{equation}
The profile count \eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:inventorylarge} gives $H_d$ in characteristic
zero or greater than $m$. It does not alone establish that pair
intersections have stabilized. The following determinant bound does.

\begin{theorem}[Rank-two stability beyond characteristic sixteen]
\label{gsr:en:44:thm:stability}
If $p>\max(m,16)$, reduction from the rational arrangement to
$\cH_{d,p}$ preserves the hyperplanes, every rank-two flat, and every
incidence between them. In particular $H_{d,p}=H_d$ and
$b_{2,d,p}=b_{2,d}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Eliminate $r_m$ using $w_m=-1$ and $w\cdot r=0$. The unnormalized
restricted integer normal is
\begin{equation}
 n(a)=(a_i+a_mw_i)_{1\le i<m}.
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:normal}
\end{equation}
For $t\le3$ normals $n(a^{(1)}),\ldots,n(a^{(t)})$, each $t$ by $t$
minor is, up to sign, the determinant of the $(t+1)$ by $(t+1)$ matrix
whose rows are $a^{(1)},\ldots,a^{(t)},w$ restricted to the chosen $t$
coordinates and coordinate $m$. This follows by adding suitable multiples
of the last row to the preceding rows and expanding at the last column.
All entries of this augmented matrix are in $\Tfortyfour$. Hadamard's inequality
therefore bounds the absolute determinant by
\[
 (t+1)^{(t+1)/2}\le16.
\]
A nonzero minor cannot become zero modulo $p>16$; a zero integer minor
remains zero. All ranks of collections of at most three normals are
preserved. Nonzero normals and proportional pairs are consequently
preserved. Membership of a third normal in the span of two independent
ones is preserved as well. These are exactly the data determining the
rank-two flats and their incident hyperplanes.

Finally $p>m$ means that every modularly balanced ternary vector is
integer-balanced, since its integer coordinate sum has absolute value at
most $m$. Thus no new normals are introduced by a modular balance
condition. This proves the whole assertion.
\end{proof}

The bound $16$ is independent of $d$ and $k$ because only three restricted
normals are needed. It does not claim that the entire intersection lattice
stabilizes at that prime. Higher-rank minors can have larger determinants.

\begin{lemma}[A uniform two-term complement expansion]
\label{gsr:en:44:lem:gexp}
For $p>\max(m,16)$,
\begin{equation}
 g_{d,p}(q)=1-\frac{H_d}{q}+\frac{b_{2,d}}{q^2}
                         +O_d(q^{-3}),
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:gexp}
\end{equation}
uniformly over the indicated finite fields. One valid absolute remainder
constant is
\begin{equation}
 C_d=(1+H_d+b_{2,d})\binom{H_d}{3}.
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:Cd}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
At a point outside all intersections of three linearly independent
hyperplane normals, the incident normals have rank at most two. If there
are $s$ incident hyperplanes of rank two, all of them contain one unique
rank-two flat and its correction is $s-1$. Thus, at every such point,
\[
 \one_{\cup H}=\sum_{H\in\cH_{d,p}}\one_H
                 -\sum_{F\in\mathcal L_2}(\nu_F-1)\one_F.
\]
The identity is also true at rank zero or one. The exceptional points
belong to a union of at most $\binom{H_d}{3}$ codimension-three
subspaces, of total relative size at most $\binom{H_d}{3}q^{-3}$.
The discrepancy of the displayed indicator formula has absolute value
at most $1+H_d+b_{2,d}$. Averaging gives the asserted error bound.
Every hyperplane has relative size $q^{-1}$ and every rank-two flat
relative size $q^{-2}$. Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:44:thm:stability} makes their coefficients
independent of the characteristic.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The coefficient to be computed]
\label{gsr:en:44:cor:second}
For fixed $k,d$, uniformly for $p>\max(2d,16)$,
\begin{align}
 \Delta_{k,d}(q)
 &=\frac{k+H_d}{q}\\
 &\quad+\frac{\binom{k}{2}+k(2^m-1-H_d)-b_{2,d}}{q^2}
          +O_{k,d}(q^{-3}).\label{gsr:en:44:eq:second}
\end{align}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For fixed $k,d$, the exact core product is
$1-S_{k,d}/q^2+O_{k,d}(q^{-4})$. Substitute this, the binomial expansion
of $(1-q^{-1})^k$, and \eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:gexp} into \eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:Phi}. Theorem
\ref{gsr:en:44:thm:sandwich} gives an $O_{k,d}(q^{-3})$ remainder uniformly in the
characteristic: the direction inventory is bounded by $3^v$, independently
of $p$. Since
$S_{k,d}-\binom{k}{2}-kH_d=\binom{k}{2}+k(2^m-1-H_d)$,
the coefficient is the one displayed.
\end{proof}

The dependence on $b_{2,d,p}$ in this corollary was already identified in
\cite{repo44b}. The new content so far is its uniform characteristic
range and the exact principal product. The next section evaluates the
remaining invariant in a number of operations polynomial in $d$.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A fixed nine-point grid computes every second coefficient\srctag{44}}]{A fixed nine-point grid computes every second coefficient}\label{gsr:en:44:sec:d7}
\srcnote{44}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:en:44:sec:grid}

\subsection{Affine profiles and rank-two flats}
For an integer-balanced ternary normal $a$, put $z=w\odot a\in\Tfortyfour^m$.
Then $w\cdot z=0$. Two nonconstant profiles define the same hyperplane
exactly when
\begin{equation}
 z'=\lambda z+\mu\one,\qquad \lambda\ne0.
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:profileequivalence}
\end{equation}
A profile using exactly two distinct values has six ternary representatives
in its affine class. A profile using all three values has two, because the
only affine symmetries of $\Tfortyfour$ over $\Q$ are identity and negation.
These representative multiplicities will be retained, rather than
replacing affine equivalence by sign equivalence.

Take an ordered pair of nonconstant balanced profiles $z,z'$ which are
independent modulo the constant line. The coordinate pairs form a set
\begin{equation}
 S=\{(z_j,z'_j):1\le j\le m\}\subseteq\mathcal G:=\Tfortyfour^2.
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:Sgrid}
\end{equation}
Independence modulo constants is equivalent to $S$ affinely spanning
$\Q^2$. Let $\mathcal S$ denote all subsets of $\mathcal G$ with this
property. There are only $2^9=512$ possible subsets before imposing it.
For $S\in\mathcal S$ define
\begin{equation}
 c_i(S)=\begin{cases}6,&\text{the $i$th projection has two values},\\
                      2,&\text{it has three values},\end{cases}
 \qquad i=1,2.
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:ci}
\end{equation}
Both projections have at least two values, since $S$ spans the plane.

Let $\nu(S)$ be the number of nonzero projective directions $(b:c)$ for
which some affine function $a+bX+cY$ maps $S$ into $\Tfortyfour$.
Every such function produces a balanced ternary profile
$a\one+bz+cz'$, because the three constituent profiles have signed sum
zero. Its class gives a hyperplane containing the codimension-two flat
defined by the original pair. Conversely every hyperplane through that
flat arises this way. Therefore $\nu(S)$ is exactly its multiplicity.

There is a small exact algorithm for $\nu(S)$. Choose any three
noncollinear points of $S$. Assign to them the $27$ ordered triples of
values in $\Tfortyfour^3$, solve for the unique affine function, and retain it if
its values at the other points are in $\Tfortyfour$. Discard constant functions
and identify proportional nonzero gradient vectors. This is an exhaustive
rational computation, since an affine function is determined by three
noncollinear values.

\subsection{Balanced coordinate sequences and lattice energies}
For any $T\subseteq\mathcal G$, let
\begin{equation}
 P_T(X,Y)=\sum_{(u,v)\in T}X^uY^v,
 \qquad E_d(T)=\CT\left(P_T(X,Y)^dP_T(X^{-1},Y^{-1})^d\right).
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:energy}
\end{equation}
This counts ordered pairs of length-$d$ sequences from $T$ with equal
vector sum. Equivalently, if $W_d^T(s)$ counts ordered $d$-step walks with
steps in $T$ and endpoint $s\in\Z^2$, then
\begin{equation}
 W_0^T(s)=\one_{s=0},\qquad
 W_{j+1}^T(s)=\sum_{t\in T}W_j^T(s-t),\qquad
 E_d(T)=\sum_s W_d^T(s)^2.
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:walk}
\end{equation}
For $d\ge1$, $E_d(\varnothing)=0$.
Define the exact-support count
\begin{equation}
 N_d(S)=\sum_{T\subseteq S}(-1)^{|S|-|T|}E_d(T).
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:exact-support}
\end{equation}
Inclusion--exclusion shows that $N_d(S)$ counts the balanced coordinate
sequences whose combined support is exactly $S$. In particular it is a
nonnegative integer, despite the alternating formula.

\begin{theorem}[Fixed-grid formula]
\label{gsr:en:44:thm:grid}
For every $d\ge2$,
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 b_{2,d}=\sum_{S\in\mathcal S}
                 \frac{N_d(S)}{\nu(S)c_1(S)c_2(S)}.}
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:gridformula}
\end{equation}
More precisely, if $f_{\nu,d}$ is the number of rank-two flats incident
with exactly $\nu$ hyperplanes, then
\begin{equation}
 f_{\nu,d}=\sum_{\substack{S\in\mathcal S\\\nu(S)=\nu}}
                 \frac{N_d(S)}{\nu(\nu-1)c_1(S)c_2(S)}.
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:flatformula}
\end{equation}
Both formulae can be evaluated through $d$ in $O(d^3)$ exact arithmetic
operations and $O(d^2)$ memory, with constants independent of $d$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Fix a rank-two flat $F$ of multiplicity $\nu$. It has $\nu(\nu-1)$ ordered
pairs of distinct incident hyperplanes. For an ordered pair, choose every
ternary representative of each of its two profiles. There are
$c(z)c(z')$ raw ordered pairs. The support $S$ of each raw pair spans the
plane; its multiplicity is $\nu$, and its two projection representative
counts are $c(z),c(z')$.

Give this raw pair weight $1/(\nu c(z)c(z'))$. All representatives of one
ordered hyperplane pair contribute $1/\nu$. All ordered hyperplane pairs
through $F$ therefore contribute $\nu-1$. On the other hand, raw balanced
pairs with a specified support $S$ are counted by $N_d(S)$: the first
$d$ coordinate pairs and the last $d$ coordinate pairs must have equal
sum. Summing the weights by support proves \eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:gridformula}.
Giving each raw pair instead weight
$1/(\nu(\nu-1)c(z)c(z'))$ proves \eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:flatformula}.

For the operation count, at step $j$ every walk endpoint lies in
$[-j,j]^2$. The recurrence \eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:walk} uses at most nine additions
per endpoint, so one step costs $O(j^2)$ operations for each of the fixed
$512$ supports. Summing for $j\le d$ costs $O(d^3)$ operations, and
only the current arrays, of total size $O(d^2)$, need be stored.
Boolean M\"obius inversion on the nine-bit subset lattice costs a fixed
number of operations for each $j$. All rational weights and template
multiplicities are independent of $d$. The final numbers are integers by
the already proved counting interpretation.
\end{proof}

The bound is an arithmetic-operation bound, not a unit-cost assertion for
arbitrarily large integers. Walk counts have $O(d)$ bits, since there
are at most $9^d$ walks; the same linear bit bound holds for the energies.
Using ordinary schoolbook integer arithmetic still gives a polynomial
bit-complexity bound. The algorithm replaces enumeration of exponentially
many hyperplanes or their quadratically many pairs by a fixed collection
of two-dimensional walk recurrences.

The formula also gives an independently checkable consistency identity:
\begin{equation}
 \sum_\nu\binom\nu2 f_{\nu,d}=\binom{H_d}{2},\qquad
 b_{2,d}=\sum_\nu(\nu-1)f_{\nu,d}.
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:pairconsistency}
\end{equation}
The first identity says that every unordered pair of hyperplanes meets
in one rank-two flat. Neither identity is used to guess the answer.

\section[{Eight lattice energies and the explicit eight-arrangement coefficient\srctag{44}}]{Eight lattice energies and the explicit eight-arrangement coefficient}\label{gsr:en:44:sec:d8}
\srcnote{44}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:en:44:sec:compact}

\subsection{A finite-certified compression of the general formula}
Define the pair-overlap deficit
\begin{equation}
 B_d=\binom{H_d}{2}-b_{2,d}.
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:deficit}
\end{equation}
This notation is distinct from the modular binary count $B_\ell(p)$,
which always has two arguments and was used only in the direction
inventory. By \eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:pairconsistency},
\begin{equation}
 B_d=\sum_{F\in\mathcal L_2}\binom{\nu_F-1}{2}
 =\sum_{S\in\mathcal S}
        \frac{\nu(S)-2}{2\nu(S)c_1(S)c_2(S)}N_d(S).
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:deficitemplates}
\end{equation}
The first equality makes positivity transparent. The second follows by
the same weighted raw-pair count as Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:44:thm:grid}.

For a Laurent polynomial $P$ define
\[
 \mathcal E_d(P)=\CT\bigl(P(X,Y)^dP(X^{-1},Y^{-1})^d\bigr).
\]
Consider the following eight polynomials, each the indicator polynomial
of a finite planar step set:
\begin{align}
 P_7&=1+X+X^{-1}+Y+Y^{-1}+XY^{-1}+X^{-1}Y,\\
 P_6&=1+X+Y+X^2+XY+Y^2,\\
 P_{5a}&=1+X+Y+XY+Y^2,\\
 P_{5b}&=1+X+X^{-1}+Y+Y^{-1},\\
 P_4&=1+X+Y+Y^2,\\
 P_3&=1+X+Y,\qquad P_2=1+X,\qquad P_1=1.
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:eightpolynomials}
\end{align}
The subscripts record the number of points, not the arrangement dimension.
In particular $\mathcal E_d(P_2)=\binom{2d}{d}$ and
$\mathcal E_d(P_1)=1$.

\begin{theorem}[Eight-shape compression; finite rational certificate]
\label{gsr:en:44:thm:compact}
For every $d\ge1$, the fixed-grid expression gives
\begin{align}
 B_d={}&\frac1{12}\mathcal E_d(P_7)
       +\frac16\mathcal E_d(P_6)
       -\frac12\mathcal E_d(P_{5a})
       +\frac18\mathcal E_d(P_{5b})\notag\\
     &-\frac12\mathcal E_d(P_4)
       +\frac76\mathcal E_d(P_3)
       -\binom{2d}{d}+\frac{19}{24}.
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:compact}
\end{align}
For $d=1$ both $H_d$ and $b_{2,d}$ are zero. The universal finite identity
reducing \eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:deficitemplates} to \eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:compact} is certified by
\gitpath{code/verify.py} and \gitpath{data/grid_certificate.json}.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof and precise finite component]
Substitute \eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:exact-support} into \eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:deficitemplates}.
For each $T\subseteq\mathcal G$, its rational coefficient is
\begin{equation}
 \alpha_T=\sum_{\substack{S\in\mathcal S\\Tfortyfour\subseteq S}}
 (-1)^{|S|-|T|}\frac{\nu(S)-2}{2\nu(S)c_1(S)c_2(S)}.
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:alphas}
\end{equation}
If two finite step sets are related by an invertible rational affine
map, their energies are equal: a pair of $d$-term sums is equal before
the map if and only if it is equal afterward. The common affine
translation cancels because both sums have length $d$.

The finite certificate evaluates \eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:alphas} on all $512$ supports,
not on a finite list of values of $d$. To classify rational affine shapes,
map every ordered noncollinear triple of a planar support to
$(0,0),(1,0),(0,1)$ and choose the lexicographically least resulting set
of rational coordinate pairs. The corresponding one-dimensional
normalization uses ordered distinct pairs; empty sets and singletons
are treated separately. Two supports have the same key exactly when
they are rationally affinely equivalent. Summing the coefficients
\eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:alphas} by these keys gives the following complete nonzero list:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lrrrrrrrrr}
\toprule
Shape & $P_7$ & $P_6$ & $P_{5a}$ & $P_{5b}$ & $P_4$ & $P_3$ & $P_2$ & $P_1$ & $\varnothing$\\
\midrule
Coefficient & $1/12$ & $1/6$ & $-1/2$ & $1/8$ & $-1/2$ & $7/6$ & $-1$ & $19/24$ & $-1/3$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
This table is the finite computational component of the theorem. Its
checker reconstructs all template directions from the $27$ affine
assignments, computes every rational coefficient, and verifies equality
of the full dictionaries of affine-shape coefficients. All zero shape
coefficients are checked as well. The empty-set energy is zero when
$d\ge1$, yielding \eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:compact}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 40--46]
At $d=8$: $H_8=2{,}585{,}444$ is source~18's $C_8$, $2^{16}-1-H_8=-2{,}519{,}909$ (checked at the write), and the second coefficient of the degenerate count is $\binom k2-2{,}519{,}909k-b_{2,8}$, $b_{2,8}=3{,}280{,}234{,}631{,}541$ (the certificate's output, reproduced on a copy at the write). At $d=2$ the formula gives source~27's $(k^2+21k-6)/2$.
\end{writenote}

The general fixed-grid theorem does not depend on this compression or
its finite certificate. Thus the main algorithm and its proof survive
even if the eight-shape identity is not used. The certificate is not a
proof-assistant theorem: it is an explicit finite exact-arithmetic
component of an otherwise conventional proof.

In the implementation the grid is ordered lexicographically and a support
is encoded by its nine-bit mask. Representative masks for the displayed
shapes are $254,95,31,124,15,11,10,8$, respectively. The certificate
includes the actual point sets, so this convention can be checked without

Their multiplicities are
\begin{equation}
 \#\{S:\nu(S)=2,3,4,6\}=178,128,76,76,
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:templatehist}
\end{equation}
and no other multiplicity occurs in the enumeration.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The exponentially smaller pair-overlap deficit\srctag{44}}]{The exponentially smaller pair-overlap deficit}\label{gsr:en:44:sec:d9}
\srcnote{44}{Section 9}
\label{gsr:en:44:sec:asymptotic}

The large count $b_{2,d}$ is close to the number of hyperplane pairs.
The difference has its own growth scale. We derive that scale directly
from the fixed-grid theorem, so the following asymptotic does not depend
on the eight-shape finite certificate.

\begin{lemma}[The dominant seven-point support]\label{gsr:en:44:lem:seven}
For every $S\in\mathcal S$, $\nu(S)\le6$. If $\nu(S)\ge3$, then
$|S|\le7$. Among seven-point supports there are exactly two with
$\nu(S)\ge3$: the central strips $|X+Y|\le1$ and $|X-Y|\le1$ inside
$\mathcal G$. Each has $\nu(S)=3$ and $c_1(S)=c_2(S)=2$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Restrict any admissible nonconstant affine function to three noncollinear
points of $S$. Modulo an affine change of its values, a nonconstant
ternary profile on three labelled points has six possibilities: three
bipartitions for two-valued profiles, and three orderings modulo reversal
for three-valued profiles. Distinct gradient directions give distinct
classes upon restriction, so $\nu(S)\le6$.

The two coordinate projections already give two directions. A third
requires a function with both gradient coordinates nonzero. If $|S|\ge8$,
at least two horizontal rows are full. The three values on one full row
are exactly $\Tfortyfour$, and the values on the other are a nonzero translate of
that set. A finite nonempty subset of $\Q$ is not invariant under a
nonzero translation. Thus $|S|\ge8$ is impossible.

If $|S|=7$, at least one row and one column are full. Their three-term
arithmetic progressions force both gradient coordinates to be $1$ or
$-1$, after the normalization that the output alphabet is $\Tfortyfour$.
The allowed grid points lie in a strip of three consecutive levels of
$X+Y$ or $X-Y$. A noncentral such strip has at most six grid points,
whereas the central strip has exactly seven. These are therefore the only
possibilities. On either central strip, the same full row and column
argument shows that the only extra non-axis direction is its defining
diagonal; the other diagonal takes more than three values. This proves
$\nu=3$. Both coordinate projections have three values, so $c_1=c_2=2$.
\end{proof}

The two seven-point supports are equivalent by reflection to the support
of $P_7$. Their combined weight in \eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:deficitemplates} is $1/12$.
Every remaining contributing support has at most six points. Since
$0\le N_d(S)\le |S|^{2d}$ and all weights in
\eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:deficitemplates} are at most $1/12$, the crude but explicit bound
\begin{equation}
 \left|B_d-\frac1{12}\mathcal E_d(P_7)\right|
                      \le44\cdot36^d
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:deficiterror}
\end{equation}
follows. Indeed there are at most $512$ remaining supports, and the
sequences on the seven-point support missing a specified point number
at most $6^{2d}$. Summing the seven missing-point bounds contributes at
most $(7/12)36^d$; $(512+7)/12<44$.

\begin{theorem}[Triangular-lattice deficit asymptotic]
\label{gsr:en:44:thm:defectasy}
As $d\to\infty$,
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 B_d=\frac{7\,49^d}{96\pi\sqrt3\,d}
          \left(1-\frac5{24d}+O(d^{-2})\right).}
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:defectasy}
\end{equation}
Furthermore,
\begin{equation}
 b_{2,d}\sim\frac{3\,81^d}{64\pi d},\qquad
 \frac{B_d}{\binom{H_d}{2}}
       \sim\frac{14}{9\sqrt3}\left(\frac{49}{81}\right)^d.
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:relativeasy}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The support of $P_7$ is centrally symmetric, so
$\mathcal E_d(P_7)=\CT P_7^{2d}$. Fourier coefficient extraction gives
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal E_d(P_7)=\frac1{(2\pi)^2}
 \int_{[-\pi,\pi]^2}
  \bigl(1+2\cos u+2\cos v+2\cos(u-v)\bigr)^{2d}\,du\,dv.
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:fourierintegral}
\end{equation}
The absolute value of the bracket is at most seven, with equality only
at $(0,0)$ on the torus. This follows from the triangle inequality for
the seven unit complex terms: equality requires all of them to have the
same phase, which the constant term forces to be one.

Put $Q_2=u^2+v^2+(u-v)^2$ and
$Q_4=u^4+v^4+(u-v)^4$. Near zero, the logarithm of the bracket divided
by seven is
\begin{equation}
 -\frac{Q_2}{7}+\frac{Q_4}{84}-\frac{Q_2^2}{98}
                         +O\bigl((u^2+v^2)^3\bigr).
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:logexpansion}
\end{equation}
After $(u,v)=\sqrt{7/(2d)}\,(s,t)$, the exponent $2d$ times this logarithm
is
\[
 -Q_2(s,t)+\frac1d
       \left(\frac7{24}Q_4(s,t)-\frac14Q_2(s,t)^2\right)
       +O\bigl(d^{-2}(s^2+t^2)^3\bigr).
\]
The Gaussian integral is
$\int_{\R^2}e^{-Q_2}\,ds\,dt=\pi/\sqrt3$.
Under the normalized Gaussian its covariance matrix is
\[
 \begin{pmatrix}1/3&1/6\\1/6&1/3\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Hence $\E Q_4=1$ and $\E Q_2^2=2$. For example each of
$s,t,s-t$ has variance $1/3$ and fourth moment $1/3$; also $Q_2$ is a
sum of two squares after linear normalization, giving the stated second
moment. The relative coefficient at order $1/d$ is therefore
$7/24-1/2=-5/24$.

Here is a remainder justification for this use of the expansion. Outside
a fixed small neighborhood of zero the integrand is bounded by
$(7-\epsilon)^{2d}$ for some $\epsilon>0$. Inside that neighborhood the
real analytic logarithm has the displayed Taylor expansion and its
quadratic form is positive definite. Restricting the scaled variables
first to a ball of radius $d^{1/20}$ makes the integrated remainder,
including the square of the fourth-order correction, bounded by
$d^{-2}$ times an integrable Gaussian times a fixed polynomial.
The remaining scaled annulus is exponentially small in $d^{1/10}$,
by the quadratic upper bound on the logarithm. Gaussian tails permit
extension to $\R^2$. These bounds justify an $O(d^{-2})$ relative error.
Thus
\[
 \mathcal E_d(P_7)=\frac{7\,49^d}{8\pi\sqrt3\,d}
                \left(1-\frac5{24d}+O(d^{-2})\right).
\]
Combine this with \eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:deficiterror}; its exponential error is
smaller than every inverse power correction on the scale $49^d/d$.

For the final assertions, the one-dimensional coefficient integral for
$T_{2d}$ has integrand $(1+2\cos u)^{2d}$. Its unique absolute maximum
is three at zero, with normalized logarithm $-u^2/3+O(u^4)$.
The same Gaussian argument gives
$T_{2d}\sim 9^d\sqrt3/(2\sqrt{2\pi d})$.
The term $\binom{2d}{d}\le4^d$ is exponentially smaller, so
$H_d\sim9^d\sqrt3/(4\sqrt{2\pi d})$.
Squaring and dividing by two gives
$\binom{H_d}{2}\sim3\,81^d/(64\pi d)$.
The deficit is exponentially smaller, giving both statements in
\eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:relativeasy}.
\end{proof}

The dominant step set is a triangular-lattice hexagon with a holding
step at its center. Its appearance is forced by the extremal grid
support argument, not introduced as an analogy after the asymptotic was
observed numerically. Further coefficients can be obtained from the same
analytic integral, but their all-orders derivation is not needed here.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Contrasting growing-dimension laws\srctag{44}}]{Contrasting growing-dimension laws}\label{gsr:en:44:sec:d10}
\srcnote{44}{Section 10}
\label{gsr:en:44:sec:growing}

The exact products allow regimes inaccessible to a fixed-order
inclusion--exclusion approximation. Their interpretation must remain
precise: $\Phi$ is the probability of avoiding the classified obstructions,
not necessarily of avoiding every ternary relation.

\begin{theorem}[Signed-collision scale]
\label{gsr:en:44:thm:birthday}
Fix $d\ge2$. Along any sequence of finite fields with $p\ge5$ and
$q\to\infty$, if $k/q\to c\in[0,\infty)$, then
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_{k,d,p}(q)\longrightarrow e^{-c-c^2}.
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:birthday}
\end{equation}
Consequently the probability of full nondegeneracy has upper limit at
most $e^{-c-c^2}$ in this regime.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The number of cross-section hyperplanes is bounded in terms of $d$ alone,
even when the characteristic varies, so $g_{d,p}(q)=1+O_d(q^{-1})$.
The nonzero-side probability converges to $e^{-c}$. With $L=2^m-1$,
\[
 \log F_{k,d,p}(q)
 =-\frac{kL+k(k-1)}{q^2}
      +O_d\left(\frac{k+k^3}{q^4}\right)
 \longrightarrow-c^2.
\]
All factors are positive for large $q$ in this regime. Multiplying proves
\eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:birthday}. Full nondegeneracy implies avoidance of the classified
obstructions, so its probability is at most $\Phi$.
\end{proof}

The linear term $c$ is the zero-side cost; the quadratic term $c^2$ is the
signed-collision cost. The finite binary offset constellation has fixed
size and does not contribute at this scale.

\begin{theorem}[Small-characteristic rank window]
\label{gsr:en:44:thm:rankwindow}
Fix $p\in\{2,3\}$, $d\ge2$, and an integer $s\ge0$. For $q=p^a$ and
$k=2a-m+1-s$, as $a\to\infty$,
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_{k,d,p}(q)\longrightarrow
                   \prod_{j=s+1}^{\infty}(1-p^{-j}).
 \label{gsr:en:44:eq:rankwindow}
\end{equation}
If $k>2a-m+1$, every arrangement is degenerate.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The last assertion is Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:44:cor:thresholds}. In the specified
window the exact core product is
\[
 \prod_{i=0}^{k-1}(1-p^{m-1+i-2a})
       =\prod_{j=s+1}^{2a-m+1}(1-p^{-j}).
\]
Its limit is the displayed convergent positive product, because
$\sum_jp^{-j}<\infty$. The cross-section product in
\eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:smallg} and the nonzero-side probability tend to one; the latter
uses $k=O(a)$ and $a/p^a\to0$.
\end{proof}

Thus the classified obstruction has a dimension scale of order $q$ in
characteristics at least five, but a rank threshold of order $\log q$ in
characteristics two and three. Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:44:thm:sandwich} does not turn
these into full nondegeneracy limits: its inventory $R_{k,d,p}$ grows
rapidly with $k$. Any such strengthening would require new control of
non-core directions, not simply another expansion of the exact product.
