\section{Source~45's chapter: energy levels and the coset range \wtag}\label{gsr:en:sec:energylevels}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the eighth write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next two sections are source~45's Sections~2--3. \emph{Logically they follow source~14's near-maximal energy material} (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:14:thm:energy-sharp-stability} and the collision results of its Section~\ref{gsr:en:14:sec:collision-stability}) and source~15's collision amplification (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:collision}); they are printed here because no number printed earlier may move. Source~45's introduction is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:45:sec:d1}; its Sections~4--5 are in Part~III (Section~\ref{gsr:cc:sec:ufourgap}).

\emph{What is proved.} For $m\ge5$ the three largest additive energies of $m$-element subsets of a torsion-free abelian group are $M_m$, $M_m-4(m-2)$ and $M_m-8(m-3)$, $M_m=(2m^3+m)/3$; the sets at the second value are the affine images of $H_m=\{0,\ldots,m-2,m\}$ (Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:45:en:top-three}, \ref{gsr:en:45:en:second-equality}, \ref{gsr:en:45:en:third-gap}), through the exact identity $(M_m-E(A))/4=\#\{x<y<z:x+z-y\notin A\}$ (Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:45:en:identity}) and a unit-defect theorem for positive Schur triples. The first gap follows from the inverse Pollard theorem and Hegyv\'ari's work, as source~45 says (Remark~\ref{gsr:en:45:en:pollard-credit}); the classification and the third gap are new here, and the third level is not classified. Source~14's envelope $|A\triangle C|\le\tau(\varepsilon)m$, proved for $\varepsilon\le1/100$, is extended to $\varepsilon<1/9$ in every abelian group, with the canonical subgroup $\{d:|A\cap(A+d)|>m/2\}$, uniqueness, and all positive equality cases, which are exactly the punctured cosets $C\setminus K$, $K$ a subcoset of index at least nine (Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:45:co:envelope}, \ref{gsr:en:45:co:equality}); a second, nested-hole envelope with optimal leading constant one (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:45:co:puncture}); for coordinate-cube collisions, equality forces one punctured coordinate (Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:45:col:stability}, \ref{gsr:en:45:col:equality}). The equality cases are the intake's punctured-coset observation recorded at item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:cosetrange}, now with all equality cases on the larger range. The largest range is open.

\emph{Relation to the formal statements} (checked at HEAD \texttt{6d4942222}). \file{theorem_7_1} and \file{theorem_7_2} (\file{Sections06\_07.lean}, lines~104 and~125) have, since the seventh write's pins, the exact companions \file{theorem_7_1_holds} and \file{theorem_7_2_holds} (\file{Proofs07FreimanClosure.lean}, lines~185 and~235); the exact energy levels and the coset envelope are different statements and are not formalized.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The first three additive-energy levels\srctag{45}}]{The first three additive-energy levels}\label{gsr:en:45:sec:d2}
\srcnote{45}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:en:45:en:section}

The opening discussion of Section~7 of Gowers's paper records an exact
extremal fact: an arithmetic progression maximizes the additive energy of a
fixed number of integers, and it is the only maximizer
\cite[Section~7, immediately before Theorem~7.2]{gowers}.
Here we examine the next two values below that maximum.  This is a different
endpoint from the subgroup-coset bound $E(A)\leq |A|^3$ used elsewhere in
this article.  The ordered setting has maximum
$(2|A|^3+|A|)/3$, and its first two positive defects have exact linear sizes.

The maximum, an endpoint-addition recurrence, and the congruence of energy
modulo four belong to the existing literature.  Hegyv\'ari explicitly
studies the set of attainable energies and computes the displaced-endpoint
examples used below \cite[Section~2.1]{hegyvari}.  The first gap also
follows from the inverse Pollard theorem \cite{pollardequality}; we give both
its provenance and an elementary proof.  The full second-level equality
classification and the exact third level are extensions developed here
beyond the statements located in the inspected sources and the pinned
repository \cite{repo45}.  We make no assertion of global publication
priority for them.  Their proofs are self-contained.

\subsection{Statement of the spectrum theorem}
\label{gsr:en:45:en:statement}

For a nonempty finite set $A\subset\R$, put
\begin{align}
 E(A)&=\#\{(a,b,c,d)\in A^4:a+b=c+d\},
 \label{gsr:en:45:en:energy-definition}\\
 M_m&=\frac{2m^3+m}{3},\qquad
 D(A)=\frac{M_m-E(A)}4,\qquad m=|A|.
 \label{gsr:en:45:en:defect-definition}
\end{align}
The notation $D(A)$ in this section denotes a quarter of the deficit from
the torsion-free maximum.  Its integrality and nonnegativity will follow
from a counting identity, rather than being assumed.

For $m\geq3$, define
\begin{equation}
 H_m=\{0,1,\ldots,m-2,m\},\qquad
 L_m=\{0,2,3,\ldots,m\}=m-H_m.
 \label{gsr:en:45:en:second-models}
\end{equation}
An affine image of a finite real set means its image under $x\mapsto u+vx$
with $v\ne0$.  In particular, reflection is allowed.

\begin{theorem}[The first three levels]
\label{gsr:en:45:en:top-three}
For every integer $m\geq5$, the three largest distinct additive energies of
$m$-element subsets of $\R$ are
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\quad
 M_m,\qquad M_m-4(m-2),\qquad M_m-8(m-3).
 \quad}
 \label{gsr:en:45:en:first-three}
\end{equation}
The maximum occurs precisely for arithmetic progressions.  The second
value occurs precisely for affine images of $H_m$.  If $A$ belongs to
neither of these two classes, then
\begin{equation}
 E(A)\leq M_m-8(m-3),
 \label{gsr:en:45:en:third-bound}
\end{equation}
and equality is attained by
$\{0,1,\ldots,m\}\setminus\{2\}$.
The same assertions hold for finite subsets of every torsion-free abelian
group, with the affine models interpreted using a nonzero group element
as their common step.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 40--46]
Checked at the write by exhaustion over the $m$-subsets of $\{0,\ldots,n\}$: the three largest energies are $85,73,69$ for $m=5$ ($n=12$) and $146,130,122$ for $m=6$ ($n=13$), as the formula gives; the intake's search through $m=8$ agrees and finds the third value also at shapes other than $J_m$ (for example $\{0,2,3,4,6\}$ at $m=5$), consistent with the third level being unclassified.
\end{writenote}

The theorem classifies every set at the second level; it does not classify
all sets at the third level.  The restriction $m\geq5$ is necessary for
the stated second-level classification.  Small-cardinality exceptions
are discussed in Subsection~\ref{gsr:en:45:en:limits}.

\subsection{An exact ordered-completion deficit}
\label{gsr:en:45:en:ordered-defect}

The following identity turns the energy deficit into a count of specific
failed completions.  It is also a convenient exact certificate for finite
computations.

\begin{proposition}[Ordered-completion identity]
\label{gsr:en:45:en:identity}
For every nonempty finite $A\subset\R$,
\begin{equation}
 D(A)=
 \#\{(x,y,z)\in A^3:x<y<z,\ x+z-y\notin A\}.
 \label{gsr:en:45:en:missing-triples}
\end{equation}
In particular $D(A)$ is a nonnegative integer and
$E(A)\equiv |A|\pmod4$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Write $A=\{a_1<\cdots<a_m\}$.  For $m\geq2$, let
$B=A\setminus\{a_m\}$, $a=a_m$, and $n=m-1$.  Define
\begin{align}
 T(B,a)&=\#\{(x,y,z)\in B^3:x+y-z=a\},
 \label{gsr:en:45:en:endpoint-T}\\
 e(B,a)&=\binom n2-T(B,a).
 \label{gsr:en:45:en:endpoint-e}
\end{align}
In every triple counted by $T(B,a)$ one has $x>z$, because
$x-z=a-y>0$.  Conversely, a pair $z<x$ in $B$ determines the only
possible value $y=a-x+z$.  Consequently
\begin{equation}
 e(B,a)=\#\{(z,x)\in B^2:z<x,\ a-x+z\notin B\}\geq0.
 \label{gsr:en:45:en:endpoint-missing}
\end{equation}

Count the additive quadruples in $A$ by their occurrences of $a$.
Quadruples with no occurrence contribute $E(B)$.  Exactly one occurrence
contributes $4T(B,a)$, one copy for each position.  If there are exactly
two occurrences, one must be on each side of the equation: placing both
on the same side would require two smaller numbers to sum to $2a$.
The remaining values must agree, giving $4n$ quadruples.  Exactly three
occurrences are impossible, and four occurrences contribute one.
Therefore
\begin{equation}
 E(A)=E(B)+4m-3+4T(B,a).
 \label{gsr:en:45:en:energy-recurrence}
\end{equation}
This endpoint recurrence is also present, in difference-multiplicity
notation, in Hegyv\'ari's proof of the congruence modulo four
\cite[proof of Theorem~2.1]{hegyvari}.

The elementary identity
\[
 M_m-M_{m-1}=4m-3+4\binom{m-1}{2}
\]
now gives
\begin{equation}
 D(A)=D(B)+e(B,a).
 \label{gsr:en:45:en:defect-recurrence}
\end{equation}
Starting with a singleton, whose deficit is zero, and iterating proves
\eqref{gsr:en:45:en:missing-triples}.  Indeed, for $z<x<a$, the completion
$a-x+z$ lies strictly between $z$ and $a$.  Its membership in $A$ is
therefore equivalent to membership in the prefix preceding $a$.
Finally $M_m\equiv m\pmod4$, since
$M_m-m=2m(m-1)(m+1)/3$ is divisible by four.  The congruence follows.
\end{proof}

The recurrence admits a useful equality statement.

\begin{lemma}[Zero endpoint defect]
\label{gsr:en:45:en:endpoint-zero}
Let $B\subset\R$ be finite and nonempty, and let $a>\max B$.
Then $e(B,a)=0$ if and only if $B\cup\{a\}$ is an arithmetic progression.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The assertion is immediate for $|B|=1$, so assume $|B|=n\geq2$ and
translate $\min B$ to zero.  Let
\[
 D^+(B)=\{x-z:x,z\in B,\ x>z\}.
\]
If $e(B,a)=0$, then $a-d\in B\setminus\{0\}$ for every
$d\in D^+(B)$.  The exclusion of zero follows from
$a-d\geq a-\max B>0$.  Hence $|D^+(B)|\leq n-1$.
The reverse inequality follows from
$B\setminus\{0\}\subset D^+(B)$, and thus
$D^+(B)=B\setminus\{0\}$.

Let $d$ be the least positive element of $B$.  Whenever $b\in B$ and
$b>d$, the difference $b-d$ is again in $B$.  Repeated subtraction must
terminate, and a positive terminal value below $d$ is impossible.  Thus
all elements are integer multiples of $d$, and all intermediate multiples
up to the largest are present.  Therefore
$B=\{0,d,\ldots,(n-1)d\}$.  The containment
$a-D^+(B)\subset B\setminus\{0\}$ is between sets of the same size,
so it is equality.  Comparing their least elements gives $a=nd$.
The converse follows directly by completing pairs in a progression.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The classical maximum]
\label{gsr:en:45:en:maximum}
For every nonempty finite real set $A$, one has $E(A)\leq M_{|A|}$,
with equality if and only if $A$ is an arithmetic progression.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The inequality follows from Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:45:en:identity}.  If $|A|\geq2$
and equality holds, then both nonnegative terms in
\eqref{gsr:en:45:en:defect-recurrence} vanish, and
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:45:en:endpoint-zero} makes $A$ a progression.  Singletons are
progressions as well.  Conversely every completion in
\eqref{gsr:en:45:en:missing-triples} succeeds for a progression.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Appending a point and the sharp first gap}
\label{gsr:en:45:en:first-gap-section}

\begin{lemma}[Appending a point to a progression]
\label{gsr:en:45:en:append-AP}
Let $B=\{0,d,\ldots,(n-1)d\}$, where $d>0$ and $n\geq2$, and
let $a>(n-1)d$.  If $a/d$ is not an integer, then $T(B,a)=0$.
If $a=qd$ for an integer $q\geq n$, then
\begin{equation}
 T(B,a)=
 \sum_{h=\max\{1,q-n+1\}}^{n-1}(n-h),
 \label{gsr:en:45:en:append-formula}
\end{equation}
where an empty sum is zero.  Consequently, if $B\cup\{a\}$ is not
a progression, then $e(B,a)\geq n-1$.  For $n\geq3$, equality in
this last bound occurs precisely when $a=(n+1)d$.
If $n\geq4$ and $a$ is neither $nd$ nor $(n+1)d$, then
\begin{equation}
 e(B,a)\geq2n-3.
 \label{gsr:en:45:en:append-second-bound}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
All values of $x+y-z$ on $B^3$ are integer multiples of $d$.
For $a=qd$, a positive difference $hd=x-z$ has exactly $n-h$
representations in $B$, and its associated completion belongs to $B$
exactly when $0\leq q-h\leq n-1$.  This proves
\eqref{gsr:en:45:en:append-formula}.

At $q=n$ the sum is $\binom n2$.  For $q\geq n+1$ it is at most
$\binom{n-1}{2}$, attained only at $q=n+1$ when $n\geq3$.
If $a/d$ is not an integer, then $e(B,a)=\binom n2\geq n-1$;
this inequality is strict for $n\geq3$.
For $q\geq n+2$, the sum is at most $\binom{n-2}{2}$, so the
deficit is at least $2n-3$.  The nonintegral case also satisfies this
bound because $\binom n2\geq2n-3$ for $n\geq4$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp first gap]
\label{gsr:en:45:en:first-gap}
If $A\subset\R$ has $m\geq3$ elements and is not an arithmetic
progression, then
\begin{equation}
 D(A)\geq m-2,
 \qquad E(A)\leq M_m-4(m-2).
 \label{gsr:en:45:en:first-gap-bound}
\end{equation}
Equality is attained by $H_m$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For $m=3$, remove the largest point.  The remaining two-point set is an
AP, and Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:45:en:append-AP} gives $D(A)=1$ unless $A$ is an AP.
Now induct on $m$.  Write $B=A\setminus\{\max A\}$.
If $B$ is an AP, Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:45:en:append-AP} gives
$D(A)=e(B,\max A)\geq m-2$.  Otherwise the induction hypothesis
gives $D(B)\geq m-3$, and Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:45:en:endpoint-zero} gives
$e(B,\max A)\geq1$.  Their sum is at least $m-2$.
For $H_m$, append $m$ to $\{0,\ldots,m-2\}$ and use the equality
case in Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:45:en:append-AP}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why the first gap is a consequence of earlier work]
\label{gsr:en:45:en:pollard-credit}
We record the precise relationship to inverse Pollard, so that the
elementary proof above is not mistaken for an assertion of novelty of the
bound.  For an integer set $A$ of size $m$, let
\[
 r_A(d)=|A\cap(A+d)|,\qquad
 S_t(A)=\sum_d\min\{t,r_A(d)\}.
\]
Embed $A$ in a sufficiently large prime cyclic group, with no new
two-sum equalities.  Pollard's inequality gives
$S_t(A)\geq t(2m-t)$.  For $2\leq t\leq m-2$, the equality
classification in \cite[Theorem~3]{pollardequality} says that a non-AP
$A$ gives strict inequality: none of the exceptional endpoint cases
applies to $(A,-A)$.  At $t=1$, use the classical equality case in
$|A-A|\geq2m-1$, or the recalled Vosper theorem in
\cite[Theorem~1]{pollardequality}.  A cyclic AP in these equality cases
pulls back to an integer AP, using its consecutive three-term relations.

Symmetry $r_A(d)=r_A(-d)$ and $r_A(0)=m$ show that $S_t(A)$ has
parity $t$, as does $t(2m-t)$.  Thus each of these $m-2$ strict
inequalities improves by at least two.  The layer-cake identity
\[
 E(A)=(2m-1)m^2-2\sum_{t=1}^{m-1}S_t(A)
\]
then gives $M_m-E(A)\geq4(m-2)$.  This is the first-gap bound.
Hegyv\'ari's formula for
$\{1,\ldots,m-1,m+k\}$ already gives the extremal example at
$k=1$ \cite[Section~2.1]{hegyvari}.

For a finite set in a torsion-free abelian group, identify its generated
subgroup with $\Z^r$ and choose an integer linear functional avoiding
the finitely many nonzero differences of its pair sums. Its restriction
is a Freiman $2$-isomorphism to an integer set. It preserves energy and
the non-AP condition: an AP in the image pulls back using consecutive
three-term relations. Thus the same prior implication covers real
sets and general torsion-free sets.
\end{remark}

\subsection{A unit deficit in the positive Schur-triple problem}
\label{gsr:en:45:en:schur-section}

The next classification provides information that the numerical first gap
alone does not supply.  Positivity is essential here; we count ordered
Schur triples with repeated entries allowed.

\begin{lemma}[Exactly one missing Schur triple]
\label{gsr:en:45:en:unit-Schur}
Let $C=\{c_1<\cdots<c_n\}\subset(0,\infty)$, and put
\[
 S(C)=\#\{(x,y,z)\in C^3:x+y=z\},\qquad
 h(C)=\binom n2-S(C).
\]
Then $h(C)\geq0$, with equality precisely when
$C=d\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ for some $d>0$.
If $n\geq4$, then
\begin{equation}
 h(C)=1
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 C=d\{1,2,\ldots,n-1,n+1\}\quad(d>0).
 \label{gsr:en:45:en:unit-Schur-classification}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $r_j$ be the number of ordered representations $x+y=c_j$ in $C$.
Both summands precede $c_j$, and each of the $j-1$ possible first
summands determines the second.  Therefore
\begin{equation}
 h(C)=\sum_{j=1}^n\bigl(j-1-r_j\bigr),
 \qquad j-1-r_j\geq0.
 \label{gsr:en:45:en:Schur-deficit-decomposition}
\end{equation}
Equality $r_j=j-1$ says exactly that the prefix
$\{c_1,\ldots,c_{j-1}\}$ is invariant under the reflection
$x\mapsto c_j-x$.  If this holds at every index, induction gives
$c_j=jd$, with $d=c_1$.  This proves the zero-deficit assertion.

Suppose now that $h(C)=1$.  There is a unique deficient index $k$,
whose contribution in \eqref{gsr:en:45:en:Schur-deficit-decomposition} is one.
Before that index, $c_i=id$.  Necessarily $k\geq2$.

First suppose $k\geq3$.  We have $r_k=k-2\geq1$, so $c_k=qd$
for an integer $q\geq k$.  The case $q=k$ has zero deficit and is
excluded.  For $k\leq q\leq2k-2$, the number of ordered pairs in
$\{1,\ldots,k-1\}^2$ summing to $q$ is $2k-1-q$; above this
range it is zero.  The equality $r_k=k-2$ therefore forces
$q=k+1$.
If $k<n$, zero deficit at the next index would require the prefix
\[
 \{d,2d,\ldots,(k-1)d,(k+1)d\}
\]
to be invariant under reflection about $c_{k+1}/2$.
Comparing its least and greatest elements gives
$c_{k+1}=(k+2)d$.  But that reflection sends the present element
$2d$ to the absent element $kd$, a contradiction.  Thus $k=n$,
giving the displayed model.

It remains to rule out $k=2$.  Here $c_2\ne2d$.  Since $n\geq4$,
zero deficit at index three gives $c_3=d+c_2$.  Zero deficit at index
four requires the three-point prefix $\{d,c_2,d+c_2\}$ to be
centrally symmetric.  Its middle point must be its center, so
\[
 2c_2=d+(d+c_2),
\]
forcing $c_2=2d$, a contradiction.
Conversely, the model in \eqref{gsr:en:45:en:unit-Schur-classification} has
$r_j=j-1$ for $j<n$ and $r_n=n-2$, and hence has deficit one.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Unit endpoint defect]
\label{gsr:en:45:en:endpoint-one}
Let $B\subset\R$ have $n\geq4$ elements and $a>\max B$.
If $e(B,a)=1$, then $B\cup\{a\}$ is an affine image of $L_{n+1}$.
More precisely, after translating $\min B$ to zero, there is a $d>0$
such that
\[
 a=(n+1)d,
 \qquad B=\{0,2d,3d,\ldots,nd\}.
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Set $C=a-B\subset(0,\infty)$.  The bijection
$(x,y,z)\mapsto(a-x,a-y,a-z)$ sends the equation $x+y-z=a$ to
the Schur equation $(a-x)+(a-y)=a-z$.  Thus $e(B,a)=h(C)$.
Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:45:en:unit-Schur}.  Once $\min B=0$, the maximum
of $C$ is $a$, so its classified form gives exactly the stated values.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The second and third levels}
\label{gsr:en:45:en:second-third}

\begin{theorem}[All second-level sets]
\label{gsr:en:45:en:second-equality}
Let $A\subset\R$ have $m\geq5$ elements.  Then
\[
 D(A)=m-2
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 A\text{ is an affine image of }H_m.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The models attain the value by Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:45:en:first-gap}.
Conversely, write $B=A\setminus\{a\}$, with $a=\max A$.
If $B$ is an AP, the equality statement in Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:45:en:append-AP}
gives an affine image of $H_m$.
If $B$ is not an AP, then Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:45:en:first-gap} and
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:45:en:endpoint-zero} give
\[
 D(B)\geq m-3,\qquad e(B,a)\geq1.
\]
Their sum is $m-2$, so $e(B,a)=1$.
Since $|B|=m-1\geq4$, Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:45:en:endpoint-one} applies
and makes $A$ an affine image of $L_m$, hence a reflected affine image
of $H_m$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The sharp third gap]
\label{gsr:en:45:en:third-gap}
If $m\geq5$ and an $m$-element real set $A$ is neither an AP nor an
affine image of $H_m$, then $D(A)\geq2m-6$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Call the APs and the affine images of $H_m$ the first two classes.
For $m=5$, Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:45:en:first-gap} and
\ref{gsr:en:45:en:second-equality} give $D(A)>3$ outside those classes.
Integrality then gives $D(A)\geq4=2m-6$.

Assume $m\geq6$, put $n=m-1$, and again let
$B=A\setminus\{a\}$, $a=\max A$.  There are three cases.

If $B$ is an AP, normalize it as $\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}$.
The values $a=n$ and $a=n+1$ would put $A$ in the first two classes.
All other values satisfy $e(B,a)\geq2n-3$ by
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:45:en:append-AP}, which is stronger than the desired
$2n-4=2m-6$.

If $B$ is a second-level set, normalize it by a translation and a
positive dilation to either
\[
 B=H_n=\{0,1,\ldots,n-2,n\}
 \quad\text{or}\quad B=L_n=\{0,2,3,\ldots,n\}.
\]
In both cases $D(B)=n-2$, and the difference one has multiplicity
$n-2$.  If $a$ is nonintegral, every positive-difference completion
$a-h$ is nonintegral, so $e(B,a)=\binom n2\geq n-2$.
If $a$ is an integer at least $n+2$, all the difference-one
completions exceed $\max B$, again giving $e(B,a)\geq n-2$.
For the remaining value $a=n+1$, the model $L_n$ would extend to
$L_{n+1}$ and is excluded by the hypothesis on $A$.
In the model $H_n$, difference two has multiplicity $n-2$ and
completion $n-1$, which is absent.  Thus $e(B,a)\geq n-2$ in
every admissible case, and $D(A)\geq2n-4$.

Finally, suppose $B$ belongs to neither of the first two classes.
Induction gives $D(B)\geq2n-6$.
Endpoint defect zero would force $A$ to be an AP by
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:45:en:endpoint-zero}, and endpoint defect one would force
$A$ into the second class by Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:45:en:endpoint-one}.
Hence $e(B,a)\geq2$, and
$D(A)\geq(2n-6)+2=2m-6$.
\end{proof}

Sharpness follows from the next exact formula, which also exhibits more
of the energy spectrum near an interval.

\begin{proposition}[Deleting one point from an interval]
\label{gsr:en:45:en:one-hole}
Let $m\geq2$ and $1\leq j\leq m-1$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 D\bigl(\{0,1,\ldots,m\}\setminus\{j\}\bigr)
 =j(m-j)-\min\{j,m-j\}.
 \label{gsr:en:45:en:one-hole-formula}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Put $A=\{0,1,\ldots,m\}\setminus\{j\}$.
For $x<y<z$ in $A$, the completion $x+z-y$ lies in $[0,m]$,
so it fails to belong to $A$ precisely when it equals $j$.
Solving for the middle element gives $y=x+z-j$.
The strict inequalities $x<y<z$ are equivalent to $x<j<z$.
There are $j(m-j)$ choices
\[
 0\leq x\leq j-1,\qquad j+1\leq z\leq m.
\]
Their determined middle value belongs to $A$ except when $y=j$,
or equivalently $x+z=2j$.
The excluded pairs are exactly $(j-t,j+t)$ with
$1\leq t\leq\min\{j,m-j\}$.
Apply Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:45:en:identity} to finish the count.
\end{proof}

At $j=1$ the formula gives $D=m-2$.  At $j=2$ and $m\geq5$ it
gives $D=2m-6$.  In the latter model the unique gap of size two is
interior, with a unit gap on each side, whereas in $H_m$ and $L_m$
that gap is first or last.  Thus it belongs to neither of the first two
classes.  Since $0<m-2<2m-6$ for $m\geq5$, the bounds and examples
prove \eqref{gsr:en:45:en:first-three} over $\R$.

\subsection{Transfer, exact rigidity, and limitations}
\label{gsr:en:45:en:limits}

\begin{proposition}[Torsion-free transfer]
\label{gsr:en:45:en:torsion-free}
Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:45:en:top-three}, \ref{gsr:en:45:en:first-gap},
\ref{gsr:en:45:en:second-equality}, and~\ref{gsr:en:45:en:third-gap} hold for finite
subsets of every torsion-free abelian group.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The subgroup generated by a finite set $A$ is a finitely generated
torsion-free abelian group, hence isomorphic to $\Z^r$ for some finite
$r$.  Choose $r$ real numbers linearly independent over $\mathbb Q$.
They define an injective additive map $\Z^r\to\R$.
This map preserves all additive quadruples, and hence $E(A)$ and $D(A)$.

It also preserves the stated equality classes in both directions.
For an image AP, the common real step is the image of the difference
between two consecutive points.  Its relations pull back by injectivity.
For an image of $H_m$ or $L_m$ with $m\geq5$, there are adjacent
model points separated by the unit step.  Their preimages again supply
an actual group element as the step, and injectivity pulls back every
listed model point.  The real theorems therefore give the asserted
group theorems.  Conversely, every nontrivial torsion-free abelian group
contains an infinite cyclic subgroup, in which all the displayed models
can be realized.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[An exact rigidity window]
\label{gsr:en:45:en:rigidity-window}
Let $A$ have $m\geq5$ elements in a torsion-free abelian group.
If
\[
 E(A)>M_m-8(m-3),
\]
then $A$ is an AP or an affine image of $H_m$.
In the latter case, deleting one point leaves an $(m-1)$-term AP.
The strict energy threshold cannot be weakened to a non-strict one.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:45:en:third-gap}; remove the isolated end point in
the $H_m$ model.  The single-hole model with $j=2$ attains the
threshold and belongs to neither permitted class.
\end{proof}

For $m=3$, every non-AP triple has energy $15=M_3-4$; the two
consecutive gaps can have any unequal ratio.  For $m=4$, the
second-level classification also has extra families.  For example,
$\{0,1,4,5\}$ has energy $36=M_4-8$, but is not an affine image
of $H_4$.  These examples explain why the equality classification and
the three-level theorem start at $m=5$.

The torsion-free assumption must be retained.  A finite subgroup of
size $m$ has energy $m^3$, exceeding $M_m$ when $m>1$.
For a subset of a finite cyclic group, the conclusions are available
only after an explicit \emph{rectification}: a Freiman isomorphism of
order two to a torsion-free set, preserving both directions of all
two-sum relations.  Merely choosing integer representatives does not
establish such an isomorphism, because modular wraparound may create
additional quadruples.  This distinction is particularly relevant to
Gowers's argument, which passes between integers and cyclic groups.

Finally, the window here has absolute width $O(m)$ around a quantity
of order $m^3$.  Its relative width is therefore $O(m^{-2})$.
It supplies exact rigidity at a fine discrete scale; it does not supply
a constant-error near-extremizer theorem or a better global bound in
Szemer\'edi's theorem.  Shao's work addresses a different structural
scale, obtaining large pieces in progressions of controlled rank from
normalized energy inequalities \cite{shao}.  The two types of result
are complementary: the present arguments resolve exact finite energy
levels and equality geometry close to Gowers's classical Section~7
endpoint.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A larger coset-stability range and the geometry of equality\srctag{45}}]{A larger coset-stability range and the geometry of equality}\label{gsr:en:45:sec:d3}
\srcnote{45}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:en:45:co:section}

The additive-energy endpoint relevant to Gowers's inverse and arrangement
arguments is a subgroup coset.  Quantitative information near that endpoint
is useful only when it controls both the ambient approximation and the
geometry of its errors.  Source~14 of the existing repository report proves
the sharp quadratic coset envelope below for defect at most $1/100$
(its delivered Theorem~4.2); its Question~4 asks for a larger validity range
and for all equality cases.  Source~15 subsequently develops
collision-sensitive arrangement amplification and equality theory, while
retaining that small-defect range.  We use those results as the local
comparison, and credit their envelope and collision framework
\cite{repo45}.  Their place in the original argument is the energy and
arrangement machinery of Gowers's proof \cite{gowers}.

This section extends the same envelope to defect strictly below $1/9$,
constructs its subgroup directly from autocorrelation, and classifies every
case of equality in that range.  An exact remainder measures two separate
obstructions to equality: points outside the closest coset, and the
additive-energy defect of the missing points inside it.  This also gives a
quantitative approximation by a coset with a subcoset removed.  Finally,
for axis-cube collisions, equality forces the removed coset to occur in a
single coordinate.  The range $1/9$ is a proved sufficient range; its
optimality is not asserted.

\subsection{Autocorrelation and an intrinsic subgroup}

Throughout this section, $G$ is an abelian group and $A\subset G$ is finite
and nonempty.  The ambient group need not be finite.  Write
\begin{equation}
 m=|A|,\qquad
 r(d)=|A\cap(A+d)|,\qquad
 E(A)=\sum_{d\in G}r(d)^2,
 \qquad
 \varepsilon=1-\frac{E(A)}{m^3}.
 \label{gsr:en:45:co:normalization}
\end{equation}
Thus $E(A)$ is the number of ordered additive quadruples in $A$.
All sums involving $r$ have finite support.  The number
$\varepsilon$ in \eqref{gsr:en:45:co:normalization} is the \emph{actual} energy
defect.  An externally supplied upper bound for it will be denoted by
$\varepsilon_0$.

For a finite subgroup coset $C$ of $G$, put
$d_C(A)=|A\triangle C|$, where $\triangle$ denotes symmetric difference.
We use the normalized distance
\begin{equation}
 \delta(A)=\frac1m\min_C d_C(A).
 \label{gsr:en:45:co:distance-definition}
\end{equation}
The minimum exists: singleton cosets provide a nonempty collection of
finite, nonnegative integer distances.  Only finite cosets need to be
considered; an infinite coset has infinite symmetric difference with $A$.
Set $E(\varnothing)=0$ when an auxiliary missing set is empty.

The elementary identities
\begin{equation}
 \sum_d r(d)=m^2,\qquad
 m^3-E(A)=\sum_{a,b\in A}\bigl(m-r(a-b)\bigr)
 \label{gsr:en:45:co:defect-identity}
\end{equation}
will be used repeatedly.  The second follows by grouping the ordered
pairs $(a,b)$ according to their difference.  We also have
\begin{equation}
 r(u-v)\ge r(u)+r(v)-m.
 \label{gsr:en:45:co:overlap-triangle}
\end{equation}
Indeed, the subsets $A\cap(A+u)$ and $A\cap(A+v)$ of $A$ have
intersection of size at least $r(u)+r(v)-m$; translation of their
intersection injects into a translate of the overlap counted by $r(u-v)$.

\begin{lemma}[A pointwise autocorrelation gap]
\label{gsr:en:45:co:pointwise-gap}
For every $d\in G$,
\begin{equation}
 \frac{r(d)}m\left(1-\frac{r(d)}m\right)\le 2\varepsilon.
 \label{gsr:en:45:co:pointwise-gap-bound}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $I=\{x\in A:x+d\in A\}$, so $|I|=r(d)$.  For $x\in I$ and
$b\in A$, inequality~\eqref{gsr:en:45:co:overlap-triangle}, applied to $x-b$ and
$x+d-b$, gives
\[
 m-r(d)\le \bigl(m-r(x-b)\bigr)+\bigl(m-r(x+d-b)\bigr).
\]
Sum over $I\times A$.  The first sum on the right is bounded by
$m^3-E(A)$ because $I\subset A$, and the second has the same bound
because $I+d\subset A$.  Consequently
\[
 m\,r(d)\bigl(m-r(d)\bigr)\le 2\bigl(m^3-E(A)\bigr).
\]
Division by $m^3$ proves the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Canonical subgroup and preliminary approximation]
\label{gsr:en:45:co:canonical}
Suppose $0\le\varepsilon<1/9$, and define
\begin{equation}
 a=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-8\varepsilon}}2,
 \qquad H=\{d\in G:r(d)>m/2\}.
 \label{gsr:en:45:co:canonical-definitions}
\end{equation}
Then $H$ is a finite subgroup.  There is a unique $H$-coset $C$
containing more than $5m/6$ points of $A$.  If
\begin{equation}
 t=|A\setminus C|,\quad u=|C\setminus A|,\quad
 x=\frac tm,\quad \delta=\frac{t+u}{m},\quad h=|H|,
 \label{gsr:en:45:co:coset-parameters}
\end{equation}
then
\begin{equation}
 0\le x\le\frac a2<\frac16,
 \qquad
 \delta\le\frac{a-2ax+2x^2}{1-a}
 \le\frac a{1-a}<\frac12.
 \label{gsr:en:45:co:rough-distance}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The parameter $a$ lies in $[0,1/3)$ and satisfies
$\varepsilon=a(1-a)/2$.  Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:45:co:pointwise-gap} gives the
dichotomy
\begin{equation}
 \frac{r(d)}m\le a
 \quad\hbox{or}\quad
 \frac{r(d)}m\ge1-a
 \qquad(d\in G).
 \label{gsr:en:45:co:two-branches}
\end{equation}
Thus $H$ consists precisely of the differences on the upper branch.
It contains zero and is finite, since it is contained in $A-A$.
If $d,e\in H$, then
\[
 \frac{r(d-e)}m\ge1-2a>a.
\]
The dichotomy forces $d-e\in H$.  A nonempty finite set closed under
differences is a subgroup.

Let $n_j$ be the sizes of the intersections of $A$ with the distinct
$H$-cosets, including only the nonempty intersections, and write
$S=\sum_j n_j^2$.  Counting pairs whose difference lies in $H$ gives
$S=\sum_{d\in H}r(d)$.  On $H$, we use $r(d)^2\le mr(d)$;
off $H$, the lower branch gives $r(d)^2\le amr(d)$.  Hence
\[
 (1-\varepsilon)m^3=E(A)
 \le mS+am(m^2-S),
\]
and therefore
\begin{equation}
 \frac S{m^2}\ge1-\frac{\varepsilon}{1-a}=1-\frac a2.
 \label{gsr:en:45:co:coset-occupancy}
\end{equation}
Because $\sum_j n_j/m=1$,
\[
 \max_j\frac{n_j}{m}\ge\sum_j\left(\frac{n_j}{m}\right)^2
 =\frac S{m^2}.
\]
Choose the maximizing coset $C$.  It contains at least $(1-a/2)m>5m/6$
points of $A$, so it is unique, and $x\le a/2$.

The upper branch on $H$ and the concentration in $C$ also give
\[
 h(1-a)m\le S\le(m-t)^2+t^2.
\]
For the second inequality, the sum of the squares of the remaining
coset occupancies is at most the square of their sum $t$.
Since $h/m=1+\delta-2x$, rearrangement yields
\[
 \delta\le\frac{a-2ax+2x^2}{1-a}.
\]
Here $0\le x\le a/2\le a$, so $-2ax+2x^2\le0$.
Finally $a<1/3$ gives $a/(1-a)<1/2$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{An exact remainder around a coset}

The next estimate is independent of the preceding construction.  It
separates the points outside a proposed coset from the points missing
inside it, and retains the energy of the latter set.

\begin{proposition}[The outlier and missing-set remainder]
\label{gsr:en:45:co:exact-remainder}
Let $C=c+H$ be any finite subgroup coset, and put
\[
 A_0=A\cap C,\quad T=A\setminus C,\quad K=C\setminus A,
 \qquad b=|A_0|,\quad t=|T|,\quad u=|K|.
\]
With $x=t/m$ and $\delta=(t+u)/m$, one has
\begin{align}
 E(A)&\le E(A_0)+6bt^2+5t^3,
 \label{gsr:en:45:co:outlier-energy}\\
 E(A_0)&=b^3-bu(b-u)-\bigl(u^3-E(K)\bigr),
 \label{gsr:en:45:co:complement-identity}
\end{align}
and consequently
\begin{equation}
 \varepsilon\ge\delta(1-\delta)
 +x\bigl(2+\delta^2-(8+\delta)x+2x^2\bigr)
 +\frac{u^3-E(K)}{m^3}.
 \label{gsr:en:45:co:full-remainder}
\end{equation}
The coefficient of $x$ in \eqref{gsr:en:45:co:full-remainder} is not asserted
nonnegative for an arbitrary proposed coset.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
An additive quadruple in $A$ cannot have exactly one entry outside $C$:
three entries in a subgroup coset force the fourth into that same coset.
Quadruples with no entries in $T$ contribute $E(A_0)$.  For exactly two
entries in $T$, there are six choices of their positions.  After their
values and one of the two inside values have been fixed, the final value
is determined.  These cases therefore contribute at most $6bt^2$.
Exactly three entries in $T$ contribute at most $4t^3$, and four entries
contribute $E(T)\le t^3$.  This proves \eqref{gsr:en:45:co:outlier-energy}.

For \eqref{gsr:en:45:co:complement-identity}, translate $C$ to $H$ and write
$h=|H|=b+u$.  Expanding the four factors of $\1_{A_0}=\1_H-\1_K$
in the additive-quadruple count gives
\[
 E(A_0)=h^3-4h^2u+6hu^2-4u^3+E(K).
\]
For example, a term with two prescribed entries in $K$ and two in $H$
has $hu^2$ solutions: one $H$-entry is free and the last is determined
in $H$.  The other mixed terms are counted in the same way, regardless
of the positions of the entries.  Substitution of $h=b+u$ gives
\eqref{gsr:en:45:co:complement-identity}.

Finally combine the two estimates, use
$b/m=1-x$ and $u/m=\delta-x$, and expand:
\begin{align*}
 \frac{m^3-E(A)}{m^3}
 &\ge 1-(1-x)^3
 +(1-x)(\delta-x)(1-\delta)
 -6(1-x)x^2-5x^3
 +\frac{u^3-E(K)}{m^3}\\
 &=\delta(1-\delta)
 +x\bigl(2+\delta^2-(8+\delta)x+2x^2\bigr)
 +\frac{u^3-E(K)}{m^3}.
\end{align*}
This is \eqref{gsr:en:45:co:full-remainder}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The sharp envelope up to defect \texorpdfstring{$1/9$}{1/9}}

For $0\le z\le1/4$, define
\begin{equation}
 \tau(z)=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4z}}2,
 \qquad \tau(z)\bigl(1-\tau(z)\bigr)=z.
 \label{gsr:en:45:co:tau}
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Expanded range of the quadratic coset envelope]
\label{gsr:en:45:co:envelope}
If $E(A)>8m^3/9$, there is a unique finite subgroup coset $C$ minimizing
$|A\triangle C|$, and
\begin{equation}
 |A\triangle C|\le\tau(\varepsilon)m.
 \label{gsr:en:45:co:envelope-bound}
\end{equation}
Its subgroup is the canonical set
$H=\{d:r(d)>m/2\}$, and $C$ is the unique $H$-coset containing more
than half of $A$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Use the coset and parameters of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:45:co:canonical}.  Define
\[
 F(\delta,x)=2+\delta^2-(8+\delta)x+2x^2.
\]
Since $x\le\delta$ and $x<1/6$, its derivative in $\delta$ is
$2\delta-x\ge0$, and therefore
\[
 F(\delta,x)\ge F(x,x)=2-8x+2x^2>\frac{13}{18}>0.
\]
The last strict inequality follows because the quadratic decreases on
$[0,1/6]$ and takes the value $13/18$ at $1/6$.
The missing-set defect $u^3-E(K)$ is nonnegative.  Hence
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:45:co:exact-remainder} gives
$\delta(1-\delta)\le\varepsilon$.  As $\delta<1/2$,
the increasing branch of this quadratic can be inverted, yielding
$\delta\le\tau(\varepsilon)$.

It remains to prove uniqueness among all finite subgroup cosets, not
merely among $H$-cosets.  Put $\tau=\tau(\varepsilon)$.  We have
\begin{equation}
 \tau<\tau(1/9)=\frac{3-\sqrt5}{6}<\frac15.
 \label{gsr:en:45:co:tau-range}
\end{equation}
Suppose that two cosets $C,C'$ both have symmetric-difference distance
at most $\tau m$ from $A$.  Then
\[
 |C\cap C'|\ge(1-2\tau)m,
 \qquad |C|,|C'|\le(1+\tau)m.
\]
Their intersection is larger than half of either coset, because
$1-2\tau>(1+\tau)/2$.  A nonempty intersection of subgroup cosets is
a coset of the intersection of their subgroups.  Its index in either
subgroup is a positive integer, so an intersection larger than half
forces both indices to equal one.  The subgroups, and then the cosets,
coincide.  Any coset closer to $A$ than the constructed $C$ would also
satisfy the same $\tau$-bound.  This proves unique global minimality.
The intrinsic description follows from Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:45:co:canonical}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 40--46]
\emph{Against source~14} (checked at the write). Source~14's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:14:thm:energy-sharp-stability} proves the same envelope and uniqueness for $\varepsilon\le1/100$; here the range is $\varepsilon<1/9$ ($\tau(1/9)=0.1273$ against $\tau(1/100)=0.0101$). Equality example recomputed exactly: $A=\Z/36\Z\setminus\{0,9,18,27\}$ has $m=32$, $E(A)=29{,}184$, $\varepsilon=7/64$ and $|A\triangle(\Z/36\Z)|/m=1/8=\tau(7/64)$. The equality cases (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:45:co:equality}) are the punctured cosets of the intake observation at item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:cosetrange}, which advances source~14's Question~4.
\end{writenote}

\end{writenote}

\begin{corollary}[A supplied upper bound for the defect]
\label{gsr:en:45:co:upper-defect}
If $0\le\varepsilon_0<1/9$ and
$E(A)\ge(1-\varepsilon_0)m^3$, the same canonical closest coset satisfies
\[
 |A\triangle C|\le\tau(\varepsilon_0)m.
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The actual defect satisfies $0\le\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0$.
Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:45:co:envelope} and the monotonicity of $\tau$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What changes from the existing result]
The function $\tau$ and its sharp small-defect interpretation are
credited to source~14 \cite{repo45}.  The subgroup construction in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:45:co:canonical} replaces its preliminary small-difference-set
argument, and makes the same envelope valid throughout
$0\le\varepsilon<1/9$.  Neither this theorem nor the comparison claims
that $1/9$ is the optimal endpoint.  The statements also hold for finite
sets in infinite abelian groups, since their canonical subgroup is
contained in the finite set $A-A$.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Every exact envelope extremizer}

From now on, $C$ is the unique closest coset from
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:45:co:envelope}, and
$\delta=\delta(A)=|A\triangle C|/m$.  Keep $x,t,u,K$ as in
\eqref{gsr:en:45:co:coset-parameters}, and define the excess over the quadratic
envelope by
\begin{equation}
 \eta=\varepsilon-\delta(1-\delta).
 \label{gsr:en:45:co:excess-definition}
\end{equation}

\begin{proposition}[A structural remainder above the envelope]
\label{gsr:en:45:co:structural-remainder}
If $\varepsilon<1/9$, then
\begin{equation}
 \eta\ge\bigl(2-8\delta+2\delta^2\bigr)x
       +\frac{u^3-E(K)}{m^3}
 \ge x+\frac{u^3-E(K)}{m^3}.
 \label{gsr:en:45:co:structural-remainder-bound}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For $0\le x\le\delta<1/5$, the polynomial $F(\delta,x)$ in the
proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:45:co:envelope} decreases in $x$:
its derivative is $-(8+\delta)+4x<0$.  Thus
\[
 F(\delta,x)\ge F(\delta,\delta)=2-8\delta+2\delta^2.
\]
Insert this in \eqref{gsr:en:45:co:full-remainder}.  The last coefficient is
itself decreasing on the relevant interval, and
\[
 2-8\tau(1/9)+2\tau(1/9)^2
 =\sqrt5-\frac{11}{9}>1.
\]
Since $\delta\le\tau(\varepsilon)<\tau(1/9)$, the second inequality
follows.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[All equality cases in the quadratic envelope]
\label{gsr:en:45:co:equality}
Suppose $\varepsilon<1/9$.  Equality
\begin{equation}
 \delta(A)=\tau(\varepsilon)
 \label{gsr:en:45:co:equality-condition}
\end{equation}
holds precisely in the following cases:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item $A$ is a finite subgroup coset, and $\varepsilon=0$;
 \item $A=C\setminus K$, where $C=c+H$ is a finite subgroup coset,
 $K$ is a coset of a subgroup $L\le H$ contained in $C$, and
 $r=[H:L]\ge9$.
\end{enumerate}
In the second case,
\begin{equation}
 \delta(A)=\frac1{r-1},\qquad
 \varepsilon=\frac{r-2}{(r-1)^2},
 \label{gsr:en:45:co:equality-values}
\end{equation}
and $C$ is the unique closest coset.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Condition~\eqref{gsr:en:45:co:equality-condition} is equivalent to $\eta=0$.
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:45:co:structural-remainder} forces $x=0$ and
$E(K)=u^3$.  Thus $A\subset C$.  If $u=0$, then $A=C$.
If $u>0$, maximal energy says that every ordered triple
$x,y,z\in K$ satisfies $x-y+z\in K$.  Translate one point of $K$
to zero.  The resulting finite set contains zero and is closed under
negation and addition, hence is a subgroup $L$.  Therefore $K$ is
a coset of $L$ inside $C$.  Writing $r=[H:L]$, we obtain
$u=|L|$, $m=(r-1)|L|$, and $\delta=1/(r-1)$.
The strict inequality $\delta<\tau(1/9)$ implies $r\ge9$.

Conversely, let $A=C\setminus K$ with the stated index.  Since
$E(K)=u^3$, identity~\eqref{gsr:en:45:co:complement-identity} gives
\[
 m^3-E(A)=mu(m-u).
\]
Consequently $\varepsilon=\delta_0(1-\delta_0)$ with
$\delta_0=u/m=1/(r-1)$.  For $r\ge9$ this defect is less than $1/9$
and $\delta_0<1/2$, so $\delta_0=\tau(\varepsilon)$.
The displayed coset $C$ satisfies the envelope bound with equality.
The uniqueness part of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:45:co:envelope} identifies it with the
closest coset, proving the converse and \eqref{gsr:en:45:co:equality-values}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The discrete equality parameters]
\label{gsr:en:45:co:discrete-equality}
Across all finite abelian groups, the nonzero equality defects in the
range $\varepsilon<1/9$ are exactly
\[
 \left\{\frac{r-2}{(r-1)^2}: r\in\N,\ r\ge9\right\}.
\]
In a fixed ambient group only indices of its finite subgroup inclusions
can occur.  In $\F_p^n$ the admissible indices are $r=p^j\ge9$,
with $1\le j\le n$.  In a prime cyclic group the nontrivial examples
in this range are complements of one point, for $p\ge11$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Necessity follows from Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:45:co:equality}.  Every integer
$r\ge9$ is realized by a cyclic group $H$ of order $r$ with
$L=\{0\}$.  The remaining assertions follow from the possible subgroup
indices in the indicated groups.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The missing-subcoset examples already appear in a write note adjoining
source~14's Question~4 \cite{repo45}.  Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:45:co:equality}
proves that they exhaust equality in the enlarged range.  In particular,
sharpness of the function $\tau$ does not mean equality is attainable at
every real defect parameter.  Equality in
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:45:co:upper-defect}, with a supplied bound
$\varepsilon_0$, additionally forces the actual defect to equal
$\varepsilon_0$, by the strict monotonicity of $\tau$.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Stability of the punctured-coset extremizers}

The exact remainder controls the outliers and the missing-set defect
through a common budget.  Applying the coset envelope to the missing
set, while keeping that budget intact, gives a second sharp envelope
for repair.  The relevant parameter is $\eta/\delta^3$, because the
missing set has size approximately $\delta m$ and energy scale
$(\delta m)^3$.

\begin{theorem}[The nested-hole envelope and all equality cases]
\label{gsr:en:45:co:puncture}
\label{gsr:en:45:co:puncture-refined}
Suppose $\varepsilon<1/9$, $\delta=\delta(A)>0$, and
\begin{equation}
 0\le s=\frac{\eta}{\delta^3}<\frac19,
 \qquad \eta=\varepsilon-\delta(1-\delta).
 \label{gsr:en:45:co:recursive-hypothesis}
\end{equation}
Let $C$ be the canonical closest coset and $K=C\setminus A$.
There is a unique closest subgroup coset $D$ to $K$; it is a
nonempty proper subcoset of $C$.  This same $D$ minimizes the repair
inside the fixed outer coset $C$.  Write
\[
 \Delta_C(A)=\frac1m\min_{\substack{D'\subsetneq C\\
                       D'\text{ a nonempty subgroup coset}}}
                   |A\triangle(C\setminus D')|.
\]
If $s>0$, then
\begin{equation}
 \Delta_C(A)
 \le \delta\tau(s)
 =\frac{\tau(s)}s\frac\eta{\delta^2}
 \le(1+2s)\frac\eta{\delta^2}.
 \label{gsr:en:45:co:puncture-refined-bound}
\end{equation}
Equality in the first bound holds precisely when
\begin{equation}
 A=C\setminus(D\setminus J)=(C\setminus D)\cup J,
 \label{gsr:en:45:co:recursive-equality}
\end{equation}
where $J\subsetneq D\subsetneq C$ are nonempty subgroup cosets
and the index of the subgroup underlying $J$ in that underlying $D$
is at least nine.  The assertion fixes the canonical outer coset $C$.
If $s=0$, then $A=C\setminus D$ and $\Delta_C(A)=0$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Keep $x=|A\setminus C|/m$ and put $k=|K|/m=\delta-x$.
The coupled remainder \eqref{gsr:en:45:co:structural-remainder-bound} gives
$x\le\eta=s\delta^3<\delta$, so $k>0$ and $K$ is nonempty.
Define its actual defect by $\zeta=1-E(K)/|K|^3$.  The same remainder
states that
\begin{equation}
 \eta\ge x+k^3\zeta.
 \label{gsr:en:45:co:coupled-hole-budget}
\end{equation}
To control the full interval of possible outlier masses, define
\[
 z(y)=\frac{\eta-y}{(\delta-y)^3}
 \qquad(0\le y\le\eta).
\]
Its denominator is positive, and
\[
 z'(y)=\frac{-\delta+3\eta-2y}{(\delta-y)^4}<0,
\]
where $3\eta=3s\delta^3<\delta/3$ uses $s<1/9$ and $\delta<1$.
Thus $0\le z(y)\le z(0)=s<1/9$ throughout the interval.
In particular \eqref{gsr:en:45:co:coupled-hole-budget} gives
$0\le\zeta\le z(x)<1/9$.

Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:45:co:envelope} to $K$ inside $C$, after translating
$C$ to its finite subgroup.  There is a closest subcoset $D\subset C$
with
\begin{equation}
 |K\triangle D|\le\tau(\zeta)|K|.
 \label{gsr:en:45:co:hole-repair}
\end{equation}
The ambient version of the same theorem makes $D$ the unique closest
coset even among those not contained in $C$.
Moreover $|K|\le\delta m<m/5$, so
\[
 |D|\le(1+\tau(\zeta))|K|<\frac54|K|<\frac m4,
 \qquad |C|\ge(1-\delta)m>\frac{4m}{5}.
\]
Hence $D$ is proper.  The outliers are disjoint from both sets
inside $C$, giving
\begin{equation}
 \Delta_C(A)=x+\frac{|K\triangle D|}{m}
 \le x+k\tau(\zeta)
 \le x+(\delta-x)\tau(z(x)).
 \label{gsr:en:45:co:recursive-chain}
\end{equation}
The equality on the left also proves the asserted minimization
property of $D$.

Suppose $s>0$ and define
\[
 F(y)=y+(\delta-y)\tau(z(y))
 \qquad(0\le y\le\eta).
\]
Write $k_y=\delta-y$ and $b_y=\tau(z(y))$.  Then
$0\le b_y<1/2$ and $b_y(1-b_y)=(\eta-y)/k_y^3$.
Differentiating gives
\begin{align*}
 F'(y)
 &=1-b_y+
       \frac{-k_y^{-2}+3b_y(1-b_y)}{1-2b_y}\\
 &=\frac{1-b_y^2-k_y^{-2}}{1-2b_y}<0,
\end{align*}
because $0<k_y\le\delta<\tau(1/9)<1$.
Thus \eqref{gsr:en:45:co:recursive-chain} implies
$\Delta_C(A)\le F(x)\le F(0)=\delta\tau(s)$.
For the simpler estimate, put $b=\tau(s)<\tau(1/9)<1/4$.  Then
\[
 \frac{\tau(s)}s=\frac1{1-b}
 =1+\frac{s}{(1-b)^2}
 \le1+\frac{16}{9}s\le1+2s.
\]
When $s=0$, Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:45:co:equality} gives the exact punctured-coset
representation, with no division by $s$ required.

Suppose next that $s>0$ and equality holds in the first bound.
Strict decrease of $F$ forces $x=0$, so $A\subset C$ and
$k=\delta$.  The exact complement identity now gives
$\eta=\delta^3\zeta$, hence $\zeta=s$.
Equality in \eqref{gsr:en:45:co:recursive-chain} therefore requires
\[
 \frac{|K\triangle D|}{|K|}=\tau(\zeta).
\]
The positive-defect equality classification in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:45:co:equality}, applied to $K$, says exactly that
$K=D\setminus J$, where $J$ is a nonempty subcoset of $D$ and
its underlying subgroup has index at least nine.
This is \eqref{gsr:en:45:co:recursive-equality}.
Conversely, under the theorem's hypotheses, such a representation
makes $D$ the unique closest coset to $K$ by the same inner equality
classification.  The complement identity gives $\zeta=s$, and
\[
 \Delta_C(A)=\frac{|K\triangle D|}{m}
            =\delta\tau(s),
\]
proving sufficiency as well.  No minimization over different outer
cosets is asserted in this equality statement.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Range extended by source~68}: outer defect below $1/4$ and inner defect $s\le1/4$, with all equality cases and an oriented form (its Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:puncture}, \ref{gsr:en:68:thm:puncture-equality}, \ref{gsr:en:68:thm:oriented-puncture}, Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:68:prop:puncture-endpoint}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{proposition}[Attainment and the sharp leading constant]
\label{gsr:en:45:co:puncture-scale}
The first bound in \eqref{gsr:en:45:co:puncture-refined-bound} is attained by
nested-hole examples for every pair of integers $r\ge10$ and $u\ge8$,
at $s=(u-1)/u^2$.  These examples have minimum repair cost exactly
one point, even if the outer coset is allowed to vary.
Consequently the scale $\eta/\delta^2$ cannot be replaced by a
little-oh bound, and the optimal uniform leading constant in
$(C_0+o(1))\eta/\delta^2$, as $\eta/\delta^3\to0$, is $C_0=1$.
The assertion of sharpness concerns these attained families; it does
not assert attainment for every real parameter.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Let the ambient group $H$ be cyclic of order $r(u+1)$, let $L\le H$
have order $u+1$, and put
\[
 K=L\setminus\{0\},\qquad A=H\setminus K,
 \qquad m=(r-1)(u+1)+1.
\]
The difference multiplicities of $K$ inside $L$ are $u$ at zero and
$u-1$ at every nonzero element.  Therefore
\[
 E(K)=u^2+u(u-1)^2=u^3-u^2+u.
\]
The exact complement identity gives
\begin{equation}
 \delta_0=\frac um,\qquad
 \eta_0=\frac{u^2-u}{m^3},\qquad
 \varepsilon=\delta_0(1-\delta_0)+\eta_0.
 \label{gsr:en:45:co:nested-family-defect}
\end{equation}
Since
\[
 \delta_0<\frac1{r-1}\le\frac19,
 \qquad \eta_0<\delta_0^2,
\]
we have $\varepsilon<\delta_0<1/9$.
Also $\delta_0<1/2$ and
$\varepsilon\ge\delta_0(1-\delta_0)$, so the coset $H$ satisfies
$|A\triangle H|/m=\delta_0\le\tau(\varepsilon)$.
Uniqueness in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:45:co:envelope} makes $H$ the canonical
closest coset.  Hence $\delta=\delta_0$, $\eta=\eta_0$, and
\[
 s=\frac\eta{\delta^3}=\frac{u-1}{u^2}
 \le\frac7{64}<\frac19,
 \qquad \tau(s)=\frac1u.
\]
The bound on $s$ uses $u\ge8$ and decrease of $(u-1)/u^2$ for $u>2$.

The punctured coset $H\setminus L$ differs from $A$ by one point.
There is no zero-edit representation $A=C'\setminus D'$ by nested
subgroup cosets in this ambient group.  Indeed $|A|>|H|/2$, so a
coset $C'$ containing $A$ must equal $H$: every proper subgroup coset
of the finite group $H$ has size at most $|H|/2$.
An exact representation would then require $D'=K$.
But a subgroup coset contained in $L$ has size dividing $|L|=u+1$,
whereas $|K|=u$ does not divide $u+1$ for $u>1$.
Thus the minimum edit count is exactly one, and
\[
 \Delta_H(A)=\frac1m=\delta\tau(s).
\]
This proves finite attainment with all the stated numerical conditions.
Finally
\begin{equation}
 \frac\eta{\delta^2}=\frac{1-1/u}{m},\qquad
 \frac{1/m}{\eta/\delta^2}=\frac u{u-1}\longrightarrow1,
 \qquad s\longrightarrow0
 \quad(u\to\infty).
 \label{gsr:en:45:co:scale-sharp-ratio}
\end{equation}
The upper bound in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:45:co:puncture-refined} has multiplier
$\tau(s)/s=1+s+O(s^2)$, which tends to one.  The attained family
proves that no smaller uniform asymptotic leading constant is possible.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Axis-cube collisions and coordinate splitting}

We now distinguish ordinary additive energy from the more restrictive
axis-cube collision count used in the arrangement framework.  Let
\[
 G=\prod_{i=1}^k G_i,\qquad k\ge1,
\]
where the $G_i$ are abelian groups.  For $g\in G$, let $e_i(g)$ denote
the element with $i$th coordinate $g_i$ and all other coordinates zero.
For $x,h\in G$, define the axis cube
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{Cube}(x,h)
 =\{x+\omega\cdot h:\omega\in\{0,1\}^k\},
 \qquad
 \omega\cdot h=(\omega_1h_1,\ldots,\omega_kh_k).
 \label{gsr:en:45:col:cube-definition}
\end{equation}
Degenerate cubes are included.  For a finite set $A\subset G$, let
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal Q(A)=
 \#\{(x,z,h):\operatorname{Cube}(x,h),
                    \operatorname{Cube}(z,h)\subset A\}.
 \label{gsr:en:45:col:collision-definition}
\end{equation}
This count is finite even if the ambient groups are infinite: the
endpoints $x$ and $x+h$ determine $h$ from two elements of $A$.

For completeness, if $\phi:A\to W$ takes values in an abelian group,
define on a cube contained in $A$
\[
 D_h\phi(x)=\sum_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^k}
                  (-1)^{|\omega|}\phi(x+\omega\cdot h).
\]
Let $\mathcal Q_\phi(A)$ count the triples in
\eqref{gsr:en:45:col:collision-definition} for which
$D_h\phi(x)=D_h\phi(z)$.  This is the label-respected collision count.
Changing all signs by a common factor changes neither the equality
condition nor the count.

\begin{lemma}[Collision and corner bounds]
\label{gsr:en:45:col:energy-corners}
For every finite nonempty $A$ of size $m$,
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal Q_\phi(A)\le\mathcal Q(A)\le E(A)\le m^3.
 \label{gsr:en:45:col:energy-chain}
\end{equation}
If
\[
 C_i(A)=\#\{(x,w)\in A^2:x+e_i(w-x)\in A\},
\]
then
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal Q(A)\le m C_i(A)\qquad(1\le i\le k).
 \label{gsr:en:45:col:corner-bound}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Send $(x,z,h)$ to $(x,z,w=x+h)$.  This map is injective.  A valid
cube pair has $x,z,w,z+w-x\in A$, so its image is an additive-energy
triple.  This proves the middle inequality in
\eqref{gsr:en:45:col:energy-chain}; the other inequalities are immediate.
For the same image, the corner $x+e_i(w-x)$ belongs to $A$.
For each admissible pair $(x,w)$ there are at most $m$ choices of $z$,
which proves \eqref{gsr:en:45:col:corner-bound}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Product-coset stability below defect $1/9$]
\label{gsr:en:45:col:stability}
Suppose
\[
 \mathcal Q(A)\ge(1-\varepsilon_0)m^3,
 \qquad 0\le\varepsilon_0<1/9.
\]
Then the unique closest finite subgroup coset to $A$ is a coordinate
product
\begin{equation}
 C=\prod_{i=1}^k(c_i+H_i),\qquad H_i\le G_i,
 \label{gsr:en:45:col:product-coset}
\end{equation}
and $|A\triangle C|\le\tau(\varepsilon_0)m$.
The conclusion also follows from the same lower bound on
$\mathcal Q_\phi(A)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By \eqref{gsr:en:45:col:energy-chain} and Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:45:co:upper-defect},
the unique closest coset $C=c+H$ exists.  Write
$h=|H|$, $t=|A\setminus C|$, $x=t/m$, and
$\delta=|A\triangle C|/m$.  Then
\[
 x\le\delta\le\tau(\varepsilon_0)<1/5,
 \qquad h/m=1+\delta-2x.
\]
We prove $e_iH\subset H$ for each $i$.

If this inclusion failed, the homomorphism
\[
 F_i:H\times H\longrightarrow G,
 \qquad F_i(y,w)=y+e_i(w-y),
\]
would have image $H+e_iH$.  Its image contains $H$ by taking $y=w$,
and contains $e_iH$ by taking $y=0$; the reverse inclusion follows
from the formula.  Since $e_iH\not\subset H$, this image has at least
$2h$ elements.  Every nonempty fiber consequently has size at most
$h/2$.

After translation by $c$, at most $mh/2$ pairs in $C^2$ have their
mixed corner in $A$.  At most $m^2-(m-t)^2$ pairs in $A^2$ are outside
$C^2$.  We infer
\begin{align*}
 \frac{C_i(A)}{m^2}
 &\le1-(1-x)^2+\frac{1+\delta-2x}{2}\\
 &=\frac12+\frac\delta2+x-x^2
 \le\frac12+\frac{3\delta}{2}<\frac45.
\end{align*}
But \eqref{gsr:en:45:col:corner-bound} and the hypothesis give
$C_i(A)/m^2\ge\mathcal Q(A)/m^3>8/9$, a contradiction.
Thus every coordinate component of every element of $H$ lies in $H$.
If $H_i$ is its projection to $G_i$, summing these coordinate components
shows $H=\prod_i H_i$.  This proves \eqref{gsr:en:45:col:product-coset}; the
distance bound and uniqueness were already obtained.  The label-respected
case follows from $\mathcal Q_\phi\le\mathcal Q$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Positive-defect equality requires one punctured coordinate}

The energy theorem allows a missing subgroup coset with an arbitrary
orientation inside the closest coset.  Collision equality is more rigid.

\begin{theorem}[All positive-defect collision-envelope extremizers]
\label{gsr:en:45:col:equality}
Let
\[
 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{cube}}=1-\frac{\mathcal Q(A)}{m^3},
 \qquad 0<\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cube}}<1/9.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \delta(A)=\tau(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cube}})
 \label{gsr:en:45:col:equality-condition}
\end{equation}
if and only if, after translation, there are finite subgroups
$H_i\le G_i$ and one coordinate $j$ such that
\begin{equation}
 A=(H_j\setminus K_j)\times\prod_{i\ne j}H_i,
 \label{gsr:en:45:col:single-puncture}
\end{equation}
where $K_j$ is a coset of a subgroup $L_j\le H_j$ and
$[H_j:L_j]\ge9$.  Its unique closest coset is
$C=\prod_i H_i$, translated back to the original coordinates.
At zero defect, $\mathcal Q(A)=m^3$ holds precisely for coordinate
product cosets.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $\varepsilon=1-E(A)/m^3$ be the actual additive-energy defect.
If \eqref{gsr:en:45:col:equality-condition} holds, then
\[
 \delta(A)\le\tau(\varepsilon)
 \le\tau(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cube}})=\delta(A).
\]
Strict monotonicity of $\tau$ forces
$\varepsilon=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cube}}$, so $E(A)=\mathcal Q(A)$.
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:45:co:equality} gives $A=C\setminus K$, where $K$ is a
subgroup coset inside $C$, and Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:45:col:stability} makes $C$
a coordinate product.

We first show that $A$ is closed under coordinate mixing.  Suppose
$x,w\in A$ and
$v=x+e_i(w-x)\notin A$.  Since $A\subset C$ and
$|C|=m(1+\delta)<2m$, there is $z\in A$ with $z+w-x\in A$:
the two relevant translates of $A$ inside $C$ have intersection of
size at least $2m-|C|>0$.  Thus $(x,z,w)$ is an additive-energy
triple, but its uniquely corresponding cube pair, with side $w-x$,
fails at the corner $v$.  The injection in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:45:col:energy-corners} is therefore not surjective, contrary
to $E(A)=\mathcal Q(A)$.  Every such mixed corner must lie in $A$.

A nonempty set closed under replacing one coordinate by the corresponding
coordinate of any other member is the Cartesian product of its coordinate
projections.  To verify this, start with any member and successively
replace coordinates to obtain any prescribed tuple from those projections.
After translating $C$ to $H=\prod_iH_i$, write
\[
 A=\prod_i A_i,\qquad A_i\subset H_i,
 \qquad K=b+L=H\setminus A.
\]
All $A_i$ are nonempty, and at least one is proper because the defect is
positive.  Suppose two coordinates have proper $A_i$.  For every
coordinate $i$, choose a different coordinate $j$ with $A_j\ne H_j$,
and fix its value in $H_j\setminus A_j$.  The entire $i$th-coordinate
fiber, with the other coordinates fixed arbitrarily, then lies in $K$.
Differences within this fiber imply $e_iH_i\subset L$.  This holds
for every $i$, so $L=H$ and $K=H$, contradicting $A\ne\varnothing$.
Exactly one coordinate, say $j$, is proper.  Therefore
\[
 K=(H_j\setminus A_j)\times\prod_{i\ne j}H_i.
\]
Projection of the coset $K$ shows that $H_j\setminus A_j$ is a
subgroup coset $K_j$.  This gives \eqref{gsr:en:45:col:single-puncture}, and
its index is the index $[H:L]\ge9$ from Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:45:co:equality}.

Conversely, let $A$ have the form \eqref{gsr:en:45:col:single-puncture}.  Both
additive energy and axis-cube collisions factor over Cartesian products.
In a full subgroup coordinate, every triple of the two bases and the
side is valid, giving $|H_i|^3$.  In the sole punctured coordinate,
a one-dimensional cube pair is exactly an additive quadruple, so its
collision count equals its energy.  Hence $\mathcal Q(A)=E(A)$.
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:45:co:equality} proves \eqref{gsr:en:45:col:equality-condition} and
identifies the closest coset.

At zero defect, \eqref{gsr:en:45:col:energy-chain} and
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:45:col:stability} force $A$ itself to be a coordinate product
coset.  Every such coset has $\mathcal Q(A)=m^3$, proving the last
assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[What equality says for labels]
\label{gsr:en:45:col:labelled-domain}
If $\varepsilon_\phi=1-\mathcal Q_\phi(A)/m^3<1/9$ and
$\delta(A)=\tau(\varepsilon_\phi)$, then
\[
 \mathcal Q_\phi(A)=\mathcal Q(A)=E(A).
\]
At positive defect the domain has the form
\eqref{gsr:en:45:col:single-puncture}; at zero defect it is a coordinate product
coset.  Constant labels attain equality on every domain in these
classifications.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The chain \eqref{gsr:en:45:col:energy-chain}, the energy envelope, and the strict
monotonicity of $\tau$ force equality of all three counts.  Apply
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:45:col:equality}.  For a constant label, the two full
alternating sums agree on every valid cube pair, so
$\mathcal Q_\phi(A)=\mathcal Q(A)$.
\end{proof}

The last corollary classifies the necessary domain geometry and supplies
sufficient constant-label examples.  It does not classify all admissible
labels.  A label classification must retain arbitrary lower-coordinate
terms, as the exact endpoint theory in sources~14--15 already emphasizes
\cite{repo45}.  Quantitative repair of those labels on the punctured
products is a further problem.

\section{Source~48's chapter: collision-aware derandomization of the restriction step \wtag}\label{gsr:en:sec:derandomization}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the ninth write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next eight sections are source~48's Sections~2--9, on the random restriction of Gowers's Lemma~9.3. \emph{Logically the chapter follows source~17's chapter} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:restriction}), whose Fej\'er restriction it makes constructive, and source~29's restriction over a fixed field (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:fixedfield}); it is printed here because no number printed earlier may move. Source~48's introduction is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:48:sec:d1}; its checks, integration notes and questions are in Part~V.

\emph{What is proved.} A rational signed combination $F$ of order-$s$ additive energies on a common set of labels, each label selected independently with a rational probability, is rounded deterministically to a set $S$ with $F(S)\ge\E F$ in $O(\costfortyeight nD)$ rational operations and $O((s+1)^2D)$ storage, $\costfortyeight=\binom{s+2}2^2$ and $D$ the total size of the ambient groups (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:48:gcr:thm:headline}). The method is an exact group-algebra inventory of partial energy counts in which a repeated label is selected once (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:48:gcr:thm:identity}), with a universal Stirling response that turns each probability replacement into translations of coefficient arrays (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:48:gcr:thm:replacement}) and a branch decision by $O(s^2)$ probes (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:48:gcr:thm:rounding}). A distinct-support profile gives the same for a uniformly random subset of any prescribed size, with no factor of that size (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:48:gcr:thm:fixed}); fixed systems of linear equations, with zero coefficients, repeated entries and composite moduli, are handled with column-type compression (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:48:gcr:thm:systems}). Applied to Lemma~9.3: for $B\subseteq\F_p$, $|B|=\beta p$, and a map $\phi$ respecting at least $\alpha n^{2s-1}$ balanced tuples, a set $B'$ with respected proportion $1-\eta$ and $\calT_s(B')\ge n^{2s-1}/(2\eta L^{2s})$ is \emph{constructed} with rational arithmetic in $O(\costfortyeight np^5)$ operations, under the threshold of source~17 (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:48:gcr:thm:source}); this is source~17's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:17:thm:main} with its retention, in the unweighted scalar case, made constructive. It answers source~17's Question~9 in its ambient-size form (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:recovery}). The bounds are polynomial in the ambient size $D$, not in $\log D$, as source~48 says; no new retention exponent is claimed.

\emph{Relation to the formal statements} (checked at HEAD \texttt{06b30ca52}). \file{lemma_9_3} (\file{Sections08\_09.lean}, line~77) has the exact companion \file{lemma_9_3_holds} (\file{Proofs09Restriction.lean}, line~376), an existence theorem; the algorithm, its complexity and the constructive theorem are not formalized.
