\section[{Sampling counts and the repeated-entry obstruction\srctag{48}}]{Sampling counts and the repeated-entry obstruction}\label{gsr:en:48:sec:d2}
\srcnote{48}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:sec:notation}

All groups are finite, abelian, written additively, and supplied in a
representation in which translations of a full group-indexed array can be
performed in linear time in its size. Products of cyclic groups have this
property. Arithmetic complexity counts rational operations separately
from the bit cost of those operations.

\begin{definition}[Partial energy counts]\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:def:partial}
For nonnegative integers $a,b$ and $h\in K$, let
\[
 N_{a,b}(S;h)=\#\left\{(i_1,\ldots,i_a,j_1,\ldots,j_b)\in S^{a+b}:
     \sum_{r=1}^a g_{i_r}-\sum_{r=1}^b g_{j_r}=h\right\}.
\]
The empty tuple has count $N_{0,0}(S;h)=\one_{h=0}$. Thus
$E_s(S;g)=N_{s,s}(S;0)$.
\end{definition}

If $S_{\boldsymbol p}$ is formed by independent label selection, a tuple
with distinct-label support $A$ survives with probability
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:support-prob}
 \prod_{i\in A}p_i.
\end{equation}
Multiplying $p_i$ once for every occurrence instead computes another
quantity. The difference persists even when the underlying group is
prime-cyclic and all label images are distinct.

\begin{example}[A one-label diagnostic]\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:ex:diagonal}
For one label selected with probability $q$, its order-$s$ energy is one
when selected and zero otherwise. Therefore
\[
 \E E_s(S_q)=q.
\]
The ordinary weighted convolution expression gives $q^{2s}$. At
$q=1/2$ and $s=8$ these are $1/2$ and $1/65536$, respectively.
An algorithm that substitutes the weighted convolution for the conditional
expectation is not merely making a small numerical error.
\end{example}

For a source function $\phi:B\to H$, use the two labelled images
\[
 g_x^{\rm dom}=x\in G,\qquad
 g_x^{\rm gr}=(x,\phi(x))\in G\oplus H.
\]
Then
\[
 \calT_s(S)=E_s(S;g^{\rm dom}),\qquad
 \calR_s(S,\phi)=E_s(S;g^{\rm gr}),\qquad
 0\le\calR_s(S,\phi)\le\calT_s(S).
\]
For $0<\eta\le1$, the useful signed statistic is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:objective}
 F_\eta(S)=\calR_s(S,\phi)-(1-\eta)\calT_s(S).
\end{equation}
Equivalently, every respected tuple contributes $\eta$ and every
unrespected tuple contributes $-(1-\eta)$.

\begin{lemma}[Surplus extraction]\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:lem:surplus}
If $F_\eta(S)\ge J>0$, then
\[
 \calR_s(S,\phi)\ge(1-\eta)\calT_s(S),\qquad
 \calT_s(S)\ge J/\eta.
\]
When $S$ is a subset of a group, not a multiset of repeated labels,
\[
 |S|\ge(J/\eta)^{1/(2s-1)}.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The first assertion is the definition of $F_\eta$. Since
$\calR_s\le\calT_s$, one also has $F_\eta\le\eta\calT_s$.
Finally, an additive $2s$-tuple is determined by its first $2s-1$ entries:
the last entry is forced in the group. Hence
$\calT_s(S)\le |S|^{2s-1}$.
\end{proof}

The positivity of a computed surplus is an exact certificate. A negative
surplus is only a failed certificate for that sampling distribution; it
is not evidence that no useful subset exists.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{An exact group-algebra inventory\srctag{48}}]{An exact group-algebra inventory}\label{gsr:en:48:sec:d3}
\srcnote{48}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:sec:inventory}

\subsection{The finite coefficient algebra}
Let $\Q[K]$ have basis symbols $[h]$, $h\in K$, with
$[h][h']=[h+h']$. Work in the finite algebra
\[
 \mathcal A_s(K)=\Q[K][u,v]/(u^{s+1},v^{s+1}).
\]
Use the divided-power basis
\[
 \dpp{u}{a}=u^a/a!,\qquad \dpp{v}{b}=v^b/b!.
\]
A coefficient array $A_{a,b}(h)$ represents
$\sum A_{a,b}(h)\dpp{u}{a}\dpp{v}{b}[h]$. Divided powers are only a convenient
basis over $\Q$; the group may have arbitrary torsion. Their multiplication
introduces the integer factors $\binom{a+c}{a}$ and $\binom{b+d}{b}$.

For one label with image $g$, define the truncated exponential
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:single-exp}
 \mathcal E_g
  =\exp(u[g]+v[-g])
  =\sum_{0\le a,b\le s}\dpp{u}{a}\dpp{v}{b}[(a-b)g].
\end{equation}
All exponentials and inverses in this section are finite formal operations
in a nilpotent ideal. There is no analytic convergence question.

\begin{definition}[Bernoulli inventory]\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:def:inventory}
Set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:inventory}
 \calI_{\boldsymbol p}
 =\prod_{i=1}^n\bigl(1+p_i(\mathcal E_{g_i}-1)\bigr)
 =\sum_{a,b,h}A_{a,b}(h)\dpp{u}{a}\dpp{v}{b}[h].
\end{equation}
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Exact coefficient identity]\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:thm:identity}
For every $0\le a,b\le s$ and $h\in K$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:identity}
 A_{a,b}(h)=\E N_{a,b}(S_{\boldsymbol p};h).
\end{equation}
In particular, $A_{s,s}(0)=\E E_s(S_{\boldsymbol p};g)$.
The assertion permits repeated entries, repeated group images, probabilities
zero or one, and arbitrary finite abelian groups.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For a deterministic subset $S$,
\[
 \prod_{i\in S}\mathcal E_{g_i}
 =\exp\left(u\sum_{i\in S}[g_i]+v\sum_{i\in S}[-g_i]\right).
\]
The coefficient of $\dpp{u}{a}\dpp{v}{b}[h]$ is
$N_{a,b}(S;h)$: expansion of the two powers lists the ordered choices of
$a$ positive and $b$ negative labels.

Let $X_i=\one_{i\in S_{\boldsymbol p}}$. Independence across labels gives
\[
 \E\prod_i\mathcal E_{g_i}^{X_i}
 =\prod_i\bigl((1-p_i)+p_i\mathcal E_{g_i}\bigr)=\calI_{\boldsymbol p}.
\]
Taking coefficients proves the identity. Alternatively, a label factor
contributes $p_i$ whenever that label occupies a nonempty collection of
positions, and contributes one otherwise, which gives
\eqref{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:support-prob} directly.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Initialization by translations, not convolution}
Multiplication of a general inventory by the factor for one label gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:init-update}
 A'_{a,b}(h)=A_{a,b}(h)+p_i
 \sum_{\substack{0\le c\le a,\ 0\le d\le b\\c+d>0}}
 \binom ac\binom bd
 A_{a-c,b-d}\bigl(h-(c-d)g_i\bigr).
\end{equation}
This is a collection of translations of lower-degree arrays. It is not a
convolution of two arbitrary arrays. Start with $A_{0,0}(0)=1$ and all
other coefficients zero, and apply \eqref{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:init-update} once per label.

\begin{lemma}[Initialization cost]\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:lem:initialization}
All coefficients of \eqref{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:inventory} can be initialized in
$O(\costfortyeight n|K|)$ rational operations with $(s+1)^2|K|$ coefficient locations.
The updates can be performed in place, in decreasing order of $a+b$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The number of quadruples $(a,b,c,d)$ with
$0\le c\le a\le s$ and $0\le d\le b\le s$ is
\[
 \left(\sum_{a=0}^s(a+1)\right)^2=\binom{s+2}{2}^{\!2}=\costfortyeight.
\]
Each nonconstant summand is a weighted translation of an array of length
$|K|$. In decreasing total degree, every source row has smaller total
degree and has not yet changed. Thus all values on the right side are old
values, exactly as required.
\end{proof}

A direct Fourier method can sometimes initialize ordinary weighted
energies more quickly. The point here is different: the same small state
will continue to give the \emph{correct} conditional expectation after
arbitrary indicators have been fixed.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Local replacement, Stirling coefficients, and bit cost\srctag{48}}]{Local replacement, Stirling coefficients, and bit cost}\label{gsr:en:48:sec:d4}
\srcnote{48}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:sec:replacement}

\subsection{A replacement that never divides by a probability}
To replace the probability of one label from $p$ to $q$, multiply the
inventory by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:ratio}
 R_{p,q}(t)=\frac{1+q(e^t-1)}{1+p(e^t-1)}
     =1+(q-p)H_p(t),\qquad
 H_p(t)=\frac{e^t-1}{1+p(e^t-1)},
\end{equation}
with $t=u[g]+v[-g]$. The denominator has constant term one even when
$p=0$ or $p=1$. This removes a common endpoint difficulty in deletion
formulas based on division by $p$ or by $1-p$.

Let $\left\{\begin{smallmatrix}k\\j\end{smallmatrix}\right\}$ denote a
Stirling number of the second kind, and write
\[
 H_p(t)=\sum_{k=1}^{2s}h_k(p)t^k/k!
 \quad\text{modulo terms of degree greater than }2s.
\]

\begin{lemma}[Explicit response polynomials]\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:lem:response}
For $k\ge1$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:response}
 h_k(p)=\sum_{j=1}^{k}(-p)^{j-1}j!
       \left\{\begin{matrix}k\\j\end{matrix}\right\}.
\end{equation}
In particular,
\[
 h_1=1,\qquad h_2=1-2p,\qquad
 h_3=1-6p+6p^2,\qquad
 h_4=1-14p+36p^2-24p^3.
\]
The degree is at most $k-1$, $h_k(0)=1$, and
$h_k(1)=(-1)^{k-1}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Expand the geometric inverse in \eqref{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:ratio}:
\[
 H_p(t)=\sum_{j\ge1}(-p)^{j-1}(e^t-1)^j.
\]
The exponential generating function for ordered partitions into $j$
nonempty blocks is
\[
 (e^t-1)^j=j!\sum_{k\ge j}
 \left\{\begin{matrix}k\\j\end{matrix}\right\}\frac{t^k}{k!}.
\]
For completeness, its coefficient counts assignments of $k$ labelled
positions to $j$ nonempty labelled boxes, which are precisely an unordered
set partition followed by an ordering of its blocks. Comparing
coefficients proves \eqref{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:response}. The endpoint $p=1$ follows
also from $H_1(t)=1-e^{-t}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact local replacement]\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:thm:replacement}
Suppose $A$ is the inventory of the current probabilities. Define
$r_0=1$ and $r_k=(q-p)h_k(p)$ for $k\ge1$. Replacing one label image $g$
from probability $p$ to probability $q$ changes the coefficients to
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:replacement}
 A'_{a,b}(h)=
 \sum_{c=0}^a\sum_{d=0}^b
 \binom ac\binom bd r_{c+d}
 A_{a-c,b-d}\bigl(h-(c-d)g\bigr).
\end{equation}
Its cost is $O(\costfortyeight|K|)$ rational operations, with an in-place descending
implementation. Moreover,
\begin{align}
 A'_{s,s}(0)&=A_{s,s}(0)+(q-p)\Delta_g,\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:probe}\\
 \Delta_g&=\sum_{\substack{0\le c,d\le s\\c+d>0}}
 \binom sc\binom sd h_{c+d}(p)
 A_{s-c,s-d}\bigl(-(c-d)g\bigr).\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:delta}
\end{align}
Thus the exact slope of the conditional expectation is obtained from
$(s+1)^2-1$ coefficient probes.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The replacement ratio in \eqref{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:ratio} cancels exactly the old
label factor and inserts the new one. After substituting
$t=u[g]+v[-g]$, the coefficient of $\dpp{u}{c}\dpp{v}{d}$ is
$r_{c+d}[(c-d)g]$. Multiplication in the divided-power basis gives
\eqref{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:replacement}. The complexity and update order follow from
the same count as Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:48:gcr:lem:initialization}. Setting $(a,b,h)=(s,s,0)$
and separating $(c,d)=(0,0)$ proves the last two identities.
\end{proof}

The response polynomials are universal: neither the group, the label,
the other probabilities, nor the source function occurs in them.
The only group operation in the formula is translation by an integer
multiple of the current image.

\subsection{Bit complexity is not hidden in an arithmetic-operation count}
\begin{proposition}[Common-denominator control]\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:prop:bits}
Suppose initially $p_i\in Q^{-1}\Z\cap[0,1]$ for an integer $Q\ge1$,
and subsequent replacements set probabilities to zero or one. A coefficient
of total degree $d=a+b$ has denominator dividing $Q^d$. The reduced
numerators and denominators in the coefficient updates have bit length
\[
 O\bigl(s(\log(n+1)+\log Q+\log(s+1))\bigr).
\]
A rational objective coefficient adds its own bit length to comparisons.
Consequently, for fixed $s$ the arithmetic bounds give polynomial bit-time
bounds in the explicit ambient sizes, $n$, $\log Q$, and the input
coefficient bit lengths.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:48:gcr:thm:identity}, each coefficient is a sum of at most
$n^d$ monomials, each a product of probabilities for at most $d$ distinct
labels. A common denominator is therefore $Q^d$.

For an intermediate summand of \eqref{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:replacement}, the lower
coefficient has degree $d-k$, where $k=c+d$ in that formula. The response
$r_k$ is a polynomial of degree at most $k$ in grid probabilities. Thus
its product with the lower coefficient still has denominator dividing
$Q^d$. The integer coefficients in $h_k$ count ordered set partitions
with signs. Their total absolute value is at most $k!2^{k-1}$: order the
$k$ elements and insert cuts between consecutive elements, an
onto representation of ordered set partitions. Binomial coefficients and
the polynomially many summands introduce at most another
$O(s\log(s+1))$ bits. This proves the stated bound.

For arbitrary rational input probabilities, one may use the least common
multiple of their denominators as $Q$. Its logarithm is at most the sum
of their denominator bit lengths, so this also gives a polynomial bound.
The statement concerns exact reduced arithmetic; it does not say that
all these operations have unit bit cost.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Deterministic signed-energy rounding\srctag{48}}]{Deterministic signed-energy rounding}\label{gsr:en:48:sec:d5}
\srcnote{48}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:sec:rounding}

The inventory records one expectation at a time, but that expectation is
for the \emph{same} random label set in all ambient groups. Thus several
inventories can be rounded together without an independence assumption
between their statistics.

\begin{theorem}[Exact signed rounding]\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:thm:rounding}
Let $F(S)=\sum_{\nu=1}^{v}c_\nu E_s(S;g^{(\nu)})$ with rational $c_\nu$,
and let $\boldsymbol p\in([0,1]\cap\Q)^n$. The following algorithm returns
$S$ with $F(S)\ge\E F(S_{\boldsymbol p})$.
Initialize the inventory in each group. For each undecided label $i$,
compute its signed derivative
\[
 \Delta_i=\sum_{\nu=1}^{v}c_\nu
 \sum_{\substack{0\le a,b\le s\\a+b>0}}
 \binom sa\binom sb h_{a+b}(p_i)
 A^{(\nu)}_{s-a,s-b}\bigl(-(a-b)g_i^{(\nu)}\bigr).
\]
Replace $p_i$ by $1$ when $\Delta_i\ge0$ and by $0$ otherwise, using the
local replacement formula to update each inventory. Return the labels
whose final probabilities equal $1$.

The cost is $O(\costfortyeight nD)$ rational operations and
$O((s+1)^2D)$ rational storage. The decision itself uses
$O((s+1)^2v)$ coefficient probes and arithmetic operations after the
universal response coefficients have been computed.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
At any stage let $J$ be the current signed expectation and let $p=p_i$.
The replacement identity gives the two conditional values
\[
 J_0=J-p\Delta_i,\qquad J_1=J+(1-p)\Delta_i.
\]
Their weighted average $(1-p)J_0+pJ_1$ equals $J$. The stated rule chooses
an endpoint no smaller than $J$. All groups use that same endpoint, so
the signed combination is genuinely evaluated on one shared subset.

The update identity preserves the exact conditional-expectation
invariant. At the last step every probability is zero or one, and the
expectation is the deterministic value $F(S)$. Induction therefore proves
the inequality. Initial probabilities zero or one are already decided
and require no branching.

Initialization and each replacement use at most a constant multiple of
$\costfortyeight D$ arithmetic operations by the preceding section. Summing over
$n$ labels gives the cost. The arrays have $(s+1)^2D$ entries. A Stirling
table through degree $2s$, the powers of $p$, and all $h_j(p)$ can be
computed in $O(s^2)$ arithmetic operations; this does not increase the
stated total. The displayed derivative uses only $(s+1)^2-1$ entries
from each group's arrays.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Constructive restriction from a supplied certificate]
\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:cor:supplied}
Let $B\subseteq G$, $\phi:B\to H$, and $0<\eta\le1$ be rational. Suppose
rational inclusion probabilities satisfy
\[
 \E\bigl[\calR_s(S,\phi)-(1-\eta)\calT_s(S)\bigr]\ge J>0.
\]
One can deterministically find $B'\subseteq B$ with
\[
 \calR_s(B',\phi)\ge(1-\eta)\calT_s(B'),\qquad
 \calT_s(B')\ge J/\eta,
\]
in $O(\costfortyeight |B|(|G|+|G||H|))$ rational operations and
$O((s+1)^2(|G|+|G||H|))$ storage.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Use two inventories, on $G$ and $G\oplus H$, with label images $x$ and
$(x,\phi(x))$, and coefficients $-(1-\eta)$ and $1$. Apply the theorem
and the surplus-to-restriction implication proved in Section~2.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What one signed objective does not imply]
A signed combination with a positive lower bound need not preserve each
of its summands separately. In particular, adding weighted Fourier or
energy statistics does not, by itself, prove several independent lower
bounds. The corollary works because one specific surplus implies both
quality and retained mass. Other simultaneous conclusions need their own
logical implication or a different potential.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Exact cardinality without a cardinality-sized state\srctag{48}}]{Exact cardinality without a cardinality-sized state}\label{gsr:en:48:sec:d6}
\srcnote{48}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:sec:fixed}

Independent rounding does not control the final size. A conventional
size-generating variable can introduce a state indexed by every possible
cardinality. Here the statistic uses only $2s$ positions, so it is enough
to record the number of \emph{distinct undecided labels used by a tuple}.
That number never exceeds $2s$, even when the desired subset is very large.

\subsection{The distinct-support inventory}
Suppose $I$ consists of already included labels and $U$ consists of
undecided labels, with $|U|=N$. Excluded labels contribute no factor. Put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:support-inventory}
 \calP_{I,U}(z)=
 \prod_{i\in I}\mathcal E_{g_i}
 \prod_{i\in U}\bigl(1+z(\mathcal E_{g_i}-1)\bigr),
 \qquad
 \mathcal E_g=\exp(u[g]+v[-g]).
\end{equation}
The exponentials are the finite truncated polynomials from Section~3.
Write $P_{a,b,j}(h)$ for the coefficient of
$u^{[a]}v^{[b]}z^j[h]$. It is a nonnegative integer counting ordered
partial tuples with difference $h$ and exactly $j$ distinct labels from
$U$; every remaining label used belongs to $I$. In particular,
$P_{a,b,j}=0$ for $j>a+b$ and for $j>N$.

For $0\le r\le N$, define a linear functional on these polynomials by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:hyper-identity}
 \calL_{N,r}(z^j)=
 \begin{cases}
  \displaystyle\frac{\binom rj}{\binom Nj}
    =\frac{(r)_j}{(N)_j},&0\le j\le r,\\[5pt]
  0,&j>r.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
The $j=0$ value is $1$, including when $N=r=0$. No denominator with
$j>N$ is used.

\begin{lemma}[Exact uniform-subset expectation]\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:lem:uniform}
If $R$ is a uniform $r$-element subset of $U$, then
\[
 \E E_s(I\cup R;g)=
 \sum_{j=0}^{2s}P_{s,s,j}(0)\calL_{N,r}(z^j).
\]
The same identity holds for every partial coefficient $(a,b,h)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A tuple using a particular $j$-element subset $J$ of $U$ survives exactly
when $J\subseteq R$. Its probability is
$\binom{N-j}{r-j}/\binom Nr=\binom rj/\binom Nj$ for $j\le r$, and zero
otherwise. Group the tuples by their distinct undecided support size.
Repeated occurrences do not add additional required labels.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Exclusion and inclusion are polynomial replacements}
For a selected undecided label with image $g$, use the formal shorthand
$t=u[g]+v[-g]$. Its old factor is $1+z(e^t-1)$. On excluding it, replace
that factor by $1$; on including it, replace it by $e^t$. Thus the two
multipliers are
\begin{align}
 R_0(t,z)&=\frac1{1+z(e^t-1)}=1-zH_z(t),\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:fixed-exclude}\\
 R_1(t,z)&=\frac{e^t}{1+z(e^t-1)}=1+(1-z)H_z(t).
 \label{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:fixed-include}
\end{align}
All inverses are finite nilpotent expansions. Their degree-$k$ divided
coefficients are respectively $-z h_k(z)$ and $(1-z)h_k(z)$, of polynomial
degree at most $k$. The constant coefficient is $1$. The translation
update from Section~4 therefore applies verbatim, now with polynomial
rather than rational entries.

\begin{theorem}[Prescribed-size signed rounding]\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:thm:fixed}
For every signed energy statistic $F$ and $0\le k\le n$, one can
construct a set $S$ of size exactly $k$ with
\[
 F(S)\ge\frac1{\binom nk}\sum_{|A|=k}F(A)
\]
in $O(\costfortyeight(2s+1)^2nD)$ rational operations and
$O((s+1)^2(2s+1)D)$ storage. The polynomial coefficient arrays themselves
can be maintained over the integers.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Start with $I=\varnothing$, $U=[n]$, and remaining quota $r=k$.
Maintain the inventory \eqref{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:support-inventory} in every group.
For one undecided label, the excluded-child expectation $J_0$ is obtained
by the $R_0$ replacement followed by $\calL_{N-1,r}$. The included-child
expectation $J_1$ uses $R_1$ followed by $\calL_{N-1,r-1}$.
These are \emph{different evaluators}; applying $\calL_{N,r}$ after both
updates would give the wrong conditional expectations.

When $0<r<N$, uniform sampling gives
\[
 J=(1-r/N)J_0+(r/N)J_1.
\]
Choose a child of maximum value. If $r=0$, only exclusion is feasible;
if $r=N$, only inclusion is feasible. In those cases the feasible
conditional value equals $J$. The update reduces $N$ by one and reduces
$r$ by one exactly when the label is included. It preserves $0\le r\le N$
and never decreases the objective. At termination, $r=N=0$, exactly $k$
labels have been included, and the conditional value is their statistic.

One may compute each child's top coefficient first, using only lower
rows of the current arrays, and then update the whole inventory for the
chosen child. No second full child inventory is necessary. Each response
and array polynomial has degree at most $2s$. Naive truncated polynomial
multiplication takes $O((2s+1)^2)$ rational operations. The translation
count is the same $\costfortyeight D$ as before. This proves the operation and
storage bounds. The response polynomials and initial arrays have integer
coefficients; rational arithmetic is needed only for evaluation and
comparison of the branch values.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Bit bounds and the two sampling laws]
An inventory coefficient counts at most $n^{a+b}$ partial tuples.
The response-polynomial coefficients are bounded by ordered-partition
counts through degree $2s$, so integer intermediate bit lengths are
$O(s(\log(n+1)+\log(s+1)))$. The ratios in
\eqref{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:hyper-identity} have $O(s\log(n+1))$ bits, and there are at
most $2s+1$ such terms per evaluation. This gives polynomial bit bounds,
including arbitrary rational signed weights.

This theorem starts from a \emph{uniform} prescribed-size subset. It does
not assert the same state size for a heterogeneous Bernoulli distribution
conditioned on its cardinality. Those distributions have different
support-inclusion probabilities; they are not interchangeable.
\end{remark}

\subsection{All sizes and several quotas}
With $I=\varnothing$ initially, let $c_j$ be the signed coefficient of
$z^j$ in the top zero-difference inventories. Then the exact profile for
all uniform subset sizes is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:fixed-profile}
 \frac1{\binom nk}\sum_{|A|=k}F(A)
   =\sum_{j=0}^{2s}c_j\frac{\binom kj}{\binom nj},
\end{equation}
where the summand is zero when $j>k$ or $j>n$. The initial profile requires
only $2s+1$ coefficients, and evaluating it at all $k$ requires $O(sn)$
arithmetic operations using successive binomial-ratio recurrences.
Producing a separately rounded set for \emph{every} $k$ can of course
require separate rounding runs; this additional output is not free.

More generally, partition the labels into $c$ specified colour classes
and prescribe one cardinality in each class. Attach a variable $z_a$ to
undecided labels in class $a$. Every tuple uses at most $2s$ distinct
labels in total, so at most $\binom{2s+c}{c}$ support monomials occur.
Uniform sampling with these quotas is independent between colour
classes, and the evaluator sends $\prod_a z_a^{j_a}$ to
\[
 \prod_a\frac{\binom{r_a}{j_a}}{\binom{N_a}{j_a}}.
\]
Branch only within the current label's colour, and use the same
conditional-average argument. For fixed $s,c$ this gives an exact
$O_{s,c}(nD)$ algorithm preserving every prescribed colour quota. This
is an exact cardinality constraint, not a general theorem about
simultaneously preserving arbitrary spectral statistics.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{General linear systems and column-type compression\srctag{48}}]{General linear systems and column-type compression}\label{gsr:en:48:sec:d7}
\srcnote{48}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:sec:systems}

\subsection{An inventory for arbitrary position-dependent increments}
Let there be $t$ labelled positions. For every input label $i$ and
position $j$, specify an increment $a_{i,j}\in K$. Define
\[
 N(S)=\#\{(i_1,\ldots,i_t)\in S^t:
                    a_{i_1,1}+\cdots+a_{i_t,t}=0\}.
\]
For example, a system $A\boldsymbol x=0$ of $d$ equations over an abelian
group $G$ uses $K=G^d$ and $a_{i,j}=A_jx_i$, where $A_j$ is column $j$.
To require a graph map to respect the same system, use
$K=(G\oplus H)^d$ and $a_{i,j}=A_j(x_i,\phi(x_i))$.

Work in the squarefree coefficient algebra
$\Q[K][z_1,\ldots,z_t]/(z_1^2,\ldots,z_t^2)$. Put
\[
 E_i=\prod_{j=1}^t(1+z_j[a_{i,j}]),\qquad
 I_{\boldsymbol p}=\prod_i(1+p_i(E_i-1)).
\]
The coefficient of $z_1\cdots z_t[0]$ is exactly $\E N(S_{\boldsymbol p})$.
Indeed, the term indexed by a subset of positions chooses all their
occurrences of one label at once, so its probability is $p_i$, not a
power of $p_i$.

\begin{theorem}[Exact system rounding]\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:thm:systems}
For a fixed number $t$ of positions, a rational signed combination of
such system counts on a common label set can be evaluated and rounded
without decreasing expectation in $O(3^t nD)$ rational operations and
$O(2^tD)$ storage. Here $D$ is the sum of the ambient group sizes of the
statistics. No nonzero-coefficient, large-characteristic, or distinct-entry
hypothesis is required.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Since the variables commute and square to zero,
$E_i=\exp(\sum_jz_j[a_{i,j}])$. Write
$a_i(U)=\sum_{j\in U}a_{i,j}$ for $U\subseteq[t]$. The same replacement
identity with $r_0=1$ and $r_k=(q-p_i)h_k(p_i)$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:system-replace}
 A'_S(h)=\sum_{U\subseteq S}r_{|U|}
                      A_{S\setminus U}(h-a_i(U)).
\end{equation}
There is no extra factorial: the coefficient of a squarefree monomial
$z_U$ in $(\sum_jz_j[a_{i,j}])^{|U|}/|U|!$ is precisely $[a_i(U)]$.
Descending subset size gives an in-place update. The number of
$(S,U)$ with $U\subseteq S\subseteq[t]$ is $3^t$, and there are $2^t$
coefficient rows. A derivative of the top coefficient requires only
$2^t-1$ probes. Apply the same signed conditional-expectation rule as in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:48:gcr:thm:rounding}.
\end{proof}

The theorem applies over composite moduli because it uses only group
addition and formal coefficient identities. A matrix coefficient may be
zero or a nonunit. Restrictions involving coefficient invertibility
belong to particular analytic existence estimates, not to this exact
counting and rounding engine.

\subsection{Identical column types reduce the exponent}
Suppose the positions split into types $1,\ldots,c$, with multiplicities
$m_1,\ldots,m_c$, and $a_{i,j}=b_{i,\tau}$ whenever position $j$ has type
$\tau$. Replace the squarefree variables by divided variables
$u_\tau^{[a_\tau]}$, $0\le a_\tau\le m_\tau$, and the label exponential by
\[
 \exp\left(\sum_{\tau=1}^c u_\tau[b_{i,\tau}]\right).
\]
A coefficient represents ordered positions within each type. The
replacement formula has a product of binomial coefficients, exactly as
in the two-type energy inventory. Its operation and storage bounds are
\begin{align}
 O\left(nD\prod_{\tau=1}^c\binom{m_\tau+2}{2}\right),
 \qquad
 O\left(D\prod_{\tau=1}^c(m_\tau+1)\right).
 \label{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:types-cost}
\end{align}
To prove the operation count, sum the number
$\prod_\tau(a_\tau+1)$ of lower multi-indices over all target
multi-indices: the sum factors as
$\prod_\tau\sum_{a=0}^{m_\tau}(a+1)$.

A balanced $2s$-tuple has two types, $+1$ and $-1$, both of multiplicity
$s$. Formula~\eqref{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:types-cost} recovers the headline bounds rather
than $3^{2s}$. In particular, at the source's order $s=8$, the inventory
has $81$ rows and the double-index translation budget is $2025$, independent
of the number of possible sixteen-tuples.

For a system over $\F_p$ of row rank $d_0$, row reduction can first replace
it by $d_0$ independent equations, leaving its zero set unchanged. With
scalar domain and codomain $\F_p^h$, the graph ambient group then has
size $p^{d_0(1+h)}$. This may still be exponentially large in an input
dimension. The result is an explicit ambient-size theorem, not a solution
to the sparse or high-dimensional representation problem.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Robust certificates and entirely rational filters\srctag{48}}]{Robust certificates and entirely rational filters}\label{gsr:en:48:sec:d8}
\srcnote{48}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:sec:rational}

\subsection{A collision-safe perturbation estimate}
The phase filters in an analytic existence proof may take irrational
values. The inventory algorithm does not need to represent these values
exactly: a quantified surplus and a rational approximation are sufficient.
The perturbation bound must again count distinct labels, not occurrences
as independent selections.

\begin{lemma}[Tuple-objective Lipschitz bound]\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:lem:lipschitz}
Let $B$ be a set of $n$ distinct group elements and $m=2s$. For the
objective $F_\eta$ of \eqref{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:objective}, $0<\eta\le1$, and two
probability vectors $\boldsymbol p,\boldsymbol q\in[0,1]^B$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:lipschitz}
 |\calJ(\boldsymbol p)-\calJ(\boldsymbol q)|
 \le m n^{m-1}\|\boldsymbol p-\boldsymbol q\|_\infty.
\end{equation}
More precisely, let $I_x$ be the number of initial additive $m$-tuples
whose distinct-entry support contains $x$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:influence}
 |\calJ(\boldsymbol p)-\calJ(\boldsymbol q)|
 \le\sum_{x\in B}I_x|p_x-q_x|,
 \qquad \sum_x I_x\le m\calT_s(B)\le mn^{m-1}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For numbers $u_1,\ldots,u_j,v_1,\ldots,v_j\in[0,1]$, a telescoping product
identity gives
\[
 \left|\prod_{r=1}^j u_r-\prod_{r=1}^j v_r\right|
       \le\sum_{r=1}^j|u_r-v_r|.
\]
Apply this to the \emph{distinct support} of each tuple. Its signed
coefficient in $F_\eta$ has absolute value at most one. Summing and
interchanging the finite sums proves the first part of
\eqref{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:influence}. Every tuple has at most $m$ distinct entries,
and its final entry is determined by the preceding $m-1$, which gives
the remaining bounds.
\end{proof}

The refined influence form permits nonuniform precision: high-influence
points must be approximated more accurately. The influences themselves
are accessible from the derivative formula applied to the unsigned domain
energy at the all-one probability vector. This gives an exact, optional
precision-allocation certificate rather than an unproved heuristic.

\begin{corollary}[Finite-family certificate]\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:cor:family}
Let $\Theta$ be a finite family of probability vectors. Suppose its exact
mean surplus is at least $J_0$, and rational vectors
$\widetilde{\boldsymbol p}^{\theta}$ satisfy
$\|\widetilde{\boldsymbol p}^{\theta}-\boldsymbol p^{\theta}\|_\infty
\le\varepsilon$ for every $\theta$. Searching the rational family and
rounding its best member returns a set with
\[
 F_\eta(S)\ge J_0-mn^{m-1}\varepsilon.
\]
The cost after constructing the rational family is
$O(\costfortyeight nD(|\Theta|+1))$ rational operations, with streaming storage
$O((s+1)^2D+n)$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The rational-family average is at least the claimed lower bound by
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:48:gcr:lem:lipschitz}. Its maximum is at least its average.
Evaluate every member with the inventory, retain its parameters if best,
and apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:48:gcr:thm:rounding} to that member. Only the best
parameters and its probability vector need be kept.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A certified rational Fej\'er table}
For $L\ge2$ define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:fejer}
 K_L(t)=\frac1{L^2}\left|\sum_{j=0}^{L-1}e^{2\pi ijt}\right|^2
 =\frac{L+2\sum_{j=1}^{L-1}(L-j)\cos(2\pi jt)}{L^2}.
\end{equation}
The first expression shows $0\le K_L\le1$.

\begin{lemma}[Rational probability table]\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:lem:kernel}
Given integers $p,L\ge2$ and $Q\ge1$, an explicitly computable table
$q_0,\ldots,q_{p-1}\in Q^{-1}\Z\cap[0,1]$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:kernel-approx}
 0\le K_L(t/p)-q_t<2/Q\qquad(0\le t<p).
\end{equation}
It can be constructed using exact rational arithmetic and certified
finite-series bounds. Its construction is polynomial in $p,L,\log(Q+1)$
in the bit model. No numerical sign oracle is required.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Put $\varepsilon=1/(16Q)$. First enclose $\pi$ in a rational interval
of width at most $\varepsilon$. One entirely elementary construction uses
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:machin}
 \pi=16\arctan(1/5)-4\arctan(1/239).
\end{equation}
For $0<x<1$, the alternating partial sums of
$\sum_{j\ge0}(-1)^j x^{2j+1}/(2j+1)$ enclose $\arctan x$, with error
bounded by the first omitted term. This follows also by integrating the
finite geometric identity for $(1+x^2)^{-1}$. Thus $O(\log(Q+1))$ terms
suffice for \eqref{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:machin}. The identity itself follows from the
tangent addition formula: for $A=\arctan(1/5)$ and
$B=\arctan(1/239)$, $\tan(4A)=120/119$ and $\tan(4A-B)=1$; the angles
locate $4A-B$ in $(0,\pi/2)$.

For each residue $r$, choose $|r|\le p/2$. Evaluate the cosine Taylor
polynomial at $2r\pi_0/p$, where $\pi_0$ is the interval midpoint, until
the Lagrange remainder is at most $\varepsilon$. Its argument has
absolute value less than $4$, so $O(\log(Q+1))$ terms are enough.
The uncertainty in the argument contributes at most
$\varepsilon/2$, since cosine is $1$-Lipschitz. We obtain rational cosine
intervals of width at most $3\varepsilon$.

Use those intervals in the second expression of \eqref{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:fejer}.
The nonconstant weights have total mass
$2\sum_{j=1}^{L-1}(L-j)/L^2=(L-1)/L<1$, so the resulting kernel interval
has width at most $3\varepsilon$. Intersect it with $[0,1]$, obtaining
$[\ell_t,u_t]$, and put $q_t=\lfloor Q\ell_t\rfloor/Q$.
Then $q_t\le K_L(t/p)$ and
\[
 K_L(t/p)-q_t<3/(16Q)+1/Q<2/Q.
\]
The value at $t=0$ may be set exactly to one.

The numbers of series terms are logarithmic in $Q+1$, and their rational
numerators, denominators and factorials have polynomial bit lengths in
$\log p$ and $\log(Q+1)$. The final table uses $O(pL)$ rational weighted
additions after the $p$ cosine intervals are prepared. This proves the
claimed bit-time statement.
\end{proof}

The supplied implementation uses this construction. Its numerical
cosine comparison in the test suite is supplementary: the certificate
comes from the rational interval and the proved remainder bounds.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A deterministic polynomial-loss restriction theorem\srctag{48}}]{A deterministic polynomial-loss restriction theorem}\label{gsr:en:48:sec:d9}
\srcnote{48}{Section 9}
\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:sec:source}

\subsection{Statement and inherited quantitative ingredient}
The following theorem is the precise constructive strengthening of the
companion's Fej\'er restriction bound. The source is Gowers's
Lemma~9.3~\cite{gowers}; the polynomial-retention estimate and translated
Fej\'er filter were established in the inspected companion
manuscript~\cite{repo48companion}. We include their short argument so that the
algorithmic conclusion does not rest on an unchecked black box.

\begin{theorem}[Fully rational constructive restriction]
\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:thm:source}
Let $m=2s\ge4$, $p$ be prime, $B\subseteq\F_p$ have size
$n=\beta p>0$, and $\phi:B\to\F_p$. Let rational
$\alpha,\eta\in(0,1]$ satisfy
\[
 \calR_s(B,\phi)\ge\alpha n^{m-1}.
\]
Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:source-params}
 L=\left\lceil\frac{m+1}{\alpha\eta}\right\rceil,
 \qquad d=\alpha+\eta-\alpha\eta,
 \qquad Q=\left\lceil\frac{4mL^m}{d}\right\rceil.
\end{equation}
Assume \eqref{gsr:fm:48:gcr:eq:intro-threshold}. A deterministic algorithm with
only rational probability arithmetic returns $B'\subseteq B$ satisfying
\eqref{gsr:fm:48:gcr:eq:intro-quality}--\eqref{gsr:fm:48:gcr:eq:intro-retention}.

Excluding the separately described rational-kernel precomputation, the
complete algorithm uses $O(\costfortyeight n p^5)$ rational operations and
$O((s+1)^2p^2+n)$ storage. Once a filter parameter triple is supplied,
exact evaluation and rounding use $O(\costfortyeight np^2)$ operations. All these
operations have polynomial bit cost in the explicit ambient model.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 47--53]
\emph{Against the formal statement} (checked at HEAD \texttt{06b30ca52}). \file{lemma_9_3} (\file{Sections08\_09.lean}, line~77) has the exact companion \file{lemma_9_3_holds} (\file{Proofs09Restriction.lean}, line~376), an existence theorem; source~17's theorem implies its prime case with an explicit threshold (note in source~17's chapter), and this theorem makes that case constructive with the same constants. The algorithm and its complexity are not formalized.
\end{writenote}

The complete algorithm first searches $p^3$ phase triples; the smaller
rounding bound is not a bound for that search. For fixed $s$ and $n\le p$,
the complete arithmetic bound is $O_s(p^6)$. It is a substantial reduction
from listing the source's additive sixteen-tuples, but not a practical
claim for the very large $p$ required by the worst-case analytic threshold.

\subsection{Signal of the filter}
The Fourier expansion of \eqref{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:fejer} is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:fejer-fourier}
 K_L(t)=\frac1L\sum_{a=-(L-1)}^{L-1}
            \left(1-\frac{|a|}{L}\right)e^{2\pi iat}.
\end{equation}
Set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:signal}
 S_{m,L}=1+2\sum_{j=1}^{L-1}(j/L)^m.
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}[Signal bounds]\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:lem:signal}
For $m\ge2$,
\[
 \frac{2L}{m+1}\le S_{m,L}\le L.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For the lower bound, the trapezoidal rule for the convex function
$f(x)=(1-x/L)^m$ on $[0,L]$ gives
\[
 \tfrac12 f(0)+\sum_{j=1}^{L-1}f(j)+\tfrac12 f(L)
       \ge\int_0^L f(x)\,dx=L/(m+1).
\]
Twice the left side is $S_{m,L}$. For the upper bound, sum $u^m\le u$
over the triangular coefficients in \eqref{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:fejer-fourier}.
Their sum is $L$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Exceptional tuples and their exact role}
Let $\epsilon=(1,\ldots,1,-1,\ldots,-1)\in\F_p^m$ with $s$ entries of
each sign. An additive tuple $x\in\F_p^m$ is called exceptional when
there exists an integer vector
$a\in[-L+1,L-1]^m$ such that
\[
 \sum_j a_j=0\pmod p,\qquad \sum_j a_jx_j=0,
 \qquad a\bmod p\notin\Span(\epsilon).
\]

\begin{lemma}[Exceptional count]\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:lem:exceptional}
There are at most
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:exceptional}
 D_0=(2L-1)^{m-1}p^{m-2}
\end{equation}
exceptional additive tuples. Every nonexceptional tuple has distinct
entries. If a vector in the indicated integer box reduces to a multiple
of $\epsilon$, it is exactly $t\epsilon$ as an integer vector, with
$|t|\le L-1$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
After choosing the first $m-1$ coefficients, the last is determined modulo
$p$ by their sum. The permitted interval contains at most one representative
because $p>2L-2$. Thus there are at most $(2L-1)^{m-1}$ coefficient
vectors. For a vector outside $\Span(\epsilon)$, the equations with rows
$a$ and $\epsilon$ are independent over $\F_p$, so have $p^{m-2}$
solutions. A union bound proves \eqref{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:exceptional}.

If $x_i=x_j$, the vector $e_i-e_j$ witnesses exceptionality: it is in the
coefficient box, its sum is zero, and it cannot be a multiple of
$\epsilon$ because $m\ge4$. Finally, if $a\equiv t\epsilon\pmod p$,
choose $t=a_1$. Each integer $a_j-\epsilon_jt$ is divisible by $p$ and
has absolute value at most $2L-2<p$, hence vanishes.
\end{proof}

Choose $u,v,c$ uniformly in $\F_p$, and, conditioned on the triple, include
$x\in B$ independently with probability
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:phase-prob}
 p_x^{u,v,c}=K_L\bigl((ux+v\phi(x)+c)/p\bigr).
\end{equation}
The numerator denotes its residue class, so the expression is independent
of the chosen lift.

\begin{lemma}[Generic survival]\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:lem:survival}
A nonexceptional additive tuple is selected with unconditional probability
$L^{-m}S_{m,L}$ if it is respected, and $L^{-m}$ otherwise.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The entries are distinct, so conditional independence gives a product of
$m$ filter values. Expand them by \eqref{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:fejer-fourier}. Averaging
over $u,v,c$ leaves exactly the coefficient vectors satisfying
\[
 \sum a_jx_j=0,\qquad \sum a_j\phi(x_j)=0,\qquad \sum a_j=0.
\]
By nonexceptionality and Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:48:gcr:lem:exceptional}, these vectors are
$t\epsilon$, $|t|\le L-1$. If the tuple is respected, all such $t$
survive, giving $L^{-m}S_{m,L}$. Otherwise only $t=0$ survives: a nonzero
$t$ in that interval cannot annihilate a nonzero scalar discrepancy in
$\F_p$. The coefficient for $t=0$ is $L^{-m}$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A surplus with enough slack for rationalization}
Put $T=\calT_s(B)$, $R=\calR_s(B,\phi)$, and $a=L^{-m}$.
Exceptional tuples may be repeated; they are not silently assigned the
generic survival probabilities. Let $D_R,D_B$ be the numbers of respected
and unrespected exceptional tuples in $B$. Their sum is at most $D_0$.
The generic-survival lemma and the bound of one on all survival
probabilities give
\begin{align}
 \E F_\eta
 &\ge\eta aS_{m,L}(R-D_R)
       -(1-\eta)a(T-R)-(1-\eta)D_B\notag\\
 &\ge a\bigl[\eta S_{m,L}R-(1-\eta)(T-R)\bigr]-D_0.
 \label{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:source-surplus}
\end{align}
The last inequality uses $aS_{m,L}\le1$.

Let $M=n^{m-1}$. We have $T\le M$, $R\ge\alpha M$, and
$\alpha\eta S_{m,L}\ge2$ by the choice of $L$. Consequently,
\begin{align}
 a[\eta S_{m,L}R-(1-\eta)(T-R)]
 &\ge a[\alpha\eta S_{m,L}-(1-\eta)(1-\alpha)]M\notag\\
 &\ge(1+d)aM,\qquad d=\alpha+\eta-\alpha\eta>0.
 \label{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:slack}
\end{align}
The size assumption is exactly a sufficient condition for
$D_0\le aM/2$. Thus
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:slack-surplus}
 \E_{u,v,c}\calJ(\boldsymbol p^{u,v,c})
    \ge(\tfrac12+d)L^{-m}M.
\end{equation}
Keeping $d$ instead of discarding it is useful: it pays for a rational
filter approximation without weakening the existing retention constant.

\subsection{Proof of the constructive theorem}
Construct the rational kernel table of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:48:gcr:lem:kernel} with
$Q$ from \eqref{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:source-params}. Replace every probability in
\eqref{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:phase-prob} by the corresponding table entry. Uniformly over
all triples,
\[
 \|\widetilde{\boldsymbol p}^{u,v,c}-\boldsymbol p^{u,v,c}\|_\infty
       <2/Q\le\frac{d}{2mL^m}.
\]
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:48:gcr:lem:lipschitz} and \eqref{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:slack-surplus} imply
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:rational-surplus}
 \E_{u,v,c}\calJ(\widetilde{\boldsymbol p}^{u,v,c})
    \ge(\tfrac12+\tfrac d2)L^{-m}M
    \ge M/(2L^m).
\end{equation}
Search all $p^3$ triples, evaluating their rational objectives with the
domain and graph inventories. Keep one attaining the largest value.
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:48:gcr:thm:rounding} produces a deterministic subset with
$F_\eta(B')\ge M/(2L^m)$. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:48:gcr:lem:surplus} proves
\eqref{gsr:fm:48:gcr:eq:intro-quality} and the first bound of
\eqref{gsr:fm:48:gcr:eq:intro-retention}. Since
$L\le(m+2)/(\alpha\eta)$, its second bound follows.

For one triple, the total group size is $p+p^2$ and initialization costs
$O(\costfortyeight n(p+p^2))$. Multiplication by $p^3$ and one final rounding gives
$O(\costfortyeight np^5)$. Streaming gives the stated storage. All rational
probabilities have common denominator $Q$, so
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:48:gcr:prop:bits} applies. Kernel precomputation is polynomial
by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:48:gcr:lem:kernel}; under the hypothesis $L<(p+2)/2$, its
$O(pL)$ table stage is also polynomial in the ambient size. This completes
the proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:48:gcr:thm:source}.

\subsection{An explicit search--threshold tradeoff}
\begin{corollary}[Two phase parameters]\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:cor:unshifted}
The same retention conclusion and rational denominator $Q$ are obtained
by searching only $(u,v)\in\F_p^2$, setting $c=0$, provided the size
hypothesis is replaced by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:unshifted-threshold}
 p>2L-2,\qquad
 p\ge2L^m(2L-1)^m\beta^{-(m-1)}.
\end{equation}
The arithmetic cost is then $O(\costfortyeight np^4)$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Define exceptionality without the coefficient-sum condition.
There are at most $(2L-1)^m$ possible coefficient vectors; the same
rank-two count gives exceptional mass at most
$(2L-1)^mp^{m-2}$. Nonexceptional tuples still have distinct entries and
the same principal-line classification. Averaging over $u,v$ now imposes
only the domain and image equations, and the generic survival
probabilities are unchanged. The larger threshold makes the new
exceptional bound at most $M/(2L^m)$. Repeat
\eqref{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:slack}--\eqref{gsr:en:48:gcr:eq:rational-surplus}. There are now $p^2$
parameter choices instead of $p^3$.
\end{proof}

This tradeoff is not simultaneously a better density threshold and a
faster search: it saves one factor $p$ in search at the cost of one factor
$2L-1$ in the sufficient ambient-size threshold.

\subsection{Exact data can outperform the worst-case certificate}
For a concrete rational kernel table, the algorithm computes
\[
 \max_{u,v,c}\calJ(\widetilde{\boldsymbol p}^{u,v,c})
 \quad\text{and, optionally,}\quad
 p^{-3}\sum_{u,v,c}\calJ(\widetilde{\boldsymbol p}^{u,v,c})
\]
exactly, including every degenerate tuple. A positive maximum is sufficient
even when \eqref{gsr:fm:48:gcr:eq:intro-threshold} fails spectacularly. The threshold
is a uniform sufficient condition, not a prerequisite for running the
algorithm. No separate enumeration of the exceptional set is required
for this exact-data certificate.

The same exact evaluation supports finite searches over $L$, $\eta$, or a
user-specified rational kernel family, as long as their costs are counted.
This implements a finite optimization procedure; it is not a proof that
Fej\'er kernels or the chosen grid are globally optimal filters.

\gsrnewfloats

\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the ninth write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next twenty-four sections are source~53's Sections~2--8, source~51's Sections~2--10 and source~52's Sections~2--9. They open this report's first chapter on Gowers's Section~13, the extraction of a bilinear square from the eight-arrangement data (Stages~13.4--13.9 and Corollary~13.10), \emph{as encoded in the repository}: all three study the Lean statements, not the paper's estimates. They are Report279--281 of the series of sources~26, 32, 41 and~42 and do not cite one another. Their introductions are Sections~\ref{gsr:fm:53:sec:d1}, \ref{gsr:fm:51:sec:d1} and~\ref{gsr:fm:52:sec:d1}; their questions, verification notes and source maps are in Part~V.

\emph{What source~53 proves (the spine).} For $0<a_0\le1$ put $N_0(a_0)=\lceil(8/c(a_0))^{1/\gamma(a_0)}\rceil$ with $c=\zeta_{13}/2$ and $\gamma(a)=2^{-386}a^{1856}2^{-13Q(a)}$, the formal \file{section13SquareExponent}. For every prime $N\ge N_0(a_0)$ and every Section~13 context of actual density $a\ge a_0$ there are proper progressions $V,W$ of the same nonzero step and length $k\ge D(a)N^{4\gamma(a)}-1\ge N^{3\gamma(a)}$, $D(a)>1/2$, and $B\subseteq A\cap(V\times W)$ of mass at least $2^{-137}a^{704}k^2$ on which the original phase is bilinear (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:53:thm:main}). Seven sufficient budgets collapse exactly to the seventh (Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:53:prop:collapse}); the short Stage~13.6 witness ($\len R\in\{m,m+1\}$) is recovered from the construction itself, not from its exported type (Section~\ref{gsr:en:53:sec:d6}); rectification inside a short parent, balanced aligned parents and an endpoint-contained cover give the side $\lceil L/2\rceil^{g}-1$ (Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:53:prop:geometry}). The analytic inputs are imported, explicitly, as proved Lean theorems at the pin. The threshold is sufficient, not optimal.

\emph{What source~51 proves.} For every large prime $N$ there are a genuine context of varying density $\alpha=\lfloor N/8\rfloor/N$, complete Stage~13.4--13.5 data, all six budgets of the budget-qualified extraction theorem and Stage~13.6--13.9 data with $\len R\le\len Q$, whose retained set $S\times U$ has $(S-S)\cap(U-U)=\{0\}$: no common-step square of side two, so the grid predicate \file{Corollary1310Grid} fails for these witnesses (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:51:thm:main}). This refutes a universal implication from retained data, not existential extraction or \file{corollary_13_10}, as source~51 says. \emph{What source~52 proves.} The two all-moduli encodings preserved in the repository, \file{lemma_13_7_without_domain} and \file{lemma_13_7_without_prime_assumption}, are false: over $N=2^k$, $k=939\cdot2^{1892}+5$, the even residues $T=\{2j:j<N/16\}$ carry the order-eight Freiman map $2j\mapsto j$, which every ambient affine map meets in at most one point, so the Stage~13.7 length and mass requirements are incompatible (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:52:thm:base}); variants add genuine Stage~13.4 data, unit input steps, and (with a non-unit step) all six numerical budgets with $R\subseteq Q$ (Theorems~\ref{gsr:fm:52:thm:strengthening}, \ref{gsr:en:52:thm:budgets}); the mechanism persists over every fixed prime-power family (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:52:thm:primepower}). The prime-corrected \file{lemma_13_7} is untouched, and the combination of a unit step with the full package is left open, as source~52 says.

\section[{The context and the quantifiers\srctag{53}}]{The context and the quantifiers}\label{gsr:en:53:sec:d2}\label{gsr:en:53:sec:context}
\srcnote{53}{Section 2}
A progression $P=P(x,d;L)$ in $\F_N$ is the indexed sequence $x+jd$ for $0\le j<L$. Its carrier is denoted by $P$ when no confusion is possible, and its length is $\len P=L$. It is proper if the indexing is injective; then $|P|=\len P$. A common-step square means the product of two proper equal-length progressions whose steps agree and are nonzero. Their starting points need not agree.

A map is order-eight Freiman on a set if it preserves equality between sums of eight elements, with repetitions allowed. A function $\phi:\F_N^2\to\F_N$ is separately order-eight Freiman on $A$ when each horizontal and vertical restriction has this property on the corresponding section of $A$.

An eight-arrangement at height $h$ consists of sixteen horizontal coordinates $x_i$ and sixteen vertical coordinates $y_i$ such that
\[
 \sum_{i=1}^{8}x_i=\sum_{i=9}^{16}x_i,
 \qquad (x_i,y_i),(x_i,y_i+h)\in A\quad(1\le i\le16).
\]
It is respected by $\phi$ if the same equality of sums holds for the sixteen values $\phi(x_i,y_i+h)-\phi(x_i,y_i)$. Let $C(h)$ count all these arrangements, and let $C_\phi(h)$ count the respected ones. These are ordinary finite counts, without normalization.

\begin{definition}[Section 13 context]
The context consists of $A\subseteq\F_N^2$, a function $\phi:\F_N^2\to\F_N$, and $a\in(0,1]$, with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:53:eq:context}
 |A|=aN^2,\qquad
 (1-2^{-44})\sum_h C(h)\le\sum_h C_\phi(h),
\end{equation}
and the separate order-eight Freiman property. These are exactly the hypotheses of the source record \codefiftythree{Section13Context}; the auxiliary parameter $\eta$ is fixed there to $2^{-44}$.
\end{definition}
The actual density is $a=|A|/N^2$ and may vary with $N$. Bilinearity in the conclusion means \eqref{gsr:fm:53:eq:bilinear} on $B$; it does not assert equality with $\phi$ everywhere on $V\times W$.

\subsection{Why the uniform order of quantifiers matters}
The older fixed-exact-density statement has the form: for every fixed $a>0$, there is $N_0(a)$ such that the conclusion holds whenever $|A|=aN^2$ and $N\ge N_0(a)$ is prime. Taken only as an exported statement, it can be eventually vacuous for each fixed $0<a<1$. If $a$ is irrational, the cardinality identity is impossible. If $a=r/s$ in lowest terms with $0<r<s$, it forces $s\mid N^2$; for prime $N$, this requires $s=N$ or $s=N^2$, and hence permits at most one prime. This observation neither disproves the fixed-density theorem nor invalidates its constructive proof.

The newer uniform source theorem and Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:53:thm:main} have the nonvacuous order
\[
 \forall a_0\in(0,1]\ \exists N_0(a_0)\
 \forall N\text{ prime}\ \forall(A,\phi,a),\quad
 a_0\le a\le1,\ N\ge N_0(a_0)\Longrightarrow\text{conclusion}.
\]
The old quantifier issue is therefore not a remaining defect in the pinned uniform source theorem. No threshold here is obtained by substituting the varying density into a pointwise existential statement.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Scalar parameters and imported analytic inputs\srctag{53}}]{Scalar parameters and imported analytic inputs}\label{gsr:en:53:sec:d3}\label{gsr:en:53:sec:inputs}
\srcnote{53}{Section 3}
The Section 10 cutoff and the Stage 13.4 scalar bounds are
\begin{align}
 \theta(a)&=2^{-59}a^{176},\label{gsr:en:53:eq:theta}\\
 t(a)&=2^{-1882}\theta(a)^{10477}
       =2^{-620025}a^{1843952},\label{gsr:en:53:eq:t}\\
 b(a)&=2^{1882}\theta(a)^{-10479}
       =2^{620143}a^{-1844304}.\label{gsr:en:53:eq:b}
\end{align}
Also put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:53:eq:Wz}
 W(a)=2^{135}a^{-704},\quad
 \kappa(a)=\lceil K(a)\rceil,\quad
 z(a)=\frac{2^{-155\kappa(a)}(a^{32}/16)^{18\kappa(a)}}{\kappa(a)}.
\end{equation}
Thus $z$ includes both the source's natural ceiling and division by that integer. In particular $z$ is not being replaced by an unrounded radius.

\subsection{Monotonicity and the relative exponent margin}
On any interval $[a_0,1]$, the functions $\theta,t,c,\beta,f,g,z,\gamma$ are nondecreasing, while $b,W,K,Q$ are nonincreasing. The explicit powers prove most assertions immediately. For $c$, increasing $a$ decreases $K$, increases $2^{-228K}$, and increases $a^{576K}$: the base increases while the positive exponent decreases and the base is at most one. For $z$, $\kappa$ decreases, so all three factors $2^{-155\kappa}$, $(a^{32}/16)^{18\kappa}$ and $1/\kappa$ increase. This reasoning does not require continuity of a ceiling-dependent function. The pinned parameter files supply these same monotonicity results.

We shall use
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:53:eq:monobounds}
 0<c(a)\le\tfrac12,\quad 0<2\beta(a)\le1,\quad
 0<f(a),g(a)\le1.
\end{equation}
For an actual positive integer spectrum count $j\le b(a)$, write
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:53:eq:uvw}
 u(a,j)=\frac{t(a)^2}{16j},\qquad
 v(j)=2^{-12j},\qquad w(j)=2^{-11j}.
\end{equation}
The letter $j$ is the actual integer count. It is distinct from the much larger real function $Q(a)$ in \eqref{gsr:fm:53:eq:KQ}.

\begin{lemma}[Uniform relative margin]\label{gsr:en:53:lem:margin}
For every $0<a\le1$ and $1\le j\le b(a)$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:53:eq:margin}
 2\beta(a)<u(a,j)v(j)\le u(a,j)w(j).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The explicit expressions give $b(a)<Q(a)/2$ and
$t(a)b(a)=\theta(a)^{-2}\ge1$. Thus, putting $Q=Q(a)$,
\[
 u\ge\frac1{16b(a)^3}\ge\frac1{2Q^3},\qquad
 v\ge2^{-6Q}.
\]
For $Q\ge2$, the elementary inequality $4Q^3<2^{7Q}$ implies
$2\cdot2^{-13Q}<2^{-6Q}/(2Q^3)\le uv$.
For example $Q\le2^Q$ for $Q\ge1$ gives $4Q^3\le2^{2+3Q}<2^{7Q}$ for $Q\ge2$. Finally $v\le w$. This is also the source's proved factor-two recurrence margin.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The analytic interface used in the proof}
We import the following source results. They are not reproved by the companion diagnostics. The source files and declarations are identified in Appendix~\ref{gsr:fz:53:app:sources}.

\paragraph{Initial progression and recurrence.}
For a context and the admissible cutoff $\theta(a)$, Stage 13.4 constructs a positive integer $j\le b(a)$ and a proper nonzero-step progression $P$. With
\[
 x=\frac{t(a)}{64\pi}N^{u(a,j)},\qquad p=\lfloor x\rfloor,
\]
one has $\len P=p$ or $\len P=p-1$, together with the full spectral and weighted-height conditions of Stage 13.4. For an odd prime $N$, Stage 13.5 then constructs the genuine progression $Q_{\mathrm{st}}\subseteq P$ and its spectral recurrence data if
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:53:eq:recurrenceconditions}
 T_2(j)<\len P,\qquad
 8\le(\len P)^{v(j)},\qquad
 160+2a^{32}\le a^{32}(\len P)^{v(j)}.
\end{equation}
The exact simultaneous quadratic threshold is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:53:eq:T2}
 T_2(j)=2^{(1+2^{321})2^{11(j-1)}}\qquad(j\ge1).
\end{equation}
It is an integer and is increasing in $j$. The Stage 13.5 output is proper with nonzero step, has
$\len Q_{\mathrm{st}}\ge(\len P)^{v(j)}/2$, and has the required recurrence error $(\len P)^{-w(j)}$. These assertions summarize the numerical interface, not replacements for the other stage conditions; the imported theorem supplies all of those conditions.

\paragraph{All-density Stage 13.6.}
For those genuine stages, and an integer $m$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:53:eq:integerbudgets}
 \begin{gathered}
 1\le m,\quad m^2\le N,\quad m+1\le\len Q_{\mathrm{st}},\quad
 c(a)N^{\beta(a)}\le m,\\
 (\len P)^{-w(j)}\le z(a)/m,
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
the all-density constructor produces genuine Stage 13.6 data with a proper progression $R$, nonzero step $\stfiftythree R=\stfiftythree Q_{\mathrm{st}}$, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:53:eq:Rbounds}
 c(a)N^{\beta(a)}\le\len R\le\len Q_{\mathrm{st}}.
\end{equation}
There is no hypothesis $a\le1/6$. Moreover its actual construction may retain
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:53:eq:Rshort}
 \len R=m\quad\hbox{or}\quad\len R=m+1.
\end{equation}
This last assertion is a strengthened existential selection, verified from the same witness construction in Section~\ref{gsr:en:53:sec:shortwitness}. It is not inferred for every witness satisfying only \eqref{gsr:en:53:eq:Rbounds}.

\paragraph{Rows and coefficients.}
Stage 13.7 constructs a proper nonzero-step progression $S\subseteq R$ of length
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:53:eq:Sbound}
 L=\len S\ge(\len R)^{f(a)}.
\end{equation}
If $L\ge W(a)$, Stage 13.8 supplies $C\subseteq A$, a set of heights $J_0\subseteq Q_{\mathrm{st}}$, an offset $y$, and scalar order-eight Freiman maps $A_c,B_c$ on $J_0$ such that, with $\delta=2^{-135}a^{704}$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:53:eq:coeffdata}
 \begin{gathered}
 C\subseteq S\times(J_0+y),\qquad |C|\ge\delta L\len Q_{\mathrm{st}},\\
 \phi(x,z)=A_c(z-y)+B_c(z-y)x\qquad((x,z)\in C).
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
The scalar Freiman assertions follow by projecting the coefficient pair in the exact Stage 13.8 predicate. These results are valid on the full density range.

The further all-scale coefficient-localization theorem will be stated precisely in Section~\ref{gsr:en:53:sec:geometry}. It is the only analytic ingredient within the geometric argument there.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Seven sufficient quantitative budgets\srctag{53}}]{Seven sufficient quantitative budgets}\label{gsr:en:53:sec:d4}\label{gsr:en:53:sec:seven}
\srcnote{53}{Section 4}
Fix $a_0\in(0,1]$. A subscript zero on a scalar function means evaluation at $a_0$. Define the fixed quantities
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:53:eq:fixed}
 q=\lfloor b_0\rfloor,\quad d_0=\frac{t_0}{64\pi},\quad d=d_0/2,
 \quad u_0=\frac{t_0^2}{16q},\quad v_0=2^{-12q}.
\end{equation}
Here $q\ge1$, $0<d<1$, and $u_0,v_0>0$. Every actual integer count $j\le b(a)$ satisfies $j\le q$, so $u(a,j)\ge u_0$ and $v(j)\ge v_0$.

Put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:53:eq:HLX}
 \begin{split}
 H&=\max\{8,\lceil160a_0^{-32}+2\rceil\},\\
 L_*&=\max\{T_2(q)+1,\lceil H^{1/v_0}\rceil\},\\
 X_*&=\max\{8,W_0,4\cdot8^{1/g_0}\}.
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
Both $H$ and $L_*$ are natural numbers. The separate $+1$ in $T_2(q)+1$ preserves the strict recurrence requirement.

Consider seven positive real thresholds:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:53:eq:seven}
 \begin{array}{ll}
 R_1=3,&R_2=((L_*+2)/d_0)^{1/u_0},\\[3pt]
 R_3=(1/c_0)^{1/\beta_0},&R_4=(4/d)^{1/\beta_0},\\[3pt]
 R_5=(1/(z_0d))^{1/\beta_0},&
 R_6=(X_*^{1/f_0}/c_0)^{1/\beta_0},\\[3pt]
 R_7=(8/c_0)^{1/\gamma_0}.&
 \end{array}
\end{equation}
Their dependence is solely on $a_0$. We first explain all seven budgets, before proving in Section~\ref{gsr:en:53:sec:collapse} that $R_7$ strictly dominates the others.

\begin{proposition}[Constructive consequences of the seven budgets]\label{gsr:en:53:prop:budgets}
If $N$ is prime and $N\ge\max_i R_i$, then every context with $a_0\le a\le1$ admits genuine Stages 13.4--13.8 satisfying \eqref{gsr:en:53:eq:coeffdata}. They may be selected with the short-parent alternative \eqref{gsr:en:53:eq:Rshort}, and they satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:53:eq:shortscales}
 2(\len R-1)<N,\qquad
 L\ge(\len R)^{f(a)}\ge\bigl(c(a)N^{\beta(a)}\bigr)^{f(a)}\ge X_*\ge W(a).
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Use the imported Stage 13.4 constructor, and abbreviate $u=u(a,j)$, $v=v(j)$, $w=w(j)$. Since $N\ge R_1$, the prime is odd. Since $N\ge R_2$,
\[
 x=\frac{t(a)}{64\pi}N^u\ge d_0N^{u_0}\ge L_*+2.
\]
The floor and optional predecessor each lose at most one unit, so
$\len P>x-2\ge L_*$; in particular $\len P\ge L_*$. Thus
\[
 T_2(j)\le T_2(q)<\len P,\qquad
 (\len P)^v\ge(\len P)^{v_0}\ge H.
\]
Because $H\ge160a_0^{-32}+2\ge160a^{-32}+2$, all three conditions in \eqref{gsr:en:53:eq:recurrenceconditions} follow. Apply the Stage 13.5 constructor.

For later use the same budget gives the stronger fixed-coefficient statement
\[
 d_0N^u\ge d_0N^{u_0}\ge L_*+2\ge4.
\]
Hence the two units of rounding loss imply
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:53:eq:Pbound}
 \len P\ge(d_0/2)N^u=dN^u.
\end{equation}
It matters here that the smaller fixed coefficient $d_0$ itself has the lower bound four, not merely the actual pre-floor quantity $x$.

Set $A_*=c(a)N^{\beta(a)}$ and $m=\lceil A_*\rceil$. The third threshold gives $A_*\ge c_0N^{\beta_0}\ge1$. Since $c(a)\le1/2$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:53:eq:mceil}
 1\le m\le A_*+1\le2A_*\le N^{\beta(a)},\qquad
 m^2\le N^{2\beta(a)}\le N.
\end{equation}
For either $s=v$ or $s=w$, \eqref{gsr:en:53:eq:Pbound}, $0<d<1$, $s\le1$, and Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:53:lem:margin} give
\[
 (\len P)^s\ge d^sN^{us}\ge dN^{2\beta(a)}.
\]
The fourth threshold implies $dN^{\beta(a)}\ge4$, whence
\[
 \len Q_{\mathrm{st}}\ge\tfrac12(\len P)^v
 \ge2N^{\beta(a)}\ge m+1.
\]
The fifth implies $z(a)dN^{\beta(a)}\ge1$, whence
$z(a)(\len P)^w\ge N^{\beta(a)}\ge m$, equivalently the last condition in \eqref{gsr:en:53:eq:integerbudgets}. Every integer and Bohr budget is now verified. Use the all-density constructor with this $m$, retaining its actual length alternative \eqref{gsr:en:53:eq:Rshort}.

The sixth threshold yields
\[
 A_*\ge c_0N^{\beta_0}\ge X_*^{1/f_0}\ge1.
\]
Since $f(a)\ge f_0$, it follows that
$A_*^{f(a)}\ge X_*$. Also $A_*\ge8$, because $X_*\ge8$ and $f_0\le1$. Thus $m\ge8$, and
\[
 2(\len R-1)\le2m<m^2\le N.
\]
Apply Stages 13.7 and 13.8. Their hypotheses hold because
$L\ge(\len R)^{f(a)}\ge A_*^{f(a)}\ge X_*\ge W_0\ge W(a)$.
Their output gives \eqref{gsr:en:53:eq:coeffdata} and \eqref{gsr:en:53:eq:shortscales}. This proves the proposition; the seventh budget will pay the final clean-exponent absorption.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The same budgets also verify the existing square API}
The sixth budget is deliberately compatible with the previously exported indexed-span square theorem. Put $X=(\len R)^{f(a)}\ge X_*$. Its three scale hypotheses are
\[
 8\le X,\qquad W(a)\le X,\qquad
 8\le\left(\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor X\rfloor}{2}\right\rfloor\right)^{g(a)}.
\]
The inner expression is natural integer division. For $X\ge8$, it is at least $X/4$, so the last inequality follows from $X_*\ge4\cdot8^{1/g_0}$ and $g(a)\ge g_0$. The source theorem then gives a square with actual-density mass and side at least
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:53:eq:baseline}
 \left(\frac{(c(a)N^{\beta(a)})^{f(a)}}4\right)^{g(a)/2}-1
 \ge\frac{c_0}{4}N^{2\gamma(a)}-1.
\end{equation}
Indeed $(c(a)^{f(a)}/4)^{g(a)/2}\ge c(a)/4\ge c_0/4$. From $N\ge R_7$ and monotonicity of $\gamma$,
$(c_0/4)N^{\gamma(a)}\ge2$, so \eqref{gsr:en:53:eq:baseline} is at least $N^{\gamma(a)}$.

This gives a direct actual-density refinement using only the already exported square API. The stronger theorem uses the same budgets but retains more of the selected geometry. No square-root loss from \eqref{gsr:en:53:eq:baseline} will be imposed on the sharper route.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The seventh threshold dominates exactly\srctag{53}}]{The seventh threshold dominates exactly}\label{gsr:en:53:sec:d5}\label{gsr:en:53:sec:collapse}
\srcnote{53}{Section 5}
We now prove that the apparent maximum in \eqref{gsr:en:53:eq:seven} is exactly $R_7$, on the entire interval $0<a_0\le1$.

\begin{proposition}[Exact threshold collapse]\label{gsr:en:53:prop:collapse}
For every $0<a_0\le1$, $R_i<R_7$ for $1\le i\le6$. Consequently
\[
 \left\lceil\max_{1\le i\le7}R_i\right\rceil
 =\lceil R_7\rceil=N_0(a_0).
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Throughout this proof only, suppress the subscript zero, set $h=\log_2(1/a_0)\ge0$, and write $K,Q,b,t,c,\beta,f,g$ for their values at $a_0$. Then
\begin{align*}
 K&=2^{114+320h},&Q&=2^{1048576+2097152h},\\
 b&=2^{620143+1844304h},&t&=2^{-620025-1843952h},\\
 f&=2^{-100-448h},&g&=2^{-284-1408h}.
\end{align*}
Introduce logarithmic losses
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:53:eq:losses}
 C=\log_2(1/c)=1+K(228+576h),\quad
 D_0=\log_2(1/d_0),\quad D_1=\log_2(1/d)=D_0+1.
\end{equation}
The logarithm of the seventh term is exactly
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:53:eq:E}
 E=\log_2R_7=\frac{4(C+3)}{\beta fg}
   =(C+3)2^{13Q+386+1856h}.
\end{equation}
All comparisons below concern positive quantities.

We use the elementary estimate
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:53:eq:hexp}
 1+h\le2^{2h}\qquad(h\ge0),
\end{equation}
which follows from $\log 2\ge1/2$ and $e^x\ge1+x$. Since $\pi<4$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:53:eq:Dsmall}
 \begin{split}
 D_0&<620033+1843952h,\\
 D_1&<620034+1843952h,\\
 D_1+2&<620036+1843952h<2^{21}(1+h)<C.
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
The last inequality follows from
$C>2^{114}(228+576h)$ by comparing both positive coefficients.

\paragraph{Terms one, three and four.}
Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:53:eq:E} gives $E>4>\log_2 3$. The third logarithm is $C/\beta$, and
\[
 \frac{E}{C/\beta}=\frac{4(C+3)}{fgC}>4.
\]
The fourth logarithm is $(D_1+2)/\beta<C/\beta$. Thus all three terms are strictly below $R_7$.

\paragraph{Term five and the rounded radius.}
The exact radius parameter is $\kappa=\lceil K\rceil$. Because $K\ge1$,
$1\le\kappa\le K+1\le2K$. From \eqref{gsr:en:53:eq:Wz},
\[
 Z:=\log_2(1/z)=\kappa(227+576h)+\log_2\kappa.
\]
For a positive integer $\kappa$, $\kappa\le2^\kappa$, so $\log_2\kappa\le\kappa$. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:53:eq:Zbound}
 Z\le\kappa(228+576h)\le2K(228+576h)=2(C-1)<2C.
\end{equation}
The fifth logarithm is $(Z+D_1)/\beta<3C/\beta<E$. This pays the integer ceiling and the denominator in the source radius without treating either as negligible.

\paragraph{Term six and the exact branch of the maximum.}
Since $2^{1408h}\ge1+704h$,
\[
 1/g=2^{284}2^{1408h}\ge2^{284}(1+704h)>135+704h=\log_2W.
\]
Also $3=\log_2 8<2+3/g$. Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:53:eq:Xexact}
 X_*=4\cdot8^{1/g},\qquad\log_2X_*=2+3/g.
\end{equation}
Writing $E_6=\log_2R_6$ and multiplying by the positive common denominator gives
\[
 E_6\beta fg=Cfg+2g+3\le C+5<4(C+3)=E\beta fg.
\]
Every branch of the maximum defining $X_*$ is therefore accounted for.

\paragraph{Term two and the strict recurrence buffer.}
Here $q=\lfloor b\rfloor\ge512$. Since $160\cdot2^{32h}+2\ge162$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:53:eq:Hlog}
 H=\lceil160\cdot2^{32h}+2\rceil
 \le160\cdot2^{32h}+3\le163\cdot2^{32h}<2^{8+32h}.
\end{equation}
Let $T=T_2(q)$ and $J=\log_2T$. Retaining the exact factor $1+2^{321}$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:53:eq:Tlog}
 J=(1+2^{321})2^{11(q-1)}
 <2^{11q+311}\le2^{12q}.
\end{equation}
Put $M=\max\{T,H^{2^{12q}}\}$. Each entry is greater than one, and both rounding losses in $L_*$ give
\[
 T+1\le M+1,\qquad
 \lceil H^{2^{12q}}\rceil\le M+1,\qquad
 L_*+2\le M+3<4M.
\]
In particular the strict source requirement has not been replaced by a non-strict one. Taking logarithms and using \eqref{gsr:en:53:eq:Hlog}--\eqref{gsr:en:53:eq:Tlog},
\[
 \log_2(L_*+2)<2+2^{12q}(8+32h).
\]
Then \eqref{gsr:en:53:eq:Dsmall} and \eqref{gsr:en:53:eq:hexp} yield
\begin{align}
 \log_2(L_*+2)+D_0
 &<2^{12q}(10+32h+D_0)\notag\\
 &<2^{12q}(620043+1843984h)\notag\\
 &<2^{12q+21}(1+h)\le2^{12q+21+2h}.\label{gsr:en:53:eq:Llog}
\end{align}
The reciprocal exponent is exactly
$1/u_0=q\,2^{1240054+3687904h}$. Hence $E_2=\log_2R_2$ satisfies
\begin{align}
 E_2&<q\,2^{12q+1240075+3687906h}\notag\\
    &\le2^{12q+1860218+5532210h},\label{gsr:en:53:eq:E2}
\end{align}
using $q\le b=2^{620143+1844304h}$.
Now
\[
 \frac b{Q/2}=2^{-428432-252848h}<1,
\]
so $12q<6Q$. The remaining affine expression is bounded by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:53:eq:polynomialQ}
 1860218+5532210h<2^{23}(1+h)
 \le2^{23+2h}<Q.
\end{equation}
Together, \eqref{gsr:en:53:eq:E2}--\eqref{gsr:en:53:eq:polynomialQ} imply
\[
 E_2<2^{7Q}<(C+3)2^{13Q+386+1856h}=E.
\]
This completes all six strict comparisons, including $h=0$.
\end{proof}

\section[{Why the all-density witness is short\srctag{53}}]{Why the all-density witness is short}\label{gsr:en:53:sec:d6}\label{gsr:en:53:sec:shortwitness}
\srcnote{53}{Section 6}
The strength of the geometric argument depends on preserving information in an actual selection. We verify that this is available throughout $0<a\le1$.

The all-density initial-stage wrapper in
\srclink{Proofs13AllDensityExtraction.lean\#L13-L49}{\codefiftythree{Proofs13AllDensityExtraction.lean}, lines 13--49}
first obtains height models from the all-density model theorem, then invokes the Bohr-model Stage 13.6 constructor with the same integer $m$ and the same budgets. The dense normalization is handled before selecting $R$; it does not change the prescribed partition size.

The Bohr-model constructor in
\srclink{Proofs13CommonStepSelection.lean\#L212-L236}{\codefiftythree{Proofs13CommonStepSelection.lean}, lines 212--236}
invokes the short-difference-rule constructor. In that file the common-step row selection, lines 92--132, explicitly returns a proper $R$ with
$\len R=m$ or $m+1$, as well as its step, linearity and mass facts. The short-difference-rule proof obtains this very $R$ and the length alternative at lines 152--154, forms its Stage 13.6 record using the same $R$ at line 160, and verifies all stage conjuncts at lines 166--181. One may therefore retain the length alternative together with the same proved conjuncts. None of these steps assumes $a\le1/6$.

The adaptive cap in the dense height model affects the preliminary fibres and their corrected mass; it does not alter the subsequent common-step partition into lengths $m$ or $m+1$. Thus \eqref{gsr:en:53:eq:Rshort} is available for suitably chosen outputs of the full all-density construction.

This is a proof-level strengthened existence statement. The weaker exported type, which records only $\len R\le\len Q_{\mathrm{st}}$, does not imply shortness for an arbitrary old witness. We never make that inference.
