\section[{Short parents and direct square geometry\srctag{53}}]{Short parents and direct square geometry}\label{gsr:en:53:sec:d7}\label{gsr:en:53:sec:geometry}
\srcnote{53}{Section 7}
This section is self-contained apart from the following explicitly stated analytic input.

\paragraph{Imported all-scale coefficient localization.}
Let $N$ be prime, $T$ a proper nonzero-step progression of positive length $v$, and $X_0$ a nonempty column set. Suppose $0<\delta\le1$, $J\subseteq T$, $A_c,B_c$ are scalar order-eight Freiman maps on $J$, and
\[
 C_0\subseteq X_0\times(J+y),\quad |C_0|\ge\delta|X_0|v,\quad
 \phi(x,z)=A_c(z-y)+B_c(z-y)x\quad((x,z)\in C_0).
\]
The source theorem
\srclink{Proofs13CoefficientPartition.lean\#L84-L127}{\codefiftythree{extract\_bilinear\_cell}}
provides a proper nonzero-step progression $U\subseteq T$ and the retained set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:53:eq:localization}
 D_0=\{(x,z)\in C_0:z-y\in U\},\qquad
 \len U\ge v^e,\quad |D_0|\ge\delta|X_0|\len U,
 \quad e=\delta^2/2^{14},
\end{equation}
on which $\phi$ is bilinear. There is no lower-scale premise such as $8\le v^e$. The exponent is the one-domain simultaneous coefficient exponent; the two scalar maps do not cause two successive exponent losses. In our application,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:53:eq:geometricg}
 \delta=2^{-135}a^{704},\qquad e=2^{-284}a^{1408}=g(a).
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}[Rectification inside a short progression]\label{gsr:en:53:lem:rectify}
Let $P$ be a proper progression in $\F_N$ of nonzero step $d$ and length $n$, with $2(n-1)<N$. If a proper progression $X$ of length at least two is contained in $P$, then, after possibly reversing only its indexing, there is a positive integer $s$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:53:eq:rectified}
 \stfiftythree X=sd,\qquad s(\len X-1)\le n-1.
\end{equation}
Its carrier and length are unchanged by the reversal.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Normalize by the affine bijection $z\mapsto(z-P.start)/d$. The successive points of $X$ have unique indices $i_j\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$. All differences $i_{j+1}-i_j$ lie in $[-(n-1),n-1]$ and represent the same residue $\stfiftythree X/d$. Their pairwise differences have absolute value at most $2(n-1)<N$, so they are equal as integers. Let the common value be $s_0$. It is nonzero because $X$ is proper and has at least two points. If it is negative, reverse the indexing, and put $s=|s_0|$. Comparing extreme indices proves \eqref{gsr:en:53:eq:rectified}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Balanced aligned parents]\label{gsr:en:53:lem:balanced}
If integers $L\ge2$, $s\ge1$ and $q_Q$ satisfy $s(L-1)<q_Q$, then the index interval $\{0,\ldots,q_Q-1\}$ partitions into step-$s$ progressions with lengths between $\lceil L/2\rceil$ and $L$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Split the interval into its $s$ residue chains. Each has length $n\ge L-1$. For a chain of length $n$, put $c=\lceil n/L\rceil$, and divide it into $c$ consecutive blocks whose lengths differ by at most one. They have length at most $L$. If $c=1$, their length is at least $L-1\ge\lceil L/2\rceil$. If $c\ge2$, then
\[
 n\ge(c-1)L+1,\qquad
 n/c\ge L-(L-1)/c\ge(L+1)/2.
\]
Thus the smallest block has length at least $\lfloor(L+1)/2\rfloor=\lceil L/2\rceil$. These blocks partition each chain and hence the whole interval.
\end{proof}
The lower bound is sharp for this partition class: a chain of length $L+1$ needs at least two blocks of length at most $L$, and one has length at most $\lceil L/2\rceil$.

\begin{lemma}[Endpoint-contained common-step cover]\label{gsr:en:53:lem:cover}
Let $S=P(x,d;L)$ and $T=P(y,e;M)$ be proper progressions in a cyclic group, with $e\ne0$ and $e=jd$ for a positive integer $j$. If an integer $k$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:53:eq:fit}
 1\le k\le M,\qquad jk\le L,
\end{equation}
and $D\subseteq S\times T$ has $|D|\ge\delta LM$ with $\delta\ge0$, there are proper progressions $V\subseteq S$ and $W\subseteq T$ of common step $e$ and length $k$ such that
\[
 |D\cap(V\times W)|\ge(\delta/4)k^2.
\]
Every restriction-invariant property of $D$, including agreement with a fixed bilinear function, persists on the intersection.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Split the indices of $S$ into their $j$ residue chains. Their lengths are at least $k$ by $jk\le L$, their steps are $jd=e$, and their total length is $L$. In any chain of $n\ge k$ points, take consecutive blocks of length $k$, then add the terminal length-$k$ block if there is a nonempty remainder. All blocks stay in the chain and cover it. Their total length is
\[
 k\lceil n/k\rceil<n+k\le2n.
\]
Thus $S$ has a contained step-$e$ cover with total capacity less than $2L$. Apply the same block construction to $T$ to get capacity less than $2M$.

The product cells cover $S\times T$, with possible overlap, and their total capacity is less than $4LM$. Counting members of $D$ with multiplicity yields at least $|D|\ge\delta LM$. Some cell therefore has density at least $\delta/4$. Each cell is proper by containment in an injective parent indexing, and has the required common step and side. Restriction proves the final assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Short-parent extraction with the full exponent]\label{gsr:en:53:prop:geometry}
Let $N$ be prime and let $R,Q_{\mathrm{st}},S$ be proper nonzero-step progressions with
\[
 \stfiftythree R=\stfiftythree Q_{\mathrm{st}},\qquad S\subseteq R,\qquad
 L=\len S\ge3,\qquad r=\len R\le\len Q_{\mathrm{st}},\qquad 2(r-1)<N.
\]
Suppose the support, mass and row identities in \eqref{gsr:en:53:eq:coeffdata} hold for some $0<\delta\le1$, with scalar order-eight Freiman coefficients on $J_0\subseteq Q_{\mathrm{st}}$. Then there is a proper common-step square, with retained set $B\subseteq C$, density at least $\delta/4$, bilinearity of the original $\phi$ on $B$, and side
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:53:eq:sharpside}
 k\ge\lceil L/2\rceil^{\delta^2/2^{14}}-1.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Rectify $S\subseteq R$ by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:53:lem:rectify}, reversing its indexing if needed. Then
\[
 \stfiftythree S=s\stfiftythree Q_{\mathrm{st}},\qquad s\ge1,\qquad
 s(L-1)\le r-1<\len Q_{\mathrm{st}}.
\]
Transport the partition of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:53:lem:balanced} through the proper indexing of $Q_{\mathrm{st}}$. It yields disjoint parents $T_i$ of step $\stfiftythree S$ and lengths $v_i$ with
$\lceil L/2\rceil\le v_i\le L$ and $\sum_i v_i=\len Q_{\mathrm{st}}$.
The sets $C_i=\{(x,z)\in C:z-y\in T_i\}$ partition $C$. Weighted averaging of their actual pair counts therefore selects a parent $T$ of length $v$ with
\[
 |C_T|\ge\delta Lv,\qquad C_T\subseteq S\times((J_0\cap T)+y).
\]
The row identity and Freiman maps restrict to $J_0\cap T$. Apply the analytic input \eqref{gsr:en:53:eq:localization} with this same density $\delta$. It gives $U\subseteq T$, length $M\ge v^e$ for $e=\delta^2/2^{14}$, and a set $D_0\subseteq C_T\cap(S\times(U+y))$ with
$|D_0|\ge\delta LM$ and bilinearity on $D_0$. No density is lost in the parent selection or in this analytic localization.

Since $L\ge3$, $v\ge2$ and $e>0$, so the integer $M$ is at least two. Further,
$2(v-1)\le2(L-1)\le2(r-1)<N$. Rectify $U\subseteq T$ with a possible indexing reversal. For a positive integer $j$ this gives
\[
 \stfiftythree U=j\stfiftythree S,\qquad j(M-1)\le v-1\le L-1.
\]
Set $k=M-1$. It is positive, $k\le M$ and $jk\le L$. Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:53:lem:cover} to $S$ and $U+y$, retaining a set $B\subseteq D_0$ of mass at least $(\delta/4)k^2$. Finally
\[
 k=M-1\ge v^e-1\ge\lceil L/2\rceil^e-1.
\]
Properness, equal nonzero step, original-domain containment and bilinearity have all been preserved.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{The original phase and the offset.}
Only carriers are restricted, or their indexing reversed. Neither operation changes the ambient variables in $\phi$. More explicitly, if the localized affine coefficients are
$A_c(h)=a_1h+a_0$ and $B_c(h)=b_1h+b_0$, substituting $h=z-y$ gives
\[
 \phi(x,z)=(a_0-a_1y)+(b_0-b_1y)x+a_1z+b_1xz.
\]
This includes both offset corrections and is a bilinear formula in the original coordinates. There is no claim that the old arbitrary Stage 13.9 witness acquired a grid; the selected $U$ is newly constructed inside a short aligned parent.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The sharper coefficient and final assembly\srctag{53}}]{The sharper coefficient and final assembly}\label{gsr:en:53:sec:d8}\label{gsr:en:53:sec:assembly}
\srcnote{53}{Section 8}
For $N\ge N_0(a_0)$, Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:53:prop:collapse} implies all seven budgets. Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:53:prop:budgets} and the verified short-parent construction provide every hypothesis of Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:53:prop:geometry}. In particular,
$L\ge W(a)\ge2^{135}$, so no singleton or two-point exception is needed.

Use $\delta=2^{-135}a^{704}$ and $g(a)=\delta^2/2^{14}$. With $A_*=c(a)N^{\beta(a)}$, \eqref{gsr:en:53:eq:sharpside} and $L\ge A_*^{f(a)}$ give
\begin{align}
 k&\ge\lceil L/2\rceil^{g(a)}-1
    \ge(L/2)^{g(a)}-1\notag\\
  &\ge2^{-g(a)}c(a)^{f(a)g(a)}N^{\beta(a)f(a)g(a)}-1
   =D(a)N^{4\gamma(a)}-1.\label{gsr:en:53:eq:exactsharp}
\end{align}
The full $\lceil L/2\rceil^{g(a)}$ estimate is retained. Replacing it by the weaker $L^{g(a)/2}$ bound would unnecessarily halve this exponent.

\begin{lemma}[Uniform coefficient bound]\label{gsr:en:53:lem:D}
For every $0<a\le1$, $D(a)>1/2$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $h=\log_2(1/a)\ge0$. Since
$\log_2(1/c(a))=1+2^{114}a^{-320}(228+576h)$, the exact loss is
\begin{align}
 \log_2(1/D(a))
 &=g(a)+f(a)g(a)\log_2(1/c(a))\notag\\
 &=2^{-284}a^{1408}+2^{-384}a^{1856}
   +2^{-270}a^{1536}(228+576h).\label{gsr:en:53:eq:Dloss}
\end{align}
Using $\log 2\ge1/2$ and $e^x\ge1+x$,
$2^{1536h}\ge1+768h$. Hence
\[
 228+576h\le228(1+768h)\le228\cdot2^{1536h},
 \qquad a^{1536}(228+576h)\le228.
\]
The loss in \eqref{gsr:en:53:eq:Dloss} is consequently at most
\[
 2^{-284}+2^{-384}+228\cdot2^{-270}
 <230\cdot2^{-270}<256\cdot2^{-270}=2^{-262}<1.
\]
Thus $\log_2(1/D(a))<1$, proving $D(a)>1/2$ uniformly, including $a=1$ and arbitrarily small positive $a$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Completion of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:53:thm:main}]
Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:53:eq:exactsharp} and Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:53:lem:D} give the first two side estimates. Put $x=N^{\gamma(a)}$. Monotonicity of $\gamma$ and $N\ge R_7$ imply
\[
 x\ge N^{\gamma(a_0)}\ge8/c(a_0)\ge16.
\]
Therefore
\[
 \tfrac12x^4-1\ge8x^3-1\ge x^3=N^{3\gamma(a)}.
\]
The cover retains density $\delta/4=2^{-137}a^{704}$ and a subset of the original $A$; all phase identities use the original $\phi$. Properness gives $|V|=|W|=k$. This proves every conclusion of the theorem. The previously established comparison $N_0\le N_{\mathrm{safe}}$ now proves Corollary~\ref{gsr:fm:53:cor:safe} as well.
\end{proof}

\section[{The exact retained interface\srctag{51}}]{The exact retained interface}\label{gsr:en:51:sec:d2}\label{gsr:en:51:sec:interface}
\srcnote{51}{Section 2}
We first translate the source interface into mathematical notation. This also fixes all normalization and indexing conventions used in the proof.

\subsection{The context and the two initial stages}
An order-eight Freiman homomorphism on a set preserves equal sums of eight elements. A function $\phi:(\Z/N\Z)^2\to\Z/N\Z$ is separately order-eight Freiman on $A$ when each of its vertical and horizontal restrictions has this property on the corresponding section of $A$.

An eight-arrangement at height $h$ consists of sixteen horizontal coordinates $x_i$ and sixteen vertical coordinates $y_i$, with
\[
 \sum_{i=1}^{8}x_i=\sum_{i=9}^{16}x_i,
 \qquad (x_i,y_i),(x_i,y_i+h)\in A\quad(1\le i\le16).
\]
It is respected when the analogous equality holds for the sixteen values
$\phi(x_i,y_i+h)-\phi(x_i,y_i)$. Let $C(h)$ count all such arrangements and let $C_{\phi}(h)$ count the respected ones. A context consists of $A,\phi,\alpha,\eta$ satisfying
\[
 0<\alpha\le1,\qquad |A|=\alpha N^2,\qquad \eta=2^{-44},
 \qquad (1-\eta)\sum_h C(h)\le\sum_h C_{\phi}(h),
\]
together with the separate Freiman property.
A height is good when $(1-2\eta)C(h)\le C_{\phi}(h)$ and strong when it is good and
$C(h)\ge\alpha^{32}N^{31}/16$.

Let
\[
 \Aedge_h=\{(x,y):(x,y),(x,y+h)\in A\},\qquad
 f_h(x)=|\{y:(x,y)\in\Aedge_h\}|.
\]
The source Fourier transform is unnormalized:
$\widehat f(\xi)=\sum_xf(x)\exp(\pm2\pi i\xi x/N)$; its sign convention does not affect any norm below. Write $\|\xi\|_N$ for the absolute value of a centered integer representative.
For $\theta>0$ put
\[
 \theta_1=2^{-1882}\theta^{10477},\qquad
 Q_{134}(\theta)=2^{1882}\theta^{-10479}.
\]
Stage 13.4 stores a positive integer $q$, an integer $m_D$, a progression $P$, a set $H_{134}$, and $q$ pairs $a_i,b_i\in\Z/N\Z$. Its complete conditions are:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{134.\arabic*}]
\item $\stfiftyone P\ne0$, $P$ proper, $H_{134}\subseteq P$, and $q\le Q_{134}(\theta)$;
\item $m_D=\lfloor\theta_1N^{\theta_1^2/(16q)}/(64\pi)\rfloor$, and either $\lenfiftyone P=m_D$ or $\lenfiftyone P+1=m_D$;
\item $\alpha^{32}N^{31}\lenfiftyone P/8\le\sum_{h\in H_{134}\cap\good}C(h)$;
\item if $h\in H_{134}$ and $|\widehat f_h(\xi)|\ge\theta N^2$, then $\xi=a_ih+b_i$ for some $i$.
\end{enumerate}
Here the floor is the exact predicate $m_D\le x<m_D+1$.
Stage 13.5 stores $Q$ and defines
\[
 \Crit=(Q\cap H_{134})\cap\{h:h\text{ is strong}\}.
\]
Its complete conditions are $\stfiftyone Q\ne0$, properness, $Q\subseteq P$, and
\begin{align}
 \tfrac12(\lenfiftyone P)^{2^{-12q}}&\le\lenfiftyone Q,\label{gsr:en:51:eq:135len}\\
 \|(a_ih+b_i)\stfiftyone Q\|_N&\le(\lenfiftyone P)^{-2^{-11q}}N
       &&(i<q,\ h\in Q),\label{gsr:en:51:eq:135freq}\\
 \alpha^{32}\lenfiftyone Q/20&\le|\Crit|.\label{gsr:en:51:eq:135mass}
\end{align}

\subsection{The six numerical budgets}
The Section 13 scalar functions and the relevant Section 10 functions are
\begin{align*}
 \kth(\alpha)&=2^{114}\alpha^{-320},&
 \zet(\alpha)&=2^{-228\kth(\alpha)}\alpha^{576\kth(\alpha)},\\
 \qth(\alpha)&=2^{2^{20}}\alpha^{-2^{21}},&
 \lambda_{10}(a)&=2^{-37}a^{11/2},\\
 k(a)&=\lceil2^{74}a^{-10}\rceil,&
 \zeta_{10}(a)&=2^{-155k(a)}a^{18k(a)}/k(a).
\end{align*}
In particular, the ceiling and the division by $k(a)$ in the last formula must both be retained. Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:51:eq:budgetnotation}
 \begin{aligned}
 c&=\zet(\alpha)/2,&\quad \beta&=2^{-13\qth(\alpha)},\\
 f&=2^{-100}\alpha^{448},& W&=2^{135}\alpha^{-704},\qquad
 z=\zeta_{10}(\alpha^{32}/16).
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Besides $N$ prime, the context, $\alpha\le1/6$, and the two complete initial-stage predicates at $\theta=\lambda_{10}(\alpha^{32}/16)$, the budget theorem assumes an integer $m$ satisfying exactly
\begin{alignat}{3}
 &0<m, &&\hspace{1.5em}m^2\le N,
 &&\hspace{1.5em}m+1\le\lenfiftyone Q,\label{gsr:en:51:eq:budgetinteger}\\
 &cN^\beta\le m, &&\hspace{1.5em}(\lenfiftyone P)^{-2^{-11q}}\le z/m,
 &&\hspace{1.5em}W\le(cN^\beta)^f.\label{gsr:en:51:eq:budgetanalytic}
\end{alignat}
These are, in order, \codefiftyone{hm}, \codefiftyone{hsize}, \codefiftyone{hupper}, \codefiftyone{hlower}, \codefiftyone{hbudget}, and \codefiftyone{hwidth}. The integer $m$ in this theorem is \emph{not} the field $m_D$ stored in Stage 13.4. In our construction they will be $n$ and $p$, respectively.

The theorem then existentially produces $F,G,H,J$, with the four subsequent stage predicates and $\lenfiftyone R\le\lenfiftyone Q$. Section~\ref{gsr:en:51:sec:later} lists every conjunct of these predicates while verifying our explicit choices. This avoids treating a weakened or obsolete version of Stage 13.7 as the current interface.

\subsection{The grid is a stronger assertion}
The source predicate \codefiftyone{Corollary1310Grid} asks for a positive finite number of product cells $V_i\times W_i$ which form a disjoint partition of all $S\times(U+y)$. For every $i$ it requires
\[
 \stfiftyone{V_i}\ne0,\quad \stfiftyone{V_i}=\stfiftyone{W_i},\quad
 V_i,W_i\text{ proper},\quad
 \lenfiftyone{V_i}=\lenfiftyone{W_i}\ge\sqrt{\lenfiftyone U}-1.
\]
Different cells may have different common steps. The counterexample will exclude even one cell of side length two, whatever that common step might be. It therefore does not depend on the extra difficulty of demanding an exact disjoint partition.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The geometric obstruction in isolation\srctag{51}}]{The geometric obstruction in isolation}\label{gsr:en:51:sec:d3}\label{gsr:en:51:sec:obstruction}
\srcnote{51}{Section 3}
\begin{lemma}[Separated difference sets]\label{gsr:en:51:lem:separation}
Let $n\ge2$ and $N>n^2-1$. In $\Z/N\Z$ put
\[
 S_n=\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\},\qquad
 U_n=\{0,n,2n,\ldots,(n-1)n\}.
\]
Then $(S_n-S_n)\cap(U_n-U_n)=\{0\}$. Hence no proper common-step square of side at least two is contained in $S_n\times U_n$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A member of the intersection has representatives $a$ and $nj$ with
$|a|\le n-1$ and $|j|\le n-1$. If $a\equiv nj\pmod N$, then
\[
 |a-nj|\le(n-1)+n(n-1)=n^2-1<N.
\]
Thus $a=nj$ as integers. Since $|a|<n$, this forces $a=j=0$.
If $V\subseteq S_n$ and $W\subseteq U_n$ are progressions with the same step $e$ and at least two terms, their first two terms put $e$ in both difference sets. The common step must therefore be zero, contrary to the required nonzero step.
\end{proof}

For a small illustration take $N=47$ and $n=5$:
\[
 S=\{0,1,2,3,4\},\qquad U=\{0,5,10,15,20\}.
\]
The two nonzero difference sets are $\{\pm1,\ldots,\pm4\}$ and
$\{\pm5,\pm10,\pm15,\pm20\}$; they are disjoint modulo $47$.
With $R=S$ and $Q=\{0,\ldots,20\}$, one has $S\subseteq R$, $U\subseteq Q$, $|R|\le|Q|$, and $\stfiftyone U=5\stfiftyone S$. Since $\sqrt5-1>1$, this also excludes the grid predicate. This example is an illustration of the geometry only: it is not presented as a full-budget witness. The main task is to embed the same mechanism into genuine initial-stage data at the much larger scales demanded by \eqref{gsr:en:51:eq:budgetinteger}--\eqref{gsr:en:51:eq:budgetanalytic}.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Uniform constants and a simultaneous prime choice\srctag{51}}]{Uniform constants and a simultaneous prime choice}\label{gsr:en:51:sec:d4}\label{gsr:en:51:sec:scales}
\srcnote{51}{Section 4}
All constants introduced before choosing $N$ in this section are fixed independently of $N$ and its eventual density. They are real numbers or integers defined symbolically; numerical expansion is neither needed nor intended.

\subsection{The fixed exponents}
Set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:51:eq:fixedconstants}
 \begin{gathered}
 K=2^{762},\qquad q=2K+1=2^{763}+1,\qquad
 T=1882+763\cdot10477=7\,995\,833,\\
 d_0=\frac{2^{-T}}{64\pi},\qquad
 c_P=\frac{d_0}{2},\qquad
 u_0=\frac{2^{-2T}}{16q},\qquad
 w=2^{-11q},\qquad r=\frac{u_0w}{4}.
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
We use $T$ for the fixed exponent to keep it distinct from an integer step multiplier later. Uniform bounds for the Section 10 and 13 functions will use
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:51:eq:uniformconstants}
 \begin{gathered}
 k_0=2^{1394},\qquad c_0=2^{-(2532k_0+1)},\qquad
 z_0=2^{-(2531k_0+1394)},\\
 \beta_0=2^{-13\cdot2^{9437184}},\qquad
 \beta_1=2^{-13\cdot2^{7340032}},\qquad
 f_0=2^{-1892},\qquad W_0=2^{2951}.
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
These extremely small or large quantities are finite and positive. They will occur only in inequalities and fixed thresholds.

\begin{lemma}[The exponent margin]\label{gsr:en:51:lem:margin}
One has $0<\beta_1<r<u_0/4<1/64$, $0<w\le1/2$, and $u_0-2r>0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Since $q<2^{764}$,
\[
 r=\frac{2^{-2T-11q}}{64q}
   >2^{-(2T+770+11q)}.
\]
The exact integer identity $2T+770=15\,992\,436<2^{25}$ and the bound
$11q<2^{768}$ imply $2T+770+11q<2^{769}$. Therefore
\[
 r>2^{-2^{769}}>2^{-13\cdot2^{7340032}}=\beta_1.
\]
The remaining inequalities follow from $q\ge1$, $0<2^{-2T}<1$,
$0<w<1$, and $u_0-2r=u_0(1-w/2)>0$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Uniformity over the actual density interval}
\begin{lemma}[Uniform scalar estimates]\label{gsr:en:51:lem:uniform}
For every $\alpha\in[1/16,1/8]$, the notation in \eqref{gsr:en:51:eq:budgetnotation} satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:51:eq:uniformbounds}
 c_0\le c\le\tfrac12,\quad
 \beta_0\le\beta\le\beta_1<r,\quad
 f_0\le f<1,\quad W\le W_0,\quad z\ge z_0>0.
\end{equation}
Also, with $\theta=\lambda_{10}(\alpha^{32}/16)$ and
$\theta_1=2^{-1882}\theta^{10477}$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:51:eq:thetabounds}
 \theta=2^{-59}\alpha^{176},\qquad
 2^{-763}\le\theta\le2^{-587}<1,\qquad
 0<\theta\le\alpha^{32}/4,\qquad \theta_1\ge2^{-T}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The identity for $\theta$ is
$2^{-37}(\alpha^{32}/16)^{11/2}=2^{-59}\alpha^{176}$.
The endpoints of the density interval give the powers $-763$ and $-587$.
Moreover $4\theta/\alpha^{32}=2^{-57}\alpha^{144}\le1$, and the definition of $T$ yields the bound on $\theta_1$.

For the Section 13 prefactor,
$\kth(\alpha)\le2^{114+4\cdot320}=k_0$. Since $\alpha\ge2^{-4}$,
\[
 \zet(\alpha)
 =2^{-228\kth(\alpha)}\alpha^{576\kth(\alpha)}
 \ge2^{-2532\kth(\alpha)}\ge2^{-2532k_0}.
\]
This gives $c\ge c_0$. Positivity and $\alpha\le1$ give $0<c\le1/2$.
Next,
\[
 2^{7340032}\le\qth(\alpha)\le2^{9437184},
\]
because $2^{20}+3\cdot2^{21}=7\,340\,032$ and
$2^{20}+4\cdot2^{21}=9\,437\,184$.
Taking the decreasing function $x\mapsto2^{-13x}$ gives the asserted bounds for $\beta$. The formulas for $f_0,W_0$ follow from
$100+4\cdot448=1892$ and $135+4\cdot704=2951$.

Finally put $a=\alpha^{32}/16$. Then $2^{-132}\le a\le2^{-100}$ and
$2^{74}a^{-10}\le2^{1394}=k_0$. Because $k_0$ is an integer, the ceiling
$k=\lceil2^{74}a^{-10}\rceil$ satisfies $1\le k\le k_0$, without an extra $+1$ loss. Retaining the division by $k$,
\[
 z=2^{-155k}a^{18k}/k
 \ge 2^{-(155+18\cdot132)k}/k
 \ge 2^{-2531k_0}/k_0=z_0.
\]
This argument uses no continuity across jumps of the ceiling.
\end{proof}

\subsection{One threshold for all subsequent requirements}
Choose a prime $N$ large enough that the following eight conditions hold:
\begin{align}
 N&\ge K^2, & d_0N^{u_0}&\ge2,\label{gsr:en:51:eq:Nconditions1}\\
 c_PN^{u_0-2r}&\ge1, & N^r&\ge5,\label{gsr:en:51:eq:Nconditions2}\\
 N^{1-r}&\ge16, & N^{1-2r}&>2,\label{gsr:en:51:eq:Nconditions3}\\
 c_P^{-w}N^{-3r}&\le z_0, & c_0N^{\beta_0}&\ge W_0^{1/f_0}.\label{gsr:en:51:eq:Nconditions4}
\end{align}
Every constant here is fixed. All growth exponents are positive by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:51:lem:margin}; the first inequality in \eqref{gsr:en:51:eq:Nconditions4} is equivalently
$N^{3r}\ge c_P^{-w}/z_0$. Thus all eight conditions hold for every real $N$ above one finite threshold. There are arbitrarily large primes beyond it.

Now set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:51:eq:actualscales}
 \begin{gathered}
 b=\lfloor N/8\rfloor,\qquad \alpha=b/N,\qquad
 \theta=2^{-59}\alpha^{176},\qquad \theta_1=2^{-1882}\theta^{10477},\\
 d=\theta_1/(64\pi),\qquad u=\theta_1^2/(16q),\qquad
 p=\lfloor dN^u\rfloor,\qquad n=\lfloor N^r\rfloor.
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
The earlier density bounds apply because $N\ge K^2\ge16$:
$b\ge N/8-1\ge N/16$, while $b\le N/8$. Hence
$1/16\le\alpha\le1/8<1/6$. In particular $d\ge d_0$, $u\ge u_0$, $d<1$, and $0<u<1/(16q)\le1/16$.

\begin{lemma}[Length and containment estimates]\label{gsr:en:51:lem:lengths}
The chosen integers satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:51:eq:scaleresults}
 \begin{gathered}
 p\ge c_PN^{u_0}\ge N^{2r}\ge n^2,\qquad 1\le p<N,\\
 5\le n\le N^r\le N/16\le b,\qquad
 n\ge N^r/2,\qquad 2n^2<N.
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The inequality $dN^u\ge d_0N^{u_0}\ge2$ permits
$\lfloor dN^u\rfloor\ge dN^u/2\ge c_PN^{u_0}$. The third threshold condition then gives $p\ge N^{2r}$. Since $d<1$, $u<1$, and $N>1$, we have $p\le dN^u<N$.
The remaining assertions follow from $N^r\ge5$, the elementary floor bound
$\lfloor x\rfloor\ge x/2$ for $x\ge2$, and \eqref{gsr:en:51:eq:Nconditions3}.
\end{proof}

This is the entire large-modulus argument. In particular, it does not invoke a theorem with a fixed-density threshold and then substitute a moving density into it. The uniform estimates prove a single threshold valid for our actual $\alpha(N)$.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A genuine strip context and the initial data\srctag{51}}]{A genuine strip context and the initial data}\label{gsr:en:51:sec:d5}\label{gsr:en:51:sec:initial}
\srcnote{51}{Section 5}
Let $X=\Z/N\Z$, let $B_0=\{0,\ldots,b-1\}\subset X$, and put
\[
 A=B_0\times X,\qquad \phi(x,y)=0,\qquad \eta=2^{-44}.
\]
The $b$ residues in $B_0$ are distinct, so $|A|=bN=\alpha N^2$.
The zero map preserves every additive relation on every horizontal or vertical section. It respects every arrangement. These facts verify each field of \codefiftyone{Section13Context}, including the global respected-arrangement proportion.

\subsection{The fixed-height arrangement count}
Let $\rho(s)$ be the number of ordered eight-tuples of elements of $B_0$ having sum $s\in X$, and write
\[
 E_8(B_0)=\sum_{s\in X}\rho(s)^2.
\]
Since $\sum_s\rho(s)=b^8$, Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:51:eq:energy}
 E_8(B_0)\ge b^{16}/N=\alpha^{16}N^{15}.
\end{equation}
For a prescribed height $h$, an arrangement has an additive sixteen-tuple of horizontal coordinates in $B_0$, and its sixteen vertical coordinates can be chosen freely and independently. Therefore the exact normalization is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:51:eq:arrangement}
 C(h)=C_{\phi}(h)=N^{16}E_8(B_0)\ge\alpha^{16}N^{31}.
\end{equation}
There is no extra factor $N$ at fixed height. Summing over heights would introduce one. Every height is good, and every height is strong because
$\alpha^{16}\ge\alpha^{32}/16$.

\subsection{A uniformly covering family of constant frequencies}
At every height, $\Aedge_h=A$ and $f_h=N\one_{B_0}$. For a nonzero frequency $\xi$, let $j=\|\xi\|_N$, so $1\le j\le N/2$. The finite geometric sum gives
\[
 \left|\sum_{x=0}^{b-1}e^{\pm2\pi i\xi x/N}\right|
 =\frac{|\sin(\pi b\xi/N)|}{|\sin(\pi\xi/N)|}
 \le\frac1{\sin(\pi j/N)}\le\frac N{2j}.
\]
The last inequality is $\sin t\ge2t/\pi$ on $[0,\pi/2]$. Thus
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:51:eq:Fourier}
 |\widehat f_h(\xi)|\le N^2/(2j).
\end{equation}
It follows that $|\widehat f_h(\xi)|\ge\theta N^2$ forces
$j\le1/(2\theta)\le2^{762}=K$. Zero frequency is included separately; no division by zero is used.

Index the integer interval $[-K,K]$ by $i=0,\ldots,q-1$, and set
$a_i=0$, $b_i=i-K\pmod N$. All Fourier coefficients at or above the threshold are on these constant graphs, for every height. The number $q$ is fixed independently of $N$, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:51:eq:qbound}
 q<2^{764}<2^{1882}\le2^{1882}\theta^{-10479}=Q_{134}(\theta).
\end{equation}
All listed frequencies have centered absolute value at most $K$, including frequencies that are unnecessary for covering the actual large spectrum.

\subsection{Every Stage 13.4 and 13.5 condition}
Take $P=Q=P(0,1;p)$ and $H_{134}=P$, with $m_D=p$ and the graph family above. Properness and nonzero step follow from $p<N$ and $N>1$. The exact floor equation is the definition of $p$ in \eqref{gsr:en:51:eq:actualscales}; the first branch $\lenfiftyone P=m_D$ of the source's length alternative holds. Since every height is good, \eqref{gsr:en:51:eq:arrangement} yields
\[
 \sum_{h\in H_{134}\cap\good}C(h)
 =pN^{16}E_8(B_0)
 \ge p\alpha^{16}N^{31}
 \ge \alpha^{32}N^{31}p/8.
\]
Together with $q>0$, \eqref{gsr:en:51:eq:qbound}, and the Fourier cover, this checks all four Stage 13.4 groups listed in Section~\ref{gsr:en:51:sec:interface}. The cutoff also satisfies $0<\theta\le\alpha^{32}/4$, the extra cutoff hypothesis in the separate statement of Lemma 13.4.

For Stage 13.5, containment $Q\subseteq P$ is equality. Since $p\ge1$ and $0<2^{-12q}\le1$, inequality \eqref{gsr:en:51:eq:135len} follows from $p^{2^{-12q}}/2\le p$. For every listed graph and every $h\in Q$,
\[
 \|(a_ih+b_i)\stfiftyone Q\|_N\le K\le\sqrt N
 \le N^{1-w}\le p^{-w}N.
\]
Here $N\ge K^2$, $w\le1/2$, and $p\le N$ were used in that order. Thus the frequency condition is verified for the whole graph family, rather than just for the graphs needed at a particular height. Finally, every height is strong and $H_{134}=Q$, so
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:51:eq:crit}
 \Crit=Q,\qquad |\Crit|=p,\qquad \alpha^{32}p/20\le p.
\end{equation}
This completes Stage 13.5 without omitting any frequency or mass condition.

\section[{Verification of all six budgets\srctag{51}}]{Verification of all six budgets}\label{gsr:en:51:sec:d6}\label{gsr:en:51:sec:budgets}
\srcnote{51}{Section 6}
Set the theorem's independent integer input to $m=n$. The first three budgets follow at once from Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:51:lem:lengths}:
\[
 n\ge5>0,\qquad n^2<N/2<N,\qquad n+1\le n^2\le p=\lenfiftyone Q.
\]
For the lower-length budget, $c\le1/2$, $\beta<r$, $N\ge1$, and $n\ge N^r/2$ give
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:51:eq:hlower}
 cN^\beta\le\tfrac12N^r\le n.
\end{equation}
Thus the floor is absorbed uniformly; no extra density-dependent threshold is hidden in this step.

The corrected Bohr budget uses the whole progression $P$ and the radius $z$, including its denominator from Section 10. Since $u_0w=4r$,
\begin{align*}
 n p^{-w}
 &\le N^r(c_PN^{u_0})^{-w}\\
 &=c_P^{-w}N^{r-u_0w}
   =c_P^{-w}N^{-3r}
 \le z_0\le z.
\end{align*}
Dividing by $n>0$ is exactly $p^{-w}\le z/n$.

For the width budget it is essential to use the lower target $cN^\beta$, not just the actual chosen integer $n$. Uniform positivity and \eqref{gsr:en:51:eq:Nconditions4} give
\[
 cN^\beta\ge c_0N^{\beta_0}\ge W_0^{1/f_0}\ge1.
\]
Because $f\ge f_0>0$, raising this base to $f$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:51:eq:hwidth}
 (cN^\beta)^f\ge(cN^\beta)^{f_0}\ge W_0\ge W.
\end{equation}
This verifies the source's actual \codefiftyone{hwidth}, a stronger check than merely arranging a wide enough final progression. Together with $\alpha<1/6$ and Section~\ref{gsr:en:51:sec:initial}, every antecedent of the budget-qualified extraction theorem is now satisfied.

\section[{The complete chosen output chain\srctag{51}}]{The complete chosen output chain}\label{gsr:en:51:sec:d7}\label{gsr:en:51:sec:later}
\srcnote{51}{Section 7}
We next construct the retained output data directly. Set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:51:eq:outputs}
 \begin{gathered}
 R=S=P(0,1;n),\qquad U=P(0,n;n),\qquad y=0,\\
 Y(h)=A\quad(h\in X),\qquad B=S\times Q,\\
 a(h)=c(h)=0\quad(h\in X),\qquad
 J_{138}=Q,\qquad C=S\times Q,\qquad D_{139}=S\times U.
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
The letters $a,c$ on the middle line denote row coefficients, not the scalar $c$ in \eqref{gsr:en:51:eq:budgetnotation}. We use $J_{138},D_{139}$ for sets so that the Stage 13.8 and 13.9 record names $H,J$ do not collide with set notation. The source fields are respectively $H.J$ and $J.D$.

The progressions $R,S$ are proper and have nonzero step one. The integer representatives of $U$ are $0,n,\ldots,(n-1)n$, all below $n^2<N$; hence $U$ is proper and has nonzero step $n$. Also
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:51:eq:containments}
 S=R\subseteq B_0,\qquad U\subseteq Q,\qquad
 \lenfiftyone R=n\le p=\lenfiftyone Q.
\end{equation}
In particular, $U\subseteq Q$ follows from $(n-1)n<n^2\le p$. None of these containment statements relies on a modular quotient estimate.

\subsection{Stage 13.6}
The source requires: the step equality $\stfiftyone R=\stfiftyone Q$, nonzero step, properness, the length bound $cN^\beta\le\lenfiftyone R$, and for every $h\in\Crit$,
\[
 Y(h)\subseteq\Aedge_h,\qquad |Y(h)|\ge2^{-43}\alpha^{224}N^2,
\]
with the vertical $\phi$-difference affine in the first coordinate on
$Y_R(h)=\{(x,y)\in Y(h):x\in R\}$. It additionally requires the two separate mass inequalities
\begin{align}
 2^{-43}\alpha^{224}\lenfiftyone R\,N|\Crit|
 &\le\sum_{h\in\Crit}|Y_R(h)|,\label{gsr:en:51:eq:136mass1}\\
 2^{-48}\alpha^{256}\lenfiftyone Q\,\lenfiftyone R\,N
 &\le\sum_{h\in\Crit}|Y_R(h)|.\label{gsr:en:51:eq:136mass2}
\end{align}
The step and length conditions follow from \eqref{gsr:en:51:eq:hlower} and the definitions. Here $Y(h)=A=\Aedge_h$, and
$|Y(h)|=\alpha N^2\ge2^{-43}\alpha^{224}N^2$ because
$2^{-43}\alpha^{223}\le1$. Since $S\subseteq B_0$,
$Y_R(h)=S\times X$, of cardinality $nN$. The vertical difference is zero, so its affine representation has both coefficients zero. Finally \eqref{gsr:en:51:eq:crit} makes the sum exactly $pnN$; both \eqref{gsr:en:51:eq:136mass1} and \eqref{gsr:en:51:eq:136mass2} follow because their scalar coefficients are at most one. The additional retained comparison $\lenfiftyone R\le\lenfiftyone Q$ was verified in \eqref{gsr:en:51:eq:containments}.

\subsection{Stage 13.7 including the original domain}
The complete current predicate requires $\stfiftyone S\ne0$, properness, $S\subseteq R$, and $(\lenfiftyone R)^f\le\lenfiftyone S$, followed by
\begin{gather*}
 B\subseteq S\times(\Crit+y),\qquad
 2^{-43}\alpha^{224}\lenfiftyone S\,|\Crit|\le|B|,\\
 2^{-48}\alpha^{256}\lenfiftyone Q\,\lenfiftyone S\le|B|.
\end{gather*}
Every row of $\phi$ on $B$ above a critical height must be affine, and one must also have $B\subseteq A$.

All progression properties hold because $S=R$. Since $n\ge1$ and $0<f<1$,
$n^f\le n$. Our support is exactly $S\times\Crit$ and $|B|=np$, so both lower mass bounds hold. Every row is zero. Crucially, $S\subseteq B_0$ gives
$B=S\times Q\subseteq B_0\times X=A$. Thus this is the full \codefiftyone{IsStage137Data}, not the earlier \codefiftyone{IsStage137DataWithoutDomain}.

\subsection{Stage 13.8 with all critical heights retained}
The row identity in the source is
$\phi(x,y+h)=a(h)+c(h)x$ on $B$ for $h\in\Crit$. Our zero coefficients satisfy it. The remaining conditions are
\begin{gather*}
 J_{138}\subseteq\Crit,\qquad
 h\mapsto(a(h),c(h))\text{ is order-eight Freiman on }J_{138},\\
 C=\{z\in B:z_2-y\in J_{138}\},\qquad
 2^{-135}\alpha^{704}\lenfiftyone Q\,\lenfiftyone S\le|C|.
\end{gather*}
They hold with $J_{138}=Q=\Crit$ and $C=B$: the coefficient pair is constant zero and $|C|=np$. Write
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:51:eq:delta}
 \delta=2^{-135}\alpha^{704}\in(0,1).
\end{equation}
The final inequality is just $\delta np\le np$.

Retaining all of $Q$ in this stage is important. Replacing $J_{138}$ prematurely by $U$ would demand $n^2\ge\delta np$, which is not a consequence of our scales. The later restriction to $U$ is made only in Stage 13.9, where its density is measured relative to $S\times U$.
The separate width hypothesis used to invoke the Stage 13.8 lemma also follows:
$W\le(cN^\beta)^f\le n^f\le n=\lenfiftyone S$.

\subsection{Stage 13.9}
The source requires nonzero step, properness, and $U\subseteq Q$, all already verified. Its step-multiple condition
\[
 \exists t\in\Z_{\ge0},\qquad \stfiftyone U=t\stfiftyone S
\]
is witnessed by the positive ordinary integer $t=n$. Let
$g=2^{-284}\alpha^{1408}\in(0,1)$. The lower length condition is
$(\lenfiftyone S)^g\le\lenfiftyone U$, which holds because $n^g\le n$.
The exact set filter in the source gives
\[
 \{z\in C:z_2-y\in U\cap J_{138}\}=S\times U=D_{139}.

Thus $|D_{139}|=n^2\ge\delta\lenfiftyone S\,\lenfiftyone U$, as required. Finally, a bilinear function means a polynomial
$c_{00}+c_{10}x+c_{01}y+c_{11}xy$ agreeing with $\phi$ on the retained set. All four coefficients zero give the required witness on $D_{139}$.
This checks every Stage 13.9 conjunct, including the exact filter identity and its density normalization.

\section[{Failure of the grid and of the new fit hypothesis\srctag{51}}]{Failure of the grid and of the new fit hypothesis}\label{gsr:en:51:sec:d8}\label{gsr:en:51:sec:failure}
\srcnote{51}{Section 8}
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:51:lem:separation} applies since $N>2n^2$. It gives \eqref{gsr:fm:51:eq:diffintersection} and excludes every proper common-step square of side at least two inside $S\times U$.

Suppose the grid predicate held. Because $n\ge5$, its real lower bound
$\sqrt n-1$ is strictly greater than one; each integral cell side length is at least two. The partition equality makes each product cell a subset of $S\times U$. Both factors of a cell are nonempty, so its first factor is a subset of $S$ and its second factor a subset of $U$. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:51:lem:separation} rules this out. The grid predicate is therefore false, proving Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:51:thm:main}.

The newer source theorem uses a positive integer $t$ with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:51:eq:upstreamfit}
 \stfiftyone U=t\stfiftyone S,\qquad t\lfloor\sqrt{\lenfiftyone U}\rfloor\le\lenfiftyone S.
\end{equation}
For our displayed progressions, every such integer step representative satisfies $t\equiv n\pmod N$. Since $0<n<N$, the least positive representative is $n$, so every positive representative has $t\ge n$. As $\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor\ge2$,
\[
 t\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor\ge2n>n=\lenfiftyone S.
\]
Hence the new fit condition fails for every positive representative. The slightly weaker sufficient condition with $\lfloor\sqrt{n-1}\rfloor$ also fails. This is fully consistent with the conditional cover theorem: its missing hypothesis does not follow for these witnesses.

Over a prime field, the mere existence of a natural-number multiplier is almost vacuous for nonzero steps. Indeed, for any $d,e\ne0$, the residue $e/d$ has a representative in $\{1,\ldots,N-1\}$ and gives $e=td$. What is not automatic is the small representative bound
$t\le\lenfiftyone S/k$ for the desired square side $k$. Separate length bounds, density bounds, and Bohr control at an earlier stage cannot be read as that integer bound without an additional argument.

\section[{A conditional covering repair and its exact scope\srctag{51}}]{A conditional covering repair and its exact scope}\label{gsr:en:51:sec:d9}\label{gsr:en:51:sec:cover}
\srcnote{51}{Section 9}
A finite cover suffices for dense-square extraction; an exact disjoint grid is unnecessary. This elementary observation is already reflected in the newer source. We give an endpoint-contained proof because it makes the integer fit particularly transparent, then compare it with the actual padded-cover implementation.

\begin{proposition}[Endpoint-contained common-step cover]\label{gsr:en:51:prop:cover}
Let $S=P(a,d;L)$ and $T=P(b,e;M)$ be proper progressions in a cyclic group. Suppose $e\ne0$, $e=td$ for a positive integer $t$, and let $k$ be an integer satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:51:eq:fit}
 1\le k\le M,\qquad tk\le L.
\end{equation}
If $D\subseteq S\times T$ and $|D|\ge\delta LM$ with $\delta\ge0$, there are proper progressions $V\subseteq S$, $W\subseteq T$, both of step $e$ and length $k$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:51:eq:coverdensity}
 |D\cap(V\times W)|\ge\frac\delta4 k^2.
\end{equation}
Any property of $D$ inherited by restriction, including agreement with a fixed bilinear function, persists on this intersection. Primality is not required.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Split the indices $0,\ldots,L-1$ of $S$ by residue modulo $t$. Since $tk\le L$, all $t$ residue chains are nonempty, and their lengths $n_a$ are either $\lfloor L/t\rfloor$ or $\lceil L/t\rceil$, hence at least $k$. Each is a proper progression of step $td=e$, inherited from the injective indexing of $S$, and $\sum_an_a=L$.

For a chain of $n\ge k$ points, write $n=Ak+r$ with $A\ge1$ and $0\le r<k$. Take the consecutive length-$k$ blocks starting at
$0,k,\ldots,(A-1)k$. If $r>0$, append the terminal length-$k$ block starting at $n-k$. These blocks cover the chain, stay inside it, and have total length
\[
 k\lceil n/k\rceil<n+k\le2n.
\]
Apply this to every residue chain of $S$. The resulting step-$e$ cover has total length $C_S<2L$. Apply the same construction directly to $T$, obtaining a step-$e$ cover with total length $C_T<2M$.

All product cells $V_i\times W_j$ are proper common-step $k\times k$ squares, and they cover $S\times T$, possibly with overlap. Counting members of $D$ with multiplicity gives
\[
 \sum_{i,j}|D\cap(V_i\times W_j)|\ge|D|\ge\delta LM,
 \qquad \sum_{i,j}|V_i\times W_j|=C_SC_T<4LM.
\]
The weighted average density is at least $\delta LM/(C_SC_T)\ge\delta/4$, so some cell has the required density. Restriction gives the final assertion.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Square root rounding and the current constants}
For $M\ge2$, put $k=\lfloor\sqrt{M-1}\rfloor$. Then $k\ge1$ and
$k^2\le M-1<(k+1)^2$. Since $M$ is an integer, this implies
$M\le(k+1)^2$, and therefore
\[
 k\ge\sqrt M-1.
\]
Consequently the additional integer budget
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:51:eq:weakerfit}
 \exists t\ge1:\quad \stfiftyone U=t\stfiftyone S,\qquad
 t\lfloor\sqrt{\lenfiftyone U-1}\rfloor\le\lenfiftyone S
\end{equation}
is sufficient, with $T=U+y$, for the intended side-length lower bound. Using the Stage 13.9 density $\delta=2^{-135}\alpha^{704}$ gives exactly the weakened Corollary 13.10 coefficient
$\delta/4=2^{-137}\alpha^{704}$. For $M=1$, the required lower side length is zero; choosing a singleton in each nonempty ambient factor and averaging handles this case directly. For $M=0$ the positive-length covering statement above is not applicable, and no such case is used in our counterexample.

The stronger fit $t(M-1)\le L$ permits $k=M-1$ when $M\ge2$. This is a conditional increase in the extracted side length, not a claim that the existing stage data imply such a fit.

\subsection{What is already present in the newer source}
The file \codefiftyone{Proofs13CommonStepCover.lean} at the later pin contains the declarations
\codefiftyone{bilinear\_\allowbreak square\_\allowbreak of\_\allowbreak integer\_\allowbreak step\_\allowbreak fit} and
\codefiftyone{corollary\_\allowbreak 13\_\allowbreak 10\_\allowbreak of\_\allowbreak integer\_\allowbreak step\_\allowbreak fit}. The former assumes a prime modulus, proper input progressions, $e\ne0$, $e=td$, and precisely $t>0$, $k>0$, $tk\le L$, $k\le M$, together with support, density, and bilinearity. It constructs equal-length common-step progressions and a retained subset $E\subseteq D$ of density at least $\delta/4$ on their product.

Its cover is padded: for each residue class it uses blocks indexed through
$\lfloor L/(tk)\rfloor$, with the final block allowed to extend beyond the original endpoint. The total indexed capacity is
\[
 t\bigl(\lfloor L/(tk)\rfloor+1\bigr)k\le L+tk\le2L.
\]
The analogous capacity for the second coordinate is at most $2M$. Properness of the padded cells follows from nonzero step and $k\le M\le N$ in a prime modulus. Thus the output progressions need not themselves be subsets of the input progressions, but the selected set remains a subset of $D$. This differs from Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:51:prop:cover}, whose cells stay inside both original factors and whose proof works without primality.

The source's Corollary 13.10 wrapper uses $k=\lfloor\sqrt M\rfloor$ and assumes \eqref{gsr:en:51:eq:upstreamfit}, together with positive $M$, the Stage 13.9 predicate, proper $S$, and the support condition. It achieves the same required bound $k\ge\sqrt M-1$ and quarter-density coefficient. We credit this as an existing source theorem, rather than presenting the covering repair as a missing formal result. We inspected the declaration and proof text but did not recompile it or perform a Lean axiom audit in this work.

Neither cover proves \codefiftyone{Corollary1310Grid}: overlapping or padded covers are sufficient for a dense-cell argument but do not supply an exact disjoint partition. The positive result in Section~\ref{gsr:en:51:sec:constructive} obtains suitable geometry for selected witnesses by preserving a short parent and choosing a new localized height progression.

\subsection{The complete fixed-density source theorem}\label{gsr:en:51:sec:completecurrent}
At commit \texttt{77f7d8c1f7506254c0b2a49ce9f80ffca8d3675c}, retrieved on 7 October 2026, \codefiftyone{Proofs13CompleteSquareExtraction.lean} already contains a full context-to-square theorem. Its declaration, lines 39--48, has the precise quantifiers
\[
 \forall\alpha\in(0,1]\ \exists N_0(\alpha)\ 
 \forall N\ge N_0(\alpha)\text{ prime}\ 
 \forall\text{ contexts of exact density }\alpha.
\]
For each such context it constructs proper equal-length progressions $V,W$ with the same nonzero step and a set $B\subseteq A\cap(V\times W)$ on which the original $\phi$ is bilinear, with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:51:eq:latestcomplete}
 \begin{gathered}
 \lenfiftyone V=\lenfiftyone W\ge N^{\gamma(\alpha)},\qquad
 |B|\ge2^{-137}\alpha^{704}\lenfiftyone V\,\lenfiftyone W,\\
 \gamma(\alpha)=\frac{2^{-386}\alpha^{1856}}{2^{13\qth(\alpha)}}
              =\frac{\beta f g}{4}>0,\qquad
 g=2^{-284}\alpha^{1408}.
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
Its lines 13--29 define the exponent and establish this closed form. All intermediate data and square geometry are constructed in that source theorem. Therefore the actual-chain square construction is not described here as missing from the latest inspected upstream source. The stage, grid and explicit budget files were re-fetched at this pin and are byte-identical to the primary snapshots used in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:51:thm:main}.

There is a useful exact comparison with the direct finite-budget repair in Section~\ref{gsr:en:51:sec:constructive}. On the original budget range $0<\alpha\le1/6$, its lower bound is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:51:eq:latestcomparison}
 (cN^\beta)^{fg/2}-1=c^{fg/2}N^{2\gamma(\alpha)}-1.
\end{equation}
For each fixed $\alpha$, the positive constant $c^{fg/2}$ and exponent $\gamma(\alpha)>0$ imply that this is at least $N^{\gamma(\alpha)}$ for sufficiently large $N$: putting $x=N^{\gamma(\alpha)}$, the inequality $c^{fg/2}x^2-1\ge x$ holds eventually. Thus the clean power in \eqref{gsr:en:51:eq:latestcomplete} is consistent with the more local, constant-bearing bound; no new optimal global exponent is claimed. The source theorem additionally covers the full density range up to one, which our original six-budget corollary does not assert.

The older fixed-density quantifier order does not itself give one threshold depending only on a positive lower density bound for all varying actual densities above it. The later uniform theorem in Section~\ref{gsr:en:51:sec:uniformcurrent} supplies that stronger quantifier order. There is a precise integrality issue with the older exact-density quantifier order. For a fixed irrational $\alpha$, the identity $|A|=\alpha N^2$ is impossible for every positive integer $N$. For a fixed rational $\alpha=a/b\in(0,1)$ in lowest terms, integrality forces $b\mid N^2$. With $N$ prime and $b>1$, this can hold only for a prime dividing the fixed denominator $b$, and hence for no sufficiently large prime. Thus the pointwise fixed-exact-density statement is eventually vacuous for every fixed $\alpha\in(0,1)$; $\alpha=1$ is the remaining case. This does not make the stated theorem false or invalidate its constructive proof. It explains why that older theorem type alone cannot provide a nonvacuous threshold uniform over the actual densities of arbitrary admissible contexts. Our strip contexts have varying actual density for arbitrarily large primes, so the finite-budget obstruction and its compatible re-selection examples do not have this vacuity. This limitation concerns the older API, not the latest uniform theorem. Reconciliation with unchanged catalogue or printed target statements remains a separate question outside this report. In particular, \eqref{gsr:en:51:eq:latestcomplete} does not assert a grid for an arbitrary previously selected Stage 13.9 witness or a side bound in terms of that witness's actual length. We inspected and byte-verified this source but did not rerun its Lean build or axiom checks. The later source amendment below completes the report's dated comparison.

\subsection{A restricted sharpness statement}
The uniform factor $1/4$ is asymptotically sharp if one insists on the prescribed step and side $M-1$. Work in an integer $M\times M$ box, with $M\ge3$, and place one unit of mass at each of its four corners. The ambient density is $4/M^2$. Every contained consecutive $(M-1)\times(M-1)$ square contains exactly one corner and has density $1/(M-1)^2$. The ratio of output to ambient density is
\[
 \frac{M^2}{4(M-1)^2}\longrightarrow\frac14.
\]
The same example embeds without wrap in a sufficiently large cyclic group. This proves only the stated fixed-step, prescribed-length sharpness. It does not prove optimality if arbitrary other steps or shorter output progressions are allowed, and it is not a sharpness statement for the square-root side length used in the source wrapper.

\section[{A direct repair for suitably selected witnesses\srctag{51}}]{A direct repair for suitably selected witnesses}\label{gsr:en:51:sec:d10}\label{gsr:en:51:sec:constructive}
\srcnote{51}{Section 10}
The obstruction identifies information that a lossy retained interface cannot recover for arbitrary witnesses. It does not prevent a better selection from carrying that information. We now prove an existential repair by preserving the short parent already used in the actual Stage 13.6 construction, localizing the coefficient extraction, and taking a final square of side $\lenfiftyone U-1$.

The geometric arguments below are self-contained. One analytic input is imported from the pinned source and is stated explicitly. We do not reprove that analytic theorem or assert a new Lean verification of the resulting repair.

\subsection{The imported all-scale coefficient input}
\paragraph{Source input.}
The theorem \codefiftyone{extract\_\allowbreak bilinear\_\allowbreak cell} in
\codefiftyone{Proofs13CoefficientPartition.lean}, lines 84--127 at commit
\texttt{2548e7fffc64de1a05eadae81b9247d9b9042c3b}, supplies the following statement. Let $N$ be prime, $T$ a proper progression of nonzero step and positive length $v$, $X_0$ a nonempty column set, and $J_0\subseteq T$. Suppose $0<\delta\le1$, the maps $A_c,B_c$ are order-eight Freiman on $J_0$, and
\[
 C_0\subseteq X_0\times(J_0+y),\qquad |C_0|\ge\delta|X_0|v,
 \qquad \phi(x,z)=A_c(z-y)+B_c(z-y)x\quad((x,z)\in C_0).
\]
Then there is a proper nonzero-step progression $U\subseteq T$ such that, with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:51:eq:analyticinput}
 e=\delta^2/2^{14},\qquad
 D=\{(x,z)\in C_0:z-y\in U\},
\end{equation}
one has
\[
 \lenfiftyone U\ge v^e,\qquad |D|\ge\delta|X_0|\lenfiftyone U,
 \qquad \phi\text{ is bilinear on }D.
\]
There is no lower-scale premise such as $8\le v^e$ in this source theorem. Its proof applies the existing all-scale simultaneous affine partition to the two coefficient maps on their one shared domain, then uses weighted selection. For $q\ge1$, the definition in \codefiftyone{Proofs07SimultaneousLinearity.lean}, lines 1075--1077, is $\codefiftyone{cor711Exponent}(\delta,q)=2^{-14}\delta^2/q$, giving the displayed one-domain exponent at $q=1$. In particular, the two maps do not incur two independent exponent losses.

\subsection{Short-carrier rectification and balanced parents}
\begin{lemma}[Rectification inside a short progression]\label{gsr:en:51:lem:rectify}
Let $P$ be a proper progression in $\F_N$ of nonzero step $d$ and length $n_P$, with $2(n_P-1)<N$. If a proper progression $X_1$ of length at least two has carrier contained in $P$, then, after possibly reversing its indexing, it has step $ad$ for a positive ordinary integer $a$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:51:eq:rectifiedspan}
 a(\lenfiftyone{X_1}-1)\le n_P-1.
\end{equation}
Reversal leaves its carrier and length unchanged.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Normalize $P$ by the affine bijection $z\mapsto(z-P.start)/d$.
The successive points of $X_1$ have unique indices $i_j\in\{0,\ldots,n_P-1\}$. Every difference $i_{j+1}-i_j$ is in $[-(n_P-1),n_P-1]$ and represents the same residue $\stfiftyone{X_1}/d$. Two such integer representatives differ in absolute value by at most $2(n_P-1)<N$, so they are equal as integers. Write their common value as $a_0$; it is nonzero because the progression is proper and has at least two points. Thus $i_j=i_0+ja_0$. Reverse the progression if $a_0<0$ and put $a=|a_0|$. The difference of its extreme indices proves \eqref{gsr:en:51:eq:rectifiedspan}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Balanced aligned parent partition]\label{gsr:en:51:lem:balanced}
Let $L\ge2$, $a\ge1$, and $a(L-1)<q_Q$ be integers. The interval
$\{0,\ldots,q_Q-1\}$ has a disjoint partition into step-$a$ progressions, each of length between $\lceil L/2\rceil$ and $L$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Split the interval into its $a$ residue chains. Since
$q_Q\ge a(L-1)+1$, every chain has length $r_a\ge L-1$, and all chains are nonempty. For one chain of length $r_a$, put $c_a=\lceil r_a/L\rceil$ and split it into $c_a$ consecutive blocks whose lengths differ by at most one. Their lengths are $\lfloor r_a/c_a\rfloor$ or $\lceil r_a/c_a\rceil$, and they are at most $L$.
If $c_a=1$, the chain length lies in $[L-1,L]$ and hence is at least $\lceil L/2\rceil$. If $c_a\ge2$, then
\[
 r_a\ge(c_a-1)L+1,\qquad
 \frac{r_a}{c_a}\ge L-\frac{L-1}{c_a}\ge\frac{L+1}{2}.
\]
Thus the smallest block has length at least
$\lfloor(L+1)/2\rfloor=\lceil L/2\rceil$. The blocks partition each chain, so together they partition the original interval.
\end{proof}
The lower bound is optimal for this class of partitions: a chain of length $L+1$ needs at least two blocks of length at most $L$, and one block then has length at most $\lfloor(L+1)/2\rfloor=\lceil L/2\rceil$. This is a statement about the parent partition, separate from the density sharpness in Section~\ref{gsr:en:51:sec:cover}.

\subsection{The direct geometric and analytic assembly}
\begin{theorem}[Short-parent square extraction]\label{gsr:en:51:thm:repair}
Let $N$ be prime. Let $R,Q,S$ be proper progressions in $\F_N$, with all three steps nonzero, $\stfiftyone R=\stfiftyone Q$, and $S\subseteq R$. Write
\[
 n_R=\lenfiftyone R,\qquad q_Q=\lenfiftyone Q,\qquad L=\lenfiftyone S.
\]
Assume $L\ge3$, $n_R\le q_Q$, and $2(n_R-1)<N$. Let $0<\delta\le1$, $J_0\subseteq Q$, and suppose
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:51:eq:repairinputs}
 \begin{gathered}
 C\subseteq S\times(J_0+y),\qquad |C|\ge\delta Lq_Q,\\
 \phi(x,z)=A_c(z-y)+B_c(z-y)x\quad((x,z)\in C).
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
where the coefficient pair $(A_c,B_c)$ is order-eight Freiman on $J_0$.
Using the source input \eqref{gsr:en:51:eq:analyticinput}, there exist a newly selected proper nonzero-step progression $U\subseteq Q$, proper common-step progressions $V\subseteq S$, $W\subseteq U+y$ of the same nonzero step and the same length $k$, and a set $E\subseteq C\cap(V\times W)$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:51:eq:repairconclusion}
 \begin{gathered}
 k=\lenfiftyone U-1\ge\lceil L/2\rceil^{\delta^2/2^{14}}-1
           \ge L^{\delta^2/2^{15}}-1,\\
 |E|\ge(\delta/4)k^2,\qquad \phi\text{ is bilinear on }E.
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:51:lem:rectify} to $S\subseteq R$. Represent the same carrier $S$, reversing its indexing if necessary, with
\[
 \stfiftyone S=a\stfiftyone Q,\qquad a\ge1,\qquad a(L-1)\le n_R-1<q_Q.
\]
Transport Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:51:lem:balanced} through the injective indexing of $Q$.
This partitions $Q$ into proper parents $T_i$ of step $\stfiftyone S$ and lengths
\[
 h:=\lceil L/2\rceil\le v_i:=\lenfiftyone{T_i}\le L.
\]
Every parent is short enough to rectify its subprogressions, since
$2(v_i-1)\le2(L-1)\le2(n_R-1)<N$.

Let $C_i=\{(x,z)\in C:z-y\in T_i\}$. This is a disjoint partition of $C$, and $\sum_i v_i=q_Q$. Weighted averaging therefore gives one parent $T=T_i$, of length $v$, with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:51:eq:weightedparent}
 |C_i|\ge\delta Lv.
\end{equation}
This uses actual pair mass, not merely the number of retained heights. Put $J_T=J_0\cap T$ and $C_T=C_i$. Its support is $S\times(J_T+y)$; the original row formula and the Freiman coefficient pair restrict to $J_T$. Projection of the pair onto either coordinate gives the two scalar Freiman maps. Also $|C_T|\le L|J_T|$, so \eqref{gsr:en:51:eq:weightedparent} implies $|J_T|\ge\delta v$, as needed within the analytic source proof.

Invoke \eqref{gsr:en:51:eq:analyticinput} with column set $S$, parent $T$, domain $J_T$, set $C_T$, and the same $y,\phi,A_c,B_c,\delta$. It supplies $U\subseteq T$ with
\[
 M:=\lenfiftyone U\ge v^e,\qquad e=\delta^2/2^{14},\qquad
 D=\{(x,z)\in C_T:z-y\in U\},\qquad |D|\ge\delta LM,
\]
and bilinearity on $D$. No density is lost in this localization. Because $U\subseteq T$ and $C$ was supported over $J_0$, the same set is exactly
\[
 D=\{(x,z)\in C:z-y\in U\cap J_0\}.
\]
Since $L\ge3$, we have $v\ge2$ and $v^e>1$, so the integer $M$ is at least two.
Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:51:lem:rectify} again to $U\subseteq T$, reversing $U$ if necessary. Its carrier and $D$ stay unchanged, while its step becomes
\[
 \stfiftyone U=b\stfiftyone S,\qquad b\ge1,\qquad b(M-1)\le v-1\le L-1.
\]
Thus Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:51:prop:cover} applies to $S$ and $U+y$ with the stronger choice $k=M-1$. It gives the asserted $V,W,E$, density, containments, and bilinearity. Finally,
\[
 k=M-1\ge v^e-1\ge\lceil L/2\rceil^e-1\ge L^{e/2}-1.
\]
The last inequality follows from $\lceil L/2\rceil^2\ge L$ for every integer $L\ge3$.
\end{proof}

For $L=1$ or $2$, positive mass makes $C$ nonempty. One point of $C$ gives a proper singleton square at any chosen nonzero step, carrying density one and a constant bilinear value. It meets the weaker effective target $L^{\delta^2/2^{15}}-1$. These cases are not needed under the actual width budget.

\subsection{The original phase and the height offset are preserved}
All selections above restrict original carriers or reverse their indexing. The phase is always the original $\phi$, evaluated in the original coordinates. To see the height offset explicitly, the analytic source proof produces affine row coefficients on $U\cap J_0$ of the form
\[
 A_c(h)=a_1h+a_0,\qquad B_c(h)=b_1h+b_0.
\]
For an actual point $(x,z)\in D$, substitute $h=z-y$ to obtain
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:51:eq:originalphase}
 \phi(x,z)=(a_0-a_1y)+(b_0-b_1y)x+a_1z+b_1xz.
\end{equation}
This is a bilinear formula in the original variables, with both intercept corrections included. Reversing $S$ or $U$ does not replace $x$ or $h$ by a new coordinate: it merely reorders the same carrier. Consequently the ambient functions and the formula \eqref{gsr:en:51:eq:originalphase} are unchanged. In the actual stage chain, $E\subseteq C\subseteq B\subseteq A$, so the original-domain containment is also preserved.

\subsection{Recovering the short parent from the actual budget construction}
The hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:51:thm:repair} can be obtained for suitably selected outputs under the existing six budgets. This requires following the actual construction, rather than taking an arbitrary witness from its lossy existential conclusion.

The source \codefiftyone{common\_\allowbreak step\_\allowbreak row\_\allowbreak selection} in
\codefiftyone{Proofs13CommonStepSelection.lean}, lines 92--132, selects $R$ with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:51:eq:shortactual}
 \lenfiftyone R=m\quad\text{or}\quad\lenfiftyone R=m+1.
\end{equation}
The proof of \codefiftyone{lemma\_\allowbreak 13\_\allowbreak 6\_\allowbreak of\_\allowbreak short\_\allowbreak difference\_\allowbreak rules} receives this fact as its local length alternative and constructs $F$ from that same $R$. The subsequent Bohr-model and initial-stage wrappers do not alter $R$, but their stated conclusions retain only $\lenfiftyone R\le\lenfiftyone Q$. Thus \eqref{gsr:en:51:eq:shortactual} can be preserved by using those same witness constructions and exporting the length alternative. It cannot be inferred for every arbitrary $F$ satisfying the wrapper's weaker conclusion.

Put $A_0=cN^\beta$, with $c,\beta,f,W$ as in \eqref{gsr:en:51:eq:budgetnotation}, and let $L=\lenfiftyone S$ for the Stage 13.7 output. The existing lower-length and width budgets, followed by the Stage 13.7 length bound, give
\[
 L\ge(\lenfiftyone R)^f\ge A_0^f\ge W=\delta^{-1}\ge2^{135},
 \qquad \delta=2^{-135}\alpha^{704}.
\]
Properness and $S\subseteq R$ give $L\le\lenfiftyone R\le m+1$, so $m\ge3$. Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:51:eq:actualshortness}
 2(\lenfiftyone R-1)\le2m<m^2\le N.
\end{equation}
The steps of $R,Q$ agree and are nonzero by Stage 13.6, while $\lenfiftyone R\le m+1\le\lenfiftyone Q$. The properness and nonzero step of $S$ are explicit Stage 13.7 conditions. The Stage 13.8 support, mass, row formula and pair Freiman property give \eqref{gsr:en:51:eq:repairinputs}. Reversing the indexing of $S$ preserves these stages: their support and row statements concern its carrier and the actual first coordinate.

\begin{corollary}[Existential square extraction under the existing budgets]\label{gsr:en:51:cor:actualrepair}
For every prime $N$, context, Stage 13.4 and 13.5 data, and integer $m$ satisfying all the hypotheses of the pinned budget theorem, its actual constructions can be used to select $F,G,H$ satisfying the exact Stage 13.6--13.8 predicates and \eqref{gsr:en:51:eq:shortactual}, and then a proper same-step bilinear square with retained set in $C\subseteq A$, density at least $2^{-137}\alpha^{704}$, and side $k$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:51:eq:effectivewidth}
 \begin{split}
 k&\ge\lceil L/2\rceil^{2^{-284}\alpha^{1408}}-1
      \ge L^{2^{-285}\alpha^{1408}}-1\\
  &\ge\bigl(cN^\beta\bigr)^{2^{-385}\alpha^{1856}}-1.
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
This is a mathematical consequence using the imported analytic source input; no new formal implementation of this corollary is asserted.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The preceding argument supplies every hypothesis of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:51:thm:repair}.
Here $e=\delta^2/2^{14}=2^{-284}\alpha^{1408}$ and $\delta/4=2^{-137}\alpha^{704}$. The last line of \eqref{gsr:en:51:eq:effectivewidth} follows from $L\ge(cN^\beta)^f$ and
$f(e/2)=2^{-385}\alpha^{1856}$.
\end{proof}

\section[{The precise retained interface\srctag{52}}]{The precise retained interface}\label{gsr:en:52:sec:d2}\label{gsr:en:52:sec:interface}
\srcnote{52}{Section 2}
We translate the source into mathematical notation before choosing witnesses. All finite counts are unnormalized, and all real exponent laws below have positive bases.

\subsection{Progressions and ambient affine maps}
A modular progression $P=(a,d,L)$ has carrier
\[
 [P]=\{a+jd:0\le j<L\}\subseteq\ZN,
 \qquad \len P=L.
\]
It is proper when $|[P]|=L$. The definition concerns injectivity of the parameterization; it does not forbid a carrier that crosses the conventional residue cut. Nonzero step is a separate condition. The predicate \codefiftyone{LinearOn} on $U\subseteq\ZN$ means
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:52:eq:ambient}
 \exists a,b\in\ZN\quad \forall x\in U,\quad f(x)=ax+b.
\end{equation}
It does not mean merely that $f(a_0+jd_0)$ is affine as a function of the integer index $j$.

\subsection{Context and arrangement normalization}
An order-eight Freiman homomorphism on $V$ preserves equality between sums of eight elements of $V$, with repetitions allowed. A context comprises $A\subseteq(\ZN)^2$, a total function $\phi:(\ZN)^2\to\ZN$, and reals $\alpha,\eta$ satisfying
\[
 0<\alpha\le1,\quad |A|=\alpha N^2,\quad \eta=2^{-44},
\]
the separate order-eight Freiman property on all horizontal and vertical sections of $A$, and the required mostly-respected inequality.

To specify the latter, an eight-arrangement at fixed height $h$ consists of sixteen $x_i$ and sixteen $y_i$ with
\[
 \sum_{i=1}^{8}x_i=\sum_{i=9}^{16}x_i,
 \qquad (x_i,y_i),(x_i,y_i+h)\in A \quad(1\le i\le16).
\]
It is respected if the first eight and last eight sums of
$\phi(x_i,y_i+h)-\phi(x_i,y_i)$ agree. Write $C(h)$ for the number of contained arrangements and $C_\phi(h)$ for the number of respected contained arrangements. The context requires
\[
 (1-\eta)\sum_h C(h)\le\sum_h C_\phi(h).
\]
A height is good if $(1-2\eta)C(h)\le C_\phi(h)$, and strong if it is good and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:52:eq:strong}
 C(h)\ge \alpha^{32}N^{31}/16.
\end{equation}
For records $D,E$, define
\[
 \Crit=([E.Q]\cap D.H)\cap\{h:h\text{ is strong}\}.
\]
This is exactly \codefiftyone{criticalHeights}.

\subsection{Stage 13.6 in full}
Write
\begin{align*}
 \delta&=2^{-43}\alpha^{224},&
 \lambda&=2^{-48}\alpha^{256},&
 \varepsilon&=2^{-100}\alpha^{448},\\
 K_{13}&=2^{114}\alpha^{-320},&
 Q_{13}&=2^{2^{20}}\alpha^{-2^{21}},&
 \zeta_{13}&=2^{-228K_{13}}\alpha^{576K_{13}},\\
 c&=\zeta_{13}/2,& \beta&=2^{-13Q_{13}}.
\end{align*}
For $h\in\ZN$, put
\[
 \edges_h=\{(x,y):(x,y),(x,y+h)\in A\},\qquad
 Y_h^R=\{(x,y)\in F.Y(h):x\in[F.R]\}.
\]
The full \codefiftyone{IsStage136Data} predicate is the conjunction of:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{136.\arabic*}]
\item $F.R$ and $E.Q$ have the same nonzero step, and $F.R$ is proper;
\item $cN^\beta\le\len(F.R)$;
\item for each $h\in\Crit$, $F.Y(h)\subseteq\edges_h$, $\delta N^2\le|F.Y(h)|$, and the vertical difference of $\phi$ is of the form $a_hx+b_h$ on $Y_h^R$;
\item $\delta\len(F.R)N|\Crit|\le\sum_{h\in\Crit}|Y_h^R|$;
\item $\lambda\len(E.Q)\len(F.R)N\le\sum_{h\in\Crit}|Y_h^R|$.
\end{enumerate}
In particular there is no conjunct $\len(F.R)\le\len(E.Q)$ and no requirement that $F.R$ lie in $E.Q$.

\subsection{The two Stage 13.7 conclusions}
A candidate output $G$ consists of $y_0\in\ZN$, a progression $S$, and $B\subseteq(\ZN)^2$. Write $L=\len S$. The weak predicate comprises:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{137.\arabic*}]
\item $S$ has nonzero step, is proper, and $[S]\subseteq[F.R]$;
\item $(\len(F.R))^\varepsilon\le L$;
\item $B\subseteq[S]\times(y_0+\Crit)$;
\item $\delta L|\Crit|\le|B|$;
\item $\lambda\len(E.Q)L\le|B|$;
\item for every $h\in\Crit$, the map $x\mapsto\phi(x,y_0+h)$ is ambient affine on $U_h=\{x\in[S]:(x,y_0+h)\in B\}$.
\end{enumerate}
The full predicate is precisely this weak predicate together with $B\subseteq A$. We will contradict only conditions 137.1--137.4 and 137.6. Dropping the second mass lower bound or the original-domain requirement cannot repair the examples.

\subsection{The genuine initial-stage predicates}\label{gsr:en:52:subsec:initial}
For the strengthening we also need the complete initial-stage interface. Define
\[
 \theta_1=2^{-1882}\theta^{10477},\qquad
 Q_{134}(\theta)=2^{1882}\theta^{-10479}.
\]
The record $D$ stores $q,m_D,P,H_{134}$ and $q$ coefficient pairs $(a_i,b_i)$. The Stage 13.4 conditions are:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{134.\arabic*}]
\item $q>0$, $P$ proper with nonzero step, and $H_{134}\subseteq[P]$;
\item $q\le Q_{134}(\theta)$;
\item $m_D\le\theta_1N^{\theta_1^2/(16q)}/(64\pi)<m_D+1$;
\item $\len P=m_D$ or $\len P+1=m_D$;
\item $\alpha^{32}N^{31}\len P/8\le\sum_{h\in H_{134},\ h\text{ good}}C(h)$;
\item for $h\in H_{134}$ and every $r$ with $|\widehat f_h(r)|\ge\theta N^2$, there is $i$ with $r=a_ih+b_i$.
\end{enumerate}
Here $f_h(x)=|\{y:(x,y)\in\edges_h\}|$, and the source transform is unnormalized:
\[
 \widehat f(r)=\sum_{x\in\ZN}f(x)\exp(\pm2\pi i rx/N).
\]
The sign convention has no effect on the bounds in this report. The separate theorem \codefiftyone{lemma\_13\_4} requires primality and $0<\theta\le\alpha^{32}/4$. Our construction verifies its conclusion predicate directly and satisfies this numerical threshold condition, but does not assert primality.

The Stage 13.5 record stores $Q$. Its predicate requires:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{135.\arabic*}]
\item $Q$ proper with nonzero step and $[Q]\subseteq[P]$;
\item $(\len P)^{2^{-12q}}/2\le\len Q$;
\item for every $i$ and $h\in[Q]$,
$\ca{(a_ih+b_i)d_Q}\le(\len P)^{-2^{-11q}}N$;
\item $\alpha^{32}\len Q/20\le|\Crit|$.
\end{enumerate}
The quantity $\ca{r}$ is the least absolute value of an integer representative of $r$. This spells out every extra premise used later.

\section[{The common dyadic strip\srctag{52}}]{The common dyadic strip}\label{gsr:en:52:sec:d3}\label{gsr:en:52:sec:strip}
\srcnote{52}{Section 3}
For this section take any integer $k\ge5$ and set
\[
 N=2^k,\quad m=2^{k-4},\quad
 T=\{2j\bmod N:0\le j<m\},\quad A=T\times\ZN.
\]
Let $P_0=(0,2,m)$ and define the total function
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:52:eq:phi}
 \phi(x,y)=\left\lfloor\frac{x.\mathrm{val}}2\right\rfloor\pmod N,
\end{equation}
where $x.\mathrm{val}\in\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$ is the canonical representative. In particular $\phi(2j,y)=j$ for $0\le j<m$, and $\phi$ is independent of $y$ everywhere.

\begin{lemma}[The context is genuine]\label{gsr:en:52:lem:context}
With $\alpha=1/16$ and $\eta=2^{-44}$, these data satisfy every field of \codefiftyone{Section13Context}. Moreover every height is strong.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The representatives $2j$ are distinct and less than $N$, so $|T|=m$ and $P_0$ is proper with nonzero step. Hence
$|A|=mN=\alpha N^2$, with $0<\alpha\le1$.

Every nonempty vertical section is the full group, and the corresponding map is constant. Empty vertical sections give a vacuous Freiman condition. For a horizontal section, take indices $j_1,\ldots,j_8,j'_1,\ldots,j'_8\in\{0,\ldots,m-1\}$ whose doubled sums agree modulo $N$. Put
\[
 \Delta=\sum_{i=1}^8j_i-\sum_{i=1}^8j'_i\in\Z.
\]
The domain equality implies $N\mid2\Delta$, hence $(N/2)\mid\Delta$. But
\[
 |\Delta|\le8(m-1)=N/2-8<N/2.
\]
Thus $\Delta=0$, and the image sums agree even as integers. This proves the order-eight condition with repeated entries allowed.

All vertical differences of $\phi$ vanish. Every contained arrangement is consequently respected, globally and at each height. Thus $C_\phi(h)=C(h)$, which implies the mostly-respected and good-height inequalities because $\eta>0$.

For the strong-height lower bound, let $r(s)$ be the number of ordered eight-tuples in $T$ with sum $s$, and put $E_8(T)=\sum_s r(s)^2$. There are $m^8$ such tuples in total. Cauchy--Schwarz over the $N$ possible sums gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:52:eq:energy}
 E_8(T)\ge m^{16}/N.
\end{equation}
For each fixed height $h$, an additive sixteen-tuple of first coordinates permits exactly $N^{16}$ independent choices of the second coordinates: both endpoints of every resulting edge belong to $A$. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:52:eq:count}
 C(h)=C_\phi(h)=N^{16}E_8(T)
 \ge m^{16}N^{15}=\alpha^{16}N^{31}
 \ge\alpha^{32}N^{31}/16.
\end{equation}
The height is fixed in this count, so there is no extra factor $N$. The sixteen second coordinates are independent, so none of those sixteen factors is missing. This proves~\eqref{gsr:en:52:eq:strong} at every height.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Uniform edge data]\label{gsr:en:52:lem:edges}
For every height, $\edges_h=A$, $f_h=N\one_T$, and the vertical difference of $\phi$ is zero. If a progression $R$ contains $T$ and $F.Y(h)=A$, then $Y_h^R=A$ and its affine difference coefficients can be taken to be zero.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The two edge endpoints lie in $A$ exactly when their common first coordinate is in $T$. All remaining assertions follow directly.
\end{proof}

At $\alpha=2^{-4}$ the constants become
\begin{align}\label{gsr:en:52:eq:constants}
 \delta&=2^{-939},&\lambda&=2^{-1072},&\varepsilon&=2^{-1892},\\
 K_{13}&=2^{1394},&Q_{13}&=2^{9\cdot2^{20}},&
 c&=2^{-2532K_{13}-1}.\nonumber
\end{align}
Indeed $43+4\cdot224=939$, $48+4\cdot256=1072$, $100+4\cdot448=1892$, $114+4\cdot320=1394$, and $228+4\cdot576=2532$. Also $2^{20}+4\cdot2^{21}=9\cdot2^{20}$. In particular
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:52:eq:easybounds}
 0<c<\alpha,\quad 0<\beta<1,\quad
 0<\delta<\alpha<1,\quad 0<\lambda<1.
\end{equation}
For every $N\ge1$, it follows that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:52:eq:Rlength}
 cN^\beta\le cN<\alpha N=m.
\end{equation}
This settles the Stage 13.6 length condition without evaluating $K_{13}$, $Q_{13}$, or $N$ numerically.

\section[{The exact step two counterexample\srctag{52}}]{The exact step two counterexample}\label{gsr:en:52:sec:d4}\label{gsr:en:52:sec:base}
\srcnote{52}{Section 4}
We now prove Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:52:thm:base}. Take its specified $k$ and the common context above. Set
\[
 D.q=1,\quad D.m=m,\quad D.P=P_0,\quad D.H=T,
 \quad D.a(0)=D.b(0)=0,
\]
\[
 E.Q=P_0,\qquad F.R=P_0,\qquad F.Y(h)=A\quad(h\in\ZN).
\]
All heights are strong, so $\Crit=T$ and $|\Crit|=m>0$.

\subsection{Every required premise}
The common step is the nonzero residue $2$, and $F.R$ is proper. Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:52:eq:Rlength} proves the progression length bound. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:52:lem:edges} gives the exact edge-domain and restricted-edge identities, and the zero affine vertical difference. Edge density follows from $|A|=\alpha N^2\ge\delta N^2$.

The sum in the last two Stage 13.6 conjuncts is exactly
\[
 \sum_{h\in T}|Y_h^R|=m|A|=m^2N.
\]
The required lower bounds are respectively $\delta m^2N$ and $\lambda m^2N$, so both hold by~\eqref{gsr:en:52:eq:easybounds}. This verifies the whole predicate, rather than appealing to the existence theorem of Stage 13.6.

The extra Stage 13.5 predicate also holds. Its geometric assertions are immediate from $Q=P=P_0$; its length condition follows from $m\ge1$ and $0<2^{-12}\le1$; all coefficient expressions vanish; and its critical-height condition is $\alpha^{32}m/20\le m$. No Stage 13.4 certificate is inferred from the record name or these checks.

\subsection{The affine obstruction}
\begin{lemma}[At most one point per row]\label{gsr:en:52:lem:one}
For any $a,b,y\in\ZN$, the equation $\phi(x,y)=ax+b$ holds at at most one point $x\in T$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If it holds at $2j$ and $2j'$ with $0\le j,j'<m$, subtraction gives
\[
 (2a-1)(j-j')=0\quad\text{in }\Z/2^k\Z.
\]
The residue $2a-1$ is odd, so it is coprime to $2^k$ and is a unit. Hence $j=j'$ modulo $N$. As $j,j'\in[0,m)$ and $m<N$, they are equal as integers. Thus the two points coincide.
\end{proof}
This argument uses the prime-power structure. For an arbitrary even composite modulus an odd residue need not be a unit; the mere fact that step $2$ is a nonunit would not justify the same proof.

\subsection{The incompatible output bounds}
Suppose a weak Stage 13.7 output existed. Its row supports $U_h$ lie in $T$, so Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:52:lem:one} and the affine row condition give $|U_h|\le1$. Translation $h\mapsto y_0+h$ is injective. The support condition therefore partitions $B$ into exactly the possible rows indexed by $T$, and
\[
 |B|=\sum_{h\in T}|U_h|\le m.
\]
The first mass lower bound yields
\[
 \delta Lm\le|B|\le m,\qquad L\le\delta^{-1}=2^{939}.
\]
The output length condition yields the strict opposite:
\begin{align*}
 L\ge m^\varepsilon
 &=\left(2^{k-4}\right)^{2^{-1892}}
  =2^{(k-4)2^{-1892}}\\
 &=2^{939+2^{-1892}}>2^{939}.
\end{align*}
This contradiction proves Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:52:thm:base}. In this particular construction, the support already implies $B\subseteq T\times\ZN=A$, so the missing original-domain conjunct is not the source of failure.
