\section[{Progressions, polynomial lists, and branch masses\srctag{50}}]{Progressions, polynomial lists, and branch masses}\label{gsr:en:50:sec:d2}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:sec:definitions}
\srcnote{50}{Section 2}

\begin{definition}[Proper progression and box]
For a prime $p$, a nonempty proper modular arithmetic progression is
\[
 I=\{a+bt:0\le t<n\}\subseteq\F_p,
 \qquad b\ne0,\quad 1\le n\le p.
\]
Its length is $n=|I|$. A product box is $I_1\times\cdots\times I_D$, and its
width is $\min_i|I_i|$. A common-step box has the same difference in all axes.
The repository uses common-step boxes. Our estimates allow independent steps
and hence apply to that narrower class.
\end{definition}

Singletons can also be represented with difference zero. This harmless
representational redundancy never affects the long-axis estimates. The empty
box is allowed when discussing universal cover predicates; its width is zero,
and it contributes no mass. All counting arguments concern nonempty cells.
Properness is essential: a formal length with repeated residues cannot be used
in place of the number of distinct points.

\begin{definition}[Cover by a polynomial list]
Let $I\subseteq\F_p$ be nonempty, let $a:I\to S\subseteq\F_p$, and let $d,q$ be
nonnegative integers. Define the unnormalized optimum
\[
 \Cov_{q,d}(a;I)=
 \max_{P_1,\ldots,P_q\in\F_p[Y],\ \deg P_i\le d}
 \left|\{y\in I:a(y)\in\{P_1(y),\ldots,P_q(y)\}\}\right|.
\]
For $q=0$ the optimum is zero. Repetitions are permitted. A list of fewer than
$q$ polynomials can be padded without reducing its covered set.
\end{definition}

Write $S=\{v_1,\dots,v_R\}$ with distinct $v_j$. The symbol counts are
\[
 b_j(I)=|\{y\in I:a(y)=v_j\}|.
\]
When order matters, write $b_{(1)}\ge\cdots\ge b_{(R)}$ and
$B_s=b_{(1)}+\cdots+b_{(s)}$, with $B_0=0$. A \emph{useful constant} is a
constant polynomial whose value belongs to $S$. We count distinct useful
constants in a list; repeated copies do not create additional branches.

For a probability vector $\pi=(\pi_1,\dots,\pi_R)$, set
\[
 M_s(\pi)=\sum_{j=1}^s\pi_{(j)},\qquad M_0(\pi)=0.
\]
The sequence $M_s$ records the greatest mass that can be retained by selecting
$s$ branches. It is the relevant complexity profile in this article. It is not
being identified with Shannon entropy or with the rank of a polynomial.

\begin{definition}[Multiaffine polynomials]
A polynomial on $\F_p^D$ is multiaffine if its degree in each coordinate is at
most one. Equivalently, it has the form
\[
 \mu(z)=\sum_{J\subseteq\{1,\dots,D\}}c_J\prod_{j\in J}z_j.
\]
Constants and lower-dimensional terms are included. This is the meaning of
\filename{IsMultilinear} in the repository~\cite{repo50definitions}.
\end{definition}

In particular, fixing every coordinate except the last gives an affine
polynomial in the last coordinate. This elementary observation is the only
property of multiaffinity needed for the main counterexample.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Exact one-dimensional cover laws\srctag{50}}]{Exact one-dimensional cover laws}\label{gsr:en:50:sec:d3}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:sec:one-dimensional}
\srcnote{50}{Section 3}

\begin{lemma}[Finite-alphabet root bound]\label{gsr:en:50:bc:lem:roots}
If $P\in\F_p[Y]$ is nonconstant of degree at most $d$ and $a:I\to S$ with
$|S|=R$, then
\[
 |\{y\in I:P(y)=a(y)\}|\le dR.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The agreement set is contained in the union, over $v\in S$, of the roots of
$P-v$. Each $P-v$ is a nonzero polynomial of degree at most $d$ and therefore
has at most $d$ roots. Summing these $R$ bounds proves the claim. The usual
root bound follows by factoring out $Y-y_0$ at each distinct root, so no
restriction on the relative sizes of $d$ and $p$ is needed for the inequality.
The bound is simply uninformative when $dR\ge|I|$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Finite cover envelope and exact optimum]\label{gsr:en:50:bc:thm:exact}
Let $a:I\to S$, $|I|=n$, $|S|=R$, and $d\ge1$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:finite-envelope}
 B_{\min(q,R)}\le \Cov_{q,d}(a;I)
 \le \min\left\{n,\max_{0\le s\le\min(q,R)}
       \bigl(B_s+(q-s)dR\bigr)\right\}.
\end{equation}
If $1\le q\le R$ and $b_{(q)}\ge dR$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:exact-spectrum}
 \Cov_{q,d}(a;I)=B_q.
\end{equation}
If $b_{(q)}>dR$, every optimal list of size $q$ consists of $q$ distinct useful
constants whose total symbol mass is $B_q$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The $\min(q,R)$ heaviest useful constants establish the lower bound. Consider
any list and let $s$ be its number of distinct useful constants. They cover at
most $B_s$ points. Each remaining nonconstant polynomial covers at most $dR$
points by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:lem:roots}; an outside-alphabet constant or an
unneeded duplicate covers no additional points and can be charged the same
upper bound. The union has size at most $B_s+(q-s)dR$. This proves
\eqref{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:finite-envelope}.

When $q\le R$, for every $s\le q$,
\[
 B_q-B_s=\sum_{j=s+1}^q b_{(j)}\ge(q-s)b_{(q)}.
\]
Consequently $B_s+(q-s)dR\le B_q$ under the stated hypothesis. The lower and
upper bounds agree. If $b_{(q)}>dR$ and $s<q$, the inequality is strict. An
optimal list must therefore have $s=q$; all its entries are distinct useful
constants, and their masses must sum to $B_q$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Quantitative optimizer deficit]\label{gsr:en:50:bc:cor:deficit}
Under $1\le q\le R$ and $b_{(q)}>dR$, a list with $s$ distinct useful constants
misses at least
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:one-d-deficit}
 (q-s)(b_{(q)}-dR)
\end{equation}
points relative to the optimum $B_q$. Thus a list covering at least $B_q-D$
points has
\[
 q-s\le \frac{D}{b_{(q)}-dR}.
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Subtract its upper bound in \eqref{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:finite-envelope} from $B_q$ and use
the preceding proof.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What is and is not sharp]
The exact-optimum conclusion, and hence the leading branch-mass profile, is
sharp because the heaviest constant graphs attain it. We do not claim that the
root envelope in \eqref{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:finite-envelope} is attained for every list,
every word, or every $n,d,R$. Its utility is that the envelope becomes an exact
answer once the individual branch masses exceed the root-counting allowance.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[Prescribed approximate masses]\label{gsr:en:50:bc:cor:profile-envelope}
Suppose $|b_j/n-\pi_j|\le\varepsilon$ for every symbol. For $q\le R$,
\begin{align}
 M_q(\pi)-q\varepsilon
 &\le \frac{\Cov_{q,d}(a;I)}{n},\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:profile-lower}\\
 \frac{\Cov_{q,d}(a;I)}{n}
 &\le \min\left\{1,\max_{0\le s\le q}
 \left(M_s(\pi)+s\varepsilon+(q-s)\frac{dR}{n}\right)\right\}.
 \label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:profile-upper}
\end{align}
For the uniform profile and $n\ge dR^2$ this gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:uniform-simple}
 \frac{\Cov_{q,d}(a;I)}{n}\le q\left(\frac1R+\varepsilon\right).
\end{equation}
If $n(1/R-\varepsilon)\ge dR$, the exact value is $B_q/n$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For any set of $s$ symbols its mass is at most $M_s(\pi)+s\varepsilon$.
Selecting the $q$ symbols of largest prescribed mass gives the lower bound.
Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:thm:exact}. In the uniform case both $1/R+\varepsilon$
and $dR/n$ are bounded by $1/R+\varepsilon$, giving
\eqref{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:uniform-simple}. The last assertion follows from
$b_{(q)}\ge n(1/R-\varepsilon)$.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Product boxes, adaptive partitions, and global rigidity\srctag{50}}]{Product boxes, adaptive partitions, and global rigidity}\label{gsr:en:50:sec:d4}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:sec:boxes}
\srcnote{50}{Section 4}

\subsection{A dimension-free lifting of the obstruction}
The following statement deliberately allows far more than multiaffine graphs.
The coefficients of the final-coordinate polynomial may depend arbitrarily on
the other coordinates.

\begin{theorem}[Product-box cover law]\label{gsr:en:50:bc:thm:product}
Let $T$ be any finite nonempty set, $I\subseteq\F_p$, and $F(h,y)=a(y)$ on
$T\times I$. Suppose each candidate graph $\mu_i(h,y)$ is, for every fixed $h$,
a polynomial of degree at most $d$ in $y$. Then the maximum number of covered
points using $q$ graphs is exactly
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:product-optimum}
 |T|\Cov_{q,d}(a;I).
\end{equation}
In particular, every list covers at most $|T|$ times the upper envelope in
\eqref{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:finite-envelope}. If $1\le q\le R$ and $b_{(q)}\ge dR$, this maximum is $|T|B_q$,
and the maximum remains the same when the graphs are required to be
multiaffine in all coordinates of a product box $T\times I$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Fix $h$ and apply the definition of $\Cov_{q,d}$. Sum over $h\in T$ for the
upper bound. A maximizing univariate list, used independently of $h$, attains
\eqref{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:product-optimum} in the stated unrestricted class. Under
$b_{(q)}\ge dR$, the heaviest constants attain it; those constants are
multiaffine as well.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Adaptive partition bound]\label{gsr:en:50:bc:cor:adaptive}
Suppose $a:\F_p\to S$ is $(\pi,\varepsilon)$-balanced on every proper modular
progression of length at least $L$. Let a nonempty finite family of pairwise disjoint
nonempty product boxes $C_u=T_u\times I_u$ have $|I_u|\ge L$. On each cell choose at most
$q$ graphs with final-coordinate degree at most $d$, allowing the partition and
the lists to depend on the entire word. The covered fraction of the union is
at most
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:adaptive-profile}
 \min\left\{1,\max_{0\le s\le\min(q,R)}
   \left(M_s(\pi)+s\varepsilon+(q-s)\frac{dR}{L}\right)\right\}.
\end{equation}
For a uniform profile, $q\le R$, and $L\ge dR^2$, it is at most
$q(1/R+\varepsilon)$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:cor:profile-envelope} and
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:thm:product} separately to each cell, and sum their cardinality
bounds. Disjointness turns this sum into the total covered mass. All estimates
were established simultaneously for every allowable final axis, so no
independence between the word, the partition, and the lists is being assumed.
\end{proof}

No bound on the number of cells is needed. The other axes can be arbitrarily
short, the common differences can change between cells, and the lists may
change between fibres. Requiring every axis to be long or the differences to
agree only restricts the adversary further.

\subsection{Global polynomial stability}
The preceding fibrewise theorem is sufficient for the counterexample. When
the candidate graphs are polynomial in the base coordinates as well, one can
also control how many \emph{globally} nonconstant graphs occur in a nearly
optimal list.

\begin{lemma}[Rectangular zero bound]\label{gsr:en:50:bc:lem:grid}
Let $P\in\F_p[X_1,\dots,X_D]$ be nonzero and satisfy
$\deg_{X_i}P\le e_i$. For nonempty finite sets $A_i\subseteq\F_p$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:grid-zero}
 \frac{|\{z\in\prod_iA_i:P(z)=0\}|}{\prod_i|A_i|}
 \le \sum_{i=1}^D\frac{e_i}{|A_i|}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Induct on $D$. In dimension one this is the root bound. Write $P$ as a
polynomial in $X_D$ and choose its nonzero leading coefficient $P_0$.
Outside the zero set of $P_0$ on the base grid, the last-coordinate polynomial
has at most $e_D$ roots. On the exceptional base points allow all last
coordinates. The induction hypothesis bounds the exceptional fraction by
$\sum_{i<D}e_i/|A_i|$. Adding $e_D/|A_D|$ proves the result.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Global-graph envelope and rigidity]\label{gsr:en:50:bc:thm:global}
Let $C=A_1\times\cdots\times A_k\times I=T\times I$, and put $F(h,y)=a(y)$.
Consider polynomial graphs with base-coordinate degrees at most $e_i$ and
final-coordinate degree at most $d\ge1$. Write $\lambda_j=b_{(j)}/|I|$ and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:global-zeta}
 z_C=\sum_{i=1}^k\frac{e_i}{|A_i|}+\frac{dR}{|I|}.
\end{equation}
Any list of $q\le R$ graphs with $s$ distinct globally useful constants covers
at most the following fraction of $C$:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:global-envelope}
 \sum_{j=1}^s\lambda_j+(q-s)z_C.
\end{equation}
If $\lambda_q\ge z_C$, the optimum is $\sum_{j=1}^q\lambda_j$. If
$\lambda_q>z_C$, a list whose covered fraction is within $\Delta$ of the optimum
satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:global-stability}
 q-s\le\frac{\Delta}{\lambda_q-z_C}.
\end{equation}
In particular, every optimal list consists of globally constant branches.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For a globally nonconstant polynomial $\mu$ and each occupied symbol $v_j$,
the polynomial $\mu-v_j$ is nonzero. Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:lem:grid} on
$T\times I_j$, where $I_j=\{y\in I:a(y)=v_j\}$. It gives at most
\[
 |T|\left(|I_j|\sum_i\frac{e_i}{|A_i|}+d\right)
\]
agreements on that subgrid. Summing over occupied symbols gives at most
$|C|z_C$ agreements. A constant outside the alphabet contributes zero. The
$s$ distinct useful constants contribute at most
$|C|\sum_{j\le s}\lambda_j$, so the union bound proves
\eqref{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:global-envelope}. The rest follows by subtracting this bound
from the mass of the $q$ heaviest constants, exactly as in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:thm:exact}.
\end{proof}

For multiaffine graphs and width at least $w$, one may use
$z_C\le(k+R)/w$. Thus on sufficiently wide balanced boxes, replacing any
constant branch by a genuinely nonconstant global polynomial creates a fixed
loss in covered mass. This strengthens an order-of-magnitude obstruction into
a classification of exact optimizers and a stability estimate.

\begin{corollary}[Stability across a partition]
Under Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:thm:global}, suppose all cells have
$\lambda_{q,u}-z_{C_u}\ge g>0$. If a cellwise list loses total mass at most
$\Delta\sum_u|C_u|$ relative to the sum of the cellwise optima, then
\[
 \frac{\sum_u|C_u|(q-s_u)}{\sum_u|C_u|}\le\frac{\Delta}{g}.
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Multiply the per-cell deficit bound by the cell cardinality and sum.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Balanced words at logarithmic scales\srctag{50}}]{Balanced words at logarithmic scales}\label{gsr:en:50:sec:d5}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:sec:balanced}
\srcnote{50}{Section 5}

\subsection{A self-contained concentration estimate}
\begin{lemma}[Bernoulli concentration]\label{gsr:en:50:bc:lem:concentration}
If $X_1,\dots,X_n$ are independent Bernoulli variables with common mean $u$, then
\[
 \Prob\left(\left|n^{-1}\sum_iX_i-u\right|>\varepsilon\right)
 \le2\exp(-2n\varepsilon^2).
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For a Bernoulli variable $X$, let
$g(t)=\log\E\exp(t(X-u))$. Then $g(0)=g'(0)=0$, and $g''(t)$ is the variance
of a Bernoulli variable under exponential tilting. Hence $0\le g''(t)\le1/4$
and $g(t)\le t^2/8$. Independence gives
\[
 \E\exp\left(t\sum_i(X_i-u)\right)\le\exp(nt^2/8).
\]
Markov's inequality with $t=4\varepsilon$ bounds the upper tail by
$\exp(-2n\varepsilon^2)$. Apply the same argument to $-\sum_i(X_i-u)$ for the
lower tail, and add the bounds. The degenerate cases $u=0,1$ are immediate.
This is the Bernoulli specialization of Hoeffding's inequality~\cite{hoeffding}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Simultaneous progression balance]\label{gsr:en:50:bc:thm:balanced}
Let $p\ge R$ be prime, let $S\subseteq\F_p$ have size $R$, and let $\pi$ be a
probability vector on $S$. For $\varepsilon>0$, put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:balance-scale}
 L(p,R,\varepsilon)=
 \left\lceil\frac{\log(4Rp^3)}{2\varepsilon^2}\right\rceil.
\end{equation}
There exists a word $a:\F_p\to S$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:balance}
 \left|\frac{|\{y\in I:a(y)=v_j\}|}{|I|}-\pi_j\right|\le\varepsilon
\end{equation}
for every symbol and every proper modular progression $I$ of length at least
$L$. If $L>p$, the assertion about such progressions is vacuous; all subsequent
applications explicitly ensure $L\le p$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Assign the symbols independently with probabilities $\pi_j$. There are at most
$p^3$ triples consisting of a start, a nonzero difference, and a length. For
one such progression and one symbol, Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:lem:concentration} bounds
the failure probability by $2e^{-2\varepsilon^2|I|}$. The union bound is at most
\[
 2Rp^3e^{-2\varepsilon^2L}\le\frac12.
\]
A word with no failures therefore exists. Repeated parameterizations of the
same set only overcount the bad events, which is harmless.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Deterministic construction with rational probabilities}
\begin{theorem}[Exact conditional-expectation construction]\label{gsr:en:50:bc:thm:derandomize}
If $\pi$ and $\varepsilon$ are rational and the expected number of balance
failures is less than one, a balanced word can be constructed deterministically
using polynomially many exact arithmetic operations in $p$ and $R$. A direct
implementation uses $O(R^2p^4+Rp^3)$ arithmetic operations after binomial-tail
precomputation, with intermediate integers of bit length polynomial in
$p$, $\log R$, and the input denominator lengths.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Enumerate the progression--symbol upper and lower bad events. At most $2Rp^3$
events are needed. After fixing an initial segment of the word, an event's
conditional probability is a binomial tail: the already fixed count is known,
and the unfixed positions of its progression remain independent Bernoulli
variables. For rational $\pi_j$ these probabilities are rational and can be
computed exactly.

Let $Z$ be the number of bad events. Initially $\E Z<1$. At a new position,
the current conditional expectation is the $\pi$-weighted average of the
conditional expectations after the possible assignments. Choose an assignment
of positive probability that does not increase that expectation. Once every
position has been assigned, the conditional expectation is the integer $Z$,
still less than one. Thus $Z=0$.

For completeness, precompute the binomial cumulative distribution tables for
all remaining lengths $0\le m\le p$ and all symbols. With a common probability
denominator $D$, every event probability can be represented on denominator
$D^p$. These tables and powers require polynomially many exact operations.
An event can then be evaluated from its fixed count and remaining length by
two table lookups. Evaluating all events for all $R$ candidates at each of $p$
positions gives $O(R^2p^4)$ operations. Progression membership is determined by
solving $y=a+bt$ and checking $0\le t<n$ in the standard representatives, so
maintaining the fixed counts also has polynomial cost. The scaled integer
scores have $O(p\log D+\log(Rp^3))$ bits. This proves the claimed arithmetic
bound; it is a bound in the field size, not in $\log p$.
\end{proof}

The algorithm can equivalently stop at the lexicographically first balanced
word found by exhaustive search. Conditional expectation is included to show
that this is not merely an unstructured existence argument. It does not make
the astronomical instance in Section~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:sec:counterexample} practical.

\subsection{An explicit threshold for power-size cells}
\begin{lemma}[A convenient threshold]\label{gsr:en:50:bc:lem:threshold}
Let $R\ge2$, $0<c\le1$, and $\varepsilon=1/(4R)$. If
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:threshold-log}
 \log p\ge \frac{128R^2}{c^2},
\end{equation}
then
\[
 p^c\ge L(p,R,\varepsilon),\qquad p^c\ge R^2,\qquad p\ge R.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Set $t=\log p$. The assumption implies $t\ge\log(4R)$ and $t\ge1$. Hence
\[
 L=\left\lceil8R^2\bigl(\log(4R)+3t\bigr)\right\rceil
 \le32R^2t+1\le33R^2t.
\]
The power-series bound $e^{ct}\ge (ct)^2/2$, together with
$c^2t\ge128R^2$, gives $p^c\ge64R^2t\ge L$ and $p^c\ge R^2$.
Since $c\le1$, $p\ge p^c\ge R^2\ge R$.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Realizing arbitrary local cover profiles\srctag{50}}]{Realizing arbitrary local cover profiles}\label{gsr:en:50:sec:d6}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:sec:profiles}
\srcnote{50}{Section 6}

\begin{theorem}[Asymptotically exact profile realization]\label{gsr:en:50:bc:thm:profile}
Fix $R,d\ge1$, a probability vector $\pi$ on $R$ symbols, and a length function
$L_p\le p$ with $L_p/\log p\to\infty$ along the primes. There are words
$a_p:\F_p\to S_p$, $|S_p|=R$, such that, for every $q\le R$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:asymptotic-profile}
 \sup_{I:\,|I|\ge L_p}
 \left|\frac{\Cov_{q,d}(a_p;I)}{|I|}-M_q(\pi)\right|\longrightarrow0.
\end{equation}
The same limit is valid for the best covered fraction of any nonempty union of disjoint
nonempty product boxes whose final axes have length at least $L_p$, allowing an adaptive
choice of the boxes and at most $q$ final-degree-$d$ graphs on each cell.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Set
\[
 \varepsilon_p=
 \sqrt{\frac{\log(4Rp^3)}{2L_p}}.
\]
The proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:thm:balanced}, with the integer minimum length
$\lceil L_p\rceil$, supplies words balanced within $\varepsilon_p$, and
$\varepsilon_p\to0$. Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:cor:profile-envelope} implies, uniformly
in the progression,
\[
 M_q(\pi)-q\varepsilon_p
 \le\frac{\Cov_{q,d}}{|I|}
 \le M_q(\pi)+q\varepsilon_p+\frac{qdR}{L_p}.
\]
The upper inequality uses $M_s\le M_q$ for $s\le q$. Both errors tend to zero.
For boxes, apply Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:cor:adaptive}; using the $q$ globally
heaviest prescribed constants in every cell gives the matching lower bound.
\end{proof}

If $\pi_{(q)}>0$, eventually
$|I|(\pi_{(q)}-\varepsilon_p)\ge dR$ on every admissible axis. The univariate
optimum is then \emph{exactly} the mass of the $q$ empirically heaviest symbols,
not merely asymptotic to it. With long base axes as well,
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:thm:global} classifies the global polynomial optimizers.

\begin{corollary}[No branch-budget reset]\label{gsr:en:50:bc:cor:no-reset}
Fix $q<R$, a loss $\eta\in(0,1)$, a degree bound $d$, and any $c>0$. If
$q/R<1-\eta$, then, for all sufficiently large primes, there is a full-domain
function of the form $F(h,y)=a(y)$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item every fixed-$y$ cross-section is constant;
\item every final-coordinate fibre is exactly covered by $R$ constant graphs;
\item no partition into boxes of width at least $p^c$ admits a cellwise cover
      by $q$ degree-at-most-$d$ final-coordinate graphs retaining a fraction
      $1-\eta$ of the full box.
\end{enumerate}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Use the uniform profile and Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:thm:profile} with $L_p=p^c$ when
$c\le1$. For $c>1$ no nonempty proper box of that width exists, so the
nonexistence conclusion is automatic. Choose the error smaller than the fixed
gap $1-\eta-q/R$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why a power-width conclusion matters]
The condition $L_p/\log p\to\infty$ is sufficient, not claimed optimal. It
includes every fixed positive power $p^c$, however small the exponent is.
Thus replacing a failed width exponent by a smaller positive constant cannot
by itself remove a branch-count obstruction. Allowing singleton cells would,
of course, change the problem completely.
\end{remark}

\subsection{A stronger scale for growing alphabets}
The deterministic root allowance $dR$ is appropriate for arbitrary words, but
can be reduced substantially when the word itself is being constructed. The
following result gives a second, affirmative quantitative refinement.

\begin{theorem}[Simultaneous avoidance of nonconstant polynomial graphs]
\label{gsr:en:50:bc:thm:growing}
Let $p$ be prime, $2\le R\le p$, $1\le d<p$, and $0<\tau<1$. Put
\begin{align}
 H&=(d+1)\log p+\log4,\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:avoid-H}\\
 T&=\left\lceil\max\{e^2d,H\}\right\rceil,
 \qquad
 L_{\rm bal}=\left\lceil\frac{4R}{\tau^2}\log(8Rp^3)\right\rceil.
 \label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:avoid-T}
\end{align}
For every alphabet $S\subseteq\F_p$ of size $R$, there exists a word
$a:\F_p\to S$ with the following simultaneous properties:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item On every proper progression $I$ with $|I|\ge L_{\rm bal}$, each symbol
has between $(1-\tau)|I|/R$ and $(1+\tau)|I|/R$ occurrences.
\item Every nonconstant polynomial of degree at most $d$ agrees with $a$ on
fewer than $T$ points of every proper progression.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently, on every progression with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:improved-scale}
 |I|\ge \max\left\{L_{\rm bal},\frac{R(T+1)}{1-\tau}\right\},
\end{equation}
the exact optimum for each $q\le R$ is the mass of the $q$ heaviest constants,
and every optimal list contains only useful constants. In particular, for
fixed $\tau$ the sufficient scale is $O(R(d+1)\log p)$, rather than the
$R^2$-type scale obtained by combining absolute symbol balance with the
worst-case root bound. These conclusions are nonvacuous when the displayed
scale is at most $p$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Choose the symbols independently and uniformly. For one symbol count on an
$n$-point progression, the mean is $\mu=n/R$. The exponential-moment proof of
the Bernoulli tail estimate gives
\[
 \Prob(|X-\mu|>\tau\mu)\le2e^{-\tau^2\mu/4}
 \qquad(0<\tau<1).
\]
Here the upper-tail exponent is
$\mu((1+\tau)\log(1+\tau)-\tau)$; its second derivative in $\tau$ is
$\mu/(1+\tau)\ge\mu/2$, so it is at least $\mu\tau^2/4$. The lower-tail
exponent is at least $\mu\tau^2/2$ by the same calculation. The union bound
over at most $Rp^3$ symbol--progression pairs is at most $1/4$ when
$n\ge L_{\rm bal}$.

Now fix a nonconstant polynomial $P$ of degree at most $d$ on the whole
field. It can take a value in $S$ on at most $dR$ points. At each such point the
random word matches it with probability $1/R$, independently. The number $X$
of matches therefore has mean at most $d$. Its exponential moment is bounded
by $\exp(d(e^u-1))$. For any integer $t\ge d$, Markov's inequality, with
$u=\log(t/d)$, yields
\[
 \Prob(X\ge t)\le(ed/t)^t.
\]
With $t=T\ge e^2d$ the right-hand side is at most $e^{-T}\le e^{-H}$.
There are at most $p^{d+1}$ coefficient lists, so the probability of any
such global failure is at most $p^{d+1}e^{-H}=1/4$. A bound for total agreement
on the field also bounds agreement on every progression. With positive
probability both (i) and (ii) hold.

On a progression satisfying \eqref{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:improved-scale}, every symbol has
at least $T+1$ occurrences, whereas each nonconstant polynomial has fewer
than $T$ agreements. Repeat the proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:thm:exact}, now
charging a nonconstant polynomial $T$ rather than $dR$. The optimum is the
sum of the $q$ largest symbol counts and strict rigidity follows. Finally,
$R\le p$ gives $\log(8Rp^3)=O(\log p)$, and
$T=O((d+1)\log p)$, proving the scale estimate.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[A sharper implicit avoidance threshold]
One may replace the convenient $T$ in \eqref{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:avoid-T} by any integer
$T\ge d$ satisfying
\[
 T\log\frac{T}{ed}\ge(d+1)\log p+\log4.
\]
For fixed $d$ its least solution is of order
$\log p/\log\log p$. No union bound over polynomial \emph{lists} is required:
a uniform bound for each nonconstant graph suffices for the list envelope.
The balanced-symbol scale may still dominate the final answer.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[A growing-alphabet regime]\label{gsr:en:50:bc:cor:growing}
Suppose $R=R(p)\le p$, $d=d(p)<p$, and
\[
 \frac{R(d+1)\log p}{L_p}\longrightarrow0,
 \qquad L_p\le p.
\]
Then words can be chosen so that, simultaneously for every $q\le R$ and every
proper progression of length at least $L_p$, the optimum is exactly the mass
of the $q$ heaviest symbols and
\[
 \left|\frac{\Cov_{q,d}(a;I)}{|I|}-\frac qR\right|=o(1).
\]
The same asymptotic cover bound holds on adaptive unions of product boxes with
those final-axis lengths, even for arbitrary dependence of the polynomial
coefficients on the base point.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Choose $\tau=\tau_p\to0$ sufficiently slowly that
$R\tau_p^{-2}\log p=o(L_p)$. For example, for large $p$ one may take
$\tau_p=(R\log p/L_p)^{1/4}$. The hypothesis also ensures
$RT=o(L_p)$ in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:thm:growing}. The scale condition eventually
holds. Each selected symbol mass lies within $\tau_p/R$ of $1/R$, so summing
$q\le R$ such masses creates error at most $\tau_p$. The fibrewise proof of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:thm:product} and summation over disjoint cells complete the
argument.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The pinned Section 16 interface\srctag{50}}]{The pinned Section 16 interface}\label{gsr:en:50:sec:d7}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:sec:interface}
\srcnote{50}{Section 7}

This section translates only the definitions needed for the application. The
source for these formulas is the pinned repository catalogue, including its
corrections and proper-box requirements~\cite{repo50section16}. Bare references
to ``Lemma 16.10'' in this section are not references to a theorem proved in
this manuscript.

\subsection{The multiple-multilinearity controls}
For a dimension $D$, define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:controls}
 E_D=2^{2^{D+8}},\qquad
 c(u,\gamma,D)=(\gamma u)^{E_D},\qquad
 q(u,\gamma,D)=(\gamma u)^{-E_D},
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:s-control}
 s(u,\gamma,D)=\left(\frac{2}{u\gamma}\right)^{2^{2^{D+6}}}.
\end{equation}
We use a lower-case $q(\cdot)$ only for this real-valued control function; an
integer list length is written $q_0$ or $Q$ in the application.

For a full-domain function $F:\F_p^D\to\F_p$, the property
$\ML_{\gamma,r}(F)$ in the catalogue says the following. For every
$0<\rho\le1$ and every proper common-step box $P$, there are a retained set
$H\subseteq P$, a proper box partition $(P_j)$ of $P$, and an integer $q_0$
such that
\begin{align}
 |H|&\ge(1-\rho)|P|,\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:ML-mass}\\
 q_0&\le q(\rho/r,\gamma,D)^r,
 \label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:ML-count}\\
 \wt(P_j)&\ge \wt(P)^{c(\rho/r,\gamma,D)^r},
 \label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:ML-width}
\end{align}
and, on $H\cap P_j$, the function agrees pointwise with one of $q_0$ globally
multiaffine polynomials. The choice of the matching polynomial can depend on
the point. This is a cover by a union of graphs, not agreement with a single
polynomial. The repository's relation-valued definition specializes to this
form on a full graph.

\begin{lemma}[An identity-partition certificate]\label{gsr:en:50:bc:lem:identity-ML}
Suppose $0<\gamma\le1$, $r\ge1$, and the image of $F$ has size at most $R$.
If
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:identity-budget}
 R\le (r/\gamma)^{E_Dr},
\end{equation}
then $\ML_{\gamma,r}(F)$ holds. In particular, every constant function has this
property.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For every $\rho$, use the identity partition $P_1=P$, retain all of $P$, and
use the constant polynomials corresponding to the image of $F$. The graph
budget is at least its value at $\rho=1$, namely the right-hand side of
\eqref{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:identity-budget}. The required width exponent is
$(\gamma\rho/r)^{E_Dr}\in(0,1]$. For an integer width $w\ge1$, $w^a\le w$
when $0<a\le1$; for $w=0$, $0^a=0$. Thus the width condition also holds.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The final-coordinate line-cover input}
Let $k\ge1$, so the ambient dimension is $k+1$. For outer parameters
$0<\theta,\gamma\le1$, put
\begin{align}
 \theta_1&=(\theta\gamma/4)^{2^{2^{k+5}}},
 &\delta&=2^{-37}(\theta_1/4)^{11/2},\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:aux-one}\\
 \zeta&=2^{-s(\theta,\gamma,k)},
 &t&=\delta^{-2}s(\theta_1/8,\delta,k),\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:aux-two}\\
 r&=(2^k-1)\gamma^{-2}s(2^{-(k+2)}\theta,\gamma,k),
 &K&=(k+1)^2\,2^{k+4}.\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:aux-three}
\end{align}
For a loss $0<\sigma\le1$, the two graph-count bounds are
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:two-counts}
 Q_\gamma(\sigma)=q(\sigma/(2r),\gamma,k+1)^r,
 \qquad
 Q_\delta(\sigma)=q(\sigma/(2t),\delta,k)^t.
\end{equation}
Given an integer $q_\delta$, the required line-cover width is
\begin{align}
 \ell(m,q_\delta)&=\frac{\zeta}{2}m^{e(\sigma,q_\delta)},
 \label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:ell}\\
 e(\sigma,q_\delta)&=
 \frac{c(\sigma/(2r),\gamma,k+1)^r
       c(\sigma/(2t),\delta,k)^t}
      {2K^{2^{k+1}q_\delta}}.
 \label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:e}
\end{align}
All auxiliary parameters are positive; $\delta,\zeta\le1$ and $r,t\ge1$ in
the cases used below.

The predicate \filename{Section16AllBoxLineCovers} requires, for every $\sigma$,
every integer $m$, and every proper $(k+1)$-box $P$ with $m\le\wt(P)$, integers
$q_\gamma\le Q_\gamma(\sigma)$ and $q_\delta\le Q_\delta(\sigma)$, together
with a proper partition $S_u=T_u\times I_u$ of $P$ and a set
$E\subseteq P$ of mass at least $(1-\sigma)|P|$. The cells have width at least
\eqref{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:ell}; on each final-coordinate fibre in $E$, the function is
covered by $q_\gamma$ globally affine functions of the final coordinate. Their
coefficients may depend on the cell and on the base point.

\begin{lemma}[Identity line covers]\label{gsr:en:50:bc:lem:identity-line}
If $F$ takes at most $R$ values and
\[
 R\le Q_\gamma(1),\qquad Q_\delta(1)\ge1,
\]
with the parameters satisfying $r,t\ge1$, $0<\gamma,\delta,\zeta\le1$, then
$F$ satisfies \filename{Section16AllBoxLineCovers}.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Use $q_\gamma=R$, $q_\delta=1$, the identity partition, $E=P$, and the $R$
constant final-coordinate affine functions. The bounds in
\eqref{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:two-counts} increase when $\sigma$ decreases, so the graph
budgets hold for every $\sigma$. Both factors in the numerator of
\eqref{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:e} lie in $(0,1]$, and its denominator is at least $2$. Thus
$0<e\le1$. For $m\ge1$, $\ell(m,1)\le m\le\wt(P)$; for $m=0$ the width
requirement is zero. The identity box has the required base/final-axis product
structure and properness. All conditions are therefore witnessed explicitly.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The precise two-input implication}
The catalogue's \filename{lemma_16_10} asserts, for a certain named full or partial
map $\phi_1$ on a domain $B_1$, that
\begin{align}
 &\left[\text{every fixed-final-coordinate section is }
 \ML_{\gamma,r_0}\right]
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \left[\text{all the line covers above exist}\right]
 \nonumber\\[-2pt]
 &\hspace{3cm}\Longrightarrow\quad \ML_{\gamma,1}(\phi_1),
 \label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:two-input-claim}\\
 &\hspace{1cm}r_0=\gamma^{-2}s(2^{-(k+2)}\theta,\gamma,k).
 \nonumber
\end{align}
The auxiliary names $B_1$ and $\phi_1$ are not unrestricted variables in the
source, so a counterexample must also realize them using the source's cube
selection construction. That realization is included in the next section.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A counterexample to the two-input form of Lemma 16.10\srctag{50}}]{A counterexample to the two-input form of Lemma 16.10}\label{gsr:en:50:sec:d8}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:sec:counterexample}
\srcnote{50}{Section 8}

\begin{theorem}[Fixed-parameter, arbitrarily large prime counterexamples]
\label{gsr:en:50:bc:thm:counterexample}
Let
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:counter-constants}
 k=1,\quad \theta=\gamma=1,\quad
 E=E_2=2^{1024},\quad Q=2^E,\quad R=4Q,\quad c=Q^{-1}.
\end{equation}
For every prime
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:prime-bound}
 p>2^{4096Q^4},
\end{equation}
there are witnesses to both premises of the pinned
\filename{lemma_16_10}, with $B_1=\F_p^2$, for which its conclusion is false.
More specifically, they can be chosen so that
$\phi_1(h,y)=a(y)$ for an $R$-valued word and every admissible target cover at
loss $\rho=1/2$ covers at most $5p^2/16$ points of the full box.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
We verify the assertion in five steps.

\paragraph{1. Construct the word.}
Choose $S=\{0,1,\dots,R-1\}\subset\F_p$ and put
$\varepsilon=1/(4R)$. Since $\log2\ge1/2$, condition
\eqref{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:prime-bound} gives
\[
 \log p>2048Q^4=\frac{128R^2}{c^2}.
\]
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:lem:threshold} implies $p\ge R$ and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:power-dominates}
 p^c\ge L(p,R,\varepsilon),\qquad p^c\ge R^2.
\end{equation}
Use Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:thm:balanced} with the uniform distribution on $S$ to choose
$a:\F_p\to S$ balanced within $\varepsilon$ on every proper progression of
length at least $L$. For a fully specified deterministic choice, order
$\F_p$ and $S$ by their integer representatives and use the least-score,
least-symbol tie-breaking rule of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:thm:derandomize}. No value of
this enormous word needs to be computed to establish its existence or the
properties proved here.

\paragraph{2. Realize the source's named map and domain.}
Take $B=\F_p^2$, $H_1=\F_p$, the anchor $x_0=0$, and
\[
 \phi(h,y)=a(y).
\]
For every sidelength $h$, let $Y_h$ consist of \emph{all} cube elements in
\filename{Section16CubeElement B h}. In dimension one such an element is a
horizontal pair of vertices with sidelength $h$, together with its final
coordinate. Because $B$ is full, every such pair is admitted, including the
pair based at $0$ with any final coordinate $y$.

The source predicate \filename{Section16GoodInducedPair} requires membership of
$h$ in $H_1$ and an element of $Y_h$ whose base is $x_0$ and whose final
coordinate is $y$. These requirements now hold for every $(h,y)$. Consequently
\[
 B_1=\text{\filename{section16GoodDomain}}\,(B,H_1,Y,x_0)=\F_p^2.
\]
The map \filename{section16PhiOne} is $\phi(x_0+h,y)$, which here equals $a(y)$.
Thus the named domain and map are genuinely realized, not substituted by an
informal surrogate.

\paragraph{3. Verify the cross-section premise.}
At the chosen parameters,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:r0-value}
 r_0=s(1/8,1,1)=16^{2^{128}}\ge2.
\end{equation}
For each fixed $y$, the map $h\mapsto a(y)$ is constant on all of $\F_p$.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:lem:identity-ML} gives $\ML_{1,r_0}$ for that section, using
one graph and retaining every point on every proper box. This proves exactly
\filename{FinalCoordinateSectionsMultiplyLinear} in the antecedent.

\paragraph{4. Verify every line-cover requirement.}
Since $k=1$, the $r$ in \eqref{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:aux-three} equals $r_0$. The auxiliary
values in \eqref{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:aux-one}--\eqref{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:aux-three} satisfy
$0<\delta,\zeta\le1$ and $t\ge1$. For every $0<\sigma\le1$,
\begin{align*}
 Q_\gamma(\sigma)
 &=\left(\frac{2r_0}{\sigma}\right)^{Er_0}
 \ge 2^{2E}=Q^2\ge4Q=R,\\
 Q_\delta(\sigma)
 &=\left(\frac{2t}{\delta\sigma}\right)^{E_1t}\ge1.
\end{align*}
Here $Q\ge4$ and $r_0\ge2$ justify the comparisons. Set $q_\gamma=R$ and
$q_\delta=1$. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:lem:identity-line} supplies all boxes, all losses,
and all integer scales $m$, with the identity partition and no exceptional
points. Therefore \filename{Section16AllBoxLineCovers} holds.

\paragraph{5. Refute the conclusion.}
Apply the asserted conclusion $\ML_{1,1}(\phi_1)$ to the full proper box
$P=\F_p^2$ represented by two length-$p$, step-one axes, at loss $\rho=1/2$.
Its graph and width requirements become
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:target-budget}
 q_0\le q(1/2,1,2)=2^E=Q,
 \qquad \wt(P_j)\ge p^{c(1/2,1,2)}=p^c.
\end{equation}
In each nonempty cell $P_j=T_j\times I_j$, the final axis is a proper modular
progression of length at least $p^c$. By \eqref{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:power-dominates} it is
long enough for the balance property and has length at least $R^2$.
Multiaffine graphs restrict to degree-at-most-one polynomials in the final
coordinate. Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:cor:adaptive} therefore bounds the covered mass,
after \emph{any} such partition, by
\[
 q_0\left(\frac1R+\frac1{4R}\right)|P|
 \le \frac{5Q}{4R}p^2=\frac5{16}p^2.
\]
Every retained point has to be covered because $B_1$ is the entire domain.
But \eqref{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:ML-mass} demands $|H|\ge p^2/2$. Since $5/16<1/2$, this
is impossible. Both premises hold and the conclusion fails.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Why the usual possible repairs do not address this example}
The example uses prime moduli, proper boxes, distinct residues, a full domain,
positive width exponents, and the allowed parameter values $\theta=\gamma=1$.
It therefore does not rely on composite-modulus torsion, zero iteration
parameters, inflated formal widths, sparse domains, or the limit
$\theta\to0$. There are counterexamples for every prime beyond the explicit
bound, so introducing an arbitrary threshold $p\ge p_0(\theta,\gamma,k)$
does not repair this two-input implication. The fibre cover is exact, so
improving its exceptional-set estimate cannot repair it either.

The obstruction is to a particular graph budget. It does not say that the
function lacks any multiple-multilinear description: the $R$ constant graphs
already provide one. What fails is replacing the permitted input branch count
by the smaller count in \eqref{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:target-budget} while retaining half the
mass on long cells.

\begin{corollary}[Hamming robustness]\label{gsr:en:50:bc:cor:robust}
Let $a$ be a word from Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:thm:counterexample}. If
$a':\F_p\to S$ differs from $a$ on fewer than $3p/16$ coordinates, then the
same two-premise counterexample is obtained from $F'(h,y)=a'(y)$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The premises are unchanged: the slices remain constant and the same $R$
constant fibre graphs cover everything. For any proposed target partition and
lists, replacing $a$ by $a'$ changes agreement at at most
$p|\{y:a(y)\ne a'(y)\}|<3p^2/16$ points. The universal $5p^2/16$ upper bound
for $a$ therefore remains strictly below $p^2/2$ for $a'$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Both orientations of coordinate sections]\label{gsr:en:50:bc:prop:all-sections}
In Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:thm:counterexample}, every one-dimensional coordinate
section, in either orientation, is $\ML_{1,r_0}$ with $r_0$ as in
\eqref{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:r0-value}. Hence adding that extra coordinate-section hypothesis
alone does not repair the assertion.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Sections with the final coordinate fixed are constant. Sections with the base
coordinate fixed equal the $R$-valued word $a$. For those, apply
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:lem:identity-ML} in dimension one. Indeed
$r_0=2^{4\cdot2^{128}}\ge2E$, so
\[
 r_0^{E_1r_0}\ge2^{r_0}\ge2^{2E}=Q^2\ge R.
\]
This verifies the necessary identity-partition graph budget.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Invisibility to horizontal differences]\label{gsr:en:50:bc:prop:invisible}
For every word $a$ and $F(h,y)=a(y)$, every positive-order alternating cube
difference in the base variables vanishes identically. In the one-dimensional
base used above, the source's induced cube map is identically zero.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
All vertices of a base-variable cube have the same final coordinate, so all
values of $F$ are equal. The sum of the alternating signs is
$(1-1)^k=0$ for a positive-dimensional cube. In dimension one the value is
simply $a(y)-a(y)=0$.
\end{proof}

This last observation explains why some additional compatibility tests may
still miss the problem. Any proposed repair must account for one-coordinate
summands that disappear under the differences it tests. This does not imply the full upstream product property. In fact,
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:prop:endpoint} proves that the witnesses fail that property
at $\gamma=1$.

\subsection{A parameter-general version}
\begin{proposition}[The obstruction is not restricted to endpoint parameters]
\label{gsr:en:50:bc:prop:general-parameters}
Fix $k\ge1$ and $0<\theta,\gamma\le1$. Put
\[
 E=E_{k+1},\qquad Q=(2/\gamma)^E,\qquad
 R=\lceil4Q\rceil,\qquad c=Q^{-1}.
\]
For all sufficiently large primes the same full-domain construction satisfies
the two premises at these parameters and violates the conclusion at loss
$1/2$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The cross-sections are constant, with the prescribed $r_0\ge1$. The line-cover
iteration $r=(2^k-1)r_0$ is at least two. Therefore
\[
 Q_\gamma(1)=(2r/\gamma)^{Er}\ge(2/\gamma)^{2E}=Q^2.
\]
Since $Q\ge5$ and $R\le4Q+1\le5Q$, we have $Q_\gamma(1)\ge R$.
The delta-side budget is at least one, so the identity line cover works.
Choose $p$ large enough for Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:lem:threshold}, use the uniform word
on $R$ symbols, and realize the full good domain by taking all cubes and
anchor zero. The target graph count is at most $Q$ and the target width
exponent is $c$. Hence the covered fraction is at most
$5Q/(4R)\le5/16$, again less than $1/2$. All parameters other than the prime
and the word are fixed in this argument.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A repair interface that retains complexity\srctag{50}}]{A repair interface that retains complexity}\label{gsr:en:50:sec:d9}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:sec:repair}
\srcnote{50}{Section 9}

\subsection{What a valid replacement must preserve}
There are two separate tasks in the Section 16 lifting argument. One is to
turn fibrewise affine data and slice information into multiaffine graph
covers. The other is to fit the resulting count and width into prescribed
control functions. Our result is a barrier to the second task when only the
bundled inputs are retained; it is not a barrier to interpolation itself.

A replacement theorem can keep its output parameters explicitly dependent on
the input branch count, use a suitably larger iteration parameter, require
extra structural hypotheses, or weaken the retained mass. Merely retaining a
formal assertion that the parameters can later be absorbed is not a repair.
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:cor:no-reset} gives a necessary check: on uniform $R$-branch
words, an output list retaining $1-\eta$ of long boxes must have at least
$(1-\eta-o(1))R$ branches.

\subsection{The full-domain endpoint product property}
The upstream product property is not merely an unspecified possible source of
additional information. At its endpoint, it can be characterized exactly. This
also verifies a concrete limit on what the counterexample disproves.

For a full-domain $G:\F_p^D\to\F_p$, the repository's product property at
parameter $\gamma$ requires the following for every finite family of parallel
coordinate restrictions $\psi_i$, every set $A\subseteq\F_p$, and nonnegative
weights $w$ on $A$:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:product-property}
 \sum_{\substack{x_1+x_2=x_3+x_4\\x_t\in A\\
           \psi_i(x_1)+\psi_i(x_2)=\psi_i(x_3)+\psi_i(x_4)\ \forall i}}
       \prod_{t=1}^4w(x_t)
 \ \ge\ \gamma^{8m}p^{-1}\left(\sum_{x\in A}w(x)\right)^4,
\end{equation}
where $m$ is the number of restrictions~\cite{repo50product}.

\begin{proposition}[Endpoint characterization]\label{gsr:en:50:bc:prop:endpoint}
For a full-domain map $G:\F_p^D\to\F_p$, $D\ge1$, the product property with
$\gamma=1$ is equivalent to $G$ being globally multiaffine. Consequently it
implies $\ML_{1,1}(G)$ with one graph. The witnesses in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:thm:counterexample} do \emph{not} have this upstream endpoint
product property.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Assume the product property at $\gamma=1$. Take one coordinate restriction
$\psi$, $A=\F_p$, and $w=1$. There are exactly $p^3$ ordered additive
quadruples, and \eqref{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:product-property} requires all $p^3$ of them to
be respected. In particular,
\[
 \psi(x)+\psi(y)=\psi(x+y)+\psi(0)\qquad(x,y\in\F_p).
\]
Thus $\psi-\psi(0)$ is additive. Since the additive group of $\F_p$ is generated
by $1$, it equals $x\mapsto sx$ for some $s\in\F_p$. Every coordinate
restriction is therefore affine.

A separately affine function on a full product of fields is multiaffine. To
verify this without a separate theorem, induct on $D$ and write
\[
 G(h,y)=G(h,0)+y\bigl(G(h,1)-G(h,0)\bigr).
\]
The two base functions are separately affine, so the induction hypothesis
expresses them as multiaffine polynomials. The displayed formula gives the
joint multiaffine representation.

Conversely, for a multiaffine $G$, every coordinate restriction is affine and
therefore respects every additive quadruple. For any finite family of them,
the sum on the left of \eqref{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:product-property} is the ordinary weighted
additive energy. Extend $w$ by zero outside $A$ and let
$r(s)=\sum_xw(x)w(s-x)$. Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
 \sum_sr(s)^2\ge p^{-1}\left(\sum_sr(s)\right)^2
 =p^{-1}\left(\sum_xw(x)\right)^4.
\]
This is exactly the product-property bound at $\gamma=1$.
The identity partition with the single graph $G$ proves $\ML_{1,1}(G)$.

Finally, our balanced word has every one of its $R$ symbols present, since
its full-field symbol masses are at least $3/(4R)$. Here $2\le R<p$.
A nonconstant affine map on $\F_p$ has image size $p$, and a constant one has
image size one. Thus $a$ is not affine. The coordinate restriction
$y\mapsto a(y)$ rules out the endpoint product property.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 47--53]
\emph{Formalized} (checked at HEAD \texttt{06b30ca52}): \file{section16_unit_product_iff_multilinear} (\file{Proofs16MultilinearProduct.lean}, line~89) proves that over a prime field the full-domain product property at $\gamma=1$ is equivalent to multilinearity, with \file{HasProductProperty.unit_multilinear} (\file{Proofs16ProductEndpoint.lean}, line~146) for the forward direction; \file{FORMALIZATION\_STATUS.txt}: it ``supplies the positive endpoint requested by source~50's plan''.
\end{writenote}

The equivalence is an elementary endpoint fact, not a claim to a new inverse
theorem. It pinpoints a genuine hypothesis lost by the two-input abstraction.
It does not establish a corrected lifting statement for $0<\gamma<1$, nor
does it show that the full product property is inherited by every intermediate
object at the same parameter. Those are different quantitative questions.

\subsection{The existing positive local lift}
The pinned repository already contains a theorem
\filename{section16_local_affine_lift} with explicit output data~\cite{repo50lift}.
Its role is important here because it avoids the false parameter reset. In a
simplified mathematical reading, start with an affine fibre cover of size
$q_{\rm in}>0$, a slice parameter $s\ge1$, losses $\tau,\epsilon\in(0,1]$,
and an integer sampling parameter $r_{\rm sam}$ satisfying
\[
 6q_{\rm in}\le r_{\rm sam}\tau^2.
\]
For a base scale $m\ge4$ and an integer $v\ge1$, the theorem assumes
\[
 v^2+1\le(m/8)^{c(\epsilon/(r_{\rm sam}s),\gamma,k)^{r_{\rm sam}s}}.
\]
It produces an integer $p_0$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:positive-p0}
 p_0\le\bigl[q(\epsilon/(r_{\rm sam}s),\gamma,k)\bigr]^{r_{\rm sam}s}.
\end{equation}
The graph-index type in that theorem has cardinality
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:positive-count}
 r_{\rm sam}p_0+r_{\rm sam}^2p_0^2.
\end{equation}
The output box width is at least $v-1$, and the retained fraction is at least
$1-2\tau-\epsilon$. For a partial domain, the coverage conclusion applies on
that domain intersected with the retained set. In a full-domain application it
is a cover of the entire retained set.

We cite this as a source theorem, not as a newly verified Lean result: no
kernel rebuild of the repository was performed for this article. The important
point is that \eqref{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:positive-count} continues to depend on the sampling
budget and therefore on $q_{\rm in}$. Its statement does not silently identify
that count with $q(\rho,\gamma,k+1)$.

The count still depends on the sampling budget, so the point made above stands.
\end{writenote}

\subsection{An elementary label-preserving interpolation lemma}
The next proposition records a transparent sufficient condition for gluing.
It is standard interpolation, not a new substitute for the source theorem.
Its purpose is to exhibit an interface in which the branch budget is visible.

\begin{proposition}[Label-preserving two-anchor gluing]\label{gsr:en:50:bc:prop:label-gluing}
Let $u\ne v$ in $\F_p$. Suppose $F$ is defined on a subset $D$ of a product
$T\times I$. For each branch $j\in\{1,\dots,R\}$, assume that its final-variable
map $\ell_{j,h}(y)$ is affine in $y$. On a common base-box partition, suppose
its anchor values $\ell_{j,h}(u)$ and $\ell_{j,h}(v)$ are covered by respective
lists of $A_j$ and $B_j$ multiaffine functions of $h$. Outside a base exceptional
set of relative mass $\beta$, assume these covers and the branch representation
of $F$ hold. Then a multiaffine cover on the corresponding product cells exists
with at most
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:50:bc:eq:label-count}
 \sum_{j=1}^R A_jB_j
\end{equation}
graphs, losing at most the base exceptional fraction $\beta$ there. A separate
pointwise representation failure of mass $\alpha$ increases the total loss by
at most $\alpha$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For every candidate pair $(U,V)$ of anchor functions for branch $j$, form
\[
 L_{j,U,V}(h,y)=\frac{v-y}{v-u}U(h)+\frac{y-u}{v-u}V(h).
\]
This is multiaffine in $h$ and affine in $y$, hence multiaffine jointly. At any
good $h$, a correct pair of candidates agrees with the two anchor values, so
its interpolant is exactly $\ell_{j,h}$ for all $y$. There are $A_jB_j$ pairs
for branch $j$. Take their union over $j$. The exceptional-set assertion
follows by multiplying the base exceptional set by the final axis and adding
any separate pointwise failures.
\end{proof}

For the model words every branch has $A_j=B_j=1$, so this construction uses
$R$ constant graphs. Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:thm:profile} shows why a general cover
cannot replace that number by an arbitrary smaller budget while keeping
almost all the mass. A degree-$d$ version uses $d+1$ distinct anchors and
$\sum_j\prod_{t=0}^d A_{j,t}$ interpolants; it follows from the same Lagrange
formula and preserves degree at most $d$ in the final variable.

\subsection{Formal interface recommendations}
Keep a local lifting theorem parameterized by the actual input count,
sampling budget, slice control, retained mass, and output width. Make any
subsequent comparison with a standard control function a separate theorem,
with all outer parameters universally quantified in its statement. The
counterexample in Section~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:sec:counterexample} should be a negative test
for proposed comparisons. No theorem label should receive a proved status
merely because a nearby interpolation theorem has been checked.

A more ambitious repair may strengthen the upstream structural assumptions.
That requires determining which of those assumptions really constrain the
one-coordinate summands in Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:prop:invisible}; it cannot be
inferred from the existence of the two bundled covers alone.

\section[{An acyclic replacement for the Section 16 cover theorem\srctag{49}}]{An acyclic replacement for the Section 16 cover theorem}\label{gsr:en:49:sec:d8}
\srcnote{49}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:en:49:ac:section}

This section proves a quantitative implication from seven finite interfaces
appearing before the closing numerical comparison in Section~16 of
Gowers's paper~\cite{gowers,repo49}. The earlier project audit did
not establish that comparison for the displayed controls. Here the term
\emph{acyclic} refers to explicit replacement recurrences in which every
recursive call strictly decreases the active dimension. The retained
global set is chosen before the local error tolerance. Graph counts, width
exponents, minimum widths, and prime thresholds are kept separate.
The result supplies a replacement for the logical conclusion of
Corollary~16.11. It does not establish the paper's printed control functions
or a new global bound for arithmetic-progression-free sets.

The sampling and shared-interpolation ingredients have already been
developed in the earlier interpolation report~\cite{repo49interpolation}.
They are restated here to make the induction complete. The additional
work is the full recurrence, its quantifier order, and its treatment of
unused coordinates. The latter point is useful: a partition in fewer
coordinates cannot simply be assumed to extend to a partition whose
common difference is synchronized in all coordinates.

\subsection{The numerical comparison being replaced}
\label{gsr:en:49:ac:budget-context}

For clarity, we reproduce the earlier project's algebraic audit
\cite{repo49interpolation}. This calculation concerns one displayed
numerical comparison, not the truth of the source's structural assertion.
Put
\[
 \mathcal A_j=2^{2^{j+8}},\qquad
 \mathcal Q(t,\gamma,j)=(\gamma t)^{-\mathcal A_j},\qquad
 \mathcal B_k=2^{2^{k+6}}.
\]
With $0<\theta,\gamma,\rho\le1$ and a sample size $r\ge1$, the
auxiliary quantities in the published closing comparison have the form
\[
 \mathcal R=\gamma^{-2}
       \left(\frac{2^{k+3}}{\theta\gamma}\right)^{\mathcal B_k},
 \qquad \Omega=4r^2\mathcal R.
\]
The comparison on printed page~575 is
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal Q(\rho/(4\Omega),\gamma,k)^\Omega
 \le\mathcal Q(\rho,\gamma,k+1).
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:old-comparison}
\end{equation}
Writing $b=\log(1/(\gamma\rho))\ge0$ and using
$\mathcal A_{k+1}=\mathcal A_k^2$, it is equivalent to
\[
 \Omega\{b+\log(4\Omega)\}\le\mathcal A_k b.
\]
But $\mathcal R\ge2^{(k+3)\mathcal B_k}>\mathcal A_k$ for every
$k\ge1$, and hence $\Omega>\mathcal A_k$. The inequality fails.
The edited transcription has a different, same-dimension version on
the left, which fails still more directly. The two versions should
not be identified with one another.

Source~50, of the same day, shows that the two-input catalogue statement \file{lemma_16_10} is itself false, not only the comparison (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:branchcover}); this section's theorem is a conditional replacement with new controls, from the stronger hypotheses I1--I7.
\end{writenote}

The smaller anchor budget from \cite{repo49interpolation} is useful,
but by itself does not justify \eqref{gsr:en:49:ac:old-comparison}. The remedy
below defines new controls from the operations actually performed.
It permits a weaker width exponent and carries a separate minimum
width, instead of trying to absorb the entire refinement into these
particular printed powers.

\subsection{Active coordinates and the product property}
\label{gsr:en:49:ac:definitions}

Throughout this section, $p$ is prime, Fourier transforms on $\mathbb F_p$
are unnormalized, and $|t|_p$ denotes the least absolute residue of
$t\in\mathbb F_p$. Thus
\[
 \widehat g(r)=\sum_{x\in\mathbb F_p}g(x)
                    \exp(-2\pi i rx/p),\qquad
 \operatorname{Bohr}(K,\rho)
 =\{t:|rt|_p\leq \rho p\text{ for all }r\in K\}.
\]
A box is a product of nonempty injective arithmetic progressions having
one common nonzero difference. Its width is the smallest side length.
A multilinear polynomial in this section means a polynomial affine in
each variable separately, so it includes all lower-degree terms.

\begin{definition}[Active-coordinate cover]\label{gsr:en:49:ac:def-cover}
Let $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb F_p^j\times\mathbb F_p$, let $D\geq j$,
and choose $j$ distinct ambient coordinates, in a specified order, with
independent fixed translations. Write
$\pi:\mathbb F_p^D\to\mathbb F_p^j$ for the resulting projection and
translation map. On a box $P\subseteq\mathbb F_p^D$, a cover with
parameters $(Q,c,T;\varepsilon)$ consists of a set
$E\subseteq P$, $|E|\geq(1-\varepsilon)|P|$, and a partition of $P$
into boxes of width at least $m^c$, where $m$ is the width of $P$ and
$m\geq T$. On each cell there are at most $Q$ polynomials depending
only on the active coordinates, multilinear in those coordinates,
whose values include every $y$ with $(\pi(z),y)\in\Lambda$ whenever
$z\in E$ belongs to that cell.
\end{definition}

The exceptional set need not depend only on the active coordinates.
The models themselves must do so. Covers are preserved by restricting
$\Lambda$, by translating active coordinates, and by permuting them.

\begin{definition}[Product property]\label{gsr:en:49:ac:def-product}
A partial map $\phi:A\subseteq\mathbb F_p^j\to\mathbb F_p$ has the
$\gamma$-product property if the following holds. Choose any coordinate
direction, any $s\geq1$ restrictions $\psi_1,\ldots,\psi_s$ to parallel
coordinate lines, any common domain $U\subseteq\mathbb F_p$, and any
weight $w:U\to[0,\infty)$. The sum of
$w(a)w(b)w(c)w(d)$ over quadruples with
\[
 a+b=c+d,\qquad
 \psi_i(a)+\psi_i(b)=\psi_i(c)+\psi_i(d)\quad(1\leq i\leq s)
\]
is at least
\[
 \gamma^{8s}p^{-1}\left(\sum_{x\in U}w(x)\right)^4.
\]
A relation $\Gamma\subseteq\mathbb F_p^j\times\mathbb F_p$ has that
property if every partial map with graph contained in $\Gamma$ does.
\end{definition}

This is the paper's product property, with the ambient prime denoted by
$p$. It is inherited by subrelations and proper coordinate sections.

\subsection{The finite interfaces used as hypotheses}
\label{gsr:en:49:ac:interfaces}

The implication below assumes the following corrected interfaces.
Their proofs are earlier parts of the source development; reproducing
all of them would amount to reproducing much of the paper. Stating the
interfaces explicitly identifies the dependency boundary of the new
induction. None invokes the conclusion being proved here.

\paragraph{I1. Order-eight extraction.}
If a map on a set of density $b$ has at least $\rho(bp)^3$ additive
quadruples, then it has a restriction to an order-eight Freiman map on
at least
\begin{equation}
 2^{-1882}\rho^{1164}bp
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-extraction-input}
\end{equation}
points.

\paragraph{I2. Bohr linearization of an exact Freiman map.}
An order-eight Freiman map on a set of density $b$ admits a set $K$ of
at most $16b^{-2}$ frequencies such that its restriction to any
progression of length at most $L$ is affine whenever its difference
$d$ satisfies
\begin{equation}
 d\in\operatorname{Bohr}\bigl(K,b/(32\pi L)\bigr).
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-bohr-input}
\end{equation}
The statement concerns the original domain's global density. No local
density assumption in the progression is required.

\paragraph{I3. Many respected arrangements.}
A $\gamma$-product map on a set of density $b$ in
$\mathbb F_p^{k+1}$, $k\geq1$, respects at least
\begin{equation}
 b^{7\cdot4^{k+1}}\gamma^{21k\cdot4^{k+1}}p^{17k+15}
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-arrangements-input}
\end{equation}
eight-arrangements. Here an eight-arrangement is an ordered family of
sixteen coordinate cubes with common side vector
$h\in\mathbb F_p^k$, the $i$th cube lying in last-coordinate section
$x_i$, where $x_1+\cdots+x_8=x_9+\cdots+x_{16}$. The arrangement is
respected if the corresponding signed cube sums of the map satisfy
the same equality. Repetitions are counted in this convention.

\paragraph{I4. Riesz selection.}
Set
\begin{equation}
 H_k=2^{\,2^{k+4}+k+3}.
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-hk}
\end{equation}
If the respected count is at least $\alpha b^{15}p^{17k+15}$ and
$0<\eta_0\leq1$, there is a subset of the original map domain
with at least
\begin{equation}
 (\alpha\eta_0/4)^{H_k}b^{15}p^{17k+15}
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-riesz-output}
\end{equation}
arrangements, at least a proportion $1-\eta_0$ respected, provided
\begin{equation}
 (\alpha\eta_0/4)^{H_k}b^{15}p
 \geq k\,3^{2^{k+4}}.
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-riesz-threshold}
\end{equation}

\paragraph{I5. A Bohr model for an almost homomorphism on a domain.}
Let a finite domain $X$ have a projection $r:X\to\mathbb F_p$, with
fibres of size at most $M$ and $|X|=bMp$. Suppose a map on $X$ respects
at least a proportion $1-2^{-43}$ of its order-eight additive
relations. Put $g(x)=|r^{-1}(x)|$ and
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 K_b&=\{t:|\widehat g(t)|\geq2^{-37}b^{11/2}Mp\},\\
 R_b&=2^{74}b^{-10},\qquad
 z_b=2^{-155R_b}b^{18R_b}/R_b.
 \end{split}
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-domain-input}
\end{equation}
Then $|K_b|\leq R_b$, and there is $Y\subseteq X$ with
$|Y|\geq b^6|X|/20000$ such that the map restricted to $Y$ is a
$\operatorname{Bohr}(K_b,z_b)$-homomorphism. In particular its value
is constant on each fibre of $Y$, and the resulting partial function
of the projected coordinate is affine on any progression of length
at most $L$ with difference in
$\operatorname{Bohr}(K_b,z_b/L)$.

\paragraph{I6. Product properties of large spectra.}
For $f:\mathbb F_p^{k+1}\to\mathbb C$ with $|f|\leq1$, define
\[
 f_h(x)=\sum_{z\in\mathbb F_p^k}
       \prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^k}
       \mathcal C^{|\omega|+k}f(z+\omega h,x),
\]
where $\mathcal C$ is complex conjugation and multiplication
$\omega h$ is coordinatewise. The relation
\begin{equation}
 \{(h,t):|\widehat f_h(t)|\geq\delta p^{k+1}\}
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-spectral-input}
\end{equation}
has the $\delta$-product property. Also, for
$f:\mathbb F_p\to\mathbb C$, $|f|\leq1$, a partial graph selecting
a Fourier coefficient of modulus at least $\gamma p$ from each
$k$-fold multiplicative derivative has the $\gamma$-product property.
The elementary large-coefficient consequence of the paper's
Lemma~3.1 is used only in Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:49:ac:cor-inverse} below.

\paragraph{I7. Simultaneous multilinear phase partition.}
For $D\geq2$ and an integer $q\geq1$, define
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 K_D&=D^2 2^{D+3},\qquad
 a_D(q)=K_D^{-2^Dq},\\
 L_D(q)&=2^{\left(2^{40D^3+1}+1\right)K_D^{2^Dq}}.
 \end{split}
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-phase-input}
\end{equation}
Given $q$ multilinear polynomials on a $D$-box of width $w\geq L_D(q)$,
there is a partition into boxes of width at least $w^{a_D(q)}$ on
each of which every polynomial has image diameter at most
$2p w^{-a_D(q)}$ in the least-residue metric.
