\subsection{Two elementary cover operations}
\label{gsr:en:49:ac:operations}

\begin{lemma}[Sequential refinement]\label{gsr:en:49:ac:lem-refinement}
Suppose $s$ relations or partial functions on one ambient box have
cover triples $(Q_i,c_i,T_i)$ at error $\varepsilon/s$. Put
$C=\prod_{i=1}^s c_i$. A simultaneous refinement has width exponent
$C$, total error at most $\varepsilon$, and a sufficient initial
width threshold is $\max_iT_i^{1/C}$. A union needs at most
$\sum_i Q_i$ graph models, and a sum of functions on a common
domain needs at most $\prod_iQ_i$ models.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Apply the cover for the first relation, then apply the second cover
inside every resulting box, and continue. At stage $i$ the width is
at least $m^{c_1\cdots c_i}$, and all previous covers remain valid
on subboxes. Since $c_i\leq1$, every input width is at least $m^C$,
which exceeds each required $T_i$. The discarded masses add, because
the boxes at any stage partition the original box. Lists concatenate
for a union; all choices of one model from each list give the models
for a sum. Models retain the union of their active coordinate sets.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Anchors, including singleton classes]
\label{gsr:en:49:ac:lem-anchors}
Let $S=T\times I$ be a nonempty box with distinguished coordinate
$x\in I$. Suppose that each row of a partial function on $S$ is
partitioned into at most $q$ classes, with the function affine on
each class. For every integer $r\geq1$, one can choose at most $r$
distinct anchors in $I$ so that, except for at most
$2q|S|/(r+1)$ points, each point is either an anchor point or belongs
to a class containing two distinct anchors. If every chosen anchor
slice has at most $v$ multilinear models after a common refinement,
then these retained points are covered by at most
\begin{equation}
 rv+\binom r2v^2
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-anchor-count}
\end{equation}
multilinear models, including the distinguished coordinate.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $|I|\leq r$, choose every point of $I$ and use the constant
extensions of the anchor slices; there is no loss. Otherwise sample
an $r$-subset uniformly. Choose a test point uniformly outside this
subset. For a fixed class $C$, let $Z$ count its points in the
resulting uniform $(r+1)$-subset. Exchangeability gives
\[
 \Pr(\text{test point is in }C,
          \text{ at most one anchor is in }C)
 =\mathbb E\left[\frac Z{r+1}\mathbf1_{Z\leq2}\right]
 \leq\frac2{r+1}.
\]
Sum over at most $q$ classes and over all rows. The nonanchor
fraction of the box is at most one, and all anchor points are
retained. Averaging therefore gives the required anchor set.

Write two distinct anchors as $x_i,x_j$. If $u_i(h),u_j(h)$ are
models for their slices, their interpolant is
\begin{equation}
 \frac{(x_j-x)u_i(h)+(x-x_i)u_j(h)}{x_j-x_i}.
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-interpolant}
\end{equation}
It is multilinear in the active $h$ coordinates and affine in $x$.
The denominator is nonzero because the anchors are distinct in a
prime field. Include all $v^2$ interpolants for each anchor pair and
all $v$ constant extensions for each anchor. On a class hit twice,
the appropriate interpolant agrees with the class's affine map.
An anchor point is covered by its slice's constant extension. This
also explains why singleton classes cause no exception to the proof.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The replacement theorem and its base case}
\label{gsr:en:49:ac:main-theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Acyclic cover theorem from I1--I7]
\label{gsr:en:49:ac:thm-main}
Assume interfaces I1--I7. The explicit recurrences below define, for
each $j\geq1$ and $0<a,\gamma\leq1$, an integer
$N_j(a,\gamma)$ and, for every $D\geq j$ and
$0<\varepsilon\leq1$, a positive integer $Q_j(a,\gamma;\varepsilon)$,
a number $c_{j,D}(a,\gamma;\varepsilon)\in(0,1]$, and a threshold
$T_{j,D}(a,\gamma;\varepsilon)\geq2$ with the following property.

If $p\geq N_j(a,\gamma)$ is prime,
$\Gamma\subseteq\mathbb F_p^j\times\mathbb F_p$ has size at most
$\gamma^{-2}p^j$ and has the $\gamma$-product property, there is a
single $J\subseteq\mathbb F_p^j$ with
$|J|\geq(1-a)p^j$ such that
$\Gamma\cap(J\times\mathbb F_p)$ has the active-coordinate cover
of Definition~\ref{gsr:en:49:ac:def-cover} with parameters
\[
 \bigl(Q_j(a,\gamma;\varepsilon),
       c_{j,D}(a,\gamma;\varepsilon),
       T_{j,D}(a,\gamma;\varepsilon);\varepsilon\bigr)
\]
for every $D$, every permitted active-coordinate map, every
$\varepsilon$, and every box whose width meets the threshold.
The set $J$ is independent of all these local choices.
\end{theorem}

The graph count does not require an ambient-dimension index. The
width exponent and threshold do. This distinction will follow from
the recurrence itself.

For the base case put
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 b_*&=2^{-1882}\gamma^{9312}a^{1165},\qquad
 q_* =\left\lceil\gamma^{-2}/b_*\right\rceil,\\
 t_*&=\left\lceil16q_*b_*^{-2}\right\rceil.
 \end{split}
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-base-constants}
\end{equation}
For every $D\geq1$ and every local error, define
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 N_1(a,\gamma)&=3,\qquad Q_1(a,\gamma;\varepsilon)=q_*,\\
 c_{1,D}(a,\gamma;\varepsilon)&=\frac1{4(t_*+1)},\\
 T_{1,D}(a,\gamma;\varepsilon)
 &=\max\left\{2^{4(t_*+1)},
       (256\pi/b_*)^{2(t_*+1)}\right\}.
 \end{split}
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-base-profile}
\end{equation}

\begin{proof}[Proof of the base case]
As long as the remaining relation has projection of density at least
$a$, choose one graph over its projection, whose actual density is
$v\geq a$. The product property gives at least
$\gamma^8v^4p^3$ additive quadruples. In I1 its normalized parameter
is $\rho=\gamma^8v$, so the extracted order-eight Freiman piece has
size at least
$2^{-1882}\gamma^{9312}v^{1165}p\geq b_*p$.
Remove the graph of this piece and repeat. There are at most $q_*$
pieces; after deleting the final remaining projection, their union
covers the relation above a set $J$ of the required size.

For each piece use its \emph{global} density in I2. The combined
spectra have at most $t_*$ frequencies. Each piece's valid Bohr
radius is at least the one obtained from $b_*$. This same finite
collection of pieces works in every ambient dimension.

Consider a $D$-box of width $m$ and common difference $d_0$, and put
\[
 L=\left\lfloor m^{1/(2(t_*+1))}\right\rfloor,
 \qquad H=\left\lceil64\pi L/b_*\right\rceil.
\]
Simultaneous pigeonholing for the combined frequencies gives
$1\leq u\leq H^{t_*}$ with
$|rd_0u|_p\leq p/H$ for every frequency $r$. The threshold in
\eqref{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-base-profile} implies
\[
 \frac m u\geq2L,
 \qquad L\geq m^{1/(4(t_*+1))}.
\]
Indeed $H\leq128\pi L/b_*$, and
$m^{1/2}\geq2(128\pi/b_*)^{t_*}$ suffices for the first inequality;
the other threshold gives the second after taking the floor.

In each side's index interval split the residue classes modulo $u$
into successive blocks with lengths in $[L,2L-1]$. Such a split is
possible for every integer length at least $L$, and every residue
class has at least $L$ points. Products of these blocks partition
the original box. They have common difference $ud_0\ne0$, because
$u\leq m/(2L)<p$, and have the required width. The Bohr condition
for I2 with length parameter $2L-1$ follows from
\[
 \frac1H\leq\frac{b_*}{64\pi L}
       \leq\frac{b_*}{32\pi(2L-1)}.
\]
Each graph piece is therefore affine in its active coordinate on
every cell. There is no local loss. Translating or choosing a
different active coordinate does not change the argument.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why the base proof uses global spectra]
The extracted Freiman pieces need not have density $b_*$ in an
arbitrary local progression. Thus one cannot simply apply the
local-density form of Corollary~7.11 with the original density
parameter. The preceding argument first obtains Bohr information
from the global sets, then localizes that information by simultaneous
pigeonholing.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Global extraction in dimension \texorpdfstring{$k+1$}{k+1}}
\label{gsr:en:49:ac:global-extraction}

Suppose the theorem is known in active dimensions $1,\ldots,k$.
Fix $a,\gamma$. All constants in the following display are global;
they are chosen before any ambient dimension or local tolerance:
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 \kappa&=a/2^{k+2},\qquad b_0=a/2,\\
 \alpha_0&=b_0^{7\cdot4^{k+1}-15}
                      \gamma^{21k\cdot4^{k+1}},\\
 \tau&=(2^{-46}\alpha_0)^{H_k}b_0^{15},\qquad u_0=\tau/4,\\
 \delta&=2^{-37}u_0^{11/2},\qquad
 R_0=\left\lceil2^{74}u_0^{-10}\right\rceil,\\
 \zeta&=2^{-155R_0}u_0^{18R_0}/R_0,\\
 \eta&=2^{-32}\tau^8,\qquad
 B_* =\left\lceil\gamma^{-2}/\eta\right\rceil.
 \end{split}
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-global-constants}
\end{equation}
Here $H_k$ was defined in \eqref{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-hk}. Keeping the exact Riesz
output $\tau$ avoids the further coarse numerical domination used
in the source's Lemma~15.6. Define the prime threshold by
\begin{equation}
 N_{k+1}(a,\gamma)=
 \left\lceil\max\left\{
 3,\frac{k3^{2^{k+4}}}{\tau},
 \max_{1\leq l\leq k}N_l(\kappa,\gamma),
 N_k(\tau/8,\delta)
 \right\}\right\rceil.
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-prime-recursion}
\end{equation}
Every dimension on its right side is smaller than $k+1$.

\begin{lemma}[A fixed graph piece]\label{gsr:en:49:ac:lem-piece}
Assume I1--I7 and the lower-dimensional induction hypotheses.
Let $p$ meet \eqref{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-prime-recursion}, and suppose a
$\gamma$-product relation of size at most $\gamma^{-2}p^{k+1}$ has
projection of density at least $a$. It contains a graph piece of
size at least $\eta p^{k+1}$ with the local profiles constructed in
Subsection~\ref{gsr:en:49:ac:local-profile}. The piece is chosen independently
of ambient dimension, local error, and local box.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose a partial map $\phi$ on a set $A$ of density at least $a$,
with graph in the relation. For each positive-dimensional proper
coordinate section, apply the corresponding lower-dimensional core
theorem with outer error $\kappa$ and parameter $\gamma$. For a
fixed set of coordinates to be held constant, its sections partition
the ambient space, so their total discarded mass is at most
$\kappa p^{k+1}$. There are fewer than $2^{k+1}$ choices. Pruning all
of them leaves a domain of density at least $b_0$, on every proper
section of which the relevant lower-dimensional core profile holds.
Those profiles hold simultaneously in all ambient dimensions and
at every local error. They persist on all further restrictions.

Apply I3 and I4 with selection error $2^{-44}$. If the actual
retained density exceeds $b_0$, the same lower bounds remain valid,
since all powers of that density are positive. The threshold in
\eqref{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-prime-recursion} gives a set $B_0$ containing at least
$\tau p^{17k+15}$ eight-arrangements, at least a proportion
$1-2^{-44}$ respected by $\phi$.

For each side vector $h$, let $C(h)$ and $G(h)$ count its
arrangements and respected arrangements. Let $X_h$ be the set of
individual cubes with that side vector, with projection to the last
coordinate $x$. Directly from the ordered arrangement definition,
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 C(h)&\leq p^{16k+15},\qquad |X_h(x)|\leq p^k,\\
 C(h)&\leq |X_h|p^{15k+14}.
 \end{split}
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-cube-domain-counts}
\end{equation}
For the last inequality, specify the first cube, the other fifteen
basepoints, and fourteen of their last coordinates; the remaining
last coordinate is determined by the additive relation.

Discard the $h$ with $G(h)<(1-2^{-43})C(h)$. Their total arrangement
mass is at most half the total, because the overall failure
proportion is at most $2^{-44}$. Then discard those with
$C(h)<(\tau/4)p^{16k+15}$. The remaining set $H$ satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{h\in H}C(h)\geq(\tau/4)p^{17k+15},\qquad
 |X_h|\geq u_0p^{k+1}\quad(h\in H).
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-good-h}
\end{equation}
The induced cube-sum map on $X_h$ respects at least a proportion
$1-2^{-43}$ of its order-eight additive relations.

Let $f=\mathbf1_{B_0}$, so that the function $f_h$ in I6 is exactly
$x\mapsto|X_h(x)|$. Apply I5 with the actual density
$b_h=|X_h|/p^{k+1}\geq u_0$. Enlarge its natural spectrum to
\begin{equation}
 K_h=\{t:|\widehat f_h(t)|\geq\delta p^{k+1}\}.
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-kh}
\end{equation}
The natural threshold is at least the threshold in this definition.
Also $R_0\geq2^{74}b_h^{-10}$, and
\[
 2^{-155R_0}u_0^{18R_0}/R_0
 \leq 2^{-155R_{b_h}}b_h^{18R_{b_h}}/R_{b_h}.
\]
Consequently the original homomorphism may be restricted to
$\operatorname{Bohr}(K_h,\zeta)$. Here $R_0$ bounds the
\emph{natural} spectrum's rank; no bound $|K_h|\leq R_0$ is being
asserted for the enlarged spectrum. We obtain $Y_h\subseteq X_h$
with
\begin{equation}
 |Y_h|\geq\frac{u_0^6}{20000}|X_h|
          \geq2^{-27}\tau^6|X_h|.
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-yh}
\end{equation}
The cube sum on $Y_h$ gives a partial function $\phi'(h,x)$, affine
along progressions of length at most $L$ whose difference lies in
$\operatorname{Bohr}(K_h,\zeta/L)$.

By I6, the spectral relation
$\Delta=\{(h,t):t\in K_h\}$ has the $\delta$-product property.
Parseval and $0\leq f_h\leq p^k$ imply
\[
 \sum_t|\widehat f_h(t)|^2
 =p\sum_x f_h(x)^2\leq p^{2k+2},
 \qquad |K_h|\leq\delta^{-2}.
\]
Thus the lower-dimensional core theorem applies to $\Delta$ with
outer error $\tau/8$. Intersect its core with $H$ and call the
result $H_1$. By \eqref{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-cube-domain-counts},
\[
 \sum_{h\in H_1}C(h)\geq(\tau/8)p^{17k+15},
 \qquad |H_1|\geq(\tau/8)p^k.
\]
Together with \eqref{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-good-h} and \eqref{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-yh}, this gives
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{h\in H_1}|Y_h|
 \geq2^{-32}\tau^8p^{2k+1}=\eta p^{2k+1}.
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-anchor-base-mass}
\end{equation}

Average over the $p^k$ possible cube basepoints. There is one fixed
$z=(z_1,\ldots,z_k)$ and a set $B_1$ of at least
$\eta p^{k+1}$ pairs $(h,x)$, with $h\in H_1$, on which
\begin{equation}
 \phi'(h,x)=\sum_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^k}
                (-1)^{|\omega|}\phi(z+\omega h,x).
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-cube-identity}
\end{equation}
All displayed map values are defined there. The all-ones term
$\phi_1(h,x)=\phi(z+h,x)$ is a translation of a restriction of
$\phi$. Solving \eqref{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-cube-identity} for it writes it as
$(-1)^k\phi'$ plus $2^k-1$ signed proper-section terms. Each proper
section of $\phi_1$ retains its lower-dimensional core profile.
All choices made so far concern finite global data. No local box,
ambient dimension, or local error has been chosen. The local proof
that follows therefore applies to this one fixed piece.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The exact local profile of an extracted piece}
\label{gsr:en:49:ac:local-profile}

Fix $D\geq k+1$ and a desired error $0<e\leq1$. The local
construction has four error allocations, each at most $e/4$.

\paragraph{Spectral freezing.}
Define
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 q_S&=Q_k(\tau/8,\delta;e/4),\\
 c_S&=c_{k,D}(\tau/8,\delta;e/4),\qquad
 T_S=T_{k,D}(\tau/8,\delta;e/4),\\
 a_S&=a_D(q_S),\qquad c_F=c_Sa_S/2,\\
 T_F&=\max\left\{T_S,L_D(q_S)^{1/c_S},
                   (16/\zeta)^{2/(c_Sa_S)}\right\}.
 \end{split}
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-freeze-profile}
\end{equation}
These expressions use only the $k$-dimensional spectral core.

\begin{lemma}[Freezing in the full ambient box]
\label{gsr:en:49:ac:lem-freeze}
On a $D$-box of width $m\geq T_F$, one may discard at most an
$e/4$ fraction and partition into boxes of width at least $m^{c_F}$
such that $\phi'(h,\cdot)$ is affine on every remaining partial
vertical row with $h\in H_1$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Apply the active-coordinate spectral cover to the $D$-box, obtaining
cells of width at least $m^{c_S}$ and a good set with loss at most
$e/4$. On a cell let its spectral models be
$\mu_1(h),\ldots,\mu_{q_S}(h)$, padding the list if necessary.
They depend only on $h$. At every good point with $h\in H_1$, the
entire set $K_h$ lies among their values.

Apply I7 \emph{in ambient dimension $D$} to
$\nu_i(h,x)=\mu_i(h)x$. These are multilinear in the ambient
coordinates. The resulting boxes have width at least
$W=m^{c_Sa_S}$ and each $\nu_i$ has image diameter at most $2p/W$.
For a child common difference $d$, compare two consecutive values
of its $x$ coordinate, keeping all other coordinates fixed. This gives
\begin{equation}
 |\mu_i(h)d|_p\leq2p/W.
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-direction-freeze}
\end{equation}
There are two such values because the threshold makes $W$ large.

Set $L=\lfloor\zeta W/8\rfloor$. Split every side into consecutive
blocks of lengths in $[L,2L-1]$, leaving the common difference
unchanged. Since $W^{1/2}\geq16/\zeta$,
\[
 L\geq\zeta W/16\geq W^{1/2}=m^{c_F}.
\]
Also $2/W\leq\zeta/(2L-1)$. Thus
\eqref{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-direction-freeze} puts $d$ in the Bohr set required
to make $\phi'(h,\cdot)$ affine on a vertical block, whenever
the original spectral good set covers $K_h$ there.

The good set is not required to be cylindrical. For any retained
point its full $K_h$ is covered by the same cell's models; those
models do not depend on $x$ or on unused coordinates. This is enough
to establish the direction condition for its row. Refining a good
set by intersection with cells creates no further loss.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{The proper-section terms.}
Write
\begin{equation}
 R=2^k-1,\qquad n_l=\binom{k}{l-1}\quad(1\leq l\leq k).
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-remainder-multiplicities}
\end{equation}
Exactly $n_l$ terms in the remainder of
\eqref{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-cube-identity} have $l$ active coordinates: $l-1$
coordinates of $h$ and the distinguished coordinate $x$. Retaining
these dimensions gives better controls than bounding every term by
the $k$-dimensional profile. Put
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 q_l&=Q_l(\kappa,\gamma;e/(4R)),\\
 c_l&=c_{l,D}(\kappa,\gamma;e/(4R)),\\
 T_R&=\max_{1\leq l\leq k}T_{l,D}(\kappa,\gamma;e/(4R)),\\
 q_0&=\prod_{l=1}^kq_l^{n_l},\qquad
 c_R=\prod_{l=1}^kc_l^{n_l}.
 \end{split}
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-remainder-profile}
\end{equation}
Successive refinement of these $R$ functions costs at most $e/4$
of the ambient mass. It changes the width exponent to $c_Fc_R$.
On each resulting vertical row, $\phi_1$ is covered by at most
$q_0$ affine functions: choose one proper-section model for each
term and add the single affine function supplied for $\phi'$.
Assign each point to the first line containing it to get disjoint
classes for Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:49:ac:lem-anchors}.

\paragraph{Anchor slices.}
Define
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 r&=\left\lceil8q_0/e\right\rceil,\\
 q_H&=Q_k(\kappa,\gamma;e/(4r)),\\
 c_H&=c_{k,D}(\kappa,\gamma;e/(4r)),\qquad
 T_H=T_{k,D}(\kappa,\gamma;e/(4r)).
 \end{split}
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-horizontal-profile}
\end{equation}
The anchor lemma loses at most $e/4$ of each ambient cell. For a
cell whose vertical side has fewer than $r$ points, take that whole
side as anchors. Each anchor slice is a restriction of a proper
section of $\phi_1$, so it has the indicated $k$-dimensional profile
\emph{in the same ambient dimension $D$}, treating the vertical
coordinate as unused. Refine all at most $r$ such slices, for another
loss of at most $e/4$. No lifting of an independently chosen
lower-dimensional partition is required.

The resulting triple for one extracted piece is
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 q_{\mathrm{piece}}(e)
    &=r q_H+\binom r2q_H^2,\\
 c_{\mathrm{piece}}(e)&=c_Fc_Rc_H^r,\\
 T_{\mathrm{piece}}(e)
    &=\max\{T_F,T_R^{1/c_{\mathrm{piece}}(e)},
                   T_H^{1/c_{\mathrm{piece}}(e)}\}.
 \end{split}
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-piece-profile}
\end{equation}
The threshold is deliberately generous: every input width in the
remainder and anchor refinements is at least
$m^{c_{\mathrm{piece}}(e)}$. The spectral threshold was already
accounted for in $T_F$. The four losses sum to at most $e$.
Formula~\eqref{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-interpolant} shows that all final models are
multilinear in the active $k+1$ coordinates. This completes the
local assertion of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:49:ac:lem-piece}.

\subsection{Closing the induction}
\label{gsr:en:49:ac:closure}

For $j=k+1$, use the global constants
\eqref{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-global-constants}. Given $\varepsilon$, set
$e=\varepsilon/B_*$ and define
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 Q_{k+1}(a,\gamma;\varepsilon)
    &=B_*q_{\mathrm{piece}}(e),\\
 c_{k+1,D}(a,\gamma;\varepsilon)
    &=c_{\mathrm{piece}}(e)^{B_*},\\
 T_{k+1,D}(a,\gamma;\varepsilon)
    &=\max\{2,T_{\mathrm{piece}}(e)^{
                       1/c_{k+1,D}(a,\gamma;\varepsilon)}\}.
 \end{split}
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-final-recursion}
\end{equation}
Equations~\eqref{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-base-constants}--\eqref{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-base-profile},
\eqref{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-global-constants}--\eqref{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-prime-recursion}, and
\eqref{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-freeze-profile}--\eqref{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-final-recursion} are the
promised explicit recurrences.

\begin{proof}[Completion of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:49:ac:thm-main}]
Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:49:ac:lem-piece} whenever the remaining relation has
projection of density at least $a$, and remove the resulting graph
piece. Each removes at least $\eta p^{k+1}$ graph points. The total
number of pieces is at most $B_*$, since the original relation has
at most $\gamma^{-2}p^{k+1}$ points. Removing a graph preserves
the product property. At termination let $J$ be the complement of
the remaining projection. Then $|J|\geq(1-a)p^{k+1}$, and the
relation above $J$ is covered by the union of the extracted pieces.

The lower-dimensional core choices, Riesz selections, domain
subsets, and cube basepoints all precede the choice of a local
parameter. Thus these pieces and $J$ work simultaneously for every
ambient dimension and local tolerance. Now fix those local choices.
Use each piece at error $\varepsilon/B_*$, refine successively,
and apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:49:ac:lem-refinement}. The graph counts add,
the width exponents multiply, and the errors sum to at most
$\varepsilon$. Padding by empty pieces if necessary gives exactly
the bounds in \eqref{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-final-recursion}.

Every profile called on the right side has active dimension at
most $k$. There is no same-dimension call whose size must be absorbed
into a previously fixed power. The recurrences are therefore well
founded. At the base $Q_1$ does not depend on $D$; the graph-count
recurrence uses only lower graph counts, whereas the spectral
freezing stage contributes one affine map per row independently
of its number of spectral models. Hence $Q_{k+1}$ also does not
depend on $D$. This finishes the induction.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Growth bounds for the new controls}
\label{gsr:en:49:ac:growth}

\begin{proposition}[Elementary envelopes]\label{gsr:en:49:ac:prop-envelopes}
For every fixed $j,D$, $D\geq j$, there is an effectively computable
$C\geq2$ such that, with $u=a\gamma\varepsilon$,
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 N_j(a,\gamma)&\leq(C/(a\gamma))^C,\\
 Q_j(a,\gamma;\varepsilon)&\leq(C/u)^C,\\
 c_{j,D}(a,\gamma;\varepsilon)&\geq
                    \exp\bigl(-(C/u)^C\bigr),\\
 T_{j,D}(a,\gamma;\varepsilon)&\leq
                    \exp\!\left(\exp\bigl((C/u)^C\bigr)\right).
 \end{split}
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-envelopes}
\end{equation}
The exact recurrences, rather than a claim of an optimal $C$, are
the numerical content of the theorem.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Use induction on the active dimension. The base constants have
polynomial upper bounds in $(a\gamma)^{-1}$; their negative width
logarithm has such a bound as well. At an inductive step, the
quantities $\kappa^{-1},\tau^{-1},\delta^{-1},\eta^{-1},B_*$
are polynomially bounded in $(a\gamma)^{-1}$ for fixed dimension.
So is $\log(1/\zeta)$: $R_0$ is polynomially bounded and the only
additional factors in its logarithm are logarithms of such
quantities. The recursion for $N_j$ therefore remains polynomial.

Every lower-dimensional parameter substituted into a $Q$ is at
least the reciprocal of a polynomial in $u^{-1}$. Consequently
the $q_l$, $q_0$, $r$, $q_H$, and the final graph count are
polynomially bounded. The negative logarithm of a width exponent
is a sum of lower negative logarithms multiplied by polynomially
bounded repetition counts. In the spectral step,
$-\log a_D(q_S)=2^Dq_S\log K_D$ is also polynomially bounded.
This proves the asserted single-exponential lower bound for $c$.

Finally, the logarithm of each threshold is bounded by an
exponential of a polynomial. This is true of $L_D(q_S)$ and of
the lower thresholds by induction. Raising such a threshold to
the reciprocal of a width exponent multiplies its logarithm by
another single exponential, preserving this form. The term
involving $1/\zeta$ obeys the same bound. Increasing $C$ finitely
many times proves all four inequalities simultaneously. This
induction can be performed directly on the explicit expressions,
so the constant is effective.
\end{proof}

The effect of preserving actual section dimensions is visible even
when the outer parameters are fixed. Define integers $A_j,B_j$ by
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 A_1=B_1&=0,\qquad
 S_k=\sum_{l=1}^k\binom{k}{l-1}A_l,\\
 A_{k+1}&=2(A_k+1)(S_k+2)-2,\\
 B_{k+1}&=(B_k+1)(S_k+2)-1.
 \end{split}
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-epsilon-degrees}
\end{equation}

\begin{proposition}[Dependence on the local error]
\label{gsr:en:49:ac:prop-epsilon}
For fixed $a,\gamma,j,D$, as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ the exact
recurrences satisfy
\begin{equation}
 Q_j=O(\varepsilon^{-A_j}),\qquad
 -\log c_{j,D}=O(\varepsilon^{-B_j}),\qquad
 \log\log T_{j,D}=O(\varepsilon^{-B_j}).
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-epsilon-asymptotics}
\end{equation}
The first four pairs $(A_j,B_j)$ are
$(0,0),(2,1),(34,11),(7698,1319)$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The statement is immediate in dimension one. At the next step,
$q_0=O(\varepsilon^{-S_k})$, so
$r=O(\varepsilon^{-(S_k+1)})$, and the horizontal error
$e/(4r)$ is bounded below by a positive constant times
$\varepsilon^{S_k+2}$. The graph bound
$r q_H+\binom r2q_H^2$ has exponent
$2(S_k+1)+2A_k(S_k+2)=A_{k+1}$.
The term $c_H^r$ has negative logarithm of order at most
\[
 \varepsilon^{-(S_k+1)-B_k(S_k+2)}
   =\varepsilon^{-B_{k+1}}.
\]
All earlier width losses have exponents at most
$\max\{A_k,B_k\}\leq B_{k+1}$. For the thresholds, the lower
horizontal threshold contributes exponent $B_k(S_k+2)$ to its
double logarithm, and taking reciprocal width powers contributes
at most $B_{k+1}$, which is larger. The other thresholds are
smaller in the same sense. The fixed number $B_*$ of global pieces
changes constants but none of these powers.
\end{proof}

Replacing all proper-section terms by the largest-dimensional
profile would instead give the pairs
$(0,0),(2,1),(46,15),(30454,5183)$. The smaller exponents above are
proved for this recurrence; no optimality is asserted.

\subsection{A replacement for the multilinear inverse conclusion}
\label{gsr:en:49:ac:inverse-consequence}

\begin{corollary}[Recursive version of the Corollary 16.11 interface]
\label{gsr:en:49:ac:cor-inverse}
Assume I1--I7 and the large-coefficient consequence of the paper's
Lemma~3.1. Let $0<\alpha\leq1/2$ and
$f:\mathbb F_p\to\mathbb C$, $|f|\leq1$, fail
$\alpha$-uniformity of degree $k+1$ in the paper's convention.
Put
\[
 a=\alpha/4,\qquad\gamma=\alpha/2,\qquad
 \varepsilon=\alpha/8,
\]
and abbreviate
$Q=Q_k(a,\gamma;\varepsilon)$ and
$c=c_{k,k}(a,\gamma;\varepsilon)$. If
\begin{equation}
 p\geq\max\{N_k(a,\gamma),T_{k,k}(a,\gamma;\varepsilon)\},
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-inverse-threshold}
\end{equation}
there is a box $P\subseteq\mathbb F_p^k$ of width at least $p^c$
and a multilinear polynomial $\mu$ on $P$ such that
\begin{equation}
 \#\{h\in P:|\widehat{\Delta_h f}(\mu(h))|
                       \geq(\alpha/2)p\}
 \geq \frac{\alpha}{8Q}|P|.
 \label{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-inverse-output}
\end{equation}
Here $\Delta_h f$ is the $k$-fold multiplicative derivative.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The large-coefficient step gives a partial graph on at least
$(\alpha/2)p^k$ side vectors, selecting Fourier coefficients of
modulus at least $(\alpha/2)p$. By I6 this graph has the
$(\alpha/2)$-product property. Apply
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:49:ac:thm-main} and then its local conclusion to the whole
box $\mathbb F_p^k$, of width $p$. Global deletion removes at most
$(\alpha/4)p^k$ points of this graph's domain; local deletion
removes at most $(\alpha/8)p^k$. At least $(\alpha/8)p^k$
domain points therefore survive. Some partition cell has surviving
relative density at least $\alpha/8$. Assign each of its surviving
points to the first model whose value is the selected coefficient.
One of at most $Q$ models receives at least the fraction
$\alpha/(8Q)$, proving \eqref{gsr:en:49:ac:eq-inverse-output}.
\end{proof}

If a common width and density parameter is wanted, one may take
$c_* =\min\{c,\alpha/(8Q)\}$. More informatively,
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:49:ac:prop-envelopes} gives a polynomial density
lower bound in $\alpha$ and a width of the form
\[
 p^{\exp(-(C/\alpha)^C)}
\]
once $p\geq\exp(\exp((C/\alpha)^C))$, with effective $C$
depending on $k$. This is a complete recursive replacement of the
local implication, with a weaker width exponent than the unsupported
printed power. Every use of a source interface and every new
quantitative dependency is displayed above. A further claim about
the downstream Sections~17--18 would require propagating these new
controls through those sections; that is not part of this theorem.

\subsection{Questions arising from the repaired recurrence}
\label{gsr:en:49:ac:questions}

The proof suggests several focused problems. First, can the repeated
slice refinement be replaced by a simultaneous theorem that keeps
the width exponent polynomial in the local error? The present
recurrence identifies precisely where the single exponential
appears: a number of anchor slices growing as a power of
$\varepsilon^{-1}$ is refined successively. Second, can the
minimum-width threshold be reduced while preserving the global
core's independence of the local tolerance? Third, one can replace
I7 by a sharper simultaneous polynomial recurrence theorem and
recompute the profiles without modifying the global extraction
argument. Finally, a formal implementation can represent the
recurrences as expression trees indexed by active dimension; the
strict decrease in every recursive call gives a direct termination
proof and avoids encoding a failed final domination as an opaque
numerical assertion.

\section{Sources~55 and~57: the polynomial-phase endpoint in every degree \wtag}\label{gsr:en:sec:phaseendpoint}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the tenth write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next eleven sections are source~55's Sections~2--11 and source~57's Section~5, on functions whose Gowers norm is close to its maximum. \emph{Logically they continue the chapters on the Proposition~6.1 endpoint} of sources~31 and~29 (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:endpoint}) and~38 (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:oddstability}); they are printed here because no number printed earlier may move. Source~55's introduction is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:55:sec:d1}; source~57's is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:57:sec:d1}, and its Section~13 chapter is Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:theoremthirteen}.

\emph{What source~55 proves.} For $|f|\le1$ on a finite abelian group $G$ and $\varepsilon=1-\norm f_{U^d}^{2^d}$, the squared normalized $L^2$ distance to the phase polynomials of degree at most $d-1$ (nonclassical ones included) satisfies $D_d(f)\le(2/q)\varepsilon+b_d(G)\varepsilon^2+R_d\varepsilon^3$ once $\varepsilon\le e_d$, $q=2^d$, with $b_d=(3^d-1)/(2q^2)$ for $|G|$ odd and $(q^2-1)/(3q^2)$ for $|G|$ even, both sharp on every nontrivial group of that parity (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:55:thm:main}); second-order saturation forces the tangent to be a conjugate pair of characters (odd order) or one order-two character (even order) (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:55:thm:rigidmain}). The local theorem is explicit (radius \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:radius}, cubic constant \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:R}; Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:55:thm:local}); the global entry $e_d$ comes from the published Eisner--Tao theorem (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:55:thm:ET}), which source~55 imports and does not make numerical. The key steps are a fifth-order real-part cancellation for bounded complex functions and a four-vertex census of the cube (Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:55:lem:fifth}, Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:55:lem:fourtypes}); the exact even-order $U^2$ modulus is $2(1-\sqrt{(1+\sqrt{1-2e})/2})$ (Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:55:prop:exactu2}). At $d=3$ the coefficients $13/64$ and $21/64$ are those of sources~38 and~31 in another class of functions (note after Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:55:thm:main}).

\emph{What source~57's Section~5 proves.} If $Q_4(f)\ge1-\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon\le2^{-10}$ on $\F_p$, one scalar $c$ gives $|\widehat{\Delta_h\Delta_kf}(chk)|\ge3/4-4\varepsilon$ on at least $(1-332\varepsilon)p^2$ pairs (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:near-u4}), with no scale threshold and no inverse theorem as input; at every order $216s+8$ in place of $332$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:prime-all-orders}), an $s$-additive frequency map on every finite abelian group (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:group-all-orders}), a cubic phase with correlation at least $\sqrt{1-6194\varepsilon}-\varepsilon$ in characteristic at least five (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:cubic-inverse}), polynomial phases of degree $k-1$ for $p\ge k$ (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:all-degree-inverse}), and the linear order of the squared error is optimal (Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:error-order}). This is the endpoint branch of its proof of Theorem~13.12 (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:theoremthirteen}).

\emph{Relation to the formal statements} (checked at HEAD \texttt{fe7165a3c}). \file{proposition_6_1} (\file{Sections06\_07.lean}, line~37) has the exact companion \file{proposition_6_1_holds} (\file{Proofs05\_10.lean}, line~505); no declaration concerns near-maximal Gowers norms in general. Source~57's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:near-u4} is formalized as the repository's own \file{endpoint_global_fourier} (\file{Proofs13EndpointGlobalFourier.lean}, line~12; density $1-332\varepsilon$, coefficient $(3/4-4\varepsilon)N$) for the proof of \file{theorem_13_12} (note in Section~\ref{gsr:en:57:sec:d5}); nothing else in this chapter is formalized.
