\section[{Main results\srctag{55}}]{Main results}\label{gsr:en:55:sec:d2}\label{gsr:en:55:sec:main}
\srcnote{55}{Section 2}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp second-order endpoint stability]\label{gsr:en:55:thm:main}
For every integer $d\ge2$ there are constants $e_d>0$ and $R_d<\infty$,
independent of the finite abelian group, such that for every $|f|\le1$ with
$\eps=1-\Ufiftyfive(f)\le e_d$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:main}
 D_d(f)\le \frac2q\eps+b_d(G)\eps^2+R_d\eps^3,
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:b}
 b_d(G)=
 \begin{cases}
 \displaystyle\frac{3^d-1}{2q^2},& |G|\text{ odd},\\[5pt]
 \displaystyle\frac{q^2-1}{3q^2},& |G|\text{ even}.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
For every nontrivial finite abelian $G$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:sharpmod}
 \mathfrak S_{d,G}(e)=\frac2q e+b_d(G)e^2+O_d(e^3)
 \quad(e\downarrow0),
\end{equation}
with a range and error constant uniform in $G$. In particular, neither the
linear nor the quadratic coefficient can be decreased.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 54--59]
\emph{Checked at the write} (exact rationals). With $C_d=(6^d-2q^2+q)/8$, $A_d=q(q-1)(q-2)/24$ and $K_{0,d}=q(q-1)/8$ (Appendix~\ref{gsr:fz:55:app:ledger}), $K_{0,d}+C_d/2=q(3^d-1)/16$ and $K_{0,d}+A_d=q(q^2-1)/24$ for $d=2,\ldots,12$, so $8K_d/q^3$ is \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:b}; the table above and $\beta_d(G)$ of Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:55:cor:normdef} follow for $d=2,\ldots,6$. \emph{Against sources~31 and~38.} Source~31's optimal fidelity bound $R(\delta)=\bigl(1-\sqrt{(1+\sqrt{1-4\delta})/2}\bigr)/2$ gives the squared distance $2(1-\sqrt{1-R(\delta)})=\delta/4+21\delta^2/64+O(\delta^3)$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:31:thm:sharp}, uniform over finite abelian groups), and source~38's odd-order modulus has squared distance $\varepsilon/4+13\varepsilon^2/64+(\sqrt2/64)\varepsilon^{5/2}+O(\varepsilon^3)$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:38:thm:odd-modulus}); at $d=3$ this theorem's coefficients are $1/4$, $13/64$ (odd order) and $21/64$ (even order). The classes differ: sources~31 and~38 take $L^2$-normalized functions and coset phases, this source $|f|\le1$ and phase polynomials on the whole group. Unimodular functions belong to both, and this source's extremizing families (\eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:evenfamily}, \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:oddfamily}) are unimodular; source~38's $\varepsilon^{5/2}$ term comes from near point masses on groups with three-torsion, which are not bounded by one after normalization, so it does not contradict the $O_d(\varepsilon^3)$ here. This source extends the two coefficients to every degree and to bounded functions; the global entry $e_d$ rests on the published Eisner--Tao theorem and is not explicit (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:near}).
\end{writenote}

An explicit admissible $R_d$ is given in equation~\eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:R}; the local radius is
explicit in equation~\eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:radius}. We do not extract a numerical value of the
global entry threshold $e_d$ from the published near-extremizer theorem.
That distinction does not make theorem~\ref{gsr:en:55:thm:main} conditional: its input is a
published theorem, not an unproved hypothesis.

\begin{corollary}[Norm-deficit normalization]\label{gsr:en:55:cor:normdef}
Writing $\delta=1-\norm f_{U^d}$ instead, the sharp expansion is
\[
 \mathfrak S_{d,G}\bigl(1-(1-\delta)^q\bigr)
 =2\delta+\beta_d(G)\delta^2+O_d(\delta^3),
\]
where
\[
 \beta_d(G)=
 \begin{cases}
 (3^d-2^{d+1}+1)/2,& |G|\text{ odd},\\
 (2^d-1)(2^d-2)/3,& |G|\text{ even}.
 \end{cases}
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Substitute $1-(1-\delta)^q=q\delta-q(q-1)\delta^2/2+O_d(\delta^3)$
into theorem~\ref{gsr:en:55:thm:main} and its matching examples.
\end{proof}

For orientation, the first coefficients in the cubical-defect normalization
are as follows.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}cccc@{}}
\toprule
$d$ & coefficient of $e$ & odd-order coefficient of $e^2$ & even-order coefficient of $e^2$\\
\midrule
2 & $1/2$ & $1/4$ & $5/16$\\
3 & $1/4$ & $13/64$ & $21/64$\\
4 & $1/8$ & $5/32$ & $85/256$\\
5 & $1/16$ & $121/1024$ & $341/1024$\\
6 & $1/32$ & $91/1024$ & $1365/4096$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\begin{theorem}[Tangent rigidity of second-order extremizers]\label{gsr:en:55:thm:rigidmain}
Fix $d\ge2$. Let $G_n$ be nontrivial finite abelian groups of the same parity,
and let $|f_n|\le1$, with $\eps_n=1-\Ufiftyfive(f_n)>0$ and $\eps_n\to0$. Suppose
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:saturate}
 D_d(f_n)=\frac2q\eps_n+b_d(G_n)\eps_n^2+o(\eps_n^2).
\end{equation}
Choose minimizing phases $P_n$, rotated so that $\E f_n\overline{P_n}\ge0$.
Then
\[
 1-\E|f_n|^2=o(\eps_n^2).
\]
If the groups have even order, there are nontrivial order-two characters
$\chi_n$ and signs $s_n\in\{-1,1\}$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:evenrigid}
 \norm{\frac{f_n\overline{P_n}-1}{\sqrt{D_d(f_n)}}-i s_n\chi_n}_2\longrightarrow0.
\end{equation}
If the groups have odd order, there are nontrivial characters $\chi_n$ and
$\zeta_n\in S^1$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:oddrigid}
 \norm{\frac{f_n\overline{P_n}-1}{\sqrt{D_d(f_n)}}
       -i\sqrt2\,\Rea(\zeta_n\chi_n)}_2\longrightarrow0.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

This is a necessity statement for second-order saturation, not a claim that
an arbitrary $o(\sqrt D)$ approximation to the displayed tangent automatically
saturates the quadratic coefficient. Quantitative control of higher-order
components is needed for that converse. Explicit saturating families will be
given in section~\ref{gsr:en:55:sec:sharpness}.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Demodulation and the bounded-function geometry\srctag{55}}]{Demodulation and the bounded-function geometry}\label{gsr:en:55:sec:d3}\label{gsr:en:55:sec:normal}
\srcnote{55}{Section 3}

Fix a phase $P$, not necessarily minimizing, and rotate it so that
$F=f\overline P$ has real nonnegative mean. For this section write
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:variables}
 m=\E F,\qquad r=F-m,\qquad
 a=1-\E|F|^2,\qquad D=\E|F-1|^2,\qquad z=D+a.
\end{equation}
The letter $r$ denotes a centered function, not a cube direction. We will use
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:identities}
 m=1-\frac z2,\qquad \E r=0,\qquad
 v:=\E|r|^2=D-\frac{z^2}{4},\qquad 0\le v\le D.
\end{equation}
The identities follow by expanding the squared distances and using
$\E|F|^2=1-a$. The number $a$ is an amplitude deficit; it vanishes precisely
when $|F|=1$ everywhere.

\begin{lemma}[Amplitude loss is visible to the cube]\label{gsr:en:55:lem:amplitude}
For every $d\ge1$ and every $|F|\le1$,
\[
 0\le a\le1-\Ufiftyfive(F).
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Any two distinct cube vertices are independent and uniform on $G$.
Taking absolute values in \eqref{gsr:fm:55:eq:cube} and discarding all but two factors
gives
\[
 \Ufiftyfive(F)\le (\E|F|)^2\le\E|F|^2.
\]
\end{proof}

The next pointwise identity will rule out an otherwise possible error of
order $D^{5/2}$.
\begin{lemma}[Real-part constraint]\label{gsr:en:55:lem:realpart}
Let $A(x)=1-|F(x)|^2\ge0$ and $u=\Rea r$. If $m>0$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:realpart}
 2m u=v+a-A-|r|^2.
\end{equation}
For every nontrivial character $\chi$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:skew}
 \abs{\widehat r(\chi)+\overline{\widehat r(-\chi)}}\le z.
\end{equation}
Here $\widehat r(\chi)=\E r\overline\chi$, and additive notation is used in
the character group.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Expand $|F|^2=|m+r|^2$ and use $1-m^2=v+a$ to obtain
\eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:realpart}. Also
\[
 2(1-\Rea F)=A+|F-1|^2.
\]
The right side is nonnegative and has mean $a+D=z$. At a nontrivial
frequency its Fourier coefficient has magnitude at most $z$.
Since constants disappear at that frequency and
$2\widehat{\Rea r}(\chi)=\widehat r(\chi)+
\overline{\widehat r(-\chi)}$, this proves \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:skew}.
\end{proof}

In particular, a small bounded perturbation of $1$ is primarily imaginary.
Crucially, \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:realpart} is an exact pointwise identity, so it remains
useful for perturbations concentrated on very small subsets. No uniform
pointwise smallness of $F-1$ will be assumed.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Four vertices of a discrete cube\srctag{55}}]{Four vertices of a discrete cube}\label{gsr:en:55:sec:d4}\label{gsr:en:55:sec:census}
\srcnote{55}{Section 4}

For $\omega\in\{0,1\}^d$, put $X_\omega=x+\omega\cdot h$, with all
$x,h_j$ independent and uniform on $G$.

\subsection{Independence of every three vertices}

\begin{lemma}[Three-wise independence]\label{gsr:en:55:lem:triple}
For any three distinct cube vertices $\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3$, the
variables $X_{\omega_1},X_{\omega_2},X_{\omega_3}$ are independent and
uniform, on every finite abelian group.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Reflect coordinates to send $\omega_1$ to $0$. This is realized on the
sampling variables by replacing suitable $h_j$ with $-h_j$ and translating
$x$, an invertible transformation preserving the uniform measure.
The remaining two vertices are distinct nonzero binary vectors $u,v$.
Their coordinate columns $(u_j,v_j)$ contain at least two distinct nonzero
members of $\{(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)\}$. The corresponding $2\times2$ determinant
is $1$ or $-1$. Including the base variable $x$ therefore gives a
$3\times3$ minor of determinant $\pm1$ in the augmented forms
$(1,\omega_i)$. Fixing every other variable, these three variables can be
solved uniquely for any prescribed triple of outputs over $G$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The complete four-vertex classification}

A four-set of cube vertices will be called \emph{ordinary} if it is an
integer parallelogram, that is, if its four distinct elements can be ordered
so that $a+b=c+e$ in $\Z^d$. It will be called \emph{exceptional} if its
xor is zero but it is not ordinary. These are precisely the additional
four-point dependencies created by two-torsion.

\begin{lemma}[Integral and binary four-point circuits]\label{gsr:en:55:lem:fourtypes}
Every four-set of distinct vertices belongs to exactly one of the following
classes.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item An ordinary parallelogram. Three associated variables are independent;
      the fourth satisfies their unique parallelogram relation.
\item An exceptional set. After reflecting and relabeling, its joint law is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:exceptionallaw}
 (x,\ x+U+V,\ x+U+W,\ x+V+W),
\end{equation}
      where $x,U,V,W$ are independent uniform elements of $G$.
\item A set with nonzero xor. All four associated variables are independent
      and uniform on $G$.
\end{enumerate}
The numbers of ordinary, total xor-zero, and exceptional four-sets are
respectively
\begin{align}
 C_d&=\frac{6^d-2\cdot4^d+2^d}{8},\label{gsr:en:55:eq:C}\\
 A_d&=\frac{q(q-1)(q-2)}{24},\label{gsr:en:55:eq:A}\\
 J_d&=A_d-C_d.\label{gsr:en:55:eq:J}
\end{align}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Reflect one vertex to $0$, and call the others $u,v,w$.
If $u+v+w\ne0$ in $\F_2^d$, these three distinct nonzero vectors are
linearly independent over $\F_2$. There is an odd $3\times3$ binary minor.
A $3\times3$ zero-one determinant has absolute value at most $2$, so this
minor is $\pm1$. The augmented four forms consequently have a unimodular
minor, which proves (iii). For completeness, if $B$ is a $3\times3$ zero-one matrix, form a
$4\times4$ matrix whose first row and column are all $1$ and whose lower
block is $1-2B$. Subtracting its first row from the other rows gives
determinant $(-2)^3\det B$. Each row has Euclidean norm $2$, so the
Hadamard determinant inequality gives $8|\det B|\le16$.

If $u+v+w=0$ in $\F_2^d$, every nonzero coordinate column is one of
$110,101,011$. At least two of these types occur. If exactly two occur,
one of $u,v,w$ is the integer sum of the other two, whose supports are
disjoint. This is an ordinary parallelogram. The independence assertion
follows from lemma~\ref{gsr:en:55:lem:triple}. If all three types occur, combine all
sampling directions of each type into a single variable. The three sums
are independent and uniform, and give \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:exceptionallaw}.
The nonzero full minors then have greatest common divisor $2$; this also
describes the relevant Smith obstruction without requiring the Smith normal
form theorem in the proof.

There are $6^d$ ordered solutions of $a+b=c+e$ in the binary cube: each
coordinate has six possibilities. The two diagonal families have size
$4^d$ each and intersection of size $2^d$. All other solutions have four
distinct entries. Each ordinary four-set contributes eight orderings,
proving \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:C}.

Finally, a xor-zero four-set is an affine two-plane in $\F_2^d$.
Any ordered triple of distinct points determines its fourth point, and each
plane has $4\cdot3\cdot2=24$ such triples. This proves \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:A} and
\eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:J}.
\end{proof}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}rrrrr@{}}
\toprule
$d$ & $\binom{2^d}{4}$ & ordinary $C_d$ & exceptional $J_d$ & independent\\
\midrule
2&1&1&0&0\\
3&70&12&2&56\\
4&1820&100&40&1680\\
5&35960&720&520&34720\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The ordinary/exceptional distinction concerns the integer coefficient
matrix. Even in an odd-order group, the exceptional four-set exists
combinatorially; its induced map is then surjective because multiplication
by $2$ is invertible. Its centered correlation consequently vanishes.

\subsection{Fourier control of the quartic coefficient}

For a centered complex function $r$, define
\begin{align}
 Q_d(r)&=\sum_{\substack{S\subseteq\{0,1\}^d\\|S|=4}}
       \E\prod_{\omega\in S}\cC^{|\omega|}r(X_\omega),\label{gsr:en:55:eq:Q}\\
 E_4(r)&=\sum_{\chi\in\widehat G}|\widehat r(\chi)|^4,\qquad
 T_4(r)=\sum_{\substack{\chi\ne0\\2\chi=0}}|\widehat r(\chi)|^4.
 \label{gsr:en:55:eq:E4}
\end{align}

\begin{proposition}[Quartic circuit bound]\label{gsr:en:55:prop:quartic}
For every centered complex $r$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:quarticbound}
 \Rea Q_d(r)\le C_d E_4(r)+J_d T_4(r).
\end{equation}
If $b$ is real and centered, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:quarticreal}
 Q_d(b)=Q_d(ib)=C_d E_4(b)+J_d T_4(b).
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Independent four-sets contribute zero. For an ordinary set, Fourier
expansion and the parallelogram relation leave one freely varying
frequency, with signs and conjugations depending on the labeling. The
resulting sum is a product of four Fourier coefficients, each of the form
$\widehat r(\chi)$, $\widehat r(-\chi)$, or its conjugate. H\"older's
inequality bounds its absolute value by $E_4(r)$.

For \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:exceptionallaw}, Fourier orthogonality forces
\[
 \chi_1+\chi_2=\chi_1+\chi_3=\chi_2+\chi_3=0,
 \qquad \chi_0+\chi_1+\chi_2+\chi_3=0.
\]
Thus all four frequencies equal the same $\chi$ with $2\chi=0$.
The zero frequency contributes nothing because $r$ is centered. The
absolute contribution is at most $T_4(r)$. Summation proves
\eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:quarticbound}.

For real $b$, an ordinary correlation is exactly $E_4(b)$. On a two-torsion
character the Fourier coefficient of a real function is real, so the
exceptional correlation is exactly $T_4(b)$. Conjugations do not change
$b$. Replacing $b$ by $ib$ multiplies a four-set contribution by
$i^4(-1)^{\sum_{\omega\in S}|\omega|}$. Every dependent four-set has xor
zero, so this sign is $1$. Independent contributions remain zero.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A cubic remainder for bounded complex perturbations\srctag{55}}]{A cubic remainder for bounded complex perturbations}\label{gsr:en:55:sec:d5}\label{gsr:en:55:sec:remainder}
\srcnote{55}{Section 5}

An ordinary application of H\"older to five small $L^2$ factors suggests an
error of order $v^{5/2}$, which is too large for a cubic error in the defect.
The pointwise geometry of the unit disk improves that estimate.

\subsection{H\"older estimates from triple independence}

\begin{lemma}[Four-, five-, and six-factor estimates]\label{gsr:en:55:lem:holder}
Let $r:G\to\C$, put $v=\E|r|^2$, and use distinct cube vertices for the
variables displayed below. Then
\begin{align}
 \E\prod_{j=1}^4|r(X_j)|&\le v^2,\label{gsr:en:55:eq:holder4}\\
 \E|r(X_1)|^2\prod_{j=2}^5|r(X_j)|&\le v^3,\label{gsr:en:55:eq:holder5}\\
 \E\prod_{j=1}^6|r(X_j)|&\le v^3.\label{gsr:en:55:eq:holder6}
\end{align}
For every nonnegative $A$ with $\E A=a$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:holderA}
 \E A(X_1)\prod_{j=2}^5|r(X_j)|\le a v^2.
\end{equation}
Statements with more vertices than the cube contains are simply unused.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Pair the four factors in \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:holder4} and use Cauchy--Schwarz and
pairwise independence. For \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:holder5}, take the six triples
$\{1,j,k\}$ with $2\le j<k\le5$. The product of
\[
 \bigl(|r(X_1)|^2|r(X_j)|^2|r(X_k)|^2\bigr)^{1/6}
\]
over these triples is precisely the integrand on the left of
\eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:holder5}. H\"older with six equal exponents and
lemma~\ref{gsr:en:55:lem:triple} gives $v^3$. Replace $|r(X_1)|^2$ by $A(X_1)$ in these
six factors to get \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:holderA}.

For \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:holder6}, use all twenty triples from six indices, with
exponent $1/20$ on each product of three squared magnitudes. Each index
occurs ten times, giving exponent one on its magnitude. Triple
independence again gives the asserted bound.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Cancellation of the potentially dangerous fifth term}

\begin{lemma}[Fifth-order real-part cancellation]\label{gsr:en:55:lem:fifth}
In the notation \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:variables}--\eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:identities}, suppose $m>0$.
For any five distinct cube vertices and any conjugation choices $s_j\in\{0,1\}$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:fifth}
 \abs{\Rea\E\prod_{j=1}^5\cC^{s_j}r(X_j)}
 \le \frac5m(v+a)v^2.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Write $r=u+ib$ with real $u,b$. A product of five factors each equal to
$ib$ or $-ib$ is purely imaginary. Telescope the difference from that
product, changing one factor at a time. Since $|b|\le|r|$, its real part
has absolute value at most
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^5\E|u(X_j)|\prod_{k\ne j}|r(X_k)|.
\]
By \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:realpart},
\[
 |u|\le\frac{v+a+A+|r|^2}{2m}.
\]
For each summand, lemma~\ref{gsr:en:55:lem:holder} bounds the three contributions in the
numerator by $(v+a)v^2$, $av^2$, and $v^3$. Their sum is
$2(v+a)v^2$. Summing over the five choices proves \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:fifth}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Explicit centered expansion]\label{gsr:en:55:thm:expansion}
Suppose $|F|\le1$ and $m=\E F$ is real with $m\ge1/2$. In the notation
above,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:expansion}
 \Ufiftyfive(F)=m^q+m^{q-4}\Rea Q_d(r)+\mathcal R,
 \qquad |\mathcal R|\le B_d(v+a)v^2,
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:B}
 B_d=10\binom q5+\sum_{s=6}^q\binom qs2^{s-6}.
\end{equation}
A binomial coefficient with lower index larger than $q$ is zero, and an
empty sum is zero. In particular, $B_2=0$ and $B_3=608$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Expand each cube factor as $m+\cC^{|\omega|}r(X_\omega)$.
Terms with one, two, or three centered factors vanish by
lemma~\ref{gsr:en:55:lem:triple}. The constant term is $m^q$ and the four-factor term is
$m^{q-4}Q_d(r)$. Taking real parts is legitimate because $\Ufiftyfive(F)$ is real.

For each five-factor term, lemma~\ref{gsr:en:55:lem:fifth} and $m\ge1/2$ give the bound
$10(v+a)v^2$; the outside factor $m^{q-5}$ is at most one whenever such
terms occur. For a term with $s\ge6$ factors, retain any six and bound the
others using $|r|\le|F|+m\le2$. Equation \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:holder6} gives
$2^{s-6}v^3\le2^{s-6}(v+a)v^2$. Summing the numbers of terms yields
\eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:B}. For $q=4$ there is no remainder.
\end{proof}

The estimate is uniform over groups and does not invoke an inverse theorem.
It applies to sparse perturbations, amplitude defects, and mixtures of the
two. Its constants are deliberately coarse; the point is the order of the
error and its explicit dependence only on $d$.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A continuous two-torsion profile\srctag{55}}]{A continuous two-torsion profile}\label{gsr:en:55:sec:d6}\label{gsr:en:55:sec:profile}
\srcnote{55}{Section 6}

Let
\[
 v_2=\sum_{\substack{\chi\ne0\\2\chi=0}}|\widehat r(\chi)|^2.
\]
This is the part of the centered variance carried by nontrivial order-two
characters. In odd order $v_2=0$.

\begin{proposition}[Fourier mass pairing]\label{gsr:en:55:prop:pairing}
Under the bounded-function hypotheses of section~\ref{gsr:en:55:sec:normal},
\begin{align}
 E_4(r)&\le v_2^2+\frac12(v-v_2)^2+z^2(v-v_2),\label{gsr:en:55:eq:pairE}\\
 T_4(r)&\le v_2^2.\label{gsr:en:55:eq:pairT}
\end{align}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:profile}
 \Rea Q_d(r)\le
 A_d v_2^2+\frac{C_d}{2}(v-v_2)^2+C_d z^2(v-v_2).
\end{equation}
Also, without using the real-part constraint,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:crudequartic}
 \Rea Q_d(r)\le A_d v^2.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Partition the nonzero characters not fixed by negation into pairs
$\{\chi,-\chi\}$. For one pair write
$x=|\widehat r(\chi)|$, $y=|\widehat r(-\chi)|$, and $s=x^2+y^2$.
Equation \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:skew} gives $|x-y|\le z$, whence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:pairalgebra}
 x^4+y^4=\frac{s^2}{2}+\frac{(x^2-y^2)^2}{2}
 \le\frac{s^2}{2}+z^2s.
\end{equation}
Indeed $(x+y)^2\le2s$. Summing, and using
$\sum s^2\le(\sum s)^2$, gives the non-fixed part of \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:pairE}.
The fixed part is bounded by $v_2^2$, proving both displayed inequalities.
Now apply \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:quarticbound} and use $C_d+J_d=A_d$.
Finally $E_4(r)\le v^2$ and $T_4(r)\le v^2$ imply
\eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:crudequartic}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Profile-sensitive endpoint bound]\label{gsr:en:55:cor:profile}
If $z\le1$, then
\begin{align}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:profilemaster}
 \Ufiftyfive(F)\le{}&\left(1-\frac z2\right)^q
 +A_d v_2^2+\frac{C_d}{2}(v-v_2)^2\\
 &\quad+C_d z^2(v-v_2)+B_d(v+a)v^2.\notag
\end{align}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Use theorem~\ref{gsr:en:55:thm:expansion} and proposition~\ref{gsr:en:55:prop:pairing}. The right side of
\eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:profile} is nonnegative, and $0<m^{q-4}\le1$.
\end{proof}

For $v>0$ write $\tau=v_2/v$. The leading quartic coefficient in
\eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:profilemaster} is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:profilefunction}
 \Phi_d(\tau)=A_d\tau^2+\frac{C_d}{2}(1-\tau)^2.
\end{equation}
Since $A_d>C_d/2>0$ for $d\ge2$, its maximum on $[0,1]$ is $A_d$,
attained only at $\tau=1$. Thus the worse even-order coefficient is not
merely a formal consequence of allowing torsion: it is attained only when
the centered Fourier energy becomes concentrated in two-torsion.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The explicit local stability theorem\srctag{55}}]{The explicit local stability theorem}\label{gsr:en:55:sec:d7}\label{gsr:en:55:sec:local}
\srcnote{55}{Section 7}

Define
\begin{align}
 K_{0,d}&=\frac{q(q-1)}8,\label{gsr:en:55:eq:K0}\\
 M_d&=\begin{cases}C_d/2,&|G|\text{ odd},\\A_d,&|G|\text{ even},\end{cases}
 \qquad
 L_d=\begin{cases}C_d,&|G|\text{ odd},\\0,&|G|\text{ even},\end{cases}
 \label{gsr:en:55:eq:ML}\\
 K_d&=K_{0,d}+M_d,\qquad H_d=B_d+L_d.\label{gsr:en:55:eq:KH}
\end{align}
For a radius and uniform inversion constant, put
\begin{align}
 K_*&=K_{0,d}+A_d,\qquad H_*=B_d+C_d,\qquad c=q/2,\label{gsr:en:55:eq:star}\\
 \rho_d&=\min\left\{\frac12,
       \frac{q}{16(K_*+1)},
       \sqrt{\frac{q}{8(B_d+2C_d+1)}}\right\},\label{gsr:en:55:eq:radius}\\
 R_d&=\frac{12K_*^2}{c^5}+\frac{24K_*H_*}{c^6}
                         +\frac{8H_*}{c^4}.\label{gsr:en:55:eq:R}
\end{align}
All these constants are explicit. In \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:ML}, the even-order choice
is valid on every group, though it is not optimal on odd-order groups.

\begin{theorem}[A posteriori local phase certificate]\label{gsr:en:55:thm:local}
Let $P\in\cP_{d-1}(G)$ and rotate it so that $m=\E f\overline P\ge0$.
Suppose $|f|\le1$ and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:localinput}
 z=2(1-m)=D+a\le\rho_d,
 \qquad D=\E|f-P|^2,\quad a=1-\E|f|^2.
\end{equation}
Then, writing $\eps=1-\Ufiftyfive(f)$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:localpoly}
 \eps\ge\frac q2D-K_dD^2-H_dD^3+\frac q4a,
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:coarse}
 D+a\le\frac4q\eps.
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:localinverse}
 D\le\frac2q\eps+\frac{8K_d}{q^3}\eps^2+R_d\eps^3.
\end{equation}
The phase $P$ need not minimize distance.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Demodulate by $P$ and use the notation of section~\ref{gsr:en:55:sec:normal}. Since
$z\le1$, theorem~\ref{gsr:en:55:thm:expansion} and proposition~\ref{gsr:en:55:prop:pairing} give the master bound
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:master}
 \Ufiftyfive(f)\le\left(1-\frac z2\right)^q+M_dD^2+B_dzD^2+L_dz^2D.
\end{equation}
For odd order use $v_2=0$, $v\le D$, and $v+a\le z$.
For even order use \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:crudequartic} instead.

Taylor's formula with a nonpositive third derivative gives
\[
 (1-z/2)^q\le1-\frac q2z+K_{0,d}z^2
 \qquad(0\le z\le1).
\]
Substitute $z=D+a$ in \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:master} and collect the terms containing
$a$ to obtain
\begin{align}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:beforeabsorb}
 \eps\ge{}&\frac q2D-K_dD^2-H_dD^3\\
 &+a\left\{\frac q2-K_{0,d}(2D+a)-B_dD^2-L_d(2D+a)D\right\}.\notag
\end{align}
Since $2D+a\le2\rho_d$, the expression in braces is at least
\[
 \frac q2-2K_{0,d}\rho_d-(B_d+2C_d)\rho_d^2\ge\frac q4.
\]
This proves \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:localpoly}. Also
\[
 K_dD+H_dD^2\le K_*\rho_d+H_*\rho_d^2
 \le\frac q{16}+\frac q8<\frac q4,
\]
which proves \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:coarse}.

For clarity, we spell out the inversion rather than hiding it in an
asymptotic notation. From \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:localpoly}, dropping the nonnegative
amplitude term, and from \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:coarse},
\[
 D\le\frac\eps c+\frac{K_d}{c}D^2+\frac{H_d}{c}D^3,
 \qquad D\le\frac{2\eps}{c}.
\]
Because $0\le\eps\le1$, it follows first that
\[
 D-\frac\eps c\le C_1\eps^2,
 \qquad C_1=\frac{4K_d}{c^3}+\frac{8H_d}{c^4}.
\]
Consequently (using the positive part if $D-\eps/c<0$)
\[
 D^2\le\frac{\eps^2}{c^2}+\frac{3C_1}{c}\eps^3,
 \qquad D^3\le\frac{8\eps^3}{c^3}.
\]
Substituting once more yields
\[
 D\le\frac\eps c+\frac{K_d}{c^3}\eps^2+
 \left(\frac{12K_d^2}{c^5}+\frac{24K_dH_d}{c^6}
       +\frac{8H_d}{c^4}\right)\eps^3.
\]
Replacing $K_d,H_d$ by $K_*,H_*$ in the cubic coefficient proves
\eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:localinverse}.
\end{proof}

The sharp coefficients simplify dramatically:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:Ksimplify}
 K_{0,d}+\frac{C_d}{2}=\frac{q(3^d-1)}{16},
 \qquad
 K_{0,d}+A_d=\frac{q(q^2-1)}{24}.
\end{equation}
Thus $8K_d/q^3$ is exactly \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:b}.

\begin{corollary}[Explicit $U^3$ certificate]\label{gsr:en:55:cor:u3}
Suppose $P$ is a quadratic phase in the difference sense,
$|f|\le1$, and after constant rotation
$2(1-\E f\overline P)=D+a\le1/44$. With
$\eps=1-\norm f_{U^3}^8$, one has
\[
 \begin{array}{ll}
 \eps\ge4D-13D^2-620D^3+2a,& |G|\text{ odd},\\[2pt]
 \eps\ge4D-21D^2-608D^3+2a,& |G|\text{ even}.
 \end{array}
\]
In either case $D+a\le\eps/2$, and
\[
 D\le\frac\eps4+
 \begin{cases}13\eps^2/64,& |G|\text{ odd},\\21\eps^2/64,& |G|\text{ even}
 \end{cases}
 +\frac{25813}{256}\eps^3.
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Here $q=8$, $C_3=12$, $A_3=14$, $B_3=608$, $K_*=21$, $H_*=620$,
$\rho_3=1/44$, and \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:R} equals $25813/256$.
\end{proof}

The radius $1/44$ is not asserted to be optimal. Unlike the quadratic
coefficient, neither this radius nor the displayed cubic error constant has
been optimized.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Uniform entry and matching extremizing families\srctag{55}}]{Uniform entry and matching extremizing families}\label{gsr:en:55:sec:d8}\label{gsr:en:55:sec:sharpness}
\srcnote{55}{Section 8}

\subsection{The published entry theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Eisner--Tao entry theorem, finite-group form]\label{gsr:en:55:thm:ET}
For fixed $d$, if $|f|\le1$ and $\norm f_{U^d}\to1$, then there is
$P\in\cP_{d-1}(G)$ with $\E|f-P|=o_d(1)$, uniformly in the finite
abelian group $G$.
\end{theorem}

This is \cite[Theorem 1.1]{eisnertao}, not a theorem newly proved here.
Since $|f-P|\le2$, its conclusion implies squared $L^2$ distance $o_d(1)$.
Also $a\le\eps$ by lemma~\ref{gsr:en:55:lem:amplitude}. For a minimizing phase, after
rotation, $z=D_d(f)+a\to0$ uniformly. Thus there is $e_d>0$ such that
$\eps\le e_d$ implies the hypothesis of theorem~\ref{gsr:en:55:thm:local}. Equations
\eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:localinverse} and \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:Ksimplify} prove the upper bound in
theorem~\ref{gsr:en:55:thm:main}.

\subsection{Separation of nonconstant phase classes}

To prove sharpness, it is not enough to calculate distance to the constant
phase: another polynomial phase could conceivably be closer. The following
uniform gap excludes that possibility.

\begin{lemma}[A uniform phase-class gap]\label{gsr:en:55:lem:gap}
If $R:G\to S^1$ is a phase polynomial of degree at most $s\ge1$ and is
not constant, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:gap}
 |\E R|\le1-\gamma_s,\qquad \gamma_s=4^{-(s-1)}.
\end{equation}
Consequently, if $|F|=1$ and
\[
 D_{\rm const}(F):=\min_{c\in S^1}\E|F-c|^2<\gamma_{d-1}/2,
\]
then $D_d(F)=D_{\rm const}(F)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $s=1$, a phase is a constant times a character, and a nonconstant
character has mean zero. Suppose the assertion known for $s-1$. If
$|\E R|>1-\gamma_s$, rotate $R$ so that its mean is positive, and write
$\eta=1-\E R<\gamma_s$. Then $\norm{R-1}_2^2=2\eta$.
For each direction $h$, the phase derivative
$\Delta_hR(x)=R(x+h)\overline{R(x)}$ has degree at most $s-1$, and
\[
 \norm{\Delta_hR-1}_2\le2\norm{R-1}_2.
\]
It follows that $\Rea\E\Delta_hR\ge1-4\eta>1-\gamma_{s-1}$.
By induction every derivative is constant. Therefore $R$ is a constant
multiple of a character. Its nonzero mean forces that character to be
trivial, a contradiction. This proves \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:gap}.

For the final assertion choose a closest constant $c$. If a nonconstant
phase $P$ had distance to $F$ at most $\sqrt{D_{\rm const}(F)}$, the triangle
inequality would give
\[
 \norm{P-c}_2\le2\sqrt{D_{\rm const}(F)}<\sqrt{2\gamma_{d-1}}.
\]
But \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:gap} implies
$\min_c\norm{P-c}_2^2=2(1-|\E P|)\ge2\gamma_{d-1}$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Even-order groups: an exact one-character family}

Every even-order finite abelian group has a nontrivial character
$\chi:G\to\{-1,1\}$. For $t$ real put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:evenfamily}
 F_t=e^{it\chi}.
\end{equation}
Its mean is $\cos t$. For sufficiently small $t$, lemma~\ref{gsr:en:55:lem:gap} gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:evenD}
 D_d(F_t)=2(1-\cos t).
\end{equation}
The additive cubical difference of $\chi$ factors exactly:
\[
 \sum_\omega(-1)^{|\omega|}\chi(x+\omega\cdot h)
 =\chi(x)\prod_{j=1}^d(1-\chi(h_j)).
\]
It vanishes unless all $\chi(h_j)=-1$, an event of probability $1/q$;
on that event it is $q\chi(x)$. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:eveneps}
 \eps(F_t)=\frac{1-\cos(qt)}q.
\end{equation}
For small positive $e$, choose
$t=q^{-1}\arccos(1-qe)$. This gives the exact attained distance
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:evencurve}
 \mathcal D^{\rm even}_d(e)
 =2\left[1-\cos\left(\frac1q\arccos(1-qe)\right)\right].
\end{equation}
Taylor expansion, or elimination of $t^2$ from
\eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:evenD}--\eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:eveneps}, gives
\[
 \mathcal D^{\rm even}_d(e)
 =\frac2q e+\frac{q^2-1}{3q^2}e^2+O_d(e^3).
\]
The choice of $t$ and the phase-gap range are independent of the group.

\subsection{Odd-order groups: a conjugate-pair family}

Let $G$ have odd order and be nontrivial. Choose a nontrivial character
$\chi$, so $\chi\ne-\chi$ in additive dual notation, and set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:oddfamily}
 b=\sqrt2\,\Rea(\zeta\chi),\qquad F_t=e^{itb},\qquad |\zeta|=1.
\end{equation}
Then $\E b=0$, $\E b^2=1$, $|b|\le\sqrt2$, and the Fourier mass of $b$
is $1/2$ at each of $\chi,-\chi$. Thus
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:oddQ}
 Q_d(b)=C_d/2.
\end{equation}
Write $\mu_4=\E b^4$ and
$S=\sum_\omega(-1)^{|\omega|}b(X_\omega)$. Triple independence gives
\begin{align}
 \E S^2&=q,\label{gsr:en:55:eq:S2}\\
 \E S^4&=q\mu_4+3q(q-1)+24Q_d(b).
 \label{gsr:en:55:eq:S4}
\end{align}
Indeed the multiplicity patterns $3+1$ and $2+1+1$ vanish, the pattern
$2+2$ contributes $6\binom q2$, and the four-distinct pattern contributes
the final term. Its signs are positive on every dependent four-set by
proposition~\ref{gsr:en:55:prop:quartic}.

The law of $S$ is symmetric: interchanging the two endpoints of the first
cube direction changes $S$ to $-S$ and preserves the sampling measure.
Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:oddexpandeps}
 \eps(F_t)=\frac q2t^2-
 \left(\frac{q\mu_4}{24}+\frac{q(q-1)}8+\frac{C_d}{2}\right)t^4
 +O_d(t^6).
\end{equation}
For sufficiently small $t$, the closest phase is a constant by
lemma~\ref{gsr:en:55:lem:gap}, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:oddexpandD}
 D_d(F_t)=2(1-|\E e^{itb}|)
         =t^2-\frac{\mu_4}{12}t^4+O(t^6).
\end{equation}
To check the latter formula, expand the mean through order four. Its real
part is $1-t^2/2+\mu_4t^4/24+O(t^6)$, while its imaginary part is
$O(t^3)$ because $\E b=0$. Taking the modulus changes it only at order
six. All error estimates are uniform because $|b|\le\sqrt2$.

Eliminating $t^2$ makes the fourth moment cancel:
\[
 \eps(F_t)=\frac q2D_d(F_t)
   -\left(K_{0,d}+\frac{C_d}{2}\right)D_d(F_t)^2+O_d(D_d(F_t)^3).
\]
Inversion gives the odd coefficient in \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:b}. The derivative of
\eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:oddexpandeps} is $qt+O_d(t^3)$, uniformly, so every sufficiently
small positive defect is attained by a positive $t$.
Together with the uniform upper bound, the two families prove
\eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:sharpmod} and complete the proof of theorem~\ref{gsr:en:55:thm:main}.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Proof of second-order rigidity\srctag{55}}]{Proof of second-order rigidity}\label{gsr:en:55:sec:d9}\label{gsr:en:55:sec:rigidity}
\srcnote{55}{Section 9}

We now prove theorem~\ref{gsr:en:55:thm:rigidmain}. All little-oh estimates in this section
are along its given sequence. Demodulate by a minimizing phase and use
$F,r,D,a,z,v,v_2$ as before, suppressing the index $n$. Write
$c=q/2$, and let $M=M_d$, $K=K_{0,d}+M$.

\subsection{Amplitude and quartic saturation}

By theorem~\ref{gsr:en:55:thm:main} and the saturation hypothesis,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:rigD}
 D=\frac\eps c+\frac K{c^3}\eps^2+o(\eps^2),
 \qquad cD-KD^2=\eps+o(\eps^2).
\end{equation}
The local theorem gives $z=O_d(\eps)$ and
\[
 \eps\ge cD-KD^2-H_dD^3+\frac q4a.
\]
Since $a\ge0$, \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:rigD} implies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:rigamp}
 a=o(\eps^2),\qquad v=D-z^2/4\sim D\sim\eps/c.
\end{equation}
The exact expansion \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:expansion}, expanded in $z$, now yields
\[
 \eps=cD-K_{0,d}D^2-\Rea Q_d(r)+o(\eps^2).
\]
Combining with \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:rigD},
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:rigQ}
 \Rea Q_d(r)=M v^2+o(v^2).
\end{equation}

\subsection{Even order: concentration at one real character}

In even order, \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:profile} and \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:rigQ} imply
\[
 A_d\le\Phi_d(v_2/v)+o(1).
\]
The unique maximum of \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:profilefunction} is at $1$, so
$v_2/v\to1$. The non-fixed Fourier mass is $o(v)$; in particular its
fourth-power sum is $o(v^2)$. Thus
\[
 E_4(r)=T_4(r)+o(v^2).
\]
Applying \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:quarticbound} once more to \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:rigQ} gives
$T_4(r)\sim v^2$. Let the squared Fourier masses on nontrivial order-two
characters be $p_\chi$. Since
\[
 \sum p_\chi\sim v,\qquad \sum p_\chi^2\sim v^2,
 \qquad \sum p_\chi^2\le(\max p_\chi)\sum p_\chi,
\]
one such character $\chi$ carries $(1-o(1))v$.
Equation \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:skew} at a fixed character gives
$|2\Rea\widehat r(\chi)|\le z=O(\eps)=o(\sqrt v)$.
Therefore for a sign $s$,
\[
 \widehat r(\chi)=i s\sqrt v+o(\sqrt v),\qquad
 \norm{r-i s\sqrt v\,\chi}_2=o(\sqrt v).
\]
Finally $m-1=O(D)=o(\sqrt D)$ and $v/D\to1$, which proves
\eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:evenrigid}.

\subsection{Odd order: concentration at one conjugate pair}

There is no nontrivial order-two character. Since $C_d>0$,
\eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:quarticbound}, \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:pairE}, and \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:rigQ} give
\[
 E_4(r)=\frac12v^2+o(v^2).
\]
Let $s_j$ be the total squared mass in the $j$th conjugate pair. The
pairwise inequality \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:pairalgebra} implies
\[
 E_4(r)\le\frac12\sum_j s_j^2+z^2v.
\]
Here $z^2v=o(v^2)$, while $\sum_j s_j=v$. Thus
$\sum_j s_j^2\sim v^2$, and one pair $\{\chi,-\chi\}$ carries
$(1-o(1))v$.
For its coefficients $\alpha=\widehat r(\chi)$ and
$\beta=\widehat r(-\chi)$, \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:skew} says
\[
 \beta=-\overline\alpha+o(\sqrt v),\qquad
 |\alpha|=|\beta|+o(\sqrt v)=\sqrt{v/2}+o(\sqrt v).
\]
Choose $\zeta\in S^1$ so that
$\alpha=i\sqrt{v/2}\,\zeta+o(\sqrt v)$. Fourier inversion and Parseval
give
\[
 \norm{r-i\sqrt{2v}\,\Rea(\zeta\chi)}_2=o(\sqrt v).
\]
As above, adding back $m-1$ and replacing $v$ by $D$ proves
\eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:oddrigid}. This completes the proof of
theorem~\ref{gsr:en:55:thm:rigidmain}.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{An exact calibration at degree two\srctag{55}}]{An exact calibration at degree two}\label{gsr:en:55:sec:d10}\label{gsr:en:55:sec:exactu2}
\srcnote{55}{Section 10}

At $d=2$ the Fourier identity allows a nonasymptotic answer on every
even-order group. This elementary calibration is useful for checking the
normalizations and the direction of the inequality; it is not being
claimed as an independent historical novelty.

\begin{proposition}[Exact even-order $U^2$ stability modulus]\label{gsr:en:55:prop:exactu2}
If $G$ is a nontrivial finite abelian group of even order, then for
$0\le e\le1/2$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:exactu2}
 \mathfrak S_{2,G}(e)
 =2\left(1-\sqrt{\frac{1+\sqrt{1-2e}}2}\right).
\end{equation}
The right side remains a valid upper bound for every finite abelian group.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Polynomial phases of degree one are constants times characters.
Let $s=\E|f|^2$ and $m=\max_\chi|\widehat f(\chi)|$. Then
\[
 D_2(f)=1+s-2m,\qquad
 \Ufiftyfive(f)=\sum_\chi|\widehat f(\chi)|^4\le m^2s\le m^2.
\]
If $\eps(f)\le e\le1/2$, it follows that $m\ge\sqrt{1-e}$ and
$D_2(f)\le2-\sqrt2$.
Demodulate by a maximizing character. With $D=D_2(f)$ and $z=D+a$,
\[
 \Ufiftyfive(f)\le m^4+v^2
 =\left(1-\frac z2\right)^4+\left(D-\frac{z^2}4\right)^2.
\]
For fixed $D$, this expression is decreasing in $z$ from $D$ to the
actual value of $z$: its derivative is
\[
 -2(1-z/2)^3-z(D-z^2/4)\le0.
\]
Both terms have the indicated sign on that interval because $m\ge0$
and the endpoint variance is nonnegative. Consequently
\[
 \eps(f)\ge g(D):=2D-\frac52D^2+D^3-\frac18D^4.
\]
Writing $u=1-D/2$, this is $g(D)=2u^2(1-u^2)$.
The function $g$ increases on $0\le D\le2-\sqrt2$, so $g(D)\le e$
implies the upper bound in \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:exactu2}.

For equality choose an order-two character and
$f=e^{it\chi}=\cos t+i\chi\sin t$, with $0\le t\le\pi/4$.
The largest Fourier coefficient is $\cos t$, so the closest phase is the
constant one. Its defect is $(1-\cos4t)/4$, covering $[0,1/2]$, and
its distance is $2(1-\cos t)$. This is exactly \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:exactu2}.
\end{proof}

In particular, the even-order example curve \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:evencurve} is
exactly optimal at $d=2$. Our higher-degree theorem proves optimality
through second order, not the full exact curve for $d\ge3$.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Consequences for phase testing and local structure\srctag{55}}]{Consequences for phase testing and local structure}\label{gsr:en:55:sec:d11}\label{gsr:en:55:sec:applications}
\srcnote{55}{Section 11}

\subsection{A sharp soundness expansion for unit-modulus cube tests}

Suppose $|f|=1$ and define the squared cubical test loss
\[
 \mathcal L_d(f)=\E\abs{
   \prod_\omega\cC^{|\omega|}f(X_\omega)-1}^2.
\]
Since the product has modulus one and its expectation is real,
$\mathcal L_d(f)=2\eps(f)$. Therefore theorem~\ref{gsr:en:55:thm:main} gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:55:eq:test}
 D_d(f)\le\frac1q\mathcal L_d(f)
       +\frac{b_d(G)}4\mathcal L_d(f)^2
       +O_d(\mathcal L_d(f)^3).
\end{equation}
Both coefficients are sharp by the same unit-modulus examples. This is
an average squared-loss statement for complex phases, not a claim about
the rejection probability of a Boolean-valued test without a conversion
of the loss convention.

\subsection{Certification after a coarse inverse step}

Suppose a separate argument supplies a polynomial phase $P$ with
$|\E f\overline P|\ge1-\rho_d/2$. Rotate $P$ and compute the cubical
loss. The local theorem immediately returns an explicit bound on
$\E|f-P|^2$, without needing the qualitative entry theorem or a new
minimization over all phases. At $d=3$, the candidate-correlation condition
is simply $|\E f\overline P|\ge1-1/88$.

This supplies a concrete endpoint interface for the extraction and
integration architecture in Gowers's proof. It does not supply such a
candidate from an arbitrary fixed positive $U^d$ norm. In particular it
should not be substituted for an open Section 16 or Section 17 catalogue
entry whose hypotheses are substantially weaker.

\subsection{Cosets and quotients}

If the same problem is posed on a coset $x_0+H$ with normalized counting
measure and all directions in $H$, translation identifies it exactly
with the theorem on $H$. The parity in the coefficient is the parity of
$|H|$, not that of an unrelated ambient group. Pullback along a surjective
homomorphism preserves every cube average and the explicit example
families. For the upper theorem no quotient reduction is necessary.

The corresponding assertion for an arbitrary Bohr set with restricted
sampling is not automatic: the proof depends on exact triple independence.
Likewise, restricting all vertices to an interval changes the underlying
sampling law. These are substantive extension questions, not harmless
changes of notation.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Near-maximal uniformity and global frequency maps\srctag{57}}]{Near-maximal uniformity and global frequency maps}\label{gsr:en:57:sec:d5}
\srcnote{57}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:en:57:ep:section}

The small interval near $\alpha=1$ in the preceding argument admits a
different, much stronger conclusion: the progressions can be the whole
prime field. We prove this directly, with explicit constants, by correcting
the dominant Fourier frequencies of multiplicative derivatives. The same
argument extends to every uniformity order. On a prime field, permutation
symmetry reduces the dependence on the number of derivative parameters to
a linear loss.

All averages and Fourier transforms in this section are normalized. Thus,
on $\Fp$, $\widehat u(r)=\E_x u(x)\ep(-rx)$, where
$\ep(t)=\exp(2\pi i t/p)$; the Fourier coefficients in Gowers's original
normalization are $p\widehat u(r)$. We write
\[
 Q_j(u)=\norm{u}_{U^j}^{2^j},\qquad
 \D_hu(x)=u(x+h)\overline{u(x)}.
\]
On a general finite abelian group, frequencies belong to its character
group, written additively. Distances between finite-valued maps mean the
proportion of inputs on which they disagree. The near-extremizer principle
that very large uniformity forces closeness to a polynomial phase is
established in much greater generality by Eisner and Tao
\cite[Theorem~1.1]{eisnertao}. The contribution here is an explicit
frequency-correction argument suited to the preceding quantitative
application, its symmetry improvement, and the constants in the resulting
prime-field estimates.

\subsection{Phase normalization and additive correction}

\begin{lemma}[Normalization without an order-dependent loss]
\label{gsr:en:57:ep:phase-rounding}
Let $G$ be finite abelian, $d\ge1$, and $|f|\le1$. Define $g=f/|f|$
where $f\ne0$, and $g=1$ at the zeros of $f$. If
$Q_d(f)\ge1-\varepsilon$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:57:ep:rounding}
 \norm{f-g}_1\le\varepsilon,
 \qquad Q_d(g)\ge1-2\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
Furthermore, for every $s\ge1$ and every choice of directions,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:57:ep:derivative-transfer}
 \norm{\D_{h_1}\cdots\D_{h_s}f-
       \D_{h_1}\cdots\D_{h_s}g}_1
 \le2^s\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For each cube, write its alternating product for $f$ as $AC$, where
$A$ is the product of the $2^d$ absolute values and $C$ is the
corresponding product for $g$. Thus $0\le A\le1$ and $|C|=1$.
For $-1\le r\le1$,
\[
 2(1-Ar)-(1-r)=1+(1-2A)r\ge1-|1-2A|\ge0.
\]
Apply this with $r=\Re C$ and average. Since the cube averages are real,
$1-Q_d(g)\le2(1-Q_d(f))$. Also
$Q_d(f)\le\E A\le\E|f|$, using any fixed cube vertex, and consequently
$\norm{f-g}_1=\E(1-|f|)\le\varepsilon$.
Finally telescope the $2^s$ factors in a multiplicative derivative.
Every other factor has modulus at most one, and translation preserves
the $L^1$ norm. This proves \eqref{gsr:en:57:ep:derivative-transfer} uniformly in
the directions.
\end{proof}

The next argument is a direct form of the classical
Blum--Luby--Rubinfeld correction method \cite{blr}; we include the
finite abelian group proof and constants.

\begin{lemma}[An elementary additive correction bound]
\label{gsr:en:57:ep:blr}
Let $A,H$ be finite abelian groups and $u:A\to H$. Put
\[
 \theta=\Prob_{x,y}[u(x+y)\ne u(x)+u(y)].
\]
If $\theta<1/6$, there is a homomorphism $v:A\to H$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:57:ep:blr-distance}
 \dist(u,v)\le\frac{\theta}{1-2\theta}\le2\theta.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Fix $x$ and put $A_x(y)=u(x+y)-u(y)$. For independent uniform $y,z$,
the addition tests at $(x+y,z-y)$ and $(y,z-y)$ each fail with
probability $\theta$: each ordered pair is uniformly distributed on
$A^2$. If both tests hold, then $A_x(y)=A_x(z)$. Thus the collision
probability of $A_x$ is at least $1-2\theta$. For any finite
probability distribution $(m_a)$, $\sum_a m_a^2\le\max_a m_a$.
The most frequent value of $A_x$ therefore has mass at least
$1-2\theta>1/2$. Denote this unique value by $v(x)$.

The exact identity
\[
 A_{x+x'}(y)=A_x(x'+y)+A_{x'}(y)
\]
and the union bound show that all three majority values occur
simultaneously with probability at least $1-6\theta>0$.
Hence $v(x+x')=v(x)+v(x')$. If $u(x)\ne v(x)$, at least
$1-2\theta$ of the original tests with first argument $x$ fail.
Writing $\delta=\dist(u,v)$ gives
$\delta(1-2\theta)\le\theta$, as required.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Symmetric bilinear correction on a prime field]
\label{gsr:en:57:ep:symmetric-bilinear}
Let $\phi:\Fp^2\to\Fp$ be symmetric, with $\phi(h,0)=0$. If
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:57:ep:bilinear-test}
 \Prob_{h,h',k}[\phi(h+h',k)\ne\phi(h,k)+\phi(h',k)]\le\tau,
\end{equation}
then some $c\in\Fp$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:57:ep:bilinear-correction}
 \Prob_{h,k}[\phi(h,k)\ne chk]\le18\tau.
\end{equation}
No smallness condition on $\tau$ is required.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For each $k$, let $\theta_k$ be the failure rate in the row
$h\mapsto\phi(h,k)$. If $\theta_k<1/6$, apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:blr};
the corrected row is $h\mapsto a(k)h$ and has distance at most
$2\theta_k$. Otherwise take $a(k)=0$, incurring distance at most
$1\le6\theta_k$. The zero row is already correct, so take $a(0)=0$.
The global distance $\delta$ from $\phi$ to $L(h,k)=a(k)h$ is at most
$6\tau$.

Symmetry gives
$D:=\Prob[L(h,k)\ne L(k,h)]\le2\delta$. Put $q=(p-1)/p$ and
\[
 m_c=\Prob[a(k)/k=c\mid k\ne0].
\]
Because $a(0)=0$, a mismatch requires $h,k\ne0$, and therefore
\[
 D=q^2\Bigl(1-\sum_c m_c^2\Bigr).
\]
Choose $c$ with maximum $m_c$. The distance between $L$ and $(h,k)\mapsto
chk$ is $q^2(1-\max_c m_c)\le D$. Consequently the distance from
$\phi$ to this bilinear map is at most $\delta+D\le3\delta\le18\tau$.
The calculation is valid also for $p=2$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{From Fourier concentration to addition tests}

\begin{lemma}[Dominant frequencies of mixed derivatives]
\label{gsr:en:57:ep:selector}
Let $G$ be finite abelian, $s\ge1$, and $g:G\to\C$ be unimodular.
Suppose $Q_{s+2}(g)\ge1-\rho$. There is a frequency map
$\phi:G^s\to\widehat G$ with the following properties.
It is symmetric in its arguments and equals zero whenever one argument
is zero. There is a function $t:G^s\to[0,1]$ with $\E t\le\rho$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:57:ep:selector-coefficient}
 \left|\widehat{\D_{h_1}\cdots\D_{h_s}g}
              \bigl(\phi(h_1,\ldots,h_s)\bigr)\right|^2
 \ge1-t(h_1,\ldots,h_s).
\end{equation}
In each coordinate, the additive-test failure rate of $\phi$ is at most
$9\rho$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write $F_{\boldsymbol h}=\D_{h_1}\cdots\D_{h_s}g$ and
$t(\boldsymbol h)=1-Q_2(F_{\boldsymbol h})$. The Gowers recursion gives
$\E t\le\rho$. Since $F_{\boldsymbol h}$ is unimodular, Parseval and
the Fourier expression for $Q_2$ give
\[
 \sum_r|\widehat F_{\boldsymbol h}(r)|^2=1,
 \qquad
 \sum_r|\widehat F_{\boldsymbol h}(r)|^4=1-t(\boldsymbol h).
\]
Hence the largest squared Fourier modulus is at least $1-t$.
Choose a maximizing frequency with one fixed ordering of $\widehat G$
to break ties. Mixed derivatives commute, so this choice is symmetric.
If one direction is zero, the derivative is identically one, and the
maximizing frequency is uniquely zero.

For suitable unit scalars $z_{\boldsymbol h}$, put
\[
 e(\boldsymbol h)=
 \norm{F_{\boldsymbol h}-z_{\boldsymbol h}\chi_{\phi(\boldsymbol h)}}_2^2
 =2-2|\widehat F_{\boldsymbol h}(\phi(\boldsymbol h))|
 \le2t(\boldsymbol h).
\]
Thus $\E e\le2\rho$. In the first coordinate the exact cocycle identity is
\[
 F_{h+h',\boldsymbol k}(x)
 =F_{h,\boldsymbol k}(x+h')F_{h',\boldsymbol k}(x).
\]
If the selected frequencies fail to add, the unit characters approximating
the two sides are orthogonal, regardless of their scalar phases. Their
$L^2$ distance is $\sqrt2$. The triangle inequality, followed by
Cauchy--Schwarz, therefore yields
\[
 \ind_{\mathrm{failure}}\le\frac32
 \bigl(e(h+h',\boldsymbol k)+e(h,\boldsymbol k)+e(h',\boldsymbol k)\bigr).
\]
Averaging bounds the failure rate by
$(9/2)\E e\le9\rho$. The other coordinates are identical.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[A global square near maximal fourth uniformity]
\label{gsr:en:57:ep:near-u4}
Let $p$ be prime and $f:\Fp\to\C$ satisfy $|f|\le1$ and
\[
 Q_4(f)\ge1-\varepsilon,\qquad 0\le\varepsilon\le1/1024.
\]
There are $c\in\Fp$ and $B\subseteq\Fp^2$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:57:ep:u4-conclusion}
 |B|\ge(1-332\varepsilon)p^2,
 \qquad
 \left|\widehat{\D_h\D_kf}(chk)\right|
 \ge\frac34-4\varepsilon\quad ((h,k)\in B).
\end{equation}
In particular $|B|\ge(173/256)p^2>p^2/2$, and every displayed Fourier
coefficient is at least $191/256>1/2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Normalize $f$ to $g$ by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:phase-rounding}. Apply
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:selector} with $s=2$ and $\rho=2\varepsilon$.
The first-coordinate test fails with probability at most
$\tau=18\varepsilon$, so Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:symmetric-bilinear} supplies
$c$ with $\phi(h,k)=chk$ except on at most $324\varepsilon$ of the pairs.
Discard also the pairs where $t(h,k)>1/4$; Markov's inequality bounds
their proportion by $4\E t\le8\varepsilon$.
On each remaining pair, \eqref{gsr:en:57:ep:selector-coefficient} gives a Fourier
modulus at least $\sqrt3/2\ge3/4$ for $\D_h\D_kg$. The uniform bound
\eqref{gsr:en:57:ep:derivative-transfer} changes this coefficient by at most
$4\varepsilon$ on returning to $f$. The exceptional proportions sum
to $332\varepsilon$. At $\varepsilon=1/1024$, the two elementary
estimates in the statement are equal to $173/256$ and $191/256$.
\end{proof}

This theorem supplies the endpoint needed in Section~13 with
$P=Q=\Fp$, represented by $0,1,\ldots,p-1$ with common step one. It
uses neither a scale threshold nor an inverse theorem as an input.
The exact endpoint $\varepsilon=0$ is included.

\subsection{Every order on a prime field}

\begin{lemma}[Correction of a symmetric table in several variables]
\label{gsr:en:57:ep:symmetric-table}
Let $\phi:\Fp^s\to\Fp$ be symmetric and vanish whenever any coordinate
is zero. If its first-coordinate additive-test failure rate is at most
$\tau$, then some $c\in\Fp$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:57:ep:table-correction}
 \Prob[\phi(h_1,\ldots,h_s)\ne c h_1\cdots h_s]\le12s\tau.
\end{equation}
There is no smallness condition on $\tau$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Correct the first-coordinate rows as in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:symmetric-bilinear}. This gives
$L(\boldsymbol h)=a(h_2,\ldots,h_s)h_1$ at global distance
$\delta\le6\tau$. Choose $a=0$ on every row for which one remaining
coordinate is zero; those original rows are identically zero.
Both $L$ and $\phi$ vanish when $h_1=0$ as well. Thus every discrepancy
lies in $\Omega=(\Fp^*)^s$, of density $q^s$, where $q=(p-1)/p$.

On $\Omega$ define
\[
 \psi(\boldsymbol h)=\frac{\phi(\boldsymbol h)}{h_1\cdots h_s}.
\]
It is symmetric and is within $\delta/q^s$ of the predictor
$a(h_2,\ldots,h_s)/(h_2\cdots h_s)$, which is independent of $h_1$.
Symmetry gives, for each coordinate $j$, a predictor independent of
$h_j$ with the same error bound.

Take independent uniform $X,Y\in\Omega$ and replace the coordinates of
$X$ by those of $Y$ successively. At replacement $j$, the corresponding
predictor agrees on the two tuples. Their $\psi$ values can differ only
if at least one prediction is wrong, with probability at most
$2\delta/q^s$. Hence
\[
 \Prob[\psi(X)\ne\psi(Y)]\le\frac{2s\delta}{q^s}.
\]
For the distribution $m_c=\Prob[\psi=c]$, the left side is
$1-\sum_c m_c^2$. A most frequent $c$ has exceptional probability
$1-\max_c m_c\le1-\sum_c m_c^2$. Multiplying the resulting estimate
by $q^s$ and including the exactly correct zero-coordinate tuples gives
\eqref{gsr:en:57:ep:table-correction}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Symmetric frequency extraction at every order]
\label{gsr:en:57:ep:prime-all-orders}
Let $p$ be prime, $s\ge1$, and $f:\Fp\to\C$ satisfy $|f|\le1$ and
$Q_{s+2}(f)\ge1-\varepsilon$. There exist $c\in\Fp$ and
$B\subseteq\Fp^s$ such that
\begin{align}
 |B|&\ge\bigl(1-(216s+8)\varepsilon\bigr)p^s,
 \label{gsr:en:57:ep:all-order-density}\\
 \left|\widehat{\D_{h_1}\cdots\D_{h_s}f}
                (c h_1\cdots h_s)\right|
 &\ge\frac34-2^s\varepsilon\qquad(\boldsymbol h\in B).
 \label{gsr:en:57:ep:all-order-coefficient}
\end{align}
A half-density set with Fourier modulus at least $1/2$ follows whenever
\[
 \varepsilon\le
 \min\left\{\frac1{432s+16},\,2^{-s-2}\right\}.
\]
For $s=2$, Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:near-u4} improves the coefficient $440$ in
\eqref{gsr:en:57:ep:all-order-density} to $332$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
After phase normalization, Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:selector} has
$\rho=2\varepsilon$ and test error at most $18\varepsilon$.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:symmetric-table} corrects the selector outside a set of
proportion $216s\varepsilon$. Removing $t>1/4$ costs a further
$8\varepsilon$. On the retained set the Fourier modulus for the phase
is at least $3/4$; \eqref{gsr:en:57:ep:derivative-transfer} gives the stated loss
$2^s\varepsilon$ for $f$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{An extension to arbitrary finite abelian groups}

The scalar division used above is specific to a one-dimensional prime
field. A separate additive-correction argument works on all finite abelian
groups, with a larger dependence on $s$.

\begin{lemma}[Correction of an approximately separately additive map]
\label{gsr:en:57:ep:separate-correction}
Let $A_1,\ldots,A_s,H$ be finite abelian groups. Suppose
$\phi:A_1\times\cdots\times A_s\to H$ has additive-test failure at most
$\tau$ in every coordinate. Put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:57:ep:Cs}
 C_1=2,\qquad C_s=6+38C_{s-1}
       =\frac{80\cdot38^{s-1}-6}{37}.
\end{equation}
If $38^{s-1}\tau<1/6$, there is a separately additive map $B$ such that
$\dist(\phi,B)\le C_s\tau$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The case $s=1$ is Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:blr}. For larger $s$, correct the
first-coordinate rows with global distance at most $6\tau$, using the
zero homomorphism on rows whose test error is at least $1/6$.
The corrected rows form a map $a$ of the remaining coordinates into
the finite abelian group $\Hom(A_1,H)$.

In any remaining coordinate, the corrected addition test, after
evaluation at a uniform element of $A_1$, can fail only if the original
test fails or one of its three values was changed. Its failure
probability is therefore at most $\tau+18\tau=19\tau$.
A nonzero homomorphism $A_1\to H$ has a proper kernel, so it is
nonzero on at least half of $A_1$. The actual homomorphism-valued
addition test for $a$ consequently fails with probability at most
$38\tau$. Apply induction in $s-1$ coordinates with this parameter.
Its premise is precisely $38^{s-1}\tau<1/6$, and the total correction
distance is at most $6\tau+38C_{s-1}\tau=C_s\tau$.
Evaluating the resulting homomorphism-valued map at the first coordinate
produces the required separately additive $B$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Frequency extraction on a finite abelian group]
\label{gsr:en:57:ep:group-all-orders}
Let $G$ be finite abelian, $s\ge1$, and $f:G\to\C$ satisfy $|f|\le1$ and
$Q_{s+2}(f)\ge1-\varepsilon$. If
$18\cdot38^{s-1}\varepsilon<1/6$, there is an $s$-additive map
$B:G^s\to\widehat G$ and a set $E\subseteq G^s$ of density at least
$1-(18C_s+8)\varepsilon$ such that
\[
 \left|\widehat{\D_{h_1}\cdots\D_{h_s}f}
                       (B(\boldsymbol h))\right|
 \ge\frac34-2^s\varepsilon
 \qquad(\boldsymbol h\in E).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Combine Lemmas~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:phase-rounding}, \ref{gsr:en:57:ep:selector}, and
\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:separate-correction} with $\tau=18\varepsilon$.
The selector-correction error is $18C_s\varepsilon$; removing $t>1/4$
costs $8\varepsilon$, and transfer back to $f$ costs
$2^s\varepsilon$ in the Fourier modulus.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 70--81]
\emph{A smaller loss for $d\ge2$} (source~72, Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:nearmaximal}): on every finite abelian group its density loss is $(6^d-1)(2^{d+2}+1)\varepsilon$, that is $45\varepsilon$, $595\varepsilon$, $7095\varepsilon$ at $d=1,2,3$ against this theorem's $44\varepsilon$, $1484\varepsilon$, $56204\varepsilon$ (its Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:72:thm:main}). Source~72 does not cite this theorem; source~57 arrived after its overlap check.
\end{writenote}

Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:group-all-orders} asserts separate additivity of a frequency
map. It does not assert that this map is a symmetric tensor or that it
integrates to one polynomial phase. Such integration requires an additional
argument. The next result carries it out in the cubic prime-field case.

\subsection{An explicit cubic inverse theorem near the maximum}

\begin{corollary}[Cubic phase approximation with an explicit error]
\label{gsr:en:57:ep:cubic-inverse}
Let $p\ge5$ be prime and $f:\Fp\to\C$ satisfy $|f|\le1$ and
\[
 Q_4(f)\ge1-\varepsilon,\qquad 0\le\varepsilon<1/17604.
\]
There is $P\in\Fp[X]$, of degree at most three, such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:57:ep:cubic-correlation}
 \left|\E_x f(x)\ep(-P(x))\right|
 \ge\sqrt{1-6194\varepsilon}-\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
For a suitable scalar $z$ of modulus one,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:57:ep:cubic-distance}
 \norm{f-z\ep(P)}_2^2
 \le2\bigl(1-\sqrt{1-6194\varepsilon}\bigr)+2\varepsilon
 \le12390\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
We first record the degree descent for a unimodular function $u$ with
$Q_4(u)\ge1-D$. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:selector} gives mean deficit at most $D$
and first-coordinate test failure at most $9D$. The symmetric bilinear
correction changes at most $162D$ of its frequencies. Therefore, using
\eqref{gsr:en:57:ep:selector-coefficient} on the agreement set and positivity on
its complement, some $c$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:57:ep:first-descent-average}
 \E_{h,k}\left|\widehat{\D_h\D_ku}(chk)\right|^2\ge1-163D.
\end{equation}
There is no thresholding of the individual deficits here.

Set $u_1(x)=u(x)\ep(-(c/6)x^3)$. The additive polynomial identity
\[
 \bigl((x+h+k)^3-(x+h)^3-(x+k)^3+x^3\bigr)c/6
 =chkx+(c/2)hk(h+k)
\]
shows that the squared modulus of $\E_x\D_h\D_ku_1(x)$ equals the
squared Fourier modulus in \eqref{gsr:en:57:ep:first-descent-average}.
The Gowers recursion consequently gives $Q_3(u_1)\ge1-163D$.

For a unimodular $v$ with $Q_3(v)\ge1-D_1$, the one-variable selector
of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:selector} has addition-test error at most $9D_1$.
If $9D_1<1/6$, Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:blr} supplies a frequency $bh$ outside
a set of proportion at most $18D_1$. The same averaging gives
\[
 \E_h\left|\widehat{\D_hv}(bh)\right|^2\ge1-19D_1.
\]
Demodulate by $\ep(-(b/2)x^2)$. Since
$((x+h)^2-x^2)b/2=bhx+(b/2)h^2$, the resulting function $v_1$ satisfies
$Q_2(v_1)\ge1-19D_1$. Parseval gives a frequency $r$ for which
$|\widehat v_1(r)|^2\ge1-19D_1$.

Now normalize the original $f$ to its unit phase $g$.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:phase-rounding} permits $D=2\varepsilon$, whence
$D_1=326\varepsilon$. The last correction requires
$2934\varepsilon<1/6$, exactly the stated bound
$\varepsilon<1/17604$, and $19D_1=6194\varepsilon$.
Undoing the demodulations gives
\[
 P(X)=(c/6)X^3+(b/2)X^2+rX,
 \qquad
 |\E g\ep(-P)|\ge\sqrt{1-6194\varepsilon}.
\]
Both divisions are legitimate because $p\ge5$.
Since $\norm{f-g}_1\le\varepsilon$, this proves
\eqref{gsr:en:57:ep:cubic-correlation}. Align a unit scalar $z$ with the
correlation and use $\E|f|^2\le1$ to obtain the first bound in
\eqref{gsr:en:57:ep:cubic-distance}. The second uses
$1-\sqrt{1-x}\le x$ for $0\le x\le1$.
\end{proof}

The scalar $z$ is necessary: a constant unit phase need not be a
$p$th root of unity. This corollary is an explicit version of a known
near-extremizer phenomenon, not a new qualitative inverse principle.
Eisner and Tao explicitly leave their effective polynomial rates
unspecified \cite[Remark~1.6]{eisnertao}. No optimality is claimed for
the constants $6194$ and $12390$.

\subsection{Explicit integration in every degree at higher characteristic}

The symmetric frequency map also integrates in every degree when the
characteristic exceeds the polynomial degree. Keeping the average squared
Fourier modulus through each descent yields an explicit factorial bound.

\begin{corollary}[Polynomial phase approximation at every order]
\label{gsr:en:57:ep:all-degree-inverse}
Let $k\ge2$, let $p\ge k$ be prime, and define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:57:ep:Kk}
 K_k=2\prod_{r=1}^{k-2}(108r+1)
 \le2\cdot109^{k-2}(k-2)!,
\end{equation}
with the empty product equal to one. Suppose $f:\Fp\to\C$ satisfies
$|f|\le1$,
$Q_k(f)\ge1-\varepsilon$, and $0\le\varepsilon\le1/K_k$.
There exists $P\in\Fp[X]$ of degree at most $k-1$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:57:ep:all-degree-correlation}
 \left|\E_x f(x)\ep(-P(x))\right|
 \ge\sqrt{1-K_k\varepsilon}-\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
For a suitable unit scalar $z$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:57:ep:all-degree-distance}
 \norm{f-z\ep(P)}_2^2
 \le2\bigl(1-\sqrt{1-K_k\varepsilon}\bigr)+2\varepsilon
 \le(2K_k+2)\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Let $u$ be unimodular with $Q_{r+2}(u)\ge1-D$, where $r\ge1$.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:selector} gives mean Fourier deficit at most $D$ and
additive-test failure at most $9D$. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:symmetric-table}
therefore supplies a scalar $c$ for which the selected frequency agrees
with $c h_1\cdots h_r$ outside a set of proportion at most $108rD$.
Using \eqref{gsr:en:57:ep:selector-coefficient} on the agreement set gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:57:ep:general-descent-average}
 \E_{\boldsymbol h}
 \left|\widehat{\D_{h_1}\cdots\D_{h_r}u}
                   (c h_1\cdots h_r)\right|^2
 \ge1-(108r+1)D.
\end{equation}

If $p>r+1$, put
$u_1(x)=u(x)\ep(-c x^{r+1}/(r+1)!)$.
The additive difference of order $r$ of $cX^{r+1}/(r+1)!$ is
\[
 c h_1\cdots h_r X+\gamma(\boldsymbol h)
\]
for some constant term $\gamma(\boldsymbol h)$. Indeed each difference
reduces the degree by one and multiplies the leading coefficient by
the previous degree and its direction. The factorial is invertible
under the stated characteristic assumption. The Gowers recursion and
\eqref{gsr:en:57:ep:general-descent-average} now give the degree descent
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:57:ep:general-descent}
 Q_{r+1}(u_1)\ge1-(108r+1)D.
\end{equation}
The symmetric-table lemma has no smallness premise, so no additional
threshold is needed at any step.

Normalize $f$ to its unit phase $g$. By
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:phase-rounding}, $Q_k(g)\ge1-2\varepsilon$.
Apply \eqref{gsr:en:57:ep:general-descent} successively for
$r=k-2,k-3,\ldots,1$. Every modulation has degree at most $k-1<p$,
and their sum is a polynomial $R$ of degree at most $k-1$.
The final function $v=g\ep(-R)$ satisfies
\[
 Q_2(v)\ge1-
 2\varepsilon\prod_{r=1}^{k-2}(108r+1)
 =1-K_k\varepsilon.
\]
When $k=2$ the sequence of modulations is empty and $R=0$.
Parseval supplies a frequency $a$ such that
$|\widehat v(a)|^2\ge Q_2(v)\ge1-K_k\varepsilon$.
Take $P=R+aX$ and return from $g$ to $f$ using
$\norm{f-g}_1\le\varepsilon$. This proves
\eqref{gsr:en:57:ep:all-degree-correlation}; scalar alignment and
$1-\sqrt{1-x}\le x$ give \eqref{gsr:en:57:ep:all-degree-distance}.
Finally, $108r+1\le109r$ for $r\ge1$ proves the upper bound in
\eqref{gsr:en:57:ep:Kk}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 70--81]
\emph{Two later phase theorems} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:nearmaximal}): on every cyclic group source~72 gives squared distance $(2A_k+1)\varepsilon$ to a periodic rational polynomial phase, $A_k=(2^k+1)6^{(k-2)(k-1)/2}$, smaller than this corollary's $(2K_k+2)\varepsilon$ for $k=3,4,5,6$ and larger for $k=2$ and $k\ge7$ (its Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:72:thm:periodicphase}); on every finite abelian group and $\varepsilon\le10^{-k}$ source~73 gives $(2/2^k)\varepsilon+O(\varepsilon^2)$, which supersedes both there (its Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:73:thm:main}).
\end{writenote}

The generic fourth-order constant is $K_4=47306$.
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:cubic-inverse} retains the sharper constant $6194$
by using the two-variable collision argument and the direct one-variable
BLR correction. The higher-characteristic condition above serves a
specific purpose: the factorials used to integrate the frequency maps
must be invertible. No analogous classical-polynomial conclusion is
asserted here in the excluded characteristics.

\begin{proposition}[The order of the squared error cannot be improved]
\label{gsr:en:57:ep:error-order}
Fix $k\ge2$ and a prime $p\ge k$. A bound $o(\varepsilon)$ cannot uniformly replace
the order $O(\varepsilon)$ of the squared $L^2$ distance in
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:all-degree-inverse}, even on this fixed field.
The same statement applies to Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:cubic-inverse} when $k=4$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Take a nonconstant real $h:\Fp\to\R$ of mean zero, put
$\sigma^2=\E h^2>0$, and let $f_t(x)=\exp(it h(x))$. There are finitely
many polynomial phase functions of degree at most $k-1$ modulo a constant
scalar. Every nonconstant one has mean of modulus strictly less than one.
At $t=0$ the constant phase is strictly closer than all these alternatives;
continuity preserves this for sufficiently small $t$. Hence
\[
 \inf_{|z|=1,\,\deg P\le k-1}\norm{f_t-z\ep(P)}_2^2
 =2-2|\E e^{it h}|=\sigma^2t^2+O(t^3).
\]
In the $k$th-order cube product, write the additive alternating sum
of the $2^k$ values of $h$ as $S$. Taylor expansion gives
$1-Q_k(f_t)=(t^2/2)\E S^2+O(t^3)$. Distinct cube vertices are
pairwise independent uniform points: the corresponding two affine
forms have rank two over $\Fp$. Their mixed products of mean-zero
$h$ average to zero, while each diagonal term contributes
$\sigma^2$. Thus $\E S^2=2^k\sigma^2$, and
\[
 1-Q_k(f_t)=2^{k-1}\sigma^2t^2+O(t^3).
\]
The ratio of the optimal squared distance to this deficit tends to
$2^{1-k}$, in particular $1/8$ for $k=4$.
This establishes the error order, without identifying an
optimal global numerical constant.
\end{proof}

\section{Sources~59 and~56: affine rigidity on larger ranges and relative repair \wtag}\label{gsr:en:sec:affinerepair}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the tenth write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next twelve sections are source~59's Sections~7--10 and source~56's Sections~2--9. \emph{Logically they continue source~11's chapter} on affine rigidity at the Section~6 endpoint (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:affine}) and source~12's extension (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:bohr}); they are printed here because no number printed earlier may move. The introductions are Sections~\ref{gsr:fm:59:sec:d1} and~\ref{gsr:fm:56:sec:d1}; source~59's Sections~2--6 are the next chapter (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:charseparation}).

\emph{What source~59 proves here.} For $f:G\to W$ at error density $t$ from any affine reference, with $\varepsilon(f)=1-\mathcal E(f)/N^3$ and $\Psi(t)=4t-10t^2+6t^3$ (source~11's $\Psi_0$): an exact signed graph expansion (Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:59:lem:signed-graph-identity}) gives $\varepsilon\ge\Psi(t)+6(t^3-E(S)/N^3)+2(1-3t)a$ for $t\le1/2$ when $W[2]=0$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:59:thm:affine-local-third}), improving source~11's colour coefficient $2(1-7t)$; averaging the signed kernel gives $\varepsilon\ge\Psi(t)$ on $t<4/9$ ($W[2]=0$) and on $t<1/2$ ($W[2]=W[3]=0$), with equality exactly for one nonzero error value on a subgroup coset (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:59:thm:affine-four-ninths}; source~11 had $t<1/7$), and both endpoints resolved (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:59:cor:affine-endpoints}). With the published correction theorem of Ben-Or, Coppersmith, Luby and Rubinfeld, as source~59 credits, it obtains recovery for $\varepsilon<2/9$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:59:thm:affine-global-two-ninths}; source~11: $1/9$), the exact non-affine energy $N^3-4N^2+10N-6$ for $N\ge16$ (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:59:cor:affine-sixteen}; source~11: $N\ge34$), and the partial-graph threshold $\alpha^4>7/9$ at Proposition~6.1 (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:59:cor:affine-partial-two-ninths}; source~11: $8/9$); a map $\Z/12\Z\to\Z/3\Z$ of energy $1296>1266$ shows that the cutoff is at least~$13$ (Section~\ref{gsr:en:59:sec:d10}). Source~59 says that these global consequences follow from the prior cubic and classical correction and are not independently novel. Its Section~\ref{gsr:en:59:sec:d10} also shows that a displayed probability estimate in the published proof of Green and Tao's Lemma~8.3 fails for an element of order five ($3/5$, not at most $1/2$): a counterexample to that estimate only, not to the lemma or to the inverse theorem, as source~59 says (note there).

\emph{What source~56 proves.} For a weight $w:G\to[0,1]$ of mean $\alpha$ on a finite abelian group with $u^4=\norm{w-\alpha}_{U^2}^4\le\alpha^5/1024$, any map to an arbitrary abelian group whose weighted additive-quadruple error is $\varepsilon\le1/1024$ agrees with a unique affine map off relative weighted mass $13\varepsilon/50$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:56:thm:main}); the domain condition does not depend on $\varepsilon$. A two-sided profile gives the coefficient $1/4+o(1)$, optimal (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:56:thm:profile-intro}, Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:56:cor:sharp-limit}); consequences are exact extension, a Fourier certificate and a four-query tester (Section~\ref{gsr:en:56:sec:d8}), and affine repair on quadratic level sets of rank $p^{R-4r}\ge2^{14}$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:56:thm:quadratic}). Linear repair is classical (Blum--Luby--Rubinfeld, Kazhdan--Ziegler), as source~56 says; its contribution is the explicit weighted relative theorem.

\emph{Relation to the formal statements} (checked at HEAD \texttt{fe7165a3c}). \file{proposition_6_1}, \file{lemma_6_2} and \file{corollary_7_6} (\file{Sections06\_07.lean}, lines~37, 47 and~197) and \file{lemma_10_9} (\file{Section10.lean}, line~335) have exact companions; source~56 says that it does not prove a stronger conclusion from the hypotheses of \file{lemma_10_9}. There is no formal counterpart of the affine-rigidity theory; nothing in this chapter is formalized.
