\section[{Signed graph expansions and stronger affine rigidity\srctag{59}}]{Signed graph expansions and stronger affine rigidity}\label{gsr:en:59:sec:d7}
\srcnote{59}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:en:59:sec:new-affine-rigidity}

The following results refine the local graph-energy analysis in source~11 of
\cite{repo59}, which quantifies the full-energy endpoint preceding
Gowers's Lemma~6.2~\cite{gowers}.

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group of order $N$ and let $W$ be an abelian
group with no nonzero element of order two. The target need not be finite:
every sum used below is supported on the finite image of the map in question.
For $f:G\to W$ write
\[
 \mathcal E(f)=\#\left\{(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)\in G^4:
 \begin{array}{c}
 x_1+x_2=x_3+x_4,\\
 f(x_1)+f(x_2)=f(x_3)+f(x_4)
 \end{array}\right\}.
\]
The normalized graph defect is
\[
 \varepsilon(f)=1-\frac{\mathcal E(f)}{N^3}.
\]
An affine map is a homomorphism plus a constant. Subtracting an affine
map preserves $\mathcal E$. Fix such a map $\ell$ and set $g=f-\ell$,
$S=\{x:g(x)\ne0\}$, $s=|S|$, $t=s/N$. For $b\ne0$ define
\[
 c_b=|g^{-1}(b)|,\quad M=\sum_b c_b^2,\quad
 A=s^2-M,\quad C=\sum_b c_b c_{-b},\quad
 Z=\sum_{a,b\ne0,\ a+b\ne0}c_a c_b c_{a+b}.
\]
Here $A$ counts ordered pairs of errors with different values, while $C$
counts ordered opposite-value pairs. Set $a=A/N^2$, $c=C/N^2$ and
$e_S=E(S)/N^3$, with $E(S)$ denoting ordinary set additive energy.
The cubic profile is
\[
 \Psi(t)=4t-10t^2+6t^3.
\]

\subsection{An exact signed expansion}

For a finitely supported real function $u$ on an abelian group define
\[
 \mathscr E(u)=\sum_{z_1+z_2=z_3+z_4}
 u(z_1)u(z_2)u(z_3)u(z_4)=\sum_z(u*u)(z)^2.
\]
In $G\times W$, let $B=1_{G\times\{0\}}$ and
\[
 D(x,w)=1_S(x)\bigl(1_{\{g(x)\}}(w)-1_{\{0\}}(w)\bigr).
\]
Thus $B+D$ is exactly the indicator of the graph of $g$.

\begin{lemma}[Signed graph identity]\label{gsr:en:59:lem:signed-graph-identity}
For every such $g$,
\begin{align}
 \mathcal E(g)={}&N^3-4sN^2+N(6s^2+4M+2C)\notag\\
 &-4s^3-8sM-4sC+4Z+\mathscr E(D).
 \label{gsr:en:59:eq:signed-graph-identity}
\end{align}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:signed-quartic-support}
 \mathscr E(D)\le6E(S).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Expand the four factors in $\mathscr E(B+D)$. The term with no $D$ is
$N^3$. For a term with one $D$, the target coordinate of that factor
must be zero, and the other two free domain coordinates contribute
$N^2$; its value is $-sN^2$, giving the linear term.

Put $m_0=-s$ and $m_b=c_b$ for $b\ne0$. With two $D$ factors in
opposite-sign positions, the contribution is $N\sum_bm_b^2=N(s^2+M)$.
There are four choices. For a same-sign pair the contribution is
$N\sum_bm_bm_{-b}=N(s^2+C)$, and there are two choices. With three
$D$ factors, the fourth domain point is uniquely determined and the
target condition gives
\[
 \sum_{a+b=c}m_am_bm_c=Z-s^3-2sM-sC.
\]
There are four identical contributions, by exchanging the two positive
positions, the two negative positions, or the two sides. The four-$D$
term is $\mathscr E(D)$. This proves the identity.

For the bound, fix a domain additive quadruple inside $S$ and let the
four nonzero signed target labels be
$y_1=g(x_1)$, $y_2=g(x_2)$, $y_3=-g(x_3)$, $y_4=-g(x_4)$.
Its contribution to $\mathscr E(D)$ is
\[
 K(y_1,y_2,y_3,y_4)=1+P-T+F,
\]
where $P$ is the number of zero-sum pairs among the four positions,
$T$ the number of zero-sum triples, and $F$ is $1$ when the sum of
all four labels is zero and $0$ otherwise. There are no singleton
terms because every $y_i$ is nonzero.

Since $W$ has no nonzero involution, the graph joining opposite labels
is a disjoint union of complete bipartite graphs. On four vertices it
has at most four edges, so $P\le4$. Thus $K\le1+4+1=6$.
There are $E(S)$ relevant domain quadruples. Summing the pointwise
upper bound proves \eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:signed-quartic-support}; individual kernel
values need not be nonnegative.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Weighted Schur bounds]\label{gsr:en:59:lem:weighted-schur-affine}
One has $0\le C\le A$ and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:schur-basic-affine}
 Z\le\frac{sA}{2}.
\end{equation}
If $W$ also has no nonzero element of order three, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:schur-no-three-affine}
 Z\le\frac{s(A-C)}{2}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Every opposite-value pair has distinct values, proving $C\le A$.
For an ordered triple of nonzero labels $(u,v,w)$, consider the three
equations $u+v=w$, $u+w=v$, $v+w=u$. At most one can hold: two of
them would force one nonzero label to have order two. Let $R$ be the
number that hold and let $U$ count unequal pairs among the three
positions. If $R=1$ then $U\ge2$, since $u=v=w$ would force the
common value to be zero. Thus $2R\le U$ pointwise. Sum with weight
$c_uc_vc_w$. The two sides sum to $6Z$ and $3sA$, respectively,
which proves \eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:schur-basic-affine}.

For the stronger assertion let $V$ count pairs that are neither equal
nor opposite. In a solution $u+v=w$, the pair $(u,v)$ is never
opposite. If $u=v$, then each of $(u,w)$ and $(v,w)$ is neither equal
nor opposite, since $w=2u$, $u\ne0$, and $3u\ne0$. If $u\ne v$,
the first pair contributes to $V$. Neither of the remaining pairs
can be equal; if both were opposite we would have $u=v=-w$, contrary
to $u\ne v$. Hence $V\ge2$. Thus $2R\le V$, whose weighted sum is
$6Z\le3s(A-C)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[A stronger local cubic and structural remainder]
\label{gsr:en:59:thm:affine-local-third}
If $0\le t\le1/2$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:affine-master-third}
 \varepsilon(f)\ge\Psi(t)+6(t^3-e_S)+2(1-3t)a.
\end{equation}
In particular, for $0<t<1/3$,
$\varepsilon(f)\ge\Psi(t)$, with equality precisely when
$g=b1_S$ for one nonzero value $b$ and $S$ is a subgroup coset.
If $W$ has no nonzero elements of orders two or three and $0<t<2/5$,
the same cubic and the same equality classification hold. More precisely,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:affine-master-no-three}
 \varepsilon(f)\ge\Psi(t)+6(t^3-e_S)
                    +(4-10t)a+(6t-2)c.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For $g_0=b1_S$ with $b\ne0$, either the same expansion or direct
support-pattern counting gives
\[
 \mathcal E(g_0)=N^3-4sN^2+10s^2N-12s^3+6E(S).
\]
Subtract \eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:signed-graph-identity} and use
\eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:signed-quartic-support} to obtain the useful intermediate bound
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:affine-color-intermediate}
 \mathcal E(g_0)-\mathcal E(g)
 \ge (N-2s)(4A-2C)-4Z.
\end{equation}
Since $s\le N/2$, the inequalities $C\le A$ and $Z\le sA/2$ imply
that its right side is at least $2(N-3s)A$. This proves
\eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:affine-master-third}.

When $s<N/3$, both remainder terms are nonnegative and the coefficient
of $A$ is positive. Equality forces $A=0$ and $E(S)=s^3$.
The first condition makes all error values equal. For completeness,
the equality $E(S)=s^3$ says that every $x-y+z$, with $x,y,z\in S$,
lies in $S$. Fixing $y$ shows that $S-y$ is a finite subgroup, so
$S$ is a coset. The converse follows from the displayed exact formula.

With no order-three elements, use \eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:schur-no-three-affine}
in \eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:affine-color-intermediate} without first replacing $C$:
\[
 (N-2s)(4A-2C)-2s(A-C)
 =(4N-10s)A+(6s-2N)C.
\]
This proves \eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:affine-master-no-three}. If $s\le N/3$, its
color part is at least $(2N-4s)A$, using $C\le A$ and
$6s-2N\le0$. If $N/3\le s<2N/5$, it is at least
$(4N-10s)A$, using $C\ge0$. In either range the coefficient is
strictly positive. Equality is therefore classified exactly as above.
\end{proof}

Relative to source~11 of \cite{repo59}, the first inequality replaces the
earlier color coefficient
$2(1-7t)$ by $2(1-3t)$ and enlarges the corresponding sufficient
support radius from $1/7$ to $1/3$. The absence of order-three elements
is visible in a further explicit remainder, rather than only in a
qualitative conclusion. These radii are sufficient radii; no optimality
assertion is made about them. Equality of the cubic is realized at every
available subgroup-coset density in the stated ranges.

\begin{corollary}[Quantitative near-equality below one third]
\label{gsr:en:59:cor:affine-near-third}
If $0<t<1/3$ and $\varepsilon(f)\le\Psi(t)+\eta$, then
\[
 t^3-e_S\le\frac{\eta}{6},\qquad
 a\le\frac{\eta}{2(1-3t)}.
\]
For some nonzero $b$, the proportion of points having nonzero error
different from $b$ is at most
$\eta/[2t(1-3t)]$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Drop the other nonnegative remainder in
\eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:affine-master-third}. If $m=\max_b c_b$, then
$\sum_b c_b^2\le sm$, so $s-m\le A/s$. Divide by $N$.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Averaging the signed kernel: radii four ninths and one half\srctag{59}}]{Averaging the signed kernel: radii four ninths and one half}\label{gsr:en:59:sec:d8}
\srcnote{59}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:en:59:sec:affine-averaged-kernel}

The exact expansion also admits a second use of the quartic term.
Averaging three choices of signs gives a cubic bound in the color
multiplicities. Retaining the contribution from missing fourth points
then preserves a support-energy remainder while enlarging the local range.

Retain all notation from Section~\ref{gsr:en:59:sec:new-affine-rigidity} and put
\[
 Z_3=\sum_{b\ne0,\,3b=0}c_b^2c_{-b},\qquad z_3=Z_3/N^3.
\]

\begin{lemma}[A torsion-resolved Schur estimate]
\label{gsr:en:59:lem:affine-schur-resolved}
One has
\[
 Z\le\frac{s(A-C)}2+Z_3,\qquad Z_3\le\frac{sC}{2}.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
In the proof of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:59:lem:weighted-schur-affine}, the only way a
Schur solution can fail to supply two pairs that are neither equal nor
opposite is to have two labels equal to $b$ and the third equal to
$-b$, where $3b=0$. For clarity, in $u+v=w$, if $u=v$ and $w=-u$
then $3u=0$; if $u\ne v$, then $(u,v)$ already contributes, and both
other pairs cannot be opposite. Thus the pointwise inequality is
$2R\le V+2J$, where $J$ indicates such an exceptional triple.
The weighted sums of $R,V,J$ are $3Z$, $3s(A-C)$ and $3Z_3$.
This proves the first inequality.

Group the nonzero order-three labels into pairs $\{b,-b\}$. Such a
pair contributes $c_bc_{-b}(c_b+c_{-b})$ to $Z_3$ and
$2c_bc_{-b}$ to $C$. Since $c_b+c_{-b}\le s$, summation proves the
second inequality.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Averaged signed-kernel bound]
\label{gsr:en:59:lem:affine-averaged-kernel}
For every finite error support and every target without nonzero
involutions,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:affine-averaged-kernel}
 \mathscr E(D)\le6s^3-2sA+sC-Z_3.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Use the kernel $K=1+P-T+F$ from the proof of
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:59:lem:signed-graph-identity}. If $P=4$, the four signed labels
are two copies of $b$ and two of $-b$ for some nonzero $b$. If
$P=3$, their opposite-pair graph must be the complete bipartite graph
$K_{1,3}$; hence the labels are three copies of $b$ and one of $-b$,
and $F=0$, since $2b\ne0$. If $P\le2$, use $F\le1$.
Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:affine-kernel-caps}
 K\le6,\qquad
 K\le4\ \text{unless the four labels are balanced copies of }\{b,-b\}.
\end{equation}
If three specified signed labels are all equal to $b$ and $3b=0$,
then $T\ge1$. The balanced case is impossible; the preceding
$P=3$ and $P\le2$ alternatives therefore both give $K\le3$.
If three specified signed labels are all equal but $3b\ne0$, they
still cannot be extended to a balanced quadruple, giving $K\le4$.

Fix an ordered triple $(x_1,x_2,x_3)\in S^3$, with nonzero error
labels $(u,v,w)$. There are three ways to designate one of these three
positions as negative and the other two as positive. In each case the
fourth domain point, in the remaining negative position, is uniquely
determined. If it is outside $S$, its contribution is zero. Otherwise
apply the kernel caps above. The caps used below are positive, so they
also bound the zero contribution when the fourth point is outside $S$.

For each designation start with the upper bound $6$ and call the
amount subtracted from this bound its guaranteed loss. Let $U$ be the
number of unequal pairs among $(u,v,w)$, let $V$ count pairs that are
neither equal nor opposite, and let $J$ indicate that the triple uses
both labels of one pair $\{b,-b\}$ with $3b=0$.
The sum of the three guaranteed losses is at least $U+V+J$:
\begin{itemize}
 \item If $u=v=w$, then $U=V=J=0$, and no loss is required.
 \item If the triple uses both labels of a single pair $\{b,-b\}$,
 exactly one of the three designations makes its three signed labels
 all equal. This designation loses at least $2$, and loses at least
 $3$ when $3b=0$. Here $U=2$, $V=0$, so the total is at least
 $U+V+J$.
 \item If the triple meets at least two distinct pairs $\{b,-b\}$,
 no designation can extend to a balanced quadruple. Every designation
 loses at least $2$, for a total loss at least $6$. Since $U\le3$,
 $V\le3$ and $J=0$, this is sufficient.
\end{itemize}

For each of the three designations separately, summing the actual
contribution over all triples in $S^3$ equals $\mathscr E(D)$: this
is just a reparametrization of the four-factor energy, with the three
free positions assigned the indicated signs. Therefore averaging the
three upper bounds gives
\[
 \mathscr E(D)\le6s^3-\frac13
   \sum_{x_1,x_2,x_3\in S}(U+V+J).
\]
The three sums are respectively $3sA$, $3s(A-C)$ and $3Z_3$.
This proves \eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:affine-averaged-kernel}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The support deficit in the averaged bound]
\label{gsr:en:59:lem:affine-kernel-support}
Under the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:59:lem:affine-averaged-kernel},
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:affine-kernel-support}
 \mathscr E(D)\le6s^3-2sA+sC-Z_3-3\bigl(s^3-E(S)\bigr).
\end{equation}
If $W$ also has no nonzero order-three elements, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:affine-kernel-support-no-three}
 \mathscr E(D)\le6s^3-2sA+sC-4\bigl(s^3-E(S)\bigr).
\end{equation}
The coefficients $3$ and $4$ cannot be increased in these respective
inequalities while keeping the other terms fixed.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
In the preceding proof let $L_i$ be the cap assigned to designation
$i\in\{1,2,3\}$ of an ordered triple, and let $K_i$ be its actual
contribution. Thus $L_i\in\{3,4,6\}$ and
\[
 \sum_{i=1}^3 L_i\le18-(U+V+J).
\]
Write $I_i=1$ when the fourth point for designation $i$ is outside
$S$, and $I_i=0$ otherwise. Since $K_i=0$ when $I_i=1$ and every
cap is at least $3$, one has $K_i\le L_i-3I_i$. For each
designation separately,
\[
 \sum_{(x_1,x_2,x_3)\in S^3} I_i=s^3-E(S).
\]
Summing the three inequalities and dividing by three proves
\eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:affine-kernel-support}. In the absence of order three, the
cap $3$ never occurs and $J=Z_3=0$. Replacing $3I_i$ by $4I_i$
proves \eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:affine-kernel-support-no-three}.

For sharpness, take $G=\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z$, $S=\{0,1\}$,
$g(0)=b\ne0$, $g(1)=-b$, and $g=0$ elsewhere. Directly,
\[
 s=2,\quad E(S)=6,\quad A=C=2,\quad\mathscr E(D)=36.
\]
For a target element $b$ of order three, $Z_3=2$ and the original
kernel bound has right side $42$; for a target without order three
it has right side $44$. Since $s^3-E(S)=2$, both stated support
coefficients attain equality in the corresponding examples.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Larger local ranges with color and support remainders]
\label{gsr:en:59:thm:affine-four-ninths}
For every target without nonzero involutions,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:affine-torsion-resolved-profile}
 \varepsilon(f)-\Psi(t)
 \ge3(t^3-e_S)+(4-8t)a+(5t-2)c-3z_3.
\end{equation}
Consequently, if $0<t<4/9$ then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:affine-four-ninths}
 \varepsilon(f)\ge\Psi(t)+3(t^3-e_S)
 +\left(2-\frac{9t}{2}\right)a
 \ge\Psi(t).
\end{equation}
If $W$ also has no nonzero order-three elements, the sufficient range
improves to $0<t<1/2$, with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:affine-half-no-three}
 \varepsilon(f)\ge\Psi(t)
 +4(t^3-e_S)+\min\{2-3t,\,4-8t\}\,a.
\end{equation}
In either range, equality with $\Psi(t)$ occurs precisely for one
nonzero error value supported on a subgroup coset.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The signed identity rearranges exactly as
\[
 N^3\bigl(\varepsilon(f)-\Psi(t)\bigr)
 =(N-2s)(4A-2C)-4Z+6s^3-\mathscr E(D).
\]
Apply Lemmas~\ref{gsr:en:59:lem:affine-schur-resolved} and
\ref{gsr:en:59:lem:affine-kernel-support}. Retaining the term
$3\bigl(s^3-E(S)\bigr)$, the remaining right side is at least
\[
 (N-2s)(4A-2C)-2s(A-C)-4Z_3+2sA-sC+Z_3
 =(4N-8s)A+(5s-2N)C-3Z_3,
\]
proving \eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:affine-torsion-resolved-profile}.
Since $Z_3\le sC/2$, this is at least
\[
 (4N-8s)A+\left(\frac{7s}{2}-2N\right)C.
\]
When $s<4N/9$, the coefficient of $C$ is negative, so $C\le A$
gives $(2N-9s/2)A$, proving \eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:affine-four-ninths}.

In the no-order-three case, use the stronger support remainder
$4\bigl(s^3-E(S)\bigr)$. The coefficient $5s-2N$ changes sign at $s=2N/5$.
Below that point use $C\le A$, giving $(2N-3s)A$; above it use
$C\ge0$, giving $(4N-8s)A$. Both coefficients are positive in the
stated range, and they agree at $s=2N/5$. This proves
\eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:affine-half-no-three}.

Equality with the cubic forces $A=0$, hence $g=b1_S$ with $b\ne0$.
The exact one-valued-error formula then gives
$\varepsilon(f)-\Psi(t)=6(t^3-e_S)$, so $E(S)=s^3$ and $S$ is a
subgroup coset. Conversely, these configurations attain equality.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 54--59]
\emph{Against source~11} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:affine}). Source~11's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:11:thm:mainlocal} proves $\varepsilon\ge\Psi_0(t)$ with coset equality on $0<t<1/7$ for targets without involutions (and $\Psi_1$ on $t<1/3$ with them); this theorem extends the first range to $t<4/9$, and to $t<1/2$ without 3-torsion, with the same equality cases, which answers the first part of source~11's question how far the radius $1/7$ extends (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:affineenvelope}); the involution case is this source's Question~\ref{gsr:fz:59:q:involutions}.
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{The whole range for elementary abelian $3$-group targets} (source~67, Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:charthree}): for these targets, which have no involutions but have $3$-torsion, $\varepsilon\ge\Psi(t)$ holds for every $t\le2/3$, with the same coset equality cases for $0<t<2/3$ and a separate affine family at $t=2/3$ (its Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:67:cthree:local}). Source~67 credits this theorem's ranges $4/9$ and $1/2$ to source~59.
\end{writenote}

\begin{lemma}[Rigidity of the averaged kernel bound]
\label{gsr:en:59:lem:affine-kernel-equality}
Assume $s>0$ and $W[2]=\{0\}$. Equality in
\eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:affine-averaged-kernel} holds if and only if
$g=b\one_S$ for a nonzero $b\in W$ and $S$ is a subgroup coset.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The proof of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:59:lem:affine-averaged-kernel} assigns each of the
three designations an upper cap belonging to $\{3,4,6\}$. Its final
deficit is a sum of nonnegative pointwise deficits: the actual
contribution is at most its assigned cap, and the sum of the three
caps is at most $18-(U+V+J)$. Equality of the total therefore forces
equality at every one of these finite comparisons.

Every cap is positive. Thus no fourth point can be outside $S$,
since its actual contribution would then be zero. It follows that
$S$ is closed under $x+y-z$, and hence is a coset. Equivalently, this
also follows from Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:59:lem:affine-kernel-support}.

If two occurring colors $u,v$ are neither equal nor opposite, use a
triple of points with colors $(u,u,v)$, allowing a repeated point for
the two copies of $u$. Every designation has cap $4$, so the sum of
caps is $12$. But $U=V=2$ and $J=0$, giving
$18-(U+V+J)=14$. This is strict slack, a contradiction. All colors
therefore belong to one pair $\{b,-b\}$.

For each occurring color $b$, let $T_b=\{x:g(x)=b\}$. On a triple
from $T_b^3$, all three caps are $6$. Equality forces the actual
kernel to be $6$, which requires a balanced quadruple. Its fourth
point therefore also has color $b$. Consequently $T_b$ is closed
under $x+y-z$, so it is a coset.

Suppose both $b$ and $-b$ occur. Choose $x\in T_b$ and
$z\in T_{-b}$. Since $S$ is a coset, $2x-z\in S$. Since $T_b$ is
a coset and $z\notin T_b$, one has $2x-z\notin T_b$, so
$g(2x-z)=-b$. In the triple $(x,x,z)$ designate $z$ as negative.
All four signed labels are then $b$. There are no zero-sum pairs,
and the four-label sum is nonzero: $4b=0$ would contradict
$W[2]=\{0\}$. The actual kernel is consequently
\[
 1-4\one_{3b=0},
\]
which is $1$ or $-3$. Its assigned cap is respectively $4$ or $3$,
again a strict deficit. Thus only one color occurs.

Conversely, if $g=b\one_S$ with $S$ a coset, then
$A=C=Z_3=0$ and $\mathscr E(D)=6E(S)=6s^3$, proving equality.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The two local endpoints]
\label{gsr:en:59:cor:affine-endpoints}
If $W[2]=\{0\}$ and $t=4/9$, then
\[
 \varepsilon(f)>\Psi(4/9).
\]
If $W[2]=W[3]=\{0\}$ and $t=1/2$, then
$\varepsilon(f)\ge\Psi(1/2)=1/4$, with equality precisely when
$g=b\one_S$ for a nonzero $b$ and an index-two subgroup coset $S$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The comparisons proving Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:59:thm:affine-four-ninths} remain
valid at their closed endpoints. At $t=4/9$ they give
\[
 \varepsilon(f)-\Psi(t)\ge3(t^3-e_S).
\]
If equality with $\Psi(t)$ held, then $E(S)=s^3$ and $S$ would be
a coset. A coset in a finite group has reciprocal-integer density,
which cannot equal $4/9$. The inequality is therefore strict.

Now assume $W[3]=\{0\}$ and $N=2s$. The exact signed identity
can be written as a sum of nonnegative terms:
\begin{align*}
 N^3\bigl(\varepsilon(f)-\Psi(t)\bigr)
 ={}&4\left(\frac{s(A-C)}2-Z\right)\\
 &+\bigl(6s^3-2sA+sC-\mathscr E(D)\bigr)+sC.
\end{align*}
The Schur bound and \eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:affine-averaged-kernel} prove
nonnegativity. Equality forces equality in the latter kernel bound.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:59:lem:affine-kernel-equality} therefore gives one nonzero
color on a coset, whose density $1/2$ makes its index two. Conversely,
the exact one-valued formula gives equality for every such map.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Near-equality on the enlarged odd-target range]
\label{gsr:en:59:cor:affine-four-ninths-near}
If $0<t<4/9$, $\eta\ge0$, and
$\varepsilon(f)\le\Psi(t)+\eta$, then
\[
 a\le\frac{2\eta}{4-9t},\qquad
 t^3-e_S\le\min\left\{\frac{\eta}{3},\,
       \frac{\eta}{6}+\frac{2(3t-1)_+\eta}{3(4-9t)}\right\}.
\]
For some nonzero $b$, the fraction of all domain points with nonzero
error different from $b$ is at most $2\eta/[t(4-9t)]$.
If $W[3]=\{0\}$, $0<t<1/2$, and
$\varepsilon(f)\le\Psi(t)+\eta$ with $\eta\ge0$, then writing $h(t)=\min\{2-3t,4-8t\}>0$, one has
\[
 a\le\frac{\eta}{h(t)},\qquad t^3-e_S\le\frac{\eta}{4},
\]
\[
 \frac1N\min_{b\ne0}|\{x:g(x)\notin\{0,b\}\}|
       \le\frac{\eta}{t h(t)}.
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The first bound and $t^3-e_S\le\eta/3$ follow from
\eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:affine-four-ninths}. Since $t<4/9<1/2$,
\eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:affine-master-third} also applies, giving
$6(t^3-e_S)\le\eta+2(3t-1)_+a$. Substitute the first bound.
The color conclusion again follows from $s-\max_b c_b\le A/s$.
The no-order-three conclusions follow in the same way from
\eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:affine-half-no-three}.
\end{proof}

The proof identifies the role of order three explicitly. Such torsion
does not change the original one-valued cubic, but it creates exceptional
Schur triples and lowers a signed-kernel cap from four to three. The
combined bookkeeping enlarges the sufficient local radius to $4/9$;
removing this torsion enlarges it further to $1/2$. The support deficits
have coefficients $3$ and $4$ in the corresponding kernel bounds, and
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:59:cor:affine-endpoints} settles equality at both endpoints.
Neither number is asserted to be the best possible universal radius.

\section[{Classical correction and global affine recovery\srctag{59}}]{Classical correction and global affine recovery}\label{gsr:en:59:sec:d9}
\srcnote{59}{Section 9}
\label{gsr:en:59:sec:affine-classical-global}


The next lemma is the classical sharp-range majority correction argument,
with its collision-to-mode estimate retained~\cite{bclr,dss}. It is included
to give a complete proof of the global consequences for the repository's
Section~6 interface. Neither majority decoding nor the $7/9$
homomorphism-test threshold is claimed as a new result.

\paragraph{Priority of the global consequences.}
The sharper published correction theorem of Ben-Or, Coppersmith, Luby,
and Rubinfeld~\cite{bclr}, restated as Theorem~4.2 by Diaconis, Shao,
and Soundararajan~\cite{dss}, gives
\[
 \Pr[F\ne L]\le\frac{3-\sqrt{9-24\rho}}{12}<\frac17
 \qquad(\rho<2/9).
\]
Consequently, the global graph-defect range $\varepsilon<2/9$ and the
exact non-affine energy formula for $N\ge16$ below already follow from
that published theorem and source~11's earlier local cubic on
$t<1/7$~\cite{repo59}. They are not independently novel global
results. Their role here is to complete and simplify an explicitly
unfinished correction/cutoff step in the pinned report. The new local
color and support estimates of the preceding sections are separate
refinements. We reproduce an elementary correction proof with a weaker
intermediate distance bound, which is sufficient for the complete
argument below.

\begin{lemma}[Majority correction in the $7/9$ range]
\label{gsr:en:59:lem:affine-correction-seven-ninths}
Let $F:G\to W$ and suppose that
\[
 \rho=\Pr_{x,y}[F(x+y)\ne F(x)+F(y)]<2/9.
\]
Put $q=(1-\sqrt{1-4\rho})/2$. There is a homomorphism $L:G\to W$
with $\Pr[F\ne L]\le q<1/3$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For fixed $h$, let $Z_h(y)=F(h+y)-F(y)$. For independent uniform
$y,z$, both
\[
 F(h+y)+F(z)=F(h+y+z),\qquad
 F(y)+F(h+z)=F(h+y+z)
\]
hold except on a set of probability at most $2\rho$. Each tested pair
is uniform on $G^2$. Thus the collision probability of $Z_h$ is at
least $1-2\rho>1/2$.

For any probability distribution with largest atom $p$, one has
$\sum p_i^2\le p$, so this largest atom exceeds $1/2$. Also
$\sum p_i^2\le p^2+(1-p)^2$, because the remaining atoms have total
mass $1-p$. Therefore $p(1-p)\le\rho$, and the branch $p>1/2$
gives $p\ge1-q$. Let $L(h)$ be this unique modal value.

Since $q<1/3$, the three identities
\[
 Z_{h+k}(x)=L(h+k),\quad Z_h(x+k)=L(h),\quad Z_k(x)=L(k)
\]
hold simultaneously for some $x$. Their exact cocycle identity proves
$L(h+k)=L(h)+L(k)$. If $F(h)\ne L(h)$, at least a fraction $1-q$
of the values $Z_h(y)$ differ from $F(h)$. Averaging yields
$\rho\ge(1-q)\Pr[F\ne L]$. Since $\rho=q(1-q)$, the conclusion
follows, including the case $\rho=0$.
\end{proof}

Let $D(u)$ be the inverse of $\Psi$ on $[0,1/7]$; this restriction is
strictly increasing. In the next statement $d(f)$ denotes the smallest
normalized Hamming distance from $f$ to an affine map.

\begin{theorem}[Global sharp-profile recovery on a larger range]
\label{gsr:en:59:thm:affine-global-two-ninths}
If $\varepsilon(f)<2/9$, then the nearest affine map is unique and
\[
 d(f)\le D(\varepsilon(f)).
\]
For positive defect, equality holds precisely when the error from that
map is one nonzero constant on a subgroup coset.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The average, over $a,x,y$, of the acceptance condition
\[
 f(a+x)+f(a+y)=f(a)+f(a+x+y)
\]
is $1-\varepsilon(f)$: the parametrization by $(a,x,y)$ is a bijection
onto ordered additive quadruples. Hence for some anchor $a$ the map
$F_a(x)=f(a+x)-f(a)$ has additive-test failure probability
$\rho\le\varepsilon(f)$. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:59:lem:affine-correction-seven-ninths}
produces an affine map within distance less than $1/3$ from $f$.

Thus $t=d(f)<1/3$, and Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:59:thm:affine-local-third} gives
$\varepsilon(f)\ge\Psi(t)$. The derivative
$\Psi'(t)=4-20t+18t^2$ has just one zero in $[1/7,1/3]$, and it is
a maximum of $\Psi$. Consequently
\[
 \min_{[1/7,1/3]}\Psi
 =\min\{132/343,4/9\}>2/9.
\]
Therefore $t<1/7$, where inversion gives the stated estimate.

Two distinct affine maps into $W$ agree either nowhere or on a coset
of the kernel of a nonzero homomorphism. The image of that homomorphism
is a nontrivial finite subgroup of $W$, hence has order at least three.
Their mutual distance is therefore at least $2/3$. Two nearest maps
within distance less than $1/3$ from $f$ must coincide. Finally, equality
in the inverse estimate is equality in the local cubic, whose equality
case has already been proved. The converse follows from the exact
one-valued-error formula.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 82--94]
\emph{Extended to defect $1/4$ for every target} by source~93 (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:recovery}), with a complete dichotomy at $1/4$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:endpoint}); source~93 credits this theorem and source~68's multilevel overlap inequality.
\end{writenote}

\begin{corollary}[Exact non-affine energy for $N\ge16$]
\label{gsr:en:59:cor:affine-sixteen}
Suppose that $W\ne\{0\}$ and $N\ge16$. Then
\[
 \max_{f\text{ non-affine}}\mathcal E(f)
 =N^3-4N^2+10N-6.
\]
The maximizers are precisely the one-point modifications of affine maps.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For $N\ge16$, monotonicity in $N$ gives
\[
 \Psi(1/N)\le\Psi(1/16)=\frac{435}{2048}<\frac29.
\]
If a non-affine map had energy greater than the claimed value, the
preceding theorem would give $d(f)<1/N$, impossible on an $N$-point
domain. At equality it gives $d(f)\le1/N$, hence $d(f)=1/N$.
Conversely, an affine map changed at one point by a nonzero value has
the displayed energy, by the exact one-valued-error formula. It is
non-affine because distinct affine maps cannot differ at a single
point when $N\ge16$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 54--59]
\emph{Checked at the write} (exact rationals). $\Psi(1/16)=435/2048<2/9$; $\Psi(1/7)=132/343$ and $\Psi(1/3)=4/9$, both above $2/9$; $\Psi'(t)=4-20t+18t^2>0$ on $[0,1/16]$; $\Psi(1/2)=1/4$, so $(1-\Psi(1/2))\cdot12^3=1296$ against $12^3-4\cdot12^2+10\cdot12-6=1266$ (Section~\ref{gsr:en:59:sec:d10}). \emph{Against source~11's cutoff} (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:11:thm:maingap}, $N\ge34$): for targets without involutions the cutoff is now $16$, and the third write's exhaustive table (Remark~\ref{gsr:en:11:rem:cutoff}: $\Z/6\to\Z/3$ and $\Z/9\to\Z/3$ fail) together with this source's $\Z/12\to\Z/3$ example puts the exact universal cutoff between $13$ and~$16$; the intake's marked derivation of the cutoff $30$ (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:smallgroups}) is superseded. This source credits the global consequence to classical correction and source~11's cubic. Source~67, placed later and not yet written in, records the maximum from $N\ge13$ with $13$ optimal for elementary abelian 3-group targets.
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
For elementary abelian $3$-group targets source~67 proves the formula from $N\ge13$, with $13$ optimal (its Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:67:cthree:nonaffine-gap}); its sharpness example at $N=12$ is this source's parity map $\Z/12\Z\to\Z/3\Z$ (energy $1296>1266$, Section~\ref{gsr:en:59:sec:d10}), which source~67 does not attribute to this source at that point, although it credits this source's ranges, recovery threshold $2/9$ and cutoff $16$ (its bibliography entry \cite{repo67charaffine}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 82--94]
\emph{Lowered to $13$ for every target} by source~93 (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:thirteen}), which answers this source's Question~\ref{gsr:fz:59:q:small-domains} at $13$, $14$ and~$15$.
\end{writenote}

This improves the pinned repository's sufficient cutoff $34$ to $16$
for targets without involutions~\cite{repo59}, as a consequence of
classical correction and the prior local cubic. It does not claim that
$16$ is the exact cutoff. Classifying the exact maximum and all
extremizers for domains of size $N<16$ remains a separate problem.

\begin{corollary}[Partial graphs and the Section 6 interface]
\label{gsr:en:59:cor:affine-partial-two-ninths}
Let $B\subseteq G$, let $\phi:B\to W$, and suppose that its graph
$\Gamma_B$ satisfies
$E(\Gamma_B)\ge(1-\varepsilon)N^3$ with $0\le\varepsilon<2/9$.
There is a unique affine map $\ell$ with at most $D(\varepsilon)N$
disagreements with $\phi$ on $B$. Moreover,
\[
 \frac{|G\setminus B|}{N}\le1-(1-\varepsilon)^{1/3}.
\]
Every arbitrary completion of $\phi$ gives the same recovered affine map.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Every completion has graph energy at least $E(\Gamma_B)$, and so the
global theorem applies. The set bound $E(\Gamma_B)\le |B|^3$ gives
$\beta=|B|/N\ge(1-\varepsilon)^{1/3}$. If two affine maps satisfy
the disagreement bound, they agree at least on
$(\beta-2D(\varepsilon))N$ points. Since
$\beta>7/9$ and $D(\varepsilon)<1/7$, this exceeds
$(7/9-2/7)N=31N/63>N/3$, impossible for two distinct affine maps
into a target without involutions. This also proves independence from
the completion.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 54--59]
Source~11's Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:11:cor:prop61} enters the high-correlation regime under $\alpha^4>8/9$; this corollary lowers it to $7/9$, as the next paragraph says.
\end{writenote}

In the prime-cyclic frequency-selection setting of Gowers's
Proposition~6.1~\cite{gowers}, its graph-energy conclusion
$E(\Gamma_B)\ge\alpha^4N^3$ therefore enters this regime as soon as
$\alpha^4>7/9$, replacing the earlier sufficient condition
$\alpha^4>8/9$. The error is at most $D(1-\alpha^4)N$.
This strengthens a high-correlation endpoint consequence of the
proposition; it changes neither its exponent four nor the general
quantitative bound in Szemer\'edi's theorem.

\section[{Examples, comparisons, and precise claim boundaries\srctag{59}}]{Examples, comparisons, and precise claim boundaries}\label{gsr:en:59:sec:d10}
\srcnote{59}{Section 10}
\label{gsr:en:59:sec:comparisons}

\subsection{A finite-field example where image size matters}

Let $H=\F_2^3$ and let $F$ consist of six of its seven nonzero elements. Here $q=6$, so the exact universal rank is two. Two suitable linear functionals have common kernel equal to the line through the omitted element. Their common fibers each have size two. The finite-image argument therefore costs only $2^2=4$, giving a guaranteed retained weight of $w(B)/4$ for any graph with that defect set and any $k$. Charging continuous arc lengths instead would give only $w(B)/(5k)^2$. The example separates the role of rank from the role of character-image size.

For a character of image order $81$, the prime-primary radius for $p=3$ is $1/6$. At order $k=8$, the exact single-coordinate factor is
\[
 \frac{\lceil81/48\rceil}{81}=\frac2{81},
\]
which improves the continuous factor $1/48$. These finite corrections are substantial when the image is small, and can still help when it is larger than the localization denominator.

\subsection{An exact small-domain obstruction}

Take $G=\Z/12\Z$, $W=\Z/3\Z$, and let $f$ equal one on odd residues and zero on even residues. Relative to the zero affine reference, its error support is an index-two coset and $t=1/2$. The one-valued formula in Section~\ref{gsr:en:59:sec:new-affine-rigidity} gives
\[
 \mathcal E(f)=\left(1-\Psi(1/2)\right)12^3
 =\frac34\,12^3=1296.
\]
The one-point formula would give $12^3-4\cdot12^2+10\cdot12-6=1266$. The map is non-affine: its image has two elements, whereas an affine map into $\Z/3\Z$ has image size one or three. Thus a size restriction in Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:59:cor:affine-sixteen} cannot simply be removed, even without target involutions. The optimal universal cutoff is at least $13$ and at most $16$; the orders between them require further analysis.

\subsection{The published order-five probability issue}
\label{gsr:en:59:sec:gt-pitfall}

Green--Tao's published separation lemma, Lemma~8.3 on page~106 of \cite{greentaoUthree}, seeks a small set of characters whose radius-$1/4$ Bohr neighborhood meets a given set only at zero. Its proof states, for a uniformly chosen character and a fixed nonzero element $f$, the estimate
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:gt-displayed-estimate}
 \Prob\bigl(\distT{\chi(f)}<1/4\bigr)\le1/2.
\end{equation}
For an element of order five, evaluation is uniform on
$\{0,1/5,2/5,3/5,4/5\}$. The arc contains $0,1/5,4/5$, so the probability is $3/5$. Hence \eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:gt-displayed-estimate}, as a statement for every nonzero element in every finite abelian group, is false. The same displayed step occurs in the inspected arXiv version.

The conclusion is deliberately limited: this is a counterexample to that probability estimate. It is not a counterexample to the lemma's conclusion with its original rank allowance, and it is not a disproof of the inverse theorem. The present article does not decide whether the original separation conclusion follows by a different argument. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:59:lem:small-ball} gives the correct order-sensitive distribution, and radius $1/5$ supplies a valid universal half-survival estimate. Combined with strict adaptive deletion, it yields the sharp statement actually proved here. No claim is made to be the first to have noticed the issue.

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 54--59]
\emph{Recorded as stated} (standing rule of 4~October 2026). The arithmetic is checked at the write: for $f$ of order five, $\chi(f)$ is uniform on $\{0,1/5,2/5,3/5,4/5\}$ and exactly $0$, $1/5$ and $4/5$ lie within $1/4$ of an integer, so the probability is $3/5>1/2$; in the exact small-ball law of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:59:lem:small-ball}, $\beta_5(1/4)=(2\lceil5/4\rceil-1)/5=3/5$. This is a counterexample to the displayed estimate \eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:gt-displayed-estimate} read as a statement for every nonzero element of every finite abelian group, not to Lemma~8.3 of Green and Tao or to their inverse theorem, as this source says; the write did not re-read the published proof, and \cite{greentaoUthree} is the report's entry for that paper.
\end{writenote}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Normalization and elementary Fourier facts\srctag{56}}]{Normalization and elementary Fourier facts}\label{gsr:en:56:sec:d2}\label{gsr:en:56:sec:prelim}
\srcnote{56}{Section 2}

Let $\widehat G$ be the character group of $G$. The Fourier transform and
convolution are normalized by
\[
\widehat f(\chi)=\E_x f(x)\overline{\chi(x)},
\qquad (f*g)(x)=\E_y f(y)g(x-y).
\]
Character orthogonality gives inversion and Parseval:
\[
f(x)=\sum_{\chi\in\widehat G}\widehat f(\chi)\chi(x),
\qquad \sum_{\chi\in\widehat G}|\widehat f(\chi)|^2=\E_x|f(x)|^2.
\]
These formulas use an ordinary sum, not an average, on the dual group.
The $U^2$ norm is
\[
\norm{f}_{U^2(G)}^4=
\E_{x,h,k}f(x)\overline{f(x+h)}\overline{f(x+k)}f(x+h+k)
=\sum_{\chi}|\widehat f(\chi)|^4.
\]
The identity follows by inserting Fourier inversion and averaging the three
independent variables. Each nonzero surviving term has all four character
indices equal.

\begin{lemma}[Energy and centering]\label{gsr:en:56:lem:energy}
For a real nonnegative $w$ of mean $\alpha$, one has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:56:eq:energy-center}
\Qcal(w)=\sum_{\chi}|\widehat w(\chi)|^4
      =\alpha^4+\norm{w-\alpha}_{U^2(G)}^4.
\end{equation}
If $0\le v\le1$ and $b=\E v$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:56:eq:trivial-energy-cap}
\Qcal(v)\le b^3,
\qquad \sum_{\chi\ne1}|\widehat v(\chi)|^4\le b^3-b^4\le b^3.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The Fourier expansion of \eqref{gsr:fm:56:eq:Q-def} gives the first equality; removing
the trivial character gives the second. For \eqref{gsr:en:56:eq:trivial-energy-cap},
bound the fourth factor $v(a+b-c)$ in the defining average by one. The
remaining three variables are independent. Subtracting the trivial Fourier
term gives the centered bound.
\end{proof}

For later use write
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:56:eq:mu-sigma}
\mu=\E w^2,\qquad
\sigma=\max_{\chi\ne1}|\widehat w(\chi)|,
\end{equation}
with $\sigma=0$ if $G$ is the trivial group. Since $0\le w\le1$,
\[
\alpha^2\le\mu\le\alpha,
\quad \sum_{\chi\ne1}|\widehat w(\chi)|^2=\mu-\alpha^2,
\quad \sigma\le u.
\]
The last inequality is the elementary comparison between the largest term
and the fourth-power sum of nonnegative terms.

\subsection{Why the weight bound matters}
The restriction $w\le1$ is used in the energy cap and in bounding
$\mu$ by $\alpha$. A general bounded nonnegative weight can first be divided
by its supremum; the test error and relative distance are invariant under
this rescaling, but the stated uniformity hypothesis must then be checked
for the rescaled weight. It would be incorrect to keep the original
$\alpha^5$ threshold unchanged under arbitrary rescaling.

\subsection{A collision-to-mode inequality}
\begin{lemma}\label{gsr:en:56:lem:mode}
If $(p_j)$ is a probability distribution with finite support and
$m=\max_jp_j$, then
\[
1-m\le1-\sum_jp_j^2.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The inequality $\sum_jp_j^2\le m\sum_jp_j=m$ is immediate.
\end{proof}
All modes in the proof have finite support, even when $H$ is infinite.
No measure-theoretic selection principle and no ordering of $H$ is required
for the mathematical existence statements. An implementation may use any
fixed tie-breaking rule.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Autocorrelation, triangle variance, and pointwise links\srctag{56}}]{Autocorrelation, triangle variance, and pointwise links}\label{gsr:en:56:sec:d3}\label{gsr:en:56:sec:moments}
\srcnote{56}{Section 3}

The domain estimates are independent of the labels. Their role is to replace
successive exceptional-set deletions by direct moment bounds.
Define
\begin{align}
r(h)&=\E_x w(x)w(x+h),\label{gsr:en:56:eq:r-def}\\
T(h,k)&=\E_x w(x)w(x+h)w(x+h+k),\label{gsr:en:56:eq:T-def}\\
D_w(x)&=\E_{y,z}w(y)w(z)w(y+z-x).\label{gsr:en:56:eq:link-def}
\end{align}
The symbol $D_w(x)$ is a domain link density, whereas $\Def_w(\phi)$ is
the label defect; they are different quantities.

\begin{lemma}[Autocorrelation identities]\label{gsr:en:56:lem:r}
One has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:56:eq:r-identities}
0\le r(h)\le\alpha,\qquad
\E_hr(h)=\alpha^2,\qquad
\E_h(r(h)-\alpha^2)^2=u^4.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Positivity is immediate and $w(x+h)\le1$ gives $r(h)\le\alpha$.
The mean follows by averaging $x$ and $x+h$ independently. The square
average $\E_hr(h)^2$ is $\Qcal(w)$, by the change of variables that identifies
two pairs of the same difference with an additive quadruple. Therefore its
variance is $\Qcal(w)-\alpha^4=u^4$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Exact triangle second moment]\label{gsr:en:56:lem:triangle}
The triangle density satisfies
\begin{align}
\E_{h,k}T(h,k)&=\alpha^3,\label{gsr:en:56:eq:T-mean}\\
\E_{h,k}T(h,k)^2&=\E_z r(z)^3.\label{gsr:en:56:eq:T-second}
\end{align}
Consequently, for
$V=\E_{h,k}(T(h,k)-\alpha^3)^2$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:56:eq:T-variance}
V\le\alpha(1+2\alpha)u^4,
\qquad \frac{\sqrt V}{\alpha^3}\le\lambda\sqrt{1+2\alpha}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The variables $(x,x+h,x+h+k)$ are independently uniform, proving
\eqref{gsr:en:56:eq:T-mean}. For the second moment introduce two base points $x,y$
and put $z=y-x$. The change of variables
\[
a=x,\qquad b=x+h,\qquad c=x+h+k
\]
is a bijection of $G^3$. Thus
\begin{align*}
\E_{h,k}T(h,k)^2
&=\E_{z,a,b,c}
 w(a)w(a+z)w(b)w(b+z)w(c)w(c+z)\\
&=\E_zr(z)^3.
\end{align*}
Write $d(z)=r(z)-\alpha^2$. Then $\E d=0$ and $\E d^2=u^4$, so
\[
V=3\alpha^2u^4+\E d^3.
\]
Since $d\le\alpha-\alpha^2$, the pointwise inequality
$d^3\le(\alpha-\alpha^2)d^2$ holds also when $d$ is negative.
This gives \eqref{gsr:en:56:eq:T-variance}. Dividing by $\alpha^6$ and using
$u^4=\lambda^2\alpha^5$ proves the normalized estimate.
\end{proof}

A slightly stronger bound replaces $\alpha(1+2\alpha)$ by
$\mu+2\alpha^2$, because Cauchy--Schwarz gives $r(h)\le\mu$.
We retain the simpler density-only form in the main constants.

\begin{lemma}[Uniform pointwise link bound]\label{gsr:en:56:lem:link}
For every $x\in G$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:56:eq:link-bound}
|D_w(x)-\alpha^3|
\le u^2\sqrt{\mu-\alpha^2}
\le\lambda\alpha^3\sqrt{1-\alpha}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Set $\widetilde w(x)=w(-x)$. Then
$D_w=w*w*\widetilde w$, whose Fourier coefficient at $\chi$ is
$\widehat w(\chi)^2\overline{\widehat w(\chi)}$.
Its trivial coefficient is $\alpha^3$. Hence Fourier inversion and
Cauchy--Schwarz give
\begin{align*}
|D_w(x)-\alpha^3|
&\le\sum_{\chi\ne1}|\widehat w(\chi)|^3\\
&\le\left(\sum_{\chi\ne1}|\widehat w(\chi)|^4\right)^{1/2}
      \left(\sum_{\chi\ne1}|\widehat w(\chi)|^2\right)^{1/2}\\
&=u^2\sqrt{\mu-\alpha^2}.
\end{align*}
Now use $\mu-\alpha^2\le\alpha(1-\alpha)$ and the definition of $\lambda$.
\end{proof}

The exponent $\alpha^{5/4}$ in the main theorem is already visible here:
controlling the triple link relative to its mean requires
$u^2\sqrt\alpha$ to be small compared with $\alpha^3$. This explains the
sufficient exponent used by this proof; it does not establish its necessity.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Weighted modal differences without discarding fibers\srctag{56}}]{Weighted modal differences without discarding fibers}\label{gsr:en:56:sec:d4}\label{gsr:en:56:sec:modal}
\srcnote{56}{Section 4}

For each $h$ with $r(h)>0$, let $\nu_h$ be the probability distribution of
\[
\phi(x+h)-\phi(x)
\]
when $x$ is sampled with weights $w(x)w(x+h)$. Choose a mode $q(h)\in H$.
When $r(h)=0$, set $q(h)=0$. Put
\[
b(h)=1-\nu_h(q(h)),\qquad
c(h)=1-\sum_{v\in H}\nu_h(v)^2,
\]
with both values zero on zero-mass fibers. By Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:56:lem:mode},
$0\le b(h)\le c(h)\le1$. The total bad-pair mass is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:56:eq:B-def}
B=\E_hr(h)b(h)
 =\E_{x,h}w(x)w(x+h)
   \ind_{\phi(x+h)-\phi(x)\ne q(h)}.
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}[Collision identity and weighted interpolation]\label{gsr:en:56:lem:weighted-interpolation}
Writing $D=\Def_w(\phi)=\eps(\alpha^4+u^4)$, one has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:56:eq:collision-defect}
D=\E_hr(h)^2c(h)
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:56:eq:B-interpolation}
\alpha^2B\le D+u^2\sqrt D.
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:56:eq:beta-bound}
\frac{B}{\alpha^2}\le
\beta:=\eps(1+\kappa)+s\sqrt{\eps(1+\kappa)}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A quadruple with the same difference on two ordered pairs can be written
as $(x+h,y,x,y+h)$. It is respected precisely when the two differences of
$\phi$ coincide. The weight of such pairs at fixed $h$ is $r(h)^2$,
which proves \eqref{gsr:en:56:eq:collision-defect}.
Since $b\le c$,
\[
\E_hr(h)^2b(h)\le D.
\]
Insert $\alpha^2=r(h)-(r(h)-\alpha^2)$ into $\alpha^2B$:
\begin{align*}
\alpha^2B
&=\E_hr(h)^2b(h)-\E_h(r(h)-\alpha^2)r(h)b(h)\\
&\le D+\left(\E_h(r(h)-\alpha^2)^2\right)^{1/2}
          \left(\E_hr(h)^2b(h)^2\right)^{1/2}\\
&\le D+u^2\sqrt D.
\end{align*}
The last step uses $b^2\le b$ and Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:56:lem:r}.
Dividing by $\alpha^4$ gives \eqref{gsr:en:56:eq:beta-bound}.
\end{proof}

The absence of a threshold on $r(h)$ is important. Selecting only shifts with
$r(h)$ above a cutoff would introduce a further exceptional-set loss. Here
both the original test and the selected difference map retain their actual
pair multiplicities.

\begin{lemma}[Triangle transfer to an ambient additive test]\label{gsr:en:56:lem:triangle-transfer}
Let
\[
R_q=\set{(h,k)\in G^2:q(h+k)\ne q(h)+q(k)},
\qquad \rho=\frac{|R_q|}{N^2},\qquad v=\frac{\sqrt V}{\alpha^3}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:56:eq:rho-root-ineq}
\rho\le3\beta+v\sqrt\rho
\end{equation}
and therefore
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:56:eq:rho-bounds}
\rho\le
\left(\frac{v+\sqrt{v^2+12\beta}}2\right)^2
\le6\beta+v^2
\le6\beta+3\lambda^2.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For any $(h,k)\in R_q$, a triangle
$(x,x+h,x+h+k)$ cannot have all three differences equal to
$q(h),q(k),q(h+k)$. Thus at least one of its three edges is a bad pair in
\eqref{gsr:en:56:eq:B-def}. An erroneous ordered pair extends to triangles with
third-vertex total weight exactly $\alpha$. This holds for each of the
three edge positions, by bijective changes of variables. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:56:eq:bad-triangle-union}
\E_{h,k}T(h,k)\ind_{R_q}(h,k)\le3\alpha B.
\end{equation}
On the other hand, Cauchy--Schwarz and \eqref{gsr:en:56:eq:T-mean} give
\[
\alpha^3\rho
\le\E_{h,k}T(h,k)\ind_{R_q}(h,k)+\sqrt V\sqrt\rho.
\]
Divide by $\alpha^3$ and apply \eqref{gsr:en:56:eq:beta-bound}.
Solving the quadratic inequality in $\sqrt\rho$ gives the first bound
in \eqref{gsr:en:56:eq:rho-bounds}. Alternatively,
$v\sqrt\rho\le(\rho+v^2)/2$ gives $\rho\le6\beta+v^2$.
Finally $1+2\alpha\le3$ in \eqref{gsr:en:56:eq:T-variance}.
\end{proof}

The square-root expression is retained for data-dependent applications.
The coarser last expression is convenient for a short rational verification
of the universal constants.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Self-correction and coarse affine reconstruction\srctag{56}}]{Self-correction and coarse affine reconstruction}\label{gsr:en:56:sec:d5}\label{gsr:en:56:sec:coarse}
\srcnote{56}{Section 5}

We include the classical self-correction argument in full because it fixes
the threshold, works for arbitrary abelian targets, and makes the subsequent
constant calculation independent of a black-box stability theorem. The
method is the homomorphism self-correction mechanism of
Blum--Luby--Rubinfeld \cite{blr}; it is not claimed as a new result.

\begin{lemma}[Ambient homomorphism self-correction]\label{gsr:en:56:lem:BLR}
Let $q:G\to H$ have additive-test error
\[
\rho=\Pp_{x,y}\bigl(q(x+y)\ne q(x)+q(y)\bigr)<\frac16.
\]
There is a homomorphism $L:G\to H$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:56:eq:BLR-distance}
\tau:=\Pp_x(q(x)\ne L(x))\le\frac{\rho}{1-2\rho}.
\end{equation}
For every $x$, the value $L(x)$ is the unique mode of
$q(x+y)-q(y)$ as $y$ ranges uniformly over $G$; that mode has mass at least
$1-2\rho$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Fix $x$ and write $d_x(y)=q(x+y)-q(y)$. For independent uniform $y,z$,
the two identities
\[
q(x+y+z)=q(x+y)+q(z),\qquad q(y+z)=q(y)+q(z)
\]
fail with combined probability at most $2\rho$. When both hold,
$d_x(y+z)=d_x(y)$. Since $(y,y+z)$ is a uniformly distributed independent
pair, the collision probability of the distribution of $d_x$ is at least
$1-2\rho$. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:56:lem:mode} supplies a mode of at least this mass.
It is unique because $1-2\rho>1/2$. Define that mode to be $L(x)$.

The exact identity
\[
d_{x+z}(y)=d_x(y)+d_z(x+y)
\]
holds for all $x,z,y$. For fixed $x,z$, each of the three quantities equals
its corresponding mode with probability at least $1-2\rho$ over $y$.
The union bound leaves a positive probability of simultaneous agreement
because $6\rho<1$. It follows that
$L(x+z)=L(x)+L(z)$ for every $x,z$.

If $q(x)\ne L(x)$, the conditional probability that $d_x(y)=q(x)$ is
at most $2\rho$. Thus the additive test fails, conditional on this $x$,
with probability at least $1-2\rho$. Averaging over such $x$ yields
$\rho\ge(1-2\rho)\tau$, proving \eqref{gsr:en:56:eq:BLR-distance}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Return to the weighted domain]\label{gsr:en:56:lem:back}
Suppose $q$ has been selected as in Section~\ref{gsr:en:56:sec:modal}, and a
homomorphism $L$ differs from $q$ on an ambient proportion $\tau$.
Then there is $c\in H$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:56:eq:back-bound}
t_w(\phi,L+c)\le\beta+\tau+s\sqrt\tau.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $S=\{h:q(h)\ne L(h)\}$. A weighted pair fails the relation
$\phi(x+h)-\phi(x)=L(h)$ only if it is a bad pair for $q$ or its shift lies
in $S$. The total bad-pair mass is at most
\begin{align*}
B+\E_h r(h)\ind_S(h)
&\le B+\alpha^2\tau+u^2\sqrt\tau.
\end{align*}
Here the last step is Cauchy--Schwarz applied to
$(r-\alpha^2)\ind_S$. After division by $\alpha^2$, the two endpoints of
a weighted pair are independently distributed with mass function
$w(x)/(N\alpha)$. Therefore the collision defect of
$\psi(x)=\phi(x)-L(x)$ under that probability measure is at most
$\beta+\tau+s\sqrt\tau$. Choose a mode $c$ of $\psi$ and apply
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:56:lem:mode} once more.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Parameterized coarse repair]\label{gsr:en:56:prop:coarse-general}
Compute $\beta$ from \eqref{gsr:en:56:eq:beta-bound} and $v=\sqrt V/\alpha^3$. Set
\[
\rho_*=
\left(\frac{v+\sqrt{v^2+12\beta}}2\right)^2.
\]
If $\rho_*<1/6$, set $\tau_*=\rho_* /(1-2\rho_*)$. There is an affine map
$\Phi$ with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:56:eq:coarse-general}
t_w(\phi,\Phi)\le\beta+\tau_*+s\sqrt{\tau_*}.
\end{equation}
One may replace $\rho_*$ throughout by any larger upper bound below $1/6$,
in particular by $6\beta+3\lambda^2$ when that quantity is below $1/6$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Combine Lemmas~\ref{gsr:en:56:lem:triangle-transfer}, \ref{gsr:en:56:lem:BLR}, and \ref{gsr:en:56:lem:back}.
The functions $x/(1-2x)$ and $x+s\sqrt x$ are increasing on their relevant
nonnegative domains.
\end{proof}

This proposition is already useful outside the fixed numerical range of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:56:thm:main}. It separates two tasks: establishing a coarse
approximation from triangle sampling, and improving that approximation
using the local error profile. Merely estimating the expression in
\eqref{gsr:en:56:eq:coarse-general} as $\eps\to0$ would leave a nonzero
uniformity-dependent error. The next section is what removes that error.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The one-error profile and linear amplification\srctag{56}}]{The one-error profile and linear amplification}\label{gsr:en:56:sec:d6}\label{gsr:en:56:sec:profile}
\srcnote{56}{Section 6}

Fix an affine map $\Phi=L+c$. Subtracting it from $\phi$ does not alter
which additive quadruples are respected. We may therefore suppose that
$\Phi=0$. Let
\[
E=\{x\in\supp w:\phi(x)\ne0\},\qquad
v_E(x)=w(x)\ind_E(x),\qquad b=\E v_E=\alpha t.
\]
The letter $v_E$ denotes a marked weight, not the normalized triangle
standard deviation from Section~\ref{gsr:en:56:sec:coarse}.

\begin{lemma}[Two marked vertices]\label{gsr:en:56:lem:two-marked}
Place $v_E$ at any two distinct coordinate positions in the ordered equation
$a+b=c+d$, and place $w$ at the other two. The resulting ambient-normalized
weighted count $M$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:56:eq:two-marked}
M\le b^2\alpha^2+u^2b^{3/2}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
There are two types of positions. If the marked variables lie on the same
side of the equation, the Fourier expression is
\[
\sum_{\chi}\widehat {v_E}(\chi)^2
                     \overline{\widehat w(\chi)^2}.
\]
If they lie on opposite sides, it is
\[
\sum_{\chi}|\widehat {v_E}(\chi)|^2|\widehat w(\chi)|^2.
\]
In either case the trivial character contributes $b^2\alpha^2$ and the
absolute value of the remaining contribution is at most
\begin{align*}
\sum_{\chi\ne1}|\widehat {v_E}(\chi)|^2|\widehat w(\chi)|^2
&\le
\left(\sum_{\chi\ne1}|\widehat {v_E}(\chi)|^4\right)^{1/2}u^2\\
&\le u^2b^{3/2},
\end{align*}
by \eqref{gsr:en:56:eq:trivial-energy-cap}. No division by two in $G$ is used.
The argument is therefore valid in groups with two-torsion as well.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Local defect profile]\label{gsr:en:56:prop:profile}
For every affine comparison map and its relative error $t$, the inequalities
\eqref{gsr:fm:56:eq:profile-lower} and \eqref{gsr:fm:56:eq:profile-upper} hold.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For an ordered additive quadruple let $K_i\in\{0,1\}$ indicate that its
$i$th coordinate lies in $E$. A quadruple with exactly one marked coordinate
is necessarily violated: the three zero residual labels cannot cancel the
single nonzero one. Pointwise on four binary indicators,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:56:eq:binary-IE}
\ind_{K_1+K_2+K_3+K_4=1}
\ge\sum_{i=1}^4K_i-2\sum_{1\le i<j\le4}K_iK_j.
\end{equation}
Indeed, for $r=0,1,2,3,4$ marked incidences, the right side is
$r-2\binom r2$, respectively $0,1,0,-3,-8$.

For each fixed coordinate position, the weighted count with that coordinate
marked is
\[
\E_xv_E(x)D_w(x)
\ge b\alpha^3(1-\lambda\sqrt{1-\alpha})
\]
by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:56:lem:link}. The six two-marked counts are bounded by
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:56:lem:two-marked}. Multiplying \eqref{gsr:en:56:eq:binary-IE} by the
quadruple weight and averaging therefore gives
\[
\Def_w(\phi)\ge
4b\alpha^3(1-\lambda\sqrt{1-\alpha})
-12b^2\alpha^2-12u^2b^{3/2}.
\]
Substitute $b=\alpha t$, $u^2=\lambda\alpha^{5/2}$, and
$\Def_w(\phi)=\eps\alpha^4(1+\lambda^2\alpha)$ to obtain
\eqref{gsr:fm:56:eq:profile-lower}.

Conversely, a violated quadruple must have at least one marked coordinate.
The union bound and the upper estimate in Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:56:lem:link} yield
\[
\Def_w(\phi)\le
4b\alpha^3(1+\lambda\sqrt{1-\alpha}),
\]
which is \eqref{gsr:fm:56:eq:profile-upper}.
\end{proof}

Repeated vertices cause no difficulty. The $K_i$ count coordinate incidences,
not distinct elements of $E$. If the same erroneous point occurs twice it
contributes two incidences, and the exact-one assertion is not applied to it.
This observation prevents an implicit nondegeneracy assumption.

\subsection{A sharper form retaining the marked energy}
The proof actually bounds each two-marked term by
\[
b^2\alpha^2+u^2\sqrt{\Qcal(v_E)-b^4}.
\]
Thus, when the error support itself has small centered energy, the
$t^{3/2}$ correction in \eqref{gsr:fm:56:eq:profile-lower} can be reduced. One fully
explicit density-only variant is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:56:eq:profile-stronger}
\eps(1+\lambda^2\alpha)\ge
4(1-\lambda\sqrt{1-\alpha})t
-12t^2-12\lambda t^{3/2}\sqrt{1-\alpha t},
\end{equation}
because \eqref{gsr:en:56:eq:trivial-energy-cap} gives
$\Qcal(v_E)-b^4\le b^3(1-b)$.
We do not need this small additional improvement for the main theorem.

\subsection{Why a coarse theorem suffices}
The right side of \eqref{gsr:fm:56:eq:profile-lower} is linear and positive for
sufficiently small $t$, with a coefficient close to four when $\lambda$ is
small. Thus a domain-dependent coarse estimate placing $t$ in that region
immediately becomes a bound proportional to $\eps$. This is the central
bootstrapping step. It avoids demanding that every intermediate approximation
already have error $O(\eps)$.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Proof of the main theorem and optimal first-order coefficient\srctag{56}}]{Proof of the main theorem and optimal first-order coefficient}\label{gsr:en:56:sec:d7}\label{gsr:en:56:sec:main-proof}
\srcnote{56}{Section 7}

\subsection{A rational constant calculation}
Assume \eqref{gsr:fm:56:eq:main-hyp}. Then
\[
\lambda\le\frac1{32},\quad
\kappa\le\frac1{1024},\quad
s\le\frac1{32},\quad
\sqrt\eps\le\frac1{32},\quad
\sqrt{1+\kappa}\le\frac{33}{32}.
\]
Consequently \eqref{gsr:en:56:eq:beta-bound} implies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:56:eq:beta-numeric}
\beta\le
\frac{1025}{1048576}+\frac{1056}{1048576}
=\frac{2081}{1048576}<\frac1{480}.
\end{equation}
By Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:56:lem:triangle-transfer},
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:56:eq:rho-numeric}
\rho\le6\beta+3\lambda^2
<\frac1{80}+\frac3{1024}
=\frac{79}{5120}<\frac1{64}<\frac16.
\end{equation}
Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:56:lem:BLR}. Since
\[
\tau\le\frac{\rho}{1-2\rho}<\frac1{62}<\frac1{60},
\qquad \sqrt\tau<\frac17,
\]
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:56:lem:back} gives an affine map with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:56:eq:coarse-numeric}
t<\frac1{480}+\frac1{60}+\frac1{224}
=\frac{13}{560}<\frac1{32}.
\end{equation}
We emphasize that no limit argument is being used; all constants are finite
and the inequalities apply also when $\eps=0$.

For $t\le1/32$, the lower profile implies
\begin{align*}
\eps(1+\kappa)
&\ge t\left[4(1-\lambda\sqrt{1-\alpha})-12t-12\lambda\sqrt t\right]\\
&\ge t\left[4\left(1-\frac1{32}\right)
             -\frac{12}{32}-\frac{12}{32\cdot4}\right]
=\frac{109}{32}t.
\end{align*}
Here $\sqrt t\le1/4$ is a convenient weaker bound than $1/\sqrt{32}$.
Since
\[
\frac{109}{32}>3\left(1+\frac1{1024}\right),
\]
we have established
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:56:eq:one-third}
t\le\frac\eps3.
\end{equation}
In particular, $\eps=0$ forces $t=0$.

For $t>0$, divide the lower profile by $t$ and then use
$12t\le4\eps$ and $12\lambda\sqrt t\le4\sqrt3\lambda\sqrt\eps$.
This proves \eqref{gsr:fm:56:eq:refined-intro}; the same conclusion holds trivially
when $t=0$. Its denominator is at least
\[
4\left(1-\frac1{32}\right)-\frac4{1024}
-4\cdot\frac74\cdot\frac1{32}\cdot\frac1{32}
=\frac{3957}{1024},
\]
where $\sqrt3<7/4$. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:56:eq:13-50}
t\le\frac{1025}{3957}\eps\le\frac{13}{50}\eps.
\end{equation}
The constant inequality $1025/3957<13/50$ is strict; the displayed
error bound is nonstrict so as to include zero error.

\subsection{Separation and uniqueness}
\begin{lemma}[Weighted affine separation]\label{gsr:en:56:lem:separation}
Suppose $\sigma\le\alpha$. Distinct affine maps $\Phi_1,\Phi_2:G\to H$
satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:56:eq:separation}
\frac{\E_xw(x)\ind_{\Phi_1(x)\ne\Phi_2(x)}}{\alpha}
\ge\frac{1-\sigma/\alpha}{2}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Their equality set is either empty or a coset of the kernel of the difference
of their linear parts. If the linear parts are equal but their constants
are different, the equality set is empty. Otherwise the kernel is a proper
subgroup $K$ of index $m\ge2$. Its annihilator $K^\perp$ has $m$ characters,
and orthogonality gives
\[
\ind_{x_0+K}(x)=\frac1m\sum_{\chi\in K^\perp}\chi(x-x_0).
\]
It follows that the relative weighted mass of this coset is at most
\[
\frac1m+\left(1-\frac1m\right)\frac\sigma\alpha
\le\frac{1+\sigma/\alpha}{2}.
\]
Taking the complement proves the lemma.
\end{proof}

Under the main hypothesis,
\[
\frac\sigma\alpha\le\frac u\alpha
=\sqrt\lambda\,\alpha^{1/4}\le\frac1{\sqrt{32}}<\frac15.
\]
Thus distinct affine maps have relative weighted distance greater than
$2/5$. Two maps each satisfying \eqref{gsr:fm:56:eq:main-bound} would have mutual
distance at most $26\eps/50\le26/(50\cdot1024)<2/5$, a contradiction.
Together with \eqref{gsr:en:56:eq:13-50}, this completes the proof of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:56:thm:main}. Taking $w=\ind_A$ gives
Corollary~\ref{gsr:fm:56:cor:subset-main}, and Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:56:prop:profile} plus the
bootstrap proves Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:56:thm:profile-intro}.

\subsection{The coefficient \texorpdfstring{$1/4$}{1/4} is asymptotically exact}
\begin{corollary}\label{gsr:en:56:cor:sharp-limit}
For any sequence of inputs satisfying \eqref{gsr:fm:56:eq:main-hyp} with actual
errors $\eps>0$, if $\eps\to0$ and $\lambda\to0$, then the repaired distances
satisfy
\[
\frac{t}{\eps}\longrightarrow\frac14.
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The upper profile gives
\[
\frac{t}{\eps}\ge
\frac{1+\lambda^2\alpha}{4(1+\lambda\sqrt{1-\alpha})}.
\]
The refined upper bound \eqref{gsr:fm:56:eq:refined-intro} gives the other side.
Both comparison expressions tend to $1/4$ uniformly in $0<\alpha\le1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[A single erroneous label]\label{gsr:en:56:ex:sharp}
Let $G=\Z/N\Z$, let $H=\Z/2\Z$, set $w=1$, and change the zero map at
one point to the nonzero element of $H$. Its distance from the zero affine
map is $t=1/N$. The two profiles with $\lambda=0$ give
\[
4t-12t^2\le\eps\le4t.
\]
For $N$ sufficiently large the main theorem applies, and affine separation
shows that the zero map is the unique nearest affine map. Hence
$t/\eps\to1/4$.
For completeness the exact error is
\[
\eps=\frac{(N-1)(4N-8)}{N^3}
=4t-12t^2+8t^3.
\]
At every nonzero shift the label-difference distribution has multiplicities
$N-2$ and $2$, which proves the formula. This elementary full-domain example
is only a sharpness witness; sharper full-domain stability profiles are
already present in the inspected repository.
\end{example}

The equality of the limiting coefficient concerns the joint limit
$\lambda,\eps\to0$. At fixed positive $\lambda$, the present upper and lower
bounds need not have the same first-order coefficient. Neither an exact
extremal profile nor an extremizer classification at fixed uniformity is
asserted.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Exact extension, spectral certificates, and testing\srctag{56}}]{Exact extension, spectral certificates, and testing}\label{gsr:en:56:sec:d8}\label{gsr:en:56:sec:corollaries}
\srcnote{56}{Section 8}

\begin{corollary}[Exact Freiman extension]\label{gsr:en:56:cor:exact}
Under $u^4\le\alpha^5/1024$, any map $\phi:\supp w\to H$ respecting every
additive quadruple of positive weight extends to a unique affine map on $G$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:56:thm:main} with $\eps=0$. Relative weighted distance zero
means equality at every point with positive weight because the domain is
finite. Uniqueness follows from Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:56:lem:separation}.
\end{proof}
This is an explicit exact-extension consequence of the same repair theorem;
no passage through arbitrarily small positive error parameters is required.

\begin{corollary}[A maximum-Fourier-coefficient certificate]\label{gsr:en:56:cor:spectral}
If
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:56:eq:spectral-hyp}
\max_{\chi\ne1}|\widehat w(\chi)|\le\frac{\alpha^2}{32},
\end{equation}
then the domain hypothesis of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:56:thm:main} holds.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Parseval yields
\[
u^4=\sum_{\chi\ne1}|\widehat w(\chi)|^4
\le\sigma^2(\mu-\alpha^2)
\le\sigma^2\alpha
\le\frac{\alpha^5}{1024}.
\]
\end{proof}
The certificate is sufficient, not equivalent to the $U^2$ condition.
Direct use of the fourth moment can be considerably better when a few
Fourier coefficients dominate the spectrum.

\subsection{Working relative to a subgroup or a coset}
Let $K\le G$ and let the domain lie in $x_0+K$. Translate by $-x_0$ and use
probability averages on $K$, not on $G$. The theorem gives a map
\[
x_0+k\longmapsto L_K(k)+c,
\qquad L_K\in\Hom(K,H),
\]
with the same estimates, provided the relative $U^2(K)$ hypothesis holds.
It does not in general extend that affine map from $x_0+K$ to all of $G$.

\begin{example}[An ambient-extension obstruction]\label{gsr:en:56:ex:subgroup}
Take $G=\Z/4\Z$, $K=\{0,2\}$, and $H=\Z/2\Z$. The map on $K$ defined by
$\phi(0)=0$, $\phi(2)=1$ is a homomorphism on $K$ and hence respects every
additive quadruple there. It has no affine extension to $G$: its constant
would have to be zero, while every homomorphism $L:G\to H$ satisfies
$L(2)=2L(1)=0$. Thus Fourier uniformity in the correct ambient group is a
substantive hypothesis, and relative extension must not be silently
identified with extension to a larger group.
\end{example}

\subsection{A four-query affine tester}
Define
\[
d_w(\phi,\Aff(G,H))=\min_{\Phi\in\Aff(G,H)}t_w(\phi,\Phi).
\]
The minimum exists: each candidate gives the mass of one of finitely many
error subsets of $G$, and at least the constant maps exist.

\begin{corollary}[Soundness with a weighted quadruple sampler]\label{gsr:en:56:cor:tester}
Assume $u^4\le\alpha^5/1024$. The test that samples a weighted additive
quadruple and checks its label relation has perfect completeness and
rejection probability
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:56:eq:tester-soundness}
\eps\ge\min\left\{\frac1{1024},\frac{50}{13}
 d_w(\phi,\Aff(G,H))\right\}.
\end{equation}
For distinct affine maps the relative weighted code distance is greater
than $2/5$ under the same hypothesis.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Affine maps respect every quadruple. If $\eps\le1/1024$,
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:56:thm:main} gives $d_w\le13\eps/50$. If
$\eps>1/1024$, the other branch of \eqref{gsr:en:56:eq:tester-soundness} is immediate.
The code-distance assertion was proved in Section~\ref{gsr:en:56:sec:main-proof}.
\end{proof}

This is a statement about \emph{four label queries per accepted configuration}.
It does not promise four membership queries to produce that configuration.
For instance, rejection sampling starts with independent uniform $a,b,c$,
sets $d=a+b-c$, and accepts with probability $w(a)w(b)w(c)w(d)$.
The expected number of ambient proposals is $1/\Qcal(w)$, which may be of
order $\alpha^{-4}$. Given an efficient weighted quadruple sampler, repeating
the test $m$ times gives false acceptance probability at most
$(1-\eps)^m\le e^{-m\eps}$.

\subsection{A local-to-global interpretation}
The conclusion can be viewed as a quantitative presentation theorem for
$G$: labels on a sufficiently uniform weighted subset that almost respect
the four-term presentation relations nearly arise from a global affine map.
The code-distance estimate gives uniqueness, whereas triangle transfer gives
existence. These are logically separate: separation by itself would not
produce a nearby global map.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Explicit affine repair on quadratic level sets\srctag{56}}]{Explicit affine repair on quadratic level sets}\label{gsr:en:56:sec:d9}\label{gsr:en:56:sec:quadratic}
\srcnote{56}{Section 9}

This section turns the Fourier hypothesis into a concrete algebraic rank
condition. The labels are tested for \emph{affinity}, even though their
domain is a quadratic level set. Repair of approximately quadratic labels
is a different problem and is not proved here.

Fix an odd prime $p$, and write $e_p(t)=\exp(2\pi i t/p)$. A quadratic
polynomial on $\F_p^n$ has the form
\[
Q(x)=x^TMx+\ell(x)+c,
\]
with $M$ symmetric. In this section its rank means the matrix rank of $M$.
The linear and constant terms do not affect this rank.

\begin{lemma}[Quadratic Fourier bound]\label{gsr:en:56:lem:gauss}
For every quadratic $Q$ with matrix rank $R_0$ and every linear functional
$\xi$, one has
\[
\left|\E_x e_p(Q(x)-\xi(x))\right|\le p^{-R_0/2}.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Absorb $-\xi$ into the linear part of $Q$. Squaring the absolute value of
the average and introducing a difference $h$ gives
\[
\left|\E_xe_p(Q(x))\right|^2
=\E_h\E_x e_p(Q(x+h)-Q(x)).
\]
The dependence on $x$ in the phase is the linear form $2x^TMh$.
Its average vanishes unless $Mh=0$, because $p$ is odd. The remaining
terms have modulus at most one. Since the kernel of $M$ has relative
size $p^{-R_0}$, the squared absolute value is at most $p^{-R_0}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Rank certificate independent of the test error]\label{gsr:en:56:thm:quadratic}
Let $r\ge1$ and let $Q_1,\ldots,Q_r:\F_p^n\to\F_p$ be quadratic
polynomials such that every nonzero linear combination has matrix rank at
least $R$. For any $b_1,\ldots,b_r\in\F_p$, put
\[
A=\{x:Q_1(x)=b_1,\ldots,Q_r(x)=b_r\}.
\]
Suppose
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:56:eq:rank-threshold}
p^{R-4r}\ge2^{14}.
\end{equation}
Then $A$ is nonempty. For every abelian group $H$ and every map
$\phi:A\to H$ with additive-quadruple error at most
$0\le\eps\le1/1024$, there is a unique affine map $\Phi:\F_p^n\to H$
agreeing with $\phi$ except on at most $13\eps|A|/50$ points.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Orthogonality gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:56:eq:quadratic-expansion}
\ind_A(x)=p^{-r}\sum_{\theta\in\F_p^r}
 e_p\left(\sum_{j=1}^r\theta_j(Q_j(x)-b_j)\right).
\end{equation}
The term $\theta=0$ has mean $p^{-r}$. By Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:56:lem:gauss},
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:56:eq:quadratic-density}
|\alpha-p^{-r}|\le(1-p^{-r})p^{-R/2}\le p^{-R/2}.
\end{equation}
At a nontrivial additive character, the $\theta=0$ term in the Fourier
transform vanishes. The same argument gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:56:eq:quadratic-sigma}
\sigma\le p^{-R/2}.
\end{equation}
The rank hypothesis implies
\[
p^{-R/2}\le\frac{p^{-2r}}{128}\le\frac{p^{-r}}2,
\]
so $\alpha\ge p^{-r}/2>0$. In particular,
\[
\sigma\le\frac{p^{-2r}}{128}\le\frac{\alpha^2}{32}.
\]
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:56:cor:spectral} and then Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:56:thm:main} apply.
Equivalently, a direct calculation is
\[
\frac{\norm{\ind_A-\alpha}_{U^2}^4}{\alpha^5}
\le\frac{p^{-R}\alpha}{\alpha^5}
\le16p^{4r-R}\le\frac1{1024}.
\]
\end{proof}

An equivalent integer rank bound is
\[
R\ge4r+\left\lceil14\log_p2\right\rceil.
\]
For example, the sufficient additional ranks are nine for $p=3$, seven
for $p=5$, and five for $p=7$, since $3^9$, $5^7$, and $7^5$ exceed
$2^{14}$ whereas the preceding powers do not. These constants are
certificates from the displayed proof, not optimal-rank assertions.
If $r=0$, the domain is the whole vector space and the theorem applies
without any rank requirement.

\subsection{Nonvacuity and sharpness at small densities}
\begin{proposition}\label{gsr:en:56:prop:sparse-sharp}
For every fixed odd prime $p$ and positive integer $r$, there are domains
with densities tending to $p^{-r}$, normalized uniformity $\lambda\to0$,
and maps with $\eps\to0$ whose nearest affine distance satisfies
$t/\eps\to1/4$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For each $M$, use $r$ disjoint blocks of $M$ variables and put
\[
Q_j(x)=\sum_{i=1}^M x_{j,i}^2,
\qquad G_M=\F_p^{rM},
\qquad A_M=\{Q_1=\cdots=Q_r=0\}.
\]
Every nonzero combination has rank at least $M$. Thus
\[
\alpha_M=p^{-r}+O(p^{-M/2}),\qquad
\lambda_M^2\le p^{-M}\alpha_M^{-4}\longrightarrow0.
\]
In particular $|A_M|\to\infty$. Give every point label zero in $\F_p$ except
one point, which receives label one. Its distance from the zero map is
$t_M=1/|A_M|$. The upper profile proves $\eps_M\to0$, and the lower profile
proves $\eps_M=4t_M(1+o(1))>0$ for large $M$.
The main theorem and affine separation identify the zero map as the unique
nearest affine map for large $M$: any other affine map disagrees with zero
on more than $2/5$ of the domain and hence cannot improve its vanishing
error. This proves the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 54--59]
\emph{Checked at the write} (exact rationals): the constant chain of Section~\ref{gsr:en:56:sec:d7}, $1025/1048576+1056/1048576=2081/1048576<1/480$, $6/480+3/1024=79/5120<1/64$, $(1/64)/(1-2/64)=1/62<1/60$, $1/60<1/49$, $1/480+1/60+1/224=13/560<1/32$, $4(31/32)-12/32-12/128=109/32>3\cdot1025/1024$, $4(31/32)-4/1024-7/1024=3957/1024$ and $1025/3957<13/50$; and the ranks of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:56:thm:quadratic}: $3^8<2^{14}\le3^9$, $5^6<2^{14}\le5^7$, $7^4<2^{14}\le7^5$, so the additional ranks are $9$, $7$ and~$5$ as stated.
\end{writenote}

Thus the limiting coefficient is not merely an artifact of the full-domain
case. It remains optimal at arbitrarily small fixed limiting densities.
The rank needed for the affine-repair corollary has no dependence on
$\log(\eps^{-1})$ or on $\eps^{-1}$. This does not establish the analogous
independence for quadratic-label repair.
