\section{Source~59's chapter: exact character separation at Section~7 \wtag}\label{gsr:en:sec:charseparation}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the tenth write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next five sections are source~59's Sections~2--6, on the extraction of a Freiman homomorphism of order $k$ (Gowers's Lemma~7.5 and Corollary~7.6). \emph{Logically they continue the chapters of sources~24 and~31 on Section~7} (Sections~\ref{gsr:en:sec:section7} and~\ref{gsr:en:sec:weighted7}) and source~10's torsion budget; they are printed here because no number printed earlier may move.

\emph{What is proved.} For a finite symmetric forbidden set with $q$ sign orbits, the exact worst-case number of characters that separate it is $\lfloor\log_2(q+1)\rfloor$ at radius $1/5$, $\lfloor\log_3(2q+1)\rfloor$ at radius $1/7$ for odd-order defects, and $\lfloor\log_p((p-1)q+1)\rfloor$ at radius $1/(2p)$ for $p$-power orders, every rank sharp (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:59:thm:sharp-separation}); the exact small-ball law of one character (Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:59:lem:small-ball}) and strict adaptive deletion (Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:59:lem:adaptive}) are the key. Weighted localization then gives exact Freiman restrictions of order $k$ over arbitrary abelian targets, $|B|/(5k)^{\lfloor\log_2(q+1)\rfloor}$ in general (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:59:thm:freiman-extraction}), with finite-image rounding (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:59:thm:finite-image}), and, from $|\Gamma-\Gamma|\le C|\Gamma|$, $|B'|\ge C^{-(2k+1)\log_2(5k)}|B|$ independently of the target (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:59:cor:doubling}); this answers source~24's mixed-torsion question (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:groups}). Every symmetric set is realized as the defect set of a graph at a prescribed order (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:59:thm:realizability}); the one-character problem contains the lonely runner conjecture, whose known bounds transfer (Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:59:prop:lonely-runner}). The separation architecture is Green and Tao's, the finite-field kernel Gowers and Mili\'cevi\'c's, as source~59 credits; the universal exponent can exceed Gowers's $4k$, and source~10's prime-cyclic bound is not improved, as it says.

\emph{Relation to the formal statements} (checked at HEAD \texttt{fe7165a3c}). \file{lemma_7_5} and \file{corollary_7_6} (\file{Sections06\_07.lean}, lines~183 and~197) have the exact companions \file{lemma_7_5_holds} (\file{Proofs07FreimanRestriction.lean}, line~267) and \file{corollary_7_6_holds} (\file{Proofs07AdditiveRestriction.lean}, line~100), stated for prime cyclic groups; nothing in this chapter is formalized.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Exact character distributions and order-sensitive radii\srctag{59}}]{Exact character distributions and order-sensitive radii}\label{gsr:en:59:sec:d2}
\srcnote{59}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:en:59:sec:distributions}

Let $H_0$ be finitely generated. By the structure theorem, its character group is a product of a finite group and a torus; equip it with normalized Haar measure. We first record exactly what a random character does to a single element. This elementary detail controls every torsion issue that follows.

\begin{lemma}[Evaluation and extension]\label{gsr:en:59:lem:character-evaluation}
If $f\in H_0$ has finite order $n$, evaluation $\chi\mapsto\chi(f)$ sends Haar measure to the uniform measure on $\T[n]$. If $f$ has infinite order, it sends Haar measure to Haar measure on $\T$. Every character on a subgroup of an abelian group extends to the full group.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
First prove the extension assertion. Suppose $\chi$ is defined on $K\le H$ and $x\notin K$. If there is a positive integer $n$ with $nx\in K$, choose the least such $n$ and choose $u\in\T$ with $nu=\chi(nx)$. The definition $\chi(k+mx)=\chi(k)+mu$ is well-defined on $K+\Z x$. If no such $n$ exists, choose $u$ arbitrarily and use the same definition. A maximal extension argument proves the assertion, using divisibility of $\T$.

Every character of $\langle f\rangle$ therefore extends to $H_0$. Evaluation is consequently onto $\T[n]$ in the finite-order case and onto $\T$ in the infinite-order case. A continuous surjective homomorphism of compact groups pushes normalized Haar measure to normalized Haar measure. Alternatively, the finite case follows from equal fiber sizes, and the infinite case follows directly by integrating over the torus coordinates of $\widehat H_0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Exact open-arc probability]\label{gsr:en:59:lem:small-ball}
For $0<\theta<1/2$ and $n\in\{2,3,\ldots\}\cup\{\infty\}$, set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:beta}
 \beta_n(\theta)=
 \begin{cases}
 (2\lceil n\theta\rceil-1)/n,&n<\infty,\\
 2\theta,&n=\infty.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
If $\ord(f)=n$, then
\[
 \Prob_{\chi}\bigl(\distT{\chi(f)}<\theta\bigr)=\beta_n(\theta).
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For finite $n$, the residues at distance strictly less than $\theta$ are zero and the pairs $\pm j/n$ with $1\le j<n\theta$. There are $2\lceil n\theta\rceil-1$ of them. For infinite order, the relevant open arc has length $2\theta$.
\end{proof}

The strict arc convention is essential. For example,
\[
 \beta_5(1/4)=\frac35,\qquad
 \beta_5(1/5)=\frac15,\qquad
 \beta_6(1/5)=\frac12.
\]
Thus one cannot replace the exact distribution by continuous circle measure when the evaluated element has small finite order.

\begin{proposition}[Optimal uniform probability cutoffs]\label{gsr:en:59:prop:probability-cutoffs}
For every integer $r\ge2$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:cutoff-all}
 \beta_n\left(\frac1{3r-1}\right)\le\frac1r
 \quad\text{for all finite }n\ge r\text{ and for }n=\infty.
\end{equation}
For every odd integer $r\ge3$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:cutoff-odd}
 \beta_n\left(\frac1{3r-2}\right)\le\frac1r
 \quad\text{for all odd finite }n\ge r\text{ and for }n=\infty.
\end{equation}
In each statement, the displayed radius is the largest radius for which that uniform probability bound holds over the stated class of finite orders.

For a prime $p$ and $a\ge1$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:cutoff-primary}
 \beta_{p^a}\left(\frac1{2p}\right)\le\frac1p,
 \qquad \beta_\infty\left(\frac1{2p}\right)=\frac1p.
\end{equation}
No larger radius gives this contraction uniformly over all $p$-power orders.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For \eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:cutoff-all}, write $j=\lceil n/(3r-1)\rceil$. If $j=1$, then $\beta_n=1/n\le1/r$. If $j\ge2$, then
\[
 n\ge(j-1)(3r-1)+1,\qquad
 n-r(2j-1)\ge(r-1)(j-2)\ge0.
\]
This proves the finite-order assertion, and $2/(3r-1)\le1/r$ handles infinite order. At order $n=3r-1$, any increase of the radius admits the two nearest nonzero roots, making the probability at least $3/(3r-1)>1/r$.

For \eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:cutoff-odd}, put $j=\lceil n/(3r-2)\rceil$. The case $j=1$ is the same. For $j\ge2$, the least odd integer strictly larger than $(j-1)(3r-2)$ is that number plus $d$, where $d=1$ if $j$ is odd and $d=2$ if $j$ is even. Hence
\[
 n-r(2j-1)\ge(r-2)(j-2)+d-2\ge0.
\]
For odd $j\ge3$ the final expression is at least $r-3$, and for even $j$ it is nonnegative directly. Infinite order again satisfies the bound. The odd order $3r-2$ proves radius optimality.

If $p$ is odd, then $p^a/(2p)$ is a half-integer, so the finite probability in \eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:cutoff-primary} equals $1/p$ exactly. For $p=2$, it is $1/2$ at $a=1$ and $1/2-1/2^a$ at $a\ge2$. Finally $\beta_{p^a}(\theta)\to2\theta$ as $a\to\infty$, which proves the last optimality assertion.
\end{proof}

Taking $r=2$ in \eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:cutoff-all} gives radius $1/5$ and contraction $1/2$. Taking $r=3$ in \eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:cutoff-odd} gives radius $1/7$ and contraction $1/3$. If the actual defects avoid all small orders, the larger values of $r$ give additional options. Those options are sufficient estimates; no corresponding exact-rank claim is made here for every composite $r$.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Adaptive character separation and matching obstructions\srctag{59}}]{Adaptive character separation and matching obstructions}\label{gsr:en:59:sec:d3}
\srcnote{59}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:en:59:sec:separation}

Choose a representative set $D\subset F$ of the sign orbits and write $q=|D|$. All sets considered in this section are finite; the containing abelian group may be arbitrary. Characters may be chosen on a finitely generated subgroup and extended by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:59:lem:character-evaluation}.

\begin{theorem}[Exact order-profile certificate]\label{gsr:en:59:thm:profile}
Choose radii $0<\theta_j<1/2$, $1\le j\le m$, and put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:profile-budget}
 P=\sum_{f\in D}\prod_{j=1}^m\beta_{\ord(f)}(\theta_j).
\end{equation}
If $P<1$, there are characters $\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_m$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:separation-condition}
 \text{for every }f\in F,\quad
 \distT{\chi_j(f)}\ge\theta_j\text{ for some }j.
\end{equation}
For $q\ge2$, the hypothesis $P\le1$ is sufficient. More generally, if $P<q$, some tuple of characters leaves at most $\lceil P\rceil-1$ representatives satisfying all the strict reverse inequalities.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Take independent Haar-uniform characters and let $X$ count representatives satisfying $\distT{\chi_j(f)}<\theta_j$ for every $j$. The exact probability formula gives $\E X=P$. All these inequalities hold on an open neighborhood of the zero character tuple, so $X=q$ on a set of positive Haar measure. If $P<q$ and $X\ge P$ everywhere, that neighborhood makes $\E X>P$, a contradiction. Thus $X<P$ somewhere; since $X$ is integral, $X\le\lceil P\rceil-1$. The assertions follow. When $P<1$ and $q=1$, the elementary expectation argument also applies directly.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why the endpoint needs an argument]
An ordinary union bound with expectation one does not exclude a survivor at every character tuple. Here the bad events have a common open intersection of positive measure, on which at least two representatives survive. That extra overlap is what permits equality in the budget. For $q=1$, a budget of one is not sufficient in general: a wide enough arc can contain the entire image of an odd-order element.
\end{remark}

\begin{lemma}[Strict adaptive deletion]\label{gsr:en:59:lem:adaptive}
Suppose every order occurring in $F$ satisfies $\beta_n(\theta)\le1/b$, where $b\ge2$ is an integer. Then $F$ can be separated at radius $\theta$ by at most
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:rank-function}
 m_b(q)=\left\lfloor\log_b\bigl((b-1)q+1\bigr)\right\rfloor
\end{equation}
characters, with $m_b(0)=0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
At a stage with $s>0$ surviving representatives, let $X$ count survivors after one new character. We have $\E X\le s/b$. A positive-measure neighborhood of zero has $X=s>s/b$, so some character has $X<s/b$. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:strict-recurrence}
 s_{\mathrm{next}}\le\left\lceil\frac{s}{b}\right\rceil-1
 =\left\lfloor\frac{s-1}{b}\right\rfloor.
\end{equation}
Writing $U(s)=(b-1)s+1$, this implies $U(s_{\mathrm{next}})\le U(s)/b$. Put $m=m_b(q)$. If the process has not terminated earlier, after $m$ steps
\[
 U(s_m)\le \frac{(b-1)q+1}{b^m}<b.
\]
Every positive integer $s$ has $U(s)\ge b$, so $s_m=0$.
\end{proof}

For perspective, $m$ steps suffice exactly throughout the range
\[
 q\le b+b^2+\cdots+b^m.
\]
Thus two universal characters handle as many as six sign orbits; two odd-order characters handle as many as twelve. The gain over taking a fixed number of independent characters is an adaptive integer gain, not a change in a continuous logarithmic approximation.

\begin{theorem}[Sharp universal, odd, and prime-primary ranks]\label{gsr:en:59:thm:sharp-separation}
Let $F\subset H\setminus\{0\}$ be finite and symmetric, with $q$ sign orbits.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item With no restriction on $H$ or $F$, radius $1/5$ is achievable with at most $m_2(q)=\lfloor\log_2(q+1)\rfloor$ characters.
\item If every finite-order element of $F$ has odd order, radius $1/7$ is achievable with at most $m_3(q)=\lfloor\log_3(2q+1)\rfloor$ characters.
\item If every finite-order element of $F$ has order a power of a fixed prime $p$, radius $1/(2p)$ is achievable with at most $m_p(q)$ characters.
\end{enumerate}
Each number of characters is best possible as a worst-case function of $q$, for every $q\ge1$. In \textup{(i)} and \textup{(ii)}, the radius cannot be increased while retaining that same rank bound for all $q$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The upper bounds follow from Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:59:prop:probability-cutoffs} and Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:59:lem:adaptive}.

For the rank lower bounds, fix $p$ and $q\ge1$, and put $m=m_p(q)$. Then
\[
 \frac{p^m-1}{p-1}\le q<\frac{p^{m+1}-1}{p-1}.
\]
Inside $V=\F_p^{m+1}$ fix an $m$-dimensional subspace $U$. From every one-dimensional subspace $L\le U$, choose a nonzero representative $v_L$ and include both $v_L$ and $-v_L$ in $F$. Add such pairs from further distinct projective lines of $V$ until there are exactly $q$ sign orbits. The displayed inequalities ensure that this is possible, also for $p=2$, when each pair is a singleton.

Characters of $V$ identify with linear functionals into $\F_p$. Any $m-1$ characters have a nonzero common kernel on $U$. That kernel contains a projective line whose chosen representative belongs to $F$. Consequently $m-1$ characters fail at every positive radius. This proves the prime-primary lower bound for every $q$; $p=2$ and $p=3$ prove the universal and odd-order lower bounds.

For universal radius sharpness, take $H=\Z/5\Z$ and $F=H\setminus\{0\}$. Here $q=2$ and $m_2(q)=1$. Every nontrivial character permutes $\T[5]$, so some forbidden element has distance $1/5$; the trivial character does worse. For the odd case, $H=\Z/7\Z$ and $F=H\setminus\{0\}$ have $q=3$, $m_3(q)=1$, and the analogous obstruction at $1/7$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Three distinct optimality assertions]\label{gsr:en:59:rem:three-sharpnesses}
The theorem proves an exact rank for each $q$. It proves an optimal radius uniformly in $q$ at those ranks in the first two cases. Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:59:prop:probability-cutoffs} proves a pointwise probability threshold for prime powers. The last assertion does not imply that $1/(2p)$ is the largest attainable prime-primary separation radius. Nor does sharp separator rank by itself prove an optimal retained proportion in a Freiman restriction.
\end{remark}

\begin{example}[Order profile versus a uniform class]
Suppose the representative orders are $2$ and $5$. At radius $1/5$ the one-character budget is $1/2+1/5=7/10<1$, so one character suffices. If there are three representatives, one of order $3$ and two of infinite order, then radius $1/7$ gives budget $1/3+2(2/7)=19/21<1$. Exact profiles retain information that is discarded by replacing every survival probability by its largest allowed value. In the adaptive version, one may use the sharper bound $\lceil\sum_f\beta_{\ord(f)}(\theta)\rceil-1$ at each stage.
\end{example}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Weighted Freiman restrictions over arbitrary abelian targets\srctag{59}}]{Weighted Freiman restrictions over arbitrary abelian targets}\label{gsr:en:59:sec:d4}
\srcnote{59}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:en:59:sec:extraction}

Let $G,H$ be abelian groups, let $B\subset G$ be finite and nonempty, and let $\phi:B\to H$. Define $\Gamma,F_k^0,F_k$ as in \eqref{gsr:fm:59:eq:intro-defect}, where $k\ge1$ is an integer. The group $H_0=\langle\phi(B)\rangle$ is finitely generated, and $F_k\subset H_0$. Let $w:B\to[0,\infty)$ and write $w(B)=\sum_{x\in B}w(x)$.

\begin{theorem}[Weighted localization]\label{gsr:en:59:thm:freiman-extraction}
Suppose $\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_m:H_0\to\T$ separate $F_k$ with radii $0<\theta_j\le1/2$, in the sense of \eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:separation-condition}. Then some $B'\subset B$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:weighted-restriction}
 w(B')\ge w(B)\prod_{j=1}^m\frac{\theta_j}{k},
\end{equation}
and $\phi|_{B'}$ is a Freiman homomorphism of order $k$. Moreover, $B$ can be partitioned into at most $\prod_j\lceil k/\theta_j\rceil$ subsets on each of which $\phi$ is such a homomorphism.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For each $j$, choose a uniformly translated half-open arc of length $\theta_j/k$, independently in each circle coordinate. Retain $x$ when every $\chi_j(\phi(x))$ lies in its corresponding arc. Every fixed $x$ is retained with probability $\prod_j\theta_j/k$, so the expected retained weight is the right-hand side of \eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:weighted-restriction}. A translate with at least that weight exists.

Suppose $x_1+\cdots+x_k=y_1+\cdots+y_k$ with all $x_i,y_i\in B'$. Its label defect
\[
 h=\phi(x_1)+\cdots+\phi(x_k)-\phi(y_1)-\cdots-\phi(y_k)
\]
belongs to $F_k^0$. Lift each character value to the real half-open interval representing its chosen arc. Each of the two $k$-term sums lies in the same interval of length $\theta_j$. Their difference therefore has absolute value strictly less than $\theta_j$, so $\distT{\chi_j(h)}<\theta_j$ for every $j$. Separation forces $h=0$.

For the partition assertion, divide circle $j$ into $L_j=\lceil k/\theta_j\rceil$ equal half-open arcs. Each arc has length at most $\theta_j/k$, and the same argument applies to every pulled-back product cell. Empty cells may be discarded. The half-open convention preserves strictness even when $1/L_j=\theta_j/k$.
\end{proof}

The assertion also covers zero total weight: one can choose any nonempty cell, or a singleton, without affecting the inequality. If $F_k$ is empty, there is no separation to perform and one takes $B'=B$.

\begin{corollary}[Explicit universal and torsion-sensitive retention]\label{gsr:en:59:cor:explicit-extraction}
Put $q=|F_k/\{\pm1\}|$. An order-$k$ Freiman restriction can retain at least the following fractions of any nonnegative weight:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.41\linewidth}c@{}}
\toprule
Defect condition & Retained fraction\\
\midrule
No restriction & $(5k)^{-m_2(q)}$\\
All finite defect orders odd & $(7k)^{-m_3(q)}$\\
All finite defect orders powers of $p$ & $(2pk)^{-m_p(q)}$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The exponent is zero when $q=0$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:59:thm:sharp-separation} and then Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:59:thm:freiman-extraction}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Exact finite-image rounding}

The continuous-arc loss is often wasteful on a finite character image. The following refinement keeps the finite arithmetic exactly.

\begin{theorem}[Finite-image gain]\label{gsr:en:59:thm:finite-image}
In Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:59:thm:freiman-extraction}, suppose $\chi_j(H_0)$ has finite order $N_j$. Its factor $\theta_j/k$ in \eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:weighted-restriction} can be replaced by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:finite-image-factor}
 a_j=\frac{\lceil N_j\theta_j/k\rceil}{N_j}.
\end{equation}
If the image is infinite, keep the factor $\theta_j/k$. All the improved factors can be multiplied, regardless of dependencies between the character coordinates.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Choose $t_j=\lceil N_j\theta_j/k\rceil$ consecutive points of the cyclic image and translate this block uniformly by that image. A fixed image point is included with probability $t_j/N_j$. The points in a block lift to a real interval of span
\[
 \frac{t_j-1}{N_j}<\frac{\theta_j}{k}.
\]
Thus the proof of exact Freiman behavior is unchanged. Make these translations independently in the ambient product of the coordinate images. They need not be induced by a common translation in $H_0$; every point still has the stated product inclusion probability. For a trivial image, $N_j=1$ and its factor is one.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Finite exponent and finite-field fibers]\label{gsr:en:59:cor:finite-exponent}
If $H_0$ has exponent $E$, the partition form of Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:59:cor:explicit-extraction} has at most $\min(E,dk)^m$ cells, where $(d,m)$ is $(5,m_2(q))$, $(7,m_3(q))$, or $(2p,m_p(q))$ in the appropriate case.

If $H_0$ has exponent $p$, an order-$k$ restriction retains at least
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:prime-fibers}
 p^{-m_p(q)}w(B).
\end{equation}
More strongly, let $r$ be the number of distinct one-dimensional $\F_p$-subspaces meeting $F_k$. Then $q$ can be replaced by $r$ in \eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:prime-fibers}.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
An exponent-$E$ character has at most $E$ values, so at most $\min(E,dk)$ equal arcs can be occupied in each coordinate.

For exponent $p$, a nontrivial character has image order $p$. At radius $1/(2p)$, formula \eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:finite-image-factor} is exactly $1/p$ for every $k\ge1$. Furthermore, a narrow-arc survivor is precisely a vector annihilated by the corresponding linear functional. Nonzero scalar multiples define the same annihilation event. Apply the adaptive argument to the $r$ projective lines, whose individual survival probability is $1/p$, and take a common fiber of the selected functionals.
\end{proof}

The linear-kernel method in this corollary is classical \cite[Lemma~3.3]{gowersmilicevicufour}. Its role here is to show that the general circle formulation includes exact finite-field fibers, rather than unnecessarily charging a factor $k$ for each character. The adaptive rank improves the rounding endpoint of the direct independent-kernel argument.

\subsection{A projection formulation}

\begin{proposition}[Exact local sections of an abelian quotient]\label{gsr:en:59:prop:projection}
Let $\pi:E\to G$ be a homomorphism of abelian groups, let $A\subset E$ be finite, and put
\[
 F=((kA-kA)\cap\ker\pi)\setminus\{0\}.
\]
If characters on $\langle A\rangle$ separate $F$ at radii $\theta_j$, the same retained-weight bound gives $A'\subset A$ on which $\pi$ is a Freiman isomorphism of order $k$ onto $\pi(A')$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The localization proof shows that any equality of two $k$-term sums after applying $\pi$ already holds in $E$. Forward preservation follows from the homomorphism property of $\pi$. If $A'$ is nonempty, pad a one-term equality using any fixed point of $A'$ to obtain injectivity; the empty case is vacuous.
\end{proof}

This formulation allows non-split extensions: the ambient abelian group need not be presented as a product. The graph case is the special case of a projection whose restriction to the initial set is already injective.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Small doubling and comparison with Lemma~7.5\srctag{59}}]{Small doubling and comparison with Lemma~7.5}\label{gsr:en:59:sec:d5}
\srcnote{59}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:en:59:sec:doubling}

\begin{lemma}[Vertical injection; classical defect budget]\label{gsr:en:59:lem:vertical-injection}
If $|\Gamma-\Gamma|\le C|\Gamma|$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:vertical-budget}
 Q_k:=|F_k^0|\le C^{2k+1}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The map
\[
 F_k^0\times\Gamma\longrightarrow (k+1)\Gamma-k\Gamma,
 \qquad (h,\gamma)\longmapsto (0,h)+\gamma
\]
is injective. Indeed, the domain projection of its value determines the unique graph point $\gamma$, and then determines $h$. Therefore
\[
 Q_k|\Gamma|\le |(k+1)\Gamma-k\Gamma|.
\]
The classical Pl\"unnecke--Ruzsa inequality says that $|A+B|\le C|A|$ implies $|rB-sB|\le C^{r+s}|A|$ for $r+s>1$; see \cite[Theorem~1.2]{petridis}. Apply it with $A=\Gamma$, $B=-\Gamma$, $r=k$, and $s=k+1$. Its conclusion concerns the full sum-difference set; no preliminary restriction of $\Gamma$ is required.
\end{proof}

The injection and this use of Pl\"unnecke--Ruzsa are already present in the finite-field precedent and in sources~10 and~24 \cite{gowersmilicevicufour,repo59}. We include them to make the quantitative interface explicit.

\begin{corollary}[Target-independent polynomial restriction]\label{gsr:en:59:cor:doubling}
Under the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:59:lem:vertical-injection}, there is an order-$k$ Freiman restriction satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:universal-doubling}
 |B'|\ge C^{-(2k+1)\log_2(5k)}|B|.
\end{equation}
If every finite-order nonzero defect has odd order, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:odd-doubling}
 |B'|\ge C^{-(2k+1)\log_3(7k)}|B|.
\end{equation}
The same conclusions hold for any fixed nonnegative weight on $B$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Universally, $q+1\le Q_k$, so
\[
 m_2(q)\le\log_2 Q_k\le(2k+1)\log_2 C.
\]
In the odd-defect case, $F_k$ has no involutions, so $2q+1=Q_k$ and $m_3(q)\le\log_3 Q_k$. Substitute these estimates into Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:59:cor:explicit-extraction}. For $C=1$, the defect set is empty and the assertion still holds.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 54--59]
\emph{Source~24's mixed-torsion question is answered} (its Question~7, item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:groups}): the bound holds for every abelian target, independently of its size, rank and invariant factors, with order-sensitive variants. Source~10's prime-cyclic bound is not improved, as this source says. Source~61, placed later and not yet written in, records the same exponent $(2m+1)\log_2(5m)$ found independently.
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Checked at the eleventh write} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:allmoduli}): source~61 finds the exponent $(2m+1)\log_2(5m)$ independently, in the partition form $|B|/(5mK^{(2m+1)\log_2(5m)})$ for some cell (its Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:61:ter:main-partition}); this corollary is sharper by the factor $5m$, and its defect-sensitive form by the separation rank $\lfloor\log_2(q+1)\rfloor\le\lceil\log_2|D|\rceil$. Source~61's pin precedes this source's placement.
\end{writenote}

For mixed finite targets, the exact order of a defect is the least common multiple of its component orders. Formula \eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:beta} therefore uses its invariant-factor information without splitting the problem into primary components. The resulting estimate is independent of target cardinality and rank. It answers source~24's mixed-torsion extension question in this explicit sense. A sharper bound for a particular group or a particular defect set can use Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:59:thm:profile}, finite-image rounding, or both.

For comparison, the exponents of $C$ in several bounds are:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}crrr@{}}
\toprule
$k$ & Gowers $4k$ & Universal $(2k+1)\log_2(5k)$ & Odd $(2k+1)\log_3(7k)$\\
\midrule
$2$ & $8$ & $16.610$ & $12.011$\\
$4$ & $16$ & $38.897$ & $27.298$\\
$8$ & $32$ & $90.473$ & $62.289$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The numerical entries are illustrative approximations. Gowers's original statement has the additional prefactor $1/(8k)$ and a prime-cyclic target; the present rows have the broader target hypotheses stated above. Source~10's prime-cyclic refinement is stronger still in that special setting. The actual $Q_k$ and the finite-image corrections should be used before this coarse table whenever they are available.

\subsection{An explicitly attributed Balog--Szemer\'edi--Gowers corollary}

For a finite subset $A$ of an abelian group, Reiher--Schoen prove that $E(A)\ge\gamma|A|^3$ and $0<\eta<1/2$ imply the existence of $A_1\subset A$ with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:reiher-schoen-input}
 |A_1|\ge(1-\eta)\gamma^{1/2}|A|,
 \qquad |A_1-A_1|\le2^{33}\eta^{-9}\gamma^{-4}|A_1|.
\end{equation}
This is their Theorem~1.2 \cite{reiherschoen}; it is an external input, not a new estimate in this article.

\begin{corollary}[From graph energy to exact restrictions]\label{gsr:en:59:cor:bsg-extraction}
Suppose $E(\Gamma)\ge\gamma|B|^3$, with $0<\gamma\le1$. Define
\[
 A_k=(2k+1)\log_2(5k).
\]
Then, for every $0<\eta<1/2$, an order-$k$ Freiman restriction satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:bsg-extraction}
 |B'|\ge (1-\eta)\,2^{-33A_k}\eta^{9A_k}
                  \gamma^{1/2+4A_k}|B|.
\end{equation}
If the target has no nonzero finite-order elements of even order, one may instead take $A_k=(2k+1)\log_3(7k)$. It is enough that all defects of the original graph have the odd-order property.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply \eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:reiher-schoen-input} to $\Gamma$. Its subset is still a graph, now over some $B_1$. Apply Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:59:cor:doubling} with $C=2^{33}\eta^{-9}\gamma^{-4}$ and multiply the retained fractions. Defects of a restricted graph form a subset of the original defect set, so the odd-order condition is inherited.
\end{proof}

For example, fixing $\eta=1/4$ writes the universal factor as
\[
 \frac34\,2^{-51A_k}\gamma^{1/2+4A_k}.
\]
This gives a fully explicit general-target analogue of the energy-to-Freiman step. It should not be described as a new record for Balog--Szemer\'edi--Gowers or as uniformly stronger than the project’s specialized prime-cyclic Corollary~7.6 refinements.

\subsection{Every symmetric forbidden set is a graph defect set}
\label{gsr:en:59:sec:realizability}

The sharp separation examples are not excluded by requiring the
forbidden set to arise from a graph. In fact, arbitrary symmetric
forbidden sets admit the following exact realization. The construction
also shows why sharp character rank does not establish sharp retained
mass.

\begin{theorem}[Exact realization with prescribed Freiman order]
\label{gsr:en:59:thm:realizability}\label{gsr:en:59:prop:realizable}
Let $H$ be an abelian group, let $F\subset H\setminus\{0\}$ be finite,
nonempty and symmetric, and let $q=|F/\{\pm1\}|$. For each $k\ge2$ there
are an abelian group $G$, a set $B\subset G$ of size $2kq$, and a map
$\phi:B\to H$ whose graph $\Gamma$ satisfies
\[
 \{h\ne0:(0,h)\in k\Gamma-k\Gamma\}=F.
\]
One may take $G=\Z^{(2k-1)q}$, or the finite group
$G=C_L^{(2k-1)q}$ for any integer $L>2k$.

There is a partition $B=B_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup B_q$, with $|B_i|=2k$,
such that a subset $B'\subset B$ supports an exact Freiman restriction
of order $k$ if and only if it omits at least one point of every $B_i$.
Consequently the largest such subset has size $(2k-1)q$. For arbitrary
nonnegative weights $w$ on $B$, the largest retained weight is exactly
\[
 w(B)-\sum_{i=1}^q\min_{x\in B_i}w(x).
\]
Moreover, $\phi$ itself is a Freiman homomorphism of every order
$1\le j<k$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Choose sign representatives $f_1,\ldots,f_q$ of $F$ and a basis
$e_{i,j}$ of $\Z^{(2k-1)q}$, indexed by $1\le i\le q$,
$1\le j\le2k-1$. In the $i$th coordinate block put
\[
 v_{i,j}=e_{i,j}\quad(1\le j<2k),\qquad
 v_{i,2k}=\sum_{j=1}^k e_{i,j}
                -\sum_{j=k+1}^{2k-1}e_{i,j}.
\]
These $2kq$ vectors are distinct. Set $B_i=\{v_{i,1},\ldots,v_{i,2k}\}$,
put $\phi(v_{i,1})=f_i$, and give all other vertices label zero. The
relation
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^k v_{i,j}=\sum_{j=k+1}^{2k}v_{i,j}
\]
has label defect $f_i$, so every element of $F$ occurs.

Conversely, consider an equality of two sums of $k$ vertices and let
$a_{i,j}$ be the multiplicity on the left minus the multiplicity on
the right. Then $\sum_{i,j}\max(a_{i,j},0)\le k$. Coordinate comparison
shows that the only integer relations in block $i$ are
\[
 (a_{i,1},\ldots,a_{i,2k})
   =t_i(\underbrace{1,\ldots,1}_{k},
         \underbrace{-1,\ldots,-1}_{k})
 \qquad(t_i\in\Z).
\]
Hence $k\sum_i|t_i|\le k$. Either every $t_i$ is zero, in which case
the two multisets are identical, or exactly one $t_i$ equals $1$ or
$-1$. In the latter case the relation uses every vertex of its block,
once on the prescribed side, and has defect $f_i$ or $-f_i$.
This proves the asserted defect set and the necessary and sufficient
condition on $B'$. Omitting a vertex of minimum weight from each block
gives the weighted optimum. Replacing the two sums of length $k$ by
sums of length $j<k$ gives $k\sum_i|t_i|\le j$, forcing every $t_i=0$.

For the finite-domain version reduce the vectors modulo $L$. They
remain distinct because their coordinate differences have absolute
value at most $2<L$. In a relation between two $k$-term sums, each
coordinate of the corresponding integer sum is
$a_{i,j}+a_{i,2k}$ or $a_{i,j}-a_{i,2k}$, and has absolute value at
most $2k<L$. If that coordinate vanishes modulo $L$, it therefore
vanishes as an integer. Thus the relations relevant to the proof are
unchanged, and all conclusions persist.
\end{proof}

For $F=\varnothing$, a one-point constant graph provides a realization.
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:59:thm:realizability} upgrades all the every-$q$ separation-rank
obstructions to graph-defect examples at any prescribed $k\ge2$.
Nevertheless their optimal retained proportion is
$1-1/(2k)$, independently of $F$.

The construction also has an explicit additive cost. Writing $M=2kq$,
\[
 |\Gamma-\Gamma|=M(M-1)+1,
 \qquad \frac{|\Gamma-\Gamma|}{|\Gamma|}=M-1+\frac1M.
\]
Indeed, for $k>2$ every two-term relation in the domain is trivial.
For $k=2$, the only nontrivial two-term relations have nonzero label
defects and therefore are not relations in $\Gamma$. Thus every
nonzero ordered difference of graph points has a unique representation;
the zero difference accounts for the remaining one element. Bare graph
realizability imposes no restriction on $F$, but requiring small
difference doubling is a substantive additional condition.

\section[{One-character restrictions and lonely runners\srctag{59}}]{One-character restrictions and lonely runners}\label{gsr:en:59:sec:d6}
\srcnote{59}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:en:59:sec:one-character}

The logarithmic rank is necessary in general because low-order torsion can force a common kernel. When the defects have infinite order, the relevant small-ball probabilities are continuous and a single character is enough for a useful linear bound.

\begin{proposition}[A one-character bound from the actual orders]\label{gsr:en:59:prop:one-character}
Let $F$ have $q\ge1$ sign representatives $D$ and put
\[
 T(F)=\sum_{\substack{f\in D\\\ord(f)<\infty}}\frac1{\ord(f)}.
\]
If $T(F)<1$, then $F$ can be separated by one character at radius
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:torsion-budget-radius}
 \theta=\frac{1-T(F)}{2q}.
\end{equation}
Consequently, for a graph with this defect set, a weighted order-$k$ Freiman restriction retains at least
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:torsion-budget-retention}
 \frac{1-T(F)}{2kq}\,w(B).
\end{equation}
In particular, when every defect has infinite order, the fraction is $1/(2kq)$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For finite $n$ and $0<\theta<1/2$,
\[
 \beta_n(\theta)=\frac{2\lceil n\theta\rceil-1}{n}
 <2\theta+\frac1n.
\]
If at least one finite-order defect occurs, the sum of the survival probabilities at \eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:torsion-budget-radius} is strictly less than $2q\theta+T(F)=1$. The profile theorem gives separation.

If all orders are infinite and $q\ge2$, the radius $1/(2q)$ makes the sum exactly one, so the endpoint assertion of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:59:thm:profile} applies. If $q=1$, define a character on the infinite cyclic subgroup generated by its representative by sending that representative to $1/2$, then extend it. This separate argument is needed because the open radius-$1/2$ arc has full Haar measure on the circle. In every case, apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:59:thm:freiman-extraction}.
\end{proof}

This is a sufficient torsion budget, not an exact criterion for one-character separation. It is useful when finite-order defects have large orders or are sparse. The exact profile in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:59:thm:profile} is normally stronger than the estimate $2\theta+1/n$ used to obtain this compact formula.

\subsection{An exact connection to the lonely runner constant}

For $q\ge1$, define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:lonely-constant}
 \Lambda(q)=\inf_{\substack{v_1,\ldots,v_q\in\Z_{>0}\\\text{distinct}}}
       \max_{t\in\T}\min_{1\le i\le q}\distT{tv_i}.
\end{equation}
The integer lonely runner conjecture is the assertion $\Lambda(q)=1/(q+1)$ for every $q$; see \cite{perarnauserrarunner}. We need no assumption of that conjecture.

\begin{proposition}[Transfer of the lonely runner constant]\label{gsr:en:59:prop:lonely-runner}
If every element of $F$ has infinite order, then one character separates $F$ at radius $\Lambda(q)$. A weighted Freiman restriction therefore retains at least $\Lambda(q)w(B)/k$. Conversely, a uniform one-character assertion at radius $1/(q+1)$ for all such sets would imply the integer lonely runner conjecture.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Work in a finitely generated subgroup $H_0$ containing $F$ and the graph labels. Write $H_0/T_0\cong\Z^d$, where $T_0$ is its finite torsion subgroup. Every defect has a nonzero image in this quotient. Choose an integer linear functional on $\Z^d$ which is nonzero on every such image and distinguishes the distinct images up to sign. This amounts to avoiding finitely many proper rational hyperplanes; such an integer functional exists, for example by evaluating at $(1,M,\ldots,M^{d-1})$ for an integer $M$ outside the finitely many roots of the resulting nonzero polynomials.

The absolute values of the projected defects give $r\le q$ distinct positive integer speeds. Some $t\in\T$ realizes a minimum distance at least $\Lambda(r)\ge\Lambda(q)$. The maximum for a fixed finite set of speeds is attained by compactness; monotonicity follows by adjoining extra speeds. Composing the functional with multiplication by $t$ gives the required character. Elements whose free images coincide or are opposite produce the same speed and cause no problem, even if the original elements differ by torsion.

For the converse take $H=\Z$ and $F=\{\pm v_1,\ldots,\pm v_q\}$. Every character has the form $n\mapsto tn$, so the asserted separation is exactly the lower bound in the conjecture. The reverse inequality $\Lambda(q)\le1/(q+1)$ follows from speeds $1,2,\ldots,q$: among $0,t,\ldots,qt$ two points have circular distance at most $1/(q+1)$, whereas $t=1/(q+1)$ attains that value.
\end{proof}

The elementary argument above gives $\Lambda(q)\ge1/(2q)$. It is not the strongest known general lower bound. Bedert's Theorem~1.3 gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:bedert}
 \Lambda(q)\ge\frac1{2q}+q^{-5/3-o(1)}
 \qquad(q\to\infty)
\end{equation}
in the cited preprint \cite{bedertrunner}. Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:59:prop:lonely-runner} immediately transfers that additional term, divided by $k$, to infinite-order graph defects. The improvement in \eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:bedert} is Bedert's, and the asymptotic $o(1)$ is not an explicit finite-$q$ constant supplied by this article.

\subsection{An explicit Riesz-product refinement under dissociativity}

There is a complementary route for a structurally restricted forbidden set. The following statement extends the elementary Riesz-product calculation in Bedert's Lemma~4.1 \cite{bedertrunner} to arbitrary abelian groups and to a specified dissociativity order. Its method is classical; the explicit formula is useful as a reusable interface.

\begin{definition}
A finite set $D$ is $\ell$-dissociated, where $\ell\ge1$ is an integer, if every relation
\[
 \sum_{f\in D}a_ff=0,\qquad a_f\in\{-\ell,\ldots,\ell\},
\]
has all coefficients zero.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[A quantitative dissociated radius]\label{gsr:en:59:prop:riesz}
Let $D$ be $\ell$-dissociated with $q=|D|\ge1$, and let $F=D\cup(-D)$. Put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:59:eq:riesz-radius}
 c_\ell=2^{-\ell}\binom{2\ell}{\ell},\qquad
 \delta_{\ell,q}=\frac1{2\pi}
 \arccos\left(1-\left(\frac{c_\ell}{q}\right)^{1/\ell}\right).
\end{equation}
One character separates $F$ at radius $\delta_{\ell,q}$. For graph defects, the resulting weighted Freiman restriction retains $\delta_{\ell,q}w(B)/k$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
On the compact dual of a finitely generated subgroup containing $D$, set
\[
 R(\chi)=\prod_{f\in D}
       \frac{(1-\cos(2\pi\chi(f)))^\ell}{c_\ell}.
\]
The constant term of $(1-\cos(2\pi x))^\ell$ is $c_\ell$. To verify it, write $z=e^{2\pi ix}$ and use
\[
 (1-\cos(2\pi x))^\ell
 =2^{-\ell}(1-z)^\ell(1-z^{-1})^\ell;
\]
the constant coefficient is $2^{-\ell}\sum_{j=0}^\ell\binom\ell j^2=c_\ell$.
Every frequency in the product has coefficients between $-\ell$ and $\ell$ on $D$. Dissociativity and character orthogonality imply that $R$, and every product obtained by deleting one factor, has integral one. This remains valid with torsion because the stated dissociativity excludes precisely the relevant zero-frequency aliases.

Let $\delta=\max_\chi\min_{f\in D}\distT{\chi(f)}$, whose maximum exists by compactness. At every character, some $f$ has distance at most $\delta$. Multiply that covering inequality by $R\ge0$ and integrate. On the event $\distT{\chi(f)}\le\delta$, its own factor is at most $(1-\cos(2\pi\delta))^\ell/c_\ell$. Removing that factor and integrating the remaining product gives
\[
 1\le q\,\frac{(1-\cos(2\pi\delta))^\ell}{c_\ell}.
\]
Solving proves \eqref{gsr:en:59:eq:riesz-radius}. The expression lies in the domain of $\arccos$: $c_\ell\le2^\ell$ and $q\ge1$. Localization gives the last assertion.
\end{proof}

For $\ell=1$, this is
\[
 \delta_{1,q}=\frac1{2\pi}\arccos(1-1/q)
 \sim\frac1{\pi\sqrt{2q}}.
\]
It substantially exceeds the elementary $1/(2q)$ radius from the infinite-order case when the full representative set is dissociated and $q$ is large. The hypothesis on the entire set is essential: finding a large dissociated subset does not by itself separate the remaining defects. Adapting the argument to partial dissociativity is a distinct research problem.

\section{Source~54's chapter: one quadratic phase at Proposition~8.1 \wtag}\label{gsr:en:sec:singlephase}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the tenth write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next eight sections are source~54's Sections~2--9, the report's first chapter on Gowers's Section~8. Source~54's introduction is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:54:sec:d1}; its integration notes and questions are in Part~V.

\emph{What is proved.} For odd $N$, $f=\one_A-\delta$, any nonempty $P\subseteq\Z/N\Z$ of size $T$ and the hypothesis $\sum_{h\in P}|D_h(\lambda h+\mu)|^2\ge\beta N^2T$ of Proposition~8.1, \emph{one} polynomial $\psi(z)=2^{-1}\lambda z^2+rz$ satisfies $\sum_s|\sum_{z\in P+s}f(z)\e(-\psi(z)/N)|\ge\beta NT/(B\sigma)\ge(27/4)\beta NT$, $\sigma=\delta(1-\delta)$, $B=\max(\delta,1-\delta)$, where Gowers's translate-dependent phases give $1/\sqrt2$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:54:thm:main}). The source is an exact mixed weighted Fourier factorization with coefficient one, optimal (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:54:thm:factor}); quadratic refinements extend it to every finite abelian group, and even order needs doubled roots (Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:54:prop:refine}, Example~\ref{gsr:en:54:ex:even}). The offset energy $\En_\eta(g)$ is at most $c_m\sigma^2$ with $c_m=1,1/2,1/3,1/4$ by the order $m$ of the offset, with all equality cases (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:54:thm:ceilings}), and near-extremizers are within $K_m\sqrt\sigma\varepsilon^{1/2}$ ($m\le4$) or $3\sqrt\sigma\varepsilon^{1/4}$ ($m\ge5$) of an extremizer, both exponents optimal (Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:54:thm:short-stability}, \ref{gsr:en:54:thm:cycle-stability}, Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:54:prop:obstruction}); several intercepts are governed by the clique number (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:54:thm:clique}, through the Motzkin--Straus theorem, credited). The constant $27/4$ is the uniform consequence of the amplitude estimate, not an optimum over balanced indicators, and no lower bound on each translate is claimed, as source~54 says.

\emph{Relation to the formal statements} (checked at HEAD \texttt{fe7165a3c}). \file{proposition_8_1} (\file{Sections08\_09.lean}, line~29) has the exact companion \file{proposition_8_1_holds} (\file{Proofs08QuadraticBias.lean}, line~1069), for odd $N$ and a progression $P$; Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:54:thm:main} implies it (note after the theorem) and is not formalized.
