\section[{An exact mixed and weighted Fourier factorization\srctag{54}}]{An exact mixed and weighted Fourier factorization}\label{gsr:en:54:sec:d2}
\srcnote{54}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:en:54:sec:factor}

\subsection{Conventions and definitions}
All groups in the article are finite and nonempty. Write $n=|G|$ and
$\E_x=n^{-1}\sum_{x\in G}$. For $u:G\to\C$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:Fourier}
 \widehat u(\xi)=\E_xu(x)\e(-\xi(x)),\quad
 u(x)=\sum_{\xi\in\widehat G}\widehat u(\xi)\e(\xi(x)),\quad
 \sum_\xi|\widehat u(\xi)|^2=\norm u_2^2.
\end{equation}
The Fourier sums are not normalized a second time.

Let $u,v:G\to\C$, $\eta\in\widehat G$, and $w:G\to[0,\infty)$.
Write $T=\sum_h w(h)$. Define
\begin{align}
 A(h)&=A_\eta(u,v)(h)
   =\E_xu(x+h)\overline{v(x)}\e(-\eta(x)),\label{gsr:en:54:eq:mixed-A}\\
 a_\xi&=\widehat u(\xi)\overline{\widehat v(\xi-\eta)},
 &\Ov_\eta(u,v)&=\sum_\xi|a_\xi|,\label{gsr:en:54:eq:overlap}\\
 \Win_{\xi,w}u(s)&=\sum_hw(h)u(s+h)\e(-\xi(h)),\label{gsr:en:54:eq:window}\\
 \Sc_{\xi,w}(u,v)&=\E_s|v(s)|\,|\Win_{\xi,w}u(s)|,
 &H&=\max_\xi\Sc_{\xi,w}(u,v),\label{gsr:en:54:eq:score}\\
 \En_{\eta,w}(u,v)&=\sum_hw(h)|A(h)|^2.\label{gsr:en:54:eq:weighted-energy}
\end{align}
In the auto-correlation case we abbreviate $u=v=g$.

\begin{lemma}[The two exact identities]\label{gsr:en:54:lem:factor}
For every $h\in G$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:A-expand}
 A(h)=\sum_\xi a_\xi\e(\xi(h)).
\end{equation}
If
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:K}
 K_\xi=\E_s\overline{v(s)}\e(-\eta(s))\Win_{\xi,w}u(s),
\end{equation}
then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:energy-factor}
 \En_{\eta,w}(u,v)=\sum_\xi\overline{a_\xi}K_\xi.
\end{equation}
The right side of \eqref{gsr:en:54:eq:energy-factor} is real and nonnegative.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Expand $u(x+h)$ and $\overline{v(x)}$ using \eqref{gsr:en:54:eq:Fourier}.
Character orthogonality in $x$ leaves exactly the pairs of frequencies
$(\xi,\xi-\eta)$, proving \eqref{gsr:en:54:eq:A-expand}. Also,
\[
 K_\xi=\sum_hw(h)A(h)\e(-\xi(h)).
\]
Substituting this expression and interchanging the finite sums gives
\[
 \sum_\xi\overline{a_\xi}K_\xi
 =\sum_hw(h)A(h)\overline{\sum_\xi a_\xi\e(\xi(h))}
 =\sum_hw(h)|A(h)|^2.
\]
There are no convergence or exchange-of-limits issues.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Common-frequency extraction]\label{gsr:en:54:thm:factor}
With the preceding notation,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:extraction}
 \En_{\eta,w}(u,v)
 \leq\Ov_\eta(u,v)\max_\xi\Sc_{\xi,w}(u,v),\qquad
 \Ov_\eta(u,v)\leq\norm u_2\norm v_2.
\end{equation}
The coefficient one in the first inequality is optimal. If $\Ov_\eta(u,v)>0$,
there is a single frequency $\xi$ with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:single-score}
 \E_s|v(s)|\,|\Win_{\xi,w}u(s)|
 \geq\frac{\En_{\eta,w}(u,v)}{\Ov_\eta(u,v)}.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:54:lem:factor}, the triangle inequality, and
$|K_\xi|\leq\Sc_{\xi,w}(u,v)$,
\[
 \En_{\eta,w}(u,v)
 \leq\sum_\xi|a_\xi|\Sc_{\xi,w}(u,v)
 \leq\Ov_\eta(u,v)H.
\]
Cauchy--Schwarz in the dual group and Parseval give the second inequality
in \eqref{gsr:en:54:eq:extraction}. A maximizer exists because the dual group is
finite. To see optimality, take $u=v=c\e(\xi_0(\cdot))$ with $c\ne0$
and $\eta=0$. Then $\En=|c|^4T$, $\Ov=|c|^2$, and $H=|c|^2T$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why the phase need not depend on the translate]
The order of operations matters. We first sum the nonnegative quantities
$|a_\xi|\Sc_{\xi,w}$ over frequencies, and only then choose a frequency.
The average over $s$ is already inside $\Sc_{\xi,w}$. Replacing this by a
pointwise maximum in $s$ would give the weaker conclusion of a different
frequency on each translate.
\end{remark}

\subsection{What spectral overlap retains}
For $u=v=g$ and $\sigma=\norm g_2^2>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:Hellinger-overlap}
 \frac{\Ov_\eta(g)}{\sigma}
 =\sum_\xi\sqrt{p_\xi p_{\xi-\eta}},\qquad
 p_\xi=\frac{|\widehat g(\xi)|^2}{\sigma}.
\end{equation}
This is the affinity of a probability distribution and its translate.
In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:affinity-deficit}
 1-\frac{\Ov_\eta(g)}{\sigma}
 =\frac12\sum_\xi(\sqrt{p_\xi}-\sqrt{p_{\xi-\eta}})^2.
\end{equation}
The inequality $\Ov_\eta(g)\leq\sigma$ is an equality precisely when
$p_\xi=p_{\xi-\eta}$ for every $\xi$. It is strict whenever the power
spectrum is not invariant under the offset. A small positive overlap
improves the extraction denominator; a zero overlap means $A\equiv0$
and hence zero input energy. There is no division by zero in any
positive-energy application.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Quadratic untwisting and the strengthened proposition\srctag{54}}]{Quadratic untwisting and the strengthened proposition}\label{gsr:en:54:sec:d3}
\srcnote{54}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:en:54:sec:quadratic}

\subsection{The sign and normalization calculation}
Return temporarily to $G=\Z/N\Z$ with $N$ odd. Interpret
$2^{-1}\lambda$ in $\Z/N\Z$, and put
\[
 q(x)=2^{-1}\lambda x^2/N\pmod1,\qquad
 g(x)=f(x)\e(-q(x)),\qquad \eta(x)=\mu x/N.
\]
The defining property of $q$ is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:quad-difference}
 q(x+h)-q(x)-q(h)=\lambda hx/N\pmod1.
\end{equation}
In \eqref{gsr:fm:54:eq:gowers-coeff}, set $x=y+h$ and use
\eqref{gsr:en:54:eq:quad-difference}. The result is the exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:untwist-sign}
 N^{-1}D_h(\lambda h+\mu)
 =\e(-q(h)-\mu h/N)A_\eta(g)(h).
\end{equation}
This calculation is useful because the sign of $h$ in the original
backward derivative need not agree with a forward-difference convention.
The harmless factor on the right has absolute value one.

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:54:thm:main}]
Choose $w=\one_P$. By \eqref{gsr:en:54:eq:untwist-sign}, the hypothesis says
$\En_{\eta,w}(g)\geq\beta T$. Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:54:thm:factor} provides one
frequency $r$ with
\[
 \E_s|g(s)|\,|\Win_{r,w}g(s)|
 \geq\beta T/\Ov_\eta(g)\geq\beta T/\sigma.
\]
Since $|g(s)|=|f(s)|$ and translation $h\mapsto z=s+h$ is a bijection,
\[
 |\Win_{r,w}g(s)|
 =\left|\sum_{z\in P+s}f(z)\e(-(2^{-1}\lambda z^2+rz)/N)\right|.
\]
Multiplication by $N$ proves \eqref{gsr:fm:54:eq:main-weighted}; then
$|f(s)|\leq B$ proves the first inequality in
\eqref{gsr:fm:54:eq:main-unweighted}. Finally let $t=\min(\delta,1-\delta)$.
Then $B\sigma=t(1-t)^2$ for $0<t\leq1/2$. Its derivative is
$(1-t)(1-3t)$, so its maximum is $4/27$, attained at $t=1/3$.
This proves the final inequality.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Sharp and non-sharp assertions]
Coefficient one is sharp in the mixed extraction theorem. The factor
$27/4$ is the exact uniform consequence of the displayed amplitude
estimate, not a proved optimum over all balanced indicators. The
constant-one extremizer used in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:54:thm:factor} is generally not
a balanced indicator on an odd-order group. Those distinctions prevent
an unwarranted sharpness claim.
\end{remark}

The new unweighted coefficient tends to $8$ as the density tends to
$1/2$ (exact half-density is impossible for odd $N$). At density
$1/3$ or $2/3$, it is $27/4$. The gain is accompanied by a strictly
stronger common-polynomial conclusion, not merely by a numerical change.
No lower bound on $N$ is required beyond the stated algebraic hypotheses.

\subsection{The form for arbitrary weights and bounded functions}
Let $f$ now be any nonzero complex function, with
$B=\norm f_\infty$, $\sigma=\norm f_2^2$, and $a=\norm f_1$.
Assume $T>0$ and $\En_{\eta,w}(g)>0$, so that
$\Ov_\eta(g)>0$. The same calculation gives, for one common phase,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:weighted-general}
 \E_s|f(s)|F(s)\geq\frac{\En_{\eta,w}(g)}{\Ov_\eta(g)},\qquad
 \E_sF(s)\geq\frac{\En_{\eta,w}(g)}{B\Ov_\eta(g)},
\end{equation}
where
\[
 F(s)=\left|\sum_hw(h)f(s+h)\e(-q(s+h)-\xi(s+h))\right|.
\]
In particular, at least one translate has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:max-translate}
 \frac{F(s)}{T}\geq
 \frac{\En_{\eta,w}(g)}{Ta\Ov_\eta(g)}.
\end{equation}
For a balanced indicator, $a=2\sigma$, so an energy lower bound
$\beta T$ yields $F(s)/T\geq\beta/(2\sigma^2)$. This is an
existence statement for one translate, not an average bound of that size.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Every finite abelian group, including even order\srctag{54}}]{Every finite abelian group, including even order}\label{gsr:en:54:sec:d4}
\srcnote{54}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:en:54:sec:refinements}

\begin{definition}
A quadratic refinement of a symmetric biadditive map
$b:G\times G\to\T$ is a function $q:G\to\T$ with $q(0)=0$ and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:refinement}
 q(x+y)-q(x)-q(y)=b(x,y).
\end{equation}
Such a function is a quadratic phase polynomial in the additive-difference
sense. It need not be represented by a polynomial with coefficients in
$\Z/N\Z$, even when $G=\Z/N\Z$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Existence and the precise ambiguity]\label{gsr:en:54:prop:refine}
Every symmetric biadditive $b:G\times G\to\T$ has a quadratic
refinement. Any two refinements differ by a character of $G$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Write $G=\bigoplus_{i=1}^d\Z/n_i\Z$ with generators $e_i$, and let
$b_{ij}=b(e_i,e_j)$. Choose $a_i\in\T$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:ai}
 n_i a_i=-\binom{n_i}{2}b_{ii}.
\end{equation}
Such a choice exists because multiplication by $n_i$ on $\T$ is
surjective. For integer representatives $x_i$, set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:coordinate-q}
 q(x)=\sum_i\left(x_i a_i+\binom{x_i}{2}b_{ii}\right)
       +\sum_{i<j}x_ix_jb_{ij}.
\end{equation}
Changing $x_i$ to $x_i+n_i$ changes this expression by
\[
 n_i a_i+\binom{n_i}{2}b_{ii}+n_ix_i b_{ii}
       +\sum_{j\ne i}n_ix_jb_{ij}=0.
\]
Here $n_ib_{ij}=0$ follows from biadditivity. Thus $q$ is well-defined
on $G$. Expanding the binomial terms verifies
\eqref{gsr:en:54:eq:refinement}. Conversely, subtracting
\eqref{gsr:en:54:eq:refinement} for two refinements proves that their difference
is additive and hence a character.
\end{proof}

For $f:G\to\C$, define the derivative coefficient selected by $b$ and
an intercept $\eta\in\widehat G$ by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:B-energy}
 C_{b,\eta}(h)=\E_xf(x+h)\overline{f(x)}
                     \e(-b(h,x)-\eta(x)).
\end{equation}
If $q$ refines $b$ and $g=f\e(-q)$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:general-untwist}
 C_{b,\eta}(h)=\e(q(h))A_\eta(g)(h).
\end{equation}
Consequently Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:54:thm:factor} and
\eqref{gsr:en:54:eq:weighted-general} hold unchanged, with a single phase
$q+\xi$ on every translate. Symmetry is the correct hypothesis:
the polarization of any function satisfying \eqref{gsr:en:54:eq:refinement} is
necessarily symmetric. No assertion about nonsymmetric selectors is
being hidden in the untwisting step.

\subsection{The even cyclic case}
On $\Z/N\Z$ with $N$ even, the function
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:even-q}
 q(x)=\frac{\lambda x^2}{2N}\pmod1
\end{equation}
is well-defined, since
$q(x+N)-q(x)=\lambda x+\lambda N/2$ is an integer. It refines
$b(x,h)=\lambda xh/N$. When $\lambda$ is odd, it generally takes values
in $(2N)^{-1}\Z/\Z$ rather than in $N^{-1}\Z/\Z$.

\begin{example}[Why the target phase class must change]\label{gsr:en:54:ex:even}
Let $G=\Z/2\Z$ and $f(0)=1$, $f(1)=i$. Take
$q(0)=0$, $q(1)=1/4$, so $f=\e(q)$ and the untwisted function is
identically one. For $b(x,h)=xh/2$ and $\eta=0$, one has
$|C_{b,0}(h)|=1$ for both shifts. On the full group, extraction by $q$
has normalized correlation one.

Every polynomial over $\Z/2\Z$, however, induces an affine function
on its two points. Its exponential therefore has values proportional
to $(1,1)$ or $(1,-1)$. The largest normalized correlation with $f$ is
$|(1\pm i)/2|=1/\sqrt2$. Thus a constant-one strengthening for general
bounded functions cannot retain the classical $\Z/2\Z$ polynomial
phase class. The doubled-root refinement is essential.
\end{example}

Changing the refinement $q$ changes it by a character and merely
reindexes the maximizing frequency $\xi$. Thus the available family of
common phases is intrinsic to $b$.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Exact global offset ceilings and equality cases\srctag{54}}]{Exact global offset ceilings and equality cases}\label{gsr:en:54:sec:d5}
\srcnote{54}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:en:54:sec:ceilings}

\begin{lemma}[Power-spectrum identity]\label{gsr:en:54:lem:power}
For every $g:G\to\C$ and $\eta\in\widehat G$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:global-power}
 \En_\eta(g)=\sum_\xi
            |\widehat g(\xi)|^2|\widehat g(\xi-\eta)|^2.
\end{equation}
In particular $\En_\eta(g)=\En_{-\eta}(g)$, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:moyal}
 \sum_{\eta\in\widehat G}\En_\eta(g)=\norm g_2^4.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Apply Parseval in $h$ to \eqref{gsr:en:54:eq:A-expand} with $u=v=g$.
The symmetry follows by reindexing $\xi$. Summing over all $\eta$
factors the resulting double sum into two copies of
$\sum_\xi|\widehat g(\xi)|^2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 54--59]
\emph{Relation to source~31.} The function $(h,\eta)\mapsto|A_\eta(g)(h)|^2/\sigma^2$ is source~31's phase-space function $q_f$ (with $f=g/\sqrt\sigma$; Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:endpoint}), and \eqref{gsr:en:54:eq:global-power} is its sum over $h$ at the fixed frequency $\eta$; summing also over $\eta$ gives \eqref{gsr:en:54:eq:moyal} and source~31's total-mass identity in Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:31:lem:moyal}. Source~54 does not cite source~31 (note in Section~\ref{gsr:fm:54:sec:d1}).
\end{writenote}

We will need an explicit triangle-free graph certificate. Besides
proving the ceiling, it will select the four frequencies from which the
stability theorem is obtained.

\begin{lemma}[A weighted triangle-free certificate]\label{gsr:en:54:lem:TF}
Let $\Gamma$ be a finite simple triangle-free graph. Assign probabilities
$p_v\geq0$ to its vertices, with $\sum_vp_v=1$, and put
\[
 F=\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E(\Gamma)}p_up_v,\qquad
 d_v=\sum_{u:\{u,v\}\in E(\Gamma)}p_u.
\]
Then $F\leq1/4$. More precisely,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:TF-identity}
 F-4F^2=
 \sum_{\{u,v\}\in E}p_up_v(1-d_u-d_v)
 +\left(\sum_vp_vd_v^2-(2F)^2\right),
\end{equation}
and both terms on the right are nonnegative. If $F>0$, some edge with
$p_up_v>0$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:edge-capture}
 1-d_u-d_v\leq1-4F.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The neighborhoods of the endpoints of an edge are disjoint because
there are no triangles. Therefore $d_u+d_v\leq1$ on every edge.
Furthermore,
\[
 \sum_vp_vd_v=2F,\qquad
 \sum_{\{u,v\}\in E}p_up_v(d_u+d_v)=\sum_vp_vd_v^2.
\]
These equations give \eqref{gsr:en:54:eq:TF-identity}; the second term is a
variance. Hence $F-4F^2\geq0$ and $F\leq1/4$. The average of
$1-d_u-d_v$ over edges with weights $p_up_v/F$ is at most $1-4F$,
which proves \eqref{gsr:en:54:eq:edge-capture}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The exact extremizers]\label{gsr:en:54:thm:ceilings}
Let $g\ne0$, $\sigma=\norm g_2^2$, $m=\ord(\eta)$, and
$p_\xi=|\widehat g(\xi)|^2/\sigma$. Then
$\En_\eta(g)\leq c_m\sigma^2$, with $c_m$ as in
\eqref{gsr:fm:54:eq:cm}. Equality is characterized by the following table.
In every row all unlisted frequencies have zero power, and the phases
of nonzero Fourier coefficients are arbitrary.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}clp{9.1cm}@{}}
\toprule
$m$ & $c_m$ & Power-spectrum description\\
\midrule
$1$ & $1$ & A single frequency has mass $1$.\\[3pt]
$2$ & $1/2$ & A single $\eta$-orbit has masses $1/2,1/2$.\\[3pt]
$3$ & $1/3$ & A single $\eta$-orbit has masses $1/3,1/3,1/3$.\\[3pt]
$4$ & $1/4$ & A single four-cycle carries all the mass; each of its two alternating pairs has total mass $1/2$.\\[3pt]
$\geq5$ & $1/4$ & For some $\xi_0$, the frequencies
$\xi_0-\eta,\xi_0,\xi_0+\eta$ carry masses
$a,1/2,1/2-a$, where $0\leq a\leq1/2$.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Translation by $\eta$ partitions $\widehat G$ into cycles of length
$m$. By Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:54:lem:power}, we must maximize
$\sum_\xi p_\xi p_{\xi-\eta}$.

If $m=1$, this is $\sum p_\xi^2\leq1$, with equality precisely for a
point mass. If $m=2$, a cycle with masses $a,b$ contributes $2ab$.
Writing $t=a+b$, one has $2ab\leq t^2/2$. Summing over cycles gives
at most $1/2$; equality requires one cycle and $a=b=1/2$.

For $m=3$, a cycle with masses $a,b,c$ contributes $ab+bc+ca$.
This is at most $(a+b+c)^2/3$, with equality when $a=b=c$.
Again all mass must belong to one cycle to attain $1/3$.

For $m\geq4$, the graph of these cycles is simple and triangle-free,
and each undirected edge appears once in the offset sum. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:54:lem:TF}
gives the upper bound $1/4$. If equality holds, choose an edge as in
\eqref{gsr:en:54:eq:edge-capture}. Its two neighborhoods carry all the mass.
When $m=4$, their union is one four-cycle. If its alternating-pair
masses are $U,V$, the energy is $UV$, so $U=V=1/2$.

When $m\geq5$, the union consists of four consecutive vertices,
inducing a path. Let their masses in path order be $a,b,c,d$.
Writing $U=a+c$ and $V=b+d$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:P4-factor}
 ab+bc+cd=UV-ad\leq\frac14.
\end{equation}
Equality forces $U=V=1/2$ and $ad=0$. Removing the zero endpoint
leaves a three-vertex star with center mass $1/2$. This gives the
last row of the table. Conversely every distribution in the table
attains the claimed bound by direct substitution.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
For general graphs, broad descriptions of every Motzkin--Straus
maximizer require care; erroneous classifications in earlier literature
have been corrected \cite{tangmotzkin}. The proof above does not appeal to
such a classification. It derives the equality cases directly from
the special cycle geometry.
\end{remark}

The constants remain optimal when one restricts to functions with
$\norm g_\infty\leq1$, provided the $L^2$ norm is not prescribed in
advance: construct a Fourier polynomial from a listed spectrum and
scale it by a sufficiently small nonzero constant. The ratio
$\En_\eta(g)/\norm g_2^4$ is unchanged. This does not prove optimality
for balanced indicators of a prescribed density.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Dimension-free stability and the fourth-root obstruction\srctag{54}}]{Dimension-free stability and the fourth-root obstruction}\label{gsr:en:54:sec:d6}
\srcnote{54}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:en:54:sec:stability}

\subsection{The cycle stability lemma}
\begin{theorem}[Recovery of a three-frequency star]\label{gsr:en:54:thm:cycle-stability}
Let $\Gamma$ be a disjoint union of cycles of a common length $m\geq5$.
Let $p$ be a probability distribution on its vertices and suppose
\[
 F=\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E}p_up_v\geq\frac14-\varepsilon,
 \qquad 0\leq\varepsilon\leq\frac1{16}.
\]
There is an extremal star distribution $q$ from the last row of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:54:thm:ceilings} for which
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:l1-star}
 \norm{p-q}_1\leq8\varepsilon+4\sqrt{3\varepsilon}.
\end{equation}
The exponent $1/2$ in this probability-distance estimate is optimal.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Since $F\geq3/16>0$, choose an edge using
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:54:lem:TF}. The union of the neighborhoods of its endpoints
is a four-vertex path $S$. Its outside mass $r$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:r-bound}
 r\leq1-4F\leq4\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
Write the masses on the path as $a,b,c,d$ in order; their sum is
$t=1-r$. Put $U=a+c$, $V=b+d$, and $D=|U-V|$.

The contribution of edges crossing from $S$ to its complement is at
most $rt$, simply by allowing every possible pair. By the
triangle-free bound applied to the outside distribution of total mass
$r$, its internal contribution is at most $r^2/4$. Consequently,
using \eqref{gsr:en:54:eq:P4-factor},
\begin{align}
 ad+\frac{D^2}{4}
 &=\frac{t^2}{4}-F+F_{\mathrm{outside}}\notag\\
 &\leq\frac{(1-r)^2}{4}-\left(\frac14-\varepsilon\right)
                 +r(1-r)+\frac{r^2}{4}\notag\\
 &=\varepsilon+\frac r2-\frac{r^2}{2}
 \leq3\varepsilon.\label{gsr:en:54:eq:ad-D}
\end{align}
Here $F_{\mathrm{outside}}$ includes both crossing and wholly outside
edges. It follows that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:endpoints}
 \min(a,d)\leq\sqrt{3\varepsilon},\qquad
 D\leq2\sqrt{3\varepsilon}.
\end{equation}

Suppose $a\leq d$; the other case is symmetric. Delete the outside
mass and the left endpoint. The retained star has center mass $c$
and total leaf mass $b+d$. Define $q$ to have center mass $1/2$
and distribute the remaining $1/2$ between the two leaves in the
same proportion as their old masses. If both old leaf masses vanish,
choose either leaf; the following distance calculation still holds.
Let $R=r+a$ be the total deleted mass. Then
\begin{align}
 \norm{p-q}_1
 &=R+|c-1/2|+|b+d-1/2|\notag\\
 &=R+\max\{R,|c-b-d|\}\notag\\
 &\leq R+\max\{R,D+a\}\notag\\
 &\leq2R+D\notag\\
 &\leq8\varepsilon+4\sqrt{3\varepsilon}.
 \label{gsr:en:54:eq:distance-calc}
\end{align}
The penultimate inequality uses $a\leq R$.
The optimality assertion is proved in Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:54:prop:obstruction}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{From powers to functions}
\begin{lemma}[Phase-preserving lifting]\label{gsr:en:54:lem:lifting}
Let $g\ne0$, $\sigma=\norm g_2^2$, and
$p_\xi=|\widehat g(\xi)|^2/\sigma$. For any probability distribution
$q$ on $\widehat G$, there is $g_q$ with Fourier powers $\sigma q$
for which
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:hellinger-lift}
 \norm{g-g_q}_2^2
 =\sigma\sum_\xi(\sqrt{p_\xi}-\sqrt{q_\xi})^2
 \leq\sigma\norm{p-q}_1.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Use the phase of $\widehat g(\xi)$ for the new coefficient
$\widehat g_q(\xi)=\sqrt{\sigma q_\xi}$ times that phase. If the old
coefficient vanishes, choose an arbitrary phase. Parseval gives the
identity. The inequality follows pointwise from
$(\sqrt a-\sqrt b)^2\leq|a-b|$ for $a,b\geq0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Fourth-root recovery]\label{gsr:en:54:cor:fourth-root}
If $m\geq5$ and
$\En_\eta(g)\geq(1/4-\varepsilon)\sigma^2$ with
$0\leq\varepsilon\leq1/16$, an exact extremizer $g_*$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:fourth-root}
 \norm{g-g_*}_2
 \leq\sqrt\sigma\sqrt{8\varepsilon+4\sqrt{3\varepsilon}}
 \leq3\sqrt\sigma\,\varepsilon^{1/4}.
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Combine Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:54:lem:power}, Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:54:thm:cycle-stability}, and
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:54:lem:lifting}. For the last inequality use
$8\varepsilon\leq2\sqrt\varepsilon$ and
$2+4\sqrt3<9$.
\end{proof}

The recovered function has the same $L^2$ norm as $g$. The proof does
not preserve an additional pointwise bound, a real-valued condition,
or the property of being a balanced indicator. Such preservation is
a separate problem and is not asserted here.

\begin{proposition}[The sharp obstruction]\label{gsr:en:54:prop:obstruction}
Fix any offset order $m\geq5$. For every $0<t\leq1/4$, there is a
function $g_t$ with $\norm{g_t}_2^2=\sigma$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:obstruction}
 \En_\eta(g_t)=\left(\frac14-t^2\right)\sigma^2,
 \qquad
 \inf_{g_*}\norm{g_t-g_*}_2\geq\sqrt\sigma\,t^{1/2},
\end{equation}
where the infimum is over all exact extremizers of the same norm.
The corresponding power distribution is at $\ell^1$ distance at least
$2t$ from every extremal power distribution. These examples may all
be chosen with $\norm{g_t}_\infty\leq1$ by fixing $\sigma=1/4$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Place the four consecutive Fourier powers
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:P4-example}
 \bigl(t,\,1/2-t,\,1/2-t,\,t\bigr)
\end{equation}
on one $\eta$-orbit and put zero elsewhere. The induced support is a
path, so its edge sum is
\[
 t(1/2-t)+(1/2-t)^2+t(1/2-t)=1/4-t^2.
\]
Every extremal star misses at least mass $t$ of this distribution:
a three-vertex star cannot contain all four consecutive vertices,
and every positive mass is at least $t$. A star centered at either
of the two internal vertices misses exactly one endpoint, so $t$
is the exact minimum omitted mass.

For functions, the omitted Fourier coefficients alone contribute at
least $\sigma t$ to squared $L^2$ distance, independent of their
phases and of any changes on the retained frequencies. For power
probabilities, deleting mass at least $t$ and restoring total mass
one costs at least $2t$ in $\ell^1$. Finally, choose Fourier
coefficients of magnitudes $\sqrt{\sigma p_\xi}$. Their absolute sum
is at most $2\sqrt\sigma$, by Cauchy--Schwarz on four frequencies.
Thus $\sigma=1/4$ ensures the desired pointwise bound.
\end{proof}

With $\varepsilon=t^2$, the lower bound is exactly of fourth-root
order. In particular, an $O(\varepsilon^{1/2})$ theorem for all
nonzero offsets is false, even for uniformly bounded functions on a
fixed cyclic group of order at least five.

\subsection{Orders at most four}
\begin{theorem}[Square-root recovery for short orbits]\label{gsr:en:54:thm:short-stability}
For $m\in\{1,2,3,4\}$, under the hypotheses of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:54:thm:overview-offset}, there is an exact extremizer of
norm $\sqrt\sigma$ satisfying the first line of
\eqref{gsr:fm:54:eq:overview-stability}.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Work with the power distribution $p$ and lift the construction by
preserving Fourier phases. All squared distances below are divided
by $\sigma$.

\emph{Order one.} Since $\sum p_\xi^2\geq1-\varepsilon$,
some $p_\xi\geq1-\varepsilon$. Lifting the point mass at that
frequency gives squared distance
$2-2\sqrt{p_\xi}\leq2\varepsilon$.

\emph{Order two.} Let $t_j$ denote orbit masses. The energy is at
most $\frac12\sum_jt_j^2$, hence a largest orbit has mass at least
$1-2\varepsilon$. Let $r\leq2\varepsilon$ be the outside mass and
$a,b$ the masses of the chosen pair. Outside orbits contribute at
most $r^2/2$, so
\[
 (a-b)^2=(1-r)^2-4ab\leq2\varepsilon-2r+2r^2\leq2\varepsilon.
\]
Replace $a,b$ by $1/2,1/2$. Using
$(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt y)^2\leq(x-y)^2/y$ for $y>0$, the inside squared
Hellinger distance is at most
\[
 2\bigl((a-1/2)^2+(b-1/2)^2\bigr)=r^2+(a-b)^2.
\]
Including the outside mass gives at most
$4\varepsilon+4\varepsilon^2\leq5\varepsilon$.

\emph{Order three.} A largest orbit has mass $t\geq1-3\varepsilon$;
put $r=1-t$. For its three masses $a_i$, let
$V=\sum_{i=1}^3(a_i-t/3)^2$. Its contribution is
$t^2/3-V/2$, while the other orbits contribute at most $r^2/3$.
The energy assumption gives $V\leq2\varepsilon$.
Replacing the three masses by $1/3$ has squared Hellinger cost at
most
\[
 r+3\sum_i(a_i-1/3)^2=r+3V+r^2
 \leq9\varepsilon+9\varepsilon^2\leq10\varepsilon.
\]

\emph{Order four.} Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:54:lem:TF} selects one four-cycle with
outside mass $r\leq4\varepsilon$. Let $U,V$ be its alternating-pair
masses. The outside energy is at most $r^2/4$, whence
\[
 (U-V)^2\leq4\varepsilon-2r+2r^2\leq4\varepsilon.
\]
Scale the two alternating-pair distributions to total mass $1/2$
each, preserving their internal proportions. The inside squared
Hellinger cost is
$(\sqrt U-1/\sqrt2)^2+(\sqrt V-1/\sqrt2)^2$, at most
$r^2+(U-V)^2$. With the outside mass, the total is at most
$8\varepsilon+16\varepsilon^2\leq9\varepsilon$.
These estimates give the four constants claimed.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Optimality of the short-orbit exponents]
\label{gsr:en:54:prop:short-sharp}
The exponent $1/2$ in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:54:thm:short-stability} cannot be
increased uniformly. For $m=1$ assume $|G|\geq2$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For $m=1$, the distribution $(1-t,t)$ has deficit
$2t-2t^2$ and every extremal point mass omits at least $t$, giving
$L^2$ distance at least $\sqrt{\sigma t}$.
For $m=2$, the pair $(1/2+t,1/2-t)$ has deficit $2t^2$.
The unique extremal powers on that orbit are $(1/2,1/2)$, and the
Hellinger distance is bounded below by a positive constant times
$|t|$ for small $t$.
For $m=3$, use $(1/3+t,1/3-t,1/3)$; the deficit is $t^2$ and the
same conclusion follows. For $m=4$, put masses $1/2+t,1/2-t$ on
one edge. The energy deficit is $t^2$, and every extremizer must
have total mass $1/2$ on each alternating pair. Cauchy--Schwarz on
each pair bounds the Hellinger distance below by that of the pair
totals, again a positive constant times $|t|$. Fourier phases can
be arbitrary, since choosing matching phases minimizes distance.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Several intercepts and the classical clique parameter\srctag{54}}]{Several intercepts and the classical clique parameter}\label{gsr:en:54:sec:d7}
\srcnote{54}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:en:54:sec:multi}
The single-offset problem has a particularly simple graph, but the
spectral identity accommodates more than one intercept without
additional analytic losses.

\begin{theorem}[Simultaneous offset energy]\label{gsr:en:54:thm:clique}
Let $S\subseteq\widehat G\setminus\{0\}$ satisfy $S=-S$.
Let $\Gamma_S$ be the simple graph on $\widehat G$ in which
$\xi,\zeta$ are adjacent exactly when $\xi-\zeta\in S$.
If its clique number is $\omega$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:clique-energy}
 \sum_{\eta\in S}\En_\eta(g)
 \leq\left(1-\frac1\omega\right)\norm g_2^4.
\end{equation}
The constant is best possible. For $S=\varnothing$, take $\omega=1$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $g\ne0$, Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:54:lem:power} writes the left side divided by
$\sigma^2$ as
\[
 2\sum_{\{\xi,\zeta\}\in E(\Gamma_S)}p_\xi p_\zeta.
\]
The classical Motzkin--Straus theorem \cite{motzkinstraus} says that the maximum
of this expression over probability distributions is $1-1/\omega$.
For completeness, its extremal-value argument is short. If two
nonadjacent vertices both have positive mass, redistribute their
combined mass entirely to whichever has the larger weighted
neighbor sum. The objective does not decrease, because it is
linear in this redistribution and there is no edge between the
two vertices. Repeating reduces the support to a clique. On a
clique of size $k\leq\omega$, the objective is
$1-\sum p_\xi^2\leq1-1/k\leq1-1/\omega$.
Uniform mass on a maximum clique attains equality, and it can be
realized as the normalized Fourier power spectrum of a function.
\end{proof}

Taking $S=\{\eta,-\eta\}$ recovers the nonzero-offset values in
\eqref{gsr:fm:54:eq:cm}, remembering that this set has one element if
$\ord(\eta)=2$. The equality classification for general $S$ is not
inferred from the support-reduction proof: existence of a
clique-supported maximizer does not imply that every maximizer
has clique support. The four-cycle row of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:54:thm:ceilings}
already demonstrates the distinction.

\begin{example}[A subgroup of intercepts]
If $H\leq\widehat G$ and $S=H\setminus\{0\}$, then $\Gamma_S$ is
a disjoint union of complete graphs on the cosets of $H$.
Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:54:eq:clique-energy} has constant $1-1/|H|$.
For $|H|>1$, equality means that the power spectrum is uniform on
one coset of $H$. Indeed, a coset of mass $t$ contributes at most
$(1-1/|H|)t^2$, with equality at equal masses, and summing forces
all the mass into one coset.
\end{example}

More generally, nonnegative symmetric weights $c_\eta=c_{-\eta}$
give the exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:weighted-graph}
 \sum_\eta c_\eta\En_\eta(g)
 =\sigma^2\sum_{\xi,\zeta}c_{\xi-\zeta}p_\xi p_\zeta.
\end{equation}
This turns any valid upper certificate for the finite quadratic
program on the right into a derivative-spectrum bound. No claim
is made that its value is always determined by an unweighted
clique number.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Localization, robustness, and many useful translates\srctag{54}}]{Localization, robustness, and many useful translates}\label{gsr:en:54:sec:d8}
\srcnote{54}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:en:54:sec:local}

\subsection{How a local hypothesis forces global structure}
Let $P\subseteq G$ have density $\rho=|P|/|G|>0$, and assume
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:local-input}
 \frac1{|P|}\sum_{h\in P}|A_\eta(g)(h)|^2\geq\beta.
\end{equation}
Positivity and the global ceiling give
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:local-ceiling}
 \rho\beta\leq\En_\eta(g)\leq c_m\sigma^2,
 \qquad
 \beta\leq\sigma^2\min\{1,c_m/\rho\}.
\end{equation}
The second bound also uses $|A_\eta(g)(h)|\leq\sigma$.
Thus, if $\rho\beta\geq(c_m-\varepsilon)\sigma^2$, the entire
function is close to the extremal Fourier family specified in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:54:thm:overview-offset}. This gives an explicit
local-to-global recovery criterion, with the same stability exponents.

\begin{corollary}[Certification that the intercept is zero]
\label{gsr:en:54:cor:zero-intercept}
In \eqref{gsr:en:54:eq:local-input}, the intercept must be zero if
$\rho\beta>\sigma^2/2$. If $|G|$ is odd, it suffices that
$\rho\beta>\sigma^2/3$. If $|G|$ is odd and $3\nmid|G|$, it
suffices that $\rho\beta>\sigma^2/4$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Every nonzero character has order at least two; on an odd-order
group it has odd order at least three; and in the last case its
order is at least five. Apply \eqref{gsr:fm:54:eq:cm}.
\end{proof}

On $\Z/p\Z$ with $p\geq5$ prime, this applies directly to the
intercept $\mu$ in the quadratic selector after untwisting. The
thresholds in the corollary are sharp as global $L^2$-normalized
statements when the corresponding character orders occur. They
are not claimed sharp for every prescribed proper subset $P$.

\begin{example}[The density factor cannot be discarded]
Take $g=\one_{\{0\}}$ on any group, let $P=\{0\}$, and choose
any nonzero character $\eta$. Then $\sigma=1/|G|$ and
$A_\eta(g)(0)=\sigma$. Thus the local ratio is
$\beta/\sigma^2=1$, despite the nonzero intercept. The global
energy is only $\sigma^2/|G|$. This bounded example rules out
applying the nonzero-offset ceiling directly to an arbitrary
local average without its coverage factor $\rho$.
\end{example}

For a weight $0\leq w\leq L$, the analogous bound is
$\En_{\eta,w}(g)\leq L|G|c_m\sigma^2$. Its effective coverage is
$T/(L|G|)$. This observation handles repeated or weighted shifts
without treating multiplicity as additional independent coverage.

\subsection{A complementary global correlation bound}
The local extraction does not lose a factor $\rho$, because it
keeps the correlation localized. A different conclusion follows
by paying that factor.
\begin{proposition}\label{gsr:en:54:prop:global-corr}
Under \eqref{gsr:en:54:eq:local-input}, some frequency $\xi$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:global-corr}
 |\widehat g(\xi)|\geq\sqrt{\rho\beta/\sigma}.
\end{equation}
For a quadratic untwisting $g=f\e(-q)$, this is a global
correlation of $f$ with the single phase $q+\xi$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
By \eqref{gsr:en:54:eq:global-power},
$\En_\eta(g)\leq\max_\xi|\widehat g(\xi)|^2\sum_\zeta
|\widehat g(\zeta-\eta)|^2
=\sigma\max_\xi|\widehat g(\xi)|^2$.
Now use $\En_\eta(g)\geq\rho\beta$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Noisy derivative data}
\begin{proposition}[An $L^2$-robust input]\label{gsr:en:54:prop:noisy}
Let $T=\sum w>0$. Suppose observations $\widetilde A(h)$ satisfy
\[
 \left(\frac1T\sum_hw(h)|\widetilde A(h)|^2\right)^{1/2}
 \geq\sqrt\beta,
 \qquad
 \left(\frac1T\sum_hw(h)|\widetilde A(h)-A_\eta(g)(h)|^2\right)^{1/2}
 \leq\zeta.
\]
Then every extraction conclusion holds with the effective energy
parameter (positive-energy denominators are used only when this is positive)
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:noise-beta}
 \beta_{\mathrm{eff}}=(\sqrt\beta-\zeta)_+^2.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The reverse triangle inequality in the weighted finite $L^2$ space
gives $\norm{A_\eta(g)}_{L^2(w/T)}\geq
(\sqrt\beta-\zeta)_+$. Squaring gives the required energy bound.
\end{proof}

This statement is about error in complex correlation data. It does
not assert that a small numerical error in a frequency label always
has a small effect; that requires a separate estimate translating
label error into correlation error. Likewise, an approximately
symmetric bilinear selector does not automatically have an exact
quadratic refinement.

For an erasure variant, if an observed collection has total weight
$T$ and the unusable shifts have weight at most $\theta T$, then
$|A_\eta(g)(h)|^2\leq\sigma^2$ shows that deleting them loses at
most $\theta\sigma^2T$ of true energy. Hence the effective lower
bound on the retained energy, still normalized by the original
$T$, is $(\beta-\theta\sigma^2)_+T$.

\subsection{Quantitative abundance for the chosen common phase}
Use the phase selected in \eqref{gsr:en:54:eq:weighted-general}, put
$Z(s)=F(s)/T$, and suppose $\En_{\eta,w}(g)\geq\beta T$.
Then $0\leq Z\leq B$ and $\E_s|f(s)|Z(s)\geq\beta/\Ov_\eta(g)$.
For $0\leq\tau<B$, let $S_\tau=\{s:Z(s)>\tau\}$. Splitting the
last average over $S_\tau$ and its complement gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:many-translates}
 \E_s|f(s)|\one_{S_\tau}(s)
 \geq\frac{(\beta/\Ov_\eta(g)-\tau\norm f_1)_+}{B-\tau},
 \qquad
 \frac{|S_\tau|}{|G|}
 \geq\frac{(\beta/\Ov_\eta(g)-\tau\norm f_1)_+}{B(B-\tau)}.
\end{equation}
This is an elementary capped-mean consequence, not a new general
selection inequality. Its useful feature here is that all selected
translates use the \emph{same} quadratic phase. For a balanced
indicator one may substitute $\norm f_1=2\sigma$ and
$\Ov_\eta(g)\leq\sigma$.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{An exact deficit and a constructive selector\srctag{54}}]{An exact deficit and a constructive selector}\label{gsr:en:54:sec:d9}
\srcnote{54}{Section 9}
\label{gsr:en:54:sec:algorithm}

\subsection{Where near equality can lose mass}
Keep the notation of Section~\ref{gsr:en:54:sec:factor}. Since
$|K_\xi|\leq\Sc_\xi\leq H$, the factorization yields the exact
nonnegative decomposition
\begin{align}
 \Ov H-\En
 &=\sum_\xi|a_\xi|(H-\Sc_\xi)
   +\sum_\xi\left(|a_\xi|\Sc_\xi
                 -\Re(\overline{a_\xi}K_\xi)\right).
 \label{gsr:en:54:eq:deficit}
\end{align}
There are two different losses. The first measures concentration
on frequencies with poor average window score. The second is
phase cancellation inside the corresponding correlations.

For $a_\xi\ne0$, set $\theta_\xi=a_\xi/|a_\xi|$ and
$Z_\xi(s)=\overline{v(s)}\e(-\eta(s))\Win_{\xi,w}u(s)$.
The second summand has the more explicit form
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:phase-deficit}
 |a_\xi|\E_s
 \left(|Z_\xi(s)|-\Re(\overline{\theta_\xi}Z_\xi(s))\right).
\end{equation}
Thus exact equality forces the nonzero $Z_\xi(s)$ to have the
required common argument whenever the corresponding spectral
weight is positive, in addition to maximal average window score.
Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:54:eq:deficit} is also a certificate for numerical or
formal implementations: no estimate is hidden between its two sides.

If $\Ov>0$, define $\pi_\xi=|a_\xi|/\Ov$. A random frequency
sampled from $\pi$ has expected score at least $\En/\Ov$.
If $H>0$ and $\En\geq(1-\varepsilon)\Ov H$, then for every
$0<\tau<1$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:54:eq:random-good}
 \pi\{\xi:\Sc_\xi<(1-\tau)H\}\leq\varepsilon/\tau.
\end{equation}
This is Markov's inequality applied to the first deficit term.
It is a useful robustness statement about extraction, separate
from the offset-energy stability theorem.

\subsection{Finite implementation}
A deterministic selector can be implemented as follows: compute
$\widehat u$ and $\widehat v$; form the products $a_\xi$; for each
frequency compute $\Win_{\xi,w}u$ and its score $\Sc_\xi$; retain
a maximizing frequency and report the values in
\eqref{gsr:en:54:eq:energy-factor} and \eqref{gsr:en:54:eq:deficit}. The group Fourier
transform and the chosen group representation are explicit input.

For $\Z/N\Z$, each window array is a cyclic correlation and can
be computed by FFT. Scanning all $N$ frequencies uses
$O(N^2\log N)$ arithmetic operations and $O(N)$ working memory
when arrays are streamed. This is an arithmetic-operation bound,
not an exact bit-complexity theorem for arbitrary complex inputs.
With exact cyclotomic data, comparisons of scores require certified
algebraic or interval arithmetic. The included implementation uses
floating point for Fourier regression tests and exact integer
arithmetic only for the graph certificates.

The stability selector for $m\geq5$ is particularly simple. Compute
neighbor masses $d_v$, choose an edge minimizing $1-d_u-d_v$ among
edges of positive weight, delete the smaller endpoint of its
four-vertex neighborhood path, and rebalance the resulting star.
All structural choices can be made from the power spectrum alone;
Fourier phases enter only when reconstructing the nearby function.

\section{Source~58's chapter: Lemma~9.3 on every cyclic group \wtag}\label{gsr:en:sec:torsionrestriction}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the tenth write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next ten sections are source~58's Sections~2--11, on the restriction step of Gowers's Lemma~9.3. \emph{Logically they continue the chapters of sources~17, 29 and~48} (Sections~\ref{gsr:en:sec:restriction}, \ref{gsr:en:sec:fixedfield} and~\ref{gsr:en:sec:derandomization}) and source~40's barrier (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:fejer}); they are printed here because no number printed earlier may move. Source~58's introduction is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:58:sec:d1}.

\emph{What is proved.} For every $N\ge1$, $B\subseteq\Z/N\Z$ with $b=|B|\ge(4/(\alpha\eta))^{54}$ and any map $\phi:B\to H$ to a finite abelian group with $\GGfiftyeight_{16}(B,\phi)\ge\alpha b^{15}$, some $B'\subseteq B$ has $\GGfiftyeight_{16}(B',\phi)\ge(1-\eta)\TT_{16}(B')$ and $\TT_{16}(B')\ge(\alpha\eta/4)^{54}b^{15}$ (\hyperref[gsr:fm:58:thm:A]{Theorem~A}); Gowers's exponent is $2^{19}$. It comes from an expectation theorem for amplified positive Fourier filters with explicit nonprincipal error $\tau_G(2D)(R_m^k-P^k)b^{m-2}$ and collision error $\binom m2R_2^kb^{m-2}$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:58:thm:expectation}), giving exponent $O(m\log m)$ for every balanced relation of length $m$ on every cyclic group (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:58:thm:polynomial}), arbitrary targets (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:58:cor:arbitrary-target}) and the quadruple input of Corollary~9.4 (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:58:cor:quadruples}). Within normalized nonnegative filters the leading principal cost is exactly $m\log m/(2\log a)$ when a discrepancy may have order $a$ (\hyperref[gsr:fm:58:thm:B]{Theorem~B}), the multi-layer counterpart of source~40's barrier. This answers source~17's composite-modulus question for one balanced relation (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:groups}). The exponent $54$ is a certified convenience, not optimal, and the prime-field exponents of sources~04 and~17 remain better there, as source~58 says.

\emph{Relation to the formal statements} (checked at HEAD \texttt{fe7165a3c}). \file{lemma_9_3} and \file{corollary_9_4} (\file{Sections08\_09.lean}, lines~77 and~91) have the exact companions \file{lemma_9_3_holds} and \file{corollary_9_4_holds} (\file{Proofs09Restriction.lean}, lines~376 and~416), on all moduli with an existential threshold and exponent $2^{19}$; source~58's counts are \file{additiveTupleCount}, \file{phiAdditiveTupleCount} and \file{GammaHomOfOrder} (\file{Definitions.lean}, lines~322, 327 and~334). Theorem~A implies \file{lemma_9_3} with $N_0=\lceil\beta^{-1}(4/(\alpha\eta))^{54}\rceil$ (Section~\ref{gsr:en:58:sec:d11}); it is not formalized.
