\section[{Counts, normalizations, and finite Fourier analysis\srctag{58}}]{Counts, normalizations, and finite Fourier analysis}\label{gsr:en:58:sec:d2}
\srcnote{58}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:en:58:sec:notation}

Fix $m=2r\ge4$ and put
\[
 \eps=(\underbrace{1,\ldots,1}_{r},
        \underbrace{-1,\ldots,-1}_{r}).
\]
Groups are written additively. For $B\subseteq G$ and $\phi:B\to H$,
define
\begin{align}
 \mathcal T_m(B)&=\{\mathbf x\in B^m:\sum_{i=1}^m\eps_i x_i=0\},\\
 \mathcal G_m(B,\phi)&=\{\mathbf x\in\mathcal T_m(B):
                       \sum_{i=1}^m\eps_i\phi(x_i)=0\}.
\end{align}
Their cardinalities are $\TT_m$ and $\GGfiftyeight_m$. The remaining tuples form
$\mathcal U_m$, with cardinality $\UU_m$. We call a tuple in
$\mathcal G_m$ \emph{respected} and one in $\mathcal U_m$ \emph{bad}.
The target discrepancy of a tuple is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:discrepancy}
 \delta(\mathbf x)=\sum_i\eps_i\phi(x_i)\in H.
\end{equation}
No injectivity hypothesis is placed on $\phi$.

\begin{lemma}[Free-variable and collision counts]\label{gsr:en:58:lem:counts}
For every finite abelian $G$ and $B\subseteq G$ of size $b$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:free-bound}
 \TT_m(B)\le b^{m-1}.
\end{equation}
The number of additive tuples with at least one repeated entry is at most
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:collision-count}
 \binom m2 b^{m-2}.
\end{equation}
Every bad tuple has at least two distinct entries.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The first $m-1$ entries determine the last, since its coefficient is a
unit $\pm1$. For the second assertion, fix a pair of positions $i<j$
that will be equal, and choose a position $h$ outside that pair. Choose
the $m-2$ entries in all positions except $j,h$; then $x_j=x_i$, and
the coefficient $\eps_h=\pm1$ determines $x_h$. At most $b^{m-2}$
tuples arise for this pair. Sum over the pairs, allowing overcounting.
Finally, if every entry equals $x$, both balanced sums of its image
equal $r\phi(x)$, so the tuple is respected.
\end{proof}

The group of characters $G\to\T=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ is denoted
$\widehat G$. With $\e(t)=\exp(2\pi it)$, character orthogonality is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:orthogonality}
 \E_{\chi\in\widehat G}\e(\chi(x))=\ind_{x=0}.
\end{equation}
Here and below uniform averages on a finite set use total mass one.
For completeness, if $x\ne0$, the finite abelian decomposition supplies
a character $\chi_0$ with $\e(\chi_0(x))\ne1$; translating the sum by
$\chi_0$ multiplies it by that number, forcing it to vanish.

On $\T$ integration always means normalized Haar integration. For
functions on a finite abelian group $V$, the unnormalized Fourier
transform is
\[
 \widehat f(\chi)=\sum_{x\in V}f(x)\e(-\chi(x)).
\]
This convention will be used only for the moment calculation in
Section~\ref{gsr:en:58:sec:interfaces}; all random-character averages are normalized
as in \eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:orthogonality}.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Admissible filters and their torsion spectrum\srctag{58}}]{Admissible filters and their torsion spectrum}\label{gsr:en:58:sec:d3}
\srcnote{58}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:en:58:sec:filters}

\begin{definition}\label{gsr:en:58:def:filter}
An admissible decreasing filter of degree $D\ge1$ is a real trigonometric
polynomial
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:filter}
 K(t)=\sum_{n=-D}^D c_n\e(nt)
\end{equation}
such that $0\le K(t)\le1$, $K(0)=1$, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:coefficients}
 c_{-n}=c_n\ge0,\qquad c_0\ge c_1\ge\cdots\ge c_D,
 \qquad c_1>0.
\end{equation}
Coefficients outside $[-D,D]$ are set equal to zero. Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:filter-parameters}
 P=\sum_n c_n^m,\qquad
 P_a=\sum_{a\mid n}c_n^m\quad(a\ge2),\qquad
 Q=P_2,\qquad R_s=\int_\T K(t)^s\,dt.
\end{equation}
\end{definition}

The normalization implies $\sum_n c_n=1$. In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:parameter-order}
 0<Q<P<1,\qquad P\le R_m\le R_2\le1.
\end{equation}
The strict inequality $Q<P$ follows from $c_1>0$; $P<1$ follows because
at least three coefficients are positive and $m>1$. To see $P\le R_m$,
expand the constant coefficient of $K^m$. Its nonnegative summands
include all vectors $\mathbf n=t\eps$, whose total weight is $P$.
The last two inequalities follow from $0\le K\le1$.

\begin{lemma}[Order spectrum]\label{gsr:en:58:lem:order-spectrum}
For every integer $a\ge2$, one has $P_a\le Q$. More generally, if
$a\ge a_0\ge2$, then $P_a\le P_{a_0}$.
If $\delta\in H$ has order $a$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:principal-order}
 \sum_{n\in\Z}c_n^m\ind_{n\delta=0}=P_a.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The exact identity follows from $n\delta=0$ if and only if $a\mid n$.
By symmetry and monotonicity,
\[
 P_a=c_0^m+2\sum_{j\ge1}c_{aj}^m
 \le c_0^m+2\sum_{j\ge1}c_{a_0j}^m=P_{a_0}.
\]
All sums are finite because the coefficients are extended by zero.
\end{proof}

This elementary spectrum is the reason small target torsion cannot be
discarded. If the order of a discrepancy exceeds $D$, only frequency
zero contributes, and $P_a=c_0^m$. If it has order two, every even
frequency contributes. Replacing this contribution by $c_0^m$ would
invalidate a uniform theorem for targets containing an element of
order two.

\begin{lemma}[Positivity ceiling]\label{gsr:en:58:lem:ceiling}
For any normalized nonnegative filter with real nonnegative Fourier
coefficients, without a monotonicity assumption, and every integer
$a\ge2$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:ceiling}
 1\le\frac{P}{P_a}\le a.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $F=K^{*m}$ be the $m$-fold normalized convolution on $\T$. It is
nonnegative, and its Fourier coefficients are $c_n^m$. The roots of
unity identity gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:convolution-ceiling}
 aP_a-P=\sum_{j=1}^{a-1}F(j/a)\ge0.
\end{equation}
Also $P_a\le P$ because it is a sub-sum of nonnegative terms.
\end{proof}

The order-two case bounds the separation of a single positive filter by
two. Increasing the degree cannot make all nonzero discrepancies
arbitrarily unlikely relative to zero discrepancy. Independent layers
are therefore a natural way to amplify a uniform separation.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A finite random selector and the good-tuple bound\srctag{58}}]{A finite random selector and the good-tuple bound}\label{gsr:en:58:sec:d4}
\srcnote{58}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:en:58:sec:selector}

Fix an integer $k\ge1$ and an integer $M>mD$. For each
$\ell=1,\ldots,k$, choose independently a uniform $\chi_\ell\in\widehat G$,
a uniform $\psi_\ell\in\widehat H$, and a shift
\[
 u_\ell\in\{0,1/M,\ldots,(M-1)/M\}
\]
with uniform distribution. Conditional on all these choices, select each
\emph{distinct point} $x\in B$ independently with probability
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:selection-probability}
 p(x)=\prod_{\ell=1}^k
 K\bigl(\chi_\ell(x)+\psi_\ell(\phi(x))+u_\ell\bigr).
\end{equation}
The selected set is denoted $B'$. This is a finite probability space:
there are finitely many parameter choices and finitely many subsets,
with real weights between zero and one. No limiting random process is
needed.

For one layer and an ordered tuple $\mathbf x$, expand the
\emph{formal occurrence product}. Character orthogonality and the shift
average give
\begin{align}
 &\E_{\chi,\psi,u}\prod_{i=1}^m
 K\bigl(\chi(x_i)+\psi(\phi(x_i))+u\bigr)\notag\\
 &\quad=
 \sum_{\mathbf n\in[-D,D]^m}
 \left(\prod_{i=1}^m c_{n_i}\right)
 \ind_{\sum_i n_i=0}
 \ind_{\sum_i n_ix_i=0}
 \ind_{\sum_i n_i\phi(x_i)=0}.
 \label{gsr:en:58:eq:fourier-expansion}
\end{align}
The first equation here is an equality in $\Z$, while the second and
third are in $G$ and $H$. Indeed, averaging the shifts first gives
$\sum_i n_i\equiv0\pmod M$, and
$|\sum_i n_i|\le mD<M$ upgrades it to the integer equality. In
particular, there is no shift-grid aliasing.

Call $\mathbf n$ \emph{principal} if $\mathbf n=t\eps$ for some integer
$t$. Since $\sum_i\eps_i=0$, every principal vector passes the shift
condition. If $\mathbf x$ is respected, it also passes both group
conditions, and its total principal weight is $P$.

\begin{proposition}[Good survival, including repetitions]\label{gsr:en:58:prop:good}
The selector \eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:selection-probability} satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:good-expectation}
 \E\GGfiftyeight_m(B',\phi)\ge P^k\GGfiftyeight_m(B,\phi).
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
All the terms in \eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:fourier-expansion} are nonnegative, so the
expected formal product for a respected tuple is at least $P$ in each
layer. Independence of the layers gives $P^k$.

If a point $x$ occurs $\mu_x$ times in the tuple, its factor in the
formal containment product is $p(x)^{\mu_x}$. Its factor in the actual
conditional containment probability is $p(x)$. Since $0\le p(x)\le1$,
\[
 \prod_{x\text{ distinct in }\mathbf x}p(x)
 \ge \prod_{i=1}^m p(x_i).
\]
Thus the lower bound remains valid with repeated entries. Summing it
over the respected tuples proves the proposition.
\end{proof}

The inequality in this proof has a direction. It does not justify an
upper bound for repeated bad tuples. Those tuples are treated separately
in Section~\ref{gsr:en:58:sec:collisions}.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Nonprincipal relations and the domain torsion cost\srctag{58}}]{Nonprincipal relations and the domain torsion cost}\label{gsr:en:58:sec:d5}
\srcnote{58}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:en:58:sec:torsion}

For a finite abelian group $G$ and an integer $d\ne0$, write
\[
 G[d]=\{x\in G:dx=0\},\qquad
 \tau_G(L)=\max_{1\le d\le L}|G[d]|.
\]
If $G=\Z/N\Z$, then $|G[d]|=\gcd(N,d)$, and therefore
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:cyclic-torsion}
 \tau_{\Z/N\Z}(2D)\le2D.
\end{equation}
This includes composite $N$ and the trivial group. If
$G\cong\bigoplus_{j=1}^s\Z/N_j\Z$, the exact formula is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:invariant-factors}
 |G[d]|=\prod_{j=1}^s\gcd(N_j,d).
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}[Two-relation completion bound]\label{gsr:en:58:lem:two-relations}
Let $\mathbf n\in[-D,D]^m\cap\Z^m$ be nonprincipal. Then the number of
$\mathbf x\in B^m$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:two-relations}
 \sum_i\eps_ix_i=0,
 \qquad \sum_i n_ix_i=0
\end{equation}
is at most $\tau_G(2D)b^{m-2}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Some two-column minor
\[
 d=\eps_i n_j-\eps_j n_i
\]
is nonzero. Otherwise $n_i/\eps_i$ would have the same integer value
for every $i$, making $\mathbf n$ principal. Also $0<|d|\le2D$.
Fix all entries except $x_i,x_j$. The first equation in
\eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:two-relations} expresses one of these as an affine function
of the other, because its coefficient is $\pm1$. Substitution into the
second leaves an equation of the form $dx=a$. Every nonempty fibre of
multiplication by $d$ is a coset of $G[d]$. Thus there are at most
$|G[d]|\le\tau_G(2D)$ completions for each of the $b^{m-2}$ choices.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Weighted nonprincipal error]\label{gsr:en:58:prop:nonprincipal}
In the $k$-layer Fourier expansion, the total contribution from arrays
containing a nonprincipal layer, summed over any subcollection of
additive tuples with distinct entries, is at most
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:nonprincipal-error}
 \tau_G(2D)(R_m^k-P^k)b^{m-2}.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Before imposing either group condition, the total coefficient weight
of a single layer satisfying the integer zero-sum condition is
\[
 \sum_{\sum_i n_i=0}\prod_i c_{n_i}=R_m.
\]
The principal part of this weight is $P$. Therefore the weight of all
$k$-layer arrays with a nonprincipal layer is exactly $R_m^k-P^k$.

For each such array choose one nonprincipal layer. Every tuple
contributing to that array satisfies the two relations in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:58:lem:two-relations}. Ignore all further group equations,
including the target equations, and use the completion bound. Sum over
the arrays with their nonnegative weights. Distinctness only reduces
the number counted. This gives \eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:nonprincipal-error}.
\end{proof}

This argument pays neither for the number of coefficient vectors nor
for a union bound over the layers. In particular, the error contains
$R_m^k-P^k$, rather than a constant independent of $k$ or an extra
factor $k$. This decay is useful when one amplifies a fixed filter many
times.

\subsection{A refined coefficient-by-coefficient torsion profile}

For a nonprincipal vector define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:tau-n}
 \tau(\mathbf n)=
 \min_{\eps_i n_j-\eps_j n_i\ne0}
 |G[\eps_i n_j-\eps_j n_i]|,
 \quad
 W_G(K)=\sum_{\substack{\sum_i n_i=0\\\mathbf n\text{ nonprincipal}}}
 \tau(\mathbf n)\prod_i c_{n_i}.
\end{equation}
The same proof, classified by the \emph{first} nonprincipal layer,
replaces \eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:nonprincipal-error} by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:weighted-profile}
 W_G(K)\frac{R_m^k-P^k}{R_m-P}\,b^{m-2}.
\end{equation}
Indeed, the first $\ell-1$ layers have total weight $P^{\ell-1}$,
layer $\ell$ contributes $W_G(K)$, and the remaining layers have
weight $R_m^{k-\ell}$. Summing the geometric progression proves the
formula. Here $R_m>P$: the positive coefficients $c_0,c_1,c_{-1}$
supply a nonprincipal zero-sum vector for $m\ge4$.

There is a related exact ambient calculation. The integer matrix with
rows $\eps$ and $\mathbf n$ has Smith invariants $(1,g_{\mathbf n})$,
where $g_{\mathbf n}$ is the greatest common divisor of its nonzero
two-column minors. Hence its kernel on $G^m$ has size
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:smith}
 |G|^{m-2}|G[g_{\mathbf n}]|.
\end{equation}
To see this, elementary unimodular row and column operations reduce the
matrix to its Smith form; the first invariant is one because the first
row contains a unit. On $G$, the resulting two diagonal equations have
respectively one and $|G[g_{\mathbf n}]|$ choices, with $m-2$ free
coordinates.

The distinction between \eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:weighted-profile} and
\eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:smith} matters. Smith operations can mix the coordinates and
need not preserve $B^m$. The gcd of all minors therefore cannot simply
replace the chosen-minor fibre bound for an arbitrary subset $B$.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Repeated bad tuples and their decaying error\srctag{58}}]{Repeated bad tuples and their decaying error}\label{gsr:en:58:sec:d6}
\srcnote{58}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:en:58:sec:collisions}

\begin{lemma}[Distinct-point H\"older bound]\label{gsr:en:58:lem:holder}
If a tuple has $d\ge2$ distinct entries, its probability of containment
in the selector is at most $R_d^k\le R_2^k$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Fix one layer and its characters. Let the phases of the $d$ distinct
points be $\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_d$. H\"older's inequality for the
finite shift average gives
\[
 \E_u\prod_{j=1}^d K(u+\theta_j)
 \le\prod_{j=1}^d
       \bigl(\E_u K(u+\theta_j)^d\bigr)^{1/d}.
\]
The translated polynomial $K(u+\theta_j)^d$ has degree at most
$dD\le mD<M$. Its grid average equals its constant coefficient,
which is $R_d$. Thus the right side is $R_d$. Averaging over the
characters preserves the bound. Independence of the layers gives
$R_d^k$, and $R_d\le R_2$ follows from $0\le K\le1$ and $d\ge2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Collision error]\label{gsr:en:58:cor:collision-error}
The expected number of repeated bad tuples retained in $B'$ is at most
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:collision-error}
 \binom m2 R_2^k b^{m-2}.
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Every bad tuple has at least two distinct entries. Apply
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:58:lem:holder} and then the collision count in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:58:lem:counts}.
\end{proof}

When the collision profile is known, one can retain more information.
Let $C_d$ be the number of bad additive tuples with exactly $d$ distinct
entries. The exact improvement is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:collision-profile}
 \sum_{d=2}^{m-1}C_dR_d^k.
\end{equation}
This may be substantially below \eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:collision-error}. A purely
combinatorial bound on $C_d$ is also possible: partition the $m$
positions into $d$ cells, and give a cell the sum of its $\eps_i$
coefficients. If all these sums vanish, every tuple with that pattern
is respected. Otherwise, solving for a cell with nonzero coefficient
$a$ gives at most $|G[a]|b^{d-1}$ assignments. Sum the best such bound
over the relevant set partitions. No such refinement is needed for
Theorem~A.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The expectation theorem and a simultaneous selection certificate\srctag{58}}]{The expectation theorem and a simultaneous selection certificate}\label{gsr:en:58:sec:d7}
\srcnote{58}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:en:58:sec:restriction}

\begin{theorem}[Central expectation estimate]\label{gsr:en:58:thm:expectation}
Let $m=2r\ge4$, let $G,H$ be finite abelian groups, and let $B\subseteq G$
have cardinality $b>0$. For an admissible decreasing filter $K$ and
$k\ge1$, the selector of Section~\ref{gsr:en:58:sec:selector} satisfies
\begin{align}
 \E\GGfiftyeight_m(B',\phi)&\ge P^k\GGfiftyeight_m(B,\phi),\label{gsr:en:58:eq:central-good}\\
 \E\UU_m(B',\phi)&\le Q^k\UU_m(B,\phi)+A_kb^{m-2},\label{gsr:en:58:eq:central-bad}
\end{align}
where
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:Ak}
 A_k=\tau_G(2D)(R_m^k-P^k)+\binom m2 R_2^k
 \le\left(\tau_G(2D)+\binom m2\right)R_2^k.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The first inequality is Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:58:prop:good}. For the second,
first consider bad tuples with distinct entries, so actual survival
equals the formal occurrence product. If the discrepancy has order
$a\ge2$, an all-principal array contributes $P_a^k\le Q^k$.
Summed over such tuples this is at most $Q^k\UU_m(B,\phi)$.
The arrays with a nonprincipal layer contribute at most
\eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:nonprincipal-error}. Finally add the repeated bad tuples,
using Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:58:cor:collision-error}. This proves
\eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:central-bad}. The simpler upper bound on $A_k$ uses
$R_m\le R_2$ and discards the nonpositive term $-\tau_G(2D)P^k$.
\end{proof}

The expectations must be converted into a single subset having both
the desired quality and the desired mass. Separate applications of
averaging to two inequalities would not establish this.

\begin{theorem}[Exact selection certificate]\label{gsr:en:58:thm:certificate}
Fix $0<\eta<1$ and abbreviate $\GGfiftyeight_m(B,\phi)=g$,
$\UU_m(B,\phi)=u$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:Psi}
 \Psi_k=\eta P^kg-(1-\eta)Q^ku-(1-\eta)A_kb^{m-2}.
\end{equation}
If $\Psi_k>0$, some subset $B'\subseteq B$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:certificate-conclusions}
 \GGfiftyeight_m(B',\phi)\ge(1-\eta)\TT_m(B'),
 \qquad \TT_m(B')\ge\frac{\Psi_k}{\eta}>0.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For each outcome of the selector, put
\[
 F=\GGfiftyeight_m(B',\phi)-(1-\eta)\TT_m(B')
   =\eta\GGfiftyeight_m(B',\phi)-(1-\eta)\UU_m(B',\phi).
\]
The expectation theorem gives $\E F\ge\Psi_k$. Thus some outcome has
$F\ge\Psi_k>0$, which proves the quality assertion. For that same
outcome,
\[
 F=\eta\TT_m(B')-\UU_m(B',\phi)\le\eta\TT_m(B'),
\]
and the mass assertion follows.
\end{proof}

The exact certificate can use observed counts $g,u$ and the refined
errors \eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:weighted-profile} or \eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:collision-profile}.
The following consequence depends only on a lower bound for $g$.

\begin{theorem}[Polynomial restriction from a spectral gap]
\label{gsr:en:58:thm:polynomial}
Suppose $0<\alpha,\eta\le1$ and
$\GGfiftyeight_m(B,\phi)\ge\alpha b^{m-1}$. Set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:k-choice}
 t=\alpha\eta,\qquad \mathcal R=\frac PQ>1,
 \qquad k=\left\lceil\frac{\log(2/t)}{\log\mathcal R}\right\rceil.
\end{equation}
If
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:exact-threshold}
 b\ge\frac{4A_k}{tP^k},
\end{equation}
then a subset $B'\subseteq B$ satisfies
\begin{align}
 \GGfiftyeight_m(B',\phi)&\ge(1-\eta)\TT_m(B'),\label{gsr:en:58:eq:general-quality}\\
 \TT_m(B')&\ge\frac{\alpha P^k}{4}b^{m-1}.\label{gsr:en:58:eq:general-mass}
\end{align}
A simpler sufficient size condition is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:coarse-threshold}
 b\ge4\left(\tau_G(2D)+\binom m2\right)t^{-1}
       \left(\frac{R_2}{P}\right)^k.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $\eta=1$, take $B'=B$; the required mass follows from the assumption
on $\GGfiftyeight_m$. Suppose $0<\eta<1$. The choice of $k$ gives
$Q^k\le(t/2)P^k$. Since $u\le\TT_m(B)\le b^{m-1}$,
\begin{align*}
 \Psi_k
 &\ge tP^kb^{m-1}-(1-\eta)\frac t2P^kb^{m-1}
                  -(1-\eta)A_kb^{m-2}\\
 &\ge\frac t2P^kb^{m-1}-(1-\eta)A_kb^{m-2}.
\end{align*}
Under \eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:exact-threshold}, the final error is at most
$tP^kb^{m-1}/4$. Thus $\Psi_k\ge tP^kb^{m-1}/4>0$. Apply
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:58:thm:certificate} and divide by $\eta$.
The coarse condition follows from \eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:Ak}.
\end{proof}

To exhibit the powers explicitly, define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:a-z}
 a_K=\frac{-\log P}{\log\mathcal R},\qquad
 z_K=\frac{\log(R_2/P)}{\log\mathcal R},\qquad
 C_G=\tau_G(2D)+\binom m2.
\end{equation}
Since $0<P<1$ and $R_2/P\ge1$, the ceiling gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:ceiling-bounds}
 P^k\ge P(t/2)^{a_K},\qquad
 (R_2/P)^k\le (R_2/P)(2/t)^{z_K}.
\end{equation}
We obtain the following power-law statement with explicit constants.

\begin{corollary}\label{gsr:en:58:cor:power-law}
Under the preceding hypotheses, the sufficient threshold
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:power-threshold}
 b\ge4C_G\frac{R_2}{P}\,2^{z_K}
        (\alpha\eta)^{-(z_K+1)}
\end{equation}
guarantees the quality conclusion and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:power-retention}
 \TT_m(B')\ge
 \frac{P}{4\cdot2^{a_K}}
 \alpha^{a_K+1}\eta^{a_K}b^{m-1}.
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}

For fixed $m$ and a fixed filter, these are polynomial dependencies on
the two accuracy parameters. In a cyclic domain, every constant is
independent of the modulus. For general finite abelian domains the
torsion factor is genuine: for example,
$\tau_{(\Z/2\Z)^s}(2D)=2^s$ when $D\ge1$. In such a family the
sufficient condition can become vacuous. We do not claim a
dimension-independent theorem for all finite abelian domains.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Powered cosine filters and the certified exponent 54\srctag{58}}]{Powered cosine filters and the certified exponent 54}\label{gsr:en:58:sec:d8}
\srcnote{58}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:en:58:sec:explicit}

For an integer $q\ge1$ use
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:cosine-kernel}
 K_q(t)=\cos^{2q}(\pi t),\qquad
 c_n=4^{-q}\binom{2q}{q+n}\quad(|n|\le q).
\end{equation}
This kernel is already used in the prime-field refinement of repository
source~04 \cite{repo58}. It satisfies all the conditions of
Definition~\ref{gsr:en:58:def:filter}, has degree $D=q$, and has exact moments
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:cosine-moments}
 R_s=4^{-qs}\binom{2qs}{qs}.
\end{equation}
The present argument chooses $q$ as a function of the relation length
and then amplifies the same filter; $q$ need not increase as $\eta$
decreases.

\subsection{An elementary uniform \texorpdfstring{$O(m\log m)$}{O(m log m)} bound}

\begin{lemma}\label{gsr:en:58:lem:central-binomial}
For every integer $q\ge1$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:central-binomial}
 4^{-q}\binom{2q}{q}\ge\frac1{2\sqrt q}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Equality holds at $q=1$. The ratio of the left sides at $q+1$ and $q$
is $(2q+1)/(2q+2)$, which is at least $\sqrt{q/(q+1)}$ after squaring.
Induction proves the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[A uniform spectral gap]\label{gsr:en:58:prop:uniform-gap}
For $m\ge4$ and the choice $q=m$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:uniform-gap}
 \frac PQ>\frac32,\qquad
 P>\frac53(2\sqrt m)^{-m}.
\end{equation}
Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:uniform-exponent}
 a_K\le
 \frac{m\log(2\sqrt m)-\log(5/3)}{\log(3/2)}
 =O(m\log m).
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Let $c_0=4^{-m}\binom{2m}{m}$. Since
\[
 \left(\frac{c_1}{c_0}\right)^m
 =\left(\frac m{m+1}\right)^m>\e^{-1}>\frac13,
\]
we have $P/c_0^m>5/3$. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:58:lem:central-binomial} gives the
claimed lower bound on $P$.

For $1\le n\le m$, write
\[
 \frac{c_n}{c_0}
 =\prod_{j=1}^n
 \frac{m+1/2-(j-1/2)}{m+1/2+(j-1/2)}.
\]
The inequality $\log((1-u)/(1+u))\le-2u$ for $0<u<1$ yields
\[
 \frac{c_n}{c_0}\le
 \exp\left(-\frac{n^2}{m+1/2}\right).
\]
Thus, extending the sum beyond the support,
\[
 \frac Q{c_0^m}
 \le1+2\sum_{j\ge1}\exp\left(-\frac{4mj^2}{m+1/2}\right)
 <1+2\sum_{j\ge1}\e^{-3j^2}<\frac{10}{9}.
\]
For the last inequality, $j^2\ge1+3(j-1)$ bounds the sum by
$\e^{-3}/(1-\e^{-9})$, and $\e^3>20$ suffices. Therefore
$P/Q>(5/3)/(10/9)=3/2$. Substitute in \eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:a-z}.
\end{proof}

Combining this proposition with Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:58:cor:power-law} proves
all-modulus polynomial restriction for every balanced even arity. The
bound $z_K\le a_K$ follows from $R_2\le1$, so the sufficient threshold
also has exponent $O(m\log m)$. Theorem~B will identify the best
possible leading retention exponent within the filter class.

\subsection{An exact certificate at \texorpdfstring{$m=16$}{m = 16}}

Choose $q=25$, and introduce the integers
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:AB}
 A=\sum_{n=-25}^{25}\binom{50}{25+n}^{16},\qquad
 B_{\mathrm{ev}}=
 \sum_{\substack{-25\le n\le25\\2\mid n}}
 \binom{50}{25+n}^{16}.
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:PQ-exact}
 P=\frac A{2^{800}},\qquad Q=\frac{B_{\mathrm{ev}}}{2^{800}},
 \qquad R_2=\frac{\binom{100}{50}}{2^{100}}.
\end{equation}
The following five inequalities are exact integer certificates. They
are verified without floating point in the accompanying program
\texttt{code/verify\_constants.py}; Appendix~\ref{gsr:fz:58:app:certificate}
also gives the complete essential computation.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule
Integer inequality & Consequence\\
\midrule
$A\ge2^{750}$ & $P\ge2^{-50}$\\[3pt]
$250A\ge481B_{\mathrm{ev}}$ & $\mathcal R=P/Q\ge481/250$\\[3pt]
$481^{53}\ge2^{50}250^{53}$ & $\mathcal R^{53}\ge2^{50}$\\[3pt]
$481^{50}\ge2^{47}250^{50}$ & $\mathcal R^{50}\ge2^{47}$\\[3pt]
$\binom{100}{50}\le2^{97}$ & $R_2\le2^{-3}$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem A for finite targets]
Set $t=\alpha\eta$ and
$k=\lceil\log_{\mathcal R}(2/t)\rceil$. In a cyclic group
$\tau_G(50)\le50$ and $\binom{16}{2}=120$, so
\eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:coarse-threshold} is implied by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:54-intermediate-threshold}
 b\ge680t^{-1}(R_2/P)^k.
\end{equation}
The certificates give $R_2/P\le2^{47}$ and
$\log_{\mathcal R}(2^{47})\le50$. Hence
\[
 (R_2/P)^k\le2^{47}(2/t)^{50},
\]
so the right side of \eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:54-intermediate-threshold} is at most
$680\cdot2^{97}t^{-51}$. Since $680<2^{11}$ and $0<t\le1$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:54-threshold-comparison}
 680\cdot2^{97}t^{-51}\le 2^{108}t^{-54}=(4/t)^{54}.
\end{equation}
Thus the hypothesis of Theorem~A ensures the size condition of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:58:thm:polynomial}.

For the retention, the other certificates imply
\[
 a_K\le53,\qquad P^k\ge P(t/2)^{a_K}
                    \ge2^{-50}(t/2)^{53}.
\]
Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:54-retention-comparison}
 \frac{\alpha P^k}{4}
 \ge2^{-105}\alpha^{54}\eta^{53}
 \ge2^{-108}\alpha^{54}\eta^{54}
 =\left(\frac{\alpha\eta}{4}\right)^{54}.
\end{equation}
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:58:thm:polynomial} proves the tuple-count conclusions.
Finally $\TT_{16}(B')\le|B'|^{15}$ gives the point-count corollary.
\end{proof}

The exact rational values, rather than their rounded certificates, give
\begin{align}
 P&\approx1.4263285575\times10^{-15},&
 \mathcal R&\approx1.9247171505,\notag\\
 a_K&\approx52.2064261968,&
 z_K&\approx48.3411887375.\label{gsr:en:58:eq:numerics16}
\end{align}
These decimals are descriptive, not the basis of the integer theorem.
For a precise nonintegral-exponent theorem, use the exact definitions
\eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:PQ-exact} in \eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:power-threshold} and
\eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:power-retention}. Degree $25$ was selected by a finite
numerical search within the powered cosine family. We do not claim
that it optimizes over all admissible filters, or even over all degrees
without a certified global search.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Further generalizations of the restriction estimate\srctag{58}}]{Further generalizations of the restriction estimate}\label{gsr:en:58:sec:d9}
\srcnote{58}{Section 9}
\label{gsr:en:58:sec:extensions}

\subsection{Targets of arbitrary cardinality}

The finite-target hypothesis can be removed for the restriction
conclusions, because only finitely many target discrepancies are relevant.

\begin{lemma}[Finite quotient preserving all relevant relations]
\label{gsr:en:58:lem:finite-quotient}
Let $B$ be finite and $\phi:B\to H$, where $H$ is any abelian group.
For a fixed balanced arity $m=2r$, there are a finite abelian group $H_0$ and a map
$\phi_0:B\to H_0$ such that every ordered tuple in $B^m$ has zero
balanced target discrepancy under $\phi$ if and only if it does under
$\phi_0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The subgroup generated by $\phi(B)$ is finitely generated, hence is
isomorphic to $\Z^s\oplus F$ with $F$ finite. Consider the finite set
of all balanced $m$-term discrepancies of points of $B$. Choose an
integer $L\ge2$ larger than the absolute value of every coordinate of
every free part in this set. Reduction of $\Z^s$ modulo $L$, keeping
$F$ unchanged, kills none of these finitely many nonzero discrepancies: an element with a
nonzero free coordinate has a nonzero coordinate modulo $L$, and an
element with zero free part has its nonzero torsion component preserved.
Compose $\phi$ with this finite quotient. Zero discrepancies remain
zero and all the relevant nonzero discrepancies remain nonzero.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{gsr:en:58:cor:arbitrary-target}
Theorem~A and the restriction conclusions of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:58:thm:polynomial} and Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:58:cor:power-law} hold for
maps to arbitrary abelian target groups, with unchanged constants.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:58:lem:finite-quotient} and the finite-target theorem.
The same quotient preserves the relevant tuple counts on every subset
of $B$, so the selected subset works for the original map.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Using the actual discrepancy-order distribution}

For a finite target let $u_a$ be the number of bad tuples in $B^m$
whose discrepancy has order $a$. The proof of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:58:thm:expectation} gives the stronger estimate
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:order-distribution}
 \E\UU_m(B',\phi)\le\sum_{a\ge2}P_a^ku_a+A_kb^{m-2}.
\end{equation}
It is harmless that the sum includes repeated tuples, since those only
enlarge the principal upper bound and their actual survival is already
charged to the collision error. Only finitely many $u_a$ are nonzero.

If every nonzero discrepancy has order at least $a_0$, monotonicity
gives $P_a\le P_{a_0}$, and all the restriction theorems hold with
$Q=P_{a_0}$. In particular, a finite target of odd order uses
$a_0\ge3$. More generally, for a nontrivial finite target its smallest prime divisor is an available
choice for $a_0$. If all nonzero discrepancies have order greater
than $D$, one can use $Q=c_0^m$. This explains why a large-characteristic
argument can have a stronger single-filter separation than an argument
uniform over targets containing elements of order two.

Coefficient monotonicity can also be relaxed. For a nonnegative
coefficient filter with $c_1>0$, use
$Q_*:=\max_{a\ge2}P_a$ instead. This is a maximum over finitely many
distinct possibilities, since $P_a=c_0^m$ for $a>D$, and $Q_*<P$
because every $P_a$ omits $c_1^m+c_{-1}^m$. The same proof applies.
The decreasing condition conveniently identifies the worst order as two.

\subsection{Different filters in different layers}

Let layer $\ell$ use an admissible filter $K_\ell$ of degree $D_\ell$,
with parameters $P_\ell,Q_\ell,R_{s,\ell}$. Take
$M>m\max_\ell D_\ell$ and set $D_*:=\max_\ell D_\ell$. Then
\begin{align}
 \E\GGfiftyeight_m(B',\phi)&\ge\Bigl(\prod_\ell P_\ell\Bigr)\GGfiftyeight_m(B,\phi),\notag\\
 \E\UU_m(B',\phi)&\le
 \Bigl(\prod_\ell Q_\ell\Bigr)\UU_m(B,\phi)\notag\\
 &\quad+\left\{\tau_G(2D_*)
   \left(\prod_\ell R_{m,\ell}-\prod_\ell P_\ell\right)
    +\binom m2\prod_\ell R_{2,\ell}\right\}b^{m-2}.
 \label{gsr:en:58:eq:mixed-filters}
\end{align}
The proof is identical: nonprincipal arrays have the difference of
the two displayed product weights, while the distinct-point H\"older
bound multiplies across layers. This flexibility may improve a
finite-size certificate even when it does not improve the asymptotic
principal exponent, as the next section shows.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Optimal leading growth of the Fourier-filter exponent\srctag{58}}]{Optimal leading growth of the Fourier-filter exponent}\label{gsr:en:58:sec:d10}
\srcnote{58}{Section 10}
\label{gsr:en:58:sec:optimality}

In this section $m$ is any integer at least two, not necessarily even.
Let $\mathcal K$ be the class of finite trigonometric polynomials
\[
 K(t)=\sum_n c_n\e(nt),\qquad 0\le K\le1,\quad K(0)=1,
 \quad c_{-n}=c_n\ge0.
\]
For a fixed integer $a\ge2$, use the notation of Theorem~B and let
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:Ima}
 I_{m,a}=\inf_{K\in\mathcal K}\mathcal A_{m,a}(K).
\end{equation}
We prove both sides of the asymptotic, uniformly over all finite
degrees in the lower bound.

\subsection{A coefficient bound from the mean of the filter}

Put $s=c_0=\int_\T K$. Continuity and $K(0)=1$ give $s>0$.
If $s=1$, then $K\equiv1$, so the exponent is infinite by convention.
We may assume $0<s<1$. The integral formula gives $c_n\le s$, and
$\sum_n c_n=1$. Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:mean-bound}
 P_m\le s^{m-1}<1,\qquad Q_{m,a}\ge s^m>0.
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}[Rearrangement bound for a nonzero coefficient]
\label{gsr:en:58:lem:bathtub}
For every nonzero integer $n$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:bathtub}
 c_n\le\frac{\sin(\pi s)}{\pi}=s\beta(s),
 \qquad \beta(s):=\frac{\sin(\pi s)}{\pi s}.
\end{equation}
Moreover
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:sinc}
 0<\beta(s)\le1-\frac{2s^2}{3}\le\exp(-2s^2/3)
 \qquad(0<s<1).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $h(t)=\cos(2\pi nt)$. Its distribution on $\T$ is the same as
that of $\cos(2\pi t)$. Let $E$ be its top level set of measure $s$,
so its boundary level is $\cos(\pi s)$. Pointwise,
\[
 (\ind_E-K)(h-\cos(\pi s))\ge0.
\]
Since $\int(\ind_E-K)=0$, integration gives
\[
 c_n=\int K(t)h(t)\,dt
 \le\int_E h(t)\,dt
 =\int_{-s/2}^{s/2}\cos(2\pi t)\,dt
 =\frac{\sin(\pi s)}{\pi}.
\]
This proves the coefficient bound directly, without an extremal
regularity assumption on $K$.

For $0\le v\le1$, concavity of sine on $[0,\pi/2]$ gives
$\sin(\pi v/2)\ge v$, hence $\cos(\pi v)\le1-2v^2$.
Integrating with $v=su$ for $0\le u\le1$ yields
\[
 \beta(s)=\int_0^1\cos(\pi su)\,du\le1-2s^2/3.
\]
The exponential bound follows from $1-x\le\e^{-x}$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The universal lower bound}

If $P_m=Q_{m,a}$, the lower bound is automatic. Otherwise let
$\mathcal R_a=P_m/Q_{m,a}>1$. By Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:58:lem:ceiling},
$\mathcal R_a\le a$. Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:mean-bound} gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:lower-one}
 \mathcal A_{m,a}(K)\ge
 \frac{-(m-1)\log s}{\log a}.
\end{equation}
On the other hand, Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:58:lem:bathtub} implies
\begin{align}
 \mathcal R_a-1
 &=\frac{P_m-Q_{m,a}}{Q_{m,a}}\notag\\
 &\le\frac{\sum_{n\ne0}c_n^m}{s^m}
 \le\frac{1-s}{s}\beta(s)^{m-1}
 \le\frac{1-s}{s}\exp\left(-\frac{2(m-1)s^2}{3}\right).
 \label{gsr:en:58:eq:ratio-tail}
\end{align}
Use $\log\mathcal R_a\le\mathcal R_a-1$ and $-\log s\ge1-s$ to get
a complementary bound,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:lower-two}
 \mathcal A_{m,a}(K)\ge
 (m-1)s\exp\left(\frac{2(m-1)s^2}{3}\right).
\end{equation}

For sufficiently large $m$, put $s_m=\sqrt{3\log m/m}<1$.
If $s\le s_m$, equation~\eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:lower-one} yields
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:lower-small-s}
 \mathcal A_{m,a}(K)\ge
 \frac{m-1}{2\log a}
 \bigl(\log m-\log\log m-\log3\bigr).
\end{equation}
If $s>s_m$, the right side of \eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:lower-two} is increasing in
$s$, and therefore
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:lower-large-s}
 \mathcal A_{m,a}(K)\ge
 (m-1)\sqrt{\frac{3\log m}{m}}\,m^{2-2/m}.
\end{equation}
For fixed $a$, this is eventually larger than
\eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:lower-small-s}. Thus, uniformly over $K\in\mathcal K$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:optimal-lower}
 I_{m,a}\ge\frac{m\log m}{2\log a}-O_a(m\log\log m).
\end{equation}
The two branches express an obstruction: a narrow filter has a small
mean and loses many good tuples, whereas a filter with larger mean has
little nonzero-frequency mass capable of separating a nonzero
discrepancy from zero.

\subsection{An explicit family attaining the leading constant}

Take
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:optimal-q}
 q=\left\lceil m(\log m)^2\right\rceil,
 \qquad K(t)=\cos^{2q}(\pi t),
 \qquad J=\left\lfloor\sqrt{q/m}\right\rfloor.
\end{equation}
For sufficiently large $m$, $J\le q/4$. For $1\le n\le J$,
\[
 \frac{c_n}{c_0}=\prod_{j=1}^n
 \left(1-\frac{2j-1}{q+j}\right).
\]
The fractions lie in $[0,1/2]$, so $\log(1-x)\ge-2x$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:cosine-ratio-lower}
 \log\frac{c_n}{c_0}
 \ge-\frac4q\sum_{j=1}^n j
 \ge-\frac{4n^2}{q}.
\end{equation}
Hence $(c_n/c_0)^m\ge\e^{-4}$ when $|n|\le J$, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:many-coefficients}
 \frac{P_m}{c_0^m}\ge1+2J\e^{-4}.
\end{equation}

Let $w_n=c_n^m$. It is even and nonincreasing for $n\ge0$. Group the
positive indices into blocks of length $a$. Each block ending at $aj$
has every value at least $w_{aj}$, so
\[
 \sum_{n\ge1}w_n\ge a\sum_{j\ge1}w_{aj}.
\]
Together with \eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:convolution-ceiling}, this proves
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:residue-defect}
 0\le aQ_{m,a}-P_m\le(a-1)c_0^m.
\end{equation}
Write $d=(aQ_{m,a}-P_m)/P_m$. By
\eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:many-coefficients},
\[
 0\le d\le\frac{a-1}{1+2J\e^{-4}}=O_a(1/\log m).
\]
It follows that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:ratio-near-a}
 \log(P_m/Q_{m,a})=\log a-\log(1+d)
                         =\log a-O_a(1/\log m).
\end{equation}
Finally, Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:58:lem:central-binomial} and $P_m\ge c_0^m$ give
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:upper-numerator}
 -\log P_m\le m\log(2\sqrt q)
   =\frac m2\log m+m\log\log m+O(m).
\end{equation}
Dividing \eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:upper-numerator} by
\eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:ratio-near-a} proves
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:optimal-upper}
 I_{m,a}\le\frac{m\log m}{2\log a}+O_a(m\log\log m).
\end{equation}
Together with \eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:optimal-lower}, this proves Theorem~B,
including the asserted additive error term.

\subsection{What the optimality statement covers}

The theorem optimizes the loss in the principal good-to-bad separation.
For identical layers this loss is exactly $\mathcal A_{m,a}(K)$:
achieving separation $L$ costs a principal good-survival factor
approximately $L^{-\mathcal A_{m,a}(K)}$. It does not optimize the
finite-size error or the ceiling in the number of layers.
Nor is it a lower bound on the actual survival of every input set:
particular inputs can benefit from additional Fourier terms or structure.

Allowing a fixed list of different independent filters cannot improve
the optimal principal exponent. If all the denominators are positive,
then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:mixed-exponent}
 \frac{\sum_\ell-\log P_{m,\ell}}
      {\sum_\ell\log(P_{m,\ell}/Q_{m,a,\ell})}
 \ge I_{m,a},
\end{equation}
because the left side is a weighted average of the individual
exponents, with nonnegative denominator weights. Layers with ratio
one contribute no separation and cannot improve this inequality.
Adaptive choices depending on earlier outcomes, filters without
nonnegative Fourier coefficients, and structural extraction arguments
are not covered by this lower bound.

For $a=2$, the theorem explains a difference from a
large-characteristic prime-field argument. The latter can exclude all
nonzero principal frequencies for every bad discrepancy in a chosen
degree range, whereas a uniform order-two argument has separation at
most two per layer. There is consequently no conflict between the
$m\log m$ barrier here and the linear-in-$m$ prime-field exponents
already present in sources~04 and~17.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Moment lifting and the Gowers--ProveIt interfaces\srctag{58}}]{Moment lifting and the Gowers--ProveIt interfaces}\label{gsr:en:58:sec:d11}
\srcnote{58}{Section 11}
\label{gsr:en:58:sec:interfaces}

We return to balanced even arity $m=2r\ge4$. The restriction theorem
accepts a density of respected $m$-tuples. In applications the input is
often a density of respected quadruples. The following standard
interpolation, already used in repository sources~04 and~17, performs
the conversion without an extra ambient-density loss.

\begin{proposition}[Graph moment lifting]\label{gsr:en:58:prop:moment-lifting}
For a nonempty finite set $A$ in a finite abelian group $V$, let
$E_r(A)$ count ordered solutions to
$a_1+\cdots+a_r=a_{r+1}+\cdots+a_{2r}$ in $A^{2r}$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:moment-lifting}
 E_r(A)\ge\frac{E_2(A)^{r-1}}{|A|^{r-2}}\qquad(r\ge2).
\end{equation}
In particular, if $\GGfiftyeight_4(B,\phi)\ge\gamma b^3$ with $0<\gamma\le1$,
then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:graph-lifting}
 \GGfiftyeight_{2r}(B,\phi)\ge\gamma^{r-1}b^{2r-1}.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Orthogonality gives
\[
 E_j(A)=\frac1{|V|}\sum_{\chi\in\widehat V}
                       |\widehat{\ind_A}(\chi)|^{2j}.
\]
Apply H\"older to the normalized Fourier average, writing
$|\widehat{\ind_A}|^4$ as the product of
$|\widehat{\ind_A}|^{2r/(r-1)}$ and
$|\widehat{\ind_A}|^{2(r-2)/(r-1)}$. For $r>2$ this gives
\[
 E_2(A)\le E_r(A)^{1/(r-1)}E_1(A)^{(r-2)/(r-1)}.
\]
Since $E_1(A)=|A|$, rearrangement proves
\eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:moment-lifting}; $r=2$ is equality.
Apply it to the graph $A=\{(x,\phi(x)):x\in B\}\subseteq G\times H$,
which has size $b$ and $E_j(A)=\GGfiftyeight_{2j}(B,\phi)$.
For arbitrary abelian targets, apply a finite quotient preserving both
the quadruple and $2r$-tuple discrepancies; the same calculation then
proves the assertion there as well.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[All-modulus quadruple-input restriction]
\label{gsr:en:58:cor:quadruples}
Let $B\subseteq\Z/N\Z$ and let $\phi:B\to H$ for any abelian group
$H$. Suppose $0<\gamma,\eta\le1$ and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:quad-hyp}
 \GGfiftyeight_4(B,\phi)\ge\gamma b^3,
 \qquad b\ge\left(\frac4{\gamma^7\eta}\right)^{54}.
\end{equation}
Then a subset $B'\subseteq B$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:quad-conclusion}
 \GGfiftyeight_{16}(B',\phi)\ge(1-\eta)\TT_{16}(B'),\qquad
 \TT_{16}(B')\ge
 \left(\frac{\gamma^7\eta}{4}\right)^{54}b^{15}.
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Use $r=8$ in Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:58:prop:moment-lifting}, and then apply
Theorem~A and Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:58:cor:arbitrary-target} with $\alpha=\gamma^7$.
\end{proof}

The improvement in moment normalization is credited to the prior
project work. The new point in this composition is the all-modulus
restriction and its explicit constants.

\subsection{An explicit replacement at Lemma 9.3}

Write $b=\beta N$ as in the original lemma. Under the nonvacuous
hypotheses one has $0<\alpha,\beta\le1$. A sufficient starting modulus
for Theorem~A is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:N0-lemma}
 N_0=\left\lceil\beta^{-1}
                   \left(\frac4{\alpha\eta}\right)^{54}\right\rceil.
\end{equation}
For every $N\ge N_0$, the conclusion becomes
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:lemma-interface}
 \TT_{16}(B')\ge
 \left(\frac{\alpha\eta}{4}\right)^{54}\beta^{15}N^{15},
 \qquad \GGfiftyeight_{16}(B',\phi)\ge(1-\eta)\TT_{16}(B').
\end{equation}
Since $0<\alpha\eta/4<1$ and $54<2^{19}$, this also implies the
retention required by the original and formal Lemma~9.3. This is a
mathematical implication of statements; it is not a claim that the
new implication has been checked in Lean.

For Corollary~9.4, the quadruple input is
$\GGfiftyeight_4(B,\phi)\ge\gamma\beta^3N^3=\gamma b^3$. We may take
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:58:eq:N0-corollary}
 N_0=\left\lceil\beta^{-1}
                   \left(\frac4{\gamma^7\eta}\right)^{54}\right\rceil,
\end{equation}
with retention $(\gamma^7\eta/4)^{54}\beta^{15}N^{15}$.
The printed coefficient contains the additional factor $\beta^6$
inside $(\gamma^7\beta^6\eta/4)^{2^{19}}$. The removal of that density
factor in the moment input was already established in the prior
prime-field refinements; the present corollary makes the resulting
restriction available for every modulus.

\subsection{Formalization and integration plan}

At the inspected commit the repository's definitions match the present
counts exactly:
\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{0.40\linewidth}L{0.52\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
Mathematical quantity & Existing Lean interface\\
\midrule
$\TT_{16}(B)$ & \texttt{additiveTupleCount 8 B}\\[4pt]
$\GGfiftyeight_{16}(B,\phi)$ & \texttt{phiAdditiveTupleCount 8 B phi}\\[4pt]
$\GGfiftyeight_{16}\ge(1-\eta)\TT_{16}$
 & \texttt{GammaHomOfOrder 8 B phi (1 - eta)}\\[4pt]
Lemma 9.3 / Corollary 9.4 statements
 & \texttt{Sections08\_09.lean}\\[4pt]
Existing exact companions
 & \texttt{lemma\_9\_3\_holds},
   \texttt{corollary\_9\_4\_holds} in
   \texttt{Proofs09Restriction.lean}\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The formal statements quantify over all nonzero moduli, not just primes.
Their premises quantify $\alpha,\beta>0$ without explicit upper bounds.
Those upper bounds follow in a nonempty instance from $b\le N$ and
$\GGfiftyeight_{16}\le b^{15}$. Thus this difference in presentation causes no
interface gap. For Corollary~9.4 the definition
\texttt{GammaAdditive B phi (gamma * beta\^{}3)} is the ambient
normalization of the quadruple condition used above.

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 54--59]
\emph{Checked at HEAD \texttt{fe7165a3c}.} \file{additiveTupleCount}, \file{phiAdditiveTupleCount}, \file{GammaHomOfOrder} and \file{GammaAdditive} are at lines~322, 327, 334 and~306 of \file{Definitions.lean}; \file{lemma_9_3} and \file{corollary_9_4} at lines~77 and~91 of \file{Sections08\_09.lean}; \file{lemma_9_3_holds} and \file{corollary_9_4_holds} at lines~376 and~416 of \file{Proofs09Restriction.lean}. No new statement with exponent~$54$ has been added to the development.
\end{writenote}

A useful implementation order is:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Prove the two-relation completion lemma for integer coefficients
      on finite abelian groups, with the cyclic gcd corollary.
\item Formalize the finite shift-grid identity and the distinction
      between products over positions and products over distinct points.
\item Establish the exact nonprincipal coefficient mass and the
      repeated-tuple H\"older bound.
\item Prove the signed expectation certificate and instantiate its
      finite probability space with the cosine coefficients.
\item Certify the five integer inequalities by exact arithmetic, then
      expose new strengthened statements with exponent $54$ and the
      explicit $N_0$; derive the existing weaker interfaces from them.
\end{enumerate}
No Lean source is included in this package, because a theorem statement
with an unproved placeholder would not be a formalization. The
accompanying source audit supplies the pinned provenance needed for
integration. The existing report can incorporate these sections as a
new contribution while preserving the earlier source identifiers and
their priority credits.

\section[{Conventions and the exact imported results\srctag{57}}]{Conventions and the exact imported results}\label{gsr:en:57:sec:d2}\label{gsr:en:57:qt:conventions}
\srcnote{57}{Section 2}

Throughout the Fourier part, $p$ is prime, $\Fp$ has normalized counting
measure, and $\ep(t)=\exp(2\pi i t/p)$. We use
\[
 \widehat f(r)=\E_{x\in\Fp}f(x)\ep(-rx),\qquad
 \D_hf(x)=f(x+h)\overline{f(x)}.
\]
Thus the Fourier transform used in Gowers's paper is $p\widehat f$.
The source uses the backward derivative
$\nabla_hf(x)=f(x)\overline{f(x-h)}$. The identity
\[
 \nabla_{h_1}\cdots\nabla_{h_s}f(x)
 =\D_{h_1}\cdots\D_{h_s}f(x-h_1-\cdots-h_s)
\]
shows that its Fourier coefficient at $r$ differs from ours by the
unit factor $\ep(-r(h_1+\cdots+h_s))$. In particular, the moduli and
frequency labels in every imported hypothesis and conclusion agree.
For a finite abelian group $G$ we instead index the normalized Fourier
transform by its character group $\widehat G$. Write
$Q_d(f)=\|f\|_{U^d(G)}^{2^d}$. The basic identities needed below are
\begin{align}
 Q_2(f)&=\sum_{\chi\in\widehat G}|\widehat f(\chi)|^4,
 &\sum_{\chi\in\widehat G}|\widehat f(\chi)|^2&=\E_x|f(x)|^2,
 \label{gsr:en:57:qt:fourier}\\
 Q_{s+2}(f)&=\E_{h_1,\ldots,h_s}
 Q_2(\D_{h_1}\cdots\D_{h_s}f).
 \label{gsr:en:57:qt:recursion}
\end{align}
All $L^r$ norms are normalized. In particular, $|f|\le1$ implies
$0\le Q_d(f)\le1$. The failure of cubic $\alpha$-uniformity in the
pinned catalogue is exactly $Q_4(f)>\alpha$.

An arithmetic progression in $\Fp$ is represented by
$P=\{x+jd:0\le j<m\}$, together with its integer length $m$.
It is \emph{proper} when these $m$ elements are distinct. We always
require $d\ne0$. The full field, represented with $m=p$ and $d=1$, is
a proper progression. A bilinear formula in the terminology of
Section~13 means
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:57:qt:multiaffine}
 \mu(h,k)=c_{00}+c_{10}h+c_{01}k+c_{11}hk .
\end{equation}
It need not be additive in either variable. We call this a
\emph{multiaffine formula} when distinguishing it from the homogeneous
bilinear map $chk$.

\subsection{Arrangements and Freiman restrictions}

A map $\phi:A\to\Fp$, where $A\subseteq\Fp^2$, is separately Freiman
of order eight if each horizontal and vertical restriction preserves
every equality between two sums of eight elements of that fibre,
with repetitions permitted.

\begin{definition}[Ordered eight-arrangements]\label{gsr:en:57:qt:arrangement}
Put $\sigma_j=1$ for $1\le j\le8$ and $\sigma_j=-1$ for $9\le j\le16$.
An ordered eight-arrangement is a tuple
\[
 (x_1,\ldots,x_{16},y_1,\ldots,y_{16},h),
 \qquad \sum_{j=1}^{16}\sigma_jx_j=0 .
\]
Its $32$ labelled vertices are
$v_{j,0}=(x_j,y_j)$ and $v_{j,1}=(x_j,y_j+h)$.
It lies in $A$ if all these vertices lie in $A$, and it is
\emph{respected} by $\phi$ if
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^{16}\sigma_j
 \bigl(\phi(x_j,y_j+h)-\phi(x_j,y_j)\bigr)=0.
\]
Denote the total and respected counts by $T(A)$ and $R(A,\phi)$.
Degenerate arrangements and repeated physical vertices are counted.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[A uniform upper count]\label{gsr:en:57:qt:total-count}
If $|A|=\beta p^2$, then $T(A)\le\beta^{15}p^{32}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For fixed $h,x$, let $n_h(x)$ count the $y$ for which both
$(x,y),(x,y+h)$ lie in $A$. Then $n_h(x)\le p$ and
$\sum_x n_h(x)\le|A|$. For each $h$, the first fifteen $x$ coordinates
determine $x_{16}$, so the number of arrangements at height $h$ is at
most $p(\sum_x n_h(x))^{15}\le p|A|^{15}$. Summing over $h$ gives
$p^2|A|^{15}=\beta^{15}p^{32}$.
\end{proof}

The following two inputs are from Gowers \cite{gowers}, with the
normalization and the exact constants recorded here.

\begin{inputtheorem}[One-fibre restriction]\label{gsr:en:57:qt:fibre-input}
Suppose $g:\Fp\to\C$ satisfies $|g|\le1$, $U\subseteq\Fp$ has density
$u>0$, and $\psi:U\to\Fp$ obeys
$|\widehat{\D_kg}(\psi(k))|\ge a$ for every $k\in U$, where $0<a\le1$.
There is $V\subseteq U$ of size at least
\[
 2^{-1882}a^{9312}u^{1165}p
\]
on which $\psi$ is a Freiman homomorphism of order eight.
\end{inputtheorem}
\begin{proof}[Derivation from the cited inputs]
The sum of the squared \emph{unnormalized} Fourier coefficients is at
least $ua^2p^3$. Proposition~6.1 gives at least $u^4a^8p^3$
$\psi$-additive quadruples. Corollary~7.6 says that a graph on a
density-$u$ set with at least $\gamma(up)^3$ additive quadruples has an
order-eight restriction of size $2^{-1882}\gamma^{1164}up$.
Taking $\gamma=ua^8$ gives the display. These are the original
constants; no strengthened Freiman theorem is being assumed.
\end{proof}

\begin{inputtheorem}[Gowers's Lemma 12.4]\label{gsr:en:57:qt:abundance-input}
Let $|f|\le1$, let $A\subseteq\Fp^2$ have density $\beta>0$, and suppose
$|\widehat{\D_k\D_lf}(\phi(k,l))|\ge a>0$ on $A$. Then
\[
 R(A,\phi)\ge\beta^{112}a^{336}p^{32}.
\]
\end{inputtheorem}

\subsection{The uniform common-square interface}

The geometric extraction is the substantial inherited part of
Section~13. It must be imported with its \emph{uniform density}
quantifiers: a lower density bound is fixed before the modulus and
before the actual input set. The statement below is precisely the
interface supplied by the pinned repository, not an assumption of
Theorem~13.12 itself.

\begin{inputtheorem}[Uniform common-square extraction]\label{gsr:en:57:qt:square-input}
For every $0<\delta\le1$ there is an integer $N_{\mathrm{sq}}(\delta)$
such that the following holds for every prime $p\ge N_{\mathrm{sq}}(\delta)$.
Suppose $A\subseteq\Fp^2$ has actual density $\beta\ge\delta$,
$\phi:A\to\Fp$ is separately Freiman of order eight, and
\[
 R(A,\phi)\ge(1-2^{-44})T(A).
\]
There are proper progressions $P,Q$ with the same nonzero step and the
same integer length $m$, a set $B\subseteq A\cap(P\times Q)$, and a
global formula \eqref{gsr:en:57:qt:multiaffine} agreeing with $\phi$ on $B$, such
that
\begin{align}
 m&\ge p^{\gamma(\delta)},&
 |B|&\ge 2^{-137}\delta^{704}m^2,\label{gsr:en:57:qt:imported-square}\\
 \gamma(\delta)&=
 \frac{2^{-386}\delta^{1856}}{2^{13\mathcal Q(\delta)}},&
 \mathcal Q(\delta)&=2^{2^{20}}\delta^{-2^{21}}.\label{gsr:en:57:qt:gamma}
\end{align}
\end{inputtheorem}

The exact Lean declaration is
\begin{center}
\small\path{section13_complete_square_extraction_uniform_density}
\end{center}
in \path{Proofs13UniformSquareExtraction.lean} \cite{repo57}.
The exponent formula is in
\path{Proofs13CompleteSquareExtraction.lean}.
The conclusion called \texttt{BilinearOn} there means agreement with
one global formula of the displayed kind. Extending that formula to
$P\times Q$ is therefore legitimate, even though agreement with the
selected frequencies is needed only on $B$.
Partial maps can be extended arbitrarily off their specified domains
when constructing the total map in the Lean context; every relevant
arrangement has all vertices inside that domain.

\begin{lemma}[Absorbing the prefactor]\label{gsr:en:57:qt:gamma-bound}
For $0<\delta\le1$,
$\gamma(\delta)\ge2^{-15\mathcal Q(\delta)}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Put $x=\delta^{-1}\ge1$. The elementary estimate $\log_2x\le2x$
follows from $\log x\le x$ and $\log2>1/2$. Since
$\mathcal Q(\delta)\ge3712\delta^{-1}$ and
$\mathcal Q(\delta)\ge386$, we obtain
\[
 386+1856\log_2(\delta^{-1})\le2\mathcal Q(\delta).
\]
Taking binary logarithms in \eqref{gsr:en:57:qt:gamma} proves the claim.
The same estimate is already proved in
\path{Proofs13ExplicitFourierExponent.lean}; the short calculation is
included to expose the quantitative dependence.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Fej\'er purification for the Section 13 arrangements\srctag{57}}]{Fej\'er purification for the Section 13 arrangements}\label{gsr:en:57:sec:d3}\label{gsr:en:57:qt:fejer-section}
\srcnote{57}{Section 3}

We reprove the precise specialization of the earlier Fej\'er selection
theorem \cite{repo57fejer} that will be used. This selection theorem is an
inherited ingredient. Its propagation through the common-square
interface, and the endpoint argument that completes the parameter
range, are the refinements developed here.

\begin{samepage}
\begin{theorem}[Specialized Fej\'er purification]\label{gsr:en:57:qt:fejer}
Let $0<\beta,\rho,\eta\le1$, let $A\subseteq\Fp^2$ have density $\beta$,
and let $\phi:A\to\Fp$ satisfy
$R(A,\phi)\ge\rho\beta^{15}p^{32}$. If
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:57:qt:fejer-threshold}
 p\ge 2\beta^{-15}
 \left(\frac{18\cdot33^2}{(\rho\eta)^2}\right)^{32},
\end{equation}
there is $A'\subseteq A$ with
\begin{align}
 R(A',\phi)&\ge
 \frac{\rho^{32}\eta^{31}}{3^{31}33^{32}}\,
 \beta^{15}p^{32},\label{gsr:en:57:qt:fejer-mass}\\
 R(A',\phi)&\ge\frac{1}{1+\eta}T(A')
 \ge(1-\eta)T(A').\label{gsr:en:57:qt:fejer-ratio}
\end{align}
\end{theorem}
\end{samepage}

\subsection{The relation isolated by one scalar feature}

Put $\lambda_{j,0}=-\sigma_j$, $\lambda_{j,1}=\sigma_j$, and use the
single feature $F(x,y)=xy$. There are $32$ free arrangement parameters:
eliminate $x_{16}$ using
$x_{16}=\sum_{j<16}\sigma_jx_j$. For a vector of coefficients
$u=(u_{j,e})\in\Fp^{32}$, the feature relation is the polynomial
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:57:qt:feature-poly}
 \mathcal P_u=
 \sum_{j=1}^{16}x_j
 \bigl((u_{j,0}+u_{j,1})y_j+u_{j,1}h\bigr)
\end{equation}
after that elimination.

\begin{lemma}[Exactly one universal relation]\label{gsr:en:57:qt:universal}
The polynomial $\mathcal P_u$ is identically zero if and only if
$u=c\lambda$ for some $c\in\Fp$. Every other $\mathcal P_u$ is a
nonzero polynomial of total degree at most two.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $j<16$, the coefficients involving $y_j$ force
$u_{j,0}+u_{j,1}=0$. The coefficient of $y_{16}$ is
$(u_{16,0}+u_{16,1})\sum_{j<16}\sigma_jx_j$, so its vanishing forces
the same identity for $j=16$. What remains is
\[
 h\sum_{j<16}(u_{j,1}+\sigma_ju_{16,1})x_j.
\]
Thus $u_{j,1}=\sigma_jc$ with $c=-u_{16,1}$, and the other
coordinates equal $-\sigma_jc$. Conversely these coefficients give
$ch\sum_j\sigma_jx_j=0$.
\end{proof}

Let
$L=\lceil66/(\rho\eta)\rceil$ and $H=L-1$.
Then $L\le99/(\rho\eta)$, and \eqref{gsr:en:57:qt:fejer-threshold} implies
$p>2H$. Reduction modulo $p$ is injective on the integer interval
$[-H,H]$. Consequently the box $[-H,H]^{32}$ meets the universal
relation line exactly in $c\lambda$, $-H\le c\le H$.

Call an arrangement exceptional if an unintended vector in that box
vanishes on its feature values. A nonzero polynomial of total degree
at most two in $32$ variables has at most $2p^{31}$ zeros. Pairing
$u$ with $-u$, which has the identical zero set, bounds the number by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:57:qt:exceptional}
 D\le\bigl((2H+1)^{32}-(2H+1)\bigr)p^{31}
 \le2(2L)^{32}p^{31}.
\end{equation}
The polynomial zero estimate follows by induction: a polynomial
whose degree in the last variable is $t$ has a leading coefficient
of degree at most $D_0-t$; at most
$(D_0-t)p^{r-2}$ base choices kill that coefficient, and every other
base choice permits at most $t$ roots. This gives the standard
$D_0p^{r-1}$ bound.

Every nonexceptional arrangement has distinct physical vertices. A
coincidence of two labels would yield a feature relation with just
one coefficient $1$ and one coefficient $-1$, which is not a multiple
of $\lambda$. This observation includes the arrangements with $h=0$.

\subsection{Positive Fourier coefficients and repeated vertices}

Define the normalized Fej\'er kernel
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:57:qt:kernel}
 K_L(z)=\left|\frac1L\sum_{n=0}^{L-1}z^n\right|^2
 =\sum_{|j|<L}c_jz^j,\qquad
 c_j=\frac{L-|j|}{L^2}.
\end{equation}
On the unit circle $0\le K_L\le1$, the coefficients are nonnegative,
$c_j=c_{-j}$, and $\sum_jc_j=1$. Put
\[
 b_K=L^{-32},\qquad
 A_K=\sum_{|j|<L}c_j^{32}=b_K R_L,\qquad
 R_L=1+2\sum_{j=1}^{L-1}(1-j/L)^{32}.
\]
Convexity of $(1-x)^{32}$ and the trapezoidal bound for its integral
on $[0,1]$ give
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:57:qt:kernel-ratio}
 R_L\ge\frac{2L}{33}\ge\frac4{\rho\eta},
 \qquad A_K\ge\frac2{33}L^{-31}.
\end{equation}

Choose independent uniform $t,u\in\Fp$. Conditional on these seeds,
retain each physical point $v\in A$ independently with probability
$K_L(\ep(t\phi(v)+uF(v)))$.
For a respected arrangement, expanding the product over its
$32$ labels and averaging over $t,u$ retains all intended terms
$c\lambda$. Their total contribution is $A_K$, since all other
surviving coefficients are nonnegative.

This is also a lower bound for the \emph{actual} survival probability
when a physical point has several labels: the labelled product
raises a weight in $[0,1]$ to a higher power, whereas actual selection
uses that weight once. Repeated vertices must be handled in this
direction; independent selection of labels would describe a different
random subset.

For a nonexceptional, unrespected arrangement the physical vertices
are distinct, and every surviving feature relation is $c\lambda$.
Its nonzero $\phi$-defect forces $c=0$, because $|c|\le H<p$.
Its survival probability is therefore exactly $b_K$. Each exceptional
bad arrangement is bounded simply by one.

\subsection{One random outcome has both required properties}

Let $X,Y$ be the numbers of respected and unrespected arrangements
in the selected subset, and put $T_0=\beta^{15}p^{32}$. Then
\[
 \E X\ge\rho A_KT_0,\qquad
 \E Y\le b_KT_0+D .
\]
The threshold \eqref{gsr:en:57:qt:fejer-threshold}, together with
$L\le99/(\rho\eta)$, gives
\[
 D\le2(2L)^{32}p^{31}\le L^{-32}\beta^{15}p^{32}=b_KT_0,
\]
since $2\cdot99^2=18\cdot33^2$. Hence
\[
 \E(X-Y/\eta)\ge(\rho A_K-2b_K/\eta)T_0
 \ge\frac{\rho A_K}{2}T_0>0.
\]
Choose an outcome with score at least its expectation. Then
$Y\le\eta X$ and
\[
 X\ge\frac{\rho A_K}{2}T_0
 \ge\frac{\rho L^{-31}}{33}T_0
 \ge\frac{\rho^{32}\eta^{31}}{3^{31}33^{32}}T_0 .
\]
These are \eqref{gsr:en:57:qt:fejer-mass}--\eqref{gsr:en:57:qt:fejer-ratio}, proving
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:qt:fejer}. No independence between different arrangements is
needed.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Improved quantitative propagation and the printed exponent\srctag{57}}]{Improved quantitative propagation and the printed exponent}\label{gsr:en:57:sec:d4}\label{gsr:en:57:qt:propagation}
\srcnote{57}{Section 4}

\subsection{Keeping the exact initial density exponent}

\begin{proposition}[Prepared frequency graph]\label{gsr:en:57:qt:prepared}
Let $0<\alpha<1$, put $a=\alpha/2$, and let $|f|\le1$ with
$Q_4(f)>\alpha$. There is a set $A_2\subseteq\Fp^2$ of density
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:57:qt:initial-density}
 \beta\ge a^b,\qquad b=14\,409\,429,
\end{equation}
and a separately order-eight Freiman map $\phi:A_2\to\Fp$ such that
$|\widehat{\D_h\D_k f}(\phi(h,k))|\ge a$ on $A_2$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For each $(h,k)$, write $M(h,k)$ for the largest Fourier modulus of
$\D_h\D_kf$. By \eqref{gsr:en:57:qt:fourier}--\eqref{gsr:en:57:qt:recursion},
\[
 \alpha<Q_4(f)\le\E_{h,k}M(h,k)^2,
\]
because the sum of the squared Fourier moduli of each second
derivative is at most one. Let $A_0=\{(h,k):M(h,k)\ge a\}$, of
density $d_0$. Then $\alpha<d_0+(1-d_0)a^2$. Since $\alpha=2a$ and
$0<a\le1/2$, this implies $d_0\ge a$. Choose a maximizing frequency
at each pair in $A_0$.

For each fixed $h$, let $u_h$ be its fibre density. Apply
Input theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:qt:fibre-input} to $g=\D_hf$ and that fibre; empty fibres
contribute zero and need no invocation. Summing the retained sizes
and using convexity gives a set of density
\[
 \beta_1\ge2^{-1882}a^{9312}\E_hu_h^{1165}
 \ge2^{-1882}a^{10477}\ge a^{12359}.
\]
The last inequality uses $a\le1/2$. Repeat the same argument in the
other coordinate. Restriction preserves the first Freiman property,
and
\begin{align*}
 \beta&\ge2^{-1882}a^{9312}\beta_1^{1165}\\
 &\ge a^{1882+9312+12359\cdot1165}
 =a^{14\,409\,429}.
\end{align*}
The Fourier lower bound survives both restrictions.
\end{proof}

The familiar rounded bound $\beta\ge a^{2^{24}}$ follows immediately.
Retaining $b$ instead of rounding it is useful: it lowers the final
power-of-two density exponent by one more factor of two.

\begin{proposition}[Improved purification density]\label{gsr:en:57:qt:purified}
Under the hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:57:qt:prepared}, suppose
$p\ge a^{-2^{37}}$. There is $A_3\subseteq A_2$ with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:57:qt:delta}
 |A_3|/p^2\ge\delta:=a^d,\qquad d=2\,996\,201\,429,
\end{equation}
such that $\phi$ remains separately Freiman of order eight,
every selected Fourier coefficient has modulus at least $a$, and
\[
 R(A_3,\phi)\ge(1-2^{-44})T(A_3).
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Put $\beta_0=a^b$, $\eta=2^{-44}$ and
$\rho_0=\beta_0^{97}a^{336}$. For the actual density $\beta\ge\beta_0$,
Input theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:qt:abundance-input} yields
\[
 R(A_2,\phi)\ge\beta^{112}a^{336}p^{32}
 \ge\rho_0\beta^{15}p^{32}.
\]
Thus the lower proportion parameter is fixed independently of the
actual density.

The right side of \eqref{gsr:en:57:qt:fejer-threshold} is largest when
$\beta=\beta_0$. Since $18\cdot33^2<2^{17}$, a sufficient upper
bound for it is
\begin{align}
 2\beta_0^{-15}
 \left(\frac{18\cdot33^2}{(\rho_0\eta)^2}\right)^{32}
 &\le a^{-(6223b+24865)}\nonumber\\
 &=a^{-89\,669\,901\,532}
 \le a^{-2^{37}}. \label{gsr:en:57:qt:threshold-arithmetic}
\end{align}
Here $2^j\le a^{-j}$ for every nonnegative integer $j$.
The field-size and characteristic requirements of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:qt:fejer} are both included in this bound.

Apply that theorem. With
$C_0=2^{-1364}/(3^{31}33^{32})\ge2^{-1618}$, its mass bound gives
\begin{align*}
 R(A_3,\phi)
 &\ge C_0\beta_0^{3104}\beta^{15}a^{10752}p^{32}\\
 &\ge a^{3119b+10752+1618}p^{32}
 =a^{44\,943\,021\,421}p^{32}.
\end{align*}
Writing $\beta'=|A_3|/p^2$, Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:57:qt:total-count} implies
$(\beta')^{15}\ge a^{44\,943\,021\,421}$. Therefore
\[
 \beta'\ge a^{44\,943\,021\,421/15}\ge a^d,
 \qquad d=\left\lceil\frac{44\,943\,021\,421}{15}\right\rceil.
\]
The ratio statement is \eqref{gsr:en:57:qt:fejer-ratio}, and the other
properties are hereditary under restriction.
\end{proof}

\subsection{An explicit all-parameter length bound}

\begin{theorem}[Quantitative extraction from the improved preparation]\label{gsr:en:57:qt:all-alpha}
For every $0<\alpha<1$, all sufficiently large primes $p$, and
every $f:\Fp\to\C$ with $|f|\le1$ and $Q_4(f)>\alpha$, there are
proper, equal-length progressions $P,Q$ with the same nonzero
step, a set $B\subseteq P\times Q$, and a formula
\eqref{gsr:en:57:qt:multiaffine}, such that, writing $m=|P|=|Q|$,
\begin{align}
 m&\ge p^{\,2^{-(2/\alpha)^{2^{53}}}},\label{gsr:en:57:qt:all-length}\\
 |B|&\ge(\alpha/2)^{2^{41}}m^2,\label{gsr:en:57:qt:all-mass}\\
 \bigl|\widehat{\D_h\D_kf}\bigl(\mu(h,k)\bigr)\bigr|
 &\ge\alpha/2\quad ((h,k)\in B).\label{gsr:en:57:qt:all-coeff}
\end{align}
More precisely, \eqref{gsr:en:57:qt:all-length}--\eqref{gsr:en:57:qt:all-mass} may be
replaced by $m\ge p^{\gamma(a^d)}$ and
$|B|\ge2^{-137}a^{704d}m^2$, with $a=\alpha/2$ and $d$ as in
\eqref{gsr:en:57:qt:delta}.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Use Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:57:qt:purified} and apply Input theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:qt:square-input} at the lower
density $\delta=a^d$. Its hypotheses use the actual density only
through the lower bound $\delta$, so the threshold is uniform in
the function and all selected sets. The exact bounds follow
directly from \eqref{gsr:en:57:qt:imported-square}.

For the simpler powers of two, Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:57:qt:gamma-bound} gives
$\gamma(a^d)\ge2^{-15\mathcal Q(a^d)}$. Since $a\le1/2$,
\begin{align}
 15\mathcal Q(a^d)
 &=15\cdot2^{2^{20}}a^{-d2^{21}}\nonumber\\
 &\le a^{-(d2^{21}+2^{20}+4)}
 \le a^{-2^{53}},\label{gsr:en:57:qt:spectral-arithmetic}
\end{align}
where the penultimate exponent is
$6\,283\,489\,820\,278\,788<2^{53}$. Also
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:57:qt:mass-arithmetic}
 2^{-137}a^{704d}
 \ge a^{137+704d}
 =a^{2\,109\,325\,806\,153}
 \ge a^{2^{41}}.
\end{equation}
Agreement with $\phi$ on $B$ transfers the Fourier lower bound.
\end{proof}

The repository has also proved the length exponent $2^{61}$ in place of $2^{70}$, with density $(\alpha/2)^{2^{42}}$, for all $0<\alpha\le1$ by the larger overlap $\alpha\le332/333$ (\file{theorem_13_12_with_improved_printed_bounds}, \file{Proofs13ImprovedPrintedBounds.lean}, line~11); that strengthening is the repository's, not this source's. \file{FORMALIZATION\_STATUS.txt} credits source~57's route.

\begin{remark}[The size threshold]\label{gsr:en:57:qt:threshold-remark}
One may take
\[
 N_0(\alpha)=
 \max\left\{2,\left\lceil(\alpha/2)^{-2^{37}}\right\rceil,
 N_{\mathrm{sq}}\bigl((\alpha/2)^d\bigr)\right\}.
\]
This is a precise uniform threshold defined using the inherited
extraction threshold. The power $(\alpha/2)^{-2^{37}}$ is an explicit
sufficient threshold for \emph{purification}; it is not asserted to
bound the whole extraction. No closed elementary expression for
$N_{\mathrm{sq}}$ is derived in this article.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Why an endpoint argument is necessary}

The length exponent in \eqref{gsr:en:57:qt:all-length} does not by itself
dominate the printed exponent for every $\alpha$ approaching one.
The factor $2/\alpha$ matters inside these powers. We retain that
distinction rather than absorbing it informally.

For $\alpha\le1-2^{-10}$, comparison of the two exponents reduces to
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:57:qt:overlap}
 (2^{17}-1)\log(1/\alpha)\ge\log2.
\end{equation}
Indeed it is equivalent to
$(2/\alpha)^{2^{53}}\le\alpha^{-2^{70}}$.
Now $\log(1/\alpha)\ge1-\alpha\ge2^{-10}$, and
$(2^{17}-1)2^{-10}>1>\log2$, so \eqref{gsr:en:57:qt:overlap} holds.

For the remaining interval, an elementary rigidity argument gives
a much stronger ambient square:
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:near-u4} proves that $Q_4(f)\ge1-\varepsilon$ implies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:57:qt:endpoint-summary}
 |B|\ge(1-332\varepsilon)p^2,\qquad
 |\widehat{\D_h\D_kf}(chk)|\ge3/4-4\varepsilon
 \quad((h,k)\in B).
\end{equation}
With $\varepsilon=1-\alpha\le2^{-10}$, these bounds are at least
$173p^2/256$ and $191/256$. Take $P=Q=\Fp$, both represented
properly with step one. Their length $p$ dominates the printed
lower bound, the coefficient exceeds $\alpha/2$, and their good-pair
density exceeds $a^{2^{41}}$.

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:57:main:extraction}]
Use Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:qt:all-alpha} and \eqref{gsr:en:57:qt:overlap} when
$0<\alpha\le1-2^{-10}$. Use \eqref{gsr:en:57:qt:endpoint-summary}, proved in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:near-u4}, when $1-2^{-10}<\alpha<1$.
The threshold in Remark~\ref{gsr:en:57:qt:threshold-remark} works for the combined
statement. At $\alpha=1$ the strict hypothesis $Q_4(f)>\alpha$ is
impossible; the non-strict equality case is separately included in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:near-u4} with $\varepsilon=0$.
\end{proof}

The new mechanism is the reduction of the density loss before the
geometric extraction. A change from $a^{2^{66}}$ to $a^d$ in that
input is amplified by the factor $\delta^{-2^{21}}$ inside
$\mathcal Q(\delta)$. The endpoint argument then removes the
remaining parameter-range obstruction. Neither step changes an
integer progression length into a real interval or assumes
unrestricted versions of the raw catalogue extraction statements.
