\section{Source~57's chapter: bounded Schur deficits and the third energy level \wtag}\label{gsr:en:sec:thirdlevel}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the tenth write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next section is source~57's Section~6. \emph{Logically it continues source~45's chapter} on the top of the torsion-free energy spectrum (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:energylevels}); it is printed here because no number printed earlier may move.

\emph{What is proved.} For a positive real set $C$ of $n$ elements with Schur deficit $h(C)=s$ and $n\ge5s-1$, $C$ is a positive dilate of $\{j+\lambda_j:1\le j\le n\}$ with $(\lambda_j)$ nondecreasing, nonnegative and summing to $s$, so there are exactly $p(s)$ classes (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:st:partitions}); for $s=2$ the threshold $n=6$ is optimal (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:st:schur-two}). For $m\ge7$ the $m$-element torsion-free sets with $E(A)=M_m-8(m-3)$, $M_m=(2m^3+m)/3$, are exactly the affine images of $J_m=\{0,\ldots,m\}\setminus\{2\}$ and $K_m=\{0,2,3,\ldots,m-1,m+1\}$; at $m=6$ there is one further class, $\{0,1,2,4,5,6\}$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:st:third-equality}). These answer source~45's first two research questions, its Questions~6.1--6.2 (Question~\ref{gsr:fz:45:q:third} and the question after it; item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:energylevels}); the energy recurrence and the first two levels are source~45's and Hegyv\'ari's, credited. The results concern ordered real and torsion-free sets; the transfer to cyclic groups needs a Freiman isomorphism, as source~57 says.

\emph{Relation to the formal statements.} No declaration concerns energy levels or Schur deficits; nothing in this chapter is formalized.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Bounded Schur defects and integer partitions\srctag{57}}]{Bounded Schur defects and integer partitions}\label{gsr:en:57:sec:d6}
\srcnote{57}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:en:57:st:section}

The ordered endpoint of Gowers's Section~7 has a discrete structure that
is invisible in a bound with an unspecified constant: an arithmetic
progression maximizes the additive energy of an $m$-element torsion-free
set, and the next attainable energies have exact linear deficits.
Source~45 of the pinned repository~\cite{repo57levels} determined the first three values and
classified the first two equality cases. It explicitly left open the
classification at the third value and a general question about positive
sets with a bounded deficit in their Schur-triple count. We answer both
questions here.

The two conclusions have different scopes. Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:st:partitions}
classifies every fixed Schur deficit by integer partitions, beyond an
explicit linear threshold in the deficit. Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:st:third-equality}
classifies every third-level energy extremizer, with the optimal threshold
of seven points. These statements concern real or torsion-free sets.
They require an explicit rectification hypothesis before being applied
to subsets of a finite cyclic group.

The maximum Schur count and its arithmetic-progression equality case are
classical; see Huczynska~\cite[Theorem~9]{huczynska}. Her paper studies
attainable counts in intervals, with its near-extremal structural section
focused on the lower endpoint. The energy recurrence and congruence used
below occur in Hegyv\'ari~\cite[Section~2.1]{hegyvari}. We reproduce
short proofs of the required earlier ingredients to make the new
classification self-contained. The additions relative to the pinned
repository are the bounded-deficit partition theorem, the complete
Schur-defect-two classification, and the third-energy equality theorem;
no worldwide publication-priority assertion is intended.

\subsection{Two consecutive perfect reflection rows}

Let $C=\{c_1<\cdots<c_n\}\subset(0,\infty)$, and define
\begin{equation}
 S(C)=\#\{(x,y,z)\in C^3:x+y=z\},\qquad
 h(C)=\binom n2-S(C).
 \label{gsr:en:57:st:schur-defect}
\end{equation}
The summands are ordered and may coincide. Write $r_j$ for the number
of ordered representations $x+y=c_j$ with $x,y\in C$, and put
\begin{equation}
 e_j=j-1-r_j.
 \label{gsr:en:57:st:row-defect}
\end{equation}
Both summands precede $c_j$, and each first summand determines the second.
Consequently $e_j\geq0$ and $h(C)=\sum_j e_j$. We call row $j$
\emph{perfect} when $e_j=0$. Equivalently, its preceding prefix is
invariant under the reflection $x\mapsto c_j-x$.

\begin{lemma}[Two perfect rows]
\label{gsr:en:57:st:two-perfect}
If rows $j$ and $j+1$ are perfect, then $c_i=id$ for
$1\leq i\leq j+1$, where $d=c_1>0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The case $j=1$ is immediate. For $j\geq2$, put
\[
 P=\{c_1,\ldots,c_{j-1}\},\quad Q=P\cup\{c_j\},\quad
 t=c_{j+1}-c_j>0.
\]
Perfectness gives $c_j-P=P$ and $c_{j+1}-Q=Q$, whence
\[
 P+t=c_{j+1}-(c_j-P)\subseteq Q.
\]
The left side has $j-1$ points and omits $\min Q=c_1$, so it equals
$Q\setminus\{c_1\}$. Comparing the increasing lists gives
$c_{i+1}=c_i+t$ for $1\leq i<j$. The first reflection also gives
$c_j=c_1+c_{j-1}$. Substitution yields $c_1=t$, and therefore
$c_i=it$ for $i\leq j+1$.
\end{proof}

In particular, after the first imperfect row there cannot be two
consecutive perfect rows. This simple observation controls the entire
finite pattern, rather than only the last representation count.

\subsection{All fixed Schur deficits are eventually partitions}

\begin{theorem}[A bounded terminal perturbation]
\label{gsr:en:57:st:terminal}
Let $s\geq1$ be an integer. If $|C|=n\geq3s+1$ and $h(C)\leq s$,
then for some $d>0$ the set $d^{-1}C$ consists of positive integers and
\begin{equation}
 \{1,\ldots,n-2s\}\subseteq d^{-1}C
 \subseteq\{1,\ldots,n+s\}.
 \label{gsr:en:57:st:terminal-inclusions}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If every row is perfect, successive reflections give $C=d\{1,\ldots,n\}$.
Otherwise let $k$ be the first imperfect row. Before it, $c_i=id$ with
$d=c_1$. The suffix of rows $k,\ldots,n$ starts with an imperfect row,
has at most $s$ imperfect rows, and has no two consecutive perfect rows
by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:57:st:two-perfect}. It therefore has at most $2s$ rows.
Thus
\[
 L:=k-1\geq n-2s\geq s+1.
\]
For every $j\geq k$,
$r_j=j-1-e_j\geq L-s\geq1$. Hence $c_j$ is a sum of two earlier
points, and induction makes $a_j=c_j/d$ an integer.

For $j\geq k$, put $g_j=a_j-a_{j-1}$. Every
$x\in\{1,\ldots,\min(g_j-1,L)\}$ is an earlier point, but
$a_j-x>a_{j-1}$, so its partner is absent. Therefore
\[
 e_j\geq\min(g_j-1,L).
\]
Since $e_j\leq s<L$, we have $g_j-1<L$ and $e_j\geq g_j-1$.
Summing over $j\geq k$ gives
\[
 a_n-n=\sum_{j=k}^n(g_j-1)\leq\sum_{j=k}^n e_j\leq s.
\]
This proves both inclusions in \eqref{gsr:en:57:st:terminal-inclusions}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Partition classification]
\label{gsr:en:57:st:partitions}
Let $s\geq1$ and $n\geq5s-1$ be integers. A positive real $n$-set
$C$ satisfies $h(C)=s$ if and only if
\begin{equation}
 C=d\{j+\lambda_j:1\leq j\leq n\}
 \label{gsr:en:57:st:partition-model}
\end{equation}
for some $d>0$ and integers
\begin{equation}
 0\leq\lambda_1\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_n,
 \qquad\sum_{j=1}^n\lambda_j=s.
 \label{gsr:en:57:st:partition-conditions}
\end{equation}
There are exactly $p(s)$ such sets up to positive dilation, where $p(s)$
is the ordinary partition function. In every model,
$\lambda_1=\cdots=\lambda_{n-s}=0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Since $5s-1\geq3s+1$, Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:st:terminal} applies. Normalize
$d=1$ and write $C=\{a_1<\cdots<a_n\}$ with integer entries. Let
$H=\{1,\ldots,a_n\}\setminus C$ be its holes. Every hole is at least
$n-2s+1$, whereas $a_n\leq n+s$. The threshold gives
\begin{equation}
 2(n-2s+1)>n+s\geq a_n.
 \label{gsr:en:57:st:no-two-holes}
\end{equation}
Thus no sum of two holes belongs to $C$.

For a point $a_j$, exactly $a_j-j$ integers below it are holes.
For each such hole $z$, the positive integer $a_j-z$ cannot be another
hole, by \eqref{gsr:en:57:st:no-two-holes}; hence it is an earlier point of $C$.
It supplies one failed reflection entry in row $j$. Conversely, every
failed entry arises in this way. Therefore
\begin{equation}
 e_j=a_j-j.
 \label{gsr:en:57:st:exact-area}
\end{equation}
Set $\lambda_j=a_j-j$. Strict increase of the integer $a_j$ makes
these numbers nonnegative and nondecreasing; their sum is $h(C)=s$.
This proves necessity.

Conversely, suppose \eqref{gsr:en:57:st:partition-conditions} holds. There are at
most $s$ positive entries, so $a_j=j$ for $j\leq n-s$ and
$a_n\leq n+s$. Every hole is at least $n-s+1$, and
$2(n-s+1)>n+s$. Again no sum of two holes belongs to $C$, so the same
argument proves \eqref{gsr:en:57:st:exact-area} and $h(C)=s$.

Finally $n>s$, so $\lambda_1=0$ and the dilation is fixed by $d=c_1$.
The positive tail of $(\lambda_j)$ is exactly an integer partition of
$s$, written in increasing order and padded by zeros. This gives the
count $p(s)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Checked at the eleventh write} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:energygap}): source~66 proves the same normal form for $n\ge3r+1$ (its Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:partition}), better than $5s-1$ for $s\ge3$; with Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:st:schur-two} and source~66's obstruction at $n=2s+1$, the optimal threshold satisfies $2s+2\le N(s)\le3s+1$ for $s\ge3$, and source~66 conjectures $2s+2$. The two sources were written the same day; neither cites the other.
\end{writenote}

For example, at deficit three the only eventual models are
\[
 \begin{split}
 &\{1,\ldots,n-1,n+3\},\\
 &\{1,\ldots,n-2,n,n+2\},\\
 &\{1,\ldots,n-3,n-1,n,n+1\},
 \end{split}
\]
up to positive dilation. The theorem supplies the sufficient threshold
$n\geq14$ in this example; it does not assert that this threshold is
optimal. For deficit two we next obtain the optimal threshold directly.

\subsection{The complete deficit-two classification}

\begin{theorem}[Two missing Schur representations]
\label{gsr:en:57:st:schur-two}
For $n\geq6$, the positive real $n$-sets with $h(C)=2$ are precisely
\begin{equation}
 d\{1,\ldots,n-1,n+2\}\quad\hbox{and}\quad
 d\{1,\ldots,n-2,n,n+1\},\qquad d>0.
 \label{gsr:en:57:st:two-models}
\end{equation}
At $n=5$ there is exactly one additional dilation class,
$d\{1,2,4,5,6\}$. Thus six is the optimal eventual threshold.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $k$ be the first imperfect row and put $d=c_1$. The preceding points
are $c_i=id$. There is either one row of defect two or two rows of
defect one.

Suppose first that $k\geq4$ and $e_k=2$. Since $r_k=k-3>0$,
$c_k=qd$ for an integer $q$. For $k\leq q\leq2k-2$, the number of
ordered pairs from $\{1,\ldots,k-1\}$ with sum $q$ is $2k-1-q$;
above this range it is zero. The condition $r_k=k-3$ therefore gives
$q=k+2$. A following row would have to be perfect. Reflection of
$\{1,\ldots,k-1,k+2\}$ would have sum $k+3$, sending the present
point $2$ to the absent point $k+1$. Hence there is no following row,
and $k=n$, giving the first model.

If $k\geq4$ and $e_k=1$, the same calculation gives $c_k=(k+1)d$.
The next row cannot be perfect: its reflection would send $2$ to the
missing $k$. Thus $e_{k+1}=1$, and all later rows must be perfect.
Normalize $d=1$. The next point $q=c_{k+1}$ is an integer, because
$r_{k+1}=k-1>0$, and $q\geq k+2$. Its representation count in
$\{1,\ldots,k-1,k+1\}$ is
\[
 \max(2k-1-q,0)
 +2\mathbf1_{\{1\leq q-k-1\leq k-1\}}
 +\mathbf1_{\{q=2k+2\}}.
\]
At $q=k+2$ this equals $k-1$. At larger $q$ it is at most $k-2$:
the interval contribution is at most $\max(k-4,0)$, the mixed
contribution is at most two, and the isolated double-summand case has
value one. Hence $q=k+2$. A further perfect row would reflect
$\{1,\ldots,k-1,k+1,k+2\}$ with sum $k+3$, sending the present
point $3$ to the missing $k$. Thus $n=k+1$, giving the second model.

For $k=3$, the first two points are $d,2d$. If $e_3=2$, the third
row has no representations. A following perfect row would make the
three-point prefix symmetric and force $c_3=3d$, a contradiction.
If $e_3=1$, then $c_3=4d$. The next row must have defect one,
and its two representations force $c_4=5d$ or $6d$. The prefix
$\{1,2,4,6\}$ is not symmetric, so the latter choice cannot continue.
The prefix $\{1,2,4,5\}$ is symmetric with sum six, allowing $c_5=6d$;
then $\{1,2,4,5,6\}$ is not symmetric. This yields exactly the extra
five-point model and no model of size six or more.

It remains to exclude $k=2$ when $n\geq5$. Write $c_1=a,c_2=b$,
where $0<a<b$ and $b\ne2a$. Here $e_2=1$. If $e_3=0$, then
$c_3=a+b$. The fourth row cannot be perfect, because symmetry of
$\{a,b,a+b\}$ would force $b=2a$. Its defect must therefore be one,
and its two representations give $c_4=2a+b$ or $a+2b$.
Neither four-point prefix is symmetric: comparison of its inner and
outer pair sums would force respectively $b=2a$ or $a=0$. If instead
$e_3=1$, its unique representation gives $c_3=2a$ or $2b$.
A subsequent perfect row requires $a+c_3=2b$. The second option is
impossible, while the first gives $b=3a/2$ and a four-point prefix
proportional to $\{2,3,4,6\}$, which again is not symmetric.
Thus no case with $k=2$ reaches five points.

The two models in \eqref{gsr:en:57:st:two-models} have final row defects
$(2)$ and $(1,1)$ respectively. The exceptional five-point model has
row defects $(0,0,1,1,0)$. This also verifies sufficiency.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Ordered energy and its first gaps}

For a nonempty real set $A$ of size $m$, define
\begin{equation}
 E(A)=\#\{(a,b,c,d)\in A^4:a+b=c+d\},\quad
 M_m=\frac{2m^3+m}{3},\quad D(A)=\frac{M_m-E(A)}4.
 \label{gsr:en:57:st:energy-defect}
\end{equation}
For $B$ of size $n$ and $a>\max B$, set
\[
 T(B,a)=\#\{(x,y,z)\in B^3:x+y-z=a\},\qquad
 e(B,a)=\binom n2-T(B,a).
\]
Each pair $z<x$ in $B$ determines the only possible completion
$y=a-x+z$. Thus $e(B,a)$ is a nonnegative integer. Counting the
occurrences of the largest point in an additive quadruple gives
\[
 E(B\cup\{a\})=E(B)+4n+1+4T(B,a),
\]
and therefore
\begin{equation}
 D(B\cup\{a\})=D(B)+e(B,a).
 \label{gsr:en:57:st:endpoint}
\end{equation}
Iterating from a singleton also gives the useful exact identity
\begin{equation}
 D(A)=\#\{x<y<z\hbox{ in }A:x+z-y\notin A\}.
 \label{gsr:en:57:st:ordered-completion}
\end{equation}
These identities prove that $D(A)$ is a nonnegative integer.

The transformation $C=a-B$ identifies $e(B,a)=h(C)$. Consequently,
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:st:partitions} already has a direct endpoint interpretation:
if $e(B,a)=s$ and $|B|\geq5s-1$, then $B\cup\{a\}$ is an affine
image of
\[
 \{0\}\cup\{j+\lambda_j:1\leq j\leq |B|\},
\]
with $(\lambda_j)$ a partition of $s$ as above. It is contained in an
arithmetic progression of length at most $|B|+1+s$ and omits at most
$s$ points from it.

We recall the short endpoint facts needed for energy equality.

\begin{lemma}[Endpoint costs zero and one]
\label{gsr:en:57:st:endpoint-small}
For $a>\max B$, one has $e(B,a)=0$ if and only if $B\cup\{a\}$
is an arithmetic progression. If $|B|=n\geq4$ and $e(B,a)=1$, then,
after translating $\min B$ to zero, for some $d>0$,
\begin{equation}
 B=d\{0,2,3,\ldots,n\},\qquad a=(n+1)d.
 \label{gsr:en:57:st:unit-endpoint}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The zero assertion follows from the zero-defect Schur classification:
$h(C)=0$ forces $C=d\{1,\ldots,n\}$ by its perfect rows. For defect
one there is a unique imperfect row $k$. Before it $c_i=id$. If
$k\geq3$, its $k-2>0$ representations force $c_k=(k+1)d$.
A following perfect row would reflect $2d$ to the missing $kd$, so
$k=n$. If $k=2$, perfect rows three and four would force first
$c_3=d+c_2$ and then $2c_2=d+c_3$, contradicting $c_2\ne2d$.
Thus $C=d\{1,\ldots,n-1,n+1\}$. Since $a=\max C$ after
$\min B=0$, this is exactly \eqref{gsr:en:57:st:unit-endpoint}.
\end{proof}

For an AP $B=d\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, a nonintegral value of $a/d$
has $T(B,a)=0$. For an integer $a/d=q\geq n$,
\begin{equation}
 T(B,a)=\sum_{h=\max(1,q-n+1)}^{n-1}(n-h).
 \label{gsr:en:57:st:ap-endpoint}
\end{equation}
Indeed a positive difference $hd$ has $n-h$ representations, and
its completion belongs to $B$ precisely when $q-h\leq n-1$.
The successive exceptional endpoints $q=n,n+1$ have costs $0,n-1$;
for $n\geq4$, every other endpoint has cost at least $2n-3$.

Define
\[
 H_m=\{0,1,\ldots,m-2,m\},\qquad
 L_m=\{0,2,3,\ldots,m\}=m-H_m.
\]
An affine model permits both positive and negative nonzero slopes.

\begin{proposition}[The preceding energy gaps]
\label{gsr:en:57:st:preceding-gaps}
The following assertions hold for real sets.
\begin{enumerate}
 \item $D(A)=0$ exactly for arithmetic progressions.
 \item For $m\geq3$, every non-AP $m$-set has $D(A)\geq m-2$.
 \item For $m\geq5$, equality $D(A)=m-2$ holds exactly for affine
 images of $H_m$.
 \item For $m\geq5$, outside the preceding two classes one has
 $D(A)\geq2m-6$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The first statement follows from \eqref{gsr:en:57:st:endpoint} and
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:57:st:endpoint-small}. For the second, induct on $m$, with
the three-point case given by \eqref{gsr:en:57:st:ap-endpoint}. If removing the
maximum leaves an AP, that same formula gives endpoint cost at least
$m-2$. Otherwise its defect is at least $m-3$, and the endpoint cost
is at least one. Equality is attained by $H_m$.

For the third assertion, an AP prefix forces the displaced endpoint
in $H_m$. A non-AP prefix forces endpoint cost one, and
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:57:st:endpoint-small} gives $L_m$.

For the fourth assertion, the case $m=5$ follows from integrality and
the strict inequality $D(A)>3$ outside the first two classes. Induct
with $n=m-1$ and $B=A\setminus\{a\}$, where $a=\max A$.
An AP prefix has cost at least $2n-3>2n-4$ by
\eqref{gsr:en:57:st:ap-endpoint}. If $B$ is second-level, normalize it as
$H_n$ or $L_n$. Its defect is $n-2$, and difference one has
multiplicity $n-2$. Noninteger endpoints have cost $\binom n2$;
integer endpoints at least $n+2$ fail on every difference-one pair.
At $a=n+1$, $L_n$ extends to another excluded second-level set,
whereas $H_n$ fails on its $n-2$ pairs of difference two. Hence all
admissible endpoints cost at least $n-2$. Finally, if $B$ is in neither
class, induction gives $D(B)\geq2n-6$ and endpoint costs zero and
one are excluded by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:57:st:endpoint-small}. Its cost is at
least two, giving $D(A)\geq2n-4=2m-6$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Every third-level extremizer}

\begin{theorem}[Complete third-energy classification]
\label{gsr:en:57:st:third-equality}
Let $m\geq7$. For every $m$-element real set $A$,
\begin{equation}
 E(A)=\frac{2m^3+m}{3}-8(m-3)
 \label{gsr:en:57:st:third-energy}
\end{equation}
if and only if $A$ is an affine image of one of
\begin{equation}
 J_m=\{0,1,\ldots,m\}\setminus\{2\},\qquad
 K_m=\{0,2,3,\ldots,m-1,m+1\}.
 \label{gsr:en:57:st:third-models}
\end{equation}
At $m=6$ the only additional affine class is
$\{0,1,2,4,5,6\}$. Thus seven is the smallest eventual threshold
for the two-class statement. These classifications also hold in every
torsion-free abelian group.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write $n=m-1$, $a=\max A$, and $B=A\setminus\{a\}$.
The target defect is $D(A)=2n-4$. If $B$ is an AP, the two exceptional
endpoints put $A$ in the first two energy classes, while every other
endpoint costs at least $2n-3$. Hence this case is impossible.

Suppose next that $B$ is second-level. Since $n\geq5$, positively
normalize it as $H_n$ or $L_n$. Its defect is $n-2$, so its endpoint
cost must be exactly $n-2$. Noninteger endpoints cost
$\binom n2>n-2$. For $H_n$, the endpoint $n+1$ fails exactly on
difference two, whose multiplicity is $n-2$. It produces a reflected
$J_m$. The endpoint $n+2$ fails on difference one with multiplicity
$n-2$ and also on difference three with positive multiplicity $n-3$.
Every endpoint at least $n+3$ fails on both differences one and two,
each of multiplicity $n-2$. Thus no other endpoint qualifies.

For $L_n$, the endpoint $n+1$ gives another second-level set and is
excluded. The endpoint $n+2$ fails exactly on difference one, of
multiplicity $n-2$, giving $K_m$. Every endpoint at least $n+3$
fails on differences one and two, again each of multiplicity $n-2$.
This exhausts the second-level prefixes.

If $B$ is in neither preceding class,
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:57:st:preceding-gaps} gives $D(B)\geq2n-6$.
Endpoint costs zero and one are excluded, so equality forces
\[
 D(B)=2n-6,\qquad e(B,a)=2.
\]
Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:st:schur-two} to $C=a-B$; here $n\geq6$.
After translating $\min B=0$, its first model gives
\[
 B=d\{0,3,4,\ldots,n+1\},\qquad a=(n+2)d.
\]
Reflection turns this $B$ into $d\{0,1,\ldots,n-2,n+1\}$.
Formula~\eqref{gsr:en:57:st:ap-endpoint} gives $D(B)=2n-5$, a contradiction.
The second model gives
\[
 B=d(\{0,1,\ldots,n\}\setminus\{2\}),\qquad a=(n+1)d,
\]
and hence $A=dJ_m$. This proves necessity.

For sufficiency, the ordered-completion identity gives, for
$1\leq j\leq m-1$,
\begin{equation}
 D(\{0,1,\ldots,m\}\setminus\{j\})
 =j(m-j)-\min(j,m-j).
 \label{gsr:en:57:st:single-hole}
\end{equation}
Indeed a failed completion must equal $j$. Its extremal entries satisfy
$x<j<z$ and its middle entry is $y=x+z-j$. Of the $j(m-j)$ choices
of $(x,z)$, precisely $\min(j,m-j)$ have $y=j$ and must be excluded.
Taking $j=2$ gives $D(J_m)=2m-6$. For $K_m$, its prefix $L_{m-1}$
has defect $m-3$, and its endpoint has exactly $m-3$ failing pairs
of difference one. Hence $D(K_m)=2m-6$.

For $m=6$, the preceding prefix analysis is unchanged except that
$|C|=5$. Its extra Schur model gives
$A=d\{0,1,2,4,5,6\}$. Formula~\eqref{gsr:en:57:st:single-hole} gives
its defect $6=2m-6$, and Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:st:schur-two} supplies no
further exceptions. Its normalized successive gaps are $(1,1,2,1,1)$,
whereas those of $J_6$ are $(1,2,1,1,1)$ up to reversal and those
of $K_6$ are $(2,1,1,1,2)$. It is therefore a distinct affine class,
proving optimality of the threshold.

Finally the subgroup generated by a finite set in a torsion-free abelian
group is isomorphic to $\mathbb Z^r$ and embeds additively into
$\mathbb R$ by choosing $r$ rationally independent real numbers.
This preserves energy. Every classified model contains a pair separated
by its unit step, so the real step is the image of an actual group
difference. Injectivity pulls back every model relation, completing
the torsion-free transfer.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 54--59]
\emph{Source~45's first two research questions are answered} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:energylevels}; item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:energylevels}): its Question~\ref{gsr:fz:45:q:third} by this theorem, with the optimal threshold $m\ge7$ and the exception $\{0,1,2,4,5,6\}$ at $m=6$, and its question on bounded Schur defect by Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:57:st:partitions} and~\ref{gsr:en:57:st:schur-two} (sufficient threshold $5s-1$; optimal values $4$, $6$, $8$ for $s=1,2,3$ are not proved in general). The finite enumerations of this source were rerun on a copy at the write with identical output. Source~66, placed after this source (\texttt{06b30ca52}) and not yet written in, records the same partition normal form with threshold $3r+1$, a third-level classification from $m\ge8$ and the fourth level (from its placement record, not checked here).
\end{writenote}

The partition theorem also gives a finite route to further energy
classifications: a bounded endpoint cost eventually permits only $p(s)$
positive dilation classes. It does not, by itself, prove that a bound
$D(A)\leq K|A|$ always provides a bounded-cost endpoint of sufficient
length. That additional localization is the next structural obstacle.

\section{Source~67's chapter: affine rigidity in characteristic three \wtag}\label{gsr:en:sec:charthree}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the eleventh write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next two sections are source~67's Sections~3--4. \emph{Logically they continue the affine-rigidity chapters} of source~11 (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:affine}) and of sources~59 and~56 (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:affinerepair}); they are printed here because no number printed earlier may move.

\emph{What is proved.} For $f:G\to W$, $G$ finite abelian of order $N$ and $W$ an elementary abelian $3$-group, at error density $t$ from an affine reference: $\varepsilon(f)\ge\Psi(t)=4t-10t^2+6t^3$ for every $t\in[0,1]$, with a nonnegative remainder $(2-3t)(2a-c)+\tfrac43b$ that measures several error colours and the target rank, and, for $0<t<2/3$, equality exactly for one nonzero error value on a subgroup coset; the endpoint $t=2/3$ has its own affine equality family (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:67:cthree:local}). Source~59 proved $\varepsilon\ge\Psi(t)$ on $t<4/9$ for every target without involutions (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:59:thm:affine-four-ninths}); elementary abelian $3$-groups have no involutions but have $3$-torsion, so source~67 extends that range to $t\le2/3$ for this target class. With a Fourier argument: a unique nearest affine map, within $D(\varepsilon)$, whenever $\varepsilon<1/4$ on arbitrary domains or $\varepsilon<4/9$ on elementary abelian $3$-domains, both thresholds sharp as universal strict thresholds (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:67:cthree:global}); and the non-affine maximum $\mathcal E(f)\le N^3-4N^2+10N-6$ from $N\ge13$, with $13$ optimal (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:67:cthree:nonaffine-gap}). \emph{Two different ``$4/9$''}: source~59's bounds the error density $t$, source~67's the defect $\varepsilon$. The recovery thresholds compare with source~11's $\varepsilon<1/9$ and source~59's $2/9$ (for all involution-free targets, through classical correction). The order-thirteen cutoff settles source~11's cutoff question for elementary abelian $3$-group targets; its sharpness example, the parity map $\Z/12\Z\to\Z/3\Z$ of energy $1296>1266$, is source~59's (Section~\ref{gsr:en:59:sec:d10}), uncited at that point (note after the corollary). The thresholds concern the four-point graph-energy test only, as source~67 says. Sources~93 and~96, placed during this write, record the recovery threshold $1/4$ and the cutoff $13$ for every abelian target (93) and the whole cubic range for every odd-order target (96); they are not checked here (note after Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:67:cthree:local}).

\emph{Relation to the formal statements} (checked at HEAD \texttt{fb9602e55}). \file{proposition_6_1} and \file{lemma_6_2} (\file{Sections06\_07.lean}, lines~37 and~47) have the exact companions \file{proposition_6_1_holds} and \file{lemma_6_2_holds} (\file{Proofs05\_10.lean}, lines~505 and~589); the affine-rigidity theory has no formal counterpart, and nothing in this chapter is formalized.

\section[{Cubic rigidity throughout the nontrivial range in characteristic three\srctag{67}}]{Cubic rigidity throughout the nontrivial range in characteristic three}\label{gsr:en:67:sec:d3}
\srcnote{67}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:en:67:cthree:section}

The cubic error profile in the preceding repository work is
\[
 \Psi(t)=4t-10t^2+6t^3=2t(1-t)(2-3t).
\]
Its nontrivial range is $0<t<2/3$.  The result below establishes this
entire range when the error values belong to an elementary abelian
$3$-group.  The domain can be any finite abelian group.  A second result
gives exact universal thresholds for unique affine recovery: graph defect
below $1/4$ on arbitrary finite abelian domains, and below $4/9$ on
elementary abelian $3$-domains.  These are strict thresholds, and explicit
examples show that neither endpoint can be included in the respective
universal recovery assertion.

The target restriction is essential to the proof.  Random linear
projections to $\mathbb F_3$ retain enough of the signed graph energy to
reduce the main inequality to a two-color autocorrelation estimate.
This is more information than a pointwise maximum of a signed
four-position kernel retains.

\subsection{Definitions and the principal local theorem}

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group of cardinality $N$, let $W$ be an
elementary abelian $3$-group, and let $f:G\to W$.  The group $W$ may be
infinite: only the finite-dimensional vector space generated by the
finitely many values used below is relevant.  Define the graph energy
and its normalized defect by
\begin{gather*}
 \mathcal E(f)=
 \#\{(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)\in G^4:
 x_1+x_2=x_3+x_4,\ f(x_1)+f(x_2)=f(x_3)+f(x_4)\},
 \\
 \varepsilon(f)=1-\frac{\mathcal E(f)}{N^3}.
\end{gather*}
An affine map means a homomorphism plus a constant.  Fix any affine
reference $\ell$, put $g=f-\ell$, and write
\[
 S=\{x:g(x)\ne0\},\quad s=|S|,\quad t=s/N,
 \qquad c_v=|\{x:g(x)=v\}|\quad(v\ne0).
\]
The reference need not be a nearest affine map.  Set
\begin{align*}
 M&=\sum_{v\ne0}c_v^2,&
 A&=s^2-M,&
 C&=\sum_{v\ne0}c_vc_{-v},\\
 Z&=\sum_{\substack{u,v\ne0\\u+v\ne0}}c_uc_vc_{u+v},&
 T&=\sum_{\substack{u,v,w\ne0\\
       \dim_{\mathbb F_3}\langle u,v,w\rangle\ge2}}c_uc_vc_w.
\end{align*}
Thus $A$ counts ordered unequal-color pairs, $C$ counts ordered
opposite-color pairs, $Z$ counts weighted Schur triples, and $T$ counts
ordered triples not contained in one one-dimensional target subspace.
Let $a=A/N^2$, $c=C/N^2$, and $b=T/N^3$.  Always $0\le C\le A$.

\begin{theorem}[Characteristic-three cubic rigidity]
\label{gsr:en:67:cthree:local}
With the preceding definitions, the following inequality holds for
every $0\le t\le1$:
\begin{equation}
 \varepsilon(f)-\Psi(t)
 \ge (2-3t)(2a-c)+\frac43 b.
 \label{gsr:en:67:cthree:master}
\end{equation}
Consequently $\varepsilon(f)\ge\Psi(t)$ for every $t\in[0,1]$.
For $0<t<2/3$, equality holds if and only if
\begin{equation}
 f(x)=\ell(x)+v\,1_{x_0+H}(x)
 \quad\hbox{for some }v\ne0\hbox{ and subgroup }H\le G.
 \label{gsr:en:67:cthree:onecolor}
\end{equation}
At $t=2/3$, equality holds if and only if $g=f-\ell$ is affine and has
an image of cardinality three containing zero.  Equivalently,
\[
 g(x)=v\bigl(\lambda(x)+j\bigr)
 \quad(v\ne0, j\in\mathbb F_3),
\]
where $\lambda:G\to\mathbb F_3$ is a surjective homomorphism.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Forward pointers} (from placement records, not checked at this write). Source~96, placed by \texttt{09f5b745a} during this write, records $\varepsilon(f)\ge\Psi(t)$ on the whole range $t\le2/3$, with the coset equality classification, for \emph{every} odd-order target, which would contain this theorem's inequality; source~93 records affine recovery below graph defect $1/4$ and the non-affine maximum from $N\ge13$ for every abelian target (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:67:cthree:global} and Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:67:cthree:nonaffine-gap} here concern elementary abelian $3$-group targets). Both are for the writes that add them.
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Extended to every odd-order target} by source~96 (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:96:thm:affine-cubic}, Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:oddaffine}), with the same coset equality below $2/3$ and an order-three classification at $t=2/3$; source~96 does not cite this source, an unplaced archive at its pin, so this theorem is the first full-range proof, for elementary abelian $3$-groups.
\end{writenote}

The inequality for $2/3<t<1$ follows simply from $\Psi(t)<0$ and
$\varepsilon(f)\ge0$.  The mathematical improvement is the whole
positive interval, the explicit color remainder in
\eqref{gsr:en:67:cthree:master}, and its rigidity statement.  In particular, no
failure of the cubic inequality beyond $2/3$ is being asserted.

\subsection{The two-color autocorrelation estimate}

For a finitely supported complex function $h$ on an abelian group put
\[
 \mathscr E(h)=\sum_d
 \left|\sum_x h(x+d)\overline{h(x)}\right|^2.
\]
For real $h$ this equals the sum of
$h(x_1)h(x_2)h(x_3)h(x_4)$ over additive quadruples.

\begin{lemma}[Two colors separated by an angle of $\pi/3$]
\label{gsr:en:67:cthree:two-color}
Let $P,Q$ be disjoint finite sets in an abelian group, of cardinalities
$x,y$, respectively.  Put $s=x+y$ and
$h=1_P+e^{i\pi/3}1_Q$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 \mathscr E(h)\le s^3-2xy\max\{x,y\}\le s^3-sxy.
 \label{gsr:en:67:cthree:two-color-bound}
\end{equation}
If $x,y>0$, equality in the second upper bound
$\mathscr E(h)\le s^3-sxy$ holds precisely when $x=y$ and $P,Q$ are
distinct cosets of the same finite subgroup $H$, with their coset
difference not of order two in the quotient group.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For a fixed direction $d$, write the autocorrelation as
$A_d+e^{i\pi/3}B_d+e^{-i\pi/3}C_d$, where $A_d$ counts the
same-color pairs and $B_d,C_d$ count the two orientations of
cross-color pairs.  Write $v=B_d+C_d$, $r=A_d+v$, and
$m=\min\{x,y\}$.  The elementary constraints are
\[
 A_d\ge0,\quad 0\le B_d,C_d\le m,\quad r\le s.
\]
Expansion of the squared modulus gives
\[
 \left|A_d+e^{i\pi/3}B_d+e^{-i\pi/3}C_d\right|^2
 =r^2-A_dv-3B_dC_d.
\]
We claim
\begin{equation}
 r(s-r)+A_dv+3B_dC_d\ge(s-m)v.
 \label{gsr:en:67:cthree:pointwise}
\end{equation}
After subtraction of the right side, the left side is
\[
 A_d(s-A_d-v)+v(m-v)+3B_dC_d.
\]
If $v\le m$, every displayed term is nonnegative.  If $v\ge m$,
then $(m-B_d)(m-C_d)\ge0$ gives
$B_dC_d\ge m(v-m)$, and hence
\[
 v(m-v)+3B_dC_d\ge(v-m)(3m-v)\ge0,
\]
since $v\le2m$.  This proves \eqref{gsr:en:67:cthree:pointwise}.
Now sum over $d$, using
$\sum_dr=s^2$ and $\sum_d(B_d+C_d)=2xy$.  The first bound in
\eqref{gsr:en:67:cthree:two-color-bound} follows; the second uses
$\max\{x,y\}\ge s/2$.

For equality in the second bound with $xy>0$, first $x=y=m=s/2$.
The proof of \eqref{gsr:en:67:cthree:pointwise} shows that a direction with a
cross-color pair has $v=m$, $B_dC_d=0$, and
$A_d\in\{0,m\}$.  The possibility $A_d=m$ would give $r=s$, so
translation by $d$ would permute $P\cup Q$.  A permutation of the
union moves equally many points from $P$ to $Q$ and from $Q$ to $P$,
contradicting $B_dC_d=0$ and $v>0$.  Therefore $A_d=0$.
For a direction with no cross-color pair, equality gives $A_d=0$ or
$A_d=s$.  Consequently every positive autocorrelation of $P$ has
value $|P|$ and the same direction preserves $Q$.  The usual equality
case of $E(P)\le|P|^3$ makes $P$ a coset of a subgroup $H$; the
preceding preservation and $|Q|=|H|$ make $Q$ another coset of $H$.
The two oriented cross differences must be distinct, excluding order
two for their difference.  Conversely, these cosets have exactly the
autocorrelation patterns just described, so they attain equality.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Signed graph energy with two nonzero ternary values]
\label{gsr:en:67:cthree:scalar-signed}
Suppose $g:G\to\mathbb F_3$ takes the values $1$ and $-1$ on
disjoint sets $P,Q$ and is zero elsewhere.  Define
\[
 D(x,w)=1_{\{g(x)\ne0\}}
       \bigl(1_{\{g(x)\}}(w)-1_{\{0\}}(w)\bigr).
\]
If $|P|=x$, $|Q|=y$, and $s=x+y$, then
\begin{equation}
 \mathscr E(D)\le6s^3-6sxy.
 \label{gsr:en:67:cthree:scalar-signed-bound}
\end{equation}
When $xy>0$, equality has exactly the coset description in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:67:cthree:two-color}.  More strongly, the term $6sxy$ can be
replaced by $12xy\max\{x,y\}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$.  Fourier expansion only in the target
coordinate gives zero for its trivial character.  For either other
character, the domain function is
$(\omega-1)1_P+(\omega^2-1)1_Q$, or its conjugate.
The two coefficients have modulus $\sqrt3$ and ratio
$e^{i\pi/3}$ or its conjugate.  Target orthogonality therefore gives
\[
 \mathscr E(D)=6\mathscr E(1_P+e^{i\pi/3}1_Q).
\]
Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:67:cthree:two-color}.
\end{proof}

For a scalar target, the stronger version and the signed identity below
already give the entirely explicit estimate
\begin{equation}
 \varepsilon(f)-\Psi(t)
 \ge \bigl(2-6\min\{|P|,|Q|\}/N\bigr)\,
          \frac{2|P||Q|}{N^2}.
 \label{gsr:en:67:cthree:scalar-imbalance}
\end{equation}
Thus an imbalance between the two nonzero error colors improves the
color penalty as well.

\subsection{Linear projection and the seven target configurations}

The passage to vector-valued targets uses an exact projection identity,
not a union bound over coordinates.  Let $V$ be the finite-dimensional
subspace of $W$ spanned by the error values, and let $\lambda$ range
uniformly over $V^*=\operatorname{Hom}(V,\mathbb F_3)$, including zero.
On $G\times V$, define
\[
 D=\sum_{x\in S}\bigl(\delta_{(x,g(x))}-\delta_{(x,0)}\bigr).
\]
Write $D_\lambda$ for the pushforward of $D$ under
$(x,w)\mapsto(x,\lambda(w))$; the two entries cancel when
$\lambda(g(x))=0$.

\begin{lemma}[Exact projected signed energy]
\label{gsr:en:67:cthree:projection}
One has
\begin{equation}
 \mathscr E(D)=\frac32\mathbb E_\lambda\mathscr E(D_\lambda).
 \label{gsr:en:67:cthree:projection-identity}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For every $v\in V$,
$\Pr_\lambda[\lambda(v)=0]=1/3+(2/3)1_{\{v=0\}}$.
Apply this to the signed target sum of each horizontal additive
quadruple in the expansion of $\mathscr E(D_\lambda)$.
The constant $1/3$ part vanishes: for every $x$,
$\sum_wD(x,w)=0$, so the unrestricted sum over its four target
coordinates factors into four zero sums.  The remaining part is
$(2/3)\mathscr E(D)$.
\end{proof}

For $a_1,a_2,a_3\in\mathbb F_3$, define $\kappa(a_1,a_2,a_3)$ to be
zero if any entry is zero, one if all three entries are equal and
nonzero, and $2/3$ otherwise.  If $x_\lambda,y_\lambda$ are the two
nonzero projected color sizes and $s_\lambda=x_\lambda+y_\lambda$,
then
\[
 \sum_{u,v,w\ne0}c_uc_vc_w
 \kappa(\lambda u,\lambda v,\lambda w)
 =s_\lambda^3-s_\lambda x_\lambda y_\lambda.
\]
Indeed, among three nonzero projected labels the number of ordered
non-monochromatic triples is $3x_\lambda y_\lambda s_\lambda$.
Lemmas~\ref{gsr:en:67:cthree:scalar-signed} and \ref{gsr:en:67:cthree:projection} now imply
\begin{equation}
 \mathscr E(D)\le
 \sum_{u,v,w\ne0}c_uc_vc_w K(u,v,w),
 \qquad
 K(u,v,w)=9\mathbb E_\lambda
              \kappa(\lambda u,\lambda v,\lambda w).
 \label{gsr:en:67:cthree:projected-kernel}
\end{equation}

For a triple of nonzero vectors, let $U$ count its unequal pairs,
$P_-$ its opposite pairs, and $R$ the equations among
$u+v=w$, $u+w=v$, and $v+w=u$.  At most one of these equations holds.
The following table is exhaustive.  In its rank-two rows,
``independent'' means that the displayed exceptional vector is
independent of the repeated or opposite pair.

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrrrrr@{}}
\toprule
Configuration & $U$ & $P_-$ & $R$ & $K$ &
$6-(2U-P_-+4R)/3-K$\\
\midrule
All three equal & $0$ & $0$ & $0$ & $6$ & $0$\\
One line, not all equal & $2$ & $2$ & $1$ & $4$ & $0$\\
Two equal, independent third & $2$ & $0$ & $0$ & $10/3$ & $4/3$\\
Opposite pair, independent third & $3$ & $1$ & $0$ & $8/3$ & $5/3$\\
Rank two, pairwise nonparallel, $R=1$ & $3$ & $0$ & $1$ & $4/3$ & $4/3$\\
Rank two, pairwise nonparallel, $u+v+w=0$ & $3$ & $0$ & $0$ & $2$ & $2$\\
Rank three & $3$ & $0$ & $0$ & $2$ & $2$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Here is a direct way to verify the numerical column without appealing
to computation.  In rank one, the nonzero functional values occur with
probability $2/3$.  In rank two, the values on a basis are the nine
equally likely pairs in $\mathbb F_3^2$.  The third row has two
nonzero monochromatic outcomes and two nonzero non-monochromatic
outcomes; the fourth has four of the latter.  For $w=u+v$ there are
two nonzero outcomes, both non-monochromatic.  For $w=-u-v$ there are
two nonzero outcomes, both monochromatic.  In rank three, among the
27 outcomes there are two nonzero monochromatic and six nonzero
non-monochromatic outcomes.  Multiplying the averages by nine gives
the table.  The rank-two classification is exhaustive because any
dependence of three pairwise nonparallel vectors over $\mathbb F_3$
has three nonzero coefficients, each equal to $1$ or $-1$.

\begin{proposition}[A signed energy bound retaining target rank]
\label{gsr:en:67:cthree:vector-signed}
With the notation of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:67:cthree:local},
\begin{equation}
 \mathscr E(D)\le
 6s^3-2sA+sC-4Z-\frac43T.
 \label{gsr:en:67:cthree:vector-signed-bound}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The table gives
\[
 K(u,v,w)\le6-\frac{2U-P_-+4R}{3}
       -\frac43\,1_{\{\dim\langle u,v,w\rangle\ge2\}}.
\]
Sum with weight $c_uc_vc_w$.  The sums of $U$, $P_-$, and $R$ are
$3sA$, $3sC$, and $3Z$, respectively.  Equation
\eqref{gsr:en:67:cthree:projected-kernel} proves the assertion.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The exact graph expansion and equality}

For completeness, the signed identity used to finish the argument is
included here.  Let $B=1_{G\times\{0\}}$, so that $B+D$ is the graph
indicator of $g$.  Expansion in the number of $D$ factors gives
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal E(g)=N^3-4sN^2+N(6s^2+4M+2C)
       -4s^3-8sM-4sC+4Z+\mathscr E(D).
 \label{gsr:en:67:cthree:signed-identity}
\end{equation}
The one-factor contribution is $-4sN^2$.  For two factors, four
opposite-sign position pairs contribute $N(s^2+M)$ each and two
same-sign pairs contribute $N(s^2+C)$ each.  For three factors, put
$m_0=-s$, $m_v=c_v$ for $v\ne0$; the target sum is
\[
 \sum_{u+v=w}m_um_vm_w=Z-s^3-2sM-sC,
\]
and there are four choices of the omitted position.  The final term
has four $D$ factors.  All these counts include repeated domain
coordinates with their correct multiplicities.

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:67:cthree:local}]
Affine subtraction preserves graph energy.  Subtracting the cubic
profile from \eqref{gsr:en:67:cthree:signed-identity} gives
\[
 N^3\bigl(\varepsilon(f)-\Psi(t)\bigr)
 =2(N-2s)(2A-C)-4Z+6s^3-\mathscr E(D).
\]
Insert Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:67:cthree:vector-signed} to obtain
\[
 N^3\bigl(\varepsilon(f)-\Psi(t)\bigr)
 \ge(2N-3s)(2A-C)+\frac43T.
\]
This is \eqref{gsr:en:67:cthree:master}.  If $0<t<2/3$, its right side is
nonnegative and its color term is at least $(2N-3s)A$.  Equality
therefore forces $A=0$, so all nonzero error values equal one $v$.
For such an error, direct substitution or support-pattern counting
gives
\begin{equation}
 \varepsilon(v1_S)=\Psi(t)
       +\frac{6(s^3-E(S))}{N^3}.
 \label{gsr:en:67:cthree:one-color-identity}
\end{equation}
The elementary inequality $E(S)\le s^3$ is an equality precisely
for subgroup cosets.  Indeed, if $r_S(d)=|S\cap(S+d)|$, then
$E(S)=\sum_dr_S(d)^2\le s\sum_dr_S(d)=s^3$; equality makes each
positive $r_S(d)$ equal $s$, and the translation stabilizer of $S$
then makes $S$ a coset.  This proves both directions of
\eqref{gsr:en:67:cthree:onecolor}.

At $t=2/3$, the profile is zero.  Full graph energy is equivalent to
affineness: the identity
\[
 \mathcal E(g)=\sum_h\sum_w
       |\{x:g(x+h)-g(x)=w\}|^2
\]
shows that full energy is equivalent to every derivative being
constant, and the derivative cocycle makes these constants a
homomorphism.  If an affine map $g$ has a zero fiber of size $N/3$,
its image is a three-element subgroup containing zero.  This gives
exactly the endpoint description in the theorem.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Attainment of the color coefficient]
\label{gsr:en:67:cthree:color-sharp}
Let $H\le G$, let $P,Q$ be distinct $H$-cosets whose difference has
order other than two in $G/H$, and let $g=v1_P-v1_Q$ for $v\ne0$.
Put $h=|H|$ and $t=2h/N$.  Then $A=C=2h^2$, $T=0$, and
\begin{equation}
 \varepsilon(g)-\Psi(t)=(2-3t)\frac{2h^2}{N^2}.
 \label{gsr:en:67:cthree:color-attainment}
\end{equation}
Thus the color coefficient in \eqref{gsr:en:67:cthree:master} cannot be
uniformly increased with the other terms fixed at these parameters.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:67:cthree:scalar-signed} has equality for these two cosets,
and their two nonzero values lie on one target line.  The projection
table also has equality on that line.  Consequently every inequality
used in deriving \eqref{gsr:en:67:cthree:master} is an equality.
\end{proof}

For example, take $G=\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z$ and $H=\{0\}$ with
$q\ge3$.  At $q=3$ the two-color example is an affine map and gives
the endpoint $t=2/3$.  At arbitrarily large $q$ it gives genuine
two-error examples and the exact color penalty at $t=2/q$.

\begin{corollary}[Color stability]
\label{gsr:en:67:cthree:color-stability}
If $0<t<2/3$ and
$\varepsilon(f)\le\Psi(t)+\eta$ with $\eta\ge0$, then
\[
 \frac{A}{N^2}\le\frac{\eta}{2-3t},\qquad
 \frac{T}{N^3}\le\frac{3\eta}{4}.
\]
There is a nonzero error value $v$ such that the proportion of domain
points with nonzero error different from $v$ is at most
$\eta/[t(2-3t)]$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The first two inequalities follow from \eqref{gsr:en:67:cthree:master}.
If $m_*=\max c_v$, then $M\le sm_*$, whence
$A\ge s(s-m_*)$.  Divide by $N^2$.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Sharp thresholds for global affine recovery\srctag{67}}]{Sharp thresholds for global affine recovery}\label{gsr:en:67:sec:d4}
\srcnote{67}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:en:67:cthree:recovery-section}

The local theorem makes no claim that its affine reference is nearest.
This section constructs a nearby affine reference from energy alone.
It also distinguishes a sharp admissible defect threshold from an
exact energy envelope at every real parameter: equality with the
cubic profile requires subgroup indices, which form a discrete set.

\subsection{A scalar Fourier argument}

Use the normalized Fourier transform on $G$,
$\widehat u(\gamma)=N^{-1}\sum_xu(x)\overline{\gamma(x)}$.
For $f:G\to\mathbb F_3$, set $u(x)=\omega^{f(x)}$.  Orthogonality
in the target and in the domain gives
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\mathcal E(f)}{N^3}
 =\frac{1+2\sum_{\gamma\in\widehat G}|\widehat u(\gamma)|^4}{3},
 \qquad \sum_\gamma|\widehat u(\gamma)|^2=1.
 \label{gsr:en:67:cthree:fourier-identity}
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}[Excluding a character of the wrong order]
\label{gsr:en:67:cthree:wrong-order}
If $u:G\to\{1,\omega,\omega^2\}$ and $\gamma^3$ is a nontrivial
character, then
\begin{equation}
 |\widehat u(\gamma)|\le\frac{\sqrt3}{2}.
 \label{gsr:en:67:cthree:wrong-order-bound}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For $z=u\overline\gamma$ one has $|z|=1$ and
$\mathbb E z^3=\mathbb E\overline\gamma^{\,3}=0$.
Put $r=\sqrt3/2$.  For every real $\theta$,
\[
 r+\frac16\cos(3\theta)-\cos\theta
 =\frac23(\cos\theta-r)^2(\cos\theta+2r)\ge0.
\]
Apply this inequality to the phase of $e^{-i\phi}z$, choosing
$\phi$ so that $e^{-i\phi}\mathbb E z$ is nonnegative real.
The third moment term averages to zero, proving the bound.
\end{proof}

For later use, if $p_0,p_1,p_2$ are the proportions of the three values
of a ternary function, then
\begin{equation}
 |p_0+p_1\omega+p_2\omega^2|^2
 =\frac{3(p_0^2+p_1^2+p_2^2)-1}{2}.
 \label{gsr:en:67:cthree:ternary-mean}
\end{equation}
In particular, a squared modulus above $3/4$ forces one $p_j>5/6$,
using $\sum p_j^2\le\max p_j$.  A squared modulus above $1/3$
forces one $p_j>2/3$: with all $p_j\le2/3$, the maximal sum of their
squares is $5/9$, attained by a permutation of $(2/3,1/3,0)$.

Let
\[
 \rho=\frac{2-\sqrt2}{3}.
\]
The cubic $\Psi$ is strictly increasing on $[0,\rho]$ and
$\Psi(\rho)=\Psi(1/3)=4/9$.  Also
\begin{equation}
 \Psi(t)\ge\frac49\quad(\rho\le t\le1/3),
 \qquad 3\rho=2-\sqrt2<\frac23.
 \label{gsr:en:67:cthree:branch-separation}
\end{equation}
These facts follow either by differentiation or from
\[
 \Psi(t)-\frac49
 =\frac29(3t-1)(9t^2-12t+2).
\]
Write $D:[0,4/9]\to[0,\rho]$ for this increasing inverse branch.

\begin{proposition}[Scalar recovery]
\label{gsr:en:67:cthree:scalar-recovery}
Let $f:G\to\mathbb F_3$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $\varepsilon(f)<1/4$, there is a unique nearest affine map
$\ell$, and its disagreement proportion is at most $D(\varepsilon(f))$.
\item If $G$ is elementary abelian of exponent three, the same
conclusion holds under the weaker hypothesis $\varepsilon(f)<4/9$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Put $q_\gamma=|\widehat u(\gamma)|^2$, $Q=\sum q_\gamma^2$, and
$M=\max q_\gamma$.  By \eqref{gsr:en:67:cthree:fourier-identity},
$Q=1-3\varepsilon(f)/2$.

In the first case $Q>5/8$.  Since $Q\le M$, one has $M>5/8$;
also $Q\le M^2+(1-M)^2$.  The latter expression is increasing for
$M\ge1/2$ and is $5/8$ at $M=3/4$, so $M>3/4$.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:67:cthree:wrong-order} shows that a character attaining $M$
has order dividing three.  It therefore equals $\omega^L$ for a
homomorphism $L:G\to\mathbb F_3$.
Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:67:cthree:ternary-mean}, applied to $f-L$, gives an
affine map $L+j$ with disagreement $t<1/6$.
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:67:cthree:local} gives $\varepsilon(f)\ge\Psi(t)$, so
$t\le D(\varepsilon(f))$.  The relevant interval is increasing;
moreover $\Psi(1/12)=77/288>1/4$, so in fact $t<1/12$.

In the second case $Q>1/3$, so some $q_\gamma>1/3$.
Every character of $G$ has order dividing three.  The second
consequence of \eqref{gsr:en:67:cthree:ternary-mean} gives an affine map with
disagreement $t<1/3$.  The local cubic and
\eqref{gsr:en:67:cthree:branch-separation} force $t<\rho$, and inversion gives
$t\le D(\varepsilon(f))$.

Finally, two distinct affine maps into $\mathbb F_3$ agree on at
most $N/3$ points: a nonconstant affine difference has equal-sized
fibers, and a nonzero constant difference has no zeros.  In both
cases $t<\rho<1/3$, so no two affine maps can both have disagreement
at most $t$.  In particular, a nearest affine map is unique and is
the map just constructed.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Synchronizing all linear projections}

\begin{theorem}[Two sharp universal recovery thresholds]
\label{gsr:en:67:cthree:global}
Let $W$ be an elementary abelian $3$-group and let $f:G\to W$ on a
finite abelian group $G$.  Then there is a unique nearest affine map
$\ell$ satisfying
\begin{equation}
 \frac{|\{x:f(x)\ne\ell(x)\}|}{N}
 \le D(\varepsilon(f))
 \label{gsr:en:67:cthree:global-inverse}
\end{equation}
whenever either
\[
 \varepsilon(f)<\frac14,
 \quad\hbox{or}\quad
 G\hbox{ is elementary abelian of exponent three and }
 \varepsilon(f)<\frac49.
\]
Neither strict defect threshold can be enlarged, or replaced by a
non-strict inequality, in its stated class of domains.
If equality holds in \eqref{gsr:en:67:cthree:global-inverse} with positive
defect, the error $f-\ell$ is precisely one nonzero constant on a
subgroup coset.  Such examples attain the cubic inverse at their
available subgroup-index parameters.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
First suppose $W$ finite-dimensional.  For each $\lambda\in W^*$,
let $f_\lambda=\lambda\circ f$ and let $\ell_\lambda$ be the
affine map supplied by Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:67:cthree:scalar-recovery}.
A failed projected quadruple is a failed original quadruple, so
$\varepsilon(f_\lambda)\le\varepsilon(f)$ and
\[
 \Pr[f_\lambda\ne\ell_\lambda]
 \le D(\varepsilon(f_\lambda))\le D(\varepsilon(f))<\rho.
\]
For $\lambda,\mu$, the affine map
$\ell_{\lambda+\mu}-\ell_\lambda-\ell_\mu$ is nonzero at a
proportion of inputs at most $3D(\varepsilon(f))<3\rho<2/3$.
A nonzero affine map into $\mathbb F_3$ is nonzero on at least
$2/3$ of the domain.  Consequently
\[
 \ell_{\lambda+\mu}=\ell_\lambda+\ell_\mu,
 \qquad \ell_0=0.
\]
Finite-dimensional duality now supplies a unique map
$\ell:G\to W$ with $\lambda\circ\ell=\ell_\lambda$ for every
$\lambda$.  Since the scalar maps are affine and linear
functionals separate points, $\ell$ is affine.

For each nonzero vector $v$, exactly $2/3$ of the functionals are
nonzero on $v$.  Hence, if $t=\Pr[f\ne\ell]$,
\[
 \frac23t
 =\mathbb E_\lambda\Pr[f_\lambda\ne\ell_\lambda]
 \le D(\varepsilon(f)).
\]
It follows that $t<(3/2)\rho<1/3$.  Apply
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:67:cthree:local} and
\eqref{gsr:en:67:cthree:branch-separation} once more: because
$\varepsilon(f)<4/9$, the interval $[\rho,1/3]$ is excluded and
$t\le D(\varepsilon(f))$.  Distinct affine maps into $W$ disagree
on at least $2N/3$ points, so the nearest map is unique.

If $W$ is infinite, let $V$ be the finite-dimensional span of $f(G)$
and apply the construction in $V$.  Any competing affine map into
$W$ whose distance is no greater than the constructed map has
distance less than $N/3$; the same affine-distance bound forces it
to coincide with the constructed map.  This proves global
uniqueness in $W$, not merely uniqueness among maps into $V$.
Equality in the inverse is equality in the local cubic and therefore
has the stated coset form.

For sharpness of the first threshold, use $G=\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$
and $f(0)=0$, $f(1)=1$ in $\mathbb F_3$.  There are six respected
quadruples, so $\varepsilon(f)=1/4$.  Every homomorphism
$\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z\to\mathbb F_3$ is zero; the constants zero
and one are distinct nearest affine maps, each at distance $1/2$.
For the second threshold, use $G=\mathbb F_3$ and
$f=(0,0,1)$.  Its graph energy is $15$, so its defect is $4/9$.
The three affine maps interpolating each pair of its three graph
points are distinct and all have distance $1/3$.
Both examples embed into any nonzero elementary abelian $3$-target
and lift to arbitrarily large domains by a product projection.
Thus the two claimed universal thresholds are sharp.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Two different ``$4/9$''} (checked at the write). Here $4/9$ bounds the \emph{defect} $\varepsilon(f)$ on elementary abelian $3$-domains; source~59's $t<4/9$ bounds the \emph{error density} in the local cubic (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:59:thm:affine-four-ninths}). The recovery threshold $1/4$ on arbitrary domains compares with source~11's $1/9$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:11:thm:mainstability}) and source~59's $2/9$ for involution-free targets (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:59:thm:affine-global-two-ninths}).
\end{writenote}

The inverse bound should be interpreted at attainable data.  At
positive equality parameters $t$ is the reciprocal of a subgroup
index.  No assertion is made that every real
$\varepsilon$ in either interval is attained with equality.

\begin{figure}[tbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=.90\textwidth]{figures/67-exact-profiles-rigidity_profile.pdf}
\caption{The local cubic profile and the two strict universal
recovery thresholds. The profile is relative to any affine
reference and is not monotone over its full positive interval.
Recovery uses its increasing branch up to
$\rho=(2-\sqrt2)/3$; the proof excludes the intervening branch
before invoking the inverse. The plot is not a claim that every
point on the curve is an attainable nearest-affine extremum.}
\label{gsr:en:67:fig:rigidity-profile}
\end{figure}

\begin{lemma}[Ternary quantization on thirteen roots]
\label{gsr:en:67:cthree:thirteen-roots}
If $u:\mathbb Z/13\mathbb Z\to\{1,\omega,\omega^2\}$ and
$\gamma$ is a nontrivial character, then
\begin{equation}
 |\widehat u(\gamma)|
 \le \frac{\sin(\pi/3)}{13\sin(\pi/39)},
 \qquad
 |\widehat u(\gamma)|^2<\frac7{10}.
 \label{gsr:en:67:cthree:thirteen-roots-bound}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write the thirteen values of $\gamma$ in their cyclic order.
For any phase $\phi$, the real part of
$e^{-i\phi}u(x)\overline{\gamma(x)}$ is at most the largest
cosine obtained by choosing one of the three possible values of $u(x)$.
Because multiplication by three permutes the residues modulo thirteen,
the character phases, reduced modulo $2\pi/3$, are thirteen equally
spaced points with spacing $\Delta=2\pi/39$.
Choose for each one its representative in $[-\pi/3,\pi/3]$ after
the common rotation by $-\phi$.  These representatives have the form
$\delta+j\Delta$ for $-6\le j\le6$, with
$|\delta|\le\Delta/2$; at a boundary either representative has the
same cosine.  Therefore their cosine sum is
\[
 \sum_{j=-6}^{6}\cos(\delta+j\Delta)
 =\cos\delta\,\frac{\sin(13\Delta/2)}{\sin(\Delta/2)}
 \le\frac{\sin(\pi/3)}{\sin(\pi/39)}.
\]
Choose $\phi$ to be the argument of $\widehat u(\gamma)$ and divide
by thirteen to obtain the first bound.

Strict concavity of sine gives
$13\sin(\pi/39)>4\sin(\pi/12)$.  Consequently
\[
 \left(\frac{\sin(\pi/3)}{13\sin(\pi/39)}\right)^2
 <\left(\frac{\sin(\pi/3)}{4\sin(\pi/12)}\right)^2
 =\frac{3(2+\sqrt3)}{16}<\frac7{10}.
\]
The last inequality is equivalent to $\sqrt3<26/15$, whose square is
$675<676$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The sharp unrestricted-domain cutoff]
\label{gsr:en:67:cthree:nonaffine-gap}
Suppose $W\ne\{0\}$ is elementary abelian of exponent three and
$|G|=N\ge13$.  Every non-affine $f:G\to W$ satisfies
\[
 \mathcal E(f)\le N^3-4N^2+10N-6.
\]
Equality holds exactly for one-point modifications of affine maps. The universal cutoff thirteen is optimal.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For $N\ge14$, $\Psi(1/N)\le\Psi(1/14)<1/4$.
If a non-affine map had larger energy, Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:67:cthree:global}
would give affine distance less than $1/N$, impossible on an
$N$-point set.  At equality the recovered distance is at most $1/N$,
and hence exactly $1/N$; the map is a one-point modification.
Conversely such a modification has the displayed energy by
\eqref{gsr:en:67:cthree:one-color-identity}.

\paragraph{The remaining order thirteen.}
For $N=13$, the domain is $G=\mathbb Z/13\mathbb Z$ and every
affine map into an elementary abelian $3$-group is constant.  The
one-point value of the graph energy is
$13^3-4\cdot13^2+10\cdot13-6=1645$.

First suppose $f:G\to\mathbb F_3$ has graph energy at least $1645$.
With $Q$ and $M$ as in Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:67:cthree:scalar-recovery},
\[
 Q\ge\frac{1369}{2197}>\frac{29}{50},\qquad Q\le M,
 \qquad Q\le M^2+(1-M)^2.
\]
Thus $M>7/10$: otherwise $M>1/2$ and the last quadratic would give
$Q\le(7/10)^2+(3/10)^2=29/50$.  By
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:67:cthree:thirteen-roots}, the maximizing character must be
trivial.  Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:67:cthree:ternary-mean} then gives
\[
 \max_j\Pr[f=j]\ge\sum_j\Pr[f=j]^2
 =\frac{2M+1}{3}>\frac45.
\]
There is therefore a constant $j$ with at most two disagreements.
If there were exactly two, Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:67:cthree:local} would imply
\[
 \varepsilon(f)\ge\Psi(2/13)=\frac{880}{2197}
 >\frac{552}{2197}=1-\frac{1645}{2197},
\]
a contradiction.  Thus $f$ differs from a constant at at most one point.

For a vector-valued $f:G\to W$ with the same energy lower bound,
restrict to the finite-dimensional span $V$ of its values.  Each
projection $\lambda\circ f$ has at least the same graph energy and
hence differs from a uniquely determined constant $j_\lambda$ at at
most one point.  For any $\lambda,\mu\in V^*$, outside the union of
their three possible error sets one has
$j_{\lambda+\mu}=j_\lambda+j_\mu$.  Such a point exists because
$13>3$.  Hence $\lambda\mapsto j_\lambda$ is linear, so there is
$w\in V$ with $j_\lambda=\lambda(w)$ for every $\lambda$.
Average the number of projected disagreements over $V^*$:
\[
 \frac23\,|\{x:f(x)\ne w\}|
 =\mathbb E_\lambda|\{x:\lambda(f(x))\ne j_\lambda\}|
 \le1.
\]
The integer on the left before multiplication by $2/3$ is consequently
at most one.  Thus a nonconstant $f$ with energy at least $1645$ is a
one-point modification of a constant.  Its energy is exactly $1645$
by \eqref{gsr:en:67:cthree:one-color-identity}.  This proves both the inequality
and its equality statement at $N=13$.

\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Credit} (standing rule of 4~October 2026). The example at $N=12$ that makes $13$ optimal is source~59's parity map $\Z/12\Z\to\Z/3\Z$ (Section~\ref{gsr:en:59:sec:d10}), which this source does not attribute to source~59 here, although it credits source~59's cutoff $16$ (\cite{repo67charaffine}). \emph{Checked at the write}: $(3/4)\cdot12^3=1296$ and $12^3-4\cdot12^2+10\cdot12-6=1266$. This settles source~11's cutoff for elementary abelian $3$-group targets at $13$ (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:smallgroups}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 82--94]
\emph{Extended to every abelian target} by source~93 (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:thirteen}), with the same optimal cutoff $13$; its quarter-range recovery likewise extends this source's elementary abelian $3$-group threshold $1/4$ to every target (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:recovery}).
\end{writenote}

The cutoff is sharp: the index-two example on $\mathbb Z/12\mathbb Z$,
with values zero and one on its two parity classes, has energy $1296$,
whereas the one-point value is $1266$. Thus no uniform cutoff at most
$12$ is possible for this class. Both numbers use the graph-energy
normalization in the theorem.

\subsection{Consequences for a partial frequency graph}

Suppose $B\subseteq G$, $\phi:B\to W$, and its graph $\Gamma_B$
has energy at least $(1-\varepsilon)N^3$.  Every completion $f:G\to W$
then has defect at most $\varepsilon$.  Under either strict threshold
in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:67:cthree:global}, the completion therefore recovers an
affine map with at most $D(\varepsilon)N$ disagreements on $B$.
Moreover this affine map is independent of the chosen completion.
Indeed, writing $\beta=|B|/N$, graph energy is at most $|B|^3$, so
$\beta\ge(1-\varepsilon)^{1/3}$.  Two recovered affine maps would
agree on at least $(\beta-2D(\varepsilon))N$ points of $B$.
Even at the larger threshold,
\[
 (5/9)^{1/3}-2\rho>\frac13,
\]
so distinct affine maps are excluded.  For an exact algebraic check,
$(5/9)^{1/3}>4/5$ and $2\rho<2/5$, giving a lower bound greater
than $2/5>1/3$.

This is an endpoint refinement of the graph-energy output used after
Gowers's Fourier selection step.  It supplies neither a mechanism for
reaching this high-energy regime from small correlation nor an
improvement to the complete quantitative Szemer\'edi iteration.

\section{Sources~68 and~66: the energy gap, the coset range and the fourth energy level \wtag}\label{gsr:en:sec:energygap}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the eleventh write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next thirteen sections are source~68's Sections~2--4 and source~66's Sections~2--11, on sets of nearly maximal additive energy. \emph{Logically they continue source~45's chapter} on energy levels and the coset range (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:energylevels}), source~14's coset envelope (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:14:thm:energy-sharp-stability}) and source~57's third level (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:thirdlevel}); they are printed here because no number printed earlier may move. Source~68's universal inequalities, valid in every abelian group, come first; source~66's ordered classification, for real and torsion-free sets, second. Their introductions are Sections~\ref{gsr:fm:68:sec:d1} and~\ref{gsr:fm:66:sec:d1}.

\emph{What source~68 proves.} For finite $A$ of size $m$ in any abelian group and every $d$, $m\,r_A(d)(m-r_A(d))\le m^3-E(A)$, with coefficient one sharp even at positive defect, with an exact mixed-set remainder, all equality cases and a weighted form (Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:pointwise}, \ref{gsr:en:68:thm:pointwise-equality}, Propositions~\ref{gsr:en:68:prop:mixed}, \ref{gsr:en:68:prop:weighted}), and the multilevel bound $E(A)\le(2m^3+\sum_ig_i^3)/3$ from attained overlap values (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:multilevel}). With $\varepsilon=1-E(A)/m^3$: for $\varepsilon\le1/4$ the set $H=\{d:r_A(d)>m/2\}$ is a subgroup and a most occupied $H$-coset $C$ has $|A\symdiff C|\le\tau(\varepsilon)m$, the threshold $1/4$ optimal even in cyclic groups (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:coset}, Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:68:prop:threshold-sharp}); the closest coset is unique below the separate optimal threshold $2/9$ (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:68:cor:unique}); all envelope equality cases are punctured cosets $C\setminus(z+L)$ of index at least four (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:coset-equality}); and nested puncture repair holds with outer defect below $1/4$ and inner defect at most $1/4$, with all equality cases and an oriented version from one nearly saturated translation (Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:puncture}, \ref{gsr:en:68:thm:puncture-equality}, \ref{gsr:en:68:thm:oriented-puncture}, Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:68:prop:puncture-endpoint}). Source~14 had the coset envelope for $\varepsilon\le1/100$ and source~45 for $\varepsilon<1/9$ with the coefficient two in the pointwise gap; this answers source~45's Questions~6.6--6.8 and source~14's Question~4 in its range and equality parts (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:cosetrange}).

\emph{What source~66 proves.} For a positive ordered set with Schur defect $\sigma(C)\le r$ and $n\ge3r+1$, $c_i=d(i+\lambda_i)$ with $(\lambda_i)$ nondecreasing, nonnegative and summing to $\sigma(C)$, so defect $r$ has exactly $p(r)$ classes (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:partition}); $n=2r+1$ does not suffice (Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:prop:obstruction}). Reflection gives bounded-hole normal forms for endpoint extensions (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:boundary}), whose energy is an exact affine function of $m$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:holeenergy}), and the sharp envelope $E(A)\le M_m-4r(m-1-r)$ with equality only for $\{0,\ldots,m\}\setminus\{r\}$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:envelope}). The four largest energies for $m\ge11$ are $M_m$, $M_m-4(m-2)$, $M_m-8(m-3)$, $M_m-8m+20$, with one, two, three and two oriented templates (Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:third}, \ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:fourth}, \ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:fourlevels}), with a recovery window, a torsion-free transfer and an affine graph consequence (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:cor:recovery}, Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:torsionfree}, Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:cor:graphs}). The first gap is implicit in the equality theory of Pollard's inequality and the first two levels are source~45's, as source~66 says.

\emph{Against source~57} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:thirdlevel}; the two were written the same day, and neither cites the other). The partition normal form is source~57's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:st:partitions} with threshold $3r+1$ in place of $5s-1$: the same for $r=1$ ($4$), and better for $r\ge3$; for $r=2$ source~57's optimal threshold $6$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:st:schur-two}) is better than $7$. So the optimal threshold $N(r)$ satisfies $2r+2\le N(r)\le3r+1$ for $r\ge3$, with $N(1)=4$ and $N(2)=6$, and source~66 conjectures $N(r)=2r+2$ (its Conjecture~\ref{gsr:fz:66:epnf:conj:threshold}). The third level: source~66's oriented templates $J_m^-$, $J_m^+$ and $C_m$ are source~57's two affine classes $J_m$ and $K_m$ (the first in its two orientations, $C_m=K_m$ symmetric); source~57's cutoff $m\ge7$ is better than source~66's $m\ge8$. The fourth level is new with source~66 (it answers source~57's Research question~\ref{gsr:fz:57:rq:levels} for the fourth level), and so are the hole energy law (its Research question~\ref{gsr:fz:57:rq:polynomials}) and the endpoint envelope (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:energylevels}).

\emph{Relation to the formal statements.} No declaration concerns additive energy levels, Schur defects or coset envelopes (checked at HEAD \texttt{fb9602e55}); nothing in this chapter is formalized.

\section[{A sharp pointwise energy inequality\srctag{68}}]{A sharp pointwise energy inequality}\label{gsr:en:68:sec:d2}
\srcnote{68}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:en:68:sec:energy}

Throughout this section, $A$ is a nonempty finite subset of an abelian
group $G$, written additively. The ambient group need not be finite.
All convolutions and sums in Sections~\ref{gsr:en:68:sec:energy}--\ref{gsr:en:68:sec:punctures}
use counting measure. Set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:energy-notation}
 m=|A|,\qquad r_A(d)=|A\cap(A+d)|,\qquad
 E(A)=\sum_{d\in G}r_A(d)^2,\qquad
 \eps=\frac{m^3-E(A)}{m^3}.
\end{equation}
The same energy is $\sum_x(\ind_A*\ind_A)(x)^2$, by reordering the
equation $a_1+a_2=a_3+a_4$. In particular, $0\le\eps<1$.
Write $q(d)=r_A(d)/m$ and
\[
 \tau(u)=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4u}}2\quad(0\le u\le1/4).
\]
Thus $\tau(u)(1-\tau(u))=u$ and $\tau$ is increasing.

\subsection{An exact nonnegative remainder}

\begin{theorem}[Universal overlap gap]\label{gsr:en:68:thm:pointwise}
For every $d\in G$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:pointwise}
 m\,r_A(d)\bigl(m-r_A(d)\bigr)\le m^3-E(A).
\end{equation}
Equivalently, $q(d)(1-q(d))\le\eps$. The coefficient $1$ is sharp,
including at positive defect.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{This answers source~45's Question~\ref{gsr:fz:45:q:pointwise}} (coefficient one, universally; source~45 had two).
\end{writenote}

We prove a mixed version, which also identifies all losses in the proof.
For finite sets $A,B$, define
$E(A,B)=\sum_x(\ind_A*\ind_B)(x)^2$.

\begin{proposition}[Mixed-set remainder]\label{gsr:en:68:prop:mixed}
Suppose $a=|A|\ge b=|B|>0$. For $d\in G$ put
\[
 C=A\cap(B+d),\quad U=A\cup(B+d),\quad
 P=A\setminus(B+d),\quad Q=(B+d)\setminus A.
\]
Let $t=|C|$, $p=a-t$, $k=b-t$, and
$w=\ind_C*\ind_U$, $v=\ind_P*\ind_Q$. Then
\begin{align}
 ab^2-E(A,B)-bt(b-t)
 &=pk^2-E(P,Q)\notag\\
 &\quad+\sum_x(t-w(x))(w(x)+2v(x))\ge0.
 \label{gsr:en:68:eq:mixed-remainder}
\end{align}
Consequently $E(A,B)\le ab^2-bt(b-t)$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The disjoint decompositions $A=C\sqcup P$ and $B+d=C\sqcup Q$ give,
using commutativity,
\[
 s:=\ind_A*\ind_{B+d}
 =\ind_C*\ind_{C\sqcup P\sqcup Q}+\ind_P*\ind_Q=w+v.
\]
Here $0\le w\le t$, $0\le v\le k$, and
\[
 \sum w=t(a+b-t),\qquad \sum v=pk,\qquad
 \sum s^2=E(A,B).
\]
Expanding the right side of \eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:mixed-remainder} gives
$pk^2+t\sum w+2t\sum v-\sum s^2$.
Its constant part is
$pk^2+t^2(a+b-t)+2tpk=ab^2-bt(b-t)$.
Finally $E(P,Q)=\sum v^2\le k\sum v=pk^2$, and every term of the
remaining sum is nonnegative.
\end{proof}

Taking $B=A$ proves Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:pointwise}. In this case
$p=k=m-t$ and the exact identity is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:self-remainder}
 m^3-E(A)-mt(m-t)
 =k^3-E(P,Q)+\sum_x(t-w(x))(w(x)+2v(x)).
\end{equation}
This union--intersection argument belongs to the classical
set-transformation approach to additive inequalities. The contribution
needed here is the precise energy remainder and its consequences; no
claim to originate that general proof mechanism is made.

\begin{example}[Sharpness at positive defect]\label{gsr:en:68:ex:punctured}
Let $L<K$ be finite subgroups with $r=[K:L]\ge3$, let $A=K\setminus L$,
and write $\ell=|L|$. Then $m=(r-1)\ell$, and
\[
 r_A(d)=
 \begin{cases}
  m,&d\in L,\\
  (r-2)\ell,&d\in K\setminus L,\\
  0,&d\notin K.
 \end{cases}
\]
Summation gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:punctured-parameters}
 \eps=\frac{r-2}{(r-1)^2}.
\end{equation}
Every $d\in K\setminus L$ attains equality in
\eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:pointwise}. Translations of these examples have the same
properties.
\end{example}

The earlier project bound was
$q(d)(1-q(d))\le2\eps$ \cite{repo68fortyfive}. Thus
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:pointwise} answers its explicit coefficient-one question.
It does so for every finite subset of every abelian group, without a
small-defect assumption.

\subsection{Several overlap levels give a stronger bound}

The next result preserves more information than one application of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:pointwise}. It is important that its truncation function
uses \emph{sum} multiplicities and its nodes come from \emph{difference}
multiplicities.

\begin{theorem}[Multilevel energy bound]\label{gsr:en:68:thm:multilevel}
Let
$0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_\ell=m$, with each internal $t_i$ an attained value
of $r_A$. Put $g_i=t_i-t_{i-1}$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:multilevel}
 E(A)\le\frac{2m^3+\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}g_i^3}{3}.
\end{equation}
Equivalently, for $a_i=t_i/m$,
\[
 \eps\ge\frac{1-\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}(a_i-a_{i-1})^3}{3}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Put $z=\ind_A*\ind_A$ and
$S(u)=\sum_x\min(z(x),u)$ for $0\le u\le m$.
For an attained value $t=r_A(d)$, the proof above has
$0\le w\le\min(s,t)$ and $\sum w=t(2m-t)$.
Since $s$ is a translate of $z$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:truncation-node}
 S(t)\ge t(2m-t).
\end{equation}
The function $S$ is concave, $S(0)=0$, and $S(m)=m^2$.
On each interval $[t_{i-1},t_i]$, it is therefore at least the chord
joining the corresponding values of $P(u)=2mu-u^2$.
The difference between $P(u)$ and that chord is
$(u-t_{i-1})(t_i-u)$; its integral is $g_i^3/6$.
Consequently
\[
 \int_0^m S(u)\,du\ge\frac{2m^3}{3}-\frac16\sum_i g_i^3.
\]
On the other hand, integrating each truncated multiplicity gives
\[
 \int_0^m S(u)\,du
 =\sum_x\left(mz(x)-\frac{z(x)^2}{2}\right)
 =m^3-\frac{E(A)}2.
\]
Combining the two formulas proves \eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:multilevel}.
\end{proof}

One internal node recovers \eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:pointwise}, since
$t^3+(m-t)^3=m^3-3mt(m-t)$.
Adding a genuinely new node decreases the right side of
\eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:multilevel}: splitting a positive gap $g=u+v$ replaces $g^3$
by $u^3+v^3=g^3-3uvg$.
Thus the full distinct overlap spectrum gives the strongest member of
this family.

\begin{example}[The interval test]
If every integer $0,1,\ldots,m$ is attained by $r_A$, then
$E(A)\le(2m^3+m)/3$. The integer interval
$A=\{0,\ldots,m-1\}\subset\Z$ attains this bound, because its
nonzero difference multiplicities are
$m,m-1,m-1,\ldots,1,1$.
The assertion is conditional on the attained spectrum. It is not an
upper bound for arbitrary sets in groups with torsion.
\end{example}

\subsection{Complete equality classification for one translation}

\begin{lemma}[The elementary three-halves lemma]\label{gsr:en:68:lem:threehalves}
If $T$ is finite and nonempty in an abelian group and
$|T-T|<3|T|/2$, then $T-T$ is a subgroup.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $n=|T|$ and $D=T-T$. For $d=a-b\in D$, the sets $T-a$ and
$T-b$ both lie in $D$, so
$r_T(d)\ge2n-|D|>n/2$.
For $d,e\in D$, the overlap triangle inequality
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:overlap-triangle}
 r_T(d-e)\ge r_T(d)+r_T(e)-n
\end{equation}
therefore gives $r_T(d-e)>0$. Thus $D$ is closed under differences.
It contains zero and is finite, so it is a subgroup.
For completeness, \eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:overlap-triangle} follows by intersecting
$T\cap(T+d)$ and $T\cap(T+e)$ inside $T$ and translating the resulting
intersection.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[All positive-gap equality cases]\label{gsr:en:68:thm:pointwise-equality}
Suppose $0<r_A(d)<m$. Equality in \eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:pointwise} holds exactly
in the following cases, up to translation of $A$.
\begin{enumerate}
 \item $A=K\setminus(z+L)$, where $L<K$ are finite subgroups,
 $z\in K$, $[K:L]\ge3$, and $d\in K\setminus L$.
 \item $A=(a+L)\sqcup(b+L)$, where $L$ is a finite subgroup,
 $b-a$ has order at least four or infinite order in $G/L$, and
 $d+L=\pm(b-a)+L$.
\end{enumerate}
The second family has $\eps=1/4$. Allowing order three in that family
duplicates the index-three examples in the first family.
If $r_A(d)\in\{0,m\}$, equality holds precisely when $A$ is a finite
subgroup coset.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write $t=r_A(d)$ and $k=m-t$, so $t,k>0$.
Equality in \eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:self-remainder} forces
$v(x)\in\{0,k\}$, $w(x)\in\{0,t\}$, and $v(x)>0$ only where
$w(x)=t$. Hence $s=w+v$ takes only the values $0,t,m$.
The set $R=\{x:s(x)=m\}$ is nonempty, since $P,Q$ are nonempty.

Let $L=\Stab(A)=\{h:A+h=A\}$, a finite subgroup, and choose $x_0\in R$.
The equation $s(x_0)=m$ says $A=x_0-(A+d)$.
The same equation at $x$ holds exactly when $x-x_0\in L$;
therefore $R=x_0+L$.
Both $P$ and $Q$ are $L$-periodic, and $P+Q\subset R$.
Fixing one element of $Q$ shows that $P$ lies in a single $L$-coset;
its nonemptiness and periodicity make it exactly that coset.
The same holds for $Q$. Thus $|L|=k$.

Pass to $G/L$, and let $T$ be the image of $A$, of size $n=m/k\ge2$.
After a fixed translation of its argument, the sum convolution of $T$
has exactly one value $n$, and all other positive values are $n-1$.
Its total mass is $n^2$, so exactly $n$ of these latter values occur:
$|T+T|=n+1$.
The full representation value also gives a reflection taking $T$ to
itself. Hence $|T-T|=|T+T|=n+1$.

For $n\ge3$, $n+1<3n/2$, and Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:68:lem:threehalves} makes
$T-T$ a subgroup of order $n+1$.
The set $T$ lies in one coset of this subgroup and misses one point.
Lifting to $G$ gives the first family, with index $n+1\ge4$.
Since $0<t<m$, the shift belongs to $K\setminus L$.
For $n=2$, write $T=\{\bar a,\bar b\}$.
Its difference has order greater than two, and the nontrivial
positive overlap occurs exactly at the two signed differences.
Order three gives the remaining case of the first family; all other
orders give the second.

Conversely, the multiplicities in Example~\ref{gsr:en:68:ex:punctured} prove
equality for the first family. For the second family they are $2|L|$
on $L$, $|L|$ on each of the two signed difference cosets, and zero
elsewhere. Thus $E(A)=6|L|^3$, $m=2|L|$, and $\eps=1/4$.

Finally, when $t=0$ or $m$, equality means $E(A)=m^3$.
Counting triples shows that every $a-b+c$, for $a,b,c\in A$, then
belongs to $A$. Translating one element to zero makes $A$ a finite
subgroup. The converse is immediate.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Bounded weights and minimum overlap}

There is a useful extension in which the correct overlap is the
minimum of two weights, rather than their product.

\begin{proposition}[Weighted overlap gap]\label{gsr:en:68:prop:weighted}
Let $f:G\to[0,1]$ have finite support and positive mass $m=\sum_xf(x)$.
Define
\[
 E(f)=\sum_x(f*f)(x)^2,\qquad
 t_f(d)=\sum_x\min(f(x),f(x-d)).
\]
Then, for every $d$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:weighted-gap}
 E(f)\le m^3-mt_f(d)(m-t_f(d)).
\end{equation}
The multilevel bound \eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:multilevel} holds with arbitrary
attained values of $t_f$ and these real-valued masses.
If $E(f)\ge3m^3/4$, the finite set
$\{d:t_f(d)>m/2\}$ is a subgroup.
More generally, for $0\le f\le M$, $M>0$, the corresponding
normalized defect is $1-E(f)/(Mm^3)$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Put $g(x)=f(x-d)$,
$c=\min(f,g)$, $u=\max(f,g)$, $p=f-c$, and $v_0=g-c$.
Then $f=c+p$, $g=c+v_0$, $u=c+p+v_0$, and commutativity gives
\[
 f*g=c*u+p*v_0.
\]
Let $t=\sum c$, $k=m-t$, $w=c*u$, and $v=p*v_0$.
Because $u,p,v_0\le1$, we have $w\le t$, $v\le k$.
Moreover $\sum w=t(2m-t)$, $\sum v=k^2$, and
$\sum(f*g)^2=E(f)$. The expansion proving
\eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:self-remainder} therefore applies without change and proves
\eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:weighted-gap}.
It also gives $\sum_x\min((f*f)(x),t)\ge t(2m-t)$ at each attained
minimum-overlap value. The concavity and integration proof of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:multilevel} uses no integrality and still applies.

Finally,
$t_f(d)=m-\frac12\|f-f(\,\cdot-d)\|_1$.
The triangle inequality for the $\ell^1$ norm gives
$t_f(d-e)\ge t_f(d)+t_f(e)-m$.
The two-node proof of the subgroup assertion in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:coset} now applies verbatim.
Replacing $f$ by $f/M$ proves the last assertion.
\end{proof}

For indicator functions, minimum overlap equals the usual
autocorrelation. For general weights it does not. In particular,
the occupancy identity $\sum_{d\in H}r_A(d)=\sum_i|A\cap C_i|^2$
used below has no direct replacement with $t_f$; the weighted
proposition does not by itself assert the set-valued coset-distance
bound.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Sharp coset rigidity and two different thresholds\srctag{68}}]{Sharp coset rigidity and two different thresholds}\label{gsr:en:68:sec:d3}
\srcnote{68}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:en:68:sec:cosets}

The pointwise gap separates overlap values into two ranges.
Using two attained values at once proves that the upper range is a
subgroup throughout the entire real range of the quadratic inverse.
This extra step is necessary: the one-value triangle argument alone
only reaches defect $2/9$.

\subsection{The canonical subgroup and the optimal existence range}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp coset existence]\label{gsr:en:68:thm:coset}
Let $A$ be as in \eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:energy-notation}, and suppose $\eps\le1/4$.
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:canonical-subgroup}
 H=\{d\in G:r_A(d)>m/2\}
\end{equation}
is a finite subgroup. If $C$ is any $H$-coset maximizing $|A\cap C|$,
then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:coset-envelope}
 \delta_C:=\frac{|A\symdiff C|}{m}\le\tau(\eps).
\end{equation}
For $\eps<1/4$, this maximizing $H$-coset is unique.
The threshold $1/4$ is optimal for both the subgroup assertion and
the guarantee that some subgroup coset has distance at most $m/2$.
Optimality already holds among finite cyclic ambient groups.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof of the subgroup assertion]
The set $H$ contains zero, is symmetric, and is finite, because
