$H\subset A-A$. Suppose $d,e\in H$ but $q(d-e)\le1/2$.
Set $c=q(d-e)$ and $b=\min(q(d),q(e))$.
The overlap triangle inequality gives
\[
 0<c\le\frac12<b\le\frac{1+c}{2}.
\]
Both $c$ and $b$ are attained normalized multiplicities.
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:multilevel}, with these two internal nodes, gives
\[
 \eps\ge F(c,b):=
 \frac{1-c^3-(b-c)^3-(1-b)^3}{3}.
\]
For fixed $c$,
$\partial F/\partial b=(1-c)(1+c-2b)$.
It is positive before the upper endpoint of the displayed interval.
As $b>1/2$ and $c>0$,
\[
 F(c,b)>F(c,1/2)
 =\frac14+\frac{c(1/2-c)}2\ge\frac14,
\]
a contradiction, including when $\eps=1/4$.
Thus $H$ is closed under differences and is a subgroup.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of the distance bound]
Write $a=\tau(\eps)$, $\beta=1-a$, and $h=|H|$.
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:pointwise} implies
\[
 q(d)\ge\beta\quad(d\in H),\qquad
 q(d)\le a\quad(d\notin H).
\]
These inequalities remain valid at $a=\beta=1/2$.
Let $p_i=|A\cap C_i|/m$ be the occupancies of the $H$-cosets, and put
$p_*=\max_i p_i$, $S_2=\sum_i p_i^2$.
Then $\sum_i p_i=1$, $S_2\le p_*$, and
\[
 \sum_{d\in H}q(d)=mS_2,\qquad
 \sum_{d\in G}q(d)=m,\qquad
 \eps=\frac1m\sum_{d\in G}q(d)(1-q(d)).
\]
For $d\in H$, $q(1-q)\ge\beta(1-q)$.
For $d\notin H$, $q(1-q)\ge\beta q$.
Summing these bounds gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:occupancy-budget}
 \eps\ge\beta\left(\frac hm+1-2S_2\right).
\end{equation}
For a maximizing coset,
$\delta_C=h/m+1-2p_*$. Since $\eps=a\beta$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:occupancy-frontier}
 \delta_C+2(p_*-S_2)\le a.
\end{equation}
This proves \eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:coset-envelope}.

To prove uniqueness among $H$-cosets when $a<1/2$, bound $q^2\le q$
on $H$ and $q^2\le aq$ off $H$. Then
\[
 1-\eps=\frac1m\sum_dq(d)^2\le S_2+a(1-S_2),
 \qquad S_2\ge1-\frac{\eps}{1-a}=1-a>\frac12.
\]
Thus $p_*\ge S_2>1/2$, and only one $H$-coset can attain $p_*$.
The optimality assertion is proved in
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:68:prop:threshold-sharp} below.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
Source~14's envelope held for $\varepsilon\le1/100$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:14:thm:energy-sharp-stability}) and source~45's for $\varepsilon<1/9$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:45:co:envelope}); $\tau(1/4)=1/2$ and $\tau(2/9)=1/3$ (checked at the write).
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{The optimal range} for $k=2$ remains this theorem's; source~101's $k=2$ part (range $1/60$) and its higher-dimensional profiles are in Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:cubestability}.
\end{writenote}

The same calculation yields an exact identity that will be useful for
stability and equality:
\begin{align}
 a-\delta_C
 &=2(p_*-S_2)\notag\\
 &\quad+\frac{1}{m\beta}
 \left(\sum_{d\in H}(q(d)-\beta)(1-q(d))
       +\sum_{d\notin H}q(d)(a-q(d))\right).
 \label{gsr:en:68:eq:rounding-remainder}
\end{align}
Every summand is nonnegative. This records both the distribution of
mass between cosets and the deviation of overlaps from the two
extreme levels.

\begin{corollary}[A sharper outlier budget]\label{gsr:en:68:cor:outlier}
Assume $\eps<1/4$, let $C$ be the canonical coset from
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:coset}, and put $x=|A\setminus C|/m$, $\delta=\delta_C$.
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:outlier-frontier}
 \delta+2x(1-2x)\le\tau(\eps)<\frac12,
 \qquad x<\frac14,\qquad \delta<\frac12.
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The largest occupancy is $1-x>1/2$, and
$S_2\le(1-x)^2+x^2$. Substitute in \eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:occupancy-frontier}.
Since $\delta\ge x$, this gives $3x-4x^2<1/2$.
On $1/4\le x<1/2$ the left side is at least $1/2$, so $x<1/4$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The sharp uniqueness range}

Here and below a subgroup coset means a coset of a \emph{finite}
subgroup, even if the ambient group is infinite. Define
\[
 \delta(A)=\min_C\frac{|A\symdiff C|}{m}.
\]
The minimum exists: the set of possible unnormalized distances is a
nonempty set of nonnegative integers.

\begin{lemma}[Separation of distinct cosets]\label{gsr:en:68:lem:coset-separation}
Distinct subgroup cosets $C,C'$ satisfy
\[
 |C\symdiff C'|\ge\min(|C|,|C'|).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If their intersection is empty the claim is immediate.
Otherwise their intersection is a coset of the intersection of their
underlying subgroups. If one coset properly contains the other, the
subgroup index is at least two, and the difference has size at least
that of the smaller coset.
If neither contains the other, the intersection has size at most half
of each; hence the symmetric difference is at least the larger size.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Optimal uniqueness threshold]\label{gsr:en:68:cor:unique}
Any coset $C$ with $|A\symdiff C|\le m/3$ is a closest coset.
If $|A\symdiff C|<m/3$, it is the unique closest coset.
In particular, if $\eps<2/9$, the canonical coset is the unique closest
coset and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:unique-envelope}
 \delta(A)=\delta_C\le\tau(\eps)<1/3.
\end{equation}
The defect threshold $2/9$ is sharp for uniqueness.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Suppose both $C$ and $C'$ have distance at most $\rho m$ from $A$.
Then $|C|,|C'|\ge(1-\rho)m$, whereas
$|C\symdiff C'|\le2\rho m$. If they are distinct,
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:68:lem:coset-separation} implies $\rho\ge1/3$.
If one distance is $m/3$ and the other is strictly smaller, the upper
bound is strictly below $2m/3$ while both sizes are at least $2m/3$,
again impossible. This proves both distance assertions.
Now use $\tau(2/9)=1/3$ and Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:coset}.

For sharpness, take $A=\{0,1,2\}\subset\Z/4\Z$.
Its difference multiplicities are $3,2,2,2$, so $E(A)=21$ and
$\eps=2/9$. Both $\Z/4\Z$ and $\{0,2\}$ are closest cosets,
each at distance $1=m/3$.
\end{proof}

Uniqueness among cosets of the \emph{canonical} subgroup persists to
$\eps<1/4$. Uniqueness when the underlying subgroup is also allowed to
vary stops at $2/9$. These are different assertions, and both
thresholds have a role in the subsequent repair theorem.

\subsection{All canonical-envelope equality cases}

\begin{theorem}[Equality in the coset envelope]\label{gsr:en:68:thm:coset-equality}
Use the canonical coset convention of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:coset}.
\begin{enumerate}
 \item If $\eps=0$, then $A=C$ is a subgroup coset.
 \item For $0<\eps<1/4$, equality $\delta_C=\tau(\eps)$ holds
 exactly when
 \[
 A=C\setminus(z+L),\qquad L<H,\quad z+L\subset C,\quad
 r=[H:L]\ge4.
 \]
 Here
 $\delta_C=1/(r-1)$ and $\eps=(r-2)/(r-1)^2$.
 These examples also satisfy $\delta(A)=\delta_C$.
 \item For $\eps=1/4$, equality $\delta_C=1/2$ holds exactly when
 $A$ is the union of two cosets of $H=\Stab(A)$ whose difference
 has order greater than two in $G/H$. There are exactly two
 maximizing $H$-cosets.
\end{enumerate}
In the uniqueness range $\eps<2/9$, the positive equality cases in
part~2 have $r\ge5$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The case $\eps=0$ follows from the maximal-energy characterization in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:pointwise-equality}.
Suppose $0<\eps<1/4$ and equality holds.
Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:rounding-remainder} forces
$p_*=S_2$. Since
$p_*-S_2=\sum_i p_i(p_*-p_i)$,
every nonzero occupancy equals $p_*$.
Also $S_2\ge\beta>1/2$, so there is only one occupied coset:
$A\subset C$.
The other remainder terms show that $q(d)\in\{\beta,1\}$ for $d\in H$.

Let $L=\Stab(A)=\{d:q(d)=1\}$ and write $\ell=|L|$.
Since $\delta_C=a$ and $A\subset C$, $h/m=1+a$.
The identity $\sum_{d\in H}q(d)=m$ now becomes
\[
 \ell+(h-\ell)\beta=m,
 \qquad \ell a=m-\beta h=ma^2.
\]
Therefore $\ell=ma=|C\setminus A|$.
The missing set is $L$-periodic and has size $|L|$, so it is a single
$L$-coset.
Moreover $h/\ell=(1+a)/a=1+1/a$ is an integer greater than three:
$r\ge4$.
Conversely Example~\ref{gsr:en:68:ex:punctured} gives the stated parameters.
For $r\ge4$ its overlaps outside $L$ but inside $H$ are strictly above
$m/2$, so the ambient coset $C$ is indeed the canonical one.
Its distance is at most $m/3$, and
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:68:cor:unique} proves it is a closest coset.

At $\eps=1/4$, the same occupancy argument gives one or two nonzero
occupancies, all equal. If there were one, the zero remainder would
force $q(d)=1$ for all $d\in H$, since $q(d)>1/2$ there.
Then $h=m$ and $\delta_C=0$, a contradiction.
There are therefore two occupancies, each $1/2$.
As $\delta_C=h/m$, equality makes $h=m/2$; each occupied coset is full.
Their quotient difference cannot have order two, since their union
would then itself be a subgroup coset of maximal energy.
For order greater than two, the multiplicities are $m$ on $H$ and
$m/2$ on the two signed difference cosets. They give $\eps=1/4$,
$\delta_C=1/2$, and $H=\Stab(A)$, as required.
\end{proof}

The curve $\tau(\eps)$ is attained at the indicated discrete
parameters. In particular, there is no canonical-envelope equality
for $2/9<\eps<1/4$. This arithmetic gap is relevant to any proposed
continuous refinement of the bound.

\subsection{Why the endpoint cannot be increased}

\begin{proposition}[Sharpness of the quarter-defect threshold]
\label{gsr:en:68:prop:threshold-sharp}
For every $\eps_0>1/4$ there is a finite subset of a finite cyclic group
with defect between $1/4$ and $\eps_0$ for which
$\{d:r_A(d)>|A|/2\}$ is not a subgroup and
$\delta(A)>1/2$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
First let $K$ be a finite abelian group of order $h\ge2$, and work in
$K\times\Z$ with
\[
 A=(K\times\{0,1\})\cup\{(0,2)\},\qquad m=2h+1.
\]
At second coordinate zero the difference multiplicity is $m$ at zero
and $2h$ at the other $h-1$ points.
At each of the two levels $\pm1$, every first coordinate has
multiplicity $h+1$.
At each level $\pm2$, every first coordinate has multiplicity $1$.
Hence
\begin{align*}
 E(A)&=(2h+1)^2+(h-1)(2h)^2+2h(h+1)^2+2h\\
 &=6h^3+4h^2+8h+1,\\
 \eps-\frac14
 &=\frac{20h^2-14h-1}{4(2h+1)^3}>0.
\end{align*}
The last expression tends to zero as $h\to\infty$.
For $d=(0,1)$, $r_A(d)=h+1>m/2$ but $r_A(2d)=1\le m/2$.
Every finite subgroup coset in $K\times\Z$ lies at one integer level,
so its maximum possible improvement over the empty-set distance is
$h$. The nearest such cosets are the two full levels, and
\[
 \delta(A)=\frac{h+1}{2h+1}>\frac12.
\]

To obtain a finite cyclic example, take $K=\Z/h\Z$ and a prime
$p>4h+3$, and replace the integer coordinate by $\Z/p\Z$.
The five difference levels remain distinct, so the energy is
unchanged. A subgroup with nonzero projection onto $\Z/p\Z$ has size
at least $p$, and each of its cosets has distance at least
$p-m>h+1$ from $A$.
A subgroup with zero projection lies in one level, where the preceding
minimum remains $h+1$.
Finally $p$ is coprime to $h$, so
$\Z/h\Z\times\Z/p\Z$ is cyclic.
Choosing $h$ sufficiently large proves the assertion.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Sharp puncture repair and a single near-saturated translation\srctag{68}}]{Sharp puncture repair and a single near-saturated translation}\label{gsr:en:68:sec:d4}
\srcnote{68}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:en:68:sec:punctures}

The coset theorem determines an ambient structure.  The next question is
whether a set close to its quadratic error envelope is close to a coset
with one subcoset removed.  Source~45 of the repository report proves the
profile below when both the outer energy defect and the normalized inner
excess are less than $1/9$ \cite{repo68fortyfive}.  We retain that profile with both
defects less than $1/4$.  We also show that near equality in the energy
inequality at one translation specifies which subgroup the repaired hole
must avoid.

The distinction between a canonical coset and a closest coset matters in
this section.  Unless a smaller range is specified, the outer coset is the
one constructed by Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:coset}.  Above defect $2/9$ it is not
silently identified with a closest coset.  All minimizations over holes
keep this outer coset fixed.

\subsection{A stronger remainder around a proposed coset}

Retain $m,E(A),\eps,q$ from \eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:energy-notation}.  For any finite
subgroup coset $C=c+H$, put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:puncture-notation}
 A_0=A\cap C,\qquad T=A\setminus C,\qquad K=C\setminus A,
 \qquad b=|A_0|,\quad t=|T|,\quad u=|K|,
\end{equation}
and define
\[
 x=\frac{t}{m},\qquad \delta=\frac{t+u}{m}.
\]
An empty auxiliary set has energy zero.

\begin{proposition}[Outlier and missing-set remainder]
\label{gsr:en:68:prop:puncture-remainder}
For every proposed coset $C$,
\begin{align}
 E(A)&\le E(A_0)+6bt^2+t^3,\label{gsr:en:68:eq:puncture-outliers}\\
 E(A_0)&=b^3-bu(b-u)-\bigl(u^3-E(K)\bigr).
 \label{gsr:en:68:eq:puncture-complement}
\end{align}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:puncture-remainder}
 \eps\ge \delta(1-\delta)+xB(\delta,x)
                  +\frac{u^3-E(K)}{m^3},
 \qquad
 B(\delta,x)=2+\delta^2-(8+\delta)x+6x^2.
\end{equation}
The polynomial $B$ need not be positive for an arbitrary proposed coset.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Count the ordered triples $(z_1,z_2,z_3)\in A^3$ whose alternating sum
$z_1-z_2+z_3$ lies in $A$, according to the number of their entries in
$T$.  Triples with no such entry contribute $E(A_0)$.  If exactly one
entry lies in $T$, the output lies outside $C$, hence in $T$.  There are
three choices of its position.  Fixing the input in $T$, the output in
$T$, and one of the two inputs in $A_0$ determines the remaining input.
These cases contribute at most $3bt^2$.  Triples with exactly two entries
in $T$ contribute at most all $3bt^2$ possible input triples, and those
with three contribute at most $t^3$.  This proves
\eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:puncture-outliers}.

Translate $C$ to $H$ and write $h=|H|=b+u$.  Expanding the four indicator
factors in the additive-quadruple count, using
$\ind_{A_0}=\ind_H-\ind_K$, gives the exact identity
\[
 E(A_0)=h^3-4h^2u+6hu^2-4u^3+E(K).
\]
For example, a term with two prescribed entries in $K$ has $hu^2$
solutions: one of the remaining entries is free in $H$, and the last is
determined there.  Substitution of $h=b+u$ gives
\eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:puncture-complement}.  Finally use
$b/m=1-x$ and $u/m=\delta-x$ in the first two assertions and expand.
The resulting polynomial is \eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:puncture-remainder}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Comparison with the predecessor remainder]
\label{gsr:en:68:rem:puncture-remainder-credit}
Source~45 bounds the outlier contribution by $6bt^2+5t^3$; its resulting
polynomial has $2x^2$ in place of $6x^2$.  Counting input triples gives the
stronger form above.  This counting argument is already implicit in
Source~14's proof of the quadratic coset envelope.  The refinement used
here combines that argument with Source~45's exact missing-set identity;
we credit those predecessor ingredients \cite{repo68fourteen,repo68fortyfive}.
\end{remark}

\subsection{The canonical outlier budget}

Suppose now that $\eps<1/4$.  Let
\[
 a=\tau(\eps),\qquad H=\{d:q(d)>1/2\},
\]
and let $C$ be the $H$-coset with largest intersection with $A$, as in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:coset}.  Define $x,\delta$ by
\eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:puncture-notation}, and put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:puncture-excess}
 \eta=\eps-\delta(1-\delta).
\end{equation}
Here $\delta$ is the distance to this specified $C$.

\begin{lemma}[Uniform canonical budget]
\label{gsr:en:68:lem:puncture-budget}
One has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:puncture-canonical-range}
 0\le x<\frac14,\qquad x\le\delta\le a<\frac12,
 \qquad
 \eta\ge\frac38x+\frac{u^3-E(K)}{m^3}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $p_j$ be the proportions of $A$ in the $H$-cosets, and write
$p_* =1-x$ for their maximum.  The canonical-coset argument gives
\[
 \sum_jp_j^2\ge1-a>\frac12,
 \qquad p_*\ge\sum_jp_j^2,
\]
so $x<1/2$ and the maximizing coset is unique.  Keeping the occupancy
loss in the same argument gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:puncture-occupancy}
 \delta+2\left(p_*-\sum_jp_j^2\right)\le a.
\end{equation}
For completeness, the pointwise gap gives $q\ge1-a$ on $H$ and
$q\le a$ off $H$, whence
\[
 \eps=\frac1m\sum_dq(d)(1-q(d))
 \ge(1-a)\left(\frac{|H|}{m}+1-2\sum_jp_j^2\right).
\]
Use $\eps=a(1-a)$ and
$\delta=|H|/m+1-2p_*$ to obtain \eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:puncture-occupancy}.

Since $\sum_jp_j^2\le(1-x)^2+x^2$, this implies
\[
 \delta+2x(1-2x)\le a<\frac12.
\]
Also $\delta\ge x$.  Thus $3x-4x^2<1/2$.  This is impossible for
$1/4\le x<1/2$, proving $x<1/4$.  For $\delta\ge x$,
\[
 \frac{\partial B}{\partial\delta}=2\delta-x\ge0,
 \qquad B(\delta,x)\ge2-8x+6x^2>\frac38.
\]
The last polynomial decreases on $[0,1/4]$ and has value $3/8$ at
$1/4$.  Insert this bound into \eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:puncture-remainder}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The exact puncture profile below the quarter threshold}

For the fixed canonical $C$, define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:puncture-distance}
 \Delta_C(A)=\frac1m
 \min_{\substack{D\subsetneq C\text{ a nonempty}\\
                 \text{subgroup coset}}}
                  |A\symdiff(C\setminus D)|.
\end{equation}
The theorem below proves that an admissible hole exists under its
hypotheses.

\begin{theorem}[Sharp canonical puncture profile]
\label{gsr:en:68:thm:puncture}
Suppose $\eps<1/4$, let $C$ be its canonical coset, and assume
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:puncture-hypotheses}
 \delta=\frac{|A\symdiff C|}{m}>0,
 \qquad 0\le s=\frac{\eta}{\delta^3}<\frac14,
 \qquad \eta=\eps-\delta(1-\delta).
\end{equation}
Then $K=C\setminus A$ is nonempty, a closest subgroup coset to $K$
exists, and every such closest coset is a nonempty proper subcoset of
$C$.  Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:puncture-profile}
 \Delta_C(A)\le\delta\tau(s).
\end{equation}
If $s<2/9$, the minimizing hole is unique.  Separately, if
$\eps<2/9$, $C$ is the unique closest outer coset to $A$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Put $c=3/8$.  The bound $\eta\ge cx$ holds even if $K$ is initially
empty.  Since
\[
 x\le\frac\eta c=\frac83s\delta^3
                <\frac23\delta^3<\frac\delta6,
\]
we have $x<\delta$, so $K$ is nonempty.  Set
\[
 k=\frac{|K|}{m}=\delta-x,
 \qquad \zeta=1-\frac{E(K)}{|K|^3}.
\]
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:68:lem:puncture-budget} gives the coupled inequality
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:puncture-hole-budget}
 \eta\ge cx+k^3\zeta.
\end{equation}

For $0\le y\le\eta/c$ define
\[
 z(y)=\frac{\eta-cy}{(\delta-y)^3}.
\]
Its denominator is positive, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:puncture-z-derivative}
 z'(y)=\frac{-c\delta+3\eta-2cy}{(\delta-y)^4}<0.
\end{equation}
Indeed $3\eta=3s\delta^3<(3/4)\delta^3<(3/16)\delta<c\delta$.
It follows that
\[
 0\le\zeta\le z(x)\le z(0)=s<\frac14.
\]
Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:coset} to $K$ within $C$, after translating
$C$ to $H$.  It supplies a subgroup coset $D\subset C$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:puncture-inner-repair}
 |K\symdiff D|\le\tau(\zeta)|K|.
\end{equation}
This $D$ is proper.  Writing $h=|C|$, we have
\[
 \frac{|K|}{h}=\frac{\delta-x}{1+\delta-2x}<\frac13,
\]
because $2\delta-x<1$.  Since $\tau(\zeta)<1/2$,
$|D|<(3/2)|K|<h/2$.

For any hole inside $C$, the outliers $T$ contribute exactly $t$ edits.
Hence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:puncture-repair-chain}
 \Delta_C(A)\le x+k\tau(\zeta)
              \le x+(\delta-x)\tau(z(x)).
\end{equation}
To optimize this coupled bound without losing a leading constant, set
\[
 F(y)=y+(\delta-y)\tau(z(y)),\qquad b_y=\tau(z(y)).
\]
Using $b_y(1-b_y)=z(y)$, direct differentiation gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:puncture-F-derivative}
 F'(y)=\frac{1-b_y^2-c/(\delta-y)^2}{1-2b_y}<0.
\end{equation}
The denominator is positive, while $\delta-y\le\delta<1/2$ gives
$c/(\delta-y)^2>3/2$.  Thus
\[
 \Delta_C(A)\le F(x)\le F(0)=\delta\tau(s),
\]
as claimed.

We justify the assertion about closest holes.  A closest subgroup coset
to $K$ exists because the nonnegative integer distances have a minimum.
It must intersect $K$: a disjoint coset has distance at least $|K|+1$,
whereas a singleton in $K$ has distance $|K|-1$.  If a closest coset $E$
were not contained in $C$, its nonempty intersection $E\cap C$ would be
a subgroup coset and would strictly decrease its distance to $K$.
Finally $E\ne C$, since $|C|-|K|>2|K|$ and a singleton is closer.
Therefore all closest cosets are admissible holes, and they minimize
\eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:puncture-distance}.

If $s<2/9$, then $\zeta\le s<2/9$ and Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:68:cor:unique}
applied to $K$ makes its closest coset unique.  The assertion about the
outer coset follows from that corollary applied to $A$.  If $s=0$, the
budget gives $x=0$ and $E(K)=|K|^3$, so $K$ itself is a coset and the
repair is exact.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[All equality cases in the puncture profile]
\label{gsr:en:68:thm:puncture-equality}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:puncture}, if $s>0$, equality
in \eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:puncture-profile} holds precisely when
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:puncture-equality}
 A=(C\setminus D)\cup J,
\end{equation}
where $J\subsetneq D\subsetneq C$ are nonempty subgroup cosets and
the subgroup of $J$ has index $r\ge4$ in the subgroup of $D$.
The assertion retains the specified canonical outer coset $C$.
For $s=0$, one has $A=C\setminus D$ exactly.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Suppose first that $s>0$ and equality holds.  In the proof of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:puncture}, use the canonical inner coset supplied by
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:coset}.  The strict decrease in
\eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:puncture-F-derivative} forces $x=0$.  Thus $A\subset C$,
$|K|/m=\delta$, and the exact complement identity gives
\[
 \eta=\delta^3\zeta,\qquad \zeta=s.
\]
The chain of inequalities can now be an equality only if the canonical
inner coset realizes equality in its own quadratic envelope.
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:coset-equality} says exactly that $K=D\setminus J$,
where the subgroup index is $r\ge4$.

Conversely, suppose the displayed configuration holds under the
theorem's hypotheses.  Write $\ell=|J|$, so $|K|=(r-1)\ell$.
The inner energy identity gives
\[
 \zeta=\frac{r-2}{(r-1)^2},
 \qquad \frac{|K\symdiff D|}{|K|}
       =\frac1{r-1}=\tau(\zeta)\le\frac13.
\]
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:68:cor:unique}, including its endpoint minimality assertion,
shows that $D$ is a closest coset to $K$; it is unique when $r\ge5$.
The complement identity then yields $\zeta=s$ and
\[
 \Delta_C(A)=\frac\ell m=\delta\tau(s).
\]
The $s=0$ case was proved at the end of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:puncture}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What is sharp]
The exact profile is attained at the discrete parameters supplied by the
subgroup indices.  This does not assert attainment at every real $s$.
For $s>0$, it can be written
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:puncture-leading}
 \delta\tau(s)=\frac{\tau(s)}s\frac\eta{\delta^2},
 \qquad
 \frac{\tau(s)}s=\frac1{1-\tau(s)}
                 =1+s+2s^2+O(s^3).
\end{equation}
The examples below prove that the uniform asymptotic leading constant
one cannot be reduced.
\end{remark}

\subsection{A translation gap determines the orientation of the hole}

For every $d\in G$ define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:translation-gap}
 \theta_d=\eps-q(d)(1-q(d))\ge0.
\end{equation}
The nonnegativity is Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:pointwise}.  The excess $\eta$
measures closeness to the coset envelope; $\theta_d$ measures closeness
to equality at one specified translation.

\begin{proposition}[Exact translation-gap decomposition]
\label{gsr:en:68:prop:translation-decomposition}
Suppose $\eps<1/4$, and use its canonical $C=c+H$.  For $d\in H$ put
\[
 z_d=\frac{r_K(d)+r_T(d)}m.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:translation-exact}
 q(d)=1-\delta+z_d,
 \qquad
 \theta_d=\eta+(1-2\delta)z_d+z_d^2.
\end{equation}
If $d\notin H$ and $\delta>0$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:translation-off-H}
 \theta_d\ge\frac\delta8.
\end{equation}
The constant in this last separation estimate is not asserted optimal.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
A difference in $H$ cannot connect $C$ to another $H$-coset.  Therefore
\[
 r_A(d)=r_{A_0}(d)+r_T(d),\qquad
 r_{A_0}(d)=|H|-2u+r_K(d).
\]
Since $|H|-2u=m-t-u=m(1-\delta)$, this proves the first identity in
\eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:translation-exact}.  Substitute it into
\eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:translation-gap} to obtain the second.

If $d\notin H$, every pair counted by $r_A(d)$ has at least one endpoint
in $T$, so $q(d)\le2x<1/2$.  The function $v(1-v)$ increases on
$[0,1/2]$.  Thus \eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:puncture-remainder} implies
\begin{align}
 \theta_d&\ge R(\delta,x),\label{gsr:en:68:eq:translation-R}\\
 R(\delta,x)
   &=\delta-\delta^2+\delta^2x-(4+\delta)x^2+6x^3.\notag
\end{align}
We claim $R(\delta,x)\ge\delta/8$ on
$0\le x\le\delta\le1/2$, $x\le1/4$.  For fixed $x$,
$R(\delta,x)-\delta/8$ is concave in $\delta$, so its minimum on
$[x,1/2]$ occurs at an endpoint.  At the first,
\[
 R(x,x)=x(1-2x)(1-3x)\ge\frac x8.
\]
At the second,
\[
 R(1/2,x)-\frac18
 =\frac{(1-4x)(1+6x-12x^2)}8\ge0,
\]
which is stronger than the required $R(1/2,x)\ge1/16$.
This proves \eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:translation-off-H}.
\end{proof}

For a subgroup coset $D$, write $L_D$ for its underlying subgroup.
For the fixed outer coset $C$, define the oriented repair distance
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:oriented-distance}
 \Delta_{C,d}(A)=\frac1m
 \min_{\substack{D\subsetneq C\text{ a nonempty subgroup coset}\\
                 d\notin L_D}}
                  |A\symdiff(C\setminus D)|.
\end{equation}
The following theorem proves that the minimizing class is nonempty.

\begin{theorem}[Sharp repair from one nearly saturated translation]
\label{gsr:en:68:thm:oriented-puncture}
Suppose $\eps<1/4$, let $C=c+H$ be the canonical coset, and assume
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:oriented-hypotheses}
 \delta=\frac{|A\symdiff C|}{m}>0,
 \qquad 0\le\sigma=\frac{\theta_d}{\delta^3}<\frac14.
\end{equation}
Then $d\in H$.  Every closest subgroup coset $D$ to $K=C\setminus A$
is a proper subcoset of $C$ and satisfies $d\notin L_D$.  In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:oriented-profile}
 \Delta_{C,d}(A)=\Delta_C(A)
       \le\delta\tau\left(\frac{\theta_d}{\delta^3}\right).
\end{equation}
If $\sigma<2/9$, the minimizing hole is unique.

For $\sigma>0$, equality in \eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:oriented-profile} holds precisely
for the nested configurations in \eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:puncture-equality}, with
inner index $r\ge4$ and $d\notin L_D$.  For $\sigma=0$, the repair is
exact: $A=C\setminus D$ and $d\in H\setminus L_D$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If $d\notin H$, Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:68:prop:translation-decomposition} gives
$\theta_d\ge\delta/8$.  But the hypotheses imply
\[
 \theta_d<\frac{\delta^3}{4}<\frac\delta{16},
\]
a contradiction.  Hence $d\in H$, and
\eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:translation-exact} gives $\eta\le\theta_d$.
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:puncture} applies with
$s=\eta/\delta^3\le\sigma$.  For any minimizing hole $D$, put
$e=\Delta_C(A)$.  Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:68:eq:oriented-repair-size}
 e\le\delta\tau(\sigma)<\frac\delta2.
\end{equation}

Suppose $d\in L_D$.  Then $D+d=D$, and intersecting $K\cap D$ with its
translate within $D$ gives
\[
 r_K(d)\ge2|K\cap D|-|D|=|K|-|K\symdiff D|.
\]
Since $e=x+|K\symdiff D|/m$, division by $m$ yields
$z_d\ge r_K(d)/m\ge\delta-e>\delta/2$.
The exact gap identity therefore implies
\[
 \theta_d\ge z_d^2>\frac{\delta^2}{4},
\]
contradicting $\theta_d<\delta^3/4<\delta^2/8$.
Thus every minimizing hole avoids $d$ in its subgroup.  All are
admissible in \eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:oriented-distance}, proving the equality of the
two minima and the bound.  If $\sigma<2/9$, then $s<2/9$ and the
uniqueness assertion of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:puncture} applies.

Suppose next that $\sigma>0$ and the profile is attained.  The chain
\[
 \Delta_C(A)\le\delta\tau(\eta/\delta^3)
              \le\delta\tau(\theta_d/\delta^3)
\]
forces $\eta=\theta_d$ and equality in the puncture profile, by strict
monotonicity of $\tau$.  Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:puncture-equality} gives
$A=(C\setminus D)\cup J$ with inner index $r\ge4$.  In this
representation $r_K(d)>0$ whenever $d\in L_D$: indeed
$r_K(d)\ge|D|-2|J|=(r-2)|J|>0$.  The equality
$\theta_d=\eta$ and \eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:translation-exact} therefore force
$d\notin L_D$.

Conversely, in such a configuration with $d\notin L_D$, the hole
$K=D\setminus J$ is disjoint from $K+d$ and there are no outliers.
Thus $z_d=0$, $\theta_d=\eta$, and
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:puncture-equality} gives equality in
\eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:oriented-profile}.  If $\sigma=0$, the same identity gives
$\eta=0$ and the exact punctured-coset representation, with the
orientation already established.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Attainment, a nonunique hole, and the sharp leading constant}

\begin{example}[A sharp model in the enlarged range]
\label{gsr:en:68:ex:puncture-twelve}
Let $G=\Z/12\Z$, $D=\{0,3,6,9\}$, $J=\{0\}$, and
$A=(G\setminus D)\cup J$.  The canonical outer coset is $C=G$.
Here
\[
 m=9,\qquad K=\{3,6,9\},\qquad
 \delta=\frac13,\qquad
 \eta=\frac{2}{243},\qquad
 \eps=\frac{56}{243}\in\left(\frac29,\frac14\right).
\]
Also $s=\eta/\delta^3=2/9$, and
\[
 \Delta_C(A)=\frac19=\delta\tau(2/9).
\]
The four-point hole $D$ and the two-point coset $\{3,9\}$ are both
closest to $K$, each at one edit.  Thus uniqueness of the hole would be
false in the larger range.  With $d=1$, both holes avoid $d$ in their
subgroup, $\theta_d=\eta$, and the oriented profile is attained too.
\end{example}

\begin{proposition}[Exact attainment and optimal leading constant]
\label{gsr:en:68:prop:puncture-sharpness}
Fix an integer $R\ge10$.  For every integer $r\ge4$, let
$G=\Z/(Rr)\Z$, let $D$ be its subgroup of order $r$, and set
\[
 J=\{0\},\qquad A=(G\setminus D)\cup J,\qquad d=1.
\]
Then all hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:oriented-puncture} hold, its
profile is attained, and
\begin{align}
 m&=(R-1)r+1,&
 \delta&=\frac{r-1}{m},\notag\\
 \theta_d=\eta&=\frac{(r-1)(r-2)}{m^3},&
 \sigma&=\frac{r-2}{(r-1)^2},\label{gsr:en:68:eq:puncture-model}\\
 \Delta_{G,d}(A)&=\frac1m
                 =\delta\tau(\sigma).&&\notag
\end{align}
Consequently the best uniform asymptotic leading constant in a bound
of the form
\[
 \Delta_{C,d}(A)\le(C_0+o(1))\frac{\theta_d}{\delta^2}
 \quad\text{as }\theta_d/\delta^3\longrightarrow0
\]
is $C_0=1$.  The corresponding statement with $\eta$ and $\Delta_C$
also has leading constant one.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The missing set is $K=D\setminus\{0\}$.  Its maximal-coset complement
calculation gives the parameters in \eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:puncture-model}.  Since
$d=1\notin D$, $r_K(d)=0$ and hence $\theta_d=\eta$.
Moreover $\delta<1/(R-1)\le1/9$ and $\eta<\delta^2$, so
\[
 \eps=\delta(1-\delta)+\eta<\delta<\frac19.
\]
The same intersection formula shows $q(h)\ge1-\delta>1/2$ for every
$h\in G$, so the canonical outer coset is indeed $G$.
For $r\ge4$ we have $\sigma\le2/9<1/4$ and
$\tau(\sigma)=1/(r-1)$.  The equality theorems give the one-edit
repair.  Finally,
\[
 \frac{\Delta_{G,d}(A)}{\theta_d/\delta^2}
 =\frac{r-1}{r-2}\longrightarrow1,
 \qquad \sigma\longrightarrow0,
\]
proving optimality of the leading constant.
\end{proof}

The new translation statement supplies information not present in an
unoriented coset approximation: a nearly saturated overlap identifies a
hole whose subgroup excludes the tested direction.  Its proof retains
the actual gap at that direction, the missing-set energy, and the
outlier mass.  It remains a local structural theorem; no improved global
Szemer\'edi bound is inferred from it alone.

\subsection{The inner endpoint and the strict outer threshold}

The inner quarter threshold can be included.  It has additional equality
cases, so we record it separately from the strict-range theorems.

\begin{proposition}[Endpoint extension and its equality cases]
\label{gsr:en:68:prop:puncture-endpoint}
Keep the strict outer hypothesis $\eps<1/4$ and the canonical coset
convention.  The puncture conclusion \eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:puncture-profile} remains
valid for
\[
 0\le s=\eta/\delta^3\le1/4,
\]
and the oriented conclusion \eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:oriented-profile}, including
admissibility of every minimizing hole, remains valid for
\[
 0\le\sigma=\theta_d/\delta^3\le1/4.
\]
At $s=1/4$, equality in the puncture profile holds precisely when
$A=C\setminus K$ and $K$ is the union of two cosets of a finite subgroup
$L$, whose difference has order greater than two in $G/L$.
At $\sigma=1/4$, equality in the oriented profile holds precisely for
these configurations with the additional condition
\[
 K\cap(K+d)=\varnothing.
\]
The strict outer hypothesis $\eps<1/4$ cannot be replaced by
$\eps\le1/4$ in either canonical repair assertion.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
If $s=1/4$, the construction in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:puncture} still gives
$x\le(2/3)\delta^3<\delta/6$, so $K$ is nonempty.  The function $z(y)$
is continuous at zero, has $z(0)=1/4$, and is strictly decreasing.
For $y>0$ its values are below $1/4$, so the derivative calculation
\eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:puncture-F-derivative} applies and is strictly negative.
Continuity of $F$ at zero therefore gives $F(x)\le F(0)$, with strict
inequality for $x>0$.  The inner coset theorem is valid at
$\zeta=1/4$, and its supplied hole has
\[
 |D|\le\frac32|K|<\frac{|C|}{2},
\]
so properness is unchanged.  The rest of the minimization argument
applies without modification.

For the oriented assertion, $\theta_d\le\delta^3/4<\delta/16$ still
forces $d\in H$.  The endpoint puncture bound gives
$e=\Delta_C(A)\le\delta/2$.  If a minimizing hole were preserved by
$d$, the same intersection argument would give $z_d\ge\delta-e\ge
\delta/2$, and consequently
\[
 \theta_d\ge z_d^2\ge\frac{\delta^2}{4}
                 >\frac{\delta^3}{4}\ge\theta_d,
\]
a contradiction.  Thus every minimizing hole is oriented correctly.

Suppose equality holds with $s=1/4$.  Strict decrease of $F$ away from
zero forces $x=0$, and the complement identity gives $\zeta=s=1/4$.
The canonical inner coset must attain its envelope.  The endpoint
classification in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:coset-equality} says exactly that
$K$ is the stated union of two $L$-cosets.

To prove the converse, write $|L|=\ell$, so $|K|=2\ell$.  Every subgroup
coset $E$ has distance at least $\ell$ from $K$.  Indeed, if $E$ meets
only one of the two $L$-cosets, their intersection has size $i\le\ell$
and
\[
 |K\symdiff E|=2\ell+|E|-2i\ge2\ell-i\ge\ell.
\]
If it meets both, each intersection has the same size
$i=|L\cap L_E|$.  When $i<\ell$, the subgroup index gives
$i\le\ell/2$, while $|E|\ge2i$, so
$|K\symdiff E|=2\ell+|E|-4i\ge\ell$.
When $i=\ell$, $E$ contains both full $L$-cosets.  Its index over $L$
is at least three: index two would make their quotient difference have
order two.  Hence the same distance is at least $\ell$.
A coset meeting neither is farther still.  The two constituent
$L$-cosets attain distance $\ell$, proving the minimum.  Thus
$\Delta_C(A)=\ell/m=\delta/2$ as required.

For oriented equality at $\sigma=1/4$, the monotone chain of the proof
of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:oriented-puncture} forces
$\eta=\theta_d$ and endpoint puncture equality.  With $x=0$,
\eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:translation-exact} makes this additional equality equivalent
to $r_K(d)=0$.  This is the displayed disjointness condition.  The
converse follows from the same identity.

Finally, let $A$ be the union of two cosets of a nontrivial finite
subgroup $H$, with quotient difference of order greater than two.
Then $\eps=1/4$, and a canonical outer coset $C$ is one of the two
constituents.  Here
\[
 \delta=1/2,\qquad \eta=0,\qquad K=C\setminus A=\varnothing.
\]
The proposed puncture bound would require zero edits, although
$A\ne C\setminus D$ for every hole $D\subset C$.
Taking a translation between the two constituents gives
$\theta_d=0$ as well, so the oriented conclusion also fails at the
outer endpoint.  For a concrete finite cyclic instance, take
$H=\{0,3\}\subset\Z/6\Z$ and $A=\{0,1,3,4\}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[Attainment at the inner endpoint]
\label{gsr:en:68:ex:puncture-inner-endpoint}
Let $G=\Z/8\Z$, $C=G$, $K=\{0,1\}$, and $A=C\setminus K$.
Then
\[
 m=6,\quad \delta=\frac13,\quad
 \eps=\frac{25}{108},\quad
 \eta=\frac1{108},\quad s=\frac14,
 \qquad \Delta_C(A)=\frac16=\delta\tau(1/4).
\]
The singleton holes $\{0\}$ and $\{1\}$ both attain the minimum.
For $d=2$, $K\cap(K+d)$ is empty, so $\theta_d=\eta$,
$\sigma=1/4$, and the oriented endpoint is attained as well.
\end{example}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Exact ordered defects and endpoint reflection\srctag{66}}]{Exact ordered defects and endpoint reflection}\label{gsr:en:66:sec:d2}
\srcnote{66}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:sec:ordered}

\begin{definition}
For a finite real set of size $m$, put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:totaldef}
 \Drm(A)=\frac{M_m-\Erm(A)}4.
\end{equation}
For the empty set, use $M_0=\Erm(\varnothing)=\Drm(\varnothing)=0$.
\end{definition}

The following identity explains why the factor four is natural.  It also
proves that $\Drm(A)$ is a nonnegative integer, which will matter when
separating successive energy levels.

\begin{lemma}[Ordered-defect identity]\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:lem:ordered}
For every finite $A\subset\R$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:tripledef}
 \Drm(A)=\#\{x<y<z:\ x,y,z\in A,\ x+z-y\notin A\}.
\end{equation}
If $A=B\cup\{a\}$, $a>\max B$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:recurrence}
 \Drm(A)=\Drm(B)+\e(B,a).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $m=|A|$ and $n=m-1=|B|$.  Among additive quadruples involving $a$,
the quadruple $(a,a,a,a)$ contributes one.  Those with exactly two
occurrences of $a$ contribute $4n$: the two occurrences lie on opposite
sides of the equation, and the remaining entries are equal.  There are
no quadruples with exactly three occurrences, and no quadruples with
two occurrences on one side and none on the other, by maximality of $a$.

A quadruple with exactly one occurrence of $a$ is obtained by choosing
an ordered pair $z<x$ in $B$ for which $y=a-x+z$ belongs to $B$, then
placing $a,z$ on one side and $x,y$ on the other.  There are four choices
for the side and position of $a$.  This count is valid also when $x=y$:
there is then one ordered choice for $x,y$, not two.  Consequently, with
\[
 T(B,a)=\#\{z<x:\ z,x\in B,\ a-x+z\in B\},
\]
we have
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:energyrecurrence}
 \Erm(A)-\Erm(B)=4m-3+4T(B,a).
\end{equation}
Since $T(B,a)+\e(B,a)=\binom n2$ and
$M_m-M_{m-1}=2m^2-2m+1$, equation~\eqref{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:recurrence} follows.

Every triple counted by \eqref{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:tripledef} either lies in $B$, or has
largest point $a$ and is exactly a failed pair in \eqref{gsr:fm:66:epnf:eq:endpointdef}.
Induction from sets of size at most two proves the identity.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Reflection]\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:lem:reflection}
Let $B$ be nonempty, let $a>\max B$, and let $C=a-B$.  Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:reflection}
 \e(B,a)=\sigma(C).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A pair $z<x$ in $B$ gives the pair $a-z>a-x$ in $C$.  The difference of
these two positive numbers is $x-z$.  Membership of $a-x+z$ in $B$ is
equivalent to membership of $x-z$ in $C$.  This is a bijection between
the two sets of failures.
\end{proof}

If $c_1<\cdots<c_n$ are the positive elements of $C$, write
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:localdef}
 e_i=\#\{j<i:c_i-c_j\notin C\},\qquad \sigma(C)=\sum_{i=1}^n e_i.
\end{equation}
A positive difference smaller than $c_i$ can belong only to
$C_{i-1}=\{c_1,\ldots,c_{i-1}\}$.  Thus $e_i$ is determined entirely by
the prefix $C_i$.  Equivalently, $\binom n2-\sigma(C)$ is the number of
ordered positive Schur representations $u+v=w$ within $C$; repeated
summands $u=v$ are allowed and are counted once for that ordered choice.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Two exact reflections force an arithmetic prefix\srctag{66}}]{Two exact reflections force an arithmetic prefix}\label{gsr:en:66:sec:d3}
\srcnote{66}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:sec:reflections}

\begin{lemma}[Consecutive zero defects]\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:lem:twozeros}
Suppose $1\le i<n$ and $e_i=e_{i+1}=0$.  With $d=c_1$, one has
\[
 C_{i+1}=\{d,2d,\ldots,(i+1)d\}.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $i=1$, the assertion is $c_2-c_1=c_1$, which follows immediately
from $e_2=0$.  Assume $i\ge2$.  Since $e_i=0$, reflection
$s\mapsto c_i-s$ permutes $C_{i-1}$.  Since $e_{i+1}=0$, reflection
$s\mapsto c_{i+1}-s$ permutes $C_i$.  Pairing the smallest and largest
elements of $C_i$ under the latter reflection gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:successorstep}
 c_{i+1}=c_i+d.
\end{equation}
For $s\in C_{i-1}$, composing the two reflections shows that
\[
 s+d=c_{i+1}-(c_i-s)\in C_i.
\]
Thus every point of $C_i$ other than its largest point has a successor
obtained by adding $d$.  Starting at any point and repeatedly adding
$d$ must eventually reach $c_i$, since the set is finite.  In particular,
starting at $d$ shows that $c_i$ is an integer multiple of $d$ and that
all intermediate multiples occur.  Starting at any other point shows
that it belongs to the same chain.  There are $i$ points, so $c_i=id$;
\eqref{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:successorstep} finishes the proof.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Zero defect]\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:cor:zero}
A positive $n$-element set has $\sigma(C)=0$ if and only if
$C=\{d,2d,\ldots,nd\}$ for some $d>0$.
Consequently, $\e(B,a)=0$ if and only if $B\cup\{a\}$ is an arithmetic
progression whose last point is $a$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The cases $n\le2$ are immediate.  For $n\ge3$, apply
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:lem:twozeros} to the final pair of indices.  The converse is
immediate from closure of the relevant positive differences.  Reflection
then proves the endpoint assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[A long initial arithmetic block]\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:lem:longblock}
Suppose $\sigma(C)\le r$, and let $L$ be the largest integer such that
$c_j=jd$ for $1\le j\le L$, where $d=c_1$.  Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:longblock}
 L\ge n-2r.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
There is nothing to prove when $L=n$.  Otherwise $e_{L+1}>0$: zero
would make reflection of $\{d,\ldots,Ld\}$ about $c_{L+1}/2$ a
permutation, forcing $c_{L+1}=(L+1)d$.  After this first positive defect,
no two consecutive $e_i$ can vanish, by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:lem:twozeros} and
maximality of $L$.  A zero--positive pattern starting with a positive
entry and containing no consecutive zeros has at most twice as many
entries as positive entries.  There are at most $r$ positive entries,
since each costs at least one in $\sum e_i$.  Hence $n-L\le2r$.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The partition normal-form theorem\srctag{66}}]{The partition normal-form theorem}\label{gsr:en:66:sec:d4}
\srcnote{66}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:sec:partitions}

\begin{theorem}[Small Schur defect]\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:partition}
Let $r\ge1$ be an integer and $n\ge3r+1$.  For a positive ordered set
$C=\{c_1<\cdots<c_n\}$, the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $\sigma(C)\le r$.
\item With $d=c_1$, there are nonnegative integers
$0\le\lambda_1\le\cdots\le\lambda_n$ such that
\[
 c_i=d(i+\lambda_i),\qquad \sum_i\lambda_i\le r.
\]
\end{enumerate}
In this situation $\sigma(C)=\sum_i\lambda_i$.  In particular, exact
defect $r$ gives precisely $p(r)$ classes up to positive dilation.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Assume (i).  Let $L$ be as in Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:lem:longblock}; then
$L\ge n-2r\ge r+1$.  If $L=n$, all conclusions hold with zero shifts.
We divide the remaining argument into three steps.

\emph{First, all points are integer multiples of $d$.}
Otherwise let $c_i$ be the first point that is not.  Every previous point
is a multiple of $d$, and every difference $c_i-c_j$, $j<i$, is not.
None belongs to the previous prefix, so $e_i=i-1\ge L>r$, a
contradiction.  Scale by $d$ and henceforth take $d=1$.

\emph{Second, all points are at most $2L+1$.}
Suppose that $i$ is the first index with $c_i\ge2L+2$.  For every earlier
index $j$, write $q_j=c_j-j$, the number of missing positive integers
below $c_j$.  All missing integers are at least $L+1$.  Since
$c_j\le2L+1$, two missing integers cannot sum to $c_j$.  Among the
$c_j-1$ ordered decompositions $u+v=c_j$ into positive integers,
exactly $q_j$ fail through $u$ and exactly $q_j$ fail through $v$, and
these failure classes are disjoint.  Thus
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:holecount}
 (j-1)-e_j=c_j-1-2q_j,\qquad e_j=q_j.
\end{equation}
Let $s=i-1-L$ be the number of earlier points beyond the initial block.
Every such point has $q_j\ge1$, hence $\sum_{j<i}e_j\ge s$.
For each $t\in\{1,\ldots,L\}$, the difference $c_i-t$ is larger than
$L$.  At most $s$ of these $L$ distinct differences can belong to the
earlier prefix.  Therefore $e_i\ge L-s$, and
\[
 \sigma(C)\ge\sum_{j<i}e_j+e_i\ge s+(L-s)=L>r,
\]
again a contradiction.

\emph{Third, the shifts have exactly the claimed total.}
Now every target is at most $2L+1$, so the same disjoint-hole count
\eqref{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:holecount} applies to every index.  Set $\lambda_i=c_i-i$.
These are nonnegative integers, and they are nondecreasing because
$c_{i+1}\ge c_i+1$.  Their sum is $\sum_i e_i=\sigma(C)$.

Conversely, assume (ii).  At most $r$ shifts are positive, so the first
$n-r$ points are $1,\ldots,n-r$ after scaling.  Also $c_n\le n+r$.
Two missing positive integers have sum at least $2(n-r+1)$, which is
larger than $n+r$ when $n\ge3r+1$.  Thus the disjoint-hole count applies
again and gives $e_i=\lambda_i$ for every $i$.

Removing the zero shifts gives a nondecreasing list of positive integers
summing to the exact defect.  Conversely, every partition of $r$ has
at most $r<n$ entries, and padding it with leading zeros constructs a
valid set.  The scale is fixed by $c_1=d$, so different lists give
different positive-dilation classes.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Against source~57} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:thirdlevel}; checked at the write). Source~57's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:st:partitions} has the same conclusion for $n\ge5s-1$ (positions among the last $s$); $3r+1\le5r-1$ with equality at $r=1$, so this theorem's threshold is better for $r\ge2$, except that source~57 proves the optimal value $6$ at $r=2$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:st:schur-two}). With Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:prop:obstruction}, the optimal threshold satisfies $2r+2\le N(r)\le3r+1$; $N(1)=4$ and $N(2)=6$ attain the lower end, as this source's Conjecture~\ref{gsr:fz:66:epnf:conj:threshold} predicts.
\end{writenote}

\begin{corollary}[A finite set of local obstructions]\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:cor:finite}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:partition}, $C$ contains
$\{d,2d,\ldots,(n-r)d\}$ and is contained in
$\{d,2d,\ldots,(n+r)d\}$.  The number of classes with defect at most
$r$ is $\sum_{j=0}^r p(j)$, where $p(0)=1$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{example}[Defects one, two, and three]\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:ex:smallr}
Suppressing leading zeros in the shift vector, the possibilities are
\[
\begin{array}{c|l}
r&\text{positive shifts}\\ \hline
1&(1)\\
2&(2),\ (1,1)\\
3&(3),\ (1,2),\ (1,1,1).
\end{array}
\]
For example, defect two gives either
$\{1,\ldots,n-1,n+2\}$ or
$\{1,\ldots,n-2,n,n+1\}$, up to dilation.
These two sets produce different boundary-hole descriptions after
reflection; the partition parameter need not be unchanged by that
reflection.
\end{example}

\begin{proposition}[A genuine size obstruction]\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:prop:obstruction}
For every $r\ge1$, the set
\[
 C_r=\intr{1}{2r+2}\setminus\{r+1\}
\]
has $2r+1$ points and $\sigma(C_r)=r$, but its shift sum is $r+1$.
Thus an unrestricted theorem of the form of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:partition} cannot start at $n=2r+1$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Every target above the missing point has one hole below it, so the
uncorrected shift sum is $r+1$.  The only target that is a sum of two
holes is $2r+2=(r+1)+(r+1)$.  At this target, the two failure classes in
the inclusion--exclusion count intersect in one ordered choice.  That
reduces the Schur defect by one.  All other targets have no such
intersection.  Therefore $\sigma(C_r)=r$.
\end{proof}

The obstruction identifies the phenomenon that the size hypothesis
prevents: \emph{two holes can repair a Schur deficit by adding to an
existing point}.  The bound $3r+1$ is proved, not asserted optimal.
The interval between $2r+2$ and $3r+1$ is a concrete further problem.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Boundary-hole normal forms for endpoint extensions\srctag{66}}]{Boundary-hole normal forms for endpoint extensions}\label{gsr:en:66:sec:d5}
\srcnote{66}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:sec:boundary}

\begin{definition}[Hole weight]
For a finite positive integer set $H=\{h_1<\cdots<h_s\}$, define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:weight}
 \wtop(H)=\sum_{j=1}^s(h_j-j+1)
       =\sum_{h\in H}h-\binom s2.
\end{equation}
The empty hole set has weight zero.  For nonempty $H$ and $N>\max H$ (or $H=\varnothing$ and $N\ge0$), put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:holemodel}
 A_H(N)=\intr{0}{N}\setminus H.
\end{equation}
\end{definition}

The numbers $\mu_j=h_j-j+1$ are positive and nondecreasing.  Conversely,
any positive nondecreasing list $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_s$ gives
$h_j=\mu_j+j-1$.  This is a bijection between hole sets of weight $r$
and partitions of $r$.  It also gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:holebounds}
 s\le r,\qquad h_s\le r.
\end{equation}
The second assertion follows directly from
$\sum_{j<s}h_j\ge\binom s2$.

\begin{theorem}[Endpoint normal forms]\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:boundary}
Let $A=B\cup\{a\}\subset\R$, where $a>\max B$, let $|B|=n$, and
suppose $\e(B,a)=r\ge1$ and $n\ge3r+1$.  Then there is a unique
normalization by translation and positive dilation for which
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:endpointmodel}
 A=A_H(N),\qquad \wtop(H)=r,\qquad N=n+|H|.
\end{equation}
In this normalization the gap between the last two points is one, and
$H\subset\intr{1}{r}$.
Conversely, every hole set of weight $r$, with $N=n+|H|$ and
$n\ge3r+1$, produces endpoint defect $r$.
Consequently, for fixed $n$ and $r$ in this range, there are exactly
$p(r)$ oriented affine classes.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Translate so that $\min B=0$, and let $d=a-\max B$.  Reflection gives
$C=a-B$ with $c_1=d$.  By Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:partition}, after dividing by
$d$ we may write $c_i=i+\lambda_i$.  Let
\[
 N=c_n=n+\lambda_n,
\]
so $a=N$.  The reflected endpoint set is
$\{N\}\cup(N-C)$, an integer interval with a hole set $H$.
Its number of holes is $s=N-n=\lambda_n$.

Let $t$ be the number of positive shifts.  The initial block of $C$
has length $n-t$.  Every hole of $C$ is at least $n-t+1$, so after
reflection every hole of $A$ is at most
\[
 N-(n-t+1)=s+t-1\le\sum_i\lambda_i=r.
\]
The inequality uses the $t-1$ other positive shifts, each at least one.
Finally, summing the points in the reflected set gives
\begin{align*}
 \sum_i\lambda_i
 &=\sum_{c\in C}c-\frac{n(n+1)}2\\
 &=nN-\left(\frac{N(N-1)}2-\sum_{h\in H}h\right)
       -\frac{n(n+1)}2\\
 &=\sum_{h\in H}h-\binom s2=\wtop(H).
\end{align*}
This proves the asserted form.  Translation is fixed by the minimum,
and dilation by the final gap $d$, so the normalization is unique.

For the converse, take $H$ of weight $r$ and $N=n+s$.  Since
$N\ge3r+1+s>2\max H$, the last gap is one.  To count failed pairs at
endpoint $N$, fix a missing completion $h\in H$ and a present point
$z$ with $0\le z<h$.  The other point is necessarily
\[
 x=N-h+z.
\]
It lies in $\intr{0}{N-1}\setminus H$: indeed,
$x\ge N-\max H>\max H$.  Conversely, every failed pair is obtained
this way.  There are $h_j-(j-1)$ choices for $z$ at the hole $h_j$.
Their sum is $\wtop(H)=r$.  The partition bijection and uniqueness of
normalization finish the proof.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Full-set containment from the local defect]\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:cor:endpointinverse}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:boundary}, $A$ is contained in
an arithmetic progression of at most $m+r$ points and contains an
arithmetic progression of at least $m-r$ points, where $m=n+1$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The containing interval has $N+1=m+s\le m+r$ points.  The terminal
interval $\intr{\max H+1}{N}$ has $N-\max H=m-1+s-\max H\ge m-r$
points, since $s\ge1$ and $\max H\le r$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[An orientation-sensitive parameter]
The reflected set of an endpoint model has the same total energy but
usually a different last-endpoint defect.  For example,
$\intr{0}{m}\setminus\{1\}$ has final defect one in the theorem's
range, whereas its reflection
$\intr{0}{m}\setminus\{m-1\}$ has final defect $m-2$.
Thus an endpoint classification must not be silently substituted for a
classification under a total-energy hypothesis.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{An exact energy law for arbitrary boundary holes\srctag{66}}]{An exact energy law for arbitrary boundary holes}\label{gsr:en:66:sec:d6}
\srcnote{66}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:sec:energylaw}

The normal-form theorem reduces an infinite real-variable problem to
finitely many hole sets.  The next formula computes the entire energy
of each such template, not only the local defect.

For $H=\{h_1<\cdots<h_s\}$ define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:pairset}
 \mathcal P(H)=\{(h,x):h\in H,\ 0\le x<h,\ x\notin H\}.
\end{equation}
It has $\wtop(H)$ elements.  For $(h,x)\in\mathcal P(H)$ let
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:overlap}
 R_H(h,x)=\#\{(u,v)\in H^2:v>h,\ v-u=h-x\}.
\end{equation}
Write $j_H(h)=\#(H\cap\intr{1}{h})$ and set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:kappadef}
 \kappa(H)=\sum_{(h,x)\in\mathcal P(H)}
 \left(h+s-j_H(h)-\#(H\cap\intr{1}{x})-R_H(h,x)\right).
\end{equation}
An interval with upper endpoint zero in the counting term is empty.
Use $\kappa(\varnothing)=0$.

\begin{theorem}[Exact boundary-hole energy]\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:holeenergy}
Let $H$ be a finite positive integer set, let $r=\wtop(H)$, and suppose
$N\ge2\max H$ when $H\ne\varnothing$.  If
$m=|A_H(N)|=N+1-|H|$, then
\begin{align}
 \Drm(A_H(N))&=r(m-1)-\kappa(H),\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:holedefect}\\
 \Erm(A_H(N))&=M_m-4r(m-1)+4\kappa(H).\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:holeenergy}
\end{align}
For $H=\varnothing$, the same formulas hold with $r=\kappa=0$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:lem:ordered}, a failed triple $x<y<z$ has a missing
completion $h=x+z-y$.  This completion lies strictly between $x$ and
$z$, hence belongs to $H$.  Conversely, choose $(h,x)\in\mathcal P(H)$
and set $t=h-x>0$.  A corresponding triple is determined by
\[
 z\in\intr{h+1}{N},\qquad y=z-t,
\]
provided both $z$ and $y$ are present.  The inequality $z>h$ gives
$y>x$, so there is no additional ordering constraint.

There are initially $N-h$ choices for $z$.  Exactly $s-j_H(h)$ are
excluded because $z\in H$.  Choices excluded because $y\in H$ are in
bijection with $u\in H$, $u>x$, by $z=u+h-x$.  All of these satisfy
$z\le N$: the hypothesis gives $u+h-x\le2\max H\le N$.
Their number is $s-\#(H\cap\intr{1}{x})$.
The overlap of the two exclusion classes is precisely $R_H(h,x)$.
Therefore the number of valid triples for this pair is
\[
 N-h-(s-j_H(h))
       -(s-\#(H\cap\intr{1}{x}))+R_H(h,x).
\]
Summing over the $r$ pairs, and using $N=m-1+s$, gives
\eqref{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:holedefect}.  The energy formula follows from the definition
of $\Drm$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why the overlap term is indispensable]
When two holes are separated by $h-x$, the same choice of $z$ is
excluded twice by the two single-hole tests.  Omitting $R_H$ therefore
changes the constant term of the energy.  For example, two distinct
weight-four partitions already have the same value of $\kappa$;
the energy law does not imply that energy alone determines the
partition.  The local normal form is strictly more informative.
\end{remark}

\subsection{The first values}
Table~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:tab:kappa} lists the complete spectrum through weight four.
The formula for $\Drm$ uses $n=m-1$ to make the endpoint interpretation
visible.  Every entry is an exact identity in the stated long-interval
range.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{ccll}
\toprule
$r$ & $H$ & $\kappa(H)$ & $\Drm(A_H(N))$ \\
\midrule
1 & $\{1\}$ & $1$ & $n-1$ \\
2 & $\{2\}$ & $4$ & $2n-4$ \\
  & $\{1,2\}$ & $3$ & $2n-3$ \\
3 & $\{3\}$ & $9$ & $3n-9$ \\
  & $\{1,3\}$ & $7$ & $3n-7$ \\
  & $\{1,2,3\}$ & $6$ & $3n-6$ \\
4 & $\{4\}$ & $16$ & $4n-16$ \\
  & $\{1,4\}$ & $12$ & $4n-12$ \\
  & $\{2,3\}$ & $11$ & $4n-11$ \\
  & $\{1,2,4\}$ & $10$ & $4n-10$ \\
  & $\{1,2,3,4\}$ & $10$ & $4n-10$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Partition-indexed endpoint templates.  The repeated constant
at weight four is an actual energy coincidence, not a rounding effect.}
\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:tab:kappa}
\end{table}

For instance, $H=\{2\}$ has pairs $(2,0),(2,1)$ and contributes two
summands equal to two in \eqref{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:kappadef}, so $\kappa=4$.
For $H=\{1,2\}$, the only pairs are $(1,0),(2,0)$.
Their contributions are respectively one and two, giving $\kappa=3$.
At $H=\{1,3\}$, the contributions of $(1,0),(3,0),(3,2)$ are
$2,3,2$, hence $\kappa=7$.  These are the constants used in the energy
classification, so none depends on numerical approximation.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A sharp all-defect endpoint envelope\srctag{66}}]{A sharp all-defect endpoint envelope}\label{gsr:en:66:sec:d7}
\srcnote{66}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:sec:envelope}

\begin{lemma}[The largest boundary constant]\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:lem:kappabound}
If $\wtop(H)=r\ge1$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:kappabound}
 \kappa(H)\le r^2,
\end{equation}
with equality if and only if $H=\{r\}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
There are $r$ summands in \eqref{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:kappadef}.  For a pair with
$h=h_j$, its summand is at most
\[
 h_j+s-j\le h_s\le r.
\]
The middle inequality follows because the $s-j$ later holes are
strictly increasing integers.  This proves \eqref{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:kappabound}.

If equality holds, every summand equals $r$ and $h_s=r$.
Equality in the elementary inequality $h_s\le\wtop(H)$ forces
$h_j=j$ for $j<s$.  If $s\ge2$, consider the pair $(1,0)$.
When $r>s$, its contribution is at most $s<r$.  When $r=s$, the hole
set is $\{1,\ldots,r\}$, and $R_H(1,0)\ge1$, so that contribution
is again smaller than $r$.  Both contradict equality.  Therefore
$s=1$ and $H=\{r\}$.  Conversely, the $r$ pairs $(r,x)$,
$0\le x<r$, each contribute $r$ for that hole set.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp endpoint-sensitive energy bound]\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:envelope}
Let $A=B\cup\{a\}\subset\R$, $a>\max B$, and $|A|=m$.  Suppose
$\e(B,a)=r\ge1$ and $m-1\ge3r+1$.  Then
\begin{align}
 \Drm(A)&\ge r(m-1-r),\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:defectenvelope}\\
 \Erm(A)&\le M_m-4r(m-1-r).\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:energyenvelope}
\end{align}
Equality in either bound holds if and only if
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:envelopeequality}
 A=b+d\bigl(\intr{0}{m}\setminus\{r\}\bigr),\qquad d>0.
\end{equation}
The coefficient and the constant term are therefore sharp for every
allowed $r$ and $m$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:boundary} gives $A_H(N)$ with $\wtop(H)=r$,
$N=m-1+|H|$, and $\max H\le r$.  Its size hypothesis implies
$N>2\max H$, so Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:holeenergy} applies.  Use
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:lem:kappabound}; its equality case gives exactly
\eqref{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:envelopeequality}.  Conversely, that model has endpoint defect
$r$ by Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:boundary}, and $\kappa(\{r\})=r^2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The smallest three endpoint defects]\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:cor:smallendpoints}
Put $n=m-1$.  For final endpoint defect one and $n\ge4$, the only
normal form is $A_{\{1\}}(n+1)$ and $\Drm=n-1$.
For defect two and $n\ge7$, the possibilities are
\[
 A_{\{2\}}(n+1),\quad \Drm=2n-4;
 \qquad A_{\{1,2\}}(n+2),\quad \Drm=2n-3.
\]
For defect three and $n\ge10$, the possibilities and their defects are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
H&\Drm\\ \hline
\{3\}&3n-9\\
\{1,3\}&3n-7\\
\{1,2,3\}&3n-6.
\end{array}
\]
In each line $N=n+|H|$.
\end{corollary}

The significance of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:envelope} is that the entire
endpoint spectrum has been replaced by a finite partition problem.
It is not merely a bound obtained by discarding a few exceptional
points.  Nevertheless, it controls a local endpoint parameter; a
separate argument is needed to infer a normal form from a large total
energy.  We give that argument for four levels next.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The known first and second levels, with complete proofs\srctag{66}}]{The known first and second levels, with complete proofs}\label{gsr:en:66:sec:d8}
\srcnote{66}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:sec:knownlevels}

The statements in this section, including the third-level lower bound,
are already recorded in the source-45 repository review
\cite{repo66levels}.  Their proofs are included to isolate the genuinely new
equality analysis in Sections~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:sec:third} and \ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:sec:fourth}.

For $m\ge5$, define the oriented models
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:PLR}
 P_m=\intr{0}{m-1},\qquad
 L_m=\intr{0}{m}\setminus\{1\},\qquad
 R_m=\intr{0}{m}\setminus\{m-1\}.
\end{equation}
They have defects $0,m-2,m-2$, respectively.

\begin{lemma}[Extending an arithmetic progression]\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:lem:APextension}
Let $B=\intr{0}{n-1}$ and $a>n-1$.  If $a\notin\Z$, then
$\e(B,a)=\binom n2$.  If $a=n+t$ with $t\in\Z_{\ge0}$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:APextension}
 \e(B,a)=\sum_{j=1}^{\min(t,n-1)}(n-j).
\end{equation}
In particular, for $0\le t\le n-1$, it equals
$tn-t(t+1)/2$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For a pair $z<x$, write $j=x-z$.  There are $n-j$ pairs of difference
$j$.  A noninteger endpoint makes every completion nonintegral.
At endpoint $n+t$, the completion belongs to $B$ exactly when
$n+t-j\le n-1$, or $j\ge t+1$.  The remaining pairs are precisely
those counted in \eqref{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:APextension}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[First gap and second equality cases]\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:prop:firstgap}
For a real $m$-element set with $m\ge3$, either $A$ is an arithmetic
progression or
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:firstgap}
 \Drm(A)\ge m-2.
\end{equation}
For $m\ge5$, equality in \eqref{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:firstgap} holds if and only if $A$
is an oriented affine copy of $L_m$ or $R_m$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For three points, the sole ordered triple has its completion in the set
exactly when the three points form an arithmetic progression.  Thus the
defect is zero or one.  Proceed by induction, writing $A=B\cup\{a\}$
and $n=|B|=m-1$.

If $B$ is an arithmetic progression, normalize it to
$\intr{0}{n-1}$.  Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:lem:APextension} gives either the next
arithmetic point, or a defect at least $n-1=m-2$.
If $B$ is not an arithmetic progression, induction gives
$\Drm(B)\ge n-2$ and Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:cor:zero} gives $\e(B,a)\ge1$.
The recurrence proves the gap.

Now let $m\ge5$ and $\Drm(A)=m-2=n-1$.  If $B$ is an arithmetic
progression, \eqref{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:APextension} shows that the only endpoint is
$a=n+1$; the noninteger value $\binom n2$ and all integer choices
$t\ge2$ are larger.  This is $R_m$.
If $B$ is not an arithmetic progression, the preceding lower bounds
force $\e(B,a)=1$.  Here $n\ge4$, so
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:cor:smallendpoints} gives $L_m$.
The asserted defects of $L_m,R_m$ follow from
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:holeenergy} and reflection.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Extending either second-level model]\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:lem:LRextension}
Let $n\ge4$, let $B=L_n$ or $R_n$, and let $a>n$.
Unless $B=L_n$ and $a=n+1$, one has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:LRlower}
 \e(B,a)\ge n-2.
\end{equation}
For later use, the following more specific statements hold:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ccl}
\toprule
$B$ & $a$ & Endpoint defect or lower bound\\
\midrule
$L_n$ & $n+1$ & $1$\\
$L_n$ & $n+2$ & $n-2$\\
$L_n$ & integer $a\ge n+3$ & at least $2n-4$\\
$R_n$ & $n+1$ & $n-2$\\
$R_n$ & $n+2$ & at least $2n-5$\\
$R_n$ & integer $a\ge n+3$ & at least $2n-4$\\
Either & noninteger $a$ & $\binom n2$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For any positive difference $j$ of $B$, every pair with that difference
fails exactly when $a-j\notin B$; its contribution is the multiplicity
$r_B(j)=\#\{z\in B:z+j\in B\}$.
Both $L_n$ and $R_n$ satisfy
\[
 r_B(1)=r_B(2)=n-2.
\]
For $L_n$ at $a=n+1$, the only failing difference is $n$, which has
multiplicity one.  At $a=n+2$, the only failing difference is one,
with multiplicity $n-2$; the missing completion one would require
difference $n+1$, which is unavailable.  At $a\ge n+3$, differences
one and two both fail.

For $R_n$ at $a=n+1$, the only failing difference is two, again with
multiplicity $n-2$.  At $a=n+2$, differences one and three fail;
their multiplicities are $n-2$ and $n-3$.  At $a\ge n+3$, differences
one and two fail.  Noninteger endpoints make every completion
nonintegral.  These observations prove the table and the lower bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Third-level exclusion bound]\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:prop:thirdbound}
Let $m\ge5$.  If $A\subset\R$ has $m$ points and is not an oriented
affine copy of $P_m,L_m,R_m$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:thirdbound}
 \Drm(A)\ge2m-6.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
At $m=5$, Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:prop:firstgap} and its equality classification
exclude defects zero through three except the listed sets.  Integrality
therefore gives $\Drm(A)\ge4=2m-6$.

For the induction step, let $m\ge6$, put $n=m-1$, and remove the last
point.  If $B$ is an arithmetic progression, the cases $t=0,1$ in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:lem:APextension} give excluded sets.  Every other endpoint
has defect at least $2n-3$, including noninteger endpoints since
$n\ge5$; this is larger than $2n-4=2m-6$.

If $B$ is a second-level model, its defect is $n-2$.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:lem:LRextension} adds at least $n-2$, except for the extension
of $L_n$ to $L_m$, which is excluded.

In the remaining case, induction gives $\Drm(B)\ge2n-6$.
Endpoint defect zero is impossible by Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:cor:zero};
endpoint defect one would make $A$ a copy of $L_m$ by
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:cor:smallendpoints}, also excluded.
Hence $\e(B,a)\ge2$, and the recurrence gives $\Drm(A)\ge2n-4$.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Complete classification of the third energy level\srctag{66}}]{Complete classification of the third energy level}\label{gsr:en:66:sec:d9}
\srcnote{66}{Section 9}
\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:sec:third}

Define three oriented templates
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:Jmodels}
 \begin{split}
 J_m^-&=\intr{0}{m}\setminus\{2\},\qquad
 J_m^+=\intr{0}{m}\setminus\{m-2\},\\
 C_m&=\intr{0}{m+1}\setminus\{1,m\}.
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
The last model has one hole near each endpoint.  It cannot be found by
looking only for the reflected single-hole construction.

\begin{theorem}[All third-level extremizers]\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:third}
Let $m\ge8$.  A real $m$-element set satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:thirdequality}
 \Drm(A)=2m-6
 \quad\text{equivalently}\quad
 \Erm(A)=M_m-8(m-3)
\end{equation}
if and only if it is an oriented affine copy of one of
$J_m^-,J_m^+,C_m$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The defect of $J_m^-$ is $2(m-1)-4=2m-6$ by
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:holeenergy}; reflection gives the same for $J_m^+$.
The model $C_m$ is obtained by extending $L_{m-1}$ at endpoint $m+1$.
The defect of the prefix is $m-3$, and
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:lem:LRextension} gives the same endpoint defect $m-3$.
Thus all three models attain \eqref{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:thirdequality}.

Conversely, put $n=m-1\ge7$ and write $A=B\cup\{a\}$ with the last
point removed.  We distinguish the three prefix types used in
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:prop:thirdbound}.

\emph{Arithmetic prefix.}  The extension is either an excluded
first- or second-level model, or has defect at least $2n-3$.
The target defect is $2n-4$, so this case gives no equality.

\emph{Second-level prefix.}  Normalize $B$ to $L_n$ or $R_n$.
Since $\Drm(B)=n-2$, equality requires endpoint defect exactly $n-2$.
For $L_n$, the endpoint $n+1$ has defect one, and the endpoint $n+2$
has defect $n-2$, yielding $C_m$.  All later integer endpoints have
defect at least $2n-4>n-2$.  Noninteger endpoints have defect
$\binom n2>n-2$.
For $R_n$, endpoint $n+1$ has defect $n-2$ and yields $J_m^+$.
The endpoint $n+2$ has defect at least $2n-5>n-2$ because $n\ge7$;
all later integer endpoints and noninteger endpoints are also too
large.  This exhausts the second-level prefixes.

\emph{Any other prefix.}  Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:prop:thirdbound} gives
$\Drm(B)\ge2n-6$, so the target forces $\e(B,a)\le2$.
Endpoint defects zero and one would make $A$ a first- or second-level
model, and are impossible.  Thus $\e(B,a)=2$.
Since $n\ge7$, Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:cor:smallendpoints} applies: the two
normal forms have total defects $2n-4$ and $2n-3$.
Only $A_{\{2\}}(n+1)=J_m^-$ has the required defect.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Against source~57} (checked at the write). Source~57's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:st:third-equality} classifies the same level for $m\ge7$, a better cutoff, as the affine images of $J_m=\{0,\ldots,m\}\setminus\{2\}$ and $K_m=\{0,2,3,\ldots,m-1,m+1\}$: this theorem's $J_m^-$ and $J_m^+$ are $J_m$ and its reflection, and $C_m$ is $K_m$, which is symmetric. Both answer source~45's Question~\ref{gsr:fz:45:q:third}.
\end{writenote}

\begin{remark}[The cutoff is not cosmetic]
At $m=6$, the set $\intr{0}{6}\setminus\{3\}$ also has defect six,
which equals $2m-6$, but is not one of the three displayed templates.
The theorem makes no claim of optimality for the sufficient cutoff
$m\ge8$.  The example explains why a small-cardinality qualification
cannot simply be omitted.  The inclusion of $C_m$ is essential even
when $m$ is arbitrarily large.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The fourth energy level and the eight-template theorem\srctag{66}}]{The fourth energy level and the eight-template theorem}\label{gsr:en:66:sec:d10}
\srcnote{66}{Section 10}
\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:sec:fourth}

Put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:Tmodels}
 T_m^-=\intr{0}{m+1}\setminus\{1,2\},\qquad
 T_m^+=\intr{0}{m+1}\setminus\{m-1,m\}.
\end{equation}
These are reflected copies of one another.

\begin{theorem}[All fourth-level extremizers]\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:fourth}
Let $m\ge11$.  A real $m$-element set satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:fourthequality}
 \Drm(A)=2m-5
 \quad\text{equivalently}\quad
 \Erm(A)=M_m-8m+20
\end{equation}
if and only if it is an oriented affine copy of $T_m^-$ or $T_m^+$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The boundary-hole formula gives
$\Drm(T_m^-)=2(m-1)-3=2m-5$, and reflection gives the same for $T_m^+$.
For the converse, put $n=m-1\ge10$ and remove the last point.

\emph{Arithmetic prefix.}  With $B=\intr{0}{n-1}$, the target defect
is $2n-3$.  Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:lem:APextension} gives that value exactly when
$a=n+2$.  Values $a=n,n+1$ give smaller defects; $a=n+t$ with $t\ge3$
gives at least $3n-6>2n-3$; and $\binom n2>2n-3$ excludes
noninteger endpoints.  The resulting set is $T_m^+$.

\emph{Second-level prefix.}  Here $\Drm(B)=n-2$, so the required
endpoint defect is $n-1$.  The table in Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:lem:LRextension}
excludes it.  For $L_n$, the first two possible integer endpoints have
defects $1,n-2$, and all later ones have at least $2n-4>n-1$.
For $R_n$, the first has defect $n-2$, the second at least
$2n-5>n-1$, and later ones at least $2n-4$.  Noninteger endpoints
are again larger.  Thus no second-level prefix contributes.

\emph{Any other prefix.}  By Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:prop:thirdbound},
$\Drm(B)\ge2n-6$, and therefore $\e(B,a)\le3$.
Defects zero and one are excluded as before.  Defect two gives the two
models of Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:cor:smallendpoints}, and only the model with
holes $\{1,2\}$ has defect $2n-3$.  It is $T_m^-$.
For endpoint defect three, that same corollary is valid since $n\ge10$.
The three possible total defects are
\[
 3n-9,\qquad 3n-7,\qquad 3n-6.
\]
All exceed $2n-3$ when $n\ge10$.  This eliminates the final case.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The first four levels]\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:fourlevels}
For every $m\ge11$, the four largest distinct additive energies of
real $m$-element sets are the values in Table~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:tab:levels}, with
exactly the indicated oriented affine models.  In particular, every
other $m$-element set has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:nextinteger}
 \Drm(A)\ge2m-4,\qquad \Erm(A)\le M_m-8m+16.
\end{equation}
The bound \eqref{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:nextinteger} is only an exclusion bound; it is not
asserted to be the fifth energy level.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The maximum and its equality case follow from the ordered-defect
identity and Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:cor:zero}, by removing the last point, or
directly from Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:prop:firstgap}.
The first gap and its equality classification give the second level.
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:prop:thirdbound} excludes every intervening defect
before the third level, and Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:third} classifies its
extremizers.  Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:fourth} classifies the next integer
value of the defect.  Each displayed model exists for all $m\ge11$,
and the four defect values are distinct.  All remaining defects are
larger integers, giving \eqref{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:nextinteger}.
\end{proof}

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{ccl}
\toprule
$\Drm(A)$ & $\Erm(A)$ & Normalized oriented models\\
\midrule
$0$ & $M_m$ & $\intr{0}{m-1}$\\[3pt]
$m-2$ & $M_m-4m+8$ & $\intr{0}{m}\setminus\{1\}$,
 $\intr{0}{m}\setminus\{m-1\}$\\[3pt]
$2m-6$ & $M_m-8m+24$ & $\intr{0}{m}\setminus\{2\}$,
 $\intr{0}{m}\setminus\{m-2\}$,\\
 & & $\intr{0}{m+1}\setminus\{1,m\}$\\[3pt]
$2m-5$ & $M_m-8m+20$ & $\intr{0}{m+1}\setminus\{1,2\}$,
 $\intr{0}{m+1}\setminus\{m-1,m\}$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{The first four energy levels for $m\ge11$.  The models are
listed up to translation and \emph{positive} dilation.  Allowing
reflection identifies the displayed pairs.}
\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:tab:levels}
\end{table}

\begin{example}[The smallest cardinality covered by all four levels]
At $m=11$, $M_m=891$, and the four energies are
\[
 891,\quad855,\quad827,\quad823.
\]
The third level includes the two one-hole sets
$\intr{0}{11}\setminus\{2\}$ and
$\intr{0}{11}\setminus\{9\}$, and the two-sided-hole set
$\intr{0}{12}\setminus\{1,11\}$.  The fourth level consists of
$\intr{0}{12}\setminus\{1,2\}$ and its reflection.
These numbers are evaluations of exact formulas, not estimates.
\end{example}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Inverse consequences and the boundary of the Ramsey application\srctag{66}}]{Inverse consequences and the boundary of the Ramsey application}\label{gsr:en:66:sec:d11}
\srcnote{66}{Section 11}
\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:sec:applications}

\subsection{Entire-set recovery, rather than a proportional subset}

\begin{corollary}[A sharp high-energy recovery window]\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:cor:recovery}
Let $A\subset\R$ have $m\ge11$ elements and suppose
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:recoveryhyp}
 \Erm(A)\ge\frac{2m^3+m}{3}-8m+20.
\end{equation}
Then $A$ is one of the eight oriented templates in Table~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:tab:levels}.
It lies in an arithmetic progression of at most $m+2$ points, contains
an arithmetic progression of at least $m-2$ points, and satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:diffbound}
 \cardbars{A-A}\le2m+3.
\end{equation}
The upper bound on the containing progression and the difference-set
bound are attained within this window.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The hypothesis is $\Drm(A)\le2m-5$, so
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:fourlevels} gives the list.  Every model is contained
in $\intr{0}{m+1}$.  The consecutive blocks giving the inner
progression have lengths respectively $m$, $m-1$, at least $m-2$,
and $m-1$ in the four rows of the table.  All differences belong to
$\intr{-(m+1)}{m+1}$ after normalization, proving \eqref{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:diffbound}.

For $T_m^-$, the interval $\intr{3}{m+1}$ supplies differences
$1,\ldots,m-2$, and subtraction from zero supplies
$3,\ldots,m+1$.  These cover all positive differences through $m+1$,
so $|T_m^--T_m^-|=2m+3$.  Moreover, it has diameter $m+1$ and contains
consecutive integer points.  Any real arithmetic progression containing
it has step at most one: the difference one must be an integer multiple
of the step.  Such a progression has at least $m+2$ points.
\end{proof}

The comparison with Gowers's Theorem~7.2 is quantitative but local.
Here the energy-density assumption is
\[
 \frac{\Erm(A)}{m^3}\ge
 \frac23-\frac{23}{3m^2}+\frac{20}{m^3}.
\]
It lies within $O(m)$ of the ordered maximum and approaches $2/3$,
whereas Gowers's extraction works at every fixed positive $c_0$.
The present corollary retains \emph{all} points, gives dimension one,
and loses at most two positions in a containing progression.  It does
not improve the general dependence on $c_0$ in Proposition~7.3.

\subsection{Torsion-free abelian groups}

\begin{theorem}[Transfer of the energy classification]\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:torsionfree}
Let $G$ be a torsion-free abelian group and $A\subset G$ have $m\ge11$
points.  The first-four-level classification and
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:cor:recovery} remain valid, with models interpreted as
\[
 b+S v=\{b+tv:t\in S\},\qquad v\in G\setminus\{0\},
\]
where $S$ is one of the integer templates.  The third-level equality
classification similarly holds for $m\ge8$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The subgroup generated by the finite set $A$ is a finitely generated
torsion-free abelian group, hence isomorphic to $\Z^d$ for some finite
$d$.  Choose $d$ real numbers linearly independent over $\Q$.  Sending
a basis to these numbers gives an injective additive map into $\R$.
It preserves every additive quadruple in both directions, so the energy
and cardinality of the image equal those of $A$.

Apply the real classification to the image.  Every displayed integer
template has two points whose parameters differ by one.  Its real
common step is therefore an actual difference of two image points,
and lifts to a group element $v$.  A model point with parameter zero
lifts to $b$.  Injectivity then pulls back every relation
$x=b+tv$, giving the whole model in $G$.  The progression and
difference-set conclusions follow from these same relations.

Only the finitely generated subgroup containing $A$ is embedded.
No embedding of an arbitrary ambient torsion-free group into $\R$
is assumed.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A graph-rigidity corollary for the inverse step}

\begin{corollary}[Affine graphs in the four-level window]\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:cor:graphs}
Let $S\subset\Z$ have $m\ge11$ elements, let
$\phi:S\to\Z^d$, and let
\[
 \Gamma=\{(x,\phi(x)):x\in S\}\subset\Z^{d+1}.
\]
If $\Erm(\Gamma)\ge M_m-8m+20$, then $\Gamma$ is a rank-one
arithmetic template from Table~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:tab:levels}.
In particular, there exist $x_0\in\Z$, $y_0\in\Z^d$,
$u\in\Z\setminus\{0\}$, $v\in\Z^d$, and a listed parameter set $I$
such that
\[
 S=\{x_0+tu:t\in I\},\qquad
 \phi(x_0+tu)=y_0+tv\quad(t\in I).
\]
Thus $\phi$ is the restriction of a rational affine map on its entire
domain $S$.
\end{corollary}
