\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:torsionfree} to $\Gamma$.  Write the direction
of the resulting one-dimensional model as $(u,v)$.  If $u=0$, two
different graph points in that model have the same first coordinate,
contradicting that $\Gamma$ is a graph.  Thus $u\ne0$, and the
stated formulas follow.  Eliminating $t$ gives
$\phi(x)=y_0+(x-x_0)v/u$ on $S$.
\end{proof}

This corollary concerns a torsion-free graph with an exceptionally high
energy.  In Gowers's proof the selected graph often lives in a cyclic
ambient group, and the available energy need not be close to this
endpoint.  Both changes of hypothesis must be justified before using
the corollary in that setting.  In particular, it supplies no missing
rectification theorem by itself.

\subsection{A safe cyclic lifting interface}

\begin{proposition}[No-wrap transfer]\label{gsr:en:66:epnf:prop:nowrap}
Let $q$ be a positive integer and let $A\subset\Z/q\Z$ have a set of
distinct integer representatives $\widetilde A\subset\intr{0}{L}$
with $q>2L$.  Then
\[
 \Erm_{\Z/q\Z}(A)=\Erm_{\Z}(\widetilde A).
\]
Consequently, every real or integer classification above applies to
$\widetilde A$ when its corresponding hypotheses hold, and reduces to
a progression-with-holes description of $A$ modulo $q$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For four representatives, the difference between the two pair sums
lies in $[-2L,2L]$.  A multiple of $q$ in that interval is zero since
$q>2L$.  Thus an additive congruence holds exactly when the integer
additive equality holds.
\end{proof}

The strict inequality $q>2L$ is essential to this simple argument;
$q>L$ alone does not prevent wraparound between pair sums.  A finite
subgroup also shows why no torsion-free endpoint statement can be
transferred without a hypothesis: it has energy $m^3$, exceeding
$M_m$ for $m>1$.

\subsection{What would be needed to improve a global progression bound}
The local theorem isolates a possible terminal branch in an inverse
argument: if a rectified graph is already in the four-level window,
its global affine structure is exact.  To improve an upper bound for
Szemer\'edi's theorem, one would still need a quantitative mechanism
forcing that branch, or showing that the complementary branch yields
a more efficient density increment.  Neither assertion is proved
here.  The all-$r$ normal form may be useful in an energy-peeling
argument because the template count depends on the local defect
rather than on the ambient size; turning this observation into a
complete iteration requires additional estimates.

\section{Sources~68, 62, 61 and~60: Lemma~9.3 on every modulus \wtag}\label{gsr:en:sec:allmoduli}

The next twenty sections are source~68's Sections~5--7, source~62's Sections~2--9, source~61's Sections~2--9 and source~60's Section~9, on the restriction step of Gowers's Lemma~9.3 (and, for source~61, the Freiman restriction of Lemma~7.5). \emph{Logically they continue source~58's chapter} on Lemma~9.3 on every cyclic group (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:torsionrestriction}), with sources~17, 29 and~48 before it (Sections~\ref{gsr:en:sec:restriction}, \ref{gsr:en:sec:fixedfield}, \ref{gsr:en:sec:derandomization}), and, for source~61, source~59's character separation (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:charseparation}); they are printed here because no number printed earlier may move. Their introductions are Sections~\ref{gsr:fm:68:sec:d1}, \ref{gsr:fm:62:sec:d1}, \ref{gsr:fm:61:sec:d1} and~\ref{gsr:fm:60:sec:d1}.

\emph{What is proved.} \emph{Source~68}: for $B$ in a finite cyclic group, $b=|B|$, $\phi:B\to H$ into any abelian group with $G_{16}(B,\phi)\ge\alpha b^{15}$ and $b\ge(4/(\alpha\eta))^{53}$, a subset $B'$ with $T_{16}(B')\ge(\alpha\eta/4)^{53}b^{15}$ and $G_{16}(B')\ge(1-\eta)T_{16}(B')$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:ff:thm:53}), by source~58's expectation theorem (reproved, Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:rf:thm:expectation}) with a degree-twelve rational filter and exact integer certificates (Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:68:ff:prop:certificates}); an asymmetric form $2^{-205/2}\alpha^{105/2}\eta^{103/2}$ above $b\ge576\cdot2^{94}(\alpha\eta)^{-49}$ (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:68:ff:cor:asymmetric}); and two-parameter bounds on the principal cost $\cI_{m,a}$, with $\cI_{m,a}/m\to1+1/(2c)$ when $a=m^{c+o(1)}$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:uf:thm:uniform}, Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:68:uf:cor:regimes}). \emph{Source~62}: for $B\subseteq\Z/N\Z$ of size $\beta N$ and $\phi:B\to\Z/M\Z$, unit-dilation averaging gives restriction with no relation between $N$ and $M$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:62:thm:main}); explicitly, retention $2^{-245}\alpha^{31}\eta^{30}|B|^{15}$ above $N\ge2^{253}(\alpha\eta)^{-31}\beta^{-15}$ (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:62:cor:polynomial8}), and $\alpha^{16}\eta^{15}$ divided by a double logarithm in the refined form (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:62:cor:loglog}), which is necessary for its detector (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:62:thm:primitive-lower}); the exact weighted degeneracy constant with limit $\zeta(m-2)/\zeta(m-1)$, not a uniform bound (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:62:thm:kappa}, Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:62:prop:smallL}). \emph{Source~61}: on arbitrary finite abelian groups, $|\Gamma-\Gamma|\le K|\Gamma|$ partitions the whole domain into at most $5mK^{(2m+1)\log_2(5m)}$ cells on which $\phi$ is an exact Freiman homomorphism of order $m$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:61:ter:main-partition}); a threshold-free exact order-eight restriction with $2^{-2193}\alpha^{911}|B|$ points and $2^{-35277}\alpha^{14655}|B|^{15}$ tuples (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:61:ter:main-eight}); and $\lfloor\log_2m\rfloor+1\le b_m\le\log_2(5m)$ for the universal avoidance-colouring exponent (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:61:ter:main-exponent}). \emph{Source~60}: a translated Fej\'er selector with an all-group certificate (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:60:rst:thm:survival}, Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:60:rst:cor:certificate}) gives, on prime moduli, source~17's retention $\alpha^m\eta^{m-1}/(2(m+2)^m)$ under $b\ge2(1+\binom m2)L^{m-1}$, $L=\lceil(m+1)/(\alpha\eta)\rceil$ (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:60:rst:cor:prime}).

\emph{Which is best in which setting} (checked at the write; the inequalities in exact arithmetic). (i) \emph{Prime moduli, $\F_p\to\F_p$}: source~60's corollary keeps the powers $\alpha^{16}\eta^{15}$ of source~17 at $m=16$ with the threshold $242L^{15}$, one power of $L$ below the intake's marked composition $2(1+\binom m2)L^m$ (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:threshold}); on fixed fields source~29 remains better. (ii) \emph{Cyclic domain and cyclic target, $\Z/N\Z\to\Z/M\Z$}: source~62's powers $\alpha^{31}\eta^{30}$ are the best explicit ones; against source~68's $(\alpha\eta/4)^{53}$ its retention is larger exactly when $2^{-245}\alpha^{31}\eta^{30}>2^{-106}\alpha^{53}\eta^{53}(1-\eta)$, that is $\alpha^{22}\eta^{23}(1-\eta)<2^{-139}$ (counting respected tuples on both sides), while its threshold $N\ge2^{253}(\alpha\eta)^{-31}\beta^{-15}$ grows like $\beta^{-15}$ where source~68's, $N\ge\beta^{-1}(4/(\alpha\eta))^{53}$, grows like $\beta^{-1}$; neither dominates. (iii) \emph{Cyclic domain, arbitrary abelian target}: source~68's exponent $53$ is the best (source~58: $54$); source~62 does not apply (its question on noncyclic targets, Section~\ref{gsr:fz:62:sec:d12}). (iv) \emph{Arbitrary finite abelian domain and target}: only source~61 applies; its restriction is exact and threshold-free, at the cost of the powers $\alpha^{911}$ and $\alpha^{14655}$. All of them improve the printed exponent $2^{19}$. \emph{Against the catalogue} (\file{lemma_9_3}, \file{Sections08\_09.lean}, line~77, all $N\ge N_0$, maps $\Z/N\Z\to\Z/N\Z$, retention $(\alpha\eta/4)^{2^{19}}\beta^{15}N^{15}$): source~68's theorem implies it with $N_0=\lceil\beta^{-1}(4/(\alpha\eta))^{53}\rceil$, source~62's with $N_0=\lceil2^{253}(\alpha\eta)^{-31}\beta^{-15}\rceil$ ($M=N$), and source~61's with $N_0=1$; source~61's Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:61:ter:cor94} also implies \file{corollary_9_4} with $N_0=1$ (notes at the corollaries). Source~60's is for prime moduli only. Both catalogue statements are already exact (\file{lemma_9_3_holds}, \file{corollary_9_4_holds}, \file{Proofs09Restriction.lean}, lines~376 and~416), and none of these theorems is formalized.

\emph{Credits.} Source~68 reproves and credits source~58's expectation theorem; source~62's pin precedes source~58's placement, so their overlap is not a lapse; source~61 finds source~59's exponent $(2m+1)\log_2(5m)$ independently, and source~59's bound is sharper by the factor $5m$ and in its defect-sensitive form (note after Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:61:ter:main-partition}); source~61's Pl\"unnecke argument is Petridis's and its energy-to-growth step a conservative Balog--Szemer\'edi--Gowers argument, credited; source~60's selector uses source~17's Fej\'er kernel and source~04's weighted rank-two count, credited.

\emph{Relation to the formal statements} (checked at HEAD \texttt{fb9602e55}). \file{lemma_9_3} and \file{corollary_9_4} (\file{Sections08\_09.lean}, lines~77 and~91) and \file{lemma_7_5}, \file{corollary_7_6} (\file{Sections06\_07.lean}, lines~183 and~197) have exact companions (\file{lemma_9_3_holds}, \file{corollary_9_4_holds} in \file{Proofs09Restriction.lean}, lines~376 and~416; \file{lemma_7_5_holds}, \file{Proofs07FreimanRestriction.lean}, line~267; \file{corollary_7_6_holds}, \file{Proofs07AdditiveRestriction.lean}, line~100); the tuple counts are \file{additiveTupleCount}, \file{phiAdditiveTupleCount} and \file{GammaHomOfOrder} (\file{Definitions.lean}, lines~322, 327 and~334). Nothing in this chapter is formalized.

\section[{A restriction estimate with decaying exceptional terms\srctag{68}}]{A restriction estimate with decaying exceptional terms}\label{gsr:en:68:sec:d5}
\srcnote{68}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:en:68:sec:restriction}

The new finite filter in Section~\ref{gsr:en:68:sec:filter} is inserted into a
restriction theorem already established in source~58~\cite{repo68fiftyeight}.
We give its proof here so that the numerical improvement can be checked
without importing an unspecified selection argument. The underlying
random-character restriction is Gowers' method
\cite[Lemma~9.3]{gowers}; the weighted nonprincipal estimate and the
decaying correction for repeated points are credited to source~58.

\subsection{Ordered counts and admissible filters}

For this section fix an even integer $m=2r\ge4$ and write
\[
 \eps=(\underbrace{1,\ldots,1}_{r},
       \underbrace{-1,\ldots,-1}_{r}).
\]
Initially $G,H$ are finite abelian groups, $B\subseteq G$ is nonempty,
$b=|B|$, and $\phi:B\to H$. Define
\begin{align}
 T_m(B)&=\bigl|\{\mathbf x\in B^m:
                     \textstyle\sum_i\eps_i x_i=0\}\bigr|,
 \label{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:T}\\
 G_m(B,\phi)&=\bigl|\{\mathbf x\in B^m:
          \textstyle\sum_i\eps_i x_i=0,
          \ \sum_i\eps_i\phi(x_i)=0\}\bigr|,
 \label{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:G}\\
 U_m(B,\phi)&=T_m(B)-G_m(B,\phi).
 \label{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:U}
\end{align}
Every count is of ordered tuples, with repetitions allowed. An additive
tuple is \emph{respected} when its target discrepancy
$\sum_i\eps_i\phi(x_i)$ is zero, and \emph{bad} otherwise.

\begin{lemma}[Free variables and repeated entries]
\label{gsr:en:68:rf:lem:counts}
One has $T_m(B)\le b^{m-1}$. The number of additive tuples having a
repeated entry is at most $\binom m2b^{m-2}$. Every bad tuple has at
least two distinct entries.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The first $m-1$ entries determine the last, whose coefficient is
$\pm1$. To count repetitions, fix positions $i<j$ with $x_i=x_j$
and choose a position $h$ outside that pair. Choose the entries in the
$m-2$ positions other than $j,h$. The equality determines $x_j$,
and the additive relation determines $x_h$. Thus there are at most
$b^{m-2}$ tuples for each pair; a union bound proves the assertion.
If every entry is the same point, both balanced target sums equal
$r\phi(x)$, so that tuple is respected.
\end{proof}

Put $e(t)=\exp(2\pi i t)$ and identify $\T$ with $\R/\Z$, equipped
with Haar measure of total mass one. A \emph{decreasing admissible
filter of degree $D$} is a real trigonometric polynomial
\begin{equation}
 K(t)=\sum_{n=-D}^{D}c_ne(nt),\qquad
 0\le K\le1,\quad K(0)=1,
 \label{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:filter}
\end{equation}
whose coefficients satisfy
\begin{equation}
 c_{-n}=c_n\ge0,\qquad c_0\ge c_1\ge\cdots\ge c_D,
 \qquad c_1>0.
 \label{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:decreasing}
\end{equation}
Coefficients outside the indicated range are zero. Define
\begin{equation}
 P=\sum_n c_n^m,\qquad
 P_a=\sum_{a\mid n}c_n^m\quad(a\ge2),\qquad
 Q=P_2,\qquad R_j=\int_\T K(t)^j\,dt.
 \label{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:parameters}
\end{equation}
Here $a$ is an integer order, whereas the subscript $j$ in $R_j$
denotes a power of the filter. In particular,
\begin{equation}
 0<Q<P<1,\qquad P\le R_m\le R_2\le1.
 \label{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:parameter-order}
\end{equation}
Indeed, $\sum c_n=1$, at least $c_{-1},c_0,c_1$ are positive, and
the sum defining $Q$ omits $c_{-1}^m+c_1^m$. The expansion of the
constant coefficient of $K^m$ contains all vectors
$(t\eps_1,\ldots,t\eps_m)$, of total weight $P$, proving $P\le R_m$.
The remaining comparisons follow from $0\le K\le1$.

\begin{lemma}[Target orders]
\label{gsr:en:68:rf:lem:orders}
If $a\ge a_0\ge2$, then $P_a\le P_{a_0}$. If an element $z\in H$
has order $a$, then
\[
 \sum_{n\in\Z}c_n^m\ind_{nz=0}=P_a\le Q.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Evenness and monotonicity give
$P_a=c_0^m+2\sum_{j\ge1}c_{aj}^m
\le c_0^m+2\sum_{j\ge1}c_{a_0j}^m$.
The exact formula follows from $nz=0$ if and only if $a\mid n$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A finite random selector}

For $x\in G$, normalized character orthogonality is
\begin{equation}
 \E_{\chi\in\widehat G}e(\chi(x))=\ind_{x=0}.
 \label{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:orthogonality}
\end{equation}
For $x\ne0$, the decomposition of a finite abelian group into cyclic
groups supplies a character that is nontrivial on $x$. Translating the
character sum by it proves that the sum vanishes.

Choose integers $k\ge1$ and $M>mD$. Independently for each
$\ell=1,\ldots,k$, choose uniform characters
$\chi_\ell\in\widehat G$, $\psi_\ell\in\widehat H$, and a uniform
shift $u_\ell\in\{0,1/M,\ldots,(M-1)/M\}$. Conditional on these
parameters, select each distinct point $x\in B$ independently with
probability
\begin{equation}
 p(x)=\prod_{\ell=1}^k
 K\bigl(\chi_\ell(x)+\psi_\ell(\phi(x))+u_\ell\bigr).
 \label{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:selector}
\end{equation}
This defines a random subset $B'$. The parameter choices and the set
of possible subsets are finite; the probabilities need not be rational.

For one layer, expansion and orthogonality give the identity
\begin{align}
 &\E_{\chi,\psi,u}\prod_{i=1}^m
 K\bigl(\chi(x_i)+\psi(\phi(x_i))+u\bigr)\notag\\
 &\quad=
 \sum_{\mathbf n\in[-D,D]^m}
 \left(\prod_i c_{n_i}\right)
 \ind_{\sum_i n_i=0}
 \ind_{\sum_i n_ix_i=0}
 \ind_{\sum_i n_i\phi(x_i)=0}.
 \label{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:expansion}
\end{align}
The first equality tested on the right is in $\Z$. The grid average
initially imposes divisibility by $M$, and
$|\sum_i n_i|\le mD<M$ makes divisibility equivalent to zero.
The other equalities are in $G$ and $H$.

Call a coefficient vector \emph{principal} if
$\mathbf n=t\eps$ for an integer $t$. For a respected additive tuple,
every principal vector passes all three tests, with total weight $P$.
For a bad additive tuple of discrepancy order $a$, its principal
weight is $P_a$. All coefficients in the expansion are nonnegative.

For tuples with distinct entries, the product in
\eqref{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:expansion}, multiplied over layers, is the actual
conditional containment probability. For repeated entries it is a
\emph{formal product over occurrences}. If $x$ occurs $\mu_x$ times,
the formal factor is $p(x)^{\mu_x}$ and the actual factor is $p(x)$.
Consequently actual containment is at least formal containment.
It follows that
\begin{equation}
 \E G_m(B',\phi)\ge P^kG_m(B,\phi),
 \label{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:good}
\end{equation}
including all repetitions. This direction of comparison cannot be used
to upper-bound bad repeated tuples; those require the next estimates.

\subsection{Nonprincipal relations and collision errors}

For $d\ne0$ put $G[d]=\{x\in G:dx=0\}$, and define
\begin{equation}
 \tau_G(L)=\max_{1\le d\le L}|G[d]|.
 \label{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:tau}
\end{equation}
For cyclic groups, including the trivial group,
\begin{equation}
 |(\Z/N\Z)[d]|=\gcd(N,d),\qquad
 \tau_{\Z/N\Z}(2D)\le2D.
 \label{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:cyclic}
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}[Completion with two relations]
\label{gsr:en:68:rf:lem:completion}
For a nonprincipal $\mathbf n\in[-D,D]^m\cap\Z^m$, at most
$\tau_G(2D)b^{m-2}$ tuples in $B^m$ satisfy both
$\sum_i\eps_i x_i=0$ and $\sum_i n_i x_i=0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
There are positions $i,j$ with
$d=\eps_i n_j-\eps_j n_i\ne0$. Otherwise all integers
$n_i/\eps_i$ would be equal, making the vector principal.
Moreover $|d|\le2D$. Fix the other $m-2$ entries. The first relation,
whose relevant coefficient is $\pm1$, expresses one remaining entry
in terms of the other. Substitution into the second gives an equation
$dx=z$, up to an immaterial sign. Every nonempty multiplication fibre
is a coset of $G[d]$. Restriction of both entries to $B$ only reduces
the number of completions.
\end{proof}

The total coefficient weight of one layer satisfying just the integer
zero-sum test is the constant coefficient of $K^m$, namely $R_m$.
Its principal part has weight $P$. Hence the total weight of all
$k$-layer coefficient arrays containing a nonprincipal layer is
$R_m^k-P^k$. For each such array choose one nonprincipal layer and
apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:68:rf:lem:completion}, discarding all other conditions.
Summing nonnegative weights proves that its total contribution over
distinct-entry additive tuples is at most
\begin{equation}
 \tau_G(2D)(R_m^k-P^k)b^{m-2}.
 \label{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:nonprincipal}
\end{equation}
Each array is counted once. There is no union bound over the layers
and no additional factor $k$.

\begin{lemma}[Containment of a tuple with repeated entries]
\label{gsr:en:68:rf:lem:holder}
A tuple with $d\ge2$ distinct entries has containment probability at
most $R_d^k\le R_2^k$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Fix the characters in one layer and write $\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_d$
for the phases of its distinct points. H\"older's inequality gives
\[
 \E_u\prod_{j=1}^d K(u+\theta_j)
 \le\prod_{j=1}^d
       \bigl(\E_uK(u+\theta_j)^d\bigr)^{1/d}=R_d.
\]
To justify the equality, each translated polynomial has degree at
most $dD\le mD<M$; its grid average therefore equals its constant
coefficient, which is $R_d$. Average over the characters and multiply
over the independent layers. Finally $K^d\le K^2$ for $d\ge2$.
\end{proof}

By Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:68:rf:lem:counts}, the expected number of retained bad
tuples with repeated entries is at most
\begin{equation}
 \binom m2R_2^kb^{m-2}.
 \label{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:collisions}
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Repeated-filter estimate; source 58]
\label{gsr:en:68:rf:thm:expectation}
For the selector \eqref{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:selector},
\begin{align}
 \E G_m(B',\phi)&\ge P^kG_m(B,\phi),\label{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:expect-good}\\
 \E U_m(B',\phi)&\le Q^kU_m(B,\phi)+A_kb^{m-2},
 \label{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:expect-bad}
\end{align}
where
\begin{equation}
 A_k=\tau_G(2D)(R_m^k-P^k)+\binom m2R_2^k
 \le C_G R_2^k,\qquad C_G=\tau_G(2D)+\binom m2.
 \label{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:Ak}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The good bound is \eqref{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:good}. For a bad distinct-entry tuple,
the all-principal part is at most $Q^k$ by
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:68:rf:lem:orders}. Sum that part over the bad tuples, add
\eqref{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:nonprincipal}, and then add \eqref{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:collisions}.
The final inequality uses $R_m\le R_2$ and drops the nonpositive term
$-\tau_G(2D)P^k$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{One subset with both quality and retained mass}

\begin{theorem}[Spectral-gap restriction; source 58]
\label{gsr:en:68:rf:thm:selection}
Suppose $0<\alpha,\eta\le1$ and
$G_m(B,\phi)\ge\alpha b^{m-1}$. Put
\begin{equation}
 t=\alpha\eta,\qquad \cR=P/Q>1,\qquad
 k=\left\lceil\frac{\log(2/t)}{\log\cR}\right\rceil.
 \label{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:k}
\end{equation}
If
\begin{equation}
 b\ge \frac{4A_k}{tP^k},
 \label{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:exact-threshold}
\end{equation}
then some $B'\subseteq B$ satisfies
\begin{equation}
 G_m(B',\phi)\ge(1-\eta)T_m(B'),\qquad
 T_m(B')\ge\frac{\alpha P^k}{4}b^{m-1}.
 \label{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:selection-conclusion}
\end{equation}
A sufficient replacement for \eqref{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:exact-threshold} is
$b\ge4C_Gt^{-1}(R_2/P)^k$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $\eta=1$, take $B'=B$ and use $T_m(B)\ge G_m(B,\phi)$.
Assume $\eta<1$. For each outcome consider the single random variable
\[
 F=G_m(B',\phi)-(1-\eta)T_m(B')
   =\eta G_m(B',\phi)-(1-\eta)U_m(B',\phi).
\]
The choice of $k$ implies $Q^k\le(t/2)P^k$. Since
$U_m(B,\phi)\le b^{m-1}$, Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:rf:thm:expectation} gives
\begin{align*}
 \E F
 &\ge tP^kb^{m-1}-(1-\eta)Q^kb^{m-1}
                      -(1-\eta)A_kb^{m-2}\\
 &\ge\frac t2P^kb^{m-1}-A_kb^{m-2}
 \ge\frac t4P^kb^{m-1}>0.
\end{align*}
Choose an outcome with $F\ge\E F$. Its positivity proves the quality
claim, and $F=\eta T_m(B')-U_m(B',\phi)\le\eta T_m(B')$ proves
the retained-mass claim. The simpler threshold follows from
\eqref{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:Ak}.
\end{proof}

Define the two real exponents
\begin{equation}
 a_K=\frac{-\log P}{\log\cR},\qquad
 z_K=\frac{\log(R_2/P)}{\log\cR}.
 \label{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:costs}
\end{equation}
Here $a_K>0$ and $z_K\ge0$. Since $k<\log(2/t)/\log\cR+1$,
\begin{equation}
 P^k\ge P(t/2)^{a_K},\qquad
 (R_2/P)^k\le(R_2/P)(2/t)^{z_K}.
 \label{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:ceiling}
\end{equation}
Thus a sufficient threshold and the resulting retention are
\begin{align}
 b&\ge4C_G(R_2/P)\,2^{z_K}(\alpha\eta)^{-(z_K+1)},
 \label{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:power-threshold}\\
 T_m(B')&\ge
 \frac{P}{4\,2^{a_K}}\alpha^{a_K+1}\eta^{a_K}b^{m-1}.
 \label{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:power-retention}
\end{align}
These are the precise interfaces used below. The powers of $\alpha$
and $\eta$ need not be rounded to the same integer.

\subsection{Arbitrary abelian target groups}

\begin{lemma}[A finite quotient preserving the tuple relations]
\label{gsr:en:68:rf:lem:finite-quotient}
For finite $B$, any map $\phi:B\to H$ to an abelian group, and a
fixed $m$, there is a finite abelian group $H_0$ and a map
$\phi_0:B\to H_0$ preserving precisely which balanced $m$-term
target discrepancies vanish. The same equivalence holds on every
subset of $B$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The subgroup generated by $\phi(B)$ is finitely generated, hence is
isomorphic to $\Z^s\oplus F$ for a finite abelian group $F$. List all
balanced $m$-term discrepancies of points of $B$. Choose an integer
$L\ge2$ strictly larger than the absolute values of all coordinates
of their free parts. Reduce the free factor modulo $L$ and retain
$F$. A nonzero free coordinate remains nonzero modulo $L$; a
nonzero discrepancy with zero free part retains its nonzero torsion
coordinate. Zero discrepancies remain zero. Every tuple in a subset
was already in the original finite list.
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:rf:thm:selection} and \eqref{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:power-threshold}--
\eqref{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:power-retention} therefore hold for arbitrary abelian
targets, with the same constants. Only the domain is required to be
finite. The general-domain torsion factor remains present: for
$G=(\Z/2\Z)^s$, already $|G[2]|=|G|$. Its bound by $2D$ is a
specific advantage of cyclic domains, rather than a property of all
finite abelian groups.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A degree-twelve filter and the exponent fifty-three\srctag{68}}]{A degree-twelve filter and the exponent fifty-three}\label{gsr:en:68:sec:d6}
\srcnote{68}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:en:68:sec:filter}

The restriction proof is now fixed. Its remaining inputs are the
coefficients of a filter and exact inequalities between their moments.
Source~58 uses $\cos^{50}(\pi t)$, of degree $25$, to obtain the common
exponent $54$ in its size threshold and retained tuple fraction
\cite{repo68fiftyeight}. The following rational filter reduces the degree to
$12$ and the common exponent to $53$. It also gives a principal cost
strictly below $103/2$, compared with approximately $52.2064$ for that
specific powered cosine. No optimum over all filters is asserted.

\subsection{An admissible polynomial with rational coefficients}

Extend the following sequence evenly and by zero outside $[-6,6]$:
\begin{equation}
 (a_0,a_1,\ldots,a_6)=(1000,942,782,558,320,124,14).
 \label{gsr:en:68:ff:eq:seed}
\end{equation}
Set
\begin{equation}
 S=\sum_{j=-6}^6a_j=6480,\qquad
 H(t)=\sum_{j=-6}^6a_je(jt),\qquad K(t)=\frac{H(t)^2}{S^2}.
 \label{gsr:en:68:ff:eq:kernel}
\end{equation}
Since the sequence is real and even, $H$ is real. Thus $K\ge0$;
the triangle inequality gives $|H(t)|\le S$, so $K\le1$; and
$H(0)=S$ gives $K(0)=1$. Write
\begin{equation}
 d=S^2=41990400,\qquad
 b_n=\sum_j a_ja_{n-j},\qquad c_n=b_n/d.
 \label{gsr:en:68:ff:eq:coefficients}
\end{equation}
The $c_n$ are the Fourier coefficients of $K$ and are nonnegative and
even. Their positive-side data are small enough to print in full.

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}rrrrrrr@{}}
\toprule
$n$&0&1&2&3&4&5\\
\midrule
$b_n$&4856448&4669952&4150460&3401728&2558308&1749968\\
\midrule
$n$&6&7&8&9&10&11\\
\midrule
$b_n$&1073460&577432&262680&94984&24336&3472\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The final coefficient is $b_{12}=196$. In particular,
$b_0>b_1>\cdots>b_{12}>0$ and $b_1>0$. Also
$\sum_{n=-12}^{12}b_n=S^2$. This proves all the conditions of
\eqref{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:filter}--\eqref{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:decreasing}, with degree exactly
$D=12$.

\subsection{Exact integer certificates}

For the rest of this section $m=16$. Introduce the integers
\begin{equation}
 A=\sum_{n=-12}^{12}b_n^{16},\qquad
 B_{\rm ev}=\sum_{\substack{-12\le n\le12\\2\mid n}}b_n^{16},
 \qquad V=\sum_{n=-12}^{12}b_n^2.
 \label{gsr:en:68:ff:eq:integers}
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}
 P=\frac{A}{d^{16}},\qquad Q=\frac{B_{\rm ev}}{d^{16}},\qquad
 \cR=\frac{A}{B_{\rm ev}},\qquad R_2=\frac{V}{d^2}.
 \label{gsr:en:68:ff:eq:exact-parameters}
\end{equation}
The last identity is the constant coefficient of $K^2$, since
$c_{-n}=c_n$. In particular $V=147141531710208$.

\begin{proposition}[Finite certificates]
\label{gsr:en:68:ff:prop:certificates}
The integers in \eqref{gsr:en:68:ff:eq:integers} satisfy all the inequalities
in the following table.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule
Exact inequality&Consequence\\
\midrule
$2^{49}A>d^{16}$&$P>2^{-49}$\\[2pt]
$250A>481B_{\rm ev}$&$\cR>481/250$\\[2pt]
$481^{52}>2^{49}250^{52}$&$\cR^{52}>2^{49}$\\[2pt]
$481^{49}>2^{46}250^{49}$&$\cR^{49}>2^{46}$\\[2pt]
$8V<d^2$&$R_2<2^{-3}$\\[2pt]
$A^{105}>d^{32}B_{\rm ev}^{103}$&$a_K<103/2$\\[2pt]
$A^{49}>B_{\rm ev}^{48}Vd^{14}$&$z_K<48$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Consequently $a_K<52$ and $z_K<49$ also hold.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The inequalities are finite integer arithmetic with the explicitly
listed coefficients. To make the certificate independently executable,
the complete essential computation is printed below; exponentiation
uses integers of arbitrary precision.
\begin{small}
\begin{verbatim}
seed = [1000, 942, 782, 558, 320, 124, 14]
a = {j: seed[abs(j)] for j in range(-6, 7)}
d = sum(a.values()) ** 2
b = {n: sum(a[j] * a.get(n-j, 0) for j in a)
     for n in range(-12, 13)}
A = sum(v ** 16 for v in b.values())
B = sum(v ** 16 for n, v in b.items() if n % 2 == 0)
V = sum(v * v for v in b.values())
checks = [
    d == 41990400,
    all(b[n] > b[n+1] for n in range(12)),
    2**49 * A > d**16,
    250 * A > 481 * B,
    481**52 > 2**49 * 250**52,
    481**49 > 2**46 * 250**49,
    8 * V < d**2,
    A**105 > d**32 * B**103,
    A**49 > B**48 * V * d**14,
]
if not all(checks):
    raise ArithmeticError("Certificate failed")
\end{verbatim}
\end{small}
The accompanying verifier executes these comparisons and additional
normalization checks. No floating-point inequality enters the
certificate.

For the last two consequences, the penultimate inequality is precisely
$P^2\cR^{103}>1$, implying
$-\log P/\log\cR<103/2$. The final inequality is precisely
$\cR^{48}P/R_2>1$, implying
$\log(R_2/P)/\log\cR<48$. These arguments only take logarithms of
strictly positive numbers and use $\cR>1$.
\end{proof}

For orientation, the values are
\begin{align}
 P&\approx2.2934630227959095\cdot10^{-15},
 &\cR&\approx1.925599333199833,\notag\\
 a_K&\approx51.44504972230757,
 &z_K&\approx47.654839268529635.
 \label{gsr:en:68:ff:eq:diagnostics}
\end{align}
These decimals describe the certified filter. The theorem below rests
on Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:68:ff:prop:certificates}.

\subsection{The resulting restriction theorem}

\begin{theorem}[A common exponent of fifty-three]
\label{gsr:en:68:ff:thm:53}
Let $G$ be any finite cyclic group, let $H$ be any abelian group, and
let $\phi:B\to H$ for a nonempty $B\subseteq G$ of cardinality $b$.
Suppose $0<\alpha,\eta\le1$ and
\[
 G_{16}(B,\phi)\ge\alpha b^{15}.
\]
If
\begin{equation}
 b\ge\left(\frac4{\alpha\eta}\right)^{53},
 \label{gsr:en:68:ff:eq:53-threshold}
\end{equation}
then a subset $B'\subseteq B$ satisfies
\begin{align}
 G_{16}(B',\phi)&\ge(1-\eta)T_{16}(B'),\notag\\
 T_{16}(B')&\ge
       \left(\frac{\alpha\eta}{4}\right)^{53}b^{15},
 \qquad
 |B'|\ge
       \left(\frac{\alpha\eta}{4}\right)^{53/15}b.
 \label{gsr:en:68:ff:eq:53-conclusion}
\end{align}
The counts include repeated entries and require no restriction on
the prime factors of $|G|$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
First assume $H$ finite and put $t=\alpha\eta$. The filter has
$D=12$, hence \eqref{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:cyclic} gives
$C_G\le24+\binom{16}{2}=144$. The first five certificates imply
\[
 P\ge2^{-49},\qquad R_2/P\le2^{46},\qquad
 a_K\le52,\qquad z_K\le49.
\]
Thus the sufficient threshold \eqref{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:power-threshold} is at
most
\[
 576\,2^{95}t^{-50}
 \le2^{106}t^{-53}=(4/t)^{53}.
\]
Here $576\le2^{11}$ and $0<t\le1$. The retained proportion in
\eqref{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:power-retention} is at least
\[
 \frac{2^{-49}}{4\,2^{52}}\alpha^{53}\eta^{52}
 =2^{-103}\alpha^{53}\eta^{52}
 \ge2^{-106}\alpha^{53}\eta^{53}.
\]
The inequalities in the powers use $0<\alpha,\eta\le1$.
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:rf:thm:selection} supplies the same subset for quality
and mass. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:68:rf:lem:counts} gives
$T_{16}(B')\le|B'|^{15}$, yielding the size conclusion.
For arbitrary $H$, apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:68:rf:lem:finite-quotient} and
transfer the selected subset back to the original map.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Against the formal statement and the other all-moduli theorems} (checked at the write). With $b=\beta N$ and $N_0=\lceil\beta^{-1}(4/(\alpha\eta))^{53}\rceil$ this theorem gives \file{lemma_9_3} (\file{Sections08\_09.lean}, line~77), since $0<\alpha\eta/4<1$ and $53<2^{19}$, on paper; the catalogue statement is already exact and this theorem is not formalized. It improves source~58's exponent $54$ (\hyperref[gsr:fm:58:thm:A]{Theorem~A}) in the same setting; for cyclic targets source~62's Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:62:cor:polynomial8} retains more when $\alpha^{22}\eta^{23}(1-\eta)<2^{-139}$ (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:allmoduli}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{corollary}[A stronger asymmetric parameter bound]
\label{gsr:en:68:ff:cor:asymmetric}
Under the same count hypothesis, the sufficient size condition
\begin{equation}
 b\ge576\,2^{94}(\alpha\eta)^{-49}
 \label{gsr:en:68:ff:eq:asymmetric-threshold}
\end{equation}
guarantees a subset with respected proportion at least $1-\eta$ and
\begin{equation}
 T_{16}(B')\ge
 2^{-205/2}\alpha^{105/2}\eta^{103/2}b^{15}.
 \label{gsr:en:68:ff:eq:asymmetric-retention}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Use $z_K\le48$ in \eqref{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:power-threshold}, together with
$C_G\le144$ and $R_2/P\le2^{46}$. Use $a_K\le103/2$ and
$P\ge2^{-49}$ in \eqref{gsr:en:68:rf:eq:power-retention}. The exponent of two
in the denominator is $49+2+103/2=205/2$.
\end{proof}

The comparison with source~58 is on the same cyclic-domain,
arbitrary-target interface and with the same tuple conventions:
the common threshold $(4/(\alpha\eta))^{54}$ and fraction
$(\alpha\eta/4)^{54}$ are both improved by replacing $54$ with $53$.
The asymmetric corollary retains more of the certified information.
These are local restriction bounds. No propagation through the full
inverse argument or density-increment iteration is supplied here.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Uniform principal costs as arity and torsion vary\srctag{68}}]{Uniform principal costs as arity and torsion vary}\label{gsr:en:68:sec:d7}
\srcnote{68}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:en:68:sec:uniform}

The preceding restriction uses discrepancy order two as its worst
case. When all nonzero target discrepancies have order at least $a$,
the principal bad weight can instead be $P_a$. Source~58 proves,
for each fixed $a\ge2$, the asymptotic
\[
 \cI_{m,a}=\frac{m\log m}{2\log a}
             +O_a(m\log\log m)
 \qquad(m\longrightarrow\infty)
\]
for the principal cost defined below \cite{repo68fiftyeight}.
We obtain a uniform estimate, allow $a$ to grow with $m$, and improve
the fixed-$a$ error. An additional term $m-1$ becomes a leading term
when $a$ is a power of $m$.

\subsection{The extremal problem and its two-parameter answer}

In this section $m\ge2$ is any integer. Evenness of $m$ is needed for
its application to a balanced relation, but is unnecessary for the
extremal problem. Let $\mathcal K$ be the class of all finite
trigonometric polynomials
\begin{equation}
 K(x)=\sum_n c_ne(nx),\qquad
 0\le K\le1,\quad K(0)=1,\quad c_n=c_{-n}\ge0.
 \label{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:class}
\end{equation}
Monotonicity of the coefficients is not required in this class. Put
\begin{equation}
 P_m(K)=\sum_n c_n^m,\qquad
 Q_{m,a}(K)=\sum_{a\mid n}c_n^m
 \quad(a\ge2),
 \label{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:moments}
\end{equation}
and define
\begin{equation}
 \costA_{m,a}(K)
   =\frac{-\log P_m(K)}{\log(P_m(K)/Q_{m,a}(K))},
 \qquad
 \cI_{m,a}=\inf_{K\in\mathcal K}\costA_{m,a}(K).
 \label{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:cost}
\end{equation}
Zero gain $P_m=Q_{m,a}$ is assigned cost $+\infty$. All logarithms
are natural.

\begin{theorem}[A uniform arity--torsion estimate]
\label{gsr:en:68:uf:thm:uniform}
For every pair of integers $m,a\ge2$,
\begin{align}
 \cI_{m,a}&\ge m-1,\label{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:baseline}\\
 \cI_{m,a}&\ge
 m-1+\frac{m(\log m-20)}{2\log a},\label{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:lower}\\
 \cI_{m,a}&\le
 m-1+\frac{m}{2\log a}
 \left[
 \log m+\log\log\!\left(e+\frac{\log m}{\log a}\right)+4
 \right].
 \label{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:upper}
\end{align}
The constants are absolute and the inequalities hold for all the
stated finite parameters. No optimality is claimed for the constants
$20$ and $4$.
\end{theorem}

The lower estimate imports the classical circle Riesz--Sobolev
inequality \cite[Theorem~1.1 and (1.8)]{christiliopoulou}. The remaining
steps, including its precise convolution consequence and the finite
approximants in the upper construction, are proved below.

\subsection{Elementary bounds and a small-gain estimate}

Write $s=c_0=\int_\T K$. Since $K$ is continuous, nonnegative, and
$K(0)=1$, one has $s>0$. If $s=1$, then $K\equiv1$ and its cost is
infinite. Otherwise $0<s<1$. The integral formula for a coefficient
and the normalization at zero give
\begin{equation}
 0\le c_n\le s,\qquad
 \sum_n c_n=1,\qquad
 P_m\le s^{m-1},\qquad Q_{m,a}\ge s^m.
 \label{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:mean}
\end{equation}
Let $P=P_m$, $Q=Q_{m,a}$, and $R=P/Q$ when the parameters are fixed.

\begin{lemma}[Gain ceilings]
\label{gsr:en:68:uf:lem:ceilings}
For every admissible filter,
\[
 1\le R\le a,\qquad R\le s^{-1}.
\]
Every positive-gain filter has $\costA_{m,a}(K)\ge m-1$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Use normalized convolution
$f*g(x)=\int_\T f(x-y)g(y)\,dy$. The function $F=K^{*m}$ is
nonnegative and has Fourier coefficients $c_n^m$. Therefore
\[
 Q=\frac1a\sum_{j=0}^{a-1}F(j/a)\ge\frac{F(0)}a=\frac Pa.
\]
The lower bound $R\ge1$ follows by deleting nonnegative terms.
Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:mean} gives $R\le1/s$. For $R>1$,
$-\log P\ge(m-1)(-\log s)$ and $\log R\le-\log s$, proving the
cost estimate.
\end{proof}

The next elementary estimate is used in source~58. We retain it
because a bound for gains bounded away from one is not by itself
sufficient to control the infimum in \eqref{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:cost}.

\begin{lemma}[A coefficient estimate and the small-gain alternative]
\label{gsr:en:68:uf:lem:bathtub}
For $n\ne0$,
\begin{equation}
 c_n\le s\,\frac{\sin(\pi s)}{\pi s}
       \le s\exp(-2s^2/3).
 \label{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:coefficient}
\end{equation}
Consequently, for $R>1$,
\begin{align}
 R-1&\le\frac{1-s}{s}\exp\!\left(-\frac{2(m-1)s^2}{3}\right),
 \label{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:small-gain}\\
 \costA_{m,a}(K)&\ge
 (m-1)s\exp\!\left(\frac{2(m-1)s^2}{3}\right).
 \label{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:large-mean-cost}
\end{align}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The distribution of $\cos(2\pi nx)$ under Haar measure is that of
$\cos(2\pi x)$. Let $E$ be its top level set of measure $s$.
The pointwise inequality
\[
 (\ind_E-K)\bigl(\cos(2\pi nx)-\cos(\pi s)\bigr)\ge0
\]
and $\int(\ind_E-K)=0$ imply
$c_n\le\int_E\cos(2\pi nx)\,dx=\sin(\pi s)/\pi$.
For $0\le v\le1$, concavity of sine gives
$\sin(\pi v/2)\ge v$, hence $\cos(\pi v)\le1-2v^2$.
Integrating with $v=su$ for $0\le u\le1$ gives
$\sin(\pi s)/(\pi s)\le1-2s^2/3\le e^{-2s^2/3}$.

The total mass of the nonzero coefficients is $1-s$. Thus
\[
 R-1\le\frac{\sum_{n\ne0}c_n^m}{s^m}
 \le\frac{1-s}{s}\exp\!\left(-\frac{2(m-1)s^2}{3}\right).
\]
Finally use $-\log P\ge(m-1)(-\log s)$,
$-\log s\ge1-s$, and $\log R\le R-1$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A convolution-concentration bound}

For a nonnegative integrable function $f$ on $\T$, let $f^\star$
be its symmetric nonincreasing rearrangement: it is even,
nonincreasing on $[0,1/2]$, and equimeasurable with $f$.
For $0\le v\le1$, let $I_v$ be the centered interval of measure $v$.
The classical inequality we use is
\begin{equation}
 \int_\T (f*g)h
 \le\int_\T(f^\star*g^\star)h^\star
 \qquad(f,g,h\ge0).
 \label{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:riesz}
\end{equation}
This is the circle case of the cited theorem; that source credits
Baernstein for this case \cite{christiliopoulou}.

Say that $f\preceq F$, with $F$ symmetric nonincreasing and of the
same integral as $f$, if
\begin{equation}
 \int_E f\le\int_{I_{|E|}}F
 \quad\hbox{for every measurable }E\subseteq\T.
 \label{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:majorization}
\end{equation}
Equivalently, the centered partial integrals of $f^\star$ are bounded
by those of $F$. By the layer-cake representation, this implies
$\int f^\star q\le\int Fq$ for every nonnegative symmetric
nonincreasing $q$.

\begin{lemma}[Convolution preserves this concentration order]
\label{gsr:en:68:uf:lem:concentration-order}
If $f\preceq F$ and $g\preceq G$, then $f*g\preceq F*G$.
In particular, for $0\le f\le1$ with $\int f=s$ and integers $m\ge2$,
\begin{equation}
 f^{*m}(x)\le \ind_{I_s}^{*m}(0)
 \quad\hbox{for every }x\in\T.
 \label{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:interval-domination}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
First, convolution of symmetric nonincreasing functions on the
circle is symmetric nonincreasing. By layer cake it suffices to
check two interval indicators. If their lengths are $\alpha,\beta$,
put $p=(\alpha+\beta)/2$ and $q=|\alpha-\beta|/2$. Their real-line
overlap at separation $x\ge0$ is
$\ell(x)=(p-x)_+-(q-x)_+$. On the circle, for $0\le x\le1/2$,
the overlap is $\ell(x)+\ell(1-x)$. The first summand has slope
$0$ or $-1$. The second can have slope $+1$ only when
$x>1-p$; then $q\le1-p<x<p$, since $p+q\le1$, so the first
has slope $-1$. Their sum is therefore nonincreasing.

For $|E|=v$, \eqref{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:riesz} gives
\[
 \int_E f*g
 \le\int_{I_v}f^\star*g^\star
 =\int_\T f^\star(g^\star*\ind_{I_v}).
\]
The parenthesized function is symmetric nonincreasing. Replace
$f^\star$ by $F$ using \eqref{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:majorization} and layer cake.
By commutativity, the resulting expression equals
$\int g^\star(F*\ind_{I_v})$. Replace $g^\star$ by $G$ in the
same way. The result is $\int_{I_v}F*G$, proving the claim.

If $0\le f\le1$ and $\int f=s$, then
$\int_E f\le\min(|E|,s)=\int_{I_{|E|}}\ind_{I_s}$.
Thus $f\preceq\ind_{I_s}$, and induction gives
$f^{*m}\preceq\ind_{I_s}^{*m}$. Apply this to intervals centered at
$x$ and let their measure decrease to zero.
The functions in this final step are continuous for $m\ge2$:
for bounded $f,g$, translation continuity in $L^1$ and
$\|f*(g(\,\cdot+h)-g)\|_\infty
\le\|f\|_\infty\|g(\,\cdot+h)-g\|_1$
give the needed continuity.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Mean-sensitive spectral concentration]
\label{gsr:en:68:uf:prop:concentration}
For every $K\in\mathcal K$, $s=\int K$, and integer $m\ge2$,
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 P_m(K)\le s^m\left(1+\frac4{s\sqrt m}\right).}
 \label{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:concentration}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Fourier convolution gives $P_m(K)=K^{*m}(0)$. The Fourier
coefficients of $\ind_{I_s}$ are $s\,\sinc(\pi ns)$, where
$\sinc z=\sin z/z$ and $\sinc0=1$. Their $m$th powers are absolutely
summable for $m\ge2$. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:68:uf:lem:concentration-order} therefore
implies
\[
 \frac{P_m(K)}{s^m}
 \le1+2\sum_{n\ge1}|\sinc(\pi ns)|^m.
\]
For $0\le x\le1$, the sine estimate from
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:68:uf:lem:bathtub} gives
$|\sinc(\pi x)|\le e^{-2x^2/3}$; for $x>1$ use
$|\sinc(\pi x)|\le(\pi x)^{-1}$. The resulting envelope
\[
 F_m(x)=
 \begin{cases}
 e^{-2mx^2/3},&0\le x\le1,\\
 (\pi x)^{-m},&x>1
 \end{cases}
\]
is nonincreasing, including its downward jump at one. Thus
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{n\ge1}|\sinc(\pi ns)|^m
 &\le\frac1s\int_0^\infty F_m(x)\,dx\\
 &\le\frac1s\left(\sqrt{\frac{3\pi}{8m}}
                       +\frac{\pi^{-m}}{m-1}\right)
 <\frac2{s\sqrt m}.
\end{align*}
For the last convenient constant, $\pi<4$ and $\pi^m\ge m$ imply
$\sqrt{3\pi/8}+\sqrt m\,\pi^{-m}/(m-1)
\le\sqrt{3/2}+1/\sqrt2<2$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Proof of the uniform lower bound}

Fix a positive-gain filter and abbreviate
$C=-\log P$, $v=-\log s$, and $R=P/Q>1$.
Suppose first that $R\ge3/2$. Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:concentration}
gives
\[
 R\le1+\frac4{s\sqrt m}.
\]
Since $R-1\ge R/3$, it follows that
$s\le12/(R\sqrt m)$. Also $4/(s\sqrt m)\ge1/2$, so
$1+4/(s\sqrt m)\le12/(s\sqrt m)$. Consequently
\begin{align}
 v&\ge\log R+\tfrac12\log m-\log12,\notag\\
 C&\ge(m-1)v+\tfrac12\log m-\log12\notag\\
  &\ge(m-1)\log R+\tfrac m2\log m-m\log12.
 \label{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:large-gain-cost}
\end{align}
If the last remainder is nonnegative, division by
$\log R\le\log a$ proves the required lower bound, with $20$
even replaceable in this case by $2\log12$.
If it is negative, the baseline $C/\log R\ge m-1$ proves
\eqref{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:lower}.

Now suppose $1<R<3/2$. If $\log m\le20$, the correction in
\eqref{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:lower} is nonpositive and the baseline suffices.
For the remaining case set $x=\log m\ge20$ and
$s_0=\sqrt{3\log m/m}<1$. When $s\le s_0$,
\begin{equation}
 \costA_{m,a}(K)\ge
 \frac{m-1}{2\log(3/2)}(x-\log x-\log3).
 \label{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:small-gain-small-mean}
\end{equation}
This is at least $m-1+mx/(2\log2)$. Here is an explicit check of
the numerical range. One has
\[
 \frac{m-1}{m}\ge\frac{99}{100},\quad
 \frac1{2\log(3/2)}>\frac65,\quad
 \frac1{2\log2}<\frac34,\quad
 \log3<\frac{11}{10},\quad \log x\le\frac x5.
\]
The logarithmic estimates follow respectively from elementary
integral or alternating-series bounds and the exponential series;
the last one holds at $x=20$ and persists by differentiation.
The left side of \eqref{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:small-gain-small-mean}, divided by $m$,
is therefore at least
$594x/625-3267/2500$, whereas the claimed comparison is at most
$1+3x/4$. The difference is
$(501x-5767)/2500>0$ for $x\ge20$.

If instead $s>s_0$, the right side of
\eqref{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:large-mean-cost} increases with $s$, and hence
\[
 \costA_{m,a}(K)
 \ge(m-1)\sqrt{3x/m}\,m^{2-2/m}
 \ge\tfrac12\sqrt{3x}\,m^{3/2}.
\]
Since $e^{x/2}\ge x$ for $x\ge20$, the last expression is at least
$mx$, which is at least $m-1+mx/(2\log2)$.
Both subcases dominate \eqref{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:lower} because $a\ge2$.
Together with Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:68:uf:lem:ceilings}, this proves both lower
estimates in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:uf:thm:uniform}.

\subsection{Theta filters and their finite approximants}

For $t>0$ put
\[
 \Theta(t)=\sum_{n\in\Z}e^{-tn^2},\qquad
 F_t(x)=\sum_{n\in\Z}e^{-tn^2}e(nx).
\]
The Gaussian Fourier integral gives the periodization identity
\begin{equation}
 F_t(x)=\sqrt{\frac\pi t}
       \sum_{j\in\Z}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\pi^2(x-j)^2}{t}\right)>0.
 \label{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:poisson-function}
\end{equation}
For completeness, the $n$th Fourier coefficient of the right side,
after combining the translated intervals into $\R$, is
$\sqrt{\pi/t}\int_\R e^{-\pi^2y^2/t}e(-ny)\,dy=e^{-tn^2}$.
Absolute convergence justifies periodization and identifies the
Fourier series. At zero this yields
\begin{equation}
 \Theta(t)=\sqrt{\frac\pi t}\,\Theta(\pi^2/t).
 \label{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:poisson}
\end{equation}

The normalized function $F_t/\Theta(t)$ is nonnegative; its
nonnegative Fourier coefficients sum to one, so its values are at
most one. It is not a finite polynomial. To remain within
\eqref{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:class}, use
\begin{equation}
 K_{t,J}(x)=
 \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{|n|\le J}
          \left(1-\frac{|n|}{J+1}\right)e^{-tn^2}e(nx)}
      {\displaystyle\sum_{|n|\le J}
          \left(1-\frac{|n|}{J+1}\right)e^{-tn^2}}
 \qquad(J\ge1).
 \label{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:fejer-approximation}
\end{equation}
The numerator is the convolution of $F_t$ with the nonnegative
Fej\'er kernel
$(J+1)^{-1}|\sum_{j=0}^Je(jx)|^2$. It is therefore nonnegative.
After normalization, its nonnegative even coefficients sum to one,
which implies $K_{t,J}\le1$ and $K_{t,J}(0)=1$.
Thus every $K_{t,J}$ belongs to the exact finite class $\mathcal K$.
Its coefficients also decrease with $|n|$, as both factors in the
numerator of \eqref{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:fejer-approximation} do. The upper
construction therefore satisfies the stronger decreasing-filter
hypotheses of Section~\ref{gsr:en:68:sec:restriction} as well.

As $J\to\infty$, their coefficient sequences converge in $\ell^1$
to $e^{-tn^2}/\Theta(t)$ by dominated convergence and convergence of
the positive normalizing denominator. The inequality
$|u^m-v^m|\le m|u-v|$ for $u,v\in[0,1]$ then gives convergence of
both $P_m$ and $Q_{m,a}$. The limiting gain is strictly positive,
because $a\ge2$ and the omitted coefficients at $n=\pm1$ are
positive. Hence
\begin{equation}
 \cI_{m,a}\le
 \frac{m\log\Theta(t)-\log\Theta(mt)}
      {\log\Theta(mt)-\log\Theta(ma^2t)}
 \qquad(t>0).
 \label{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:theta-cost}
\end{equation}
This use of a limit proves an upper bound for the infimum over
finite polynomials; it does not enlarge the admissible class.

\subsection{Proof of the uniform upper bound}

Put
\begin{equation}
 A=\log a,\quad L=\log m,\quad u=L/A,\quad
 h=\log(e+u),\qquad t=\frac1{ma^2h}.
 \label{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:theta-choice}
\end{equation}
In particular $h\ge1$. For $v\ge1$, the inequality
$n^2\ge1+3(n-1)$ for $n\ge1$ gives
\begin{equation}
 \Theta(v)\le1+\frac{2e^{-v}}{1-e^{-3v}}
             \le1+3e^{-v}.
 \label{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:theta-tail}
\end{equation}
Write $\delta=\log\Theta(\pi^2h)$. Since $\pi^2>9$,
\begin{equation}
 0\le\delta\le3e^{-\pi^2h}\le3(e+u)^{-9}.
 \label{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:delta}
\end{equation}
By \eqref{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:poisson}, the denominator in
\eqref{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:theta-cost} is
\[
 A+\log\Theta(\pi^2a^2h)-\log\Theta(\pi^2h)\ge A-\delta>0.
\]
The numerator is
\begin{align*}
 &(m-1)A+\tfrac m2L+\tfrac{m-1}{2}\log(\pi h)\\
 &\hspace{16mm}
 +m\log\Theta(\pi^2ma^2h)-\log\Theta(\pi^2a^2h).
\end{align*}
Its last positive correction is at most
$3me^{-36m}<1$, by $a^2\ge4$, $h\ge1$, and
\eqref{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:theta-tail}; its last negative correction can be
discarded. Using $\log\pi<2$ gives the upper bound
$(m-1)A+B_\star$, where
\[
 B_\star=\tfrac m2L+\tfrac m2\log h+m.
\]
Consequently
\begin{equation}
 \cI_{m,a}-(m-1)
 \le\frac{B_\star+(m-1)\delta}{A-\delta}.
 \label{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:upper-preconstant}
\end{equation}

We include the elementary constant budget to retain full uniformity
in $a$. Since $A>1/2$, $e+u>2$, and
$\delta<3/512<1/8$, one has $A-\delta\ge A/2$. Therefore
\begin{align*}
 \frac{A(B_\star+(m-1)\delta)}{A-\delta}
 &\le B_\star+m\delta+\frac{2\delta}{A}(B_\star+m\delta)\\
 &\le B_\star+
 m\bigl[\delta+\delta u+2\delta\log h+4\delta(1+\delta)\bigr]\\
 &\le B_\star+m.
\end{align*}
For the last line,
$\delta\le3/512$, $\delta u\le3/256$, and
$\delta\log h\le\delta h\le3/256$ follow from
\eqref{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:delta} and $\log(e+u)\le e+u$.
Also $4\delta(1+\delta)<1/32$. The bracket is thus less than
$37/512<1$. Inserting this bound into
\eqref{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:upper-preconstant} proves
\[
 \cI_{m,a}\le
 m-1+\frac{(m/2)L+(m/2)\log h+2m}{A},
\]
which is exactly \eqref{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:upper}.
The proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:uf:thm:uniform} is complete.

\subsection{Consequences and scope of the cost comparison}

\begin{corollary}[The arity--torsion regimes]
\label{gsr:en:68:uf:cor:regimes}
Let $m\to\infty$ through integers and let $a=a(m)\ge2$ be integral.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item If $\log a/\log m\to c\in(0,\infty)$, then
$\cI_{m,a}/m\to1+1/(2c)$.
\item If $\log a/\log m\to\infty$, then $\cI_{m,a}/m\to1$.
\item If $\log a=o(\log m)$, then
$\cI_{m,a}\sim m\log m/(2\log a)$.
\item For each fixed $a\ge2$,
\[
 \cI_{m,a}=\frac{m\log m}{2\log a}
       +O_a\bigl(m(1+\log\log\log m)\bigr).
\]
For each fixed $m\ge2$, one has
$\lim_{a\to\infty}\cI_{m,a}=m-1$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Set $u=\log m/\log a$ in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:uf:thm:uniform}.
When $u$ stays bounded, the logarithmic correction
$\log\log(e+u)$ stays bounded and $\log a\to\infty$.
This proves (i) and (ii). If $u\to\infty$, then $m-1=o(mu)$,
and
$[1+\log\log(e+u)]/\log m\to0$, because
$u\le\log m/\log2$. This proves (iii). At fixed $a$, the upper
correction grows as $\log\log\log m$; the lower error is $O_a(m)$,
and the term $m-1$ is absorbed in the stated error. At fixed $m$,
the upper correction tends to zero as $a\to\infty$, whereas the
baseline remains $m-1$.
\end{proof}

In particular, uniformly whenever $\log a\ge c\log m$ for a fixed
$c>0$, the theorem gives the more precise expression
\[
 \cI_{m,a}
 =m-1+\frac{m\log m}{2\log a}
       +O_c\!\left(\frac m{\log a}\right).
\]
The limiting coefficient is thus $2$ when $a$ is approximately
$\sqrt m$, $3/2$ when $a$ is approximately $m$, and $5/4$ when
$a$ is approximately $m^2$. These coefficients concern the principal
filter cost; they are not asserted to be the exponents of a completed
Szemer\'edi bound.

Independent heterogeneous filters do not escape this particular
lower bound. If layer $\ell$ has $P_\ell,Q_\ell$ and positive gain,
the total principal cost is
\[
 \frac{\sum_\ell-\log P_\ell}
      {\sum_\ell\log(P_\ell/Q_\ell)}
 =
 \sum_\ell
 \frac{\log(P_\ell/Q_\ell)}
      {\sum_j\log(P_j/Q_j)}\,\costA_{m,a}(K_\ell)
 \ge\cI_{m,a}.
\]
Zero-gain layers add nonnegative cost and no gain. This is a
statement about the specified principal certificate. It gives no
lower bound on the survival of a particular input set, which can
benefit from extra Fourier relations or structure.

Finally, the finite approximants in
\eqref{gsr:en:68:uf:eq:fejer-approximation} may require a large degree. Their
cost estimate alone does not control the torsion term, collision
error, or ambient threshold in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:rf:thm:selection}.
The degree-twelve theorem supplies a separate finite certificate
where all of those terms are retained. The sharpness of the
triple-logarithmic upper correction at fixed $a$ remains open in
this manuscript.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Notation and the main restriction theorem\srctag{62}}]{Notation and the main restriction theorem}\label{gsr:en:62:sec:d2}
\srcnote{62}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:en:62:sec:main}

Let $k\ge2$ and put $m=2k$. Write
\[
 \sigma=(\underbrace{1,\ldots,1}_{k},
          \underbrace{-1,\ldots,-1}_{k}).
\]
For a subset $B\subseteq\Z/N\Z$, define
\[
 \Rcal_m(B)=\{(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in B^m:\sigma\cdot x=0\},
 \qquad T_m(B)=|\Rcal_m(B)|.
\]
Tuples are ordered and repetitions are included. For
$\phi:B\to\Z/M\Z$, let
\[
 S_m(B,\phi)=|\{x\in\Rcal_m(B):\sigma\cdot\phi(x)=0\}|.
\]
The nonzero element $\delta(x)=\sigma\cdot\phi(x)$ is the \emph{defect}
of an unrespected tuple. We call $\phi$ a $(1-\eta)$-homomorphism of order
$k$ on $B$ when
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:homdef}
 S_m(B,\phi)\ge(1-\eta)T_m(B).
\end{equation}
The elementary bound
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:countcap}
 T_m(B)\le |B|^{m-1}
\end{equation}
follows by specifying the first $m-1$ coordinates and solving for the last.

For $L\ge2$, define two modulus-independent envelopes:
\begin{align}
 H_{\rm el}(L)&=1+3\log_2 L,\label{gsr:en:62:eq:Hel}\\
 H_{\rm RS}(L)&=4+2\log\bigl(3\log(2L)\bigr).
 \label{gsr:en:62:eq:HRS}
\end{align}
All unmarked logarithms are natural. The elementary envelope requires no
external number-theoretic estimate. The second uses \cite[Theorem 15]{rosserschoenfeld}.
Either can be used below, as can their minimum.

Set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:Km}
 C_m=\binom m2,\qquad
 K_m=1+\left(\frac54\right)^{m-1}2^{-(m-2)}
          \left(1+\frac2{m-3}\right)+2^{4-m}.
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:K16}
 K_{16}<1.003<2,\qquad C_{16}=120.
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Polynomial-loss restriction for arbitrary cyclic moduli]
\label{gsr:en:62:thm:main}
Let $N,M\ge2$, $m=2k\ge4$, and $0<\alpha,\beta,\eta\le1$.
Suppose $B\subseteq\Z/N\Z$ has cardinality $\beta N$ and
$\phi:B\to\Z/M\Z$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:inputS}
 S_m(B,\phi)\ge\alpha|B|^{m-1}.
\end{equation}
Choose an integer $L\ge2$ and an envelope $H$ from
\eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:Hel}--\eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:HRS} such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:Lcondition}
 L\ge\frac{2(m+1)H(L)}{\alpha\eta}.
\end{equation}
If
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:Ncondition}
 N\ge
 \frac{2(m+1)(K_m+C_m)L^{m-1}}
      {\alpha\eta\beta^{m-1}},
\end{equation}
then there is $B'\subseteq B$ for which
\begin{align}
 S_m(B',\phi)&\ge
       \frac{\alpha}{(m+1)L^{m-1}}|B|^{m-1},\label{gsr:en:62:eq:retention}\\
 S_m(B',\phi)&\ge(1-\eta)T_m(B').\label{gsr:en:62:eq:quality}
\end{align}
There is no relation required between $N$ and $M$.
\end{theorem}

The fact that \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:retention} counts \emph{respected} tuples is slightly
stronger than a lower bound only for all additive tuples. The theorem also
implies a direct set-size estimate:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:size}
 |B'|\ge
 \frac{\alpha^{1/(m-1)}}{(m+1)^{1/(m-1)}L}|B|.
\end{equation}
Indeed, combine \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:retention} with \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:countcap} for $B'$.

\Needspace{14\baselineskip}
\begin{corollary}[Near-prime-scale retention]
\label{gsr:en:62:cor:loglog}
For each fixed even $m\ge4$, there are positive constants $c_m,D_m$ with the
following property. Put
\[
 x=\alpha\eta,\qquad \ell(x)=\log\log(\e^{\e}/x).
\]
Under \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:inputS}, it is sufficient that
\[
 N\ge D_m\,\beta^{-(m-1)}x^{-m}\ell(x)^{m-1}
\]
to obtain \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:quality} and
\[
 S_m(B',\phi)\ge
 c_m\frac{\alpha^m\eta^{m-1}}{\ell(x)^{m-1}}|B|^{m-1}.
\]
Using only $H_{\rm el}$ gives the analogous statement with
$\ell(x)$ replaced by $1+\log(1/x)$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For fixed $m$, an integer $L$ of order
$x^{-1}\ell(x)$ satisfies \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:Lcondition} with $H_{\rm RS}$.
To see this as $x\downarrow0$, take
$L$ to be an integer between $D x^{-1}\ell(x)$ and twice that quantity.
Then $H_{\rm RS}(L)=(2+o(1))\ell(x)$, so any sufficiently large constant
$D$ depending on $m$ works. Increasing $D$ handles the remaining compact
range of $x\in(0,1]$. Substitute in \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:Ncondition} and
\eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:retention}. The elementary version follows in the same way from
$H_{\rm el}(L)=O(1+\log(1/x))$.
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:62:thm:main} is proved in Section~\ref{gsr:en:62:sec:proof}. The next three
sections establish its analytic and arithmetic ingredients.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The unit-dilation detector\srctag{62}}]{The unit-dilation detector}\label{gsr:en:62:sec:d3}
\srcnote{62}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:en:62:sec:detector}

\subsection{A normalized Fej\'er filter}

On $\T=\mathbb R/\Z$, let
\begin{align}
 F_L(t)&=\frac1{L^2}\left|\sum_{j=0}^{L-1}\eexp{jt}\right|^2
       =\sum_{|c|<L}w_L(c)\eexp{ct},\label{gsr:en:62:eq:FL}\\
 w_L(c)&=\frac{L-|c|}{L^2},\qquad
 b_L(c)=Lw_L(c)=1-\frac{|c|}{L}\quad(|c|<L).
\end{align}
Outside this range, both weights are zero. Thus
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:weightfacts}
 0\le F_L\le1,\quad w_L(c)\ge0,\quad
 \sum_c w_L(c)=1.
\end{equation}
The last equality can also be viewed probabilistically: $w_L$ is the law of
$U-V$ for independent uniform $U,V\in\{0,\ldots,L-1\}$.

Define the detector kernel and its value at zero by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:Pkernel}
 P_{m,L}(t)=\sum_{|c|<L}b_L(c)^m\eexp{ct},\qquad
 A_{m,L}=P_{m,L}(0).
\end{equation}
Although individual cosine terms may be negative, the entire kernel is not.

\begin{lemma}[Positivity and central mass]\label{gsr:en:62:lem:positive}
For every positive integer $m$,
$P_{m,L}(t)\ge0$. For $m\ge1$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:A-lower}
 A_{m,L}=1+2\sum_{c=1}^{L-1}(1-c/L)^m
 \ge \frac{2L}{m+1}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The Fourier coefficients of $LF_L$ are $b_L(c)$. Therefore
$P_{m,L}$ is the $m$-fold convolution of the nonnegative function $LF_L$
with itself, where convolution uses probability Haar measure on $\T$.
This proves positivity.

For the second assertion, the function
$f(t)=(1-t/L)^m$ on $[0,L]$ is convex. The trapezoidal rule for a convex
function gives
\[
 \frac12f(0)+\sum_{j=1}^{L-1}f(j)+\frac12f(L)
 \ge\int_0^L f(t)\,dt=\frac{L}{m+1}.
\]
Use $f(0)=1$ and $f(L)=0$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The response of a nonzero defect}

Write $\Urm_q=(\Z/q\Z)^\times$ and let $\varphi(q)=|\Urm_q|$ be Euler's
totient function. Define the primitive response
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:primitive}
 B_{m,L}(q)=\frac1{\varphi(q)}\sum_{a\in\Urm_q}P_{m,L}(a/q)
 \quad(q\ge2).
\end{equation}
For convenience set $B_{m,L}(1)=A_{m,L}$.
The Ramanujan sum is
\[
 c_q(n)=\sum_{a\in\Urm_q}\eexp{an/q}.
\]
The standard orthogonality calculation gives the exact rational formula
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:Ramanujan-profile}
 B_{m,L}(q)=1+2\sum_{c=1}^{L-1}(1-c/L)^m\frac{c_q(c)}{\varphi(q)}.
\end{equation}
In particular, exact computation of this response does not require numerical
trigonometry.

\begin{lemma}[Ramanujan identity]\label{gsr:en:62:lem:Ramanujan}
If $g=\gcd(q,n)$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:Ramanujan}
 \frac{c_q(n)}{\varphi(q)}
   =\frac{\mu(q/g)}{\varphi(q/g)}.
\end{equation}
Also $\varphi(v)\ge\sqrt{v/2}$ for every positive integer $v$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Insert $\ind_{\gcd(a,q)=1}=\sum_{d\mid\gcd(a,q)}\mu(d)$ in the defining
sum and apply geometric-sum orthogonality. This yields
$c_q(n)=\sum_{d\mid\gcd(q,n)}d\mu(q/d)$. Evaluating this formula on prime
powers, and using multiplicativity, gives \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:Ramanujan}.

For the totient bound, write
\[
 \frac{\varphi(v)^2}{v}
 =\prod_{p^a\parallel v}p^{a-2}(p-1)^2.
\]
Each factor for an odd prime is at least one. The factor at $2$, if present,
is at least $1/2$. The product is therefore at least $1/2$.
\end{proof}

The relation between this kernel and the restriction procedure is exact.
Choose $r$ uniformly in $\Z/N\Z$ and $s$ uniformly in $\Urm_M$.
For each $x\in B$, put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:px}
 p_{r,s}(x)=F_L\bigl(rx/N+s\phi(x)/M\bigr).
\end{equation}
Residue representatives do not affect this expression.
For an additive tuple, the Fourier coefficient vectors
$c=\lambda\sigma$ contribute
$L^{-m}A_{m,L}$ if the tuple is respected, and
$L^{-m}B_{m,L}(q)$ if its defect has order $q$.
To justify the latter assertion, write the defect as $(M/q)a$ with
$\gcd(a,q)=1$. The map $\Urm_M\to\Urm_q$ is surjective with equal-size fibres,
so $s\delta/M$ is uniform on the primitive $q$th roots.
Surjectivity follows prime-power by prime-power from the Chinese remainder
theorem.

The other coefficient vectors are the arithmetic error. They cannot simply
be discarded: averaging over units may give negative Ramanujan sums.
Section~\ref{gsr:en:62:sec:weighted} bounds their total absolute contribution.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Uniform primitive-response bounds\srctag{62}}]{Uniform primitive-response bounds}\label{gsr:en:62:sec:d4}
\srcnote{62}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:en:62:sec:primitive-bounds}

\begin{lemma}[A sampling inequality]\label{gsr:en:62:lem:sampling}
For every $q\ge2$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:sampling}
 0\le B_{m,L}(q)\le\frac{q}{\varphi(q)}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Positivity follows from Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:62:lem:positive}. Orthogonality on the
$q$-point grid gives
\[
 \sum_{a=0}^{q-1}P_{m,L}(a/q)
 =q\left(1+2\sum_{1\le j<L/q}(1-jq/L)^m\right).
\]
Since the summand is decreasing in $j$,
\[
 q\sum_{1\le j<L/q}(1-jq/L)^m
 \le\int_0^L(1-t/L)^m\,dt=\frac{L}{m+1}.
\]
Subtracting $P_{m,L}(0)=A_{m,L}$ and using \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:A-lower} shows
\[
 0\le\sum_{a=1}^{q-1}P_{m,L}(a/q)\le q.
\]
The primitive points form a subset of these nonzero points, and the terms
are nonnegative. Division by $\varphi(q)$ proves the assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Modulus-independent envelopes]\label{gsr:en:62:prop:envelopes}
For all $q\ge2$, $L\ge2$, and positive integers $m$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:envelopes}
 B_{m,L}(q)\le H_{\rm el}(L).
\end{equation}
Using the explicit totient estimate of Rosser--Schoenfeld also gives
$B_{m,L}(q)\le H_{\rm RS}(L)$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
First suppose $q\ge L^3$. For $1\le c<L$, Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:62:lem:Ramanujan} gives
\[
 \left|\frac{c_q(c)}{\varphi(q)}\right|
 \le\sqrt{\frac{2\gcd(q,c)}q}\le\sqrt{\frac{2L}q}.
\]
Consequently, by \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:Ramanujan-profile},
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:largeq}
 B_{m,L}(q)\le1+2(L-1)\sqrt{2L/q}<1+2\sqrt2<4.
\end{equation}

For $q<L^3$, let $p_1<\cdots<p_t$ be its distinct prime divisors.
Since $p_i\ge i+1$,
\[
 \frac q{\varphi(q)}
 =\prod_{i=1}^t\frac{p_i}{p_i-1}
 \le\prod_{i=1}^t\frac{i+1}{i}=t+1
 \le1+\log_2q<1+3\log_2L.
\]
Combine this with Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:62:lem:sampling}. Because $L\ge2$, the last
expression is at least four, which also covers \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:largeq}.

For the sharper envelope, use the classical inequality
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:RS}
 \frac q{\varphi(q)}
 <\e^\gamma\log\log q+
   \frac{2.50637}{\log\log q}\qquad(q\ge3),
\end{equation}
from \cite[Theorem 15]{rosserschoenfeld}.
If $q\ge30$, then $\log\log q>1$, $\e^\gamma<2$, and the right-hand side
is less than $2\log\log q+3$.
For $q<L^3$ this is at most
$2\log(3\log L)+3<H_{\rm RS}(L)$.
For $2\le q<30$, direct use of the prime divisors gives
$q/\varphi(q)\le3<4$.
Finally, \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:largeq} is again below four.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The role of the external input]
Only the improvement from a single logarithm to a double logarithm uses
\eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:RS}. The main theorem with $H_{\rm el}$, the explicit powers in
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:62:cor:polynomial8}, the exact gcd formula, and the detector
obstructions are proved here without it.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Weighted short relations over composite cyclic groups\srctag{62}}]{Weighted short relations over composite cyclic groups}\label{gsr:en:62:sec:d5}
\srcnote{62}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:en:62:sec:weighted}

A union bound over every coefficient vector in $[-L,L]^m$ wastes the
normalization $\sum_c w_L(c)=1$. We retain that normalization throughout.
The resulting quantity has an exact arithmetic interpretation.

Let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_m$ be independent with distribution $w_L$, and put
\[
 p_{L,d}(a)=\Prob(Z_1\equiv a\pmod d),\qquad
 R_{m,L}=\Prob(Z_1=\cdots=Z_m)=\sum_cw_L(c)^m.
\]
Notice $R_{m,L}=L^{-m}A_{m,L}$; this is a collision probability, not a new
filter parameter. For $N\ge1$, define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:kappaN}
 \kappa_{N,m,L}
 =\E\left[\gcd(N,Z_1-Z_m,\ldots,Z_{m-1}-Z_m)
       \ind_{\{\exists i<m:\,Z_i\ne Z_m\}}\right].
\end{equation}
The exclusion of constant coefficient vectors is essential.

\begin{theorem}[Exact weighted degeneracy constant]\label{gsr:en:62:thm:kappa}
Let $m\ge4$ and $L\ge2$. Then
\begin{align}
 \kappa_{N,m,L}
 &=\sum_{\substack{d\mid N\\1\le d\le2L-2}}\varphi(d)
       \left(\sum_{a\bmod d}p_{L,d}(a)^m-R_{m,L}\right),
       \label{gsr:en:62:eq:kappa-formula}\\
 \kappa^*_{m,L}:=\sup_{N\ge1}\kappa_{N,m,L}
 &=\sum_{d=1}^{2L-2}\varphi(d)
       \left(\sum_{a\bmod d}p_{L,d}(a)^m-R_{m,L}\right).
       \label{gsr:en:62:eq:kappastar}
\end{align}
The supremum is attained by every multiple of
$\lcm(1,2,\ldots,2L-2)$. Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:Kbound}
 0\le\kappa_{N,m,L}\le\kappa^*_{m,L}\le K_m,
\end{equation}
where $K_m$ is given in \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:Km}, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:kappalimit}
 \lim_{L\to\infty}\kappa^*_{m,L}
 =\sum_{d=1}^{\infty}\frac{\varphi(d)}{d^{m-1}}
 =\frac{\zeta(m-2)}{\zeta(m-1)}.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For a nonconstant tuple, the gcd of its integer differences is a positive
integer at most $2L-2$. Apply
$g=\sum_{d\mid g}\varphi(d)$ to the gcd in \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:kappaN}.
The event that all differences are divisible by $d$ is the event that all
$Z_i$ have the same residue modulo $d$, with probability
$\sum_a p_{L,d}(a)^m$. Subtract the probability $R_{m,L}$ of an actually
constant tuple. This proves \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:kappa-formula}.
All bracketed terms are nonnegative. Dropping $d\mid N$ gives
\eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:kappastar}, and making $N$ a multiple of every $d\le2L-2$
achieves equality.

We next bound the residue probabilities. Write $L=ud+r$ with $0\le r<d$.
The residue counts of a uniform variable in $\{0,\ldots,L-1\}$ are $u$ or
$u+1$. Since $Z_1$ is a difference of two such variables, Cauchy--Schwarz
shows that its largest residue probability is attained at zero. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:resmax}
 \max_a p_{L,d}(a)=p_{L,d}(0)
 =\frac1d+\frac{r(d-r)}{dL^2}
 \le\frac1d+\frac d{4L^2}.
\end{equation}
For $d\le L$ this is at most $5/(4d)$.
For $d>L$, the original uniform variable has $L$ distinct residues, and
$p_{L,d}(0)=1/L$.

The term $d=1$ in \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:kappastar} is at most one.
Use $\sum_a p_a^m\le(\max_a p_a)^{m-1}$ for the other terms, and discard
the nonnegative subtraction $R_{m,L}$ to get
\begin{align*}
 \kappa^*_{m,L}
 &\le1+\left(\frac54\right)^{m-1}
       \sum_{d=2}^{L}\frac{\varphi(d)}{d^{m-1}}
       +L^{-(m-1)}\sum_{d=L+1}^{2L-2}\varphi(d)\\
 &\le1+\left(\frac54\right)^{m-1}
       \sum_{d=2}^{\infty}d^{-(m-2)}+2L^{3-m}.
\end{align*}
The integral estimate
\[
 \sum_{d=2}^{\infty}d^{-(m-2)}
 \le2^{-(m-2)}+\int_2^\infty t^{-(m-2)}\,dt
 =2^{-(m-2)}\left(1+\frac2{m-3}\right)
\]
and $L\ge2$ prove \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:Kbound}.

For the limit, fix $d$. Formula \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:resmax}, or the underlying residue
counts, shows $p_{L,d}(a)\to1/d$. Also $R_{m,L}=O_m(L^{1-m})\to0$.
For $d\le L$, the summands are bounded by a constant depending on $m$
times $d^{-(m-2)}$, a summable sequence. The contribution from $d>L$ is
at most $2L^{3-m}\to0$. Truncation at a fixed $d$, followed by the
summable tail bound, proves the first equality of \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:kappalimit}.
The last equality follows by multiplying the absolutely convergent Euler
products, or from $\varphi(n)=n\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)/d$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Why the gcd is the correct finite-ring count}

\begin{lemma}[Two linear equations]\label{gsr:en:62:lem:linearcount}
For $c\in\Z^m$ not an integer multiple of $\sigma$, the number of
$x\in(\Z/N\Z)^m$ satisfying
$\sigma\cdot x=c\cdot x=0$ equals
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:linearcount}
 N^{m-2}\gcd(N,d_1,\ldots,d_{m-1}),\qquad
 d_i=c_i-c_m\sigma_i/\sigma_m.
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:weighted-equations}
 \sum_{c\notin\Z\sigma}\left(\prod_{j=1}^mw_L(c_j)\right)
 \#\{x:\sigma\cdot x=c\cdot x=0\}
 =N^{m-2}\kappa_{N,m,L}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Because $\sigma_m=\pm1$, solve the first equation for $x_m$.
The second becomes $\sum_{i<m}d_i x_i=0$.
The image of this homomorphism from $(\Z/N\Z)^{m-1}$ to $\Z/N\Z$ has
size $N/g$, where $g=\gcd(N,d_1,\ldots,d_{m-1})$.
Its kernel therefore has size $N^{m-1}/(N/g)=gN^{m-2}$.
This uses no field structure.

Multiply each coefficient $c_i$ by $\sigma_i$. The distribution is unchanged
because $w_L$ is symmetric. The differences in the gcd become differences
from the last transformed coefficient, up to sign, and
$c\in\Z\sigma$ becomes the event that all transformed coefficients are
equal. Averaging \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:linearcount} gives
\eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:weighted-equations}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Exact small lengths and a false limiting-constant shortcut}

\begin{proposition}\label{gsr:en:62:prop:smallL}
For every integer $m\ge4$,
\begin{align}
 \kappa^*_{m,2}&=1-4^{1-m},\label{gsr:en:62:eq:kappa2}\\
 \kappa^*_{m,3}&=
 1+\frac{5^m+4^m+2\cdot3^m-6\cdot2^m-12}{9^m}.
 \label{gsr:en:62:eq:kappa3}
\end{align}
In particular, at $m=16$ the limit in \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:kappalimit} is
\emph{not} a valid bound for every finite $L$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For $L=2$, the weights at $-1,0,1$ are $1/4,1/2,1/4$.
A nonconstant tuple has integer gcd two exactly when all its entries are
in $\{-1,1\}$ and both signs occur. All other nonconstant tuples have gcd
one. This gives \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:kappa2}.

For $L=3$, the integer weight numerators are $(1,2,3,2,1)$, with denominator
nine. The residue-power numerators for $d=1,2,3,4$ are respectively
\[
 9^m,\quad5^m+4^m,\quad3\cdot3^m,\quad3^m+3\cdot2^m.
\]
The constant-tuple numerator is $3^m+2\cdot2^m+2$.
Insert these into \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:kappastar} with totient weights $1,1,2,2$.

Finally,
\[
 \frac{\zeta(14)}{\zeta(15)}
 =1+\sum_{d=2}^{\infty}\frac{\varphi(d)}{d^{15}}
 \le1+2^{-14}\left(1+\frac2{13}\right)
 <\kappa^*_{16,3}.
\]
The last inequality follows directly from the integer expression
\eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:kappa3}; it is also checked as a rational inequality by the
accompanying verifier.
\end{proof}

This distinction matters when inserting constants into a formal argument.
The exact asymptotic coefficient is not automatically a uniform finite-size
coefficient. In decimal form,
$\kappa^*_{16,3}\approx1.0000847096$, whereas
$\zeta(14)/\zeta(15)\approx1.0000306590$.
The safe rational envelope \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:Km} gives
$K_{16}\approx1.0022457446$.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The restriction proof, including repeated vertices\srctag{62}}]{The restriction proof, including repeated vertices}\label{gsr:en:62:sec:d6}
\srcnote{62}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:en:62:sec:proof}

For a family $\mathcal Q\subseteq\Rcal_m(B)$, define its weighted count at fixed
$r,s$ by
\[
 W_{\mathcal Q}(r,s)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal Q}\prod_{j=1}^mp_{r,s}(x_j).
\]
The product here has one factor per \emph{position}, even when coordinates
repeat. This convention is useful for Fourier expansion, but differs from
actual subset selection. We keep the two operations separate.

\begin{lemma}[Weighted main term and error]\label{gsr:en:62:lem:weighted-main}
Let $G$ be the respected tuple family in $B$, and let $Y_q$ count the
unrespected tuples whose defect has order $q$. Then
\begin{align}
 \left|\E W_G-L^{-m}A_{m,L}S_m(B,\phi)\right|
 &\le\kappa_{N,m,L}N^{m-2},\label{gsr:en:62:eq:weighted-good}\\
 \left|\E W_{\Rcal_m(B)\setminus G}
       -L^{-m}\sum_{q\mid M,\ q>1}B_{m,L}(q)Y_q\right|
 &\le\kappa_{N,m,L}N^{m-2}.\label{gsr:en:62:eq:weighted-bad}
\end{align}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Expand the product using \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:FL} and average over $r$.
A coefficient vector $c$ survives this average exactly when $c\cdot x=0$
in $\Z/N\Z$. Vectors $c=\lambda\sigma$ yield the main terms calculated
in Section~\ref{gsr:en:62:sec:detector}.

For every other $c$, the remaining average over $s$ is a complex number of
absolute value at most one. Thus its absolute contribution, summed over any
subfamily of additive tuples, is bounded by
\[
 \sum_{c\notin\Z\sigma}\left(\prod_j w_L(c_j)\right)
 \#\{x\in(\Z/N\Z)^m:\sigma\cdot x=c\cdot x=0\}.
\]
Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:62:lem:linearcount}. The argument is valid separately for the
good and the bad subfamilies. In particular, no positivity of the individual
Ramanujan coefficients has been assumed.
\end{proof}

Now, conditional on $r,s$, include each \emph{distinct point} $x\in B$ in
$B'$ independently with probability $p_{r,s}(x)$.
Let $G'$ and $Y'$ be the actual respected and unrespected tuple counts in
$B'$. A repeated point is included once, not independently once per position.

\begin{lemma}[Rounding correction]\label{gsr:en:62:lem:rounding}
The above procedure satisfies
\begin{align}
 \E G'&\ge L^{-m}A_{m,L}S_m(B,\phi)
                   -\kappa_{N,m,L}N^{m-2},\label{gsr:en:62:eq:EG}\\
 \E Y'&\le L^{-m}\sum_{q\mid M,\ q>1}B_{m,L}(q)Y_q
                   +(\kappa_{N,m,L}+C_m)N^{m-2}.
                   \label{gsr:en:62:eq:EY}
\end{align}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For a tuple with distinct support $D$, its conditional survival probability
is $\prod_{x\in D}p_{r,s}(x)$. Because $0\le p_{r,s}(x)\le1$, this is at
least the position-by-position product. This proves the favourable inequality
for the good family.

For a tuple with no repetitions the two products agree. Their difference is
at most one otherwise. For any fixed pair of distinct positions $i,j$, the
number of additive tuples satisfying $x_i=x_j$ is $N^{m-2}$: identify the two
variables and solve the additive relation for one of the other variables,
whose coefficient is still $1$ or $-1$. Such another variable exists because
$m\ge4$. A union bound gives at most $C_mN^{m-2}$ repeated tuples.
Combine this with Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:62:lem:weighted-main}.
\end{proof}

The following theorem is the full data-sensitive form of the method.

\begin{theorem}[Restriction retaining the defect-order profile]
\label{gsr:en:62:thm:profile-restriction}
Fix $L\ge2$ and $0<\eta\le1$. Write $S=S_m(B,\phi)$, and let $Y_q$ be as
above. Define
\begin{align}
 \Pi&=L^{-m}\left(\eta A_{m,L}S
           -(1-\eta)\sum_{q\mid M,\ q>1}B_{m,L}(q)Y_q\right),\\
 \Delta&=\bigl(\kappa_{N,m,L}+(1-\eta)C_m\bigr)N^{m-2}.
\end{align}
If $\Pi>\Delta$, there is $B'\subseteq B$ satisfying
\eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:quality} and
\[
 S_m(B',\phi)\ge\frac{\Pi-\Delta}{\eta}.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Use the linear objective
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:objective}
 Z=\eta G'-(1-\eta)Y'=\eta(G'+Y')-Y'.
\end{equation}
Lemmas~\ref{gsr:en:62:lem:weighted-main}--\ref{gsr:en:62:lem:rounding} imply
$\E Z\ge\Pi-\Delta>0$.
Some realization therefore has $Z\ge\Pi-\Delta$.
The inequality $Z\ge0$ is exactly $Y'\le\eta(G'+Y')$.
Also $Z\le\eta G'$, so $G'\ge(\Pi-\Delta)/\eta$.
Both assertions follow.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:62:thm:main}]
Put $b=|B|$ and $S=S_m(B,\phi)$. By \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:countcap},
$\sum_qY_q\le b^{m-1}$. Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:62:prop:envelopes} and
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:62:lem:rounding}, applied to \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:objective}, give
\[
 \E Z\ge
 L^{-m}\bigl(\eta\alpha A_{m,L}-(1-\eta)H(L)\bigr)b^{m-1}
 -(K_m+C_m)N^{m-2}.
\]
By \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:A-lower} and \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:Lcondition},
$\alpha\eta A_{m,L}\ge4H(L)$. Hence the first term is at least
$\tfrac34\eta\alpha A_{m,L}L^{-m}b^{m-1}$.
On the other hand, \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:Ncondition}, $b=\beta N$, and
\eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:A-lower} give
\[
 (K_m+C_m)N^{m-2}
 \le\frac{\alpha\eta}{2(m+1)L^{m-1}}b^{m-1}
 \le\frac14\eta\alpha A_{m,L}L^{-m}b^{m-1}.
\]
It follows that
\[
 \E Z\ge\frac12\eta\alpha A_{m,L}L^{-m}b^{m-1}>0.
\]
Choose a realization with at least this value. As in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:62:thm:profile-restriction}, it has the required quality and
\[
 G'\ge\frac12\alpha A_{m,L}L^{-m}b^{m-1}
 \ge\frac{\alpha}{(m+1)L^{m-1}}b^{m-1}.
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[No exceptional-set deletion]
The proof never asserts that every selected tuple is nondegenerate.
It controls the total signed error from all extra short relations and then
separately controls repeated vertices. This is why the filter length does
not appear in the constant $K_m$.
\end{remark}
