\section[{An explicit order-eight strengthening\srctag{62}}]{An explicit order-eight strengthening}\label{gsr:en:62:sec:d7}
\srcnote{62}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:en:62:sec:order8}

The main theorem can be used with exact integer parameter choices.
For $x=\alpha\eta$, let $e\ge1$ be the least integer satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:dyadicchoice}
 2^e\ge\frac{34(1+3e)}{x},\qquad L=2^e.
\end{equation}
Such an integer exists because exponential growth dominates linear growth.

\begin{corollary}[A rationally checkable parameter recipe]
\label{gsr:en:62:cor:dyadic8}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:62:thm:main} with $m=16$, the sufficient
condition
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:4148}
 N\ge\frac{4148 L^{15}}{\alpha\eta\beta^{15}}
\end{equation}
with $L$ from \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:dyadicchoice} gives a subset $B'$ satisfying
\[
 S_{16}(B',\phi)\ge\frac{\alpha}{17L^{15}}|B|^{15},
 \qquad S_{16}(B',\phi)\ge(1-\eta)T_{16}(B').
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
At dyadic $L$, $H_{\rm el}(L)=1+3e$, so \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:dyadicchoice} is exactly
\eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:Lcondition}. Use $K_{16}<2$, $C_{16}=120$, and
$2\cdot17\cdot122=4148$ in \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:Ncondition}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Fully explicit polynomial powers]\label{gsr:en:62:cor:polynomial8}
Let $0<\alpha,\beta,\eta\le1$, let $B\subseteq\Z/N\Z$ have size $\beta N$,
and let $\phi:B\to\Z/M\Z$ respect at least $\alpha|B|^{15}$ additive
sixteen-tuples. If
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:coarseN}
 N\ge2^{253}(\alpha\eta)^{-31}\beta^{-15},
\end{equation}
then some $B'\subseteq B$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:coarseR}
 S_{16}(B',\phi)\ge2^{-245}\alpha^{31}\eta^{30}|B|^{15},
 \qquad S_{16}(B',\phi)\ge(1-\eta)T_{16}(B').
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Again write $x=\alpha\eta$ and put $y=136/x$. Choose an integer
$j=\lceil2\log_2y\rceil$, so that
$y^2\le2^j<2y^2$ and $j\le2\log_2y+1$.
For $y\ge4$,
\[
 1+\tfrac32\log_2y\le y;
\]
this holds at $y=4$ and the difference of the right and left sides is
increasing thereafter. Thus
\[
 \frac{34(1+3j)}x
 \le y\bigl(1+\tfrac32\log_2y\bigr)\le y^2\le2^j.
\]
Minimality in \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:dyadicchoice} gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:coarseL}
 L\le2^j<2(136/x)^2<2^{16}x^{-2}.
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\[
 \frac{\alpha}{17L^{15}}
 >2^{-245}\alpha x^{30}
 =2^{-245}\alpha^{31}\eta^{30},
\]
because $17<2^5$. Also
\[
 \frac{4148L^{15}}{x\beta^{15}}
 <2^{253}x^{-31}\beta^{-15},
\]
because $4148<2^{13}$. Apply Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:62:cor:dyadic8}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Checked at the write.} With $M=N$, $|B|=\beta N$ and $0<\alpha,\eta\le1$: $(\alpha\eta/4)^{2^{19}}\le2^{-2^{20}}(\alpha\eta)^{2^{19}}\le2^{-245}\alpha^{31}\eta^{30}$, so this corollary implies \file{lemma_9_3} with $N_0=\lceil2^{253}(\alpha\eta)^{-31}\beta^{-15}\rceil$, on paper. Against source~68's exponent-$53$ theorem, whose retention of respected tuples is at least $(1-\eta)(\alpha\eta/4)^{53}b^{15}$, this corollary retains more exactly when $\alpha^{22}\eta^{23}(1-\eta)<2^{-139}$; its threshold grows like $\beta^{-15}$, source~68's like $\beta^{-1}$ (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:allmoduli}).
\end{writenote}

\subsection{Comparison with the repository interface}

The formal interface \texttt{lemma\_9\_3} asks for a retained additive count
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:old}
 (\alpha\eta/4)^{2^{19}}\,\beta^{15}N^{15}
\end{equation}
and a $(1-\eta)$-homomorphism of order eight \cite{repo62statement}.
Our new lower bound is larger throughout the nonvacuous parameter range.
Indeed, since $x=\alpha\eta\le1$ and $\alpha\ge x$,
\[
 2^{-245}\alpha^{31}\eta^{30}
 =2^{-245}\alpha x^{30}
 \ge2^{-245}x^{31}
 \ge(x/4)^{2^{19}}.
\]
The assertion for $\alpha>1$ is vacuous by \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:countcap}; similarly,
$\beta>1$ cannot describe a subset of $\Z/N\Z$.
Thus the written theorem implies the full old interface, with an explicit
size threshold, and considerably stronger retention.

The coarse powers $31,30$ are not the strongest output. They are useful
because they contain no implicit scale choice and use only the elementary
response envelope. The data-sensitive theorem and
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:62:cor:loglog} retain the near-prime exponents $16,15$, at the cost
of a double-logarithmic denominator.

\section[{Torsion obstructions and the scope of optimality\srctag{62}}]{Torsion obstructions and the scope of optimality}\label{gsr:en:62:sec:d8}
\srcnote{62}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:en:62:sec:obstructions}

\subsection{Why averaging all scalars is insufficient}

Suppose the target dilation $s$ were uniform on all of $\Z/M\Z$, rather
than its unit group. For a defect of order $q$, the proportional-vector
response would be
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:allscalar}
 B^{\rm all}_{m,L}(q)
 =\sum_{\substack{|c|<L\\q\mid c}}b_L(c)^m.
\end{equation}
For fixed $q$ and $m$, Riemann sums show
\[
 A_{m,L}=\frac{2L}{m+1}+O_m(1),\qquad
 B^{\rm all}_{m,L}(q)=\frac{2L}{q(m+1)}+O_m(1).
\]
Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:plateau}
 \lim_{L\to\infty}\frac{A_{m,L}}{B^{\rm all}_{m,L}(q)}=q.
\end{equation}
For an order-two defect the gain saturates at two. A filter-length increase
alone cannot provide the arbitrarily large gain needed as
$\alpha\eta\to0$. This is a failure of that averaging calculation, not a
counterexample to the restriction theorem.

In contrast, the unit response for each fixed $q>1$ tends to zero.
Here is a useful quantitative estimate that makes this precise.

\begin{lemma}[Suppression of a fixed torsion order]\label{gsr:en:62:lem:fixedq}
For $t\notin\Z$,
\[
 P_{m,L}(t)\le\frac{m}{L\sin^2(\pi t)}.
\]
Consequently, for fixed $m,q$,
$B_{m,L}(q)=O_{m,q}(L^{-1})$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $a_n=(1-n/L)^m$ for $0\le n\le L$, and $a_n=0$ afterwards.
Convexity gives $d_n=a_{n-1}-2a_n+a_{n+1}\ge0$ for $n\ge1$, with
$\sum_{n\ge1}d_n=a_0-a_1$.
Multiplication of the symmetric Fourier series by
$2-2\cos(2\pi t)$ gives
\[
 4\sin^2(\pi t)P_{m,L}(t)
 =2(a_0-a_1)-2\sum_{n\ge1}d_n\cos(2\pi nt)
 \le4(a_0-a_1)\le4m/L.
\]
Average over the finite set of primitive $q$th roots.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A necessary double logarithm for this detector}

The fixed-$q$ estimate cannot be made uniform with a constant independent
of $q$ and $L$.

\begin{theorem}[Primorial lower bound for the primitive response]
\label{gsr:en:62:thm:primitive-lower}
For every fixed positive integer $m$, there is an unbounded sequence of
integers $L$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:primitive-lower}
 \sup_{q\ge2}B_{m,L}(q)
 \ge\frac{\log\log(6L)}{6(m+1)}.
\end{equation}
Together with Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:62:prop:envelopes}, this identifies the
worst-case double-logarithmic order, up to constants, along that sequence.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $Q$ be the product of all primes at most an integer $y\ge5$, and put
$L=Q/6$. The residues $1$ and $Q-1$ are units. For $|c|<L=Q/6$,
$\cos(2\pi c/Q)\ge1/2$, so
\[
 P_{m,L}(1/Q)\ge\tfrac12 A_{m,L}.
\]
By positivity, the two primitive residues just mentioned give
\[
 B_{m,L}(Q)\ge\frac{A_{m,L}}{\varphi(Q)}
 \ge\frac{Q}{3(m+1)\varphi(Q)}.
\]
No prime number theorem is needed for the remaining estimate.
The Euler product
\[
 \frac Q{\varphi(Q)}=\prod_{p\le y}(1-p^{-1})^{-1}
\]
expands as the reciprocal sum over positive integers all of whose prime
factors are at most $y$. It includes every integer up to $y$, whence
$Q/\varphi(Q)\ge\sum_{n=1}^y1/n\ge\log y$.
Also $Q\le y!\le y^y$, and therefore
$\log\log Q\le\log y+\log\log y\le2\log y$.
Combining the last three inequalities yields
\eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:primitive-lower}. Infinitely many primes ensure that these $L$
are unbounded.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What has, and has not, been shown sharp]
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:62:thm:primitive-lower} rules out an absolute bound for
$B_{m,L}(q)$ for the specific kernels \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:Pkernel} and primitive-unit
averaging. It does not prove that every restriction theorem needs a double
logarithm. A different kernel, several coordinated tests, or a structural
restriction argument might avoid it. Nor does the theorem assert sharpness
of the powers of $\alpha$ and $\eta$ in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:62:thm:main}.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Extensions and constructive content\srctag{62}}]{Extensions and constructive content}\label{gsr:en:62:sec:d9}
\srcnote{62}{Section 9}
\label{gsr:en:62:sec:extensions}

\subsection{Different domain and target moduli}

The whole proof allows $\Z/N\Z$ as domain and $\Z/M\Z$ as target.
The character detecting a domain relation is chosen independently from the
unit dilation detecting a target defect. Domain degeneracy depends only on
$N$, while the defect response depends only on the order of the target
error. Thus neither coprimality of $N,M$ nor a bound on the target order is
needed. A trivial target has no bad tuples and can be handled by $B'=B$.

This separation is useful when an auxiliary cyclic group records a discrete
phase or label but the original configuration lives in another cyclic group.
It is not an assertion about general noncyclic targets: those do not possess
a single unit orbit with the same primitive-character property.

\subsection{Labelled domains and multifunctions}

Let $X$ be a finite set of labels, let $r:X\to\Z/N\Z$ be a base map, and
let $\phi:X\to\Z/M\Z$ be a target map. Suppose
$|r^{-1}(a)|\le R$ for every $a$, where $R\ge1$ is an integer, and
$|X|=\beta RN$.
Define additive and respected tuples using $r(x_j)$ in the domain equation
and $\phi(x_j)$ in the target equation. These are tuples of labels, not
unlabelled base points.

\begin{theorem}[Bounded-fibre labelled restriction]\label{gsr:en:62:thm:labels}
Let $m=2k\ge4$, $N,M\ge2$, and $0<\alpha,\beta,\eta\le1$.
Suppose at least $\alpha R|X|^{m-1}$ labelled additive tuples are respected.
Choose $L$ as in \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:Lcondition}. It is sufficient that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:62:eq:labelthreshold}
 N\ge\frac{2(m+1)(K_m+C_m/R)L^{m-1}}
              {\alpha\eta\beta^{m-1}}
\end{equation}
to obtain $X'\subseteq X$ that respects at least a proportion $1-\eta$ of its
labelled additive tuples and contains at least
\[
 \frac{\alpha}{(m+1)L^{m-1}}R|X|^{m-1}
\]
respected labelled tuples.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The additive tuple cap is now $R|X|^{m-1}$, since the last base coordinate
is determined but has at most $R$ labels. Apply the filter
\[
 F_L\bigl(u r(x)/N+s\phi(x)/M\bigr)
\]
and round independently for each label.

For a fixed base tuple satisfying two linear equations, there are at most
$R^m$ label lifts. Thus the error in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:62:lem:weighted-main} is at most
$\kappa_{N,m,L}R^mN^{m-2}$.
For a specified equality of two labels, the number of additive tuples is at
most $R^{m-1}N^{m-2}$: after identifying the labels, solve the base equation
for one remaining label, and use the fibre cap. Hence the rounding correction
is at most $C_mR^{m-1}N^{m-2}$.

The objective \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:objective} therefore has error at most
$(K_m+C_m/R)R^mN^{m-2}$. The main scale is
$R|X|^{m-1}=\beta^{m-1}R^mN^{m-1}$.
The proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:62:thm:main}, with these substitutions, gives
\eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:labelthreshold} and the claimed conclusion.
\end{proof}

The normalization by $R$ is necessary. Omitting it would incorrectly use
the graph bound \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:countcap} in a setting where several labels can
have the same base coordinate. This version fits the multifunction viewpoint
used later in Gowers' argument, but by itself supplies no statement about
higher-dimensional arrangements.

\subsection{Finite conditional-expectation construction}

The existence proof is constructive in a finite, though not necessarily
practical, sense. First enumerate the pairs
$(r,s)\in\Z/N\Z\times\Urm_M$ and choose one whose conditional expectation
of \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:objective} is at least the unconditional mean. Then decide
membership in $B'$ one point at a time. Conditional on all previous
decisions, the remaining objective has an expectation affine in the next
membership indicator, so at least one of the decisions zero or one does not
decrease that expectation.

All filter values belong to a cyclotomic number field and are real algebraic
numbers, so the required comparisons can in principle be made exactly.
The proof does not establish an attractive bit-complexity bound for this
implementation. In particular, it should not be confused with a fast
algorithm for finding long arithmetic progressions.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Notation and the exact relation interface\srctag{61}}]{Notation and the exact relation interface}\label{gsr:en:61:sec:d2}
\srcnote{61}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:notation}

For subsets of an abelian group, $A+B=\{a+b:a\in A,b\in B\}$ and $A-B$ is defined similarly. The set $mA$ is the $m$-fold sumset; repetitions are permitted, and $0A=\{0\}$. Unless otherwise specified, all sums over group elements use counting measure. For nonempty $A$, translating by a fixed element shows $|A-A|\geq|A|$, so every difference ratio below is at least one.

\begin{definition}[Freiman homomorphism of order $m$]
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:freiman-def}
A map $\phi:B\to H$ is a Freiman homomorphism of order $m$ if, for all $x_1,\ldots,x_m,y_1,\ldots,y_m\in B$,
\[
\sum_{i=1}^m x_i=\sum_{i=1}^m y_i
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\sum_{i=1}^m\phi(x_i)=\sum_{i=1}^m\phi(y_i).
\]
Only preservation is required; injectivity of $\phi$ is not required.
\end{definition}

Repetitions are essential. Removing repeated variables changes the statement and destroys the torsion obstructions below. If $B$ is nonempty, an order-$m$ homomorphism is an order-$s$ homomorphism for every $1\leq s\leq m$: append $m-s$ copies of a fixed element to both sides.

\begin{definition}[Relation energies]
For $s\geq1$ and $A\subseteq G$, set
\[
\Energy_s(A)=
\#\{(x_1,\ldots,x_s,y_1,\ldots,y_s)\in A^{2s}:
\textstyle\sum_i x_i=\sum_i y_i\}.
\]
For $\phi:B\to H$, set
\begin{align*}
\Energy_s^\phi(B)
=\#\{(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)\in B^{2s}:\ &\textstyle\sum_i x_i=\sum_i y_i,\\[-2pt]
&\textstyle\sum_i\phi(x_i)=\sum_i\phi(y_i)\}.
\end{align*}
Equivalently, $\Energy_s^\phi(B)=\Energy_s(\Gamma)$.
\end{definition}

The tuples are ordered and may be degenerate. Specifying the first $2s-1$ entries determines the last, if it belongs to the set. Hence
\begin{equation}
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:energy-cap}
\Energy_s^\phi(B)\leq\Energy_s(B)\leq n^{2s-1}.
\end{equation}
If $\phi$ is exact of order $s$, the first inequality is equality.

For functions $u,v:G\to\C$, use convolution
\[
(u*v)(z)=\sum_{x\in G}u(x)v(z-x).
\]
If $w$ is supported on $A$, define
\begin{equation}
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:weighted-energy-def}
\Energy_s(w)=\sum_{z\in G}|w^{*s}(z)|^2.
\end{equation}
This equals the corresponding sum over equal-sum tuples, weighted by
$\prod_i w(x_i)\overline{w(y_i)}$. For $w=\one_A$ it is $\Energy_s(A)$.
The graph weight $\widetilde w$ is defined by
$\widetilde w(x,\phi(x))=w(x)$ and zero elsewhere.

\begin{lemma}[Weighted exactness]
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:weighted-exactness}
If $\phi|_A$ is a Freiman homomorphism of order $m$, then
\[
\Energy_s(w)=\Energy_s(\widetilde w)
\qquad(1\leq s\leq m)
\]
for every complex weight $w$ supported on $A$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $A$ is empty both energies vanish. Otherwise expand both energies into ordered pairs of $s$-tuples. The graph sum is subject to the additional equality of image sums. Exactness and padding show that this additional condition holds for every base relation. The indexing sets and their weights therefore agree term by term.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Separating every nonzero defect with few characters\srctag{61}}]{Separating every nonzero defect with few characters}\label{gsr:en:61:sec:d3}
\srcnote{61}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:characters}

Write $\T=\R/\Z$, and let $\|t\|_{\T}$ be the distance to zero. A character is an additive homomorphism $\chi:H\to\T$. Its exponential form is $\exp(2\pi i\chi(x))$. The finite dual group is denoted $\widehat H$.

\begin{lemma}[A uniform root-grid estimate]
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:root-grid}
Let $h\ne0$ have order $q$ in a finite abelian group $H$. For a uniformly chosen $\chi\in\widehat H$,
\begin{equation}
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:half-character}
\Pr\bigl(\|\chi(h)\|_{\T}<1/5\bigr)
=\frac{2\ceil{q/5}-1}{q}\leq\frac12.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Evaluation at $h$ maps $\widehat H$ onto the cyclic group of $q$-th roots in $\T$. One way to check surjectivity is to write $H$ as a product of cyclic groups. The possible evaluations in each coordinate form a cyclic subgroup of order equal to the order of that coordinate of $h$; together they generate a subgroup of order $q$. Every fiber of a surjective homomorphism between finite groups has the same size. Thus the evaluation is uniform on $\{j/q:0\leq j<q\}$.

A residue has distance strictly less than $1/5$ precisely when its signed representative has absolute value strictly less than $q/5$. There are $2\ceil{q/5}-1$ such residues. For $q\geq10$,
\[
2\ceil{q/5}-1<2q/5+1\leq q/2.
\]
For $q=2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9$ the numerators are, respectively,
$1,1,1,1,3,3,3$, which also satisfy the required inequality.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{A misprint in the proof} (standing rule of 4~October 2026; checked at the write). The list ``$1,1,1,1,3,3,3$'' has seven numerators for the eight orders $q=2,\ldots,9$; the values of $2\lceil q/5\rceil-1$ are $1,1,1,1,3,3,3,3$, the last ($q=9$) missing. All eight satisfy $2\lceil q/5\rceil-1\le q/2$ (with equality at $q=2$ and $q=6$), so the lemma holds as stated.
\end{writenote}

The strict inequality at radius $1/5$ is deliberate. Replacing it by a closed ball would include three of the five roots when $q=5$, invalidating the one-half bound. No large-order approximation is being used.

\begin{lemma}[Greedy separation]
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:separation}
For $D\subseteq H\setminus\{0\}$ there are characters
$\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_r$ with
\[
r\leq\ceil{\log_2(|D|+1)}
\]
such that every $d\in D$ satisfies
$\|\chi_j(d)\|_{\T}\geq1/5$ for at least one $j$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $D$ is empty, take no characters. Otherwise, apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:61:ter:root-grid} and linearity of expectation to the current unseparated set. Some character leaves at most half that set inside the open radius-$1/5$ ball. Choose such a character and continue. After $r$ choices the remaining number is at most $|D|2^{-r}$. For $r=\ceil{\log_2(|D|+1)}$ this is strictly less than one, hence zero. The argument is a finite greedy construction; independence between the defects is unnecessary.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Universal higher-order avoidance coloring]
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:avoidance}
Let $H$ be a finite abelian group, $D\subseteq H\setminus\{0\}$, and $m\geq1$. There is a partition of $H$ into at most
\begin{equation}
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:avoidance-colors}
(5m)^{\ceil{\log_2(|D|+1)}}
\leq5m(|D|+1)^{\log_2(5m)}
\end{equation}
nonempty cells $S$ such that $(mS-mS)\cap D=\varnothing$.
Symmetry of $D$ is not needed.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Choose the characters in Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:61:ter:separation}, and represent every character value in $[0,1)$. Partition $[0,1)$ into the $5m$ half-open intervals
\[
I_a=[a/(5m),(a+1)/(5m)),\qquad 0\leq a<5m.
\]
Color $x\in H$ by the tuple of intervals containing its character values. There are at most $(5m)^r$ colors.

Suppose $x_1,\ldots,x_m,y_1,\ldots,y_m$ lie in one color cell. For every chosen character, all $2m$ representatives lie in an interval of length $1/(5m)$, so the difference of the two real sums has absolute value strictly less than $1/5$. Consequently
\[
\left\|\chi_j\left(\sum_i x_i-\sum_i y_i\right)\right\|_{\T}<1/5
\quad\text{for every }j.
\]
This difference cannot belong to $D$, by separation. The final inequality in \eqref{gsr:en:61:ter:avoidance-colors} follows from $\ceil t\leq t+1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Mass and one scalar functional]
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:avoidance-mass}
Let an avoidance partition have $R$ cells. For every nonnegative weight $\mu$ on $H$, some cell has mass at least $\sum_H\mu/R$. For every complex-valued function $z$ on $H$, some cell satisfies
\[
\left|\sum_{x\in S}z(x)\right|\geq
\frac1R\left|\sum_{x\in H}z(x)\right|.
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The first assertion is averaging, and the second is the triangle inequality over the partition.
\end{proof}

The favorable cell may depend on the weight or scalar functional. The corollary does not assert simultaneous preservation of an arbitrary list of unrelated correlations.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Small differences and a vertical-defect budget\srctag{61}}]{Small differences and a vertical-defect budget}\label{gsr:en:61:sec:d4}
\srcnote{61}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:sumsets}

We include the standard growth ingredients to make the exponents in the restriction theorem independently checkable. The minimal-growth argument is due to Petridis \cite{petridis}; it is used here as a known theorem with a reproduced proof, not as a new ingredient.

\begin{lemma}[Minimal-growth lemma]
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:petridis}
Let $A,B$ be finite nonempty subsets of an abelian group. Choose a nonempty $X\subseteq A$ minimizing $|X+B|/|X|$, and write $\kappa=|X+B|/|X|$. Then for every finite $C$,
\[
|X+B+C|\leq\kappa|X+C|.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The empty case is immediate. Otherwise order $C=\{c_1,\ldots,c_t\}$, and define
\[
X_i=\{x\in X:x+c_i\notin X+\{c_1,\ldots,c_{i-1}\}\}.
\]
The newly added parts $X_i+c_i$ are disjoint and cover $X+C$, so
$|X+C|=\sum_i|X_i|$.

Every point of $(X\setminus X_i)+B+c_i$ is already in
$X+B+\{c_1,\ldots,c_{i-1}\}$. Indeed, an equality
$x+c_i=x'+c_j$ with $j<i$ remains an equality after addition of the same $b\in B$. Thus the number of new points contributed by $X+B+c_i$ is at most
\[
|X+B|-|(X\setminus X_i)+B|.
\]
By minimality, $|(X\setminus X_i)+B|\geq\kappa|X\setminus X_i|$, with the empty case interpreted as zero. The number of new points is therefore at most $\kappa|X_i|$. Summing over $i$ proves the lemma.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Ruzsa triangle inequality]
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:triangle}
If $U,V,X$ are finite subsets of an abelian group and $X\ne\varnothing$, then
\[
|U-V|\,|X|\leq|U+X|\,|V+X|.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For each $d\in U-V$ choose one representation $d=u_d-v_d$. The map
\[
(d,x)\longmapsto(u_d+x,v_d+x)
\]
is injective into $(U+X)\times(V+X)$. The difference of the two coordinates recovers $d$, and then either coordinate recovers $x$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Pl\"unnecke--Ruzsa difference estimate]
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:plunnecke}
Let $A$ be finite nonempty and $|A-A|\leq K|A|$. Then for all nonnegative integers $r,s$,
\begin{equation}
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:PR}
|rA-sA|\leq K^{r+s}|A|.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:61:ter:petridis} with $B=-A$ and a minimizing nonempty $X\subseteq A$. Its growth ratio satisfies $\kappa\leq K$. Repeated application, with $C=(j-1)B$, gives
\[
|X+jB|\leq\kappa^j|X|\qquad(j\geq0).
\]
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:61:ter:triangle} now gives
\[
|rB-sB|\leq\frac{|X+rB|\,|X+sB|}{|X|}
\leq\kappa^{r+s}|X|
\leq K^{r+s}|A|.
\]
Negation identifies the cardinality on the left with $|rA-sA|$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Disjoint graph translates]
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:vertical}
Let $\Gamma$ be the graph of $\phi:B\to H$, where $B\subseteq G$ is nonempty. If $|\Gamma-\Gamma|\leq K|B|$, then
\begin{equation}
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:vertical-bound}
|\Def_m(\Gamma)|\leq K^{2m+1}.
\end{equation}
More precisely,
\[
|B|\,|\Def_m(\Gamma)|\leq|(m+1)\Gamma-m\Gamma|.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For different $h\in H$, the vertical translates $\Gamma+(0,h)$ are pairwise disjoint. If
$(x,\phi(x)+h)=(y,\phi(y)+h')$, the first coordinate gives $x=y$, and then the second gives $h=h'$. For $h\in\Def_m(\Gamma)$ each translate lies in $(m+1)\Gamma-m\Gamma$. Counting their disjoint union proves the precise statement; Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:61:ter:plunnecke} gives \eqref{gsr:en:61:ter:vertical-bound}.
\end{proof}

This packing step uses the fact that $\Gamma$ is a graph. Applying only
$|m\Gamma-m\Gamma|\leq K^{2m}|\Gamma|$ would leave an unwanted factor $|B|$ in the defect budget. The extra translate removes that dependence at the cost of one power of $K$.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Exact Freiman partitions and retention statements\srctag{61}}]{Exact Freiman partitions and retention statements}\label{gsr:en:61:sec:d5}
\srcnote{61}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:partition-proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:61:ter:main-partition}]
The defect set $\Def_m(\Gamma)$ contains zero and is symmetric. Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:61:ter:avoidance} in $H$ to
$D=\Def_m(\Gamma)\setminus\{0\}$, and pull its color classes back by $\phi$.
Discard empty inverse images. The resulting partition of $B$ uses at most
$(5m)^{\ceil{\log_2|\Def_m(\Gamma)|}}$ cells.

Suppose $x_1,\ldots,x_m,y_1,\ldots,y_m$ lie in a cell $B_j$ and have equal base sums. Their image defect
\[
h=\sum_i\phi(x_i)-\sum_i\phi(y_i)
\]
belongs to $\Def_m(\Gamma)$ by definition. All the image points lie in one avoidance cell, so $h\notin D$. Hence $h=0$, proving exactness. Finally Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:61:ter:vertical} and \eqref{gsr:en:61:ter:avoidance-colors} give $R\leq5mK^{a_m}$. Averaging the cardinalities gives the size assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Balanced bounded-coefficient systems]
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:coefficients}
In each cell supplied by Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:61:ter:main-partition}, $\phi$ preserves every integer-coefficient equation
\[
\sum_{i=1}^t c_i x_i=0,
\qquad \sum_i c_i=0,
\qquad \sum_{c_i>0}c_i\leq m.
\]
It preserves any finite system of such equations on the same cell.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
If all coefficients vanish, the assertion is immediate. Otherwise expand positive and negative coefficients as repetitions, obtaining an equal-sum relation of order at most $m$. Pad both sides equally to order $m$. Applying exactness gives the asserted image equation. The same cell is exact for every order-$m$ relation, so the assertion holds for a whole system.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Several maps with a joint hypothesis]
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:joint}
Let $\phi_i:B\to H_i$ for $1\leq i\leq t$, and let $\Phi=(\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_t)$. If the joint graph in $G\times\prod_iH_i$ has difference ratio at most $K$, the bound in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:61:ter:main-partition} supplies one partition on which every $\phi_i$ is exact of order $m$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply the theorem with codomain $\prod_iH_i$ and project the resulting image-sum equalities onto each coordinate.
\end{proof}

There is no extra factor depending on $t$ once the joint hypothesis is given. Separate small-difference or energy bounds for the individual graphs do not establish that hypothesis.

\begin{proposition}[Weighted energy retained by a partition]
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:energy-retention}
Let $B=\bigsqcup_{j=1}^R B_j$ be a partition with $R\geq1$, let $w:B\to\C$, and put $w_j=w\one_{B_j}$. Then, for every $s\geq1$,
\begin{equation}
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:partition-energy}
\sum_{j=1}^R\Energy_s(w_j)\geq R^{1-2s}\Energy_s(w),
\qquad
\max_j\Energy_s(w_j)\geq R^{-2s}\Energy_s(w).
\end{equation}
If the cells are exact restrictions of $\phi$ of order $m$, then for $s\leq m$ every energy on the left also equals its graph-weighted counterpart.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Define $\widehat w(\chi)=\sum_{x\in G}w(x)\exp(-2\pi i\chi(x))$. Orthogonality and the convolution identity give
\[
\Energy_s(w)=\frac1{|G|}\sum_{\chi\in\widehat G}|\widehat w(\chi)|^{2s}.
\]
Minkowski's inequality for this normalized $L^{2s}$ norm, followed by H\"older's inequality for the finite sum over cells, gives
\begin{align*}
\Energy_s(w)^{1/(2s)}
&\leq\sum_j\Energy_s(w_j)^{1/(2s)}\\
&\leq R^{1-1/(2s)}\left(\sum_j\Energy_s(w_j)\right)^{1/(2s)}.
\end{align*}
Raise to the power $2s$, and then average to obtain the maximum bound. Weighted exactness is Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:61:ter:weighted-exactness}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[One correlation and a nonnegative budget]
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:correlation}
For the partition in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:61:ter:main-partition}, every function $z:B\to\C$ admits an exact cell satisfying
\[
\left|\sum_{x\in B_j}z(x)\right|\geq
\frac{1}{5mK^{a_m}}\left|\sum_{x\in B}z(x)\right|.
\]
Every nonnegative mass admits the analogous retention inequality.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Use the triangle inequality and averaging as in Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:61:ter:avoidance-mass}, with $R\leq5mK^{a_m}$.
\end{proof}

For example, one can take $z(x)=f(x)\exp(-2\pi i\psi(x))$ for a specified test phase $\psi$. This preserves that single scalar sum on one exact restriction. It does not preserve all such tests at once, and it does not guarantee that an earlier energy-to-growth selection has retained the original test sum. These are separate issues.

\subsection{An elementary lower energy bound}

\begin{lemma}[Energy from sumset support]
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:CS-energy}
For every nonempty finite $A$ and $s\geq1$,
\[
\Energy_s(A)\geq\frac{|A|^{2s}}{|sA|}.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The representation function $r_s=\one_A^{*s}$ is supported on $sA$ and has total mass $|A|^s$. Cauchy--Schwarz gives
$|A|^{2s}\leq|sA|\sum_zr_s(z)^2$.
\end{proof}

This inequality will allow the same restriction to satisfy both the cardinality and energy conclusions in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:61:ter:main-eight}. It avoids selecting different favorable cells for the two criteria.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A self-contained energy-to-growth input\srctag{61}}]{A self-contained energy-to-growth input}\label{gsr:en:61:sec:d6}
\srcnote{61}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:bsg}

The next proposition is a conservative version of a standard Balog--Szemer\'edi--Gowers step. Its proof uses the familiar popular-difference graph and common-neighborhood method. We include it so that no unverified numerical estimate in another research manuscript is needed for the principal constants. This is not an improvement over the strongest versions available in the inspected research collection \cite{repo61research}.

\begin{proposition}[A conservative BSG estimate]
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:bsg-prop}
Let $A$ be a nonempty finite subset of an abelian group, $n=|A|$, and $0<c\leq1$. If $\Energy_2(A)\geq cn^3$, there exists $A_1\subseteq A$ such that
\begin{equation}
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:bsg-result}
|A_1|\geq cn/8,
\qquad
|A_1-A_1|\leq2^{21}c^{-9}n.
\end{equation}
In particular, $A_1$ is nonempty and has difference ratio at most $2^{24}c^{-10}$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Let
\[
r(d)=\#\{(a,b)\in A^2:a-b=d\},\qquad
P=\{d:r(d)\geq cn/2\},\qquad \delta=c/2.
\]
We have $\sum_dr(d)=n^2$ and $\sum_dr(d)^2=\Energy_2(A)$. The contribution from $d\notin P$ is at most
$(cn/2)\sum_dr(d)=cn^3/2$. Since $r(d)\leq n$,
\begin{equation}
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:popular}
\sum_{d\in P}r(d)\geq cn^2/2=\delta n^2,
\qquad |P|\leq2n/c=n/\delta.
\end{equation}

Form a bipartite graph whose two vertex classes are copies of $A$, joining a left vertex $a$ to a right vertex $b$ when $a-b\in P$. Write $N(a)$ for the right neighborhood of a left vertex. Call an ordered pair $(a,a')$ of left vertices bad if
\[
|N(a)\cap N(a')|<t,
\qquad t=\delta^2n/32.
\]
The pair may have equal entries; all counts remain ordered.

Choose a right vertex $v$ uniformly and let $U$ be its left neighborhood. By \eqref{gsr:en:61:ter:popular}, $\E|U|\geq\delta n$. If $b(U)$ is the number of ordered bad pairs in $U^2$, then
\[
\E b(U)=\frac1n\sum_{(a,a')\,\mathrm{bad}}|N(a)\cap N(a')|
\leq tn.
\]
Therefore
\[
\E\left(|U|-\frac{16b(U)}{\delta n}\right)
\geq\delta n-\frac{16t}{\delta}=\frac{\delta n}{2}.
\]
Fix $v$ with score at least $\delta n/2$, and write $M=|U|$. It follows that
\begin{equation}
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:core-score}
M\geq\delta n/2,
\qquad b(U)\leq\frac{\delta nM}{16}\leq\frac{M^2}{8}.
\end{equation}
Delete from $U$ every vertex with more than $M/4$ bad partners in $U$. Since badness is symmetric and the pairs are ordered, summing the bad-partner counts gives exactly $b(U)$. At most $4b(U)/M\leq M/2$ vertices are deleted. Denote the remaining left vertices by $A_1$. Then
\[
|A_1|\geq M/2\geq\delta n/4=cn/8.
\]

For any $u,v\in A_1$, at least $M/2$ vertices $w\in U$ are good partners of both endpoints. Each such $w$ has at least $t$ common right neighbors with $u$ and at least $t$ with $v$. Thus there are at least
\begin{equation}
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:walk-count}
\frac{M t^2}{2}\geq\frac{\delta^5n^3}{4096}
\end{equation}
length-four walks $u-b-w-b'-v$. Repeated vertices are allowed, as they are throughout this proof.

For each $d\in A_1-A_1$, fix endpoints $u_d,v_d\in A_1$ with $u_d-v_d=d$. Encode a walk between these endpoints by
\[
(p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4)
=(u_d-b,\ w-b,\ w-b',\ v_d-b')\in P^4.
\]
The label tuple determines the walk once its endpoints are fixed: recover $b$ from $u_d,p_1$, then $w$ from $b,p_2$, and then $b'$ from $w,p_3$. Moreover
\[
p_1-p_2+p_3-p_4=d,
\]
so label sets arising from different differences $d$ are disjoint. Using \eqref{gsr:en:61:ter:popular} and \eqref{gsr:en:61:ter:walk-count},
\[
|A_1-A_1|\frac{\delta^5n^3}{4096}
\leq |P|^4\leq(n/\delta)^4.
\]
Rearranging gives
$|A_1-A_1|\leq2^{12}\delta^{-9}n=2^{21}c^{-9}n$.
Dividing by $|A_1|\geq cn/8$ yields the final ratio bound.
\end{proof}

No asymptotic qualification is hidden in this argument. The threshold $t$ and the score may be nonintegral; comparisons with the integer counts are literal real inequalities. The argument remains valid when $n$ is small and when the group has elements of order two.

\begin{lemma}[High energy controls ordinary additive energy]
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:young}
For a finite set $A$ of size $n$ and every $m\geq2$,
\begin{equation}
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:young-energy}
\Energy_m(A)\leq n^{2m-4}\Energy_2(A).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The inequality $\|u*v\|_2\leq\|u\|_2\|v\|_1$ follows by the triangle inequality applied to the sum of translates of $u$, weighted by $v$. Apply it repeatedly to
$\one_A^{*m}=(\one_A*\one_A)*\one_A^{*(m-2)}$. Since $\|\one_A\|_1=n$,
\[
\|\one_A^{*m}\|_2\leq n^{m-2}\|\one_A*\one_A\|_2.
\]
Squaring proves the result, including equality of the two expressions when $m=2$.
\end{proof}

Thus the hypothesis $\Energy_m^\phi(B)\geq\alpha n^{2m-1}$ implies $\Energy_2(\Gamma)\geq\alpha n^3$. Applying Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:61:ter:bsg-prop} to the graph, rather than to the domain alone, is crucial: the extracted small-difference set must still encode the map.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Polynomial exact restriction of high relation energy\srctag{61}}]{Polynomial exact restriction of high relation energy}\label{gsr:en:61:sec:d7}
\srcnote{61}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:high-energy}

\begin{theorem}[General-order energy restriction]
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:general-energy}
Let $m\geq2$, $B\subseteq G$ be nonempty with $|B|=n$, and $\phi:B\to H$. Suppose $0<\alpha\leq1$ and either
\[
\Energy_m^\phi(B)\geq\alpha n^{2m-1}
\quad\text{or}\quad
\Energy_2^\phi(B)\geq\alpha n^3.
\]
Put
\[
a_m=(2m+1)\log_2(5m),\qquad
\theta_m=2ma_m+m,\qquad K=2^{24}\alpha^{-10}.
\]
There is an exact order-$m$ restriction $B'\subseteq B$ satisfying simultaneously
\begin{align}
|B'|&\geq\frac{\alpha n}{8(5m)K^{a_m}},
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:general-size}\\
\Energy_m(B')=\Energy_m^\phi(B')
&\geq(5m)^{-2m}K^{-\theta_m}
\left(\frac{\alpha n}{8}\right)^{2m-1}.
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:general-energy-bound}
\end{align}
Equivalently, the energy lower bound is
\begin{equation}
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:general-constant}
\Energy_m(B')\geq C_m\alpha^{p_m}n^{2m-1},
\quad
\begin{cases}
p_m=2m-1+10\theta_m,\\
C_m=(5m)^{-2m}2^{-3(2m-1)-24\theta_m}.
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
In particular, $p_m=O(m^2\log m)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:61:ter:young} reduces the first hypothesis to the second. Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:61:ter:bsg-prop}, applied to $\Gamma$, gives a subset $\Gamma_1$ of size $M\geq\alpha n/8$ and difference ratio at most $K$. Because it is a subset of a graph, $\Gamma_1$ is the graph of $\phi$ restricted to a subset $B_1\subseteq B$.

Partition $B_1$ by Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:61:ter:main-partition}, and choose a largest cell $B'$. Then $|B'|\geq M/R$, where $R\leq5mK^{a_m}$. This proves \eqref{gsr:en:61:ter:general-size}. Projection onto $G$ and Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:61:ter:plunnecke} give
\[
|mB'|\leq|m\Gamma_1|\leq K^mM.
\]
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:61:ter:CS-energy} therefore yields
\begin{align*}
\Energy_m(B')
&\geq\frac{(M/R)^{2m}}{K^mM}
 =R^{-2m}K^{-m}M^{2m-1}\\
&\geq(5m)^{-2m}K^{-(2ma_m+m)}
\left(\frac{\alpha n}{8}\right)^{2m-1}.
\end{align*}
Every relation is respected by exactness. Substitution of $K=2^{24}\alpha^{-10}$ gives \eqref{gsr:en:61:ter:general-constant}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A plug-in interface for stronger BSG inputs}

\begin{proposition}[Modular transfer]
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:modular-transfer}
Let $m\geq2$, $0<\alpha\leq1$, and use $a_m,\theta_m$ from Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:61:ter:general-energy}. Suppose an energy-to-growth theorem applicable to $\Gamma$ supplies a subgraph $\Gamma_1$ with
\[
M=|\Gamma_1|\geq c_0\alpha^u n,
\qquad
|\Gamma_1-\Gamma_1|\leq C\alpha^{-v}M,
\]
where $c_0>0$, $u,v\geq0$, and $C\geq1$. Then an exact order-$m$ restriction satisfies simultaneously
\begin{align}
|B'|&\geq\frac{c_0}{5mC^{a_m}}\alpha^{u+va_m}n,
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:transfer-size}\\
\Energy_m(B')&\geq
\frac{c_0^{2m-1}}{(5m)^{2m}C^{\theta_m}}
\alpha^{u(2m-1)+v\theta_m}n^{2m-1}.
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:transfer-energy}
\end{align}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Repeat the last proof with $K=C\alpha^{-v}$ and $M\geq c_0\alpha^u n$. Nothing else changes.
\end{proof}

This is the correct place to import a stronger established energy-to-growth theorem. A statement bounding $|\Gamma_1-\Gamma_1|$ relative to the \emph{original} size $n$ must first be converted to a bound relative to $M$. Losing this distinction changes both the constant and the exponent. The present unconditional numerical results use only Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:61:ter:bsg-prop}; the modular statement does not certify the hypotheses of another source.

\subsection{The order-eight calculation}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:61:ter:main-eight}]
Use the preceding proof with $m=8$. The exact integer inequality
\[
40^{17}<2^{91}
\]
gives $a_8=17\log_2 40<91$. Consequently
\[
R\leq40K^{a_8}\leq2^6K^{91},
\qquad M\geq\alpha n/8,
\qquad K=2^{24}\alpha^{-10}.
\]
The largest cell therefore has
\[
|B'|\geq\frac{M}{R}
\geq2^{-9}\alpha nK^{-91}
=2^{-(9+24\cdot91)}\alpha^{1+10\cdot91}n
=2^{-2193}\alpha^{911}n.
\]
The same cell has energy at least
\begin{align*}
R^{-16}K^{-8}M^{15}
&\geq2^{-96}K^{-(16\cdot91+8)}(\alpha n/8)^{15}\\
&=2^{-141}K^{-1464}\alpha^{15}n^{15}\\
&=2^{-(141+24\cdot1464)}\alpha^{15+10\cdot1464}n^{15}\\
&=2^{-35277}\alpha^{14655}n^{15}.
\end{align*}
Exactness gives equality of the base and respected energy counts. The proof starts equally well from either hypothesis in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:61:ter:main-eight}.
\end{proof}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule
Quantity & Value used in the order-eight proof\\
\midrule
Graph-core size & $M\geq\alpha n/8$\\
Graph-core difference ratio & $K\leq2^{24}\alpha^{-10}$\\
Partition size & $R\leq2^6K^{91}$\\
Sumset support & $|8B'|\leq K^8M$\\
Size exponents & $9+24\cdot91=2193$, $1+10\cdot91=911$\\
Energy exponents & $141+24\cdot1464=35277$\\
& $15+10\cdot1464=14655$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\section[{Consequences for Gowers's restriction lemmas\srctag{61}}]{Consequences for Gowers's restriction lemmas}\label{gsr:en:61:sec:d8}
\srcnote{61}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:gowers}

\subsection{Lemma 7.5: a generalization, not a prime-field constant improvement}

Gowers's Lemma 7.5 extracts an order-$m$ Freiman restriction from a graph with small difference set. The original proof uses scalar multiplication and an interval in the codomain. The inspected formal statement explicitly requires the modulus to be prime \cite{gowers,repo61statements}.

Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:61:ter:main-partition} replaces the prime scalar by a short list of characters and replaces the single selected interval by a complete partition. Its codomain can be, for example,
\[
H=(\Z/8\Z)^{r_1}\times(\Z/9\Z)^{r_2}
\times(\Z/25\Z)^{r_3},
\]
with no explicit rank or exponent factor. The domain need not be cyclic either.

The cost is visible: the exponent $a_m=(2m+1)\log_2(5m)$ is larger than $4m$ for the relevant values of $m$. The uniform theorem is not advertised as a numerical improvement in the prime-modulus case. Its output is stronger in generality and in the partition structure, and its precise defect-budget version can be much better than its worst-case $K$ bound.

\subsection{Lemma 9.3: exactness and removal of the threshold}

\begin{corollary}[A strengthened cyclic Lemma 9.3]
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:lemma93}
Let $N\geq1$, $B\subseteq\Z/N\Z$ be nonempty, $|B|=\beta N$, and $\phi:B\to\Z/N\Z$. Suppose
\[
\Energy_8^\phi(B)\geq\alpha\beta^{15}N^{15},
\qquad \alpha>0.
\]
Then there is an exact order-eight restriction $B'\subseteq B$ with
\[
\Energy_8(B')\geq2^{-35277}\alpha^{14655}\beta^{15}N^{15}.
\]
For every $0<\eta\leq1$, this implies the numerical and approximate-respect conclusions of the inspected statement of Lemma 9.3, with $N_0=1$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The energy cap \eqref{gsr:en:61:ter:energy-cap} implies $\alpha\leq1$. Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:61:ter:main-eight} with $n=\beta N$. Exactness implies any requirement that at least a proportion $1-\eta$ of the additive tuples be respected. Finally,
\begin{align*}
(\alpha\eta/4)^{2^{19}}
&=2^{-1048576}\alpha^{524288}\eta^{524288}\\
&\leq2^{-35277}\alpha^{14655},
\end{align*}
since $0<\alpha,\eta\leq1$, $1048576\geq35277$, and $524288\geq14655$. No restriction on $N$ beyond positivity was used.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]

For nonempty $B$ the hypothesis forces $\alpha\le1$, and for $0<\alpha,\eta\le1$ one has $(\alpha\eta/4)^{2^{19}}\le2^{-2^{20}}\alpha^{2^{19}}\le2^{-35277}\alpha^{14655}$, since $2^{20}=1{,}048{,}576\ge35{,}277$ and $2^{19}=524{,}288\ge14{,}655$; exactness gives \file{GammaHomOfOrder}~$8$~$B'$~$\phi$~$(1-\eta)$. So this corollary implies \file{lemma_9_3} (\file{Sections08\_09.lean}, line~77) with $N_0=1$, on paper; the catalogue statement is already exact (\file{lemma_9_3_holds}), and this corollary is not formalized.

The conclusion is stronger in three separate senses: its displayed coefficient is larger throughout the stated parameter range, it asserts exact order-eight respect, and it has no large-modulus premise. The proof does not assert that its coefficient dominates the sharper \emph{prime-field} bounds in other project reports. Those comparisons involve different hypotheses and different outputs.

\Energy_2^\phi(B)\geq\gamma |B|^3,

\Energy_8(B')\geq2^{-35277}\gamma^{14655}|B|^{15}.

\subsection{Why the original density normalization survives}

If one knew only $|B'|\geq\rho|B|$, the elementary ambient-group bound would give
\[
\Energy_8(B')\geq\frac{|B'|^{16}}{|G|},
\]
which in a cyclic group is of scale $\rho^{16}\beta^{16}N^{15}$. This has an extra factor of $\beta$ compared with the normalization in Lemma 9.3. The proof above instead uses
$|8B'|\leq K^8M$, where $M$ is the size of the selected \emph{graph core}. It therefore produces a multiple of $M^{15}$ and, ultimately, of $|B|^{15}$. This support estimate is the quantitative reason the restriction can retain the desired relation-energy scale.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Torsion obstructions and the optimal logarithmic scale\srctag{61}}]{Torsion obstructions and the optimal logarithmic scale}\label{gsr:en:61:sec:d9}
\srcnote{61}{Section 9}
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:torsion}

The absence of an ambient-order parameter in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:61:ter:avoidance} does not mean that torsion is harmless. Rather, torsion is paid for by the exponent of the defect budget. The following examples show that logarithmic growth of that exponent in $m$ is necessary.

\subsection{A coloring problem requiring singleton cells}

Let $\chi_m(H,D)$ denote the least number of cells in a partition of $H$ satisfying $(mS-mS)\cap D=\varnothing$ for every cell $S$.

\begin{proposition}[An exact $2$-primary obstruction]
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:coloring-lower}
Let $e\geq1$, $r\geq1$, and $2^{e-1}\leq m$. Set
\[
H=(\Z/2^e\Z)^r,
\quad T=H[2]=2^{e-1}H,
\quad D=T\setminus\{0\}.
\]
Then every admissible cell is a singleton, and
\begin{equation}
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:coloring-exact}
\chi_m(H,D)=2^{er}=(|D|+1)^e.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Let $x\ne y$. Their difference has order $2^j$ for some $1\leq j\leq e$. Put $q=2^{j-1}\leq m$. Then $q(x-y)$ is a nonzero element of $H[2]$, hence belongs to $D$.

If a cell contains $x,y$, the difference $q(x-y)$ belongs to $mS-mS$: use $q$ copies of $x$ against $q$ copies of $y$, and append the same $m-q$ copies of $y$ to both sides. Thus any two distinct elements in one cell violate avoidance. Singleton cells are admissible because $m\{x\}-m\{x\}=\{0\}$. Their number is $|H|=2^{er}$, while $|D|+1=2^r$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:61:ter:main-exponent}]
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:61:ter:avoidance} gives the upper bound with constant $C_m=5m$. For the lower bound choose $e=\floor{\log_2m}+1$, so that $2^{e-1}\leq m$, and let $r$ tend to infinity in Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:61:ter:coloring-lower}. If a universal bound with exponent $b<e$ held, it would require
\[
2^{er}\leq C_m2^{br}
\quad\text{for every }r,
\]
which is impossible. The limiting statements follow because the two bounds differ from $\log_2m$ by bounded amounts.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The case $m=1$]
For symmetric $D$, the ordinary Cayley graph with differences in $D$ has maximum degree $|D|$. A greedy vertex coloring uses at most $|D|+1$ colors. Taking $D=H\setminus\{0\}$ forces singleton cells. Thus the analogous exponent is exactly $b_1=1$. The character bound remains valid but is not sharp in this case.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[A $p$-primary variant]
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:p-primary}
Let $p$ be prime, $p^{e-1}\leq m$, $H=(\Z/p^e\Z)^r$, and $D=H[p]\setminus\{0\}$. Then
\[
\chi_m(H,D)=p^{er}=(|D|+1)^e.
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For $x\ne y$ with difference of order $p^j$, multiply the difference by $p^{j-1}\leq m$. It becomes a nonzero element of $H[p]$. The padding argument and the singleton upper bound are identical to those above.
\end{proof}

The prime $2$ yields the largest lower exponent from this family for a given $m$. The obstruction uses increasing rank and fixed exponent; it cannot be removed simply by checking sufficiently large moduli.

\subsection{Graph restrictions that must be singletons}

The preceding coloring example allows an arbitrary forbidden set. The next construction shows that related torsion obstructions actually arise from graphs, and quantifies their graph difference ratio and energy.

\begin{theorem}[Canonical-section graph obstruction]
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:graph-obstruction}
Let $e\geq2$, $L=2^{e-1}\leq m$, and $r\geq1$. Define
\[
G=(\Z/L\Z)^r,
\qquad H=(\Z/(2L)\Z)^r,
\]
and let $\phi:G\to H$ take each coordinate to its representative in $\{0,\ldots,L-1\}$. With $\Gamma$ its graph and $n=L^r$,
\begin{align}
|\Gamma-\Gamma|&=(2L-1)^r,
&K&=(2-1/L)^r,
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:section-diff}\\
\Energy_2(\Gamma)&=\left(\frac{2L^3+L}{3}\right)^r,
&\frac{\Energy_2(\Gamma)}{n^3}
&=\left(\frac23+\frac1{3L^2}\right)^r.
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:section-energy}
\end{align}
Every exact Freiman restriction of order $m$ has at most one point.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
First consider one coordinate. The graph differences are precisely
\[
(t\bmod L,\ t\bmod 2L),\qquad -(L-1)\leq t\leq L-1.
\]
These $2L-1$ pairs are distinct. Taking independent coordinates proves \eqref{gsr:en:61:ter:section-diff}.

For two-term sums, all representative sums lie between $0$ and $2L-2$. Equality modulo $2L$ is therefore equality as integers, which also implies equality modulo $L$. The one-coordinate graph energy is the additive energy of the interval $\{0,\ldots,L-1\}$:
\[
L^2+2\sum_{j=1}^{L-1}j^2
=L^2+\frac{(L-1)L(2L-1)}3
=\frac{2L^3+L}{3}.
\]
Multiplication over the coordinates proves \eqref{gsr:en:61:ter:section-energy}.

Now let $x\ne y$ in $G$ and put $d=\phi(x)-\phi(y)\in H$. This difference is nonzero. Its order is $2^j$ for some $j\leq e$. In fact $j\geq2$: every nonzero element of order two has some coordinate equal to $L$ modulo $2L$, whereas each representative coordinate difference lies between $-(L-1)$ and $L-1$.

Set $q=2^{j-1}\leq L\leq m$. Then $qd$ is a nonzero element of $H[2]$, and $H[2]$ is the kernel of reduction from $H$ to $G$. Consequently
\[
q(x-y)=0\quad\text{in }G,
\qquad q(\phi(x)-\phi(y))\ne0\quad\text{in }H.
\]
This is an unrespected order-$q$ relation using only $x,y$. Padding gives an unrespected order-$m$ relation on the same pair. No exact restriction can contain both points.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Necessary exponents for graph extraction]
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:graph-lower-exponents}
Fix $m\geq2$ and a power of two $L\leq m$, $L\geq2$.
If a universal theorem guarantees an exact order-$m$ restriction of size at least
$c_mK^{-a}|B|$ whenever the graph difference ratio is at most $K$, with $c_m>0$ independent of the groups, then necessarily
\begin{equation}
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:K-necessary}
a\geq\frac{\log L}{\log(2-1/L)}.
\end{equation}
If a universal theorem instead guarantees size at least $c_m\gamma^u|B|$ under
$\Energy_2^\phi(B)\geq\gamma|B|^3$, then necessarily
\begin{equation}
\label{gsr:en:61:ter:gamma-necessary}
u\geq\frac{\log L}{-\log(2/3+1/(3L^2))}.
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply the proposed guarantee to Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:61:ter:graph-obstruction}, and let $r\to\infty$. Since every exact restriction has size at most one, the bases in
\[
c_m\bigl[L(2-1/L)^{-a}\bigr]^r\leq1,
\qquad
c_m\bigl[L(2/3+1/(3L^2))^u\bigr]^r\leq1
\]
must be at most one. Taking logarithms gives the conclusions.
\end{proof}

Choosing the largest power of two below $m$ makes both necessary exponents of order $\log m$. For the $K$ exponent, the leading scale is $\log_2m$. The proven upper graph exponent is $a_m=O(m\log m)$, leaving a factor of order $m$ unresolved. The matching leading logarithm in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:61:ter:main-exponent} belongs to the \emph{defect-coloring} problem, not to this stronger graph-extraction optimization.

\begin{example}[The order-eight section]
For $m=8$, take $L=8$. Then $G=(\Z/8\Z)^r$, $H=(\Z/16\Z)^r$, $n=8^r$,
\[
K=(15/8)^r,
\qquad \gamma=(43/64)^r.
\]
Every exact order-eight restriction is a singleton. This gives a concrete test family for any proposed improvement to the order-eight size exponent. It is not a counterexample to Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:61:ter:main-eight}; the lower bounds there are compatible with singleton output on this family.
\end{example}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A translated Fej\'er restriction theorem\srctag{60}}]{A translated Fej\'er restriction theorem}\label{gsr:en:60:sec:d9}
\srcnote{60}{Section 9}
\label{gsr:en:60:rst:sec:restriction}

The restriction step in Section~9 of Gowers's proof turns a map that
respects many additive relations into one that respects nearly all
relations on a smaller set~\cite{gowers}.
Source~04 replaces repeated elementary filters by one positive Fourier
kernel and retains the Fourier weights of unwanted relations~\cite{repo60four}.
Source~17 uses a Fej\'er kernel whose amplification grows linearly with its
bandwidth~\cite{repo60seventeen}.  We combine those two features with an independent
translation of the phase.  The translation reduces the \emph{total weight}
of unwanted coefficient relations by a factor of the bandwidth.  The same
factor controls the survival of repeated tuples, so it is not lost when
the selected set is interpreted as an actual subset.

The resulting prime-cyclic theorem has the retention coefficient of
source~17, with a size threshold of degree $m-1$ in the inverse accuracy
parameter for $m$-term relations.  The proposed composition of sources~04
and~17 had degree $m$.  We also prove a finite-data certificate on arbitrary
finite abelian groups, with small-order torsion and repeated tuples
explicitly accounted for.  The improvement is local to the restriction
step; no later inverse-theorem parameter comparison is assumed.

\subsection{Relations, the kernel, and the finite probability space}

Let $G,H$ be finite abelian groups, let $\varnothing\ne B\subseteq G$,
write $b=|B|$, and let $\phi:B\to H$.
Fix an even integer $m=2r\ge4$ and put
\[
 \varepsilon=(\underbrace{1,\ldots,1}_{r},
              \underbrace{-1,\ldots,-1}_{r}).
\]
An ordered tuple $\mathbf x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in B^m$ is
\emph{additive} if $\sum_i\varepsilon_i x_i=0$ in $G$, and is
\emph{respected} if also
\[
 \Delta_\phi(\mathbf x):=\sum_i\varepsilon_i\phi(x_i)=0
 \quad\hbox{in }H.
\]
Let $T_m(B)$ count all additive tuples and let $G_m(B,\phi)$ count the
respected ones.  Repeated coordinates are included in both counts.
For the current input abbreviate
\[
 T=T_m(B),\qquad G_0=G_m(B,\phi),\qquad U=T-G_0,
\]
and let $U_{\rm rep}$ count the unrespected additive tuples with at least
one repeated coordinate.  The elementary bounds
\begin{equation}
 T\le b^{m-1},\qquad
 U_{\rm rep}\le\binom m2 b^{m-2}
 \label{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:elementary-counts}
\end{equation}
hold on every finite abelian group.  For the first, the last coordinate is
uniquely determined by the preceding ones.  For the second, prescribe an
equality $x_i=x_j$ and choose a position $k\notin\{i,j\}$.  Fixing the
$m-2$ positions outside $\{j,k\}$ determines $x_j$ by the equality and
$x_k$ by its coefficient $\varepsilon_k=\pm1$ in the additive relation.
A union bound over the pairs proves the assertion, without any torsion
hypothesis.

Write $\mathbb T=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ and $e(t)=\exp(2\pi i t)$.
For an integer $L\ge2$ define
\begin{equation}
 K_L(t)=\frac1{L^2}\left|\sum_{j=0}^{L-1}e(jt)\right|^2
       =\sum_{n=1-L}^{L-1}a_n e(nt),
 \qquad a_n=\frac{L-|n|}{L^2}.
 \label{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:kernel}
\end{equation}
Then $0\le K_L\le1$, the coefficients are nonnegative,
$\sum_n a_n=1$, and $\int_{\mathbb T}K_L=1/L$.
Set
\begin{align}
 a&=L^{-m},\notag\\
 S=S_{m,L}
  &=\sum_{|t|<L}\left(1-\frac{|t|}{L}\right)^m,
  \label{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:signal}\\
 J=J_{m,L}&=\int_{\mathbb T}K_L(t)^m\,dt.
  \label{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:moment}
\end{align}
The useful bounds are
\begin{equation}
 \frac{2L}{m+1}\le S\le L,
 \qquad aS\le J\le\frac1L.
 \label{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:kernel-bounds}
\end{equation}
The lower bound for $S$ is the trapezoidal inequality for the convex
function $(1-t/L)^m$ on $[0,L]$; its upper bound follows by replacing the
$m$th power by the first power.  The inequality $J\le1/L$ follows from
$K_L^m\le K_L$.  In the nonnegative Fourier expansion for $J$, the
coefficient vectors $n=t\varepsilon$ all have coordinate sum zero and
have total weight $aS$, proving the remaining inequality.

An exact formula, useful when optimizing finite parameters, is
\begin{equation}
 J_{m,L}=L^{-2m}\sum_{j=0}^{m}(-1)^j\binom{2m}{j}
             \binom{(m-j)L+m-1}{2m-1}.
 \label{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:moment-exact}
\end{equation}
Here a binomial coefficient is zero when its nonnegative upper argument
is smaller than its lower argument.  Indeed $L^{2m}J_{m,L}$ is the
coefficient of $z^{m(L-1)}$ in $(1+z+\cdots+z^{L-1})^{2m}$; expanding
$(1-z^L)^{2m}(1-z)^{-2m}$ gives~\eqref{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:moment-exact}.

For a positive integer $q$ define the leakage signal
\begin{equation}
 S_{m,L}[q]=\sum_{\substack{|t|<L\\q\mid t}}
                  \left(1-\frac{|t|}{L}\right)^m.
 \label{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:leakage}
\end{equation}
In particular $S_{m,L}[q]=1$ when $q>L-1$.  For a finite abelian group put
\begin{equation}
 G[d]=\{x\in G:dx=0\},\qquad
 \tau_G(L)=\max_{1\le d\le2L-2}|G[d]|.
 \label{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:torsion}
\end{equation}
For $G=\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ this is
$\max_{1\le d\le2L-2}\gcd(n,d)$.  It is $1$ whenever multiplication by
every integer between $1$ and $2L-2$ is injective on $G$.

All random choices can be finite.  Put
\begin{equation}
 Q=m(L-1)+1.
 \label{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:finite-shift}
\end{equation}
Choose independently a uniform character $\chi\in\widehat G$, a uniform
character $\psi\in\widehat H$, and a uniform integer
$j\in\{0,\ldots,Q-1\}$.  We regard characters additively as maps to
$\mathbb T$.  Conditional on these choices, include each point $x\in B$
independently in a random subset $B'$ with probability
\begin{equation}
 p(x)=K_L\bigl(\chi(x)+\psi(\phi(x))+j/Q\bigr).
 \label{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:selector}
\end{equation}
The bound $0\le K_L\le1$ makes these valid Bernoulli probabilities.
Let $X$ and $Y$ be the numbers of respected and unrespected additive
$m$-tuples in $B'$, respectively.

\subsection{An exact finite-group survival estimate}

\begin{theorem}[Translated-kernel survival estimates]
\label{gsr:en:60:rst:thm:survival}
With the definitions above, on arbitrary finite abelian groups $G,H$,
\begin{align}
 \mathbb E X&\ge aS G_0,
 \label{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:good-survival}\\
 \mathbb E Y&\le
  a\sum_{\substack{\mathbf x\in B^m\text{ additive}\\
                         \Delta_\phi(\mathbf x)\ne0}}
       S_{m,L}[\operatorname{ord}(\Delta_\phi(\mathbf x))]\notag\\
 &\quad+\tau_G(L)(J-aS)b^{m-2}
   +(L^{-1}-a)U_{\rm rep}.
 \label{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:bad-survival}
\end{align}
In particular, if every nonzero discrepancy appearing among the
unrespected tuples has order greater than $L-1$, then
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb E Y\le aU+
       \frac{\tau_G(L)+\binom m2}{L}\,b^{m-2}.
 \label{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:bad-simple}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For a fixed tuple $\mathbf x$, write
\[
 P(\mathbf x)=\prod_{i=1}^{m}p(x_i),\qquad
 R(\mathbf x)=\prod_{z\in\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}}p(z).
\]
The first product includes multiplicities.  The second is the true
conditional probability that every point of the tuple is selected.
Thus $R\ge P$, and equality holds when the coordinates are distinct.

For $n=(n_1,\ldots,n_m)\in\{1-L,\ldots,L-1\}^m$, put
$w_n=\prod_i a_{n_i}$.  Expanding the first product and applying
orthogonality of the two finite dual groups and of the $Q$ shifts gives
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb E P(\mathbf x)
  =\sum_n w_n\,
     1_{\{\sum_i n_i=0\text{ in }\mathbb Z\}}
     1_{\{\sum_i n_i x_i=0\text{ in }G\}}
     1_{\{\sum_i n_i\phi(x_i)=0\text{ in }H\}}.
 \label{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:orthogonality}
\end{equation}
To justify the integer condition, the shift average initially requires
$Q\mid\sum_i n_i$, whereas
$|\sum_i n_i|\le m(L-1)<Q$.  Hence divisibility is equivalent to exact
integer equality.  In particular, there is no assumption here that the
group exponents exceed the kernel bandwidth.

Call $n=t\varepsilon$ an integer principal-line vector.  On every
respected additive tuple all these vectors contribute to
\eqref{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:orthogonality}, and their total weight is $aS$.
The inequality $R\ge P$ therefore proves~\eqref{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:good-survival},
including for tuples with repeated coordinates.
On an unrespected tuple a principal-line vector contributes exactly when
$t\Delta_\phi(\mathbf x)=0$.  Its total contribution is
$aS_{m,L}[\operatorname{ord}(\Delta_\phi(\mathbf x))]$.

Suppose next that $n$ is not on the integer principal line.  Some
$2$-by-$2$ minor of the two integer rows $\varepsilon,n$ is then a
nonzero integer $d$ with $|d|\le2L-2$.  After fixing the other $m-2$
coordinates in $B$, elimination using a coefficient $\varepsilon_i=\pm1$
reduces the equations
\[
 \sum_i\varepsilon_i x_i=0,\qquad \sum_i n_i x_i=0
\]
to an equation $dz=z_0$ for one remaining coordinate.  Such an equation
has either no solutions or $|G[d]|$ solutions, with the other coordinate
uniquely determined.  Thus there are at most
$\tau_G(L)b^{m-2}$ additive tuples satisfying the additional domain
relation.  Imposing the image relation, or restricting to unrespected
tuples, cannot increase this count.

The total weight of all vectors with $\sum_i n_i=0$ is $J$.
Subtracting the principal-line weight shows that the nonprincipal vectors
have total weight $J-aS$.  Summing first over tuples and then over these
vectors consequently bounds their total contribution by
$\tau_G(L)(J-aS)b^{m-2}$.

It remains to compare multiplicity products with actual survival.
For any chosen coordinate $x_i$ one has $R(\mathbf x)\le p(x_i)$.
For fixed $\chi,\psi$, averaging over the $Q$ shifts gives
$\mathbb E_j p(x_i)=1/L$, since $Q>L-1$.  Thus
$\mathbb E R(\mathbf x)\le1/L$.
The zero coefficient vector in~\eqref{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:orthogonality} contributes
$a$ on every tuple, so $\mathbb E P(\mathbf x)\ge a$.  Therefore
\[
 0\le\mathbb E\bigl(R(\mathbf x)-P(\mathbf x)\bigr)
       \le L^{-1}-a.
\]
This difference is zero for distinct-coordinate tuples.  Summing it over
the $U_{\rm rep}$ unrespected repeated tuples proves
\eqref{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:bad-survival}.  Finally use
\eqref{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:elementary-counts}, $J-aS\le1/L$, and
$S_{m,L}[q]=1$ for $q>L-1$ to obtain~\eqref{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:bad-simple}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[A finer domain torsion statistic]
\label{gsr:en:60:rst:rem:weighted-torsion}
The factor $\tau_G(L)(J-aS)$ in~\eqref{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:bad-survival} can be
replaced by
\[
 \sum_{\substack{n\notin\mathbb Z\varepsilon\\\sum_i n_i=0}}
 w_n\min_{\substack{i<j\\d_{ij}\ne0}}|G[d_{ij}]|,
 \qquad d_{ij}=\varepsilon_i n_j-\varepsilon_j n_i.
\]
The proof simply chooses the best nonzero minor separately for each
coefficient vector.  The actual image-discrepancy orders and $U_{\rm rep}$
can likewise be retained.  Thus the theorem gives a certificate sensitive
to the input's torsion and relation statistics, rather than requiring
every one of them to be replaced by a uniform maximum.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Restriction with a simultaneous count guarantee}

\begin{corollary}[Finite-data certificate]
\label{gsr:en:60:rst:cor:certificate}
Let $0<\eta\le1$ and define
\begin{align*}
 \Psi_L={}&\eta aS G_0
 -a\sum_{\substack{\mathbf x\in B^m\text{ additive}\\
                          \Delta_\phi(\mathbf x)\ne0}}
       S_{m,L}[\operatorname{ord}(\Delta_\phi(\mathbf x))]\\
 &\quad-\tau_G(L)(J-aS)b^{m-2}-(L^{-1}-a)U_{\rm rep}.
\end{align*}
If $\Psi_L>0$, some $B'\subseteq B$ satisfies
\begin{equation}
 T_m(B')\ge\frac{\Psi_L}{\eta}>0,
 \qquad
 \frac{G_m(B',\phi)}{T_m(B')}\ge\frac1{1+\eta}\ge1-\eta.
 \label{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:certificate-output}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:60:rst:thm:survival} gives
$\mathbb E(\eta X-Y)\ge\Psi_L$.
Choose a realization with $\eta X-Y\ge\Psi_L$.  Then $Y\le\eta X$ and
\[
 T_m(B')=X+Y\ge X\ge\frac{\eta X-Y}{\eta}
                         \ge\frac{\Psi_L}{\eta}.
\]
These inequalities prove the simultaneous proportion and count claims.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[An explicit polynomial restriction]
\label{gsr:en:60:rst:thm:polynomial}
Suppose $0<\alpha,\eta\le1$ and
$G_m(B,\phi)\ge\alpha b^{m-1}$.  Put
\[
 L=\left\lceil\frac{m+1}{\alpha\eta}\right\rceil,
 \qquad C=\tau_G(L)+\binom m2.
\]
Assume that every nonzero discrepancy on an unrespected additive tuple
has order greater than $L-1$, and that
\begin{equation}
 b\ge2C L^{m-1}.
 \label{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:size-threshold}
\end{equation}
Then there is a subset $B'\subseteq B$ such that
\begin{align}
 \frac{G_m(B',\phi)}{T_m(B')}&\ge\frac1{1+\eta}\ge1-\eta,
 \label{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:proportion}\\
 T_m(B')&\ge\frac{b^{m-1}}{2\eta L^m}
 \ge\frac{\alpha^m\eta^{m-1}}{2(m+2)^m}\,b^{m-1}.
 \label{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:retention}
\end{align}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By~\eqref{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:kernel-bounds}, $\eta\alpha S\ge2$.
The elementary upper bound for $T$ and~\eqref{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:bad-simple} give
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb E(\eta X-Y)
 &\ge a(\eta\alpha S-1)b^{m-1}-\frac{C}{L}b^{m-2}\\
 &\ge a b^{m-1}-\frac{C}{L}b^{m-2}
 \ge\frac a2 b^{m-1}.
\end{align*}
The last inequality is exactly~\eqref{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:size-threshold}.
The signed-objective argument of Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:60:rst:cor:certificate}
proves the first bound in~\eqref{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:retention} and the proportion
claim.  Finally
$L\le(m+2)/(\alpha\eta)$ gives the second retention bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Prime cyclic groups]
\label{gsr:en:60:rst:cor:prime}
Let $B\subseteq\mathbb F_p$ and $\phi:B\to\mathbb F_p$, where $p$ is
prime.  Under the hypothesis $G_m(B,\phi)\ge\alpha b^{m-1}$, define $L$
as in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:60:rst:thm:polynomial}.  The sole size condition
\begin{equation}
 b\ge2\left(1+\binom m2\right)L^{m-1}
 \label{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:prime-threshold}
\end{equation}
implies the conclusions~\eqref{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:proportion}--\eqref{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:retention}.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The condition implies $p\ge b>2L-2$.  Consequently $\tau_G(L)=1$ and
every nonzero image discrepancy has order $p>L-1$.  Apply
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:60:rst:thm:polynomial}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Against the intake's marked composition and the catalogue} (checked at the write). Item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:threshold} records, as an unproved composition of sources~04 and~17, source~17's retention $1/(2\eta L^m)$ under $|B|\ge2(1+\binom m2)L^m$; this corollary proves it with the smaller threshold $2(1+\binom m2)L^{m-1}$, one power of $L$ less, on every prime modulus. At $m=16$, $2(1+\binom{16}2)=242$ and $(m+2)^m=18^{16}$, as in Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:60:rst:cor:sixteen}. The catalogue's \file{lemma_9_3} (\file{Sections08\_09.lean}, line~77) quantifies over all moduli, so this prime-modulus corollary does not imply it; it is not formalized.
\end{writenote}

The same conclusion holds for arbitrary finite abelian $G,H$ whenever
multiplication by $1,\ldots,2L-2$ is injective on $G$ and every nonzero
element of $H$ has order greater than $L-1$.  For example, composite
cyclic groups whose prime factors exceed $2L-2$ satisfy both requirements
when used as both domain and codomain.  The general certificate in
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:60:rst:cor:certificate} remains valid with small torsion
present; its positivity is then an explicit additional condition.

\subsection{Finite deterministic extraction}

For a rational tolerance $\eta$, the existence proof can be made
deterministic without an appeal to a limiting probability space.
Enumerate the $|G||H|Q$ choices of $(\chi,\psi,j)$ and compute the
conditional expectation of $\eta X-Y$ under the independent point
selections.  At least one choice has conditional expectation at least
the unconditional expectation.  Fix a maximizing choice.

Expose the membership of the points of $B$ one at a time.  At each step
the current conditional expectation is a convex combination of the two
conditional expectations obtained by including or excluding the next
point.  Choose a branch with at least the current value.  If its
Bernoulli probability is $0$ or $1$, use the forced branch.  Once every
point is exposed, the resulting set has $\eta X-Y$ at least the proved
lower bound.

All comparisons can be exact.  The kernel probabilities belong to a
cyclotomic field with conductor dividing
\[
 \operatorname{lcm}\bigl(\exp(G),\exp(H),Q\bigr),
\]
and their relevant real algebraic values can be compared exactly.
Direct enumeration of additive tuples suffices to compute each
conditional expectation; its survival factor is the product over
\emph{distinct} unexposed points.  This supplies a finite extraction
procedure.  It is not a claim that the numerical thresholds or the
straightforward implementation are practical at very small tolerances.

\subsection{Sixteen-term relations and comparison of thresholds}

The density-sensitive moment input used in sources~04 and~17 is valid on
every finite abelian group.  For completeness, if $A$ is a nonempty
finite subset of an abelian group and $E_j(A)$ counts its additive
$2j$-tuples, then
\begin{equation}
 E_j(A)\ge\frac{E_2(A)^{j-1}}{|A|^{j-2}}
 \qquad(j\ge2).
 \label{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:moment-interpolation}
\end{equation}
Using unnormalized Fourier coefficients on the ambient group, define a
probability distribution on its dual with weights proportional to
$|\widehat{1_A}(\chi)|^2$.  Its $(j-1)$st moment of
$|\widehat{1_A}(\chi)|^2$ is $E_j(A)/|A|$, and its first moment is
$E_2(A)/|A|$.  Jensen's inequality proves
\eqref{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:moment-interpolation}.

Apply this to the graph $\{(x,\phi(x)):x\in B\}$.
If $\phi$ respects at least $\gamma b^3$ additive quadruples, then it
respects at least $\gamma^7b^{15}$ additive sixteen-tuples.
Consequently Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:60:rst:cor:prime} gives the following explicit
form of the order-eight restriction step.

\begin{corollary}[Order eight]
\label{gsr:en:60:rst:cor:sixteen}
Let $B\subseteq\mathbb F_p$ and $\phi:B\to\mathbb F_p$ respect at least
$\gamma b^3$ additive quadruples, where $0<\gamma\le1$.
For $0<\eta\le1$, set
\[
 L=\left\lceil\frac{17}{\gamma^7\eta}\right\rceil.
\]
If $b\ge242L^{15}$, there is $B'\subseteq B$ for which at least a
proportion $1/(1+\eta)$ of all additive sixteen-tuples is respected and
\begin{equation}
 T_{16}(B')\ge\frac{b^{15}}{2\eta L^{16}}
       \ge\frac{\gamma^{112}\eta^{15}}{2\cdot18^{16}}\,b^{15}.
 \label{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:sixteen-output}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}

The comparison uses the same normalization, the number of available
points $b$, and the same $L$.  Source~17's retained coefficient is
$[2(m+2)^m]^{-1}$, exactly the coefficient in
\eqref{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:retention}.  The proposed combination of its Fej\'er signal
with source~04's weighted rank-two estimate would require
$2(1+\binom m2)L^m$ points.  Our proof replaces that by
$2(1+\binom m2)L^{m-1}$, a factor $L$ smaller.

At $m=16$ the two combined thresholds are therefore $242L^{16}$ and
$242L^{15}$.  Source~17's original exceptional-vector count has bandwidth
degree $31$ before its additional density dependence is removed, while
source~04's order-eight theorem has threshold
\[
 242\cdot3200^8(\gamma^7\eta)^{-16}
\]
and retention coefficient $(2\cdot3200^8)^{-1}$.
The new theorem has degree $15$ in the inverse parameter
$\gamma^7\eta$ and the larger retained coefficient
$(2\cdot18^{16})^{-1}$; indeed $18^{16}=324^8<3200^8$.
These comparisons strengthen the stated local inputs
of~\cite{repo60four,repo60seventeen}, rather than an already completed global bound.

The threshold exponent $m-1$ is not asserted optimal.  On groups with
persistent small-order torsion, a one-kernel selector can have substantial
principal-line leakage: for fixed $q$, the ratio $S_{m,L}[q]/S_{m,L}$
tends to $1/q$ as $L\to\infty$.  Removing such leakage, or obtaining a
much lower threshold uniformly over growing prime cyclic groups,
requires an additional argument.  Formula~\eqref{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:bad-survival}
identifies precisely which relation statistics that argument must control.

\section{Source~60's chapter: the arrangement polynomial of every order \wtag}\label{gsr:en:sec:arrangementpolynomial}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the eleventh write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next six sections are source~60's Sections~3--8, on Gowers's respected arrangements of Section~12 near complete agreement on a full product. \emph{Logically they continue source~33's chapter} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:arrangements}), whose questions they answer in part; they are printed here because no number printed earlier may move. Source~60's introduction is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:60:sec:d1}; its coarse decoder is its Appendix~A, in Part~V.

\emph{What is proved.} For every even number $s\ge4$ of vertical differences and distance $0<\delta\le1/4$ to the exact models $a(x)+B(x,y)+\ell(y)$, the failure probability satisfies $\varepsilon_s\ge B_s(\delta)=(1-(1-4\delta)^s)/4-2^{2s-3}\delta^{s-1}(1-2\delta)$, a polynomial that strictly improves source~33's for $s\ge6$ and is source~33's cubic $4\delta-24\delta^2+32\delta^3$ at $s=4$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:60:arr:local}); equality for $0<\delta<1/4$ holds exactly for $a\one_C(x)\lambda(y)$ after adding an exact model, with $2a=0\ne a$, $C$ a coset of index $n\ge3$ and $\lambda$ onto $\Z/2\Z$, at $\delta=1/(2n)$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:60:arr:equality}); under source~33's activation threshold the inverse branch gives every Taylor coefficient of the repair bound optimally in succession, $\delta\le\varepsilon/16+(15/128)\varepsilon^2+(155/512)\varepsilon^3+O(\varepsilon^4)$ for Gowers's eight-arrangements (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:60:arr:repair}, Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:60:arr:coefficients}). The auxiliary-label profile behind it holds without conditions on the groups (Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:60:aux:profile}, \ref{gsr:en:60:aux:equality}). Odd targets and the common prime: the bracket $(s-1)/s^2\le c_s^{\mathrm{prime}}\le(3s-2)/(2s^2)$, against source~33's $(3s-2)/(4s^2)$ and $2(s-1)/s^2$ (Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:60:arr:odd-target}, \ref{gsr:en:60:arr:prime-obstruction}). Two directions: if $\eta=\dist(f,\Vcal)+\dist(f,\HH)<1/4$, then $\dist(f,\A)\le J(\eta)=(1+\eta-\sqrt{1-2\eta})/2$, optimal (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:60:two:intersection}), and biaffine repair with every inverse coefficient through degree $s-2$ optimal (Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:60:two:repair}, \ref{gsr:en:60:two:sharpness}). These answer source~33's Questions~2, 3 (the equality part) and~8 (locally), and improve both ends of its Question~1 (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:arrangerepair}). The majority correction is Blum--Luby--Rubinfeld's and the coarse decoder source~33's, credited; the theorems concern full products, not the sparse domains Gowers needs (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:endpoint}). Source~96, placed during this write and not yet written in, proves the odd-target repair and the bracket $[15/256,23/256]$ independently, in a version with no cubic term and no smallness condition (from its placement record, not checked here; note after Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:60:arr:prime-obstruction}).
