\section[{Respected arrangements and their normalization\srctag{60}}]{Respected arrangements and their normalization}\label{gsr:en:60:sec:d3}
\srcnote{60}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:en:60:arr:setup}

Throughout this section, $G,H,K$ are finite abelian groups and $s=2m\ge4$.
All probabilities use uniform measures, independently unless a relation is
specified. For $f:G\times H\to K$, write
\[
 D_hf(x,y)=f(x,y+h)-f(x,y).
\]
The vertical $s$-difference test chooses $h\in H$, independent base points
$y_1,\ldots,y_s\in H$, and a uniform tuple $(x_1,\ldots,x_s)$ subject to
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:arr:balance}
 x_1+\cdots+x_m=x_{m+1}+\cdots+x_s.
\end{equation}
It accepts precisely when
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:arr:test}
 \sum_{i=1}^{m}D_hf(x_i,y_i)
 =\sum_{i=m+1}^{s}D_hf(x_i,y_i).
\end{equation}
Its failure probability is $\varepsilon_s(f)$.
The ordered-query convention includes $h=0$, repeated coordinates, and
coinciding vertices. There are exactly
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:arr:normalization}
 |G|^{s-1}|H|^{s+1}
\end{equation}
query tuples. If $G=H=\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$, this is $N^{2s}$.
In the arrangement terminology of Gowers's Section~12, $s=2k$ corresponds
to a $k$-arrangement; in particular, eight-arrangements have $s=16$.
These are the conventions of the earlier full-product repair report
\cite{repo60thirtythree}, derived from Gowers's framework~\cite{gowers}.

Let
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:arr:model-class}
 \mathcal V(G,H;K)=
 \{(x,y)\mapsto a(x)+B(x,y)+\ell(y):
       B\text{ biadditive},\ \ell\text{ additive}\},
\end{equation}
where $a:G\to K$ is arbitrary. Uniform Hamming distance is denoted by
$d$, and
\[
 \delta=\delta_{\mathcal V}(f)
       :=\min_{\psi\in\mathcal V}d(f,\psi).
\]
Every member of $\mathcal V$ passes every test: its derivative is
$B(x,h)+\ell(h)$, and \eqref{gsr:en:60:arr:balance} cancels the biadditive terms.
Thus adding a member of $\mathcal V$ changes neither the test outcome nor
the distance to $\mathcal V$. The converse, that a function passing every
test belongs to $\mathcal V$, follows from the coarse decoder reproduced
in Appendix~\ref{gsr:fz:60:decode:section}.

\begin{lemma}[Independence of proper coordinate families]
\label{gsr:en:60:arr:independence}
Every proper subfamily of the coordinates in a uniform tuple satisfying
\eqref{gsr:en:60:arr:balance} is independent and uniform. The same holds for the
pairs $(x_i,y_i)$, conditional on any fixed increment $h$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
After prescribing any proper coordinate family, choose one unprescribed
coordinate to solve for. All other unprescribed coordinates are free,
and the coefficient of the final coordinate is $1$ or $-1$. There are
therefore exactly $|G|^{s-|I|-1}$ completions after prescribing the
coordinates in $I$, independently of their values. The labels $y_i$
are independently uniform by definition.
\end{proof}

The preceding independence is almost complete, but the omitted last
degree matters for sharp bounds. The next theorem retains it through
Fourier coefficients instead of discarding arrangements with several
erroneous differences.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A sharp spectral inequality with independent labels\srctag{60}}]{A sharp spectral inequality with independent labels}\label{gsr:en:60:sec:d4}
\srcnote{60}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:en:60:aux:section}

Let $S$ be a finite nonempty set and $F:G\times S\to K$.
Choose the horizontal coordinates as in \eqref{gsr:en:60:arr:balance} and labels
$u_1,\ldots,u_s\in S$ independently. Write $e_s(F)$ for the probability
that
\[
 \sum_{i\le m}F(x_i,u_i)\ne\sum_{i>m}F(x_i,u_i).
\]
This auxiliary test does not itself involve derivatives.

For a character $\chi\in\widehat K$, put
\[
 g_\chi(x)=\mathbb E_{u\in S}\chi(F(x,u)),\qquad
 \widehat g_\chi(\xi)=\mathbb E_{x\in G}
                 g_\chi(x)\overline{\xi(x)}.
\]
The horizontal Fourier transform is normalized; the sum over
$\widehat G$ below is not normalized. The average over $\widehat K$ is
normalized.

\begin{lemma}[Moment identity]\label{gsr:en:60:aux:moment}
For every even $s\ge4$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:aux:moment-equation}
 1-e_s(F)=\mathbb E_{\chi\in\widehat K}
             \sum_{\xi\in\widehat G}|\widehat g_\chi(\xi)|^s.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Character orthogonality on $K$ expresses acceptance as the character
average of the signed sum. Averaging the independent labels leaves
$g_\chi(x_i)$ on the first half and its complex conjugate on the second.
Expand each function in horizontal characters. Orthogonality in the
$s-1$ free coordinates forces one common frequency in all $s$ factors,
giving \eqref{gsr:en:60:aux:moment-equation}.
\end{proof}

Define, for $0\le t\le1/2$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:aux:profile-definition}
 E_s(t)=\frac{1-(1-2t)^s}{2}
             -2^{s-1}t^{s-1}(1-t).
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Auxiliary-label profile]\label{gsr:en:60:aux:profile}
If $t=\mathbb P_{x,u}[F(x,u)\ne0]\le1/2$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:aux:bound}
 e_s(F)\ge E_s(t).
\end{equation}
No condition on the exponent of any group or on the number of labels is
required.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The case $t=0$ is immediate. Suppose $t>0$, put $q=2t$ and
$b=(1-q)^2$, and write
\[
 a_\chi=\mathbb E_{x,u}\chi(F(x,u)),\qquad
 v_\chi=|a_\chi|^2.
\]
Because $F=0$ with probability $1-t$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:aux:constant-range}
 |a_\chi-1|\le2t,
 \qquad b\le v_\chi\le1.
\end{equation}
For a nontrivial horizontal character,
\[
 \widehat g_\chi(\xi)
 =\mathbb E_{x,u}\mathbf1_{\{F\ne0\}}
       (\chi(F(x,u))-1)\overline{\xi(x)},
\]
so $|\widehat g_\chi(\xi)|\le q$. Parseval and $|g_\chi|\le1$ give
\begin{align}
 \sum_{\xi\ne1}|\widehat g_\chi(\xi)|^s
 &\le q^{s-2}\sum_{\xi\ne1}|\widehat g_\chi(\xi)|^2
 \nonumber\\
 &\le q^{s-2}(1-v_\chi).
 \label{gsr:en:60:aux:tail}
\end{align}

Set
\[
 C=\frac{1-b^m}{1-b}=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}b^j.
\]
The chord of the convex function $z\mapsto z^m$ on $[b,1]$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:aux:chord}
 v_\chi^m\le1-C(1-v_\chi).
\end{equation}
Combining the last two inequalities yields
\[
 1-\sum_\xi|\widehat g_\chi(\xi)|^s
 \ge(C-q^{s-2})(1-v_\chi).
\]
The factor $C-q^{s-2}$ is nonnegative for $0<q\le1$, and is positive
when $q<1$. If $P(z)=\mathbb P[F=z]$, character orthogonality gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:aux:collision}
 \mathbb E_\chi v_\chi=\sum_zP(z)^2
 \le(1-t)^2+t^2.
\end{equation}
Hence the moment identity implies
\begin{align*}
 e_s(F)&\ge2t(1-t)(C-q^{s-2})\\
 &=\frac{1-(1-2t)^s}{2}
       -2^{s-1}t^{s-1}(1-t),
\end{align*}
as required. At $t=1/2$, the same calculation has $b=0$, $C=1$, and
gives the valid endpoint bound zero.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[All interior equality cases]\label{gsr:en:60:aux:equality}
Suppose $0<t<1/2$. Equality in \eqref{gsr:en:60:aux:bound} holds if and only if
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:aux:equality-model}
 F(x,u)=a\mathbf1_C(x),
\end{equation}
where $a\in K$ is a nonzero element of order two and $C$ is a coset of
a subgroup of $G$, with density $t$. In particular, the labels have no
effect and $t$ is the reciprocal of an integer at least three.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
All slack terms in the preceding proof are nonnegative. Since
$C-q^{s-2}>0$, equality forces equality in \eqref{gsr:en:60:aux:collision}.
The mass outside zero must therefore be concentrated at one nonzero
element $a$. Thus $F$ takes only the values $0,a$.

The chord inequality \eqref{gsr:en:60:aux:chord} is strict in the interior of
$[b,1]$, because $m\ge2$. Consequently
\[
 |1-t+t\chi(a)|^2\in\{(1-2t)^2,1\}
       \quad(\chi\in\widehat K).
\]
This is equivalent to $\chi(a)\in\{1,-1\}$ for every character.
Characters separate points, so $2a=0$; since $a\ne0$, its order is two.
Choose a character with $\chi(a)=-1$.

For this character, equality in the final step of \eqref{gsr:en:60:aux:tail}
forces $|g_\chi(x)|=1$ for every $x$: the multiplier $q^{s-2}$ is
positive. But $g_\chi(x)$ is the average of the signs distinguishing
$F(x,u)=0$ and $F(x,u)=a$. Thus these signs, and hence $F(x,u)$, are
independent of $u$ at each $x$. Let $C$ be the nonzero support.

Equality in the first step of \eqref{gsr:en:60:aux:tail} now says that every
nontrivial Fourier coefficient of $\mathbf1_C$ has modulus either zero
or $t$. The trivial coefficient has modulus $t$ as well. Fix $c\in C$
and let $J$ be the subgroup generated by $C-C$. Equality in the triangle
inequality for $\widehat{\mathbf1_C}(\xi)$ says that its modulus is $t$
exactly when $\xi$ is constant on $C$, equivalently when
$\xi\in J^\perp$. Therefore its Fourier support is precisely
$J^\perp$. Fourier inversion gives
\[
 \mathbf1_C(x)=t\sum_{\xi\in J^\perp}\xi(x-c)
              =t|J^\perp|\mathbf1_{c+J}(x).
\]
Evaluation at $c$ proves $t|J^\perp|=1$ and $C=c+J$.

Conversely, for a function of the form \eqref{gsr:en:60:aux:equality-model}, half
the characters of $K$ satisfy $\chi(a)=1$ and give $g_\chi=1$.
The other half give $g_\chi=1-2\mathbf1_C$. If $n=[G:J]=1/t$, this
function has constant Fourier coefficient $1-2t$ and $n-1$ other
nonzero coefficients, each of modulus $2t$. Thus
\[
 e_s(F)=\frac12\{1-(1-2t)^s-(n-1)(2t)^s\}=E_s(t),
\]
which proves sufficiency.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Monotone profile ratio]\label{gsr:en:60:aux:ratio}
The ratio $E_s(t)/t$, extended at zero by the value $s$, is strictly
decreasing on $[0,1/2]$. Its value at $1/2$ is zero. In particular,
$E_s(t)>0$ for $0<t<1/2$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For positive $t$,
\[
 \frac{E_s(t)}t=
 \sum_{j=0}^{s-1}(1-2t)^j-2^{s-1}t^{s-2}(1-t).
\]
The first term is strictly decreasing; its $j=1$ summand already is.
The derivative of $t^{s-2}(1-t)$ is
$t^{s-3}((s-2)-(s-1)t)>0$ on $(0,1/2]$. This proves strict
decrease. The endpoint values follow by substitution and continuity.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The complete polynomial and its equality cases\srctag{60}}]{The complete polynomial and its equality cases}\label{gsr:en:60:sec:d5}
\srcnote{60}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:en:60:arr:local-section}

Choose a nearest model $\psi$ and put $r=f-\psi$. Its arbitrary row
constants can be optimized separately. We may therefore suppose zero
is a most frequent value of $r(x,\cdot)$ in every row. Define
\begin{align}
 p_x(z)&=\mathbb P_y[r(x,y)=z],&
 \delta_x&=1-p_x(0),\nonumber\\
 t_h&=\mathbb P_{x,y}[D_hr(x,y)\ne0],&
 \overline t&=\mathbb E_h t_h.
 \label{gsr:en:60:arr:row-profile}
\end{align}
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:arr:profile-basic}
 \delta=\mathbb E_x\delta_x,\qquad
 0\le t_h\le2\delta,\qquad
 \overline t=\mathbb E_x\left(1-\sum_zp_x(z)^2\right)\ge\delta.
\end{equation}
Indeed, a nonzero derivative has at least one nonzero endpoint.
For the average, $(y,y+h)$ is uniformly independent, and
$\sum_zp_x(z)^2\le\max_zp_x(z)=p_x(0)$.
If $\delta_x\le\kappa\le1/2$ for every row, one also has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:arr:row-cap}
 \overline t\ge2(1-\kappa)\delta,
\end{equation}
because $\sum_zp_x(z)^2\le(1-\delta_x)^2+\delta_x^2$.

Define
\begin{align}
 B_s(d)&=\frac12E_s(2d)\nonumber\\
 &=\frac{1-(1-4d)^s}{4}
       -2^{2s-3}d^{s-1}(1-2d)\label{gsr:en:60:arr:polynomial}\\
 &=\frac{1-(1-q)^s-2q^{s-1}+q^s}{4},\qquad q=4d.
 \nonumber
\end{align}
The terms of degree $s$ cancel, so $B_s$ has degree $s-1$.

\begin{theorem}[Sharp all-order local polynomial]\label{gsr:en:60:arr:local}
For every even $s\ge4$ and every $f$ with $0<\delta\le1/4$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:arr:local-bound}
 \varepsilon_s(f)\ge\frac{\overline t}{\delta}B_s(\delta)
                         \ge B_s(\delta).
\end{equation}
Under the row cap $\delta_x\le\kappa\le1/2$, the stronger conclusion is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:arr:local-row-cap}
 \varepsilon_s(f)\ge2(1-\kappa)B_s(\delta).
\end{equation}
The unprofiled bound also holds at $\delta=0$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
At each fixed increment, apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:60:aux:profile} to
$F_h(x,y)=D_hr(x,y)$ with label set $H$. Since $t_h\le2\delta\le1/2$,
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:60:aux:ratio} implies
\[
 \varepsilon_s(f)\ge\mathbb E_hE_s(t_h)
 \ge\frac{E_s(2\delta)}{2\delta}\overline t
 =\frac{\overline t}{\delta}B_s(\delta).
\]
Now use \eqref{gsr:en:60:arr:profile-basic} or \eqref{gsr:en:60:arr:row-cap}.
\end{proof}

For orientation, the first two polynomials are
\begin{align}
 B_4(d)&=4d-24d^2+32d^3,\label{gsr:en:60:arr:b4}\\
 B_6(d)&=6d-60d^2+320d^3-960d^4+1024d^5.
 \label{gsr:en:60:arr:b6}
\end{align}
The first is the sharp cubic already proved in \cite{repo60thirtythree}. The
second and the higher polynomials close the gap left by that report's
one-error estimate. More explicitly, its conditional polynomial is
\[
 L_s(t)=st(1-t)((1-t)^{s-2}-t^{s-2}),
\]
and direct parity expansion gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:arr:strict-improvement}
 E_s(t)-L_s(t)=
 \sum_{\substack{3\le j\le s-3\\j\ \mathrm{odd}}}
 \binom{s}{j}
 \{t^j(1-t)^{s-j}-t^{s-1}(1-t)\}.
\end{equation}
Every summand is positive for $0<t<1/2$. The sum is empty for $s=4$
and nonempty for every even $s\ge6$. Therefore the new polynomial
strictly improves the earlier one throughout $0<d<1/4$ in those
higher orders.

\begin{lemma}[Distance of a single coset spike to affine maps]
\label{gsr:en:60:arr:coset-spike}
Let $J\le G$ have index $n\ge3$, let $C$ be a coset of $J$, and let
$v$ be a nonzero element of an abelian group $M$. The distance of
$x\mapsto v\mathbf1_C(x)$ to the affine maps $G\to M$ is exactly $1/n$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The zero map gives the upper bound. Consider an affine map $\Lambda$
with additive part $L$. If $L|_J$ is nonzero, the proportion matching
any constant target in each $J$-coset is at most $1/2$, because a
nonempty fiber of $L|_J$ has index at least two. Thus the disagreement
is at least $1/2$.

If $L|_J=0$, descend to $G/J$, whose order is $n$. A constant affine
map cannot improve on zero. For a nonconstant affine map, let $r\ge2$
be the size of its additive image; then $r$ divides $n$. It matches
zero on at most $n/r$ quotient points and the exceptional nonzero
target on at most one further point. If $n\ge4$,
$n/r+1\le n/2+1\le n-1$. If $n=3$, necessarily $r=3$, and the same
bound is $n/r+1=2=n-1$. At least one quotient point is therefore
wrong, giving disagreement at least $1/n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Classification of equality in the local polynomial]
\label{gsr:en:60:arr:equality}
Let $s\ge4$ be even and $0<\delta_{\mathcal V}(f)<1/4$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:arr:equality-condition}
 \varepsilon_s(f)=B_s(\delta_{\mathcal V}(f))
\end{equation}
if and only if there exist $\psi\in\mathcal V$, a nonzero element
$a\in K$ of order two, a surjective homomorphism
$\lambda:H\to\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$, and a coset $C$ of a subgroup
$J\le G$ with index $n\ge3$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:arr:equality-form}
 f(x,y)=\psi(x,y)+a\mathbf1_C(x)\lambda(y).
\end{equation}
The last product denotes $0$ or $a$ according to the binary values.
Every such function has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:arr:equality-distance}
 \delta_{\mathcal V}(f)=\frac1{2n},
\end{equation}
and attains equality simultaneously for every even $s\ge4$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
First assume equality and choose the modal nearest residual $r$ used
above. Since $B_s(\delta)>0$ and the ratio in Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:60:aux:ratio}
is strictly decreasing, every step in \eqref{gsr:en:60:arr:local-bound} can be
an equality only if
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:arr:equality-profile}
 \overline t=\delta,\qquad t_h\in\{0,2\delta\}
                       \quad\text{for every }h.
\end{equation}
Moreover, equality holds in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:60:aux:profile} at each active
increment, meaning each $h$ with $t_h>0$. By
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:60:aux:equality}, $D_hr(x,y)$ is independent of $y$ at
every active increment. It is zero everywhere at every inactive
increment. Thus every derivative of each row is independent of its
base point, and
\[
 r(x,y)=c(x)+L_x(y)
\]
for homomorphisms $L_x:H\to K$.

The common kernel
\[
 H_0=\{h:L_x(h)=0\text{ for every }x\}
\]
is exactly the set of inactive increments. Equation
\eqref{gsr:en:60:arr:equality-profile} says that the active proportion is $1/2$,
so $[H:H_0]=2$. Let $\lambda:H\to\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$ have kernel
$H_0$. Every $L_x$ factors through $\lambda$. Fix one active increment
$h_0$. Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:60:aux:equality} gives
\[
 L_x(h_0)=a\mathbf1_C(x),
\]
where $a$ has order two and $C$ is a subgroup coset of density
$2\delta$. Consequently $L_x(y)=a\mathbf1_C(x)\lambda(y)$.
Absorbing $c(x)$ into the model proves \eqref{gsr:en:60:arr:equality-form}.
The index is greater than two because $\delta<1/4$.

For the converse, it suffices to treat
$f_0(x,y)=a\mathbf1_C(x)\lambda(y)$, since adding a model changes
neither distance nor test outcomes. Compare $f_0$ with an arbitrary
model $b(x)+B(x,y)+\ell(y)$. Its row slope is the affine map
\[
 \Lambda:G\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}(H,K),\qquad
 \Lambda(x)=B(x,\cdot)+\ell.
\]
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:60:arr:coset-spike}, applied to the nonzero homomorphism
$a\lambda$, says that these slopes disagree with those of $f_0$ on
at least $1/n$ of the rows. In every such row, the difference is a
nonconstant affine map of $H$, whose zero set has density at most
$1/2$. Even after optimizing all row constants, the distance is
therefore at least $1/(2n)$. The zero model attains that distance.

For half the increments, $\lambda(h)=0$ and the test always accepts.
For the other half,
$D_hf_0(x,y)=a\mathbf1_C(x)$, and Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:60:aux:equality} gives
failure $E_s(1/n)$. Averaging proves
$\varepsilon_s(f_0)=E_s(1/n)/2=B_s(1/(2n))$.
\end{proof}

This classification includes even subgroup indices. The earlier
example in \cite{repo60thirtythree} used odd cyclic orders to simplify the
nearest-model argument. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:60:arr:coset-spike} removes that
restriction. It also shows the exact scope of the word sharp: the
polynomial is attained at the classified distances $1/(2n)$, including
a sequence tending to zero. The theorem does not claim that it is the
best pointwise bound at every other feasible distance.


\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/60-fourier-limits-arrangement_profiles.pdf}
\caption{Left: the new $s=16$ polynomial and the earlier $F_{16}$ on
$0\le\delta\le1/4$. Markers are equality examples at $\delta=1/(2n)$,
$3\le n\le24$; the shaded interval is the increasing branch used below.
The full polynomial is not globally increasing. Right: a classified
equality map on $\mathbb Z_{12}\times\mathbb Z_8$ with target $\mathbb Z_2$,
$C=\{0,4,8\}$ and $\ell_2(y)=y\bmod2$. The dark cells have value one.
Its distance is $1/8$, illustrating an even subgroup index.}
\label{gsr:en:60:fig:profiles}
\end{figure}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A repair modulus sharp to every asymptotic order\srctag{60}}]{A repair modulus sharp to every asymptotic order}\label{gsr:en:60:sec:d6}
\srcnote{60}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:en:60:arr:inverse-section}

To invert a local polynomial one must first locate the nearest model
on its small branch. We use the previously established elementary
decoder from \cite{repo60thirtythree}, whose proof is included in
Appendix~\ref{gsr:fz:60:decode:section}:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:arr:coarse-input}
 \varepsilon_4(f)<\frac1{216}
       \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \delta_{\mathcal V}(f)\le60\varepsilon_4(f).
\end{equation}
The moment identity also implies
$\varepsilon_4(f)\le\varepsilon_s(f)$: every Fourier coefficient has
modulus at most one, so the acceptance moment decreases with $s$.

\begin{lemma}[An explicit increasing branch]\label{gsr:en:60:arr:branch}
The polynomial $B_s$ is strictly increasing on
$[0,1/(4(s-1))]$, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:arr:branch-endpoint}
 B_s\left(\frac1{4(s-1)}\right)>\frac{23}{216}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
With $q=4d$,
\[
 B_s'(d)=s(1-q)^{s-1}-2(s-1)q^{s-2}+sq^{s-1}.
\]
For $0\le q\le1/(s-1)$ this is at least
\[
 s\left(\frac{s-2}{s-1}\right)^{s-1}
                  -\frac2{(s-1)^{s-3}}>0.
\]
The final inequality is equivalent to
$s(s-2)^{s-1}>2(s-1)^2$. For $s\ge4$ it follows from
$(s-2)^{s-1}\ge(s-2)^3$, $s(s-2)>2(s-1)$, and
$(s-2)^2\ge s-1$.

At the endpoint $q=1/(s-1)$, Bernoulli's inequality gives
$(1-q)^s\le1/(1+sq)<1/2$. Also $2q^{s-1}\le2/27$.
Substitution in \eqref{gsr:en:60:arr:polynomial}, retaining the nonnegative
$q^s$ term or discarding it, proves
\[
 B_s\left(\frac1{4(s-1)}\right)
       >\frac14\left(\frac12-\frac2{27}\right)=\frac{23}{216}.
\]
\end{proof}

Let $\rho_s$ denote the inverse branch of $B_s$ with values in
$[0,1/(4(s-1))]$.

\begin{theorem}[All-order repair]\label{gsr:en:60:arr:repair}
If
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:arr:activation}
 \varepsilon_s(f)\le\frac1{240(s-1)},
\end{equation}
then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:arr:repair-bound}
 \delta_{\mathcal V}(f)\le\rho_s(\varepsilon_s(f)).
\end{equation}
The activation threshold is the same sufficient threshold as in
\cite{repo60thirtythree}; no optimality of that threshold is asserted.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The moment comparison and \eqref{gsr:en:60:arr:coarse-input} give
\[
 \delta\le60\varepsilon_s(f)\le\frac1{4(s-1)}.
\]
The coarse decoder applies because
$1/(240(s-1))\le1/720<1/216$.
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:60:arr:local} gives $B_s(\delta)\le\varepsilon_s(f)$.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:60:arr:branch} places this error in the domain of $\rho_s$ and
permits inversion on the branch containing $\delta$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Optimal higher coefficients]\label{gsr:en:60:arr:coefficients}
For every even $s\ge6$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:arr:inverse-cubic}
 \rho_s(u)=\frac us+\frac{2(s-1)}{s^2}u^2
       +\frac{8(s-1)(2s-1)}{3s^3}u^3+O_s(u^4).
\end{equation}
For $s=4$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:arr:inverse-four}
 \rho_4(u)=\frac u4+\frac38u^2+u^3+\frac{105}{32}u^4+O(u^5).
\end{equation}
Every Taylor coefficient of $\rho_s$ is optimal in succession for
uniform asymptotic repair estimates over finite abelian groups.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For $s\ge6$, the correction term in \eqref{gsr:en:60:arr:polynomial} begins at
degree $s-1\ge5$, so
\[
 B_s(d)=sd-2s(s-1)d^2
           +\frac83s(s-1)(s-2)d^3+O_s(d^4).
\]
Substituting a power series into $B_s(\rho_s(u))=u$ yields
\eqref{gsr:en:60:arr:inverse-cubic}. The case $s=4$ instead uses the whole cubic
\eqref{gsr:en:60:arr:b4}, giving \eqref{gsr:en:60:arr:inverse-four}.

The inverse is analytic near zero because $B_s'(0)=s>0$.
For each $n\ge3$, take $G=\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$, $H=K=\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$,
$C=\{0\}$, and $f_n(x,y)=\mathbf1_C(x)y$.
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:60:arr:equality} gives
\[
 \delta_n=\frac1{2n},\qquad
 \varepsilon_s(f_n)=B_s(\delta_n).
\]
For sufficiently large $n$, these examples lie on the inverse branch
and satisfy $\delta_n=\rho_s(\varepsilon_s(f_n))$ exactly. Since their
errors tend to zero, reducing any coefficient while keeping all earlier
coefficients fixed contradicts these equalities at the first changed
order. The statement allows the remainder constant to depend on fixed
$s$, but not on the groups or the function.
\end{proof}

For example,
\begin{align*}
 \rho_6(u)&=\frac u6+\frac5{18}u^2+\frac{55}{81}u^3+O(u^4),\\
 \rho_{16}(u)&=\frac u{16}+\frac{15}{128}u^2
                           +\frac{155}{512}u^3+O(u^4).
\end{align*}
At $s=16$, the quadratic inverse in \cite{repo60thirtythree} has cubic coefficient
$225/512$; the sharp value is $155/512$. More generally, classical
Lagrange inversion gives a reproducible formula for every coefficient:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:arr:lagrange}
 [u^j]\rho_s(u)=\frac1j[z^{j-1}]
                         \left(\frac z{B_s(z)}\right)^j.
\end{equation}
Thus the higher-arrangement coefficient question in \cite{repo60thirtythree} is
answered to every order. The exact equality portion of its cubic
classification question is answered by Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:60:arr:equality};
quantitative near-equality is a separate problem.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Odd targets and a sharper common-prime coefficient interval\srctag{60}}]{Odd targets and a sharper common-prime coefficient interval}\label{gsr:en:60:sec:d7}
\srcnote{60}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:en:60:arr:prime-section}

The equality family uses two-torsion, so it does not determine the
optimal second coefficient when $G=H=K=\mathbb F_p$ with $p$ odd.
The earlier report \cite{repo60thirtythree} placed that optimal coefficient
between $(3s-2)/(4s^2)$ and $2(s-1)/s^2$. We improve both ends.
An expansion through two erroneous queries gives a stronger repair
upper bound whenever the target has odd order. A block of rows
carrying a two-valued interval function gives a larger lower
obstruction over a common prime field. The resulting interval is
still not a determination of the optimal coefficient.

\begin{lemma}[A uniform expansion through two errors]\label{gsr:en:60:arr:three-error}
Let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_s$ be $K$-valued random variables, where $s=2m\ge4$.
Suppose every three-coordinate subfamily is independent, each
marginal is zero with probability $1-t$, and the conditional
distribution outside zero is $q$. Put
\[
 c(q)=\sum_{z\ne0}q(z)^2,\qquad
 d(q)=\sum_{z\ne0}q(z)q(-z),\qquad
 D_s=(s^2+1)\binom{s}{3}.
\]
For $m$ positive signs and $m$ negative signs, the failure probability
$e=\mathbb P[\sum_i\sigma_iZ_i\ne0]$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:arr:second-expansion}
 \left|e-st+
   \left\{\binom{s}{2}+m^2c(q)+m(m-1)d(q)\right\}t^2\right|
 \le D_st^3.
\end{equation}
If $t=0$, the conclusion is interpreted as $e=0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $t>0$, put $I_i=\mathbf1_{\{Z_i\ne0\}}$ and
$C_{ij}=\mathbf1_{\{\sigma_iZ_i+\sigma_jZ_j=0\}}$.
The expression
\[
 T=\sum_iI_i-\sum_{i<j}(1+C_{ij})I_iI_j
\]
equals the failure indicator whenever at most two variables are
nonzero. Opposite-sign pairs cancel with conditional probability
$c(q)$; there are $m^2$ such pairs. Same-sign pairs cancel with
conditional probability $d(q)$; there are $m(m-1)$ of them. Pairwise
independence therefore gives
\[
 \mathbb ET=st-
   \left\{\binom{s}{2}+m^2c(q)+m(m-1)d(q)\right\}t^2.
\]
At every outcome, the absolute discrepancy between $T$ and the
failure indicator is at most $s^2+1$. The probability of at least
three nonzero variables is at most $\binom{s}{3}t^3$, by the union
bound and three-coordinate independence. This proves the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[A stronger quadratic repair coefficient for odd targets]
\label{gsr:en:60:arr:odd-target}
Suppose $K$ has odd order, and set
\[
 C_s=\frac{s(3s-2)}4,\qquad
 Q_s(d)=sd-2C_sd^2-4D_sd^3,
 \qquad D_s=(s^2+1)\binom{s}{3}.
\]
For the auxiliary test of Section~\ref{gsr:en:60:aux:section}, without a
smallness assumption on $t=\mathbb P[F\ne0]$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:arr:odd-auxiliary}
 e_s(F)\ge st-C_st^2-D_st^3.
\end{equation}
For arrangements, if $\delta=\delta_{\mathcal V}(f)\le1/(4s^2)$,
then $\varepsilon_s(f)\ge Q_s(\delta)$. If
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:arr:odd-activation}
 \varepsilon_s(f)\le\frac1{240s^2},
\end{equation}
the inverse branch of $Q_s$ on $[0,1/(4s^2)]$ gives the uniform bound
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:arr:odd-repair}
 \delta_{\mathcal V}(f)
 \le\frac{\varepsilon_s(f)}s
       +\frac{3s-2}{2s^2}\varepsilon_s(f)^2
       +O_s(\varepsilon_s(f)^3).
\end{equation}
No claim of sharpness is made for the quadratic coefficient in
\eqref{gsr:en:60:arr:odd-repair} or for the convenient cubic remainder and
activation threshold.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Because $K$ has no nonzero element of order two, its nonzero elements
partition into distinct pairs $\{z,-z\}$. Therefore
\[
 c(q)+d(q)=\sum_{\{z,-z\}}(q(z)+q(-z))^2\le1,
\]
and
\[
 m^2c(q)+m(m-1)d(q)\le m^2.
\]
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:60:arr:three-error}, with
$\binom{s}{2}+m^2=C_s$, proves \eqref{gsr:en:60:arr:odd-auxiliary}.

For arrangements, take the modal nearest residual and the profile
\eqref{gsr:en:60:arr:row-profile}. Apply \eqref{gsr:en:60:arr:odd-auxiliary} at each
increment. Since $t_h\le2\delta$,
\begin{align*}
 \varepsilon_s(f)
 &\ge s\overline t-C_s\mathbb E_ht_h^2-D_s\mathbb E_ht_h^3\\
 &\ge(s-2C_s\delta-4D_s\delta^2)\overline t.
\end{align*}
The multiplier is positive in the stated range, so
$\overline t\ge\delta$ gives $\varepsilon_s(f)\ge Q_s(\delta)$.
For completeness, both this positivity and the increasing inverse
branch follow from one estimate. Since $C_s\le3s^2/4$ and
$D_s\le s^5/3$, for $0\le d\le1/(4s^2)$ one has
\begin{align*}
 Q_s'(d)&=s-4C_sd-12D_sd^2\\
 &\ge s-\frac34-\frac s4
 \ge\frac{9s}{16}>\frac s2.
\end{align*}
The multiplier above is at least $Q_s'(\delta)$.

Under \eqref{gsr:en:60:arr:odd-activation}, the coarse decoder gives
$\delta\le60\varepsilon_s(f)\le1/(4s^2)$. Its own threshold is
automatically satisfied. Moreover,
$Q_s(1/(4s^2))\ge1/(8s)>1/(240s^2)$, so the inverse is defined on
the whole required error interval. Inverting $Q_s$ gives the first
two coefficients $1/s$ and $2C_s/s^3=(3s-2)/(2s^2)$, proving
\eqref{gsr:en:60:arr:odd-repair} with a uniform remainder.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Proved again, independently,} by source~96 (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:96:thm:arr-odd}, Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:oddarrangements}), which did not know this source: its profile $\varepsilon\ge sd-s(3s-2)d^2/2$ holds for every full-domain map, with no cubic remainder and no smallness hypothesis; this theorem has priority and the all-order inverse coefficients.
\end{writenote}

\begin{theorem}[Improved common-prime obstruction]\label{gsr:en:60:arr:prime-obstruction}
Fix an even $s\ge4$. There are functions
$f_p:\mathbb F_p^2\to\mathbb F_p$, with $p$ tending to infinity through
odd primes and $\delta_p=\delta_{\mathcal V}(f_p)\to0$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:arr:prime-defect}
 \varepsilon_s(f_p)=s\delta_p-s(s-1)\delta_p^2+O_s(\delta_p^3).
\end{equation}
Consequently, every uniform common-prime repair estimate of the form
\[
 \delta_{\mathcal V}(f)\le\frac{\varepsilon_s(f)}s
           +c\varepsilon_s(f)^2
           +O_s(\varepsilon_s(f)^3),
\]
with a remainder constant independent of $p$ and $f$, must have
$c\ge(s-1)/s^2$. If $c_s^{\mathrm{prime}}$ denotes the infimum of
admissible coefficients in such uniform estimates, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:arr:prime-bracket}
 \frac{s-1}{s^2}\le c_s^{\mathrm{prime}}
                         \le\frac{3s-2}{2s^2}.
\end{equation}
The upper bound in this bracket is the odd-target theorem; the lower
bound is the new obstruction. Both improve the corresponding
endpoints recorded in \cite{repo60thirtythree}.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $R=\lfloor\sqrt p\rfloor$, choose any $S_p\subset\mathbb F_p$ of
size $R$, and put
\[
 A_p=\{0,1,\ldots,(p-3)/2\},\qquad
 f_p(x,y)=\mathbf1_{S_p}(x)\mathbf1_{A_p}(y).
\]
The indicators are regarded as elements of $\mathbb F_p$. Write
$r=R/p$ and $\alpha=(p-1)/(2p)$.

For zero slope, each row is best approximated by the constant zero:
in the active rows, $\alpha<1/2$. Its distance is $r\alpha$.
To rule out other slopes, note that every model over the common prime
field has the form $a(x)+(bx+c)y$. If $(b,c)\ne(0,0)$, its slope is
nonzero in at least $p-1$ rows, and on each such row its distance from
zero is at least $1-1/p$, independently of $a(x)$. Thus that model's
distance from zero is at least $(1-1/p)^2$. By the triangle inequality,
its distance from $f_p$ is at least $(1-1/p)^2-r\alpha$, which exceeds
$r\alpha$ for all sufficiently large $p$. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:arr:prime-distance}
 \delta_p=r\alpha=\frac{R(p-1)}{2p^2}.
\end{equation}

Use representatives $h=0,\ldots,p-1$ and define
\[
 \rho_h=\mathbb P_y[
       \mathbf1_{A_p}(y+h)\ne\mathbf1_{A_p}(y)]
       =\frac{2\min(h,p-h)}p.
\]
The two nonzero derivative values $1,-1$ occur equally often. For
fixed $h$, a uniformly sampled derivative of $f_p$ therefore has
probabilities $1-r\rho_h,r\rho_h/2,r\rho_h/2$ at $0,1,-1$.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:60:arr:independence} gives three-coordinate independence,
even when $s=4$. Here the nonzero conditional law assigns probability
$1/2$ to each of $1,-1$, so $c(q)=d(q)=1/2$. Applying
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:60:arr:three-error} conditionally and then averaging yields
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:arr:prime-uniform-remainder}
 \left|\varepsilon_s(f_p)-sr\mathbb E_h\rho_h
       +\frac34s(s-1)r^2\mathbb E_h\rho_h^2\right|
 \le(s^2+1)\binom{s}{3}r^3.
\end{equation}
The error constant here is independent of $p$ and of the choice of
$S_p$.

The interval has two shifts of each length $1,\ldots,(p-1)/2$, so the
elementary sums of the first powers and squares give the exact moments
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:arr:rho-moments}
 \mathbb E_h\rho_h=\frac{p^2-1}{2p^2},\qquad
 \mathbb E_h\rho_h^2=\frac{p^2-1}{3p^2}.
\end{equation}
Substitution, followed by \eqref{gsr:en:60:arr:prime-distance}, gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:arr:prime-preasymptotic}
 \varepsilon_s(f_p)=s\delta_p\left(1+\frac1p\right)
   -s(s-1)\delta_p^2\frac{p+1}{p-1}+O_s(r^3).
\end{equation}
Since $R=\lfloor\sqrt p\rfloor$, one has $r=O(\delta_p)$ and
$p^{-1}=O(\delta_p^2)$. Thus \eqref{gsr:en:60:arr:prime-preasymptotic} implies
\eqref{gsr:en:60:arr:prime-defect}, with a uniform remainder.

Reversing the expansion proves
\[
 \delta_p=\frac{\varepsilon_s(f_p)}s
            +\frac{s-1}{s^2}\varepsilon_s(f_p)^2
            +O_s(\varepsilon_s(f_p)^3),
\]
which forces the lower bound in \eqref{gsr:en:60:arr:prime-bracket}.
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:60:arr:odd-target} supplies its upper bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{A later independent proof} (forward pointer, not checked at this write). Source~96, placed by \texttt{09f5b745a} during this write and not yet written in, proves the odd-target repair and the common-prime bracket $[15/256,23/256]$ at $s=16$ independently, in a version with no cubic term and no smallness condition, according to its placement record; it is to be written with source~96. This source arrived first, and the results are printed once, in its form.
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{The same construction} is source~96's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:96:thm:arr-prime-obstruction}, found independently; the bracket $[15/256,23/256]$ at $s=16$ is this source's first.
\end{writenote}

The growing number of active rows is essential to the second-order
calculation. With a single active row, the unavoidable odd-prime
imbalance between the two row values contributes at second order.
Here it contributes only to the uniform cubic remainder. For
eight-arrangements the improved bracket is
\[
 \frac{15}{256}\le c_{16}^{\mathrm{prime}}\le\frac{23}{256},
\]
in place of the earlier interval $[23/512,15/128]$. Determining the
optimal value inside the new interval remains open.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Two-direction testing and sharp robust intersection\srctag{60}}]{Two-direction testing and sharp robust intersection}\label{gsr:en:60:sec:d8}\label{gsr:en:60:sec:two-direction}
\srcnote{60}{Section 8}

The vertical test is invariant under adding an arbitrary function of $x$. Consequently a vertical repair theorem cannot, by itself, produce a fully biaffine map. The horizontal analogue removes this freedom, but only after the two approximate models have been synchronized. The following argument gives an exact robust-intersection modulus before bringing in the arrangement tests.

\subsection{The model classes and their separation}

For finite abelian $G,H,K$, let
\begin{align*}
 \Vcal&=\{a(x)+B(x,y)+\ell(y)\},\\
 \HH&=\{b(y)+C(x,y)+m(x)\},\\
 \A&=\{c+D(x,y)+m(x)+\ell(y)\},
\end{align*}
where $a:G\to K$ and $b:H\to K$ are arbitrary, $B,C,D$ are biadditive, $m:G\to K$ and $\ell:H\to K$ are homomorphisms, and $c\in K$. Clearly $\A\subseteq\Vcal\cap\HH$. The proof below also establishes the reverse inclusion.

\begin{lemma}[Separation of different bilinear parts]\label{gsr:en:60:two:bilinear-separation}
Suppose $v\in\Vcal$ and $w\in\HH$ have respective biadditive parts $B$ and $C$. If $B\ne C$, then
\[
 \dist(v,w)\ge\frac14.
\]
The constant $1/4$ cannot be increased in general.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Write $D=B-C$ and $v(x,y)-w(x,y)=D(x,y)+a_0(x)-b_0(y)$. Choose $u\in G$ such that the homomorphism $y\mapsto D(u,y)$ is nonzero. For each $x$, let
\[
 S_x=\{y:v(x,y)=w(x,y)\}.
\]
If $y\in S_x\cap S_{x+u}$, subtraction gives
\[
 D(u,y)+a_0(x+u)-a_0(x)=0.
\]
The solution set is empty or a coset of the kernel of a nonzero homomorphism, so it has density at most $1/2$. It follows that
\[
 \frac{|S_x|}{|H|}+\frac{|S_{x+u}|}{|H|}
 \le 1+\frac{|S_x\cap S_{x+u}|}{|H|}\le\frac32.
\]
Average over $x$ to obtain an agreement fraction at most $3/4$. For sharpness, the map $xy$ on $\Z_2\times\Z_2$ differs from the zero map at exactly one of the four points.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp robust intersection]\label{gsr:en:60:two:intersection}
Let $f:G\times H\to K$, and put
\[
 d_v=\dist(f,\Vcal),\qquad d_h=\dist(f,\HH),\qquad \eta=d_v+d_h.
\]
If $0\le\eta<1/4$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:two:J}
 \dist(f,\A)\le J(\eta)
 :=\frac{1+\eta-\sqrt{1-2\eta}}2.
\end{equation}
There are exact equality examples for a dense set of $\eta\in(0,1/4)$. In particular, no strictly smaller continuous upper bound as a function of $\eta$ alone is valid for all finite abelian groups.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Choose nearest models $v\in\Vcal$ and $w\in\HH$. Since
$\dist(v,w)\le\eta<1/4$, Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:60:two:bilinear-separation} forces their biadditive parts to agree. Subtract the common biaffine function $B(x,y)+m(x)+\ell(y)$ from $f,v,w$. After this subtraction the two approximants have the form $A(x)$ and $E(y)$, and their distances from the new $f$ are still $d_v,d_h$.

Let $p$ and $q$ be the value distributions of $A(x)$ and $E(y)$. The inputs $x,y$ are independent, so
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:two:agreement}
 \sum_zp(z)q(z)=\Prob[A(x)=E(y)]\ge1-\eta.
\end{equation}
Each distribution has an atom of mass at least $1-\eta$, because their inner product is at most either largest atom. These atoms have the same location $c$. Indeed, if their locations were different, the agreement probability would be at most the sum of their two tail masses, hence at most $2\eta<1-\eta$.

Write $r=1-p(c)$ and $t=1-q(c)$. Then $0\le r,t\le\eta<1/4$, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:two:mismatch}
 \eta\ge\Prob[A\ne E]
 \ge r+t-2rt.
\end{equation}
The last inequality bounds the mass of equal nonmodal values by $rt$. Pointwise,
\[
 \1_{\{f\ne c\}}
 \le\1_{\{f\ne A(x)\}}+\1_{\{f\ne E(y)\}}
       +\1_{\{A(x)=E(y)\ne c\}}.
\]
Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:two:eta-rt}
 \dist(f,c)\le\eta+rt.
\end{equation}
Put $z=\sqrt{rt}<1/2$. By the arithmetic--geometric mean inequality and \eqref{gsr:en:60:two:mismatch},
\[
 2z-2z^2\le r+t-2rt\le\eta.
\]
The function $2z-2z^2$ increases on $[0,1/2]$, so
\[
 z\le\frac{1-\sqrt{1-2\eta}}2.
\]
Substitution in \eqref{gsr:en:60:two:eta-rt} gives $\eta+z^2\le J(\eta)$. Adding back the common biaffine function gives \eqref{gsr:en:60:two:J}.

For equality, take $G=H=\Z_n$ with $n$ odd and $K=\Z_2$. Choose $S\subseteq G$ and $T\subseteq H$ with the same density $u$, where
\[
 0<u<\frac{1-1/\sqrt2}{2}.
\]
Let $f$ be the indicator of $(S\times H)\cup(G\times T)$. There are no nonzero homomorphisms from the odd-order groups to $\Z_2$, so $\Vcal$ consists of row functions, $\HH$ of column functions, and $\A$ of constants. Optimizing a modal value in every row or column gives
\[
 d_v=d_h=u(1-u),\qquad
 \dist(f,\A)=2u-u^2=J\bigl(2u(1-u)\bigr).
\]
Rational $u$ with odd denominators are dense in the indicated interval. Their values of $\eta=2u(1-u)$ are dense in $(0,1/4)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The separation example in Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:60:two:bilinear-separation} proves sharpness of that lemma's threshold. It does not assert that the conclusion of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:60:two:intersection} fails at precisely $\eta=1/4$. Extending the modulus beyond its present range is a separate question. Taking $\eta=0$ proves $\Vcal\cap\HH=\A$.
\end{remark}

\subsection{A variance bound that uses both directions}

Let $\eps_s^v(f)$ be the vertical arrangement failure probability from the preceding section. Define $\eps_s^h(f)$ by exchanging the two input groups: choose a common horizontal increment $g\in G$, choose a uniform balanced relation among the $y_i$, and independently choose the $x_i$. The tested values are $D_g^x f(x_i,y_i)=f(x_i+g,y_i)-f(x_i,y_i)$. Thus both tests have their own balanced coordinates and their own independent labels.

\begin{lemma}[Two conditional collision defects]\label{gsr:en:60:two:variance}
Let $r:G\times H\to K$ satisfy $\Prob[r=0]=1-\delta$. Set
\[
 t_h^v=\Prob_{x,y}[D_h^y r(x,y)\ne0],\qquad
 t_g^h=\Prob_{x,y}[D_g^x r(x,y)\ne0].
\]
Then $0\le t_h^v,t_g^h\le2\delta$, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:two:variance-bound}
 \E_h t_h^v+\E_g t_g^h\ge2\delta(1-\delta).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The cap follows because a nonzero difference requires at least one of its endpoints to be nonzero. For the sum, let $Z(x,y)=e_{r(x,y)}$ in the Euclidean space with orthonormal basis $(e_z)_{z\in K}$. Independence of $x,y$ gives the orthogonal decomposition
\[
 Z=\E Z+(\E[Z\mid x]-\E Z)+(\E[Z\mid y]-\E Z)+W,
\]
where $W$ is orthogonal to all functions of $x$ and to all functions of $y$. Consequently
\begin{align*}
 \E\norm{Z-\E[Z\mid x]}_2^2
 +\E\norm{Z-\E[Z\mid y]}_2^2
 &\ge\E\norm{Z-\E Z}_2^2.
\end{align*}
If $p_x(z)=\Prob_y[r(x,y)=z]$, the first term equals
$\E_x(1-\sum_zp_x(z)^2)=\E_h t_h^v$, since $y$ and $y+h$ are independent uniform after averaging $h$. The other conditional variance is $\E_g t_g^h$. The total variance is $1-\sum_zp(z)^2$, where $p$ is the global value distribution of $r$. Finally,
\[
 \sum_zp(z)^2\le (1-\delta)^2+\delta^2,
\]
because all nonzero masses sum to $\delta$. This proves \eqref{gsr:en:60:two:variance-bound}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Two-direction local defect profile]\label{gsr:en:60:two:profile}
For even $s\ge4$, let $\delta=\dist(f,\A)\le1/4$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:two:P}
 \eps_s^v(f)+\eps_s^h(f)
 \ge P_s(\delta):=2(1-\delta)B_s(\delta).
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Subtract a nearest biaffine map and call the residual $r$. Each test is invariant under this subtraction, and $\Prob[r=0]=1-\delta$. For $\delta=0$ the claim is immediate. Otherwise apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:60:aux:profile} to $D_h^y r$ with labels $y$, and to $D_g^x r$ with labels $x$. Since $E_s(t)/t$ decreases on $[0,1/2]$ and every derivative defect is at most $2\delta$, the sum of the two failures is at least
\[
 \frac{E_s(2\delta)}{2\delta}
   \left(\E_h t_h^v+\E_g t_g^h\right)
 \ge (1-\delta)E_s(2\delta)=P_s(\delta).
\]
Here Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:60:two:variance} supplies the second inequality. The residual need not be modal in every row: only its global zero mass is used.
\end{proof}

\subsection{An activated inverse and optimal coefficients}

\begin{theorem}[Local biaffine repair]\label{gsr:en:60:two:repair}
Let $s\ge4$ be even, and set $e=\eps_s^v(f)+\eps_s^h(f)$. If
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:two:activation}
 0\le e\le\frac1{1920s},
\end{equation}
then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:two:repair-bound}
 \dist(f,\A)\le\sigma_s(e),
\end{equation}
where $\sigma_s$ is the inverse of $P_s$ on $[0,1/(16s)]$. In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:two:series}
 \sigma_s(e)=\frac e{2s}+\frac{2s-1}{4s^2}e^2+O_s(e^3).
\end{equation}
For $s\ge6$, the cubic coefficient is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:two:cubic}
 \sigma_s(e)=\frac e{2s}+\frac{2s-1}{4s^2}e^2
       +\frac{8s^2-3s-2}{12s^3}e^3+O_s(e^4).
\end{equation}
For $s=4$ the cubic coefficient of this upper bound is $21/128$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By the coarse decoder in Appendix~\ref{gsr:fz:60:decode:section} and the monotonicity $\eps_4\le\eps_s$,
\[
 d_v+d_h\le60e<\frac14.
\]
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:60:two:intersection} applies. For $0\le\eta<1/4$, its proof gives $J(\eta)\le\eta+\eta^2\le2\eta$. Hence
\[
 \delta:=\dist(f,\A)\le120e\le\frac1{16s}.
\]
This is the required choice of inverse branch.

We verify that the branch is increasing. Write $q=4\delta\le1/(4s)$. Differentiation gives
\[
 B_s'(\delta)
 =s(1-q)^{s-1}-2(s-1)q^{s-2}+s q^{s-1}.
\]
Bernoulli's inequality makes the first term at least $3s/4$. Since $s\ge4$ and $q\le1/(4s)$, the absolute value of the negative term is at most $2(s-1)/(16s^2)<s/4$. Thus $B_s'\ge s/2$. Also $B_s(\delta)\le s\delta$, by $1-(1-4\delta)^s\le4s\delta$ and the nonnegative correction subtracted in $B_s$. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:two:positive-derivative}
 P_s'(\delta)
 =2\bigl((1-\delta)B_s'(\delta)-B_s(\delta)\bigr)
 \ge s(1-3\delta)>0.
\end{equation}
Integrating shows that $P_s(1/(16s))>1/(1920s)$, so the inverse exists on the whole output range in \eqref{gsr:en:60:two:activation}. Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:60:two:profile} then gives \eqref{gsr:en:60:two:repair-bound}.

Finally, $B_s(\delta)=s\delta-2s(s-1)\delta^2+O_s(\delta^3)$, so
\[
 P_s(\delta)=2s\delta-2s(2s-1)\delta^2+O_s(\delta^3).
\]
For $s\ge6$ the cubic coefficient of $P_s$ is
$\tfrac43s(s-1)(4s-5)$, obtained by expanding \eqref{gsr:en:60:arr:polynomial}. Reversal of these series gives \eqref{gsr:en:60:two:series} and \eqref{gsr:en:60:two:cubic}. Directly using $B_4=4\delta-24\delta^2+32\delta^3$ gives the stated exceptional cubic coefficient.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp coefficients through degree $s-2$]\label{gsr:en:60:two:sharpness}
In the uniform expansion of the two-direction repair bound, every coefficient of $\sigma_s$ through degree $s-2$ is optimal in succession, with preceding coefficients fixed. Thus both coefficients in \eqref{gsr:en:60:two:series} are optimal for all $s\ge4$, and the cubic in \eqref{gsr:en:60:two:cubic} is optimal for $s\ge6$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Take $G=H=\Z_n$, $n$ odd, $K=\Z_2$, and $f(x,y)=\1_{\{0\}}(x)$. There are no nonzero homomorphisms from either domain group to $K$, so the biaffine maps are constants and
\[
 \delta=\dist(f,\A)=\frac1n.
\]
All vertical tests pass. A horizontal increment $g=0$ also always passes. For $g\ne0$, the derivative is supported on exactly two $x$-values. The $x_i$ in the horizontal test are independent, so its $s$ tested derivatives are independent Bernoulli random variables with parameter $2/n$ in $\Z_2$. The balanced condition constrains only their $y$-coordinates. Thus the failure is odd parity, and exactly
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:two:Cs}
 e=C_s(\delta):=\frac{1-\delta}{2}
                     \bigl(1-(1-4\delta)^s\bigr).
\end{equation}
Comparison with $P_s$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:60:two:gap}
 C_s(\delta)-P_s(\delta)
 =2^{2s-2}\delta^{s-1}(1-\delta)(1-2\delta).
\end{equation}
Both functions have derivative $2s$ at zero. Their inverse power series therefore agree through degree $s-2$. Letting odd $n\to\infty$ gives examples with $e\to0$ on which each of those coefficients is attained. A reduction of the first differing coefficient, with earlier ones fixed, would contradict this sequence.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The factor in \eqref{gsr:en:60:two:gap} begins at degree $s-1$. The proof therefore does not establish optimality at degree $s-1$ or beyond. In particular, the cubic $21/128$ at $s=4$ is a valid upper-bound coefficient, not a claimed sharp one. Nor is $P_s$ asserted to be the full finite-error envelope.
\end{remark}

\subsection{How often should each direction be tested?}

\begin{corollary}[Optimal fixed allocation at leading order]\label{gsr:en:60:two:allocation}
Suppose a tester chooses the vertical arrangement test with probability $p\in(0,1)$ and the horizontal test with probability $1-p$. Write
\[
 \eps_{\rm mix}=p\eps_s^v+(1-p)\eps_s^h,
 \qquad a=\min\{p,1-p\}.
\]
If $\eps_{\rm mix}\le a/(1920s)$, then
\[
 \dist(f,\A)\le\sigma_s(\eps_{\rm mix}/a)
 =\frac{\eps_{\rm mix}}{2sa}+O_{s,p}(\eps_{\rm mix}^2).
\]
The leading coefficient $1/(2sa)$ is optimal for each fixed $p$. It is minimized by $p=1/2$, where it equals $1/s$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Since $\eps_{\rm mix}\ge a(\eps_s^v+\eps_s^h)$, Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:60:two:repair} applies. The sparse-row example of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:60:two:sharpness}, or its transpose, puts all failure in the less frequently tested direction. Its error is $\eps_{\rm mix}=a C_s(\delta)=2sa\delta+O_s(\delta^2)$, proving the lower obstruction. Maximizing $\min(p,1-p)$ gives the stated allocation.
\end{proof}

\statusline{This section resolves the local full-product two-direction repair problem with sharp first-order constants and more precise asymptotics. Sparse domains, optimal finite-error envelopes, and stability of the robust-intersection equality examples remain open.}

\section{Source~67's Section~5: the interpolation count at Lemma~16.10 \wtag}\label{gsr:en:sec:interpolationcost}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the eleventh write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next section is source~67's Section~5. \emph{Logically it continues source~39's chapter} on shared anchors at Lemma~16.10 (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:sharedanchor}) and source~19's sampling sections; it is printed here because no number printed earlier may move.

\emph{What is proved.} If anchor $i$ carries a list of $L_i$ base functions and fibre classes have degree below $t$, then for $1\le t\le r$ every certified point (sampled, or with $t$ anchors in its class) is covered by at most $E_t(L_1,\ldots,L_r)$ functions (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:67:interp:thm:anchor-upper}): the ordinary $t$-anchor interpolants also cover the sampled points, so source~39's count $\sum_iL_i+E_t$ loses its first term (for affine fibres, $rL+\binom r2L^2$ becomes $\binom r2L^2$). The complete formula, with empty lists, is Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:67:interp:thm:anchor-all-cases}. The count is exact for the local interface: dense examples over large prime fields force all $E_t$ candidates even against candidates of arbitrary fixed degree in the base variable (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:67:interp:thm:anchor-lower}), with a product lower bound on the uncovered mass, so that $M\ge(1-\delta-o(1))E_t$ when a fraction $\delta$ may be deleted (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:67:interp:cor:anchor-asymptotic}), and a cell-count trade-off (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:67:interp:cor:anchor-partitions}). The elementary symmetric counting is credited to source~39, as source~67 says. The closing comparison of Lemma~16.10 is not addressed.

\section[{The exact number of interpolation candidates\srctag{67}}]{The exact number of interpolation candidates}\label{gsr:en:67:sec:d5}
\srcnote{67}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:en:67:interp:sec:anchor-optimality}

The shared-anchor argument in Gowers's Lemma~16.10~\cite{gowers} has two logically
separate costs: finding anchors that certify most points, and converting
the slice lists at those anchors into a list on the whole base cell.
Sources~19 and~39 in the existing ProveIt report~\cite{repo67anchor} substantially improve
the first cost and preserve the labels of the second. Source~39's
Section~10 gives, for degree less than $t$, the candidate bound
\[
 \sum_{i=1}^r L_i+
 \sum_{\substack{I\subseteq[r]\\|I|=t}}\prod_{i\in I}L_i,
\]
and its further-research section asks whether algebraic coincidences can
compress these lists and whether a matching lower-bound model exists.
Here the direct-anchor term is removed, and the remaining elementary
symmetric polynomial is shown to be the exact universal answer for
the fixed-cell interface. A quantitative lower bound continues to hold
after deletion of points, and gives a tradeoff between the number of
further cells and their list sizes.

This is a local assertion with a concrete optimality scope. The
construction satisfies the same slice-list and polynomial-fibre
hypotheses, with one class in every fibre and a domain of density
arbitrarily close to one. It is not asserted to satisfy every additional
product-property hypothesis of the full Gowers induction. The ordinary
interpolation count is closely related to polynomial list recovery at
the minimum agreement threshold; no priority claim for Lagrange
interpolation or for the general coding-theoretic viewpoint is intended.

\subsection{The local interface and the smaller upper bound}

Let $\mathbb F$ be a field, let $J\subseteq\mathbb F$ be finite, and fix
distinct anchors $a_1,\ldots,a_r\in J$. Write $R=\{a_1,\ldots,a_r\}$.
Let $H$ be a finite base set and let $V\subseteq\mathbb F^H$ be a linear
space. A partial function
\[
 \phi:B\longrightarrow\mathbb F,\qquad B\subseteq H\times J,
\]
has fibre $B_h=\{y:(h,y)\in B\}$. In every fibre suppose that $B_h$ is
partitioned into classes, and on each class $C$ the function
$y\mapsto\phi(h,y)$ agrees with a polynomial $P_{h,C}$ of degree less
than $t$. The number of classes will not enter the candidate theorem.

At each anchor $a_i$ suppose that a nonempty list
\[
 \mu_{i,1},\ldots,\mu_{i,L_i}\in V,\qquad L_i\ge1,
\]
covers the partial slice: whenever $(h,a_i)\in B$, its value is
$\mu_{i,j}(h)$ for at least one $j$. A common good subset of $H$ can
simply be substituted for $H$; the theorem makes no additional deletion.

A point of $B$ is \emph{certified} if it is itself sampled, or if its
class contains at least $t$ distinct anchors. This is the certification
rule of source~39: sampled points are retained even when their class
has fewer than $t$ anchors. Put
\[
 E_t(L_1,\ldots,L_r)
 :=\sum_{\substack{I\subseteq[r]\\|I|=t}}\prod_{i\in I}L_i.
\]

\begin{theorem}[No separate direct-anchor candidates]
\label{gsr:en:67:interp:thm:anchor-upper}
Suppose $1\le t\le r$. All certified points are covered by at most
\begin{equation}
 T=E_t(L_1,\ldots,L_r)
 \label{gsr:en:67:interp:eq:anchor-T}
\end{equation}
functions in
\[
 V\otimes\operatorname{Poly}_{<t}(J)
 =\left\{\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}v_j(h)y^j:v_j\in V\right\}.
\]
In particular, if every $L_i\le L$, the count is at most
$\binom rtL^t$. For affine fibres and separately affine base lists,
the count is $\binom r2L^2$, and every candidate is separately affine
in all base variables and in $y$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For a $t$-subset $I\subseteq[r]$ and one index $j_i\in[L_i]$ for each
$i\in I$, form the Lagrange interpolant
\begin{equation}
 F_{I,(j_i)}(h,y)
 =\sum_{i\in I}\mu_{i,j_i}(h)
      \prod_{\substack{k\in I\\k\ne i}}
                  \frac{y-a_k}{a_i-a_k}.
 \label{gsr:en:67:interp:eq:anchor-lagrange}
\end{equation}
All denominators are nonzero and all coefficients in the $y$-expansion
belong to $V$. There are $T$ indexed choices, possibly with repetitions.

For a nonsampled certified point, choose $t$ anchors from its class and
a correct list member at each of them. The two polynomials in $y$,
the class polynomial and the candidate evaluated at $h$, have degree
less than $t$ and agree at $t$ distinct points. They therefore coincide.

For a sampled point $(h,a_i)$, choose \emph{any} $t$-subset $I$
containing $i$, select a correct list member at $i$, and select arbitrary
members of the other nonempty lists. At $y=a_i$, all other Lagrange
coefficients vanish and the $i$th coefficient is one. Thus this
candidate covers the sampled point. Values at the other chosen anchors
need not belong to the same class, or even to the domain of $\phi$;
their candidate functions are nevertheless defined on the whole base
cell. This is precisely why the direct-anchor candidates are redundant.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Formalized since its arrival}, in the affine case and in the repository's own form (checked at HEAD \texttt{fb9602e55}): \file{Section16SampledOrAnchoredOn.compressed_multilinear_cover} (\file{Proofs16CompressedInterpolation.lean}, line~56; \texttt{081abc4d3}) gives a family of $\max(p,\binom r2p^2)$ candidates for arbitrary samples with replacement, and \file{section16_compressed_budget_lt_old} (\file{Proofs16CompressedCandidateBounds.lean}, line~42) the strict comparison with $rb+r^2b^2$; \file{FORMALIZATION\_STATUS.txt} cites this theorem. The case $t\ge3$ and the lower constructions are not formalized. Source~39's count is its Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:39:thm:labelled} and Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:39:cor:affine-list}.
\end{writenote}

\begin{theorem}[All anchor counts, including empty lists]
\label{gsr:en:67:interp:thm:anchor-all-cases}
Allow $r\ge0$, $t\ge1$, and $L_i\ge0$. Let
$A=\{i:L_i>0\}$ and $a=|A|$. With the same certification and
slice-cover hypotheses, every certified point is covered by at most
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal L_t(L_1,\ldots,L_r)=
 \begin{cases}
 0,&a=0,\\
 \max_iL_i,&0<a<t,\\
 E_t(L_1,\ldots,L_r),&a\ge t
 \end{cases}
 \label{gsr:en:67:interp:eq:anchor-all-cases}
\end{equation}
candidates in $V\otimes\operatorname{Poly}_{<t}(J)$.
For $t=1$ this becomes $\sum_iL_i$, including the all-empty case.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
An anchor with an empty covering list cannot meet the domain $B$ at
any base point under consideration. Removing those anchors changes
neither the sampled domain points nor the number of anchors in a
class. If none remain, there are no certified points. If at least
$t$ remain, apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:67:interp:thm:anchor-upper}; terms involving an
empty list vanish from $E_t$.

If $0<a<t$, no class can meet $t$ anchors, so all certified points
are sampled. Put $L_* =\max_iL_i$. Pad every nonempty list by repeating
its last member until it has length $L_*$. For each $1\le j\le L_*$,
interpolate the $j$th members across all $a$ active anchors. The
resulting polynomial in $y$ has degree at most $a-1<t$, with coefficients
in $V$. At each active anchor the $L_*$ candidates include every member
of that anchor's list. They therefore cover all sampled points.
\end{proof}

The change at $a=t$ reflects the certification rule. Below the
threshold, only anchor values must be covered, and their lists can
be aligned. At the threshold, the rule certifies nonsampled values,
and all independent interpolation choices may become necessary.

\subsection{Generic finite-field lists}

The lower bound requires genuinely different interpolants. The next
elementary lemma supplies them over an explicit range of prime fields.
For $u>r$, use the convention $E_u(L_1,\ldots,L_r)=0$.

\begin{lemma}[Lists with no interpolation collisions]
\label{gsr:en:67:interp:lem:anchor-generic}
Fix integers $r\ge t\ge1$ and $L_1,\ldots,L_r\ge1$, and set
\begin{equation}
 D=L_{i_*}-1+E_t\bigl((L_i)_{i\ne i_*}\bigr),
 \qquad L_{i_*}=\max_iL_i.
 \label{gsr:en:67:interp:eq:anchor-collision-count}
\end{equation}
Let $p$ be a prime with $p>\max\{r,D\}$. For any distinct
$a_1,\ldots,a_r\in\mathbb F_p$, one can choose sets
$A_i\subseteq\mathbb F_p$ of cardinality $L_i$ such that the following
hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item no polynomial of degree less than $t$ takes values in $A_i$ at
more than $t$ of the anchors;
\item the interpolants obtained by choosing a $t$-subset $I$ and one
value from each $A_i$, $i\in I$, are all distinct. There are exactly
$T=E_t(L_1,\ldots,L_r)$ of them.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Process the anchors in an order for which
$L_1\le\cdots\le L_r$, after relabelling if needed. Suppose the
lists at the previous anchors have been chosen. At anchor $a_i$,
forbid the values at $a_i$ of all polynomials interpolated from
$t$ of the previous lists. There are at most
$E_t(L_1,\ldots,L_{i-1})$ forbidden values. Since
\[
 L_i+E_t(L_1,\ldots,L_{i-1})
 \le L_r+E_t(L_1,\ldots,L_{r-1})=D+1\le p,
\]
one can choose $L_i$ distinct allowed values. This gives a
deterministic construction: for example, choose the first available
residues in increasing order.

If a polynomial of degree less than $t$ meets the final lists at
$t+1$ distinct anchors, consider the last of those anchors in the
construction. Its value was forbidden by the preceding $t$ anchors,
a contradiction. This proves the first conclusion. For the second, suppose
two indexed interpolants coincide. If their anchor sets coincide,
their values at each anchor force their ordinate selections to coincide.
If their anchor sets differ, their common polynomial meets the lists
at every anchor in their union, which has at least $t+1$ members.
This contradicts the first conclusion.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Meaning of the generic condition]
For $t=2$, the condition says that no nonvertical line through chosen
points on two anchor lines passes through a chosen point on a third
anchor line. Thus all cross-anchor secants are different. The lemma
gives a deterministic finite construction, not an unspecified
asymptotic genericity assumption. It is not intended to optimize
the true minimum field size. An independent union-bound proof would
give the sufficient condition
$p>\sum_i\binom{L_i}{2}+E_{t+1}(L_1,\ldots,L_r)$, usually larger.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[The best order for the greedy cardinality bound]
\label{gsr:en:67:interp:prop:anchor-greedy-order}
Among all anchor orders, the maximum of the stepwise upper bounds
\[
 L_i-1+E_t(L_1,\ldots,L_{i-1})
\]
is minimized by a nondecreasing order of the list sizes, and its value
there is $D$ from \eqref{gsr:en:67:interp:eq:anchor-collision-count}.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Consider adjacent sizes $x\le y$ after a fixed prefix, and put
$A=E_t(\text{prefix})$, $B=E_{t-1}(\text{prefix})$, with $E_0=1$.
The maximum of their two costs in the order $x,y$ is
$A+y+xB-1$. In the order $y,x$ it is
$A+\max\{y,x+yB\}-1$. If $B=0$ the maxima coincide. If $B\ge1$,
$y+xB\le x+yB$ because $(y-x)(B-1)\ge0$. Thus removing an inversion
cannot increase the maximum. All later prefix elementary symmetric
polynomials are unchanged. Repeated adjacent swaps prove optimality.
For a nondecreasing order the stepwise bounds are nondecreasing, so
the last equals the maximum, namely $D$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Exact optimality and deletion robustness}

Write $x_+=\max\{x,0\}$. A polynomial has bidegree at most $(d,t-1)$
if it has degree at most $d$ in the base variable $h$ and degree at most
$t-1$ in the fibre variable $y$, separately.

\begin{theorem}[Dense sharp examples and an explicit uncovered-mass bound]
\label{gsr:en:67:interp:thm:anchor-lower}
Fix $r\ge t\ge1$, $L_1,\ldots,L_r\ge1$, $d\ge1$, and $n\ge1$.
Let $T$ and $D$ be defined in \eqref{gsr:en:67:interp:eq:anchor-T} and
\eqref{gsr:en:67:interp:eq:anchor-collision-count}, and suppose that $p$ is prime with
\begin{equation}
 p>\max\{r,D,Tn-1\}.
 \label{gsr:en:67:interp:eq:anchor-field}
\end{equation}
There exist an interval $H\subseteq\mathbb F_p$ of size $Tn$,
$r$ anchors in $J=\mathbb F_p$, and a partial function
$\phi:B\to\mathbb F_p$ with $B\subseteq H\times J$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}
\item every fibre has one polynomial class of degree less than $t$;
\item the slice at anchor $i$ is covered by $L_i$ constant functions;
\item every point of $B$ is certified by the $r$ anchors;
\item the domain density is
\begin{equation}
 \frac{|B|}{|H|p}=1-\frac{r-t}{p};
 \label{gsr:en:67:interp:eq:anchor-domain-density}
\end{equation}
\item for every list of $M$ polynomials of bidegree at most $(d,t-1)$,
the number $U$ of domain points covered by none of them satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\quad
 U\ \ge\ (T-M)_+(n-dM)_+
                   \bigl(p-r-(t-1)M\bigr)_+ .\quad}
 \label{gsr:en:67:interp:eq:anchor-robust-lower}
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
Consequently, if
\begin{equation}
 n>d(T-1),\qquad p-r>(t-1)(T-1),
 \label{gsr:en:67:interp:eq:anchor-exact-range}
\end{equation}
every exact list cover requires at least $T$ candidates. Exactly $T$
are sufficient. In particular, the universal bound
$\binom r2L^2$ for affine fibres is best possible already for one base
variable, even if the competing candidates may have any fixed base
degree $d$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Take the lists $A_i$ from Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:67:interp:lem:anchor-generic}, and enumerate
their $T$ distinct interpolants as $P_1,\ldots,P_T$. Let $I_\nu$ be
the $t$ anchors used to define $P_\nu$. Set
\[
 H=\{0,1,\ldots,Tn-1\}\subseteq\mathbb F_p,
 \qquad
 H_\nu=\{(\nu-1)n,\ldots,\nu n-1\}.
\]
The size hypothesis makes these disjoint $n$-element blocks. Let
$S=\mathbb F_p\setminus R$, so $|S|=p-r$. For $h\in H_\nu$ put
\begin{equation}
 B_h=S\cup\{a_i:i\in I_\nu\},
 \qquad \phi(h,y)=P_\nu(y)\quad(y\in B_h).
 \label{gsr:en:67:interp:eq:anchor-example}
\end{equation}
The whole fibre is one polynomial class and contains exactly $t$
anchors. Thus it is entirely certified. At an anchor $a_i$ the only
defined values are elements of $A_i$, so $A_i$ supplies a list of
$L_i$ constant functions. Every fibre has size $p-r+t$, proving
\eqref{gsr:en:67:interp:eq:anchor-domain-density}.

Let the proposed cover be $F_1(h,y),\ldots,F_M(h,y)$. A candidate can
coincide as a polynomial with at most one of the distinct targets
$P_\nu(y)$. Hence at least $(T-M)_+$ targets have no identical
candidate. Fix such a target.

For each $j$, the difference
\[
 F_j(h,y)-P_\nu(y)=\sum_{b=0}^{t-1}c_{j,b}(h)y^b
\]
is a nonzero polynomial, and some coefficient $c_{j,b}$ is a nonzero
polynomial of degree at most $d$. There are at most $d$ values of $h$
at which every coefficient vanishes, that is, at which $F_j(h,\cdot)$
and $P_\nu$ agree identically in $y$. Across all $M$ candidates,
at most $dM$ rows have such a full-row coincidence. On each of the
remaining at least $(n-dM)_+$ rows of $H_\nu$, each candidate differs
from $P_\nu$ by a nonzero polynomial of degree at most $t-1$ in $y$.
It agrees at at most $t-1$ points of $S$. Their union therefore covers
at most $(t-1)M$ of the $p-r$ nonsampled columns on that row. At least
$(p-r-(t-1)M)_+$ points remain uncovered. Sum over the unmatched
targets. All counted points belong to $H\times S\subseteq B$, which
proves \eqref{gsr:en:67:interp:eq:anchor-robust-lower}.

If $M<T$, conditions~\eqref{gsr:en:67:interp:eq:anchor-exact-range} make every factor
strictly positive, so exact coverage is impossible. Conversely, the
list $P_1(y),\ldots,P_T(y)$ covers $B$ and has the required bidegree.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A single explicit sufficient prime condition]
\label{gsr:en:67:interp:cor:anchor-prime}
With $T,D,r,t,d$ fixed, put $n=d(T-1)+1$. Every prime
\[
 p>\max\{D,\ T[d(T-1)+1]-1,\ r+(t-1)(T-1)\}
\]
admits an example with exact minimum $T$ candidates. For the affine
case and separately affine candidates, one may take $t=2$, $d=1$,
$n=T$, and any prime
\[
 p>\max\left\{
 L_{i_*}-1+\sum_{\substack{i<j\\i,j\ne i_*}}L_iL_j,
 \ T^2-1,\ r+T-1
 \right\}.
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The displayed inequalities give \eqref{gsr:en:67:interp:eq:anchor-field} and
\eqref{gsr:en:67:interp:eq:anchor-exact-range}. In the general formula the last term
is at least $r$, as required by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:67:interp:lem:anchor-generic}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Asymptotically exact cost with permitted deletion]
\label{gsr:en:67:interp:cor:anchor-asymptotic}
Fix $r,t,L_1,\ldots,L_r,d$ and $0\le\varepsilon<1$. There are examples
of the preceding type with domain density tending to one such that
every list of $M<T$ bidegree-$(d,t-1)$ candidates leaves an ambient
fraction at least
\begin{equation}
 \left(1-\frac MT\right)
 \left(1-\frac{dM}{n}\right)
 \left(1-\frac{r+(t-1)M}{p}\right)
 \label{gsr:en:67:interp:eq:anchor-ambient-fraction}
\end{equation}
uncovered, whenever the displayed factors are nonnegative. In
particular, for $n\to\infty$ and primes $p\ge Tn$ tending to infinity,
an ambient deletion allowance of $\varepsilon$ forces
\[
 M\ge (1-\varepsilon-o(1))T.
\]
Conversely, retaining any $M$ of the target polynomials covers all
points in the corresponding $M$ row blocks and possibly further points, so
deleting at most a fraction $1-M/T$ of $B$ always suffices. Thus the
leading deletion--list tradeoff is sharp.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Divide \eqref{gsr:en:67:interp:eq:anchor-robust-lower} by $|H|p=Tnp$. The two last
factors tend to one uniformly over the finite range $0\le M<T$.
The upper comparison deletes all unselected blocks; these blocks
have the same domain mass because every row has $p-r+t$ points.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Sharpness below the anchor threshold]
\label{gsr:en:67:interp:prop:anchor-small-r-sharp}
Suppose that exactly $a$ lists are nonempty, where $0<a<t$, and put
$L_* =\max_iL_i$. Fix $d\ge1$ and choose $n>d(L_*-1)$.
Over every sufficiently large prime field, there is an example
satisfying the slice-list and certification hypotheses whose exact
minimum number of bidegree-$(d,t-1)$ candidates is $L_*$. Empty
lists and the all-empty case are therefore handled by the sharp
piecewise budget in \eqref{gsr:en:67:interp:eq:anchor-all-cases}.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
It suffices to take a prime
$p>\max\{r,L_*,L_*n-1\}$ and $r$ distinct anchors. Partition the
interval of $L_*n$ base points into blocks $H_0,\ldots,H_{L_*-1}$ of
size $n$. For every active anchor $i$, use the list of constant
functions $0,1,\ldots,L_i-1$. At a row $h\in H_\nu$, define the
domain to consist of just the $a$ active anchors and put
\[
 \phi(h,a_i)=\min\{\nu,L_i-1\}.
\]
These $a$ values lie on one polynomial of degree at most $a-1<t$,
so the whole fibre can again be one polynomial class. Every domain
point is sampled. The interpolation construction in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:67:interp:thm:anchor-all-cases} supplies $L_*$ candidates.

Choose an anchor $i_*$ with $L_{i_*}=L_*$. At this column, the
values on the successive blocks are the $L_*$ distinct constants
$0,\ldots,L_*-1$. For any $M<L_*$ proposed candidates,
at least $L_*-M$ of these constants are not identically equal to
any of the univariate polynomials $h\mapsto F_j(h,a_{i_*})$.
On the block for such a constant, each difference is a nonzero
polynomial of degree at most $d$, and the union of the $M$ candidates
matches at at most $dM<n$ rows. Exact coverage is impossible.
When all lists are empty there are no certified points, so the
correct minimum is zero.
\end{proof}

\subsection{What additional partitioning can and cannot save}

The fixed-cell lower bound should not be confused with a prohibition
on making more cells. In fact the construction explicitly shows the
natural exchange: the $T$ consecutive base blocks can each be assigned
one candidate. The correct invariant of unrestricted further
partitioning is total candidate occurrences.

\begin{corollary}[Cell-count versus list-size tradeoff]
\label{gsr:en:67:interp:cor:anchor-partitions}
Use an example from Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:67:interp:thm:anchor-lower}. Partition its base
rectangle into finitely many cells, and on cell $j$ permit a list of
$M_j$ functions that are restrictions of ambient polynomials of
bidegree at most $(d,t-1)$. Put $M=\sum_jM_j$.
The uncovered-mass bound \eqref{gsr:en:67:interp:eq:anchor-robust-lower} still holds
with this $M$. Under \eqref{gsr:en:67:interp:eq:anchor-exact-range}, an exact cover
requires
\begin{equation}
 \sum_jM_j\ge T.
 \label{gsr:en:67:interp:eq:anchor-total-budget}
\end{equation}
Consequently, $b$ cells with at most $Q$ candidates each require
$bQ\ge T$. This product bound is attainable whenever the $T$ target
blocks can be grouped into $b$ groups of size at most $Q$; consecutive
groups give ordinary rectangular arithmetic-progression cells.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Choose an ambient polynomial extension of every local candidate.
Discarding the cell restrictions can only increase coverage. This
gives a global cover with at most $M$ candidates, to which
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:67:interp:thm:anchor-lower} applies. For attainment, group consecutive
blocks $H_\nu$, retain all columns, and list the target polynomials
belonging to each group. Every graph point in that cell is covered.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Higher base dimensions]
For the separately affine case, take a Cartesian product of the example
with any finite sets of additional base coordinates and let $\phi$
ignore those coordinates. For every fixed choice of their values,
each competing separately affine candidate becomes bidegree $(1,t-1)$
in the original base and fibre variables. Applying the same bound on
every slice proves identical proportional lower bounds in any positive
base dimension. This does not impose an exponential penalty in the
number of added coordinates.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Consequences for the Section 16 interface}

For affine fibres, source~39's labelled refinement gives a common
per-anchor list bound
\[
 L=Q\!\left(\frac{\epsilon}{rb},\gamma,k\right)^b,
\]
where $b$ is the inherited slice complexity and the base scale is
controlled separately. At every final base cell with $r\ge2$, the
new upper theorem replaces the old expression
\[
 rL+\binom r2L^2
\]
by $\binom r2L^2$, with exactly the same anchors, base partition,
exceptional set, and admissibility hypotheses. Its proof uses no
geometric synchronization step. If a later synchronization only
restricts already constructed candidates, the improvement survives
unchanged.

The exact lower bound answers source~39's question about a generic
matching lower-bound model: the remaining elementary-symmetric cost
cannot universally be lowered from only those slice-list and
certification hypotheses. This remains true with one polynomial class
per fibre, nearly full domain, arbitrary fixed extra degree in the base
variable, and a small allowed deletion fraction. Compression therefore
needs a stronger premise, for example more than $t$ compatible anchors
per target polynomial, relations tying choices at different anchors,
or information from the product property. The example identifies which
information the present interface has discarded.

The theorem does not close Gowers's numerical recurrence. The source
controls still require an independent audit of scale, outside error,
and list size through Lemmas~16.9--16.11. The result settles the local
candidate optimum and states the precise partition tradeoff; it makes
no assertion of a new bound for $r_k(N)$ or for van der Waerden numbers.

\subsection{Further questions opened by the sharp interface}

\begin{enumerate}
\item Suppose each target class has at least $u>t$ valid anchors and
each such anchor is covered by its labelled list. Determine a sharp
candidate bound that uses this surplus agreement. A first comparison
is $E_t(L)/\binom ut$ when a globally compatible polynomial is already
specified by its anchor values, but a pointwise base-dependent choice
must not be silently replaced by such global compatibility.
\item In Gowers's full product-property setting, can the generic
collision-free examples be excluded quantitatively? A positive result
should provide a verifiable relation among the anchor lists and a
concrete improvement over the exact fixed-interface optimum.
\item For prescribed bounded prime fields, determine the maximum
number of distinct $t$-anchor interpolants when the sufficient
 genericity condition $p>D$ is unavailable. This is a finite
incidence/list-recovery problem rather than an asymptotic permission
to choose an arbitrarily large field.
\item Optimize the finite deletion bound
\eqref{gsr:en:67:interp:eq:anchor-robust-lower}. Its asymptotic leading term is sharp,
but the factors $dM$ and $(t-1)M$ are union bounds; incidences shared
between candidates can improve the finite correction.
\item Impose a lower width on every further arithmetic cell, rather
than merely charging total candidate occurrences. Determine the
best tradeoff between width, number of cells, deletion, and local
list size. The elementary construction here permits $T$ consecutive
blocks of width $n$, so any stronger lower bound needs a row-label
placement that prevents such inexpensive separation.
\end{enumerate}
