\section{Sources~72 and~73: near-maximal Gowers norms in every order and an explicit polynomial-phase entry \wtag}\label{gsr:en:sec:nearmaximal}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the twelfth write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next seventeen sections are source~72's Sections~2--10 and source~73's Sections~2--9, on functions whose Gowers norm is close to its maximum. \emph{Logically they continue the chapter of sources~55 and~57} on the polynomial-phase endpoint (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:phaseendpoint}), which itself continues the Proposition~6.1 endpoint chapters of sources~31, 29 (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:endpoint}) and~38 (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:oddstability}); they are printed here because no number printed earlier may move. The introductions are Sections~\ref{gsr:fm:72:sec:d1} and~\ref{gsr:fm:73:sec:d1}. Four sections of source~73 (Sections~\ref{gsr:en:73:sec:d3}, \ref{gsr:en:73:sec:d4}, \ref{gsr:en:73:sec:d6} and~\ref{gsr:en:73:sec:d9}) are source~55's text, credited by source~73, and are printed once, in source~55's chunks; their places keep the heading, the sentences source~55 lacks and a note. Source~70's near-maximal branch at Theorem~13.12, which works at the same endpoint for $U^4$, is in the next chapter but one (Section~\ref{gsr:en:70:sec:d9} and its Appendix~A, Section~\ref{gsr:en:70:sec:dA}).

\emph{What source~72 proves.} For every finite abelian group $G$, every $d\ge1$ and $|f|\le1$ with $\norm f_{U^{d+2}}^{2^{d+2}}>1-\varepsilon$, $0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_d=[20\cdot6^{d-1}(2^{d+2}+1)]^{-1}$, there are a separately additive $\Phi:G^d\to\widehat G$ and a set of density greater than $1-(6^d-1)(2^{d+2}+1)\varepsilon>7/10$ on which the normalized Fourier coefficient of the $d$-fold derivative at $\Phi$ exceeds $\sqrt{4/5}-2^d\varepsilon>3/4$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:72:thm:main}); on $\Z/N\Z$, $N\ge2$, $\Phi=c\,a_1\cdots a_d$ on full cycles (Corollary~\ref{gsr:fm:72:cor:cyclic}). The engine is a dense-extension induction through homomorphism-valued slices with loss $C_d=(6^d-1)/5$ (Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:72:lem:dense}). Further: the sharp support gap $2^{-d}$ for nonzero separately additive maps (Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:72:lem:support}), uniqueness and symmetry of $\Phi$ at a stronger threshold (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:72:thm:symmetry}), a near-one selected-energy bound (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:72:thm:unitenergy}), and on every cyclic group proximity $\norm{f-z\,e(P)}_2^2\le(2A_k+1)\varepsilon$, $A_k=(2^k+1)6^{(k-2)(k-1)/2}$, to a \emph{periodic rational} polynomial phase for $\varepsilon\le3/(10A_k)$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:72:thm:periodicphase}), with ordinary residue-ring phases when $\gcd((k-1)!,N)=1$ (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:72:thm:classical}); a two-element example shows that the ordinary target fails in general (Example~\ref{gsr:en:72:ex:torsion}). The near-extremizer phenomenon is Eisner and Tao's, and the dense extension is source~12's mechanism, both credited by source~72.

\emph{What source~73 proves.} For every $d\ge2$, every nontrivial finite abelian group and $|f|\le1$ with $\varepsilon=1-\norm f_{U^d}^{q}\le10^{-d}$, $q=2^d$, the squared distance to the phase polynomials of degree at most $d-1$, nonclassical ones included, satisfies $D_d(f)\le(2/q)\varepsilon+b_d(G)\varepsilon^2+R'_d\varepsilon^3$ with $R'_d<3q^3$ and the local radius at least $q^{-5/2}$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:73:thm:main}, Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:73:prop:constants}). The linear and quadratic coefficients are source~55's sharp ones; the new parts are a correlation-preserving entry induction whose error coefficient does not grow with $d$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:73:thm:fidelity}, a quantitative form of Eisner and Tao's small-cocycle argument), a polar reduction without a cube-vertex loss (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:73:thm:diskentry}) and a convex-interpolation remainder $B'_d=10\binom q5+\binom q6$ in place of source~55's $10\binom q5+\sum_{s\ge6}\binom qs2^{s-6}$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:73:thm:expansion}). \emph{This answers source~55's Question~\ref{gsr:fz:55:q:entry}}: the entry threshold, the radius and the cubic coefficient are singly exponential in $d$ (note after that question).

\emph{How the near-maximal results compare} (computed at the write from the printed constants). \emph{Frequency maps:} source~57's Section~5 (Section~\ref{gsr:en:57:sec:d5}), which arrived after source~72's overlap check and is not cited by it, has the finite-abelian all-order extraction with density loss $(18C_s+8)\varepsilon$, $C_1=2$, $C_s=6+38C_{s-1}$, that is $44\varepsilon$, $1484\varepsilon$, $56204\varepsilon$ at $d=1,2,3$, against source~72's $(6^d-1)(2^{d+2}+1)\varepsilon=45\varepsilon$, $595\varepsilon$, $7095\varepsilon$: source~72 has the smaller loss on general finite abelian groups for every $d\ge2$, source~57 at $d=1$; on prime fields source~57's $(216d+8)\varepsilon$ and its $332\varepsilon$ at $d=2$ are smaller still. \emph{Phase approximation:} on prime fields $p\ge k$ source~57 has squared distance at most $(2K_k+2)\varepsilon$ with $K_k=2\prod_{r=1}^{k-2}(108r+1)$ (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:all-degree-inverse}); source~72's $(2A_k+1)\varepsilon$ is smaller for $k=3,4,5,6$ ($109$, $7345$, $3079297$ and $7860602881$ against $438$, $94614$, $30748902$ and $13314273702$) and larger for $k=2$ and every $k\ge7$; source~72 alone covers composite moduli. Both are superseded on $\varepsilon\le10^{-k}$ by source~73's expansion, whose linear coefficient is $2/q$; since $3/(10A_k)<10^{-k}$ for every $k\ge4$, source~72's cyclic phase theorem keeps only the ranges $10^{-k}<\varepsilon\le3/(10A_k)$ at $k=2,3$ and its explicit periodic rational polynomials. \emph{At $U^4$ on cyclic groups:} source~72's Corollary~\ref{gsr:fm:72:cor:cyclic} at $d=2$ gives density $1-595\varepsilon$ and coefficient $\sqrt{4/5}-4\varepsilon$ for $\varepsilon\le1/2040$ on every $\Z/N\Z$, against source~70's $1-9792\varepsilon$ and $\sqrt{63/64}-4\varepsilon$ for $\varepsilon\le2^{-16}$ (its Appendix~A, every $N\ge2$) and the formal $1-332\varepsilon$ and $3/4-4\varepsilon$ on prime moduli (below).

\emph{Relation to the formal statements} (checked at HEAD \texttt{0c4f9054d}). \file{endpoint_global_fourier} (\file{Proofs13EndpointGlobalFourier.lean}, line~12) is the prime-field case $d=2$ in source~57's form (density $1-332\varepsilon$, coefficient $(3/4-4\varepsilon)N$, no threshold); it is used for \file{theorem_13_12} (\file{theorem_13_12_near_one}, \file{Proofs13EndpointPrintedTheorem.lean}, line~12). Nothing else in this chapter is formalized: no declaration concerns higher-order near-maximal Gowers norms, noncyclic groups, periodic rational phases or source~55's expansion, and source~55's own formalization plan is unexecuted. Source~72 says that its result is not an inverse theorem at arbitrary uniformity and therefore does not bear on the open \file{theorem_18_1}.

\section[{Normalization and polar reduction\srctag{72}}]{Normalization and polar reduction}\label{gsr:en:72:sec:d2}\label{gsr:en:72:sec:normalization}
\srcnote{72}{Section 2}
\subsection{Cube averages and degree indexing}
Let $\mathcal C$ denote conjugation. For $k\geq1$,
\begin{align}
 Q_k(f)
 &=\E_{x,h_1,\ldots,h_k}
 \prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^k}
 \mathcal C^{|\omega|}f\left(x-\sum_{j=1}^k\omega_jh_j\right)\label{gsr:en:72:eq:cube}\\
 &=\E_{h_1,\ldots,h_{k-1}}
 \abs{\E_xD_{h_1}\cdots D_{h_{k-1}}f(x)}^2.\label{gsr:en:72:eq:squared}
\end{align}
To verify \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:squared}, first expand the differences. For any $u:G\to\C$,
\[
 \E_{x,h}u(x)\conjbar{u(x-h)}=\abs{\E_xu(x)}^2,
\]
since $(x,x-h)$ is uniformly distributed on $G^2$. Average the final difference. This also proves that $Q_k(f)$ is real and nonnegative. Replacing all $h_j$ by $-h_j$ shows that the positive-shift cube convention has the same average.

The operators $D_a$ commute even if $f$ is not unit-valued. For example,
\[
 D_aD_bf(x)=f(x)\conjbar{f(x-a)}\conjbar{f(x-b)}f(x-a-b).
\]
It follows immediately from the cube expansion that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:72:eq:derivativeU2}
 Q_{d+2}(f)=\E_{\ba\in G^d}\norm{D_{\ba}f}_{U^2}^4.
\end{equation}
Finite character orthogonality gives Parseval and the $U^2$ identity:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:72:eq:parseval}
 \sum_{\gamma\in\widehat G}|\Fcal_g(\gamma)|^2=\E_x|g(x)|^2,
 \qquad
 \norm{g}_{U^2}^4=\sum_{\gamma\in\widehat G}|\Fcal_g(\gamma)|^4.
\end{equation}
For the second identity, the Fourier transform of the correlation
$x\mapsto\E_y g(y)\conjbar{g(y-x)}$ is $|\Fcal_g|^2$; applying Parseval gives the result.

For comparison with the pinned repository definitions~\cite{repo72defs}, on $\Z/N\Z$ the condition called \texttt{UniformOfDegree} $f\,\alpha\,(d+1)$ is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:72:eq:repositoryindex}
 \sum_{\ba\in G^{d+1}}\abs{\sum_xD_{\ba}f(x)}^2
 \leq\alpha N^{d+3}.
\end{equation}
Dividing by $N^{d+3}$ gives $Q_{d+2}(f)\leq\alpha$. Thus the negation is the near-maximal hypothesis with $\eps=1-\alpha$, when $\alpha$ lies in the stated range. The uniformity degree is $d+1$, Gowers order $d+2$, Gowers power $2^{d+2}$, and unnormalized squared-sum exponent $d+3$. For $d=2$, these are respectively $3$, $4$, $16$, and $5$. No extra power of $N$ is hidden in the notation.

\subsection{Normalize once and control every derivative}
\begin{lemma}\label{gsr:en:72:lem:polar}
Suppose $|f|\leq1$ and $Q_k(f)>1-\eps$, with $\eps>0$. Define
\[
 v(x)=\begin{cases}f(x)/|f(x)|,&f(x)\ne0,\\1,&f(x)=0.\end{cases}
\]
Then $|v|=1$, and, writing $\delta=\norm{v-f}_1$,
\begin{align}
 \delta&=\E_x(1-|f(x)|)<\eps,\label{gsr:en:72:eq:polardelta}\\
 Q_k(v)&>1-(2^k+1)\eps,\label{gsr:en:72:eq:polarQ}\\
 \norm{D_{\ba}v-D_{\ba}f}_1&\leq2^d\delta<2^d\eps
 \qquad(\ba\in G^d).\label{gsr:en:72:eq:polarD}
\end{align}
Consequently each fixed normalized Fourier coefficient of a $d$-fold derivative changes by less than $2^d\eps$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Each factor of the cube product has modulus at most one. Its absolute value is therefore at most $|f(x)|$ at the base vertex. As $Q_k$ is real and nonnegative,
\[
 0\leq Q_k(f)\leq\E_x|f(x)|\leq1,
\]
which proves \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:polardelta}. If $|z_j|,|w_j|\leq1$, telescoping products gives
\[
 \abs{\prod_{j=1}^m z_j-\prod_{j=1}^m w_j}
 \leq\sum_{j=1}^m|z_j-w_j|.
\]
Apply this to the $2^k$ factors in each cube. Every vertex argument is uniform as $x$ varies, even when some vertices coincide, so
\[
 |Q_k(v)-Q_k(f)|\leq2^k\delta.
\]
This proves \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:polarQ}. The same argument for the $2^d$ factors in a fixed derivative proves \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:polarD}, uniformly in the directions. Fourier coefficient differences are bounded by the $L^1$ difference.
\end{proof}
The uniformity in \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:polarD} is important: returning to $f$ will not discard a further set of directions. For both cyclic phase conclusions, polar normalization is performed only once, before any demodulation.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Good tuples and exact partial additivity\srctag{72}}]{Good tuples and exact partial additivity}\label{gsr:en:72:sec:d3}\label{gsr:en:72:sec:rigidity}
\srcnote{72}{Section 3}
Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:72:lem:polar} with $k=d+2$ and write $h_{\ba}=D_{\ba}v$. These functions are unit-valued. Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:72:eq:goodset}
 T=\left\{\ba\in G^d:\norm{h_{\ba}}_{U^2}^4\geq\frac45\right\},
 \qquad \eta=1-\dens(T).
\end{equation}
From \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:derivativeU2} and \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:polarQ}, the average defect
$1-\norm{h_{\ba}}_{U^2}^4$ is less than $M_d\eps$. Each bad tuple has defect greater than $1/5$, so
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:72:eq:badset}
 \eta<5M_d\eps.
\end{equation}
If there are no bad tuples this is still strict because $\eps>0$.

\begin{lemma}\label{gsr:en:72:lem:dominant}
For each $\ba\in T$ there is a unique $\phi(\ba)\in\widehat G$ with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:72:eq:dominant}
 |\Fcal_{h_{\ba}}(\phi(\ba))|\geq\sqrt{4/5}.
\end{equation}
For some $z_{\ba}\in\T$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:72:eq:error}
 \norm{h_{\ba}-z_{\ba}\chi_{\phi(\ba)}}_2^2
 =2-2|\Fcal_{h_{\ba}}(\phi(\ba))|
 \leq e^2:=2-2\sqrt{4/5}.
\end{equation}
Moreover $3e<\sqrt2$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Set $a_\gamma=|\Fcal_{h_{\ba}}(\gamma)|^2$. Parseval gives $\sum a_\gamma=1$, while the $U^2$ identity gives $\sum a_\gamma^2\geq4/5$. Since $\sum a_\gamma^2\leq\max a_\gamma$, some $a_\gamma\geq4/5$. Two such frequencies would contribute at least $8/5$ to $\sum a_\gamma$, so the frequency is unique. Choose $z_{\ba}$ to be the phase of this Fourier coefficient and expand the squared $L^2$ norm. Finally,
\[
 (3e)^2=18(1-\sqrt{4/5})<2,
\]
because $\sqrt{4/5}>8/9$, equivalently $4/5-64/81=4/405>0$. The individual errors are bounded by $e$; they need not equal it.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{gsr:en:72:lem:partial}
The map $\phi:T\to\widehat G$ is separately partially additive. Namely, if three tuples have all coordinates in common except one, whose entries are $u$, $v$, and $u+v$, and all three belong to $T$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:72:eq:partial}
 \phi(\ldots,u+v,\ldots)
 =\phi(\ldots,u,\ldots)+\phi(\ldots,v,\ldots).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For every unit-valued $w$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:72:eq:cocycle}
 D_{u+v}w(x)=D_uw(x)D_vw(x-u).
\end{equation}
The cancellation uses $|w(x-u)|=1$; the formula is not valid for general disk-valued functions. Take $w$ to be the product of the other $d-1$ difference operators applied to $v$. Commutation of differences gives the same identity for the three $h$ functions in question.

Products of unit functions obey
\[
 \norm{g_1g_2-q_1q_2}_2
 \leq\norm{g_1-q_1}_2+\norm{g_2-q_2}_2,
\]
and translation preserves $L^2$ distance. The character approximation to the right side of \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:cocycle} has frequency
$\phi(\ldots,u,\ldots)+\phi(\ldots,v,\ldots)$, since
$\chi_\gamma(x-u)=\chi_\gamma(-u)\chi_\gamma(x)$.
It lies within $2e$ of the right side. The left side has a character approximation within $e$. Thus the two unit-multiple characters are within $3e<\sqrt2$ of one another. Distinct characters, multiplied by arbitrary unit scalars, have $L^2$ distance exactly $\sqrt2$ by orthogonality. Their frequencies coincide, proving \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:partial}.
\end{proof}
This is exact partial additivity, with no rounding in $G$ and no Fourier-sign change. The passage through unit-valued $v$ is what makes the cocycle identity exact.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Dense extension in one and several variables\srctag{72}}]{Dense extension in one and several variables}\label{gsr:en:72:sec:d4}\label{gsr:en:72:sec:extension}
\srcnote{72}{Section 4}
\subsection{The one variable difference map}
\begin{lemma}\label{gsr:en:72:lem:onevar}
Let $G$ be a finite abelian group, let $H$ be any abelian group, and let $A\subseteq G$ satisfy $|A|>3|G|/4$. Suppose $F:A\to H$ satisfies
$F(x+y)=F(x)+F(y)$ whenever $x,y,x+y\in A$. Then $F$ extends uniquely to a homomorphism $L:G\to H$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
First prove that $F$ preserves additive quadruples. Suppose $x,y,z,w\in A$ and $x+y=z+w=s$. The intersection
\[
 A\cap(A-x)\cap(A-z)\cap(A-s)
\]
is nonempty because the complement is contained in four sets each of size less than $|G|/4$. Choose $t$ in that intersection. Partial additivity, only on triples lying in $A$, gives
\begin{align*}
 F(s+t)&=F(x+t)+F(y)=F(x)+F(t)+F(y),\\
 F(s+t)&=F(z+t)+F(w)=F(z)+F(t)+F(w).
\end{align*}
Cancel $F(t)$. Thus $F(x)+F(y)=F(z)+F(w)$ without requiring $s\in A$.

For any $h\in G$, choose $u,u+h\in A$, possible because $|A|>|G|/2$, and define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:72:eq:diffmap}
 L(h)=F(u+h)-F(u).
\end{equation}
If $v,v+h\in A$ is another choice, the equality $(u+h)+v=u+(v+h)$ and the quadruple property show that \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:diffmap} is independent of the choice. For $h,k\in G$, the intersection of the three sets imposing $u,u+h,u+h+k\in A$ is nonempty because $|A|>2|G|/3$. Telescoping then gives
\[
 L(h+k)=F(u+h+k)-F(u)=L(k)+L(h).
\]
For $a\in A$, choose $u,u+a\in A$. Original partial additivity yields $L(a)=F(a)$. Finally $A-A=G$, so any homomorphic extension must have the values \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:diffmap}. No assumption that $0\in A$ was used.
\end{proof}
The difference-map mechanism is established. Source 12 of the pinned canonical article proves an affine extension from a dense Freiman map with density greater than $2/3$~\cite{srctwelve}. Here the four-translate argument first converts partial additivity into that quadruple property. We include all details so the different hypothesis and the $3/4$ threshold remain explicit.

\subsection{Homomorphism valued slice induction}
\begin{lemma}\label{gsr:en:72:lem:dense}
Let $d\geq1$, let $G$ be finite abelian, and let $H$ be any abelian group. Suppose $T\subseteq G^d$ has missing density $\eta$ and $\phi:T\to H$ satisfies separate partial additivity as in \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:partial}. If
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:72:eq:densecondition}
 6^{d-1}\eta<\frac14,
\end{equation}
then there are a separately additive $L:G^d\to H$ and $B\subseteq T$ such that $L=\phi$ on $B$ and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:72:eq:denseconclusion}
 1-\dens(B)\leq C_d\eta,\qquad C_d=\frac{6^d-1}{5}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
We induct on $d$, for all abelian codomains simultaneously. At $d=1$, \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:densecondition} gives $|T|>3|G|/4$. Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:72:lem:onevar}, take $B=T$, and use $C_1=1$.

Suppose $d\geq2$. Write a tuple as $(x,y)$, with $x\in G$ and $y\in G^{d-1}$. Define
\[
 A_y=\{x:(x,y)\in T\},\quad
 S=\{y:|A_y|>5|G|/6\},\quad
 \sigma=1-\dens(S).
\]
Every discarded slice misses at least $|G|/6$ points. Averaging missing slice sizes gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:72:eq:sigma}
 \sigma\leq6\eta.
\end{equation}
For $y\in S$, Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:72:lem:onevar} gives a unique homomorphism $L_y:G\to H$ extending $x\mapsto\phi(x,y)$, since $5/6>3/4$. Regard $y\mapsto L_y$ as a map from $S$ to the abelian group $\Hom(G,H)$ under pointwise addition.

We claim that this map is separately partially additive. Fix a tail coordinate, and let $y,y',y''\in S$ have identical other coordinates and selected entries satisfying $y''_i=y_i+y'_i$. The intersection
\[
 I=A_y\cap A_{y'}\cap A_{y''}
\]
has size strictly greater than $|G|/2$: each missing slice proportion is strictly less than $1/6$. On $I$, original partial additivity gives
\[
 L_{y''}(x)-L_y(x)-L_{y'}(x)=0.
\]
The left side is a homomorphism from $G$ to $H$. If nonzero, its kernel would be a proper subgroup of finite $G$, hence have index at least two and size at most $|G|/2$. Thus it is zero on all of $G$, proving
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:72:eq:sliceadd}
 L_{y''}=L_y+L_{y'}.
\end{equation}
This kernel argument uses neither primality nor a finite codomain.

By \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:densecondition} and \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:sigma},
\[
 6^{d-2}\sigma\leq6^{d-1}\eta<\frac14.
\]
Apply the induction hypothesis to the map $S\to\Hom(G,H)$. There is a separately additive
\[
 M:G^{d-1}\longrightarrow\Hom(G,H)
\]
and a set $B'\subseteq S$ such that $M(y)=L_y$ for $y\in B'$ and $1-\dens(B')\leq C_{d-1}\sigma$. Define
\[
 L(x,y)=M(y)(x),\qquad B=T\cap(G\times B').
\]
The first coordinate is additive because $M(y)$ is a homomorphism. Each tail coordinate is additive because $M$ is separately additive and evaluation at fixed $x$ is a homomorphism. On $B$, $L(x,y)=L_y(x)=\phi(x,y)$. Finally,
\begin{align*}
 1-\dens(B)&\leq\eta+C_{d-1}\sigma
 \leq(1+6C_{d-1})\eta\\
 &=\frac{6^d-1}{5}\eta.
\end{align*}
The recurrence $C_d=1+6C_{d-1}$ with $C_1=1$ gives the closed form. This completes the induction.
\end{proof}
\begin{remark}
The non-strict estimate $\sigma\leq6\eta$ suffices; strictness of the retained slice condition supplies the essential intersection size greater than $|G|/2$. If $\eta=0$, the proof gives $B=T=G^d$. If $G$ is trivial, the density condition forces $T=G^d$, and partial additivity forces the sole value to be zero. In higher dimensions the lemma does not assert agreement on all of $T$, nor does its proof require global uniqueness.
\end{remark}

\section[{Proof of the Fourier theorem and cyclic specialization\srctag{72}}]{Proof of the Fourier theorem and cyclic specialization}\label{gsr:en:72:sec:d5}\label{gsr:en:72:sec:completion}
\srcnote{72}{Section 5}
\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:72:thm:main}]
By \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:badset} and the upper bound on $\eps$,
\[
 6^{d-1}\eta<5\cdot6^{d-1}M_d\eps\leq\frac14.
\]
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:72:lem:dense} applies to the frequency map of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:72:lem:partial}. It gives $\Phi$ and $B\subseteq T$ with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:72:eq:missingfinal}
 1-\dens(B)\leq C_d\eta<(6^d-1)M_d\eps.
\end{equation}
The last inequality remains strict when $\eta=0$ because $\eps>0$. At the permitted endpoint,
\[
 (6^d-1)M_d\eps_d
 =\frac{6^d-1}{20\cdot6^{d-1}}
 =\frac3{10}-\frac1{20\cdot6^{d-1}},
\]
which proves \eqref{gsr:fm:72:eq:maindensity}. On $B$ we have $\Phi=\phi$, so Lemmas~\ref{gsr:en:72:lem:polar} and \ref{gsr:en:72:lem:dominant} imply
\[
 \abs{\Fcal_{D_{\ba}f}(\Phi(\ba))}
 >\sqrt{4/5}-2^d\eps.
\]
Finally,
\[
 2^d\eps\leq\frac{2^d}{20\cdot6^{d-1}(2^{d+2}+1)}
 <\frac1{80\cdot6^{d-1}}\leq\frac1{80},
\]
and hence
\[
 \sqrt{4/5}-2^d\eps>\frac45-\frac1{80}=\frac{63}{80}>\frac34.
\]
Every conclusion concerns the original function $f$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Corollary~\ref{gsr:fm:72:cor:cyclic}]
Every homomorphism $\Z/N\Z\to\Z/N\Z$ is multiplication by its value at $1$. Apply this successively in each argument of $\Phi$ to obtain
\[
 \Phi(a_1,\ldots,a_d)=a_1\cdots a_d\Phi(1,\ldots,1).
\]
Set $c=\Phi(1,\ldots,1)$. This is well-defined modulo $N$ without any division or primality assumption. The unnormalized transform is $N$ times the normalized one, proving \eqref{gsr:fm:72:eq:cycliccoeff}. The map $i\mapsto i\bmod N$, $0\leq i<N$, is injective and has image $G$, verifying the full-cycle properness assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{gsr:en:72:cor:coarseenergy}
For the map in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:72:thm:main}, using the unnormalized character transform on $G$,
\[
 \sum_{\ba\in G^d}\abs{\widehat{D_{\ba}f}(\Phi(\ba))}^2
 >\frac{63}{160}|G|^{d+2}.
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Retain only $B$, whose density exceeds $7/10$, and use squared normalized coefficients greater than $9/16$. Multiply the resulting tuple-average bound by $|G|^{d+2}$.
\end{proof}
This is an analytic energy conclusion. Any use in an additional local-box or density-increment interface needs a separate check of that interface's hypotheses.

\begin{tabular}{@{}cccc@{}}
\toprule
$d$ & $M_d$ & $\eps_d$ & endpoint density lower expression\\
\midrule
$1$ & $9$ & $1/180$ & $3/4$\\
$2$ & $17$ & $1/2040$ & $17/24$\\
$3$ & $33$ & $1/23760$ & $101/144$\\
$4$ & $65$ & $1/280800$ & $605/864$\\

\section[{Exact extremizers and a small characteristic obstruction\srctag{72}}]{Exact extremizers and a small characteristic obstruction}\label{gsr:en:72:sec:d6}\label{gsr:en:72:sec:torsion}
\srcnote{72}{Section 6}
\begin{proposition}\label{gsr:en:72:prop:exact}
If $|f|\leq1$ and $Q_{d+2}(f)=1$, then $|f|=1$ everywhere, and there is a separately additive $\Phi:G^d\to\widehat G$ such that every $D_{\ba}f$ is a unit scalar multiple of $\chi_{\Phi(\ba)}$. Thus every selected normalized coefficient has magnitude $1$, and every selected unnormalized coefficient has magnitude $|G|$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The inequality $Q_{d+2}(f)\leq\E|f|\leq1$ forces $|f|=1$ at every point of the finite group. In \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:derivativeU2}, each summand lies in $[0,1]$ and the average is $1$, so every summand is $1$. Parseval then forces all squared Fourier mass of each derivative onto a unique frequency. The exact cocycle gives separate additivity on all tuples, either directly or by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:72:lem:partial} with zero error.
\end{proof}
The strict hypothesis in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:72:thm:main} is impossible at $\eps=0$. Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:72:prop:exact} is a separate statement, rather than an insertion of $\eps=0$ into a strict density inequality.

\begin{example}\label{gsr:en:72:ex:torsion}
For any $d\geq1$, let $G=\Z/2\Z$ and
\[
 f(0)=1,\qquad f(1)=\exp\left(\frac{2\pi i}{2^{d+1}}\right).
\]
This is an exact extremizer for $Q_{d+2}$, with frequency map
$\Phi(a_1,\ldots,a_d)=a_1\cdots a_d\in\Z/2\Z$. Yet it is not a scalar multiple of $e_2(P)$ for any ordinary $\Z/2\Z$-valued polynomial $P$.
\end{example}
\begin{proof}
A zero direction makes a derivative of a unit function identically one, and subsequent differences remain one. If all directions are $1$, induction in $s\geq1$, with $x$ represented by $0$ or $1$, gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:72:eq:torsiondiff}
 D_1^sf(x)=\exp\left(2\pi i\,
 \frac{2^{s-1}(2x-1)}{2^{d+1}}\right).
\end{equation}
For $s=1$ this is the definition of the difference. Switching $x$ with $x-1\bmod2$ negates $2x-1$, so another difference doubles the exponent, proving the induction. At $s=d$ the values are $-i,i$, namely $-i$ times the nontrivial character. At $s=d+1$ the derivative is the constant $-1$; at $s=d+2$ it is identically $1$. Hence the cube average is $1$ and the stated frequency map follows for every tuple. On the other hand $f(1)/f(0)$ is neither $1$ nor $-1$, whereas every ratio of two values of a scalar multiple of $e_2(P)$ must belong to $\{1,-1\}$.
\end{proof}
This does not contradict proximity to $\mathbb R/\Z$-valued polynomial maps. Section~\ref{gsr:en:72:sec:demodulation} constructs periodic rational polynomial phases on every cyclic group, and Section~\ref{gsr:en:72:sec:classical} explicitly realizes the $d=2$ example by such a cubic. The obstruction concerns ordinary residue-ring polynomial phases; dividing by $(d+1)!$ in that ring would be unjustified without invertibility.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Sharp support gaps and uniqueness\srctag{72}}]{Sharp support gaps and uniqueness}\label{gsr:en:72:sec:d7}\label{gsr:en:72:sec:uniqueness}
\srcnote{72}{Section 7}
\subsection{Support of a nonzero separately additive map}
\begin{lemma}\label{gsr:en:72:lem:support}
Let $G_1,\ldots,G_d$ be finite abelian groups and $H$ any abelian group. A nonzero separately additive map $A:G_1\times\cdots\times G_d\to H$ has
\[
 \dens(\supp A)\geq2^{-d}.
\]
The constant is sharp.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $d=1$, the kernel of a nonzero homomorphism is a proper subgroup, so it occupies at most half the finite domain. Suppose $d\geq2$. Let $V$ be the abelian group of separately additive maps $G_2\times\cdots\times G_d\to H$. The slice map
\[
 G_1\to V,\qquad x_1\mapsto A(x_1,\cdot)
\]
is a nonzero homomorphism. At least half its slices are nonzero. By induction, each such slice has support density at least $2^{-(d-1)}$. Averaging gives $2^{-d}$. Neither $H$ nor $V$ must be finite, since only the domain kernel index is used. If a factor is trivial, no such nonzero map exists. Sharpness is attained by $A(x)=x_1\cdots x_d$ on $(\Z/2\Z)^d$ with values in $\Z/2\Z$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{gsr:en:72:cor:uniqueagreement}
Suppose two separately additive maps $L_1,L_2$ agree with a partially defined function $\phi$ on sets $B_1,B_2$ in its domain. If their missing densities $\delta_1,\delta_2$ in the whole product satisfy
\[
 \delta_1+\delta_2<2^{-d},
\]
then $L_1=L_2$ everywhere.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The support of $L_1-L_2$ lies outside $B_1\cap B_2$, whose missing density is at most $\delta_1+\delta_2$. A nonzero difference would contradict Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:72:lem:support}.
\end{proof}
In Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:72:lem:dense}, the condition $C_d\eta<2^{-d-1}$ therefore makes the extension unique among all maps satisfying its agreement-density guarantee. This does not assert uniqueness among less accurate approximations.

\subsection{An intrinsic Fourier witness and its symmetry}
\begin{proposition}\label{gsr:en:72:prop:intrinsic}
Let $|f|\leq1$ on a finite abelian group. Suppose separately additive maps $\Psi_1,\Psi_2:G^d\to\widehat G$ each admit a set $E_i$ of density strictly greater than $1-2^{-d-1}$ on which
\[
 |\Fcal_{D_{\ba}f}(\Psi_i(\ba))|>3/4.
\]
Then $\Psi_1=\Psi_2$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
At a tuple in $E_1\cap E_2$, two distinct selected frequencies would contribute more than $2(3/4)^2=9/8$ to the squared Fourier mass. Parseval bounds that mass by $1$ because $|D_{\ba}f|\leq1$. Thus the maps agree on the intersection. Their difference has support density less than $2^{-d}$, so Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:72:lem:support} makes it zero.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}\label{gsr:en:72:thm:symmetry}
In Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:72:thm:main}, assume the stronger bound
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:72:eq:symthreshold}
 0<\eps\leq\eps_d^{\rm sym}
 :=\frac1{2^{d+1}(6^d-1)M_d}.
\end{equation}
There is exactly one separately additive map admitting original-$f$ Fourier coefficients greater than $3/4$ on a set of density greater than $1-2^{-d-1}$. The map furnished by Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:72:thm:main} is that map and is symmetric under all permutations of its $d$ arguments.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The stronger threshold is at most $\eps_d$, since
\[
 6^d-1\geq5\cdot6^{d-1},\qquad 2^{d+1}\geq4.
\]
By \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:missingfinal},
\[
 1-\dens(B)<(6^d-1)M_d\eps\leq2^{-d-1}.
\]
Thus Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:72:thm:main} supplies a witness in the class of Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:72:prop:intrinsic}, which proves uniqueness. For any permutation $\pi$, the map
$\Phi_\pi(a_1,\ldots,a_d)=\Phi(a_{\pi(1)},\ldots,a_{\pi(d)})$
is separately additive. Since differences commute, permuting the good set gives another set of the same density with the same coefficient guarantee. Therefore $\Phi_\pi=\Phi$ by intrinsic uniqueness.
\end{proof}
One can equivalently use the permutation invariance of $T$ and its unique dominant frequency, together with Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:72:cor:uniqueagreement}. Indeed $C_d\eta<(6^d-1)M_d\eps\leq2^{-d-1}$.

Symmetry is only in the derivative directions. The $(d+1)$-variable quantity $\chi_{\Phi(\ba)}(x)$ is not asserted to be symmetric between $x$ and the $a_i$. On a cyclic group symmetry already follows from $c\prod_i a_i$; the stronger threshold additionally makes $c$ unique within the stated dense-witness class. For $d=1,2,3,4$, the stronger thresholds are
\[
 \frac1{180},\quad\frac1{4760},\quad\frac1{113520},\quad\frac1{2693600}.
\]
The support bound is sharp, but that does not show that these Fourier thresholds are optimal.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Near one selected Fourier energy\srctag{72}}]{Near one selected Fourier energy}\label{gsr:en:72:sec:d8}\label{gsr:en:72:sec:energy}
\srcnote{72}{Section 8}
\begin{theorem}\label{gsr:en:72:thm:unitenergy}
Let $d\geq1$ and $v:G\to\C$ be unit-valued. If
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:72:eq:unitenergyhyp}
 Q_{d+2}(v)>1-\tau,\qquad
 0<\tau\leq\frac1{20\cdot6^{d-1}},
\end{equation}
there is a separately additive $\Phi:G^d\to\widehat G$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:72:eq:unitenergy}
 \E_{\ba}|\Fcal_{D_{\ba}v}(\Phi(\ba))|^2>1-6^d\tau.
\end{equation}
The same construction provides $B\subseteq G^d$ with
\[
 \dens(B)>1-(6^d-1)\tau,\qquad
 |\Fcal_{D_{\ba}v}(\Phi(\ba))|\geq\sqrt{4/5}\quad(\ba\in B).
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
No polar reduction is needed. Define $T$ as in \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:goodset}; its missing density obeys $\eta<5\tau$. The dominant-frequency and cocycle lemmas give separate partial additivity. Since $6^{d-1}\eta<1/4$, the dense extension lemma applies, yielding $B$ with missing density less than $(6^d-1)\tau$.

The additional step is to retain the actual fourth moment on $B$. For $h=D_{\ba}v$ with $\ba\in B$, the selected coefficient is the unique largest one, since its squared magnitude is at least $4/5$ and the total squared mass is $1$. Thus
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:72:eq:actualmoment}
 |\Fcal_h(\Phi(\ba))|^2
 =\max_\gamma|\Fcal_h(\gamma)|^2
 \geq\sum_\gamma|\Fcal_h(\gamma)|^4
 =\norm h_{U^2}^4.
\end{equation}
All $U^2$ fourth powers lie in $[0,1]$. Retaining $B$ in the nonnegative selected-energy average gives
\begin{align*}
 \E_{\ba}|\Fcal_{D_{\ba}v}(\Phi(\ba))|^2
 &\geq\E_{\ba}1_B(\ba)\norm{D_{\ba}v}_{U^2}^4\\
 &\geq Q_{d+2}(v)-(1-\dens(B))\\
 &>1-\tau-(6^d-1)\tau=1-6^d\tau.
\end{align*}
The tuples outside $B$ may have arbitrary selected coefficients; their nonnegative contribution can only improve the bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{gsr:en:72:cor:diskenergy}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:72:thm:main}, its construction can be made with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:72:eq:diskenergy}
 \E_{\ba}|\Fcal_{D_{\ba}f}(\Phi(\ba))|^2
 >1-\bigl[6^d(2^{d+2}+1)+2^{d+1}\bigr]\eps.
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The polar function satisfies $Q_{d+2}(v)>1-M_d\eps$. Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:72:thm:unitenergy} with $\tau=M_d\eps$, using the same good-set construction. By Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:72:lem:polar}, corresponding coefficients differ by less than $2^d\eps$. Since both magnitudes are at most $1$,
\[
 \bigl||z|^2-|w|^2\bigr|\leq(|z|+|w|)|z-w|\leq2|z-w|.
\]
The squared-coefficient loss is therefore less than $2^{d+1}\eps$, uniformly in the tuple. Average and use \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:unitenergy}.
\end{proof}
For the \emph{sum} over all tuples of squared unnormalized coefficients, multiply \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:unitenergy} or \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:diskenergy} by $|G|^{d+2}$. For the \emph{tuple average} of squared unnormalized coefficients, multiply only by $|G|^2$. Both energy results hold for every finite abelian group with no factorial or symmetry assumption.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Cyclic demodulation by periodic rational phases\srctag{72}}]{Cyclic demodulation by periodic rational phases}\label{gsr:en:72:sec:d9}\label{gsr:en:72:sec:demodulation}
\srcnote{72}{Section 9}

Write $e(t)=\exp(2\pi i t)$. A \emph{periodic rational polynomial phase}
on $\Z/N\Z$ is represented by $q(x)=e(P(x))$, where $P\in\mathbb Q[x]$
and $P(x+N)-P(x)\in\Z$ for every $x\in\Z$. The polynomial itself need not
be periodic. If $\deg P\leq s$, its induced $\mathbb R/\Z$-valued map has
additive-difference degree at most $s$: ordinary rational differences of order $s+1$ vanish, so every corresponding multiplicative derivative of the phase is one.

\begin{lemma}[Rational shift antiderivative]\label{gsr:en:72:lem:rationalshift}
Let $N\geq2$, $m\geq2$, and $c\in\Z$. There is a unique
$P_{N,m,c}\in\mathbb Q[x]$ of degree at most $m$, with $P_{N,m,c}(0)=0$,
such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:72:eq:rationalshift}
 P_{N,m,c}(x+N)-P_{N,m,c}(x)=c\binom{x}{m-1}.
\end{equation}
Its coefficient of $x^m$ is $c/(m!N)$, and $e(P_{N,m,c})$ is $N$-periodic
on all of $\Z$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The map $P\mapsto P(x+N)-P(x)$ from rational polynomials of degree at most
$m$ modulo constants to rational polynomials of degree at most $m-1$ has
triangular matrix with diagonal $N,2N,\ldots,mN$, because
\[
 (x+N)^j-x^j=jN x^{j-1}+\text{terms of degree at most }j-2.
\]
It is therefore an isomorphism. The condition $P(0)=0$ fixes the constant,
and comparison of top coefficients proves the stated $x^m$ coefficient,
including when $c=0$.

Explicitly, write $c\binom{x}{m-1}=\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}b_rx^r$ and
$P=\sum_{j=1}^m a_jx^j$. Descending from $r=m-1$ to $r=0$, set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:72:eq:rationalrecursion}
 a_{r+1}=\frac{b_r-\sum_{j=r+2}^m a_j\binom jr N^{j-r}}{(r+1)N}.
\end{equation}
These divisions take place in $\mathbb Q$, not in $\Z/N\Z$.
The polynomial $\binom{x}{m-1}$ is integer-valued at every integer,
including negatives: $\binom{-r}{j}=(-1)^j\binom{r+j-1}{j}$ for $r>0$.
Thus \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:rationalshift} makes the exponential periodic. Iterating
in either direction gives $P(x+tN)-P(x)\in\Z$ for all integers $x,t$.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{A Newton basis formula.}
There is also a second exact construction. Set $F(t)=c\binom{Nt}{m-1}$ and
\[
 b'_j=\sum_{i=0}^j(-1)^{j-i}\binom ji F(i),\qquad
 P(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}b'_j\binom{x/N}{j+1}.
\]
The Newton expansion $F(t)=\sum_j b'_j\binom tj$ follows by successive forward differences, since $\binom tj$ form a degree-ordered basis. Pascal's identity gives the required shift equation, and every $\binom{0}{j+1}$ is zero. Uniqueness identifies this polynomial with the triangular construction. The companion compares the two constructions exactly over its stated finite ranges.

\begin{lemma}[All-cyclic demodulation]\label{gsr:en:72:lem:periodicdemodulation}
Let $N\geq2$ and $d\geq1$. Choose an integer lift $c$ of a frequency in
$\Z/N\Z$, put $P=P_{N,d+1,c}$ and $q=e(P)$. For all integer increments
$a_1,\ldots,a_d$ there is $\beta_{\ba}\in\mathbb Q$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:72:eq:rationallinear}
 \delta_{a_1}\cdots\delta_{a_d}P(x)
 =\frac cN(a_1\cdots a_d)x+\beta_{\ba},\qquad
 \delta_aP(x)=P(x)-P(x-a).
\end{equation}
Consequently, for every complex-valued $v$ on $\Z/N\Z$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:72:eq:demodidentity}
 Q_{d+1}(v\conjbar q)
 =\E_{\ba}\abs{\Fcal_{D_{\ba}v}(c a_1\cdots a_d)}^2.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A backward difference of a degree-$j$ monomial with coefficient $a_j$
has $x^{j-1}$ coefficient $j a a_j$. The coefficient of $x^{d+1}$ in
$P$ is $c/((d+1)!N)$. After $d$ differences the coefficient of $x$ is
therefore $(c/N)\prod_i a_i$, and all other terms are constant. This
proves \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:rationallinear}, also for negative or zero increments.

Since $q$ is $N$-periodic, these calculations are valid for arbitrary
integer representatives of $x$ and the increments, and give
\[
 D_{\ba}q(x)=e(\beta_{\ba})\chi_{c\prod_i a_i}(x).
\]
Changing an increment by $N$ does not change the derivative; its character
frequency also stays the same modulo $N$. The scalar $e(\beta_{\ba})$ is determined by evaluation at $x=0$, so it too is representative-independent. A different lift of $c$ may
change $q$, but gives the same required frequency. No canonical choice
of $q$ depending only on the residue of $c$ is asserted.

Multiplicative differences distribute over products and conjugation,
including for non-unit $v$. Hence
\[
 \abs{\E_xD_{\ba}(v\conjbar q)(x)}
 =\abs{\E_xD_{\ba}v(x)\conjbar{\chi_{c\prod_i a_i}(x)}}.
\]
Square and average, using \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:squared} at order $d+1$, to obtain
\eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:demodidentity}. The backward sign is positive and the conjugated
demodulator matches the negative-sign Fourier transform.
\end{proof}

The next construction retains the narrower residue-ring target when
factorial inversion is available.

\begin{lemma}\label{gsr:en:72:lem:factorial}
Let $N\geq2$, $d\geq1$, and $\gcd((d+1)!,N)=1$. Given $c\in\Z/N\Z$, put
\[
 p(x)=c\bigl((d+1)!\bigr)^{-1}x^{d+1},\qquad q(x)=e_N(p(x)).
\]
For every $\ba\in(\Z/N\Z)^d$, there is $b_{\ba}\in\Z/N\Z$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:72:eq:polylinear}
 \delta_{a_1}\cdots\delta_{a_d}p(x)
 =c(a_1\cdots a_d)x+b_{\ba},\qquad
 \delta_a p(x)=p(x)-p(x-a).
\end{equation}
Consequently \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:demodidentity} holds for this $q$ as well,
for every complex-valued $v$ on $\Z/N\Z$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For a polynomial with leading term $a_mx^m$, the binomial theorem gives
\[
 a_m\bigl(x^m-(x-a)^m\bigr)=m a a_m x^{m-1}
 +\text{terms of degree at most }m-2.
\]
Lower-degree terms contribute degree at most $m-2$ after the difference. This identity is first an integer polynomial identity and can be reduced in any residue ring. Repeating it $d$ times for a degree-$d+1$ monomial gives leading coefficient $(d+1)!$ times the original coefficient times $a_1\cdots a_d$. The stated inverse makes this coefficient $c\prod_i a_i$, proving \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:polylinear}; if a leading coefficient vanishes, the same polynomial identity still holds. The remaining term has degree at most zero.

Thus $D_{\ba}q(x)=e_N(b_{\ba})\chi_{c\prod_i a_i}(x)$. Multiplicative differences distribute over products and conjugation, even for non-unit inputs. Therefore
\[
 \abs{\E_xD_{\ba}(v\conjbar q)(x)}
 =\abs{\E_xD_{\ba}v(x)\conjbar{\chi_{c\prod_i a_i}(x)}}.
\]
Square and average, using \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:squared} at order $d+1$, to obtain \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:demodidentity}.
\end{proof}
The sign in \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:polylinear} is positive because the difference is $p(x)-p(x-a)$. Demodulation multiplies by $\conjbar q$, and the Fourier convention uses a negative sign. These three choices agree.

For unit $v$ satisfying \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:unitenergyhyp}, combine Corollary~\ref{gsr:fm:72:cor:cyclic}'s scalar description with Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:72:thm:unitenergy} and Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:72:lem:periodicdemodulation} to get
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:72:eq:descent}
 Q_{d+1}(v\conjbar q)>1-6^d\tau.
\end{equation}
The function $v\conjbar q$ is still unit-valued. Thus repeated descent has no additional polar-normalization loss.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Explicit near extremizers on every cyclic group\srctag{72}}]{Explicit near extremizers on every cyclic group}\label{gsr:en:72:sec:d10}\label{gsr:en:72:sec:classical}
\srcnote{72}{Section 10}
\begin{theorem}\label{gsr:en:72:thm:periodicphase}
Let $k\geq2$ and $N\geq2$. Write
\[
 R=\frac{(k-2)(k-1)}2,\qquad A_k=(2^k+1)6^R.
\]
If $|f|\leq1$ on $\Z/N\Z$ and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:72:eq:classhyp}
 Q_k(f)>1-\eps,\qquad0<\eps\leq\frac3{10A_k},
\end{equation}
then there are $P\in\mathbb Q[x]$ of degree at most $k-1$, with $P(0)=0$
and $e(P)$ $N$-periodic on $\Z$, and $z\in\C$, $|z|=1$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:72:eq:classbound}
 \norm{f-z e(P)}_2^2
 <2\bigl[1-\sqrt{1-A_k\eps}\bigr]+\eps
 \leq(2A_k+1)\eps.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Normalize once, obtaining unit-valued $v$ from Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:72:lem:polar} with
\[
 \E(1-|f|)<\eps,\qquad Q_k(v)>1-(2^k+1)\eps.
\]
Set $r=k-2$, $\Delta=A_k\eps\leq3/10$, and, for $0\leq d\leq r$, define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:72:eq:budgets}
 t_d=\Delta\,6^{-d(d+1)/2}.
\end{equation}
Then $t_r=(2^k+1)\eps$, $t_0=\Delta$, and $6^dt_d=t_{d-1}$. Every positive-dimensional stage is admissible for Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:72:thm:unitenergy}, because
\begin{align}
 20\cdot6^{d-1}t_d
 &\leq20\cdot6^{d-1}\frac3{10}6^{-d(d+1)/2}\notag\\
 &=6^{-d(d-1)/2}\leq1.\label{gsr:en:72:eq:budgetcheck}
\end{align}
The most restrictive stage is $d=1$; no recursive threshold is omitted.

At stage $d=r,r-1,\ldots,1$, the current unit function $u$ has $Q_{d+2}(u)>1-t_d$. Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:72:thm:unitenergy} supplies the scalar frequency $c_d\prod_i a_i$. Choose any integer lift of $c_d$, and define
\[
 P_d=P_{N,d+1,c_d},\qquad q_d=e(P_d)
\]
using Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:72:lem:rationalshift}. No factorial inverse modulo $N$ is needed.
By \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:descent}, the unit function $u\conjbar{q_d}$ satisfies
\[
 Q_{d+1}(u\conjbar{q_d})>1-6^dt_d=1-t_{d-1}.
\]
This is the next induction hypothesis. At the end, with
\[
 P_{\rm high}=\sum_{d=1}^r P_d,\qquad
 w=v e(-P_{\rm high}),
\]
we have $|w|=1$, $\deg P_{\rm high}\leq k-1$, $P_{\rm high}(0)=0$,
$e(P_{\rm high})$ $N$-periodic, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:72:eq:finalU2}
 Q_2(w)>1-\Delta.
\end{equation}
For $k=2$, the sum is empty and \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:finalU2} is the initial polar estimate. The exact accumulated stage multiplier is
$\prod_{d=1}^r6^d=6^{r(r+1)/2}=6^R$.

Parseval and the $U^2$ identity yield a frequency $b$ with
\[
 |\Fcal_w(b)|^2\geq Q_2(w)>1-\Delta>0.
\]
Choose $z=\Fcal_w(b)/|\Fcal_w(b)|$. Then
\[
 \norm{w-z\chi_b}_2^2=2-2|\Fcal_w(b)|
 <2\bigl(1-\sqrt{1-\Delta}\bigr).
\]
Multiplication by $e(P_{\rm high})$ preserves $L^2$ distance. Choosing
an integer lift of $b$, put $P=P_{\rm high}+(b/N)x$ and $W=z e(P)$.
The polynomial $P$ has the claimed rational degree and normalization,
and $e(P)$ is $N$-periodic. We have the same bound for $\norm{v-W}_2^2$.

Finally write $f=\rho v$, with $\rho=|f|\in[0,1]$. Pointwise, as $|v|=|W|=1$,
\begin{align}
 |\rho v-W|^2
 &=\rho|v-W|^2+(1-\rho)^2\notag\\
 &\leq|v-W|^2+(1-\rho).\label{gsr:en:72:eq:diskidentity}
\end{align}
Average and use $\E(1-\rho)<\eps$ to get the first inequality in \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:classbound}. Since $\sqrt{1-\Delta}\geq1-\Delta$ for $0\leq\Delta\leq1$, the right side is at most $2\Delta+\eps=(2A_k+1)\eps$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 70--81]
\emph{Superseded on $\varepsilon\le10^{-k}$} by source~73 (Section~\ref{gsr:en:73:sec:d2} onward), on every finite abelian group, whose distance bound $(2/2^k)\varepsilon+O(\varepsilon^2)$ is measured to all phase polynomials of degree at most $k-1$, nonclassical ones included, which on $\Z/N\Z$ contain the periodic rational phases used here. Since $3/(10A_k)<10^{-k}$ for $k\ge4$ (checked at the write), this theorem keeps only the ranges $10^{-2}<\varepsilon\le3/50$ ($k=2$) and $10^{-3}<\varepsilon\le1/180$ ($k=3$) and its explicit periodic rational polynomial. On prime fields with $p\ge k$ source~57's Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:all-degree-inverse} gives the squared distance $(2K_k+2)\varepsilon$ with $K_k=2\prod_{r\le k-2}(108r+1)$; this theorem's $2A_k+1$ is smaller for $k=3,4,5,6$ and larger for $k=2$ and every $k\ge7$.
\end{writenote}
For $k=2,3,4$, the thresholds $3/(10A_k)$ are $3/50$, $1/180$, and $1/12240$, while $2A_k+1$ equals $11$, $109$, and $7345$. The $k=2$ threshold is a convenient common sufficient condition; direct Fourier analysis permits a better result. The theorem gives $L^2$ distance less than $\sqrt{(2A_k+1)\eps}$, with squared distance linear in the \emph{cube-average} defect, not the norm defect.

\begin{corollary}[Classical target under factorial invertibility]\label{gsr:en:72:thm:classical}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:72:thm:periodicphase}, if additionally
$\gcd((k-1)!,N)=1$, there are $p\in(\Z/N\Z)[x]$ of degree at most $k-1$
and $z\in\T$ satisfying the bound \eqref{gsr:en:72:eq:classbound} with $z e_N(p)$
in place of $z e(P)$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
In the same descent, use Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:72:lem:factorial} to choose
$q_d=e_N(p_d)$, where $p_d=c_d((d+1)!)^{-1}x^{d+1}$. The required inverses
exist because $(d+1)!$ divides $(k-1)!$. The energy identity and all
budgets are identical. At the last Fourier step set $p=\sum_d p_d+bx$.
\end{proof}

The scalar $z$ is unrestricted on the unit circle and is recorded separately
from the polynomial. Factorial invertibility holds, for example, for primes
$N\geq k$, and for some composite moduli. Example~\ref{gsr:en:72:ex:torsion} prevents
removing the restriction while keeping ordinary residue-ring phases;
it does not obstruct the periodic rational target in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:72:thm:periodicphase}. For example, its case $N=2,d=2$ is exactly
\[
 P_{2,3,1}(x)=\frac{x^3}{12}-\frac{3x^2}{8}+\frac{5x}{12},\qquad
 P_{2,3,1}(1)=\frac18,
\]
with $P(x+2)-P(x)=\binom{x}{2}$ and
$\delta_1^2P(x)=x/2-5/4$, so $D_1^2 e(P)=-i\chi_1$.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A correlation preserving entry theorem\srctag{73}}]{A correlation preserving entry theorem}\label{gsr:en:73:sec:d2}\label{gsr:en:73:sec:entry}
\srcnote{73}{Section 2}
Put $T_hu(x)=u(x-h)$ and $\e(t)=\exp(2\pi it)$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:73:eq:eta}
 \eta_2=1,\qquad
 \eta_k=\frac1{180\cdot10^{k-3}}\quad(k\ge3).
\end{equation}
\begin{theorem}[Unit phase fidelity]\label{gsr:en:73:thm:fidelity}
For any finite abelian group, $k\ge2$, and $|v|=1$, if
$\delta=1-Q_k(v)\le\eta_k$, there exists $p\in\cP_{k-1}(G)$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:73:eq:fidelity}
 |\E v\overline p|^2\ge Q_k(v)=1-\delta.
\end{equation}
After a constant rotation,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:73:eq:unitdistance}
 \norm{v-p}_2^2\le2(1-\sqrt{1-\delta})\le2\delta.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
The constant in the final error is independent of $k$; only the
admissible defect threshold decreases with $k$.

\begin{lemma}[Separation of phase classes]\label{gsr:en:73:lem:separation}
If $u\in\cP_s(G)$, $s\ge1$, and
$\norm{u-1}_2<2^{3/2-s}$, then $u$ is constant.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $s=1$, write $u=z\chi$ with $|z|=1$ and a character $\chi$.
A nonconstant character has mean zero, hence $\norm{z\chi-1}_2^2=2$.
For $s\ge2$, each derivative $T_hu/u$ has degree at most $s-1$ and
\[
 \norm{T_hu/u-1}_2\le2\norm{u-1}_2<2^{3/2-(s-1)}.
\]
Induction makes every derivative constant. Therefore $u$ has degree at
most one, and the base case applies since $2^{3/2-s}\le\sqrt2$.
\end{proof}
This is the standard separation argument used in the near-extremizer
method; the displayed threshold follows by retaining its base constant.

\begin{proof}[Proof of theorem~\ref{gsr:en:73:thm:fidelity}]
We induct on $k$. Fourier transform is normalized by
$\widehat v(\chi)=\E v\overline\chi$. For $k=2$, Parseval gives
\[
 \sum_\chi|\widehat v(\chi)|^2=1,\qquad
 Q_2(v)=\sum_\chi|\widehat v(\chi)|^4.
\]
It follows that some $\chi$ satisfies
$|\widehat v(\chi)|^2\ge Q_2(v)$, proving the base case.

Suppose $k\ge3$. For each $h\in G$ set
\[
 w_h=(T_hv)\overline v,\qquad
 \delta_h=1-Q_{k-1}(w_h).
\]
The cube recursion gives $\E_h\delta_h=\delta$, and all $\delta_h\ge0$.
For $\delta>0$ let $A=\{h:\delta_h\le10\delta\}$, so $|A|/|G|\ge9/10$.
The thresholds ensure $10\delta\le\eta_{k-1}$: when $k=3$,
$10\eta_3=1/18\le\eta_2$, and thereafter $10\eta_k=\eta_{k-1}$.
For $h\in A$, induction supplies a phase $p_h\in\cP_{k-2}(G)$.
Rotate it so that $\E w_h\overline{p_h}\ge0$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:73:eq:goodderivative}
 |\E w_h\overline{p_h}|^2\ge1-\delta_h,
 \qquad \norm{w_h-p_h}_2^2\le2\delta_h.
\end{equation}

Keep $q_h=p_h$ on $A$. For $h\notin A$, the set
$I_h=A\cap(h-A)$ has density at least $4/5$. Since
$\E_a(\delta_a+\delta_{h-a})=2\delta$, its restricted average is at most
$(5/2)\delta$. Choose $a,b\in A$ with $a+b=h$ and
$\delta_a+\delta_b\le(5/2)\delta$, and put
$q_h=(T_ap_b)p_a$. The exact identity
$w_{a+b}=(T_aw_b)w_a$ and the squared triangle inequality yield
\[
 \norm{w_h-q_h}_2^2
 \le2\bigl(\norm{w_a-p_a}_2^2+\norm{w_b-p_b}_2^2\bigr)
 \le4(\delta_a+\delta_b)\le10\delta<\delta_h.
\]
For unit phases $u,p$ and $z=\E u\overline p$, one has
$1-|z|^2\le2-2\Rea z=\norm{u-p}_2^2$.
Consequently, for every $h$ simultaneously,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:73:eq:repairedfamily}
 1-|\E w_h\overline{q_h}|^2\le\delta_h,
 \qquad \norm{w_h-q_h}_2^2\le20\delta=:s_0^2.
\end{equation}
When $\delta=0$, every $\delta_h=0$; induction gives exact phases for all
$h$, and \eqref{gsr:en:73:eq:repairedfamily} holds with $s_0=0$ without using $A$.

Define a degree-at-most $k-2$ phase
\[
 R_{h,t}=\frac{q_{h+t}}{(T_hq_t)q_h}.
\]
Comparison with the exact cocycle law for the $w_h$ gives
$\norm{R_{h,t}-1}_2\le3s_0$. By \eqref{gsr:en:73:eq:eta},
\[
 3s_0\le10^{-(k-3)/2}\le2^{-(k-3)}
 <\sqrt2\,2^{-(k-3)}=2^{3/2-(k-2)}.
\]
Thus lemma~\ref{gsr:en:73:lem:separation} makes every $R_{h,t}$ constant, and also
$3s_0\le1$. Write $R_{h,t}=\e(c(h,t))$ with the principal lift
$c(h,t)\in[-1/2,1/2)$. Since $|\e(c)-1|\le1$, we have
$|c(h,t)|\le1/6$. Associativity of the translated products implies
\[
 c(h,t)+c(h+t,u)-c(h,t+u)-c(t,u)\in\Z.
\]
Its absolute value is at most $2/3$, so the integer is zero. Averaging
in $u$ and setting $b(h)=\E_u c(h,u)$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:73:eq:coboundary}
 c(h,t)=b(h)+b(t)-b(h+t).
\end{equation}
Set $q'_h=\e(b(h))q_h$. The sign in this definition and
\eqref{gsr:en:73:eq:coboundary} give the exact law
\[
 q'_{h+t}=(T_hq'_t)q'_h.
\]
Integrate it explicitly by defining $p_0(x)=q'_{-x}(0)$. Evaluating the
law with indices $-x,h$ at $0$ gives
$p_0(x-h)=q'_h(x)p_0(x)$. Hence $q'_h=T_hp_0/p_0$ for every $h$, so
$p_0\in\cP_{k-1}(G)$.

For $g=v/p_0$, the scalar correction $q'_h/q_h$ does not change the
magnitude of the derivative correlation. Therefore
\[
 Q_2(g)=\E_h|\E T_hg\overline g|^2
 =\E_h|\E w_h\overline{q_h}|^2
 \ge1-\E_h\delta_h=1-\delta.
\]
A final application of Parseval supplies a character $\chi$ with
$|\E g\overline\chi|^2\ge Q_2(g)$. The phase $p=p_0\chi$ proves
\eqref{gsr:en:73:eq:fidelity}. Rotating its correlation to the nonnegative real axis
proves \eqref{gsr:en:73:eq:unitdistance}, since $1-\sqrt{1-\delta}\le\delta$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A polar reduction without a cube vertex loss}
\begin{theorem}[Disk valued entry]\label{gsr:en:73:thm:diskentry}
For $k\ge2$, $|f|\le1$, and $\eps=1-Q_k(f)\le\eta_k/2$, there is
$p\in\cP_{k-1}(G)$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:73:eq:diskentry}
 \norm{f-p}_2^2\le2(1-\sqrt{1-2\eps})+\eps\le5\eps.
\end{equation}
Also $a=1-\E|f|^2\le\eps$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Put $\rho=|f|$ and $v=f/\rho$ where $\rho>0$, and $v=1$ otherwise.
For one cube write $V$ for its unit phase product and $R$ for the product
of its $2^k$ amplitudes. Thus $|V|=1$, $0\le R\le1$,
$Q_k(f)=\E VR$, $Q_k(v)=\E V$, and $Q_k(\rho)=\E R$.
The reality and nonnegativity of the cube averages give
\[
 Q_k(\rho)\ge Q_k(f),\qquad
 |Q_k(v)-Q_k(f)|\le\E(1-R)=1-Q_k(\rho)\le\eps.
\]
It follows that $1-Q_k(v)\le2\eps\le\eta_k$.
The product of the cube amplitudes is at most the amplitude at any one
vertex, so $Q_k(f)\le\E\rho$ and $\E(1-\rho)\le\eps$.
Apply theorem~\ref{gsr:en:73:thm:fidelity} and rotate $p$ to make its correlation with $v$
nonnegative. Pointwise,
\[
 |\rho v-p|^2=\rho|v-p|^2+(1-\rho)^2
 \le|v-p|^2+1-\rho.
\]
Averaging proves the first inequality in \eqref{gsr:en:73:eq:diskentry}; the second
uses $1-\sqrt{1-2\eps}\le2\eps$ for $0\le2\eps\le1$.
Finally two distinct cube vertices are independent and uniform. Retaining
only their amplitudes gives
$Q_k(f)\le(\E\rho)^2\le\E\rho^2$, proving $a\le\eps$.
\end{proof}
The two-unit-factor identity behind this reduction is important: a
term-by-term telescoping estimate over all $2^k$ vertices would introduce
an unnecessary factor depending on $k$.

\section[{Fifth cancellation and convex interpolation\srctag{73}}]{Fifth cancellation and convex interpolation}\label{gsr:en:73:sec:d5}\label{gsr:en:73:sec:remainder}
\srcnote{73}{Section 5}

The moment bounds and fifth-order cancellation in the next two subsections are imported from source 55\,\cite[Section 5]{srcfiftyfive}; the subsequent interpolation step refines its tail estimate.

An ordinary application of H\"older to five small $L^2$ factors suggests an
error of order $v^{5/2}$, which is too large for a cubic error in the defect.
The pointwise geometry of the unit disk improves that estimate.

\subsection{H\"older estimates from triple independence}

\begin{lemma}[Four-, five-, and six-factor estimates]\label{gsr:en:73:lem:holder}
Let $r:G\to\C$, put $v=\E|r|^2$, and use distinct cube vertices for the
variables displayed below. Then
\begin{align}
 \E\prod_{j=1}^4|r(X_j)|&\le v^2,\label{gsr:en:73:eq:holder4}\\
 \E|r(X_1)|^2\prod_{j=2}^5|r(X_j)|&\le v^3,\label{gsr:en:73:eq:holder5}\\
 \E\prod_{j=1}^6|r(X_j)|&\le v^3.\label{gsr:en:73:eq:holder6}
\end{align}
For every nonnegative $A$ with $\E A=a$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:73:eq:holderA}
 \E A(X_1)\prod_{j=2}^5|r(X_j)|\le a v^2.
\end{equation}
Statements with more vertices than the cube contains are simply unused.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Pair the four factors in \eqref{gsr:en:73:eq:holder4} and use Cauchy--Schwarz and
pairwise independence. For \eqref{gsr:en:73:eq:holder5}, take the six triples
$\{1,j,k\}$ with $2\le j<k\le5$. The product of
\[
 \bigl(|r(X_1)|^2|r(X_j)|^2|r(X_k)|^2\bigr)^{1/6}
\]
over these triples is precisely the integrand on the left of
\eqref{gsr:en:73:eq:holder5}. H\"older with six equal exponents and
lemma~\ref{gsr:en:55:lem:triple} gives $v^3$. Replace $|r(X_1)|^2$ by $A(X_1)$ in these
six factors to get \eqref{gsr:en:73:eq:holderA}.

For \eqref{gsr:en:73:eq:holder6}, use all twenty triples from six indices, with
exponent $1/20$ on each product of three squared magnitudes. Each index
occurs ten times, giving exponent one on its magnitude. Triple
independence again gives the asserted bound.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Cancellation of the potentially dangerous fifth term}

\begin{lemma}[Fifth-order real-part cancellation]\label{gsr:en:73:lem:fifth}
In the notation \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:variables}--\eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:identities}, suppose $m>0$.
For any five distinct cube vertices and any conjugation choices $s_j\in\{0,1\}$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:73:eq:fifth}
 \abs{\Rea\E\prod_{j=1}^5\cC^{s_j}r(X_j)}
 \le \frac5m(v+a)v^2.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Write $r=u+ib$ with real $u,b$. A product of five factors each equal to
$ib$ or $-ib$ is purely imaginary. Telescope the difference from that
product, changing one factor at a time. Since $|b|\le|r|$, its real part
has absolute value at most
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^5\E|u(X_j)|\prod_{k\ne j}|r(X_k)|.
\]
By \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:realpart},
\[
 |u|\le\frac{v+a+A+|r|^2}{2m}.
\]
For each summand, lemma~\ref{gsr:en:73:lem:holder} bounds the three contributions in the
numerator by $(v+a)v^2$, $av^2$, and $v^3$. Their sum is
$2(v+a)v^2$. Summing over the five choices proves \eqref{gsr:en:73:eq:fifth}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Convex interpolation remainder]\label{gsr:en:73:thm:expansion}
Suppose $|F|\le1$, $m=\E F\in[1/2,1]$, and use the notation of
section~\ref{gsr:en:55:sec:normal}. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:73:eq:expansion}
 \Ufiftyfive(F)=m^q+m^{q-4}\Rea \mathcal Q_d(r)+\mathcal R,
 \qquad |\mathcal R|\le B'_d(v+a)v^2,
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:73:eq:B}
 B'_d=10\binom q5+\binom q6.
\end{equation}
Binomial coefficients vanish when their lower index exceeds $q$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For real $t\in[0,1]$ put
$F_t=m+tr=(1-t)m+tF$ and $H(t)=\Ufiftyfive(F_t)$.
Convexity of the unit disk implies $|F_t|\le1$. The function $H$ is a
polynomial of degree at most $q$ in the real variable $t$.
For $q\ge6$, six differentiations give
\begin{align*}
 H^{(6)}(t)=6!\sum_{|S|=6}\E
 \left(\prod_{\omega\in S}\cC^{|\omega|}r(X_\omega)\right)
 \left(\prod_{\omega\notin S}\cC^{|\omega|}F_t(X_\omega)\right).
\end{align*}
Every six-set occurs in exactly $6!$ orders, and no affine factor can be
differentiated twice. Taking absolute values, discarding the bounded
undifferentiated factors, and using lemma~\ref{gsr:en:73:lem:holder} gives
\[
 |H^{(6)}(t)|\le6!\binom q6v^3.
\]
Taylor's formula at $t=0$, evaluated at $t=1$, has integral remainder
\[
 T=\frac1{5!}\int_0^1(1-t)^5H^{(6)}(t)\,dt,
 \qquad |T|\le\binom q6v^3.
\]
The coefficients of degrees one, two, and three vanish by centeredness
and triple independence. The fourth coefficient is $m^{q-4}\mathcal Q_d(r)$.
The real part of each fifth coefficient is at most
$10(v+a)v^2$ by lemma~\ref{gsr:en:73:lem:fifth}, since $m\ge1/2$ and
$m^{q-5}\le1$ whenever such terms occur. Also $v^3\le(v+a)v^2$.
Taking real parts proves the result. If $q=4$, the cube polynomial has
degree four and the expansion is exact, with $B'_2=0$.
\end{proof}
Source 55 instead used
$10\binom q5+\sum_{s=6}^q\binom qs2^{s-6}$.
Keeping the undifferentiated factors as bounded interpolants avoids
expanding their exponentially many subsets. No assumption that
$\norm{F-1}_\infty$ is small is used.

\section[{The explicit local stability theorem\srctag{73}}]{The explicit local stability theorem}\label{gsr:en:73:sec:d7}\label{gsr:en:73:sec:local}
\srcnote{73}{Section 7}

Define
\begin{align}
 K_{0,d}&=\frac{q(q-1)}8,\label{gsr:en:73:eq:K0}\\
 M_d&=\begin{cases}C_d/2,&|G|\text{ odd},\\A_d,&|G|\text{ even},\end{cases}
 \qquad
 L_d=\begin{cases}C_d,&|G|\text{ odd},\\0,&|G|\text{ even},\end{cases}
 \label{gsr:en:73:eq:ML}\\
 K_d&=K_{0,d}+M_d,\qquad H'_d=B'_d+L_d.\label{gsr:en:73:eq:KH}
\end{align}
For a radius and uniform inversion constant, put
\begin{align}
 K_*&=K_{0,d}+A_d,\qquad H'_*=B'_d+C_d,\qquad c=q/2,\label{gsr:en:73:eq:star}\\
 \rho'_d&=\min\left\{\frac12,
       \frac{q}{16(K_*+1)},
       \sqrt{\frac{q}{8(B'_d+2C_d+1)}}\right\},\label{gsr:en:73:eq:radius}\\
 R'_d&=\frac{12K_*^2}{c^5}+\frac{24K_*H'_*}{c^6}
                         +\frac{8H'_*}{c^4}.\label{gsr:en:73:eq:R}
\end{align}
All these constants are explicit. In \eqref{gsr:en:73:eq:ML}, the even-order choice
is valid on every group, though it is not optimal on odd-order groups.

\begin{theorem}[A posteriori local phase certificate]\label{gsr:en:73:thm:local}
Let $P\in\cP_{d-1}(G)$ and rotate it so that $m=\E f\overline P\ge0$.
Suppose $|f|\le1$ and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:73:eq:localinput}
 z=2(1-m)=D+a\le\rho'_d,
 \qquad D=\E|f-P|^2,\quad a=1-\E|f|^2.
\end{equation}
Then, writing $\eps=1-\Ufiftyfive(f)$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:73:eq:localpoly}
 \eps\ge\frac q2D-K_dD^2-H'_dD^3+\frac q4a,
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:73:eq:coarse}
 D+a\le\frac4q\eps.
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:73:eq:localinverse}
 D\le\frac2q\eps+\frac{8K_d}{q^3}\eps^2+R'_d\eps^3.
\end{equation}
The phase $P$ need not minimize distance.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Demodulate by $P$ and use the notation of section~\ref{gsr:en:55:sec:normal}. Since
$z\le1$, theorem~\ref{gsr:en:73:thm:expansion} and proposition~\ref{gsr:en:55:prop:pairing} give the master bound
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:73:eq:master}
 \Ufiftyfive(f)\le\left(1-\frac z2\right)^q+M_dD^2+B'_dzD^2+L_dz^2D.
\end{equation}
For odd order use $v_2=0$, $v\le D$, and $v+a\le z$.
For even order use \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:crudequartic} instead.

Taylor's formula with a nonpositive third derivative gives
\[
 (1-z/2)^q\le1-\frac q2z+K_{0,d}z^2
 \qquad(0\le z\le1).
\]
Substitute $z=D+a$ in \eqref{gsr:en:73:eq:master} and collect the terms containing
$a$ to obtain
\begin{align}\label{gsr:en:73:eq:beforeabsorb}
 \eps\ge{}&\frac q2D-K_dD^2-H'_dD^3\\
 &+a\left\{\frac q2-K_{0,d}(2D+a)-B'_dD^2-L_d(2D+a)D\right\}.\notag
\end{align}
Since $2D+a\le2\rho'_d$, the expression in braces is at least
\[
 \frac q2-2K_{0,d}\rho'_d-(B'_d+2C_d)(\rho'_d)^2\ge\frac q4.
\]
This proves \eqref{gsr:en:73:eq:localpoly}. Also
\[
 K_dD+H'_dD^2\le K_*\rho'_d+H'_*(\rho'_d)^2
 \le\frac q{16}+\frac q8<\frac q4,
\]
which proves \eqref{gsr:en:73:eq:coarse}.

For clarity, we spell out the inversion rather than hiding it in an
asymptotic notation. From \eqref{gsr:en:73:eq:localpoly}, dropping the nonnegative
amplitude term, and from \eqref{gsr:en:73:eq:coarse},
\[
 D\le\frac\eps c+\frac{K_d}{c}D^2+\frac{H'_d}{c}D^3,
 \qquad D\le\frac{2\eps}{c}.
\]
Because $0\le\eps\le1$, it follows first that
\[
 D-\frac\eps c\le C_1\eps^2,
 \qquad C_1=\frac{4K_d}{c^3}+\frac{8H'_d}{c^4}.
\]
Consequently (using the positive part if $D-\eps/c<0$)
\[
 D^2\le\frac{\eps^2}{c^2}+\frac{3C_1}{c}\eps^3,
 \qquad D^3\le\frac{8\eps^3}{c^3}.
\]
Substituting once more yields
\[
 D\le\frac\eps c+\frac{K_d}{c^3}\eps^2+
 \left(\frac{12K_d^2}{c^5}+\frac{24K_dH'_d}{c^6}
       +\frac{8H'_d}{c^4}\right)\eps^3.
\]
Replacing $K_d,H'_d$ by $K_*,H'_*$ in the cubic coefficient proves
\eqref{gsr:en:73:eq:localinverse}.
\end{proof}

The sharp coefficients simplify dramatically:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:73:eq:Ksimplify}
 K_{0,d}+\frac{C_d}{2}=\frac{q(3^d-1)}{16},
 \qquad
 K_{0,d}+A_d=\frac{q(q^2-1)}{24}.
\end{equation}
Thus $8K_d/q^3$ is exactly \eqref{gsr:fm:73:eq:b}.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Singly exponential radius and the completed entry argument\srctag{73}}]{Singly exponential radius and the completed entry argument}\label{gsr:en:73:sec:d8}\label{gsr:en:73:sec:combine}
\srcnote{73}{Section 8}
\begin{proposition}[Uniform numerical constants]\label{gsr:en:73:prop:constants}
The constants in equations~\eqref{gsr:en:73:eq:radius} and \eqref{gsr:en:73:eq:R} satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:73:eq:radiuslower}
 \rho'_d\ge q^{-5/2}=2^{-5d/2},\qquad R'_d<3q^3=3\cdot8^d.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The four-set census gives $0\le C_d\le A_d\le q^3/24$. Also
$K_*=q(q^2-1)/24\le q^3/24$. Since $q\ge4$,
\[
 K_*+1\le q^3/24+1\le q^3/12.
\]
Using $\binom qs\le q^s/s!$ gives
\begin{align*}
 B'_d+2C_d+1
 &\le q^5/12+q^6/720+q^3/12+1\\
 &\le q^6\left(\frac1{48}+\frac1{720}+\frac1{768}+\frac1{4096}\right)
 =\frac{4381}{184320}q^6<\frac{q^6}{40}.
\end{align*}
Thus the second entry in the minimum defining $\rho'_d$ is at least
$3/(4q^2)\ge q^{-5/2}$, since $\sqrt q\ge2$.
The third is at least $\sqrt5\,q^{-5/2}$, and the first is $1/2\ge q^{-5/2}$.
This proves the radius assertion.

For the cubic constant a slightly tighter estimate is useful:
\begin{align*}
 H'_* =B'_d+C_d
 &\le q^5/12+q^6/720+q^3/24\\
 &\le q^6\left(\frac1{48}+\frac1{720}+\frac1{1536}\right)
 =\frac{527}{23040}q^6<\frac{q^6}{40}.
\end{align*}
Substitute $K_*\le q^3/24$, $H'_*\le q^6/40$, and $c=q/2$ into
\eqref{gsr:en:73:eq:R}. This gives
\[
 R'_d\le\frac23q+\frac85q^3+\frac{16}5q^2
 \le\left(\frac1{24}+\frac85+\frac45\right)q^3
 =\frac{293}{120}q^3<3q^3.
\]
All estimates hold for every real $q\ge4$ where the displayed polynomial
bounds are used; no finite numerical search is needed.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:73:thm:main}]
Assume $\eps\le10^{-d}$. This is at most $\eta_d/2$:
for $d=2$ it is $1/100\le1/2$, and for $d\ge3$ the ratio is
\[
 \frac{10^{-d}}{\eta_d/2}=\frac{360}{1000}=\frac9{25}.
\]
By theorem~\ref{gsr:en:73:thm:diskentry}, a phase $P$ satisfies $D=\E|f-P|^2\le5\eps$.
Rotate $P$ so that $m=\E f\overline P\ge0$, which only decreases $D$.
Since $a\le\eps$, we obtain $z=D+a\le6\eps$.
For $d\ge4$,
\[
 6\cdot10^{-d}\le q^{-5/2}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 36\le(25/8)^d.
\]
The latter holds at $d=4$ because $36\cdot8^4=147456<390625=25^4$,
and its right side increases with $d$.
For the two remaining degrees the exact radius formula gives
$\rho'_2=1/14$ and $\rho'_3=1/44$; hence
$6/100\le1/14$ and $6/1000\le1/44$.
Thus $z\le\rho'_d$ in every case. Apply theorem~\ref{gsr:en:73:thm:local} and
\eqref{gsr:en:73:eq:Ksimplify}, followed by proposition~\ref{gsr:en:73:prop:constants}.
Finally $D_d(f)\le D$, so no minimizing-phase selection was needed.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Low degree ledger}
The exact radius and cubic formula can be much sharper than their clean
uniform bounds. The following entries use equations~\eqref{gsr:en:73:eq:B}, \eqref{gsr:en:73:eq:radius} and \eqref{gsr:en:73:eq:R};
they are also reproduced by the companion code.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}rrrrrr@{}}
\toprule
$d$ & $B'_d$ & $K_*$ & $H'_*$ & $\rho'_d$ & $R'_d$\\
\midrule
2 & 0 & $5/2$ & 1 & $1/14$ & $121/32$\\
3 & 588 & 21 & 600 & $1/44$ & $25023/256$\\
4 & 51688 & 170 & 51788 & $1/171$ & $3759139/4096$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
For example, in degree three a quadratic phase candidate with
$D+a\le1/44$ satisfies
\[
 \begin{array}{ll}
 \eps\ge4D-13D^2-600D^3+2a,&|G|\text{ odd},\\
 \eps\ge4D-21D^2-588D^3+2a,&|G|\text{ even}.
 \end{array}
\]
In both cases $D+a\le\eps/2$, and
\[
 D\le\frac\eps4+
 \begin{cases}13\eps^2/64,&|G|\text{ odd},\\21\eps^2/64,&|G|\text{ even}
 \end{cases}
 +\frac{25023}{256}\eps^3.
\]
The new fifth-and-higher remainder coefficient is $588$, compared with
$608$ in source 55. Its radius $1/44$ happens to remain unchanged.
The improvement becomes larger at higher degrees.

\section{Sources~75--81: hereditary relative energy and the Section~6 endpoint \wtag}\label{gsr:en:sec:hereditary}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the twelfth write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next fifty-eight sections are source~75's Sections~9--14 (the second Part of its manuscript), source~76's Sections~2--8, source~77's Sections~2--10, source~78's Sections~2--11 and Appendix~A, source~79's Sections~2--9 and Appendix~A, source~80's Sections~2--8 and source~81's Sections~2--10. \emph{Logically they continue source~11's chapter} on affine rigidity at the Section~6 endpoint (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:affine}) and the chapter of sources~59 and~56 (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:affinerepair}), and they stand beside source~67's characteristic-three chapter (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:charthree}); they are printed here because no number printed earlier may move. The seven sources are one chain, Reports~287--293 of the series, each citing its predecessor (sources~77--81 by the SHA-256 of its \TeX{} source, all recomputed and matching at the write), and they are printed in that order. Source~76's Section~2 is source~78's Section~2 word for word and source~80's Sections~5--7 are source~81's Sections~8--10; each is printed once, in the later source (Sections~\ref{gsr:en:76:sec:d2} and~\ref{gsr:en:80:sec:d5}--\ref{gsr:en:80:sec:d7} keep the heading and a note). Source~76's Section~3, a self-contained proof of its cyclic lemma that differs from source~78's Section~3 in text and proof, is printed as a second route, as is source~75's arbitrary-target theorem. The introductions are Sections~\ref{gsr:fm:75:sec:d1}--\ref{gsr:fm:81:sec:d1}.

\emph{The invariant.} For a map $a:G\to H$ defined on \emph{all} of an abelian group $G$, with values in an abelian group $H$, and a finitely supported weight $w\ge0$, let $\Eadd(w)$ count additive quadruples of $G$ with weights and $\Ea(w)$ those also respected by $a$; $r(a)=\inf_w\Ea(w)/\Eadd(w)$, and $\rind(a)$ is the same infimum over indicators of finite sets. For an indicator $\ind_A$, $\Ea(\ind_A)$ is the repository's \file{phiAdditiveCount}~$A\,a$. \emph{This is not source~11's statistic}: source~11, source~59 and source~67's characteristic-three chapter study the energy of the whole graph normalized by $N^3$, $\Energy(f)/N^3=\Ea(\ind_G)/\Eadd(\ind_G)$ on a finite group, one test among all those taken here; a single changed value costs at most $4/N$ of that average (source~78's Section~\ref{gsr:en:78:sec:d11}, item~5), while on $\Z/N\Z\to\Z/N\Z$ it already forces $r\le8/11$ (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:75:cor:sparsegap}). The thresholds of those chapters ($1/4$ and $4/9$ in source~67's, $2/9$ and $4/9$ in source~59's) bound the defect $1-\Energy(f)/N^3$ of the whole-graph energy and are not comparable with the thresholds $3/4$, $19/27$, $\rho$ here, which bound infima of the relative ratio. Source~56 uses the same fixed-weight relative statistic under a Fourier-uniformity hypothesis and approximate repair, as sources~75, 76 and~78 say. None of sources~75--81 cites source~11 or source~67.

\emph{What is proved, strongest first.} \emph{Classification} (source~78): every $a$ is exactly one of: affine, with $r=\rind=1$; the division-free index-two family $a(k)=\beta+\psi(k)$, $a(t+k)=\beta+u+\psi(k)$ on an index-two subgroup $K$ with defect $\eta=2u-\psi(2t)\ne0$, with $r=\rind=3/4$; or a finite indicator of ratio at most $19/27$, which is optimal ($a(j)=j$ on $C_3\to\Z$) (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:78:thm:classification}, Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:78:prop:C3lower}). Under the increment equation (P), the third class has $\rind\le5/8$, sharp (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:78:thm:P}), with a genuine order-four obstruction ($35/128$ on $C_8^2\to C_4$); the index-two subgroup is intrinsic (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:78:cor:canonical}) and the attainment criteria of source~77 hold for every endpoint map (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:78:cor:attainment}). \emph{Weighted cutoff} (source~79): the third class has $r\le\rho=(\sqrt6-1)/(\sqrt6-1+\sqrt{\sqrt6-2})=0.6837442484\ldots$, optimal, with the unique minimizer $(1,\tau,1)$, $\tau=\sqrt{\sqrt6-2}$, on $C_3\to\Z$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:79:thm:gap}); every nonzero-defect index-three affine cut has $r=\rho$, attained iff $G\setminus K$ contains an element of finite order (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:79:thm:three-main}); $\lfloor j/3\rfloor$ on $\Z$ has infimum $\rho$, never attained. \emph{Elementary abelian $3$-groups} (sources~80 and~81): on $\F_3$-spaces of any dimension and any target, $r>5/8$ iff $a$ is affine or a translated index-three cut iff every indicator on at most nine points has ratio above $53/81$, sharp (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:80:thm:main}); outside these families the optimal uniform weighted bound is $\lambda=(11+6\sqrt6)/(11+6\sqrt6+7\sqrt{6\sqrt6-8})=0.5865294215\ldots$, attained by one order-two spike on $\F_3^2$, with every other plane map outside the favourable families at most $677/1161$, and nine support points necessary at the threshold $\lambda$ (Theorems~\ref{gsr:fm:81:thm:main}, \ref{gsr:fm:81:thm:plane-equality}). \emph{Witness sizes} (sources~76 and~77): indicators on at most $\max\{6,2\lceil3/\sqrt{32\varepsilon}\rceil\}$ points reach $3/4+\varepsilon$, exponent $1/2$ optimal (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:76:thm:witnesses}); weights need $\Theta(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ points, with leading constant between $1/\log16$ and $\pi/(8\mathsf G)$, the latter sharp for containing intervals (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:77:thm:main-gap}, Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:77:cyclo-interval-lower}). \emph{The first steps} (sources~75 and~76): for maps $\Z/N\Z\to\Z/N\Z$, $r\in[0,8/11]\cup\{3/4,1\}$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:75:thm:classification}); on arbitrary abelian groups $r>3/4$ iff affine, with integer parity on $\Z$ at $3/4$ never attained (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:76:thm:main}).

\emph{Superseded within the chain} (stated where they are printed, by dated notes): source~75's $8/11$ by $19/27$ (indicators) and $\rho$ (weights), both optimal over all abelian targets; source~76's $3/4$ dichotomy and its conditional $5/8$ for cyclic-coset-affine maps by source~78's trichotomy and its (P)-branch theorem; source~76's question on the weighted support order by source~77; source~78's weighted question by source~79; source~80's weighted bound $\gamma=0.6244659979\ldots$ by source~81's $\lambda$. \emph{Two scope warnings.} The constants $19/27$, $\rho$, $\lambda$ are optimal uniformly over targets; for one fixed target they are upper bounds (for $\F_3$-spaces source~82, placed and not yet written, gives $5/9$ when the target has no element of order two; for maps $\Z/N\Z\to\Z/N\Z$, the setting of source~75, see the note after its Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:75:thm:classification}).
