\section[{The classification and the sharp threshold\srctag{75}}]{The classification and the sharp threshold}\label{gsr:en:75:sec:d9}\label{gsr:en:75:sec:relative}
\srcnote{75}{Section 9}
In this part $N\ge1$ is arbitrary and $a:\G\to\G$ is a total map. We use the energies and ratio in \eqref{gsr:fm:75:eq:ordinary-intro}--\eqref{gsr:fm:75:eq:ratio-intro}. For a nonempty subset $U\subseteq\G$, let $1_U$ denote its indicator, and define
\[
 r_{\rm ind}(a)=\min_{\varnothing\ne U\subseteq\G}
 \frac{\Eng(a,1_U)}{\Eng_{\rm add}(1_U)}.
\]
Always $0\le r(a)\le r_{\rm ind}(a)\le1$. The denominator in $r(a)$ is positive, since a nonzero weight supplies a positive diagonal term. Homogeneity permits normalization $\sum w=1$. On this compact simplex the denominator is at least $1/N$, so the ratio is continuous and its infimum is attained. Adding an affine map to $a$ changes neither respected quadruples nor these ratios.

\begin{theorem}[Hereditary cyclic classification]\label{gsr:en:75:thm:classification}
For every positive integer $N$, the following assertions hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $r_{\rm ind}(a)>8/11$, then $a$ is affine, or $N$ is even and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:75:eq:parityform}
 a(x)=\alpha x+\beta+\delta\varepsilon(x),\qquad \alpha,\beta,\delta\in\G,
\end{equation}
where $\varepsilon(x)\in\{0,1\}$ is the parity of the residue $x$. A parity-form map is affine exactly when $2\delta=0$.
\item An affine map has $r(a)=r_{\rm ind}(a)=1$. A non-affine parity-form map has
\[
 r(a)=r_{\rm ind}(a)=3/4.
\]
\item Both ratios belong to $[0,8/11]\cup\{3/4,1\}$. In particular,
\[
 r(a)>3/4\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 r_{\rm ind}(a)>3/4\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a\text{ is affine}.
\]
\end{enumerate}
The threshold $3/4$ is sharp across all cyclic moduli and for each even $N\ge4$. No optimality claim is made for the secondary constant $8/11$ or for the odd-modulus threshold.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 70--81]
\emph{Superseded uniformly over targets, and what remains for $\Z/N\Z\to\Z/N\Z$} (checked at the write). Over arbitrary abelian groups the third class has indicator ratio at most $19/27$ and weighted infimum at most $\rho=0.6837\ldots$, both optimal (sources~78 and~79, Theorems~\ref{gsr:fm:78:thm:classification} and~\ref{gsr:fm:79:thm:gap}), so the secondary constant $8/11$ is superseded and the gap $(8/11,3/4)$ contains no value of $r$ or $\rind$. The optimal examples ($C_3\to\Z$) do not have this theorem's target $\Z/N\Z$: an exhaustive computation at the write over all maps $\Z/N\Z\to\Z/N\Z$ for $N=3,\ldots,7$ gives the largest $\rind$ outside the affine and parity forms as $5/9$, $5/8$, $69/125$, $73/105$ and $19/31$, attained at $N=6$ by $73/105=0.695\ldots<19/27$. Whether $19/27$ (or $8/11$) is approached in this setting as $N$ grows is open (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:hereditary}).
\end{writenote}

The distinction between an implication at a strict threshold and classification at an attained value matters. For every $8/11<c\le3/4$, the maps satisfying $\Eng(a,w)\ge c\Eng_{\rm add}(w)$ for all nonnegative weights are exactly the affine and parity-form maps. For $3/4<c\le1$, only affine maps remain. We prove the theorem in three steps: four consecutive points for $N\ge7$, direct small-modulus arguments, and an exact identity for all weights.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Four-point tests and the exceptional small moduli\srctag{75}}]{Four-point tests and the exceptional small moduli}\label{gsr:en:75:sec:d10}
\srcnote{75}{Section 10}
\begin{lemma}[Four consecutive points]\label{gsr:en:75:lem:fourpoints}
Let $N\ge7$. If $r_{\rm ind}(a)>8/11$, then the first differences
$d(x)=a(x+1)-a(x)$ satisfy $d(x+2)=d(x)$ for every $x\in\G$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Fix $x$ and take $U=\{x,x+1,x+2,x+3\}$. Write the four images as $a_0,a_1,a_2,a_3$. The pair sums have multiplicities
\[
 1,2,3,4,3,2,1,
 \qquad \Eng_{\rm add}(1_U)=1+4+9+16+9+4+1=44,
\]
since the seven residues $0,\ldots,6$ are distinct modulo $N$. Set
\[
 A=a_0+a_2-2a_1,\quad B=a_1+a_3-2a_2,
 \quad M=a_0+a_3-a_1-a_2.
\]
The identity $M=A+B$ holds in $\G$. If $M\ne0$, at least one of $A,B$ is nonzero. The failure of $M=0$ destroys eight ordered quadruples comparing the two ordered representations of $\{0,3\}$ with those of $\{1,2\}$, in either order. The failure of $A=0$, or of $B=0$, destroys four further ordered quadruples comparing the endpoint pair with the repeated midpoint. These families have distinct ordinary pair sums. Hence
\[
 \Eng(a,1_U)\le44-8-4=32,
 \qquad \frac{\Eng(a,1_U)}{\Eng_{\rm add}(1_U)}\le\frac8{11},
\]
a contradiction. Therefore $M=0$ for every $x$, which is exactly $d(x+2)=d(x)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Integrating two-periodic differences]\label{gsr:en:75:lem:integrate}
If $d(x+2)=d(x)$ on $\G$, then $a$ is affine for odd $N$ and has the form \eqref{gsr:en:75:eq:parityform} for even $N$. Such a form is affine exactly when $2\delta=0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For odd $N$, translation by $2$ generates $\G$, so $d$ is constant and summation gives $a(x)=a(0)+xd(0)$.

Let $N=2m$. Put $t=d(0)+d(1)$. Summing all $2m$ increments gives $mt=0$ modulo $2m$. An integer representative of $t$ is therefore even. Choose $\alpha\in\G$ with $2\alpha=t$, and set $\beta=a(0)$ and $\delta=a(1)-a(0)-\alpha$. The increments of \eqref{gsr:en:75:eq:parityform} are $\alpha+\delta$ and $\alpha-\delta$, agreeing with $d(0)$ and $d(1)$. The value at zero also agrees, proving the representation. These increments are constant exactly when $2\delta=0$, and a map on a cyclic group is affine exactly when its first differences are constant.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Small cyclic moduli]\label{gsr:en:75:lem:small}
For $1\le N\le6$, the condition $r_{\rm ind}(a)>8/11$ has the same classification as in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:75:thm:classification}.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $h,v\in\G$, put
\[
 n_h(v)=|\{x\in\G:a(x+h)-a(x)=v\}|,
 \qquad Q_h=\sum_v n_h(v)^2.
\]
Parametrizing an additive quadruple by equal domain differences gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:75:eq:histogram}
 \Eng(a,1_{\G})=\sum_hQ_h,\qquad
 \Eng_{\rm add}(1_{\G})=N^3,\qquad Q_0=N^2,
 \qquad Q_{-h}=Q_h.
\end{equation}
The sum of the $N$ increments in direction $h$ is zero. A nonconstant histogram cannot have multiplicities $N-1$ and $1$: if the values were $v$ repeated $N-1$ times and $u$ once, their sum would be $Nv+(u-v)=u-v$, forcing $u=v$ in $\G$. Thus for $N\ge4$, every nonconstant histogram satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:75:eq:hist-bound}
 Q_h\le(N-2)^2+4.
\end{equation}
Indeed its largest multiplicity is at most $N-2$, and concentrating the remaining mass as far as possible maximizes the sum of squares. If $h$ generates $\G$, a constant increment in direction $h$ makes $a$ affine.

For $N=1,2$, every map is affine. For $N=3$, a non-affine map has nonconstant histograms at $h=1,2$. The only permitted multiplicity partition is $1+1+1$, so
\[
 r_{\rm ind}(a)\le\frac{9+3+3}{27}=\frac59<\frac8{11}.
\]
For $N=4$, a constant increment $a(x+2)-a(x)$ gives two-periodic first differences and hence Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:75:lem:integrate}. Otherwise $a$ is non-affine, all three nonzero-direction histograms are nonconstant, and
\[
 r_{\rm ind}(a)\le\frac{16+3\cdot8}{64}=\frac58<\frac8{11}.
\]
For $N=5$, every nonzero direction generates the group. A non-affine map therefore has
\[
 r_{\rm ind}(a)\le\frac{25+4\cdot13}{125}=\frac{77}{125}<\frac8{11}.
\]
For $N=6$, a constant increment in direction $2$ again gives Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:75:lem:integrate}. Otherwise $Q_2=Q_4\le20$, and $Q_1=Q_5\le20$ because a constant generating increment would make $a$ affine. The remaining bound $Q_3\le36$ suffices:
\[
 r_{\rm ind}(a)\le\frac{36+20+20+36+20+20}{216}
 =\frac{19}{27}<\frac8{11}.
\]
All these are analytical bounds, not conclusions from a finite search.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The exact parity energy identity\srctag{75}}]{The exact parity energy identity}\label{gsr:en:75:sec:d11}\label{gsr:en:75:sec:sos}
\srcnote{75}{Section 11}
\begin{proposition}[Parity sum of squares]\label{gsr:en:75:prop:sos}
Suppose $N$ is even and $a$ has the form \eqref{gsr:en:75:eq:parityform} with $2\delta\ne0$. For a nonnegative weight $w$, let $e$ and $o$ be its restrictions to the even and odd cosets, extended by zero. Convolution, norms, and inner products use counting measure on $\G$. Define
\[
 R(h)=\sum_x e(x)o(x+h).
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:75:eq:sos}
 \Eng(a,w)-\frac34\Eng_{\rm add}(w)
 =\frac14\norm{e*e-o*o}_2^2
 +\frac12\sum_h\bigl(R(h)-R(-h)\bigr)^2.
\end{equation}
Equality holds exactly when $e*e=o*o$ and $R(h)=R(-h)$ for every $h$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Remove the affine part of $a$. In any ordinary additive quadruple, the integer parity sums on the two sides lie in $\{0,1,2\}$ and agree modulo $2$. Unequal sums must be $0$ and $2$, whose image sums differ by $\pm2\delta\ne0$. Thus precisely the quadruples with equal integer parity sums are respected.

Write
\[
 U=\norm{e*e}_2^2,\qquad V=\norm{o*o}_2^2,
 \qquad C=\ip{e*e}{o*o},\qquad D=\norm{e*o}_2^2.
\]
The first two convolutions are supported on the even coset, and $e*o$ on the odd coset. Consequently
\begin{align}
 \Eng_{\rm add}(w)&=U+V+2C+4D,\label{gsr:en:75:eq:parityordinary}\\
 \Eng(a,w)&=U+V+4D.\label{gsr:en:75:eq:parityrespected}
\end{align}
Expanding and relabeling the four variables gives
\[
 C=\sum_hR(h)R(-h),\qquad D=\sum_hR(h)^2.
\]
For the first identity, an equation $x+y=u+v$ with $x,y$ even and $u,v$ odd is parametrized by $u=x+h$, $v=y-h$. For the second, the mixed equation is parametrized by the common displacement from an even point to an odd point. Hence
\[
 D-C=\frac12\sum_h\bigl(R(h)-R(-h)\bigr)^2.
\]
Subtracting three quarters of \eqref{gsr:en:75:eq:parityordinary} from \eqref{gsr:en:75:eq:parityrespected} yields
\[
 \frac14(U+V-2C)+(D-C),
\]
which is exactly \eqref{gsr:en:75:eq:sos}. The equality conditions follow from its two nonnegative square terms.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Completion of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:75:thm:classification}]
Lemmas~\ref{gsr:en:75:lem:fourpoints}--\ref{gsr:en:75:lem:small} prove the asserted forms under the indicator hypothesis. Affine maps respect every ordinary additive quadruple, so both ratios equal one.

For a non-affine parity form, Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:75:prop:sos} gives $r(a)\ge3/4$. Taking $w=1_{\G}$ and $m=N/2$, all four quantities $U,V,C,D$ above equal $m^3$. Therefore
\[
 \Eng_{\rm add}(1_{\G})=8m^3=N^3,\qquad
 \Eng(a,1_{\G})=6m^3=\frac34N^3.
\]
This proves $r(a)=r_{\rm ind}(a)=3/4$. If either ratio exceeds $8/11$, the classification applies, so its value is $3/4$ or one. Finally, for every even $N\ge4$, the map $a(x)=\varepsilon(x)$ has $2\delta=2\ne0$ in $\G$, and is a non-affine example with ratio $3/4$. This proves all threshold and sharpness assertions.
\end{proof}

The proof uses particularly few indicator tests. For $N\ge7$, the $N$ consecutive four-point sets force two-periodic differences, and the full-group indicator separates non-affine parity forms from affine maps. For $N\le6$, the full-group indicator and the direct small-modulus argument suffice. Arbitrary weights are essential to the exact all-weight lower bound, but are not needed to force the classification.

\section[{Sparse modifications and the proposed relative repair\srctag{75}}]{Sparse modifications and the proposed relative repair}\label{gsr:en:75:sec:d12}
\srcnote{75}{Section 12}
\begin{lemma}[Affine agreement of parity forms]\label{gsr:en:75:lem:parityagreement}
A non-affine parity-form map on $\Z/N\Z$ agrees with any affine map on at most $N/2$ points.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Write $N=2m$ and subtract the affine comparison. The difference has the form
\[
 sx+t+\delta\varepsilon(x),\qquad 2\delta\ne0.
\]
On $x=2j$ and $x=2j+1$, the zero conditions are respectively
\[
 2sj=-t,\qquad 2sj=-t-s-\delta.
\]
These are fibres of the homomorphism $j\mapsto2sj$ from $\Z/m\Z$ to $\G$. If this homomorphism is nonconstant, each fibre has at most $m/2$ elements, so the total agreement is at most $m$. If it is constant, each parity coset contributes zero or $m$ points. Both could contribute only if the original map equalled the affine comparison everywhere, contrary to non-affinity. The bound is again $m=N/2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A fixed gap for defects below half density]\label{gsr:en:75:cor:sparsegap}
If $a$ differs nontrivially from an affine map on fewer than $N/2$ points, then
\[
 r(a)\le r_{\rm ind}(a)\le8/11.
\]
For $N\ge7$, some four consecutive residues already give an indicator witness with respected-to-ordinary energy ratio at most $8/11$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Agreement on more than $N/2$ points excludes a non-affine parity form by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:75:lem:parityagreement}. It also excludes a different affine map: the agreement set of two different affine maps is empty or a fibre of a nonzero cyclic homomorphism, and therefore has at most $N/2$ points. Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:75:thm:classification} proves the bound. For $N\ge7$, if every four-point window satisfied its middle-pair identity, Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:75:lem:integrate} would give precisely one of the excluded forms. Thus at least one window supplies the stated witness.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The deletion examples fail relative energy]\label{gsr:en:75:cor:joined}
Every map in Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:75:thm:baseline} and~\ref{gsr:en:75:thm:optimized} can be chosen with a nonzero slice $a$ supported on fewer than $N/2$ points. It then has $r(a)\le8/11$, while its full-dimensional map has the stated full weighted product properties, named data, and positive minimum deletion cost.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The parameter proofs give $0<\lambda<1/2$, so $m\le\lambda N<N/2$. Also $m^{c_\rho}\ge L_0$ and $c_\rho\le1$ imply $m\ge L_0$. Apply the balanced-symbol conclusion of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:75:lem:word} on $J$: the symbol $1\in S$ occurs at least $7m/(8R)>0$ times. Thus $a$ is nonzero and vanishes outside $J$. Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:75:cor:sparsegap} applies relative to the zero affine map; the remaining properties were proved in the first part.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Translation to the product parameter}
For $0\le\gamma\le1$, replacing the one-restriction ambient test by
\[
 \Eng(a,w)\ge\gamma^8\Eng_{\rm add}(w)\qquad(w\ge0)
\]
has the following full-domain cyclic consequences:
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $\gamma^8>3/4$, equivalently $\gamma>(3/4)^{1/8}$, then $a$ is affine.
\item At $\gamma^8=3/4$, non-affine parity forms remain for each even $N\ge4$.
\item If $\gamma^8>8/11$, every qualifying map is affine or a parity form; every nontrivial modification of an affine map on fewer than $N/2$ points fails the hypothesis.
\end{enumerate}
This answers the proposed denominator change for a single full-domain slice. It does not establish that a simultaneous-family version is preserved under any specific restriction or selection procedure.

\subsection{Why the full domain matters}
On a subset whose unordered pair sums are all distinct, every additive quadruple is trivial, and every map preserves it. A concrete example is $A=\{0,1,3\}\subseteq\Z/7\Z$, whose unordered pair sums are $0,1,2,3,4,6$. The map with values $a(0)=a(1)=0$ and $a(3)=1$ has respected energy equal to ordinary energy for every weight supported on $A$, but cannot extend to an affine map of $\Z/7\Z$: the first two values force the zero affine map. Thus a partial-domain affine-extension statement requires more hypotheses.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The sharp threshold for arbitrary abelian targets\srctag{75}}]{The sharp threshold for arbitrary abelian targets}\label{gsr:en:75:sec:d13}\label{gsr:en:75:sec:abelian}
\srcnote{75}{Section 13}
The target $\G$ was used in the small-modulus bounds and in dividing an even residue by two. The sharp $3/4$ affine threshold itself has a broader form. Here an affine map into an abelian group $H$ means $a(x)=\beta+\phi(x)$ for a homomorphism $\phi:\G\to H$; the relative energies use equality in $H$ for the image condition.

\begin{theorem}[Arbitrary abelian target]\label{gsr:en:75:thm:abeliantarget}
Let $N\ge1$, let $H$ be any abelian group, and let $a:\Z/N\Z\to H$. If all nonempty subset indicators have respected-to-ordinary energy ratio greater than $3/4$, then $a$ is affine. In particular $r(a)>3/4$ if and only if $a$ is affine.

For $N=2m$, a map with two-periodic consecutive increments has the division-free form
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:75:eq:divisionfree}
 a(2j)=\beta+jd,\qquad a(2j+1)=\beta+jd+u,
 \qquad md=0\quad(j\in\Z/m\Z).
\end{equation}
It is affine exactly when $d=2u$, and otherwise has $r(a)=3/4$. The threshold is sharp uniformly over cyclic domains and abelian targets, including infinite targets; sharpness for every fixed target is not asserted. The $8/11$ classification of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:75:thm:classification} remains stated for target $\Z/N\Z$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The four-point proof in Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:75:lem:fourpoints} uses only abelian addition in the target. For $N\ge7$ the stronger-than-$3/4$ indicator hypothesis therefore forces two-periodic increments. For odd $N$, they are constant, say $v$, and summing around the cycle gives $Nv=0$, so the map is affine. For $N=2m$, take $\beta=a(0)$, $u=a(1)-a(0)$, and $d=a(2)-a(0)$. Summation gives \eqref{gsr:en:75:eq:divisionfree} and $md=0$. Its consecutive increments are $u$ and $d-u$, so affinity is equivalent to $d=2u$; in that case $Nu=md=0$ as required.

For the non-affine even case, write a pair of residues as $x_i=2j_i+\varepsilon_i$ and let $p=\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2\in\{0,1,2\}$. Equal domain sums force $p$ and the other pair's parity sum $p'$ to agree modulo two. If $p=p'$, the $j$-sums agree modulo $m$, hence the image sums agree because $md=0$. Otherwise $\{p,p'\}=\{0,2\}$; the $j$-sums differ by one modulo $m$, and the image sums differ by $\pm(2u-d)\ne0$. Thus precisely the same parity classes as in Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:75:prop:sos} are respected. Its exact sum-of-squares proof applies without change and the full-group indicator gives equality at $3/4$.

It remains to check $N\le6$ without assuming $Nh=0$ for target elements $h\in H$. The histogram identities \eqref{gsr:en:75:eq:histogram} remain valid, since each histogram has finite support. A nonconstant histogram has square sum at most $(N-1)^2+1$. If its multiplicity type $(N-1,1)$ is excluded, the bound improves to $(N-2)^2+4$.

Two cycle observations provide the required exclusions. For an involutive shift, increments come in pairs $v,-v$. If $v\ne-v$, their counts coincide; if $v=-v$, its count is even. Therefore a nonconstant histogram of type $(N-1,1)$ is impossible when $N$ is even. For shift $2$ on $\Z/6\Z$, the two cycles have length three. A histogram with five copies of $v$ and one of $u$ has an all-$v$ cycle, giving $3v=0$, and its other cycle gives $2v+u=0$, hence $u=v$, a contradiction.

For $N=1$ every map is affine. For $N=2$, every map already has \eqref{gsr:en:75:eq:divisionfree} with $d=0$, so the preceding parity calculation applies. For $N=3$, a non-affine map has two nonconstant generating histograms, giving uniform ratio at most
\[
 \frac{9+2\cdot5}{27}=\frac{19}{27}<\frac34.
\]
For $N=4$, constant $\Delta_2a$ gives two-periodic first differences. Otherwise $Q_2\le8$ by the involution observation, while $Q_1=Q_3\le10$, giving
\[
 \frac{16+8+2\cdot10}{64}=\frac{44}{64}<\frac34.
\]
For $N=5$, all nonzero shifts generate the group, so a non-affine map has uniform ratio at most
\[
 \frac{25+4\cdot17}{125}=\frac{93}{125}<\frac34.
\]
For $N=6$, constant $\Delta_2a$ again gives the even normal form. Otherwise $Q_2=Q_4\le20$ by the three-cycle observation and $Q_1=Q_5\le26$. If $\Delta_3a$ is nonconstant, the involution observation gives $Q_3\le20$, so the ratio is at most
\[
 \frac{36+2\cdot20+2\cdot26+20}{216}=\frac{148}{216}<\frac34.
\]
If $\Delta_3a$ is constant, then $Q_3=36$ and $\Delta_1a$ is three-periodic. Its multiplicities are even and it is nonconstant, so $Q_1=Q_5\le20$. The bound becomes
\[
 \frac{36+2\cdot20+2\cdot20+36}{216}=\frac{152}{216}<\frac34.
\]
These bounds exhaust the remaining non-affine cases. They use the full-group indicator, so the indicator hypothesis suffices throughout. Finally, take $H=\Z$ and $a(x)=\varepsilon(x)$ on any even cyclic domain, including $N=2$. Then \eqref{gsr:en:75:eq:divisionfree} has $d=0$, $u=1$, and ratio exactly $3/4$, proving uniform sharpness.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 70--81]
Contained in source~76's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:76:thm:main} (arbitrary abelian domains as well as targets) and in source~78's classification; this cyclic-domain proof, with its division-free form, is a second route (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:hereditary}).
\end{writenote}

The target-independent histogram bound used for $N=5$ is $93/125$, which exceeds $8/11$. The argument therefore does not silently extend the same-cyclic secondary gap to arbitrary targets. The domain remains cyclic in every assertion above.

\section[{A deterministic certificate from local tests\srctag{75}}]{A deterministic certificate from local tests}\label{gsr:en:75:sec:d14}\label{gsr:en:75:sec:certificate}
\srcnote{75}{Section 14}
\begin{corollary}[Linear scan certificate]\label{gsr:en:75:cor:certificate}
Given the values of $a:\G\to\G$, a deterministic procedure using $O(N)$ arithmetic operations in $\G$ returns one of the following certificates:
\begin{enumerate}
\item coefficients of an affine representation, proving $r(a)=1$;
\item coefficients of a non-affine parity representation and the full-group indicator, proving $r(a)=3/4$;
\item an indicator witness with respected-to-ordinary energy ratio at most $8/11$.
\end{enumerate}
For $N\ge7$, the third certificate uses four consecutive residues. For $N\le6$, the full-group indicator suffices. The operation count is an arithmetic-operation count, not a bit-complexity analysis.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For $N\ge7$, scan the $N$ middle relations
$a(x)+a(x+3)=a(x+1)+a(x+2)$. Any failure yields the four-point certificate of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:75:lem:fourpoints}; its energies can be counted on a set of size four. If all pass, integrate the two-periodic differences using Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:75:lem:integrate}, and test $2\delta=0$ in the even case. The represented values can be checked in a further linear pass. Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:75:prop:sos} and the full-group identity certify the corresponding exact ratio symbolically, without enumerating $N^3$ quadruples.

For $N\le6$, test affine and parity representations directly; outside these forms, Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:75:lem:small} gives the uniform certificate. This costs a fixed number of operations because $N\le6$. No search over weights or randomized witness selection is involved.
\end{proof}

\section[{A self-contained cyclic lemma\srctag{76}}]{A self-contained cyclic lemma}\label{gsr:en:76:sec:d3}\label{gsr:en:76:sec:cyclic}
\srcnote{76}{Section 3}
\begin{lemma}[Cyclic domains and arbitrary targets]\label{gsr:en:76:lem:cyclic}
Every nonaffine map from a cyclic group, finite or infinite, to an arbitrary abelian group has $\rind\le3/4$. On a finite cyclic domain some indicator attains a ratio at most $3/4$. More specifically, either there is an indicator of at most six points with ratio strictly below $3/4$, or the map has the nonzero-defect form~\eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:cyclic-form}.
\end{lemma}

\subsection{Four consecutive points}
First consider $\Z$ or $\Z/N$ with $N\ge7$. The four distinct points $x,x+1,x+2,x+3$ have pair-sum multiplicities $1,2,3,4,3,2,1$: all seven integer sums remain distinct modulo $N$. Their ordinary energy is $44$. Write $a_i=a(x+i)$ and
\[
 A=a_0+a_2-2a_1,\quad B=a_1+a_3-2a_2,\quad
 M=a_0+a_3-a_1-a_2=A+B.
\]
If $M\ne0$, comparisons between the two ordered pairs of type $\{0,3\}$ and the two of type $\{1,2\}$ lose eight ordered quadruples at sum $3$. At least one of $A,B$ is nonzero, losing four additional comparisons at sum $2$ or $4$. The indicator ratio is therefore at most
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:76:eq:four-window}
 \frac{44-12}{44}=\frac8{11}<\frac34.
\end{equation}
This argument is an implication in arbitrary $H$ and uses no cancellation of an integer factor.

If every window has $M=0$, let $b(x)=a(x+1)-a(x)$. Then $b(x+2)=b(x)$. On an odd cycle $b$ is constant, making $a$ affine. On an even cycle or on $\Z$, set $\beta=a(0)$, $u=b(0)$ and $d=b(0)+b(1)$. Summing the two-periodic increments gives~\eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:cyclic-form}, with $nd=0$ in order $2n$. A nonaffine form has $\eta\ne0$ and is handled in Section~\ref{gsr:en:78:subsec:cyclic-endpoint}.

\subsection{Difference histograms for the small orders}
For $G=\Z/N$, define
\[
 \Delta_h a(x)=a(x+h)-a(x),\quad
 n_h(v)=|\{x:\Delta_h a(x)=v\}|,\quad Q_h=\sum_v n_h(v)^2.
\]
Only finitely many $v\in H$ occur, even when $H$ is infinite. Reindexing an additive quadruple as $(x+h,y,x,y+h)$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:76:eq:histogram}
 \Ea(\ind_G)=\sum_{h\in G}Q_h,\qquad
 \Eadd(\ind_G)=N^3,\qquad Q_0=N^2,\quad Q_{-h}=Q_h.
\end{equation}
A constant derivative in a generating direction makes $a$ affine, since summing around the cycle annihilates the increment. A nonconstant histogram with total $N$ has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:76:eq:histogram-bounds}
 Q_h\le(N-1)^2+1.
\end{equation}
If the multiplicity pattern $(N-1,1)$ is impossible, then for $N\ge4$ the bound improves to $(N-2)^2+4$. Indeed, among nonnegative integer multiplicities with given sum, moving a unit from a smaller positive entry to a larger one increases the sum of squares. The maximum is therefore the most concentrated allowed partition, $(N-1,1)$ or $(N-2,2)$ respectively.

Two restrictions on such partitions will be used. If $h$ is an involution, points are paired as $x,x+h$, with derivative values $v,-v$. A non-self-negative value and its negative have equal multiplicity; each self-negative value has even multiplicity. Thus a nonconstant $(N-1,1)$ histogram is impossible for even $N$. For $h=2$ in $\Z/6$, the two derivative cycles each have length three. A hypothetical five occurrences of $v$ and one of $u$ would force an all-$v$ cycle with $3v=0$ and a second cycle with $2v+u=0$. This forces $u=v$, again impossible.

Here are all orders not covered by the four-point argument.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{\(N=\arabic*\).},start=1]
\item Every map on the one-point group is affine.
\item Every map has form~\eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:cyclic-form}, with $n=1$ and $d=0$.
\item For a nonaffine map both nonzero shifts generate, so $Q_1=Q_2\le5$. The full ratio is at most $19/27<3/4$.
\item If $\Delta_2a$ is constant, then $b(x+2)=b(x)$, giving~\eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:cyclic-form}. Otherwise $Q_2\le8$ by involution pairing and $Q_1=Q_3\le10$, so the full ratio is at most $44/64<3/4$.
\item Every nonzero shift generates. Nonaffinity gives $Q_h\le17$ for $h\ne0$, and full ratio at most $93/125<3/4$.
\item If $\Delta_2a$ is constant, use~\eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:cyclic-form}. Otherwise $Q_2=Q_4\le20$ by the two three-cycles, and $Q_1=Q_5\le26$. If $\Delta_3a$ is nonconstant, involution pairing gives $Q_3\le20$, and the total is at most $148$, out of $216$. If $\Delta_3a$ is constant, then $b(x+3)=b(x)$. The nonconstant histogram of $b$ now has even multiplicities, so $Q_1=Q_5\le20$, whereas $Q_3=36$. The total is at most $152$, out of $216$. Both ratios are below $3/4$.
\end{enumerate}
To justify the constant-$\Delta_2$ reductions, subtract its values at $x+1$ and $x$; the result is $b(x+2)-b(x)=0$. The same calculation with $\Delta_3$ gives three-periodicity. All exceptional witnesses above are full indicators of groups of order at most six. This finishes Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:76:lem:cyclic}.

\begin{remark}
The number $8/11$ in~\eqref{gsr:en:76:eq:four-window} is the value of one local witness bound. It is not a general arbitrary-target or arbitrary-domain spectral classification. The argument needs only that this bound, and each exceptional small-order bound, is strictly below $3/4$.
\end{remark}

\section[{Jensen structure on finitely generated subgroups\srctag{76}}]{Jensen structure on finitely generated subgroups}\label{gsr:en:76:sec:d4}\label{gsr:en:76:sec:jensen}
\srcnote{76}{Section 4}
A map is affine on a cyclic coset $x+\langle y\rangle$ if its values are a constant plus a homomorphism on that cyclic subgroup. Normalize $f=a-a(0)$, so $f(0)=0$.

\begin{lemma}[Cyclic-coset affinity and Jensen]\label{gsr:en:76:lem:jensen}
Cyclic-coset affinity is equivalent to
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:76:eq:jensen}
 f(x+y)+f(x-y)=2f(x)\qquad(x,y\in G).
\end{equation}
For every solution with $f(0)=0$,
\begin{align}
 f(-y)&=-f(y),\label{gsr:en:76:eq:oddness}\\
 2f(x+y)&=2f(x)+2f(y),\label{gsr:en:76:eq:double-additive}\\
 f(x+2y)&=f(x)+2f(y).\label{gsr:en:76:eq:even-shift}
\end{align}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Affinity on $x+\langle y\rangle$ gives~\eqref{gsr:en:76:eq:jensen}. Conversely, apply~\eqref{gsr:en:76:eq:jensen} along that coset to get
\[
 f(x+(j+1)y)-f(x+jy)=f(x+jy)-f(x+(j-1)y).
\]
Successive increments are constant for all integers $j$. If $y$ has finite order, going once around the cycle annihilates the increment. Thus the restriction is genuinely affine on the cyclic group, not merely on its integer parametrization.

Putting $x=0$ gives~\eqref{gsr:en:76:eq:oddness}. Exchange $x,y$ in~\eqref{gsr:en:76:eq:jensen} and use oddness to obtain
$f(x+y)-f(x-y)=2f(y)$. Add this to~\eqref{gsr:en:76:eq:jensen} to get~\eqref{gsr:en:76:eq:double-additive}. Finally apply Jensen at $(x+y,y)$ and then~\eqref{gsr:en:76:eq:double-additive} to obtain~\eqref{gsr:en:76:eq:even-shift}.
\end{proof}

The normalization, oddness and cyclic recurrence are classical Jensen-equation ingredients; see Stetk\ae r~\cite{stetkaer}. We record the arbitrary-target algebra explicitly because target $2$-torsion must be retained. A torsion-free conclusion cannot simply be used for a general $H$; compare the explicit $2$-torsion-free hypothesis in Sabour--Kabbaj~\cite[Theorem~3.3]{sabourkabbaj}.

\begin{proposition}[Local torsion-aware form]\label{gsr:en:76:prop:local-form}
Let $f$ satisfy~\eqref{gsr:en:76:eq:jensen} and $f(0)=0$. On each finitely generated subgroup $L\le G$ there are a homomorphism $\phi:L\to H$ and a map $g:L/2L\to H[2]$, where
$H[2]=\{h\in H:2h=0\}$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:76:eq:local-form}
 f|_L=\phi+g\circ\pi,\qquad g(0)=0,
 \qquad \pi:L\longrightarrow L/2L.
\end{equation}
Conversely, every such expression on $L$ satisfies Jensen's equation there.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Use the structure theorem for finitely generated abelian groups~\cite[Theorem~4.56]{knapp} to write $L$ as a finite direct sum of finite or infinite cyclic groups, with generators $e_i$. If a summand has finite order $n_i$, the cyclic recurrence gives $n_i f(e_i)=0$. Therefore the prescriptions $\phi(e_i)=f(e_i)$ define a homomorphism into $H$; infinite summands impose no relation.

By~\eqref{gsr:en:76:eq:double-additive}, $2f$ is a homomorphism, and it agrees with $2\phi$ on the generators. Thus $b=f|_L-\phi$ has $2b=0$. Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:76:eq:even-shift} gives
\[
 b(x+2y)=b(x)+2b(y)=b(x).
\]
So $b$ is constant on $2L$-cosets and takes values in $H[2]$. This proves~\eqref{gsr:en:76:eq:local-form}. Conversely, $\pi(x+y)=\pi(x-y)$; the two corresponding $g$-values sum to zero, as does $2g(\pi x)$. The homomorphism part satisfies Jensen, proving the converse.
\end{proof}

The choice of $\phi$ depends on a cyclic decomposition and need not be canonical. We use this proposition only for finitely generated $L$. No decomposition of an arbitrary abelian $G$ into cyclic summands, and no global splitting of $f$ in the form~\eqref{gsr:en:76:eq:local-form}, is required or asserted.

\subsection{A nonzero defect uses two generators}
If $f$ is not a homomorphism, choose $x,y$ with
$f(x+y)\ne f(x)+f(y)$, and let $L=\langle x,y\rangle$. Apply Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:76:prop:local-form}. The vector space $V=L/2L$ over $\F_2$ has dimension at most two. In dimension zero or one every map $g:V\to H[2]$ vanishing at zero is additive, which would make $f|_L$ additive. Therefore $V\cong\F_2^2$ and $g$ is nonadditive.

In coordinates $(s,t)\in\F_2^2$, write
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:76:eq:quadratic-remainder}
 g(s,t)=s h_1+t h_2+st\delta,\qquad
 h_1=g(1,0),\quad h_2=g(0,1),\quad
 0\ne\delta=g(1,1)-h_1-h_2\in H[2].
\end{equation}
The linear terms cancel on additive quadruples, and $\delta$ has order exactly two. Respectedness is consequently exactly that of the scalar map $q(s,t)=st$ into $\F_2$.

\begin{lemma}[The four-point quotient]\label{gsr:en:76:lem:klein}
For the nonadditive remainder~\eqref{gsr:en:76:eq:quadratic-remainder}, the full quotient has $64$ additive quadruples, of which $40$ are respected. A quadruple fails precisely when its four entries are all distinct.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
An additive quadruple in $\F_2^2$ has either one value four times, two values twice each, or all four values once. The first two patterns are respected because every image lies in $H[2]$. For the last pattern the sum of its four image values is $\delta\ne0$, so it fails. There are $4!=24$ such ordered quadruples and $4^3=64$ quadruples in total. Equivalently, quotient sum zero contributes $16$ respected comparisons; each of the three nonzero sums contributes $8$.
\end{proof}

A two-generated abelian group with $\dim(L/2L)=2$ has two invariant-factor cyclic coordinates, each of even finite order or infinite order. In particular it is finite, $\Z\times\Z/(2q)$ for some $q\ge1$, or $\Z^2$. This is a use of the finite-generation structure theorem on $L$ alone. If $L$ is finite, each quotient quadruple has $|2L|^3$ additive lifts: choose its first three entries in their fibers and determine the fourth. The homomorphism part cancels on those lifts. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:76:eq:finite-subgroup}
 \frac{\Ea(\ind_L)}{\Eadd(\ind_L)}
 =\frac{40|2L|^3}{64|2L|^3}=\frac58.
\end{equation}
This is the exact two-generated \emph{finite} subgroup witness. The infinite cases require finite supports and are treated next.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Exact infinite-box limits\srctag{76}}]{Exact infinite-box limits}\label{gsr:en:76:sec:d5}\label{gsr:en:76:sec:boxes}
\srcnote{76}{Section 5}
\subsection{Parity-resolved interval counts}
Keep $U_m=(2m^3+m)/3$ and $C_m=U_m-m$. For
$\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_4)\in\{0,1\}^4$ with
$\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2=\varepsilon_3+\varepsilon_4$ modulo two, count additive quadruples in $\{0,\ldots,2m-1\}$ with these parities. Writing $x_i=2j_i+\varepsilon_i$ reduces the condition to
\[
 j_1+j_2-j_3-j_4
 =\frac{\varepsilon_3+\varepsilon_4-\varepsilon_1-\varepsilon_2}{2},
 \qquad 0\le j_i<m.
\]
Six of the eight admissible patterns have equal integer parity sums and count $U_m$. The other two, $0011$ and $1100$, have count $C_m$. Thus the total is $8U_m-2m$, and each individual pattern count divided by $U_m$ tends to one.

For a full cyclic factor $\Z/(2q)$ each admissible parity pattern has exactly $q^3$ lifts, by choosing three entries in their parity fibers. These elementary counts, rather than a general equidistribution assertion, give the limits below. Intervals and boxes are standard finite averaging constructions; the connection with F\o lner sets is background~\cite{taoamenability}, not an additional theorem invoked in the proof.

\subsection{One infinite coordinate}
For $L\cong\Z\times\Z/(2q)$ take
$A_m=\{0,\ldots,2m-1\}\times\Z/(2q)$. Its ordinary energy is
\[
 \Eadd(\ind_{A_m})=(8U_m-2m)(2q)^3.
\]
For the quadratic remainder, the failures are the $24$ quotient quadruples using all four parity vectors. In their first coordinate, each of the six patterns with two zeroes and two ones occurs four times. Two patterns contribute $C_m$ and four contribute $U_m$, so
\[
 \Eadd(\ind_{A_m})-\Ea(\ind_{A_m})
 =4(2C_m+4U_m)q^3=8(C_m+2U_m)q^3.
\]
Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:76:eq:cylinder}
 \frac{\Ea(\ind_{A_m})}{\Eadd(\ind_{A_m})}
 =\frac{5U_m-m}{8U_m-2m}
 =\frac{5m^2+1}{8m^2+1}
 =\frac58+\frac3{64m^2+8}\longrightarrow\frac58.
\end{equation}
Already $m=1$ gives $2/3<3/4$, although the finite factor may have arbitrarily many points.

\subsection{Two infinite coordinates}
For $L\cong\Z^2$ take
\[
 A_{m_1,m_2}=\{0,\ldots,2m_1-1\}\times\{0,\ldots,2m_2-1\},
 \qquad U_i=U_{m_i},\quad C_i=C_{m_i}.
\]
Then
\begin{align}
 \Eadd(\ind_A)&=(8U_1-2m_1)(8U_2-2m_2),\label{gsr:en:76:eq:box-energy}\\
 \Eadd(\ind_A)-\Ea(\ind_A)&=8(C_1U_2+U_1C_2+U_1U_2).\label{gsr:en:76:eq:box-failures}
\end{align}
For clarity, in each coordinate of an all-distinct quotient quadruple there are two zeroes and two ones. Of its six patterns, two are type $C$ and four are type $U$. If both coordinates are type $C$, the four parity vectors cannot all be distinct. Of the $24$ all-distinct quadruples, eight have each of the types $(C,U)$, $(U,C)$ and $(U,U)$. This proves~\eqref{gsr:en:76:eq:box-failures}.

With $b_i=m_i^2$, substitution yields the exact formula
\begin{align}
 \frac{\Ea(\ind_A)}{\Eadd(\ind_A)}
 &=\frac{40b_1b_2+8b_1+8b_2+7}{(8b_1+1)(8b_2+1)}\label{gsr:en:76:eq:box-ratio}\\
 &=\frac58+\frac{3(8b_1+8b_2+17)}{8(8b_1+1)(8b_2+1)}.
 \label{gsr:en:76:eq:box-error}
\end{align}
Both $m_1$ and $m_2$ must tend to infinity for the displayed error to tend to zero. Letting only one side grow need not suffice. Examples are $23/33$ at $(m_1,m_2)=(1,2)$ and $79/121$ at $(2,2)$, both below $3/4$.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Completion and sharpness of the two gaps\srctag{76}}]{Completion and sharpness of the two gaps}\label{gsr:en:76:sec:d6}\label{gsr:en:76:sec:completion}
\srcnote{76}{Section 6}
\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorems~\ref{gsr:fm:76:thm:main} and~\ref{gsr:fm:76:thm:conditional}]
If a cyclic-coset restriction of $a$ is nonaffine, Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:76:lem:cyclic} and restriction~\eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:restriction} give $\rind(a)\le3/4$. Otherwise $a$ is affine on every cyclic coset. If $a$ is not globally affine, the Jensen reduction produces the two-generated subgroup above. Its finite full indicator~\eqref{gsr:en:76:eq:finite-subgroup}, cylinder sequence~\eqref{gsr:en:76:eq:cylinder}, or box sequence~\eqref{gsr:en:76:eq:box-error} gives $\rind(a)\le5/8$. This proves the nonaffine upper bounds. Affine maps have $r=\rind=1$, so the equivalences follow. The index-two examples give sharpness of $3/4$.
\end{proof}

To verify sharpness of the \emph{conditional} $5/8$ bound for all weights, take $G=\F_2^2$, $H=\F_2$, and $a(s,t)=st$. Every cyclic coset has at most two points, so this map is affine on every such coset. Write the four point weights as $a_0,a_1,a_2,a_3\ge0$ and $P=a_0a_1a_2a_3$. The multiplicity classification from Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:76:lem:klein} gives
\begin{align*}
 \Eadd(w)&=\sum_{i=0}^3a_i^4
       +6\sum_{0\le i<j\le3}a_i^2a_j^2+24P,\\
 \Ea(w)&=\Eadd(w)-24P.
\end{align*}
AM--GM yields $\sum_i a_i^4\ge4P$ and $\sum_{i<j}a_i^2a_j^2\ge6P$. Hence $\Eadd(w)\ge64P$ and $\Ea(w)\ge(5/8)\Eadd(w)$. Equal positive weights attain equality. Thus $r(a)=\rind(a)=5/8$.

For finite $G$, the proof always supplies a finite indicator with ratio at most $3/4$. The analogous attainment assertion on infinite $G$ is false by integer parity. Neither proof classifies all maps whose infimum is $3/4$ or all equality cases of the conditional gap.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Indicator witnesses with optimal support exponent\srctag{76}}]{Indicator witnesses with optimal support exponent}\label{gsr:en:76:sec:d7}\label{gsr:en:76:sec:indicator}
\srcnote{76}{Section 7}
We now bound witness cardinality independently of the groups. The cyclic branch needs a wrapping estimate; the Jensen branch needs a small product set rather than the potentially large full finite subgroup.

\subsection{Even intervals including modular wrapping}\label{gsr:en:76:subsec:wrapping}
Fix $\epsilon>0$ and let
\[
 m=\ceil{\frac3{\sqrt{32\epsilon}}}\ge1.
\]
For~\eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:cyclic-form} on $\Z$, the interval of length $2m$ has error at most $\epsilon$ by~\eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:interval-ratio}. On $\Z/(2n)$, if $n<m$, use the full group, of size $2n<2m$, with exact ratio $3/4$. If $n\ge m$, use the residues $A=\{0,\ldots,2m-1\}$.

In the even-coordinate group $\Z/n$ let $I=\{0,\ldots,m-1\}$ and $f=\ind_I*\ind_I$. The odd part is the translate of the even part by one in $\Z/(2n)$, so the quantities~\eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:UVCD} satisfy
\[
 U=V=D=\norm f_2^2,\qquad C=\ip f{f(\,\cdot-1)}.
\]
Set $d_0=U-C$. Telescoping the interval convolution gives
\[
 f(s)-f(s-1)=\ind_I(s)-\ind_I(s-m),
\]
including $m=n$, where both sides vanish. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:76:eq:wrapped-difference}
 d_0=\frac12\norm{f-f(\,\cdot-1)}_2^2
 =\frac12|I\mathbin\triangle(I+m)|
 =\min(m,n-m)\le m.
\end{equation}
The last equality follows by counting the overlap of the two length-$m$ cyclic intervals. Also, $f$ is the periodization modulo $n$ of the nonnegative integer triangular convolution. Collecting nonnegative coefficients before squaring can only increase its squared norm, so
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:76:eq:wrapped-U}
 U\ge U_m=(2m^3+m)/3.
\end{equation}
The excess $3d_0/[2(8U-2d_0)]$ increases with $d_0$ and decreases with $U$. Equations~\eqref{gsr:en:76:eq:wrapped-difference} and~\eqref{gsr:en:76:eq:wrapped-U} therefore give
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:76:eq:wrapped-ratio}
 \frac{\Ea(\ind_A)}{\Eadd(\ind_A)}
 =\frac{6U}{8U-2d_0}
 \le\frac34+\frac9{32m^2+4}\le\frac34+\epsilon.
\end{equation}
This treats wrapping without assuming that the interval is shorter than half the modulus.

\subsection{Six points for a Jensen defect}
On the two-generated subgroup $L$ of Section~\ref{gsr:en:76:sec:jensen}, use its two cyclic coordinates, of even finite order $N_i$ or infinite order. In the first coordinate take $A_1=\{0,1\}$. In the second take $A_2=\{0,1,2\}$, except that $A_2=\{0,1\}$ when $N_2=2$. The product $A=A_1\times A_2$ has at most six points.

Let $e_i,o_i$ be the even and odd indicator parts in coordinate $i$, and define $U_i,V_i,C_i,D_i$ as in~\eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:UVCD}. No equality among $U_i,V_i,D_i$ is assumed here. Independence of the coordinate sums gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:76:eq:six-energy}
 \Eadd(\ind_A)=(U_1+V_1+2C_1+4D_1)(U_2+V_2+2C_2+4D_2).
\end{equation}
Every failed quotient quadruple uses two zeroes and two ones in each coordinate. Of the six such coordinate patterns, $0011$ and $1100$ have lift count $C_i$, and the other four have lift count $D_i$. The $24$ all-distinct quotient quadruples comprise eight patterns each of the types $(C,D)$, $(D,C)$ and $(D,D)$, with none of type $(C,C)$. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:76:eq:six-loss}
 \Eadd(\ind_A)-\Ea(\ind_A)=8(C_1D_2+D_1C_2+D_1D_2).
\end{equation}

In the first coordinate $(U_1,V_1,C_1,D_1)=(1,1,c,1)$, where $c=1$ if $N_1=2$ and $c=0$ otherwise. In the second coordinate,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:76:eq:six-coordinate}
 (U_2,V_2,C_2,D_2)=\begin{cases}
 (1,1,1,1),&N_2=2,\\
 (8,1,2,2),&N_2=4,\\
 (6,1,2,2),&N_2\ge6\text{ even, or }N_2=\infty.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
These are all wrapping cases: first-coordinate pair sums lie between zero and two; second-coordinate pair sums lie between zero and four. For $N_2\ge4$ or $N_2=\infty$, the even-even convolution is the triangle $(1,2,1)$ at positions $0,2,4$. Its norm squared is six unless order four identifies its two endpoints, making it eight. The odd-odd convolution has its single unit at position two, giving $V_2=1$, $C_2=2$; the mixed convolution has two unit coefficients, giving $D_2=2$.

Substituting in~\eqref{gsr:en:76:eq:six-energy}--\eqref{gsr:en:76:eq:six-loss} yields all six possibilities:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|r|r|c}
 c&N_2&\Eadd(\ind_A)&\Ea(\ind_A)&\Ea(\ind_A)/\Eadd(\ind_A)\\ \hline
 0&2&48&32&2/3\\
 1&2&64&40&5/8\\
 0&4&126&94&47/63\\
 1&4&168&120&5/7\\
 0&\ge6\text{ or }\infty&114&82&41/57\\
 1&\ge6\text{ or }\infty&152&104&13/19
\end{array}
\]
In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:76:eq:six-ratio}
 |A|\le6,\qquad
 \frac{\Ea(\ind_A)}{\Eadd(\ind_A)}\le\frac{47}{63}
 =\frac34-\frac1{252}<\frac34.
\end{equation}
No optimality of six or of $47/63$ is asserted.

Combining this six-point set with the at-most-six-point cyclic witnesses and the length-$2m$ interval proves Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:76:thm:witnesses}(a)'s upper bound. In particular the main rigidity implication itself can be witnessed at uniformly bounded size once a fixed positive tolerance is specified; the longer boxes are needed to identify the sharper conditional infimum $5/8$.

\subsection{A lower bound for every parity indicator}
Take integer parity~\eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:integer-parity}, and let $A\subset\Z$ be finite nonempty with $|A|=s$. Let $e,o$ be its even and odd indicator parts. Use Laurent polynomials, so negative elements of $A$ are allowed:
\[
 F(z)=\sum_{j\in A}z^j,\quad
 E(z)=\sum_{\substack{j\in A\\j\text{ even}}}z^j,\quad
 O(z)=\sum_{\substack{j\in A\\j\text{ odd}}}z^j.
\]
Then $E^2-O^2=F(z)F(-z)$. Reducing coefficients modulo two and using characteristic-two squaring gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:76:eq:modtwo}
 F(z)F(-z)\equiv F(z)^2\equiv F(z^2)\pmod2.
\end{equation}
For each of the $s$ distinct $j\in A$, the coefficient at $z^{2j}$ is odd, hence has squared absolute value at least one. The coefficient vector is $e*e-o*o$, so
\[
 \norm{e*e-o*o}_2^2\ge s.
\]
There are at most $s^3$ additive quadruples on $A$, since the first three entries determine the fourth. The sum of squares therefore yields
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:76:eq:indicator-lower}
 \frac{\Ea(\ind_A)}{\Eadd(\ind_A)}-\frac34
 \ge\frac{s}{4\Eadd(\ind_A)}\ge\frac1{4s^2}.
\end{equation}
Thus error at most $\epsilon$ requires $s\ge1/(2\sqrt\epsilon)$. Together with the uniform upper bound, this proves optimality of the indicator exponent $1/2$. The argument uses integral indicator coefficients; it gives no analogous lower bound for arbitrary real weights.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Binomial weights and logarithmic support\srctag{76}}]{Binomial weights and logarithmic support}\label{gsr:en:76:sec:d8}\label{gsr:en:76:sec:weighted}
\srcnote{76}{Section 8}
Only the nonzero-defect cyclic branch needs a new weight: every other nonaffine branch already has an indicator of at most six points and ratio below $3/4$. Fix an integer $m\ge1$.

\subsection{The exact integer formula}
For a nonzero-defect cyclic form on $\Z$, take
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:76:eq:binomial-weight}
 w(j)=\binom{2m}{j}\quad(0\le j\le2m),\qquad w(j)=0\text{ otherwise}.
\end{equation}
The support has $2m+1$ points. If $E,O$ are its even and odd generating polynomials, then
\[
 E+O=(1+z)^{2m},\qquad E-O=(1-z)^{2m},\qquad
 E^2-O^2=(1-z^2)^{2m}.
\]
Vandermonde's identity, obtained by taking the central coefficient of $(1+z)^r(1+z)^r$, gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:76:eq:binomial-norms}
 \norm{e*e-o*o}_2^2=\binom{4m}{2m},\qquad
 \Eadd(w)=\sum_{j=0}^{4m}\binom{4m}{j}^{\!2}=\binom{8m}{4m}.
\end{equation}
Reflection $j\mapsto2m-j$ preserves both parity parts. Substituting this reflection in $R(h)=\sum_j e(j)o(j+h)$ gives $R(h)=R(-h)$. The second sum of squares vanishes exactly, and hence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:76:eq:binomial-exact}
 \frac{\Ea(w)}{\Eadd(w)}
 =\frac34+\frac14\frac{\binom{4m}{2m}}{\binom{8m}{4m}}.
\end{equation}
This formula is exact for every nonzero-defect form~\eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:cyclic-form} on $\Z$, because its respectedness pattern is the same as integer parity.

\subsection{Folding into an even finite cycle}
Let the cyclic group have even order $N$. If $N\le2m+1$, its full indicator has at most $2m+1$ points and ratio exactly $3/4$. Otherwise reduce~\eqref{gsr:en:76:eq:binomial-weight} modulo $N$. Its input positions remain distinct. Reflection about $m$ still preserves parity modulo the even number $N$, so $R(h)=R(-h)$ remains valid.

The ordinary convolution is a periodization of a nonnegative coefficient sequence, giving
$\Eadd(w)\ge\binom{8m}{4m}$. The signed difference convolution is the periodization of $(1-z^2)^{2m}$, supported on exponents between $0$ and $4m$. Since $N>2m$, at most two coefficients fall in each residue class. The elementary inequality $(a+b)^2\le2(a^2+b^2)$ gives
\[
 \norm{e*e-o*o}_2^2\le2\binom{4m}{2m}.
\]
Therefore, in either cyclic setting the excess is at most
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:76:eq:folded-excess}
 \frac12\frac{\binom{4m}{2m}}{\binom{8m}{4m}}\le\frac12\,4^{-m}.
\end{equation}
For the last inequality, Vandermonde gives
$\binom{8m}{4m}\ge\binom{4m}{2m}^2$, while
\[
 \binom{4m}{2m}=\prod_{j=1}^{2m}\frac{2m+j}{j}\ge2^{2m}=4^m.
\]
Restriction transports these weights to any nonaffine cyclic-coset branch. The remaining branches use the indicators of at most six points already proved. This completes Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:76:thm:witnesses}(b).

For a prescribed error $\epsilon>0$, one can take
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:76:eq:m-epsilon}
 m=\max\left\{1,\ceil{\log_4\frac1{2\epsilon}}\right\}.
\end{equation}
The distinction from indicator witnesses is substantive: weighting permits the logarithmic support upper bound, whereas every integer-parity indicator obeys~\eqref{gsr:en:76:eq:indicator-lower}. This comparison concerns the number of support points only; it is not a bit-complexity or query-complexity bound, and it supplies no optimal lower bound for weighted support.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Pair counting and a sum of squares\srctag{77}}]{Pair counting and a sum of squares}\label{gsr:en:77:sec:d2}\label{gsr:en:77:sec:SOS}
\srcnote{77}{Section 2}
Every $x\in G$ has a unique expression $\alpha t+k$ with $\alpha\in\{0,1\}$ and $k\in K$. For a pair, let $p\in\{0,1,2\}$ be the integer sum of its two labels $\alpha$. Pairs with the same domain sum have the same $p$ modulo two. Equal integer $p$ gives equal image sums; unequal $p$ means $0$ versus $2$, and the image sums differ by $\eta$ or $-\eta$. As $\eta\ne0$, exactly the even-even versus odd-odd comparisons fail.

Use counting-measure convolution and the real inner product:
\[
 (f*g)(s)=\sum_x f(x)g(s-x),\qquad
 \norm f_2^2=\sum_x f(x)^2,\qquad \ip fg=\sum_xf(x)g(x).
\]
Set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:77:eq:UVCD}
 U=\norm{e*e}_2^2,\quad V=\norm{o*o}_2^2,\quad
 C=\ip{e*e}{o*o},\quad D=\norm{e*o}_2^2,\quad
 R(h)=\sum_xe(x)o(x+h).
\end{equation}
Mixed pairs have odd domain sum, and unmixed pairs have even domain sum. The preceding classification yields
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:77:eq:split}
 \Eadd(w)=U+V+2C+4D,\qquad \Ea(w)=U+V+4D.
\end{equation}
Direct finite reindexing gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:77:eq:correlation}
 D=\sum_hR(h)^2,\qquad C=\sum_hR(h)R(-h).
\end{equation}
For the second identity, a summand is $e(x)e(y)o(x+h)o(y-h)$, whose two even and two odd entries have equal sums. For the first, $e(x)e(y)o(x+h)o(y+h)$ corresponds to the equal mixed sums $x+(y+h)=y+(x+h)$; the change of variables is bijective.

\begin{proposition}[Exact positive defect]\label{gsr:en:77:prop:SOS}
For every weight in~\eqref{gsr:fm:77:eq:family},
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:77:eq:SOS}
 \Delta(w)\Eadd(w)=
 \frac14\norm{e*e-o*o}_2^2
 +\frac12\sum_h\bigl(R(h)-R(-h)\bigr)^2.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The first term is $(U+V-2C)/4$. The second is $D-C$ by~\eqref{gsr:en:77:eq:correlation}. Their sum is $(U+V)/4+D-3C/2$, which equals the left-hand side by~\eqref{gsr:en:77:eq:split}. All sums are finite.
\end{proof}

This identity proves the lower endpoint $3/4$ without a finiteness assumption on $G$. For context, the endpoint is the infimum for every map in this family. Indeed, $\langle t\rangle$ is either infinite cyclic or cyclic of even finite order. In the finite case its full indicator attains, as proved in Section~\ref{gsr:en:77:sec:existence}. In the infinite case the binomial weights of Section~\ref{gsr:en:77:sec:binomial}, transferred along $j\mapsto jt$, approach $3/4$. Domain and image pair comparisons are preserved under this transfer.

\subsection{Translation and the local group}\label{gsr:en:77:subsec:translation}
Translate the weight to $L$ by $w_0(l)=w(x_0+l)$. Translation preserves all domain pair-sum comparisons. It either preserves the two original parity classes or interchanges them, according to $\pi(x_0)$, and the distinction between equal and unequal integer pair-label sums is unchanged. Hence both energies in~\eqref{gsr:en:77:eq:split} are preserved. The signed self-convolution changes only by translation and possibly a sign, so its norm is unchanged too.

The appropriate group is the difference-generated $L$ in~\eqref{gsr:fm:77:eq:local}, not necessarily the group generated by the original support. This removes a base-point torsion component that has no bearing on the additive pattern. All Fourier arguments below are carried out on $L=\Z^d\oplus T$, never on the full arbitrary ambient group. If $\pi|_L=0$, only one original parity occurs and the ratio is one; the subsequent formulas include this case.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Exact finite-torsion classification\srctag{77}}]{Exact finite-torsion classification}\label{gsr:en:77:sec:d3}\label{gsr:en:77:sec:classification}
\srcnote{77}{Section 3}
For $L=\Z^d\oplus T$, its dual is explicitly $\T^d\times\widehat T$, where $\T$ is the complex unit circle. Use normalized Lebesgue measure on each circle and normalized counting measure on the finite character group $\widehat T$. For a finite function define
\[
 \widehat f(z,\chi)=\sum_{n\in\Z^d}\sum_{v\in T}f(n,v)z^n\chi(v).
\]
Character orthogonality gives Parseval and converts convolution into multiplication. These facts follow by expanding the finite sums: $\int_{\T^d}z^n\,dz$ vanishes unless $n=0$, and $|T|^{-1}\sum_\chi\chi(v)$ vanishes unless $v=0$. In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:77:eq:parseval}
 \norm f_2^2=\frac1{|T|}\sum_{\chi\in\widehat T}
 \int_{\T^d}|\widehat f(z,\chi)|^2\,dz.
\end{equation}
Complex conjugates enter the expansion of the squared modulus in the usual way.

\begin{lemma}[One convolution equation suffices]\label{gsr:en:77:lem:one-equation}
Equality $\Delta(w)=0$ holds if and only if $e*e=o*o$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Necessity follows from the first square in~\eqref{gsr:en:77:eq:SOS}. Conversely, if $e*e=o*o$, then $(\widehat e)^2=(\widehat o)^2$ at every dual point, so $|\widehat e|=|\widehat o|$. In the notation~\eqref{gsr:en:77:eq:UVCD}, the convolution equality gives $U=V=C$. Parseval also gives
\[
 D=\int|\widehat e|^2|\widehat o|^2
   =\int|\widehat e|^4=U,
\]
where the integral abbreviates the normalized torus integral and finite average. Thus $U=V=C=D$, and~\eqref{gsr:en:77:eq:split} gives ratio $6U/(8U)=3/4$. Here $U>0$: if $U=0$, then $e=0$ and the assumed equality forces $o=0$, contradicting $w\ne0$.
\end{proof}

Write the parity character on $L$ as
\[
 \sigma(n,v)=(-1)^{\pi(n,v)}=\lambda(n)\varepsilon(v),
\]
where $\lambda:\Z^d\to\{\pm1\}$ and $\varepsilon:T\to\{\pm1\}$ are characters. For $\chi\in\widehat T$, put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:77:eq:Pchi}
 P_\chi(z)=\sum_n\left(\sum_{v\in T}w_0(n,v)\chi(v)\right)z^n,
 \qquad S=\{\chi:P_\chi\not\equiv0\}.
\end{equation}
For each free coordinate $n$, the inner coefficient is the torsion Fourier transform of the fiber $v\mapsto w_0(n,v)$. Thus $S$ is the union of those fiberwise Fourier supports. Let $\lambda z$ denote the substitution $z_j\mapsto\lambda(e_j)z_j$, where $e_j$ is the $j$th free generator.

\begin{theorem}[Pair-free torsion spectrum]\label{gsr:en:77:thm:spectral}
For any splitting $L=\Z^d\oplus T$,
\[
 \Delta(w)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \text{for every }\chi\in\widehat T,\quad
 P_\chi\equiv0\text{ or }P_{\chi\varepsilon}\equiv0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad S\cap(S\varepsilon)=\varnothing.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
As $e+o=w$ and $e-o=\sigma w$, commutativity gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:77:eq:signed-convolution}
 e*e-o*o=w*(\sigma w).
\end{equation}
The torsion transform of $\sigma w_0$ is $P_{\chi\varepsilon}(\lambda z)$. By Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:77:lem:one-equation}, equality holds exactly when
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:77:eq:product-zero}
 P_\chi(z)P_{\chi\varepsilon}(\lambda z)\equiv0
 \qquad\text{for every }\chi.
\end{equation}
Here vanishing at all torus points is equivalent to vanishing as a Laurent polynomial, by coefficient orthogonality. The ring $\C[z_1^{\pm1},\ldots,z_d^{\pm1}]$ is an integral domain: multiply factors by monomials and use the integral-domain property of the ordinary polynomial ring. The sign substitution is an automorphism. Therefore~\eqref{gsr:en:77:eq:product-zero} is equivalent to one of its two polynomial factors being identically zero, which is the asserted criterion. If $d=0$, the ring is $\C$ and the same argument applies.
\end{proof}

Although the polynomials use a splitting, the criterion is equivalent to the intrinsic convolution equation, so its truth does not depend on that choice. It couples the Fourier supports of \emph{all} free-coordinate fibers; a separate disjointness test within each fiber would be weaker and is not the theorem.

\begin{corollary}[Necessary local torsion and fiber balance]\label{gsr:en:77:cor:balance}
If $\Delta(w)=0$, then $\varepsilon\ne1$. Moreover, for every free coordinate $n$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:77:eq:balance}
 \sum_{v:\varepsilon(v)=1}w_0(n,v)
 =\sum_{v:\varepsilon(v)=-1}w_0(n,v).
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Nonnegativity and $w_0\ne0$ imply $P_1\not\equiv0$. The criterion forces $P_\varepsilon\equiv0$ and therefore $\varepsilon\ne1$. Equating each coefficient of $P_\varepsilon$ to zero gives~\eqref{gsr:en:77:eq:balance}.
\end{proof}
The balance equations are necessary, not sufficient. The full condition remains the pair-free union of torsion spectra in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:77:thm:spectral}.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Existence of an attaining weight\srctag{77}}]{Existence of an attaining weight}\label{gsr:en:77:sec:d4}\label{gsr:en:77:sec:existence}
\srcnote{77}{Section 4}
\begin{theorem}[Torsion dichotomy]\label{gsr:en:77:thm:torsion}
For~\eqref{gsr:fm:77:eq:family}, a finite attaining weight exists if and only if a finite attaining indicator exists, and this happens if and only if $G\setminus K$ contains a finite-order element.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If a finite attaining weight exists, Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:77:cor:balance} produces $v\in T=\Tor(L)$ with $\pi(v)=1$. This is a finite-order element in the required coset, even in the subgroup generated by support differences.

Conversely, let $v\in G\setminus K$ have finite order $N$. The homomorphism $\pi$ shows $N$ is even, say $N=2r$. On the finite cyclic subgroup $C=\langle v\rangle$, choose $w=\ind_C$. Its even and odd parts each have $r$ points. Every even sum has exactly $r$ even-even and $r$ odd-odd ordered representations, and every odd sum has exactly $r$ even-odd representations. Therefore $U=V=C=D=r^3$. Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:77:eq:split} gives ratio $6r^3/(8r^3)=3/4$. Translation gives the same result on every coset of $C$. Indicators are weights, completing the equivalence.
\end{proof}

Equivalently, existence means $\pi|_{\Tor(G)}$ is nontrivial. If ambient torsion is parity-trivial, no finite weight attains, even if $G$ has much torsion. If it is parity-nontrivial, some weight attains; this says nothing automatic about a separately specified weight.

\subsection{Ambient torsion does not replace local torsion}
In $G=\Z/2\Z\oplus\Z$ take parity from the first coordinate. The ambient involution $(1,0)$ lies outside $K$, so an attaining indicator exists. But the points
\[
 (0,0),\ (1,1),\ (0,2)
\]
lie in the infinite cyclic subgroup generated by $(1,1)$. Their difference-generated group is torsion-free. Every positive weighting of these three points has a strictly positive gap, by Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:77:thm:main-gap}; the exact optimum is also covered by Section~\ref{gsr:en:77:sec:three}. The same remains true after any common translation, including a translation with nontrivial torsion component.

Nor is local parity-nontrivial torsion sufficient for a \emph{fixed} weight. On $\Z/4\Z$, the indicator of $\{0,1\}$ has ratio one: its only additive comparisons are the same unordered pair, possibly reordered. Yet its support differences generate all of $\Z/4\Z$, with parity-nontrivial torsion. This example separates the necessary local condition from the exact spectral criterion.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Equality weights beyond subgroup invariance\srctag{77}}]{Equality weights beyond subgroup invariance}\label{gsr:en:77:sec:d5}\label{gsr:en:77:sec:examples}
\srcnote{77}{Section 5}
\subsection{A rational nonperiodic example on six points}
On $G=\Z/6\Z$ with ordinary parity, define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:77:eq:C6}
 (w(0),\ldots,w(5))=(6,5,3,2,3,5).
\end{equation}
Equivalently, $w(j)=4+2\cos(2\pi j/6)$. Its Fourier support is $\{0,1,5\}$; multiplication by the parity character shifts frequencies by $3$, giving $\{3,4,2\}$. They are disjoint, so Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:77:thm:spectral} gives equality. All six weights are positive, and the unique maximum at $0$ rules out every nonzero translation period.

Here is a direct integer certificate, with coordinates listed from $0$ to $5$:
\begin{align*}
 e*e=o*o&=(54,0,45,0,45,0),\\
 e*o=R&=(0,51,0,42,0,51),\\
 w*w&=(108,102,90,84,90,102),\\
 U=V=C=D&=6966,\\
 \Eadd(w)&=55728,\qquad \Ea(w)=41796.
\end{align*}
Thus equality does not require uniform weights on a subgroup or invariance under a nonzero translation.

\subsection{An attaining support below the least order outside the parity kernel}
On $G=\Z/8\Z$, take
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:77:eq:C8}
 w(j)=1+\cos(2\pi j/8),\qquad 0\le j<8.
\end{equation}
The weights are nonnegative, with a unique zero at $j=4$, so the support has seven points. Its Fourier support is $\{0,1,7\}$, disjoint from its parity shift $\{4,5,3\}$. Hence it attains. Every parity-one element of $\Z/8\Z$ has order eight. Therefore the smallest possible attaining support need not equal the least order of a parity-one element. This only gives an upper bound of seven for the former quantity in this group; it is not a proof that seven is minimal.

The values in~\eqref{gsr:en:77:eq:C8} belong to $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)$. The companion checks the convolution equality exactly in that quadratic field, including positivity and the single zero, rather than relying on floating-point trigonometry.

\subsection{Why the union over free fibers is necessary}
On $\Z\oplus\Z/6\Z$ with parity from the torsion coordinate, put
\[
 w(0,\cdot)=(6,5,3,2,3,5),\qquad
 w(1,\cdot)=(6,3,3,6,3,3),
\]
and zero on other free fibers. The two torsion Fourier supports are
$\{0,1,5\}$ and $\{0,2,4\}$. Each is separately disjoint from its shift by $3$, so each fiber alone attains. Their union is not disjoint from that shift. Directly,
\[
 (e*e-o*o)(1,0)=24,\qquad
 (e*e-o*o)(1,2)=(e*e-o*o)(1,4)=-12.
\]
Thus the combined weight does not attain. The example explains concretely why Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:77:thm:spectral} tests the union of spectra, rather than testing each free fiber separately.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The sparse Mahler input\srctag{77}}]{The sparse Mahler input}\label{gsr:en:77:sec:d6}\label{gsr:en:77:sec:mahler}
\srcnote{77}{Section 6}
We now prove the quantitative gap. This is an application of an established coefficient theorem, not a new Mahler-measure theorem. For a nonzero Laurent polynomial on $\T^d$, write
\[
 M(P)=\exp\left(\int_{\T^d}\log|P(z)|\,dz\right).
\]
The logarithm is integrable; monomial factors have measure one. Mahler measure is multiplicative and invariant under torus translations, directly from its definition. For $d=0$, set $M(c)=|c|$ for a nonzero constant.

\begin{lemma}[Akhtari--Vaaler]\label{gsr:en:77:lem:AV}
Let $B=\{b_0,\ldots,b_{m-1}\}\subset\Z^d$ be ordered by an injective real homomorphism. If $P(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}c_jz^{b_j}$ is nonzero, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:77:eq:AV}
 |c_j|\le\binom{m-1}{j}M(P)\qquad(0\le j<m).
\end{equation}
Coefficients may be complex or zero, so $B$ may contain the coefficient support strictly.
\end{lemma}
This is Theorem~1.2 of Akhtari--Vaaler~\cite{akhtarivaaler}; in one variable use Theorem~1.1 and Corollary~1.1 after ordering the integer exponents. The input depends on the number of exponents, not their maximum size. Its proof is imported, not reproduced. No arithmetic restriction on the weights is needed.

For completeness, an injective homomorphism $\Z^d\to\R$ is obtained by dot product with $d$ real numbers linearly independent over $\mathbb Q$. If $d=0$, then $B=\{0\}$ and~\eqref{gsr:en:77:eq:AV} is the constant identity, requiring no external theorem.

\begin{lemma}[A fourth-moment comparison]\label{gsr:en:77:lem:moment}
For $P$ as above and any coordinatewise sign vector $\lambda\in\{\pm1\}^d$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:77:eq:moment}
 \int_{\T^d}|P(z)P(\lambda z)|^2\,dz
 \ge\frac{\displaystyle\int_{\T^d}|P(z)|^4\,dz}
 {4^{m-1}\binom{2m-2}{m-1}}.
\end{equation}
The same inequality holds for $P\equiv0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For nonzero $P$, summing~\eqref{gsr:en:77:eq:AV} and its squares gives
\begin{align}
 \norm P_\infty&\le\sum_j|c_j|\le 2^{m-1}M(P),\label{gsr:en:77:eq:infty}\\
 \int|P|^2&=\sum_j|c_j|^2
 \le\binom{2m-2}{m-1}M(P)^2.\label{gsr:en:77:eq:L2}
\end{align}
The last step uses $\sum_j\binom{m-1}{j}^2=\binom{2m-2}{m-1}$. Thus
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:77:eq:L4}
 \int|P|^4\le\norm P_\infty^2\int|P|^2
 \le4^{m-1}\binom{2m-2}{m-1}M(P)^4.
\end{equation}
The integral arithmetic--geometric mean inequality and torus-translation invariance give
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:77:eq:AGM}
 \int|P(z)P(\lambda z)|^2\,dz
 \ge M\bigl(P(z)P(\lambda z)\bigr)^2=M(P)^4.
\end{equation}
Combining the two estimates proves~\eqref{gsr:en:77:eq:moment}. If $P=0$, both sides are zero. The logarithmic singularities of a nonzero polynomial do not obstruct~\eqref{gsr:en:77:eq:AGM}; its logarithm is integrable and the usual integral geometric mean applies.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A torsion-local positive gap\srctag{77}}]{A torsion-local positive gap}\label{gsr:en:77:sec:d7}\label{gsr:en:77:sec:gap}
\srcnote{77}{Section 7}
\begin{proof}[Proof of the gap in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:77:thm:main-gap}]
Use the translated local group and the polynomials~\eqref{gsr:en:77:eq:Pchi}. By hypothesis $\pi$ vanishes on $T$, so $\varepsilon=1$ and the Fourier transform of $\sigma w_0$ is $P_\chi(\lambda z)$ in torsion component $\chi$.

Let $B=q(A)\subseteq\Z^d$, so $|B|=m$. The exponent support of every $P_\chi$ is contained in this same set $B$, though cancellation may remove coefficients. Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:77:lem:moment} separately at each $\chi$ and average. Parseval and convolution multiplication give
\begin{align*}
 \norm{w_0*(\sigma w_0)}_2^2
 &=\frac1{|T|}\sum_{\chi}\int|P_\chi(z)P_\chi(\lambda z)|^2\,dz\\
 &\ge\frac{1}{4^{m-1}\binom{2m-2}{m-1}}
 \frac1{|T|}\sum_{\chi}\int|P_\chi(z)|^4\,dz\\
 &=\frac{\Eadd(w_0)}{4^{m-1}\binom{2m-2}{m-1}}.
\end{align*}
By~\eqref{gsr:en:77:eq:signed-convolution}, translation invariance, and the first term of~\eqref{gsr:en:77:eq:SOS}, dividing by $4\Eadd(w)$ proves the first bound of~\eqref{gsr:fm:77:eq:main-gap}. The clean bound follows from $\binom{2m-2}{m-1}\le4^{m-1}$. Since $m\le s$ and $4^m\binom{2m-2}{m-1}$ increases with the positive integer $m$, the bound with $s$ follows too.
\end{proof}

The averaging order is important. Each torsion character first supplies a comparison between its signed and unsigned fourth moments; only then are the comparisons averaged. Collapsing all torsion fibers to one positive weight and comparing energies afterward would introduce an unnecessary multiplicity loss.

\begin{corollary}[Ambient parity-trivial torsion]\label{gsr:en:77:cor:ambient-gap}
If $\pi$ vanishes on $\Tor(G)$, every nonzero finite weight in~\eqref{gsr:fm:77:eq:family} has a positive gap satisfying~\eqref{gsr:fm:77:eq:main-gap}. In particular no such weight attains the endpoint.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Every finite-order element of $L\le G$ is a finite-order element of $G$, so $\pi|_{\Tor(L)}=0$. Apply the theorem.
\end{proof}

This includes torsion-free $G$, but is strictly more general. For example, take $G=\Z\oplus T$ with arbitrary finite $T$ and parity from the integer coordinate. The estimate depends on the number of occupied integer coordinates, even if every such coordinate carries many torsion points. If $m=1$, all support points have the same parity, the ratio is one, and the bound $\Delta\ge1/4$ is exact.

\subsection{The one-variable proof in direct form}
For integer parity, let $F(z)=\sum_jw(j)z^j$, $W=\sum_jw(j)$ and $Q=\sum_jw(j)^2$. The sparse coefficient inequality yields
\[
 W\le2^{s-1}M(F),\qquad Q\le\binom{2s-2}{s-1}M(F)^2.
\]
The polynomial of $e*e-o*o$ is
\[
 F(z)F(-z)=(E_0(z)+O_0(z))(E_0(z)-O_0(z))
 =E_0(z)^2-O_0(z)^2,
\]
where $E_0,O_0$ are the even and odd parts of $F$. Parseval and the geometric mean give $\norm{e*e-o*o}_2^2\ge M(F)^4$. The triangle inequality for $w*w=\sum_x w(x)w(\,\cdot-x)$ gives
\[
 \Eadd(w)=\norm{w*w}_2^2\le W^2Q
 \le4^{s-1}\binom{2s-2}{s-1}M(F)^4.
\]
The first square of~\eqref{gsr:en:77:eq:SOS} again proves the claimed gap. This form displays explicitly why neither widely separated exponents nor arbitrary positive real coefficient values escape the support bound.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Binomial witnesses and optimal logarithmic order\srctag{77}}]{Binomial witnesses and optimal logarithmic order}\label{gsr:en:77:sec:d8}\label{gsr:en:77:sec:binomial}
\srcnote{77}{Section 8}
\begin{proposition}[Exact binomial excess]\label{gsr:en:77:prop:binomial}
For integer parity and $h\ge1$, put $w_h(j)=\binom{2h}{j}$ on $0\le j\le2h$, and zero elsewhere. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:77:eq:binomial}
 \Delta(w_h)=\frac14\frac{\binom{4h}{2h}}{\binom{8h}{4h}}
 <\frac12\,16^{-h}.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The unsigned polynomial is $(1+z)^{2h}$ and its signed product is $(1-z^2)^{2h}$. Vandermonde's identity therefore gives
\[
 \Eadd(w_h)=\binom{8h}{4h},\qquad
 \norm{e*e-o*o}_2^2=\binom{4h}{2h}.
\]
Reflection $j\mapsto2h-j$ preserves both parity parts and their weights. Substituting that reflection in the correlation sum gives $R(v)=R(-v)$, so the second square in~\eqref{gsr:en:77:eq:SOS} vanishes. This proves the equality in~\eqref{gsr:en:77:eq:binomial}.

For the strict estimate, set $B_n=\binom{2n}{n}$. Since $B_n/B_{n-1}=4-2/n$,
\[
 \frac{B_{4h}}{B_{2h}}
 =16^h\prod_{k=2h+1}^{4h}\left(1-\frac1{2k}\right).
\]
Induction gives $\prod_k(1-u_k)\ge1-\sum_ku_k$ for $u_k\in[0,1]$. Here
\[
 \sum_{k=2h+1}^{4h}\frac1{2k}\le\frac{2h}{4h+2}<\frac12.
\]
Hence $B_{4h}/B_{2h}>16^h/2$, proving~\eqref{gsr:en:77:eq:binomial}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The integer-parity support function}
Define
\[
 n(\epsilon)=\min\left\{|\supp w|:0\ne w\ge0\text{ finitely supported on }\Z,
 \ \Delta(w)\le\epsilon\right\}.
\]
For $\epsilon>0$ this is a minimum over a nonempty set of positive integers, by the binomial construction. If $\epsilon\ge1/4$, then $n(\epsilon)=1$. For $0<\epsilon<1/4$, the clean lower bound gives
\[
 \frac1{4\cdot16^{s-1}}\le\epsilon
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad s\ge1+\log_{16}\frac1{4\epsilon}.
\]
For the upper bound take $h=\ceil{\log_{16}(1/(2\epsilon))}\ge1$ in Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:77:prop:binomial}. Its support has $2h+1$ points and its excess is strictly less than $\epsilon$. This proves~\eqref{gsr:fm:77:eq:n-bounds-main} and the logarithmic order. The lower bound can be rounded upward, since $n(\epsilon)$ is an integer.

The central-binomial denominator yields the stronger necessary condition
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:77:eq:exact-integer-bound}
 4^s\binom{2s-2}{s-1}\ge\frac1\epsilon.
\end{equation}
This is suitable for exact rational checking, without logarithmic rounding. It improves the clean lower estimate. The binomial comparison alone leaves the factor-two gap in~\eqref{gsr:fm:77:eq:n-bounds-main}; Section~\ref{gsr:en:77:cyclo-weights} improves the upper constant further.

\subsection{Worst-case witnesses for arbitrary nonaffine maps}
For a nonaffine full-domain map $a:G\to H$, let $n_a(\epsilon)$ be the least support size of a nonnegative finite weight with ratio at most $3/4+\epsilon$. Report~288's quantitative theorem gives, for $0<\epsilon<1/4$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:77:eq:universal-upper}
 n_a(\epsilon)\le
 \max\left\{6,\,2\ceil{\log_4\frac1{2\epsilon}}+1\right\}.
\end{equation}
This is the earlier general theorem, used as an explicitly identified input; the present report does not repeat its full cyclic and Jensen reduction. Taking the supremum over all such maps and using integer parity as one member gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:77:eq:worst-case}
 1+\log_{16}\frac1{4\epsilon}
 \le\sup_{G,H,a\text{ nonaffine}}n_a(\epsilon)
 \le\max\left\{6,\,2\ceil{\log_4\frac1{2\epsilon}}+1\right\}.
\end{equation}
Thus the weighted worst-case order is exactly logarithmic. The sharper $16^{-h}$ estimate in~\eqref{gsr:en:77:eq:binomial} is asserted for the stated binomial construction; no unproved replacement of the general bound~\eqref{gsr:en:77:eq:universal-upper} is made.

This settles the weighted-order question left by Report~288. It does not imply that every nonaffine map requires growing support: some have a fixed small witness at or below $3/4$. It also does not change the larger, square-root order for worst-case indicator witnesses established there.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Cyclotomic weights and the Catalan exponential rate\srctag{77}}]{Cyclotomic weights and the Catalan exponential rate}\label{gsr:en:77:sec:d9}
\srcnote{77}{Section 9}
\label{gsr:en:77:cyclo-weights}

Put
\[
 \mathsf G=\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^r}{(2r+1)^2},
 \qquad \kappa_{\rm C}=\frac{8\mathsf G}{\pi}.
\]
For orientation, $e^{\kappa_{\rm C}}=10.303536978\ldots$ and
$\kappa_{\rm C}^{-1}=0.4287268912\ldots$.
In this section $\delta(w)=\Delta(w)$, and $n$ denotes polynomial degree, so the support size is $n+1$. The positive factors used below belong to the classical polynomial
factor-norm examples of Boyd and Borwein
\cite{boydfactor,borweinfactor}.  We apply them to weighted parity
energy; no novelty claim for the polynomial family itself is intended.

\begin{proposition}[Cyclotomic parity witnesses]
\label{gsr:en:77:cyclo-witnesses}
For every even integer $n\ge2$, define
\[
 \alpha_j=\frac{(j+1/2)\pi}{n}\quad(0\le j<n/2),\qquad
 F_n(z)=\prod_{j=0}^{n/2-1}
       \bigl(z^2+2\sin(\alpha_j)z+1\bigr)
       =\sum_{k=0}^n w_kz^k.
\]
The coefficients are strictly positive real algebraic numbers,
$w_k=w_{n-k}$, and
\begin{equation}
 F_n(z)F_n(-z)=1+z^{2n}.
 \label{gsr:en:77:cyclo-factor}
\end{equation}
For integer-valued parity on $\mathbb Z$, this weight has support size
$n+1$ and excess
\begin{equation}
 \delta_n=\frac1{2E_n},\qquad
 E_n=\sum_{k=0}^{2n}\bigl([z^k]F_n(z)^2\bigr)^2.
 \label{gsr:en:77:cyclo-exact}
\end{equation}
As $n\to\infty$ through even integers,
\begin{align}
 E_n&=\frac{e^{\kappa_{\rm C}n}}{2\sqrt{2n}}
       \left(1+\frac{13\pi}{96n}+O(n^{-2})\right),
       \label{gsr:en:77:cyclo-E}\\
 \delta_n&=\sqrt{2n}\,e^{-\kappa_{\rm C}n}
       \left(1-\frac{13\pi}{96n}+O(n^{-2})\right).
       \label{gsr:en:77:cyclo-delta}
\end{align}
Moreover, for every even $n\ge2$,
\begin{equation}
 \frac{2e^{-\pi^2/24}}{3\sqrt\pi}\sqrt n\,
 e^{-\kappa_{\rm C}n}
 \le\delta_n\le
 \frac{128\pi}{81}\sqrt n\,e^{-\kappa_{\rm C}n}.
 \label{gsr:en:77:cyclo-uniform}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The roots of $z^{2n}+1$ in the open left half-plane have arguments
\[
 \frac\pi2+\frac{(j+1/2)\pi}{n},\qquad 0\le j<n.
\]
For even $n$, no root lies on the imaginary axis. Pairing conjugate
roots gives the displayed quadratic factors. Each factor has strictly
positive coefficients and is reciprocal, which proves positivity and
palindromicity. The roots are roots of unity, so the coefficients are
algebraic. Negation interchanges the left and right root sets, and
both factors in \eqref{gsr:en:77:cyclo-factor} are monic because $n$ is even.
This proves \eqref{gsr:en:77:cyclo-factor} exactly.

Write $e_k=w_k\mathbf1_{2\mathbb Z}(k)$,
$o_k=w_k\mathbf1_{2\mathbb Z+1}(k)$, and
$R(h)=\sum_xe_xo_{x+h}$. Reflection $k\mapsto n-k$ preserves
both parity parts and gives $R(h)=R(-h)$. The signed convolution
$e*e-o*o$ has generating polynomial $F_n(z)F_n(-z)$, hence squared
norm $2$. The sum-of-squares identity
\[
 \delta_n E_n=\frac14\|e*e-o*o\|_2^2+
 \frac12\sum_h(R(h)-R(-h))^2
\]
now proves \eqref{gsr:en:77:cyclo-exact}.

We supply global bounds before using Laplace's method. Put
$s_j=\sin\alpha_j$. On the unit circle,
\[
 H_n(t):=\frac{|F_n(e^{it})|^4}{F_n(1)^4}
       =\prod_j\left|\frac{\cos t+s_j}{1+s_j}\right|^4,
 \qquad -\pi\le t\le\pi.
\]
Every factor is at most one. At least $n/4$ of the $s_j$ are at
least $1/2$: writing $n=2m$, the number is
$m-\lceil m/3-1/2\rceil\ge m/2$, with the two cases $m=1,2$
checked directly. For $s\in[1/2,1]$,
\[
 1-\left(\frac{\cos t+s}{1+s}\right)^2
 =\frac{(1-\cos t)(1+\cos t+2s)}{(1+s)^2}
 \ge\frac49(1-\cos t).
\]
Consequently
\begin{equation}
 H_n(t)\le
 \exp\left(-\frac{2n}{9}(1-\cos t)\right)
 \le\exp\left(-\frac{4nt^2}{9\pi^2}\right).
 \label{gsr:en:77:cyclo-global}
\end{equation}
In the last step we used $1-\cos t\ge2t^2/\pi^2$ on
$[-\pi,\pi]$. Thus no other part of the circle contributes a
competing peak, including neighborhoods of the roots.
On $|t|\le n^{-1/2}$ each factor before the fourth power is at
least $1-1/(2n)$, so
$H_n(t)\ge(1-1/(2n))^{2n}\ge81/256$. Parseval and the Gaussian
upper bound therefore give
\begin{equation}
 \frac{81}{256\pi\sqrt n}\le
 \frac{E_n}{F_n(1)^4}
 =\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}H_n(t)\,dt
 \le\frac{3\sqrt\pi}{4\sqrt n}.
 \label{gsr:en:77:cyclo-integral-uniform}
\end{equation}

For the value at one, let $f(x)=\log(2(1+\sin x))$. The identity
$2(1+\sin x)=4\cos^2(x/2-\pi/4)$ gives
\[
 \int_0^{\pi/2}f(x)\,dx=2\mathsf G.
\]
One elementary verification uses the Abel-damped Fourier series for
$\log(2\cos u)$ on $0\le u\le\pi/4$: termwise integration and passage to the limit give
$\int_0^{\pi/4}\log(2\cos u)\,du=\mathsf G/2$.
The substitution $u=\pi/4-x/2$ gives the displayed identity.
Since $f'(0)=1$, $f'(\pi/2)=0$, midpoint Euler--Maclaurin with
step $h=\pi/n$ yields
\begin{equation}
 \log F_n(1)=\frac{2\mathsf G n}{\pi}
              +\frac{\pi}{24n}+O(n^{-3}).
 \label{gsr:en:77:cyclo-at-one}
\end{equation}
Also $f''(x)=-1/(1+\sin x)$, so concavity and the elementary
midpoint error estimate give the uniform bound
\[
 0\le\log F_n(1)-\frac{2\mathsf G n}{\pi}
       \le\frac{\pi^2}{48n}.
\]
Combining this with \eqref{gsr:en:77:cyclo-integral-uniform} and
$\delta_n=1/(2E_n)$ proves \eqref{gsr:en:77:cyclo-uniform}.

For the first asymptotic correction, set
$T_r=\sum_j(1+s_j)^{-r}$. Midpoint quadrature gives
\[
 T_1=\frac n\pi+O(n^{-1}),\qquad
 T_2=\frac{2n}{3\pi}+O(n^{-1}),
\]
since the corresponding integrals on $[0,\pi/2]$ are $1$ and
$2/3$. Uniformly in a fixed neighborhood of $t=0$,
\[
 \log H_n(t)
 =-2T_1t^2+\left(\frac{T_1}{6}-\frac{T_2}{2}\right)t^4
   +O(nt^6).
\]
This Taylor remainder is uniform in $n$ because the factor
$\cos t+s_j$ stays uniformly positive there. With $t=u/\sqrt n$,
\[
 \log H_n(u/\sqrt n)
 =-\frac{2u^2}{\pi}-\frac{u^4}{6\pi n}
  +O\left(\frac{u^2+u^6}{n^2}+\frac{u^4}{n^3}\right).
\]
Integrate first over $|t|\le n^{-2/5}$. Taylor expansion of the
exponential there has an integrable Gaussian-times-polynomial
remainder of relative order $O(n^{-2})$. The complementary integral
is exponentially small by \eqref{gsr:en:77:cyclo-global}. Since the normalized
fourth moment of $e^{-2u^2/\pi}$ is $3\pi^2/16$, it follows that
\[
 \frac{E_n}{F_n(1)^4}
 =\frac1{2\sqrt{2n}}
   \left(1-\frac{\pi}{32n}+O(n^{-2})\right).
\]
Equation \eqref{gsr:en:77:cyclo-at-one} contributes $\pi/(6n)$ after
taking the fourth power; $\pi/6-\pi/32=13\pi/96$. This proves
\eqref{gsr:en:77:cyclo-E}, and inversion proves \eqref{gsr:en:77:cyclo-delta}.
\end{proof}
