\paragraph{Even finite cyclic domains.}
Let the cyclic order $N$ be even. If $N>n$, place the same weights
on the distinct residues $0,\ldots,n$. The reflection $k\mapsto n-k$
modulo $N$ still preserves parity and both weight parts. The signed
convolution is $1+z^{2n}$ modulo $z^N-1$, so its squared norm is
$2$ unless $N\mid2n$, when it is $4$. Under $N>n$, the latter
case is exactly $N=2n$. Ordinary convolution is nonnegative
periodization of the convolution on $\mathbb Z$, so its squared
norm cannot decrease. Thus the excess is at most $\delta_n$ when
$N\ne2n$, and at most $2\delta_n$ in all cases. If $N\le n$,
constant weight on the full cyclic group has excess zero and
support at most $n$.
In particular, the cyclic-or-six-point reduction proved in Report~288~\cite{srcseventysix} gives
weighted witnesses of support at most $\max\{6,n+1\}$ at excess
at most $2\delta_n$. Its upper support bound therefore has leading
coefficient $\pi/(8\mathsf G)$ in $\log(1/\epsilon)$; the factor
of two in excess does not change that coefficient. More explicitly, with
$y=\log(1/\epsilon)\to\infty$, choosing the next even degree above
$(y+\tfrac12\log y+C)/\kappa_{\rm C}$ for a sufficiently large fixed $C$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:77:cyclo-universal-support}
 \sup_{G,H,a\text{ nonaffine}}n_a(\epsilon)
 \le\frac{y+\tfrac12\log y}{\kappa_{\rm C}}+O(1).
\end{equation}
Indeed the uniform upper bound~\eqref{gsr:en:77:cyclo-uniform} makes
$2\delta_n\le\epsilon$ with that choice, and even rounding costs at most two degrees. Together with the sparse lower bound, the remaining leading-coefficient range is $[1/\log16,\,1/\kappa_{\rm C}]$.

\paragraph{Rational or integer approximations.}
The exact coefficients above need not be rational. If rational
weights are required, approximate half the positive vector by
positive rationals and reflect to preserve palindromicity. The
energy ratio is continuous on nonzero nonnegative vectors, so the
excess can be approximated arbitrarily closely with unchanged
support. Clearing denominators then gives positive integer weights
with the same ratio. To obtain a prescribed inequality, choose
first a strict margin below its threshold. The exact identity
\eqref{gsr:en:77:cyclo-factor} is not asserted for these approximations,
and no bound on their heights is claimed.

\begin{proposition}[Sharp exponential rate under an interval constraint]
\label{gsr:en:77:cyclo-interval-lower}
For every nonzero nonnegative weight on $\mathbb Z$ supported
inside an interval of $n+1$ consecutive integers,
\begin{equation}
 \delta(w)\ge\frac{e^{-\kappa_{\rm C}n}}{4(n+1)}.
 \label{gsr:en:77:cyclo-interval-bound}
\end{equation}
Consequently, among witnesses with such an interval constraint,
the optimal exponential rate is $\kappa_{\rm C}$. Equivalently,
the minimum length of a containing integer interval for excess
at most $\epsilon$ is
$\bigl(\pi/(8\mathsf G)+o(1)\bigr)\log(1/\epsilon)$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
After translating, the generating polynomial $F$ has degree
$d\le n$. Translation preserves the energy ratio, including when
it swaps the two parity classes. Put $Q(z)=F(z)F(-z)$ and
$B=\|Q\|_2^2$, with normalized circle measure. Boyd's
factor-norm inequality \cite{boydfactor} states
\[
 \|P\|_\infty\|Q_0\|_\infty
 \le C_2^{\deg P+\deg Q_0}\|PQ_0\|_\infty,
 \qquad C_2=e^{2\mathsf G/\pi},
\]
for arbitrary nonzero complex polynomials. Nonnegative
coefficients give $\|F\|_\infty=\|F(-z)\|_\infty=F(1)$.
Moreover $Q$ is even with at most $d+1$ coefficient positions,
so coefficient Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
 F(1)^4\le C_2^{4d}\|Q\|_\infty^2
          \le C_2^{4d}(d+1)B.
\]
With $E=\Eadd(w)$, the inequalities $E\le F(1)^4$ and $\delta E\ge B/4$ prove
\[
 \delta\ge\frac{e^{-\kappa_{\rm C}d}}{4(d+1)}
         \ge\frac{e^{-\kappa_{\rm C}n}}{4(n+1)}.
\]
For an explicit inversion, put $y=\log(1/\epsilon)$. The lower bound implies
$d\ge(y-\log y)/\kappa_{\rm C}-O(1)$ for any qualifying weight as $y\to\infty$; if $d>y/\kappa_{\rm C}$ this is immediate, and otherwise bound $\log(4(d+1))$ by $\log y+O(1)$. The upper bound in~\eqref{gsr:en:77:cyclo-uniform}, choosing the next even degree, supplies a witness with
$d\le(y+\tfrac12\log y)/\kappa_{\rm C}+O(1)$. The same inequalities apply to containing interval length $d+1$ after changing the bounded terms. Dividing by $y$ proves the stated limiting coefficient.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Scope of the constant.}
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:77:cyclo-interval-lower} concerns degree or
containing interval length. It is not a bound in terms of the
number of positive weights alone when gaps are unrestricted.
The unrestricted sparse-support problem still has the separate
lower bound established earlier; the present construction improves
its upper constant but does not identify the unrestricted optimum.
The cyclotomic vector is also not claimed to minimize the excess
at every fixed support size.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The exact three-point integer minimum\srctag{77}}]{The exact three-point integer minimum}\label{gsr:en:77:sec:d10}\label{gsr:en:77:sec:three}
\srcnote{77}{Section 10}
\begin{theorem}[Smallest nontrivial weighted optimization]\label{gsr:en:77:thm:three}
For integer parity, weights supported on at most two points have ratio one. Among weights supported on exactly three integer points, the minimum ratio is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:77:eq:three-min}
 \frac{9+\sqrt6}{15}
 =\frac34+\frac{4\sqrt6-9}{60}.
\end{equation}
Equality holds exactly on an odd-step three-term arithmetic progression, with weights proportional to $(1,6^{1/4},1)$ in increasing order.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
On at most two integer points, equal pair sums compare the same unordered pair, so every additive quadruple is respected. For a support $x<y<z$, the only possible equality between distinct unordered pair sums is $x+z=2y$. If it fails, the ratio is one. If it holds with even step, all three points have the same parity, again giving ratio one. For odd step, the endpoints share parity and the middle has opposite parity.

Let the endpoint weights be $a,c>0$ and the middle weight $b>0$. The failed quadruple mass is $4acb^2$: the endpoint pair has two orders, the middle pair has one, and the two sides can be interchanged. Set
\[
 p=ac,\qquad q=b^2,\qquad v=a^2+c^2\ge2p.
\]
Counting the five possible pair sums gives
\begin{align}
 \Eadd(w)&=v^2+2p^2+q^2+4q(v+p),\label{gsr:en:77:eq:three-energy}\\
 \frac{\Ea(w)}{\Eadd(w)}
 &=1-\frac{4pq}{v^2+2p^2+q^2+4q(v+p)}.\label{gsr:en:77:eq:three-ratio}
\end{align}
For fixed positive $p,q$, the denominator increases strictly with $v\ge2p$. Thus the ratio is minimized only when $v=2p$, or $a=c$.

Write $X=q/p>0$ and $r=\sqrt6$. The resulting failed fraction is $4X/(X^2+12X+6)$. The exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:77:eq:three-certificate}
 \frac4{12+2r}-\frac{4X}{X^2+12X+6}
 =\frac{4(X-r)^2}{(12+2r)(X^2+12X+6)}\ge0
\end{equation}
shows that its unique maximum occurs at $X=r$. Its value is $(6-\sqrt6)/15$, so subtraction from one gives~\eqref{gsr:en:77:eq:three-min}. Finally $a=c$ and $b^2/a^2=\sqrt6$ mean $b/a=6^{1/4}$, as asserted. All denominators in~\eqref{gsr:en:77:eq:three-certificate} are positive; this is an exact algebraic certificate, not a numerical optimization.
\end{proof}

For the binomial three-point weight $(1,2,1)$, the excess is $3/140$; it is not the minimizing three-point weight. Thus the binomial family proves the asymptotic upper order but need not optimize a given small support size. The theorem also implies $n(\epsilon)=3$ whenever
\[
 \frac{4\sqrt6-9}{60}\le\epsilon<\frac14,
\]
since one or two points have excess $1/4$. Below this interval the exact function remains undetermined here.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Restriction and a division-free index-two family\srctag{78}}]{Restriction and a division-free index-two family}\label{gsr:en:78:sec:d2}\label{gsr:en:78:sec:index-two}
\srcnote{78}{Section 2}
\subsection{Restriction to a translated subgroup}
Let $C\le G$, $z\in G$, and $b(c)=a(z+c)$. Translating a weight on $C$ to $z+C$ preserves both energies: the two domain sums each gain $2z$, and the image sums are those of $b$. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:restriction}
 r(a)\le r(b),\qquad \rind(a)\le\rind(b).
\end{equation}
This holds without any finiteness assumption on $C$. Adding an affine map to $a$, where defined on a group, also leaves respectedness of additive quadruples unchanged.

\subsection{A common homomorphism on two cosets}
Let $K\le G$ have index two, choose $t\notin K$, and let $\psi:K\to H$ be a homomorphism. For $\beta,u\in H$, define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:index-two-form}
 a(k)=\beta+\psi(k),\qquad
 a(t+k)=\beta+u+\psi(k)\quad(k\in K),
 \qquad \eta=2u-\psi(2t).
\end{equation}
The element $2t$ belongs to $K$, so the defect $\eta$ is defined. The map is affine exactly when $\eta=0$. Necessity follows by evaluating a putative homomorphism at $2t$; sufficiency follows by adding points in the two cosets, the only extra relation being $2u=\psi(2t)$. No extension of $\psi$ is assumed and no division by two in $H$ is used.

Assume $\eta\ne0$. Write each point uniquely as $\varepsilon t+k$ with $\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}$. For a pair of points let $p\in\{0,1,2\}$ be its \emph{integer} sum of the two $\varepsilon$-values. Two pairs with the same domain sum have congruent $p$ modulo two. If their integer $p$-values agree, their image sums agree. Otherwise the values are $0$ and $2$, and the image sums differ by $\eta$ or $-\eta$. Thus precisely these comparisons fail.

For a finite weight $w$, let $e=w\ind_K$ and $o=w\ind_{t+K}$. Convolution and norms use counting measure:
\[
 (f*g)(s)=\sum_x f(x)g(s-x),\qquad \norm f_2^2=\sum_x f(x)^2.
\]
Put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:UVCD}
 U=\norm{e*e}_2^2,\quad V=\norm{o*o}_2^2,\quad
 C=\ip{e*e}{o*o},\quad D=\norm{e*o}_2^2,
 \quad R(h)=\sum_x e(x)o(x+h).
\end{equation}
Even and odd pair sums have disjoint supports. The pair classification gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:energy-split}
 \Eadd(w)=U+V+2C+4D,\qquad \Ea(w)=U+V+4D.
\end{equation}
Expanding finite sums and reindexing yields
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:correlation}
 C=\sum_h R(h)R(-h),\qquad D=\sum_hR(h)^2.
\end{equation}
For example, the first right-hand side sums
$e(x)e(y)o(x+h)o(y-h)$ over $x,y,h$, exactly the configurations with equal even-even and odd-odd sums. The second identity expresses an equal mixed-pair sum by the common difference of its two even entries and its two odd entries.

\begin{proposition}[Exact sum of squares]\label{gsr:en:78:prop:SOS}
For every nonzero finite weight in the nonzero-defect family~\eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:index-two-form},
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:SOS}
 \Ea(w)-\frac34\Eadd(w)
 =\frac14\norm{e*e-o*o}_2^2
  +\frac12\sum_h\bigl(R(h)-R(-h)\bigr)^2\ge0.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
By~\eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:correlation}, the second term on the right is $D-C$. The first is $(U+V-2C)/4$. Their sum is $(U+V)/4+D-3C/2$, which is the difference on the left by~\eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:energy-split}. Every sum is finite.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Finite and infinite cyclic endpoint calculations}\label{gsr:en:78:subsec:cyclic-endpoint}
On $\Z$ or $\Z/(2n)$, the two-coset form becomes
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:cyclic-form}
 a(2j)=\beta+jd,\qquad a(2j+1)=\beta+jd+u,
 \qquad \eta=2u-d.
\end{equation}
For a finite cycle $j$ is taken modulo $n$ and $nd=0$; on $\Z$ there is no relation on $d$. If $\eta=0$, the map is affine; suppose otherwise.

On the finite cycle, the full indicator has $U=V=C=D=n^3$. Its ratio is exactly $6n^3/(8n^3)=3/4$. On $\Z$, use
\[
 A_m=\{0,1,\ldots,2m-1\},\qquad
 U_m=\frac{2m^3+m}{3},\qquad C_m=U_m-m \quad(m\ge1).
\]
The convolution of $\ind_{\{0,\ldots,m-1\}}$ with itself is the triangle
$1,2,\ldots,m-1,m,m-1,\ldots,1$. Summing its squares gives $U_m$; taking its inner product with a one-step translate gives $C_m$. Thus $U=V=D=U_m$, $C=C_m$, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:interval-ratio}
 \frac{\Ea(\ind_{A_m})}{\Eadd(\ind_{A_m})}
 =\frac{6U_m}{8U_m-2m}
 =\frac34+\frac9{32m^2+4}\longrightarrow\frac34.
\end{equation}
Together with~\eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:SOS}, these calculations give $r=\rind=3/4$ for every nonzero-defect cyclic form.

They also settle~\eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:index-two-form} on arbitrary $G$. The subgroup $\langle t\rangle$ is infinite cyclic or finite cyclic of even order, because its image in $G/K$ is nonzero. Its restriction is~\eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:cyclic-form} with $d=\psi(2t)$ and the same nonzero defect. Restriction gives the upper bound and~\eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:SOS} gives the lower bound. We have proved:
\begin{corollary}[An exact endpoint family]\label{gsr:en:78:cor:index-two}
Every map~\eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:index-two-form} with $\eta\ne0$ satisfies
$r(a)=\rind(a)=3/4$, for arbitrary abelian $G,H$.
\end{corollary}

This family includes cases where $\psi$ does not extend to $G$. For example, take $G=\Z/4$, $H=\Z/2$, $K=\{0,2\}$, $t=1$, $\psi(2)=1$, and $\beta=u=0$. The values are $0,0,1,1$, and $\eta=1$. Every homomorphism $G\to H$ sends $2$ to zero, so a formula requiring an extension of $\psi$ would miss this example.

\subsection{Strict nonattainment on the integers}\label{gsr:en:78:subsec:strict}
For~\eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:cyclic-form} on $\Z$ with $\eta\ne0$, every individual finite-weight ratio is strictly greater than $3/4$. If only one of $e,o$ is nonzero, its ratio is one. Otherwise let $p=\max\supp(e)$ and $q=\max\supp(o)$. These integers have different parity and hence are unequal. Positivity of the endpoint coefficients gives
\[
 \max\supp(e*e)=2p,\qquad \max\supp(o*o)=2q.
\]
Consequently $e*e\ne o*o$, and the first term of~\eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:SOS} is positive.

In particular, take $H=\Z$ and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:integer-parity}
 a(j)=\begin{cases}0&j\text{ even},\\1&j\text{ odd}.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
This nonaffine map has defect $2$, both infima equal to $3/4$, and no finite weight attaining that value. This proves the individual-strictness distinction discussed in Section~\ref{gsr:fm:78:sec:main}.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Cyclic failure of the increment equation\srctag{78}}]{Cyclic failure of the increment equation}\label{gsr:en:78:sec:d3}\label{gsr:en:78:sec:cyclic}
\srcnote{78}{Section 3}
\begin{lemma}[A preliminary cyclic witness]\label{gsr:en:78:lem:cyclic-preliminary}
If \eqref{gsr:fm:78:eq:P} fails for some $x,h\in G$, a subset of $x+\langle h\rangle$ of at most six points has indicator ratio at most $8/11$. The target $H$ may have arbitrary torsion.
\end{lemma}
We first prove the $8/11$ witness bound, then strengthen it to $19/27$. The preliminary small-order estimates will also justify a curvature rule in short cyclic directions during the stronger proof.

\subsection{The four-point window}
Suppose $h$ has infinite order or finite order $N\ge7$. The four distinct points $x,x+h,x+2h,x+3h$ have pair-sum multiplicities
\[
 1,2,3,4,3,2,1,
\]
so their ordinary energy is $44$. The seven possible sums remain distinct in the domain. Put $a_i=a(x+ih)$ and
\[
 A=a_0+a_2-2a_1,\quad B=a_1+a_3-2a_2,\quad
 M=a_0+a_3-a_1-a_2=A+B.
\]
Failure of \eqref{gsr:fm:78:eq:P} means $M\ne0$. At the central sum, the two ordered pairs of type $\{0,3\}$ and the two of type $\{1,2\}$ have different target sums. This loses $2\cdot2\cdot2=8$ ordered comparisons. Since $A+B\ne0$, at least one of $A,B$ is nonzero. The corresponding comparison of a repeated pair with a two-order pair at sum $2$ or $4$ loses another four. These losses occur in different sum fibers. Thus
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:window}
 \Ea(\ind_{\{x,x+h,x+2h,x+3h\}})\le32,
 \qquad\frac{\Ea}{\Eadd}\le\frac{32}{44}=\frac8{11}.
\end{equation}
No integer multiple has been cancelled in $H$; the only implication used is that $A+B\ne0$ forces one summand to be nonzero.

\subsection{Histogram identities and restrictions}
For a map on $C_N=\Z/N\Z$, write
\[
 \Delta_h a(y)=a(y+h)-a(y),\qquad
 n_h(v)=|\{y:\Delta_h a(y)=v\}|,\qquad Q_h=\sum_vn_h(v)^2.
\]
Only finitely many target values occur. Every additive quadruple has the unique form $(y+h,z,y,z+h)$, giving
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:histogram}
 \Ea(\ind_{C_N})=\sum_{h\in C_N}Q_h,\quad
 \Eadd(\ind_{C_N})=N^3,\quad Q_0=N^2,\quad Q_{-h}=Q_h.
\end{equation}
A derivative that is constant in a generating direction makes the map affine: repeated addition gives $a(jh)=a(0)+jv$, and going around the cycle gives $Nv=0$.

A nonconstant histogram of mass $N$ has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:partition-bound}
 Q_h\le(N-1)^2+1.
\end{equation}
For $N\ge4$, if the partition $(N-1,1)$ is impossible, the bound improves to $(N-2)^2+4$. To see both assertions, transferring a unit from a smaller positive part to a larger one strictly increases the sum of squares. Among the permitted nonconstant partitions the most concentrated one maximizes it.

There are two useful restrictions. If $h$ has order two, the points come in pairs $y,y+h$ with derivative values $v,-v$. Non-self-negative values occur with the same multiplicities as their negatives, and each self-negative value has even multiplicity. A nonconstant partition $(N-1,1)$ is therefore impossible for even $N$. For the step $h=2$ on $C_6$, there are two derivative cycles of length three. Five occurrences of $v$ and one of $u$ would give one all-$v$ cycle with $3v=0$ and a second with $2v+u=0$. Subtraction gives $u=v$, a contradiction.

\subsection{Orders one through six}
Translate the cyclic coset and parametrize it by $C_N$. Write $b(j)=a(j+1)-a(j)$. The equation at step one is exactly $b(j+2)=b(j)$. A constant $\Delta_2a$ implies this by subtracting its values at $j+1$ and $j$. Likewise, a constant $\Delta_3a$ implies $b(j+3)=b(j)$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{Order \arabic*.},start=1]
 \item The equation is automatic on the trivial group.
 \item Since $2h=0$, the equation is automatic.
 \item Failure of the equation implies nonaffinity. Both nonzero directions generate, so $Q_1=Q_2\le5$ and the full ratio is at most
 \[
 (9+2\cdot5)/27=19/27<8/11.
 \]
 \item Failure makes $\Delta_2a$ nonconstant. Involution pairing gives $Q_2\le8$, and the generating derivatives satisfy $Q_1=Q_3\le10$. The full ratio is at most
 \[
 (16+2\cdot10+8)/64=11/16<8/11.
 \]
 \item The sharpened argument below gives $17/25<8/11$ for every nonaffine map, in particular for every failure of the equation.
 \item Failure again makes $\Delta_2a$ nonconstant. The two three-cycles give $Q_2=Q_4\le20$, while $Q_1=Q_5\le26$. If $\Delta_3a$ is nonconstant, involution pairing gives $Q_3\le20$; hence the energy is at most
 \[
 36+2\cdot26+2\cdot20+20=148.
 \]
 If $\Delta_3a$ is constant, $b$ is three-periodic, and its nonconstant histogram has even multiplicities. Thus $Q_1=Q_5\le20$, whereas $Q_3=36$, and the energy is at most
 \[
 36+2\cdot20+2\cdot20+36=152.
 \]
 Both ratios are at most $152/216=19/27<8/11$.
\end{enumerate}
All these witnesses are the full cyclic coset, with at most six points. Together with \eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:window}, they prove Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:78:lem:cyclic-preliminary}, once the five-cycle calculation is supplied.

\begin{proposition}[Sharp full-indicator bound on the five-cycle]\label{gsr:en:78:prop:C5}
For every nonaffine $a:C_5\to H$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:C5}
 \Ea(\ind_{C_5})\le85,\qquad
 \frac{\Ea(\ind_{C_5})}{\Eadd(\ind_{C_5})}\le\frac{17}{25}.
\end{equation}
The bound is sharp for this full-indicator statistic.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Every nonzero direction generates. Thus the relevant histograms are nonconstant, and $Q_1,Q_2\le17$. The only partition of five with square sum exceeding $13$ is $(4,1)$, with square sum $17$.

Suppose $Q_1=17$. Four increments equal $v$ and the remaining increment equals $u\ne v$. Telescoping gives $4v+u=0$, so $u=-4v$ and $5v\ne0$. Rotate the cycle so the exceptional increment is the closing edge from position four to zero. For $0\le j\le4$ the map is then $a(j)=\beta+jv$. The step-two derivative equals $2v$ three times and $-3v$ twice. These two values are distinct because $5v\ne0$, and therefore $Q_2=13$.

If instead $Q_2=17$, use $2$ as generator. The same calculation gives $Q_4=13$; as $Q_4=Q_1$, it again yields $Q_1+Q_2=30$. If neither square sum is $17$, their sum is at most $26$. Consequently \eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:histogram} gives
\[
 \Ea(\ind_{C_5})=25+2Q_1+2Q_2\le25+2\cdot30=85.
\]
For sharpness, take $a(j)=j\in\Z$ for the standard representatives $0,\ldots,4$. Its respected energy is the ordinary integer-interval energy
\[
 1^2+2^2+3^2+4^2+5^2+4^2+3^2+2^2+1^2=85.
\]
The ordinary domain energy remains $5^3=125$.
\end{proof}
This proof establishes sharpness for the full indicator. It makes no claim about the weighted infimum of that example. The companion additionally checks all 31 nonempty subsets of this particular five-point map; that finite check is separate from the general proposition.

\subsection{The sharp cyclic witness}
\begin{lemma}[The sharp universal cyclic cutoff]\label{gsr:en:78:lem:cyclic}
If \eqref{gsr:fm:78:eq:P} fails for some $x,h\in G$, some subset of $x+\langle h\rangle$ of at most ten points has indicator ratio at most $19/27$. This holds for every abelian target.
\end{lemma}
The bounds already proved cover orders at most six. We next prove orders seven through nine by histograms, then exclude all larger orders by a complete finite symbolic certificate. The certificate classifies arbitrary target collisions; it is not a search over maps into selected finite targets.

\subsubsection{An arithmetic-cut histogram}
Suppose a generating derivative on $C_N$ has multiplicities $(N-1,1)$. Rotate that generator so its exceptional increment closes the cycle. The values then have the form $a(j)=\beta+jv$, $0\le j<N$, with $Nv\ne0$. In direction $d$, the derivative takes the distinct values $dv$ and $(d-N)v$ with multiplicities $N-d$ and $d$. Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:arithmetic-cut}
 \frac{\Ea(\ind_{C_N})}{N^3}
 =\frac{N^2+\sum_{d=1}^{N-1}((N-d)^2+d^2)}{N^3}
 =\frac{2N^2+1}{3N^2}.
\end{equation}
If this partition is absent, every nonconstant histogram has square sum at most $(N-2)^2+4$.

A useful global observation is that a constant $\Delta_2a$ on a cyclic group makes the unit increments two-periodic. The sum of every two consecutive increments is then constant, and so $\Delta_{2h}a$ is constant for every integer direction $h$, including negative ones. Thus \eqref{gsr:fm:78:eq:P} holds in every direction. Any failure of \eqref{gsr:fm:78:eq:P} on a cyclic group therefore makes $\Delta_2a$ nonconstant.

\subsubsection{Orders seven through nine}
\textbf{Order seven.} Every nonzero direction generates. If one histogram is $(6,1)$, equation~\eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:arithmetic-cut} gives ratio $33/49<19/27$. Otherwise all six nonzero square sums are at most $5^2+2^2=29$, and
\[
 \Ea\le49+6\cdot29=223<231,\qquad231/343=33/49.
\]
This applies to every nonaffine map on $C_7$.

\textbf{Order eight.} Suppose \eqref{gsr:fm:78:eq:P} fails. An odd-direction histogram $(7,1)$ gives arithmetic-cut ratio $43/64<19/27$. Otherwise all four odd-direction derivatives are nonconstant and have $Q_h\le40$. The nonconstant $\Delta_2a$ cannot have partition $(7,1)$: one of its two four-cycles would give $4v=0$, and the other $3v+u=0$, forcing $u=v$. Hence $Q_2=Q_6\le40$.

If $\Delta_4a$ is nonconstant, involution pairing excludes $(7,1)$ and gives $Q_4\le40$, so $\Ea\le64+7\cdot40=344<352$. Otherwise $\Delta_4a\equiv c$ for some $c$. Every derivative is then four-periodic, since $\Delta_h a(x+4)=\Delta_h a(x)$, and all its multiplicities are even. If no odd-direction histogram is $(6,2)$, each odd $Q_h\le4^2+4^2=32$, giving
\[
 \Ea\le64+64+4\cdot32+2\cdot40=336<352.
\]
In the remaining case choose an odd generator with histogram $(6,2)$. A four-term period of its increments has three copies of $v$ and one of $u\ne v$. Adjacent two-step sums are $2v$ and $v+u$, each four times on $C_8$, so $Q_2=Q_6=32$. Moreover
\[
 \Delta_3a(x)=c-\Delta_1a(x-1),
\]
so the four odd-direction square sums are all $40$. The total is $64+64+4\cdot40+2\cdot32=352$, and $352/512=11/16<19/27$. Reparametrizing by the chosen generator only permutes directions.

\textbf{Order nine.} For a nonaffine map the six generating derivatives are nonconstant. If any has partition $(8,1)$, equation~\eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:arithmetic-cut} gives $163/243<19/27$. Otherwise all six have square sum at most $53$. If $\Delta_3a$ is nonconstant, its three three-cycles exclude $(8,1)$: an all-$v$ cycle gives $3v=0$, and a cycle with one exceptional $u$ gives $2v+u=0$, again forcing $u=v$. Thus $Q_3=Q_6\le53$, and $\Ea\le81+8\cdot53=505<513$.

If $\Delta_3a$ is constant, every derivative is three-periodic and has multiplicities divisible by three. Each generating square sum is at most $6^2+3^2=45$, whereas $Q_3=Q_6=81$. Therefore $\Ea\le81+2\cdot81+6\cdot45=513$, and $513/729=19/27$.

\subsection{The curvature rule and the ten-point branch tree}\label{gsr:en:78:subsec:branch}
Suppose, towards a contradiction, that \eqref{gsr:fm:78:eq:P} fails but every nonempty indicator on at most ten points of the relevant cyclic coset has ratio greater than $19/27$. After translating the coset, we may work on the cyclic group itself. The preceding cases make its failure direction have order $N\ge10$ or infinite order.

For any four-term progression set
\[
 A=a_0-2a_1+a_2,\qquad B=a_1-2a_2+a_3,\qquad M=A+B.
\]
In a direction of order at least seven, if $A,B,M$ were all nonzero, the three separate pair-sum fibers would lose $4+4+8=16$ comparisons out of $44$. The ratio would be at most $28/44=7/11<19/27$. In a direction of order at most six, the earlier full-coset estimates imply \eqref{gsr:fm:78:eq:P} under the present hypothesis, so $M=0$. Thus, in \emph{every} direction,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:curvature-rule}
 A=0\quad\hbox{or}\quad B=0\quad\hbox{or}\quad A+B=0.
\end{equation}
This includes direction $2h$ when $h$ has order ten or twelve; no four-point calculation with incorrectly distinct pair sums is used there.

At the chosen failure $M\ne0$, exactly one of $A,B$ is zero. Reverse the progression if necessary to make $A=0$, and translate its base point to index zero. Put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:normalization-ten}
 d=a_1-a_0,\qquad b_i=a_i-a_0-id\quad(0\le i\le9).
\end{equation}
Then $(b_0,b_1,b_2,b_3)=(0,0,0,u)$ with $u\ne0$. These ten indices represent actual distinct points. For finite $N$, the term $id$ is only an integer-parameter normalization: it need not descend to a homomorphism on $C_N$. All uses of \eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:curvature-rule} are integer-balanced and remain valid, while energy comparisons will retain the wrap slope $v=Nd$ explicitly.

For four values $(p,q,r,s)$ with $p-2q+r\ne0$, rule~\eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:curvature-rule} forces
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:extension-choice}
 s=2r-q\quad\hbox{or}\quad s=r+q-p.
\end{equation}
The following tree is exhaustive. Each indicated nonzero curvature is $u$ or $-u$; no assumption on $2u$ is needed.
\begin{enumerate}
 \item On indices $(1,2,3,4)$, values $(0,0,u,b_4)$ give $b_4\in\{u,2u\}$. Certificate row 1 below excludes $2u$, so $b_4=u$.
 \item On $(2,3,4,5)$, values $(0,u,u,b_5)$ give $b_5\in\{u,2u\}$. Row 2 excludes $2u$, so $b_5=u$.
 \item On $(0,2,4,6)$ and $(1,3,5,7)$, rule~\eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:extension-choice} gives $b_6,b_7\in\{u,2u\}$. Rows 3, 4, 5 exclude respectively $(u,u),(u,2u),(2u,u)$; hence $(b_6,b_7)=(2u,2u)$.
 \item On $(5,6,7,8)$, values $(u,2u,2u,b_8)$ give $b_8\in\{2u,3u\}$. Row 6 excludes $3u$, so $b_8=2u$.
 \item On $(3,5,7,9)$, values $(u,u,2u,b_9)$ give $b_9\in\{2u,3u\}$. Rows 7 and 8 exclude both possibilities, a contradiction.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Complete arbitrary-target branch certificates}\label{gsr:en:78:subsec:certificates}
For each row write $b_i=c_i u$. A digit string in the following table lists $c_0,c_1,\ldots$ in order. Let $D_t$ count ordered quadruples in the specified test set $S$ with
\[
 i+j=k+l,\qquad c_i+c_j-c_k-c_l=t.
\]
The complete nonzero data satisfy $D_t=D_{-t}$ and are as follows; omitted defects have zero count.
\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{c l l r r r c}
\hline
Row & $(c_i)$ & $S$ & $D_0$ & $D_1$ & $D_2$ & Upper ratio\\\hline
1 & 00012 & $0,\ldots,4$ & 53 & 14 & 2 & $57/85$\\
2 & 000112 & $0,\ldots,5$ & 98 & 24 & 0 & $49/73$\\
3 & 00011111 & $1,2,3,4,5,7$ & 90 & 20 & 0 & $9/13$\\
4 & 00011112 & $2,\ldots,7$ & 98 & 24 & 0 & $49/73$\\
5 & 00011121 & $0,\ldots,7$ & 204 & 64 & 6 & $27/43$\\
6 & 000111223 & $0,\ldots,8$ & 321 & 84 & 0 & $107/163$\\
7 & 0001112222 & $2,3,4,5,6,7,9$ & 139 & 36 & 0 & $139/211$\\
8 & 0001112223 & $0,\ldots,9$ & 470 & 100 & 0 & $47/67$\\\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
These are elementary coefficient counts. One way to verify every entry by hand is to form, for each integer pair sum $s$, the polynomial
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:pair-polynomial}
 F_s(X)=\sum_{\substack{i,j\in S\\i+j=s}}X^{c_i+c_j}.
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:D-generator}
 \sum_tD_tX^t=\sum_sF_s(X)F_s(X^{-1}).
\end{equation}
All input vectors and test sets are printed above, so this completely specifies the finite calculation. The companion recomputes it by both ordered quadruples and independent pair-sum multiplication.

Since $u\ne0$, defects $\pm u$ never vanish and $\pm2u$ vanish exactly when $u$ has order two. The ordinary energy is $D_0+2D_1+2D_2$, and the numerator is at most $D_0+2D_2$. This proves the displayed no-wrap bounds for every abelian target. Their maximum is $47/67<19/27$. For $N\ge19$ or infinite order, all pair sums lie between zero and eighteen, so there is no wrapping and these bounds finish the branch exclusions.

For $10\le N\le18$, put $v=Nd$ and define
\[
 C_N(z,t)=\bigl|\{(i,j,k,l)\in S^4:i+j-k-l=zN,\ c_i+c_j-c_k-c_l=t\}\bigr|.
\]
Here $z\in\{-1,0,1\}$, $C_N(-z,-t)=C_N(z,t)$, and the original target defect is exactly
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:wrap-defect}
 zv+tu.
\end{equation}
The zero-wrap coefficients are the $D_t$ above. Define the positive-wrap polynomial
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:positive-wrap}
 P_N(X)=\sum_tC_N(1,t)X^t
       =\sum_sF_{s+N}(X)F_s(X^{-1}).
\end{equation}
Appendix~\ref{gsr:en:78:app:certificate} prints all 31 nonzero polynomials for these eight rows and nine cyclic orders; every unlisted polynomial is zero. The exact ordinary energy is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:wrap-denominator}
 E_N=D_0+2D_1+2D_2+2P_N(1).
\end{equation}

Every printed polynomial has exponent support of diameter at most three. A positive-wrap coefficient $t$ is respected exactly when $v=-tu$. Two such coefficients $t,t'$ can be respected together exactly when $(t-t')u=0$. Thus every possible target is covered by just three collision types. Put
\begin{align}
 W_2&=\max_{r\bmod2}\sum_{t\equiv r\ (2)}C_N(1,t),&
 W_3&=\max_{r\bmod3}\sum_{t\equiv r\ (3)}C_N(1,t),\label{gsr:en:78:eq:wrap-residue}\\
 W_\infty&=\max_t C_N(1,t),&&\nonumber
\end{align}
with all three values zero for an empty polynomial. Order two permits exactly the parity collisions and also respects $\pm2u$ in the zero-wrap part. Order three permits exactly the residue-three collisions. Order at least four, or infinite order, permits no collision between distinct printed exponents. Therefore the respected numerator is bounded by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:wrap-numerator}
 U_N=\max\{D_0+2D_2+2W_2,\ D_0+2W_3,\ D_0+2W_\infty\}.
\end{equation}
If $v\notin\langle u\rangle$, no nonzero-wrap term is respected and the same bound applies. The negative-wrap contribution equals the positive one by the symmetry of $C_N$. No cyclicity assumption on the whole target, and no division, has entered.

Appendix~\ref{gsr:en:78:app:certificate} lists all 72 rational bounds $U_N/E_N$ obtained from these explicit polynomials. Their largest is $59/84$, strictly below $19/27$ because $59\cdot27=1593<1596=19\cdot84$. This proves every finite-wrap branch exclusion. The ten-point tree is impossible, so a required witness exists. Together with the full-coset cases of orders at most nine, this proves Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:78:lem:cyclic}.

\section[{The elementary-two classification\srctag{78}}]{The elementary-two classification}\label{gsr:en:78:sec:d4}\label{gsr:en:78:sec:elementary}
\srcnote{78}{Section 4}
Let $V$ be a vector space over $\F_2$, possibly of infinite dimension. In this section all target values remain in an arbitrary abelian group.

\begin{lemma}[The four-point trichotomy]\label{gsr:en:78:lem:plane}
On a four-point affine plane $P\subseteq V$, the respected full-indicator energy is either $64$, $48$, or at most $40$. In the first case the restriction is affine. In the second, the doubled target values form two distinct classes of size two; the unique unrespected opposite-pair partition pairs within these classes.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Write $P=\{x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3\}$, where $x_0+x_1+x_2+x_3=0$, and put $A_i=a(x_i)$. Define
\[
 D=|\{(i,j):2A_i=2A_j\}|,
\]
and let $k$ be the number of true equalities among
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:three-partitions}
 A_0+A_1=A_2+A_3,\quad A_0+A_2=A_1+A_3,\quad A_0+A_3=A_1+A_2.
\end{equation}
The zero-sum fiber has four repeated pairs and contributes $D$. Each of the three remaining fibers has two ordered copies of each of two unordered pairs, contributing $8$ if the corresponding equality fails and $16$ if it holds. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:plane-energy}
 \Eadd(\ind_P)=64,\qquad \Ea(\ind_P)=D+24+8k.
\end{equation}
If $k=3$, subtraction of the equalities gives equal doubled values, so $D=16$ and the energy is $64$. After subtracting $A_0$, the three other values have order dividing two and satisfy the addition relation on the translated two-dimensional vector space. Thus the restriction is affine.

If $k=2$, relabel so the first two equalities hold. Normalize $A_0=0$ and write $B=A_1$, $C=A_2$. They give
\[
 A_3=B-C=C-B,\qquad 2B=2C.
\]
The third equality is equivalent to $2B=0$, so its failure makes the doubled-value classes exactly $\{0,3\}$ and $\{1,2\}$. Therefore $D=8$ and the energy is $48$. The missing partition is the one pairing within the doubled-value classes, as asserted.

If $k=1$, doubling the one equality gives an equality between sums of doubled values. A multiplicity pattern $(3,1)$ is impossible, because cancelling the three common doubled values forces the exceptional one to agree as well. If all doubled values agreed, normalization would put all four values in $H[2]=\{v:2v=0\}$; in this group any one equality in \eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:three-partitions} implies all three. Thus the only remaining doubled-value multiplicities have square sum at most $2^2+2^2=8$, and the energy is at most $40$. If $k=0$, the direct bound $D\le16$ gives the same conclusion.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Global gluing on an elementary-two domain]\label{gsr:en:78:thm:elementary}
Every $a:V\to H$ is affine, has the nonzero-defect index-two form, or has a four-point affine plane of indicator ratio at most $5/8$. This includes dimensions zero and one, where the third possibility cannot occur.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Assume every plane has energy $48$ or $64$. Subtract $a(0)$, so $a(0)=0$, and put $b(x)=2a(x)$. On every plane, $b$ is constant or takes two distinct values twice each. Any three distinct points lie in an affine plane. It follows that $b$ has at most two values globally; this is immediate as well when $|V|\le2$.

If $b$ is constant, it is zero. Every plane is then affine by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:78:lem:plane}. For distinct nonzero $x,y$, the plane $\{0,x,y,x+y\}$ gives $a(x+y)=a(x)+a(y)$. The repeated-argument case follows from $2a(x)=0$, and a zero argument is immediate. Thus $a$ is a homomorphism.

Otherwise the doubled values are $0,c$, with $c\ne0$. Define $\chi:V\to\F_2$ by $2a(x)=c$ exactly when $\chi(x)=1$. Every plane contains an even number of points with $\chi=1$. The plane through $0,x,y,x+y$ yields additivity for distinct nonzero arguments; the remaining arguments are automatic. Hence $\chi$ is a nonzero homomorphism and $K=\ker\chi$ has index two.

On $K$ all doubled values are zero, so the same plane argument and the repeated-argument case show that $\psi=a|_K$ is a homomorphism. Choose $t\notin K$ and set $u=a(t)$, so $2u=c\ne0$. For nonzero $k\in K$, the plane $\{0,k,t,t+k\}$ has doubled values $0,0,c,c$. By Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:78:lem:plane}, its missing partition is the within-class partition, and both cross-class partitions are respected. In particular
\[
 a(0)+a(t+k)=a(k)+a(t),
\]
so $a(t+k)=u+\psi(k)$. The identity is immediate for $k=0$. Restoring the constant gives the stated family, with $2t=0$ and defect $2u\ne0$. Section~\ref{gsr:en:78:sec:index-two} gives its exact infima $3/4$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Sharpness at five eighths]\label{gsr:en:78:prop:sharp}
The map $a(s,t)=st:\F_2^2\to\F_2$ satisfies $r(a)=\rind(a)=5/8$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Every doubled target value is zero and none of the three opposite-pair equalities holds. Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:plane-energy} gives $40/64=5/8$ for the full indicator. For arbitrary nonnegative weights $w_0,w_1,w_2,w_3$, let $P=w_0w_1w_2w_3$. An additive quadruple either repeats one point four times, repeats two points twice each, or uses all four points. Only the last type fails under $a$, so the failed mass is $24P$, and
\[
 \Eadd(w)=\sum_iw_i^4+6\sum_{i<j}w_i^2w_j^2+24P.
\]
AM--GM gives $\sum_iw_i^4\ge4P$ and $\sum_{i<j}w_i^2w_j^2\ge6P$, also when $P=0$. Thus $\Eadd(w)\ge64P$ and the respected ratio is at least $1-24/64=5/8$. On an exponent-two domain \eqref{gsr:fm:78:eq:P} is automatic, proving the sharpness statement of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:78:thm:P} as well.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The two-dimensional grid and its order-four torsion\srctag{78}}]{The two-dimensional grid and its order-four torsion}\label{gsr:en:78:sec:d5}\label{gsr:en:78:sec:grid}
\srcnote{78}{Section 5}
Assume \eqref{gsr:fm:78:eq:P}, fix $h,k\in G$, and set
\[
 F(i,j)=a(ih+jk)\qquad(i,j\in\Z).
\]
There is no assumption that $h,k$ are independent. This integer grid is an algebraic device for deriving identities; indicators will later be chosen in the actual subgroup $\langle h,k\rangle$.

\begin{lemma}[Grid expansion and obstruction]\label{gsr:en:78:lem:grid}
There are $c_{\epsilon,\delta},P_0,P_1,Q_0,Q_1,R\in H$, with $\epsilon,\delta\in\{0,1\}$, such that for all integers $m,n$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:grid-expansion}
 F(2m+\epsilon,2n+\delta)
 =c_{\epsilon,\delta}+mP_\delta+nQ_\epsilon+mnR.
\end{equation}
With $s=P_1-P_0$, one has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:grid-torsion}
 Q_1-Q_0=-s,\qquad R=2s=-2s,\qquad4s=0,
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:grid-derivatives}
 \Delta_{2h}a(ih+jk)=P_0+js,\qquad
 \Delta_{2k}a(ih+jk)=Q_0-is.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The first-axis equation says the unit increments have period two. Hence
\[
 F(2m+\epsilon,j)=F(\epsilon,j)+mP(j),\qquad
 P(j)=F(2,j)-F(0,j),
\]
where the two-step increment $P(j)$ is the same for both values of $\epsilon$. Apply the second-axis recurrence to $F(0,j)$, $F(1,j)$, and to $P(j)=F(2,j)-F(0,j)$. It gives \eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:grid-expansion}, with
\begin{align*}
 c_{\epsilon,\delta}&=F(\epsilon,\delta),&
 P_\delta&=F(2,\delta)-F(0,\delta),\\
 Q_\epsilon&=F(\epsilon,2)-F(\epsilon,0),&
 R&=F(2,2)-F(2,0)-F(0,2)+F(0,0).
\end{align*}
The same $R$ works on all parity classes because it is the common two-step increment of $P(j)$. Backwards recurrence proves the formula for negative integers too; it needs no division.

Put $t=Q_1-Q_0$. Apply \eqref{gsr:fm:78:eq:P} in grid direction $(1,1)$ at bases $(0,0),(1,0),(0,1)$. Substitution in \eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:grid-expansion} gives, in this order,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:diagonal-substitutions}
 s+t=0,\qquad s-t+R=0,\qquad -s+t+R=0.
\end{equation}
For example, at base $(0,0)$ the four entries are $F(3,3),F(2,2),F(1,1),F(0,0)$; the $c$-terms and $R$ cancel, leaving $(P_1-P_0)+(Q_1-Q_0)$. The other bases retain one $R$ and give the two other displayed expressions. Thus $t=-s$ and both $R=2s$ and $R=-2s$, proving \eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:grid-torsion}.

At $(i,j)=(2m+\epsilon,2n+\delta)$, the first two-step derivative is $P_\delta+nR=P_0+(2n+\delta)s=P_0+js$. The second is $Q_\epsilon+mR=Q_0-\epsilon s+2ms=Q_0-is$, where $2s=-2s$ is used in the last equality. This proves \eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:grid-derivatives} without replacing order four by order two.
\end{proof}

The possibility that $s$ has order four is genuine. A useful finite example is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:order-four-example}
 \begin{split}
 G&=C_8\times C_8,\qquad H=C_4,\\
 a(2m+\epsilon,2n+\delta)&=m\delta-n\epsilon+2mn\pmod4,
 \qquad\epsilon,\delta\in\{0,1\}.
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
Its values are well defined modulo eight in the two domain coordinates. Here the basic grid has $P_0=Q_0=0$, $P_1=1$, $Q_1=-1$, $R=2$, so $s=1\in C_4$.

For completeness, its equation \eqref{gsr:fm:78:eq:P} has a direct algebraic verification. Substituting $m\mapsto m+p$ and $n\mapsto n+q$ in \eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:order-four-example}, and using $2=-2$ modulo four, gives
\[
 \Delta_{(2p,2q)}a(i,j)=pj-qi+2pq\pmod4.
\]
Translating $(i,j)$ by $(p,q)$ changes this expression by $pq-qp=0$. Hence $\Delta_{(p,q)}\Delta_{(2p,2q)}a=0$, exactly \eqref{gsr:fm:78:eq:P}. The companion independently checks all $64\cdot64=4096$ pairs $(x,h)$ and finds full ratio $35/128$. The main theorem does not depend on this example; it illustrates why discarding the order-four possibility would be unsafe.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Exact boxes and balanced translations\srctag{78}}]{Exact boxes and balanced translations}\label{gsr:en:78:sec:d6}\label{gsr:en:78:sec:boxes}
\srcnote{78}{Section 6}
We now count within the original finitely generated group, so no noninjective grid parametrization is used as an indicator. By the structure theorem write
\[
 L\cong\Z^r\oplus T,\qquad |T|<\infty,
\]
and fix one such identification. For $N\ge0$, put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:boxes}
 B_N=\{-N,\ldots,N\}^r\times T,\qquad m=2N+1.
\end{equation}
If $r=0$, this means $B_N=L$ for every $N$.

\begin{lemma}[Exact energy and boundary error]\label{gsr:en:78:lem:boundary}
The ordinary energy of \eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:boxes} is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:box-energy}
 E_N:=\Eadd(\ind_{B_N})
 =|T|^3\left(\frac{2m^3+m}{3}\right)^r.
\end{equation}
For any fixed balanced tuple $(v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4)\in L^4$, meaning $v_1+v_2=v_3+v_4$, coordinatewise translation is a bijection on all additive quadruples. If $r>0$, at most $O(m^{3r-1})=o(E_N)$ quadruples enter or leave $B_N^4$ under this translation. The same bound applies to any prescribed subfamily and its translated image. For $r=0$ the error is exactly zero.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
An interval of length $m$ has triangular pair-sum multiplicities $1,2,\ldots,m-1,m,m-1,\ldots,1$. Their squared sum is
\[
 m^2+2\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}j^2=(2m^3+m)/3.
\]
The full finite group $T$ has energy $|T|^3$, because the first three entries determine the fourth. Energies multiply for Cartesian products, proving \eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:box-energy}.

Write the free coordinates of $v$ as $(v_1',\ldots,v_r')$. The symmetric difference of the free box and its translate has at most
\[
 2\left(\sum_{j=1}^r|v_j'|\right)m^{r-1}
\]
points: translate one coordinate at a time and use the union bound. Including $T$ gives $O(m^{r-1})$. Torsion translations preserve the full torsion factor.

Balanced translation preserves the additive equation and is invertible. If membership in $B_N^4$ changes, some coordinate lies in a fixed symmetric-difference boundary of size $O(m^{r-1})$. Two further coordinates can be selected in fixed translates or unions of translates of $B_N$, each of size $O(m^r)$; the fourth is forced by the additive equation. Summing over the four possible boundary coordinates gives $O(m^{3r-1})$. This upper bound also bounds the change for any subfamily under the same bijection. Formula~\eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:box-energy} gives $E_N\asymp m^{3r}$, so the relative error tends to zero. In a finite group the full box is translation invariant, giving exact equality.
\end{proof}
The constants here may depend on the selected group identification and fixed translations. The proof does not assert a uniform effective witness size across all groups and all maps.

\begin{lemma}[Uniform finite-quotient patterns]\label{gsr:en:78:lem:patterns}
Let $\pi:L\to P$ be a surjective homomorphism onto a fixed finite abelian group. Every additive pattern $(p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4)\in P^4$ has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:pattern-count}
 \frac{E_N}{|P|^3}+o(E_N)
\end{equation}
additive lifts in $B_N^4$. For each $v\in P$, the quadruples with $\pi(x_1-x_3)=v$ number
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:difference-count}
 \frac{E_N}{|P|}+o(E_N).
\end{equation}
For $r=0$ both formulas hold without error.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Given two additive patterns, choose lifts $v_1,v_2,v_3\in L$ of the differences of their first three coordinates, and set $v_4=v_1+v_2-v_3$. Additivity of the patterns makes its quotient the required fourth difference. This fixed balanced translation carries one pattern class bijectively to the other among all additive quadruples. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:78:lem:boundary} makes their counts in the box differ by $o(E_N)$.

There are $|P|^3$ additive patterns, and their counts sum to $E_N$. Since the number of patterns is fixed, each count must be \eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:pattern-count}. For a fixed difference $v$, choose $p_3,p_2$ freely, then put $p_1=p_3+v$ and $p_4=p_2+v$. Thus exactly $|P|^2$ patterns have that difference. Summing their counts gives \eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:difference-count}. No homomorphic section of $\pi$ was assumed.
\end{proof}
These are relative-energy statements for the explicitly chosen boxes. They do not follow merely from ordinary pointwise equidistribution, and no claim about arbitrary F\o lner sequences is needed.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A nonzero grid obstruction forces a gap\srctag{78}}]{A nonzero grid obstruction forces a gap}\label{gsr:en:78:sec:d7}\label{gsr:en:78:sec:obstruction}
\srcnote{78}{Section 7}
\begin{proposition}[The obstruction estimate]\label{gsr:en:78:prop:obstruction}
Assume \eqref{gsr:fm:78:eq:P}. If the element $s$ of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:78:lem:grid} is nonzero for some $h,k$, then $\rind(a)\le5/8$. If $s$ has order four, the proof gives the stronger bound $\rind(a)\le11/32$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Let $q=\ord(s)\in\{2,4\}$ and $L=\langle h,k\rangle$. Any relation $ih+jk=0$ forces $js=0$ by the first formula in \eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:grid-derivatives}, on comparing its value at that point with its value at zero. The second formula similarly gives $is=0$. Thus $q$ divides both $i,j$, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:grid-quotient}
 \pi:L\longrightarrow(\Z/q\Z)^2,\qquad
 \pi(ih+jk)=(i,j)\pmod q
\end{equation}
is well defined and surjective. Other relations in $L$ cause no problem.

Write an additive quadruple uniquely as $(x+g,y,x,y+g)$, and its target defect as
\[
 D=a(x+g)+a(y)-a(x)-a(y+g).
\]
Restrict to the difference class $\pi(g)=(i,j)$. The balanced translation $(2h,0,2h,0)$ changes the defect by
\[
 \Delta_{2h}a(x+g)-\Delta_{2h}a(x)=js,
\]
using \eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:grid-derivatives}. The translation $(2k,0,2k,0)$ changes it by $-is$. Both translations preserve $g$ itself, and therefore preserve the difference class. Fixed combinations of these two translations realize all elements of
\[
 C_{i,j}=\langle is,js\rangle\le H,
 \qquad d_{i,j}:=|C_{i,j}|=\frac q{\gcd(q,i,j)}.
\]
Each such translation maps the defect-zero subfamily bijectively to the specified defect-$c$ subfamily among all quadruples of the difference class. Their counts in $B_N^4$ consequently differ by $o(E_N)$, by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:78:lem:boundary}. These $d_{i,j}$ defect classes are disjoint. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:78:lem:patterns} therefore bounds the respected count in this difference class by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:class-bound}
 \frac1{d_{i,j}}\frac{E_N}{q^2}+o(E_N).
\end{equation}
Summing over the fixed $q^2$ difference classes and dividing by $E_N$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:obstruction-average}
 \limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{\Ea(\ind_{B_N})}{E_N}
 \le\frac1{q^2}\sum_{i,j\bmod q}\frac1{d_{i,j}}.
\end{equation}
For $q=2$, there is one class with $d=1$ and three with $d=2$, giving
\[
 \frac{1+3/2}{4}=\frac58.
\]
For $q=4$, there is one with $d=1$, three with $d=2$, and twelve with $d=4$, giving
\[
 \frac{1+3/2+12/4}{16}=\frac{11}{32}.
\]
Every $B_N$ is a genuine finite subset of the original subgroup $L\le G$. Restriction gives the claimed infimum bounds. If $L$ is finite, all counting errors vanish and its full indicator satisfies the same bound. If $L$ is infinite, the conclusion is an infimum bound; exact finite attainment at that limiting number is not asserted.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Removing a common homomorphism without division\srctag{78}}]{Removing a common homomorphism without division}\label{gsr:en:78:sec:d8}\label{gsr:en:78:sec:pushout}
\srcnote{78}{Section 8}
Assume \eqref{gsr:fm:78:eq:P} and $\rind(a)>5/8$. Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:78:prop:obstruction} forces every base-zero grid obstruction to vanish. Since $s=P_1-P_0$, its vanishing says precisely
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:common-derivative}
 \Delta_{2h}a(k)=\Delta_{2h}a(0)\qquad(h,k\in G).
\end{equation}
Subtract $a(0)$, preserving all energy ratios, and write the normalized map again as $a$.

\begin{lemma}[The homomorphism on the doubling subgroup]\label{gsr:en:78:lem:2G}
There is a homomorphism $\psi:2G\to H$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:2G-law}
 \psi(z)=a(z),\qquad a(x+z)=a(x)+\psi(z)\quad(x\in G,\ z\in2G).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Every $z\in2G$ equals $2h$ for some $h$. Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:common-derivative} and $a(0)=0$ give $a(x+z)-a(x)=a(z)$. The definition $\psi(z)=a(z)$ therefore makes no choice of a half of $z$ and is unambiguous. Taking $x,z\in2G$ proves its additivity directly.
\end{proof}
The next construction is the standard pushout of $2G\hookrightarrow G$ and $\psi$; we prove the needed facts explicitly~\cite{stacks}. It extends a homomorphism by enlarging its target, rather than assuming an extension into $H$ exists.

\begin{lemma}[An injective target enlargement]\label{gsr:en:78:lem:pushout}
Set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:pushout}
 H'=(H\oplus G)/J,\qquad J=\{(-\psi(z),z):z\in2G\}.
\end{equation}
Then $\iota:H\to H'$, $\iota(u)=[(u,0)]$, is injective, and $\phi:G\to H'$, $\phi(x)=[(0,x)]$, is a homomorphism extending $\iota\psi$ on $2G$. The formula
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:residual}
 b(x+2G)=\iota(a(x))-\phi(x)
\end{equation}
defines a map $b:G/2G\to H'$ with $b(0)=0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The set $J$ is already a subgroup, because $\psi$ is a homomorphism. If $(u,0)\in J$, equality of the second coordinates forces $z=0$, and equality of the first then forces $u=0$. This proves injectivity. The map $\phi$ is visibly a homomorphism, and
\[
 [(0,z)]=[(\psi(z),0)]\qquad(z\in2G),
\]
so it extends $\iota\psi$. On replacing $x$ by $x+z$ in \eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:residual}, equation~\eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:2G-law} adds $\iota\psi(z)$ to the first term and $\phi(z)=\iota\psi(z)$ to the second. Thus the difference is well defined on the quotient. Its value at zero is zero.
\end{proof}
On any additive quadruple in $G$, the $\phi$ contributions cancel. Since $\iota$ is injective, equality of the original target sums is equivalent to equality of the residual target sums. In particular both equality and inequality are preserved. This is the exact reason that enlarging the target does not lose the energy information.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Transferring quotient planes and descending structure\srctag{78}}]{Transferring quotient planes and descending structure}\label{gsr:en:78:sec:d9}\label{gsr:en:78:sec:completion}
\srcnote{78}{Section 9}
The quotient $V=G/2G$ is a vector space over $\F_2$. The map $b$ in \eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:residual} therefore fits Section~\ref{gsr:en:78:sec:elementary}, but its bad-plane conclusion must first be transferred to actual finite subsets of $G$.

\begin{lemma}[Transfer from a quotient plane]\label{gsr:en:78:lem:plane-transfer}
Let $v+W\subseteq V$ be a four-point affine plane, with $\dim W=2$. There are a two-generated subgroup $L\le G$, a translate $z+L$, and finite boxes $B_N\subseteq L$ as in \eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:boxes} for which
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:plane-transfer}
 \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{\Ea(\ind_{z+B_N})}{\Eadd(\ind_{z+B_N})}
 =\frac{\mathcal E_{b|_{v+W}}(\ind_{v+W})}{64}.
\end{equation}
If $L$ is finite, the equality is exact for its full coset indicator.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Lift $v$ to $z\in G$ and a basis of $W$ to $h,k\in G$. Put $L=\langle h,k\rangle$; the quotient map $\pi:L\to W$ is surjective. Its kernel is $L\cap2G$, which need not equal $2L$, and no such equality is required.

Translate the boxes of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:78:lem:boundary} by $z$. Domain additivity is preserved because both sums gain $2z$. On additive quadruples, the homomorphism $\phi$ cancels, so respectedness is exactly the corresponding relation between the four residual values in $v+W$. There are $|W|^3=64$ additive quotient patterns. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:78:lem:patterns} says each has $E_N/64+o(E_N)$ additive lifts. Summing those counts over precisely the respected quotient patterns proves \eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:plane-transfer}. In the finite case there is no error.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:78:thm:P}]
It suffices to show that \eqref{gsr:fm:78:eq:P} together with $\rind(a)>5/8$ forces one of the first two structural classes. Propositions~\ref{gsr:en:78:prop:obstruction} and Lemmas~\ref{gsr:en:78:lem:2G}--\ref{gsr:en:78:lem:pushout} give the normalized residual map $b:V\to H'$. By Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:78:lem:plane-transfer}, a quotient plane of ratio at most $5/8$ would imply $\rind(a)\le5/8$, a contradiction. Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:78:thm:elementary} therefore makes $b$ affine or of index-two form. This also covers $\dim V\le1$, with no plane to transfer.

If $b$ is affine, its normalization $b(0)=0$ makes it a homomorphism. Thus
\[
 \iota a=\phi+b\circ q,\qquad q:G\to G/2G,
\]
is a homomorphism. Injectivity of $\iota$ implies that the normalized $a$ is a homomorphism into the original target $H$.

Otherwise let $\overline K\le V$ be the hyperplane supplied by the elementary-two theorem and put $K=q^{-1}(\overline K)$. On $\overline K$, the normalized $b$ is a homomorphism, and on its other coset it has the same homomorphism plus one offset. Consequently $\iota(a|_K)$ is a homomorphism, and for $t\notin K$, $k\in K$,
\[
 \iota(a(t+k))=\iota(a(t))+\iota(a(k)).
\]
Injectivity descends both conclusions to $H$: $\psi=a|_K$ is a homomorphism and $a(t+k)=a(t)+\psi(k)$.

The defect is nonzero in the original target as well. If $\overline u=b(q(t))$, then $2\overline u\ne0$ by Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:78:thm:elementary}, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:nonzero-descent}
 \iota\bigl(2a(t)-a(2t)\bigr)=2\overline u\ne0.
\end{equation}
Indeed $q(2t)=0$, $b(0)=0$, and $\phi(2t)=2\phi(t)$. Thus $u=a(t)$ and $\eta=2u-\psi(2t)$ give the required nonzero defect. Restoring $\beta=a(0)$ yields \eqref{gsr:fm:78:eq:family-main}. This proves the dichotomy above $5/8$; its contrapositive is the asserted third-case bound. Sharpness is Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:78:prop:sharp}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:78:thm:classification}]
If \eqref{gsr:fm:78:eq:P} fails, Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:78:lem:cyclic} gives \eqref{gsr:fm:78:eq:universal-witness}. If \eqref{gsr:fm:78:eq:P} holds and $a$ is outside the first two structural classes, Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:78:thm:P} gives $\rind(a)\le5/8$. Since $5/8<19/27$, the defining approximation property of an infimum gives a finite indicator with ratio strictly less than $19/27$. Thus the third conclusion is an actual finite witness, even though the intermediate $5/8$ conclusion may be only a limit.

The first class has both infima one, while Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:78:cor:index-two} gives both infima $3/4$ in the nonzero-defect class. The three alternatives are disjoint because $19/27<3/4<1$. Finally $r(a)\le\rind(a)$ excludes weighted endpoint $3/4$ in the third class. This proves both endpoint classifications.
\end{proof}

\subsection{An intrinsic and unique index-two subgroup}
\begin{corollary}[Canonical kernel and defect]\label{gsr:en:78:cor:canonical}
For a nonaffine endpoint map, define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:canonical-defect}
 J_a(x)=a(2x)-2a(x)+a(0).
\end{equation}
Then $J_a$ takes exactly the two values $0,-\eta$, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:canonical-kernel}
 K=\{x:J_a(x)=0\}
\end{equation}
is the unique index-two subgroup for which $a$ has form \eqref{gsr:fm:78:eq:family-main}. Its normalized homomorphism is $\psi(k)=a(k)-a(0)$. The nonzero defect $\eta$ is independent of the choice of $t\notin K$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
In that form $a(0)=\beta$. For $k\in K$,
\[
 J_a(k)=\psi(2k)-2\psi(k)=0.
\]
For $x=t+k$,
\[
 J_a(t+k)=\psi(2t)+2\psi(k)-2u-2\psi(k)=-\eta.
\]
Since $\eta\ne0$, the zero set is exactly $K$. Any other representation has the same intrinsic zero set, proving uniqueness. Replacing $t$ by $t+k_0$ changes $u$ by $\psi(k_0)$ and $\psi(2t)$ by $2\psi(k_0)$, leaving the defect unchanged.
\end{proof}
In particular, the endpoint character $\pi:G\to\F_2$ with kernel $K$ is intrinsic. The criterion is a theorem about maps already known to be endpoint maps: an arbitrary map with a two-valued diagonal defect still needs its common-homomorphism law checked.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Finite attainment for every hereditary endpoint map\srctag{78}}]{Finite attainment for every hereditary endpoint map}\label{gsr:en:78:sec:d10}\label{gsr:en:78:sec:attainment}
\srcnote{78}{Section 10}
Report~289 proved the following fixed-weight and existential criteria for the division-free family~\cite[Theorem 1.2 and Sections 3--4]{srcseventyseven}. Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:78:thm:classification} removes the family restriction when the hypothesis is that the \emph{hereditary infimum} equals $3/4$. It does not assert that every map having one weight of ratio $3/4$ is an endpoint map; a map with a smaller infimum can also have such a weight.

\begin{corollary}[Complete endpoint attainment criteria]\label{gsr:en:78:cor:attainment}
Suppose $r(a)=3/4$, equivalently $\rind(a)=3/4$, and let $K$ and $\pi:G\to\F_2$ be its canonical subgroup and character. For any nonzero nonnegative finite weight $w$, put $e=w\ind_K$ and $o=w\ind_{G\setminus K}$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:equality-convolution}
 \frac{\Ea(w)}{\Eadd(w)}=\frac34\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad e*e=o*o.
\end{equation}
To state the spectral version, choose $x_0\in\supp w$, translate $w$ to $w_0$ on
\[
 L=\langle\supp w-\supp w\rangle\cong\Z^d\oplus T,
 \qquad T=\Tor(L),
\]
and let $S\subseteq\widehat T$ be the union of the Fourier supports of the finite torsion fibers $v\mapsto w_0(n,v)$, over all free coordinates $n\in\Z^d$. Put $\varepsilon=(-1)^{\pi|_T}$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:78:eq:equality-spectrum}
 \frac{\Ea(w)}{\Eadd(w)}=\frac34\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 S\cap(S\varepsilon)=\varnothing.
\end{equation}
Moreover, the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
 \item some nonzero nonnegative finite weight attains $3/4$;
 \item some nonempty finite indicator attains $3/4$;
 \item $G\setminus K$ contains a finite-order element;
 \item $\pi|_{\Tor(G)}$ is nontrivial.
\end{enumerate}
For a particular attaining weight, $\pi|_{\Tor(L)}$ must already be nontrivial. This necessary local torsion condition alone is not sufficient for that weight.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:78:thm:classification} puts $a$ in the nonzero-defect family, with the canonical $K$ of Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:78:cor:canonical}. The fixed-weight convolution criterion, its equivalent pair-free torsion-spectrum formulation, and the existential torsion dichotomy are exactly the cited results of Report~289 for this family. Their hypotheses permit arbitrary abelian $G,H$ and arbitrary finite nonnegative weights, so they apply without any further restriction.

For clarity, the role of the spectral condition is independent of the choice of splitting. Writing
\[
 P_\chi(z)=\sum_n\left(\sum_{v\in T}w_0(n,v)\chi(v)\right)z^n
\]
gives $S=\{\chi:P_\chi\not\equiv0\}$. The signed convolution equation becomes
\[
 P_\chi(z)P_{\chi\varepsilon}(\lambda z)\equiv0
 \quad(\chi\in\widehat T),
\]
where $\lambda$ is the restriction of the parity sign to the free factor. The Laurent polynomial ring over $\C$ is an integral domain and sign substitution is an automorphism, so this is precisely \eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:equality-spectrum}. The intrinsic convolution criterion makes its truth splitting-independent.

Nonnegativity implies $P_1\not\equiv0$, so the spectral criterion forces $\varepsilon\ne1$, proving the necessary local torsion statement and the necessity in the existential criterion. Conversely, a finite-order element outside $K$ has even order; the full indicator of its cyclic subgroup has ratio $3/4$ by Section~\ref{gsr:en:78:subsec:cyclic-endpoint}. Finally finite-order elements are exactly the elements of $\Tor(G)$, proving the last equivalence.
\end{proof}

This completes the conceptual link between the two reports without changing Report~289. Its theorem was stated for a specified family, and remains valid in that scope; the present classification proves that every hereditary endpoint map belongs to that family. Quantitative positive-gap estimates from Report~289 likewise apply whenever its stated local torsion hypothesis is satisfied. No new optimal weighted-support constant is asserted here.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Examples and limits of the conclusions\srctag{78}}]{Examples and limits of the conclusions}\label{gsr:en:78:sec:d11}\label{gsr:en:78:sec:examples}
\srcnote{78}{Section 11}
\begin{proposition}[Sharpness of the universal indicator cutoff]\label{gsr:en:78:prop:C3lower}
For $a:C_3\to\Z$ defined by $a(j)=j$ for $j=0,1,2$, one has $\rind(a)=19/27$. Consequently $19/27$ is the optimal universal indicator upper bound for the third class.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The full domain has ordinary energy $27$ and respected energy equal to the integer-interval energy $1+4+9+4+1=19$. Every proper nonempty subset has at most two points. For two distinct points of $C_3$, the three unordered pair sums are distinct, so every additive quadruple compares the same unordered pair and is respected. All proper-subset ratios are therefore one. This proves the indicator infimum. The map is nonaffine, and $C_3$ has no index-two subgroup, so it lies in the third class.
\end{proof}
The same map with weights $(1,2/3,1)$ has respected energy $934/81$ and ordinary energy $1366/81$, hence ratio $467/683<19/27$. Thus its indicator extremality does not prove weighted sharpness.

Several further examples separate the theorem's hypotheses and quantifiers.
\begin{enumerate}
 \item \textbf{An extension into the original target may fail.} On $C_4\to C_2$, the values $0,0,1,1$ have endpoint $3/4$. The common homomorphism on $K=\{0,2\}$ sends $2$ to $1$, while every homomorphism $C_4\to C_2$ sends $2$ to zero. Thus replacing the division-free form with a homomorphism on all of $G$ plus a scalar parity term would lose valid endpoint maps.
 \item \textbf{The endpoint need not be attained.} Integer-valued parity on $\Z$ has exact infima $3/4$, but every finite-weight ratio is strictly larger. This is consistent with the torsion criterion, since $\Z$ has no nonzero finite-order element.
 \item \textbf{The equation alone does not give endpoint structure.} The quadratic map $st:\F_2^2\to\F_2$ satisfies \eqref{gsr:fm:78:eq:P} automatically and has exact infima $5/8$. The order-four model \eqref{gsr:en:78:eq:order-four-example} gives a different obstruction. An energy hypothesis is essential when eliminating these possibilities.
 \item \textbf{Local torsion matters for a prescribed weight.} Take $G=C_2\oplus\Z$ with parity from $C_2$. An attaining weight exists on the order-two subgroup. But a weight on $\{(0,0),(1,1),(0,2)\}$ has torsion-free support-difference group and cannot attain. Conversely, on $C_4$, the indicator of $\{0,1\}$ has ratio one although its differences generate a parity-nontrivial torsion group. Existence and fixed-weight attainment have different criteria.
 \item \textbf{Uniform acceptance is a different hypothesis.} Modifying one value of an affine map on a finite group of order $N$ can spoil at most $4/N$ of uniformly sampled additive quadruples, by the union bound on the four coordinates. Such maps may be nonaffine while full-group acceptance tends to one. The main theorem tests every finite indicator, rather than only the full-group average.
\end{enumerate}
The classification asserts equality $r=\rind$ only in its first two classes. It does not identify the relationship between the two infima below the universal gap. Nor does a sharp full-indicator estimate for one small group determine the global subthreshold spectrum.
