\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Completion of the theorem and consequences\srctag{80}}]{Completion of the theorem and consequences}\label{gsr:en:80:sec:d8}\label{gsr:en:80:sec:completion}
\srcnote{80}{Section 8}
We now assemble the geometric and analytic parts, including the low-rank cases.

If $\dim V=0$, the domain consists of one point. Every map is affine, and every admissible weight has ratio one. The line and plane conditions are vacuous and consistent with the conclusion.

If $\dim V=1$, the whole domain is a three-point line. Failure of the arithmetic-progression condition gives ratio $5/9$ by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:80:lem:line}. Otherwise choose an affine ordering and write
\[
 a(x_0+rt)=\beta+ru,\qquad r\in\{0,1,2\}.
\]
If $3u=0$, this is affine; if $3u\ne0$, it is a cut with $K=\{0\}$. There are no affine planes in this dimension, so a plane-only condition would be vacuous and false as a characterization.

For dimension at least two, Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:81:prop:gluing} says that an outside-family global map has an outside-family plane restriction. Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:80:prop:plane} supplies one of the three listed indicator witnesses on that plane. By~\eqref{gsr:en:80:eq:restriction}, the energies are unchanged in the ambient group. This proves Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:80:thm:witness} in every rank. Extending the local weighted witnesses by zero also proves Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:80:thm:weighted-witness}; in rank one the line witness already has the smaller ratio $5/9$.

Affine maps respect every additive quadruple, so their ratio is one for every weight. Section~\ref{gsr:en:81:sec:analytic} proves that cuts have ratio infimum $\rho>c>5/8>\gamma$. Thus condition~(i) of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:80:thm:main} implies~(ii). The weighted obstruction theorem gives~(ii)$\Rightarrow$(i), including the equivalent threshold $5/8$. Also (i)$\Rightarrow$(iii) because every indicator ratio is at least the weighted infimum, and Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:80:thm:witness} gives~(iii)$\Rightarrow$(i). Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:81:prop:gluing}, the restriction argument for lines, and the low-rank discussion establish (i)$\Leftrightarrow$(iv). This completes the main classification and both obstruction theorems.

\subsection{The strict quantifier is handled by structure}
A pointwise assertion that every individual test has ratio greater than a number does not ordinarily imply that the infimum is strictly greater than that number. The implication (iii)$\Rightarrow$(ii) does not make that invalid inference. It first uses finite witnesses to obtain the structural classification, and then obtains the uniform lower bound $\rho>c$ from the classified formulas.

Indeed, the proof gives the stronger implication
\[
 \bigl[R_a(S)>c\text{ for all nonempty }|S|\le9\bigr]
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \bigl[\Ea(f)\ge\rho\EaddV(f)\text{ for all finite }f\ge0\bigr].
\]
The passage from finitely many points per local test to all finite weights is mathematical content, not an exchange of an infimum with a strict inequality.

\begin{corollary}[The upper weighted spectrum]\label{gsr:en:80:cor:spectrum}
For arbitrary $V$ over $\F_3$ and abelian $H$,
\[
 r(a)\in[0,\gamma]\cup\{\rho,1\}.
\]
Moreover $r(a)=1$ exactly for affine maps, and $r(a)=\rho$ exactly for translated nonaffine index-three cuts.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Any value above $\gamma$ belongs to the two classified families, whose exact values are $1$ and $\rho$. Conversely those families have the indicated values. They are disjoint because $3u\ne0$ makes a transversal nonaffine.
\end{proof}
This corollary is confined to elementary abelian three-group domains. It does not settle the equality classification for arbitrary abelian source groups in Report~291.

\begin{corollary}[A finite small-integer recognition test]\label{gsr:en:80:cor:integer}
Membership in the two families is equivalent to the assertion that every nonzero weight supported on at most nine points, with positive values in $\{5,8\}$, has ratio greater than $\eta$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Family maps have all ratios at least $\rho>\eta$. An outside-family map has an integer-weight certificate with ratio at most $\eta$ by Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:80:thm:weighted-witness}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Targets without two-torsion]\label{gsr:en:80:cor:no-two}
If $H$ has no nonzero element of order two, every outside-family map has a three-point indicator witness of ratio $5/9$ or a nine-point plane witness of ratio at most $49/81$. In particular $r(a)\le\rind(a)\le49/81$ outside the two families. No optimality is asserted for this improved bound.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:80:lem:hist} makes the $Q_h=53$ branch impossible. The remaining plane branches are the failed line test, the all-low full-plane test, or a constant derivative giving a family map. The same gluing and low-rank arguments transfer the witnesses to $V$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Targets annihilated by three]\label{gsr:en:80:cor:three-target}
If $3H=0$, every nonaffine map has a three-point indicator witness of ratio $5/9$. The uniform outside-affine bound $5/9$ is sharp both for $r$ and for $\rind$, already for a map $C_3\to C_3$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
In this target, a midpoint relation on a line is equivalent to the sum of its three values being zero. Hence if every line passes the progression test, every such sum vanishes. Put $g=a-a(0)$. A line through zero gives $g(-x)=-g(x)$. For distinct $x,y$, the third point of their line is $-x-y$, so the zero-sum identity gives $g(x+y)=g(x)+g(y)$. For $x=y$, this follows from $g(2x)=g(-x)=-g(x)=2g(x)$. The case $x=y=0$ is immediate. Thus $g$ is a homomorphism and $a$ is affine. By contraposition a nonaffine map has a failed line, whose indicator ratio is $5/9$.

For sharpness, take the map $C_3\to C_3$ with values $(0,0,1)$. It fails every midpoint relation. For nonnegative weights $(x,y,z)\ne(0,0,0)$, put
\[
 N=x^4+y^4+z^4+4(x^2y^2+y^2z^2+z^2x^2),
 \qquad P=xyz(x+y+z).
\]
The respected energy is $N$ and the ordinary energy is $N+4P$. The identities
\begin{align*}
 x^4+y^4+z^4+x^2y^2+y^2z^2+z^2x^2-2P
   &=(x^2-yz)^2+(y^2-zx)^2+(z^2-xy)^2,\\
 x^2y^2+y^2z^2+z^2x^2-P
   &=\tfrac12\bigl((xy-yz)^2+(yz-zx)^2+(zx-xy)^2\bigr)
\end{align*}
imply $N\ge5P$, and therefore $N/(N+4P)\ge5/9$. Equal positive weights attain $5/9$, so both infima are exactly $5/9$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{What the obstruction shapes do and do not say}
The bound of nine points is a universal sufficient witness bound, not a proof of minimal possible support. The six-point spike calculation explains why testing only the full indicator of each plane is too weak: the normalized spike has full-plane ratio $505/729>c$, but its two-line indicator has ratio exactly $53/81=c$. More generally, indicator witnesses and weighted minimizers perform different jobs. The obstruction theorem uses only indicators, while the family value $\rho$ is attained with an irrational middle weight.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The unrestricted minimum of an order two spike\srctag{81}}]{The unrestricted minimum of an order two spike}\label{gsr:en:81:sec:d2}\label{gsr:en:81:sec:spike}
\srcnote{81}{Section 2}
Write $G=\F_3^2$, and for this section let $a(0)=1$ and $a(x)=0$ for $x\ne0$, with values in $\Z/2\Z$. We prove the lower bound for nine independently varying nonnegative real weights, including all zero-coordinate boundary cases.

For real functions on $G$, use unnormalized convolution and inner product,
\[
 (v*w)(s)=\sum_xv(x)w(s-x),\qquad
 \langle v,w\rangle=\sum_xv(x)w(x).
\]
Then $\EaddV(f)=\norm{f*f}_2^2$. Write $f=t\delta_0+g$, with $t\ge0$, $g\ge0$ and $g(0)=0$. Define
\begin{align}
 S(g)&=\sum_xg(x)^2,& P(g)&=\sum_xg(x)g(-x),\notag\\
 A(g)&=4S(g)+2P(g),& B(g)&=\norm{g*g}_2^2,\label{gsr:en:81:eq:ABC}\\
 C(g)&=\langle g,g*g\rangle
       =\sum_{x,y}g(x)g(y)g(x+y).&&\notag
\end{align}
The same formulas define $A,B,C,S,P$ for arbitrary real, possibly signed functions.

\subsection{Separating the retained and lost energy}
A quadruple is respected by the spike if and only if its number of zero entries is even. No additive quadruple has exactly three zero entries and a fourth nonzero entry. The lost quadruples thus have exactly one zero entry. Expanding
\[
 f*f=t^2\delta_0+2tg+g*g
\]
and using $g(0)=0$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:NL}
 N:=\Ea(f)=t^4+t^2A(g)+B(g),\qquad
 L:=\EaddV(f)-\Ea(f)=4tC(g).
\end{equation}
In particular, $N+L=\EaddV(f)>0$, and $L\ge0$. The eventual inequality $N\ge\kappa_*L$ is equivalent to the desired ratio bound even when $L=0$.

\subsection{Centering all eight ordinary weights}
Let
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:center}
 b=1-\delta_0,\qquad m=\frac18\sum_{x\ne0}g(x),\qquad g=mb+h.
\end{equation}
Then $m\ge0$, $h(0)=0$, and $\sum_xh(x)=0$. The signed function $h$ records all seven independent deviations of the ordinary weights from their mean. No symmetry restriction has been imposed.

The identities
\[
 b*b=7\cdot1+\delta_0=:q,\qquad b*h=-h,\qquad
 \norm q_2^2=456
\]
imply
\begin{align}
 A(g)&=48m^2+A(h),\label{gsr:en:81:eq:centerA}\\
 C(g)&=56m^3-\tfrac12mA(h)+C(h),\label{gsr:en:81:eq:centerC}\\
 B(g)&=456m^4+m^2A(h)-4mC(h)+B(h).\label{gsr:en:81:eq:centerB}
\end{align}
Here are the mixed terms explicitly. Since $h(0)=\sum h=0$, the mixed terms in $S$ and $P$ vanish. Moreover,
\[
 \langle b,q\rangle=56,\quad \langle h,q\rangle=\langle b,h\rangle=0,
 \quad\langle b,h*h\rangle=-P(h),\quad
 \langle q,h*h\rangle=P(h).
\]
Substituting $g*g=m^2q-2mh+h*h$ yields~\eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:centerC} and~\eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:centerB}. Thus, for any real $\kappa$,
\begin{align}
 N-\kappa L={}&t^4+48t^2m^2+456m^4-224\kappa tm^3\notag\\
 &+A(h)(t^2+m^2+2\kappa tm)
       -4(m+\kappa t)C(h)+B(h).\label{gsr:en:81:eq:master}
\end{align}

\subsection{A centered Fourier inequality}
\begin{lemma}\label{gsr:en:81:lem:centered}
For every real $h:G\to\R$ with $h(0)=0$ and $\sum_xh(x)=0$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:centered-lemma}
 C(h)^2\le\frac19A(h)B(h).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Use
\[
 \widehat h(\xi)=\sum_{x\in G}h(x)e^{-2\pi i\langle\xi,x\rangle/3}.
\]
Orthogonality gives inversion and Parseval with factor $1/9$, and convolution becomes multiplication. The zero coefficient vanishes. Since $h$ is real, the other eight coefficients form four conjugate pairs. Choose representatives $z_i=a_i+ib_i$, $1\le i\le4$. Inversion at zero gives $\sum_i a_i=0$.

Set
\[
 q_i=a_i^2+b_i^2,\quad X=\sum_i a_i^2,\quad R=\sum_iq_i,
 \quad T=\sum_iq_i^2,\quad U=\sum_i a_iq_i.
\]
The precise Fourier identities are
\begin{align}
 S(h)&=\tfrac29R,&P(h)&=\tfrac29(2X-R),\notag\\
 A(h)&=\tfrac49(2X+R),&B(h)&=\tfrac29T,&C(h)&=\tfrac29U.\label{gsr:en:81:eq:fourier-ABC}
\end{align}
For the cubic, Parseval gives $\frac19\sum_\xi\overline{\widehat h(\xi)}\widehat h(\xi)^2$, whose paired terms are $\frac29a_i|z_i|^2$. This uses the real part of $|z_i|^2z_i$, not the real part of $z_i^3$.

If $X=0$, then all $a_i=0$ and $U=C(h)=0$, proving the assertion. Otherwise $R\ge X>0$ and $T>0$. From $\sum_i a_i=0$ and Cauchy's inequality,
\[
 a_i^2\le3\sum_{j\ne i}a_j^2=3(X-a_i^2),\qquad a_i^2\le\tfrac34X.
\]
Also $b_i^2\le R-X$, so
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:Tbound}
 q_i\le R-\tfrac14X,
 \qquad T\le R(R-X/4).
\end{equation}
Centering the four numbers $q_i$ and using Cauchy's inequality again gives
\[
 U^2=\left[\sum_i a_i(q_i-R/4)\right]^2
 \le X\left(T-R^2/4\right).
\]
Consequently,
\begin{align*}
 \frac{C(h)^2}{A(h)B(h)}
 &=\frac{U^2}{2(2X+R)T}\\
 &\le\frac{X}{2(2X+R)}\left(1-\frac{R^2}{4T}\right)
 \le\frac{X(3R-X)}{2(2X+R)(4R-X)}\le\frac19.
\end{align*}
The middle step uses~\eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:Tbound} in the correct direction: at fixed $R$, the expression $1-R^2/(4T)$ increases with $T>0$. The last step follows from
\[
 2(2X+R)(4R-X)-9X(3R-X)=(R-X)(8R-5X)\ge0.
\]
All divided quantities are positive in the case under consideration.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A proved averaging inequality and its strictness}
For $t,m\ge0$ and $0\le\kappa\le3/2$, put
\[
 \alpha=t^2+m^2+2\kappa tm,\qquad \beta=m+\kappa t.
\]
The elementary estimate $|P(h)|\le S(h)$ shows
\[
 A(h)\ge2S(h)\ge0,
\]
with strict positivity when $h\ne0$. Also $B(h)\ge0$. Since $\beta\ge0$, Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:81:lem:centered} yields
\begin{align}
 A(h)\alpha-4\beta C(h)+B(h)
 &\ge A(h)\alpha-\tfrac43\beta\sqrt{A(h)B(h)}+B(h)\notag\\
 &=\left(\sqrt{B(h)}-\tfrac23\beta\sqrt{A(h)}\right)^2
     +A(h)q_\kappa(t,m),\label{gsr:en:81:eq:averaging}
\end{align}
where
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:q}
 q_\kappa(t,m)=\left(1-\frac49\kappa^2\right)t^2
             +\frac59m^2+\frac{10}{9}\kappa tm\ge0.
\end{equation}
If $m>0$ and $h\ne0$, this remainder is strictly positive, because $q_\kappa(t,m)\ge5m^2/9>0$. This proves the reduction to equal ordinary weights as an inequality for every signed deviation $h$. It is not an assumption that averaging improves a quotient, nor an assertion that averaging improves the cubic term separately.

\subsection{The scalar square factorization}
For $s>0$ define
\[
 F(s)=\frac{s^4+48s^2+456}{224s},\qquad
 F'(s)=\frac{3s^4+48s^2-456}{224s^2}.
\]
The numerator of $F'$ is strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$, starts negative and tends to infinity. Its unique zero is $s=u_*$, because $u_*^2=6\sqrt6-8$. Direct simplification gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:kappastar}
 F(u_*)=\kappa_*=\frac{u_*(u_*^2+24)}{56},\qquad
 0<\kappa_*\le F(2)=\frac{83}{56}<\frac32.
\end{equation}
This applicability check does not use the averaging inequality. In particular,~\eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:averaging} is available at $\kappa=\kappa_*$.

The root relation and the value in~\eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:kappastar} give
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:scalar-factorization}
 \begin{split}
 &t^4+48t^2m^2+456m^4-224\kappa_*tm^3\\
 &\hspace{8mm}=(t-u_*m)^2
       \bigl(t^2+2u_*tm+(3u_*^2+48)m^2\bigr).
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
Indeed, $3u_*^4+48u_*^2=456$ and $224\kappa_*=4u_*(u_*^2+24)$ make the coefficients agree. The second factor is positive on the closed quadrant $t,m\ge0$ except at $(0,0)$. Equations~\eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:master}, \eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:averaging} and~\eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:scalar-factorization} prove $N\ge\kappa_*L$ for every nonnegative weight.

\begin{proposition}[Exact spike minimum and all equality weights]\label{gsr:en:81:prop:spike}
For the order-two spike, $r(a)=\lambda$, and the weights attaining it are exactly~\eqref{gsr:fm:81:eq:minimizer} with $p=0$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Since $N+L>0$,
\[
 N\ge\kappa_*L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \frac{N}{N+L}\ge\frac{\kappa_*}{1+\kappa_*}=\lambda.
\]
If $m=0$, nonnegativity of $g$ gives $g=h=0$, and a nonzero weight is supported only at zero. If $t=0$, the spike is outside the support. In both cases $L=0$ and the ratio is $1$, so equality at $\lambda<1$ is impossible.

For equality, therefore, $t,m>0$. Strictness in~\eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:averaging} forces $h=0$, and~\eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:scalar-factorization} forces $t=u_*m$. Conversely these conditions make every remainder vanish. Thus the infimum is attained on exactly one positive scaling ray, with full support. There are no additional boundary or nonsymmetric minimizers.
\end{proof}
Target translation, addition of an affine map and affine source changes preserve every respected quadruple. Replacing $1\in\Z/2\Z$ by any nonzero element of order two therefore preserves this conclusion, as does moving the spike to any point.


\subsection{An explicit stability estimate for the weights}\label{gsr:en:81:sec:weight-stability}
Uniqueness can be strengthened quantitatively for this fixed plane map. This concerns perturbations of the weights, not a distance classification of arbitrary maps.

\begin{corollary}[Nonoptimal quantitative weight stability]\label{gsr:en:81:cor:stability}
Let $a$ be an affine-plus-order-two-spike map on $G$, with spike at $p$. Normalize $f\ge0$ by $\sum_xf(x)=1$, and put
\[
 f_*(p)=\frac{u_*}{u_*+8},\qquad f_*(x)=\frac1{u_*+8}\quad(x\ne p),
 \qquad c_*=1-\frac{4\kappa_*^2}{9}.
\]
Then, with the unnormalized Euclidean norm on the nine coordinates,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:weight-stability}
 \frac{\Ea(f)}{\EaddV(f)}-\lambda
 \ge\frac{2c_*}{65(1+\kappa_*)}\norm{f-f_*}_2^2.
\end{equation}
The coefficient is positive, approximately $0.0013440882$, and is not claimed optimal.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Translate $p$ to zero. In the notation above, $t+8m=1$. Direct radical simplification gives
\[
 \kappa_*^2=1+\frac{81\sqrt6}{196},\qquad
 c_*=\frac59-\frac{9\sqrt6}{49}.
\]
The bounds $2<\sqrt6<5/2$ give $0<c_*<1/2<5/9$. Combining~\eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:averaging} and~\eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:scalar-factorization}, and discarding the nonnegative square, gives
\[
 N-\kappa_*L\ge(t-u_*m)^2(t^2+m^2)
                    +2c_*\norm h_2^2(t^2+m^2).
\]
Here the scalar second factor is at least $t^2+m^2$, and $A(h)\ge2\norm h_2^2$. Since
\[
 1=(t+8m)^2\le65(t^2+m^2),
\]
we obtain
\[
 N-\kappa_*L\ge\frac{(t-u_*m)^2+2c_*\norm h_2^2}{65}.
\]
Write $t_*=u_* /(u_*+8)$ and $m_*=1/(u_*+8)$. Then
\[
 (t-u_*m)^2=\frac{(u_*+8)^2}{64}(t-t_*)^2
       \ge\frac98(t-t_*)^2,
\]
since $u_*>2$. Orthogonality of the mean and centered parts gives
\[
 \norm{f-f_*}_2^2=\frac98(t-t_*)^2+\norm h_2^2.
\]
Since $2c_*<1$, the last two displays give $N-\kappa_*L\ge(2c_*/65)\norm{f-f_*}_2^2$. Finally,
\[
 \frac{N}{N+L}-\lambda
 =\frac{N-\kappa_*L}{(1+\kappa_*)\EaddV(f)},\qquad
 0<\EaddV(f)\le\left(\sum_xf(x)\right)^4=1.
\]
This proves the estimate, including the boundary of the simplex; no coordinate was divided by.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Plane reductions and derivative histograms\srctag{81}}]{Plane reductions and derivative histograms}\label{gsr:en:81:sec:d3}\label{gsr:en:81:sec:reductions}
\srcnote{81}{Section 3}
We now prove the upper bound for an arbitrary map $a:G\to H$ on $G=\F_3^2$. A target relation is always manipulated as an equality in an abelian group. Torsion assumptions will be derived when needed, never imposed globally.

\subsection{Invariance and the three point test}
Subtracting an affine map preserves each respectedness condition: its pair sums agree whenever the source pair sums agree. An affine source bijection preserves the source equation as well, since a translation contributes the same twice-translated vector on each side. These operations preserve every energy ratio. If the respected quadruples of one map form a subset of those of another, its respected energy is no larger for every nonnegative weight.

For a full three-point affine line, $\EaddV(\ind)=27$. At each source sum, the ordered pairs consist of one diagonal pair and the two orderings of the other pair. Without a target collision the contribution is $1^2+2^2=5$; a collision adds $4$. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:line}
 \Ea(\ind)=15+4m,
\end{equation}
where $m$ is the number of true midpoint equalities among the three choices of midpoint. If $m=0$, this gives ratio $5/9$. Otherwise the three target values form an arithmetic progression in some ordering. For a cyclic three-point line this is equivalent to at least two of the three cyclic increments agreeing. This equivalence uses no division in $H$.

Until further notice, assume every line is such an arithmetic progression. We call this the \emph{linewise progression condition}.

\subsection{Constant directions and the histogram identity}
For $h\in G$ define
\[
 D_h(x)=a(x+h)-a(x),\qquad
 Q_h=\sum_{v\in H}|\{x:D_h(x)=v\}|^2.
\]
Only finitely many terms occur. The parameterization of additive quadruples as $(x+h,y,x,y+h)$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:histogram}
 \Ea(1_G)=\sum_{h\in G}Q_h=81+2\sum_{d}Q_d,\qquad
 \EaddV(1_G)=729,
\end{equation}
where $d$ ranges over four representatives of the nonzero directions modulo sign. Indeed $Q_0=81$, and $D_{-h}(x)=-D_h(x-h)$ gives $Q_{-h}=Q_h$.

\begin{lemma}[A constant derivative gives a favorable map]\label{gsr:en:81:lem:constant}
Under the linewise progression condition, if $D_h$ is constant for some nonzero direction $h$, then $a$ is affine or a translated index-three affine cut.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let the constant value be $v$, which may be zero. Summing around an $h$-cycle gives $3v=0$. With $K=\langle h\rangle$ and $\psi(jh)=jv$, one has $a(x+k)=a(x)+\psi(k)$ for all $k\in K$. Choose a transversal line. Its values can be ordered as $\beta,\beta+u,\beta+2u$. Every permutation of the three elements of $\F_3$ is affine, so a translated basepoint and an orientation of the transversal realize that order. The $K$-translation law now gives~\eqref{gsr:fm:81:eq:cut}. It is affine when $3u=0$ and a cut otherwise.
\end{proof}
Thus an outside-family map surviving the line test has no constant derivative in a nonzero direction. In particular, a derivative with constant value zero is excluded as well.

\begin{lemma}[The derivative multiplicity gap]\label{gsr:en:81:lem:histogram}
Under the linewise progression condition, every nonconstant $D_h$ satisfies $Q_h\le45$ or $Q_h=53$. In the latter case its values are $v$ at seven points and $v+\delta$ at two points on one $h$-parallel line, with $3v=0$, $\delta\ne0$, and $2\delta=0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The translation $x\mapsto x+h$ has three disjoint three-cycles. On each cycle the increments sum to zero and at least two agree. A multiplicity partition of nine with largest part at most six has square sum at most $6^2+3^2=45$. Thus a nonconstant partition with larger square sum must be $(8,1)$, $(7,2)$, or $(7,1,1)$.

Let $v$ be the dominant value. In the $(8,1)$ case, an untouched cycle gives $3v=0$, and the exceptional cycle gives $2v+u=0$, forcing $u=v$. In the $(7,1,1)$ case, exceptions on different cycles force the same contradiction; exceptions on the same cycle give three distinct increments there, contradicting the progression condition. For $(7,2)$, exceptions on different cycles are likewise impossible. Both occur on one cycle. The other cycles give $3v=0$, and the exceptional cycle gives $v+2u=0$. Hence $\delta=u-v$ is nonzero and $2\delta=0$, while $Q_h=7^2+2^2=53$.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A high derivative and its exact target branches\srctag{81}}]{A high derivative and its exact target branches}\label{gsr:en:81:sec:d4}\label{gsr:en:81:sec:high}
\srcnote{81}{Section 4}
Suppose some $Q_h=53$. Subtract the directional homomorphism with slope $v$ from Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:81:lem:histogram}. Two parallel rows become constant, and the third row has two equal values and one value differing by $\delta$. After source and target translations, write the array as
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:high-normal}
 \begin{matrix}0&0&0\\ b&b&b\\ c&c&c+\delta\end{matrix},
 \qquad \delta\ne0,\quad2\delta=0.
\end{equation}
Each transversal line has values $(0,b,c)$ or $(0,b,c+\delta)$. For $(0,b,z)$ the three midpoint alternatives are
\[
 z=-b,\qquad z=2b,\qquad b=2z.
\]
The third is identical for $z=c$ and $z=c+\delta$. If it holds, $b=2c$. If it fails, the first two alternatives must hold in opposite order, since the same one for both triples would force $\delta=0$. Thus these three possibly overlapping branches exhaust every target:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:high-branches}
 \begin{array}{ll}
 \mathrm{I}:&b=2c,\\
 \mathrm{II}:&c=-b,\quad\delta=3b,\\
 \mathrm{III}:&c=2b,\quad\delta=-3b.
 \end{array}
\end{equation}

\subsection{The spike branch and the generic strict case}
In branch I interchange rows $1$ and $2$, an affine source permutation. With integer row labels $j=0,1,2$, the map becomes
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:row-spike}
 a(i,j)=jc+\varepsilon(i,j)\delta,
\end{equation}
where $\varepsilon$ is $1$ at a single point $p$ of row $1$ and $0$ elsewhere. Put $d=3c$. For two source-equal pairs, the difference of their integer row sums is $3k$, with $k\in\{-1,0,1\}$. The target-sum difference is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:km}
 kd+m\delta,
\end{equation}
where $m$ is the difference in their numbers of occurrences of $p$.

If $d=0$, the row baseline is a homomorphism, and respectedness is exactly the spike parity condition. Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:81:prop:spike} gives $r(a)=\lambda$ and all minimizing weights.

If $d\notin\{0,\delta\}$,~\eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:km} is zero exactly when $k=0$ and $m$ is even. For $k=\pm1$, an equality would force $d\in\{0,\delta\}$. Thus respectedness is contained in that of the pure spike. Its optimal positive weight already gives a ratio at most $\lambda$. We record a stronger full-indicator count, needed for a uniform separated remainder:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:generic361}
 \Ea(1_G)=361,\qquad\frac{\Ea(1_G)}{\EaddV(1_G)}=\frac{361}{729}.
\end{equation}
To verify the numerator without a bounded-target sample, count integer pair row sums separately, since $k=0$ is required. For row sums $0$ and $4$, there are three pairs at each of three horizontal sums, all of even spike parity, giving $27$ each. For row sums $1$ and $3$, the row types are $(0,1),(1,0)$ or $(1,2),(2,1)$. At each horizontal sum their parity classes have sizes $4$ and $2$, giving $3(4^2+2^2)=60$ each.

At integer row sum $2$, pair types $(0,2),(2,0)$ supply six even-parity pairs at each horizontal sum. Type $(1,1)$ supplies three more even pairs at sum $2p$, because the pair $(p,p)$ uses the spike twice. At each other horizontal sum it supplies one even pair and two odd pairs. The contribution is therefore $9^2+2(7^2+2^2)=187$. Summing gives $27+60+187+60+27=361$, equivalently $87+87+187$ by source row sum modulo three.

If $d=\delta$, let $v'=c+\delta$. Then $3v'=0$. Subtracting the row homomorphism $j\mapsto jv'$ leaves $\delta$ at the two nonexceptional points of row $1$, and zero elsewhere. This is a two-point binary coloring. Put weight $2$ on its containing line and weight $1$ elsewhere. Direct pair counting gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:two-witness}
 \Ea(f)=1330,\qquad\EaddV(f)=2322,
 \qquad\frac{\Ea(f)}{\EaddV(f)}=\frac{665}{1161}.
\end{equation}

\subsection{The two cross branches}
Branches II and III give $6b=0$. The slope $-2b$ therefore defines a row homomorphism. Subtracting it leaves, respectively,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:crosspatterns}
 \begin{matrix}0&0&0\\1&1&1\\1&1&0\end{matrix}
 \qquad\hbox{or}\qquad
 \begin{matrix}0&0&0\\1&1&1\\0&0&1\end{matrix},
\end{equation}
where $1$ denotes the actual nonzero order-two element $\delta$. These are line-plus-point colorings or their complements after an affine source change. Put weight $1$ on the first two rows and weight $2$ on the last row. Both patterns have
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:cross-witness}
 \Ea(f)=1354,\qquad\EaddV(f)=2322,
 \qquad\frac{\Ea(f)}{\EaddV(f)}=\frac{677}{1161}.
\end{equation}
For~\eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:two-witness} and~\eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:cross-witness}, the counts can be obtained by grouping all ordered pairs first by source sum and then by target sum; the energy is the sum of squares of the resulting pair weights. The public integer companion independently checks these counts by both ordered-pair grouping and all $729$ ordered source quadruples. Only the two actual target values $0,\delta$ occur after normalization, and $\delta\ne0$, so no additional target relation changes these counts.

\subsection{The explicit spike witness}
For clarity, the spike weight with value $t$ at $p$ and $1$ elsewhere has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:spikepoly}
 \Ea(f)=t^4+48t^2+456,
 \qquad\EaddV(f)=t^4+48t^2+456+224t.
\end{equation}
This also follows from~\eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:NL} with $g=b$. The unique positive minimum of this one-variable quotient occurs at $t=u_*$, by~\eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:kappastar}. The unrestricted lower proof was essential: this one-variable computation alone would not establish that arbitrary nonsymmetric weights have ratio at least $\lambda$.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{All low derivative cases\srctag{81}}]{All low derivative cases}\label{gsr:en:81:sec:d5}\label{gsr:en:81:sec:low}
\srcnote{81}{Section 5}
Assume now there is no $Q_h=53$, and no derivative is constant in a nonzero direction. If some $Q_h=45$, its multiplicity partition must be $(6,3)$. Indeed largest part at most five gives at most $5^2+4^2=41$, and Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:81:lem:histogram} has excluded the larger parts. Write its values as $v$ six times and $u$ three times, with $u\ne v$.

On each of the three parallel cycles let $k$ count occurrences of $u$. The three counts sum to three, so their unordered list is $(0,0,3)$, $(0,1,2)$, or $(1,1,1)$. The mixed list is impossible: its $k=0$ cycle gives $3v=0$, and its $k=1$ cycle gives $2v+u=0$, hence $u=v$. Exactly two cases remain:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{\Alph*.}]
\item two all-$v$ cycles and one all-$u$ cycle, with $3v=3u=0$;
\item each cycle has increments $(v,v,u)$ in some cyclic order, where $u=-2v$ and $3v\ne0$.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Case A and its order nine target}
Subtracting the homomorphism with slope $v$ leaves constant rows $0,b$ and a row with value set $\{c,c+\delta,c+2\delta\}$, where $\delta=u-v$ has exact order three. Every one of these three distinct values $z$ satisfies one of
\[
 z=-b,\qquad z=2b,\qquad2z=b.
\]
Each alternative covers at most one of the three values. For the third this follows because multiplication by two is injective on a coset of an order-three subgroup. Thus the three alternatives must cover three different values. In particular $-b$ and $2b$ are distinct in the same $\delta$-coset, so $3b=\pm\delta$ and $b$ has exact order nine.

Write a member of that coset as $-b+k(3b)$, with $k$ taken modulo three. The equation $2z=b$ gives $2k=1$ modulo three, so $k=2$ and $z=5b$. With $q=5b$ one has $b=2q$ and $q$ of exact order nine. After an affine horizontal coordinate change the array is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:order9}
 \begin{matrix}0&0&0\\2&2&2\\1&4&7\end{matrix}
 \quad\hbox{in the subgroup }\langle q\rangle\cong\Z/9\Z.
\end{equation}
Every permutation of three horizontal coordinates is affine and leaves the other two constant rows unchanged. The four $Q$-values of~\eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:order9} are $(45,33,33,33)$, giving
\[
 \frac{\Ea(1_G)}{729}=\frac{81+2(45+33+33+33)}{729}=\frac{41}{81}.
\]
The exact order-nine conclusion matters: a further target quotient cannot collapse this pattern while retaining $\delta\ne0$.

\subsection{Case B and the alignment dichotomy}
Each row is, in cyclic order and up to a row constant, $(0,v,2v)$, with one exceptional edge of increment $-2v$. The edge is unique since $3v\ne0$. Let $e_j\in\F_3$ be its tail coordinate in row $j$. If the function $j\mapsto e_j$ is affine, a shear and translation align all exceptional edges. If it is not affine, a shear aligns the first two, and the third differs from them by $1$ or $-1$. Reversing the horizontal coordinate interchanges these two possibilities, replacing the common increment $v$ by $-v$ if needed.

For precision, under $i_{\rm old}=\varepsilon i_{\rm new}+rj+s$ the new tail is $e_j-rj-s$ when $\varepsilon=1$, and $rj+s-e_j-1$ when $\varepsilon=-1$. The final $-1$ accounts for reversal of an oriented edge. Thus there are exactly two normal forms, represented by tails $(2,2,2)$ and $(2,2,1)$. This uses a single affine change of the plane, not unrelated permutations within the rows.

\subsection{Aligned edges}
After alignment, the baseline column is an arithmetic progression. Reorder the rows affinely to put it in progression order, yielding
\[
 a(i,j)=iv+ju,\qquad i,j\in\{0,1,2\},\qquad3v\ne0.
\]
The transversal triples $(u,v+2u,2v)$ and $(0,v+2u,2v+u)$ have midpoint differences, respectively,
\[
 (-3v,3u,3v-3u),\qquad(-3v-3u,3u,3v).
\]
The progression condition therefore requires
\[
 3u=0\ \hbox{or}\ 3u=3v,
 \qquad
 3u=0\ \hbox{or}\ 3u=-3v.
\]
If $3u=0$, the $j$ direction has constant derivative and Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:81:lem:constant} applies. Otherwise $\delta=3u=3v$ is nonzero with $2\delta=0$. Both $u+\delta$ and $v+\delta$ are annihilated by three. Subtracting the corresponding homomorphism leaves the binary array
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:cap}
 \begin{matrix}0&1&0\\1&0&1\\0&1&0\end{matrix}.
\end{equation}
Its four one-points are an affine cap. Its $Q$-values are $(45,45,41,41)$, giving full-indicator ratio
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:cap-ratio}
 \frac{81+2(45+45+41+41)}{729}=\frac{425}{729}.
\end{equation}

\subsection{Nonaligned edges and all transversal conditions}\label{gsr:en:81:sec:nonaligned}
The nonaligned form, after target translation and absorption of row constants, is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:nonaligned}
 \begin{matrix}
 0&v&2v\\
 b&b+v&b+2v\\
 c+v&c+2v&c
 \end{matrix},\qquad3v\ne0.
\end{equation}
All horizontal rows are already progressions. A transversal line chooses coordinate $i+js$ in row $j$, for $i,s\in\F_3$. Subtracting its first target value produces exactly these six distinct formal triples:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:sixtriples}
 \begin{array}{lll}
 T_1=(0,b,c+v),&T_2=(0,b,c-2v),\\
 T_3=(0,b+v,c),&T_4=(0,b-2v,c),\\
 T_5=(0,b+2v,c+2v),&T_6=(0,b-v,c-v).
 \end{array}
\end{equation}
The nine lines, grouped by slopes $s=0,1,2$, give $(T_1,T_1,T_2)$, $(T_3,T_3,T_4)$, and $(T_5,T_6,T_6)$ respectively. Hence no line condition has been omitted.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The complete integer relation certificate\srctag{81}}]{The complete integer relation certificate}\label{gsr:en:81:sec:d6}\label{gsr:en:81:sec:lattices}
\srcnote{81}{Section 6}
The sole enumerated arbitrary-target branch is~\eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:nonaligned}. It is a finite problem in integer relations, not a survey of selected target groups. We give its exact input, output, and verification criterion.

For a triple $(A,B,C)$, its midpoint alternatives are $2A-B-C=0$, $2B-A-C=0$, and $2C-A-B=0$. With formal variable order $(v,b,c)$, the triples in~\eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:sixtriples} produce these vectors:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{c r r r}
\toprule
Triple & First midpoint & Second midpoint & Third midpoint\\
\midrule
$T_1$&$(-1,-1,-1)$&$(-1,2,-1)$&$(2,-1,2)$\\
$T_2$&$(2,-1,-1)$&$(2,2,-1)$&$(-4,-1,2)$\\
$T_3$&$(-1,-1,-1)$&$(2,2,-1)$&$(-1,-1,2)$\\
$T_4$&$(2,-1,-1)$&$(-4,2,-1)$&$(2,-1,2)$\\
$T_5$&$(-4,-1,-1)$&$(2,2,-1)$&$(2,-1,2)$\\
$T_6$&$(2,-1,-1)$&$(-1,2,-1)$&$(-1,-1,2)$\\

\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Choose one vector in each row. There are exactly $3^6=729$ choices. For a choice, let $M$ be the $3\times6$ matrix with those vectors as columns, and let $L=M\Z^6\le\Z^3$.

\begin{proof}[Exact certificate and verification]
The public companion constructs all choices directly from the six formal triples and records their integer matrices. Its stored six-row input matrix is $M^{\mathsf T}$ in our notation. For each $M$, it reduces the rows of $M^{\mathsf T}$ by swaps, sign changes and addition of an integer multiple of one row to another. It retains the transformation matrix $U$ and checks, entry by entry,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:unimodular}
 U M^{\mathsf T}=R,\qquad \det U\in\{1,-1\}.
\end{equation}
The nonzero rows of $R$ consequently generate exactly the original lattice; they are not merely a basis of its rational span or its saturation. Each displayed candidate basis is transposed and reduced by the same explicitly verified type of transformations. Equality of the reduced bases identifies its integer lattice. The counts in the table then follow by grouping the $729$ checked choices; they sum to $729$. The three rank-two cases are retained and checked.

All input choices, transformation matrices and products are retained in the companion certificate. Verification uses integers only and does not require a computer algebra system. An independent alternative check used integer-coordinate containment in each candidate basis and equality of the maximal determinantal divisors. For equal-rank nested lattices in the same rational span, the ratio of these divisors is the lattice index; equality forces index one. The public unimodular certificate does not need this alternative as an assumption.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Why this proves a statement for every target.}
An actual triple $(v,b,c)$ in any abelian group $H$ defines a homomorphism $\Z^3\to H$. For each of the six progression triples choose one true midpoint relation. At least one exists by hypothesis; if several hold, any one supplies a choice in the exhaustive list. Every vector of its lattice $L$ lies in the kernel of $\Z^3\to H$. Hence every displayed lattice consequence is an equality in the actual target. This covers infinite targets and unbounded torsion directly.

The first four lattices force $3v=0$, contradicting~\eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:nonaligned}. The $36$ remaining choices have bases of the form
\[
 \begin{pmatrix}6&s&k\\0&3&1\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad s\in\{0,3\},\quad k\in\{1,4\}.
\]
Thus
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:six-torsion}
 6v=0,\qquad 3b=-sv,\qquad c=-b-kv,
 \qquad6b=6c=0.
\end{equation}
Put $\delta=3v\ne0$. Then $2\delta=0$ and $3b,3c\in\{0,\delta\}$. Further relations in $H$ can only add equalities; they cannot invalidate~\eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:six-torsion}. A quotient killing $\delta$ is incompatible with $3v\ne0$. The next step takes place in the actual target, so there is no unsupported claim that passing to a quotient preserves an upper energy bound.

\subsection{Removing the three torsion part}
Every value in~\eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:nonaligned} is annihilated by six. The map $a-3a=-2a$ therefore has values in an exponent-three subgroup of $H$ and remains linewise a progression, since multiplication by $-2$ is a target homomorphism.

A linewise-progression map into an exponent-three abelian group is affine. Indeed, subtract its value at zero and call the result $g$. In such a target, every midpoint relation is equivalent to the sum of the three line values being zero. Lines through zero give $g(2x)=2g(x)$. For $x\ne y$, the third point on their line is $z=-x-y$, and
\[
 g(x)+g(y)=-g(z)=2g(z)=g(2z)=g(x+y).
\]
The case $x=y$ follows from $g(2x)=2g(x)$, and pairs involving zero are immediate. Thus $g$ is a homomorphism.

Subtracting the affine map $a-3a$ leaves exactly $3a$ without changing any respected quadruple or any derivative histogram. Its four binary possibilities are
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:binary-nonaligned}
 \begin{matrix}
 0&1&0\\
 e&e+1&e\\
 f+1&f&f
 \end{matrix},\qquad e,f\in\{0,1\},
\end{equation}
where entries are multiples of $\delta$ and are added modulo two. The exact counts are
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{c c r}
\toprule
$(e,f)$ & Sorted derivative square sums & $\Ea(1_G)$\\
\midrule
$(0,0)$&$(41,41,41,45)$&417\\
$(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)$&$(45,45,45,53)$&457\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The first is a noncollinear three-point coloring; the other three are line-plus-point colorings or their complements. In the current no-$Q=53$ branch only the first remains. Its full-indicator ratio is $417/729=139/243$.

\section[{Affine geometry in arbitrary dimension\srctag{81}}]{Affine geometry in arbitrary dimension}\label{gsr:en:81:sec:d8}\label{gsr:en:81:sec:geometry}
\srcnote{81}{Section 8}
The plane alternative alone does not yet supply a single global kernel or a single slope. We establish the geometry needed to synchronize them. Every argument below is finite-dimensional at the point where it is used, but its conclusion is global; no finite-dimensional induction or limiting choice of compatible normal forms is needed.

\begin{lemma}[Plane sections determine a hyperplane]\label{gsr:en:81:lem:geometry}
Assume $\dim V\ge2$. Let $A$ be a nonempty proper subset of $V$. Suppose that for every affine plane $P\subseteq V$, the section $A\cap P$ is empty, is all of $P$, is an affine line, or is the complement in $P$ of an affine line. Then $A$ is an affine hyperplane or the complement of an affine hyperplane.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The hypothesis is invariant under complementation. We divide the proof according to whether some affine line has exactly two points in $A$.

\emph{Case 1.} Let $L$ have exactly two points in $A$, let $r$ be its remaining point, and put $B=V\setminus A$. Then $B\cap L=\{r\}$. For any $s\in B\setminus\{r\}$, the point $s$ is outside $L$. The affine plane $P$ spanned by $L$ and $s$ has a $B$-section meeting $L$ in precisely one point. Among the four permitted types, only an affine line can meet $L$ in one point. Indeed, a complement of a line meets $L$ in $0$, $2$, or $3$ points, according as the deleted line equals $L$, crosses it, or is parallel and distinct. Consequently $B\cap P$ is the line through $r,s$. We have proved that the entire line through $r$ and each $s\in B$ lies in $B$.

Translate $r$ to zero. Then $B$ is closed under scalar multiplication. For independent $s,t\in B$, the section on $\Span(s,t)$ contains the two distinct lines $\langle s\rangle$ and $\langle t\rangle$. It cannot be empty or a line. It cannot be the complement of a line either: every affine line in this plane intersects at least one of the two distinct-direction lines through zero. The section must therefore be the whole plane. This gives closure under sums of independent vectors; dependent pairs are handled by scalar closure. Thus $B$ is a linear subspace after the translation.

If its codimension were at least two, choose two vectors whose classes in $V/B$ are linearly independent. Their span meets $B$ only at zero, yielding a forbidden singleton plane section. Properness rules out codimension zero. Hence $B$ has codimension one, and $A$ is the complement of an affine hyperplane.

\emph{Case 2.} No affine line has exactly two points in $A$. Thus the entire line through any two distinct points of $A$ lies in $A$. Translate a point of $A$ to zero. The line through $0$ and $x$ gives $-x\in A$ whenever $x\in A$. For distinct $x,y\in A$, the third point of the line through $-x,-y$ is $x+y$, so $x+y\in A$. If $x=y$, then $x+y=-x\in A$ as well. Therefore $A$ is a linear subspace after translation. The same quotient-plane argument excludes codimension at least two, and properness excludes codimension zero. Thus $A$ is an affine hyperplane.

The quotient-plane argument chooses only two independent quotient vectors, and applies without a dimension bound on $V$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[A partition has one common direction]\label{gsr:en:81:lem:partition}
Let $F:V\to H$ be nonconstant, with $\dim V\ge2$. Suppose each nonempty fiber is an affine hyperplane or the complement of an affine hyperplane. Then a linear hyperplane $K\le V$ exists such that $F$ is constant on each of the three cosets of $K$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Two disjoint affine hyperplanes are parallel. To see this in arbitrary dimension, write them as prescribed levels of two nonzero linear functionals $\ell_1,\ell_2:V\to\F_3$. If their kernels differ, the functionals are independent. The map $(\ell_1,\ell_2):V\to\F_3^2$ is onto, because a proper image would be annihilated by a nonzero linear functional on $\F_3^2$, contradicting independence. The two prescribed levels must then meet. We also use the fact that one affine hyperplane contained in another equals it: translate a common point and compare their nested codimension-one direction spaces.

Suppose first that a fiber is $V\setminus M$ for an affine hyperplane $M$. Every other fiber $B$ is contained in $M$. Such a $B$ cannot equal $V\setminus N$ for an affine hyperplane $N$, since this would give $V\setminus M\subseteq N$. The left side contains two distinct hyperplanes parallel to $M$. An affine hyperplane containing either one equals it, and so cannot contain both. Thus $B$ is itself a hyperplane. Containment in $M$ gives $B=M$. There are exactly two fibers, and the direction of $M$ is the desired $K$.

If no fiber is a complement, all fibers are hyperplanes. They are disjoint, hence parallel, with a common direction $K$. Since they partition $V$, they are precisely the three cosets of $K$. This proves the lemma without any prior assumption that $F$ has finite range.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Gluing the plane descriptions\srctag{81}}]{Gluing the plane descriptions}\label{gsr:en:81:sec:d9}\label{gsr:en:81:sec:gluing}
\srcnote{81}{Section 9}
Assume $\dim V\ge2$ and every affine plane restriction of $a$ is affine or a nonaffine translated cut. We prove a global normal form using the map
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:F}
 F(x)=3a(x).
\end{equation}
This is integer multiplication in the arbitrary group $H$; we will never cancel a factor of three.

\subsection{The level sets of the triple map}
On an affine plane where $a$ is affine, $F$ is constant, since every homomorphism from its direction space has image annihilated by three. On a plane cut,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:Fcut}
 F(x_0+k+rt)=3\beta+rq,\qquad q=3u\ne0.
\end{equation}
The first two and the last two of these three stripe values are distinct. The first and last coincide precisely when $2q=0$. Hence every plane fiber of $F$ is empty, full, a line, or a complement of a line. The complement case is necessary for order-two $q$.

If $F$ is nonconstant, every nonempty global fiber is proper. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:81:lem:geometry} applies to each one, and Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:81:lem:partition} yields a single linear hyperplane $K$ such that $F$ factors through $V/K$. It is nonconstant on that three-element quotient.

If $F$ is constant, no plane restriction can be a nonaffine cut, since~\eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:Fcut} has distinct first two values. Thus $a$ is affine on every affine plane. Put $g(x)=a(x)-a(0)$. Any $x,y\in V$ lie in a linear plane, including when they are dependent because $\dim V\ge2$. On that plane $g$ is a homomorphism: it is affine and vanishes at zero. Therefore
\[
 g(x+y)=g(x)+g(y)\qquad(x,y\in V),
\]
and $a$ is globally affine. It remains to handle the nonconstant case.

\subsection{Transverse planes identify the kernel direction}
Call $P=p+W$ \emph{transverse to $K$} when $W\not\subseteq K$. The quotient map $W\to V/K$ is onto and has one-dimensional kernel $W\cap K$. Thus $P$ meets each $K$-coset in one affine line and sees all three quotient values of $F$. Since these values are not all equal, $F|_P$ is nonconstant and $a|_P$ must be a nonaffine cut.

Its local kernel direction is exactly $W\cap K$. Indeed, any nonconstant triple has a value occurring precisely once. That value has a fiber in $P$ equal to a complete line in direction $W\cap K$. In the local cut description, a fiber of $3a|_P$ with three points is a line in the local kernel direction. Equality of these two lines identifies the directions. This argument covers both three distinct quotient values and the case of a repeated endpoint value. It does not assume a common choice of local stripe labels.

\subsection{One derivative works on all three cosets}
Fix $0\ne h\in K$. On any transverse plane whose direction contains $h$, the preceding argument makes $h$ a local kernel direction. The cut formula therefore makes $D_h a$ constant throughout that entire plane, across all three stripes.

For arbitrary $x,y\in V$, first suppose $y-x\notin K$. The vectors $h,y-x$ are independent, and
\[
 P=x+\Span(h,y-x)
\]
is transverse to $K$ and contains both points. Hence $D_h a(x)=D_h a(y)$. If instead $y-x\in K$, choose $z$ with $z-x\notin K$. Then $z-y\notin K$ as well. Applying the preceding comparison to $(x,z)$ and $(y,z)$ gives the same equality. We have proved that $D_h a$ is globally constant for every $h\in K$.

Write that constant as $\psi(h)$ and set $\psi(0)=0$. The cocycle identity gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:psi}
 \psi(h+k)=D_{h+k}a(x)=D_h a(x)+D_k a(x+h)
 =\psi(h)+\psi(k)
\end{equation}
for all $h,k\in K$, including zero cases. Thus $\psi:K\to H$ is a homomorphism and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:global-slope}
 a(x+k)=a(x)+\psi(k)\qquad(x\in V,\ k\in K).
\end{equation}
The same $\psi$ works on all three cosets. This is stronger than saying that each coset separately supports an affine map, which would leave a genuine compatibility gap.

\subsection{The quotient progression and its basepoint}
Every affine line lies in an affine plane. Restricting an affine plane map gives an arithmetic-progression value triple. For a plane cut with local transversal generator $t_0$, a kernel-parallel line is affine. A transverse line can be written in cut coordinates as
\[
 x_0+k_0+r(k_1+t_0),\qquad r\in\{0,1,2\},
\]
and its values are
\[
 \beta+\psi(k_0)+r\bigl(\psi(k_1)+u\bigr).
\]
This is an arithmetic progression in the chosen order. The identity is valid when coordinates wrap modulo three because $3\psi(k_1)=0$.

Now choose $t\notin K$. The values at $0,t,2t$ have an arithmetic-progression ordering. As in the plane proof, every permutation of these three points is affine. Choose a starting point $x_0$ on this transversal and replace $t$ by $-t$ if needed so that its values are $\beta,\beta+u,\beta+2u$. Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:global-slope} gives
\[
 a(x_0+k+rt)=\beta+\psi(k)+ru
 \qquad(k\in K,\ r\in\{0,1,2\}).
\]
If $3u=0$, then $F$ would be constant, contrary to the current case. Hence $3u\ne0$, and the global map is a translated nonaffine cut.

\begin{proposition}[Exact local-to-global statement]\label{gsr:en:81:prop:gluing}
In dimension at least two, a map $a:V\to H$ is affine or a translated index-three affine cut if and only if every affine plane restriction belongs to those two families.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The forward implication follows by restriction. For detail, a plane with direction contained in $K$ lies in one global coset and has an affine restriction. A transverse plane has kernel direction $W\cap K$. Choose its basepoint in $x_0+K$ and a transverse generator $t+k_1$. Its local increment is $u+\psi(k_1)$ and has triple $3u\ne0$. It is therefore a nonaffine local cut. Affine global maps restrict affinely. The reverse implication is the preceding construction.
\end{proof}
Nothing in the construction assumes a finite basis for $V$, a finite range for $a$, or a torsion-free target. The hyperplane is obtained from global fibers, and the common homomorphism is obtained from globally constant derivatives.


\subsection{Transferring a small witness to the whole group}
Taking the contrapositive of Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:81:prop:gluing}, every outside-family map in rank at least two has an affine plane restriction outside the favorable plane families. The plane theorem supplies a weight on that plane with ratio at most $\lambda$. Extend it by zero to $V$. An affine plane identification preserves $x+y=z+w$, and quadruples using points outside the support have product zero. Both energies are therefore unchanged. The support has at most nine points.

In rank one, either the full three-point line has no midpoint relation, giving the $5/9$ witness, or its values have a progression ordering. Every such ordering is affine on the source. Writing the values as $\beta,\beta+u,\beta+2u$ gives an affine map if $3u=0$ and a translated cut with $K=\{0\}$ otherwise. Rank zero is entirely affine. Thus the universal upper-bound and support assertions of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:81:thm:main} hold in every rank, without a compactness argument.

Sharpness of this uniform upper bound follows from the rank-two map of Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:81:prop:spike}, which is outside the favorable families by the derivative argument in Section~\ref{gsr:en:81:sec:finish-plane}. The claimed sharpness uses this rank-two example; no higher-rank equality assertion is required.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The exact weighted value of a cut\srctag{81}}]{The exact weighted value of a cut}\label{gsr:en:81:sec:d10}\label{gsr:en:81:sec:analytic}
\srcnote{81}{Section 10}
For completeness, we give the lower bound as well as the three-point attaining test. This is the exponent-three specialization of the index-three energy theorem in Report~291~\cite{srcseventynine}, also included in Report~292~\cite{srceighty}. Here the Fourier group can always be taken finite, so neither a limiting argument nor compact-group measure theory is needed.

For this section only, write
\[
 \tau=\sqrt{\sqrt6-2},\qquad
 \kappa=\frac{\sqrt6-1}{\tau},\qquad \rho=\frac{\kappa}{1+\kappa}.
\]
The unstarred $\kappa$ is the cut constant, distinct from the spike parameter $\kappa_*$.

\subsection{A sharp complex quartic}
For $A,B,C\in\C$, define
\begin{align}
 N(A,B,C)&=|A|^4+|C|^4+4|B|^2(|A|^2+|C|^2)+|2AC+B^2|^2,\label{gsr:en:81:eq:N}\\
 T(A,B,C)&=A^2\overline B\,\overline C+AB\overline C^{\,2},\qquad
 X(A,B,C)=4\operatorname{Re}T(A,B,C).\label{gsr:en:81:eq:X}
\end{align}
\begin{lemma}[Complex quartic lower bound]\label{gsr:en:81:lem:quartic}
For every $A,B,C\in\C$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:quartic}
 N(A,B,C)\ge4\kappa|T(A,B,C)|\ge\kappa X(A,B,C).
\end{equation}
The constant $\kappa$ is sharp, with equality at $(A,B,C)=(1,\tau,1)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If any entry vanishes, then $T=0$ and the inequality is immediate. Otherwise put $x=|A|>0$, $y=|B|>0$, $z=|C|>0$, and
\[
 q=\cos(\arg A+\arg C-2\arg B),\quad
 R^2=x^2+z^2+2xzq,\quad
 J=(x^2+z^2+y^2)^2+2x^2z^2.
\]
Expansion gives $N=J+2y^2R^2$ and $|T|=xyzR$. When $R=0$, the inequality is again immediate. For positive $R$, the derivative in $R$ of
\[
 \frac{J+2y^2R^2}{4xyzR}
\]
has the sign of $2y^2R^2-J$. Since $R\le x+z$ and
\[
 J-2y^2(x+z)^2=(y^2-2xz)^2+x^4+z^4>0,
\]
that quotient decreases strictly as $R$ increases through its allowed range. Its minimum over phases is at $R=x+z$, namely at $q=1$.

It remains to minimize the real expression
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:real-quartic}
 \frac{x^4+z^4+4y^2(x^2+z^2)+(2xz+y^2)^2}{4xyz(x+z)}.
\end{equation}
Normalize $x+z=1$ by homogeneity and put $p=xz\in(0,1/4]$. The numerator becomes
\[
 6p^2-4p+1+4y^2(1-p)+y^4.
\]
At fixed $y$, the derivative of this numerator divided by $p$ has the sign of
\[
 6p^2-(1+4y^2+y^4)<0,
\]
because $6p^2\le3/8<1$. Therefore~\eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:real-quartic} is minimized at $p=1/4$, that is, at $x=z$. Rescale to $x=z=1$. The remaining quotient is
\[
 h(y)=\frac{y^4+12y^2+6}{8y}.
\]
Its derivative has the sign of $3y^4+12y^2-6$, which is strictly increasing for $y>0$ and has its unique zero at $y=\tau$. The quotient tends to infinity as $y\to0$ or $y\to\infty$, and
\[
 h(\tau)=\frac{8(\sqrt6-1)}{8\tau}=\kappa.
\]
This proves $N\ge4\kappa|T|$. The second inequality in~\eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:quartic} is $\operatorname{Re}T\le|T|$. The triple $(1,\tau,1)$ attains both, proving sharpness.
\end{proof}
The phases are essential: the Fourier transforms used below are complex even when all original weights are nonnegative.

\subsection{The exact pair-convolution splitting}
Normalize $x_0=0$ by translating the domain. Fix a cut~\eqref{gsr:fm:81:eq:cut} and an arbitrary nonzero finitely supported nonnegative weight $f$. Let
\[
 f_r(k)=f(k+rt),\qquad k\in K,\quad r\in\{0,1,2\}.
\]
All convolutions in this subsection are on $K$. Since $3t=0$, the ordinary pair-convolution functions on the three output cosets are
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:convolutions}
 f_0*f_0+2f_1*f_2,\qquad
 2f_0*f_1+f_2*f_2,\qquad
 2f_0*f_2+f_1*f_1.
\end{equation}
At a fixed sum $\ell\in K$, the pair types $(0,0)$ and $(1,2),(2,1)$ have target sums $2\beta+\psi(\ell)$ and $2\beta+\psi(\ell)+3u$. These are distinct because $3u\ne0$. At a fixed sum $\ell+t$, the types $(0,1),(1,0)$ and $(2,2)$ again differ by $3u$. At a fixed sum $\ell+2t$, the types $(0,2),(2,0)$ and $(1,1)$ have equal target sums. Thus
\begin{align}
 \Ea(f)={}&\norm{f_0*f_0}_2^2+4\norm{f_1*f_2}_2^2
 +4\norm{f_0*f_1}_2^2+\norm{f_2*f_2}_2^2\notag\\
 &+\norm{2f_0*f_2+f_1*f_1}_2^2.\label{gsr:en:81:eq:respected-conv}
\end{align}
The ordinary energy is the sum of the squared norms of the three expressions in~\eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:convolutions}. No injectivity of $\psi$ is used, and the order of the nonzero element $3u$ can be two, three, any larger finite number, or infinite. At each fixed source sum only a single nonzero copy of $3u$ distinguishes the relevant pair classes.

\subsection{Finite Fourier analysis and the uniform lower bound}
Let $L\le K$ be the linear span of the supports of $f_0,f_1,f_2$. It is a finite-dimensional vector space over $\F_3$, hence a finite group. All the convolutions above are supported on $L$.

Its characters are homomorphisms $\chi:L\to\{1,\omega,\omega^2\}$, where $\omega=\exp(2\pi i/3)$. After choosing a basis, they are indexed by the linear forms on $L$. For $g:L\to\C$, put
\[
 \widehat g(\chi)=\sum_{k\in L}g(k)\chi(k).
\]
The orthogonality identity
\[
 \frac1{|L|}\sum_{\chi}\chi(k)\overline{\chi(\ell)}=\ind_{k=\ell}
\]
follows by factoring the sum over basis coordinates, using $1+\omega+\omega^2=0$. Expansion then gives Parseval,
\[
 \norm{g}_2^2=\frac1{|L|}\sum_{\chi}|\widehat g(\chi)|^2,
 \qquad \widehat{g*h}=\widehat g\,\widehat h.
\]
Write $A=\widehat f_0(\chi)$, $B=\widehat f_1(\chi)$, $C=\widehat f_2(\chi)$. Equations~\eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:convolutions}--\eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:respected-conv} become
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:fourier-energies}
 \Ea(f)=\frac1{|L|}\sum_\chi N(A,B,C),\qquad
 \EaddV(f)=\frac1{|L|}\sum_\chi\bigl(N(A,B,C)+X(A,B,C)\bigr).
\end{equation}
The cross terms of the first two squared norms are exactly $4\operatorname{Re}(A^2\overline B\overline C+AB\overline C^{\,2})$; the third norm is already included in $N$. Integrating here means only averaging over finitely many characters.

Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:81:lem:quartic} at each character and add. This yields
\[
 \Ea(f)\ge\kappa\bigl(\EaddV(f)-\Ea(f)\bigr),
 \qquad \frac{\Ea(f)}{\EaddV(f)}\ge\frac{\kappa}{1+\kappa}=\rho.
\]
The inequality holds for every finite weight, uniformly in its support. Infinite dimension introduces no extra step: a separate finite group $L$ suffices for each test.

\subsection{Three-point attainment and separation of constants}
On the transversal $0,t,2t$, use weights $(1,s,1)$ and target values $(0,u,2u)$ after discarding the target constant. Direct pair counting gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:81:eq:attain-polynomials}
 \Ea(f)=6+12s^2+s^4,\qquad
 \EaddV(f)=6+8s+12s^2+s^4.
\end{equation}
At source sum zero the respected contribution is $1+4s^2$, at source sum $t$ it is $4s^2+1$, and at source sum $2t$ it is $(2+s^2)^2$. The first two mixed classes differ by $3u$, so this count covers arbitrary target torsion.

For $s=\tau$, the numerator is $8(1+\tau^2)$ by $\tau^4+4\tau^2-2=0$, and the ratio is
\[
 \frac{1+\tau^2}{1+\tau^2+\tau}=\rho.
\]
Translating back places the support at $x_0,x_0+t,x_0+2t$. Together with the lower bound, this proves $r(a)=\rho$ and exact finite attainment.

For an exact separation, $\sqrt6<49/20$ gives $0<\tau<7/10$. The polynomial $8s^2-17s+8$ decreases on $[0,7/10]$ and equals $1/50>0$ at $7/10$. Therefore $8(1+\tau^2)>17\tau$, which is equivalent to $\rho>17/25$. On the other hand,~\eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:kappastar} gives
\[
 \lambda\le\frac{83}{139}<\frac{17}{25}<\rho<1.
\]
Every affine map respects every quadruple and has $r(a)=1$. This completes Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:81:thm:main}, including the equivalence between $r(a)>\lambda$ and the favorable structural alternatives.

\begin{corollary}[An excluded interval in the weighted spectrum]
Across all the source and target groups considered here, every map satisfies
\[
 r(a)\in[0,\lambda]\cup\{\rho,1\}.
\]
The endpoint $\lambda$ is attained, and no value lies strictly between $\lambda$ and $\rho$ or strictly between $\rho$ and $1$.
\end{corollary}
The display is a containment, not a claim that every point of $[0,\lambda]$ is attained. The existence of a finite local witness for outside-family maps does not assert that every such map has a finite weight attaining its own infimum.

\section{Sources~71 and~70: Section~13 again, on fixed prime support and the printed Theorem~13.12 \wtag}\label{gsr:en:sec:sectionthirteenagain}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the twelfth write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next twenty-one sections are source~71's Sections~2--11 and source~70's Sections~2--11 and Appendix~A. \emph{Logically source~71 continues the ninth write's Section~13 chapter} after source~52 (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:sectionthirteen}), and \emph{source~70 continues source~57's chapter on Theorem~13.12} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:theoremthirteen}); they are printed here because no number printed earlier may move. Both are Reports of the series of sources~26, 32, 41, 42 and~51--53 (Reports~283 and~282); their introductions are Sections~\ref{gsr:fm:71:sec:d1} and~\ref{gsr:fm:70:sec:d1}.

\emph{What source~71 proves.} Fix $r\ge2$ and $s$ with $r^s\ge8r$, $a=r^{-s}$. For every large $N$ with $r^s\mid N$ and every prime divisor of $N$ dividing $r$, the strip context $A=T\times\Z/N\Z$, $T$ the first $N/r^s$ multiples of $r$, with $\phi(x,y)=\lfloor x.\mathrm{val}/r\rfloor$, carries a selected genuine Stage~13.4--13.6 package with all six numerical budgets, yet \emph{every} genuine initial pair at the exact cutoff admits no Stage~13.6 record with even a weak Stage~13.7 continuation, and every such Stage~13.5 step is divisible by $r$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:71:thm:main}). The key facts are a global agreement cap ($\lfloor x/r\rfloor$ meets every ambient affine map in at most $r$ points when the radical of $N$ divides $r$; Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:71:lem:affine}) and the sharp subgroup radius $1/3$ (Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:71:lem:subgroup}). This extends source~52's obstruction over $N=2^k$ (one selected package) to every fixed mixed prime support, for example every large $2^e3^f$ with $e,f\ge3$, and to all initial reselections; source~52's threshold over prime powers is unchanged.

\emph{What source~70 proves, and what is superseded.} \emph{Its headline is superseded.} It recovers the printed Theorem~13.12 (side $N^{2^{-\alpha^{-2^{70}}}}$, mass $(\alpha/2)^{2^{76}}$, all large primes) as an asymptotic statement (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:70:thm:printed}). Before it arrived, that statement had been proved in writing by source~57 (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:57:main:extraction}) and formally as \file{theorem_13_12_holds} (below), and the repository had improved the printed powers $2^{70}$ and $2^{76}$ to $2^{61}$ and $2^{42}$; source~70's last status check (\texttt{7d0199a11}) predates both. \emph{What survives.} (1) A lower-range side exponent one exponential level better than every proved one, \emph{conditional on Lau's simultaneous-recurrence theorem} (a preprint, with a non-numerical starting threshold): $E_{\mathrm L}(\alpha)=2^{-3100876}(\alpha/2)^{9222672\cdot2^{66}}$, so $-\log_2E_{\mathrm L}(\alpha)=3100876+9222672\cdot2^{66}(1+\log_2(1/\alpha))$ is linear in $\log(1/\alpha)$, against $(2/\alpha)^{2^{53}}$ for the formal Fej\'er exponent and $\alpha^{-2^{70}}$ printed (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:70:thm:local}, Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:70:prop:compare}); its mass $2^{-137}\delta_\alpha^{704}$ is no better than the printed one and much weaker than the formal $(\alpha/2)^{2^{42}}$. (2) The near-maximal branch on \emph{every} cyclic modulus $N\ge2$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:70:thm:near} and its Appendix~A, Section~\ref{gsr:en:70:sec:dA}): mass $(1-9792\varepsilon)N^2$ and coefficient $(\sqrt{63/64}-4\varepsilon)N$ for $\varepsilon=1-\alpha\le2^{-16}$, where source~57 and the formal theorem have primes only, with the better mass $1-332\varepsilon$ and range, and the smaller coefficient $(3/4-4\varepsilon)N$; source~72 (previous chapter but one) has density $1-595\varepsilon$ at coefficient $(\sqrt{4/5}-4\varepsilon)N$ on every cyclic group for $\varepsilon\le1/2040$. Its prime-field branch is an independent proof of source~57's: source~70's pin precedes source~57's arrival. (3) A Maynard-only variant with an unspecified absolute constant (Section~\ref{gsr:en:70:sec:d11}). Its formal route (its Question~5) has been taken by the repository in a different way.

\emph{Relation to the formal statements} (checked at HEAD \texttt{0c4f9054d}). \file{theorem_13_12} (\file{Sections12\_13.lean}, line~718) is an exact companion, \file{theorem_13_12_holds} (\file{Proofs13EndpointPrintedTheorem.lean}, line~73; \texttt{d48e8af00}, 6~October 2026, 23:55): Fej\'er extraction away from one (\file{theorem_13_12_away_from_one}, \file{Proofs13FejerPrintedRange.lean}, line~39) and the near-maximal branch \file{theorem_13_12_near_one} (\file{Proofs13EndpointPrintedTheorem.lean}, line~12) from \file{endpoint_global_fourier} (\file{Proofs13EndpointGlobalFourier.lean}, line~12; prime $N$); \file{theorem_13_12_with_fejer_explicit_bound} (\file{Proofs13FejerExplicitExponent.lean}, line~55) and \file{theorem_13_12_with_improved_printed_bounds} (\file{Proofs13ImprovedPrintedBounds.lean}, line~11). No Lau or Maynard input occurs in the Lean tree, and nothing of source~70 is formalized. \file{lemma_13_7} (line~558) is exact on prime moduli; the all-moduli encodings \file{lemma_13_7_without_domain} and \file{lemma_13_7_without_prime_assumption} (lines~526 and~534) are preserved and unasserted, refuted in writing by sources~52 and~71, and their negations are not formalized; the preserved \file{lemma_13_5_without_prime_assumption} and \file{lemma_13_6_without_preceding_context} (lines~411 and~468) are not refuted by source~71, which constructs Stage~13.5 and~13.6 records. The line numbers that source~71 quotes refer to its pin \texttt{5c9a442d2}.

\section[{Complete retained interface\srctag{71}}]{Complete retained interface}\label{gsr:en:71:sec:d2}\label{gsr:en:71:sec:interface}\label{gsr:en:71:complete-retained-interface}
\srcnote{71}{Section 2}

Let \(Z=\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\). A progression \(P=(x,d,L)\) has carrier \([P]=\{x+jd:0\le j<L\}\), length \(L\in\mathbb N\), and step \(d\in Z\). It is proper when \(|[P]|=L\). This is cardinal injectivity, not a prohibition on crossing the canonical residue cut. Write \(\|r\|_N\) for the least absolute value of an integer representative of \(r\in Z\). Ambient affinity on \(U\) means \(f(x)=\xi x+\tau\) on \(U\) for one pair \(\xi,\tau\in Z\).

An order-eight Freiman map preserves equality between two sums of eight domain elements, with repetitions allowed. The context requires \(0<a\le1\), \(|A|=aN^2\), \(\eta=2^{-44}\), separate order-eight Freiman behavior of \(\phi\) on all horizontal and vertical sections of \(A\), and the mostly-respected arrangement inequality.

At fixed height \(h\), an arrangement consists of sixteen \(x_i\), with the first eight summing to the last eight, and sixteen independent \(y_i\), with \((x_i,y_i),(x_i,y_i+h)\in A\). It is respected when the same equality holds for the sixteen vertical differences of \(\phi\). Let \(C(h)\) and \(C_\phi(h)\) be these unnormalized counts. The context requires \[
(1-\eta)\sum_h C(h)\le\sum_h C_\phi(h).
\] A height is good if \((1-2\eta)C(h)\le C_\phi(h)\), and strong if it is good and \(a^{32}N^{31}/16\le C(h)\). For fixed \(S_0,D,E\), put \[
\mathcal H=([E.Q]\cap D.H)\cap\{h:h\text{ is strong}\}.
\tag{2.1}
\]

Use the exact source constants \[
\begin{aligned}
\delta&=2^{-43}a^{224},&
\lambda&=2^{-48}a^{256},&
\varepsilon&=2^{-100}a^{448},\\
K&=2^{114}a^{-320},&
Q_{13}&=2^{2^{20}}a^{-2^{21}},&
c&=\tfrac12\,2^{-228K}a^{576K},\\
\beta&=2^{-13Q_{13}},&
W&=2^{135}a^{-704}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2.2}
\] Here \(\beta\) is the source exponent sometimes called \(\beta_{\rm old}\). It is not strengthened. Set \[
\kappa=\left\lceil2^{74}(a^{32}/16)^{-10}\right\rceil=\lceil K\rceil,
\qquad
z=\frac{2^{-155\kappa}(a^{32}/16)^{18\kappa}}{\kappa}.
\tag{2.3}
\] This retains the exact ceiling and denominator of section10Zeta. Here \(K=2^{114}r^{320s}\) is a positive integer, so \(\kappa=K\) and \[
z=2^{-227K}a^{576K}/K>0.
\tag{2.4}
\]

\subsection{Stage 13.4}\label{gsr:en:71:stage-13.4}

For a cutoff \(\theta>0\), set \[
\theta_1=2^{-1882}\theta^{10477},
\qquad b=2^{1882}\theta^{-10479}.
\tag{2.5}
\] The record \(D\) stores \(q,m_D,P,H\) and \(q\) coefficient pairs \((A_i,B_i)\in Z^2\). Its full predicate requires:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \(q>0\), \(P\) proper with nonzero step, and \(H\subseteq[P]\).
\item
  \(q\le b\).
\item
  \(m_D\le \theta_1N^{\theta_1^2/(16q)}/(64\pi)<m_D+1\).
\item
  \(\operatorname{len}(P)=m_D\) or \(\operatorname{len}(P)+1=m_D\).
\item
  \(a^{32}N^{31}\operatorname{len}(P)/8\le\sum_{h\in H,\ h\text{ good}}C(h)\).
\item
  If \(h\in H\) and \(|\widehat f_h(\omega)|\ge\theta N^2\), then \(\omega=A_ih+B_i\) for some \(i\). Here \(f_h(x)\) counts the \(y\) such that \((x,y),(x,y+h)\in A\), and the Fourier transform is unnormalized.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Stage 13.5}\label{gsr:en:71:stage-13.5}

Write \(v=2^{-12q}\), \(w=2^{-11q}\); these exponents mean \(-(12q)\) and \(-(11q)\). The record \(E\) stores \(Q\). Its full predicate requires:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \(Q\) proper with nonzero step and \([Q]\subseteq[P]\).
\item
  \(\operatorname{len}(P)^v/2\le\operatorname{len}(Q)\).
\item
  \(\|(A_ih+B_i)\operatorname{step}(Q)\|_N\le\operatorname{len}(P)^{-w}N\), for all \(i\) and \(h\in[Q]\).
\item
  \(a^{32}\operatorname{len}(Q)/20\le|\mathcal H|\).
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Stage 13.6}\label{gsr:en:71:stage-13.6}

Let \(\mathcal E_h=\{(x,y):(x,y),(x,y+h)\in A\}\). The record \(F\) stores a progression \(R\) and sets \(Y_h\subseteq Z^2\). Put \(Y_h^R=\{(x,y)\in Y_h:x\in[R]\}\). Its full predicate requires:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \(R\) proper with the same nonzero step as \(Q\).
\item
  \(cN^\beta\le\operatorname{len}(R)\).
\item
  For every \(h\in\mathcal H\), \(Y_h\subseteq\mathcal E_h\), \(\delta N^2\le|Y_h|\), and \(\phi(x,y+h)-\phi(x,y)=\xi_hx+\tau_h\) on \(Y_h^R\), for some \(\xi_h,\tau_h\in Z\).
\item
  \(\delta\operatorname{len}(R)N|\mathcal H|\le\sum_{h\in\mathcal H}|Y_h^R|\).
\item
  \(\lambda\operatorname{len}(Q)\operatorname{len}(R)N\le\sum_{h\in\mathcal H}|Y_h^R|\).
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Weak Stage 13.7}\label{gsr:en:71:weak-stage-13.7}

The record \(G\) stores \(y\in Z\), a progression \(S\) of length \(L\), and \(B\subseteq Z^2\). Its weak predicate requires:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \(S\) proper with nonzero step and \([S]\subseteq[R]\).
\item
  \(\operatorname{len}(R)^\varepsilon\le L\).
\item
  \(B\subseteq[S]\times(y+\mathcal H)\).
\item
  \(\delta L|\mathcal H|\le|B|\).
\item
  \(\lambda\operatorname{len}(Q)L\le|B|\).
\item
  For each \(h\in\mathcal H\), \(x\mapsto\phi(x,y+h)\) is ambient affine on \(\{x\in[S]:(x,y+h)\in B\}\).
\end{enumerate}

The full predicate adds \(B\subseteq A\); excluding the weak one excludes the full one.

\subsection{The six numerical budgets}\label{gsr:en:71:the-six-numerical-budgets}

Besides \(a\le1/6\) and the genuine initial-stage predicates, the source budget theorem assumes \[
0<M,\quad M^2\le N,\quad M+1\le\operatorname{len}(Q),\quad
cN^\beta\le M,\quad
\operatorname{len}(P)^{-w}\le z/M,\quad
W\le(cN^\beta)^\varepsilon.
\tag{2.6}
\] It separately assumes primality, which will be false here.

\section[{Uniform scalar margins and constant separation\srctag{71}}]{Uniform scalar margins and constant separation}\label{gsr:en:71:sec:d3}\label{gsr:en:71:sec:scalar}
\srcnote{71}{Section 3}
Choose the exact cutoff
\[
 \theta=2^{-37}(a^{32}/16)^{11/2}=2^{-59}a^{176}.
 \tag{3.1}
\]
Since $0<a\le1/(8r)\le1/16$, we have $0<\theta<a<1$ and
$\theta/(a^{32}/4)=2^{-57}a^{144}<1$. In particular the usual numerical cutoff admissibility bound holds.

Let $q$ be any positive integer with $q\le b$. This includes every genuine Stage 13.4 record at the fixed cutoff. Define
\[
 u(q)=\frac{\theta_1^2}{16q},\quad v(q)=2^{-12q},\quad w(q)=2^{-11q},
 \qquad d=\frac{\theta_1}{64\pi},\quad c_P=d/2.
 \tag{3.2}
\]
All bases and constants are positive, and
\[
 0<d,c_P<1,\qquad0<u(q)<1/16,\qquad0<v(q)<w(q)\le1/2.
\]
The following scalar estimate is uniform in $q$; no modulus assumption is involved.

\begin{lemma}[Uniform relative margin]\label{gsr:en:71:lem:margin}
For every integer $1\le q\le b$,
\[
 2\beta<u(q)v(q),\qquad\beta<u(q),\qquad\beta<u(q)w(q).
 \tag{3.3}
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
We reproduce the elementary argument of Report281, Lemma 3.1~\cite{srcfiftythree}. Expanding the constants gives
\[
 \theta_1=2^{-620025}a^{1843952},\qquad
 b=2^{620143}a^{-1844304},
 \tag{3.4}
\]
and hence
\[
 \frac{b}{Q_{13}/2}=2^{-428432}a^{252848}<1,
 \qquad\theta_1b=\theta^{-2}\ge1.
 \tag{3.5}
\]
Thus $1\le q\le b<Q_{13}/2$ and $\theta_1\ge1/b$, so
\[
 u(q)\ge\frac1{16b^3}\ge\frac1{2Q_{13}^3},\qquad
 v(q)\ge2^{-6Q_{13}}.
 \tag{3.6}
\]
For every real $Q\ge2$, one has $Q\le2^Q$. Indeed, if $j=\lfloor Q\rfloor\ge1$, then $Q\le j+1\le2^j\le2^Q$, using the inductive inequality $j+1\le2^j$. Consequently
$4Q^3\le2^{2+3Q}<2^{7Q}$. Since $Q_{13}>2$,
\[
 2\beta=2\cdot2^{-13Q_{13}}
 <\frac{2^{-6Q_{13}}}{2Q_{13}^3}\le u(q)v(q).
\]
Finally $v(q)<1$ and $v(q)<w(q)$ give the other two assertions.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Constant separation]\label{gsr:en:71:lem:separation}
For the literal source constants,
\[
 0<c<d/8<1,\qquad0<\delta\le a<1,\qquad0<\lambda<1,
 \qquad\varepsilon>0.
 \tag{3.7}
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The last three comparisons are immediate from (2.2) and $0<a\le1$. For the first,
\[
 d=2^{-620031}a^{1843952}/\pi,
 \qquad d/8>2^{-620036}a^{1843952},
\]
where the strict inequality uses $\pi<4$. Since $K\ge2^{114}$,
\[
 1+228K>620036,\qquad576K\ge1843952.
\]
As $0<a\le1$, we obtain
\[
 c=2^{-(1+228K)}a^{576K}
 <2^{-620036}a^{1843952}<d/8.
\]
The bound $d<1$ follows from its definition. In particular $c<1/2$.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Selected parameters and eight thresholds\srctag{71}}]{Selected parameters and eight thresholds}\label{gsr:en:71:sec:d4}\label{gsr:en:71:sec:thresholds}
\srcnote{71}{Section 4}
For the selected initial records, set
\[
 J=\left\lfloor\frac1{2r\theta}\right\rfloor,
 \qquad q_0=r(2J+1),\qquad
 u_0=u(q_0),\quad v_0=v(q_0),\quad w_0=w(q_0),\quad
 \sigma=u_0v_0/2.
\]
Since $\theta^{-1}=2^{59}a^{-176}\ge8r$, we have $J\ge4$ and $q_0>0$. The exact floor estimate gives
\[
 q_0\le\theta^{-1}+r\le2\theta^{-1}
 \le2^{1882}\theta^{-10479}=b.
 \tag{4.1}
\]
The final comparison is equivalent to $1\le2^{1881}\theta^{-10478}$. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:71:lem:margin} therefore applies to $q_0$, giving
\[
 \beta<\sigma<u_0,\qquad2\sigma=u_0v_0<1,
 \qquad\sigma<u_0w_0<1.
\]
All these constants depend only on $r,s$. The floor-based definition is exact; in this particular family one may also simplify
\[
 J=2^{58}r^{176s-1},\qquad q_0=2^{59}r^{176s}+r.
\]
These integers are left symbolic, and the proof does not need this optional simplification.

Choose $N$ to satisfy the same eight positive-power conditions:
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
\mathrm{(T1)}\quad N\ge r^{s+1},
&\mathrm{(T2)}\quad N^{u_0}\ge2/d,\\
\mathrm{(T3)}\quad N^{1-u_0}\ge d/a,
&\mathrm{(T4)}\quad N^{u_0-\sigma}\ge2/c_P,\\
\mathrm{(T5)}\quad N^\sigma\ge2,
&\mathrm{(T6)}\quad N\ge(rJ)^2,\\
\mathrm{(T7)}\quad N^{u_0w_0-\sigma}\ge c_P^{-w_0}/z,
&\mathrm{(T8)}\quad N^{\beta\varepsilon}\ge Wc^{-\varepsilon}.
\end{array}\tag{4.2}
\]
Write these as $N^{\rho_i}\ge C_i$, including the exponent-one conditions. All $\rho_i$ are strictly positive, and all $C_i$ are positive finite numbers. One sufficient integer threshold is
\[

\subsection{The source floor forces a nonempty critical set}

\]

\]

\subsection{The global affine agreement bound}
\begin{lemma}[One agreement per residue class]\label{gsr:en:71:lem:affine}
Suppose $r\mid N$ and $\operatorname{rad}(N)\mid r$. The total function
$f(x)=\lfloor x.\mathrm{val}/r\rfloor\bmod N$ agrees with any ambient affine map $x\mapsto\xi x+\tau$ at at most one point in each residue class modulo $r$. Its global agreement set has at most $r$ points.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
In the canonical class $t\in\{0,\ldots,r-1\}$, write $x=rj+t$, where $0\le j<N/r$; then $f(x)=j$. If two points with indices $j,j'$ agree with the same affine map, subtraction gives
\[
 (r\xi-1)(j-j')=0\quad\text{in }\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z.
 \tag{9.4}
\]
For every prime $\ell\mid N$, the support hypothesis gives $\ell\mid r$, so $r\xi-1\equiv-1\pmod\ell$. Consequently $\gcd(r\xi-1,N)=1$, and $r\xi-1$ is a unit modulo $N$. Cancel it to obtain $j=j'\pmod N$. The canonical index range gives equality as integers and hence equality of the points. Summing the one-point bound over the $r$ residue classes gives the global cap.
\end{proof}
This invertibility argument is the sole use of $\operatorname{rad}(N)\mid r$ in the obstruction and construction. Integrality, no-wrap divisibility, the exact $r$-element kernel and all selected-stage checks require only $r\mid N$ or the stronger divisibility $r^s\mid N$ already stated. The total extension of $\phi$ ensures the lemma applies to weak output rows even outside $A$.

\subsection{The direct all-choice contradiction}

\]
The row-affinity conjunct supplies one ambient coefficient pair on $B_h$, allowed to depend on $h$. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:71:lem:affine} gives $|B_h|\le r$. Translation $h\mapsto G.y+h$ is injective, and weak support accounts for every point of $G.B$, so
\[
 |G.B|=\sum_{h\in\mathcal H}|B_h|\le r|\mathcal H|.
\]
The first weak mass bound and (9.3) yield $\delta L\le r$. On the other hand, width and the two length lower bounds give
\[
 W\le(cN^\beta)^\varepsilon
 \le\operatorname{len}(F.R)^\varepsilon\le L\le r/\delta.
 \tag{9.5}
\]
This is impossible because
\[
 W\delta=2^{135-43}a^{-704+224}
 =2^{92}a^{-480}=2^{92}r^{480s}>r.
 \tag{9.6}
\]
For example, $a^{-1}=r^s\ge8r$ makes the last strict inequality immediate.

The proof does not analyze the alternative steps or require $F.R\subseteq T$, $F.R\subseteq E.Q$, $F.R\subseteq D.P$, $G.B\subseteq A$, a particular starting point, or absence of wrapping. It does not use the second weak mass bound or an upper bound on the length of $F.R$. It excludes the weak output before any of those extra conditions could help.

\begin{lemma}[Sharp finite subgroup radius]\label{gsr:en:71:lem:subgroup}
A nontrivial finite subgroup of $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ of order $t\ge2$ has maximum centered absolute value
\[

\]

This is an ordinary mathematical statement on positive moduli. It does not claim that deleting a primality typeclass binder from a Lean declaration leaves a well-typed declaration. \begin{corollary}[Every fixed prime-power family with unchanged threshold]
Fix a prime $p$ and an integer $s$ with $p^s\ge8p$. For every $k$ satisfying the original eight-threshold exponent specification (4.4) with $r=p$, the context at $N=p^k$ has the selected full-budget package and excludes every weak continuation for every genuine initial pair at the exact cutoff.
