\subsection{Mixed prime support with independent exponents}
For $r=6$, one may take $s=3$ because $6^3\ge8\cdot6$. The theorem applies to every sufficiently large $N=2^e3^f$ with $e,f\ge3$. There is no requirement $e=f$. For $r=10$, $s=2$ suffices and the moduli include every sufficiently large $2^e5^f$ with $e,f\ge2$. If $r$ itself has repeated prime factors, the lower exponent requirements are correspondingly $f_\ell\ge s e_\ell$.

The factorization support is fixed before the threshold is selected. The theorem gives neither a threshold uniform in $r,s$ nor examples at squarefree moduli. Indeed $r^s\mid N$ with $s\ge2$ forces at least exponent two at each prime dividing $r$.

\subsection{Why outside support is a real boundary}
The other construction steps use only divisibility, but the global affine cap can fail if $N$ has an additional prime divisor. For example, let $r=2$, $s=4$ and $N=80$. Then $r^s=16$ divides $N$, but the extra prime factor $5$ does not divide $r$. The affine map $3x$ agrees with $\lfloor x.\mathrm{val}/2\rfloor$ at $x=0,32,64$, all in the same residue class modulo $2$. Writing $x=2j$, agreement is $5j=0\pmod{80}$, which holds at $j=0,16,32$ in $0\le j<40$.

Thus both the single-class cap one and the global cap $r=2$ can fail outside the support hypothesis. This is a finite algebraic boundary example, not a full-budget witness at $N=80$, a counterexample to the actual prime theorem, or a classification of what other arguments might prove outside the present families.

\section[{The context and the imported analytic interfaces\srctag{70}}]{The context and the imported analytic interfaces}\label{gsr:en:70:sec:d2}\label{gsr:en:70:sec:inputs}
\srcnote{70}{Section 2}

\subsection{Section 13 contexts}
Let $N$ be prime. A map $F$ is order-eight Freiman on a finite set if it preserves equalities between sums of eight elements, with repetitions allowed. A map $\phi:G^2\to G$ is separately order-eight Freiman on $A\subseteq G^2$ when its horizontal and vertical restrictions have this property on their respective sections of $A$.

An eight-arrangement at height $h$ is a choice of sixteen horizontal coordinates $x_i$ and sixteen vertical coordinates $y_i$ with
\[
 \sum_{i=1}^8x_i=\sum_{i=9}^{16}x_i,
 \qquad (x_i,y_i),(x_i,y_i+h)\in A\quad(1\le i\le16).
\]
It is respected by $\phi$ when the equality also holds between the sums of the sixteen values $\phi(x_i,y_i+h)-\phi(x_i,y_i)$. Let $C(h)$ and $C_\phi(h)$ count all and respected arrangements, respectively.

\begin{definition}[Section 13 context]\label{gsr:en:70:def:context}
A context consists of $A\subseteq G^2$, $\phi:G^2\to G$, and its actual density $a\in(0,1]$ such that
\[
 |A|=aN^2,\qquad
 (1-\eta)\sum_hC(h)\le\sum_hC_\phi(h),\qquad \eta=2^{-44},
\]
and $\phi$ is separately order-eight Freiman on $A$.
\end{definition}
A height is good if $C_\phi(h)\ge(1-2\eta)C(h)$, and strong if it is good and $C(h)\ge a^{32}N^{31}/16$. These are the exact source predicates.

\subsection{Scalar parameters}
Throughout the local proof define
\begin{align}
 \theta(a)&=2^{-59}a^{176},&
 t(a)&=2^{-620025}a^{1843952},&
 b(a)&=2^{620143}a^{-1844304},\label{gsr:en:70:eq:tb}\\
 K(a)&=2^{114}a^{-320},&
 c(a)&=\tfrac12\,2^{-228K(a)}a^{576K(a)},\label{gsr:en:70:eq:c}\\
 \kappa(a)&=\lceil K(a)\rceil,&
 z(a)&=\frac{2^{-155\kappa(a)}(a^{32}/16)^{18\kappa(a)}}{\kappa(a)},\label{gsr:en:70:eq:z}\\
 f_*(a)&=2^{-100}a^{448},&g_*(a)&=2^{-284}a^{1408},&W(a)&=2^{135}a^{-704}.\label{gsr:en:70:eq:fg}
\end{align}
The notation $f_*,g_*$ distinguishes exponents from the Fourier input function $f$. The radius $z(a)$ is the actual rounded Section 10 radius, including division by $\kappa(a)$; it is not replaced by the unrounded prefactor $2c(a)$.

On $[a_0,1]$, the positive quantities $\theta,t,c,z,f_*,g_*$ are nondecreasing, while $b,W,K,\kappa$ are nonincreasing. For $c$, the base $a$ increases while its positive exponent $576K(a)$ decreases; both changes increase $a^{576K(a)}$ for $a\le1$. For $z$, each of its three factors increases as $a$ increases and $\kappa$ decreases. No continuity through a ceiling is needed. We also have $c(a)\le1/2$.

\subsection{Initial progression and weighted spectral data}
The source result \codefiftythree{lemma\_13\_4\_holds} supplies an integer $1\le q\le b(a)$, a proper nonzero-step progression $P$, a set $H\subseteq P$, and coefficients $a_i,b_i\in G$ for $1\le i\le q$. Put
\[
 u=\frac{t(a)^2}{16q},\qquad x=\frac{t(a)}{64\pi}N^u,\qquad m_P=\lfloor x\rfloor.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:initial}
 \len P=m_P\ \text{or}\ m_P-1,\qquad
 \sum_{h\in H,\ h\text{ good}}C(h)\ge\frac{a^{32}}8N^{31}\len P.
\end{equation}
Whenever $h\in H$ and the vertical-edge fibre has Fourier coefficient at least $\theta(a)N^2$ at $r$, some $i$ has $r=a_i h+b_i$. The exact corrected cutoff has $N^2$, not $N$.
The source also proves the arrangement cap
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:cap}
 0\le C(h)\le N^{31}.
\end{equation}
The chosen $\theta(a)$ satisfies the required $0<\theta(a)\le a^{32}/4$.

\subsection{Height models and short difference rules}
For a strong height $h$, let the vertical-edge domain consist of pairs $v=(x,y)$ with $(x,y),(x,y+h)\in A$. Its phase difference is
\[
 \phi_h(v)=\phi(x,y+h)-\phi(x,y).
\]
The imported all-density height-model theorem supplies $Y_h$ in this domain with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:Ymass}
 |Y_h|\ge\delta_{\rm row}N^2,\qquad\delta_{\rm row}=2^{-43}a^{224},
\end{equation}
and a scalar Bohr-difference model with radius $z(a)$ and spectrum $\mathcal K_h$. Every $r\in\mathcal K_h$ satisfies the spectral cutoff used in the preceding paragraph. There is no $a\le1/6$ restriction: the source's adaptive fibre normalization already removes it.

Write $|r|_N$ for centered absolute residue, and
\[
 \operatorname{Bohr}(\mathcal K,\rho)
 =\{d\in G:|rd|_N\le\rho N\text{ for every }r\in\mathcal K\}.
\]
Corollary 10.14, applied to the supplied scalar model, states that if $m\ge1$ is an integer and $d\in\operatorname{Bohr}(\mathcal K_h,z(a)/m)$, then a scalar $\lambda_h\in G$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:shortdiff}
 \phi_h(v)-\phi_h(w)=\lambda_h(v_1-w_1)
\end{equation}
for $v,w\in Y_h$ whenever $v_1-w_1=jd$ for some integer $-m\le j\le m$. There is no further scale requirement in this corollary.

The imported \codefiftythree{common\_step\_row\_selection} says that if $d\ne0$, $m>0$, $m^2\le N$, and \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:Ymass} and \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:shortdiff} hold for a finite height set $I$, then there is a proper progression $R$ of step $d$ and length
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:Rshort}
 \len R=m\quad\text{or}\quad m+1
\end{equation}
on whose restricted $Y_h$ sections $\phi_h$ is affine in the first coordinate, with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:rowaggregate}
 \sum_{h\in I}|\{v\in Y_h:v_1\in R\}|
 \ge\delta_{\rm row}\len R\,N|I|.
\end{equation}
We use this constructor directly, preserving the selected witness's exact alternative \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:Rshort}.

\subsection{Row extraction and coefficient localization}
The exact Stage 13.6 predicate includes the source's old length bound
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:oldbeta}
 c(a)N^{\beta_{\rm old}(a)}\le\len R,
 \qquad \beta_{\rm old}(a)=2^{-13Q_*(a)},\quad
 Q_*(a)=2^{1048576}a^{-2097152},
\end{equation}
as well as the row masses, row linearity, and an aggregate mass coefficient $2^{-48}a^{256}$. From genuine Stage 13.6 data, the all-scale Stage 13.7 theorem supplies a proper nonzero-step $S\subseteq R$ with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:S}
 L=\len S\ge(\len R)^{f_*(a)}.
\end{equation}
Its retained domain is contained in the original $A$. If $L\ge W(a)$, Stage 13.8 supplies $C\subseteq A$, $J_0\subseteq Q$, an offset $y$, and scalar order-eight Freiman maps $A_c,B_c$ on $J_0$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:coeffdata}
 \begin{gathered}
 C\subseteq S\times(J_0+y),\qquad |C|\ge\delta L\len Q,
 \qquad\delta=2^{-135}a^{704},\\
 \phi(x,z)=A_c(z-y)+B_c(z-y)x\quad((x,z)\in C).
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
Primality, original-domain containment, and the width condition are all retained here.

Finally we import the all-scale \codefiftythree{extract\_bilinear\_cell}. If $T$ is a proper nonzero-step progression of positive length $v$, $X_0$ is a nonempty column set, $J\subseteq T$, the two coefficient maps are order-eight Freiman on $J$, and
\[
 C_0\subseteq X_0\times(J+y),\quad |C_0|\ge\delta|X_0|v,\quad
 \phi(x,z)=A_c(z-y)+B_c(z-y)x\quad((x,z)\in C_0),
\]
with $0<\delta\le1$, then there is a proper nonzero-step $U\subseteq T$, of length $M$, for which
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:localized}
 M\ge v^{\delta^2/2^{14}},\qquad
 D=\{(x,z)\in C_0:z-y\in U\},\qquad
 |D|\ge\delta|X_0|M,
\end{equation}
and the original $\phi$ is bilinear on $D$. This is the simultaneous one-domain coefficient exponent, with no second exponent loss for the two maps and no lower-scale premise such as $8\le v^{\delta^2/2^{14}}$.

\paragraph{What is imported.}
The analytic assertions of this section, including their existence claims, are imported from the pinned declarations identified in Appendix~\ref{gsr:fz:70:app:map}. The subsequent elementary arguments verify how those interfaces compose; they do not independently reprove every Section 7--13 analytic result or replay Lean.

\section[{From simultaneous recurrence to own-step partitions\srctag{70}}]{From simultaneous recurrence to own-step partitions}\label{gsr:en:70:sec:d3}\label{gsr:en:70:sec:partition}
\srcnote{70}{Section 3}
This section restates the finite mechanism of canonical source 16 \cite{srcsixteen}. Its role is to expose the finite hypotheses paid by the recurrence theorem, including the strict source threshold and the actual step of each output cell.

\begin{lemma}[Rectangular Dirichlet approximation]\label{gsr:en:70:lem:dirichlet}
If $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_q\in\Tquot$, $0<\delta_i\le1/2$, $J_i=\lceil2/\delta_i\rceil$, and $T=\prod_iJ_i$, there is an integer $1\le t\le T$ such that
\[
 \|t\xi_i\|_{\Tquot}\le\delta_i/2\quad(1\le i\le q).
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Partition the $i$th unit interval into $J_i$ equal half-open intervals. The $T+1$ points $n(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_q)$ for $0\le n\le T$ occupy $T$ rectangular boxes. Subtract two in the same box. Their positive index difference is at most $T$, and the $i$th circle distance is at most $1/J_i\le\delta_i/2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Finite own-step certificate]\label{gsr:en:70:lem:certificate}
Fix integers $q\ge1$, $R\ge1$, $L\ge2$, torus coefficients $A_i,B_i$, and $0<\delta_i\le1/2$. Put
\[
 J_i=\lceil2/\delta_i\rceil,\quad T=\prod_iJ_i,\quad
 \eta_i=\frac{\delta_i}{4LT^2},\quad Q_0=\left\lfloor\frac R{LT}\right\rfloor.
\]
If an integer $1\le s\le Q_0$ obeys $\|A_i s^2\|_{\Tquot}\le\eta_i$ for all $i$, then $\{0,\ldots,R-1\}$ has an exact disjoint partition into progressions $X$ of lengths between $L$ and $2L-1$ such that, for their own integer steps $d_X$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:ownstepindex}
 \|(A_i n+B_i)d_X\|_{\Tquot}\le\delta_i
 \quad(n\in X,\ 1\le i\le q).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Each residue chain modulo $s$ has at least $LT$ points. Any chain of $n\ge K$ points partitions into consecutive blocks of lengths $K$ through $2K-1$: take $\lfloor n/K\rfloor$ blocks and distribute its remainder among them. Apply this with $K=LT$.

On one such block write its points as $x+sj$, $0\le j<n<2LT$. By Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:70:lem:dirichlet}, some $1\le t\le T$ satisfies
\[
 \|t(A_i x+B_i)s\|_{\Tquot}\le\delta_i/2\quad\text{for all }i.
\]
Split the block's $j$-indices into residue chains modulo $t$. Each has at least $L$ points because $n\ge LT$ and $t\le T$. Partition each chain into blocks with lengths $L$ through $2L-1$. The resulting progression has its actual step $d_X=st$. For any of its indices,
\[
 \begin{split}
 \|(A_i(x+sj)+B_i)st\|_{\Tquot}
 &\le\|t(A_i x+B_i)s\|_{\Tquot}+jt\|A_is^2\|_{\Tquot}\\
 &\le\delta_i/2+2LT^2\eta_i=\delta_i.
 \end{split}
\]
All operations were partitions, so there is no endpoint deletion or discarded mass.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Transport to a cyclic progression]\label{gsr:en:70:lem:transport}
Let $P=P(h_0,d_0;R)$ be proper in $\Z/N\Z$ and $a_i,b_i\in\Z/N\Z$. Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:70:lem:certificate} with
\[
 A_i=a_id_0^2/N\pmod1,\qquad
 B_i=(a_ih_0+b_i)d_0/N\pmod1.
\]
Its transported cells $Q$ partition the carrier of $P$, are proper of the same lengths, have nonzero step, and satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:ownstepcyclic}
 |(a_i h+b_i)\stfiftythree Q|_N\le\delta_iN\qquad(h\in Q).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Represent the coefficients by integers when forming torus classes. If an index cell has step $st$, its transported step is $d_0st$. For $h=h_0+d_0n$ the identity
\[
 \frac{(a_i h+b_i)d_0st}{N}=(A_i n+B_i)st\pmod1
\]
proves \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:ownstepcyclic}. Every transported indexing is a restriction of the injective indexing of $P$, hence proper. Each has at least $L\ge2$ points, so its step cannot be zero. No inverse of $d_0$, $2$, or $4$ is used in this transfer.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The external recurrence input}
For each $q\ge1$, Lau's Theorem 1.1 \cite{lau}, specialized to degree two, supplies a constant $X_0(q)>2$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:Lauinput}
 \begin{gathered}
 X>X_0(q),\quad 0<\eta_i\le1/100,\quad
 \prod_i\eta_i^{-1}\le X^{1/22}\\
 \Longrightarrow\quad
 \exists s\in\Z:\quad 1\le s<X,\quad
 \|A_i s^2\|_{\Tquot}\le\eta_i\ \text{for all }i.
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
The constant is uniform over the coefficient tuple and the individual tolerances. Here is the numerical specialization. Take Lau's parameters $\varepsilon=1/16$ and $M=6$, with dimension $q$ and degree $2$. The required lower bound $M\ge\max\{4,1/2+\log(\varepsilon^{-1})/(2\log2)\}$ holds. His denominator is
\[
 2c_2=\frac{169}{8}+\frac9{32q^5}\le\frac{685}{32}<22.
\]
Thus the stronger product hypothesis in \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:Lauinput} suffices. For torus coefficients choose any real lifts; integer changes of lift do not affect the conclusion. Neither the input nor this report assigns a numerical value to $X_0(q)$.

In Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:70:lem:certificate}, $T\ge4$ and $L\ge2$, so
\[
 0<\eta_i\le\frac{1/2}{4\cdot2\cdot16}=\frac1{256}<\frac1{100}.
\]
Writing $\Delta=\prod_i\delta_i$, the two finite sufficient hypotheses are exactly
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:finitecriteria}
 Q_0>X_0(q),\qquad Q_0\ge(4LT^2)^{22q}\Delta^{-22}.
\end{equation}
Indeed $\prod_i\eta_i^{-1}=(4LT^2)^q\Delta^{-1}$. The external output $s<Q_0$ is more than the certificate needs. Crucially, the second inequality does not replace the first strict threshold.

\subsection{Balanced powers and a finite symbolic threshold}
Put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:rq}
 r_q=\frac1{128q^2},\qquad L=\lceil R^{r_q}\rceil,
 \qquad\delta_i=R^{-r_q}.
\end{equation}
The available exponent margin is
\[
 (q+1)(44q+1)r_q\le\frac{45}{64}<1,
\]
because $90q^2-(q+1)(44q+1)=(q-1)(46q+1)\ge0$.
Define positive exponents and constants
\begin{align}
 s_q&=1-(q+1)r_q,&v_q&=1-(q+1)(44q+1)r_q,\label{gsr:en:70:eq:sqvq}\\
 A_q&=4\cdot3^q(8\cdot3^{2q})^{22q},&
 B_q&=8\cdot3^q(X_0(q)+1),\notag\\
 R_q&=\max\{2^{1/r_q},A_q^{1/v_q},B_q^{1/s_q}\}.\label{gsr:en:70:eq:Rq}
\end{align}
If an integer $R\ge R_q$, then $R^{r_q}\ge2$, $L\le2R^{r_q}$, and $T\le3^qR^{qr_q}$. Moreover
\[
 \frac R{LT}\ge\frac{R^{s_q}}{2\cdot3^q}\ge4(X_0(q)+1)>2.
\]
The floor is at least half its argument, so
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:Q0floor}
 Q_0\ge\frac{R^{s_q}}{4\cdot3^q}\ge2(X_0(q)+1)>X_0(q).
\end{equation}
Also
\[
 (4LT^2)^{22q}\Delta^{-22}
 \le(8\cdot3^{2q})^{22q}R^{44q(q+1)r_q}
 \le\frac{R^{s_q}}{4\cdot3^q}\le Q_0,
\]
where the middle inequality is precisely $R^{v_q}\ge A_q$. This proves both conditions in \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:finitecriteria}.

\subsection{Critical heights without a partition loss}
In the Stage 13.4 progression define
\[
 w(h)=C(h)\,1_{\{h\in H\text{ and }h\text{ good}\}}.
\]
By \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:initial} and \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:cap}, its mean is at least $(a^{32}/8)N^{31}$ and its values lie in $[0,N^{31}]$. The exact own-step partition therefore has a cell $Q$ with at least that mean. At the smaller cutoff $(a^{32}/16)N^{31}$ the bounded-variable inequality gives a high-value fraction at least
\[
 \frac{a^{32}/8-a^{32}/16}{1-a^{32}/16}
 =\frac{a^{32}}{16-a^{32}}\ge\frac{a^{32}}{16}.
\]
Since the cutoff is positive, these points lie in $H$, are good, and meet the strong-height threshold. Thus the set $I$ of critical heights in $Q$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:critical}
 |I|\ge\frac{a^{32}}{16}\len Q,
 \qquad \len Q\ge(\len P)^{r_q},\qquad
 |(a_i h+b_i)\stfiftythree Q|_N\le(\len P)^{-r_q}N.
\end{equation}
The last estimate holds on every point of $Q$, not only on $I$.

\section[{One threshold for every actual density\srctag{70}}]{One threshold for every actual density}\label{gsr:en:70:sec:d4}\label{gsr:en:70:sec:threshold}
\srcnote{70}{Section 4}
The local quantitative improvement is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:betanew}
 \beta(a)=\frac{t(a)^2}{4096b(a)^3}
 =2^{-3100491}a^{9220816},\qquad
 e(a)=\frac{\beta(a)f_*(a)g_*(a)}2
 =2^{-3100876}a^{9222672}.
\end{equation}
Both are increasing, positive, and $\beta(a)<1/2$ on $(0,1]$.

\begin{theorem}[Uniform local extraction]\label{gsr:en:70:thm:local}
Fix $0<a_0\le1$. There is a threshold $N_{\rm loc}(a_0)$, specified in \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:Nloc}, such that every prime $N\ge N_{\rm loc}(a_0)$ and every Section 13 context of actual density $a\in[a_0,1]$ admit proper equal-length progressions $V,W$ with the same nonzero step, a set $B\subseteq A\cap(V\times W)$, and a global function $\mu$ of the form \eqref{gsr:fm:70:eq:bilinear}, for which
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:localconclusion}
 \len V=\len W\ge N^{e(a)},\qquad
 |B|\ge2^{-137}a^{704}\len V\len W,\qquad
 \phi|_B=\mu|_B.
\end{equation}
Only the threshold uses $a_0$; the exponent and retained density use the actual $a$.
\end{theorem}

\subsection{The finite maximum}
A subscript zero denotes evaluation at $a_0$. Since $1\le q\le b(a)\le b_0$, only finitely many recurrence constants occur. Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:Rstar}
 R_* =\max_{1\le q\le\lfloor b_0\rfloor}R_q,
 \qquad d_0=\frac{t_0}{128\pi},\quad
 u_0=\frac{t_0^2}{16b_0},\quad z_0=z(a_0),\quad W_0=W(a_0).
\end{equation}
The maximum exists without any monotonicity assumption on $X_0(q)$. In particular it is uniform over all possible actual densities and coefficient tuples. Now set
\begin{align}
 H_0&=\max\left\{2,\frac3{c_0},\frac2{d_0},\frac1{d_0z_0},
                    \frac{W_0^{1/f_{*,0}}}{c_0}\right\},\label{gsr:en:70:eq:H0}\\
 N_{\rm loc}(a_0)&=
 \left\lceil\max\left\{2,
       (R_*/d_0)^{1/u_0},H_0^{1/\beta_0},3^{1/e_0}\right\}\right\rceil.\label{gsr:en:70:eq:Nloc}
\end{align}
Every quantity is positive and $d_0<1$. These expressions keep huge powers symbolic. They constitute a finite formula in the unspecified $X_0(q)$; calling \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:Nloc} a numerical effective bound would be incorrect.

\subsection{Initial floors and the improved exponent}
Fix $N\ge N_{\rm loc}(a_0)$ and an actual density $a\in[a_0,1]$. Use the initial progression from Section~\ref{gsr:en:70:sec:inputs}. Since $u=t(a)^2/(16q)\ge u_0$, the threshold gives
\[
 d_0N^u\ge d_0N^{u_0}\ge R_*\ge2.
\]
With $x=t(a)N^u/(64\pi)$ we have $x\ge4$. The two possible integer losses in \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:initial} give $\len P>x-2\ge x/2$, hence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:Plower}
 \len P\ge\frac{t(a)}{128\pi}N^u\ge d_0N^u\ge R_*.
\end{equation}
Thus the partition and critical-height construction applies. Its exact exponent identity is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:urbeta}
 ur_q=\frac{t(a)^2}{2048q^3}\ge2\beta(a).
\end{equation}
As $0<r_q\le1$ and $0<d_0<1$, this implies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:Qlower}
 \len Q\ge(\len P)^{r_q}
 \ge d_0^{r_q}N^{ur_q}\ge d_0N^{2\beta(a)}.
\end{equation}

Choose the new integer row length
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:m}
 m=\lceil c(a)N^{\beta(a)}\rceil.
\end{equation}
Since $N^{\beta(a)}\ge N^{\beta_0}\ge H_0$, all of the following hold:
\begin{align}
 m&\ge c(a)N^{\beta(a)}\ge c_0N^{\beta_0}\ge3,\label{gsr:en:70:eq:budget1}\\
 m&\le c(a)N^{\beta(a)}+1\le N^{\beta(a)},\label{gsr:en:70:eq:budget2}\\
 m^2&\le N^{2\beta(a)}\le N,\label{gsr:en:70:eq:budget3}\\
 m+1&\le2N^{\beta(a)}\le d_0N^{2\beta(a)}\le\len Q,\label{gsr:en:70:eq:budget4}\\
 m(\len P)^{-r_q}&\le\frac1{d_0N^{\beta(a)}}\le z_0\le z(a),\label{gsr:en:70:eq:budget5}\\
 c(a)N^{\beta(a)}&\ge W_0^{1/f_{*,0}},\label{gsr:en:70:eq:budget6}\\
 N^{e(a)}&\ge N^{e_0}\ge3.\label{gsr:en:70:eq:budget7}
\end{align}
For \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:budget2}, use $c(a)\le1/2$ and $N^{\beta(a)}\ge2$. The fourth and fifth bounds are paid by $2/d_0$ and $1/(d_0z_0)$ in $H_0$. The sixth will pay every actual-density Stage 13.8 width requirement; the last will absorb both a constant and the final subtraction by one.

\subsection{Compatibility with the source stage predicates}
For the Lau choice, the new $Q$ also satisfies the old Stage 13.5 accuracy and length inequalities. Indeed
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:rlegacy}
 r_q>2^{-11q}\ge2^{-12q}\qquad(q\ge1).
\end{equation}
The first inequality is equivalent to $2^{11q}>128q^2$. It holds at $q=1$, and when $q$ increases by one the exponential multiplies by $2048$, while $(q+1)^2/q^2\le4$. The new critical-height fraction $a^{32}/16$ also dominates the old $a^{32}/20$.

We need the old Stage 13.6 lower-length conjunct, but will not use its hardcoded Bohr wrapper. To verify the conjunct, put $h=\log_2(1/a)\ge0$. Then
\[
 \begin{split}
 -\log_2\beta(a)&=3100491+9220816h
 <2^{24}(1+h)\\
 &\le2^{24+2h}<2^{1048576+2097152h}=Q_*(a)<13Q_*(a).
 \end{split}
\]
Here $1+h\le2^{2h}$ for $h\ge0$, for example from the exponential series and $2\log2>1$. Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:betacompare}
 \beta(a)>\beta_{\rm old}(a),\qquad
 c(a)N^{\beta_{\rm old}(a)}\le m.
\end{equation}
This checks precisely the legacy length condition required downstream.

\section[{The direct row constructor and the selected parent\srctag{70}}]{The direct row constructor and the selected parent}\label{gsr:en:70:sec:d5}\label{gsr:en:70:sec:constructor}
\srcnote{70}{Section 5}
Fix a critical height $h\in I$ and its all-density model from Section~\ref{gsr:en:70:sec:inputs}. If $r\in\mathcal K_h$, its fibre identity gives the cutoff $\theta(a)N^2$, and $h\in H$ lets Stage 13.4 write $r=a_i h+b_i$. Since $h\in Q$, the new own-step estimate and \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:budget5} give
\[
 |r\stfiftythree Q|_N\le(\len P)^{-r_q}N\le\frac{z(a)}mN.
\]
Therefore, directly from the definition,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:directbohr}
 \stfiftythree Q\in\operatorname{Bohr}(\mathcal K_h,z(a)/m).
\end{equation}
Apply Corollary 10.14 to obtain \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:shortdiff} with $d=\stfiftythree Q$. The model's adaptive normalization is unchanged by the new value of $m$.

\paragraph{Why an old wrapper is not enough.}
The source helper \codefiftythree{stage136\_common\_step\_mem\_bohr} asks for the different numerical premise
\[
 (\len P)^{-2^{-11q}}\le z(a)/m.
\]
Our better actual step bound does not prove that weaker exponent's numerical inequality at the larger $m$. The same fixed exponent is inherited by \codefiftythree{lemma\_13\_6\_of\_bohr\_models} and the corresponding initial-stages wrapper. Calling those helpers unchanged would leave an unjustified hypothesis. Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:directbohr} and the direct short-difference route avoid it.

Now apply \codefiftythree{common\_step\_row\_selection} with the actual nonzero step $d=\stfiftythree Q$, the height set $I$, the original $\phi_h$, and the sets $Y_h$. Bounds \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:budget1} and \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:budget3} provide $m>0$ and $m^2\le N$. We retain the constructor's witness $R$ with
\[
 \stfiftythree R=\stfiftythree Q\ne0,\quad R\text{ proper},\quad
 \len R=m\ \text{or}\ m+1,
\]
and \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:rowaggregate}. The lower length condition follows from \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:betacompare}. By \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:critical}, the aggregate mass is at least

 =2^{-47}a^{256}\len Q\len R\,N,

Let $n_R=\len R$. The retained alternative and $m\ge3$ imply
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:shortparent}
 2(n_R-1)\le2m<m^2\le N.
\end{equation}
This is information about the selected constructor witness, not a conclusion about every arbitrary Stage 13.6 witness.

The all-scale Stage 13.7 theorem now gives $S\subseteq R$ with
\[

\]
By \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:budget6}, $f_*(a)\ge f_{*,0}$ and $W_0\ge1$, so $L\ge W_0\ge W(a)$. Stage 13.8 therefore gives exactly \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:coeffdata}. This explicitly pays its width condition and preserves its original-domain hypothesis.

\section[{Short-parent geometry without an exponent loss\srctag{70}}]{Short-parent geometry without an exponent loss}\label{gsr:en:70:sec:d6}\label{gsr:en:70:sec:geometry}
\srcnote{70}{Section 6}
We next turn \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:coeffdata} into a common-step square. The only analytic input within this section is the stated coefficient localization \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:localized}.

\begin{lemma}[Rectification inside a short progression]\label{gsr:en:70:lem:rectify}
Let $P$ be a proper nonzero-step progression in $\F_N$, of length $n$, with $2(n-1)<N$. If a proper progression $X\subseteq P$ has length at least two, then, after possibly reversing only its indexing, there is an integer $s\ge1$ with
\[
 \stfiftythree X=s\stfiftythree P,\qquad s(\len X-1)\le n-1.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Normalize by the affine bijection $z\mapsto(z-P.start)/(\stfiftythree P)$. The successive points of $X$ have unique indices $i_j\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$. The differences $i_{j+1}-i_j$ all represent one residue and lie in $[-(n-1),n-1]$. Any two differ by an integer of absolute value less than $N$, so they are equal as integers. Their common value is nonzero because $X$ is proper and has at least two points. Reverse its indexing if that value is negative. Comparing the extreme indices gives the bound. Carrier, length, and function values do not change.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Balanced aligned parents]\label{gsr:en:70:lem:balanced}
If integers $L\ge2$, $s\ge1$, and $q_Q$ satisfy $s(L-1)<q_Q$, the interval $\{0,\ldots,q_Q-1\}$ partitions into step-$s$ progressions whose lengths lie between $\lceil L/2\rceil$ and $L$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Every residue chain modulo $s$ has length $n\ge L-1$. Put $c=\lceil n/L\rceil$ and divide the chain into $c$ consecutive blocks with lengths differing by at most one. The upper bound is $L$. If $c=1$, the lower bound is $L-1\ge\lceil L/2\rceil$. If $c\ge2$, then $n\ge(c-1)L+1$ and
\[
 n/c\ge L-(L-1)/c\ge(L+1)/2.
\]
Thus the smallest integer block length is at least $\lfloor(L+1)/2\rfloor=\lceil L/2\rceil$. All blocks are disjoint and cover the interval.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Contained common-step covers]\label{gsr:en:70:lem:cover}
Let $S=P(x,d;L)$ and $T=P(y,e;M)$ be proper progressions in a cyclic group, where $e=jd\ne0$ and $j\ge1$ is an integer. If $1\le k\le M$, $jk\le L$, and $D\subseteq S\times T$ has $|D|\ge\delta LM$ with $\delta\ge0$, there are proper $V\subseteq S$, $W\subseteq T$, of common step $e$ and length $k$, such that
\[
 |D\cap(V\times W)|\ge(\delta/4)k^2.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Split $S$ into its index residue chains modulo $j$. Each has at least $k$ points and their lengths sum to $L$. On a chain of $n\ge k$ points take consecutive $k$-blocks and, if a nonempty remainder remains, add the terminal $k$-block. They stay in the parent and cover the chain, with total indexed capacity
\[
 k\lceil n/k\rceil<n+k\le2n.
\]
This gives a step-$e$ cover of $S$ of capacity less than $2L$. The same endpoint construction on $T$ gives a step-$e$ cover of capacity less than $2M$. Their products cover $S\times T$ with total capacity less than $4LM$. Count actual elements of $D$ with multiplicity in the cover. Some cell has density at least $\delta/4$. Properness is inherited from the parent indexings; no extension outside either parent is used.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The square from a selected short parent]\label{gsr:en:70:prop:geometry}
Suppose \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:coeffdata} holds with $0<\delta\le1$, $L\ge3$, $S\subseteq R$, $\stfiftythree R=\stfiftythree Q\ne0$, $n_R\le\len Q$, and $2(n_R-1)<N$. There is a proper common-step square of side $k$, with retained set $B\subseteq C$ and original-phase bilinearity, such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:geoside}
 |B|\ge(\delta/4)k^2,\qquad
 k\ge\lceil L/2\rceil^{\delta^2/2^{14}}-1.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Rectify $S\subseteq R$, reversing its indexing if necessary. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:70:lem:rectify} gives
\[
 \stfiftythree S=s\stfiftythree Q,\qquad s\ge1,\qquad
 s(L-1)\le n_R-1<\len Q.
\]
Transport Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:70:lem:balanced} through the proper indexing of $Q$. It partitions $Q$ into proper parents $T_i$ of step $\stfiftythree S$, lengths $v_i$ in $[\lceil L/2\rceil,L]$, and total length $\len Q$. The restrictions
\[
 C_i=\{(x,z)\in C:z-y\in T_i\}
\]
partition $C$. Averaging their actual pair counts selects a parent $T$, of length $v$, with $|C_T|\ge\delta Lv$. The coefficient maps restrict to $J_0\cap T$ and remain order-eight Freiman; the row formula persists.

Apply \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:localized} with $X_0=S$ and this same $\delta$. It gives $U\subseteq T$, length $M\ge v^g$ where $g=\delta^2/2^{14}$, and $D\subseteq C_T\cap(S\times(U+y))$ with $|D|\ge\delta LM$ and original-phase bilinearity. No density was lost in either selection. Since $L\ge3$, $v\ge2$, $g>0$, and $M$ is an integer, $M\ge2$.

Also $2(v-1)\le2(L-1)\le2(n_R-1)<N$. Rectify $U\subseteq T$, again allowing only indexing reversal. Then
\[
 \stfiftythree U=j\stfiftythree S,\qquad j\ge1,\qquad j(M-1)\le v-1\le L-1.
\]
Set $k=M-1$. It is positive, $k\le M$, and $jk\le L$. Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:70:lem:cover} to $S$ and $U+y$ to obtain $B\subseteq D$ with mass at least $(\delta/4)k^2$. Finally $k\ge v^g-1\ge\lceil L/2\rceil^g-1$. All output carriers stay in the corresponding parents, so $B\subseteq C\subseteq A$. Original-phase bilinearity is restriction-invariant.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{The height offset is not discarded.}
If the localized coefficients are $A_c(h)=a_1h+a_0$ and $B_c(h)=b_1h+b_0$, their original-coordinate formula is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:offset}
 \phi(x,z)=(a_0-a_1y)+(b_0-b_1y)x+a_1z+b_1xz.
\end{equation}
Both offset corrections are present. Restricting carriers and reversing indexings do not change $\phi$ or the ambient variables. We are constructing a suitable localized $U$, rather than asserting new geometry for every arbitrary Stage 13.9 witness.

\section[{Finishing the local power bound\srctag{70}}]{Finishing the local power bound}\label{gsr:en:70:sec:d7}\label{gsr:en:70:sec:locfinish}
\srcnote{70}{Section 7}
In our application $\delta=2^{-135}a^{704}$ and
\[
 \frac{\delta^2}{2^{14}}=2^{-284}a^{1408}=g_*(a).
\]
Equations \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:S}, \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:m}, and \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:geoside} yield the coefficient-bearing lower bound
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:coeffside}
 k\ge 2^{-g_*(a)}c(a)^{f_*(a)g_*(a)}
           N^{\beta(a)f_*(a)g_*(a)}-1.
\end{equation}
The coefficient is uniformly greater than $1/2$, despite the very small $c(a)$.

\begin{lemma}[Uniform coefficient control]\label{gsr:en:70:lem:coefficient}
For every $0<a\le1$,
\[
 D(a)=2^{-g_*(a)}c(a)^{f_*(a)g_*(a)}>1/2.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Put $h=\log_2(1/a)\ge0$. From \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:c},
\[
 \log_2(1/c(a))=1+2^{114}a^{-320}(228+576h).
\]
Consequently
\[
 -\log_2D(a)
 =2^{-284}a^{1408}+2^{-384}a^{1856}
    +2^{-270}a^{1536}(228+576h).
\]
Since $\log2\ge1/2$, the exponential series gives
\[
 2^{1536h}\ge1+768h,\qquad
 228+576h\le228(1+768h).
\]
The density-logarithm factor is therefore at most $228$, and the entire loss is less than $230\cdot2^{-270}<1$. Exponentiating proves the claim.
\end{proof}

By \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:budget7}, $x=N^{e(a)}\ge3$. Since $\beta f_*g_*=2e$, \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:coeffside} gives
\[
 k\ge\tfrac12x^2-1\ge x=N^{e(a)}.
\]
The last inequality holds for $x\ge3$, for instance because $x^2-2x-2\ge9-6-2>0$ there and is increasing. The mass in \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:geoside} is
\[
 (\delta/4)k^2=2^{-137}a^{704}k^2.
\]
Together with the containment and formula \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:offset}, this proves Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:70:thm:local}.

The source theorem \codefiftythree{lemma\_13\_11\_holds} has the following exact asymptotic input-output form. For each $0<\alpha\le1$, there is a threshold $N_{11}(\alpha)$ such that, for every prime $N\ge N_{11}(\alpha)$ and every disc-valued $f$ with $\|f\|_{U^4}^{16}>\alpha$, there are $A\subseteq G^2$ and $\psi:G^2\to G$ satisfying

 \begin{gathered}
 |A|\ge\delta_\alpha N^2,\quad
 \delta_\alpha=(\alpha/2)^{2^{66}},\\
 \psi\text{ separately order-eight Freiman on }A,\qquad
 (1-2^{-44})\sum_hC(h)\le\sum_hC_\psi(h),\\
 |\widehat{D_aD_bf}(\psi(a,b))|\ge\alpha N/2
 \quad((a,b)\in A).
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
This is another imported analytic theorem; its own $\alpha$-dependent threshold is retained.

Use the actual density $a=|A|/N^2\in[\delta_\alpha,1]$ to form a context. Take
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:NFourier}
 N_{\mathrm L}(\alpha)
 =\max\{N_{11}(\alpha),N_{\rm loc}(\delta_\alpha)\}.

\[
 N^{e(a)}\ge N^{e(\delta_\alpha)}=N^{E_{\mathrm L}(\alpha)}.

It gives a global bilinear $\mu$ agreeing with $\psi$ on the retained $B$. Use $\Phi=\mu$ on the full progression square. Thus the output function is bilinear on the entire square, while the equality needed to preserve Fourier coefficients is used only on $B$. We do not assert that the original extracted $\psi$ becomes bilinear everywhere.

The mass satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:masscompare}
 2^{-137}a^{704}\ge2^{-137}\delta_\alpha^{704}
 \ge(\alpha/2)^{2^{76}}.

For an explicit check, write $h=\log_2(1/\alpha)\ge0$. The base-two logarithmic loss on the middle expression is
\[
 137+704\cdot2^{66}(1+h)
 \le(137+704\cdot2^{66})(1+h)<2^{76}(1+h).

Finally $B\subseteq A$ and $\Phi=\psi$ there preserve exactly the Fourier coefficients in \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:lemma1311}. This proves all target conclusions with the recurrence exponent.

\begin{proposition}[Comparison with the printed exponent]\label{gsr:en:70:prop:compare}
For $0<\alpha\le2^{-2^{-63}}$, $E_{\mathrm L}(\alpha)>E(\alpha)$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Put $h=\log_2(1/\alpha)$, $C=3100876<2^{22}$, and

\[
 -\log_2E_{\mathrm L}(\alpha)=C+D(1+h),\qquad

In either case the negative logarithm of $E_{\mathrm L}$ is smaller, proving the stated direction.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Near-maximal branch]\label{gsr:en:70:thm:near}

\begin{align}
 |B|&>(1-9792\varepsilon)N^2\ge\frac{871}{1024}N^2,\label{gsr:en:70:eq:nearmass}\\

\end{align}
With $P=Q=P(0,1;N)$ and $\Phi(a,b)=cab$, every output condition in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:70:thm:printed} follows, with no extra large-modulus threshold in this range.
\end{theorem}

\subsection{Normalization and the cube identities}
Use normalized averages and normalized $L^1,L^2$ norms. For a function $g$, write
\[
 F_g(r)=\E_xg(x)e^{-2\pi i rx/N},\qquad
 \chi_r(x)=e^{2\pi i rx/N}.
\]
Character orthogonality and Parseval give
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:U2Fourier}
 \|g\|_{U^2}^{4}
 =\E_c|\E_xD_cg(x)|^2
 =\sum_r|F_g(r)|^4,\qquad
 \sum_r|F_g(r)|^2=\E_x|g(x)|^2.
\end{equation}
For example, $\E_xD_cg(x)=\sum_r|F_g(r)|^2\chi_r(c)$; averaging its squared modulus proves the first identity. Expanding a squared derivative average adds one cube direction, so
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:U4decomp}
 \|f\|_{U^4}^{16}=\E_{a,b}\|D_aD_bf\|_{U^2}^{4}
\end{equation}
is also the ordinary normalized sixteen-vertex cube average. Its nonnegativity is immediate from \eqref{gsr:fm:70:eq:U4}.

Every cube product has absolute value at most $|f(x)|$ at its base vertex, because all sixteen factors have modulus at most one. Taking absolute values and then averages gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:amplitude}
 0\le\|f\|_{U^4}^{16}\le\E_x|f(x)|\le1,
 \qquad \E_x(1-|f(x)|)<\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
This also proves the vacuity of $\alpha=1$.

Define $v(x)=f(x)/|f(x)|$ when $f(x)\ne0$, and $v(x)=1$ otherwise. Then $|v|=1$ everywhere and
\[
 \|v-f\|_1=\E(1-|f|)<\varepsilon.
\]
For complex factors of modulus at most one, a telescoping product estimate bounds the difference of two products by the sum of the factor differences. Applying it to the sixteen cube vertices, each uniformly distributed after averaging the base point, gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:phaseU4}
 |\|v\|_{U^4}^{16}-\|f\|_{U^4}^{16}|
 \le16\|v-f\|_1,
 \qquad \|v\|_{U^4}^{16}>1-17\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
Applying the four-factor version to each fixed pair $a,b$ gives the uniform estimate
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:uniformreturn}
 \|D_aD_bv-D_aD_bf\|_1\le4\|v-f\|_1<4\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
This holds for every pair, including those selected later. A normalized Fourier coefficient changes by less than $4\varepsilon$ under this replacement.

\subsection{Good pairs and a unique character}
Put $h_{a,b}=D_aD_bv$, a unit-modulus function, and define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:goodpairs}
 T=\{(a,b):\|h_{a,b}\|_{U^2}^4\ge63/64\},
 \qquad \eta_*=1088\varepsilon=64\cdot17\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
The average of the nonnegative defect $1-\|h_{a,b}\|_{U^2}^4$ is less than $17\varepsilon$ by \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:phaseU4} and \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:U4decomp}. Markov's inequality therefore gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:badpairs}
 |G^2\setminus T|<\eta_*N^2.
\end{equation}
If no bad pairs exist, the strict inequality still holds because $\varepsilon>0$.

For a good pair, \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:U2Fourier} gives
\[
 \sum_r|F_{h_{a,b}}(r)|^2=1,
 \qquad\sum_r|F_{h_{a,b}}(r)|^4\ge63/64.
\]
Since the fourth-power sum is at most the largest squared coefficient times the squared-coefficient sum, some frequency $\varphi(a,b)$ has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:dominant}
 |F_{h_{a,b}}(\varphi(a,b))|\ge\sqrt{63/64}.
\end{equation}
It is unique: two such coefficients would contribute at least $126/64>1$ to Parseval. Choose the unit scalar $z_{a,b}$ with the same argument as that nonzero coefficient. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:L2close}
 \|h_{a,b}-z_{a,b}\chi_{\varphi(a,b)}\|_2^2
 =2-2|F_{h_{a,b}}(\varphi(a,b))|
 \le2(1-\sqrt{63/64})\le1/32.
\end{equation}
No product-set structure of $T$ is assumed.

\subsection{Cocycles force exact partial additivity}
For a unit function $w$ the identity
\[
 D_{a+a'}w(x)=D_aw(x)D_{a'}w(x-a)
\]
holds because the middle values of $w$ cancel with their conjugates. Apply it with $w=D_bv$; commutativity gives the second identity below:
\begin{align}
 h_{a+a',b}(x)&=h_{a,b}(x)h_{a',b}(x-a),\label{gsr:en:70:eq:cocyclea}\\
 h_{a,b+b'}(x)&=h_{a,b}(x)h_{a,b'}(x-b).\label{gsr:en:70:eq:cocycleb}
\end{align}
Suppose $(a,b),(a',b),(a+a',b)\in T$. Replace the three functions in \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:cocyclea} by their character approximants. Translation preserves the $L^2$ error and multiplies a character only by a unit scalar. Products of unit functions satisfy the triangle bound for the sum of the factor errors. Thus a unit multiple of $\chi_{\varphi(a+a',b)}$ and a unit multiple of $\chi_{\varphi(a,b)+\varphi(a',b)}$ have $L^2$ distance at most
\[
 3/\sqrt{32}<\sqrt2.
\]
Unit multiples of distinct characters have distance exactly $\sqrt2$, by orthogonality. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:partiala}
 \varphi(a+a',b)=\varphi(a,b)+\varphi(a',b).
\end{equation}
The same reasoning with \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:cocycleb} gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:partialb}
 \varphi(a,b+b')=\varphi(a,b)+\varphi(a,b')
\end{equation}
whenever the relevant three pairs are good. These are exact identities in $G$, not an informal rounding of approximate frequencies. The unconstrained unit phase constants do not affect the separation argument.

\subsection{A dense partial-additive map extends}
\begin{lemma}[Dense partial-additive extension]\label{gsr:en:70:lem:denseextension}
Let $A$ be a subset of a finite abelian group $G$ with $|A|>3|G|/4$, and let $F:A\to H$ take values in an abelian group. If
\[
 F(x+y)=F(x)+F(y)\quad\text{whenever }x,y,x+y\in A,
\]
then $F$ is the restriction of a unique homomorphism $L:G\to H$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
First obtain the Freiman-two relation. If $x,y,z,w\in A$ and $x+y=z+w=s$, the intersection of the four translates imposing
\[
 t,\ x+t,\ z+t,\ s+t\in A
\]
has positive cardinality, because each complement has size less than $|G|/4$. For such $t$, every term used in the following partial-additivity identities lies in $A$:
\[
 \begin{split}
 F(s+t)&=F(x+t)+F(y)=F(x)+F(t)+F(y),\\
 F(s+t)&=F(z+t)+F(w)=F(z)+F(t)+F(w).
 \end{split}
\]
Cancel $F(t)$ to obtain $F(x)+F(y)=F(z)+F(w)$.

For $h\in G$ choose $u,u+h\in A$, possible since $|A|>|G|/2$, and set $L(h)=F(u+h)-F(u)$. If $v,v+h\in A$ is another choice, the Freiman relation applied to $(u+h)+v=u+(v+h)$ proves independence of the choice. For $h,k\in G$, choose $u,u+h,u+h+k\in A$, possible since $|A|>2|G|/3$. Telescoping gives $L(h+k)=L(h)+L(k)$. If $a\in A$, choose $u,u+a\in A$ and use partial additivity to get $L(a)=F(a)$. Finally every $h$ is a difference of two members of $A$, so any extension must have this value. This proves uniqueness.
\end{proof}
The difference-map and triangle mechanism is familiar; canonical source 12 already contains the sharper affine extension of a Freiman map from density greater than $2/3$ \cite{srctwelve}. Here the preliminary four-translate step is essential: our initial hypothesis is partial additivity, so the Freiman property must first be established. We do not present the extension lemma as a new theorem of additive combinatorics.

\subsection{Extend columns and then their slopes}
For $b\in G$ put $A_b=\{a:(a,b)\in T\}$ and
\[
 S_* =\{b:|A_b|>7N/8\}.
\]
Every $b\notin S_*$ contributes at least $N/8$ missing pairs. By \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:badpairs},
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:badcolumns}
 |G\setminus S_*|<8\eta_*N.
\end{equation}
For each $b\in S_*$, Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:70:lem:denseextension} applies to $a\mapsto\varphi(a,b)$ by \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:partiala}. Every homomorphism from the cyclic group $G$ to itself is multiplication by its value at one, so a unique $k_b\in G$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:slopes}
 \varphi(a,b)=k_ba\qquad(a\in A_b).
\end{equation}
If $b,b',b+b'\in S_*$, then $A_b\cap A_{b'}\cap A_{b+b'}$ has more than $5N/8$ elements. Since $N>3$, it contains a nonzero $a$. Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:partialb} and \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:slopes} give
\[
 (k_{b+b'}-k_b-k_{b'})a=0.
\]
This is the one place in this main proof where field cancellation is used. Hence $k_{b+b'}=k_b+k_{b'}$.

The numerical hypothesis gives
\[
 \eta_*\le17/1024,\qquad 8\eta_*\le17/128<1/4.
\]
Thus \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:badcolumns} implies $|S_*|>3N/4$. Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:70:lem:denseextension} a second time, now to $b\mapsto k_b$. There is $c\in G$ with $k_b=cb$ for every $b\in S_*$. Consequently
\[
 \varphi(a,b)=cab\quad\text{on}\quad B=T\cap(G\times S_*).
\]
The missing-pair count is at most the bad-pair count plus $N$ times the bad-column count. Hence
\[
 |B|>(1-9\eta_*)N^2=(1-9792\varepsilon)N^2.
\]
At $\varepsilon=2^{-16}$ this lower proportion is exactly
$1-9792/65536=871/1024$, proving \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:nearmass}.

\subsection{Return to the original function and the full square}
For every $(a,b)\in B$, \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:dominant} and the uniform estimate \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:uniformreturn} imply
\[
 |F_{D_aD_bf}(cab)|>\sqrt{63/64}-4\varepsilon
 \ge\sqrt{63/64}-2^{-14}>3/4.
\]
The final inequality needs no decimal approximation: both sides of
$\sqrt{63/64}>3/4+2^{-14}$ are positive and their squares have the same strict ordering. Multiply by $N$ to get \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:nearcoef}. This coefficient belongs to $f$, not only to its phase normalization $v$.

Choose $P=Q=P(0,1;N)$. Its carrier is $G$, its cardinality and length are $N$, and its step is nonzero. The total-domain map $\Phi(a,b)=cab$ is of the form \eqref{gsr:fm:70:eq:bilinear} with only $c_{11}=c$ nonzero. For $0<\alpha\le1$,
\[
 0<E(\alpha)\le1/2\le1,
 \qquad (\alpha/2)^{2^{76}}\le1/2<871/1024.
\]
Thus $N^{E(\alpha)}\le N$, the mass bound implies \eqref{gsr:fm:70:eq:targetmass}, and $3N/4\ge\alpha N/2$ implies \eqref{gsr:fm:70:eq:targetFourier}. This proves every assertion of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:70:thm:near}.

\paragraph{Relation to near-extremizer theory.}
Eisner--Tao's Theorem 1.1(2) gives proximity to polynomial phases near maximal Gowers norm; their Remark 1.6 discusses effective polynomial rates without specifying the constants used here. Their phase normalization, character separation, and cocycle extension are primary antecedents of this mechanism. Our argument stops at the bilinear frequency interface and does not integrate $cab$ to an approximating cubic phase. Every constant in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:70:thm:near} has been calculated above.

\srcnote{70}{Section 10}
The lower-range comparison in Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:70:prop:compare} ends at $2^{-2^{-63}}$. Since $1-e^{-x}<x$ for $x>0$ and $\log2<1$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:overlap}
 1-2^{-2^{-63}}<(\log2)2^{-63}<2^{-63}<2^{-16}.
\end{equation}
Hence $2^{-2^{-63}}>1-2^{-16}$, and the two proved intervals overlap.

For definiteness, one can choose
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:Npiecewise}
 N_{\mathrm F}(\alpha)=
 \begin{cases}
 N_{\mathrm L}(\alpha),&0<\alpha<1-2^{-16},\\
 5,&1-2^{-16}\le\alpha<1,\\
 2,&\alpha=1.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
The first branch lies entirely within the range of Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:70:prop:compare}; the second uses Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:70:thm:near}; the third is vacuous by \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:amplitude}. Each threshold depends only on $\alpha$. This proves Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:70:thm:printed}.

The order of quantifiers is important. In the recurrence branch we first fix $\delta_\alpha$, then take a finite maximum over the possible integer spectrum counts and the source threshold $N_{11}(\alpha)$. Only after that do we quantify over $N$, $f$, and their resulting actual density. We never replace a pointwise threshold $N_0(a)$ by an uncontrolled value at a varying $a=|A|/N^2$.

The conclusion recovers the exact numerical exponent, mass, and Fourier constants in the repository's asymptotic target. It leaves two distinct issues untouched: removing the lower-range large-$N$ qualification, and replacing the non-numerical external starting constants by numerical estimates. Neither is implied by the displayed power exponent alone.

\section[{A published-only recurrence alternative\srctag{70}}]{A published-only recurrence alternative}\label{gsr:en:70:sec:d11}\label{gsr:en:70:sec:maynard}
\srcnote{70}{Section 11}
This optional section explains precisely what can be retained using Maynard's published theorem alone. It is not needed for Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:70:thm:printed}.

Maynard's Theorem 1.1 \cite{maynard} gives an absolute $C_2>2$, depending only on the degree two, and starting constants $X_{\mathrm M}(q)>2$, depending only on the degree and number of polynomials, such that
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 X>X_{\mathrm M}(q),\quad 0<\eta_i\le1/100,\quad
 \prod_i\eta_i^{-1}\le X^{1/C_2}\\
 \Longrightarrow\quad
 \exists s\in\Z:\quad 1\le s<X,\quad
 \|A_i s^2\|_{\Tquot}\le\eta_i\ \text{for all }i.
 \end{gathered}
\]
The constants are uniform in coefficients and tolerances. The published remarks do not supply a proved numerical upper bound on $C_2$ or a numerical starting threshold. A tentative numerical suggestion concerning a corollary is not such a bound.

Reapply the elementary certificate with $C=C_2$, rather than invoking a specifically Lau-labelled $C>21$ corollary. Put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:maynardr}
 r_{\mathrm M}(q)=\frac1{8(C_2+1)q^2}.
\end{equation}
The power budget satisfies
\[
 (q+1)(2C_2q+1)r_{\mathrm M}(q)
 \le\frac{2C_2+1}{4(C_2+1)}<\frac12.
\]
Thus formulas \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:sqvq}--\eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:Rq} apply with $22$ replaced by $C_2$, $r_q$ by $r_{\mathrm M}(q)$, and $X_0$ by $X_{\mathrm M}$. They yield the same exact partition and the same critical-height fraction. Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:70:eq:maynardbeta}
 \beta_{\mathrm M}(a)=\frac{t(a)^2}{256(C_2+1)b(a)^3}
 =\frac{16}{C_2+1}\beta(a),\qquad
 e_{\mathrm M}(a)=\frac{2^{-3100872}}{C_2+1}a^{9222672}.
\end{equation}
Then $ur_{\mathrm M}(q)\ge2\beta_{\mathrm M}(a)$ and
$e_{\mathrm M}=\beta_{\mathrm M}f_*g_*/2$.

Two compatibility problems must be addressed. From $C_2>2$ alone one cannot infer either $r_{\mathrm M}(q)\ge2^{-11q}$ or $\beta_{\mathrm M}(a)\ge\beta_{\rm old}(a)$. An unspecified absolute constant may be arbitrarily large relative to the displayed numerical constants. Simply replacing $22$ by $C_2$ in an old Stage 13.5 or Stage 13.6 wrapper is therefore insufficient.

\subsection{The repaired two-branch construction}
For an actual density with $\beta_{\mathrm M}(a)\ge\beta_{\rm old}(a)$, retain the new $Q$ as the raw source record, without claiming the old Stage 13.5 predicate. The height models require only strong heights; direct Bohr membership needs the Stage 13.4 cover, critical-height membership, and the actual new own-step estimate. The direct common-row constructor needs its nonzero step, row mass, short-difference identities, and $m^2\le N$. It does not need the legacy Stage 13.5 exponent.

With $m=\lceil c(a)N^{\beta_{\mathrm M}(a)}\rceil$, the threshold calculation of Section~\ref{gsr:en:70:sec:threshold}, with the new exponents, pays these hypotheses. The branch inequality pays the one remaining old lower-length conjunct. Reconstruct all Stage 13.6 facts directly, exactly as in Section~\ref{gsr:en:70:sec:constructor}. The Stage 13.7 and 13.8 interfaces then consume those facts, so the geometry proves side at least $N^{e_{\mathrm M}(a)}$ and mass $2^{-137}a^{704}$.

For actual densities with $\beta_{\rm old}(a)>\beta_{\mathrm M}(a)$, use the previously proved old all-density short-parent construction of Report281 \cite{srcfiftythree}. We state its additional input explicitly. With
\[
 \gamma_{\rm old}(a)=\frac{\beta_{\rm old}(a)f_*(a)g_*(a)}4,
\]
that construction, uniformly for $a\in[a_0,1]$, gives the same mass, properness, common step, original-domain containment, and original-phase bilinearity, with side at least $N^{3\gamma_{\rm old}(a)}$, at the threshold
\[
 N_{281}(a_0)=
 \left\lceil\left(\frac8{c(a_0)}\right)^{1/\gamma_{\rm old}(a_0)}\right\rceil.
\]
This optional argument imports that old-scale quantitative result; the main Lau proof does not need it. In the present branch,
\[
 3\gamma_{\rm old}(a)=\tfrac34\beta_{\rm old}(a)f_*(a)g_*(a)
 >\tfrac12\beta_{\mathrm M}(a)f_*(a)g_*(a)=e_{\mathrm M}(a).
\]
So the old construction implies the desired weaker Maynard target.

Taking the maximum of $N_{281}(a_0)$ and the symbolic new-route threshold gives one threshold for all actual densities. The branch choice may depend on $a$; the threshold does not. This repairs both legacy conditions, not only the lower-length comparison. Fourier assembly then yields exponent $e_{\mathrm M}(\delta_\alpha)$ with the same mass and Fourier conclusions.

\paragraph{Its limitation.}
Without a numerical upper bound on $C_2$, this alternative does not certify the specific overlap comparison with $2^{-\alpha^{-2^{70}}}$ on the interval used in Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:70:prop:compare}. For each fixed finite $C_2$ it dominates that printed exponent sufficiently far toward $\alpha=0$, but this alone need not meet the explicit near-maximal interval. The stated all-$\alpha$ recovery therefore uses Lau's numerical exponent input; the Maynard-only consequence retains its unspecified absolute coefficient and non-numerical threshold.

\section[{A separate all-cyclic near-maximal strengthening\srctag{70}}]{A separate all-cyclic near-maximal strengthening}\label{gsr:en:70:sec:dA}\label{gsr:en:70:app:cyclic}
\srcnote{70}{Appendix A}
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:70:thm:near} has a useful strengthening that does not alter the frozen prime-branch argument: its same estimates hold on $G=\Z/N\Z$ for every integer $N\ge2$. Only the field-cancellation paragraph requires replacement.

After extending the dense columns, all homomorphisms $\Z/N\Z\to\Z/N\Z$ still have the form $a\mapsto k_ba$. If $b,b',b+b'\in S_*$, set
\[
 I=A_b\cap A_{b'}\cap A_{b+b'},\qquad
 d=k_{b+b'}-k_b-k_{b'}.
\]
The frequency identities hold at every $a\in I$, so $da=0$ for all such $a$. We have $|I|>5N/8>N/2$. If $d\ne0$, multiplication by $d$ is a nonzero homomorphism, since it sends $1$ to $d$. Its kernel is a proper subgroup and therefore has index at least two, hence cardinality at most $N/2$. This contradicts $I\subseteq\ker(a\mapsto da)$. Consequently $d=0$ even without an invertible element in $I$.

All remaining steps use finite character orthogonality, cube identities, unit-modulus cocycles, the finite-abelian dense-extension lemma, and relative cardinality estimates. They hold for every $N$, including $N=2,3$. The full cycle has nonzero step $1$ precisely when $N\ge2$, and $cab$ still has the required bilinear polynomial form. Thus the conclusion \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:nearmass}--\eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:nearcoef} and all Fourier-square output predicates hold in this enlarged near-maximal range. This does not extend the lower-$\alpha$ analytic extraction branch to composite moduli.

\section[{Affine lists on long modular progressions\srctag{74}}]{Affine lists on long modular progressions}\label{gsr:en:74:sec:d2}
\srcnote{74}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:en:74:sec:word}

\subsection{How often an affine orbit enters a short interval}

\begin{lemma}[Active positions]\label{gsr:en:74:lem:active}
Suppose $N\ge3R$, $R\ge2$, and $P$ is a proper progression of length
$L\ge2$. If $f(x)=\alpha x+\beta$ is nonconstant on $P$, then
\[
 A=|\{0\le t<L:f(x_0+dt)\in S\}|\le L/2+R.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Write $f(x_0+dt)=v+\Delta t$, where $v=\alpha x_0+\beta$ and
$\Delta=\alpha d$. Because $L\ge2$, the restriction is nonconstant exactly
when $\Delta\ne0$. Let $\ell=\ord(\Delta)=N/\gcd(N,\Delta)\ge2$.
A full period visits each element of $v+\langle\Delta\rangle$ exactly once.
With $h=N/\ell$, that coset is one residue class modulo $h$, so its
intersection with $S$ has size $a_0$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:74:eq:coset}
 a_0\le\left\lceil\frac{R}{h}\right\rceil
 =\left\lceil\frac{R\ell}{N}\right\rceil
 \le\lceil\ell/3\rceil\le\ell/2,
 \qquad a_0\le R.
\end{equation}
For the last ceiling inequality, $\ell=2,3$ are immediate. For
$\ell=3k,3k+1,3k+2$ with $\ell\ge4$, it respectively reduces to
$k\le3k/2$, $k+1\le(3k+1)/2$ with $k\ge1$, and
$k+1\le(3k+2)/2$.

Write $L=u\ell+r$, $0\le r<\ell$. Each full period contributes $a_0$
active positions, and the remaining positions have distinct values.
Thus
\[
 A\le u a_0+\min(r,a_0)
 \le (L-r)/2+a_0\le L/2+R.
\]
No injectivity of $f$ on the whole progression is assumed: the period
may be smaller or larger than $L$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Elementary concentration estimates}

We include the estimates so that the word existence theorem does not
rely on a concentration result with unspecified constants.

\begin{lemma}[Three tail bounds]\label{gsr:en:74:lem:tails}
Let $X$ be a sum of independent Bernoulli variables with mean $\mu$.
For $0<\varepsilon<1$ and $t>0$,
\begin{align}
 \Pr(X\le(1-\varepsilon)\mu)&\le
       \exp(-\mu\varepsilon^2/2),\label{gsr:en:74:eq:lower}\\
 \Pr(X\ge(1+\varepsilon)\mu)&\le
       \exp(-\mu\varepsilon^2/(2+\varepsilon)),\label{gsr:en:74:eq:upper}\\
 \Pr(X-\mu\ge t)&\le
       \exp\!\left(-\frac{t^2}{2(\mu+t/3)}\right).
       \label{gsr:en:74:eq:bernstein}
\end{align}
The last bound is trivial if $\mu=0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For every real $\lambda$, independence and $\log(1+z)\le z$ for $z>-1$
give
\[
 \mathbb E e^{\lambda X}\le\exp(\mu(e^\lambda-1)).
\]
Exponential Markov with $\lambda=\log(1-\varepsilon)<0$ gives the
lower-tail exponent
$\mu((1-\varepsilon)\log(1-\varepsilon)+\varepsilon)$.
Its bracket is at least $\varepsilon^2/2$: the difference is zero at zero
and has derivative $-\log(1-\varepsilon)-\varepsilon\ge0$.
The same calculation with $\lambda=\log(1+\varepsilon)>0$ gives
$\mu((1+\varepsilon)\log(1+\varepsilon)-\varepsilon)$.
The inequality
\[
 \log(1+\varepsilon)\ge\frac{2\varepsilon}{2+\varepsilon}
\]
follows by differentiating and comparing at zero. The derivative of
$\varepsilon^2/(2+\varepsilon)$ is
$\varepsilon(4+\varepsilon)/(2+\varepsilon)^2$, at most
$2\varepsilon/(2+\varepsilon)$. Integration proves \eqref{gsr:en:74:eq:upper}.

For $0<\lambda<3$, the power series and
$j!\ge2\cdot3^{j-2}$ for $j\ge2$ imply
\[
 e^\lambda-1-\lambda\le
 \frac{\lambda^2}{2(1-\lambda/3)}.
\]
Therefore
$\mathbb E e^{\lambda(X-\mu)}\le
\exp(\mu\lambda^2/(2(1-\lambda/3)))$.
Substitute $\lambda=t/(\mu+t/3)<3$ and apply exponential Markov.
The resulting exponent is $-t^2/(2(\mu+t/3))$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Existence and agreement bounds in theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:74:thm:word}]
Assign the $N$ letters $b(x)$ independently and uniformly from $S$.
Fix a proper progression $P$ of length $L\ge L_0$. Its domain points
are distinct, so the sampled letters are independent.
For a fixed symbol $v$, its count is $\operatorname{Bin}(L,1/R)$ with
mean $L/R$. Taking $\varepsilon=1/8$ in \eqref{gsr:en:74:eq:lower} and
$\varepsilon=1/4$ in \eqref{gsr:en:74:eq:upper} gives
\begin{align*}
 \Pr\bigl(b_v(P)<7L/(8R)\bigr)&\le e^{-L/(128R)},\\
 \Pr\bigl(b_v(P)>5L/(4R)\bigr)&\le e^{-L/(36R)}
 \le e^{-L/(128R)}.
\end{align*}

For a fixed affine map with nonconstant restriction, agreement is possible
only at the $A$ positions of lemma~\ref{gsr:en:74:lem:active}. Its agreement count $Y$
is $\operatorname{Bin}(A,1/R)$, even when affine values repeat: independence
belongs to the distinct domain letters. Since $L\ge8R$,
\[
 \mu_Y=A/R\le L/(2R)+1\le5L/(8R).
\]
Put $t=L/(8R)$. The event $Y>3L/(4R)$ implies $Y-\mu_Y>t$, and
\eqref{gsr:en:74:eq:bernstein} gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:74:eq:affine-tail}
 \Pr(Y>3L/(4R))\le
 \exp(-3L/(256R))\le\exp(-L/(128R)),
\end{equation}
using the exact identity
$(1/8)^2/[2(5/8+(1/8)/3)]=3/256$.
Strict failure events are bounded by the corresponding weak events, so
nonintegral thresholds cause no rounding loss.

There are at most $N^3$ progression presentations: $N$ choices each for
start, difference, and positive length at most $N$. There are $N^2$
affine coefficient pairs. Thus at most $2RN^3+N^5=K$ bad events are
being excluded. Improper presentations and short progressions are omitted;
repeated presentations only overcount. The union bound is
\[
 \Pr(\text{some bad event})\le K e^{-L_0/(128R)}\le\frac12.
\]
At least one word satisfies all the assertions at once. In particular,
the progression or cover may subsequently be chosen as a function of
that word. No additional union bound over affine lists is needed.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The exact optimum and its deficit}

\begin{proof}[List conclusions in theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:74:thm:word}]
Set $B_0=0$. Consider a list of $q$ affine maps, $1\le q\le R$,
allowing repeated entries. Let $C\subseteq S$ be its set of distinct
useful constant restricted values, and let $s=|C|$. Choose one entry
representing each value of $C$. Their union covers precisely the letters
in $C$, at most $B_s$ points. Each remaining entry is nonconstant on $P$,
constant outside $S$, or a duplicate useful constant. In those three
cases its \emph{additional} mass is at most $3L/(4R)$, zero, or zero,
respectively. Hence the whole union has mass at most
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:74:eq:list-upper}
 B_s+(q-s)\frac{3L}{4R}.
\end{equation}
All symbol counts are at least $7L/(8R)$, so
\[
 B_q-B_s\ge(q-s)\frac{7L}{8R}.
\]
Subtracting \eqref{gsr:en:74:eq:list-upper} proves the deficit
$(q-s)L/(8R)$. The $q$ heaviest ordinary constant maps attain $B_q$.
If $s<q$, the deficit is positive, so an optimizer must have $s=q$.
Every entry is consequently a distinct useful constant restriction, and
its selected mass must be $B_q$. The converse is immediate.

A constant restriction in $S$ agrees at at most $5L/(4R)$ points,
a constant outside $S$ nowhere, and a nonconstant restriction at at most
$3L/(4R)$. This proves the stated single-map bound. For any integer
$q\ge0$, including $q>R$, a union therefore covers at most
$\min\{L,5qL/(4R)\}$ points.
\end{proof}

The restricted-constant condition for $L\ge2$ is exactly
\[
 \alpha_i d=0\pmod N,\qquad
 v_i=\alpha_i x_0+\beta_i\in S.
\]
There is no requirement that $\alpha_i=0$. For even $N$, on the even
residues the ambient map $x\mapsto(N/2)x$ is constantly zero. Adding a
symbol yields the same restricted graph as that ordinary constant map.
This is why a statement classifying ambient slopes as zero would be false.

\subsection{A nonvacuous range and the alphabet boundary}

\begin{proposition}\label{gsr:en:74:prop:nonvacuous}
If $R\ge2$ and $N\ge1024R\log(1024R)$, then the threshold in
\eqref{gsr:fm:74:eq:word-threshold} satisfies $L_0\le N$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Let $A=\log(1024R)$ and $N_*=1024RA$. Then
$A\ge\log2048>2\log4$ and $N_*>640R$, in particular $N_*\ge3R$.
For $N\ge3R$, $2R\le N^2$ and hence $K\le2N^5$.
At $N=N_*$,
\[
 \frac{N_*}{128R}=8A,\qquad
 \log4+5\log N_* =\log4+5A+5\log A\le8A.
\]
Here $\log A\le A/2$ for $A\ge2$, which follows by minimizing
$A/2-\log A$, and $\log4\le A/2$.
The derivative of $N/(128R)-\log4-5\log N$ is nonnegative for
$N\ge640R$. Thus $128R\log(2K)\le N$ for all $N\ge N_*$.
Since $N$ is integral, the ceiling is still at most $N$; also $8R\le N$.
\end{proof}

If $L_0>N$, the theorem remains correct but tests no progression.
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:74:prop:nonvacuous} prevents this. For example, exact rational
logarithm enclosures in the companion give $L_0=13486$ for $N=32768$
and $R=2$. Even the nonunit-step progression of even residues then has
length $N/2\ge L_0$. This checks a usable scale, not the computation of
a universally satisfactory word.

The interval alphabet is essential to the arithmetic argument and to any
unqualified rigidity claim. For even $N\ge4$, replace it by the subgroup
alphabet $S'=\{0,N/2\}$. The two ambient affine maps
\[
 f(x)=(N/2)x,\qquad g(x)=(N/2)x+N/2
\]
are nonconstant on $\GN$ and take the two distinct alphabet values at
every $x$. Their union covers every $S'$-valued word, so they form an
optimal nonconstant two-list on the full group. For an exactly balanced
word, their agreement counts sum to $N$, so one agrees at at least $N/2$,
the best constant mass. If the single-map maximum exceeds $N/2$, no
constant attains it; if it equals $N/2$, a nonconstant attains it. Thus
even one-list optimizer rigidity fails for this alphabet. This is a
specific obstruction, not a classification of all possible alphabets.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Weighted energy with an arbitrary sparse defect\srctag{74}}]{Weighted energy with an arbitrary sparse defect}\label{gsr:en:74:sec:d3}
\srcnote{74}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:en:74:sec:sparse}

For $a:\GN\to\GN$ and a nonnegative weight $w:\GN\to\R$, define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:74:eq:energy}
 \Eng(a,w)=
 \sum_{\substack{x_1+x_2=x_3+x_4\\
                  a(x_1)+a(x_2)=a(x_3)+a(x_4)}}
       w(x_1)w(x_2)w(x_3)w(x_4).
\end{equation}
All quadruples are ordered. A tested subset can be absorbed by making
$w$ zero outside it.

\begin{lemma}[Sparse weighted restoration]\label{gsr:en:74:lem:sparse}
Let $J\subseteq\GN$ have size $m\ge1$, and suppose $a$ vanishes outside
$J$, with arbitrary values on $J$. Write
\[
 A=\sum_{x\notin J}w(x),\qquad B=\sum_{x\in J}w(x),\qquad W=A+B.
\]
Then
\begin{align}
 \Eng(a,w)&\ge\frac{A^4}{N}+\frac{B^4}{m^2}\label{gsr:en:74:eq:two-mass}\\
 &\ge\frac{W^4}{(N^{1/3}+m^{2/3})^3}
 =\frac{W^4}{N}\bigl(1+(m^2/N)^{1/3}\bigr)^{-3}.
 \label{gsr:en:74:eq:sparse-coefficient}
\end{align}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $w_0=w1_{\GN\setminus J}$. Every additive quadruple in its support
is respected because $a=0$ there. Its contribution is
\[
 \sum_{s\in\GN}\left(\sum_xw_0(x)w_0(s-x)\right)^2
 \ge\frac1N\left(\sum_s\sum_xw_0(x)w_0(s-x)\right)^2
 =\frac{A^4}{N}
\]
by Cauchy--Schwarz. Independently, all diagonal quadruples $(x,y,x,y)$
with $x,y\in J$ are respected by every map and contribute
\[
 \left(\sum_{x\in J}w(x)^2\right)^2\ge\frac{B^4}{m^2}.
\]
The two families are disjoint. Every other summand is nonnegative, giving
\eqref{gsr:en:74:eq:two-mass}. H\"older's inequality applied to
\[
 A+B=(A/N^{1/4})N^{1/4}+(B/m^{1/2})m^{1/2}
\]
with exponents $4$ and $4/3$ gives
\[
 (A+B)^4\le
 (A^4/N+B^4/m^2)(N^{1/3}+m^{2/3})^3.
\]
This proves \eqref{gsr:en:74:eq:sparse-coefficient}, including $W=0$.
\end{proof}

The minimization in the last step is exact for the two-mass expression,
with $A:B=N^{1/3}:m^{2/3}$ when both are nonzero. This does not claim
that the total respected energy has no additional contributions or that
the displayed universal coefficient is optimal. The proof uses no balance,
interval structure of $J$, or primality. When $m=o(\sqrt N)$ its coefficient
tends to one, although the values on $J$ remain arbitrary.

\subsection{The full family and relation quantifiers}

The source's \filename{HasProductProperty} requires the following~\cite{repo74product}.
For every finite family of $t$ parallel coordinate restrictions
$\psi_1,\ldots,\psi_t$ of a partial map, every common test set $U$ within
their domains, and every nonnegative weight $w$ on $U$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:74:eq:product}
 \sum_{\substack{x_1+x_2=x_3+x_4,\ x_j\in U\\
       \psi_i(x_1)+\psi_i(x_2)=\psi_i(x_3)+\psi_i(x_4)\ \forall i}}
       \prod_{j=1}^4w(x_j)
 \ge\frac{\gamma^{8t}}{N}\left(\sum_{x\in U}w(x)\right)^4.
\end{equation}
The natural number $t$ may be zero. The relation property requires this
for every partial function whose graph is contained in the relation.

\begin{corollary}\label{gsr:en:74:cor:product}
Let $0<\gamma\le1$ and $F(h,y)=a(y)$ on $\GN^2$, with $a$ as in
lemma~\ref{gsr:en:74:lem:sparse}. If
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:74:eq:gamma-condition}
 \gamma^8\le\bigl(1+(m^2/N)^{1/3}\bigr)^{-3},
\end{equation}
then $F$ has the full product property and its full graph has the relation
product property. The graph has exactly $N^2$ elements.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
All restrictions in the first coordinate are constant and respect every
additive quadruple. All restrictions in the second coordinate are the
same map $a$. For $t\ge1$, simultaneous additivity in that direction
therefore imposes exactly the single condition in \eqref{gsr:en:74:eq:energy}.
Extend the tested weight by zero and use lemma~\ref{gsr:en:74:lem:sparse},
\eqref{gsr:en:74:eq:gamma-condition}, and $\gamma^{8t}\le\gamma^8$.
For $t=0$ there is no additivity constraint on images: ordinary convolution
Cauchy--Schwarz gives coefficient one, as required by $\gamma^0=1$.
The same ordinary bound handles the first coordinate for any $t$.

If a partial function has graph contained in the full graph of $F$, it
agrees with $F$ at every point in its domain. Every permitted common test
set therefore sees the very same restrictions as the full map. The
inequality just proved applies unchanged, including the empty-family
case. Finally, the graph projection is a bijection onto $\GN^2$.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The pinned local cover interface\srctag{74}}]{The pinned local cover interface}\label{gsr:en:74:sec:d4}
\srcnote{74}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:en:74:sec:interface}

We now state the controls used in the counterexample rather than treating
``multiple-linearity'' as a qualitative label. The pin is commit
\filename{17f048dfa919de04a1989035a2d680ec0865c774}; the exact public source
snapshots and byte identities are listed in appendix~\ref{gsr:fz:74:sec:sources}.

For integer $d\ge0$ set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:74:eq:controls}
 E_d=2^{2^{d+8}},\quad
 C(\tau,\gamma,d)=(\gamma\tau)^{E_d},\quad
 \mathcal Q(\tau,\gamma,d)=C(\tau,\gamma,d)^{-1},\quad
 \mathcal S(\tau,\gamma,d)=\left(\frac2{\tau\gamma}\right)^{2^{2^{d+6}}}.
\end{equation}
These are \filename{multipleC}, \filename{multipleQ}, and \filename{multipleS}.
The printed controls on journal page~567 of Gowers's paper agree with
this exponent nesting~\cite{gowers}. No omitted outer exponential is
being inserted to alter the comparison.

\begin{definition}[The quantitative cover predicate]\label{gsr:en:74:def:ML}
For $0<\gamma\le1$ and $r\ge1$, let $\ML_{\gamma,r}(\Gamma)$ denote
\filename{MultiplyLinear gamma r} for a relation
$\Gamma\subseteq\GN^d\times\GN$. For each $0<\rho\le1$ and every
proper box $P$, it requires a retained set $H\subseteq P$ of size at least
$(1-\rho)|P|$, a partition of $P$ into proper boxes $P_j$, a common natural
graph count $q$, and multiaffine maps $\mu_{ji}$ such that
\begin{align}
 q&\le\mathcal Q(\rho/r,\gamma,d)^r,\label{gsr:en:74:eq:ML-count}\\
 \operatorname{width}(P_j)&\ge
 \operatorname{width}(P)^{C(\rho/r,\gamma,d)^r},\label{gsr:en:74:eq:ML-width}\\
 x\in H\cap P_j,\ (x,y)\in\Gamma&\implies y=\mu_{ji}(x)
       \text{ for some }i.\label{gsr:en:74:eq:ML-cover}
\end{align}
For a function, the relation is its graph on the recorded domain.
\end{definition}

The retained mass is measured against the whole input box, even for a
partial relation; the covering implication only concerns relation points.
For our full-domain counterexample every retained point must be covered.
The cells partition the whole box, not only its retained subset.

\begin{lemma}[A finite image at a large iteration]\label{gsr:en:74:lem:image}
A function on a full or partial domain with image of size at most $R$
has $\ML_{\gamma,r}$ in dimension $d$ whenever
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:74:eq:image-budget}
 R\le(r/\gamma)^{E_dr},\qquad 0<\gamma\le1,\quad r\ge1.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Use the identity partition, retain all of $P$, and take constant maps
at each image value, padding if necessary to $R$ maps. Their number is
bounded at every loss because
$\mathcal Q(\rho/r,\gamma,d)^r=(r/(\gamma\rho))^{E_dr}$
is minimized at $\rho=1$. The exponent
$C(\rho/r,\gamma,d)^r$ lies in $(0,1]$. If the integral width $w\ge1$,
then $w^{C^r}\le w$; if $w=0$, its positive real power is zero.
This includes the source's dimension-zero convention. All maps are
multiaffine and every relevant graph value is covered.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Both independent graph counts and the line width}

In this subsection and in sections~\ref{gsr:en:74:sec:obstruction} and \ref{gsr:en:74:sec:realization}, fix
$k=1$, $\theta=1$, and $E=E_2=2^{1024}$. Put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:74:eq:downstream-parameters}
 \begin{split}
 s&=\gamma^{-2}\mathcal S(1/8,\gamma,1)
      =\gamma^{-2}(16/\gamma)^{2^{128}},\\
 \theta_1&=(\gamma/4)^{2^{64}},\qquad
 \delta=2^{-37}(\theta_1/4)^{11/2},\qquad
 \zeta=2^{-\mathcal S(1,\gamma,1)},\\
 t&=\delta^{-2}\mathcal S(\theta_1/8,\delta,1).
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
These satisfy $s,t\ge1$ and $0<\theta_1,\delta,\zeta\le1$.
The gamma-side iteration \filename{section16Lemma9R} is exactly $s$,
since $2^k-1=1$. For a local loss $0<\sigma\le1$, the separate count
ceilings are
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:74:eq:line-counts}
 Q_\gamma(\sigma)=\left(\frac{2s}{\gamma\sigma}\right)^{Es},
 \qquad
 Q_\delta(\sigma)=\left(\frac{2t}{\delta\sigma}\right)^{E_1t}.
\end{equation}
The two natural witness counts are denoted $q_\gamma,q_\delta$.
The latter, not the former, occurs in the required width
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:74:eq:line-width}
 \ell(n,q_\delta)=\frac\zeta2 n^{e(\sigma,q_\delta)},\qquad
 e(\sigma,q_\delta)=
 \frac{(\gamma\sigma/(2s))^{Es}(\delta\sigma/(2t))^{E_1t}}
      {2\cdot128^{4q_\delta}}.
\end{equation}
Indeed the source has $\operatorname{section16K}(1)=128$ and
$2^{k+1}=4$.

The all-box premise quantifies over every $\sigma$, every natural input
scale $n$, and every proper $P$ with width at least $n$. It asks for those
two counts within \eqref{gsr:en:74:eq:line-counts}, a retained set of mass at least
$(1-\sigma)|P|$, a proper partition into product boxes of width at least
\eqref{gsr:en:74:eq:line-width}, and at most $q_\gamma$ globally affine maps on each
final-coordinate fibre covering the retained function values. The maps
may depend arbitrarily on the first-coordinate point. This is exactly
\filename{Section16AllBoxLineCovers}, through \filename{Section16LineCover}.

\begin{lemma}[An image bound supplies every line-cover test]
\label{gsr:en:74:lem:line}
With the parameters above, if the image has size at most $R$ and
$R\le Q_\gamma(1)$, then the all-box line-cover premise holds.
One may take $q_\gamma=R$ and $q_\delta=1$ for every test.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The delta-side bound is at least one, and both ceilings in
\eqref{gsr:en:74:eq:line-counts} increase when $\sigma$ decreases. Retain the whole
box, use its identity partition and its actual first and last coordinate
factors, and use the $R$ constant affine maps on every fibre.
The exponent in \eqref{gsr:en:74:eq:line-width} lies in $(0,1]$. If $n\ge1$,
$\ell(n,1)\le n\le\operatorname{width}(P)$; if $n=0$, it is zero.
Properness and the common-difference product identities are preserved
by the identity partition. Thus all tests, including width zero, are met.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Construction and failure of the parameter reset\srctag{74}}]{Construction and failure of the parameter reset}\label{gsr:en:74:sec:d5}
\srcnote{74}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:en:74:sec:obstruction}

\subsection{The quantitative scale is nonempty}

For now take $k=1$, so $E=E_2=2^{1024}$ and $E_1=2^{512}$.
Use the corresponding parameters in theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:74:thm:main}. In particular $Q\ge5$,
$R\le4Q+1\le5Q\le Q^2$, and $0<c\le1$. The first inequality in
\eqref{gsr:fm:74:eq:threshold} implies $N\ge\max(8,3R)$ and $u=\log N\ge1$:
its right side exceeds both $\log8$ and $\log(3R)$, using
$\log x\le x$ and $R\ge2$. For the $K$ of \eqref{gsr:fm:74:eq:word-threshold},
\[
 K\le2N^5,\qquad \log(2K)\le\log4+5u\le7u.
\]
Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:74:eq:L0-upper}
 L_0\le897Ru,
\end{equation}
since $\lceil128R\log(2K)\rceil\le896Ru+1\le897Ru$ and
$8R\le897Ru$.

As $N\ge8$, $m\ge N^{1/3}/2$. Using $c\le1$ and
$e^z\ge z^2/2$ for $z\ge0$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:74:eq:scale}
 m^c\ge\tfrac12 e^{cu/3}\ge\frac{c^2u^2}{36}
 \ge\frac{32768}{36}Ru>897Ru\ge L_0.
\end{equation}
The strict comparison is the integer inequality
$32768-36\cdot897=476>0$. Thus $L_0<m^c\le m\le N$.
The word theorem is being used on a genuine length range. Unlike the
prime-field injectivity argument, no additional $m^c\ge R^2$ condition
is required.

\subsection{Choose the word and restore all weighted tests}

Take $b$ from theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:74:thm:word} and set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:74:eq:def-a}
 a(y)=\begin{cases}b(y),&y\in J,\\0,&y\notin J,\end{cases}
 \qquad F(h,y)=a(y).
\end{equation}
The image has at most $R$ values because $0\in S$. Every progression
contained in $J$ inherits the agreement bounds of $b$.
The second threshold in \eqref{gsr:fm:74:eq:threshold} ensures
\[
 (m^2/N)^{1/3}\le N^{-1/9}\le\gamma^{-8/3}-1.
\]
Rearrangement gives \eqref{gsr:en:74:eq:gamma-condition}. Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:74:cor:product}
proves the full weighted function and relation properties, not only an
unweighted energy estimate or a fixed family of restrictions.

\subsection{Large iteration controls survive}

Every fixed-final-coordinate section of $F$ is constant. It has one graph
on the identity partition for every proper box and every loss, at the
prescribed iteration $s$. Other proper coordinate sections in dimension
two are either copies of $a$ or zero-dimensional constants.

For the one-dimensional copies of $a$, note first that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:74:eq:s-large}
 s\ge16^{2^{128}}=2^{4\cdot2^{128}}\ge2E_1.
\end{equation}
Also $s\ge2$, so
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:74:eq:section-budget}
 (s/\gamma)^{E_1s}\ge(2/\gamma)^{2E_1^2}=Q^2\ge R.
\end{equation}
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:74:lem:image} proves all those covers. Zero-dimensional sections are
constant and need only one graph; their width condition is zero.
Thus the stronger \filename{ProperCrossSectionsMultiplyLinear} holds, and
so does the fixed-final-coordinate premise of Lemma~16.10.

The minimum gamma-side count bound also satisfies
\[
 Q_\gamma(1)=(2s/\gamma)^{Es}\ge(2/\gamma)^{2E}=Q^2\ge R.
\]
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:74:lem:line} supplies the exact all-box premise with
$(q_\gamma,q_\delta)=(R,1)$. This verification is independent of
whether the numbered Lemma~16.9 is available at the modulus in question.

\subsection{An adaptive target cover still misses too much}

Suppose for contradiction that $\ML_{\gamma,1}(F)$ holds. Test
definition~\ref{gsr:en:74:def:ML} on the proper common-step box $P=J\times J$ at loss
$\rho=1/2$. It requires a retained set $H$ with $|H|\ge m^2/2$,
at most $Q$ multiaffine graphs per cell, and proper cells of width
at least $m^c$.

This width is strictly positive, so each cell has two nonempty axes.
Because its carrier is contained in $J\times J$, fixing a point on one
axis shows that the other axis is contained in $J$. Hence its final axis
$I$ is a proper progression inside $J$ with
$|I|\ge m^c>L_0$. This explicitly avoids an inference from containment
of an empty Cartesian product.

Fix a first-coordinate point in the cell. A multiaffine map restricts
on that fibre to $y\mapsto\alpha y+\beta$. If its restriction to $I$
is constant, it agrees with $a$ at at most $5|I|/(4R)$ points; a constant
outside $S$ agrees nowhere. If its restriction is nonconstant,
theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:74:thm:word} bounds agreement by $3|I|/(4R)$.
This classification does not assume a nonzero ambient slope is invertible
or nonconstant on $I$.

At most $Q$ graphs therefore cover at most $5Q|I|/(4R)$ points on the
fibre. Sum over the first-axis points, then over the disjoint cells:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:74:eq:contradiction}
 \text{covered mass}\le\frac{5Q}{4R}|P|
 \le\frac5{16}m^2<\frac12m^2.
\end{equation}
The word was chosen simultaneously for all proper progressions and all
affine restrictions; the partition and its graphs are free to depend on
it. Since the domain is full, every point of $H$ must be covered.
Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:74:eq:contradiction} is impossible. This proves the main
negative conclusion, once the named-domain realization below is checked.
