\section[{Realization of the named upstream data\srctag{74}}]{Realization of the named upstream data}\label{gsr:en:74:sec:d6}
\srcnote{74}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:en:74:sec:realization}

The previous proof can be realized by the actual good-domain and
all-ones-map definitions, with no surrogate objects. Set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:74:eq:witnesses}
 \begin{gathered}
 B=\GN^2,\qquad\phi=F,\qquad H=J_{\rm base}=H_1=\GN,\\
 x_0=0,\qquad Y_h=X_h,\qquad\phi'(h,y)=0,\qquad\psi_h(y)=0.
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
Here $X_h$ is the full finite type \filename{Section16CubeElement B h}, and
$Y_h$ consists of all its elements. It is not the short interval $J$;
$J_{\rm base}$ denotes the separate spectrum-selection base set.
We check the exact objects used in the pinned definitions~\cite{repo74section16}.

\subsection{Structured pairs and arrangement masses}

For $k=1$, a horizontal cube with side $h$, base $x$, and final coordinate
$y$ has vertices $(x,y)$ and $(x+h,y)$. Its alternating value is
\[
 \phi(x,y)-\phi(x+h,y)=a(y)-a(y)=0.
\]
Every general arrangement is therefore respected. A full 8-arrangement
has one horizontal side, sixteen horizontal basepoints, and sixteen final
coordinates subject to one additive relation. The last coordinate is
uniquely determined by the other fifteen, with coefficient $1$ or $-1$.
Thus, over every $\GN$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:74:eq:arrangement-counts}
 \operatorname{generalArrangementCount}(8,B)=N^{32},\qquad
 \operatorname{countAtSide}(8,B,h)=N^{31}.
\end{equation}
There is no nonunit division in this count. Respecting all arrangements,
the proper-section covers from equation~\eqref{gsr:en:74:eq:section-budget}, and
$0<\theta_1\le1$ imply
\filename{Section16StructuredPair 1 gamma B phi}: its two mass inequalities
are $\theta_1N^{32}\le N^{32}$ and
$(1-2^{-44})N^{32}\le N^{32}$.

The domain $X_h$ has $N^2$ elements, one choice of base and one of final
coordinate. Consequently the recorded Lemma~16.5 conclusions hold:
\[
 \frac{\theta_1}{4}N^{32}\le\sum_{h\in H}N^{31}=N^{32},
 \qquad
 2^{-27}\theta_1^6|X_h|\le|Y_h|=N^2.
\]
For \filename{HasBohrDifferenceModel} the map $\psi_h=0$ is a Freiman
homomorphism on every Bohr set, and every induced difference is zero.
Therefore its required indexed-difference identity holds exactly,
regardless of the radius~\cite{repo74bohr}.

\subsection{The actual spectrum and induced selection}

For the indicator of the full $B$, the higher cube correlation is the
constant $N$: each of its $N$ horizontal bases contributes one.
The source uses unnormalized cyclic Fourier transform, so its Fourier
values are $N^2$ at frequency zero and zero elsewhere. To see the latter
without primality, the sum of a nontrivial cyclic character is a finite
geometric series with ratio different from $1$, whose $N$th power is one; its sum is zero.
Since $0<\delta\le1$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:74:eq:spectrum}
 \begin{gathered}
 K_h=\operatorname{section16LargeSpectrum}(B,h,\delta)=\{0\},\\
 \operatorname{section16SpectrumRelation}(B,\delta)=\{(h,0):h\in\GN\}.
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
This relation has $\ML_{\delta,t}$ with one constant graph and the
identity partition. Restriction to $J_{\rm base}=\GN$ changes nothing.

The value clause in \filename{Section16InducedSelection} says precisely that
$\phi'$ equals the induced cube value on each chosen element. Both are
zero. Its other clause requires affinity on certain short Bohr
progressions intersected with the induced domain. The zero function is
affine on every set, so this clause holds for all its parameters, including
all lengths and steps admitted by the definition. In fact the induced
domain is the full $\GN\times\GN$.

\subsection{Good pairs and the alternating identity}

The three recorded size antecedents in Lemma~16.7 reduce to
\[
 \frac{\theta_1}{8}N\le N,\qquad
 \frac{\theta_1}{4}N^2\le N^2,\qquad
 2^{-27}\theta_1^6N^2\le N^2.
\]
For every $(h,y)$, the cube based at $x_0=0$ with side $h$ and final
coordinate $y$ belongs to $Y_h$. This remains true for $h=0$; these are
cube objects, with no properness requirement on the side. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:74:eq:good-domain}
 \begin{gathered}
 \operatorname{section16GoodInducedPairCount}(B,H_1,Y,0)=N^2,\\
 B_1=\operatorname{section16GoodDomain}(B,H_1,Y,0)=\GN^2.
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
The lower bound uses $\theta_2=2^{-32}\theta_1^8\le1$ and is immediate;
the promised value identity again reads $0=0$.

The source's all-ones vertex function is
\[
 \phi_1(h,y)=\phi(x_0+h,y)=a(y)=F(h,y).
\]
For $k=1$ there is only one other vertex. The signed remainder in the
actual definition is
$-(-1)^{1+0}\phi(x_0,y)=a(y)$. Therefore
\filename{Section16PhiOneIdentity} is the exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:74:eq:phi-identity}
 a(y)=(-1)^1\cdot0+a(y).
\end{equation}
Its required remainder cover is in dimension two at iteration $s$.
Since $s\ge2$,
\[
 (s/\gamma)^{Es}\ge(2/\gamma)^{2E}=Q^2\ge R,
\]
and lemma~\ref{gsr:en:74:lem:image} proves that cover on the actual $B_1$.
This completes the named realization and the two-dimensional case of
theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:74:thm:main}.

\subsection{What this verification does and does not assert}

For prime $N$, all the displayed algebraic, size, selection, and cover
antecedents in the numbered Lemma~16.9 are satisfied. Its prime-modulus
assumption is not inferred for composite $N$. The predicate
\filename{Section16AllBoxLineCovers} and Lemma~16.10 itself require only
$N\ne0$ in the pin, so the direct witnesses in lemma~\ref{gsr:en:74:lem:line} suffice
in every modulus claimed here.

The structured-pair witness is the recorded \emph{output} of the
Lemma~16.4 selection. We have not established its separately quantified
induction-family assumption, namely the lower-dimensional Theorem~16.2
family. Nor do we claim that every possible choice of the earlier
selections must be this witness. A universal implication from these
recorded predicates is falsified; an existential assertion of better
selection remains a different statement.

\section[{Every positive induction dimension\srctag{74}}]{Every positive induction dimension}\label{gsr:en:74:sec:d7}
\srcnote{74}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:en:74:sec:dimension-lift}

We now prove the stated extension to every fixed $k\ge1$. The two-dimensional
argument was presented separately to expose the source witnesses without
indices. No new probabilistic estimate or additional word is needed.

\begin{proposition}[Dimension lift]\label{gsr:en:74:prop:dimension}
For every fixed $k\ge1$, the construction and all conclusions of
theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:74:thm:main} hold with the parameters in \eqref{gsr:fm:74:eq:main-parameters}
and the same thresholds \eqref{gsr:fm:74:eq:threshold}.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Use $E=E_{k+1}$, and define $Q,c,R,N,m,J,b,a$ exactly as before.
The scale argument \eqref{gsr:en:74:eq:L0-upper}--\eqref{gsr:en:74:eq:scale} uses only
$R\ge2$, $0<c\le1$, and the displayed threshold, so it is unchanged.
Set $F(h,y)=a(y)$ on $\GN^k\times\GN$. All $k$ horizontal coordinate
restrictions are constant, and every final-coordinate restriction is $a$.
The proof of corollary~\ref{gsr:en:74:cor:product} applies verbatim, including every family
size and every graph-contained partial function. Its graph has $N^{k+1}$
elements.

The prescribed proper-section iteration is now
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:74:eq:general-r0}
 B_k=2^{2^{k+6}},\qquad
 r_0=\gamma^{-2}\left(\frac{2^{k+3}}\gamma\right)^{B_k},
 \qquad r=(2^k-1)r_0.
\end{equation}
We claim $r_0\ge2E_{k+1}$. Indeed $2^{k+6}\ge k+10$ for all $k\ge1$,
as follows from its value at $k=1$ and induction. Therefore
$B_k\ge2^{k+10}$, and
\[
 \log_2 r_0\ge(k+3)B_k\ge2^{k+10}
 \ge1+2^{k+9}=\log_2(2E_{k+1}).
\]
In particular $r\ge r_0\ge2$. For any positive-dimensional proper face
of dimension $l\le k$, $E_l\ge1$ and hence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:74:eq:general-face}
 (r_0/\gamma)^{E_l r_0}\ge(2/\gamma)^{2E_{k+1}}=Q^2\ge R.
\end{equation}
A coordinate-face pullback has image size at most $R$, so lemma~\ref{gsr:en:74:lem:image}
provides all prescribed proper-section covers. A zero-dimensional face
is constant. Fixing the final coordinate also gives a constant function
of all $k$ horizontal variables, satisfying the first premise directly.

The general source parameters are
\[
 \theta_1=(\gamma/4)^{2^{2^{k+5}}},\quad
 \delta=2^{-37}(\theta_1/4)^{11/2},\quad
 \zeta=2^{-\mathcal S(1,\gamma,k)},\quad
 t=\delta^{-2}\mathcal S(\theta_1/8,\delta,k).
\]
They again have $0<\theta_1,\delta,\zeta\le1$ and $t\ge1$.
The two count bounds become
\[
 Q_\gamma(\sigma)=(2r/(\gamma\sigma))^{E_{k+1}r},\qquad
 Q_\delta(\sigma)=(2t/(\delta\sigma))^{E_kt}.
\]
Thus $Q_\gamma(1)\ge Q^2\ge R$ and $Q_\delta(1)\ge1$.
With $K_k=(k+1)^2 2^{k+4}$, the required line-width exponent is
\[
 \frac{(\gamma\sigma/(2r))^{E_{k+1}r}
       (\delta\sigma/(2t))^{E_kt}}
      {2K_k^{2^{k+1}q_\delta}}\in(0,1].
\]
The identity partition, full retained set and constant affine maps,
with $(q_\gamma,q_\delta)=(R,1)$, give every all-box line-cover witness,
exactly as in lemma~\ref{gsr:en:74:lem:line}.

For the target, take $P=J^{k+1}$ at loss $1/2$.
Each proper output cell has all $k+1$ axes nonempty, width at least $m^c$,
and each axis contained in $J$. On fixing its first $k$ coordinates, every
multiaffine graph is affine in $y$. The same one-dimensional agreement
bound gives at most $5Q/(4R)$ of that cell's mass. Summing yields
$5m^{k+1}/16<m^{k+1}/2$, the required contradiction.

It remains to verify the named data in the larger dimension. In
\eqref{gsr:en:74:eq:witnesses}, take $B=\GN^{k+1}$ and
$H=J_{\rm base}=H_1=\GN^k$, with $Y_h$ again the full cube domain,
$x_0=0$, and zero induced and Bohr maps. Each horizontal cube has
alternating value
\[
 a(y)\sum_{\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}^k}(-1)^{|\varepsilon|}
 =a(y)(1-1)^k=0,
\]
where $k\ge1$ is essential. Thus every arrangement is respected.
There are $N^k$ sides, $N^{16k}$ choices of horizontal basepoints, and
$N^{15}$ choices of independent final coordinates, giving
\[
 N^{17k+15}\text{ arrangements},\qquad
 N^{16k+15}\text{ at each side},\qquad |X_h|=|Y_h|=N^{k+1}.
\]
All size inequalities follow by multiplying these equalities by the same
factors at most one as in section~\ref{gsr:en:74:sec:realization}. The full indicator's
cube correlation is the constant $N^k$, so its Fourier transform is
$N^{k+1}$ at zero and zero elsewhere. The spectrum is $\{0\}$, its
relation has a one-constant-graph $\ML_{\delta,t}$ cover, and the zero
maps verify every Bohr-model and induced-selection condition.

For each $(h,y)$, the cube based at zero belongs to $Y_h$, so the good
domain is the full $\GN^{k+1}$ and the good-pair count is $N^{k+1}$.
Every translated vertex has value $a(y)$, including the all-ones vertex.
The sum of $(-1)^{k+|\varepsilon|}$ over all vertices is zero, while the
all-ones summand is one. The sum over the other vertices is therefore
$-1$. The source remainder equals $a(y)$, and the alternating identity
reads $a(y)=(-1)^k0+a(y)$. Finally,
\[
 (r/\gamma)^{E_{k+1}r}\ge(2/\gamma)^{2E_{k+1}}=Q^2\ge R,
\]
so lemma~\ref{gsr:en:74:lem:image} gives its dimension-$(k+1)$ remainder cover at the
actual required iteration $r$. This proves every named assertion, with
the same prime-only numbered-lemma and independent-induction-family
qualifications already stated.
\end{proof}

The theorem does not include $k=0$: the horizontal alternating sum then
has one term and no cancellation. The ambient deletion in the next section
has density $m/N$ in every dimension, so increasing $k$ does not alter the
reselection boundary.

\section[{The endpoint and the reselection boundary\srctag{74}}]{The endpoint and the reselection boundary}\label{gsr:en:74:sec:d8}
\srcnote{74}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:en:74:sec:boundaries}

\begin{proposition}[The full-domain endpoint]\label{gsr:en:74:prop:endpoint}
For $N\ge2$ and $D\ge1$, a full-domain map $G:\GN^D\to\GN$ has the
product property at $\gamma=1$ if and only if it is globally multiaffine.
It then has $\ML_{1,1}$ with one graph.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Take a single coordinate restriction $\psi$, the entire test group, and
weight one. There are exactly $N^3$ additive quadruples. The endpoint
lower bound is $N^{-1}N^4=N^3$, so every quadruple must be respected.
In particular,
\[
 \psi(x)+\psi(y)=\psi(x+y)+\psi(0).
\]
The map $\psi-\psi(0)$ is additive on the cyclic group, hence equals
$x\mapsto\alpha x$ with $\alpha=\psi(1)-\psi(0)$.
Every coordinate restriction is affine. Induct on $D$ using
\[
 G(h,y)=G(h,0)+y\bigl(G(h,1)-G(h,0)\bigr).
\]
The two functions of $h$ are separately affine, so induction gives their
multiaffine representations and then one for $G$. This uses only the
cyclic additive structure, not a field inverse.

Conversely, every coordinate restriction of a multiaffine map is affine
and respects all additive quadruples. For any tested family, its
simultaneous energy is ordinary weighted additive energy. Extending
weights by zero and applying convolution Cauchy--Schwarz gives coefficient
one. The identity partition with the graph $G$ verifies $\ML_{1,1}$:
its width exponent $\rho^{E_D}$ lies in $(0,1]$ and its graph budget
$\rho^{-E_D}$ is at least one.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 70--81]
On prime fields this endpoint is formalized as \file{section16_unit_product_iff_multilinear} (\file{Proofs16MultilinearProduct.lean}, line~89; checked at HEAD \texttt{0c4f9054d}), source~50's Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:50:bc:prop:endpoint}; the cyclic-ring version is not formalized.
\end{writenote}

Source~50 proves this endpoint characterization for prime fields; the
proof above repeats its argument and observes that it also works for a
cyclic ring~\cite{srcfifty}. It is not presented as a new inverse theorem.
Our threshold \eqref{gsr:fm:74:eq:threshold} explicitly excludes $\gamma=1$.
The distinction between the endpoint and every fixed smaller parameter
is therefore substantive rather than a missing limit argument.

\subsection{Deleting the slab changes the order of quantifiers}

For the maps in theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:74:thm:main}, deleting $\GN^k\times J$ costs exactly
$m/N\le N^{-2/3}$ of the ambient domain and leaves the zero map. The
remaining relation has a one-constant-graph cover on every box. The
retained set inside the cover definition may still be the whole box:
only relation points need coverage, and the remaining ones have value zero.
Thus these witnesses cannot rule out a theorem that first chooses a
suitable global core and then promises local covers on that restricted
relation. This is the retained-core quantifier order already present in
source~49's conditional theorem.

Theorem~16.2 itself permits a global retained set and uses a larger
iteration parameter. Our counterexample does not contradict it. It also
does not refute the full contextual proof of Gowers's main theorem or
any global bound in Szemer\'edi's theorem. The only claimed obstruction
is to the pinned parameter-one implication and to attempted repairs
that merely add the specific satisfied predicates.

\subsection{What would constitute further progress}

A repair preserving the target budget must introduce information that
excludes the present witnesses or modify the selection and retention
quantifiers. Allowing a different complexity budget is another option.
The following questions are suggestions for further work, not assertions
of established open status.

\begin{question}[An adequate local hypothesis]
Which quantitative local condition, compatible with the upstream Fourier
selection, prevents arbitrary sparse slabs while still being inherited
by the selected relation?
\end{question}
Ambient-normalized energy alone is insufficient by lemma~\ref{gsr:en:74:lem:sparse}.
A stronger energy condition relative to the tested set is a possible
object of study. We do not assert that our chosen word fails any such
condition without a separate proof, or that such a condition alone repairs
the cover theorem.

\begin{question}[A retained core with explicit controls]
Can the allowed global deletion be chosen before every local loss and
box while improving source~49's conditional graph, width, and threshold
profiles under its certified interfaces?
\end{question}
The prior conditional theorem already exists. Merely restating its
acyclic recurrence would not answer this quantitative question, and the
failure of a comparison of upper bounds is not a lower bound on every
possible cover.

\begin{question}[Alphabet geometry and higher degree]
For which subsets of a cyclic group can the coset-intersection estimate
be replaced by a useful uniform active-position bound? What is the
correct substitute for higher-degree restrictions or products of cyclic
groups?
\end{question}
The affine proof uses a periodic coset orbit. Polynomial values need not
have that structure, and the subgroup-alphabet example rules out ignoring
alphabet geometry. Neither the exact arbitrary-word cover law nor a
product-group profile invariant is proved here.

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 70--81]
\emph{Progress since} (within this arrival): for full-domain one-variable maps, the hereditary relative energy of source~75's second Part and of sources~76--81 is such a local condition: a lower bound above $3/4$ forces affinity on every abelian group (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:76:thm:main}), and a sparse slab fails it (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:75:cor:sparsegap}); its inheritance through the Section~16 selections, the actual question, is not proved by any of them. Source~75's first Part answers the deletion side: a fixed-density slab forces a positive deletion fraction (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:slabs}). These questions are merged into items~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:closure} and~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:branchprofiles}.
\end{writenote}

\section[{Parameters and the exact local predicate\srctag{75}}]{Parameters and the exact local predicate}\label{gsr:en:75:sec:d2}\label{gsr:en:75:sec:predicate}
\srcnote{75}{Section 2}
Fix an integer $k\ge1$, put $d=k+1$, and fix $0<\gamma<1$. Write
\[
 \G=\Z/N\Z,\qquad E_j=2^{2^{j+8}},\qquad E=E_d,
 \qquad Q_0=(2/\gamma)^E,
 \qquad \eta=(\gamma^{-8/3}-1)^3>0.
\]
In particular $E\ge2^{1024}>16$ and $\eta<\gamma^{-8}$.
A proper modular progression is a presentation
$\{x_0+jt:0\le j<L\}$ having $L$ distinct elements. Its difference need not be a unit. A proper box is a product of such progressions with a common difference. Its width is the minimum axis length. The source's dimension-zero width is zero. Multiaffine maps are polynomials
$\mu(x)=\sum_{A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}}c_A\prod_{i\in A}x_i$
with coefficients in $\G$; constant terms are allowed. These conventions follow the pinned definitions~\cite{repo74defs,repo74section16}.

At the source pin
\filename{17f048dfa919de04a1989035a2d680ec0865c774},
\filename{MultiplyLinear gamma r}, in the range $r\ge1$ used here, for a relation
$\Gamma\subseteq\G^j\times\G$ requires the following for every
$0<\rho\le1$ and every proper input box $P$. There are a set
$H\subseteq P$ with $|H|\ge(1-\rho)|P|$, a partition of the \emph{whole}
$P$ into proper boxes $P_a$, a common natural graph count $q$, and multiaffine maps $\mu_{ai}$, such that
\begin{align}
 q&\le\bigl((r/(\gamma\rho))^{E_j}\bigr)^r,\label{gsr:en:75:eq:count}\\
 \operatorname{width}(P_a)&\ge\operatorname{width}(P)^{((\gamma\rho/r)^{E_j})^r},\label{gsr:en:75:eq:width}\\
 x\in H\cap P_a,\ (x,y)\in\Gamma&\Longrightarrow
 y=\mu_{ai}(x)\quad\hbox{for some }i.\label{gsr:en:75:eq:cover}
\end{align}
For a domain $D\subseteq\G^j$ and total ambient map $F$, the partial-function predicate is precisely this relation predicate for
$\Gamma_D=\{(x,F(x)):x\in D\}$.
Crucially, $|H|$ is measured against $|P|$, but a point of $P\setminus D$ has no graph value requiring coverage.

For $F:\G^d\to\G$, define its minimum deletion fraction by
\[
 \Delta_{\gamma}(F)=
 \min_{\substack{D\subseteq\G^d\\ \ML_{\gamma,1}(\Gamma_D)}}
 \frac{N^d-|D|}{N^d}.
\]
The minimum exists because the ambient set is finite and the empty graph is admissible. As projection is a bijection on a function graph, this is also the minimum fraction of graph pairs that must be deleted. It is \emph{not} a minimum over changes to values or additions of new graph pairs.


The full weighted function product property at parameter $\gamma$ requires the following. For every finite family of $t$ parallel coordinate restrictions $\psi_1,\ldots,\psi_t$ of the partial function, every common test set $U$ in their domains, and every nonnegative weight on $U$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:75:eq:full-product}
 \sum_{\substack{x_1+x_2=x_3+x_4,\ x_i\in U\\
 \psi_j(x_1)+\psi_j(x_2)=\psi_j(x_3)+\psi_j(x_4)\ \forall j}}
 \prod_{i=1}^4w(x_i)
 \ge\frac{\gamma^{8t}}N\left(\sum_{x\in U}w(x)\right)^4.
\end{equation}
The family may be empty. The relation product property requires this for every partial function whose graph lies in the relation. This is the source's \filename{HasProductProperty} convention~\cite{repo74product}.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A self-contained long-progression word estimate\srctag{75}}]{A self-contained long-progression word estimate}\label{gsr:en:75:sec:d3}
\srcnote{75}{Section 3}
\begin{lemma}\label{gsr:en:75:lem:word}
Let integers $R\ge2$ and $N\ge3R$ be given. Set
\[
 S=\{0,\ldots,R-1\}\subseteq\G,\quad
 K=2RN^3+N^5,\quad
 L_0=\max\{8R,\ceil{128R\log(2K)}\}.
\]
There is a word $b:\G\to S$ such that on every proper progression $I$ of length $L\ge L_0$ every symbol has count in
$[7L/(8R),5L/(4R)]$, and every affine restriction nonconstant on $I$ agrees with $b$ at at most $3L/(4R)$ points. Consequently every single affine restriction agrees at at most $5L/(4R)$ points, and every list of at most $q$ affine restrictions covers at most $5qL/(4R)$ points.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
First fix a nonconstant restriction
$f(x_0+jt)=v+j\Delta$, where $\Delta\ne0$ and its additive order is $\ell\ge2$. A complete period visits a coset of the subgroup with spacing $h=N/\ell$. The number $a_0$ of values of this coset in $S$ obeys
\[
 a_0\le\ceil{R/h}=\ceil{R\ell/N}\le\ceil{\ell/3}\le\ell/2,
 \qquad a_0\le R.
\]
For $\ell=2,3$ the penultimate comparison is direct; for each of the three residue classes modulo $3$ it follows immediately for $\ell\ge4$.
Writing $L=u\ell+r$, $0\le r<\ell$, the number $A$ of positions at which $f$ has a value in $S$ is at most
$u a_0+\min(r,a_0)\le L/2+R$.

Choose the $b(x)$ independently and uniformly from $S$.
For a sum $X$ of independent Bernoulli variables of mean $\mu$, the elementary exponential moment bound
$\E e^{\lambda X}\le\exp(\mu(e^\lambda-1))$ gives
\begin{align*}
 \Pr(X\le(1-\varepsilon)\mu)&\le e^{-\mu\varepsilon^2/2},\\
 \Pr(X\ge(1+\varepsilon)\mu)&\le e^{-\mu\varepsilon^2/(2+\varepsilon)},\\
 \Pr(X-\mu\ge t)&\le\exp\left(-\frac{t^2}{2(\mu+t/3)}\right).
\end{align*}
Here $0<\varepsilon<1$, $t>0$, with the last estimate trivial at $\mu=0$. For completeness, use exponential Markov with
$\lambda=\log(1-\varepsilon)$ or $\log(1+\varepsilon)$ for the first two estimates. The required inequalities
$(1-\varepsilon)\log(1-\varepsilon)+\varepsilon\ge\varepsilon^2/2$
and
$(1+\varepsilon)\log(1+\varepsilon)-\varepsilon\ge\varepsilon^2/(2+\varepsilon)$
follow by differentiating from zero; for the second use
$\log(1+\varepsilon)\ge2\varepsilon/(2+\varepsilon)$.
For the third estimate, $j!\ge2\cdot3^{j-2}$ for $j\ge2$ gives
$e^\lambda-1-\lambda\le\lambda^2/(2(1-\lambda/3))$ for $0<\lambda<3$; substitute $\lambda=t/(\mu+t/3)$.

On a fixed proper progression, a given symbol count has mean $L/R$. Its failures below $7L/(8R)$ or above $5L/(4R)$ each have probability at most $e^{-L/(128R)}$, using respectively $\varepsilon=1/8$ and $1/4$.
A fixed nonconstant affine agreement count has distribution
$\operatorname{Bin}(A,1/R)$ because the domain points are distinct, even if affine values repeat. As $L\ge8R$, its mean is at most $5L/(8R)$. The third tail bound, with $t=L/(8R)$, bounds failure above $3L/(4R)$ by
$e^{-3L/(256R)}\le e^{-L/(128R)}$.
There are at most $N^3$ progression presentations and $N^2$ affine maps. Thus at most $K$ bad events are excluded, and their union has probability at most
$K e^{-L_0/(128R)}\le1/2$.
A word avoiding all failures exists. A constant restriction in $S$ uses its symbol-count upper bound; a constant outside $S$ never agrees. Summing the single-map bound proves the list bound without an independence assumption or another union bound.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Graph-convolution restoration of weighted energy\srctag{75}}]{Graph-convolution restoration of weighted energy}\label{gsr:en:75:sec:d4}
\srcnote{75}{Section 4}
For a map $a:\G\to\G$ and nonnegative $w:\G\to\R$, write
\[
 \Eng(a,w)=\sum_{\substack{x_1+x_2=x_3+x_4\\a(x_1)+a(x_2)=a(x_3)+a(x_4)}}
 \prod_{i=1}^4w(x_i).
\]
All sums are unnormalized and quadruples ordered.
\begin{lemma}\label{gsr:en:75:lem:energy}
Suppose $a=0$ outside a nonempty $J\subseteq\G$ and $a(J)\subseteq S$. Put
$A=\sum_{x\notin J}w(x)$, $B=\sum_{x\in J}w(x)$, and
$M=|J+J|\,|S+S|$. Then
\begin{align}
 \Eng(a,w)&\ge A^4/N+B^4/M,\label{gsr:en:75:eq:mass}\\
 \Eng(a,w)&\ge\frac{(A+B)^4}{N}
 \left(1+(M/N)^{1/3}\right)^{-3}.\label{gsr:en:75:eq:coeff}
\end{align}
If $J=\{0,\ldots,m-1\}$ and $S=\{0,\ldots,R-1\}$, then
$M\le(2m-1)(2R-1)<4mR$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The all-outside quadruples are respected because $a=0$ there. Ordinary convolution Cauchy--Schwarz gives their contribution at least $A^4/N$.
Define a nonnegative function on $\G\times\G$ by
$g(x,z)=w(x)1_J(x)1_{\{a(x)\}}(z)$.
Its convolution $g*g$ is supported on $(J+J)\times(S+S)$, and
$\sum_{s,t}(g*g)(s,t)=B^2$. Hence
\[
 \sum_{s,t}(g*g)(s,t)^2\ge B^4/M.
\]
The left side is exactly the all-inside respected-quadruple contribution. The inside and outside families are disjoint and all remaining summands nonnegative, proving \eqref{gsr:en:75:eq:mass}.
H\"older gives
$(A+B)^4\le(A^4/N+B^4/M)(N^{1/3}+M^{1/3})^3$,
which proves \eqref{gsr:en:75:eq:coeff}. An interval of $m$ residues has at most $2m-1$ pair sums; similarly for $S$.
\end{proof}
The minimization of the two-mass expression is exact at
$A:B=N^{1/3}:M^{1/3}$, but neither this energy lower bound nor its ensuing deletion bounds are asserted to be optimal for the actual word. One may also use $\min\{m^2,M\}$ in place of $M$, by the original diagonal-quadruple argument.

\begin{corollary}\label{gsr:en:75:cor:product}
If $4mR/N\le\eta$ and $F(h,y)=a(y)$ on $\G^k\times\G$, then $F$ has the full weighted function product property at parameter $\gamma$, and its full graph has the relation product property.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The energy coefficient in \eqref{gsr:en:75:eq:coeff} is at least
$(1+\eta^{1/3})^{-3}=\gamma^8$.
For every family of $t\ge1$ parallel final-coordinate restrictions, all restrictions are the same $a$. On any common test set, extend the test weight by zero. Simultaneous respected energy therefore has coefficient at least $\gamma^8\ge\gamma^{8t}$. Horizontal restrictions are constant, so ordinary convolution gives coefficient one. For $t=0$ there is no image constraint, and the same ordinary bound supplies exactly the required coefficient one. Every partial map with graph in the full graph agrees with $F$ on its domain; every common test set therefore obeys the same estimates. This is the source's full relation quantifier, not merely an unweighted or fixed-family version.
\end{proof}
A sharper exact finite sufficient energy test is $M/N\le\eta$. If $2m-1\le N$ and $2R-1\le N$, it becomes
$(2m-1)(2R-1)\le\eta N$, equivalently
$m\le\floor{(1+\eta N/(2R-1))/2}$.
This is an exact algebraic threshold for the displayed sufficient estimate, not a necessary condition for the product property.

\section[{Arbitrary retained domains: the deletion inequality\srctag{75}}]{Arbitrary retained domains: the deletion inequality}\label{gsr:en:75:sec:d5}
\srcnote{75}{Section 5}
Choose $b$ from Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:75:lem:word}, put $J=\{0,\ldots,m-1\}$, and define
\[
 a(y)=\begin{cases}b(y)&y\in J,\\0&y\notin J,\end{cases}
 \qquad F(h,y)=a(y).
\]
For a local loss $0<\rho<1$, write
\[
 q_\rho=(\gamma\rho)^{-E},\quad c_\rho=(\gamma\rho)^E,
 \quad \beta(\rho,R)=1-\rho-\frac{5q_\rho}{4R}.
\]
\begin{theorem}[General finite deletion profile]\label{gsr:en:75:thm:profile}
Assume $N\ge3R$, $1\le m\le N$, and $m^{c_\rho}\ge L_0$. Every retained domain $D\subseteq\G^d$ satisfying
$\ML_{\gamma,1}(\Gamma_D)$ obeys
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:75:eq:delete}
 \frac{|\G^d\setminus D|}{N^d}
 \ge \left[1-\rho-\frac{5\floor{q_\rho}}{4R}\right]_+\frac mN
 \ge[\beta(\rho,R)]_+\frac mN.
\end{equation}
Here $[x]_+=\max\{x,0\}$. Conversely,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:75:eq:sandwich}
 \Delta_\gamma(F)\le m/N.
\end{equation}
Thus whenever $\beta(\rho,R)>0$, the minimum deletion fraction is bounded between $\beta(\rho,R)m/N$ and $m/N$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Test the local predicate on the proper common-step-one box
$P=\G^k\times J$, which has width $m$ and size $N^k m$.
Every output cell has width at least $m^{c_\rho}\ge L_0>0$, so all its axes are nonempty. Since its carrier lies in $P$, fixing points on all other axes shows that its final axis $I$ lies in $J$; it is proper and has length at least $L_0$.
After fixing its first $k$ coordinates, each multiaffine graph is affine in the final variable. At most $\floor{q_\rho}$ such maps cover at most
$5\floor{q_\rho}|I|/(4R)$ points on that fibre. Sum over horizontal fibres and disjoint cells. If $C$ is the set of points of $P$ whose full-map value $F(x)$ is covered, then
$|C|\le5\floor{q_\rho}|P|/(4R)$.
The covering condition for the partial graph states
$H\cap D\subseteq C$. Consequently
\[
 (1-\rho)|P|\le|H|\le|P\setminus D|+|C|.
\]
This explicitly includes the deleted points, which may enter $H$ freely. It yields
$|P\setminus D|\ge(1-\rho-5\floor{q_\rho}/(4R))|P|$.
As $|\G^d\setminus D|\ge|P\setminus D|$, division by $N^d$ proves \eqref{gsr:en:75:eq:delete}.

For the upper bound retain $D_0=\G^k\times(\G\setminus J)$. Its partial graph has value zero wherever it is defined. On every proper box and at every loss take $H$ to be the \emph{whole} box, the identity partition, and one constant-zero graph. Its count is permitted because $(\gamma\rho)^{-E}\ge1$; its width is permitted because $(\gamma\rho)^E\in(0,1]$ (with the source's width-zero convention when necessary). The cover implication concerns only defined points and is satisfied. Exactly $N^k m$ domain points, or the same number of graph pairs, have been removed.
\end{proof}
The same lower proof applies to any graph subrelation: every subrelation of a single-valued full graph is uniquely $\Gamma_D$. No Cartesian, fibrewise, random, or slab-shaped assumption is made on $D$.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Explicit positive-density scales\srctag{75}}]{Explicit positive-density scales}\label{gsr:en:75:sec:d6}
\srcnote{75}{Section 6}
\begin{lemma}[Elementary nonvacuity threshold]\label{gsr:en:75:lem:scale}
Let $R\ge2$, $0<c\le1$, and $0<\lambda<1/2$. Set $m=\floor{\lambda N}$. If
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:75:eq:scale}
 \log N\ge8192R/c^2,\qquad N\ge(2/\lambda)^2,
\end{equation}
then $N\ge3R$, $m\ge\lambda N/2\ge\sqrt N$, and $m^c>L_0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Put $u=\log N$. Its lower bound implies $u\ge1$ and $u\ge\log(3R)$, since $8192R\ge3R\ge\log(3R)$. Thus $N\ge3R$ and
$K=2RN^3+N^5\le2N^5$, so
$\log(2K)\le\log4+5u\le7u$.
It follows that $L_0\le897Ru$: the rounded logarithmic term is at most $896Ru+1\le897Ru$, and $8R\le897Ru$.
The second size bound gives $\lambda N\ge2\sqrt N\ge2$, so
$m\ge\lambda N/2\ge\sqrt N$.
Finally,
\[
 m^c\ge e^{cu/2}\ge c^2u^2/8\ge1024Ru>897Ru\ge L_0,
\]
using $e^z\ge z^2/2$ for $z\ge0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Positive-density continuation with the original alphabet]\label{gsr:en:75:thm:baseline}
Take
\[
 R=\ceil{4Q_0},\quad c_0=(\gamma/2)^E,\quad
 \lambda=\eta/(4R),\quad m=\floor{\lambda N}.
\]
Every integer $N$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:75:eq:baselineN}
 \log N\ge8192R/c_0^2,\qquad N\ge(8R/\eta)^2
\end{equation}
admits the above full-domain $F$ with the full weighted function and relation product properties, all the named source data specified below, and
\begin{align}
 \frac{3m}{16N}&\le\Delta_\gamma(F)\le\frac mN,\label{gsr:en:75:eq:half}\\
 \Delta_\gamma(F)&\ge\frac{3\eta}{128R}>0.
\end{align}
Indeed the same construction and thresholds satisfy the stronger bounds
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:75:eq:improved}
 \frac{3m}{8N}\le\Delta_\gamma(F)\le\frac mN,
 \qquad \Delta_\gamma(F)\ge\frac{3\eta}{64R}.
\end{equation}
All constants here are independent of $N$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Because $R\ge4(2/\gamma)^E$ and $\eta<\gamma^{-8}$,
$0<\lambda<\gamma^{E-8}/(16\cdot2^E)<1/2$.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:75:lem:scale} applies with $c=c_0$, while
$4mR/N\le4\lambda R=\eta$ gives the product properties.
At loss $\rho=1/2$, $q_\rho=Q_0$ and the agreement fraction is at most $5/16$, giving $\beta\ge3/16$. This proves \eqref{gsr:en:75:eq:half}. Use $m/N\ge\lambda/2$ for its positive constant bound.
For \eqref{gsr:en:75:eq:improved}, take $\rho=3/5$. Its width exponent is larger than $c_0$, so the same threshold works. Its agreement fraction is at most
$(5/16)(5/6)^E$. Since $(5/6)^4=625/1296<1/2$ and $E\ge16$,
$(5/6)^E<1/16$. The deletion fraction within the slab is therefore greater than
$2/5-5/256=487/1280>3/8$.
\end{proof}
For this same alphabet one may instead choose
\[
 \rho_E=\tfrac12(5E/8)^{1/(E+1)},\qquad
 \beta_E=1-\frac{E+1}{2E}(5E/8)^{1/(E+1)}.
\]
Here $1/2\le\rho_E<1$: $5E/8\ge1$ and $5E/8<2^{E+1}$ for $E\ge2$. The general profile gives
$\Delta_\gamma(F)\ge\beta_E m/N$, because the derivative of
$1-\rho-(5/16)(2\rho)^{-E}$ vanishes at this $\rho_E$ and its second derivative is negative. The width exponent is at least $c_0$. The value $\beta_E$ tends to $1/2$ as $E\to\infty$. This optimizes the displayed conservative loss profile for fixed original $R$, not the true minimum deletion problem.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Optimizing the alphabet and the loss\srctag{75}}]{Optimizing the alphabet and the loss}\label{gsr:en:75:sec:d7}
\srcnote{75}{Section 7}
For fixed $\gamma,E$, disregard rounding for one moment and set $m/N=\eta/(4R)$. The lower-bound surrogate from Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:75:thm:profile} is
\[
 \frac\eta4\left(\frac{1-\rho}{R}-\frac{5q_\rho}{4R^2}\right).
\]
For fixed $\rho$, elementary differentiation gives its maximum at
\[
 R_{\rm cont}=\frac{5q_\rho}{2(1-\rho)},
\]
with value $\eta\gamma^E\rho^E(1-\rho)^2/20$.
The logarithmic derivative of $\rho^E(1-\rho)^2$ is
$E/\rho-2/(1-\rho)$, giving the unique maximizer
$\rho_*=E/(E+2)$ and continuous maximum
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:75:eq:surrogate}
 \frac{\eta\gamma^E E^E}{5(E+2)^{E+2}}.
\end{equation}
Only this elementary surrogate within this construction family is optimized.

\begin{theorem}[Rounded optimized positive barrier]\label{gsr:en:75:thm:optimized}
Put
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \rho_* =\frac E{E+2},\qquad
 q_*=(\gamma\rho_*)^{-E},\qquad c_*=q_*^{-1},\\
 R=\ceil{\frac{5(E+2)q_*}{4}},\qquad
 \lambda=\frac\eta{4R},\qquad m=\floor{\lambda N}.
 \end{gathered}
\]
Every integer $N$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:75:eq:optimizedN}
 \log N\ge8192R/c_*^2,\qquad N\ge(8R/\eta)^2
\end{equation}
admits such an $F$ with all the same weighted product and named upstream properties, and
\begin{align}
 \frac{m}{N(E+2)}&\le\Delta_\gamma(F)\le\frac mN,\label{gsr:en:75:eq:optimizedsandwich}\\
 \Delta_\gamma(F)&\ge\frac{\eta}{8R(E+2)}
 \ge\frac{\eta\gamma^E}{12e^2(E+2)^2}>0.\label{gsr:en:75:eq:optimizedconstant}
\end{align}
The sharper unrounded-in-$N$ estimate is
\[
 \Delta_\gamma(F)\ge\frac{\eta}{4R(E+2)}-\frac1{N(E+2)}.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The choice of $R$ gives
$5q_* /(4R)\le1/(E+2)$, while
$1-\rho_*=2/(E+2)$. Thus $\beta(\rho_*,R)\ge1/(E+2)$.
Also
\[
 0<\lambda<\frac{\gamma^{-8}}{5(E+2)q_*}
 =\frac{\gamma^{E-8}\rho_*^E}{5(E+2)}<\frac12.
\]
Here the actual $E\ge8$ is used; an abstract assumption $E\ge4$ would not alone justify this inequality uniformly in $\gamma$.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:75:lem:scale}, Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:75:cor:product}, and Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:75:thm:profile} prove \eqref{gsr:en:75:eq:optimizedsandwich} and the first inequality of \eqref{gsr:en:75:eq:optimizedconstant}.
Set $T=(E+2)q_*\ge4$. Since $R\le5T/4+1\le3T/2$,
\[
 \frac{\eta}{8R(E+2)}\ge\frac{\eta}{12(E+2)^2q_*}
 =\frac{\eta\gamma^E\rho_*^E}{12(E+2)^2}
 \ge\frac{\eta\gamma^E}{12e^2(E+2)^2}.
\]
The last inequality follows from
$(1+2/E)^E\le e^2$, itself a consequence of $\log(1+x)\le x$.
Finally $m\ge\lambda N-1$ gives the displayed sharper estimate.
\end{proof}

\section[{Transfer of the pinned source predicates\srctag{75}}]{Transfer of the pinned source predicates}\label{gsr:en:75:sec:d8}\label{gsr:en:75:sec:transfer}
\srcnote{75}{Section 8}
The construction admits the same named data as Report 286. We verify that claim directly at the pinned interface, beginning with its image budget. In the baseline construction $R\le4Q_0+1\le Q_0^2$ because $Q_0\ge5$. In the optimized construction,
\[
 q_* =\gamma^{-E}(1+2/E)^E<8\gamma^{-E},
\]
so
\[
 R\le10(E+2)\gamma^{-E}+1
 \le11(E+2)\gamma^{-E}\le4^E\gamma^{-2E}=Q_0^2.
\]
For the last comparison use $\gamma^{-E}\le\gamma^{-2E}$ and
$11(E+2)\le4^E$ for integers $E\ge4$: it holds at $4$ and is preserved by incrementing $E$. Thus both variants satisfy the same sufficient image budget
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:75:eq:imagebudget}
 R\le Q_0^2.
\end{equation}

\subsection{Image bounds, proper sections, and all-box line covers}
A partial function with at most $R$ image values has
$\ML_{\gamma,r}$ in dimension $j$ whenever
$R\le(r/\gamma)^{E_jr}$, $r\ge1$. Indeed use all $R$ constant values, the identity partition, and the entire box as $H$. The graph ceiling is smallest at loss one, and the width exponent lies in $(0,1]$; zero width causes no problem.

The source iterations for $k\ge1$ are
\[
 B_k=2^{2^{k+6}},\quad
 r_0=\gamma^{-2}(2^{k+3}/\gamma)^{B_k},\quad
 r=(2^k-1)r_0.
\]
They satisfy $r\ge r_0\ge2E$. To see this, $2^{k+6}\ge k+10$ implies $B_k\ge2^{k+10}$, and
$\log_2r_0\ge(k+3)B_k\ge2^{k+10}\ge1+2^{k+9}=\log_2(2E)$.
A positive-dimensional proper face has dimension $j\le k$ and image size at most $R$, so
\[
 (r_0/\gamma)^{E_jr_0}\ge(2/\gamma)^{2E}=Q_0^2\ge R.
\]
Zero-dimensional faces are constant. Every fixed-final-coordinate section is constant in all horizontal coordinates. These facts give
\filename{ProperCrossSectionsMultiplyLinear} and the fixed-final-coordinate premise of the pinned \filename{lemma_16_10}.

Write the source's remaining parameters as
\[
 \theta_1=(\gamma/4)^{2^{2^{k+5}}},\quad
 \delta=2^{-37}(\theta_1/4)^{11/2},\quad
 \zeta=2^{-\mathcal S(1,\gamma,k)},\quad
 t=\delta^{-2}\mathcal S(\theta_1/8,\delta,k),
\]
where $\mathcal S(\tau,\gamma,j)=(2/(\tau\gamma))^{2^{2^{j+6}}}$.
Then $0<\theta_1,\delta,\zeta\le1$ and $t\ge1$.
At a line-cover loss $\sigma$, the two independent graph ceilings are
$(2r/(\gamma\sigma))^{Er}$ and
$(2t/(\delta\sigma))^{E_kt}$.
The first is at least $Q_0^2\ge R$, the second at least one. Set their natural witness counts to $(q_\gamma,q_\delta)=(R,1)$.
With $K_k=(k+1)^2 2^{k+4}$, the line-width requirement is
\[
 \frac\zeta2 n^{e},\qquad
 e=\frac{(\gamma\sigma/(2r))^{Er}(\delta\sigma/(2t))^{E_kt}}
 {2K_k^{2^{k+1}q_\delta}}\in(0,1].
\]
For any proper box of width at least the natural number $n$, use its identity partition, retain it entirely, and use the $R$ constant affine functions on each final-coordinate fibre. For $n\ge1$, the required width is at most $n$; for $n=0$ it is zero. This supplies the exact \filename{Section16AllBoxLineCovers} predicate, including both graph budgets and the delta-side dependence of the width. It does not require a prime modulus.

\subsection{The named full-domain realization}
Take $B=\G^{k+1}$, $\phi=F$, horizontal side/base-selection sets
$H=J_{\rm base}=H_1=\G^k$, basepoint $x_0=0$, and for each side $h$ take $Y_h=X_h$ to be the full finite type \filename{Section16CubeElement B h}. The notation $J_{\rm base}$ is unrelated to the short final-coordinate interval $J$.
Choose both the induced map $\phi'$ and every Bohr-model map $\psi_h$ to be zero.
Every horizontal alternating cube value is
\[
 a(y)\sum_{\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}^k}(-1)^{|\varepsilon|}
 =a(y)(1-1)^k=0.
\]
Hence every general arrangement is respected. For an 8-arrangement, there are $N^k$ sides, $N^{16k}$ horizontal base choices, and $N^{15}$ independent final coordinates, because the sixteenth is determined with coefficient $1$ or $-1$. Thus the total arrangement count is $N^{17k+15}$, its per-side count $N^{16k+15}$, and
$|X_h|=|Y_h|=N^{k+1}$.
The structured-pair inequalities multiply these full counts by factors at most one, including $\theta_1$ and $1-2^{-44}$. Together with the proper-section covers this gives \filename{Section16StructuredPair 1 gamma B phi}. The recorded Lemma 16.5 size conclusions also follow immediately, their factors being $\theta_1/4$ and $2^{-27}\theta_1^6$.

The full indicator's higher cube correlation is the constant $N^k$; its unnormalized Fourier transform is $N^{k+1}$ at zero and zero elsewhere. The nonzero-frequency vanishing is the cyclic geometric-series identity and does not require primality. The actual large spectrum is therefore $\{0\}$, and the spectrum relation is the graph of zero. It has a one-constant-graph $\ML_{\delta,t}$ cover. Zero is a Freiman homomorphism on every Bohr set~\cite{repo74bohr}; all induced differences vanish, giving \filename{HasBohrDifferenceModel}. The value and short-Bohr-progression affinity clauses of \filename{Section16InducedSelection} hold identically.

For every $(h,y)$, the cube based at zero belongs to $Y_h$. Thus the actual good domain is all of $\G^{k+1}$ and the good-pair count is $N^{k+1}$; its size lower bounds again have factors at most one (in particular $\theta_2=2^{-32}\theta_1^8\le1$). The actual all-ones vertex value is $a(y)=F(h,y)$. The sum of $(-1)^{k+|\varepsilon|}$ over all vertices is zero and the all-ones term is one, so the other terms sum to $-1$. The source remainder is consequently $a(y)$, and
\filename{Section16PhiOneIdentity} reads $a(y)=(-1)^k0+a(y)$.
Its required remainder cover is available because
$(r/\gamma)^{Er}\ge Q_0^2\ge R$.
These calculations are independent of the size of $J$ and use only the image budget \eqref{gsr:en:75:eq:imagebudget}.

The full graph has exactly $N^{k+1}\le\gamma^{-2}N^{k+1}$ elements. For prime $N$, the named antecedents of the source's actual numbered Lemma 16.9 are available. For composite $N$, only the displayed predicates and direct all-box line-cover witnesses are asserted; the prime-only numbered lemma is not applied. The separately quantified lower-dimensional Theorem 16.2 induction-family assumption upstream of the selection is not proved here. The structured pair is a valid recorded output, not a claim that every contextual selection must choose this output.

\section{Sources~82, 83 and~85: target torsion, fourth norms of the reflection and spectral saturation \wtag}\label{gsr:en:sec:spikes}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the thirteenth write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next twenty-nine sections are source~82's Sections~2--9, source~83's Sections~2--13 and source~85's Sections~2--10 (Reports~294, 295 and~297). \emph{Logically they continue the hereditary chain of sources~75--81} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:hereditary}): the same invariant, the infimum $r(a)$ over finitely supported weights of the respected fraction $\Ea/\Eadd$ of additive quadruples, for maps defined on a whole abelian group; it is not source~11's whole-graph energy (that chapter's guide). The three sources form a chain of their own (source~82 imports source~81's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:81:thm:main}, source~85 imports source~83's reflection theorem, each by the SHA-256 of the predecessor's \TeX{} source; all match). The introductions are Sections~\ref{gsr:fm:82:sec:d1}, \ref{gsr:fm:83:sec:d1} and~\ref{gsr:fm:85:sec:d1}.

\emph{What source~82 proves.} Fix an $\F_3$-space $V$ of dimension at least two and a nontrivial abelian target $H$. Among maps outside the affine maps and the translated index-three cuts, the largest $r(a)$ is exactly $5/9$ when $H$ has no element of order two and source~81's $\lambda=(11+6\sqrt6)/(11+6\sqrt6+7\sqrt{6\sqrt6-8})=0.5865294215\ldots$ otherwise, both attained for every fixed pair $(V,H)$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:82:thm:main}): $5/9$ by a pulled-back three-value map, also for indicators, $\lambda$ by the codimension-two spike $\delta\ind_{\ker\pi}$ with every product weight $f_0\otimes h$. Without two-torsion every bad map has a three-point line witness of ratio $5/9$ or a nine-point plane witness of ratio at most $41/81$, at most $361/729$ when no derivative has square sum $45$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:82:thm:no2}, Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:82:prop:q45}). The lower bound for spikes comes from the sharp complex fourth-power inequality $\norm{R_9z}_4^4\ge(2\lambda-1)\norm z_4^4$ for $R_9=I-2J/9$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:82:thm:reflection}) and a nine-frequency block lift. The upper bound $\lambda$ with two-torsion is source~81's, imported; the bound $5/9$ is source~82's own.

\emph{What source~83 proves.} For every $n\ge3$ and $\gamma>0$ every real $\ell^4$-maximizer of $I-\gamma J/n$ takes at most two values and complex maximizers are complex multiples of real ones (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:83:thm:general}), with a finite quintic reduction (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:83:thm:quintic}) and an exact threshold $\gamma_n\uparrow\gamma_\infty=(3+\sqrt3+\sqrt{2\sqrt3})/2$ above which constants maximize (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:83:thm:threshold}, Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:83:cor:gamma-infty}); this proves the $p=4$ case of Conjecture~5.6 of Bouthat, Mashreghi and Morneau-Gu\'erin. For the reflection $H_n=I-2J/n$, $C_n=\norm{H_n}_{4\to4}^4=(1+k_n)/(1-k_n)$ with at most two candidate multiplicities near $np_*$, $p_*=(1-\sqrt{2/3})/2$, $C_n<3+2\sqrt2$ and $\norm{H_n}_{4\to4}\to\sqrt{1+\sqrt2}$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:83:thm:reflection-overview}). Through the parity identity, the point spike of order two on any abelian group of order $n$ has $r\ge\eta_n=1/(1+k_n)$ (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:83:cor:spectral-bound}), attained iff an optimal multiplicity divides $n$, with all equality weights (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:83:thm:attainment}), and the same for subgroup spikes by index (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:83:thm:subgroup-spike}). \emph{Source~82's reflection theorem is the case $n=9$} ($m_9=1$, $k_9=k_*$, $\eta_9=\lambda$; checked at the write); the two proofs are independent and both are printed.

\emph{What source~85 proves.} The integer comparator $W(n,m)=m(n-m)(n-2m)^4$ orders the two candidates and adjacent candidates never tie, so the optimal multiplicity $m_n$ is unique for every $n\ge3$ (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:85:cor:unique}), which answers source~83's question on ties; exactly $77$ orders $n\ge3$ saturate, the largest $583=11\cdot53$, the same list for subgroup indices; rational or indicator equality occurs only at order or index four (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:85:thm:main}, Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:85:cor:rational}).

\emph{Checked at the write} (\file{verify13.py}). The constants $\lambda$, $\mu=2\lambda-1$, $\norm{R_9}_{4\to4}=\mu^{-1/4}=1.5504278\ldots$; $k_9=k_*$ and $t_9=u_*$; $C_n<3+2\sqrt2$ for $n\le400$; $\gamma_n$ increasing to $\gamma_\infty$; the uniqueness of $m_n$ for $n\le700$ against all multiplicities, and the comparator on the two candidates up to $n=200000$, giving exactly the $77$ orders of Table~\ref{gsr:fm:85:tab:classification}. The spike of order two on $\F_3^2$ with weights $(u_*,1,\ldots,1)$ has ratio exactly $\lambda$ (to $45$ digits), and product weights on $\F_3^3$ keep it. \emph{Per target, in dimension one} (a relation the brief asked for): for maps $\F_3\to\Z/3\Z$ and $\F_3\to\Z/7\Z$ the largest indicator infimum outside the two families is $5/9$ (exhaustive), as source~82's theorem states for every positive dimension when the target has no two-torsion; for $\Z/3\Z\to\Z/3\Z$ this is the value $5/9$ that the twelfth write computed for fixed targets $\Z/N\Z\to\Z/N\Z$ (note after source~75's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:75:thm:classification}). The other values computed there, $5/8$, $69/125$, $73/105$, $19/31$ for $N=4,\ldots,7$, have cyclic domains that are not $\F_3$-spaces: source~82 does not apply to them, and $19/31>5/9$ at $N=7$ shows that its $5/9$ is specific to $\F_3$-space domains. Relative to source~80's indicator cutoff $53/81$ (the nine-point spike over its $511$ supports): without two-torsion source~82's indicator witnesses give at most $5/9<53/81$, so the cutoff $53/81$ is attained only with two-torsion.

\emph{Which $5/8$} (the scope warning of Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:hereditary}). \section[{Lines and plane derivatives\srctag{82}}]{Lines and plane derivatives}\label{gsr:en:82:sec:d2}\label{gsr:en:82:sec:plane-start}
\srcnote{82}{Section 2}
For this section and Sections~\ref{gsr:en:82:sec:q45}--\ref{gsr:en:82:sec:finish-plane}, assume $H[2]=\{0\}$. Equivalently, multiplication by two is injective on $H$. Elements of order three, nine, other odd orders, or infinite order are all permitted.

A target triple is called a progression if it has some ordering $A,B,C$ with $2B=A+C$. Distinctness of these values is not required.

\begin{lemma}[The three-point line test]\label{gsr:en:82:lem:line}
For an affine line $L\subset V$, let $m$ be the number of its three true target midpoint equalities. Then
\[\EaddV(\ind_L)=27,\qquad\Ea(\ind_L)=15+4m.\]
Thus a line without a progression ordering has indicator ratio $5/9$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
At each of the three source sums there is one diagonal ordered pair and the two orderings of the other unordered pair. If their target sums agree, the respected contribution is $3^2=9$; otherwise it is $1^2+2^2=5$. Add over the three source sums.
\end{proof}
In a cyclic source ordering of the line, a progression ordering is equivalent to at least two of the three successive target increments being equal. For example, equality of the first two increments is a midpoint relation at their common vertex; all three alternatives arise this way. The increments always sum to zero. This observation uses neither division nor an ordering on $H$.

We may therefore restrict attention to a plane $G=\F_3^2$ on which every line has a progression ordering. For $h\ne0$, set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:derivatives}
 D_h(x)=a(x+h)-a(x),\qquad
 Q_h=\sum_{v\in H}|\{x\in G:D_h(x)=v\}|^2.
\end{equation}
Only finitely many terms in this sum are nonzero. Translation by $h$ partitions the plane into three cycles of length three; on each cycle the three derivative values sum to zero and at least two agree. Also $Q_{-h}=Q_h$, since $D_{-h}(x)=-D_h(x-h)$.

The parameterization $(x+h,y,x,y+h)$ of source additive quadruples gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:energy-Q}
 \Ea(\ind_G)=\sum_{h\in G}Q_h
       =81+2\sum_dQ_d,\qquad\EaddV(\ind_G)=9^3=729,
\end{equation}
where $d$ runs over representatives of the four unoriented directions. Indeed, the target relation for that quadruple is $D_h(x)=D_h(y)$, and $Q_0=81$.

Affine source changes, target translations and subtraction of an affine map preserve which source additive quadruples are respected. In particular, they preserve the energy ratios; subtraction of a homomorphism translates each derivative histogram without changing its multiplicities.

\begin{lemma}[A constant derivative forces an allowed plane map]\label{gsr:en:82:lem:constant}
If every line in $G$ is a progression and some $D_h$ with $h\ne0$ is constant, then $a$ is affine or a translated index-three affine cut.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Write $D_h=v$. Going around an $h$-cycle gives $3v=0$. With $K=\langle h\rangle$, define $\psi(ih)=iv$; then $a(x+k)=a(x)+\psi(k)$. A transversal line has a progression ordering. Every permutation of its three points is an affine permutation of $\F_3$, so choose a basepoint $x_0$ and an orientation $t$ giving transversal values $\beta,\beta+u,\beta+2u$. Thus~\eqref{gsr:fm:82:eq:cut} holds. It is affine when $3u=0$ and a cut otherwise.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[No directional square sum exceeds forty five]\label{gsr:en:82:lem:qbound}
For a plane map outside the two families and with every line a progression, $Q_h\le45$ for every $h\ne0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A nonconstant multiset of nine entries with square-multiplicity sum greater than $45$ has partition $(8,1)$, $(7,2)$ or $(7,1,1)$. A constant multiset is excluded by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:82:lem:constant}. Let $v$ denote the majority value.

For $(8,1)$, an all-$v$ cycle gives $3v=0$, and the exceptional cycle gives $2v+u=0$, hence $u=v$. In $(7,1,1)$, exceptions in separate cycles yield the same contradiction; putting both exceptions in one cycle creates three distinct increments and violates the progression condition. For $(7,2)$, separate exceptional cycles are again impossible. In a common cycle their values are $(v,u,u)$; ordinary cycles give $3v=0$, and $v+2u=0$ then gives $2(u-v)=0$. Injectivity of doubling gives $u=v$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The square sum forty five branch\srctag{82}}]{The square sum forty five branch}\label{gsr:en:82:sec:d3}\label{gsr:en:82:sec:q45}
\srcnote{82}{Section 3}
The only partition of nine with square sum $45$ is $(6,3)$. Write its derivative values as $v$ six times and $u$ three times, with $u\ne v$. The numbers of $u$ entries in the three cycles form one of
\[(0,0,3),\qquad(0,1,2),\qquad(1,1,1).
\]
The middle possibility is excluded by the equations $3v=0$ and $2v+u=0$. There remain two cases:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item two all-$v$ cycles and one all-$u$ cycle, with $3v=3u=0$;
 \item all three cycles of type $(v,v,u)$, with $u=-2v$ and $3v\ne0$.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Two constant rows and an order nine pattern}
In the first case subtract the homomorphism of slope $v$ in the chosen direction and translate the target. The rows become
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:row-order9}
 \begin{matrix}
 0&0&0\\ b&b&b\\ c&c+\delta&c+2\delta
 \end{matrix},\qquad\delta=u-v\ne0,\quad3\delta=0.
\end{equation}
Every exceptional-row value $z$ belongs to a transversal triple $(0,b,z)$, whose three midpoint alternatives are
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:zchoices}
 z=-b,\qquad z=2b,\qquad 2z=b.
\end{equation}
The three row values are distinct. Each alternative covers at most one of them, including the third because doubling is injective. Hence all alternatives occur. In particular, $-b$ and $2b$ differ by a nonzero element of $\langle\delta\rangle$, so $3b=\delta$ or $-\delta$ and $b$ has exact order nine. If $2q=b$ denotes the third value, then $q=-b+j(3b)$ for some $j\in\{0,1,2\}$. The equation $2q=b$ gives $(6j-3)b=0$, hence $j=2$ and $q=5b$. Thus $q$ also has order nine and $b=2q$.

Permute the three horizontal coordinates, an affine operation, to write the map as
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:order9}
 \begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\2&2&2\\1&4&7\end{pmatrix}q.
\end{equation}
Its directional square sums are $(45,33,33,33)$. For an explicit count, use the equivalent exceptional row $(7,1,4)q$. In the horizontal direction the increments are $0$ six times and $3q$ three times. In each other direction, up to simultaneous sign reversal, the values are $2q$ five times, $-q$ twice and $-4q$ twice. They are distinct because $q$ has order nine. Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:energy-Q} gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:369}
 \Ea(\ind_G)=81+2(45+3\cdot33)=369,
 \qquad\frac{\Ea(\ind_G)}{729}=\frac{41}{81}.
\end{equation}

\subsection{Aligned exceptional edges}
In the second case each row has a unique edge with increment $-2v$ and two edges with increment $v$. Let its exceptional-edge position be a function of the row label in $\F_3$. If that function is affine, a source shear aligns the exceptional edges. The row baselines have a progression ordering, and an affine permutation of rows then gives
\[a(i,j)=iv+ju,\qquad i,j\in\{0,1,2\},\quad3v\ne0.
\]
The transversal triples $(u,v+2u,2v)$ and $(0,v+2u,2v+u)$ must be progressions. Their midpoint alternatives, discarding the impossible alternatives $3v=0$, respectively give
\[3u=0\ \text{or}\ 3u=3v,\qquad
  3u=0\ \text{or}\ 3u=-3v.
\]
If $3u\ne0$, then $6v=0$, and injectivity of doubling contradicts $3v\ne0$. Hence $3u=0$; the $j$-derivative is constant and Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:82:lem:constant} applies. This case cannot be outside the two families.

\subsection{Nonaligned exceptional edges}
Otherwise an affine shear aligns two exceptional edges and leaves the third shifted by $1$ or $-1$. Reversing the horizontal coordinate if needed and absorbing row constants gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:nonaligned}
 \begin{matrix}
 0&v&2v\\ b&b+v&b+2v\\ c+v&c+2v&c
 \end{matrix},\qquad3v\ne0.
\end{equation}
The nine transversal lines have horizontal coordinate $i+js$ in row $j$, with $i,s\in\F_3$. Subtracting their first values yields the six distinct triples
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:sixtriples}
 \begin{array}{lll}
 T_1=(0,b,c+v),&T_2=(0,b,c-2v),\\
 T_3=(0,b+v,c),&T_4=(0,b-2v,c),\\
 T_5=(0,b+2v,c+2v),&T_6=(0,b-v,c-v).
 \end{array}
\end{equation}
Grouped by slopes $s=0,1,2$, the nine lines produce $(T_1,T_1,T_2)$, $(T_3,T_3,T_4)$ and $(T_5,T_6,T_6)$. Thus all transversal conditions are represented.

\begin{lemma}[Six progression triples force six torsion]\label{gsr:en:82:lem:sixv}
In any abelian group, if all six triples in~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:sixtriples} have a progression ordering, then $6v=0$.
\end{lemma}
The lemma does not require injective doubling. Its exact finite proof is given in Section~\ref{gsr:en:82:sec:certificate}; this is the sole computer-assisted relation branch needed for the target-refined upper theorem. Applying it here and cancelling the injective factor two gives $3v=0$, a contradiction. We have therefore proved:

\begin{proposition}[The forty five branch]\label{gsr:en:82:prop:q45}
An outside-family plane map into a group with injective doubling, all of whose lines are progressions, and with some $Q_h=45$, is equivalent under the stated affine operations to~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:order9}. Its full-plane indicator ratio is $41/81$.
\end{proposition}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The square sums forty one and thirty nine\srctag{82}}]{The square sums forty one and thirty nine}\label{gsr:en:82:sec:d4}\label{gsr:en:82:sec:finish-plane}
\srcnote{82}{Section 4}
The next branches are necessary for the stronger $361/729$ bound when $45$ does not occur. They also show where other odd torsion orders can and cannot affect the calculation.

\subsection{The partition five four is impossible}
The partitions of nine with square sum $41$ are $(5,4)$ and $(6,2,1)$. Suppose the former occurs, with $v$ five times and $u$ four times. Set $d=u-v\ne0$. A cycle with $k$ copies of $u$ obeys $3v+kd=0$. The possible sorted triples of such counts are
\[(0,1,3),\qquad(0,2,2),\qquad(1,1,2).
\]
Subtracting cycle equations gives $d=0$ in the first and third cases, and $2d=0$ in the second. All are impossible when doubling is injective.

\subsection{The partition six two one has an exact form}
Let the derivative values be $v$ six times, $u$ twice and $w$ once, all distinct. The cycle containing $w$ cannot have three distinct increments. Hence it is either $(v,v,w)$ or $(u,u,w)$.

If it is $(v,v,w)$, the remaining two cycles contain four $v$'s and two $u$'s. Either they are an all-$v$ cycle and a $(v,u,u)$ cycle, or they are two $(v,v,u)$ cycles. In the first case, $3v=0$ and $v+2u=0$ imply $2(u-v)=0$, contrary to distinctness. In the second, $2v+u=2v+w=0$ implies $u=w$.

Thus the exceptional cycle is $(u,u,w)$ and the other two are all $v$. In particular $3v=0$ and $2u+w=0$. Subtracting the homomorphism of slope $v$ and translating yields
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:q41rows}
 \begin{matrix}0&0&0\\b&b&b\\c&c+d&c+2d\end{matrix},
 \qquad d=u-v\ne0,\quad3d\ne0.
\end{equation}
The last inequality follows from $u\ne w=-2u$ and $3v=0$. The three exceptional values are distinct, since $d\ne0$ and $2d\ne0$.

As in~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:zchoices}, the three values must exhaust $-b$, $2b$ and the unique solution $q$ of $2q=b$. Thus their set is $\{-2q,q,4q\}$. An affine permutation of horizontal coordinates gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:q41normal}
 \begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\2&2&2\\-2&1&4\end{pmatrix}q.
\end{equation}
In this ordering the horizontal increments are $0$ six times, $3q$ twice and $-6q$ once, still of partition $(6,2,1)$. In particular $9q\ne0$. In each other direction the increments, up to simultaneous sign reversal, are
\[2q\ \text{five times},\qquad -q\ \text{twice},\qquad-4q\ \text{twice}.
\]
Any collision among them would force $3q=0$ or $6q=0$, and injective doubling would imply $3q=0$, contradicting $9q\ne0$. The horizontal values are likewise distinct. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:361exact}
 (Q_d)_d=(41,33,33,33),\qquad
 \Ea(\ind_G)=81+2(41+3\cdot33)=361.
\end{equation}
This proof does not assume $q$ has infinite order. The only relevant coefficient differences are $3$, $6$ and $9$, so no other odd-order collision was omitted.

\subsection{The remaining square sums}
The complete list of partitions of nine with square sum greater than $35$ is
\begin{gather*}
 (9),\ (8,1),\ (7,2),\ (7,1,1),\ (6,3),\\
 (6,2,1),\ (6,1,1,1),\ (5,4).
\end{gather*}
It follows by separating the largest part: at most four gives square sum at most $4^2+4^2+1=33$; largest part five gives at most $41$, with the next largest case $5^2+3^2+1=35$; largest part at least six leaves precisely the listed possibilities above $35$.

Only $(6,1,1,1)$, of square sum $39$, remains untreated. Let $v$ occur six times, with distinct singleton values $u,w,z$. A cycle containing two different singletons would have three distinct increments, even if its third increment were $v$, and hence violate the progression condition. Thus each singleton belongs to a cycle with two $v$'s. The equations
\[2v+u=2v+w=2v+z=0
\]
force $u=w=z$, a contradiction. This exclusion does not even require injective doubling.

If a direction has square sum $45$, Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:82:prop:q45} applies. If not, but one has square sum $41$, equation~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:361exact} applies. If neither occurs, every direction has $Q_d\le35$, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:361bound}
 \Ea(\ind_G)\le81+2\cdot4\cdot35=361.
\end{equation}
Together with Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:82:lem:line}, this proves the entire plane assertion in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:82:thm:no2}. Notice that $369/729=41/81<5/9$, so a line failing the progression test is the only branch needed to reach the final sharp constant.

\section[{The exact six triple relation lemma\srctag{82}}]{The exact six triple relation lemma}\label{gsr:en:82:sec:d5}\label{gsr:en:82:sec:certificate}
\srcnote{82}{Section 5}
We give the precise finite input and verification criterion for Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:82:lem:sixv}. This is a calculation in $\Z^3$ that proves a statement for every abelian group; testing a bounded list of target groups would not suffice.

For a formal triple $(A,B,C)$, the midpoint relations are $2A-B-C$, $2B-A-C$ and $2C-A-B$. In formal variable order $(v,b,c)$, the six triples~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:sixtriples} give the following vectors:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{c r r r}
\toprule
Triple & First midpoint & Second midpoint & Third midpoint\\
\midrule
$T_1$&$(-1,-1,-1)$&$(-1,2,-1)$&$(2,-1,2)$\\
$T_2$&$(2,-1,-1)$&$(2,2,-1)$&$(-4,-1,2)$\\
$T_3$&$(-1,-1,-1)$&$(2,2,-1)$&$(-1,-1,2)$\\
$T_4$&$(2,-1,-1)$&$(-4,2,-1)$&$(2,-1,2)$\\
$T_5$&$(-4,-1,-1)$&$(2,2,-1)$&$(2,-1,2)$\\
$T_6$&$(2,-1,-1)$&$(-1,2,-1)$&$(-1,-1,2)$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Call the vector in row $i$ and column $j$ $R_{i,j}$, indexing $i=1,\ldots,6$ and $j=0,1,2$. There are exactly $729$ possible choices $\varepsilon\in\{0,1,2\}^6$ of one relation per row. The finite assertion needed is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:cert-identity}
 \text{for every }\varepsilon\in\{0,1,2\}^6,\quad
 \exists(c_1,\ldots,c_6)\in\Z^6:\quad
 \sum_{i=1}^6c_iR_{i,\varepsilon_i}=(6,0,0).
\end{equation}
The distributed file \filename{companion/midpoint_certificate.json} supplies one explicit coefficient vector for each choice, using a canonical permutation of the six groups and sign-normalized relations. The checker verifies the correspondence with the actual transversal triples. Undoing those permutations and signs gives exactly~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:cert-identity}, without changing coefficient magnitudes. The public checker reconstructs the triples and their relation vectors rather than accepting copied vectors from the certificate. It verifies that every one of the $729$ choices occurs exactly once, that all coefficient entries are integers of absolute value at most six, and that the three coordinates of~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:cert-identity} agree exactly. All arithmetic is integer arithmetic. No normal-form routine, floating-point rank decision or external algebra package is needed for this certificate.

\begin{proof}[Proof of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:82:lem:sixv} from the exhaustive certificate]
Define the homomorphism $\Phi:\Z^3\to H$ by
\[\Phi(p,q,r)=pv+qb+rc.
\]
For each of the six progression triples, select a true midpoint equality. This produces one choice $\varepsilon$, and $\Phi(R_{i,\varepsilon_i})=0$ for all $i$. Apply $\Phi$ to the verified identity~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:cert-identity} for that choice. The result is $6v=0$.

If several midpoint equalities hold for a triple, choosing any one is sufficient. Additional relations in $H$ only enlarge the kernel of $\Phi$ and cannot invalidate the conclusion. Thus infinite targets and torsion of unbounded order are covered without any finite-target extrapolation.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{What is and is not computer assisted.}
The existence of the $729$ displayed certificate identities is a finite component of the proof. The package contains their complete data and a verifier; it does not merely record a count or a PASS label. The reduction from arbitrary abelian groups to those identities is the preceding argument. The line and derivative reductions, the three-fiber inequality, the reflection moment proof and the infinite-dimensional arguments are mathematical proofs in the text. Other exact companion calculations are diagnostics for their algebra and finite counts, not substitutes for those proofs.
