\section[{Why affine planes suffice in every dimension\srctag{82}}]{Why affine planes suffice in every dimension}\label{gsr:en:82:sec:d6}\label{gsr:en:82:sec:gluing}
\srcnote{82}{Section 6}
We reproduce the qualitative part of the preceding report's gluing theorem~\cite{srceightyone}. It is valid for every abelian target, irrespective of its two torsion. Its numerical upper bound is not used in this section.

\begin{lemma}[Hyperplanes from plane sections]\label{gsr:en:82:lem:sections}
Let $\dim V\ge2$ and let $A$ be a nonempty proper subset of $V$. If every affine-plane section of $A$ is empty, full, a line, or the complement of a line, then $A$ is an affine hyperplane or the complement of one.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The hypothesis is invariant under complementation. Suppose first that some affine line $L$ has exactly two points in $A$. Put $B=V\setminus A$, and let $r$ be the unique point of $B\cap L$. For any $s\in B\setminus\{r\}$, the point $s$ is outside $L$. In the plane spanned by $L$ and $s$, the $B$-section meets $L$ once. Among the allowed section types only a line can do so: a complement of a line meets $L$ in zero, two or three points. Consequently the entire line through $r,s$ lies in $B$.

Translate $r$ to zero. Then $B$ is closed under scalar multiplication. For independent $s,t\in B$, its section on $\Span(s,t)$ contains two different lines through zero. It cannot be a line. It cannot be the complement of a line either, because every affine line in this plane intersects at least one of those two lines. Thus the section is the whole plane, giving closure under addition of independent vectors. Dependent vectors are handled by scalar closure, so $B$ is a subspace after translation. If its codimension were at least two, the span of two independent quotient representatives would meet $B$ in a singleton, a forbidden plane section. Its codimension is therefore one.

If no line has exactly two points in $A$, the line through any two of its distinct points lies wholly in $A$. Translate a point of $A$ to zero. Lines through zero give negation closure; the third point of the line through $-x,-y$ is $x+y$ for distinct $x,y\in A$. Equal vectors are handled by $2x=-x$. Hence $A$ is a subspace after translation. The same quotient-plane argument forces codimension one. All choices here involve only finitely many vectors, so the reasoning covers infinite dimension.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The fibers have a common direction]\label{gsr:en:82:lem:fibers}
If a nonconstant map $F:V\to H$ has every nonempty fiber an affine hyperplane or the complement of one, then $F$ is constant on the three cosets of a single linear hyperplane $K$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Disjoint affine hyperplanes are parallel. Indeed, hyperplanes of different directions are prescribed levels of independent linear functionals; the map given by the two functionals is onto $\F_3^2$, so those levels meet. One affine hyperplane contained in another must equal it.

If a fiber is $V\setminus M$, every other fiber is contained in $M$. Such a fiber cannot be the complement of a hyperplane $N$, for then $N$ would contain the two distinct hyperplanes constituting $V\setminus M$, which is impossible. Hence that fiber is itself a hyperplane and must equal $M$. There are exactly two fibers, and $K$ is the direction of $M$. If no fiber is a complement, the disjoint hyperplane fibers are parallel and constitute the three cosets of their common direction.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Qualitative local to global theorem]\label{gsr:en:82:prop:gluing}
A full map $a:V\to H$, with $\dim V\ge2$, belongs to one of the two families in Definition~\ref{gsr:fm:82:def:families} if and only if each affine-plane restriction does.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For the nontrivial direction, suppose every affine plane is allowed and put $F=3a$. On an affine plane restriction, $F$ is constant. On a cut plane its stripe values are $3\beta$, $3\beta+q$ and $3\beta+2q$ with $q=3u\ne0$. The consecutive values differ; the endpoints can coincide only when $2q=0$. Thus every plane fiber of $F$ is empty, full, a line, or a line complement.

If $F$ is constant, no plane can be a nonaffine cut. Then $g(x)=a(x)-a(0)$ restricts to a homomorphism on every linear plane. Any pair of vectors lies in a linear plane, after enlargement when dependent, so $g(x+y)=g(x)+g(y)$ globally.

If $F$ is nonconstant, Lemmas~\ref{gsr:en:82:lem:sections} and~\ref{gsr:en:82:lem:fibers} give a hyperplane $K$ such that $F$ is constant on its three cosets. A plane $P=p+W$ transverse to $K$ sees all three coset values, so its restriction is a nonaffine cut. Its local kernel direction is $W\cap K$. To check this even when the endpoint values of $F$ repeat, choose a value occurring just once in the nonconstant three-value quotient. Its fiber on $P$ is a full line in direction $W\cap K$ and also a local-kernel line, identifying the directions.

Fix $0\ne h\in K$. On every transverse plane whose direction contains $h$, the derivative $D_h a$ is constant across the whole plane. If $y-x\notin K$, the plane $x+\Span(h,y-x)$ compares $D_h a(x)$ and $D_h a(y)$. If $y-x\in K$, choose $z$ outside their common $K$-coset and make the comparison through $z$. Hence $D_h a$ is globally constant. Denote that constant by $\psi(h)$ and set $\psi(0)=0$. The derivative cocycle gives
\[\psi(h+k)=D_{h+k}a(x)=D_ha(x)+D_ka(x+h)=\psi(h)+\psi(k).
\]
Thus $\psi:K\to H$ is a homomorphism and $a(x+k)=a(x)+\psi(k)$ for every $x\in V$.

Every line restriction of an allowed plane has a progression ordering. For a cut this follows by using the affine $K$-coordinate on a kernel-parallel line, or the quotient coordinate on a transverse line; the identity $3\psi=0$ takes care of coordinate wraparound. Choose a transversal line to $K$, reorder it affinely, and write its values as $\beta,\beta+u,\beta+2u$. The global derivative formula extends this to~\eqref{gsr:fm:82:eq:cut}. If $3u=0$, then $F$ would be constant, contrary to the present case. This gives a global cut.

Conversely, affine maps restrict affinely. A plane parallel to the kernel of a global cut is affine. A transverse plane has kernel direction $W\cap K$ and increment $u+\psi(k_1)$ for a suitable kernel vector $k_1$; its triple is $3u\ne0$, so it is a local cut. This proves the converse.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[All-rank upper bound in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:82:thm:no2}]
In dimension at least two, the contrapositive of Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:82:prop:gluing} provides an outside-family affine plane. If some line in it fails the progression test, use Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:82:lem:line}. Otherwise Sections~\ref{gsr:en:82:sec:q45}--\ref{gsr:en:82:sec:finish-plane} supply the full-plane witness and its refined bound. Extend the indicator by zero to the ambient $V$; every nonzero energy summand still lies in its original support, so both energies are unchanged.

In dimension one, a progression-valued triple can be ordered by an affine source permutation and is affine or a translated cut. Hence an outside-family map has a failed-progression line. No compactness or limiting passage is needed in infinite dimension.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Sharp five ninths attainment through every kernel\srctag{82}}]{Sharp five ninths attainment through every kernel}\label{gsr:en:82:sec:d7}\label{gsr:en:82:sec:five-nine}
\srcnote{82}{Section 7}
The upper bound does not by itself prove sharpness at a fixed higher rank. We prove a lower bound for all weights on an explicit full map, including weights whose three kernel fibers differ arbitrarily.

\begin{lemma}[Three-variable sum of squares]\label{gsr:en:82:lem:sos}
For nonnegative $a,b,c$, let
\[N(a,b,c)=a^4+b^4+c^4+4(a^2b^2+a^2c^2+b^2c^2).
\]
Then
\begin{align}
 N(a,b,c)-5abc(a+b+c)
 ={}&\frac12\bigl((a^2-b^2)^2+(b^2-c^2)^2+(c^2-a^2)^2\bigr)\notag\\
 &+\frac52\bigl((ab-bc)^2+(bc-ca)^2+(ca-ab)^2\bigr)\ge0.
 \label{gsr:en:82:eq:sos}
\end{align}
Equality holds at $a=b=c$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Expand the six squares. The first bracket contributes $a^4+b^4+c^4-(a^2b^2+b^2c^2+c^2a^2)$; the second contributes five times the latter pair-square sum minus $5abc(a+b+c)$.
\end{proof}

Choose $0\ne t\in H$ with $H[2]=\{0\}$. Then $0,t,2t$ are pairwise distinct. Let $b:\F_3\to H$ have values $(0,0,t)$. None of its three midpoint relations holds: two would require $t=0$, and the third would require $2t=0$. Thus it is an outside-family map. For weights $(x,y,z)$, separating the diagonal and off-diagonal pair classes gives
\[\mathcal E_b=N(x,y,z),\qquad
  \mathcal E_{\F_3}=N(x,y,z)+4xyz(x+y+z).
\]
Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:sos} gives a ratio at least $5/9$, attained by the line indicator. This is the rank-one calculation; the next argument is needed for every higher rank.

Let $\pi:V\to\F_3$ be surjective and linear, let $K=\ker\pi$, and let $a=b\circ\pi$. First suppose $V$ is finite. Choose $e$ with $\pi(e)=1$ and write the three fiber functions as
\[f_r(k)=f(k+re),\qquad k\in K,\quad r\in\{0,1,2\}.
\]
All convolutions in this section are on $K$, and $\norm{g}_2^2=\sum_{k\in K}|g(k)|^2$. At source quotient sum zero the two target-sum classes are $f_0*f_0$ and $2f_1*f_2$. At quotient sum one they are $f_2*f_2$ and $2f_0*f_1$; at sum two they are $f_1*f_1$ and $2f_0*f_2$. They remain distinct because the relevant target sums are $0,t,2t$. Consequently
\begin{align}
 \Ea(f)&=\sum_{r=0}^2\norm{f_r*f_r}_2^2
                 +4\sum_{0\le r<s\le2}\norm{f_r*f_s}_2^2,\label{gsr:en:82:eq:three-retained}\\
 \EaddV(f)&=\norm{f_0*f_0+2f_1*f_2}_2^2
       +\norm{f_1*f_1+2f_0*f_2}_2^2
       +\norm{f_2*f_2+2f_0*f_1}_2^2.\label{gsr:en:82:eq:three-ordinary}
\end{align}

Use the unnormalized Fourier transform on $K$,
\[\widehat g(\chi)=\sum_{k\in K}g(k)\overline{\chi(k)}.
\]
Character orthogonality gives $\widehat{g*h}=\widehat g\,\widehat h$ and Parseval with factor $1/|K|$. For each character write $A=\widehat f_0(\chi)$, $B=\widehat f_1(\chi)$, $C=\widehat f_2(\chi)$. The summands of~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:three-retained} and~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:three-ordinary}, before the common factor, are respectively
\begin{align}
 N_\chi&=|A|^4+|B|^4+|C|^4+4(|AB|^2+|AC|^2+|BC|^2),\label{gsr:en:82:eq:complexN}\\
 E_\chi&=|A^2+2BC|^2+|B^2+2AC|^2+|C^2+2AB|^2\notag\\
 &=N_\chi+4\operatorname{Re}\bigl(A^2\overline{BC}+B^2\overline{AC}
                                      +C^2\overline{AB}\bigr).\label{gsr:en:82:eq:complexE}
\end{align}
Apply~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:sos} to $(|A|,|B|,|C|)$ and bound each real part by its modulus. This yields the pointwise inequality for every complex triple
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:complex59}
 E_\chi\le N_\chi+4|ABC|(|A|+|B|+|C|)\le\frac95N_\chi.
\end{equation}
Summing over characters proves
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:59lower}
 \Ea(f)\ge\frac59\EaddV(f)
\end{equation}
for every nonnegative weight, with no restriction on its fiber shapes. Complex Fourier coefficients cause no loss because~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:complex59} was proved for arbitrary complex $A,B,C$.

If $f(k+re)=h(k)$ for every $r$, where $h\ge0$ is nonzero, equations~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:three-retained}--\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:three-ordinary} become $15\norm{h*h}_2^2$ and $27\norm{h*h}_2^2$. Thus every such product weight attains $5/9$. Taking $h=\ind_{\{0\}}$ supplies a three-point indicator attaining it.

For infinite-dimensional $V$, let $f$ be any admissible weight and enlarge the span of its support by a vector $e$ with $\pi(e)=1$. The resulting subspace is finite-dimensional and the restricted quotient remains onto. Both energies are unchanged, so~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:59lower} applies. Product weights with finitely supported $h$ still attain equality. Finally, a transversal line has values $(0,0,t)$ and fails the progression test; since every line of either allowed family is a progression, $a\in\Ufam$. This completes the sharpness assertions of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:82:thm:no2} for every positive rank.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The sharp complex nine point reflection\srctag{82}}]{The sharp complex nine point reflection}\label{gsr:en:82:sec:d8}\label{gsr:en:82:sec:reflection}
\srcnote{82}{Section 8}
Let $J$ be the $9\times9$ all-ones matrix and let
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:Rdef}
 R_9=I-\frac29J.
\end{equation}
Thus $R_9$ subtracts twice the coordinate mean and satisfies $R_9^2=I$. The analytic assertion needed for the higher-rank spike is a sharp inequality on arbitrary complex vectors, not only on Fourier transforms of specially chosen weights.

\begin{theorem}[Exact fourth-power reflection ratio]\label{gsr:en:82:thm:reflection}
With the constants in~\eqref{gsr:fm:82:eq:constants},
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:reflection}
 \inf_{z\in\C^9\setminus\{0\}}
 \frac{\norm{R_9z}_4^4}{\norm z_4^4}=\mu=2\lambda-1.
\end{equation}
The same infimum holds over real vectors. Its nonzero real equality vectors are precisely the real scalar multiples of permutations of
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:zminus}
 z_-=(u_*+8,u_*-1,\ldots,u_*-1).
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:operatornorm}
 \norm{R_9}_{4\to4}=\mu^{-1/4}=1.5504278145502\ldots
\end{equation}
over both the real and complex scalars. No classification of all complex equality vectors is asserted.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 82--94]
\emph{The case $n=9$ of source~83's reflection theorem} (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:83:thm:reflection-overview}; source~83 credits this source): there $m_9=1$ and $k_9=k_*$, so $\norm{H_9}_{4\to4}^4=(1+k_*)/(1-k_*)=\mu^{-1}$ and $\eta_9=\lambda$ (checked at the write). The two proofs are independent and both are printed.
\end{writenote}

\subsection{Two classical moment bounds with their equality information}
Write a real vector as $z=m\ind+w$, where $m=\E z_i$ and $\E w_i=0$, and let
\[\sigma^2=\E w_i^2,\qquad M_3=\E w_i^3,\qquad M_4=\E w_i^4.
\]
Here $\E$ is the average over the nine coordinates. If $\sigma=0$, the nonzero vector is constant, $R_9z=-z$, and the ratio is one. The zero vector satisfies the homogeneous inequality trivially. For $\sigma>0$, put $Y_i=w_i/\sigma$ and $s=|\E Y^3|$. Then $\E Y=0$ and $\E Y^2=1$.

The Pearson moment inequality~\cite{pearsonskew} follows directly from the square
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:Pearson}
 0\le\E\bigl(Y^2-(\E Y^3)Y-1\bigr)^2
    =\E Y^4-(\E Y^3)^2-1.
\end{equation}
Thus $\E Y^4\ge1+s^2$. We will also need the finite equal-atom skewness bound, a special case of the sample bound recorded by Kirby~\cite{kirbyskew},
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:skew}
 s\le\frac7{\sqrt8}.
\end{equation}
For completeness, maximize or minimize $\sum_iY_i^3$ on the compact set
\[\sum_iY_i=0,\qquad\sum_iY_i^2=9.
\]
The two constraint gradients are independent: dependence would make $Y$ constant, incompatible with mean zero and unit variance. At any extremum the Lagrange equations therefore take the form
\[3Y_i^2=\alpha+2\beta Y_i.
\]
There are at most two distinct coordinate values, and there must be exactly two of opposite sign. If the positive value occurs $j$ times, the constraints force the two values to be
\[\sqrt{\frac{9-j}{j}},\qquad-\sqrt{\frac j{9-j}},\qquad1\le j\le8.
\]
Their third moment and its square are
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:skewvalues}
 \frac{9-2j}{\sqrt{j(9-j)}},\qquad
 \frac{81}{j(9-j)}-4.
\end{equation}
The square is maximized exactly at $j=1$ or $8$, proving~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:skew}. Equality is therefore attained only by permutations and sign reversals of
\[Y=(8,-1,\ldots,-1)/\sqrt8.
\]
For this vector the Pearson square also vanishes. Hence the two separate moment relaxations can be equalities simultaneously.

\subsection{A global scalar maximization}
Define
\[A=m^4+6m^2\sigma^2+M_4,\qquad B=4mM_3.
\]
We claim
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:momentbound}
 |B|\le k_*A.
\end{equation}
For $\sigma>0$, put $r=|m|/\sigma$. Equations~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:Pearson}--\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:skew} give
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:Frs}
 \frac{|B|}{A}\le F(r,s):=\frac{4rs}{r^4+6r^2+1+s^2},
 \qquad r\ge0,\quad0\le s\le7/\sqrt8.
\end{equation}
If $s=0$, the expression is zero. If $s>0$, its derivative in $r$ has the sign of $1+s^2-6r^2-3r^4$. This decreases strictly for positive $r$, starts positive and tends to minus infinity. Thus the unique positive critical point is the global maximum, since $F$ is zero at $r=0$ and tends to zero at infinity. In terms of $y=r^2$, it is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:yscalar}
 y=-1+\sqrt{(4+s^2)/3},\qquad s^2=3y^2+6y-1.
\end{equation}
At that point the squared maximum is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:Gscalar}
 G(y)=\frac{3y^2+6y-1}{y(y+3)^2},\qquad
 G'(y)=\frac{-3(y-1)(y+1)^2}{y^2(y+3)^3}.
\end{equation}
The relevant $y$-interval is from $-1+2/\sqrt3$ to
\[y_*=-1+\sqrt{27/8}=-1+\frac{3\sqrt6}{4}=u_*^2/8<1.
\]
It lies in $(0,1)$, so $G$ is strictly increasing there. Hence the global maximum in~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:Frs} occurs at $s=7/\sqrt8$ and $r=u_*/\sqrt8$, with value
\[F(u_*/\sqrt8,7/\sqrt8)=\frac{7u_*}{11+6\sqrt6}=k_*.
\]
This proves~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:momentbound}. Also $0<k_*<1$, since $k_*^2=G(y_*)<G(1)=1/2$. No local-optimizer assumption or numerical comparison is involved.

\subsection{The real inequality and its equality rays}
Expansion about the mean gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:AB}
 \frac19\norm z_4^4=A+B,\qquad
 \frac19\norm{R_9z}_4^4=A-B.
\end{equation}
For nonzero $z$, $A>0$. With $\mu=(1-k_*)/(1+k_*)$, equation~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:momentbound} implies
\[(A-B)-\mu(A+B)=(1+\mu)(k_*A-B)\ge0.
\]
This proves the real lower bound. For $z_-$ in~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:zminus}, the mean is $u_*$, the centered coordinates are $(8,-1,\ldots,-1)$, and
\[\sigma^2=8,\qquad M_3=56,\qquad B=224u_*>0.
\]
All inequalities are equalities with the required positive sign $B=k_*A$, so the lower constant is sharp.

Conversely, a nonzero real equality vector cannot have zero variance, zero mean or zero third centered moment, since those cases give ratio one and $0<\mu<1$. Equality forces the endpoint in~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:skew}, equality in Pearson, $|m|/\sigma=u_*/\sqrt8$, and $mM_3>0$. Thus its centered part is a nonzero real scalar multiple of a permutation of $(8,-1,\ldots,-1)$, and its mean is the same scalar times $u_*$. This is precisely the claimed family of real equality vectors.

\subsection{Phase averaging and the complex inequality}
For any $w\in\C$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:phase}
 \frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\bigl(\operatorname{Re}(e^{i\theta}w)\bigr)^4
                      \,d\theta=\frac38|w|^4.
\end{equation}
Because $R_9$ has real entries, it commutes with taking $\operatorname{Re}(e^{i\theta}\,\cdot\,)$. Apply the real inequality to this real vector for each $\theta$, sum the coordinates and integrate. The factor $3/8$ cancels, proving
\[\norm{R_9z}_4^4\ge\mu\norm z_4^4\qquad(z\in\C^9).
\]
The real equality vector already lies in $\C^9$, so the complex constant is equally sharp. This is the standard phase-averaging mechanism behind real-to-complex $L_p$ norm equality; the general theorem of Holtz and Karow applies in particular to $p=q=4$~\cite{holtzkarow}. No novelty is claimed for this complexification step.

Finally $R_9^2=I$. Substituting $z=R_9w$ in the lower inequality gives the reciprocal upper inequality. Equality for the upper norm occurs at $R_9z_-$, proving~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:operatornorm}. The quantities are distinct:
\[\inf\frac{\norm{R_9z}_4}{\norm z_4}=\mu^{1/4},\qquad
 \inf\frac{\norm{R_9z}_4^4}{\norm z_4^4}=\mu,\qquad
 \norm{R_9}_{4\to4}=\mu^{-1/4}.
\]
This completes Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:82:thm:reflection}.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Nine frequency blocks and all rank spike attainment\srctag{82}}]{Nine frequency blocks and all rank spike attainment}\label{gsr:en:82:sec:d9}\label{gsr:en:82:sec:spike-lift}
\srcnote{82}{Section 9}
Assume now that $0\ne\delta\in H$ and $2\delta=0$. Let $\pi:V\to\F_3^2$ be a surjective linear map, put $K=\ker\pi$, and define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:pullback}
 a(x)=\delta\ind_K(x),\qquad s(x)=1-2\ind_K(x).
\end{equation}
The linearity requirement on $\pi$ is essential to the theorem as stated: it makes $K$ a subgroup of index nine and gives the annihilator and splitting used below. An arbitrary surjection of sets need not have either property.

\subsection{The parity identity}
On a source additive quadruple, the target relation is
\[(\ind_K(x)+\ind_K(y)-\ind_K(z)-\ind_K(w))\delta=0.
\]
Since $\delta$ has exact order two, this holds precisely when the total number of entries in $K$ is even. Its indicator is
\[\frac{1+s(x)s(y)s(z)s(w)}2.
\]
For real $f$, define the ordinary quartic form by~\eqref{gsr:fm:82:eq:energy}, allowing signed entries. Summing the preceding identity gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:parity}
 \Ea(f)=\frac{\EaddV(f)+\EaddV(sf)}2.
\end{equation}
Only nonnegative weights are needed for $r(a)$, but the homogeneous identity itself holds for all real $f$.

\subsection{The block multiplier on a finite source}
First suppose $V$ is finite and write $N=|V|$. For characters $\xi\in\widehat V$, use
\[\widehat f(\xi)=\sum_{x\in V}f(x)\overline{\xi(x)}.
\]
Character orthogonality and convolution give, for real $f$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:fourth-Fourier}
 \EaddV(f)=\norm{f*f}_2^2=\frac1N\sum_{\xi\in\widehat V}|\widehat f(\xi)|^4.
\end{equation}
The equality uses the squared real convolution; it is not an assertion about an unconjugated quartic on arbitrary complex physical weights.

Let $W=K^\perp\le\widehat V$. Since $[V:K]=9$, $|W|=9$, and
\[\widehat{\ind_K}=|K|\ind_W.
\]
The Fourier transform of a pointwise product is $N^{-1}$ times convolution on the dual group. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:block}
 \widehat{sf}(\xi)=\widehat f(\xi)-\frac29
                   \sum_{\eta\in W}\widehat f(\xi+\eta).
\end{equation}
The minus sign in the usual convolution formula can be replaced by a plus sign because $W=-W$. The cosets $\xi+W$ partition $\widehat V$ into nine-element blocks, and on each block formula~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:block} is exactly the action of $R_9$.

Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:82:thm:reflection} to the arbitrary complex coefficient vector on every block. Add and use~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:fourth-Fourier} for both $f$ and $sf$ to obtain
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:signedlower}
 \EaddV(sf)\ge\mu\EaddV(f).
\end{equation}
The parity identity then gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:lambdalower}
 \Ea(f)\ge\frac{1+\mu}{2}\EaddV(f)=\lambda\EaddV(f).
\end{equation}
This is an all-weight lower bound on the full higher-rank source, rather than an inequality restricted to constant fibers or one-parameter test weights.

\subsection{Product fibers give exact attainment}
Choose a linear splitting $V\cong\F_3^2\oplus K$ compatible with $\pi$. For the quotient weight $f_0$ defined by
\[f_0(0)=u_*,\qquad f_0(q)=1\quad(q\ne0),
\]
the unnormalized Fourier coefficient vector is $z_-$ in~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:zminus}: the zero coefficient is $u_*+8$, and every nonzero coefficient is $u_*-1$. This is exactly a reflection equality vector. Equations~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:parity} and~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:fourth-Fourier} therefore give quotient energy ratio $\lambda$.

An independent direct count for the weight $f_T$ taking value $T$ at zero and one elsewhere gives the useful normalization check
\begin{align}
 \mathcal E_{\F_3^2}(f_T)&=T^4+48T^2+224T+456,\label{gsr:en:82:eq:spikepoly}\\
 \mathcal E_{\delta\ind_{\{0\}}}(f_T)&=T^4+48T^2+456.\notag
\end{align}
At $T=u_*$,
\[u_*^4+48u_*^2+456=32(11+6\sqrt6),
\]
so the quotient of the two lines is $1/(1+k_*)=\lambda$, agreeing with the reflection proof.

For every nonzero nonnegative $h$ on $K$, put $f(q,k)=f_0(q)h(k)$. The source additive equation splits into independent equations in the two factors, and the target relation depends only on the quotient. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:82:eq:product}
 \EaddV(f)=\mathcal E_{\F_3^2}(f_0)\mathcal E_K(h),\qquad
 \Ea(f)=\mathcal E_{\delta\ind_{\{0\}}}(f_0)\mathcal E_K(h).
\end{equation}
Since $\mathcal E_K(h)>0$, the kernel factor cancels and $f$ attains $\lambda$. The weight $h$ can have arbitrary nonnegative values and arbitrary support; a constant kernel weight is only one special case of this product family.

\subsection{Infinite dimension and exclusion of the allowed families}
If $V$ has infinite dimension, every admissible weight is supported in a finite-dimensional subspace. Enlarge that subspace by preimages of the two standard basis vectors of $\F_3^2$. The restricted map $\pi$ remains surjective, and every nonzero energy summand is unchanged. Thus the finite proof yields~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:lambdalower} for the original weight. Conversely, a linear splitting exists by choosing those preimages; any finitely supported nonzero $h$ in~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:product} gives a finitely supported equality weight. In particular, taking $h=\ind_{\{0\}}$ gives a nine-point attaining weight.

The full map in~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:pullback} is outside the two families. Restrict it to a two-dimensional linear complement on which $\pi$ is an isomorphism. This is a single-point order-two spike. For each nonzero direction on that plane, its derivative equals zero at seven points and $\delta$ at two points, so no nonzero derivative is constant. An affine map has all derivatives constant, and a plane cut has a constant derivative in its kernel direction. Thus the plane restriction is unfavorable. Since either allowed global family restricts to allowed planes by Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:82:prop:gluing}, the full map is unfavorable as well.

We have now proved its exact value $r(a)=\lambda$: the lower bound is~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:lambdalower}, and the product weights attain it. This proof does not require the universal upper bound to establish the value of the construction.

\begin{proof}[Completion of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:82:thm:main}]
If $H[2]=\{0\}$, Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:82:thm:no2} supplies $r(a)\le5/9$ for every unfavorable map, and Section~\ref{gsr:en:82:sec:five-nine} supplies an unfavorable map with attained value $5/9$ for this fixed $V,H$. If $H[2]\ne\{0\}$, the imported Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:82:thm:imported} supplies $r(a)\le\lambda$ for every unfavorable map, and the construction just proved supplies an unfavorable map of attained value $\lambda$ for this same fixed $V,H$. Thus both suprema are actual maxima, with precisely the claimed quantifiers.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The fixed-mean two-value theorem\srctag{83}}]{The fixed-mean two-value theorem}\label{gsr:en:83:sec:d2}\label{gsr:en:83:sec:two-values}
\srcnote{83}{Section 2}
We first establish strict inequality over the identity and then use second variation on a single affine hyperplane. Keeping only one linear constraint makes the sign argument especially direct.

\begin{lemma}[Strict inequality and nonzero mean]\label{gsr:en:83:lem:strict}
For $n\ge3$ and $\gamma>0$, $C_{n,\gamma}>1$. A real maximizing vector exists and has nonzero mean.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $w=(1,1,-2,0,\ldots,0)$, so that $\sum_iw_i=0$ and $\sum_iw_i^3=-6$. Put $h=1-\gamma$. Along $w+t\ind$ the fourth-power ratio is
\[R(t)=\frac{\sum_i(w_i+ht)^4}{\sum_i(w_i+t)^4}.\]
Its denominator at zero is $18$, and
\[R(0)=1,\qquad R'(0)=-\frac{4\gamma\sum_iw_i^3}{\sum_iw_i^4}=\frac{4\gamma}{3}>0.\]
For sufficiently small positive $t$, $R(t)>1$. Compactness of the real $\ell_4$ unit sphere gives an actual maximum. Every mean-zero vector is fixed by $T_\gamma$, so no nonzero such vector maximizes a norm strictly greater than one.
\end{proof}

Fix $C=C_{n,\gamma}$ and define the homogeneous quartic gap
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:gap}
 Q_C(y)=C\sum_i y_i^4-\sum_i(y_i-\gamma\bar y)^4.
\end{equation}
It is nonnegative on all of $\R^n$ and vanishes at every real maximizing vector.

\begin{proof}[Proof of the real assertion in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:83:thm:general}]
Fix a maximizing vector $x$ with mean $\mu\ne0$. On the affine hyperplane $\sum_i y_i=n\mu$, expansion gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:fixed-mean}
 Q_C(y)=\sum_i f(y_i)-n\gamma^4\mu^4,
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:separable-f}
 f(t)=(C-1)t^4+4\gamma\mu t^3-6\gamma^2\mu^2t^2+4\gamma^3\mu^3t.
\end{equation}
Thus $x$ is a constrained global minimum of $\sum_i f(y_i)$. The first-order condition yields a common real number $\nu$ with $f'(x_i)=\nu$ for every $i$. Since
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:cubic-stationarity}
 f'(t)-\nu=4(C-1)t^3+12\gamma\mu t^2-12\gamma^2\mu^2t+4\gamma^3\mu^3-\nu
\end{equation}
has degree three, at most three distinct coordinate values can occur.

Suppose three occur, $r_1<r_2<r_3$, with multiplicities $j,s,\ell$. Write $U=r_2-r_1>0$ and $V=r_3-r_2>0$. These are exactly the three distinct roots of~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:cubic-stationarity}. Differentiating its factored form gives
\begin{align}
 f''(r_1)&=4(C-1)U(U+V),\label{gsr:en:83:eq:second-values}\\
 f''(r_2)&=-4(C-1)UV,\notag\\
 f''(r_3)&=4(C-1)V(U+V).\notag
\end{align}
At a constrained minimum, $\sum_i f''(x_i)v_i^2$ must be nonnegative for every $v$ with $\sum_i v_i=0$. If $s\ge2$, choose opposite perturbations on two middle coordinates. Their second variation is negative. Therefore $s=1$.

Now choose the tangent vector with value $-V/j$ on the $r_1$ group, value $U+V$ on the unique middle coordinate, and value $-U/\ell$ on the $r_3$ group. Its sum is zero, and its second variation is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:second-factor}
 4(C-1)UV(U+V)\left[\frac Vj-(U+V)+\frac U\ell\right].
\end{equation}
The bracket equals
\[-V\frac{j-1}{j}-U\frac{\ell-1}{\ell},\]
which is strictly negative unless $j=\ell=1$. Thus the only remaining possibility is $n=3$, with all three values occurring once. Vieta's formula then gives
\[r_1+r_2+r_3=-\frac{3\gamma\mu}{C-1},\]
whereas the mean constraint gives $r_1+r_2+r_3=3\mu$. Since $\mu\ne0$, this forces $C-1=-\gamma$, contrary to $C>1$ and $\gamma>0$. Three values are impossible.
\end{proof}

This proof excludes the zero-second-variation case separately; it does not mistake semidefiniteness for a sufficient minimum condition. Repeated roots of the stationary cubic cause no exception, because the contradiction is needed only when three distinct coordinate values occur. Nor does the argument divide by individual coordinates, which may be zero.

\begin{corollary}\label{gsr:en:83:cor:exactly-two}
If $0<\gamma\le2$, every real maximizing vector has exactly two distinct values. In particular, this holds for centering and reflection.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
A constant vector has fourth-power ratio $|1-\gamma|^4\le1<C_{n,\gamma}$.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Complex equality and common phase\srctag{83}}]{Complex equality and common phase}\label{gsr:en:83:sec:d3}\label{gsr:en:83:sec:complex}
\srcnote{83}{Section 3}
The equality of real and complex norms follows from phase averaging. The special action on the mean-zero hyperplane then determines the phase of every equality vector.

\begin{lemma}[Fourth-power phase average]\label{gsr:en:83:lem:phase}
For every $z\in\C^n$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:phase-average}
 \frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\norm{\Rea(e^{i\theta}z)}_4^4\,d\theta
 =\frac38\norm z_4^4.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For a scalar $z_j=\rho e^{i\alpha}$, its contribution is $\rho^4$ times the average of $\cos^4(\theta+\alpha)$, namely $3/8$. Sum over coordinates.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of the complex assertion in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:83:thm:general}]
The matrix $T_\gamma$ is real, so it commutes with real phase projections. Integrate the real inequality
\[\norm{T_\gamma\Rea(e^{i\theta}z)}_4^4\le C\norm{\Rea(e^{i\theta}z)}_4^4.\]
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:83:lem:phase} proves the same inequality for complex $z$. Real inputs prove equality of the two operator norms.

If $z\ne0$ attains equality, the continuous nonnegative function
\[\theta\longmapsto Q_C(\Rea(e^{i\theta}z))\]
has zero integral and hence vanishes at every phase. Choose $\theta$ so that $\Rea(e^{i\theta}\mu(z))=0$, where $\mu(z)=n^{-1}\sum_i z_i$ denotes the coordinate mean. The real projection $u=\Rea(e^{i\theta}z)$ is mean-zero, so $T_\gamma u=u$ and
\[Q_C(u)=(C-1)\norm u_4^4.\]
Since $C>1$, $u=0$. Thus $e^{i\theta}z$ is purely imaginary in every coordinate, and $z$ is a complex scalar multiple of a real vector. Homogeneity makes that real vector a maximizer. Conversely every such complex multiple is a maximizer.
\end{proof}

The argument also excludes a nonzero complex maximizer of mean zero: in that case every phase projection would vanish.

\begin{proposition}[Finite exponents and common phase]\label{gsr:en:83:prop:finite-p}
Let $n\ge3$, $\gamma>0$, and $1\le p<\infty$ with $p\ne2$. The real and complex $\ell_p$ norms of $T_\gamma$ agree and are strictly larger than one. Every complex maximizing vector is a complex multiple of a real maximizing vector.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Replace $3/8$ in the phase-average identity by the positive constant
\[c_p=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|\cos\theta|^p\,d\theta.\]
It remains to prove strict inequality over one. Take $w=(n-1,-1,\ldots,-1)$. The derivative at zero of the $p$th-power ratio along $w+t\ind$ equals
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:p-derivative}
 -\frac{p\gamma((n-1)^{p-1}-(n-1))}{(n-1)^p+(n-1)}.
\end{equation}
Because $n-1>1$, this is nonzero exactly when $p\ne2$. At $p=1$ the derivative is legitimate: all coordinates of input and output stay away from zero for sufficiently small $|t|$. A suitable sign of $t$ gives a ratio greater than one. Phase averaging and a mean-zero phase projection now give the same proof as above, with $\norm{T_\gamma}_{p\to p}^p-1>0$.
\end{proof}
This proposition makes no assertion that real maximizing vectors have two values for arbitrary $p$, and makes no common-phase assertion at $p=\infty$. At $p=2$ the mean-zero eigenspace can supply genuinely complex equality vectors, so excluding that exponent is substantive.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The exact finite quintic reduction\srctag{83}}]{The exact finite quintic reduction}\label{gsr:en:83:sec:d4}\label{gsr:en:83:sec:quintic}
\srcnote{83}{Section 4}
Write $h=1-\gamma<1$. For $1\le m\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, let $w_m$ have $m$ coordinates $\sqrt{(n-m)/m}$ and $n-m$ coordinates $-\sqrt{m/(n-m)}$. Set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:dk-kappa}
 d_m=\frac{n-2m}{\sqrt{m(n-m)}},\qquad \kappa_m=1+d_m^2.
\end{equation}
Direct calculation of uniform empirical moments gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:two-moments}
 \E w_m=0,\quad\E w_m^2=1,\quad\E w_m^3=d_m,\quad\E w_m^4=\kappa_m.
\end{equation}
Every nonconstant real two-valued vector is, up to permutation, $c(r\ind+w_m)$ for some such $m$, some $c\ne0$, and some $r\in\R$. Indeed, if its values on groups of sizes $m,n-m$ are $a,b$, then
\[c=(a-b)\frac{\sqrt{m(n-m)}}n,\qquad r=\frac{ma+(n-m)b}{nc}.\]
Choose the smaller group for $m$; a negative $c$ handles either ordering of the values. The balanced split also fits this parameterization.

Using~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:two-moments}, the fourth-power ratio on this branch is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:Rk}
 R_m(r)=\frac{h^4r^4+6h^2r^2+4hd_mr+\kappa_m}
 {r^4+6r^2+4d_mr+\kappa_m}.
\end{equation}
Denote the denominator by $D_m(r)$. It is the empirical fourth moment of a nonconstant vector, hence $D_m(r)>0$ for every real $r$. We have $R_m(0)=1$ and $R_m(r)\to h^4$ as $|r|\to\infty$.

\begin{theorem}[Finite formula and full equality set]\label{gsr:en:83:thm:quintic}
Define
\begin{align}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:Gk}
 G_m(r)={}&3h^2(h+1)r^5+3d_mh(h^2+h+1)r^4\notag\\
 &+\kappa_m(h+1)(h^2+1)r^3+6d_mhr^2\notag\\
 &+3\kappa_m(h+1)r+\kappa_md_m.
\end{align}
Discard a branch only when $h=-1$ and $d_m=0$, and let $Z_m$ be the real roots of $G_m$ for every remaining branch. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:finite-formula}
 C_{n,\gamma}=\max\left(\{h^4\}\cup\{R_m(r):G_m\not\equiv0,\ r\in Z_m\}\right).
\end{equation}
The real maximizing lines are exactly the constant line if $h^4=C_{n,\gamma}$, together with all permutations of lines generated by $r\ind+w_m$ for pairs in~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:finite-formula} with $R_m(r)=C_{n,\gamma}$. All complex equality vectors are the nonzero complex multiples of these representatives.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Differentiate~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:Rk} and collect powers to obtain
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:R-derivative}
 R_m'(r)=\frac{4(h-1)G_m(r)}{D_m(r)^2}.
\end{equation}
The linear coefficient of $G_m$ is $3\kappa_m(h+1)$, so $G_m\equiv0$ forces $h=-1$. Its constant coefficient then forces $d_m=0$; substitution proves the converse. This exceptional branch is exactly a balanced reflection branch, with $R_m\equiv1$, so it cannot maximize $C_{n,\gamma}>1$.

Every other branch has only finitely many real critical points. By Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:83:thm:general}, an actual real maximizing vector is constant or lies at a finite point of one of these branches. In the latter case differentiability forces $G_m(r)=0$. Constants realize $h^4$. Conversely every listed candidate is the ratio of an actual vector, so none exceeds the induced norm. This proves the formula and its real equality classification. The complex classification follows from Section~\ref{gsr:en:83:sec:complex}.
\end{proof}
The formula is a finite exact reduction for every real $\gamma>0$. It is algebraic when the parameter is algebraic, but it is not a general formula by radicals for quintic roots. No division by $h$, by $r$, or by a vector coordinate occurs.

\subsection{Distinguished parameters and balanced branches}
At centering, $\gamma=1$ and $h=0$, so
\[G_m(r)=\kappa_m(r^3+3r+d_m).\]
Its derivative with respect to $r$ is $3\kappa_m(r^2+1)>0$, hence it has one real root. At reflection, $\gamma=2$ and $h=-1$,
\[G_m(r)=d_m(\kappa_m-6r^2-3r^4),\]
which leads to the radical calculation below.

When $d_m=0$, $\kappa_m=1$, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:balanced-factor}
 G_m(r)=(h+1)r\bigl(3h^2r^4+(h^2+1)r^2+3\bigr).
\end{equation}
Away from $h=-1$ its only real critical point is $r=0$, of ratio one. Thus no nonconstant balanced branch contributes a maximizing vector for the parameters of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:83:thm:general}.

At $\gamma=n$, $-T_n=J_n-I$ and Jensen's inequality gives
\begin{align*}
 \sum_i\left|\sum_{j\ne i}x_j\right|^4
 &\le(n-1)^3\sum_i\sum_{j\ne i}|x_j|^4\\
 &=(n-1)^4\sum_j|x_j|^4.
\end{align*}
For real equality, strict convexity forces the $n-1$ coordinates excluding each index to agree. Any pair is jointly excluded by another index because $n\ge3$, so all coordinates agree. Constants attain the bound, proving
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:zero-diagonal}
 \norm{T_n}_{4\to4}=n-1,
\end{equation}
with constant-only real and complex equality.

\subsection{A second finiteness check}
Normalize a real maximizer to mean one and write it on a fixed two-group pattern as $\ind+t w_m$. Its gap divided by $n$ is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:mean-one-gap}
 (C-1)\kappa_mt^4+4d_m(C-h)t^3+6(C-h^2)t^2+(C-h^4).
\end{equation}
This is a nonnegative nonzero quartic with positive leading coefficient. Each real zero has even multiplicity, so at most two distinct real zeros occur. There are finitely many patterns. The real equality set is therefore a finite union of lines, together with zero. This confirms the finite character of the answer independently of the root count in~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:Gk}; the complex proof did not require it.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The exact constant-vector transition\srctag{83}}]{The exact constant-vector transition}\label{gsr:en:83:sec:d5}\label{gsr:en:83:sec:threshold}
\srcnote{83}{Section 5}
For $\gamma\le2$, Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:83:cor:exactly-two} has already excluded constants. Now assume $\gamma>2$ and put $s=\gamma-1=-h>1$. Constants have ratio $s^4$. The quartic gap at this trial value factors as
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:transition-gap}
 \frac1nQ_{s^4}(\ind+t w_m)
 =t^2\bigl[(s^4-1)\kappa_mt^2+4d_m(s^4+s)t+6s^2(s^2-1)\bigr].
\end{equation}
The leading and constant coefficients of the bracketed quadratic are positive.

\begin{lemma}[The discriminant criterion]\label{gsr:en:83:lem:discriminant}
Constants maximize exactly when
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:beta-F}
 \frac{d_m^2}{\kappa_m}\le F(s)
 :=\frac32\frac{(s-1)^2(s^2+1)}{(s^2-s+1)^2}
\end{equation}
for every $1\le m\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A quadratic with the stated positive leading coefficient is nonnegative on $\R$ exactly when its discriminant is nonpositive. Applying this to~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:transition-gap} and simplifying yields~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:beta-F}. If the inequalities hold, every nonzero-mean two-valued vector has ratio at most $s^4$, and every mean-zero vector has ratio one. If any vector exceeded $s^4$, an actual norm maximizer would do so, and Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:83:thm:general} would make it constant or two-valued, a contradiction. Conversely a negative quadratic gap produces a two-valued vector exceeding the constant ratio. This use of the all-maximizer theorem at the actual norm does not assume that the trial gap is globally nonnegative in advance.
\end{proof}

Write $K_m=n^2-3nm+3m^2$. The left side is
\[\beta_{n,m}:=\frac{(n-2m)^2}{K_m}.\]
Its maximum occurs uniquely at $m=1$ in the smaller-group convention, because
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:strict-beta}
 \beta_{n,1}-\beta_{n,m}
 =\frac{n^2(m-1)(n-1-m)}{(n^2-3n+3)K_m}.
\end{equation}
Let
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:beta-n}
 \beta_n=\beta_{n,1}=\frac{(n-2)^2}{n^2-3n+3},\qquad 0<\beta_n<1.
\end{equation}
The reciprocal-symmetric form and derivative of $F$ are
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:F-reciprocal}
 F(s)=\frac32\left(1-\frac1{(s+s^{-1}-1)^2}\right),\qquad
 F'(s)=\frac{3s(s-1)(s+1)}{(s^2-s+1)^3}>0.
\end{equation}
Thus $F$ increases from zero to $3/2$ as $s$ runs from $1$ to infinity.

\begin{theorem}[Threshold and complete transition equality]\label{gsr:en:83:thm:threshold}
Define
\begin{align}
 u_n&=1+\sqrt{\frac{3(n^2-3n+3)}{n^2-n+1}},\label{gsr:en:83:eq:un}\\
 \gamma_n&=1+\frac{u_n+\sqrt{u_n^2-4}}2.\label{gsr:en:83:eq:gamma-n}
\end{align}
Then $2<\gamma_n<n$, and the equality classification is as follows.
\begin{enumerate}
 \item For $0<\gamma<\gamma_n$, every maximizing vector is nonconstant and exactly two-valued, up to the common complex phase established above.
 \item For $\gamma>\gamma_n$, the only maximizing vectors are nonzero constants.
 \item At $\gamma=\gamma_n$, set $s=\gamma_n-1$, $d=d_1$, $\kappa=\kappa_1$, and
 \begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:tstar}
 t_*=-\frac{2d(s^4+s)}{(s^4-1)\kappa}.
 \end{equation}
 The real maximizing vectors are precisely the nonzero real multiples of $\ind$ and of permutations of $\ind+t_*w_1$. All complex maximizing vectors are their nonzero complex multiples.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:83:lem:discriminant} reduces constant maximality to $F(s)\ge\beta_n$. Strict monotonicity gives a unique threshold. Solving $F(s)=\beta_n$ first for $s+s^{-1}$ gives $u_n$; choosing the root $s>1$ gives~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:gamma-n}. In particular, $\gamma_n>2$. Also
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:gamma-upper}
 F(n-1)-\beta_n=\frac{n^2(n-2)^2}{2(n^2-3n+3)^2}>0,
\end{equation}
so $\gamma_n<n$.

Above the threshold every discriminant is strictly negative. Thus~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:transition-gap} vanishes only at $t=0$, and the all-maximizer theorem leaves constants alone. At the threshold the unique extremal split $m=1$ has a double quadratic root, exactly $t_*$ in~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:tstar}; it is nonzero because $d_1>0$. Every other split has strictly negative discriminant and yields only $t=0$. Below the threshold a negative gap on the $m=1$ split excludes constant maximality. Mean-zero vectors are never maximizing, so normalization to mean one loses no equality case. The complex classification is already proved.
\end{proof}

For an exact algebraic check, $s=\gamma_n-1$ is the unique root larger than one of the threshold equation
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:threshold-polynomial}
 (n^2-n+1)(s^2-s+1)^2-3(n^2-3n+3)s^2=0.
\end{equation}
The uniqueness here is on the interval $s>1$; the reciprocal symmetry produces the corresponding root below one. Approximate values are $\gamma_3\approx2.4389349902$, $\gamma_9\approx3.0404152910$, and $\gamma_{30}\approx3.2236846011$. These decimals orient the transition and play no role in the proof.

\begin{corollary}[Sharp dimension-free constant threshold]\label{gsr:en:83:cor:gamma-infty}
The sequence $\gamma_n$ increases strictly to
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:gamma-infty}
 \gamma_\infty=\frac{3+\sqrt3+\sqrt{2\sqrt3}}2.
\end{equation}
Consequently, if $\gamma\ge\gamma_\infty$, every maximizing vector is constant in every finite dimension $n\ge3$. If $0<\gamma<\gamma_\infty$, constants fail to maximize in some sufficiently large finite dimension.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For real $n>2$,
\[\beta_n=1-\frac{n-1}{n^2-3n+3},\qquad
 \frac{d\beta_n}{dn}=\frac{n(n-2)}{(n^2-3n+3)^2}>0.\]
Thus $\beta_n\uparrow1$, and the strictly increasing inverse of $F$ gives $\gamma_n\uparrow\gamma_\infty$. Substitution of $u=1+\sqrt3$ into~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:gamma-n} gives~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:gamma-infty}, since $u^2-4=2\sqrt3$. Each finite threshold is strictly below the limit, so the first assertion uses the constant-only regime, including when $\gamma=\gamma_\infty$. The second follows from eventual $\gamma<\gamma_n$.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Reflection and scalar optimization\srctag{83}}]{Reflection and scalar optimization}\label{gsr:en:83:sec:d6}\label{gsr:en:83:sec:reflection}
\srcnote{83}{Section 6}
We now specialize to $H_n=T_2$. For $n=1$, $H_1=-I$. For $n=2$,
\[H_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}.\]
Both are signed coordinate permutations, so every nonzero real or complex vector has ratio one. Their equality sets must be kept separate from those for $n\ge3$.

Assume $n\ge3$. The general theorem proves that every real upper equality vector is exactly two-valued. Since $H_n^2=I$, the smallest fourth-power ratio over nonzero vectors is $C_n^{-1}$, and $H_n$ maps upper equality vectors bijectively to lower equality vectors.

Fix a multiplicity $1\le m<n/2$, and abbreviate
\[d=d_{n,m}>0,\qquad \kappa=1+d^2,\qquad v=w_m.\]
For a translated, scaled two-valued vector $a\ind+\sigma v$ with $\sigma>0$, the moments~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:two-moments} give
\begin{align}
 \frac1n\norm{a\ind+\sigma v}_4^4
 &=a^4+6a^2\sigma^2+4a\sigma^3d+\sigma^4\kappa,\label{gsr:en:83:eq:reflection-moments}\\
 \frac1n\norm{H_n(a\ind+\sigma v)}_4^4
 &=a^4+6a^2\sigma^2-4a\sigma^3d+\sigma^4\kappa.\notag
\end{align}
The ratio exceeds one only if $a<0$. With $r=|a|/\sigma$, define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:scalar-asymmetry}
 b_d(r)=\frac{4rd}{r^4+6r^2+1+d^2},\qquad r\ge0.
\end{equation}
For the upper orientation the ratio is $(1+b_d(r))/(1-b_d(r))$, which is increasing in $b_d(r)$. Its denominator is positive because it is a positive fourth moment. In particular $b_d(r)<1$.

\begin{lemma}[Unique optimum for each unbalanced split]\label{gsr:en:83:lem:scalar-optimum}
For $d>0$, the function in~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:scalar-asymmetry} has a unique maximum at $r=\sqrt y$, where
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:y-critical}
 y=-1+\sqrt{\frac{4+d^2}{3}}>0.
\end{equation}
Its maximum is $d/[\sqrt y(y+3)]$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
After removal of a positive denominator, the derivative has the sign of
\[1+d^2-6r^2-3r^4.\]
This expression decreases strictly from a positive value to minus infinity as $r$ runs from zero to infinity. Its unique positive zero is described by~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:y-critical}. At that zero,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:critical-identity}
 1+d^2=6y+3y^2.
\end{equation}
Therefore the denominator of~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:scalar-asymmetry} at $r=\sqrt y$ is $4y(y+3)$, proving the asserted value.
\end{proof}
For $d=d_{n,m}$, the identity
\[4+d^2=\frac{n^2}{m(n-m)}\]
turns~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:y-critical} into $y=y_{n,m}$ from~\eqref{gsr:fm:83:eq:reflection-parameters}. A balanced split has $d=0$ and contributes ratio one throughout, so it never maximizes $C_n>1$. Including its value $k_{n,m}=0$ in the finite maximum is harmless. The radical $y_{n,m}$ is positive even in this case: $y_{n,m}\ge2/\sqrt3-1>0$.

Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:83:thm:general}, Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:83:lem:scalar-optimum}, and the realizability of every two-valued branch now prove~\eqref{gsr:fm:83:eq:reflection-main}. This is a complete optimization, not an assumption that a symmetric vector is norming.

\begin{theorem}[Every reflection equality vector]\label{gsr:en:83:thm:reflection-equality}
For $n\ge3$, let
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:Mn}
 \mc_n=\{m:1\le m\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor,\ k_{n,m}=k_n\}.
\end{equation}
For $m\in\mc_n$, let $v_{n,m}$ have $m$ entries $\sqrt{(n-m)/m}$ and $n-m$ entries $-\sqrt{m/(n-m)}$. Then every real upper equality vector, and only such a vector, is a nonzero real multiple of a permutation of
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:upper-reflection-vector}
 v_{n,m}-\sqrt{y_{n,m}}\ind,\qquad m\in\mc_n.
\end{equation}
Every real lower equality vector is a nonzero real multiple of a permutation of
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:lower-reflection-vector}
 v_{n,m}+\sqrt{y_{n,m}}\ind,\qquad m\in\mc_n.
\end{equation}
For complex vectors, replace the nonzero real multiples by nonzero complex multiples. All possible ties in $\mc_n$ are retained.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The real two-value theorem covers every upper equality vector. The scalar optimum on an unbalanced branch is unique, and its upper orientation is the negative mean in~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:upper-reflection-vector}. Arbitrary real scaling and permutations cover both signs and all coordinate placements. Conversely these vectors attain the computed norm for each maximizing multiplicity. Applying $H_n$ changes the minus sign to plus and transfers upper equality to lower equality. The common-phase theorem gives precisely the complex multiples and excludes additional complex equality vectors.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Two candidate multiplicities and the universal limit\srctag{83}}]{Two candidate multiplicities and the universal limit}\label{gsr:en:83:sec:d7}\label{gsr:en:83:sec:multiplicity}
\srcnote{83}{Section 7}
The remaining discrete optimization has a unimodal continuous interpolation. At the critical point~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:critical-identity},
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:G-y}
 k^2=\Phi(y):=\frac{3y^2+6y-1}{y(y+3)^2},\qquad
 \Phi'(y)=-\frac{3(y-1)(y+1)^2}{y^2(y+3)^3}.
\end{equation}
For $p=m/n\in(0,1/2]$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:y-p}
 y(p)=\frac1{\sqrt{3p(1-p)}}-1
\end{equation}
decreases strictly from infinity to $2/\sqrt3-1$. The expression $\Phi$ is nonnegative on this domain, so maximizing $k$ is equivalent to maximizing $k^2$.

\begin{proposition}[Exact two-candidate rule]\label{gsr:en:83:prop:candidates}
Let
\[c_- =\max\{1,\min\{\lfloor n/2\rfloor,\lfloor np_*\rfloor\}\},\qquad
 c_+ =\max\{1,\min\{\lfloor n/2\rfloor,\lceil np_*\rceil\}\}.
\]
Then $\mc_n\subseteq\{c_-,c_+\}$, and $k_n$ is the larger of their radical values, retaining both if equal.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
By~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:G-y}, $\Phi$ increases on $y<1$ and decreases on $y>1$. Because $y(p)$ decreases, $k(p)$ increases up to the unique point where $y=1$ and decreases thereafter. Solving $p(1-p)=1/12$ in $(0,1/2]$ gives $p=p_*$. Every grid point strictly farther along one side than the adjacent grid point has a smaller value. Thus only the clipped neighboring grid points can maximize.
\end{proof}
This rule does not assert that the two adjacent values are always different. The equality theorem is written to accommodate any tie, without depending on whether ties can occur.

\begin{proof}[Proof of the universal bound and limit in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:83:thm:reflection-overview}]
At the unique continuous optimum $y=1$, $k=1/\sqrt2$. Hence
\[\frac{1+k}{1-k}\le\frac{1+1/\sqrt2}{1-1/\sqrt2}=3+2\sqrt2.\]
For finite $n\ge3$, equality would require $m/n=p_*$, impossible because $m/n$ is rational and $p_*$ irrational. The isometric cases $n=1,2$ also satisfy the strict bound. Choosing the neighboring grid points gives $m_n/n\to p_*$; continuity proves $k_n\to1/\sqrt2$ and the full sequence limit~\eqref{gsr:fm:83:eq:reflection-limit}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Divisibility monotonicity]\label{gsr:en:83:prop:divisibility}
If $n$ divides $N$, then $\norm{H_N}_{4\to4}\ge\norm{H_n}_{4\to4}$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Repeat every coordinate $N/n$ times. This preserves the coordinate mean and multiplies both fourth moments by $N/n$, so it embeds every $n$-coordinate reflection ratio into the $N$-coordinate problem.
\end{proof}
The sequence need not increase at consecutive integers. The proof of the limit requires no such monotonicity. The norm formula depends only on the rational split proportion for each individual branch, which explains exact equalities across different dimensions when their optimal proportions agree.
