\section[{Exact finite illustrations\srctag{83}}]{Exact finite illustrations}\label{gsr:en:83:sec:d8}\label{gsr:en:83:sec:finite-examples}
\srcnote{83}{Section 8}
The general proofs above are analytic. This section singles out finite comparisons whose exact arithmetic certificates are shipped with the report. A decimal approximation is never used to choose a maximizing branch.

At $n=4$, the winning split is $m=1$, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:n4}
 y_{4,1}=\frac13,\qquad k_{4,1}=\frac35,\qquad C_4=4,
 \qquad\norm{H_4}_{4\to4}=\sqrt2.
\end{equation}
The upper representative has one coordinate $2/\sqrt3$ and three coordinates $-2/\sqrt3$; after scaling, it is $(1,-1,-1,-1)$. Its lower representative is a multiple of $(2,0,0,0)$, consistent with direct application of $H_4$.

The candidate rule gives only $m=1$ for $3\le n\le10$. Exact interval comparisons give $m=1$ for $11\le n\le15$, but $m=2$ at $n=16$. For the last comparison, the winning-minus-losing gap satisfies
\begin{align}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:n16-certificate}
 k_{16,2}-k_{16,1}&>\frac{6733144914351667150626599968633112005256310887392941}{10^{55}},\\
 k_{16,2}-k_{16,1}&<\frac{6733144914351667150626599968633112005256310887392942}{10^{55}}.\notag
\end{align}
Both endpoints are strictly positive rational numbers. This is the exact interval certificate, rather than a floating-point optimization result. Since the winning proportions are $2/16=1/8$, the formula gives the exact equality
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:n8-n16}
 C_{16}=C_8=5.69082685348779\ldots.
\end{equation}
The decimal is illustrative; the equality follows from the identical rational proportion.

At $n=9$, the winning split is $m=1$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:n9-constants}
 u=\sqrt{6\sqrt6-8},\qquad
 \lambda_9=\frac{11+6\sqrt6}{11+6\sqrt6+7u}.
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:n9-energy-constant}
 \frac{1+C_9^{-1}}2=\lambda_9
 =0.5865294215371423896783162434\ldots.
\end{equation}
This is the nine-point weighted constant used in Report~294~\cite{srceightytwo}. The all-order formula here extends the operator calculation; the ensuing energy application explains when a finite-group nonnegative weight can actually realize its spectral lower bound.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Parity energy and the spectral lower bound\srctag{83}}]{Parity energy and the spectral lower bound}\label{gsr:en:83:sec:d9}\label{gsr:en:83:sec:energy}
\srcnote{83}{Section 9}
Let $G$ be a finite abelian group of order $n\ge3$, written additively. Let $A$ be an abelian target group with an element $\delta\ne0$ satisfying $2\delta=0$. The point spike is the full-domain map
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:point-spike}
 a(x)=\delta\ind_{\{0\}}(x).
\end{equation}
For $f:G\to[0,\infty)$, define unnormalized ordered energies
\begin{align}
 \Eng(f)&=\sum_{x+y=z+w}f(x)f(y)f(z)f(w),\label{gsr:en:83:eq:energy-definition}\\
 \Ea(f)&=\sum_{\substack{x+y=z+w\\a(x)+a(y)=a(z)+a(w)}}f(x)f(y)f(z)f(w).\label{gsr:en:83:eq:retained-definition}
\end{align}
Repeated entries are included. For $f\ne0$ the diagonal quadruple at any point with $f>0$ makes the energies positive. Put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:energy-ratio-inf}
 r_G(a)=\inf_{f\ge0,\ f\ne0}\frac{\Ea(f)}{\Eng(f)},\qquad
 \eta_n=\frac{1+C_n^{-1}}2=\frac1{1+k_n}.
\end{equation}
The symbol $\eta_n$ is distinct from the transition parameter $\beta_n$ in~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:beta-n}.

Write $\widehat G$ for the character group, with trivial character $1$. Use the convention
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:Fourier-convention}
 F(\chi)=\widehat f(\chi)=\sum_{x\in G}f(x)\overline{\chi(x)},\qquad
 f(x)=\frac1n\sum_{\chi\in\widehat G}F(\chi)\chi(x).
\end{equation}
For real $h$, including signed $h$, convolution and character orthogonality give
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:Fourier-energy}
 \Eng(h)=\sum_{u\in G}(h*h)(u)^2
 =\frac1n\sum_{\chi\in\widehat G}|\widehat h(\chi)|^4.
\end{equation}
Indeed $h*h$ is real, $\widehat{h*h}=(\widehat h)^2$, and Parseval yields the last expression.

\begin{lemma}[Parity identity]\label{gsr:en:83:lem:parity}
For $s=1-2\ind_{\{0\}}$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:parity-identity}
 \Ea(f)=\frac{\Eng(f)+\Eng(sf)}2,\qquad
 \widehat{sf}=H_nF.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Because $\delta$ has order two, a source additive quadruple is respected exactly when the total number of its zero entries is even. Signs in the target relation do not change parity. Its indicator is therefore $(1+s(x)s(y)s(z)s(w))/2$, which gives the first identity. The second follows from
\[\widehat{sf}(\chi)=F(\chi)-2f(0),\qquad f(0)=\frac1n\sum_{\psi\in\widehat G}F(\psi).\]
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Spectral energy bound]\label{gsr:en:83:cor:spectral-bound}
For the point spike on every finite abelian $G$ of order $n\ge3$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:spectral-bound}
 \frac{\Ea(f)}{\Eng(f)}
 =\frac12\left(1+\frac{\norm{H_nF}_4^4}{\norm F_4^4}\right)\ge\eta_n.
\end{equation}
Equality holds exactly when $F$ is a lower reflection equality vector from Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:83:thm:reflection-equality}.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Combine~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:Fourier-energy} and~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:parity-identity}, then apply the lower reflection inequality $\norm{H_nF}_4^4\ge C_n^{-1}\norm F_4^4$. This is the only inequality in the argument.
\end{proof}
For completeness, a point spike on a group of order $n=1$ or $2$ has retained energy equal to ordinary energy for every weight. The same Fourier calculation applies, and $H_1,H_2$ are isometries, so the ratio is one. The multiplicity criterion below is needed only for $n\ge3$.

The sharp complex operator inequality alone does not guarantee equality for a nonnegative weight. Fourier transforms of such weights satisfy positivity constraints. The next section gives their exact consequence.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{When a point spike attains the spectral bound\srctag{83}}]{When a point spike attains the spectral bound}\label{gsr:en:83:sec:d10}\label{gsr:en:83:sec:attainment}
\srcnote{83}{Section 10}
Retain $\mc_n$ from~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:Mn}. For every integer $q\ge3$, set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:tq}
 t_q=\sqrt{q\sqrt{\frac{q-1}{3}}-(q-1)}.
\end{equation}
This is positive, since $q^2-3q+3>0$.

\begin{theorem}[Saturation and every nonnegative equality weight]\label{gsr:en:83:thm:attainment}
For the point spike~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:point-spike}, $r_G(a)=\eta_n$ if and only if some $m\in\mc_n$ divides $n$. All nonzero nonnegative weights attaining the spectral bound are exactly the following:
choose such an $m$, set $q=n/m$, choose a subgroup $L\le G$ of order $q$, and choose $c>0$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:all-weight-equality}
 f(x)=\begin{cases}
 ct_q,&x=0,\\
 c,&x\in L\setminus\{0\},\\
 0,&x\notin L.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
If no $m\in\mc_n$ divides $n$, then $r_G(a)>\eta_n$. Thus the possibility of spectral saturation depends only on $n$, not on the isomorphism type of $G$.
\end{theorem}

\subsection{The Fourier high-level set}
Suppose $f\ge0$ is nonzero and attains equality. By Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:83:thm:reflection-equality}, for some $m\in\mc_n$, some $S\subseteq\widehat G$ with $|S|=m$, and some $z\in\C\setminus\{0\}$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:Fourier-two-levels}
 F(\chi)=z\bigl(B+(A-B)\ind_S(\chi)\bigr),
\end{equation}
where, abbreviating $y=y_{n,m}$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:AB-levels}
 A=\sqrt{\frac{n-m}{m}}+\sqrt y,\qquad
 B=-\sqrt{\frac m{n-m}}+\sqrt y.
\end{equation}
Every $m\in\mc_n$ is unbalanced because $k_n>0$, so $m<n/2$. We have
\[A-B=\frac n{\sqrt{m(n-m)}}>0,\qquad A+B=d_{n,m}+2\sqrt y>0.\]
Therefore $A>0$ and $A>|B|$, whether $B$ is positive, zero, or negative.

Nonnegativity of $f$ implies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:Fourier-positivity}
 F(1)=\sum_xf(x)>0,\qquad |F(\chi)|\le F(1)\quad(\chi\in\widehat G).
\end{equation}
If $1\notin S$, a high-level coordinate would violate this inequality. Hence $1\in S$, and $F(1)=zA>0$ forces $z>0$ real. Define
\[K_S(x)=\sum_{\chi\in S}\chi(x).\]
Inversion gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:character-sum-inversion}
 f(x)=zB\ind_{\{0\}}(x)+\frac{z(A-B)}nK_S(x).
\end{equation}
For $x\ne0$, this shows $K_S(x)\ge0$ and real. At $x=0$, $K_S(0)=m>0$, so the same conclusion holds everywhere. The possible negative low Fourier level causes no exception.

\subsection{An elementary nonnegative character-sum lemma}
\begin{lemma}\label{gsr:en:83:lem:character-subgroup}
If $S\subseteq\widehat G$ contains $1$ and $K_S(x)$ is real and nonnegative for all $x\in G$, then $S$ is a subgroup of $\widehat G$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Set $\mu(x)=K_S(x)/n$. Orthogonality gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:mu-identities}
 \mu(x)\ge0,\qquad \sum_x\mu(x)=1,\qquad
 \sum_x\mu(x)\overline{\chi(x)}=\ind_S(\chi).
\end{equation}
For $\chi\in S$, the last expression is one. Consequently
\[\sum_x\mu(x)|\chi(x)-1|^2
 =2-2\Rea\sum_x\mu(x)\chi(x)=0.\]
Thus $\chi(x)=1$ on the support of $\mu$. Products and inverses of characters with this property retain it, and their Fourier averages in~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:mu-identities} are therefore one. They belong to $S$. Since $1\in S$, this proves the claim.
\end{proof}

Apply the lemma and let
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:annihilator}
 L=S^\perp=\{x\in G:\chi(x)=1\text{ for every }\chi\in S\}.
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:character-sum-subgroup}
 K_S(x)=m\ind_L(x).
\end{equation}
To verify the zero case, choose $\chi_0\in S$ with $\chi_0(x)\ne1$. Multiplication by $\chi_0$ permutes $S$, so $K_S(x)=\chi_0(x)K_S(x)$ and the sum vanishes. On $L$, every summand is one. Summing~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:character-sum-subgroup} over $G$ gives $m|L|=n$, because $1\in S$. Thus
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:divisibility-necessary}
 m\mid n,\qquad |L|=q=n/m.
\end{equation}

\subsection{Recovering the weight and proving the converse}
The mean of the Fourier vector~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:Fourier-two-levels} is $z\sqrt y$, so $f(0)=z\sqrt y>0$. For $x\in L\setminus\{0\}$,~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:character-sum-inversion} gives
\[f(x)=\frac{z(A-B)m}{n}=z\sqrt{\frac m{n-m}}=:c>0,\]
and $f(x)=0$ off $L$. Since $q=n/m$,
\[y=\frac q{\sqrt{3(q-1)}}-1,\qquad
 \frac{f(0)}c=\sqrt{(q-1)y}=t_q.\]
This proves the necessity and the claimed complete equality form.

Conversely, a weight~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:all-weight-equality} has Fourier transform
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:weight-Fourier-converse}
 F(\chi)=c(t_q-1)+cq\ind_{L^\perp}(\chi),\qquad |L^\perp|=n/q=m.
\end{equation}
With $z=c\sqrt{q-1}$, the two levels are exactly $zA,zB$ in~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:AB-levels}. Thus $F$ is a lower equality vector and Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:83:cor:spectral-bound} gives equality.

Every finite abelian group has a subgroup of each divisor order. One elementary proof is induction on the desired divisor $d$. If $d>1$, choose a prime $p\mid d$ and an order-$p$ subgroup $P$ by Cauchy's theorem. Apply the induction hypothesis to the divisor $d/p$ of $|G/P|$; the inverse image of that subgroup has order $d$. This works because $G$ is abelian and $G/P$ is a group. Thus divisibility in~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:divisibility-necessary} always supplies the needed $L$.

\subsection{Why nonsaturation is a strict gap}
By homogeneity, restrict to the compact simplex
\[\Delta_G=\{f:G\to[0,\infty):\sum_xf(x)=1\}.\]
For $f\in\Delta_G$, $F(1)=1$ and~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:Fourier-energy} gives $\Eng(f)\ge1/n$. Therefore the energy ratio is continuous on the entire simplex and attains its minimum. If no optimal multiplicity divides $n$, the preceding classification excludes equality at every point of the simplex, so its minimum is strictly larger than $\eta_n$. This completes the proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:83:thm:attainment}. It does not quantify the positive excess or compute the true minimum in the nonsaturating case.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Direct energy formulas and two finite consequences\srctag{83}}]{Direct energy formulas and two finite consequences}\label{gsr:en:83:sec:d11}\label{gsr:en:83:sec:energy-examples}
\srcnote{83}{Section 11}
A direct check helps separate the optimal weight profile from the Fourier classification. On a group of order $q$, take weight $t\ge0$ at zero and weight one elsewhere. Its Fourier values are $t+q-1$ at the trivial character and $t-1$ at every other character. Hence
\begin{align}
 E_q(t)&=\frac{(t+q-1)^4+(q-1)(t-1)^4}{q}\notag\\
 &=t^4+6(q-1)t^2+4(q-1)(q-2)t\notag\\
 &\hspace{15mm}+(q-1)(q^2-3q+3),\label{gsr:en:83:eq:direct-E}\\
 E_{a,q}(t)&=\frac{E_q(t)+E_q(-t)}2\notag\\
 &=t^4+6(q-1)t^2+(q-1)(q^2-3q+3).\label{gsr:en:83:eq:direct-Ea}
\end{align}
For $q>2$, minimizing $E_{a,q}(t)/E_q(t)$ is equivalent to maximizing
\[\frac{t}{t^4+6(q-1)t^2+(q-1)(q^2-3q+3)}.\]
The unique positive critical point solves
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:tq-stationarity}
 3t^4+6(q-1)t^2=(q-1)(q^2-3q+3),
\end{equation}
and its positive solution is $t=t_q$. All these energy identities remain valid for extension by zero from a subgroup to $G$; every contributing additive quadruple then lies in that subgroup. Multiplication by $c$ multiplies both energies by $c^4$. This calculation verifies the profile, but by itself would neither classify all minimizers nor prove the divisibility obstruction.

\subsection{Order twenty seven and the failure of nearest rounding}
The exact two candidates at $n=27$ are $m=2,3$. Rational interval arithmetic in the companion proves
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:M27}
 \mc_{27}=\{3\}.
\end{equation}
In particular, ordinary nearest-integer rounding would fail here: $27p_*=2.477296\ldots$ but the winning multiplicity is three. Since $3/27=1/9$, the formulas give exactly $C_{27}=C_9$ and $\eta_{27}=\lambda_9$ from~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:n9-constants}.

For every abelian group $G$ of order $27$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:order27}
 r_G(\delta\ind_{\{0\}})=\lambda_9.
\end{equation}
All minimizing weights equal $cu$ at zero, equal $c$ on the other eight points of a subgroup of order nine, and vanish outside that subgroup, with $c>0$ and $u=\sqrt{6\sqrt6-8}$. This applies equally to $\Z/27\Z$, $\Z/9\Z\times\Z/3\Z$, and $(\Z/3\Z)^3$. The classification comes from Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:83:thm:attainment}, rather than from testing only these three examples.

\subsection{Order eighty one and strict spectral nonsaturation}
The exact candidates at $n=81$ are $m=7,8$. The companion certifies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:M81}
 \mc_{81}=\{7\}.
\end{equation}
Since $7$ does not divide $81$, Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:83:thm:attainment} gives, for every abelian group of order $81$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:order81}
 \eta_{81}<r_G(\delta\ind_{\{0\}})\le\lambda_9.
\end{equation}
The upper bound follows by using the nine-point weight on any subgroup of order nine. Numerically,
\[\eta_{81}=0.5858505206117180012297191566\ldots,\qquad
 \lambda_9=0.5865294215371423896783162434\ldots.\]
The strict lower inequality is a compactness consequence of the exact divisibility obstruction; it is not inferred from these decimals. Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:order81} does not assert that the true minimum equals $\lambda_9$, or that it is the same for different groups of order $81$.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Spikes on subgroups of finite index\srctag{83}}]{Spikes on subgroups of finite index}\label{gsr:en:83:sec:d12}\label{gsr:en:83:sec:subgroup-spikes}
\srcnote{83}{Section 12}
Let $G$ now be any finite abelian group, let $K\le G$ have index $n\ge3$, and define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:subgroup-spike}
 a_K(x)=\delta\ind_K(x).
\end{equation}
No direct-product decomposition of $G$ is assumed.

\begin{theorem}[Index controls the spectral bound and its saturation]\label{gsr:en:83:thm:subgroup-spike}
One has $r_G(a_K)\ge\eta_n$. Equality is attainable if and only if some $m\in\mc_n$ divides $n$. If none does, $r_G(a_K)>\eta_n$.

If a nonzero nonnegative $f$ attains equality, its quotient fiber-mass weight
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:fiber-masses}
 g(x+K)=\sum_{k\in K}f(x+k)
\end{equation}
is a point-spike equality weight on $G/K$ of the form~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:all-weight-equality}. Conversely, constant-fiber lifts of any such quotient weight attain equality on $G$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Set $N=|G|$ and $W=K^\perp\le\widehat G$, so $|W|=n$. Because $\widehat{\ind_K}=|K|\ind_W$, multiplication by $s_K=1-2\ind_K$ transforms $F=\widehat f$ according to
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:Fourier-block}
 \widehat{s_Kf}(\chi)=F(\chi)-\frac2n\sum_{\eta\in W}F(\chi\eta).
\end{equation}
An inverse on $\eta$ makes no difference because $W$ is a subgroup. The cosets of $W$ partition $\widehat G$ into $n$-element blocks. On each block~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:Fourier-block} is $H_n$. Sum the lower fourth-power reflection inequality over the blocks and use the parity identity with $s_K$ to obtain the claimed lower bound.

For necessity of the saturation criterion, equality in the sum forces equality in every nonzero block, since each block gap is nonnegative. The identity block $W$ is nonzero because $F(1)>0$. Identifying $\widehat{G/K}$ with $W$, the Fourier transform of~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:fiber-masses} is precisely $F|_W$. Thus $g$ is a point-spike equality weight on the quotient, and Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:83:thm:attainment} proves both divisibility and the necessary fiber-mass form.

For sufficiency, let $h$ be any attaining quotient weight and set $f(x)=h(x+K)$. Each additive quadruple in $G/K$ has exactly $|K|^3$ lifts satisfying the additive relation in $G$: choose the first three lifts freely and the fourth is determined. Respect by $a_K$ depends only on the quotient. Therefore
\[\Eng_G(f)=|K|^3\Eng_{G/K}(h),\qquad
 \mathcal E_{a_K}(f)=|K|^3\mathcal E_{\delta\ind_{\{0\}}}(h),\]
and the ratio is $\eta_n$. Finally, compactness on the finite $G$ unit-mass simplex proves strictness whenever saturation is impossible.
\end{proof}
For index $n=1$ or $2$, the block calculation instead gives $\mathcal E_{a_K}(f)=\Eng(f)$ for every nonnegative weight, since the corresponding reflection blocks are isometries.

The theorem does not classify all equality weights when $K$ is nontrivial. The necessary fiber-mass condition alone need not ensure equality on the other Fourier blocks. The constant-fiber construction proves existence and requires no splitting of the group extension. No infinite-group equality statement is asserted.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{What the energy result says about indicator witnesses\srctag{83}}]{What the energy result says about indicator witnesses}\label{gsr:en:83:sec:d13}\label{gsr:en:83:sec:scope}
\srcnote{83}{Section 13}
The weights in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:83:thm:attainment} need not be indicators. Define the indicator-restricted quantity
\[r_{G,\mathrm{ind}}(a)=\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq G}
 \frac{\Ea(\ind_S)}{\Eng(\ind_S)}.\]
Always $r_G(a)\le r_{G,\mathrm{ind}}(a)$, and the same spectral lower bound applies to every indicator. The weighted attainment theorem cannot be transferred automatically to indicators: its origin value is $ct_q$, rather than necessarily $c$.

The group-order-$27$ example illustrates this distinction precisely. Its full weighted equality classification has $t_9=\sqrt{6\sqrt6-8}>1$, so none of the minimizing weights is a scalar multiple of an indicator. Since there are only finitely many nonempty subsets of $G$, it follows that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:83:eq:indicator-27}
 r_{G,\mathrm{ind}}(\delta\ind_{\{0\}})>\lambda_9\qquad(|G|=27).
\end{equation}
This conclusion is restricted to the stated point spike and finite group; it does not classify the indicator minimum.

For a general map, the reflection-norm application here assumes its nonaffine part is an order-two point or subgroup spike. The operator calculation supplies no universal upper bound for arbitrary maps or arbitrary targets. In particular, the result is a local weighted additive-energy statement that can enter an energy or uniformity argument once the appropriate spike structure has been proved. It is not a new global bound in Ramsey theory or Szemeredi's theorem, and it does not alter the separately established global hypotheses or upper bounds in earlier reports.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The reflection input from Report 295\srctag{85}}]{The reflection input from Report 295}\label{gsr:en:85:sec:d2}\label{gsr:en:85:sec:input}
\srcnote{85}{Section 2}
Write $\ind=(1,\ldots,1)$, $J_n=\ind\ind^T$, and $H_n=I-2J_n/n$. Counting measure is used in
\[\norm{x}_4^4=\sum_{i=1}^n|x_i|^4.\]
The following is the exact analytic input from Report 295~\cite{srceightythree}; its proof of the all-maximizer theorem is not repeated here.

\begin{proposition}[Inherited reflection theorem]\label{gsr:en:85:prop:inherited}
For $n\ge3$, one has $0<k_n<1$, $\norm{H_n}_{4\to4}^4=C_n>1$ over both scalar fields, and the complete upper and lower equality sets are as follows. Let $v_{n,m}$ have $m$ coordinates $\sqrt{(n-m)/m}$ and $n-m$ coordinates $-\sqrt{m/(n-m)}$. Every nonzero upper equality vector is a permutation and nonzero scalar multiple of
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:85:eq:upper}
 v_{n,m}-\sqrt{y_{n,m}}\ind,\qquad m\in\mc_n,
\end{equation}
and every nonzero lower equality vector is a permutation and nonzero scalar multiple of
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:85:eq:lower}
 v_{n,m}+\sqrt{y_{n,m}}\ind,\qquad m\in\mc_n.
\end{equation}
The scalars are real for real equality and complex for complex equality. The lower ratio is $C_n^{-1}$, since $H_n^2=I$.
\end{proposition}
This is the combination of Report 295's all-real-maximizer theorem, common-phase theorem, scalar reflection optimization, and complete reflection equality theorem. In that report, the relevant statements are Theorems 1.1, 1.2 and 6.2, with the arguments in Sections 2, 3 and 6. The statement imported here is explicitly displayed above, so the present finite-order arguments do not depend on unexplained notation from the earlier report.

For orientation, $v=v_{n,m}$ has normalized moments
\[\E v=0,\quad\E v^2=1,\quad\E v^3=d_{n,m},\quad\E v^4=1+d_{n,m}^2.\]
On an unbalanced two-valued branch $m<n/2$, so $d>0$, the upper fourth-power ratio for $v-r\ind$ is $(1+b_d(r))/(1-b_d(r))$, where
\[b_d(r)=\frac{4rd}{r^4+6r^2+1+d^2},\qquad r\ge0.\]
Its derivative has the sign of $1+d^2-6r^2-3r^4$, so its unique positive maximum is at $r=\sqrt{y_{n,m}}$. Substitution gives $k_{n,m}$. For the balanced branch $d=0$, the function $b_d$ is identically zero and its ratio is one, so it cannot maximize $C_n>1$. This explains the radicals in~\eqref{gsr:fm:85:eq:parameters}; the substantial inherited assertion is that these branches cover \emph{every} real and complex equality vector.

Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:85:thm:main} removes the remaining ambiguity in $m$. It does not make the equality set a single vector: permutations and nonzero scalar multiples remain, and point-spike weights can be supported on different subgroups.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{An integer comparator and the exact candidates\srctag{85}}]{An integer comparator and the exact candidates}\label{gsr:en:85:sec:d3}\label{gsr:en:85:sec:comparator}
\srcnote{85}{Section 3}
The radical formula has a particularly simple order-preserving polynomial.

\begin{lemma}[Exact comparator]\label{gsr:en:85:lem:comparator}
At fixed $n$, the complete ordering of the nonnegative numbers $k_{n,m}$, including ties, is the ordering of
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:85:eq:W}
 W(n,m)=m(n-m)(n-2m)^4.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Put $u=m(n-m)$ and $s=\sqrt{3u}$. Since $u\le n^2/4$, we have $0<s<n$. Substituting $y=(n-s)/s$ and $y+3=(n+2s)/s$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:85:eq:k-rationalize}
 k_{n,m}^2=\frac{3(n^2-4u)s}{(n-s)(n+2s)^2}.
\end{equation}
Every denominator is positive. Using $s^2=3u$, expand
\[(n-s)(n+2s)^2=n^3+3n^2s-4s^3=n^3+3(n^2-4u)s.\]
Thus, with $A=3(n^2-4u)s\ge0$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:85:eq:W-k}
 k_{n,m}^2=\frac{A}{n^3+A},\qquad A^2=27u(n^2-4u)^2=27W(n,m).
\end{equation}
Both $W\mapsto\sqrt{27W}$ and $A\mapsto A/(n^3+A)$ are strictly increasing on the nonnegative half-line. As $k_{n,m}\ge0$, the conclusion follows, including the balanced branch $W=0$.
\end{proof}
In particular, no comparison of radicals and no decimal decision are needed to select a split. The lemma gives the exact alternative formula
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:85:eq:k-from-W}
 k_{n,m}=\sqrt{\frac{\sqrt{27W(n,m)}}{n^3+\sqrt{27W(n,m)}}}.
\end{equation}

\begin{proposition}[Unimodality and two candidates]\label{gsr:en:85:prop:candidates}
Put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:85:eq:pstar}
 p_* =\frac{1-\sqrt{2/3}}2.
\end{equation}
Every maximizing multiplicity is the floor or ceiling of $np_*$, clipped to $[1,\lfloor n/2\rfloor]$, with duplicate candidates removed.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The continuous interpolation of~\eqref{gsr:en:85:eq:W} is
\[\frac{W(n,m)}{n^6}=F(m/n),\qquad F(p)=p(1-p)(1-2p)^4.\]
If $t=p(1-p)$, then $F=t(1-4t)^2$ and
\[\frac{dF}{dt}=(1-4t)(1-12t).\]
As $t$ increases strictly with $p$ on $(0,1/2)$, $F$ increases strictly on $(0,p_*)$ and decreases strictly on $(p_*,1/2)$. Only the adjacent grid points around $p_*$ can maximize. Clipping accounts for the lower endpoint when $np_*<1$.
\end{proof}
For an integer implementation, no square root is needed even for the candidates:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:85:eq:candidate-test}
 m<np_*\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad3(n-2m)^2>2n^2,
 \qquad 0\le2m\le n.
\end{equation}
Both sides before squaring are nonnegative, which is essential for this equivalence. The irrationality of $p_*$ excludes an equality endpoint.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Why the maximizing multiplicity never ties\srctag{85}}]{Why the maximizing multiplicity never ties}\label{gsr:en:85:sec:d4}\label{gsr:en:85:sec:no-ties}
\srcnote{85}{Section 4}
Unimodality reduces the question to two adjacent integers. A divisibility argument resolves it in every dimension.

\begin{lemma}[No adjacent ties]\label{gsr:en:85:lem:no-tie}
If $1\le m<m+1\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, then $W(n,m)\ne W(n,m+1)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Set $x=n-2m$ and $z=x-2=n-2(m+1)$, so $x>z\ge0$. If $z=0$, the second value is zero and the first is positive. Suppose $z>0$ and assume equality. Because $4m(n-m)=n^2-x^2$, we get
\[(n^2-x^2)x^4=(n^2-z^2)z^4,\]
and hence
\begin{align}
 n^2&=\frac{x^6-z^6}{x^4-z^4}
 =\frac{x^4+x^2z^2+z^4}{x^2+z^2}\notag\\
 &=x^2+z^2-\frac{x^2z^2}{x^2+z^2}.\label{gsr:en:85:eq:tie-equation}
\end{align}
If $x,z$ are odd, they are coprime because their difference is two. Thus
\[\gcd(x^2+z^2,x^2z^2)=1.\]
The integrality of $n^2$ in~\eqref{gsr:en:85:eq:tie-equation} would force $x^2+z^2$ to divide $x^2z^2$, so $x^2+z^2=1$, impossible for positive $x,z$.

If $x,z$ are even, write $x=2a$, $z=2b$. Then $a,b$ are positive consecutive integers, and~\eqref{gsr:en:85:eq:tie-equation} becomes
\[n^2=4(a^2+b^2)-\frac{4a^2b^2}{a^2+b^2}.\]
Now $\gcd(a^2+b^2,a^2b^2)=1$, so integrality forces $a^2+b^2\mid4$. But $a\ge2$, $b\ge1$ give $a^2+b^2\ge5$. This is again impossible.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[All-order uniqueness]\label{gsr:en:85:cor:unique}
For every $n\ge3$, there is exactly one optimal multiplicity $m_n$. Therefore~\eqref{gsr:en:85:eq:upper} and~\eqref{gsr:en:85:eq:lower}, with $m=m_n$, give a single permutation-and-scaling family for each of the upper and lower reflection equality sets.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
A maximum exists in the finite multiplicity set. Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:85:prop:candidates} restricts all maxima to either one candidate or two adjacent candidates. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:85:lem:no-tie} excludes the latter tie.
\end{proof}
The proof is independent of any finite search. It does not assert that arbitrary nonadjacent nonmaximizing branches can never tie. Nor does it replace exact comparison of the two candidates by nearest-integer rounding: for $n=27$, the candidates are $2,3$ and
\[W(27,3)-W(27,2)=10{,}582>0,\]
although $27p_*<5/2$. The exact comparison $27p_*<5/2$ follows from $27\sqrt{2/3}>22$, whose positive squared difference is $486-484=2$.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The energy bound and complete point-spike equality\srctag{85}}]{The energy bound and complete point-spike equality}\label{gsr:en:85:sec:d5}\label{gsr:en:85:sec:energy}
\srcnote{85}{Section 5}
We now give a concise self-contained derivation of the energy saturation criterion from Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:85:prop:inherited}. This identifies precisely why a divisibility condition enters the classification.

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group of order $n$, and let an abelian target contain an element $\delta\ne0$ with $2\delta=0$. Consider the full-domain point spike $a(x)=\delta\ind_{\{0\}}(x)$. For a nonzero nonnegative weight $f$ on $G$, set
\begin{align}
 \Eng(f)&=\sum_{x+y=z+w}f(x)f(y)f(z)f(w),\label{gsr:en:85:eq:energy}\\
 \Ea(f)&=\sum_{\substack{x+y=z+w\\a(x)+a(y)=a(z)+a(w)}}f(x)f(y)f(z)f(w),\label{gsr:en:85:eq:retained}\\
 r_G(a)&=\inf_{f\ge0,\ f\ne0}\frac{\Ea(f)}{\Eng(f)}.\label{gsr:en:85:eq:infimum}
\end{align}
The sums are ordered and include repeated entries. With the convention
\[\widehat f(\chi)=\sum_{x\in G}f(x)\overline{\chi(x)},\qquad
 f(x)=\frac1n\sum_{\chi\in\widehat G}\widehat f(\chi)\chi(x),\]
Parseval and convolution give, for every real $h$, including signed weights,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:85:eq:Fourier-energy}
 \Eng(h)=\sum_u(h*h)(u)^2=\frac1n\sum_{\chi\in\widehat G}|\widehat h(\chi)|^4.
\end{equation}
Write $s=1-2\ind_{\{0\}}$ and $F=\widehat f$. A source additive quadruple is respected by $a$ exactly when the total number of its zero entries is even. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:85:eq:parity}
 \Ea(f)=\frac{\Eng(f)+\Eng(sf)}2,\qquad \widehat{sf}=H_nF.
\end{equation}
The latter identity uses $f(0)=n^{-1}\sum_\chi F(\chi)$. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:85:eq:spectral}
 \frac{\Ea(f)}{\Eng(f)}
 =\frac12\left(1+\frac{\norm{H_nF}_4^4}{\norm F_4^4}\right)
 \ge\frac{1+C_n^{-1}}2=\eta_n.
\end{equation}
Equality holds exactly when $F$ is a lower equality vector. The sharp operator bound alone is insufficient to guarantee such an $F$ is the Fourier transform of a nonnegative weight.

\begin{theorem}[Point-spike saturation and every equality weight]\label{gsr:en:85:thm:attainment}
For $n\ge3$, the point spike attains $\eta_n$ if and only if $m_n\mid n$. Put $q=n/m_n$ when this holds and define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:85:eq:tq}
 t_q=\sqrt{q\sqrt{\frac{q-1}{3}}-(q-1)}.
\end{equation}
All nonzero nonnegative equality weights, and only those, have the form
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:85:eq:profile}
 f(x)=\begin{cases}
 ct_q,&x=0,\\
 c,&x\in L\setminus\{0\},\\
 0,&x\notin L,
 \end{cases}
 \qquad c>0,\quad L\le G,\quad |L|=q.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The maximizing split is unbalanced: $W(n,1)>0$ for $n\ge3$, while a balanced split has zero comparator. Abbreviate $m=m_n$, $y=y_{n,m}$. If equality holds, Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:85:prop:inherited} yields a set $S\subseteq\widehat G$ of size $m$ and a nonzero complex scalar $z$ with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:85:eq:two-Fourier}
 F(\chi)=z\bigl(B+(A-B)\ind_S(\chi)\bigr),\quad
 A=\sqrt{\frac{n-m}{m}}+\sqrt y,\quad
 B=-\sqrt{\frac m{n-m}}+\sqrt y.
\end{equation}
We have $A>0$, $A-B>0$ and $A+B=d_{n,m}+2\sqrt y>0$, so $A>|B|$. Nonnegativity gives
\[F(1)=\sum_xf(x)>0,\qquad |F(\chi)|\le F(1).\]
Thus $1\in S$ and $z>0$ is real. Let $K_S(x)=\sum_{\chi\in S}\chi(x)$. Fourier inversion gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:85:eq:inversion}
 f(x)=zB\ind_{\{0\}}(x)+\frac{z(A-B)}nK_S(x).
\end{equation}
Consequently $K_S$ is real and nonnegative away from zero; at zero it equals $m>0$.

Set $\mu(x)=K_S(x)/n$. Orthogonality gives $\sum_x\mu(x)=1$ and $\widehat\mu=\ind_S$. For $\chi\in S$,
\[\sum_x\mu(x)|\chi(x)-1|^2=2-2\Rea\sum_x\mu(x)\chi(x)=0.\]
Thus every such $\chi$ equals one on $\supp\mu$. Products and inverses retain this property and have Fourier average one, so belong to $S$. As $1\in S$, the set $S$ is a subgroup.

Let $L=S^\perp$. Character orthogonality within $S$ gives $K_S=m\ind_L$. Summing over $G$ gives $m|L|=n$, hence $m\mid n$ and $|L|=q$. Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:85:eq:inversion} now yields the off-origin value
\[c=z\sqrt{\frac m{n-m}}>0,\]
while the mean of the Fourier vector is $f(0)=z\sqrt y$. Their ratio is $\sqrt{(q-1)y}=t_q$, proving~\eqref{gsr:en:85:eq:profile}.

Conversely, the Fourier transform of~\eqref{gsr:en:85:eq:profile} is
\[F(\chi)=c(t_q-1)+cq\ind_{L^\perp}(\chi),\qquad |L^\perp|=m.\]
With $z=c\sqrt{q-1}$, these are exactly the two levels in~\eqref{gsr:en:85:eq:two-Fourier}; therefore the weight attains~\eqref{gsr:en:85:eq:spectral}. Every finite abelian group has a subgroup of every divisor order: choose an order-$p$ subgroup for a prime $p\mid q$, use induction in the quotient for $q/p$, and take the inverse image. This proves existence whenever $m\mid n$.
\end{proof}
This argument recalls the complete point-spike theorem from Report 295, now with its unique multiplicity. It does not derive Fourier positivity from the integer comparator; the character-sum step is indispensable.

\begin{corollary}[Strict nonsaturation]\label{gsr:en:85:cor:strict}
If $m_n\nmid n$, then $r_G(a)>\eta_n$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
By homogeneity restrict to the compact simplex $\sum_xf(x)=1$, $f\ge0$. Here $F(1)=1$ and~\eqref{gsr:en:85:eq:Fourier-energy} gives $\Eng(f)\ge1/n$. The ratio is continuous, so attains its minimum. Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:85:thm:attainment} excludes equality everywhere on that simplex, proving strict inequality.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A finite cutoff with exact endpoint control\srctag{85}}]{A finite cutoff with exact endpoint control}\label{gsr:en:85:sec:d6}\label{gsr:en:85:sec:cutoff}
\srcnote{85}{Section 6}
Suppose $m_n\mid n$ and write $q=n/m_n$. The split is unbalanced, so $q\ge3$. Every clipped candidate satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:85:eq:distance}
 |m_n-np_*|<1.
\end{equation}
Indeed, $p_*<1/3$ and $n/3\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ for $n\ge3$, so $np_*$ lies strictly below the upper endpoint; neither floor nor ceiling needs upper clipping. If the floor is clipped from zero to one, then $0<np_*<1$ and~\eqref{gsr:en:85:eq:distance} still holds. Otherwise it follows from irrationality and the floor/ceiling definitions.

Since $m_n=n/q$,~\eqref{gsr:en:85:eq:distance} gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:85:eq:reciprocal-distance}
 n\left|\frac1q-p_*\right|<1.
\end{equation}
The unique closest reciprocal $1/q$ with integer $q\ge3$ is $1/11$. To verify this without rounding, first note $1/11<p_*<1/10$. Within $q\ge11$, $1/11$ is closest; within $3\le q\le10$, $1/10$ is closest. Their midpoint is $21/220$, and $p_*<21/220$ selects $1/11$. After squaring positive quantities, the three exact differences are
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:85:eq:cutoff-integers}
 3\cdot81-2\cdot121=1,\quad
 2\cdot25-3\cdot16=2,\quad
 2\cdot110^2-3\cdot89^2=437.
\end{equation}
It follows that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:85:eq:cutoff}
 n<\frac1{p_*-1/11}=594+242\sqrt6<1187.
\end{equation}
The last inequality follows from $593^2-6\cdot242^2=265>0$. Also $6\cdot242^2-592^2=920>0$, so the irrational cutoff lies strictly between $1186$ and $1187$.

Thus only $n=3,\ldots,1186$ need checking. One complete route compares \emph{every} allowed branch at these $1184$ orders, a total of
\[\sum_{n=3}^{1186}\lfloor n/2\rfloor=351{,}648\]
integer values. Retaining the maximum and testing $m_n\mid n$ yields Table~\ref{gsr:fm:85:tab:classification}. The companion performs this full search independently of its candidate calculation and records every winner, candidate value, runner-up and positive gap. The next section proves the same classification with a much smaller finite certificate.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A compact completeness proof by fixed quotient\srctag{85}}]{A compact completeness proof by fixed quotient}\label{gsr:en:85:sec:d7}\label{gsr:en:85:sec:compact}
\srcnote{85}{Section 7}
Fix an integer $q\ge3$, write $n=qm$, and put $p=1/q$. We test whether the branch with multiplicity $m$ is optimal. The interpolation $F$ from Section~\ref{gsr:en:85:sec:comparator} has one strict maximum, at $p_*$. This makes the winning values of $m$ an initial interval.

\subsection{Quotients from three through ten}
For $3\le q\le10$, $p>p_*$. Every later branch has larger proportion and smaller value. The branch $m=1$ is therefore optimal automatically. For $m\ge2$, optimality is equivalent to
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:85:eq:previous}
 F(p)>F\left(p-\frac1{qm}\right),\quad\hbox{or}\quad
 W(qm,m)-W(qm,m-1)>0.
\end{equation}
Necessity is clear from the preceding competitor and absence of ties. For sufficiency, if that competitor has smaller value, its proportion must lie below $p_*$, since on the right-hand side of the maximum a preceding point has larger value. Every still earlier point is then smaller by strict increase to the left, and every later point is smaller by strict decrease to the right.

There is exactly one $r_-\in(0,p_*)$ with $F(r_-)=F(p)$. For $0\le r<p$, one has $F(r)<F(p)$ exactly when $r<r_-$. The preceding proportion
\[p-\frac1{qm}=p\left(1-\frac1m\right)\]
increases strictly to $p$ as $m$ grows. Therefore the winning integers form a finite initial interval beginning at one. A last-winner and first-loser test determine it completely.

\subsection{Quotients at least eleven}
For $q\ge11$, $p<p_*$. The following branch is always allowed, since $m+1\le qm/2$. By the analogous unimodality argument, the branch is optimal exactly when
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:85:eq:following}
 F(p)>F\left(p+\frac1{qm}\right),\quad\hbox{or}\quad
 W(qm,m)-W(qm,m+1)>0.
\end{equation}
All preceding points are smaller. If the following point is smaller, it must lie beyond $p_*$, and every later point is smaller too. There is a unique $r_+\in(p_*,1/2)$ with $F(r_+)=F(p)$, and for $p<r\le1/2$ the condition $F(r)<F(p)$ is exactly $r>r_+$. The following proportion
\[p+\frac1{qm}=p\left(1+\frac1m\right)\]
decreases strictly to $p$. Again the winners form a finite initial interval, now possibly empty.

For every $q\ge22$ and $m\ge1$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:85:eq:tail}
 p<p+\frac1{qm}\le\frac2q\le\frac1{11}<p_*.
\end{equation}
The following branch is then strictly better. Consequently only $q=3,\ldots,21$ require boundary comparisons.

\subsection{The twenty-seven integer comparisons}
Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:85:eq:D}
 D_q(m)=\begin{cases}
 W(qm,m)-W(qm,m-1),&3\le q\le10,\\
 W(qm,m)-W(qm,m+1),&q\ge11.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
The first formula is used only for $m\ge2$; at $m=1$ the win is automatic. Table~\ref{gsr:en:85:tab:gaps} lists exact values at the last winner and the first loser. For an empty winning interval, the first loser is $m=1$.

\begin{proof}[Completion of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:85:thm:main}]
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:85:cor:unique} proves uniqueness. The initial-interval arguments and Table~\ref{gsr:en:85:tab:gaps} yield exactly Table~\ref{gsr:fm:85:tab:classification}. Its number of pairs is

This compact proof does not require the exhaustive cutoff search. \section[{Consequences and representative orders\srctag{85}}]{Consequences and representative orders}\label{gsr:en:85:sec:d8}\label{gsr:en:85:sec:examples}
\srcnote{85}{Section 8}
At the last saturating order, $n=583$, the unique multiplicity is $m_n=53$ and $q=11$. Every equality weight is supported on an order-eleven subgroup and has origin-to-other-point ratio $t_{11}$. This applies to every abelian group of order $583$. For all $n\ge584$, spectral equality is impossible and the compactness argument gives a strict, unquantified gap.

At $n=27$, the winner is $m_n=3$, so $q=9$ and equality weights occupy a subgroup of order nine. At $n=81$, the exact candidates are $7,8$, and
\[W(81,7)-W(81,8)=13{,}515{,}678>0.\]
Since $7\nmid81$, spectral equality is impossible in every group of order $81$. Neither example uses numerical rounding or a search over weights. The actual order-$81$ minimum is not computed here.

For any listed order $n=qm$, its optimal proportion is $1/q$. The definitions in~\eqref{gsr:fm:85:eq:parameters} depend only on this proportion, so $k_n=k_q$, $C_n=C_q$ and $\eta_n=\eta_q$. Indeed every listed $q$ itself has optimal multiplicity one. Thus the $77$ orders arise from only the $13$ displayed quotient values $q=3,\ldots,15$. Equality of constants at repeated proportions does not imply equality of the dimensions or of the weight supports.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Subgroup spikes and the limit of the classification\srctag{85}}]{Subgroup spikes and the limit of the classification}\label{gsr:en:85:sec:d9}\label{gsr:en:85:sec:subgroups}
\srcnote{85}{Section 9}
Let $K\le G$ have index $n$, and set $a_K(x)=\delta\ind_K(x)$, with the same nonzero order-two value $\delta$. The additive energies are defined as in~\eqref{gsr:en:85:eq:energy}--\eqref{gsr:en:85:eq:retained} with $a_K$ in place of $a$.

\Needspace{11\baselineskip}
\begin{theorem}[Index criterion and quotient fibers]\label{gsr:en:85:thm:subgroup}
For $n\ge3$, the spectral lower bound is $r_G(a_K)\ge\eta_n$, and equality is attainable if and only if $n$ is in Table~\ref{gsr:fm:85:tab:classification}. If $f\ge0$ attains equality, its fiber-mass function
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:85:eq:fiber}
 g(x+K)=\sum_{k\in K}f(x+k)
\end{equation}
is a point-spike equality weight on $G/K$, of the form~\eqref{gsr:en:85:eq:profile}. Conversely, constant-fiber lifts of such quotient profiles attain equality. If $n$ is unlisted, $r_G(a_K)>\eta_n$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Put $N=|G|$ and $V=K^\perp\le\widehat G$, so $|V|=n$. Since $\widehat{\ind_K}=|K|\ind_V$, multiplication by $s_K=1-2\ind_K$ acts on $F=\widehat f$ by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:85:eq:block}
 \widehat{s_Kf}(\chi)=F(\chi)-\frac2n\sum_{\eta\in V}F(\chi\eta).
\end{equation}
Thus each coset of $V$ is an $n$-coordinate reflection block. Apply the lower fourth-power inequality to every block, sum, and use the parity identity. This gives the bound.

Equality forces every nonzero block to be a lower equality vector. The identity block $V$ is nonzero because $F(1)>0$, and it is precisely the Fourier transform of $g$ in~\eqref{gsr:en:85:eq:fiber}, identified with a function on $G/K$. The point-spike theorem therefore forces the classification and the necessary fiber profile.

For sufficiency let $h$ be any equality profile on $G/K$ and put $f(x)=h(x+K)$. Every quotient additive quadruple has $|K|^3$ lifts satisfying the additive relation in $G$: choose three lifts freely and the fourth is determined. Both energies are multiplied by $|K|^3$, so the quotient ratio is preserved. Compactness on the unit-mass simplex proves strictness when equality is impossible.
\end{proof}
No direct-product decomposition of $G$ is needed. These assertions reproduce the subgroup criterion of Report 295 with its finite index list now explicit. They do \emph{not} classify every equality weight for nontrivial $K$: the necessary fiber masses need not guarantee equality on the other Fourier blocks. The constant-fiber construction supplies sufficient examples, not a claimed complete equality family.

For index one or two the reflection blocks are isometries. In those cases every nonnegative weight has retained energy equal to ordinary energy. There is no infinite-group equality claim here.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Rational weights and indicator attainment\srctag{85}}]{Rational weights and indicator attainment}\label{gsr:en:85:sec:d10}\label{gsr:en:85:sec:rational}
\srcnote{85}{Section 10}
The distinction between spectral attainment and an infimum is especially important for rational weights.

\begin{lemma}[Rationality among classified support orders]\label{gsr:en:85:lem:rational-t}
For the support orders $q$ appearing in Table~\ref{gsr:fm:85:tab:classification}, the number $t_q$ is rational if and only if $q=4$, in which case $t_4=1$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Suppose $t_q\in\Q$. Then
\[\sqrt{(q-1)/3}=\frac{t_q^2+q-1}{q}\in\Q.\]
Writing this square root as $a/b$ in lowest positive terms gives $3a^2=(q-1)b^2$, so coprimality forces $b^2\mid3$, hence $b=1$. Thus $q=1+3a^2$. The classified support orders satisfy $3\le q\le15$, leaving only $q=4$ and $q=13$. Direct substitution gives $t_4=1$ and $t_{13}=\sqrt{14}$. A rational square root of an integer must be an integer, while $3^2<14<4^2$, so the latter value is irrational.
\end{proof}

\Needspace{11\baselineskip}
\begin{corollary}[Exact rational and indicator attainment]\label{gsr:en:85:cor:rational}
Among group orders $n\ge3$, a point spike has a nonzero rational-valued spectral equality weight if and only if $n=4$. At that order its rational equality weights are exactly the positive rational constant weights. A nonempty indicator attains the spectral bound exactly when $n=4$ and it is the indicator of the whole group.

For subgroup spikes of index $n\ge3$, a nonzero rational-valued spectral equality weight exists if and only if $n=4$. A nonempty indicator equality weight exists if and only if $n=4$. These existence statements do not classify all equality weights with a nontrivial kernel.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For a point-spike equality profile, $q\ge3$, so some nonzero point of $L$ has weight $c$. Rationality of all weights makes $c$ and $ct_q$ rational; since $c>0$, it forces $t_q\in\Q$. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:85:lem:rational-t} gives $q=4$, and the classification table forces $m=1$, $n=4$ and $L=G$. The profile is constant. Conversely every positive rational constant weight at order four attains equality. An indicator has $c=1$, so exactly the full-group indicator works.

For a rational subgroup-spike equality weight, every quotient fiber mass is rational. The necessary quotient profile in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:85:thm:subgroup} therefore forces index four. Indicators are rational-valued and satisfy the same obstruction. Conversely the constant weight one on $G$ is a constant-fiber lift of the full-group quotient indicator when the index is four, so it attains equality.
\end{proof}

Define the rational and indicator restrictions by
\begin{align*}
 r_{G,\Q}(a)&=\inf_{f:G\to\Q_{\ge0},\ f\ne0}\frac{\Ea(f)}{\Eng(f)},\\
 r_{G,\mathrm{ind}}(a)&=\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq G}\frac{\Ea(\ind_S)}{\Eng(\ind_S)}.
\end{align*}
The corollary implies a strict indicator gap at every $n\ge3$ other than four, and the corresponding subgroup-spike statement at every index $n\ge3$ other than four: only finitely many nonempty subsets are involved, and none attains the bound.

The rational infimum behaves differently. Rational points are dense in the nonnegative unit-mass simplex, and the ratio is continuous there with positive denominator. Every real weight can therefore be approximated in ratio by rational weights, so
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:85:eq:rational-inf}
 r_{G,\Q}(a)=r_G(a).
\end{equation}
This density argument applies to subgroup spikes as well. In particular, at the other $76$ saturating orders or indices, every individual nonzero rational weight has ratio strictly above $\eta_n$, but rational weights approach $\eta_n$ arbitrarily closely. Nonattainment by rational weights does not produce a positive gap in their infimum. The strict indicator gap does not determine the indicator minimum.
