\section{Sources~93 and~90: affine recovery below graph defect \texorpdfstring{$1/4$}{1/4}, the universal cutoff~\texorpdfstring{$13$}{13} and one cyclic direction \wtag}\label{gsr:en:sec:quarter}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the thirteenth write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next two sections are source~93's Section~8 and source~90's Section~6. \emph{Logically they continue source~11's chapter} on affine rigidity at the Section~6 endpoint (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:affine}), the chapter of sources~59 and~56 (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:affinerepair}) and source~67's characteristic-three chapter (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:charthree}), and they use source~68's multilevel overlap inequality (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:energygap}); the statistic is the whole-graph energy $\mathcal E(f)$ and its defect $\varepsilon=1-\mathcal E(f)/N^3$, \emph{not} the hereditary infimum of the two preceding chapters.

\emph{What source~93 proves here.} For $f:G\to W$, $G$ finite abelian of order $N$ and $W$ any abelian group: if $\varepsilon(f)<1/4$ there is a unique nearest affine map, at distance at most $D_\kappa(\varepsilon)$, the inverse of source~11's cubic $\Psi_\kappa(t)=4t-(10+2\kappa)t^2+(6+2\kappa)t^3$ on $[0,1/7]$, $\kappa=1$ iff $W$ has an involution (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:recovery}); at $\varepsilon=1/4$ a complete dichotomy (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:endpoint}); and for $N\ge13$ every non-affine map has $\mathcal E(f)\le N^3-4N^2+(10+2\kappa)N-(6+2\kappa)$, equality exactly for one-point modifications (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:thirteen}). \emph{This settles the cutoff} that sources~11, 59 and~67 left open: $34$ with involutions (source~11), $16$ without (source~59's Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:59:cor:affine-sixteen}), $13$ for elementary abelian $3$-targets (source~67's Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:67:cthree:nonaffine-gap}): it is $13$ for every target, and $13$ is optimal for both kinds of target (checked at the write: the exhaustive maximum over non-affine $\Z/13\Z\to\Z/2\Z$ is $1669$, the one-point value; at $N=12$ the map $(0,0,1,1,\ldots)$ into $\Z/2\Z$ and the index-two coset indicator into $\Z/3\Z$ have energy $1296$, above $1288$ and $1266$). It extends source~59's recovery range $\varepsilon<2/9$ and source~68's set version to $\varepsilon<1/4$ for every target, credited by source~93, and gives the larger high-correlation range $\alpha^4>3/4$ in Proposition~6.1 (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:gowers}). The quarter threshold concerns the four-point affine test; the familiar $2/9$ of the three-point homomorphism test is another statistic, as source~93 says.

\emph{What source~90 proves here.} For $N\ge12$ and every map $f:C_N\to W$ into an abelian group, the mean over directions of the derivative collision probability satisfies $D(f)\le\frac{N+1}6d_1(f)$, with all equality cases (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:90:thm:cycle}); generic cut expansion gives the leading constant $1/4$ in place of $1/6$. Checked exhaustively at the write for $C_{12},C_{13},C_{14}\to C_2$: no violation, and non-affine equality only for $N=13$.

\emph{Relation to the formal statements} (checked at HEAD \texttt{bf285410b}). \file{proposition_6_1} and \file{lemma_6_2} (\file{Sections06\_07.lean}, lines~37 and~47) are exact (\file{proposition_6_1_holds}, \file{lemma_6_2_holds}, \file{Proofs05\_10.lean}, lines~505 and~589); source~93's Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:gowers} is a consequence of their outputs and changes no statement. The quarter recovery, the cutoff~$13$ and the directional comparison are not formalized.
\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Sharp affine recovery and the universal order-thirteen cutoff\srctag{93}}]{Sharp affine recovery and the universal order-thirteen cutoff}\label{gsr:en:93:sec:d8}
\srcnote{93}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:en:93:rig:section}

This section combines the overlap-spectrum inequality of
\cite{srcsixtyeight} with the local graph-energy profiles of
\cite{srceleven,srcfiftynine}.  The resulting recovery theorem
holds for every abelian target, including infinite targets and groups
with mixed torsion.  It extends the quarter-defect recovery theorem
previously proved for elementary abelian three-groups in
\cite{srcsixtyseven}; the earlier general-target recovery range in
\cite{srcfiftynine} was $\varepsilon<2/9$.
We also classify the obstruction at the quarter endpoint and prove the
optimal universal cutoff thirteen for the largest non-affine graph
energy.  The cutoff thirteen was already known for elementary abelian
three-targets by \cite{srcsixtyseven}; the extension to arbitrary
abelian targets is proved below.

The underlying overlap transformation, the majority-subgroup argument,
the cubic profiles, and their local equality families are credited to
these predecessors.  We include the needed proofs to make the present
combination independently checkable.  All counts use ordered tuples
and include repeated entries.

\subsection{Definitions and the recovery statement}

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group, write $N=|G|$, and let $W$ be an
arbitrary abelian group.  For a finite subset $A$ of an abelian group,
write
\[
 r_A(z)=|A\cap(A+z)|,
 \qquad E(A)=\sum_z r_A(z)^2.
\]
For $f:G\to W$, put $\Gamma_f=\{(x,f(x)):x\in G\}$ and
\begin{align}
 \mathcal E(f)&=E(\Gamma_f)\notag\\
 &=\#\{(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)\in G^4:
 x_1+x_2=x_3+x_4,\ 
 f(x_1)+f(x_2)=f(x_3)+f(x_4)\},
 \label{gsr:en:93:rig:graph-energy}\\
 \varepsilon(f)&=1-\frac{\mathcal E(f)}{N^3},
 \qquad
 d(f,\operatorname{Aff})=
 \min_{\ell\ {\rm affine}}\frac{|\{x:f(x)\ne\ell(x)\}|}{N}.
 \label{gsr:en:93:rig:distance}
\end{align}
An affine map is a homomorphism plus a constant.  The minimum in
\eqref{gsr:en:93:rig:distance} exists even when $W$ is infinite: constants give
a nonempty comparison family, and the possible unnormalized distances
belong to $\{0,1,\ldots,N\}$.

Let $\kappa=1$ if $W$ contains a nonzero element of order two, and let
$\kappa=0$ otherwise.  Define
\begin{equation}
 \Psi_\kappa(t)=4t-(10+2\kappa)t^2+(6+2\kappa)t^3.
 \label{gsr:en:93:rig:cubics}
\end{equation}
Both polynomials are strictly increasing on $[0,1/7]$, and
$\Psi_\kappa(1/7)\ge120/343>1/4$.  Throughout this section,
$D_\kappa$ denotes the inverse of this restricted branch; in
particular, it is defined on $[0,1/4]$.

\begin{theorem}[Sharp universal quarter-defect recovery]
\label{gsr:en:93:rig:recovery}
If $\varepsilon(f)<1/4$, then $f$ has a unique nearest affine map
$\ell:G\to W$, and
\begin{equation}
 d(f,\operatorname{Aff})\le D_\kappa(\varepsilon(f)).
 \label{gsr:en:93:rig:recovery-bound}
\end{equation}
The homomorphism part $L$ of $\ell$ is the strict derivative majority:
for every $h\in G$, $L(h)$ is the unique value $w\in W$ satisfying
\begin{equation}
 \#\{x\in G:f(x+h)-f(x)=w\}>N/2.
 \label{gsr:en:93:rig:derivative-majority}
\end{equation}
The constant part of $\ell$ is the strict majority value of $f-L$.

At positive distance, equality in \eqref{gsr:en:93:rig:recovery-bound} holds
exactly when
\begin{equation}
 f=\ell+b\,1_{x_0+H},
 \label{gsr:en:93:rig:coset-errors}
\end{equation}
where $H\le G$ and $b\ne0$; when $\kappa=1$, the element $b$ must
have order two.  The strict defect threshold $1/4$ is optimal as a
universal assertion in each of the two target-torsion classes.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 82--94]
\emph{Against the earlier ranges.} Source~59 recovered below defect $2/9$ for every target (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:59:thm:affine-global-two-ninths}) and source~67 below $1/4$ for elementary abelian $3$-group targets (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:67:cthree:global}); source~68 has the set version (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:multilevel}). This theorem gives $1/4$ for every abelian target, as source~93 says, crediting them.
\end{writenote}

The equality family in \eqref{gsr:en:93:rig:coset-errors} is the inherited local
one from \cite{srceleven,srcfiftynine}.  Equality parameters
are constrained by subgroup indices; the theorem does not assert
attainment at every real value of $\varepsilon$.

\subsection{The inherited overlap inequality and majority subgroup}

The following two lemmas are the overlap-spectrum and subgroup
arguments of \cite{srcsixtyeight}, in the forms needed here.

\begin{lemma}[Multilevel overlap inequality]
\label{gsr:en:93:rig:multilevel}
Let $A$ be a finite nonempty subset of an abelian group, with
$m=|A|$.  Suppose
$0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_j=m$, and every internal $t_i$ is an attained
value of $r_A$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 E(A)\le\frac{2m^3+\sum_{i=1}^j(t_i-t_{i-1})^3}{3}.
 \label{gsr:en:93:rig:multilevel-bound}
\end{equation}
In particular, if $\varepsilon=1-E(A)/m^3$ and $q(z)=r_A(z)/m$,
then
\begin{equation}
 q(z)(1-q(z))\le\varepsilon\qquad\text{for every }z.
 \label{gsr:en:93:rig:overlap-gap}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Fix a shift $z$ with $r_A(z)=t$, and put
\[
 C=A\cap(A+z),\quad U=A\cup(A+z),\quad
 P=A\setminus(A+z),\quad Q=(A+z)\setminus A.
\]
The disjoint decompositions and commutativity of convolution give
\[
 1_A*1_{A+z}=1_C*1_U+1_P*1_Q.
\]
The first summand is between zero and $t$, and its total mass is
$t(2m-t)$.  If
\[
 S(u)=\sum_x\min\{(1_A*1_A)(x),u\}\qquad(0\le u\le m),
\]
the translation of the convolution argument has no effect on this
sum, so $S(t)\ge t(2m-t)$.

The function $S$ is concave, $S(0)=0$, and $S(m)=m^2$.
On each interval $[t_{i-1},t_i]$ it therefore dominates the chord
joining the corresponding values of $P(u)=2mu-u^2$.
The area between this parabola and that chord is
$(t_i-t_{i-1})^3/6$.  Consequently
\[
 \int_0^m S(u)\,du
 \ge\frac{2m^3}{3}-\frac16\sum_{i=1}^j(t_i-t_{i-1})^3.
\]
On the other hand, direct integration of each truncated multiplicity
gives
\[
 \int_0^m S(u)\,du=m^3-\frac{E(A)}2.
\]
These two expressions prove \eqref{gsr:en:93:rig:multilevel-bound}.
For one internal node $t$, use
$t^3+(m-t)^3=m^3-3mt(m-t)$ to obtain
\eqref{gsr:en:93:rig:overlap-gap}.  Its endpoint cases $t=0,m$ are immediate.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Majority subgroup through the closed quarter endpoint]
\label{gsr:en:93:rig:majority-subgroup}
Under the notation of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:multilevel}, if
$\varepsilon\le1/4$, then
\begin{equation}
 K=\{z:r_A(z)>m/2\}
 \label{gsr:en:93:rig:canonical-subgroup}
\end{equation}
is a finite subgroup.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The set $K$ contains zero, is symmetric, and is finite because it
lies in $A-A$.  Suppose $d,e\in K$ but $d-e\notin K$.
The overlap triangle inequality
\[
 r_A(d-e)\ge r_A(d)+r_A(e)-m
\]
follows by intersecting $A\cap(A+d)$ and $A\cap(A+e)$ inside $A$.
Thus, with $c=q(d-e)$ and $b=\min\{q(d),q(e)\}$,
\[
 0<c\le\frac12<b\le\frac{1+c}{2}.
\]
The normalized internal nodes $c,b$ in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:multilevel} give
\[
 \varepsilon\ge F(c,b):=
 \frac{1-c^3-(b-c)^3-(1-b)^3}{3}.
\]
For fixed $c$, the derivative in $b$ is
$(1-c)(1+c-2b)$, which is positive before the upper endpoint of
the displayed interval.  Hence
\[
 F(c,b)>F(c,1/2)
 =\frac14+\frac{c(1/2-c)}2\ge\frac14,
\]
a contradiction.  Closure under differences proves the assertion.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Local cubic profiles and their equality cases}

We give the local estimates needed for the recovery and order-thirteen
arguments.  The no-involution estimate is the one-third-range
refinement in \cite{srcfiftynine}; the two-torsion estimate and
the exact one-color formulas are from \cite{srceleven}.
Only the range $t<1/3$ is needed in this section.

Subtract an affine reference $\ell$ and put $g=f-\ell$,
$S=\{x:g(x)\ne0\}$, $s=|S|$, and $t=s/N$.  For $b\ne0$, set
\begin{equation}
 c_b=|g^{-1}(b)|,
 \quad M=\sum_{b\ne0}c_b^2,
 \quad A=s^2-M,
 \quad C=\sum_{b\ne0}c_bc_{-b}.
 \label{gsr:en:93:rig:color-statistics}
\end{equation}
These sums have finite support.  Write $e_S=E(S)/N^3$ and
$a=A/N^2$.  The letters $A$ and $C$ in
\eqref{gsr:en:93:rig:color-statistics} are scalar color statistics, not the
ambient sets in the preceding subsection.

\begin{lemma}[Exact one-color defect and maximal set energy]
\label{gsr:en:93:rig:one-color}
For any $b\ne0$,
\begin{align}
 N^3-\mathcal E(b1_S)
 &=4sN^2-10s^2N+12s^3-6E(S),&&2b\ne0,
 \label{gsr:en:93:rig:one-odd}\\
 N^3-\mathcal E(b1_S)
 &=4sN^2-12s^2N+16s^3-8E(S),&&2b=0.
 \label{gsr:en:93:rig:one-even}
\end{align}
For nonempty $S$, $E(S)\le s^3$, with equality precisely when $S$
is a coset of a subgroup of $G$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Inclusion--exclusion counts additive quadruples with exactly one
position in $S$, exactly three positions in $S$, or exactly two
same-side positions in $S$, respectively, as
\begin{align*}
 Q_1&=4sN^2-12s^2N+12s^3-4E(S),\\
 Q_3&=4s^3-4E(S),\\
 Q_{2,\mathrm{same}}&=2s^2N-4s^3+2E(S).
\end{align*}
For example, a prescribed position in $S$ with the other three
outside contributes
$sN^2-3s^2N+3s^3-E(S)$.  A prescribed triple in $S$ with the
remaining position outside contributes $s^3-E(S)$.  A prescribed
same-side pair with the other two outside contributes
$s^2N-2s^3+E(S)$; there are two such pairs.

For $2b\ne0$, the failed patterns are exactly those counted by
$Q_1+Q_3+Q_{2,\mathrm{same}}$.  For $2b=0$, they are exactly
those counted by $Q_1+Q_3$.  This proves
\eqref{gsr:en:93:rig:one-odd}--\eqref{gsr:en:93:rig:one-even}.

Finally,
\[
 E(S)=\sum_d r_S(d)^2\le s\sum_d r_S(d)=s^3.
\]
At equality, every positive $r_S(d)$ is $s$.
If $L=\{d:S+d=S\}$ and $x\in S$, this implies
$S-x\subset L$, while invariance gives $x+L\subset S$.
Thus $S=x+L$, and $L$ is a finite subgroup.  The converse follows
directly from the difference multiplicities of a coset.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Signed expansion without target involutions]
\label{gsr:en:93:rig:signed-expansion}
Suppose $W$ has no nonzero element of order two.  Define
\[
 Z=\sum_{\substack{u,v\ne0\\u+v\ne0}}c_uc_vc_{u+v},
 \qquad
 D(x,w)=1_S(x)\bigl(1_{\{g(x)\}}(w)-1_{\{0\}}(w)\bigr).
\]
For a finitely supported real function $v$ on an abelian group, put
$\mathcal E(v)=\sum_z(v*v)(z)^2$.  Then
\begin{align}
 \mathcal E(g)
 ={}&N^3-4sN^2+N(6s^2+4M+2C)\notag\\
 &-4s^3-8sM-4sC+4Z+\mathcal E(D),
 \label{gsr:en:93:rig:signed-identity}\\
 \mathcal E(D)&\le6E(S),
 \qquad 0\le C\le A,
 \qquad Z\le\frac{sA}{2}.
 \label{gsr:en:93:rig:signed-bounds}
\end{align}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The graph indicator of $g$ is $B+D$, where
$B=1_{G\times\{0\}}$.  Expand its four-factor energy.
The term with no $D$ is $N^3$, and each of the four one-factor
terms is $-sN^2$.
For two $D$ factors, each of the four opposite-side pairs
contributes $N(s^2+M)$ and each of the two same-side pairs
contributes $N(s^2+C)$.
For three factors, set $m_0=-s$ and $m_b=c_b$ for $b\ne0$.
The target-coordinate sum is
\[
 \sum_{u+v=w}m_um_vm_w=Z-s^3-2sM-sC.
\]
There are four choices of the omitted position.  The four-factor
term is $\mathcal E(D)$, proving \eqref{gsr:en:93:rig:signed-identity}.

For its upper bound, fix a horizontal additive quadruple in $S^4$.
Its four nonzero signed target labels are
$y_1=g(x_1)$, $y_2=g(x_2)$, $y_3=-g(x_3)$, and $y_4=-g(x_4)$.
Its contribution to $\mathcal E(D)$ is
$1+P-T+F$, where $P$ counts zero-sum pairs of positions, $T$
counts zero-sum triples, and $F$ indicates that all four labels
sum to zero.  There are no zero-sum singleton terms.
Because the target has no nonzero involution, the graph joining
opposite labels is a disjoint union of complete bipartite graphs.
On four vertices it has at most four edges.  Thus $P\le4$ and
$1+P-T+F\le6$.  Summing over the $E(S)$ horizontal quadruples
gives $\mathcal E(D)\le6E(S)$.

Every opposite-label pair has unequal labels, proving $C\le A$.
For an ordered triple $(u,v,w)$ of nonzero labels, let $R$ count
the equations $u+v=w$, $u+w=v$, and $v+w=u$, and let $U$ count
its unequal pairs.  At most one equation holds: two would force
a nonzero label to have order two.  If one holds, at least two
pairs are unequal, so $2R\le U$.  Summing with weights
$c_uc_vc_w$ gives $6Z\le3sA$ and proves the last assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Inherited local cubic profiles]
\label{gsr:en:93:rig:local-cubic}
With the preceding notation, suppose $0<t<1/3$.
If $W$ has no nonzero involution, then
\begin{equation}
 \varepsilon(f)\ge\Psi_0(t)+6(t^3-e_S)+2(1-3t)a.
 \label{gsr:en:93:rig:local-odd}
\end{equation}
If $W$ has a nonzero involution, put $J=M-C\ge0$ and
$j=J/N^2$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 \varepsilon(f)\ge\Psi_1(t)+8(t^3-e_S)
             +6(1-3t)a+2(1-2t)j.
 \label{gsr:en:93:rig:local-even}
\end{equation}
In either case $\varepsilon(f)\ge\Psi_\kappa(t)$, with equality
exactly for \eqref{gsr:en:93:rig:coset-errors}, requiring $2b=0$ when
$\kappa=1$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Affine subtraction preserves energy.  In the no-involution case,
rearrange \eqref{gsr:en:93:rig:signed-identity} as
\[
 N^3\bigl(\varepsilon(f)-\Psi_0(t)\bigr)
 =(N-2s)(4A-2C)-4Z+6s^3-\mathcal E(D).
\]
Since $s<N/3<N/2$, Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:signed-expansion} bounds this
below by
\[
 6\bigl(s^3-E(S)\bigr)+2(N-2s)A-2sA
 =6\bigl(s^3-E(S)\bigr)+2(N-3s)A.
\]
Division by $N^3$ proves \eqref{gsr:en:93:rig:local-odd}.

For the second case, first
\[
 J=M-C=\frac12\sum_{b\ne0}(c_b-c_{-b})^2\ge0.
\]
Choose a nonzero involution $b_0\in W$ and compare $g$ with
$g_0=b_01_S$.  Put $T_0=s^3-\sum_{b\ne0}c_b^3$.
A non-monochromatic ordered triple has at least two unequal
pairs, so counting unequal pairs with the remaining entry gives
$T_0\le3sA/2$.

For exactly two error positions, $g_0$ always respects the
quadruple.  For each opposite-side pair, $g$ fails on the $A$
ordered unequal-label assignments.  For each same-side pair it
fails on $s^2-C=A+J$ assignments.  Each fixed assignment has at
least $N-2s$ completions with its other two positions outside
$S$: either remaining position excludes at most $s$ values of
the free parameter.  Thus the two-error gain is at least
$(N-2s)(6A+2J)$.
For exactly three errors, $g_0$ fails.  Any gain for $g$ requires
a non-monochromatic triple, so its total gain is at most
$4T_0\le6sA$.  With zero, one, or four errors, $g_0$ cannot
lose.  Consequently
\[
 \mathcal E(g_0)-\mathcal E(g)
 \ge6(N-3s)A+2(N-2s)J.
\]
Together with \eqref{gsr:en:93:rig:one-even}, this is
\eqref{gsr:en:93:rig:local-even}.

All remainder terms in the relevant displayed inequality are
nonnegative, and their color coefficients are positive.
Equality therefore forces $A=0$ and $E(S)=s^3$; in the
two-torsion case it also forces $J=0$.
The condition $A=0$ says that one nonzero value $b$ occurs.
For one value, $J=0$ is exactly $b=-b$.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:one-color} identifies $S$ as a subgroup coset
and verifies every converse equality case.
\end{proof}

\subsection{From the majority subgroup to a global affine map}

For the remainder of the section, the majority subgroup attached to a
graph is always
\begin{equation}
 K_f=\{(h,w)\in G\times W:r_{\Gamma_f}(h,w)>N/2\}.
 \label{gsr:en:93:rig:graph-majority-subgroup}
\end{equation}
The identity
\[
 r_{\Gamma_f}(h,w)=\#\{x:f(x+h)-f(x)=w\}
\]
connects this notation with \eqref{gsr:en:93:rig:derivative-majority}.

\begin{lemma}[Graph projection and quantitative entry]
\label{gsr:en:93:rig:graph-entry}
Suppose $\varepsilon(f)\le1/4$.
The subgroup $K_f$ is the graph of a homomorphism $L:H_0\to W$
on a subgroup $H_0\le G$.
If $\varepsilon(f)<1/4$, then $H_0=G$.
Whenever $H_0=G$, there is a unique strict majority value $c$ of
$f-L$, and, for $\ell=L+c$ and
$t=|\{x:f(x)\ne\ell(x)\}|/N$,
\begin{equation}
 t\le B(\varepsilon(f))
 :=\frac{1-\sqrt{(1+\sqrt{1-4\varepsilon(f)})/2}}{2}
 \le\frac{1-1/\sqrt2}{2}<\frac16.
 \label{gsr:en:93:rig:entry-bound}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:majority-subgroup} makes $K_f$ a finite subgroup.
Its vertical intersection is trivial, since
$r_{\Gamma_f}(0,w)=0$ for $w\ne0$.
Projection to $G$ is consequently injective on $K_f$; its image
is a subgroup $H_0$, and $K_f$ is the graph of a homomorphism
$L:H_0\to W$.

Put $h=|H_0|=|K_f|$, and let
$p_i=|\Gamma_f\cap C_i|/N$ be the occupancies of its cosets.
Each $p_i\le h/N$, because a $K_f$-coset projects onto an
$H_0$-coset and $\Gamma_f$ has only one point over each input.
Set $S_2=\sum_i p_i^2$.  Counting pairs in the same coset gives
\[
 \sum_{z\in K_f}r_{\Gamma_f}(z)=N^2S_2,
 \qquad \sum_zr_{\Gamma_f}(z)=N^2.
\]
The bounds $r\le N$ on $K_f$ and $r\le N/2$ off $K_f$ imply
\begin{equation}
 1-\varepsilon(f)=\frac{\mathcal E(f)}{N^3}
 \le\frac{1+S_2}{2}.
 \label{gsr:en:93:rig:occupancy-energy}
\end{equation}
If $H_0$ is proper, then $h\le N/2$ and
$S_2\le\max_i p_i\le1/2$.  Thus
\eqref{gsr:en:93:rig:occupancy-energy} gives $\varepsilon(f)\ge1/4$,
proving surjectivity in the strict case.

Now suppose $H_0=G$.  Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:93:rig:occupancy-energy}
gives $S_2\ge1/2$, and in fact $S_2>1/2$.
Otherwise equality throughout that equation would force
$r(z)^2=Nr(z)$ for every $z\in K_f$.
Since $r(z)>N/2$ there and $|K_f|=N$, all these multiplicities
would be $N$, giving $S_2=1$, a contradiction.
Hence $p_*:=\max_i p_i>1/2$.  The cosets of the full graph of
$L$ correspond exactly to values of $f-L$, so there is a unique
strict majority value $c$ and $p_*=1-t$ with $t<1/2$.

Abbreviate $\varepsilon=\varepsilon(f)$ and set
\[
 a=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4\varepsilon}}2,
 \qquad \beta=1-a.
\]
By \eqref{gsr:en:93:rig:overlap-gap}, the normalized overlap
$q=r_{\Gamma_f}/N$ is at least $\beta$ on $K_f$ and at most
$a$ off $K_f$.  On these two regions, respectively,
$q(1-q)\ge\beta(1-q)$ and $q(1-q)\ge\beta q$.
Using $|K_f|=N$ and the preceding coset identities gives
\[
 \varepsilon=\frac1N\sum_zq(z)(1-q(z))
 \ge2\beta(1-S_2).
\]
All fibers except the largest have total proportion $t$, whence
$S_2\le(1-t)^2+t^2$.  Therefore
\[
 \varepsilon\ge4\beta t(1-t).
\]
As $\varepsilon=a\beta$ and $t<1/2$, solving this quadratic
inequality proves \eqref{gsr:en:93:rig:entry-bound}.  The proof includes
$a=\beta=1/2$ at the closed quarter endpoint.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:recovery}]
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:graph-entry} supplies a full homomorphism $L$, a
majority constant $c$, and an affine map $\ell=L+c$ with
disagreement proportion $t<1/6$.
If $t=0$, the conclusion is immediate.
Otherwise Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:local-cubic} gives
$\varepsilon(f)\ge\Psi_\kappa(t)$.
Both cubics are strictly increasing on $[0,1/6]$, and
$\Psi_\kappa(1/7)>1/4$, so $t<1/7$ and
$t\le D_\kappa(\varepsilon(f))$.

Two distinct affine maps into any abelian target agree on at most
$N/2$ inputs: the zero fiber of their nonzero affine difference is
either empty or a coset of the kernel of a nonzero homomorphism.
If an affine map were as close to $f$ as $\ell$, the two maps
would differ on at most $2tN<N/2$ inputs, so they would coincide.
Thus $\ell$ is the unique nearest affine map.
Its majority description is part of
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:graph-entry}, and equality is exactly the local
equality case in Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:local-cubic}.

For sharpness without target involutions, take
$f:\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z$ with values
$(0,1)$.  It respects six of the eight additive quadruples, so
$\varepsilon(f)=1/4$.  Its two closest affine maps are the two
corresponding constants, each at distance $1/2$.
For the class with target involutions, take
$f:\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$ with values
$(0,0,1,1)$.  Its four derivative collision counts are
$16,8,16,8$, giving energy $48$ and again defect $1/4$.
Each of the four affine maps has distance $1/2$.
Lifting either example through a product projection preserves
the normalized defect and gives the same obstruction on
arbitrarily large domains.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The complete obstruction at defect one quarter}

\begin{theorem}[Quarter-endpoint dichotomy]
\label{gsr:en:93:rig:endpoint}
Suppose $\varepsilon(f)=1/4$.  Exactly one of the following
alternatives holds.
\begin{enumerate}
 \item The subgroup $K_f$ projects onto $G$.  There is a unique
 nearest affine map and
 \[
 d(f,\operatorname{Aff})\le D_\kappa(1/4).
 \]
 \item The subgroup $K_f$ is the graph of a homomorphism
 $L:H_0\to W$ on an index-two subgroup $H_0<G$, and
 $\Gamma_f$ is the disjoint union of two $K_f$-cosets.
 Their difference in $(G\times W)/K_f$ has order greater
 than two, or infinite order.  Every global affine map agrees
 with $f$ on at most $N/2$ inputs.
\end{enumerate}
Conversely, every graph satisfying the description in the second
alternative has defect $1/4$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If the projection of $K_f$ is all of $G$, the entry bound in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:graph-entry}, Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:local-cubic},
and affine separation prove the first alternative exactly as in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:recovery}.

If the projection is proper, use the notation in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:graph-entry}.  Then
\[
 \frac34\le\frac{1+S_2}{2}\le\frac34.
\]
Thus $S_2=1/2$.  Since $S_2\le h/N\le1/2$, one has
$h=N/2$.  Moreover each positive occupancy must equal $1/2$:
the equality $\sum_i p_i^2=(1/2)\sum_i p_i$ forces
$p_i(1/2-p_i)=0$ for every $i$.
There are exactly two occupied cosets, and both are full.

If their quotient difference had order two, their union would
itself be a subgroup coset and would have energy $N^3$,
contrary to the hypothesis.  For every other possible order,
the autocorrelation is $N$ on $K_f$, $N/2$ on each of the two
distinct signed difference cosets, and zero elsewhere.
Its energy is $6(N/2)^3=3N^3/4$, proving the converse.

For the agreement assertion, compare $f$ with an affine map
$c+M$ on $G$.  The restriction of $f$ to each $H_0$-coset has
the same homomorphism part $L$.
If $L-M|_{H_0}$ is nonzero, its finite image has cardinality
$q\ge2$.  On either half-coset there are at most
$|H_0|/q$ agreements, so there are at most $N/2$ in total.
If that difference is zero, either every point or no point of
each half-coset agrees.  Agreement on both would make $f$
affine and give energy $N^3$.  Thus agreement is again at most
$N/2$.  The two alternatives are mutually exclusive because
the first has distance below $1/7$, whereas the second has
distance at least $1/2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The no-involution endpoint in global coordinates]
\label{gsr:en:93:rig:endpoint-odd}
Suppose $W$ has no nonzero involution.
The second alternative of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:endpoint} is
equivalent to
\begin{equation}
 f=\ell+b1_{x_0+H_0},\qquad [G:H_0]=2,\quad b\ne0,
 \label{gsr:en:93:rig:binary-boundary}
\end{equation}
for a global affine map $\ell$.
Exactly $\ell$ and $\ell+b$ are nearest affine maps, both at
distance $1/2$; every other affine map agrees with $f$ on at
most $N/3$ inputs.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Let $L:H_0\to W$ be the homomorphism in the second alternative
and choose $x_0\notin H_0$.
Multiplication by two is injective, hence bijective, on the
finite group $L(H_0)$.  Choose $v\in L(H_0)$ with
$2v=L(2x_0)$.  Define
\[
 M(h)=L(h),\qquad M(x_0+h)=v+L(h)\qquad(h\in H_0).
\]
The identity $2v=L(2x_0)$ checks additivity when both inputs
are outside $H_0$; the other cases follow from additivity of
$L$.  Thus $M$ is a global homomorphism extending $L$.
Subtract $M$ and the constant on the first half-coset.
The remaining function is zero on $H_0$ and has one value
$b\ne0$ on its complement, giving \eqref{gsr:en:93:rig:binary-boundary}.
The converse is also immediate from the derivative counts,
or from Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:one-color} with $t=1/2$ and coset support.

An affine competitor whose homomorphism restriction to $H_0$
differs from $L$ has a nonzero image of size at least three,
since $W$ has no involution.  The preceding proof then bounds
its agreement by $N/3$.
If the restriction agrees, the global homomorphism must equal
$M$: their difference factors through $G/H_0$, of order two,
and no such nonzero map to $W$ exists.
Only the two constants in \eqref{gsr:en:93:rig:binary-boundary} then
give any agreements.  They each give exactly $N/2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why the target hypothesis cannot be dropped]
\label{gsr:en:93:rig:nonextension}
The endpoint function $(0,0,1,1)$ from
$\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z$ to $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$ has
$L(2)=1$ on $H_0=\{0,2\}$.
This homomorphism does not extend to the whole domain, since
every homomorphism to $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$ vanishes at $2$.
It is therefore essential to retain the graph-subgroup
description in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:endpoint} for general targets.
There are four nearest affine maps in this example, rather
than the two in Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:endpoint-odd}.
\end{remark}

\subsection{The exact non-affine maximum for all orders at least thirteen}

\begin{theorem}[Optimal universal cutoff]
\label{gsr:en:93:rig:thirteen}
Let $W$ be nontrivial abelian and $G$ finite abelian of order
$N\ge13$.  Every non-affine map $f:G\to W$ satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal E(f)\le
 N^3-4N^2+(10+2\kappa)N-(6+2\kappa).
 \label{gsr:en:93:rig:maximum}
\end{equation}
Equality holds exactly for an affine map modified at one
point by a nonzero value; that value must have order two
when $\kappa=1$.
The universal cutoff thirteen is optimal both for targets
without involutions and for targets containing involutions.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For $N\ge14$,
\[
 \Psi_\kappa(1/N)\le\Psi_0(1/14)
 =\frac{650}{2744}<\frac14.
\]
If a non-affine map has energy at least the right side of
\eqref{gsr:en:93:rig:maximum}, Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:recovery} gives
$d(f,\operatorname{Aff})\le1/N$.
The distance of a non-affine map is an integer multiple of
$1/N$ and is positive, so the map is a one-point modification.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:one-color} gives its exact energy and proves
the asserted equality description.
The same argument treats $N=13$, $\kappa=1$, since
$\Psi_1(1/13)=528/2197<1/4$.

It remains to treat $N=13$ without target involutions.
The domain is then cyclic of prime order.
Suppose
\[
 \mathcal E(f)\ge1645=13^3-4\cdot13^2+10\cdot13-6,
 \qquad 13^3-\mathcal E(f)\le552.
\]
Put $A=\Gamma_f$ and $K=\{z:r_A(z)\ge7\}$.
We first show that $K$ is a subgroup, even though the defect
bound here is slightly greater than $1/4$.
If closure under differences failed, the proof of
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:majority-subgroup} would give attained integer
multiplicities $c,b$ with
\[
 1\le c\le6,\qquad 7\le b\le(13+c)/2.
\]
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:multilevel} would then imply
\begin{equation}
 13^3-E(A)
 \ge\frac{13^3-c^3-(b-c)^3-(13-b)^3}{3}
 \ge588.
 \label{gsr:en:93:rig:thirteen-closure-certificate}
\end{equation}
For the last comparison, fix $c$.
The expression on the right is nondecreasing in $b$ over
the indicated interval, so it is minimized at $b=7$.
The convex expression $c^3+(7-c)^3$ on $1\le c\le6$
is maximized at $c=1$ or $6$.  Its value, after adding
$6^3$, is $433$, and $(2197-433)/3=588$.
This contradicts the available defect $552$.

As before, $K$ has trivial vertical intersection.
Its projection is a subgroup of $\mathbb Z/13\mathbb Z$,
so it is either trivial or the full group.
If $K=\{0\}$, every nonzero difference multiplicity is
at most six and
\[
 E(A)\le13^2+6(13^2-13)=1105<1645,
\]
which is impossible.
Thus $K$ is the graph of a global homomorphism $L$.
Let $c_w$ be the fiber cardinalities of $f-L$.
Using $r_A\le13$ on $K$ and $r_A\le6$ outside it gives
\begin{equation}
 E(A)\le7\sum_wc_w^2+6\cdot13^2.
 \label{gsr:en:93:rig:thirteen-fiber-bound}
\end{equation}
If every fiber has size at most eight, convexity of the square
function under $\sum_wc_w=13$ yields
$\sum_wc_w^2\le8^2+5^2=89$.
Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:93:rig:thirteen-fiber-bound} would give
$E(A)\le7\cdot89+1014=1637<1645$.
Hence a fiber has size at least nine.
After subtracting its affine map, the error support has
cardinality $s\le4$, with $s/13\le4/13<1/3$.

Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:local-cubic} now applies.
For the four possible positive support sizes its lower
bounds on the unnormalized defect are
\[
 \begin{array}{c|rrrr}
  s&1&2&3&4\\ \hline
  13^3\Psi_0(s/13)&552&880&1020&1008.
 \end{array}
\]
All cases $s=2,3,4$ contradict defect at most $552$.
The non-affine assumption excludes $s=0$, so $s=1$.
The one-point formula completes the proof of
\eqref{gsr:en:93:rig:maximum} and its equality case at order thirteen.

For optimality in the no-involution class, take
$f:\mathbb Z/12\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z$
equal to zero on the even inputs and one on the odd inputs.
Its energy is $1296$, whereas the proposed one-point bound
at $N=12$ would be $1266$.
For targets with an involution, take
$f:\mathbb Z/12\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$ with
$f(x)=\lfloor(x\bmod4)/2\rfloor$.
Its energy is also $1296$, exceeding the corresponding
one-point value $1288$.
Both are quotient lifts of the endpoint examples in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:recovery}, and both are non-affine.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 82--94]
\emph{This settles the cutoff} of source~11's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:11:thm:maingap} ($N\ge34$), source~59's Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:59:cor:affine-sixteen} ($N\ge16$ without involutions) and source~67's Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:67:cthree:nonaffine-gap} ($N\ge13$ for elementary abelian $3$-targets), and answers source~59's Question~\ref{gsr:fz:59:q:small-domains} at $13$, $14$, $15$. \emph{Checked at the write}: the maximum over all non-affine $\Z/13\Z\to\Z/2\Z$ is $1669=13^3-4\cdot13^2+12\cdot13-8$ (exhaustive); at $N=12$ the formula fails for both kinds of target ($1296>1288$ for $(0,0,1,1,\ldots)$ into $\Z/2\Z$; $1296>1266$ for the index-two coset indicator into $\Z/3\Z$), so $13$ is optimal for both.
\end{writenote}

\subsection{Partial domains and Proposition 6.1}

The next consequence retains the ambient normalization in the
Gowers interface.  It does not assume that a sparse graph of
energy close to $|B|^3$ extends to the full domain.

\begin{corollary}[Partial-domain recovery]
\label{gsr:en:93:rig:partial}
Let $B\subseteq G$ and $\phi:B\to W$, and suppose
\[
 E(\Gamma_\phi)\ge(1-\varepsilon)N^3,
 \qquad 0\le\varepsilon<1/4.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 |B|\ge(1-\varepsilon)^{1/3}N,
 \label{gsr:en:93:rig:partial-size}
\end{equation}
and there is a unique nearest global affine map on $B$.
It disagrees with $\phi$ on at most $D_\kappa(\varepsilon)N$
points of $B$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The elementary bound $E(\Gamma_\phi)\le|B|^3$ gives
\eqref{gsr:en:93:rig:partial-size}.
Extend $\phi$ arbitrarily to a map $f:G\to W$.
Every respected partial quadruple remains respected, so
$\varepsilon(f)\le\varepsilon$.
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:recovery}, and monotonicity of $D_\kappa$,
give an affine map with at most $D_\kappa(\varepsilon)N$
errors on $B$.

Two global affine maps meeting this error bound agree on
at least $|B|-2D_\kappa(\varepsilon)N$ inputs.
Since $(3/4)^{1/3}>6/7$ and $D_\kappa(\varepsilon)<1/7$,
this number is greater than $4N/7>N/2$.
Affine separation forces the two maps to coincide.
In particular, the result is independent of the arbitrary
completion, and any affine map minimizing the error on
$B$ is this same map.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A larger high-correlation range in Proposition 6.1]
\label{gsr:en:93:rig:gowers}
Let $G=W=\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$, let $F:G\to\mathbb C$
satisfy $|F|\le1$, and let $\phi:B\to W$ for $B\subseteq G$.
Use
\[
 \partial_hF(x)=F(x)\overline{F(x-h)},\qquad
 \widehat u(r)=\sum_{x\in G}u(x)e^{-2\pi i rx/N}.
\]
Suppose $\alpha>0$ and
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{h\in B}|\widehat{\partial_hF}(\phi(h))|^2
 \ge\alpha N^3,
 \qquad \alpha^4>3/4.
 \label{gsr:en:93:rig:gowers-hypothesis}
\end{equation}
Then $\phi$ has a unique nearest global affine map on $B$,
with at most
\[
 D_\kappa(1-\alpha^4)N
\]
disagreements there, and $|B|\ge\alpha N$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Each squared Fourier coefficient is at most $N^2$, so the hypothesis gives
$|B|\ge\alpha N$ and hence $\alpha\le1$.
Gowers's Proposition~6.1 \cite{gowers} gives
$E(\Gamma_\phi)\ge\alpha^4N^3$.
Apply Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:partial} with
$\varepsilon=1-\alpha^4$.
\end{proof}

This improves the sufficient high-correlation condition from
$\alpha^4>7/9$ in \cite{srcfiftynine}, and from the older
$\alpha^4>8/9$ application in \cite{srceleven}, to
$\alpha^4>3/4$.
It preserves the fourth power in Proposition~6.1 and concerns its
high-agreement endpoint.  No improved global bound in
Szemer\'edi's theorem follows merely from this substitution.
The underlying test here is four-point affine consistency;
the classical three-point homomorphism test has a different
defect parameter and threshold.

\subsection{Deterministic recovery and a corruption certificate}

\begin{proposition}[A deterministic decoder]
\label{gsr:en:93:rig:decoder}
Assume the full input table of $f$ is given, together with
constant-time group operations, equality tests, and table access.
Under $\varepsilon(f)<1/4$, the affine map in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:recovery} can be recovered with $O(N^2)$
group operations and equality tests, storing $O(N)$ group
elements.  No hashing or order relation on $W$ is required.

Moreover, if $f'$ is obtained by changing at most $\sigma N$
values of $f$, and
\begin{equation}
 D_\kappa(\varepsilon(f))+\sigma<1/4,
 \label{gsr:en:93:rig:corruption-margin}
\end{equation}
the same decoder applied to $f'$ recovers the original affine
map, whether or not $\varepsilon(f')<1/4$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For each $h\in G$, run the Boyer--Moore pair-cancellation
majority pass on the sequence
$(f(x+h)-f(x))_{x\in G}$, then make a second pass to verify
that its candidate occurs more than $N/2$ times.
The first pass maintains one candidate and a counter,
discarding pairs of unequal values; a strict majority cannot
be eliminated by such pair cancellations.
The verified candidate is $L(h)$ by
\eqref{gsr:en:93:rig:derivative-majority}.
Store these $N$ values and use the same two-pass procedure
on $f(x)-L(x)$ to recover and verify the constant part.
Each derivative row costs $O(N)$ operations and equality
tests with constant additional storage; the residual row
costs $O(N)$.  This proves the stated complexity.

For robustness, the original affine map $\ell=L+c$ differs
from $f'$ on fewer than $N/4$ inputs by
\eqref{gsr:en:93:rig:corruption-margin}.
For any fixed $h$, a derivative entry can differ from $L(h)$
only if $x$ or $x+h$ is one of those erroneous inputs.
Fewer than $N/2$ derivative entries are therefore wrong.
Every derivative row still has strict majority $L(h)$,
and the residual row still has strict majority $c$.
The same verified pair-cancellation procedure recovers
$\ell$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Computational and formal status]
The accompanying exact verifier checks the majority subgroup,
the recovery and endpoint statements, and the order-thirteen
scalar comparisons.  It includes exhaustive small-domain maps
and specified larger sparse-error examples, with its precise
scope recorded in the verification output.
These computations supplement the proofs above; they are not
an exhaustive classification in unrestricted sizes and do not
constitute Lean verification.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[Recovery in given product coordinates]
\label{gsr:en:93:rig:coordinate-decoder}
Under the hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:decoder}, if the domain is
supplied in coordinates $G=\prod_{i=1}^r\Z/n_i\Z$, with $r\ge1$ and
$n_i\ge2$, the decoder can use
$O(Nr)$ group operations and equality tests and $O(N)$ stored group
elements. In particular this is $O(N\log N)$.
The same conclusion holds under the corruption hypothesis of
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:decoder}.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Compute and verify derivative majorities only for the $r$ coordinate
generators. They give the values of the homomorphism already guaranteed
by Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:recovery}, or of the original homomorphism under
the corruption certificate. Precompute the $n_i$ successive multiples
of each generator image, then evaluate $L(x)$ using at most $r$
additions per input. Finally find and verify the majority of $f-L$.
The derivative passes cost $O(Nr)$; precomputation costs
$O(\sum_i n_i)$; evaluating all inputs costs $O(Nr)$.
For $n_i\ge2$, $\sum_i n_i\le N$ (including the one-factor case),
and $r\le\log_2N$. The stated storage and time bounds follow.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{An exact comparison for a single cyclic direction\srctag{90}}]{An exact comparison for a single cyclic direction}\label{gsr:en:90:sec:d6}
\srcnote{90}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:en:90:sec:directional}

Let $C_N=\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$, let $W$ be an abelian group, and let
$f:C_N\to W$. The target need not be finite: every distribution used below
has finite support. Write
\[
 d_h(f)=\Pr_{x,y\in C_N}
 [f(x+h)-f(x)\ne f(y+h)-f(y)],
 \qquad
 D(f)=\frac1N\sum_{h\in C_N}d_h(f).
\]
All variables displayed without a specified law are uniform and independent.
Then $d_{-h}(f)=d_h(f)$ and $d_0(f)=0$. Thus $d_1(f)$ is the failure
probability when the sampled direction is uniformly chosen from
$\{1,-1\}$. It is a four-query test and does not involve the anchored
three-query BLR equation.

For the graph $\Gamma_f=\{(x,f(x)):x\in C_N\}$, one has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:90:dir:eq:energy}
 E(\Gamma_f)=N^3(1-D(f)).
\end{equation}
Indeed, an additive quadruple can be parameterized by
$(x+h,y,x,y+h)$, and its image is additive exactly when the two
displayed derivatives agree. This is the full-domain graph-energy
interface of Gowers' Lemma~6.2~\cite{gowers}.

\begin{theorem}[Sharp amplification from one cyclic direction]
\label{gsr:en:90:thm:cycle}
Suppose $N\ge12$. Then every map $f:C_N\to W$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:90:dir:eq:sharpcycle}
 \boxed{D(f)\le \frac{N+1}{6}\,d_1(f).}
\end{equation}
Equality holds precisely in the following cases:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $f$ is affine, so both sides vanish;
\item the cyclic increment sequence $f(i+1)-f(i)$ has $N-1$ copies of
some $a\in W$ and one copy of $-(N-1)a$, where $Na\ne0$.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently $(N+1)/6$ is the optimal constant uniformly over abelian
targets. For any fixed target containing an $a$ with $Na\ne0$, it is
also the optimal constant for that target.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 82--94]
\emph{Checked at the write} (\file{verify13.py}): exhaustively for all maps $C_{12},C_{13},C_{14}\to C_2$ with $f(0)=0$, no violation; non-affine equality occurs only for $N=13$ ($13$ maps with $f(0)=0$), and not when $N$ annihilates the target, as the equality classification says. The statistic is a directional collision rate, not source~93's graph-energy defect (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:quarter}).
\end{writenote}

The hypothesis $N\ge12$ is the range of the proof below; no claim is
made that twelve is the least possible cutoff. In particular, sharpness
does not require $W$ to have characteristic zero: $W=C_p$ works whenever
$p\nmid N$. If $NW=0$, the second equality case is impossible.

\subsection{Two exact circular-window probabilities}

For $x\in C_N$ and $0\le h<N$, put
\[
 I_{x,h}=\{x,x+1,\ldots,x+h-1\}\subset C_N.
\]
For a position $i$, let $B_i$ be the event that $i$ belongs to exactly
one of $I_{x,h}$ and $I_{y,h}$, where $x,y,h$ are independent and uniform.

\begin{lemma}[Window marginals and pair intersections]
\label{gsr:en:90:dir:lem:windows}
For every $N\ge2$ and every position $i$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:90:dir:eq:singlewindow}
 \Pr(B_i)=P_N:=\frac{N^2-1}{3N^2}.
\end{equation}
For two distinct positions at cyclic separation $1\le d\le N/2$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:90:dir:eq:pairwindow}
 \Pr(B_i\cap B_j)=J_N(d):=
 \frac{N^3-6dN^2+18d^2N-16d^3+4d-N}{3N^3}
 \ge\frac18.
\end{equation}
Equality in the last inequality occurs exactly when $4\mid N$ and
$d=N/4$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For fixed $h$, a given position belongs to a random length-$h$ window
with probability $h/N$. Hence
\[
 \Pr(B_i\mid h)=\frac{2h(N-h)}{N^2}.
\]
Averaging and using
$\sum_{h=0}^{N-1}h(N-h)=N(N^2-1)/6$ proves
\eqref{gsr:en:90:dir:eq:singlewindow}.

For the pair, translate the positions to $0,d$ with $1\le d\le N/2$.
For a single uniform window, the probabilities of the membership
patterns $11,10,01,00$ are respectively
\[
 r_h,\quad h/N-r_h,\quad h/N-r_h,\quad 1-2h/N+r_h,
 \qquad
 r_h=\frac{(h-d)_++(h-(N-d))_+}{N}.
\]
Both disagreement events occur precisely when the two windows have
complementary membership patterns. Their conditional probability is
\[
 2r_h(1-2h/N+r_h)+2(h/N-r_h)^2.
\]
This equals $2h^2/N^2$ for $0\le h<d$,
$2((h-d)(N-h-d)+d^2)/N^2$ for $d\le h\le N-d$, and
$2(N-h)^2/N^2$ for $N-d<h<N$. Summing these three quadratic pieces gives
\eqref{gsr:en:90:dir:eq:pairwindow}.

For the lower bound put $z=4d-N$. Direct factorization gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:90:dir:eq:pairfactor}
 J_N(d)-\frac18
 =\frac{z^2(3N-2z)+8z}{24N^3}.
\end{equation}
If $z\ge0$, then $z\le N$ and $3N-2z\ge N$, so the expression is
nonnegative and vanishes only at $z=0$. If $z<0$, write $z=-m$ with
the positive integer $m$. The numerator becomes
$m(m(3N+2m)-8)$, which is strictly positive for $N\ge3$.
The remaining case $N=2,d=1$ gives $J_2(1)=1/4$ directly.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[A union estimate with pair overlap]
\label{gsr:en:90:dir:lem:union}
For $s\ge1$ distinct marked positions,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:90:dir:eq:union}
 \Pr\left(\bigcup_{i\in S} B_i\right)
 \le sP_N-\frac{s-1}{8}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $K$ count the events $B_i$ that occur. For $0\le K\le s$,
\[
 \mathbf1_{K>0}\le K-\frac{2}{s}\binom K2.
\]
For $1\le K\le s$ the right-hand side minus one is
$(K-1)(s-K)/s\ge0$; at $K=0$ both sides vanish. Taking expectations
and applying Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:90:dir:lem:windows} gives
\[
 \Pr(K>0)\le sP_N-\frac2s\binom{s}{2}\frac18
 =sP_N-\frac{s-1}{8}.
\]
\end{proof}

\subsection{Proof of the sharp comparison and all equality cases}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:90:thm:cycle}]
Put $a_i=f(i+1)-f(i)$ and let $n_w=|\{i:a_i=w\}|$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:90:dir:eq:histogram}
 d_1(f)=1-\frac1{N^2}\sum_w n_w^2.
\end{equation}
If all increments equal $a$, their sum is zero, so $Na=0$ and
$f(i)=f(0)+ia$ is affine. Suppose the increments are not constant.

First assume $\max_w n_w\le N/2$. Since
$\sum_w n_w^2\le(\max_w n_w)\sum_w n_w\le N^2/2$, we have
$d_1(f)\ge1/2$. Consequently
$((N+1)/6)d_1(f)\ge13/12>1\ge D(f)$.

Otherwise there is a unique majority increment $a$. Let $S$ be its
exceptional positions and write $s=|S|$, so $1\le s<N/2$. The
histogram identity gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:90:dir:eq:histlower}
 d_1(f)\ge\frac{2s(N-s)}{N^2},
\end{equation}
because all minority class sizes sum to $s$ and their squares sum to
at most $s^2$. For fixed $h$,
\[
 f(x+h)-f(x)=ha+\sum_{i\in I_{x,h}\cap S}(a_i-a).
\]
If none of the $B_i$, $i\in S$, occurs, the exceptional increments
included by the two windows are identical, and the derivatives agree.
Thus Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:90:dir:lem:union} implies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:90:dir:eq:minoritybound}
 D(f)\le s\frac{N^2-1}{3N^2}-\frac{s-1}{8}.
\end{equation}

For $2\le s\le4$, the difference between the right-hand side of
\eqref{gsr:en:90:dir:eq:minoritybound} and
$((N+1)/6)\,2s(N-s)/N^2$ is
\[
 (s-1)\left(\frac{s(N+1)}{3N^2}-\frac18\right)<0.
\]
Indeed $8s(N+1)\le32(N+1)<3N^2$ for $N\ge12$; at $N=12$ the final
integer comparison is $416<432$, and the difference increases
thereafter. These cases satisfy \eqref{gsr:en:90:dir:eq:sharpcycle} strictly.

For $s\ge5$, use $s<N/2$ and the monotonicity of $s(N-s)$ on
$[0,N/2]$. Then
\[
 \frac{N+1}{6}\,d_1(f)
 \ge\frac{5(N+1)(N-5)}{3N^2}>1\ge D(f).
\]
The strict inequality is equivalent to
$2N^2-20N-25>0$, which holds for every $N\ge12$.

It remains to consider $s=1$. Write the exceptional increment as
$a+u$, with $u\ne0$. Since the increments sum to zero, $Na+u=0$,
so $u=-Na$ and $Na\ne0$. The length-$h$ derivative takes exactly two
distinct values, $ha$ and $ha+u$, with probabilities
$(N-h)/N$ and $h/N$. Therefore
\[
 d_h(f)=\frac{2h(N-h)}{N^2},\qquad
 d_1(f)=\frac{2(N-1)}{N^2},\qquad
 D(f)=\frac{N^2-1}{3N^2}
 =\frac{N+1}{6}d_1(f).
\]
This proves the inequality, sharpness, and the equality classification.
\end{proof}

After rotating the exceptional increment to the edge from $N-1$ to
$0$, every non-affine equality case has the explicit form
\[
 f(j)=b+ja,\qquad 0\le j<N,\qquad Na\ne0.
\]
The formula uses these integer representatives; it is not an affine
map of $C_N$. This distinction is precisely the obstruction detected
by the equality case.

\subsection{Why generic expansion loses an exact factor}

For a symmetric probability measure $\mu$ on a finite abelian group,
define the balanced cut constant
\[
 \beta(\mu)=\min_{\varnothing\ne A\ne G}
 \frac{\Pr_{x\in G,h\sim\mu}[x\in A,\ x+h\notin A]}
 {( |A|/|G|)(1-|A|/|G|)}.
\]
For a finite-valued $g$, sum the defining cut inequality over its
fibers. This proves
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:90:dir:eq:categorical}
 \Pr_{x,h\sim\mu}[g(x+h)\ne g(x)]
 \ge\beta(\mu)\Pr_{x,y}[g(x)\ne g(y)].
\end{equation}
The constant is optimal for unrestricted categorical functions, by
taking $g$ to be the indicator of a minimizing cut.

For the nearest-neighbor law on $C_N$, every nontrivial cut has at
least two boundary edges, so
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:90:dir:eq:cyclecut}
 \beta(\tfrac12(\delta_1+\delta_{-1}))
 =\frac{N}{\lfloor N^2/4\rfloor}.
\end{equation}
Intervals with $\lfloor N/2\rfloor$ points attain equality.
For each $t$, apply \eqref{gsr:en:90:dir:eq:categorical} to
$g_t(x)=f(x+t)-f(x)$ and then average over $t$. One obtains only
\[
 D(f)\le\frac{\lfloor N^2/4\rfloor}{N}d_1(f).
\]
The sharp coefficient in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:90:thm:cycle} improves the
limiting coefficient from $1/4$ to $1/6$. The improvement uses that the
fiber maps arise as derivatives of a single cyclic function. It is
not an improvement to the categorical cut inequality itself.
The ordinary spectral gap $1-\cos(2\pi/N)$ would give the much weaker
quadratic-in-$N$ coefficient. Expander-based affine testing is
classical; see Shpilka--Wigderson~\cite[Theorems~1.4--1.5]{shpilkawigderson}.
The present exact fixed-cycle coefficient and its equality cases
should be distinguished from that general testing principle.


\subsection{An exact twelve-point example}

Take $N=12$, $W=C_5$, and $f(j)=j\bmod5$ for the representatives
$0\le j<12$. Eleven cyclic increments equal $1$, while the increment
from $11$ to $0$ equals $-11\equiv4\pmod5$. Hence
\[
 d_1(f)=\frac{11}{72},\qquad
 D(f)=\frac{143}{432},\qquad
 \frac{D(f)}{d_1(f)}=\frac{13}{6}.
\]
There are exactly $22$ rejected ordered pairs among the $12^2$
queries at direction one and $572$ rejected configurations among
all $12^3$ uniformly sampled parallelograms. Thus
$E(\Gamma_f)=1156$. The sharp comparison gives the exact defect
$143/432$, while the categorical cut comparison gives only
$D(f)\le11/24$.

The example also explains why a claim of global affine recovery
cannot be inferred merely from the size of the factor in
\eqref{gsr:en:90:dir:eq:sharpcycle}. On the target $\mathbb Z$, the same
representative formula $f(j)=j$ has distance $1-1/N$ from every
nearest affine map, since all homomorphisms $C_N\to\mathbb Z$ vanish.
Yet $D(f)=(N^2-1)/(3N^2)<1/3$. Any separate recovery theorem must
retain its own domain, target, and defect-range hypotheses.

\subsection{What the theorem changes at the graph interface}

Combining \eqref{gsr:en:90:dir:eq:energy} and \eqref{gsr:en:90:dir:eq:sharpcycle} gives
\[
 E(\Gamma_f)\ge
 N^3\left(1-\frac{N+1}{6}d_1(f)\right).
\]
Thus a specified one-direction derivative collision estimate can
certify an explicit amount of full additive graph energy, with the
optimal all-target loss for $N\ge12$. The number of points queried
remains four. The theorem changes the distribution of the direction
and the exact conversion constant; it does not establish sparse-domain
extraction or a new quantitative Szemer\'edi bound.

For a different generating direction $u\in C_N$, multiplication by
$u$ is a permutation of $C_N$, so the identical argument gives
$D(f)\le((N+1)/6)d_u(f)$. Averaging proves the same comparison for any
probability law supported on generating directions. If two distinct
unoriented generating directions receive positive mass, non-affine
equality is impossible: a sawtooth equality case for one direction
has derivative multiplicities $k,N-k$ in the other, where
$2\le k\le N-2$, and so cannot have the required multiplicities
$N-1,1$ there. No claim that $(N+1)/6$ remains the optimal coefficient
for each such multi-direction law is made.

The introduction is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:88:sec:d1}.
