\section[{Definitions and normalization\srctag{88}}]{Definitions and normalization}\label{gsr:en:88:sec:d2}
\srcnote{88}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:en:88:sec:notation}

\subsection{Coordinate groups and the product property}

Let $K_1,\ldots,K_k$ be finite abelian groups, written additively, and
put $X=\prod_{j=1}^kK_j$ and $M=|X|$.
Let $V$ be any abelian group and let $\phi:B\to V$ be a partial map,
where $B\subseteq X$. A coordinate-$j$ restriction is the function of
$t\in K_j$ obtained by fixing all coordinates except the $j$th, on
the set where that coordinate line meets $B$.

\begin{definition}[Coordinate product property]
\label{gsr:en:88:def:PP}
Fix $0<\gamma_j\le1$ for each coordinate.
We say that $\phi$ has these product-property parameters if, for every
coordinate $j$, every positive integer $p$, every family of $p$
coordinate-$j$ restrictions $\psi_1,\ldots,\psi_p$, every common domain
$E\subseteq K_j$, and every $\theta:E\to[0,\infty)$,
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{\substack{a,b,c,d\in E\,;\ a+b=c+d\\
        \psi_i(a)+\psi_i(b)=\psi_i(c)+\psi_i(d)\ (1\le i\le p)}}
 \theta(a)\theta(b)\theta(c)\theta(d)
 \ge \frac{\gamma_j^{8p}}{|K_j|}
       \left(\sum_{t\in E}\theta(t)\right)^4.
 \label{gsr:en:88:eq:PP}
\end{equation}
When every parameter equals $\gamma$, we write $\PP_\gamma$.
Repeated restrictions are allowed.
\end{definition}

The property is inherited by restriction of the domain and by passage
to a coordinate fibre. This follows directly: a family of restrictions
of the smaller map, on a common smaller domain, is still an allowed
family for the original map. We will only need finitely many family
sizes $p$, specified by the proofs.

Definition~\ref{gsr:en:88:def:PP} agrees with Gowers' product property when all
coordinate and value groups are $\Z/N\Z$. In the original proof,
Lemmas~14.2 and~14.3 supply the property from large Fourier coefficients
of suitable derivative functions \cite{gowers}. Our counting
theorems require the product property as stated; they do not add a
primality, equal-order, or torsion-free assumption.

\begin{lemma}[A nonvacuous universal parameter]
\label{gsr:en:88:lem:weak-PP}
If $V$ is finite of cardinality $v$, every partial map has
$\PP_{v^{-1/8}}$. A constant map has $\PP_1$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For the chosen restrictions place mass $\theta(t)$ at
$(t,\psi_1(t),\ldots,\psi_p(t))\in K_j\times V^p$ and call the
resulting measure $\mu$. The left side of \eqref{gsr:en:88:eq:PP} is
$\sum_z(\mu*\mu)(z)^2$. Cauchy--Schwarz bounds it below by
$|K_j|^{-1}v^{-p}(\sum\theta)^4$.
If the map is constant, the value equations are automatic and the
same proof uses only $K_j$. This elementary observation also appears
in the prior collision-amplification chapter \cite{srcfifteen}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Cubes, configurations, and vertex weights}

For $x,h\in X$ and $\omega\in\{0,1\}^k$, write
$x+\omega\odot h=(x_j+\omega_jh_j)_{j=1}^k$.
The ordered axis cube with base $x$ and side $h$ has these vertices.
It is admissible if all its vertices lie in $B$; its mixed label is
\begin{equation}
 D_h\phi(x)=\sum_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^k}
                  (-1)^{|\omega|}\phi(x+\omega\odot h).
 \label{gsr:en:88:eq:mixed-label}
\end{equation}
A parallel cube pair is the ordered triple $(x,y,h)\in X^3$.
It is respected if both constituent cubes are admissible and
$D_h\phi(x)=D_h\phi(y)$.

A configuration is the ordered triple $(x,g,h)\in X^3$ with vertices
$x+\epsilon\odot g+\eta\odot h$, for
$\epsilon,\eta\in\{0,1\}^k$.
It is respected if all its vertices lie in $B$ and, after fixing every
local state outside coordinate $j$, its four values in that coordinate
satisfy
\begin{equation}
 z_{00}+z_{11}=z_{10}+z_{01}.
 \label{gsr:en:88:eq:face-relation}
\end{equation}
This condition is imposed in every coordinate and at every choice of
the other local states.

For $w:X\to[0,\infty)$ supported on $B$, define
\begin{align}
 \mathcal F_k(w)&=
 \sum_{\substack{(x,g,h)\in X^3\\\text{configuration respected}}}
 \prod_{\epsilon,\eta\in\{0,1\}^k}
 w(x+\epsilon\odot g+\eta\odot h),
 \label{gsr:en:88:eq:weighted-configuration}\\
 \mathcal C_k(w)&=
 \sum_{\substack{(x,y,h)\in X^3\\\text{cube pair respected}}}
 \prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^k}
 w(x+\omega\odot h)w(y+\omega\odot h).
 \label{gsr:en:88:eq:weighted-pair}
\end{align}
Thus $\mathcal F_k=\mathcal F_k(\mathbf1_B)$ and
$\mathcal C_k=\mathcal C_k(\mathbf1_B)$ are ordinary counts.
The normalized average $\E_X$ always gives each element of $X$ mass
$M^{-1}$.

All parameters are ordered, and zero sides and repeated physical
vertices are retained. In a weighted count, a repeated vertex
contributes once for each occurrence. This convention is essential:
the two weighted constructions in Section~\ref{gsr:en:88:sec:counting} compare
products with their multiplicities. No division by a number of cube
symmetries or by a factorial is made anywhere.

For induction, the zero-coordinate product is a singleton.
Its configuration weight is $\mathcal F_0(w)=w$ and its pair weight
is $\mathcal C_0(w)=w^2$. These conventions give the correct base
cases without any exception to the weighted formulas.


% ===== RANK =====

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{An exact basis for the configuration constraints\srctag{88}}]{An exact basis for the configuration constraints}\label{gsr:en:88:sec:d3}
\srcnote{88}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:en:88:rank:section}
\label{gsr:en:88:sec:rank}

The product-property argument pays for a list of coordinate-line
restrictions. Some of those restrictions are already integer linear
combinations of others on the common domain under consideration.
The appropriate count is therefore the number of vertex values needed
to specify a labeling satisfying the previously imposed face relations.
We determine that count over arbitrary abelian value groups. Working
integrally is useful: a rank computation over a field alone would not
justify the same conclusion in targets with torsion.

\subsection{Product grids with one relation in each coordinate}

Let $S_1,\ldots,S_k$ be finite sets, with $|S_i|=q_i\ge2$.
For each $i$, fix integers $r_{i,s}$, $s\in S_i$, and a distinguished
symbol $p_i\in S_i$ such that
\[
 r_{i,p_i}=\epsilon_i\in\{1,-1\}.
\]
Set
\[
 S=\prod_{i=1}^k S_i,\qquad
 T_i=S_i\setminus\{p_i\},\qquad
 T=\prod_{i=1}^k T_i,\qquad
 D=|T|=\prod_{i=1}^k(q_i-1).
\]
An $A$-valued labeling $f:S\to A$, where $A$ is an abelian group,
is \emph{admissible} if, for every coordinate $i$ and every choice
of all its other coordinates,
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{s_i\in S_i}r_{i,s_i}
 f(s_1,\ldots,s_i,\ldots,s_k)=0.
 \label{gsr:en:88:rank:relations}
\end{equation}
Integer multiplication is interpreted as repeated group addition.
No multiplication of two elements of $A$ is used.

\begin{theorem}[Integral product-grid interpolation]
\label{gsr:en:88:rank:interpolation}
For every abelian group $A$, restriction from $S$ to $T$ is an
isomorphism from the group of admissible labelings onto $A^T$.
In particular, any prescribed values on $T$ extend uniquely.

More explicitly, for $t\in T_i$ define
\[
 c_i(s,t)=
 \begin{cases}
  1,&s=t,\\
  0,&s\in T_i\setminus\{t\},\\
  -\epsilon_i r_{i,t},&s=p_i.
 \end{cases}
\]
The extension of $b:T\to A$ is
\begin{equation}
 f(s)=\sum_{t\in T}
       \left(\prod_{i=1}^k c_i(s_i,t_i)\right)b(t).
 \label{gsr:en:88:rank:extension}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The formula agrees with $b$ at every point of $T$. For each
coordinate $i$ and $t_i\in T_i$,
\[
 \sum_{s_i\in S_i}r_{i,s_i}c_i(s_i,t_i)
 =r_{i,t_i}+\epsilon_i(-\epsilon_i r_{i,t_i})=0.
\]
Distributing the finite sums in \eqref{gsr:en:88:rank:extension} therefore
verifies \eqref{gsr:en:88:rank:relations}, so the formula gives an extension.

For uniqueness, relation \eqref{gsr:en:88:rank:relations} determines a value
whose $i$th coordinate is $p_i$ from values with the same other
coordinates and with $i$th coordinate in $T_i$:
\[
 f(s_1,\ldots,p_i,\ldots,s_k)
 =-\epsilon_i\sum_{t_i\in T_i}r_{i,t_i}
 f(s_1,\ldots,t_i,\ldots,s_k).
\]
Induction on the number of pivot coordinates of $s$ determines
every value from $b$. Both restriction and extension preserve
addition, establishing the asserted isomorphism.
\end{proof}

The isomorphism is uniform in the target group. In particular, the
same basis works for every finite abelian group, including groups
with elements of order two or three.

\subsection{Exactly how many face relations are independent}

Let $\mathbb Z^S$ have standard basis $e_s$, and let
$\mathcal R\le\mathbb Z^S$ be generated by all the formal face
relations appearing in \eqref{gsr:en:88:rank:relations}. Thus admissible
$A$-valued labelings are exactly the homomorphisms
\[
 \operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb Z^S/\mathcal R,A).
\]

\begin{theorem}[An integral basis of the relation module]
\label{gsr:en:88:rank:relation-basis}
The quotient $\mathbb Z^S/\mathcal R$ is free abelian of rank $D$,
and the classes of $e_t$, $t\in T$, form a basis. The relation
module is free of rank
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{rank}\mathcal R
 =\prod_{i=1}^kq_i-\prod_{i=1}^k(q_i-1).
 \label{gsr:en:88:rank:relation-rank}
\end{equation}
Moreover, an integral basis of $\mathcal R$ can be selected from
the original face relations, allowing multiplication by $-1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For each $s\in S\setminus T$, choose one coordinate $i(s)$ at
which $s_{i(s)}=p_{i(s)}$. Let $R_s$ be $\epsilon_{i(s)}$ times
the face relation in that coordinate with the other coordinates
fixed by $s$. Its coefficient at $e_s$ is one, and all its other
terms have one fewer pivot coordinate than $s$.

These $|S|-D$ relations are linearly independent over $\mathbb Z$.
Indeed, in a nonzero linear combination choose the greatest number
of pivot coordinates occurring among its indices with nonzero
coefficient. The corresponding basis vector $e_s$ occurs in its
own leading term and in no other term at that level. Its coefficient
cannot cancel.

Eliminating pivot coordinates with the $R_s$ reduces every $e_s$
to the integer linear combination of the $e_t$, $t\in T$, given
by \eqref{gsr:en:88:rank:extension}. All original face relations reduce to
zero, by the identity for the $c_i$ used in the preceding proof.
Consequently the $R_s$ generate all of $\mathcal R$, and the
classes of the $e_t$ span the quotient. They are independent:
the map sending $e_s$ to its coefficient vector in
\eqref{gsr:en:88:rank:extension} kills every face relation and sends each
$e_t$ to its distinct standard basis vector in $\mathbb Z^T$.
This proves all assertions.
\end{proof}

For equal coordinate sizes $q_i=q$, there are $kq^{k-1}$ displayed
face relations. Their rank is $q^k-(q-1)^k$, so the dimension of
their relation space is
\[
 kq^{k-1}-q^k+(q-1)^k.
\]
The difference is not an asymptotic estimate: it is the exact
number of redundant equations in this formal product-grid system.

\subsection{The parallelogram configuration}

Take
\[
 S_i=\{00,10,01,11\},\qquad p_i=11,
\]
with the local relation
\begin{equation}
 f(00)-f(10)-f(01)+f(11)=0.
 \label{gsr:en:88:rank:parallelogram}
\end{equation}
The configuration basis is
\[
 T=\{00,10,01\}^k.
\]

\begin{lemma}[Exact configuration rank]
\label{gsr:en:88:rank:fourstate}
An abelian-group-valued labeling of the $4^k$ formal vertices of
a $k$-coordinate configuration, satisfying every coordinate-face
parallelogram identity, is uniquely determined by its $3^k$ values
on $T$. The face-relation module has rank $4^k-3^k$.

There is no universal set of fewer than $3^k$ raw vertex values
that determines every such labeling. This failure already occurs
for every prime-field target $A=\mathbb F_p$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The positive assertions follow from
Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:88:rank:interpolation}--\ref{gsr:en:88:rank:relation-basis}.
For the lower assertion fix any $U\subset S$ with $|U|<3^k$ and
any prime $p$. The admissible $\mathbb F_p$-valued labelings form
a vector space of dimension $3^k$. Evaluation on $U$ is a linear
map to $\mathbb F_p^U$, so its kernel is nonzero. A nonzero
labeling in that kernel agrees with the zero labeling on $U$ and
differs elsewhere.
\end{proof}

When two formal vertices represent the same ambient group element,
there can be extra dependencies. The corollary provides a universal
upper bound valid also in that situation. Its lower assertion
concerns unrestricted formal configurations; it is realized by
configurations with distinct vertices, for example by using the
four coordinates $0,1,2,3$ in a cyclic group of order at least five.

\subsection{Exact certificates for additive quadruples}

Here is the form needed when imposing the product property.
Let $E$ be a subset of an abelian group $H$. For every $s\in S$,
let $\psi_s:E\to A$ be a restriction. Suppose that for every
$u\in E$, the horizontal array
\[
 s\longmapsto\psi_s(u)
\]
satisfies the face relations \eqref{gsr:en:88:rank:relations}.

\begin{theorem}[A smallest universal list of restriction tests]
\label{gsr:en:88:rank:tests}
For every $u_1,u_2,u_3,u_4\in E$ with
$u_1+u_2=u_3+u_4$, the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item
$\psi_s(u_1)+\psi_s(u_2)=\psi_s(u_3)+\psi_s(u_4)$ for every
$s\in S$;
\item
the same identity holds for every $s\in T$.
\end{enumerate}
The number $D$ of restrictions in the second condition is the
smallest possible size of a universal list of raw restrictions.
In the parallelogram case it is exactly $3^k$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The defect array
\[
 d(s)=\psi_s(u_1)+\psi_s(u_2)
      -\psi_s(u_3)-\psi_s(u_4)
\]
is admissible because its face relations are integer linear
combinations of those of the four horizontal arrays. By
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:88:rank:interpolation}, it vanishes on all of $S$ if and
only if it vanishes on $T$.

For minimality, fix any list $U\subset S$ with $|U|<D$.
For any prime $p$, the dimension argument in the proof of
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:88:rank:fourstate} gives a nonzero admissible
array $z:S\to\mathbb F_p$ that vanishes on $U$.
Take $H=E=\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z$, and put
\[
 \psi_s(0)=\psi_s(2)=0,\qquad \psi_s(1)=z(s).
\]
Each horizontal array is admissible, while every selected
restriction $\psi_s$, $s\in U$, is identically zero and hence
respects every additive quadruple. For the quadruple
$(u_1,u_2,u_3,u_4)=(0,0,1,2)$, which is additive in $H$,
the defect is $-z(s)$ and is nonzero at some unselected vertex.
Thus no smaller raw list is a universal certificate.
\end{proof}

The theorem is about the number of coordinate restrictions
required by this certificate. It does not prove optimality of a
final exponent in a counting theorem. A different averaging
argument can use less information than full configuration
respect and can therefore improve the counting exponent further.

\subsection{The reference cube: exactly which tests are necessary}

The direct cube-pair argument uses less information than complete
configuration respect. Its common domain says that a reference
cube and a comparison cube have the same alternating value at
each level. It is therefore appropriate to ask for the fewest
raw restriction tests that force the common alternating value
to respect an additive quadruple.

Let $\Omega=\{0,1\}^r$, put $d=2^r$, and write
$\sigma_\omega=(-1)^{|\omega|}$. For an abelian group $A$,
consider pairs of arrays $a,b\in A^\Omega$ satisfying
\begin{equation}
 L(a)=L(b),\qquad
 L(a)=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}\sigma_\omega a_\omega.
 \label{gsr:en:88:rank:equal-mixed}
\end{equation}
The common value $L(a)=L(b)$ is the quantity to be forced to zero.

\begin{theorem}[Exact raw-test complexity for an equal-mixed cube pair]
\label{gsr:en:88:rank:reference}
Let $U\subseteq\{\mathrm{ref},\mathrm{cmp}\}\times\Omega$ be
a set of selected raw coordinates. The implication
\begin{equation}
 \left.
 \begin{gathered}
   L(a)=L(b),\\
   a_\omega=0\quad((\mathrm{ref},\omega)\in U),\\
   b_\omega=0\quad((\mathrm{cmp},\omega)\in U)
 \end{gathered}
 \right\}
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad L(a)=0
 \label{gsr:en:88:rank:reference-implication}
\end{equation}
holds for every abelian group $A$ if and only if $U$ contains
all $d$ coordinates of one of the two cubes. In particular,
the smallest universal raw-test list has size exactly $2^r$.
The necessity already holds for every prime-field target.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If all coordinates of either array vanish, its alternating
value vanishes; equality in \eqref{gsr:en:88:rank:equal-mixed} proves
sufficiency.

Conversely, suppose $U$ omits a reference coordinate $\omega_0$
and a comparison coordinate $\nu_0$. In $\mathbb F_p$, for
any prime $p$, set
\[
 a_{\omega_0}=\sigma_{\omega_0},\qquad
 b_{\nu_0}=\sigma_{\nu_0},
\]
and set all other coordinates to zero. Every selected
coordinate vanishes, but
\[
 L(a)=\sigma_{\omega_0}^2=1
     =\sigma_{\nu_0}^2=L(b).
\]
Thus \eqref{gsr:en:88:rank:reference-implication} fails. The argument
also works in characteristic two, where both signs equal one.
\end{proof}

This is a statement about additive-quadruple defects as well.
Suppose that reference restrictions $\psi_\omega:E\to A$
and comparison restrictions $\theta_\omega:E\to A$ satisfy
\[
 \sum_\omega\sigma_\omega\psi_\omega(u)
 =\sum_\omega\sigma_\omega\theta_\omega(u)
 \qquad(u\in E).
\]
For a fixed additive quadruple in $E$, their raw defects form
arrays $a,b$ satisfying \eqref{gsr:en:88:rank:equal-mixed}. Enforcing
the additive identity at the $2^r$ reference vertices forces
the common mixed-value defect to vanish. Fewer raw tests
cannot give a universal implication under only the displayed
horizontal equality: place the counterexample arrays of the
theorem at level $1$ of $\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z$ and zero
arrays at levels $0,2$. The quadruple $(0,0,1,2)$ then has
nonzero common mixed-value defect, while every selected
restriction is identically zero.

The horizontal equality does not reduce the number of free
reference values. Every choice of the reference array is
permitted, since the same choice for the comparison array
satisfies it. The theorem's lower example also permits
different reference and comparison arrays and covers tests
drawn from both cubes. This is why a count of all $2^{r+1}$
raw values is unnecessary, while a claim that fewer than
$2^r$ suffice would need an additional hypothesis.

Actual configurations with repeated physical vertices can
have further identities. The sharp universal statement is
realized without those coincidences: for $r\ge1$, in each
horizontal coordinate use cube side $1$, reference base $0$,
and comparison base $2$ in a cyclic group of order at least
five. The two cubes have distinct vertices and common side.
For $r=0$, the statement has one reference value, and equality
identifies the single comparison value with it.

As in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:88:rank:tests}, the lower bound applies to
this universal raw-test certificate. It does not exclude a
different analytic argument that avoids requiring the same
intermediate conclusion.

\subsection{Why a unit pivot is the correct integral hypothesis}

There is a useful distinction between intrinsic rank and recovery
from raw coordinates. If a local relation vector $r_i$ is merely
primitive, meaning that its coefficients have greatest common
divisor one, then
\[
 \mathbb Z^{S_i}/\mathbb Zr_i
\]
is still free of rank $q_i-1$. Consequently the product quotient
by all coordinate-face relations is free of rank
$\prod_i(q_i-1)$. This follows either by extending each primitive
vector to an integral basis, or from the elementary quotient
identity
\[
 \mathbb Z^S/\mathcal R
 \cong\bigotimes_{i=1}^k
       \left(\mathbb Z^{S_i}/\mathbb Zr_i\right).
\]
It need not follow that exactly that many \emph{raw} vertex
coordinates determine every labeling over every finite abelian
target.

For example, the primitive relation $2a+3b=0$ has intrinsic
rank one. The value $a$ alone does not determine $b$ over
$\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z$, while $b$ alone does not determine $a$
over $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$. Both raw coordinates are necessary
for recovery uniform in all finite abelian targets.

More generally, write $M=\mathbb Z^S/\mathcal R$. A selected
set $U$ of raw vertices determines all admissible labelings
over every finite abelian target if and only if the classes
$[e_u]$, $u\in U$, generate $M$ as an abelian group. Sufficiency
is immediate. For necessity, if the subgroup they generate is
$L\ne M$, the nonzero finitely generated group $M/L$ has a
nonzero finite quotient. Composing the quotient map with
$M\to M/L$ gives a nonzero admissible finite-group-valued
labeling that vanishes on $U$.

In the unit-pivot theorem, the chosen coordinate classes form
an integral basis, so the generation condition is automatic.
This explains both the exact $(q-1)^k$ generalization and the
absence of hidden characteristic assumptions in the
parallelogram application.


% ===== COUNTING =====

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Smaller determining families in the configuration argument\srctag{88}}]{Smaller determining families in the configuration argument}\label{gsr:en:88:sec:d4}
\srcnote{88}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:en:88:count:configuration-section}
\label{gsr:en:88:sec:counting}

The original induction for Lemma~14.4 applies the product property to
every vertex of an already respected horizontal configuration.  Those
vertex values satisfy linear relations.  After using the relations,
the number of necessary tests is $3^{k-1}$ instead of $4^{k-1}$ at the
$k$th induction step.  A second change is possible for Corollary~14.5:
one can construct a parallel cube pair directly, and then only the
$2^{k-1}$ vertices of one reference cube have to be tested.  The two
changes give different counting theorems.  The stronger cube-pair
exponent below is not asserted for full configurations.

Throughout this section, all ordered parameter choices are counted,
including choices with zero sides or repeated vertices.  A repeated
vertex contributes its weight once for each occurrence.  Extend the
nonnegative weight $w$ by zero outside $B$.

\subsection{The configuration bound}

We use the following consequence of the four-state determining lemma.
Suppose that four tensors on
$\{00,10,01,11\}^{d}$ each satisfy the relation
$z_{00}+z_{11}=z_{10}+z_{01}$ on every coordinate face.  Their signed sum
does too.  Thus, to prove that their signed sum vanishes everywhere, it
is enough to test it on
\[
 \{00,10,01\}^{d}.
\]
Indeed, a coordinate equal to $11$ can be eliminated by
$z_{11}=z_{10}+z_{01}-z_{00}$, one coordinate at a time.  This argument
uses integer linear combinations and is valid for every abelian target
group, including groups with torsion.

\begin{theorem}[Configuration count with a determining family]
\label{gsr:en:88:count:configuration}
Let $\pi$ be an ordering of the $k$ coordinate groups.  Under the
coordinate product properties with parameters $\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_k$,
every nonnegative weight $w$ supported on $B$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:88:count:configuration-anisotropic}
 \frac{\mathcal F_k(w)}{M^3}
 \ge
 (\E_X w)^{4^k}
 \prod_{i=1}^{k}
 \gamma_{\pi(i)}^{\,8\cdot3^{i-1}4^{k-i}}.
\end{equation}
In particular, when all parameters equal $\gamma$ and $B$ has density
$\beta$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:88:count:configuration-indicator}
 \mathcal F_k(\mathbf1_B)
 \ge M^3\beta^{4^k}\gamma^{8(4^k-3^k)}.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Reorder the coordinates according to $\pi$ and use induction.  For zero
coordinates the ambient space is a singleton, the configuration has
one vertex, and the assertion is the identity
$\mathcal F_0(w)=w$.

For the induction step write $X=Z\times T$, with $|Z|=M_0$ and
$|T|=n$, and let $\gamma_T$ be the parameter for the last coordinate.
A potential horizontal configuration $q$ consists of a base and two
side vectors in $Z$, so there are exactly $M_0^3$ possible $q$.
Let $E_q\subseteq T$ consist of those levels $t$ at which $q$ is
contained in $B_t$ and respected by $\phi_t$.  On this common domain put
\[
 \theta_q(t)
 =\prod_{v\in\{00,10,01,11\}^{k-1}}w(q(v),t).
\]
The product includes vertex multiplicities.  Set $\theta_q(t)=0$ off
$E_q$.

Apply the vertical product property only to the restrictions through
the $3^{k-1}$ positions in $\{00,10,01\}^{k-1}$.  It yields a weighted
count of at least
\[
 \frac{\gamma_T^{8\cdot3^{k-1}}}{n}
 \left(\sum_t\theta_q(t)\right)^4
\]
of additive quadruples $a+b=c+d$ whose value defect is zero at those
positions.  All four horizontal configurations at $a,b,c,d$ are
respected, by the definition of $E_q$.  Their signed difference is a
tensor satisfying the horizontal face relations, and hence its defect
is zero at every omitted position too.  This supplies every vertical
face identity.  The horizontal identities were already supplied by
membership in $E_q$.

For completeness, regard $a,c,d,b$ as the vertical states
$00,10,01,11$, respectively.  Their base is $a$, their two increments
are $c-a$ and $d-a$, and $a+(c-a)+(d-a)=b$.  Thus the resulting
configuration is recovered uniquely from the source parameters, and
every occurrence of a vertex has exactly the required weight.
Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:88:count:configuration-step}
 \mathcal F_k(w)
 \ge \frac{\gamma_T^{8\cdot3^{k-1}}}{n}
       \sum_q\left(\sum_t\theta_q(t)\right)^4.
\end{equation}

Write $A_{k-1}$ for the product of the horizontal parameter factors in
the induction hypothesis.  The first moment is exactly
\[
 \sum_{q,t}\theta_q(t)
 =\sum_t\mathcal F_{k-1}(w_t).
\]
The induction hypothesis, followed by Jensen's inequality in $t$, gives
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{q,t}\theta_q(t)
 &\ge M_0^3 A_{k-1}
       \sum_t(\E_Zw_t)^{4^{k-1}}\\
 &\ge M_0^3n A_{k-1}(\E_Xw)^{4^{k-1}}.
\end{align*}
Another application of Jensen, now over the $M_0^3$ possible $q$, gives
\[
 \sum_q\left(\sum_t\theta_q(t)\right)^4
 \ge \frac{\bigl(\sum_{q,t}\theta_q(t)\bigr)^4}{M_0^9}.
\]
Substitution in \eqref{gsr:en:88:count:configuration-step} proves the induction
with new factor $A_{k-1}^{4}\gamma_T^{8\cdot3^{k-1}}$.
This is exactly the product in
\eqref{gsr:en:88:count:configuration-anisotropic}.  For equal parameters, its
total exponent is
\[
 8\sum_{i=1}^k3^{i-1}4^{k-i}=8(4^k-3^k).
\]
Taking $w=\mathbf1_B$ proves
\eqref{gsr:en:88:count:configuration-indicator}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Scope of the determining lemma]
The horizontal face-relation space has dimension $3^d$ over every
field: arbitrary values on $\{00,10,01\}^d$ extend uniquely by the
elimination rule.  Therefore a test using fewer than $3^d$ scalar
coordinate evaluations cannot certify vanishing for every tensor in
that space.  This proves optimality of the determining-family size in
this local argument.  It does not prove that the exponent in
\eqref{gsr:en:88:count:configuration-indicator} is the optimal consequence of the
full product property.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Direct and weighted parallel cube-pair forcing\srctag{88}}]{Direct and weighted parallel cube-pair forcing}\label{gsr:en:88:sec:d5}
\srcnote{88}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:en:88:count:cube-section}

The configuration theorem retains all $4^k$ occurrences of a
configuration.  A pair of parallel $k$-cubes has only $2^{k+1}$ vertex
occurrences.  The direct argument uses agreement of two horizontal
mixed values, without first requiring every horizontal configuration
face.  The saving is visible already at dimension two: the configuration
proof needs three vertical lines, whereas the direct pair construction
needs the two endpoints of a reference edge.

\subsection{The gluing map}

\begin{lemma}[Two orientations of a respected pair]
\label{gsr:en:88:count:gluing}
Write $X=Z\times T$, where $Z$ has $k-1$ coordinates.  Fix two
horizontal cubes $\kappa,\kappa'$ of the same side $h$, with bases
$x,x'$.  Suppose $a+b=c+d$ in $T$; both cubes are admissible and have
equal mixed values at each of the four levels; and the value functions
at every vertex of the reference cube $\kappa$ respect this additive
quadruple.  Put
\[
 t=c-a=b-d.
\]
Then both ordered cube pairs
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:88:count:two-orientations}
 \bigl((x,a),(x',d);(h,t)\bigr),
 \qquad
 \bigl((x',a),(x,d);(h,t)\bigr)
\end{equation}
are contained and respected.  For either orientation separately, the
map from $(x,x',h,a,b,c,d)$ to its ordered output pair is injective.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
At every admitted level $u$, write
\[
 L(u)=D_h\phi(\kappa,u)=D_h\phi(\kappa',u).
\]
Taking the alternating sum of the reference-vertex equations gives
$L(a)+L(b)=L(c)+L(d)$.  Equivalently,
\[
 L(a)-L(c)=L(d)-L(b).
\]
These are the mixed values of the first pair in
\eqref{gsr:en:88:count:two-orientations}, and the same argument applies to the
second pair.  The necessary vertices belong to the assumed horizontal
cubes at the four levels.

For the first orientation the ordered output recovers
$x,x',h,a,d,t$.  Then $c=a+t$ and $b=d+t$ recover the rest of the input.
For the second orientation the same recovery applies after swapping
$x$ and $x'$.  This proves injectivity without a nondegeneracy
assumption.
\end{proof}

In the unweighted case, fix $(x,x',h)$ and let $E$ be the levels at
which the lower-dimensional pair is contained and respected.  The
product property on the $2^{k-1}$ reference-vertex lines supplies many
additive quadruples in $E$.  Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:88:count:gluing} maps them
injectively into full cube pairs.  The first moment over all choices
of $(x,x',h)$ is the lower-dimensional pair count.  The two Jensen
steps from the configuration argument then give the recurrence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:88:count:cube-recurrence}
 e_0=0,\qquad e_k=4e_{k-1}+8\cdot2^{k-1}.
\end{equation}
The next theorem retains exact homogeneity for arbitrary nonnegative
weights, using both orientations of the same construction.

\subsection{A homogeneous weighted theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Weighted parallel cube-pair count]
\label{gsr:en:88:count:cubepairs}
Let $\pi$ order the $k$ coordinate groups, and suppose the coordinate
product properties have parameters $\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_k$.
For every nonnegative weight $w$ supported on $B$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:88:count:weighted-cubes-anisotropic}
 \frac{\mathcal C_k(w)}{M^3}
 \ge
 \left(\E_X w^{2^{1-k}}\right)^{4^k}
 \prod_{i=1}^{k}
 \gamma_{\pi(i)}^{8\cdot2^{i-1}4^{k-i}}.
\end{equation}
In particular, for a common parameter $\gamma$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:88:count:weighted-cubes-isotropic}
 \mathcal C_k(w)
 \ge M^3
 \left(\E_X w^{2^{1-k}}\right)^{4^k}
 \gamma^{4(4^k-2^k)}.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
After reordering coordinates, induct on $k$.  For zero coordinates,
the two zero-dimensional cubes consist of the same singleton, so
$\mathcal C_0(w)=w^2$.  Formula
\eqref{gsr:en:88:count:weighted-cubes-anisotropic} has exponent $2^{1-0}=2$ and
is exactly this identity.

At a positive-dimensional induction step write $X=Z\times T$,
$|Z|=M_0$, $|T|=n$.  A potential ordered horizontal pair is
$q=(x,x',h)$, of which there are $M_0^3$.  Let $E_q\subseteq T$
consist of the levels where its two cubes $\kappa,\kappa'$ are
admissible and have equal mixed values.  Set
\[
 P_q(u)=\prod_{\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}^{k-1}}
              w(\kappa(\varepsilon),u),
 \qquad
 P'_q(u)=\prod_{\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}^{k-1}}
              w(\kappa'(\varepsilon),u),
\]
and use the weight
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:88:count:sqrt-weight}
 \theta_q(u)=\sqrt{P_q(u)P'_q(u)}\,\mathbf1_{E_q}(u).
\end{equation}
All square roots here are of nonnegative real numbers; the target group
requires no divisibility assumption.

Apply the vertical product property to the $2^{k-1}$ vertex lines of
$\kappa$, with common domain $E_q$ and weight $\theta_q$.  Call the
resulting quadruples admitted.  For an admitted quadruple $a+b=c+d$,
the weights of the two output pairs in Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:88:count:gluing} are
\begin{align*}
 U&=P_q(a)P_q(c)P'_q(d)P'_q(b),\\
 U'&=P'_q(a)P'_q(c)P_q(d)P_q(b).
\end{align*}
Their geometric mean is exactly
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:88:count:geometric-identity}
 \sqrt{UU'}
 =\theta_q(a)\theta_q(b)\theta_q(c)\theta_q(d).
\end{equation}
The two orientations are each injective on the same set of admitted
data.  Consequently their total weights each satisfy
\[
 \sum_{q,\,\mathrm{admitted}}U\le\mathcal C_k(w),
 \qquad
 \sum_{q,\,\mathrm{admitted}}U'\le\mathcal C_k(w).
\]
We do not assert that the two sums are equal.  The arithmetic--geometric
mean inequality suffices:
\begin{align}
 \mathcal C_k(w)
 &\ge \sum_{q,\,\mathrm{admitted}}\sqrt{UU'}\notag\\
 &\ge \frac{\gamma_T^{8\cdot2^{k-1}}}{n}
       \sum_q\left(\sum_u\theta_q(u)\right)^4.
 \label{gsr:en:88:count:weighted-step}
\end{align}

The square-root weight was chosen to make its first moment exact:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:88:count:weighted-first-moment}
 \sum_{q,u}\theta_q(u)
 =\sum_{u\in T}\mathcal C_{k-1}(\sqrt{w_u}).
\end{equation}
Put $s_k=2^{1-k}$ and let $A_{k-1}$ denote the horizontal parameter
product.  Since $s_{k-1}/2=s_k$, the induction hypothesis and Jensen
give
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{q,u}\theta_q(u)
 &\ge M_0^3 A_{k-1}
       \sum_u\left(\E_Z w_u^{s_k}\right)^{4^{k-1}}\\
 &\ge M_0^3n A_{k-1}
       \left(\E_X w^{s_k}\right)^{4^{k-1}}.
\end{align*}
Jensen over the $M_0^3$ potential $q$ gives
\[
 \sum_q\left(\sum_u\theta_q(u)\right)^4
 \ge\frac{\bigl(\sum_{q,u}\theta_q(u)\bigr)^4}{M_0^9}.
\]
Substituting in \eqref{gsr:en:88:count:weighted-step}, and using
$M_0^{12}n^4/(nM_0^9)=M_0^3n^3=M^3$, proves the induction with
parameter product $A_{k-1}^4\gamma_T^{8\cdot2^{k-1}}$.
This gives \eqref{gsr:en:88:count:weighted-cubes-anisotropic}.  The sum of the
parameter exponents in the common-parameter case is
\[
 8\sum_{i=1}^k2^{i-1}4^{k-i}=4(4^k-2^k),
\]
which proves \eqref{gsr:en:88:count:weighted-cubes-isotropic}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The stronger replacement for Corollary 14.5]
\label{gsr:en:88:count:indicator}
If $B$ has density $\beta$ and $\phi$ has the common product-property
parameter $\gamma$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:88:count:indicator-cubes-formula}
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 \mathcal C_k(\mathbf1_B)
 \ge M^3\beta^{4^k}\gamma^{4(4^k-2^k)}.}
\end{equation}
For $0\le w\le1$, the weaker but simpler weighted lower bound
$\mathcal C_k(w)\ge
 M^3(\E w)^{4^k}\gamma^{4(4^k-2^k)}$ also holds.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
For an indicator, $w^{2^{1-k}}=w$.  For $k\ge1$ and $0\le w\le1$,
$w^{2^{1-k}}\ge w$ pointwise.  Apply
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:88:count:cubepairs}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 82--94]
\emph{Against the formal statement} (checked at HEAD \texttt{bf285410b}). \file{corollary_14_5} (\file{Sections14\_15.lean}, line~253) has the exponent $2k4^k$, and $4(4^k-2^k)\le2k4^k$ with equality only at $k=1$; read at the definition level, this corollary implies it, and \file{corollary_14_5_holds} (\file{Proofs14Configurations.lean}, line~942) is already exact.
\end{writenote}

\begin{remark}[Homogeneity and the weight restriction]
The fractional moment in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:88:count:cubepairs} is part of
the statement.  Its total degree in $w$ is
\[
 2^{1-k}4^k=2^{k+1},
\]
exactly the number of vertex occurrences in a cube pair.  Therefore the
theorem remains valid under arbitrary rescaling of $w$.  Replacing that
moment by $\E w$ for unbounded weights would generally be false by
homogeneity when $k\ge2$.  The last statement of
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:88:count:indicator} explicitly uses $w\le1$.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Quantitative comparison and the local limitation}

The common-parameter exponents are as follows.  The original
configuration bound also supplied the original cube-pair bound.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{r|r|r|r}
 $k$ & Original $2k4^k$
     & Configurations $8(4^k-3^k)$
     & Direct pairs $4(4^k-2^k)$\\
 \hline
 1 & 8 & 8 & 8\\
 2 & 64 & 56 & 48\\
 3 & 384 & 296 & 224\\
 4 & 2048 & 1400 & 960\\
 5 & 10240 & 6248 & 3968
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
For every $k\ge2$ both changes are strict.  This follows term by term
in the sums for the exponents: the original induction has cost
$8\cdot4^{i-1}$ at step $i$, the determining-family induction has
$8\cdot3^{i-1}$, and the direct pair induction has
$8\cdot2^{i-1}$; each is subsequently raised to the power $4^{k-i}$.
Thus the factor $k$ in the old exponent is removed, while the density
exponent $4^k$ is retained.

There is a corresponding limitation of the present interface.
On an abstract reference cube, its $2^d$ vertex values have no face
relations imposed.  Their alternating sum is a linear functional with
a nonzero coefficient at every vertex, over every field, including
characteristic two.  If the available tests consist only of individual
vertex defects, omitting any one test cannot force that alternating
sum to be zero: put a nonzero defect at the omitted vertex and zero
elsewhere.  Equality of the two horizontal mixed values does not
remove this freedom, since the partner cube can copy the reference
values.  Hence $2^d$ is the smallest universal set of individual tests
for this direct construction.  A better global exponent would have to
use more than this local determining argument, such as a stronger
consequence of the product property or information retained between
successive side vectors.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Different coordinate parameters and finite product profiles\srctag{88}}]{Different coordinate parameters and finite product profiles}\label{gsr:en:88:sec:d6}
\srcnote{88}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:en:88:count:profiles-section}

The anisotropic forms above have a useful consequence: a weak coordinate
need not incur the largest exponent.  The order of induction can be
chosen from the supplied parameters.

\begin{proposition}[Best order for scalar coordinate parameters]
\label{gsr:en:88:count:order}
Among the bounds of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:88:count:configuration}, and separately
among those of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:88:count:cubepairs}, an optimal coordinate
order satisfies
\[
 \gamma_{\pi(1)}\ge\gamma_{\pi(2)}\ge\cdots\ge\gamma_{\pi(k)}.
\]
Thus the strongest product-property parameter is used first.  If all
parameters are distinct, this is the unique optimal order.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The negative logarithm of either parameter product has the form
\[
 \sum_{i=1}^k a_i x_{\pi(i)},\qquad
 x_j=-\log\gamma_j,
\]
where $a_i=8\cdot3^{i-1}4^{k-i}$ for configurations and
$a_i=8\cdot2^{i-1}4^{k-i}$ for cube pairs.  In both cases
$a_1>\cdots>a_k>0$.  If $i<j$ but
$x_{\pi(i)}>x_{\pi(j)}$, swapping those two entries lowers the cost by
\[
 (a_i-a_j)(x_{\pi(i)}-x_{\pi(j)})>0.
\]
Eliminating all such inversions proves the proposition.  Equal
parameters may be permuted without changing the bound.
\end{proof}

For example, in three horizontal coordinates the direct-pair parameter
factor is
\[
 \gamma_{\pi(1)}^{128}
 \gamma_{\pi(2)}^{64}
 \gamma_{\pi(3)}^{32}.
\]
This dependence is supplied by the theorem itself and does not require
replacing all three parameters by their minimum.

\subsection{Only finitely many product tests are needed}

The following formulation identifies exactly which part of the full
product property enters the proof.  Suppose a coordinate $j$ comes with
coefficients $\eta_j(p)\in[0,1]$, and the weighted product-property
inequality for a family of $p$ parallel restrictions has lower factor
$\eta_j(p)/|K_j|$ in place of $\gamma_j^{8p}/|K_j|$.
The coefficient may depend on the family size without having a power
form.

\begin{theorem}[Product-profile version]
\label{gsr:en:88:count:profiles}
Fix a coordinate order $\pi$.
If the product inequalities hold at the family sizes
$p=3^{i-1}$ in coordinate $\pi(i)$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:88:count:profile-config}
 \frac{\mathcal F_k(w)}{M^3}
 \ge (\E_Xw)^{4^k}
       \prod_{i=1}^k
       \eta_{\pi(i)}(3^{i-1})^{4^{k-i}}.
\end{equation}
If they hold at the family sizes $p=2^{i-1}$ in coordinate $\pi(i)$,
then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:88:count:profile-cubes}
 \frac{\mathcal C_k(w)}{M^3}
 \ge \left(\E_Xw^{2^{1-k}}\right)^{4^k}
       \prod_{i=1}^k
       \eta_{\pi(i)}(2^{i-1})^{4^{k-i}}.
\end{equation}
No product inequality at another family size is required for the
corresponding conclusion.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
In the proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:88:count:configuration}, the newly added
coordinate is tested once, on $3^{i-1}$ lines, and its supplied
coefficient is raised to the fourth power at each subsequent induction
step.  Substituting $\eta_{\pi(i)}(3^{i-1})$ at that occurrence proves
\eqref{gsr:en:88:count:profile-config}.  The proof of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:88:count:cubepairs} has the same structure with
$2^{i-1}$ reference-vertex lines, giving
\eqref{gsr:en:88:count:profile-cubes}.  Restriction to a coordinate slice preserves
each of the needed inequalities, since every tested family remains a
family of restrictions of the original partial map.
\end{proof}

For positive coefficients, optimizing either displayed bound is the
finite assignment problem with costs
\[
 -4^{k-i}\log\eta_j(3^{i-1}),
 \qquad\text{or}\qquad
 -4^{k-i}\log\eta_j(2^{i-1}),
\]
respectively.  Unlike the scalar-parameter case, a general profile need
not admit a single sorting rule: its quality at one family size may
differ from its quality at another.

\subsection{The collision input with the fibre profile retained}

\begin{corollary}[Horizontal collision profile]
\label{gsr:en:88:count:collision-profile}
Let $B\subseteq X\times T$, with $|X|=M$, $|T|=n$, and let
$\beta_t=|B_t|/M$.  Define the normalized horizontal collision count
\[
 \chi=\frac{1}{M^3n}\sum_{t\in T}
                   \mathcal C_k(\mathbf1_{B_t}).
\]
For any horizontal coordinate order $\pi$, put
\[
 A_\pi=\prod_{i=1}^k
       \gamma_{\pi(i)}^{8\cdot2^{i-1}4^{k-i}}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:88:count:collision-profile-formula}
 \chi\ge A_\pi\E_{t\in T}\beta_t^{4^k}
       \ge A_\pi\beta^{4^k},
 \qquad \beta=\frac{|B|}{Mn}.
\end{equation}
For weights, the exact horizontal analogue is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:88:count:weighted-collision-profile}
 \frac{1}{M^3n}\sum_t\mathcal C_k(w_t)
 \ge A_\pi\E_t
       \left(\E_X w_t^{2^{1-k}}\right)^{4^k}.
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:88:count:cubepairs} on each horizontal fibre and
average.  The second inequality in
\eqref{gsr:en:88:count:collision-profile-formula} is Jensen's inequality.
\end{proof}

The arrangement step can therefore retain the common collision
parameter before substituting its improved lower bound.  This order of
substitution preserves the cancellation used in the earlier coupled
amplification argument.


% ===== ARRANGEMENTS =====

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{From the stronger cube bound to higher arrangements\srctag{88}}]{From the stronger cube bound to higher arrangements}\label{gsr:en:88:sec:d7}
\srcnote{88}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:en:88:sec:arrangements}

We now keep the improved horizontal cube-pair count through the
collision-sensitive argument of source~15 \cite{srcfifteen}. This section
rederives that argument with all normalizations visible. Its purpose is
to establish the stronger combined theorem, not to reassign the prior
moment inequalities.

\subsection{The collision measure}

Let $X=\prod_{j=1}^kK_j$, $M=|X|$, and let $T$ be a finite abelian
group of size $n$. Suppose $B\subseteq X\times T$ and
$\phi:B\to V$. For $t\in T$, write
\[
 B_t=\{x:(x,t)\in B\},\qquad
 \beta_t=|B_t|/M,\qquad \beta=\E_t\beta_t.
\]
For $h\in X$, $t\in T$, and $v\in V$, set
\begin{equation}
 m_h(t,v)=
 \#\{x\in X:(x+\omega\odot h,t)\in B\text{ for all }\omega,
             \ D_h\phi(x,t)=v\}.
 \label{gsr:en:88:eq:collision-multiplicity}
\end{equation}
The notation $D_h\phi(x,t)$ means the alternating sum only in the
$k$ horizontal coordinates. Define
\begin{equation}
 C_h=\sum_{t,v}m_h(t,v)^2,\qquad
 C=\sum_h C_h,\qquad
 \chi=\frac{C}{M^3n}.
 \label{gsr:en:88:eq:collision-definitions}
\end{equation}
The integer $C$ counts respected horizontal cube pairs in the same
vertical fibre. In particular
\begin{equation}
 C=\sum_{t\in T}\mathcal C_k(\mathbf1_{B_t}).
 \label{gsr:en:88:eq:collision-fibres}
\end{equation}

\begin{corollary}[Improved collision input]
\label{gsr:en:88:arr:collision}
Assume the horizontal coordinate parameters are
$\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_k$. For an ordering $\pi$, put
\[
 H_\pi=\prod_{i=1}^k
       \gamma_{\pi(i)}^{8\,2^{i-1}4^{k-i}}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \chi\ge H_\pi\E_t\beta_t^{4^k}
       \ge H_\pi\beta^{4^k}.
 \label{gsr:en:88:eq:improved-collision}
\end{equation}
With a common parameter, $H_\pi=\gamma^{4(4^k-2^k)}$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The product property is inherited by each fibre. Apply
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:88:count:cubepairs} with its indicator weight, sum
\eqref{gsr:en:88:eq:collision-fibres}, and use Jensen's inequality for
$u\mapsto u^{4^k}$.
\end{proof}

For later interpretation, the useful upper bound on the same parameter is
\begin{equation}
 0<\chi\le\E_t\beta_t^3\le\beta\le1
 \qquad(B\ne\varnothing).
 \label{gsr:en:88:eq:collision-upper}
\end{equation}
Indeed, forgetting the label condition and sending $(x,y,h)$ to
$(x,x+h,y)$ injects admissible cube pairs in $B_t$ into $B_t^3$.
The strict positivity follows by taking $h=0$ and an occupied fibre.
One must not reverse the first inequality or replace
$\E_t\beta_t^3$ by $\beta^3$ without an additional hypothesis.

\subsection{Ordered arrangements and exact moment interpolation}

\begin{definition}[Respected $d$-arrangements]
\label{gsr:en:88:def:arrangements}
For an integer $d\ge1$, an ordered $d$-arrangement consists of a common
horizontal side $h$, $2d$ horizontal bases $x_1,\ldots,x_{2d}$, and
$2d$ levels $t_1,\ldots,t_{2d}$ satisfying
\[
 t_1+\cdots+t_d=t_{d+1}+\cdots+t_{2d}.
\]
Every cube $(x_i,h,t_i)$ must be contained in $B$.
The arrangement is respected when also
\[
 \sum_{i=1}^dD_h\phi(x_i,t_i)
 =\sum_{i=d+1}^{2d}D_h\phi(x_i,t_i).
\]
Let $R_d(h)$ and $R_d=\sum_hR_d(h)$ count these objects with a fixed
side and with all sides, respectively, and put
\[
 a_d=\frac{R_d}{M^{2d+1}n^{2d-1}}.
\]
Thus $R_1=C$, $a_1=\chi$, and $R_2$ is the respected
parallelepiped-pair count.
\end{definition}

There are exactly $M^{2d+1}n^{2d-1}$ ambient arrangement parameters:
choose $h$, the $2d$ bases, and the first $2d-1$ levels; the final
level is forced. This count uses only the group law.

\begin{lemma}[Moment interpolation with the collision denominator]
\label{gsr:en:88:arr:moment}
For $d\ge2$ and $C>0$,
\begin{equation}
 R_d\ge\frac{R_2^{d-1}}{C^{d-2}},\qquad
 a_d\ge\frac{a_2^{d-1}}{\chi^{d-2}}.
 \label{gsr:en:88:eq:moment-amplification}
\end{equation}
The same first inequality holds at a fixed side $h$ whenever $C_h>0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
View $m_h$ as a finitely supported nonnegative measure on $T\times V$.
Its $d$-fold convolution satisfies
\[
 R_d(h)=\sum_z\bigl(m_h^{*d}(z)\bigr)^2.
\]
Put $V_0=\langle\phi(B)\rangle\le V$ and $H=T\times V_0$, using
the same group for every $h$. This group is finitely generated abelian,
and every $m_h$ is supported on $H$. With the unnormalized transform
$\widehat m_h(\xi)=\sum_{z\in H}m_h(z)\overline{\xi(z)}$,
on the compact dual of $H$ with probability Haar measure,
Plancherel gives
\[
 R_d(h)=\int |\widehat m_h(\xi)|^{2d}\,d\xi.
\]
For a finite target this is just finite character orthogonality; for
a general target it is the same identity for finite Fourier sums on
a product of circles and finite groups.

Let $U(h,\xi)=|\widehat m_h(\xi)|^2$ and integrate with counting measure
in $h$ and Haar measure in $\xi$. For $d>2$, H\"older gives
\[
 R_2=\int
       (U^d)^{1/(d-1)}U^{(d-2)/(d-1)}
 \le R_d^{1/(d-1)}C^{(d-2)/(d-1)}.
\]
For $d=2$ the assertion is equality. Rearranging proves the count
inequality. Its normalizing factor is correct because
\[
 \frac{(M^5n^3)^{d-1}}{(M^3n)^{d-2}}
       =M^{2d+1}n^{2d-1}.
\]
The proof with $h$ fixed omits the sum in that variable.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The vertical product property with the collision retained}

\begin{lemma}[Reference-cube amplification, prior collision form]
\label{gsr:en:88:arr:vertical}
Suppose the vertical coordinate has parameter $\gamma_T$. Then
\begin{align}
 R_2(h)&\ge
  \frac{\gamma_T^{8\cdot2^k}C_h^4}{nM^4},
 \label{gsr:en:88:eq:vertical-fixed-side}\\
 R_2&\ge\frac{\gamma_T^{8\cdot2^k}C^4}{nM^7},\qquad
 a_2\ge\gamma_T^{8\cdot2^k}\chi^4.
 \label{gsr:en:88:eq:vertical-global}
\end{align}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Fix a side $h$ and a reference base $y\in X$. On the set of levels
where the reference cube is contained in $B$, define
\[
 \theta_y(t)=m_h(t,D_h\phi(y,t)),
\]
and put this function equal to zero elsewhere. Apply the vertical
product property to the $2^k$ restrictions through the reference
vertices, with weight $\theta_y$.
The resulting weighted number of additive level quadruples is at least
\[
 \frac{\gamma_T^{8\cdot2^k}}n
       \left(\sum_t\theta_y(t)\right)^4.
\]
At each of the four levels choose a cube with the same mixed label as
the reference cube; the number of such choices is $\theta_y(t)$.
Adding the vertex equations with alternating signs shows that the
four chosen cubes form a respected $2$-arrangement.

For the fixed reference $y$, this construction is injective into the
arrangements counted by $R_2(h)$: their four levels and four bases
recover all the choices. Consequently the displayed lower bound
holds for every $y$. Average this inequality over the $M$ reference
bases and apply Jensen. The first-moment identity is
\[
 \sum_{y,t}\theta_y(t)=\sum_{t,v}m_h(t,v)^2=C_h.
\]
This proves \eqref{gsr:en:88:eq:vertical-fixed-side}. Averaging is necessary:
different reference bases can describe the same final arrangement.
We have not asserted an injection that forgets the reference base.

Sum over the $M$ possible sides and use
$\sum_hC_h^4\ge C^4/M^3$. Dividing by $M^5n^3$ gives
\eqref{gsr:en:88:eq:vertical-global}.
\end{proof}

Lemmas~\ref{gsr:en:88:arr:moment} and~\ref{gsr:en:88:arr:vertical} are the collision forms
proved in source~15 \cite[Theorems~3.3 and~5.5]{srcfifteen}.
The new ingredient is the stronger value of the input
\eqref{gsr:en:88:eq:improved-collision}.

\begin{theorem}[Improved product-property amplification]
\label{gsr:en:88:arr:main}
Suppose $B\subseteq X\times T$ has density $\beta>0$ and $\phi$ has
the coordinate parameters $\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_k,\gamma_T$.
For every integer $d\ge2$ and every horizontal order $\pi$,
\begin{align}
 a_d&\ge\gamma_T^{8(d-1)2^k}\chi^{3d-2},
 \label{gsr:en:88:eq:arrangement-chi}\\
 a_d&\ge
 \left(\E_t\beta_t^{4^k}\right)^{3d-2}
 H_\pi^{3d-2}\gamma_T^{8(d-1)2^k}.
 \label{gsr:en:88:eq:arrangement-profile}
\end{align}
In particular, under $\PP_\gamma$,
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 R_d\ge M^{2d+1}n^{2d-1}
  \beta^{(3d-2)4^k}
  \gamma^{(12d-8)4^k-4d\,2^k}.}
 \label{gsr:en:88:eq:arrangement-new}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
First couple the two inequalities while retaining $\chi$:
\[
 a_d\ge\frac{a_2^{d-1}}{\chi^{d-2}}
 \ge\frac{(\gamma_T^{8\cdot2^k}\chi^4)^{d-1}}{\chi^{d-2}}
 =\gamma_T^{8(d-1)2^k}\chi^{3d-2}.
\]
The exponent $3d-2$ is positive. Hence the lower bound
\eqref{gsr:en:88:eq:improved-collision} may now be substituted into this expression,
proving \eqref{gsr:en:88:eq:arrangement-profile}.
With equal parameters, the exponent on $\gamma$ is
\begin{align*}
 (3d-2)\,4(4^k-2^k)+8(d-1)2^k
 &=4(3d-2)4^k-4d\,2^k\\
 &=(12d-8)4^k-4d\,2^k.
\end{align*}
Jensen applied to the fibre densities finishes the proof.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The denominator must be coupled before substitution]
The proof does not insert a lower bound for $\chi$ directly into
the denominator of \eqref{gsr:en:88:eq:moment-amplification}. That would move
the denominator in the wrong direction. It first uses the positive
fourth power in \eqref{gsr:en:88:eq:vertical-global}, leaving the positive power
$3d-2$. This point matters when the improved cube estimate is integrated
into a formal proof or a symbolic parameter calculation.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[A stronger eight-arrangement input]
\label{gsr:en:88:arr:eight}
If all coordinate groups are $\Z/N\Z$, $B\subseteq(\Z/N\Z)^{k+1}$
has density $\beta$, and $\phi$ has $\PP_\gamma$, then
\begin{equation}
 R_8\ge
 \beta^{22\cdot4^k}\gamma^{88\cdot4^k-32\cdot2^k}N^{17k+15}.
 \label{gsr:en:88:eq:eight-new}
\end{equation}
This conclusion does not require $N$ prime.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Set $d=8$, $M=N^k$, and $n=N$ in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:88:arr:main}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 82--94]
\emph{Against source~15 and the formal statement} (checked at the write). Source~15's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:15:thm:coupled} has $\gamma^{44k4^k+56\cdot2^k}$ at the same density exponent; the gain is $\gamma^{-44((k-2)4^k+2^{k+1})}$, one at $k=1$. The formal \file{lemma_14_8} (\file{Sections14\_15.lean}, line~292) has $\beta^{28\cdot4^k}\gamma^{84k4^k}$; since $22\cdot4^k\le28\cdot4^k$ and $88\cdot4^k-32\cdot2^k\le84k4^k$ for every $k\ge1$, this corollary implies it for $\beta,\gamma\le1$, and \file{lemma_14_8_holds} (\file{Proofs14ProductToArrangements.lean}, line~18) is already exact.
\end{writenote}

\subsection{Comparison with both relevant baselines}

The corrected statement of Lemma~14.8 in the inspected repository is
\begin{equation}
 R_8\ge\beta^{28\cdot4^k}\gamma^{84k4^k}N^{17k+15}.
 \label{gsr:en:88:eq:eight-formal-baseline}
\end{equation}
It is this supported statement, not the smaller exponent in the
original printed Corollary~14.6, that provides the baseline for the
formal interface \cite{repo88,srcfifteen}. The stronger source~15
theorem is
\begin{equation}
 R_8\ge\beta^{22\cdot4^k}
              \gamma^{44k4^k+56\cdot2^k}N^{17k+15}.
 \label{gsr:en:88:eq:eight-project-baseline}
\end{equation}
The density saving from $28\cdot4^k$ to $22\cdot4^k$ already belongs
to that earlier coupled argument. The additional frequency saving
in \eqref{gsr:en:88:eq:eight-new} is the contribution of the present cube-pair
theorem.

For general $d$, source~15's frequency exponent is
$(6d-4)k4^k+8(d-1)2^k$.
Its excess over the present exponent is
\begin{equation}
 (6d-4)\bigl((k-2)4^k+2^{k+1}\bigr).
 \label{gsr:en:88:eq:general-frequency-saving}
\end{equation}
This is zero at $k=1$ and positive for $k\ge2$.
For fixed $d$ as $k$ grows, the ratio of the new frequency exponent
to the preceding one is asymptotic to $2/k$.

\subsection{Side profiles and limits of the conclusion}

For completeness, the argument can preserve the side distribution as
well as the fibre distribution. Set $\chi_h=C_h/(M^2n)$, so that
$\chi=\E_h\chi_h$. The fixed-side versions of
Lemmas~\ref{gsr:en:88:arr:moment} and~\ref{gsr:en:88:arr:vertical} yield
\begin{equation}
 a_d\ge\gamma_T^{8(d-1)2^k}
            \E_h\chi_h^{3d-2}.
 \label{gsr:en:88:eq:side-profile}
\end{equation}
Sides with $C_h=0$ contribute zero and require no division.
Formula~\eqref{gsr:en:88:eq:side-profile} is useful when the collision mass is
concentrated on a small collection of sides. The profile retention
itself is part of the earlier collision method; the new count can
be used without discarding it.

The minimal determining-family theorems do not classify extremizers
of \eqref{gsr:en:88:eq:arrangement-new}. They only show that the stated raw
vertex tests cannot be further reduced using the same local linear
information. A proof that keeps additional compatibility between
different horizontal pairs or different side vectors may improve the
global exponents again. The remaining density exponent $4^k$ is
another concrete target, discussed in Section~\ref{gsr:fz:88:sec:research}.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Propagation through the degree-weighted selection step\srctag{88}}]{Propagation through the degree-weighted selection step}\label{gsr:en:88:sec:d8}
\srcnote{88}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:en:88:sel:section}
\label{gsr:en:88:sec:selection}

The new arrangement estimate can be passed through the next restriction
step with every exponent and size condition retained.  The selector used
in this section is the existing degree-weighted Fej\'er theorem of
ProveIt source~35 \cite{srcthirtyfive}.  Our contribution here is its
composition with Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:88:arr:main}, and the resulting comparison
with the earlier inputs to the same selector.  This distinction matters:
an improvement already obtained by the selection theorem is not a new
consequence of the present cube-pair argument.

\subsection{The precise selection interface}

Let $k\ge1$, let $q$ be a prime power of characteristic $p$, and let
$B\subseteq\F_q^{k+1}$ have density $\beta>0$.  We use the ordered
eight-arrangement count from the preceding section, specialized to
$X=\F_q^k$ and $T=\F_q$.  Denote the count without a respect condition
by $T(B)$ and the respected count by $G_\phi(B)$, for
$\phi:B\to\F_q$.  Set
\begin{equation}
 s=2^{k+4},\qquad M_k=17k+15,\qquad
 T_0=\beta^{15}q^{M_k}.
 \label{gsr:en:88:sel:normalization}
\end{equation}
Thus $s$ is the number of labelled vertex occurrences.  All counts
include zero side coordinates and repeated physical vertices.
The elementary upper bound
\begin{equation}
 T(B)\le T_0
 \label{gsr:en:88:sel:count-upper}
\end{equation}
follows by choosing the common horizontal side, the first fifteen
origin vertices in $B$, and the last horizontal origin.  The balanced
relation uniquely determines the last level.  This gives at most
$q^{2k}|B|^{15}=T_0$ possibilities.

For $0\le t\le k$, define
\begin{equation}
 D_t=16\sum_{j=0}^{t}\binom{k}{j}-\binom{k}{t},\qquad
 C_k=120\,3^k,\qquad
 \omega_t=1+\mathbf1_{\{t=1\}}+C_k\mathbf1_{\{t=k\}}.
 \label{gsr:en:88:sel:dimensions}
\end{equation}
In particular, $D_0=15$ and $D_k=s-1$.  The symbols $D_t$ and $\omega_t$ belong to the coefficient
stratification of the selector; $D_t$ does not denote a mixed difference.

\begin{theorem}[The prior degree-weighted selection theorem]
\label{gsr:en:88:sel:prior-selector}
Suppose $0<\alpha,\beta,\eta\le1$ and
$G_\phi(B)\ge\alpha T_0$.  Put
\begin{equation}
 L=\left\lceil\frac{s+1}{\alpha\eta}\right\rceil.
 \label{gsr:en:88:sel:bandwidth-general}
\end{equation}
Assume
\begin{equation}
 p>2(L-1),\qquad
 q\ge
 \max_{0\le t\le k}
 \left(2(k+1)\omega_t\beta^{-15}L^{D_t}\right)^{1/(t+1)}.
 \label{gsr:en:88:sel:threshold-general}
\end{equation}
Then some $B'\subseteq B$ satisfies
\begin{align}
 \frac{G_\phi(B')}{T(B')}
 &\ge\frac1{1+\eta}\ge1-\eta,
 \label{gsr:en:88:sel:purity-general}\\
 G_\phi(B')
 &\ge\frac{T_0}{2\eta L^s}
 \ge\frac{\alpha^s\eta^{s-1}}{2(s+2)^s}\,T_0,
 \label{gsr:en:88:sel:mass-general}\\
 \frac{|B'|}{q^{k+1}}
 &\ge\beta\left(\frac1{2\eta L^s}\right)^{1/15}.
 \label{gsr:en:88:sel:density-general}
\end{align}
For a prime field $q=p$, the size condition on $q$ in
\eqref{gsr:en:88:sel:threshold-general} already implies its characteristic
condition.
\end{theorem}

This is the $m=16$ specialization of the explicit corollary in
source~35 \cite{srcthirtyfive}.  We record the full statement because both
the characteristic condition and the normalization affect its
composition with an improved input.  The last assertion follows from
the $t=0$ condition:
\[
 p\ge2(k+1)\beta^{-15}L^{15}\ge4L^{15}>2(L-1).
\]
For extension fields, a large cardinality $q$ does not imply a large
characteristic, so that condition remains separate.

For clarity, the quantitative mechanism behind the displayed threshold
can be summarized without changing the theorem being imported.  The
source's exact signal and normalized error are
\begin{align*}
 R_s(L)&=1+2\sum_{u=1}^{L-1}(1-u/L)^s,\\
 \mathcal K(L,q)&=\sum_{t=0}^kL^{D_t}Q_t(q)
                    +C_kL^{s-1}q^{-k-1},
\end{align*}
where $Q_0=q^{-1}$, $Q_1=q^{-2}+(q-1)q^{-16}$, and
$Q_t=q^{-t-1}$ for $t\ge2$.  Since $Q_1\le2q^{-2}$, the size
condition makes $\mathcal K(L,q)\le\beta^{15}/2$.  Convexity and
the trapezoidal rule give $R_s(L)\ge2L/(s+1)$.  Consequently the
source's signed expectation score
\[
 \alpha\eta R_s(L)-(1-\alpha)-\beta^{-15}\mathcal K(L,q)
\]
is larger than $1/2$.  Its selection argument then gives the first
count in \eqref{gsr:en:88:sel:mass-general}; the second uses
$L\le(s+2)/(\alpha\eta)$.  The Fourier selection and the
degree-stratified certificate estimates underlying that signed score
are precisely the prior theorem, not additional claims of this article.

\subsection{The improved Lemma~15.6 input and output}

Define
\begin{equation}
 A_k=22\,4^k-15,\qquad
 g_k=88\,4^k-32\,2^k,\qquad
 c_s=\frac{2^{-44(s-1)-1}}{(s+2)^s}.
 \label{gsr:en:88:sel:new-exponents}
\end{equation}
The subtraction of fifteen in $A_k$ is forced by
\eqref{gsr:en:88:sel:normalization}.  In particular, the horizontal collision
exponent $4^k$ is not the exponent of the eight-arrangement density.
The latter is $22\,4^k$ after the coupling in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:88:arr:main}.

\begin{corollary}[An explicit improved output at the Lemma~15.6 interface]
\label{gsr:en:88:sel:new-output}
Let $B\subseteq\F_q^{k+1}$ have density $0<\beta\le1$, where
$k\ge1$, and suppose $\phi:B\to\F_q$ has the product property with
parameter $0<\gamma\le1$.  Put
\begin{equation}
 L_{\mathrm{new}}=
 \left\lceil
 2^{44}(s+1)\beta^{-A_k}\gamma^{-g_k}
 \right\rceil.
 \label{gsr:en:88:sel:new-bandwidth}
\end{equation}
Assume \eqref{gsr:en:88:sel:threshold-general} with $L=L_{\mathrm{new}}$.
Then there exists $B'\subseteq B$ such that
\begin{align}
 \frac{G_\phi(B')}{T(B')}
 &\ge\frac1{1+2^{-44}}>1-2^{-44},
 \label{gsr:en:88:sel:new-purity}\\
 G_\phi(B')
 &\ge2^{43}L_{\mathrm{new}}^{-s}\beta^{15}q^{17k+15},
 \label{gsr:en:88:sel:new-exact-count}\\
 G_\phi(B')
 &\ge
 c_s\beta^{sA_k+15}\gamma^{sg_k}q^{17k+15},
 \label{gsr:en:88:sel:new-count}\\
 \frac{|B'|}{q^{k+1}}
 &\ge
 \beta\left(2^{43}L_{\mathrm{new}}^{-s}\right)^{1/15}
 \ge c_s^{1/15}\beta^{(sA_k+15)/15}\gamma^{sg_k/15}.
 \label{gsr:en:88:sel:new-density}
\end{align}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:88:arr:main} with $d=8$ gives
\[
 G_\phi(B)\ge
 \beta^{22\,4^k}\gamma^{88\,4^k-32\,2^k}q^{17k+15}
 =\alpha_{\mathrm{new}}T_0,
 \qquad
 \alpha_{\mathrm{new}}=\beta^{A_k}\gamma^{g_k}.
\]
Both $A_k$ and $g_k$ are positive for $k\ge1$, so
$0<\alpha_{\mathrm{new}}\le1$.  Apply
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:88:sel:prior-selector} with this parameter and
$\eta=2^{-44}$.  It gives \eqref{gsr:en:88:sel:new-purity},
\eqref{gsr:en:88:sel:new-exact-count}, and the first density bound.
Since
\[
 L_{\mathrm{new}}
 \le2^{44}(s+2)\beta^{-A_k}\gamma^{-g_k},
\]
substitution proves \eqref{gsr:en:88:sel:new-count} and the second density
bound.  Every count here uses the same ordered arrangement parameter
space as \eqref{gsr:en:88:sel:normalization}, so no conversion or collision
factor is introduced at this interface.
\end{proof}

If a sufficient threshold without a ceiling inside its formula is
preferred, define
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal N_k(\beta,\gamma)=
 \max_{0\le t\le k}
 \left[
 2(k+1)\omega_t\bigl(2^{44}(s+2)\bigr)^{D_t}
 \beta^{-15-A_kD_t}\gamma^{-g_kD_t}
 \right]^{1/(t+1)}.
 \label{gsr:en:88:sel:threshold-ceiling-free}
\end{equation}
For every prime $q\ge\lceil\mathcal N_k(\beta,\gamma)\rceil$,
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:88:sel:new-output} applies.  For extension fields one
additionally retains $p>2(L_{\mathrm{new}}-1)$.  The exact bandwidth
condition \eqref{gsr:en:88:sel:threshold-general} can be smaller than this
convenient sufficient replacement.

\begin{example}[Two horizontal coordinates]
\label{gsr:en:88:sel:k2}
For $k=2$,
\[
 s=64,\quad A_k=337,\quad g_k=1280,\quad
 (D_0,D_1,D_2)=(15,46,63),\quad C_k=1080.
\]
Thus
\[
 L=\left\lceil65\,2^{44}\beta^{-337}\gamma^{-1280}\right\rceil
\]
and the size requirement is
\begin{equation}
 q\ge\max\left\{
 6\beta^{-15}L^{15},\quad
 (12\beta^{-15}L^{46})^{1/2},\quad
 (6486\beta^{-15}L^{63})^{1/3}
 \right\}.
 \label{gsr:en:88:sel:k2-threshold}
\end{equation}
The respected count is at least
\begin{equation}
 2^{-2773}66^{-64}\beta^{21583}\gamma^{81920}q^{49},
 \label{gsr:en:88:sel:k2-count}
\end{equation}
and its proportion among all arrangements in the selected subset is
at least $1/(1+2^{-44})$.  These are explicit theoretical bounds;
their size is not presented as practical.
\end{example}

\subsection{Pointwise comparisons using the same selector}

The closest previously proved input is the coupled estimate of
source~15 \cite{srcfifteen}:
\begin{equation}
 G_\phi(B)\ge
 \beta^{22\,4^k}\gamma^{g_k^{(15)}}q^{17k+15},
 \qquad
 g_k^{(15)}=44k4^k+56\,2^k.
 \label{gsr:en:88:sel:old15}
\end{equation}
Its density exponent agrees with the new one.  The decrease in the
product-property exponent is exactly
\begin{equation}
 \Delta_k=g_k^{(15)}-g_k
 =44\bigl((k-2)4^k+2^{k+1}\bigr).
 \label{gsr:en:88:sel:delta}
\end{equation}
This is zero for $k=1$ and positive for every $k\ge2$.

\begin{proposition}[Both the count guarantee and its hypotheses improve]
\label{gsr:en:88:sel:comparison}
Use $\eta=2^{-44}$ and Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:88:sel:prior-selector} for both
\eqref{gsr:en:88:sel:old15} and the new input.  For all
$0<\beta,\gamma\le1$, the new bandwidth is no larger than the old
bandwidth, every size requirement in
\eqref{gsr:en:88:sel:threshold-general} is no stronger, and its separate
characteristic requirement is no stronger.  The ratio of the new
monomial lower bound \eqref{gsr:en:88:sel:new-count} to the old monomial lower
bound produced by that same theorem is
\begin{equation}
 \gamma^{-s\Delta_k}.
 \label{gsr:en:88:sel:count-ratio15}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:88:sel:delta} gives
$\alpha_{\mathrm{new}}\ge\alpha_{15}$, where
$\alpha_{15}=\beta^{A_k}\gamma^{g_k^{(15)}}$.  The ceiling of
$(s+1)/(\alpha\eta)$ is nonincreasing in $\alpha$, and each
quantity on the right of \eqref{gsr:en:88:sel:threshold-general} is
nondecreasing in $L$.  This proves the hypothesis comparison and
also compares the exact $L$-based count guarantees.  The monomial
guarantees have the same coefficient $c_s$ and the same power of
$\beta$; dividing them gives \eqref{gsr:en:88:sel:count-ratio15}.
\end{proof}

The ratio in \eqref{gsr:en:88:sel:count-ratio15} is strictly larger than one
when $k\ge2$ and $\gamma<1$.  This strict statement concerns the
displayed monomial guarantees.  The exact ceiling-based guarantees
can coincide when the two bandwidth ceilings coincide.

For comparison with source~35's actual downstream substitution, its
input was the corrected Gowers estimate \cite{gowers,srcthirtyfive}
with exponents
\[
 b_k^{(G)}=28\,4^k,\qquad g_k^{(G)}=84k4^k.
\]
Here the respective improvements before selection are
\[
 b_k^{(G)}-22\,4^k=6\,4^k,\qquad
 g_k^{(G)}-g_k=(84k-88)4^k+32\,2^k>0.
\]
At fields meeting the older hypotheses, the ratio of the new and old
monomial guarantees through the same degree-weighted selector is
\begin{equation}
 \beta^{-6s4^k}
 \gamma^{-s\{(84k-88)4^k+32\,2^k\}}.
 \label{gsr:en:88:sel:count-ratio-gowers}
\end{equation}
The sufficient field and characteristic thresholds decrease as well,
by the same monotonicity argument.  In particular, the saving in the
retained density exponent is $6s4^k=96\,8^k$.

\subsection{The field-size saving and its order of limits}

The coefficient geometry of the prior selector is measured by
\begin{equation}
 E_{k,16}=\max_{0\le t\le k}\frac{D_t}{t+1}.
 \label{gsr:en:88:sel:E}
\end{equation}
This quantity is unchanged.  Source~35 proves
$E_{k,16}\sim2s/k$ as $k\to\infty$ \cite{srcthirtyfive}.
For each fixed $k$, fixed $\beta>0$, and fixed purity target, let
$\gamma\downarrow0$.  Since
$L_{\mathrm{new}}\asymp_{k,\beta}\gamma^{-g_k}$, the right side
of the exact cardinality threshold has logarithmic growth exponent
\begin{equation}
 \lim_{\gamma\downarrow0}
 \frac{\log\!\left[
 \max_{0\le t\le k}
 \left(2(k+1)\omega_t\beta^{-15}L_{\mathrm{new}}^{D_t}\right)^{1/(t+1)}
 \right]}{\log(1/\gamma)}
 =E_{k,16}g_k.
 \label{gsr:en:88:sel:fixed-k-threshold-exponent}
\end{equation}
The earlier source~15 input gives $E_{k,16}g_k^{(15)}$ instead.
Taking $k\to\infty$ in these already identified exponents yields
\begin{align}
 E_{k,16}g_k&\sim\frac{2816}{k}\,8^k,&
 E_{k,16}g_k^{(15)}&\sim1408\,8^k,
 \label{gsr:en:88:sel:threshold-asymptotic}\\
 s g_k&=1408\,8^k-512\,4^k,&
 s g_k^{(15)}&=704k\,8^k+896\,4^k.
 \label{gsr:en:88:sel:retention-asymptotic}
\end{align}
Thus both ratios of new to earlier product-property exponents are
asymptotic to $2/k$.  The order of limits is explicit: these formulas
do not assert an estimate with untracked constants uniform in all
of $k$, $\beta$, and $\gamma$.

For the illustrative choice $\beta=\gamma=1/2$, the bandwidths are
integers without rounding loss:
\[
 L_{\mathrm{new}}=(s+1)2^{44+A_k+g_k}.
\]
At $k=2$, the $t=1$ branch governs both the new and source~15
thresholds.  Hence the bandwidth decreases by $2^{352}$, the
right side of the field-size threshold decreases by exactly
$2^{23\cdot352}=2^{8096}$, and the monomial respected-count
guarantee increases by $2^{64\cdot352}=2^{22528}$.
The exact-arithmetic companion verifies the governing branch by
raising candidate thresholds to common integer powers, rather than
relying on rounded logarithms.  It also reports illustrative base-two
logarithms for $k=2,3$.

\subsection{Keeping fibre profiles and the boundary of the result}

The preceding statements can retain the stronger density profile from
the horizontal cube-pair theorem.  Write
$\beta_z=|B_z|/q^k$ and
\[
 \rho_k=\E_z\beta_z^{4^k}.
\]
The arrangement input is then
$G_\phi(B)\ge\rho_k^{22}\gamma^{g_k}q^{17k+15}$.
One may therefore replace $\alpha_{\mathrm{new}}$ throughout by
\begin{equation}
 \alpha_{\mathrm{profile}}=
 \beta^{-15}\rho_k^{22}\gamma^{g_k}.
 \label{gsr:en:88:sel:profile}
\end{equation}
This is a valid selection parameter: $\rho_k\le\beta$ implies
$\alpha_{\mathrm{profile}}\le\beta^7\le1$, while Jensen gives
$\rho_k\ge\beta^{4^k}$ and hence
$\alpha_{\mathrm{profile}}\ge\alpha_{\mathrm{new}}$.
The exact formulas \eqref{gsr:en:88:sel:bandwidth-general}--
\eqref{gsr:en:88:sel:density-general} preserve that improvement automatically.
The same substitution works with the anisotropic coordinate product
from the preceding section in place of the scalar
$\gamma^{g_k}$.

This completes a quantitative passage from the new Section~14 input
through the adjacent Section~15 selection interface.  A global
Szemer\'edi bound would also require the later modeling, interpolation,
and density-increment recursions, with compatible largeness conditions
throughout.  Those additional conclusions are not supplied by the
composition proved here.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Sharp density obstructions and the remaining gap\srctag{88}}]{Sharp density obstructions and the remaining gap}\label{gsr:en:88:sec:d9}
\srcnote{88}{Section 9}
\label{gsr:en:88:sec:sharpness}

The local test counts in Section~\ref{gsr:en:88:sec:rank} are exact. There is a
second, different sharpness question: what power of the domain density
can occur in a universal lower bound? A random-domain argument gives
a useful answer without making any assumption about the optimal
frequency exponent.

\begin{lemma}[Random-domain counts for finite patterns]
\label{gsr:en:88:sharp:random-pattern}
Fix $0<\beta<1$. For each $N$, let $Y_N$ be a finite set whose size
tends to infinity, and let $\mathcal P_N$ be a nonempty finite family
of ordered patterns, each having $m$ labelled vertex occurrences in
$Y_N$. Suppose that every fixed occurrence is uniformly distributed
in $Y_N$ when a pattern is chosen uniformly, and that the proportion
of patterns with any repeated physical vertex tends to zero.

Then there are subsets $B_N\subseteq Y_N$ with
\begin{equation}
 \frac{|B_N|}{|Y_N|}\longrightarrow\beta,
 \qquad
 \frac{\#\{P\in\mathcal P_N:P\subseteq B_N\}}{|\mathcal P_N|}
       \longrightarrow\beta^m.
 \label{gsr:en:88:eq:random-pattern-limit}
\end{equation}
The same subsets can be chosen for any fixed finite collection of
pattern families satisfying these assumptions, and one may require
$|B_N|=\lfloor\beta|Y_N|\rfloor$ exactly.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Include every point of $Y_N$ independently with probability $\beta$.
Let $Z_N$ be the normalized contained-pattern count. For a pattern
with $r$ distinct physical vertices its survival probability is
$\beta^r$. All but an $o(1)$ fraction have $r=m$, so
$\E Z_N=\beta^m+o(1)$.

Two pattern survival indicators are independent whenever their sets
of physical vertices are disjoint. If $P,Q$ are chosen independently
and uniformly, a specified occurrence of $P$ equals a specified
occurrence of $Q$ with probability $1/|Y_N|$, by their uniform
marginals and the independence of the parameter choices. A union
bound therefore gives
\[
 \operatorname{Var}(Z_N)
 \le\Pr(P\text{ and }Q\text{ share a vertex})
 \le\frac{m^2}{|Y_N|}.
\]
Also
$\operatorname{Var}(|B_N|/|Y_N|)=\beta(1-\beta)/|Y_N|$.
Both quantities converge in probability to their displayed limits.
For finitely many families the same statement follows from a finite
union bound. Choosing an outcome for each sufficiently large $N$
establishes the simultaneous deterministic sequences.
Finally, changing $u$ points changes a normalized pattern count by
at most $mu/|Y_N|$, by the uniform marginal at each occurrence.
Adding or deleting $o(|Y_N|)$ points to obtain the required exact
cardinality therefore preserves all the limits.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Necessary density exponents]
\label{gsr:en:88:sharp:density}
Fix $k\ge1$ and $d\ge2$. In universal bounds under the product
property, with a positive leading constant independent of $\beta$,
the following restrictions are necessary:
\begin{align}
 \mathcal F_k&\ge c_kM^3\beta^b\gamma^g
       \quad\Longrightarrow\quad b\ge4^k,
 \label{gsr:en:88:eq:density-obstruction-configuration}\\
 \mathcal C_k&\ge c_kM^3\beta^b\gamma^g
       \quad\Longrightarrow\quad b\ge2^{k+1},
 \label{gsr:en:88:eq:density-obstruction-pair}\\
 a_d&\ge c_{k,d}\beta^b\gamma^g
       \quad\Longrightarrow\quad b\ge2d\,2^k.
 \label{gsr:en:88:eq:density-obstruction-arrangement}
\end{align}
Here the constants $c_k,c_{k,d}>0$ and exponents are fixed independently
of the ambient group and the density. In particular, the density
exponent $4^k$ in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:88:count:configuration} is optimal.
At this exponent its coefficient one cannot be increased uniformly.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Take all coordinate groups to be $\Z/N\Z$, with $N$ tending to
infinity through primes, and use the constant labeling $\phi=0$ on
every sampled domain. By Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:88:lem:weak-PP}, this map has
$\PP_1$. Every contained object is respected.

For configurations in $(\Z/N\Z)^k$, the pattern has $m=4^k$
occurrences. Every occurrence is uniform because the base is
uniform. For a fixed pair of distinct formal vertices, their
difference has a nonzero coefficient $1$ or $-1$ in at least one
side coordinate. Hence its vanishing has probability at most $1/N$.
A union bound over the finitely many vertex pairs shows that the
fraction with repetitions tends to zero. The ambient configuration
count is $N^{3k}$. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:88:sharp:random-pattern} gives domains
of density tending to $\beta$ with
$\mathcal F_k/N^{3k}\to\beta^{4^k}$.

For parallel cube pairs the same proof uses $m=2^{k+1}$.
Two occurrences in the same cube can coincide only when at least
one specified side coordinate is zero. For occurrences from
different cubes, the independent base difference makes their
coincidence probability $N^{-k}$. Thus again the repetition
probability is $O_k(N^{-1})$, and
$\mathcal C_k/N^{3k}\to\beta^{2^{k+1}}$.

For $d$-arrangements in $(\Z/N\Z)^{k+1}$, use
$m=2d\,2^k$ occurrences and ambient count $N^{(2d+1)k+2d-1}$.
Each occurrence is uniform: each horizontal base is free, and each
level is uniform under the balanced level equation.
Within one cube a coincidence has probability at most $1/N$.
Between two different cubes, the horizontal bases are independent;
moreover the difference of their levels is a nonzero linear form
on the balanced level space when $2d\ge4$.
There is a level coordinate outside the chosen pair, so this
nonzero form has a coefficient $1$ or $-1$ after eliminating one
level. Consequently the coincidence probability tends to zero.
The random-pattern lemma yields $a_d\to\beta^{2d2^k}$.

If one of the asserted universal bounds holds, pass to its
corresponding limit with $\gamma=1$. It implies
$\beta^m\ge c\beta^b$ for every fixed $0<\beta<1$.
If $b<m$, letting $\beta\downarrow0$ contradicts $c>0$.
This proves all three restrictions. At $b=m$, the same limit forces
$c\le1$. Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:88:count:configuration}
attains the first necessary exponent with constant one.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What is sharp and what is still separated]
For configurations, the density exponent is settled even though the
optimal frequency exponent remains open. For cube pairs, the proved
density exponent and the necessary one give the interval
\[
 2^{k+1}\ \le\ b_k^{\mathrm{possible}}\ \le\ 4^k,
\]
where the upper endpoint is witnessed by the present theorem with
an explicit frequency exponent. This notation records a feasible
range, not the existence of a minimizing exponent with every other
parameter fixed. At $k=1$ the two endpoints coincide; for $k\ge2$
they do not. Likewise the necessary density exponent for
arrangements is substantially smaller than $(3d-2)4^k$.

These elementary random-domain obstructions explain why exact
configuration interpolation does not by itself settle the cube-pair
problem. The target object has fewer vertex occurrences. The direct
pair proof already exploits this difference for the frequency loss;
it may still be possible to exploit it for the density loss.
\end{remark}

The homogeneity of the weighted theorem supplies a separate useful
check. For $w\equiv c$ on the full product and $\phi=0$,
\[
 \mathcal C_k(w)=M^3c^{2^{k+1}},\qquad
 \left(\E_Xw^{2^{1-k}}\right)^{4^k}=c^{2^{k+1}}.
\]
Thus the theorem is exactly scaled at every $c>0$ when $\gamma=1$.
Replacing its fractional moment by $(\E_Xw)^{4^k}$ for arbitrary
unbounded $w$ would fail already for a constant $c>1$ and $k\ge2$.
