\section[{The exact geometric and quantitative conventions\srctag{87}}]{The exact geometric and quantitative conventions}\label{gsr:en:87:sec:d2}\label{gsr:en:87:sec:definitions}
\srcnote{87}{Section 2}
We give the definitions needed to read the counterexample without relying on informal names. A point of dimension $j$ is an element of $\F_N^j$. A modular arithmetic progression is a presentation
\[
 T=\{a+nb:0\le n<\ell\}\subseteq\F_N.
\]
It is \emph{proper} if the displayed parameterization is injective. In that case $|T|=\ell\le N$. Arbitrary starts and steps, including wrapping progressions, are allowed. A zero step is proper only for length at most one. A box is a product of such progressions whose steps are equal within that box. Its width is the minimum formal axis length, with width defined to be zero in dimension zero. A proper box has cardinality equal to the product of its axis lengths. Different cells in a partition may have different common steps.

The source's \filename{IsMultilinear} means a multiaffine polynomial, including its constant term:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:multiaffine}
 \mu(z)=\sum_{e\in\{0,1\}^j} a_e\prod_{i:e_i=1}z_i.
\end{equation}
Thus constant functions qualify, and fixing every coordinate but one produces an affine function of the remaining variable. The definition is algebraic over $\F_N$ and is independent of a box's progression parameterization. These conventions are in \srclineeightyseven{Definitions}{228}{the polynomial and box definitions}.

\subsection{Multiple multilinearity}
Write the source's three controls as
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:controls}
 c(\rho,\gamma,j)=(\gamma\rho)^{A_j},\qquad
 q(\rho,\gamma,j)=c(\rho,\gamma,j)^{-1},\qquad
 s(\rho,\gamma,j)=\left(\frac2{\rho\gamma}\right)^{2^{2^{j+6}}}.
\end{equation}
These are \filename{multipleC}, \filename{multipleQ}, and \filename{multipleS}. For a relation $\Gamma\subseteq\F_N^j\times\F_N$, the property $\ML_{\gamma,r}(\Gamma)$ means: for every real loss $0<\rho\le1$ and every proper input box $P$, there exist a finite proper box partition $(Q_u)_{u<M}$, a set $G\subseteq P$, a natural graph count $q_0$, and multiaffine maps $\mu_{u,i}$, $i<q_0$, with
\begin{align}
 |G|&\ge(1-\rho)|P|,\label{gsr:en:87:eq:MLmass}\\
 q_0&\le q(\rho/r,\gamma,j)^r,\label{gsr:en:87:eq:MLcount}\\
 \operatorname{width}(Q_u)&\ge
 \operatorname{width}(P)^{c(\rho/r,\gamma,j)^r},\label{gsr:en:87:eq:MLwidth}\\
 (x,y)\in\Gamma,\ x\in G\cap Q_u&\ \Longrightarrow\
 y=\mu_{u,i}(x)\text{ for some }i<q_0.\label{gsr:en:87:eq:MLcover}
\end{align}
A single natural $q_0$ works across all cells, although the maps vary freely with the cell. There is no a priori bound on the number of cells. For a partial function $(B,\phi)$, $\ML_{\gamma,r}(B,\phi)$ is the property of its graph. Crucially, points of $G\setminus B$ require no graph coverage. Our testing box will lie entirely inside $B$, excluding that escape.

\subsection{A reusable finite-value certificate}\label{gsr:en:87:subsec:constantcover}
Suppose a partial map in dimension $j$ takes values in a finite alphabet of size $m$. For fixed $0<\gamma\le1$ and $r\ge1$, it has $\ML_{\gamma,r}$ whenever, for every $0<\rho\le1$,
\[
 m\le q(\rho/r,\gamma,j)^r.
\]
Indeed, take the original box as the sole partition cell, retain its entire carrier, and use the $m$ constant graphs. The width exponent $(\gamma\rho/r)^{A_jr}$ lies in $(0,1]$. An integer width $w\ge1$ satisfies $w^{\lambda}\le w$ for such $\lambda$; a width of zero satisfies $0^\lambda=0$. The latter also covers dimension zero. Empty alphabets are handled by zero graphs, and constant maps by one graph. We use this elementary certificate for all proper coordinate faces and for the actual spectrum relation. It is distinct from the unit cover that eventually fails.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The slab and a word balanced on every long progression\srctag{87}}]{The slab and a word balanced on every long progression}\label{gsr:en:87:sec:d3}\label{gsr:en:87:sec:word}
\srcnote{87}{Section 3}
Fix the constants in~\eqref{gsr:fm:87:eq:mainconst}. For prime $N\ge N_*$ let
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:intervals}
 L=\floor{\frac{N}{4R}},\qquad E=\{0,\ldots,L-1\},\qquad
 S=\{0,\ldots,R-1\},\qquad \alpha=\frac LN.
\end{equation}
We regard $E$ and $S$ as subsets of the prime field. The threshold implies $N\ge(8R)^2$ and $R<N$, so these embeddings are injective and $L>0$. Since $N/(4R)>2$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:density}
 \frac1{8R}<\alpha\le\frac1{4R};
 \qquad\text{in particular}\qquad \theta\le\alpha.
\end{equation}
Only the weak lower bound is needed for the common-base fields; the strict bound also places the graph on the non-small-projection side of extraction.

Set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:beta}
 t_0=N^{1/(2K)},\qquad \varepsilon=\frac1{32K},\qquad
 \beta=\frac1R+\varepsilon=\frac9{32K}.
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}[Simultaneous progression balance]\label{gsr:en:87:lem:balance}
There is a function $f:\F_N\to S$ such that, for every proper modular progression $T$ with $|T|\ge t_0$ and every $c\in\F_N$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:balance}
 |\{x\in T:f(x)=c\}|\le\beta|T|.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose the $f(x)$ independently and uniformly from $S$. On a proper progression of $n$ points, the count of a fixed symbol is a sum of $n$ independent Bernoulli variables with mean $1/R$. Hoeffding's inequality gives the upper-tail bound
\[
 \Pr\bigl(|\{x\in T:f(x)=c\}|>(1/R+\varepsilon)n\bigr)
 \le \exp(-2\varepsilon^2n)=\exp\left(-\frac n{512K^2}\right).
\]
There are at most $N^2(N+1)\le2N^3$ progression presentations with lengths from zero to $N$. This includes arbitrary directions and wrapping progressions; duplicate presentations only enlarge the count. Union-bounding over the $R$ symbols gives failure probability at most
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:unionbound}
 2RN^3\exp\left(-\frac{t_0}{512K^2}\right).
\end{equation}
It is strictly less than one. Indeed $t_0\ge2^{26}K^6$ and $\sqrt{t_0}\ge8192K^3$. For $K\ge1$ and $t_0\ge1$,
$\log(8K)\le3K$ and $\log t_0\le\sqrt{t_0}$. Therefore
\begin{align*}
 \log(2RN^3)&=\log(8K)+6K\log t_0\\
 &\le9K\sqrt{t_0}<16K\sqrt{t_0}
 \le\frac{t_0}{512K^2}.
\end{align*}
This proves the strict probability estimate. Symbols outside $S$ occur zero times. A realization with no failure has the asserted property.
\end{proof}

This argument is the established concentration ingredient used in the pinned \srceightyseven{Proofs16BalancedFieldWord}{balanced-field-word development}. We include it to make the explicit threshold self-contained; the result is existential. Neither the article nor its finite companion constructs a word at an astronomical theorem-scale modulus.

\begin{lemma}[The width budget]\label{gsr:en:87:lem:width}
With $W=L^{1/K}$, one has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:width}
 W\ge N^{1/(2K)}=t_0\ge32KR.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The floor estimate gives $L\ge N/(8R)$. The inequality $N\ge(8R)^2$ implies $N/(8R)\ge\sqrt N$; raising to $1/K$ proves the first inequality. Finally
$t_0\ge2^{26}K^6\ge128K^2=32KR$.
All these claims already follow from the much stronger displayed $N_*$: in particular $N_*\ge2^{26}K^6\ge(32K)^2$.
\end{proof}

From now on choose any balanced word supplied by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:87:lem:balance} and define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:input}
 B=\F_N^k\times E,\qquad \phi(h,x)=f(x)
 \quad(h\in\F_N^k,\ x\in\F_N).
\end{equation}
The function is defined on the entire ambient space, exactly as required by the source interface. It is its partial graph over $B$ that will have the endpoint product property.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The original weighted product property at the endpoint\srctag{87}}]{The original weighted product property at the endpoint}\label{gsr:en:87:sec:d4}\label{gsr:en:87:sec:product}
\srcnote{87}{Section 4}
For a finite domain $F\subseteq\F_N$, a nonnegative weight $w$ and a family of maps $(g_i)_{i<m}$, define the simultaneous weighted additive energy
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:energy}
 \mathcal E_F(w;(g_i))=
 \sum_{\substack{x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4\in F\\x_1+x_2=x_3+x_4\\
 g_i(x_1)+g_i(x_2)=g_i(x_3)+g_i(x_4)\ (i<m)}}
 \prod_{a=1}^4w(x_a).
\end{equation}
The exact \srclineeightyseven{Sections14_15}{52}{product property} tests every $m\in\N$, every coordinate direction, every family of parallel restrictions of $\phi$, and every common finite domain $F$ contained in all the corresponding sections of $B$. It requires
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:producttarget}
 \mathcal E_F(w;(g_i))\ge\gamma^{8m}N^{-1}
 \left(\sum_{x\in F}w(x)\right)^4.
\end{equation}
The normalization is by $N$, not by $|F|$. The case $m=0$ is part of the definition: both common-section containment and simultaneous image additivity are then vacuous.

\begin{lemma}[Weighted graph-sumset bound]\label{gsr:en:87:lem:energy}
Let $A,S\subseteq\F_N$, let $g:A\to S$, and suppose
$|A+A|\,|S+S|\le N$. For every $F\subseteq A$ and every nonnegative real weight $w$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:graphenergy}
 \mathcal E_F(w;(g))\ge N^{-1}\left(\sum_{x\in F}w(x)\right)^4.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $(u,v)\in\F_N^2$, define
\[
 r(u,v)=\sum_{\substack{x,y\in F\\x+y=u\\g(x)+g(y)=v}}w(x)w(y).
\]
Then $\sum r=(\sum_Fw)^2$, $\sum r^2=\mathcal E_F(w;(g))$, and the support of $r$ lies in $(A+A)\times(S+S)$. If the total weight is positive, the support is nonempty and Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
 \mathcal E_F(w;(g))\ge
 \frac{(\sum_Fw)^4}{|\operatorname{supp}r|}
 \ge\frac{(\sum_Fw)^4}{N}.
\]
If the total weight is zero, nonnegativity makes the assertion immediate. Empty domains cause no exception.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}\label{gsr:en:87:prop:product}
The input~\eqref{gsr:en:87:eq:input} satisfies \filename{HasProductProperty B phi 1}.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Our embedded intervals satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:sumset}
 |E+E|\,|S+S|\le(2L-1)(2R-1)<4LR\le N.
\end{equation}
This estimate would remain valid as an upper bound even if the sums wrapped; here the threshold makes the interval lengths smaller than the modulus.

First take a nonempty family of parallel restrictions in the final coordinate. Each restriction is the same map $f$, regardless of the first-coordinate anchor. The common-domain condition forces $F\subseteq E$. Requiring additivity after every restriction is therefore equivalent to requiring it after $f$ once. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:87:lem:energy}, with $A=E$, yields~\eqref{gsr:en:87:eq:producttarget} at $\gamma=1$ for every family size $m\ge1$ and all allowed weights.

Next take one of the first $k$ coordinate directions. Every restriction is constant along that coordinate. The constants may depend on the anchor, but every additive quadruple respects every constant. If $r_0(u)=\sum_{x+y=u}w(x)w(y)$, then ordinary Cauchy--Schwarz on the $N$ possible sums yields
\[
 \sum_{u\in\F_N}r_0(u)^2\ge\frac1N\left(\sum_Fw\right)^4.
\]
This proves the desired bound in these directions.

Finally, if $m=0$, the common-domain condition does not force $F\subseteq E$, even in the final direction. There is also no image constraint. The same ordinary weighted-energy inequality applies on any $F\subseteq\F_N$. This proves the zero-family case separately and completes every quantifier in the source definition.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Relation form]\label{gsr:en:87:cor:relation}
The partial graph over $B$ has the relation product property at parameter one. Its cardinality is $\alpha N^d\le N^d$, and its projection cardinality is $\alpha N^d>\theta N^d$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Any partial graph contained in $\Gamma$ agrees with $\phi$ throughout its own domain, which is a subset of $B$. Every family of tested restrictions therefore satisfies the same estimates in Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:87:prop:product}; no statement about the arbitrary total extension outside that domain is needed. The two cardinalities follow from $|B|=N^kL$ and~\eqref{gsr:en:87:eq:density}.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Why endpoint rigidity does not apply.}
Full-domain product property at $\gamma=1$ has stronger rigidity consequences in the recorded development. Our domain is a slab, so endpoint weighted energy only tests final-coordinate sets contained in $E$ when the family is nonempty. Its graph-sumset support fits within $N$ locations, allowing the exact ambient-normalized lower bound despite arbitrary finite-alphabet oscillation. This is the mechanism that reaches $\gamma=1$.

\section[{All three structured-pair hypotheses\srctag{87}}]{All three structured-pair hypotheses}\label{gsr:en:87:sec:d5}\label{gsr:en:87:sec:structured}
\srcnote{87}{Section 5}
For our fixed $\gamma=1$, put
\begin{align}
 \theta_1&=\left(\frac\theta4\right)^{2^{2^{k+5}}},\label{gsr:en:87:eq:theta1}\\
 s_0&=s(2^{-(k+2)}\theta,1,k)
 =\left(\frac{2^{k+3}}\theta\right)^{2^{2^{k+6}}}.
 \label{gsr:en:87:eq:s0}
\end{align}
These are exactly the arrangement parameter and common face parameter of \srclineeightyseven{Section16}{186}{the structured-pair definition}. We shall use
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:basicparameters}
 0<\theta_1\le\theta^{16}\le\alpha^{16},\qquad
 s_0\ge\frac1\theta=8R\ge R.
\end{equation}
For the first inequality, $k\ge1$ makes $2^{2^{k+5}}\ge16$, and $0<\theta\le1$.

\subsection{Every proper coordinate face}
Let $0\le j<d$ and choose any coordinate-face embedding with arbitrary fixed coordinates. Its pullback of $\phi$ is still $S$-valued on its partial domain, even when the final coordinate is among the free coordinates. For every loss $0<\rho\le1$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:facebudget}
 q(\rho/s_0,1,j)^{s_0}
 =\left(\frac{s_0}{\rho}\right)^{A_js_0}\ge R.
\end{equation}
The finite-value certificate in Section~\ref{gsr:en:87:subsec:constantcover}, using the original box, its entire carrier, and the $R$ constant graphs, proves the exact face property $\ML_{1,s_0}$. It applies to every allowed dimension and every face, not just final-coordinate sections. In dimension zero the source's width is zero and the positive width exponent makes the identity partition valid. For empty boxes in positive dimension, the same observation applies. Thus the first structured-pair conjunct is fully verified.

\subsection{The required arrangement count}
A source $8$-arrangement consists of one common side vector, sixteen base vectors, and sixteen final coordinates satisfying an eight-versus-eight additive relation. In the slab, containment imposes exactly that all final coordinates lie in $E$; the base vectors and side are unrestricted. Let
\[
 T_8(E)=\#\{(x_1,\ldots,x_{16})\in E^{16}:
 x_1+\cdots+x_8=x_9+\cdots+x_{16}\}.
\]
Then the count is exactly
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:arrcount}
 \operatorname{generalArrangementCount}(8,B)=N^{17k}T_8(E).
\end{equation}
The exponent $17k$ accounts for the common side and all sixteen independent bases. If $r_8(u)$ counts eight-tuples from $E$ of sum $u$, then $\sum_ur_8(u)=L^8$. Consequently
\[
 T_8(E)=\sum_ur_8(u)^2\ge\frac{L^{16}}N.
\]
Combining this with~\eqref{gsr:en:87:eq:basicparameters} gives exactly
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:arrlower}
 \operatorname{generalArrangementCount}(8,B)
 \ge\alpha^{16}N^{17k+15}\ge\theta_1N^{17k+15}.
\end{equation}
The stronger comparison $\theta_1\le\alpha^{16}$ is essential; the weaker inequality $\theta_1\le\alpha$ alone would not establish the arrangement field.

\subsection{Every arrangement is respected}
For any side $h$, base $a$ and final coordinate $x$, the alternating value of its $k$-cube is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:zerosum}
 \sum_{e\in\{0,1\}^k}(-1)^{|e|}\phi(a+e\cdot h,x)
 =f(x)\sum_e(-1)^{|e|}=f(x)(1-1)^k=0.
\end{equation}
The equality holds for degenerate sides as well. Thus all sixteen cube values in any arrangement are zero; their additive relation is automatic. Every contained arrangement is respected, so the required fraction $1-2^{-44}$ is satisfied with room to spare. This is the only place where $k\ge1$ is indispensable to the construction: the alternating sum in dimension zero is not zero. All three conjuncts of \filename{Section16StructuredPair theta 1 B phi} now hold.

\section[{The actual common-base structure\srctag{87}}]{The actual common-base structure}\label{gsr:en:87:sec:d6}\label{gsr:en:87:sec:commonbase}
\srcnote{87}{Section 6}
A common-base witness has five data fields
\[
 H,\quad J,\quad (Y_h)_{h\in\F_N^k},\quad\phi',\quad x_0
\]
and eight proof fields, in the exact source order:
\filename{Hmass}, \filename{intersect_mass}, \filename{cube_mass},
\filename{selected_mass}, \filename{selection}, \filename{spectrum},
\filename{good_mass}, and \filename{identity}. The selection field itself has two conjuncts. We now realize all these fields with shared, concrete data, rather than satisfying disconnected proxy hypotheses.

For a side $h\in\F_N^k$, let $X_h$ be the source's cube domain. Its elements are cubes of side $h$ together with a final coordinate, all of whose vertices belong to $B$. For the slab,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:cubedomain}
 X_h\ \cong\ \F_N^k\times E,\qquad |X_h|=N^kL=\alpha N^{k+1}.
\end{equation}
The bijection records the arbitrary cube base and final coordinate; the side is fixed. Choose
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:badwitness}
 H=J=\F_N^k,\qquad Y_h=X_h\text{ for every }h,\qquad
 \phi'(h,x)=0,\qquad x_0=0.
\end{equation}
In the source, $Y_h$ is a finite subset of the subtype of valid cube-domain elements; ``$Y_h=X_h$'' means all elements of that subtype.

A good induced pair $(h,x)$ means $h\in H\cap J$ and $Y_h$ contains the cube with base $x_0$, side $h$, and final coordinate $x$. With~\eqref{gsr:en:87:eq:badwitness}, this holds precisely when $x\in E$. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:badgooddomain}
 B_1(D_{\rm bad})=B,\qquad
 \phi_1(D_{\rm bad})(h,x)=\phi(x_0+h,x)=f(x),\qquad
 \#\{\text{good pairs}\}=N^kL.
\end{equation}
These equalities follow from the named definitions, including the actual common base $x_0$; they are not stipulated replacements for those definitions.

\subsection{All mass fields}
The first four proof fields reduce to
\begin{align}
 \tfrac14\theta_1N^k&\le N^k=|H|,\label{gsr:en:87:eq:Hmass}\\
 \tfrac18\theta_1N^k&\le N^k=|H\cap J|,\label{gsr:en:87:eq:intersectmass}\\
 \tfrac14\theta_1N^{k+1}&\le\alpha N^{k+1}=|X_h|,\label{gsr:en:87:eq:cubemass}\\
 2^{-27}\theta_1^6|X_h|&\le|X_h|=|Y_h|.\label{gsr:en:87:eq:selectedmass}
\end{align}
All hold because $0<\theta_1\le\theta\le\alpha\le1$. The good-mass parameter is exactly
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:theta2}
 \theta_2=2^{-32}\theta_1^8.
\end{equation}
Since $\theta_2\le\theta_1\le\alpha$, the source's required good-pair lower bound $\theta_2N^{k+1}$ follows from~\eqref{gsr:en:87:eq:badgooddomain}.

\subsection{The two selection clauses}
The value clause requires $\phi'(h,x)$ to equal the induced alternating cube value on every selected cube. Both sides are zero by~\eqref{gsr:en:87:eq:zerosum}. For the progression clause, put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:delta-zeta}
 \delta=2^{-37}(\theta_1/4)^{11/2},\qquad
 \zeta=2^{-s(\theta,1,k)}.
\end{equation}
For each $h$, each positive integer $m$, each step in the actual Bohr set
$\operatorname{Bohr}(K_h,\zeta/m)$ and each progression of that step and length at most $m$, the source asks that $\phi'(h,\cdot)$ be affine on its intersection with the induced domain. The global zero function is affine on every set, using coefficients zero and zero. Thus this clause is true for the actual spectrum $K_h$, the actual $\zeta$, all permitted steps and domains, without any estimate on the Bohr set's size. It would be incorrect to omit this compatibility clause merely because the value identity is simple.

\subsection{The corrected alternating identity}
The source's all-ones function is $\phi_1(h,x)=\phi(x_0+h,x)$, and its remainder is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:remainder}
 \phi_{\rm rem}(h,x)=
 -\sum_{e\ne\one}(-1)^{k+|e|}\phi(x_0+e\cdot h,x).
\end{equation}
Solving the alternating cube identity for the all-ones term gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:identity}
 \phi_1=(-1)^k\phi'+\phi_{\rm rem}\quad\text{on }B_1.
\end{equation}
For the present input, every vertex value is $f(x)$. Since
$\sum_e(-1)^{k+|e|}=0$ and the coefficient of the all-ones term is $1$,
$\sum_{e\ne\one}(-1)^{k+|e|}=-1$ and $\phi_{\rm rem}=f(x)$. Thus~\eqref{gsr:en:87:eq:identity} reads $f(x)=0+f(x)$ with exactly the source signs. This verifies the identity field in every dimension, rather than extrapolating the $k=1$ sign pattern.

\section[{The genuine spectrum relation and its cover\srctag{87}}]{The genuine spectrum relation and its cover}\label{gsr:en:87:sec:d7}\label{gsr:en:87:sec:spectrum}
\srcnote{87}{Section 7}
The spectrum field is part of the common-base structure and cannot be replaced by a convenient artificial relation. Here its exact form is elementary. The source uses the unnormalized Fourier transform
\[
 \widehat g(r)=\sum_{x\in\F_N}g(x)\exp(-2\pi i rx/N).
\]
Its higher cube correlation of the indicator of $B$ is, for every $h$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:correlation}
 \operatorname{higherCubeCorrelation}(\one_B,h)(x)=N^k\one_E(x).
\end{equation}
Indeed, for fixed $x\in E$ each of the $N^k$ base choices contributes one to the cube product, including all conjugated factors; for $x\notin E$ every product is zero. This also handles degenerate sides.

The large-spectrum threshold is $\delta N^{k+1}$. By~\eqref{gsr:en:87:eq:correlation}, it reduces to $|\widehat{\one_E}(r)|\ge\delta N$. Thus define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:spec}
 K_{\rm spec}=\{r\in\F_N:|\widehat{\one_E}(r)|\ge\delta N\}.
\end{equation}
The actual spectrum relation is exactly $\F_N^k\times K_{\rm spec}$ and is independent of $h$. Restricting it to $J=\F_N^k$ changes nothing.

Parseval in this normalization gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:parseval}
 |K_{\rm spec}|\delta^2N^2
 \le\sum_r|\widehat{\one_E}(r)|^2=NL,
 \qquad |K_{\rm spec}|\le\alpha\delta^{-2}\le\delta^{-2}.
\end{equation}
The factor $N$ in $NL$ is necessary; a normalized-transform convention would give the wrong threshold calculation. The general source spectrum bound is recorded in \srceightyseven{Proofs16SpectrumInduction}{the spectrum induction file}; here we have computed the actual relation directly.

The precise iteration parameter in the structure is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:specT}
 T=\delta^{-2}s(\theta_1/8,\delta,k).
\end{equation}
Since $0<\delta\le1$ and $T\ge1$, every loss $0<\rho\le1$ has graph budget
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:specbudget}
 q(\rho/T,\delta,k)^T
 =\left(\frac{T}{\delta\rho}\right)^{A_kT}
 \ge\delta^{-A_kT}\ge\delta^{-2}\ge|K_{\rm spec}|.
\end{equation}
Here $A_kT\ge2$. Use the constant graphs indexed by $K_{\rm spec}$, the original input box as the sole cell, and retain the whole carrier. The width exponent $(\delta\rho/T)^{A_kT}$ lies in $(0,1]$, so the identity partition works exactly as in Section~\ref{gsr:en:87:subsec:constantcover}. This proves the required $\ML_{\delta,T}$ spectrum field. In conjunction with Section~\ref{gsr:en:87:sec:commonbase}, every field of $D_{\rm bad}$ is now established.

\paragraph{The previously proved cover inputs still hold.}
The source\textquotesingle s \srceightyseven{Proofs16CommonBaseLineCovers}{common-base cover-input theorem} applies to these very data and the structured pair. It supplies the genuine final-section and all-box line-cover hypotheses, with the distinct graph-count parameters already built into those statements. Thus the failure below does not arise from substituting weaker abstract cover premises for the actual upstream product, selection and spectrum conditions. It persists after all of them have been verified.

\section[{Why every admissible unit cover fails\srctag{87}}]{Why every admissible unit cover fails}\label{gsr:en:87:sec:d8}\label{gsr:en:87:sec:failure}
\srcnote{87}{Section 8}
At loss $\rho=1/2$ in dimension $d=k+1$, the source controls have the exact values
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:unitcontrols}
 q(1/2,1,d)=2^{A_d}=K,\qquad c(1/2,1,d)=K^{-1}.
\end{equation}
Take the proper step-one input box
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:testbox}
 P=E^d,\qquad |P|=L^d>0,\qquad\operatorname{width}(P)=L.
\end{equation}
Every point of $P$ belongs to $B_1(D_{\rm bad})=\F_N^k\times E$.

Suppose $\ML_{1,1}(B_1(D_{\rm bad}),\phi_1)$ held. Its witnesses at this loss and box would supply a proper partition $(Q_u)$, a retained set $G\subseteq P$ with $|G|\ge|P|/2$, and $q_0\le K$ multiaffine maps per cell, with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:outputwidth}
 \operatorname{width}(Q_u)\ge L^{1/K}=W.
\end{equation}
The partition may depend on $f$, and so may every candidate map. We show the bound uniformly over all those choices.

Fix a cell $Q_u$ and any choice $h$ of its first $k$ coordinates. Its final-coordinate fibre is a proper progression $T$ with
\[
 |T|\ge\operatorname{width}(Q_u)\ge W\ge t_0.
\]
Restrict a candidate $\mu_{u,i}$ to this fibre. By~\eqref{gsr:en:87:eq:multiaffine} it becomes an affine map $x\mapsto ax+b$ on $\F_N$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $a=0$, balance~\eqref{gsr:en:87:eq:balance} bounds its agreement with $f$ by $\beta|T|$, also when its constant value is outside $S$
\item If $a\ne0$, primeness of $N$ makes the map injective, so at most $R$ points of $T$ can have $ax+b\in S$. Agreement with the $S$-valued word $f$ is therefore at most $R$
\end{enumerate}
A union bound valid for either type and any mixture gives
\begin{align}
 \#\{x\in T:f(x)=\mu_{u,i}(h,x)\text{ for some }i<q_0\}
 &\le q_0(\beta|T|+R)\notag\\
 &\le\left(K\beta+\frac{KR}{W}\right)|T|\notag\\
 &\le\left(\frac9{32}+\frac1{32}\right)|T|
 =\frac5{16}|T|.\label{gsr:en:87:eq:fibrebound}
\end{align}
The final inequality is exactly Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:87:lem:width}. Summing over first-coordinate fibres yields at most $5|Q_u|/16$ covered points in the cell. Summing over the disjoint partition cells then gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:contradiction}
 |G|\le\frac5{16}\sum_u|Q_u|=\frac5{16}|P|
 <\frac12|P|\le|G|,
\end{equation}
a contradiction. Every point of $G$ needed coverage because $P\subseteq B_1$.

\paragraph{Potential degeneracies.}
An empty cell has width zero and cannot meet the positive lower bound $W$ in positive dimension. Zero graphs cover no points; zero cells cannot partition nonempty $P$. Properness prevents repetitions from inflating the formal widths. Arbitrary common differences in different cells and wrapping axes are already covered by simultaneous progression balance. The proof does not restrict the number of cells, prescribe a partition, or require the candidate maps to be chosen before the word. It is the established finite-alphabet $5/16$ mechanism, now applied to an input satisfying all contextual fields at the endpoint.

\begin{proof}[Conclusion of the universal negation]
For the fixed $\theta>0$ and $\gamma=1$ in~\eqref{gsr:fm:87:eq:mainconst}, every prime $N\ge N_*$ has the bad witness just constructed. Given any proposed threshold $N_0$ in~\eqref{gsr:fm:87:eq:universal}, choose a prime at least $\max(N_0,N_*)$, possible by unboundedness of primes. The input meets both hypotheses, but one universally quantified witness fails its conclusion. Thus no $N_0$ works. This proves the final assertion of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:87:thm:main} for each $k\ge1$.
\end{proof}

\section[{A good witness for exactly the same input\srctag{87}}]{A good witness for exactly the same input}\label{gsr:en:87:sec:d9}\label{gsr:en:87:sec:good}
\srcnote{87}{Section 9}
Choose a modal symbol $c\in S$ on the interval $E$, and put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:modal}
 E_c=\{x\in E:f(x)=c\},\qquad |E_c|\ge\frac LR.
\end{equation}
Keep $B,\phi,H,J,\phi',x_0$, the actual spectrum relation, and all quantitative parameters unchanged. Only replace $Y_h$ by the cube-domain elements whose final coordinate lies in $E_c$. Call the resulting data $D_{\rm good}$.

For each side, $|Y_h|=N^k|E_c|\ge|X_h|/R$. The selection threshold is small enough:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:goodselection}
 2^{-27}\theta_1^6\le\theta\le\frac1R.
\end{equation}
The value and Bohr-progression clauses remain true for the zero induced function. The common-base good-pair count is $N^k|E_c|\ge(\alpha/R)N^{k+1}$. Its required lower bound still follows since
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:goodmass}
 \theta_2=2^{-32}\theta_1^8\le\theta^2
 =\frac\theta{8R}\le\frac\theta R\le\frac\alpha R.
\end{equation}
The fields concerning $H$, $H\cap J$, cube-domain size, and spectrum are literally unchanged. The identity still holds on the smaller domain by the same zero alternating sum. Hence $D_{\rm good}$ belongs to the same common-base data type as $D_{\rm bad}$.

Its named good domain and translated function are
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:gooddomain}
 B_1(D_{\rm good})=\F_N^k\times E_c,\qquad
 \phi_1(h,x)=c\quad((h,x)\in B_1(D_{\rm good})).
\end{equation}
For any proper input box and any $0<\rho\le1$, take the identity partition, retain the entire carrier and use the one constant graph $c$. The unit graph budget is $\rho^{-A_d}\ge1$, and its positive width exponent is $\rho^{A_d}\le1$. Thus this is an exact $\ML_{1,1}$ certificate, including boxes not contained in the partial domain.

The two witnesses make the quantifier distinction concrete. The input is neither excluded by the source hypotheses nor intrinsically incapable of giving a unit-cover subrelation. The all-selected witness retains too many unrelated final-coordinate values, whereas a permitted modal selection removes that obstruction within the recorded mass budget. The modal argument proves existence only for this family of inputs.

\section[{A sufficient existential repair and its limitations\srctag{87}}]{A sufficient existential repair and its limitations}\label{gsr:en:87:sec:d10}\label{gsr:en:87:sec:repair}
\srcnote{87}{Section 10}
In this section fix $k\ge1$ and return to arbitrary admissible $\theta,\gamma$. Here the source mass parameters are
\[
 \theta_1=(\theta\gamma/4)^{2^{2^{k+5}}},\qquad
 \theta_2=2^{-32}\theta_1^8.
\]
Define a new, presently unproved interface $\operatorname{ELift}(k)$ by preserving the first five quantifier groups and both hypotheses of~\eqref{gsr:fm:87:eq:universal}, and replacing its final clause by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:existential}
 \exists D\in\CB_{\theta,\gamma}(B,\phi):
 \ML_{\gamma,1}\bigl(B_1(D),\phi_1(D)\bigr).
\end{equation}
More explicitly, its threshold is still uniform in $B,\phi$, and it ranges over every sufficiently large prime modulus. The selection $D$ may depend on the structured input. This is a new proposed theorem to prove, not an asserted consequence of the current common-base constructor.

\begin{proposition}[Conditional transport to a large piece]\label{gsr:en:87:prop:transport}
Assume the structured-pair extraction theorem with the preceding-dimensional induction hypotheses, and assume $\operatorname{ELift}(k)$. Then the existing large-piece argument in dimension $k+1$ obtains a unit-multiply-linear subrelation with the same good-mass parameter $\theta_2$ as in the source common-base transport.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Fix admissible $\theta,\gamma$ and take the maximum of $3$, the extraction threshold and the new existential-lifting threshold. For any later prime modulus and a relation $\Gamma$ with the required product property and a projection too large for the small-support alternative, structured extraction yields a partial graph $(B,\phi)$ contained in $\Gamma$ and satisfying $\SP_{\theta,\gamma}$. The relation product property supplies $\PPop_\gamma(B,\phi)$. Apply~\eqref{gsr:en:87:eq:existential} to select $D$ with the unit cover.

Let $U=B_1(D)$, and let $t=(x_0,0)\in\F_N^{k+1}$. Every good pair witnesses a selected cube based at $x_0$. Its all-ones vertex therefore lies in $B$, so $z+t\in B$ for $z\in U$, and $\phi_1(z)=\phi(z+t)$. Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:87:eq:transportrelation}
 \Gamma_D=\{(z+t,\phi_1(z)):z\in U\}\subseteq\Gamma.
\end{equation}
Translation is bijective, the partial graph has one value per point, and the named good-domain cardinality equals the named good-pair count. Thus
\[
 |\Gamma_D|=|U|=\#\{\text{good pairs of }D\}\ge\theta_2N^{k+1}.
\]
Finally, translating boxes preserves properness, widths, partition cardinalities and retained mass. Composing a multiaffine map with a coordinate translation remains multiaffine by expanding~\eqref{gsr:en:87:eq:multiaffine}. Translating the given $\ML_{\gamma,1}$ certificate therefore proves $\ML_{\gamma,1}(\Gamma_D)$ without parameter or mass loss. These are exactly the named statements in \srceightyseven{Proofs16GoodDomainTransport}{the good-domain transport file} and the mass-transport invocation in \srceightyseven{Proofs16ContextualInduction}{the contextual large-piece proof}.
\end{proof}

The original proof first invokes a separate constructor to obtain some common-base witness and then applies a universal lift to that witness. Under~\eqref{gsr:en:87:eq:existential}, that intermediate arbitrary choice and its separate construction threshold are unnecessary: the existential lift already returns compatible data and a cover. The extraction threshold and the new lift threshold suffice for this step, together with the standard $N\ge3$ condition. With the other recorded large-piece-to-induction results as inputs, the same route conditionally yields the corresponding induction step. No general existence proof for~\eqref{gsr:en:87:eq:existential} is supplied here.

\subsection{Other possible changes of interface}
A second possible route would select a witness and then pass to a further good subdomain, with an explicit mass loss and a compatible cover. Any such loss must be propagated into the large-piece bound; it cannot be silently absorbed into the unchanged $\theta_2$. A third route could strengthen the common-base data by a condition forcing the relevant cross-coordinate compatibility. That condition would need an independent construction theorem, and must exclude $D_{\rm bad}$ without excluding all suitable witnesses. A fourth route could weaken the target complexity by allowing a larger iteration parameter. The finite-value certificates show why additional complexity can cover the slab, but this report does not establish an induction with modified quantitative parameters.

These are distinct mathematical tasks. Adding back the product property, spectrum field, all proper-face covers, or the named line-cover input is insufficient: the bad witness already has all of them.

\section[{Comparison with the earlier obstruction\srctag{87}}]{Comparison with the earlier obstruction}\label{gsr:en:87:sec:d11}\label{gsr:en:87:sec:comparison}
\srcnote{87}{Section 11}
The earlier unnumbered sparse-defect note is logically relevant and must be distinguished from the present result. Its source pin was

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 82--94]
\emph{The earlier note is this report's source~74} (Report~286, \emph{Sparse Defects and Local Cover Obstructions}), which has the same pin \texttt{17f048dfa} and proves the obstruction for \emph{every} $k\ge1$ and every $\gamma<1$ on the two-premise interface of Lemma~16.10 (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:74:thm:main}), not only for $k=1$; its witnesses also refute \file{Section16ContextualLiftAt} at every $\gamma<1$ (twelfth write, Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:slabs}). The SHA-256 \texttt{d277529f}\ldots{} recorded for the note is not that of source~74's \TeX{} source and matches no delivered file; the note itself was not delivered.
\end{writenote}
\begin{center}\small\filename{17f048dfa919de04a1989035a2d680ec0865c774}.\end{center}
Its identity is recorded in the companion source manifest. For fixed $0<\gamma<1$, it takes a full-domain map on $\F_N^2$ that is zero away from an interval $J$ of length $\lfloor N^{1/3}\rfloor$ in the final coordinate. A balanced finite word is placed on $J$.

For arbitrary weights, splitting their total mass into $a$ off $J$ and $b$ on $J$ produces the lower bound
\[
 \frac{a^4}{N}+\frac{b^4}{|J|^2}
 \ge\frac{(a+b)^4}{N}
 \left(1+(|J|^2/N)^{1/3}\right)^{-3}.
\]
The coefficient tends to one as $N\to\infty$, so it eventually dominates a fixed $\gamma^8<1$. This proves the original product-property tests while a local box inside $J$ still defeats the unit cover. The full common-base, spectrum, induced-selection and remainder data are also realized there. Consequently that note already rules out a universal implication from the recorded fields; the existence of such an obstruction is not a novelty claim of Report~299.

The present graph-sumset inequality is different: on a partial slab the energy coefficient is exactly one because $|E+E||S+S|<N$. It does not approach one through a vanishing defect. Once $k$ is fixed, $R$ and $\theta$ are fixed and
\[
 \theta<\frac{|E|}{N}\le\frac1{4R}=2\theta
\]
for all sufficiently large primes. The construction works in every positive cube dimension because all initial-coordinate differences vanish. The actual spectrum ceases to be merely the zero frequency, but its finite constant-graph cover remains within the prescribed spectrum budget. Finally, the explicit modal witness identifies a permissible selection repairing this example, rather than relying solely on the logical distinction between a universal and an existential statement.

The concentration method and finite-alphabet obstruction appear in the
\srceightyseven{Proofs16BalancedFieldWord}{balanced-field-word},

\srceightyseven{Proofs16FiniteAlphabetBoxCover}{finite-alphabet box-cover} source files.
The contribution assembled here is their compatibility with the endpoint product property and every actual contextual field. Neither an exhaustive literature-priority claim nor an optimized threshold is intended.

\section[{Conventions and the affine four-point test\srctag{96}}]{Conventions and the affine four-point test}\label{gsr:en:96:sec:d2}
\srcnote{96}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:en:96:sec:affine-definitions}

All groups in the article are written additively. Averages and
probabilities are uniform unless another measure is stated. Additive
energies and convolutions in the next three sections are
\emph{unnormalized}; Fourier coefficients and uniformity averages in
the later sections are normalized. This distinction is essential.

Let $G,K$ be finite abelian groups and put $N=|G|$. An affine map is
\[
 \ell(x)=L(x)+b,\qquad L\in\Hom(G,K),\quad b\in K.
\]
For $f:G\to K$, define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:affine-defect}
 \varepsilon(f)=\Prob_{x,y,z\in G}
 [f(x)+f(y)\ne f(z)+f(x+y-z)].
\end{equation}
Equivalently, if $\Gamma_f=\{(x,f(x)):x\in G\}$ and
\[
 E(\Gamma_f)=\#\{(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4):x_1+x_2=x_3+x_4,
 \ f(x_1)+f(x_2)=f(x_3)+f(x_4)\},
\]
then $\varepsilon(f)=1-E(\Gamma_f)/N^3$. Repeated points are included.
Subtracting an affine map leaves this defect unchanged.

Fix any affine reference $\ell$, put $r=f-\ell$, and write
\[
 S=\{x:r(x)\ne0\},\qquad s=|S|,\qquad t=s/N.
\]
The reference need not be a nearest affine map. For $a\in K\setminus\{0\}$
let $S_a=\{x:r(x)=a\}$ and $n_a=|S_a|$, with $n_0=0$ by convention.
Introduce
\begin{align}
 M&=\sum_a n_a^2,& A&=s^2-M, & C&=\sum_a n_a n_{-a},\label{gsr:en:96:eq:label-stats}\\
 Z&=\sum_{a+b=c}n_a n_b n_c,&
 \Delta&=s^3-E(S),\label{gsr:en:96:eq:support-stats}
\end{align}
where $E(S)=\#\{(x,y,z,w)\in S^4:x+y=z+w\}$.
Thus $A$ counts ordered pairs of support points carrying distinct error
labels, $C$ counts those carrying opposite labels, and $\Delta$ counts
ordered triples $x,y,z\in S$ for which $x+y-z$ falls outside $S$.
All five quantities are nonnegative.

\begin{lemma}[Elementary support-energy bound]\label{gsr:en:96:lem:coset-energy}
For a nonempty finite set $S$ in an abelian group, $E(S)\le s^3$,
with equality if and only if $S$ is a coset of a subgroup.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Every triple $(x,y,z)\in S^3$ has at most one fourth point $x+y-z$,
so the inequality is immediate. In the equality case this fourth
point always belongs to $S$. Fix $z_0\in S$. The translated set
$H=S-z_0$ contains zero and is closed under $u+v-w$; hence it is
closed under addition and negation and is a subgroup. The converse
follows directly from closure in a coset.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Odd-target label inequalities]\label{gsr:en:96:lem:label-inequalities}
If $K$ has no nonzero element of order two, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:schur-bounds}
 0\le C\le A,\qquad 2Z\le sA.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Nonzero opposite labels are distinct, so the pairs counted by $C$
form a subset of the pairs counted by $A$.
For any three nonzero labels $a,b,c$, at most one of
$a+b=c$, $a+c=b$, and $b+c=a$ can hold: two such equations would
give a nonzero element annihilated by two. If exactly two labels
coincide, the sum of the three equation indicators is at most one;
if all three coincide, it is zero. In all cases,
\[
 2\bigl(\one_{a+b=c}+\one_{a+c=b}+\one_{b+c=a}\bigr)
 \le \one_{a\ne b}+\one_{a\ne c}+\one_{b\ne c}.
\]
Multiply by $n_a n_b n_c$ and sum. The two sides become $6Z$ and
$3sA$, respectively.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A signed-graph identity and a new coupled bound\srctag{96}}]{A signed-graph identity and a new coupled bound}\label{gsr:en:96:sec:d3}
\srcnote{96}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:en:96:sec:signed-graph}

For real functions on a finite abelian group, write
$(u*v)(z)=\sum_xu(x)v(z-x)$ and $\ip uv=\sum_xu(x)v(x)$.
For a set, the same letter inside a convolution denotes its indicator.
On $G\times K$ put
\[
 P=\one_{\{(x,r(x)):x\in S\}},\quad B=\one_{S\times\{0\}},
 \quad D=P-B,\quad L_0=\one_{G\times\{0\}}.
\]
The full graph indicator is $L_0+D$. Set $E_D=\norm{D*D}_2^2$.

\begin{lemma}[Exact signed-graph identity]\label{gsr:en:96:lem:signed-identity}
With the preceding notation,
\begin{align}
 E(\Gamma_r)={}&N^3-4sN^2+N(6s^2+4M+2C)\nonumber\\
 &-4s^3-8sM-4sC+4Z+E_D.
 \label{gsr:en:96:eq:signed-identity}
\end{align}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $\mu:K\to\Z$ have $\mu(0)=-s$ and $\mu(a)=n_a$ for $a\ne0$.
Then $L_0*L_0=NL_0$, $L_0*D(x,a)=\mu(a)$, and
$\sum_x(D*D)(x,a)=(\mu*\mu)(a)$.
Expand the squared norm of
\[
 (L_0+D)*(L_0+D)=NL_0+2L_0*D+D*D.
\]
The constant term is $N^3$, the first cross term is $-4sN^2$,
and the two quadratic terms are $4N(s^2+M)$ and $2N(s^2+C)$.
The remaining cross term is
\[
 4\sum_a\mu(a)(\mu*\mu)(a)
 =4Z-8sM-4sC-4s^3.
\]
The last square is $E_D$. Combining the terms proves the identity.
\end{proof}

The identity is already implicit in the signed-graph treatment of source
59. The improvement is to bound its last term while retaining the
\emph{same missing triples} that enter $Z$.

Define $W$ to count triples $(x,y,z)\in S^3$ satisfying both
\[
 r(x)+r(y)=r(z),\qquad x+y-z\in S.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:missing-triples}
 0\le Z-W\le\min\{Z,\Delta\}.
\end{equation}
The second restriction excludes a subset of precisely the $\Delta$
triples missing from the support energy. Bounding these two losses
independently would discard this information.

\begin{lemma}[Coupled signed-energy bound]\label{gsr:en:96:lem:coupled-energy}
For arbitrary finite abelian $G,K$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:coupled-energy}
 E_D\le2E(S)+4sM+2sC-4W.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Expand $\norm{P*P-2P*B+B*B}_2^2$.
The supports of $P*B$ and $B*B$ have disjoint target coordinates,
since all labels on $S$ are nonzero. The resulting exact expression is
\begin{align*}
 E_D={}&E(\Gamma_{r|S})+E(S)
 +4\sum_a\norm{S_a*S}_2^2\\
 &+2\sum_a\ip{S_a*S_{-a}}{S*S}-4W.
\end{align*}
Projection to $G$ gives $E(\Gamma_{r|S})\le E(S)$.
For the mixed energy, use the difference representation:
\[
 \norm{S_a*S}_2^2
 =\sum_h |S_a\cap(S_a+h)|\,|S\cap(S+h)|\le s n_a^2.
\]
Also $(S*S)(z)\le s$, whence
$\ip{S_a*S_{-a}}{S*S}\le s n_a n_{-a}$.
Substitution proves the stated upper bound. The negative term $-4W$
has been retained exactly.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Coupled support and label remainder]\label{gsr:en:96:thm:affine-remainder}
Let $K$ have odd order, let $f:G\to K$, and let $\ell$ be any affine
reference. With the statistics of Section~\ref{gsr:en:96:sec:affine-definitions},
\begin{align}
 N^3\bigl(\varepsilon(f)-\Psi(t)\bigr)
 \ge{}&2\Delta+2(N-s)(2A-C)-4\min\{Z,\Delta\}
 \label{gsr:en:96:eq:remainder-before-schur}\\
 ={}&(2N-3s)A+2(N-s)(A-C)+(sA-2Z)
        +2|\Delta-Z|\nonumber\\
 \ge{}&(2N-3s)A+|2\Delta-sA|+2(N-s)(A-C).
 \label{gsr:en:96:eq:affine-remainder}
\end{align}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Subtract the cubic from the defect in \eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:signed-identity}:
\begin{align*}
 N^3(\varepsilon-\Psi(t))
 =6s^3+(4N-8s)A+(4s-2N)C-4Z-E_D.
\end{align*}
Insert \eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:coupled-energy}, use $E(S)=s^3-\Delta$,
and simplify. This gives
\[
 2\Delta+2(N-s)(2A-C)-4(Z-W),
\]
which proves \eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:remainder-before-schur} by
\eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:missing-triples}. Now use $Z\le sA/2$ from
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:96:lem:label-inequalities} and the elementary identity
\[
 2\Delta-4\min\{\Delta,sA/2\}=|2\Delta-sA|-sA.
\]
This yields \eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:affine-remainder}. All steps remain valid when
$S$ is empty.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The affine cubic: full range, equality, and stability\srctag{96}}]{The affine cubic: full range, equality, and stability}\label{gsr:en:96:sec:d4}
\srcnote{96}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:en:96:sec:affine-consequences}

\begin{theorem}[The full positive range of the affine cubic]
\label{gsr:en:96:thm:affine-cubic}
Suppose $K$ has odd order. For every $f:G\to K$ and every affine
reference $\ell$, with $t=\Prob[f\ne\ell]$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:global-cubic}
 \boxed{\varepsilon(f)\ge4t-10t^2+6t^3.}
\end{equation}
If $0<t<2/3$, equality holds if and only if
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:affine-equality}
 f(x)=\ell(x)+b\one_{x_0+H}(x)
\end{equation}
for a subgroup $H\le G$, a coset $x_0+H$, and a nonzero $b\in K$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $t\le2/3$, every term on the right of
\eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:affine-remainder} is nonnegative: $2N-3s\ge0$,
$A\ge C$, and $N\ge s$. This proves the inequality there.
For $t\ge2/3$, $\Psi(t)=2t(1-t)(2-3t)\le0$, while
$\varepsilon(f)\ge0$, proving it on the remaining range.

If $0<t<2/3$ and equality holds, the coefficient of $A$ in
\eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:affine-remainder} is positive, so $A=0$. Thus there is
exactly one nonzero error label $b$. The absolute-value term then
forces $\Delta=0$, and Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:96:lem:coset-energy} makes $S$ a coset.
Conversely, if $r=b\one_S$ and $S$ is a coset, then $M=s^2$,
$C=Z=0$, and $E_D=6E(S)=6s^3$. The factor $6$ follows from
\[
 (\delta_b-\delta_0)*(\delta_b-\delta_0)
 =\delta_{2b}-2\delta_b+\delta_0:
\]
its three positions are distinct because $b\ne0$ and $2b\ne0$.
Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:signed-identity} now gives equality in the cubic.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Place in the report} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:oddaffine}). This answers both halves of source~59's Question~\ref{gsr:fz:59:q:affine-range}, with no condition on the three-torsion of the target. \emph{Source~67 proved the full range first for elementary abelian $3$-groups} (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:67:cthree:local}); this source, which does not cite source~67 (an unplaced archive at its pin), extends it to every odd-order target. Checked at the write, exhaustively: no violation on $58{,}078$ maps of ten (domain, odd target) pairs with every affine reference at $t\le2/3$, and a violation $-1/4$ for $\Z/4\Z\to\Z/2\Z$ (\file{verify14.py}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{corollary}[The endpoint $t=2/3$]\label{gsr:en:96:cor:affine-endpoint}
At $t=2/3$, equality in \eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:global-cubic} holds exactly when
$f-\ell$ is affine, its linear part has image of order three, and
its affine image contains zero. In particular, equality is impossible
at this endpoint if either $G$ or $K$ has order coprime to three.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Here $\Psi(t)=0$, so equality means the four-point test never fails.
Taking $z=0$ shows that $r(x)-r(0)$ is a homomorphism; conversely
an affine map passes every test. A nonempty zero fiber of an affine
map has size $N/|\operatorname{im}L|$. Since its zero fraction is
$1/3$, the image of its linear part has order three. The affine image must
contain zero, and these conditions are also sufficient.
\end{proof}

This endpoint also explains the natural limit of the nontrivial range:
a nonconstant affine map with a three-element image may disagree with
the zero affine reference at exactly $2/3$ of the domain and still
have zero defect. The theorem therefore cannot force positive rejection
at every positive disagreement with an arbitrary reference.

\begin{corollary}[Quantitative information near equality]
\label{gsr:en:96:cor:affine-near-equality}
Suppose $0<t<2/3$ and put $\rho=\varepsilon(f)-\Psi(t)$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:affine-stability}
 \frac{A}{N^2}\le\frac{\rho}{2-3t},\qquad
 \frac{\Delta}{N^3}\le\frac{\rho}{2}
             \max\left\{1,\frac{t}{2-3t}\right\}.
\end{equation}
Some nonzero label $b$ occurs on all but at most
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:modal-error}
 \frac{\rho}{t(2-3t)}N
\end{equation}
points of the error support. In particular,
\[
 E(S)\ge s^3\left(1-\frac{\rho}{2t^3}
             \max\left\{1,\frac{t}{2-3t}\right\}\right).
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Divide \eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:affine-remainder} by $N^3$ and write
$a=A/N^2$, $\delta=\Delta/N^3$. It gives
$\rho\ge(2-3t)a$ and, retaining that first term when estimating
the absolute value, $2\delta\le\rho+(4t-2)a$.
If $t\le1/2$, the latter is at most $\rho$. If $t\ge1/2$, use
$a\le\rho/(2-3t)$ to obtain $2\delta\le t\rho/(2-3t)$.
If $n_b=\max_a n_a$, then $M\le n_b s$, so
$s-n_b\le A/s$. This proves \eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:modal-error} and the remaining claim.
\end{proof}

The stability statement deliberately stops at a label concentration and
an additive-energy conclusion. Converting near-maximal set energy into
a particular edit distance from a coset requires another theorem with its
own constants. The exact equality classification needed no such input.

\begin{example}[Sharpness and the importance of odd targets]
For $G=\Z/n\Z$, a singleton error $r=b\one_{\{0\}}$ gives
\[
 \varepsilon(r)=\frac4n-\frac{10}{n^2}+\frac6{n^3}
\]
for every nonzero odd-order label $b$. Thus the coefficients of the
cubic are met along arbitrarily small nonzero error fractions. More
generally, every coset gives equality at its reciprocal-index density.
If $G=K=\Z/2\Z$ and $r$ is the identity homomorphism, then
$t=1/2$ and $\varepsilon(r)=0<\Psi(1/2)=1/4$. Hence the target
hypothesis cannot be deleted.
\end{example}

\subsection{Stability and a positive gap at the endpoint}
\label{gsr:en:96:sec:affine-endpoint-stability}

The equality statement at $t=2/3$ has a quantitative counterpart.
The correction input in this subsection is classical: it is
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:96:boot:cor:sharp-affine}, with its proof and attribution
in Appendix~\ref{gsr:en:96:boot:sec:sharp-correction}. The deductions below
combine that correction theorem with the cubic proved here and the
possible sizes of affine zero fibers.

For $0\le e<2/9$, let $\omega(e)$ be the unique number in
$[0,1/4]$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:endpoint-inverse}
 \Psi(\omega(e))=e,
 \qquad \Psi(u)=4u-10u^2+6u^3.
\end{equation}
This is well defined: $\Psi(0)=0$, $\Psi(1/4)=15/32>2/9$,
and $\Psi'(u)\ge1/8$ on $[0,1/4]$.

\begin{proposition}[Order-three structure near the endpoint]
\label{gsr:en:96:prop:affine-endpoint-stability}
Let $G,K$ be finite abelian groups with $|K|$ odd. Let $f:G\to K$,
let $\ell$ be any affine reference, and put
\[
 r=f-\ell,\qquad t=\Prob[r\ne0],\qquad
 \delta=|t-2/3|,\qquad e=\varepsilon(f).
\]
If $e<2/9$, there is an affine map $a:G\to K$ with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:endpoint-corrected-distance}
 \Prob[r\ne a]\le\omega(e).
\end{equation}
If also
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:endpoint-radius}
 \delta+\omega(e)<\frac{2}{15},
\end{equation}
then $a$ has a linear part with image of order three and its affine
image contains zero. Its zero set is a coset of an index-three
subgroup, and it differs from the zero set of $r$ on at most
$\omega(e)|G|$ points.

In particular, when $t=2/3$, all these conclusions hold for every
$e<2/9$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Subtracting $\ell$ preserves the rejection probability. Classical
affine correction gives an affine $a$ with
\[
 u:=\Prob[r\ne a]\le B(e)<\frac19<\frac14.
\]
Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:96:thm:affine-cubic} to $r$ with reference $a$.
It gives $e\ge\Psi(u)$. The monotonicity on $[0,1/4]$ therefore
implies $u\le\omega(e)$.

Let $q=\Prob[a=0]$. The two zero indicators differ only where
$r\ne a$, so
\[
 |q-1/3|\le |\Prob[r=0]-1/3|+u
             \le\delta+\omega(e).
\]
Under \eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:endpoint-radius}, this gives $1/5<q<7/15$.
In particular, the zero fiber is nonempty. Write $a(x)=L(x)+c$.
Its zero fiber has density $1/j$, where
$j=|\operatorname{im}L|$ is odd because $|K|$ is odd.
The only reciprocal of a positive odd integer in $(1/5,7/15)$
is $1/3$. Hence $j=3$, proving the structural conclusions.

At the exact endpoint $\delta=0$, the radius condition is automatic:
\[
 \Psi(2/15)=\frac{416}{1125}>\frac29>e,
\]
so monotonicity gives $\omega(e)<2/15$.
\end{proof}

The inverse modulus also records the small-error scale:
\[
 \omega(e)=\frac e4+\frac{5e^2}{32}
                    +\frac{11e^3}{64}+O(e^4).
\]
This is a derived endpoint consequence, rather than a new general
homomorphism-correction threshold.

\begin{corollary}[Gap when an order-three image is impossible]
\label{gsr:en:96:cor:affine-endpoint-gap}
In the same setting, suppose $3\nmid|G|$ or $3\nmid|K|$.
If $\delta=|t-2/3|<2/15$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:affine-endpoint-gap}
 \varepsilon(f)\ge
 \min\left\{\frac29,\,
       \Psi\left(\frac{2}{15}-\delta\right)\right\}.
\end{equation}
In particular, if $t=2/3$ and $3\nmid|K|$, then
$\varepsilon(f)\ge2/9$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The conclusion is immediate if $e\ge2/9$. Otherwise use the affine
approximant from the preceding proof, with $u<1/4$. Every affine
zero fiber is either empty or has density $1/j$ for a positive odd
integer $j$. The hypotheses rule out $j=3$, so its distance from
$1/3$ is at least $2/15$. The zero-indicator comparison gives
\[
 u\ge\frac{2}{15}-\delta.
\]
Both sides lie in $[0,1/4]$. The cubic and its monotonicity give
$e\ge\Psi(u)\ge\Psi(2/15-\delta)$, proving the bound.
At $\delta=0$, use $\Psi(2/15)=416/1125>2/9$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{The endpoint gap.} With the example of Section~\ref{gsr:en:96:sec:d4} ($8/27$ for $\Z/3\Z\to\Z/5\Z$, rechecked at the write) the infimum at $t=2/3$ with $3\nmid|K|$ lies in $[2/9,8/27]$. The intake found $8/27$ as the least value in every small case it enumerated ($\Z/3\Z\to\Z/5\Z$, $\Z/6\Z\to\Z/5\Z$, $\Z/3\Z\to\Z/7\Z$); that is evidence, not a proof (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:affineenvelope}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{example}[Sharp radius and an upper endpoint obstruction]
\label{gsr:en:96:ex:affine-endpoint-obstructions}
The strict radius $2/15$ in \eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:endpoint-radius} cannot be
increased, or made non-strict, uniformly over these groups. Take
$G=K=\Z/5\Z$, $\ell=0$, and $r(x)=x$. Then $e=\omega(e)=0$,
$t=4/5$, and $|t-2/3|=2/15$, while no order-three linear image
is possible.

For a different obstruction at the exact endpoint, take
$G=\Z/3\Z$, $K=\Z/5\Z$, $\ell=0$, and
$r(0)=0$, $r(1)=1$, $r(2)=-1$. Then $t=2/3$. For horizontal
difference zero, the graph-difference multiplicity is $3$; for each
of the other two differences, the multiplicities are $2$ and $1$.
Thus the graph energy is $3^2+2(2^2+1^2)=19$ and
\[
 \varepsilon(r)=1-\frac{19}{27}=\frac{8}{27}.
\]
Consequently the infimum of the endpoint defect over all such maps
into odd-order targets with $3\nmid|K|$ lies in
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:affine-endpoint-bracket}
 \left[\frac29,\frac{8}{27}\right].
\end{equation}
The exact endpoint gap is not determined here. A sharper research
question is to determine this infimum and the structure of maps
approaching it, and to determine the optimal endpoint stability
modulus and its range beyond the present $e<2/9$ correction regime.
\end{example}

\subsection{A weighted extension with independent labels}
\label{gsr:en:96:sec:affine-weighted}

The argument also permits a probability distribution on the target at
each domain point. Let $p_x(a)\ge0$ for $x\in G$, $a\in K$, with
$\sum_a p_x(a)=1$. Define
\[
 E(p)=\sum_{x+y=z+w}\ \sum_{a+b=c+d}
          p_x(a)p_y(b)p_z(c)p_w(d),\qquad
 \varepsilon(p)=1-\frac{E(p)}{N^3}.
\]
This is the rejection probability when the four labels are drawn
independently at their four occurrences, including repeated domain
coordinates. Relative to an affine reference $\ell$, put
\[
 S_a(x)=p_x(\ell(x)+a)\quad(a\ne0),\qquad
 S(x)=1-p_x(\ell(x)),\qquad s=\sum_xS(x),\quad t=s/N.
\]
Define $n_a=\sum_xS_a(x)$ and $M,A,C,Z$ as in
Section~\ref{gsr:en:96:sec:affine-definitions}. For the weighted support use
$E(S)=\sum_{x+y=z+w}S(x)S(y)S(z)S(w)$ and $\Delta=s^3-E(S)$.

\begin{theorem}[Weighted affine stability]\label{gsr:en:96:thm:affine-weighted}
If $K$ has odd order, the complete remainder
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:96:thm:affine-remainder} holds with these definitions.
Consequently $\varepsilon(p)\ge\Psi(t)$.
For $0<t<2/3$, equality holds exactly for deterministic distributions
concentrated on a map of the form
$\ell+b\one_{x_0+H}$, where $b\ne0$ and $H\le G$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Replace the graph and support indicators by their nonnegative weights
in the convolution expansions. The zero-label weight is $1-S$,
so the signed identity is unchanged. The bounds for mixed energies
continue to hold because $0\le S\le1$; for example
$\sum_xS(x)S(x+h)\le s$. Dropping the relation on four labels bounds
the weighted nonzero graph energy by $E(S)$. The mass of compatible
three-label patterns that fails to complete into the weighted support is
at most
\[
 \sum_{x,y,z} S(x)S(y)S(z)\bigl(1-S(x+y-z)\bigr)
     =s^3-E(S)=\Delta,
\]
and is also at most $Z$. The two label inequalities hold for
nonnegative real masses by their identical weighted counting proofs.
All the algebra in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:96:thm:affine-remainder} therefore applies.

In a positive-range equality case it forces $A=0$ and $\Delta=0$.
Write $r_S(h)=\sum_xS(x)S(x+h)$. Equality in
$\sum_h r_S(h)^2\le s\sum_hr_S(h)=s^3$, and $r_S(0)>0$, force
$r_S(0)=s$. Hence $\sum_xS(x)^2=\sum_xS(x)$, making $S$ an
indicator. Since $A=0$, all nonzero-label mass is concentrated at one
label, and the row sums make every distribution deterministic.
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:96:thm:affine-cubic} completes the equality classification.
\end{proof}

The sampling convention matters. Drawing one random function and
reusing its label at every repeated coordinate generally gives a
different energy. That correlated model is not asserted here.

\gsrnewfloats
\section{Source~98: third-energy rigidity and the index-two fingerprints \wtag}\label{gsr:en:sec:thirdenergy}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the fourteenth write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next eight sections are source~98's Sections~2--9. \emph{Logically they close the hereditary block} of sources~75--81 (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:hereditary}) and~82, 83, 85 (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:spikes}): for a full-domain map $a:G\to H$ between abelian groups, $r_m(a)$ is the infimum over finitely supported weights of the fraction of additive $2m$-tuples whose equality of sums $a$ respects, and $r_{m,\mathrm{ind}}$ the same over indicator weights; the hereditary chain studied $r=r_2$. The introduction, with the three main theorems, is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:98:sec:d1}.

\emph{What is proved.} $a$ is affine iff $r_3(a)>5/8$ iff $r_{3,\mathrm{ind}}(a)>5/8$, sharp on~$\Z$ (integer parity has $r_3=5/8$, never attained; Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:98:he:main}); in the index-two family, a defect of order two has $r_m=1/2+2^{-m}$ and a defect of order $d>m/2$ has $r_m=2^{1-2m}\binom{2m}m$, so the fourth energy separates the defect orders that the second and third do not (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:98:he:fingerprints}); maps affine on every cyclic coset satisfy $r_m\le J_m=1/2+2^{1-2m}$, sharp at $st$ on $\F_2^2$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:98:he:jensen-main}). One step is computer-assisted: a finite certificate on cyclic domains of orders three to five, with a proved reduction to arbitrary targets (Section~\ref{gsr:en:98:sec:d6}); it is listed with the report's other finite certificates as a trust boundary.

\emph{Credits.} Source~98 credits Report~288, which is source~76: at $m=2$ its formulas give back source~76's $3/4$ and conditional $5/8$. Its sum-of-squares equality case $e*e=o*o$ is source~77's fixed-weight criterion, and $J_2=5/8$ is also source~78's $(P)$-branch bound; its \TeX{} cites neither (dated notes below). \emph{The constant $5/8$, by energy order}: source~76's conditional bound is $J_2$ and source~85's $\eta_4$ (the point spike of order two), both for $m=2$ and the same extremal object (thirteenth write); source~80's $5/8$ is the fixed-target maximum at $N=4$, also $m=2$; source~98's threshold is for $m=3$.

\emph{Checked at the write} (\file{verify14.py}): $Q_{m,d}=2^{1-2m}\sum_\ell\binom{2m}{m+2d\ell}$ equals $1/2+2^{-m}$ at $d=2$ and $2^{1-2m}\binom{2m}m$ for $d>m/2$ ($m\le15$), so $r_3=5/8$ for every defect order and $r_4=9/16$ or $35/64$, and $Q_{6,3}=463/1024$ lies in the open intermediate range; on $\F_2^2$ with $a(s,t)=st$ the indicator minimum is exactly $J_m$ for $m=2,\ldots,5$. The intake found no nonaffine map above $5/8$ at $m=3$ on $31$ small group pairs, and none above $9/16$ at $m=4$ on $22$ (evidence for source~98's Question~1, not proof).

\emph{Formal status} (HEAD \texttt{a0c3e9b67}): only the order-two count is formal, \file{phiAdditiveCount} (\file{Definitions}:301) with \file{IsPhiAdditive} (\file{Definitions}:295), and Gowers's Proposition~6.1 and Lemma~6.2 (exact). No hereditary infimum, higher-order respected-tuple count or index-two family is formalized. Its questions are merged into item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:hereditary}.
