Finally, $\BBsf(\one_{b+K})=0$ is equivalent to $K+2H=H$, or equivalently to $H/K$ having odd order. This proves both directions.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Exact separation of torsion and geometry]
Formula~\eqref{gsr:en:103:eq:identity} has three independent pieces of information: $\BBsf$ records parity imbalance, $e$ records failure of the holes to be a coset, and $\WWsf$ records the extra forbidden five-, six-, and seven-hit patterns. It is stronger than a single upper bound. In odd order the first obstruction vanishes, while the other two are nonnegative in the small-hole range.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Recovery of the exact coset-deletion formula}
Let $R=b+K\subset H$, put $r=\abs K$, $q=\abs{H/K}$, and $\tau=\abs{(H/K)[2]}$. For the characters trivial on $K$, the fourth power of the signed mass is $r^4$, and the other characters contribute zero. Thus
\[
 \BBsf(\one_R)=(\tau-1)r^4.
\]
Since $e=\WWsf=0$, Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:103:thm:identity} gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:103:eq:cosetdelete}
 \CkS_3(H\setminus R)=r^4\bigl(q^4-8q^3+28q^2-44q+21+2\tau\bigr).
\end{equation}
Writing $n=(q-1)r$ and $\delta=1/(q-1)$, this becomes
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:103:eq:parityprofile}
 \eps_3(H\setminus R)=P(\delta)-2(\tau-1)\delta^4.
\end{equation}
This exact deletion formula was already available in \cite{srconehundredone}; it is recovered here as a transparent special case, not claimed as a new result. What is new in our argument is the decomposition controlling arbitrary and fractional hole functions around it.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Why the coefficient 35 cannot be lowered\srctag{103}}]{Why the coefficient 35 cannot be lowered}\label{gsr:en:103:sec:d5}\label{gsr:en:103:sec:optimal35}
\srcnote{103}{Section 5}

\begin{theorem}[Optimal universal tail-energy coefficient]\label{gsr:en:103:thm:35}
For a subset $R$ of any finite abelian group, with $r=\abs R$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:103:eq:35ineq}
 \TT(R)+35r^4\le35r\bigl(r^3-\EEsf(R)\bigr).
\end{equation}
No constant smaller than $35$ can replace the coefficient on the right uniformly, even if the groups are restricted to odd cyclic groups.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The inequality is an immediate rearrangement of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:103:thm:tail}. For sharpness, take
\[
 R_m=\{1,B,B^2,\ldots,B^{m-1}\}\subset\Z/N_m\Z,
\]
where $B=10$ and $N_m$ is odd and larger than $20B^m$. All relations used below then lift to integer relations without wraparound. Uniqueness of base-$B$ expansions gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:103:eq:sparseenergy}
 \EEsf(R_m)=2m^2-m.
\end{equation}
Indeed, equal sums of two powers have the same unordered pair of exponents.

Every five-subset correlation is $O(m^3)$. For the forty-eight sets in $\mathcal P_5$, this follows from $N_S=m\EEsf(R_m)$. For the eight other sets, cube symmetry reduces to the cap $\{000,100,010,001,111\}$. Prescribing its values produces the relation
\[
 a+b+c=d+2e.
\]
Base-$B$ uniqueness requires equality of exponent multisets. If $d=e$ there are $m$ possibilities. If $d\ne e$, there are $m(m-1)$ choices of $(d,e)$ and three placements of $d$ on the left. Thus the cap correlation is exactly
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:103:eq:sparsecap}
 3m^2-2m.
\end{equation}
Since $0\le b(k)\le\binom{k}{5}$ for $0\le k\le8$, equation~\eqref{gsr:en:103:eq:tailpattern} yields $\abs{\TT(R_m)}=O(m^3)$. Therefore
\[
 \frac{\TT(R_m)+35m^4}{m(m^3-\EEsf(R_m))}
 =\frac{35m^4+O(m^3)}{m^4-2m^3+m^2}\longrightarrow35.
\]
A smaller universal coefficient is impossible.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Optimality of this coefficient does not imply optimality of the density cutoff $12/35$ in Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:103:cor:complement}. A better inequality could use additional structure relating $e$ and $\WWsf$, rather than only their separate nonnegativity.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A weighted subgroup-boundary inequality\srctag{103}}]{A weighted subgroup-boundary inequality}\label{gsr:en:103:sec:d6}\label{gsr:en:103:sec:boundary}
\srcnote{103}{Section 6}
The set version of the next estimate, with the same constant, is an antecedent from \cite{srconehundredone}. We give a proof that also handles fractional exterior weights.

\begin{theorem}[Weighted boundary estimate]\label{gsr:en:103:thm:boundary}
Let $H$ be a finite subgroup of an abelian group, $h=\abs H$, and let $d:G\to[0,1]$ be finitely supported outside $H$, with mass $s$. For every $k\ge1$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:103:eq:boundary}
 \CkS_k(\one_H+d)\le h^{k+1}+(2^{k+1}-2)hs^k+s^{k+1}.
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:103:eq:boundary3}
 \CkS_3(\one_H+d)-h^4\le14hs^3+s^4.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The case $k=1$ is the identity $(h+s)^2=h^2+2hs+s^2$. The case $s=0$ is immediate, so suppose $s>0$. Set $a=\one_H+d$ and $a_t(x)=a(x)a(x+t)$. Then
\[
 \CkS_k(a)=\sum_t\CkS_{k-1}(a_t).
\]
Put
\[
 z_t=\sum_xd(x)d(x+t),\qquad R_H=\sum_{t\in H}z_t.
\]
One has $0\le z_t\le s$, $\sum_tz_t=s^2$, and $R_H\le s^2$.
For $t\in H$, $a_t=\one_H+d(x)d(x+t)$, so induction gives, with $c_{k-1}=2^k-2$,
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{t\in H}\CkS_{k-1}(a_t)
 &\le h^{k+1}+c_{k-1}h\sum_{t\in H}z_t^{k-1}
       +\sum_{t\in H}z_t^k\\
 &\le h^{k+1}+c_{k-1}hs^{k-2}R_H+s^{k-1}R_H.
\end{align*}
Here $k\ge2$, so all exponents are nonnegative.

For $t\notin H$, the mass of $a_t$ is $c_t+z_t$, where
\[
 c_t=\sum_x\bigl(\one_H(x)d(x+t)+d(x)\one_H(x+t)\bigr).
\]
We claim $c_t+2z_t\le2s$. Indeed,
\[
 z_t\le\sum_{x\notin H,\ x+t\notin H}d(x),\qquad
 z_t\le\sum_{x\notin H,\ x+t\notin H}d(x+t),
\]
and the omitted masses in these two sums are exactly the two terms in $c_t$. Also $\sum_{t\notin H}c_t=2hs$.

Convexity on the triangle $c,z\ge0$, $c+2z\le2s$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:103:eq:triangle}
 (c+z)^k\le(2s)^{k-1}c+s^{k-1}z.
\end{equation}
To see this directly, express $(c,z)$ as a convex combination of $(0,0)$, $(2s,0)$ and $(0,s)$ and apply convexity of $(c+z)^k$. By Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:103:lem:domination},
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{t\notin H}\CkS_{k-1}(a_t)
 &\le\sum_{t\notin H}(c_t+z_t)^k\\
 &\le2^khs^k+s^{k-1}(s^2-R_H).
\end{align*}
Combining the two ranges cancels the $s^{k-1}R_H$ terms. The remaining contribution $c_{k-1}hs^{k-2}R_H$ is at most $c_{k-1}hs^k$. Since $c_{k-1}+2^k=2^{k+1}-2$, the induction closes.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The exact local inequality, with all defects retained\srctag{103}}]{The exact local inequality, with all defects retained}\label{gsr:en:103:sec:d7}\label{gsr:en:103:sec:local}
\srcnote{103}{Section 7}
Translate the comparison coset to $H$. For $a:G\to[0,1]$, define its holes and exterior part by
\[
 f=(1-a)|_H,\qquad d=a\one_{G\setminus H},\qquad
 r=\sum_Hf,\quad s=\sum_{G\setminus H}d.
\]
Thus
\[
 n=M(a)=h-r+s,\qquad \delta=\frac{r+s}{n},\qquad y=\frac sn.
\]
The definitions of $e(f),\BBsf(f),\WWsf(f)$ refer to the group $H$.

\begin{theorem}[Local defect refinement, arbitrary torsion]\label{gsr:en:103:thm:localdefect}
If $n>0$ and $\delta\le1/50$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:103:eq:localdefect}
 \eps_3(a)\ge P(\delta)+\frac72\delta\frac sn
 +\frac{(12h-35r)e(f)+\WWsf(f)-2\BBsf(f)}{n^4}.
\end{equation}
Moreover $12h-35r>11h$ in this range.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Separate cubes lying wholly inside $H$ from those with an exterior vertex. For the latter, increasing the values inside $H$ to one can only increase their contribution. Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:103:thm:boundary} and the exact complement identity imply
\begin{align}\label{gsr:en:103:eq:localupper}
 \CkS_3(a)\le\Psf(h,r)+14hs^3+s^4
       +2\BBsf(f)-(12h-35r)e(f)-\WWsf(f).
\end{align}
Set $x=r/n$ and $y=s/n$. Then $x+y=\delta$, $h/n=1+x-y$, and $(h-r)/n=1-y$. The polynomial part of the right-hand side, divided by $n^4$, is
\begin{align}\label{gsr:en:103:eq:F}
 F(x,y)={}&(1-y)^4-4x(1-y)^3+10x^2(1-y)^2-8x^3(1-y)\notag\\
          &+14(1+x-y)y^3+y^4.
\end{align}
One has $F(\delta,0)=1-P(\delta)$ and the exact factorization
\begin{align}\label{gsr:en:103:eq:G}
 \frac{F(\delta-y,y)-F(\delta,0)}y
 ={}&-8\delta+4y+4\delta^2+4\delta y+10y^2\notag\\
    &+8\delta^3-14\delta^2y+22\delta y^2-28y^3
\end{align}
when $y\ne0$, with the natural polynomial interpretation at $y=0$. For $0\le y\le\delta\le1/50$, drop the negative cubic terms and use $y\le\delta$ to obtain
\[
 \frac{F(\delta-y,y)-F(\delta,0)}y
 \le-\delta(4-18\delta-30\delta^2)\le-\frac72\delta.
\]
Thus $F(x,y)\le1-P(\delta)-(7/2)\delta y$, proving \eqref{gsr:en:103:eq:localdefect}.

Finally $h\ge(1-\delta)n$ and $r\le\delta n$, so $r/h\le\delta/(1-\delta)\le1/49$. Hence $12h-35r\ge(12-35/49)h>11h$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:103:thm:main}]
Odd order gives $\BBsf(f)=0$. Every correction term in \eqref{gsr:en:103:eq:localdefect} is then nonnegative, proving the bound. If $\delta>0$ and equality holds, the exterior term forces $s=0$. The strictly positive coefficient of $e(f)$ forces $e(f)=0$, so $f$ is a nonempty subgroup-coset indicator by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:103:lem:energyzero}. Conversely, deleting such a coset in odd order gives $s=0$, $e=\WWsf=\BBsf=0$, and \eqref{gsr:en:103:eq:polym} gives equality exactly. The case $\delta=0$ follows from the definition of the distance.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Parity-balanced extension]\label{gsr:en:103:cor:balanced}
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:103:thm:main} remains valid without an odd-order assumption on $H$ whenever the hole mass is equally distributed among the cosets of $2H$. In the equality case, the deleted subgroup coset has odd index in $H$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The balance condition is equivalent to $\BBsf(f)=0$. Apply the same proof and Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:103:cor:complement}.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Self-contained rounding from near-maximal energy\srctag{103}}]{Self-contained rounding from near-maximal energy}\label{gsr:en:103:sec:d8}\label{gsr:en:103:sec:rounding}
\srcnote{103}{Section 8}
This section supplies the global entry point into the local theorem. The set argument is an explicit form of the elementary near-maximal-energy method used in \cite{srconehundredone}; we include its proof to keep the dependencies of the weighted extension transparent.

\subsection{A small-difference lemma}
\begin{lemma}\label{gsr:en:103:lem:smallD}
If $B$ is a nonempty finite subset of an abelian group and
$\abs{B-B}<3\abs B/2$, then $B-B$ is a subgroup.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Put $D=B-B$. If $t=b_1-b_2\in D$, both $B-b_1$ and $B-b_2$ lie in $D$, so their intersection has size at least $2\abs B-\abs D>\abs B/2$. Thus
\[
 \abs{B\cap(B+t)}>\frac{\abs B}{2}\qquad(t\in D).
\]
For $s,t\in D$, the subsets $\{x\in B:x-s\in B\}$ and $\{x\in B:x+t\in B\}$ each have more than half the elements of $B$, so intersect. For such an $x$, $(x+t)-(x-s)=s+t\in D$. The set $D$ contains zero and is symmetric, hence is a subgroup.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Indicator rounding}
For a nonempty finite set $A$ of size $n$, write
\[
 u(t)=\abs{A\cap(A+t)},\qquad d_A(t)=n-u(t),\qquad
 \eps_2(A)=1-\frac{\EEsf(A)}{n^3}.
\]
The function $d_A$ is subadditive, since $2d_A(t)=\abs{A\symd(A+t)}$. Also
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:103:eq:pairdefect}
 n^3-\EEsf(A)=\sum_{a,b\in A}d_A(b-a).
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Explicit set rounding]\label{gsr:en:103:thm:setrounding}
If $\eps_2(A)<1/60$, there exists a finite subgroup coset $C$ such that, with
$\delta_C=\abs{A\symd C}/n$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:103:eq:setrounding}
 \delta_C\le\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4\eps_2(A)}}2
 <\frac1{50},\qquad \delta_C\le2\eps_2(A).
\end{equation}
The coset $C$ is the unique nearest finite subgroup coset.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By \eqref{gsr:en:103:eq:pairdefect}, choose $a\in A$ with
$\sum_{b\in A}d_A(b-a)\le\eps_2n^2$. Put
\[
 B=\{b\in A:d_A(b-a)\le n/12\}.
\]
Markov's inequality gives $\abs B\ge(1-12\eps_2)n>4n/5$. For $t\in B-B$, subadditivity gives $d_A(t)\le n/6$, hence $u(t)\ge5n/6$. Since $\sum_tu(t)=n^2$, the difference set $D=B-B$ has size at most $6n/5<3\abs B/2$. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:103:lem:smallD} makes it a subgroup $H$.

Since $a\in B$, the coset $C=a+H$ contains $B$. Write
\[
 m=\abs{A\cap C},\quad r=\abs{C\setminus A},\quad s=\abs{A\setminus C},\quad
 h=m+r,\quad n=m+s.
\]
The construction gives $m>4n/5$, $h\le6n/5$, $s/m<1/4$, and
$\delta_C=(r+s)/n<3/5$.

Translate $C$ to $H$ and let $R=H\setminus A$. Expanding four factors gives
\[
 \EEsf(H\setminus R)=h^3-4rh^2+6r^2h-4r^3+\EEsf(R)
 \le m^3-rm(m-r),
\]
using $\EEsf(R)\le r^3$. A parallelogram cannot have exactly one vertex outside $H$. Each of its six placements of two outside vertices contributes at most $ms^2$, each of four placements of three outside vertices contributes at most $s^3$, and the all-outside term contributes at most $s^3$. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:103:eq:roughenergy}
 \EEsf(A)\le m^3-rm(m-r)+6ms^2+5s^3.
\end{equation}
Let $D_0=r+s$. Direct algebra gives
\begin{align*}
 n^3-\EEsf(A)
 &\ge D_0n(n-D_0)
 +s(2m^2-4sm-4s^2+r^2+rs)\\
 &\ge D_0n(n-D_0)+\tfrac34sm^2.
\end{align*}
The last step uses $s/m<1/4$ and $r\ge0$. Dividing by $n^3$ yields
\[
 \eps_2(A)\ge\delta_C(1-\delta_C).
\]
The larger root branch is impossible because $\delta_C<3/5$ and $\eps_2<1/60$. Thus the smaller-root bound in \eqref{gsr:en:103:eq:setrounding} holds. It is less than $1/50$ because $(1/50)(49/50)>1/60$, and is at most $2\eps_2$ since the smaller root is less than $1/2$. Uniqueness and nearestness follow from Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:103:lem:unique} below.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Uniqueness of a close coset]\label{gsr:en:103:lem:unique}
Let $a:G\to[0,1]$ have finite support and positive mass $n$. There is at most one finite subgroup coset $C$ with $\norm{a-\one_C}_1<n/3$. If such a coset exists, it is the unique nearest finite subgroup coset.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Suppose $C,D$ both satisfy the strict bound. Write $h_C=\abs C$ and $m_C=\sum_Ca$. The identity
\[
 \norm{a-\one_C}_1=n+h_C-2m_C
\]
and the bounds $m_C\le h_C$, $m_C\le n$ imply $2n/3<h_C<4n/3$ and $m_C>2n/3$. The same holds for $D$, so $C\cap D$ is nonempty. Translate an intersection point to zero, writing the two cosets as subgroups for the purpose of cardinality comparisons.

If one is properly contained in the other, the larger has at least twice the cardinality of the smaller, contradicting the two size bounds. If neither contains the other, their intersection has size at most half the smaller subgroup, so $\abs{C\symd D}\ge\max(h_C,h_D)>2n/3$. But the triangle inequality gives $\abs{C\symd D}<2n/3$, another contradiction. Thus $C=D$.

Any competing coset with distance no greater than that of an existing close coset also has distance less than $n/3$, so it is equal to that coset. This proves nearestness without assuming an abstract minimizer exists in advance.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Global set version]\label{gsr:en:103:cor:globalset}
If $A$ is a nonempty subset of a finite odd-order abelian group and $\eps_3(A)<1/60$, then there is a unique nearest subgroup coset $C$ with
\[
 \delta=\frac{\abs{A\symd C}}{\abs A}<\frac1{50},\qquad
 \eps_3(A)\ge P(\delta).
\]
The equality cases are exactly those in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:103:thm:main}.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:103:lem:domination} implies $\eps_2(A)\le\eps_3(A)$. Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:103:thm:setrounding}, then Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:103:thm:main}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Weighted rounding and proof of the global theorem}
\begin{theorem}[Weighted rounding in any abelian group]\label{gsr:en:103:thm:weightedrounding}
Let $a:G\to[0,1]$ have finite support and mass $n>0$. If
$\eps=1-\CkS_3(a)/n^4<1/2000$, there is a unique nearest finite subgroup coset $C$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:103:eq:weightedrounding}
 \norm{a-\one_C}_1\le35\eps n<\frac n{50}.
\end{equation}
No odd-order assumption is needed for this rounding statement.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:103:lem:domination} gives $\EEsf(a)\ge(1-\eps)n^3$. Combining this with \eqref{gsr:en:103:eq:l2},
\[
 I:=\sum_xa(x)(1-a(x))\le\eps n.
\]
Let $B=\{x:a(x)\ge1/2\}$, $m=\abs B$, and $d=\norm{a-\one_B}_1$. Since $\min(t,1-t)\le2t(1-t)$ on $[0,1]$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:103:eq:threshold}
 d\le2I\le2\eps n,\qquad (1-2\eps)n\le m\le(1+2\eps)n.
\end{equation}
In particular $m>0$.

A four-factor telescoping expansion of the energy gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:103:eq:Elipschitz}
 \abs{\EEsf(a)-\EEsf(B)}\le4d\max(n,m)^2.
\end{equation}
For each telescoping term, retain the absolute difference at one vertex, choose two other independent parallelogram vertices, and bound the fourth factor by one. The three retained arguments are independent, giving at most $d\max(n,m)^2$.

It follows that
\[
 \EEsf(B)\ge\bigl[1-\eps-8\eps(1+2\eps)^2\bigr]n^3.
\]
The bracket is positive in the stated range. Dividing by $m^3\le(1+2\eps)^3n^3$ therefore yields
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:103:eq:epsB}
 \eps_2(B)\le
 \frac{15\eps+44\eps^2+40\eps^3}{(1+2\eps)^3}
 \le16\eps<\frac1{60}.
\end{equation}
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:103:thm:setrounding} supplies a coset $C$ with
\[
 \abs{B\symd C}\le2\eps_2(B)m\le32\eps(1+2\eps)n.
\]
Using \eqref{gsr:en:103:eq:threshold} and the triangle inequality,
\[
 \norm{a-\one_C}_1\le(34\eps+64\eps^2)n\le35\eps n.
\]
This is less than $n/50$, so Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:103:lem:unique} gives uniqueness and nearestness.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:103:thm:globalintro}]
Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:103:thm:weightedrounding}. In an odd-order ambient group the resulting subgroup has odd order. Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:103:thm:main} then gives the exact local profile and its equality characterization.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The inverse profile and near-equality rigidity\srctag{103}}]{The inverse profile and near-equality rigidity}\label{gsr:en:103:sec:d9}\label{gsr:en:103:sec:rigidity}
\srcnote{103}{Section 9}

\subsection{Exact inverse, including higher coefficients}
On $[0,1/50]$,
\[
 P'(\delta)=4(1-2\delta)(1-3\delta)>0.
\]
Let $\rho$ denote the inverse of $P$ on this interval. Whenever a preceding global theorem gives a nearest-coset distance $\delta$ and $\eps$ lies in $[0,P(1/50)]$, it follows that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:103:eq:inverse}
 \delta\le\rho(\eps).
\end{equation}
For small $\eps$, exact formal series reversion gives
\begin{align}\label{gsr:en:103:eq:series}
 \rho(\eps)={}&\frac\eps4+\frac{5\eps^2}{32}+\frac{21\eps^3}{128}
 +\frac{425\eps^4}{2048}\notag\\
 &+\frac{2371\eps^5}{8192}+\frac{28105\eps^6}{65536}+O(\eps^7).
\end{align}
The displayed coefficients are checked by substituting the polynomial through degree six into $4\rho-10\rho^2+8\rho^3$. Analyticity follows from $P'(0)=4\ne0$.

These coefficients are sharp along admissible subgroup indices. Take an odd integer $q\ge51$, let $H$ be any odd-order abelian group with a subgroup $K$ of index $q$, and set $A=H\setminus K$. Then
\[
 \delta=\frac1{q-1}\le\frac1{50},\qquad \eps_3(A)=P(\delta).
\]
As $q\to\infty$ through odd values, the distance tends to zero and equality holds in \eqref{gsr:en:103:eq:inverse}. We do not assert that every real value of $\delta$ is realized by a finite set; subgroup indices impose arithmetic discreteness.

\subsection{A quantitative near-extremal classification}
The complete defect terms also quantify the structure of a near-equality set.

\begin{theorem}[Two-level coset rigidity]\label{gsr:en:103:thm:rigidity}
Let $A$ be a nonempty finite subset of an abelian group, let $C=x_0+H$ be a coset of a finite odd-order subgroup, and suppose
\[
 0<\delta=\frac{\abs{A\symd C}}{n}\le\frac1{50},\qquad n=\abs A.
\]
Set $\gamma=\eps_3(A)-P(\delta)\ge0$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:103:eq:exteriorrigidity}
 \frac{\abs{A\setminus C}}n\le\frac{2\gamma}{7\delta}.
\end{equation}
If additionally $\gamma\le\delta^3/1000$, there is a coset $L$ of a subgroup of $H$, contained in $C$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:103:eq:rigidity}
 \frac{\abs{A\symd(C\setminus L)}}n\le\frac{2\gamma}{\delta^2}.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Translate $C$ to $H$ and use the notation $r=\abs{H\setminus A}$, $s=\abs{A\setminus H}$, $x=r/n$, $y=s/n$. Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:103:thm:localdefect} gives
\[
 \gamma\ge\frac72\delta y+\frac{11h\,e(\one_{H\setminus A})}{n^4},
\]
which proves \eqref{gsr:en:103:eq:exteriorrigidity}. Under the additional assumption,
$y\le2\delta^2/7000<\delta/2$, so $x\ge\delta/2>0$. Let $R=H\setminus A$. Since $h\ge(1-\delta)n$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:103:eq:holedefect}
 \eps_2(R)=\frac{e(\one_R)}{r^3}
 \le\frac{\gamma}{11(1-\delta)x^3}
 \le\frac{8}{11000(1-\delta)}<\frac1{60}.
\end{equation}
Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:103:thm:setrounding} \emph{inside $H$}. It gives a subgroup coset $L\subset H$ with
\begin{align*}
 \frac{\abs{R\symd L}}n
 &\le\frac{2e(\one_R)}{r^2n}
 \le\frac{2\gamma}{11(1-\delta)x^2}
 \le\frac{8\gamma}{11(1-\delta)\delta^2}
 <\frac{\gamma}{\delta^2}.
\end{align*}
Finally,
\[
 \frac{\abs{A\symd(H\setminus L)}}n
 =y+\frac{\abs{R\symd L}}n
 \le\frac{2\gamma}{7\delta}+\frac{\gamma}{\delta^2}
 \le\frac{2\gamma}{\delta^2}.
\]
Translate back to $C$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What the two scales mean]
The exterior mass is controlled on the scale $\gamma/\delta$, while the structural error of the holes is controlled on the scale $\gamma/\delta^2$. This follows from the coefficient of $e(f)$ in the exact identity and from the cubic normalization of hole energy. The theorem supplies upper bounds with explicit constants; it does not prove that both rates or constants are optimal.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Examples, scope, and failure modes\srctag{103}}]{Examples, scope, and failure modes}\label{gsr:en:103:sec:d10}\label{gsr:en:103:sec:examples}
\srcnote{103}{Section 10}

\subsection{An exact odd-order equality family}
Take $H=\Z/51\Z$, $K=\{0\}$, and $A=H\setminus K$. Then $n=50$, $\delta=1/50$, and
\[
 \eps_3(A)=\frac4{50}-\frac{10}{50^2}+\frac8{50^3}=0.076064.
\]
Thus $\CkS_3(A)=50^4(1-0.076064)=5{,}774{,}600$. The comparison coset is unique by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:103:lem:unique}. This example lies at the local theorem's distance cutoff, although its deficit is larger than the sufficient threshold in the global rounding theorem. Local and global hypotheses must not be conflated.

For a global equality example choose an odd index $q$ large enough that $P(1/(q-1))<1/2000$, such as $q=10001$. Deleting a singleton in $\Z/q\Z$ then meets the weighted global theorem's hypothesis as well.

\subsection{Even-order groups really need the parity term}
Take an elementary abelian two-group $H$ of order $q\ge64$ and delete one point. Here $r=1$, $\tau=q$, and $\delta=1/(q-1)<1/50$. Formula~\eqref{gsr:en:103:eq:parityprofile} gives
\[
 \eps_3(H\setminus\{0\})
 =P(\delta)-2(q-1)\delta^4
 =4\delta-10\delta^2+6\delta^3.
\]
Thus the odd-order polynomial is false without a torsion hypothesis, even arbitrarily close to a coset. This is a structural obstruction, not a weakness of the proof. More generally the exact fourth-moment correction $2\BBsf(f)$ measures the necessary adjustment.

\subsection{Fractional holes versus Boolean extremizers}
Let $f\equiv\theta$ on a finite group $H$. Then
\[
 r=\theta h,\qquad \EEsf(f)=\theta^4h^3,\qquad
 e(f)=\theta^3(1-\theta)h^3.
\]
Every nontrivial character sum vanishes, so $\BBsf(f)=0$. For $0<\theta<1$ the energy defect is positive; whenever $\theta<12/35$, Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:103:cor:complement} is strict. This is consistent with, and illustrates, the Boolean equality classification in the weighted theorem.

\subsection{The mass normalization is part of the theorem}
The reference quantity is $M(a)^4$, not the fourth power of the ambient group order and not an unconstrained critical-$L^p$ normalization. For finite $G$, the usual normalized Gowers expression satisfies
\[
 \norm{a}_{U^3(G)}^8=\frac{\CkS_3(a)}{\abs G^4}
\]
for real nonnegative $a$. Hence $\eps_3(a)=1-\norm{a}_{U^3(G)}^8/(M(a)/\abs G)^4$. The cap $a\le1$ is essential to the elementary cube domination and the equality classification.

\subsection{No automatic progression-counting consequence}
The proof does not assert that a near-maximal local cube count appears at the required scale of a progression argument. To obtain a quantitative Szemer\'edi improvement, one would still need a mechanism that produces the relevant local configuration, controls restriction losses, transports the density increment and iterates it. The current result closes a finite extremal problem and provides an exact structural tool; it does not supply those global steps.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{An optimal comparison of energy and cube deficits\srctag{104}}]{An optimal comparison of energy and cube deficits}\label{gsr:en:104:sec:d2}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:sec:comparison}
\srcnote{104}{Section 2}
\subsection{Elementary identities}
For $A_t=A\cap(A-t)$, fixing the last increment gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:recursion}
 \cC_1(A)=|A|^2,\qquad \cC_k(A)=\sum_{t\in G}\cC_{k-1}(A_t)\quad(k\ge2).
\end{equation}
All sums over an infinite group have finite support. The first three star-vertex values must complete a parallelogram, whereas the other $k-2$ star values have at most $|A|$ choices each. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:energy-upper}
 \cC_k(A)\le |A|^{k-2}E(A),\qquad \eps_2(A)\le\eps_k(A).
\end{equation}
Also, $E(A)=|A|^3$ if and only if every $u,v,w\in A$ satisfies $u-v+w\in A$. Translating a fixed point of $A$ to zero then gives a set closed under subtraction, hence a finite subgroup. Thus, for every $k\ge2$, the exact nonempty maximizers of $\cC_k(A)\le|A|^{k+1}$ are the finite subgroup cosets.

\subsection{The first-failure injection}
\begin{theorem}[Optimal all-dimensional comparison]\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:thm:comparison}
For every nonempty finite set $A$ in an abelian group and every $k\ge2$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:comparison}
 \eps_2(A)\le\eps_k(A)\le(2^k-k-1)\eps_2(A).
\end{equation}
The upper constant is optimal, even when restricted to finite odd-order groups.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The lower bound is \eqref{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:energy-upper}. Put $n=|A|$. Choose the $k+1$ star values
$a_0,a_1,\ldots,a_k\in A$. The value at a subset $S\subseteq[k]$ is
\[
 v_S=\sum_{i\in S}a_i-(|S|-1)a_0;
 \qquad v_\varnothing=a_0.
\]
There are $n^{k+1}$ such choices, of which exactly $\cC_k(A)$ give a full cube in $A$.

Order the subsets of size at least two by increasing size, breaking ties once and for all. For a failed cube, let $S$ be its first failed subset. Fix distinct indices $i,j\in S$ as deterministic functions of $S$, and put $T=S\setminus\{j\}$. Then $v_T\in A$, and
\[
 v_S=v_T-a_0+a_j\notin A.
\]
There are exactly $n^3-E(A)=\de(A)$ possible bad triples $(v_T,a_0,a_j)$ in $A^3$.

Given this triple and all the other original star values except $a_i$, the value $a_i$ is uniquely recovered from
\[
 a_i=v_T+(|T|-1)a_0-\sum_{\ell\in T\setminus\{i\}}a_\ell.
\]
The remaining free original values number $k-2$. Thus for each prescribed first-failure subset $S$, at most $n^{k-2}\de(A)$ star assignments are possible. There are $2^k-k-1$ nonbasic subsets. Summing and dividing by $n^{k+1}$ gives the upper bound.

For sharpness let $A_q=\Z/q\Z\setminus\{0\}$, with $q$ odd and tending to infinity. Every single labelled cube vertex is uniform; every pair of distinct labelled vertices is jointly uniform. The first two Bonferroni inequalities therefore give
\[
 \cC_k(A_q)=q^{k+1}-2^kq^k+O_k(q^{k-1}).
\]
Since $|A_q|=q-1$, this yields
\[
 \eps_k(A_q)=\frac{2^k-k-1}{q}+O_k(q^{-2}),\qquad
 \eps_2(A_q)=\frac1q+O(q^{-2}).
\]
Their ratio tends to the asserted constant.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{New}, and checked at the write on $\Z/q\Z$ minus a point: $\varepsilon_3/\varepsilon_2=3.80$, $3.90$ and $\varepsilon_4/\varepsilon_2=9.31$, $10.12$ for $q=31$, $61$, approaching $4$ and $11$.
\end{writenote}

\begin{corollary}[The cubic completion estimate]\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:cor:cubic-completion}
For every finite $R$ with $r=|R|$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:cubic-completion}
 r^4-\cC_3(R)\le4r\bigl(r^3-E(R)\bigr).
\end{equation}
The assertion includes $r=0$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}
The proof is an injection into failed ternary closure tests, not an appeal to an inverse theorem. A naive union bound over arbitrary affine expressions would not identify a uniformly distributed bad triple. The first-failure ordering ensures that the predecessor vertex belongs to $A$, and the coefficient-one recovery of $a_i$ avoids division and all torsion restrictions.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{An exact odd-order complement identity\srctag{104}}]{An exact odd-order complement identity}\label{gsr:en:104:sec:d3}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:sec:complement}
\srcnote{104}{Section 3}
\subsection{The Boolean three-cube census}
Let $V=\{0,1\}^3$, with vertices numbered in binary as $0,1,\ldots,7$. Associate to $\omega\in V$ the row $(1,\omega)\in\Z^4$.
\begin{lemma}[Four-vertex census]\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:lem:census}
Every set of at most three distinct vertices extends to a unimodular affine basis of four cube vertices. Among the seventy four-element subsets, twelve are affine parallelograms, fifty-six have determinant of absolute value one, and two have determinant of absolute value two. Every five-element subset contains a unimodular four-element subset.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Flip coordinates so that one of three given vertices is zero. For two distinct nonzero $0$--$1$ vectors $u,v$, some $2\times2$ coordinate minor has determinant $\pm1$: their nonempty supports are either nested, or each has a coordinate outside the other. Adjoin the coordinate vector in the unused coordinate to obtain a unimodular basis. The cases of one or two prescribed vertices follow by extending first to a triple.

For completeness the four-element subsets have the following orbits under coordinate permutations and coordinate flips. Each row gives a representative, its orbit size, and its absolute determinant.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrr@{}}\toprule
Representative vertex numbers & Orbit size & $|\det|$\\\midrule
$\{0,1,2,3\}$ & 6 & 0\\
$\{0,1,2,4\}$ & 8 & 1\\
$\{0,1,2,5\}$ & 24 & 1\\
$\{0,1,2,7\}$ & 24 & 1\\
$\{0,1,6,7\}$ & 6 & 0\\
$\{0,3,5,6\}$ & 2 & 2\\\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
These orbits are distinct, as can also be checked from their pairwise Hamming distances and face incidences; their sizes sum to seventy. The two singular orbits are the six faces and six diagonal rectangles. The determinant-two orbit consists of the two parity tetrahedra.

Finally, split any five chosen vertices between a pair of opposite faces. One face contains at least three of them, and the other contains at least one. Three vertices of a square form a unimodular affine basis in that face; adjoining a vertex in the opposite face gives a unimodular four-vertex basis.
\end{proof}

When $H$ has odd order, every full-rank matrix in this census acts invertibly on $H^4$: its determinant is $\pm1$ or $\pm2$, and multiplication by two is an automorphism of $H$. Consequently, prescribing any full-rank four vertex values leaves exactly one parameter tuple. Prescribing at most three leaves the expected power of $h=|H|$ choices. For an affine parallelogram, its four values contribute $hE(R)$ when constrained to $R$.

\subsection{Occupancy remainders}
For $R\subseteq H$, let $N_j(R;H)$ count parameter tuples in $H^4$ for which exactly $j$ of the eight \emph{labelled} cube vertices belong to $R$. If a vertex value repeats, each occurrence is counted. Abbreviate $N_j=N_j(R;H)$, and define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:T}
 T(h,r)=h^4-8rh^3+28r^2h^2-44r^3h+23r^4.
\end{equation}
\begin{theorem}[Exact odd-order occupancy identity]\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:thm:occupancy}
For every subset $R$ of a finite odd-order abelian group $H$,
\begin{align}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:occupancy}
 T(h,r)-\cC_3(H\setminus R)
 ={}&12h\de(R)-35\bigl(r^4-\cC_3(R)\bigr)\\
 &+N_5+5N_6+15N_7.\nonumber
\end{align}
In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:complement-remainder}
 \cC_3(H\setminus R)\le T(h,r)-(12h-140r)\de(R)-N_5-5N_6-15N_7.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The inclusion--exclusion sum through order four, by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:104:ocb:lem:census}, is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:B4}
 B_4=h^4-8rh^3+28r^2h^2-56r^3h+12hE(R)+58r^4.
\end{equation}
For a parameter tuple having occupancy $j>0$, its contribution to this truncated sum is
\[
 \sum_{i=0}^4(-1)^i\binom ji=\binom{j-1}{4},
\]
where a binomial coefficient is zero when its lower index exceeds its upper index. For occupancy zero the contribution is one. Thus the exact correction to $B_4$ is
\[
 N_5+5N_6+15N_7+35N_8.
\]
Since $N_8=\cC_3(R)$, substituting \eqref{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:B4} and rearranging proves \eqref{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:occupancy}. Applying Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:104:ocb:cor:cubic-completion} gives \eqref{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:complement-remainder}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{The same identity as source~103's} Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:103:thm:identity}, in occupancy form (note there); checked at the write on $861$ subsets of odd groups.
\end{writenote}

\begin{corollary}[Sharp odd-order complement bound]\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:cor:complement}
If $0<r<3h/35$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:complement}
 \cC_3(H\setminus R)\le T(h,r).
\end{equation}
Equality holds exactly when $R$ is a subgroup coset in $H$. The inequality also holds for $r=0$ and for $r=3h/35$ when the latter is an integer.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The coefficient $12h-140r$ is positive in the strict range. Equality therefore forces $\de(R)=0$, so $R$ is a coset. Conversely let $R=b+K$. It has maximal energy and cube count. A cube with at least five labelled vertices in $R$ has a full-rank four-vertex subset in $R$. In the odd-order quotient $H/K$, the corresponding invertible matrix forces every vertex to equal $b+K$. Hence $N_5=N_6=N_7=0$, and the identity gives equality.
\end{proof}

For $m=h-r$, the polynomial simplifies to
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:T-m}
 T(h,r)=m^4-4rm^3+10r^2m^2-8r^3m.
\end{equation}
This exact cancellation is the reason the final distance profile is cubic rather than quartic.

\begin{remark}[Why the earlier fourth-order loss disappears]
Stopping at $B_4$ and discarding all higher occupancies leaves a $35r^4$ error after normalization. It is not necessary to estimate every five-, six-, and seven-vertex pattern separately. Retaining the full-cube contribution $35\cC_3(R)$ cancels that error for coset holes, and \eqref{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:cubic-completion} charges its failure to the already available energy deficit. The remaining occupancy counts have favorable signs. This is the new step beyond the fourth-order Bonferroni argument in \cite{srconehundredone}.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Sharp subgroup boundaries without quotient two-torsion\srctag{104}}]{Sharp subgroup boundaries without quotient two-torsion}\label{gsr:en:104:sec:d4}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:sec:boundary}
\srcnote{104}{Section 4}
\subsection{A universal boundary estimate}
We first record the unrestricted estimate needed when the nearby subgroup has odd order but the ambient quotient may have two-torsion. This is a reusable estimate from \cite{srconehundredone}; its proof is included to make the dependency explicit.
\begin{lemma}[Unrestricted boundary]\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:lem:universal-boundary}
For a finite subgroup $H$ and finite $D\subseteq G\setminus H$, writing $h=|H|$, $s=|D|$, one has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:universal-boundary}
 \cC_k(H\cup D)\le h^{k+1}+(2^{k+1}-2)hs^k+s^{k+1}\qquad(k\ge1).
\end{equation}
Consequently, with the notation of \eqref{gsr:fm:104:ocb:eq:parameters},
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:boundary-holes}
 \cC_k(A)\le\cC_k(H\setminus R)+(2^{k+1}-2)hs^k+s^{k+1}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The case $s=0$ is immediate, and $k=1$ is the identity $(h+s)^2=h^2+2hs+s^2$. Put $B=H\cup D$, $z_t=|D\cap(D-t)|$, and
\[
 R_H=\sum_{t\in H}z_t\le s^2.
\]
For $t\in H$, $B\cap(B-t)=H\cup(D\cap(D-t))$. If $c_{k-1}=2^k-2$, induction and $z_t\le s$ give
\[
 \sum_{t\in H}\cC_{k-1}(B\cap(B-t))
 \le h^{k+1}+c_{k-1}hs^{k-2}R_H+s^{k-1}R_H.
\]
For $t\notin H$, let $c_t$ count ordered pairs of difference $t$ with one endpoint in $H$ and the other in $D$. Then
\[
 |B\cap(B-t)|=c_t+z_t,\qquad c_t+2z_t\le2s.
\]
The capacity inequality follows by counting the uses of $D$ as first and second endpoints. Convexity of the $k$th power, on the triangle with vertices $(0,0),(2s,0),(0,s)$, gives
\[
 (c_t+z_t)^k\le(2s)^{k-1}c_t+s^{k-1}z_t.
\]
Since $\sum_{t\notin H}c_t=2hs$ and $\sum_{t\notin H}z_t=s^2-R_H$, the outside contribution to the recursion is at most
\[
 2^khs^k+s^{k+1}-s^{k-1}R_H.
\]
The final terms involving $R_H$ cancel, and $R_H\le s^2$ gives $c_k=c_{k-1}+2^k=2^{k+1}-2$.

Every cube of $A$ not entirely in $H$ is also a cube of $H\cup D$ not entirely in $H$. Subtracting the $h^{k+1}$ inside cubes proves \eqref{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:boundary-holes}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{An exact identity for one occupied outside coset}
The singleton version in $H\times\Z/3\Z$ already appears in \cite{srconehundredone}. The following identity extends it to an arbitrary subset of a single outside fiber; the subsequent theorem supplies the matching uniform upper bound even when many outside fibers are occupied.
\begin{proposition}[One-fiber identity]\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:prop:one-fiber}
Suppose $D\subseteq b+H$ and $2b\notin H$. Then for every $k\ge2$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:one-fiber}
 \cC_k(H\cup D)=h^{k+1}+2kh\cC_{k-1}(D)+\cC_k(D).
\end{equation}
In particular, if $D=b+K$ with $K\le H$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:one-fiber-coset}
 \cC_k(H\cup D)=h^{k+1}+2khs^k+s^{k+1}.
\end{equation}
No size condition on $s/h$ is needed for this identity.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Project a cube to $G/H$. Its vertex values lie in $\{0,b+H\}$. At a base vertex in $H$, every nonzero quotient increment must equal $b+H$. Two such increments would produce $2b+H$, which is neither allowed value. At a base vertex in $b+H$, the same argument uses $-b+H$. Thus a nonconstant quotient cube has exactly one changing coordinate.

The constant quotient cubes contribute $h^{k+1}$ and $\cC_k(D)$. For a nonconstant one, choose the changing coordinate and its orientation in $2k$ ways. The outside facet is a $(k-1)$-cube in $D$. For each such facet, the transverse increment has exactly $h$ choices making the other facet lie in $H$, and then every vertex of that other facet automatically lies in $H$. This proves the identity. A coset of size $s$ has $s^{j+1}$ cubes of dimension $j$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Quotient-fiber dispersion and cross capacity}
Assume henceforth that $(G/H)[2]=\{0\}$. For a nonzero quotient element $q$, let
\[
 d_q=|D\cap\pi^{-1}(q)|,\qquad
 P=s^2-\sum_{q\ne0}d_q^2,
\]
where $\pi:G\to G/H$ is the quotient map. The quantity $P$ counts ordered pairs of points of $D$ lying in different $H$-cosets. In terms of the preceding correlations,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:RH-P}
 R_H=\sum_{t\in H}z_t=\sum_qd_q^2=s^2-P.
\end{equation}
For $t\notin H$ with $\pi(t)=q$, the cross count is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:cross-capacity}
 c_t=d_q+d_{-q}\le s,\qquad c_t+2z_t\le2s.
\end{equation}
Here $q\ne-q$ is precisely where the quotient hypothesis is used.

\begin{lemma}[A secant bound]\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:lem:secant}
Let $s>0$, $0\le c\le s$, and $0\le z\le s-c/2$. For $k\ge2$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:secant}
 (c+z)^k\le c^k+\beta_ks^{k-1}z,
 \qquad \beta_k=2\bigl((3/2)^k-1\bigr).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $z>0$,
\[
 \frac{(c+z)^k-c^k}{z}
 =\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}(c+z)^{k-1-i}c^i.
\]
Since $c\le s$ and $c+z\le3s/2$, this is at most
\[
 s^{k-1}\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}(3/2)^{k-1-i}
 =2\bigl((3/2)^k-1\bigr)s^{k-1}.
\]
The case $z=0$ is immediate.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The boundary theorem with remainders}
Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:boundary-deficit}
 B_k(H,D)=h^{k+1}+2khs^k+s^{k+1}-\cC_k(H\cup D),
 \qquad a_k=2(k-1)h-(\beta_k-1)s.
\end{equation}
\begin{theorem}[Dispersion and energy remainders]\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:thm:boundary-remainders}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:104:ocb:thm:boundary-main}, with $s/h\le\alpha_k$, one has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:dispersion-remainder}
 B_k(H,D)\ge a_ks^{k-2}P.
\end{equation}
For $k\ge3$ one also has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:energy-remainder}
 B_k(H,D)\ge a_ks^{k-3}\de(D).
\end{equation}
Both are uniform in the ambient group and in the ratio $h/s$ within the stated range.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The sufficient radii $\alpha_k$ decrease with $k$. Indeed, writing $t=(3/2)^k$, the comparison $\alpha_{k+1}\le\alpha_k$ is equivalent to
\[
 (k-3)t+3\ge0,
\]
which holds for $k=2$ and for every $k\ge3$. We may therefore induct on dimension, starting from the exact dimension-one identity. If $t\in H$, the induction hypothesis applies to $D\cap(D-t)$ because $z_t/h\le s/h\le\alpha_k\le\alpha_{k-1}$; for $k=2$ no radius is needed at dimension one. An empty outside intersection contributes exactly the inside-coset count. Summing yields
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:inside-odd}
 \sum_{t\in H}\cC_{k-1}((H\cup D)\cap((H\cup D)-t))
 \le h^{k+1}+2(k-1)hs^{k-2}R_H+s^{k-1}R_H.
\end{equation}

For $t\notin H$, the cardinality bound and Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:104:ocb:lem:secant} give
\[
 \cC_{k-1}((H\cup D)\cap((H\cup D)-t))
 \le(c_t+z_t)^k\le c_t^k+\beta_ks^{k-1}z_t.
\]
Partition the nonzero quotient elements into unordered pairs $\{q,-q\}$. Put $w_{\{q,-q\}}=d_q+d_{-q}$. Their sum is $s$, and every quotient element has $h$ lifts. Therefore
\[
 \sum_{t\notin H}c_t^k
 =2h\sum_{\{q,-q\}}w_{\{q,-q\}}^k\le2hs^k.
\]
Also $\sum_{t\notin H}z_t=P$. Adding the outside estimate to \eqref{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:inside-odd} and using $R_H=s^2-P$ proves
\[
 \cC_k(H\cup D)\le h^{k+1}+2khs^k+s^{k+1}
       -\bigl(2(k-1)h-(\beta_k-1)s\bigr)s^{k-2}P.
\]
Since $a_k\ge0$ is exactly the assumed ratio condition, this proves the induction and \eqref{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:dispersion-remainder}.

For the energy remainder, suppose $k\ge3$ and set
\[
 E_H=\sum_{t\in H}z_t^2,\qquad J=sR_H-E_H\ge0.
\]
In the inside sum, improve the power bounds to
$z_t^{k-1}\le s^{k-3}z_t^2$ and $z_t^k\le s^{k-2}z_t^2$. Compared with \eqref{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:inside-odd}, this saves
\[
 \bigl(2(k-1)h+s\bigr)s^{k-3}J.
\]
Thus we have the stronger joint remainder
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:joint-remainder}
 B_k(H,D)\ge a_ks^{k-2}P+\bigl(2(k-1)h+s\bigr)s^{k-3}J.
\end{equation}
Since $2(k-1)h+s\ge a_k$, the right side is at least
$a_ks^{k-3}(sP+J)$. Finally,
\[
 \de(D)=s^3-E(D)
 =sP+J-\sum_{t\notin H}z_t^2\le sP+J.
\]
This proves \eqref{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:energy-remainder}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Completion of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:104:ocb:thm:boundary-main}]
The inequality follows from the nonnegative dispersion remainder. If the ratio is strict, then $a_k>0$, so equality forces $P=0$. All of $D$ lies in a single outside coset $b+H$. Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:104:ocb:prop:one-fiber} gives
\[
 B_k(H,D)=2kh\bigl(s^k-\cC_{k-1}(D)\bigr)
              +\bigl(s^{k+1}-\cC_k(D)\bigr).
\]
Both terms are nonnegative. Equality forces $\cC_k(D)=s^{k+1}$, hence $D$ is a coset $b'+K$. Since it lies in $b+H$, its difference subgroup $K$ is contained in $H$. Conversely every such subcoset gives equality by the same identity.

For sharpness take $G=\F_3^{m+1}$, $H=\F_3^m\times\{0\}$, and $D=\{b\}$ with $b\notin H$. Then $s/h=3^{-m}\to0$ and the count is exactly $h^{k+1}+2kh+1$. A smaller coefficient fails for every member of this family.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A quantitative inverse theorem for the boundary}
We use the elementary rounding result proved in Appendix~\ref{gsr:en:104:ocb:sec:rounding}: if $\eps_2(D)<1/60$, then $D$ lies within relative distance at most $2\eps_2(D)$ of a finite coset.
\begin{theorem}[Boundary near-extremizers]\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:thm:boundary-inverse}
Let $k\ge3$, $(G/H)[2]=\{0\}$, $s>0$, and $s/h<\alpha_k$. Set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:inverse-parameters}
 \gamma=2(k-1)-(\beta_k-1)s/h>0,\qquad
 \eta=\frac{B_k(H,D)}{hs^k},\qquad \zeta=\frac\eta\gamma.
\end{equation}
If $\zeta<1/60$, there are $b\notin H$ and $K\le H$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:boundary-inverse}
 \frac{|D\symd(b+K)|}{s}
 \le\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4\zeta}}2\le2\zeta.
\end{equation}
Moreover some outside $H$-coset already contains at least $(1-\zeta)s$ points of $D$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The two remainders imply
\[
 \frac P{s^2}\le\zeta,\qquad \frac{\de(D)}{s^3}\le\zeta.
\]
If $p_q=d_q/s$, then $\sum p_q^2\ge1-\zeta$, whereas
$\sum p_q^2\le\max p_q$. Thus a coset $b+H$ contains at least $(1-\zeta)s$ points of $D$.

Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:104:ocb:lem:rounding} to $D$ in $G$. It gives a finite coset $L$ with
\[
 u:=|D\symd L|/s\le(1-\sqrt{1-4\zeta})/2\le2\zeta.
\]
The intersection of $L$ with $b+H$ has size at least $(1-\zeta-u)s$, while $|L|\le(1+u)s$. Since $\zeta<1/60$ and $u\le2\zeta$, this intersection has more than $|L|/2$ elements. A nonempty intersection of two finite cosets is a coset of the intersection of their underlying subgroups. Its size can exceed half of $|L|$ only if the subgroup underlying $L$ is contained in $H$. Thus $L$ itself lies in $b+H$, and has the required form.
\end{proof}

The factor $\gamma^{-1}$ records deterioration near the sufficient ratio endpoint. Neither that deterioration nor the numerical constant in \eqref{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:boundary-inverse} is asserted to be optimal. The conclusion is stronger than ambient coset approximation: it identifies a subcoset of the original subgroup in an outside fiber.

\section[{The exact odd-order cubic profile and its rigidity\srctag{104}}]{The exact odd-order cubic profile and its rigidity}\label{gsr:en:104:sec:d5}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:sec:cubic}
\srcnote{104}{Section 5}
\subsection{Mixed holes and outside points}
\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:104:ocb:thm:cubic-main}]
Translate $C$ to $H$. If $\delta\le1/50$, then
\[
 \frac rh\le\frac\delta{1-\delta}\le\frac1{49}<\frac3{35}.
\]
The complement estimate applies. By \eqref{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:T-m} and the unrestricted boundary estimate in dimension three,
\begin{align*}
 \cC_3(A)\le{}&m^4-4rm^3+10r^2m^2-8r^3m+14hs^3+s^4\\
 &-(12h-140r)\de(R)-N_5-5N_6-15N_7.
\end{align*}
Here the occupancy counts are taken inside $H$ for the hole set $R$; cubes meeting $D$ have been bounded separately.

Set $x=r/n$, $y=s/n$, and $\delta=x+y$. The polynomial part divided by $n^4$ is
\begin{align*}
 F(x,y)={}&(1-y)^4-4x(1-y)^3+10x^2(1-y)^2-8x^3(1-y)\\
          &+14(1+x-y)y^3+y^4.
\end{align*}
Its exact difference from the pure-deletion endpoint is
\begin{align}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:mixed-polynomial}
 F(\delta-y,y)-F(\delta,0)=y\bigl(&-8\delta+4y+4\delta^2+4\delta y+10y^2\\
 &+8\delta^3-14\delta^2y+22\delta y^2-28y^3\bigr).\nonumber
\end{align}
Since $0\le y\le\delta$, this is at most
\[
 -\delta y\bigl(4-18\delta-30\delta^2\bigr)
 \le-\tfrac72\delta y\qquad(\delta\le1/50).
\]
Finally $F(\delta,0)=1-4\delta+10\delta^2-8\delta^3$. This proves \eqref{gsr:fm:104:ocb:eq:cubic-main}; it also shows that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:occupancy-extra}
 \frac{N_5+5N_6+15N_7}{n^4}
\end{equation}
may be added to its right-hand side.

For $\delta>0$, equality in the profile forces $s=0$. The coefficient $12h-140r$ is positive, so equality also forces $\de(R)=0$. The hole set is therefore a subcoset. Conversely, Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:104:ocb:cor:complement} and \eqref{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:T-m} give equality for every such deletion in the stated interval.

For the nearest-coset assertion, $\eps_2(A)\le\eps_3(A)<1/60$, so Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:104:ocb:lem:rounding} gives a unique nearest coset with $\delta<1/50$. Its order is odd in a finite odd-order ambient group.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A quantitative nested-coset theorem}
The earlier manuscript gives asymptotic rigidity for sharp sequences. The new remainder gives a finite, explicit conclusion at the natural cubic scale.
\begin{theorem}[Quantitative rigidity near the cubic profile]\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:thm:cubic-rigidity}
Suppose $C=a+H$ has odd order, $0<\delta=\delta_C\le1/50$, and put
\[
 g=\eps_3(A)-\po_3(\delta).
\]
If $g\le\delta^3/100$, there exists a coset $L$ of a subgroup of $H$, contained in $C$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:cubic-rigidity}
 \frac{|A\symd(C\setminus L)|}{n}\le\frac{g}{\delta^2}.
\end{equation}
More precisely,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:cubic-rigidity-parts}
 \frac sn\le\frac{2g}{7\delta},\qquad
 \frac{|R\symd L|}{n}\le\frac{8g}{9\delta^2}.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Translate to $C=H$. Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:104:ocb:thm:cubic-main} gives the first bound in \eqref{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:cubic-rigidity-parts}. In particular
\[
 y\le\frac{\delta^2}{350}<\frac\delta2,\qquad x=\delta-y\ge\frac\delta2>0.
\]
Also
\[
 \frac{12h-140r}{n}=12-128x-12y\ge12-128\delta>9.
\]
The energy remainder therefore implies
\[
 \eps_2(R)=\frac{\de(R)}{r^3}
 \le\frac{g}{9x^3}
 \le\frac{8g}{9\delta^3}\le\frac8{900}<\frac1{60}.
\]
Apply the rounding lemma to $R$ in the group $H$. For some subcoset $L\subseteq H$,
\[
 \frac{|R\symd L|}{r}\le2\eps_2(R),\qquad
 \frac{|R\symd L|}{n}\le\frac{2g}{9x^2}\le\frac{8g}{9\delta^2}.
\]
The outside part $D$ and the error inside $H$ are disjoint. Their total relative size is at most
\[
 \left(\frac89+\frac{2\delta}{7}\right)\frac{g}{\delta^2}
 \le\frac{g}{\delta^2},
\]
as required.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Asymptotically sharp sequences]\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:cor:sharp-sequences}
Let $A_j$ have odd-order nearby cosets $C_j$ and distances $0<\delta_j\to0$. If
\[
 \eps_3(A_j)=4\delta_j-10\delta_j^2+8\delta_j^3+o(\delta_j^3),
\]
then $|A_j\setminus C_j|=o(\delta_j^2|A_j|)$, and the hole sets are within $o(\delta_j|A_j|)$ of subcosets of $C_j$.
\end{corollary}

\subsection{The inverse stability modulus}
The polynomial $\po_3$ is strictly increasing on $[0,1/50]$, because
\[
 (\po_3)'(u)=4-20u+24u^2>0.
\]
Thus the nearest-coset bound can also be written
$\delta\le(\po_3)^{-1}(\eps_3)$ under the near-maximal hypothesis $\eps_3<1/60$. Reversion at zero yields
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:inverse-series}
\begin{split}
 (\po_3)^{-1}(e)={}&\frac e4+\frac{5e^2}{32}+\frac{21e^3}{128}
 +\frac{425e^4}{2048}+\frac{2371e^5}{8192}+O(e^6).
\end{split}
\end{equation}
The series identity is verified by substitution; the implicit function theorem gives convergence in a neighborhood of zero. Exact subcoset deletions realize the inverse bound along a sequence tending to zero, so the successive coefficients cannot be lowered while keeping the preceding ones unchanged.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Higher-dimensional exact local profiles\srctag{104}}]{Higher-dimensional exact local profiles}\label{gsr:en:104:sec:d6}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:sec:higher}
\srcnote{104}{Section 6}
\subsection{An explicit cost for holes}
For $k\ge4$ put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:higher-constants}
 q=k+1,\qquad M=2^k,\qquad A_k=M-2q>0,\qquad
 S_k=\binom q2+\binom M2.
\end{equation}
Choose
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:rho}
 \eta_k=\min\left\{\frac1q,\frac{A_k}{6S_k},\frac{\alpha_k}{2}\right\},
 \qquad
 \rho_k=\min\left\{\frac1{50},\frac{\eta_k}{1+\eta_k}\right\}.
\end{equation}
The factor $1/2$ on $\alpha_k$ keeps the boundary argument strictly inside its sufficient radius, including in the equality classification.

\begin{lemma}[Hole cost]\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:lem:hole-cost}
Let $H$ be any finite abelian group, $R\subseteq H$, $r=|R|$, $m=|H|-r>0$. If $r/m\le\eta_k$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:hole-cost}
 \cC_k(H\setminus R)\le(m-r)^{k+1}-\frac{A_k}{2}rm^k.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Any two distinct labelled cube vertices are independent uniform coordinates in $H$. To see this integrally, flip one vertex to zero. If the other is a nonzero $0$--$1$ vector $v$, select a coordinate where $v$ is one and append all the other coordinate vectors. This gives a unimodular affine basis. The second-order Bonferroni inequality therefore gives
\[
 \cC_k(H\setminus R)\le h^{k+1}-Mrh^k+\binom M2r^2h^{k-1}.
\]
Divide by $m^q$ and put $t=r/m$, so $h=m(1+t)$. The resulting upper bound is
\[
 (1+t)^q-Mt(1+t)^{q-1}+\binom M2t^2(1+t)^{q-2}.
\]
Taylor's theorem bounds its first term above by
$1+qt+\binom q2t^2(1+t)^{q-2}$; the negative term is at most $-Mt$. Since $t\le1/q$, we have $(1+t)^{q-2}<3$. Hence the expression is at most
\[
 1-(M-q)t+3S_kt^2
 \le1-qt-\frac{A_k}{2}t
 \le(1-t)^q-\frac{A_k}{2}t.
\]
The last step is Bernoulli's inequality, valid since $0\le t<1$. Multiplying by $m^q$ proves the assertion. This hole estimate is the same elementary ingredient used in the unrestricted theory of \cite{srconehundredone}; the boundary contribution will now be sharper.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Why all holes are suboptimal in higher dimensions}
\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:104:ocb:thm:higher-main}, general $k$]
Translate $C$ to $H$. Under $\delta\le\rho_k$,
\[
 \frac rm\le\frac\delta{1-\delta}\le\eta_k,
 \qquad \frac sh\le\frac\delta{1-\delta}\le\eta_k\le\frac{\alpha_k}{2}.
\]
The boundary theorem applies to $H\cup D$, and the argument for \eqref{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:boundary-holes} now gives
\[
 \cC_k(A)\le\cC_k(H\setminus R)+2khs^k+s^{k+1}.
\]
If $s=0$, this assertion follows directly without invoking a nonempty-boundary hypothesis. Combining with Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:104:ocb:lem:hole-cost} and normalizing yields
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:higher-mixed}
 \frac{\cC_k(A)}{n^{k+1}}
 \le(1-\delta)^{k+1}-\frac{A_k}{2}x(1-y)^k
      +2k(1+\delta-2y)y^k+y^{k+1}.
\end{equation}
For fixed $\delta$, the last two terms increase with $y$ on $[0,\delta]$ when $\delta\le1/50$. Their derivative, for $y>0$, is
\[
 y^{k-1}\bigl(2k^2(1+\delta)-(4k-1)(k+1)y\bigr)>0;
\]
the endpoint follows by continuity. Thus these terms are at most
$2k(1-\delta)\delta^k+\delta^{k+1}$. Since $(1-y)^k\ge(1-\delta)^k$, \eqref{gsr:fm:104:ocb:eq:higher-main} follows.

If equality holds in the profile at $\delta>0$, its positive hole penalty forces $r=0$, so $A=H\cup D$ with $D\ne\varnothing$. Equality is then exactly the strict-range equality case of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:104:ocb:thm:boundary-main}. Conversely an outside subcoset gives equality by Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:104:ocb:prop:one-fiber}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The full rounded neighborhood in dimension four}
The general radius is conservative. When $k=4$ the hole estimate can be checked on a larger interval without weakening the penalty.
\begin{lemma}[Four-dimensional improvement]\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:lem:four-hole}
For $k=4$, the conclusion of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:104:ocb:lem:hole-cost} holds whenever $r/m\le1/49$, with $A_4/2=3$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The difference between the normalized second-order Bonferroni bound and $(1-t)^5$ is exactly
\[
 t\bigl(-6+56t+284t^2+296t^3+106t^4\bigr).
\]
For $0\le t\le1/49$, the sum of the four positive terms in parentheses is less than $3$, as follows by substituting $1/49$. Thus the difference is at most $-3t$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Completion of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:104:ocb:thm:higher-main}]
For $k=4$ and $\delta\le1/50$, one has $r/m,s/h\le1/49$. This lies inside both the improved hole range and the strict boundary range $\alpha_4=16/19$. The preceding mixed proof therefore applies unchanged. Expanding $\po_4$ gives \eqref{gsr:fm:104:ocb:eq:four-profile}.

In a finite odd-order ambient group, $\eps_4(A)<1/60$ supplies the unique nearest coset with $\delta<1/50$ by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:104:ocb:lem:rounding} and the energy comparison. This proves the final assertion.
\end{proof}

For general $k\ge4$, the analogous sufficient near-maximal hypothesis is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:higher-eps-threshold}
 \eps_k(A)<\min\{1/60,\rho_k(1-\rho_k)\}.
\end{equation}
Indeed, rounding gives $\delta\le(1-\sqrt{1-4\eps_k})/2<\rho_k$. In a finite odd-order group this gives the nearest-coset form of the theorem with no additional structural hypothesis.

\subsection{Comparison with the unrestricted profiles}
The unrestricted higher-dimensional profile in \cite{srconehundredone} has boundary coefficient $2^{k+1}-2$. Consequently our improvement in a finite odd-order group is exactly
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:torsion-gap}
 \bigl(2^{k+1}-2-2k\bigr)(1-\delta)\delta^k.
\end{equation}
For $k=4$, the unrestricted polynomial is
\[
 5\delta-10\delta^2+10\delta^3-35\delta^4+30\delta^5,
\]
and the improvement is $22(1-\delta)\delta^4$. The difference first appears in the fourth-order coefficient, not in the leading linear cost.

The leading perturbation costs explain the dimension transition. A small deletion costs $(2^k-k-1)\delta+O_k(\delta^2)$, while a small addition costs $(k+1)\delta+O_k(\delta^2)$. Deletion is cheaper in dimension two, the linear costs tie in dimension three, and addition is cheaper for every $k\ge4$. The exact cubic calculation resolves the tied case in favor of deletion. Torsion then affects the cubic coefficient for $k=3$ and the order-$k$ boundary coefficient for $k\ge4$.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Sharp examples, obstructions, and the meaning of sharpness\srctag{104}}]{Sharp examples, obstructions, and the meaning of sharpness}\label{gsr:en:104:sec:d7}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:sec:examples}
\srcnote{104}{Section 7}
\subsection{Odd-order deletion families}
Let $K\le H$ with $H$ of odd order, let $R=b+K$, and put $q=[H:K]$, $r=|K|$. Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:104:ocb:cor:complement} gives an exact identity for such holes, even when the sufficient small-hole condition is not imposed: its proof for cosets uses the exact occupancy identity directly. Namely,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:deletion-example}
 \cC_3(H\setminus R)=r^4(q^4-8q^3+28q^2-44q+23).
\end{equation}
For $q\to\infty$ through odd values,
\[
 \delta=\frac1{q-1},\qquad
 \eps_3=4\delta-10\delta^2+8\delta^3.
\]
The ambient coset is the unique nearest one once $\delta<1/3$, by the uniqueness argument in Appendix~\ref{gsr:en:104:ocb:sec:rounding}. These examples establish exact equality at distances approaching zero, both for the profile and for its inverse expansion.

\subsection{Odd-order addition families}
Take $G=\F_3^{m+1}$, $H=\F_3^m\times\{0\}$, and $D=\{b\}$ outside $H$. More generally, lift this construction through a subgroup $K$. If $|H/K|=q$, then $h=qs$, $n=(q+1)s$, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:addition-example}
 \delta=\frac1{q+1},\qquad
 \cC_k(H\cup(b+K))=h^{k+1}+2khs^k+s^{k+1}.
\end{equation}
For fixed $k\ge4$ and sufficiently large $q=3^m$, these are exact equality cases in the higher-dimensional local theorem. Thus the coefficient $2k$ and the resulting polynomial cannot be successively improved near zero.

\subsection{Two different two-torsion obstructions}
The odd-order condition in the cubic complement theorem is genuine. For $H=\Z/64\Z$ and $A=H\setminus\{0\}$, direct counting gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:even-obstruction}
 \eps_3(A)-\po_3(1/63)=-\frac{2}{63^4}<0.
\end{equation}
One may verify this without a large enumeration: the same census for a singleton hole in any finite abelian $H$ gives
\[
 \cC_3(H\setminus\{0\})=h^4-8h^3+28h^2-44h+21+2|H[2]|.
\]
Each parity tetrahedron has $|H[2]|$ solutions with all four values zero; each unimodular tetrahedron has one. A cube with five zero labelled vertices is entirely zero, by the final part of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:104:ocb:lem:census}, so the only higher-occupancy correction is 35. For $C_{64}$, $|H[2]|=2$, proving \eqref{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:even-obstruction}.

Here $1/63<1/50$, so the proposed odd profile fails inside the stated local interval when the odd-order hypothesis is removed. The extra solutions arise from the determinant-two tetrahedra.

The quotient hypothesis in the boundary theorem is also genuine, even at arbitrarily small $s/h$. Let $G=\F_2^{m+1}$, let $H$ be a hyperplane, and take $D=\{b\}$ outside it. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:binary-boundary}
 \cC_k(H\cup\{b\})=h^{k+1}+(2^{k+1}-2)h+1.
\end{equation}
To count the mixed cubes, view a cube as an affine map from $\F_2^k$. Its projection to $G/H$ is a nonconstant affine Boolean function, of which there are $2(2^k-1)$. Requiring all vertices on its outside hyperplane to map to $b$ leaves one freely chosen value in $H$. The two constant projections contribute $h^{k+1}$ and one. For $k\ge2$, \eqref{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:binary-boundary} exceeds the proposed $2k$ boundary bound, while $s/h=2^{-m}\to0$.

\subsection{A size obstruction even in odd order}
The small-boundary condition cannot simply be deleted. Take $G=\Z/3\Z$, $H=\{0\}$, and $D=\{1,2\}$. In dimension three,
\[
 \cC_3(G)=3^4=81,
 \qquad h^4+6hs^3+s^4=1+48+16=65.
\]
Thus the $2k$ coefficient is not a global bound for arbitrary $s/h$. The exact optimal radius remains an independent extremal question.

\subsection{What the results do not determine}
The equality distances in \eqref{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:deletion-example} and \eqref{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:addition-example} are discrete. A universal polynomial bound with equality along a sequence does not determine the exact extremal envelope at every prescribed real distance, or at every integer pair $(|A|,|A\symd C|)$. It determines a sharp local universal inequality and all its equality configurations in the proved range.

Likewise, the comparison theorem is an optimal bound between normalized deficits, not a classification of all its equality cases. The quantitative inverse estimates are explicit but not claimed to have optimal constants. The sufficient radii $3/35$, $1/50$, $\alpha_k$, and $\rho_k$ serve different steps of the proofs and are not proposed as the largest possible radii.

Finally, support stability for indicator functions is not phase stability for arbitrary complex functions. No assertion about approximate polynomial phases, characteristic-independent inverse theorems, or an improved global progression bound is implicit in the present results.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Self-contained coset rounding\srctag{104}}]{Self-contained coset rounding}\label{gsr:en:104:sec:dA}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:sec:rounding}
\srcnote{104}{Appendix A}
This appendix reproves the rounding input and its constants from \cite{srconehundredone}. It is included so that none of the new inverse theorems depends on an unverified external stability assertion.

\subsection{Translation defect and a small-difference-set lemma}
For $A\ne\varnothing$, $n=|A|$, set
\[
 u_A(t)=|A\cap(A+t)|,\qquad
 d_A(t)=n-u_A(t)=\tfrac12|A\symd(A+t)|.
\]
Double counting and translation invariance give
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:translation-identities}
 \sum_tu_A(t)=n^2,\qquad E(A)=\sum_tu_A(t)^2,\qquad
 \de(A)=\sum_{a,b\in A}d_A(a-b),
\end{equation}
and the triangle inequality gives $d_A(t+v)\le d_A(t)+d_A(v)$.

If $B$ is finite and nonempty with $|B-B|<3|B|/2$, then $B-B$ is a subgroup. Indeed, putting $T=B-B$, for $t=b_1-b_2$ the sets $B-b_1$ and $B-b_2$ both lie in $T$, so
\[
 u_B(t)\ge2|B|-|T|>|B|/2.
\]
For $s,t\in T$, the sets $B\cap(B+s)$ and $B\cap(B-t)$ have a common point, and such a point witnesses $s+t\in B-B$. Symmetry and the presence of zero complete the proof.

\subsection{Coarse rounding}
Let $e=\eps_2(A)<1/60$. By \eqref{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:translation-identities}, choose $a\in A$ with
\[
 \sum_{b\in A}d_A(b-a)\le en^2.
\]
Set $B=\{b\in A:d_A(b-a)\le n/12\}$. Markov's inequality gives
$|B|\ge(1-12e)n>4n/5$. For $b,c\in B$, subadditivity implies $u_A(b-c)\ge5n/6$. Thus
\[
 |B-B|\le6n/5<3|B|/2,
\]
and $H=B-B$ is a subgroup. Since $a\in B$, the coset $C=a+H$ contains $B$. In the notation of \eqref{gsr:fm:104:ocb:eq:parameters},
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:coarse-rounding}
 h\le6n/5,\qquad m>4n/5,\qquad s/m<1/4,\qquad |A\symd C|<3n/5.
\end{equation}

\subsection{The exact energy comparison near a coset}
Expansion of the four parallelogram indicators gives, for $R\subseteq H$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:energy-complement}
 E(H\setminus R)=h^3-4rh^2+6r^2h-4r^3+E(R)
 \le m^3-rm(m-r).
\end{equation}
Every three vertices of a parallelogram form independent coordinates; this proves the identity without a characteristic restriction. Equality in the inequality holds exactly when $R$ is empty or a coset.

An additive quadruple cannot have exactly one vertex outside $H$. Quadruples with two outside vertices contribute at most $6ms^2$: for each of the six position choices, two outside values and one inside value determine the fourth. Those with three outside vertices contribute at most $4s^3$, and those with four contribute at most $s^3$. Hence
\[
 E(A)\le m^3-rm(m-r)+6ms^2+5s^3.
\]
Writing $d=r+s$, direct expansion gives
\begin{align}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:energy-local}
 n^3-E(A)&\ge dn(n-d)+s(2m^2-4sm-4s^2+r^2+rs)\\
          &\ge dn(n-d)+\tfrac34sm^2\quad\text{if }s\le m/4.\nonumber
\end{align}

\subsection{Uniqueness and the final bound}
There cannot be two distinct cosets $C_1,C_2$ satisfying $|A\symd C_i|<n/3$. Their sizes lie between $2n/3$ and $4n/3$, and they intersect because each contains more than $2n/3$ points of $A$. If one underlying subgroup were properly contained in the other, their size ratio would be at least two, which is impossible. Otherwise their intersection has size at most half of each coset. Thus, if they were distinct,
\[
 |C_1\symd C_2|\ge\max(|C_1|,|C_2|)>2n/3,
\]
contrary to the triangle inequality. In particular, any coset within $n/3$ of $A$ is its unique nearest coset: any better coset would also be within $n/3$.

\begin{lemma}[Explicit energy rounding]\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:lem:rounding}
If $\eps_2(A)=e<1/60$, there is a unique nearest finite coset $C$, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:rounding}
 \delta(A)\le\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4e}}2<\frac1{50},\qquad
 \delta(A)\le2e.
\end{equation}
Moreover $e\ge\delta-\delta^2$, with equality at positive distance exactly for a deletion of a subcoset from $C$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The coarse coset satisfies $\delta_C<3/5$ and, by \eqref{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:energy-local}, $e\ge\delta_C(1-\delta_C)$. The larger root of $u(1-u)=e<1/60$ exceeds $3/5$, so $\delta_C$ lies below the smaller root, which is less than $1/50$. Uniqueness follows from the preceding argument. The rationalized smaller root is
$2e/(1+\sqrt{1-4e})\le2e$. Equality in the profile forces $s=0$ in \eqref{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:energy-local}, and then equality in \eqref{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:energy-complement} forces the holes to be a coset. The converse follows by direct substitution.
\end{proof}

\section{Source~99: exponential rank dependence of Bohr boundaries in prime cyclic groups \wtag}\label{gsr:en:sec:primebohr}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the fourteenth write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next nine sections are source~99's Sections~2--9 and Appendix~A. \emph{Logically they continue the Section~10 chapter of sources~28 and~30} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:section10}), immediately after source~30's exponential-rank obstruction (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:30:cor:exponential}), and source~12's Bohr-radius chapter (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:bohr}). The introduction is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:99:sec:d1}.

\emph{What is proved.} For every $r\ge2$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there are fixed distinct frequencies $a_0,\ldots,a_{r-1}$ (as close in ratio as one likes) and a rational radius such that in every sufficiently large prime cyclic group the Bohr set has exactly $2^r-1$ cyclic runs and normalized boundary ratio above $(1-\varepsilon)(2^r-1)/2$, every constraint essential (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:99:thm:main}); with source~30's escape-tube upper bound, $(2^r-1)/2\le c_r^{\mathrm{prime}}\le c_r^{\mathrm{fin}}\le3^r-1$, and $c_1=1/2$ (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:99:cor:constants}). Also an exact arc classification, a closed mass formula, a radius window on which the run count persists, and a total-variation approximation/translation tradeoff. \emph{Against source~30}: source~30 had $\mathcal L_{2s+1}\ge3^s/2$ by a product spike in \emph{composite} cyclic groups and said the prime case and the optimal base were unsettled; source~99 gives $(2^r-1)/2$ for every $r$ in prime cyclic groups, which exceeds $3^s/2$ at every odd rank $r=2s+1\ge3$. So source~30's Question~2 (prime order) is answered and the lower rank base of its Question~1 rises from $\sqrt3$ to~$2$; the base $2$ against $3$ is open (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:fixedradius}). In rank one $\mathcal L_1=c_1=1/2$ (source~30 had $\mathcal L_1\le2$). The radius $\rho=1/(2T)$ depends on the rank and the accuracy, so the problem at a radius fixed independently of $r$ is untouched (source~99's Question~2). Normalizations agree: source~30's $t=\max_i\normT{\chi_i(d)}/\rho_i$ with individual widths, source~99's common radius a special case; both use the one-sided boundary $b_B(d)=|B\setminus(B+d)|$.

\emph{Checked at the write} (\file{verify14.py}): Appendix~A's instance, frequencies $11$, $12$ and radius $1/20$ in $\Z/10007\Z$: $|B|=105$, three runs, $K=10007/8400$; $(2^{2s+1}-1)/2>3^s/2$ for $s\ge1$.

\emph{Formal status} (HEAD \texttt{a0c3e9b67}): source~99's sets are literally \file{bohr} (\file{Definitions}:282) on \file{ZMod p} with $K=\{a_j\}$ and $\delta=\rho$, the domain of Gowers's Lemma~10.10, \file{lemma_10_10} (\file{Section10}:362), exact as \file{lemma_10_10_holds} (\file{Proofs10Bohr}:277); its family satisfies that upper bound trivially (its ratio is far below $2^{r+1}r\rho^{1-r}$). No lower bound, escape tube or spike is formalized; \file{corollary_10_11} and \file{theorem_10_13} are unchanged by it.
