\section[{Definitions and main results\srctag{99}}]{Definitions and main results}\label{gsr:en:99:sec:d2}\label{gsr:en:99:sec:main}
\srcnote{99}{Section 2}

We write $\T=\R/\Z$ and $\normT{t}=\min_{n\in\Z}|t-n|$. Characters are additive homomorphisms $\chi:G\to\T$. For a finite abelian group $G$, a nonempty finite set $\Gamma$ of characters and $0<\rho\le1/4$, put
\[
 B(\Gamma,\rho)=\{x\in G:\normT{\chi(x)}\le\rho\text{ for all }\chi\in\Gamma\}.
\]
The \emph{defining rank} is $|\Gamma|$. It is a number of constraints, not the dimension of the subgroup generated by the characters. In a prime cyclic group the latter distinction is essential.

For $d\in G$, define the one-sided boundary and normalized step by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:99:eq:definitions}
 b_B(d)=|B\setminus(B+d)|,
 \qquad
 \eta_\Gamma(d)=\frac{\max_{\chi\in\Gamma}\normT{\chi(d)}}{\rho}.
\end{equation}
Translation invariance of cardinality gives
\[
 b_B(d)=|\{x\in B:x+d\notin B\}|=b_B(-d),
 \qquad |B\mathbin\triangle(B+d)|=2b_B(d).
\]
Whenever $\eta_\Gamma(d)>0$, set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:99:eq:ratio}
 K(B,d)=\frac{b_B(d)}{\eta_\Gamma(d)|B|}.
\end{equation}
An absolute angular step $\zeta$ corresponds to $\eta=\zeta/\rho$; these normalizations must not be interchanged in comparing inequalities.

\begin{theorem}[Prime-cyclic exponential obstruction]\label{gsr:en:99:thm:main}
For every integer $r\ge2$ and every $0<\eps<1$, there exist distinct positive integers $a_0,\ldots,a_{r-1}$ and a rational $0<\rho<1/4$ with the following properties. For every sufficiently large prime $p$, let
\[
 B_p=\{x\in\Z/p\Z:\normT{a_jx/p}\le\rho\text{ for }0\le j<r\}.
\]
Then $B_p$ has exactly $2^r-1$ nonempty cyclic runs, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:99:eq:main-bound}
 b_{B_p}(1)=2^r-1,
 \qquad
 K(B_p,1)>(1-\eps)\frac{2^r-1}{2}.
\end{equation}
The frequencies and radius are fixed before $p$ tends to infinity, and $\eta_\Gamma(1)\to0$. Moreover, every defining inequality is individually essential for all sufficiently large $p$. For any prescribed $\kappa>0$, the construction can also ensure
\[
 \frac{\max_j a_j}{\min_j a_j}<1+\kappa.
\]
\end{theorem}

Here a cyclic run is a connected component in the cycle graph with edges $x\sim x+1$. A nonempty proper set with $M$ such components has one exit edge per component and therefore boundary $M$.

\begin{remark}[Quantifiers about the radius]
For each fixed $r$ and accuracy $\eps$, the theorem uses a single radius for all sufficiently large primes. It does \emph{not} assert one radius uniform in $r$ and $\eps$. The construction's radii tend to zero when its sharpness parameter tends to infinity. Section~\ref{gsr:en:99:sec:robust} nevertheless gives a nonzero interval of radii on which the component count persists.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[Asymptotic extremal constants]
Let $c_r^{\mathrm{fin}}$ be
\[
 \lim_{\tau\downarrow0}\ \sup\{K(B,d): G\text{ finite abelian},\ |\Gamma|\le r,
 \ 0<\rho\le1/4,\ 0<\eta_\Gamma(d)\le\tau\}.
\]
Define $c_r^{\mathrm{prime}}$ by restricting $G$ to prime cyclic groups. The limits exist in $[0,\infty]$ because the suprema decrease as $\tau$ decreases.
\end{definition}

\begin{corollary}[Rank bounds]\label{gsr:en:99:cor:constants}
For every $r\ge1$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:99:eq:constants}
 \frac{2^r-1}{2}\le c_r^{\mathrm{prime}}
 \le c_r^{\mathrm{fin}}\le3^r-1.
\end{equation}
In rank one, $c_1^{\mathrm{prime}}=c_1^{\mathrm{fin}}=1/2$.
Consequently no polynomial $P(r)$ can bound $K(B,d)$ uniformly at small positive steps, even if only prime cyclic groups are allowed.
\end{corollary}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Against source~30} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:primebohr}). Source~30 had $\mathcal L_{2s+1}\ge3^s/2$ in composite cyclic groups (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:30:cor:exponential}) and $\mathcal L_1\le2$; with $c_r^{\mathrm{prime}}\le\mathcal L_r\le c_r^{\mathrm{fin}}$ this corollary answers source~30's prime-order question, raises the lower rank base from $\sqrt3$ to~$2$ and gives $\mathcal L_1=1/2$; the base $2$ against $3$ is open (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:fixedradius}). The Bohr sets are the Lean \file{bohr} on \file{ZMod p} (\file{Definitions}:282), the domain of \file{lemma_10_10_holds}.
\end{writenote}

The upper estimate is an attributed consequence of the fixed-radius package, reproved here for completeness. It is not claimed to be sharp. Our construction closes neither the base-$2$ versus base-$3$ gap in \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:constants} nor the fixed-radius-uniform-in-rank problem.

\begin{theorem}[Approximation--translation tradeoff]\label{gsr:en:99:thm:tradeoff-intro}
Fix $r\ge1$ and let $C_r,D_r\ge0$. Suppose there is $\tau_r>0$ and a rule assigning a probability measure $\nu$ to every prime-cyclic instance of defining rank at most $r$ with $0<\eta\le\tau_r$, in such a way that
\[
 \dTV(\nu,\mu_B)\le D_r\eta,
 \qquad
 \dTV(\tau_d\nu,\nu)\le C_r\eta,
 \qquad \mu_B=\frac{\ind_B}{|B|}.
\]
Here $\tau_d\nu(x)=\nu(x-d)$ and $\eta=\eta_\Gamma(d)$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:99:eq:tradeoff-main}
 C_r+2D_r\ge\frac{2^r-1}{2}.
\end{equation}
In particular both costs cannot be polynomial in $r$.
\end{theorem}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{From circle arcs to prime cyclic groups\srctag{99}}]{From circle arcs to prime cyclic groups}\label{gsr:en:99:sec:d3}\label{gsr:en:99:sec:discretization}
\srcnote{99}{Section 3}

The discretization mechanism needs no equidistribution estimate or theorem on primes in short intervals. The elementary uniform grid suffices.

\begin{lemma}[Arc-counting and run-counting]\label{gsr:en:99:lem:grid}
Let $E\subset\T$ be a union of $M$ pairwise disjoint closed arcs of positive lengths less than one, with positive gaps between consecutive arcs. Let $\mu(E)$ be their total length. For an integer $n\ge2$, put
\[
 E_n=\{x\in\Z/n\Z:x/n\in E\}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:99:eq:discrepancy}
 \bigl||E_n|-n\mu(E)\bigr|\le M.
\end{equation}
If every arc has length greater than $2/n$ and every gap has length greater than $1/n$, then $E_n$ has exactly $M$ cyclic runs and $b_{E_n}(1)=M$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Lift a particular arc to an interval $[\alpha,\beta]\subset\R$ of length less than one. Its grid points are represented by integers in $[n\alpha,n\beta]$; reduction modulo $n$ is injective on them. Their number is
\[
 \lfloor n\beta\rfloor-\lceil n\alpha\rceil+1,
\]
unless the interval contains no integer, in which case it is zero. In either case the difference from $n(\beta-\alpha)$ has absolute value at most one. Summing over the disjoint arcs proves \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:discrepancy}. An arc of length greater than $2/n$ contains grid points forming a nonempty consecutive block. An open gap of length greater than $1/n$ contains a grid point, so distinct blocks do not merge. This proves the run count, including the component that crosses zero.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Boundary ratio under discretization]\label{gsr:en:99:prop:discretization}
Let $a_0,\ldots,a_{r-1}$ be distinct positive integers, let $a_* =\max_j a_j$, and suppose
\[
 E=\{t\in\T:\normT{a_jt}\le\rho\text{ for all }j\}
\]
is a union of $M$ positive-length arcs separated by positive gaps. For every sufficiently large integer $n$,
\[
 b_{E_n}(1)=M,\qquad \eta_n=\frac{a_*}{\rho n},
\]
and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:99:eq:grid-limit}
 \lim_{n\to\infty}K(E_n,1)=\frac{\rho M}{a_*\mu(E)}.
\end{equation}
The same limit holds along primes. If $n\mu(E)>M$ and the run-count hypotheses hold, then, writing $K_\infty=\rho M/(a_*\mu(E))$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:99:eq:grid-error}
 \frac{K_\infty}{1+M/(n\mu(E))}
 \le K(E_n,1)\le
 \frac{K_\infty}{1-M/(n\mu(E))}.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For $n>2a_*$, $\normT{a_j/n}=a_j/n$, and the frequencies remain distinct and nonzero modulo $n$. Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:99:lem:grid}; then
\[
 K(E_n,1)=\frac{\rho M n}{a_*|E_n|}.
\]
The discrepancy bound gives both the limit and \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:grid-error}. There are arbitrarily large primes, and the assertions hold for all large integers, so restriction to primes introduces no additional analytic input.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{An explicit near-parallel frequency system\srctag{99}}]{An explicit near-parallel frequency system}\label{gsr:en:99:sec:d4}\label{gsr:en:99:sec:parameters}
\srcnote{99}{Section 4}

Fix $r\ge2$ and put $s=r-1$. Set $D=s!$ and choose an integer $T$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:99:eq:T}
 T\equiv1\pmod D,\qquad T\ge2sD+4.
\end{equation}
For $D=1$, the congruence places no restriction. Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:99:eq:parameters}
 q_i=T+iD\quad(1\le i\le s),\qquad
 A=\prod_{i=1}^s q_i,\qquad \rho=\frac1{2T},
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:99:eq:frequencies}
 a_0=A,\qquad a_i=A+\frac{A}{q_i}\quad(1\le i\le s).
\end{equation}
The circle model is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:99:eq:circle}
 \B=\{t\in\T:\normT{a_it}\le\rho\ (0\le i\le s)\}.
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}[Arithmetic properties]\label{gsr:en:99:lem:arithmetic}
The $q_i$ are pairwise coprime. The $a_i$ are distinct positive integers, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:99:eq:frequency-ratio}
 a_*=a_1=A\left(1+\frac1{q_1}\right),\qquad
 \frac{a_*}{a_0}=1+\frac1{q_1}.
\end{equation}
Also $T\ge6$, $q_i>T$, and $q_s+1\le2T$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If a prime $\ell$ divides both $q_i$ and $q_j$, with $i<j$, then it divides $(j-i)D$. Every prime factor of $j-i$ divides $s!=D$. Thus $\ell\mid D$. But $q_i\equiv T\equiv1\pmod\ell$, a contradiction. The remaining assertions follow immediately from the definitions and \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:T}.
\end{proof}

The first constraint in \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:circle} partitions the problem into disjoint narrow cells. Every point satisfying it has a unique representation
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:99:eq:cell-representation}
 t=\frac{x+u}{A}\pmod1,
 \qquad x\in\Z/A\Z,\qquad -\rho\le u\le\rho.
\end{equation}
Uniqueness follows from $2\rho<1$. Write $y_i$ for a centered integer representative of $x\bmod q_i$. Substituting \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:cell-representation} into \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:frequencies} gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:99:eq:residual}
 a_it\equiv\frac{y_i}{q_i}+\left(1+\frac1{q_i}\right)u\pmod1.
\end{equation}
The Chinese remainder theorem permits the residues $y_i$ to be prescribed independently. Its use here is \emph{inside an auxiliary circle model}; the final finite ambient modulus is prime, not $A$.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Exact component classification\srctag{99}}]{Exact component classification}\label{gsr:en:99:sec:d5}\label{gsr:en:99:sec:components}
\srcnote{99}{Section 5}

Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:99:eq:LU}
 L_i=\frac{1-\rho q_i}{q_i+1},\qquad
 U_i=\frac{\rho q_i}{q_i+1}.
\end{equation}
Both numbers are positive. The sequence $L_i$ decreases with $i$, while $U_i$ increases with $i$.

\begin{lemma}[Three residue values and one sign]\label{gsr:en:99:lem:residues}
If \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:cell-representation} belongs to $\B$, then every $y_i$ lies in $\{-1,0,1\}$. Residues of both signs cannot occur in the same noncentral cell: $y_i=-1$ forces $u>0$, while $y_i=1$ forces $u<0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
By the triangle inequality on $\T$ and \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:residual},
\[
 \frac{|y_i|}{q_i}=\normT{y_i/q_i}
 \le\rho+\left(1+\frac1{q_i}\right)|u|
 \le\left(2+\frac1{q_i}\right)\rho.
\]
Consequently
\[
 |y_i|\le(2q_i+1)\rho
 =1+\frac{iD+1/2}{T}<2.
\]
Since $y_i$ is an integer, it is $-1$, $0$, or $1$. For these residues,
\[
 \left|\frac{y_i}{q_i}+\left(1+\frac1{q_i}\right)u\right|
 \le\frac1{T+1}+\frac{1+1/(T+1)}{2T}<\frac12.
\]
Thus the modular inequality unwraps to an ordinary absolute-value inequality. Since $\rho q_i<1$, the lower endpoint of the permissible $u$-interval for $y_i=-1$ is $L_i>0$. Reflection gives the assertion for $y_i=1$.
\end{proof}

For each nonempty $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,s\}$, let $x_S\in\Z/A\Z$ be the unique residue satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:99:eq:CRT-pattern}
 x_S\equiv\begin{cases}-1\pmod{q_i},&i\in S,\\0\pmod{q_i},&i\notin S.\end{cases}
\end{equation}
Set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:99:eq:subset-endpoints}
 \ell_S=L_{\min S},\qquad
 v_S=\begin{cases}U_{\min S^c},&S\ne\{1,\ldots,s\},\\
 \rho,&S=\{1,\ldots,s\}.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
The notation $\min S^c$ is used only when the complement is nonempty.

\begin{theorem}[Complete list of arcs]\label{gsr:en:99:thm:arcs}
The circle set $\B$ consists of exactly $M=2^{s+1}-1=2^r-1$ pairwise disjoint positive-length closed arcs:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:99:eq:arcs}
 \left[-\frac{U_1}{A},\frac{U_1}{A}\right],\qquad
 \left[\frac{x_S+\ell_S}{A},\frac{x_S+v_S}{A}\right],\qquad
 -\left[\frac{x_S+\ell_S}{A},\frac{x_S+v_S}{A}\right]
 \quad(\varnothing\ne S\subseteq[s]),
\end{equation}
where intervals are read on $\T$. Every arc has length at least $1/(4AT^2)$, and every gap has length at least $(1-2\rho)/A$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
When all $y_i=0$, the inequalities in \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:residual} become $|u|\le U_i$, so the central interval is $[-U_1,U_1]$ in the $u$-coordinate. If $u>0$, Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:99:lem:residues} permits precisely the patterns $y_i=-1$ for $i\in S$, $y_i=0$ otherwise. For $i\in S$, the allowed interval is
\[
 L_i\le u\le \frac{1+\rho q_i}{q_i+1}.
\]
Its upper endpoint exceeds $\rho$, since its difference from $\rho$ is $(1-\rho)/(q_i+1)>0$. For $i\notin S$, the only additional restriction is $u\le U_i$. Intersecting these inequalities with $0<u\le\rho$ gives exactly \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:subset-endpoints}. Reflection supplies all negative-sign patterns. No other patterns are possible.

We verify positive lengths quantitatively. From \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:parameters} and \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:LU},
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:99:eq:LU-differences}
 \rho-L_i=\frac{2iD+1}{2T(q_i+1)},\qquad
 \rho-U_j=\frac1{2T(q_j+1)}.
\end{equation}
For a proper nonempty $S$, write $i=\min S$ and $j=\min S^c$. Since $q_i+1\le2T$ and $q_j+1\ge T$,
\[
 v_S-\ell_S
 =\frac{2iD+1}{2T(q_i+1)}-\frac1{2T(q_j+1)}
 \ge\frac{2D-1}{4T^2}\ge\frac1{4T^2}.
\]
For $S=[s]$, only the first positive term occurs, and the same lower bound holds. The central length $2U_1$ is also at least $1/(4T^2)$. Division by $A$ proves the arc-length bound.

The CRT patterns are distinct: the zero pattern, the nonempty negative patterns, and their positive reflections cannot coincide because $q_i>2$. Thus different arcs lie in different first-constraint cells. Consecutive such cells have gaps at least $(1-2\rho)/A$, even if intervening cells are unoccupied. This proves disjointness and the gap bound. The number of arcs is $1+2(2^s-1)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Geometry of the obstruction]
For fixed $s$, the central arc has $u$-length of order $T^{-1}$, while each noncentral arc has length of order $T^{-2}$. Nevertheless each noncentral arc contributes one exit on a sufficiently fine cyclic grid. The number of these small components is exponential in the number of constraints. Their masses become negligible without their boundary contributions disappearing. Near-parallel frequencies therefore do not imply a single interval-like Bohr set.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Exact mass and the prime-order lower bound\srctag{99}}]{Exact mass and the prime-order lower bound}\label{gsr:en:99:sec:d6}\label{gsr:en:99:sec:mass}
\srcnote{99}{Section 6}

\begin{theorem}[Closed mass formula]\label{gsr:en:99:thm:mass}
The Haar probability measure $\mu=\mu(\B)$ equals
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:99:eq:mass-general}
 A\mu=2\rho+2\sum_{i=1}^s2^{s-i}\frac{2\rho q_i-1}{q_i+1}.
\end{equation}
In particular, define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:99:eq:F}
 F_s(T)=1+2D\sum_{i=1}^s\frac{i2^{s-i}}{T+iD+1}.
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:99:eq:mass-special}
 \mu=\frac{F_s(T)}{AT},\qquad
 1\le F_s(T)\le1+\frac{2D(2^{s+1}-s-2)}{T}.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Among the nonempty subsets $S$, exactly $2^{s-i}$ have $\min S=i$. Hence
\[
 \sum_{S\ne\varnothing}\ell_S=\sum_{i=1}^s2^{s-i}L_i.
\]
The complements of nonempty proper subsets range over nonempty proper subsets. Removing the full complement subtracts $U_1$, while $S=[s]$ contributes $\rho$. Therefore
\[
 \sum_{S\ne\varnothing}v_S=\rho+\sum_{i=1}^s2^{s-i}U_i-U_1.
\]
Adding the central length $2U_1$ and twice the noncentral positive lengths gives
\[
 A\mu=2\rho+2\sum_{i=1}^s2^{s-i}(U_i-L_i),
\]
which is \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:mass-general}. Now $2\rho q_i-1=iD/T$, proving \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:mass-special}. Finally
\[
 \sum_{i=1}^s i2^{s-i}=2^{s+1}-s-2
\]
follows by induction (or by differentiating a finite geometric sum), and every denominator in \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:F} is at least $T$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Finite-prime formula]\label{gsr:en:99:thm:finite-prime}
For the parameters in Section~\ref{gsr:en:99:sec:parameters}, every prime
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:99:eq:prime-threshold}
 p>8AT^2
\end{equation}
satisfies
\begin{align}
 b_{B_p}(1)&=M=2^r-1,\label{gsr:en:99:eq:finite-boundary}\\
 \bigl||B_p|-pF_s(T)/(AT)\bigr|&\le M,\label{gsr:en:99:eq:finite-card}\\
 \eta_p&=\frac{2TA(1+1/q_1)}p.\label{gsr:en:99:eq:finite-eta}
\end{align}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:99:eq:K-limit}
 \lim_{\substack{p\to\infty\\p\ \mathrm{prime}}}K(B_p,1)
 =K_r(T):=\frac{2^r-1}{2(1+1/q_1)F_s(T)}.
\end{equation}
Whenever $p\mu>M$, the two-sided error estimate \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:grid-error} holds with $K_\infty=K_r(T)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Under \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:prime-threshold}, the shortest arc in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:99:thm:arcs} has length greater than $2/p$. The gaps exceed $1/p$ because $(1-2\rho)/A\ge(5/6)/A$ and $T\ge6$. Also $p>2a_*$. Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:99:lem:grid}, Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:99:prop:discretization} and Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:99:thm:mass}. Substitution into $\rho M/(a_*\mu)$ gives \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:K-limit}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of the main numerical assertion in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:99:thm:main}]
For fixed $r$, $F_s(T)\to1$ and $1+1/q_1\to1$ as $T\to\infty$ through \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:T}. Thus
\[
 K_r(T)\longrightarrow\frac{2^r-1}{2}.
\]
Choose $T$ large enough that $K_r(T)>(1-\eps/2)(2^r-1)/2$, and then choose the prime cutoff large enough that the finite-prime ratio is greater than $(1-\eps)(2^r-1)/2$. The same frequencies and radius work for every prime beyond this cutoff. Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:finite-eta} proves $\eta_p\to0$, and \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:frequency-ratio} proves the optional near-parallel requirement after enlarging $T$ further. Irredundancy is established in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:99:thm:irredundancy} below.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[An explicit choice for an accuracy target]\label{gsr:en:99:prop:accuracy}
Let $0<\eps<1$ and put $H=2^r-r-1$. Choose $T$ satisfying \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:T} and
\[
 T\ge\frac{4(1+2DH)}\eps.
\]
Then $K_r(T)\ge(1-\eps/2)M/2$. If in addition
\[
 p>\max\{8AT^2,\ 2MAT/\eps\},
\]
then $K(B_p,1)>(1-\eps)M/2$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Using $q_1\ge T$ and \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:mass-special},
\[
 (1+1/q_1)F_s(T)
 \le(1+1/T)(1+2DH/T)
 \le1+\frac{2(1+2DH)}T\le1+\eps/2.
\]
Here $T\ge1$ suffices for the middle bound. Since $(1+x)^{-1}\ge1-x$ for $x\ge0$, the first claim follows. Also $\mu\ge1/(AT)$, so $M/(p\mu)<\eps/2$. The lower half of \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:grid-error} yields
\[
 K(B_p,1)\ge\frac M2\frac{1-\eps/2}{1+\eps/2}>\frac M2(1-\eps).
\]
\end{proof}

The exact formula is increasing in $T$ if the factorial $D$ and rank are held fixed: every nonconstant positive factor in its denominator decreases. Thus $M/2$ is the supremum of the limiting ratios \emph{within this family}. This observation must not be read as a universal optimality statement.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Robust radii and irredundant defining constraints\srctag{99}}]{Robust radii and irredundant defining constraints}\label{gsr:en:99:sec:d7}\label{gsr:en:99:sec:robust}
\srcnote{99}{Section 7}

\subsection{A full radius interval}
The small components are not merely isolated grid points created by a closed-endpoint convention.

\begin{theorem}[Persistence under radius perturbation]\label{gsr:en:99:thm:robust}
Keep $q_i,A,a_i$ fixed and replace $\rho=1/(2T)$ by a radius $\rho'$ with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:99:eq:radius-window}
 |\rho'-\rho|\le\frac1{16T^2}.
\end{equation}
The same CRT patterns describe exactly $M=2^r-1$ positive-length arcs. Each arc has length at least $1/(8AT^2)$, and each gap has length at least $(1-2\rho')/A$. Their measure is an affine function of $\rho'$:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:99:eq:affine-mass}
 A\mu(\rho')=2\rho'M
 -2(2\rho'+1)\sum_{i=1}^s\frac{2^{s-i}}{q_i+1}.
\end{equation}
Consequently every sufficiently fine prime grid has the same exact boundary $M$ throughout this radius window; the sufficient uniform condition $p>16AT^2$ works.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $T\ge6$ and $q_i\le T+sD\le3T/2-2$, the perturbed radius still satisfies
\[
 0<\rho'<\tfrac14,\qquad \rho'q_i<1,
 \qquad (2q_i+1)\rho'<2.
\]
For example $\rho'\le1/(2T)+1/(16T^2)<9/(16T)$ and $q_i<3T/2$, so the second product is less than $27/32$. Also
\[
 (2q_i+1)\rho'
 \le(3T-3)\left(\frac1{2T}+\frac1{16T^2}\right)<2.
\]
The unwrapping estimate remains valid because
\[
 \frac1{T+1}+\left(1+\frac1{T+1}\right)\rho'<\frac12.
\]
Therefore the residue restriction and the exclusion of mixed signs remain unchanged.

The endpoint formulas remain $L_i(\rho')=(1-\rho'q_i)/(q_i+1)$ and $U_i(\rho')=\rho'q_i/(q_i+1)$, with the same monotonicity in $i$. Each endpoint has derivative in $\rho'$ of absolute value at most one, including the endpoint $\rho'$ itself. Thus every noncentral $u$-length changes by at most $2|\rho'-\rho|\le1/(8T^2)$. Its original length is at least $1/(4T^2)$, so its perturbed length is at least $1/(8T^2)$. The central length satisfies the same estimate. Distinct arcs still occupy distinct first-constraint cells, proving the gap statement. Repeating the subset sum in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:99:thm:mass}, now using
\[
 U_i(\rho')-L_i(\rho')
 =2\rho'-\frac{2\rho'+1}{q_i+1},
\]
gives \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:affine-mass}. The final statement follows from Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:99:lem:grid}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Every frequency does work}
\begin{theorem}[Individual essentiality]\label{gsr:en:99:thm:irredundancy}
For the original radius $\rho=1/(2T)$, deleting any one of the $r$ defining inequalities strictly enlarges the circle Bohr set. In each case there is a nonempty open interval on which all the retained inequalities hold strictly and the deleted inequality fails strictly. Hence all $r$ inequalities are individually essential on every sufficiently fine prime grid.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
First delete $a_i$ for some $1\le i\le s$. Choose $x\in\Z/A\Z$ with residues $x\equiv2\pmod{q_i}$ and $x\equiv0\pmod{q_j}$ for $j\ne i$, and take $u=0$. The $a_0$-constraint and all retained constraints have residual zero. The deleted constraint has residual $2/q_i$, which is less than $1/2$ and greater than $\rho$. These inequalities are strict and persist on an open neighborhood.

Next delete $a_0$. Let $x$ have residue $-1$ modulo every $q_i$, and choose
\[
 u=\rho+\frac{1-\rho}{2(q_s+1)}.
\]
For each $i$, the allowable interval under the $a_i$-constraint is
\[
 L_i<u<\rho+\frac{1-\rho}{q_i+1}.
\]
The chosen $u$ lies strictly inside every such interval, but $u>\rho$, so the $a_0$-constraint fails. Also $u<1/2$, so this failure is genuinely modular, not an unwrapping artifact. Again an open neighborhood witnesses strict enlargement. A nonempty open interval contains a point of every sufficiently fine grid. Taking the largest of the finitely many required cutoffs proves the finite statement.
\end{proof}

Individual essentiality rules out padding the example with unused frequencies. It does not claim that no entirely different system with fewer constraints and another radius can describe the same finite set; that stronger minimization problem is not needed here.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Upper comparison and rank-one calibration\srctag{99}}]{Upper comparison and rank-one calibration}\label{gsr:en:99:sec:d8}\label{gsr:en:99:sec:upper}
\srcnote{99}{Section 8}

This section records the upper side of \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:constants}. The escape-tube argument and exponential packing estimate are already part of the inspected fixed-radius package \cite{srcthirty}; their inclusion here fixes conventions and makes the comparison self-contained.

\begin{lemma}[No immediate re-entry]\label{gsr:en:99:lem:no-reentry}
Suppose $0<\rho\le1/4$, $m\ge1$, and
\[
 \normT{\chi(d)}\le\frac\rho{2m}\quad(\chi\in\Gamma).
\]
If $x\in B=B(\Gamma,\rho)$ but $x+d\notin B$, then $x+jd\notin B$ for every $1\le j\le2m$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose a character causing the first exit. Write its centered value at $x$ as $v\in[-\rho,\rho]$ and its centered value at $d$ as $h$, with $|h|\le\rho/(2m)$. There is no wrap on the first step since $|v+h|\le3\rho/2<1/2$. After changing the sign of this character if necessary, $h>0$ and $v+h>\rho$. For $1\le j\le2m$,
\[
 \rho<v+jh\le\rho+2mh\le2\rho\le\tfrac12.
\]
Its distance to the nearest integer is therefore greater than $\rho$ at every such step, including a possible value $1/2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Escape-tube inequality]\label{gsr:en:99:prop:escape}
Under the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:99:lem:no-reentry},
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:99:eq:escape}
 2m\,b_B(d)\le |B(\Gamma,3\rho/2)|-|B|
 \le(3^r-1)|B|,
 \qquad r=|\Gamma|.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Let $E_+=\{x\in B:x+d\notin B\}$ and $E_-=\{x\in B:x-d\notin B\}$. They have the same size $b_B(d)$. Consider the $2m$ translated sets
\[
 E_++jd,\quad E_--jd\qquad(1\le j\le m).
\]
They lie outside $B$ by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:99:lem:no-reentry}. Two sets of the same sign cannot intersect: a collision would place a point of $B$ at a positive return time at most $m-1$ from an exit point. A collision of opposite signs would give a return time $j+k\le2m$. All are impossible. The triangle inequality places every translated point in $B(\Gamma,3\rho/2)$, proving the first inequality.

For the second, choose centered coordinate representatives of each point in the enlarged Bohr set. Each coordinate lies in $[-3\rho/2,3\rho/2]$. Partition that interval into three sets of diameter at most $\rho$, assigning shared endpoints consistently. This partitions the enlarged Bohr set into at most $3^r$ cells. In a nonempty cell choose one point $x_0$. For every point $x$ of the cell, $x-x_0\in B(\Gamma,\rho)$. The map $x\mapsto x-x_0$ is injective, so each cell has at most $|B|$ points. Hence the enlarged set has size at most $3^r|B|$.
\end{proof}

If $0<\eta\le1/2$, take $m=\lfloor1/(2\eta)\rfloor$. Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:escape} gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:99:eq:upper-finite}
 K(B,d)\le\frac{3^r-1}{2\eta\lfloor1/(2\eta)\rfloor}.
\end{equation}
The denominator tends to one as $\eta\downarrow0$; more uniformly it is at least $1-2\eta$. This proves $c_r^{\mathrm{fin}}\le3^r-1$.

\begin{proposition}[Exact asymptotic rank-one constant]\label{gsr:en:99:prop:rankone}
For a single defining character and $0<\eta\le1$, one has
\[
 K(B,d)\le\frac1{2-\eta}.
\]
Consequently $c_1^{\mathrm{fin}}=c_1^{\mathrm{prime}}=1/2$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The character's image is a cyclic subgroup of $\T$ of order $q$. Its fibers have equal size, so they cancel from $K(B,d)$. Put $z=\rho q$ and $n=\lfloor z\rfloor$. The image of $B$ is $[-n,n]\subset\Z/q\Z$. Write the centered step as $\pm k/q$ with $1\le k\le q/2$. Since $\eta=k/z\le1$, $k\le n$. There is no collision with a wrapped copy of the interval, since $2n+k\le3\rho q\le3q/4<q$. Thus the one-sided boundary is $k$, and
\[
 K(B,d)=\frac{z}{2\lfloor z\rfloor+1}
 \le\frac z{2z-1}=\frac1{2-1/z}\le\frac1{2-\eta}.
\]
The denominator is positive because $z\ge k\ge1$. For the matching limit, take the character $x\mapsto x/p$, a fixed radius in $(0,1/4]$, and step one as primes $p\to\infty$. The interval has one cyclic run and its normalized ratio tends to $1/2$.
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:99:thm:main}, Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:99:prop:rankone}, and \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:upper-finite} prove Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:99:cor:constants} completely.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Functional consequences and the limits of smoothing shortcuts\srctag{99}}]{Functional consequences and the limits of smoothing shortcuts}\label{gsr:en:99:sec:d9}\label{gsr:en:99:sec:functional}
\srcnote{99}{Section 9}

For probability measures on a finite set we use
\[
 \dTV(\mu,\nu)=\frac12\sum_x|\mu(x)-\nu(x)|.
\]

\begin{lemma}[Exact testing norm]\label{gsr:en:99:lem:TV}
For every nonempty finite $B\subset G$,
\begin{align}
 \dTV(\tau_d\mu_B,\mu_B)
 &=\frac{b_B(d)}{|B|},\label{gsr:en:99:eq:TV}\\
 \sup_{0\le f\le1}\left|\sum_xf(x)(\tau_d\mu_B(x)-\mu_B(x))\right|
 &=\frac{b_B(d)}{|B|}.\label{gsr:en:99:eq:testnorm}
\end{align}
For real $f$ with $|f|\le1$, the analogous supremum is $2b_B(d)/|B|$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The two uniform probability masses agree on $B\cap(B+d)$ and have difference $1/|B|$ in absolute value on their symmetric difference, which has size $2b_B(d)$. This proves \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:TV}. Taking $f$ to be the indicator of one one-sided difference attains the supremum for $0\le f\le1$; the total positive and total negative mass are both $b_B(d)/|B|$. A function equal to the sign of the signed difference attains the last supremum.
\end{proof}

Thus Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:99:thm:main} is not just a statement about a combinatorial boundary convention. It gives an exact testing-norm interpretation of the obstruction to translating averages against a sharp Bohr probability measure.

\begin{proposition}[Finite-instance tradeoff]\label{gsr:en:99:prop:tradeoff}
For any probability measure $\nu$ on $G$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:99:eq:finite-tradeoff}
 \dTV(\tau_d\nu,\nu)+2\dTV(\nu,\mu_B)
 \ge\frac{b_B(d)}{|B|}.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The triangle inequality and invariance of total variation under translation give
\[
 \dTV(\tau_d\mu_B,\mu_B)
 \le\dTV(\tau_d\mu_B,\tau_d\nu)
   +\dTV(\tau_d\nu,\nu)+\dTV(\nu,\mu_B)
 =2\dTV(\nu,\mu_B)+\dTV(\tau_d\nu,\nu).
\]
Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:99:lem:TV}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:99:thm:tradeoff-intro}]
Apply \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:finite-tradeoff} to the rule in the theorem and divide by $\eta$. For every instance covered by the rule,
\[
 C_r+2D_r\ge K(B,d).
\]
Use Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:99:thm:main}, first taking arbitrarily large primes for a fixed construction and then taking $T$ arbitrarily large. The rank-one case follows from Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:99:prop:rankone}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{What this means for the two research programs}
A proposed replacement for a Bohr localization step cannot assert, at every radius and for every bounded test function, a translation error $\operatorname{poly}(r)\eta$ for the sharp uniform measure. Nor can it evade the obstruction by introducing a probability kernel that stays within $\operatorname{poly}(r)\eta$ in total variation while also having translation error $\operatorname{poly}(r)\eta$.

There are several legitimate ways around the hypotheses. A proof can choose a regular radius, allow a larger approximation error, use positive smooth cutoffs rather than approximate the sharp uniform measure at the step scale, or exploit special structure of the test functions. These are genuinely different interfaces. In particular, \eqref{gsr:fm:99:eq:certificate} does not demand an $O(\operatorname{poly}(r)\eta)$ total-variation approximation to an arbitrary sharp cell. The OpenAI setup's padding, translation averaging and target discount therefore are not contradicted by our theorem. Their role is made more precise: the unrestricted sharp-indicator shortcut would be false even in the prime-cyclic linear model.

The examples are not constructed to be progression-free. Consequently the extremal test in \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:testnorm} is not an obstruction to every possible estimate specialized to a progression-free density-increment input. Such a specialization would need its own assumptions and proof. Similarly, a large family-dependent frequency bound or prime cutoff here is not a new upper or lower bound for $r_k(N)$.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A worked rank-two example\srctag{99}}]{A worked rank-two example}\label{gsr:en:99:sec:dA}\label{gsr:en:99:app:example}
\srcnote{99}{Appendix A}

Take $r=2$, $s=D=1$, $T=10$. Then
\[
 q_1=A=11,\qquad (a_0,a_1)=(11,12),\qquad \rho=1/20.
\]
The central $u$-interval has endpoints $\pm11/240$, so the central circle arc is $[-1/240,1/240]$. The nonempty subset is $S=\{1\}$, for which $x_S=10$, $\ell_S=3/80$ and $v_S=1/20$. The positive-sign arc in the chosen lift is
\[
 \left[\frac{803}{880},\frac{201}{220}\right],
\]
and the third arc is its reflection. Each noncentral arc has length $1/880$. Consequently
\[
 \mu=\frac1{120}+\frac2{880}=\frac7{660},\qquad
 K_2(10)=\frac{(1/20)\,3}{12\,(7/660)}=\frac{33}{28}.
\]
The sufficient grid cutoff is $p>8\cdot11\cdot10^2=8,800$. For the prime $p=10,007$, direct enumeration gives $|B_p|=105$ and boundary three. The exact normalized ratio is
\[
 K(B_p,1)=\frac{3\cdot10,007}{240\cdot105}=\frac{10,007}{8,400}.
\]
This is slightly larger than the limiting ratio because the finite-grid cardinality fluctuates within the discrepancy bound. No monotonicity in $p$ is asserted. Increasing $T$ in this rank-two family, rather than merely increasing $p$, is what makes the limiting ratio approach $3/2$.

\section{Source~96: odd-target arrangement repair, the common-prime bracket and erasures \wtag}\label{gsr:en:sec:oddarrangements}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the fourteenth write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next three sections are source~96's Sections~5--6 and Appendix~A, on the high-agreement repair of respected arrangements. \emph{Logically they continue source~33's chapter} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:arrangements}) and source~60's arrangement polynomial (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:arrangementpolynomial}).

\emph{A duplicate, printed as a second route.} Source~96's Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:96:thm:arr-odd} and~\ref{gsr:en:96:thm:arr-prime-obstruction} prove the odd-target repair bound and the half-interval common-prime obstruction, hence the bracket $(s-1)/s^2\le c_s^{\mathrm{prime}}\le(3s-2)/(2s^2)$, $[15/256,23/256]$ at $s=16$, in place of source~33's $[23/512,15/128]$. \emph{Source~60 proved the same pair first} (Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:60:arr:odd-target} and~\ref{gsr:en:60:arr:prime-obstruction}; arrival \texttt{0d93c1eac}, 6~October, 22:07), and neither cites the other (source~60 was an unplaced archive at source~96's pin). The mechanisms are the same (odd-target cancellation of two errors; half-interval rows over $\lfloor\sqrt p\rfloor$ rows), but the proofs differ: source~60 expands through two errors with a cubic remainder under $\delta\le1/(4s^2)$, while source~96 uses the exact pointwise inequality $\one\ge L-\binom L2-C$, which gives the profile $\varepsilon\ge sd-s(3s-2)d^2/2$ for every full-domain map, with no remainder and no smallness hypothesis. So the section is printed whole, as a credited second route, with source~60's priority and its all-order inverse coefficients noted; the remainder-free profile is source~96's own. Appendix~A is a self-contained proof of source~33's coarse decoder, as source~60's Appendix~A is; the two are independent re-proofs of the same inherited lemma.

\emph{New in source~96}: the erasure theorem (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:96:thm:arr-erasure}). Source~33's erasure-robust repair $R_s(E)/(1-\tau)$ keeps an additive floor $1-\lambda$ as the observed disagreement $\eta\to0$; source~96's bound $d\le(T+\sqrt{T^2+4\kappa\tau T})/2$, with $T\le80\lambda\eta/(79s)$, vanishes with $\eta$, at the optimal square-root order, and is linear when rows are thick (Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:96:prop:arr-thin-sharp} shows the thin-row regimes sharp). This advances item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:erasures}. Neither source~60 nor any source~01--95 has it.

\section[{Arrangement repair: an odd-target improvement\srctag{96}}]{Arrangement repair: an odd-target improvement}\label{gsr:en:96:sec:d5}
\srcnote{96}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:en:96:sec:arrangement-repair}

We now study the high-agreement arrangement problem of source~33 in the
repository collection \cite{repo96}. There are two refinements. Keeping
track of which erroneous edges can cancel improves the quadratic repair
coefficient for odd targets. Keeping track of which erroneous edges are
actually observed removes the additive erasure floor of the earlier
partial-domain statement.

\subsection{The test, its exact models, and the inherited decoder}

Let $G,H,K$ be finite abelian groups and let $s=2m\ge4$ be even.
A random arrangement chooses $h\in H$ uniformly, chooses
$x_1,\ldots,x_s\in G$ uniformly subject to
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-horizontal}
 x_1+\cdots+x_m=x_{m+1}+\cdots+x_s,
\end{equation}
and independently chooses uniform $y_1,\ldots,y_s\in H$. Put
$\sigma_i=1$ for $i\le m$ and $\sigma_i=-1$ otherwise. The test accepts
$\phi:G\times H\to K$ when
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-test}
 \sum_{i=1}^s\sigma_iD_h\phi(x_i,y_i)=0,
 \qquad D_h\phi(x,y)=\phi(x,y+h)-\phi(x,y).
\end{equation}
Repetitions and $h=0$ are included. There are
$|G|^{s-1}|H|^{s+1}$ ordered arrangements. For common cyclic groups,
$s=16$ is Gowers's eight-arrangement, with $N^{32}$ possible choices.

The exact model class is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-model}
 \Vmodel(G,H;K)=
 \{\psi(x,y)=a(x)+B(x,y)+\ell(y):
       B\text{ biadditive},\ \ell\in\Hom(H,K)\},
\end{equation}
where $a:G\to K$ is arbitrary. Every model passes every test:
$D_h\psi(x,y)=B(x,h)+\ell(h)$, and
\eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-horizontal} cancels the resulting sum. The arbitrary row
function is essential, since vertical differences cannot detect it.
Write $\epsilon_s(\phi)$ for the rejection probability and $d(\phi)$ for
normalized Hamming distance to $\Vmodel$.

Every proper subfamily of the $x_i$ in \eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-horizontal} is
independent and uniform. Indeed, after prescribing it, choose all but
one of the remaining coordinates freely and solve for the last, whose
coefficient is $1$ or $-1$. Consequently any proper collection of edge
variables $(x_i,y_i)$ is independent at fixed $h$. This statement concerns
the sampling law and does not exclude realized coincidences.

We use the following existing theorem solely to place a nearest model
on the small-error branch. Its proof is source~33's full-product decoder,
not a new assertion of this article \cite{repo96}. A self-contained proof
is included in Appendix~\ref{gsr:en:96:boot:sec:decoder}.

\begin{lemma}[Existing full-product repair]\label{gsr:en:96:lem:arr-existing}
If $\epsilon=\epsilon_s(\phi)\le1/[240(s-1)]$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-existing}
 d(\phi)\le R_s(\epsilon),\qquad
 R_s(u)=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-8(s-1)u/s}}{4(s-1)}.
\end{equation}
In particular $R_s(u)\le2u/s$ on this interval.
\end{lemma}

\subsection{Counting one error and canceling pairs}

\begin{theorem}[Odd-target quadratic repair]\label{gsr:en:96:thm:arr-odd}
Suppose $|K|$ is odd. For every full-domain map, with
$d=d(\phi)$ and $\epsilon=\epsilon_s(\phi)$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-odd-profile}
 \epsilon\ge sd-\frac{s(3s-2)}2d^2.
\end{equation}
Under $\epsilon\le1/[240(s-1)]$, this gives
\begin{align}
 d&\le R_s^{\mathrm{odd}}(\epsilon)
   :=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-2(3s-2)\epsilon/s}}{3s-2},
       \label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-odd-inverse}\\
 R_s^{\mathrm{odd}}(u)
   &=\frac us+\frac{3s-2}{2s^2}u^2+O_s(u^3).
       \label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-odd-series}
\end{align}
The domain groups $G,H$ need not have odd order.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Choose a nearest model and subtract it. For its fixed $B,\ell$, optimize
each row constant. Thus for the residual $r$ we may assume that
$p_x(0)=\max_zp_x(z)$, where $p_x(z)=\Prob_y[r(x,y)=z]$. Put
\[
 t_h=\Prob_{x,y}[D_hr(x,y)\ne0],\qquad
 \overline t=\E_h t_h.
\]
A nonzero difference has a nonzero endpoint, so $t_h\le2d$.
Averaging over $y,h$ gives independent uniform endpoints, hence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-row-profile}
 \overline t=\E_x\left(1-\sum_zp_x(z)^2\right)\ge d.
\end{equation}

Fix $h$ and write $Z_i=D_hr(x_i,y_i)$. Let $L$ count the nonzero
$Z_i$, and let $C$ count unordered pairs $\{i,j\}$ for which both
values are nonzero and $\sigma_iZ_i+\sigma_jZ_j=0$. Pointwise,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-pair-pointwise}
 \one_{\{\sum_i\sigma_iZ_i\ne0\}}
       \ge L-\binom L2-C.
\end{equation}
For $L=0,1,2$ this is an equality; for $L\ge3$ its right-hand side is
nonpositive. This is an exact inequality without a discarded remainder.

For $z\ne0$ write $p(z)=\Prob[Z_i=z]$ and $t=\sum_{z\ne0}p(z)=t_h$.
Pairwise independence gives
\[
 \E L=st,\qquad \E\binom L2=\binom s2t^2,
\]
and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-cancellation}
 \E C=m^2c_-+m(m-1)c_+,
 \qquad
 c_-:=\sum_{z\ne0}p(z)^2,\quad
 c_+:=\sum_{z\ne0}p(z)p(-z).
\end{equation}
The orientation matters: the $m^2$ pairs with opposite signs cancel
when their values are equal, while the $m(m-1)$ pairs with equal signs
cancel when their values are opposite.

Since $K$ has odd order, its nonzero elements split into disjoint pairs
$\{z,-z\}$. If such a pair has masses $a,b$, its contribution to
\eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-cancellation} is
\[
 m^2(a^2+b^2)+2m(m-1)ab
       =m^2(a+b)^2-2mab\le m^2(a+b)^2.
\]
Summing shows $\E C\le m^2t^2$. Thus, conditionally on $h$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-conditional-odd}
 \epsilon_h\ge st_h-A_st_h^2,
 \qquad A_s=\binom s2+m^2=\frac{s(3s-2)}4.
\end{equation}
Averaging and using $t_h\le2d$ yields
$\epsilon\ge(s-2A_sd)\overline t$. When this coefficient is nonnegative,
use \eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-row-profile}; otherwise the proposed lower bound is
negative and follows from $\epsilon\ge0$. This proves
\eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-odd-profile} for all $d$.

Under the activation hypothesis, Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:96:lem:arr-existing} gives
$d\le2\epsilon/s<1/(3s-2)$, the vertex of the new quadratic. The
smaller root is therefore the correct inverse branch, proving
\eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-odd-inverse}. Expanding the square root gives
\eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-odd-series}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{A second route to source~60's theorem.} Source~60's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:60:arr:odd-target} proved the odd-target repair bound first (arrival \texttt{0d93c1eac}, 6~October), with the same coefficient $(3s-2)/(2s^2)$, through an expansion with a cubic remainder under $\delta\le1/(4s^2)$; this source, written without knowledge of it, proves the profile for every full-domain map, with no remainder and no smallness hypothesis, from the exact pointwise inequality~\eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-pair-pointwise}. Source~60 also has every coefficient of the inverse expansion (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:60:arr:coefficients}).
\end{writenote}

The earlier all-target quadratic inverse coefficient was
$2(s-1)/s^2$. The new coefficient $(3s-2)/(2s^2)$ is strictly smaller
for every $s\ge4$. This improvement arises from the absence of nonzero
self-inverse error labels; it is not an assumption about the domain's
torsion.

\subsection{A stronger obstruction in the common-prime setting}

The earlier single-row linear-label example from source~33 leaves room
below the new upper bound. A different example improves the lower bound
as well.

\begin{theorem}[Half-interval rows over a common prime]
\label{gsr:en:96:thm:arr-prime-obstruction}
For every fixed even $s\ge4$, there are maps
$\phi_p:\F_p\times\F_p\to\F_p$, with $p$ tending to infinity through
odd primes and $d_p=d(\phi_p)\to0$, such that
\begin{align}
 \epsilon_s(\phi_p)&=sd_p-s(s-1)d_p^2+o_s(d_p^2),
       \label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-prime-expansion}\\
 d_p&=\frac{\epsilon_s(\phi_p)}s+
       \frac{s-1}{s^2}\epsilon_s(\phi_p)^2
       +o_s(\epsilon_s(\phi_p)^2).
       \label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-prime-inverse-obstruction}
\end{align}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Choose $S_p\subset\F_p$ with $k_p=|S_p|\to\infty$ and $k_p/p\to0$;
for example take $k_p=\lfloor\sqrt p\rfloor$. Put
\[
 I_p=\{0,\ldots,(p-3)/2\},\qquad
 \phi_p(x,y)=\one_{S_p}(x)\one_{I_p}(y),\qquad \nu=k_p/p.
\]
Every exact model has the form $a_x+(bx+c)y$. The model with $b=c=0$
and $a_x=0$ has distance
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-prime-distance}
 d_p=\nu\frac{p-1}{2p}.
\end{equation}
If $(b,c)\ne(0,0)$, at most one row has zero slope. On every other
row an affine function of nonzero slope can match the binary-valued
label function at at most two points, one for each possible value.
Such a model has at most $p+2(p-1)=3p-2$ matches. For $p\ge7$ the
zero-slope model has at least $p^2/2>3p-2$ matches. Optimizing its row
constants chooses zero, since $|I_p|<p/2$. Thus
\eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-prime-distance} is the exact nearest-model distance.

At fixed $h$, the derivative of $\one_{I_p}$ takes values $1,-1$ with
equal probabilities $r_h/p$, where
$r_h=|I_p\setminus(I_p-h)|$. Hence $D_h\phi_p$ has probabilities
$t_h/2$ at each of $1,-1$, where $t_h=\nu q_h$ and $q_h=2r_h/p$.
For the random variables in \eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-pair-pointwise}, the difference
between the left-hand side and the right-hand side vanishes for
$L\le2$ and has absolute value at most $s^2+1$ otherwise.
Proper-coordinate independence, including at $s=4$, gives
\[
 \Prob[L\ge3]\le\binom s3t_h^3.
\]
Every pair of nonzero signed values cancels with probability $1/2$.
Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-prime-conditional}
 \epsilon_h=st_h-\frac{3s(s-1)}4t_h^2+R_h,
 \qquad |R_h|\le(s^2+1)\binom s3t_h^3.
\end{equation}
Possible modular cancellations involving three or more errors are
already included in this remainder.

Writing $a=(p-1)/2$, we have $r_0=0$ and $r_{\pm j}=j$ for
$1\le j\le a$. The sums of the first two powers of the integers give
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-interval-moments}
 \E_hq_h=\frac{1-p^{-2}}2,
 \qquad \E_hq_h^2=\frac{1-p^{-2}}3.
\end{equation}
Combining \eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-prime-conditional}--\eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-interval-moments}
with \eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-prime-distance} gives the more precise formula
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-prime-precise}
 \epsilon_s(\phi_p)
   =sd_p(1+1/p)
    -s(s-1)d_p^2\frac{p+1}{p-1}+O_s(d_p^3).
\end{equation}
The remainder is uniform in $p$ and $S_p$: $0\le q_h\le1$ and
$\nu\le3d_p$. Since $k_p\to\infty$, we have $d_p/p=o(d_p^2)$.
This proves \eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-prime-expansion}; eliminating $d_p$ in the
series gives \eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-prime-inverse-obstruction}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{The same construction as source~60's} Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:60:arr:prime-obstruction} (half-interval labels on $\lfloor\sqrt p\rfloor$ rows), found independently; the bracket $[15/256,23/256]$ at $s=16$ is source~60's first. Both improve source~33's $[23/512,15/128]$ (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:arrangerepair}).
\end{writenote}

For precision, define the optimal common-prime second coefficient by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-prime-coefficient}
 c_s^{\mathrm{prime}}=
 \lim_{\zeta\downarrow0}\sup
 \left\{\frac{d(\phi)-\epsilon_s(\phi)/s}{\epsilon_s(\phi)^2}:
 \begin{array}{l}
 p\text{ odd prime},\ \phi:\F_p^2\to\F_p,\\
 0<\epsilon_s(\phi)\le\zeta
 \end{array}\right\}.
\end{equation}
The uniform upper expansion and the constructed sequence give
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-prime-bracket}
 \frac{s-1}{s^2}\le c_s^{\mathrm{prime}}
                    \le\frac{3s-2}{2s^2}.
\end{equation}
In particular, for eight-arrangements,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-eight-bracket}
 \boxed{\frac{15}{256}\le c_{16}^{\mathrm{prime}}
                         \le\frac{23}{256}}.
\end{equation}
Source~33 recorded $23/512\le c_{16}^{\mathrm{prime}}\le15/128$
\cite{repo96}. Both sides are improved. The exact coefficient remains open.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Erasure-sensitive arrangement repair\srctag{96}}]{Erasure-sensitive arrangement repair}\label{gsr:en:96:sec:d6}
\srcnote{96}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:en:96:sec:arrangement-erasures}

The full-product theorem also admits an extension in which the repair
error vanishes with the rejection rate among observed arrangements.
The geometry of thin rows determines the resulting modulus.

\subsection{Observed configurations and the main theorem}

Let $A\subset G\times H$ and $\phi:A\to K$. Write
\[
 \alpha=\frac{|A|}{|G||H|}=1-\tau,
 \qquad \alpha_x=\frac{|A_x|}{|H|}.
\]
Let $\lambda$ be the probability that all $2s$ point occurrences of a
sampled arrangement lie in $A$, and let $\eta$ be its rejection
probability conditional on that event. Put $\theta=\lambda\eta$.
The union bound and the uniformity of any one designated point give
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-validity}
 1-2s\tau\le\lambda\le\alpha.
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Repair with erasures and arbitrary row densities]
\label{gsr:en:96:thm:arr-erasure}
Let $q=|K|\ge2$, $\kappa=1-q^{-1}$, and suppose
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-erasure-activation}
 E:=\theta+1-\lambda\le\frac1{240(s-1)}.
\end{equation}
Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-erasure-parameters}
 D=R_s(E),\qquad b=1-2(s-1)(D+\tau),
 \qquad T=\frac{\theta}{sb}.
\end{equation}
Then $b\ge79/80$. There is a model $\psi\in\Vmodel(G,H;K)$ such that,
with
\[
 d_x=\frac{|\{y\in A_x:\phi(x,y)\ne\psi(x,y)\}|}{|H|},
 \qquad d=\E_xd_x,
\]
we have
\begin{align}
 d&\le D, & \E_x\alpha_xd_x&\le T,
          \label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-erasure-weighted}\\
 d&\le\frac{T+\sqrt{T^2+4\kappa\tau T}}2.
          \label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-erasure-root}
\end{align}
If every nonempty row has density at least $\beta>0$, then also
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-erasure-thick}
 d\le T/\beta.
\end{equation}
Relative disagreement on $A$ is $d/\alpha$. In these bounds $T$ may
be replaced by $80\lambda\eta/(79s)$. In particular, $\eta=0$ implies
exact extension to a model. A sufficient activation condition is
$\eta+2s\tau\le1/[240(s-1)]$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Extend $\phi$ arbitrarily to $G\times H$. The extension can fail only
on a valid failed arrangement or an invalid arrangement, so its full
defect is at most $E$. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:96:lem:arr-existing} supplies a model
with ambient observed distance at most $D$. Choose a nearest model on
$A$, so its distance $d$ also satisfies $d\le D$.

For this model's fixed $B,\ell$, optimize each row constant. For the
observed residual $r=\phi-\psi$, put
\[
 p_x(z)=\Prob_y[(x,y)\in A\text{ and }r(x,y)=z].
\]
Then $\sum_zp_x(z)=\alpha_x$, $p_x(0)=\max_zp_x(z)$, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-observed-modal}
 d_x=\alpha_x-p_x(0)\le\kappa\alpha_x.
\end{equation}

For each $h$ let $u_h$ be the ambient probability that the edge
$(x,y),(x,y+h)$ is observed and has nonzero residual difference, and
let $v_h$ be its probability of being unobserved. A union bound gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-observed-edge-caps}
 u_h\le2d,\qquad v_h\le2\tau.
\end{equation}
At fixed $h$, let $F_i$ mean that edge $i$ is observed with nonzero
difference, and let $Z_i$ mean that it is observed with zero difference.
Proper-coordinate independence gives, for each $i$,
\begin{align*}
 \Prob[F_i\text{ and all }Z_j\ (j\ne i)]
 &\ge\Prob[F_i]-\sum_{j\ne i}\Prob[F_i\text{ and not }Z_j]\\
 &=u_h-(s-1)u_h(u_h+v_h).
\end{align*}
These events are disjoint as $i$ varies and each forces a valid failed
test. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-marked-observed-error}
 \theta\ge s\E_h[u_h(1-(s-1)(u_h+v_h))]
       \ge s(1-2(s-1)(d+\tau))\E_hu_h.
\end{equation}

The pair $(y,y+h)$ becomes independent uniform after averaging. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-observed-collision}
 \E_hu_h
   =\E_x\left(\alpha_x^2-\sum_zp_x(z)^2\right)
   \ge\E_x\alpha_xd_x.
\end{equation}
Here $\sum_zp_x(z)^2\le p_x(0)\alpha_x$ by the modal choice.
From \eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-validity}, $\tau\le1-\lambda\le E$, and
$D\le2E/s$ by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:96:lem:arr-existing}. Consequently
\[
 b\ge1-2(s-1)E(1+2/s)
   \ge1-\frac{1+2/s}{120}\ge\frac{79}{80}.
\]
Thus the coefficient in \eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-marked-observed-error} is positive,
and \eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-observed-collision} proves
$\E_x\alpha_xd_x\le\theta/(sb)=T$.

Set $d_x/\alpha_x=0$ on empty rows. Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
 d^2\le(\E_x\alpha_xd_x)\left(\E_x\frac{d_x}{\alpha_x}\right).
\]
On a positive row, \eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-observed-modal} gives
\[
 \frac{d_x}{\alpha_x}-d_x
   =\frac{d_x(1-\alpha_x)}{\alpha_x}
   \le\kappa(1-\alpha_x).
\]
The corresponding upper bound remains valid on empty rows under the
stated convention. Therefore $d^2\le T(d+\kappa\tau)$, whose positive
root is \eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-erasure-root}. A row-density lower bound instead
gives $\E_x\alpha_xd_x\ge\beta d$, proving
\eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-erasure-thick}.

Finally, $\lambda>0$ follows from \eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-erasure-activation};
no undefined conditional probability occurs. Also
$E=\eta+(1-\eta)(1-\lambda)\le\eta+2s\tau$. At $\eta=0$ we have
$T=0$ and hence $d=0$. The case $|K|=1$, omitted from the statement,
is trivial.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{New against source~33} (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:33:ras:thm:erasures}): that theorem's bound keeps an additive floor $1-\lambda$ as the observed disagreement tends to zero; this one vanishes with it, at the square-root order shown optimal in Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:96:prop:arr-thin-sharp}. Neither source~60 nor any other source has it (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:erasures}).
\end{writenote}

Source~33's earlier erasure statement gives only
$d\le R_s(\lambda\eta+1-\lambda)$ \cite{repo96}. For fixed erasures
that bound can remain positive at zero observed rejection.
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:96:thm:arr-erasure} uses it to choose a nearby model and
then counts observed errors directly. The result remains a near-full
domain theorem: the activation hypothesis has not been removed.

\subsection{Optimal order and the necessity of row thickness}

\begin{corollary}[A bound using the entire row-density profile]
\label{gsr:en:96:cor:arr-full-row-profile}
Under Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:96:thm:arr-erasure}, the same model also satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-profile-dual}
 d\le \inf_{\mu\ge0}
 \left\{\mu T+\kappa\,\E_x\alpha_x(1-\mu\alpha_x)_+\right\}.
\end{equation}
The infimum is the exact maximum permitted by the relaxed constraints
$0\le d_x\le\kappa\alpha_x$ and $\E_x\alpha_xd_x\le T$.
It can be evaluated by sorting the positive row densities, or by
checking $\mu=0$ and the finitely many values $\mu=1/\alpha_x$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For every $\mu\ge0$ and every row,
\[
 d_x\le\mu\alpha_xd_x+
          \kappa\alpha_x(1-\mu\alpha_x)_+.
\]
If $\mu\alpha_x\ge1$, the first term already dominates $d_x$.
Otherwise the inequality follows from $d_x\le\kappa\alpha_x$.
Average and use $\E_x\alpha_xd_x\le T$ to obtain
\eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-profile-dual}.

For the relaxation, each unit assigned to $d_x$ has cost $\alpha_x$
in the weighted constraint and the same benefit in the objective.
An exchange from a thicker row to an unfilled thinner row cannot
increase cost. Thus an optimum fills rows in increasing order of
$\alpha_x$, with at most one density level partially filled.
Choosing $\mu$ to be the reciprocal of that level makes the
displayed rowwise inequalities equalities and makes the cost
constraint tight. If every row can be filled, $\mu=0$ is optimal.
The case $T=0$ follows by taking $\mu$ at least the reciprocal of
the least positive density. This also proves the finite evaluation
claim. Exact attainability by arrangement labelings is not asserted.
\end{proof}

For fixed $\tau>0$ and $T\to0$, the new root is
\[
 \sqrt{\kappa\tau T}+\frac T2+O_{\kappa,\tau}(T^{3/2}).
\]
When $\tau=0$ it equals $T$ exactly. The change of order is forced by
actual thin-row examples.

\begin{proposition}[Sharp thin-row regimes]\label{gsr:en:96:prop:arr-thin-sharp}
Fix $s\ge4$ even and a finite abelian target $K$ of cardinality $q\ge2$.
For an arbitrarily small fixed positive erasure budget, there are
examples satisfying \eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-erasure-activation} for which
$d\asymp\sqrt\eta$ and $d/\eta\to\infty$.
Moreover there are joint limits with $\tau\to0$ and $d/\tau\to0$ in
which
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-thin-sharp-ratios}
 \frac{\theta\kappa\tau}{sd^2}\longrightarrow1,
 \qquad \frac{ds\beta}{\theta}\longrightarrow1,
 \qquad b\longrightarrow1.
\end{equation}
Thus the leading square-root coefficient and the row-thickness factor
in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:96:thm:arr-erasure} are attained in these joint regimes.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Let $G=\Z_n$ with $n\ge3$, put $\nu=1/n$, and let $H=\Z_M$, where
$M>2q$ and $\gcd(M,q)=1$. All rows are fully observed and labeled zero,
except $x=0$: retain only $T_0=\{0,\ldots,q-1\}$ there, and label its
$q$ points by a bijective listing of $K$. Since every homomorphism
$\Z_M\to K$ is zero, the model class consists precisely of arbitrary
row constants. Hence the exact nearest-model distance and erasure
density are
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-thin-distance}
 d=\frac{\nu(q-1)}M,\qquad
 \tau=\nu(1-q/M),\qquad \beta=q/M.
\end{equation}

Let $P_j$ be the probability that exactly $j$ horizontal coordinates
are zero. Inclusion--exclusion and proper-coordinate independence give
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-horizontal-patterns}
 P_j=\binom sj\left[\nu^j(1-\nu)^{s-j}
                  +(-1)^j(\nu^{s-1}-\nu^s)\right].
\end{equation}
Indeed all proper specified zero events have their independent
probabilities, while the all-zero event has probability $\nu^{s-1}$.
In particular
\[
 P_0=(1-\nu)^s+\nu^{s-1}-\nu^s>0,
\]
and
\[
 P_1=s[\nu(1-\nu)^{s-1}-\nu^{s-1}(1-\nu)]>0.
\]
Write $r_h=|T_0\cap(T_0-h)|$. With exactly one exceptional horizontal
coordinate, a valid test fails precisely when that edge's two points
are distinct. The identities
$\sum_hr_h=q^2$ and $\sum_{h\ne0}r_h=q(q-1)$ therefore give the
leading terms
\begin{align}
 \theta&=\frac{P_1q(q-1)}{M^2}+O_{s,n,q}(M^{-3}),
       \label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-thin-theta}\\
 \lambda&=P_0+\frac{P_1q^2}{M^2}+O_{s,n,q}(M^{-3}).
       \label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-thin-lambda}
\end{align}
To bound the remainders, a configuration with at least two exceptional
coordinates can be valid only for at most $2q-1$ increments, and at
least two independent vertical bases must lie in intersections of size
at most $q$. Its contribution is $O(M^{-3})$. This also accounts for
every possible cancellation of its labels.

For fixed $n$, these formulas prove $d\asymp\sqrt\eta$ and
$d/\eta\to\infty$. Choosing $n>480s(s-1)$ makes the activation
hypothesis hold for all sufficiently large $M$, since
$E\to1-P_0\le s/n$. The erasure densities remain below the fixed
budget $1/n$.

Next let $n\to\infty$ after taking the indicated large-$M$ limits.
Since $P_1/(s\nu)\to1$, substitution of
\eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-thin-distance} into
\eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-thin-theta} proves both ratios in
\eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-thin-sharp-ratios}. Also $E\to0$, so $D,\tau\to0$ and
$b\to1$. Equivalently one may take a sufficiently rapidly growing
diagonal sequence with $\gcd(M,q)=1$. This proves sharpness of the
specified leading regimes, without asserting optimality of the whole
finite-error root or of the activation threshold.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[An exact binary check]
For $q=2$ and odd $M$, only $h=1,-1$ can reject in the construction
above. At either increment a valid test rejects exactly when the number
of exceptional horizontal coordinates is odd. Thus the exact formulas are
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-binary-exact}
 \theta=\frac2M\sum_{\substack{1\le j<s\\j\text{ odd}}}\frac{P_j}{M^j},
 \qquad
 \lambda=P_0+\sum_{j=1}^s\frac{(2^j+2)P_j}{M^{j+1}}.
\end{equation}
These rational identities are included in the verification supplement.
They are also convenient for checking examples within the small
activation interval without enumerating every arrangement.
\end{remark}

The two arrangement questions left by these results are concrete.
First, determine the exact coefficient in
\eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-prime-bracket}, which requires using more of the joint
derivative distribution than the present pair estimate. Second, replace
the near-full-domain bootstrap by a relative or pseudorandom-domain
decoder while preserving \eqref{gsr:en:96:eq:arr-observed-collision}. Any such
statement must retain row-thickness information or allow the
square-root loss demonstrated above.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The inherited full-product arrangement decoder, with proof\srctag{96}}]{The inherited full-product arrangement decoder, with proof}\label{gsr:en:96:sec:dA}
\srcnote{96}{Appendix A}
\label{gsr:en:96:boot:sec:decoder}

This appendix supplies a self-contained proof of
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:96:lem:arr-existing}. The theorem and the ingredients reproduced
here are prior work from source~33 of the repository collection
\cite{repo96}; they are included so that the new arrangement refinements
can be checked without consulting that large combined document. The
majority correction is the classical homomorphism-testing mechanism of
Blum, Luby and Rubinfeld \cite{blr}, with independent auxiliary labels
retained explicitly. No result in this appendix is claimed as a new
contribution.

The groups $G,H,K$, the balanced arrangement law, the derivative
$D_h\phi(x,y)=\phi(x,y+h)-\phi(x,y)$, the model class $\Vmodel$, and
$d(\phi)$ are those of Section~\ref{gsr:en:96:sec:arrangement-repair}. All groups
are finite abelian, and every average below is normalized unless it is
displayed as a sum over characters.

\subsection{Monotonicity of the arrangement rejection probability}

For a finite abelian group $L$, let $\widehat L$ denote its character
group, whose elements take values in the complex unit circle. Use the
normalized transform
\[
 \widehat g(\xi)=\E_{x\in G}g(x)\overline{\xi(x)}.
\]
For $\chi\in\widehat K$ and $h\in H$, set
\[
 g_{\chi,h}(x)=\E_{y\in H}\chi(D_h\phi(x,y)).
\]

\begin{lemma}[Arrangement moment identity]\label{gsr:en:96:boot:lem:moment}
For every even $s\ge4$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:boot:eq:moment}
 1-\epsilon_s(\phi)
   =\E_{h\in H}\E_{\chi\in\widehat K}
          \sum_{\xi\in\widehat G}|\widehat g_{\chi,h}(\xi)|^s.
\end{equation}
In particular $\epsilon_4(\phi)\le\epsilon_s(\phi)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Character orthogonality on $K$ writes the acceptance indicator as the
average, over $\chi\in\widehat K$, of the character of the signed sum
of differences. At fixed $h,\chi$, averaging the independent $y_i$
leaves
\[
 \E_{\substack{x_1+\cdots+x_m=x_{m+1}+\cdots+x_s}}
   \prod_{i\le m}g_{\chi,h}(x_i)
   \prod_{i>m}\overline{g_{\chi,h}(x_i)},\qquad s=2m.
\]
Expanding each factor in its Fourier series and averaging the $s-1$
free horizontal coordinates forces all Fourier frequencies to coincide.
The surviving expression is
$\sum_\xi|\widehat g_{\chi,h}(\xi)|^s$, proving
\eqref{gsr:en:96:boot:eq:moment}. The character average over $\widehat K$ is
normalized; the displayed sum over $\widehat G$ is not.

Since $|g_{\chi,h}(x)|\le1$, each Fourier coefficient has modulus at
most one. Each summand therefore decreases as the even exponent rises
from $4$ to $s$, giving the stated monotonicity.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Noisy homomorphisms and affine maps}

\begin{lemma}[Homomorphism correction with independent labels]
\label{gsr:en:96:boot:lem:noisy-hom}
Let $U,V$ be finite abelian groups, let $S$ be a finite nonempty set,
and let $F:U\times S\to V$. Suppose the independently sampled noisy
homomorphism test has error
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:boot:eq:noisy-error}
 e=\Prob_{u,v,\alpha,\beta,\gamma}
   [F(u,\alpha)+F(v,\beta)\ne F(u+v,\gamma)]<\frac16.
\end{equation}
Then there is a homomorphism $L:U\to V$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:boot:eq:noisy-correction}
 \Prob_{u,\alpha}[F(u,\alpha)\ne L(u)]\le\frac{e}{1-2e}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Fix $z\in U$ and consider
\[
 A_z(y;\alpha,\beta)=F(z+y,\alpha)-F(y,\beta).
\]
Two independent copies agree with probability at least $1-2e$.
Indeed, introduce one more independent label $\gamma$ and compare
\begin{align*}
 F(z+y,\alpha)+F(y',\beta')&=F(z+y+y',\gamma),\\
 F(y,\beta)+F(z+y',\alpha')&=F(z+y+y',\gamma).
\end{align*}
Each equality has failure probability $e$: even with $z$ fixed, its
two group inputs are independent uniform elements, and its three labels
are independent. If both hold, the two copies of $A_z$ agree.

Writing $p_z(t)=\Prob[A_z=t]$, we obtain
\[
 \max_t p_z(t)\ge\sum_t p_z(t)^2\ge1-2e.
\]
Thus $A_z$ has a unique modal value $L(z)$ and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:boot:eq:uniform-mode}
 \Prob[A_z=L(z)]\ge1-2e\qquad\text{for every }z\in U.
\end{equation}
There is an exact cocycle identity
\[
 A_{z+z'}(y;\alpha,\beta)
   =A_z(y+z';\alpha,\gamma)+A_{z'}(y;\gamma,\beta).
\]
For fixed $z,z'$, each of these three variables misses its mode with
probability at most $2e$. Since $6e<1$, there is a choice of the common
random variables for which all three equal their modes. Hence
$L(z+z')=L(z)+L(z')$, so $L$ is a homomorphism.

Finally, the original test can be written as the comparison
\[
 F(u,\alpha)=A_u(v;\gamma,\beta).
\]
Conditional on $u,\alpha$, if $F(u,\alpha)\ne L(u)$, the event that
the right-hand side equals $L(u)$ forces rejection. That event has
probability at least $1-2e$, and its random variables are independent of
$\alpha$. Therefore
$e\ge(1-2e)\Prob[F(u,\alpha)\ne L(u)]$, proving
\eqref{gsr:en:96:boot:eq:noisy-correction}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Affine correction with independent labels]
\label{gsr:en:96:boot:lem:noisy-affine}
Let $F:G\times S\to K$, with $S$ finite and nonempty. Let $e$ be the
probability that
\[
 F(x_1,\alpha_1)+F(x_2,\alpha_2)
      \ne F(x_3,\alpha_3)+F(x_4,\alpha_4),
\]
where $x_1+x_2=x_3+x_4$ is uniformly sampled and all labels are
independent uniform elements of $S$. There is an affine map
$A:G\to K$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:boot:eq:affine-six}
 \Prob_{x,\alpha}[F(x,\alpha)\ne A(x)]\le6e.
\end{equation}
When $e<1/6$, the stronger upper bound $e/(1-2e)$ holds.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If $e\ge1/6$, any affine map gives \eqref{gsr:en:96:boot:eq:affine-six}.
Otherwise fix an anchor $(x_4,\alpha_4)=(z,t)$ whose conditional
rejection probability $e_0$ is at most $e$. Conditional on this anchor,
write $x_1=z+u$, $x_2=z+v$, and $x_3=z+u+v$, with $u,v$ independent
uniform. The map
\[
 Q(u,\alpha)=F(z+u,\alpha)-F(z,t)
\]
has noisy homomorphism error $e_0$. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:96:boot:lem:noisy-hom}
supplies a homomorphism $L$ with error at most
$e_0/(1-2e_0)\le e/(1-2e)$. Translating back gives the affine map
$A(x)=L(x-z)+F(z,t)$. Since $e<1/6$, the stronger error bound is at
most $3e/2$, which in particular is at most $6e$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Separation of distinct affine maps]
\label{gsr:en:96:boot:lem:separation}
Distinct affine maps $A,A':G\to K$ disagree on at least half of $G$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Their difference has the form $L(x)+c$ for a homomorphism $L$.
If $L=0$ and $c\ne0$, it never vanishes. If $L\ne0$, its zero set is
empty or a coset of $\ker L$, whose index is at least two. In every
case its zero set has density at most $1/2$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Synchronizing corrected derivatives}

\begin{proposition}[The coarse full-product decoder]
\label{gsr:en:96:boot:prop:coarse}
If $\epsilon_4(\phi)<1/216$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:boot:eq:coarse}
 d(\phi)\le6\epsilon_4(\phi)
       +\frac{36\epsilon_4(\phi)}{1-72\epsilon_4(\phi)}
       \le60\epsilon_4(\phi).
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Let $e_h$ be the conditional rejection probability of the four-difference
test at increment $h$. Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:96:boot:lem:noisy-affine} to
$F_h(x,y)=D_h\phi(x,y)$, with $H$ as the auxiliary-label set. Choose
an affine map $A_h:G\to K$ such that
\[
 \rho_h:=\Prob_{x,y}[D_h\phi(x,y)\ne A_h(x)]\le6e_h,
 \qquad \rho:=\E_h\rho_h\le6\epsilon_4(\phi)<\frac1{36}.
\]
The exact derivative cocycle is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:boot:eq:derivative-cocycle}
 D_{h+k}\phi(x,y)=D_h\phi(x,y+k)+D_k\phi(x,y).
\end{equation}
When all three affine predictions at these inputs are correct,
$A_{h+k}(x)=A_h(x)+A_k(x)$. Every prediction has average error $\rho$,
since all the shifted inputs have the appropriate uniform marginals.
Thus a union bound gives
\[
 \Prob_{h,k,x}[A_{h+k}(x)\ne A_h(x)+A_k(x)]\le3\rho.
\]
Let $\operatorname{Aff}(G,K)$ denote the finite abelian group of affine
maps under pointwise addition. By Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:96:boot:lem:separation},
\[
 \eta_0:=\Prob_{h,k}[A_{h+k}\ne A_h+A_k
                   \text{ as functions on }G]
       \le6\rho<\frac16.
\]
Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:96:boot:lem:noisy-hom} to $h\mapsto A_h$, with target
$\operatorname{Aff}(G,K)$ and a singleton label set. It produces a
homomorphism $\mathcal A:H\to\operatorname{Aff}(G,K)$ with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:boot:eq:synchronization-error}
 q_0:=\Prob_h[A_h\ne\mathcal A(h)]
   \le\frac{\eta_0}{1-2\eta_0}
   \le\frac{6\rho}{1-12\rho}.
\end{equation}

Define
\[
 \ell(y)=\mathcal A(y)(0),\qquad
 B(x,y)=\mathcal A(y)(x)-\mathcal A(y)(0).
\]
The homomorphism property of $\mathcal A$ makes $\ell$ additive and
$B$ additive in $y$; the fact that each $\mathcal A(y)$ is affine makes
$B$ additive in $x$. Hence $B$ is biadditive. For
$r(x,y)=\phi(x,y)-B(x,y)-\ell(y)$, we have
\[
 \Prob_{h,x,y}[D_hr(x,y)\ne0]\le\rho+q_0.
\]
Indeed, unless the original derivative prediction is wrong or
$A_h\ne\mathcal A(h)$, the residual derivative vanishes.

For each $x$, put $p_x(z)=\Prob_y[r(x,y)=z]$. Averaging the two
independent endpoints $y,y+h$ gives
\[
 \Prob_{h,y}[D_hr(x,y)\ne0]
       =1-\sum_zp_x(z)^2\ge1-\max_zp_x(z).
\]
Choose $a(x)$ to be a modal value of that row. Then
$a(x)+B(x,y)+\ell(y)$ is an exact model at distance at most
$\rho+q_0$. Using \eqref{gsr:en:96:boot:eq:synchronization-error},
$\rho\le6\epsilon_4$, and the monotonicity of the displayed rational
function proves the first bound in \eqref{gsr:en:96:boot:eq:coarse}.
Finally, $\epsilon_4<1/216$ gives $1-72\epsilon_4>2/3$, so the
fraction is at most $54\epsilon_4$. Adding $6\epsilon_4$ proves the
coarse constant $60$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{A re-proof of source~33's decoder}, as source~60's Appendix~\ref{gsr:fz:60:sec:dA} is; the two re-proofs are independent of each other.
\end{writenote}

\subsection{The small-branch quadratic inverse}

\begin{lemma}[One-error quadratic profile]
\label{gsr:en:96:boot:lem:quadratic}
If $d=d(\phi)\le1/[2(s-1)]$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:boot:eq:quadratic}
 \epsilon_s(\phi)\ge Q_s(d):=sd-2s(s-1)d^2.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Subtract a nearest model and optimize its row constants so that zero
is a modal residual value on every row. For the residual $r$, write
\[
 t_h=\Prob_{x,y}[D_hr(x,y)\ne0],\qquad
 \overline t=\E_ht_h.
\]
The endpoint union bound gives $t_h\le2d$. Writing
$p_x(z)=\Prob_y[r(x,y)=z]$, the modal choice gives
$\sum_zp_x(z)^2\le p_x(0)$, and averaging the independent endpoints
therefore yields
\[
 \overline t=\E_x\left(1-\sum_zp_x(z)^2\right)
       \ge\E_x(1-p_x(0))=d.
\]

At fixed $h$, let $Z$ count the nonzero differences among the $s$
queried edges. Any test with $Z=1$ rejects, in every abelian target.
For every nonnegative integer $Z$,
\[
 \one_{\{Z=1\}}\ge Z-Z(Z-1).
\]
Pairwise independence of the queried edge variables consequently gives
\[
 \epsilon_h\ge\Prob[Z=1]
      \ge st_h-s(s-1)t_h^2.
\]
Averaging, using $t_h\le2d$, and then $\overline t\ge d$ yields
\[
 \epsilon_s(\phi)
   \ge s(1-2(s-1)d)\overline t
   \ge s(1-2(s-1)d)d.
\]
The assumed upper bound on $d$ makes the multiplier nonnegative,
justifying the last step.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:96:lem:arr-existing}]
Write $\epsilon=\epsilon_s(\phi)\le1/[240(s-1)]$.
By Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:96:boot:lem:moment},
\[
 \epsilon_4(\phi)\le\epsilon
      \le\frac1{720}<\frac1{216}.
\]
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:96:boot:prop:coarse} therefore applies and gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:boot:eq:branch-entry}
 d(\phi)\le60\epsilon_4(\phi)\le60\epsilon
                      \le\frac1{4(s-1)}.
\end{equation}
On this interval the quadratic $Q_s$ from
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:96:boot:lem:quadratic} is increasing, from zero to
$s/[8(s-1)]$. That lemma gives $Q_s(d(\phi))\le\epsilon$.
Since $\epsilon<s/[8(s-1)]$, solving on this increasing branch gives
\[
 d(\phi)\le
 \frac{1-\sqrt{1-8(s-1)\epsilon/s}}{4(s-1)}=R_s(\epsilon).
\]
Rationalization yields
\[
 R_s(\epsilon)=
 \frac{2\epsilon}{s\bigl(1+\sqrt{1-8(s-1)\epsilon/s}\bigr)}
 \le\frac{2\epsilon}{s}.
\]
All square roots are real in the stated interval; explicitly,
$8(s-1)\epsilon/s\le1/(30s)<1$.
The coarse step \eqref{gsr:en:96:boot:eq:branch-entry} is what makes inversion
legitimate: the local quadratic alone would also permit a large-distance
branch and would not prove the decoder.
\end{proof}


\subsection{The classical \texorpdfstring{$2/9$}{2/9} correction threshold}
\label{gsr:en:96:boot:sec:sharp-correction}

For the endpoint analysis we also record the sharper classical
homomorphism-correction threshold of Ben-Or, Coppersmith, Luby and
Rubinfeld \cite{bclr}. The independent-label formulation below follows
from the same majority argument. The threshold and the correction
function are prior work; the proof is included to make the subsequent
endpoint deductions self-contained.

\begin{lemma}[Sharp classical correction with independent labels]
\label{gsr:en:96:boot:lem:sharp-noisy}
Let $U,V$ be finite abelian groups, let $S$ be a finite nonempty set,
and let $F:U\times S\to V$. Suppose
\[
 e=\Prob_{u,v,\alpha,\beta,\gamma}
 [F(u,\alpha)+F(v,\beta)\ne F(u+v,\gamma)]<\frac29,
\]
with independent uniform $u,v,\alpha,\beta,\gamma$. Then there is a
homomorphism $L:U\to V$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:en:96:boot:eq:sharp-noisy}
 \Prob_{u,\alpha}[F(u,\alpha)\ne L(u)]
 \le B(e):=\frac{3-\sqrt{9-24e}}{12}
 \le\frac e2<\frac19.
\end{equation}
The inequality $B(e)<e/2$ is strict when $e>0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:96:boot:lem:noisy-hom}, fix $z$ and put
\[
 A_z(y;\alpha,\beta)=F(z+y,\alpha)-F(y,\beta).
\]
Two independent copies of $A_z$ agree with probability at least
$1-2e$. Thus its largest atom has mass at least $1-2e>1/2$.
Let $L(z)$ be its unique modal value and let $e_z$ be the probability
of missing this value. In particular, $e_z<1/2$. The collision
probability is at most $(1-e_z)^2+e_z^2$, because the total mass of
all the other atoms is $e_z$. Consequently
\[
 e_z(1-e_z)\le e,
 \qquad e_z\le r_e:=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4e}}2<\frac13.
\]
The exact identity
\[
 A_{z+z'}(y;\alpha,\beta)
 =A_z(y+z';\alpha,\gamma)+A_{z'}(y;\gamma,\beta)
\]
has, with positive probability, all three terms equal to their modes:
the union bound for the three exceptional events is at most
$3r_e<1$. Therefore $L(z+z')=L(z)+L(z')$.

Write $d=\Prob[F(u,\alpha)\ne L(u)]$. Comparing the original test
with $A_u(v;\gamma,\beta)$, whose labels are independent of
$\alpha$, gives
\[
 e\ge(1-r_e)d,
 \qquad d\le\frac{e}{1-r_e}=r_e<\frac13.
\]
Now count incorrect labels in the three queries relative to $L$.
Their indicators are pairwise independent and each has expectation
$d$: the three group inputs $u,v,u+v$ are pairwise independent,
and the auxiliary labels are independent even when group inputs
coincide. If exactly one query is incorrect, the test rejects.
For their sum $Z$, the pointwise inequality
$\one_{\{Z=1\}}\ge Z-Z(Z-1)$ therefore yields
\[
 e\ge3d-6d^2.
\]
The larger root of $3d-6d^2=e$ is greater than $1/3$ for
$e<2/9$. The already established $d<1/3$ excludes that branch,
so $d\le B(e)$. Finally, rationalization gives
\[
 B(e)=\frac{2e}{3+\sqrt{9-24e}}\le\frac e2,
\]
strictly when $e>0$, since $\sqrt{9-24e}>1$ in the stated range.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Classical affine correction]
\label{gsr:en:96:boot:cor:sharp-affine}
In the independently labelled affine test of
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:96:boot:lem:noisy-affine}, if its rejection probability is
$e<2/9$, there is an affine map $A$ with disagreement at most
$B(e)$. This includes the ordinary four-point test by taking the
label set to be a singleton.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Use the same anchor $(z,t)$ as in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:96:boot:lem:noisy-affine}, whose conditional rejection
probability $e_0$ is at most $e$. The translated map
$F(z+u,\alpha)-F(z,t)$ has noisy homomorphism error $e_0$.
Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:96:boot:lem:sharp-noisy} and translate its homomorphism
back to an affine map. Since $B$ is increasing on $[0,2/9)$, the
disagreement is at most $B(e_0)\le B(e)$.
\end{proof}
