Source~20's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:20:thm:index} gives the general directional-to-global comparison with the optimal constant for each subgroup tuple, and its Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:20:prop:pair} the sharp pair correction $\sqrt{m-1}$ (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:torsion}).
\end{writenote}

The $L^p$ exponents assigned to the non-target functions are $1$ for
$k=2$, then $(2,2)$, $(2,4,4)$, $(2,4,8,8)$, and so forth.  Their
reciprocals sum to one.  The functions and coefficients can be reordered
before applying the theorem, provided a coefficient with invertible
difference from the target is left immediately before it.  This permits
optimization of the norm product when the functions have different
densities or sizes.

\begin{corollary}[Every target in an arithmetic progression]
\label{gsr:cc:10:cor:torsion-ap-target}
Let $k\geq2$, let $f_0,\ldots,f_{k-1}:G\to\mathbb C$ satisfy
$|f_i|\leq1$, and let $0\leq j\leq k-1$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 \left|\mathbb E_{x,d}\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}f_i(x+id)\right|
 \leq
 \left(\prod_{i\ne j}\kappa_G(i-j)\right)^{1/2^{k-1}}
                  \|f_j\|_{U^{k-1}}.
 \label{gsr:cc:10:eq:torsion-arbitrary-target}
\end{equation}
In particular, for an endpoint target the factor is
$\bigl(\prod_{r=1}^{k-1}\kappa_G(r)\bigr)^{1/2^{k-1}}$.
It is one whenever the exponent of $G$ is coprime to $(k-1)!$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Every target has a neighboring coefficient with difference $1$ or $-1$.
Place that neighbor last among the non-target functions and apply
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:10:thm:torsion-mixed-lp}.  Its $L^p$ product is at most one.
The endpoint formula and the coprimality assertion follow directly.
\end{proof}

For the internal target $j$, the kernel product is
\[
 \left(\prod_{r=1}^j\kappa_G(r)\right)
 \left(\prod_{r=1}^{k-1-j}\kappa_G(r)\right).
\]
Thus coprimality of the exponent of $G$ with
$j!(k-1-j)!$ suffices for that individual estimate.  The endpoint result
in particular extends the prime-modulus statement to composite cyclic
groups with no prime factor below $k$, and to arbitrary finite abelian
groups satisfying the same restriction on their prime divisors.

The invertible-neighbor hypothesis in the general-coefficient theorem
is essential to the theorem as stated.  For $k=2$, coefficients $(0,2)$
on $G=\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$, and opposite nontrivial characters, the
multilinear average is one whereas the target $U^1$ seminorm is zero.

\subsection{Sharpness and an explicit obstruction}

\begin{proposition}[Sharp torsion growth]
\label{gsr:cc:10:prop:torsion-sharpness}
For three-term progressions on $G=(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^n$, the
endpoint factor $|G|^{1/4}$ in
\eqref{gsr:cc:10:eq:torsion-arbitrary-target} is exactly sharp.
More generally, for $k=p+1$ on
$G=(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^n$, with $p$ prime, the endpoint factor
$|G|^{1/2^p}$ has the optimal order in $|G|$, up to constants depending
only on $p$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
First let $G=(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^n$, $N=2^n$, and set
\[
 g(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=i^{x_1+\cdots+x_n},
\]
using representatives $x_i\in\{0,1\}$.  Every normalized Fourier
coefficient of $g$ has absolute value $N^{-1/2}$: in each coordinate
the Fourier factors are $(1+i)/2$ and $(1-i)/2$.  Therefore
\[
 \|g\|_{U^2}^4=\sum_{\chi}|\widehat g(\chi)|^4=N^{-1}.
\]
Take the two endpoint functions to be $\overline g,g$, and the middle
function to be one.  Since $2d=0$, the progression average equals one.
The upper bound is exactly $N^{1/4}N^{-1/4}=1$.

For the general assertion write $s=p$ and $N=p^n$.  Choose independent
uniform unit-circle phases $g(z)$ for the points $z\in G$.  For a fixed
$s$-dimensional cube, the expectation of its alternating product is
either zero or one, according as the exponents of these independent
phases fail to cancel or all cancel.  If its $2^s$ vertices are all
distinct, the expectation is zero.  Each pair of distinct cube vertices
coincides with probability $1/N$, because their difference contains a
coefficient $1$ or $-1$ on at least one independent uniform increment.
The union bound gives
\[
 \mathbb E_g\|g\|_{U^s}^{2^s}
 \leq\frac{\binom{2^s}{2}}N.
\]
There is consequently a circle-valued $g$ with at most this Gowers
power.  Put $\overline g,g$ at the two endpoints of the $(p+1)$-term
pattern and put one at every intermediate position.  The average is
again one because $pd=0$.  Hence any factor valid for all such functions
is at least
\[
 \left(\frac{N}{\binom{2^p}{2}}\right)^{1/2^p}.
\]
The kernel product in the upper bound is exactly $N$, since the
differences $1,\ldots,p-1$ are invertible.  This proves the asserted
optimal order.  The random estimate is useful for large $N$; for small
$N$ its right-hand side may exceed the trivial upper bound one.
\end{proof}

A small explicit example also illustrates why the modulus restriction
in the source theorem matters.  On $\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z$ take
$g=(1,1,-1)$ and the four functions $(\overline g,1,1,g)$.  Their
four-term average is one.  However,
\[
 \|g\|_{U^3}^8=\frac{49}{81}<1.
\]
Indeed, the zero derivative is one, and each nonzero derivative is a
translate of $(1,-1,-1)$, whose $U^2$ fourth power is
$(1/3)^4+2(2/3)^4=11/27$.  The recursion gives
$(1+2\cdot11/27)/3=49/81$.
\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 06--10]
Rechecked at the second write: $(1/3)^4+2(2/3)^4=33/81=11/27$ and $(1+22/27)/3=49/81$. The $\Z/2\Z$ torsion examples of sources~03 and~04 (Part~III above) are of the same kind; here the factor is quantified and shown sharp on $(\Z/2\Z)^n$.
\end{writenote}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Density-sensitive counting and modular progression criteria\srctag{10}}]{Density-sensitive counting and modular progression criteria}\label{gsr:cc:10:sec:d6}
\srcnote{10}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:cc:10:sec:density-counting}

For convenience write
\[
 \Lambda_k(F_1,\ldots,F_k)
 =\mathbb E_{x,d}\prod_{i=1}^kF_i(x+(i-1)d).
\]
The following replacement for the counting step keeps the densities
and uses only $k-2$ error terms.

\begin{theorem}[A density-weighted telescoping estimate]
\label{gsr:cc:10:thm:density-telescoping}
Let $k\geq3$ and let $A_1,\ldots,A_k\subseteq G$.  Put
$F_i=\mathbf1_{A_i}$, $\delta_i=\mathbb EF_i$, and
$b_i=F_i-\delta_i$.  For $3\leq j\leq k$ set
\[
 \tau_j(G)=\left(\prod_{r=1}^{j-1}\kappa_G(r)\right)^{1/2^{j-1}},
 \quad
 B_j=\left(\prod_{i=1}^{j-2}\delta_i^{1/2^i}\right)
                   \delta_{j-1}^{1/2^{j-2}},
 \quad
 D_j=\prod_{i=j+1}^k\delta_i.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \left|\Lambda_k(F_1,\ldots,F_k)-\prod_{i=1}^k\delta_i\right|
 \leq\sum_{j=3}^kD_jB_j\tau_j(G)\|b_j\|_{U^{j-1}}.
 \label{gsr:cc:10:eq:density-telescoping}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $L_i=x+(i-1)d$ use the pointwise identity
\[
 \prod_{i=1}^kF_i(L_i)-\prod_{i=1}^k\delta_i
 =\sum_{j=1}^k
   \left(\prod_{i<j}F_i(L_i)\right)b_j(L_j)
   \left(\prod_{i>j}\delta_i\right).
\]
The averaged term with $j=1$ vanishes because $\mathbb Eb_1=0$.
The averaged term with $j=2$ also vanishes: the two adjacent forms are
jointly uniform on $G^2$, so its average factors and contains
$\mathbb Eb_2=0$.  Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:10:thm:torsion-mixed-lp} in natural
coefficient order to every remaining $j$-term average.  The target is
$b_j$, its kernel factor is $\tau_j(G)$, and
$\|\mathbf1_{A_i}\|_{L^p}=\delta_i^{1/p}$ makes its mixed norm
product exactly $B_j$.  The triangle inequality proves the claim.
\end{proof}

For one or two forms the count equals its product of densities exactly.
If the exponent of $G$ is coprime to $(k-1)!$, all the factors
$\tau_j(G)$ are one.  In particular, under the uniformity assumptions
of Corollary~3.3 of the source paper, one has
$\|b_j\|_{U^{j-1}}\leq\alpha$, and its error term can be replaced by
\[
 \alpha\sum_{j=3}^kD_jB_j\leq(k-2)\alpha.
\]
The displayed density-dependent sum is often appreciably smaller.

\begin{corollary}[One-set counting]
\label{gsr:cc:10:cor:one-set-counting}
Let $k\geq3$, let $A\subseteq G$ have density $\delta$, and put
\[
 \eta=\|\mathbf1_A-\delta\|_{U^{k-1}},\qquad
 T_{k,G}(\delta)=\sum_{j=3}^k\delta^{k-j}\tau_j(G).
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 |\Lambda_k(A)-\delta^k|
 \leq\delta\eta T_{k,G}(\delta).
 \label{gsr:cc:10:eq:one-set-torsion-count}
\end{equation}
In the coprime case, put
\[
 S_k(\delta)=\sum_{m=0}^{k-3}\delta^m.
\]
Then $T_{k,G}(\delta)=S_k(\delta)$ and
\begin{equation}
 |\Lambda_k(A)-\delta^k|\leq\delta S_k(\delta)\eta.
 \label{gsr:cc:10:eq:one-set-coprime-count}
\end{equation}
For $0\leq\delta<1$,
$S_k(\delta)=(1-\delta^{k-2})/(1-\delta)$, while
$S_k(1)=k-2$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The reciprocals in the definition of $B_j$ sum to one, so $B_j=\delta$
when all the sets are $A$.  Gowers norm monotonicity gives
$\|\mathbf1_A-\delta\|_{U^{j-1}}\leq\eta$ for $j\leq k$.
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:10:thm:density-telescoping} now gives both estimates.

For completeness, monotonicity follows from two applications of
Cauchy--Schwarz.  Writing
$g=\Delta_{h_1}\cdots\Delta_{h_{s-1}}f$, one has
\[
 |\mathbb Eg|^4
 =\left|\mathbb E_t\mathbb E_x
                 g(x)\overline{g(x+t)}\right|^2
 \leq\mathbb E_t\left|\mathbb E_x
                 g(x)\overline{g(x+t)}\right|^2
 =\|g\|_{U^2}^4.
\]
Average this inequality over the $h_i$, and use
$(\mathbb E_h|\mathbb Eg|^2)^2
 \leq\mathbb E_h|\mathbb Eg|^4$.
The two sides identify with the appropriate cube forms and yield
$\|f\|_{U^s}\leq\|f\|_{U^{s+1}}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[An explicit modular progression criterion]
\label{gsr:cc:10:cor:improved-modular-criterion}
Let $k\geq3$, suppose that the exponent of $G$ is coprime to $(k-1)!$,
and let $A\subseteq G$ have positive density $\delta$.  With $\eta$ as
above, the number of ordered pairs $(x,d)$ for which all $k$ terms are
distinct and lie in $A$ is at least
\begin{equation}
 \delta N^2
   \left(\delta^{k-1}-S_k(\delta)\eta-\frac1N\right).
 \label{gsr:cc:10:eq:proper-ap-lower-bound}
\end{equation}
In particular, $A$ contains such a progression if
\[
 N\bigl(\delta^{k-1}-S_k(\delta)\eta\bigr)>1.
\]
A simpler sufficient pair of conditions is
\begin{equation}
 \eta\leq\frac{\delta^{k-1}}{2S_k(\delta)},
 \qquad N>2\delta^{1-k}.
 \label{gsr:cc:10:eq:improved-ap-sufficient-pair}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
There are exactly $|A|=\delta N$ counted pairs with $d=0$.
If $d\ne0$ and two terms coincide, then $rd=0$ for some
$1\leq r\leq k-1$, contradicting invertibility of multiplication by
$r$.  Subtracting these exactly $\delta N$ degenerate pairs from
\eqref{gsr:cc:10:eq:one-set-coprime-count}, after multiplying by $N^2$, proves
\eqref{gsr:cc:10:eq:proper-ap-lower-bound}.  Either displayed condition makes
this lower bound strictly positive.
\end{proof}

In the notation of the source paper, being $\alpha$-uniform of degree
$k-2$ means $\eta^{2^{k-1}}\leq\alpha$.  Thus the sufficient
uniformity condition in \eqref{gsr:cc:10:eq:improved-ap-sufficient-pair} can be
written
\[
 \alpha\leq
  \left(\frac{\delta^{k-1}}{2S_k(\delta)}\right)^{2^{k-1}},
 \qquad N>2\delta^{1-k}.
\]
These improve the local modular-counting requirements.  Incorporating
them into a global quantitative Szemer\'edi argument also requires the
later inverse, density-increment, and interval-transfer steps to be
recomputed with their own hypotheses.
\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 06--10]
Compared with the criteria of sources~03, 04 and~06 in the note after source~04's Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:04:prog:super}: the error here is $\delta$ times theirs, and in $\alpha$ terms the power of $\delta$ is $(k-1)2^{k-1}$, between source~06's $(k-\frac12)2^{k-2}$ and source~04's $k2^{k-1}$. Not formalized.
\end{writenote}

\subsection{Repeated terms and the appropriate main term}

The torsion-sensitive estimate also gives a distinct-point criterion
without a coprimality assumption.  Define
\[
 \mathcal D_k(G)=\bigcup_{r=1}^{k-1}G[r].
\]
A progression repeats a point exactly when
$d\in\mathcal D_k(G)$.  For each such difference, at most $\delta N$
choices of $x$ can contribute, since the first point must belong to
$A$.  Hence a sufficient criterion for a progression with $k$ distinct
points in an arbitrary finite abelian group is
\begin{equation}
 \delta^{k-1}-\eta T_{k,G}(\delta)
 >\frac{|\mathcal D_k(G)|}{N}.
 \label{gsr:cc:10:eq:general-torsion-proper-criterion}
\end{equation}

In small characteristic it is sometimes preferable to reduce the
pattern before estimating it.  On $(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^n$, if
$k>p$, the homogeneous indicator product is exactly the $p$-term
product, since coefficients repeat modulo $p$ and indicators are
idempotent.  For a Bernoulli random set with inclusion probability
$\delta$, the exact expected normalized count is then
\[
 \left(1-\frac1N\right)\delta^p+\frac{\delta}{N}.
\]
Its leading independent-membership term is $\delta^p$.  This coefficient
collision explains why a dimension-independent error tending to zero
around $\delta^k$ cannot describe that pattern.

\paragraph{Further questions specific to these estimates.}
The sharpness argument determines the correct group-size order for
$k=p+1$; exact constants for larger $k$ and general torsion profiles
remain open within this investigation.  A natural next problem is to
retain the restricted images $cG$ in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:10:lem:torsion-fibre-average}, instead of replacing each by all
of $G$, and to exploit the overlap of these images.  For heterogeneous
sets, the telescoping order and the assignment of the $L^p$ exponents
can be optimized jointly; when all coefficient differences are
invertible, the rearrangement inequality assigns the largest reciprocal
exponents to the smallest densities within a fixed prefix.  The finite
fibre identity, mixed-norm induction, telescoping identity, and exact
degenerate-pair count are also natural separate formalization targets.

\section[{An exact dimension threshold for polynomial colorings\srctag{10}}]{An exact dimension threshold for polynomial colorings}\label{gsr:cc:10:sec:d9}
\srcnote{10}{Section 9}
\label{gsr:cc:10:sec:polynomial-obstruction}

There is a useful restricted question behind the recent constructions of
sets with fewer arithmetic progressions than their uniformity might suggest:
how many coordinates can a polynomial coloring control while forbidding
reflection symmetry along every nontrivial progression?  The construction
of Shi and Dong uses a sum of odd-degree field norms
\cite{shidong}.  We give an exact answer when the number of
field-valued color coordinates and their total degrees are prescribed.
The obstruction is a direct Chevalley--Warning argument
\cite{chevalley,warning}; an analogous argument involving all
homogeneous degrees appears in F\"uhrer and Taranchuk
\cite{fuehrertaranchuk}.  Our purpose is to state the precise degree
budget, prove its optimality, and identify the limit it places on this
construction method.  We make no claim of first discovery of these
polynomial-method consequences.

Throughout this section, let $k=2m\ge4$ and let $p>k$ be prime.  A coloring
$Q:\mathbb F_p^d\to\mathbb F_p^r$ is \emph{polynomial with coordinate
degree bounds $D_1,\ldots,D_r$} if its $\ell$th coordinate is represented
by a polynomial $Q_\ell$ of total degree at most $D_\ell$.
A progression $(a,a+h,\ldots,a+(k-1)h)$ is \emph{symmetrically colored}
if
\begin{equation}
 Q(a+ih)=Q(a+(k-1-i)h)\qquad(0\le i<m).
 \label{gsr:cc:10:eq:poly-symmetric-ap}
\end{equation}
It is nontrivial when $h\ne0$.  The assumption $p>k$ guarantees that all
$k$ of its points are then distinct.

\subsection{Odd coefficients encode reflection symmetry}

Fix a center $z\in\mathbb F_p^d$ and introduce formal variables
$H=(H_1,\ldots,H_d)$ and $T$.  For a polynomial $P$ of total degree at
most $D$, write
\begin{equation}
 P(z+TH)=\sum_{j=0}^{D} C_{j,z}(H)T^j.
 \label{gsr:cc:10:eq:poly-taylor-coefficients}
\end{equation}
The polynomial $C_{j,z}$ is homogeneous of degree $j$, or is zero.
Indeed, in the expansion of a monomial, selecting the coefficient of
$T^j$ selects exactly $j$ factors from the coordinates of $H$.
This coefficient definition needs no differentiation or division by
factorials.

\begin{lemma}[Reflection and the odd coefficient equations]
\label{gsr:cc:10:lem:poly-odd-coefficients}
Suppose $1\le D\le k$ and put $s=\lceil D/2\rceil$.
For $z,h\in\mathbb F_p^d$, the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The progression with center $z$ and direction $h$ is symmetrically
      colored by $P$.
\item $C_{1,z}(h)=C_{3,z}(h)=\cdots=C_{2s-1,z}(h)=0$.
\item The polynomial $P(z+Th)$ is even in $T$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Put $\alpha_i=i-\tfrac12\in\mathbb F_p$ for $1\le i\le m$.
The progression with center $z$ has points
$z\pm\alpha_1h,\ldots,z\pm\alpha_mh$.  Its reflection equalities are
$P(z+\alpha_i h)=P(z-\alpha_i h)$.

The $\alpha_i$ are nonzero, and their squares are pairwise distinct:
for $i\ne j$, the quantities
$\alpha_i-\alpha_j=i-j$ and $\alpha_i+\alpha_j=i+j-1$ are nonzero
modulo $p$.  In particular, $1\le i+j-1\le k-1<p$.

Subtracting the two evaluations in
\eqref{gsr:cc:10:eq:poly-taylor-coefficients} cancels all even powers, leaving
\[
 P(z+TH)-P(z-TH)
   =2\sum_{j=1}^{s}C_{2j-1,z}(H)T^{2j-1}.
\]
Its degree is at most $2s-1\le k-1$, even when $D=k$.
After division by $2\alpha_i$, the reflection equalities become
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^{s}C_{2j-1,z}(h)(\alpha_i^2)^{j-1}=0
 \qquad(1\le i\le m).
\]
Since $s\le m$, the first $s$ equations form a square Vandermonde
system with determinant
\[
 \prod_{1\le i<j\le s}(\alpha_j^2-\alpha_i^2)\ne0.
\]
Thus all its unknown odd coefficients vanish.  Conversely, vanishing of
these coefficients makes the polynomial even and implies every required
reflection equality.
\end{proof}

The important distinction is that the degree budget contains only
$1,3,\ldots,2s-1$.  An even top degree contributes no new reflection
equation.  This is why degree bounds $2s-1$ and $2s$ lead to the same
dimension threshold.

\subsection{The zero-count obstruction}

We recall the short finite-field proof of the form of Chevalley--Warning
that we need.

\begin{lemma}[Chevalley--Warning in the needed form]
\label{gsr:cc:10:lem:poly-chevalley-warning}
Let $F_1,\ldots,F_t\in\mathbb F_p[H_1,\ldots,H_d]$ vanish at the
origin.  Omit zero polynomials from the degree sum.  If
$\sum_{j=1}^{t}\deg F_j<d$, the number of their common zeros in
$\mathbb F_p^d$ is divisible by $p$.  Consequently there are at least
$p$ common zeros, including at least $p-1$ nonzero common zeros.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By Fermat's theorem, the polynomial function
\[
 I(H)=\prod_{j=1}^{t}\bigl(1-F_j(H)^{p-1}\bigr)
\]
equals the indicator of the common zero set.  Its total degree is less
than $d(p-1)$.  Every monomial of $I$ therefore has at least one variable
whose exponent $e$ satisfies $0\le e<p-1$.  For that exponent,
\[
 \sum_{u\in\mathbb F_p}u^e=0\quad\text{in }\mathbb F_p.
\]
For $e=0$ this is $p=0$; for $1\le e<p-1$ it is the usual finite-field
power sum.  Summation of each monomial over $\mathbb F_p^d$ factors
into the corresponding one-variable sums, and hence gives zero.
It follows that $\sum_h I(h)=0$ in $\mathbb F_p$, which is the required
divisibility.  The zero count is positive because the origin is a common
zero, so it is at least $p$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact dimension threshold with heterogeneous degrees]
\label{gsr:cc:10:thm:poly-exact-dimension}
Let $r\ge1$, let $1\le D_\ell\le k$ for $1\le\ell\le r$, and put
\[
 s_\ell=\left\lceil\frac{D_\ell}{2}\right\rceil,
 \qquad B=\sum_{\ell=1}^{r}s_\ell^2.
\]
There exists a polynomial coloring
$Q:\mathbb F_p^d\to\mathbb F_p^r$, with
$\deg Q_\ell\le D_\ell$, having no nontrivial symmetrically colored
$k$-term arithmetic progression if and only if $d\le B$.

If $d>B$, then for every such $Q$ and every center $z$, the number of
directions giving a symmetrically colored progression centered at $z$,
including the zero direction, is divisible by $p$.  In particular,
there are at least $p-1$ nonzero such directions at every center.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For necessity, fix $z$ and apply
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:10:lem:poly-odd-coefficients} to each color coordinate.
Reflection symmetry is equivalent to the common vanishing of
\[
 C_{\ell,1,z}(h),\ C_{\ell,3,z}(h),\ldots,
 C_{\ell,2s_\ell-1,z}(h)
 \qquad(1\le\ell\le r).
\]
These homogeneous polynomials vanish at the origin and have total
degree sum at most
\[
 \sum_{\ell=1}^{r}\sum_{j=1}^{s_\ell}(2j-1)
   =\sum_{\ell=1}^{r}s_\ell^2=B.
\]
If $d>B$, Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:10:lem:poly-chevalley-warning} gives the asserted
divisibility and nonzero directions.  Thus avoidance requires $d\le B$.

For sufficiency we use the odd-degree norm construction of Shi and
Dong~\cite[Sections 3--4]{shidong}, allowing a different top degree
in each coordinate.  For a positive odd integer $t$, identify
$\mathbb F_p^t$ linearly with $\mathbb F_{p^t}$ and let
$N_t:\mathbb F_p^t\to\mathbb F_p$ be the field norm.  In degree one,
take $N_1(u)=u$.  We need that $N_t$ is homogeneous of degree $t$ and
that $N_t(u)=0$ holds exactly when $u=0$.

Here is a polynomial description of those properties.  If
$\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_t$ is a basis of $\mathbb F_{p^t}$ over
$\mathbb F_p$, then
\[
 N_t(u_1,\ldots,u_t)
   =\prod_{a=0}^{t-1}
       \left(\sum_{j=1}^{t}u_j\beta_j^{p^a}\right).
\]
This is a product of $t$ linear forms, and Frobenius permutes its
factors, so its coefficients lie in $\mathbb F_p$.  Its value is the
norm of $\sum_j u_j\beta_j$, which is nonzero precisely when that
field element is nonzero.  In particular, its formal total degree is
$t$, despite the alternative large-exponent expression for a field norm.

For color coordinate $\ell$, introduce disjoint variable blocks
\[
 u_\ell^{(1)}\in\mathbb F_p,\quad
 u_\ell^{(3)}\in\mathbb F_p^3,\quad\ldots,\quad
 u_\ell^{(2s_\ell-1)}\in\mathbb F_p^{2s_\ell-1}.
\]
There are $s_\ell^2$ variables in that coordinate's collection of
blocks.  On their full $B$-dimensional product define
\begin{equation}
 Q_\ell(u)=\sum_{j=1}^{s_\ell}
             N_{2j-1}\bigl(u_\ell^{(2j-1)}\bigr).
 \label{gsr:cc:10:eq:poly-layered-norm}
\end{equation}
Its total degree is $2s_\ell-1\le D_\ell$.

Suppose a progression with center $z$ and direction $h$ is symmetrically
colored.  Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:10:lem:poly-odd-coefficients} says that every
$Q_\ell(z+Th)$ is even.  If $h$ has a nonzero block in coordinate
$\ell$, let $t$ be the largest odd index with
$h_\ell^{(t)}\ne0$.  All higher-index blocks contribute constants,
because their directions vanish; all lower-index blocks have degree
less than $t$.  The coefficient of $T^t$ in $Q_\ell(z+Th)$ is therefore
exactly
\[
 N_t\bigl(h_\ell^{(t)}\bigr)\ne0.
\]
Since $t$ is odd, this contradicts evenness.  Thus every direction
block vanishes, and $h=0$.  This proves avoidance at $d=B$.

For $d<B$, restrict the construction to any linear embedding of
$\mathbb F_p^d$ into $\mathbb F_p^B$.  A nonzero direction remains
nonzero under the embedding, and composition with a linear map does
not increase total degree, so all the required properties are preserved.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 11--14]
Source~14 reproves this threshold and determines the exact minimum count above it, $q^d(q^{\max(d-B,0)}-1)$ over every $\F_q$ with $p>k$, with subspace equality and a prime-field gap (its Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:14:thm:coloring-exact-supersaturation}); the quintic question remains open (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:colhigh}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Two later uses} (Part~III, sources~64 and~67): source~64's dimension barrier $n\le tk^2/4$ for degree $k-1$ (its Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:64:thm:polynomial-barrier}) is this theorem at $D_\ell=k-1$, uncited there; source~67 removes the degree cap for sums of independent norm blocks, whose dimension is at most $rm^2$ for $2m$-term progressions (its Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:67:norm:classification}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{corollary}[Equal degree bounds and optimal coordinate budget]
\label{gsr:cc:10:cor:poly-equal-degrees}
For $1\le D\le k$, a coloring by $r$ polynomial coordinates of total
degree at most $D$ can avoid all nontrivial symmetrically colored
$k$-APs on $\mathbb F_p^d$ exactly when
\[
 d\le r\left\lceil D/2\right\rceil^2.
\]
In particular, for degree at most $k=2m$ the exact condition is
$d\le rm^2$, and for $d\geq1$ the least possible number of polynomial coordinates
is $\lceil d/m^2\rceil$.
\end{corollary}

At the equality dimension $d=B$, the coloring
\eqref{gsr:cc:10:eq:poly-layered-norm} is surjective onto $\mathbb F_p^r$.
Indeed, each coordinate contains its own independent linear variable
$u_\ell^{(1)}$.  After choosing all other variables, the $r$ linear
variables are uniquely determined by the desired color.  Thus every
color class has exactly $p^{B-r}$ points.

\subsection{An upper bound for arbitrary degree budgets}

When the degree exceeds the progression length, the reflection equations
can vanish without all odd coefficients vanishing.  Nevertheless, they
give a useful explicit dimension bound.

\begin{proposition}[A dimension bound in every degree]
\label{gsr:cc:10:prop:poly-arbitrary-degree}
For a positive integer $s$, define
\[
 B_m(s)=
 \begin{cases}
  s^2,&s\le m,\\
  m(2s-m),&s\ge m.
 \end{cases}
\]
Let $D_1,\ldots,D_r\ge1$ be arbitrary, put
$s_\ell=\lceil D_\ell/2\rceil$, and suppose
$Q:\mathbb F_p^d\to\mathbb F_p^r$ is polynomial with
$\deg Q_\ell\le D_\ell$.  If
\[
 d>\sum_{\ell=1}^{r} B_m(s_\ell),
\]
then at every prescribed center there are at least $p-1$ nonzero
directions producing symmetrically colored $k$-term progressions.
Thus avoidance requires
$d\le\sum_{\ell=1}^{r}B_m(s_\ell)$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Fix a center $z$ and write the odd coefficients of one coordinate as
$C_{2j+1,z}(H)$, for $0\le j<s$, with $s=\lceil D/2\rceil$.
Let $y_i=\alpha_i^2$ for the nonzero half-integer parameters used in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:10:lem:poly-odd-coefficients}, and put
$v_j=(y_i^j)_{i=1}^{m}\in\mathbb F_p^m$.
After dividing each reflection equality by $2\alpha_i$, the vector of
reflection equations is
\[
 E(H)=\sum_{j=0}^{s-1}v_j C_{2j+1,z}(H)=0.
\]
If $s\le m$, these are equivalent to the individual odd coefficient
equations, whose total degree sum is $s^2$.

If $s>m$, form the square matrix
\[
 V=(v_{s-m},v_{s-m+1},\ldots,v_{s-1}).
\]
It is the usual Vandermonde matrix multiplied on the left by the
invertible diagonal matrix with entries $y_i^{s-m}$, so it is
invertible.  The equivalent system $V^{-1}E(H)=0$ has equations
\[
 F_j(H)=C_{2(s-m+j)+1,z}(H)
       +\sum_{q=0}^{s-m-1}b_{j,q}C_{2q+1,z}(H)=0,
       \qquad 0\le j<m,
\]
for scalars $b_{j,q}\in\mathbb F_p$.
Every coefficient in the second sum has strictly smaller degree than
the displayed first coefficient.  Consequently
\[
 \deg F_j\le 2(s-m+j)+1,\qquad
 \sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\deg F_j\le m(2s-m).
\]
Zero polynomials may again be omitted.  Although the transformed
equations need not be homogeneous, they all vanish at the origin.
Applying this procedure independently to each color coordinate
produces a system equivalent to reflection symmetry with total degree
sum at most $\sum_\ell B_m(s_\ell)$.  The conclusion follows from
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:10:lem:poly-chevalley-warning}.
\end{proof}

For four-term progressions and a scalar degree bound $D=5$ or $6$,
Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:10:prop:poly-arbitrary-degree} gives $d\le8$.
The cubic construction already attains dimension $4$, so the
corresponding maximum dimension lies between $4$ and $8$.
Determining that maximum is a concrete question beyond the exact
low-degree theorem.  No matching construction is asserted for the
arbitrary-degree bound.

\subsection{An explicit four-dimensional example}

For $k=4$, both scalar degree bounds $D=3$ and $D=4$ have exact
dimension threshold $4$.  Over $\mathbb F_5$, the polynomial
$T^3+T+1$ has no root and is therefore irreducible.  If
$\theta^3+\theta+1=0$, the norm of $a+b\theta+c\theta^2$ is
\begin{align}
 N_3(a,b,c)
  &=\det\begin{pmatrix}
       a&-c&-b\\
       b&a-c&-b-c\\
       c&b&a-c
     \end{pmatrix} \notag\\
  &=a^3-2a^2c+ac^2+ab^2+3abc-b^3-bc^2+c^3
       \pmod5.
 \label{gsr:cc:10:eq:poly-explicit-cubic}
\end{align}
The determinant is that of multiplication by
$a+b\theta+c\theta^2$ in the basis $1,\theta,\theta^2$.
Consequently
\[
 Q(x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3)=x_0+N_3(x_1,x_2,x_3)
\]
is a five-coloring of $\mathbb F_5^4$ with five color classes of
$125$ points and no nontrivial symmetrically colored $4$-AP.

The accompanying exact-arithmetic verification checks the determinant
formula, the absence of nonzero norm zeros, and all
$625\cdot624=390{,}000$ ordered nontrivial progressions.  It finds no
symmetrically colored progression.  This finite check verifies the
displayed example; the theorem in arbitrary dimension and characteristic
follows from the preceding proof.

\subsection{What the threshold does and does not settle}

The same result holds for any prescribed centrally symmetric pattern
$\{\pm\alpha_1,\ldots,\pm\alpha_m\}$ in $\mathbb F_p$ with
$\alpha_i\ne0$ and pairwise distinct $\alpha_i^2$.
The conditions
$Q(z+\alpha_i h)=Q(z-\alpha_i h)$ are again equivalent to the same
odd coefficient equations, by the same Vandermonde argument.  Hence the
optimal dimension depends on the degree budgets and the number of
reflection pairs, rather than on equal spacing itself.

For degree at most $k$, the theorem shows that the formal palette
$\mathbb F_p^r$ must satisfy $r/d\ge4/k^2$, and the equality
construction uses all $p^r$ colors.  This is a sharp statement about a
prescribed number of polynomial color coordinates.  It is not a lower
bound on the actual image size of arbitrary maps with redundant color
coordinates, nor an optimality theorem for unrestricted colorings of
intervals or cyclic groups.  In particular, the auxiliary digit colors
in Shi and Dong's cyclic construction are outside this polynomial
coordinate model.  The possibility of $N^{o(1)}$ colors in the
Deng--Tidor--Zhao symmetric-progression problem remains outside the
conclusion~\cite{dengtidorzhao}.

The restriction $D_\ell\le k$ also matters.  With higher odd degrees,
agreement at the $k$ progression parameters need not make the entire odd
polynomial vanish.  Thus higher-degree constructions and nonpolynomial
color data provide specific directions beyond the class solved here.
Within the stated class, however, both sides of the optimization problem
are complete: the odd-degree sum gives a universal obstruction, and the
known norm construction attains it.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Centered cube counts and their spectral decomposition\srctag{13}}]{Centered cube counts and their spectral decomposition}\label{gsr:cc:13:sec:d7}\label{gsr:cc:13:sec:cubes}
\srcnote{13}{Section 7}

Lemma 3.10 bounds the normalized number of $d$-dimensional cubes in a set of density $\delta$ by $(\delta+\eta)^{2^d}$, where $\eta$ is the appropriate uniformity norm of its balanced function. The triangle inequality proves that bound, but it treats all terms in the binomial expansion as possible. Mean zero forces many of them to vanish exactly.

In this section let $G=\F_p^n$, where $p$ is an odd prime, and let $f:G\to\R$ have mean zero. Initially no absolute bound on $f$ is required. Put $V_d=\{0,1\}^d$, $m=2^d$, and
\[
 L_v(x,h)=x+v\cdot h,\qquad
 I_S(f)=\E_{x,h}\prod_{v\in S}f(L_v(x,h)),\qquad I_\varnothing=1.
\]
For $\delta\ge0$, define
\[
 \mathcal Q_d(\delta+f)
 =\E_{x,h}\prod_{v\in V_d}(\delta+f(L_v(x,h)))
 =\Un{\delta+f}{d}^{m}.
\]
The last equality uses real-valuedness. For $f=\ind_A-\delta$, this is the normalized count of all additive cubes, including degenerate ones, exactly as in the source lemma.

\subsection{Cancellation from an affine coloop}

Associate to each vertex $v$ the column $\widetilde v=(1,v)\in\F_p^{d+1}$. A vertex $v\in S$ is a \emph{coloop of $S$} if its column is not in the span of the other columns in $S$. Call $S$ \emph{coloopless} if it has no coloop, with the empty set included by convention. This is the standard vector-matroid language for the affine dependencies of the cube; that matroid is a classical object \cite{dasilva}. The role of the terminology here is simply to identify a factor that can be averaged independently.

\begin{lemma}[Coloop cancellation]\label{gsr:cc:13:lem:coloop}
If $S$ has a coloop, then $I_S(f)=0$. For every $S\subset V_d$,
\[
 |I_S(f)|\le\Un{f}{d}^{|S|}.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $v$ is a coloop, elementary linear algebra gives $w\in\F_p^{d+1}$ such that $\widetilde v\cdot w=1$ and $\widetilde u\cdot w=0$ for all other $u\in S$. For each $t\in G$, translate the $(d+1)$ variables by $(w_0t,\ldots,w_dt)$. Uniform measure is invariant under this translation. It changes only the factor at $v$, replacing it by $f(L_v+t)$. Average in $t$; its average is zero. The norm bound follows from \eqref{gsr:dt:13:eq:gcs}, placing $f$ at vertices in $S$ and the constant $1$ elsewhere.
\end{proof}

Let $c_{d,p}(j)$ count the coloopless $j$-subsets of $V_d$ and write $\eta=\Un{f}{d}$. Direct expansion gives the exact formula
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:13:eq:coloopsum}
 \mathcal Q_d(\delta+f)
 =\sum_{S\text{ coloopless}}\delta^{m-|S|}I_S(f).
\end{equation}
Thus the relevant coefficient polynomial is determined by the actual coefficient matroid over $\F_p$. For higher dimensions, one must not silently substitute characteristic-zero ranks.

\subsection{The quartic term in every dimension}

\begin{lemma}[Four-vertex classification]\label{gsr:cc:13:lem:fourvertices}
Every three distinct cube vertices are affinely independent. In odd characteristic, an affinely dependent four-subset is exactly an ordinary parallelogram of the binary cube. Its expectation $I_S(f)$ is $\rho^4$, where $\rho=\Un{f}{2}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Reflect coordinates to move one vertex to $0$. Two distinct nonzero binary vectors cannot be proportional: at a coordinate where the first is $1$, the proportionality factor must be $1$, forcing equality. This proves independence of three vertices.

For four dependent vertices, reflect one to $0$ and call the others $u,v,w$. In a nonzero relation $\lambda u+\mu v+\nu w=0$, each of $\lambda,\mu,\nu,\lambda+\mu+\nu$ is nonzero; otherwise three vertices would be dependent. A nonzero coordinate pattern among $(u_i,v_i,w_i)$ can therefore only be $110,101$, or $011$: singleton patterns and $111$ are excluded. At least two pair patterns occur, or the vectors would coincide. Relabel so that $110$ and $101$ occur. They force $\mu=\nu=-\lambda$. Since $2\lambda\ne0$, pattern $011$ cannot occur. Consequently $u=v+w$ with disjoint supports for $v,w$. The four vertices form an ordinary parallelogram.

Any three forms belonging to that parallelogram are jointly uniform on $G^3$; their coefficient matrix has rank three. Hence
\[
 I_S(f)=\E_{a,b,c}f(a)f(b)f(c)f(a+b-c)
 =\sum_\chi|\widehat f(\chi)|^4=\rho^4.
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The exact quartic coefficient]\label{gsr:cc:13:prop:quartic}
The number of four-vertex parallelograms in $V_d$ is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:13:eq:quarticcount}
 P_d=\frac{6^d-2\cdot4^d+2^d}{8}.
\end{equation}
For $d\ge2$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:13:eq:quarticbound}
 \left|\mathcal Q_d(\delta+f)-\delta^m
 -P_d\delta^{m-4}\rho^4\right|
 \le\sum_{j=5}^{m}c_{d,p}(j)\delta^{m-j}\eta^j.
\end{equation}
An empty sum is zero; in particular $\mathcal Q_2(\delta+f)=\delta^4+\rho^4$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Coordinatewise, there are six ordered solutions to $a+b=c+e$ in $\{0,1\}$. Thus the binary cube has $6^d$ ordered solutions. The degenerate ones, with the same two vertices on both sides, number $2\cdot4^d-2^d$. Every nondegenerate parallelogram has eight orderings, proving \eqref{gsr:cc:13:eq:quarticcount}. The values $0,1,2$ remain distinct in odd characteristic. Equation \eqref{gsr:cc:13:eq:quarticbound} now follows from lemmas~\ref{gsr:cc:13:lem:coloop} and \ref{gsr:cc:13:lem:fourvertices} and \eqref{gsr:cc:13:eq:coloopsum}.
\end{proof}

In particular, the error from the random-density main term starts at fourth order, rather than at first order. The exact quartic coefficient cannot be reduced for bounded real weights: replace $f$ by $t g$ for any fixed nonzero mean-zero real $g$, fix $0<\delta<1$, and let $t\downarrow0$. For small $t$, the function $\delta+t g$ lies in $[0,1]$. The quartic term is $P_d\delta^{m-4}t^4\Un{g}{2}^4$, and all remaining terms have order at least $t^5$. This is a weighted sharpness statement; it does not by itself assert an extremal theorem restricted to indicators at a fixed finite group size.

\subsection{All surviving subsets of the three-cube}

\begin{proposition}[The three-dimensional coefficient table]\label{gsr:cc:13:prop:cubetable}
For every odd $p$, the values $c_{3,p}(j)$, $j=0,\ldots,8$, are
\[
 (1,0,0,0,12,8,28,8,1).
\]
Consequently, with $\eta=\Un{f}{3}$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:13:eq:cubepolynomial}
 \mathcal Q_3(\delta+f)
 \le\delta^8+12\delta^4\eta^4+8\delta^3\eta^5
 +28\delta^2\eta^6+8\delta\eta^7+\eta^8.
\end{equation}
The quartic term may be replaced by $12\delta^4\rho^4$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The first four entries and the twelve four-subsets follow from lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:13:lem:fourvertices} and proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:13:prop:quartic}. Every affine hyperplane in $\F_p^3$ contains at most four binary vertices: choose a variable with a nonzero coefficient, assign the other two bits, and solve for that variable. Therefore any five vertices have full affine rank four after homogenization.

A five-subset has a coloop exactly when it contains a parallelogram. Each parallelogram extends to four five-subsets, and no five-subset contains two parallelograms. To justify the latter statement, two four-subsets of a five-set share three vertices, while three cube vertices complete to at most one parallelogram. After reflection, the possible completions of $0,u,v$ are $u+v,u-v,v-u$; at most one can be binary, according as the supports are disjoint or one strictly contains the other. Thus $12\cdot4=48$ of the $\binom85=56$ five-subsets have a coloop, leaving eight.

Deleting a vertex from a subset of size at least six still leaves at least five vertices and hence full rank. Every such subset is coloopless. Their counts are $28,8,1$. Apply \eqref{gsr:cc:13:eq:coloopsum}, lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:13:lem:coloop}, and $\rho\le\eta$.
\end{proof}

For comparison, the source bound $(\delta+\eta)^8$ has nonzero coefficients in the first three orders. Its quartic coefficient is $70$, and its fifth coefficient is $56$. Centering removes the first three nonconstant orders and reduces the next two coefficients to $12$ and $8$. These are exact combinatorial cancellations.

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 11--14]
\emph{Credit.} The quartic coefficient $P_d$ is source~03's $R_d$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:03:cube:main}), source~04's $P_d$, source~08's $R_d$ and source~09's $P_d$; on odd-order groups the three-cube table $(1,0,0,0,12,8,28,8,1)$ is source~04's support count (Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:04:cub:supports}), source~08's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:08:thm:three-exact} and source~14's Appendix~A (Section~\ref{gsr:cc:14:sec:dA}). Here it is stated over $\F_p^n$; those sources prove it on every group of odd order (source~03 on every finite abelian group, with the order-two correction).
\end{writenote}

\subsection{A complete spectral identity}

Write $a_\xi=\widehat f(\xi)$, so $a_{-\xi}=\overline{a_\xi}$, and put
\[
 \sigma^2=\E f^2=\sum_\xi|a_\xi|^2,
 \quad\rho^4=\sum_\xi|a_\xi|^4,
 \quad\zeta=\max_\xi|a_\xi|,
 \quad\eta=\Un{f}{3}.
\]
Define the real quantities
\begin{align}
 T_5&=\sum_\xi |a_\xi|^2 a_\xi^2\overline{a_{2\xi}},\label{gsr:cc:13:eq:T5}\\
 B_1&=\sum_{\xi,\nu}|a_\xi|^2|a_\nu|^2|a_{\xi+\nu}|^2,\label{gsr:cc:13:eq:B1}\\
 B_2&=\sum_{\xi,\nu}|a_\xi|^2a_\nu^2a_{\xi-\nu}\overline{a_{\xi+\nu}},\label{gsr:cc:13:eq:B2}\\
 B_3&=\sum_{\xi,\nu}a_\xi^2a_\nu^2a_{-\xi-\nu}^2.\label{gsr:cc:13:eq:B3}
\end{align}
Finally let $T_7$ be the common expectation $I_S(f)$ of a seven-subset of the cube. Cube symmetries show that it is independent of the omitted vertex.

\begin{theorem}[Exact centered three-cube decomposition]\label{gsr:cc:13:thm:cubeidentity}
For every real mean-zero $f$ on $\F_p^n$, $p$ odd,
\begin{align}
 \mathcal Q_3(\delta+f)
 ={}&\delta^8+12\delta^4\rho^4+8\delta^3T_5\notag\\
 &+\delta^2(12B_1+12B_2+4B_3)
 +8\delta T_7+\eta^8.\label{gsr:cc:13:eq:cubeidentity}
\end{align}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:13:eq:circuitbounds}
 |T_5|\le\zeta\rho^4,\qquad
 |B_2|,|B_3|\le B_1\le\eta^6,\qquad
 |T_7|\le\eta^4\sqrt{B_1}.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The eight five-circuits are the sets consisting of a vertex, its three graph neighbors, and its antipode. They form one symmetry orbit. Their unique affine relation is the sum of the three neighbors minus twice the vertex minus the antipode. Fourier expansion therefore gives \eqref{gsr:cc:13:eq:T5} for every five-circuit.

The six-subsets split into three symmetry orbits, according to whether their omitted pair has Hamming distance one, two, or three. There are $12,12,4$ such pairs, respectively. Fourier expansion imposes one equation for each of $x,h_1,h_2,h_3$. The following kernel parametrizations, in lexicographic order of the retained vertices, verify the corresponding products:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}clc@{}}
\toprule
Omitted pair & Six Fourier indices & Contribution\\
\midrule
$000,001$ & $(u+v,-u-v,-u,u,-v,v)$ & $B_1$\\
$000,011$ & $(u+v,-u-v,v,-u-2v,u,v)$ & $B_2$\\
$000,111$ & $(v,u,-u-v,-u-v,u,v)$ & $B_3$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
For the middle row set $\xi=u+v$, $\nu=v$. Each parametrization solves the four constraints and has two free coordinates; its integer pivot minor is a unit. Thus the calculation is valid over every odd field without a hidden divisor. The seven-subsets contribute $8\delta T_7$, and the full subset contributes $\eta^8$. This proves \eqref{gsr:cc:13:eq:cubeidentity}.

The first bound in \eqref{gsr:cc:13:eq:circuitbounds} follows termwise from \eqref{gsr:cc:13:eq:T5}. The bound $|B_3|\le B_1$ also follows by taking absolute values. For $B_2$, Cauchy--Schwarz bounds its absolute value by
\[
 \left(\sum_{\xi,\nu}|a_\xi|^2|a_\nu|^2|a_{\xi-\nu}|^2\right)^{1/2}
 \left(\sum_{\xi,\nu}|a_\xi|^2|a_\nu|^2|a_{\xi+\nu}|^2\right)^{1/2}
 =B_1,
\]
using $|a_{-\nu}|=|a_\nu|$. Gowers--Cauchy--Schwarz applied to the corresponding six-subset gives $B_1\le\eta^6$.

To bound $T_7$, set
\[
 A(h,k)=\E_x f(x+h)f(x+k)f(x+h+k),
\]
\[
 B(h,k)=\E_x f(x)f(x+h)f(x+k)f(x+h+k).
\]
Splitting the cube into parallel faces gives $T_7=\E_{h,k}A(h,k)B(h,k)$. Expanding $\E A^2$ gives a cube missing an adjacent pair, so $\E A^2=B_1$. Expanding $\E B^2$ gives the full cube, so $\E B^2=\eta^8$. Cauchy--Schwarz proves the final bound.
\end{proof}


\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 11--14]
\emph{Credit.} The identity \eqref{gsr:cc:13:eq:cubeidentity} is source~08's complete odd-order three-cube expansion (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:08:thm:three-exact}), which holds on every finite abelian group of odd order; here it is proved over $\F_p^n$, $p$ odd. New in this source: the orbit moments $B_1,B_2,B_3,T_7$ with the bounds \eqref{gsr:cc:13:eq:circuitbounds}, the spectral deficit below, and the sign examples.
\end{writenote}
\subsection{A further sharp spectral deficit}

The zero Fourier coefficient is absent because $\E f=0$. Keeping this absence improves the elementary estimate $B_1\le\sigma^2\rho^4$.

\begin{proposition}[A spectral upper bound with the zero-frequency loss]\label{gsr:cc:13:prop:spectraldeficit}
If $\sigma^2>0$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:13:eq:spectraldeficit}
 B_1\le\sigma^2\rho^4-\frac{\rho^8}{\sigma^2}.
\end{equation}
Equality is attained when $|\widehat f(\xi)|^2$ is constant for every nonzero $\xi$, including for a scalar multiple of $|G|\ind_{\{0\}}-1$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Put $b_\xi=|a_\xi|^2$, so $b_0=0$ and $b_{-\xi}=b_\xi$. Translation gives the exact identity
\[
 \sigma^2\rho^4-B_1
 =\frac12\sum_\nu b_\nu\sum_\xi(b_\xi-b_{\xi+\nu})^2.
\]
For each nonzero $\nu$, retain only the two terms $\xi=0,-\nu$. They contribute $2b_\nu^2$, whence the right side is at least $\sum_\nu b_\nu^3$. Cauchy--Schwarz yields
\[
 (\rho^4)^2=\left(\sum_\nu b_\nu^2\right)^2
 \le\left(\sum_\nu b_\nu\right)\left(\sum_\nu b_\nu^3\right)
 =\sigma^2\sum_\nu b_\nu^3.
\]
This proves \eqref{gsr:cc:13:eq:spectraldeficit}. If all nonzero $b_\nu$ are equal, the discarded translation terms vanish and the final Cauchy--Schwarz inequality is an equality.
\end{proof}

For a balanced indicator, $\sigma^2=\delta(1-\delta)$ is known exactly. The right side of \eqref{gsr:cc:13:eq:spectraldeficit} is nonnegative, since $\rho^4\le\sigma^4$. Combining the proposition with theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:13:thm:cubeidentity} gives, for $\sigma>0$,
\[
 B_1\le\mathcal B:=\min\left\{\eta^6,
 \sigma^2\rho^4-\rho^8/\sigma^2\right\}.
\]
The case $\sigma=0$ means $f=0$ and is immediate.

One convenient two-sided consequence of the exact identity is
\begin{align}
 &\left|\mathcal Q_3(\delta+f)-\delta^8
 -12\delta^4\rho^4-12\delta^2B_1-\eta^8\right|\notag\\
 &\hspace{12mm}\le
 8\delta^3\zeta\rho^4+16\delta^2B_1
 +8\delta\eta^4\sqrt{B_1}.\label{gsr:cc:13:eq:sharpcubeerror}
\end{align}
If only an upper bound is wanted, theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:13:thm:cubeidentity} instead gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:13:eq:cubeobservableupper}
 \mathcal Q_3(\delta+f)
 \le\delta^8+12\delta^4\rho^4+8\delta^3\zeta\rho^4
 +28\delta^2\mathcal B+8\delta\eta^4\sqrt{\mathcal B}+\eta^8.
\end{equation}
This retains more information than the one-parameter polynomial \eqref{gsr:cc:13:eq:cubepolynomial}; it is useful when the ordinary Fourier norm is much smaller than the higher uniformity norm.

\subsection{Signs, characteristic, and the scope of sharpness}

Odd-order circuit terms cannot simply be discarded. On $\Z/p\Z$, $p\ge7$, take
\[
 g(x)=\cos(2\pi x/p)-u\cos(4\pi x/p),\qquad u>0.
\]
Its only relevant Fourier modes are $\pm1,\pm2$, and \eqref{gsr:cc:13:eq:T5} gives $T_5(g)=-u/16$. Replacing $g$ by $-g$ reverses that sign. Multiplying by a sufficiently small number and adding a fixed $\delta\in(0,1)$ makes this a valid $[0,1]$-valued weight. Likewise, for $g(x)=\cos(2\pi x/p)+u\sin(4\pi x/p)$, one has
\[
 B_3=-3u^2/32=-B_1.
\]
Thus the possible negative contribution in \eqref{gsr:cc:13:eq:sharpcubeerror} is real, even for elementary two-frequency examples.

The coloop cancellation mechanism is valid over every finite field, but the explicit odd-characteristic table is not. In characteristic two, the three-cube table is $1,0,0,0,14,0,28,8,1$. Already its quartic coefficient differs. In larger dimensions one should compute $c_{d,p}(j)$ over the actual field and then apply \eqref{gsr:cc:13:eq:coloopsum}. These rank questions connect the analytic problem to classical cube matroids \cite{dasilva}, while control of more general linear systems belongs to the wider theory of true complexity \cite{gowerswolf}.

Finally, neither the surviving-subset polynomial nor its spectral upper bound is asserted to be jointly optimal at every parameter tuple. We proved exact cancellation, exact identities, an exact leading coefficient, and explicitly stated inequalities with their own equality cases. Those are stronger and more precise claims than a numerical estimate, but they do not identify all simultaneous extremizers of the $U^3$ norm.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Interval discrepancy with the sharp length exponent\srctag{13}}]{Interval discrepancy with the sharp length exponent}\label{gsr:cc:13:sec:d8}\label{gsr:cc:13:sec:interval}
\srcnote{13}{Section 8}

The proof of Lemma 3.5 bounds an interval's Fourier coefficient by frequency decay and explicitly discards the additional bound by the interval's length \cite{gowers,repo13paper}. Retaining both estimates gives a stronger local statement and an exact dual constant.

\begin{theorem}[Exact and explicit interval discrepancy bounds]\label{gsr:cc:13:thm:interval}
Let $N\ge2$, $I\subset\Z/N\Z$ be an interval of length $M$, $0\le M\le N$, and let $f$ have mean zero. Put $\rho=\Un{f}{2}$, $\beta=M/N$, and $b=\min(\beta,1-\beta)$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:13:eq:intervalexact}
 |\E f\ind_I|\le\rho D_N(M),
 \qquad
 D_N(M)=\left(\sum_{r=1}^{N-1}
 \left|\frac{\sin(\pi Mr/N)}{N\sin(\pi r/N)}\right|^{4/3}\right)^{3/4}.
\end{equation}
This constant is optimal over mean-zero real bounded functions. If $0<M<N$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:13:eq:intervalfinite}
 D_N(M)\le\left(4b^{1/3}-3N^{-1/3}\right)^{3/4}
 \le2\sqrt2\,b^{1/4}.
\end{equation}
For $M=0$ or $M=N$, discrepancy is zero. The exponent $1/4$ cannot be replaced by a larger one, even for balanced indicators.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The geometric-series formula gives the absolute value of the normalized interval Fourier coefficient displayed in \eqref{gsr:cc:13:eq:intervalexact}. Since $\widehat f(0)=0$, Parseval and H\"older yield
\[
 |\E f\ind_I|
 \le\left(\sum_{r\ne0}|\widehat f(r)|^4\right)^{1/4}
 \left(\sum_{r\ne0}|\widehat{\ind_I}(r)|^{4/3}\right)^{3/4}.
\]
This proves the exact upper bound. For its optimality, prescribe the Fourier coefficients of a test function by
\[
 \widehat f(r)=\widehat{\ind_I}(r)
 |\widehat{\ind_I}(r)|^{-2/3}\quad(r\ne0),
 \qquad\widehat f(0)=0,
\]
with zero used when the interval coefficient vanishes. These coefficients are conjugate symmetric, so $f$ is real. They attain equality in H\"older. Scale $f$ to have absolute value at most $1$; the quotient of discrepancy by $\rho$ is unchanged.

For the explicit estimate, nonzero coefficients are unchanged in absolute value when $I$ is replaced by its complementary interval, so
\[
 |\widehat{\ind_I}(r)|\le\min\{b,(2|r|)^{-1}\},
\]
where $|r|$ is the least positive centered frequency magnitude. The first bound is the interval length; the second follows from $|\sin(\pi r/N)|\ge2|r|/N$. Let $F(x)=\min\{b,(2x)^{-1}\}^{4/3}$. This function is decreasing. Pair opposite frequencies, possibly overcounting the frequency $N/2$, and compare each summand with the integral on its preceding unit interval:
\[
 \sum_{r\ne0}|\widehat{\ind_I}(r)|^{4/3}
 \le2\sum_{r=1}^{\lfloor N/2\rfloor}F(r)
 \le2\int_0^{N/2}F(x)\,dx.
\]
For a nontrivial interval $b\ge1/N$, the transition point $1/(2b)$ is at most $N/2$. Evaluation gives
\[
 2\left[\frac12b^{1/3}
 +2^{-4/3}\int_{1/(2b)}^{N/2}x^{-4/3}\,dx\right]
 =4b^{1/3}-3N^{-1/3}.
\]
Taking the $3/4$ power proves \eqref{gsr:cc:13:eq:intervalfinite}.

To prove the exponent is best possible, take $A=I$ with $\beta\to0$ and $f=\ind_I-\beta$. Then $\E f\ind_I=\beta(1-\beta)$, whereas Parseval and $|\widehat{\ind_I}(r)|\le\beta$ give $\rho^4\le\beta^3(1-\beta)$. An estimate $|\E f\ind_I|\le C\rho\beta^\gamma$ with fixed $C$ would therefore force $\gamma\le1/4$ as $\beta\downarrow0$.
\end{proof}

For $f=\ind_A-\delta$ and the source convention of degree-one $\alpha$-uniformity, $\rho\le\alpha^{1/4}$. Multiplying the normalized estimate by $N$ gives
\[
 \bigl||A\cap I|-\delta|I|\bigr|
 \le2\sqrt2\,\alpha^{1/4}N
 \min\left\{\frac{|I|}{N},1-\frac{|I|}{N}\right\}^{1/4}.
\]
The repository's repaired Lemma 3.5 has the length-independent constant $3$; the new expression improves it for every nontrivial interval and vanishes at both endpoint lengths. The exact dual constant is available if numerical constants matter. The same assertion holds for affine images of intervals under invertible slopes, because those maps permute Fourier frequencies. \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 11--14]} The repaired Lemma~3.5 is the formal \file{lemma_3_5} (\file{Sections01\_03.lean}, line~299; exact companion \file{lemma_3_5_holds}, \file{Proofs03Interval.lean}, line~412, at HEAD \texttt{e1db00e99}). No other source of this report treats Lemma~3.5.

\begin{proposition}[The small-relative-length limit]\label{gsr:cc:13:prop:sinclimit}
If $M\to\infty$ and $M/N\to0$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:13:eq:sinclimit}
 \frac{D_N(M)}{(M/N)^{1/4}}
 \longrightarrow
 \left(\int_{\R}\left|\frac{\sin\pi t}{\pi t}\right|^{4/3}\,dt\right)^{3/4},
\end{equation}
where the integrand takes its continuous value $1$ at $0$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Write $\beta=M/N$ and rescale frequencies by $t=\beta r$. For bounded $t$, $r/N=t/M\to0$, so the interval coefficient divided by $\beta$ tends uniformly on compact sets to $\sin(\pi t)/(\pi t)$ in absolute value. The frequency mesh is $\beta\to0$, giving the Riemann sum on every compact interval. The bound $(2|r|)^{-1}$ gives a tail, after division by $\beta^{1/3}$, of order $A^{-1/3}$ for $|r|>A/\beta$, uniformly in $M,N$. Let the compact cutoff $A$ increase after taking the limit. The omission of frequency zero costs only $\beta$ in the rescaled sum and disappears. Finally take the $3/4$ power.
\end{proof}

This is the usual scaling analysis of a Dirichlet kernel, written here to identify the limiting optimal constant. The gain in the source lemma comes from retaining a parameter it had intentionally discarded.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Progression counting by telescoping\srctag{13}}]{Progression counting by telescoping}\label{gsr:cc:13:sec:d9}\label{gsr:cc:13:sec:counting}
\srcnote{13}{Section 9}

The $2^k$ factor in Corollary 3.3 comes from expanding every indicator into its mean and balanced part. A telescoping expansion needs only $k-2$ errors, because the first two affine forms are exactly independent. We also record the precise group hypothesis needed by the argument.

\begin{lemma}[Endpoint generalized von Neumann inequality]\label{gsr:cc:13:lem:gvn}
Let $k\ge2$, and let $G$ be a finite abelian group on which multiplication by each integer $1,\ldots,k-1$ is an automorphism. If $|f_i|\le1$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:13:eq:gvn}
 \left|\E_{x,r\in G}\prod_{i=1}^k f_i(x+(i-1)r)\right|
 \le\Un{f_k}{k-1}.
\end{equation}
The convention at $k=2$ is $\Un{f}{1}=|\E f|$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $k=2$, the map $(x,r)\mapsto(x,x+r)$ is bijective, and the average factors. Suppose the result holds at $k-1$. Apply Cauchy--Schwarz in $x$ and use $|f_1|\le1$. Expand the remaining square, write the two step variables as $r$ and $r+u$, and replace $x+r$ by a new basepoint. With $\Delta_hf(y)=f(y)\overline{f(y+h)}$, this gives
\[
 |\Lambda_k(f_1,\ldots,f_k)|^2
 \le\E_u\left|\Lambda_{k-1}
 (\Delta_uf_2,\Delta_{2u}f_3,\ldots,\Delta_{(k-1)u}f_k)\right|.
\]
The induction hypothesis bounds the right side by $\E_u\Un{\Delta_{(k-1)u}f_k}{k-2}$. The power-mean inequality and bijectivity of multiplication by $k-1$ bound this by
\[
 \left(\E_h\Un{\Delta_hf_k}{k-2}^{2^{k-2}}\right)^{1/2^{k-2}}
 =\Un{f_k}{k-1}^{2}.
\]
The final equality is the defining derivative identity for Gowers norms. Take square roots. This is the normalized induction underlying Gowers' Theorem 3.2 \cite{gowers}.
\end{proof}

The hypothesis holds on $\F_p^n$ whenever $p\ge k$, and on $\Z/N\Z$ whenever $\gcd(N,(k-1)!)=1$. Thus primality is a sufficient condition, not the underlying requirement. The condition cannot simply be dropped: on $\Z/3\Z$, take $k=4$, $f_1=f_4=(1,1,-1)$, and $f_2=f_3=1$. The progression average is $1$, since $x+3r=x$ and $f_1(x)f_4(x)=1$, whereas $\Un{f_4}{3}^8=49/81<1$. This gives an explicit failure of \eqref{gsr:cc:13:eq:gvn} without coefficient invertibility.

\begin{theorem}[A density-weighted telescoping bound]\label{gsr:cc:13:thm:telescoping}
Under the group hypothesis of lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:13:lem:gvn}, let $g_i:G\to[0,1]$, $\delta_i=\E g_i$, and $f_i=g_i-\delta_i$. For $k\ge3$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:13:eq:telescoping}
 \left|\Lambda_k(g_1,\ldots,g_k)-\prod_{i=1}^k\delta_i\right|
 \le\sum_{j=3}^k\Un{f_j}{j-1}\prod_{i=j+1}^k\delta_i.
\end{equation}
In particular, if all the displayed norms are at most $\eta$, the error is at most $(k-2)\eta$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Replace $g_k$ by $\delta_k+f_k$, then $g_{k-1}$ by $\delta_{k-1}+f_{k-1}$ in the term containing $\delta_k$, and continue. This is the exact identity
\[
 \Lambda_k(g_1,\ldots,g_k)
 =\left(\prod_{i=3}^k\delta_i\right)\Lambda_2(g_1,g_2)
 +\sum_{j=3}^k\left(\prod_{i=j+1}^k\delta_i\right)
 \Lambda_j(g_1,\ldots,g_{j-1},f_j).
\]
The first term equals $\prod_i\delta_i$ by two-form independence. Each balanced function is bounded by $1$ in absolute value, so lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:13:lem:gvn} bounds the $j$th error by $\Un{f_j}{j-1}$. Since each density is at most $1$, there are at most $k-2$ such errors.
\end{proof}

The uniformity assumptions in the repository's Corollary 3.3 say exactly that $\Un{f_j}{j-1}\le\alpha$ for $j\ge3$. Therefore \eqref{gsr:cc:13:eq:telescoping} replaces its factor $2^k$ by
\[
 \sum_{j=3}^k\prod_{i=j+1}^k\delta_i\le k-2.
\]
For unnormalized counts, multiply by $|G|^2$. \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 11--14] Credit:} the generalized von Neumann bound and this telescope are source~03's Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:03:ap:gvn} and Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:03:ap:telescoping} and source~04's Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:04:prog:gvn} and Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:04:prog:telescoping}, and also source~06's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:06:uni:first-telescope} and source~10's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:10:thm:density-telescoping}; the corollary below is source~03's criterion (Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:03:ap:criterion}; this $S_k$ is its $S_{k-2}$). Sources~06 (quadratic in the norm) and~10 (error $\delta S_k\eta$) are stronger. Reversing the order gives a second valid bound with terms $\Un{f_j}{k-j}\prod_{i<j}\delta_i$, $1\le j\le k-2$, but those norms require their own hypotheses; they are not supplied automatically by the forward assumptions.

\begin{corollary}[An explicit modular existence criterion]\label{gsr:cc:13:cor:modexistence}
Under the group hypothesis of lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:13:lem:gvn}, let $k\ge3$, let $A\subset G$ have density $\delta>0$, let $\eta=\Un{\ind_A-\delta}{k-1}$, and set
\[
 S_k(\delta)=\sum_{j=0}^{k-3}\delta^j.
\]
If
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:13:eq:modcriterion}
 \delta^k-\eta S_k(\delta)>\frac{\delta}{|G|},
\end{equation}
then $A$ contains a $k$-term progression with nonzero difference. Under the group hypothesis, its terms are distinct. A convenient sufficient pair of conditions is
\[
 \eta\le\frac{\delta^k}{2S_k(\delta)},\qquad
 |G|>2\delta^{1-k}.
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Monotonicity of Gowers norms gives $\Un{\ind_A-\delta}{j-1}\le\eta$ for $3\le j\le k$. Apply theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:13:thm:telescoping}. Exactly $|A|$ pairs $(x,r)$ have $r=0$ and every term in $A$; their normalized contribution is $\delta/|G|$. Inequality \eqref{gsr:cc:13:eq:modcriterion} leaves a nonzero-step pair. If two of its terms coincided, multiplication by an integer from $1$ to $k-1$ would kill the nonzero difference, contradicting the automorphism hypothesis.
\end{proof}

This is explicitly a modular/group conclusion. It does not, by itself, rectify a progression into the integer interval $[N]$. The source development has separate transfer modules for that purpose, and a global integer theorem must retain those steps.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The exact secondary term in the three-cube extremal problem\srctag{14}}]{The exact secondary term in the three-cube extremal problem}\label{gsr:cc:14:sec:d2}
\srcnote{14}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:cc:14:sec:secondary-cube}

All averages are normalized. For a finite abelian group $G$ and a real
function $W:G\to\mathbb R$, put
\[
 Q_3(W)=\mathbb E_{x,h_1,h_2,h_3\in G}
       \prod_{v\in\{0,1\}^3}W(x+v\cdot h)=\|W\|_{U^3}^8.
\]
Throughout, $|G|$ is coprime to $6$. The earlier leading-term result and
its two-harmonic example left a gap: after subtracting
$6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4$, the coefficient at $\delta^{8/3}u^{16/3}$ was
bounded below by $(9/4)^{1/3}$ and above by $6$. We determine it exactly.

\begin{theorem}[Exact secondary coefficient, uniformly in the group]
\label{gsr:cc:14:thm:secondary-exact}
Put $C_*=(9/4)^{1/3}$. There are absolute constants $c,C>0$ such that,
whenever $\delta>0$, $f:G\to\mathbb R$ has mean zero, and
$u=\|f\|_{U^3}\leq c\delta$,
\begin{equation}
 Q_3(\delta+f)\leq
 \delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4+
 C_*\delta^{8/3}u^{16/3}+C\delta^{7/3}u^{17/3}.
 \label{gsr:cc:14:eq:secondary-uniform-upper}
\end{equation}
No pointwise bound on $f$ is needed.

For $0<\delta<1$, define
\[
 M_\delta(u)=
 \sup_{\substack{G\ {\rm finite\ abelian},\ (|G|,6)=1\\
                 W:G\to[0,1],\ \mathbb E W=\delta\\
                 \|W-\delta\|_{U^3}\leq u}} Q_3(W).
\]
Then, as $u\downarrow0$,
\begin{equation}
 M_\delta(u)=\delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4+
       C_*\delta^{8/3}u^{16/3}+O_\delta(u^{17/3}).
 \label{gsr:cc:14:eq:secondary-extremal-expansion}
\end{equation}
The upper constants are independent of $G$, even for varying groups.
\end{theorem}

This is a theorem about the local extremal cube problem. It does not by
itself improve the final quantitative bound in Szemer\'edi's theorem.



\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 11--14]
\emph{Source~04's Question~1 is settled.} See Remark~\ref{gsr:cc:14:rem:q1} at the end of this section for the deduction in source~04's normalization. The ``earlier project note'' with the gap $[(9/4)^{1/3},6]$ is source~04 (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:04:cub:fractional}, Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:04:cub:two-frequency}); its leading term $6\sqrt2$ and the norm gap \eqref{gsr:cc:14:eq:old-norm-gap} are source~04's Theorems~\ref{gsr:cc:04:cub:main} and~\ref{gsr:cc:04:cub:norm-gap}, reproved below; the centered expansion \eqref{gsr:cc:14:eq:centered-three-cube} is in sources~03, 04, 08, 09 and~13 (Appendix~A, Section~\ref{gsr:cc:14:sec:dA}, is its certificate here).
\end{writenote}
\subsection{Fourier preliminaries and the previous leading estimate}

Write the dual group additively, and put
\[
 a_r=\widehat f(r)=\mathbb E_xf(x)\overline{r(x)},\qquad
 a_{-r}=\overline{a_r},\qquad a_0=0.
\]
We use the exact identities
\begin{align}
 \|f\|_{U^2}^4&=\sum_r|a_r|^4=:S,\\
 \|f\|_{U^3}^8&=\sum_{s,t}|T(s,t)|^2,\qquad
 T(s,t)=\sum_r a_r\overline{a_{r+s}}\,
                       \overline{a_{r+t}}a_{r+s+t},\label{gsr:cc:14:eq:T-Fourier}\\
 B_5(f)&:=\mathbb E_{x,h_1,h_2,h_3}
       f(x)f(x+h_1)f(x+h_2)f(x+h_3)f(x+h_1+h_2+h_3)\\
       &=\sum_r a_{2r}a_{-r}^3a_r.\label{gsr:cc:14:eq:B5-Fourier}
\end{align}
The sum in \eqref{gsr:cc:14:eq:T-Fourier} is unnormalized. On inserting Fourier
inversion in the cube, the four orthogonality equations say that the
parity-adjusted frequency labels form an affine three-cube; grouping
its two parallel faces gives the identity.

The centered expansion is
\begin{equation}
 Q_3(\delta+f)=\delta^8+12\delta^4S+8\delta^3B_5(f)+R_6+R_7+u^8,
 \qquad |R_6|\leq28\delta^2u^6,\quad |R_7|\leq8\delta u^7.
 \label{gsr:cc:14:eq:centered-three-cube}
\end{equation}
Indeed, one, two, or three distinct cube forms are jointly uniform, so
their centered terms vanish. The twelve four-element parallelograms
contribute $S$ each; all other four-element supports are independent.
The eight surviving five-element supports are cube-symmetric copies
of $\{000,100,010,001,111\}$ and give $B_5(f)$. Bound the $28$ sextic
and $8$ septic supports by cube Cauchy--Schwarz. Odd order suffices:
the nonzero minors in these support arguments are $\pm1$ or $\pm2$.

Let $\lambda_r=|a_r|^2$ and $M=\sum_r|a_r|^8$. The coordinate axes
in \eqref{gsr:cc:14:eq:T-Fourier} contribute
\[
 2\mathcal E(\lambda)-S^2,\qquad
 \mathcal E(\lambda)=\sum_{r+s=t+w}\lambda_r\lambda_s\lambda_t\lambda_w.
\]
Retaining the union of
\[
 (r=t,\ s=w),\quad (r=w,\ s=t),\quad (s=-r,\ w=-t)
\]
in this positive energy sum gives $3S^2-3M$. Each family weighs $S^2$,
each pairwise intersection weighs $M$, and the triple intersection
has $2r=0$ and zero weight. Consequently,
\begin{equation}
 \|f\|_{U^3}^8\geq5S^2-6M\geq2S^2.\label{gsr:cc:14:eq:old-norm-gap}
\end{equation}
The final inequality uses conjugate pairing, which gives $M\leq S^2/2$.
Equality for nonzero $f$ forces exactly one conjugate pair.

Choose a largest pair $\{\xi,-\xi\}$, and write
\begin{equation}
 \rho=|a_\xi|,\qquad
 D=\sum_{r\notin\{\xi,-\xi\}}|a_r|^4,\qquad
 b=|a_{2\xi}|,\qquad S=2\rho^4+D.
 \label{gsr:cc:14:eq:dominant-pair-notation}
\end{equation}
There is no order-three character, so the pairs $\{\pm\xi\}$ and
$\{\pm2\xi\}$ are disjoint, and $2b^4\leq D$. The axes estimate yields
\begin{equation}
 \text{axes contribution}\geq
 8\rho^8+20\rho^4D+2D^2=2S^2+12\rho^4D,\label{gsr:cc:14:eq:axes-local}
\end{equation}
because the tail eighth-power mass is at most $D^2/2$.
Maximality of $\rho$ also gives
\begin{equation}
 \|f\|_{U^3}^8\geq(2+3D/S)S^2,\label{gsr:cc:14:eq:old-localization}
\end{equation}
by using $M\leq\rho^4S=(S-D)S/2$ in \eqref{gsr:cc:14:eq:old-norm-gap}.

\subsection{Eight additional Fourier slots}

\begin{lemma}[The off-axis correction]\label{gsr:cc:14:lem:eight-slots}
With the notation above,
\begin{equation}
 \|f\|_{U^3}^8\geq
 2S^2+12\rho^4D+8\rho^4b^4
       -16\rho^3D^{5/4}-16\rho^2D^{3/2}.
 \label{gsr:cc:14:eq:eight-slots-bound}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Besides the axes, retain the eight slots
\[
       (s,t)\in\{(\pm\xi,\pm3\xi),(\pm3\xi,\pm\xi)\}.
\]
They are distinct and off the axes: $3\xi\ne0$ and $\xi\ne\pm3\xi$.
Their $T$-values have the same modulus, by
$T(s,t)=T(t,s)$ and $T(-s,t)=\overline{T(s,t)}$.

Let $a'_r=a_r$ off $\{\xi,-\xi\}$ and $a'_r=0$ on that pair. There
is an exact decomposition
\begin{equation}
 T(\xi,3\xi)=
 \rho^2b^2+
 2\operatorname{Re}\!\left(a_\xi\overline{a_{2\xi}}\,
                            \overline{a_{4\xi}}a_{5\xi}\right)
 +T_{a'}(\xi,3\xi).
 \label{gsr:cc:14:eq:T-key-decomposition}
\end{equation}
The base $r=-2\xi$ gives labels $(-2\xi,-\xi,\xi,2\xi)$ and
contributes $\rho^2b^2$. The only other nonzero summands involving
a dominant label have bases $r=\xi$ and $r=-5\xi$; they are conjugates.
The other possible bases force a zero label.

To check small torsion explicitly, the four offsets are $0,1,3,4$.
Two dominant labels differ by $\pm2\xi$. Offset difference $2$ gives
the displayed main term. The only extra coincidence in an order
coprime to $6$ is order $5$, where offset difference $3$ equals $-2$;
both extra summands contain $a_0$. For order $5$ the middle term in
\eqref{gsr:cc:14:eq:T-key-decomposition} vanishes as well, since $5\xi=0$.
For all other allowed orders, its three other labels are in the tail.

Each tail coefficient is at most $(D/2)^{1/4}$. H\"older gives
$|T_{a'}(\xi,3\xi)|\leq D$. Thus
\[
 |T(\xi,3\xi)-\rho^2b^2|\leq2\rho(D/2)^{3/4}+D.
\]
Using $|A+E|^2\geq A^2-2A|E|$ for $A\geq0$,
\begin{align*}
 8|T(\xi,3\xi)|^2
 &\geq8\rho^4b^4
       -32\rho^3b^2(D/2)^{3/4}-16\rho^2b^2D\\
 &\geq8\rho^4b^4-16\rho^3D^{5/4}-16\rho^2D^{3/2}.
\end{align*}
The last line uses $b^2\leq(D/2)^{1/2}$ and rounds constants upward.
Add this to \eqref{gsr:cc:14:eq:axes-local}.
\end{proof}

If the tail consists of the doubled pair alone, $D=2b^4$.
The axes penalty above $2S^2$ is then $24\rho^4b^4$; the eight
additional terms raise it to $32\rho^4b^4$, the exact leading
penalty in the two-harmonic model.

\subsection{Uniform localization and optimization}

\begin{proof}[Proof of the upper estimate]
The zero case is immediate. Scale to
$g=f/u$, $\|g\|_{U^3}=1$, and $t=u/\delta$, so that
$Q_3(\delta+f)=\delta^8Q_3(1+tg)$. In this proof the Fourier variables
refer to $g$. Put
\[
 S_0=1/\sqrt2,\quad \eta=S_0-S\geq0,\quad
 F=Q_3(1+tg)-1-6\sqrt2\,t^4.
\]
For $0<t\leq1$, the centered expansion gives
\begin{equation}
 F=-12\eta t^4+8t^5B_5(g)+R,\qquad |R|\leq37t^6.
 \label{gsr:cc:14:eq:F-localization}
\end{equation}
If $F\leq0$, the desired upper bound is immediate. Assume $F>0$.

First $|B_5(g)|\leq\rho S<1$. Hence $\eta=O(t)$ uniformly, and
$S\geq S_0/2$ for sufficiently small absolute $t$. By
\eqref{gsr:cc:14:eq:old-localization},
\[
 3DS\leq1-2S^2=2\eta(S_0+S)\leq2\sqrt2\,\eta,\qquad
 D\leq(8/3)\eta.
\]
The selected pair in $B_5$ contributes at most
$2\rho^4(D/2)^{1/4}$, while the other terms contribute at most
$\rho D$. Since $2\rho^4\leq S\leq S_0<1$, $D<1$, and $\rho<1$,
each of these two contributions is at most $D^{1/4}$. Thus
$|B_5(g)|\leq2D^{1/4}$. Therefore
\[
 12\eta\leq16tD^{1/4}+37t^2
 \leq16(8/3)^{1/4}t\eta^{1/4}+37t^2.
\]
If $\eta\leq(37/6)t^2$ the desired stronger localization follows
already. Otherwise subtract $37t^2\leq6\eta$ and divide by
$\eta^{1/4}$. Both cases give, for example,
\begin{equation}
             \eta\leq7t^{4/3},\qquad D\leq19t^{4/3},
 \label{gsr:cc:14:eq:quantified-localization}
\end{equation}
for all sufficiently small absolute $t$.

Substitute $\rho^4=(S_0-\eta-D)/2$ into
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:14:lem:eight-slots}, and use $2b^4\leq D$:
\begin{align*}
 2\sqrt2\,\eta\geq&
 3\sqrt2\,D+2\sqrt2\,b^4
 -(6D+4b^4)(\eta+D)\\
 &-16\rho^3D^{5/4}-16\rho^2D^{3/2}.
\end{align*}
Here the nonnegative term $2\eta^2$ was discarded. By
\eqref{gsr:cc:14:eq:quantified-localization}, all errors are uniformly
$O(t^{5/3})$, so
\begin{equation}
          \eta\geq\tfrac32 D+b^4-O(t^{5/3}).
 \label{gsr:cc:14:eq:sharp-deficit}
\end{equation}
If $a_\xi=\rho e^{i\theta}$, the selected quintic term is exactly
$2\rho^4\operatorname{Re}(a_{2\xi}e^{-2i\theta})$. Thus
\[
       B_5(g)\leq2\rho^4b+\rho D\leq S_0b+D.
\]
Consequently,
\begin{align*}
 F&\leq-18Dt^4-12b^4t^4+4\sqrt2\,bt^5+O(t^{17/3})\\
  &\leq-48b^4t^4+4\sqrt2\,bt^5+O(t^{17/3}).
\end{align*}
The error scales are $t^4t^{5/3}=t^{17/3}$,
$t^5D=O(t^{19/3})$, and $t^6=O(t^{17/3})$.
Finally,
\[
 \sup_{b\geq0}(4\sqrt2\,tb-48b^4)
   =C_*t^{4/3},\qquad
 b=\beta_*t^{1/3},\quad
 \beta_*=\left(\frac{\sqrt2}{48}\right)^{1/3}.
\]
Indeed $b^3=\sqrt2 t/48$, and
$3\sqrt2\,\beta_*=(9/4)^{1/3}$. Rescaling proves
\eqref{gsr:cc:14:eq:secondary-uniform-upper}, including uniformity in $G$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The matching model and the supremum}

On a character of order greater than $8$, take
$a_{\pm\xi}=\rho$, $a_{\pm2\xi}=b$, all positive, and no others.
There is no aliasing in frequency parallelograms, whose two-label sums
lie in $[-4,4]$. Here is an explicit enumeration certificate. In the
Fourier cube identity, every frequency belongs to
$\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}$; the absence of aliasing means that all the face
parallelograms close over the integers. Hence the frequency labels are
integer affine cubes in this five-point interval.

Reflect each direction with negative increment. This makes all three
increments nonnegative without changing the numbers of vertices of each
absolute frequency. Their sum is at most $4$. The possible multisets
of positive increments are
\[
 \varnothing,\ (1),\ (2),\ (3),\ (4),\
 (1,1),\ (1,2),\ (1,3),\ (2,2),\
 (1,1,1),\ (1,1,2).
\]
For a multiset of $k$ positive increments with sum $H$ and multiplicities
$m_1,m_2,\ldots$, choose the coordinate positions and the original signs
in
\[
       \frac{3!}{(3-k)!\prod_jm_j!}\,2^k
\]
ways. The minimum vertex ranges over the integers $-2,\ldots,2-H$.
This gives the following complete table, where $n_j$ counts the vertices
of absolute frequency $j$:
\[
\begin{array}{c|r}
(n_0,n_1,n_2)&\text{number of frequency cubes}\\ \hline
(8,0,0)&1\\
(4,4,0)&24\\
(4,0,4)&24\\
(3,4,1)&16\\
(2,4,2)&96\\
(0,8,0)&8\\
(0,4,4)&48\\
(0,0,8)&8
\end{array}
\]
Each row contributes its count times $\delta^{n_0}\rho^{n_1}b^{n_2}$.
Consequently,
\begin{align}
 \|f\|_{U^3}^8&=8\rho^8+48\rho^4b^4+8b^8,\label{gsr:cc:14:eq:model-norm}\\
 Q_3(\delta+f)&=\delta^8+24\delta^4(\rho^4+b^4)
 +16\delta^3\rho^4b+96\delta^2\rho^4b^2+\|f\|_{U^3}^8.
 \label{gsr:cc:14:eq:model-Q}
\end{align}
These are the earlier cosine identities with amplitudes $2\rho,2b$.
Choose
\[
 b=\beta_*\delta^{-1/3}u^{4/3},\qquad
 \rho^4=-3b^4+\sqrt{u^8/8+8b^8}.
\]
Then $\|f\|_{U^3}=u$ exactly and
$\rho^4=u^4/(2\sqrt2)-3b^4+O(b^8/u^4)$. Substitution gives
\[
 Q_3(\delta+f)=\delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4
 +C_*\delta^{8/3}u^{16/3}+O_\delta(u^{20/3}).
\]
For fixed $0<\delta<1$ these are $[0,1]$ weights for small $u$.
A fixed prime cyclic group of order $17$ supplies them. This proves
the matching lower bound in \eqref{gsr:cc:14:eq:secondary-extremal-expansion}.
For norms smaller than the stated budget $u$, apply the upper estimate
at the actual norm and use monotonicity of its positive displayed powers.

\subsection{Rigidity at the secondary scale}

\begin{theorem}[Two-harmonic rigidity]\label{gsr:cc:14:thm:secondary-rigidity}
Fix $\delta>0$. Let $G_j$ have order coprime to $6$ and let $f_j$ be
real and centered, with $u_j=\|f_j\|_{U^3}\downarrow0$. Suppose
\[
 Q_3(\delta+f_j)=\delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u_j^4
 +C_*\delta^{8/3}u_j^{16/3}+o_\delta(u_j^{16/3}).
\]
Then largest pairs $\{\pm\xi_j\}$, with
$a_{j,\xi_j}=\rho_j e^{i\theta_j}$, satisfy
\begin{align}
 |a_{j,2\xi_j}|&\sim\beta_*\delta^{-1/3}u_j^{4/3},\\
 \frac{a_{j,2\xi_j}}{|a_{j,2\xi_j}|}e^{-2i\theta_j}&\longrightarrow1,\\
 \sum_{r\notin\{\pm\xi_j,\pm2\xi_j\}}|a_{j,r}|^4
       &=o_\delta(u_j^{16/3}),\\
 \rho_j^4&=\frac{u_j^4}{2\sqrt2}
      -3\beta_*^4\delta^{-4/3}u_j^{16/3}+o_\delta(u_j^{16/3}).
\end{align}
After removing the two conjugate pairs, the remainder is
$o_\delta(u_j^{4/3})$ in $U^2$. No $L^2$ approximation is asserted.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Use the normalized variables above. Put
$\beta=b/t^{1/3}$ and $e=(D-2b^4)/t^{4/3}\geq0$.
Retaining both the phase and the unused tail in the upper proof gives
\[
 \frac{F}{t^{16/3}}\leq
 4\sqrt2\,\beta\cos\phi-48\beta^4-18e+o(1),
 \qquad\phi=\arg a_{2\xi}-2\arg a_\xi.
\]
Here replacing $2\rho^4b\cos\phi$ by $S_0b\cos\phi$ is an approximation
with absolute error at most $(\eta+D)b$, because
$2\rho^4=S_0-\eta-D$. We use this error estimate, rather than a
one-sided inequality whose direction could depend on $\cos\phi$.
After the $t^5$ factor and division by $t^{16/3}$, its contribution
is $O(t^{4/3})=o(1)$ by localization.
Localization bounds $\beta,e$. The polynomial
$4\sqrt2\beta-48\beta^4$ has unique maximum $C_*$ at $\beta_*>0$.
Asymptotic equality forces
$\beta\to\beta_*$, $e\to0$, and $\cos\phi\to1$.
The exact centered expansion then gives
\[
 \eta/t^{4/3}\to
 (4\sqrt2\beta_*-C_*)/12=4\beta_*^4,\qquad
 D/t^{4/3}\to2\beta_*^4.
\]
Use $\rho^4=(S_0-\eta-D)/2$ and rescale. The Fourier formula
for $U^2$ gives the claimed remainder norm.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Indicator sharpness}

\begin{proposition}
For every $0<\delta<1$, there are prime cyclic groups and subsets $A_j$
with densities $\delta_j\to\delta$ and
$v_j=\|1_{A_j}-\delta_j\|_{U^3}\downarrow0$, such that
\[
 \frac{Q_3(1_{A_j})-\delta_j^8-6\sqrt2\,\delta_j^4v_j^4}
 {\delta_j^{8/3}v_j^{16/3}}\longrightarrow C_*.
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Take the two-harmonic weights at $u_j=2^{-j}u_0$, for a sufficiently
small fixed $u_0>0$, on sufficiently large
primes $p_j$. Their exact formulas do not depend on the prime once it
exceeds $8$. Include points independently with the prescribed weights.
At most $28/p_j$ of normalized three-cubes have a repeated vertex.
Elsewhere independence gives the weighted expectation exactly, for
both the indicator cube polynomial and the product centered at the
fixed mean $\delta$. Expectation errors are therefore $O(1/p_j)$.
Changing one inclusion decision changes either polynomial by at most
$8/p_j$, so a bounded-difference variance estimate gives $O(1/p_j)$
variance. The density has variance at most $1/(4p_j)$. Therefore, for
large enough $p_j$, some realization approximates all three statistics
simultaneously to any prescribed error. Recentring at the actual
density costs at most $8|\delta_j-\delta|$.

Take errors $o(u_j^{28/3})$. Then
$v_j^8=u_j^8+o(u_j^{28/3})$, whence
$v_j^4=u_j^4+o(u_j^{16/3})$. The model expansion transfers with its
exact secondary coefficient, including the replacements of $\delta$
by $\delta_j$. Since $v_j/u_j\to1$ and $u_{j+1}/u_j=1/2$,
the actual norms $v_j$ decrease strictly after discarding finitely
many initial indices.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why boundedness alone cannot give $L^2$ rigidity]
The indicator examples also supply an explicit obstruction to replacing
the $U^2$ remainder in Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:14:thm:secondary-rigidity} by an
$L^2$ remainder tending to zero.  For those examples,
\[
 \|1_{A_j}-\delta_j\|_2^2
       =\delta_j(1-\delta_j)\longrightarrow\delta(1-\delta)>0.
\]
Let $P_j$ be any Fourier projection onto at most four frequencies,
including a projection onto two conjugate pairs.  Each Fourier
coefficient has modulus at most $v_j=\|1_{A_j}-\delta_j\|_{U^3}$,
by \eqref{gsr:cc:14:eq:old-norm-gap}.  Thus Parseval gives
$\|P_j\|_2^2\le4v_j^2\to0$ and, by orthogonality,
\[
 \|1_{A_j}-\delta_j-P_j\|_2^2
       \longrightarrow\delta(1-\delta).
\]
Thus even exact asymptotic secondary extremality among bounded weights
does not imply small $L^2$ distance from the two-harmonic projection.
\end{remark}



\begin{writeremarkc}[Source~04's Question~1; added at the third write, 6~October 2026]\label{gsr:cc:14:rem:q1}
\emph{Claim.} In source~04's normalization the limit in its display~(Q1) exists and equals $C_*=(9/4)^{1/3}$: for $0<\delta<1$, with $M^{04}_\delta(u)$ the supremum of $Q_3(W)$ over prime cyclic groups of order greater than $16$ and weights $0\le W\le1$ with $\E W=\delta$ and $\|W-\delta\|_{U^3}=u$,
\[
 \lim_{u\downarrow0}\frac{M^{04}_\delta(u)-\delta^8-6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4}{\delta^{8/3}u^{16/3}}=(9/4)^{1/3}.
\]
\emph{Proof.} Every prime $p>16$ is coprime to $6$, and $\|W-\delta\|_{U^3}=u$ implies $\le u$, so $M^{04}_\delta(u)\le M_\delta(u)$, the supremum of Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:14:thm:secondary-exact}; by \eqref{gsr:cc:14:eq:secondary-extremal-expansion} the $\limsup$ of the displayed quotient is at most $C_*$. Source~04's Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:04:cub:two-frequency} gives, on $\Z/p\Z$ with $p>16$ and norm exactly $u$, the quotient $(9/4)^{1/3}+o(1)$, so the $\liminf$ is at least $(9/4)^{1/3}=C_*$. \emph{The normalizations agree:} source~04's model $f=a\cos(2\pi x/p)+b\cos(4\pi x/p)$ has Fourier coefficients $a/2$ and $b/2$, so this source's $\rho,b$ are source~04's $a/2,b/2$; substituting $\rho=a/2$, $b=b_{04}/2$ in \eqref{gsr:cc:14:eq:model-norm}--\eqref{gsr:cc:14:eq:model-Q} gives source~04's identity \eqref{gsr:cc:04:cub:two-frequency-complete} term by term, and $\beta_*=(\sqrt2/48)^{1/3}$ is half of source~04's $c=(\sqrt2/6)^{1/3}$. (Checked at the write: the model identity against a direct cube sum on $\Z/17\Z$ at two parameter points, agreement to $10^{-15}$; the normalized quotient along the model at $\delta=1/4$ is $1.3104628$ at $u=10^{-4}$ and $1.3103709$ at $u=10^{-6}$, against $C_*=1.3103707$.) This is a new result of source~14, not a second route; it is unrefereed and not formalized. The constants $c,C$ of the upper bound are not explicit (source~14's Question~3). The concentration question of source~04's Question~2 is answered in $U^2$ by Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:14:thm:secondary-rigidity} and fails in $L^2$ by the remark above.
\end{writeremarkc}
