\section[{Order five changes the next exponent\srctag{14}}]{Order five changes the next exponent}\label{gsr:cc:14:sec:d3}
\srcnote{14}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:cc:14:sec:order-five}

Even after excluding order-three characters, short additive resonances
still matter. In particular,
order five produces a further distinction: on groups of exponent five,
the correction of order $u^{16/3}$ vanishes, and the next exponent is $6$.
The optimal coefficient at $u^6$ is not determined here.

\begin{lemma}[An order-five energy penalty]\label{gsr:cc:14:lem:order-five-penalty}
If the largest Fourier character $\xi$ has order $5$, then
\begin{equation}
             \|f\|_{U^3}^8\geq2S^2+16\rho^6b^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:14:eq:order-five-penalty}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
In addition to the three energy families retained in the norm-gap proof,
retain the additive quadruple
\[
               (\xi,\xi,-\xi,-2\xi).
\]
It is additive because $2\xi=-3\xi$. Interchanging the sides, interchanging
the unequal entries on a side, and negating all entries produces eight
distinct quadruples, all outside the previous three families. Each has
weight $\rho^6b^2$. Thus
$\mathcal E(\lambda)\geq3S^2-3M+8\rho^6b^2$.
The axes bound and $M\leq S^2/2$ prove the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp correction exponent in exponent five]
\label{gsr:cc:14:thm:exponent-five}
Let $\delta>0$, and let $G$ be a nontrivial finite abelian group of
exponent $5$. Uniformly
over such groups and real centered functions,
\[
 Q_3(\delta+f)\leq
 \delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4+O(\delta^2u^6)
 \qquad (u/\delta\downarrow0).
\]
For $0<\delta<1$, the exponent $6$ cannot be increased, even on the fixed
group $\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z$. This group has $[0,1]$ weights of mean
$\delta$, with centered norm $u$, satisfying
\begin{equation}
 Q_3(W_u)=\delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4
       +\frac{2^{3/4}}3\,\delta^2u^6+O_\delta(u^8).
 \label{gsr:cc:14:eq:order-five-model-asymptotic}
\end{equation}
The coefficient $2^{3/4}/3$ is a lower bound, not a claim of optimality.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Uniform upper estimate]
Normalize by $g=f/u$, $t=u/\delta$, as in the preceding proof, and use
$F,\eta,D,\rho,b$ there. If $F\leq0$ there is nothing to prove.
Otherwise the first localization step gives $\eta=O(t)$ and $D=O(\eta)$.
Thus $\rho^4=(S_0-\eta-D)/2$ is bounded below by a positive absolute
constant. By Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:14:lem:order-five-penalty},
$b^2=O(\eta)$, since $1-2S^2\leq2\sqrt2\,\eta$.
The quintic estimate becomes
\[
       |B_5(g)|\leq2\rho^4b+\rho D=O(\eta^{1/2}+\eta).
\]
The centered cube expansion gives
\[
       \eta\leq C_1t\eta^{1/2}+C_2t\eta+C_3t^2.
\]
For small $t$, absorb the middle term. The resulting quadratic
inequality in $\sqrt\eta$ gives $\eta=O(t^2)$.
Consequently $B_5(g)=O(t)$, and $F=O(t^6)$ uniformly.
Rescaling proves the assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Exact model and positive order-six correction]
On $\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z$, choose the Fourier coefficients
\[
 a_1=\rho e^{i\pi/10},\qquad a_2=b e^{i\pi/5},\qquad
 a_{-1}=\overline{a_1},\quad a_{-2}=\overline{a_2}.
\]
The constant coefficient of $W=\delta+f$ is $\delta$.
Put $z=e^{i\pi/10}$, so $z^5=i$. The six symmetry types of $T(s,t)$
are as follows; multiplicities total $25$.
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|l}
(s,t)&\text{multiplicity}&T(s,t)\\ \hline
(0,0)&1&\delta^4+2\rho^4+2b^4\\
(0,1)&4&2\delta^2\rho^2+2\rho^2b^2+b^4\\
(0,2)&4&2\delta^2b^2+2\rho^2b^2+\rho^4\\
(1,1)&4&\delta^2\rho^2+2\delta\rho^2b\\
(2,2)&4&\delta^2b^2\\
(1,2)&8&\rho^2b^2+2\delta\rho^2b
\end{array}
\]
Each entry follows by summing the five bases $r$ in
\eqref{gsr:cc:14:eq:T-Fourier}; terms with phase $z^5=i$ cancel with conjugates.
Squaring these entries and summing with their multiplicities proves
\begin{align}
 \|f\|_{U^3}^8
 &=8\rho^8+16\rho^6b^2+48\rho^4b^4+16\rho^2b^6+8b^8,
 \label{gsr:cc:14:eq:order-five-exact-norm}\\
 Q_3(\delta+f)
 &=\delta^8+24\delta^4(\rho^4+b^4)+16\delta^3\rho^4b
    +96\delta^2\rho^4b^2+48\delta^2\rho^2b^4\notag\\
 &\hspace{14mm}+32\delta\rho^4b^3+\|f\|_{U^3}^8.
 \label{gsr:cc:14:eq:order-five-exact-Q}
\end{align}
Choose
\[
             b=\kappa\delta^{-1}u^2,\qquad
             \kappa=2^{5/4}/12,
\]
and choose the unique positive $\rho$ making
\eqref{gsr:cc:14:eq:order-five-exact-norm} equal $u^8$.
Existence follows for small $u$ from strict increase in $\rho$.
The expansion is
\[
 \rho^4=\frac{u^4}{2\sqrt2}-2^{-3/4}u^2b^2+O_\delta(u^8).
\]
The order-six coefficient in \eqref{gsr:cc:14:eq:order-five-exact-Q} is therefore
\[
 -24\,2^{-3/4}\kappa^2+4\sqrt2\,\kappa=\frac{2^{3/4}}3.
\]
All other terms are $O_\delta(u^8)$. The real weights are in $[0,1]$
for small $u$, since $\rho,b\to0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{The coefficient is now determined} by sources~21 and~23, independently: $2^{3/4}/3$ is optimal, uniformly over all nontrivial groups of exponent five, with an absolute $O(u^8)$ remainder for $u\le c\delta$ (source~21's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:21:thm:main}, source~23's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:23:five:main}; Section~\ref{gsr:cc:sec:charfive}). ``The coefficient $2^{3/4}/3$ is a lower bound, not a claim of optimality'' stands as this source's statement. On $\Z/5\Z$ the next coefficient is $20/9$ (source~21's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:21:thm:five-point-next}); the universal eighth-order coefficient is open (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:eighth}).
\end{writenote}

The same upper argument applies whenever a largest character has order
$5$, even if the ambient group, still of order coprime to $6$, has
characters of other orders. Hence an asymptotically
optimal family for the coefficient $C_*$ cannot eventually use an
order-five largest pair: its rigidity conclusion has
$b\asymp t^{1/3}$ and $\eta\asymp t^{4/3}$, while the order-five
penalty would force $\eta\gg b^2\asymp t^{2/3}$.

\subsection{The fixed-group classification}

For a fixed nontrivial $G$ of order coprime to $6$, let $M_{\delta,G}(u)$
denote the weighted supremum with that group held fixed.
If the exponent of $G$ is not $5$, its dual has a character of order at
least $7$. For order greater than $8$, the positive two-harmonic model
in \eqref{gsr:cc:14:eq:model-norm}--\eqref{gsr:cc:14:eq:model-Q} applies without change.

Here is a complete uncentered certificate for order $7$, which is the
only additional small case needed. Take
$a_{\pm1}=\rho$, $a_{\pm2}=b$, and $a_0=\delta$ in $\mathbb Z/7\mathbb Z$.
Under sign changes and interchange of $s,t$, the following ten types
exhaust all $49$ slots:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|l}
(s,t)&\text{multiplicity}&T(s,t)\\ \hline
(0,0)&1&\delta^4+2\rho^4+2b^4\\
(0,1)&4&2\delta^2\rho^2+2\rho^2b^2\\
(0,2)&4&2\delta^2b^2+\rho^4\\
(0,3)&4&b^4+2\rho^2b^2\\
(1,1)&4&\delta^2\rho^2+2\delta\rho^2b\\
(1,2)&8&2\delta\rho^2b\\
(1,3)&8&\rho^2b^2\\
(2,2)&4&\delta^2b^2\\
(2,3)&8&0\\
(3,3)&4&2\rho b^3
\end{array}
\]
Squaring and summing gives
\begin{align*}
 \|f\|_{U^3}^8&=8\rho^8+48\rho^4b^4+32\rho^2b^6+8b^8,\\
 Q_3(\delta+f)&=\delta^8+24\delta^4(\rho^4+b^4)
     +16\delta^3\rho^4b+96\delta^2\rho^4b^2+\|f\|_{U^3}^8.
\end{align*}
Thus order seven adds only $32\rho^2b^6$ to the centered norm formula
and to the final norm term of the cube count.

At $b=\beta_*\delta^{-1/3}u^{4/3}$, choose $\rho$ so that the actual
norm equals $u$. The extra term is $O_\delta(u^{10})$ in the eighth
power and changes $\rho^4$ by $O_\delta(u^6)$. It therefore changes
the cube count only by $O_\delta(u^6)$, which is smaller than the
secondary scale $u^{16/3}$. All these models lift along a character
to the original fixed group, preserving normalized averages.

Consequently, if the exponent of $G$ is not $5$,
\[
 M_{\delta,G}(u)=\delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4
        +C_*\delta^{8/3}u^{16/3}+O_\delta(u^{17/3}).
\]
If $G$ has exponent $5$, the first correction has sharp exponent $6$,
and its coefficient remains to be determined. The trivial group is
excluded because its only centered function is zero.

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
The coefficient is now determined: it is $2^{3/4}/3$, uniformly (sources~21 and~23; note after Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:14:thm:exponent-five}).
\end{writenote}

\section[{Exact supersaturation and rigidity for polynomial colorings\srctag{14}}]{Exact supersaturation and rigidity for polynomial colorings}\label{gsr:cc:14:sec:d6}
\srcnote{14}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:cc:14:sec:coloring-supersaturation}

The dimension obstruction for low-degree polynomial colorings has a
stronger counting form.  Once the dimension exceeds the obstruction
budget, the least possible number of symmetrically colored progressions
can be determined exactly, at each prescribed center and in total.
Equality also has a geometric consequence: the permitted directions at
each center form a linear subspace.  The classical ingredients are
Warning's second theorem and the minimum-support theorem for polynomial
functions on a finite field.  We prove the ingredients needed here;
their application gives an exact extremal answer in the specified
polynomial-coordinate model.  Neither the polynomial minimum-support
theorem nor the norm construction is claimed as new.

This is a related finite-field problem, rather than a direct replacement
for Gowers's Corollary~8.3.  That corollary concerns monochromatic
four-term progressions in colorings of an interval.  A symmetrically
colored four-term progression may have two different colors, in the
order $a,b,b,a$.  The repository's \texttt{HasMonochromaticAP} and
\texttt{corollary\_8\_3} definitions encode the former condition;
the finite-field symmetry condition below needs a separate definition.

\subsection{The extremal question and its exact answer}

Let $\mathbb F_q$ have characteristic $p$, and assume
\[
 k=2m\ge4,\qquad p>k,\qquad r\ge1,\qquad
 1\le D_\ell\le k\quad(1\le\ell\le r).
\]
The restriction concerns the characteristic, not just the cardinality
$q$ of the field.  Put
\[
 s_\ell=\left\lceil D_\ell/2\right\rceil,
 \qquad B=\sum_{\ell=1}^r s_\ell^2.
\]
Consider polynomial maps
$Q=(Q_1,\ldots,Q_r):\mathbb F_q^d\to\mathbb F_q^r$
with $\deg Q_\ell\le D_\ell$.  At a center $z$, define
\begin{equation}
 S_z(Q)=\left\{h\in\mathbb F_q^d:
 Q\bigl(z+(i-\tfrac12)h\bigr)
 =Q\bigl(z-(i-\tfrac12)h\bigr)
 \text{ for }1\le i\le m\right\}.
 \label{gsr:cc:14:eq:coloring-Sz}
\end{equation}
The zero direction is included.  For $h\ne0$, the resulting $k$ points
are distinct because $p>k$.  Let
\[
 A_k^{\mathrm{sym}}(Q)
 =\#\{(a,h)\in\mathbb F_q^d\times(\mathbb F_q^d\setminus\{0\}):
     Q(a+ih)=Q(a+(k-1-i)h)\ (0\le i<m)\}.
\]
This is a count of ordered pairs $(a,h)$; no quotient by changes of
orientation or by different parametrizations is implicit.

\begin{theorem}[Exact polynomial-coloring supersaturation]
\label{gsr:cc:14:thm:coloring-exact-supersaturation}
For every admissible $Q$ and every center $z$,
\begin{equation}
 |S_z(Q)|\ge q^{\max\{d-B,0\}}.
 \label{gsr:cc:14:eq:coloring-pointwise-min}
\end{equation}
There is one admissible $Q$ attaining equality simultaneously at every
center.  Consequently
\begin{equation}
 \min_Q A_k^{\mathrm{sym}}(Q)
 =q^d\bigl(q^{\max\{d-B,0\}}-1\bigr).
 \label{gsr:cc:14:eq:coloring-total-min}
\end{equation}
If $d\ge B$ and equality holds in \eqref{gsr:cc:14:eq:coloring-pointwise-min}
at a particular $z$, then $S_z(Q)$ is an $\mathbb F_q$-linear subspace
of dimension $d-B$.  Equality in \eqref{gsr:cc:14:eq:coloring-total-min} therefore
implies this subspace conclusion at every center.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
Source~22 extends the pointwise statement to every equality pattern and every degree at a prescribed centre (its Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:22:thm:pattern-minimum} and Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:22:cor:symmetric}, which recovers the low-degree case here), and shows that the quintic and sextic pointwise budget for symmetric four-term progressions is exactly eight (Section~\ref{gsr:cc:22:sec:d7}).
\end{writenote}

The previous existence threshold $d\le B$ is recovered by asking when
the right side of \eqref{gsr:cc:14:eq:coloring-total-min} is zero.  Above the
threshold, the conclusion strengthens the first Chevalley--Warning
argument, which supplies only $p-1$ nonzero directions over a prime
field.  In dimension $d=B+e$, the exact unavoidable number is
$q^e-1$ at every center.

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 11--14]
\emph{Credit.} The threshold case (the minimum is $0$ exactly when $d\le B$) is source~10's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:10:thm:poly-exact-dimension}, the ``separate project report'' of Section~\ref{gsr:fm:14:sec:d1}; it is reproved here. New: the exact counts above the threshold over every $\F_q$ with $p>k$, the subspace geometry of equality, and the prime-field gap. Source~10's quintic question ($4\le d\le8$) is not answered (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:colhigh}).
\end{writenote}


\subsection{A self-contained minimum-support lemma}

A polynomial in $n$ variables is called reduced if its degree in each
individual variable is at most $q-1$.  Replacing $X_i^q$ by $X_i$
repeatedly gives the unique reduced polynomial representing a given
polynomial function on $\mathbb F_q^n$.  Reduction cannot increase
total degree.  Uniqueness follows by induction from the fact that a
nonzero one-variable polynomial of degree less than $q$ cannot vanish
at every element of $\mathbb F_q$.

\begin{lemma}[Minimum support]
\label{gsr:cc:14:lem:coloring-min-support}
Let $F$ be a nonzero reduced polynomial on $\mathbb F_q^n$ with total
degree at most $R<n(q-1)$.  Write
$R=a(q-1)+b$, with $0\le b<q-1$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 \#\{x:F(x)\ne0\}\ge(q-b)q^{n-a-1}.
 \label{gsr:cc:14:eq:coloring-rm-weight}
\end{equation}
In particular, for $0\le B\le n$, degree at most $B(q-1)$ and
nonempty support imply support size at least $q^{n-B}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Successively take the leading coefficient in the last variable.  More
explicitly, if
$F(X',X_n)=\sum_{j=0}^t F_j(X')X_n^j$ and $F_t\ne0$,
then above every point where $F_t$ is nonzero, at least $q-t$
values of $X_n$ make $F$ nonzero.  Induction on the number of variables
therefore produces exponents $e_1,\ldots,e_n$, each between $0$ and
$q-1$, such that
\[
 \sum_i e_i\le R,
 \qquad \#\operatorname{supp}F\ge\prod_i(q-e_i).
\]
These exponents form a monomial of $F$, obtained by the successive
leading-coefficient choices.

It remains to minimize the product under the displayed constraints.
We may increase some $e_i$ until their sum is $R$, since this only
decreases the product.  If $0<e_i\le e_j<q-1$, transferring one unit
from $e_i$ to $e_j$ changes the corresponding two factors from
$(q-e_i)(q-e_j)$ to
$(q-e_i+1)(q-e_j-1)$, decreasing their product.  Repeating this
operation leaves at most one exponent strictly between $0$ and $q-1$.
The minimum is attained by $a$ exponents equal to $q-1$, one equal
to $b$, and the others equal to zero.  Its value is exactly
$(q-b)q^{n-a-1}$.  For $B=n$, the final assertion is simply that
nonempty support has at least one point.
\end{proof}

The next equality case is the $b=0$ part of the classical
minimum-weight Reed--Muller classification; see Leducq's account
\cite{leducq}.  A short slicing proof is included to make the
geometric conclusion of Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:14:thm:coloring-exact-supersaturation}
independent of a coding-theory black box.

\begin{lemma}[Rigidity of minimum support]
\label{gsr:cc:14:lem:coloring-min-support-rigidity}
If a nonzero reduced polynomial of degree at most $B(q-1)$ on
$\mathbb F_q^n$ has exactly $q^{n-B}$ nonzero values, where
$0\le B\le n$, its support is an affine subspace of dimension $n-B$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The cases $B=0$ and $B=n$ are immediate.  Set $e=n-B\ge1$ and write
$S=\operatorname{supp}F$.  An invertible affine change of variables,
followed by reduction, preserves the degree bound and the support size.
Fix any family of $q$ parallel affine hyperplanes and take them to be
$X_1=c$.  Let $t$ be the number of these hyperplanes missing $S$.

If $1\le t\le q-2$, then
\[
 F(X)=\prod_{c:\,S\cap\{X_1=c\}=\varnothing}(X_1-c)\,G(X)
\]
as a polynomial.  To see the factorization, the restriction to a missing
hyperplane is a reduced polynomial that vanishes on the entire field
grid, hence is the zero polynomial; the factor theorem applies to each
distinct $c$.  We have
\[
 \deg G\le B(q-1)-t
       =(B-1)(q-1)+(q-1-t).
\]
On each of the other $q-t$ hyperplanes, $G$ has nonempty support and
its nonzero values occur exactly where $F$ is nonzero.  Applying
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:14:lem:coloring-min-support} in $n-1$ variables gives at least
$(t+1)q^{e-1}$ points on each such hyperplane.  Consequently
\[
 |S|\ge(q-t)(t+1)q^{e-1}>q^e,
\]
because $(q-t)(t+1)-q=t(q-t-1)>0$.  This is impossible.
Thus every parallel family has either no missing member or exactly
$q-1$ missing members.

In a family with no missing member, applying the minimum-support bound
to every restriction shows that each hyperplane contains at least
$q^{e-1}$ points of $S$.  The total is $q^e$, so every member contains
exactly $q^{e-1}$ points.

Some family must have a missing member.  Otherwise every affine
hyperplane would contain exactly $q^{e-1}$ points of $S$.  Choose
$x\notin S$ and count pairs $(H,y)$ with $H$ a hyperplane through $x$
and $y\in H\cap S$.  There are $(q^n-1)/(q-1)$ hyperplanes through
$x$, whereas each $y\ne x$ lies with $x$ in
$(q^{n-1}-1)/(q-1)$ hyperplanes.  The two counts would give
\[
 q^{e-1}(q^n-1)=q^e(q^{n-1}-1),
\]
which would imply $q^{e-1}=q^e$.  Hence a family has exactly one member
meeting $S$, and $S$ is contained in a hyperplane.

Take that hyperplane to be $X_1=0$.  Uniqueness of reduced
representatives gives
\[
 F(X_1,X')=(1-X_1^{q-1})G(X'),\qquad G(X')=F(0,X').
\]
Because $G\ne0$, the degree of the right side is
$q-1+\deg G$, so $\deg G\le(B-1)(q-1)$.  Its support still has size
$q^e$.  Induction with $n-1$ variables and budget $B-1$ shows that this
support is an affine $e$-dimensional subspace of the hyperplane.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Warning's second theorem, with an equality case]
\label{gsr:cc:14:cor:coloring-warning-second}
Suppose polynomials $F_1,\ldots,F_t$ on $\mathbb F_q^n$ have a
nonempty common zero set $Z$, and their total degree sum is at most
$B\le n$.  Then $|Z|\ge q^{n-B}$.  If equality holds, $Z$ is an
affine subspace of dimension $n-B$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The polynomial function
\[
 I(X)=\prod_{j=1}^t\bigl(1-F_j(X)^{q-1}\bigr)
\]
is the indicator of $Z$.  Its degree is at most $B(q-1)$, and it is
nonzero since $Z$ is nonempty.  Reduce $I$ and apply the two lemmas.
\end{proof}

The numerical inequality is precisely the classical second theorem
of Warning \cite{warning}.  Its equality statement here is a
consequence of the classical minimum-support classification.

\subsection{Odd Taylor coefficients and the sharp construction}

For fixed $z$, define the coefficient polynomials by
\[
 Q_\ell(z+TH)=\sum_{j=0}^{D_\ell}C_{\ell,j,z}(H)T^j.
\]
Each nonzero $C_{\ell,j,z}$ is homogeneous of degree $j$ in $H$.
This definition uses polynomial expansion and requires no division
by factorials.

\begin{lemma}[The reflection equations]
\label{gsr:cc:14:lem:coloring-reflection-coefficients}
Under the hypotheses above,
\[
 S_z(Q)=\{h:
 C_{\ell,2j-1,z}(h)=0\text{ for all }
       1\le\ell\le r,\ 1\le j\le s_\ell\}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Put $\alpha_i=i-\tfrac12$.  The $\alpha_i$ are nonzero and their
squares are pairwise distinct: for $i\ne j$ both $i-j$ and $i+j-1$
are nonzero in characteristic $p>k$.  Subtracting the evaluations at
$T=\alpha_i$ and $T=-\alpha_i$, then dividing by $2\alpha_i$, gives
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^{s_\ell}
 C_{\ell,2j-1,z}(h)(\alpha_i^2)^{j-1}=0
 \qquad(1\le i\le m).
\]
Since $s_\ell\le m$, the first $s_\ell$ equations have an invertible
Vandermonde matrix.  They are equivalent to vanishing of all the
listed coefficients.  The converse follows by substitution.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:14:thm:coloring-exact-supersaturation}]
The coefficient polynomials vanish at $h=0$ and have total degree sum
at most
\[
 \sum_{\ell=1}^r\sum_{j=1}^{s_\ell}(2j-1)
 =\sum_{\ell=1}^r s_\ell^2=B.
\]
For $d\ge B$, Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:14:cor:coloring-warning-second} therefore
gives $|S_z(Q)|\ge q^{d-B}$.  For $d<B$, the zero direction alone
gives the asserted bound.  If $d\ge B$ and equality holds, the same
corollary says that $S_z(Q)$ is an affine subspace.  It contains zero,
so it is a linear subspace.

For sharpness, for each positive odd $t$ let
$N_t:\mathbb F_q^t\to\mathbb F_q$ be the norm from
$\mathbb F_{q^t}$ to $\mathbb F_q$ in a fixed linear coordinate basis.
It is a homogeneous polynomial of degree $t$, and
$N_t(u)=0$ if and only if $u=0$.  These facts follow, for example, by
writing
\[
 N_t(u_1,\ldots,u_t)
 =\prod_{a=0}^{t-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^t u_i\beta_i^{q^a}\right),
\]
where the $\beta_i$ form a field basis.  Frobenius permutes the factors,
so the coefficients lie in $\mathbb F_q$.

Use disjoint blocks
$u_\ell^{(2j-1)}\in\mathbb F_q^{2j-1}$, altogether $B$ coordinates,
and set
\begin{equation}
 Q_\ell(u)=\sum_{j=1}^{s_\ell}
             N_{2j-1}\bigl(u_\ell^{(2j-1)}\bigr).
 \label{gsr:cc:14:eq:coloring-sharp-norm-map}
\end{equation}
This is the odd norm-layer construction used in the recent coloring
literature \cite{shidong}.  Its degree is at most $D_\ell$.
Suppose a direction has a nonzero block in coordinate $\ell$, and let
$t$ be its largest nonzero block index.  In $Q_\ell(z+Th)$ the
coefficient of $T^t$ is exactly $N_t(h_\ell^{(t)})\ne0$: larger blocks
have zero direction and contribute constants, whereas smaller blocks
have degree less than $t$.  Since $t$ is odd, the reflection-coefficient
lemma rules out this direction.  Thus the map on $\mathbb F_q^B$ has
$S_z=\{0\}$ at every center.

For $d\ge B$, use this map on the first $B$ coordinates and ignore the
remaining $d-B$ coordinates.  Its symmetric-direction set is exactly
the kernel of that projection, with size $q^{d-B}$ at every center.
For $d<B$, restrict the map along a linear injection
$\mathbb F_q^d\hookrightarrow\mathbb F_q^B$; every nonzero direction
remains nonzero, so $S_z=\{0\}$.

Finally, the change of variables
$z=a+(k-1)h/2$ is a bijection between start-direction pairs and
center-direction pairs.  Hence
\[
 A_k^{\mathrm{sym}}(Q)=\sum_{z\in\mathbb F_q^d}(|S_z(Q)|-1).
\]
Summing the pointwise bound and using the construction proves the
exact minimum.  If the sum attains its lower bound, every nonnegative
pointwise excess is zero, proving the final equality assertion.
\end{proof}

There is also an adaptive version: if at a particular center some of
the odd coefficient polynomials vanish identically, their degrees
should be omitted.  With
\[
 B_z=\sum_{\ell,j:\,C_{\ell,2j-1,z}\ne0}(2j-1),
\]
the same proof gives $|S_z(Q)|\ge q^{\max\{d-B_z,0\}}$.
In particular, equality at the universal bound in a dimension
$d\ge B$ forces $B_z=B$.

\subsection{A sharp gap in the first supercritical dimension}

Over a prime field, homogeneity and the elementary Chevalley--Warning
divisibility give considerably more than an increment of one above
the minimum when $d=B+1$.

\begin{proposition}[First-supercritical gap and stability]
\label{gsr:cc:14:prop:coloring-first-gap}
Work over $\mathbb F_p$ with $p>k$ and $d=B+1$.  At every center,
\begin{equation}
 |S_z(Q)|=p\quad\hbox{or}\quad |S_z(Q)|\ge p^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:14:eq:coloring-gap}
\end{equation}
Both values $p$ and $p^2$ occur for admissible maps, simultaneously
at all centers in their respective examples.

Let $E$ be the number of centers with $|S_z(Q)|>p$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 A_k^{\mathrm{sym}}(Q)
 \ge p^d(p-1)+(p^2-p)E.
 \label{gsr:cc:14:eq:coloring-stability-count}
\end{equation}
In particular, if the left side is at most
$p^d(p-1)+\varepsilon p^d(p^2-p)$, at least
$(1-\varepsilon)p^d$ centers have exactly one projective direction
of reflection symmetry: their $S_z(Q)$ is a one-dimensional linear
subspace.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The defining coefficient equations are homogeneous, so their nonzero
common zeros form scalar orbits of size $p-1$.  Thus
$|S_z(Q)|\equiv1\pmod{p-1}$.
The degree sum is at most $B<d$, so
$p\mid |S_z(Q)|$ by Chevalley--Warning.  For completeness, this
divisibility follows by summing the indicator polynomial from
Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:14:cor:coloring-warning-second}: its total degree is less
than $d(p-1)$, and every monomial has a coordinate exponent less than
$p-1$.  Its sum in that coordinate is zero in $\mathbb F_p$, including
exponent zero, where the sum is $p=0$.

Writing $|S_z(Q)|=pt$, the two congruences yield
$t\equiv1\pmod{p-1}$.  Since $t\ge1$, either $t=1$ or $t\ge p$.
This proves \eqref{gsr:cc:14:eq:coloring-gap}.
The norm construction controlling $B$ coordinates leaves one free
coordinate and gives $p$ directions.  Restrict that avoiding norm map
to a $(B-1)$-dimensional subspace, then ignore two coordinates in the
$d=B+1$ dimensional domain; this gives exactly $p^2$ directions.
All degrees remain within the same upper bounds.  Summing the local
gap gives \eqref{gsr:cc:14:eq:coloring-stability-count}; the last assertion uses
the equality geometry in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:14:thm:coloring-exact-supersaturation}.
\end{proof}

The prime-field restriction in this proposition is deliberate.
Warning's second theorem over $\mathbb F_q$ gives the exact minimum
$q^{d-B}$, but the elementary divisibility proof just used supplies
divisibility by the characteristic $p$.  It does not by itself justify
replacing every occurrence of $p$ in the gap argument by a nonprime $q$.

\subsection{Examples and boundaries}

For scalar degree at most three or four and $k=4$, the budget is
$B=4$.  Consequently
\[
 \min_Q A_4^{\mathrm{sym}}(Q)
 =\begin{cases}
   0,&d\le4,\\
   q^d(q^{d-4}-1),&d\ge4.
  \end{cases}
\]
At $q=5,d=6$, this is $5^6(5^2-1)=375\,000$ ordered nontrivial
progressions.  The example is $Q=x_0+N_3(x_1,x_2,x_3)$ with two
additional free coordinates.  Each center has exactly $25$ symmetric
directions, including zero.  At $q=5,d=5$, every center has either
exactly five or at least twenty-five symmetric directions.

The equality subspaces may vary with the center.  For example,
$Q(x,y)=x+y^2$ has degree at most two, $B=1$, and
\[
 S_{(a,b)}(Q)=\{(u,v):u+2bv=0\}.
\]
There are $q$ directions at every center, attaining the minimum in
dimension two; the one-dimensional kernel changes with $b$.
Consequently equality does not, in general, imply that $Q$ factors
through a single fixed linear projection of dimension $B$.

The higher-degree question remains distinct.  For a scalar quintic and
$k=4$, write
$P(z+TH)=\sum_{j=0}^5 C_{j,z}(H)T^j$.  Reflection at the two
parameters $1/2$ and $3/2$ is equivalent to
\[
 C_{1,z}=\frac9{16}C_{5,z},\qquad
 C_{3,z}=-\frac52 C_{5,z}.
\]
Thus the odd coefficients need not vanish individually, and the
argument giving the low-degree budget $B=9$ cannot be used as an
avoidance construction for four-term progressions.  Conversely, the
same equations are equivalent to
\[
 C_{3,z}+\frac{40}{9}C_{1,z}=0,\qquad
 C_{5,z}-\frac{16}{9}C_{1,z}=0.
\]
These two polynomials have degrees at most three and five,
respectively.  Their degree sum is therefore at most $3+5=8$,
giving the necessary bound $d\le8$ for avoidance.
The cubic construction gives $d\ge4$.  Nothing in the present
supersaturation theorem determines the maximum within $4\le d\le8$.

\begin{proposition}[Failure of the first norm extension in characteristic five]
\label{gsr:cc:14:prop:coloring-artin-schreier-obstruction}
For every prime $p$, the degree-$p$ field norm
$N:\mathbb F_{p^p}\to\mathbb F_p$ is constant on a nontrivial affine
$\mathbb F_p$-line.  In particular, at $p=5$ a quintic norm in five
variables does not avoid symmetrically colored four-term progressions.
Adding independent lower-degree norm blocks does not remove this
counterexample.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Choose a root $\theta$ of $X^p-X-1$ in an algebraic closure.
Then $\theta^p=\theta+1$, and induction gives
$\theta^{p^j}=\theta+j$ for $0\le j\le p$.  The first $p$ elements
are distinct, and the $p$th iterate returns to $\theta$.  Thus
$X^p-X-1$ is irreducible over $\mathbb F_p$, and $\theta$ lies in
$\mathbb F_{p^p}$.  The points $\theta+a$, for $a\in\mathbb F_p$,
are precisely its Frobenius conjugates, and
\[
 N(\theta+a)
 =\prod_{b\in\mathbb F_p}(\theta+a+b)
 =\theta^p-\theta=1.
\]
They form the required affine line.  In a direct sum of norm blocks,
fix every other block and vary only this line in the degree-$p$ block;
the total color remains constant.
\end{proof}

This obstruction concerns a proposed construction, not every polynomial
of degree five.  It therefore does not improve the upper bound eight
or disprove the possibility of a different five-dimensional coloring.

\section[{Quantitative examples and what the refinements measure\srctag{14}}]{Quantitative examples and what the refinements measure}\label{gsr:cc:14:sec:d7}
\srcnote{14}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:cc:14:sec:examples}

\subsection{Convergence of the sharp cube model}

The sharp secondary term comes from a competition between two
effects.  A small coefficient at twice the dominant frequency
creates a positive quintic contribution, linear in the secondary
amplitude.  Keeping the centered $U^3$ norm fixed requires
decreasing the dominant amplitude, producing a quartic penalty
in that same secondary amplitude.  In normalized variables the
competition is exactly
\[
 4\sqrt2\,t b-48b^4.
\]
The balance $b\asymp t^{1/3}$ explains the fractional power:
the outer quartic scale $t^4$ is multiplied by $t^{4/3}$.
The coefficient is determined by the penalty as well as the
positive correlation.  Retaining only the coordinate axes of
the Fourier identity misses the eight extra penalty terms and
therefore misses the sharp coefficient.

For the positive two-harmonic model, define
\[
 \mathcal R_\delta(u)=
 \frac{Q_3(\delta+f_u)-\delta^8-6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4}
 {\delta^{8/3}u^{16/3}}.
\]
At $\delta=1/4$, the exact polynomial formulas give the following
values, rounded from 90-digit decimal arithmetic.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{rrr}
\toprule
$u$ & $\mathcal R_{1/4}(u)$ & $C_*=(9/4)^{1/3}$\\
\midrule
$10^{-2}$ & $1.3532657043$ & $1.3103706971$\\
$10^{-3}$ & $1.3123554554$ & $1.3103706971$\\
$10^{-4}$ & $1.3104628080$ & $1.3103706971$\\
$10^{-6}$ & $1.3103708955$ & $1.3103706971$\\
$10^{-9}$ & $1.3103706971$ & $1.3103706971$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/14-sharp-extremals-cube_convergence.pdf}
\caption{The exact two-harmonic model at density $1/4$.
The left panel displays the normalized secondary coefficient;
the right displays its positive excess over $C_*$ on logarithmic
axes.  These are evaluations of the proved polynomial identities,
not fitted evidence for the theorem.  The model's error after
normalization is $O_\delta(u^{4/3})$; the uniform upper theorem
allows a larger remainder because it controls all functions.}
\label{gsr:cc:14:fig:cube-convergence}
\end{figure}

On an exponent-five group, the additional penalty is quadratic
in $b$, rather than quartic at the relevant scale.  The balance
there is $b\asymp t$, giving a correction $t^6$.  This explains
why a torsion assumption is substantive even after order three
has been excluded.  It also distinguishes a proved exponent
from an optimal coefficient: the order-six exponent is sharp,
while its best coefficient remains a concrete open problem.

\subsection{A sharp stability example and a computable moment gain}

Take $A=\mathbb F_{101}\setminus\{0\}$.  Then $m=100$ and
\[
 E(A)=990\,100=(1-0.0099)m^3.
\]
The nearest coset is the whole field, at distance one.  Thus
\[
 \frac{|A\triangle\mathbb F_{101}|}{|A|}
 =0.01=\tau(0.0099).
\]
Taking a Cartesian product with full additional coordinates
preserves both normalized ratios.  This gives a transparent
sharpness example in every cube dimension.

The same example shows why a denominator depending only on
the sizes of the cross-sections can already improve a moment
bound.  A section of size $100$ in a prime-coordinate space
cannot be a coordinate coset, since such a coset has size
$101^a$.  The cardinality defect in
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:14:cor:cardinality-profile-defect} is $0.01$,
yielding an energy deficit $0.0099$ without inspecting
individual points.  If every nonempty section has this same
normalized defect, the eighth-arrangement lower bound gains
the factor
\[
 (1-0.0099)^{-6}>1.06
\]
over the cubic-profile denominator.  The gain is local and
explicit; whether it survives subsequent steps depends on
the parameter regime of the full argument.

\subsection{How fast polynomial supersaturation grows}

For one cubic or quartic color coordinate and symmetric
four-term progressions, $B=4$.  Over $\mathbb F_5$ the theorem
gives the exact values below.  Directions include zero in
the middle column and exclude it in the final column.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{rrr}
\toprule
Dimension $d$ & Minimum directions at each center &
Minimum ordered nontrivial four-APs\\
\midrule
$4$ & $1$ & $0$\\
$5$ & $5$ & $12\,500$\\
$6$ & $25$ & $375\,000$\\
$7$ & $125$ & $9\,687\,500$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The norm construction attains every row.  Adding one dimension
beyond the threshold does not merely force one progression
somewhere: it forces four nonzero directions at every center.
In the first supercritical dimension the next possible local
count is at least twenty-five including zero, so a near-minimum
global count strongly limits the number of exceptional centers.
The equality kernels can still vary with the center, as the
quadratic example in Section~\ref{gsr:cc:14:sec:coloring-supersaturation}
demonstrates.

\section[{A finite certificate for the centered cube expansion\srctag{14}}]{A finite certificate for the centered cube expansion}\label{gsr:cc:14:sec:dA}
\srcnote{14}{Appendix A}
\label{gsr:cc:14:app:centering}

Associate to a cube vertex $\omega\in\{0,1\}^3$ the row
$(1,\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3)$.  A vertex in a chosen support
is called a \emph{coloop} if deleting its row lowers the rank of
the rows.  If a support has a coloop, its product of centered
functions has zero average: one may average the corresponding
linear form independently of all the others.

Here is the full support classification.  Ranks are over the
rationals; the relevant nonzero four-by-four minors are $\pm1$
and $\pm2$, so the same independence argument is valid over every
finite abelian group of odd order.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{rrrrl}
\toprule
Size & Total & With a coloop & Remaining & Contribution\\
\midrule
$0$ & $1$ & $0$ & $1$ & Constant term\\
$1$ & $8$ & $8$ & $0$ & Zero\\
$2$ & $28$ & $28$ & $0$ & Zero\\
$3$ & $56$ & $56$ & $0$ & Zero\\
$4$ & $70$ & $58$ & $12$ & Parallelogram moment $S$\\
$5$ & $56$ & $48$ & $8$ & Five-point moment $B_5$\\
$6$ & $28$ & $0$ & $28$ & At most $u^6$ each\\
$7$ & $8$ & $0$ & $8$ & At most $u^7$ each\\
$8$ & $1$ & $0$ & $1$ & $u^8$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

For four vertices, the dependent supports are the six faces
and six diagonal parallelograms.  Every other four-vertex support
has full rank.  For five vertices, the complement is a three-vertex
set.  Up to cube symmetries, its three pairwise Hamming distances
are $(1,1,2)$, $(1,2,3)$, or $(2,2,2)$.  These types have
respectively $24$, $24$, and $8$ realizations.  In the first two
types the five-vertex support has a coloop; the final type is
the set of three neighbors of a cube vertex.  Its complement
is a cube-symmetric copy of
$\{000,100,010,001,111\}$.

For example, the complements of
$\{000,100,010\}$ and $\{000,100,111\}$ have coloops $110$
and $011$, respectively.  In the remaining case the five
forms satisfy the unique full-support dependence
\[
 2L_{000}-L_{100}-L_{010}-L_{001}+L_{111}=0,
 \qquad L_\omega=x+\omega\cdot h.
\]
Orthogonality then gives the Fourier expression for $B_5$ used
in Equation~\eqref{gsr:cc:14:eq:B5-Fourier}.  Generalized cube
Cauchy--Schwarz, obtained by successive Cauchy--Schwarz in
the cube directions, bounds a support of size $j$ by
$\|f\|_{U^3}^j$ after inserting constant ones at the other
vertices.  This proves the exact expansion and the two
remainder bounds in Equation~\eqref{gsr:cc:14:eq:centered-three-cube}.

The file \leanfile{verify_certificates.py} enumerates all
$255$ nonempty supports using exact rational row reduction,
checks the coloop counts and the minor values, and verifies
the five-vertex description.  It also checks all $25$ and
$49$ Fourier slots in the order-five and order-seven tables
with exact integer polynomial coefficients.  Thus no floating
point computation is needed for these certificates.
