\section[{Exact fourth- and fifth-order cube corrections in every dimension\srctag{16}}]{Exact fourth- and fifth-order cube corrections in every dimension}\label{gsr:cc:16:sec:d8}
\srcnote{16}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:cc:16:cub:section}\label{gsr:cc:16:sec:cubes}

Gowers's Lemma~3.10 bounds the number of cubes by applying the triangle
inequality to a constant plus a balanced function.  The resulting binomial
bound includes many terms which vanish identically.  We determine all
terms through degree five in every dimension.  The answer includes a
three-torsion contribution which first occurs in dimension four.

\subsection{Notation and the expansion}

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group, with normalized averages, and let
$f:G\to\mathbb R$ satisfy $\mathbb E f=0$.  Put $m=2^d$ and define
\[
 \mathcal Q_d(g)=
 \mathbb E_{x,h_1,\ldots,h_d\in G}
       \prod_{v\in\{0,1\}^d}g(x+v\cdot h).
\]
For real $g$, this is $\|g\|_{U^d}^{m}$.  Write $a_\chi=\widehat f(\chi)$,
using the normalization
$f(x)=\sum_{\chi\in\widehat G}a_\chi\chi(x)$ and additive notation for
$\widehat G$.  Thus $a_{-\chi}=\overline{a_\chi}$ and $a_0=0$.  Set
\begin{align}
 Q(f)&=\sum_{\chi\in\widehat G}|a_\chi|^4
                  =\|f\|_{U^2}^{4},\label{gsr:cc:16:cub:qdef}\\
 Q_2(f)&=\sum_{2\chi=0}|a_\chi|^4,\nonumber\\
 D(f)&=\sum_{\chi\in\widehat G}a_{2\chi}a_\chi a_{-\chi}^3,
                  \label{gsr:cc:16:cub:ddef}\\
 D_3(f)&=\sum_{3\chi=0}a_\chi^4a_{-\chi}.\nonumber
\end{align}
All four quantities are real.  The first two are nonnegative; the last two
can have either sign.  In each sum the trivial character contributes zero.
Define
\begin{align}
 P_d&=\frac{6^d-2\cdot4^d+2^d}{8},&
 T_d&=\frac{8^d-3\cdot6^d+3\cdot4^d-2^d}{24},\label{gsr:cc:16:cub:counts}\\
 F_d&=4T_d,&
 H_d&=\frac{10^d-4\cdot8^d+6\cdot6^d-4\cdot4^d+2^d}{24}.
 \nonumber
\end{align}

\begin{theorem}[The low-order cube expansion]
\label{gsr:cc:16:cub:main}
Let $d\geq2$, and let $f:G\to\mathbb R$ have mean zero.
The coefficients of $t,t^2,t^3$ in $\mathcal Q_d(\delta+tf)$ vanish.
Over every finite abelian group, the coefficient of $t^4$ is
\begin{equation}
 \delta^{m-4}\bigl(P_dQ(f)+T_dQ_2(f)\bigr).
 \label{gsr:cc:16:cub:quartic}
\end{equation}
If $G$ has odd order and $d\geq3$, then
\begin{align}
 \mathcal Q_d(\delta+tf)
  ={}&\delta^m+P_d\delta^{m-4}Q(f)t^4\nonumber\\
    &+\delta^{m-5}\bigl(F_dD(f)+H_dD_3(f)\bigr)t^5
       +R_d(\delta,t,f).\label{gsr:cc:16:cub:expansion}
\end{align}
Writing $\tau=\|f\|_{U^d}$, the remainder satisfies
\begin{equation}
 |R_d(\delta,t,f)|\leq
 \sum_{k=6}^{m}\binom{m}{k}|\delta|^{m-k}|t|^k\tau^k.
 \label{gsr:cc:16:cub:remainder}
\end{equation}
For $d=2$ the exact formula is
$\mathcal Q_2(\delta+tf)=\delta^4+t^4Q(f)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{Credit.} An independent third derivation of source~09's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:09:thm:main} (on every finite abelian group; this $F_d$, $H_d$ are source~09's $Q_d$, $S_d$, this $P_d$ is source~03's $R_d$), also proved by source~18 (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:18:cube:thm-fifth}); the quartic part is source~03's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:03:cube:main} and source~08's. The restriction of the quintic formula to odd order is not needed: the intake found the same formula on $\Z/2$, $\Z/4$, $\Z/6$, $\Z/8$ and $(\Z/2)^2$, as source~09's all-groups theorem implies. The $\Z/3\Z$ example ($200$ and $352$) is also in source~18's Section~\ref{gsr:fz:18:sec:d8}. \emph{Notation:} $D$ here is source~04's $B_5$ and source~09's $\Mfive$; $D_3$ is source~09's $\Tthree$.
\end{writenote}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{c|rrrr}
$d$&$P_d$&$T_d$&$F_d$&$H_d$\\\hline
2&1&0&0&0\\
3&12&2&8&0\\
4&100&40&160&16\\
5&720&520&2080&480\\
6&4816&5600&22400&8960
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

For example, in dimension four and odd order,
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal Q_4(\delta+tf)
 =\delta^{16}+100\delta^{12}Q(f)t^4
  +\delta^{11}\bigl(160D(f)+16D_3(f)\bigr)t^5+R_4.
 \label{gsr:cc:16:cub:four}
\end{equation}
The term $16D_3(f)$ cannot generally be dropped: it is present on groups
with three-torsion.  On groups of order coprime to six, only $Q$ and $D$
occur through degree five.

\begin{example}[A nonzero three-torsion correction]
On $\Z/3\Z$, let $f=(2,-1,-1)$. Its two nontrivial normalized
Fourier coefficients are both one, so $Q(f)=D(f)=D_3(f)=2$.
Formula~\eqref{gsr:cc:16:cub:four} begins
\[
 \mathcal Q_4(\delta+tf)
  =\delta^{16}+200\delta^{12}t^4+352\delta^{11}t^5+O(t^6).
\]
Omitting the order-three term would instead give $320$ as the quintic
coefficient. This is an exact algebraic distinction, not a limiting effect.
\end{example}

\subsection{Vertex systems and the quartic term}

For a vertex subset $S=\{v_1,\ldots,v_k\}\subseteq\{0,1\}^d$, put
\[
 M_f(S)=\mathbb E_{x,h}\prod_{i=1}^k f(x+v_i\cdot h).
\]
Fourier orthogonality gives
\begin{equation}
 M_f(S)=
 \sum_{\substack{\xi_1+\cdots+\xi_k=0\\
        \sum_i v_{i,j}\xi_i=0\ (1\leq j\leq d)}}
       \prod_{i=1}^k a_{\xi_i}.
 \label{gsr:cc:16:cub:fourier}
\end{equation}
The constraints are the kernel equations of the integer matrix with
columns $(1,v_i)$.  Consequently the Taylor coefficient of degree $k$ is
$\delta^{m-k}\sum_{|S|=k}M_f(S)$.

\begin{lemma}
\label{gsr:cc:16:cub:small}
Any one, two, or three distinct Boolean vertices have a maximal affine
minor equal to $1$ or $-1$.  Thus $M_f(S)=0$ for $1\leq |S|\leq3$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Reflect coordinates to put one vertex at zero.  Coordinate reflection
preserves the average: reflect coordinate $j$ by replacing $x$ with
$x+h_j$ and $h_j$ with $-h_j$.  For three vertices, the two remaining
nonzero distinct binary columns have at least two distinct nonzero row
patterns from $10,01,11$.  Any two such patterns have determinant $\pm1$.
The cases of one or two vertices are immediate.  The corresponding linear
evaluation map onto $G^{|S|}$ is therefore surjective, so its outputs are
independent uniform variables.  Their product average is
$(\mathbb E f)^{|S|}=0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Four-vertex classification]
\label{gsr:cc:16:cub:fourclass}
For four distinct Boolean vertices, exactly one of the following applies:
\begin{enumerate}
\item They form a real parallelogram, and $M_f(S)=Q(f)$.
\item Their affine matrix has full rank and an affine minor $\pm1$,
      and $M_f(S)=0$.
\item They form an affine $\mathbb F_2$ plane which is not a real
      parallelogram, and $M_f(S)=Q_2(f)$.
\end{enumerate}
The numbers of configurations in the first and third cases are $P_d$ and
$T_d$, respectively.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Reflect one vertex to zero, leaving three binary columns.  Their rational
rank is two or three.  In rank two, project injectively onto two suitable
coordinates.  The four images are all of the two-cube; hence the original
vertices form a parallelogram with primitive affine relation
$(1,1,-1,-1)$.  Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:16:cub:small} supplies a unimodular subsystem, so
the frequency kernel is exactly $(\chi,\chi,-\chi,-\chi)$, in a suitable
ordering.  Formula~\eqref{gsr:cc:16:cub:fourier} gives $Q(f)$.

In rank three, each three-by-three binary determinant is $0,\pm1$, or
$\pm2$.  A minor $\pm1$ makes the evaluation map surjective and gives
zero.  The sole determinant-two binary pattern, up to row and column
permutations, has rows $110,101,011$.  Adding any other nonzero binary row
produces a determinant-one minor with two of these rows.  Therefore, if no
minor $\pm1$ exists, every coordinate row is $000,110,101$, or $011$, and
all three nonzero types occur.  The kernel equations force all four
frequencies to be the same $\chi$ with $2\chi=0$.  Since $a_\chi$ is real
on such characters, their contribution is $Q_2(f)$.

To count parallelograms, choose their common midpoint.  If $r$ coordinates
vary between the endpoints of an opposite pair, there are $2^{d-r}$
choices for the fixed coordinates and $2^{r-1}$ distinct opposite pairs
about that midpoint.  Thus their number is
\[
 \sum_{r=2}^d\binom dr2^{d-r}\binom{2^{r-1}}2
   =\frac{6^d-2\cdot4^d+2^d}{8}=P_d.
\]
There are
$2^d(2^d-1)(2^d-2)/24$ affine two-planes in $\mathbb F_2^d$.
Subtracting $P_d$ gives $T_d$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Five-vertex circuits and the three-torsion term}

\begin{lemma}[Five-vertex classification in odd order]
\label{gsr:cc:16:cub:fiveclass}
Suppose that $G$ has odd order.  For a five-element vertex subset $S$, the
only possibly nonzero contributions are the following:
\begin{enumerate}
\item A rational affine circuit with relation
      $2v_0+v_4=v_1+v_2+v_3$, contributing $D(f)$.
      There are $F_d$ such subsets.
\item An affinely independent configuration which is a signed
      combinatorial embedding of
      $\{0000,1110,1101,1011,0111\}$, contributing $D_3(f)$.
      There are $H_d$ such subsets.
\end{enumerate}
Every other five-element subset has $M_f(S)=0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A rational affine $r$-plane contains at most $2^r$ Boolean vertices:
projection onto $r$ suitable coordinates is injective on that plane.
Hence the affine dimension of $S$ is three or four.

First suppose it is three, and project injectively onto three coordinates.
Every five vertices of a three-cube contain a unimodular four-vertex
subsystem.  Indeed, their affine rank modulo two is three because an
affine $\mathbb F_2$ plane has only four points.  Some affine minor is
therefore odd; all such minors have absolute value at most two, so this
minor is $\pm1$.  The frequency kernel is the free rank-one kernel of the
primitive rational relation, with no additional torsion.  Extra ambient
coordinate rows impose no further constraints, because the same integer
relation annihilates each of them.

If four vertices form a parallelogram, the unique relation has a zero
coefficient at the remaining vertex.  Its frequency is consequently zero,
and $a_0=0$ makes the contribution vanish.  Otherwise the relation has full
support.  The three-cube has precisely eight five-point circuits, namely a
vertex, its three neighbors, and its antipode.  To see exhaustion, classify
the omitted triple by its Hamming distances: the only types are
$(1,1,2)$, $(1,2,3)$, and $(2,2,2)$.  For the first two types take the
representatives $\{000,100,010\}$ and $\{000,100,111\}$; their complements
contain the parallelograms $\{001,011,101,111\}$ and
$\{001,010,101,110\}$, respectively.  The third type leaves one of the
stated circuits.  Its primitive relation is
$2v_0+v_4=v_1+v_2+v_3$.  Thus the frequency kernel is
$(2\chi,-\chi,-\chi,-\chi,\chi)$, and
\eqref{gsr:cc:16:cub:fourier} gives $D(f)$.

For the count, $v_0$ is the unique vertex with coefficient two and $v_4$ is
also determined; $v_1,v_2,v_3$ have $3!$ possible orderings.  In any
coordinate the relation allows eight binary row patterns: two constants
and three complementary pairs of nonconstant patterns.  All three
nonconstant types must occur to give affine dimension three.  By
inclusion--exclusion, the number of subsets is
\[
 \frac{2^d}{6}\bigl(4^d-3\cdot3^d+3\cdot2^d-1\bigr)=F_d.
\]

Now suppose the affine dimension is four.  Some five-by-five affine minor
is nonzero and has absolute value at most three.  In fact, replacing the
four binary coordinate rows by sign rows multiplies the determinant by
$2^4$, while Hadamard's inequality bounds the resulting determinant by
$5^{5/2}$; hence the original integer determinant has absolute value at
most $\lfloor5^{5/2}/16\rfloor=3$.

A minor of absolute value one or two gives a surjective evaluation map on
an odd-order group and therefore contributes zero.  Otherwise every
nonzero affine minor has absolute value three.  Modulo three, a row basis
can be extended from the nonzero constant row; rank five would therefore
give an affine minor nonzero modulo three.  The augmented rank modulo
three is exactly four: any four of these affinely independent
vertices remain independent modulo three, since their nonzero affine
minors have absolute value at most two.  Its one-dimensional mod-three
kernel has full support.  Its five nonzero coefficients are $\pm1$, and
their sum is zero modulo three.  Four coefficients therefore have one
sign and the remaining coefficient has the other sign.

Let $v_0$ be the uniquely distinguished vertex.  Reflect it to zero.
Every coordinate row of the other four vertices has either zero or three
ones.  All four weight-three patterns must occur, or the rational affine
rank would be smaller than four.  This is precisely the configuration in
the statement.  Its frequency equations force $\xi_i=\chi$ for
$1\leq i\leq4$, $\xi_0=-\chi$, and $3\chi=0$.  Thus its contribution is
$D_3(f)$.  In particular, only three-torsion occurs, not characters of
order nine: the equations, or the adjugate of a determinant-three
subsystem, give $3\chi=0$.

There are now ten permitted coordinate patterns: two constants and four
complementary pairs of nonconstant patterns.  All four nonconstant types
must occur.  The distinguished vertex is unique and the other four have
$4!$ possible orderings.  Their number is therefore
\[
 \frac{2^d}{24}
  \bigl(5^d-4\cdot4^d+6\cdot3^d-4\cdot2^d+1\bigr)=H_d.
\]
This exhausts both possible rational affine dimensions.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:16:cub:main}]
Expand the product defining $\mathcal Q_d(\delta+tf)$ by its vertex
subsets.  Lemmas~\ref{gsr:cc:16:cub:small}--\ref{gsr:cc:16:cub:fiveclass} determine every
coefficient through degree five.  For a subset $S$ of cardinality $k$,
apply Gowers--Cauchy--Schwarz with $f$ on $S$ and the constant function one
on its complement.  This gives $|M_f(S)|\leq\tau^k$.  Summing the remaining
terms gives~\eqref{gsr:cc:16:cub:remainder}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The embedding count]
\label{gsr:cc:16:cub:stirling}
If $\left\{\begin{smallmatrix}n\\r\end{smallmatrix}\right\}$ denotes a
Stirling number of the second kind, the number of signed combinatorial
$r$-subcubes in a $d$-cube is
\[
 E_{d,r}=2^{d-r}
        \left\{\begin{matrix}d+1\\r+1\end{matrix}\right\}.
\]
Partition the varying coordinates into $r$ nonempty blocks, copy or
complement one latent variable on each block, and fix the remaining
coordinates.  The extra element in the Stirling number marks the block
of fixed coordinates.  The formulas above become
$P_d=E_{d,2}$, $T_d=2E_{d,3}$, $F_d=8E_{d,3}$, and $H_d=16E_{d,4}$.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Consequences, sharp moment bounds, and limits}

\begin{corollary}[A refined version of the cube-counting upper bound]
\label{gsr:cc:16:cub:bound}
Let $d\geq3$, let $G$ have odd order, let $A\subseteq G$ have density
$\delta$, and put $f=1_A-\delta$.  If $\|f\|_{U^d}^{m}\leq\alpha$, then
\begin{align*}
 \mathcal Q_d(1_A)\leq{}&
 \delta^m+P_d\delta^{m-4}Q(f)
 +\delta^{m-5}\bigl(F_dD(f)+H_dD_3(f)\bigr)\\
 &+\sum_{k=6}^m\binom{m}{k}\delta^{m-k}\alpha^{k/m}.
\end{align*}
\end{corollary}

If only $\alpha$ is available, monotonicity gives $Q(f)\leq\alpha^{4/m}$.
The following estimates bound the fifth-order terms as well.  In
particular, at fixed $d$ and positive $\delta$, the leading error is of
order $\alpha^{4/m}$ instead of the order $\alpha^{1/m}$ appearing in
the direct Minkowski bound.  The exact expression retains more useful
information whenever $Q,D$, or $D_3$ can be estimated separately.

\begin{proposition}[Sharp bounds for the quintic moment]
\label{gsr:cc:16:cub:dbounds}
For real mean-zero functions on odd-order groups,
\[
 |D(f)|\leq 2^{-1/4}Q(f)^{5/4},\qquad
 |D_3(f)|\leq 2^{-1/4}Q(f)^{5/4}.
\]
If the group has no three-torsion, then
\[
 |D(f)|\leq 2^{-1/2}Q(f)^{5/4}.
\]
The constants are sharp in their stated classes.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Pair nonzero frequencies into $\{\chi,-\chi\}$.  Put
$b_i=|a_\chi|$ for one representative of each pair.  Doubling permutes
these pairs, say by $\sigma$, because the group has odd order.  Then
\[
 |D(f)|\leq2\sum_i b_i^4b_{\sigma(i)},\qquad
 Q(f)=2\sum_i b_i^4.
\]
Bounding each $b_{\sigma(i)}$ by $(\sum_jb_j^4)^{1/4}$ proves the first
inequality.  The same argument restricted to three-torsion proves the
bound for $D_3$.  Equal positive Fourier coefficients on an order-three
character pair attain both constants.

If three-torsion is absent, $\sigma$ has no fixed points.  Normalize
$\sum_i b_i^4=1$ and let $u=\max_i b_i$.  If $u^4\leq1/2$, the sum is
at most $u\leq2^{-1/4}$.  Otherwise put $v=(1-u^4)^{1/4}$.  The largest
coordinate is sent to another coordinate, at most $v$, while all other
coordinates are sent to values at most $u$.  Hence
\[
 \sum_i b_i^4b_{\sigma(i)}\leq u^4v+v^4u\leq2^{-1/4}.
\]
For the last inequality, the function
$(r^4+r)/(r^4+1)^{5/4}$ has its maximum $2^{-1/4}$ at $r=1$:
the sign of its derivative is the sign of
\[
 (1-r)(r^6+r^5+r^4+5r^3+r^2+r+1).
\]
Restoring the normalization proves the second constant.  Equal positive
Fourier coefficients on the four nontrivial characters of an order-five
quotient attain it.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{Credit.} The bound with $2^{-1/4}$ is source~04's bound on $B_5$ (Section~\ref{gsr:cc:04:sec:d6}); the constant $2^{-1/2}$ without three-torsion, sharp, is new in this report (the intake's adversarial search found no exceedance).
\end{writenote}

\begin{remark}[Higher torsion and the scope of the improvement]
\label{gsr:cc:16:cub:scope}
The low-order proof suggests organizing subsequent coefficients by the
integer kernels and Smith normal forms of affine Boolean vertex
matrices.  A full-rank $k$-vertex subsystem has a nonzero affine minor of
absolute value at most $\lfloor k^{k/2}/2^{k-1}\rfloor$.  Primes larger
than this cannot produce a new torsion kernel for that subsystem.
For $k=4,5$ this bound gives exactly the possible primes two and three.

An explicit family in dimension $r\geq3$ consists of the $r+1$ vertices
$0,\boldsymbol1-e_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol1-e_r$.  Its affine determinant is
$r-1$ and its correlation is
\[
 \sum_{(r-1)\chi=0}a_{-\chi}a_\chi^r.
\]
The coordinate equations force all nonzero-vertex frequencies to equal
$\chi$ and then force $(r-1)\chi=0$.  This family need not exhaust the
configurations or locate the first occurrence of a given prime.

The results above are explicit local improvements to the cube-counting
step.  They do not, by themselves, improve a global quantitative
Szemer\'edi bound.  Their proofs are independent of the accompanying
finite calculations; the exact computations serve only as reproducible
checks of classification counts, signs, and normalization.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Optimality of the exponent for sets}
\label{gsr:cc:16:cub:sets}

The fourth-order term also gives an obstruction for genuine subsets of
cyclic groups, rather than only for weighted functions.

\begin{proposition}[Sharp order of the small-uniformity error]
\label{gsr:cc:16:cub:sharpness}
Fix $d\geq2$ and put $m=2^d$.  There are odd cyclic groups $G_n$ and
subsets $A_n\subseteq G_n$ of density exactly $\delta=1/3$ such that,
writing $\alpha_n=\|1_{A_n}-\delta\|_{U^d}^m$, one has
\[
 \alpha_n\longrightarrow0,
 \qquad
 \frac{\mathcal Q_d(1_{A_n})-\delta^m}{\alpha_n^{4/m}}
       \longrightarrow c_d>0.
\]
Consequently a bound with a uniform error $o(\alpha^{4/m})$ is impossible,
even at this fixed density and on odd cyclic groups.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
On $G_0=\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z$, take $f_0=(2,-1,-1)$ and
$w_t=1/3+tf_0$, where $0<t<1/3$.  This is a function into $[0,1]$ of mean
$1/3$.  The two nontrivial Fourier coefficients of $f_0$ are one, so
$Q(f_0)=2$.
Let $B_d=\|f_0\|_{U^d}^m>0$.  Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:16:cub:main} gives
\begin{align}
 \mathcal Q_d(w_t)&=\delta^m+
        2P_d\delta^{m-4}t^4+O_d(t^5),\label{gsr:cc:16:cub:weighted-sharp}\\
 \mathcal Q_d(w_t-\delta)&=B_dt^m.\nonumber
\end{align}
For $d=2$ the first identity is exact without the error term.

We explain carefully how to realize these two moments by sets.
Let $p\ne3$ be an odd prime and independently select each
$(x,y)\in G_0\times\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z$ with probability $w_t(x)$.
For a random cube, two distinct vertices have the same second coordinate
with probability $1/p$, because their difference is a nonzero binary
linear form with a coefficient $1$ or $-1$.  Away from these collisions,
the selected-point variables at its vertices are independent.  Thus, for
$j=1,2$, the expected value of
\[
 T_1=\mathcal Q_d(1_A),\qquad T_2=\mathcal Q_d(1_A-\delta)
\]
differs from the corresponding weighted moment in
\eqref{gsr:cc:16:cub:weighted-sharp} by at most $2\binom m2/p$.

Likewise, products associated with two cubes are independent unless they
share a selected-point variable.  A union bound over their $m^2$ pairs of
vertices gives
\[
 \operatorname{Var}(T_j)\leq\frac{2m^2}{p}.
\]
The density has expectation $\delta$ and variance at most $1/(12p)$.
Consequently, for any $\varepsilon>0$ and sufficiently large $p$, a
realization exists whose density differs from $\delta$ by at most
$\varepsilon$ and whose two moments differ from their weighted targets
by at most $2\varepsilon$.  This follows directly from Chebyshev's
inequality and a union bound.

Change at most an $\varepsilon$ fraction of the points to make the
cardinality exactly $p$, hence the density exactly $1/3$.  A telescoping
product and uniformity of each vertex marginal show that this changes
each $T_j$ by at most $m\varepsilon$.  Choose
$\varepsilon=t^{m+1}$ and then choose $p=p(t)$ sufficiently large.
The resulting set, still denoted by $A_t$, satisfies
\begin{align*}
 \mathcal Q_d(1_{A_t})-\delta^m
     &=2P_d\delta^{m-4}t^4+O_d(t^5),\\
 \|1_{A_t}-\delta\|_{U^d}^{m}
     &=B_dt^m+O_d(t^{m+1}).
\end{align*}
Taking any sequence $t\downarrow0$ and using
$G_0\times\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z\cong\mathbb Z/(3p)\mathbb Z$ proves the
claim, with
\[
 c_d=2P_d\delta^{m-4}B_d^{-4/m}>0.
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{Credit.} Sharpness of the exponent $4/2^d$ for sets is source~03's Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:03:cube:setsharpness}, source~04's Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:04:cub:rounding}, source~09's Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:09:prop:sharp4} with Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:09:cor:transfer}, and source~18's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:18:cube:thm-indicator-sharpness}; new here is only the packaging for sets of exact density $1/3$ in odd cyclic groups. At $d=2$ the ratio is identically one, so that case is trivial.
\end{writenote}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Exact fourth and fifth order cube counts\srctag{18}}]{Exact fourth and fifth order cube counts}\label{gsr:cc:18:sec:d3}
\srcnote{18}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:cc:18:cube:sec-expansion}

Gowers' Lemma~3.10 applies the triangle inequality to the cube norm.
The resulting estimate is convenient, but it treats the constant and
balanced parts as if the first mixed term could already be nonzero.
Centering actually eliminates all terms of degrees one, two, and three.
We now compute the next two degrees exactly, in every dimension and on
every finite abelian group.  The answer distinguishes ordinary affine
circuits from the extra relations created by two- and three-torsion.

Throughout this section, $G$ is a finite abelian group, averages are
normalized, and the dual group $\widehat G$ is written additively.  Our
Fourier convention is
\[
 \widehat f(\gamma)
   =\mathbb E_{x\in G}f(x)\overline{\gamma(x)},
 \qquad
 \widehat G[p]=\{\gamma\in\widehat G:p\gamma=0\}.
\]
For a real function $g$, define
\[
 \mathcal C_d(g)
   =\mathbb E_{x,h_1,\ldots,h_d\in G}
       \prod_{v\in\{0,1\}^d}g(x+v\cdot h)
   =\|g\|_{U^d}^{2^d}.
\]
Thus $|G|^{d+1}\mathcal C_d(1_A)$ counts parameterized cubes in $A$,
including cubes with repeated vertices.  Real-valuedness is essential
to the simple identical-function expansion used below; complex cube
norms carry the usual alternating conjugations.

\subsection{The coefficient theorem}

For $d\geq 3$, put $m=2^d$ and define
\begin{align}
 R_d&=\frac{6^d-2\cdot4^d+2^d}{8},
 &B_d&=\frac{2^d(2^d-1)(2^d-2)}{24},\label{gsr:cc:18:cube:eq-RB}\\
 Q_d&=\frac{8^d-3\cdot6^d+3\cdot4^d-2^d}{6},
 &S_d&=\frac{10^d-4\cdot8^d+6\cdot6^d-4\cdot4^d+2^d}{24}.
 \label{gsr:cc:18:cube:eq-QS}
\end{align}
For a real mean-zero function $f:G\to\mathbb R$, set
\begin{align}
 V_4(f)&=\sum_{\gamma\in\widehat G}|\widehat f(\gamma)|^4
            =\|f\|_{U^2}^4,\label{gsr:cc:18:cube:eq-V4}\\
 E_2(f)&=\sum_{\gamma\in\widehat G[2]}\widehat f(\gamma)^4,
 \label{gsr:cc:18:cube:eq-E2}\\
 T_5(f)&=\sum_{\gamma\in\widehat G}
       \widehat f(2\gamma)\widehat f(\gamma)
       \widehat f(-\gamma)^3,\label{gsr:cc:18:cube:eq-T5}\\
 E_3(f)&=\sum_{\gamma\in\widehat G[3]}
       \widehat f(-\gamma)\widehat f(\gamma)^4.
 \label{gsr:cc:18:cube:eq-E3}
\end{align}
These quantities are real: replacing $\gamma$ by $-\gamma$ conjugates
each summand.  Moreover, $V_4(f)$ and $E_2(f)$ are nonnegative.  In the
latter sum, every Fourier coefficient is real because $2\gamma=0$.
The zero character contributes zero to all four expressions.

\begin{theorem}[Exact expansion through degree five]
\label{gsr:cc:18:cube:thm-fifth}
Let $G$ be any finite abelian group, $d\geq3$, $m=2^d$, and let
$f:G\to\mathbb R$ have mean zero.  For all real $\delta,t$,
\begin{align}
 \mathcal C_d(\delta+tf)
   ={}&\delta^m
    +\delta^{m-4}t^4
        \bigl(R_dV_4(f)+(B_d-R_d)E_2(f)\bigr)\notag\\
    &+\delta^{m-5}t^5
        \bigl(Q_dT_5(f)+S_dE_3(f)\bigr)
    +\mathcal R_d(\delta,t;f),\label{gsr:cc:18:cube:eq-fifth-expansion}
\end{align}
where, writing $\eta=\|f\|_{U^d}$,
\begin{equation}
 |\mathcal R_d(\delta,t;f)|
 \leq\sum_{j=6}^{m}\binom mj
          |\delta|^{m-j}|t|^j\eta^j.
 \label{gsr:cc:18:cube:eq-fifth-remainder}
\end{equation}
In particular, the coefficients of $t,t^2,t^3$ vanish identically.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{Credit.} The coefficients are those of source~09's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:09:thm:main} on every finite abelian group ($Q_d=2^d\,S(d+1,4)$, $S_d=2^d\,S(d+1,5)$ with Stirling numbers, as source~09 writes them), also derived independently by source~16 (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:16:cub:main}, odd order for the quintic part); the quartic part is source~03's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:03:cube:main} and source~08's. So this is the fourth independent derivation in the report; source~18 could see none of the other three (sources~09 and~16 were not in the repository at its pin). New in method: the Smith-form and Hadamard-minor argument showing that only the primes $2$ and~$3$ enter through order five (Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:18:cube:cor-small-smith}). \emph{Notation:} $R_d$ is source~03's $R_d$ (source~04's, 09's and~16's $P_d$), $B_d-R_d$ is $T_d$; this $Q_d$ is a five-circuit count (= source~09's $Q_d$ = source~16's $F_d$), not a cube count.
\end{writenote}

\begin{remark}[Small torsion and low dimensions]
If $G$ has no nonzero element killed by $2$, then $E_2(f)=0$.
If $G$ has no nonzero element killed by $3$, then $E_3(f)=0$.
The fifth order identity therefore needs no exclusion of two-torsion.
For $d=2$ the whole expansion reduces to the familiar exact identity
\[
 \mathcal C_2(\delta+tf)=\delta^4+t^4\|f\|_{U^2}^4.
\]
\end{remark}

The first coefficient values are
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrr}
 d&R_d&B_d&Q_d&S_d\\\hline
 3&12&14&8&0\\
 4&100&140&160&16\\
 5&720&1240&2080&480
\end{array}
\]
The twelve four-point circuits and eight five-point circuits in the
ordinary three-dimensional cube are classical; they are listed, for
example, by Beerenwinkel, Pachter, and Sturmfels~\cite{bps}.
Here the aim is an explicit all-dimensional cube-moment formula,
including the contributions of small torsion and a norm-controlled
remainder.  The circuit interpretation itself is not a novelty claim.

\subsection{Fourier constraints and integer minors}

For a set $W=\{v_1,\ldots,v_s\}\subseteq\{0,1\}^d$, let
\[
 M_W=\begin{pmatrix}1&\cdots&1\\v_1&\cdots&v_s\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Fourier inversion and character orthogonality give
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb E_{x,h}\prod_{v\in W}f(x+v\cdot h)
 =\sum_{\substack{\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_s\in\widehat G\\
                  M_W\gamma=0}}
       \prod_{i=1}^s\widehat f(\gamma_i).
 \label{gsr:cc:18:cube:eq-fourier-kernel}
\end{equation}
The matrix acts by integer multiplication in the abelian group
$\widehat G$.  Rational rank alone does not determine this kernel:
the integer invariant factors must also be controlled.

\begin{lemma}[Small minors of Boolean affine matrices]
\label{gsr:cc:18:cube:lem-small-minors}
For a Boolean affine matrix $M_W$, any $k\times k$ minor containing
the row of ones has absolute value at most $1,1,1,2,3$ for
$k=1,2,3,4,5$, respectively.  Every three distinct columns have a
$3\times3$ minor equal to $\pm1$.  Every five distinct columns have
a $4\times4$ minor equal to $\pm1$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For a minor containing the row of ones, reflect each selected
coordinate in which the first selected vertex equals one.  At the
matrix level this replaces a coordinate row by the row of ones minus
that row.  The first selected vertex now has all selected coordinates
zero.  Subtracting its column from the other columns reduces the
determinant, up to sign, to that of a binary $(k-1)\times(k-1)$ matrix.

If $D$ is a binary $r\times r$ matrix, the matrix
\[
 H=\begin{pmatrix}1&\boldsymbol1^{\mathsf T}\\
                 \boldsymbol1&J-2D\end{pmatrix}
\]
has entries in $\{-1,1\}$ and determinant $(-2)^r\det D$.
Hadamard's inequality gives
\[
 |\det D|\leq\frac{(r+1)^{(r+1)/2}}{2^r}.
\]
For $r=1,2,3,4$, taking integer parts gives $1,1,2,3$.

Three distinct points of $\mathbb F_2^d$ have affine rank three,
because an affine line contains only two points.  Extend the nonzero
row of ones to a row basis over $\mathbb F_2$ and select three
independent columns.  The resulting minor is odd and has absolute
value at most one, so it is $\pm1$.

Similarly, five distinct points have affine rank at least four over
$\mathbb F_2$, because an affine plane contains only four points.
Extending the row of ones to four independent rows and selecting four
independent columns produces an odd minor of absolute value at most
two.  It too must equal $\pm1$.
\end{proof}

We use the elementary Smith normal form principle that unimodular
integer row and column operations induce automorphisms over every
abelian group.  If a full-column-rank integer matrix has invariant
factors $1,\ldots,1,p$, its kernel over an abelian group $H$ is a copy
of $H[p]$.  For prime $p$, its coordinates are the multiples of a
vector spanning the one-dimensional kernel modulo $p$.

\begin{corollary}[Only two small primes can occur]
\label{gsr:cc:18:cube:cor-small-smith}
For four distinct cube vertices, the rational rank is three or four.
In rank three the nonzero Smith invariants are $1,1,1$; in rank four
they are $1,1,1,D$ with $D\in\{1,2\}$.

For five distinct cube vertices, the rational rank is four or five.
In rank four the nonzero invariants are $1,1,1,1$; in rank five they
are $1,1,1,1,D$ with $D\in\{1,2,3\}$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The unit minors in Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:18:cube:lem-small-minors} make the third
determinantal divisor equal to one for a four-point set and the fourth
determinantal divisor equal to one for a five-point set.  In full
column rank, extend the row of ones to a rational row basis.  A
nonzero maximal minor containing that row has absolute value at most
two or three.  The final determinantal divisor divides this minor.
The stated lists follow.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The four-point coefficient}

\begin{lemma}[Four-point classification]
\label{gsr:cc:18:cube:lem-four-classification}
For four distinct Boolean cube vertices, exactly the following
possibilities can contribute to~\eqref{gsr:cc:18:cube:eq-fourier-kernel}:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item An ordinary rectangle, with primitive relation
       $u+v=w+z$, contributes $V_4(f)$.
 \item Four rationally independent vertices whose XOR is zero
       contribute $E_2(f)$.
\end{enumerate}
All other four-point sets have zero correlation.
There are $R_d$ sets of the first type and $B_d-R_d$ of the second.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Suppose first that the rational rank is three.  Its unique affine
dependence has nonzero coefficients, since three distinct vertices
are independent.  The positive and negative coefficients split as
two and two: a cube vertex cannot be a strict convex combination of
other cube vertices.  Write
\[
 a u+b v=c w+e z,\qquad a+b=c+e,
\]
with all coefficients positive.  Reflect coordinates so that $u=0$.
In every nonconstant coordinate, $v=1$ and a nonempty proper subset
of $\{c,e\}$ sums to $b$.  Affine dimension two requires both
possible nonconstant patterns.  Therefore $b=c=e$ and then $a=b$.
The primitive dependence is $u+v=w+z$.  The unit Smith invariants
show that the Fourier kernel consists exactly of the tuples
$(\gamma,\gamma,-\gamma,-\gamma)$, giving $V_4(f)$.

In rational rank four, the kernel is trivial unless the final Smith
invariant is two.  Modulo two, the unique dependence must involve all
four columns because every three are independent.  It is therefore
the XOR relation.  The Fourier kernel is exactly
\[
 \{(\gamma,\gamma,\gamma,\gamma):2\gamma=0\},
\]
giving $E_2(f)$.  A trivial Fourier kernel gives a product containing
$\widehat f(0)=0$.

To count rectangles, there are six binary coordinate patterns
satisfying $u+v=w+z$.  The two degenerate matchings each give $4^d$
ordered tuples, and their intersection gives $2^d$.  Every
nondegenerate rectangle has eight labelings of this form: choose
which opposite pair is on the left and order the two pairs.  This
gives $R_d$ in~\eqref{gsr:cc:18:cube:eq-RB}.

An unordered four-set has XOR zero precisely when it is an affine
plane in $\mathbb F_2^d$.  Choose its origin, then an ordered basis,
and divide by the four origins and six ordered bases of one plane.
The count is
\[
 \frac{2^d(2^d-1)(2^d-2)}{4\cdot6}=B_d.
\]
Of these, $R_d$ are ordinary rectangles, leaving $B_d-R_d$ of the
second type.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The five-point coefficient}

\begin{lemma}[Ordinary five-point circuits]
\label{gsr:cc:18:cube:lem-five-circuits}
Every five-point circuit of the real affine Boolean cube has,
after relabeling and common sign, the primitive relation
\begin{equation}
 2u+v=x+y+z.
 \label{gsr:cc:18:cube:eq-five-relation}
\end{equation}
There are exactly $Q_d$ such circuits, and each contributes $T_5(f)$
over every finite abelian group.  Every rational rank-four
five-point set that is not a circuit contributes zero.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
In rational rank four, Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:18:cube:cor-small-smith} gives a
unit rank-four minor.  The character kernel over any $\widehat G$
is therefore generated by the primitive integer dependence vector,
without additional torsion parameters.  If this vector has a zero
coefficient, its support consists of four points forming a
rectangle.  The remaining Fourier coordinate is zero, so the
correlation vanishes.

Otherwise, all five coefficients are nonzero.  Their signs split
as two and three, again because every cube vertex is extreme.
Write the positive dependence as
\[
 a u+b v=c x+e y+q z,
 \qquad a+b=c+e+q,
\]
where all five coefficients are positive.  Reflect coordinates so
that $u=0$.  Every nonconstant coordinate has $v=1$ and corresponds
to a nonempty proper subset of $\{c,e,q\}$ whose sum is $b$.
Affine dimension three requires at least three distinct such
patterns.

For three positive numbers, three distinct proper nonempty subsets
can have a common sum only if all three numbers are equal.  Indeed,
equal-sum subsets form an antichain.  A three-element antichain of
proper nonempty subsets of a three-element set is either the three
singletons or the three pairs: a singleton and a pair omitting it
leave no third subset incomparable with both.  Equality of the
three singleton sums or three pair sums forces $c=e=q$.  Thus
$b=c$ or $b=2c$, and $a=2c$ or $a=c$, respectively.  Interchanging
$u,v$ if necessary proves~\eqref{gsr:cc:18:cube:eq-five-relation}.

Its Fourier kernel is
\[
 (\gamma_u,\gamma_v,\gamma_x,\gamma_y,\gamma_z)
     =(2\gamma,\gamma,-\gamma,-\gamma,-\gamma),
\]
which gives~\eqref{gsr:cc:18:cube:eq-T5}.

For the count, the coefficient-two vertex and the same-sign
coefficient-one vertex are uniquely distinguished; the other three
vertices have $3!$ orderings.  Each coordinate row satisfying
\eqref{gsr:cc:18:cube:eq-five-relation} is one of eight patterns: two
constants and three nonconstant types together with their
complements.  After reflecting to $u=0$, the three types are
\[
 (0,1,1,0,0),\quad (0,1,0,1,0),\quad (0,1,0,0,1).
\]
Together with the row of ones, they are independent.  Rational rank
four holds exactly when all three types occur.  Inclusion-exclusion
therefore gives
\[
 Q_d=\frac{8^d-3\cdot6^d+3\cdot4^d-2^d}{3!}.
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The additional three-torsion circuits]
\label{gsr:cc:18:cube:lem-three-torsion}
Among rationally independent five-point subsets, exactly $S_d$
can give nonzero centered correlation.  Each has a unique
dependence modulo three with coefficient pattern
$(-1,1,1,1,1)$, up to common sign and relabeling, and contributes
$E_3(f)$.  The subsets with a nontrivial invariant factor two
contribute zero.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $D$ be the last Smith invariant in
Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:18:cube:cor-small-smith}.  If $D=1$, the Fourier kernel
is trivial and the correlation is zero.

If $D=2$, the unique dependence modulo two has even support because
the first row consists of ones.  Its support has size at least four
and at most five, so it has size four.  The Smith kernel consists
of two-torsion multiples of this vector.  One Fourier coordinate
is consequently zero, and mean zero again kills the correlation.

Suppose $D=3$.  Any four columns are rationally independent, and a
nonzero four-by-four minor containing the row of ones has absolute
value one or two.  They are therefore independent modulo three.
The unique dependence modulo three involves all five columns, with
coefficients in $\{1,-1\}$.  Their sum is zero modulo three.  After
a common sign, exactly one is negative and the other four are
positive.  The Fourier kernel is parameterized by
\[
 (-\gamma,\gamma,\gamma,\gamma,\gamma),
 \qquad 3\gamma=0,
\]
and its correlation is $E_3(f)$.

For counting, label the distinguished negative vertex $u$ and the
others $v_1,\ldots,v_4$.  Coordinatewise the relation is
\[
 -u+v_1+v_2+v_3+v_4=0\pmod3.
\]
There are ten binary row patterns: two constants and four
nonconstant types together with their complements.  After
reflection to $u=0$, the nonconstant rows are
$(0,\boldsymbol1-e_j)$ for $1\leq j\leq4$.  The four vectors
$\boldsymbol1-e_j$ are independent over the rationals because
$\det(J-I)=-3$.  Thus rational rank five holds exactly when all
four nonconstant types occur.  Inclusion-exclusion gives
\[
 10^d-4\cdot8^d+6\cdot6^d-4\cdot4^d+2^d
\]
ordered tuples.  The distinguished vertex is unique, and the other
four have $4!$ orderings.  Division by $4!$ proves the formula for
$S_d$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:18:cube:thm-fifth}]
Expand the $m$-fold product defining $\mathcal C_d(\delta+tf)$.
A subset of $j$ vertices contributes $\delta^{m-j}t^j$ times its
$f$-correlation.  For $j=1,2,3$, the corresponding affine matrices
have unit full-column-rank minors; character orthogonality forces
zero Fourier coordinates, so the correlations vanish.  Lemmas
\ref{gsr:cc:18:cube:lem-four-classification},
\ref{gsr:cc:18:cube:lem-five-circuits}, and
\ref{gsr:cc:18:cube:lem-three-torsion} give the fourth and fifth coefficients.

For every subset of $j$ vertices, Gowers--Cauchy--Schwarz, applied
to $f$ at those vertices and the constant function one at the
others, bounds the absolute correlation by $\|f\|_{U^d}^{j}$.
Summing this bound over all subsets with $j\geq6$ gives
\eqref{gsr:cc:18:cube:eq-fifth-remainder}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Characteristic two and characteristic three]
If $G$ has exponent two, then $T_5(f)=0$ because
$\widehat f(2\gamma)=\widehat f(0)=0$, and $E_3(f)=0$ as well.
Every fifth order term vanishes.  If $G$ has exponent three, then
$T_5(f)=E_3(f)$, after replacing $\gamma$ by $-\gamma$ in one sum.
The fifth coefficient is then
\[
 (Q_d+S_d)E_3(f),\qquad
 Q_d+S_d=\frac{10^d-6\cdot6^d+8\cdot4^d-3\cdot2^d}{24}.
\]
These identities explain why an odd-order hypothesis suffices for
the ordinary fourth coefficient but does not remove the extra
fifth order contribution.
\end{remark}

\subsection{A quantitative strengthening of Lemma 3.10}

\begin{corollary}[Centered cube bound]
\label{gsr:cc:18:cube:cor-improved-bound}
Let $g:G\to\mathbb R$ have mean $\delta\geq0$, set $f=g-\delta$,
and suppose $\|f\|_{U^d}\leq\varepsilon$, with $d\geq3$ and
$m=2^d$.  Then
\begin{align}
 \mathcal C_d(g)\leq{}&\delta^m
     +B_d\delta^{m-4}\varepsilon^4
     +(Q_d+S_d)\delta^{m-5}\varepsilon^5\notag\\
     &+\sum_{j=6}^{m}\binom mj
          \delta^{m-j}\varepsilon^j.
 \label{gsr:cc:18:cube:eq-improved-bound}
\end{align}
If $G$ has no two-torsion, $B_d$ may be replaced by $R_d$.
If $G$ has no three-torsion, $Q_d+S_d$ may be replaced by $Q_d$.
The stronger signed spectral formula
\eqref{gsr:cc:18:cube:eq-fifth-expansion} remains available in every case.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Use Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:18:cube:thm-fifth} with $t=1$.  The fourth coefficient
is a sum of $B_d$ correlations, each of absolute value at most
$\varepsilon^4$.  The nonzero fifth types number $Q_d+S_d$, each
of absolute value at most $\varepsilon^5$.  These estimates follow
from the same Gowers--Cauchy--Schwarz inequality as the remainder
bound.  The stated torsion exclusions remove the corresponding
terms from the exact formula.
\end{proof}

For a set $A$ of density $\delta$, the balanced function is
$f=1_A-\delta$.  In Gowers' normalization, degree-$(d-1)$
$\alpha$-uniformity means
$\|f\|_{U^d}^{m}\leq\alpha$.  Thus
\eqref{gsr:cc:18:cube:eq-improved-bound} improves the first possible error
from the order $\alpha^{1/m}$ supplied by
$(\delta+\alpha^{1/m})^m$ to order $\alpha^{4/m}$, at fixed
positive density and fixed $d$.  This is a local improvement of
the cube-counting lemma.  An improvement of the terminal
Szemer\'edi bound would require propagating it through an argument
that uses this estimate quantitatively.

\subsection{Sharpness, including genuine indicator sets}

The unrestricted finite-group leading constant $B_d$ is optimal.
The first step is an exact weighted example; a Bernoulli
approximation then transfers its leading behavior to sets.

\begin{proposition}[Exact order-two character example]
\label{gsr:cc:18:cube:prop-character-extremizer}
Let $\chi:G\to\{-1,1\}$ be a nontrivial character, $d\geq2$,
and $m=2^d$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal C_d(\delta+t\chi)
 =\frac{(\delta+t)^m+(\delta-t)^m
        +(2m-2)(\delta^2-t^2)^{m/2}}{2m}.
 \label{gsr:cc:18:cube:eq-character-exact}
\end{equation}
Moreover, $\|t\chi\|_{U^d}=|t|$.  At fixed $\delta>0$,
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal C_d(\delta+t\chi)
  =\delta^m+B_d\delta^{m-4}t^4+O_{d,\delta}(t^6).
 \label{gsr:cc:18:cube:eq-character-asymptotic}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The values of $\chi(x),\chi(h_1),\ldots,\chi(h_d)$ are independent
uniform signs.  Consequently the signs on the cube are the
evaluations of a uniformly random affine Boolean function on
$\mathbb F_2^d$.  Of its $2^{d+1}=2m$ possible affine functions,
two are constant and the other $2m-2$ are balanced.  A constant
function contributes $(\delta+t)^m$ or $(\delta-t)^m$; a balanced
one contributes $(\delta+t)^{m/2}(\delta-t)^{m/2}$.  This proves
\eqref{gsr:cc:18:cube:eq-character-exact}.

Every $d$-fold cube derivative of a character is one for $d\geq2$,
so its $U^d$ norm is one.  In the even polynomial
\eqref{gsr:cc:18:cube:eq-character-exact}, the quadratic coefficient is
zero and the quartic coefficient is
\[
 \frac{2\binom m4+(2m-2)\binom{m/2}{2}}{2m}
 =\frac{m(m-1)(m-2)}{24}=B_d.
\]
This proves the expansion.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Approximation of weights by sets in cube norm]
\label{gsr:cc:18:cube:lem-bernoulli}
Fix $d\geq2$, put $m=2^d$, and let $G=\mathbb F_2^n$, of order
$N$.  For every function $w:G\to[0,1]$, there is a set $A\subseteq G$
such that
\begin{equation}
 \|1_A-w\|_{U^d}
 \leq\left(\frac{m-1}{N}\right)^{1/m}.
 \label{gsr:cc:18:cube:eq-bernoulli-bound}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Include each $y\in G$ in $A$ independently with probability $w(y)$,
and write $z=1_A-w$.  For a cube whose $m$ sites are distinct,
independence and centering give
\[
 \mathbb E_A\prod_{v\in\{0,1\}^d}z(x+v\cdot h)=0.
\]
Every other product has absolute value at most one.  A collision
occurs only if $a\cdot h=0$ for some nonzero
$a\in\mathbb F_2^d$.  For fixed nonzero $a$, this has probability
$1/N$.  A union bound over $m-1$ choices gives
\[
 0\leq\mathbb E_A\|z\|_{U^d}^{m}\leq\frac{m-1}{N}.
\]
Some realization is at most this average, proving the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Optimal unrestricted leading coefficient for sets]
\label{gsr:cc:18:cube:thm-indicator-sharpness}
Fix $d\geq3$ and $\delta\in(0,1)$.  There are finite groups
$G_k=\mathbb F_2^{n_k}$ and sets $A_k\subseteq G_k$, with densities
$\delta_k\to\delta$ and balanced norms
$\varepsilon_k=\|1_{A_k}-\delta_k\|_{U^d}\to0$, such that
\begin{equation}
 \lim_{k\to\infty}
 \frac{\mathcal C_d(1_{A_k})-\delta_k^{m}}
      {\delta_k^{m-4}\varepsilon_k^4}=B_d.
 \label{gsr:cc:18:cube:eq-indicator-sharpness}
\end{equation}
Therefore $B_d$ in the unrestricted finite-group leading term of
\eqref{gsr:cc:18:cube:eq-improved-bound} cannot be decreased, even when the
functions being counted are indicators.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $t_k>0$ tend to zero, with
$t_k\leq\min(\delta,1-\delta)$.  Choose $N_k=2^{n_k}$ sufficiently
large that
\[
 \left(\frac{m-1}{N_k}\right)^{1/m}\leq t_k^5.
\]
On $G_k$, choose a nontrivial sign character $\chi_k$ and set
$w_k=\delta+t_k\chi_k$.  This weight lies in $[0,1]$ and has mean
$\delta$.  Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:18:cube:lem-bernoulli} gives a set $A_k$ with
$z_k=1_{A_k}-w_k$ satisfying $\|z_k\|_{U^d}\leq t_k^5$.

The mean is bounded by the cube norm, so
\[
 \delta_k=\delta+\mathbb E z_k=\delta+O(t_k^5).
\]
The balanced function of $A_k$ is
\[
 1_{A_k}-\delta_k
   =t_k\chi_k+z_k-\mathbb E z_k.
\]
The triangle inequality and its reverse give
$\varepsilon_k=t_k+O(t_k^5)$.  Also,
$\|1_{A_k}\|_{U^d},\|w_k\|_{U^d}\leq1$, because both functions
take values in $[0,1]$.  Hence
\[
 |\mathcal C_d(1_{A_k})-\mathcal C_d(w_k)|
 \leq m\|1_{A_k}-w_k\|_{U^d}\leq m t_k^5.
\]
Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:18:cube:prop-character-extremizer} now yields
\[
 \mathcal C_d(1_{A_k})-\delta_k^m
 =B_d\delta^{m-4}t_k^4+O_{d,\delta}(t_k^5).
\]
Since
$\delta_k^{m-4}\varepsilon_k^4
 =\delta^{m-4}t_k^4(1+o(1))$,
division proves~\eqref{gsr:cc:18:cube:eq-indicator-sharpness}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{Credit.} Sharpness of $B_d$ for sets is source~03's Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:03:cube:setsharpness} (with exact rational densities in its Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:03:cube:exactdensity}); proved again here by rounding. The best coefficient on odd-order groups, which Section~\ref{gsr:fz:18:sec:d9} asks for (``especially in dimension four''), is settled at $d=3$ by source~04's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:04:cub:norm-gap} ($c_3^{\mathrm{odd}}=2^{-1/2}$, note there); open for $d\ge4$ (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:normgap}).
\end{writenote}

This sharpness statement uses groups with two-torsion.  It leaves
open the best leading coefficient when multiplication by two is
invertible, especially for $d\geq4$.  The exact coefficient in that
case is $R_d\|f\|_{U^2}^4$, so the remaining optimization concerns
the strongest possible comparison between the centered real
$U^2$ and $U^d$ norms.

\section{Source~20's chapter: quadratic counting errors at Section~3 \wtag}\label{gsr:cc:sec:quadratic}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the fourth write, 6~October 2026.}}\par
The next seven sections are source~20, a manuscript on the passage from uniformity to counting in Gowers's Section~3 (Theorem~3.2, Corollary~3.3). It keeps two functions through the last Cauchy--Schwarz step, which gives an error quadratic in the balanced uniformity norm. \emph{Logically the chapter stands beside source~06's Section~\ref{gsr:cc:06:sec:d3}}, which proves the quadratic error first, and source~10's Section~\ref{gsr:cc:10:sec:d5} on torsion; source~20 could see neither (only source~04's manuscript, whose telescope is linear). It is printed here, at the end of Part~III, because no number printed earlier may move. Its introduction is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:20:sec:d1}; its formalization notes, questions, conclusion and source audit are in Part~V (Sections~\ref{gsr:fz:20:sec:d9}--\ref{gsr:fz:20:sec:dA}). Its notation is in the table at the head of this Part.

\emph{What is proved, in one paragraph.} For surjective homomorphisms of finite abelian groups, two marked functions bounded by directional seminorms and one $L^2$ factor (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:20:thm:two}; source~06's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:06:uni:two-functions} for slope systems); the directional-to-global comparison with the optimal constant for every subgroup tuple (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:20:thm:index}) and a collapsed-pair obstruction; quadratic counting with unequal densities (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:20:thm:count}) and, for one set, $|\Lambda_k(1_A)-\delta^k|\le B_k(\delta)u^2$ (Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:20:cor:symmetric}) with $B_k$ strictly below source~06's coefficient (proved at the write, note there); the sharp pair correction $\sqrt{m-1}$ (Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:20:prop:pair}); supersaturation (Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:20:cor:super}); and sharpness of the exponent $2$ for three-term counts of indicator sets of density near $1/2$ on $\F_{29}^{2m}$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:20:thm:indicator-sharpness}; new in this report). Not claimed: sharpness for $k\ge4$ or for prime cyclic groups, a substitute for the asymmetric Corollary~3.3, a global bound.

\emph{Relation to the formal statements} (checked at HEAD \texttt{0b4890a1c}). \file{theorem_3_2} and \file{corollary_3_3} (\file{Sections01\_03.lean}, lines~258, 276) are exact companions for prime $N$ and $k\le N$. Nothing in this chapter is formalized.

\section[{Normalized cubes and subgroup directions\srctag{20}}]{Normalized cubes and subgroup directions}\label{gsr:cc:20:sec:d2}
\srcnote{20}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:cc:20:sec:cubes}

All groups in this article are finite abelian groups, written additively.
Every expectation uses the uniform probability measure on its indicated
finite set. We put $\Delta_h f(x)=f(x)\overline{f(x+h)}$. Complex
conjugation is denoted by $\cc$, so $\cc^0z=z$ and $\cc^1z=\bar z$.
The $L^p$ norms also use normalized measure.

\begin{definition}[Directional cube seminorm]
For subgroups $H_1,\ldots,H_s\le G$, $s\ge1$, define
\begin{equation}
 D_{H_1,\ldots,H_s}(f)^{2^s}
 =\E_{x\in G}\E_{h_r\in H_r}
       \prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^s}
       \cc^{|\omega|}f(x+\omega\cdot h).
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:directional}
\end{equation}
Its nonnegative $2^s$-th root is intended. When every $H_r=G$, this is
$\Useminorm{f}{s}$. In particular $\Useminorm{f}{1}=|\E f|$.
\end{definition}

The direction list is symmetric: a permutation of its entries simply
renames the cube coordinates. Directions may coincide or be trivial.
For $s=1$,
\begin{equation}
 D_H(f)^2=\E_{q\in G/H}\abs{\E_{x\in q}f(x)}^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:relative-one}
\end{equation}
Thus a trivial direction is meaningful and should not be discarded.

\begin{lemma}[Positivity, mixed Cauchy--Schwarz, and phase invariance]
\label{gsr:cc:20:lem:gcs}
The quantity in \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:directional} is nonnegative. For functions
$f_\omega:G\to\C$,
\begin{equation}
 \abs{\E_{x\in G}\E_{h_r\in H_r}
       \prod_\omega\cc^{|\omega|}f_\omega(x+\omega\cdot h)}
 \le\prod_\omega D_{H_1,\ldots,H_s}(f_\omega).
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:mixed}
\end{equation}
The resulting $D$ satisfies the triangle inequality. If $s\ge2$ and
$\chi$ is a character of $G$, then $D(f\chi)=D(f)$, and in particular
$\Useminorm{f\chi}{s}=\Useminorm{f}{s}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Averaging the last derivative first gives
\begin{equation}
 D_{H_1,\ldots,H_s}(f)^{2^s}
 =\E_{h_1,\ldots,h_{s-1}}\E_{q\in G/H_s}
   \abs{\E_{x\in q}\Delta_{h_1}\cdots\Delta_{h_{s-1}}f(x)}^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:positivity}
\end{equation}
This proves positivity directly, including $s=1$.

For the mixed inequality introduce independent $t_r^0,t_r^1\in H_r$
and an independent $z\in G$. Set $h_r=t_r^1-t_r^0$ and
$x=z+\sum_r t_r^0$. The resulting $(x,h)$ is uniformly distributed,
so the mixed expression becomes
\[
 \E_z\E_{t_r^0,t_r^1}
 \prod_\omega\cc^{|\omega|}
 f_\omega\left(z+\sum_r t_r^{\omega_r}\right).
\]
For fixed $z$ this is a product-space box form. The box
Cauchy--Schwarz inequality follows by applying ordinary
Cauchy--Schwarz successively to the $s$ coordinates. At coordinate $r$
one regards all other variables as parameters, squares the average over
$t_r$, and introduces its independent copy. After all $s$ steps, the
factor belonging to each $\omega$ is its diagonal box form to the power
$1/2^s$. This argument also proves positivity of each diagonal box form.
Applying H\"older in $z$, with $2^s$ equal exponents, gives
\eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:mixed}, because the average of each diagonal box form is
exactly \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:directional}.

Expanding the diagonal cube for $f+g$ and applying \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:mixed} to
its $2^{2^s}$ terms gives
$D(f+g)^{2^s}\le(D(f)+D(g))^{2^s}$.
Finally, an alternating cube of a character is identically one when
$s\ge2$: both its constant exponent and each linear increment exponent
cancel. This proves phase invariance.
\end{proof}

For reference, normalized Fourier coefficients are
\[
 \widehat f(\chi)=\E_x f(x)\overline{\chi(x)}.
\]
Orthogonality gives Parseval and the fourth-moment identity
\begin{equation}
 \sum_\chi|\widehat f(\chi)|^2=\norm f_2^2,
 \qquad
 \Useminorm f2^4=\sum_\chi|\widehat f(\chi)|^4.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:fourier-u2}
\end{equation}
The second identity follows by expanding all four factors of the
parallelogram and averaging the three independent variables. Their
character constraints leave one freely chosen frequency. These
normalizations are used throughout the sharpness argument.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The two-function directional estimate\srctag{20}}]{The two-function directional estimate}\label{gsr:cc:20:sec:d3}
\srcnote{20}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:cc:20:sec:two}

Let $\Omega$ be a finite abelian parameter group, and let
$L_1,\ldots,L_k:\Omega\to G$ be surjective homomorphisms. Write
\begin{equation}
 \La_L(f_1,\ldots,f_k)=\E_{z\in\Omega}\prod_{i=1}^k f_i(L_i z),
 \quad K_j=\kerop L_j,
 \quad H_{ij}=L_i(K_j)\quad(i\ne j).
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:system}
\end{equation}
For a fixed position $i$, set
\begin{equation}
 D_i(f)=D_{(H_{ij})_{j\ne i}}(f).
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:Di}
\end{equation}
This is an order $k-1$ directional seminorm. There is no pairwise
independence assumption in this definition.

\subsection{The last two coordinates have a common quotient}

\begin{lemma}[Joint fibers]
\label{gsr:cc:20:lem:joint}
For distinct $i,j$, there is an isomorphism
\[
 \theta_{ij}:G/H_{ij}\longrightarrow G/H_{ji}
\]
such that the uniform law of $(L_i z,L_j z)$ can be sampled as follows:
choose $q\in G/H_{ij}$ uniformly, then choose independently a uniform
$u\in q$ and a uniform $v\in\theta_{ij}(q)$. Consequently
\begin{equation}
 \E_z F(L_i z)Q(L_j z)
 =\E_q\left(\E_{u\in q}F(u)\right)
          \left(\E_{v\in\theta_{ij}(q)}Q(v)\right).
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:joint}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $J=(L_i,L_j)(\Omega)\le G\times G$. Both projections of $J$ are
surjective. Its horizontal kernel is $H_{ij}\times\{0\}$ and its
vertical kernel is $\{0\}\times H_{ji}$. If $(u,v)\in J$, the class of
$v$ modulo $H_{ji}$ depends only on the class of $u$ modulo $H_{ij}$:
two choices differ by a horizontal or vertical kernel element. This
constructs an isomorphism $\theta_{ij}$; symmetry supplies its inverse.
For each $q$, the elements of $J$ above $q$ are precisely the Cartesian
product $q\times\theta_{ij}(q)$. These products all have the same size.
A homomorphism from $\Omega$ to $J$ has equal-size fibers, so uniform
$z$ induces uniform measure on $J$. Formula \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:joint} follows.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[One kernel-averaging step]
\label{gsr:cc:20:lem:kernel}
Let $L:\Omega\to G$ be surjective, $K=\kerop L$, and let $a:G\to\C$.
For any $F:\Omega\to\C$,
\begin{equation}
 \abs{\E_z a(Lz)F(z)}^2
 \le\norm a_2^2\,
      \E_{z\in\Omega}\E_{h\in K}F(z)\overline{F(z+h)}.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:kernel-step}
\end{equation}
The expression on the right after $\norm a_2^2$ is real and nonnegative.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Disintegrate uniform measure on $\Omega$ over the fibers of $L$.
The left-hand average is
$\E_{v\in G}a(v)\E_{z\in L^{-1}(v)}F(z)$.
Cauchy--Schwarz bounds its square by $\norm a_2^2$ times the average of
the squared fiber means. Two independent points in the same fiber have
the form $(z,z+h)$ with $h$ uniform in $K$, proving the identity and
nonnegativity.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Two marked functions, with an $L^2$ gain]
\label{gsr:cc:20:thm:two}
Assume $k\ge3$. For any three distinct positions $i,j,\ell$ and any
functions $f_1,\ldots,f_k:G\to\C$,
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\quad
 |\La_L(f_1,\ldots,f_k)|
 \le D_i(f_i)D_j(f_j)\norm{f_\ell}_2
       \prod_{r\notin\{i,j,\ell\}}\norm{f_r}_\infty.
 \quad}
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:two}
\end{equation}
For $k=2$, the corresponding assertion is
$|\La_L(f_1,f_2)|\le D_1(f_1)D_2(f_2)$.
The numerical constant one is best possible.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If an unmarked factor is identically zero, there is nothing to prove.
By homogeneity, normalize all factors outside $\{i,j,\ell\}$ to have
supremum norm at most one. Eliminate the $r=k-2$ unmarked positions in
an order $a_1=\ell,a_2,\ldots,a_r$.

After $t$ eliminations let $h_b\in K_{a_b}$, $1\le b\le t$, and put
\[
 F_q^{(t)}(z;h)
 =\Delta_{L_qh_1}\cdots\Delta_{L_qh_t}f_q(L_qz),
 \qquad
 A_t=\E_{h_1,\ldots,h_t,z}
       \prod_{q\notin\{a_1,\ldots,a_t\}}F_q^{(t)}(z;h).
\]
Thus $A_0=\La_L(f)$. Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:20:lem:kernel}, first with $L_\ell$,
gives $|A_0|^2\le\norm{f_\ell}_2^2 A_1$.
At a later step, the factor $F_{a_{t+1}}^{(t)}$ is invariant under
$z\mapsto z+h_{t+1}$ for $h_{t+1}\in K_{a_{t+1}}$, and is
one-bounded. Apply the same averaging and Cauchy--Schwarz argument on
the product probability space of $z$ and all previous $h_b$.
It gives $|A_t|^2\le A_{t+1}$. Each $A_{t+1}$ so obtained is
nonnegative. Iteration yields
\begin{equation}
 |\La_L(f)|^{2^r}\le\norm{f_\ell}_2^{2^r} A_r.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:after-r}
\end{equation}
Only $i,j$ remain in $A_r$.

For a fixed list $h=(h_1,\ldots,h_r)$ apply
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:20:lem:joint} to their derivative functions. Define
\[
 M_i(h,q)=\E_{x\in q}
       \Delta_{L_i h_1}\cdots\Delta_{L_i h_r}f_i(x),
\]
and define $M_j$ using the corresponding coset $\theta_{ij}(q)$.
Then $A_r=\E_{h,q}M_i(h,q)M_j(h,\theta_{ij}(q))$.
Cauchy--Schwarz on this joint probability space gives
\[
 |A_r|\le
 \bigl(\E_{h,q}|M_i(h,q)|^2\bigr)^{1/2}
 \bigl(\E_{h,q}|M_j(h,\theta_{ij}(q))|^2\bigr)^{1/2}.
\]
The first squared moment is exactly
\[
 \E_{h_1,\ldots,h_r}\E_{x\in G}\E_{t\in H_{ij}}
 \Delta_{L_i h_1}\cdots\Delta_{L_i h_r}f_i(x)
 \overline{\Delta_{L_i h_1}\cdots\Delta_{L_i h_r}f_i(x+t)}
 =D_i(f_i)^{2^{r+1}}.
\]
Indeed $L_i h_b$ is uniform in $H_{i,a_b}$, and these images are
independent for different $b$. The same computation gives
$D_j(f_j)^{2^{r+1}}$ for the other moment. Combining with
\eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:after-r} and taking the $2^r$-th root proves \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:two}.
Restoring the normalized supremum norms gives the stated homogeneous
form.

For $k=2$, apply Cauchy--Schwarz directly to \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:joint} and use
\eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:relative-one}. Taking every function to be the constant one
shows that the numerical constant cannot be decreased.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{Credit.} For admissible slope systems this is source~06's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:06:uni:two-functions}, display \eqref{gsr:cc:06:uni:two-l2-bound}; here for arbitrary surjective homomorphisms, with directional seminorms. The one-function form is Gowers's Theorem~3.2 (\file{theorem_3_2}, \file{Sections01\_03.lean}, line~258; exact companion \file{theorem_3_2_holds}, \file{Proofs03ProgressionAverage.lean}, line~381, at HEAD \texttt{0b4890a1c}, for prime $N$ and $k\le N$).
\end{writenote}

\begin{corollary}[Pair-independent systems]
\label{gsr:cc:20:cor:independent}
If $(L_i,L_j):\Omega\to G^2$ is surjective for every $i\ne j$, then
\begin{equation}
 |\La_L(f)|\le
 \Useminorm{f_i}{k-1}\Useminorm{f_j}{k-1}\norm{f_\ell}_2
 \prod_{r\notin\{i,j,\ell\}}\norm{f_r}_\infty.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:global-two}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Pair surjectivity is equivalent to $H_{ij}=G$ for all distinct pairs,
so all directional norms in Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:20:thm:two} are global norms.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why two functions survive]
The last step in a one-function proof bounds the penultimate function
by one. In \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:after-r} we stop one step earlier and estimate the
two remaining conditional means symmetrically. Their squares supply the
last direction for both marked functions. This is why the output is a
product, not merely the smaller of two one-function bounds.
\end{remark}

For $k=3$ and the usual progression forms, Fourier inversion gives a
useful independent check:
\[
 \La_3(f,g,h)=\sum_\chi
       \widehat f(\chi)\widehat g(\chi^{-2})\widehat h(\chi).
\]
When multiplication by two is invertible, H\"older with exponents
$4,4,2$, and Parseval, gives any appropriate two $U^2$ factors and one
$L^2$ factor. Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:20:thm:two} extends this mechanism beyond the
Fourier-linear case and records the exact subgroups when invertibility
fails.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Sharp conversion from directional to global norms\srctag{20}}]{Sharp conversion from directional to global norms}\label{gsr:cc:20:sec:d4}
\srcnote{20}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:cc:20:sec:index}

\begin{theorem}[Finite-index comparison, with equality examples]
\label{gsr:cc:20:thm:index}
Let $s\ge2$, let $H_1,\ldots,H_s\le G$, and put $m_r=[G:H_r]$.
For every $f:G\to\C$,
\begin{equation}
 D_{H_1,\ldots,H_s}(f)
 \le \left(\prod_{r=1}^s m_r\right)^{1/2^s}\Useminorm f s.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:index}
\end{equation}
For this fixed subgroup tuple, the displayed constant is optimal.
In fact equality holds for every nonzero function supported on a single
coset of $H_*:=\bigcap_rH_r$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The annihilator $H_r^\perp$ consists of the $m_r$ characters trivial on
$H_r$. Orthogonality gives
\[
 m_r1_{H_r}(h)=\sum_{\chi\in H_r^\perp}\chi(h).
\]
Insert these identities into the normalized directional cube. Its
$2^s$-th power becomes a sum of $\prod_r m_r$ full-group cube forms,
each twisted by $\prod_r\chi_r(h_r)$. The twist can be absorbed into
characters multiplying the vertex functions, since
$\chi_r(h_r)=\chi_r(x+h_r)\overline{\chi_r(x)}$.
More explicitly, multiply the origin function by
$\prod_r\overline{\chi_r}$ and the function at singleton vertex $e_r$
by $\overline{\chi_r}$; conjugation at the singleton supplies the
required positive character. All other vertex functions remain $f$.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:20:lem:gcs} bounds the absolute value of each twisted form by
$\Useminorm f s^{2^s}$, using $s\ge2$ for character invariance. Summing proves
\eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:index}.

If $\supp f\subset x_0+H_*$, every nonzero cube integrand has its
origin and each singleton vertex in that coset. Hence every increment
lies in $H_*$, and in particular in its prescribed $H_r$.
The unrestricted and restricted cube sums therefore have identical
nonzero summands. Only their normalizations differ, by exactly
$\prod_r[G:H_r]$. This proves equality of the powers and thus equality
in \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:index}. The all-zero list of the first $s-1$ increments in
\eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:positivity} shows that $U^s(f)>0$ for nonzero $f$ when
$s\ge2$. Thus these examples prove optimality of the constant.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{Relation to source~10.} Source~10's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:10:thm:torsion-mixed-lp} pays a kernel factor $K^{1/2^{k-1}}$ for non-invertible coefficient differences, sharp on $(\Z/2\Z)^n$ (Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:10:prop:torsion-sharpness}); this theorem is the general directional-to-global conversion, with the optimal constant for every fixed subgroup tuple. With Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:20:prop:pair} it answers source~06's Question~7 for the norm-conversion step (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:torsion}); the full multilinear optimum stays open (this source's Section~\ref{gsr:fz:20:sec:d10}).
\end{writenote}

The restriction $s\ge2$ is necessary: a nontrivial character trivial
on a proper $H$ has $D_H(f)=1$ but $U^1(f)=0$.
Optimality in Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:20:thm:index} concerns norm conversion. It does
not imply that multiplying two such constants gives the best possible
constant in every multilinear counting inequality; the two equality
conditions may be incompatible with the other functions.

\begin{corollary}[Global two-function estimate with explicit costs]
\label{gsr:cc:20:cor:kappa}
For the system \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:system} with $k\ge3$, put
\begin{equation}
 \kappa_i=\left(\prod_{j\ne i}[G:H_{ij}]\right)^{1/2^{k-1}}.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:kappa}
\end{equation}
Then the right-hand side of \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:global-two}, multiplied by
$\kappa_i\kappa_j$, bounds $|\La_L(f)|$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:20:thm:index} to each of the two directional norms in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:20:thm:two}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Scalar progressions and composite moduli}

For $L_i(x,y)=x+c_i y$, one has
\begin{equation}
 H_{ij}=(c_i-c_j)G,\qquad
 [G:H_{ij}]=|G[c_i-c_j]|,
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:scalar}
\end{equation}
where $G[d]=\{x\in G:dx=0\}$. The second identity is the finite
kernel--image formula. In particular, on $\Z/N\Z$,
\begin{equation}
 \kappa_i=
 \left(\prod_{j\ne i}\gcd(N,c_i-c_j)\right)^{1/2^{k-1}}.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:cyclic-kappa}
\end{equation}
This formula remains meaningful with repeated slopes, with
$\gcd(N,0)=N$. For consecutive slopes labeled $0,\ldots,k-1$,
\begin{equation}
 \kappa_i\le
 \bigl(i!(k-1-i)!\bigr)^{1/2^{k-1}}.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:factorial}
\end{equation}
Indeed each positive greatest common divisor is at most the corresponding
nonzero integer difference. The central positions minimize this crude
factorial envelope; this need not identify the minimizing positions for
the actual gcd product for a given modulus.

As a small example, the slopes $0,1,2$ on $\Z/6\Z$ have
$\kappa_0=\kappa_2=2^{1/4}$ and $\kappa_1=1$. A bound using the
middle position and either endpoint has conversion cost $2^{1/4}$;
a bound using both endpoints has cost $\sqrt2$. Choosing the marked
positions is therefore a genuinely quantitative decision when the
available norm bounds are unequal.

\subsection{Why a torsion-independent global bound can fail}

\begin{proposition}[A collapsed-pair obstruction]
\label{gsr:cc:20:prop:obstruction}
For fixed $s\ge2$ there are one-bounded functions on groups
$G_n=\F_2^n$ whose $U^s$ norms tend to zero but for which a
three-term progression average with two such marked functions is one.
Thus no group-size-independent global two-function bound can ignore
collapsed directions in arbitrary finite abelian groups.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Assign independent uniform unit-circle phases $v(x)$ to points of a
group $G$ of size $N$. In the expected $s$-cube product, a nonzero
contribution requires every point to occur equally often at even and
odd vertices. In particular the even origin must agree with some odd
vertex. For each of the $2^{s-1}$ odd vertices $\omega$,
$\omega\cdot h=0$ has probability $1/N$, because at least one
coefficient is one. A union bound gives
\[
 \E_v\Useminorm v s^{2^s}\le 2^{s-1}/N.
\]
There is therefore a choice $v_n$ with $U^s(v_n)\to0$ on $G_n$.
Take $f_0=v_n$, $f_1=1$, $f_2=\overline{v_n}$. In characteristic two,
$x+2y=x$, so their three-term average is
$\E_{x,y}|v_n(x)|^2=1$. Both marked norms tend to zero. The subgroup
$H_{02}=\{0\}$ is precisely the collapsed direction that the
directional theorem retains.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Second-order telescoping and counting\srctag{20}}]{Second-order telescoping and counting}\label{gsr:cc:20:sec:d5}
\srcnote{20}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:cc:20:sec:count}

Let $a_i:G\to[0,1]$, let $\delta_i=\E a_i$, and put
$b_i=a_i-\delta_i$ and $\sigma_i=\norm{b_i}_2$.
Then $\norm{a_i}_2\le\sqrt{\delta_i}$ and
$\sigma_i\le\sqrt{\delta_i(1-\delta_i)}$.
For indicator functions the latter inequality is equality.

\begin{lemma}[First-two-residual identity]
\label{gsr:cc:20:lem:telescoping}
For any scalars $a_i=\delta_i+b_i$, $1\le i\le k$,
\begin{align}
 \prod_{r=1}^k a_r
 ={}&\prod_{r=1}^k\delta_r
 +\sum_{i=1}^k b_i\prod_{r\ne i}\delta_r\nonumber\\
 &+\sum_{1\le i<j\le k}
 \left(\prod_{\substack{r<j\\r\ne i}}\delta_r\right)
 b_i b_j\prod_{r>j}a_r.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:second-telescope}
\end{align}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Expand the product by the set of positions at which $b$ is chosen.
The empty set and singleton sets give the first two terms. Every other
set has unique first two elements $i<j$. All preceding positions except
$i$ contribute $\delta$, the positions $i,j$ contribute $b$, and the
remaining positions are unrestricted choices of $\delta$ or $b$,
summing to $\prod_{r>j}a_r$. This partitions all terms exactly once.
\end{proof}

Write
\begin{equation}
 w_{ij}=\prod_{\substack{r<j\\r\ne i}}\delta_r,
 \qquad u_i=\Useminorm{b_i}{k-1}.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:weights}
\end{equation}
Surjectivity of $L_i$ kills every singleton term after averaging.
When the system is pair-independent, it also kills the term with only
$b_i,b_j$ and no tail.

\begin{theorem}[Quadratic counting, unequal densities]
\label{gsr:cc:20:thm:count}
For arbitrary surjective $L_1,\ldots,L_k$ with $k\ge3$,
\begin{equation}
 \abs{\La_L(a_1,\ldots,a_k)-\prod_r\delta_r}
 \le\sum_{i<j}w_{ij}\kappa_i\kappa_j u_i u_j.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:count-torsion}
\end{equation}
If the system is pair-independent, define, for $j<k$,
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal R_j=\min\left\{
       \min_{\ell>j}\sqrt{\delta_\ell},\quad
       \sum_{\ell>j}\left(\prod_{j<r<\ell}\delta_r\right)\sigma_\ell
                         \right\}.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:tail}
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\quad
 \abs{\La_L(a_1,\ldots,a_k)-\prod_r\delta_r}
 \le\sum_{i<j<k}w_{ij}u_i u_j\mathcal R_j.
 \quad}
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:count-independent}
\end{equation}
Every permutation of the positions gives another valid bound.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Apply \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:second-telescope} to $a_r(L_rz)$ and average. Each
summand after the singleton terms is
\begin{equation}
 w_{ij}\E_z b_i(L_i z)b_j(L_jz)\prod_{r>j}a_r(L_rz).
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:term}
\end{equation}
Insert constant-one functions at the unused positions. Corollary
\ref{gsr:cc:20:cor:kappa} bounds its absolute value by
$w_{ij}\kappa_i\kappa_j u_i u_j$, since all unmarked factors are
one-bounded. Summing proves \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:count-torsion}.

Now assume pair independence. When $j=k$, the average in
\eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:term} factors as $(\E b_i)(\E b_j)=0$. For $j<k$, choose
any $\ell>j$ as the $L^2$ factor in Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:20:cor:independent}.
This gives the first bound $u_i u_j\min_{\ell>j}\sqrt{\delta_\ell}$
for the average in \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:term}.

For the second bound use the exact first-residual identity in the tail:
\[
 \prod_{r>j}a_r
 =\prod_{r>j}\delta_r+
   \sum_{\ell>j}\left(\prod_{j<r<\ell}\delta_r\right)
       b_\ell\prod_{r>\ell}a_r.
\]
The constant-tail contribution vanishes by pair independence. In each
remaining contribution use $b_\ell$ as the $L^2$ factor, retaining
$b_i,b_j$ as marked functions. This gives the second expression in
\eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:tail}. Taking the smaller bound for each $(i,j)$ and summing
proves \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:count-independent}. The proof is unchanged by a
permutation of the positions.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Order-sensitive norms]
In \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:count-independent}, $u_i u_j$ can be replaced term by term
by
$\Useminorm{b_i}{k-j+1}\Useminorm{b_j}{k-j+1}$.
Indeed the active subsystem in \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:term} has $k-j+2$ positions,
and the same proof applies to it. The tail expansion does not increase
that number of active positions. Equivalently one may retain constant-one
positions within that subsystem. The uniform highest-order version is
simpler to state; the order-sensitive version can be useful in a formal
or numerical optimization of the bound.
\end{remark}

\subsection{A single set and an explicit coefficient}

\begin{corollary}[Symmetric quadratic counting]
\label{gsr:cc:20:cor:symmetric}
Let $A\subset G$ have density $0<\delta<1$, and assume pair independence
of the $k$ forms. Put $u=\Useminorm{1_A-\delta}{k-1}$. Then
\[
 \abs{\La_L(1_A,\ldots,1_A)-\delta^k}\le B_k(\delta)u^2,
\]
with $B_k$ as in \eqref{gsr:fm:20:eq:B-intro}. Equations
\eqref{gsr:fm:20:eq:B-simple} and \eqref{gsr:fm:20:eq:B-small} hold.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
There are $j-1$ choices of $i<j$, each with
$w_{ij}=\delta^{j-2}$. The two tail bounds in \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:tail} become
$\sqrt\delta$ and
$\sigma\sum_{r=0}^{k-j-1}\delta^r$. This proves the formula for $B_k$.
For $k=3$ only $j=2$ occurs, and the smaller tail bound is $\sigma$.
Using $R_m\le\sqrt\delta$ and the positive series
$\sum_{r\ge0}(r+1)\delta^r=(1-\delta)^{-2}$ proves
\eqref{gsr:fm:20:eq:B-simple}.

For $0<\delta\le1/2$ and $m\ge2$,
\[
 \frac{\sigma(1+\delta+\cdots+\delta^{m-1})}{\sqrt\delta}
 \ge\sqrt{1-\delta}(1+\delta)\ge1.
\]
The last inequality follows on squaring from
$\delta(1-\delta-\delta^2)\ge0$ in this range. Thus $R_m=\sqrt\delta$
for $m\ge2$, whereas $R_1=\sigma$. Separating the last term of the
sum gives \eqref{gsr:fm:20:eq:B-small}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{Against source~06} (proved at the write). Source~06's Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:06:uni:homogeneous} has the coefficient $\sqrt\delta\,B^{(06)}_k(\delta)$ with $B^{(06)}_k(\delta)=\sum_{t=0}^{k-3}(t+1)\delta^t$ \eqref{gsr:cc:06:uni:coefficients}. Since $R_m(\delta)\le\sqrt\delta$, putting $t=j-2$ in \eqref{gsr:fm:20:eq:B-intro} gives $B_k(\delta)\le\sqrt\delta\sum_{t=0}^{k-3}(t+1)\delta^t=\sqrt\delta\,B^{(06)}_k(\delta)$. The inequality is strict for every $k\ge3$ and $0<\delta<1$: the term $j=k-1$ carries $R_1(\delta)=\sigma<\sqrt\delta$ with the positive weight $(k-2)\delta^{k-3}$. For $k=3$ the coefficient is $\sigma$, source~06's sharp Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:06:uni:three-term}. Ratios: $0.8536$ at $k=4$, $\delta=1/2$; $\sqrt{0.7}=0.8367$ at $k=3$, $\delta=0.3$. This advances source~06's Question~6 without settling it (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:density}).
\end{writenote}

This coefficient is the best obtained by the two explicitly specified
tail estimates at each term of this fixed telescoping identity. No claim
is made that it is the optimal coefficient among all counting arguments.
