\subsection{A torsion-inclusive symmetric statement}

Without pair independence, Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:20:cor:kappa} and
\eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:count-torsion} give
\begin{equation}
 \abs{\La_L(1_A,\ldots,1_A)-\delta^k}
 \le C_{L,\delta}u^2,
 \quad
 C_{L,\delta}=\sum_{j=2}^k\delta^{j-2}\kappa_j\sum_{i<j}\kappa_i.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:C-torsion}
\end{equation}
In particular
$C_{L,\delta}\le\kappa_{\max}^2/(1-\delta)^2$.
This is an explicit bound on every finite abelian group. It may be weak
when a direction collapses, and Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:20:prop:obstruction}
explains why some loss is then unavoidable.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Pair correlations as an exact torsion correction\srctag{20}}]{Pair correlations as an exact torsion correction}\label{gsr:cc:20:sec:d6}
\srcnote{20}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:cc:20:sec:pair}

The directional estimate can be complemented by an exact Fourier
description of the first obstruction to a product-density baseline.

\begin{proposition}[Pair correction and its sharp constant]
\label{gsr:cc:20:prop:pair}
Let $f,g:G\to\C$ have mean zero, let $d$ be an integer, and put
$H=dG$, $m=[G:H]$. Then
\begin{align}
 Q_d(f,g)&:=\E_{x,y}f(x)g(x+dy)
 =\sum_{\substack{\chi\in H^\perp\\\chi\ne1}}
       \widehat f(\chi)\widehat g(\chi^{-1}),
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:pair-fourier}\\
 |Q_d(f,g)|&\le\sqrt{m-1}\,\Useminorm f2\Useminorm g2.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:pair-bound}
\end{align}
For $m>1$, the constant $\sqrt{m-1}$ is optimal, also when the functions
are required to be real and one-bounded.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Fourier inversion and averaging $x$ force the two frequencies to be
inverses. Averaging $dy$, uniform in $H$, forces the surviving character
to lie in $H^\perp$. The zero-frequency term vanishes by centering.
H\"older on the remaining $m-1$ frequencies, with exponents $4,4,2$,
and \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:fourier-u2} prove \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:pair-bound}.
For sharpness take
\[
 f=g=t\sum_{\substack{\chi\in H^\perp\\\chi\ne1}}\chi
   =t(m1_H-1),\qquad 0<t\le1/(m-1).
\]
These are real, centered and one-bounded. Their pair correlation is
$(m-1)t^2$, while each fourth power of the $U^2$ norm is $(m-1)t^4$.
The ratio is exactly $\sqrt{m-1}$.
\end{proof}

For $a_i=\delta_i+b_i$, the full balanced expansion separates an exact
pair contribution
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{i<j}\left(\prod_{r\notin\{i,j\}}\delta_r\right)
 Q_{c_j-c_i}(b_i,b_j)
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:pair-baseline}
\end{equation}
from terms with at least three balanced factors. Thus on a non-admissible
cyclic group, keeping \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:pair-baseline} can be preferable to
regarding it as error. In the admissible case every summand is zero.
The finite-index factors and this quotient-frequency correction describe
the same obstruction in different languages: one is suited to
Cauchy--Schwarz iteration, the other isolates the precise pair bias.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Supersaturation and the uniformity parameter\srctag{20}}]{Supersaturation and the uniformity parameter}\label{gsr:cc:20:sec:d7}
\srcnote{20}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:cc:20:sec:super}

A \emph{proper ordered progression} is a pair $(x,y)$ whose $k$ entries
$x,x+y,\ldots,x+(k-1)y$ are distinct and belong to $A$.
Let $T_k^*(A)$ denote their number.

\begin{corollary}[Admissible supersaturation]
\label{gsr:cc:20:cor:super}
Suppose the consecutive progression system is admissible, $k\ge3$,
$|G|=N$, and $A\subset G$ has density $0<\delta<1$. With
$u=\Useminorm{1_A-\delta}{k-1}$,
\begin{equation}
 T_k^*(A)\ge
 N^2\bigl(\delta^k-B_k(\delta)u^2\bigr)-\delta N.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:super}
\end{equation}
In particular $T_k^*(A)>0$ whenever
\begin{equation}
 u^2\le\frac{\delta^k}{2B_k(\delta)},
 \qquad N>2\delta^{1-k}.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:threshold}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The normalized count includes all $N^2$ parameter pairs. A repeated
entry implies $(r-s)y=0$ for $0<|r-s|<k$, hence $y=0$ by
admissibility. Exactly $|A|=\delta N$ counted pairs have zero difference.
Subtract these from the lower bound supplied by
Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:20:cor:symmetric}. Conditions \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:threshold} make
the resulting lower bound strictly positive.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{Comparison} (at the write). Source~06's Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:06:uni:existence} needs $u^2\le\delta^{k-1/2}/(2B^{(06)}_k(\delta))=\delta^k/(2\sqrt\delta B^{(06)}_k(\delta))$; since $B_k(\delta)\le\sqrt\delta B^{(06)}_k(\delta)$, the condition \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:threshold} is weaker, so this criterion is the stronger one; for the other criteria of this report see the note after Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:04:prog:super}.
\end{writenote}

In Gowers's degree-$k-2$ convention, the power parameter corresponding
to the normalized cube norm is
\begin{equation}
 \alpha=u^{2^{k-1}}.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:alpha}
\end{equation}
Thus the new counting error is
$B_k(\delta)\alpha^{1/2^{k-2}}$, and the sufficient condition becomes
\begin{equation}
 \alpha\le
 \left(\frac{\delta^k}{2B_k(\delta)}\right)^{2^{k-2}}.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:alpha-threshold}
\end{equation}
For $0<\delta\le1/2$, the convenient bound
$B_k(\delta)\le4\sqrt\delta$ gives the simpler sufficient condition
\begin{equation}
 \alpha\le
 \left(\frac{\delta^{k-1/2}}8\right)^{2^{k-2}}.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:alpha-simple}
\end{equation}
This improves the local symmetric threshold derived from
\eqref{gsr:fm:20:eq:old}, which is
$\alpha\le(\delta^k/(2S_{k-2}(\delta)))^{2^{k-1}}$.
The comparison keeps the same normalized $u$ and distinguishes a
cube norm from its $2^{k-1}$-th power.

\subsection{Removing degenerate progressions with torsion}

For an arbitrary finite abelian group put
\[
 D_k(G)=\abs{\bigcup_{r=1}^{k-1}G[r]}.
\]
The difference $y$ gives a repeated entry precisely when its order is
less than $k$. For each such difference at most $|A|$ starting points
can contribute. Therefore \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:C-torsion} gives
\begin{equation}
 T_k^*(A)\ge
 N^2\bigl(\delta^k-C_{L,\delta}u^2\bigr)-\delta N D_k(G).
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:torsion-super}
\end{equation}
For cyclic groups this degeneracy count has the exact formula
\begin{equation}
 D_k(\Z/N\Z)=\sum_{\substack{d\mid N\\d<k}}\varphi(d),
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:degenerate}
\end{equation}
since there are $\varphi(d)$ elements of order $d$. This includes the
zero difference through $d=1$.

\subsection{The no-wrap distinction}

\begin{lemma}[A sufficient lifting condition]
\label{gsr:cc:20:lem:nowrap}
Suppose $A\subset\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ is embedded in $\Z/N\Z$ and
$2(n-1)<N$. Any nonconstant modular progression of length at least three
contained in $A$ is an ordinary integer progression; reversing its order
if necessary gives positive difference.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $a_0,\ldots,a_{k-1}$ be its integer representatives. Their consecutive
differences are congruent modulo $N$. Each lies between $-(n-1)$ and
$n-1$, so the difference between any two has absolute value less than
$N$ and must be zero. They are all the same integer, which is nonzero
for a nonconstant progression.
\end{proof}

The lemma does not show that cutting an arbitrary uniform set down to a
short interval preserves its balanced norm. Such a localization step can
introduce unbalanced cutoff functions at precisely the positions where
our quadratic argument needs small norms. This is one reason
\eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:alpha-threshold} is not silently promoted to a new global
Szemer\'edi estimate. The inverse theorem, density increment, iteration
losses, and localization must all be analyzed together.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A sharp quadratic obstruction for three-term counts\srctag{20}}]{A sharp quadratic obstruction for three-term counts}\label{gsr:cc:20:sec:d8}
\srcnote{20}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:cc:20:sec:sharp}

We now prove that quadratic dependence in \eqref{gsr:fm:20:eq:headline} is the
correct uniform exponent when $k=3$, not just an artifact of stopping
Cauchy--Schwarz early. The construction is explicit for bounded weights;
a second argument transfers its scale to actual subsets.

\subsection{An elementary even-dimensional Gauss identity}

Let $p=29$, let $G=\F_p^{2m}$, $N=p^{2m}$, and set
$Q(x)=x_1^2+\cdots+x_{2m}^2$. Write $e_p(t)=\exp(2\pi it/p)$.

\begin{lemma}[Gauss averages]
\label{gsr:cc:20:lem:gauss}
For every nonzero $t\in\F_p$,
\begin{equation}
 \E_{x\in G}e_p(tQ(x))=N^{-1/2},
 \qquad
 \abs{\widehat{e_p(tQ)}(\xi)}=N^{-1/2}
 \quad(\xi\in\widehat G).
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:gauss}
\end{equation}
More generally, if a quadratic form in two scalar variables over $\F_p$
has rank $r$, its sum over $2m$ independent coordinate copies has
normalized exponential average $N^{-r/2}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $g(t)=\sum_{z\in\F_p}e_p(tz^2)$. If $\chi$ is the quadratic
character, counting square roots gives $g(t)=\chi(t)g(1)$ for $t\ne0$.
The change of variables $(z,w)\mapsto(z-w,z+w)$ is invertible and gives
$|g(t)|^2=\sum_{z,w}e_p(t(z^2-w^2))=p$.
Also $\overline{g(1)}=g(-1)=\chi(-1)g(1)=g(1)$ because $p\equiv1$
modulo four. Hence $g(t)^2=p$, irrespective of its possible sign.
The product over $2m$ coordinates is $p^m$, and normalization gives the
first assertion of \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:gauss}. Completing the square for each
linear Fourier twist proves the magnitude assertion.

Every symmetric quadratic matrix over this odd-characteristic field
is diagonalizable by an invertible linear change of variables. A rank-$r$
form has $r$ nonzero diagonal coefficients; zero directions contribute
one. For each nonzero coefficient the $2m$ coordinate copies contribute
$p^{-m}=N^{-1/2}$. Their product is $N^{-r/2}$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Four phases and an exact rank census}

Set $a=1/16$ and
\begin{equation}
 h(x)=a\sum_{t\in\{-2,-1,1,2\}}e_p(tQ(x)),\qquad
 f(x)=h(x)-4aN^{-1/2},\qquad w(x)=\tfrac12+f(x).
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:weight}
\end{equation}
The conjugate pairs make $h,f,w$ real. Their means are
$\E h=4aN^{-1/2}$, $\E f=0$, and $\E w=1/2$.
Moreover $|f|\le4a(1+N^{-1/2})\le1/2$, so $0\le w\le1$.

\begin{proposition}[Exact weighted excess]
\label{gsr:cc:20:prop:weight}
For the functions in \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:weight},
\begin{align}
 \Useminorm f2^4&\le (4a)^4/N,\label{gsr:cc:20:eq:weight-u}\\
 \La_3(w)-\tfrac18
 &=a^3\left(2N^{-1/2}+62N^{-1}-64N^{-3/2}\right).
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:weight-excess}
\end{align}
Consequently, as $m\to\infty$, $\Useminorm f2\to0$ and
\begin{equation}
 \La_3(w)-\tfrac18\ge\frac1{128}\,\Useminorm f2^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:weight-sharp}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Centering removes the zero Fourier coefficient. Every other coefficient
of $f$ has absolute value at most $4aN^{-1/2}$, by
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:20:lem:gauss}. There are at most $N$ coefficients, so
\eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:fourier-u2} proves \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:weight-u}.

Expand $\La_3(h)$ by a triple $(t_0,t_1,t_2)\in\{-2,-1,1,2\}^3$.
At each coordinate, the quadratic form in $(x,y)$ has symmetric matrix
\begin{equation}
 M_t=\begin{pmatrix}
 t_0+t_1+t_2&t_1+2t_2\\
 t_1+2t_2&t_1+4t_2
 \end{pmatrix},
 \quad
 \det M_t=t_0t_1+4t_0t_2+t_1t_2.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:matrix}
\end{equation}
Its determinant has absolute value at most $24$, so vanishing modulo
$29$ is equivalent to integer vanishing. The only vanishing triples are
$(-1,2,-1)$ and $(1,-2,1)$. To check this without a search oracle,
solve
\[
 t_1(t_0+t_2)=-4t_0t_2.
\]
If $t_0+t_2=0$, the right side is nonzero. For equal endpoints the
solution is $t_1=-2t_0$, which is allowed exactly for $t_0=\pm1$.
For unequal endpoints of the same sign the required middle value has
magnitude $8/3$; for unequal endpoints of opposite signs it has magnitude
$8$. Neither is allowed. These exhaust the possible endpoint pairs.
No matrix has rank zero: subtracting its off-diagonal entry from the
bottom-right entry would give $2t_2=0$. Thus two of the $64$ matrices
have rank one and $62$ have rank two. Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:20:lem:gauss} gives
\[
 \La_3(h)=a^3(2N^{-1/2}+62N^{-1}).
\]
Any two progression positions are independent because $p$ is odd.
Expanding the centered triple therefore gives
$\La_3(f)=\La_3(h)-(\E h)^3$. The singleton and pair terms in
$\La_3(1/2+f)$ vanish. This proves \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:weight-excess}.
For $N\ge2$, its right-hand side is at least $2a^3N^{-1/2}$, whereas
\eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:weight-u} implies $\Useminorm f2^2\le16a^2N^{-1/2}$.
Their ratio is at least $a/8=1/128$.
\end{proof}

This construction supplies small global $U^2$ norm through the large
rank of the quadratic phase, while the two rank-one combinations in
\eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:matrix} preserve a larger three-term correlation. Scaling a
fixed cosine alone would not establish the same exponent: it would give
a cubic correlation in its small amplitude.

\subsection{Rounding without losing the critical scale}

A naive assertion that a random rounding is ``close'' is insufficient:
the excess itself is of order $N^{-1/2}$. We need simultaneous control
of a positive count excess and a fourth power of the norm of order
$N^{-1}$. The following argument supplies that control explicitly.

\begin{theorem}[Quadratic sharpness for indicator sets]
\label{gsr:cc:20:thm:indicator-sharpness}
There are subsets $A_m\subset\F_{29}^{2m}$, for all sufficiently large
$m$, with densities $\delta_m\to1/2$ and
$u_m=\Useminorm{1_{A_m}-\delta_m}{2}\to0$, such that
\begin{equation}
 \La_3(1_{A_m})-\delta_m^3\ge c_*u_m^2
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:indicator-sharp}
\end{equation}
for an absolute $c_*>0$. Consequently, for every $\eta>0$, no constant
$C_\eta$ can bound all these errors by $C_\eta u_m^{2+\eta}$.
The failure also holds uniformly for densities in any fixed neighborhood
of $1/2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Include each $x$ independently with probability $w(x)$ from
\eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:weight}. Let $B_x=1_A(x)$, $\delta_A=\E_x B_x$, and put
\[
 X_A=\La_3(1_A)-\delta_A^3,
 \qquad S_A=\Useminorm{1_A-\delta_A}{2}^{4}.
\]
We first show, for all sufficiently large $N$, that
\begin{equation}
 \E_A X_A\ge cN^{-1/2},\qquad
 \E_A S_A\le C/N,
 \quad c=a^3,\quad C=8((4a)^4+2)=513/32.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:round-moments}
\end{equation}

All three points of a progression are distinct unless $y=0$.
Off that diagonal, independence gives the product of the three
probabilities. On the diagonal, $B_x^3=B_x$ and $w(x)\ge w(x)^3$.
Therefore $\E_A\La_3(1_A)\ge\La_3(w)$.
Writing $\xi_x=B_x-w(x)$ and expanding the cube of their average gives
\begin{equation}
 \E_A\delta_A^3
 =\delta^3+\frac{3\delta}{N}\E_x w(x)(1-w(x))
 +\frac1{N^2}\E_x w(x)(1-w(x))(1-2w(x)),
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:density-third}
\end{equation}
where $\delta=1/2$. Since $w(1-w)\le1/4$, Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:20:prop:weight}
yields
\[
 \E_A X_A\ge 2a^3N^{-1/2}-\frac{3}{8N}-\frac1{4N^2}
 \ge a^3N^{-1/2}
\]
for sufficiently large $N$.

For the second assertion, note that
$1_A-\delta_A=f+(\xi-\E_x\xi_x)$.
By \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:fourier-u2}, subtracting the mean removes a nonnegative
term from the fourth power of a $U^2$ norm. Also
\begin{equation}
 \E_A\Useminorm\xi2^4\le2/N.
 \label{gsr:cc:20:eq:noise}
\end{equation}
To prove \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:noise}, expand the parallelogram. Independence and
$\E_A\xi_x=0$ kill any term with a point appearing exactly once.
In an odd-order group, a parallelogram with no singleton among its four
vertices must have $h=0$ or $k=0$. Indeed its three possible pairings
give respectively $h=0$, $k=0$, or $h=k$ and $2h=0$; the last case is
also zero. The union has normalized measure at most $2/N$, and the
absolute value of each expected product is at most one.
The triangle inequality and $(v+w)^4\le8(v^4+w^4)$ now give
\[
 \E_A S_A\le8\left(\Useminorm f2^4+\E_A\Useminorm\xi2^4\right)
 \le C/N,
\]
which proves \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:round-moments}.

The already proved three-term counting inequality implies
$|X_A|\le\sqrt{S_A}$ for every realization (in fact the prefactor is
at most $1/2$). Let
$E=\{X_A\ge c/(2\sqrt N)\}$. By Cauchy--Schwarz,
\[
 \frac c{\sqrt N}\le\E_A X_A
 \le\frac c{2\sqrt N}+\E_A(1_E\sqrt{S_A})
 \le\frac c{2\sqrt N}+\sqrt{C/N}\sqrt{\Pr(E)}.
\]
Consequently $\Pr(E)\ge c^2/(4C)$.
Set $K=8C^2/c^2$. Markov's inequality gives
$\Pr(S_A>K/N)\le c^2/(8C)$.
Finally $\Var(\delta_A)\le1/(4N)$, so
\[
 \Pr(|\delta_A-1/2|>N^{-1/4})\le1/(4\sqrt N).
\]
For all sufficiently large $N$, these estimates leave a positive
probability of all three events
\[
 X_A\ge c/(2\sqrt N),\qquad S_A\le K/N,\qquad
 |\delta_A-1/2|\le N^{-1/4}.
\]
Choose one such realization for each large $m$.
Then $u_m^2=\sqrt{S_{A_m}}\le\sqrt{K/N}$ and
\eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:indicator-sharp} holds with
$c_*=c/(2\sqrt K)>0$.
The norm cannot be zero when $X_A>0$. Dividing by $u_m^{2+\eta}$
now yields a lower bound $c_*u_m^{-\eta}\to\infty$, proving the
claimed impossibility.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
New in this report: source~06's three-term coefficient is sharp only at singletons ($\delta=1/N$); this theorem shows that the exponent $2$ cannot be raised at fixed density near $1/2$, for indicator sets on $\F_{29}^{2m}$. Not for prime cyclic groups or $k\ge4$ (the source's non-claims; item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:density}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Every length, prime cyclic groups} (source~100, Section~\ref{gsr:cc:sec:quadbarrier}): the quadratic exponent is sharp for every fixed $k\ge3$ and norm order $d\ge2$, on every large $\Z/Q\Z$ and on $\F_p^n$ for each fixed $p>k$, with exact cardinalities and either sign (Theorems~\ref{gsr:cc:100:thm:prime}, \ref{gsr:cc:100:thm:field}); this answers this source's Questions~1 and~3.
\end{writenote}

The constant $c_*$ is intentionally crude. The theorem determines an
exponent, not the optimal coefficient in the indicator-set extremal
problem. The finite check of the weight construction uses $m=1$;
the existence proof for the rounded sets is asymptotic and does not
claim that its crude probability thresholds are useful computationally.

\section{Source~21's chapter: the exponent-five coefficient, with source~23's second route \wtag}\label{gsr:cc:sec:charfive}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the fifth write, 6~October 2026.}}\par
The next ten sections settle the question that source~14's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:14:thm:exponent-five} left open: on groups of exponent five, the first correction after $6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4$ in the centered three-cube problem has exponent six, and its coefficient is now known. Sections~\ref{gsr:cc:21:sec:d2}--\ref{gsr:cc:21:sec:d9} are source~21, the main source; Sections~\ref{gsr:cc:23:sec:d7}--\ref{gsr:cc:23:sec:dA} are source~23's Section~7 and Appendix~A, an independent proof of the same theorem, written the same day from a pin three minutes later, printed here as a credited second route. Neither source cites the other; both cite source~14's manuscript. \emph{Logically the chapter follows source~14's Section~\ref{gsr:cc:14:sec:d3}}; it is printed here, at the end of Part~III, because no number printed earlier may move. Source~21's introduction, with the main theorem (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:21:thm:main}), is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:21:sec:d1}; its repository interface, questions and appendices are in Part~V (Sections~\ref{gsr:fz:21:sec:d10}--\ref{gsr:fz:21:sec:dB}). Source~23's introduction is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:23:sec:d1}. Their notation is in the table at the head of this Part.

\emph{What is proved, in one paragraph.} For real centered $f$ on any nontrivial finite abelian group of exponent five and $u=\norm f_{U^3}\le c\delta$, $Q_3(\delta+f)\le\delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4+C_5\delta^2u^6+Cu^8$ with $C_5=2^{3/4}/3$ and absolute $c$, $C$, sharp on every fixed such group (source~21's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:21:thm:main}, Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:21:cor:pullback}; source~23's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:23:five:main}). The mechanism is the same in both: a positive cubic statistic controls the sixth- and seventh-degree terms through the Fourier tail, and the order-five resonance makes the cost of the second harmonic quadratic. Source~21 also proves the phase envelope $C_5(\cos\theta)_+^2/(1+\cos^2\phi)$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:21:thm:phase}), rigidity of near-extremizers (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:21:thm:rigidity}; source~23's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:23:five:rigidity} is equivalent), the next coefficient $20/9$ on $\Z/5\Z$ for the maximum (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:21:thm:five-point-next}; source~23's Appendix~A computes $20/9$ for one model, a lower bound), indicator sharpness through $u^8$ as lower examples (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:21:thm:indicator}; source~23 through $u^6$) and a projection consequence of cube Cauchy--Schwarz (Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:21:prop:projection}). The universal coefficient of $u^8$ is open (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:eighth}).

\emph{Relation to the formal statements} (checked at HEAD \texttt{2dfe46f44}). \file{lemma_3_10} (\file{Sections01\_03.lean}, line~340) is an exact companion (\file{lemma_3_10_holds}, \file{Proofs03CubeUpper.lean}, line~82), as source~21 records; no characteristic-five or cube-expansion declaration exists. Nothing in this chapter is formalized.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Fourier identities and the sharp quartic deficit\srctag{21}}]{Fourier identities and the sharp quartic deficit}\label{gsr:cc:21:sec:d2}
\srcnote{21}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:cc:21:sec:fourier}

For $f:G\to\C$, our Fourier convention is
\[
 a_r=\widehat f(r)=\E_{x\in G}f(x)\overline{r(x)},
 \qquad f(x)=\sum_{r\in\widehat G}a_r r(x).
\]
Throughout the main argument $f$ is real and centered, so
$a_{-r}=\overline{a_r}$ and $a_0=0$.  Set
\begin{equation}
 \lambda_r=|a_r|^2,\qquad S=\sum_r|a_r|^4=\|f\|_{U^2}^4,
 \qquad M=\sum_r|a_r|^8.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:fourier-statistics}
\end{equation}
All sums on the dual group are unnormalized.

\begin{lemma}[A sum of Fourier squares]
\label{gsr:cc:21:lem:fourier-squares}
Define
\begin{equation}
 T(s,t)=\sum_r a_r\overline{a_{r+s}}\,
                 \overline{a_{r+t}}a_{r+s+t}.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:T}
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}
                 \|f\|_{U^3}^8=\sum_{s,t}|T(s,t)|^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:squares}
\end{equation}
For real $f$, $T(s,t)$ is real, is symmetric in $s,t$, and is unchanged
by replacing either $s$ or $t$ by its negative.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Insert Fourier inversion in the eight-vertex cube.  Averaging over
$x,h_1,h_2,h_3$ imposes the four equations
\[
 \sum_\omega r_\omega=0,
 \qquad \sum_\omega\omega_j r_\omega=0\quad(1\le j\le3).
\]
Their solutions are precisely the parity-adjusted affine frequency
cubes.  Grouping two opposite faces gives the expansion of the
right side of \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:squares}.  Equivalently, one can expand the
right side and use its four free frequencies as parameters for the
same four equations.  This parameterization uses only invertible
integer changes of variables, so the identity holds on every finite
abelian group.

In \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:T}, the substitution $r\mapsto-r-s-t$ pairs each
summand with its complex conjugate because $a_{-r}=\overline{a_r}$.
Hence $T$ is real.  Interchanging $s,t$ is immediate; shifting the
base $r$ after changing the sign of one increment conjugates $T$,
and so leaves it unchanged in the real case.
\end{proof}

Define the positive energy
\[
 \mathcal E(\lambda)=\sum_{r+s=t+w}
             \lambda_r\lambda_s\lambda_t\lambda_w
             =\sum_v(\lambda*\lambda)(v)^2,
\]
where the convolution is an unnormalized sum.  Since $\lambda$ is
even, $T(0,t)=\sum_r\lambda_r\lambda_{r+t}$, and $T(0,0)=S$.
The two axes of \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:squares} therefore contribute exactly
\begin{equation}
                 2\mathcal E(\lambda)-S^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:axes}
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}[Quartic comparison and concentration]
\label{gsr:cc:21:lem:quartic-gap}
For every real centered $f$ on an odd-order finite abelian group,
\begin{equation}
 u^8\ge5S^2-6M\ge2S^2,
 \qquad u=\|f\|_{U^3}.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:quartic-gap}
\end{equation}
If $f\ne0$, choose a largest conjugate pair $\{\xi,-\xi\}$ and put
\begin{equation}
 \rho=|a_\xi|,
 \qquad D=\sum_{r\notin\{\xi,-\xi\}}|a_r|^4,
 \qquad S=2\rho^4+D.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:tail}
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}
             u^8\ge2S^2+3DS.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:largest-pair-gap}
\end{equation}
In particular, equality in $u^8\ge2S^2$ for nonzero $f$ forces exactly
one conjugate Fourier pair.  In exponent five, every such pair gives
equality.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write the energy as a sum over $r+s+t+w=0$.  Retain the union of the
three families obtained by pairing the four entries into opposite
pairs.  Each family has weight $S^2$, every pairwise intersection has
weight $M$, and the triple intersection has weight zero: it requires
$2r=0$, and the zero Fourier coefficient vanishes.  Thus
$\mathcal E(\lambda)\ge3S^2-3M$.  Combine this with
\eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:axes}.

The nonzero Fourier coefficients come in conjugate pairs.  If their
fourth-power masses are $x_j=2|a_{r_j}|^4$, then
$S=\sum_jx_j$ and $M=\frac12\sum_jx_j^2\le S^2/2$.
This proves the second inequality and its necessary equality case.
Maximality also gives $M\le\rho^4S=(S-D)S/2$, yielding
\eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:largest-pair-gap}.  For a pure pair of order five,
directly evaluating \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:squares} gives $u^8=8\rho^8=2S^2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Credit.} The inequality $u^8\ge2S^2$ for real centered $f$ on odd-order groups is source~04's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:04:cub:norm-gap}; source~14 reproves it (its display~\eqref{gsr:cc:14:eq:old-norm-gap}). The refinement \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:largest-pair-gap} with the tail $D$ is the form used below.
\end{writenote}

The last sufficiency statement was restricted deliberately.  For
example, short resonances at order three change the norm of a pure
pair.  The present report does not silently extend an exponent-five
equality formula to all odd orders.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Higher centered coefficients with a retained Fourier tail\srctag{21}}]{Higher centered coefficients with a retained Fourier tail}\label{gsr:cc:21:sec:d3}
\srcnote{21}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:cc:21:sec:centered}

The following exact expansion introduces the terms whose crude
treatment prevented the earlier coefficient from being identified.

\begin{lemma}[Centered cube expansion]
\label{gsr:cc:21:lem:centered}
On an exponent-five group,
\begin{equation}
 Q_3(\delta+f)=\delta^8+12\delta^4S+8\delta^3B_5(f)
                  +\delta^2 C_6(f)+\delta C_7(f)+u^8,
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:centered}
\end{equation}
where $C_j$ is the sum of all $j$-vertex centered terms and
\begin{equation}
               B_5(f)=\sum_r a_{2r}a_{-r}^{3}a_r.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:B5}
\end{equation}
The number $B_5(f)$ is real.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Expand the product over subsets of the eight vertices.  One, two,
or three distinct cube forms are jointly uniform, so centering kills
their expectations.  Among the $70$ four-element supports, the $12$
parallelograms have a one-dimensional relation and contribute $S$;
the other $58$ supports are independent over $\F_5$.

Of the $56$ five-element supports, $48$ have a relation with a zero
coefficient, forcing a factor $a_0$ in their Fourier expectation.
The remaining eight are cube-symmetric copies of
$\{000,100,010,001,111\}$.  If the frequency at $111$ is $r$,
the four orthogonality equations force frequencies
$2r,-r,-r,-r,r$ on this support.  This proves \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:B5}.
Negating $r$ conjugates a summand, so the sum is real.

The support counts may also be checked by row reduction of the
columns $(1,\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3)$, as described in
Appendix~\ref{gsr:fz:21:app:certificates}.  The nonzero determinants needed for
these classifications have absolute value at most two; in
characteristic five their ranks agree with the stated ranks.
\end{proof}

Cube Cauchy--Schwarz alone gives $|C_6|\le28u^6$ and
$|C_7|\le8u^7$.  The first of these bounds is too large to
determine the coefficient of $u^6$.  We instead use the positive
statistic
\begin{equation}
             H=\sum_{r+s+t=0}\lambda_r\lambda_s\lambda_t.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:H}
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Sextic and septic profile inequalities]
\label{gsr:cc:21:thm:six-seven}
For every real centered $f$ on an exponent-five group,
\begin{equation}
              |C_6(f)|\le28H,
              \qquad |C_7(f)|\le8u^4\sqrt H.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:six-seven}
\end{equation}
For a largest pair and tail $D$ as in \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:tail},
\begin{equation}
 H\le3\sqrt{D\mathcal E(\lambda)}
       \le\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}u^4\sqrt D.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:H-tail}
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{align}
 |C_6(f)|&\le42\sqrt3\,u^4D^{1/2},\notag\\
 |C_7(f)|&\le8\sqrt{3\sqrt3/2}\,u^6D^{1/4}.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:tail-six-seven}
\end{align}
No bound on $\|f\|_\infty$ is assumed.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Classify a six-vertex support by the two omitted vertices.  Their
Hamming distance is one, two, or three.  The respective numbers of
unordered pairs are $12,12,4$.  Fourier orthogonality gives the
following representatives, with all frequency sums over $\widehat G$:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}ccl@{}}
\toprule
Omitted vertices&Multiplicity&Six-vertex expectation\\
\midrule
$000,001$&$12$&$H$\\
$000,011$&$12$&$\displaystyle J=\sum_{r,s}\lambda_r a_s^2
                                  a_{r-s}\overline{a_{r+s}}$\\
$000,111$&$4$&$\displaystyle K=\sum_{r+s+t=0}a_r^2a_s^2a_t^2$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Each formula follows by solving the same four equations used in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:21:lem:fourier-squares}, now with the omitted frequencies
set to zero.  Clearly $|K|\le H$.  For $J$, Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\begin{align*}
 |J|&\le\sum_{r,s}\lambda_r\lambda_s
                 \sqrt{\lambda_{r-s}\lambda_{r+s}}\\
 &\le\left(\sum_{r,s}\lambda_r\lambda_s\lambda_{r-s}\right)^{1/2}
       \left(\sum_{r,s}\lambda_r\lambda_s\lambda_{r+s}\right)^{1/2}
 =H,
\end{align*}
using evenness of $\lambda$.  This proves the sextic bound.

For the septic bound, replace the zero Fourier coefficient in $T$ by
a real variable $\delta$ and differentiate at $\delta=0$.  The
derivative is
\begin{equation}
 L(s,t)=2\Rea(a_sa_t\overline{a_{s+t}})
       +2\Rea(a_s\overline{a_t}\,\overline{a_{s-t}}).
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:L}
\end{equation}
This is the sum of the four terms obtained by choosing which of
the four factors contains the differentiated zero coefficient.
If indices coincide, the extra zero coefficients make the
corresponding terms vanish, so the formula still applies.
Each of these four cubic terms has squared $\ell^2$ norm $H$.
Thus $\|L\|_2\le4\sqrt H$.  Differentiating the sum of squares gives
\[
 C_7(f)=2\Rea\langle T,L\rangle,
 \qquad |C_7(f)|\le2\|T\|_2\|L\|_2\le8u^4\sqrt H.
\]

Finally, no triple drawn from $\{\xi,-\xi\}$ sums to zero because
$\xi$ has order five.  Every nonzero summand in $H$ contains at
least one tail index.  Therefore
\[
 H\le3\sum_{r\notin\{\xi,-\xi\}}
            \lambda_r(\lambda*\lambda)(-r)
   \le3\sqrt{D\mathcal E(\lambda)}.
\]
The axes in \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:squares} give
$\mathcal E(\lambda)\le(u^8+S^2)/2$.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:21:lem:quartic-gap} gives $S^2\le u^8/2$,
proving \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:H-tail} and \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:tail-six-seven}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why the two improvements must be used together]
The new bounds express the higher coefficients in terms of the
same tail $D$ that lowers the quartic contribution.  A merely
qualitative statement that $C_6$ tends to zero near a pure pair would
give a sharp coefficient with an unspecified little-oh error.  The
powers $D^{1/2}$ and $D^{1/4}$ allow the explicit $O(u^8)$ remainder.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The characteristic-five resonance and a finite bound\srctag{21}}]{The characteristic-five resonance and a finite bound}\label{gsr:cc:21:sec:d4}
\srcnote{21}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:cc:21:sec:resonance}

For a largest pair, set $b=|a_{2\xi}|$.  The pair
$\{2\xi,-2\xi\}$ is distinct from $\{\xi,-\xi\}$, so
$2b^4\le D$.  When $b>0$, write
\begin{equation}
 a_\xi=\rho e^{i\alpha},\qquad a_{2\xi}=b e^{i\beta},
 \qquad \theta=2\alpha-\beta,
 \qquad \phi=3\alpha+\beta.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:angles}
\end{equation}
These phases are understood modulo $2\pi$.  Notice the useful
identity $\theta+\phi=5\alpha$.

\begin{theorem}[A joint norm penalty]
\label{gsr:cc:21:thm:joint-gap}
With the preceding notation,
\begin{equation}
 u^8\ge2S^2+12\rho^4D+16\rho^6b^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:joint-gap}
\end{equation}
Let $D_{\rm out}=\sum_{r\notin\langle\xi\rangle}|a_r|^4$.
If $b>0$, the stronger finite inequality is
\begin{equation}
 u^8\ge2S^2+12\rho^4D+16\rho^6b^2
       +4\pos{2\rho^3b|\cos\phi|-D_{\rm out}}^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:phase-gap}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
In the four-frequency zero-sum representation of
$\mathcal E(\lambda)$, retain, in addition to the three
opposite-pair families, all permutations of
$(\xi,\xi,\xi,2\xi)$ and of its negative.
There are eight such ordered tuples, each with weight
$\rho^6b^2$.  They sum to zero because $5\xi=0$, and none belongs
to a retained opposite-pair family.  Thus
\[
 u^8\ge5S^2-6M+16\rho^6b^2.
\]
Conjugate pairing in the tail gives
$M\le2\rho^8+D^2/2$.  Expanding $S=2\rho^4+D$ now yields
\[
 5S^2-6M\ge8\rho^8+20\rho^4D+2D^2
               =2S^2+12\rho^4D.
\]

For the stronger statement retain the four off-axis slots
$(s,t)=(\pm2\xi,\pm2\xi)$ in \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:squares}.
They are distinct, and all have the same $T$ value.  The contribution
from bases in $\langle\xi\rangle$ is
\[
 T(2\xi,2\xi)=a_\xi^3a_{2\xi}
             +\overline{a_\xi^3a_{2\xi}}+E
             =2\rho^3b\cos\phi+E.
\]
For a base outside $\langle\xi\rangle$, all four shifted indices
remain outside it.  H\"older's inequality therefore gives
$|E|\le D_{\rm out}$.  The four retained squares contribute at
least the final term in \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:phase-gap}.
\end{proof}

The extra term $16\rho^6b^2$ is the decisive order-five resonance.
Without such a quadratic cost in the second harmonic, balancing a
quartic tail cost against the quintic gain can produce fractional
powers, as in the earlier $u^{16/3}$ result.  Here the balance is
quadratic and forces the smaller second harmonic $b\asymp u^2/\delta$.

\begin{proposition}[Explicit finite Fourier-profile bound]
\label{gsr:cc:21:prop:finite-profile}
For every $\delta\ge0$ and every nonzero real centered $f$ on an
exponent-five group,
\begin{align}
 Q_3(\delta+f)\le{}&\delta^8+12\delta^4S
       +16\delta^3\rho^4b\cos\theta+8\delta^3\rho D\notag\\
 &+42\sqrt3\,\delta^2u^4D^{1/2}
       +8\sqrt{3\sqrt3/2}\,\delta u^6D^{1/4}+u^8.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:finite-profile}
\end{align}
If $b=0$, its cosine term is interpreted as zero.  This bound and
the constraints \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:joint-gap}--\eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:phase-gap} are finite
inequalities, with no asymptotic qualification.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The two selected summands $r=\pm\xi$ in \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:B5} give
$2\rho^4b\cos\theta$ exactly.  Every other summand has absolute
value at most $\rho|a_r|^4$, because $\rho$ is the largest Fourier
amplitude.  Hence
\begin{equation}
 B_5(f)=2\rho^4b\cos\theta+E_5,
 \qquad |E_5|\le\rho D.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:B5-tail}
\end{equation}
Use this identity and Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:21:thm:six-seven} in
\eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:centered}.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Sharp uniform optimization and the phase envelope\srctag{21}}]{Sharp uniform optimization and the phase envelope}\label{gsr:cc:21:sec:d5}
\srcnote{21}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:cc:21:sec:optimization}

We now prove Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:21:thm:main}.  The proof first locates the
Fourier mass and then absorbs the remaining higher-degree terms.
This order is necessary: dropping the negative tail term too early
would lose the eighth-order remainder.

\begin{lemma}[Uniform localization]
\label{gsr:cc:21:lem:localization}
Let $\|g\|_{U^3}=1$, let $t>0$, and put
\[
 S_0=2^{-1/2},\qquad \eta=S_0-S,\qquad
 F=Q_3(1+tg)-1-6\sqrt2\,t^4,
\]
where the Fourier statistics refer to $g$.  If $F>0$ and $t$ is
sufficiently small, then, with absolute implied constants,
\begin{equation}
          \eta=O(t^2),\qquad D=O(t^2),\qquad b=O(t).
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:localization}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
First $S\le S_0$ by Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:21:lem:quartic-gap}.  Cube
Cauchy--Schwarz and \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:centered} give
\[
 F=-12\eta t^4+8B_5(g)t^5+R,
 \qquad |R|\le28t^6+8t^7+t^8\le37t^6\quad(t\le1).
\]
Also $|B_5(g)|\le\rho S\le1$.  Thus $F>0$ implies
$\eta=O(t)$, and $S$ is bounded below by a positive constant for
small $t$.  Equation~\eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:largest-pair-gap} yields
\[
 3DS\le1-2S^2=2\eta(S_0+S),
\]
so $D=O(\eta)$.  It follows that
$\rho^4=(S_0-\eta-D)/2$ is bounded below.  The resonance penalty
in \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:joint-gap} now gives $b^2=O(\eta)$.

Equation~\eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:B5-tail} gives
$|B_5(g)|=O(\sqrt\eta+\eta)$.  Substituting in the preceding
expression for $F$ gives
\[
 \eta\le A t\sqrt\eta+B t\eta+C t^2
\]
with absolute constants.  For small $t$, absorb $Bt\eta$.
The resulting quadratic inequality in $\sqrt\eta$ implies
$\sqrt\eta=O(t)$, proving all three claims.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:21:thm:main}, upper bound]
If $u=0$, the norm property gives $f=0$.  Otherwise set
$g=f/u$ and $t=u/\delta$.  Then
$Q_3(\delta+f)=\delta^8Q_3(1+tg)$.
If $F\le0$, the asserted upper bound is immediate, so assume $F>0$.
All the following Fourier variables refer to $g$.

By localization,
\[
 \rho^4=2^{-3/2}+O(t^2),\qquad
 \rho^6=2^{-9/4}+O(t^2).
\]
Expand \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:joint-gap}, using
$1-2S^2=2\sqrt2\eta-2\eta^2$, to obtain
\begin{equation}
           \eta\ge\frac32D+2^{1/4}b^2-O(t^4).
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:deficit}
\end{equation}
The constants are absolute.  Use
$B_5(g)\le S_0b+D$ and \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:tail-six-seven} to get
\begin{align}
 F\le{}&-18Dt^4-12\,2^{1/4}b^2t^4+4\sqrt2\,bt^5+8Dt^5
           \notag\\
 &+K_6t^6D^{1/2}+K_7t^7D^{1/4}+O(t^8),
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:before-absorption}
\end{align}
where $K_6=42\sqrt3$ and $K_7=8\sqrt{3\sqrt3/2}$.

For sufficiently small $t$, $-18D+8Dt\le-17D$.
Set $D=t^4y$.  All the terms involving $D$ in
\eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:before-absorption} are then bounded above by
\[
       t^8\bigl(-17y+K_6\sqrt y+K_7y^{1/4}\bigr)=O(t^8),
\]
because the continuous expression in parentheses tends to $-\infty$
as $y\to\infty$.  Finally,
\begin{equation}
 \sup_{b\ge0}\{-12\,2^{1/4}b^2t^4+4\sqrt2\,bt^5\}
        =C_5t^6,
 \qquad b=\beta_5t.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:quadratic-optimum}
\end{equation}
Rescaling by $\delta^8$ proves \eqref{gsr:fm:21:eq:main-upper}.  The error is
$O(\delta^8t^8)=O(u^8)$ with an absolute constant, not merely
an unspecified density-dependent error.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp phase-dependent coefficient]
\label{gsr:cc:21:thm:phase}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:21:thm:main}, choose a largest
conjugate pair.  If $b>0$ and the phases are as in
\eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:angles}, then, with absolute $c,C>0$,
\begin{equation}
 Q_3(\delta+f)\le\delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4
   +C_5\frac{(\cos\theta)_+^2}{1+\cos^2\phi}\,\delta^2u^6
   +Cu^8\quad(u\le c\delta).
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:phase-envelope}
\end{equation}
For $b=0$, the same assertion holds with the $u^6$ coefficient zero.
For each prescribed pair of phases, the coefficient in
\eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:phase-envelope} is attained asymptotically by weights on
$\Z/5\Z$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
As before, the case $F\le0$ is immediate.  In the case $F>0$,
localization applies.  The elementary inequality
$(x-y)_+^2\ge x^2-2xy$ for $x,y\ge0$ turns
\eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:phase-gap} into
\[
 \eta\ge\frac32D+2^{1/4}(1+\cos^2\phi)b^2
                    -O(t^4+bD).
\]
The selected quintic term is $2\rho^4b\cos\theta$.
Replacing $2\rho^4$ by $S_0$ here introduces an absolute error
$O((\eta+D)b)=O(t^3)$, regardless of the sign of the cosine;
after multiplication by $t^5$ this is $O(t^8)$.
The extra $O(bD)t^4$ is absorbed against the negative tail term
because $b=O(t)$.  The other tail terms are treated exactly as
in \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:before-absorption}.

The remaining one-variable optimization is
\[
 \sup_{b\ge0}\{-12\,2^{1/4}(1+\cos^2\phi)b^2t^4
                    +4\sqrt2\,b\cos\theta\,t^5\}
 =C_5\frac{(\cos\theta)_+^2}{1+\cos^2\phi}t^6.
\]
The maximizing scale is
\begin{equation}
        b=\beta_5t\,
              \frac{(\cos\theta)_+}{1+\cos^2\phi}.
 \label{gsr:cc:21:eq:phase-b}
\end{equation}
For fixed phases with $\cos\theta>0$, the exact five-point
formulas in Section~\ref{gsr:cc:21:sec:five-point-next}, with unnormalized
second amplitude
$\beta_5\delta^{-1}u^2(\cos\theta)_+/(1+\cos^2\phi)$,
give a matching coefficient and an $O_\delta(u^8)$ error.
The first amplitude is chosen to make the centered norm exactly $u$.
If $\cos\theta\le0$, take a positive second amplitude
$o(\delta^{-1}u^2)$ with the specified phase.  The coefficient is
then zero; for example $b=\delta^{-3}u^4$ gives an $O_\delta(u^8)$
error.  The case $b=0$ follows directly from the same absorption
argument with no selected quintic term.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Real Fourier coefficients lose a factor of two]
For a positive real dominant coefficient and a positive real second
coefficient, $\theta=\phi=0$.  The phase factor in
\eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:phase-envelope} is $1/2$.  The full coefficient requires
$\theta=0$ and $\cos\phi=0$, which can be achieved by
$a_\xi=\rho e^{i\pi/10}$ and $a_{2\xi}=b e^{i\pi/5}$.
The extremizing physical-space function is still real: the negative
Fourier coefficients are the complex conjugates of the positive ones.
\end{remark}


\begin{figure}[tbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=.96\textwidth]{figures/21-characteristic-five-phase_envelope.pdf}
\caption{The exact phase factor in Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:21:thm:phase}.
The marked point $\theta=0$, $\phi=\pi/2$ gives the full sharp
coefficient; positive real coefficients give the value $1/2$ at
$\theta=\phi=0$.  The factor vanishes when $\cos\theta\le0$.}
\label{gsr:cc:21:fig:phase}
\end{figure}
