\section[{A quantitative global obstruction to the high-degree norm construction\srctag{22}}]{A quantitative global obstruction to the high-degree norm construction}\label{gsr:cc:22:sec:d10}\label{gsr:cc:22:sec:norm-obstruction}
\srcnote{22}{Section 10}

Let $q$ be a power of an odd prime $p$.  Write $E_t=\mathbb F_{q^t}$,
regarded as a $t$-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb F_q$, and write
$N_t=N_{E_t/\mathbb F_q}$.  The function $N_t$ is represented by a
homogeneous polynomial of degree $t$ in any linear coordinate basis.
All progressions below are ordered start--direction pairs; directions
are not identified up to scaling or orientation.

\begin{lemma}[Exact constant-line ratios for the degree-$p$ norm]\label{gsr:cc:22:lem:norm-lines}
Define
\[
 \mathcal T=\{\theta\in E_p:\theta^q-\theta\in\mathbb F_p^*\}.
\]
Then $|\mathcal T|=q(p-1)$, every element of $\mathcal T$ is nonzero,
and for $\theta\in E_p$ the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $N_p(\theta+j)$ is independent of $j\in\mathbb F_p$;
\item $\theta\in\mathcal T$;
\item as a polynomial in $T$,
\[
 N_p(\theta+T)=T^p-T+\theta^p-\theta.
\]
\end{enumerate}
Consequently, the number of pairs $(a,h)\in E_p\times E_p^*$ for which
$N_p(a+jh)$ is constant for every $j\in\mathbb F_p$ is exactly
\[
                 (q^p-1)q(p-1).
\]
For each fixed $a\ne0$, there are exactly $q(p-1)$ such directions;
for $a=0$, there are none.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For $c\in\mathbb F_p^*$ the polynomial $X^q-X-c$ has $q$ distinct
roots in an algebraic closure, since its derivative is $-1$.  If
$\theta$ is a root, iteration gives
$\theta^{q^j}=\theta+jc$, and hence $\theta^{q^p}=\theta$.
Thus all these roots lie in $E_p$.  The root sets for different $c$
are disjoint, proving $|\mathcal T|=q(p-1)$.  They avoid zero.
For such a $\theta$, its $p$ Frobenius conjugates are exactly
$\theta+\mathbb F_p$, because $c\ne0$.  Therefore
\[
 N_p(\theta+T)
   =\prod_{j\in\mathbb F_p}(\theta+T+j)
   =(\theta+T)^p-(\theta+T)
   =T^p-T+\theta^p-\theta.
\]
This proves (ii)$\Rightarrow$(iii)$\Rightarrow$(i).

Conversely, put $P(T)=N_p(\theta+T)$, a monic polynomial of degree
$p$ over $\mathbb F_q$.  If (i) holds, $P(T)-P(0)$ vanishes at all
$p$ elements of $\mathbb F_p$; it is monic of degree $p$, so
$P(T)-P(0)=T^p-T$.  In particular $P$ is separable.  If
$\theta\in\mathbb F_q$ then $P(T)=(T+\theta)^p$, a contradiction.
Since $[E_p:\mathbb F_q]=p$, the element $\theta$ therefore has
degree $p$ over $\mathbb F_q$.  The roots of $P$ are both its
distinct Frobenius conjugates $-\theta^{q^j}$ and the translates
$-\theta+\mathbb F_p$.  Hence $\theta^q-\theta\in\mathbb F_p$;
this difference is nonzero because $\theta\notin\mathbb F_q$.
Thus (i)$\Rightarrow$(ii).

For $h\ne0$, multiplicativity of the norm shows that the progression
condition is equivalent to $a/h\in\mathcal T$.  There are $q^p-1$
choices of $h$ and $q(p-1)$ choices of this ratio.  For fixed $a\ne0$,
the directions are $h=a/\theta$, $\theta\in\mathcal T$, and are
distinct; $a=0$ gives ratio zero and therefore no direction.
\end{proof}

The word ``exact'' in this lemma concerns constancy on the full
$p$-point prime-field progression.  It does not assert an exact count
for the weaker reflection equalities on $\ell<p$ points.

\begin{proposition}[Every norm block of degree divisible by the characteristic]
Suppose $p\mid t$.  At every $a\in E_t^*$ there are at least
$q(p-1)$ distinct $h\in E_t^*$ such that $N_t(a+jh)$ is constant
for all $j\in\mathbb F_p$.  Hence this norm has at least
\[
                     (q^t-1)q(p-1)
\]
ordered nonconstant-direction progressions on which its value is constant.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The subfield $E_p\subset E_t$ exists because $p\mid t$.  Use
$\mathcal T\subset E_p^*$ from the lemma.  For $x\in E_p$,
transitivity of the norm gives
\[
 N_t(x)=N_p(x)^{t/p}.
\]
For each $a\ne0$ and $\theta\in\mathcal T$, put $h=a/\theta$.
Then
\[
 N_t(a+jh)=N_t(h)N_p(\theta+j)^{t/p},
\]
which is independent of $j$.  Distinct $\theta$ give distinct
directions.  Counting over the nonzero starts proves the assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Quantitative excess for a layered norm map]\label{gsr:cc:22:thm:norm-excess}
Consider a direct-sum norm construction on $B$ controlled coordinates,
with any number $f\ge0$ of additional ignored coordinates, so the domain
has dimension $n=B+f$.  Each controlled block has dimension $t$ and
contributes its norm $N_t$ to one specified coordinate of the coloring.
Different blocks use disjoint coordinates.  Let $\mathcal J$ be any
collection of its blocks whose degrees $t_j$ are divisible by $p$.
For any even $\ell<p$, let $S_z$ denote the directions producing reflection
symmetry about $z$ on the standard centered $\ell$-term progression, including
zero.  Then
\[
 |S_z|\ge q^f\prod_{j\in\mathcal J}
 \left(1+q(p-1)\,1_{\{z_j\ne0\}}\right).
\]
Consequently the number $A_\ell^{\rm sym}$ of ordered nontrivial symmetric
$\ell$-term progressions satisfies
\[
 A_\ell^{\rm sym}\ge q^n\left[
 q^f\prod_{j\in\mathcal J}
 \left(1+q(p-1)(1-q^{-t_j})\right)-1\right].
\]
In particular, the presence of one such block of degree $t$ forces an
excess of at least
\[
 q^{2n-B-t}(q^t-1)q(p-1)
\]
above the value $q^n(q^f-1)$ supplied solely by ignored coordinates.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
At a fixed center, set the direction in every unselected controlled
block to zero.  In a selected block $j$, always allow direction zero;
when $z_j\ne0$, additionally allow the $q(p-1)$ directions given by
the preceding proposition.  Each selected block then has a constant
norm along every prime-field parameter, so their sums in each output
coordinate are constant too.  The centered parameters for the standard
even $\ell$-term progression belong to $\mathbb F_p$.  Every chosen direction
therefore satisfies all the required reflection equalities.  The ignored
coordinates admit arbitrary directions, giving $q^f$ choices.
All these choices are independent and distinct.  This proves the local
product bound.

The starts and centered parametrizations are in bijection.  Sum
$|S_z|-1$ over centers.  For each selected block, $z_j$ is independently
uniform in its $q^{t_j}$-element space; its nonzero probability is
$1-q^{-t_j}$.  The averaged product gives the displayed global bound.
Taking one block and using $f=n-B$ gives the final expression.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{The first high-degree four-term example.}
Take $q=p=5$, $\ell=4$, and $Q=N_3+N_5$ on
$\mathbb F_5^3\oplus\mathbb F_5^5$.  The highest-two-odd-degree
construction attains $S_0=\{0\}$: the two reflection equations at
$\pm1/2$ and $\pm3/2$ form an invertible matrix on the cubic and quintic
norm values.  Nevertheless the degree-five block forces at least
\[
 5^3(5^5-1)\,5(5-1)=7\,810\,000
\]
ordered nontrivial symmetric four-term progressions.  Indeed, at every
center whose quintic block is nonzero, it supplies at least twenty
nonzero directions with the cubic block frozen.  There are
$5^3(5^5-1)$ such centers.  This distinguishes sharpness at one prescribed
center from simultaneous global sharpness of a particular construction.
It does not preclude a different degree-five polynomial from avoiding
these patterns.

\section{Sources~29 and~28: the odd-order constants \texorpdfstring{$c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}$}{c(d,odd)} \wtag}\label{gsr:cc:sec:oddconstant}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the sixth write, 6~October 2026.}}\par
The next four sections are about $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}=\sup\norm f_{U^2}^4/\norm f_{U^d}^4$ over real centered $f$ on groups of odd order, source~03's Research question~1 and source~04's Question~3, settled for $d=3$ by source~04's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:04:cub:norm-gap} ($c_3^{\mathrm{odd}}=2^{-1/2}$) and open for $d\ge4$. \emph{Logically the chapter follows source~04's Section~\ref{gsr:cc:04:sec:d6}}; it is printed here because no number printed earlier may move. Sections~\ref{gsr:cc:29:sec:d2}--\ref{gsr:cc:29:sec:d4} are source~29's, the main source; Section~\ref{gsr:cc:28:sec:d8} is source~28's, written from the same pin; neither cites the other.

\emph{What is proved, in one paragraph.} For real $f$ with no Fourier mass on self-inverse characters, $\norm f_{U^d}^{2^d}\ge2^{-m}\binom{2m}m\norm f_{U^2}^{2^d}$, $m=2^{d-2}$ (source~29's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:moment-theorem}; the moment inequality is sharp, the norm comparison is not claimed sharp), so $c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le(8/35)^{1/4}=0.6914416$ and $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}\le B_d\downarrow1/2$ (Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:cd-upper}); an interval model gives $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}\ge1/3$ for every $d$, so the limit lies in $[1/3,1/2]$ (Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:one-third}); with self-inverse mass the profile $K_m(\tau)$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:torsion-profile}). Source~28 proves the weaker universal $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}\le\sqrt{160/323}$ for $d\ge4$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:28:uq:main-gap}), the lower bound $c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\ge0.5587294$ by an exact two-harmonic witness (Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:28:uq:witness}), and that a single cosine is not a local extremizer for any $d\ge4$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:28:uq:all-d-obstruction}). The intake's exact certificate on $\Z/7\Z$ gives $c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\ge0.5587725$ (note after Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:28:uq:witness}). The bracket printed here is therefore $0.5587725\le c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le0.6914416$, among sources~01--33; sources~34, 35 and~45, placed and not yet written, record upper coefficients $81/16$, $5$ and $4795/832$, that is $c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le2/3$ and $\le0.6454070$ (note after Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:cd-upper}). In the quartic cube term the coefficient $100/\sqrt2=70.71$ at $d=4$ becomes $100(8/35)^{1/4}=69.14$ (source~29's \eqref{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:quartic-improvement}; source~28's corollary has $70.38$).

\emph{Relation to the formal statements.} \file{lemma_3_10} (\file{Sections01\_03.lean}, line~340) has the exact companion \file{lemma_3_10_holds} (\file{Proofs03CubeUpper.lean}, line~82, at HEAD \texttt{5d4718772}); no declaration concerns $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}$. Nothing in this chapter is formalized.

\section[{Notation and elementary Fourier identities\srctag{29}}]{Notation and elementary Fourier identities}\label{gsr:cc:29:sec:d2}
\srcnote{29}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:notation}

Let \(G\) be a finite abelian group. Averages over \(G\) are normalized:
\(\E_x F(x)=|G|^{-1}\sum_{x\in G}F(x)\). Sums over its character group
\(\widehat G\) use counting measure. We write characters multiplicatively
and set
\[
 \widehat f(\chi)=\E_x f(x)\overline{\chi(x)},\qquad
 \Delta_h f(x)=f(x)\overline{f(x-h)}.
\]
For \(d\ge1\), define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:gowers-definition}
 \|f\|_{U^d}^{2^d}
 =\E_{x,h_1,\ldots,h_d}
   \prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^d}
       \mathcal C^{|\omega|}f(x-\omega\cdot h),
\end{equation}
where \(\mathcal C\) is complex conjugation. In particular,
\(\|f\|_{U^1}=|\E f|\). The sign of the increments is immaterial under
uniform averaging. For \(d\ge2\), the recursive identity, together
with the Fourier identity for \(U^2\), is
\begin{align}
 \|f\|_{U^d}^{2^d}
 &=\E_h\|\Delta_hf\|_{U^{d-1}}^{2^{d-1}},\label{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:recursion}\\
 \|f\|_{U^2}^4
 &=\sum_{\chi\in\widehat G}|\widehat f(\chi)|^4.\label{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:u2-fourier}
\end{align}
Repeated Cauchy--Schwarz gives the usual monotonicity
\(\|f\|_{U^1}\le\|f\|_{U^2}\le\cdots\) and the multilinear
Gowers--Cauchy--Schwarz inequality. These elementary norm properties are
also developed in Gowers's Section~3 \cite{gowers}.

For a real function \(f\), define its autocorrelation and Fourier masses
by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:autocorrelation}
 c_f(h)=\E_x f(x)f(x-h)
       =\sum_\chi\lambda_\chi\chi(h),\qquad
 \lambda_\chi=|\widehat f(\chi)|^2.
\end{equation}
Then \(\lambda_\chi\ge0\) and
\(\lambda_{\chi^{-1}}=\lambda_\chi\). In particular, although
\(c_f\) need not be pointwise nonnegative, its Fourier coefficients
are nonnegative. We use
\[
 S=\sum_\chi\lambda_\chi^2=\|f\|_{U^2}^4.
\]
When \(f\ne0\), \(S>0\). The subgroup of self-inverse characters is
\(\widehat G[2]=\{\chi:\chi^2=1\}\). On an odd-order group it consists
only of the trivial character, so a centered function has zero Fourier
mass on \(\widehat G[2]\).

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Positive autocorrelation moments and higher norm bounds\srctag{29}}]{Positive autocorrelation moments and higher norm bounds}\label{gsr:cc:29:sec:d3}
\srcnote{29}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:moments}

\begin{samepage}
\begin{theorem}[Central-binomial autocorrelation bound]
\label{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:moment-theorem}
Let \(f:G\to\R\), and suppose
\(\widehat f(\chi)=0\) whenever \(\chi^2=1\). For every integer \(m\ge1\),
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:central-moment}
 \E_h c_f(h)^{2m}
 \ge \binom{2m}{m}\left(\frac S2\right)^m.
\end{equation}
Consequently, for every \(d\ge2\), with \(m=2^{d-2}\),
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:norm-bound}
 \|f\|_{U^d}^{2^d}
 \ge C_m\|f\|_{U^2}^{2^d},\qquad
 C_m=2^{-m}\binom{2m}{m}.
\end{equation}
The constant in \eqref{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:central-moment} is optimal uniformly over
finite abelian groups. Sharpness is not asserted for
\eqref{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:norm-bound} when \(d\ge3\).
\end{theorem}
\end{samepage}

\begin{proof}
Choose one character \(\chi_j\) from each nonzero inverse pair, and
write \(b_j=\lambda_{\chi_j}\). Thus \(S=2\sum_jb_j^2\).
The zero function is immediate, so assume at least one pair occurs.
Expanding the Fourier series of \(c_f^{2m}\) and averaging retains
precisely the monomials whose product character is trivial. Their
coefficients are nonnegative. We may therefore retain only monomials
that use \(\chi_j\) and \(\chi_j^{-1}\) equally often for every \(j\).
If each occurs \(k_j\) times, where \(\sum_jk_j=m\), the contribution is
\[
 \frac{(2m)!}{\prod_j(k_j!)^2}\prod_j b_j^{2k_j}.
\]
Hence
\begin{align}
 \E c_f^{2m}
 &\ge \binom{2m}{m}
   \sum_{\sum k_j=m}\binom{m}{k_1,k_2,\ldots}^{\!2}
        \prod_j b_j^{2k_j}\nonumber\\
 &\ge \binom{2m}{m}
   \sum_{\sum k_j=m}\binom{m}{k_1,k_2,\ldots}
        \prod_j b_j^{2k_j}\nonumber\\
 &=\binom{2m}{m}\left(\sum_jb_j^2\right)^m.
 \label{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:balanced-expansion}
\end{align}
The second inequality only uses the fact that each multinomial
coefficient is an integer at least one.

By \eqref{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:recursion} and \(\|g\|_{U^{d-1}}\ge|\E g|\),
\[
 \|f\|_{U^d}^{2^d}
 \ge\E_h|c_f(h)|^{2^{d-1}}.
\]
Here \(2^{d-1}=2m\), and \(S^m=\|f\|_{U^2}^{2^d}\), proving the
norm comparison. To see moment sharpness, take a character of order
greater than \(2m\) and \(f=2\Rea(a\chi)\), with \(a\ne0\). The only
surviving monomials in \(c_f^{2m}\) then contain the two characters
equally often, and equality holds.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Equality and stability at the moment level}

The moment argument contains more information than its last scalar
bound. It quantifies the cost of distributing Fourier fourth-power
mass among several inverse pairs.

\begin{samepage}
\begin{proposition}[Pair concentration]
\label{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:moment-stability}
Under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:moment-theorem}, let
\(f\ne0\), \(m\ge2\), and
\[
 p_j=\frac{2\lambda_{\chi_j}^2}{S},\qquad \sum_jp_j=1.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:stability-moment}
 \frac{\E c_f^{2m}}{C_mS^m}
 \ge m-(m-1)\sum_jp_j^m.
\end{equation}
If the left side is at most \(1+\varepsilon\), where
\(0\le\varepsilon<m-1\), some inverse pair has mass
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:pair-mass}
 p_j\ge
 \left(1-\frac{\varepsilon}{m-1}\right)^{1/(m-1)}.
\end{equation}
For that pair, putting \(a=\widehat f(\chi_j)\),
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:pair-distance}
 \|f-2\Rea(a\chi_j)\|_{U^2}^4
 \le S\left[1-
 \left(1-\frac{\varepsilon}{m-1}\right)^{1/(m-1)}\right].
\end{equation}
Equality in \eqref{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:central-moment}, for \(m\ge2\), holds exactly
when the Fourier support is one inverse pair and, for its character
order \(n\), \(n/\gcd(n,2)>m\).
\end{proposition}
\end{samepage}

\begin{proof}
For a composition \(k\) of \(m\), the multinomial coefficient is one
if all mass is in a single coordinate, and is at least \(m\) otherwise.
The normalized balanced sum in \eqref{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:balanced-expansion} is
the expectation of this multinomial coefficient under the multinomial
distribution with probabilities \(p_j\). The probability of a pure
composition is \(\sum_jp_j^m\). This proves
\eqref{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:stability-moment}. It gives
\(\sum_jp_j^m\ge1-\varepsilon/(m-1)\), whereas
\(\sum_jp_j^m\le(\max_jp_j)^{m-1}\). Removing the largest pair and
using \eqref{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:u2-fourier} proves the distance statement.

At equality every mixed composition must vanish, so just one pair
remains. For that pair the extra monomials have exponent
\(2j-2m\), \(0\le j\le2m\), on the chosen character. A nonzero such
exponent can be divisible by \(n\) exactly when
\(n/\gcd(n,2)\le m\). Its coefficient is positive. This proves the
stated criterion.
\end{proof}

This is stability for the autocorrelation moment and approximation in
\(U^2\). It neither asserts approximation in \(L^2\) nor classifies
near-minimizers of \(\|f\|_{U^d}/\|f\|_{U^2}\). The first inequality
in the norm proof can have its own nonzero gap.

\subsection{An explicit profile for self-inverse Fourier mass}

The absence of order-two characters is essential for a uniform
improvement over one: a nontrivial real character has all Gowers norms
equal to one. Its contribution can nevertheless be tracked exactly in
the moment method.

\begin{samepage}
\begin{theorem}[Torsion-dependent moment profile]
\label{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:torsion-profile}
Let \(f:G\to\R\) be nonzero, with no restriction on its mean or on
\(G\). Set
\[
 \tau=\frac{\sum_{\chi^2=1}\lambda_\chi^2}{S}\in[0,1],
\]
and define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:profile-polynomial}
 K_m(\tau)=\sum_{k=0}^m
 \binom{2m}{2k}\binom{2k}{k}\,
 \tau^{m-k}\left(\frac{1-\tau}{2}\right)^k.
\end{equation}
For every integer \(m\ge1\),
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:torsion-moment}
 \E_h c_f(h)^{2m}\ge K_m(\tau)S^m.
\end{equation}
For \(m=2^{d-2}\), it follows that
\(\|f\|_{U^d}^{2^d}\ge K_m(\tau)\|f\|_{U^2}^{2^d}\).
For each \(m\) and each \(\tau\), the moment constant in
\eqref{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:torsion-moment} is attained on some finite abelian group.
\end{theorem}
\end{samepage}

\begin{proof}
Separate the self-inverse frequencies from the remaining inverse
pairs. In the Fourier expansion retain terms in which every
self-inverse frequency occurs an even number of times and each
non-self-inverse pair occurs in equal numbers. These terms are exactly
the moment of
\[
 X+Y=\sum_i a_i\epsilon_i+\sum_j2b_j\cos\theta_j,
\]
where the \(\epsilon_i\) are independent uniform signs and the
\(\theta_j\) are independent uniform circle variables, all mutually
independent. Their variances are
\(\E X^2=\tau S\) and \(\E Y^2=(1-\tau)S\).
All other actual Fourier terms are nonnegative, so discarding them is
legitimate even when the original characters have extra relations.

Odd proxy moments vanish. Jensen's inequality gives
\(\E X^{2r}\ge(\tau S)^r\), including \(r=0\). The balanced
multinomial calculation gives
\(\E Y^{2k}\ge\binom{2k}{k}((1-\tau)S/2)^k\).
Expanding \(\E(X+Y)^{2m}\) and applying these two estimates gives
\eqref{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:profile-polynomial}.

For sharpness, use \(G=C_2\times C_p\), with \(p\) an odd prime
greater than \(2m\). Put Fourier squared mass
\(\lambda_\sigma=\sqrt{\tau S}\) on the nontrivial character of
\(C_2\), and
\(\lambda_\chi=\lambda_{\chi^{-1}}
=\sqrt{(1-\tau)S/2}\) on one pair from \(C_p\). A real function with
these squared Fourier coefficients exists by taking nonnegative square
roots as Fourier coefficients. Only the retained moments survive, and
both component estimates are equalities.
\end{proof}

The endpoints are \(K_m(0)=C_m\) and \(K_m(1)=1\).
The profile need not be monotone between them: for example,
\(K_2(\tau)=\tfrac32+3\tau-\tfrac72\tau^2\).
It describes how Fourier mass in both sectors can increase an even
moment; it is not a monotone penalty for torsion alone.

\section[{Consequences for the unresolved higher norm constants\srctag{29}}]{Consequences for the unresolved higher norm constants}\label{gsr:cc:29:sec:d4}
\srcnote{29}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:constants}

For \(d\ge3\), define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:cd-definition}
 c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}=
 \sup_{\substack{|G|\text{ odd},\ f:G\to\R\\
                  \E f=0,\ f\ne0}}
 \frac{\|f\|_{U^2}^4}{\|f\|_{U^d}^4}.
\end{equation}
The supremum ranges over finite groups as well as functions. The
existing report proves \(c_3^{\mathrm{odd}}=2^{-1/2}\)
\cite{repo29report}. Monotonicity alone therefore gives that same upper
bound for every \(d\ge3\). In norm-power form its coefficient is
\(2^{m/2}\), where \(m=2^{d-2}\).

\begin{samepage}
\begin{corollary}[A strict improvement from dimension four onward]
\label{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:cd-upper}
For \(d\ge4\) and \(m=2^{d-2}\),
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:cd-upper-bound}
 c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}\le B_d
 :=\frac{2}{\binom{2m}{m}^{1/m}}<2^{-1/2}.
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:u4-gap}
 \|f\|_{U^4}^{16}\ge\frac{35}{8}\|f\|_{U^2}^{16}
\end{equation}
for real centered \(f\) on odd-order groups.
The bounds \(B_d\) decrease to \(1/2\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
\emph{The best upper coefficient among sources~01--33, not the best known.} Among sources~01--33, $35/8$ is the best coefficient for real centered $f$ on odd-order groups at $d=4$ (source~28's universal bound gives $(323/160)^2=4.0754\ldots$, note after its Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:28:uq:main-gap}). Sources placed in this directory and not yet written in record larger coefficients: source~35 records $5$, source~34 records $81/16$, that is $c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le2/3$, and source~45 records $4795/832$, that is $c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le(832/4795)^{1/4}=0.6454070$ (their placements, checked at intake; for the writes that add them). With source~28's lower bound and the intake's certificate the bracket printed by this write is $0.5587725\le c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le(8/35)^{1/4}=0.6914416$ (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:normgap}). The decimals of the table were recomputed at the write.
\end{writenote}

\begin{proof}
The norm theorem gives \(c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}\le C_m^{-1/m}=B_d\).
At \(m=4\), \(C_4=35/8>4=2^{4/2}\).
Vandermonde's identity includes the central summand
\(\binom{4m}{2m}\ge\binom{2m}{m}^2\); hence
\(C_{2m}\ge C_m^2\). Induction along powers of two proves the strict
comparison with \(2^{m/2}\), and also the monotonicity of \(B_d\).
Finally \(4^m/(2m+1)\le\binom{2m}{m}\le4^m\), which gives the limit.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A lower bound uniform in the dimension}

\begin{samepage}
\begin{proposition}[A uniform interval model]
\label{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:one-third}
For every \(d\ge3\), \(c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}\ge1/3\). Consequently the
nonincreasing sequence \(c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}\) has a limit in
\([1/3,1/2]\).
\end{proposition}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
This answers the part of source~28's Research question on the asymptotic constants that asks for a positive lower bound uniform in $d$ (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:normgap}); checked at the write: the ratio $n(n^2+n+1)/(3(n+1)^3)$ is $0.278$, $0.327$, $0.3327$ at $n=10,100,1000$.
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{The limit is $1/3$} (source~63, Section~\ref{gsr:cc:sec:oddlimit}): $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}\le1/3+10\cdot2^{-\lfloor d/8\rfloor}$ for $d\ge80$ (its Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:63:norm:main}), from the sharp bounded inequality $\norm f_{U^2}^4\le\norm f_\infty^4/3$ on odd-order groups; source~60 had shown that the limit is at most $0.3464533951$.
\end{writenote}
\end{samepage}

\begin{proof}
On \(G=\Z/(2n+1)\Z\), let \(A=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\),
\(\delta=n/(2n+1)\), and \(f=2(\one_A-\delta)\).
There is no wraparound in sums of two members of \(A\).
The additive energy is
\[
 E(A)=n^2+2\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}j^2=\frac{2n^3+n}{3}.
\]
By Fourier orthogonality,
\[
 \|f\|_{U^2}^4
 =16\left(\frac{E(A)}{(2n+1)^3}-\delta^4\right),
 \qquad
 \|f\|_\infty=\frac{2(n+1)}{2n+1}.
\]
Since \(\|f\|_{U^d}\le\|f\|_\infty\),
\[
 \frac{\|f\|_{U^2}^4}{\|f\|_{U^d}^4}
 \ge\frac{n(n^2+n+1)}{3(n+1)^3}\longrightarrow\frac13.
\]
This works for each fixed \(d\), with a bound independent of \(d\).
Monotonicity and Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:cd-upper} prove the limit assertion.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A more informative lower bound in dimension four}

For a prime \(p>16\) and \(f=a\chi+\overline a\chi^{-1}\) on
\(\Z/p\Z\), with \(\chi\) nontrivial, one has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:cosine-u4}
 \|f\|_{U^4}^{16}=222|a|^{16},\qquad
 \|f\|_{U^2}^{16}=16|a|^{16}.
\end{equation}
Here is a finite combinatorial verification of the coefficient. A
surviving Fourier monomial chooses eight positive-sign vertices of
\(\{0,1\}^4\), with four ones in each coordinate. Split by the fourth
coordinate into four-subsets of the three-cube. If \(n(v)\) counts
four-subsets with coordinate-sum vector \(v\), complementing a subset
shows \(n(4\one-v)=n(v)\), and the required number is
\(\sum_v n(v)^2\). The following complete classification uses coordinate
permutations and coordinate reflections:
\[
\begin{array}{c|r|r}
 \text{sorted }(|v_1-2|,|v_2-2|,|v_3-2|)
   &\text{number of vectors }v&n(v)\\\hline
 (0,0,0)&1&8\\
 (0,0,1)&6&4\\
 (0,0,2)&6&1\\
 (0,1,1)&12&2\\
 (1,1,1)&8&1
\end{array}
\]
For example, a coordinate sum zero or four determines a full face;
for sums \((1,2,2)\), the unique point on one side of the first
coordinate determines the omitted point on the other side, giving four
choices. For \((1,1,2)\), separating whether the first two coordinate
ones occur at the same point gives two choices. For \((1,1,1)\) the
subset is forced. The balanced case \((2,2,2)\) consists of six unions
of two antipodal pairs and two parity tetrahedra. Thus the sum is
\(64+96+6+48+8=222\). The condition \(p>16\) prevents nonzero integer
exponents from vanishing modulo \(p\).

It follows that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:c4-bracket}
 \left(\frac8{111}\right)^{1/4}
 \le c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}
 \le\left(\frac8{35}\right)^{1/4}.
\end{equation}
The endpoints are approximately \(0.518133595\) and \(0.691441569\).
The interval has not been closed. In particular, the number \(35/8\)
is a rigorously improved coefficient, not the asserted sharp answer.

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
The lower end of \eqref{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:c4-bracket} is the single-cosine value. Source~28, from the same pin, raises it to $0.5587294$ by an exact two-harmonic witness (Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:28:uq:witness}), and the intake's certificate on $\Z/7\Z$ to $0.5587725$ (note there); source~28's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:28:uq:all-d-obstruction} shows that a single inverse pair is not extremal for any $d\ge4$.
\end{writenote}

\begin{figure}[ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/29-moment-stability-norm_bounds.pdf}
\caption{Left: the proved upper bounds for \(c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}\),
with the dimension-independent lower bound \(1/3\) and the sharper
cosine lower bound at \(d=4\). Right: the full fourth-dimensional
moment profile, expressed as \(K_4(\tau)^{-1/4}\). The curve is a
valid bound from the moment method, not a claimed sharp Gowers-norm
constant.}
\label{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:norm-figure}
\end{figure}

\subsection{How the coefficient enters centered cube counting}

For \(Q_d(F)=\|F\|_{U^d}^{2^d}\) and real centered \(f\), expansion
of \(Q_d(\delta+f)\) has no terms with one, two, or three selected
vertices: at those vertices the affine forms are independent. On
odd-order groups the fourth-degree term is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:quartic-term}
 P_d\delta^{2^d-4}\|f\|_{U^2}^4,\qquad
 P_d=2^{d-3}(3^d-2^{d+1}+1).
\end{equation}
This coefficient and the torsion qualifications are proved in the
existing cube-expansion reports \cite{repo29report,repo29cube}.
The new norm estimate therefore changes the available bound on this
term to
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:quartic-improvement}
 P_d B_d\delta^{2^d-4}\|f\|_{U^d}^4,\qquad d\ge4.
\end{equation}
For \(d=4\), \(P_4=100\): the coefficient improves from
\(100/\sqrt2\approx70.710678\) to
\(100(8/35)^{1/4}\approx69.144157\).
This is an explicit improvement to one local coefficient. Terms of
higher degree and subsequent inverse and localization losses still
have to be controlled before a final progression-free-set bound could
change.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A stronger real norm gap and a higher-order obstruction\srctag{28}}]{A stronger real norm gap and a higher-order obstruction}\label{gsr:cc:28:sec:d8}
\srcnote{28}{Section 8}
\gsrsrcpart{Strict norm gaps and the failure of cosine extremality}
\label{gsr:cc:28:uq:section}

The earlier repository report proves the sharp real, mean-zero comparison
$\|f\|_{U^3}^{8}\ge 2\|f\|_{U^2}^{8}$ on odd-order groups, with equality
precisely for a single conjugate pair of nonzero Fourier coefficients
\cite{repo28four}.
Its higher-order analogue was left open.  We improve the available
universal bound at every order at least four, and show that the
single-character equality model does not extend to these orders.
The two conclusions are independent: the universal estimate is a lower
bound for a norm, whereas the explicit examples give lower bounds for
the extremal ratio.

All expectations in this section use the uniform probability measure.
For a real function on a finite abelian group, our convention is
\begin{equation}
 \|f\|_{U^d}^{2^d}
 =\mathbb E_{x,h_1,\ldots,h_d}
   \prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^d}f(x+\omega\cdot h).
 \label{gsr:cc:28:uq:norm-convention}
\end{equation}
The usual conjugations in the complex definition have no effect here.
Fourier coefficients are normalized by
$\widehat f(\xi)=\mathbb E_x f(x)\overline{\xi(x)}$.
In particular,
$\|f\|_{U^2}^{4}=\sum_\xi|\widehat f(\xi)|^4$.
Write
\begin{equation}
 c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}
 =\sup_{\substack{G\ \text{finite abelian of odd order}\\
                  f:G\to\mathbb R,\ \mathbb E f=0,\ f\ne0}}
     \frac{\|f\|_{U^2}^{4}}{\|f\|_{U^d}^{4}}.
 \label{gsr:cc:28:uq:extremal-constant}
\end{equation}
No boundedness restriction changes this supremum, since the ratio is
invariant under multiplying $f$ by a nonzero scalar.

\begin{theorem}[Explicit improvement beyond the third norm]
\label{gsr:cc:28:uq:main-gap}
For every finite abelian group of odd order, every real mean-zero
function $f$, and every integer $d\ge4$,
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\quad
 \|f\|_{U^d}^{4}\ge
       \sqrt{\frac{323}{160}}\,\|f\|_{U^2}^{4}.
 \quad}
 \label{gsr:cc:28:uq:universal-gap}
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\quad
 \left(\frac{133153321267264}{1366299579065739}\right)^{1/4}
 \le c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}
 \le\sqrt{\frac{160}{323}}.
 \quad}
 \label{gsr:cc:28:uq:c4-bracket}
\end{equation}
The endpoints are approximately $0.558729390985$ and
$0.703815343078$, respectively.  The upper endpoint strictly improves
the previously available $2^{-1/2}=0.707106781187\ldots$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
\emph{Superseded the same day by source~29.} The universal bound \eqref{gsr:cc:28:uq:universal-gap} is $\norm f_{U^4}^{16}\ge(323/160)^2\norm f_{U^2}^{16}=4.0754\ldots\norm f_{U^2}^{16}$ at $d=4$; source~29's Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:cd-upper}, written from the same pin and citing neither this source nor being cited by it, gives $\norm f_{U^4}^{16}\ge(35/8)\norm f_{U^2}^{16}$, hence $c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le(8/35)^{1/4}=0.6914416$ against $\sqrt{160/323}=0.7038153$ here, and $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}\le B_d<0.6914416$ for every $d\ge5$. The sentence that the upper endpoint ``strictly improves the previously available $2^{-1/2}$'' was true at the pin. The lower endpoint $0.5587294$ is this source's own; it is improved slightly by the intake's certificate (note after Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:28:uq:witness}). The bracket is item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:normgap}; later placed sources record further upper bounds (note after source~29's Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:cd-upper}).
\end{writenote}

We give all ingredients below.  The numerical displays are descriptive;
the assertions use the exact rational quantities in the formulas.
Neither endpoint is asserted to be sharp.

\subsection{A short bounded example on five points}
\label{gsr:cc:28:uq:five-point-subsection}

\begin{proposition}[A rational counterexample to the cosine value]
\label{gsr:cc:28:uq:five-point}
On $\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z$, let
\[
 (f(0),f(1),f(2),f(3),f(4))=(0,1,1,-1,-1).
\]
Then $\mathbb E f=0$, $|f|\le1$, and
\begin{equation}
 \|f\|_{U^2}^{4}=\frac{36}{125},\qquad
 \|f\|_{U^4}^{16}=\frac{52}{625},\qquad
 \frac{\|f\|_{U^4}^{16}}{\|f\|_{U^2}^{16}}
     =\frac{5078125}{419904}<\frac{111}{8}.
 \label{gsr:cc:28:uq:five-point-values}
\end{equation}
A single real character pair of odd order at least five has the ratio
$111/8$.  Thus it cannot describe the general fourth-order optimum.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The unnormalized autocorrelations of $f$ are $(4,1,-3,-3,1)$.
Their squared sum is $36$, giving the first identity.
For $h,k\in\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z$, put
\[
 g_{h,k}(x)=f(x)f(x+h)f(x+k)f(x+h+k).
\]
Twice applying the derivative identity for Gowers norms gives
$\|f\|_{U^4}^{16}=\mathbb E_{h,k}\|g_{h,k}\|_{U^2}^{4}$.
For an integer-valued $g$, write
\[
 E(g)=\sum_t\left(\sum_x g(x)g(x+t)\right)^2,
 \qquad \|g\|_{U^2}^{4}=E(g)/125.
\]
The possibilities are
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lrr}
\toprule
Condition on $(h,k)$ & Number of pairs & $E(g_{h,k})$\\
\midrule
$h=k=0$ & 1 & 52\\
Exactly one of $h,k$ is zero & 8 & 19\\
$h,k\ne0$ and $h=\pm k$ & 8 & 6\\
$h,k\ne0$ and $h\ne\pm k$ & 8 & 1\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Indeed, the first function is the indicator of a four-point set.  In the
second case it is the indicator of a three-point set.  Its nonzero-shift
intersection counts are $2,2,1,1$, so its energy is
$3^2+2\cdot2^2+2\cdot1^2=19$.  In the last two cases its
support has size two and one, respectively, with values in $\{-1,1\}$;
the corresponding energies are $6$ and $1$, independently of the signs.
The sum of the energies is $52+8\cdot19+8\cdot6+8=260$.
Dividing by $5^5$ gives $52/625$, and the ratio follows.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The exact fourth-order dual function of a cosine}
\label{gsr:cc:28:uq:dual-subsection}

For a real function $g$, define
\begin{equation}
 D_4g(x)=\mathbb E_{h_1,h_2,h_3,h_4}
       \prod_{\substack{\omega\in\{0,1\}^4\\\omega\ne0}}
          g(x+\omega\cdot h).
 \label{gsr:cc:28:uq:dual-definition}
\end{equation}
The Gowers--Cauchy--Schwarz inequality implies
\begin{equation}
 |\mathbb E_x f(x)D_4g(x)|
       \le\|f\|_{U^4}\|g\|_{U^4}^{15}.
 \label{gsr:cc:28:uq:dual-cs}
\end{equation}
This finite multilinear inequality, rather than an unproved description
of a dual norm, is all that is needed.

\begin{lemma}[Exact cosine counts]
\label{gsr:cc:28:uq:cosine-dual}
Let $\chi$ be a character of odd order at least five, let
$\theta\in\mathbb R$, and write
$g_j=e^{ij\theta}\chi^j+e^{-ij\theta}\chi^{-j}$.
Then
\begin{equation}
 \|g_1\|_{U^4}^{16}=222,
 \qquad
 D_4g_1=111g_1+27g_3+g_5.
 \label{gsr:cc:28:uq:exact-dual}
\end{equation}
The formula remains valid when $\chi$ has order five; in that case
$g_5$ is constant.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Expand each factor in characters.  In the average defining $D_4g_1$,
the coefficient choices are signs on the fifteen nonzero Boolean
vertices.  Each direction average requires the sum of eight signs to
be divisible by the order of $\chi$.  Such a sum is even and has absolute
value at most eight.  For an odd order at least five, it must therefore
be zero as an integer.  The same observation applies to both halves of
a full four-dimensional cube; its total frequency is then also zero.

First count the full-cube choices.  Split the cube into two
three-dimensional faces.  Each face has four plus signs.  If $n(t)$ is
the number of four-subsets of $\{0,1\}^3$ whose coordinate sum is
$t=(t_1,t_2,t_3)$, the full count is $\sum_t n(t)^2$.
The required finite generating identity is
\begin{align}
 [z^4]\prod_{\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^3}(1+z x^\epsilon)
 &=x_1x_2x_3\prod_{j=1}^3(1+x_j)^2
   +\sum_{i=1}^3(1+x_i^4)\prod_{j\ne i}x_j^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:28:uq:seventy-identity}
\end{align}
Here $x^\epsilon=\prod_jx_j^{\epsilon_j}$.  This identity follows by
multiplying the eight binomials and collecting the coefficient of
$z^4$.  It gives the following complete table:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lrr}
\toprule
Type of $t$ & Number of such $t$ & $n(t)$\\
\midrule
One coordinate $0$ or $4$, the other two $2$ & 6 & 1\\
All three coordinates in $\{1,3\}$ & 8 & 1\\
Two in $\{1,3\}$, one equal to $2$ & 12 & 2\\
One in $\{1,3\}$, two equal to $2$ & 6 & 4\\
$(2,2,2)$ & 1 & 8\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Thus the count is
$6+8+12\cdot4+6\cdot16+64=222$.
The factor $e^{i\theta\sum_\omega s_\omega}$ is one for every such
choice, so this proves the first identity in \eqref{gsr:cc:28:uq:exact-dual}.

For the dual function, a choice of signs on the fifteen nonzero vertices
contributes frequency $\sum s_\omega$.  The counts at frequencies $1$
and $-1$ are both $111$: adjoining the missing sign at the origin
produces the $222$ full-cube assignments, divided equally by its sign.
The counts at frequencies $3$ and $-3$ are both $27$, as follows.
Place a frequency $3$ at the missing origin, so that the other fifteen
signs must have total $-3$.  Their six plus-sign vertices form a set
$P$ with four selected vertices on each coordinate face.
After complementing all four coordinates, we obtain six distinct
vertices, excluding $(1,1,1,1)$, with coordinate sums all equal to two.
Let $a_j$ count their vertices of Hamming weight $j$.
Then
\[
 a_0+a_1+a_2+a_3=6,\qquad a_1+2a_2+3a_3=8,
 \qquad a_0\in\{0,1\},\quad a_1\le4.
\]
Exactly three possibilities remain:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{rrrrr}
\toprule
$a_0$ & $a_1$ & $a_2$ & $a_3$ & Number\\
\midrule
0 & 4 & 2 & 0 & 3\\
1 & 2 & 3 & 0 & 12\\
1 & 3 & 1 & 1 & 12\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
In the first case the two edges form a perfect matching on four
coordinates.  In the second, choose the two singleton coordinates in
six ways; the three edges form a path with those endpoints, in two ways.
In the third, choose the triple in four ways and choose which of its three
coordinates has no singleton; the edge is then forced.
This proves $27=3+12+12$.

At frequency $-5$, the five plus-sign vertices must have a total of
sixteen coordinate incidences.  The only possibility is the vertex of
weight four together with the four vertices of weight three.  Hence the
count is one; the frequency $5$ count is also one.  Frequencies of
absolute value at least seven are impossible, since four distinct
vertices have at most $4+3+3+3=13$ incidences.  These counts exhaust all
odd frequencies, and prove the dual formula.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 34--39]
Also proved by source~34 (Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:34:norm:dual-polynomial}) and recounted by source~35 (Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:35:ng:cosine-dual}), neither citing this source.
\end{writenote}

\begin{lemma}[The order-three case]
\label{gsr:cc:28:uq:order-three}
If $\chi$ has order three, then for $g=e^{i\theta}\chi+e^{-i\theta}\chi^{-1}$,
\begin{align}
 \|g\|_{U^4}^{16}
 &=286+32\cos(6\theta)+16\cos(12\theta)\notag\\
 &=262+32\bigl(\cos(6\theta)+\tfrac12\bigr)^2\ge262.
 \label{gsr:cc:28:uq:order-three-formula}
\end{align}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $P$ be the plus-sign vertices in a character expansion of the
four-cube.  The congruences require $|P|\equiv2\pmod3$ and require each
coordinate face to contain $1$, $4$, or $7$ vertices of $P$.
The possibilities are
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{rrr}
\toprule
$|P|$ & Total frequency $2|P|-16$ & Number\\
\midrule
2 & $-12$ & 8\\
5 & $-6$ & 16\\
8 & 0 & 286\\
11 & 6 & 16\\
14 & 12 & 8\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
For two vertices, every coordinate must occur once, so the vertices
are antipodal, giving eight pairs.  For five vertices, reflect every
coordinate having four selected vertices.  Each coordinate now occurs
once, forcing the set consisting of the zero vertex and the four unit
vertices.  Its sixteen reflected copies are distinct.
For eight vertices with four on every face, the count is $222$ by
\eqref{gsr:cc:28:uq:seventy-identity}.  Otherwise some coordinate has one or seven
selected vertices.  Reflect to make this number one.  The set is one
entire three-face, with one vertex removed, and the corresponding
vertex inserted across that coordinate.  The remaining coordinate
counts must all be four.  There are $4\cdot2\cdot8=64$ such sets, each
with exactly one exceptional coordinate.  This gives $222+64=286$.
Taking complements supplies the last two rows.
Summing the associated phases proves the first line of
\eqref{gsr:cc:28:uq:order-three-formula}; the second follows from the double-angle
identity.
\end{proof}

\subsection{An explicit universal improvement}
\label{gsr:cc:28:uq:universal-proof-subsection}

We recall precisely which earlier estimate is used.  Let $f\ne0$ be
real and mean-zero on an odd-order group, set
\[
 S=\sum_\xi |\widehat f(\xi)|^4=\|f\|_{U^2}^4,
 \qquad
 p=\max_{\xi\ne0}\frac{2|\widehat f(\xi)|^4}{S}.
\]
The nonzero Fourier coefficients occur in distinct conjugate pairs,
so $0<p\le1$.

\begin{lemma}[Two bounds retaining the largest pair]
\label{gsr:cc:28:uq:pair-bounds}
With this notation, put $R=\|f\|_{U^4}^{16}/S^4$.
Then
\begin{equation}
 R\ge(5-3p)^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:28:uq:first-pair-bound}
\end{equation}
If a maximizing character has order at least five, also
\begin{equation}
 R\ge\frac{111}{8}
  \left[p^{1/4}-\frac{28}{111}(1-p)^{1/4}\right]_+^{16},
 \label{gsr:cc:28:uq:dual-pair-bound}
\end{equation}
where $[t]_+=\max(t,0)$.  If it has order three, then
\begin{equation}
 R\ge\frac{131}{8}p^4.
 \label{gsr:cc:28:uq:order-three-pair-bound}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The prior real $U^2$--$U^3$ argument retains the stronger intermediate
inequality
\[
 \|f\|_{U^3}^{8}\ge 5S^2-6M,
 \qquad M=\sum_\xi|\widehat f(\xi)|^8.
\]
For completeness, write $\lambda_\xi=|\widehat f(\xi)|^2$.
Writing $a_r=\widehat f(r)$, the exact Fourier identity is
\[
 \|f\|_{U^3}^{8}=\sum_{s,t}
   \left|\sum_r a_r\overline{a_{r+s}}\,\overline{a_{r+t}}
                         a_{r+s+t}\right|^2.
\]
Retaining its two coordinate axes gives
$\|f\|_{U^3}^{8}\ge2E(\lambda)-S^2$.
In the additive energy $E(\lambda)$, retain the union of
$r=t,s=w$; $r=w,s=t$; and $s=-r,w=-t$.
Each contributes $S^2$, each pairwise intersection contributes $M$,
and their triple intersection has zero weight because the group has odd
order and $\widehat f(0)=0$.  Thus
$E(\lambda)\ge3S^2-3M$, proving the displayed estimate.
If $p_j$ are the normalized conjugate-pair fourth-power masses, then
$2M/S^2=\sum_jp_j^2\le\max_jp_j=p$.
Consequently $\|f\|_{U^3}^{8}\ge(5-3p)S^2$.
Norm monotonicity $\|f\|_{U^4}\ge\|f\|_{U^3}$ proves
\eqref{gsr:cc:28:uq:first-pair-bound}.

Choose a maximizing character $\chi$ and write
$\widehat f(\chi)=a e^{i\theta}$, where $a=(pS/2)^{1/4}$.
If its order is at least five, apply \eqref{gsr:cc:28:uq:dual-cs} to the
function $g_1$ in Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:28:uq:cosine-dual}.
The frequencies $\chi^{\pm3}$ and $\chi^{\pm5}$ do not coincide
with the maximizing pair.  A trivial fifth power contributes zero
because $f$ is centered.  Every remaining coefficient has modulus at
most $((1-p)S/2)^{1/4}$.  Therefore
\[
 \mathbb E fD_4g_1
 \ge222(pS/2)^{1/4}-56((1-p)S/2)^{1/4}.
\]
Since $\|g_1\|_{U^4}^{16}=222$, inequality
\eqref{gsr:cc:28:uq:dual-cs}, followed by taking the sixteenth power and dividing
by $S^4$, gives \eqref{gsr:cc:28:uq:dual-pair-bound}.

If $\chi$ has order three, average $f$ over translates by
$\ker\chi$.  This operation does not increase a Gowers norm, by its
triangle inequality and translation invariance.  The quotient has three
points, and the centered averaged function is exactly
$a(e^{i\theta}\chi+e^{-i\theta}\chi^{-1})$.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:28:uq:order-three} gives
$\|f\|_{U^4}^{16}\ge262a^{16}=(131/8)p^4S^4$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Upper bound in Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:28:uq:main-gap}]
The zero function is immediate.  Otherwise use
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:28:uq:pair-bounds} and split at $p_0=159/160$.
If $p\le p_0$, then
\[
 R\ge(5-3p_0)^2=(323/160)^2.
\]
If $p>p_0$ and the maximizing character has order three,
\[
 R\ge(131/8)(159/160)^4>(323/160)^2.
\]
In the remaining case use the exact rational comparisons
\[
 (599/600)^4<159/160,
 \qquad 1/160<(9/32)^4.
\]
They imply
\[
 p^{1/4}-\frac{28}{111}(1-p)^{1/4}
 >\frac{599}{600}-\frac{28}{111}\frac9{32}
 =\frac{5147}{5550}.
\]
Finally,
\[
 \frac{111}{8}\left(\frac{5147}{5550}\right)^{16}
 >\left(\frac{323}{160}\right)^2.
\]
For example, the last comparison is the integer inequality
$111\cdot3200\cdot5147^{16}>104329\cdot5550^{16}$.
Thus $R\ge(323/160)^2$ in every case, which is
\eqref{gsr:cc:28:uq:universal-gap} for $d=4$.  Norm monotonicity extends it to
all $d\ge4$.  Rearranging proves the upper bound for $c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A smaller local quartic cube coefficient]
\label{gsr:cc:28:uq:cube-coefficient}
Let $d\ge4$, $q=2^d$, $\delta\ge0$, and let $f$ be real and centered
on an odd-order group.  Put $u=\|f\|_{U^d}$ and
\[
 P_d=2^{d-3}(3^d-2^{d+1}+1).
\]
The exact quartic expansion established in the earlier repository report
\cite{repo28four}
now gives
\begin{align}
 \left|\mathbb E_{x,h}\prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^d}
       (\delta+f(x+\omega\cdot h))-\delta^q\right|
 &\le P_d\sqrt{\frac{160}{323}}\,\delta^{q-4}u^4
      +\sum_{r=5}^{q}\binom qr\delta^{q-r}u^r.
 \label{gsr:cc:28:uq:cube-improvement}
\end{align}
For $d=4$, the available leading coefficient decreases from
$100/\sqrt2$ to $100\sqrt{160/323}$, approximately $70.3815343$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The existing exact quartic term is
$P_d\delta^{q-4}\|f\|_{U^2}^4$.  Substitute
\eqref{gsr:cc:28:uq:universal-gap}.  The higher support terms retain their original
Gowers--Cauchy--Schwarz bounds.
\end{proof}

\subsection{An exact two-harmonic family and a stronger lower bound}
\label{gsr:cc:28:uq:two-harmonics-subsection}

Let $\chi$ have order greater than $24$, and set
\begin{equation}
 f_b=\chi+\chi^{-1}+b(\chi^3+\chi^{-3}),\qquad b\in\mathbb R.
 \label{gsr:cc:28:uq:two-harmonic-family}
\end{equation}
These functions are real and centered.  Orthogonality immediately gives
\begin{equation}
 \|f_b\|_{U^2}^{4}=2(1+b^4).
 \label{gsr:cc:28:uq:two-harmonic-u2}
\end{equation}

\begin{proposition}[Exact fourth-norm polynomial]
\label{gsr:cc:28:uq:polynomial}
For \eqref{gsr:cc:28:uq:two-harmonic-family},
\begin{equation}
 \|f_b\|_{U^4}^{16}=P(b)=\sum_{j=0}^{16}c_jb^j,
 \label{gsr:cc:28:uq:polynomial-formula}
\end{equation}
where the coefficients are
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{rrrr}
\toprule
$j$ & $c_j$ & $j$ & $c_j$\\
\midrule
0 & 222 & 9 & 28320\\
1 & 864 & 10 & 24160\\
2 & 4080 & 11 & 4256\\
3 & 9120 & 12 & 5920\\
4 & 25640 & 13 & 0\\
5 & 31808 & 14 & 0\\
6 & 55120 & 15 & 0\\
7 & 49280 & 16 & 222\\
8 & 52360 & & \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
In particular, if
$R_4(b)=\|f_b\|_{U^4}^{16}/\|f_b\|_{U^2}^{16}$, then
\begin{equation}
 R_4(0)=\frac{111}{8},\qquad R_4'(0)=54>0.
 \label{gsr:cc:28:uq:first-variation}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
A Fourier choice attaches $s_\omega\in\{-3,-1,1,3\}$ to each
four-cube vertex and has weight $b^{\#\{\omega:|s_\omega|=3\}}$.
Orthogonality requires
\[
 \sum_\omega s_\omega=0,\qquad
 \sum_\omega\omega_i s_\omega=0\quad(1\le i\le4),
\]
initially as congruences modulo the character order.
Each half-cube sum has absolute value at most $24$.
The total and first-coordinate congruences imply that both first-coordinate
half sums are zero integers; the other coordinate sums are also zero
integers.  Thus the order assumption removes every congruence alias.

Here is a finite generating identity for all the displayed coefficients,
so their calculation can be reproduced without enumerating $4^{16}$
full cubes.  For $v\in\mathbb Z^3$, let
\begin{align}
 F_v(b)
 &=[z^0y^v]\prod_{\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^3}
 \left(zy^\epsilon+z^{-1}y^{-\epsilon}
             +bz^3y^{3\epsilon}+bz^{-3}y^{-3\epsilon}\right).
 \label{gsr:cc:28:uq:face-generating-function}
\end{align}
The expressions are Laurent polynomials.  Splitting the four-cube into
its two three-faces gives the exact identity
\begin{equation}
 P(b)=\sum_{v\in\mathbb Z^3}F_v(b)F_{-v}(b)
     =\sum_{v\in\mathbb Z^3}F_v(b)^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:28:uq:face-square-identity}
\end{equation}
Only $v\in[-12,12]^3$ can occur, and $F_{-v}=F_v$ by negating all
frequency choices.  Multiplication of the eight four-term factors in
\eqref{gsr:cc:28:uq:face-generating-function}, followed by
\eqref{gsr:cc:28:uq:face-square-identity}, gives the table.
This is an exact finite coefficient identity; the supplied verifier uses
integer counts to reproduce every entry.

The first two coefficients also have the independent counts already
proved above: $c_0=222$, and
$c_1=16\cdot2\cdot27=864$, because there are sixteen positions for the
unique third harmonic, two choices of its sign, and twenty-seven
completions.  Formula \eqref{gsr:cc:28:uq:two-harmonic-u2} gives
$R_4(b)=P(b)/(16(1+b^4)^4)$, proving
\eqref{gsr:cc:28:uq:first-variation}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Explicit improved witness]
\label{gsr:cc:28:uq:witness}
For any character of order greater than $24$, put
\[
 F=7(\chi+\chi^{-1})-(\chi^3+\chi^{-3}).
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \|F\|_{U^2}^{4}=4804,\qquad
 \|F\|_{U^4}^{16}=5465198316262956,
 \label{gsr:cc:28:uq:witness-norms}
\end{equation}
so
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\|F\|_{U^4}^{16}}{\|F\|_{U^2}^{16}}
 =\frac{1366299579065739}{133153321267264}
 =10.2611002569\ldots <\frac{111}{8}.
 \label{gsr:cc:28:uq:witness-ratio}
\end{equation}
The rescaled witness $F/16$ is bounded by one in absolute value.
Consequently \eqref{gsr:cc:28:uq:witness-ratio} proves the lower bound in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:28:uq:main-gap}; one may take $G=\mathbb Z/29\mathbb Z$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Substitute $b=-1/7$ in Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:28:uq:polynomial} and multiply
by the appropriate powers of seven.  The bound $|F|\le16$ is immediate
from the triangle inequality.  Both normalized ratios are unchanged by
rescaling.
\end{proof}

$\|F\|_{U^4}^{16}=5465448865508028$.
Its ratio is
$1366362216377007/133153321267264$, approximately $10.2615706719$.
This difference is a useful check on the characteristic hypothesis:
the generic polynomial must not be substituted at a small character order.

\subsection{The obstruction persists in every higher dimension}
\label{gsr:cc:28:uq:all-d-subsection}

\begin{theorem}[Single characters are not local extremizers for $d\ge4$]
\label{gsr:cc:28:uq:all-d-obstruction}
Let $d\ge4$ and let $\chi$ have order greater than $3\cdot2^{d-1}$.
For
\[
 f_{b,\theta}
 =e^{i\theta}\chi+e^{-i\theta}\chi^{-1}
       +b\bigl(e^{3i\theta}\chi^3+e^{-3i\theta}\chi^{-3}\bigr),
\]
the derivative at $b=0$ of
\begin{equation}
 R_d(b)=\frac{\|f_{b,\theta}\|_{U^d}^{2^d}}
                   {\|f_{b,\theta}\|_{U^2}^{2^d}}
 \label{gsr:cc:28:uq:general-ratio}
\end{equation}
is strictly positive.  Hence every sufficiently small negative $b$
strictly increases
$\|f_{b,\theta}\|_{U^2}^4/\|f_{b,\theta}\|_{U^d}^4$.
In particular, a nonzero single real character pair of such order is not
a local maximizer for the higher-order extremal problem.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $C_{d,j}$ count assignments
$s:\{0,1\}^d\to\{-3,-1,1,3\}$ having exactly $j$ third harmonics
and satisfying the integer equations
\begin{equation}
 \sum_\omega s_\omega=0,
 \qquad \sum_\omega\omega_i s_\omega=0\quad(1\le i\le d).
 \label{gsr:cc:28:uq:general-frequency-constraints}
\end{equation}
The same half-cube argument as above shows that the character-order
hypothesis turns all orthogonality congruences into these integer
equations.  The phase factor is then
$e^{i\theta\sum_\omega s_\omega}=1$.
Thus
\[
 \|f_{b,\theta}\|_{U^d}^{2^d}=\sum_j C_{d,j}b^j,
 \qquad
 R_d(b)=\frac{\sum_jC_{d,j}b^j}
              {[2(1+b^4)]^{2^{d-2}}}.
\]
All $C_{d,j}$ are nonnegative integers, and $C_{4,1}=864$.
There are pure-sign solutions in every dimension at least two, for
example $s_\omega=(-1)^{\omega_1+\cdots+\omega_d}$, so $C_{d,0}>0$.
Place a solution with one third harmonic on one $d$-face and an
independent pure-sign solution on the other.  Their separate moment
conditions imply all the $(d+1)$-dimensional conditions.
Either face can contain the unique third harmonic, and the resulting
assignments are distinct.  Therefore
\begin{equation}
 C_{d+1,1}\ge2C_{d,1}C_{d,0}>0.
 \label{gsr:cc:28:uq:positive-linear-recursion}
\end{equation}
It follows that
$R_d'(0)=C_{d,1}/2^{2^{d-2}}>0$.
The desired inverse ratio is $R_d(b)^{-1/2^{d-2}}$, which decreases
strictly with $R_d(b)$, proving the assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
\emph{Answers two questions.} Together with Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:28:uq:five-point} and the witness above, this theorem answers, for $d\ge4$, the sub-question of source~03's Research question~\ref{gsr:fz:03:question:oddconstant} whether the odd-order constant is attained by real parts of characters: no (for $d=3$ it is, by source~04's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:04:cub:norm-gap}). It also answers the second sentence of source~29's Question~\ref{gsr:fz:29:gmsr:q-c4} (``Is a single Fourier inverse pair extremal?''): no. Item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:normgap}.
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 34--39]
At $d=4$ source~34 gives a global form: every function supported on one inverse pair of a character of odd order at least five has ratio at most $(8/111)^{1/4}$, below the witness above (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:34:norm:main} and the note there).
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 40--46]
Source~45 also re-derives the single-pair non-extremality at $d=4$ (its Section~\ref{gsr:cc:45:sec:d4}, with the dual identity and order three), without citing this source or source~34.

\subsection{What is settled and what remains open}
\label{gsr:cc:28:uq:scope}

The proved bound \eqref{gsr:cc:28:uq:universal-gap} improves the prior general
comparison for every $d\ge4$.  The exact examples give a stronger lower
bound for the fourth-order constant, and
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:28:uq:all-d-obstruction} rules out extending the third-order
single-character equality model to higher order in general.
These conclusions do not identify the sharp value of
$c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}$, establish that two harmonics suffice at an optimum,
or classify maximizing sequences.  The recurrence
\eqref{gsr:cc:28:uq:positive-linear-recursion} proves the sign of a first variation;
it does not determine an optimal higher-dimensional constant.

A natural next problem is to optimize the two complementary bounds in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:28:uq:pair-bounds}, retaining the separate fourth-power masses at
$\chi^3$ and $\chi^5$.  A more substantial improvement would use dual
functions of a two-harmonic trial function instead of a cosine, together
with compatible concentration estimates.  Another precise question is
whether the global fourth-order supremum is attained on a finite cyclic
group or requires a limiting spectral profile.  Any such investigation
must keep small-order aliases separate from integer frequency relations.

The exact quartic-count consequence \eqref{gsr:cc:28:uq:cube-improvement} is local.
It does not by itself improve a final Szemer\'edi bound.  The supplied
standard-library program verifies the finite generating identities,
the two explicit finite-group examples, the rational comparisons in the
universal estimate, and a finite set of the constructive higher-dimensional
certificates.  The general proofs are those above; no numerical
optimization or proof-assistant verification is claimed as a substitute.

\section[{A stronger fourth-dimensional norm comparison\srctag{34}}]{A stronger fourth-dimensional norm comparison}\label{gsr:cc:34:sec:d10}
\srcnote{34}{Section 10}
\label{gsr:cc:34:norm:section}

The torsion analysis and the analytic norm comparison address different
losses in a centered cube expansion.  We now improve the analytic
coefficient.  Throughout this section, $G$ is a finite abelian group
of odd order, physical averages are normalized, and Fourier sums use
counting measure. In this section we also use additive notation for
frequency labels: $-\xi$ denotes $\xi^{-1}$ and $j\chi$ denotes
$\chi^j$. For real, centered, nonzero $f$, recall
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:34:norm:definition}
 c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}
 =\sup_{G,f}\frac{\|f\|_{U^2}^4}{\|f\|_{U^d}^4}.
\end{equation}
The merged repository report proves
$c_3^{\mathrm{odd}}=2^{-1/2}$, with equality precisely for one
conjugate Fourier pair \cite{repo34}.  The subsequently received
moment manuscript already improves the fourth-dimensional bracket to
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:34:norm:old-bracket}
 (8/111)^{1/4}\le c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}
 \le (8/35)^{1/4},
\end{equation}
whose endpoints are approximately $0.518133595$ and $0.691441569$
\cite{repo34moments}.  That later manuscript is the relevant
baseline for the following improvement.

\begin{theorem}[Improved fourth-dimensional bracket]
\label{gsr:cc:34:norm:main}
Every real centered function on every finite abelian group of odd
order satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:34:norm:rational-main}
 \|f\|_{U^2}^4\le\frac23\|f\|_{U^4}^4.
\end{equation}
More precisely,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:34:norm:new-bracket}
 \frac{4804}{5465198316262956^{1/4}}
 \le c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le\frac23.
\end{equation}
The lower endpoint is approximately $0.558729391$.  It is attained
as a lower-bound certificate by a function with two conjugate Fourier
pairs on $\Z/29\Z$.  In contrast, every function supported on one
conjugate Fourier pair has ratio at most $(8/111)^{1/4}$.
\end{theorem}
