\subsection{Retaining the dominant-pair moment profile}
\label{gsr:cc:34:norm:moments}

Write $a_\xi=\widehat f(\xi)$, so
$a_{-\xi}=\overline{a_\xi}$ and $a_0=0$.  Set
\[
 S=\sum_\xi |a_\xi|^4=\|f\|_{U^2}^4,
 \qquad
 p_j=\frac{2|a_{\xi_j}|^4}{S},
 \qquad p=\max_jp_j,
\]
where one $\xi_j$ is chosen from each nonzero inverse pair.  Thus
$\sum_jp_j=1$.  The incoming moment argument
\cite{repo34moments} begins with the positive Fourier expansion
of the autocorrelation
\[
 c_f(h)=\E_x f(x)f(x-h)
       =\sum_\xi |a_\xi|^2\xi(h).
\]
We reproduce that argument and retain the additional information
needed to combine it with a dual-function estimate.

\begin{lemma}[A profile for a specified Fourier pair]
\label{gsr:cc:34:norm:moment-profile}
For $m\ge1$, put
\[
 C_m=2^{-m}\binom{2m}{m},\qquad
 H_m(p)=\sum_{k=0}^m\binom mk^2p^k(1-p)^{m-k}.
\]
For any selected pair of mass $p$, one has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:34:norm:moment-bound}
 \E_h c_f(h)^{2m}\ge C_mS^mH_m(p).
\end{equation}
Consequently, when $m=2^{d-2}$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:34:norm:profile-norm}
 \frac{\|f\|_{U^d}^4}{S}
 \ge \bigl(C_mH_m(p)\bigr)^{1/m}.
\end{equation}
For $m=4$ this gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:34:norm:A}
 \frac{\|f\|_{U^4}^4}{S}\ge A(p)
 :=\left[\frac{35}{8}
 \{1+12p(1-p)+6p^2(1-p)^2\}\right]^{1/4}.
\end{equation}
If the largest pair has $p\le1/2$, one additionally has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:34:norm:diffuse}
 \frac{\|f\|_{U^4}^4}{S}
 \ge (1015/64)^{1/4}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Put $b_j=|a_{\xi_j}|^2$, so $S=2\sum_jb_j^2$.  In the Fourier
expansion of $c_f^{2m}$, every coefficient is nonnegative.  Retain
only monomials using each $\xi_j$ and $-\xi_j$ equally often.
Writing their common multiplicity as $k_j$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:34:norm:balanced-sum}
 \E c_f^{2m}
 \ge C_mS^m
 \sum_{\sum_j k_j=m}
       \binom{m}{k_1,k_2,\ldots}^{\!2}
       \prod_j p_j^{k_j}.
\end{equation}
This is the positive balanced-monomial step of
\cite{repo34moments}.  Group its terms according to the
multiplicity $k$ of the specified pair.  The remaining multinomial
coefficient is an integer at least one, so its square is at least
itself.  The multinomial theorem therefore bounds the contribution
of the other pairs below by $(1-p)^{m-k}$.  This proves
\eqref{gsr:cc:34:norm:moment-bound}.

The recursive norm identity and monotonicity give
\[
 \|f\|_{U^d}^{2^d}
 =\E_h\|f(\cdot)f(\cdot-h)\|_{U^{d-1}}^{2^{d-1}}
 \ge\E_h|c_f(h)|^{2^{d-1}}.
\]
Since $2^{d-1}=2m$ and $S^m=\|f\|_{U^2}^{2^d}$, this proves
\eqref{gsr:cc:34:norm:profile-norm}.  Direct expansion gives
$H_4(p)=1+12p(1-p)+6p^2(1-p)^2$.

For the last claim, interpret the normalized balanced sum in
\eqref{gsr:cc:34:norm:balanced-sum} as the expected multinomial coefficient
under the multinomial distribution of four trials with probabilities
$p_j$.  That coefficient is one for a pure composition and at least
four for every mixed composition.  Hence the sum is at least
$4-3\sum_jp_j^4$.  Because
$\sum_jp_j^4\le p^3\sum_jp_j\le1/8$, the lower bound is $29/8$.
Multiplication by $C_4=35/8$ proves \eqref{gsr:cc:34:norm:diffuse}.
\end{proof}

Thus near the old moment endpoint, almost all Fourier fourth-power
mass lies in one pair.  The next step uses information that the
moment estimate alone discarded: a one-pair function has a
substantially larger fourth Gowers norm than that endpoint permits.

\subsection{The exact fourth dual function of a real character}
\label{gsr:cc:34:norm:dual-subsection}

For real $h$, define
\[
 \mathcal D_4h(x)=
 \E_{t_1,t_2,t_3,t_4}
 \prod_{\substack{v\in\{0,1\}^4\\v\ne0}}
 h(x+v\cdot t).
\]
The Gowers--Cauchy--Schwarz inequality supplies the dual certificate
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:34:norm:dual-inequality}
 |\E f\mathcal D_4h|
 \le\|f\|_{U^4}\|h\|_{U^4}^{15},
 \qquad
 \E h\mathcal D_4h=\|h\|_{U^4}^{16}.
\end{equation}
The general use of a dual function is standard.  The useful input
here is its exact value on a real character, including the two
additional harmonics.

\begin{lemma}[The fifteen-vertex dual polynomial]
\label{gsr:cc:34:norm:dual-polynomial}
Let $\chi$ have odd order at least five, let $\theta\in\R$, and put
\[
 \phi_j=e^{ij\theta}\chi^j+e^{-ij\theta}\chi^{-j}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:34:norm:dual-exact}
 \mathcal D_4\phi_1=111\phi_1+27\phi_3+\phi_5,
 \qquad \|\phi_1\|_{U^4}^{16}=222.
\end{equation}
These identities hold for arbitrary $\theta$, including when the
character order is five or seven.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Expand the fifteen factors into their two character terms.  For
each coordinate, orthogonality requires a sum of eight signs to
vanish modulo the order of $\chi$.  This sum is even and has absolute
value at most eight.  Since that order is odd and at least five,
the sum must vanish as an integer.

The positive-sign subset $T$ of the fifteen nonorigin vertices
therefore has exactly four ones in every coordinate.  If $|T|=k$,
its output harmonic is $2k-15$.  The complete count is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:34:norm:dual-counts}
 \begin{array}{c|rrrrrr}
 k&5&6&7&8&9&10\\\hline
 \#T&1&27&111&111&27&1.
 \end{array}
\end{equation}
Here is an elementary verification.  Replace each selected vertex
by its set of zero coordinates, a proper subset of $\{1,2,3,4\}$.
For five selected vertices each coordinate must occur once among
these zero sets.  The only five distinct sets with total size four
are the empty set and the four singletons, giving one choice.

For six selected vertices every coordinate has degree two.  If the
empty set is absent, the four singleton sets and a perfect matching
are forced, giving three choices.  If it is present, either the
three pair sets form a Hamilton path, with singleton sets at the
two endpoints (twelve choices), or there are one triple, one pair,
and three singletons.  In the latter case the vertex without a
singleton belongs to both the pair and triple, and the other
endpoint of the pair is the omitted vertex of the triple.  There
are $4\cdot3=12$ choices.  The total is $27$.

For seven selected vertices every coordinate has degree three.
Let $z\in\{0,1\}$ record the empty set, and let $u,e,t$ be the
numbers of singleton, pair, and triple sets.  The complete list is
\[
 \begin{array}{c|rrr|r}
 z&t&u&e&\text{number}\\\hline
 0&0&2&5&6\\
 0&1&3&3&4+24\\
 0&2&4&1&6\\
 1&0&0&6&1\\
 1&1&1&4&12+12\\
 1&2&2&2&18+24\\
 1&3&3&0&4
 \end{array}
\]
To verify completeness, the degree and cardinality equations give
$e=5+z-2t$ and $u=2-2z+t$.  If $T_0$ is the set of vertices
omitted by the triples and $U_0$ is the set of singleton vertices,
the graph formed by the pairs must have degree
$3-t+\mathbf1_{T_0}(v)-\mathbf1_{U_0}(v)$ at $v$.
The rows count, respectively: a missing edge in $K_4$; a star or a
Hamilton path with prescribed internal vertices; a prescribed edge;
$K_4$; a four-cycle or the complement of a two-edge path; a perfect
matching or a two-edge path; and equal sets $T_0=U_0$.  The entries
sum to $111$.

Complementation within all fifteen vertices preserves the four
coordinate counts and exchanges $k$ with $15-k$.  Sizes at most
four are impossible: four distinct vertices cannot all have a one
in every coordinate.  This proves \eqref{gsr:cc:34:norm:dual-counts}, hence
the dual identity.  Finally, character orthogonality in
$\E\phi_1\mathcal D_4\phi_1$ leaves just $222$.  In orders five
and seven the third and fifth harmonics still do not overlap the
first; in order five $\phi_5$ is constant, which causes no change.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 34--39]
The identity and the value $222$ are also source~28's Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:28:uq:cosine-dual}, proved there by a face-splitting count; source~35's Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:35:ng:cosine-dual} recounts them by a third decomposition. All three sources were written on the same day; none cites another for this identity.
\end{writenote}

The order-three case requires its own calculation, since additional
sign sums can vanish modulo three.

\begin{lemma}[The order-three endpoint]
\label{gsr:cc:34:norm:order-three}
For a character $\chi$ of order three and
$\phi=e^{i\theta}\chi+e^{-i\theta}\chi^{-1}$, let
$r=2\cos(3\theta)$.  Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:34:norm:order-three-formula}
 \|\phi\|_{U^4}^{16}
 =270-16r^2+8r^4
 =262+8(r^2-1)^2\ge262.
\end{equation}
If $\widehat f(\chi)=\rho e^{i\theta}$, then
$\|f\|_{U^4}\ge\rho\|\phi\|_{U^4}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The three values $a,b,c$ of $\phi$ satisfy
$a+b+c=0$, $ab+bc+ca=-3$, and $abc=r$.  Flipping cube coordinates
shows that the average associated with a step vector depends only
on its number of nonzero coordinates.  Their multiplicities are
$1,8,24,32,16$.  Consequently, after also averaging the basepoint,
\begin{align*}
 243\|\phi\|_{U^4}^{16}
 ={}&\sum a^{16}+8\sum (ab)^8
       +24r^4\sum a^4+32r^4\sum (ab)^2
       +16r^5\sum a,
\end{align*}
where each sum has three cyclic terms.  Newton recurrences give
\[
 \sum a^4=18,\quad \sum(ab)^2=9,\quad
 \sum a^{16}=13122+11664r^2+360r^4,
\]
and
$\sum(ab)^8=6561-1944r^2+108r^4$.
Substitution proves \eqref{gsr:cc:34:norm:order-three-formula}.

Conditional expectation onto the quotient defined by $\chi$ is
averaging over translations in its kernel, hence is a contraction
for the $U^4$ norm.  Since $f$ is centered, this conditional
expectation is exactly $\rho\phi$.  This proves the last claim.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Coupling the moment and dual certificates}
\label{gsr:cc:34:norm:coupling}

\begin{proposition}[A second lower bound from the largest pair]
\label{gsr:cc:34:norm:dual-profile}
Put
\[
 K=\frac{222^{1/4}}2,
 \qquad b=\frac{82^{3/4}}{111},
 \qquad
 B(p)=K\bigl[p^{1/4}-b(1-p)^{1/4}\bigr]_+^4,
\]
where $[x]_+=\max(x,0)$.  On every odd-order group,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:34:norm:B}
 \frac{\|f\|_{U^4}^4}{S}\ge B(p).
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Choose a largest pair and write
$a_\chi=\rho e^{i\theta}$, where $\rho=(pS/2)^{1/4}$.
If its order is at least five, Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:34:norm:dual-polynomial}
and centering give
\[
 \E f\mathcal D_4\phi_1
 \ge222\rho-54|a_{3\chi}|-2|a_{5\chi}|.
\]
The nonzero pairs $\{\pm3\chi\}$ and $\{\pm5\chi\}$ are distinct
from each other and from $\{\pm\chi\}$.  If $5\chi=0$, its
coefficient vanishes.  H\"older therefore yields
\begin{align*}
 54|a_{3\chi}|+2|a_{5\chi}|
 &\le (54^{4/3}+2^{4/3})^{3/4}
       (|a_{3\chi}|^4+|a_{5\chi}|^4)^{1/4}\\
 &\le 2\,82^{3/4}\bigl(S(1-p)/2\bigr)^{1/4}.
\end{align*}
Apply \eqref{gsr:cc:34:norm:dual-inequality}, using
$\|\phi_1\|_{U^4}^{16}=222$, and raise to the fourth power.
This gives precisely \eqref{gsr:cc:34:norm:B}.

If the selected character has order three,
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:34:norm:order-three} instead gives
\[
 \frac{\|f\|_{U^4}^4}{S}
 \ge \frac{262^{1/4}}2p\ge Kp\ge B(p).
\]
Thus no group-exponent restriction has been omitted.
\end{proof}

The two separate profiles already improve the incoming bound, but
their interaction gives a larger gain.  The third and fifth
harmonics that weaken the dual certificate also force additional
\emph{positive} monomials in the autocorrelation moment.

\begin{lemma}[The resonance cost of the dual error]
\label{gsr:cc:34:norm:resonance}
Suppose the selected character $\chi$ has odd order at least five.
Define
\[
 q_3=\frac{2|a_{3\chi}|^4}{S},\qquad
 q_5=\frac{2|a_{5\chi}|^4}{S},\qquad
 L=27q_3^{1/4}+q_5^{1/4},
\]
with $q_5=0$ when $5\chi=0$.  Then, writing
$R=\|f\|_{U^4}^4/S$, one has simultaneously
\begin{align}
 R&\ge K[p^{1/4}-L/111]_+^4,
 \label{gsr:cc:34:norm:raw-dual}\\
 R^4&\ge\frac{35}{8}H_4(p)
       +p^{7/2}(21\sqrt{q_3}+7\sqrt{q_5})
 \ge\frac{35}{8}H_4(p)+\frac7{244}p^{7/2}L^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:34:norm:resonant-moment}
\end{align}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The first inequality is the proof of
Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:34:norm:dual-profile} before applying H\"older to the
two unwanted harmonics.  For the second, return to the expansion
of $c_f^8$.  In addition to all pair-balanced monomials retained
in Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:34:norm:moment-profile}, retain those containing one
$3\chi$, two $\chi$, and five $-\chi$, and their inverses.
Their total contribution is
\[
 2\frac{8!}{5!\,2!}|a_\chi|^{14}|a_{3\chi}|^2
 =336|a_\chi|^{14}|a_{3\chi}|^2.
\]
Likewise, the monomials containing one $5\chi$, one $\chi$, and
six $-\chi$, together with their inverses, contribute
$112|a_\chi|^{14}|a_{5\chi}|^2$.
These are valid zero-sum frequency tuples by the integer relations
$3+2-5=0$ and $5+1-6=0$.  They are disjoint from the pair-balanced
monomials and from each other: each uses exactly one occurrence
from a different nonzero pair.  In order five the second family
has zero coefficient; in order seven the pairs remain distinct.
Any further modular relations only add nonnegative terms.

Divide by $S^4$ and use
$|a_\chi|^{14}|a_{j\chi}|^2=(S/2)^4p^{7/2}\sqrt{q_j}$.
The moment lower bound for $R^4$ follows.  Finally, weighted
Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
 (27q_3^{1/4}+q_5^{1/4})^2
 \le\left(\frac{27^2}{21}+\frac17\right)
      (21\sqrt{q_3}+7\sqrt{q_5})
 =\frac{244}{7}(21\sqrt{q_3}+7\sqrt{q_5}),
\]
which proves the last inequality.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of the upper bound in Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:34:norm:main}]
The zero function is immediate, so suppose $S>0$ and put
$R=\|f\|_{U^4}^4/S$.  If $p\le1/2$,
\eqref{gsr:cc:34:norm:diffuse} gives $R>3/2$.  On $[1/2,1]$, $A$ is
decreasing, and for $p_0=49/50$ exact arithmetic gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:34:norm:low-p-certificate}
 A(p_0)^4-\frac{81}{16}
 =\frac{1757921}{5000000}>0.
\end{equation}
Hence $1/2\le p\le p_0$ also implies $R>3/2$.

It remains to consider $p\ge p_0$.  If the selected character has
order three, Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:34:norm:order-three} gives
$R\ge Kp> (193/100)(49/50)>3/2$.
Suppose instead that its order is at least five and, towards a
contradiction, $R\le3/2$.  The following rational comparisons are
elementary:
\[
 p^{1/4}>\frac{99}{100},\qquad
 K>\frac{193}{100},\qquad
 \left(\frac{3}{2K}\right)^{1/4}<\frac{47}{50}.
\]
Indeed $(99/100)^4<49/50$,
$(193/100)^4<222/16$, and $(47/50)^4>150/193$.
By \eqref{gsr:cc:34:norm:raw-dual}, these comparisons force
\[
 \frac{L}{111}>
 \frac{99}{100}-\frac{47}{50}=\frac1{20},
 \qquad L>\frac{111}{20}.
\]
Since $H_4(p)\ge1$ and $p^{7/2}\ge p^4\ge(49/50)^4$,
\eqref{gsr:cc:34:norm:resonant-moment} now yields
\begin{align}
 R^4-\frac{81}{16}
 &>\frac{35}{8}+
   \frac7{244}\left(\frac{49}{50}\right)^4
             \left(\frac{111}{20}\right)^2-\frac{81}{16}
 \nonumber\\
 &=\frac{77821791847}{610000000000}>0,
 \label{gsr:cc:34:norm:high-p-certificate}
\end{align}
contradicting $R\le3/2$.  Thus $R>3/2$ for nonzero $f$, which
proves the stated uniform inequality.
\end{proof}

\subsection{An explicit two-pair improvement and the variational obstruction}
\label{gsr:cc:34:norm:two-pair-subsection}

\begin{proposition}[An exact two-harmonic polynomial]
\label{gsr:cc:34:norm:two-pair}
On $\Z/29\Z$, let $\chi(x)=e^{2\pi ix/29}$ and
\[
 f_t=\chi+\chi^{-1}+t(\chi^3+\chi^{-3}),\qquad t\in\R.
\]
Then $\|f_t\|_{U^2}^4=2(1+t^4)$ and
\begin{align}
 P(t):=\|f_t\|_{U^4}^{16}
 ={}&222+864t+4080t^2+9120t^3+25640t^4\nonumber\\
 &+31808t^5+55120t^6+49280t^7+52360t^8\nonumber\\
 &+28320t^9+24160t^{10}+4256t^{11}
       +5920t^{12}+222t^{16}.
 \label{gsr:cc:34:norm:two-pair-polynomial}
\end{align}
In particular $7^{16}P(-1/7)=5465198316262956$, which proves
the lower bound in \eqref{gsr:cc:34:norm:new-bracket}.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The $U^2$ identity is Fourier orthogonality.  For the second identity,
split the four-cube into its two three-dimensional faces.  An
expanded term assigns a frequency in $\{-3,-1,1,3\}$ to each
vertex.  Orthogonality in the fourth step and the basepoint requires
the total frequency on each face to be zero.  These and all remaining
coordinate conditions hold over the integers: each relevant sum
has eight terms and absolute value at most $24<29$.

For $v\in\{0,1\}^3$ assign a frequency $r_v$, and define
\[
 A_m(t)=
 \sum_{\substack{r_v\in\{-3,-1,1,3\}\\
                 \sum_vr_v=0,\ \sum_vr_vv=m}}
 t^{\#\{v:|r_v|=3\}},\qquad m\in\Z^3.
\]
The exact finite identity is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:34:norm:face-certificate}
 P(t)=\sum_{m\in\Z^3}A_m(t)A_{-m}(t).
\end{equation}
It supplies a short exhaustive integer certificate for
\eqref{gsr:cc:34:norm:two-pair-polynomial}: enumerate the $4^8$ assignments
on one face, discard those with nonzero total, and group the others
by their three integer moments and their count of frequencies of
absolute value three.  Multiplying opposite-moment polynomials
gives the coefficients displayed in
\eqref{gsr:cc:34:norm:two-pair-polynomial}.  The accompanying standard-library
verification program implements exactly this finite sum, using
integers and rational arithmetic only.  Thus the polynomial
certificate requires neither sampling nor numerical optimization.

Finally,
\[
 \frac{\|f_{-1/7}\|_{U^2}^4}{\|f_{-1/7}\|_{U^4}^4}
 =\frac{2(1+7^{-4})}{P(-1/7)^{1/4}}
 =\frac{4804}{5465198316262956^{1/4}}.
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 34--39]
\emph{This is source~28's example} (Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:28:uq:witness}): the same functions on $\Z/29\Z$, the same polynomial and the same witness $7^{16}P(-1/7)=5465198316262956$. The intake found that the best member of the family, at $t\approx-0.145611$, gives $0.5587462$, and the batch-121 intake's certificate on $\Z/7\Z$ gives $0.5587725$ (note after source~28's corollary); neither is claimed by a source as optimal.
\end{writenote}

The full polynomial is useful for an explicit certificate, but the
failure of one-pair extremality follows already from the dual
function.  At $t=0$, its third harmonic gives
$P'(0)=16\cdot2\cdot27=864>0$, whereas
$\frac{d}{dt}\|f_t\|_{U^2}^4|_{t=0}=0$.  Therefore small negative
$t$ strictly increases the ratio.  This mechanism persists for
arbitrary initial phase and every character order at least five:
the third harmonic lies outside the original pair and is nonzero.

To compare with every one-pair model, if
$f=\rho(e^{i\theta}\chi+e^{-i\theta}\chi^{-1})$ then
$\|f\|_{U^2}^4=2\rho^4$.  For character order at least five,
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:34:norm:dual-polynomial} gives ratio $2/222^{1/4}$;
for order three, Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:34:norm:order-three} gives ratio at most
$2/262^{1/4}$, which is smaller.  Thus the two-pair certificate
exceeds every one-pair model on every finite odd-order group.

\begin{remark}[What a genuine optimizer must satisfy]
\label{gsr:cc:34:norm:stationarity}
On a fixed finite group, minimize $\|f\|_{U^4}^{16}$ subject to
$\|f\|_{U^2}^4=1$ and $\E f=0$.  A minimizer exists by
finite-dimensional compactness.  The Lagrange-multiplier equation is
\[
 \mathcal D_4f=\lambda\mathcal D_2f+\mu,
 \qquad
 \widehat{\mathcal D_2f}(\xi)=|a_\xi|^2a_\xi,
\]
for real constants $\lambda,\mu$.  The extra third harmonic in
\eqref{gsr:cc:34:norm:dual-exact} prevents a one-pair function of character
order at least five from satisfying this equation.  Order three
is an exception to that stationarity statement, since its centered
function space already consists of one Fourier pair.
\end{remark}

\subsection{The resulting fourth-dimensional cube coefficient}
\label{gsr:cc:34:norm:counting}

Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:34:prop:quartic-expansion}, recalling the established
odd-order centered expansion \cite{repo34,repo34moments}, gives
\[
 Q_4(\delta+f)=\delta^{16}+100\delta^{12}\|f\|_{U^2}^4+R,
 \qquad
 |R|\le\sum_{j=5}^{16}\binom{16}{j}
                  \delta^{16-j}\|f\|_{U^4}^j,
\]
for $\delta\ge0$.  The theorem therefore gives the following
direct refinement of the coefficient used at Lemma~3.10.

\begin{corollary}[A smaller leading coefficient]
\label{gsr:cc:34:norm:cube-corollary}
Let $u=\|f\|_{U^4}$.  Under the preceding hypotheses,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:34:norm:cube-bound}
 Q_4(\delta+f)
 \le\delta^{16}+\frac{200}{3}\delta^{12}u^4
       +\sum_{j=5}^{16}\binom{16}{j}\delta^{16-j}u^j.
\end{equation}
The coefficient $200/3\approx66.666667$ replaces the audited incoming
coefficient
$100(8/35)^{1/4}\approx69.144157$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 34--39]
The leading coefficient at $d=4$ is now $200/3=66.667$ (against $100\cdot5^{-1/4}=66.874$ for source~35, $100(8/35)^{1/4}=69.144$ for source~29, $70.382$ for source~28 and $100/\sqrt2=70.711$ from source~04's comparison); recomputed at the write.
\end{writenote}

If $u^{16}\le\alpha$, the leading correction in
\eqref{gsr:cc:34:norm:cube-bound} is
$(200/3)\delta^{12}\alpha^{1/4}$ and the remaining terms have
powers $\alpha^{j/16}$, $j\ge5$.  The two-pair example implies
that the optimal universal leading coefficient is at least
$100\cdot4804/5465198316262956^{1/4}\approx55.872939$:
scale that fixed example to zero amplitude while keeping a
positive density fixed.  At sufficiently small amplitude it also
gives a weight in $[0,1]$.  This is a local counting improvement;
the subsequent density-increment losses have not been recomputed.

\begin{remark}[The same coupling in a few higher dimensions]
\label{gsr:cc:34:norm:higher}
For $m=2^{d-2}$, Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:34:norm:moment-profile} and monotonicity
$\|f\|_{U^d}\ge\|f\|_{U^4}$ combine the profiles
$(C_mH_m(p))^{1/m}$ and $B(p)$.  The identity
\[
 H_m(p)=\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}
 \binom m{2j}\binom{2j}j\{p(1-p)\}^j
\]
follows by extracting the coefficient of $z^m$ in
$(\sqrt{p(1-p)}+z+\sqrt{p(1-p)}z^2)^m$; it shows that the first
profile decreases on $[1/2,1]$.  When $p\le1/2$,
the balanced-composition argument gives the stronger bound
\[
 \frac{\|f\|_{U^d}^4}{S}
 \ge\bigl[C_m\{m-(m-1)2^{-(m-1)}\}\bigr]^{1/m}.
\]
For $m=4,8,16,32,64$, this last bound exceeds $K$, while
$C_m^{1/m}<K$.  Both comparisons become rational inequalities
after raising to the $m$th power; the accompanying certificate
checks them exactly. For each $d\in\{5,6,7,8\}$, let $p_d$ be
the unique point of $[1/2,1]$ satisfying
\[
 (C_mH_m(p_d))^{1/m}=B(p_d),\qquad
 \beta_d=(C_mH_m(p_d))^{-1/m}.
\]
The decreasing and increasing profiles meet once: their endpoint
order is opposite, and the diffuse branch is stronger than $K$.
Their maximum is at least their common value at $p_d$, proving
$c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}\le\beta_d$. The following are rounded
approximations to these exact implicit bounds:
\[
 \begin{array}{c|cc}
 d&\text{incoming moment bound}&\text{coupled bound}\\\hline
 5&0.612819643&0.609912380\\
 6&0.565388162&0.564904412\\
 7&0.537413970&0.537382843\\
 8&0.5211683364&0.5211682954
 \end{array}
\]
These are consequences of the same two proved profiles, not
applications of the weaker uniform bound $2/3$.  The fourth
dual certificate alone does not improve the incoming moment bound
in dimensions $d\ge9$.
\end{remark}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 34--39]
Recomputed at intake by bisection: the four coupled bounds and the four bounds of source~29 are reproduced to the printed digits; the gain over source~29's $B_d$ is about $3\cdot10^{-3}$ at $d=5$ and $4\cdot10^{-8}$ at $d=8$, and none for $d\ge9$, as stated. So for $5\le d\le8$ the best upper bounds among sources~01--39 are the $\beta_d$ here; for $d\ge9$ they are source~29's $B_d$ (Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:cd-upper}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 47--53]
Source~49's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:49:ng:main} gives $c_5^{\mathrm{odd}}\le29/50=0.58$, below $\beta_5=0.6099124$ here; for $d=6,7,8$ the coupled bounds $\beta_d$ of this remark remain the best (they are below $0.58$).
\end{writenote}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A stronger gap between real centered uniformity norms\srctag{35}}]{A stronger gap between real centered uniformity norms}\label{gsr:cc:35:sec:d6}
\srcnote{35}{Section 6}
\gsrsrcpartof{35}{A stronger real fourth-order uniformity gap}
\label{gsr:cc:35:ng:section}

We use normalized counting measure on a finite abelian group $G$:
$\E_x u(x)=|G|^{-1}\sum_{x\in G}u(x)$.
Let $\mathcal C$ denote complex conjugation, so
$\mathcal C z=\overline z$. For $f:G\to\C$, the normalized
Gowers quantity is
\begin{equation}
 \norm{f}_{U^d(G)}^{2^d}
 =\E_{x,h_1,\ldots,h_d\in G}
   \prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^d}
   \mathcal C^{|\omega|}f(x+\omega\cdot h),
 \qquad \omega\cdot h=\sum_{i=1}^d\omega_i h_i.
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:gowers-definition}
\end{equation}
This defines a norm for $d\ge2$; at $d=1$ it is the seminorm
$|\E f|$. For a character $\xi\in\widehat G$, our Fourier
normalization is
\begin{equation}
 \widehat f(\xi)=\E_{x\in G}f(x)\overline{\xi(x)}.
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:fourier-definition}
\end{equation}
We suppress $G$ in the norm subscript when the ambient group is fixed.
For real functions the conjugations in
\eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:gowers-definition} have no effect.

The original Gowers inequalities compare successive uniformity norms by
monotonicity \cite{gowers}. Realness and centering permit a strict
comparison on odd-order groups. The earlier research compilation proves
\[
 \norm{f}_{U^3}^{8}\ge 2\norm{f}_{U^2}^{8}
\]
for real mean-zero functions, with equality precisely for a single
conjugate Fourier pair \cite{repo35merged}. The subsequent manuscript
\emph{Logarithmic Selection, Local Freiman Models, and Higher Uniformity}
shows that this equality model does not persist at order four, and obtains
\[
 \norm{f}_{U^d}^{4}\ge
 \sqrt{\frac{323}{160}}\,\norm{f}_{U^2}^{4}
 \qquad(d\ge4)
\]
\cite{repo35higher}. More recently, the positive-autocorrelation
moment argument of \cite{repo35moments} gives the stronger fourth-order
bound
\[
 \norm{f}_{U^4}^{16}\ge\frac{35}{8}\norm{f}_{U^2}^{16}.
\]
We increase its coefficient from $35/8$ to $5$. The additional information
is a positive term counting three-term progressions in the Fourier
amplitude distribution. Its third-harmonic specialization controls the
principal negative direction in the fourth-order dual function of a
cosine.

\begin{theorem}[A stronger real centered fourth-order norm gap]
\label{gsr:cc:35:ng:main}
Let $G$ be a finite abelian group of odd order, and let $f:G\to\R$
have mean zero. Then
\begin{equation}
 \norm{f}_{U^4}^{16}\ge 5\norm{f}_{U^2}^{16}.
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:fourth-power-form}
\end{equation}
In fact \eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:fourth-power-form} is strict for nonzero $f$.
Consequently, for every integer $d\ge4$,
\begin{equation}
 \norm{f}_{U^d}^{4}\ge 5^{1/4}\norm{f}_{U^2}^{4}.
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:main-inequality}
\end{equation}
The constant $5$ is not asserted to be optimal. The improvement over
the strongest inspected prior estimates is at $d=4$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 34--39]
\emph{Superseded the same day by source~34.} Source~34's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:34:norm:main}, written from the same pin and not cited here, gives the coefficient $81/16=5.0625>5$, that is $c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le2/3$ against $5^{-1/4}=0.6687403$ here; source~45 (placed, not yet written) records $4795/832$. The statement that $5$ improves ``the strongest inspected $U^4$ coefficient $35/8$'' was true at the pin. The energy inequality of Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:35:ng:progression-energy} is a separate result that source~34 does not contain. The intake re-derived the proof and recomputed every rational comparison of the scalar certificate exactly.
\end{writenote}

Define the extremal constants
\begin{equation}
 c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}
 =\sup_{\substack{G\text{ finite abelian, }|G|\text{ odd}\\
                  f:G\to\R,\ \E f=0,\ f\ne0}}
 \frac{\norm{f}_{U^2}^{4}}{\norm{f}_{U^d}^{4}}.
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:extremal-constant}
\end{equation}
The new fourth-order bound gives
\begin{equation}
 c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le 5^{-1/4}
 =0.668740304976\ldots,
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:constant-bound}
\end{equation}
improving $(8/35)^{1/4}=0.691441569\ldots$ from
\cite{repo35moments}, and also the earlier
$\sqrt{160/323}=0.703815343078\ldots$.
The known rational lower example from
\cite{repo35higher} consequently gives the smaller interval
\begin{equation}
 \left(\frac{133153321267264}{1366299579065739}\right)^{1/4}
 \le c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le5^{-1/4}.
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:interval}
\end{equation}
The left endpoint is approximately $0.558729390985$.
We import that example only for comparison; the proof of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:35:ng:main} does not use it.

The propagation to $d\ge5$ in \eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:main-inequality} is valid,
but is weaker than the prior central-binomial estimate at those
orders. The combined statement, with $q=2^{d-2}$, is
\begin{equation}
 c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}\le
 \min\left\{5^{-1/4},\frac{2}{\binom{2q}{q}^{1/q}}\right\}
 \qquad(d\ge4).
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:combined-bounds}
\end{equation}
The second entry is the bound of \cite{repo35moments}; at $d=5$
it is approximately $0.612819643$. Thus no new higher-dimensional
record is inferred merely from monotonicity.

\subsection{The Fourier identity and the retained energy terms}
\label{gsr:cc:35:ng:energy-section}

All averages use normalized counting measure. We write the dual group
additively and put
\[
 a_r=\widehat f(r),\qquad
 \lambda_r=|a_r|^2,\qquad
 S=\sum_r\lambda_r^2=\norm{f}_{U^2}^{4},\qquad
 M=\sum_r\lambda_r^4.
\]
Thus $a_{-r}=\overline{a_r}$ and $a_0=0$. The sums over the dual group
are ordinary, unnormalized sums; this convention is necessary because
the Fourier coefficients themselves are normalized.

The exact Fourier identity for the third uniformity norm is
\begin{align}
 \norm{f}_{U^3}^{8}
 &=\sum_{s,t\in\widehat G}|T(s,t)|^2,
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:fourier-identity}\\
 T(s,t)
 &=\sum_{r\in\widehat G}
 a_r\overline{a_{r+s}}\,\overline{a_{r+t}}a_{r+s+t}.
 \nonumber
\end{align}
For example, Fourier expansion of the original cube imposes four
orthogonality equations. Solving these equations expresses its frequency
variables as an affine cube; grouping its parallel faces gives
\eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:fourier-identity}. The solution uses additions and subtractions,
so it introduces no torsion assumption.

On the two coordinate axes,
\[
 T(0,t)=T(t,0)=\sum_r\lambda_r\lambda_{r+t}.
\]
If
\[
 E(\lambda)
 =\sum_{r+s=t+w}\lambda_r\lambda_s\lambda_t\lambda_w,
\]
retaining those axes in the nonnegative sum gives
\begin{equation}
 \norm{f}_{U^3}^{8}\ge2E(\lambda)-S^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:axes}
\end{equation}
The term $S^2$ corrects the double counting of $(s,t)=(0,0)$.

\begin{theorem}[A Fourier progression refinement]
\label{gsr:cc:35:ng:progression-energy}
Let $f$ be real and centered on a finite abelian group of odd order,
and define
\[
 J(\lambda)=\sum_{r,t}\lambda_r^2\lambda_t\lambda_{2r-t}.
\]
Then
\begin{align}
 \norm{f}_{U^3}^{8}
 &\ge 5S^2-10M+4J(\lambda),
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:full-progression-bound}\\
 \norm{f}_{U^3}^{8}
 &\ge 5S^2-6M
       +8\sum_r|a_r|^6|a_{3r}|^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:all-third-harmonics}
\end{align}
In particular, for any character $\xi$ of odd order at least five,
with $A=|a_\xi|$ and $B=|a_{3\xi}|$,
\begin{equation}
 \norm{f}_{U^3}^{8}\ge5S^2-6M+16A^6B^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:third-harmonic}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
In $E(\lambda)$ retain the union of the three families
\[
 \mathcal A=\{r=t,\ s=w\},\qquad
 \mathcal B=\{r=w,\ s=t\},\qquad
 \mathcal C=\{s=-r,\ w=-t\}.
\]
Each contributes $S^2$, using the evenness of $\lambda$ for
$\mathcal C$. Every pairwise intersection contributes $M$.
The triple intersection has $r=-r$, hence $r=0$ because the group
has odd order. Its weight is zero because $\lambda_0=0$.
The union therefore has weight $3S^2-3M$.

Next retain every nonconstant repeated-entry quadruple
\begin{equation}
 (r,r;t,2r-t),\qquad t\ne r,
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:repeated-quadruples}
\end{equation}
and its side reversal. Odd group order ensures that the two entries
on the unequal side are distinct: $t=2r-t$ would imply $t=r$.
Thus these ordered quadruples are distinct from their side reversals,
and have total weight $2(J-M)$. No positive-weight quadruple in this
new family belongs to $\mathcal A$ or $\mathcal B$, since that would
force $t=r$. Membership in $\mathcal C$ would force $r=-r$, hence
$r=0$ and zero weight. Consequently
\[
 E(\lambda)\ge3S^2-5M+2J(\lambda).
\]
Combining this with \eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:axes} proves
\eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:full-progression-bound}.

For each nonzero $r$, retain in $J$ the diagonal $t=r$ and the
additional indices $t=-r,3r$. They are distinct: a coincidence
requires $2r=0$ or $4r=0$. The $r=0$ terms have zero weight.
It follows that
\[
 J(\lambda)\ge M+2\sum_r\lambda_r^3\lambda_{3r},
\]
which proves \eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:all-third-harmonics}. If $3r=0$, the new
summand vanishes, so the statement includes groups with three-torsion.
Finally the terms $r=\xi,-\xi$ in that sum are equal and have value
$A^6B^2$, proving \eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:third-harmonic}.
\end{proof}

For a direct view of the last refinement, its extra energy configurations
are obtained from
\[
 (\xi,\xi;-\xi,3\xi),\qquad
 (-\xi,-\xi;\xi,-3\xi)
\]
by interchanging sides and ordering the unequal side. These are eight
distinct configurations outside $\mathcal A\cup\mathcal B\cup\mathcal C$,
each of weight $A^6B^2$. The factor $16$ in
\eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:third-harmonic} includes the additional factor two from
\eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:axes}.

\subsection{Two inequalities retaining the largest Fourier pair}
\label{gsr:cc:35:ng:largest-pair-section}

Assume $f\ne0$ and choose $\xi$ maximizing $|a_\xi|$. Set
\[
 A=|a_\xi|,\qquad p=\frac{2A^4}{S},\qquad D=1-p.
\]
Here $p$ is the fraction of Fourier fourth-power mass carried by the
pair $\{\xi,-\xi\}$. In particular $0<p\le1$.
After multiplying $f$ by a positive scalar we may suppose $S=1$;
then $A=(p/2)^{1/4}$.

If $p_j$ are the corresponding masses of the other conjugate pairs,
then $\sum_jp_j=D$ and
\begin{equation}
 M=\frac12\left(p^2+\sum_jp_j^2\right)
 \le\frac{p^2+D^2}{2},
 \qquad M\le\frac p2.
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:moment-bounds}
\end{equation}
The second estimate uses the maximality of $p$.
The energy argument without its new positive term gives
\begin{equation}
 \norm{f}_{U^3}^{8}\ge5-3p.
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:coarse-pair-bound}
\end{equation}
If the order of $\xi$ is at least five,
\eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:third-harmonic} and the first inequality of
\eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:moment-bounds} give
\begin{equation}
 \norm{f}_{U^3}^{8}\ge2+6pD+16A^6B^2,
 \qquad B=|a_{3\xi}|.
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:refined-pair-bound}
\end{equation}

The quadratic dependence on $B$ is the useful new feature.
An estimate using only the residual fourth-power mass would permit
$B$ as large as $(D/2)^{1/4}$. Formula
\eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:refined-pair-bound} imposes a further cost even when that
mass is small.

\subsection{The exact dual function of a cosine}
\label{gsr:cc:35:ng:dual-section}

For a real function $g$ put
\[
 D_4g(x)=\E_{h_1,h_2,h_3,h_4}
 \prod_{\substack{\omega\in\{0,1\}^4\\\omega\ne0}}
 g(x+\omega\cdot h).
\]
Cube Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\begin{equation}
 \left|\E_x f(x)D_4g(x)\right|
 \le\norm{f}_{U^4}\norm{g}_{U^4}^{15}.
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:dual-cs}
\end{equation}
The following finite identity was established in
\cite{repo35higher}. We give the counting proof because its
coefficients are essential to the numerical improvement.

\begin{lemma}[Fourth-order cosine identity]
\label{gsr:cc:35:ng:cosine-dual}
Let $\chi$ be a character of odd order at least five and let
$\theta\in\R$. Write
$g_j=e^{ij\theta}\chi^j+e^{-ij\theta}\chi^{-j}$. Then
\begin{equation}
 \norm{g_1}_{U^4}^{16}=222,
 \qquad D_4g_1=111g_1+27g_3+g_5.
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:cosine-identities}
\end{equation}
When $\chi$ has order five, $g_5$ is constant and the formula still holds.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Expand the factors into characters. Each direction equation requires
a sum of eight signs to be divisible by the odd order of $\chi$.
The sum is even and lies between $-8$ and $8$, so for an odd order
at least five it must be zero as an integer. The counting is therefore
unchanged for character orders five, seven, or larger.

For the full cube, each of two opposite three-faces has four plus
signs. Let $n(t)$ count four-subsets of $\{0,1\}^3$ with coordinate
sum $t=(t_1,t_2,t_3)$. Splitting into these faces gives the total
count $\sum_tn(t)^2$. The coefficient identity
\begin{align}
 [z^4]\prod_{\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^3}(1+zx^\epsilon)
 ={}&x_1x_2x_3\prod_{j=1}^3(1+x_j)^2
 \nonumber\\
 &+\sum_{i=1}^3(1+x_i^4)\prod_{j\ne i}x_j^2
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:subset-generating-identity}
\end{align}
gives the complete table
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lrr}
\hline
Type of $t$ & Number of $t$ & $n(t)$\\
\hline
One coordinate $0$ or $4$, the other two $2$ & 6 & 1\\
All three coordinates in $\{1,3\}$ & 8 & 1\\
Two in $\{1,3\}$, one equal to $2$ & 12 & 2\\
One in $\{1,3\}$, two equal to $2$ & 6 & 4\\
$(2,2,2)$ & 1 & 8\\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Thus the count is $6+8+12\cdot4+6\cdot16+64=222$.
All surviving full-cube assignments have total frequency zero,
which proves the first identity of \eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:cosine-identities}.

For the dual function, adjoining the missing origin sign shows that
the coefficients at frequencies $1$ and $-1$ are each $111$.
At frequency $-3$, the six plus-sign vertices among the fifteen
nonzero vertices must place four selected vertices on each coordinate
face. Complement all four coordinates. The resulting six vertices
exclude $1111$ and have coordinate sums $(2,2,2,2)$.
If $a_j$ counts their vertices of Hamming weight $j$, the possible
profiles and counts are
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{rrrrr}
\hline
$a_0$ & $a_1$ & $a_2$ & $a_3$ & Count\\
\hline
0 & 4 & 2 & 0 & 3\\
1 & 2 & 3 & 0 & 12\\
1 & 3 & 1 & 1 & 12\\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
In the first case the two edges form a perfect matching. In the
second, choose two singleton endpoints in six ways and a three-edge
path between them in two ways. In the third, choose the triple in
four ways and the coordinate of that triple without its singleton in
three ways; the remaining edge is forced. Hence the coefficient is
$3+12+12=27$. Sign reversal gives the same coefficient at $3$.

At frequency $-5$, the five plus-sign vertices must have sixteen
coordinate incidences. The unique possibility consists of the
weight-four vertex and all four weight-three vertices. Its sign
reversal gives frequency $5$. Four distinct vertices have at most
thirteen incidences, so no frequency of absolute value at least seven
survives. This proves the dual identity.
\end{proof}

Choose $\theta$ with $a_\xi=Ae^{i\theta}$ and apply the lemma to
the corresponding character. Put $C=|a_{5\xi}|$.
The pairs $\{\pm3\xi\}$ and $\{\pm5\xi\}$ are distinct and
outside $\{\pm\xi\}$; the sole exception is $5\xi=0$ at order
five, in which case $C=0$. The excluded coincidences would require
$2\xi=0$, $4\xi=0$, $6\xi=0$, or $8\xi=0$.
Consequently
\begin{equation}
 2B^4+2C^4\le D.
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:tail-budget}
\end{equation}
The dual pairing satisfies
\[
 \E fD_4g_1\ge2(111A-27B-C).
\]
Therefore, with $R=\norm{f}_{U^4}^{16}$ under the normalization
$S=1$, \eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:dual-cs} gives
\begin{equation}
 R\ge222\left[A-\frac{27}{111}B-\frac1{111}C\right]_+^{16},
 \qquad [x]_+=\max(x,0).
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:dual-pair-bound}
\end{equation}

\subsection{The character of order three}
\label{gsr:cc:35:ng:order-three-section}

The previous dual identity has a different form at order three.
We treat that case directly, rather than imposing a stronger
restriction on the ambient group.

\begin{lemma}[The ternary cosine]
\label{gsr:cc:35:ng:ternary}
For a character $\chi$ of order three and
$g=e^{i\theta}\chi+e^{-i\theta}\chi^{-1}$,
\begin{align}
 \norm{g}_{U^4}^{16}
 &=286+32\cos(6\theta)+16\cos(12\theta)
 \nonumber\\
 &=262+32\left(\cos(6\theta)+\frac12\right)^2\ge262.
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:ternary-value}
\end{align}
If a largest Fourier pair of $f$ has order three, then
\begin{equation}
 R\ge\frac{131}{8}p^4.
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:ternary-bound}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
In the character expansion of the full cube, the possible numbers
of plus signs are $2,5,8,11,14$. Their multiplicities are respectively
$8,16,286,16,8$, as follows. At size two the vertices must be
antipodal. At size five, reflect every coordinate that occurs four
times; the result is the origin together with the four unit vertices,
giving sixteen copies. At size eight, the $222$ configurations from
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:35:ng:cosine-dual} have four selected vertices on every
coordinate face. Every remaining one consists of a whole three-face
with a single vertex moved across the perpendicular direction.
There are $4\cdot2\cdot8=64$ of these, each with exactly one
exceptional direction. Taking complements gives sizes eleven and
fourteen. The frequencies are $-12,-6,0,6,12$, so summing their
phases proves the first line of \eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:ternary-value}. The
double-angle identity proves the second.

For \eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:ternary-bound}, average $f$ over the kernel of the
chosen order-three character. Translation invariance and the triangle
inequality make this averaging contractive for $U^4$. On the
three-element quotient the projected function is exactly $Ag$,
because $f$ is centered. Hence
$R\ge262A^{16}=(131/8)p^4$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A scalar certificate using exact rational bounds}
\label{gsr:cc:35:ng:scalar-section}

We now prove the constant $5$. The proof reduces to two elementary
one-variable estimates. Its few rational comparisons are also checked
by the accompanying standard-library program
\texttt{verification/verify\_norm\_gap.py}.

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:35:ng:main}]
The zero function is immediate. Otherwise rescale to $S=1$, so
$R=\norm{f}_{U^4}^{16}$. Suppose for a contradiction that $R\le5$.
Monotonicity and the rational comparison $\sqrt5<56/25$ give
\[
 \norm{f}_{U^3}^{8}\le\norm{f}_{U^4}^{8}
 \le\sqrt5<\frac{56}{25}.
\]
Equation~\eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:coarse-pair-bound} implies $p>23/25$.
If the chosen character has order three,
\eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:ternary-bound} yields
\[
 R>\frac{131}{8}\left(\frac{23}{25}\right)^4>5,
\]
a contradiction. Its order is therefore at least five.

Since $p>1/2$ and $p(1-p)$ decreases on $[1/2,1]$,
\eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:refined-pair-bound} implies $p>19/20$.
Indeed, $p\le19/20$ would give
$6p(1-p)\ge57/200>6/25$, contradicting that equation.
Thus
\begin{equation}
 0\le D<\frac1{20},\qquad
 B^2<\frac{6/25-(57/10)D}{16A^6}.
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:scalar-B-bound}
\end{equation}
In particular $D<4/95$.

Put $a=2^{-1/4}$. For $0\le D\le1/20$,
\begin{equation}
 A=a(1-D)^{1/4}\ge a(1-D/3).
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:linear-A-bound}
\end{equation}
To check this, differentiate
$(1-D)^{1/4}-(1-D/3)$. Its derivative is positive on this
interval because $(1-D)^{3/4}\ge19/20>3/4$.
We shall prove
\begin{equation}
 A-\frac{27}{111}B-\frac1{111}C>\frac{789}{1000}.
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:target-bracket}
\end{equation}
This contradicts \eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:dual-pair-bound} and $R\le5$, since
\begin{equation}
 222\left(\frac{789}{1000}\right)^{16}>5.
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:final-rational-check}
\end{equation}

First suppose $0\le D\le1/300$. H\"older's inequality and
\eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:tail-budget} give
\[
 27B+C\le
 (27^{4/3}+1)^{3/4}(B^4+C^4)^{1/4}
 \le82^{3/4}(D/2)^{1/4}.
\]
The exact comparisons
\[
 a>\frac{21}{25},\qquad
 82^{3/4}<\frac{273}{10},\qquad
 (1/600)^{1/4}<\frac{203}{1000}
\]
and \eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:linear-A-bound} show that the left side of
\eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:target-bracket} is greater than
\begin{equation}
 \frac{21}{25}\frac{899}{900}
 -\frac1{111}\frac{273}{10}\frac{203}{1000}
 =\frac{18879}{22500}-\frac{55419}{1110000}
 >\frac{789}{1000}.
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:small-D-check}
\end{equation}

It remains to consider $1/300\le D<4/95$.
Equations~\eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:scalar-B-bound}, \eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:linear-A-bound},
and $C\le(D/2)^{1/4}$ show that the left side of
\eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:target-bracket} is at least
\begin{align}
 F(D)={}&a(1-D/3)
 -\frac{27}{444a^3}(1-D/3)^{-3}
       \sqrt{6/25-57D/10}
 \nonumber\\
 &-\frac1{111}(D/2)^{1/4}.
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:scalar-F}
\end{align}
For
$h(D)=(1-D/3)^{-3}\sqrt{6/25-57D/10}$, differentiation gives
\[
 -h'(D)
 =(1-D/3)^{-4}
   \frac{261/100+(19/4)D}{\sqrt{6/25-57D/10}}>5.
\]
The last inequality follows from $\sqrt{6/25-57D/10}<1/2$
and $(1-D/3)^{-4}\ge1$.
Use $a^3<3/5$, $a<1$, and $300^{3/4}<73$ to obtain
\begin{equation}
 F'(D)>
 \frac{225}{444}-\frac13-\frac{73}{444}
 =\frac1{111}>0.
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:F-increasing}
\end{equation}
Here the last negative term bounds the derivative of
$(D/2)^{1/4}/111=aD^{1/4}/111$ for $D\ge1/300$.

It suffices to evaluate $F$ at $D=1/300$. The exact bounds
\begin{align*}
 a\frac{899}{900}&>\frac{4199}{5000},\\
 \frac{\sqrt{221/1000}}
      {4a^3(899/900)^3}&<\frac15,\\
 (1/600)^{1/4}&<\frac{203}{1000}
\end{align*}
give
\begin{equation}
 F(1/300)>
 \frac{4199}{5000}-\frac{27/5+203/1000}{111}
 =\frac{4199}{5000}-\frac{5603}{111000}
 >\frac{789}{1000}.
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:large-D-check}
\end{equation}
For the first bound use $a>1051/1250$. For the second,
squaring reduces it to
\[
 \frac{221}{1000}
 <\frac{16}{25}a^6\left(\frac{899}{900}\right)^6,
\]
which holds already with $a$ replaced by $21/25$.
Thus every comparison in the proof reduces to integer arithmetic
after clearing positive denominators and, where necessary, taking
fourth powers.

Equations~\eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:F-increasing} and \eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:large-D-check}
finish \eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:target-bracket}, contradicting $R\le5$.
Undoing the normalization proves
$\norm{f}_{U^4}^{16}>5S^4$ for $f\ne0$.
Taking fourth roots yields
$\norm{f}_{U^4}^{4}\ge5^{1/4}S$.
Finally $\norm{f}_{U^d}\ge\norm{f}_{U^4}$ for $d\ge4$
proves \eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:main-inequality} with exactly the asserted exponents.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The cube-count consequence and the remaining extremal problem}
\label{gsr:cc:35:ng:consequence-section}

For a real function $F$ on $G$, write
\[
 Q_d(F)=\E_{x,h_1,\ldots,h_d}
 \prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^d}F(x+\omega\cdot h).
\]
The fourth-order expansion proved in \cite{repo35merged} says that,
on odd-order groups, for $f=F-\delta$, $\E f=0$, $m=2^d$, and
$u=\norm{f}_{U^d}$,
\begin{align}
 Q_d(F)
 &=\delta^m+R_d\delta^{m-4}\norm{f}_{U^2}^{4}
   +\mathcal R_d,
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:cube-expansion}\\
 |\mathcal R_d|
 &\le\sum_{j=5}^{m}\binom mj\delta^{m-j}u^j,
 \qquad
 R_d=\frac{6^d-2\cdot4^d+2^d}{8}.
 \nonumber
\end{align}
This statement assumes $\delta\ge0$.

\begin{corollary}[An improved leading cube-count bound]
\label{gsr:cc:35:ng:cube-corollary}
Let $d\ge4$, let $G$ have odd order, and let $F:G\to\R$ have mean
$\delta\ge0$. With $f=F-\delta$, $m=2^d$, and $u=\norm{f}_{U^d}$,
\begin{equation}
 Q_d(F)\le\delta^m
 +5^{-1/4}R_d\delta^{m-4}u^4
 +\sum_{j=5}^{m}\binom mj\delta^{m-j}u^j.
 \label{gsr:cc:35:ng:cube-upper}
\end{equation}
In particular, at $d=4$ the quartic multiplier is
$100\cdot5^{-1/4}=66.8740304976\ldots$, improving the strongest
inspected prior multiplier
$100(8/35)^{1/4}=69.1441569\ldots$ from \cite{repo35moments}.
For $d\ge5$, retain instead the smaller multiplier supplied by
the minimum in \eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:combined-bounds}.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Substitute Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:35:ng:main} into the exact quartic term of
\eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:cube-expansion}, leaving the established remainder unchanged.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 34--39]
Source~34's Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:34:norm:cube-corollary} has $200/3=66.667$ in place of $100\cdot5^{-1/4}=66.874$ here (recomputed at the write).
\end{writenote}

For a set $A\subseteq G$ satisfying
$\norm{\1_A-\delta}_{U^d}^{m}\le\alpha$, replace $u^j$ in
\eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:cube-upper} by $\alpha^{j/m}$. Multiplication by
$|G|^{d+1}$ converts the normalized average into the parameterized
cube count used in the paper. This is a refinement of the local
Lemma~3.10 interface. It neither changes the order of the quartic
error nor supplies an optimal coefficient for $d\ge4$.

\paragraph{Methods and limitations.}
The new input is the explicit retention of repeated-entry additive
quadruples in Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:35:ng:progression-energy}. The cosine dual
identity and the preceding norm-gap framework are credited to the
earlier reports and reproved where used. All constants in the final
scalar argument are certified by exact arithmetic; the program also
enumerates the sign counts behind
Lemmas~\ref{gsr:cc:35:ng:cosine-dual} and~\ref{gsr:cc:35:ng:ternary}.
The proof is mathematical rather than Lean-formalized. It provides a
new bound relative to the inspected repository materials, with no
claim of an exhaustive literature-priority determination.

\begin{problem}[The next quantitative and structural questions]
\label{gsr:cc:35:ng:questions}
Can the full statistic $J(\lambda)$, or further nonnegative terms in
\eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:fourier-identity}, determine the optimal $c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}$?
Does an extremizer live on a finite cyclic quotient, or only arise as
a limit? At higher orders, can the additional harmonics in $D_d$ of
a cosine yield constants that improve with $d$, rather than the
single fourth-order constant propagated by monotonicity?
The negative third-harmonic examples in
\cite{repo35higher} show that any proposed classification
must retain Fourier phases as well as amplitude masses.
\end{problem}

\section{Source~34's chapter: prime torsion in cube expansions \wtag}\label{gsr:cc:sec:torsion}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the seventh write, 6~October 2026.}}\par
The next eight sections are source~34's Sections~2--9, on when a prime $p$ first enters the centered expansion of a cube count through Smith torsion of a Boolean configuration. \emph{Logically the chapter follows source~09's support-lattice material} (Sections~\ref{gsr:cc:09:sec:d4} and~\ref{gsr:cc:09:sec:d9}: integer value lattices, the order-five obstruction and the all-prime family with $h(\ell)\le\ell+2$) and source~21's order-five certificates; it is printed here because no number printed earlier may move. Source~34's introduction is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:34:sec:d1}; its Section~10 is in the chapter on $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}$ (Section~\ref{gsr:cc:34:sec:d10}).

\emph{What is proved, in one paragraph.} The least support $h(p)$ of an affinely independent Boolean configuration admitting a full-support characteristic-$p$ relation is $D_{\mathrm{div}}(p)+1$, where $D_{\mathrm{div}}(p)$ is the least order of a nonsingular binary matrix with determinant divisible by $p$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:34:thm:reduction}); $h(7)=7$ and $h(11)=h(13)=h(17)=8$, with exhaustive certificates for $11$ and $13$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:34:thm:small-primes}); every integer up to $\exp(\frac12N\log N-N\log\log N-4N)$ is eventually the sole nonunit Smith factor of a binary matrix of order $N$, through Shitov's composition and the Alon--Vu matrices (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:34:det:thm:range}); hence $h(p)\sim\hc(p)\sim2\log p/\log\log p$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:34:asy:thm:main}); universal nonnegativity of cyclic moments holds exactly for inverse-paired coefficients, and $h_{\mathrm{pos}}(m)\sim4\log m/\log\log m$ (Theorems~\ref{gsr:cc:34:pos:classification}, \ref{gsr:cc:34:pos:asymptotic}); the exact quartic term is recalled with proof (Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:34:prop:quartic-expansion}). This answers source~09's prime-onset question (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:onset}).
