\section[{Fourier identities and the retained energy defect\srctag{38}}]{Fourier identities and the retained energy defect}\label{gsr:cc:38:sec:d2}
\srcnote{38}{Section 2}
\gsrsrcpartof{38}{Exact characteristic-five cube extremizers}
\label{gsr:cc:38:sec:fourier}

This section records the background identities in the form needed by
the new projection argument. The fourth-order expansion and its
leading norm gap were established in preceding project reports
\cite{repo38collected,repo38five}; they are reproved here so the main result
has no dependence on an unquoted computation.

For $f:G\to\C$, use
\[
 a_r=\widehat f(r)=\E_x f(x)\overline{r(x)},\qquad
 f(x)=\sum_{r\in\widehat G}a_r r(x).
\]
For real centered $f$, one has $a_{-r}=\overline{a_r}$ and $a_0=0$.
Set
\[
 \lambda_r=|a_r|^2,\quad
 S=\sum_r|a_r|^4,\quad M=\sum_r|a_r|^8,\quad
 \mathcal E(\lambda)=\sum_{r+s=t+w}\lambda_r\lambda_s\lambda_t\lambda_w.
\]
The Gowers--Cauchy--Schwarz inequality bounds a cube with eight
possibly different functions by the product of their $U^3$ norms.
It follows by applying Cauchy--Schwarz successively in the three
directions and expanding each resulting square
\cite[Lemma~3.8]{gowers}. Its homogeneous form requires no
$L^\infty$ hypothesis. Expanding a sum in the cube form then gives
the triangle inequality. In particular, translation averages are
contractive for $U^3$.

\begin{lemma}[Fourier squares and their axes]
\label{gsr:cc:38:lem:fourier-squares}
Put
\[
 T_f(s,t)=\sum_r a_r\overline{a_{r+s}}\,
                       \overline{a_{r+t}}a_{r+s+t}.
\]
Then
\[
 \|f\|_{U^3}^8=\sum_{s,t}|T_f(s,t)|^2.
\]
For real $f$, $T_f$ is real, symmetric in its two arguments, and
unchanged by reversing either argument. Its two coordinate axes,
with their common origin counted once, contribute exactly
\[
 2\mathcal E(\lambda)-S^2.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Expand $|T_f(s,t)|^2$ and sum over $s,t$. Fourier expansion of the
physical cube imposes the base and three direction equations on
its eight frequencies. Their solutions are parametrized by a
parity-adjusted affine frequency cube; grouping its two opposite
faces gives precisely the displayed sum of squares. This can also
be checked directly by using the two base frequencies and the two
increments in the expanded square as its four free variables.
No division by a group element is used.

For real $f$, substitution $r\mapsto-r-s-t$ pairs every summand in
$T_f$ with its conjugate. Interchange of $s,t$ and translation of
$r$ give the other symmetries. Finally
\[
 T_f(0,t)=\sum_r\lambda_r\lambda_{r+t},\qquad T_f(0,0)=S.
\]
The squared sum on either axis is $\mathcal E(\lambda)$; subtract
one copy of $S^2$ at their intersection.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Odd-order quartic gap]
\label{gsr:cc:38:lem:quartic-gap}
For real centered $f$ on a finite abelian group of odd order,
\[
 \|f\|_{U^3}^8\ge5S^2-6M\ge2S^2.
\]
If $\{\xi,-\xi\}$ is a largest conjugate Fourier pair and
$D_{\rm pair}=\sum_{r\notin\{\xi,-\xi\}}|a_r|^4$, then
\[
 \|f\|_{U^3}^8\ge2S^2+3SD_{\rm pair}.
\]
A pure conjugate pair whose character has order five attains
$\|f\|_{U^3}^8=2S^2$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Write the energy as a sum over zero-sum quadruples and retain the
three families obtained by pairing the four positions into opposite
pairs. Each family has weight $S^2$, and every pairwise intersection
has weight $M$. The triple intersection requires $2r=0$; it has
zero weight because the order is odd and $a_0=0$. Thus
$\mathcal E(\lambda)\ge3S^2-3M$. Retaining the axes in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:38:lem:fourier-squares} proves the first inequality.

If $x_j$ are the total fourth-power masses of the conjugate pairs,
then $S=\sum_jx_j$ and $M=\frac12\sum_jx_j^2\le S^2/2$.
For a largest pair with coefficient modulus $\rho$,
$M\le\rho^4 S=(S-D_{\rm pair})S/2$, proving the stronger bound.
For a pure pair of order five, the only nonzero Fourier-square
slots are $(0,0)$ and the four axis slots with increment
$\pm2\xi$. They contribute $4\rho^8+4\rho^8=8\rho^8=2S^2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Complete centered expansion through degree seven]
\label{gsr:cc:38:lem:centered-expansion}
Assume $G$ has odd order and $f$ is real and centered. Then
\[
 \Qthirtyeight(\delta+f)=\delta^8+12\delta^4S+8\delta^3B_5(f)
                      +\delta^2 C_6(f)+\delta C_7(f)+\|f\|_{U^3}^8,
\]
where
\[
 B_5(f)=\sum_r a_{2r}a_{-r}^3a_r,\qquad
 C_6(f)=12H_f+12J_f+4K_f,
\]
with
\begin{align*}
 H_f&=\sum_{r+s+t=0}\lambda_r\lambda_s\lambda_t,\\
 J_f&=\sum_{r,s}\lambda_r a_s^2a_{r-s}\overline{a_{r+s}},\\
 K_f&=\sum_{r+s+t=0}a_r^2a_s^2a_t^2.
\end{align*}
These statistics are real. If
\[
 L_f(s,t)=2\Rea(a_sa_t\overline{a_{s+t}})
       +2\Rea(a_s\overline{a_t}\,\overline{a_{s-t}}),
\]
then $C_7(f)=2\Rea\langle T_f,L_f\rangle$, with counting measure
in this inner product. In particular
\[
 |B_5(f)|\le\|f\|_{U^3}^5,\quad
 |C_6(f)|\le28\|f\|_{U^3}^6,\quad
 |C_7(f)|\le8\|f\|_{U^3}^7.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Expand the eight-vertex product by the support of its centered
factors. A support of size one, two, or three consists of independent
cube forms whose coefficient equations have unit pivots, so centering kills it. For four vertices,
the twelve parallelogram supports contribute $S$ each; all other
supports are independent. For five vertices, forty-eight supports
force a zero Fourier coefficient. The other eight are cube
symmetries of
$\{000,100,010,001,111\}$, whose relation has coefficients
$(2,-1,-1,-1,1)$; their contribution is $B_5$.

For clarity, these assertions follow by solving the four equations
\[
 \sum_\omega r_\omega=0,\qquad
 \sum_\omega\omega_jr_\omega=0\quad(1\le j\le3),
\]
with frequencies outside the chosen support set equal to zero.
All the relation systems here can be solved using only unit pivots
and division by two. The latter is available in every group of odd
order; in particular, these identities do not require exponent five.
For six vertices classify the two omitted vertices by their Hamming
distance:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{omitted representative}&\text{number}&\text{contribution}\\ \hline
000,001&12&H_f\\
000,011&12&J_f\\
000,111&4&K_f.
\end{array}
\]
Solving the same equations gives the displayed formulas.
Their reality also follows from the real spatial cube products.

Replace $a_0$ by a real variable and differentiate the
Fourier-square identity at zero. Differentiating its four factors
gives exactly the four cubic summands in $L_f$; differentiating the
squared norm gives $2\Rea\langle T_f,L_f\rangle$. Repeated indices
cause no extra terms because the remaining zero coefficient then
vanishes. Finally each support is bounded by cube
Cauchy--Schwarz, with constants at its complementary vertices.
There are $28$ six-vertex and $8$ seven-vertex supports.
\end{proof}

The new argument will use these exact formulas to compare a function
with its projection. Bounding $C_7$ only by the product of norms
would lose a square root of the projection deficit. The exact
derivative formula avoids that loss.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Exact reduction to a five-point quotient\srctag{38}}]{Exact reduction to a five-point quotient}\label{gsr:cc:38:sec:d3}
\srcnote{38}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:cc:38:sec:quotient}

Write $N(f)=\|f\|_{U^3}^8=\Qthirtyeight(f)$ for real functions.  All
Fourier transforms are normalized, while frequency sums are unnormalized.
The following proves more than the formerly open universal eighth-order
coefficient: at sufficiently small centered norm, the entire extremal
problem reduces exactly to $\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z$.

\begin{theorem}[Exact dimension reduction; explicit sufficient range]
\label{gsr:cc:38:thm:exact-reduction}
Let $G\ne0$ be a finite abelian group with $5G=0$.  For $\delta>0$ and
$0<u\le10^{-5}\delta$, the maximum of $\Qthirtyeight(\delta+f)$ over real centered
functions $f:G\to\mathbb R$ with $\|f\|_{U^3}=u$ is identical to the
corresponding maximum on $\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z$.  Every maximizing $f$
factors through a nonzero homomorphism $G\to\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z$.
The same conclusion for the maximum holds with norm at most $u$;
the unrestricted profile is strictly increasing throughout this range.
For $0<\delta<1$, weights satisfying $0\le\delta+f\le1$ have
the same maximum if, additionally, $4u\le\min\{\delta,1-\delta\}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 34--39]
\emph{Answers two of source~21's questions} (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:eighth}): the universal coefficient of $u^8$ exists in the stated range (for $u/\delta\le10^{-5}$ and interior weights) and is $20/9$, the value source~21 proves on $\Z/5\Z$ (its Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:21:cor:pullback}), and it is the same on every fixed $\F_5^n$, with every maximizer factoring through $\Z/5\Z$. The cutoff $10^{-5}$ is a sufficient certificate; the reduction itself is not numerically testable at the scales the intake could afford (a $24$-parameter probe on $(\Z/5\Z)^2$ was stopped unfinished; no result is claimed from it).
\end{writenote}

The threshold $10^{-5}$ is only a convenient certificate and is not
asserted sharp.  We prove the norm-equality, unrestricted-real assertion
first; norm-ball monotonicity and bounded Fourier support then give
the last two statements.

\begin{proof}
Normalize $f=uF$, $\|F\|_{U^3}=1$, and $t=u/\delta$.  Thus the objective,
after dividing by $\delta^8$, is $\Qthirtyeight(1+tF)$.  Let
\[
 a_r=\widehat F(r),\quad \lambda_r=|a_r|^2,\quad
 S=\sum_r|a_r|^4,\quad S_0=2^{-1/2}.
\]
The exact centered expansion is
\[
 \Qthirtyeight(1+tF)=1+12St^4+8B_5(F)t^5+C_6(F)t^6+C_7(F)t^7+t^8,
 \qquad B_5(F)=\sum_r a_{2r}a_{-r}^3a_r.
\]
The standard cube Cauchy--Schwarz inequalities give
$|B_5(F)|\le1$, $|C_6(F)|\le28$, and $|C_7(F)|\le8$.
The real centered norm gap gives
\[
 1\ge5S^2-6\sum_r|a_r|^8\ge2S^2.
\]

\subsection{Localization requiring only the leading extremal term}

A normalized pure Fourier pair gives exactly
$1+6\sqrt2\,t^4+t^8$.  We may therefore assume the candidate $F$
has at least this value.  Set $\eta=S_0-S$.  For $t\le1$, the displayed
expansion implies
\[
 0\le\eta\le\frac23t+\frac73t^2+\frac23t^3\le4t.
\]
Choose a largest conjugate pair $\{\xi,-\xi\}$, put
$a=|a_\xi|$, and let
$D_{\rm pair}=\sum_{r\notin\{\xi,-\xi\}}|a_r|^4$.  Since
$\sum_r|a_r|^8\le a^4S=(S-D_{\rm pair})S/2$,
\[
 1\ge2S^2+3SD_{\rm pair}.
\]
When $S\ge S_0/2$, this yields $D_{\rm pair}\le2\eta\le8t$.
Let $L=\langle\xi\rangle$ and let $g$ be the Fourier projection of
$F$ to $L$, equivalently the subgroup average over $\ker\xi$.
Write $h=F-g$, $b=|a_{2\xi}|$, and
\[
 S_g=\sum_{r\in L}|a_r|^4,
 \quad D=\sum_{r\notin L}|a_r|^4,
 \quad v=\|g\|_{U^3},\quad \Delta=1-v^8.
\]
Then
\[
 S_g\ge S_0-12t,\qquad b\le(4t)^{1/4},\qquad
 a\le2^{-3/8}.
\]
Subgroup averaging is contractive for the Gowers norm, so $\Delta\ge0$.

\subsection{Coercivity of the norm loss outside the principal line}

Set
\[
 T_F(s,t)=\sum_r a_r\overline{a_{r+s}}
                     \overline{a_{r+t}}a_{r+s+t},
 \qquad N(F)=\sum_{s,t}|T_F(s,t)|^2.
\]
For $s,t\in L$, the base frequency $r$ remains in a single coset of
$L$ throughout the parallelogram, and hence
\[
 T_F(s,t)=T_g(s,t)+T_h(s,t),\qquad |T_h(s,t)|\le D.
\]
Let
\[
 R=\sum_{\substack{s,t\in L\\s\ne0, t\ne0}}|T_g(s,t)|.
\]
The elementary five-point slot enumeration gives
\[
 R\le8a^3b+8a^2b^2+8ab^3.
\]
Indeed the nonaxis slots, up to independent sign changes and interchange,
are $(\xi,\xi)$ with multiplicity four and modulus at most $2ab^3$,
$(2\xi,2\xi)$ with multiplicity four and modulus at most $2a^3b$,
and $(\xi,2\xi)$ with multiplicity eight and modulus $a^2b^2$.

Let $\mathcal E(\lambda)=\sum_{r+s=t+w}\lambda_r\lambda_s\lambda_t\lambda_w$.
The axes in the $T$ sum contribute $2\mathcal E(\lambda)-S^2$.
Write $\lambda_g=\lambda\ind_L$ and $\lambda_h=\lambda\ind_{L^c}$.
In addition to all entirely inside and entirely outside energy tuples,
retain the mixed tuples in the three families
\[
 r=t, s=w;\qquad r=w, s=t;\qquad s=-r, w=-t.
\]
Each family has mixed weight $2S_gD$.  Their pairwise intersections
contain no mixed tuple, because $L$ and its complement are stable under
negation.  All terms are nonnegative.  Consequently
\[
 \mathcal E(\lambda)\ge\mathcal E(\lambda_g)
       +\mathcal E(\lambda_h)+6S_gD.
\]
The usual three-family argument on the even sequence $\lambda_h$ gives
$\mathcal E(\lambda_h)\ge3D^2-3\sum\lambda_h^4\ge\tfrac32D^2$;
the last inequality uses conjugate pairing and odd group order.
Subtracting $S^2=(S_g+D)^2$ gives the axes estimate
\[
 2\mathcal E(\lambda)-S^2
 \ge2\mathcal E(\lambda_g)-S_g^2+10S_gD+2D^2.
\]
The nonaxis slots in $L^2$ lose at most $2RD$ relative to those of $g$,
by $|T_g+T_h|^2\ge|T_g|^2-2|T_g|D$; all other slots are nonnegative.
We have therefore proved the exact finite inequality
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\quad \Delta\ge(10S_g-2R)D+2D^2.\quad}
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:projection-coercivity}
\end{equation}

For $t\le10^{-5}$, we have $S_g\ge2/3$ and the rational bounds
$a<193/250$ and $b<2/25$. Indeed $8(193/250)^8>1$ and
$(2/25)^4>4\cdot10^{-5}$. Direct rational substitution gives
\[
 8(193/250)^3(2/25)+8(193/250)^2(2/25)^2
       +8(193/250)(2/25)^3<1/3.
\]
Thus $R<1/3$, $10S_g-2R\ge6$, and
\[
 D\le\Delta/6,
 \qquad v^8\ge2S_g^2\ge8/9,
 \qquad0\le\Delta\le1/9.
\]

\subsection{Quantitative subgroup projection}

We use the general estimate
\begin{equation}
 \|h\|_{U^3}^8\le2^8\Delta.
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:projection-convexity}
\end{equation}
For completeness, Gowers--Cauchy--Schwarz and the expansion of
$\|f+g\|_{U^3}^8+\|f-g\|_{U^3}^8$ give Clarkson's inequality
\[
 \left\|\frac{f+g}{2}\right\|_{U^3}^8+
 \left\|\frac{f-g}{2}\right\|_{U^3}^8
 \le\frac{\|f\|_{U^3}^8+\|g\|_{U^3}^8}{2}.
\]
To see the constant directly, the odd mixed terms cancel, each even
mixed term is bounded by the product of the corresponding norms, and
weighted arithmetic--geometric mean bounds the resulting scalar sum
by $2^7(\|f\|_{U^3}^8+\|g\|_{U^3}^8)$. Dividing by $2^8$
gives the displayed inequality, in agreement with the general
norm-geometric perspective of \cite{hatami}.
Apply it to $F$ and each translate $T_yF$, $y\in\ker\xi$.
Projection of their midpoint is $g$, so contractivity bounds the first
term below by $v^8$.  This gives
$\|F-T_yF\|_{U^3}\le2\Delta^{1/8}$; average over $y$ and use the
triangle inequality to obtain \eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:projection-convexity}.

\subsection{Sixth-degree differences are linear in the norm loss}

Put
\[
 H_F=\sum_{r+s+t=0}\lambda_r\lambda_s\lambda_t.
\]
The exact sixth-degree decomposition is
\[
 C_6(F)=12H_F+12J_F+4K_F,
\quad
 J_F=\sum_{r,s}\lambda_r a_s^2a_{r-s}\overline{a_{r+s}},
\quad
 K_F=\sum_{r+s+t=0}a_r^2a_s^2a_t^2.
\]
In the $J$ sum, the entirely inside part is exactly the restriction
$(r,s)\in L^2$.  Cauchy--Schwarz on the complementary domain gives
\[
 |J_F-J_g|\le H_F-H_g.
\]
Indeed its two squared bounds are the sums of
$\lambda_r\lambda_s\lambda_{r-s}$ and
$\lambda_r\lambda_s\lambda_{r+s}$ over $(r,s)\notin L^2$;
both equal $H_F-H_g$, using evenness and $s\mapsto-s$.
Also $|K_F-K_g|\le H_F-H_g$.  Hence
\[
 |C_6(F)-C_6(g)|\le28(H_F-H_g).
\]
A zero-sum triple cannot have exactly one frequency outside $L$.
Writing $A_g=\sum_{r\in L}|a_r|^2$, note that $g$ has at most
four nonzero Fourier coefficients, so $A_g^2\le4S_g\le4$ and $A_g\le2$.
We obtain
\[
 H_F-H_g\le3A_gD+H_h.
\]
The first term comes from the three choices of an inside frequency;
for each such frequency, the remaining convolution is at most $D$
by Cauchy--Schwarz.  For the entirely outside term,
\[
 H_h\le\sqrt{D\mathcal E(\lambda_h)}
 \le\sqrt{D\bigl(128\Delta+D^2/2\bigr)},
\]
because the axes inequality gives
$\mathcal E(\lambda_h)\le(\|h\|_{U^3}^8+D^2)/2$ and \eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:projection-convexity} applies.
Using $D\le\Delta/6$ and $\Delta\le1$ therefore yields
\begin{equation}
 H_F-H_g\le6\Delta,
 \qquad |C_6(F)-C_6(g)|\le168\Delta.
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:six-linear-loss}
\end{equation}

\subsection{Seventh-degree differences are also linear in the norm loss}

Define
\[
 L_F(s,t)=2\operatorname{Re}(a_sa_t\overline{a_{s+t}})
       +2\operatorname{Re}(a_s\overline{a_t}\overline{a_{s-t}}).
\]
Differentiating the sum-of-squares identity with respect to the zero
Fourier coefficient gives
$C_7(F)=2\operatorname{Re}\langle T_F,L_F\rangle$.
For $s,t\in L$ one has $L_F(s,t)=L_g(s,t)$ exactly, because all
its indices then belong to $L$.  Thus the contribution to the difference
from $L^2$ has modulus at most
\[
 2D\sum_{L^2}|L_g|\le200D\le\frac{100}{3}\Delta.
\]
Here $|a_r|\le1$, so each of the 25 values of $L_g$ has modulus at
most four.

For the complement of $L^2$, the same expansion of the norm gives
\[
 \sum_{(s,t)\notin L^2}|T_F(s,t)|^2\le\Delta+2RD
 \le\frac43\Delta.
\]
The axes cross terms within $L^2$ are nonnegative, and the remaining
cross terms lose at most $2RD$, which proves this inequality.
Each of the four cubic summands of $L_F$ has squared norm on the
complement of $L^2$ equal to $H_F-H_g$.  Consequently
\[
 \sum_{(s,t)\notin L^2}|L_F(s,t)|^2
 \le16(H_F-H_g)\le96\Delta.
\]
Cauchy--Schwarz bounds their contribution by $16\sqrt2\,\Delta$.
Adding the two regions proves
\begin{equation}
 |C_7(F)-C_7(g)|\le60\Delta.
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:seven-linear-loss}
\end{equation}
The linear estimate \eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:seven-linear-loss} is essential for exact localization; a generic
mixed cube bound would give only $O(\sqrt\Delta)$ and would settle
the eighth-order coefficient without proving exact reduction.

\subsection{Rescaling the projection strictly improves every off-line candidate}

Doubling preserves $L$ and its complement, so
$B_5(F)-B_5(g)=B_5(h)$ exactly.  Therefore
\[
 |B_5(F)-B_5(g)|\le D^{5/4}\le D\le\Delta/6.
\]
Let $g_* = g/v$; then $\|g_*\|_{U^3}=1$.
Since $0\le\Delta\le1/9<1/2$, for $k=5,6,7$ the mean value theorem
gives
\[
 |v^{-k}-1|=|(1-\Delta)^{-k/8}-1|\le4\Delta.
\]
Combining this with \eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:six-linear-loss}, \eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:seven-linear-loss}, homogeneity, and cube
Cauchy--Schwarz on $g$, one obtains
\[
 |B_5(F)-B_5(g_*)|\le5\Delta,\qquad
 |C_6(F)-C_6(g_*)|\le280\Delta,\qquad
 |C_7(F)-C_7(g_*)|\le92\Delta.
\]
At fourth degree,
\begin{align*}
 12t^4(S-S_{g_*})
 &=12t^4\bigl[D-S_g((1-\Delta)^{-1/2}-1)\bigr]\\
 &\le12t^4(D-S_g\Delta/2)
 \le-2t^4\Delta.
\end{align*}
The eighth-degree terms cancel exactly because $F$ and $g_*$ have
the same norm.  Hence
\begin{equation}
 \Qthirtyeight(1+tF)-\Qthirtyeight(1+tg_*)
 \le t^4\Delta(-2+40t+280t^2+92t^3)
 \le-t^4\Delta
 \quad(0<t\le10^{-5}).
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:strict-projection-gain}
\end{equation}
If $F$ has any nonzero off-line coefficient, then $D>0$, and \eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:projection-coercivity}
implies $\Delta>0$.  Thus its projected and rescaled competitor is
strictly better.  If the candidate was initially below the pure-pair
value, the pure-pair competitor already improves it.  Every maximum
therefore occurs on a five-point quotient.  Conversely, every function
on the five-point group pulls back along any nontrivial character and
preserves its mean, all Gowers norms, and its cube count.  This proves
the equality of maxima and the assertion about every maximizer.

For completeness, the norm-ball conclusion does not require an
unspecified smaller analytic neighborhood.  Let $F$ be a normalized
maximizer at norm $0<r\le10^{-5}$.  Localization gives $S\ge2/3$.
For $r\le s\le10^{-5}$, direct differentiation of the centered
polynomial gives
\[
 \frac{d}{ds}\Qthirtyeight(1+sF)
 \ge s^3(48S-40s-168s^2-56s^3)>0.
\]
Thus scaling a lower-norm maximizer strictly increases its objective
throughout the range.  The norm-zero value is strictly smaller by the pure-pair benchmark.
The norm-equality maximum is strictly increasing, and the norm-ball
maximum occurs on its boundary.


For interval-valued weights, every Fourier coefficient of a maximizer
has modulus at most its $U^3$ norm $u$. Its support has at most four
frequencies, so $\|f\|_\infty\le4u$. Thus the unrestricted maximizing
function is feasible for the interval constraint in the stated range;
the reverse inequality between maxima is immediate from inclusion.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Quantitative stability of quotient dependence}

\begin{corollary}[Off-quotient control by the extremal deficit]
\label{gsr:cc:38:cor:quotient-stability}
Assume the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:38:thm:exact-reduction} and that
$f$ has at least the pure-pair benchmark,
\[
 \Qthirtyeight(\delta+f)\ge\delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4+u^8.
\]
Let
$\mathscr D=\mathcal M_{\delta,G}(u)-\Qthirtyeight(\delta+f)$.
There is a nonzero character $\xi$, with
$P$ the average over its kernel, such that
\begin{align}
 \|f-Pf\|_{U^2}^4
     &\le\frac{\mathscr D}{6\delta^4},\label{gsr:cc:38:eq:quotient-stability-u2}\\
 \|f-Pf\|_{U^3}^8
     &\le\frac{256u^4\mathscr D}{\delta^4}.
       \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:quotient-stability-u3}
\end{align}
The constants do not depend on $G$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply the construction in the proof with $F=f/u$.
The rescaled projection is an admissible competitor, so
\eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:strict-projection-gain} gives
$\mathscr D\ge\delta^8t^4\Delta=\delta^4u^4\Delta$.
Now use $D\le\Delta/6$, the Fourier identity
$\|f-Pf\|_{U^2}^4=u^4D$, and
\eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:projection-convexity}.
\end{proof}

For fixed $\delta>0$, attaining the extremal expansion with error
$o(u^8)$ therefore forces an off-quotient $U^2$ error
$o(u^2/\delta)$ and an off-quotient $U^3$ error
$o(u^{3/2}/\delta^{1/2})$. The benchmark assumption is automatic for
such a family at sufficiently small $u$, because the sharp $u^6$
coefficient is positive. The conclusion concerns uniformity norms.
It does not assert that indicator approximations have vanishing
$L^2$ distance from a nonconstant fractional weight.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The five-point profile and its analytic expansion\srctag{38}}]{The five-point profile and its analytic expansion}\label{gsr:cc:38:sec:d4}
\srcnote{38}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:cc:38:sec:five-profile}

Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:38:thm:exact-reduction} reduces the dimension-uniform extremal
problem to a fixed, four-dimensional real space of centered functions.
We now solve its local optimization, including the phase variables.
The coefficient $20/9$ was calculated for this fixed group in the
preceding characteristic-five report \cite{repo38five}; it is reproduced
below as part of the calculation of two additional terms.

Write $\mathcal M_{\delta,5}(u)=\mathcal M_{\delta,\Z/5\Z}(u)$.
The interval restriction $0\le\delta+f\le1$ is temporarily absent.
This permits the exact scaling relation
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal M_{\delta,5}(u)=\delta^8\mathcal M_{1,5}(u/\delta).
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-scaling}
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[The extremal profile through twelfth order]
\label{gsr:cc:38:thm:pf-series}
There are absolute constants $\eta,C>0$ such that, for every
nontrivial finite abelian group $G$ with $5G=0$, every $\delta>0$,
and $0<u/\delta<\eta$,
\begin{align}
 \mathcal M_{\delta,G}(u)
 ={}&\delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4
       +\frac{2^{3/4}}3\delta^2u^6+\frac{20}{9}u^8\notag\\
 &+\frac{869}{216\,2^{3/4}}\frac{u^{10}}{\delta^2}
       +\frac{65759}{5832\,2^{3/2}}\frac{u^{12}}{\delta^4}
       +E_\delta(u),
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-series}
\end{align}
where $|E_\delta(u)|\le C u^{14}/\delta^6$.
More generally, $\delta^{-8}\mathcal M_{\delta,G}(\delta t)$ is
represented near zero by a convergent power series in $t^2$.
The constants and the neighborhood are independent of the ambient
dimension.  All sufficiently small maximizers on the five-point group
are obtained from one real analytic family by translations, reflection,
and the choice of a generating character.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 34--39]
\emph{Answers source~21's question on further terms on the five-point group} (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:eighth}): $c_{10}=869/(216\cdot2^{3/4})=2.39218$, $c_{12}=65759/(5832\cdot2^{3/2})=3.98651$ (decimals recomputed at the write). The intake confirmed them on $\Z/5\Z$ by direct optimization of the cube average over two Fourier coefficients: $(M-1-6\sqrt2u^4-(2^{3/4}/3)u^6-(20/9)u^8)/u^{10}=2.4079$, $2.4121$, $2.4248$, $2.4412$, $2.4610$ at $u=0.05,\ldots,0.13$ against $c_{10}+c_{12}u^2=2.4021,\ldots,2.4596$ (evidence, not proof).
\end{writenote}

The analytic neighborhood in this theorem may be smaller than the
explicit range $u/\delta\le10^{-5}$ of exact quotient reduction.
The asymptotic calculation does not require a numerical lower bound
for its radius of convergence.

\subsection{A complete Fourier certificate}

Identify the dual of $\Z/5\Z$ with $\Z/5\Z$.  After choosing a
generator so that a largest Fourier pair is $\{1,-1\}$, write
\[
 a_0=\delta,\qquad
 a_1=\rho e^{i\alpha},\quad a_2=b e^{i\beta},\quad
 a_{-r}=\overline{a_r},\qquad \rho\ge b\ge0.
\]
For $b>0$ define
\[
 \theta=2\alpha-\beta,\qquad
 \phi=3\alpha+\beta,\qquad
 \psi=\phi-\theta=\alpha+2\beta.
\]
If $b=0$, any choice of the unused phase gives the same formulas.
For these five Fourier coefficients set
\[
 T_\delta(s,t)=\sum_{r\in\Z/5\Z}
      a_r\overline{a_{r+s}}\,\overline{a_{r+t}}a_{r+s+t}.
\]
The sum-of-squares identity in Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:38:lem:fourier-squares}
gives $\Qthirtyeight(\delta+f)=\sum_{s,t}|T_\delta(s,t)|^2$.
Realness of the underlying function makes $T_\delta$ real and
invariant under independent sign changes of its two arguments and
their interchange.  The following six rows therefore account for
all $25$ slots.

\begin{center}
\begingroup\small\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.5}\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\begin{tabular}{@{}ccP{.70\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Representative & Multiplicity & Value of $T_\delta(s,t)$\\
\midrule
$(0,0)$ & $1$ & $\delta^4+2\rho^4+2b^4$\\
$(0,1)$ & $4$ & $2\delta^2\rho^2+2\rho^2b^2+b^4$\\
$(0,2)$ & $4$ & $2\delta^2b^2+2\rho^2b^2+\rho^4$\\
$(1,1)$ & $4$ & $\delta^2\rho^2+2\delta\rho^2b\cos\theta
                         +2\rho b^3\cos(2\theta-\phi)$\\
$(2,2)$ & $4$ & $\delta^2b^2+2\delta\rho b^2\cos\psi
                         +2\rho^3b\cos\phi$\\
$(1,2)$ & $8$ & $\rho^2b^2+2\delta\rho^2b\cos\theta
                         +2\delta\rho b^2\cos\psi$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\endgroup
\end{center}

Each row follows by substituting $r=0,1,2,-2,-1$ in the defining sum;
thus the table is a finite algebraic certificate, including arbitrary
Fourier phases.  In particular the centered norm is exactly
\begin{align}
 N(\rho,b,\theta,\phi):=\|f\|_{U^3}^8
 ={}&8\rho^8+16(1+\cos^2\phi)\rho^6b^2+48\rho^4b^4\notag\\
 &+16\bigl(1+\cos^2(2\theta-\phi)\bigr)\rho^2b^6+8b^8.
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-exact-norm}
\end{align}
Squaring all six rows gives the full objective
\begin{align}
 \Qthirtyeight(\delta+f)
 ={}&\delta^8+24\delta^4(\rho^4+b^4)\notag\\
 &+16\delta^3\bigl(\rho^4b\cos\theta
                      +\rho b^4\cos\psi\bigr)\notag\\
 &+24\delta^2\Bigl((3+\cos2\theta)\rho^4b^2
                    +(3+\cos2\psi)\rho^2b^4\notag\\
 &\hspace{37mm}+2\rho^3b^3
                         \bigl(\cos\phi+\cos(2\theta-\phi)\bigr)\Bigr)\notag\\
 &+16\delta\Bigl(\rho^4b^3
                     \bigl(3\cos\theta+\cos(2\phi-\theta)\bigr)\notag\\
 &\hspace{31mm}+\rho^3b^4
                     \bigl(3\cos\psi+\cos(3\theta-\phi)\bigr)\Bigr)
       +N(\rho,b,\theta,\phi).
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-exact-objective}
\end{align}
All optimization below uses these exact expressions.  In particular,
the phases are not fixed in advance.

\subsection{Localization of every maximum at the secondary scale}

By \eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-scaling}, take $\delta=1$ and put $t=u$.
The norm sphere of centered real functions on the five-point group is
compact, so the maximum exists.  Since $\rho\ge b$, the nonnegative
terms in \eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-exact-norm} imply
\begin{equation}
 8\rho^8\le t^8\le128\rho^8.
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-amplitude-bounds}
\end{equation}
Thus $\rho\asymp t$ uniformly in the phases, and both amplitudes are
$O(t)$.

\begin{lemma}[Uniform secondary localization]
\label{gsr:cc:38:lem:pf-secondary-localization}
Every five-point maximizer has $b=O(t^2)$ as $t\downarrow0$, with an
absolute implied constant.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Put $S=2(\rho^4+b^4)$.  Equation~\eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-exact-norm} gives
$t^8-2S^2\ge16\rho^6b^2$.  Therefore
\begin{align*}
 6\sqrt2\,t^4-12S
 &=\frac{6(t^8-2S^2)}{t^4/\sqrt2+S}
 \ge c t^2b^2
\end{align*}
for an absolute $c>0$, using \eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-amplitude-bounds} and
$S\le t^4/\sqrt2$.  The fifth-, sixth-, and seventh-degree parts
of \eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-exact-objective} have moduli at most, respectively,
$C t^4b$, $C t^4b^2$, and $C t^4b^3$.  For example
$\rho b^4\le\rho^4b$, $\rho^2b^4\le\rho^4b^2$, and
$\rho^3b^3\le\rho^4b^2$, because $b\le\rho$.
The constants are absolute because the displayed polynomial has
finitely many terms with bounded trigonometric factors.

The pure-pair function $b=0$ has value
$1+6\sqrt2\,t^4+t^8$.  For a maximizer, comparison with this function
and absorption of $Ct^4b^2+Ct^4b^3$ into $ct^2b^2/2$, for small $t$,
give
\[
 0\le\Qthirtyeight(1+f)-1-6\sqrt2\,t^4-t^8
       \le-\tfrac c2 t^2b^2+C t^4b.
\]
If $b>0$, division by $t^2b$ yields $b\le(2C/c)t^2$;
the claim is immediate if $b=0$.
\end{proof}

This lemma supplies the compactness needed for a perturbative maximum.
It rules out functions whose second harmonic leaves every bounded
region at the scale relevant to the next coefficient.

\subsection{Analytic optimization with both phases retained}

Set
\[
 q_0=2^{-3/4},\qquad b=kt^2,\qquad \rho^2=t^2R.
\]
After dividing the norm equation by $t^8$, one obtains
\begin{align}
 1={}&8R^4+16(1+\cos^2\phi)R^3k^2t^2+48R^2k^4t^4\notag\\
 &+16\bigl(1+\cos^2(2\theta-\phi)\bigr)Rk^6t^6+8k^8t^8.
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-normalized-norm}
\end{align}
At $t=0$, the positive solution is $R=q_0$, and the derivative of
the right side with respect to $R$ is $32q_0^3>0$.
The implicit function theorem gives a positive real analytic solution
$R(t,k,\theta,\phi)$ near zero.  It is analytic in $t^2$, uniformly
for bounded $k$ and all phases: this follows either from a finite
cover of the phase torus or directly from the uniform nonzero
derivative at $R=q_0$.

Define
\begin{equation}
 H(t,k,\theta,\phi)
   =\frac{\Qthirtyeight(1+f)-1-6\sqrt2\,t^4}{t^6},
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-normalized-objective}
\end{equation}
with $\rho=t\sqrt R$ for positive $t$.  The apparent singularity at
$t=0$ is removable, as substitution in
\eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-exact-objective} shows.  The resulting expression has
a real analytic continuation to signed $t$ using this same formula
for $\rho$.  Its expansion begins
\begin{equation}
 H=H_0+t^2H_2+t^3H_3+O(t^4),
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-H-expansion}
\end{equation}
where, writing $A=1+\cos^2\phi$,
\begin{align}
 H_0&=-24q_0 A k^2+16q_0^2k\cos\theta,
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-H0}\\
 H_2&=1+24(A^2-2)k^4-16q_0Ak^3\cos\theta
                   +24(3+\cos2\theta)q_0^2k^2,
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-H2}\\
 H_3&=16\sqrt{q_0}\,k^4\cos(\phi-\theta)
       +48q_0^{3/2}k^3
             \bigl(\cos(2\theta-\phi)+\cos\phi\bigr).
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-H3}
\end{align}
For example the first two corrections in the norm solution are
\[
 R=q_0-\frac A2k^2t^2
          +\frac{3(A^2-4)}{8q_0}k^4t^4+O(t^6),
\]
which already verify \eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-H0} and \eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-H2}.

\begin{proposition}[All local maximizing branches]
\label{gsr:cc:38:prop:pf-analytic-branches}
For sufficiently small positive $t$, every global maximum is on an
analytic critical branch converging, in the coordinates
$(k,\theta,\phi)$, to one of
\begin{equation}
 y_+=(q_0/3,0,\pi/2),\qquad
 y_-=(q_0/3,0,3\pi/2),
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-leading-classes}
\end{equation}
with phases understood modulo $2\pi$.  There is exactly one critical
branch near each class.  They have equal objective values.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For $k\ge0$,
\[
 H_0\le-24q_0k^2+16q_0^2k
       \le\frac{8q_0^3}{3}=\frac{2^{3/4}}3.
\]
Equality in the second inequality requires $k=q_0/3>0$.
Equality in the first then forces $\cos\theta=1$ and
$\cos\phi=0$, yielding exactly \eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-leading-classes}.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:38:lem:pf-secondary-localization} confines all maximizers
to a fixed compact set of $k$ and the phase torus.  On that set
$H\to H_0$ uniformly.  Each of the points in
\eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-leading-classes}, together with its analytic norm
solution, is an admissible competitor for small positive $t$.
Compactness therefore forces every sequence of maximizers with
$t\downarrow0$ to approach one of these two classes.

At either class the Hessian of $H_0$, in coordinates
$(k,\theta,\phi)$, is
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{diag}\left(-48q_0,-\frac{16q_0^3}{3},
                                     -\frac{16q_0^3}{3}\right).
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-hessian}
\end{equation}
It is negative definite.  Apply the implicit function theorem to
$\nabla_{k,\theta,\phi}H=0$ at each point.  This gives one analytic
critical branch in a neighborhood of each class, and its Hessian
remains negative definite.  The preceding compactness argument,
applied to these smaller neighborhoods, shows that these branches
exhaust the global maxima.  Their amplitude constraints are inactive:
$k$ remains positive and bounded, while $b/\rho=O(t)$.
Conjugating the Fourier coefficients sends $(\theta,\phi)$ to
$(-\theta,-\phi)$ and interchanges the branches without changing
the objective, so their values agree.
\end{proof}

The map $(\alpha,\beta)\mapsto(\theta,\phi)$ has determinant $5$.
Its five lifts on the two-dimensional phase torus correspond exactly
to translations of the five-point function.  Choosing the other
largest-pair generator is a group automorphism, and conjugation of the Fourier coefficients is reflection.  This proves the symmetry assertion in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:38:thm:pf-series}.

\subsection{Evenness and a recursion for all further coefficients}

Use the branch near $y_+$ and view $\phi-\pi/2$ as a local real
coordinate.  The exact normalized equations have the symmetry
\begin{equation}
 (t,k,\theta,\phi)\longmapsto(-t,k,-\theta,\pi-\phi).
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-parity-symmetry}
\end{equation}
To check it, note that $\cos\theta$, $\cos2\theta$,
$\cos2\psi$, and $\cos(2\phi-\theta)$ are unchanged, whereas
$\cos\psi$, $\cos\phi$, $\cos(2\theta-\phi)$, and
$\cos(3\theta-\phi)$ change sign.  The latter factors occur
precisely with the odd powers of signed $t$ in the normalized
objective.  Both squared cosine factors in
\eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-normalized-norm} are unchanged.

The involution fixes $y_+$.  Uniqueness of the analytic critical
branch thus implies that $k(t)$ is even, $\theta(t)$ is odd,
$\phi(t)-\pi/2$ is odd, and its objective value is even.
Consequently the extremal profile is analytic in $t^2$, rather
than merely possessing a finite asymptotic expansion.

This gives an effective recursion.  First solve
\eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-normalized-norm} coefficient by coefficient for $R$;
the coefficient to be solved is multiplied by $32q_0^3$.
Then expand $\nabla H=0$.  At each successive order, the new
coefficient vector of $(k,\theta,\phi)$ is multiplied by the fixed
invertible matrix \eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-hessian}; all other terms are already
known from lower orders.  Every coefficient is therefore determined
by finite algebraic operations.  The analytic implicit function
theorem proves convergence of the recursively obtained series.

\subsection{Fourth, sixth, eighth, and tenth orders}

At the limiting phases $\theta=0$, $\phi=\pi/2$, put
$z=k^2t^2/q_0$ and write $R=q_0X(z)$.  The exact norm becomes
\begin{equation}
 X^4+2zX^3+6z^2X^2+2z^3X+z^4=1,
 \qquad X(0)=1.
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-X-equation}
\end{equation}
Coefficient comparison gives
\begin{equation}
 X=1-\frac12z-\frac98z^2+\frac34z^3
                        +\frac{39}{128}z^4+O(z^5).
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-X-series}
\end{equation}
At these phases the objective simplifies to
\begin{equation}
 \Qthirtyeight(1+f)=1+24(\rho^4+b^4)+16\rho^4b
          +96\rho^4b^2+48\rho^2b^4+32\rho^4b^3+t^8.
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-fixed-phase-objective}
\end{equation}
Its first coefficient beyond the leading quartic term is the maximum
$8q_0^3/3=2^{3/4}/3$ of $H_0$.
At these fixed phases the next coefficients of $H$ are
\begin{align}
 H_2(k)&=1-24k^4-16q_0k^3+96q_0^2k^2,
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-H2-fixed}\\
 H_4(k)&=\frac{63k^6}{q_0}-32k^5-48q_0k^4+32q_0^2k^3,
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-H4-fixed}\\
 H_6(k)&=\frac{27k^8}{q_0^2}+\frac{42k^7}{q_0}
                              -216k^6-32q_0k^5.
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-H6-fixed}
\end{align}
Here $H_j(k)$ denotes the coefficient of $t^j$ after the phases
are set to their limiting values; the arbitrary-phase functions
$H_2,H_3$ remain those in \eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-H2}--\eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-H3}.

Let $k_0=q_0/3$.  Since $q_0^4=1/8$,
\begin{equation}
 H_2(k_0)=1-\frac1{27}-\frac2{27}+\frac43=\frac{20}{9}.
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-eighth-coefficient}
\end{equation}
The analytic maximizing coordinates have no term of order $t$,
because \eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-H-expansion} has none and the Hessian is
invertible.  Equation~\eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-H2} shows that its phase gradient
vanishes at $y_+$.  Thus the displacement at order $t^2$ occurs
only in the amplitude coordinate:
\begin{equation}
 k(t)=k_0+k_2t^2+O(t^4),\qquad
 k_2=-\frac{H_2'(k_0)}{H_0''(k_0)}
       =\frac{31q_0^2}{27},
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-k-displacement}
\end{equation}
where
\[
 H_2'(k_0)=\frac{496q_0^3}{9},\qquad H_0''(k_0)=-48q_0.
\]
The optimized coefficient at order $t^4$ in $H$, hence at order
$t^{10}$ in the original objective, is
\begin{align}
 K_{10}
 &=H_4(k_0)+\frac{(H_2'(k_0))^2}{96q_0}\notag\\
 &=\frac{133q_0^5}{243}+\frac{7688q_0^5}{243}
   =\frac{869q_0}{216}
   =\frac{869}{216\,2^{3/4}}.
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-tenth-coefficient}
\end{align}
The phase displacement begins at order $t^3$, so it cannot affect
this coefficient.  The next subsection computes its first effect.

\subsection{The first phase adjustment and the twelfth-order coefficient}

At $y_+$, differentiation of \eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-H3} gives
\begin{equation}
 \nabla_{\theta,\phi}H_3(y_+)
       =\frac{304q_0^{9/2}}{81}(1,-1),
 \qquad \partial_kH_3(y_+)=0.
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-phase-gradient}
\end{equation}
The phase part of the Hessian is $-(16q_0^3/3)I$.
The order-$t^3$ critical-point equations therefore yield
\begin{align}
 \theta(t)&=d_3t^3+O(t^5),\notag\\
 \phi(t)&=\frac\pi2-d_3t^3+O(t^5),
 \qquad d_3=\frac{19q_0^{3/2}}{27}.
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-phase-displacement}
\end{align}
The absence of fourth-order phase terms follows from
\eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-parity-symmetry}.  In the original phases, one lift
has
\[
 \alpha(t)=\frac\pi{10}+O(t^5),\qquad
 \beta(t)=\frac\pi5-\frac{19q_0^{3/2}}{27}t^3+O(t^5).
\]
Thus keeping both phases permanently at their limiting values is
already insufficient for the twelfth-order extremal coefficient.

We give the coefficient calculation with its optimization terms
retained.  Write $y(t)=y_++t^2y_2+t^3y_3+t^4y_4+\cdots$, where
$y_2=(k_2,0,0)$ and $y_3=(0,d_3,-d_3)$.
The coefficient of $t^6$ in $H(t,y(t))$ is
\begin{align}
 K_{12}={}&H_6(k_0)+k_2H_4'(k_0)
                    +\frac12 k_2^2H_2''(k_0)\notag\\
 &-\frac12\bigl(\nabla_{\theta,\phi}H_3(y_+)\bigr)^{\mathsf T}
      \bigl(\nabla^2_{\theta,\phi}H_0(y_+)\bigr)^{-1}
      \nabla_{\theta,\phi}H_3(y_+).
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-twelfth-optimization}
\end{align}
To justify this formula, the terms containing the unknown $y_4$
cancel because $\nabla^2H_0\,y_2+\nabla H_2=0$.
The cubic derivative of $H_0$ in the direction $y_2$ is zero,
since its restriction to the amplitude coordinate is quadratic.
The terms involving $y_3$ complete the displayed quadratic form,
using $\nabla^2H_0\,y_3+\nabla H_3=0$.  No term involving $H_5$
contributes at this order: the coordinate displacement starts at
$t^2$, and $H_5$ has prefactor $t^5$.
These observations account for every possible term through $t^6$.

The needed fixed-phase values are
\[
 H_6(k_0)=-\frac{295q_0^6}{729},\qquad
 H_4'(k_0)=\frac{254q_0^4}{81},\qquad
 H_2''(k_0)=128q_0^2.
\]
The amplitude contribution in \eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-twelfth-optimization}
and the phase contribution are, respectively,
\[
 k_2H_4'(k_0)+\tfrac12k_2^2H_2''(k_0)
       =\frac{192386q_0^6}{2187},
 \qquad
 \frac{5776q_0^6}{2187}.
\]
Consequently
\begin{equation}
 K_{12}=\frac{65759q_0^6}{729}
        =\frac{65759}{5832\,2^{3/2}}.
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-twelfth-coefficient}
\end{equation}
The phase contribution is strictly positive.  It quantifies the
first improvement obtained by optimizing the phases beyond their
limiting values.

\begin{proof}[Completion of Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:38:thm:pf-series}]
Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:38:prop:pf-analytic-branches} identifies all maxima
near zero with the analytic branches just computed.  Symmetry
\eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-parity-symmetry} makes their common value even.
Equations~\eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-eighth-coefficient},
\eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-tenth-coefficient}, and
\eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-twelfth-coefficient} therefore give an error $O(t^{14})$
after restoring the constant and quartic terms in
\eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-normalized-objective}.  Its constant is absolute,
because this is an analytic function on a fixed finite-dimensional
neighborhood.  Scale by \eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-scaling} and apply
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:38:thm:exact-reduction}.  This proves the claimed remainder
and its independence of the ambient dimension.
\end{proof}

\Needspace{12\baselineskip}
\subsection{Sharp realization by bounded weights and exact verification}

\begin{corollary}[Weighted extremizers]
\label{gsr:cc:38:cor:pf-weights}
Let $0<\delta<1$ and let $G$ be nontrivial with $5G=0$.
If $0<u\le10^{-5}\delta$ and
$4u\le\min\{\delta,1-\delta\}$, then
$\mathcal M_{\delta,G}(u)$ is attained by a weight $W:G\to[0,1]$
of mean $\delta$.  The same maximum is obtained when the centered
norm constraint is $\|W-\delta\|_{U^3}\le u$.
In particular, all coefficients in Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:38:thm:pf-series} are
sharp for bounded weights as well as for unrestricted real functions.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Every five-point centered function has at most four nonzero Fourier
coefficients.  Each coefficient has modulus at most its $U^2$ norm,
and hence at most its $U^3$ norm.  Thus $\|f\|_\infty\le4u$ for
a centered five-point function of norm $u$.  The hypotheses place
$\delta+f$ in $[0,1]$.  Pullback along a nontrivial character of $G$
preserves the mean, the norm, and the cube count.  The unrestricted
upper bound then proves equality for weights.  The norm-ball
assertion follows from the strict monotonicity in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:38:thm:exact-reduction}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[An indicator version of the cube-count bound]
\label{gsr:cc:38:cor:pf-indicator-bound}
Let $G$ be nontrivial with $5G=0$, let $A\subseteq G$ have density
$\delta>0$, and suppose
\[
 \|\ind_A-\delta\|_{U^3}^8\le\alpha,
 \qquad \alpha^{1/8}\le10^{-5}\delta.
\]
The number of ordered cube parameters $(x,h_1,h_2,h_3)\in G^4$
whose eight vertices all belong to $A$ is at most
\begin{equation}
 |G|^4\mathcal M_{\delta,5}(\alpha^{1/8}).
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-indicator-exact-bound}
\end{equation}
Here $\mathcal M_{\delta,5}(0)=\delta^8$ by continuous extension.
Repeated vertices and zero increments are included.  As
$\alpha^{1/8}/\delta\to0$, its normalized upper bound is
\begin{align}
 \Qthirtyeight(\ind_A)\le{}&\delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4\alpha^{1/2}
       +\frac{2^{3/4}}3\delta^2\alpha^{3/4}
       +\frac{20}{9}\alpha\notag\\
 &+\frac{869}{216\,2^{3/4}}\delta^{-2}\alpha^{5/4}
       +\frac{65759}{5832\,2^{3/2}}\delta^{-4}\alpha^{3/2}
       +C\delta^{-6}\alpha^{7/4},
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-indicator-series-bound}
\end{align}
for an absolute $C$, on a sufficiently small absolute range of
$\alpha^{1/8}/\delta$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Apply the norm-ball form of Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:38:thm:exact-reduction} to
$\ind_A-\delta$, and multiply its normalized cube count by $|G|^4$.
If $\alpha=0$, the centered function vanishes and the assertion is
immediate.  Otherwise Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:38:thm:pf-series}, with
$u=\alpha^{1/8}$, gives the displayed powers and the positive
remainder bound.
\end{proof}

Gowers' Lemma~3.10 gives the normalized bound
$(\delta+\alpha^{1/8})^8$ in this notation
\cite[Lemma~3.10]{gowers}.  Its first error is of order
$\alpha^{1/8}$ at fixed positive density, whereas
\eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-indicator-series-bound} begins at $\alpha^{1/2}$.
The sharp leading coefficient $6\sqrt2$ was already obtained in the
preceding project reports \cite{repo38collected,repo38five}; the additions
here are exact quotient reduction and the dimension-uniform higher
coefficients.  The corollary is an upper bound for indicators;
the exact extremizers and sharp realizations proved above are weights.

The program \file{code/verify_twelfth_order.py} checks
\eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:pf-X-series}, all the displayed $H_j$ coefficients, the
Hessian and phase displacements, and both optimized higher
coefficients by exact symbolic arithmetic.  It records the checks
in \file{data/twelfth_order_checks.json}.  A separate high-precision
stationary-branch calculation in the same program compares the
twelfth-order residual at decreasing positive values of $t$.
That numerical calculation checks the analytic branch; it is not
used to establish global optimality or the size of its neighborhood.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Cyclic reduction for every fixed odd exponent\srctag{38}}]{Cyclic reduction for every fixed odd exponent}\label{gsr:cc:38:sec:d5}
\srcnote{38}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:cc:38:sec:bounded-odd-exponent}

The mechanism behind exact reduction is not exclusive to
characteristic five.  The finite size of the cyclic frequency group
generated by a dominant character is what bounds the potentially
negative cross terms.  The following version keeps the dependence
on that size explicit.

\begin{theorem}[Exact cyclic reduction at bounded odd exponent]
\label{gsr:cc:38:thm:bounded-odd-cyclic}
Let $m\ge3$ be odd, let $G$ be a finite abelian group of exponent
exactly $m$, and put $c_m=10^{-8}m^{-8}$.  For every $\delta>0$,
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal M_{\delta,G}(u)=\mathcal M_{\delta,\Z/m\Z}(u)
       \qquad(0<u\le c_m\delta).
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:bounded-odd-profile}
\end{equation}
Every maximizing function on $G$ factors through a cyclic quotient
of odd order dividing $m$.  The same identity of maxima holds with
the norm constraint replaced by $\|f\|_{U^3}\le u$.
For $0<\delta<1$, these unrestricted maxima are attainable by weights
in $[0,1]$ if also $mu\le\min\{\delta,1-\delta\}$.
\end{theorem}

The threshold is a sufficient bound; neither its constant nor its
power of $m$ is claimed optimal.  In particular, this theorem does
not supply a threshold independent of all odd exponents.

\begin{proof}
Normalize $f=uF$, $\|F\|_{U^3}=1$, and $t=u/\delta$.
We first verify the pure-pair benchmark used in localization.
For a real function with Fourier support $\{\xi,-\xi\}$ and
coefficients $\rho e^{i\alpha}$ and its conjugate, the centered
norm is $8\rho^8$ for every nonzero odd-order character.
Indeed a two-point subset of an odd group has no parallelogram with
both increments nonzero, so only the axes of the Fourier-square
formula contribute.  If the character has order greater than three,
the fifth-, sixth-, and seventh-degree terms vanish.  For the sixth
and seventh degrees this follows from the statistic $H$: no three
frequencies from this pair sum to zero.

If the character has order three, the terms are instead
\[
 B_5=2\rho^5\cos3\alpha,\qquad
 C_6=(24+8\cos6\alpha)\rho^6,\qquad C_7=0.
\]
These identities follow directly from the $H,J,K$ and $T,L$ formulas:
here $H=2\rho^6$, $J=0$, $K=2\rho^6\cos6\alpha$, and the nonzero
slots of $L$ are disjoint from those of $T$.
Choosing $\alpha=0$ makes both additional terms positive.
Thus every nontrivial odd-order group has a normalized pure-pair
competitor of value at least $1+6\sqrt2\,t^4+t^8$.

For any maximizing candidate put
$S=\sum_r|\widehat F(r)|^4$ and $S_0=2^{-1/2}$.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:38:lem:centered-expansion}, cube Cauchy--Schwarz, and the
benchmark imply $0\le S_0-S\le4t$.
Choose a largest Fourier pair, generated by $\xi$, and put
$D_{\rm pair}=\sum_{r\notin\{\xi,-\xi\}}|\widehat F(r)|^4$.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:38:lem:quartic-gap} gives
\[
 1\ge2S^2+3SD_{\rm pair},
 \qquad D_{\rm pair}\le8t
\]
in the present range.  Let $L=\langle\xi\rangle$, of size at most
$m$, let $g$ be the Fourier projection to $L$, and write $h=F-g$.
As in the exact reduction proof, put
\[
 S_g=\sum_{r\in L}|\widehat F(r)|^4,\quad
 D=\sum_{r\notin L}|\widehat F(r)|^4,\quad
 v=\|g\|_{U^3},\quad \Delta=1-v^8.
\]
Then $S_g\ge S_0-12t$.

Let $p$ denote the Fourier projection of $g$ onto the principal pair.
For $s,t\in L$ with $s,t\ne0$, the preceding two-point observation
gives $T_p(s,t)=0$.  Telescope the four factors of $T_g-T_p$ and
apply $\ell^4$ H\"older to each of the four terms.  Each unchanged
factor has norm at most one, whereas the changed factor has norm
at most $D_{\rm pair}^{1/4}$.  Therefore
\[
 |T_g(s,t)|\le4D_{\rm pair}^{1/4},\qquad
 R:=\sum_{\substack{s,t\in L\\s,t\ne0}}|T_g(s,t)|
       \le4m^2(8t)^{1/4}.
\]
For $t\le c_m$, this is at most $4\,8^{1/4}/100<1/3$.
Also $S_g\ge2/3$.  The energy argument proving
\eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:projection-coercivity} uses only odd order and a subgroup
$L$, before its final five-point bound on $R$ is inserted.
It therefore gives here
\begin{equation}
 \Delta\ge(10S_g-2R)D+2D^2\ge6D,
 \qquad 0\le\Delta\le1/9.
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:bounded-odd-coercivity}
\end{equation}
The last bound follows from $v^8\ge2S_g^2\ge8/9$.
The subgroup-projection estimate
\eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:projection-convexity} still gives
$\|h\|_{U^3}^8\le256\Delta$.

We spell out the dependence of the higher-degree estimates on $m$.
Write $H_F,H_g$ for the nonnegative triple statistics of the two
functions.  Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
 A_g:=\sum_{r\in L}|\widehat F(r)|^2
       \le\sqrt{|L|S_g}\le\sqrt m.
\]
Exactly as in the proof of \eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:six-linear-loss},
\begin{align*}
 H_F-H_g
 &\le3A_gD+\sqrt{D(128\Delta+D^2/2)}\\
 &\le C_H\Delta,\qquad C_H=5+\frac{\sqrt m}{2}\le3m.
\end{align*}
Thus $|C_6(F)-C_6(g)|\le28C_H\Delta$.
For the seventh-degree difference the part on $L^2$ is at most
$8|L|^2D\le(4/3)m^2\Delta$, because each value of $L_g(s,t)$
has modulus at most four.  On the complement, the two squared norms
in the Cauchy--Schwarz estimate are at most
$(4/3)\Delta$ and $16C_H\Delta$.  Therefore
\[
 |C_7(F)-C_7(g)|
 \le\left(\frac43m^2+\frac{16}{\sqrt3}\sqrt{C_H}\right)\Delta.
\]
This is the same linear estimate as
\eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:seven-linear-loss}, now with its dependence on $m$ retained.

Multiplication by two preserves both $L$ and its complement, because
the group has odd order.  Consequently
$B_5(F)-B_5(g)=B_5(h)$ and its modulus is at most
$D^{5/4}\le\Delta/6$.
Set $g_*=g/v$.  For $k=5,6,7$, the rescaling estimate
$|v^{-k}-1|\le4\Delta$ remains valid.  Combining it with the preceding
bounds and cube Cauchy--Schwarz yields
\begin{align*}
 |B_5(F)-B_5(g_*)|&\le5\Delta,\\
 |C_6(F)-C_6(g_*)|&\le(28C_H+112)\Delta\le122m\Delta,\\
 |C_7(F)-C_7(g_*)|&\le10m^2\Delta.
\end{align*}
For the last simplification, $C_H\le3m$ and $m\ge3$ give
$16\sqrt{C_H/3}\le16\sqrt m\le10m$; the remaining terms are
$(4/3)m^2+32$, whose sum with $10m$ is less than $10m^2$.

The fourth-degree improvement is at least $2t^4\Delta$, by
\eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:bounded-odd-coercivity}, and the eighth-degree terms
cancel because both functions have norm one.  Hence
\[
 \Qthirtyeight(1+tF)-\Qthirtyeight(1+tg_*)
 \le t^4\Delta(-2+40t+122mt^2+10m^2t^3)\le-t^4\Delta.
\]
The coefficient in parentheses is strictly less than $-1$ throughout $t\le10^{-8}m^{-8}$;
substitution bounds the three positive terms by
$40\cdot10^{-8}m^{-8}$, $122\cdot10^{-16}m^{-15}$, and
$10\cdot10^{-24}m^{-22}$, respectively, with sum less than one.
If $D>0$, the improvement is strict.  Every maximizer consequently
has Fourier support in a cyclic group $L$ of order $d\mid m$.

The dual of $G$ has an element of order $m$, so $G$ has a cyclic
quotient of that order.  Conversely every function on a cyclic group
of order $d\mid m$ pulls back to $\Z/m\Z$ with its mean, norm, and
objective preserved.  These two pullback statements prove
\eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:bounded-odd-profile}.

For the norm-ball assertion, let $F$ be normalized and maximizing
at centered norm $0<r\le c_m$.  The localization above gives
$S\ge2/3$.  For $r\le s\le c_m$, the centered polynomial satisfies
\[
 \frac{d}{ds}\Qthirtyeight(1+sF)
       \ge s^3(48S-40s-168s^2-56s^3)>0.
\]
Scaling a positive lower-norm maximizer therefore proves strict monotonicity
throughout the range. The norm-zero value is strictly smaller by the
pure-pair benchmark.  The ball maximum is attained at its boundary.
Finally, a centered function on $\Z/m\Z$ has at most $m-1$
nonzero Fourier coefficients, each of modulus at most $u$.
The additional bound $mu\le\min\{\delta,1-\delta\}$ puts its
maximizing weight in $[0,1]$, and pullback concludes the proof.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Extremal values and the order of individual quotients]
\label{gsr:cc:38:rem:bounded-odd-order}
The equality of extremal values with $\Z/m\Z$ does not say that
every maximizing function itself factors through an order-$m$
quotient.  A lower-order character need not lie in a cyclic subgroup
of order $m$: in the dual of $\Z/9\Z\times\Z/3\Z$, for example,
the character represented by $(0,1)$ is not contained in any cyclic
subgroup of order nine.  The theorem gives cyclic dependence of
each extremizer, while the extremal value is compared by pullbacks
between the resulting cyclic groups.
\end{remark}

\section{Source~38's Part~III: six-term norm-extension defects \wtag}\label{gsr:cc:sec:sixterm}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the seventh write, 6~October 2026.}}\par
The next section is source~38's Section~7, its delivered Part~III. \emph{Logically it follows source~22's chapter on polynomial colourings} (Section~\ref{gsr:cc:sec:colourings}), whose cubic-core defect and zero-defect classification it extends, and the norm-colouring material of sources~10 and~14; it is printed here because no number printed earlier may move. For a layered linear--cubic--quintic norm colouring plus an arbitrary function of independent coordinates it counts the symmetric six-term progressions exactly; the excess over the surjectivity count is governed by centered third and fifth differences and a quadratic-character statistic (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:38:thm:six-ap-defect}). The layered construction is Shi and Dong's; no better colouring exponent is claimed, and the quintic four-term dimension question stays open (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:colhigh}). Nothing in this section is formalized.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{An exact six-term extension defect and its quadratic-character term\srctag{38}}]{An exact six-term extension defect and its quadratic-character term}\label{gsr:cc:38:sec:d7}
\srcnote{38}{Section 7}
\gsrsrcpartof{38}{Exact six-term norm-extension defects}
\label{gsr:cc:38:sec:six-ap-defect}

Gowers' Conjecture~4.2 proposed a random-density lower bound for
even-length progressions under a weaker uniformity hypothesis
\cite{gowers}.  Symmetric-progression colorings are relevant to the
limits of such a principle.  In particular, Shi and Dong use layered
odd-degree field norms to construct colorings avoiding symmetric
progressions, with applications to counterexamples to the conjecture
\cite{shidong}.  The question studied here is an exact counting problem
inside that construction method: what happens after a function of new,
independent coordinates is added to a complete norm core?

The preceding degree-stratification report \cite{repo38degrees} proves
that such an addition cannot preserve avoidance, and gives an exact
third-difference formula for the linear--cubic core.  It asks for exact
formulas beyond that case.  We answer the next case.  The
six-term core contains both a cubic and a quintic norm; after one averages
over its centers, their interaction is governed by the value distribution
of a nondegenerate quadratic form on a five-dimensional extension field.
The resulting formula applies to an arbitrary added function, without
a polynomial-degree assumption.

\subsection{Fields, extension degrees, and norm fibers}

Fix a prime power $q=p^r$ of characteristic $p>5$.  Let $N_j$ denote the
norm from $\F_{q^j}$ to $\F_q$.  The subscripts $3$ and $5$ below are
\emph{extension degrees over $\F_q$}; neither is the characteristic.
The base field need not be prime.  The assumption concerns $p$, not
merely $q$: it guarantees six distinct progression points in every
nonzero direction, the invertibility of $120$, and the nonvanishing
trace $\operatorname{Tr}_{\F_{q^5}/\F_q}(1)=5$.

\begin{lemma}[Norm presentation and fibers]
\label{gsr:cc:38:lem:six-norm-fibers}
After any linear identification $\F_{q^j}\cong\F_q^j$, the norm $N_j$
is represented by a homogeneous polynomial of total degree $j$.
Its zero fiber is $\{0\}$, and each nonzero scalar has exactly
\[
 L_j=\frac{q^j-1}{q-1}
\]
preimages.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
In a basis $b_1,\dots,b_j$, write $x=\sum_iX_i b_i$.  Then
\[
 N_j(x)=\prod_{s=0}^{j-1}\left(\sum_iX_i b_i^{q^s}\right).
\]
This is a product of $j$ linear forms.  Frobenius permutes the factors,
so its coefficients belong to $\F_q$.  The product vanishes precisely
when $x=0$.  On $\F_{q^j}^*$ it is the homomorphism $x\mapsto x^{L_j}$.
The multiplicative group is cyclic of order $q^j-1$, and the norm of
a generator has order $q-1$.  Thus the map is onto $\F_q^*$ and has
kernel of size $L_j$, which gives every nonzero fiber size.
\end{proof}

In particular, put
\[
 L_3=q^2+q+1,\qquad L_5=q^4+q^3+q^2+q+1,
 \qquad \chi:\F_q\longrightarrow\{-1,0,1\},
\]
where $\chi$ is the quadratic character extended by $\chi(0)=0$.
For an integer $e\ge0$ and an arbitrary function $R:\F_q^e\to\F_q$,
consider
\[
 P(a,u,v,w)=a+N_3(u)+N_5(v)+R(w).
\]
Here $(a,u,v,w)\in\F_q\times\F_{q^3}\times\F_{q^5}\times\F_q^e$,
so its domain has dimension $9+e$ over $\F_q$.
Write $A_6^{\mathrm{sym}}(P)$ for the
number of ordered center--direction pairs $(z,h)$ with $h\ne0$ such that
\[
 P(z+h/2)=P(z-h/2),\quad
 P(z+3h/2)=P(z-3h/2),\quad
 P(z+5h/2)=P(z-5h/2).
\]
This counts ordered nontrivial six-term arithmetic progressions with
the three stated symmetric color equalities.  The
direction is the common difference, and no quotient by sign or by
rescaling is taken.

For $b,g\in\F_q^e$, define the centered odd differences
\begin{align*}
 D_3(b,g)&=\Delta_g^3R(b-3g/2),\\
 D_5(b,g)&=\Delta_g^5R(b-5g/2),
\end{align*}
where $\Delta_gR(x)=R(x+g)-R(x)$.  Define three finite statistics
\begin{align*}
 T_0&=\#\{(b,g):D_5(b,g)=0,\ D_3(b,g)\ne0\},\\
 T_1&=\#\{(b,g):D_5(b,g)\ne0\},\\
 S&=\sum_{\substack{b,g\\D_5(b,g)\ne0}}
      \chi\!\left(\frac{40D_3(b,g)}{D_5(b,g)}-5\right).
\end{align*}
All quotients are taken in $\F_q$.  The integers appearing in
the character argument are reduced in the same field.

\begin{theorem}[Exact six-term defect]
\label{gsr:cc:38:thm:six-ap-defect}
With the notation above,
\begin{align}
 A_6^{\mathrm{sym}}(P)
 ={}&q^{9+e}(q^e-1)+q^9(q^2+q)T_0\notag\\
 &+q^9(q^2L_5-1)T_1-q^7(q+1)L_5S.
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:six-ap-defect}
\end{align}
In particular the general surjectivity lower bound
$q^{9+e}(q^e-1)$ is attained exactly when all pure third additive
differences of $R$ vanish.  Equivalently, after regarding its domain
as a vector space over $\F_p$, the function $R$ has the form
\[
 R(x)=c+L(x)+B(x,x),
\]
where $L$ is $\F_p$-linear and $B$ is symmetric
$\F_p$-bilinear, with values in $\F_q$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 34--39]
\emph{In this report.} This extends source~22's exact cubic-core defect and zero-defect classification (Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:22:cor:zero-defect}) to the linear--cubic--quintic core with an independent addition; source~22's question on defect formulas for more odd norm layers (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:patterns}) is advanced for three layers. The layered construction is Shi and Dong's, as the source says; no better colouring exponent is claimed. The exact finite checks over the fields of orders $7$ and $13$ were rerun on a copy at the write.
\end{writenote}

The formula gives a sharper hierarchy than the statement that every
added direction has at least one matching core direction.  A nonzero
third difference with zero fifth difference contributes $q^2+q$ extra
core directions on average.  A nonzero fifth difference contributes
approximately $q^6$ extra core directions on average; its exact deviation
has a quadratic-character sign.  The conclusion concerns this specified
independent extension of a norm coloring.  It does not improve the
unrestricted symmetric-progression coloring exponent or the global
Szemer\'edi bound.

\subsection{The quadratic coefficient of the quintic norm}

For $x\in E=\F_{q^5}$, write
\[
 N_5(x+T)=T^5+e_1(x)T^4+e_2(x)T^3+e_3(x)T^2+e_4(x)T+e_5(x).
\]
Expanding the square of the sum of the five Frobenius conjugates gives
\[
 e_2(x)=\frac{(\operatorname{Tr}x)^2-\operatorname{Tr}(x^2)}2.
\]

\begin{lemma}[Exact value distribution]
\label{gsr:cc:38:lem:quintic-e2-distribution}
For every $c\in\F_q$,
\[
 \#\{x\in E:e_2(x)=c\}=q^4+q^2\chi(2c).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Choose an $\F_q$-basis $b_1,\ldots,b_5$ of $E$, and let
$T=(\operatorname{Tr}(b_i b_j))_{i,j}$ be the trace-pairing matrix.
The pairing is nondegenerate: for $x\ne0$, pairing with $x^{-1}$ gives
$\operatorname{Tr}(1)=5\ne0$.  Its determinant is a nonzero square in
$\F_q$.  Indeed, if $M=(b_j^{q^i})_{0\le i\le4,1\le j\le5}$,
then $T=M^{\mathsf T}M$; moreover Frobenius acts on $M$ by a five-cycle
of its rows, so $(\det M)^q=\det M$.  Thus $\det M\in\F_q^*$
and $\det T=(\det M)^2$.

The quadratic form $e_2$ is represented relative to the trace pairing by
the self-adjoint operator
\[
 \tfrac12(1\otimes\operatorname{Tr}-I).
\]
The operator in parentheses has eigenvalue $4$ on the span of $1$ and
eigenvalue $-1$ on the trace-zero subspace.  These subspaces are
complementary because $\operatorname{Tr}(1)=5\ne0$.  Hence its
determinant is $4$, and the determinant of a matrix for $e_2$ is
\[
 2^{-5}\cdot4\det T=\frac{\det T}{8}.
\]
In particular, $e_2$ is nondegenerate of rank five and its determinant
has quadratic character $\chi(2)$.

For completeness, the standard odd-rank quadratic-form count follows
by diagonalization and additive-character orthogonality.  For a
nontrivial additive character $\psi$, put
$G=\sum_{x\in\F_q}\psi(x^2)=\sum_t\chi(t)\psi(t)$.
The identity $G^2=\chi(-1)q$ follows by writing the two nonzero
variables in $G^2$ as $u,ut$: the sum over $u\ne0$ of
$\psi(u(1+t))$ is $q-1$ at $t=-1$ and $-1$ otherwise.
If $Q$ is a nondegenerate quadratic form of rank five with matrix $A$,
then
\[
 \sum_x\psi(sQ(x))=\chi(s)\chi(\det A)G^5\qquad(s\ne0).
\]
Orthogonality gives $q^4$ solutions when $c=0$.  When $c\ne0$, use
$\sum_{s\ne0}\chi(s)\psi(-sc)=\chi(-c)G$ to obtain
\[
 \#\{x:Q(x)=c\}
 =q^4+q^{-1}\chi(\det A)\chi(-c)G^6
 =q^4+q^2\chi(c\det A).
\]
Applying this with $\chi(\det A)=\chi(2)$ proves the result.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The exact averaged reflection fibers}

For fixed $(b,g)$, let $\beta_1,\beta_3,\beta_5$ be the unique
coefficients such that
\[
 R(b+\alpha g)-R(b-\alpha g)
 =2(\beta_1\alpha+\beta_3\alpha^3+\beta_5\alpha^5)
 \qquad\left(\alpha=\tfrac12,\tfrac32,\tfrac52\right).
\]
The matrix is invertible because the three nonzero squared parameters
are distinct when $p>5$.  This is interpolation on six points, so it
does not assert that $R$ is a polynomial.  Direct finite-difference
calculation yields
\begin{equation}
 \beta_5=D_5/120,\qquad
 \beta_3=D_3/6-D_5/48.
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:six-beta-differences}
\end{equation}
In fact $D_3=6\beta_3+15\beta_5$ and $D_5=120\beta_5$.

Let $b_3=-\beta_3$, $b_5=-\beta_5$ be the target cubic and quintic
coefficients that the core must supply.  Its linear coefficient can
always be set by a unique direction in the $a$ coordinate.  If the
quintic direction is $h$, it must satisfy $N_5(h)=b_5$.  When $h\ne0$,
its contribution to the cubic coefficient at quintic center $v$ is
\[
 N_5(h)e_2(v/h)=b_5e_2(v/h).
\]
The remaining cubic direction must therefore lie in the norm fiber
\[
 N_3(h_3)=b_3-b_5e_2(v/h).
\]
The cubic norm has one preimage of zero and $L_3$ preimages of every
nonzero scalar; write this fiber size as
\[
 \nu_3(t)=1+(q^2+q)1_{\{t\ne0\}}.
\]

If $b_5=0$, the quintic direction is zero, and the reflection fiber
has size $\nu_3(b_3)$ at every core center.  If $b_5\ne0$, there are
$L_5$ possible quintic directions.  For each such direction,
$v\mapsto v/h$ is a bijection of $E$.  Consequently the sum of the
fiber size over all $q^5$ quintic centers is exactly
\begin{align*}
 H(b_3,b_5)
 &=L_5\sum_{x\in E}\nu_3(b_3-b_5e_2(x))\\
 &=L_5\left[q^5+(q^2+q)
    \left(q^5-q^4-q^2\chi(2b_3/b_5)\right)\right]\\
 &=L_5\left[q^7-(q^4+q^3)\chi(2b_3/b_5)\right].
\end{align*}
Thus the mean reflection fiber over all core centers is
\begin{equation}
 \mu(b_3,b_5)=
 \begin{cases}
  1+(q^2+q)1_{\{b_3\ne0\}},&b_5=0,\\[2pt]
  L_5\bigl[q^2-(q^{-1}+q^{-2})\chi(2b_3/b_5)\bigr],&b_5\ne0.
 \end{cases}
 \label{gsr:cc:38:eq:six-mean-fiber}
\end{equation}
This is an average; it need not be an integer.  The integer quantity
$H$ above is the sum over quintic centers.  It is not claimed that
the fiber has size $\mu$ at each individual center.

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:38:thm:six-ap-defect}]
The coefficients in the cubic and linear core centers affect only
the unique final linear adjustment and do not change the preceding
count.  There are $q^4$ choices of these centers.  Therefore the total
number of symmetric center--direction pairs, including zero directions,
is
\[
 q^9\sum_{b,g}\mu(-\beta_3(b,g),-\beta_5(b,g)).
\]
By \eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:six-beta-differences}, when $D_5\ne0$ the character in
\eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:six-mean-fiber} is
\[
 \chi(2\beta_3/\beta_5)=\chi(40D_3/D_5-5).
\]
Split the sum into $D_3=D_5=0$, the $T_0$ cases, and the $T_1$ cases.
Subtract the exactly $q^{9+e}$ zero-direction pairs, one at each center.
This gives \eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:six-ap-defect}.

For $q\ge7$, every value of the second line of
\eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:six-mean-fiber} is greater than one.  The first line equals
one precisely when $b_3=0$.  Hence equality with the baseline holds
precisely when $D_3=D_5=0$ for every $(b,g)$, which is equivalent to
vanishing of all pure third differences: a fifth difference is a
second difference of a third difference.

For completeness, we prove the prime-field classification.  Fix an
$\F_p$-basis of the additive domain $\F_q^e$, so it becomes
$\F_p^{re}$.  The function $R$ has a unique reduced polynomial
presentation with coefficients in $\F_q$,
\[
 R(X)=\sum_a c_aX^a,\qquad 0\le a_i<p.
\]
The restriction of $R$ to each prime-field line has reduced degree at
most two.  To see this, a reduced one-variable polynomial of degree
$d\in\{3,\dots,p-1\}$ has a nonzero third forward difference: its
leading coefficient is multiplied by $d(d-1)(d-2)\ne0$.  Thus the
assumed vanishing of every pure third difference excludes such a degree.

It follows that the coefficient of $T^3$ in $R(X+TH)$, after reducing
$T$ modulo $T^p-T$, vanishes as a function of $(X,H)$ on
$\F_p^{re}\times\F_p^{re}$.  Suppose $c_a\ne0$ and $|a|\ge3$.
Choose a multi-index $b\le a$ with $|b|=3$.  This coefficient contains
\[
 c_a\binom a b X^{a-b}H^b.
\]
Every $X$- and $H$-coordinate exponent is already below $p$; moreover
$\binom a b\ne0$ in characteristic $p$.  Different pairs $(a,b)$
give distinct monomials $X^{a-b}H^b$.  Contributions with larger
$|b|\equiv3\pmod{p-1}$, which arise on reducing the parameter $T$,
also have different $H$-monomials.  The displayed term therefore
cannot cancel.  Uniqueness of the reduced polynomial as a function
of $(X,H)$ gives a contradiction.  Hence $R$ has total degree at most
two in the prime-field coordinates.

Conversely, every such quadratic has zero pure third differences.
Because $p$ is odd, its quadratic part is $B(x,x)$ for a symmetric
$\F_p$-bilinear map $B$, and its degree-one part is an
$\F_p$-linear map $L$.  This proves the classification, including
proper extension fields and the zero-dimensional domain.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Explicit added monomials and exact finite checks}

For one added coordinate $w\in\F_q$, all three elementary monomial
extensions have closed formulas.

\begin{corollary}[Three exact monomial counts]
\label{gsr:cc:38:cor:six-monomials}
Write $P_j(a,u,v,w)=a+N_3(u)+N_5(v)+w^j$.  Then
\begin{align*}
 A_6^{\mathrm{sym}}(P_3)&=q^{10}(q-1)L_3,\\
 A_6^{\mathrm{sym}}(P_4)&=q^{12}(q-1),\\
 A_6^{\mathrm{sym}}(P_5)&=q^7(q-1)L_5
                  \bigl[q^5-(q^2-1)\chi(5)\bigr].
\end{align*}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The statistics in Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:38:thm:six-ap-defect} are
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccc}
R(w)&T_0&T_1&S\\ \hline
w^3&q(q-1)&0&0\\
w^4&(q-1)^2&0&0\\
w^5&0&q(q-1)&(q-1)^2\chi(5).
\end{array}
\]
For $R=w^3$, we have $D_3=6g^3$ and $D_5=0$; for $R=w^4$,
we have $D_3=24bg^3$ and $D_5=0$.  These give the first two rows.
For $R=w^5$, the interpolated coefficients are
$\beta_5=g^5$ and $\beta_3=10b^2g^3$.  Thus $D_5\ne0$ exactly
when $g\ne0$, and the character
$\chi(2\beta_3/\beta_5)=\chi(20(b/g)^2)$ is zero for $b=0$
and is $\chi(5)$ whenever $b,g\ne0$.  This proves the last row.
Substitution into \eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:six-ap-defect} and simplification gives
the displayed counts.
\end{proof}

The standard-library program \file{code/verify_six_ap_defect.py}
constructs irreducible finite-field presentations and forms $e_2$
independently as the sum of pairwise Frobenius conjugates.  It exhausts
all $7^5+13^5=388100$ quintic-field elements, checks the entire $e_2$
distribution, and directly verifies cubic norm fibers on all
$7^3+13^3=2540$ cubic-field elements.  It then verifies all
$7\cdot6+13\cdot12=198$ pairs of cubic targets and nonzero quintic
targets by an independent weighted-fiber sum, including all three
quadratic-character values.  For example, for $q=7$ the three integer
sums $H$ are
\[
 H_{+1}=2299057999,\qquad H_0=2306743943,\qquad H_{-1}=2314429887.
\]
For $q=13$ they are
\[
 H_{+1}=1940550181219,\quad H_0=1941501864497,\quad
 H_{-1}=1942453547775.
\]
Finally it evaluates the added monomials at the actual six progression
nodes and verifies the aggregate formula.  The resulting ordered
nontrivial progression counts are
\[
\begin{array}{c|r|r}
R(w)&q=7&q=13\\ \hline
w^3&96606535158&302737248100404\\
w^4&83047723206&279577021469772\\
w^5&233281014955590&8654306689055041404.
\end{array}
\]
These are exact factorized counts.  The script does not enumerate all
center--direction pairs in the ten-dimensional domain, and no such
enumeration is needed for the proof.

\paragraph{What remains.}
For an eight-term core, the next norm layer has degree seven.  The same
descending procedure forces joint value distributions of several
polarized coefficients, rather than one quadratic form.  Determining
whether those distributions admit comparably explicit character
formulas is a concrete next problem.  The global quintic avoidance
dimension for symmetric four-term progressions, between four and eight
in the preceding reports \cite{repo38degrees}, remains unresolved here.

\section{Source~45's chapter: the real fourth-uniformity gap \wtag}\label{gsr:cc:sec:ufourgap}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the eighth write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next two sections are source~45's Sections~4--5. \emph{Logically they continue the chapter on the odd-order constants} (Section~\ref{gsr:cc:sec:oddconstant}), after source~34's Section~10 and source~35's Section~6; they are printed here because that chapter is no longer the last of Part~III and no number printed earlier may move.

\emph{What is proved.} For real centered $f$ on a finite abelian group of odd order, $\norm f_{U^4}^{16}\ge(4795/832)\norm f_{U^2}^{16}$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:45:un:main}), so $c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le(832/4795)^{1/4}=0.6454070$, the best upper bound among sources~01--46 (source~49, placed by \texttt{f8bc5e2ec} and not yet written in, records $29/4$, that is $c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le(4/29)^{1/4}=0.6094183$ (for its write)). The proof applies a mean-sensitive $U^3$ bound $Q_3(g)\ge v^2+10vw+2w^2$ (Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:45:un:mean-lemma}; the three-pairing count of sources~21, 35 and~38 with the zero frequency kept) to the derivatives $f\cdot f(\cdot+h)$, the even-moment bounds of the autocorrelation (sources~29's and~34's $C_m$), $W\ge V-1$, and the scalar certificate $P(t)=-t^2/4+(33/26)t-99/676$ with $10t^2-4P=11(t-3/13)^2$. Section~\ref{gsr:cc:45:sec:d5} multiplies source~04's quartic coefficient $P_d$ by $(832/4795)^{1/4}$ for $d\ge4$ (Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:45:ap:improved}) and computes the defect of rectified holes.
