\section[{A quantitative real fourth-uniformity gap\srctag{45}}]{A quantitative real fourth-uniformity gap}\label{gsr:cc:45:sec:d4}
\srcnote{45}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:cc:45:un:section}

The real, centered setting retains information that is lost in the ordinary
monotonicity of Gowers norms.  The pinned report~\cite{repo45} establishes
the sharp comparison
\[
 \norm{f}_{U^3}^{8}\ge 2\norm{f}_{U^2}^{8}
\]
for real functions of mean zero on finite abelian groups of odd order.  It
also asks for the corresponding optimal comparison with $U^d$ when
$d\ge4$.  We give a strictly stronger fourth-order comparison, an exact
finite lower bound for its optimal constant, and a structural obstruction
to carrying the third-order extremizers into dimension four.

Our argument uses the Fourier and cube identities underlying Gowers's
proof~\cite{gowers}, together with an elementary moment count and a
rational inequality certificate.  The broader theory of functions whose
Gowers norms are near an extremal value under $L^p$ or $L^\infty$
constraints is developed, for example, by Eisner and Tao~\cite{eisnertao}.
The quotient considered here imposes realness and centering and compares
two different uniformity norms.  We state the exact remaining uncertainty:
the numerical constant proved below is a certified lower bound for the
fourth-order norm gap, and its optimal value is not determined in this
article.

\subsection{Normalization and the results}
\label{gsr:cc:45:un:normalization}

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group, written additively.  Averages over $G$
and its powers are normalized.  Characters take values on the unit circle,
and the dual group $\widehat G$ is also written additively.  For a function
$f:G\to\C$, write
\begin{equation}
 a_\xi=\widehat f(\xi)
   =\E_{x\in G}f(x)\overline{\xi(x)},
 \qquad
 f(x)=\sum_{\xi\in\widehat G}a_\xi\xi(x).
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:fourier-convention}
\end{equation}
The Fourier sums in this section are \emph{unnormalized}; in particular,
the normalization is already incorporated in $a_\xi$.

Let $\mathcal C$ denote complex conjugation.  For $d\ge1$ set
\begin{equation}
 Q_d(f)=\norm{f}_{U^d}^{2^d}
 =\E_{x,h_1,\ldots,h_d}
   \prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^d}
       \mathcal C^{|\omega|}f(x+\omega\cdot h).
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:cube-definition}
\end{equation}
Here $\norm f_{U^1}=\abs{\E f}$; for $d\ge2$ this is a norm.  For real
functions, every conjugation in~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:cube-definition} can be omitted.
The recursion, with $\Delta_hf(x)=f(x)\overline{f(x+h)}$, is
\begin{equation}
 Q_{d+1}(f)=\E_h Q_d(\Delta_h f).
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:recursion}
\end{equation}
Orthogonality gives
\begin{equation}
 S(f):=Q_2(f)=\sum_\xi\abs{a_\xi}^4.
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:second-fourier}
\end{equation}
If $f$ is real, $a_{-\xi}=\overline{a_\xi}$; if it is centered,
$a_0=0$.  Odd group order ensures that every nonzero character belongs to
a distinct pair $\{\xi,-\xi\}$.

\begin{theorem}[Explicit real fourth-order gap]
\label{gsr:cc:45:un:main}
Let $G$ be a finite abelian group of odd order and let $f:G\to\R$ satisfy
$\E f=0$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 Q_4(f)\ge\frac{4795}{832}\,S(f)^4.}
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:main-inequality}
\end{equation}
Consequently, for every $d\ge4$,
\begin{equation}
 \norm f_{U^2}^4
 \le \left(\frac{832}{4795}\right)^{1/4}\norm f_{U^d}^4.
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:higher-comparison}
\end{equation}
No bound on $\norm f_\infty$ is required.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 40--46]
\emph{Where this stands} (checked at the write). In source~29's normalization $\norm f_{U^4}^{16}\ge C\norm f_{U^2}^{16}$ the coefficients are $(323/160)^2$ (28), $35/8$ (29), $5$ (35), $81/16$ (34) and $4795/832=5.7632212$ (here), that is $c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le0.7038153$, $0.6914416$, $0.6687403$, $2/3$ and $(832/4795)^{1/4}=0.6454070$; $4795/832-81/16=583/832$. So this is the best upper bound among sources~01--46 (source~49, placed by \texttt{f8bc5e2ec} and not yet written in, records $29/4$, that is $c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le(4/29)^{1/4}=0.6094183$ (for its write)), and $0.5587725\le c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le(832/4795)^{1/4}=0.6454070$, the lower end being the batch-121 intake's certificate on $\Z/7\Z$ (note after source~28's Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:28:uq:witness}). The intake re-derived the proof and checked every identity of the certificate in exact rationals ($10t^2-4P=11(t-3/13)^2$, the final quadratic in $V$) and every intermediate inequality on 47 functions over nine odd groups. Local numerical minimization puts the truth near $C\approx10.2571$ (dossier~122; evidence only).
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 47--53]
\emph{Superseded by source~49} (now printed, Section~\ref{gsr:cc:sec:dualtest}): its Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:49:ng:main} has the coefficient $29/4>4795/832$ (the difference is $1237/832$), so $c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le(4/29)^{1/4}=0.6094183$ and the bracket among sources~01--53 is $0.5587725\le c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le0.6094183$; source~49 was written before this source arrived and does not cite it. The statement ``best among sources~01--46'' above stays true for those sources.
\end{writenote}

The theorem is homogeneous.  Thus it also applies to the $1$-bounded
functions used in density arguments, and imposing $\norm f_\infty\le1$
does not alter the optimal quotient below: every nonzero function on a
finite group can be rescaled to satisfy that condition.

Define
\begin{equation}
 c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}
 =\sup\left\{
  \frac{\norm f_{U^2}^4}{\norm f_{U^d}^4}:
  \begin{array}{l}
   G\text{ finite abelian of odd order},\\
   f:G\to\R,\quad \E f=0,\quad f\ne0
  \end{array}\right\}.
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:optimal-constant}
\end{equation}

\begin{corollary}[A rigorous interval for the optimal constant]
\label{gsr:cc:45:un:interval}
One has
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 \left(\frac{39037448}{404304625}\right)^{1/4}
 \le c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}
 \le\left(\frac{832}{4795}\right)^{1/4}.}
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:interval-equation}
\end{equation}
Numerically, the two endpoints are
\[
 0.5574336443118301
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 0.6454070108505990.
\]
Moreover, no function of the form $2\operatorname{Re}(c\xi)$, with
$c\ne0$ and $\xi$ a nontrivial character, attains the supremum defining
$c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}$.
\end{corollary}

The upper endpoint is proved in
Section~\ref{gsr:cc:45:un:certificate}.  The exact five-point example providing the
lower endpoint appears in Section~\ref{gsr:cc:45:un:five-points}.  The exclusion of
the single-character class is proved in Section~\ref{gsr:cc:45:un:cosines}.

Each of the three restrictions in Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:45:un:main} matters.  A
nontrivial complex character is centered and has $U^j$ norm equal to $1$
for every $j\ge2$, so realness cannot be dropped.  A nonzero constant function
shows that centering cannot be dropped.  On $\Z/2\Z$, the nontrivial real
character is centered and again has $U^j$ norm equal to $1$ for every $j\ge2$,
so an unrestricted even-order version is false.

For completeness, ordinary monotonicity follows directly from the cube
identities.  With $j-1$ derivatives grouped into $F_h$, one has
\[
 Q_j(f)=\E_h\abs{\E_xF_h(x)}^2,
 \qquad
 Q_{j+1}(f)=\E_h\norm{F_h}_{U^2}^4.
\]
By~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:second-fourier},
$\norm{F_h}_{U^2}^4\ge\abs{\E F_h}^4$, and Cauchy--Schwarz therefore
gives $Q_{j+1}(f)\ge Q_j(f)^2$.  This proves
$\norm f_{U^{j+1}}\ge\norm f_{U^j}$ and the passage from dimension four
to~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:higher-comparison}.  Combining only monotonicity with the
third-order result in~\cite{repo45} would give the weaker constant
$1/\sqrt2$.

\subsection{A third-order inequality retaining the mean}
\label{gsr:cc:45:un:mean-sensitive}

The essential first step is to retain the zero Fourier coefficient when
performing the third-order argument.  Derivatives of a centered function
need not be centered; their means are its autocorrelations.  Discarding
those means before the next averaging would lose the improvement.

\begin{lemma}[Fourier face identity]
\label{gsr:cc:45:un:face-identity}
For every complex function $g$ on a finite abelian group, with normalized
Fourier coefficients $a_r$, one has
\begin{align}
 Q_3(g)&=\sum_{s,t\in\widehat G}\abs{T(s,t)}^2,
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:duality}\\
 T(s,t)&=\sum_{r\in\widehat G}
       a_r\overline{a_{r+s}}\,
       \overline{a_{r+t}}a_{r+s+t}.
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:face-sum}
\end{align}
The identity requires no assumption on the order of the group.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Expand~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:cube-definition} for $d=3$ using Fourier inversion.  For
the term with frequency labels $r_\omega$, orthogonality in $x,h_1,h_2,h_3$
imposes exactly
\begin{equation}
 \sum_\omega(-1)^{|\omega|}r_\omega=0,
 \qquad
 \sum_\omega(-1)^{|\omega|}\omega_i r_\omega=0
 \quad(1\le i\le3).
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:frequency-constraints}
\end{equation}
These equations are equations in $\widehat G$, so they must be solved
without dividing by an integer.  Subtract the $h_3$ equation from the
$x$ equation.  The result is
\[
 r_{000}-r_{100}-r_{010}+r_{110}=0.
\]
Subtracting the $h_2$ and $h_1$ equations in the same way determines
$r_{101}$ and $r_{011}$.  Substitution in any one of the $h_i$ equations
then determines $r_{111}$.  Thus, writing
\[
 r=r_{000},\quad s=r_{100}-r,\quad
 t=r_{010}-r,\quad u=r_{001}-r,
\]
all solutions are exactly
\[
 r_\omega=r+\omega_1s+\omega_2t+\omega_3u.
\]
Conversely these labels satisfy~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:frequency-constraints}, as direct
substitution shows.  There are no multiplicities or divisibility factors.

For fixed $s,t$, put
\[
 P_{s,t}(r)=a_r\overline{a_{r+s}}\,
              \overline{a_{r+t}}a_{r+s+t}.
\]
The two parallel frequency faces contribute
$P_{s,t}(r)\overline{P_{s,t}(r+u)}$.  Summing over $r,u$ is therefore
$\abs{\sum_rP_{s,t}(r)}^2$.  The remaining sum over $s,t$ proves the
identity.  All averages used in orthogonality equal either zero or one;
this accounts for the unnormalized sums in~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:duality}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Mean-sensitive real third-order bound]
\label{gsr:cc:45:un:mean-lemma}
Let $G$ have odd order and let $g:G\to\R$ be arbitrary.  Set
\begin{equation}
 v=\abs{\E g}^4,
 \qquad w=Q_2(g)-v\ge0.
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:vw-definition}
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{Q_3(g)\ge v^2+10vw+2w^2.}
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:mean-bound}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Put
\[
 \lambda_r=\abs{a_r}^2,\qquad
 H=\sum_r\lambda_r^2=v+w,\qquad
 M=\sum_r\lambda_r^4.
\]
Because $g$ is real, $\lambda_{-r}=\lambda_r$ and
$\lambda_0^2=v$.  Introduce the unnormalized additive energy of the
nonnegative weights $\lambda$:
\[
 \mathcal E(\lambda)
 =\sum_{r+s=t+u}\lambda_r\lambda_s\lambda_t\lambda_u.
\]
On either coordinate axis in~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:duality},
\[
 T(0,t)=\sum_r\lambda_r\lambda_{r+t}.
\]
The squared sums on one axis add up to $\mathcal E(\lambda)$.
Retaining the union of the two axes, and subtracting their common origin
once, gives
\begin{equation}
 Q_3(g)\ge2\mathcal E(\lambda)-H^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:axes}
\end{equation}

Every summand of $\mathcal E(\lambda)$ is nonnegative.  Retain the union
of these three families of solutions of $r+s=t+u$:
\[
 \begin{array}{lll}
 \mathcal A:&r=t,&s=u,\\
 \mathcal B:&r=u,&s=t,\\
 \mathcal D:&s=-r,&u=-t.
 \end{array}
\]
Each family has total weight $H^2$.  Each pairwise intersection has total
weight $M$.  In the triple intersection all four indices coincide and
$2r=0$.  Odd group order makes $r=0$ its only possibility, so the triple
intersection has weight $\lambda_0^4=v^2$.  Inclusion--exclusion yields
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal E(\lambda)\ge3H^2-3M+v^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:three-pairings}
\end{equation}

For representatives of the nonzero opposite pairs write
$b_j=\lambda_{r_j}^2$.  Then
\[
 w=2\sum_jb_j,
 \qquad
 M=v^2+2\sum_jb_j^2
 \le v^2+\frac12w^2.
\]
Substitution into~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:axes} and~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:three-pairings} gives
\begin{align*}
 Q_3(g)
 &\ge5(v+w)^2-6\left(v^2+\frac12w^2\right)+2v^2\\
 &=v^2+10vw+2w^2,
\end{align*}
as required.
\end{proof}

When $g$ is centered this reduces to the third-order factor $2$.
The extra mixed term in~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:mean-bound} is what permits the
fourth-order improvement.  Notice also why the zero frequency could not
be omitted in the proof: it contributes the triple intersection
$v^2$ in~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:three-pairings}.

\subsection{Positive Fourier coefficients and even autocorrelation moments}
\label{gsr:cc:45:un:moments}

For a real centered function $f$, define its autocorrelation by
\begin{equation}
 R(h)=\E_x f(x)f(x+h).
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:autocorrelation}
\end{equation}
Fourier inversion and realness give
\begin{equation}
 R(h)=\sum_{\xi}\lambda_\xi\xi(h),
 \qquad
 \lambda_\xi=\abs{\widehat f(\xi)}^2,
 \qquad
 \lambda_{-\xi}=\lambda_\xi,\quad\lambda_0=0.
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:positive-spectrum}
\end{equation}
Thus $R$ is real, even, and has nonnegative Fourier coefficients.  Also
\begin{equation}
 \E_hR(h)^2=\sum_\xi\lambda_\xi^2=S(f).
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:correlation-second}
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}[All even moments of the autocorrelation]
\label{gsr:cc:45:un:moment-lemma}
If $G$ has odd order, $f:G\to\R$ is centered, and $k\ge1$ is an integer,
then
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 \E_hR(h)^{2k}\ge
       \frac{\binom{2k}{k}}{2^k}\,S(f)^k.}
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:moment-bound}
\end{equation}
For $k=1$ equality always holds.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Choose one character from each nonzero opposite pair.  With $b_j\ge0$
we may write
\[
 R(h)=\sum_jb_j\bigl(\chi_j(h)+\chi_j(h)^{-1}\bigr),
 \qquad S(f)=2\sum_jb_j^2.
\]
In the expansion of $\E R^{2k}$, each character word averages to zero or
one.  Its scalar coefficient is nonnegative.  Retain those words that
contain the same number $k_j$ of occurrences of $\chi_j$ and
$\chi_j^{-1}$, for every $j$.  These words certainly average to one,
irrespective of any other relations among the characters.  Their total
contribution is
\begin{equation}
 (2k)!\sum_{\sum_jk_j=k}
                  \prod_j\frac{b_j^{2k_j}}{(k_j!)^2}.
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:balanced-words}
\end{equation}
For every multi-index in this sum, the multinomial coefficient
$k!/\prod_jk_j!$ is a positive integer.  Consequently
\[
 \prod_j\frac1{(k_j!)^2}
 \ge\frac1{k!}\prod_j\frac1{k_j!}.
\]
Using the multinomial theorem in~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:balanced-words}, we obtain
\begin{align*}
 \E R^{2k}
 &\ge\frac{(2k)!}{k!}
       \sum_{\sum_jk_j=k}\prod_j\frac{b_j^{2k_j}}{k_j!}\\
 &=\binom{2k}{k}\left(\sum_jb_j^2\right)^k
 =\frac{\binom{2k}{k}}{2^k}S(f)^k.
\end{align*}
For $k=1$, this is precisely~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:correlation-second}.
\end{proof}

The lemma does not require the character representatives to be independent
or dissociated.  Additional additive relations contribute further
nonnegative terms; none invalidates the selected family of balanced
words.  This observation is particularly useful for handling small odd
torsion uniformly.

We shall use the four instances
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
 \E R^2&=S,&
 \E R^4&\ge\frac32S^2,\\
 \E R^6&\ge\frac52S^3,&
 \E R^8&\ge\frac{35}{8}S^4,
 \end{aligned}
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:four-moments}
\end{equation}
where $S=S(f)$.  These particular numerical coefficients are not arbitrary
estimates: they are $\binom{2k}{k}/2^k$ at $k=1,2,3,4$.

\subsection{A rational certificate for the fourth-order gap}
\label{gsr:cc:45:un:certificate}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:45:un:main}]
If $f=0$, the result is immediate.  Otherwise $S(f)>0$ by Fourier
inversion.  Replace $f$ by $S(f)^{-1/4}f$; it is enough to prove the
statement under the normalization $S(f)=1$.

For each $h\in G$ let
\begin{equation}
 g_h(x)=f(x)f(x+h),\qquad
 t(h)=R(h)^2,\qquad
 w(h)=Q_2(g_h)-t(h)^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:derivative-variables}
\end{equation}
The zero Fourier coefficient of $g_h$ is $R(h)$, so
$w(h)\ge0$.  Introduce the scalar moments
\begin{equation}
 V=\E t^2,\qquad B=\E t^3,\qquad
 A=\E t^4,\qquad W=\E w.
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:scalar-moments}
\end{equation}
By~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:four-moments},
\begin{equation}
 \E t=1,\qquad V\ge\frac32,\qquad
 B\ge\frac52,\qquad A\ge\frac{35}{8}.
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:moment-constraints}
\end{equation}

There is one more constraint linking $W$ and $V$.  The cube recursion
gives
\[
 V+W=\E_hQ_2(g_h)=Q_3(f).
\]
Apply the axis estimate~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:axes} directly to $f$.  Here its $H$
equals $S(f)=1$, and Fourier orthogonality with the even weights
$\lambda_\xi$ gives
\[
 \mathcal E(\lambda)=\E_hR(h)^4=V.
\]
Therefore
\begin{equation}
 V+W\ge2V-1,\qquad W\ge V-1.
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:W-constraint}
\end{equation}

Now apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:45:un:mean-lemma} to each $g_h$.  Its variable $v$ is
$R(h)^4=t(h)^2$, and its variable $w$ is exactly that
in~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:derivative-variables}.  Averaging the result yields
\begin{equation}
 Q_4(f)\ge\E\bigl[t^4+10t^2w+2w^2\bigr].
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:averaged-polynomial}
\end{equation}

We finish with a scalar inequality, retaining the mean and the next three
moments of $t$.  Set
\begin{equation}
 a=\frac{99}{676},\qquad b=\frac{33}{26},\qquad
 P(t)=-\frac14t^2+bt-a.
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:P-definition}
\end{equation}
The exact identity
\begin{equation}
 10t^2-4P(t)=11\left(t-\frac3{13}\right)^2
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:pointwise-certificate}
\end{equation}
and $w\ge0$ imply
\begin{equation}
 t^4+10t^2w+2w^2
 \ge t^4+2(w+P(t))^2-2P(t)^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:completion-square}
\end{equation}
The pointwise difference is
$11w(t-3/13)^2$, so the direction of this inequality does not depend on
the sign of $P(t)$.

Expand the nonsquare terms:
\begin{equation}
 t^4-2P(t)^2
 =\frac78t^4+\frac{33}{26}t^3
  -\frac{2277}{676}t^2+4ab\,t-2a^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:expanded-certificate}
\end{equation}
Taking expectations and applying Jensen only to the displayed square
in~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:completion-square}, we obtain
\begin{align}
 Q_4(f)\ge{}&\frac78A+\frac{33}{26}B
       -\frac{2277}{676}V+4ab-2a^2\nonumber\\
 &\quad+2\left(W-\frac14V+b-a\right)^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:jensen-certificate}
\end{align}
The coefficients of $A$ and $B$ are positive, permitting substitution of
their lower bounds in~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:moment-constraints}.  The expression in the
last square is also positive, because
\begin{equation}
 W-\frac14V+b-a
 \ge\frac34V+\frac{83}{676}>0.
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:square-monotonicity}
\end{equation}
It is therefore legitimate to replace $W$ by its lower bound $V-1$ in
that square.  After these substitutions, the right side
of~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:jensen-certificate} is exactly
\begin{equation}
 \frac{4795}{832}
 +\frac38\left(V-\frac32\right)
 +\frac98\left(V-\frac32\right)^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:final-certificate}
\end{equation}
This last equality is a rational polynomial identity, obtained by
substituting the two fractions in~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:P-definition}; the supplementary
verifier checks it using exact fraction arithmetic.

Since $V\ge3/2$, both additional terms
in~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:final-certificate} are nonnegative.  We have proved
$Q_4(f)\ge4795/832$ under $S(f)=1$.  Restoring the scale proves
\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:main-inequality}, and monotonicity proves
\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:higher-comparison}.
\end{proof}

Several losses in this proof are visible and independently nonnegative:
the discarded terms in the Fourier face sum, the unselected terms in the
autocorrelation moments, $11w(t-3/13)^2$, and the variance discarded by
Jensen.  Their equality conditions have not been jointly optimized.
Accordingly, $4795/832$ is presented as an explicit improved certificate,
not as the optimal fourth-order factor.

\subsection{Why one Fourier pair ceases to be extremal}
\label{gsr:cc:45:un:cosines}

The exact third-order comparison in~\cite{repo45} is attained by real
parts of characters.  The fourth-order cube has more surviving frequency
patterns, and these produce a first-order direction of improvement away
from that family.

Let $\xi$ have odd order $q\ge3$ and fix $\theta\in\R$.  For each integer
$j$ define the real function
\begin{equation}
 \phi_j(x)=e^{ij\theta}\xi(x)^j+
                   e^{-ij\theta}\xi(x)^{-j}.
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:phi-definition}
\end{equation}
The index $j$ is an integer exponent, not a claim that all these Fourier
pairs are distinct.  In particular, the possible aliases at orders five
and seven will be treated explicitly by orthogonality.

For a real function $u$, define its fourth cube dual function by
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal D_4u(x)
 =\E_{h_1,h_2,h_3,h_4}
    \prod_{\substack{\omega\in\{0,1\}^4\\\omega\ne0}}
       u(x+\omega\cdot h).
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:dual-definition}
\end{equation}
Then $Q_4(u)=\E_xu(x)\mathcal D_4u(x)$.

\begin{lemma}[Dual polynomial for a real character pair]
\label{gsr:cc:45:un:dual-cosine}
If $q\ge5$ is odd, then
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal D_4\phi_1=111\phi_1+27\phi_3+\phi_5.
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:dual-polynomial}
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}
 Q_2(\phi_1)=2,\qquad Q_4(\phi_1)=222,
 \qquad \E\phi_3\mathcal D_4\phi_1=54.
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:cosine-values}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Expand the fifteen factors in~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:dual-definition}.  A term is
indexed by signs $\sigma_\omega\in\{-1,1\}$, one for each nonzero vertex.
If $j=\sum_{\omega\ne0}\sigma_\omega$, that term contributes
$e^{ij\theta}\xi(x)^j$ precisely when
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{\omega\ne0}\omega_i\sigma_\omega\equiv0\pmod q
 \qquad(1\le i\le4).
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:dual-sign-constraints}
\end{equation}
Each sum in~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:dual-sign-constraints} consists of eight signs and
is an even integer between $-8$ and $8$.  For odd $q\ge5$, a nonzero
multiple of $q$ in this range cannot be even: the first possible nonzero
even multiple has absolute value $2q\ge10$.  Thus the congruences are
integer equalities, uniformly in all such $q$.

The number of integer-balanced sign assignments is recorded in
Table~\ref{gsr:cc:45:un:dual-counts}.  An exact polynomial certificate for the
count is
\begin{align}
 &[z_1^4z_2^4z_3^4z_4^4]
  \prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^4\setminus\{0\}}
       \left(1+y\prod_{i=1}^4z_i^{\omega_i}\right)
 \nonumber\\
 &\hspace{18mm}
 =y^5+27y^6+111y^7+111y^8+27y^9+y^{10}.
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:dual-generating-certificate}
\end{align}
Indeed, a chosen subset of positive-sign vertices must contain four
vertices with coordinate $i$ equal to one, for each $i$.  If the chosen
subset has size $k$, its total sign sum is $j=2k-15$.

For clarity, the coefficient evaluation in
\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:dual-generating-certificate} can be performed by the following
finite integer recurrence.  Begin with the coefficient $1$ at
$(k,u_1,u_2,u_3,u_4)=(0,0,0,0,0)$.  For each successive nonzero vertex
$\omega$, copy each current coefficient to the unchanged index and add
it at $(k+1,u_1+\omega_1,\ldots,u_4+\omega_4)$.  Terms having some
$u_i>4$ may be discarded.  After fifteen steps, the coefficients at
$(k,4,4,4,4)$ are respectively $1,27,111,111,27,1$ for
$k=5,6,7,8,9,10$, and zero otherwise.  This specifies an exact integer
evaluation of the displayed finite product; the supplied program also
checks it independently by enumerating all $2^{15}$ sign assignments.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{c|rrrrrr}
Total sign sum $j$&$-5$&$-3$&$-1$&$1$&$3$&$5$\\\hline
Number of assignments&$1$&$27$&$111$&$111$&$27$&$1$
\end{tabular}
\caption{The fifteen-vertex integer-balanced sign count.}
\label{gsr:cc:45:un:dual-counts}
\end{table}

Grouping the opposite values of $j$ proves
\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:dual-polynomial}, even when some resulting characters alias in
the cyclic subgroup generated by $\xi$.

We now justify each orthogonality assertion required for
\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:cosine-values}.  The two characters $\xi$ and $\xi^{-1}$ are
distinct, so $Q_2(\phi_1)=2$ and $\E\phi_1^2=2$.
The exponents in $\phi_1\phi_3$ are $\pm2,\pm4$, and those in
$\phi_1\phi_5$ are $\pm4,\pm6$.  No odd $q\ge5$ divides any of these
nonzero exponents.  Hence
\[
 \E\phi_1\phi_3=\E\phi_1\phi_5=0,
 \qquad Q_4(\phi_1)=111\cdot2=222.
\]
Similarly $q$ does not divide $6$, so $\E\phi_3^2=2$.  The exponents in
$\phi_3\phi_5$ are $\pm2,\pm8$; again no odd $q\ge5$ divides them.
It follows that $\E\phi_3\phi_5=0$ and
\[
 \E\phi_3\mathcal D_4\phi_1=27\cdot2=54.
\]
In particular, at $q=5$ the function $\phi_5$ is constant, but its
pairing with either centered $\phi_1$ or $\phi_3$ still vanishes.  At
$q=7$ some exponent pairs are represented by negative residues; the
divisibility checks just made show that this causes no additional
nonzero pairing.  No independence assumption about
$\phi_1,\phi_3,\phi_5$ has been used.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[A strict direction of improvement]
\label{gsr:cc:45:un:cosine-descent}
For every odd $q\ge5$, the real centered functions
$f_\varepsilon=\phi_1-\varepsilon\phi_3$ satisfy
\begin{align}
 Q_2(f_\varepsilon)&=2(1+\varepsilon^4),
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:cosine-S-variation}\\
 Q_4(f_\varepsilon)&=222-864\varepsilon+O(\varepsilon^2)
 \quad(\varepsilon\to0).
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:cosine-Q-variation}
\end{align}
Consequently $Q_2(f_\varepsilon)/Q_4(f_\varepsilon)^{1/4}$ is strictly
larger than $2/222^{1/4}$ for all sufficiently small positive
$\varepsilon$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The character pairs $\{\xi,\xi^{-1}\}$ and
$\{\xi^3,\xi^{-3}\}$ are disjoint: an intersection would imply
$q\mid2$ or $q\mid4$.  The second pair consists of two nontrivial,
distinct characters because $q\nmid3,6$.  Fourier inversion therefore
gives~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:cosine-S-variation} exactly, including when $q=5$.

For any real functions $u,v$, differentiating the finite polynomial
$Q_4(u+\varepsilon v)$ gives sixteen terms, according to the vertex at
which $v$ replaces $u$.  Each equals $\E v\mathcal D_4u$.
To see this directly, if that vertex is $\eta$, change variables by
\[
 x'=x+\eta\cdot h,\qquad
 h_i'=(-1)^{\eta_i}h_i.
\]
This is a bijection of $G^5$ and relabels the vertices by coordinatewise
flipping at $\eta$.  Since the functions are real, no conjugation changes
the product.  Thus
\begin{equation}
 \left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}Q_4(u+\varepsilon v)
       \right|_{\varepsilon=0}
   =16\E v\mathcal D_4u.
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:first-variation}
\end{equation}
Taking $u=\phi_1$, $v=-\phi_3$ and using
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:45:un:dual-cosine} gives the derivative $-16\cdot54=-864$.
This proves~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:cosine-Q-variation}.  The numerator in the quotient
has derivative zero at the origin, while its positive denominator has a
strictly negative derivative.  The asserted improvement follows.
\end{proof}

The notation $O(\varepsilon^2)$ here hides no limiting group argument:
for each fixed function pair, $Q_4(f_\varepsilon)$ is an ordinary real
polynomial of degree at most sixteen.  The nonzero first derivative alone
establishes a strict improvement on that same finite group.

\begin{lemma}[Order-three characters]
\label{gsr:cc:45:un:order-three}
If $\xi$ has order three, then
\begin{equation}
 Q_4(\phi_1)
 =286+32\cos(6\theta)+16\cos(12\theta)
 =262+32\left(\cos(6\theta)+\frac12\right)^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:order-three-polynomial}
\end{equation}
In particular $Q_4(\phi_1)\ge262$, whereas $Q_2(\phi_1)=2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
At order three the integer-equality reduction used in
\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:dual-sign-constraints} is unavailable, so expand the full
sixteen-vertex cube instead.  A sign assignment contributes precisely
when its total sign sum and each of its four coordinate sign sums vanish
modulo three.  Its phase is $e^{ij\theta}$, where $j$ is the total sign
sum.  Since $j$ is even and $|j|\le16$, the only possible values are
$-12,-6,0,6,12$.  Their counts are
\begin{equation}
 \begin{array}{c|rrrrr}
 j&-12&-6&0&6&12\\\hline
 \text{count}&8&16&286&16&8.
 \end{array}
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:order-three-counts}
\end{equation}

Here is an exact recurrence evaluating these five integers.  Enumerate the
sixteen vertices as $\omega^{(1)},\ldots,\omega^{(16)}$.  Let
$N_j(s,r)$ count sign choices on the first $j$ vertices with total integer
sign sum $s$ and four coordinate sums $r\in(\Z/3\Z)^4$.  Begin with
$N_0(0,0)=1$ and all other entries zero.  At a new vertex $\omega$, add
each entry $N_j(s,r)$ to both
\[
 N_{j+1}(s+1,r+\omega)
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 N_{j+1}(s-1,r-\omega).
\]
After sixteen steps, retain $N_{16}(s,0)$ for $3\mid s$; this gives
exactly~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:order-three-counts}.  The recurrence is the signed
counterpart of~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:dual-generating-certificate} and uses only
integer additions.  Exhaustive enumeration of the $2^{16}$ choices in
the supplementary program independently reproduces the same table.

The opposite values of $j$ now combine to give the first expression
in~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:order-three-polynomial}.  Substituting
$\cos(12\theta)=2\cos(6\theta)^2-1$ gives its completed-square form.
The second-order statement follows from the two distinct Fourier
coefficients of modulus one.
\end{proof}

Every nonzero real single-character function is a positive scalar
multiple of some $\phi_1$ in~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:phi-definition}.  Combining the
last two lemmas shows
\begin{equation}
 \sup_{\substack{G\text{ odd},\ \xi\ne0\\c\ne0}}
 \frac{\norm{2\operatorname{Re}(c\xi)}_{U^2}^{4}}
      {\norm{2\operatorname{Re}(c\xi)}_{U^4}^{4}}
 =\frac2{222^{1/4}}
 =0.5181335948243558\ldots.
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:single-pair-envelope}
\end{equation}
The upper value is attained whenever the character order is at least
five, but Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:45:un:cosine-descent} gives an improving
perturbation.  The order-three class has an even smaller upper bound
$2/262^{1/4}$.  Thus the same character-pair extremizer description that
works at order three fails at order four.

\subsection{An exact five-point certificate}
\label{gsr:cc:45:un:five-points}

We now give a fixed rational-valued function realizing a quotient larger
than the whole class in~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:single-pair-envelope}.  Its verification
uses integer cube products and requires neither numerical Fourier
transforms nor an optimization routine.

\begin{proposition}[A rational lower bound]
\label{gsr:cc:45:un:five-point-proposition}
On $G=\Z/5\Z$, set
\begin{equation}
 \bigl(f(0),f(1),f(2),f(3),f(4)\bigr)=(2,1,-2,-2,1).
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:five-point-function}
\end{equation}
Then $\E f=0$ and
\begin{equation}
 Q_2(f)=\frac{94}{25},\qquad
 Q_3(f)=\frac{19208}{625},\qquad
 Q_4(f)=\frac{6468874}{3125}.
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:five-point-cubes}
\end{equation}
Consequently
\begin{equation}
 \left(\frac{\norm f_{U^2}^4}{\norm f_{U^4}^4}\right)^4
 =\frac{39037448}{404304625}>\frac8{111}.
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:five-point-ratio}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The five values sum to zero.  For dimension $d$, enumerate the
$5^{d+1}$ tuples $(x,h_1,\ldots,h_d)$ and form the integer
\[
 p(x,h)=\prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^d}
                f(x+\omega\cdot h\bmod5).
\]
Let $H_d(z)$ be the number of tuples with $p(x,h)=z$.  This defines a
finite exact certificate:
\begin{equation}
 \sum_zH_d(z)=5^{d+1},\qquad
 Q_d(f)=5^{-d-1}\sum_z zH_d(z).
 \label{gsr:cc:45:un:histogram-definition}
\end{equation}

For $d=2$, the nonzero entries of this histogram are
\[
 \begin{array}{c|rrrrrrr}
 z&-8&-4&-2&1&4&8&16\\\hline
 H_2(z)&8&24&8&6&36&24&19.
 \end{array}
\]
Their weighted sum is $470$, hence $Q_2=470/125=94/25$.
For $d=3$ the nonzero entries are
\[
 \begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrrr}
 z&-32&-16&1&4&16&32&64&128&256\\\hline
 H_3(z)&96&80&8&32&168&64&128&16&33.
 \end{array}
\]
They have total multiplicity $625$ and weighted sum $19208$.
The fourth-dimensional histogram is given in
Table~\ref{gsr:cc:45:un:five-point-histogram}.  Its multiplicities sum to $3125$,
and their product-weighted sum is $6468874$.  Equation
\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:histogram-definition} therefore gives all three identities
in~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:five-point-cubes}.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{r|r}
Cube product $z$&Multiplicity $H_4(z)$\\\hline
$-2048$&$160$\\
$-1024$&$320$\\
$-512$&$160$\\
$-64$&$32$\\
$1$&$10$\\
$16$&$80$\\
$256$&$760$\\
$512$&$320$\\
$1024$&$800$\\
$2048$&$32$\\
$4096$&$320$\\
$16384$&$80$\\
$65536$&$51$\\\hline
Total multiplicity&$3125$
\end{tabular}
\caption{Exact fourth-cube certificate for~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:five-point-function}.}
\label{gsr:cc:45:un:five-point-histogram}
\end{table}

For an explicit algorithm generating these tables, start each histogram
empty; run $x,h_1,\ldots,h_d$ independently through $0,1,2,3,4$; initialize
a product to one; for every binary vector $\omega$ multiply it by the
corresponding entry of~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:five-point-function}; and increase the
resulting product's histogram count by one.  This enumerates every
normalized cube tuple exactly once and performs only exact integer
operations.  The complete implementation is included with the article.

Finally, using~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:five-point-cubes} and reducing the fraction gives
\[
 \frac{(94/25)^4}{6468874/3125}
 =\frac{39037448}{404304625}.
\]
Cross-multiplication shows that this exceeds $8/111$, which is the fourth
power of~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:single-pair-envelope}.  This proves
\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:five-point-ratio}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 40--46]
Recomputed at the write in exact rationals: $Q_2=94/25$, $Q_4=6468874/3125$, $Q_2^4/Q_4=39037448/404304625$, fourth root $0.5574336$. Sources~28 and~34 give $0.5587294$ and the batch-121 certificate $0.5587725$.
\end{writenote}

The function has only two nontrivial Fourier pairs.  To see its connection
with Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:45:un:cosine-descent}, choose
$\xi(x)=e^{2\pi i x/5}$ and $\theta=0$.  Its coefficients at the two
opposite pairs have values
\[
 a_1=\frac{5+3\sqrt5}{10},\qquad
 a_2=\frac{5-3\sqrt5}{10}.
\]
Here $a_2<0$, and on $\Z/5\Z$ the real functions $\phi_2$ and $\phi_3$
coincide at this phase.  Thus
\[
 f=a_1\bigl(\phi_1-\varepsilon\phi_3\bigr),\qquad
 \varepsilon=-\frac{a_2}{a_1}=\frac{7-3\sqrt5}{2}>0.
\]
This identifies the exact rational example as a concrete member of the
improving two-pair family.  Its cube values, however, were established
above without relying on radicals or trigonometric rounding.  Dividing
$f$ by two gives a real centered $1$-bounded example with the same
quotient.

\begin{proof}[Proof of Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:45:un:interval}]
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:45:un:main} bounds every quotient in
\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:optimal-constant} by $(832/4795)^{1/4}$.
Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:45:un:five-point-proposition} supplies the lower endpoint.
Its strict inequality~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:five-point-ratio}, together with the full
single-pair envelope~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:single-pair-envelope}, excludes every real
single-character function as a global maximizer.  This proves all parts
of the corollary.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Reproducibility and the remaining problem}
\label{gsr:cc:45:un:reproducibility}

The mathematical upper bound is proved for every finite odd-order abelian
group by the preceding inequalities.  Its validity does not depend on a
search over groups or functions.  The finite computations serve two
specific purposes: evaluating the explicit cosine sign-count identities
and verifying the exact five-point example.  The rational scalar
certificate is also checked independently.

From the extracted package directory, run
\begin{verbatim}
python3 code/verify_u4.py --json certificates/u4_certificate.json
\end{verbatim}
The program uses the Python standard library.  Integer sums and
\texttt{fractions.Fraction} carry all mathematical checks; floating-point
approximations are unnecessary.  It refuses to run under
\texttt{python -O} or \texttt{python -OO}, so its assertions cannot be
silently disabled.  The deterministic JSON report records the rational
certificate, the cosine coefficient tables, and the complete cube
histograms and weighted sums.  Direct sign enumeration and coefficient
dynamic programming independently verify
\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:dual-generating-certificate}.

The following questions remain specific to this norm comparison.
First, determine the exact value of $c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}$ and whether the
supremum over all finite groups is attained.  Second, classify the
frequency support and phases of any extremizing functions: the
single-pair classification valid at order three has now been excluded at
order four.  Third, retain more of the nonnegative remainders in
\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:duality}, \eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:balanced-words}, and
\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:completion-square} to improve the explicit upper endpoint.
Fourth, determine dimension-dependent bounds for $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}$,
rather than using the same fourth-order bound for every $d\ge4$.

The results here resolve the sharpness question for the single-character
candidate and tighten a quantitative question posed in the pinned report.
They do not determine the optimal fourth-order constant, assert a global
publication-priority claim for the comparison, or provide a new global
bound for progression-free sets.  The exact scope of the progress is the
proved interval~\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:interval-equation}, the universal inequality
\eqref{gsr:cc:45:un:main-inequality}, and the strict improving direction in
Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:45:un:cosine-descent}.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Applications to cube counting and structured holes\srctag{45}}]{Applications to cube counting and structured holes}\label{gsr:cc:45:sec:d5}
\srcnote{45}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:cc:45:sec:applications}

We make the relationship with Gowers's Lemma~3.10 explicit. The
cancellation and exact quartic coefficient in the next proposition are
credited inputs from the previous ProveIt reports, especially sources
03, 04, 08, and 09 \cite{repo45}. A short proof is included to make the
new numerical substitution self-contained.

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group of odd order, let $d\ge2$, and put
$q=2^d$. For a real function $W$, write
\[
 Q_d(W)=\E_{x,h_1,\ldots,h_d}
          \prod_{v\in\{0,1\}^d}W(x+v\cdot h)
        =\|W\|_{U^d}^{q}.
\]
Suppose $W=\rho+f$, where $\rho\ge0$, $f:G\to\R$, and $\E f=0$.
Set $u=\|f\|_{U^d}$.

\begin{proposition}[Credited exact fourth-order expansion]
\label{gsr:cc:45:ap:quartic}
With the preceding notation,
\begin{align}
 Q_d(\rho+f)
 &=\rho^q+P_d\rho^{q-4}\|f\|_{U^2}^4+R_d,
 \label{gsr:cc:45:ap:expansion}\\
 P_d&=\frac{6^d-2\cdot4^d+2^d}{8},
 \label{gsr:cc:45:ap:pd}\\
 |R_d|&\le\sum_{r=5}^{q}\binom qr\rho^{q-r}u^r.
 \label{gsr:cc:45:ap:remainder}
\end{align}
The sum in \eqref{gsr:cc:45:ap:remainder} is zero if its index set is empty.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For a subset $S$ of the Boolean vertices, expand the product by choosing
$f$ at the vertices in $S$ and $\rho$ elsewhere. Any three distinct
Boolean vertices give jointly uniform affine forms on every finite
abelian group. To verify this, reflect coordinates to move one vertex
to zero. The two other row vectors are distinct nonzero Boolean
vectors. Their supports supply a $2\times2$ minor of determinant
$1$ or $-1$: if neither support contains the other use one coordinate
from each difference; if they are nested use one coordinate in the
smaller support and one in the difference. The one- and two-vertex
cases are immediate. Thus every centered term of degree one, two, or
three vanishes.

Four distinct Boolean vertices that are affinely dependent over $\R$
form an ordinary parallelogram. Indeed their affine span is a plane,
because any three are independent, and projection onto two suitable
coordinates is injective on that plane. The four projected points must
be the four Boolean corners of a square. The affine inverse preserves
their parallelogram relation. Any three of the corresponding forms
are jointly uniform, so the fourth-order correlation is exactly
$\|f\|_{U^2}^4$.

If the four vertices are affinely independent, reflect the first to
zero and select a nonsingular $3\times3$ Boolean minor $B$ from the
other rows. Its determinant has absolute value at most two. For
completeness, border $B$ by a row and column of ones and replace its
entries by $1-2B_{ij}$. Subtracting the first row shows that the new
$4\times4$ determinant has absolute value $8|\det B|$, whereas
Hadamard's inequality bounds it by $16$. Hence $\det B=\pm1$ or
$\pm2$. These integers act invertibly on an odd-order group; the
adjugate identity makes the selected coordinate map invertible.
Consequently the four forms are jointly uniform and their centered
correlation is zero.

There are six solutions to $a+b=c+e$ in $\{0,1\}$, hence $6^d$
ordered solutions on the Boolean cube. The solutions with identical
unordered pairs on both sides number $2\cdot4^d-2^d$. Every remaining
solution uses four distinct vertices. Every parallelogram support has
eight orderings and a unique pairing into opposite vertices, proving
\eqref{gsr:cc:45:ap:pd}. Finally, cube Cauchy--Schwarz bounds a term supported on
$r$ vertices by $u^r$, since the other factors are one. Summing over
supports of size at least five gives \eqref{gsr:cc:45:ap:remainder}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Improved leading coefficient for $d\ge4$]
\label{gsr:cc:45:ap:improved}
Put $\kappa=(832/4795)^{1/4}$. If $d\ge4$, then
\begin{equation}
 0\le Q_d(\rho+f)-\rho^q
 \le \kappa P_d\rho^{q-4}u^4
       +\sum_{r=5}^{q}\binom qr\rho^{q-r}u^r.
 \label{gsr:cc:45:ap:new-bound}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The lower bound follows from $\|\rho+f\|_{U^d}\ge|\E(\rho+f)|=\rho$.
The fourth-uniformity inequality of Section~\ref{gsr:cc:45:un:section} and
monotonicity imply
\[
 \|f\|_{U^2}^4\le\kappa\|f\|_{U^4}^4
                   \le\kappa\|f\|_{U^d}^4.
\]
Substitute this into \eqref{gsr:cc:45:ap:expansion} and use the remainder bound.
\end{proof}

The first values are $P_2=1$, $P_3=12$, $P_4=100$, and $P_5=720$.
In dimension four, \eqref{gsr:cc:45:ap:new-bound} has leading coefficient
\[
 100\kappa=64.5407010850\ldots,
\]
where using only $c_3^{\mathrm{odd}}=1/\sqrt2$ would give
$100/\sqrt2=70.7106781187\ldots$. This is an improvement of about
$8.73\%$ in that coefficient. The cancellation of the first three
orders and the value $P_4=100$ were already present in the report;
the smaller multiplier is the present contribution. The best possible
quartic coefficient for this uniformity comparison is $P_dc_d^{\mathrm{odd}}$,
which is still unknown when $d\ge4$.

\subsection{The indicator and uniformity-parameter formulation}

For $A\subset G$, let $N=|G|$, $\rho=|A|/N$, and
$f=\1_A-\rho$. The number of ordered additive $d$-cubes in $A$,
including degenerate cubes, is $N^{d+1}Q_d(\1_A)$. If
$\|f\|_{U^d}^{q}\le\alpha$, then for $d\ge4$,
\begin{equation}
 \#\{\text{ordered additive $d$-cubes in }A\}
 \le N^{d+1}\left[
 \rho^q+\kappa P_d\rho^{q-4}\alpha^{4/q}
 +\sum_{r=5}^{q}\binom qr\rho^{q-r}\alpha^{r/q}
 \right].
 \label{gsr:cc:45:ap:indicator}
\end{equation}
The displayed uniformity condition is $\alpha$-uniformity of degree
$d-1$ in the normalization of Gowers's lemma and the inspected
repository definitions.
This is a finite-parameter inequality, with an explicit remainder.
It does not merely assert a formal asymptotic expansion. At fixed
$\rho>0$, the leading excess has exponent $4/q$ in $\alpha$.
Gowers's Minkowski estimate uses
$N^{d+1}(\rho+\alpha^{1/q})^q$ \cite[Lemma~3.10]{gowers}; the
improved exponent from centering is credited to the preceding reports,
and \eqref{gsr:cc:45:ap:indicator} tightens its leading constant.

\subsection{How far this reaches in the original proof}

The torsion-free results refine the extremal discussion immediately
before Gowers's Theorem~7.2. If
$E(A)>M_m-8(m-3)$ and $m\ge5$, they identify $A$ exactly as a progression
or a progression with an endpoint-adjacent hole. This is substantially
more precise information in that narrow regime than a general
large-subset structural conclusion. The hypothesis is correspondingly
much closer to the maximum. It supplies no improved exponent in the
general Balog--Szemer\'edi reduction.

The coset and collision results concern the regime where an additive
triple almost always completes, and distinguish exact puncture
extremizers from other high-energy sets. They provide useful rigidity
statements for the energy-conversion step. They do not identify a large
linear or multilinear piece under an arbitrary fixed positive energy
density. In particular, the present collision equality theorem is a
domain theorem; additional label-compatibility hypotheses must be
retained when a graph or a derivative label is part of an application.

To obtain a new global bound for Szemer\'edi's theorem one would have to
show that a sharper local estimate changes a parameter that survives
all the later restriction, recurrence, and density-increment losses.
That propagation is not supplied here. The proven improvements are
the explicit local inequalities and classifications stated above.

\subsection{A bridge between the two energy endpoints}

The ordered energy theorem also describes the first defect levels when
the hole of a dense set is rectified. A \emph{Freiman $2$-isomorphism}
is a bijection that preserves, in both directions, every relation
$a+b=c+d$ among four elements of its domain.

\begin{corollary}[Rectified holes]
\label{gsr:cc:45:ap:rectified-holes}
Let $C$ be a finite subgroup coset, $K\subset C$, $|K|=u\ge5$, and
$A=C\setminus K\ne\varnothing$, with $|A|=m$. Suppose that $K$ admits
a Freiman $2$-isomorphism $\iota$ to a subset of a torsion-free abelian
group. Put $\delta=u/m$ and
\[
 \varepsilon_0(m,u)
 =\delta(1-\delta)+\frac{u^3-M_u}{m^3}
 =\delta(1-\delta)+\frac{\delta^3}{3}
                           -\frac{\delta}{3m^2}.
\]
Then the actual defect $\varepsilon=1-E(A)/m^3$ obeys the following
alternatives:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item If $\iota(K)$ is an arithmetic progression, then
$\varepsilon=\varepsilon_0(m,u)$.
\item If $\iota(K)$ is a second-level model from
Section~\ref{gsr:en:45:en:section}, then
$\varepsilon=\varepsilon_0(m,u)+4(u-2)/m^3$.
\item In all other cases,
$\varepsilon\ge\varepsilon_0(m,u)+8(u-3)/m^3$.
\end{enumerate}
All three lower values are attained, for example, when $C$ is cyclic
of order $m+u>2u+2$, by placing the three model holes in an interval
without additive wraparound.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The complement identity proved in Section~\ref{gsr:en:45:co:section} is exact:
\[
 \varepsilon=\delta(1-\delta)+\frac{u^3-E(K)}{m^3}.
\]
Energy is preserved by $\iota$. Substitute the three alternatives of
the torsion-free theorem. For attainment, the integer holes
$\{0,\ldots,u-1\}$, $H_u=\{0,\ldots,u-2,u\}$, and
$J_u=\{0,\ldots,u\}\setminus\{2\}$ lie in $[0,u]$. Their pair sums
lie in $[0,2u]$, so reduction modulo $m+u>2u+2$ preserves all additive
quadruples. Their complements give the stated values.
\end{proof}

For example, a rectified hole of relative size $\delta$ has a forced
additional defect asymptotic to $\delta^3/3$ beyond the coset envelope,
whereas a subgroup-coset hole has no such additional defect. This gives
a precise way to distinguish two possible geometries of the deleted
part. No rectification is inferred from the energy hypothesis alone.

\section{Source~49's chapter: two-harmonic dual tests and \texorpdfstring{$c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le(4/29)^{1/4}$}{c(4,odd) at most 0.6094183} \wtag}\label{gsr:cc:sec:dualtest}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the ninth write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next section is source~49's Section~7. \emph{Logically it continues the chapter on the odd-order constants} (Section~\ref{gsr:cc:sec:oddconstant}) and source~45's chapter (Section~\ref{gsr:cc:sec:ufourgap}); it is printed here because no number printed earlier may move.

\emph{What is proved.} For real centered $f$ on a finite abelian group of odd order, $\norm f_{U^4}^{16}\ge(29/4)\norm f_{U^2}^{16}$, $\norm f_{U^5}^4\ge(50/29)\norm f_{U^2}^4$, and $\norm f_{U^4}^{16}\ge(15/2)\norm f_{U^2}^{16}$ if a largest Fourier coefficient has order other than five (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:49:ng:main}): so $c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le(4/29)^{1/4}=0.6094183$, the best upper bound among sources~01--53, and $c_5^{\mathrm{odd}}\le29/50$. The proof tests $f$ against $g_t=\phi_1+t\phi_3$ ($t=-1/7$; $-7/50$ at order five), whose fourth dual function is computed exactly by a finite integer certificate, and covers diffuse spectra by source~34's balanced-moment profile (Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:49:ng:balanced}). It does not know source~45's $4795/832$, which it supersedes (note after the theorem). The bracket is now $0.5587725\le c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le(4/29)^{1/4}=0.6094183$ (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:normgap}); the lower end is the batch-121 certificate.

\section[{Two-harmonic dual tests and stronger real uniformity gaps\srctag{49}}]{Two-harmonic dual tests and stronger real uniformity gaps}\label{gsr:cc:49:sec:d7}
\srcnote{49}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:cc:49:ng:section}

The real, centered norm comparison is a particularly concrete place where
an explicit dual function improves a local constant in Gowers's
framework. The earlier project reports prove the sharp inequality
$\|f\|_{U^3}^{8}\ge 2\|f\|_{U^2}^{8}$ and successively obtain
$\|f\|_{U^4}^{16}\ge5\|f\|_{U^2}^{16}$ and
$\|f\|_{U^2}^{4}\le(2/3)\|f\|_{U^4}^{4}$; see
\cite{repo49graded,repo49primegap}. The last report also shows that a
single Fourier pair is not extremal. Its negative third-harmonic example
suggests a better \emph{test function}, which is what we use here.

The new ingredient is the complete fourth dual function of
$\phi_1-\phi_3/7$, together with its small-order variants. Its unwanted
Fourier coefficients are much smaller, relative to its principal
coefficient, than those of the dual function of $\phi_1$ alone.
This permits a stronger comparison for an arbitrary function, not only
for a two-harmonic example.

\begin{theorem}[Fourth and fifth real norm gaps]
\label{gsr:cc:49:ng:main}
Let $G$ be a finite abelian group of odd order and let $f:G\to\mathbb R$
have mean zero. Then
\begin{align}
 \|f\|_{U^4}^{16}&\ge\frac{29}{4}\|f\|_{U^2}^{16},
 \label{gsr:cc:49:ng:universal-fourth}\\
 \|f\|_{U^5}^{4}&\ge\frac{50}{29}\|f\|_{U^2}^{4}.
 \label{gsr:cc:49:ng:fifth}
\end{align}
If a Fourier coefficient of largest nonzero magnitude can be chosen at
 a character whose order is not five, then
\begin{equation}
 \|f\|_{U^4}^{16}\ge\frac{15}{2}\|f\|_{U^2}^{16}.
 \label{gsr:cc:49:ng:non-five}
\end{equation}
In particular, \eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:non-five} holds whenever $5\nmid|G|$.
All three displayed inequalities are strict for nonzero $f$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Improved} by source~96 (Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:96:norm:optional-843}, Section~\ref{gsr:cc:sec:oddquartic}): $\norm f_{U^4}^{16}\ge(843/100)\norm f_{U^2}^{16}$, so $c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le(100/843)^{1/4}=0.5868716$, and the quartic cube coefficient at $d=4$ is $58.687$.
\end{writenote}

Consequently, with the earlier project's definition
\[
 c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}
 =\sup_{G,f}\frac{\|f\|_{U^2}^{4}}{\|f\|_{U^d}^{4}},
\]
where $G$ has odd order and $f$ is nonzero, real, and centered, we have
\begin{equation}
 c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le(4/29)^{1/4}=0.6094183098\ldots,
 \qquad c_5^{\mathrm{odd}}\le\frac{29}{50}=0.58.
 \label{gsr:cc:49:ng:constants}
\end{equation}
For groups of order prime to five the fourth constant is at most
$(2/15)^{1/4}=0.6042750794\ldots$. These constants are not claimed to be
sharp. In particular, the exact fourth-order extremal problem remains
open. The fifth-order gain comes from its own autocorrelation moment
combined with the new dual test, rather than merely propagating
\eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:universal-fourth} by monotonicity.

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 47--53]
\emph{Where this stands} (checked at the write). In source~29's normalization $\norm f_{U^4}^{16}\ge C\norm f_{U^2}^{16}$ the coefficients are $(323/160)^2$ (28), $35/8$ (29), $5$ (35), $81/16$ (34), $4795/832$ (45) and $29/4$ (here; $15/2$ when a largest coefficient has order other than five), that is $c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le0.7038153$, $0.6914416$, $0.6687403$, $2/3$, $0.6454070$ and $(4/29)^{1/4}=0.6094183$ (respectively $(2/15)^{1/4}=0.6042751$); $29/4-4795/832=1237/832$. So this is the best upper bound among sources~01--53, and $0.5587725\le c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le(4/29)^{1/4}=0.6094183$, the lower end being the batch-121 certificate (note after source~28's Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:28:uq:witness}). For $d=5$, $c_5^{\mathrm{odd}}\le29/50=0.58$ improves source~34's coupled bound $\beta_5=0.6099124$ (Remark~\ref{gsr:cc:34:norm:higher}) and the monotone bound $c_5^{\mathrm{odd}}\le c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le0.6094183$; since $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}$ decreases in $d$, it also bounds $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}$ for $d\ge6$, where source~34's $\beta_6=0.5649044$, $\beta_7$, $\beta_8$ and source~29's $B_d$ for $d\ge9$ are smaller. The intake recomputed every dual coefficient $d_{k,n}(t)$ ($n=5,7,9,11,\infty$) by an independent enumeration, and all seventeen rational comparisons exactly; its local numerical minima of the ratio stay above $29/4$ (near $10.2571$, evidence only).
\end{writenote}

\paragraph{Proof status.}
The arguments below apply to every finite abelian group of odd order.
One finite coefficient lemma is established by an exhaustive integer
certificate: five expansions with $4^8+4^7=81\,920$ face assignments each.
Every comparison is in rational arithmetic. Thus the coefficient lemma
is a computer-assisted finite proof, not a numerical optimization or a
sampling assertion. The accompanying \texttt{verify\_dual\_gap.py}
regenerates the coefficients directly from the displayed finite
formula, and \texttt{dual\_gap\_certificate.json} records them and the
exact rational margins. No floating-point computation is used in the
certificate. The decimals in the text are descriptive only.

\subsection{Balanced moments and their dependence on a dominant pair}
\label{gsr:cc:49:ng:balanced-section}

We use normalized counting measure and normalized Fourier coefficients
$a_\xi=\mathbb E_x f(x)\overline{\xi(x)}$; Fourier sums are unnormalized.
Write the dual group additively. For real centered $f$,
$a_{-\xi}=\overline{a_\xi}$ and $a_0=0$. Nonzero frequencies occur in
distinct inverse pairs because $|G|$ is odd. Put
\[
 S=\sum_\xi |a_\xi|^4=\|f\|_{U^2}^{4},\qquad
 p_j=\frac{2|a_{\xi_j}|^4}{S},\qquad p=\max_jp_j,
\]
when $f\ne0$, choosing one representative from each nonzero inverse
pair. Thus $\sum_jp_j=1$. The selected largest pair will be denoted
$\{\chi,-\chi\}$, and
\[
 a_\chi=Ae^{i\theta},\qquad A=(pS/2)^{1/4}.
\]

The next lemma is the balanced-moment profile of
\cite{repo49primegap}; we include its proof because it is an essential
input to both new constants.

\begin{lemma}[Balanced-moment profile]
\label{gsr:cc:49:ng:balanced}
For an integer $m\ge1$, define
\[
 C_m=2^{-m}\binom{2m}{m},\qquad
 H_m(p)=\sum_{k=0}^m\binom mk^2p^k(1-p)^{m-k}.
\]
For any selected Fourier pair of mass $p$,
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb E_h c_f(h)^{2m}\ge C_m S^m H_m(p),
 \qquad c_f(h)=\mathbb E_x f(x)f(x-h).
 \label{gsr:cc:49:ng:moment}
\end{equation}
When $m=2^{d-2}$ and $d\ge2$, this implies
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\|f\|_{U^d}^{4}}{S}
 \ge\{C_m H_m(p)\}^{1/m}.
 \label{gsr:cc:49:ng:moment-profile}
\end{equation}
If the selected pair is largest and $p\le1/2$, then also
\begin{equation}
 \left(\frac{\|f\|_{U^d}^{4}}S\right)^m
 \ge C_m\{m-(m-1)2^{-(m-1)}\}.
 \label{gsr:cc:49:ng:diffuse}
\end{equation}
For $p\in[1/2,1]$, the right side of
\eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:moment-profile} is nonincreasing in $p$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Set $b_j=|a_{\xi_j}|^2$. Fourier inversion gives
$c_f(h)=\sum_\xi |a_\xi|^2\xi(h)$. All monomials in its Fourier
expansion have nonnegative coefficients. Retain those in which each
$\xi_j$ and $-\xi_j$ occurs the same number $k_j$ of times. Their total
contribution is
\[
 (2m)!\sum_{\sum k_j=m}\prod_j\frac{b_j^{2k_j}}{(k_j!)^2}
 =C_mS^m\sum_{\sum k_j=m}
       \binom m{k_1,k_2,\ldots}^{\!2}\prod_jp_j^{k_j}.
\]
Group by the multiplicity $k$ of the selected pair. In the remaining
sum a squared multinomial coefficient is at least that coefficient.
The multinomial theorem bounds this remaining sum below by
$(1-p)^{m-k}$, proving \eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:moment}.

The recursive identity and the elementary bound
$\|g\|_{U^{d-1}}\ge|\mathbb Eg|$ give
\[
 \|f\|_{U^d}^{2^d}
 =\mathbb E_h\|f(\cdot)f(\cdot-h)\|_{U^{d-1}}^{2^{d-1}}
 \ge\mathbb E_h |c_f(h)|^{2^{d-1}}.
\]
This proves \eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:moment-profile}. For \eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:diffuse}, interpret
 the normalized balanced sum as the expected multinomial coefficient
of an $m$-trial multinomial distribution with probabilities $p_j$.
That coefficient is one for a pure composition and at least $m$ for
every mixed composition. Hence the sum is at least
$m-(m-1)\sum_jp_j^m$. Since
$\sum_jp_j^m\le p^{m-1}\sum_jp_j\le2^{-(m-1)}$,
\eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:diffuse} follows.

Finally, coefficient extraction gives the identity
\[
 H_m(p)=\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}
       \binom m{2j}\binom{2j}j\{p(1-p)\}^j.
\]
Its coefficients are nonnegative, and $p(1-p)$ decreases on
$[1/2,1]$, proving the last assertion.
\end{proof}

For the fourth norm, $m=4$, and the profile specializes to
\begin{equation}
 F(p):=\frac{35}{8}
    \{1+12p(1-p)+6p^2(1-p)^2\}
 \le\frac{\|f\|_{U^4}^{16}}{S^4}.
 \label{gsr:cc:49:ng:F}
\end{equation}
If $p\le1/2$, \eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:diffuse} also gives the uniform lower bound
$1015/64$ for the same ratio.

\subsection{An exact dual polynomial and its modular aliases}
\label{gsr:cc:49:ng:dual-section}

For a real function $g$, let
\[
 D_4g(x)=\mathbb E_{h_1,h_2,h_3,h_4}
       \prod_{\substack{\omega\in\{0,1\}^4\\\omega\ne0}}
                  g(x+\omega\cdot h).
\]
Gowers--Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\begin{equation}
 |\mathbb E fD_4g|\le\|f\|_{U^4}\|g\|_{U^4}^{15},
 \qquad \mathbb E gD_4g=\|g\|_{U^4}^{16}.
 \label{gsr:cc:49:ng:duality}
\end{equation}
These standard multilinear facts are part of the uniformity-norm
machinery of \cite{gowers}.

For a character $\chi$ of odd order $n\ge5$, write
\[
 \phi_j(x)=e^{ij\theta}\chi(x)^j+e^{-ij\theta}\chi(x)^{-j},
 \qquad g_t=\phi_1+t\phi_3.
\]
To specify the complete dual polynomial, introduce the Laurent
polynomial
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal P_t(X,Z)
 =\prod_{\substack{\omega\in\{0,1\}^4\\\omega\ne0}}
 \left(XZ^\omega+X^{-1}Z^{-\omega}
             +tX^3Z^{3\omega}+tX^{-3}Z^{-3\omega}\right),
 \label{gsr:cc:49:ng:CT-polynomial}
\end{equation}
where $Z^\omega=\prod_{j=1}^4Z_j^{\omega_j}$.
Let $\operatorname{CT}_n$ retain every monomial whose four $Z$
exponents are divisible by $n$, and then set these $Z$ monomials
equal to one. Define
\[
 \operatorname{CT}_n\mathcal P_t(X,Z)
       =\sum_k d_{k,n}(t)X^k.
\]
The notation $n=\infty$ means the ordinary constant term in all four
$Z$ variables. Equivalently,
\begin{equation}
 d_{k,n}(t)=
 \sum_{\substack{r_\omega\in\{-3,-1,1,3\}\ (\omega\ne0)\\
                 \sum_\omega r_\omega=k\\
                 \sum_\omega\omega_jr_\omega\equiv0\pmod n\ (1\le j\le4)}}
       t^{\#\{\omega:|r_\omega|=3\}}.
 \label{gsr:cc:49:ng:finite-coefficients}
\end{equation}
At $n=\infty$ the congruences mean integer equalities.
Thus $d_{k,n}$ is an explicit integer polynomial of degree at most
fifteen, and $d_{-k,n}=d_{k,n}$. Character orthogonality gives the
exact identity
\begin{equation}
 D_4g_t=\sum_{k>0}d_{k,n}(t)\phi_k.
 \label{gsr:cc:49:ng:exact-dual}
\end{equation}
Only positive odd $k$ occur: fifteen odd integers have odd sum.

\begin{lemma}[The integer range and the small-order certificate]
\label{gsr:cc:49:ng:certificate}
For every odd $n\ge13$, $d_{k,n}=d_{k,\infty}$ and these polynomials
vanish for $|k|>15$. For the choices of $t$ in
Table~\ref{gsr:cc:49:ng:table}, define $M,E,W$ as follows.
First, put
\begin{align}
 M={}&d_{1,n}(t)
 -\sum_{\substack{k>0,\ k\ne1\\k\equiv\pm1\pmod n}}
                      |d_{k,n}(t)|,
 \label{gsr:cc:49:ng:M}\\
 E={}&\sum_{\substack{k>0\\k\not\equiv0,1,-1\pmod n}}
                      |d_{k,n}(t)|.
 \label{gsr:cc:49:ng:E}
\end{align}
To define $W$, collect the following exact expression as
$b_0+\sum_{\ell>0}b_\ell\cos(\ell\theta)$:
\begin{align}
 \|g_t\|_{U^4}^{16}
 =2\sum_{k>0}d_{k,n}(t)\bigl(&
 \mathbf1_{n\mid k-1}\cos((k-1)\theta)
 +\mathbf1_{n\mid k+1}\cos((k+1)\theta)\nonumber\\
 &+t\mathbf1_{n\mid k-3}\cos((k-3)\theta)
 +t\mathbf1_{n\mid k+3}\cos((k+3)\theta)\bigr),
 \label{gsr:cc:49:ng:norm-cosine}
\end{align}
and put $W=b_0+\sum_{\ell>0}|b_\ell|$. In the integer case, congruence
means equality; thus $M=d_{1,\infty}(t)$,
$E=\sum_{k>1}|d_{k,\infty}(t)|$, and
$W=2(d_{1,\infty}(t)+td_{3,\infty}(t))$.

The table gives strict rational bounds $M>m_-/1000$,
$E<e_+/1000$, and $W<w_+/1000$. Consequently
\begin{equation}
 \begin{array}{ll}
 \displaystyle\frac{(2M)^{16}}{16W^{15}}>\frac{242}{25},\quad
                 \frac EM<\frac1{200},& n=5,\\[6pt]
 \displaystyle\frac{(2M)^{16}}{16W^{15}}>\frac{1033}{100},\quad
                 \frac EM<\frac{63}{10000},&
                  n=7,9,11,\infty.
 \end{array}
 \label{gsr:cc:49:ng:certificate-ratios}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{c|c|r|r|r}
$n$ & $t$ & $m_-$ & $e_+$ & $w_+$\\\hline
$5$ & $-7/50$ & $82581$ & $389$ & $165863$\\
$7$ & $-1/7$ & $82256$ & $503$ & $164459$\\
$9$ & $-1/7$ & $82255$ & $509$ & $164452$\\
$11$ & $-1/7$ & $82255$ & $515$ & $164452$\\
$\infty$ & $-1/7$ & $82255$ & $516$ & $164452$
\end{tabular}
\caption{Exact rational bounds for the two-harmonic dual certificate.
The integer row applies to all odd character orders at least thirteen;
its tail bound allows aliases and constants by overcounting them.}
\label{gsr:cc:49:ng:table}
\end{table}

\begin{proof}
Each step exponent in \eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:CT-polynomial} is a sum of eight odd
integers of absolute value at most three. It is even and lies in
$[-24,24]$. For odd $n\ge13$, divisibility by $n$ therefore forces
it to be zero as an integer. This proves agreement with the integer
constant term. If all four step sums vanish, then
\[
 k=\sum_{\omega\ne0}\left(1-\frac{|\omega|}{2}\right)r_\omega.
\]
The absolute values of the displayed coefficients sum to
$4/2+4/2+1=5$, by grouping the vertices of weights one, two,
three and four. Hence $|k|\le15$.

Formula \eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:norm-cosine} follows by inserting
\eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:exact-dual} into $\mathbb E g_tD_4g_t$ and using character
orthogonality. It gives the phase-uniform bound
$\|g_t\|_{U^4}^{16}\le W$.

Here is the complete finite procedure establishing the table.
Split the punctured four-cube into the upper face
$(v,1)$, $v\in\{0,1\}^3$, and the seven nonzero lower-face vertices
$(v,0)$, $v\ne0$. Enumerate the $4^8$ upper assignments. Discard those
whose total frequency is not zero modulo $n$, and group the rest by
 their three coordinate sums modulo $n$, their integer total frequency,
and their number of frequencies of absolute value three. Enumerate
the $4^7$ lower assignments and match the negatives of their three
coordinate sums to the upper groups. Add their integer totals and
their counts of absolute-three frequencies. This counts each assignment
in \eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:finite-coefficients} exactly once: the fourth-step equation
is the upper-face total, and the other three equations are exactly
the matching conditions. For $n=\infty$, use integer sums throughout.
There are no random choices and no omitted configurations.

The supplied verifier implements these two enumerations with integer
counters, substitutes the rational value of $t$, forms
\eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:M}--\eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:norm-cosine}, and verifies all table entries by
integer comparisons after clearing denominators. It then verifies
\eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:certificate-ratios} using just the three rational bounds
printed in each row. The JSON certificate includes every coefficient
of every $d_{k,n}$, rather than only the successful comparisons.
For illustration, the generic principal polynomial is
\begin{align*}
 d_{1,\infty}(t)={}&111+405t+1785t^2+3705t^3+9615t^4
 +10934t^5+17225t^6\\
 &+13860t^7+13090t^8+6195t^9+4530t^{10}
 +665t^{11}+740t^{12},
\end{align*}
and the exact generic norm check is
\[
 W\big|_{t=-1/7}=\frac{5465198316262956}{7^{16}}.
\]
The same norm value appears in the earlier two-harmonic example
\cite{repo49primegap}; the complete dual and the phase-uniform small-order
bounds are the additional certificate used here.
\end{proof}

The role of the order cutoff deserves emphasis. Although harmonics
such as $11\chi$ and $15\chi$ may coincide up to sign at order thirteen,
this does not invalidate the certificate. For odd $n\ge13$ none of the
odd frequencies $3,5,\ldots,15$ is congruent to $1$ or $-1$ modulo $n$:
the relevant difference or sum is even and has absolute value at most
sixteen, whereas the first nonzero even multiple of $n$ is at least
twenty-six. Tail--tail aliases are allowed in the sum of absolute
values $E$, and constant harmonics have zero pairing with centered $f$.
The integer row is thus a valid uniform bound for all these orders,
including thirteen and fifteen.

\subsection{A phase-uniform comparison for every Fourier profile}
\label{gsr:cc:49:ng:profile-section}

\begin{proposition}[Two-harmonic dual profiles]
\label{gsr:cc:49:ng:dual-profile}
Let $f\ne0$ be real and centered on an odd-order group, and choose a
largest pair of mass $p$ and character order $n$. If $n\ge5$, put
$C=(2M)^{16}/(16W^{15})$ and $\eta=E/M$ using
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:49:ng:certificate}. Then
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\|f\|_{U^4}^{16}}{S^4}
 \ge C\bigl[p^{1/4}-\eta(1-p)^{1/4}\bigr]_+^{16}.
 \label{gsr:cc:49:ng:raw-profile}
\end{equation}
For $n\ge13$ the integer row may be used. For all odd character
orders, including three, the following common profile is valid:
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\|f\|_{U^4}^{4}}S
 \ge\left(\frac{242}{25}\right)^{1/4}
 \left[p^{1/4}-\frac{63}{10000}(1-p)^{1/4}\right]_+^4.
 \label{gsr:cc:49:ng:common-profile}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Choose the phase in the test function so that
$a_\chi=Ae^{i\theta}$. Then $\mathbb E f\phi_1=2A$.
Every other harmonic in the principal inverse pair has pairing of
absolute value at most $2A$. For a nonconstant harmonic outside that
pair,
\[
 |a_{k\chi}|\le\{S(1-p)/2\}^{1/4}.
\]
This bound holds separately for every occurrence, so no assumption of
distinct tail frequencies is needed. Equations
\eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:exact-dual} and \eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:M}--\eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:E} give
\[
 \mathbb E fD_4g_t
 \ge2M(S/2)^{1/4}
       \{p^{1/4}-(E/M)(1-p)^{1/4}\}.
\]
Apply \eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:duality}, use $\|g_t\|_{U^4}^{16}\le W$, and raise
to the sixteenth power when the bracket is positive. This proves
\eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:raw-profile}; a nonpositive bracket gives the trivial lower
bound zero. The factor sixteen in the definition of $C$ comes from
$(S/2)^4=S^4/16$.

For an order-three character, average $f$ over its kernel. Averaging
translations is contractive for $U^4$, since this is a
translation-invariant norm. The resulting centered function on the
three-point quotient is exactly $A\phi_1$. Direct character expansion
of the full four-cube gives
\begin{align*}
 \|\phi_1\|_{U^4}^{16}
 &=286+32\cos(6\theta)+16\cos(12\theta)\\
 &=262+32\{\cos(6\theta)+1/2\}^2\ge262.
\end{align*}
For completeness, the counts at total frequencies
$-12,-6,0,6,12$ are $8,16,286,16,8$; the same exact verifier regenerates
them from the $2^{16}$ sign assignments. Hence
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\|f\|_{U^4}^{16}}{S^4}\ge\frac{131}{8}p^4
 \qquad(n=3).
 \label{gsr:cc:49:ng:order-three}
\end{equation}
This order-three calculation was already established in
\cite{repo49graded,repo49primegap}. It dominates
\eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:common-profile}, because $131/8>242/25$ and subtracting the
nonnegative tail term only decreases the latter profile.
For $n\ge5$, \eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:common-profile} follows directly from the bounds
\eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:certificate-ratios}. This completes all possible character
orders on an odd-order group.
\end{proof}

There is also a convenient general formulation. For $d\ge4$ and
$m=2^{d-2}$, the same proofs give the pointwise envelope
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\|f\|_{U^d}^{4}}S\ge
 \max\left\{
   \{C_mH_m(p)\}^{1/m},\quad
   \left(\frac{242}{25}\right)^{1/4}
   \left[p^{1/4}-\frac{63}{10000}(1-p)^{1/4}\right]_+^4
      \right\}.
 \label{gsr:cc:49:ng:envelope}
\end{equation}
For $p\le1/2$, one may also take the maximum with the bound in
\eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:diffuse}. Order-specific constants from
\eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:certificate-ratios} improve the second entry. Formula
\eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:envelope} keeps the entire Fourier concentration parameter;
it is stronger information than a single uniform constant.

\subsection{Rational certificates for the uniform constants}
\label{gsr:cc:49:ng:final-proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:49:ng:main}]
The zero function is immediate. Assume $f\ne0$, and write
$R=\|f\|_{U^4}^{16}/S^4$. We first prove the stronger
\eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:non-five} when a selected largest pair has order different
from five.

If $p\le1/2$, the diffuse bound gives $R\ge1015/64>15/2$.
If $1/2\le p\le15/16$, monotonicity of $F$ gives
\[
 R\ge F(15/16)=\frac{1976905}{262144}>\frac{15}{2}.
\]
Suppose $p\ge15/16$. For a character of order three,
\eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:order-three} gives
$R\ge(131/8)(15/16)^4>15/2$. Otherwise the character order is at
least seven, and the appropriate row of
\eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:certificate-ratios} applies. The exact comparisons
\[
 (9839/10000)^4<15/16,\qquad (1-p)^{1/4}\le1/2
\]
show that the bracket in \eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:raw-profile} is greater than
\[
 \frac{9839}{10000}-\frac{63}{10000}\cdot\frac12
 =\frac{3923}{4000}.
\]
Consequently
\[
 R>\frac{1033}{100}\left(\frac{3923}{4000}\right)^{16}
 >\frac{15}{2}.
\]
The last rational lower bound is approximately $7.56891$.
This proves \eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:non-five} without a restriction on the other
Fourier coefficients.

It remains to treat a largest pair of order five. If $p\le1/2$,
the preceding diffuse bound suffices. If $1/2\le p\le16/17$,
\[
 R\ge F(16/17)>\frac{29}{4}.
\]
For $p\ge16/17$, the order-five row gives
$C>242/25$ and $\eta<1/200$. Since
\[
 (9849/10000)^4<16/17,\qquad 1/17<(1/2)^4,
\]
the bracket in \eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:raw-profile} is greater than
\[
 \frac{9849}{10000}-\frac1{200}\cdot\frac12=\frac{614}{625}.
\]
Thus
\[
 R>\frac{242}{25}\left(\frac{614}{625}\right)^{16}
 >\frac{29}{4}.
\]
The last lower bound is approximately $7.28600$.
All these inequalities are included as exact fraction comparisons in
the verifier. This proves the universal fourth-order statement.
If $5\nmid|G|$, no character can have order five, proving the stated
corollary as well.

For the fifth norm put $R_5=\|f\|_{U^5}^{4}/S$. Use
\eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:envelope} with $m=8$. If $p\le1/2$,
\eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:diffuse} is already greater than $50/29$ after taking the
eighth root. If $1/2\le p\le99/100$, the balanced profile gives
\[
 R_5^8\ge C_8H_8(99/100)>(50/29)^8.
\]
The left side of the last comparison is approximately $80.24185$;
the strict comparison itself is rational. Finally suppose $p\ge99/100$.
By monotonicity, $\|f\|_{U^5}\ge\|f\|_{U^4}$, and
\eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:common-profile} applies. The rational inequalities
\[
 (997/1000)^4<99/100,\qquad (8/25)^4>1/100
\]
bound its bracket below by
\[
 \frac{997}{1000}-\frac{63}{10000}\cdot\frac8{25}
 =\frac{124373}{125000}.
\]
Therefore
\[
 R_5^4>\frac{242}{25}
            \left(\frac{124373}{125000}\right)^{16}
 >(50/29)^4.
\]
This proves \eqref{gsr:cc:49:ng:fifth} and the asserted strictness.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{What has and has not been settled.}
The new comparisons improve the project's explicit fourth- and
fifth-order norm bounds, and the dominant-order condition identifies
where the loss in the universal fourth-order certificate occurs.
It does not prove that five-torsion worsens the true extremal
constant. The lower constants supplied by actual two-harmonic examples
remain below these upper bounds. An exact value of
$c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}$, a classification of its extremizers, and a uniform
family of optimized dual tests at all orders remain open. The
certificate deliberately states only the constants its exact rational
comparisons establish.


\subsection{How the two estimates cover the critical Fourier profiles}
\label{gsr:cc:49:ng:figure-section}

Figure~\ref{gsr:cc:49:fig:dual-profiles} displays the two competing lower estimates
near the largest-pair masses used in the proof. The moment estimate
falls as a single pair dominates, while the dual estimate rises.
The proof uses rational thresholds on the two sides of this transition;
the figure is explanatory and is not used to certify an inequality.
The lower-bound constants and tail ratios in the plot are the printed
rational constants, not numerical fits to coefficient data.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering

\section{Sources~63 and~60: the limit of the odd-order constants \wtag}\label{gsr:cc:sec:oddlimit}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the eleventh write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next five sections are source~63's Sections~2--5 and source~60's Section~2, on $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}=\sup\norm f_{U^2}^4/\norm f_{U^d}^4$ over real centered $f$ on groups of odd order, the constant of Section~\ref{gsr:cc:sec:oddconstant}. \emph{Logically they continue that chapter} (sources~29, 28, 34, 35) and its continuations by sources~45 and~49 (Sections~\ref{gsr:cc:sec:ufourgap} and~\ref{gsr:cc:sec:dualtest}); they are printed here because no number printed earlier may move. Source~63's limit supersedes source~60's bracket, so source~63 comes first; source~60's section is a second route with its own connected-limit theorem. Source~63's Section~2 also fixes the conventions of its Section~6 (Section~\ref{gsr:fp:sec:facecover}).

\emph{What is proved.} \emph{Source~63}: for real centered $f$ on any abelian group of odd order $N\ge3$, $\norm f_{U^2}^4\le(1/3-4/(3N^2)+1/N^3)\norm f_\infty^4$, with equality on $\Z/N\Z$, so this is the best bound depending only on $N$, and $1/3$ is sharp uniformly (Theorems~\ref{gsr:cc:63:bounded:sharp}, \ref{gsr:cc:63:bounded:finite}; a compact-group version, Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:63:bounded:compact}); then $\lim_dc_d^{\mathrm{odd}}=1/3$ with $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}\le1/3+10\cdot2^{-\lfloor d/8\rfloor}$ for $d\ge80$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:63:norm:main}), an explicit finite-parameter bound and threshold (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:63:norm:finite}, Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:63:norm:epsilon}), the limit $b(G)$ on each fixed group (Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:63:norm:fixed-group}), and for the quartic cube coefficient $A_d=P_dc_d^{\mathrm{odd}}\sim6^d/24$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:63:cube:optimal}). \emph{Source~60}: $\lim_dc_d^{\mathrm{odd}}=\beta_{\mathrm{odd}}$, the bounded Fourier extremum, with $1/3\le\beta_{\mathrm{odd}}\le1/2-8/\pi^2+64/\pi^4=0.3464533951$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:60:norm:thm:main}), and the joint limit $1/3$ when the least prime divisor also grows, through the Riesz--Sobolev inequality of Christ and Iliopoulou (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:60:norm:thm:large-characteristic}). Source~63's inequality gives $\beta_{\mathrm{odd}}=1/3$, so source~60's limit theorem now reads $\lim_dc_d^{\mathrm{odd}}=1/3$ and its bracket is superseded; source~60's statements are correct as printed (note after Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:63:bounded:finite}). This answers the limit questions of sources~28 and~29 and source~60's Research questions~1--2 and the first half of~3 (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:normgap}). At fixed $d$ the bracket of the report stands: $0.5587725\le c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le(4/29)^{1/4}=0.6094183$ (the batch-121 certificate and source~49), and source~63's rate is compatible with it; neither source determines $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}$ at any fixed $d\ge4$, as both say. Sources placed during this write record $c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le0.5868716$ (source~96) and a rate $O(d2^{-d/2})$ (source~93); they are not checked here (note after Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:63:norm:main}). Source~63 does not cite source~60, nor conversely; both pins precede the other's arrival.
