\section[{Conventions and standard tools\srctag{63}}]{Conventions and standard tools}\label{gsr:cc:63:sec:d2}\label{gsr:cc:63:prelim:section}
\srcnote{63}{Section 2}

Unless specified otherwise, $G$ is a finite abelian group written
additively, with normalized averaging
$\E_{x\in G}=|G|^{-1}\sum_{x\in G}$. A function is \emph{centered}
if its mean is zero. We use $\mathcal C z=\overline z$ and
$\omega\cdot h=\sum_i\omega_i h_i$. All logarithms without a
subscript are natural. A factorial with argument zero is $1$.

For $r\ge1$, the normalized Gowers expression is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:63:prelim:gowers}
 \|f\|_{U^r(G)}^{2^r}
 =\E_{x,h_1,\ldots,h_r}
       \prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^r}
          \mathcal C^{|\omega|}f(x+\omega\cdot h).
\end{equation}
For $r=1$, this is $|\E f|^2$, and for $r\ge2$ its
$2^r$th root is a norm. With
$\Delta_h f(x)=f(x)\overline{f(x+h)}$, the recursion is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:63:prelim:recursion}
 \|f\|_{U^{r+1}}^{2^{r+1}}
       =\E_h\|\Delta_hf\|_{U^r}^{2^r}.
\end{equation}
For real $f$, all conjugations may be omitted, but the resulting
individual cube products can still be negative.

We use the mixed Gowers--Cauchy--Schwarz inequality
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:63:prelim:gcs}
 \left|\E_{x,h}\prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^r}
       \mathcal C^{|\omega|}f_\omega(x+\omega\cdot h)\right|
       \le\prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^r}\|f_\omega\|_{U^r}.
\end{equation}
This is the normalized form of Gowers' Lemma~3.8. Iterated
Cauchy--Schwarz in the cube coordinates proves it; expanding the
cube of $f+g$ and applying \eqref{gsr:cc:63:prelim:gcs} gives the norm
triangle inequality of his Lemma~3.9. The same identities yield
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:63:prelim:monotone}
 |\E f|\le\|f\|_{U^2}\le\|f\|_{U^3}\le\cdots\le\|f\|_\infty.
\end{equation}
These facts hold on every finite abelian group. Gowers' original
presentation and Tao's account provide the standard proofs
\cite{gowers,taohigher}. We use them as established tools; the
new estimates appear in the subsequent sections.

For a character $\chi\in\widehat G$, let
$\widehat f(\chi)=\E_x f(x)\overline{\chi(x)}$. Fourier inversion,
orthogonality, and normalized convolution give
\begin{align}
 f(x)&=\sum_{\chi\in\widehat G}\widehat f(\chi)\chi(x),
 &\E|f|^2&=\sum_\chi|\widehat f(\chi)|^2,
 \label{gsr:cc:63:prelim:fourier}\\
 (f*\mu)(x)&=\E_y f(x-y)\mu(y),
 &\widehat{f*\mu}(\chi)&=\widehat f(\chi)\widehat\mu(\chi).
 \label{gsr:cc:63:prelim:convolution}
\end{align}
In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:63:prelim:u2}
 \|f\|_{U^2}^4=\sum_\chi|\widehat f(\chi)|^4.
\end{equation}
For real $f$, $\widehat f(\chi^{-1})=
\overline{\widehat f(\chi)}$. If $G$ has odd order, each
nontrivial character is distinct from its inverse. These conjugate
pairs are central to the uniform Fourier-tail argument.

The local phase-removal section deliberately uses unnormalized cube
sums $\mathsf C_r(f)=|G|^{r+1}\|f\|_{U^r}^{2^r}$, because its
input Fourier sums and progression sizes are unnormalized. The
conversion is always displayed. The letter $d$ denotes a norm order
outside that section; inside the local problem it also denotes the
common difference of the input progressions, as in Gowers' statement.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A sharp bound for bounded real functions\srctag{63}}]{A sharp bound for bounded real functions}\label{gsr:cc:63:sec:d3}
\srcnote{63}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:cc:63:bounded:section}

The first ingredient is a pointwise constraint on autocorrelations. It
uses both real-valuedness and the bounded range of the function. The
constraint is stronger than positive definiteness alone.

\begin{lemma}[The doubling constraint]\label{gsr:cc:63:bounded:doubling}
Let $G$ be a finite abelian group and let $f:G\to[-1,1]$ be real.
For
\[
 R_f(h)=\E_{x\in G} f(x)f(x+h)
\]
one has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:63:bounded:tent}
 1+R_f(2h)\ge 2|R_f(h)|\qquad(h\in G).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For real $u,v,w\in[-1,1]$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:63:bounded:threevariables}
 uv+vw-uw\le1,\qquad -uv-vw-uw\le1.
\end{equation}
The first expression is affine separately in each variable, so its
maximum on the cube is attained at a vertex. At a vertex with $u=w$,
it is $2uv-1\le1$; at a vertex with $u=-w$, it equals $1$.
The second inequality follows by replacing $v$ by $-v$.
Apply these inequalities to
$(u,v,w)=(f(x),f(x+h),f(x+2h))$ and average over $x$.
Translation invariance gives
$\pm2R_f(h)-R_f(2h)\le1$, which is the assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The sharp bounded centered inequality]\label{gsr:cc:63:bounded:sharp}
Let $G$ be a finite abelian group of odd order and let $f:G\to\R$
have mean zero. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:63:bounded:third}
 \|f\|_{U^2(G)}^4\le\frac13\|f\|_\infty^4.
\end{equation}
The constant $1/3$ cannot be decreased uniformly over such groups.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The zero function is immediate; otherwise scale to $\|f\|_\infty=1$.
Write $R=R_f$ and $S=\E_hR(h)^2=\|f\|_{U^2}^4$.
Both sides of \eqref{gsr:cc:63:bounded:tent} are nonnegative, so
\[
 (1+R(2h))^2\ge4R(h)^2.
\]
Doubling is a bijection on a finite group of odd order. Moreover,
$\E_hR(h)=(\E f)^2=0$. Averaging the last display therefore gives
$1+S\ge4S$, and hence $S\le1/3$.
Sharpness follows from the exact cyclic example in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:63:bounded:finite} below, by letting the odd order tend
to infinity.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The precise role of odd order]\label{gsr:cc:63:bounded:even}
On an even-order abelian group there is a nontrivial character with
values in $\{-1,1\}$. It is real and centered, and both its supremum
norm and its $U^d$ norm are $1$ for every $d\ge2$.
Thus neither \eqref{gsr:cc:63:bounded:third} nor the limiting odd-order
comparison proved below extends unchanged to all finite groups.
The proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:63:bounded:sharp} uses odd order exactly to
make averaging over $h$ and $2h$ agree.
\end{remark}

\subsection{An exact finite-order correction}

The value $1/3$ is a supremum over group orders. At each fixed odd
order there is a sharp strict correction. The identity behind the
proof makes it possible to determine that correction without
classifying all autocorrelation sequences.

\begin{theorem}[Sharp universal bound at an odd order]\label{gsr:cc:63:bounded:finite}
Let $N\ge3$ be odd, let $G$ be an abelian group of order $N$, and let
$f:G\to\R$ have mean zero. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:63:bounded:finitebound}
 \|f\|_{U^2(G)}^4
 \le\left(\frac13-\frac4{3N^2}+\frac1{N^3}\right)
       \|f\|_\infty^4.
\end{equation}
For every odd $N$, equality is attained on $G=\Z/N\Z$.
Consequently this is the best bound depending only on the order $N$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Normalize as before, put $r=\E f^2$, and define the nonnegative slack
\[
 D_f(h)=(1+R_f(2h))^2-4R_f(h)^2.
\]
The averaging argument gives the exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:63:bounded:slackidentity}
 1-3\|f\|_{U^2}^4=\E_hD_f(h).
\end{equation}
At the identity element,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:63:bounded:zeroslack}
 D_f(0)=(1-r)(1+3r).
\end{equation}

We first establish $r\le1-1/N$. Consider the compact polytope
\[
 \mathcal P_N=\{(t_1,\ldots,t_N)\in[-1,1]^N:
                                      t_1+\cdots+t_N=0\}.
\]
At an extreme point, at most one coordinate lies strictly between
$-1$ and $1$: two such coordinates could be perturbed in opposite
directions. The other $N-1$ coordinates have values $\pm1$ and
an even integer sum. Its negative must lie in $[-1,1]$, so the
remaining coordinate is $0$ and the sum of the others is $0$.
The convex function $\sum t_i^2$ has a maximum at an extreme point,
where its value is $N-1$. This proves the claim.

The concave function $(1-r)(1+3r)$ takes its minimum on
$[0,1-1/N]$ at an endpoint. Its endpoint values are $1$ and
$4/N-3/N^2$, and the latter is at most $1$ for $N\ge3$.
Thus, by \eqref{gsr:cc:63:bounded:slackidentity}--\eqref{gsr:cc:63:bounded:zeroslack},
\[
 1-3\|f\|_{U^2}^4
 \ge\frac{D_f(0)}N\ge\frac4{N^2}-\frac3{N^3}.
\]
This is \eqref{gsr:cc:63:bounded:finitebound}.

For attainment, write $N=2m+1$ and define on $\Z/N\Z$
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:63:bounded:squarewave}
 f_N(0)=0,\qquad
 f_N(j)=1\ (1\le j\le m),\qquad
 f_N(j)=-1\ (m+1\le j\le2m).
\end{equation}
This function is centered and has supremum norm $1$.
For $1\le h\le m$, two terms in
$\sum_xf_N(x)f_N(x+h)$ vanish, and exactly $2h-1$ of the
remaining terms are negative. Consequently
\[
 R_{f_N}(0)=1-\frac1N,\qquad
 R_{f_N}(h)=1-\frac{4h}N\ (1\le h\le m),\qquad
 R_{f_N}(-h)=R_{f_N}(h).
\]
The formulas for the sums of the first $m$ integers and their
squares now give
\[
 \|f_N\|_{U^2}^4
 =\frac1N\left[\left(1-\frac1N\right)^2
                +2\sum_{h=1}^m\left(1-\frac{4h}N\right)^2\right]
 =\frac13-\frac4{3N^2}+\frac1{N^3}.
\]
This proves sharpness at every odd order.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Checked at the write} (exact rationals). $1/3-4/(3N^2)+1/N^3=(N^3-4N+3)/(3N^3)$, which is source~60's conjectured cyclic value, and it equals source~60's exhaustive maxima $2/9$, $36/125$, $106/343$, $232/729$, $430/1331$, $716/2197$, $1106/3375$, $1616/4913$ for $N=3,5,\ldots,17$; on $\Z_3\times\Z_3$ the maximum $56/243$ is below the bound $232/729$, so equality depends on the group, not only on $N$. \emph{Consequences in this report:} source~60's $\beta_{\mathrm{odd}}$ equals $1/3$, so its bracket $[1/3,0.3464533951]$ is superseded, and its Research questions~\ref{gsr:fz:60:q:beta} and~\ref{gsr:fz:60:q:finite-beta} (first part) are answered (notes there).
\end{writenote}

\begin{remark}[What the finite theorem classifies]
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:63:bounded:finite} determines the optimal bound uniform
over groups of the specified order and supplies exact extremizers.
It does not assert that every abelian group of that order attains
the bound, or classify all equality cases on a fixed group.
Those are distinct structural questions. The finite correction is
also separate from the $U^d$ denominator problem: controlling
$\|f\|_\infty$ by $\|f\|_{U^d}$ with an error uniform over arbitrary
groups requires the arguments of Section~\ref{gsr:cc:63:norm:section}.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Compact groups and a defect identity}

\begin{corollary}[A compact-group version]\label{gsr:cc:63:bounded:compact}
Let $G$ be a compact abelian group such that $x\mapsto2x$ is
surjective. With normalized Haar measure and the essential supremum
norm, every bounded measurable real centered function satisfies
\[
 \|f\|_{U^2(G)}^4\le\frac13\|f\|_\infty^4.
\]
On $G=\R/\Z$ equality is attained by
$f(x)=\operatorname{sgn}(\sin(2\pi x))$, with arbitrary values at
its two zeros.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The pushforward of normalized Haar measure under a surjective
continuous homomorphism is normalized Haar measure. Therefore the
proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:63:bounded:sharp}, including Fubini's theorem
for the correlation average, applies verbatim.
For the displayed square wave the autocorrelation is
$R(h)=1-4\|h\|_{\R/\Z}$. Thus
\[
 \|f\|_{U^2}^4=2\int_0^{1/2}(1-4t)^2\,dt=\frac13.
\]
\end{proof}

The proof gives more than an upper bound. For a centered real
$1$-bounded function on either class of groups,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:63:bounded:factoreddefect}
 1-3\|f\|_{U^2}^4
 =\E_h\bigl(1+R_f(2h)-2|R_f(h)|\bigr)
          \bigl(1+R_f(2h)+2|R_f(h)|\bigr).
\end{equation}
Both factors are nonnegative. Hence a function close to the sharp
bound must nearly saturate the doubling constraint for most
increments on which the second factor is bounded away from zero.
For example, if $1-3\|f\|_{U^2}^4\le\varepsilon$, then for all
$a,b>0$,
\[
 \Pr\bigl(1+R_f(2h)-2|R_f(h)|\ge a,\quad
          1+R_f(2h)+2|R_f(h)|\ge b\bigr)
 \le\frac{\varepsilon}{ab}.
\]
This is an exact analytic starting point for stability. It does not
by itself imply proximity of $f$ to a cyclic square wave.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The exact high-order odd-group comparison constant\srctag{63}}]{The exact high-order odd-group comparison constant}\label{gsr:cc:63:sec:d4}
\srcnote{63}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:cc:63:norm:section}

For each integer $d\ge2$, define
\begin{equation}
 c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}
 :=\sup_{\substack{G\text{ finite abelian},\ |G|\text{ odd}\\
                  f:G\to\R,\ \E f=0,\ f\ne0}}
       \frac{\norm{f}_{U^2}^{4}}{\norm{f}_{U^d}^{4}}.
 \label{gsr:cc:63:norm:definition}
\end{equation}
The supremum includes the group.  Consequently, convergence of Gowers
norms for a fixed finite group would not by itself determine the limit
of these constants.  The purpose of this section is to establish the
required uniformity.

\begin{theorem}[Exact limiting constant and a uniform rate]
\label{gsr:cc:63:norm:main}
The constants in \eqref{gsr:cc:63:norm:definition} satisfy
\begin{equation}
 \lim_{d\to\infty}c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}=\frac13.
 \label{gsr:cc:63:norm:limit}
\end{equation}
More explicitly, for every integer $d\ge80$,
\begin{equation}
 \frac13\le c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}
 \le\frac13+10\,2^{-\lfloor d/8\rfloor}.
 \label{gsr:cc:63:norm:rate}
\end{equation}
Neither the exponent $1/8$ nor the coefficient $10$ in this rate is
asserted optimal.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]

At fixed $d$ it is compatible with the report's bracket $0.5587725\le c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le0.6094183$ (sources~28, 49 and the batch-121 certificate) and with source~49's $c_5^{\mathrm{odd}}\le29/50$; no fixed-$d$ value is claimed. \emph{Forward pointers} (from placement records, not checked at this write): source~93 records a rate $c_d(F)-D(F)=O(d2^{-d/2})$ uniformly over odd-order families, which would supersede the rate here; source~96 records $\norm f_{U^4}^{16}\ge(843/100)\norm f_{U^2}^{16}$, that is $c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le0.5868716$, below source~49's $0.6094183$. Both are for the writes that add them.
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 82--94]
\emph{A faster rate, without an explicit constant} (source~93, Section~\ref{gsr:cc:sec:fasterlimit}): $0\le c_d(\mathcal F)-D(\mathcal F)\le Cd2^{-d/2}$ uniformly over families of odd-order groups (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:93:norm:uniform-rate}), which supersedes the order of the rate here, while this theorem's $10\cdot2^{-\lfloor d/8\rfloor}$ remains the only explicit one; no family-uniform rate beats order $d2^{-d}$ (the $\Z/3\Z$ obstruction there). Source~93 does not cite this source; it credits the limit to an undelivered manuscript (Section~\ref{gsr:dt:sec:phifour}). This is the first proof of the limit in this report.
\end{writenote}

The earlier repository report established
$1/3\le\lim_d c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}\le1/2$ by an interval construction and
central-binomial autocorrelation moments
\cite{repo63}.  Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:63:norm:main} identifies the missing
endpoint.  Its proof combines the bounded-function inequality of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:63:bounded:sharp} with three uniform estimates.  High even
moments control the tail of the Fourier fourth powers.  A positive
convolution kernel retains the important coefficients and has finite
Fourier support.  Finally, small increments in a Bohr set recover the
supremum norm of this smoothed function from a sufficiently high Gowers
norm.  Every estimate below is independent of the order and exponent
of the finite group.

\subsection{Uniform control of the Fourier tail}

We use normalized Fourier coefficients
$\widehat f(\chi)=\E_x f(x)\overline{\chi(x)}$.
For real $f$, its autocorrelation
\begin{equation}
 R_f(h)=\E_x f(x)f(x+h)
       =\sum_{\chi\in\widehat G}|\widehat f(\chi)|^2\chi(h)
 \label{gsr:cc:63:norm:autocorrelation}
\end{equation}
has nonnegative Fourier coefficients.  This positivity permits us to
retain selected words in each even-moment expansion.  The following
estimate specifically controls mass spread over many small
coefficients; a bound on the largest coefficient would not suffice.

\begin{lemma}[Fourier-tail estimate]
\label{gsr:cc:63:norm:tail}
Suppose $G$ has odd order, $f:G\to\R$ is centered, and
$\norm f_{U^d}=1$.  Choose one representative $\xi_j$ from each
nonzero conjugate Fourier pair, ordered so that
$|\widehat f(\xi_j)|$ decreases, and put
\[
 v_j=2|\widehat f(\xi_j)|^4,
 \qquad S=\sum_jv_j=\norm f_{U^2}^4\le1.
\]
For integers $1\le r\le2^{d-2}$ and $K\ge1$, let
\begin{equation}
 G_r=(2r-1)!!=\frac{(2r)!}{2^r r!},\qquad
 \tau(r,K)=\max\left\{
       \frac{r(r-1)}{K+1},
       \left(\frac2{G_r}\right)^{1/r}\right\}.
 \label{gsr:cc:63:norm:tau}
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}
                  \sum_{j>K}v_j\le\tau(r,K).
 \label{gsr:cc:63:norm:tail-bound}
\end{equation}
An empty tail is interpreted as zero.  In particular, for $r\ge16$,
\begin{equation}
                  \tau(r,r^3)\le\frac3r.
 \label{gsr:cc:63:norm:tail-special}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Put $n=2^{d-2}$.  The derivative recursion and the inequality
$\norm g_{U^{d-1}}\ge|\E g|$ give
\[
 1=\norm f_{U^d}^{2^d}\ge\E_h|R_f(h)|^{2n}.
\]
Monotonicity of probability-space $L^p$ norms therefore gives
$\E R_f^{2r}\le1$ for $r\le n$.

Write $\lambda_j=|\widehat f(\xi_j)|^2$, so
$R_f=\sum_j\lambda_j(\xi_j+\xi_j^{-1})$ and
$v_j=2\lambda_j^2$.  Each surviving word in the expansion of
$\E R_f^{2r}$ has a nonnegative coefficient.  Retain only words
using $r$ distinct tail pairs, each once in each orientation.  For a
fixed set of pairs their coefficient is $(2r)!$.  Thus, with $e_r$
denoting the elementary symmetric polynomial,
\begin{equation}
 1\ge\E R_f^{2r}
   \ge\frac{(2r)!}{2^r}\,
             e_r(v_{K+1},v_{K+2},\ldots).
 \label{gsr:cc:63:norm:distinct-pairs}
\end{equation}
Additional character relations can only add nonnegative terms, so no
independence or restriction on odd torsion has entered this argument.

Set $v=\sum_{j>K}v_j$.  If $v=0$ there is nothing to prove.  Draw
$r$ independent tail indices with probabilities $v_j/v$.  A union
bound for collisions gives
\[
 \frac{r!e_r(v_{K+1},\ldots)}{v^r}
 \ge1-\binom r2\sum_{j>K}\left(\frac{v_j}{v}\right)^2
 \ge1-\binom r2\frac{v_{K+1}}v.
\]
Since the $v_j$ decrease and their sum is at most one,
$v_{K+1}\le1/(K+1)$.  If $v\ge r(r-1)/(K+1)$, the last
display is at least $1/2$.  Substitution in
\eqref{gsr:cc:63:norm:distinct-pairs} yields $1\ge G_rv^r/2$.  If that
hypothesis fails, the other term of \eqref{gsr:cc:63:norm:tau} already bounds
$v$.  This proves \eqref{gsr:cc:63:norm:tail-bound}.

For $K=r^3$, the first term of \eqref{gsr:cc:63:norm:tau} is at most $1/r$.
The elementary integral estimate
\[
 \log(r!)\ge\int_1^r\log x\,dx\ge r\log r-r
\]
and $G_r\ge r!$ give
$(2/G_r)^{1/r}\le2^{1/r}e/r<3/r$ for $r\ge16$.
For example, $e<11/4$ and $2^{1/16}<12/11$ justify the last
strict inequality without any asymptotic estimate.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A positive smoothing kernel with a finite spectrum}

We next preserve a prescribed collection of Fourier coefficients.
Using a product of trigonometric sums, rather than assuming that the
chosen characters are independent, is essential on arbitrary finite
groups.

\begin{lemma}[Positive finite-spectrum smoothing]
\label{gsr:cc:63:norm:smoothing}
Let $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_\ell$ be characters of a finite abelian group,
where $1\le\ell\le K$, and let $J\ge1$ be an integer.  Define
\begin{equation}
 P(x)=\prod_{j=1}^{\ell}\left(\sum_{a=0}^J\xi_j(x)^a\right),
 \qquad
 \mu(x)=\frac{|P(x)|^2}{\E|P|^2}.
 \label{gsr:cc:63:norm:kernel}
\end{equation}
Then $\mu\ge0$, $\E\mu=1$, and its Fourier support is contained in
\begin{equation}
 \Gamma=\left\{\prod_{j=1}^{\ell}\xi_j^{a_j}:
                                  -J\le a_j\le J\right\},
 \qquad |\Gamma|\le(2J+1)^K.
 \label{gsr:cc:63:norm:gamma-spectrum}
\end{equation}
For each selected character,
\begin{equation}
              \widehat\mu(\xi_j)\ge\frac J{J+1}.
 \label{gsr:cc:63:norm:multiplier}
\end{equation}
All Fourier coefficients of $\mu$ are nonnegative real numbers.
For $g=f*\mu$, normalized convolution satisfies
\begin{equation}
              \norm g_{U^d}\le\norm f_{U^d}\qquad(d\ge2).
 \label{gsr:cc:63:norm:contraction}
\end{equation}
If $f$ is real and centered, so is $g$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The Fourier coefficients of $P$ are nonnegative integers, including
when different exponent vectors represent the same character.  Thus
$\E|P|^2>0$, and every coefficient of $|P|^2$ is nonnegative
real.  Its spectrum is contained in \eqref{gsr:cc:63:norm:gamma-spectrum}.

Fix $j$, and let $P_j$ be the product in \eqref{gsr:cc:63:norm:kernel} with
its $j$th factor removed.  Every correlation
$\langle P_j,\chi P_j\rangle$ is nonnegative real, by the same
Fourier-coefficient observation.  Consequently,
\begin{align*}
 \norm P_2^2&\ge(J+1)\norm{P_j}_2^2,\\
 \norm{P-\xi_jP}_2^2
 &=\norm{(1-\xi_j^{J+1})P_j}_2^2
 \le2\norm{P_j}_2^2.
\end{align*}
Here $\norm P_2$ denotes the normalized $L^2$ norm.  Since
\[
 1-\widehat\mu(\xi_j)
 =\frac{\norm{P-\xi_jP}_2^2}{2\norm P_2^2},
\]
the multiplier bound follows.  This computation explicitly retains
all aliases caused by relations among the selected characters.
Finally, convolution with $\mu$ is an average of translates with
nonnegative weights.  The triangle inequality and translation
invariance of $U^d$ prove \eqref{gsr:cc:63:norm:contraction}.  The assertions
about reality and the mean follow directly from convolution.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Uniform recovery of a supremum norm}

The next lemma supplies the uniformity needed when the order of the
group varies.  The point of using a square of a parallel-face average
is that the full cube integrand may have either sign.

\begin{lemma}[Finite-spectrum recovery]
\label{gsr:cc:63:norm:recovery}
Suppose $g:G\to\R$ has Fourier support contained in
\eqref{gsr:cc:63:norm:gamma-spectrum} and satisfies $\norm g_{U^d}\le1$,
where $d\ge2$.  Put
\begin{equation}
 M=(2J+1)^K,\qquad L=2\pi M KJ.
 \label{gsr:cc:63:norm:complexity}
\end{equation}
For a real parameter $0<\eta\le1/16$, define
\begin{align}
 \beta&=\left(\frac{\eta}{2L}\right)^K,
 &\gamma&=\left(\frac{\eta}{2(d-1)L}\right)^K,
 &s&=2^{d-1},\label{gsr:cc:63:norm:balls}\\
 F&=\gamma^{(d-1)/2^d}(\beta/2)^{2/2^d}.
 &&&&\label{gsr:cc:63:norm:F}
\end{align}
If
\begin{equation}
                       3^{-s}\le\beta/2,
 \label{gsr:cc:63:norm:activation}
\end{equation}
then
\begin{equation}
                       \norm g_\infty\le2\eta+F^{-1}.
 \label{gsr:cc:63:norm:sup-recovered}
\end{equation}
All quantities on the right depend only on $K,J,\eta,d$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For $z\in\Tquot$, write $\norm z_{\Tquot}$ for its distance to zero,
and put
\[
 \rho(y)=\max_{1\le j\le\ell}\norm{\arg\xi_j(y)/(2\pi)}_{\Tquot},
 \qquad B(t)=\{y:\rho(y)\le t\}.
\]
The argument of each character is interpreted as an element of
$\Tquot$, so no choice of a real branch is involved.  For $0<t\le1$,
\begin{equation}
                      \frac{|B(t)|}{|G|}\ge(t/2)^K.
 \label{gsr:cc:63:norm:bohr-volume}
\end{equation}
Indeed, partition each of the $\ell$ circle coordinates into
$\lceil1/t\rceil$ equal half-open intervals.  Some product cell
contains at least $\lceil1/t\rceil^{-\ell}$ of the image measure.
Translate its preimage by one of its points; the resulting differences
lie in $B(t)$.  Now use $\lceil1/t\rceil\le2/t$ and $\ell\le K$.

Every Fourier coefficient of $g$ has modulus at most
$\norm g_{U^2}\le1$.  Select for each member of $\Gamma$ one
representation in \eqref{gsr:cc:63:norm:gamma-spectrum}.  The triangle
inequality on the circle gives
\begin{equation}
                 |g(x+y)-g(x)|\le L\rho(y).
 \label{gsr:cc:63:norm:lipschitz}
\end{equation}
There are at most $M$ coefficients, and each chosen frequency has
total word length at most $KJ$, which proves this estimate with
the value of $L$ in \eqref{gsr:cc:63:norm:complexity}.

Let $A=\norm g_\infty$.  If $A<1/2$,
\eqref{gsr:cc:63:norm:sup-recovered} is immediate because $F\le1$.
Otherwise, choose $x_0$ with $|g(x_0)|=A$.  On
$x_0+B(\eta/L)$ we have $|g(x)|\ge A-\eta$; this set has
measure at least $\beta$ by \eqref{gsr:cc:63:norm:bohr-volume}.

Restrict each of $h_1,\ldots,h_{d-1}$ to
$B(\eta/((d-1)L))$.  The measure of each allowed increment set
is at least $\gamma$.  For every cube vertex $\omega$, the
subadditivity of $\rho$ and \eqref{gsr:cc:63:norm:lipschitz} give
\[
 |g(x+\omega\cdot h)-g(x)|\le\eta.
\]
If $|g(x)|\ge\eta$, the $s$ factors share the same weak sign.
Since $s$ is even, their product is nonnegative and is at least
$(|g(x)|-\eta)^s$.  If $|g(x)|<\eta$, every factor has modulus
at most $2\eta$, so the product is at least $-(2\eta)^s$.
Thus the entire parallel-face average, including the region away
from $x_0$, satisfies
\begin{align*}
 A_h&:=\E_x\prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^{d-1}}g(x+\omega\cdot h)\\
 &\ge\beta(A-2\eta)^s-(2\eta)^s
 \ge\frac\beta2(A-2\eta)^s.
\end{align*}
For the last inequality, $A\ge1/2$ and $\eta\le1/16$ imply
$2\eta/(A-2\eta)\le1/3$, and
\eqref{gsr:cc:63:norm:activation} applies.

The exact parallel-face identity for a real function is
\[
 \norm g_{U^d}^{2^d}
       =\E_{h_1,\ldots,h_{d-1}}|A_h|^2.
\]
Its summands are nonnegative.  Retaining the restricted increments
therefore gives
\[
 1\ge\norm g_{U^d}^{2^d}
 \ge\gamma^{d-1}(\beta/2)^2(A-2\eta)^{2^d}.
\]
Taking $2^d$th roots proves \eqref{gsr:cc:63:norm:sup-recovered}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A finite-parameter comparison theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Explicit finite-parameter bound]
\label{gsr:cc:63:norm:finite}
Let $d\ge2$, $1\le r\le2^{d-2}$, $K,J\ge1$ be integers,
and $0<\eta\le1/16$.  Define $\tau$ by \eqref{gsr:cc:63:norm:tau}, and
$M,L,\beta,\gamma,F$ by
\eqref{gsr:cc:63:norm:complexity}--\eqref{gsr:cc:63:norm:F}.  If
\eqref{gsr:cc:63:norm:activation} holds, then
\begin{equation}
 c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}
 \le\frac13\left(1+\frac1J\right)^4
                 (2\eta+F^{-1})^4+\tau(r,K).
 \label{gsr:cc:63:norm:finite-bound}
\end{equation}
This is a finite inequality, with no limiting qualification.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Take any admissible $G,f$, and use homogeneity to normalize
$\norm f_{U^d}=1$.  Set $S=\norm f_{U^2}^4$ and select the first
$K$ nonzero Fourier pairs as in Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:63:norm:tail}.  If fewer
than $K$ pairs occur, select all of them and use their actual number
$\ell\le K$ in the kernel.  All complexity bounds remain valid
with $K$ in place of $\ell$.

Let $g=f*\mu$, using Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:63:norm:smoothing}.  Its multiplier
bound and the Fourier formula for $U^2$ imply
\[
 \norm g_{U^2}^4
 \ge\left(\frac J{J+1}\right)^4
              \sum_{j\le K}2|\widehat f(\xi_j)|^4
 \ge\left(\frac J{J+1}\right)^4(S-\tau(r,K)).
\]
The function $g$ is real centered and satisfies
$\norm g_{U^d}\le1$.  Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:63:bounded:sharp} and then
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:63:norm:recovery} to obtain
\[
 \norm g_{U^2}^4\le\frac13\norm g_\infty^4
                  \le\frac13(2\eta+F^{-1})^4.
\]
Rearrange and take the supremum over $G,f$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of the limiting assertion in Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:63:norm:main}]
First fix a sufficiently large integer $r$, and take $K=r^3$.
Then $\tau(r,K)\le3/r$.  Next choose $J$ large and $\eta>0$
small.  These parameters are fixed independently of the group.
As $d\to\infty$, \eqref{gsr:cc:63:norm:activation} eventually holds, and
\[
 -\log F
   =O_{K,J,\eta}\!\left(\frac{d\log d}{2^d}\right)
   \longrightarrow0.
\]
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:63:norm:finite} therefore implies
\[
 \limsup_{d\to\infty}c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}
 \le\frac13(1+J^{-1})^4(1+2\eta)^4+\frac3r.
\]
Let $J,r\to\infty$ and $\eta\downarrow0$.  This proves the upper
bound $1/3$, without interchanging a fixed-group limit with a
supremum.

For completeness, recall the lower construction from the repository
\cite{repo63}.  On $G=\Z/(2n+1)\Z$, let
$A=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, $\delta=n/(2n+1)$, and
$f=2(\one_A-\delta)$.  There is no wraparound in sums of two
members of $A$, so its unnormalized additive energy is
\[
 E(A)=n^2+2\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}j^2=\frac{2n^3+n}{3}.
\]
Fourier orthogonality and direct evaluation give
\[
 \norm f_{U^2}^4
    =16\left(\frac{E(A)}{(2n+1)^3}-\delta^4\right),
 \qquad \norm f_\infty=\frac{2(n+1)}{2n+1}.
\]
Since $\norm f_{U^d}\le\norm f_\infty$, for every $d\ge2$,
\[
 \frac{\norm f_{U^2}^4}{\norm f_{U^d}^4}
 \ge\frac{n(n^2+n+1)}{3(n+1)^3}\longrightarrow\frac13.
\]
Hence $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}\ge1/3$ for every $d$, completing the
proof of \eqref{gsr:cc:63:norm:limit}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{An explicit convergence rate}

The finite theorem allows many parameter choices.  The following
deliberately simple choice proves \eqref{gsr:cc:63:norm:rate}; optimizing this
construction is a separate question.

\begin{proof}[Proof of the quantitative assertion in Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:63:norm:main}]
Let $k\ge10$ be an integer and put
\begin{equation}
 d=8k,\qquad r=2^k,\qquad K=r^3,\qquad J=r,\qquad\eta=r^{-1}.
 \label{gsr:cc:63:norm:rate-parameters}
\end{equation}
Then $r\le2^{d-2}$, $\eta\le1/16$, and
$\tau(r,K)\le3/r$.  Write
\[
 H=\log(2L/\eta),\qquad t=-\log F.
\]
Since $\log(2\pi)<3$, $\log(2r+1)\le k+2$, and
$\log r\le k$, the explicit definitions yield
\begin{align}
 H&\le r^3(k+2)+5k+4,\label{gsr:cc:63:norm:H-bound}\\
 t&=\frac{(8k+1)r^3H+(8k-1)r^3\log(8k-1)+2\log2}{r^8}.
 \label{gsr:cc:63:norm:t-exact}
\end{align}
For every $k\ge10$,
\begin{align*}
 (8k+1)(5k+4)+(8k-1)\log(8k-1)+2&\le2^{3k},\\
 (8k+1)(k+2)+1&\le2^k.
\end{align*}
These inequalities can be checked elementarily.  In the first,
replace $\log(8k-1)$ by $8k-1$ and compare the resulting
quadratic polynomial with $2^{3k}$, starting at $k=10$.
For the second, the initial comparison is $973\le1024$, and the
quadratic polynomial grows by less than a factor of two at each
subsequent step.  Substitution in
\eqref{gsr:cc:63:norm:H-bound}--\eqref{gsr:cc:63:norm:t-exact} gives
\begin{equation}
                  0\le t\le\frac{(8k+1)(k+2)+1}{r^2}
                            \le\frac1r.
 \label{gsr:cc:63:norm:t-bound}
\end{equation}

We also check the activation condition.  From
\eqref{gsr:cc:63:norm:H-bound}, $H\le r^3(k+3)$, and hence
\[
 -\log(\beta/2)=r^3H+\log2\le r^6(k+4).
\]
On the other hand,
$2^{d-1}\log3>r^8/2\ge r^6(k+4)$.
Thus \eqref{gsr:cc:63:norm:activation} holds.

For $0\le x\le1$, $e^x\le1+x+x^2$.  Since $r\ge1024$,
\begin{align*}
 \left(1+\frac1r\right)\left(\frac2r+e^{1/r}\right)
 &\le1+\frac4r+\frac4{r^2}+\frac1{r^3}
 \le1+\frac5r,\\
 \left(1+\frac5r\right)^4&\le1+\frac{21}r.
\end{align*}
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:63:norm:finite} and \eqref{gsr:cc:63:norm:t-bound} now imply
\[
 c_{8k}^{\mathrm{odd}}
 \le\frac13\left(1+\frac{21}r\right)+\frac3r
 =\frac13+\frac{10}r.
\]
Finally, norm monotonicity makes $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}$
nonincreasing in $d$.  For arbitrary $d\ge80$, take
$k=\lfloor d/8\rfloor$ and use $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}
\le c_{8k}^{\mathrm{odd}}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A constructive dimension threshold]
\label{gsr:cc:63:norm:epsilon}
For $\varepsilon>0$, set
\[
 d_\varepsilon
 =8\max\left\{10,
       \left\lceil\log_2\frac{10}{\varepsilon}\right\rceil\right\}.
\]
For every $d\ge d_\varepsilon$, every finite odd-order abelian group,
and every real centered $f$ on that group,
\[
 \norm f_{U^2}^4
       \le\left(\frac13+\varepsilon\right)\norm f_{U^d}^4.
\]
\end{corollary}

The threshold is uniform in both the function and the group.  It
therefore supplies the quantifier order required by the original
extremal question.  It does not determine the optimal constant at any
fixed $d\ge4$, and the parameter choices in
\eqref{gsr:cc:63:norm:rate-parameters} should not be read as evidence for an
optimal exponential rate.

\begin{corollary}[Exact limits on a fixed finite group]
\label{gsr:cc:63:norm:fixed-group}
For a fixed finite abelian group $G$ of odd order $N\ge3$, put
\[
 b(G)=\sup_{\substack{f:G\to\R,\ \E f=0\\f\ne0}}
                 \frac{\norm f_{U^2}^4}{\norm f_\infty^4},
 \qquad
 c_d(G)=\sup_{\substack{f:G\to\R,\ \E f=0\\f\ne0}}
                 \frac{\norm f_{U^2}^4}{\norm f_{U^d}^4}.
\]
Then, for every $d\ge2$,
\begin{equation}
 b(G)\le c_d(G)\le b(G)N^{4(d+1)/2^d},
 \qquad \lim_{d\to\infty}c_d(G)=b(G).
 \label{gsr:cc:63:norm:fixed-rate}
\end{equation}
In particular, on every odd cyclic group,
\begin{equation}
 \lim_{d\to\infty}c_d(\Z/N\Z)
       =\frac13-\frac4{3N^2}+\frac1{N^3}.
 \label{gsr:cc:63:norm:cyclic-limit}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The inequality $\norm f_{U^d}\le\norm f_\infty$ gives the lower
bound in \eqref{gsr:cc:63:norm:fixed-rate}.  For the upper bound, use the
parallel-face square identity and retain only the increments
$h_1=\cdots=h_{d-1}=0$.  Since $2^{d-1}$ is even,
\[
 \norm f_{U^d}^{2^d}
 \ge N^{-(d-1)}\left(\E_x f(x)^{2^{d-1}}\right)^2
 \ge N^{-(d+1)}\norm f_\infty^{2^d}.
\]
Thus $\norm f_\infty^4\le
N^{4(d+1)/2^d}\norm f_{U^d}^4$, proving the upper bound after
taking the supremum.  The multiplier tends to one for fixed $N$.
The cyclic value of $b(G)$ is exactly
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:63:bounded:finite}.
\end{proof}

The dependence on $N$ in \eqref{gsr:cc:63:norm:fixed-rate} explains why this
short fixed-group argument does not prove
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:63:norm:main}: its error can be arbitrarily large when
the group order varies with $d$.  The Fourier-tail and smoothing
arguments remove that dependence.
