\section[{An asymptotically sharp quartic cube coefficient\srctag{63}}]{An asymptotically sharp quartic cube coefficient}\label{gsr:cc:63:sec:d5}
\srcnote{63}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:cc:63:cube:section}

The uniform comparison theorem has a direct consequence for the
small-perturbation expansion of Gowers cube counts.  The quartic
coefficient itself was computed in the earlier ProveIt reports
\cite{repo63}.  The new conclusion is the exact limiting value of
the optimal coefficient when that expansion is expressed in terms of
the higher uniformity norm.  This is a local refinement of the
counting estimates surrounding Lemma~3.10 of Gowers's paper
\cite{gowers}.

For a real function $g$ on a finite abelian group, put
\begin{equation}
 Q_d(g)=\E_{x,h_1,\ldots,h_d}
       \prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^d}g(x+\omega\cdot h)
       =\norm g_{U^d}^{2^d}.
 \label{gsr:cc:63:cube:definition}
\end{equation}
All averages are normalized.  Write
\begin{equation}
 q=2^d,\qquad
 P_d=\frac{6^d-2\cdot4^d+2^d}{8}.
 \label{gsr:cc:63:cube:parallelogram-number}
\end{equation}
The integer $P_d$ counts the four-vertex parallelograms in the
discrete $d$-cube.  In particular, $P_2=1$ and $P_3=12$.

\subsection{Why odd torsion introduces no quartic correction}

The following elementary observation supplies the arithmetic detail
needed to work over every odd-order abelian group, including groups
with elements of order three.

\begin{lemma}[Small binary minors]
\label{gsr:cc:63:cube:binary-minors}
Every $3$-by-$3$ matrix with entries in $\{0,1\}$ has determinant
of absolute value at most two.  Every nonzero $2$-by-$2$ binary
determinant has absolute value one.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The second assertion follows directly from the determinant formula.
For the first, a row with no ones gives determinant zero, and a row
with one one reduces the determinant to a $2$-by-$2$ minor.  In the
remaining case every row is one of
\[
                    110,\quad101,\quad011,\quad111.
\]
Repeated rows give zero.  If the three distinct rows include $111$,
coordinate and row permutations reduce to the rows $111,110,101$,
whose determinant has absolute value one.  Otherwise the rows are
$110,101,011$, whose determinant has absolute value two.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Four-vertex classification]
\label{gsr:cc:63:cube:four-vertices}
Let $V\subseteq\{0,1\}^d$ have four elements.  Exactly one of the
following holds:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $V$ is a parallelogram: its elements can be labeled so that
      $v_1+v_2=v_3+v_4$ in $\Z^d$.
\item The four affine forms $x+v\cdot h$, $v\in V$, are jointly
      uniform on $G^4$ when $x,h_1,\ldots,h_d$ are independent and
      uniform in any finite abelian group $G$ of odd order.
\end{enumerate}
Any set of at most three distinct cube vertices gives jointly uniform
forms on every finite abelian group.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Reflect coordinates to move one selected vertex to the origin.
This operation preserves the assertions: a reflection in coordinate
$i$ replaces the variables by $x'=x+h_i$, $h_i'=-h_i$, an invertible
change of uniform variables.  The remaining vertex vectors now have
entries in $\{0,1\}$.

Two distinct nonzero binary vectors are linearly independent over
$\R$.  Otherwise one would be a scalar multiple of the other; a
coordinate equal to one forces the scalar to be one and the vectors
to coincide.  Their rank-two matrix therefore has a nonzero binary
$2$-by-$2$ minor, which is a unit by
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:63:cube:binary-minors}.  This proves the assertion for three
vertices, and the smaller cases follow in the same way.

For four vertices, consider the rank of the three nonzero vectors.
If it is three, a $3$-by-$3$ coordinate minor has determinant
$\pm1$ or $\pm2$.  Such a matrix acts invertibly on $G^3$ when
$|G|$ is odd: its adjugate supplies an inverse after division by its
determinant, and multiplication by two is an automorphism of $G$.
Together with the base variable $x$, this proves joint uniformity
of the four forms.

If the rank is two, project the vertex set onto two coordinates for
which the plane has rank two.  The projection is injective on the
plane, so the four projected vertices are all of $\{0,1\}^2$.
Each remaining coordinate is an affine function on this square
taking only the values zero and one.  Such a function is constant,
one of the two coordinate functions, or its complement: its values
at the four corners obey the parallelogram identity.  Consequently
the original four vertices obey that identity as well.  This also
shows that a parallelogram cannot fall into the rank-three case.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Exact quartic expansion with a controlled remainder]
\label{gsr:cc:63:cube:expansion}
Let $d\ge2$, let $G$ be a finite abelian group of odd order, and let
$f:G\to\R$ satisfy $\E f=0$.  For every $\delta\ge0$, with
$u=\norm f_{U^d}$,
\begin{equation}
 Q_d(\delta+f)
 =\delta^q+P_d\delta^{q-4}\norm f_{U^2}^4
              +\mathcal R_d(\delta,f),
 \label{gsr:cc:63:cube:exact-expansion}
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}
 |\mathcal R_d(\delta,f)|
 \le\sum_{j=5}^{q}\binom qj\delta^{q-j}u^j.
 \label{gsr:cc:63:cube:remainder}
\end{equation}
An empty sum is zero, and a zeroth power is one, including when
$\delta=0$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Expand the product in \eqref{gsr:cc:63:cube:definition}, choosing the vertices
at which the factor $f$ is used.  The empty choice contributes
$\delta^q$.  Every choice of one, two, or three vertices contributes
zero by joint uniformity and $\E f=0$.

For a four-vertex choice of affine rank three, the contribution is
again zero by Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:63:cube:four-vertices}.  For a parallelogram,
the three free vertex forms are jointly uniform by the same lemma,
and the fourth is determined by their parallelogram relation.
Its contribution is therefore
\[
 \E_{a,b,c}f(a)f(b)f(c)f(a+b-c)=\norm f_{U^2}^4.
\]

To count these choices, there are $6^d$ ordered quadruples of binary
vertices satisfying $v_1+v_2=v_3+v_4$: in each coordinate there are
six allowed bit patterns.  The trivial pairings
$(v_1,v_2)=(v_3,v_4)$ and $(v_1,v_2)=(v_4,v_3)$ account for
$2\cdot4^d-2^d$ quadruples, with their overlap counted once.
Every repeated-entry solution is one of these: if a repeated entry
lies on both sides it cancels, while $2v_1=v_3+v_4$ forces
$v_1=v_3=v_4$ coordinatewise.  Every remaining unordered
parallelogram is counted eight times, by interchanging its two
diagonals and ordering each diagonal.  This gives
\eqref{gsr:cc:63:cube:parallelogram-number} and proves the quartic term.

Finally, for a choice of $j\ge5$ vertices, fill those positions
with $f$ and the other cube positions with the constant function
one.  The mixed Gowers--Cauchy--Schwarz inequality bounds the
absolute value of the resulting average by $u^j$.
There are $\binom qj$ such choices.  Summing their bounds proves
\eqref{gsr:cc:63:cube:remainder}.
\end{proof}

The centered expansion and its quartic coefficient are credited to
the earlier reports \cite{repo63}; the short proof above makes
the torsion hypotheses explicit.  The remainder can have either
sign.  In particular, \eqref{gsr:cc:63:cube:exact-expansion} does not imply
the lower bound obtained by deleting it.  The earlier reports give
counterexamples to that deletion already at $d=3$.

\subsection{The optimal coefficient in uniformity-norm units}

\begin{definition}
\label{gsr:cc:63:cube:optimal-definition}
Let $A_d$ be the infimum of constants $A\ge0$ for which
\begin{equation}
 Q_d(\delta+f)
 \le\delta^q+A\delta^{q-4}u^4
       +\sum_{j=5}^{q}\binom qj\delta^{q-j}u^j,
 \qquad u=\norm f_{U^d},
 \label{gsr:cc:63:cube:upper-template}
\end{equation}
holds for every finite abelian group of odd order, every real
centered function $f$, and every $\delta\ge0$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Exact reduction and asymptotically sharp coefficient]
\label{gsr:cc:63:cube:optimal}
For every $d\ge2$,
\begin{equation}
                       A_d=P_dc_d^{\mathrm{odd}}.
 \label{gsr:cc:63:cube:optimal-identity}
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}
 \frac{A_d}{P_d}\longrightarrow\frac13,
 \qquad
 A_d\sim\frac{6^d}{24}\qquad(d\to\infty).
 \label{gsr:cc:63:cube:optimal-limit}
\end{equation}
For every $d\ge80$,
\begin{equation}
 \frac{P_d}{3}\le A_d
 \le P_d\left(\frac13+10\,2^{-\lfloor d/8\rfloor}\right).
 \label{gsr:cc:63:cube:optimal-rate}
\end{equation}
The same coefficient is necessary even when sharpness is tested only
on perturbations $\delta+t f$ taking values in $[0,1]$, with a fixed
$0<\delta<1$ and sufficiently small $t>0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The definition of $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}$ gives
$\norm f_{U^2}^4\le c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}u^4$.
Substitution into Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:63:cube:expansion} proves
\eqref{gsr:cc:63:cube:upper-template} with $A=P_dc_d^{\mathrm{odd}}$.

Conversely, suppose a constant $A$ satisfies
\eqref{gsr:cc:63:cube:upper-template}.  Fix an admissible nonzero $f$,
fix $0<\delta<1$, and replace $f$ by $tf$.  The finite expansion
gives, as $t\downarrow0$,
\[
 Q_d(\delta+tf)
 =\delta^q+P_d\delta^{q-4}t^4\norm f_{U^2}^4+O_{d,\delta,f}(t^5).
\]
The assumed upper bound has fourth-order term
$A\delta^{q-4}t^4\norm f_{U^d}^4$ and a remainder of order
$t^5$.  Subtract $\delta^q$, divide by
$\delta^{q-4}t^4$, and let $t\downarrow0$.  This yields
\[
                   P_d\norm f_{U^2}^4
                    \le A\norm f_{U^d}^4.
\]
Taking the supremum over the group and $f$ proves the reverse
inequality in \eqref{gsr:cc:63:cube:optimal-identity}.
Since the group is finite, $f$ is bounded, and sufficiently small
$t$ makes $0\le\delta+tf\le1$ pointwise.  Thus the restricted
sharpness assertion follows from the same argument.  It concerns
real-valued perturbations, without asserting indicator-valued
sharpness.

Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:63:norm:main} now proves
\eqref{gsr:cc:63:cube:optimal-limit} and \eqref{gsr:cc:63:cube:optimal-rate}; here
$P_d\sim6^d/8$ by \eqref{gsr:cc:63:cube:parallelogram-number}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
In the report's terms this is the best odd-order leading quartic coefficient of item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:normgap}, now asymptotic to $P_d/3$ with $P_d=(6^d-2\cdot4^d+2^d)/8$ (source~04's $P_d$, source~55's $C_d$); at $d=4$ it is $P_4c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}$ with the bracket above.
\end{writenote}

For $\delta>0$, writing $\varepsilon=u/\delta$ displays the
small-uniformity scale explicitly:
\begin{equation}
 \frac{Q_d(\delta+f)}{\delta^q}
 \le1+A_d\varepsilon^4
            +\sum_{j=5}^{q}\binom qj\varepsilon^j.
 \label{gsr:cc:63:cube:relative-expansion}
\end{equation}
For each fixed $d$, the sum after the quartic term is
$O_d(\varepsilon^5)$ as $\varepsilon\to0$.  The asymptotic result
\eqref{gsr:cc:63:cube:optimal-limit} determines how the optimal fourth-order
coefficient subsequently behaves as $d$ grows.  A simultaneous limit
in $d$ and $\varepsilon$ must retain the explicit binomial remainder.
This refinement does not by itself change a final quantitative bound
in Szemer\'edi's theorem; such a conclusion would require carrying
the improved local estimate through the later inverse and
density-increment arguments.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The limiting real Gowers norm constant\srctag{60}}]{The limiting real Gowers norm constant}\label{gsr:cc:60:sec:d2}
\srcnote{60}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:cc:60:norm:section}

The higher-dimensional comparison between real centered Gowers norms has
two distinct sources of difficulty: the function may change as the order of
the norm increases, and its ambient group may change as well.  Taking the
limit on each fixed finite group does not justify interchanging that limit
with the supremum over groups.  We resolve this interchange by controlling
the Fourier fourth-power mass and then constructing a compact-group limit.

The resulting theorem identifies the asymptotic comparison constant with
a bounded Fourier extremal problem.  It also narrows the interval
$[1/3,1/2]$ obtained in source~29 of the repository to
$[1/3,0.3464533951\ldots]$.  When the least prime divisor of the group order
tends to infinity together with the Gowers norm order, the asymptotic
constant is exactly $1/3$.  The latter statement uses the published
Riesz--Sobolev inequality of Christ and Iliopoulou; the former bound and the
compactness reduction have the self-contained proofs below, apart from
standard Fourier analysis and Pontryagin duality.

We use the normalized Gowers norms introduced in
\cite{gowers}.  Questions concerning their extremizers and nearly
extremal functions belong to the broader setting of
\cite{eisnertao}.  The use of varying compact groups as limit objects
has substantial precedent, including \cite{szegedylimits}; we do not claim
a new general framework for limits of functions on groups.  The specific
new input here is the Fourier tail estimate
\eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:tail}, which allows the starting functions to be unbounded
in the supremum norm while their increasingly high Gowers norms remain
bounded.

\subsection{Definitions and statements}
\label{gsr:cc:60:norm:subsec:statements}

All groups in this section are abelian.  Finite groups carry uniform
probability measure; compact groups carry Haar probability measure.
For a real function $f$ define
\begin{equation}
 Q_d(f)=
 \mathbb E_{x,h_1,\ldots,h_d}
 \prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^d}f(x+\omega\cdot h),
 \qquad
 \|f\|_{U^d}=Q_d(f)^{1/2^d}.
 \label{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:definition}
\end{equation}
The standard complex definition inserts conjugation at the odd vertices;
for real functions it reduces to \eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:definition}.  We use the
usual triangle inequality, translation invariance, recursion, and
monotonicity of these norms.  In particular, for $d\ge2$, convolution with
a nonnegative kernel of integral one contracts $U^d$.

The normalized Fourier coefficient at a character $\chi$ is
$\widehat f(\chi)=\mathbb E_x f(x)\overline{\chi(x)}$.  The basic identity
is
\begin{equation}
 \|f\|_{U^2}^4=\sum_{\chi}|\widehat f(\chi)|^4.
 \label{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:u2}
\end{equation}
The sum on the dual group uses counting measure.  A function is
\emph{centered} if its integral is zero.

For $d\ge2$ set
\begin{align}
 c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}
 &=\sup_{\substack{G\text{ finite},\ |G|\text{ odd}\\
                   f:G\to\mathbb R,\ \mathbb E f=0,\ f\ne0}}
      \frac{\|f\|_{U^2}^4}{\|f\|_{U^d}^4},
 \label{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:cd}\\
 \beta_{\mathrm{odd}}
 &=\sup_{\substack{G\text{ finite},\ |G|\text{ odd}\\
                   f:G\to\mathbb R,\ \mathbb E f=0,\ f\ne0}}
      \frac{\|f\|_{U^2}^4}{\|f\|_\infty^4}.
 \label{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:beta}
\end{align}
Both quotients are invariant under nonzero scalar multiplication.
Thus the second supremum can equivalently be taken over centered real
functions with $|f|\le1$.

\begin{theorem}[Asymptotic reduction and improved bracket]
\label{gsr:cc:60:norm:thm:main}
The sequence $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}$ is nonincreasing and
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 \lim_{d\to\infty}c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}=\beta_{\mathrm{odd}}.}
 \label{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:limit}
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 \frac13\le\beta_{\mathrm{odd}}
 \le B:=\frac12-\frac8{\pi^2}+\frac{64}{\pi^4}
 =0.3464533951610953\ldots.}
 \label{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:bracket}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Superseded by source~63} (Section~\ref{gsr:cc:sec:oddlimit}): its Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:63:bounded:sharp} gives $\norm f_{U^2}^4\le\norm f_\infty^4/3$ for every real centered $f$ on every finite group of odd order, so $\beta_{\mathrm{odd}}=1/3$ and the limit in \eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:limit} is $1/3$; source~63 also gives the rate. This theorem is correct as printed; only the bracket \eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:bracket} is no longer the best statement.
\end{writenote}

The exact identity $\beta_{\mathrm{odd}}=1/3$ is not proved here.
Equation~\eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:limit} makes it equivalent to the exact
asymptotic question for the Gowers norm comparison.  The upper bound is
qualitative as a statement about $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}$: for every
$\varepsilon>0$ there exists $d_0$ such that
$c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}\le B+\varepsilon$ for $d\ge d_0$, but the argument
below supplies no effective value of $d_0$.  It therefore makes no new
claim about the fourth-order coefficient $4795/832$ in source~45.

For a nontrivial finite group $G$, write $p_*(G)$ for the least prime
divisor of $|G|$.

\begin{theorem}[Exact limit as small prime torsion disappears]
\label{gsr:cc:60:norm:thm:large-characteristic}
Suppose $d_n\to\infty$, $p_*(G_n)\to\infty$, and
$f_n:G_n\to\mathbb R$ are nonzero centered functions.  Then
\begin{equation}
 \limsup_{n\to\infty}
 \frac{\|f_n\|_{U^2}^4}{\|f_n\|_{U^{d_n}}^4}\le\frac13.
 \label{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:large-characteristic}
\end{equation}
The constant is sharp.  More explicitly, if
\begin{equation}
 C(d,P)=\sup_{\substack{G\text{ finite},\ p_*(G)\ge P\\
                   f:G\to\mathbb R,\ \mathbb E f=0,\ f\ne0}}
     \frac{\|f\|_{U^2}^4}{\|f\|_{U^d}^4},
 \label{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:joint-constant}
\end{equation}
then
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\displaystyle\lim_{\substack{d\to\infty\\P\to\infty}}
 C(d,P)=\frac13}
 \label{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:joint-limit}
\end{equation}
in the joint sense: for every $\varepsilon>0$, some $d_0,P_0$ work for
all $d\ge d_0$ and $P\ge P_0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
Contained in source~63's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:63:norm:main}: if $p_*(G)\ge3$ then $|G|$ is odd, so $C(d,P)\le c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}\le1/3+10\cdot2^{-\lfloor d/8\rfloor}$ for $d\ge80$ and every $P\ge3$, with no condition on $P$ (checked at the write). The Riesz--Sobolev route remains a second proof of the joint limit.
\end{writenote}

Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:60:norm:thm:large-characteristic} concerns a simultaneous
limit.  It does not assert $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}\le1/3$ at a fixed order,
nor a bound $1/3$ uniform in $d$ for a fixed finite prime modulus.

\subsection{Positive moments prevent escape of Fourier mass}
\label{gsr:cc:60:norm:subsec:tightness}

For a real function $f$ on a finite group, its autocorrelation
\begin{equation}
 r_f(h)=\mathbb E_x f(x)f(x+h)
 \label{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:autocorrelation}
\end{equation}
has Fourier coefficients $|\widehat f(\chi)|^2\ge0$.
Consequently every surviving term in the Fourier expansion of an even
autocorrelation moment has a nonnegative coefficient.  Source~29 uses
balanced words in this expansion to obtain the central-binomial moment
bound.  Here we retain words using \emph{distinct} conjugate pairs; this
controls the tail of the spectrum rather than only its total mass.

\begin{lemma}[Uniform Fourier tail estimate]
\label{gsr:cc:60:norm:lem:tail}
Let $f:G\to\mathbb R$ be centered, let $|G|$ be odd, and suppose
$\|f\|_{U^D}\le1$, where $D\ge2$.  Choose one character $\chi_j$ from
each nontrivial inverse pair, ordering the pairs so that
\[
 x_j:=|\widehat f(\chi_j)|^4
 \quad\text{satisfies}\quad x_1\ge x_2\ge\cdots.
\]
Append zero values if the list is finite.  For every integer $L\ge0$
and every integer $1\le m\le2^{D-2}$,
\begin{align}
 2\sum_{j>L}x_j
 &\le
 2\left(\frac{m!}{(2m)!}\right)^{1/m}
 +\frac{m-1}{L+1}
 \notag\\
 &\le\frac2{m+1}+\frac{m-1}{L+1}.
 \label{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:tail}
\end{align}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The group has no nontrivial self-inverse characters, and centering
removes the trivial one.  Thus
\begin{equation}
 2\sum_jx_j=\|f\|_{U^2}^4\le1.
 \label{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:pair-total}
\end{equation}
Put $M=2^{D-2}$.  The derivative recursion and
$\|g\|_{U^{D-1}}\ge|\mathbb E g|$ imply
\[
 \mathbb E_h|r_f(h)|^{2M}
 \le\|f\|_{U^D}^{2^D}\le1.
\]
Monotonicity of the $L^p$ norms on a probability space gives
$\mathbb E|r_f|^{2m}\le1$ for every $m\le M$.

In the Fourier expansion of this last moment, retain those words that
choose $m$ distinct pairs from indices greater than $L$ and use each
character and its inverse exactly once.  If $e_m$ denotes the elementary
symmetric polynomial, their contribution is
$ (2m)!e_m(x_{L+1},x_{L+2},\ldots)$.  Therefore
\begin{equation}
 1\ge\frac{(2m)!}{m!}\mathcal D_m,
 \qquad
 \mathcal D_m=
 \sum_{\substack{j_1,\ldots,j_m>L\\j_1,\ldots,j_m\text{ distinct}}}
 x_{j_1}\cdots x_{j_m}.
 \label{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:distinct-moment}
\end{equation}
Extra character relations create further nonnegative terms, so they do
not invalidate this lower bound.

Write
\[
 T=\sum_{j>L}x_j,
 \qquad a=\max_{j>L}x_j\le\frac1{2(L+1)},
\]
where the last bound follows from the ordering and
\eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:pair-total}.  If $T>(m-1)a$, successive choices of
distinct indices leave total mass at least $T-ja$ after $j$ choices.
Induction gives
\[
 \mathcal D_m\ge\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}(T-ja)
 \ge\bigl(T-(m-1)a\bigr)^m.
\]
Combining this with \eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:distinct-moment} yields
\[
 T\le\left(\frac{m!}{(2m)!}\right)^{1/m}+(m-1)a.
\]
If $T\le(m-1)a$, the same conclusion is immediate.  Multiplication by
two proves the first inequality in \eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:tail}.  For the
second, use
$(2m)!/m!=\prod_{j=m+1}^{2m}j\ge(m+1)^m$.
\end{proof}

For a sequence $D_n\to\infty$, the right side of
\eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:tail} tends to zero uniformly in all sufficiently large
$n$ by first choosing $m$ large and then $L$ large.  This is the precise
tightness statement needed below.  Choosing $m$ of order $\sqrt L$
also gives an explicit tail of order $L^{-1/2}$ whenever $D$ is large
enough to permit that choice of $m$.

\subsection{The limit of the norms on a fixed compact group}
\label{gsr:cc:60:norm:subsec:fixed-group}

The next lemma is used only for real trigonometric polynomials.  Its
proof keeps track of signs; restricting a cube average to a set of
directions without doing so would not be legitimate.

\begin{lemma}[Fixed trigonometric polynomials]
\label{gsr:cc:60:norm:lem:fixed-group}
If $g$ is a real trigonometric polynomial on a compact abelian group $K$,
then
\begin{equation}
 \lim_{d\to\infty}\|g\|_{U^d}=\|g\|_\infty.
 \label{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:fixed-limit}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $M=\|g\|_\infty$.  The zero case is immediate.  Fix
$0<\varepsilon<M/4$, and let
\[
 E=\{x:|g(x)|\ge M-\varepsilon\},\qquad u=\mu(E)>0.
\]
The positivity of $u$ follows from continuity and the full support of
Haar measure.  Write $g=\sum_{j=1}^r a_j\chi_j$ and put
$A=\sum_j|a_j|$.  Choose a fixed $0<\eta<1/8$ with
$2\pi A\eta<\varepsilon$.  Define
\[
 B_d=\{h:\|\chi_j(h)\|_{\mathbb R/\mathbb Z}<\eta/d
                 \text{ for }1\le j\le r\},
\]
where a unit complex number is identified with its phase modulo one.
If $h_1,\ldots,h_{d-1}\in B_d$, then for every
$\omega\in\{0,1\}^{d-1}$ and every $x$,
\begin{equation}
 |g(x+\omega\cdot h)-g(x)|<\varepsilon.
 \label{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:small-shifts}
\end{equation}
Indeed the displacement of each character along a sum is bounded by
the sum of its displacements along the individual increments.

We shall use the elementary estimate
\begin{equation}
 \mu(B_d)\ge\left(\frac{\eta}{3d}\right)^r.
 \label{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:bohr-volume}
\end{equation}
To see this, divide each coordinate of the image of $K$ in
$(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^r$ into
$N=\lceil2d/\eta\rceil$ intervals.  One inverse image of a box has
measure at least $N^{-r}$.  Subtracting any point in that inverse image
places its translate inside $B_d$.  Thus
$\mu(B_d)\ge N^{-r}\ge(\eta/(3d))^r$.

For $k=2^{d-1}$ and a tuple of directions $h$ put
\[
 R(h)=\mathbb E_x
       \prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^{d-1}}g(x+\omega\cdot h).
\]
If the directions lie in $B_d$ and $|g(x)|>\varepsilon$, all factors
have the same sign by \eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:small-shifts}.  Since $k$ is even
for $d\ge2$, their product is nonnegative.  On $E$ its value is at least
$(M-2\varepsilon)^k$.  Where $|g(x)|\le\varepsilon$, its negative part
is at most $(2\varepsilon)^k$.  Consequently
\[
 R(h)\ge u(M-2\varepsilon)^k-(2\varepsilon)^k
       \ge\frac u2(M-2\varepsilon)^k
\]
for all sufficiently large $d$ and all $h\in B_d^{d-1}$.

Averaging the final direction in the cube gives the exact identity
\begin{equation}
 Q_d(g)=\mathbb E_{h_1,\ldots,h_{d-1}}R(h)^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:final-direction}
\end{equation}
Indeed the two parallel faces have base points $x$ and $x+h_d$, which
become independent uniform points after averaging $x,h_d$.  We may
therefore restrict this nonnegative square average to $B_d^{d-1}$.
By \eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:bohr-volume},
\[
 \|g\|_{U^d}\ge
 (M-2\varepsilon)
 \left[
   \left(\frac{\eta}{3d}\right)^{r(d-1)}
   \left(\frac u2\right)^2
 \right]^{1/2^d}.
\]
The factor in brackets raised to $1/2^d$ tends to one.  The opposite
bound $\|g\|_{U^d}\le M$ is immediate from the definition.  Letting
$\varepsilon$ tend to zero proves the claim.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A compact limit from high-order norm control}
\label{gsr:cc:60:norm:subsec:compactness}

We now prove the main compactness statement.  The limit group can have
elements of order two; for example, the circle does.  The property
preserved from odd-order finite groups is instead that its
\emph{discrete dual} has no nonzero element of order two.  Keeping this
distinction explicit is essential for the finite approximation later.

\begin{theorem}[Compactness with preservation of the second norm]
\label{gsr:cc:60:norm:thm:compactness}
Let $G_n$ be finite odd-order abelian groups, let $D_n\to\infty$, and
let $f_n:G_n\to\mathbb R$ be centered with
$\|f_n\|_{U^{D_n}}\le1$.  Pass to a subsequence on which
$\|f_n\|_{U^2}^4$ converges.  There exist a compact metrizable abelian
group $K$, whose discrete dual has no nonzero element of order two, and
a measurable centered real function $f$ with $|f|\le1$ almost everywhere,
such that
\begin{equation}
 \|f\|_{U^2}^4=\lim_{n\to\infty}\|f_n\|_{U^2}^4.
 \label{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:compactness-mass}
\end{equation}
If additionally $p_*(G_n)\to\infty$, $K$ can be taken connected.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If the orders $|G_n|$ remain bounded, take a further subsequence with a
fixed finite group.  Every Fourier coefficient has modulus at most one,
so there is a coefficientwise limit $f$.  For every fixed $d$, eventually
$D_n\ge d$, whence $\|f_n\|_{U^d}\le1$ and therefore
$\|f\|_{U^d}\le1$.  Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:60:norm:lem:fixed-group} gives
$\|f\|_\infty\le1$; all other claims follow by finite Fourier
continuity.  We may henceforth assume $|G_n|\to\infty$.

\paragraph{Step 1: stabilize the character relations.}
For each $n$, choose representatives $\chi_{n,j}$ of the nontrivial
inverse pairs in decreasing order of
$|\widehat f_n(\chi_{n,j})|$.  Pad the infinite list by trivial
characters after all genuine pairs have been listed.  Every fixed
initial segment consists of distinct nontrivial inverse pairs for all
sufficiently large $n$.

Let $F=\bigoplus_{j\ge1}\mathbb Z e_j$ be a countable free abelian
group, and let
\[
 \phi_n:F\longrightarrow\widehat G_n,
 \qquad\phi_n(e_j)=\chi_{n,j}.
\]
The group $F$ is countable.  Since every Fourier coefficient has modulus
at most one, a diagonal subsequence has the following two properties
for every $w\in F$: the truth value of $\phi_n(w)=0$ is eventually
constant, and $\widehat f_n(\phi_n(w))$ converges.
Let
\[
 R=\{w\in F:\phi_n(w)=0\text{ for all sufficiently large }n\},
 \qquad \Gamma=F/R.
\]
The set $R$ is a subgroup.  If $2w\in R$, oddness of $|G_n|$ forces
$w\in R$, so $\Gamma$ has no nonzero element of order two.  Set
$K=\widehat\Gamma$.  This is compact and metrizable.  For
$\gamma=w+R$ define
\begin{equation}
 b_\gamma=\lim_{n\to\infty}\widehat f_n(\phi_n(w)).
 \label{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:limit-coefficients}
\end{equation}
This is independent of the representative.  Moreover
$b_0=0$ and $b_{-\gamma}=\overline{b_\gamma}$.

\paragraph{Step 2: positive polynomial kernels produce bounded limits.}
Write $\gamma_j=e_j+R$, viewing $\gamma_j$ also as a character on $K$.
For fixed positive integers $J,t$, define
\begin{equation}
 P_{J,t}(x)=
 \prod_{j=1}^J\left|\frac{1+\gamma_j(x)}2\right|^{2t},
 \qquad K_{J,t}=\frac{P_{J,t}}{\int_K P_{J,t}}.
 \label{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:kernel}
\end{equation}
The denominator is positive: $P_{J,t}$ is continuous and equals one
at the identity.  The kernel is real, nonnegative, has integral one,
and has finite Fourier support.

Substituting $\chi_{n,j}$ for $\gamma_j$ in the same expression gives a
nonnegative kernel on $G_n$, normalized to have mean one, denoted
$K_{n,J,t}$.  Only finitely many words in $F$ occur in the polynomial.
Their relations stabilize.  Hence the normalizing constants are
eventually the same as the constant in \eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:kernel}, and all
identifications of frequencies in these polynomials eventually agree.

The functions
$g_n=f_n*K_{n,J,t}$ satisfy $\|g_n\|_{U^d}\le1$ for every fixed $d$
and all large $n$.  This follows from the norm triangle inequality and
translation invariance, because the kernel is a probability kernel and
$D_n\ge d$.  Their Fourier support is contained in a fixed finite set
of formal words.  The coefficients converge to those of the real
trigonometric polynomial $g_{J,t}$ on $K$ defined by
\begin{equation}
 \widehat g_{J,t}(\gamma)
       =b_\gamma\widehat K_{J,t}(\gamma).
 \label{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:smoothed-coefficients}
\end{equation}
For each fixed $d$, expansion of a $d$-cube average in these finitely
many Fourier coefficients involves finitely many character relations.
All such relations have stabilized.  Fourier orthogonality therefore
gives
$Q_d(g_n)\to Q_d(g_{J,t})$ and
$\|g_{J,t}\|_{U^d}\le1$.  This holds for every fixed $d$.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:60:norm:lem:fixed-group} now yields
\begin{equation}
 \|g_{J,t}\|_\infty\le1.
 \label{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:smoothed-bound}
\end{equation}

\paragraph{Step 3: remove the smoothing.}
For fixed $J$, write the numerator of \eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:kernel} as
$v_J(x)^t$, where $0\le v_J\le1$ and $v_J=1$ exactly on
\[
 H_J=\{x:\gamma_j(x)=1\text{ for }1\le j\le J\}.
\]
Outside any fixed neighborhood of $H_J$, the continuous function $v_J$
is at most some $c<1$.  On a smaller neighborhood of the identity of
positive measure, it exceeds a number $c'$ with $c<c'<1$.  It follows
that the normalized kernel mass outside the first neighborhood is at
most a constant times $(c/c')^t$.  Thus, whenever
$\gamma\in\langle\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_J\rangle$,
\begin{equation}
 \widehat K_{J,t}(\gamma)\longrightarrow1
 \quad(t\to\infty).
 \label{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:kernel-convergence}
\end{equation}

Every element of $\Gamma$ belongs to one of these finitely generated
subgroups.  A diagonal choice of $J$ and $t$ produces a sequence of
kernels for which \eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:kernel-convergence} holds at every
$\gamma\in\Gamma$.  The associated polynomials $g_{J,t}$ are centered
and real, and satisfy \eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:smoothed-bound}.  The unit ball of
$L^\infty(K)$ is weak-star compact.  Since $K$ is compact metrizable,
$L^1(K)$ is separable, so we may take a weak-star convergent subsequence.
Its limit $f$ is real centered, has $|f|\le1$ almost everywhere, and
has Fourier coefficients $b_\gamma$.

\paragraph{Step 4: recover all the Fourier fourth-power mass.}
The elements $\gamma_j$ are distinct, nonzero, and no two are inverses:
these properties hold for each fixed initial list in all sufficiently
large finite groups, so they hold after stabilization.
If $b_\gamma\ne0$, choose $\varepsilon>0$ smaller than its modulus.
The corresponding coefficient of $f_n$ has modulus at least
$\varepsilon$ for all large $n$.  Its inverse pair must lie among at
most $1/(2\varepsilon^4)$ of the ordered pairs, because
$\|f_n\|_{U^2}^4\le1$.  Stabilization forces
$\gamma=\gamma_j$ or $\gamma=-\gamma_j$ for some $j$ in this fixed
finite list.  Indeed if none of these finitely many equalities held in
$\Gamma$, all would eventually fail in the finite groups, a
contradiction.  Thus all nonzero coefficients $b_\gamma$ occur in the
listed pairs.

For each fixed $m,L$, Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:60:norm:lem:tail} applies to all
sufficiently large $n$.  First choose $m$ so that $2/(m+1)$ is small,
then choose $L$ so that $(m-1)/(L+1)$ is small.  The tails of the
Fourier fourth-power sums are therefore uniformly small.  Passing to
the limit in finite initial sums and then removing the tails gives
\[
 \sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma}|b_\gamma|^4
 =\lim_{n\to\infty}
      2\sum_j|\widehat f_n(\chi_{n,j})|^4.
\]
Using \eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:u2} proves
\eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:compactness-mass}.

Finally, if $p_*(G_n)\to\infty$ and $mw\in R$ for a fixed positive
integer $m$, then $m$ is coprime to $|G_n|$ for all large $n$.
Consequently $w\in R$.  The group $\Gamma$ is now torsion-free.
Pontryagin duality says that $\widehat\Gamma$ is connected exactly in
this situation, proving the last assertion.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Finite odd groups approximate the bounded limit problem}
\label{gsr:cc:60:norm:subsec:finite-approximation}

\begin{lemma}[Finite approximation]
\label{gsr:cc:60:norm:lem:finite-approximation}
Let $K$ be a compact abelian group whose discrete dual has no nonzero
element of order two.  If $f$ is centered real and $|f|\le1$ almost
everywhere, then
\begin{equation}
 \|f\|_{U^2}^4\le\beta_{\mathrm{odd}}.
 \label{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:finite-approximation}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Choose finitely many Fourier coefficients whose fourth powers sum to
at least $\|f\|_{U^2}^4-\varepsilon$, and let $H$ be the subgroup of
$\widehat K$ that they generate.  Conditional expectation over the
annihilator of $H$ yields a function on $\widehat H$ preserving these
coefficients, the mean, realness, and the bound one.
The structure theorem for finitely generated abelian groups gives
\[
 H\cong\mathbb Z^r\oplus T,
 \qquad
 \widehat H\cong(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^r\times\widehat T,
\]
where $T$ is finite of odd order.  Oddness follows from the absence of
order-two elements in $H$.

Convolution with positive finite Fourier kernels, for example the
kernels \eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:kernel} formed from a finite generating set of
$H$, gives a continuous real centered function $h$ on $\widehat H$
with $|h|\le1$ and with the selected Fourier coefficients arbitrarily
close to their previous values.  We may therefore arrange
\[
 \|h\|_{U^2}^4\ge\|f\|_{U^2}^4-2\varepsilon.
\]
For odd integers $N\to\infty$, restrict $h$ to the finite subgroups
\[
 H_N=\bigl((1/N)\mathbb Z/\mathbb Z\bigr)^r\times\widehat T.
\]
Riemann sums converge to Haar integrals for $h$ and its continuous
two-cube product.  If $\mu_N$ is the mean of $h|_{H_N}$, then
$\mu_N\to0$, and
\[
 h_N=\frac{h|_{H_N}-\mu_N}{1+|\mu_N|}
\]
is centered real and bounded by one.  Its second Gowers norm converges
to that of $h$.  Since each $H_N$ has odd order, the definition of
$\beta_{\mathrm{odd}}$ gives
$\beta_{\mathrm{odd}}\ge\|f\|_{U^2}^4-2\varepsilon$.
Let $\varepsilon$ tend to zero.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of \eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:limit}]
Monotonicity of the Gowers norms makes $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}$
nonincreasing.  The bound
$\|f\|_{U^d}\le\|f\|_\infty$ gives
$c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}\ge\beta_{\mathrm{odd}}$ for every $d$.
Let $c$ be the limit of this decreasing sequence.

Choose $D_n\to\infty$ and functions whose ratios in
\eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:cd} tend to $c$.  Rescale them so that
$\|f_n\|_{U^{D_n}}=1$.  Then $\|f_n\|_{U^2}^4\to c$.
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:60:norm:thm:compactness} gives a centered real function
$f$ bounded by one on a compact group with no dual order-two element,
such that $\|f\|_{U^2}^4=c$.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:60:norm:lem:finite-approximation} gives
$c\le\beta_{\mathrm{odd}}$, proving equality.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The bounded Fourier extremum}
\label{gsr:cc:60:norm:subsec:bounded-fourier}

The numerical upper bound in Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:60:norm:thm:main} uses a sharp
single-coefficient estimate together with the fact that real Fourier
coefficients occur in inverse pairs.  Centering is essential for the
sharp finite-order estimate.

\begin{lemma}[A sharp centered coefficient bound]
\label{gsr:cc:60:norm:lem:coefficient}
Let $f$ be real centered on a finite group, with $|f|\le1$.  If a
character $\chi$ has odd order $q\ge3$, then
\begin{equation}
 |\widehat f(\chi)|
 \le a_q:=\frac1q\cot\frac{\pi}{2q}<\frac2\pi.
 \label{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:coefficient}
\end{equation}
The finite-$q$ constant is attained.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Conditional expectation on the quotient generated by $\chi$ reduces
the question to a vector $(v_0,\ldots,v_{q-1})$ with
$v_j\in[-1,1]$ and $\sum_jv_j=0$.  Write $q=2n+1$.
The extreme points of this polytope have $n$ coordinates equal to one,
$n$ equal to minus one, and one equal to zero.  At most one coordinate
can lie strictly inside $[-1,1]$ at an extreme point, since otherwise
two coordinates can be perturbed in opposite directions.  The zero sum
and the odd number of coordinates then force the remaining coordinate
to be zero and the two signs to occur equally often.

Fix an angle $\theta$ and maximize
\[
 \sum_{j=0}^{q-1}v_j\cos(2\pi j/q-\theta).
\]
A maximizing extreme point places its positive coordinates at the $n$
largest cosines, its negative coordinates at the $n$ smallest, and its
zero at a median.  The $n$ largest cosines correspond to an arc of $n$
consecutive roots of unity, and a median root is adjacent to that arc.
This follows by ordering the roots by circular distance from $\theta$;
ties can be broken in this way without changing the maximum.

Up to rotation and reflection, its Fourier numerator is therefore
\begin{equation}
 1+2\sum_{j=1}^{n}e^{2\pi i j/q}
       =i\cot\frac{\pi}{2q}.
 \label{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:cotangent-sum}
\end{equation}
Taking $\theta$ to be the phase of any candidate Fourier coefficient
shows that its modulus is at most the modulus in
\eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:cotangent-sum}, divided by $q$.
The vector with zero at $0$, positives at $1,\ldots,n$, and negatives
at the remaining indices attains the bound.  Finally
$\cot t<1/t$ for $0<t<\pi/2$ proves the last inequality.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The Fourier mass cap]
\label{gsr:cc:60:norm:prop:cap}
Every centered real function $f$ on a finite odd-order group satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \|f\|_{U^2}^4
 \le\left(\frac12-\frac8{\pi^2}+\frac{64}{\pi^4}\right)
       \|f\|_\infty^4.
 \label{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:cap}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Normalize $\|f\|_\infty=1$, ignoring the zero function.  Choose one
representative of each nontrivial inverse pair and set
$\lambda_j=|\widehat f(\chi_j)|^2$.  Parseval and centering give
\[
 \sum_j\lambda_j=\frac12\|f\|_2^2\le\frac12.
\]
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:60:norm:lem:coefficient} gives
$\lambda_j\le A:=4/\pi^2$, with $1/4<A<1/2$.

If $\lambda_{\max}\le1/4$, then
$2\sum_j\lambda_j^2\le\lambda_{\max}\le1/4$.
Otherwise write $a=\lambda_{\max}\in[1/4,A]$.  The remaining mass is
at most $1/2-a$, so
\[
 2\sum_j\lambda_j^2\le2\left[a^2+(1/2-a)^2\right]
 \le2\left[A^2+(1/2-A)^2\right].
\]
The second inequality uses that the expression is increasing for
$a\in[1/4,1/2]$; its value at $A$ exceeds $1/4$, so it covers the first
case as well.  By \eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:u2}, the left side is
$\|f\|_{U^2}^4$.  Expanding the final expression proves
\eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:cap}.
\end{proof}

The lower bound $1/3$ admits a bounded finite witness with an error of
order $q^{-2}$.  On $G=\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z$, where $q=2n+1$, set
\begin{equation}
 f_q(0)=0,\qquad
 f_q(j)=1\ (1\le j\le n),\qquad
 f_q(j)=-1\ (n+1\le j\le2n).
 \label{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:lower-witness}
\end{equation}
This function is centered and has supremum norm one.  Its unnormalized
autocorrelation $R(h)=\sum_xf_q(x)f_q(x+h)$ is
\[
 R(0)=q-1,\qquad R(h)=R(q-h)=q-4h\quad(1\le h\le n).
\]
Indeed for such a nonzero $h$, exactly two terms contain the zero entry.
Among the other $q-2$ terms there are $2h-1$ pairs of opposite signs:
the two sign intervals meet after translation across their two boundaries,
with $h$ crossings at one boundary and $h-1$ at the boundary containing
the zero.  Thus $R(h)=(q-2)-2(2h-1)=q-4h$.
It follows that
\[
 \sum_hR(h)^2
 =(q-1)^2+2\sum_{h=1}^n(q-4h)^2
 =\frac{q^3-4q+3}{3}.
\]
Here the sum of squares is obtained directly from
$\sum_{h=1}^nh=n(n+1)/2$ and
$\sum_{h=1}^nh^2=n(n+1)(2n+1)/6$.
Fourier orthogonality, or the autocorrelation form of $U^2$, now gives
\begin{equation}
 \|f_q\|_{U^2}^4
 =\frac{q^3-4q+3}{3q^3}
 =\frac13-\frac4{3q^2}+\frac1{q^3}
 \longrightarrow\frac13.
 \label{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:interval-lower}
\end{equation}
Since $\|f_q\|_{U^d}\le1$, the right side is also a lower bound for
the ratio against $U^d$, for every $d$.  This has a smaller finite-size
error than the scaled centered-interval model of source~29, which has
an error of order $q^{-1}$.  No global optimality of this cyclic witness
is needed or asserted.  Together with Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:60:norm:prop:cap}
and \eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:limit}, it completes the proof of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:60:norm:thm:main}.

\subsection{An exact connected-group bound and the joint limit}
\label{gsr:cc:60:norm:subsec:connected}

The next step imports precisely one rearrangement inequality.  Theorem~1.2,
equation~(1.5), of Christ and Iliopoulou
\cite{christiliopoulou} states that, for measurable sets $A,B,C$ in
a compact connected abelian group, with measures $a,b,c$ satisfying
\[
 |a-b|\le c\le a+b,\qquad a+b+c\le2,
\]
one has
\begin{equation}
 \int_C\mathbf 1_A*\mathbf 1_B
 \le ab-\frac14(a+b-c)^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:riesz-import}
\end{equation}
Their formulation is an equivalent form of an earlier inequality of
Tao, as explained in that paper.  We use the inequality as an established
result and give the consequence needed here in full.

\begin{lemma}[Bounded centered functions on connected groups]
\label{gsr:cc:60:norm:lem:connected}
If $K$ is compact connected abelian and $f$ is real centered with
$|f|\le1$ almost everywhere, then
\begin{equation}
 \|f\|_{U^2}^4\le\frac13.
 \label{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:connected-bound}
\end{equation}
The constant is attained on the circle.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
First suppose $f=2\mathbf1_A-1$, where $\mu(A)=1/2$, and put
$u=\mathbf1_A*\mathbf1_{-A}$.  Then $0\le u\le1/2$.
For any measurable $C$ with $\mu(C)=c$, the hypotheses of
\eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:riesz-import} hold with $a=b=1/2$, so
\begin{equation}
 \int_Cu\le\frac c2-\frac{c^2}{4}.
 \label{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:halfset}
\end{equation}
For $0\le t\le1/2$, the variational formula for the positive part gives
\begin{align*}
 \int_K(u-t)_+
 &=\sup_C\left(\int_Cu-t\mu(C)\right)\\
 &\le\max_{0\le c\le1}
       \left((1/2-t)c-c^2/4\right)
 =(1/2-t)^2.
\end{align*}
Integrating this inequality in $t$ yields
\[
 \int_Ku^2
 =2\int_0^{1/2}\int_K(u-t)_+\,dt
 \le2\int_0^{1/2}(1/2-t)^2\,dt=\frac1{12}.
\]
Since the zero Fourier coefficient of $\mathbf1_A$ is $1/2$,
\[
 \|2\mathbf1_A-1\|_{U^2}^4
 =16\left(\int_Ku^2-\frac1{16}\right)\le\frac13.
\]

For general $f$, write $g=(f+1)/2$ and form the measurable subgraph
\[
 A=\{(x,t)\in K\times(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z):0\le t<g(x)\},
\]
using representatives $t\in[0,1)$.  This set has Haar measure $1/2$,
and the product group is compact connected.  Averaging
$2\mathbf1_A-1$ over translations in the circle subgroup gives the
function $(x,t)\mapsto f(x)$.  Such averaging contracts $U^2$.
The sign-function case just proved therefore gives
\eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:connected-bound}.  For a half-circle interval, its
autocorrelation is the triangular function and the inequalities above
are equalities; equivalently, the centered circle square wave has
Fourier fourth-power sum $1/3$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:60:norm:thm:large-characteristic}]
Normalize $\|f_n\|_{U^{d_n}}=1$ and extract a subsequence on which
$\|f_n\|_{U^2}^4$ converges to the limsup in question.
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:60:norm:thm:compactness} gives a compact-group limit $f$
bounded by one, preserving this fourth power.  Its dual is torsion-free
because $p_*(G_n)\to\infty$, so its group is connected.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:60:norm:lem:connected} proves the upper bound $1/3$.

The cyclic construction \eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:interval-lower} may be taken
along odd primes $2n+1\to\infty$.  Since
$\|f_n\|_{U^{d_n}}\le\|f_n\|_\infty$, its ratios against the
increasing-order Gowers norms have liminf at least $1/3$, for any
accompanying sequence $d_n\to\infty$.  The upper bound already proved
then forces convergence to $1/3$.
For every fixed $d,P$, the same interval examples show $C(d,P)\ge1/3$.
If the joint upper limit in \eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:joint-limit} exceeded
$1/3$, one could choose near-maximizers with $d_n\ge n$ and
$p_*(G_n)\ge n$ violating \eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:large-characteristic}.
This proves the joint formulation.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A bounded-exponent variant}
\label{gsr:cc:60:norm:subsec:exponent}

The compactness argument also records persistent torsion rather than
discarding it.  Fix an odd integer $q\ge3$.  Define $c_d(q)$ and
$\beta(q)$ as in \eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:cd}--\eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:beta}, restricting
to finite groups whose exponent divides $q$.

\begin{corollary}[Fixed exponent]
\label{gsr:cc:60:norm:cor:exponent}
For each fixed odd $q\ge3$,
\begin{equation}
 \lim_{d\to\infty}c_d(q)=\beta(q)
 \le\frac12-2A_q+4A_q^2,
 \qquad
 A_q=\left(\frac1q\cot\frac{\pi}{2q}\right)^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:exponent}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
In the marked-dual construction every relation $qe_j=0$ is preserved,
so the limit dual also has exponent dividing $q$.  Its finitely
generated subgroups are finite with exponent dividing $q$.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:60:norm:lem:finite-approximation} therefore returns to finite
groups in the same class, with no torus approximation needed.  The
proof of \eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:limit} gives the asserted equality.

Every nontrivial character has odd order at most $q$.  The quantity
$a_r=r^{-1}\cot(\pi/(2r))$ is increasing in $r$: after putting
$t=\pi/(2r)$, this follows from
\[
 \frac{d}{dt}(t\cot t)
 =\frac{\sin t\cos t-t}{\sin^2t}<0.
\]
Thus Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:60:norm:lem:coefficient} bounds every pair mass by $A_q$.
Since $1/4<A_q<1/2$, the same mass-cap calculation as in
Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:60:norm:prop:cap} proves \eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:exponent}.
\end{proof}

For example, the upper bounds for $q=3,5,7$ are respectively
\[
 \frac5{18}=0.277777\ldots,
 \qquad0.3164458247200069\ldots,
 \qquad0.3303703837266131\ldots.
\]
These are bounds for the limits within fixed exponent classes and are
not asserted sharp.  Their being below $1/3$ is consistent with
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:60:norm:thm:large-characteristic}: the latter allows the
characteristic to tend to infinity, whereas these classes keep it fixed.


The compactness proof separates Fourier tail control, algebraic relations,
and boundedness of the limit. The resulting extremal and quantitative
questions are developed in Section~\ref{gsr:fz:60:sec:questions}.
