\section[{Fourier fibers and the progression operator\srctag{94}}]{Fourier fibers and the progression operator}\label{gsr:cc:94:sec:d2}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:sec-fibers}
\srcnote{94}{Section 2}

\subsection{Fourier conventions}
Let $\Gamma=\widehat G$ and $\Delta=\widehat D$, written additively.
For $\xi\in\Gamma$,
\[
 \widehat f(\xi)=\stE_{x\in G}f(x)\overline{\xi(x)},\qquad
 f(x)=\sum_{\xi\in\Gamma}\widehat f(\xi)\xi(x).
\]
Thus Parseval gives
$\stnorm f_{L^2}^2=\sum_\xi|\widehat f(\xi)|^2$.
The normalized $U^2$ norm is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:u2-definition}
 \stnorm f_{U^2}^4
 =\stE_{x,h_1,h_2}f(x)\overline{f(x+h_1)f(x+h_2)}f(x+h_1+h_2)
 =\sum_\xi|\widehat f(\xi)|^4.
\end{equation}
The last identity follows by Fourier expansion and character
orthogonality; it also proves that the cube average is nonnegative.

Let $a=A^*: \Gamma\to\Delta$ and $b=B^*: \Gamma\to\Delta$ be the dual
homomorphisms. Set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:subgroups}
 U=\stker a,\quad V=\stker b,\quad L=U\cap V,\quad K=U+V,
 \quad W=\stker(a-b),\quad I=\stim a\cap\stim b.
\end{equation}
We have $|U|=u$, $|V|=v$, $|L|=\ell$, and $|K|=k$.
Indeed, $U=A(D)^\perp$, $V=B(D)^\perp$, and
$L=(A(D)+B(D))^\perp$. Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:k-image}
 K=(A(D)\cap B(D))^\perp,\qquad k=[G:A(D)\cap B(D)].
\end{equation}
For completeness, the latter equality follows because $U+V$ is contained
in the indicated annihilator and the two groups have the same cardinality,
using $|U+V|=|U||V|/|U\cap V|$ and the analogous identity for the image
subgroups.

\begin{lemma}[Fourier identity]\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:lem-fourier}
Writing $F=\widehat f_0$, $G_1=\widehat f_1$, and $G_2=\widehat f_2$, one has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:fourier-identity}
 \stLa(f_0,f_1,f_2)
 =\sum_{\substack{\beta,\gamma\in\Gamma\\a\beta+b\gamma=0}}
 F(-\beta-\gamma)G_1(\beta)G_2(\gamma).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Expanding the three functions introduces frequencies
$\alpha,\beta,\gamma$. Averaging over $x$ imposes
$\alpha+\beta+\gamma=0$, and averaging over $d$ imposes
$a\beta+b\gamma=0$. Both averages are exactly $1$ when the respective
character is trivial and $0$ otherwise. There is no additional factor
of $|G|$ or $|D|$.
\end{proof}

For $F:\Gamma\to\stC$, define a matrix with counting-measure row and
column spaces $\ell^2(\Gamma)$ by
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:matrix}
 M_F(\beta,\gamma)=
 F(-\beta-\gamma)\stind_{a\beta+b\gamma=0}.
\end{equation}
We use the Hermitian inner product
$\stip{r}{s}=\sum\overline r\,s$. Explicitly,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:matrix-pairing}
 \stLa(f_0,f_1,f_2)
 =\stip{\overline{G_1}}{M_FG_2}.
\end{equation}
Equivalently, the right side is
$\sum_{\beta,\gamma}G_1(\beta)M_F(\beta,\gamma)G_2(\gamma)$.

\subsection{The rectangular blocks}
For each $t\in I$, define
\[
 R_t=a^{-1}(t),\qquad C_t=b^{-1}(-t).
\]
The nonzero part of $M_F$ is a direct sum of rectangular blocks with rows
$R_t$ and columns $C_t$. Rows or columns not belonging to these sets are
zero. Choose $\beta_t\in R_t$, $\gamma_t\in C_t$ and put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:accessible-coset}
 S_t=-\beta_t-\gamma_t+K.
\end{equation}
This coset is independent of the choices. After permuting rows and
columns, the block takes the form
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:hankel-block}
 H_{F,s}(u_0,v_0)=F(s+u_0+v_0),\qquad (u_0,v_0)\in U\times V,
\end{equation}
where $s+K=S_t$. The permutations are obtained by writing
$\beta=\beta_t-u_0$ and $\gamma=\gamma_t-v_0$ and adjusting $s$ within
its coset if needed.

\begin{lemma}[Uniform fiber multiplicity]\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:lem-fiber}
Every element of $s+K$ occurs exactly $\ell$ times in the array
$F(s+u_0+v_0)$. Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:HS-fiber}
 \stnorm{H_{F,s}}_{\stHS}^2
 =\ell\sum_{\alpha\in s+K}|F(\alpha)|^2.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The map $U\times V\to K$ sending $(u_0,v_0)$ to $u_0+v_0$ is onto and
has kernel $\{(z,-z):z\in L\}$, of cardinality $\ell$. All fibers of a
homomorphism have its kernel cardinality. Summing squared entry
magnitudes gives \eqref{gsr:cc:94:st3:HS-fiber}.
\end{proof}

Define the accessible frequency subgroup
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:sigma}
 \Sigma=\{-\beta-\gamma:a\beta+b\gamma=0\}\le\Gamma.
\end{equation}
It contains $K$, and the distinct block supports are precisely the
cosets in $\Sigma/K$.

\begin{proposition}[Multiplicity of a support coset]\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:prop-multiplicity}
Every coset in $\Sigma/K$ occurs as $S_t$ for exactly
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:multiplicity}
 m=|W|/\ell
\end{equation}
values of $t\in I$. All blocks with the same support coset are row and
column permutations of one another.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The map $I\to\Gamma/K$, $t\mapsto S_t$, is a homomorphism, and its image
is $\Sigma/K$. To compute its kernel, suppose $S_t=K$. Adjust
$\beta_t$ by an element of $U$ and $\gamma_t$ by an element of $V$ to
arrange $\gamma_t=-\beta_t$. The constraint then says
$(a-b)\beta_t=0$, so $t\in a(W)$. Conversely, $\beta\in W$ yields the
pair $(\beta,-\beta)$ and hence the zero support coset. Thus the kernel
is $a(W)$. The kernel of $a|_W$ is $L$, proving
$|a(W)|=|W|/\ell$.

If two representatives $s,s'$ lie in the same $K$-coset, write
$s'-s=u_1+v_1$ with $u_1\in U$, $v_1\in V$. Translating the row
variable by $u_1$ and the column variable by $v_1$ identifies the two
arrays in \eqref{gsr:cc:94:st3:hankel-block}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The sharp constant will depend on $U,V,L$, but the multiplicity $m$
remembers the additional map $a-b$. Thus identical increment images do
not imply identical equality spaces or identical blind frequencies.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The exact Fourier-norm diagram\srctag{94}}]{The exact Fourier-norm diagram}\label{gsr:cc:94:sec:d3}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:sec-constants}
\srcnote{94}{Section 3}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp constants for all $p$]\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:thm-constants}
For arbitrary finite abelian $G,D$, arbitrary homomorphisms $A,B:D\to G$,
and $1\le p\le\infty$, the least constant in
\eqref{gsr:fm:94:st3:headline-p} is \eqref{gsr:fm:94:st3:headline-cp}. The constant remains
optimal when all three inputs are required to be subgroup indicators.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
It is enough to estimate $\stnorm{M_F}_{\stOp}$ in terms of
$\stnorm F_{\ell^p}$, since Fourier transformation is an isometry from
normalized $L^2$ to counting-measure $\ell^2$.

Suppose first that $2\le p\le\infty$. A matrix has operator norm at
most its Hilbert--Schmidt norm. For a block supported on $S=s+K$,
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:94:st3:lem-fiber} and finite-set H\"older give
\begin{align}
 \stnorm{H_{F,s}}_{\stOp}
 &\le\sqrt\ell\left(\sum_{\alpha\in S}|F(\alpha)|^2\right)^{1/2}
 \label{gsr:cc:94:st3:block-bound}\\
 &\le\sqrt\ell\,k^{1/2-1/p}
       \left(\sum_{\alpha\in S}|F(\alpha)|^p\right)^{1/p}
 \le (uv)^{1/2}k^{-1/p}\stnorm F_{\ell^p}.
 \nonumber
\end{align}
At $p=\infty$ the middle expression has its usual supremum interpretation.
Taking the maximum over blocks proves the upper bound for $p\ge2$.

For $1\le p\le2$, fix unit vectors $r,q\in\ell^2(\Gamma)$ and collect
coefficients of $F$ in $\langle r,M_Fq\rangle$:
\[
 z(\alpha)=\sum_{\substack{\beta+\gamma=-\alpha\\a\beta+b\gamma=0}}
                 \overline{r(\beta)}q(\gamma).
\]
For fixed $\alpha$, the sum is over part of the bijection
$\gamma=-\alpha-\beta$, so Cauchy--Schwarz gives
$\stnorm z_{\ell^\infty}\le1$. The already proved $p=2$ bound, by
finite-dimensional duality, gives $\stnorm z_{\ell^2}\le\sqrt\ell$.
If $p'$ is conjugate to $p$, then $p'\ge2$ and
\[
 \stnorm z_{\ell^{p'}}
 \le \stnorm z_{\ell^\infty}^{1-2/p'}
       \stnorm z_{\ell^2}^{2/p'}
 \le\ell^{1/p'}.
\]
For finite $p'$, the first inequality follows simply by summing
$|z|^{p'}\le\stnorm z_\infty^{p'-2}|z|^2$; $p'=\infty$ is immediate.
H\"older now bounds $|\langle r,M_Fq\rangle|$ by
$\ell^{1-1/p}\stnorm F_{\ell^p}$. Taking the supremum over $r,q$
proves the remaining upper bounds.

We prove sharpness directly with physical-space indicators. Write
$H_A=A(D)$ and $H_B=B(D)$. For $p\ge2$, take
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:large-p-witness}
 f_0=\stind_{H_A\cap H_B},\qquad
 f_1=\stind_{H_A},\qquad f_2=\stind_{H_B}.
\end{equation}
If $x\in H_A\cap H_B$, the other two indicators equal $1$ for every
$d$; otherwise $f_0(x)=0$. Therefore the average is $1/k$.
The Fourier transform of a subgroup indicator of index $j$ equals
$j^{-1}$ on its annihilator and $0$ elsewhere. Hence
\[
 \stnorm{\widehat f_0}_{\ell^p}=k^{1/p-1},\qquad
 \stnorm{f_1}_{L^2}=u^{-1/2},\qquad
 \stnorm{f_2}_{L^2}=v^{-1/2}.
\]
The resulting ratio is $(uv)^{1/2}k^{-1/p}$.

For $p\le2$, take all three inputs to be
$\stind_{H_A+H_B}$. The average is $1/\ell$, the marked Fourier norm
is $\ell^{1/p-1}$, and the product of the two $L^2$ norms is
$1/\ell$. The ratio is $\ell^{1-1/p}$. These calculations also apply
at $p=1,2,\infty$ with the stated conventions.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 82--94]
\emph{In this report.} The endpoint factor $|G[2]|^{1/4}$ of source~10 (Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:10:prop:torsion-sharpness} and its Section~\ref{gsr:cc:10:sec:d6}) is the case $(A,B)=(1,2)$ on even cyclic groups, where $u=\ell=1$, $v=2$ (checked at the write); in cyclic form the $U^2$ constant is $(\gcd(N,r)\gcd(N,s)\gcd(N,r,s))^{1/4}$. This answers source~20's question on the full operator norm (its Question~4) for three-term systems (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:torsion}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{corollary}[Sharp generalized von Neumann estimate]\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:cor-u2}
For every system \eqref{gsr:fm:94:st3:def-lambda}, inequality
\eqref{gsr:fm:94:st3:headline-u2} holds and is sharp, including within the class of
indicator inputs. No hypothesis on $A-B$ is required.
\end{corollary}

\subsection{A genuine improvement over a coarse universal estimate}
The elementary entrywise bound on a $u\times v$ block gives
\[
 |\stLa(f_0,f_1,f_2)|
 \le\sqrt{uv}\stnorm{\widehat f_0}_{\ell^\infty}
                     \stnorm{f_1}_{L^2}\stnorm{f_2}_{L^2}.
\]
Replacing the Fourier maximum by the Fourier $\ell^4$ norm in this
inequality would retain $\sqrt{uv}$. The sharp $U^2$ coefficient improves
that coefficient by the factor
\[
 \frac{\sqrt{uv}}{(uv\ell)^{1/4}}=k^{1/4}.
\]
This is an arbitrarily large improvement as the system varies, not merely
an optimization of a decimal constant. The underlying reason is uniform
fiber multiplicity, rather than a repeated use of the largest entry.

\subsection{Cyclic and product systems}
For $G=D=\stZ/N\stZ$, $Ad=rd$ and $Bd=sd$, the exact $U^2$ coefficient is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:cyclic}
 C_4=\bigl(\gcd(N,r)\gcd(N,s)\gcd(N,r,s)\bigr)^{1/4}.
\end{equation}
We use $\gcd(N,0)=N$. In particular, coincident or zero slopes cause
no exceptional case in the statement.

\begin{example}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:ex-commonkernel}
For $(N,r,s)=(12,4,6)$, the parameters are
$(u,v,\ell,k)=(4,6,2,12)$ and $C_4=48^{1/4}$.
Omitting the common-kernel factor would give $24^{1/4}$ and would be
false. The indicators of $\{0\}$, $\{0,4,8\}$ and $\{0,6\}$ attain
$48^{1/4}$.
\end{example}

If $A=B$ is surjective, then $u=v=\ell=1$, and the coefficient is $1$,
even though $A-B=0$. Thus a kernel factor involving $A-B$ cannot simply
be multiplied into the sharp constant. When $A=B=0$, the coefficient is
$|G|^{3/4}$; all three point indicators attain it.

\begin{corollary}[Exact tensorization]\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:cor-tensor}
For a direct product of two increment systems, the optimal constant
$C_p$ is the product of the two optimal constants, for every
$1\le p\le\infty$. This holds for arbitrary functions on the product,
not only for tensor-product inputs.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The kernel cardinalities $u,v,\ell$ multiply under direct products, so
both formulas in \eqref{gsr:fm:94:st3:headline-cp} multiply. Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:94:st3:thm-constants}
already bounds arbitrary inputs, and product subgroup indicators attain
the result.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The complete singular spectrum\srctag{94}}]{The complete singular spectrum}\label{gsr:cc:94:sec:d4}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:sec-spectrum}
\srcnote{94}{Section 4}

The coefficient in Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:94:st3:thm-constants} is an extremal statement
over $F$. For an individual $F$, it may be very wasteful. We now give an
exact formula which is also the structural input for stability.

\subsection{Fourier decomposition along the common kernel}
Choose representatives $r_i$ for $U/L$ and $t_j$ for $V/L$. Every element
of $K$ has a unique representation
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:unique-coordinates}
 r_i+t_j+z,\qquad z\in L.
\end{equation}
Indeed, the natural map $(U/L)\oplus(V/L)\to K/L$ is an isomorphism.
No group-theoretic splitting of $L$ inside $U$ or $V$ is being assumed;
we only choose set-theoretic representatives.

For $s+K\in\Sigma/K$ and $\chi\in\widehat L$, form the
$(u/\ell)\times(v/\ell)$ matrix
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:small-matrix}
 T_{s,\chi}(i,j)
 =\frac1\ell\sum_{z\in L}
       F(s+r_i+t_j+z)\overline{\chi(z)}.
\end{equation}
Changing representatives changes these matrices by diagonal unitary
factors, row or column permutations, and the corresponding equivalent
coordinate identifications. Their singular values, taken together, are
therefore independent of the choices; this also follows directly from
the next proof.

\begin{theorem}[Exact singular-spectrum formula]\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:thm-spectrum}
The nonzero singular values of $M_F$ are the nonzero singular values of
all matrices $\ell T_{s,\chi}$, for $s+K\in\Sigma/K$ and
$\chi\in\widehat L$, each repeated $m=|W|/\ell$ times. In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:exact-op}
 \stnorm{M_F}_{\stOp}
 =\ell\max_{s+K\in\Sigma/K}\max_{\chi\in\widehat L}
                         \stnorm{T_{s,\chi}}_{\stOp}.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Consider a single block $H_{F,s}$. Its rows have unique coordinates
$r_i+z_1$, and its columns have unique coordinates $t_j+z_2$, with
$z_1,z_2\in L$. Fourier inversion on $L$ gives
\[
 H_{F,s}(r_i+z_1,t_j+z_2)
 =\sum_{\chi\in\widehat L}T_{s,\chi}(i,j)\chi(z_1)\chi(z_2).
\]
For a vector $q=(q_j)$, put
$v(t_j+z_2)=\ell^{-1/2}q_j\overline{\chi(z_2)}$.
Then direct summation over $z_2$ gives
\[
 (H_{F,s}v)(r_i+z_1)
 =\ell^{-1/2}\chi(z_1)\bigl(\ell T_{s,\chi}q\bigr)_i.
\]
For different $\chi$, the input spaces are orthogonal and the output
spaces are orthogonal. The two Fourier coordinate changes are unitary
for counting-measure $\ell^2$. Thus the block is unitarily equivalent,
with possibly different input and output unitaries, to the direct sum
of $\ell T_{s,\chi}$ over $\chi$.

Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:94:st3:prop-multiplicity} says that each support coset
contributes $m$ permutation-equivalent blocks. Combining the block
spectra proves the theorem, including the multiplicities. Zero rows,
zero columns, and zero singular values introduce no additional nonzero
values.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The exact progression-control seminorm]\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:cor-control}
Define
\[
 \stV(f)=\sup_{\stnorm g_{L^2}=\stnorm h_{L^2}=1}
                         |\stLa(f,g,h)|.
\]
Then $\stV(f)=\stnorm{M_{\widehat f}}_{\stOp}$, given explicitly by
\eqref{gsr:cc:94:st3:exact-op}. Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:blind}
 \stV(f)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
             \widehat f(\alpha)=0\text{ for every }\alpha\in\Sigma.
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The supremum equals the matrix operator norm by Parseval and
\eqref{gsr:cc:94:st3:matrix-pairing}. If $\widehat f$ vanishes on $\Sigma$, every
entry is zero. Conversely, every $\alpha\in\Sigma$ occurs as an entry,
so a nonzero coefficient there gives a nonzero matrix.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Size of the exact calculation}
There are $|\Sigma/K|\ell$ reduced matrices, each with
$(u/\ell)(v/\ell)$ entries. Their total number of entries is
\[
 |\Sigma/K|\ell\frac{uv}{\ell^2}=|\Sigma|.
\]
Consequently the reduction reorganizes exactly the accessible Fourier
coefficients, rather than introducing a new ambient square matrix.
The repeated multiplicity $m$ need not be materialized when computing
an operator norm. Fourier transformation on $L$ and singular-value
calculations on the reduced matrices suffice.

This is not a claim of a uniform fast algorithm for every representation
of every finite group. It is an exact algebraic reduction once the
finite group, the homomorphisms, and the Fourier coefficients are given.
The supplied implementation uses explicit finite coordinates rather
than asymptotically optimized group algorithms.

\subsection{A worked nontrivial common-kernel example}
For $(N,r,s)=(12,4,6)$ from Example~\ref{gsr:cc:94:st3:ex-commonkernel},
\[
 U=\{0,3,6,9\},\quad V=\{0,2,4,6,8,10\},\quad L=\{0,6\}.
\]
There is one support coset, $K=\stZ/12\stZ$, and $m=1$.
Take $r_i\in\{0,3\}$ and $t_j\in\{0,2,4\}$. The two reduced matrices
are
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:worked-matrix}
 T_\pm=\frac12
 \begin{pmatrix}
 F(0)\pm F(6)&F(2)\pm F(8)&F(4)\pm F(10)\\
 F(3)\pm F(9)&F(5)\pm F(11)&F(7)\pm F(1)
 \end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation}
The exact control seminorm is $2\max(\stnorm{T_+}_{\stOp},
\stnorm{T_-}_{\stOp})$. A $4\times6$ constrained Fourier block has
become two $2\times3$ matrices, with all multiplicities accounted for.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{All complex extremizers above the Hilbert exponent\srctag{94}}]{All complex extremizers above the Hilbert exponent}\label{gsr:cc:94:sec:d5}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:sec-equality}
\srcnote{94}{Section 5}

\begin{definition}[Compatible separated phase]\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:def-phase}
Fix $s+K\in\Sigma/K$ and representatives as in
\eqref{gsr:cc:94:st3:unique-coordinates}. A unimodular function $\Phi:s+K\to\stT$
is a compatible separated phase if
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:phase}
 \Phi(s+r_i+t_j+z)=\rho_i\sigma_j\chi(z),
 \qquad |\rho_i|=|\sigma_j|=1,\quad\chi\in\widehat L.
\end{equation}
This property is independent of the representatives. Equivalently,
the full $U\times V$ matrix $\Phi(s+u_0+v_0)$ has rank one.
\end{definition}

We justify the equivalence as part of the following lemma; it is
important that arbitrary functions on the sum coset are \emph{not}
automatically separated phases.

\begin{lemma}[Rank-one compatibility]\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:lem-rank-one}
For a nonzero function $F$ supported on $s+K$, the matrix $H_{F,s}$
has rank one if and only if exactly one matrix $T_{s,\chi}$ is nonzero
and that matrix has rank one. If in addition $|F|$ is constant on the
coset, then $F$ is a scalar multiple of a compatible separated phase.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Unitary equivalence in Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:94:st3:thm-spectrum} gives
\[
 \strank H_{F,s}=\sum_{\chi\in\widehat L}\strank T_{s,\chi}.
\]
Thus rank one is equivalent to precisely one nonzero rank-one character
sector. Fourier inversion gives
$F(s+r_i+t_j+z)=c_i d_j\chi(z)$ in that case. If the modulus of $F$
is a positive constant, every $c_i$ and $d_j$ is nonzero and
$|c_i||d_j|$ is independent of $i,j$. It follows separately that
$|c_i|$ is constant in $i$ and $|d_j|$ is constant in $j$. Dividing
by these magnitudes gives \eqref{gsr:cc:94:st3:phase}. Conversely, the formula
\eqref{gsr:cc:94:st3:phase} is visibly a rank-one array after writing rows and
columns in their $L$-coset coordinates.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Equality classification]\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:thm-equality}
Let $2<p<\infty$ and $\stnorm F_{\ell^p}=1$. Then
$\stnorm{M_F}_{\stOp}=C_p$ if and only if there is a coset
$S=s+K\in\Sigma/K$ and a compatible separated phase $\Phi$ on $S$ such
that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:extremal-F}
 F=k^{-1/p}\Phi\stind_S.
\end{equation}
For such an $F$, the operator $J=M_F/C_p$ is a partial isometry of rank
$m=|W|/\ell$. A normalized pair $g,h\in\ell^2(\Gamma)$ satisfies
$|\langle g,M_Fh\rangle|=C_p$ if and only if
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:extremal-pair}
 h\text{ lies in the initial space of }J,
 \qquad g=\zeta Jh\quad\text{for some }|\zeta|=1.
\end{equation}
Together with $g=\overline{\widehat f_1}$ and $h=\widehat f_2$,
these conditions classify all normalized complex extremizing triples.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If the operator norm equals $C_p$, some block attains equality in every
step of \eqref{gsr:cc:94:st3:block-bound}. Equality in the last step, with $p$
finite, forces all Fourier $\ell^p$ mass onto that block's support
coset $S$. Equality in the finite-set $\ell^2$--$\ell^p$ comparison,
with $p>2$, forces constant modulus on all $k$ points of $S$.
Equality between operator and Hilbert--Schmidt norm forces rank one.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:94:st3:lem-rank-one} now gives \eqref{gsr:cc:94:st3:extremal-F}.

Conversely, \eqref{gsr:cc:94:st3:extremal-F} gives a rank-one block whose
Hilbert--Schmidt norm equals $C_p$. Every block on the same support
coset is permutation-equivalent; all other blocks vanish. There are
exactly $m$ such blocks. Each contributes one singular value $C_p$,
so $M_F/C_p$ is a rank-$m$ partial isometry.

For a partial isometry, $\stnorm{Jh}\le\stnorm h$ with equality
exactly on its initial space. Equality in
$|\langle g,Jh\rangle|\le\stnorm g\,\stnorm{Jh}\le1$ then gives
\eqref{gsr:cc:94:st3:extremal-pair}, and the converse is immediate.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Two instructive special cases}
If $L=\{0\}$, then $K=U\oplus V$. A compatible separated phase has
arbitrary unimodular factors on $U$ and $V$; it need not be a group
character. When $U=V=L$, by contrast, both quotient sets have one
point, so the compatible phases on $s+L$ are exactly a constant times
a character of $L$.

For $G=\stZ/12\stZ$, compare $(r,s)=(4,4)$ and $(4,8)$. Both have
$u=v=\ell=k=4$ and therefore the same sharp coefficient $4^{3/4}$.
In the first system, $|W|=12$, $m=3$, and $\Sigma=K$: only one support
coset is accessible, repeated three times. In the second system,
$|W|=4$, $m=1$, and $\Sigma=\Gamma$: all three $K$-cosets are
accessible, once each. Equality spaces and invisible frequencies are
different despite identical sharp constants.

\begin{remark}[Why the endpoints $p=2,\infty$ are excluded]
At $p=2$, the finite-set norm comparison is an identity and does not
force flat modulus. At $p=\infty$, coefficients outside an extremizing
coset need not vanish. The equality theorem is intentionally stated
only for $2<p<\infty$; its $p=4$ case is the one needed below.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Dimension-free stability with optimal exponents\srctag{94}}]{Dimension-free stability with optimal exponents}\label{gsr:cc:94:sec:d6}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:sec-stability}
\srcnote{94}{Section 6}

Set $C=C_4=(uv\ell)^{1/4}$, so that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:C-square}
 C^2=\ell\sqrt k.
\end{equation}
We work first in Fourier space, where the estimates are most transparent.

\begin{theorem}[Quantitative stability]\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:thm-stability}
Suppose $\stnorm F_{\ell^4}=\stnorm g_{\ell^2}=
\stnorm h_{\ell^2}=1$ and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:near-equality}
 |\langle g,M_Fh\rangle|\ge(1-\varepsilon)C,
 \qquad 0\le\varepsilon\le1/64.
\end{equation}
Then there exist $F^\star,g^\star,h^\star$ with the same three
normalizations and
\[
 |\langle g^\star,M_{F^\star}h^\star\rangle|=C
\]
such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:stability-bounds}
 \stnorm{F-F^\star}_{\ell^4}\le4\varepsilon^{1/4},\qquad
 \stnorm{g-g^\star}_{\ell^2}\le7\sqrt\varepsilon,\qquad
 \stnorm{h-h^\star}_{\ell^2}\le7\sqrt\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
The marked extremizer is supported on a single accessible coset $S$,
and that coset also satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:stability-localization}
 \sum_{\alpha\notin S}|F(\alpha)|^4\le4\varepsilon,
 \qquad
 \stnorm{|F|^2-k^{-1/2}\stind_S}_{\ell^2}\le2\sqrt\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
All constants are independent of the groups and homomorphisms.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If $\varepsilon=0$, Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:94:st3:thm-equality} applies. Assume
$\varepsilon>0$. We give the estimates in separate steps, keeping the
normalizations explicit.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{Step 1: choose a large block and localize its mass.}
By \eqref{gsr:cc:94:st3:near-equality}, the largest singular value of $M_F$ is at
least $(1-\varepsilon)C$. Choose a block $H=H_{F,s}$ containing such a
largest singular value $\sigma$, and put $S=s+K$. We have
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:sigma-chain}
 (1-\varepsilon)C\le\sigma\le\stnorm H_{\stHS}
 =\left(\ell\sum_S|F|^2\right)^{1/2}
 \le C\left(\sum_S|F|^4\right)^{1/4}\le C.
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:mass-bounds}
 \sum_S|F|^4\ge(1-\varepsilon)^4,
 \qquad
 \sum_S|F|^2\ge(1-\varepsilon)^2\sqrt k.
\end{equation}
The first inequality gives the first claim of
\eqref{gsr:cc:94:st3:stability-localization}. For the second claim, expand the
square, using $\sum_\Gamma|F|^4=1$:
\begin{align}
 \stnorm{|F|^2-k^{-1/2}\stind_S}_{\ell^2}^2
 &=2-2k^{-1/2}\sum_S|F|^2\nonumber\\
 &\le2\bigl(1-(1-\varepsilon)^2\bigr)\le4\varepsilon.
 \label{gsr:cc:94:st3:squared-amplitude}
\end{align}

\medskip\noindent\textbf{Step 2: choose a compatible best rank-one matrix.}
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:94:st3:thm-spectrum} decomposes $H$ into orthogonal character
sectors. Choose a top singular pair in one sector attaining $\sigma$.
Its rank-one lift has the form
\[
 R=\sigma ef^*,\qquad\stnorm{e}_{\ell^2}=\stnorm{f}_{\ell^2}=1,
\]
where, in $L$-coset coordinates,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:sector-vectors}
 e(r_i+z)=\ell^{-1/2}p_i\chi(z),\qquad
 f(t_j+z)=\ell^{-1/2}q_j\overline{\chi(z)}
\end{equation}
for some unit vectors $p,q$ and $\chi\in\widehat L$.
The singular-value identity gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:rank-one-error}
 \stnorm{H-R}_{\stHS}^2
 =\stnorm H_{\stHS}^2-\sigma^2
 \le(2\varepsilon-\varepsilon^2)C^2\le2\varepsilon C^2.
\end{equation}

\medskip\noindent\textbf{Step 3: flatten within that same character sector.}
Let $c=k^{-1/4}$. Replace $p_i$ and $q_j$ by their phases and flatten
the moduli of the full vectors to $|U|^{-1/2}$ and $|V|^{-1/2}$.
At a zero coordinate, choose any phase on that quotient coordinate and
extend using the same character in \eqref{gsr:cc:94:st3:sector-vectors}. Denote the
resulting unit vectors by $e_0,f_0$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:Q-block}
 Q=C e_0f_0^*.
\end{equation}
Every entry of $Q$ has modulus
$C/\sqrt{uv}=c$. Its phase is the entrywise phase of $R$ wherever
$R$ is nonzero, and its character compatibility is exact. Thus $Q$ is
$H_{F^\star,s}$ for a function $F^\star$ of the form
\eqref{gsr:cc:94:st3:extremal-F}, supported on $S$ and normalized in $\ell^4$.

We first bound the amplitude discrepancy of $H$. Since
$||z|-c|\le c^{-1}\bigl||z|^2-c^2\bigr|$, fiber multiplicity and
\eqref{gsr:cc:94:st3:squared-amplitude} give
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:flat-amplitude}
 \stnorm{|H|-c}_{\stHS}^2
 =\ell\sum_S(|F|-c)^2
 \le4\varepsilon\ell\sqrt k=4\varepsilon C^2.
\end{equation}
The reverse triangle inequality for complex numbers now yields
\begin{align}
 \stnorm{R-Q}_{\stHS}
 &=\stnorm{|R|-c}_{\stHS}
 \le\stnorm{H-R}_{\stHS}+\stnorm{|H|-c}_{\stHS}
 \le(\sqrt2+2)C\sqrt\varepsilon,
 \label{gsr:cc:94:st3:R-Q}\\
 \stnorm{H-Q}_{\stHS}
 &\le(2\sqrt2+2)C\sqrt\varepsilon
 <5C\sqrt\varepsilon.
 \label{gsr:cc:94:st3:H-Q}
\end{align}
The identity in the first line remains true at zero entries because
$|Q|=c$ there.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{Step 4: obtain a dimension-free Fourier $\ell^4$ estimate.}
By fiber multiplicity, \eqref{gsr:cc:94:st3:H-Q} implies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:F-l2}
 \stnorm{F\stind_S-F^\star}_{\ell^2}
 <5k^{1/4}\sqrt\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
The factor $k^{1/4}$ must not be mistaken for a dimension-free
$\ell^4$ bound. We remove it explicitly. Put
$D_0=F\stind_S-F^\star$ and $X=\stnorm{D_0}_{\ell^4}^2$.
Pointwise on $S$,
$|D_0|^2\le2(|F|^2+c^2)$. Therefore
\begin{align}
 X^2
 &\le4c^2\stnorm{D_0}_{\ell^2}^2
   +2\sum_S|D_0|^2\bigl(|F|^2-c^2\bigr)\nonumber\\
 &\le100\varepsilon+4X\sqrt\varepsilon.
 \label{gsr:cc:94:st3:X-quadratic}
\end{align}
The last step uses Cauchy--Schwarz and
\eqref{gsr:cc:94:st3:squared-amplitude}. Solving the quadratic inequality gives
\[
 X\le(2+\sqrt{104})\sqrt\varepsilon<13\sqrt\varepsilon.
\]
The mass outside $S$ is at most $4\varepsilon$, so
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:marked-final}
 \stnorm{F-F^\star}_{\ell^4}^4
 <169\varepsilon+4\varepsilon
 <256\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
This proves the marked estimate with constant $4$.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{Step 5: compare the singular vectors before and after flattening.}
Choose the phases of $e_0,f_0$ as above. Then
$r=\langle e,e_0\rangle$ and $t=\langle f,f_0\rangle$ are real numbers
in $[0,1]$. Squaring \eqref{gsr:cc:94:st3:R-Q} and using $\sqrt2+2<\sqrt{12}$
gives
\[
 (\sigma-C)^2+2\sigma C(1-rt)
 =\stnorm{R-Q}_{\stHS}^2<12\varepsilon C^2.
\]
Since $\sigma\ge(1-\varepsilon)C$,
\[
 1-rt\le\frac{6\varepsilon}{1-\varepsilon}<7\varepsilon.
\]
As $r,t\in[0,1]$, each of $1-r$ and $1-t$ is at most $1-rt$.
Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:singular-vector-flat}
 \stnorm{e-e_0}_{\ell^2},\quad\stnorm{f-f_0}_{\ell^2}
 \le\sqrt{14\varepsilon}<4\sqrt\varepsilon.
\end{equation}

\medskip\noindent\textbf{Step 6: control all blocks, not just one.}
There are $m$ blocks with support $S$, and they are permutation-equivalent.
In each of them choose the corresponding translated singular pair
$(e_t,f_t)$. The top singular value $\sigma$ is simple inside each block:
indeed the sum of squares of the other singular values is at most
$2\varepsilon C^2$, whereas $\sigma^2\ge(1-\varepsilon)^2C^2$.
Let $P_h$ project onto the span of the $f_t$, let $P_g$ project onto the
span of the $e_t$, and let $J_0f_t=e_t$. These vectors have disjoint
block supports and form orthonormal families. On these spaces,
$M_FP_h=\sigma J_0P_h$.

Every other singular value of a block supported on $S$ is at most
$\sqrt{2\varepsilon}\,C$. Every block supported on a different coset
has, by \eqref{gsr:cc:94:st3:block-bound} at $p=4$ and the outside-mass bound,
operator norm at most $(4\varepsilon)^{1/4}C$.
Thus every singular value outside the chosen top spaces is at most
$\rho C$, where
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:rho}
 \rho=(4\varepsilon)^{1/4},\qquad
 \rho^2=2\sqrt\varepsilon\le1/4.
\end{equation}
From $\stnorm{M_Fh}\ge(1-\varepsilon)C$ and the spectral decomposition,
\[
 (1-\varepsilon)^2
 \le\stnorm{P_hh}^2+\rho^2\stnorm{(1-P_h)h}^2.
\]
The analogous inequality follows for $g$ using $M_F^*$. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:pair-outside}
 \stnorm{(1-P_h)h}^2,\quad\stnorm{(1-P_g)g}^2
 \le\frac{2\varepsilon-\varepsilon^2}{1-\rho^2}
 \le\frac83\varepsilon<3\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
This is the step that preserves the $\sqrt\varepsilon$ exponent for
both unmarked functions. Merely replacing $M_F$ by a nearby matrix in
operator norm would lose powers.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{Step 7: align and flatten the entire pair.}
Multiply $g$ by a unimodular scalar so that
$\langle g,M_Fh\rangle$ is real and nonnegative. We undo this scalar
at the end. The contribution from the orthogonal complementary spaces
has modulus at most $3\rho\varepsilon C$ by
\eqref{gsr:cc:94:st3:pair-outside}. Therefore
\[
 \operatorname{Re}\langle P_gg,J_0P_hh\rangle
 \ge1-(1+3\rho)\varepsilon.
\]
Let $n=\stnorm{P_hh}>0$, $h_R=P_hh/n$, and $g_R=J_0h_R$.
Both are unit vectors, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:pair-R}
 \stnorm{h-h_R}^2=2(1-n)\le6\varepsilon,
 \qquad
 \stnorm{g-g_R}^2\le2(1+3\rho)\varepsilon\le5\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
In deriving the second inequality, division by $n\le1$ can only
increase the positive real inner product just bounded below.

Write $h_R=\sum_t c_tf_t$ with $\sum_t|c_t|^2=1$.
For each support-$S$ block, use the translated flat vectors
$(e_{0,t},f_{0,t})$ from Step~3 and define
\[
 h^\star=\sum_t c_tf_{0,t},\qquad
 g^\star=\sum_t c_te_{0,t}.
\]
These are a unit extremizing pair for $M_{F^\star}$ because
$M_{F^\star}f_{0,t}=Ce_{0,t}$ in each block. Disjoint supports and
\eqref{gsr:cc:94:st3:singular-vector-flat} give
$\stnorm{h_R-h^\star},\stnorm{g_R-g^\star}<4\sqrt\varepsilon$.
Combining with \eqref{gsr:cc:94:st3:pair-R} gives the two bounds with constant $7$.
Finally undo the initial unimodular rotation of $g$ and apply it to
$g^\star$ as well. Distances and absolute equality are unchanged.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Physical-space form]\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:cor-physical-stability}
Under the normalizations in Section~1.1,
a triple satisfying
$|\stLa(f_0,f_1,f_2)|\ge(1-\varepsilon)C$ admits a normalized exact
extremizing triple with the bounds \eqref{gsr:fm:94:st3:headline-stability}.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Use $F=\widehat f_0$, $g=\overline{\widehat f_1}$ and $h=\widehat f_2$
in Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:94:st3:thm-stability}, then apply Fourier inversion,
Parseval, and \eqref{gsr:cc:94:st3:u2-definition}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[No unproved preservation assertion]
The repaired triple is a complex extremizer with the stated norm
normalizations. The theorem does not assert that it remains pointwise
bounded by $1$, real-valued, or an indicator triple when the original
triple has one of those properties. Sharpness within indicators and
stability to an indicator extremizer are different questions.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Optimality of the stability exponents}
\begin{proposition}[The powers cannot be improved]\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:prop-optimal-exponents}
In a theorem uniform over all systems, the marked exponent $1/4$ in
\eqref{gsr:cc:94:st3:stability-bounds} cannot be replaced by any larger exponent.
Neither unmarked exponent $1/2$ can be replaced by a larger exponent.
These obstructions already occur on $\stZ/5\stZ$ with $A=1$, $B=2$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For this system, $U=V=L=K=\{0\}$ and $\Sigma=\Gamma$.
The constrained matrix has one entry per row and column, and its
singular values are the numbers $|F(\alpha)|$. The equality theorem
says that a normalized marked extremizer is supported at a single
frequency with modulus $1$.

Choose two distinct frequencies $\alpha_0,\alpha_1$ and put
\[
 F_t=(1-t^4)^{1/4}\stind_{\{\alpha_0\}}+
                     t\stind_{\{\alpha_1\}},\qquad0<t<1/2.
\]
Choose the other two unit vectors to select the entry at $\alpha_0$.
The deficit is $\varepsilon_t=1-(1-t^4)^{1/4}\sim t^4/4$.
Every marked exact extremizer differs from $F_t$ in $\ell^4$ norm by
at least $t$: for support $\alpha_0$ this follows from the second
coefficient, and every other support misses the first coefficient,
whose modulus is greater than $t$. A bound with exponent greater than
$1/4$ is impossible.

For the unmarked exponent, keep $F=\stind_{\{\alpha_0\}}$ and its
unit row singular vector $g_0$. Let $h_0$ be its unit column singular
vector and $h_1$ a unit coordinate vector orthogonal to it. Set
$h_t=\sqrt{1-t^2}h_0+th_1$ and $g=g_0$. The deficit is
$1-\sqrt{1-t^2}\sim t^2/2$. Any exact triple close to the marked
function and to $g_0$ must use the same frequency block; its last
vector is a unimodular multiple of $h_0$, at distance at least $t$
from $h_t$. An exact triple using another block stays a fixed positive
distance away in the marked norm or the row norm. Thus no simultaneous
stability theorem with all errors tending to zero can improve the
last-vector exponent. Perturbing the row vector instead gives the
same conclusion for the first unmarked vector.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Ordinary progressions and quotient-corrected counting\srctag{94}}]{Ordinary progressions and quotient-corrected counting}\label{gsr:cc:94:sec:d7}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:sec-counting}
\srcnote{94}{Section 7}

Write
\[
 \Lambda_3(f_0,f_1,f_2)=\stE_{x,d\in G}f_0(x)f_1(x+d)f_2(x+2d),
 \qquad\tau=|G[2]|.
\]
Let $\Gamma[2]=\{\xi\in\Gamma:2\xi=0\}$; it has cardinality
$\tau$ and is the annihilator of $2G$.

\subsection{Exact endpoint and middle seminorms}
\begin{proposition}[Endpoint]\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:prop-endpoint}
For arbitrary complex $f$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:endpoint-exact}
 \sup_{\stnorm g_{L^2}=\stnorm h_{L^2}=1}|\Lambda_3(f,g,h)|
 =\max_{\eta\in2\Gamma}
        \left(\sum_{2\xi=\eta}|\widehat f(\xi)|^2\right)^{1/2}.
\end{equation}
Consequently the exact scalar $U^2$ coefficient at either endpoint is
$\tau^{1/4}$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Here $a=1$, $b=2$, so $U=\{0\}$, $V=\Gamma[2]$ and $L=\{0\}$.
Each block is a row vector indexed by a fiber of doubling. Its
operator norm is its Euclidean norm. Alternatively,
\[
 \Lambda_3(f,g,h)=\sum_\xi\widehat f(\xi)\widehat g(-2\xi)
                                      \widehat h(\xi)
\]
exhibits those fibers directly. Each has size $\tau$, and finite-set
H\"older gives $\tau^{1/4}\stnorm{\widehat f}_{\ell^4}$; the sharpness
also follows from Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:94:st3:thm-constants}. Reversing the
progression gives the same result at the other endpoint.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Middle]\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:prop-middle}
For arbitrary complex $f$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:middle-exact}
 \sup_{\stnorm g_{L^2}=\stnorm h_{L^2}=1}|\Lambda_3(g,f,h)|
 =\max_{\eta\in2\Gamma}|\widehat f(\eta)|.
\end{equation}
In particular, the middle $U^2$ coefficient is $1$ on every finite
abelian group, and all frequencies outside $2\Gamma$ are invisible
in the middle position.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Use the basepoint $y=x+d$. The marked middle function is evaluated at
$y$, and the other two arguments are $y-d$ and $y+d$. Thus the two
dual maps are $-1$ and $1$, both with trivial kernel, while
$\Sigma=2\Gamma$. Every block is $1\times1$, with entry a coefficient
of $f$ at a doubled frequency. The matrix norm is the displayed
maximum. Frequency multiplicities do not change an operator norm.
\end{proof}

The invisibility statement also has a physical explanation. Replacing
$d$ by $d+t$ for $t\in G[2]$ keeps the two endpoints fixed and moves
the middle by $t$. Hence only
$\stE_{t\in G[2]} f(y+t)$ matters in the middle.

\subsection{Three different sets and the correct main term}
Let $\mathcal A,\mathcal B,\mathcal C\subseteq G$, with densities
$\alpha,\beta,\gamma$. For a coset $q\in G/2G$, write
\[
 \alpha_q=\stE_{x\in q}\stind_{\mathcal A}(x),\qquad
 \gamma_q=\stE_{x\in q}\stind_{\mathcal C}(x).
\]
Define the within-coset variances
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:variances}
 V_{\mathcal A}=\alpha-\stE_q\alpha_q^2,\qquad
 V_{\mathcal C}=\gamma-\stE_q\gamma_q^2,
\end{equation}
and the visible nonconstant middle Fourier maximum
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:rho-B}
 \rho_{\mathcal B}
 =\max_{\eta\in2\Gamma\setminus\{0\}}
                       |\widehat{\stind_{\mathcal B}}(\eta)|,
\end{equation}
with maximum $0$ when the indexing set is empty.

\begin{theorem}[Quotient-corrected counting]\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:thm-counting}
For every finite abelian $G$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:counting}
 \left|\Lambda_3(\stind_{\mathcal A},\stind_{\mathcal B},
                          \stind_{\mathcal C})
       -\beta\stE_q\alpha_q\gamma_q\right|
 \le\rho_{\mathcal B}\sqrt{V_{\mathcal A}V_{\mathcal C}}.
\end{equation}
Let $\delta_{\mathcal A\cap\mathcal C}=|\mathcal A\cap\mathcal C|/|G|$.
The normalized number of ordered progressions with three distinct
vertices is at least
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:94:st3:proper-count}
 \beta\stE_q\alpha_q\gamma_q
 -\rho_{\mathcal B}\sqrt{V_{\mathcal A}V_{\mathcal C}}
 -\frac{\tau}{|G|}\delta_{\mathcal A\cap\mathcal C}.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Put $F=\widehat{\stind_{\mathcal A}}$, $H=\widehat{\stind_{\mathcal C}}$,
and $B_0=\widehat{\stind_{\mathcal B}}$. Fourier expansion gives
\[
 \Lambda_3=\sum_{\xi\in\Gamma}F(\xi)B_0(-2\xi)H(\xi).
\]
For $\xi\in\Gamma[2]$, the middle coefficient is $\beta$.
On this subgroup $-\xi=\xi$, so Fourier orthogonality on $G/2G$
gives
\[
 \sum_{\xi\in\Gamma[2]}F(\xi)H(\xi)
 =\stE_q\alpha_q\gamma_q.
\]
Equivalently, the left side is
$\stE_{x,d}\stind_{\mathcal A}(x)\stind_{\mathcal C}(x+2d)$,
because doubling sends uniform measure on $G$ to uniform measure
on $2G$.

The remaining middle coefficients have modulus at most
$\rho_{\mathcal B}$. Cauchy--Schwarz bounds the remaining sum by
\[
 \rho_{\mathcal B}
 \left(\sum_{\xi\notin\Gamma[2]}|F(\xi)|^2\right)^{1/2}
 \left(\sum_{\xi\notin\Gamma[2]}|H(\xi)|^2\right)^{1/2}.
\]
The two squared masses are exactly \eqref{gsr:cc:94:st3:variances}, by Parseval
and conditional expectation onto the $2G$-cosets. This proves
\eqref{gsr:cc:94:st3:counting}.

The vertices $x,x+d,x+2d$ fail to be pairwise distinct exactly when
$2d=0$. For each such $d$, the two endpoint indicators require
$x\in\mathcal A\cap\mathcal C$, and the middle indicator is at most
$1$. Thus the normalized number of degenerate progressions is at
most $(\tau/|G|)\delta_{\mathcal A\cap\mathcal C}$. Subtracting this
upper bound from the lower bound supplied by \eqref{gsr:cc:94:st3:counting}
proves \eqref{gsr:cc:94:st3:proper-count}.
\end{proof}

If $G$ has odd order, then $2G=G$, and the main term is
$\alpha\beta\gamma$, with
$V_{\mathcal A}=\alpha(1-\alpha)$ and
$V_{\mathcal C}=\gamma(1-\gamma)$.
If $G$ has exponent two, then $2G=\{0\}$,
$V_{\mathcal A}=V_{\mathcal C}=0$, and the formula becomes the exact
identity
\[
 \Lambda_3(\stind_{\mathcal A},\stind_{\mathcal B},\stind_{\mathcal C})
 =\beta\,\delta_{\mathcal A\cap\mathcal C}.
\]
All progressions in that case have repeated endpoints. Treating
$\alpha\beta\gamma$ as the universal main term would obscure this
basic obstruction.

For one set of density $\delta$, let
$M_2=\stE_q\delta_q^2$. The all-progressions lower bound is
$\delta M_2-(\delta-M_2)\rho_{\mathcal A}$, and the proper-progressions
lower bound subtracts $\tau\delta/|G|$. These are local sufficient
conditions for a progression, not a replacement for density-increment
arguments. They are also not claimed to dominate every existing
fourth-moment error bound in the single-set, odd-order setting.

\section{Source~93: a faster passage to the bounded endpoint of the odd-order constants \wtag}\label{gsr:cc:sec:fasterlimit}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the thirteenth write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next two sections are source~93's Sections~6--7. \emph{Logically they continue the chapter of sources~63 and~60} on the limit of the odd-order constants (Section~\ref{gsr:cc:sec:oddlimit}) and, before it, the chapter of sources~29 and~28 (Section~\ref{gsr:cc:sec:oddconstant}). Source~93 does not cite source~63, which was in \file{docs/incoming} at its pin; it credits the limit $1/3$ and an earlier rate $O(\sqrt d\,2^{-d/4})$ to the undelivered manuscript of Section~\ref{gsr:dt:sec:phifour} and reprints the inputs it takes from it (its Section~\ref{gsr:cc:93:sec:d6}). \emph{Source~63 is this report's first proof of the limit} (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:63:norm:main}: $1/3\le c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}\le1/3+10\cdot2^{-\lfloor d/8\rfloor}$ for $d\ge80$).

\emph{What source~93 proves here.} For every family $\mathcal F$ of finite odd-order abelian groups, $0\le c_d(\mathcal F)-D(\mathcal F)\le Cd2^{-d/2}$ with an absolute constant (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:93:norm:uniform-rate}), where $D(\mathcal F)$ is the bounded endpoint; a lower obstruction $c_d(\{\Z/3\Z\})-2/9\ge\frac89 2^{-d}((d+1)\log3-\log(2(d+1)))$ from $\norm{(0,1,-1)}_{U^d}^{2^d}=2(d+1)/3^{d+1}$, so no family-uniform rate beats $d2^{-d}$; and for each odd prime $c_d(\{\Z/p\Z\})=D_p+4D_p\log p\,d2^{-d}+O_p(\log d\,2^{-d})$, $D_p=(p^3-4p+3)/(3p^3)$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:93:norm:prime-rate}), through an exact cube polynomial for punctured sign functions (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:93:newnorm:prime-cube-polynomial}). \emph{Against source~63} (computed at the write): $D_p$ is source~63's bounded constant $b(\Z/p\Z)=1/3-4/(3p^2)+1/p^3$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:63:bounded:finite}); source~93's rate supersedes source~63's in order, $d2^{-d/2}$ against $2^{-\lfloor d/8\rfloor}$, but its constant $C$ is not explicit (finite parameter choices are certified), so source~63's explicit bound remains the only numerical one; and source~63's elementary fixed-group bound $c_d(G)\le b(G)N^{4(d+1)/2^d}=b(G)(1+4\log N\,(d+1)2^{-d}+O(d^24^{-d}))$ (its Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:63:norm:fixed-group}) has exactly source~93's first-order coefficient $4D_p\log p$ at $G=\Z/p\Z$, so source~93's theorem shows that this bound is sharp to first order on prime cyclic groups.

\emph{Relation to the formal statements} (checked at HEAD \texttt{bf285410b}). \file{gowersNorm} and \file{UniformOfDegree} (\file{Definitions.lean}, lines~178 and~167) define the norms; no declaration concerns the constants $c_d$, the bounded endpoint or their rates. Nothing in this chapter is formalized.

\section[{The bounded uniformity problem and its prior ingredients\srctag{93}}]{The bounded uniformity problem and its prior ingredients}\label{gsr:cc:93:sec:d6}
\srcnote{93}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:cc:93:sec:norm-prior}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 82--94]
\emph{Prior work in this report.} The bounded endpoint and the limit $1/3$ that this section takes from an undelivered manuscript (Section~\ref{gsr:dt:sec:phifour}) were proved earlier in this report by source~63, which this source does not cite: $\norm f_{U^2}^4\le(1/3-4/(3N^2)+1/N^3)\norm f_\infty^4$ on odd-order groups (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:63:bounded:finite}) and $1/3\le c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}\le1/3+10\cdot2^{-\lfloor d/8\rfloor}$ for $d\ge80$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:63:norm:main}). The section reproves what it uses.
\end{writenote}

\subsection{Normalization and the previously established bounded endpoint}

All group averages are normalized.  For a real function on a finite abelian
group, write
\[
 Q_d(f)=\mathbb E_{x,h_1,\ldots,h_d}
       \prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^d}f(x+\omega\cdot h),
 \qquad\|f\|_{U^d}=Q_d(f)^{1/2^d}.
\]
Our Fourier coefficients are
$\widehat f(\chi)=\mathbb E_x f(x)\overline{\chi(x)}$; thus
$\|f\|_{U^2}^4=\sum_\chi|\widehat f(\chi)|^4$.
We use the standard Gowers Cauchy--Schwarz inequality, normhood for $d\ge2$,
translation invariance and monotonicity, all from the classical
framework~\cite{gowers}.

For a family $\mathcal F$ of odd-order finite abelian groups containing at
least one nontrivial group, define
\begin{align*}
 c_d(\mathcal F)
 &=\sup_{\substack{G\in\mathcal F,\ f:G\to\mathbb R\\
                    \mathbb E f=0,\ f\ne0}}
       \frac{\|f\|_{U^2}^4}{\|f\|_{U^d}^4},\\
 D(\mathcal F)
 &=\sup_{\substack{G\in\mathcal F,\ f:G\to[-1,1]\\
                    \mathbb E f=0}}\|f\|_{U^2}^4.
\end{align*}
Write $D(G)=D(\{G\})$ and $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}$ for the family of all such
groups.  The endpoint and two approximation lemmas in this subsection are
established in \emph{Sharp Extremal Thresholds and Uniform Limits in Gowers'
Framework}, Section 2~\cite{extremallimits}.  We reproduce their arguments to make the new rate
proof independently readable; none of these ingredients is claimed new here.

\begin{proposition}[Prior bounded endpoint and its defect]
If $|G|=N$ is odd and $f:G\to[-1,1]$ is real and centered, put
$R(h)=\mathbb E_x f(x)f(x+h)$.  Then
\begin{align*}
 2|R(h)|&\le1+R(2h),\\
 1-3\|f\|_{U^2}^4
 &=\mathbb E_h\bigl((1+R(2h))^2-4R(h)^2\bigr)\ge0.
\end{align*}
For odd $N\ge3$,
\[
 D(G)\le D_N:=\frac{N^3-4N+3}{3N^3},
 \qquad D(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z)=D_N.
\]
Consequently the bounded endpoint for all odd-order groups is $1/3$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For $a,c\in[-1,1]$,
$(1+ac)^2-(a+c)^2=(1-a^2)(1-c^2)\ge0$, and $1+ac\ge0$.
Hence $|b(a+c)|\le1+ac$ whenever also $|b|\le1$.
Substitute $a=f(x)$, $b=f(x+h)$, $c=f(x+2h)$, average, and use the
triangle inequality.  This proves the pointwise correlation bound.
Its square can be averaged because both sides are nonnegative.  Doubling
permutes $G$, while $\mathbb E R=(\mathbb E f)^2=0$ and
$\mathbb E R^2=\|f\|_{U^2}^4$, giving the defect identity.

Set $r=R(0)=\mathbb E f^2$.  Choose signs $s_x\in\{-1,1\}$ agreeing
with $f(x)$ at nonzero values.  Since $N$ is odd and $\sum f=0$,
\[
 \sum_x(1-|f(x)|)=\sum_x|s_x-f(x)|
 \ge\left|\sum_xs_x\right|\ge1.
\]
It follows that $r\le1-1/N$.  The zero-direction defect is
$1+2r-3r^2$, a concave quadratic on $[0,1-1/N]$.  Its minimum there is
at least $(4N-3)/N^2$ for $N\ge3$.  Retaining only this direction in
the nonnegative defect average gives
$1-3\|f\|_{U^2}^4\ge(4N-3)/N^3$, proving the finite bound.

For $N=2s+1$ define $f_N(0)=0$, $f_N(j)=1$ for $1\le j\le s$, and
$f_N(j)=-1$ for $s+1\le j\le2s$.  This function is centered.  Directly,
its unnormalized autocorrelation has values $C(0)=N-1$ and
$C(h)=C(-h)=N-4h$ for $1\le h\le s$.  Therefore
\[
 \|f_N\|_{U^2}^4
 =\frac{(N-1)^2+2\sum_{h=1}^s(N-4h)^2}{N^3}
 =D_N.
\]
Letting odd $N$ tend to infinity proves the universal endpoint.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The previously established Fourier-tail estimate}

\begin{lemma}[Prior uniform tail estimate]
Let $0<\tau\le1/2$, $k=\lceil8/\tau\rceil$, and suppose
$2^{d-2}\ge k+1$.  For a centered real $f$ on an odd-order group with
$\|f\|_{U^d}=1$, all but less than $2\tau$ of
$\sum_\chi|\widehat f(\chi)|^4$ lies in its $k$ largest opposite
Fourier pairs.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If there are at most $k$ nontrivial Fourier pairs, the assertion is
immediate.  Assume there are at least $k+1$.
Choose one representative $\chi_j$ per nontrivial pair
$\{\chi,\chi^{-1}\}$ and order
$\lambda_j=|\widehat f(\chi_j)|^2$ decreasingly.  Such pairs have
two distinct elements because the group has odd order.  The autocorrelation
is
\[
 R(h)=\sum_j\lambda_j(\chi_j(h)+\chi_j(h)^{-1}),
 \qquad 2\sum_j\lambda_j^2=\|f\|_{U^2}^4\le1.
\]
For $M=2^{d-2}$, the derivative recursion and monotonicity give
\[
 \mathbb E|R|^{2M}
 \le\mathbb E_h\|f\,T_hf\|_{U^{d-1}}^{2^{d-1}}=1.
\]
Every coefficient in the character expansion of $R^{2M}$ is nonnegative.
Keeping words balanced separately in the first $k+1$ pairs, and comparing
with independent circle coordinates, gives
\begin{align*}
 1&\ge\int_{\mathbb T^{k+1}}
       \left(2\sum_{j=1}^{k+1}\lambda_j\cos(2\pi\theta_j)\right)^{2M}
           d\boldsymbol\theta\\
  &\ge3^{-(k+1)}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{k+1}\lambda_j\right)^{2M}.
\end{align*}
For the last step restrict all coordinates to $[-1/6,1/6]$; the even
power is nonnegative everywhere.  Additional character relations on the
original group only add nonnegative terms.  Since $M\ge k+1$,
$\sum_{j\le k+1}\lambda_j\le\sqrt3$, so
$\max_{j>k}\lambda_j^2\le3/(k+1)^2$.

Let $T=\sum_{j>k}\lambda_j^2$ and assume $T\ge\tau$.
Set $m=\lceil4/\tau\rceil\le M$.  Monotonicity of ordinary $L^p$ norms
gives $\mathbb E R^{2m}\le1$.  Keeping words using $m$ distinct tail
pairs once in each direction yields
\[
 1\ge(2m)!\,e_m((\lambda_j^2)_{j>k}).
\]
For probability weights $p_j=\lambda_j^2/T$,
\[
 \max_jp_j\le\frac{3}{(k+1)^2\tau}
       \le\frac{3\tau}{64}\le\frac1{2m}.
\]
Here $m\le4.5/\tau$.  In $m$ independent draws, each draw after distinct
predecessors avoids them with probability at least $1/2$.
Consequently
$m!e_m((\lambda_j^2)_{j>k})\ge2^{-m}T^m$.  This would imply
\[
 1\ge\frac{(2m)!}{2^m m!}T^m
 \ge\left(\frac{m\tau}{2}\right)^m\ge2^m>1,
\]
a contradiction.  Thus $T<\tau$, and including both characters in
each pair gives the claimed $2\tau$ bound.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The previously established positive smoothing construction}

\begin{lemma}[Bohr volume]
For $k$ characters and $0<\delta\le1$, the set
$B(\delta)=\{x:|\chi_j(x)-1|\le\delta\ \forall j\}$ has density at
least $(\delta/8)^k$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Partition each circle into $q=\lceil2\pi/\delta\rceil$ equal arcs.
One of the $q^k$ coordinate cells has preimage of density at least
$q^{-k}$.  Translate that preimage by one of its points with opposite sign.
The translated set lies in $B(\delta)$ because coordinate differences
have chord distance at most $2\pi/q\le\delta$.  Finally $q\le8/\delta$.
No independence or absence of character relations is required.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Prior positive finite-spectrum smoothing]
Given $k\ge1$ characters and $0<\kappa<1/2$, set
\[
 \rho=\kappa/2,\qquad
 \beta=\left(\frac\rho{8\sqrt{2k}}\right)^k,
 \qquad
 L\ge\frac{8k}{\rho^2}\log\frac4{\kappa\beta},
\]
where $L$ is an integer.  There exists a real kernel $K\ge0$ with
$\mathbb E K=1$ such that $|1-\widehat K(\chi_j)|\le\kappa$ for all $j$.
Every support character is a product $\prod_j\chi_j^{n_j}$ with
$\sum_j|n_j|\le L$.  Moreover $0\le\widehat K(\chi)\le1$ for every
character and $\|f*K\|_{U^d}\le\|f\|_{U^d}$ for $d\ge2$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Put
\[
 H=\frac12+\frac1{2k}\sum_j\operatorname{Re}\chi_j,
 \qquad K=\frac{H^L}{\mathbb E H^L}.
\]
Then $0\le H\le1$.  On $B(\rho/\sqrt{2k})$, whose density is at least
$\beta$, one has $H\ge1-\rho^2/(8k)$.  Outside $B(\rho)$ one has
$H\le1-\rho^2/(4k)$.  Hence
\[
 \mathbb E K\,1_{G\setminus B(\rho)}
 \le\beta^{-1}\exp(-L\rho^2/(8k))\le\kappa/4.
\]
This gives
$|1-\widehat K(\chi_j)|\le\rho+2(\kappa/4)=\kappa$.
The expansion of $H^L$ has the required support, with nonnegative
Fourier coefficients, even if different monomials represent the same
character.  Positivity of $K$ and its mean one imply
$|\widehat K(\chi)|\le1$, proving the multiplier range.
Finally $f*K$ is a convex combination of translates of $f$; the norm
triangle inequality and translation invariance prove the contraction.
\end{proof}

The original smoothing lemma did not need to emphasize the nonnegative
Fourier multiplier range.  It is an immediate property of the same
kernel and is recorded here for the bounded-approximation corollary.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A faster uniform passage to the bounded endpoint\srctag{93}}]{A faster uniform passage to the bounded endpoint}\label{gsr:cc:93:sec:d7}
\srcnote{93}{Section 7}

The previous manuscript \emph{Sharp Extremal Thresholds and Uniform Limits
in Gowers' Framework}, Section 2~\cite{extremallimits}, proves
\[
 0\le c_d(\mathcal F)-D(\mathcal F)
      =O\bigl(\sqrt d\,2^{-d/4}\bigr)
\]
uniformly over families of finite odd-order abelian groups.  Its Fourier-tail
lemma and positive smoothing construction will be retained.  The two
inefficient steps in its supremum-norm comparison can be replaced.  The
result is
\[
 \boxed{0\le c_d(\mathcal F)-D(\mathcal F)
      =O\bigl(d\,2^{-d/2}\bigr).}
\]
In particular,
\[
 c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}=\frac13+O\bigl(d\,2^{-d/2}\bigr).
\]
The implied constants are absolute and no closure assumption on the family
is needed.  This does not assert optimality of the new rate.

\subsection{A translation estimate independent of the size of the spectrum}

\begin{lemma}[An explicit small-arc multiplier]
For $0<\sigma\le1$ there exists a continuous $2\pi$-periodic function
$F_\sigma$ with absolutely summable Fourier coefficients such that
\[
 F_\sigma(\theta)=e^{i\theta}-1\quad(|\theta|\le\sigma),
 \qquad \sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}|\widehat F_\sigma(n)|\le8\sigma.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $-\pi\le\theta\le\pi$, put
\[
 \eta_\sigma(\theta)=
 \begin{cases}
 1,&|\theta|\le\sigma,\\
 2-|\theta|/\sigma,&\sigma<|\theta|\le2\sigma,\\
 0,&2\sigma<|\theta|\le\pi,
 \end{cases}
 \qquad F_\sigma(\theta)=(e^{i\theta}-1)\eta_\sigma(\theta).
\]
The periodic extension is continuous because $2\sigma<\pi$.
Since $|e^{i\theta}-1|\le|\theta|$,
\[
 |\widehat F_\sigma(n)|\le
 \frac1{2\pi}\int_{-2\sigma}^{2\sigma}|\theta|\,d\theta
 =\frac{2\sigma^2}{\pi}.
\]
The distributional second derivative is the finite complex measure
\[
 F_\sigma''=-e^{i\theta}\eta_\sigma
       +2ie^{i\theta}\eta_\sigma'
       +(e^{i\theta}-1)\eta_\sigma''.
\]
The first term has total variation at most $3\sigma$; the second at most
$4$.  The jumps of $\eta_\sigma'$ occur at $-2\sigma,-\sigma,\sigma,2\sigma$
and have absolute size $1/\sigma$.  Their contributions after multiplication
by $e^{i\theta}-1$ have total variation at most $2+1+1+2=6$.
Consequently $\|F_\sigma''\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le3\sigma+10\le13$, and for $n\ne0$,
\[
 |\widehat F_\sigma(n)|\le\frac{13}{2\pi n^2}.
\]
Take $K=\lceil1/\sigma\rceil$.  The low-frequency and tail estimates give
\begin{align*}
 \sum_n|\widehat F_\sigma(n)|
 &\le(2K+1)\frac{2\sigma^2}{\pi}
       +\frac{13}{\pi}\sum_{n>K}\frac1{n^2}\\
 &\le\frac{10\sigma}{\pi}+\frac{13}{\pi K}
 \le\frac{23}{\pi}\sigma<8\sigma.
\end{align*}
Absolute convergence proves that its Fourier series represents $F_\sigma$
everywhere: it represents a continuous function with the same Fourier
coefficients, and uniqueness gives the assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Uniform discrete Bernstein estimate]
Let $G$ be a finite abelian group, let $\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_k$ be characters,
and let $g:G\to\mathbb C$ have Fourier support among products
$\chi_1^{n_1}\cdots\chi_k^{n_k}$ with $\sum_j|n_j|\le L$, where $L\ge1$.
If $0<\delta\le1/(2L)$ and
\[
 h\in B(\delta):=\{x:|\chi_j(x)-1|\le\delta\ \text{for all }j\},
\]
then
\[
 \|T_hg-g\|_\infty\le16L\delta\,\|g\|_\infty.
\]
Neither the order of $G$, the relations among the $\chi_j$, nor the number
of actual Fourier coefficients appears in the estimate.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose principal arguments $\theta_j\in[-\pi,\pi]$ of $\chi_j(h)$.
The chord bound gives $|\theta_j|\le(\pi/2)\delta\le2\delta$.
For every actual support character choose a representation of length at
most $L$.  Its eigenvalue under the translation $T_h$ therefore has an
argument in $[-\sigma,\sigma]$, where $\sigma=2L\delta\le1$.
Writing $c_n=\widehat F_\sigma(n)$, the preceding lemma gives the exact
identity
\[
 (T_h-I)g=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}c_nT_{nh}g.
\]
It holds on each support character, and the operator series converges
absolutely in supremum norm.  Every translation is an isometry, whence
\[
 \|(T_h-I)g\|_\infty\le\sum_n|c_n|\|g\|_\infty
 \le8\sigma\|g\|_\infty.
\]
This proof takes the supremum on the original finite group throughout;
it does not replace it by the supremum of a lifted torus polynomial.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Sign control for nearly constant cubes}

\begin{lemma}[Even products of nearby real numbers]
Let $m$ be even, $a\in[-1,1]$, and $b_1,\ldots,b_m\in[-1,1]$ with
$|b_j-a|\le t$.  Then
\[
 \prod_{j=1}^m b_j\ge(|a|-t)_+^m-(2t)^m.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $|a|\ge t$, all nonzero $b_j$ have the sign of $a$, so evenness gives
$\prod b_j\ge(|a|-t)^m$.  If $|a|<t$, every $|b_j|<2t$, so the product
is at least $-(2t)^m$ while the positive-part term is zero.
\end{proof}

For a real function, the identity
\[
 \|g\|_{U^d}^{2^d}
 =\mathbb E_{h_1,\ldots,h_{d-1}}
    \left|\mathbb E_x\prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^{d-1}}
            g(x+\omega\cdot h)\right|^2
\]
allows restriction to any chosen direction set.  The next theorem uses
this nonnegative square, rather than assuming individual cube products
are nonnegative.

\begin{theorem}[Uniform finite-spectrum comparison]
Let $g$ be real and have the spectrum in the preceding Bernstein lemma.
Set
\[
 n=2^d,\quad m=n/2,\quad A=16L,\quad d\ge2.
\]
Choose $0<t<1/4$ for which
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:93:newnorm:positivity-condition}
 \left(\frac{2t}{1-2t}\right)^m
       \le\frac12\left(\frac{t}{8A}\right)^k.
\end{equation}
Then
\[
 \|g\|_\infty\le\exp(E_d(k,L;t))\|g\|_{U^d},
\]
where
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:93:newnorm:finite-spectrum-E}
 E_d(k,L;t)=-\log(1-2t)
  +\frac{k(d+1)}n\log\frac{8A}{t}
  +\frac{k(d-1)}n\log(d-1)+\frac{2\log2}n.
\end{equation}
All constants are independent of $G$ and the relations between the
generating characters.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Normalize $\|g\|_\infty=1$; the zero function is trivial.  The elementary
Bohr volume estimate $\mathbb P(B(u))\ge(u/8)^k$ holds for $0<u\le1$.
At a point $x_0$ with $|g(x_0)|=1$, the Bernstein lemma gives
$|g(x_0+h)|\ge1-t$ on $B(t/A)$, a set of density at least
$b=(t/(8A))^k$.  Its parameter is at most $1/(2L)$ as required.

Restrict every first $d-1$ direction to $B(\delta)$, where
$\delta=t/[A(d-1)]$.  Translating successively and using the triangle
inequality, every factor $g(x+\omega\cdot h)$ differs from $g(x)$ by
at most $t$.  The product lemma and the preceding high-value set imply
\[
 \mathbb E_x\prod_\omega g(x+\omega\cdot h)
 \ge\mathbb E_x(|g(x)|-t)_+^m-(2t)^m
 \ge b(1-2t)^m-(2t)^m
 \ge\tfrac12b(1-2t)^m.
\]
The final inequality is exactly \eqref{gsr:cc:93:newnorm:positivity-condition}.
Restricting the squared cube identity to those directions now gives
\[
 \|g\|_{U^d}^{n}\ge
 \left(\frac{t}{8A(d-1)}\right)^{k(d-1)}
       \frac{b^2(1-2t)^n}{4}.
\]
Taking the $n$th root proves the theorem.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[An explicit optimized form]
In the spectral setting of the preceding theorem, put $a=k(d+1)/2^d$
and assume $0<a<1$.  Suppose
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:93:newnorm:optimized-condition}
 \left(\frac{2^d}{2}-k\right)\log\frac1a
       \ge k\log\bigl(256L(1+a)\bigr)+\log2.
\end{equation}
Then
\[
 \|g\|_\infty\le e^{\mathcal E_d(k,L)}\|g\|_{U^d},
\]
where
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:93:newnorm:optimized-E}
 \mathcal E_d(k,L)
 =\log(1+a)+a\log\frac{256L(1+a)}a
   +\frac{k(d-1)}{2^d}\log(d-1)+\frac{2\log2}{2^d}.
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The unique minimizer of the right side of
\eqref{gsr:cc:93:newnorm:finite-spectrum-E} is $t=a/[2(1+a)]$, which is less than
$1/4$ when $a<1$.  Substituting it into
\eqref{gsr:cc:93:newnorm:positivity-condition} gives
\eqref{gsr:cc:93:newnorm:optimized-condition}; substitution into the error gives
\eqref{gsr:cc:93:newnorm:optimized-E}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Transfer to the bounded problem}

Retain exactly the prior Fourier-tail and smoothing parameters:
\[
 0<\tau\le\frac12,\quad0<\kappa<\frac12,
 \quad k=\lceil8/\tau\rceil,\quad\rho=\kappa/2,
 \quad\beta=\left(\frac\rho{8\sqrt{2k}}\right)^k,
\]
and choose an integer
\[
 L\ge\frac{8k}{\rho^2}\log\frac4{\kappa\beta}.
\]
Provided $2^{d-2}\ge k+1$, the prior tail lemma captures all but $2\tau$
of the Fourier fourth-power mass in $k$ opposite pairs.  Its positive
kernel $K$ satisfies $\mathbb E K=1$, has spectrum of total exponent
length at most $L$ in these $k$ generators, and obeys
$|1-\widehat K(\chi_j)|\le\kappa$.

\begin{theorem}[Improved explicit transfer]\label{gsr:cc:93:norm:transfer}
In addition to the preceding assumptions, impose
\eqref{gsr:cc:93:newnorm:optimized-condition} and $0<a<1$.  Then for every
nontrivial family $\mathcal F$ of finite odd-order abelian groups,
\[
 D(\mathcal F)\le c_d(\mathcal F)\le
 \frac{e^{4\mathcal E_d(k,L)}}{(1-\kappa)^4}D(\mathcal F)+2\tau.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Normalize $\|f\|_{U^d}=1$ and form $g=f*K$ from the selected Fourier
pairs.  If there are fewer than $k$ pairs, repeat one selected nontrivial
character to obtain a list of length $k$; a nonzero centered function
has at least one such character.  Repetition leaves the tail assertion
valid and is allowed by the smoothing lemma.
Positivity of $K$ and norm convexity imply $\|g\|_{U^d}\le1$.
The tail and multiplier estimates give
\[
 \|f\|_{U^2}^4\le(1-\kappa)^{-4}\|g\|_{U^2}^4+2\tau.
\]
Since $g$ remains real and centered on the same group,
\[
 \|g\|_{U^2}^4\le D(\mathcal F)\|g\|_\infty^4
       \le D(\mathcal F)e^{4\mathcal E_d(k,L)}.
\]
Take the supremum.  The lower bound is the elementary
$\|f\|_{U^d}\le\|f\|_\infty$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The improved uniform rate]\label{gsr:cc:93:norm:uniform-rate}
Uniformly over those families,
\[
 0\le c_d(\mathcal F)-D(\mathcal F)
   \le C d\,2^{-d/2}\qquad(d\ge2),
\]
with an absolute constant $C$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Put $\tau=\kappa=\varepsilon$ and choose the least allowed integer $L$.
The prior explicit formulas give, with absolute constants,
\[
 k=O(\varepsilon^{-1}),\quad
 L=O(\varepsilon^{-4}\log(1/\varepsilon)),\quad
 \log L=O(\log(1/\varepsilon)).
\]
Choose $\varepsilon=Bd2^{-d/2}$ with a sufficiently large absolute $B$.
For all sufficiently large $d$, it is less than $1/4$ and the tail-degree
condition holds.  Moreover
\[
 a=\frac{k(d+1)}{2^d}=O(B^{-1}2^{-d/2})\to0,
 \qquad \log L=O(d),\quad\log(1/a)=O(d).
\]
The left side of \eqref{gsr:cc:93:newnorm:optimized-condition} has order $2^d d$,
whereas its right side is $O(kd)=O(B^{-1}2^{d/2})$.  Thus that condition
also holds for sufficiently large $d$.
Using $\log(1+a)\le a$ in \eqref{gsr:cc:93:newnorm:optimized-E},
\[
 \mathcal E_d(k,L)
 \le C_0\frac{k d^2}{2^d}
 \le C_1\frac{d^2}{\varepsilon2^d}
 =\frac{C_1}{B^2}\varepsilon.
\]
Take $B$ large enough that this is at most $\varepsilon$.
The transfer factor then equals $1+O(\varepsilon)$, with absolute
constants; $D(\mathcal F)\le1$ gives the claimed estimate.
Increase $C$ to cover the finitely many smaller $d$, using
$0\le c_d(\mathcal F)-D(\mathcal F)\le1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 82--94]
\emph{Against source~63} (Section~\ref{gsr:cc:sec:fasterlimit}): the order $d2^{-d/2}$ supersedes source~63's $2^{-\lfloor d/8\rfloor}$, but the constant $C$ is not explicit, so source~63's bound remains the only numerical one; by the lower obstruction below no family-uniform rate beats order $d2^{-d}$.
\end{writenote}

\subsection{A bounded approximation and a quantitative endpoint defect}

\begin{theorem}[Approximation with retained Fourier mass]
Use the parameters of the improved transfer theorem, write
$E=\mathcal E_d(k,L)$, and normalize a real centered $f$ by
$\|f\|_{U^d}=1$.  There is a real centered $h:G\to[-1,1]$ such that
\begin{align*}
 \|f-h\|_{U^2}
   &\le(\kappa^4+2\tau)^{1/4}+E,\\
 \|h\|_{U^2}^4
   &\ge e^{-4E}(1-\kappa)^4
                (\|f\|_{U^2}^4-2\tau).
\end{align*}
If furthermore $\|f\|_{U^2}^4\ge1/3-\eta$, with $\eta\ge0$, and
$R_h(x)=\mathbb E_yh(y)h(y+x)$, then
\begin{align*}
 0\le 1-3\|h\|_{U^2}^4
 &\le3\eta+6\tau+4\kappa+4E,\\
 \bigl\|1+R_h(2\,\cdot)-2|R_h|\bigr\|_{L^2(G)}
 &\le(3\eta+6\tau+4\kappa+4E)^{1/2}.
\end{align*}
For the asymptotic parameter choice $\tau=\kappa=\varepsilon$ and
$E\le\varepsilon=O(d2^{-d/2})$, the approximation is
$O(d^{1/4}2^{-d/8})$ in $U^2$ and the last defect bound is
$O((\eta+d2^{-d/2})^{1/2})$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The smoothing kernel is $K=H^L/\mathbb E H^L$, where
$H=1/2+(1/(2k))\sum_j\operatorname{Re}\chi_j$.
Every Fourier coefficient of $H$, hence of $H^L$, is nonnegative even
when some characters coincide.  Thus $0\le\widehat K(\chi)\le1$ for
every character; the upper bound also follows from positivity and
$\mathbb E K=1$.  Put $g=f*K$ and $h=e^{-E}g$.  The finite-spectrum
comparison ensures $\|h\|_\infty\le1$.  On each retained Fourier pair,
$|1-\widehat K|\le\kappa$, and on its complement it is at most one.
The Fourier-tail estimate and $\|f\|_{U^2}^4\le1$ therefore give
\[
 \|f-g\|_{U^2}^4
   =\sum_\chi|\widehat f(\chi)|^4|1-\widehat K(\chi)|^4
   \le\kappa^4+2\tau.
\]
Also $\|g\|_{U^2}\le\|g\|_{U^d}\le1$, so
$\|g-h\|_{U^2}\le1-e^{-E}\le E$.  The triangle inequality proves the
approximation estimate.  The retained Fourier coefficients give the
second displayed inequality directly.

Let $c=e^{-4E}(1-\kappa)^4\in[0,1]$.  The mass estimate implies
\[
 1-3\|h\|_{U^2}^4
 \le1-c+c(3\eta+6\tau)
 \le4E+4\kappa+3\eta+6\tau.
\]
Here $1-c\le(1-e^{-4E})+(1-(1-\kappa)^4)\le4E+4\kappa$.
The prior bounded-endpoint identity, which applies to $h$, says
\[
 1-3\|h\|_{U^2}^4
  =\mathbb E_x\bigl((1+R_h(2x))^2-4R_h(x)^2\bigr).
\]
Set $z(x)=1+R_h(2x)-2|R_h(x)|\ge0$ by the pointwise correlation
inequality.  The integrand is $z(x)^2+4z(x)|R_h(x)|\ge z(x)^2$.
This proves the $L^2$ defect bound.  Substitute the asymptotic parameters
for the final claims.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The exact first correction on every fixed prime cyclic group}

The preceding uniform rate can be complemented by a sharp first-order
asymptotic when the group is fixed and has prime order.  This answers
the rate part of the previous manuscript's fixed-group question for
prime cyclic groups; it does not determine $c_d$ at any given finite
$d\ge4$.

\begin{lemma}[An elementary fixed-cardinality comparison]
If $G$ has order $N$ and $f:G\to\mathbb R$, then for $d\ge2$,
\[
 \|f\|_{U^d}\ge N^{-(d+1)/2^d}\|f\|_\infty.
\]
Consequently, for a fixed odd-order group with $N\ge3$,
\[
 D(G)\le c_d(\{G\})\le
 D(G)\exp\!\left(\frac{4(d+1)\log N}{2^d}\right).
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
In the squared cube identity, retain the event that all first $d-1$
directions are zero.  Writing $m=2^{d-1}$, which is even,
\[
 \|f\|_{U^d}^{2^d}
 \ge N^{-(d-1)}(\mathbb E f^m)^2
 \ge N^{-(d+1)}\|f\|_\infty^{2^d}.
\]
The consequence follows from the definition of $D(G)$ and homogeneity.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact cube polynomial for a punctured sign function]
Let $p$ be an odd prime and let $f:\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z\to\{-1,0,1\}$
have exactly one zero.  The signs at its other points are arbitrary.
For $j\ge0$ and $\mathbf h=(h_1,\ldots,h_j)$, put
\[
 S(\mathbf h)=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^j\omega_i h_i:
                         \omega_i\in\{0,1\}\right\},
 \qquad
 A_{p,j}=\sum_{\mathbf h\in((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)\setminus\{0\})^j}
                (p-|S(\mathbf h)|).
\]
The empty sumset is $\{0\}$, so $A_{p,0}=p-1$.
Then for every $d\ge p-1$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:93:newnorm:prime-cube-polynomial}
 \|f\|_{U^d}^{2^d}
   =p^{-(d+1)}\sum_{j=0}^{p-2}\binom dj A_{p,j}.
\end{equation}
Moreover $A_{p,p-2}>0$, so the polynomial in $d$ on the right has
degree exactly $p-2$.  In fact
\[
 A_{p,p-2}=(p-1)2^{p-3}.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $S$ is a nonempty proper subset of $\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z$ and
$h\ne0$, then $S+h\ne S$: invariance would imply invariance under the
generator $h$, forcing $S$ to be the whole group.  Therefore
$|S\cup(S+h)|\ge|S|+1$.  Applying this successively to the subset sums
shows that any $p-1$ nonzero directions produce the whole group.

Now consider a $d$-cube and let $j$ be its number of nonzero directions.
If $j\ge p-1$, its vertex set is the whole group and one factor is zero.
If $j\le p-2$, then $d\ge p-1$ ensures at least one zero direction.
Every vertex arising from the nonzero directions then occurs with an
even multiplicity, so the product is one exactly when the cube avoids
the unique zero of $f$, and is zero otherwise.  For fixed nonzero
directions $\mathbf h$, precisely $p-|S(\mathbf h)|$ base points avoid
that zero.  Choose the $j$ nonzero coordinate positions, sum over their
values, and divide by $p^{d+1}$.  This proves the identity.

To see positivity of the leading coefficient, take all $p-2$ directions
equal to any fixed $h\ne0$.  Its subset sumset has exactly $p-1$ points,
so this tuple contributes one to $A_{p,p-2}$.

For the exact coefficient, a contributing tuple of $p-2$ nonzero
directions must increase the sumset size by exactly one at each step.
After the first step its sumset is an interval of length two in the
first direction $h_1$.  If $I$ is an interval of length $s$ in that
direction with $2\le s\le p-2$, only the steps $h_1$ and $-h_1$ can
make $|I\cup(I+h)|=s+1$.  To check this, rescale to
$I=\{0,\ldots,s-1\}$ and represent $h$ by $u\in\{1,\ldots,p-1\}$.
Then
\[
 |I\cap(I+u)|=\max(0,s-u)+\max(0,s-(p-u)).
\]
This equals $s-1$ only for $u=1,p-1$: if both summands are positive,
their sum is $2s-p<s-1$, and if exactly one is positive the assertion
is immediate.  Induction therefore forces all directions into the
same pair $\{h_1,-h_1\}$.  Conversely, every such tuple has $p-1$
subset sums.  Choosing one of $(p-1)/2$ pairs and $p-2$ independent
signs gives $(p-1)2^{p-3}$.  When $p=3$, there is one direction and
the same formula gives $A_{3,1}=2$ directly.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Sharp dimension threshold and small-prime formulas]
The threshold $d\ge p-1$ for independence from the nonzero signs is
best possible.  Compare the functions with values $(0,1,\ldots,1)$
and $(0,-1,1,\ldots,1)$ at $d=p-2$.  Every nonzero cube product of
the first is one.  For the second all such products are at most one,
and the cube with base point one and every direction one has product
minus one: it visits all nonzero residues, and visits the negative
residue one exactly once.  Thus their cube averages differ.

The first three polynomials are
\begin{align*}
 P_3(d)&=2(d+1),\\
 P_5(d)&=4+12d+24\binom d2+16\binom d3
       =\frac43(d+1)(2d^2+d+3),\\
 P_7(d)&=6+30d+120\binom d2+288\binom d3
                 +288\binom d4+96\binom d5\\
       &=\frac25(d+1)(2d^4+8d^3+2d^2+18d+15).
\end{align*}
The exact dynamic-programming and derivative-recursion certificates
verify these identities and higher coefficients for $p=11,13$.
In particular, for any punctured sign function on $\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z$
and $d\ge4$,
\[
 \|f\|_{U^d}^{2^d}
       =\frac{4(d+1)(2d^2+d+3)}{3\cdot5^{d+1}}.
\]
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp first-order prime-cyclic convergence]\label{gsr:cc:93:norm:prime-rate}
For each fixed odd prime $p$, put
\[
 D_p=\frac{p^3-4p+3}{3p^3}.
\]
Then
\begin{align*}
 c_d(\{\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z\})
 &=D_p+4D_p\log p\,\frac d{2^d}
      +O_p\!\left(\frac{\log d}{2^d}\right),\\
 \lim_{d\to\infty}\frac{2^d}{d}
       \bigl(c_d(\{\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z\})-D_p\bigr)
 &=4D_p\log p.
\end{align*}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The bounded-endpoint theorem gives $D(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)=D_p$, attained
by the centered interval sign function $f_p$ with exactly one zero.
Write
\[
 P_p(d)=\sum_{j=0}^{p-2}\binom dj A_{p,j}.
\]
The preceding theorem gives a polynomial of degree $p-2$ with positive
leading coefficient, hence
\[
 \log P_p(d)=(p-2)\log d+O_p(1).
\]
Testing the ratio on $f_p$ yields
\[
 c_d(\{\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z\})
 \ge D_p\exp\!\left(
  \frac{4(d+1)\log p-4\log P_p(d)}{2^d}\right).
\]
Together with the fixed-cardinality upper bound, this sandwiches the
logarithm of $c_d/D_p$ between
\[
 \frac{4(d+1)\log p-4(p-2)\log d+O_p(1)}{2^d}
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \frac{4(d+1)\log p}{2^d}.
\]
Both equal $4\log p\,d2^{-d}+O_p(\log d\,2^{-d})$.
Exponentiating gives the claimed expansion, since
$d^2 2^{-2d}=O(\log d\,2^{-d})$.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 82--94]
\emph{Checked at the write.} $D_p$ is source~63's $b(\Z/p\Z)$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:63:bounded:finite}); and source~63's elementary bound $c_d(G)\le b(G)N^{4(d+1)/2^d}$ (Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:63:norm:fixed-group}) expands as $b(G)+4b(G)\log N\,(d+1)2^{-d}+O(d^24^{-d})$, whose leading correction at $G=\Z/p\Z$ is exactly the first-order term here: that bound is sharp to first order on prime cyclic groups.
\end{writenote}

\begin{corollary}[A lower obstruction for every family-uniform rate]
For $f=(0,1,-1)$ on $\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z$ and every $d\ge2$,
\[
 \|f\|_{U^d}^{2^d}=\frac{2(d+1)}{3^{d+1}}.
\]
In particular,
\[
 c_d(\{\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z\})-\frac29
 \ge\frac89\,2^{-d}
       \bigl((d+1)\log3-\log(2(d+1))\bigr).
\]
No error estimate valid uniformly for all families can be
$o(d2^{-d})$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The exact cube polynomial has $A_{3,0}=A_{3,1}=2$.
Its $U^2$ fourth power is $D_3=2/9$.  Test the defining ratio on $f$
and use $e^x-1\ge x$.  The expression in parentheses is positive for
$d\ge2$ and asymptotic to $d\log3$.
\end{proof}


\subsection{Certified numerical consequences}

The improved transfer is explicit even though the asymptotic theorem
uses an absolute unspecified constant. For the even dimensions below,
choose
\[
 \tau=(3d+10)2^{-d/2},\qquad \kappa=5\,2^{-d/2},
\]
then take $k=\lceil8/\tau\rceil$ and the certified upper-rounded
integer $L$ in the smoothing construction. The accompanying program
checks every hypothesis of the transfer theorem. All logarithms and
exponentials are enclosed by rational series, so the following strict
bounds are rounded outward, rather than inferred from floating-point
optimization.

\begin{tabular}{@{}rrr@{}}
\toprule
$d$ & Upper bound for $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}$ & Upper bound for
$c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}-1/3$\\
\midrule
24 & $0.415863478988$ & $8.253014566\cdot10^{-2}$\\
32 & $0.339838862352$ & $6.505529019\cdot10^{-3}$\\
40 & $0.333831986965$ & $4.986536314\cdot10^{-4}$\\

These are usable upper bounds, not estimates of the true excess.
In particular, the fixed-prime lower obstruction concerns convergence

Determining the latter excess remains a separate problem.

\section{Source~100: the quadratic barrier in progression counting, every length, prime cyclic groups \wtag}\label{gsr:cc:sec:quadbarrier}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the fourteenth write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next ten sections are source~100's Sections~2--10 and Appendix~B. \emph{Logically they continue source~20's chapter} (Section~\ref{gsr:cc:sec:quadratic}), after its sharp three-term obstruction (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:20:thm:indicator-sharpness}). The introduction is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:100:sec:d1}.

\emph{What is proved.} For every fixed $k\ge3$, norm order $d\ge2$ and density $0<\delta<1$, every large prime cyclic group $\Z/Q\Z$ (and $\F_p^n$ for every fixed $p>k$) contains sets of exactly $\lfloor\delta Q\rfloor$ points whose balanced $U^d$ norm tends to zero while $\Lambda_k-\delta_Q^k$ is asymptotic, with either sign, to a nonzero constant times the squared norm (Theorems~\ref{gsr:cc:100:thm:prime}, \ref{gsr:cc:100:thm:field}): no counting error $o(u^2)$ is possible (Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:100:cor:barrier}). The mechanism is a centred sine of a normalized sum of independent coordinate observables, a first-dependent-subset partition formula (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:100:thm:partition}) whose cube constants $P_d$ count partitions of $\{0,1\}^d$ into parallelograms ($P_2,P_3,P_4=1,6,635$), a signed-radix transfer to $\Z/Q\Z$ and probabilistic rounding; one sequence works for all fixed lengths and norm orders at once (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:100:thm:universal}).

\emph{Against sources~20 and~06.} Source~20 proved the quadratic estimate $|\Lambda_k-\delta^k|\le B_k(\delta)u^2$ and its sharpness for $k=3$ on $\F_{29}^{2m}$, and asked for $k\ge4$ and for prime cyclic groups (its Questions~1 and~3, item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:quadexp}); \emph{source~100 answers both}, for every $k\ge3$ and every $d\ge2$, by a mechanism other than the phase-rank degeneracies source~20 suggested, and advances item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:density} with explicit attainable coefficients. The quadratic counting estimate itself is not source~20's first: source~06's Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:06:uni:homogeneous} proved it, with the three-term factor $\sqrt{\delta(1-\delta)}$ sharp at singletons (Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:06:uni:three-term}); source~100 cites only source~20 (dated note). Source~06's singleton sharpness has density tending to zero, which is why fixed-density sharpness is the content of sources~20 and~100. Source~100's upper benchmark (Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:100:prop:upper}) is self-contained and not claimed to improve source~20's $B_k(\delta)$. \emph{Notation}: source~100's amplitude $\theta=\lambda e^{-1/2}$ is not source~20's exponent $\theta$ of item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:quadexp}; its $\mathcal B_k(\delta)$ (Question~1) is the optimal coefficient, of which source~20's $B_k(\delta)$ and source~06's $B^{(06)}_k$ are upper bounds.

\emph{Checked at the write} (\file{verify14.py}): $|\scrR_d|=(6^d-2\cdot4^d+2^d)/8=1,12,100,720$ for $d=2,\ldots,5$ by brute force, and $P_2,P_3,P_4=1,6,635$ by an exact count; $P_5=108{,}019{,}500$, which source~100 does not print (the intake's datum for its question on the growth of $P_d$, recounted). The intake also found the relative error of the pure triple and cube moments to decay like $n^{-1}$, faster than the proved $n^{-1/2}$ (one configuration; evidence).

\emph{Formal status} (HEAD \texttt{a0c3e9b67}): only the linear counting interface is formal, \file{theorem_3_2} (\file{Sections01_03}:258) and \file{corollary_3_3} (\file{Sections01_03}:276), exact as \file{theorem_3_2_holds} (\file{Proofs03ProgressionAverage}:381) and \file{corollary_3_3_holds} (\file{Proofs03ProgressionCount}:349); no quadratic estimate (sources~06, 20 or~100), no Gowers norm on $\F_p^n$ and no cumulant expansion.
