\section[{Main theorems and their consequences\srctag{100}}]{Main theorems and their consequences}\label{gsr:cc:100:sec:d2}\label{gsr:cc:100:sec:main}
\srcnote{100}{Section 2}

For a finite abelian group, or a compact abelian group with normalized Haar measure, define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:U}
 \Unorm{g}{d}^{2^d}
 =\E_{x,h_1,\ldots,h_d}
   \prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^d}\cc^{|\omega|}
        g(x+\omega_1h_1+\cdots+\omega_dh_d).
\end{equation}
Here $\cc$ denotes complex conjugation. All constructed functions are real, so the conjugations in their cube products disappear. We use only $d\ge2$.

Let $\scrR_d$ be the family of four-element subsets of $\{0,1\}^d$ whose vertices form an affine parallelogram, with all four vertices distinct. Let
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:Pdef}
 P_d=\#\{\text{partitions of $\{0,1\}^d$ into members of $\scrR_d$}\}.
\end{equation}
In particular, $P_d\ge1$, and
\[
 P_2=1,\qquad P_3=6,\qquad P_4=635.
\]
Section~\ref{gsr:cc:100:sec:cubegeometry} proves the geometry and supplies an exact recurrence for these integers.

Fix a target density $0<\delta<1$, and put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:parameters}
 b=\min(\delta,1-\delta),\qquad
 \lambda=\frac b4,\qquad \theta=\lambda e^{-1/2},\qquad
 D_k=\left\lfloor\frac{(k-1)^2}{4}\right\rfloor.
\end{equation}
The particular choice of $\lambda$ leaves a uniform margin for recentering; no optimality of this amplitude is asserted.

\begin{theorem}[Prime-cyclic saturation, every fixed length]\label{gsr:cc:100:thm:prime}
Fix $k\ge3$, $d\ge2$, and $0<\delta<1$, and let $M=2^d$.
For every sufficiently large prime $Q$, there are sets
$A_Q^+,A_Q^-\subseteq\Z/Q\Z$ with
\[
 |A_Q^+|=|A_Q^-|=\lfloor\delta Q\rfloor,
 \qquad \delta_Q=\frac{\lfloor\delta Q\rfloor}{Q},
\]
and integers $n=n(Q)\to\infty$ such that
\begin{align}
 \Unorm{\ind_{A_Q^\pm}-\delta_Q}{d}
 &=\frac{\theta P_d^{1/M}}{\sqrt2}\,n^{-1/4}
       \bigl(1+O(n^{-1/2})\bigr),\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:primeU}\\
 \La_k(\ind_{A_Q^\pm})-\delta_Q^k
 &=\pm\frac{D_k}{4}\delta^{k-3}\theta^3 n^{-1/2}
       +O(n^{-1}).\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:primeAP}
\end{align}
One can arrange
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:nQ}
 n(Q)\sim\frac{\log Q}{\log\log Q}.
\end{equation}
All implicit constants depend only on the fixed parameters. In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:primeratio}
 \frac{\La_k(\ind_{A_Q^\pm})-\delta_Q^k}
      {\Unorm{\ind_{A_Q^\pm}-\delta_Q}{d}^{2}}
 \longrightarrow
 \pm\frac{\theta\delta^{k-3}D_k}{2P_d^{2/M}}.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{What this answers} (Section~\ref{gsr:cc:sec:quadbarrier}): source~20's Questions~1 and~3 (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:quadexp}), for every $k\ge3$ and every $d\ge2$. \emph{Credit}: the quadratic counting bound that this theorem shows sharp was proved first by source~06 (Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:06:uni:homogeneous}), which this source does not cite; source~20 proved the three-term sharpness on $\F_{29}^{2m}$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:20:thm:indicator-sharpness}). The amplitude $\theta$ here is not source~20's exponent $\theta$.
\end{writenote}

The theorem is stronger than the particular choice $d=k-1$: any fixed norm order $d\ge2$ has the displayed behavior on these examples. This is a lower-bound statement about these functions, not a claim that $U^d$ controls all $k$-term counts when $d<k-1$.

\begin{corollary}[The quadratic exponent cannot be improved]\label{gsr:cc:100:cor:barrier}
For every $k\ge3$ and every target density $0<\delta<1$, there is no function $\eta(t)\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$ such that
\[
 \abs{\La_k(\ind_A)-\delta_A^k}
 \le \eta\bigl(\Unorm{\ind_A-\delta_A}{k-1}\bigr)
          \Unorm{\ind_A-\delta_A}{k-1}^{2}
\]
holds for all prime cyclic groups and all sets $A$ of cardinality
$\lfloor\delta |G|\rfloor$ with sufficiently small positive balanced norm.
In particular, no uniform $O(u^{2+\eps})$ replacement is possible for any $\eps>0$. This failure holds separately for upper and lower signed counting errors.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Take $d=k-1$ in Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:100:thm:prime}. The norm tends to zero, while the absolute ratio in \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:primeratio} tends to a strictly positive constant. The signed assertions use the two choices of sign.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Fixed-field saturation]\label{gsr:cc:100:thm:field}
Fix $k\ge3$, $d\ge2$, a prime $p>k$, and $0<\delta<1$. Put $M=2^d$ and $N=p^n$. There are sets $A_n^\pm\subseteq\F_p^n$ of cardinality $\lfloor\delta N\rfloor$, with $\delta_n=|A_n^\pm|/N$, satisfying
\begin{align}
 \Unorm{\ind_{A_n^\pm}-\delta_n}{d}
 &=\theta P_d^{1/M}(p-1)^{-1/4}n^{-1/4}
       \bigl(1+O(n^{-1/2})\bigr),\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:fieldU}\\
 \La_k(\ind_{A_n^\pm})-\delta_n^k
 &=\pm\binom{k}{3}\delta^{k-3}\theta^3(p-1)^{-1/2}n^{-1/2}
       +O(n^{-1}).\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:fieldAP}
\end{align}
Thus the ratio of the signed discrepancy to the squared norm tends to
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:fieldratio}
 \pm\theta\binom{k}{3}\delta^{k-3}P_d^{-2/M}.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

The leading field ratio is independent of $p$ once the characteristic is large enough for the progression length. This does not mean that the error terms are uniform in $p$; throughout this theorem $p$ is fixed. If $\delta=a/p^s$ with integers $0<a<p^s$, then $\delta_n=\delta$ exactly for all $n\ge s$, so the field theorem also gives exact-density sharpness for this class of densities.

\subsection{Small-length constants}
For the prime-cyclic construction and $d=k-1$, the limits in \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:primeratio} are
\[
 \pm\frac\theta2\quad(k=3),\qquad
 \pm\frac{\theta\delta}{6^{1/4}}\quad(k=4),\qquad
 \pm\frac{2\theta\delta^2}{635^{1/8}}\quad(k=5).
\]
They are explicit attainable coefficients, not the optimal coefficients in a universal counting inequality. Section~\ref{gsr:cc:100:sec:improvingconstants} improves them within a larger family of observables.

\subsection{Why this does not improve the global density bound}
The examples have fixed positive density and many progressions. Their discrepancy from the random benchmark is small, though as large as a quadratic norm bound permits in order of magnitude. They are not progression-free constructions and say nothing by themselves about a sharper upper or lower bound for $r_k(N)$.

The exact conclusion is narrower and useful: replacing the square in the general symmetric counting estimate by a higher power cannot be the source of a stronger density-increment proof. To obtain a better conclusion one must exploit additional structure, alter another stage, or improve constants rather than this universal exponent.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A self-contained quadratic upper benchmark\srctag{100}}]{A self-contained quadratic upper benchmark}\label{gsr:cc:100:sec:d3}\label{gsr:cc:100:sec:upper}
\srcnote{100}{Section 3}

We include an upper bound to make the word ``sharp'' independent of trusting the earlier research manuscript. Its coefficient is deliberately not optimized and is not a claimed improvement over source 20.

\begin{definition}
A finite abelian group is \emph{$k$-admissible} if multiplication by every integer $1,\ldots,k-1$ is an automorphism. A prime cyclic group of order greater than $k$, and $\F_p^n$ for $p>k$, are $k$-admissible.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Two marked factors]\label{gsr:cc:100:lem:twomarked}
Let $a_0,\ldots,a_{r-1}$ be distinct integers such that multiplication by every $a_i-a_j$, $i\ne j$, is invertible on a finite abelian group $G$. For $r\ge3$ and arbitrary functions $f_i:G\to\C$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:twomarked}
 \abs{\E_{x,y}\prod_{i=0}^{r-1}f_i(x+a_i y)}
 \le \Unorm{f_0}{r-1}\Unorm{f_1}{r-1}\norm{f_2}_2
          \prod_{i=3}^{r-1}\norm{f_i}_\infty.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $r=3$, Fourier expansion gives a sum of the form
\[
 \sum_{\chi\in\widehat G}
 \widehat f_0(c_0\chi)\widehat f_1(c_1\chi)
 \widehat f_2(c_2\chi),
\]
where each $c_i$ is a difference of two of the $a_j$, up to a sign. All three maps on the dual group are permutations. H\"older with exponents $4,4,2$, the identity $\Unorm f2^4=\sum_\chi|\widehat f(\chi)|^4$, and Parseval prove the base case.

For the induction step, normalize all unmarked factors $f_i$, $i\ge3$, to have supremum norm at most one; a zero factor is trivial. Choose an unmarked index $\ell$. Change variables to $t=x+a_\ell y$ and apply Cauchy--Schwarz in $t$ to remove $f_\ell$. With $\Delta_h f(z)=f(z)\overline{f(z+h)}$, this yields
\[
 |T_r|^2\le\E_h\abs{T_{r-1}\bigl(
      \Delta_{(a_i-a_\ell)h}f_i:i\ne\ell\bigr)}.
\]
Apply the induction hypothesis, preserving indices $0,1,2$ in their roles. Set $s=2^{r-2}$ and $q=s/(s-2)$, so $1/s+1/s+1/q=1$ and $1\le q\le2$. H\"older in $h$ bounds the right side by
\[
 (\E_h A_h^s)^{1/s}(\E_h B_h^s)^{1/s}
       (\E_h C_h^q)^{1/q},
\]
where $A_h=\Unorm{\Delta_{(a_0-a_\ell)h}f_0}{r-2}$,
$B_h$ is defined similarly, and
$C_h=\norm{\Delta_{(a_2-a_\ell)h}f_2}_2$.
Invertibility of the differences and the cube recursion give
\[
 (\E_h A_h^s)^{1/s}=\Unorm{f_0}{r-1}^2,
 \qquad (\E_h B_h^s)^{1/s}=\Unorm{f_1}{r-1}^2.
\]
Since $q\le2$,
\[
 (\E_h C_h^q)^{1/q}\le(\E_h C_h^2)^{1/2}
 =\left(\E_{z,h}|f_2(z)|^2|f_2(z+h)|^2\right)^{1/2}
 =\norm{f_2}_2^2.
\]
Taking square roots completes the induction. Homogeneity restores the supremum norms of the other factors.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[A quadratic symmetric count]\label{gsr:cc:100:prop:upper}
Let $G$ be $k$-admissible, let $A\subseteq G$ have density $0<\delta<1$, and set
\[
 u=\Unorm{\ind_A-\delta}{k-1},\quad
 \sigma=\sqrt{\delta(1-\delta)},\quad b_*=\max(\delta,1-\delta).
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:upper}
 \abs{\La_k(\ind_A)-\delta^k}
 \le C_k(\delta)u^2,
 \qquad
 C_k(\delta)=\sigma\sum_{r=3}^k
      \binom{k}{r}\delta^{k-r}b_*^{r-3}.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Write $g=\ind_A-\delta$ and expand the product. Terms with one $g$ vanish because $\E g=0$. Terms with two vanish because the map
$(x,y)\mapsto(x+iy,x+jy)$ is a bijection when $i\ne j$. For a term with $r\ge3$ occurrences of $g$, apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:100:lem:twomarked}, then the monotonicity of Gowers norms, to obtain
\[
 \abs{\E_{x,y}\prod_{j\in S}g(x+jy)}
 \le \Unorm g{r-1}^2\norm{g}_2\norm{g}_\infty^{r-3}
 \le u^2\sigma b_*^{r-3}.
\]
There are $\binom kr$ such terms, each with coefficient $\delta^{k-r}$. Summation proves the assertion. The Fourier identity, cube recursion, norm monotonicity, and triangle inequality used here are the standard Cauchy--Schwarz properties of the norms in \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:U} \cite{gowers}; the specific two-marked estimate has been proved above.
\end{proof}

Combining Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:100:prop:upper} and Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:100:cor:barrier} proves sharpness of the exponent, without claiming sharpness of $C_k(\delta)$ or of the stronger $B_k(\delta)$ from source 20.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{An analytic first-dependent-subset formula\srctag{100}}]{An analytic first-dependent-subset formula}\label{gsr:cc:100:sec:d4}\label{gsr:cc:100:sec:partition}
\srcnote{100}{Section 4}

The leading-order mechanism is a finite, exactly centered cumulant calculation. A qualitative central limit theorem would only imply that the moments tend to zero; it would not identify the first nonzero power or its coefficient.

\subsection{Statement}
\begin{theorem}[Partition formula]\label{gsr:cc:100:thm:partition}
Let $V$ be a finite set of size $m$, let $q\ge3$ divide $m$, and let
$X=(X_v)_{v\in V}$ be a bounded real random vector. Assume that each coordinate has mean zero and variance one, and that every set of fewer than $q$ distinct coordinates is jointly independent.

Take independent copies $X^{(1)},\ldots,X^{(n)}$ of the entire vector, and define, for a fixed real $\tau>0$,
\[
 S_{n,v}=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{r=1}^n X_v^{(r)},\qquad
 Y_{n,v}=\sin(\tau S_{n,v})-\E\sin(\tau S_{n,v}),\qquad
 a=\tau e^{-\tau^2/2}.
\]
If $\scrP_q(V)$ denotes the partitions of $V$ into $q$-element blocks, then
\begin{align}
 \E\prod_{v\in V}Y_{n,v}
 &=a^m n^{-m(1/2-1/q)}
    \sum_{\pi\in\scrP_q(V)}\prod_{B\in\pi}
        \E\prod_{v\in B}X_v\notag\\
 &\hspace{1cm}+O\left(n^{-m(1/2-1/q)-1/2}\right).
 \label{gsr:cc:100:eq:partition}
\end{align}
The implicit constant may depend on the fixed law, $V,q$, and $\tau$.
\end{theorem}

\subsection{Analytic setup and exact centering}
\begin{proof}
Put $\eps=n^{-1/2}$, and introduce the joint moment-generating function
\[
 \psi(z)=\E\exp\left(\sum_{v\in V}z_vX_v\right).
\]
Boundedness makes $\psi$ entire. Since $\psi(0)=1$, its logarithm has an analytic branch near zero, chosen to vanish at zero. Write its convergent expansion as
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:cumulants}
 \log\psi(z)=\sum_{\alpha\ne0}\frac{\kappa_\alpha}{\alpha!}z^\alpha.
\end{equation}
This equation can serve as the definition of the joint cumulants. The support of a multi-index $\alpha$ is the set of coordinates with positive exponent, and its total degree is $|\alpha|$.

Let $\psi_v$ be the one-coordinate moment-generating functions. The normalized sums have joint generating function $\psi(\eps z)^n$. Factor the marginal contributions exactly:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:factor}
 \psi(\eps z)^n
 =\prod_{v\in V}A_v(\eps,z_v)\exp H(\eps,z),
 \quad
 A_v(\eps,z_v)=\exp\{\eps^{-2}\log\psi_v(\eps z_v)\}.
\end{equation}
Zero means remove the apparent singularity at $\eps=0$, so the $A_v$ extend analytically there, with
\[
 A_v(0,z_v)=e^{z_v^2/2}.
\]
The interaction logarithm consists only of mixed cumulants:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:H}
 H(\eps,z)=
 \sum_{\substack{\alpha:\,|\supp\alpha|\ge q}}
       \frac{\kappa_\alpha}{\alpha!}\eps^{|\alpha|-2}z^\alpha.
\end{equation}
Indeed, restriction to any set of fewer than $q$ coordinates factors into independent marginals; its logarithm is a sum of one-variable logarithms. Hence every mixed cumulant supported on fewer than $q$ coordinates vanishes, even if some coordinate is repeated in that cumulant.

For $z_v\in\{i\tau,-i\tau,0\}$ set
\[
 c_v(i\tau)=\frac1{2i},\quad c_v(-i\tau)=-\frac1{2i},
 \quad c_v(0)=-m_v(\eps),
\]
where
\[
 m_v(\eps)=\frac{A_v(\eps,i\tau)-A_v(\eps,-i\tau)}{2i}.
\]
For the sequence $\eps=n^{-1/2}$ this is exactly
$\E\sin(\tau S_{n,v})$. Define the finite linear transform
\[
 \mathcal T_\eps P
 =\sum_{z\in\{0,i\tau,-i\tau\}^V}
       \prod_v c_v(z_v)A_v(\eps,z_v)\,P(z).
\]
Expanding the centered sines gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:transform}
 \E\prod_vY_{n,v}=\mathcal T_\eps(e^{H(\eps,z)}).
\end{equation}
Most importantly, if a polynomial $P(z)$ misses any variable $z_v$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:annihilate}
 \mathcal T_\eps P=0,
\end{equation}
since the sum in that variable is
$\sum_{z_v}c_v(z_v)A_v(\eps,z_v)=0$ exactly. This cancellation is valid before taking any asymptotic limit.

\subsection*{The support-cost argument}
Consider a product of mixed monomials from \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:H}. Let their supports be $S_1,\ldots,S_t$ and their total degrees be $r_1,\ldots,r_t$. Its power of $\eps$ is
\[
 J=\sum_{j=1}^t(r_j-2).
\]
Only products covering $V$ can survive \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:annihilate}. Since
$r_j\ge|S_j|\ge q$, every surviving product obeys
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:cost}
 J\ge\left(1-\frac2q\right)\sum_{j=1}^t|S_j|
 \ge m\left(1-\frac2q\right)=:J_0.
\end{equation}
Equality in both inequalities is possible only if
$r_j=|S_j|=q$ for all $j$ and the supports partition $V$. Conversely, any such partition has cost $J_0$.

For a block $B$ of $q$ distinct coordinates, the coefficient of
$\prod_{v\in B}z_v$ in the logarithm is
$\kappa_B=\E\prod_{v\in B}X_v$. To see this directly, the usual expansion of the logarithm expresses this coefficient as the raw moment minus terms indexed by proper partitions. Every proper block has size less than $q$, so its centered joint moment factors and vanishes. Thus only the raw $q$-moment remains.

In the exponential $e^H$, the $1/t!$ cancels the orderings of the $t=m/q$ distinct blocks of a partition. Therefore, among the monomials that use every variable, the coefficient at cost $J_0$ is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:leadingpoly}
 \left(\sum_{\pi\in\scrP_q(V)}\prod_{B\in\pi}\kappa_B\right)
       \prod_{v\in V}z_v.
\end{equation}
For this monomial the transform separates:
\[
 \mathcal T_\eps\prod_vz_v
 =\prod_v\left[\tau\Re A_v(\eps,i\tau)\right]
 =a^m+O(\eps).
\]
The last equality follows from analyticity of each marginal factor at zero.

\subsection*{Remainder control}
Because $q\mid m$, $J_0=m-2m/q$ is an integer. On the finite grid used in \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:transform}, the functions in \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:factor} and $e^H$ are analytic for $\eps$ in a common neighborhood of zero. Taylor-expand $e^H$ through degree $J_0$. Every Taylor coefficient is a polynomial in $z$: at any fixed cost only finitely many cumulant monomials can occur. All coefficients below $J_0$ are annihilated by \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:annihilate}; at cost $J_0$, the surviving part is \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:leadingpoly}. The finite transform has uniformly bounded operator norm near $\eps=0$. Its action on the Taylor remainder is therefore $O(\eps^{J_0+1})$.

Combining these facts with \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:transform} gives
\[
 \E\prod_vY_{n,v}
 =a^m\eps^{J_0}\sum_{\pi\in\scrP_q(V)}\prod_{B\in\pi}\kappa_B
     +O(\eps^{J_0+1}),
\]
which is \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:partition}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The first progression terms]\label{gsr:cc:100:lem:tripleexpansion}
Suppose a fixed bounded random vector $(X_1,\ldots,X_r)$ has centered, variance-one coordinates, and every two distinct coordinates are independent. Form centered sine sums $Y_{n,j}$ as above. Then
\[
 \E Y_{n,i}=0,\qquad \E Y_{n,i}Y_{n,j}=0\quad(i\ne j),
\]
while for three distinct indices
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:tripleexpansion}
 \E Y_{n,i}Y_{n,j}Y_{n,\ell}
 =a^3\E(X_iX_jX_\ell)n^{-1/2}+O(n^{-1}).
\end{equation}
For any fixed subset of at least four distinct coordinates,
its centered sine product is $O(n^{-1})$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Pairwise independence persists under independent coordinatewise summation and measurable transformation. The triple assertion is Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:100:thm:partition} with $q=m=3$. For a subset of at least four coordinates, the interaction logarithm starts at order $\eps$, and a monomial of cost one has total degree three and support at most three. It cannot cover the subset. The constant term and the cost-one term are therefore annihilated, and the same analytic proof gives $O(\eps^2)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why centering cannot be omitted]
A nonsymmetric coordinate law usually gives $\E\sin S_n=O(n^{-1/2})$. Subtracting this mean only approximately can create lower-order terms in large cube products. The exact marginal factorization and exact identity \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:annihilate} prevent that error. They are also the reason that a direct uncentered Gaussian heuristic is insufficient here.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Cube geometry and local circuit moments\srctag{100}}]{Cube geometry and local circuit moments}\label{gsr:cc:100:sec:d5}\label{gsr:cc:100:sec:cubegeometry}
\srcnote{100}{Section 5}

\subsection{Four-circuits of a binary cube}
Associate to a vertex $v\in\{0,1\}^d$ the row vector $(1,v)$ and the linear form
\[
 L_v(x,h_1,\ldots,h_d)=x+v_1h_1+\cdots+v_dh_d.
\]
Linear independence of these rows is equivalent to affine independence of the vertices.

\begin{lemma}[The first binary-cube dependencies]\label{gsr:cc:100:lem:cubegeometry}
Over $\R$, and over every field of odd prime characteristic, any three distinct binary-cube vertices are affinely independent. Four distinct vertices are affinely dependent if and only if they can be labeled $v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4$ so that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:rectangle}
 v_1+v_2=v_3+v_4.
\end{equation}
In the dependent case the relation space is one-dimensional, generated by a vector with two entries $1$ and two entries $-1$. There are
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:Rcount}
 |\scrR_d|=\frac{6^d-2\cdot4^d+2^d}{8}
\end{equation}
such four-element subsets.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Suppose a third binary vertex lies on the line through two distinct binary vertices, say $v=(1-t)v_1+tv_2$. Choose a coordinate in which $v_1$ and $v_2$ differ. In that coordinate, being binary forces $t\in\{0,1\}$, so the third vertex is not distinct. This proves the three-vertex assertion.

For four dependent distinct vertices, take a nonzero affine relation
$\sum_{i=1}^4a_iv_i=0$, $\sum_i a_i=0$. All $a_i$ are nonzero, because there is no three-vertex dependence. In any nonconstant binary coordinate, the indices with coordinate one must have coefficient sum zero. Such a subset has size two: sizes one and three would force one coefficient to vanish. If every nonconstant coordinate selected the same pair partition, two of the vertices would agree in all coordinates. Thus at least two different pair partitions occur. Their zero-sum equations force the coefficients, after scaling and relabeling, to be $(1,1,-1,-1)$. This proves \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:rectangle}. Conversely that equation is a dependence. The relation is unique up to scale because any three rows are independent.

In odd characteristic, the two sides of a binary coordinate equation in \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:rectangle} are integers from $0$ to $2$, so equality modulo the characteristic is also integer equality. Hence the same family $\scrR_d$ works over every odd prime field.

For the count, the number of ordered quadruples satisfying $a+b=c+d$ in the binary cube is $6^d$, by independent choices in each coordinate. Exactly $2\cdot4^d-2^d$ are trivial, with $(c,d)=(a,b)$ or $(b,a)$. Every nontrivial quadruple has four distinct vertices. Each unordered four-circuit has eight ordered representations. Subtract and divide by eight.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Exact partition recurrence]\label{gsr:cc:100:prop:Prec}
For a subset $S\subseteq\{0,1\}^d$, let $p_d(S)$ count its partitions into members of $\scrR_d$. Then
\[
 p_d(\varnothing)=1,
 \qquad
 p_d(S)=\sum_{\substack{B\in\scrR_d:\,v\in B\subseteq S}}
                   p_d(S\setminus B)\quad(S\ne\varnothing),
\]
where $v$ is any fixed element of $S$. In particular $P_d=p_d(\{0,1\}^d)$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Every partition has exactly one block containing $v$. Removing that block is a bijection to a partition of the complement. Different blocks give disjoint alternatives.
\end{proof}

Tiling the cube by faces in its first two coordinates proves $P_d\ge1$.
The recurrence gives the following exact small values:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{rrrr}
\toprule
$d$ & Vertices & Four-circuits & $P_d$\\
\midrule
2&4&1&1\\
3&8&12&6\\
4&16&100&635\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
For $d=3$, each of the six circuits through a fixed vertex leaves one circuit. For $d=4$, the 25 circuits through a fixed vertex leave complements with 21 partitions in 15 cases and 32 partitions in 10 cases. Thus $P_4=15\cdot21+10\cdot32=635$. The included exact recurrence code verifies these finite counts; none is inferred from numerical approximation.

\subsection{A circle observable}
Let $\T=\R/\Z$ with normalized Haar measure, and set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:circleh}
 h(t)=\cos(2\pi t)+\cos(4\pi t)
      =\frac12\sum_{\xi\in\{-2,-1,1,2\}}\eexpe{\xi t}.
\end{equation}
It has mean zero, variance one, and absolute value at most two.

\begin{lemma}[Circle local moments]\label{gsr:cc:100:lem:circlemoments}
For uniform $(x,y)\in\T^2$, any two distinct evaluations $h(x+iy)$ and $h(x+jy)$ are independent. For $0\le i<j<\ell$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:circletriple}
 \E h(x+iy)h(x+jy)h(x+\ell y)
 =\begin{cases}1/4,&i+\ell=2j,\\0,&i+\ell\ne2j.\end{cases}
\end{equation}
For a uniform cube parameter in $\T^{d+1}$, any three distinct evaluations $h(L_v)$ are jointly independent. For four distinct vertices $B$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:circlefour}
 \E\prod_{v\in B}h(L_v)
 =\begin{cases}1/4,&B\in\scrR_d,\\0,&B\notin\scrR_d.\end{cases}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
An integer matrix of full row rank defines a surjective homomorphism from a torus to the target torus: its dual integer map is injective. Its Haar pushforward is therefore uniform. This proves the independence statements from the row ranks, using Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:100:lem:cubegeometry} for cubes.

Fourier orthogonality makes a joint moment equal to the sum of products of Fourier coefficients over frequency vectors in the integer relation space. For three progression rows $(1,i),(1,j),(1,\ell)$, its primitive generator has entries
\[
 \left(\frac{\ell-j}{g},-\frac{\ell-i}{g},\frac{j-i}{g}\right),
 \qquad g=\gcd(j-i,\ell-j).
\]
A nonzero integer multiple can have every entry in $\{-2,-1,1,2\}$ only when the two positive entries are one and the negative entry is minus two, or the overall negative of this vector. This is precisely the equal-gap condition. There are then two contributions of size $1/8$, proving \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:circletriple}.

For four cube vertices outside $\scrR_d$, the rows are independent, so the moment is zero. On a four-circuit the primitive relation has coefficients $(1,1,-1,-1)$ after relabeling. Its four allowable nonzero multiples have scalar $\pm1,\pm2$, each contributing $(1/2)^4$. This gives $1/4$.
\end{proof}

The number of equal-gap triples among $0,\ldots,k-1$ is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:Dcount}
 \sum_{r=1}^{\lfloor(k-1)/2\rfloor}(k-2r)
 =\left\lfloor\frac{(k-1)^2}{4}\right\rfloor=D_k.
\end{equation}
Thus every $k\ge3$ has at least one positive triple contribution, while all the other triple contributions vanish rather than canceling it.

\subsection{A fixed-field observable}
For a fixed prime $p$, define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:spikeh}
 h_p(t)=\frac{p\ind_{\{0\}}(t)-1}{\sqrt{p-1}},\qquad t\in\F_p.
\end{equation}
It also has mean zero and variance one. Its bound depends on the fixed $p$.

\begin{lemma}[Rank formula for spike moments]\label{gsr:cc:100:lem:spikemoments}
For nonzero linear forms $L_1,\ldots,L_r$ on a uniformly sampled finite-dimensional $\F_p$-space, write $Z_j=p\ind_{\{L_j=0\}}-1$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:rankformula}
 \E\prod_{j=1}^rZ_j
 =\sum_{T\subseteq\{1,\ldots,r\}}
        (-1)^{r-|T|}p^{|T|-\rank(L_j:j\in T)}.
\end{equation}
If the $r$ rows form a circuit, meaning rank $r-1$ with every proper subset independent, the moment in \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:rankformula} is $p-1$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Expand the product. The simultaneous vanishing probability for the forms indexed by $T$ is $p^{-\rank(L_T)}$. Multiplication by $p^{|T|}$ gives \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:rankformula}. For a circuit every proper-subset term is the same as for an independent family, whose entire alternating sum is zero. The full-subset term changes from one to $p$, leaving $p-1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Field local moments]\label{gsr:cc:100:cor:fieldmoments}
Suppose $p>k$. For $k$ progression slots over $\F_p$, pairs of the variables $h_p(x+jy)$ are independent, and every distinct triple has moment $(p-1)^{-1/2}$.
For cube slots over $\F_p$, every three distinct variables are independent, and a distinct four-variable moment is $(p-1)^{-1}$ on a member of $\scrR_d$, and zero otherwise.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The progression rows are distinct and any two have full rank; every triple has rank two. Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:100:lem:spikemoments} and divide by $(p-1)^{3/2}$. The cube statements follow from Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:100:lem:cubegeometry}; divide its circuit moment by $(p-1)^2$. Independent rows yield independent uniform form values, so all smaller centered moments vanish.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The weighted saturation construction\srctag{100}}]{The weighted saturation construction}\label{gsr:cc:100:sec:d6}\label{gsr:cc:100:sec:weighted}
\srcnote{100}{Section 6}

Let $H$ be either $\T$ with observable \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:circleh}, or $\F_p$ with observable \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:spikeh}. On $H^n$ define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:weighted}
 S_n(z)=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{r=1}^n h(z_r),\quad
 m_n=\E_z\sin S_n(z),\quad
 g_n(z)=\sin S_n(z)-m_n,\quad
 f_n^\pm(z)=\delta\pm\lambda g_n(z).
\end{equation}
Here and below $h$ denotes the applicable observable. The mean of $f_n^\pm$ is exactly $\delta$, not just asymptotically so. Since $|g_n|\le2$ and $\lambda=b/4$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:margin}
 \frac b2\le f_n^\pm\le1-\frac b2.
\end{equation}

\begin{proposition}[Weighted asymptotics]\label{gsr:cc:100:prop:weighted}
Fix $k\ge3$ and $d\ge2$, with $M=2^d$. Let $\mu_4$ be the four-circuit moment and let $T_k$ be the sum of the progression triple moments. Then
\begin{align}
 \Unorm{f_n^\pm-\delta}{d}^{M}
 &=\theta^M P_d\mu_4^{M/4}n^{-M/4}
       +O(n^{-M/4-1/2}),\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:weightedcube}\\
 \La_k(f_n^\pm)-\delta^k
 &=\pm\delta^{k-3}\theta^3T_k n^{-1/2}+O(n^{-1}),
       \label{gsr:cc:100:eq:weightedAP}
\end{align}
where
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:localconstants}
 (\mu_4,T_k)=
 \begin{cases}
 (1/4,D_k/4),&H=\T,\\
 ((p-1)^{-1},\binom{k}{3}(p-1)^{-1/2}),&H=\F_p,\ p>k.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
In both cases the leading coefficients are nonzero.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Under a uniformly sampled cube parameter on $H^n$, different physical coordinates $r=1,\ldots,n$ give independent copies of the base random vector $(h(L_v))_{v\in\{0,1\}^d}$. Every fewer-than-four subset is independent. Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:100:thm:partition} with $q=4$, $m=M$, and $\tau=1$. The nonzero four-block moments are exactly the members of $\scrR_d$, each of value $\mu_4$. The partition sum is therefore $P_d\mu_4^{M/4}$. Multiplication by $\lambda^M$ proves \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:weightedcube}. Since $M$ is even, the choice of sign has no effect.

For a progression, expand
\[
 \prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(\delta\pm\lambda g_n(x+jy)).
\]
The singleton and pair terms vanish exactly. Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:100:lem:tripleexpansion} gives the leading triple contribution
$\pm\delta^{k-3}\lambda^3 e^{-3/2}T_kn^{-1/2}$. Every subset of size at least four contributes $O(n^{-1})$, and there are finitely many such subsets because $k$ is fixed. The local-moment lemmas give \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:localconstants}.
\end{proof}

Taking $M$-th roots in \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:weightedcube}, which is legitimate because $P_d\mu_4^{M/4}>0$, yields
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:weightedU}
 \Unorm{f_n^\pm-\delta}{d}
 =\theta P_d^{1/M}\mu_4^{1/4}n^{-1/4}
       (1+O(n^{-1/2})).
\end{equation}
The square of this quantity has order $n^{-1/2}$, exactly the order of the progression error. This is the basic saturation mechanism.

\subsection{Why the mechanism persists for longer progressions}
A longer progression has more triples, not a higher minimal dependence size: any three distinct rank-two progression rows are dependent. On the circle, the chosen small Fourier support retains precisely the equal-gap triples, all with positive moment. On a fixed field, the spike observable retains every triple, again with positive moment. There is therefore no leading-order cancellation as $k$ increases.

The Gowers cube behaves differently. Its first dependencies have four vertices, whatever the fixed dimension $d$. Covering all $M=2^d$ vertices at the cheapest interaction cost requires $M/4$ disjoint four-circuits. Each costs $n^{-1}$, so the cube moment has order $n^{-M/4}$ and its $M$-th root always has order $n^{-1/4}$. Merely increasing the norm order does not remove this particular obstruction.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A signed-radix transfer to prime cyclic groups\srctag{100}}]{A signed-radix transfer to prime cyclic groups}\label{gsr:cc:100:sec:d7}\label{gsr:cc:100:sec:transfer}
\srcnote{100}{Section 7}

The circle construction alone is not a finite cyclic example. This section transfers a finite collection of its moments without relying on an abstract modeling theorem or an asymptotic equidistribution assertion.

\subsection{Exact transfer of bounded Fourier polynomials}
Consider finitely many systems of integer linear forms
\[
 L_\nu(t_1,\ldots,t_r)=\sum_{\ell=1}^r b_{\nu\ell}t_\ell.
\]
Let $C\ge1$ be an integer bounding the sum of the absolute coefficients in every parameter column of every system:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:Cbound}
 \sum_\nu|b_{\nu\ell}|\le C.
\end{equation}
Allow different polynomials at different slots.

\begin{lemma}[Exact bounded-frequency transfer]\label{gsr:cc:100:lem:transfer}
Let $P_\nu$ be trigonometric polynomials on $\T^n$ with each coordinate frequency in $[-L,L]$, where $L\ge1$ is an integer. Put
\[
 B=2CL+1,\qquad a_j=B^{j-1}\quad(1\le j\le n).
\]
For an integer $Q>B^n$, define
\[
 \iota_Q(x)=(a_1x/Q,\ldots,a_nx/Q)\pmod1,
 \qquad x\in\Z/Q\Z.
\]
For each of the systems in \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:Cbound},
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:exacttransfer}
 \E_{t\in(\Z/Q\Z)^r}\prod_\nu P_\nu(\iota_Q(L_\nu(t)))
 =\E_{z\in(\T^n)^r}\prod_\nu P_\nu(L_\nu(z)).
\end{equation}
The same holds with any prescribed conjugations in the product.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Expand every polynomial in its finite Fourier series. A chosen tuple of frequencies contributes to the torus average precisely when, for every coordinate $j$ and every parameter column $\ell$,
\[
 c_{\ell j}:=\sum_\nu b_{\nu\ell}\xi_{\nu j}=0.
\]
On the cyclic group, orthogonality instead requires
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^nc_{\ell j}B^{j-1}\equiv0\pmod Q
\]
for every $\ell$. The column bound gives $|c_{\ell j}|\le CL=(B-1)/2$. Thus
\[
 \abs{\sum_{j=1}^nc_{\ell j}B^{j-1}}
 \le\frac{B^n-1}{2}<Q.
\]
The congruence is an integer equality. Reduction modulo $B$ forces $c_{\ell1}=0$, since $|c_{\ell1}|<B$; division by $B$ and repetition force all the other digits to vanish. Hence the two orthogonality conditions agree term by term. Conjugation only reverses some frequency signs and changes no bound.
\end{proof}

The map $\iota_Q$ is a homomorphism from a finite group into a torus, but need not have any uniform distribution property for arbitrary test functions. The exact conclusion concerns only the bounded-frequency family, which is all that the argument needs.

\subsection{An explicit approximation schedule}
For the circle observable \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:circleh}, $|S_n|\le2\sqrt n$. Let $T_n=2n+1$ and take the Taylor polynomial of sine through degree $T_n$. Its uniform error on this range is at most
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:eta}
 \eta_n=\frac{(2\sqrt n)^{2n+2}}{(2n+2)!}
       =\exp\{-n\log n+O(n)\}.
\end{equation}
As a polynomial in the coordinate exponentials, its frequency in each coordinate is at most
\[
 L_n=2T_n=4n+2.
\]
Subtracting $m_n$ and forming $f_n^\pm$ do not increase the Fourier support. We therefore have a trigonometric polynomial $P_n^\pm$ approximating $f_n^\pm$ uniformly within $\lambda\eta_n$.

To transfer the mean, the $k$-term progression count, and the $d$-cube moment, take
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:BCschedule}
 C=\max\{1,k,k(k-1)/2,2^d\},\qquad
 B_n=2CL_n+1.
\end{equation}
For every prime $Q>B_n^n$, Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:100:lem:transfer} applies to all three systems. Product telescoping shows that replacing each polynomial by $f_n^\pm$ changes the averages by $O_{k,d,\delta}(\eta_n)$; the polynomial suprema stay bounded because the functions are bounded. In particular, the pullback
\[
 F_{n,Q}^\pm(x)=f_n^\pm(\iota_Q(x))
\]
has mean $\delta+O(\eta_n)$ and preserves the required count and centered cube moment up to $O(\eta_n)$.

Recenter by a constant:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:recenterpullback}
 \widetilde F_{n,Q}^\pm
 =F_{n,Q}^\pm+\delta-\E F_{n,Q}^\pm.
\end{equation}
For all sufficiently large $n$, the margin \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:margin} ensures
$\widetilde F_{n,Q}^\pm\in[0,1]$. Its mean is exactly $\delta$, and recentering changes all the fixed moments by $O(\eta_n)$. Since $\eta_n$ is smaller than every fixed negative power of $n$, the asymptotics of Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:100:prop:weighted} hold for these cyclic functions with the same leading coefficients and the same stated polynomial error orders.

\begin{proposition}[Weighted prime-cyclic asymptotics at every large prime]\label{gsr:cc:100:prop:primeweighted}
For fixed $k,d,\delta$, choose $n(Q)$ to be the largest positive integer with $B_n^n<Q$, with $B_n$ as in \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:BCschedule}. Then $n(Q)\to\infty$ along primes and
\[
 n(Q)\sim\frac{\log Q}{\log\log Q}.
\]
The functions $\widetilde F_{n(Q),Q}^\pm$ have mean $\delta$ and satisfy the circle versions of \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:weightedAP} and \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:weightedU}.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The preceding argument gives the moment statements. Also $B_n=8Cn+O(1)$, so
\[
 \log(B_n^n)=n\log n+O(n).
\]
The threshold is increasing, and consecutive logarithmic thresholds differ by $O(\log n)$. The maximal choice therefore has
$\log Q=n\log n+O(n+\log n)$, which is equivalent to the claimed asymptotic relation.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Rounding, exact cardinalities, and completion of the main proofs\srctag{100}}]{Rounding, exact cardinalities, and completion of the main proofs}\label{gsr:cc:100:sec:d8}\label{gsr:cc:100:sec:rounding}
\srcnote{100}{Section 8}

\subsection{A quantitative rounding lemma}
\begin{lemma}[Rounding finitely many counts and norms]\label{gsr:cc:100:lem:rounding}
Let $G$ be a $k$-admissible finite abelian group of order $N$, let $f:G\to[0,1]$ have mean $\delta$, and fix $d\ge2$, with $M=2^d$. For all sufficiently large $N$ there is a set $A\subseteq G$ such that
\begin{align}
 |A|&=\lfloor\delta N\rfloor,\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:roundsize}\\
 \Unorm{\ind_A-f}{d}&=O_{k,d}(N^{-1/(4M)}),\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:roundU}\\
 \abs{\La_k(\ind_A)-\La_k(f)}&=O_k(N^{-1/4}).\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:roundAP}
\end{align}
The same conclusion can be imposed simultaneously for any fixed finite list of progression lengths and norm orders, provided $G$ is admissible for each requested progression length, with constants depending on the list.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose independent Bernoulli variables $I(x)$ with expectations $f(x)$, and put $r(x)=I(x)-f(x)$. Thus $|r(x)|\le1$ and $\E_I r(x)=0$.

For a cube with distinct vertices, independence of the point samples makes the expectation over $I$ of its $r$-product zero. Each possible pair of cube vertices coincides with probability $1/N$ under a uniform cube parameter: the difference is a linear form containing a coefficient $1$ or $-1$. By the union bound,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:noiseU}
 \E_I\Unorm r d^M\le\frac{\binom M2}{N}.
\end{equation}
The left side is nonnegative, as it is an expectation of a Gowers norm power. Markov's inequality makes
$\Unorm r d\le N^{-1/(2M)}$ fail with probability at most
$\binom M2 N^{-1/2}$.

The density has variance at most $1/(4N)$, so
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:densityround}
 \abs{\E_x I(x)-\delta}\le N^{-1/4}
\end{equation}
fails with probability at most $\tfrac14N^{-1/2}$.

The expected progression count differs from $\La_k(f)$ by at most $1/N$. Indeed, all entries of a progression with nonzero difference are distinct by admissibility, and the only possible bias comes from the $N$ constant progressions. To bound its variance, two progression products are independent unless their vertex sets meet. For each pair of positions, the probability of equality of those vertices in two independent uniform progression parameters is $1/N$. Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:varround}
 \Var_I\La_k(I)\le\frac{k^2}{N}.
\end{equation}
Chebyshev's inequality now gives
$|\La_k(I)-\La_k(f)|\le N^{-1/4}+N^{-1}$ outside an event of probability at most $k^2N^{-1/2}$.

For all sufficiently large $N$, the union of these failure events has probability below one. Choose a realization satisfying all three bounds. Add or remove points to obtain exactly $\lfloor\delta N\rfloor$ points. By \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:densityround}, the modification changes at most $N^{3/4}+1$ points; let $e=\ind_A-I$ and $\rho=\E|e|=O(N^{-1/4})$.

Since $|e|\le1$, dropping all but one factor in the absolute cube product gives
\[
 \Unorm e d^M\le\E|e|=\rho.
\]
The triangle inequality yields
\[
 \Unorm{\ind_A-f}{d}\le\Unorm r d+\Unorm e d
 =O(N^{-1/(4M)}).
\]
Product telescoping, and the uniform marginal distribution of each progression slot, bound the change in the count by $k\rho$. This proves \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:roundAP}. A union bound over any fixed finite list gives the last assertion; the same single cardinality correction works for all members of the list.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Completion of the fixed-field theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:100:thm:field}]
Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:100:lem:rounding} to $f_n^\pm$ on $\F_p^n$. Since $N=p^n$, every rounding error is exponentially small in $n$, with fixed $p,k,d$. The actual density differs from $\delta$ by at most $1/N$. The Gowers norm of a constant is its absolute value, so the triangle inequality also bounds the cost of replacing $\delta$ by $\delta_n$ by $1/N$. These errors are smaller than the remainders in \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:weightedAP} and \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:weightedU}. Substitute the field constants from \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:localconstants} to obtain \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:fieldU} and \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:fieldAP}; division gives \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:fieldratio}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Completion of the prime-cyclic theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:100:thm:prime}]
For each sufficiently large prime $Q$, take $n(Q)$ and $\widetilde F_{n,Q}^\pm$ from Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:100:prop:primeweighted}. Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:100:lem:rounding} on $\Z/Q\Z$. Here $Q>k$ for large $Q$, so admissibility holds. Since $Q>B_n^n$ and $B_n\asymp n$, both $Q^{-1/4}$ and $Q^{-1/(4M)}$ are smaller than every fixed negative power of $n$. The same is true of the approximation error \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:eta}. Thus all transfer, recentering, rounding, and cardinality errors are negligible compared with the stated remainders.

The circle constants in \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:localconstants} now give \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:primeU} and \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:primeAP}. Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:100:prop:primeweighted} gives \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:nQ}, and division gives \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:primeratio}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Nonconstant progressions}
The normalized count includes zero common difference. For an indicator set in a $k$-admissible group, exactly $|A|$ counted parameter pairs have zero difference; every nonzero difference produces distinct entries. Hence the number $T_k^*(A)$ of ordered nonconstant progressions is
\[
 T_k^*(A)=N^2\La_k(\ind_A)-|A|.
\]
After division by $N^2$, the correction is $O(1/N)$ and is negligible in every asymptotic above. The sharpness result is therefore not an artifact of counting degenerate progressions.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{One sequence for all fixed lengths and norm orders\srctag{100}}]{One sequence for all fixed lengths and norm orders}\label{gsr:cc:100:sec:d9}\label{gsr:cc:100:sec:universal}
\srcnote{100}{Section 9}

The fixed-parameter transfer can also be diagonalized. This gives a common family of examples rather than a different conceptual construction for each $k$.

\begin{theorem}[Simultaneous saturation]\label{gsr:cc:100:thm:universal}
Fix $0<\delta<1$. There are increasing primes $Q_n$ and sets
$A_n^\pm\subseteq\Z/Q_n\Z$, each of cardinality $\lfloor\delta Q_n\rfloor$, such that for \emph{every fixed} $k\ge3$ and $d\ge2$,
\begin{align*}
 \Unorm{\ind_{A_n^\pm}-\delta_n}{d}
 &=\frac{\theta P_d^{1/2^d}}{\sqrt2}\,n^{-1/4}(1+O_{d,\delta}(n^{-1/2})),\\
 \La_k(\ind_{A_n^\pm})-\delta_n^k
 &=\pm\frac{D_k}{4}\delta^{k-3}\theta^3 n^{-1/2}+O_{k,\delta}(n^{-1}).
\end{align*}
Here $\delta_n=\lfloor\delta Q_n\rfloor/Q_n$. No quantitative relation between $Q_n$ and $n$ is asserted in this simultaneous version.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Use the same torus functions \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:weighted} for every $n$. At stage $n$, consider the finite family of progression counts of lengths $3,\ldots,n+3$ and cube moments of orders $2,\ldots,n+2$, together with the mean. Approximate the torus functions by Fourier polynomials with enough accuracy that all transferred moments, after recentering, differ by less than $n^{-n}$. The required approximation exists by the sine Taylor expansion, choosing its degree as large as necessary; the degree need not remain $2n+1$.

Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:100:lem:transfer} to that finite family, then choose a prime $Q_n$ sufficiently large, and larger than $Q_{n-1}$, that the simultaneous rounding errors in Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:100:lem:rounding}, including the final norm errors, are also less than $n^{-n}$. Such primes exist because there are arbitrarily large primes. For any fixed $k,d$, the relevant system occurs in all sufficiently late stages, and $n^{-n}$ is negligible compared with all its fixed polynomial error scales. Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:100:prop:weighted} therefore supplies the claimed asymptotics.
\end{proof}

The quantifier ``every fixed'' is essential. Neither the central analytic expansion nor its error bounds have been made uniform when $k$ or $d$ grows with $n$. The diagonal construction does not silently establish such a uniform assertion.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Improving the attainable coefficient on prime cyclic groups\srctag{100}}]{Improving the attainable coefficient on prime cyclic groups}\label{gsr:cc:100:sec:d10}\label{gsr:cc:100:sec:improvingconstants}
\srcnote{100}{Section 10}

The two-frequency circle observable is convenient but not best even within a simple explicit class. Let $R\ge2$ be fixed and define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:hR}
 h_R(t)=\frac1{\sqrt{2R}}\sum_{1\le|m|\le R}\eexpe{mt}.
\end{equation}
This is real, centered, and of variance one. It is bounded by $\sqrt{2R}$, which is sufficient for the analytic argument with fixed $R$. For $R=2$ it is precisely \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:circleh}.

\begin{proposition}[A divisor-sum coefficient]\label{gsr:cc:100:prop:largerR}
Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:JK}
 J_{k,R}=\sum_{0\le i<j<\ell<k}
       \left\lfloor\frac{R\gcd(j-i,\ell-j)}{\ell-i}\right\rfloor,
 \qquad
 K_k=\sum_{0\le i<j<\ell<k}\frac{\gcd(j-i,\ell-j)}{\ell-i}.
\end{equation}
For the construction based on $h_R$, followed by the same prime-cyclic transfer and indicator rounding, the signed discrepancy-to-squared-$U^d$ ratio tends to
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:Rratio}
 \pm\frac{\theta\delta^{k-3}}{P_d^{2/2^d}}\frac{J_{k,R}}R.
\end{equation}
If $R$ is a positive multiple of $\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,k-1)$, then $J_{k,R}/R=K_k$, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:100:eq:Kdivisors}
 K_k=\sum_{s=2}^{k-1}(k-s)
             \sum_{\substack{m\mid s\\m>1}}\frac{\varphi(m)}m.
\end{equation}
In particular the larger attainable limits are
\[
 \pm\frac{\theta\delta^{k-3}K_k}{P_d^{2/2^d}}.
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
On a cube four-circuit, all nonzero frequencies must be scalar multiples of the primitive relation $(1,1,-1,-1)$. There are $2R$ such frequency choices, each with coefficient $(2R)^{-2}$, so
\[
 \mu_4=\frac1{2R}.
\]
For a progression triple $i<j<\ell$, the largest absolute entry of its primitive relation is $(\ell-i)/\gcd(j-i,\ell-j)$. The number of nonzero multiples lying in the Fourier support is therefore
$2\lfloor R\gcd(j-i,\ell-j)/(\ell-i)\rfloor$. Thus the sum of triple moments is
\[
 T_k=\frac{2J_{k,R}}{(2R)^{3/2}}.
\]
Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:100:prop:weighted} and division by the squared norm give
$\theta\delta^{k-3}T_k/(P_d^{2/2^d}\sqrt{\mu_4})$, which simplifies to \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:Rratio}.

The transfer proof changes only its fixed frequency bound and Taylor remainder constants: the degree-$T_n$ polynomial has coordinate frequencies at most $RT_n$, and $|S_n|\le\sqrt{2Rn}$. The error still equals $\exp\{-n\log n+O_R(n)\}$. Hence the conclusion applies to every sufficiently large prime, with the same asymptotic order for $n(Q)$.

When the stated divisibility condition on $R$ holds, every quantity inside the floors is an integer, so the floor loss vanishes. Group the sum for $K_k$ by the endpoint span $s=\ell-i$. For a given span there are $k-s$ positions of the left endpoint, and the middle gap ranges over $a=1,\ldots,s-1$. Since $\gcd(a,s-a)=\gcd(a,s)$,
\[
 \sum_{a=1}^{s-1}\frac{\gcd(a,s)}s
 =\sum_{\substack{m\mid s\\m>1}}\frac{\varphi(m)}m,
\]
by grouping according to $m=s/\gcd(a,s)$. This proves \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:Kdivisors}.
\end{proof}

For reference,
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{rcccccc}
\toprule
$k$&3&4&5&6&7&8\\
\midrule
$D_k/2$&$1/2$&$1$&$2$&$3$&$9/2$&$6$\\
$K_k$&$1/2$&$5/3$&$23/6$&$34/5$&$169/15$&$1742/105$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The equal-gap triples contribute $D_k/2$ to $K_k$, and the other triples contribute positively. The coefficient is therefore strictly improved for $k\ge4$. This is an improvement \emph{within the present lower-bound construction}. It is not a determination of the optimal universal coefficient in \eqref{gsr:fm:100:eq:source20}.

\section[{A finite calculation underlying the numerical evaluator\srctag{100}}]{A finite calculation underlying the numerical evaluator}\label{gsr:cc:100:sec:dB}
\srcnote{100}{Appendix B}
For the spike observable, a one-coordinate sign vector
$\sigma\in\{-1,0,1\}^m$ gives
\[
 \E_t\exp\left\{\frac{i}{\sqrt{n(p-1)}}
       \sum_{j=1}^m\sigma_j(p\ind_{\{L_j(t)=0\}}-1)\right\}.
\]
The characteristic function of the normalized sum over $n$ independent physical coordinates is the $n$th power of this finite average. Let
$Z_\sigma(t)=\sum_j\sigma_j\ind_{\{L_j(t)=0\}}$ and $s=\sum_j\sigma_j$. Its one-coordinate expression is
\[
 e^{-is/\sqrt{n(p-1)}}\sum_{r=-m}^m
       \Pp(Z_\sigma=r)e^{ipr/\sqrt{n(p-1)}}.
\]
The histogram of $Z_\sigma$ is computed by exact enumeration of the one-coordinate parameter space. Grouping identical histograms and the same values of $s$ and $|\supp\sigma|$ reduces the number of high-precision exponential evaluations. The coefficients are exactly those obtained from writing each sine as $(e^{iz}-e^{-iz})/(2i)$ and retaining its exact centering constant. This explains both why the computation handles very large $n$ and why it is a direct check of the same centering used in the proof.

\section{Source~96: \texorpdfstring{$c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le(100/843)^{1/4}$}{c(4,odd) at most 0.5868716} and the quartic cube coefficient \wtag}\label{gsr:cc:sec:oddquartic}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the fourteenth write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next two sections are source~96's Sections~7--8. \emph{Logically they continue} the chapters on the odd-order constants $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}$ of sources~28 and~29 (Section~\ref{gsr:cc:sec:oddconstant}), 45 (Section~\ref{gsr:cc:sec:ufourgap}) and~49 (Section~\ref{gsr:cc:sec:dualtest}), and the quartic cube expansion of sources~03, 04, 08 and~09.

\emph{What is proved.} For real centred $f$ on a finite abelian group of odd order, $\norm f_{U^4}^{16}\ge(42/5)\norm f_{U^2}^{16}$ by a profiled moment argument (Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:96:norm:main}), and $(843/100)\norm f_{U^2}^{16}$ with a rational dual certificate (Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:96:norm:optional-843}), so $c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le(100/843)^{1/4}=0.5868716\ldots$, against source~49's $(4/29)^{1/4}=0.6094183$; the concentration profile $F(p)$ has $F(1)=4795/832$, source~45's constant. The bracket after source~49 was $0.5587725\le c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le0.6094183$; it is now $[0.5587725,0.5868716]$, and the quartic coefficient of the $d=4$ cube expansion falls from $60.94$ to $100(100/843)^{1/4}=58.687$ (Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:96:cube:improved-quartic}; the printed $100/\sqrt2=70.71$ before source~49). Source~96 credits sources~28, 29, 34, 45 and~49. No source~01--95 and no later arrival improves $29/4$ except this one. The intake's numerical search found the least $Q_4/S^4$ near $10.2571$ ($c_4\approx0.558783$), so the truth lies near the lower end and the gap is the dual certificate's slack, not a wrong bound (evidence, not proof). The coefficient lemma behind the certificate is computer-assisted (a complete rational enumeration), rerun at this write.

\emph{Checked at the write} (\file{verify14.py}): $(100/843)^{1/4}=0.5868716172\ldots$; $843/100-29/4=59/50$, a relative gain $118/725$; $F(4793/5000)=8.4386>843/100$; $P_4=(6^4-2\cdot4^4+2^4)/8=100$. \emph{Formal status} (HEAD \texttt{a0c3e9b67}): Gowers's cube upper bound \file{lemma_3_10} (\file{Sections01_03}:340) is exact as \file{lemma_3_10_holds} (\file{Proofs03CubeUpper}:82); source~96's Corollary~\ref{gsr:fz:96:cor:gowers-cube} strengthens its bound for odd $N$ and $d\ge4$ on paper, through the analytic $843/100$ profile. No $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}$ constant is formalized. Questions: item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:normgap}.

\section[{A stronger real fourth-uniformity comparison\srctag{96}}]{A stronger real fourth-uniformity comparison}\label{gsr:cc:96:sec:d7}
\srcnote{96}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:section}

This section improves the odd-order coefficient $29/4$ recorded in
source~49 \cite{srcfortynine} to $843/100$. We first prove the cleaner
factor $42/5$, then sharpen the crossover in
Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:96:norm:optional-843}. The proof has two complementary
parts. A Fourier mass profile strengthens the use of the mean-sensitive
third-order inequality of source~45 \cite{repo96}. A dual test then treats
functions whose fourth Fourier mass is concentrated on one opposite pair.
For characters of order five, keeping the common phase of the test's
principal coefficient, norm, and residual coefficient substantially
improves the earlier certificate. For the other orders, a new rational
choice of the test parameter supplies the required bound.

\subsection{Statement and normalization}

For a real function $f$ on a finite abelian group $G$, write
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:Q-definition}
 Q_d(f)=\E_{x,h_1,\ldots,h_d}
       \prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^d}f(x+\omega\cdot h)
       =\norm f_{U^d}^{2^d}.
\end{equation}
The real-valued convention makes conjugations unnecessary in this
formula. All averages are normalized. Our Fourier transform is
\[
 \widehat f(\xi)=\E_x f(x)\overline{\xi(x)},\qquad
 S(f)=Q_2(f)=\sum_{\xi\in\widehat G}\abs{\widehat f(\xi)}^4.
\]
The dual group is written multiplicatively when we discuss characters
and additively in the Fourier face identity below.

\begin{theorem}[Odd-order fourth-uniformity gap]
\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:main}
For every finite abelian group $G$ of odd order and every real function
$f:G\to\R$ with $\E f=0$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:main-bound}
 \boxed{Q_4(f)\ge\frac{42}{5}S(f)^4.}
\end{equation}
Consequently, for every $d\ge4$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:all-d}
 \norm f_{U^2}^{4}\le
 \left(\frac5{42}\right)^{1/4}\norm f_{U^d}^{4}.
\end{equation}
The finite coefficient lemma in the proof is certified by complete
integer and rational enumeration in the accompanying verifier.
\end{theorem}

Thus, with the existing collection's convention
\[
 c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}=
 \sup_{G,f}\frac{\norm f_{U^2}^4}{\norm f_{U^d}^4},
\]
where the supremum is over nonzero real centered functions on finite
odd-order abelian groups, the theorem gives
$c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le(5/42)^{1/4}=0.5873949\ldots$.
The old upper bound from $29/4$ was $0.6094183\ldots$.
Neither constant is claimed optimal. In particular, monotonicity does
not give a new best $U^5$ comparison: source~49 already establishes
$c_5^{\mathrm{odd}}\le29/50$, which is smaller than $(5/42)^{1/4}$.

We assume $f\ne0$ until the final scaling step and normalize $S(f)=1$.
Since $G$ has odd order, every nonzero character belongs to an opposite
pair of distinct characters. Choose representatives $\xi_j$ and put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:pair-masses}
 p_j=2\abs{\widehat f(\xi_j)}^4,
 \qquad \sum_jp_j=1,\qquad p=\max_jp_j.
\end{equation}
The parameter $p$ measures the concentration relevant to the proof.

\subsection{Balanced autocorrelation moments with two blocks}

Define the real autocorrelation
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:autocorrelation}
 R(h)=\E_x f(x)f(x+h)
     =\sum_j b_j\bigl(\xi_j(h)+\xi_j(h)^{-1}\bigr),
 \qquad b_j=\abs{\widehat f(\xi_j)}^2\ge0.
\end{equation}
Here $2\sum_jb_j^2=1$ and $\E R^2=1$.

\begin{lemma}[Two-block moment profile]
\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:balanced}
Partition the opposite pairs into two blocks of total masses $s$ and
$1-s$. For every integer $k\ge1$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:balanced-profile}
 \E R^{2k}\ge C_k H_k(s),\qquad
 C_k=2^{-k}\binom{2k}{k},\qquad
 H_k(s)=\sum_{j=0}^{k}\binom{k}{j}^{\!2}s^j(1-s)^{k-j}.
\end{equation}
In particular, if $p\ge1/2$ and $x=p(1-p)$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:three-moments}
 \begin{split}
 V:=\E R^4&\ge\frac32+3x,\\
 B:=\E R^6&\ge\frac52+15x,\\
 A:=\E R^8&\ge\frac{35}{8}(1+12x+6x^2).
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Expand $R^{2k}$ using \eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:autocorrelation}. Character
orthogonality makes each averaged word either zero or one, and its
scalar coefficient is nonnegative. Retain only words having equal
numbers of $\xi_j$ and $\xi_j^{-1}$ for each $j$. Their contribution is
\[
 (2k)!\sum_{\sum_j k_j=k}\prod_j\frac{b_j^{2k_j}}{(k_j!)^2}.
\]
For the first block, fixing $\sum k_j=r$, use
$r!/\prod_jk_j!\ge1$ to obtain
\[
 \sum_{\sum k_j=r}\prod_j\frac{b_j^{2k_j}}{(k_j!)^2}
 \ge\frac1{(r!)^2}\left(\sum_j b_j^2\right)^r
 =\frac{(s/2)^r}{(r!)^2}.
\]
The corresponding estimate for the second block gives
\[
 \E R^{2k}\ge(2k)!\sum_{r=0}^k
 \frac{(s/2)^r((1-s)/2)^{k-r}}{(r!)^2((k-r)!)^2},
\]
which is \eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:balanced-profile}. Additional relations between
the characters can only add nonnegative terms; no dissociation
assumption has entered. Isolating a largest pair as the first block
and expanding $H_2,H_3,H_4$ proves \eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:three-moments}.
\end{proof}

These balanced moment arguments are inherited from sources~29, 34,
and~49 \cite{repo96,srcfortynine}. Their simultaneous use in the next scalar
estimate is the new step.

There is a convenient separate bound when $p\le1/2$. Greedily collect
pairs until their mass first reaches $1/4$. The resulting block has
mass $s\in[1/4,3/4]$, because the last added mass is at most $1/2$.
The derivative recursion and $U^3\ge U^1$ give $Q_4(f)\ge\E R^8$.
Since $s(1-s)\ge3/16$, Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:96:norm:balanced} yields
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:diffuse}
 Q_4(f)\ge\frac{35}{8}
     \left(1+12\frac3{16}+6\left(\frac3{16}\right)^2\right)
 =\frac{15505}{1024}>\frac{42}{5}.
\end{equation}

\subsection{Keeping the mean in the third-order inequality}

We include the following source~45 estimate and its proof to make the
dependence of the new profile explicit.

\begin{lemma}[Mean-sensitive real $U^3$ estimate]
\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:mean-sensitive}
Let $g:G\to\R$ be arbitrary and let $G$ have odd order. Set
$v=\abs{\E g}^4$ and $w=Q_2(g)-v$. Then $w\ge0$ and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:mean-bound}
 Q_3(g)\ge v^2+10vw+2w^2.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write $a_r=\widehat g(r)$, $\lambda_r=\abs{a_r}^2$,
$H=\sum_r\lambda_r^2$, and $M=\sum_r\lambda_r^4$. The Fourier face
identity is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:face-identity}
 Q_3(g)=\sum_{s,t}
 \left|\sum_r a_r\overline{a_{r+s}}\,
                    \overline{a_{r+t}}a_{r+s+t}\right|^2.
\end{equation}
Use the usual alternating conjugation convention in the Fourier
expansion; the actual frequency at vertex $\omega$ is
$(-1)^{|\omega|}r_\omega$. Orthogonality in the four variables of
the three-cube then imposes four additive constraints on its eight
labels. Their solutions
are exactly the affine labels $r_\omega=r+\omega\cdot h$, a
parametrization obtained using only addition and subtraction. For
fixed two frequency directions, summing over the base point and the
third direction gives the squared face sum in
\eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:face-identity}. No division, or order hypothesis, is needed
for this identity.

Let
\[
 \mathcal E(\lambda)=
 \sum_{r+s=t+u}\lambda_r\lambda_s\lambda_t\lambda_u.
\]
Retaining the two coordinate axes in \eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:face-identity}, and
subtracting their common origin once, gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:axes}
 Q_3(g)\ge2\mathcal E(\lambda)-H^2.
\end{equation}
In the nonnegative sum $\mathcal E(\lambda)$ retain the union of
\[
 (r=t,\ s=u),\qquad (r=u,\ s=t),\qquad(s=-r,\ u=-t).
\]
Each family has weight $H^2$ because $\lambda_{-r}=\lambda_r$.
Each pairwise intersection has weight $M$. The triple intersection
requires $2r=0$; odd order makes its weight $\lambda_0^4=v^2$.
Inclusion--exclusion therefore gives
\[
 \mathcal E(\lambda)\ge3H^2-3M+v^2.
\]
Finally, $H=v+w$ and pairing nonzero opposite frequencies gives
$M\le v^2+w^2/2$. Substitute these two facts into
\eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:axes} to obtain \eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:mean-bound}.
\end{proof}

Apply this lemma to $g_h=f\,f(\cdot+h)$. Put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:scalar-variables}
 t(h)=R(h)^2,\qquad w(h)=Q_2(g_h)-t(h)^2\ge0,
 \qquad W=\E_h w(h).
\end{equation}
We have $\E t=1$, and $V,B,A$ from \eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:three-moments} are
$\E t^2,\E t^3,\E t^4$, respectively. The derivative recursion and
\eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:axes} applied directly to $f$ give
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:W-constraint}
 V+W=Q_3(f)\ge2V-1,\qquad W\ge V-1.
\end{equation}
Here $H=S(f)=1$, and $\mathcal E(\abs{\widehat f}^2)=\E R^4=V$.
Averaging \eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:mean-bound} for the derivatives gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:derivative-bound}
 Q_4(f)\ge\E\bigl[t^4+10t^2w+2w^2\bigr].
\end{equation}

\begin{proposition}[A stronger concentration profile]
\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:profile}
Under $S(f)=1$ and $p\ge1/2$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:F}
 Q_4(f)\ge F(p):=
 \frac{4795+54996p(1-p)+27534p^2(1-p)^2}{832}.
\end{equation}
The function $F$ is decreasing on $[1/2,1]$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Use the scalar polynomial of source~45,
\[
 a=\frac{99}{676},\qquad b=\frac{33}{26},\qquad
 P(t)=-\frac14t^2+bt-a.
\]
The exact identity
$10t^2-4P(t)=11(t-3/13)^2$, together with $w\ge0$, implies
\[
 t^4+10t^2w+2w^2
 \ge t^4+2(w+P(t))^2-2P(t)^2.
\]
Expand, average, and apply Jensen to the square to obtain
\begin{align}
 Q_4(f)\ge{}&\frac78A+\frac{33}{26}B-\frac{2277}{676}V
             +4ab-2a^2\nonumber\\
 &\quad+2\left(W-\frac14V+b-a\right)^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:96:norm:scalar-certificate}
\end{align}
By \eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:W-constraint}, the expression inside the square is
at least $3V/4+83/676>0$. We may replace $W$ by $V-1$. The remaining
dependence on $V$ has derivative
\[
 -\frac{2277}{676}+3\left(\frac34V+\frac{83}{676}\right)
 =\frac38+\frac94\left(V-\frac32\right)>0
 \qquad(V\ge3/2).
\]
The coefficients of $A$ and $B$ in
\eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:scalar-certificate} are positive as well. Hence all
three lower bounds in \eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:three-moments} may be substituted.
Writing $x=p(1-p)$, the result is exactly
\[
 \frac{4795}{832}+\frac{13749}{208}x+\frac{1059}{32}x^2,
\]
which proves \eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:F}. All coefficients are positive and
$p(1-p)$ is decreasing on $[1/2,1]$.
\end{proof}

At $p=1$ this profile returns source~45's constant $4795/832$.
Its gain in the crossover region comes from retaining the mass profile
in all three moments before completing the scalar argument.

\subsection{Dual tests and a finite coefficient interface}

For a character $\chi$ of odd order $n$ and a real phase $\theta$, put
\[
 \phi_j=e^{ij\theta}\chi^j+e^{-ij\theta}\chi^{-j},\qquad
 g_\tau=\phi_1+\tau\phi_3.
\]
Its real fourth dual function is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:dual-definition}
 D_4g(x)=\E_{h_1,\ldots,h_4}
    \prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^4\setminus\{0\}}g(x+\omega\cdot h).
\end{equation}
Gowers--Cauchy--Schwarz \cite{gowers} gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:dual-holder}
 \abs{\E fD_4g}\le\norm f_{U^4}\norm g_{U^4}^{15}.
\end{equation}

We specify the finite coefficients before using their bounds. Assign
$r_\omega\in\{-3,-1,1,3\}$ to every vertex of the punctured four-cube.
Let $j$ count those with $\abs{r_\omega}=3$, and let
$k=\sum_\omega r_\omega$ as an integer. Retain an assignment when
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:step-constraints}
 \sum_{\omega\ne0}\omega_i r_\omega\equiv0\pmod n
 \quad(1\le i\le4).
\end{equation}
Let $c_{k,j,n}$ count the retained assignments and set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:dual-coefficients}
 d_{k,n}(\tau)=\sum_jc_{k,j,n}\tau^j.
\end{equation}
Character orthogonality then gives the exact expression
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:dual-expansion}
 D_4g_\tau=\sum_kd_{k,n}(\tau)e^{ik\theta}\chi^k,
 \qquad d_{-k,n}=d_{k,n}.
\end{equation}
Every output $k$ is odd. For $n=\infty$, notation means that the
constraints in \eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:step-constraints} hold as integer equalities.

The following finite procedure regenerates all coefficients without
enumerating $4^{15}$ full assignments. Split the punctured cube into
the upper face $(v,1)$, $v\in\{0,1\}^3$, and the seven nonzero lower
vertices $(v,0)$. Enumerate the $4^8$ upper assignments. Require their
total to vanish modulo $n$, and group them by their three other
coordinate sums, integer total, and count of frequencies of absolute
value three. Enumerate the $4^7$ lower assignments and match the
negatives of their coordinate sums to those groups. Sum integer totals
and counts in the matched assignments. The fourth-step equation is
the upper total; the remaining equations are precisely the matching
conditions. Each solution is counted exactly once. This is the
face-split algorithm of source~49, reproduced and credited in the
standalone verifier.

\begin{lemma}[Reduction to five coefficient tables]
\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:orders}
For every odd order $n\ge13$, the integer table $n=\infty$ applies
to \eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:dual-expansion}. Its nonzero output frequencies are
among $\pm1,\pm3,\ldots,\pm15$. None of the latter frequencies other
than $\pm1$ aliases the principal pair $\{\chi,\chi^{-1}\}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Each step sum consists of eight odd integers of magnitude at most
three, so is even and lies in $[-24,24]$. A nonzero even multiple of
odd $n\ge13$ has magnitude at least $26$. Thus congruence in
\eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:step-constraints} is equivalent to integer equality.
On an integer solution,
\[
 k=\sum_{\omega\ne0}\left(1-\frac{\abs{\omega}}2\right)r_\omega.
\]
The absolute values of the scalar coefficients sum to $5$, so
$\abs{k}\le15$. For an odd $k\in\{3,5,\ldots,15\}$, the nonzero
integers $k\pm1$ are even and have magnitude at most $16$, so cannot
be divisible by such $n$. Aliases among tail frequencies are permitted;
the triangle inequality used below remains valid. A tail harmonic
that is constant has zero pairing with centered $f$.
\end{proof}

For orders $7,9,11,\infty$, define, using positive output frequencies,
\begin{align}
 M&=d_1-\sum_{\substack{k\ne1\\k\equiv\pm1\ (n)}}\abs{d_k},
 \label{gsr:cc:96:norm:ordinary-M}\\
 E&=\sum_{k\not\equiv0,\pm1\ (n)}\abs{d_k}.
 \label{gsr:cc:96:norm:ordinary-E}
\end{align}
For $\infty$, congruence means integer equality. Form the cosine
polynomial $\E g_\tau D_4g_\tau$ by multiplying
\eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:dual-expansion} by $g_\tau$. Let $W$ be its constant
coefficient plus the absolute values of its other coefficients. Then
$Q_4(g_\tau)\le W$ uniformly in $\theta$.

\begin{lemma}[Retuned dual certificate]
\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:retuned}
For $\tau=-1441/10000$, each of the four tables
$n=7,9,11,\infty$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:retuned-table}
 M>\frac{164447}{2000},\qquad
 E<\frac{313}{1000},\qquad
 W<\frac{1644551}{10000}.
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:common-constants}
 \frac{(2M)^{16}}{16W^{15}}>\frac{1027}{100},\qquad
 \frac EM<\frac{381}{100000}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Exact finite certificate]
Apply the exhaustive face split to
\eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:dual-coefficients}, evaluate each polynomial at
$-1441/10000$, and compute \eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:ordinary-M} and
\eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:ordinary-E}. To compute $W$, for every positive $k$,
$j\in\{1,3\}$, and sign $\sigma\in\{-1,1\}$, retain
$k+\sigma j$ when it is divisible by $n$, and add
$2b_jd_k$ to the coefficient of
$\cos((k+\sigma j)\theta)$, where $b_1=1,b_3=\tau$.
This proves the norm polynomial formula directly from character
orthogonality. The accompanying program verifies all three strict
rational inequalities in \eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:retuned-table}, independently
for each of the four tables.

For orientation, their approximate values are shown in
Table~\ref{gsr:cc:96:norm:retuned-decimals}; the program stores the exact
fractions, and none of the rounded values is used in an assertion.
The common three rational bounds imply
\eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:common-constants} by the exact comparisons
\[
 (2\cdot164447/2000)^{16}
 >16\frac{1027}{100}(1644551/10000)^{15},\qquad
 \frac{313}{1000}<\frac{381}{100000}\frac{164447}{2000}.
\]
\end{proof}

\subsection{An order-five certificate retaining the entire phase}

The previous argument treats its principal coefficient and its test
norm separately. At order five, retaining their dependence on one
common phase gives a substantially stronger estimate with the same
test parameter $\tau=-7/50$ used in source~49.

For this subsection only, put $u=\cos(10\theta)$ and define
\begin{align}
 M(u)&=\Rea\bigl(e^{-i\theta}\widehat{D_4g_\tau}(\chi)\bigr),
 \label{gsr:cc:96:norm:phase-M}\\
 Q(u)&=Q_4(g_\tau),\qquad
 T(u)=\abs{\widehat{D_4g_\tau}(\chi^3)}^2.
 \label{gsr:cc:96:norm:phase-QT}
\end{align}
The letters $M,Q,T$ denote these phase-dependent quantities throughout
this subsection. Let $\mathsf T_r$ be the Chebyshev polynomial,
with $\mathsf T_{-r}=\mathsf T_r$. Set
$d_k=d_{k,5}(-7/50)$ and $b_{\pm1}=1$, $b_{\pm3}=-7/50$.
The exact coefficient formulas are
\begin{align}
 M(u)&=\sum_{k\equiv1\ (5)}
       d_k\mathsf T_{(k-1)/10}(u),
 \label{gsr:cc:96:norm:phase-M-poly}\\
 Q(u)&=\sum_{j\in\{\pm1,\pm3\}}
       \sum_{k+j\equiv0\ (5)}
       b_jd_k\mathsf T_{(k+j)/10}(u),
 \label{gsr:cc:96:norm:phase-Q-poly}\\
 T(u)&=\sum_{k,l\equiv3\ (5)}
       d_kd_l\mathsf T_{(k-l)/10}(u).
 \label{gsr:cc:96:norm:phase-T-poly}
\end{align}
The Chebyshev indices are integers: the relevant exponents are even
and divisible by five. All sums include negative output frequencies.
The degrees of $M,Q,T$ are $4,4,7$, respectively.

\begin{lemma}[Phase-coupled order-five bounds]
\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:phase-certificate}
For every real phase $\theta$, equivalently every $u\in[-1,1]$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:phase-bounds}
 M(u)>0,\quad Q(u)>0,\quad
 \frac{(2M(u))^{16}}{16Q(u)^{15}}>\frac{10297}{1000},\quad
 \frac{\sqrt{T(u)}}{M(u)}<\frac{31}{10000}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write $M=\sum_{j=0}^4m_ju^j$, $Q=\sum_{j=0}^4q_ju^j$, and
$T=\sum_{j=0}^7e_ju^j$. The rational coefficients are regenerated
from \eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:phase-M-poly}--\eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:phase-T-poly} and stored
in the certificate. The following is the complete small-degree
certificate used to turn them into uniform inequalities.

First, every $m_j$ and $q_j$ is positive, and exact evaluation gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:phase-positive}
 m_0-m_1-m_3>\frac{82581}{1000},\qquad q_0-q_1-q_3>0.
\end{equation}
Dropping the positive even powers and bounding the odd powers below
proves $M>82581/1000$ and $Q>0$ on $[-1,1]$.

Next put $L(u)=2M(u)-15Q(u)/16=\sum_{j=0}^4\ell_ju^j$.
Every $\ell_j$ for $j\ge1$ is negative, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:tangent-value}
 L(1)=\frac{25140503941235240913418195507}
 {2441406250000000000000000000}
 >\frac{10297}{1000}.
\end{equation}
As $u^j\le1$, this implies $L(u)\ge L(1)$. The elementary tangent
inequality $z^{16}\ge16z-15$ for $z\ge0$, applied to $z=2M/Q$, gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:tangent-dual}
 \frac{(2M)^{16}}{16Q^{15}}
 =\frac Q{16}(2M/Q)^{16}\ge2M-15Q/16=L(u).
\end{equation}
This proves the principal bound in \eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:phase-bounds} using
only a degree-four sign certificate.

For the residual coefficient the exact signs and inequalities are
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:tail-signs}
 \begin{gathered}
 e_1,e_2<0,\qquad e_j>0\quad(3\le j\le7),\\
 e_2+\sum_{j=3}^7e_j>0,\qquad
 e_1+e_2+\sum_{j=3}^7e_j<0.
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
If $0\le u\le1$, then
\[
 T(u)\le e_0+e_1u+
 \left(e_2+\sum_{j=3}^7e_j\right)u^2\le e_0.
\]
If $-1\le u\le0$, set $v=-u$. Drop the negative odd powers of
degree at least three and bound the positive even powers by $v^2$.
With $a=-e_1$ and $b=-(e_2+e_4+e_6)$, the exact certificate gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:tail-quadratic}
 b>0,\qquad
 T(u)\le e_0+av-bv^2\le e_0+\frac{a^2}{4b}
 <\frac{651}{10000}.
\end{equation}
The bound also holds on $[0,1]$. Finally,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:tail-final}
 \frac{651}{10000}<
 \left(\frac{31}{10000}\right)^2
 \left(\frac{82581}{1000}\right)^2.
\end{equation}
Together with \eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:phase-positive}, this proves the tail
bound in \eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:phase-bounds}.

Every coefficient sign and rational inequality in
\eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:phase-positive}, \eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:tangent-value}, and
\eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:tail-signs}--\eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:tail-final} is checked by exact
fractions in the verifier. The generation formulas
\eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:phase-M-poly}--\eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:phase-T-poly}, rather than a
preloaded polynomial table, are the inputs to those checks.
\end{proof}

The improvement is substantial at this finite interface. For the
same order-five test, source~49's separate bounds gave $C>9.68$ and
$\eta<0.005$. Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:96:norm:phase-certificate} gives uniformly
$C>10.297$ and $\eta<0.0031$. This concerns available certificates;
it does not prove that order-five characters worsen the true norm
extremum.

\subsection{A common dual profile in every odd order}

\begin{proposition}[Uniform concentrated-spectrum profile]
\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:dual-profile}
For every nonzero real centered function on an odd-order group,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:D}
 \frac{Q_4(f)}{S(f)^4}\ge D(p):=
 \frac{1027}{100}
 \left[p^{1/4}-\frac{381}{100000}(1-p)^{1/4}\right]_+^{16},
\end{equation}
where $p$ is its largest opposite-pair mass after normalizing by
$S(f)$. The function $D$ is increasing on $[0,1]$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Select a largest pair represented by $\chi$ and choose $\theta$ so
that $\widehat f(\chi)=A e^{i\theta}$ with $A>0$.
For every nonconstant frequency outside this pair, realness gives
\[
 \abs{\widehat f(\xi)}\le
 \left(\frac{S(f)(1-p)}2\right)^{1/4},
 \qquad A=\left(\frac{S(f)p}{2}\right)^{1/4}.
\]
If the order is $7,9,11$ or at least $13$, apply
Lemmas~\ref{gsr:cc:96:norm:orders} and~\ref{gsr:cc:96:norm:retuned}. The principal
aliases and the tail are bounded by
\eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:ordinary-M}--\eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:ordinary-E}, so
\[
 \E fD_4g_\tau\ge
 2M(S(f)/2)^{1/4}
 \left[p^{1/4}-(E/M)(1-p)^{1/4}\right].
\]
Use \eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:dual-holder}, $Q_4(g_\tau)\le W$, and raise to the
sixteenth power if the bracket is positive. This gives
\[
 \frac{Q_4(f)}{S(f)^4}\ge
 \frac{(2M)^{16}}{16W^{15}}
 \left[p^{1/4}-(E/M)(1-p)^{1/4}\right]_+^{16}.
\]
The constants in \eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:common-constants} imply
\eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:D}. The factor $16$ in the denominator comes from
$(S(f)/2)^4=S(f)^4/16$.

For order five the test has, apart from its principal pair and the
constant mode, only the opposite pair $\{\chi^3,\chi^{-3}\}$.
Its principal pairing is exactly $2A M(u)$ and its residual pairing
has magnitude at most
$2\sqrt{T(u)}(S(f)(1-p)/2)^{1/4}$. Any Fourier coefficients of $f$
outside the cyclic subgroup generated by $\chi$ have zero pairing
with the test. Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:96:norm:phase-certificate} and
\eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:dual-holder} therefore imply \eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:D} as well,
because $10297/1000>1027/100$ and $31/10000<381/100000$.

For order three, average $f$ over $\ker\chi$. Translation
invariance and norm convexity make this averaging contractive in
$U^4$. The resulting centered quotient function is $A\phi_1$.
The exact full-cube expansion gives
\begin{align*}
 Q_4(\phi_1)&=286+32\cos(6\theta)+16\cos(12\theta)\\
 &=262+32\bigl(\cos(6\theta)+1/2\bigr)^2\ge262.
\end{align*}
For completeness, the integer total-frequency counts at
$-12,-6,0,6,12$ are $8,16,286,16,8$. They follow by applying the
four step constraints and the base-point constraint modulo three
to all $2^{16}$ sign assignments, and are regenerated by the
verifier. Thus
\[
 Q_4(f)/S(f)^4\ge\frac{131}{8}p^4,
\]
which dominates \eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:D} since $131/8>1027/100$.
All possible nontrivial character orders have now been covered.
Finally, $p^{1/4}-(381/100000)(1-p)^{1/4}$ is increasing in $p$,
so its positive-part sixteenth power is increasing.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The crossover certificate and consequences}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:96:norm:main}]
The zero function is immediate. Scale a nonzero function so that
$S(f)=1$. If $p\le1/2$, use \eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:diffuse}. If
$1/2\le p\le23/24$, Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:96:norm:profile} gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:moment-cutoff}
 Q_4(f)\ge F(23/24)>\frac{42}{5}.
\end{equation}
The rational expression on the left is $8.4554355762\ldots$;
the strict comparison is checked exactly.

If $p\ge23/24$, the exact inequalities
\[
 (4947/5000)^4<23/24,\qquad (113/250)^4>1/24
\]
and Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:96:norm:dual-profile} give
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:dual-cutoff}
 Q_4(f)>
 \frac{1027}{100}
 \left(\frac{4947}{5000}-
       \frac{381}{100000}\frac{113}{250}\right)^{16}
 >\frac{42}{5}.
\end{equation}
The middle expression is $8.4220086382\ldots$, and again the
comparison is rational. This proves the desired inequality under
$S(f)=1$. Homogeneity restores $S(f)^4$. Monotonicity
$\norm f_{U^d}\ge\norm f_{U^4}$ for $d\ge4$ proves
\eqref{gsr:cc:96:norm:all-d}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The stronger numerical bound]
\label{gsr:cc:96:norm:optional-843}
For every real centered function on a finite odd-order abelian group,
\[
 Q_4(f)\ge\frac{843}{100}S(f)^4,\qquad
 c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le\left(\frac{100}{843}\right)^{1/4}
      =0.5868716172\ldots.
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Use the same profiles with $p_0=4793/5000$. The verifier checks
\[
 F(p_0)>\frac{843}{100},\qquad
 (24737/25000)^4<p_0,\qquad
 (4511/10000)^4>1-p_0,
\]
and
\[
 \frac{1027}{100}
 \left(\frac{24737}{25000}-
       \frac{381}{100000}\frac{4511}{10000}\right)^{16}
 >\frac{843}{100}.
\]
The same increasing/decreasing crossover argument proves the claim.
The diffuse-spectrum estimate also exceeds $843/100$, and the
zero function is immediate. Scaling and taking fourth roots give
the norm consequence.
\end{proof}
