\section[{Normalization and the exact cube identity\srctag{36}}]{Normalization and the exact cube identity}\label{gsr:fp:36:sec:d2}\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:sec:normalization}
\srcnote{36}{Section 2}

\begin{lemma}[Fourier-square expansion]\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:lem:square}
For every $g:V\to\C$ and $\xi\in V^*$,
\begin{equation}
 |\widehat g(\xi)|^2
   =\E_{x,y}g(x+y)\overline{g(x)}e_p(-\xi(y)).
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:square}
\end{equation}
Consequently
\begin{equation}
 \A_f(\sigma)=\E_{x,\hh,y}
       \partial_{h_1,\ldots,h_k,y}f(x)e_p(-T(\hh,y)).
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:twistedcube}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Expand the square as an average over two independent points $z,x$,
then substitute $z=x+y$. Apply the resulting identity to
$g=\partial_{\hh}f$. Commutation of multiplicative derivatives gives
\eqref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:twistedcube}.
\end{proof}

For $d\geq2$, the normalized Gowers power is
\begin{equation}
 \norm f_{U^d}^{2^d}
  =\E_{x,h_1,\ldots,h_d}\partial_{h_1,\ldots,h_d}f(x)
  =\E_{h_1,\ldots,h_{d-1}}
           \abs{\E_x\partial_{h_1,\ldots,h_{d-1}}f(x)}^2.
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:gowers}
\end{equation}
The second identity proves the nonnegativity needed in this article.
No triangle inequality for $U^d$ is used below.

The off-by-one in the notation has mathematical content. A $k$-fold
derivative has a linear frequency if its phase originally had degree
$k+1$. Accordingly there are $k+1$ variables in $T$, the polynomial in
\eqref{gsr:fm:36:ssc:eq:canonical} has degree at most $k+1$, and the final norm is
$U^{k+1}$. The following table can serve as a normalization check.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}llll@{}}
\toprule
Derivative order & Selector & Total form & Extracted phase / norm\\
\midrule
$1$ & linear & bilinear & quadratic / $U^2$\\
$2$ & bilinear & trilinear & cubic / $U^3$\\
$3$ & trilinear & four-linear & quartic / $U^4$\\
$k$ & $k$-linear & $(k+1)$-linear & degree $k+1$ / $U^{k+1}$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The sharp bilinear estimate\srctag{36}}]{The sharp bilinear estimate}\label{gsr:fp:36:sec:d3}\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:sec:bilinear}
\srcnote{36}{Section 3}

\subsection{Statement and a direct operator proof}
Let $B:V\times V\to\Fp$ be bilinear. Its alternating part is
\begin{equation}
 \Omega(h,x)=B(h,x)-B(x,h).
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:omega}
\end{equation}
The rank of $\Omega$, as a map $V\to V^*$, is even; write it as $2r$.
For two functions $g,v:V\to\C$ define
\begin{equation}
 \Qthirtysix_B(g,v)=\E_h\abs{\E_xg(x+h)\overline{v(x)}e_p(-B(h,x))}^2,
 \qquad \Qthirtysix_B(g)=\Qthirtysix_B(g,g).
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:bilinearq}
\end{equation}
The $L^2$ norms below use normalized counting measure.

\begin{theorem}[Alternating-rank orthogonality]\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:thm:bilinear}
For arbitrary complex functions $g,v$,
\begin{equation}
 \Qthirtysix_B(g,v)\leq p^{-r}\norm g_2^2\norm v_2^2.
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:bilinearbound}
\end{equation}
In particular $\Qthirtysix_B(g)\leq p^{-r}\norm g_2^4$. For each $B$ the
factor $p^{-r}$ is attained with $g=v$ and $|g|=1$ everywhere.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 34--39]
This is the sharp, rank-sensitive form of source~31's Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:31:lem:twirl} (note in Section~\ref{gsr:fm:36:sec:d1}). Independent checks of the intake: on $21$ random triples over $\F_3^2$, $\F_5^2$, $\F_3^3$, $\F_3^4$ the normalized ratio stayed below $0.49$; the value $1/p$ is attained at $p=3,5,7$; over all $6{,}561$ trilinear forms on $\F_3^2$ with $f=1$ the maximum of the tested energy over the nonsymmetric forms is exactly $5/9=1-(2/3)^2$, the threshold of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:36:ssc:thm:main} at $k=2$.
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 40--46]
Source~43's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:orthogonality} proves the bound $d_B^{-1}$, $d_B=\sqrt{|G/R_B|}$, for every biadditive form on every finite abelian group, without division by two (checked at the write on small groups; note in Section~\ref{gsr:fm:43:sec:d1}).
\end{writenote}

We first establish the only representation-theoretic fact required for
the inequality. Inner products are linear in the first argument.

\begin{lemma}[Minimum dimension of an invariant subspace]\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:lem:multiplicity}
Suppose unitary operators $(U_h)_{h\in V}$ on a finite-dimensional
complex Hilbert space satisfy
\begin{equation}
 U_hU_l=e_p(\Omega(h,l)/2)U_{h+l},\qquad U_0=I.
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:cocycle}
\end{equation}
Every nonzero subspace invariant under all $U_h$ has dimension at least
$D=p^r$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
An alternating form of rank $2r$ has vectors
$a_1,\ldots,a_r,b_1,\ldots,b_r$ with
$\Omega(a_i,b_j)=\delta_{ij}$ and all pairings within the $a$-family or
within the $b$-family zero. To obtain them, select $a,b$ with
$\Omega(a,b)\ne0$, scale $b$ to make the value one, split off their
nondegenerate two-dimensional span, and repeat on its orthogonal
complement. This also proves evenness of the rank.

Put $X_i=U_{a_i}$ and $Z_i=U_{b_i}$. The $Z_i$ commute, $Z_i^p=I$, and
\[
 X_iZ_j=e_p(\delta_{ij})Z_jX_i.
\]
Let $E$ be a nonzero invariant subspace. It is invariant under the
inverses as well, because those are among the $U_h$ up to scalars.
The commuting unitary restrictions $Z_i|_E$ have a common nonzero
eigenvector $z$. For each $t=(t_1,\ldots,t_r)\in\Fp^r$, the vector
$X_1^{t_1}\cdots X_r^{t_r}z$ belongs to $E$. Its simultaneous $Z_i$
eigenvalues are those of $z$ multiplied by $e_p(-t_i)$.
Different $t$ give different joint eigenspaces, which are orthogonal.
There are $p^r$ such nonzero vectors. The case $r=0$ is immediate.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of the inequality in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:thm:bilinear}]
Work on $\Hh=L^2(V)$ and put
\begin{align}
 W_hg(x)&=g(x+h)e_p(-B(h,x)),\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:weyl}\\
 U_h&=e_p(-B(h,h)/2)W_h.\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:gauge}
\end{align}
A direct multiplication gives
$W_hW_l=e_p(-B(l,h))W_{h+l}$; substituting
\eqref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:gauge} yields \eqref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:cocycle}.
For $u\in\Hh$ let $P_u$ be the positive rank-one operator
$P_u(z)=\inner z u\,u$. Its trace is $\|u\|_2^2$.
Define the positive operator
\begin{equation}
 M_g=\E_h P_{U_hg}.\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:twirl}
\end{equation}
Translation of the index $h$, together with the cocycle law, gives
$U_lM_gU_l^{-1}=M_g$ for all $l$. Each eigenspace of $M_g$ is therefore
invariant. If $\lambda>0$ is its largest eigenvalue, the corresponding
eigenspace has dimension at least $D$ by
Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:lem:multiplicity}. Thus
\[
 D\lambda\leq\tr(M_g)=\norm g_2^2.
\]
Finally, multiplication by the scalar in \eqref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:gauge} does not
change the absolute value of a matrix coefficient, and
\[
 \Qthirtysix_B(g,v)=\inner{M_gv}{v}\leq\lambda\norm v_2^2.
\]
If $M_g=0$ the conclusion is automatic. This proves
\eqref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:bilinearbound} without an irreducible-representation
classification.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Sharp unit-modulus examples}
The symplectic splitting in the preceding proof yields independent
functionals $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r,\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_r\in V^*$
such that
\begin{equation}
 \Omega(h,x)=\sum_{j=1}^r
   \bigl(\alpha_j(h)\beta_j(x)-\beta_j(h)\alpha_j(x)\bigr).
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:symplecticnormal}
\end{equation}
Set $B_0(h,x)=\sum_j\alpha_j(h)\beta_j(x)$. Then $S=B-B_0$ is symmetric.
With $P_B(x)=S(x,x)/2$ and $g(x)=e_p(P_B(x))$, direct expansion gives
\begin{equation}
 \E_x\partial_hg(x)e_p(-B(h,x))
  =e_p(S(h,h)/2)\E_x e_p(-B_0(h,x)).
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:extremizercoefficient}
\end{equation}
The last average is one when all $\alpha_j(h)$ vanish and zero otherwise,
by character orthogonality. That event has probability $p^{-r}$.
This proves the sharpness assertion of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:thm:bilinear}, including the $1$-bounded setting.

For instance, on $\Fp^2$ take $B(h,x)=h_1x_2$ and $g=1$.
The alternating rank is two, and $\Qthirtysix_B(g)=1/p$. On $\Fp^{2r}$, taking
$B(h,x)=\sum_{j=1}^r h_{2j-1}x_{2j}$ and $g=1$ gives $p^{-r}$.
A bound based only on whether the alternating part vanishes would lose
all information distinguishing these examples.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The derivative rank profile\srctag{36}}]{The derivative rank profile}\label{gsr:fp:36:sec:d4}\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:sec:profile}
\srcnote{36}{Section 4}

Fix $i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$. Let $\uu$ denote the other $k-1$ increments,
inserted in their original slots, and set
\begin{align}
 g_{i,\uu}(x)&=\partial_{h_1,\ldots,\widehat{h_i},\ldots,h_k}f(x),
   &m_i(\uu)&=\norm{g_{i,\uu}}_2^2,\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:frozen}\\
 B_{i,\uu}(a,b)&=T(h_1,\ldots,h_{i-1},a,h_{i+1},\ldots,h_k,b),
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:sliceb}\\
 \Omega_{i,\uu}(a,b)&=B_{i,\uu}(a,b)-B_{i,\uu}(b,a),
   &r_i(\uu)&=\tfrac12\rk\Omega_{i,\uu}.
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:slicerank}
\end{align}
For $k=1$ the tuple $\uu$ is empty, has probability one, and
$g_{i,\uu}=f$. These conventions avoid a separate base case later.

\begin{theorem}[Amplitude-sensitive rank-profile bound]\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:thm:profile}
For every multilinear selector and every complex $f$,
\begin{equation}
 \A_f(\sigma)\leq
       \min_{1\leq i\leq k}\E_{\uu}p^{-r_i(\uu)}m_i(\uu)^2.
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:weightedprofile}
\end{equation}
For $1$-bounded $f$ this implies
\begin{equation}
 \A_f(\sigma)\leq
       \min_i\E_{\uu}p^{-r_i(\uu)}.
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:profile}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Fix $i$ and average last over $h_i=a$. Commutation of derivatives gives
$\partial_{\hh}f=\partial_a g_{i,\uu}$. Therefore
\[
 \A_f(\sigma)=\E_{\uu}\Qthirtysix_{B_{i,\uu}}(g_{i,\uu}).
\]
Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:thm:bilinear} to each slice. If $|f|\leq1$, then
$|g_{i,\uu}|\leq1$ and $m_i(\uu)\leq1$. Since the calculation applies
to every $i$, both minima follow.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Quantitative low-rank consequences]\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:cor:ranktail}
Assume $|f|\leq1$ and $\A_f(\sigma)\geq a$. For every $i$ and integer
$t\geq1$,
\begin{align}
 \Prb_{\uu}(r_i(\uu)\geq t)
       &\leq\frac{1-a}{1-p^{-t}},\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:ranktail}\\
 \Prb_{\uu}(r_i(\uu)<t)
       &\geq\frac{a-p^{-t}}{1-p^{-t}}.
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:rankpopular}
\end{align}
The second bound is informative when $a>p^{-t}$. If $r_i\geq t$ on a
set of tuples of density at least $\rho$, then
\begin{equation}
 \A_f(\sigma)\leq1-\rho(1-p^{-t}).\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:rankobstruction}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The profile average is at most
$\Prb(r_i<t)+p^{-t}\Prb(r_i\geq t)$. Rearrange and use
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:thm:profile}.
\end{proof}

The amplitude information should not be discarded unnecessarily. If a
frozen derivative has small $L^2$ mass, it is expensive to attribute
energy to that slice even when its alternating rank is zero. Conversely,
a large unweighted set of rank-zero slices need not carry appreciable
energy. Formula~\eqref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:weightedprofile} keeps these distinctions.

As a simple scale check, for $p=101$, $k=2$, an energy of $0.05$ is above
$\vartheta_{2,101}=201/10201$. It therefore certifies symmetry. For $p=5$
the same energy is below $\vartheta_{2,5}=9/25$ and does not do so.
The rank profile may still give useful information in the latter case.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Proof and sharpness of the symmetry threshold\srctag{36}}]{Proof and sharpness of the symmetry threshold}\label{gsr:fp:36:sec:d5}\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:sec:threshold}
\srcnote{36}{Section 5}

\subsection{A support lemma}
\begin{lemma}[Nonzero multilinear maps have positive support]\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:lem:support}
Let $F:V_1\times\cdots\times V_m\to W$ be a nonzero multilinear map of
finite-dimensional $\Fp$-vector spaces. Then
\begin{equation}
 \Prb(F\ne0)\geq(1-1/p)^m.\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:support}
\end{equation}
The convention for $m=0$ is a nonzero constant, with support probability
one. The same bound holds when $F$ is separately affine.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For a nonzero linear map in one variable, its kernel has codimension at
least one, so its zero probability is at most $1/p$. A nonzero affine
map either has no zeros or has a zero set which is a translate of a
proper linear kernel, giving the same bound.

For the induction, regard $F$ as a map in its first $m-1$ variables
with values in the vector space of linear maps $V_m\to W$ (or the
vector space of affine maps in the separately affine case).
This new map is nonzero and of the same separate type. By induction,
it takes a nonzero value on at least a fraction $(1-1/p)^{m-1}$ of
tuples. Conditional on such a tuple, the remaining nonzero linear or
affine map is nonzero at a fraction at least $1-1/p$ of its inputs.
Multiplying the two fractions proves the assertion.
\end{proof}

The bound is attained by $F(v_1,\ldots,v_m)=
\ell_1(v_1)\cdots\ell_m(v_m)w$, where the $\ell_j$ are nonzero
functionals and $w\ne0$. Vector-valued output is important in the
application: the output will be a whole alternating bilinear form,
not its value at a preselected pair.

\subsection{Certification}
\begin{proof}[Proof of the inequality in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:36:ssc:thm:main}]
The transpositions $(i,k+1)$, $1\leq i\leq k$, generate the symmetric
group on the $k+1$ slots. Therefore, if $T$ is not fully symmetric,
there is some $i$ for which
\[
 T(h_1,\ldots,h_i,\ldots,h_k,y)
 -T(h_1,\ldots,y,\ldots,h_k,h_i)
\]
is nonzero as a multilinear form. In the notation of
\eqref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:slicerank}, this says that
$\uu\mapsto\Omega_{i,\uu}$ is a nonzero $(k-1)$-linear map into the
vector space of alternating bilinear forms on $V$.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:lem:support} gives
\[
 \rho:=\Prb_{\uu}(\Omega_{i,\uu}\ne0)
             \geq(1-1/p)^{k-1}.
\]
Every nonzero alternating form has rank at least two, so
$r_i(\uu)\geq1$ on this event. Hence
\begin{align*}
 \A_f(\sigma)
 &\leq\E_{\uu}p^{-r_i(\uu)}\\
 &\leq(1-\rho)+\rho/p\\
 &\leq1-(1-1/p)^k.
\end{align*}
This includes $k=1$ because the nonzero defect is then a fixed
alternating bilinear form.
\end{proof}

The proof combines two independent exact obstructions: a nonzero
multilinear defect cannot hide on too few slices, and on every defective
slice noncommutation forces a factor at most $1/p$. Treating the
alternating defect as an arbitrary scalar polynomial would obscure the
second obstruction and lose the sharp constant.

\subsection{Endpoint construction}
\begin{proof}[Proof of sharpness in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:36:ssc:thm:main}]
Assume $\dim V\geq2$ and choose linearly independent $a,c\in V^*$.
Set $f=1$ and
\begin{equation}
 \sigma(h_1,\ldots,h_k)=\left(\prod_{j=1}^k a(h_j)\right)c.
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:endpointselector}
\end{equation}
This selector is symmetric in its $k$ inputs. Choose $u,v\in V$ with
$a(u)=1$, $c(u)=0$, $a(v)=0$, $c(v)=1$.
Then $T(u,\ldots,u,v)=1$, whereas swapping the first and last entries
makes the value zero. Thus $T$ is not fully symmetric.

Every multiplicative derivative of $f$ is one. Its Fourier coefficient
at a frequency is one exactly when that frequency is zero. Therefore
\begin{equation}
 \A_1(\sigma)
   =\Prb\!\left(\prod_{j=1}^k a(h_j)=0\right)
   =1-(1-1/p)^k.
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:endpointenergy}
\end{equation}
For a fixed $i$, the alternating slice is a scalar multiple of
$a\otimes c-c\otimes a$. Its rank is zero when
$\prod_{j\ne i}a(h_j)=0$ and two otherwise. Thus the rank-profile
bound and the support lemma are simultaneously equalities.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The strict inequality cannot be relaxed]
The implication in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:36:ssc:thm:main} uses $>$, not $\geq$.
It remains sharp after imposing symmetry in the derivative slots or
restricting to unit-modulus functions. In dimension one every scalar
multilinear form is already fully symmetric, so the nonsymmetric
extremal class is empty there.
\end{remark}

For reference, the first three thresholds are as follows. These are
symmetry thresholds; classical integration separately requires $p>k+1$.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}c c c c@{}}
\toprule
$p$ & $k=1$ & $k=2$ & $k=3$\\
\midrule
$3$ & $1/3$ & $5/9$ & $19/27$\\
$5$ & $1/5$ & $9/25$ & $61/125$\\
$17$ & $1/17$ & $33/289$ & $817/4913$\\
$101$ & $1/101$ & $201/10201$ & $30301/1030301$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Equality structure and stability of the bilinear step\srctag{36}}]{Equality structure and stability of the bilinear step}\label{gsr:fp:36:sec:d6}\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:sec:stability}
\srcnote{36}{Section 6}

The short operator proof suffices for the main threshold. A fuller
orthogonality identity explains how close-to-extremal slices look. This
section is a refinement of the bilinear step, not a classification of
all extremizers of the higher-order threshold.

\subsection{Block decomposition and an exact identity}
Retain $B$, $\Omega$, $r$, $D=p^r$, and the operators $U_h$ from
Section~\ref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:sec:bilinear}. Put $R=\Rthirtysix\Omega$ and choose a
nondegenerate complement $W$, so $V=R\oplus W$ and $|W|=D^2$.
The $U_z$, $z\in R$, form an ordinary commuting representation of the
additive group $R$. Consequently
\begin{equation}
 \Hh=\bigoplus_{\chi\in R^*_{\mathrm{char}}}\Hh_\chi,
 \qquad U_z|_{\Hh_\chi}=\chi(z)I.
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:blocks}
\end{equation}
Here $R^*_{\mathrm{char}}$ denotes its complex character group. Zero
blocks may be omitted for a general representation; for the concrete
representation on $L^2(V)$ every block below is nonzero.

\begin{lemma}[Explicit Weyl decomposition]\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:lem:weyldecomposition}
There are unitary identifications
\begin{equation}
 \Hh_\chi\simeq\C^D\otimes\C^D
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:tensorblocks}
\end{equation}
under which $U_w$, $w\in W$, acts on the first factor and trivially on
the second. Writing its first-factor action as $A_{\chi,w}$, the
$D^2$ matrices $D^{-1/2}A_{\chi,w}$ form an orthonormal basis of
$\operatorname{Mat}_D(\C)$ for the Hilbert--Schmidt inner product.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose symplectic generators $X_i,Z_i$ as in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:lem:multiplicity}. Within a fixed block, the common
$Z_i$ eigenspaces are permuted transitively by the $X_i$, so they have
a common dimension, say $m_\chi$. Choose an orthonormal basis of the
joint eigenspace with all eigenvalues one, and transport it by the
$X_i$. That eigenspace exists whenever the block is nonzero, because
the $X_i$ shift any joint eigenvalue tuple to $(1,\ldots,1)$.
In the resulting basis the $X_i$ shift the $D$ eigenvalue labels and
the $Z_i$ multiply them by characters, without affecting the basis
index within the original eigenspace. This constructs
$\Hh_\chi\simeq\C^D\otimes\C^{m_\chi}$.

For the concrete $U_h$ on $L^2(V)$, the trace of $U_h$ is zero for
$h\ne0$: it is a scalar times a modulated nonzero translation and
has zero diagonal in the point-mass basis. The projector onto
$\Hh_\chi$ is
$|R|^{-1}\sum_{z\in R}\overline{\chi(z)}U_z$.
Its trace is $|V|/|R|=D^2$. Thus $m_\chi=D$ for every $\chi$.

If $w\ne0$ lies in $W$, nondegeneracy provides $u\in W$ with
$\Omega(u,w)\ne0$. Conjugation by $A_{\chi,u}$ multiplies
$A_{\chi,w}$ by $e_p(\Omega(u,w))\ne1$, so its trace is zero.
The cocycle law then gives
$\tr(A_{\chi,w}A_{\chi,w'}^*)=0$ for $w\ne w'$, and equals $D$
for $w=w'$. There are $D^2$ orthogonal matrices in the $D^2$-dimensional
matrix space, proving the last assertion.
\end{proof}

Identify a vector in each tensor block with its coefficient matrix.
Write $G_\chi$ and $V_\chi$ for the matrices of the projections of
$g$ and $v$. Their Hilbert--Schmidt norms equal the Hilbert norms of
those projections.

\begin{proposition}[Exact matrix-coefficient formula]\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:prop:exactq}
With the preceding identifications,
\begin{equation}
 \Qthirtysix_B(g,v)=\frac1D\sum_\chi\norm{G_\chi V_\chi^*}_{\HS}^2.
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:exactq}
\end{equation}
In particular, with $\rho_\chi=G_\chi G_\chi^*$,
\begin{equation}
 D\Qthirtysix_B(g)=\sum_\chi\tr(\rho_\chi^2),\qquad
 \sum_\chi\tr\rho_\chi=\norm g_2^2.
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:purity}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Write $h=z+w$ with $z\in R$, $w\in W$. Since $\Omega(z,w)=0$,
$U_h=U_zU_w$. The matrix coefficient in question is
\[
 \sum_\chi\chi(z)\tr(G_\chi V_\chi^*A_{\chi,w}).
\]
Averaging its squared modulus over $z$ eliminates all cross terms
between different $\chi$. By the orthonormal-basis assertion in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:lem:weyldecomposition}, for every $D\times D$ matrix $K$,
\[
 \E_{w\in W}|\tr(KA_{\chi,w})|^2=D^{-1}\norm K_{\HS}^2.
\]
Averaging over $w$ proves \eqref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:exactq}. Set $v=g$ to obtain
\eqref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:purity}.
\end{proof}

The mixed inequality also follows from
$\|GV^*\|_{\HS}\leq\|G\|_{\HS}\|V\|_{\HS}$ and
$\sum_\chi a_\chi b_\chi\leq(\sum_\chi a_\chi)(\sum_\chi b_\chi)$
for nonnegative sequences. This gives a second proof of its exact
normalization.

\subsection{Rigidity and a dimension-free stability estimate}
\begin{theorem}[Bilinear equality and stability]\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:thm:stability}
Let $\norm g_2=1$. Equality $\Qthirtysix_B(g)=D^{-1}$ holds if and only if
$g$ is supported in one block $\Hh_\chi$ and is a simple tensor there.
Equivalently, exactly one $G_\chi$ is nonzero and it has rank one.

If $0\leq\varepsilon\leq1$ and
$\Qthirtysix_B(g)\geq(1-\varepsilon)/D$, there is a unit vector $g_0$ with
$\Qthirtysix_B(g_0)=1/D$ such that
\begin{equation}
 \norm{g-g_0}_2^2\leq2\bigl(1-\sqrt{1-\varepsilon}\bigr).
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:stability}
\end{equation}
When $0\leq\varepsilon<1/2$, the right-hand side can be improved to
\begin{equation}
 2\left(1-\sqrt{\frac{1+\sqrt{1-2\varepsilon}}2}\right).
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:stabilityimproved}
\end{equation}
These are assertions in $L^2(V)$; $g_0$ is not asserted to be $1$-bounded.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Collect all eigenvalues of all the positive matrices $\rho_\chi$ into
one finite list $(\lambda_j)$. Their sum is one, and
$D\Qthirtysix_B(g)=\sum_j\lambda_j^2$. This sum is one precisely when one
$\lambda_j$ is one and the others are zero. This proves the equality
classification.

Let $\lambda$ be the largest eigenvalue in the list. Since
$\sum_j\lambda_j^2\leq\lambda\sum_j\lambda_j=\lambda$, we have
$\lambda\geq1-\varepsilon$. A singular value decomposition of the
corresponding $G_\chi$ supplies a unit rank-one tensor $g_0$ whose
inner product with $g$ has modulus $\sqrt\lambda$. Choose its scalar
phase to make that inner product nonnegative. Then
$\|g-g_0\|_2^2=2(1-\sqrt\lambda)$, proving
\eqref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:stability}.

If $\varepsilon<1/2$, the same argument shows $\lambda>1/2$.
All other eigenvalues sum to $1-\lambda$, whence
\[
 1-\varepsilon\leq\sum_j\lambda_j^2
       \leq\lambda^2+(1-\lambda)^2.
\]
On $[1/2,1]$ this implies
$\lambda\geq(1+\sqrt{1-2\varepsilon})/2$ and yields
\eqref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:stabilityimproved}.
\end{proof}

The last scalar bound is sharp when two orthogonal Schmidt components
are available: take their squared coefficients to be $\lambda$ and
$1-\lambda$. That is a statement about the purity argument, not a
claim that every such example obeys a pointwise bound.
For higher-order derivative spectra, the simple tensors arising in
different frozen slices must also be compatible with one common $f$.
That compatibility is not supplied by this stability theorem.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Lossless polarization and the Section 17 interface\srctag{36}}]{Lossless polarization and the Section 17 interface}\label{gsr:fp:36:sec:d7}\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:sec:polarization}
\srcnote{36}{Section 7}

\subsection{A self-contained polarization calculation}
For an additive-valued function $P$, write
$\Delta_hP(x)=P(x+h)-P(x)$, using a capital delta to distinguish it
from the multiplicative derivative.

\begin{lemma}[Diagonal integration]\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:lem:polarization}
Let $d\geq2$, $p>d$, and let $T:V^d\to\Fp$ be symmetric and
$d$-linear. If $P(x)=T(x,\ldots,x)/d!$, then
\begin{equation}
 \Delta_{h_1}\cdots\Delta_{h_d}P(x)=T(h_1,\ldots,h_d).
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:polarization}
\end{equation}
Moreover, with $d=k+1$,
\begin{equation}
 \Delta_{h_1}\cdots\Delta_{h_k}P(x)
       =T(h_1,\ldots,h_k,x)+C(\hh),
 \quad C(\hh)=\Delta_{\hh}P(0).
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:linearpart}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Expand the $d$-fold difference as an alternating sum over subsets
$S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}$ of
$P(x+\sum_{j\in S}h_j)$. Multilinearity expands each term into
ordered choices of $d$ inputs from $x,h_1,\ldots,h_d$. A term missing
some $h_j$ cancels upon summing over whether $j$ is in $S$.
Thus only terms containing every $h_j$ survive. There are $d!$ of
them, they contain no $x$, and symmetry makes all of them equal to
$T(h_1,\ldots,h_d)$. Division by $d!$ gives
\eqref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:polarization}.

For the second assertion, set $F(x)=\Delta_{\hh}P(x)$. The first
assertion says $F(x+y)-F(x)=T(\hh,y)$. Taking $x=0$ gives
$F(y)=T(\hh,y)+F(0)$, which is \eqref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:linearpart}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:36:ssc:thm:extraction}]
Multiplicative derivatives distribute over products. Therefore, by
\eqref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:linearpart},
\begin{align}
 \partial_{\hh}(f e_p(-P))(x)
 &=\partial_{\hh}f(x)e_p(-\Delta_{\hh}P(x))\notag\\
 &=e_p(-C(\hh))\partial_{\hh}f(x)e_p(-\sigma(\hh)(x)).
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:pointwisederivative}
\end{align}
Average over $x$ and take absolute values. This is
\eqref{gsr:fm:36:ssc:eq:pointwise}. Squaring and averaging over $\hh$, then using
\eqref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:gowers}, gives \eqref{gsr:fm:36:ssc:eq:lossless}.
\end{proof}

The proof does not use a choice among $2^{k+1}$ candidate phases or
introduce an additional Cauchy--Schwarz power. In a homogeneous global
model the phase is read directly from the diagonal of $T$.
One may add any polynomial of degree at most $k$ to $P$ without changing
the pointwise magnitudes: its $k$-fold derivative is constant in $x$.
Thus ``canonical'' denotes the specified homogeneous representative,
not uniqueness among all possible phases.

\subsection{Exact scalar specialization}
\begin{corollary}[Equality-form replacement for the global scalar step]
\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:cor:scalar}
Let $V=\Fp$, $p>k+1$, and $\sigma(h_1,\ldots,h_k)=c h_1\cdots h_k$.
For every $f:V\to\C$, with
$P(x)=c x^{k+1}/(k+1)!$ and $g=f e_p(-P)$,
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{\hh\in V^k}\abs{\sum_{x\in V}
   \partial_{\hh}f(x)e_p(-c h_1\cdots h_kx)}^2
 =\sum_{\hh\in V^k}\abs{\sum_{x\in V}\partial_{\hh}g(x)}^2.
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:scalarunnormalized}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The total form is $c h_1\cdots h_ky$, hence is fully symmetric.
Apply \eqref{gsr:fm:36:ssc:eq:pointwise} and multiply both sides after averaging
by $p^{k+2}$.
\end{proof}

This is the scale $N^{k+2}$ used in Proposition 17.2. The original
paper uses backward cubes
\[
 \prod_{\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^k}\mathcal C^{|\epsilon|}
 f(s-\epsilon\cdot\hh),
\]
where $\mathcal C$ denotes conjugation.
Our forward cube is its translate by $h_1+\cdots+h_k$; its Fourier
coefficient differs only by a unit scalar. Thus the squared quantities
in \eqref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:scalarunnormalized} match the source convention.
The corrected repository already raises the phase degree to $k+1$
and includes the characteristic restriction; these are not newly
reported defects here \cite{repo36}.

\begin{example}[Why the degree must be $k+1$]\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:ex:degree}
Take $k=1$, $V=\Fp$, $a\ne0$, $f(x)=e_p(ax^2)$, and
$\sigma(h)(x)=2ahx$. Every tested Fourier coefficient has modulus one,
so $\A_f(\sigma)=1$. Twisting by any linear polynomial preserves the
quadratic coefficient. For such a twist $g$, $\E_x\partial_hg(x)$
vanishes for $h\ne0$ and has modulus one for $h=0$. Hence
$\|g\|_{U^2}^4=1/p$, not one. The quadratic phase in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:36:ssc:thm:extraction} is necessary.
\end{example}

\subsection{An elementary complete quadratic inverse consequence}
\begin{corollary}\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:cor:quadraticinverse}
Suppose $p>2$, $k=1$, $|f|\leq1$, and
$\A_f(\sigma)=a>1/p$. There is a polynomial $Q$ of degree at most two
such that
\begin{equation}
 \abs{\E_x f(x)e_p(-Q(x))}
       \geq\sqrt{a/\norm f_2^2}\geq\sqrt a.
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:quadraticinverse}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Theorems~\ref{gsr:fm:36:ssc:thm:main} and~\ref{gsr:fm:36:ssc:thm:extraction} give a quadratic
$P$ with $g=f e_p(-P)$ and $\|g\|_{U^2}^4=a$.
Finite character orthogonality, applied to the Fourier expansion of $g$,
gives Parseval and the fourth-moment identity
\[
 \sum_{\xi\in V^*}|\widehat g(\xi)|^2=\norm g_2^2,
 \qquad \sum_{\xi\in V^*}|\widehat g(\xi)|^4=\norm g_{U^2}^4.
\]
For completeness, in the latter identity substitute
$g(x)=\sum_\xi\widehat g(\xi)e_p(\xi(x))$ into the parallelogram
average; orthogonality in its three variables forces the four
frequencies to agree. Hence
$a\leq\max_\xi|\widehat g(\xi)|^2\norm g_2^2$.
Choose a maximizing $\xi$ and put $Q=P+\xi$.
\end{proof}

For larger $k$, the lossless identity supplies an input to a
$U^{k+1}$-inverse theorem. It does not itself prove the required
lower-order inverse theorem or its quantitative bounds.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Robust and local variants\srctag{36}}]{Robust and local variants}\label{gsr:fp:36:sec:d8}\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:sec:robust}
\srcnote{36}{Section 8}

\subsection{Errors in a frequency selector}
The expression $\A_f(\phi)$ in \eqref{gsr:fm:36:ssc:eq:energy} makes sense for an
arbitrary map $\phi:V^k\to V^*$, whether or not it is multilinear.

\begin{proposition}[Selector disagreement costs at most its density]
\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:prop:noise}
If $|f|\leq1$ and $\phi,\sigma:V^k\to V^*$ disagree on a set of
density at most $\eta$, then
\begin{equation}
 |\A_f(\phi)-\A_f(\sigma)|\leq\eta.
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:noise}
\end{equation}
If $\sigma$ is multilinear, $\A_f(\phi)\geq a$, and
$a-\eta>\thresh$, its total form is symmetric. If also $p>k+1$,
the canonical phase satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \norm{f e_p(-P)}_{U^{k+1}}^{2^{k+1}}\geq a-\eta.
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:noisyextraction}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
On agreement tuples the summands coincide. On each remaining tuple,
both squared magnitudes lie in $[0,1]$, so their difference in absolute
value is at most one. Average, then apply the main theorems.
\end{proof}

This is an agreement assumption on the selectors, not a claim that a
multilinear fit can be found efficiently from arbitrary noisy data.
Obtaining the fit remains a separate structural or algorithmic problem.
The inequality also allows deterministic rather than random corruption.

\subsection{A dense set of large coefficients}
\begin{corollary}[Dense-domain extraction]\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:cor:dense}
Let $H\subseteq V^k$ have density $\beta$, let $\sigma$ be a global
multilinear selector, and suppose
$|\widehat{\partial_{\hh}f}(\sigma(\hh))|\geq\gamma$ for every
$\hh\in H$. If $|f|\leq1$, then
\begin{equation}
 \A_f(\sigma)\geq\beta\gamma^2.
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:denseenergy}
\end{equation}
If $\beta\gamma^2>\thresh$, the form $T$ is symmetric. If additionally
$p>k+1$, its canonical phase obeys
\begin{equation}
 \norm{f e_p(-P)}_{U^{k+1}}
              \geq(\beta\gamma^2)^{1/2^{k+1}}.
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:denseextraction}
\end{equation}
A sufficient characteristic condition for both conclusions is
$p>\max\{k+1,k/(\beta\gamma^2)\}$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Retain only the nonnegative summands indexed by $H$. The characteristic
condition follows from \eqref{gsr:fm:36:ssc:eq:thresholdexpansion}.
\end{proof}

It is essential that $\sigma$ is defined multilinearly on all of
$V^k$. Values on $H$ alone do not supply such an extension. In
particular, a local multilinear pattern on an arithmetic box in the
cyclic-group argument cannot be inserted into this corollary without
an additional extension theorem.

\subsection{Common selectors on affine cosets}
Let $W\leq V$, choose a set $\mathcal C$ of representatives of affine
cosets of $W$, and assign nonnegative weights $\mu(c)$ of total one.
For $c\in\mathcal C$, put $f_c(w)=f(c+w)$. Let a single multilinear
$\sigma:W^k\to W^*$ be used in every coset and define
\begin{equation}
 \A_{\mu,f}(\sigma)=\sum_{c\in\mathcal C}\mu(c)\A_{f_c}(\sigma).
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:cosetenergy}
\end{equation}

\begin{proposition}[Weighted coset version]\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:prop:coset}
If $|f|\leq1$ and $\A_{\mu,f}(\sigma)>\thresh$, the total form of
$\sigma$ on $W$ is symmetric. If $p>k+1$ and $P$ is the canonical
polynomial on $W$, then
\begin{equation}
 \A_{\mu,f}(\sigma)=\sum_c\mu(c)
               \norm{f_c e_p(-P)}_{U^{k+1}(W)}^{2^{k+1}}.
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:cosetidentity}
\end{equation}
The weighted rank-profile estimate holds with
$m_i(\uu)^2$ replaced by
$\sum_c\mu(c)\|\partial_{\uu}f_c\|_2^4$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
If the common total form were nonsymmetric, each coset's energy would
be at most $\thresh$ by Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:36:ssc:thm:main}; average the
inequalities. The identity and the profile assertion follow by
applying their corresponding theorems separately on $W$ and summing.
\end{proof}

These are local norms on a subspace with its uniform counting measure.
The proposition does not assert that the resulting piecewise function
is a low-degree polynomial on the full ambient space. Such a gluing
statement requires additional compatibility between cosets.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Multiaffine selectors and extension fields\srctag{36}}]{Multiaffine selectors and extension fields}\label{gsr:fp:36:sec:d9}\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:sec:extensions}
\srcnote{36}{Section 9}

\subsection{Multiaffine frequency patterns}
A separately affine selector has a unique decomposition
\begin{equation}
 \sigma(\hh)=\sum_{S\subseteq[k]}\sigma_S((h_j)_{j\in S}),
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:multiaffinedecomposition}
\end{equation}
where $\sigma_S$ is multilinear in the indicated inputs and
$\sigma_\varnothing$ is constant. One can obtain this decomposition
by successive subtraction of the values at zero in each slot; the
same procedure proves uniqueness.

For fixed $i$ and $\uu$, write
\begin{equation}
 \sigma(h_1,\ldots,a,\ldots,h_k)=L_{i,\uu}(a)+\xi_{i,\uu}.
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:affineslice}
\end{equation}
Define $B_{i,\uu}(a,b)=L_{i,\uu}(a)(b)$ and its alternating rank as
before. These ranks refer to the linear part in the unfrozen input,
not to the affine offset.

\begin{theorem}[Multiaffine coefficient certification]\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:thm:multiaffine}
For a separately affine selector and arbitrary complex $f$, the
amplitude-sensitive estimate \eqref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:weightedprofile} still
holds with the ranks just defined. If $|f|\leq1$ and
$\A_f(\sigma)>\thresh$, then for every nonempty $S\subseteq[k]$
the form
\begin{equation}
 ((h_j)_{j\in S},y)\longmapsto\sigma_S((h_j)_{j\in S})(y)
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:componentform}
\end{equation}
is fully symmetric in its $|S|+1$ variables. No restriction on the
constant component is asserted.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For a fixed slice set $g=\partial_{\uu}f$ and
$v(x)=e_p(\xi_{i,\uu}(x))g(x)$. The slice energy is exactly
$\Qthirtysix_{B_{i,\uu}}(g,v)$, and $\|v\|_2=\|g\|_2$.
The mixed form of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:thm:bilinear} proves the profile.

The map $\uu\mapsto\Omega_{i,\uu}$ is separately affine into the
space of alternating bilinear forms. If it is nonzero, the affine
version of Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:lem:support} and the rank profile imply
$\A_f(\sigma)\leq\thresh$ exactly as before. Thus under the strict
energy hypothesis every such map is zero.

Expand it using \eqref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:multiaffinedecomposition}. For fixed $i$
its component indexed by $S\setminus\{i\}$, with $i\in S$, is
precisely the alternating defect obtained by swapping $h_i$ and $y$
in \eqref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:componentform}. Uniqueness of the decomposition
forces each component defect to vanish. For any fixed nonempty $S$,
the swaps between its inputs and $y$ generate all permutations of
these $|S|+1$ slots. The component form is therefore fully symmetric.
\end{proof}

The homogeneous top part can consequently be integrated when
$p>k+1$. One must not conclude that its diagonal polynomial removes
the lower-order components of the frequency selector. The following
example shows a failure of the naive equality-form extension.

\begin{example}[An affine offset survives]\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:ex:offset}
Let $V=\mathbb F_{17}$, $k=1$, $\xi(x)=x$, and
$f(x)=(1+e_{17}(x))/2$. Take the constant selector $\sigma(h)=\xi$.
It is separately affine, its linear part is zero, and
\[
 \partial_hf(x)=\tfrac14\bigl(1+e_{17}(h)+e_{17}(x+h)+e_{17}(-x)\bigr).
\]
Thus $\A_f(\sigma)=1/16>1/17$, although
$\|f\|_{U^2}^4=1/8$. Integrating the zero top part gives $P=0$, so
$\A_f(\sigma)=\|f e_{17}(-P)\|_{U^2}^4$ would be false.
There is no contradiction with Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:thm:multiaffine},
which certifies the symmetry of nonconstant components, not this
extra identity.
\end{example}

\subsection{Finite extensions of the prime field}
\begin{corollary}[Odd prime-power fields]\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:cor:primepower}
Let $q=p^e$ with $p$ odd, let $V=\Fq^n$, and let
$\psi:\Fq\to\C^\times$ be a nontrivial additive character.
Use $\Fq$-linear duals and replace $e_p$ by $\psi$ in the definitions.
The rank-profile bound becomes
\begin{equation}
 \A_f(\sigma)\leq\min_i\E_{\uu}q^{-r_i(\uu)}m_i(\uu)^2,
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:qprofile}
\end{equation}
where ranks are over $\Fq$. The sharp symmetry threshold is
$1-(1-1/q)^k$. If the total form is symmetric and the
\emph{characteristic} satisfies $p>k+1$, the canonical polarization
and lossless identities hold over $\Fq$ as well.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Write $\psi(t)=e_p(\operatorname{Tr}_{\Fq/\Fp}(ct))$ for some
$c\ne0$. A bilinear alternating form $\Omega$ of $\Fq$-rank $2r$
induces the $\Fp$-bilinear alternating form
$\operatorname{Tr}(c\Omega)$ of rank $2er$. Indeed the radicals
are the same sets: if $h$ is outside the $\Fq$-radical, the
$\Fq$-linear map $x\mapsto\Omega(h,x)$ is onto $\Fq$, and the
nonzero trace functional does not vanish on its entire image.
The dimension of the common radical is multiplied by $e$ when
scalars are restricted. Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:thm:bilinear}, on the
underlying $\Fp$-space, therefore gives the factor $p^{-er}=q^{-r}$.

A nonzero $\Fq$-linear map has a kernel of relative size at most
$1/q$, so the support induction uses $(1-1/q)^{k-1}$. The endpoint
construction uses two independent $\Fq$-linear functionals and has
the same zero-product probability with $q$ in place of $p$.
Finally, the polarization proof only requires invertibility of
$(k+1)!$, which is ensured by $p>k+1$, not by the weaker condition
$q>k+1$.
\end{proof}

The character parametrization used here follows from nondegeneracy of
the trace pairing: its nonzero scalar multiples give $q$ different
characters of the additive group of $\Fq$, hence all of them.
For example, nontriviality of the trace map follows since the polynomial
$X+X^p+\cdots+X^{p^{e-1}}$ is nonzero of degree less than $q$; multiplication
by a nonzero field element then proves nondegeneracy.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Small characteristic and other exact boundaries\srctag{36}}]{Small characteristic and other exact boundaries}\label{gsr:fp:36:sec:d10}\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:sec:limits}
\srcnote{36}{Section 10}

\subsection{Full symmetry does not guarantee classical integration}
The symmetry theorem is valid for every odd $p$, regardless of $k$.
The integration theorem is more restrictive. At the boundary
$p\leq k+1$, division by the factorial may fail for a substantive
reason, not merely because the displayed formula is inconvenient.

\begin{example}[Perfect energy without classical integration]
\label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:ex:nonclassical}
On $V=\mathbb F_3$, let $[x]\in\{0,1,2\}$ be the integer representative
and put
\begin{equation}
 f(x)=\exp(2\pi i[x]/9),\qquad
 T(a,b,c)=-abc,\qquad \sigma(a,b)(x)=-abx.
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:nonclassical}
\end{equation}
Then $T$ is symmetric, and
\begin{equation}
 \partial_{a,b,c}f(x)=e_3(-abc),\qquad\A_f(\sigma)=1.
 \label{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:nonclassicalenergy}
\end{equation}
There is no function $Q:\mathbb F_3\to\mathbb F_3$ whose third
additive derivative is $T$.
\end{example}
\begin{proof}
Let $F(x)=[x]$ as an integer-valued function, computing differences
modulo $9$. If one increment is zero the triple difference vanishes.
For three increments equal to one, write $S$ for translation by one.
Since $S^3=I$,
\[
 (S-I)^3F=3(S-S^2)F\equiv-3\pmod9,
\]
because $(S-S^2)F$ has values $-1,2,-1$.
For a negative increment, the difference operator obeys
$\Delta_{-1}=-S^{-1}\Delta_1$. Triple differences therefore have
value $-3abc$ modulo $9$ for all $a,b,c\in\mathbb F_3$; translations
of the constant triple difference do not change it.
Exponentiating proves the first identity in
\eqref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:nonclassicalenergy}; inserting it in
\eqref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:twistedcube} proves the second.

Every function $\mathbb F_3\to\mathbb F_3$ is represented by a
polynomial of degree at most two, by interpolation at the three field
points. Each additive difference lowers its degree by at least one,
so every third derivative is zero. Since $T(1,1,1)\ne0$, no such $Q$
exists.
\end{proof}

The phase $[x]/9$ is a nonclassical polynomial: its third difference is
constant and its fourth difference vanishes in $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$.
This example illustrates an established distinction in finite-field
inverse theory, rather than discovering that distinction. Tidor's
integration theorem \cite{tidor} incorporates additional
low-characteristic identities; it must not be read as integration of
all ordinary symmetric tensors into classical phases. Also, exact
integration of a prescribed derivative is stronger than merely finding
correlation with some classical polynomial phase. Our example only
rules out the former.

\subsection{Other limitations}
\paragraph{Boundedness is a real hypothesis.}
Scaling $f$ by $M$ scales $\A_f$ by $|M|^{2^{k+1}}$. Without a
pointwise bound, a nonsymmetric selector can therefore carry arbitrary
energy. The amplitude-sensitive estimate remains correct because its
right side has the same homogeneity.

\paragraph{One repeated function is special.}
The reduction to $\Qthirtysix_B(g)$ uses the fact that all cube vertices come
from derivatives of the same $f$. An arbitrary array of different
vertex functions need not have that structure. The mixed bilinear
estimate is useful for affine offsets, but it does not justify
substituting our threshold into a general mixed higher-order
correlation theorem.

\paragraph{Small energy is not exact symmetry.}
The endpoint construction already gives a substantial nonsymmetric
energy. Below the threshold, only rank-profile consequences are
proved. General approximate symmetry is a different issue: the
bounded-partition-rank approximation statement proposed in Tidor's
work is false in general, as shown by Mili\'cevi\'c's four-linear
counterexamples over $\mathbb F_2$ \cite{milicevicforms}. We do not
relabel that disproved general statement as an open question or claim
that our odd-characteristic criterion rescues it.

\paragraph{No end-to-end Ramsey estimate.}
A global selector, a finite-field domain, and sufficient energy are
inputs to this manuscript. Constructing the selector from an
arithmetic-progression obstruction, managing interval boundaries,
and iterating a density increment are not outputs. The local result
cannot by itself alter the final quantitative theorem in the
repository.

\section{Sources~46 and~43: exact binary cubic norms and Boolean phase integration \wtag}\label{gsr:fp:sec:binary}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the eighth write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next sixteen sections are source~46's Sections~2--9 and then source~43's Sections~2--9, on Gowers's phase-extraction step (Lemma~17.1 and Proposition~17.2) in characteristic two, where division by the factorial is impossible and symmetry is not the whole integrability condition. \emph{Logically the chapter stands beside source~36's chapter} (Section~\ref{gsr:fp:sec:symmetry}), which treats odd characteristic and excludes characteristic two; it is printed here because no number printed earlier may move. Their introductions are Sections~\ref{gsr:fm:46:sec:d1} and~\ref{gsr:fm:43:sec:d1}.

\emph{The common theorem, proved twice.} For a symmetric trilinear form $T$ over $\F_2^n$ let $r$ be the rank of the alternating form $T(a,a,b)+T(a,b,b)$ (source~46's $C_T$, source~43's $\Omega_T$). Then the $T$-twisted cubic average of eight $1$-bounded functions has modulus at most $2^{-r/2}$, attained with all eight functions equal to one nonclassical cubic phase with values among the eighth roots of unity, and $r/2$ is the least codimension of a subspace on which $T$ integrates (source~46's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:46:thm:sharp}; source~43's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:cubic-exact} for one function, with an amplitude factor). The seven-function correlation is at most $2^{-r/4}$, so correlation $\delta$ forces an integrable restriction of codimension at most $2\log_2(1/\delta)$, against $8\log_2(1/\delta)$ in Tidor's Proposition~4.6 (source~46's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:46:thm:seven}; source~43's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:mixed-repair}). The two proofs differ: source~46 converts the cube into quadratic convolution operators and a symplectic decomposition; source~43 uses a shear identity and its division-free orthogonality theorem. Source~46's eight-function statement contains source~43's one-function maximum, so source~46 is printed first; source~43 is a credited second route, printed whole with its further results.

\emph{Further results.} Source~46: an exact agreement threshold $(1+2^{-r/2})/2$ and a spectral stability identity (Corollary~\ref{gsr:fp:46:cor:agreement}, Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:46:prop:stability}); constructive integration and the optimal phase order; an all-characteristic scalar polarization with the optimal root-of-unity alphabet (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:46:thm:scalar-polarization}); the classification of exact nonclassical integrability of the trace tensors $\Tr(ch_1\cdots h_d)$ over $\F_{p^n}$ with their obstruction ranks and repair costs (Theorems~\ref{gsr:fp:46:thm:trace-classification}, \ref{gsr:fp:46:thm:trace-rank}, \ref{gsr:fp:46:thm:repair}). Source~43: the sharp orthogonality $\QB_B(g,h)\le d_B^{-1}\norm g_2^2\norm h_2^2$ on every finite abelian group, without division by two (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:orthogonality}); the exact symmetry threshold $1-(1-1/p_*(G))^k$ on every noncyclic finite abelian group (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:group-symmetry}), which extends source~36's threshold and its bilinear estimate; an explicit Boolean primitive (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:integration}); the sharp certification threshold $1-2^{1-d}$ in every degree (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:boolean-certification}); the fourth-power triangle bound in place of the eighth power of Tidor's Lemma~4.1 (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:triangle}); the quartic reduction and the value $11/16$ on $\F_2^2$ (Theorems~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:quartic-reduction}, \ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:quartic-two}). The four claims of source~43 that the intake did not check (orthogonality, certification threshold, fourth power, $11/16$) were checked at the write (note in Section~\ref{gsr:fm:43:sec:d1}). The integration criterion itself is Tao--Ziegler's and Tidor's, as both sources say; source~46 does not cite source~36, and source~43 cites it.

\section[{Conventions and the first integration obstruction\srctag{46}}]{Conventions and the first integration obstruction}\label{gsr:fp:46:sec:d2}\label{gsr:fp:46:sec:integration}
\srcnote{46}{Section 2}

Throughout, $p$ is prime and $V$ is a finite-dimensional $\F_p$-vector space.
All averages are normalized. We write $\T=\R/\Z$, $e(t)=\exp(2\pi i t)$,
and $\iota(a)=|a|/p\pmod1$, where $|a|\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}$ is the standard
integer representative. The map $\iota:\F_p\to\T$ is additive. A function is
\emph{1-bounded} if its modulus is at most one everywhere.

For $P:V\to\T$, put
\[
 D_hP(x)=P(x+h)-P(x).
\]
A nonclassical polynomial of degree at most $d$ is a function for which every
$(d+1)$-fold additive derivative vanishes. A symmetric $d$-linear form
$T:V^d\to\F_p$ \emph{integrates} if
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:integrates}
 D_{h_1}\cdots D_{h_d}P(x)=\iota(T(h_1,\ldots,h_d))
\end{equation}
for all $x,h_1,\ldots,h_d$. Such a $P$ automatically has degree at most $d$.
We refer to integration by a function with values in a coset of
$p^{-R}\Z/\Z$ as integration with phase order $p^R$. Constants are immaterial.
Classical integration means that $R=1$ suffices.

\begin{proposition}[Known integration criterion]\label{gsr:fp:46:prop:knowncriterion}
For symmetric $d$-linear $T$, a necessary and sufficient condition for
nonclassical integration is the following repeated-variable condition whenever
$d\geq p+1$:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:pbalance}
 T(\underbrace{a,\ldots,a}_{p},b,z_1,\ldots,z_{d-p-1})
 =T(a,\underbrace{b,\ldots,b}_{p},z_1,\ldots,z_{d-p-1}).
\end{equation}
For $d\leq p$ there is no additional condition. A necessary condition for
classical integration when $d\geq p$ is vanishing whenever $p$ arguments
coincide.
\end{proposition}

The general equivalence is the Tao--Ziegler/Tidor criterion
\cite{taozieglerlow,tidor}; we do not reprove its general sufficiency. The necessity and
the sufficiency for $d\leq p+1$ needed throughout this article are proved
below and in Section~\ref{gsr:fp:46:sec:construct}.

\begin{lemma}[Repeated-variable necessity]\label{gsr:fp:46:lem:balance-necessary}
Every total derivative satisfies \eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:pbalance}.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $I$ be the augmentation ideal of the integral group ring $\Z[V]$,
acting on functions by translations, and put $\delta_a=[a]-[0]$.
Because $pa=0$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:group-ring}
 \delta_a^p=-\sum_{j=1}^{p-1}\binom pj\delta_a^j.
\end{equation}
In particular $pI^s\subseteq I^{s+p-1}+pI^{s+1}$ for $s\geq1$.
Iterating this inclusion modulo $I^{d+1}$ shows that $pI^s$ annihilates every
degree-at-most-$d$ polynomial whenever $s+p-1>d$.

Subtract \eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:group-ring} multiplied by $\delta_b$ from its version
with $a,b$ interchanged and the corresponding factor $\delta_a$.
The $j=1$ terms cancel. Each remaining term, after multiplication by the
$d-p-1$ other differences, belongs to $pI^{d-p+j}$ with $j\geq2$.
It therefore annihilates $P$. This gives
$\delta_a^p\delta_b\prod\delta_{z_i}P
=\delta_a\delta_b^p\prod\delta_{z_i}P$, as required. For $p=2$ the sum of
remaining terms is empty. On $\F_p$-valued functions, more strongly,
$\delta_a^p=[pa]-[0]=0$, which proves the stated classical necessity.
\end{proof}

At the first obstructed degree $d=p+1$, define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:obstruction}
 C_T(a,b)=T(a,\ldots,a,b)-T(a,b,\ldots,b),
\end{equation}
with $p$ repeated arguments in each term. Symmetry and the divisibility of
$\binom pj$ by $p$ show that $C_T$ is bilinear. It is alternating because
$C_T(a,a)=0$.

\begin{proposition}[First-obstruction test]\label{gsr:fp:46:prop:first-obstruction}
A symmetric $(p+1)$-linear form integrates if and only if $C_T=0$.
For a subspace $W\leq V$, its restriction integrates if and only if
$C_T|_{W\times W}=0$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Necessity is Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:46:lem:balance-necessary}. An explicit coordinate
integrator proving sufficiency is given in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:46:thm:coordinate-integration}; the same construction on a basis of
$W$ proves the restriction statement.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Used again} by source~95 (Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:prop:prime}, via Tidor), for pairs of tensors at degree $p+1$ (Section~\ref{gsr:fp:sec:pencils}); source~95 calls this source's work ``a parallel cubic treatment'', after the README's summary that the thirteenth write corrected.
\end{writenote}

\begin{lemma}[Alternating-form geometry]\label{gsr:fp:46:lem:symplectic}
If an alternating bilinear form $C$ on an $n$-dimensional vector space has
rank $r$, then $r=2m$ is even. Its largest totally isotropic subspace has
dimension $n-m$. Moreover, $C$ is a sum of $m$ elementary wedges of linear
functionals, and no fewer such wedges suffice.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $C\ne0$, choose $u,v$ with $C(u,v)=1$. Their span is nondegenerate.
Subtract appropriate multiples of $u,v$ from every other vector to split
this plane orthogonally, and iterate. This gives $m$ hyperbolic planes and
a radical of dimension $n-2m$. Taking the radical and one line from each
plane gives an isotropic subspace of dimension $n-m$.

In the quotient by the radical, an isotropic subspace $U$ is contained in
its orthogonal complement, so $\dim U\leq m$. This proves maximality in
$V$ as well. The dual-coordinate expression of the hyperbolic planes gives
$m$ wedges. Each wedge has rank at most two, so rank subadditivity proves
the lower bound on their number.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The exact binary mixed cubic norm\srctag{46}}]{The exact binary mixed cubic norm}\label{gsr:fp:46:sec:d3}\label{gsr:fp:46:sec:sharp}
\srcnote{46}{Section 3}

In this section $V=\F_2^n$ and $T:V^3\to\F_2$ is symmetric and trilinear.
Thus
\[
 C_T(a,b)=T(a,a,b)+T(a,b,b),\qquad r=\rank C_T=2m.
\]
For eight functions $f_\eps:V\to\C$, indexed by
$\eps\in\{0,1\}^3$, define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:cube}
 \Lambda_T((f_\eps))=
 \E_{x,a,b,c}\prod_{\eps\in\{0,1\}^3}
 \conjop^{|\eps|} f_\eps(x+\eps_1a+\eps_2b+\eps_3c)
 (-1)^{T(a,b,c)},
\end{equation}
where $\conjop$ denotes complex conjugation. Allowing different functions
at all vertices is important: the result is stronger than a bound for one
repeated function.

\begin{theorem}[Sharp mixed cubic bound]\label{gsr:fp:46:thm:sharp}
For all 1-bounded $f_\eps$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:sharp}
 \abs{\Lambda_T((f_\eps))}\leq2^{-r/2}.
\end{equation}
The bound is attained. In fact there is a nonclassical polynomial
$P:V\to\frac18\Z/\Z$ of degree at most three such that, on setting all
$f_\eps=e(P)$, the average equals $2^{-r/2}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 40--46]
Source~43's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:cubic-exact} proves the one-function case independently (with an amplitude factor), by a shear identity and its division-free orthogonality theorem; here the bound holds for eight different functions. The value $2^{-r/2}$ and the codimension $r/2$ agree.
\end{writenote}

\subsection{A quadratic spectral calculation}
For a real-valued function $\kappa$ on $V$, normalized convolution is
\[
 (K_\kappa H)(x)=\E_y\kappa(x+y)H(y).
\]
The characters are $(-1)^{\xi(x)}$ for $\xi\in V^*$, with eigenvalues
$\widehat\kappa(\xi)=\E_x\kappa(x)(-1)^{\xi(x)}$.

\begin{lemma}[Flat nonzero quadratic spectrum]\label{gsr:fp:46:lem:quadratic}
Let $Q:V\to\F_2$ satisfy $Q(0)=0$, with alternating polar form
$C(x,h)=Q(x+h)+Q(x)+Q(h)$ of rank $r$. For any linear $L:V\to\F_2$,
the function $\kappa(x)=(-1)^{Q(x)+L(x)}$ has Walsh coefficients in
$\{0,2^{-r/2},-2^{-r/2}\}$. Consequently
$\norm{K_\kappa}_{2\to2}=2^{-r/2}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Changing variables in the square of a Walsh coefficient gives
\begin{align*}
 |\widehat\kappa(\xi)|^2
 &=\E_{x,h}(-1)^{Q(x)+Q(x+h)+(L+\xi)(h)}\\
 &=\E_h(-1)^{Q(h)+(L+\xi)(h)}\E_x(-1)^{C(x,h)}.
\end{align*}
The inner average is the indicator of $R=\rad C$. The restriction $Q|_R$
is linear. Averaging its character against $L+\xi$ therefore gives either
zero or $|R|/|V|=2^{-r}$. The coefficients are real, proving the assertion.
At least one is nonzero, by Parseval. Diagonalization in the character basis
proves the operator-norm formula.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Proof of the upper bound}
Make the invertible change of variables
\[
 b=a+A,\qquad c=a+B,\qquad y=x+a.
\]
The four even-parity vertices become $x,x+A,x+B,x+A+B$; the four
odd-parity vertices become $y,y+A,y+B,y+A+B$. Define
\begin{align*}
 F_{A,B}(x)&=f_{000}(x)f_{110}(x+A)f_{101}(x+B)f_{011}(x+A+B),\\
 G_{A,B}(y)&=f_{100}(y)f_{010}(y+A)f_{001}(y+B)f_{111}(y+A+B).
\end{align*}
Both functions have $L^2$ norm at most one. Multilinearity gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:kernel}
 T(a,a+A,a+B)=Q(a)+L_{A,B}(a),
\end{equation}
where
\[
 Q(a)=T(a,a,a),\qquad
 L_{A,B}(a)=T(a,a,A)+T(a,a,B)+T(a,A,B).
\]
Each term in $L_{A,B}$ is linear in $a$: the cross terms in two equal
slots cancel in characteristic two. The polar form of $Q$ is precisely
$C_T$. Therefore, with
$\kappa_{A,B}(a)=(-1)^{Q(a)+L_{A,B}(a)}$,
\[
 \Lambda_T=\E_{A,B}\E_{x,y}
 F_{A,B}(x)\overline{G_{A,B}(y)}\kappa_{A,B}(x+y).
\]
Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:46:lem:quadratic} and the Hilbert-space Cauchy--Schwarz inequality
bound the absolute value of each inner pairing by
$2^{-r/2}\norm{F_{A,B}}_2\norm{G_{A,B}}_2\leq2^{-r/2}$.
Averaging proves \eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:sharp}.

\subsection{Construction of extremizers}
For linear forms $\ell,m:V\to\F_2$, set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:elementary-binary}
 S_{\ell,m}(a,b,c)=\ell(a)m(b)m(c)+m(a)\ell(b)m(c)+m(a)m(b)\ell(c).
\end{equation}
This is symmetric and
\[
 C_{S_{\ell,m}}(a,b)=\ell(b)m(a)+\ell(a)m(b).
\]
By Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:46:lem:symplectic}, choose $m=r/2$ independent pairs
$(\ell_i,m_i)$ whose wedges sum to $C_T$. Put $S=\sum_i S_{\ell_i,m_i}$.
Then $R=T-S$ has $C_R=0$ and therefore integrates. The explicit binary
construction in Section~\ref{gsr:fp:46:sec:construct} gives an integrator
$P:V\to\frac18\Z/\Z$ of degree at most three.

For $f=e(P)$, the cubical product in \eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:cube} equals $(-1)^{R(a,b,c)}$.
Thus
\[
 \Lambda_T(f,\ldots,f)=\E_{a,b,c}(-1)^{S(a,b,c)}.
\]
In each symplectic coordinate pair, averaging over $c$ leaves the condition
\[
 m(a)m(b)=0,\qquad \ell(a)m(b)+m(a)\ell(b)=0.
\]
Exactly eight of the sixteen choices for
$(\ell(a),m(a),\ell(b),m(b))$ satisfy these two equations: four with
$m(a)=m(b)=0$, two with $(m(a),m(b))=(1,0)$, and two with $(0,1)$.
The block average is consequently $1/2$. The coordinate pairs are jointly
independent under uniform averaging. Their product gives $2^{-m}$, proving
sharpness and completing Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:46:thm:sharp}.

\begin{remark}
The proof does not estimate the rank of the original trilinear tensor. It
uses the rank of its repeated-variable obstruction. Tensors of very different
ordinary tensor ranks can therefore have exactly the same twisted cube norm.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Restriction, exact agreement, and stability\srctag{46}}]{Restriction, exact agreement, and stability}\label{gsr:fp:46:sec:d4}\label{gsr:fp:46:sec:consequences}
\srcnote{46}{Section 4}

\subsection{A factor-four improvement of the symmetric seven-function bound}
For seven 1-bounded functions indexed by the nonempty subsets of
$\{1,2,3\}$, put
\begin{align}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:seven}
 \Gamma_T=\E_{a,b,c}&\ b_1(a)b_2(b)b_3(c)b_{12}(a+b)b_{13}(a+c)\notag\\
 &\hspace{28mm}\cdot b_{23}(b+c)b_{123}(a+b+c)(-1)^{T(a,b,c)}.
\end{align}

\begin{theorem}[Improved symmetric restriction estimate]\label{gsr:fp:46:thm:seven}
Let $T:V^3\to\F_2$ be symmetric and trilinear, with $\rank C_T=r$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:seven-sharpish}
 |\Gamma_T|\leq2^{-r/4}.
\end{equation}
If $|\Gamma_T|\geq\delta>0$, there is a subspace $W\leq V$ with
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:codim-improved}
 \codim W=\frac r2\leq2\log_2(1/\delta)
\end{equation}
on which $T$ integrates to a nonclassical cubic polynomial. Among all
integrable restrictions of this particular $T$, the codimension $r/2$ is
minimal.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Cauchy--Schwarz in $(b,c)$ removes the product
$b_2(b)b_3(c)b_{23}(b+c)$ and gives
\begin{align*}
 |\Gamma_T|^2\leq\E_{b,c}\Big|
 \E_a b_1(a)b_{12}(a+b)b_{13}(a+c)b_{123}(a+b+c)(-1)^{T(a,b,c)}
 \Big|^2.
\end{align*}
Expand the square with the second variable $a+h$. The tensor factor becomes
$(-1)^{T(h,b,c)}$. The resulting expression is an eight-function cube average
with basepoint $a$, directions $(h,b,c)$, and assignments
\begin{align*}
 f_{000}=f_{100}&=b_1,&
 f_{010}=f_{110}&=\overline{b_{12}},\\
 f_{001}=f_{101}&=\overline{b_{13}},&
 f_{011}=f_{111}&=b_{123}.
\end{align*}
It is bounded by $2^{-r/2}$ by Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:46:thm:sharp}. Taking square roots
proves \eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:seven-sharpish}. Hence $r\leq4\log_2(1/\delta)$.
A largest isotropic subspace for $C_T$ has codimension $r/2$ by
Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:46:lem:symplectic}, and is exactly an integrable restriction by
Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:46:prop:first-obstruction}. These same facts give minimality.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 40--46]
Source~43's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:mixed-repair} gives the same bound $2^{-r/4}$ and codimension $\lfloor2\log_2(1/\delta)\rfloor$ through its fourth-power triangle estimate. Neither source claims the coefficient two optimal.
\end{writenote}

\paragraph{Comparison with the published bound.}
Tidor's Proposition~4.6 \cite{tidor} has the identical seven-function
hypothesis and concludes $\codim W\leq8\log_2(1/\delta)$.
There are two improvements in the preceding argument: the spectral cube
estimate gives $r\leq4\log_2(1/\delta)$, and one restricts to a maximal
isotropic subspace rather than to the full radical. The latter saves another
factor of two in codimension. No symmetry assumption has been dropped.
For a nonsymmetric tensor one must still pay for symmetrization; we do not
claim here a replacement for the constants in Tidor's nonsymmetric
Corollary~4.8 or in a full inverse theorem. Nor does sharpness of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:46:thm:sharp} establish sharpness of
\eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:seven-sharpish}: one Cauchy--Schwarz step intervenes.

\subsection{Exact derivative-spectrum maximum}
For a single 1-bounded $f:V\to\C$, define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:moment}
 M_T(f)=\E_{a,b}\left|
 \E_x f(x)\overline{f(x+a)}\,\overline{f(x+b)}f(x+a+b)
 (-1)^{T(a,b,x)}\right|^2.
\end{equation}
This is a squared Fourier-coefficient moment of the second multiplicative
derivative, evaluated at the linear frequency $x\mapsto T(a,b,x)$.

\begin{corollary}[Exact cubic spectral moment]\label{gsr:fp:46:cor:moment}
For $r=\rank C_T$,
\[
 \sup_{\norm f_\infty\leq1}M_T(f)=2^{-r/2}.
\]
The supremum is attained by the eighth-root phase in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:46:thm:sharp}.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
In \eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:moment}, expand the square with the second basepoint $x+c$.
The product is precisely the eight-vertex product in \eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:cube}, and
$T(a,b,x)+T(a,b,x+c)=T(a,b,c)$. Thus
$M_T(f)=\Lambda_T(f,\ldots,f)$. Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:46:thm:sharp}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Optimal approximate polarization}
Let $P_\eps:V\to\T$ be completely arbitrary functions, not assumed to be
polynomials. For uniform $(x,a,b,c)$, compare
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:agreement-identity}
 \sum_{\eps\in\{0,1\}^3}(-1)^{|\eps|}
 P_\eps(x+\eps_1a+\eps_2b+\eps_3c)
 \quad\text{with}\quad \iota(T(a,b,c)).
\end{equation}
Equality is in $\T$.

\begin{corollary}[Exact agreement and squared-error thresholds]\label{gsr:fp:46:cor:agreement}
Writing $m=\rank C_T/2$, the maximum probability of equality in
\eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:agreement-identity}, over all eight functions $P_\eps$, is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:agreement}
 \frac{1+2^{-m}}2.
\end{equation}
The minimum mean squared distance between the corresponding unit complex
numbers is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:error}
 2(1-2^{-m}).
\end{equation}
Both optima are attained with all $P_\eps$ equal to one nonclassical cubic
with values in $\frac18\Z/\Z$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Let $Z$ be the exponential of the difference between the two sides of
\eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:agreement-identity}. Then $|Z|=1$ and
$|\E Z|\leq2^{-m}$ by Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:46:thm:sharp}.
If $s=\Pr(Z=1)$, then $\operatorname{Re}\E Z\geq2s-1$. This proves the
upper bound for agreement. Also
$\E|Z-1|^2=2-2\operatorname{Re}\E Z\geq2(1-2^{-m})$.
For the extremizer constructed above, $Z=(-1)^{S(a,b,c)}$ and
$\E Z=2^{-m}$. Since $Z$ takes only the values $1,-1$, equality holds in
both bounds.
\end{proof}

Thus independent choices at the vertices cannot conceal a genuine
integration obstruction. The conclusion quantifies this failure, whereas a
formal factorial calculation only indicates that one particular formula is
unavailable.

\subsection{A spectral stability identity}
The proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:46:thm:sharp} retains information about near equality.
For a common function $f$, let
\[
 F_{A,B}(x)=f(x)f(x+A)f(x+B)f(x+A+B),\qquad \lambda=2^{-r/2}.
\]
The kernel $\kappa_{A,B}$ in \eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:kernel} has three possible eigenvalues:
$+\lambda,0,-\lambda$. Let $\Pi^+_{A,B},\Pi^0_{A,B},\Pi^-_{A,B}$ be the
orthogonal projections onto these three Walsh spectral subspaces. Set
\[
 A_f=\E_{A,B}\norm{F_{A,B}}_2^2,\qquad
 \mu_\sigma=\E_{A,B}\norm{\Pi^\sigma_{A,B}F_{A,B}}_2^2
 \quad(\sigma\in\{+,0,-\}).
\]

\begin{proposition}[Exact defect decomposition]\label{gsr:fp:46:prop:stability}
For every 1-bounded $f$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:stability}
 1-\frac{M_T(f)}\lambda=(1-A_f)+\mu_0+2\mu_-.
\end{equation}
In particular, if $M_T(f)\geq(1-\eps)\lambda$, then
\begin{align*}
 \E_x|f(x)|^2&\geq1-\eps,\\
 \E_{A,B}\norm{F_{A,B}-\Pi^+_{A,B}F_{A,B}}_2^2&\leq\eps,\\
 \mu_-&\leq\eps/2.
\end{align*}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For a common function, the two functions $F_{A,B},G_{A,B}$ in the upper-bound
proof coincide. Parseval and the real eigenvalues give
$M_T(f)=\lambda(\mu_+-\mu_-)$, whereas
$A_f=\mu_++\mu_0+\mu_-$. Subtraction proves
\eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:stability}. Every term on its right is nonnegative because
$A_f\leq1$. Moreover $A_f\leq\E|f|^2$, since three of the four factors in
$|F_{A,B}(x)|^2$ can be bounded by one. The conclusions follow.
\end{proof}

This is stability of the transformed four-point functions in a completely
specified spectral space. It is not yet a classification of $f$ itself near
a polynomial-phase extremizer; recovering such a classification is a
separate problem.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Constructive integration and optimal phase order\srctag{46}}]{Constructive integration and optimal phase order}\label{gsr:fp:46:sec:d5}\label{gsr:fp:46:sec:construct}
\srcnote{46}{Section 5}

We now supply the explicit integrators used above, and formulate an
all-characteristic scalar replacement for Gowers' polarization identity.
This also distinguishes higher-root phenomena from true obstructions.

\subsection{A finite-difference calculation on the prime field}
For $1\leq a\leq p-1$, write $L_a(x)=|x|^a$ on $\F_p$, viewed first as an
integer-valued periodic function. Let $\delta f(x)=f(x+1)-f(x)$.

\begin{lemma}[Valuation and leading difference]\label{gsr:fp:46:lem:scalar-diff}
For $k\geq0$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:valuation}
 v_p(\delta^kL_a(x))\geq
 \max\left\{0,\left\lceil\frac{k-a}{p-1}\right\rceil\right\}
\end{equation}
uniformly in $x$, with $v_p(0)=+\infty$.
If $d=a+s(p-1)$, then
\begin{align}
 \delta^d L_a(x)&\equiv(-1)^s p^s a!\pmod{p^{s+1}},\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:leading-diff}\\
 \delta^{d+1}L_a(x)&\equiv0\pmod{p^{s+1}}.\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:next-diff}
\end{align}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $k<p$, ordinary polynomial differencing modulo $p$ proves
\eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:valuation}: when $k>a$, the reduction modulo $p$ vanishes.
Since the translation has order $p$, $(1+\delta)^p=1$, hence
\[
 \delta^k=-\sum_{j=1}^{p-1}\binom pj\delta^{k-p+j}\qquad(k\geq p).
\]
Strong induction on $k$ proves \eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:valuation}, using $p\mid\binom pj$
and observing that the smallest resulting valuation is the $j=1$ bound.
For \eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:leading-diff}, use induction on $s$. At $s=0$ the familiar
$a$th difference of $x^a$ is $a!$ modulo $p$. At
$d=a+s(p-1)$, the $j=1$ term is $-p\delta^{d-(p-1)}L_a$.
Every term with $j\geq2$ is divisible by $p^{s+1}$ by
\eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:valuation}, giving the induction step. Equation
\eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:next-diff} is another direct instance of that valuation bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Optimal scalar integrator in every degree]\label{gsr:fp:46:thm:scalar}
Given $d\geq1$, write uniquely
\[
 d=a+s(p-1),\qquad 1\leq a\leq p-1,\quad s\geq0.
\]
Choose an integer $u$ with $u(-1)^s a!\equiv1\pmod p$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:scalar-Q}
 Q_d(x)=\frac{u|x|^a}{p^{s+1}}\pmod1
\end{equation}
has degree at most $d$ and satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:scalar-top}
 D_{h_1}\cdots D_{h_d}Q_d(x)=\iota(h_1\cdots h_d).
\end{equation}
The smallest possible phase order for any integrator of this nonzero tensor
is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:min-order}
 p^{s+1}=p^{\lceil d/(p-1)\rceil}.
\end{equation}
The lower bound allows arbitrary functions, provided their values lie in a
coset of the indicated finite subgroup of $\T$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Every difference $D_h$ on $\F_p$ is an integer-polynomial multiple of
$\delta$. Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:46:lem:scalar-diff} therefore shows that $Q_d$ has degree
at most $d$. Its top derivative is independent of $x$ and additive in each
direction: the identity $D_{h+k}=D_h+D_k+D_hD_k$ leaves an error of order
$d+1$. As an additive map out of $\F_p$ in each slot, it is determined by
its value on $(1,\ldots,1)$, which is $1/p$ by
\eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:leading-diff} and the choice of $u$. This proves
\eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:scalar-top}.

For optimality, subtract a constant from any proposed integrator with
values in a coset of $p^{-R}\Z/\Z$. Its numerator is a function
$\F_p\to\Z/p^R\Z$. The evaluation matrix for
$1,|x|,\ldots,|x|^{p-1}$ is a Vandermonde matrix whose determinant is a unit
modulo $p$, and hence modulo $p^R$. These functions therefore interpolate
all possible numerators. By \eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:valuation}, each
$|x|^a/p^R$ has degree at most $a+(R-1)(p-1)\leq R(p-1)$; the constant
has degree zero. Thus every such function has degree at most $R(p-1)$.
A nonzero $d$th derivative requires $d\leq R(p-1)$, proving the lower bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[Binary scalar phases]
For $p=2$, one may take $Q_d(x)=(-1)^{d-1}|x|/2^d$. In particular a
nonzero cubic tensor on $\F_2$ requires eighth roots, even though its total
derivative takes only the values $0,1/2$. The issue is phase depth, not a
failure of integrability.
\end{example}

\subsection{Multivariate coordinate integration through degree \texorpdfstring{$p+1$}{p+1}}
We will also use the following multivariate consequence of the valuation
argument. If $0\leq a_i<p$ and $A=\sum_i a_i>0$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:monomial-degree}
 x\longmapsto\frac{\prod_i|x_i|^{a_i}}{p^{s+1}}
 \quad\text{has degree at most } A+s(p-1).
\end{equation}
Indeed the coordinate augmentation ideal is generated by the coordinate
differences $\delta_i$. A product $\prod_i\delta_i^{k_i}$ acts separately
on the factors. The sum of the lower bounds
$\max(0,\lceil(k_i-a_i)/(p-1)\rceil)$ is at least $s+1$ whenever
$\sum_i k_i>A+s(p-1)$. This proves \eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:monomial-degree}; coordinates
with $a_i=0$ cause no difficulty, since any difference in such a coordinate
annihilates that factor.

Fix a basis $e_1,\ldots,e_n$ of $V$. For $\alpha\in\Z_{\geq0}^n$ with
$|\alpha|=d$, let
\[
 b_\alpha=T(e_1^{\alpha_1},\ldots,e_n^{\alpha_n}),
\]
where superscripts denote repetitions, not multiplication.
A symmetric multilinear form is determined by these coefficients.
For coefficients in formulas below, division by a factorial means inversion
in $\F_p$, followed by the standard integer representative.

\begin{theorem}[Explicit low-degree integration]\label{gsr:fp:46:thm:coordinate-integration}
Every symmetric $d$-linear form with $d\leq p$ integrates. A symmetric
$(p+1)$-linear form integrates if $C_T=0$. Integrators can be constructed as
follows.

For every $\alpha$ with all $\alpha_i<p$, include the classical term
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:classical-term}
 \frac{1}{p}\left|\frac{b_\alpha}{\prod_i\alpha_i!}\right|
 \prod_i|x_i|^{\alpha_i}.
\end{equation}
When $d=p$, include additionally $|b_{pe_i}|Q_p(x_i)$ for each pure
coefficient. When $d=p+1$, instead include the pure terms
$|b_{(p+1)e_i}|Q_{p+1}(x_i)$ and, for every $i<j$, the term
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:paired-term}
 -\frac{|b_{pe_i+e_j}|\,|x_i||x_j|}{p^2}.
\end{equation}
The last prescription is valid because $C_T=0$ makes
$b_{pe_i+e_j}=b_{e_i+pe_j}$. Summing these terms modulo one gives an
integrator.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The total derivative of \eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:classical-term} has exactly the prescribed
$\alpha$ component, by ordinary differentiation in the prime-field
polynomial algebra; all the relevant factorials are invertible.
The scalar terms are handled by Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:46:thm:scalar}. Their derivatives
vanish whenever a direction from another coordinate occurs.

It remains to check the paired term. Modulo $p^2$, the recurrence for
$\delta_i^p$ acting on $|x_i|$ has only the term $-p\delta_i|x_i|$ remaining:
for $2\leq j<p$, $\delta_i^j|x_i|$ is divisible by $p$.
Thus the $pe_i+e_j$ and $e_i+pe_j$ components of
$-|x_i||x_j|/p^2$ are both $1/p$. Its pure components vanish by the
scalar degree bound. If both multiplicities are between $2$ and $p-1$,
each coordinate difference contributes a factor $p$, so that component
vanishes modulo one. Any component involving a third coordinate vanishes
identically. The degree is at most $p+1$ by
\eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:monomial-degree}.

For $d=p+1$ these are all possible multiplicity patterns: a pure
$(p+1)$, a pair $(p,1)$, or multiplicities all smaller than $p$.
The equality of paired coefficients is exactly $C_T(e_i,e_j)=0$.
Matching every basis component proves the theorem.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The binary cubic integrator]\label{gsr:fp:46:cor:binary-integrator}
If $R:V^3\to\F_2$ is symmetric and $C_R=0$, then, writing
$r_i=R(e_i,e_i,e_i)$,
$r_{ij}=R(e_i,e_i,e_j)=R(e_i,e_j,e_j)$, and
$r_{ijk}=R(e_i,e_j,e_k)$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:binary-integrator}
 P(x)=\sum_i\frac{r_i|x_i|}{8}
       -\sum_{i<j}\frac{r_{ij}|x_i||x_j|}{4}
       +\sum_{i<j<k}\frac{r_{ijk}|x_i||x_j||x_k|}{2}\pmod1
\end{equation}
has $D_aD_bD_cP=\iota(R(a,b,c))$.
\end{corollary}
The coefficients are binary representatives. This formula makes the
extremizer construction in Section~\ref{gsr:fp:46:sec:sharp} completely effective.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{An all-characteristic replacement of scalar polarization\srctag{46}}]{An all-characteristic replacement of scalar polarization}\label{gsr:fp:46:sec:d6}\label{gsr:fp:46:sec:polarization}
\srcnote{46}{Section 6}

\subsection{Independent vertex functions do not remove exact obstructions}
The following observation applies in every characteristic and does not
require any regularity of the vertex functions.

\begin{lemma}[Vertex separation forces integration]\label{gsr:fp:46:lem:vertex-separation}
Let $T:V^d\to\F_p$ be multilinear. Suppose functions
$P_\eps:V\to\T$ satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:separated-identity}
 \iota(T(h_1,\ldots,h_d))=
 \sum_{\eps\in\{0,1\}^d}(-1)^{|\eps|}
 P_\eps(s-\eps\cdot h)
\end{equation}
for all $s,h_1,\ldots,h_d$. Then $P_{(1,\ldots,1)}$ integrates $T$.
Conversely, an integrator gives \eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:separated-identity} by taking every
vertex function equal to it.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For each $i$, apply the operator that subtracts the expression with $h_i=0$.
The left side is unchanged by multilinearity. Every vertex missing at least
one direction is annihilated. For the all-ones vertex, the alternating
expansion that remains is
\[
 \sum_{J\subseteq[d]}(-1)^{|J|}P_{(1,\ldots,1)}
 \left(s-\sum_{j\in J}h_j\right)
 =D_{h_1}\cdots D_{h_d}P_{(1,\ldots,1)}
 \left(s-\sum_i h_i\right).
\]
This proves the first assertion. The same identity proves the converse.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Scalar multi-affine polarization with optimal roots}
Let
\[
 \sigma(x_1,\ldots,x_k)=\sum_{J\subseteq[k]}c_J\prod_{j\in J}x_j
 \qquad(c_J\in\F_p).
\]
This is separately affine in every variable; the constant monomial is
allowed. Put $Q_0=1/p$, and use the functions $Q_j$ of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:46:thm:scalar} for $j\geq1$.

\begin{theorem}[All-characteristic scalar polarization]\label{gsr:fp:46:thm:scalar-polarization}
Define, for $\eps\in\{0,1\}^k$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:vertex-formula}
 P_\eps(s)=\sum_{J\supseteq\supp\eps}|c_J|Q_{|J|}(s).
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:scalar-polarization}
 \iota(\sigma(x))=\sum_{\eps\in\{0,1\}^k}
 (-1)^{|\eps|}P_\eps(s-\eps\cdot x)
\end{equation}
for all $x,s$. For $k\geq1$, all $P_\eps$ have degree at most $k$ and
values in $p^{-R}\Z/\Z$, where
$R=\lceil k/(p-1)\rceil$. This exponent is the optimal universal choice.
If $k<p$, the construction can be taken entirely in $p^{-1}\Z/\Z$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For a fixed $J$, its contribution to the right side is
\[
 |c_J|\sum_{\supp\eps\subseteq J}(-1)^{|\eps|}
 Q_{|J|}(s-\eps\cdot x)
 =\iota\left(c_J\prod_{j\in J}x_j\right)
\]
by \eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:scalar-top}, including the empty-set case. Summing proves the
identity. The degree and phase-order claims follow from
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:46:thm:scalar}. For the monomial $\prod_{i=1}^k x_i$,
Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:46:lem:vertex-separation} makes the all-ones vertex an integrator.
The lower bound in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:46:thm:scalar} therefore proves optimality even
among unrelated vertex functions with a common finite phase alphabet.
\end{proof}

This removes the condition $k<p$ from the \emph{existence of a phase-valued}
scalar polarization identity. It does not remove it while retaining the
original classical polynomial codomain. Conflating those statements would
produce an incorrect extension of Gowers' lemma.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Complete classification of trace-multiplication tensors\srctag{46}}]{Complete classification of trace-multiplication tensors}\label{gsr:fp:46:sec:d7}\label{gsr:fp:46:sec:trace}
\srcnote{46}{Section 7}

Let $F=\F_q$ with $q=p^n$, viewed additively as an $n$-dimensional
$\F_p$-space. For $c\in F^\times$ and $d\geq1$, set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:trace-tensor}
 T_{c,d}(h_1,\ldots,h_d)=\Tr_{F/\F_p}(c h_1\cdots h_d).
\end{equation}
It is symmetric and $\F_p$-multilinear. The trace pairing is nondegenerate:
$\Tr(uv)=0$ for every $v\in F$ implies $u=0$. We use also the Frobenius
adjoint identity
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:trace-adjoint}
 \Tr(u b^p)=\Tr(u^{p^{n-1}}b),
\end{equation}
which follows from invariance of trace under Frobenius.

\begin{theorem}[Exact trace integration classification]\label{gsr:fp:46:thm:trace-classification}
For nonzero $c$, the tensor $T_{c,d}$ integrates precisely in the following
cases:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule
Extension degree & Tensor degree & Integrability condition\\
\midrule
$n=1$ & every $d\geq1$ & always\\
$n>1$ & $d\leq p$ & always\\
$n>1$ & $d=p+1$ & $n=2$ and $c\in\F_p^\times$\\
$n>1$ & $d\geq p+2$ & never\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
For all $n$, classical integration is possible exactly when $d<p$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $n=1$, Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:46:thm:scalar} applies, multiplied by the nonzero
coefficient. For $d\leq p$, use Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:46:thm:coordinate-integration}.

At $d=p+1$, the obstruction is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:trace-C}
 C_c(a,b)=\Tr\bigl(c(a^p b-a b^p)\bigr).
\end{equation}
By \eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:trace-adjoint} and nondegeneracy, $C_c=0$ is equivalent to
\[
 c a^p=(ca)^{p^{n-1}}\quad\text{for every }a\in F.
\]
Raising to the $p$th power gives the equivalent condition
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:trace-condition}
 c^p a^{p^2}=ca\quad\text{for every }a\in F.
\end{equation}
Taking $a=1$ forces $c^p=c$. With $c\ne0$, the remaining condition is
