$a^{p^2}=a$ for all $a$, which is equivalent to $n\mid2$.
For $n>1$ this gives exactly $n=2$ and $c\in\F_p^\times$.
Sufficiency follows from Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:46:prop:first-obstruction}.

If $d\geq p+2$, apply the necessary repeated-variable identity and set all
but one of the extra directions equal to one. Their product $z$ is arbitrary.
The identity requires $C_{cz}=0$ for every $z\in F$. For $n>1$, the preceding
classification shows that not every nonzero coefficient has vanishing
obstruction. Since $cF^\times=F^\times$, this is impossible.

For classical integration with $d\geq p$, a total derivative must vanish
when $p$ directions are equal. Setting all remaining directions to one
would force $\Tr(ca^p)=0$ for every $a$. Frobenius is bijective and the trace
pairing is nondegenerate, a contradiction. Conversely, for $d<p$ the
classical terms \eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:classical-term} suffice.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Optimal phase orders in the admissible trace cases]\label{gsr:fp:46:cor:trace-order}
For $n=1$ the minimum phase order is $p^{\lceil d/(p-1)\rceil}$.
For $n>1$, it is $p$ when $d<p$, and $p^2$ when $d=p$.
In the exceptional case $n=2$, $d=p+1$, $c\in\F_p^\times$, it is also
$p^2$, including $p=2$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The scalar assertion is Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:46:thm:scalar}. For $n>1$ and $d\leq p$,
the coordinate construction gives the upper bounds, and the classical
nonintegrability in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:46:thm:trace-classification} proves optimality
at $d=p$.

For the exceptional case with $p\geq3$, the pure term $Q_{p+1}$ already has
phase order $p^2$, so the full coordinate construction does also. If $p=2$,
the potentially eighth-root pure terms have coefficient
$\Tr(ca^3)=0$ for every $a\in\F_4$, because $a^3$ is the norm into $\F_2$
and the trace of an element of $\F_2$ from $\F_4$ is zero. Only the paired
fourth-root terms remain. The impossibility of classical integration proves
the lower bound in both cases.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[The smallest extension distinguishes three phenomena]\label{gsr:fp:46:ex:F4}
Let $F=\F_4=\F_2[\theta]/(\theta^2+\theta+1)$, and write $z=x+y\theta$.
For $c=1$, the cubic trace tensor integrates to
\[
 P(z)=-|x||y|/4\pmod1.
\]
Thus fourth roots suffice, even though a nonzero scalar cubic on $\F_2$
requires eighth roots. For $c=\theta$, however,
\[
 C_\theta(1,\theta)=\Tr(\theta^2)-\Tr(\theta^3)=1.
\]
No circle-valued cubic integrator exists, regardless of phase alphabet.
The mixed cube norm is nevertheless exactly $1/2$, by
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:46:thm:sharp}. An explicit common-function extremizer is
\[
 f(x+y\theta)=\exp\!\left(\frac{2\pi i(|x|+|y|)}8\right).
\]
Its cubic phase integrates the residual diagonal tensor, not $T_\theta$
itself; the remaining elementary obstruction block has bias $1/2$.
This separates classical failure, higher-root repair, and genuine
nonintegrability in one very small field.
\end{example}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Exact restriction dimensions and repair costs\srctag{46}}]{Exact restriction dimensions and repair costs}\label{gsr:fp:46:sec:d8}\label{gsr:fp:46:sec:rank}
\srcnote{46}{Section 8}

\subsection{The obstruction rank for trace tensors}
Continue at the first obstructed degree $d=p+1$, and write $C_c$ for
\eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:trace-C}.

\begin{theorem}[Explicit radical and maximal integrable subspace]\label{gsr:fp:46:thm:trace-rank}
Let $t_c=\dim_{\F_p}\rad C_c$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:radical-dimension}
 t_c=\begin{cases}
 1,&n\text{ odd},\\
 2,&n\text{ even and }c^{(q-1)/(p+1)}=1,\\
 0,&n\text{ even and }c^{(q-1)/(p+1)}\ne1.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:restriction-exact}
 \rank C_c=n-t_c,\qquad
 \max_{W:\,T_{c,p+1}|_W\text{ integrates}}\dim W=\frac{n+t_c}{2}.
\end{equation}
For even $n$, precisely $(q-1)/(p+1)$ nonzero coefficients have $t_c=2$;
the other $p(q-1)/(p+1)$ have $t_c=0$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The trace-pairing calculation leading to \eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:trace-condition}, now
with $a$ fixed, shows that the radical is the kernel of
\[
 a\longmapsto c^p a^{p^2}-ca.
\]
A nonzero radical element therefore satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:radical-power}
 a^{p^2-1}=c^{1-p}.
\end{equation}
In the cyclic group $F^\times$, the power map on the left has kernel of size
$\gcd(p^2-1,p^n-1)=p^{\gcd(2,n)}-1$.

If $n$ is odd, this size is $p-1$ and the solvability condition is automatic:
$(c^{1-p})^{(q-1)/(p-1)}=1$. There are $p-1$ nonzero solutions and the zero
solution, so the radical has dimension one. If $n$ is even, the kernel size
is $p^2-1$, and solvability is equivalent to
$c^{(q-1)/(p+1)}=1$. There are then $p^2$ radical elements including zero;
otherwise there is only zero. This proves \eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:radical-dimension}.

The rank formula follows. By Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:46:prop:first-obstruction}, an
integrable restriction is precisely an isotropic subspace for $C_c$.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:46:lem:symplectic} proves the maximum in
\eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:restriction-exact}. Finally the coefficient condition defines a
subgroup of $F^\times$ of order $(q-1)/(p+1)$, giving the counts.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Explicit sharp binary trace moments]\label{gsr:fp:46:cor:trace-moment}
For $p=2$, $q=2^n$, and $T_c(a,b,x)=\Tr(cabx)$, the moment
\eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:moment} satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:trace-moment}
 \sup_{\norm f_\infty\leq1}M_{T_c}(f)=
 \begin{cases}
 2^{-(n-1)/2},&n\text{ odd},\\
 2^{-(n-2)/2},&n\text{ even},\ c^{(2^n-1)/3}=1,\\
 2^{-n/2},&n\text{ even},\ c^{(2^n-1)/3}\ne1.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
Every value in this formula is attained by an eighth-root cubic phase.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Combine Corollary~\ref{gsr:fp:46:cor:moment} and Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:46:thm:trace-rank}.
\end{proof}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}ccccc@{}}
\toprule
$n$ & Number of coefficients & $r$ & Largest $\dim W$ & $\sup M_{T_c}$\\
\midrule
2 & $1$ & $0$ & $2$ & $1$\\
2 & $2$ & $2$ & $1$ & $1/2$\\
3 & $7$ & $2$ & $2$ & $1/2$\\
4 & $5$ & $2$ & $3$ & $1/2$\\
4 & $10$ & $4$ & $2$ & $1/4$\\
5 & $31$ & $4$ & $3$ & $1/4$\\
6 & $21$ & $4$ & $4$ & $1/4$\\
6 & $42$ & $6$ & $3$ & $1/8$\\
7 & $127$ & $6$ & $4$ & $1/8$\\
8 & $85$ & $6$ & $5$ & $1/8$\\
8 & $170$ & $8$ & $4$ & $1/16$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The table is a specialization of the proved formulas, not a numerical
extrapolation. It shows that exact integration of arbitrary trace tensors
cannot be recovered by a dimension-independent codimension loss. This does
not contradict inverse theorems: the associated maximal correlations become
small as the required codimension increases.

\subsection{An exact elementary symmetric repair invariant}
For any prime $p$, and $\ell,m\in V^*$, define the symmetric $(p+1)$-linear
form
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:elementary-general}
 S_{\ell,m}(h_1,\ldots,h_{p+1})=
 \sum_{j=1}^{p+1}\ell(h_j)\prod_{t\ne j}m(h_t).
\end{equation}
A direct evaluation, using $u^p=u$ in $\F_p$, gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:elementary-defect}
 C_{S_{\ell,m}}(a,b)=\ell(b)m(a)-\ell(a)m(b).
\end{equation}
Define the \emph{elementary symmetric repair number} of a symmetric
$(p+1)$-linear $T$ as the least number of forms
\eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:elementary-general} whose subtraction makes $T$ integrable.
Scalar coefficients are absorbed into $\ell$.

\begin{theorem}[Exact elementary repair number]\label{gsr:fp:46:thm:repair}
For every symmetric $(p+1)$-linear $T$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:repair}
 \text{elementary symmetric repair number}(T)
 =\frac{\rank C_T}{2}
 =\min\{\codim W:T|_W\text{ integrates}\}.
\end{equation}
In particular, for $T_{c,p+1}$ this number is $(n-t_c)/2$ with $t_c$ given
by \eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:radical-dimension}.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Write $C_T$ as a sum of $r/2$ wedges by
Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:46:lem:symplectic}, choosing their orientations to match
\eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:elementary-defect}. Subtract the corresponding $S_{\ell,m}$.
The residual form has zero obstruction and integrates by
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:46:thm:coordinate-integration}. Conversely, each elementary form
has obstruction rank at most two. Subtracting fewer than $r/2$ cannot cancel
a rank-$r$ obstruction, by rank subadditivity. The equality with minimum
codimension follows again from the isotropic characterization.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 82--94]
\emph{Proved again, independently, by sources~89 and~92} (Section~\ref{gsr:fp:sec:critical}), neither citing this source: with all maximal repairs (preimages of Lagrangians of $C_T$ modulo its radical, $\prod_{i\le r}(p^i+1)$ of them), minimum integrating covers of kernel $p^r$, lossless phase removal on cosets and a sharp quotient moment. This theorem and the first-obstruction test before it hold for every prime, not only in characteristic two; the README's earlier summary of this source as characteristic-two work is corrected in this write.
\end{writenote}

\subsection{Ordinary slice-rank repair is related but different}
A slice of a $d$-linear form is a term that is linear in one chosen slot and
multilinear in the other $d-1$ slots. The slice rank is the minimum number of
such terms. Define
\[
 \rho(T)=\min\{\srank(T-R):R\text{ is symmetric and integrates}\}.
\]

\begin{proposition}[Slice-rank repair bounds]\label{gsr:fp:46:prop:slice-repair}
For symmetric $(p+1)$-linear $T$ with $r=\rank C_T$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:slice-bounds}
 r/2\leq\rho(T)\leq r.
\end{equation}
If $r=2$, then $\rho(T)=2$. For $p=2$, slice rank here equals partition rank.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Each elementary correction in \eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:elementary-general} has slice rank
at most two: separate the $j=1$ term, and factor $m(h_1)$ from all remaining
terms. Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:46:thm:repair} gives the upper bound.

Suppose $T-R$ is a sum of $s$ slices. Intersect the kernels of all $s$
singleton linear factors, and call this subspace $U$. Then
$\codim U\leq s$ and $(T-R)|_{U^d}=0$. Since $R|_U$ integrates, $T|_U$
does also. The exact minimum-codimension statement gives $s\geq r/2$.

To handle $r=2$, a nonzero symmetric slice-rank-one tensor must be a scalar
multiple of a pure power $\ell^{\otimes d}$. Indeed, write it as
$\ell(h_1)B(h_2,\ldots,h_d)$ and choose $v$ with $\ell(v)=1$.
Symmetry in the first two slots shows that $B$ is divisible by $\ell$ in
its first slot; repeating this argument proves the pure-power assertion.
For $d=p+1$, such a tensor has zero obstruction, because
$\ell(a)^p\ell(b)=\ell(a)\ell(b)^p$. Thus a rank-two obstruction cannot be
repaired by one slice. The upper bound is two.
Finally, every bipartition of three slots has a singleton side, so slice and
partition rank coincide for trilinear tensors.
\end{proof}

The factor-two interval in \eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:slice-bounds} is not asserted to close
in general. The exactly determined quantity in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:46:thm:repair} is
the \emph{specified elementary symmetric} repair number, not unrestricted
tensor rank or unrestricted partition rank in higher degree.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Returning to Gowers' derivative-spectrum step\srctag{46}}]{Returning to Gowers' derivative-spectrum step}\label{gsr:fp:46:sec:d9}\label{gsr:fp:46:sec:gowers}
\srcnote{46}{Section 9}

The preceding results concern exactly the type of polynomial untwisting
that appears near the end of Gowers' argument. We spell out the analytic
translation to avoid confusing an integration theorem with a full inverse
theorem.

\subsection{A homogeneous frequency gives an exact norm identity}
For $h=(h_1,\ldots,h_j)$, use the backward-cube convention
\[
 \mathcal B_h f(x)=\prod_{\eps\in\{0,1\}^j}
 \conjop^{|\eps|}f(x-\eps\cdot h).
\]
This convention makes the additive phase identity
\[
 \sum_\eps(-1)^{|\eps|}P(x-\eps\cdot h)
 =D_{h_1}\cdots D_{h_j}P\left(x-\sum_i h_i\right)
\]
valid with a positive sign. It gives the usual Gowers norm after averaging:
$\norm f_{U^j}^{2^j}=\E_{x,h}\mathcal B_hf(x)$.

Let $F=\F_{p^n}$, $\chi(z)=e(\Tr(z)/p)$, and $d\geq2$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:general-moment}
 \mathcal M_{c,d}(f)=\E_{h_1,\ldots,h_{d-1}}
 \left|\E_x\mathcal B_{(h_1,\ldots,h_{d-1})}f(x)
 \overline{\chi(c h_1\cdots h_{d-1}x)}\right|^2.
\end{equation}

\begin{proposition}[Exact homogeneous untwisting]\label{gsr:fp:46:prop:untwist}
If $P$ integrates $T_{c,d}$, then for every function $f:F\to\C$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:exact-untwist}
 \mathcal M_{c,d}(f)=\norm{f e(-P)}_{U^d}^{2^d}.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Expand the square in \eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:general-moment} and write its second
basepoint as $x-h_d$. The character factor is
$\overline{\chi(c h_1\cdots h_d)}$, and the function product is
$\mathcal B_{(h_1,\ldots,h_d)}f(x)$. Therefore
\[
 \mathcal M_{c,d}(f)=\E_{x,h_1,\ldots,h_d}
 \mathcal B_h f(x)e\bigl(-\iota(T_{c,d}(h))\bigr).
\]
The defining equation for $P$ identifies the integrand with
$\mathcal B_h(fe(-P))(x)$. Averaging proves
\eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:exact-untwist}.
\end{proof}

In admissible trace cases, this is an equality rather than merely a
correlation-to-norm implication. In nonintegrable cases there is no exact
vertex-separated replacement, by Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:46:lem:vertex-separation}.
For binary cubics the substitute is not an unspecified error: it is the
exact ceiling in Corollary~\ref{gsr:fp:46:cor:trace-moment}.

\subsection{General scalar multi-affine frequencies}
For a separately affine $\sigma:\F_p^{d-1}\to\F_p$, define
\[
 \mathcal M_\sigma(f)=\E_{h\in\F_p^{d-1}}
 \left|\E_x\mathcal B_hf(x)e\bigl(-\iota(\sigma(h)x)\bigr)\right|^2.
\]
The phase after squaring is $\iota(h_d\sigma(h_1,\ldots,h_{d-1}))$, which
is separately affine in the $d$ directions.

\begin{theorem}[Scalar phase-valued extension of the untwisting step]\label{gsr:fp:46:thm:general-untwist}
For $d\geq2$, there are nonclassical polynomials
$P_\eps:\F_p\to\T$, of degree at most $d$ and phase order dividing
$p^{\lceil d/(p-1)\rceil}$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:46:eq:general-untwist}
 \mathcal M_\sigma(f)
 \leq\prod_{\eps\in\{0,1\}^d}\norm{f e(-P_\eps)}_{U^d}
 \leq\max_\eps\norm{f e(-P_\eps)}_{U^d}^{2^d}.
\end{equation}
Thus a lower bound $\mathcal M_\sigma(f)\geq\alpha$ is preserved as the
same lower bound for the $2^d$th power of a suitably twisted $U^d$ norm.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Expand the square as in Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:46:prop:untwist}. Apply
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:46:thm:scalar-polarization} to $h_d\sigma(h_1,\ldots,h_{d-1})$,
using $s=x$. This absorbs the character into a separate phase at each
vertex, producing the mixed cube average of the functions
$f e(-P_\eps)$. Gowers--Cauchy--Schwarz bounds its absolute value by the
product in \eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:general-untwist}; the second inequality is immediate.
The left side is nonnegative, so this is the stated inequality.
\end{proof}

The Gowers--Cauchy--Schwarz step is standard \cite{gowers}, and arbitrary
vertex-phase absorption is already treated in the repository's local
refinement material \cite{repo46notes}. The contribution here is the
existence, explicit construction, and optimal universal phase alphabet of
the phases in small characteristic, together with the exact obstruction
analysis showing why the same statement cannot simply be transferred to
arbitrary extension-field trace tensors.

\paragraph{Classical correlation is a different question.}
Failure of a classical total-derivative representation does not automatically
mean that classical phases cannot provide the correlation required by an
inverse theorem. These are different assertions. The distinction is central
in the work of Berger--Sah--Sawhney--Tidor \cite{bsst}, and it is respected
throughout this paper. In particular, the trace classification is a theorem
about exact total derivatives, not a counterexample to an inverse theorem.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Cube identities and phase invariance\srctag{43}}]{Cube identities and phase invariance}\label{gsr:fp:43:sec:d2}\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:sec:identities}
\srcnote{43}{Section 2}

\subsection{The finite-abelian normalization}
Let $G$ be a finite abelian group, written additively. For this section
and Sections~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:sec:orthogonality}--\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:sec:symmetry}, a
multiadditive form takes values in $\Torus$. Define
\begin{equation}
 \en_T(f)=\E_{\hh\in G^{d-1}}
 \abs{\E_x\partial_{\hh}f(x)e(-T(\hh,x))}^2.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:general-energy}
\end{equation}
In the Boolean specialization we use $T/2$ in this formula and retain
the notation $\en_T$. This convention accounts for all factors of two.

\begin{lemma}[Exact selected-cube identity]\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:lem:cube}
For every complex-valued $f$ and every multiadditive $T$,
\begin{equation}
 \en_T(f)=\E_{x,h_1,\ldots,h_d}
     \partial_{h_1}\cdots\partial_{h_d}f(x)e(-T(h_1,\ldots,h_d)).
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:cube}
\end{equation}
In particular the right side is real and nonnegative, even if $T$ is
not symmetric.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For fixed $\hh$, put $g=\partial_{\hh}f$. Expanding the square in
\eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:general-energy} and replacing the two base points by
$x+y$ and $x$ gives
\[
 \abs{\E_xg(x)e(-T(\hh,x))}^2
 =\E_{x,y}g(x+y)\overline{g(x)}e(-T(\hh,y)).
\]
Average over $\hh$. Multiplicative differences commute, so the product
is the $d$-fold difference in \eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:cube}.
\end{proof}

We define the Gowers quantity by
\begin{equation}
 \norm f_{U^d}^{2^d}=\E_{x,\hh\in G^d}\partial_{\hh}f(x).
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:gowers-definition}
\end{equation}
Only this finite identity is needed below. Its nonnegativity follows
from Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:lem:cube} with $T=0$. For $1$-bounded $f$, each
selected Fourier coefficient has modulus at most one, so
$0\le\en_T(f)\le1$.

\begin{lemma}[Gauge invariance]\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:lem:gauge}
Suppose $P:G\to\Torus$ has constant $d$-fold derivative $S:G^d\to\Torus$.
Then
\begin{equation}
 \en_{T+S}(f e(P))=\en_T(f).
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:gauge}
\end{equation}
If $S=T$, then
\begin{equation}
 \en_T(f)=\norm{f e(-P)}_{U^d}^{2^d}.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:lossless}
\end{equation}
Moreover the corresponding selected Fourier magnitudes agree for each
individual $(d-1)$-tuple of directions, before averaging.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Multiplicative differences distribute over products. Thus the extra
factor in the cube identity for $f e(P)$ is $e(S)$, which cancels the
extra tensor in the phase. For the pointwise assertion, the function
$q_{\hh}(x)=\Delta_{\hh}P(x)$ satisfies
$q_{\hh}(x+y)-q_{\hh}(x)=T(\hh,y)$. Taking $x=0$ shows
$q_{\hh}(x)=c_{\hh}+T(\hh,x)$ for a constant $c_{\hh}$.
Consequently
\[
 \E_x\partial_{\hh}(f e(-P))(x)
 =e(-c_{\hh})\E_x\partial_{\hh}f(x)e(-T(\hh,x)).
\]
Taking absolute values proves the assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Amplitude and conjugation]
No step in these identities divides by $f$ or assumes $|f|=1$.
In particular they remain valid at zeros. This matters in the shear
argument, where the new function is a product of two translates of $f$.
The scale of $\en_T$ is $2^d$: replacing $f$ by $c f$ multiplies the
energy by $|c|^{2^d}$.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Division-free finite-abelian orthogonality\srctag{43}}]{Division-free finite-abelian orthogonality}\label{gsr:fp:43:sec:d3}\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:sec:orthogonality}
\srcnote{43}{Section 3}

\subsection{Alternating bicharacters and their dimensions}
Let $B:G\times G\to\Torus$ be biadditive. Define
\begin{equation}
 \kappa_B(a,b)=e(B(a,b)-B(b,a)),\qquad
 R_B=\{a:\kappa_B(a,b)=1\text{ for every }b\},
 \quad d_B=\sqrt{|G/R_B|}.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:radical}
\end{equation}
The pairing $\kappa_B$ is alternating: $\kappa_B(a,a)=1$, and
$\kappa_B(a,b)=\kappa_B(b,a)^{-1}$. This formulation uses no division
by two, including when $G$ has even order.

\begin{lemma}[Finite symplectic decomposition]\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:lem:lagrangian}
The number $d_B$ is an integer. There is a subgroup $H\supseteq R_B$
such that $H=H^\perp$ for $\kappa_B$ and $[G:H]=d_B$.
More precisely,
\begin{equation}
 G/R_B\cong\bigoplus_j(C_{m_j}\oplus C_{m_j}),\qquad d_B=\prod_jm_j,
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:symplectic-decomposition}
\end{equation}
with orthogonal nondegenerate alternating pairings on the summands.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Pass to $K=G/R_B$, where the pairing is nondegenerate. The map
$K\to\widehat K$ it induces is injective and hence bijective. Choose
$x\in K$ of maximum order $m$, which is also the exponent of $K$.
The character $\kappa_B(x,\cdot)$ has order $m$ by injectivity. Choose
$y$ such that $\kappa_B(x,y)$ is a primitive $m$th root of unity.
Then $y$ also has order $m$.

Pairing a relation $a x+b y=0$ with $x$ and $y$ shows that $a$ and $b$
are both zero modulo $m$. The subgroup $L=\langle x,y\rangle$ is
therefore $C_m\oplus C_m$, and its restricted pairing is nondegenerate.
For any $z\in K$, appropriate multiples of $x,y$ subtract the two
pairings with $x,y$; hence $K=L\oplus L^\perp$. Induction on $|K|$
gives \eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:symplectic-decomposition}. In each block, take the
cyclic subgroup generated by its first basis vector. Their direct sum
is self-annihilating. Its inverse image in $G$ is the required $H$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The mixed orthogonality theorem}
Use the normalized Hilbert space inner product
$\inner gh=\E_xg(x)\overline{h(x)}$, linear in its first argument.
Define
\begin{equation}
 \QB_B(g,h)=\E_a\abs{\E_xg(x+a)\overline{h(x)}e(-B(a,x))}^2.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:Qmixed}
\end{equation}
Write $\QB_B(g)=\QB_B(g,g)$.

\begin{theorem}[Sharp mixed orthogonality]\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:orthogonality}
For every finite abelian $G$, every biadditive $B$, and all $g,h:G\to\C$,
\begin{equation}
 \QB_B(g,h)\le d_B^{-1}\norm g_2^2\norm h_2^2.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:orthogonality}
\end{equation}
For each $B$ there is a function $g$ with $|g(x)|=1$ at every $x$ for
which $\QB_B(g)=d_B^{-1}$. Thus the coefficient is sharp even in the
one-function, pointwise-unit-modulus class.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Introduce unitaries
\begin{equation}
 (U_ag)(x)=e(-B(a,x))g(x+a).
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:operators}
\end{equation}
Direct multiplication gives
\begin{equation}
 U_aU_b=e(-B(b,a))U_{a+b},\qquad
 U_aU_b=\kappa_B(a,b)U_bU_a.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:projective-law}
\end{equation}
Let $M_g$ be the positive operator
\[
 M_gv=\E_a\inner{v}{U_ag}\,U_ag.
\]
It has trace $\norm g_2^2$. The projective multiplication law shows that
conjugation by each $U_b$ merely permutes its summands, so $M_g$ commutes
with every $U_b$.

We claim that every nonzero subspace invariant under all $U_b$ has
dimension at least $d_B$. Choose $H$ as in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:lem:lagrangian}. The unitaries $U_h$, $h\in H$, commute,
so they have a common eigenvector in any such subspace. If its joint
eigenvalue function is $\lambda(h)$, then $U_t$ transports it to the
joint eigenvalue function $\kappa_B(h,t)\lambda(h)$. Two such functions
agree precisely when the corresponding $t$'s differ by an element of
$H^\perp=H$. Distinct joint eigenvalue functions belong to orthogonal
subspaces. Representatives of $G/H$ therefore give $d_B$ independent
vectors, proving the claim.

Each nonzero eigenspace of $M_g$ is invariant under the $U_b$. Every
positive eigenvalue consequently has multiplicity at least $d_B$, and
\[
 \norm{M_g}_{\rm op}\le\frac{\tr M_g}{d_B}=d_B^{-1}\norm g_2^2.
\]
Finally,
$\QB_B(g,h)=\inner{M_gh}h\le\norm{M_g}_{\rm op}\norm h_2^2$.

For sharpness, choose a common projective eigenvalue function $\lambda$
for the commuting $U_h$, $h\in H$, and construct a $\lambda$-eigenvector
of modulus one on every coset of $H$. Here is why this is possible.
On a single coset, a joint eigenspace has dimension at most one, since
translations by $H$ determine all its coordinates from one coordinate.
A nonzero eigenvector has constant, nonzero modulus on that coset.
There are $|H|$ distinct joint eigenvalue functions on each coset.
The ratio of any two eigenvalue functions with the same projective
multiplication law is an ordinary character of $H$. There are exactly
$|H|$ such ratios. Thus every coset has the same complete set of joint
eigenvalue functions. Normalize and assemble their $\lambda$-vectors
to obtain a global $g$ with $|g|=1$.

For $a\in H$, $U_ag=\lambda(a)g$, so $|\inner{U_ag}g|=1$.
For $a\notin H$, choose $h\in H$ with $\kappa_B(h,a)\ne1$.
The vectors $g$ and $U_ag$ have different $U_h$-eigenvalues and are
orthogonal. It follows that
$\QB_B(g)=|H|/|G|=d_B^{-1}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Self-cube form]\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:cor:selfQ}
For every $g$,
\begin{equation}
 \E_{a,b,x}\partial_a\partial_b g(x)e(-B(a,b))
 =\QB_B(g)\le d_B^{-1}\norm g_2^4.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:selfQ}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Expand the square in \eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:Qmixed}, replace the two base points
by $x+b$ and $x$, and use biadditivity. Then apply
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:orthogonality}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Fields, elementary divisors, and a composite example}
If $G=\F_p^n$ and $B$ is represented by a matrix $M$ through
$B(a,b)=a^{\mathsf T}Mb/p$, then
\begin{equation}
 d_B=p^{\rk(M-M^{\mathsf T})/2}.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:field-rank}
\end{equation}
An alternating bilinear form has even rank also in characteristic two;
this is the vector-space case of Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:lem:lagrangian}.

For $G=(\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z)^n$, let $M$ be an integer matrix and
$B(a,b)=a^{\mathsf T}Mb/m\pmod1$. If $s_1,\ldots,s_n$ are the Smith
invariants of the integer matrix $M-M^{\mathsf T}$, including zeros, then
\begin{equation}
 d_B=\left(\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{m}{\gcd(m,s_i)}\right)^{1/2},
 \qquad \gcd(m,0)=m.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:smith}
\end{equation}
Indeed unimodular row and column operations remain invertible modulo
$m$, and multiplication by $s_i$ has kernel of size $\gcd(m,s_i)$.
The square root is an integer by the preceding theorem.

For example, $B(a,b)=s a_1b_2/m$ on $(\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z)^2$ has
$d_B=m/\gcd(m,s)$. The constant function already gives
$\QB_B(1)=\gcd(m,s)/m$. At $m=12$, the factors for $s=1,2,3,4,6$
are respectively $1/12,1/6,1/4,1/3,1/2$. A rank computation over only
one residue field cannot distinguish this arithmetic profile.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Sharp symmetry thresholds on finite abelian groups\srctag{43}}]{Sharp symmetry thresholds on finite abelian groups}\label{gsr:fp:43:sec:d4}\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:sec:symmetry}
\srcnote{43}{Section 4}

\subsection{Alternating slices}
Let $T:G^{k+1}\to\Torus$ be multiadditive, with $k\ge1$. Fix a slot
$i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$, and freeze the other $k-1$ derivative directions
at $\zz$. Let $B_{i,\zz}(a,b)$ be the bilinear form obtained by putting
$a$ in slot $i$ and $b$ in the last slot of $T$.

\begin{theorem}[Amplitude-sensitive slice profile]\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:slice-profile}
For every such slot,
\begin{equation}
 \en_T(f)=\E_{\zz}\QB_{B_{i,\zz}}(\partial_{\zz}f)
 \le\E_{\zz}d_{B_{i,\zz}}^{-1}\norm{\partial_{\zz}f}_2^4.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:slice-profile}
\end{equation}
For $1$-bounded $f$ the final norm factors may be omitted.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Use Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:lem:cube}, freeze the other directions, and use
commutation of multiplicative differences. The inner average is exactly
\eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:selfQ}. Each frozen derivative is $1$-bounded when $f$ is.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Support of a multiadditive map]\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:lem:support}
Let $P$ be a nontrivial finite abelian $p$-group and let
$F:P^r\to A$ be a nonzero multiadditive map to an abelian group. Then
\begin{equation}
 \Prb(F(z_1,\ldots,z_r)\ne0)\ge(1-1/p)^r.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:support}
\end{equation}
For $r=0$, a nonzero constant has support probability one.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A nonzero homomorphism out of $P$ has image of size at least $p$;
its kernel therefore occupies at most $1/p$ of $P$.
For the induction, view $F$ as a map of the first $r-1$ variables into
$\operatorname{Hom}(P,A)$. This multiadditive map is nonzero. On the
at least $(1-1/p)^{r-1}$ fraction where its value is a nonzero
homomorphism, the last argument is nonzero in the image with
probability at least $1-1/p$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Prime-power symmetry gap]\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:cor:p-gap}
If $G$ is a finite abelian $p$-group and $T$ is not invariant under
interchanging slot $i$ and the last slot, then
\begin{equation}
 \en_T(f)\le 1-(1-1/p)^k.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:p-gap}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The alternating bicharacter of $B_{i,\zz}$ is a nonzero
$(k-1)$-variable multiadditive map into the group of bicharacters.
It is nontrivial on a fraction at least $(1-1/p)^{k-1}$ of the tuples.
On those tuples its nondegenerate quotient has order at least $p^2$
by Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:lem:lagrangian}; hence $d_{B_{i,\zz}}^{-1}\le1/p$.
On the other tuples the factor is one. The total loss is at least
$(1-1/p)^k$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Primary factorization and the exact group threshold}
Write $G=\bigoplus_pG_p$. Multiadditivity implies
\begin{equation}
 T(h_1,\ldots,h_{k+1})=\sum_p T_p(h_{1,p},\ldots,h_{k+1,p}).
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:primary-tensor}
\end{equation}
To see this, expand each argument into primary components. A term
containing inputs of two different prime-power orders is annihilated by
two coprime integers and is therefore zero in $\Torus$.

Let $\mathcal P_i$ be the primes for which the slot-$i$ alternating
defect of $T_p$ is nonzero. The radical indices multiply, and averaging
over the independent primary coordinates yields
\begin{equation}
 \E_{\zz}d_{B_{i,\zz}}^{-1}
 =\prod_p\E_{\zz_p}d_{B_{i,\zz_p}}^{-1}
 \le\prod_{p\in\mathcal P_i}\bigl[1-(1-1/p)^k\bigr].
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:primary-profile}
\end{equation}
The energy itself need not factor for an arbitrary $f$. It is the
\emph{upper rank profile} in \eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:primary-profile} that factors.

\begin{theorem}[Exact universal symmetry threshold]\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:group-symmetry}
Suppose $G$ is not cyclic, and let $p_*(G)$ be the least prime $p$ for
which $G$ has a quotient isomorphic to $\F_p^2$. Then
\begin{equation}
 \en_T(f)>1-(1-1/p_*(G))^k
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad T\text{ is fully symmetric}.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:group-threshold}
\end{equation}
The threshold is attained by a nonsymmetric $T$ and $f=1$, even when
$T$ is symmetric in its first $k$ slots. If $G$ is cyclic, every
multiadditive $T:G^{k+1}\to\Torus$ is already symmetric.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
On a cyclic group with generator $g$, multilinearity gives
\[T(a_1g,\ldots,a_{k+1}g)=a_1\cdots a_{k+1}T(g,\ldots,g).\]
This expression is symmetric. Thus a nonzero alternating defect must occur on a noncyclic
primary component. Such a component has a quotient $\F_p^2$, so
$p\ge p_*(G)$. The function $1-(1-1/p)^k$ decreases as $p$ increases.
Corollary~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:cor:p-gap} and \eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:primary-profile} now
bound the energy of any nonzero slot defect by the right threshold.
The transpositions of the last slot with each other slot generate all
permutations. Absence of these defects is full symmetry.

For sharpness, choose independent linear forms $u,v$ on a quotient
$\F_p^2$ with $p=p_*(G)$, pull them back to $G$, and set
\begin{equation}
 T(h_1,\ldots,h_k,y)=\frac{u(h_1)\cdots u(h_k)v(y)}p\pmod1.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:nonsymmetric-extremizer}
\end{equation}
It is nonsymmetric: choose an input where all the $u(h_j)$ and $v(y)$
are one, while $u(y)=0$ and one of the exchanged $v(h_j)$ is zero.
For $f=1$ a selected coefficient is one precisely when
$u(h_1)\cdots u(h_k)=0$, and is zero otherwise. This has probability
$1-(1-1/p)^k$. The first $k$ slots are symmetric by construction.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 40--46]
For $G=\F_p^n$, $p$ odd, this is source~36's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:36:ssc:thm:main}; here it holds on every finite abelian group, characteristic two included, with $p_*(G)$ in place of $p$, and the orthogonality factor $d_B^{-1}$ of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:orthogonality} extends source~36's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:thm:bilinear} (credited by the source). This advances source~36's composite-modulus question (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:IV:lowchar}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{remark}[Two independent kinds of sharpness]
Taking sums of \eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:nonsymmetric-extremizer} on distinct primary
components and $f=1$ attains the product in
\eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:primary-profile}. For a fixed bilinear form, the exact
factor $d_B^{-1}$ is attained by the construction in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:orthogonality}. Neither claim requires that an
arbitrary multilinear rank profile be simultaneously attainable by one
function; such a claim would be stronger and is not made here.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Boolean nonclassical integration, explicitly\srctag{43}}]{Boolean nonclassical integration, explicitly}\label{gsr:fp:43:sec:d5}\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:sec:integration}
\srcnote{43}{Section 5}

This section supplies a self-contained Boolean form of the existing
nonclassical integration theorem. Its role is to specify exactly which
algebraic conditions the new spectral estimates must certify.

\begin{definition}\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:def:ncs}
Write $\sym^d(V)$ for the space of symmetric $d$-linear maps
$V^d\to\Ftwo$. For $d\ge3$, define $\ncs^d(V)$ to be the subspace
satisfying
\begin{equation}
 T(a,a,b,\zz)=T(a,b,b,\zz)
 \quad\text{for every }a,b\in V,\ \zz\in V^{d-3}.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:transfer}
\end{equation}
For $d=2$ put $\ncs^2(V)=\sym^2(V)$.
The notation denotes a space of symmetric \emph{multilinear maps};
no identification with symmetric tensor coinvariants in characteristic
two is being assumed.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Constructive Boolean integration]\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:integration}
A $d$-linear form $T:V^d\to\Ftwo$, $d\ge2$, has a nonclassical
primitive of degree at most $d$ if and only if $T\in\ncs^d(V)$.
Fix coordinates $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ with basis $e_1,\ldots,e_n$.
For each nonempty $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ with $|S|\le d$, let
$c_S$ be the value of $T$ on any length-$d$ basis tuple whose set of
indices is exactly $S$. This value is well defined, and a primitive is
\begin{equation}
 P_T(x)=\sum_{\substack{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq[n]\\|S|\le d}}
       \frac{c_S\prod_{i\in S}|x_i|}{2^{d-|S|+1}}\pmod1,
 \qquad |x_i|\in\{0,1\}.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:primitive-formula}
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}
 \dim_{\Ftwo}\ncs^d(V)=\sum_{s=1}^{\min(n,d)}\binom ns.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:ncs-dimension}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $S_a$ be translation by $a$ on additive functions. Because $2a=0$,
$S_a^2=I$, and consequently
\begin{equation}
 \Delta_a^2=(S_a-I)^2=-2\Delta_a,\qquad
 \Delta_a^2\Delta_b=\Delta_a\Delta_b^2.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:operator-transfer}
\end{equation}
The second identity follows since both sides equal
$-2\Delta_a\Delta_b$. Additive differences commute. A constant top
derivative is therefore symmetric and satisfies
\eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:transfer}. This proves necessity.

Now assume $T\in\ncs^d(V)$. By symmetry, a coefficient on basis
vectors depends only on their multiplicities. If two distinct indices
$i,j$ are present and $i$ occurs at least twice, the identity
\eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:transfer} changes one occurrence of $i$ into one of $j$
without changing the coefficient. For any fixed support $S$, all
positive multiplicity vectors of total $d$ are connected by these
moves: move excess occurrences into a chosen index of $S$, then
redistribute to the desired multiplicities. Thus $c_S$ is well defined.
When $d=2$ this assertion requires no moves.

It remains to check the proposed monomials, including their degree.
For a set $S$ of size $s$, put
\[
 P_S(x)=2^{-(d-s+1)}\prod_{i\in S}|x_i|\pmod1.
\]
On a single Boolean coordinate, repeated application of
\eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:operator-transfer} gives
$\Delta_{e_i}^{t}=(-2)^{t-1}\Delta_{e_i}$ for $t\ge1$.
Also
\begin{equation}
 \Delta_h=\prod_{i:h_i=1}(I+\Delta_{e_i})-I.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:coordinate-difference}
\end{equation}
Expanding any $(d+1)$ differences by
\eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:coordinate-difference} produces products of at least
$d+1$ coordinate differences. If any used coordinate lies outside
$S$, the term is zero. Otherwise, if $r\le s$ distinct coordinates
occur among $t\ge d+1$ differences, the numerator is divisible by
$2^{t-r}$. Since $t-r\ge d-s+1$, its quotient by the denominator is
integer-valued. It vanishes in $\Torus$. Thus $P_S$ has degree at most
$d$.

Apply exactly $d$ coordinate differences to $P_S$. If their support
contains an index outside $S$, the answer is zero. If their support is
a proper subset $R\subsetneq S$, of size $r<s$, the numerator is
divisible by $2^{d-r}$, giving an integer quotient because
$d-r\ge d-s+1$. If their support is exactly $S$, the result is
$\pm1/2\pmod1=1/2$, independent of the base point. Hence the top
derivative on a basis tuple has value $1/2$ exactly when that tuple's
support is $S$.

For completeness, the top derivative of any degree-at-most-$d$
polynomial is multiadditive. The identity
$\Delta_{a+b}=\Delta_a+\Delta_b+\Delta_a\Delta_b$ shows that its
failure of additivity is a $(d+1)$-fold derivative and therefore zero.
It is independent of the base point for the same reason. Agreement on
basis tuples now proves that the top derivative of
\eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:primitive-formula} is $T/2$ everywhere.
The support coefficients are independent, as the same basis-tuple
calculation isolates each one. Counting them proves
\eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:ncs-dimension}.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[Why fourth and eighth roots are unavoidable]
On $\Ftwo$, $P(x)=|x|/4$ has second derivative $ab/2$, and
$P(x)=|x|/8$ has third derivative $abc/2$. Thus symmetric diagonal
terms integrate perfectly, but not generally into $\Ftwo$-valued
classical phases. Already the quadratic diagonal requires fourth
roots of unity. This is not an obstruction to the value group
$\Torus$ used throughout the manuscript.
\end{example}

\begin{remark}[Dependence on coordinates]
The primitive in \eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:primitive-formula} is a chosen section of
the top-derivative map, not a coordinate-free canonical polynomial.
Two primitives differ by a polynomial of degree at most $d-1$.
Their use in phase removal yields the same selected energy because
such a difference has zero top derivative.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The shear identity and sharp Boolean certification\srctag{43}}]{The shear identity and sharp Boolean certification}\label{gsr:fp:43:sec:d6}\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:sec:shear}
\srcnote{43}{Section 6}

\subsection{A bilinear form hidden in a repeated direction}
We return to a symmetric $d$-linear form $T:V^d\to\Ftwo$, $d\ge3$.
For $\zz\in V^{d-3}$ define $\Omega_{\zz}$ by
\eqref{gsr:fm:43:bpi:eq:defect-intro}.

\begin{lemma}\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:lem:defect-bilinear}
Each $\Omega_{\zz}$ is an alternating bilinear form. The map
$\zz\mapsto\Omega_{\zz}$ is multilinear with values in
$\Alt^2(V)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
In characteristic two, symmetry cancels the two cross terms when
$a$ is replaced by $a+a'$ in $T(a,a,b,\zz)$; hence this expression
is linear in $a$. The same argument applies to the repeated $b$.
The remaining occurrences are already linear. Finally
$\Omega_{\zz}(a,a)=2T(a,a,a,\zz)=0$, and multilinearity in the
frozen variables is immediate.
\end{proof}

For a function $f$, write $\tau_wf(x)=f(x+w)$.
The elementary identity responsible for the stronger estimates is
\begin{equation}
 \partial_a\partial_{a+w}f
 =\overline{\partial_a(f\,\tau_wf)}.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:shear-pointwise}
\end{equation}
Indeed both sides at $x$ equal
$f(x)f(x+w)\overline{f(x+a)f(x+a+w)}$.
This identity has no exceptional set where $f$ vanishes.

\begin{theorem}[Exact shear and repeated-variable rank profile]
\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:shear}
Put
\begin{align}
 g_{\zz,w}&=\partial_{\zz}(f\,\tau_wf),\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:shear-g}\\
 B_{\zz,w}(a,b)&=T(a,a,b,\zz)+T(a,b,\zz,w).
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:shear-B}
\end{align}
The form $B_{\zz,w}$ is bilinear and
$B_{\zz,w}(a,b)+B_{\zz,w}(b,a)=\Omega_{\zz}(a,b)$.
In the notation where Boolean bilinear forms are embedded in
$\Torus$ by division by two, one has the exact identity
\begin{equation}
 \en_T(f)=\E_{\zz,w}\QB_{B_{\zz,w}}(g_{\zz,w}).
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:shear-exact}
\end{equation}
Consequently, for arbitrary complex $f$,
\begin{equation}
 \en_T(f)\le
 \E_{\zz,w}2^{-\rk\Omega_{\zz}/2}\norm{g_{\zz,w}}_2^4.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:shear-amplitude}
\end{equation}
For $1$-bounded $f$ this gives
\begin{equation}
 \en_T(f)\le\E_{\zz}2^{-\rk\Omega_{\zz}/2}.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:shear-profile}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Write the cube variables in Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:lem:cube} as $a,b,\zz,c$,
and make the invertible substitution $c=a+w$. Multilinearity gives
\[
 T(a,b,\zz,a+w)=T(a,a,b,\zz)+T(a,b,\zz,w)=B_{\zz,w}(a,b).
\]
The first term is bilinear in $a,b$ by the cancellation used in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:lem:defect-bilinear}; the second term is bilinear and
symmetric in $a,b$. Its alternating part cancels.

Apply the remaining differences $\partial_b\partial_{\zz}$ to
\eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:shear-pointwise}. They commute with complex conjugation.
The resulting inner average over $a,b,x$ is the complex conjugate of
$\QB_{B_{\zz,w}}(g_{\zz,w})$, by
Corollary~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:cor:selfQ}. That quantity is real and nonnegative,
so its conjugate is itself. This proves
\eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:shear-exact}. The orthogonality factor is
$2^{-\rk\Omega_{\zz}/2}$ by \eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:field-rank}. Applying
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:orthogonality} gives
\eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:shear-amplitude}. If $f$ is $1$-bounded, so is
$g_{\zz,w}$, and the norm factors are at most one.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A strict gap for the additional obstruction]
\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:cor:integration-gap}
If $T$ is symmetric but not in $\ncs^d(V)$, then
\begin{equation}
 \en_T(f)\le1-2^{2-d}.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:integration-gap}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The multilinear map $\zz\mapsto\Omega_{\zz}$ is nonzero.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:lem:support} says that its support has measure at least
$2^{-(d-3)}$. A nonzero alternating form has rank at least two, so its
factor in \eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:shear-profile} is at most $1/2$.
The average loses at least $2^{-(d-3)}/2=2^{2-d}$ from one.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The sharp all-degree theorem}
\begin{theorem}[Sharp Boolean phase-integration criterion]
\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:boolean-certification}
Let $d\ge2$ and let $T:V^d\to\Ftwo$ be multilinear, without an
assumed symmetry. If
\begin{equation}
 \en_T(f)>1-2^{1-d},
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:boolean-threshold}
\end{equation}
then $T\in\ncs^d(V)$. The polynomial $P_T$ in
\eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:primitive-formula} exists and satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \en_T(f)=\norm{f e(-P_T)}_{U^d}^{2^d}.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:boolean-lossless}
\end{equation}
The threshold cannot be lowered in any dimension $n\ge2$, even when
$T$ is assumed symmetric in its first $d-1$ variables.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:group-symmetry}, with $p=2$ and $k=d-1$,
forces full symmetry. For $d=2$ this already gives integrability.
For $d\ge3$, failure of integrability would imply
\eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:integration-gap}. But
$1-2^{2-d}<1-2^{1-d}$, contradicting
\eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:boolean-threshold}. Integration follows from
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:integration}, and the exact identity follows from
Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:lem:gauge}. The nonsymmetric endpoint in
\eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:nonsymmetric-extremizer}, using two independent Boolean
linear forms, has precisely energy $1-2^{1-d}$ and cannot be a top
derivative. This proves sharpness.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The two thresholds should not be conflated]
The universal threshold for a prescribed multilinear selector is
$1-2^{1-d}$. For a tensor already known to be symmetric, the sufficient
threshold $1-2^{2-d}$ is smaller. The latter is proved optimal here
only for $d=3$; Section~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:sec:quartic} shows it is not optimal
for quartics in dimension two. In dimension one all symmetric
multilinear tensors integrate, so the dimension-independent sharpness
examples necessarily use at least two coordinates.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Corrupted selectors and finite margins}
\begin{proposition}[Robust certification]\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:prop:robust}
Let $\rho:V^{d-1}\to V^*$ be an arbitrary selector, and suppose it
agrees outside a fraction $\eta$ of tuples with
$\sigma(\hh)=T(\hh,\cdot)$ for a multilinear $T$. Define
$\en_\rho(f)$ by the corresponding selected Fourier energy. Then
\begin{equation}
 |\en_\rho(f)-\en_T(f)|\le\eta.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:corruption}
\end{equation}
If a certified lower bound $L$ on $\en_\rho(f)$ satisfies
$L-\eta>1-2^{1-d}$, then $T$ integrates and
\begin{equation}
 \norm{f e(-P_T)}_{U^d}^{2^d}\ge L-\eta.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:robust-energy}
\end{equation}
If $T$ is known symmetric, $1-2^{2-d}$ may replace the threshold for
$d\ge3$. In the symmetric cubic case, every $L-\eta>0$ also gives
an integrable restriction of codimension at most
$\lfloor\log_2(1/(L-\eta))\rfloor$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Each squared selected Fourier coefficient lies in $[0,1]$. The summands
agree off the exceptional set, so their average difference is at most
its measure. Apply the preceding theorems; the cubic assertion uses
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:cubic-exact} below.
\end{proof}

The hypothesis supplies a genuine multilinear model and a certified
energy bound. It does not assert that noisy samples automatically
recover such a model. Numerical error in a computed lower bound must
be subtracted before using the strict margin.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Exact cubic obstruction ranks and optimal repair\srctag{43}}]{Exact cubic obstruction ranks and optimal repair}\label{gsr:fp:43:sec:d7}\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:sec:cubic}
\srcnote{43}{Section 7}

\subsection{The amplitude-sensitive inequality}
\begin{theorem}[Cubic obstruction bound]\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:cubic-bound}
Let $T:V^3\to\Ftwo$ be symmetric, and write
$\rk\Omega_T=2m$. For every $f:V\to\C$,
\begin{equation}
 \en_T(f)\le2^{-m}\norm{|f|^2}_{U^2}^4.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:cubic-amplitude}
\end{equation}
In particular, if $|f|\le1$ and $\mu=\E_x|f(x)|^2$, then
\begin{equation}
 \en_T(f)\le2^{-m}\mu^3\le2^{-m}.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:cubic-mass}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
In Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:shear}, there are no frozen variables $\zz$.
The rank factor is constant, and $g_w=f\tau_wf$. Thus the remaining
factor is
\[
 \E_w\norm{f\tau_wf}_2^4
 =\E_w\left(\E_x|f(x)|^2|f(x+w)|^2\right)^2
 =\norm{|f|^2}_{U^2}^4.
\]
For $a=|f|^2\in[0,1]$, put $c(w)=\E_xa(x)a(x+w)$.
Then $0\le c(w)\le\mu$ and $\E_wc(w)=\mu^2$.
Consequently $\E_wc(w)^2\le\mu\E_wc(w)=\mu^3$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A normal form modulo integrable tensors}
For two linear forms $u,v$, define the symmetric trilinear tensor
\begin{equation}
 C_{u,v}(a,b,c)=u(a)u(b)v(c)+u(a)v(b)u(c)+v(a)u(b)u(c).
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:canonical-cubic}
\end{equation}
A direct substitution gives
\begin{equation}
 \Omega_{C_{u,v}}(a,b)=u(a)v(b)+v(a)u(b).
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:cubic-wedge}
\end{equation}

\begin{proposition}[The cubic obstruction quotient]
\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:prop:cubic-quotient}
The linear map
\[
 \Omega:\sym^3(V)\longrightarrow\Alt^2(V),\qquad T\longmapsto\Omega_T,
\]
is surjective and has kernel $\ncs^3(V)$. It induces a
$\operatorname{GL}(V)$-equivariant isomorphism
\begin{equation}
 \sym^3(V)/\ncs^3(V)\cong\Alt^2(V).
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:quotient}
\end{equation}
If $\rk\Omega_T=2m$, there are independent forms
$u_1,v_1,\ldots,u_m,v_m$ such that
\begin{equation}
 T=S+C_m,\qquad S\in\ncs^3(V),\qquad
 C_m=\sum_{j=1}^m C_{u_j,v_j}.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:cubic-normal}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The kernel assertion is precisely the repeated-variable identity.
Every alternating bilinear form has a symplectic decomposition
$\sum_j(u_j\otimes v_j+v_j\otimes u_j)$; this is the vector-space
proof in Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:lem:lagrangian}, with additional radical
coordinates. Formula~\eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:cubic-wedge} gives a preimage of
each block and proves \eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:cubic-normal}. The definition of
$\Omega_T$ commutes with every linear change of coordinates, proving
equivariance.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Canonical cubic energy]\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:lem:canonical-energy}
For the tensor $C_m$ in \eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:cubic-normal},
\begin{equation}
 \en_{C_m}(1)=2^{-m}.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:canonical-energy}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For a constant function, the energy is the probability that the
selected linear functional $C_m(a,b,\cdot)$ vanishes. Different
symplectic coordinate pairs are independent, so it suffices to count
one pair. Write $a=(a_1,a_2)$ and $b=(b_1,b_2)$. The functional is
\[
 y\longmapsto a_1b_1 y_2+(a_1b_2+a_2b_1)y_1.
\]
For $a=(0,0)$, all four $b$'s work. For $a=(0,1)$, two work.
For each of $a=(1,0)$ and $(1,1)$, exactly one works. There are
$4+2+1+1=8$ successful pairs out of sixteen, giving $1/2$ per block.
Radical coordinates impose no condition. Multiplication over $m$
blocks proves the result.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The exact extremal and repair theorem}
\begin{theorem}[Exact cubic energy and optimal codimension]
\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:cubic-exact}
For every symmetric trilinear $T:V^3\to\Ftwo$ with
$\rk\Omega_T=2m$,
\begin{equation}
 \MM(T)=2^{-m},\qquad
 \min_{\substack{U\le V\\T|_{U^3}\in\ncs^3(U)}}\codim U=m.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:cubic-exact}
\end{equation}
The maximum is attained by a nonclassical cubic phase of modulus one.
An optimal subspace and an explicit primitive on it are constructible
by finite linear algebra. Hence, for $0<a\le\en_T(f)$,
\begin{equation}
 m\le\lfloor\log_2(1/a)\rfloor.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:cubic-repair}
\end{equation}
The coefficient one in this logarithmic repair law is sharp.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The upper bound is Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:cubic-bound}.
Write $T=S+C_m$ by Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:prop:cubic-quotient}, and
integrate $S$ to a cubic $P_S$. Gauge invariance and
Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:lem:canonical-energy} give
\[
 \en_T(e(P_S))=\en_{C_m}(1)=2^{-m}.
\]
This proves the exact extremum and its phase attainment.

By Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:integration}, $T|_{U^3}$ integrates precisely
when $\Omega_T|_{U\times U}=0$, that is, when $U$ is isotropic.
If $R=\rad\Omega_T$, then $\dim R=n-2m$. The image of an isotropic
$U$ in the nondegenerate symplectic quotient $V/R$ has dimension at
most $m$. Indeed in a nondegenerate alternating space of dimension
$2m$, an isotropic subspace $L$ satisfies $L\subseteq L^\perp$ and
$\dim L+\dim L^\perp=2m$. Thus
\[
 \dim U\le\dim R+m=n-m.
\]
Equality is obtained by adjoining the radical to a Lagrangian of the
quotient. One can take
$U=\bigcap_{j=1}^m\ker u_j$ in the normal form. Integrate the
restriction using \eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:primitive-formula} on a basis of $U$.
Finally $a\le2^{-m}$ gives \eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:cubic-repair}. For every
$m$, the example $T=C_m$, $f=1$ has $a=2^{-m}$ and requires exactly
codimension $m$, so no smaller universal coefficient can replace one.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 40--46]
This is source~46's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:46:thm:sharp} for one function, proved independently the same day; source~46's statement for eight functions contains the value $2^{-\rk\Omega_T/2}$, and both identify the optimal codimension $\rk\Omega_T/2$.
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 82--94]
\emph{The case $p=2$ of a conjecture} of sources~89 and~92 (Section~\ref{gsr:fp:sec:critical}): they conjecture that the one-block constant-function energy $1-2(1-1/p)^p$ is the maximum and tensorizes for odd $p$; at $p=2$ this theorem gives the energy $2^{-r}$, the conjectured value.
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Credited and reproved} by source~95 (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:scalar}), the scalar case of its simultaneous theorem for two cubics (Section~\ref{gsr:fp:sec:pencils}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{corollary}[A low-partition-rank global correction]
\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:cor:partition-repair}
There is $S\in\ncs^3(V)$ with
\begin{equation}
 \prank(T-S)\le2m\le2\lfloor\log_2(1/a)\rfloor
 \quad\text{whenever }\en_T(f)\ge a>0.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:partition-repair}
\end{equation}
Here partition rank means the least number of summands, each factoring
into a function of one nonempty set of variables and a function of
its complementary set.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Use the normal form, and write each block as
\[
 C_{u,v}(a,b,c)
 =u(a)\bigl(u(b)v(c)+v(b)u(c)\bigr)+v(a)u(b)u(c).
\]
This gives two partition-rank-one summands per block.
The assertion is an upper bound; optimality of this partition-rank
coefficient is not asserted.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Concentration, tensor products, and what stability is available}
The amplitude inequality also has concentrated extremizers. Choose an
optimal isotropic subspace $U$ of codimension $m$ and a primitive $P_U$
of $T|_{U^3}$. Define $f=1_U e(P_U)$ on $U$ and zero elsewhere.
A nonzero cube contribution requires all its vertices in $U$; this is
equivalent to $x,a,b,c\in U$. Every such contribution is one after
the tensor twist. With $\mu=|U|/|V|=2^{-m}$,
\begin{equation}
 \en_T(f)=\mu^4=2^{-m}\mu^3.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:concentrated-extremizer}
\end{equation}
Thus the mass factor in \eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:cubic-mass} can also be attained.

For direct sums of symmetric cubic tensors, alternating ranks add.
The exact theorem therefore gives the multiplicative law
\begin{equation}
 \MM(T_1\oplus T_2)=\MM(T_1)\MM(T_2).
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:tensorization}
\end{equation}
This identity is a consequence of the proved extremal formula, not an
assumption that arbitrary optimizing functions factor.

A first quantitative stability consequence concerns amplitudes. If
$\en_T(f)\ge(1-\varepsilon)2^{-m}$ with $0\le\varepsilon\le1$, then
\begin{equation}
 \E_x(1-|f(x)|^2)\le1-(1-\varepsilon)^{1/3}.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:amplitude-stability}
\end{equation}
This follows immediately from \eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:cubic-mass}.
It does not classify the phases of near-extremizers. A phase-stability
claim would require information about simultaneous equality in the
projective spectral inequalities and is left for further research.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Mixed correlations: an optimal fourth power and a smaller repair bound\srctag{43}}]{Mixed correlations: an optimal fourth power and a smaller repair bound}\label{gsr:fp:43:sec:d8}
\srcnote{43}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:sec:mixed}

The one-function cube structure is stronger than an arbitrary mixed
correlation. Nevertheless the \emph{mixed} orthogonality theorem also
improves a published local estimate without changing its hypotheses.

\subsection{The triangle correlation}
For a finite abelian group and a biadditive $B:G^2\to\Torus$, put
\begin{equation}
 L_B(u,v,w)=\E_{a,b}u(a)v(b)w(a+b)e(B(a,b)).
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:triangle-definition}
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp fourth-power bilinear estimate]
\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:triangle}
For arbitrary complex $u,v,w$,
\begin{equation}
 |L_B(u,v,w)|\le d_B^{-1/2}\norm u_2\norm v_2\norm w_2.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:triangle-L2}
\end{equation}
Consequently, for $1$-bounded functions,
\begin{equation}
 |L_B(u,v,w)|^4
 \le\E_{a,b}e(B(a,b)-B(b,a))=d_B^{-2}.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:triangle-fourth}
\end{equation}
The exponent four in \eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:triangle-fourth} is optimal as a
uniform assertion, already on $\Ftwo^2$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Write $B^{\mathsf t}(a,b)=B(b,a)$, and use the operators associated to
$B^{\mathsf t}$. Replacing $a$ by $x-b$ gives
\[
 \E_a u(a)w(a+b)e(B(a,b))
 =e(-B(b,b))\inner{U_{-b}^{B^{\mathsf t}}u}{\overline w}.
\]
Cauchy--Schwarz in $b$, followed by
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:orthogonality}, yields
\[
 |L_B|^2\le\norm v_2^2\,
 \QB_{B^{\mathsf t}}(u,\overline w)
 \le d_B^{-1}\norm u_2^2\norm v_2^2\norm w_2^2.
\]
The radical indices of $B$ and $B^{\mathsf t}$ agree.
Averaging the alternating character in its second variable is one
when the first variable is in $R_B$ and zero otherwise. Hence its
bias is $|R_B|/|G|=d_B^{-2}$, proving
\eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:triangle-fourth}.

For sharpness, take $G=\Ftwo^2$ and
$B(a,b)=a_1b_2/2$. Then $d_B=2$. Let $\zeta=e^{\pi i/4}$ and choose
\begin{equation}
 u(a)=1,\qquad w(x)=i^{x_1},\qquad
 v(b)=\begin{cases}
  \zeta^{-1},&b_2=0,\\
  \zeta(-1)^{b_1},&b_2=1.
 \end{cases}
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:triangle-extremizer}
\end{equation}
The inner average over $a$ is $\zeta/\sqrt2$ when $b_2=0$, and
$(-1)^{b_1}\zeta^{-1}/\sqrt2$ when $b_2=1$.
Multiplying by $v(b)$ makes it $1/\sqrt2$ in both cases.
Thus $|L_B|=2^{-1/2}$ and $|L_B|^4=1/4=d_B^{-2}$.
Any exponent smaller than four would fail for this example.
\end{proof}

Tidor's Lemma 4.1 \cite{tidor} gives the eighth-power version of
this estimate over finite fields. The fourth-power statement above is
therefore a strict local refinement of that displayed estimate, as well
as a finite-abelian extension. It makes no claim about priority among
all possible earlier formulations of projective orthogonality.

\subsection{A transposition defect under seven-function correlation}
For $T:V^3\to\F_p$ and $1$-bounded $b_1,\ldots,b_7$, write
\begin{align}
 \Gamma_T(b_1,\ldots,b_7)=\Big|\E_{x,y,z}
 &b_1(x)b_2(y)b_3(z)b_4(x+y)\notag\\[-2pt]
 &\cdot b_5(x+z)b_6(y+z)b_7(x+y+z)e_p(T(x,y,z))\Big|,
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:seven}
\end{align}
where $e_p(t)=e(t/p)$. Let
$T_{(12)}(x,y,z)=T(y,x,z)$.

\begin{proposition}[Fourth-power control of each transposition]
\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:prop:transposition-mixed}
If $\Gamma_T\ge\delta>0$, then
\begin{equation}
 \E_{x,y,z}e_p\bigl(T(x,y,z)-T(y,x,z)\bigr)\ge\delta^4.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:mixed-transposition}
\end{equation}
The same conclusion holds for each transposition of the three slots.
Equivalently, the analytic rank of each such defect is at most
$4\log_p(1/\delta)$, where analytic rank is minus the base-$p$
logarithm of the bias.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Freeze $z$. The inner expression is a triangle correlation in $x,y$:
combine $b_1(x)b_5(x+z)$, $b_2(y)b_6(y+z)$, and
$b_4(x+y)b_7(x+y+z)$ into the three functions.
If $K_z$ is the alternating part of the bilinear form $T(\cdot,\cdot,z)$,
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:triangle} gives the upper bound
$p^{-\rk K_z/4}$. The triangle inequality and concavity of the fourth
root give
\[
 \delta\le\E_zp^{-\rk K_z/4}
 \le\left(\E_zp^{-\rk K_z}\right)^{1/4}.
\]
The average on the right is precisely the bias in
\eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:mixed-transposition}. Permuting the variables permutes
the seven allowed arguments and proves the other cases.
\end{proof}

This proposition only controls analytic rank. It does not silently
replace analytic rank by partition rank for general trilinear tensors.
Such a conversion is a separate input in a full inverse argument.

\subsection{Refining the symmetric trilinear repair lemma}
\begin{theorem}[Seven-function repair with coefficient two]
\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:mixed-repair}
Let $T:V^3\to\Ftwo$ be symmetric, and let
$\rk\Omega_T=2m$. For every seven $1$-bounded functions,
\begin{equation}
 \Gamma_T(b_1,\ldots,b_7)\le2^{-m/2}.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:mixed-cubic-bound}
\end{equation}
Thus $\Gamma_T\ge\delta>0$ implies that $T$ integrates on a subspace
of codimension at most
\begin{equation}
 \left\lfloor2\log_2(1/\delta)\right\rfloor.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:mixed-codim}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Make the same shear $z=x+w$ used in the repeated-variable argument.
For a fixed $w$, combine the seven factors into
\[
 g_w(x)=b_1(x)b_3(x+w),\quad
 h_w(y)=b_2(y)b_7(y+w),\quad
 k_w(t)=b_4(t)b_6(t+w),
\]
leaving a scalar factor $b_5(w)$. The tensor becomes
\[
 A_w(x,y)=T(x,x,y)+T(x,y,w).
\]
It is bilinear, and its alternating part is $\Omega_T$, independent
of $w$. Its radical index parameter is therefore $d_{A_w}=2^m$.
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:triangle} bounds each inner triangle correlation
by $2^{-m/2}$. Averaging over $w$ proves
\eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:mixed-cubic-bound}. It follows that
$m\le2\log_2(1/\delta)$. An isotropic subspace of codimension $m$
exists and has an integrable restriction, by the algebraic part of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:cubic-exact}.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 40--46]
The same codimension $\lfloor2\log_2(1/\delta)\rfloor$ is source~46's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:46:thm:seven}, by a different route. Tidor's Proposition~4.6 (re-read at the write in the arXiv HTML of version~2) gives codimension at most $8\log_2(1/\delta)$ for symmetric trilinear forms over $\F_2$ under a seven-function correlation hypothesis; the hypotheses were compared only as displayed there, as both sources compare them.
\end{writenote}

Tidor's Proposition 4.6 \cite{tidor} has the same symmetric tensor
and seven-function hypothesis, with codimension at most
$8\log_2(1/\delta)$. Here the fourth-power estimate controls the
alternating rank more tightly, and an isotropic subspace replaces the
full radical. The combined result is \eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:mixed-codim}.
Optimality of the coefficient two for this seven-function problem is
not established. In contrast, coefficient one in the one-function
energy problem \eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:cubic-repair} is proved optimal.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The quartic frontier: an exact small quotient and a global reduction\srctag{43}}]{The quartic frontier: an exact small quotient and a global reduction}\label{gsr:fp:43:sec:d9}
\srcnote{43}{Section 9}
\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:sec:quartic}

\subsection{A useful nonintegrable family in every degree}
For independent $u,v\in V^*$ and $d\ge3$, put
\begin{equation}
 C_d(h_1,\ldots,h_d)=\sum_{i=1}^d v(h_i)\prod_{j\ne i}u(h_j).
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:Cd}
\end{equation}

\begin{proposition}[Explicit lower bounds]\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:prop:lower-family}
The tensor $C_d$ is symmetric and nonintegrable, and
\begin{align}
 \Omega_{\zz}(a,b)
 &=\left(\prod_{j=1}^{d-3}u(z_j)\right)
       \bigl(u(a)v(b)+v(a)u(b)\bigr),\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:Cd-defect}\\
 \en_{C_d}(1)&=1-\frac{d+1}{2^d}.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:Cd-energy}
\end{align}
Consequently the dimension-independent symmetric nonintegrable extremum
satisfies
\begin{equation}
 1-\frac{d+1}{2^d}
 \le\sup_{\substack{n\ge2,\ T\in\sym^d(\Ftwo^n)\setminus\ncs^d(\Ftwo^n)\\
                         \norm f_\infty\le1}}\en_T(f)
 \le1-2^{2-d}.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:symmetric-interval}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
In the two repeated evaluations, the terms where $v$ is placed in
one of the two repeated positions cancel in pairs. The terms where
$v$ is placed in a frozen position cancel between the two evaluations.
The two remaining terms give \eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:Cd-defect}, which is
nonzero for appropriate arguments.

For the constant function, the selected frequency is zero precisely
when both coefficients in
\[
 y\longmapsto v(y)\prod_{j=1}^{d-1}u(h_j)
 +u(y)\sum_{i=1}^{d-1}v(h_i)\prod_{j\ne i}u(h_j)
\]
are zero. Put $k=d-1$. If at least two of the $u(h_j)$ are zero,
both coefficients vanish. If exactly one is zero, the remaining
condition is one independent unbiased bit, so half the tuples work.
If none is zero, the coefficient of $v(y)$ is one and the frequency
cannot vanish. Therefore the success probability is
\[
 1-2^{-k}-\tfrac12k2^{-k}=1-(d+1)2^{-d}.
\]
The upper bound in \eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:symmetric-interval} is
Corollary~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:cor:integration-gap}.
\end{proof}

For $d=3$ the bounds coincide at $1/2$. For $d=4$ they give
$11/16\le M\le3/4$. The next results explain why the fourth-degree
problem is concentrated in one specific tensor rather than an
unrestricted search over quartic coefficients.

\subsection{High-energy quartics have one rank-two defect}
For a symmetric quartic, $z\mapsto\Omega_z$ is a linear map
$V\to\Alt^2(V)$. Denote its image dimension by $r$.

\begin{theorem}[Quartic defect dichotomy and normal form]
\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:quartic-reduction}
Let $T:V^4\to\Ftwo$ be symmetric and nonintegrable. If
$\en_T(f)>5/8$, then there are independent $u,v\in V^*$ and
$S\in\ncs^4(V)$ such that
\begin{equation}
 T=S+C_4,
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:quartic-normal}
\end{equation}
where $C_4$ is \eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:Cd} for these two forms.
More precisely, failure of this defect normal form implies the
uniform bound $\en_T(f)\le5/8$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Since $T$ is nonintegrable, $r\ge1$. If $r\ge2$, the zero fiber of
$z\mapsto\Omega_z$ has measure $2^{-r}\le1/4$. Every nonzero value
has rank at least two. Hence the profile theorem gives
\[
 \en_T(f)\le 2^{-r}+(1-2^{-r})/2\le5/8.
\]
Thus energy greater than $5/8$ forces $r=1$. Write
$\Omega_z=\ell(z)\Omega_0$ for nonzero $\ell$ and $\Omega_0$.
If $\rk\Omega_0\ge4$, then
$\en_T(f)\le(1+1/4)/2=5/8$. We must therefore have
$\rk\Omega_0=2$, so
\[
 \Omega_0(a,b)=u_0(a)v_0(b)+v_0(a)u_0(b)
\]
for independent $u_0,v_0$.

Symmetry of the original quartic imposes the identity
\begin{equation}
 \Omega_c(a,b)+\Omega_b(a,c)+\Omega_a(b,c)=0.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:quartic-bianchi}
\end{equation}
Indeed, expansion gives six quartic terms, paired equally by
symmetry. If $\ell$ were not in the span of $u_0,v_0$, choose
$c\in\ker u_0\cap\ker v_0$ with $\ell(c)=1$, and choose $a,b$
with $\Omega_0(a,b)=1$. Then the first term of
\eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:quartic-bianchi} would be one and the others zero,
a contradiction. Thus $\ell\in\operatorname{span}(u_0,v_0)$.

Set $u=\ell$. Because the scalar field is $\Ftwo$, one can choose
$v$ in the same two-dimensional span so that
$\Omega_0=u\otimes v+v\otimes u$. Formula
\eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:Cd-defect} for $d=4$ shows that $C_4$ has exactly the
same defect map as $T$. Their difference is symmetric and has zero
repeated-variable defect, and hence lies in $\ncs^4(V)$.
\end{proof}

The identity \eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:quartic-bianchi} is important: a generic
linear family of rank-two alternating forms need not be the defect
of a symmetric quartic. Ignoring this compatibility would leave an
unnecessarily large search space.

\subsection{The exact two-dimensional quartic extremum}
\begin{theorem}[The quartic value $11/16$ on $\Ftwo^2$]
\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:quartic-two}
For the tensor $C_4$ on $V=\Ftwo^2$ with $u(x)=x_1$ and $v(x)=x_2$,
\begin{equation}
 \max_{\norm f_\infty\le1}\en_{C_4}(f)=\frac{11}{16}.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:quartic-two}
\end{equation}
The same maximum holds for every symmetric nonintegrable quartic on
$\Ftwo^2$, after an integrable phase twist and a linear change of
coordinates.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Label the four points $0,e_1,e_2,e_1+e_2$ by $0,1,2,3$, and put
$z_i=f(i)^4$. We first establish the exact polynomial identity
\begin{align}
 1024\en_{C_4}(f)={}&\abs{z_0^2+z_1^2+z_2^2+z_3^2}^2
       +28\sum_{i<j}|z_i z_j|^2+480\prod_{i=0}^3|z_i|\notag\\
 &+24\operatorname{Re}\bigl(z_0z_1\overline{z_2z_3}
                       +z_0z_3\overline{z_1z_2}\bigr)
       -8\operatorname{Re}\bigl(z_0z_2\overline{z_1z_3}\bigr).
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:quartic-polynomial}
\end{align}
A short cube census proves the formula without assumptions on the
amplitudes. Here are all its cases.

If the four directions are all zero, their four possible base points
give the diagonal terms of $|\sum_i f(i)^8|^2$. If the directions
are all the same nonzero vector, their base points give its
off-diagonal terms. All these tensor signs are positive.
For a fixed nonzero vector, the fourteen remaining tuples in
$\{0,h\}^4$ use both $0$ and $h$. Each vertex of a two-point coset
then occurs four times with each conjugation parity. The two possible
base points per coset give the coefficient $28$ of each
$|f(i)f(j)|^8$.

It remains to consider direction tuples spanning $\Ftwo^2$.
The cube map $\varepsilon\mapsto\sum_j\varepsilon_jh_j$ has
four-point fibers. Unless the parity $\sum_j\varepsilon_j$ factors
through that map, every fiber contains two even and two odd vertices,
giving the common monomial $\prod_i|f(i)|^4$.
Parity factors precisely when all four directions lie in a single
two-element affine hyperplane not containing zero. They must use both
of its points. For a pair of distinct nonzero directions $a,b$, the
fourteen such tuples have multiplicity patterns $3+1$, $2+2$, and
$1+3$. Their signed sum is
\[
 4(-1)^{C_4(a,a,a,b)}+6(-1)^{C_4(a,a,b,b)}
       +4(-1)^{C_4(a,b,b,b)}.
\]
For the pairs $(e_1,e_2)$, $(e_1,e_1+e_2)$,
$(e_2,e_1+e_2)$, these sums are $6,-2,6$, respectively.
Each orientation of the associated two-pair partition has two base
points, giving coefficients $12,-4,12$ and their conjugates.
These are the three real-part terms in
\eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:quartic-polynomial}.

Finally, the sum of the tensor signs over all direction tuples is
$256(11/16)=176$ by Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:prop:lower-family}.
The rank-zero and rank-one tuples contribute $1+3(15)=46$;
the parity-factoring rank-two tuples contribute $6-2+6=10$.
The remaining signed sum is therefore $176-46-10=120$.
Their four base points give the coefficient $480$. This completes
the derivation of \eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:quartic-polynomial}.

The map $f(i)\mapsto z_i=f(i)^4$ maps the closed unit disc onto
itself. The right side of \eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:quartic-polynomial} is
subharmonic separately in each $z_i$: the first term is a squared
modulus of a holomorphic polynomial, the next two terms are
nonnegative multiples of $|z_i|^2$ and $|z_i|$, and the remaining
terms are harmonic in that variable. The disc maximum principle,
applied one coordinate at a time, shows that its maximum is attained
when every $|z_i|=1$. This use of the maximum principle can also be
seen directly from the Poisson mean inequality for the squared
modulus and the nonnegative radial terms.

Write $z_i=e^{i\theta_i}$, and put
\[
 c=\cos(\theta_0-\theta_2),\quad r=\cos(\theta_1-\theta_3),\quad
 q=\cos(\theta_0+\theta_2-\theta_1-\theta_3).
\]
The second and third terms of
\eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:quartic-polynomial} contribute $168+480=648$.
The remaining expression is
\begin{equation}
 4(c^2+r^2)+48cr+8q(cr-1).
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:quartic-cosines}
\end{equation}
Since $cr\le1$ and $-1\le q\le1$,
\[
 4(c^2+r^2)+48cr+8q(cr-1)
 \le4(c^2+r^2)+40cr+8\le56.
\]
Thus $1024\en_{C_4}(f)\le704$, or
$\en_{C_4}(f)\le11/16$. The constant function attains this value.

On a two-dimensional space, $\Alt^2(V)$ is one-dimensional.
The nonzero defect map of any nonintegrable symmetric quartic
therefore has image dimension one and nonzero rank two.
The algebraic part of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:quartic-reduction} applies
without an energy assumption. It gives the stated normal form;
gauge invariance and a linear change of variables preserve the
maximum energy.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The remaining higher-dimensional question is one fixed tensor}
Let $C_{4,n}$ denote the pullback of $C_4$ to
$\Ftwo^n=\Ftwo^2\oplus\Ftwo^{n-2}$, and define
\[
 M_{4,n}=\max_{\substack{T\in\sym^4(\Ftwo^n)\setminus\ncs^4(\Ftwo^n)\\
                         \norm f_\infty\le1}}\en_T(f).
\]

\begin{corollary}[Exact reduction of the quartic optimization]
\label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:cor:quartic-fixed}
For every $n\ge2$,
\begin{equation}
 M_{4,n}=\MM(C_{4,n}),\qquad
 \frac{11}{16}\le M_{4,n}\le\frac34,\qquad
 M_{4,2}=\frac{11}{16}.
 \label{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:quartic-fixed}
\end{equation}
The sequence $M_{4,n}$ is nondecreasing. Thus the full quartic
extremal problem reduces to asking whether adjoining directions on
which $C_4$ is zero increases its optimal tested energy.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The explicit tensor has energy $11/16>5/8$ at the constant function.
Any tensor whose defect does not have the normal form has energy at
most $5/8$, so it cannot determine the maximum. Every remaining
tensor is, after gauge and coordinates, exactly $C_{4,n}$.
This proves the equality of optimization problems. The lower and
upper bounds follow from the explicit example and the shear profile.
An optimizer on dimension $n$ may be pulled back while ignoring an
additional coordinate, proving monotonicity.
\end{proof}

We do not infer $M_{4,n}=M_{4,2}$ from the fact that the tensor uses
only two coordinates. The optimizing function may depend on all the
coordinates. Ruling out such a gain is the precise additional theorem
that would be needed. The cubic tensorization theorem does not settle
this quartic question.

\section{Source~47's chapter: exact Boolean obstruction energies \wtag}\label{gsr:fp:sec:boolenergy}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the ninth write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next eight sections are source~47's Sections~2--9. \emph{Logically they continue source~43's part of the binary chapter} (Section~\ref{gsr:fp:sec:binary}), whose quartic question they answer; they are printed here because no number printed earlier may move. Source~47's introduction is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:47:sec:d1}.

\emph{What is proved.} Over $V=\F_2^n$, for the canonical symmetric tensor $C_d=\sum_iv(h_i)\prod_{j\ne i}u(h_j)$ with independent $u,v$, the maximum selected energy is exactly $1-(d+1)/2^d$ in every degree $d\ge3$ and every dimension $n\ge2$, attained by the constant function; optimizers may use all coordinates (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:47:boe:thm:main-canonical}). The key is that every even sum of derivative directions is an exact period, which forbids frequencies (Section~\ref{gsr:fp:47:sec:d4}). For all symmetric nonintegrable tensors the maximum energy lies between $1-(d+1)/2^d$ and $1-\min\{d+1,7\}/2^d$, so the thresholds are exactly $1/2$, $11/16$, $13/16$, $57/64$ in degrees three to six (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:47:boe:thm:main-universal}), through a pure-defect classification and a sharp $7/32$ support bound for non-pure symmetric trilinear maps (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:47:boe:thm:trilinear-support}); above the threshold the tensor integrates and phase removal is lossless. A nonnegative deficit recursion and robust certification for corrupted selectors (Propositions~\ref{gsr:fp:47:boe:prop:deficit}, \ref{gsr:fp:47:boe:prop:corruption}). At $d=4$ this is source~43's quartic question, answered (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:IV:binary}); the septic value is open ($120/128\le M^{\mathrm{sym}}_{7,n}\le121/128$).

\emph{Relation to the formal statements} (checked at HEAD \texttt{06b30ca52}). \file{lemma_17_1} and \file{proposition_17_2} (\file{Sections17\_18.lean}, lines~38 and~48) have the exact companions \file{lemma_17_1_holds} (\file{Proofs17Phase.lean}, line~374) and \file{proposition_17_2_holds} (\file{Proofs17PhaseRemoval.lean}, line~373); they are stated on $\Z/N\Z$ with $N$ prime, so characteristic two lies outside them, as source~47 says. Nothing in this chapter is formalized.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Finite calculus and nonclassical integration\srctag{47}}]{Finite calculus and nonclassical integration}\label{gsr:fp:47:sec:d2}\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:sec:calculus}
\srcnote{47}{Section 2}

\subsection{The cube identity and exact slicing}
\begin{lemma}[Selected cube identity]\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:lem:cube}
For every complex $f$ and every multilinear $T$,
\begin{equation}
 \En_T(f)=\E_{x,h_1,\ldots,h_d}
    \partial_{h_1}\cdots\partial_{h_d}f(x)(-1)^{T(h_1,\ldots,h_d)}.
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:cube}
\end{equation}
For symmetric $T$ and $d\ge3$, if
$T_z(h_1,\ldots,h_{d-1})=T(h_1,\ldots,h_{d-1},z)$, then
\begin{equation}
 \En_T(f)=\E_z\En_{T_z}(\partial_z f).
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:slicing}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Fix $\hh=(h_1,\ldots,h_{d-1})$ and write
$g=\partial_{h_1}\cdots\partial_{h_{d-1}}f$.  Expanding the squared
Fourier coefficient and substituting one base point as the other plus $y$
gives
\[
 \left|\E_xg(x)(-1)^{T(\hh,x)}\right|^2
 =\E_{x,y}g(x+y)\overline{g(x)}(-1)^{T(\hh,y)}.
\]
Multiplicative derivatives commute.  Averaging proves
\eqref{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:cube}.  In the symmetric case freeze the last direction as
$z$, commute its derivative to the function, and apply the cube identity
in degree $d-1$.  This proves \eqref{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:slicing}.
\end{proof}
The cube average is real and nonnegative because its original expression
is an average of squares.  Define
\[
 \norm f_{U^d}^{2^d}=\En_0(f).
\]
For the purposes of this article, only this identity is needed, not the
full norm theory.

\begin{lemma}[Gauge invariance]\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:lem:gauge}
If $S\in\Ical_d(V)$ and $P$ satisfies \eqref{gsr:fm:47:boe:eq:primitive} with $S$
in place of $T$, then
\begin{equation}
 \En_{T+S}(f e(P))=\En_T(f).
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:gauge}
\end{equation}
In particular $\Mcal(T+S)=\Mcal(T)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The $d$-fold derivative of $e(P)$ is $(-1)^S$.  In the cube identity the
extra two factors $(-1)^S$ cancel.  Multiplication by $e(P)$ is a bijection
of the unit polydisc of functions, proving the assertion about maxima.
\end{proof}
These identities remain valid when $f$ vanishes; there is no division by
$f$ anywhere in the argument.

\subsection{The precise integration criterion}
For $d\ge3$, define the repeated-variable defect of symmetric $T$ by
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_T(z_1,\ldots,z_{d-3})(a,b)
 =T(a,a,b,z_1,\ldots,z_{d-3})+
  T(a,b,b,z_1,\ldots,z_{d-3}).
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:defect}
\end{equation}
For $d=3$ this is simply an alternating bilinear form $\Omega_T(a,b)$.

\begin{theorem}[Boolean nonclassical integration]\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:thm:integration}
A symmetric $d$-linear tensor, $d\ge3$, is in $\Ical_d(V)$ if and only if
$\Phi_T=0$.  Every symmetric bilinear tensor is integrable.  In coordinates
$x_1,\ldots,x_n$, a primitive can be chosen as
\begin{equation}
 P_T(x)=\sum_{\substack{\varnothing\ne A\subseteq[n]\\|A|\le d}}
 \frac{c_A\prod_{i\in A}|x_i|}{2^{d-|A|+1}}\pmod1,
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:explicit-primitive}
\end{equation}
where $c_A$ is the value of $T$ on any length-$d$ basis tuple whose set of
indices is exactly $A$, and $|x_i|\in\{0,1\}$.
\end{theorem}
This is the Boolean specialization of the known nonclassical integration
criterion~\cite[Definition~3.1 and Proposition~3.5]{tidor}; we give a direct
coordinate proof rather than invoke that result as a black box.
\begin{proof}
On functions taking values in $\Tcirc$, translation by $a$ has square the
identity.  Consequently
\begin{equation}
 \Delta_a^2=-2\Delta_a,\qquad
 \Delta_a^2\Delta_b=\Delta_a\Delta_b^2.
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:additive-repetition}
\end{equation}
Commuting additive differences proves symmetry and the required
repeated-variable identity for every top derivative.  This proves necessity.

Conversely, assume $\Phi_T=0$.  Symmetry makes a basis coefficient depend
only on its multiplicities.  When two indices $i,j$ occur and $i$ occurs
at least twice, the identity $T(e_i,e_i,e_j,\zz)=T(e_i,e_j,e_j,\zz)$ moves
one occurrence from $i$ to $j$ without changing the coefficient.  All
positive multiplicity lists of total $d$ on a fixed support are connected
by these moves.  Thus $c_A$ is well defined.

For a set $A$ of size $a$, consider
$P_A(x)=2^{-(d-a+1)}\prod_{i\in A}|x_i|$.  Repeated coordinate
differences satisfy
$\Delta_{e_i}^{t}=(-2)^{t-1}\Delta_{e_i}$ for $t\ge1$.  Moreover
\begin{equation}
 \Delta_h=\prod_{i:h_i=1}(I+\Delta_{e_i})-I.
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:coordinate-differences}
\end{equation}
A term in the expansion of $d+1$ differences contains at least $d+1$
