coordinate differences.  If a coordinate outside $A$ occurs, the term is
zero.  Otherwise, if $r\le a$ distinct coordinates occur among $t\ge d+1$
differences, its numerator is divisible by $2^{t-r}$, hence by
$2^{d-a+1}$.  It vanishes modulo one.  Therefore $P_A$ has degree at most
$d$.

Apply exactly $d$ coordinate differences.  A support properly contained
in $A$ again produces an integer, and a coordinate outside $A$ produces
zero.  On a tuple of support exactly $A$, the result is
$\pm1/2=1/2\pmod1$, independent of the base point.  Thus the top derivative
of \eqref{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:explicit-primitive} has the required basis coefficients.
The top derivative of a degree-at-most-$d$ polynomial is multiadditive:
$\Delta_{a+b}=\Delta_a+\Delta_b+\Delta_a\Delta_b$, and the error in
additivity is a $(d+1)$-fold derivative.  It is independent of the base
point for the same reason.  Agreement on basis tuples proves the result.
For $d=2$ the same construction works without a multiplicity-transfer
condition.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Pure powers integrate]\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:cor:pure-integrates}
For $u\in V^*$ and $m\ge2$, set $U_m(h_1,\ldots,h_m)=\prod_i u(h_i)$.
Then
\begin{equation}
 P_{u,m}(x)=\frac{|u(x)|}{2^m}\pmod1
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:pure-primitive}
\end{equation}
is a primitive of $U_m$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply the one-coordinate case of
\eqref{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:explicit-primitive} and pull back along $u$.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The spectral obstruction supplied by the defect\srctag{47}}]{The spectral obstruction supplied by the defect}\label{gsr:fp:47:sec:d3}\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:sec:spectral}
\srcnote{47}{Section 3}
This section reconstructs the shear method of the preceding
draft~\cite{repo47prior}.  It supplies the cubic base case and a profile estimate
used later.  The new improvements will come from preserving derivative
constraints and from stronger information about the support of the defect.

\subsection{A finite projective orthogonality bound}
Let $B:V\times V\to\Ftwo$ be bilinear, and put
\[
 \Omega_B(a,b)=B(a,b)+B(b,a),\qquad \rk\Omega_B=2r.
\]
An alternating bilinear form has even rank over $\Ftwo$, as is seen by
successively splitting off a pair $a,b$ with $\Omega_B(a,b)=1$.
Define
\begin{equation}
 \Qcal_B(g,h)=\E_a\left|\E_xg(x+a)\overline{h(x)}(-1)^{B(a,x)}\right|^2,
 \qquad \Qcal_B(g)=\Qcal_B(g,g).
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:Q}
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}[Projective orthogonality]\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:lem:orthogonality}
For arbitrary complex functions $g,h$,
\begin{equation}
 \Qcal_B(g,h)\le2^{-r}\norm g_2^2\norm h_2^2.
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:orthogonality}
\end{equation}
Also
\begin{equation}
 \E_{a,b,x}\partial_a\partial_b g(x)(-1)^{B(a,b)}=\Qcal_B(g).
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:Q-cube}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Use the normalized Hilbert space inner product
$\ipthirtyone gh=\E_xg(x)\overline{h(x)}$, linear in the first variable.  The
operators
\[
 (U_ag)(x)=(-1)^{B(a,x)}g(x+a)
\]
are unitary and satisfy
\[
 U_aU_b=(-1)^{B(b,a)}U_{a+b},\qquad
 U_aU_b=(-1)^{\Omega_B(a,b)}U_bU_a.
\]
The positive operator
\[
 M_gv=\E_a\ipthirtyone{v}{U_ag}U_ag
\]
has trace $\norm g_2^2$ and commutes with every $U_b$: conjugation by $U_b$
permutes its rank-one summands, and the scalar signs disappear.

Choose a subspace $H$ containing the radical of $\Omega_B$ whose image in
the symplectic quotient is Lagrangian.  Then $H=H^\perp$ and
$[V:H]=2^r$.  Every nonzero common invariant subspace of the $U_a$ has
dimension at least $2^r$.  Indeed the commuting unitaries $U_h$, $h\in H$,
have a common eigenvector in that subspace.  Its translates by representatives
of $V/H$ have different joint eigenvalues, since their ratios are the
characters $h\mapsto(-1)^{\Omega_B(h,a)}$.  They are pairwise orthogonal.

Every nonzero eigenspace of $M_g$ is such an invariant subspace.  Thus each
positive eigenvalue has multiplicity at least $2^r$, and
$\norm{M_g}_{\mathrm{op}}\le2^{-r}\tr M_g$.  Since
$\Qcal_B(g,h)=\ipthirtyone{M_gh}h$, this proves
\eqref{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:orthogonality}.  Finally, expand the square in
\eqref{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:Q} and change one base point to the other plus $b$.
The resulting average is the complex conjugate of the left side of
\eqref{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:Q-cube}; it is real because it equals $\Qcal_B(g)$.
This proves the identity.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The exact shear and its rank profile}
\begin{lemma}[Bilinearity of the defect]\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:lem:defect-alternating}
For symmetric $T$, the map $\Phi_T:V^{d-3}\to\Alt^2(V)$ is symmetric
multilinear in its frozen variables.  For each frozen tuple its value is
an alternating bilinear form in $a,b$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
In $T(a+a',a+a',b,\zz)$ the two cross terms cancel by symmetry.  This
proves additivity in the repeated variable, and the other variables are
already linear.  The same argument applies to the repeated $b$.  The
value at $a=b$ is zero.  Linearity and symmetry in the frozen variables
are inherited directly from $T$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Shear profile]\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:thm:shear}
Let $T$ be symmetric of degree $d\ge3$.  With $\tau_wf(x)=f(x+w)$, put
\[
 g_{\zz,w}=\partial_{z_1}\cdots\partial_{z_{d-3}}(f\tau_wf),\qquad
 B_{\zz,w}(a,b)=T(a,a,b,\zz)+T(a,b,\zz,w).
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \En_T(f)=\E_{\zz,w}\Qcal_{B_{\zz,w}}(g_{\zz,w}).
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:shear-exact}
\end{equation}
Consequently, for $\norm f_\infty\le1$,
\begin{equation}
 \En_T(f)\le\E_{\zz}2^{-\rk\Phi_T(\zz)/2}.
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:rank-profile}
\end{equation}
For $d=3$ the right side is $2^{-\rk\Omega_T/2}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The pointwise identity
\begin{equation}
 \partial_a\partial_{a+w}f
  =\overline{\partial_a(f\tau_wf)}
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:shear-pointwise}
\end{equation}
follows by multiplying the four factors.  In the selected cube identity,
write the directions as $a,b,\zz,c$ and substitute $c=a+w$.
Multilinearity gives the form $B_{\zz,w}$ above.  It is bilinear by the
same cancellation as in Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:47:boe:lem:defect-alternating}, and its
alternating part is $\Phi_T(\zz)$, since the term containing $w$ is
symmetric in $a,b$.  Apply the remaining derivatives to
\eqref{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:shear-pointwise} and then use
\eqref{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:Q-cube}.  Its reality removes the conjugation and proves
\eqref{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:shear-exact}.  Orthogonality bounds each summand by
$2^{-\rk\Phi_T(\zz)/2}\norm{g_{\zz,w}}_2^4$.  The last norm is at most one.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Support-to-energy inequality]\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:cor:support-energy}
For symmetric nonintegrable $T$ of degree $d\ge4$,
\begin{equation}
 \En_T(f)\le1-\tfrac12\Prb_{\zz}[\Phi_T(\zz)\ne0].
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:support-energy}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Every nonzero alternating form has rank at least two and thus contributes
at most $1/2$ to \eqref{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:rank-profile}.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Derivative periods and forbidden frequencies\srctag{47}}]{Derivative periods and forbidden frequencies}\label{gsr:fp:47:sec:d4}\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:sec:periods}
\srcnote{47}{Section 4}

\subsection{The even span is an exact period space}
For $\hh=(h_1,\ldots,h_r)$ define
\begin{equation}
 H_{\mathrm{ev}}(\hh)=
 \left\{\sum_{i=1}^r\eps_i h_i:\eps_i\in\Ftwo,
                          \ \sum_{i=1}^r\eps_i=0\right\}.
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:even-span}
\end{equation}
It is the span of $h_1+h_i$ for $2\le i\le r$.

\begin{lemma}[Exact period constraint]\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:lem:period}
For every complex $f$, including functions with zeros, and $r\ge1$, let
$F_{\hh}=\partial_{h_1}\cdots\partial_{h_r}f$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 F_{\hh}(x+h_i)=\overline{F_{\hh}(x)}\quad(1\le i\le r),\qquad
 F_{\hh}(x+w)=F_{\hh}(x)\quad(w\in H_{\mathrm{ev}}(\hh)).
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:period}
\end{equation}
In particular, for a frequency $\xi\in V^*$,
\begin{equation}
 \widehat{F_{\hh}}(\xi)\ne0
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \xi(h_1)=\xi(h_2)=\cdots=\xi(h_r).
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:frequency-support}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The product formula for $F_{\hh}(x)$ has one factor at every labelled cube
vertex, conjugated according to the parity of $r-|\eps|$.
Translation by $h_i$ toggles the $i$th vertex coordinate and reverses
conjugation parity.  It therefore conjugates the whole product.
Two such translations preserve the product, proving invariance under
the even span.  This is an identity of products, even when some labelled
vertices coincide.

If $w\in H_{\mathrm{ev}}(\hh)$ and $\xi(w)=1$, translation by $w$
changes the sign of the Fourier character while leaving the function
unchanged.  The coefficient equals its negative and is zero.  Annihilating
the generators $h_1+h_i$ is exactly the condition in
\eqref{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:frequency-support}.
\end{proof}
For two directions the identity has the particularly transparent form
\[
 \partial_a\partial_z f(x)
 =f(x)f(x+a+z)\overline{f(x+a)f(x+z)}
 =\partial_a\partial_z f(x+a+z).
\]
No approximation, exceptional set, or unit-modulus hypothesis is involved.

\begin{corollary}[A support bound for arbitrary selectors]
\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:cor:selector-support}
For an arbitrary selector $\sigma:V^r\to V^*$ and $\norm f_\infty\le1$,
\begin{align}
 &\E_{\hh}\left|\widehat{\partial_{\hh}f}(\sigma(\hh))\right|^2\notag\\
 &\qquad\le
 \E_{\hh}\ind_{\{\sigma(\hh)|_{H_{\mathrm{ev}}(\hh)}=0\}}
                 \norm{\partial_{\hh}f}_2^2
 \le \Prb_{\hh}[\sigma(\hh)|_{H_{\mathrm{ev}}(\hh)}=0].
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:selector-support}
\end{align}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The inadmissible coefficients vanish by Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:47:boe:lem:period}.
For each admissible coefficient apply Cauchy--Schwarz, and then use
$|\partial_{\hh}f|\le1$.
\end{proof}
The bound can be weaker than the shear profile if applied indiscriminately
to the original tensor.  Its decisive use here is on a slice that is known
to be a derivative of the \emph{same} original function.

\subsection{The sharp derivative-constrained rank-one estimate}
\begin{theorem}[A rank-one tensor tested on a fixed derivative]
\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:thm:fixed-derivative}
Let $u\in V^*$ be nonzero, $m\ge2$, and $z\in\ker u$.  For every
$\norm f_\infty\le1$,
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\quad
 \En_{U_m}(\partial_z f)\le1-2^{1-m},\qquad
 U_m(h_1,\ldots,h_m)=\prod_i u(h_i).
 \quad}\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:fixed-derivative}
\end{equation}
The bound is attained by $f=1$, for every such $z$ and in every dimension.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
In the selected-energy definition for $U_m$, the frequency is $u$ when
$u(h_i)=1$ for all $1\le i\le m-1$, and is zero otherwise.  On the former
set the function being transformed is
\[
 \partial_{h_1}\cdots\partial_{h_{m-1}}\partial_z f.
\]
It is invariant under $h_1+z$, while $u(h_1+z)=1$.  Its selected coefficient
therefore vanishes.  The excluded set has probability $2^{-(m-1)}$;
all remaining squared coefficients are at most one.  This proves the
bound.  For $f=1$ all derivatives are one, so every zero-frequency
coefficient is one and every nonzero-frequency coefficient is zero.
Equality follows.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why unrestricted slice optimization loses the answer]
The tensor $U_m$ itself is integrable, so $\Mcal(U_m)=1$, attained by
$e(P_{u,m})$.  Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:47:boe:thm:fixed-derivative} says that this value
cannot be attained inside the constrained family
$\{\partial_z f:|f|\le1\}$ when $u(z)=0$.  Replacing a derivative slice by
an arbitrary bounded function erases a loss of exactly $2^{1-m}$.
For the quartic problem, that loss occurs on one quarter of the slices
and supplies the missing $1/16$.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Exact canonical energies in every degree\srctag{47}}]{Exact canonical energies in every degree}\label{gsr:fp:47:sec:d5}\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:sec:canonical}
\srcnote{47}{Section 5}

\subsection{The defect and the lower bound}
\begin{lemma}[Canonical defect and constant energy]\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:lem:canonical-data}
For $d\ge3$,
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_{C_d}(\zz)(a,b)
 =\left(\prod_{j=1}^{d-3}u(z_j)\right)
      \bigl(u(a)v(b)+v(a)u(b)\bigr),
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:canonical-defect}
\end{equation}
with the empty product equal to one.  In particular $C_d$ is not integrable.
Moreover
\begin{equation}
 \En_{C_d}(1)=1-\frac{d+1}{2^d}=b_d.
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:canonical-lower}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
In $C_d(a,a,b,\zz)$, the two terms placing $v$ in a repeated $a$ slot
cancel.  The terms placing $v$ in a frozen slot cancel against their
counterparts in $C_d(a,b,b,\zz)$.  The two remaining terms give
\eqref{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:canonical-defect}.  Independence of $u,v$ makes the defect
nonzero.

For the constant function, the energy is the probability that
$C_d(h_1,\ldots,h_{d-1},\cdot)$ is the zero functional.  Its coefficients
of $v$ and $u$ are respectively
\[
 A=\prod_{j=1}^{d-1}u(h_j),\qquad
 B=\sum_{i=1}^{d-1}v(h_i)\prod_{j\ne i}u(h_j).
\]
If at least two of the $u(h_j)$ vanish, both coefficients vanish.  If
exactly one vanishes, $A=0$ and $B$ is the corresponding independent
unbiased $v$ bit.  If none vanishes, $A=1$.  With $k=d-1$, the failure
probability is therefore
$2^{-k}+\frac12k2^{-k}=(d+1)2^{-d}$.
\end{proof}
This lower-bound computation and the canonical defect were already present
in the preceding draft~\cite{repo47prior}.  The upper bound that follows is the
additional all-dimensional result.

\subsection{The inductive upper bound}
\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:47:boe:thm:main-canonical}]
For $d=3$, the alternating defect is $u\otimes v+v\otimes u$, of rank two.
The shear profile gives $\En_{C_3}(f)\le1/2=b_3$.  The lower bound is
Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:47:boe:lem:canonical-data}.

Assume the result in degree $m=d-1\ge3$.  Exact slicing gives
\begin{equation}
 \En_{C_d}(f)=\E_z
 \En_{\,u(z)C_m+v(z)U_m}(\partial_z f),
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:canonical-slicing}
\end{equation}
since each term of $C_d$ either places $v$ in the last slot or does not.
The four pairs $(u(z),v(z))$ are equidistributed.

On the quarter $(0,0)$ the tensor is zero and the slice energy is at most
one.  On the quarter $(0,1)$ it is $U_m$, and
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:47:boe:thm:fixed-derivative} gives the sharper bound
$1-2^{1-m}$ because $u(z)=0$.  On the half $u(z)=1$, the tensor is either
$C_m$ or $C_m+U_m$.  In the latter case remove the integrable tensor
$U_m$ using Corollary~\ref{gsr:fp:47:boe:cor:pure-integrates} and gauge invariance.
The resulting function is still one-bounded, so the induction hypothesis
gives $b_m$ in both cases.

It follows that
\begin{align}
 \En_{C_d}(f)
 &\le \frac14+\frac14(1-2^{2-d})+\frac12b_{d-1}\notag\\
 &=\frac14+\frac14-2^{-d}
       +\frac12\left(1-\frac{d}{2^{d-1}}\right)
 =1-\frac{d+1}{2^d}.
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:canonical-recurrence}
\end{align}
Together with the constant lower bound, this proves equality in every
degree.  Gauge invariance gives the assertion for $C_d+S$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The quartic stabilization question, explicitly}
The preceding draft left open whether the pullback $C_{4,n}$ of its
binary quartic to $\Ftwo^n$ could gain energy from extra coordinates in $f$.
For $d=4$, the preceding proof specializes to
\begin{equation}
 \En_{C_{4,n}}(f)
 \le\frac14\cdot1+\frac14\cdot\frac34
               +\frac12\cdot\frac12=\frac{11}{16}.
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:quartic-three-slices}
\end{equation}
The $3/4$ term is the constrained pure-cubic slice, not an unrestricted
cubic maximum.  Thus this argument supplies exactly the missing theorem;
no assertion about the dependence of an optimizer on the inactive
coordinates is needed.  The same mechanism gives $13/16$ in degree five
and $57/64$ in degree six for the canonical family before any classification
of other tensors is considered.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The geometry of low-complexity defects\srctag{47}}]{The geometry of low-complexity defects}\label{gsr:fp:47:sec:d6}\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:sec:geometry}
\srcnote{47}{Section 6}

\subsection{A compatibility identity}
\begin{lemma}[Bianchi-type identity]\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:lem:bianchi}
For $d\ge4$ and each fixed tuple $\mathbf w\in V^{d-4}$,
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_T(c,\mathbf w)(a,b)+\Phi_T(b,\mathbf w)(a,c)
                       +\Phi_T(a,\mathbf w)(b,c)=0.
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:bianchi}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Expand the three defects.  There are six values of $T$; symmetry pairs
them equally, so their sum is zero in $\Ftwo$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[A one-form compatibility test]\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:lem:wedge}
Let $u\in V^*$ be nonzero and $\Omega\in\Alt^2(V)$.  If
\begin{equation}
 u(c)\Omega(a,b)+u(b)\Omega(a,c)+u(a)\Omega(b,c)=0
 \quad\text{for all }a,b,c,
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:one-form}
\end{equation}
then $\Omega=u\otimes v+v\otimes u$ for some $v\in V^*$.
If $\Omega\ne0$, $u,v$ are independent and $\rk\Omega=2$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose $c_0$ with $u(c_0)=1$ and set $v(x)=\Omega(x,c_0)$.
Substitute $c=c_0$ into \eqref{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:one-form}.  It gives exactly
$\Omega(a,b)=u(a)v(b)+v(a)u(b)$.  A nonzero form of this shape has rank two.
\end{proof}
Thus a rank-four alternating form cannot occur with just one nonzero
linear frozen factor.  The compatibility identity is stronger than merely
knowing that each defect value is alternating.

\subsection{Pure symmetric maps and the canonical class}
\begin{definition}[Pure symmetric multilinear map]\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:def:pure}
A nonzero symmetric $s$-linear map $F:V^s\to W$ between finite-dimensional Boolean vector
spaces is \emph{pure} if
\begin{equation}
 F(z_1,\ldots,z_s)=A\prod_{i=1}^s u(z_i)
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:pure-map}
\end{equation}
for some nonzero $A\in W$ and nonzero $u\in V^*$.  For $s=1$, this means
that $F$ has rank one.  A nonzero map that is not pure is called non-pure.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Pure defects are exactly canonical obstructions]
\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:thm:pure-defect}
Let $d\ge4$ and $T\in\sym^d(V)$ be nonintegrable.  The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),topsep=3pt,itemsep=1pt]
\item $\Phi_T:V^{d-3}\to\Alt^2(V)$ is pure;
\item $T=C_d^{u,v}+S$ for independent $u,v\in V^*$ and $S\in\Ical_d(V)$;
\item the first-slot radical of $\Phi_T$ has codimension one.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Put $s=d-3$.  If $\Phi_T(\zz)=\Omega\prod_i u(z_i)$, choose all the
$s-1$ remaining frozen directions to have $u$ value one in
\eqref{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:bianchi}.  Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:47:boe:lem:wedge} gives
$\Omega=u\otimes v+v\otimes u$ with $u,v$ independent.  By
\eqref{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:canonical-defect}, $T-C_d^{u,v}$ has zero defect and is
integrable.  This proves (i)$\Rightarrow$(ii); the reverse implication is
the same explicit defect formula.

For any symmetric multilinear map, its first-slot radical is a radical in
every slot.  If that radical has codimension one, the map descends to an
$s$-linear map on a one-dimensional quotient and necessarily has the form
\eqref{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:pure-map}.  Conversely a nonzero pure map has radical
$\ker u$, proving the equivalence with (iii).
\end{proof}
In particular, being pure is much stronger than having a one-dimensional
\emph{image} when $s>1$.  The latter case still admits a useful description.

\begin{theorem}[One-dimensional defect images have two active coordinates]
\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:thm:binary-image}
Let $d\ge4$ and suppose the linear span of the values of $\Phi_T$ is
one-dimensional and nonzero.  Then there is a surjection $q:V\to\Ftwo^2$,
a symmetric $d$-linear $T_0$ on $\Ftwo^2$, and $S\in\Ical_d(V)$ such that
\begin{equation}
 T=S+q^*T_0.
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:binary-reduction}
\end{equation}
The common nonzero alternating value of the defect has rank two.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Write $\Phi_T(\zz)=F(\zz)\Omega_0$, where $F$ is a nonzero scalar
symmetric $(d-3)$-linear map.  Some first-slot contraction
$\ell(z)=F(z,\mathbf w)$ is nonzero.  By the Bianchi identity and
Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:47:boe:lem:wedge}, $\Omega_0$ has rank two.  Write
$\Omega_0=u\otimes v+v\otimes u$ with $u,v$ independent, and put
$R=\ker u\cap\ker v$.

Every first-slot contraction $\ell$ of $F$ vanishes on $R$.
Indeed, for $c\in R$ choose $a,b$ with $\Omega_0(a,b)=1$ in
\eqref{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:one-form}; the identity gives $\ell(c)=0$.
Symmetry gives the same conclusion in every frozen slot.  Thus the whole
defect, including its alternating pair, factors through
$q=(u,v):V\to\Ftwo^2$.

Choose a linear section $j:\Ftwo^2\to V$ and let $T_0=j^*T$.
The defect of $q^*T_0$ is the same as that of $T$, since $qj$ is the
identity and the defect factors through $q$.  Their difference is
integrable by Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:47:boe:thm:integration}.
\end{proof}
This reduces the \emph{tensor}, not the optimizing function.  It must not
be used to infer $\Mcal(q^*T_0)=\Mcal(T_0)$ for general $T_0$.
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:47:boe:thm:main-canonical} establishes that equality for the
canonical family by an additional argument.

\subsection{A retained radical-sensitive profile}
Let $F:V^s\to W$ be nonzero and symmetric, and let $r$ be the codimension
of its first-slot radical.  A nonzero $t$-linear map over $\Ftwo$ is nonzero
on at least a $2^{-t}$ fraction of its inputs: freeze all but one variable
and induct.  Consequently
\begin{equation}
 \Prb[F\ne0]\ge(1-2^{-r})2^{-(s-1)}.
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:radical-support}
\end{equation}
Applying this to $F=\Phi_T$, $s=d-3$, gives
\begin{equation}
 \En_T(f)\le1-2^{3-d}(1-2^{-r}).
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:radical-energy}
\end{equation}
This bound can be stronger than our dimension-independent bound when $r$
is large.  For $r=1$, the exact canonical result is stronger and should be
used instead.  The next section improves the small-$r$, non-pure case.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Support bounds for non-pure symmetric multilinear maps\srctag{47}}]{Support bounds for non-pure symmetric multilinear maps}\label{gsr:fp:47:sec:d7}
\srcnote{47}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:sec:support}
The following finite-field estimates are independent of Fourier analysis.
They apply to vector-valued maps, which is essential when the target is
$\Alt^2(V)$.

\subsection{Two structural reductions}
\begin{lemma}[Distinct pure factors do not add to a pure tensor]
\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:lem:pure-sum}
Let $m\ge2$, $A,B\ne0$ in $W$, and let $u,v\in V^*$ be distinct nonzero
forms.  Then $A u^{\otimes m}+B v^{\otimes m}$ is neither zero nor pure.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Over $\Ftwo$, $u,v$ are independent.  Choose $a,b$ with
$(u(a),v(a))=(1,0)$ and $(u(b),v(b))=(0,1)$.
If the sum were $D w^{\otimes m}$, evaluation on $(a,\ldots,a)$ and
$(b,\ldots,b)$ would force $D=A=B\ne0$ and $w(a)=w(b)=1$.
Evaluation on a tuple containing both $a$ and $b$ would then give zero
on the left and $D$ on the right.  The same first evaluation rules out
the zero tensor.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Non-purity survives a scalar projection]
\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:lem:projection}
If $s\ge2$ and $F:V^s\to W$ is non-pure, some linear functional
$\lambda\in W^*$ makes $\lambda\circ F$ non-pure.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Suppose every scalar projection is zero or pure.  The image of
$W^*\to\sym^s(V)$ is a linear subspace.  It cannot contain two distinct
nonzero pure scalar tensors, because their sum is non-pure by
Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:47:boe:lem:pure-sum}.  Hence that image has dimension at most one.
Since $F\ne0$, it is generated by some $u^{\otimes s}$, and separation
by linear functionals gives $F=A u^{\otimes s}$ for some $A\ne0$.
This contradicts non-purity.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Non-purity survives a contraction]\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:lem:contraction}
If $s\ge3$ and $F:V^s\to W$ is symmetric and non-pure, there exists $z$
such that $F_z=F(z,\cdot,\ldots,\cdot)$ is non-pure.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Suppose all nonzero slices are pure.  Since $z\mapsto F_z$ is linear,
Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:47:boe:lem:pure-sum} implies that their pure factors are all the
same nonzero $u\in V^*$.  Thus
$F_z=A_z u^{\otimes(s-1)}$, where $z\mapsto A_z$ is linear.
Choose $w$ with $u(w)=1$.  Symmetry gives
\[
 A_z=F(z,w,\ldots,w)=F(w,z,w,\ldots,w)=u(z)A_w.
\]
It follows that $F=A_wu^{\otimes s}$, contradicting non-purity.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Support lifting]\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:lem:lift}
For a multilinear map $F:V^s\to W$ and any fixed $z$,
\begin{equation}
 \Prb[F\ne0]\ge\tfrac12\Prb[F_z\ne0].
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:support-lift}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Fix the other inputs.  If their slice has a nonzero value at $z$, the
linear map in the first input is nonzero and hence nonzero on at least
half the first inputs.  Average this pointwise implication.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The sharp bilinear and trilinear support bounds}
\begin{proposition}[Non-pure bilinear support]\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:prop:bilinear-support}
A symmetric non-pure bilinear map $F:V^2\to W$ is nonzero on at least a
$3/8$ fraction of its inputs.  The constant is sharp.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The first-slot radical cannot have codimension one, since symmetry would
then make $F$ pure.  Thus its codimension $r$ is at least two, and
\eqref{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:radical-support} gives
$(1-2^{-r})/2\ge3/8$.  The scalar form
$u(a)u(b)+v(a)v(b)$ for independent $u,v$ has exactly this support.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The binary trilinear census]\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:lem:census}
For a scalar symmetric trilinear form on $\Ftwo^2$, write
\[
 A=F(e_1,e_1,e_1),\quad B=F(e_1,e_1,e_2),\quad
 C=F(e_1,e_2,e_2),\quad D=F(e_2,e_2,e_2).
\]
If the form is nonzero and non-pure, its support has size at least $14$
out of $64$ input triples.  The complete census is as follows.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}clc@{}}
\toprule
Support size & Coefficient strings $ABCD$ & Description\\
\midrule
$0$ & $0000$ & zero\\
$8$ & $0001,\ 1000,\ 1111$ & pure\\
$14$ & $0111,\ 1001,\ 1110$ & non-pure\\
$16$ & $0010,\ 0011,\ 0100,\ 0101,\ 1010,\ 1100$ & non-pure\\
$18$ & $0110,\ 1011,\ 1101$ & non-pure\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A triple with a zero input contributes zero.  Write the three nonzero
vectors as $a,b,c=a+b$.  The three constant triples have values
$A,D,A+B+C+D$.  The six types with a repeated input have values
$B,C,A+B,A+C,B+D,C+D$, each with multiplicity three.  The all-distinct
type has value $B+C$ and multiplicity six.  Therefore the support size is
\begin{align}
 &[A]+[D]+[A+B+C+D]\notag\\
 &\quad+3\bigl([B]+[C]+[A+B]+[A+C]+[B+D]+[C+D]\bigr)+6[B+C],
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:census-formula}
\end{align}
where brackets denote the $0$--$1$ representative of a Boolean value.
Substitution of the sixteen coefficient strings gives the displayed table.
The three nonzero pure forms are exactly
$u^{\otimes3}$ for the three nonzero linear forms $u$ on $\Ftwo^2$.
This is a complete finite arithmetic proof; the accompanying program
independently checks every row.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp non-pure trilinear support]\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:thm:trilinear-support}
For every symmetric non-pure trilinear map $F:V^3\to W$,
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\quad \Prb[F\ne0]\ge\frac7{32}.\quad}
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:trilinear-support}
\end{equation}
The coefficient is sharp, even for scalar-valued maps on $\Ftwo^2$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:47:boe:lem:projection}, choose a non-pure scalar projection
$G=\lambda\circ F$.  Its support is contained in that of $F$, so it is
enough to treat $G$.  Let $r$ be the codimension of its first-slot radical.
For $r=1$, symmetry would make it pure, which is excluded.
For $r\ge3$, \eqref{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:radical-support} yields
\[
 \Prb[G\ne0]\ge(1-2^{-r})\cdot\frac14\ge\frac7{32}.
\]
For $r=2$, symmetry makes $G$ descend in all slots to a two-dimensional
quotient.  Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:47:boe:lem:census} gives the same bound.

For sharpness, take $G=u^{\otimes3}+v^{\otimes3}$ with $u,v$ independent.
The two products equal one with probability $1/8$ each and simultaneously
with probability $1/64$.  Their sum is nonzero with probability
$1/8+1/8-2/64=7/32$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A uniform higher-degree consequence}
\begin{theorem}[Non-pure support in arbitrary degree]\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:thm:high-support}
For $s\ge3$, every symmetric non-pure map $F:V^s\to W$ satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \Prb[F\ne0]\ge\frac7{2^{s+2}}.
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:high-support}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Use Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:47:boe:lem:contraction} repeatedly to obtain a non-pure
trilinear contraction after fixing $s-3$ inputs.  Its support is at least
$7/32$ by Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:47:boe:thm:trilinear-support}.  Lift support back
$s-3$ times using Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:47:boe:lem:lift}:
$\Prb[F\ne0]\ge2^{-(s-3)}(7/32)=7/2^{s+2}$.
\end{proof}
Sharpness is established for $s=3$, not claimed for every $s>3$.
The improvement over the elementary nonzero-map bound $2^{-s}$ is the
factor $7/4$, and it uses symmetry and the exclusion of pure tensors.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Universal thresholds and exact phase removal\srctag{47}}]{Universal thresholds and exact phase removal}\label{gsr:fp:47:sec:d8}\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:sec:thresholds}
\srcnote{47}{Section 8}

\subsection{The noncanonical alternative}
\begin{theorem}[A quantitative obstruction dichotomy]
\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:thm:dichotomy}
Let $T$ be symmetric and nonintegrable and $\norm f_\infty\le1$.
Either $T=C_d^{u,v}+S$ for independent $u,v$ and integrable $S$, in which
case $\Mcal(T)=b_d$, or
\begin{equation}
 \En_T(f)\le
 \begin{cases}
  1/4,&d=3,\\
  1-6/2^d,&d=4,5,\\
  1-7/2^d,&d\ge6.
 \end{cases}
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:noncanonical-bound}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $d=3$, if the nonzero alternating defect has rank two it is
$u\otimes v+v\otimes u$, so subtracting $C_3^{u,v}$ leaves an integrable
tensor.  Otherwise its rank is at least four, and the shear profile gives
$\En_T(f)\le1/4$.

Let $d\ge4$ and $s=d-3$.  If $\Phi_T$ is pure,
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:47:boe:thm:pure-defect} gives the canonical alternative.
Otherwise it is non-pure.  For $s=1$ it is a linear map of rank at least
two, so its support has measure at least $3/4$.  For $s=2$ the support is
at least $3/8$ by Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:47:boe:prop:bilinear-support}.  For $s\ge3$
it is at least $7/2^{s+2}$ by Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:47:boe:thm:high-support}.
Apply \eqref{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:support-energy} in the three cases to obtain,
respectively, $5/8$, $13/16$, and $1-7/2^{s+3}=1-7/2^d$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:47:boe:thm:main-universal}]
The lower bound is the canonical example.  In degree three the two
alternatives in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:47:boe:thm:dichotomy} have upper bounds $1/2$
and $1/4$; in degree four they have $11/16$ and $5/8$.
In degree five both are at most $13/16$, and in degree six both are at
most $57/64$.  For $d\ge7$, the noncanonical upper bound
$1-7/2^d$ is at least the canonical value $1-(d+1)/2^d$.
This proves \eqref{gsr:fm:47:boe:eq:main-universal} and the four exact values.

Energy strictly above the universal nonintegrable upper bound forces
$T\in\Ical_d(V)$.  The explicit primitive exists by
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:47:boe:thm:integration}, and gauge invariance with $T=0$
gives the lossless identity.  The tensors $C_d$, $d=3,4,5,6$, with
$f=1$ are nonintegrable and attain the stated thresholds, proving sharpness.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Where the sextic constant comes from}
For a sextic tensor the frozen defect is trilinear.  The two routes to
$57/64$ are genuinely different.  A pure defect is repaired to the
canonical tensor and is handled by the derivative-period induction.
A non-pure defect is nonzero on at least $7/32$ of the frozen triples,
and each such triple costs at least $1/2$ in the rank profile.  The total
loss is therefore at least $7/64$.

This explains why merely repeating the earlier nonzero-map support estimate
would not suffice.  That estimate gives support only $1/8$ and hence loss
$1/16$, leaving the old upper bound $15/16$.  Even the simpler non-pure
bilinear contraction argument yields loss only $6/64$.  The sharp
trilinear support census supplies the additional $1/64$ needed for the
exact sextic result.

\subsection{Strict margins, not conclusions at equality}
For $d=4,5,6$, respectively, the implications are
\begin{align*}
 \En_T(f)>11/16&\ \Longrightarrow\ T\in\Ical_4(V),\\
 \En_T(f)>13/16&\ \Longrightarrow\ T\in\Ical_5(V),\\
 \En_T(f)>57/64&\ \Longrightarrow\ T\in\Ical_6(V).
\end{align*}
The assumption of symmetry includes the final frequency-evaluation slot.
Without that assumption these are not established criteria.  At equality
there are nonintegrable examples, so replacing $>$ by $\ge$ is false.
Neither the quintic nor the sextic proof classifies all endpoint tensors
or all maximizing functions; the canonical examples prove sharpness
without asserting uniqueness.

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{For the canonical tensor in degree $d\ge4$ the maximizing functions are now classified} by source~97 (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:97:thm:classification}, Section~\ref{gsr:fp:sec:boolendpoint}): exactly $e(P+\theta|u|)$ with $\deg P\le d-1$; the endpoint tensors were classified by sources~65 and~69.
\end{writenote}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Deficits, noisy selectors, and retained constraints\srctag{47}}]{Deficits, noisy selectors, and retained constraints}\label{gsr:fp:47:sec:d9}\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:sec:robust}
\srcnote{47}{Section 9}

\subsection{A nonnegative canonical deficit recursion}
For $d\ge4$, let $m=d-1$ and $g_z=\partial_z f$.  On $u(z)=1$ put
\[
 \widetilde g_z=g_z e\bigl(-v(z)P_{u,m}\bigr).
\]
Use conditional normalized averages over the indicated nonempty sets to
define
\begin{align}
 D_{00}&=\E_{z:u(z)=v(z)=0}\bigl(1-\En_0(g_z)\bigr),\notag\\
 D_{01}&=\E_{z:u(z)=0,\ v(z)=1}
                    \bigl(1-2^{1-m}-\En_{U_m}(g_z)\bigr),\notag\\
 D_1&=\E_{z:u(z)=1}\bigl(b_m-\En_{C_m}(\widetilde g_z)\bigr).
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:deficits}
\end{align}

\begin{proposition}[Exact deficit decomposition]\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:prop:deficit}
Each quantity in \eqref{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:deficits} is nonnegative, and
\begin{equation}
 b_d-\En_{C_d}(f)=\tfrac14D_{00}+\tfrac14D_{01}+\tfrac12D_1.
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:deficit-recursion}
\end{equation}
In particular, if $\En_{C_d}(f)\ge b_d-\eps$, then
$D_{00},D_{01}\le4\eps$ and $D_1\le2\eps$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Nonnegativity is exactly the three bounds in the proof of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:47:boe:thm:main-canonical}.  Subtract the exact sliced energy
from the matching sum of slice caps in
\eqref{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:canonical-recurrence}.  Gauge invariance on $u(z)=1$ gives
\eqref{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:deficit-recursion}.  The last assertions follow because
all terms are nonnegative.
\end{proof}
On the $(0,1)$ quarter, let $a_{z,\hh}$ be the squared selected coefficient
in the definition of $\En_{U_m}(g_z)$, and let $A$ be the set where not
all $u(h_i)$ equal one.  The forbidden coefficients are exactly zero, so
\[
 D_{01}=\E_{z:u=0,v=1}\E_{\hh}\ind_A(1-a_{z,\hh}).
\]
Thus for $0<\tau\le1$, under $\En_{C_d}(f)\ge b_d-\eps$,
\begin{equation}
 \Prb\bigl[a_{z,\hh}\le1-\tau\mid u(z)=0,v(z)=1,\ \hh\in A\bigr]
 \le\frac{4\eps}{(1-2^{1-m})\tau}.
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:slice-stability}
\end{equation}
This is a dimension-independent necessary condition on near-extremizers.
It does not yet reconstruct a single phase that simultaneously accounts
for all the nearly extremal slices.

\subsection{Corrupted frequency selectors}
For an arbitrary selector $\rho:V^{d-1}\to V^*$, define $\En_\rho(f)$ by
replacing $T(\hh,\cdot)$ with $\rho(\hh)$ in
\eqref{gsr:fm:47:boe:eq:energy}.  Suppose $\rho$ agrees with the selector of a
symmetric multilinear $T$ outside a set of measure at most $\eta$.

\begin{proposition}[Robust sharp certification]\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:prop:corruption}
For $\norm f_\infty\le1$,
\begin{equation}
 |\En_\rho(f)-\En_T(f)|\le\eta.
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:corruption}
\end{equation}
Put $\theta_d=1-\min\{d+1,7\}/2^d$.  If a certified lower bound $L$ for
$\En_\rho(f)$ satisfies $L-\eta>\theta_d$, then $T$ is integrable and
\begin{equation}
 \norm{f e(-P_T)}_{U^d}^{2^d}\ge L-\eta.
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:robust-conclusion}
\end{equation}
For $d=3,4,5,6$ the underlying uncorrupted thresholds are sharp.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Every squared coefficient lies in $[0,1]$.  The summands agree outside
the exceptional set, proving \eqref{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:corruption}.  The universal
threshold and exact phase removal then give
\eqref{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:robust-conclusion}.
\end{proof}
A numerical error budget must be subtracted in forming the certified
lower bound $L$.  The proposition assumes an actual symmetric multilinear
model; it does not construct one from noisy observations.

\subsection{Approximate periods with an explicit error term}
\begin{lemma}[Stable forbidden-frequency bound]\label{gsr:fp:47:boe:lem:approx-period}
For a complex function $G$, a shift $w$, and a character
$\chi_\xi(x)=(-1)^{\xi(x)}$ with $\xi(w)=1$,
\begin{equation}
 |\widehat G(\xi)|^2\le\tfrac14\norm{G-\tau_wG}_2^2.
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:approx-period}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Translation gives
$2\widehat G(\xi)=\E_x(G(x)-G(x+w))\chi_\xi(x)$.
Apply Cauchy--Schwarz.
\end{proof}
Consequently, in a family of one-bounded test functions with a set $B$ of
nominally forbidden coefficients, if a suitable period error is at most
$\delta_b$ for each $b\in B$, then
\begin{equation}
 \text{average squared coefficient}
 \le1-\Prb(B)+\frac14\E_b\ind_B\delta_b^2.
 \label{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:approx-average}
\end{equation}
The exact derivative theorem is the case $\delta_b=0$.
This formulation keeps analytic perturbations distinct from corruption
of the selector, which is controlled by \eqref{gsr:fp:47:boe:eq:corruption} instead.

\gsrnewfloats
\section{Sources~65 and~69: Boolean phase integration in every degree \wtag}\label{gsr:fp:sec:alldegree}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the eleventh write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next fifteen sections are source~65's Sections~2--8 and then source~69's Sections~2--9, on Gowers's phase-removal step (Proposition~17.2) in characteristic two. \emph{Logically they continue source~47's chapter} (Section~\ref{gsr:fp:sec:boolenergy}), whose degree-seven and all-degree questions they answer, and the binary chapter of sources~46 and~43 (Section~\ref{gsr:fp:sec:binary}); they are printed here because no number printed earlier may move. Their introductions are Sections~\ref{gsr:fm:65:sec:d1} and~\ref{gsr:fm:69:sec:d1}.

\emph{The common theorem, proved twice.} For every $d\ge3$ and $n\ge2$ the largest selected energy of a nonintegrable symmetric $d$-linear tensor on $\F_2^n$ is exactly $1-(d+1)/2^d$, every extremal tensor is the canonical $C_d^{u,v}$ modulo an integrable tensor, and energy above $1-(d+1)/2^d$ certifies integrability, with lossless phase removal (source~65's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:65:bsi:thm:main}; source~69's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:69:bad:thm:main}, with the classification for $d\ge4$ and the cubic law for $d=3$). Every other nonintegrable tensor has energy at most $1-3d/2^{d+1}$ (both), and at most $1-(1-2^{-r})d/2^{d-1}$ when the radical of integrable contractions has codimension $r$ (source~65's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:65:bsi:thm:gap}). The key in both is that the directions with integrable contractions form exactly the radical of the repeated-variable defect (source~65's $K_T$, source~69's $R(T)$; note the different letters), so that a noncanonical tensor keeps at least three quarters of its contractions nonintegrable and induction on the degree closes. Source~47 had proved the canonical maximum in every degree and the universal value only through degree six ($1-\min\{d+1,7\}/2^d$); its Research questions~\ref{gsr:fz:47:boe:q:septic} and~\ref{gsr:fz:47:boe:q:all-degree} and the tensor part of~\ref{gsr:fz:47:boe:q:endpoints} are answered (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:IV:boolenergy}): the septic value is $15/16$. The two sources were written independently on the same day and neither cites the other; source~65 is printed first because its statement covers $d=3$ and carries the radical-sensitive cap, and source~69 is a credited second route, printed whole with its further results. The integration criterion is Tao--Ziegler's and Tidor's, the cubic law and canonical family sources~43 and~47's, credited by both and reproved.

\emph{Further results.} Source~65: complete repair geometry ($T|_{H^d}$ integrable iff $H$ lies in $\ker u$, $\ker v$ or $\ker(u+v)$, Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:thm:repair}), the exact number of extremal classes, $(2^n-1)(2^n-2)/6$ for $d=3$ and $(2^n-1)(2^{n-1}-1)$ for $d\ge4$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:thm:count}), dimension-independent amplitude stability (Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:prop:amplitude}), robust certification and a retained contraction profile (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:thm:robust}, Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:prop:profile}). Source~69: the extremal classes are the flags $\ell\subset\Pi$ in $V^*$, also $(2^n-1)(2^{n-1}-1)$ in number (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:69:bad:thm:flags}; the counts agree, checked at the write), the exact minimal quotient $\eff(T)=\codim K(T)\le\rho+\sum_{j=1}^{\min(\rho,d-2)}\binom\rho j$, sharp for every $d\ge4$ and $\rho\ge1$ (Theorems~\ref{gsr:fm:69:bad:thm:model-intro}, \ref{gsr:fp:69:bad:thm:minimal-quotient}, \ref{gsr:fp:69:bad:thm:sharp-model}), a fixed-radical normal form (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:69:bad:thm:normal-form}) and energy bounds on the contraction rank (Corollary~\ref{gsr:fp:69:bad:cor:energy-complexity}).

\emph{Relation to the formal statements} (checked at HEAD \texttt{fb9602e55}). \file{lemma_17_1} and \file{proposition_17_2} (\file{Sections17\_18.lean}, lines~38 and~48) have the exact companions \file{lemma_17_1_holds} (\file{Proofs17Phase.lean}, line~374) and \file{proposition_17_2_holds} (\file{Proofs17PhaseRemoval.lean}, line~373); they are stated on $\Z/N\Z$ with $N$ prime, so characteristic two lies outside them, as both sources say. Nothing in this chapter is formalized.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Finite calculus and the integration criterion\srctag{65}}]{Finite calculus and the integration criterion}\label{gsr:fp:65:sec:d2}\label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:sec:calculus}
\srcnote{65}{Section 2}

\subsection{Cube expansion and phase changes}
\begin{lemma}[Selected cube identity and slicing]\label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:lem:cube}
For a multilinear tensor $T$ and an arbitrary complex function $f$,
\begin{equation}
 \En_T(f)=\E_{x,h_1,\ldots,h_d}
   \partial_{h_1}\cdots\partial_{h_d}f(x)
       (-1)^{T(h_1,\ldots,h_d)}.
 \label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:cube}
\end{equation}
If $T$ is symmetric and $d\ge3$, then, with
$T_z(h_1,\ldots,h_{d-1})=T(h_1,\ldots,h_{d-1},z)$,
\begin{equation}
 \En_T(f)=\E_z\En_{T_z}(\partial_zf).
 \label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:slicing}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For a fixed tuple $\hh=(h_1,\ldots,h_{d-1})$ let
$g=\partial_{h_1}\cdots\partial_{h_{d-1}}f$ and
$\xi(x)=T(\hh,x)$. Expanding the squared Fourier coefficient and changing
one base point to the other plus $y$ gives
\[
 \left|\E_xg(x)(-1)^{\xi(x)}\right|^2
 =\E_{x,y}g(x+y)\overline{g(x)}(-1)^{\xi(y)}.
\]
Average over $\hh$ to obtain \eqref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:cube}. Multiplicative
differences commute, as follows either from their four-factor expansion
or from the cube product. Freeze the last direction as $z$, commute its
difference onto $f$, and use symmetry to put the remaining evaluation
slot in the required position. This gives \eqref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:slicing}.
\end{proof}
All these are identities of products and finite sums. They remain valid
when $f$ has zeros; no quotient by $f$ is involved.

\begin{lemma}[Gauge invariance]\label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:lem:gauge}
If $S\in\I_d(V)$ and $P$ is a primitive of $S$, then
\begin{equation}
 \En_{T+S}(f e(P))=\En_T(f),\qquad \M(T+S)=\M(T).
 \label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:gauge}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The top multiplicative derivative of $e(P)$ is $(-1)^S$.
The two extra factors of $(-1)^S$ in \eqref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:cube} cancel.
Multiplication by $e(P)$ is a bijection of the unit polydisc of functions.
\end{proof}
In particular an integrable tensor has maximum one, and gauge invariance
with $T=0$ gives the identity \eqref{gsr:fm:65:bsi:eq:phase-removal}.

\subsection{A self-contained Boolean integration proof}
\begin{theorem}[Repeated-variable integration criterion]
\label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:thm:integration}
For a symmetric $d$-linear tensor with $d\ge3$,
\begin{equation}
 T\in\I_d(V)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\Phi_T=0.
 \label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:criterion}
\end{equation}
Every symmetric bilinear tensor is integrable. In a basis with coordinate
bits $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, an integrable tensor has an explicit primitive
\begin{equation}
 P_T(x)=\sum_{\substack{\varnothing\ne A\subseteq[n]\\|A|\le d}}
     \frac{c_A\prod_{i\in A}|x_i|}{2^{d-|A|+1}}\pmod1,
 \label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:primitive}
\end{equation}
where $|x_i|\in\{0,1\}$ and $c_A$ is the value of $T$ on any length-$d$
basis tuple whose set of occurring indices is $A$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Translation by a Boolean direction $a$ squares to the identity. Thus, on
circle-valued functions,
\begin{equation}
 \Delta_a^2=-2\Delta_a,\qquad
 \Delta_a^2\Delta_b=\Delta_a\Delta_b^2.
 \label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:operator-repetition}
\end{equation}
Commutation and \eqref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:operator-repetition} prove the necessary
repeated-variable relation for the top derivative of any primitive.

Conversely suppose $\Phi_T=0$. By symmetry a basis coefficient depends
on its multiplicities. If both $i$ and $j$ occur and $i$ occurs at least
twice, the identity
$T(e_i,e_i,e_j,\zz)=T(e_i,e_j,e_j,\zz)$ transfers one occurrence from
$i$ to $j$. All positive multiplicity lists of total $d$ on a given
support are connected by these transfers. Hence $c_A$ is well defined.

For $a=|A|$, consider the summand
$P_A=2^{-(d-a+1)}\prod_{i\in A}|x_i|$ in
\eqref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:primitive}. We use
\[
 \Delta_{e_i}^t=(-2)^{t-1}\Delta_{e_i}\quad(t\ge1),
 \qquad
 \Delta_h=\prod_{i:h_i=1}(I+\Delta_{e_i})-I.
\]
A term in the expansion of $d+1$ differences has at least $d+1$
coordinate differences. If a coordinate outside $A$ occurs, the term
vanishes. Otherwise, with $r\le a$ distinct coordinates among $t\ge d+1$
differences, its numerator is divisible by $2^{t-r}$ and therefore by
$2^{d-a+1}$. It is zero modulo one. This proves degree at most $d$.

For exactly $d$ coordinate differences, a support properly contained in
$A$ again gives an integer, and a coordinate outside $A$ gives zero.
On a tuple with support exactly $A$, the value is $\pm1/2=1/2$ modulo
one, independent of the base point. Thus \eqref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:primitive} has the
required basis coefficients in its top derivative. A top derivative of
a degree-at-most-$d$ polynomial is independent of the base point. It is
also multiadditive, because the error term in
$\Delta_{a+b}=\Delta_a+\Delta_b+\Delta_a\Delta_b$ is an extra difference.
Agreement on basis tuples proves \eqref{gsr:fm:65:bsi:eq:integrable}.
For $d=2$ no multiplicity transfer is needed and the same construction
applies to every symmetric tensor.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Dimension of the integrable space]\label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:cor:Idim}
The dimension over $\Ftwo$ is
\begin{equation}
 q_d(n):=\dim\I_d(V)=\sum_{j=1}^{\min(d,n)}\binom nj.
 \label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:Idim}
\end{equation}
For a nonzero $u\in V^*$ the pure tensor
$U_m=u^{\otimes m}$ has primitive $P_{u,m}(x)=|u(x)|/2^m$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The independent bits $c_A$ parameterize all integrable tensors uniquely.
For the final assertion apply the one-coordinate construction and pull
back along $u$.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The cubic spectral base case\srctag{65}}]{The cubic spectral base case}\label{gsr:fp:65:sec:d3}\label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:sec:cubic}
\srcnote{65}{Section 3}
The only spectral input needed for the new all-degree induction is the
cubic estimate. This section supplies a complete finite-dimensional proof
of the estimate used in the earlier drafts.

\subsection{Projective translations}
Let $B:V\times V\to\Ftwo$ be bilinear and set
$\Omega_B(a,b)=B(a,b)+B(b,a)$. This is alternating. Its rank is even:
if it is nonzero, choose $a,b$ with $\Omega_B(a,b)=1$, split off the
nondegenerate two-dimensional span of $a,b$, and repeat on its orthogonal
complement. Write $\rk\Omega_B=2s$.

For complex $g,h$ define
\begin{equation}
 Q_B(g,h)=\E_a\left|\E_xg(x+a)\overline{h(x)}(-1)^{B(a,x)}\right|^2,
 \qquad Q_B(g)=Q_B(g,g).
 \label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:Q}
\end{equation}
\begin{lemma}[Finite projective orthogonality]\label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:lem:orthogonality}
For arbitrary complex $g,h$,
\begin{equation}
 Q_B(g,h)\le2^{-s}\norm g_2^2\norm h_2^2,
 \qquad
 Q_B(g)=\E_{x,a,b}\partial_a\partial_b g(x)(-1)^{B(a,b)}.
 \label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:orthogonality}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Use the normalized inner product
$\ip gh=\E_xg(x)\overline{h(x)}$, linear in its first argument. The
operators
\[
 (U_ag)(x)=(-1)^{B(a,x)}g(x+a)
\]
are unitary and satisfy
\[
 U_aU_b=(-1)^{B(b,a)}U_{a+b},\qquad
 U_aU_b=(-1)^{\Omega_B(a,b)}U_bU_a.
\]
The positive operator
\[
 M_gv=\E_a\ip{v}{U_ag}U_ag
\]
has trace $\norm g_2^2$ and commutes with every $U_b$: conjugation
permutes its rank-one summands, and the scalar signs cancel.

Choose a maximal isotropic subspace $H$ containing the radical of
$\Omega_B$. The elementary symplectic decomposition above gives
$H=H^\perp$ and $[V:H]=2^s$. Every nonzero subspace invariant under all
$U_a$ has dimension at least $2^s$. To see this, simultaneously diagonalize
the commuting unitaries $U_h$, $h\in H$, on that invariant subspace and
choose a nonzero joint eigenvector $w$. The vectors $U_aw$ for
representatives of $V/H$ have distinct joint eigenvalues: their ratios
on $H$ are $h\mapsto(-1)^{\Omega_B(h,a)}$, and distinct cosets give
distinct characters since $H^\perp=H$. Joint eigenvectors of commuting
unitaries with distinct joint eigenvalues are orthogonal.

Each positive eigenspace of $M_g$ is invariant under all $U_a$, hence has
dimension at least $2^s$. Positivity and the trace identity imply
$\norm{M_g}_{\rm op}\le2^{-s}\norm g_2^2$. Since
$Q_B(g,h)=\ip{M_gh}h$, this proves the inequality.

For the second identity expand the square in \eqref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:Q}, and replace
one base point by the other plus $b$. The character factor becomes
$(-1)^{B(a,b)}$. The product of the four function values is the conjugate
of $\partial_a\partial_b g(x)$. The resulting cube average is real,
because it equals the real number $Q_B(g)$ after conjugation, so the
stated identity follows.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The exact shear}
\begin{theorem}[Exact cubic obstruction law]\label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:thm:cubic}
For every symmetric trilinear $T$,
\begin{equation}
 \M(T)=2^{-\rk\Omega_T/2}.
 \label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:cubic-law}
\end{equation}
In particular a nonintegrable cubic has maximum at most $1/2$, and it
has maximum $1/2$ exactly when it is canonical modulo integration.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The map $a\mapsto T(a,a,b)$ is additive: the two cross terms in the
expansion at $a+a'$ cancel by symmetry. It follows that $\Omega_T$ is
alternating bilinear. The following identity is valid pointwise for every
complex $f$:
\begin{equation}
 \partial_a\partial_{a+w}f
     =\overline{\partial_a(f\,\tau_wf)},\qquad
 \tau_wf(x)=f(x+w).
 \label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:shear}
\end{equation}
Indeed both sides are the product
$f(x)f(x+w)\overline{f(x+a)f(x+a+w)}$.
In the cubic average \eqref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:cube}, substitute $c=a+w$. The tensor
factor becomes the bilinear form
\[
 B_w(a,b)=T(a,a,b)+T(a,b,w).
\]
Its alternating part is $\Omega_T$, since the term containing $w$ is
symmetric in $a,b$. Apply the remaining difference to
\eqref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:shear} and use the real self-cube identity in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:lem:orthogonality}. This gives
\[
 \En_T(f)=\E_wQ_{B_w}(f\,\tau_wf)
       \le2^{-\rk\Omega_T/2}
                 \E_w\norm{f\,\tau_wf}_2^4
       \le2^{-\rk\Omega_T/2}.
\]

For equality, symplectic coordinates express a rank-$2s$ form as
$\Omega_T=\sum_{j=1}^s(u_j\otimes v_j+v_j\otimes u_j)$, with the
$2s$ coordinate forms independent. Direct calculation gives
$\Omega_{C_3^{u_j,v_j}}=u_j\otimes v_j+v_j\otimes u_j$. Therefore
$S=T-\sum_jC_3^{u_j,v_j}$ is integrable. At the constant function, the
energy of one block $C_3^{u,v}$ is $1/2$: its selected frequency vanishes
on exactly half of the pairs of input vectors. Independent blocks give
independent selected-frequency conditions, so the energy of their sum
at $f=1$ is $2^{-s}$. Gauge invariance supplies an extremizer for $T$.
For $s=0$ the tensor is integrable and the value is one. For $s=1$ this
also proves precisely the final canonical characterization.
\end{proof}
The block calculation concerns an explicit extremizer. It is not an
argument that arbitrary optimizing functions factor as products; the
spectral upper bound already handled every bounded function.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The canonical energy in every degree\srctag{65}}]{The canonical energy in every degree}\label{gsr:fp:65:sec:d4}\label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:sec:canonical}
\srcnote{65}{Section 4}
The all-degree canonical result is an ingredient from~\cite{repo65boe}, not
a new claim of this manuscript. Its short proof is included because the
universal theorem needs its exact value, including stability under adding
coordinates that the tensor does not use.

\subsection{Exact derivative periods}
\begin{lemma}[Even-direction periods]\label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:lem:periods}
For $r\ge1$, $F=\partial_{h_1}\cdots\partial_{h_r}f$ satisfies
\begin{equation}
 F(x+h_i)=\overline{F(x)}\quad(1\le i\le r),\qquad
 F(x+w)=F(x)\quad
 \left(w\in\left\{\sum_i\eps_i h_i:\sum_i\eps_i=0\right\}\right).
 \label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:periods}
\end{equation}
Consequently $\widehat F(\xi)\ne0$ implies
$\xi(h_1)=\cdots=\xi(h_r)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The cube product for $F(x)$ has one labelled factor at each Boolean
vertex, with conjugation parity $r-|\eps|$. Translation by $h_i$
toggles the corresponding vertex coordinate, reversing conjugation
parity. This conjugates the full product. Two such translations preserve
it; their sums generate the even-direction space in
\eqref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:periods}. If a character is nontrivial on one of these
periods, translation changes the sign of its Fourier coefficient without
changing the transformed function. The coefficient is therefore zero.
This proof also covers coincident vertices and zeros of $f$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[A pure tensor on a constrained derivative]
\label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:lem:constrained}
Let $u\ne0$, $m\ge2$, and $u(z)=0$. Then
\begin{equation}
 \En_{U_m}(\partial_zf)\le1-2^{1-m},
 \qquad U_m=u^{\otimes m},\quad\norm f_\infty\le1.
 \label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:constrained}
\end{equation}
The constant function $f=1$ attains equality.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
In the selected-energy test for $U_m$, the selected frequency is $u$
exactly when all $m-1$ sampled directions satisfy $u(h_i)=1$; otherwise
it is zero. On that first set the transformed function is
$\partial_{h_1}\cdots\partial_{h_{m-1}}\partial_zf$. It has period
$h_1+z$, but $u(h_1+z)=1$. The selected coefficient vanishes by
Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:lem:periods}. The excluded set has measure $2^{-(m-1)}$;
all remaining squared coefficients are at most one. For $f=1$ they equal
one exactly when the selected frequency is zero, giving equality.
\end{proof}
Although $U_m$ integrates and has unrestricted maximum one, the fixed
slice $\partial_zf$ cannot attain that maximum when $u(z)=0$.
This derivative constraint is the essential extra loss in the canonical
induction.

\subsection{The sharp canonical formula}
\begin{proposition}[Canonical defect and constant energy]
\label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:prop:canonical-data}
For $d\ge3$ and independent $u,v$,
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_{C_d^{u,v}}(\zz)(a,b)
  =\left(\prod_{j=1}^{d-3}u(z_j)\right)
     \bigl(u(a)v(b)+v(a)u(b)\bigr),
 \qquad
 \En_{C_d^{u,v}}(1)=b_d.
 \label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:canonical-data}
\end{equation}
In particular $C_d^{u,v}$ is nonintegrable.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
In the two repeated-variable evaluations the terms placing $v$ in either
repeated slot cancel, as do the terms placing $v$ in a frozen slot. The
two remaining terms give the displayed defect. It is nonzero.

Set $k=d-1$. The selected frequency for the constant function has the form
$Av+Bu$, with
\[
 A=\prod_{j=1}^ku(h_j),\qquad
 B=\sum_{i=1}^kv(h_i)\prod_{j\ne i}u(h_j).
\]
It is zero when at least two of the $u(h_j)$ vanish. When exactly one
vanishes, $A=0$ and $B$ is its independent unbiased $v$ bit. When none
vanishes, $A=1$. The probability of a nonzero selected frequency is
$2^{-k}+k2^{-k}/2=(d+1)/2^d$, proving the energy formula.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Canonical maximum, with arbitrary inactive coordinates]
\label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:thm:canonical}
For every $d\ge3$, independent $u,v\in V^*$, and $S\in\I_d(V)$,
\begin{equation}
 \M(C_d^{u,v}+S)=b_d.
 \label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:canonical-max}
\end{equation}
There is no assumption that the tested function factors through $(u,v)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Gauge invariance reduces to $S=0$. The cubic case is
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:thm:cubic}. Suppose the result holds in degree $m=d-1$.
Directly from the definition,
\[
 (C_d^{u,v})_z=u(z)C_m^{u,v}+v(z)U_m.
\]
Slice the energy as in \eqref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:slicing}. The four pairs
$(u(z),v(z))$ occur with probability $1/4$ each. On $(0,0)$ the slice
cap is one. On $(0,1)$ use the derivative-constrained cap
$1-2^{1-m}$ from Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:lem:constrained}. On the half where
$u(z)=1$, the slice tensor is $C_m$ plus an integrable tensor, so gauge
invariance and the induction hypothesis give cap $b_m$. Consequently
\begin{align}
 \En_{C_d}(f)
 &\le \tfrac14+\tfrac14(1-2^{2-d})+\tfrac12b_{d-1}\notag\\
 &=1-\frac{d+1}{2^d}=b_d.
 \label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:canonical-recursion}
\end{align}
Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:prop:canonical-data} supplies equality. Every sliced
function, including a phase-twisted one, was allowed to depend on all of
$V$, so no quotient-factorization assumption has entered the argument.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Defect geometry and the integrable-slice identity\srctag{65}}]{Defect geometry and the integrable-slice identity}\label{gsr:fp:65:sec:d5}\label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:sec:radical}
\srcnote{65}{Section 5}
This section isolates the algebra that turns the canonical theorem into
a universal theorem. The distinction between a defect's image and its
first-slot radical is indispensable.

\subsection{Alternation and compatibility}
\begin{lemma}[Defect compatibility]\label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:lem:compatibility}
For $d\ge3$, $\Phi_T$ is a symmetric $(d-3)$-linear map to $\Alt^2(V)$.
For $d\ge4$ and a tuple $\mathbf w\in V^{d-4}$,
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_T(c,\mathbf w)(a,b)+\Phi_T(b,\mathbf w)(a,c)
        +\Phi_T(a,\mathbf w)(b,c)=0.
 \label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:bianchi}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Additivity in a repeated variable follows because its two cross terms
cancel in characteristic two. The value at $a=b$ is zero. The other
multilinearity and symmetry assertions follow immediately from those
of $T$. Expanding \eqref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:bianchi} yields six terms of $T$, which
pair equally by symmetry and cancel.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[A one-form compatibility identity]\label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:lem:wedge}
If $u\ne0$ and $\Omega\in\Alt^2(V)$ satisfy
\[
 u(c)\Omega(a,b)+u(b)\Omega(a,c)+u(a)\Omega(b,c)=0
 \quad\text{for all }a,b,c,
\]
then $\Omega=u\otimes v+v\otimes u$ for some $v\in V^*$. When
$\Omega\ne0$, $u,v$ are independent and $\rk\Omega=2$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose $c_0$ with $u(c_0)=1$ and put $v(x)=\Omega(x,c_0)$.
The identity with $c=c_0$ gives the formula. Its nonzero case has rank
two by an immediate two-coordinate calculation.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Radical codimension one is the canonical case}
\begin{proposition}[Canonical recognition]\label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:prop:recognition}
For symmetric nonintegrable $T$ of degree $d\ge4$, the following are
equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $r(T)=1$;
\item $\Phi_T(\zz)=\Omega\prod_j u(z_j)$ for nonzero $u$ and nonzero
      $\Omega\in\Alt^2(V)$;
\item $T=C_d^{u,v}+S$ for independent $u,v$ and $S\in\I_d(V)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
By symmetry of $\Phi_T$, its first-slot radical is a radical in every
frozen slot. If it has codimension one, the map descends in each frozen
slot to $V/K_T$, which is one-dimensional. Thus it has the form in (ii).
Conversely such a nonzero map has first-slot radical $\ker u$.

Set every frozen variable other than the one displayed in
\eqref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:bianchi} equal to a vector on which $u$ is one. The identity
becomes the hypothesis of Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:lem:wedge}. Hence
$\Omega=u\otimes v+v\otimes u$ with $u,v$ independent.
By \eqref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:canonical-data}, $T-C_d^{u,v}$ has zero defect and is
integrable. This proves (ii)$\Rightarrow$(iii). The reverse implication
follows from that same defect formula and the integration criterion.
\end{proof}
This recognition result is the pure-defect classification of~\cite{repo65boe},
expressed in the radical notation needed for the next lemma. A map with
one-dimensional \emph{image} need not have radical codimension one;
no inference of that kind is used here.

\subsection{The exact set of integrable contractions}
\begin{lemma}[Integrable-slice identity]\label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:lem:slice-kernel}
For $d\ge4$ and $T\in\Sym^d(V)$,
\begin{equation}
 \{z\in V:T_z\in\I_{d-1}(V)\}=K_T,
 \qquad
 \Prob_z[T_z\in\I_{d-1}(V)]=2^{-r(T)}.
 \label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:slice-kernel}
\end{equation}
Here $K_T=V$ and $r(T)=0$ when $T$ is integrable.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For a fixed direction $z$,
\begin{align*}
 \Phi_{T_z}(z_2,\ldots,z_{d-3})(a,b)
 &=T(a,a,b,z_2,\ldots,z_{d-3},z)\\
 &\quad+T(a,b,b,z_2,\ldots,z_{d-3},z)\\
 &=\Phi_T(z,z_2,\ldots,z_{d-3})(a,b).
\end{align*}
The equivalence in \eqref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:slice-kernel} is exactly
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:thm:integration} in degree $d-1$. This includes $d=4$,
when the slice is cubic and its defect has no frozen variables.
The map $z\mapsto\Phi_T(z,\cdot)$ is linear, so $K_T$ is a subspace of
size $2^{n-r(T)}$. Dividing by $|V|$ proves the probability formula.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[One-step transfer of a universal bound]
\label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:prop:transfer}
Let $d\ge4$. Suppose every nonintegrable symmetric $(d-1)$-linear tensor
has maximum at most $B$. Then every symmetric $d$-linear tensor satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \En_T(f)\le2^{-r(T)}+(1-2^{-r(T)})B,
 \qquad \norm f_\infty\le1.
 \label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:transfer}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Use exact slicing \eqref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:slicing}. When $z\in K_T$, the slice
energy is at most one. When $z\notin K_T$, the slice tensor is
nonintegrable by Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:lem:slice-kernel}, and
$\norm{\partial_zf}_\infty\le1$, so its energy is at most $B$.
Average and use the exact slice proportions.
\end{proof}
No replacement of the common function by independent functions is made in
the identity. The inequality subsequently relaxes each nonintegrable
slice to an arbitrary bounded function, which is legitimate for an upper
bound. The canonical case, where this relaxation would lose too much,
was already treated separately in Section~\ref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:sec:canonical}.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Closing the induction in every degree\srctag{65}}]{Closing the induction in every degree}\label{gsr:fp:65:sec:d6}\label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:sec:closure}
\srcnote{65}{Section 6}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorems~\ref{gsr:fm:65:bsi:thm:main} and~\ref{gsr:fm:65:bsi:thm:gap}]
The cubic theorem supplies the base $b_3=1/2$ and the cubic endpoint
classification. Fix $d\ge4$ and assume that every nonintegrable symmetric
tensor of degree $d-1$ has maximum at most $b_{d-1}$.

Let $T$ be a nonintegrable symmetric $d$-linear tensor. Its defect is
nonzero, so $r(T)\ge1$. If $r(T)=1$, canonical recognition and
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:thm:canonical} give $\M(T)=b_d$.

If $r=r(T)\ge2$, Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:prop:transfer} with $B=b_{d-1}$
gives
\begin{align}
 \M(T)
 &\le2^{-r}+(1-2^{-r})\left(1-\frac d{2^{d-1}}\right)\notag\\
 &=1-(1-2^{-r})\frac d{2^{d-1}}\notag\\
 &\le1-\frac{3d}{2^{d+1}}
 =b_d-\frac{d-2}{2^{d+1}}<b_d.
 \label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:closing-induction}
\end{align}
This proves the universal upper bound and the stated radical-sensitive
cap. The canonical example gives the matching lower bound. Induction
therefore proves the universal formula for all degrees.

The strict final inequality in \eqref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:closing-induction} also
proves the endpoint classification: a noncanonical tensor cannot attain
$b_d$. Conversely every canonical tensor modulo integration does attain
$b_d$. The cubic case was already classified by its alternating rank.
Finally, energy strictly above $b_d$ excludes nonintegrability; the
primitive and exact phase-removal identity follow from the integration
criterion and gauge invariance. At $T=C_d$, $f=1$ the energy is exactly
$b_d$ and $T$ does not integrate, so the threshold is strict and sharp.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Why the prior support bottleneck disappears}
A direct estimate based on nonzero values of the repeated defect can
forget how many \emph{whole contractions} remain nonintegrable.
The preceding manuscript propagated a fixed trilinear support coefficient
through higher frozen degree. That yielded the loss $7/2^d$ beyond
degree six. The transfer in \eqref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:transfer} instead propagates the
\emph{sharp degree-dependent extremal loss} $d/2^{d-1}$.
The distinction is decisive: the factor $3/4$ beats the target loss,
since
\[
 \frac34\frac d{2^{d-1}}-\frac{d+1}{2^d}
       =\frac{d-2}{2^{d+1}}>0.
\]
There is consequently no need to solve the separate problem of optimal
non-pure multilinear support in each degree. That problem remains
interesting but is not a missing hypothesis of the theorem.

\subsection{Septic and endpoint consequences explicitly}
For $d=7$ the prior interval $[120/128,121/128]$ collapses to
\[
 M^{\rm sym}_{7,n}=120/128=15/16\qquad(n\ge2).
\]
A noncanonical septic obeys the stronger cap $235/256$, whereas the
extremal value is $240/256$. For quintics the old noncanonical cap
$13/16$ is replaced by $49/64<52/64$; for sextics the old cap $57/64$
is replaced by $55/64$. Thus the previously undecided noncanonical
endpoint branches are excluded without an equality analysis of the
old support estimates.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Rigidity, repair geometry, and exact counting\srctag{65}}]{Rigidity, repair geometry, and exact counting}\label{gsr:fp:65:sec:d7}\label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:sec:rigidity}
\srcnote{65}{Section 7}

\subsection{A finite rigidity window}
Set
\begin{equation}
 \gamma_3=\tfrac14,\qquad
 \gamma_d=\frac{d-2}{2^{d+1}}\quad(d\ge4),\qquad
 \eta_d=b_d-\gamma_d.
 \label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:window}
\end{equation}
\begin{corollary}[Exact tensor rigidity near the endpoint]
\label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:cor:rigidity}
If $T$ is symmetric and $\En_T(f)>\eta_d$, then either $T$ is integrable
or $T$ is canonical modulo integration. In particular, if $T$ is known
to be nonintegrable and
\[
 \En_T(f)\ge b_d-\eps,\qquad0\le\eps<\gamma_d,
\]
then $T=C_d^{u,v}+S$ exactly, with $S$ integrable.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The noncanonical alternatives of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:65:bsi:thm:gap} have energy
at most $\eta_d$. Exclude them.
\end{proof}
This is exact rigidity of a discrete tensor class, not a claim that the
function $f$ is close to one particular phase. The strict window is a
proved sufficient window; its optimal width is not established.

\subsection{All integrable restrictions of an endpoint tensor}
\begin{theorem}[Complete repair geometry]\label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:thm:repair}
Let $d\ge3$ and $T=C_d^{u,v}+S$ with $u,v$ independent and $S$ integrable.
For any subspace $H\le V$,
\begin{equation}
 T|_{H^d}\text{ is integrable}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \dim\spanof\{u|_H,v|_H\}\le1.
 \label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:repair}
\end{equation}
Equivalently, $H$ is contained in at least one of
\begin{equation}
 \ker u,\qquad\ker v,\qquad\ker(u+v).
 \label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:three-hyperplanes}
\end{equation}
These three distinct hyperplanes are exactly the maximal integrable
restriction subspaces. The minimum repair codimension is one.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
An integrable tensor remains integrable on restriction, so remove $S$.
The restricted defect is
\[
 \left(\prod_j u|_H(z_j)\right)
     \bigl(u|_H(a)v|_H(b)+v|_H(a)u|_H(b)\bigr).
\]
It vanishes when the two restricted forms are dependent. If they are
independent, their alternating product is nonzero; for $d>3$ choose
each frozen direction with $u|_H(z_j)=1$. The defect is then nonzero.
For $d=3$ the product is empty and the same conclusion follows directly.
The integration criterion proves \eqref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:repair}.

Two forms over $\Ftwo$ are dependent precisely when $u|_H=0$, $v|_H=0$,
or $(u+v)|_H=0$. This proves the containment characterization.
The three ambient kernels are distinct hyperplanes, all integrable on
restriction. Every integrable subspace is contained in one of them, so
these and only these are maximal. Codimension zero is impossible because
$T$ is nonintegrable; codimension one is achieved.
\end{proof}
For $d\ge4$, $\ker u$ is distinguished by the frozen radical of the
defect. That does \emph{not} make it the unique optimal repair hyperplane:
there are always the three in \eqref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:three-hyperplanes}.

\subsection{Uniqueness of the recovered parameters}
\begin{proposition}[Canonical obstruction parameters]\label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:prop:parameters}
For $d\ge4$, the integrable equivalence class of $C_d^{u,v}$ uniquely
determines $u$ and the coset $v+\spanof\{u\}$. Conversely these data
uniquely determine its integrable equivalence class.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The defect determines $K_T=\ker u$. Over $\Ftwo$ a hyperplane determines its
nonzero defining form uniquely. Choose $z_0$ with $u(z_0)=1$. Evaluation
of all frozen slots at $z_0$ recovers $\Omega=u\otimes v+v\otimes u$.
If $u\otimes w+w\otimes u=0$, substituting a vector with $u=1$ shows
$w\in\spanof\{u\}$. Thus $\Omega$ determines precisely the claimed
coset of $v$.

Conversely, replacing $v$ by $v+u$ changes $C_d^{u,v}$ by
$(d\bmod2)U_d$, which is integrable. Equal defects mean an integrable
difference by Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:thm:integration}. This proves both claims.
\end{proof}
For cubics the distinguished $u$ disappears: the class is determined by
$u\wedge v$, hence by the two-dimensional subspace spanned by $u,v$.
For higher degrees it is a two-dimensional subspace together with a
specified nonzero one-dimensional subspace inside it.

\begin{theorem}[Exact number of extremal tensor classes]
\label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:thm:count}
For $n\ge2$, the number of nonintegrable classes modulo $\I_d(V)$ with
maximum $b_d$ is
\begin{equation}
 e_d(n)=
 \begin{cases}
 \displaystyle\frac{(2^n-1)(2^n-2)}6,&d=3,\\[5pt]
 (2^n-1)(2^{n-1}-1),&d\ge4.
 \end{cases}
 \label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:class-count}
\end{equation}
The number of actual extremal tensors is $e_d(n)2^{q_d(n)}$, where
$q_d(n)$ is given by \eqref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:Idim}.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $d\ge4$ there are $2^n-1$ choices for $u$. The quotient
$V^*/\spanof\{u\}$ has $2^{n-1}-1$ nonzero cosets available for $v$.
Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:prop:parameters} makes these parameters injective
and exhaustive.

For $d=3$, a rank-two alternating form is $u\wedge v$ for an independent
ordered pair. Its associated two-dimensional subspace has six ordered
bases, and every invertible two-by-two matrix over $\Ftwo$ has determinant
one, so all six bases give the same nonzero alternating form. Distinct
such subspaces give distinct forms. This gives $(2^n-1)(2^n-2)/6$.
Each integrable class contains exactly $2^{q_d(n)}$ tensors.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Against source~69} (checked at the write): $(2^n-1)(2^{n-1}-1)$ is the number of flags $\ell\subset\Pi$ of a line in a plane in $V^*$, source~69's count (its Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:69:bad:thm:flags}); at $d=3$, $(2^n-1)(2^n-2)/6$ is the number of planes, the line not being determined by the class.
\end{writenote}
In dimension two there is one cubic extremal class and three extremal
classes in each degree at least four. Since $q_d(2)=3$, this gives eight
cubic extremal tensors and twenty-four in every higher degree. In
dimension three there are seven cubic classes and twenty-one higher-degree
classes; quartics therefore have $21\cdot128=2688$ extremal tensors.
These count \emph{tensors admitting an extremizer}, not tensors whose
extremizer must be the constant function.

\subsection{A necessary amplitude condition}
\begin{proposition}[Dimension-independent amplitude stability]
\label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:prop:amplitude}
Let $d\ge4$ and $T$ be a canonical tensor modulo integration. If
$\En_T(f)\ge b_d-\eps$ and $\norm f_\infty\le1$, then
\begin{equation}
 \E_x|f(x)|^2\ge1-4\eps.
 \label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:amplitude}
\end{equation}
In particular every endpoint function for a nonintegrable tensor in
these degrees has modulus one at every point.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Remove the integrable correction by a phase twist, preserving $|f|$.
In the canonical induction the three slice caps are attained in sum
exactly at $b_d$, and each slice lies below its cap. Therefore the
contribution of the $(u(z),v(z))=(0,0)$ quarter gives
\[
 b_d-\En_{C_d}(f)
 \ge\tfrac14\E_{z:u(z)=v(z)=0}
      \bigl(1-\En_0(\partial_zf)\bigr).
\]
For any one-bounded $g$ and $m\ge2$, the cube product, the triangle
inequality, and arithmetic--geometric mean give
\[
 \En_0(g)\le\E_x|g(x)|^{2^m}\le\E_x|g(x)|^2.
\]
Indeed apply arithmetic--geometric mean to the $2^m$ nonnegative vertex
factors raised to the $2^m$th power, then average; each vertex is uniform.
For $g=\partial_zf$ the last mean is at most $\E_x|f(x)|^2$.
Substitution proves \eqref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:amplitude}. At $\eps=0$, an average of
numbers in $[0,1]$ is one, so every modulus is one.
\end{proof}
The coefficient four is not claimed optimal. This statement is about
amplitudes only; phases can still have nontrivial freedom.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Robust certification and retained contraction profiles\srctag{65}}]{Robust certification and retained contraction profiles}\label{gsr:fp:65:sec:d8}
\srcnote{65}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:sec:robust}

\subsection{Corrupted selectors and measurement error}
For a selector $\rho:V^{d-1}\to V^*$, define $\En_\rho(f)$ by replacing
$T(\hh,\cdot)$ in \eqref{gsr:fm:65:bsi:eq:energy} by $\rho(\hh)$.

\begin{theorem}[Robust all-degree phase certification]
\label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:thm:robust}
Suppose $\rho(\hh)=T(\hh,\cdot)$ outside a fraction $\delta$ of tuples,
where $T$ is symmetric and $d\ge3$. Then
\begin{equation}
 |\En_\rho(f)-\En_T(f)|\le\delta.
 \label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:selector-error}
\end{equation}
If $L$ is a certified lower bound on $\En_\rho(f)$, then
\begin{align}
 L-\delta>b_d
 &\quad\Longrightarrow\quad T\in\I_d(V),\quad
       \norm{f e(-P_T)}_{U^d}^{2^d}\ge L-\delta;
       \label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:robust-integrate}\\
 L-\delta>\eta_d
 &\quad\Longrightarrow\quad T\text{ is integrable or canonical modulo integration}.
       \label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:robust-rigid}
\end{align}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Each squared coefficient lies in $[0,1]$. The two summands agree on the
uncorrupted tuples, proving \eqref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:selector-error}. Apply the
sharp threshold and the rigidity window to $\En_T(f)\ge L-\delta$.
\end{proof}
The theorem assumes an actual symmetric tensor model. It does not
construct or verify that model from noisy data. Any numerical error in
an energy estimate must already have been subtracted when forming $L$.

\begin{lemma}[Perturbing the function]\label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:lem:function-error}
For one-bounded $f,g$ and any multilinear $T$,
\begin{equation}
 |\En_T(f)-\En_T(g)|\le2^d\norm{f-g}_1.
 \label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:function-error}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
In \eqref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:cube}, telescope the difference of the two products over
its $2^d$ labelled vertices. Every other factor has modulus at most one;
the factor being replaced contributes $|f-g|$ at that vertex. Each
vertex is uniform after averaging over $x$, even when some vertices
coincide. Summing gives the bound.
\end{proof}
For a test performed on $g$ rather than $f$, subtract the additional
$2^d\norm{f-g}_1$ before applying the certification thresholds. No
optimality of this perturbation constant is asserted.

\subsection{A stronger computable profile}
Define a tensor cap $A_m(S)$ for symmetric tensors of degree $m\ge3$ by
\begin{equation}
 A_m(S)=
 \begin{cases}
 1,&S\in\I_m(V),\\
 2^{-\rk\Omega_S/2},&m=3,\\
 b_m,&m\ge4,\ r(S)=1,\\
 1-(1-2^{-r(S)})m/2^{m-1},&m\ge4,\ r(S)\ge2.
 \end{cases}
 \label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:computable-cap}
\end{equation}
The cases in the displayed order remove any overlap at an integrable
cubic. The main theorems prove $\M(S)\le A_m(S)$.

\begin{proposition}[Retained contraction profile]\label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:prop:profile}
For $d\ge4$,
\begin{equation}
 \En_T(f)\le\E_z A_{d-1}(T_z).
 \label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:profile}
\end{equation}
For nonintegrable $T$ of degree $d\ge5$, let
\[
 \mu_T=\Prob_z[T_z\text{ is nonintegrable and noncanonical}].
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \M(T)\le1-(1-2^{-r(T)})\frac d{2^{d-1}}
                      -\mu_T\gamma_{d-1}.
 \label{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:profile-gap}
\end{equation}
For $d=4$ the same conclusion holds with
$\mu_T=\Prob_z[\rk\Omega_{T_z}\ge4]$ and $\gamma_3=1/4$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Bound each term in the exact slicing identity by its cap. For the second
claim, the $2^{-r(T)}$ integrable fraction has cap one, the remaining
fraction has cap $b_{d-1}$, and on the indicated subfraction the strict
noncanonical cap subtracts at least $\gamma_{d-1}$. This is exactly
\eqref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:profile-gap}.
\end{proof}
This profile can be iterated further or combined with the unsliced cap
by taking their minimum. It is a valid finite certificate hierarchy,
not a claim that independent optimal slice functions are mutually
compatible or that the hierarchy computes the exact maximum.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Finite calculus and the integrable tensor space\srctag{69}}]{Finite calculus and the integrable tensor space}\label{gsr:fp:69:sec:d2}
\srcnote{69}{Section 2}
\label{gsr:fp:69:bad:sec:calculus}

\subsection{Cube expansion, slicing, and phase twisting}
\begin{lemma}[Exact cube and slicing identities]
\label{gsr:fp:69:bad:lem:cube}
For a multilinear tensor and a complex function,
\begin{equation}
 \En_T(f)=\E_{x,h_1,\ldots,h_d}
     \partial_{h_1}\cdots\partial_{h_d}f(x)(-1)^{T(h_1,\ldots,h_d)}.
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:cube}
\end{equation}
For symmetric $T$ and $d\ge3$,
\begin{equation}
 \En_T(f)=\E_z\En_{T_z}(\partial_z f).
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:slicing}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Fix $\hh=(h_1,\ldots,h_{d-1})$, and write
$g=\partial_{h_1}\cdots\partial_{h_{d-1}}f$ and
$\xi(x)=T(\hh,x)$.  Expand the squared Fourier coefficient and set one base
point equal to the other plus $y$:
\[
 \left|\E_x g(x)(-1)^{\xi(x)}\right|^2
   =\E_{x,y}g(x+y)\overline{g(x)}(-1)^{\xi(y)}.
\]
Averaging over $\hh$ proves \eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:cube}.  Multiplicative derivatives
commute, as follows by expanding their factors.  Freeze a cube direction as
$z$, move its derivative next to $f$, and use symmetry to put $z$ in the
contracted slot of $T$.  Applying the cube identity in degree $d-1$ gives
\eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:slicing}.
\end{proof}
