No cancellation divides by $f$, so these identities hold at zero amplitudes.
We use the normalization
\begin{equation}
 \norm f_{U^d}^{2^d}=\En_0(f).
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:Unorm}
\end{equation}
Only this cube expression is needed below.

\begin{lemma}[Gauge invariance]
\label{gsr:fp:69:bad:lem:gauge}
If $S\in\In_d(V)$ has primitive $P$, then
\begin{equation}
 \En_{T+S}(f e(P))=\En_T(f),\qquad \Ma(T+S)=\Ma(T).
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:gauge}
\end{equation}
In particular, if $T$ is integrable,
\begin{equation}
 \En_T(f)=\norm{f e(-P_T)}_{U^d}^{2^d}.
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:removal}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The $d$-fold multiplicative derivative of $e(P)$ equals $(-1)^S$.
In \eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:cube} its sign cancels the added $S$ in the tensor.
Multiplication by a unit-modulus phase permutes the unit polydisc of functions.
This proves both identities in \eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:gauge}, and the case with residual
tensor zero gives \eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:removal}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The integration criterion, with a coordinate proof}
\begin{theorem}[Boolean nonclassical integration]
\label{gsr:fp:69:bad:thm:integration}
For $d\ge3$, a symmetric tensor $T$ is integrable if and only if $\Phi_T=0$.
Every symmetric bilinear tensor is integrable.  In a chosen basis, the
integrable tensors are exactly those whose basis coefficients depend only
on the nonempty set of indices occurring, not on their positive multiplicities.
The coefficient and primitive descriptions also apply at $d=2$.
Consequently
\begin{equation}
 \dim_{\Ftwo}\In_d(\Ftwo^n)=\sum_{j=1}^{\min(n,d)}\binom nj.
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:Idim}
\end{equation}
If $c_A$ is the coefficient indexed by the support $A$, a primitive is
\begin{equation}
 P_T(x)=\sum_{\substack{\varnothing\ne A\subseteq[n]\\|A|\le d}}
 \frac{c_A\prod_{i\in A}|x_i|}{2^{d-|A|+1}}\pmod1,
 \qquad |x_i|\in\{0,1\}.
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:primitive-explicit}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
This is the characteristic-two instance of the established nonclassical
integration theorem \cite{tidor}.  The following proof also records the
explicit basis used later in the sharp model construction.
\begin{proof}
Since translation by $a$ has order two, additive difference operators on
circle-valued functions satisfy
\begin{equation}
 \Delta_a^2=-2\Delta_a,\qquad
 \Delta_a^2\Delta_b=\Delta_a\Delta_b^2.
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:repetition}
\end{equation}
They commute.  Every top derivative is therefore symmetric and obeys the
repetition relation defining $\Phi_T=0$.

Conversely, in a symmetric tensor with zero defect, the relation
\[
 T(e_i,e_i,e_j,\zz)=T(e_i,e_j,e_j,\zz)
\]
moves one occurrence from $i$ to $j$ whenever both occur and $i$ has at least
two occurrences.  Any two positive multiplicity lists of a fixed total on a
fixed support can be joined by such transfers.  The coefficient is consequently
a well-defined $c_A$.  Conversely, support-dependent coefficients satisfy all
these relations.  For bilinear tensors the support already determines the
multiplicity list, so no condition is needed.

It remains to check the primitive.  For $a=|A|$, put
$P_A(x)=2^{-(d-a+1)}\prod_{i\in A}|x_i|$.  Coordinate differences satisfy
$\Delta_{e_i}^{t}=(-2)^{t-1}\Delta_{e_i}$ for $t\ge1$, and
\begin{equation}
 \Delta_h=\prod_{i:h_i=1}(I+\Delta_{e_i})-I.
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:coordinate-expansion}
\end{equation}
A term in an expansion of $d+1$ differences contains at least $d+1$
coordinate differences.  A coordinate outside $A$ kills the term.  If the
term uses $r\le a$ distinct coordinates a total of $t\ge d+1$ times, its
numerator has a factor $2^{t-r}$ and hence is divisible by the denominator
$2^{d-a+1}$.  Thus it vanishes modulo one.

For exactly $d$ coordinate differences, an index outside $A$ again gives zero.
If the support is a proper subset of $A$, the same divisibility argument
gives an integer.  If the support is exactly $A$, the value is
$\pm1/2=1/2\pmod1$, independent of $x$.
The top difference of a degree-at-most-$d$ function is multilinear and
base-point independent: the formula
$\Delta_{a+b}=\Delta_a+\Delta_b+\Delta_a\Delta_b$ makes the additivity error
a $(d+1)$-fold difference.  Hence agreement on basis tuples proves that
\eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:primitive-explicit} has top derivative $T/2$.
Finally, there is one freely chosen bit for each nonempty support of size
at most $d$, proving \eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:Idim}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Contraction and diagonal lowering preserve integrability]
\label{gsr:fp:69:bad:lem:lowering}
If $S\in\In_{m+1}(V)$ and $m\ge2$, then both
\begin{equation}
 S_a(h_1,\ldots,h_m)=S(a,h_1,\ldots,h_m),\qquad
 D(S)(h_1,\ldots,h_m)=S(h_1,h_1,h_2,\ldots,h_m)
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:lowering}
\end{equation}
belong to $\In_m(V)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $P$ is a primitive of $S$, then $\Delta_aP$ is a degree-at-most-$m$
primitive of $S_a$; equivalently, the repetition relation persists on
freezing one slot.

For $D(S)$, the two cross terms in the repeated slot cancel, so the map
is multilinear.  The repetition relation for $S$ moves the doubled variable
between slots, proving symmetry of $D(S)$.  On a basis tuple, duplicating
one index does not change its support.  Therefore the coefficients of
$D(S)$ depend only on support, and Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:69:bad:thm:integration} gives
integrability.  In fact $D$ retains exactly the support coefficients of
sizes at most $m$ and discards those of size $m+1$.
\end{proof}
The diagonal-lowering observation will control the \emph{dimension} of a space
of defects, rather than merely provide another integration test.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The defect and the cubic spectral base case\srctag{69}}]{The defect and the cubic spectral base case}\label{gsr:fp:69:sec:d3}
\srcnote{69}{Section 3}
\label{gsr:fp:69:bad:sec:cubic}

\subsection{Alternation and compatibility}
\begin{lemma}[Structure of the repeated defect]
\label{gsr:fp:69:bad:lem:bianchi}
For symmetric $T$, the map
$\Phi_T:V^{d-3}\to\Alt^2(V)$ is symmetric multilinear.  For $d\ge4$ it satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_T(c,\mathbf w)(a,b)+\Phi_T(b,\mathbf w)(a,c)
                         +\Phi_T(a,\mathbf w)(b,c)=0,
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:bianchi}
\end{equation}
where $\mathbf w\in V^{d-4}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
In $T(a+a',a+a',b,\zz)$ the two cross terms agree by symmetry and cancel in
$\Ftwo$.  The same holds for the repeated $b$ term.  The defect is bilinear in
$a,b$, is symmetric in that pair, and vanishes when $a=b$; hence it is
alternating.  Linearity and symmetry in the frozen variables are inherited
from $T$.  Expanding \eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:bianchi} produces six tensor values.
Symmetry pairs them into three equal pairs, so the sum is zero.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A projective orthogonality estimate}
The next argument is the finite-dimensional spectral method used in the
preceding project manuscripts \cite{repo69bpi,repo69boe}.  We include it to make the cubic
base case independent of an unreviewed reference.

For a bilinear $B:V^2\to\Ftwo$, put
$\Omega_B(a,b)=B(a,b)+B(b,a)$ and define
\begin{equation}
 Q_B(g,h)=\E_a\left|\E_xg(x+a)\overline{h(x)}(-1)^{B(a,x)}\right|^2,
 \qquad Q_B(g)=Q_B(g,g).
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:QB}
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}[Projective orthogonality]
\label{gsr:fp:69:bad:lem:projective}
If the alternating form $\Omega_B$ has rank $2r$, then
\begin{equation}
 Q_B(g,h)\le2^{-r}\norm g_2^2\norm h_2^2.
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:orthogonal}
\end{equation}
Also
\begin{equation}
 Q_B(g)=\E_{x,a,b}\partial_a\partial_b g(x)(-1)^{B(a,b)}.
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:Qcube}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Use the normalized Hilbert space with inner product
$\ip gh=\E_xg(x)\overline{h(x)}$, linear in its first argument.  Define
\[
 (U_ag)(x)=(-1)^{B(a,x)}g(x+a).
\]
These operators are unitary and satisfy
\[
 U_aU_b=(-1)^{B(b,a)}U_{a+b},\qquad
 U_aU_b=(-1)^{\Omega_B(a,b)}U_bU_a.
\]
The positive operator
\[
 M_gv=\E_a\ip{v}{U_ag}U_ag
\]
has trace $\norm g_2^2$.  It commutes with every $U_b$, since conjugation by
$U_b$ permutes its rank-one summands and the scalar signs cancel.

An alternating form splits into $r$ nondegenerate two-dimensional pairs and
its radical.  This follows by choosing $a,b$ with pairing one, taking the
orthogonal complement of their span, and inducting.  In particular the rank
is even.  Choose a subspace $H$ containing the radical and one isotropic
line from each pair.  Then $H=H^\perp$ and $[V:H]=2^r$.
Every nonzero common invariant subspace for the $U_a$ has dimension at least
$2^r$: the commuting unitaries $U_h$, $h\in H$, have a common eigenvector,
and its translates by representatives of $V/H$ have distinct joint
eigenvalues.  Their eigenvalue ratios on $h$ are
$(-1)^{\Omega_B(h,a)}$.  Distinct cosets give distinct ratios, hence
orthogonal vectors.

Every positive eigenspace of $M_g$ is such an invariant subspace.
Therefore each positive eigenvalue has multiplicity at least $2^r$, and
$\norm{M_g}_{\mathrm{op}}\le2^{-r}\tr M_g$.
Since $Q_B(g,h)=\ip{M_gh}{h}$, this proves \eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:orthogonal}.
Expanding the square in \eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:QB} and replacing its second base point
by $x+b$ gives the complex conjugate of the right side of
\eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:Qcube}.  It is real because it equals $Q_B(g)$, so the
conjugation can be removed.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact cubic obstruction law]
\label{gsr:fp:69:bad:thm:cubic}
For $T\in\SM_3(V)$ let
$\Omega_T(a,b)=T(a,a,b)+T(a,b,b)$ have rank $2r$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 \Ma(T)=2^{-r}.
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:cubic-law}
\end{equation}
In particular, a nonintegrable symmetric cubic has energy at most $1/2$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Write $\tau_wf(x)=f(x+w)$.  The product identity
\begin{equation}
 \partial_a\partial_{a+w}f
       =\overline{\partial_a(f\tau_wf)}
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:shear}
\end{equation}
is valid even when $f$ vanishes.  In the cubic expression
\eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:cube}, put the third direction equal to $a+w$.  The sign is
then given by
\[
 B_w(a,b)=T(a,a,b)+T(a,b,w).
\]
This is bilinear, and its alternating part is $\Omega_T$ because the term
containing $w$ is symmetric in $a,b$.  Identity \eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:shear} and
Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:69:bad:lem:projective} give
\[
 \En_T(f)=\E_w Q_{B_w}(f\tau_wf)
       \le2^{-r}\E_w\norm{f\tau_wf}_2^4\le2^{-r}.
\]

For equality, split $\Omega_T$ into independent symplectic pairs
$\sum_{i=1}^r(u_i\otimes v_i+v_i\otimes u_i)$.
The tensor $\sum_i C_3^{u_i,v_i}$ has exactly this defect, as one checks by
substitution.  Their difference is integrable by
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:69:bad:thm:integration}.  For the constant function, the cube
average for the sum of these tensors factors over the independent pairs.
On one pair its value is $1/2$: the selected frequency is nonzero on half
of the pairs of directions.  Thus the product has energy $2^{-r}$.
Twisting by a primitive of the integrable difference gives equality for
$T$.  This use of a product gives a lower bound by an explicit function;
it makes no assertion that arbitrary optimizing functions factor.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Rank-one defects and canonical energies\srctag{69}}]{Rank-one defects and canonical energies}\label{gsr:fp:69:sec:d4}
\srcnote{69}{Section 4}
\label{gsr:fp:69:bad:sec:canonical}

\subsection{The contraction radical and its rank-one case}
For $d\ge4$, Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:69:bad:thm:integration} gives
\begin{equation}
 R(T)=\{z:\Phi_T(z,z_2,\ldots,z_{d-3})=0
                     \text{ for every }z_2,\ldots,z_{d-3}\}.
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:radical-frozen}
\end{equation}
It is a linear subspace.  By symmetry it is a radical in every frozen slot.
It equals $V$ precisely when $T$ is integrable.  Hence a nonintegrable tensor
has $\rho(T)\ge1$.

\begin{lemma}[A one-form compatibility identity]
\label{gsr:fp:69:bad:lem:wedge}
If $u\ne0$ and $\Omega\in\Alt^2(V)$ satisfy
\[
 u(c)\Omega(a,b)+u(b)\Omega(a,c)+u(a)\Omega(b,c)=0
 \quad\text{for every }a,b,c,
\]
then $\Omega=u\otimes v+v\otimes u$ for some $v\in V^*$.
If $\Omega\ne0$, $u,v$ are independent and $\Omega$ has rank two.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose $c_0$ with $u(c_0)=1$ and put $v(x)=\Omega(x,c_0)$.
Substitution of $c_0$ gives the claimed identity.  The nonzero form has a
two-dimensional nondegenerate quotient, namely that detected by $u,v$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Rank-one classification; preceding project result]
\label{gsr:fp:69:bad:prop:rank-one}
For $T\in\SM_d(V)\setminus\In_d(V)$, $d\ge4$, the following are equivalent:
$\rho(T)=1$; the defect has the form
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_T(\zz)=\Omega\prod_i u(z_i),\qquad \Omega\ne0,\ u\ne0;
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:pure}
\end{equation}
and $T=C_d^{u,v}+S$ for independent $u,v$ and integrable $S$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
If the frozen radical has codimension one, multilinearity makes the defect
descend in all frozen slots to the one-dimensional quotient.  Hence it has
form \eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:pure}.  Conversely that form has frozen radical $\ker u$.
In \eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:bianchi}, set the other frozen variables to vectors on which
$u$ equals one.  Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:69:bad:lem:wedge} gives
$\Omega=u\otimes v+v\otimes u$.
A direct expansion of \eqref{gsr:fm:69:bad:eq:canonical} gives
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_{C_d^{u,v}}(\zz)(a,b)
 =\left(\prod_i u(z_i)\right)
             \bigl(u(a)v(b)+v(a)u(b)\bigr).
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:canonical-defect}
\end{equation}
Indeed the two terms placing $v$ in repeated $a$ slots cancel, as do the
two copies of every term placing $v$ in a frozen slot.  The surviving terms
are exactly the displayed ones.  Thus $T-C_d^{u,v}$ has zero defect and is
integrable.  Formula \eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:canonical-defect} also proves the converse.
\end{proof}
This proposition was proved in \cite{repo69boe}.  The improvement below comes from
how the higher-rank alternative is handled.

\subsection{Periods of derivatives}
\begin{lemma}[Exact even-direction periods]
\label{gsr:fp:69:bad:lem:periods}
Let $F=\partial_{h_1}\cdots\partial_{h_t}f$, $t\ge1$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 F(x+h_i)=\overline{F(x)},\qquad
 F(x+w)=F(x)\quad\text{if }w\in
 \Span\{h_1+h_i:2\le i\le t\}.
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:periods}
\end{equation}
Consequently a Fourier coefficient of $F$ at $\xi\in V^*$ can be nonzero
only if $\xi(h_1)=\cdots=\xi(h_t)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The cube product defining $F$ has a factor at each labelled vertex, with
conjugation parity given by the vertex parity and $t$.  Translation by
$h_i$ toggles vertex coordinate $i$ and reverses every conjugation parity.
This conjugates the product.  Two such translations leave it unchanged,
which proves the period assertion, including when vertices coincide or
amplitudes vanish.  Translating a Fourier sum by a period $w$ with
$\xi(w)=1$ changes its sign without changing $F$, so that coefficient is zero.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[A pure tensor on a constrained derivative]
\label{gsr:fp:69:bad:lem:fixed-derivative}
Let $U_m(h_1,\ldots,h_m)=\prod_i u(h_i)$ with $u\ne0$ and $m\ge2$.
If $z\in\ker u$ and $f$ is one-bounded, then
\begin{equation}
 \En_{U_m}(\partial_z f)\le1-2^{1-m}.
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:fixed-derivative}
\end{equation}
The constant function attains this value.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The selected frequency for $U_m$ is $u$ exactly when all $m-1$ directions
$h_i$ have $u(h_i)=1$; otherwise it is zero.  On the first event the
function being transformed is
$\partial_{h_1}\cdots\partial_{h_{m-1}}\partial_zf$.
It is invariant under $h_1+z$, but $u(h_1+z)=1$.  Its selected coefficient
therefore vanishes by Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:69:bad:lem:periods}.  The event has probability
$2^{1-m}$, and every remaining squared coefficient is at most one.  For
$f=1$, zero-frequency coefficients are one and nonzero-frequency coefficients
are zero, proving equality.
\end{proof}
Without the constraint that the tested function is $\partial_zf$, the
maximum for $U_m$ is one: it has primitive $|u(x)|/2^m$.  This distinction is
essential to the canonical extremum and was the key advance of \cite{repo69boe}.

\subsection{The dimension-free canonical maximum}
\begin{theorem}[Canonical maximum; preceding project result]
\label{gsr:fp:69:bad:thm:canonical}
For independent $u,v$, every $d\ge3$, and any ambient dimension,
\begin{equation}
 \Ma(C_d^{u,v})=\En_{C_d^{u,v}}(1)=b_d.
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:canonical-max}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For the constant function, the selected frequency has the form $A v+B u$,
where, with $t=d-1$,
\[
 A=\prod_{j=1}^t u(h_j),\qquad
 B=\sum_{i=1}^t v(h_i)\prod_{j\ne i}u(h_j).
\]
If at least two $u(h_j)$ vanish, both coefficients vanish.  If exactly one
vanishes, $A=0$ and $B$ is an independent unbiased bit.  If none vanishes,
$A=1$.  Thus the probability of a nonzero frequency is
$2^{-t}+t2^{-t-1}=(d+1)/2^d$, giving the claimed lower bound.

The cubic upper bound follows from Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:69:bad:thm:cubic} and the rank-two
defect in \eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:canonical-defect}.  Suppose the upper bound is known
in degree $m=d-1\ge3$.  The exact tensor contraction is
\[
 (C_d^{u,v})_z=u(z)C_m^{u,v}+v(z)U_m.
\]
The four pairs $(u(z),v(z))$ occur equally often.  On $(0,0)$ the slice energy
is at most one.  On $(0,1)$ it is at most $1-2^{1-m}$ by
Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:69:bad:lem:fixed-derivative}.  On the half with $u(z)=1$, remove the
integrable tensor $v(z)U_m$ by gauge invariance and use the inductive bound
$b_m$.  Slicing therefore gives
\begin{align}
 \En_{C_d^{u,v}}(f)
 &\le\frac14+\frac14(1-2^{2-d})+\frac12b_{d-1} \notag\\
 &=1-\frac{d+1}{2^d}.
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:canonical-recursion}
\end{align}
This proof allows $f$ to depend on every ambient coordinate.  It never
reduces the optimization problem to a two-dimensional space.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The contraction-integrability induction\srctag{69}}]{The contraction-integrability induction}\label{gsr:fp:69:sec:d5}
\srcnote{69}{Section 5}
\label{gsr:fp:69:bad:sec:induction}

\subsection{A general one-step inequality}
\begin{lemma}[Counting nonintegrable contractions]
\label{gsr:fp:69:bad:lem:one-step}
Fix $d\ge4$, and suppose that every nonintegrable symmetric tensor of degree
$d-1$ on $V$ has maximum energy at most $\beta$.  For a symmetric tensor
$T$ with $\rho(T)=r$,
\begin{equation}
 \En_T(f)\le 2^{-r}+(1-2^{-r})\beta.
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:one-step}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The subspace $R(T)$ has proportion $2^{-r}$ in $V$.  Its contractions are
integrable, so the trivial bound one suffices there.  Every contraction
outside it is nonintegrable and has energy at most $\beta$ when tested on
$\partial_zf$, which is still one-bounded.  Average these two bounds in
\eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:slicing}.
\end{proof}
The test of whether $T_z$ is integrable is an \emph{identity} on all its
remaining variables.  Replacing it by the probability that a randomly
completed defect is nonzero would give a different, weaker estimate.

\subsection{Proof of the all-degree theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:69:bad:thm:main}]
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:69:bad:thm:cubic} gives the universal bound $b_3=1/2$.
Proceed by induction on $d\ge4$.  Let $T$ be nonintegrable.
If $\rho(T)=1$, Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:69:bad:prop:rank-one} and
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:69:bad:thm:canonical}, followed by gauge invariance, give
$\Ma(T)=b_d$.

If $\rho(T)\ge2$, apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:69:bad:lem:one-step} with
$\beta=b_{d-1}=1-d/2^{d-1}$.  It gives the more precise estimate
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 \En_T(f)\le1-\frac{d}{2^{d-1}}(1-2^{-\rho(T)}).}
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:rank-energy}
\end{equation}
Since $1-2^{-\rho(T)}\ge3/4$,
\[
 \En_T(f)\le1-\frac{3d}{2^{d+1}}
 =b_d-\frac{d-2}{2^{d+1}}<b_d.
\]
This proves the inductive universal bound and excludes every higher-rank
tensor from equality.  The canonical example attains $b_d$ and is
nonintegrable by \eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:canonical-defect}.  It proves sharpness in
every $n\ge2$ and completes the classification.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why a long support census is unnecessary here]
The preceding proof of \eqref{gsr:fm:69:bad:eq:old} uses a support bound for non-pure
symmetric multilinear defects.  That bound treats a nonzero contraction by
how rarely its \emph{values} can be nonzero.  In contrast, once the lower-degree
energy theorem is available, every nonintegrable contraction already costs a
full loss $1-b_{d-1}$.  Unless the frozen radical is a hyperplane, at least
three quarters of all contractions are of this type.  The hyperplane case is
exactly the canonical family, for which the separate derivative-period
argument is sharp.  These two alternatives close the induction without a
new tensor-support estimate.
\end{remark}

\subsection{A rank-sensitive statement and a one-step deficit identity}
Estimate \eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:rank-energy} is valid even when $\rho=1$, although it is
then weaker than the exact canonical bound.  At a fixed degree it improves
the rank-one alternative for every $\rho\ge2$.
For $r=\rho(T)$, write
\[
 c_d(r)=2^{-r}+(1-2^{-r})b_{d-1}.
\]
The proof supplies an exact nonnegative decomposition:
\begin{align}
 c_d(r)-\En_T(f)
 &=\E_z\,\mathbf1_{R(T)}(z)
           \bigl(1-\En_{T_z}(\partial_zf)\bigr)\notag\\
 &\quad+\E_z\,\mathbf1_{V\setminus R(T)}(z)
           \bigl(b_{d-1}-\En_{T_z}(\partial_zf)\bigr).
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:deficit}
\end{align}
Both integrands are nonnegative.  Thus, for example, if
$\En_T(f)\ge c_d(r)-\delta$, the fraction of all directions outside $R(T)$
whose slice energy is less than $b_{d-1}-t$ is at most $\delta/t$.
This is a direct finite averaging consequence, not a phase-stability theorem.

\begin{corollary}[Exact phase-removal certificate]
\label{gsr:fp:69:bad:cor:certificate}
If $T\in\SM_d(V)$ and $\En_T(f)>b_d$, then $T\in\In_d(V)$ and the explicit
primitive in \eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:primitive-explicit} satisfies
\[
 \norm{f e(-P_T)}_{U^d}^{2^d}=\En_T(f).
\]
For $d\ge3$ and $n\ge2$, the strict threshold cannot be lowered.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:69:bad:thm:main} excludes nonintegrability, and gauge invariance
then gives equality.  At the threshold $C_d^{u,v}$ and $f=1$ remain
nonintegrable, proving optimality.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Extremal flags and quantitative tensor rigidity\srctag{69}}]{Extremal flags and quantitative tensor rigidity}\label{gsr:fp:69:sec:d6}
\srcnote{69}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:fp:69:bad:sec:flags}

\subsection{Flags, rather than merely two-dimensional quotients}
Two tensors are \emph{gauge-equivalent} when their difference belongs to
$\In_d(V)$.  By Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:69:bad:thm:integration}, this is equivalent to
having identical defects.

\begin{theorem}[Enumeration of extremal gauge classes]
\label{gsr:fp:69:bad:thm:flags}
For $d\ge4$, the gauge classes attaining the nonintegrable maximum $b_d$
are in bijection with flags
\begin{equation}
 \ell\subset\Pi\subset V^*,\qquad \dim\ell=1,\quad\dim\Pi=2.
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:flags}
\end{equation}
Their number is
\begin{equation}
 (2^n-1)(2^{n-1}-1).
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:flag-count}
\end{equation}
The class represented by $C_d^{u,v}$ corresponds to
$\ell=\Span(u)$ and $\Pi=\Span(u,v)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The radical of a canonical defect is $\ker u$, so the defect determines
the nonzero functional $u$ uniquely over $\Ftwo$.  Choose $w$ with $u(w)=1$.
Evaluating every frozen slot at $w$ recovers the alternating form
$\Omega=u\otimes v+v\otimes u$.  For fixed $u$, this determines $v$ modulo
$\Span(u)$: if $u\wedge(v+v')=0$, choose $c$ with $u(c)=1$ and evaluate at
$(c,x)$ to get $v+v'=(v(c)+v'(c))u$.
Thus the defect determines exactly the stated flag.  Conversely a flag
specifies $u$ and $v$ modulo $u$, and formula \eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:canonical-defect}
then specifies the same defect.  Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:69:bad:thm:main} proves that these
are all extremal classes.
There are $2^n-1$ choices of $u\ne0$ and $2^{n-1}-1$ nonzero cosets of
$\Span(u)$ in $V^*$.  This proves \eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:flag-count}.
\end{proof}
For $d=3$ there is no frozen slot to distinguish a line inside the plane.
The maximal nonintegrable cubic classes are the rank-two alternating forms,
indexed by planes in $V^*$.  Each plane has three lines, so the cubic count
is $(2^n-1)(2^{n-1}-1)/3$.  Confusing these two classifications would overcount
the cubic endpoint by a factor of three.

\subsection{A discrete rigidity band}
\begin{corollary}[High-energy tensor dichotomy]
\label{gsr:fp:69:bad:cor:dichotomy}
Let $d\ge4$.  If
\begin{equation}
 \En_T(f)>1-\frac{3d}{2^{d+1}},
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:band}
\end{equation}
then either $T$ is integrable or it is gauge-equivalent to exactly one
extremal flag class.  In particular, a nonintegrable tensor whose energy lies
at distance strictly less than $(d-2)/2^{d+1}$ from $b_d$ must already have the exact canonical defect.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
A nonintegrable tensor outside the canonical classes satisfies
\eqref{gsr:fm:69:bad:eq:separation}.  Strict inequality excludes that alternative;
uniqueness of the flag follows from Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:69:bad:thm:flags}.
\end{proof}
This is rigidity of a discrete tensor invariant.  It does not assert that the
function $f$ is close to a particular phase.  Such a conclusion would require
an analysis of equality and stability inside the canonical spectral problem.

\subsection{A small exact example}
On $V=\Ftwo^3$, symmetric quartic tensors have $\binom64=15$ free coefficients.
The integrable subspace has dimension $3+3+1=7$.  There are $21$ extremal
gauge classes and therefore $21\cdot2^7=2688$ rank-one-defect tensors.
The accompanying exhaustive coefficient calculation gives
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}crr@{}}
\toprule
$\rho(T)$ & Number of tensors & $\eff(T)$\\
\midrule
$0$ & $128$ & $0$\\
$1$ & $2688$ & $2$\\
$2$ & $19712$ & $3$\\
$3$ & $10240$ & $3$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The first two counts also follow from the preceding proofs.  The last two are
reported as exact finite computations, not used in any general theorem.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The minimal obstruction quotient\srctag{69}}]{The minimal obstruction quotient}\label{gsr:fp:69:sec:d7}
\srcnote{69}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:fp:69:bad:sec:quotient}

\subsection{The complete defect radical}
The frozen radical $R(T)$ need not annihilate the two alternating slots.
A direction can be invisible when used as a frozen variable but still enter
the obstruction through one of those slots.  This is why $\rho(T)$ alone
need not equal the minimal model dimension.
The subspace $K(T)$ in \eqref{gsr:fm:69:bad:eq:K} imposes both requirements.  Symmetry
of the frozen slots and alternation of the last pair make it precisely the
common radical of the defect in \emph{every} slot.

\begin{theorem}[Exact minimal quotient]
\label{gsr:fp:69:bad:thm:minimal-quotient}
For $d\ge4$,
\begin{equation}
 \eff(T)=\codim_V K(T).
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:exact-quotient}
\end{equation}
Moreover the quotient $q:V\to V/K(T)$ itself supports a model
$T=S+q^*T_0$ with $S$ integrable.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $T=S+q^*T_0$ and $S$ is integrable, then
$\Phi_T=q^*\Phi_{T_0}$.  Every vector in $\ker q$ kills the defect in all
slots.  Thus $\ker q\subseteq K(T)$ and the target dimension is at least
$\codim K(T)$.

Conversely, multilinearity and the definition of $K(T)$ show that the defect
descends in every slot to $V/K(T)$.  Choose a linear section
$j:V/K(T)\to V$ of the quotient map and define $T_0=j^*T$.
The defect of $q^*T_0$ equals $\Phi_T$, since every vector $x$ and $jq(x)$
differ by an element of the complete radical.  Therefore
$S=T-q^*T_0$ has zero defect and is integrable.  This produces a model in
exactly the lower-bound dimension.
\end{proof}
A different section may change the representative $T_0$, but not the minimal
dimension or the defect on the quotient.  Importantly, the theorem is about
representing the \emph{tensor modulo integrable tensors}.  It does not imply
that optimizing functions descend to this quotient, nor that
$\Ma(q^*T_0)=\Ma(T_0)$ for arbitrary $T_0$.

\subsection{Two radical arguments force zero}
\begin{lemma}[The defect vanishes on two frozen-radical directions]
\label{gsr:fp:69:bad:lem:two-radical}
If $a,b\in R(T)$, then $\Phi_T(\zz)(a,b)=0$ for every frozen tuple.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Take the first frozen variable to be $c$ and the remaining ones to be
$\mathbf w$.  Equation \eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:bianchi} expresses
$\Phi_T(c,\mathbf w)(a,b)$ as the sum of two terms having either $a$ or
$b$ in a frozen slot.  Both terms vanish by \eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:radical-frozen}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The integrable-valued radical map}
Choose a complement $H$ with $V=H\oplus R(T)$ and $\dim H=\rho(T)$.
For $a\in R(T)$ define a map on $H^{d-2}$ by
\begin{equation}
 \Psi_a(h_1,\ldots,h_{d-2})
   =\Phi_T(h_2,\ldots,h_{d-2})(a,h_1).
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:Psi}
\end{equation}

\begin{proposition}[An integrable-valued linear map]
\label{gsr:fp:69:bad:prop:Psi}
The assignment
\begin{equation}
 \Psi:R(T)\longrightarrow\In_{d-2}(H),\qquad a\longmapsto\Psi_a
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:Psi-map}
\end{equation}
is linear and has kernel $K(T)$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Linearity in $a$ follows from bilinearity of the alternating pair in the
defect.  Since $a\in R(T)$, the tensor $S_a=T_a$ is integrable of degree
$d-1$.  Expanding the definition gives, with $\zz=(h_2,\ldots,h_{d-2})$,
\begin{equation}
 \Psi_a(h_1,\zz)=S_a(a,h_1,\zz)+S_a(h_1,h_1,\zz).
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:Psi-lowering}
\end{equation}
The first summand is an ordinary contraction of $S_a$, and the second is
its diagonal lowering.  Both are integrable by
Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:69:bad:lem:lowering}; restriction to $H$ preserves that property.
Thus \eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:Psi-map} has exactly the indicated, smaller target space.

If $a\in K(T)$, then certainly $\Psi_a=0$.  Conversely suppose
$a\in R(T)$ and $\Psi_a=0$.  Every frozen variable may be reduced to its
$H$ component, because its $R(T)$ component is in a frozen radical.
The other alternating variable may also be reduced to $H$, since its
$R(T)$ component pairs with $a\in R(T)$ and vanishes by
Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:69:bad:lem:two-radical}.  The remaining values are exactly those of
$\Psi_a$, hence all zero.  Therefore $a\in K(T)$.
\end{proof}
The assertion that $\Psi_a$ is integrable, not merely symmetric multilinear,
is the point that saves coordinates.  Bounding its target by all symmetric
$(d-2)$-linear tensors would give
$\rho+\binom{\rho+d-3}{d-2}$ instead of \eqref{gsr:fm:69:bad:eq:model-bound}.

\begin{proof}[Proof of the upper bound in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:69:bad:thm:model-intro}]
Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:69:bad:prop:Psi} and rank--nullity give the identity
\begin{equation}
 \eff(T)=\codim K(T)
 =\rho(T)+\rk\bigl(\Psi:R(T)\to\In_{d-2}(H)\bigr).
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:effective-exact-rank}
\end{equation}
Apply the dimension formula \eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:Idim} to the target.  This proves
\eqref{gsr:fm:69:bad:eq:model-bound}, including the integrable case $\rho=0$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A complete normal form for a prescribed radical}
The preceding map is part of a more precise description of the quotient by
integrable tensors.  Here the radical is only \emph{prescribed to contain} a
fixed subspace; it need not be exactly that subspace.

\begin{theorem}[Fixed-radical normal form]
\label{gsr:fp:69:bad:thm:normal-form}
Fix a splitting $V=H\oplus R_0$, put $r=\dim H$ and $t=\dim R_0$, and let
\[
 \mathcal W_d(H,R_0)=\{T\in\SM_d(V):R_0\subseteq R(T)\},\qquad d\ge4.
\]
For $a\in R_0$ define $\Psi_a$ by \eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:Psi}, using $H$ as written.
There is a linear isomorphism
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal W_d(H,R_0)/\In_d(V)
 \ \cong\ \bigl(\SM_d(H)/\In_d(H)\bigr)
       \oplus\operatorname{Hom}_{\Ftwo}(R_0,\In_{d-2}(H)),
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:normal-form}
\end{equation}
given by $[T]\mapsto([T|_{H^d}],\Psi)$.
In particular its dimension is
\begin{equation}
 \binom{r+d-1}{d}-\sum_{j=1}^{\min(r,d)}\binom rj
       +t\sum_{j=1}^{\min(r,d-2)}\binom rj.
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:normal-dim}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The space $\In_d(V)$ is contained in $\mathcal W_d(H,R_0)$, and both
restriction and $\Psi$ respect addition of an integrable tensor.
The proof of Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:69:bad:prop:Psi} shows that $\Psi_a$ is integrable
for every $a\in R_0$; only the inclusion $R_0\subseteq R(T)$ is needed.
Thus the displayed map is well defined and linear.

If its image is zero, the defect vanishes with all arguments in $H$, and
also when one alternating argument belongs to $R_0$ and the other to $H$.
It vanishes when both alternating arguments belong to $R_0$ by the Bianchi
identity, and whenever a frozen argument belongs to $R_0$ by hypothesis.
Expand every argument into its $H$ and $R_0$ components.  These cases cover
all terms, proving $\Phi_T=0$.  Hence the map is injective.

For surjectivity, choose a representative $A\in\SM_d(H)$ of the desired
first component and a map $L:R_0\to\In_{d-2}(H)$ for the second component.
The diagonal-lowering map
$D:\In_{d-1}(H)\to\In_{d-2}(H)$ is surjective: retain the prescribed
support coefficients of sizes at most $d-2$ and set the support coefficients
of size $d-1$ equal to zero.  Choose a basis $r_1,\ldots,r_t$ of $R_0$ and
lifts $S_i\in\In_{d-1}(H)$ with $D(S_i)=L(r_i)$.
Define a symmetric tensor $B$ to be zero on basis tuples with zero or at
least two $R_0$ slots, and set
\[
 B(r_i,h_1,\ldots,h_{d-1})=S_i(h_1,\ldots,h_{d-1})
\]
on the remaining basis tuples.  The contractions $B_{r_i}$ are pullbacks
of the integrable tensors $S_i$, so $R_0\subseteq R(B)$.
Moreover $B|_{H^d}=0$, and the term containing two $R_0$ slots vanishes in
\eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:Psi-lowering}.  Thus $\Psi^B_{r_i}=D(S_i)=L(r_i)$.
Adding the pullback of $A$ along $V\to H$ produces exactly the desired
pair of components.  This proves surjectivity.  The dimensions of the two
factors, using \eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:Idim}, give \eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:normal-dim}.
\end{proof}
The theorem gives a full linear parameterization before imposing changes of
coordinates.  Requiring $R(T)=R_0$, rather than just containment, is an
additional nondegeneracy condition on the pair of parameters.  The sharpness
construction below enforces this condition with singleton support tensors.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A construction attaining every dimension bound\srctag{69}}]{A construction attaining every dimension bound}\label{gsr:fp:69:sec:d8}
\srcnote{69}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:fp:69:bad:sec:sharp-model}

\subsection{Support-basis construction}
Fix $d\ge4$ and $r\ge1$, put $m=d-2$, and let $H=\Ftwo^r$ with basis
$e_1,\ldots,e_r$.  Index the family
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal A=\{A\subseteq[r]:1\le|A|\le m\},\qquad
 L=|\mathcal A|=\sum_{j=1}^{\min(r,m)}\binom rj.
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:A-family}
\end{equation}
For each $A\in\mathcal A$ let $S_A\in\In_{d-1}(H)$ be the support-basis
tensor whose coefficient on a $(d-1)$-tuple of basis vectors is one exactly
when the set of its indices is $A$.
Let $R_0$ have basis $\{r_A:A\in\mathcal A\}$, and take $V=H\oplus R_0$.
Define $T\in\SM_d(V)$ by its unordered basis coefficients as follows:
\begin{equation}
 T(r_A,e_{i_1},\ldots,e_{i_{d-1}})=S_A(e_{i_1},\ldots,e_{i_{d-1}});
 \quad
 T=0\text{ on tuples with zero or at least two }R_0\text{ slots}.
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:sharp-construction}
\end{equation}
Extend symmetrically and multilinearly.  This is a complete explicit
specification of a tensor on $r+L$ coordinates.

\begin{theorem}[Sharpness of the effective-dimension bound]
\label{gsr:fp:69:bad:thm:sharp-model}
The tensor in \eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:sharp-construction} satisfies
\begin{equation}
 R(T)=R_0,\qquad \rho(T)=r,\qquad K(T)=0,\qquad
 \eff(T)=r+L=B_d(r).
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:sharp-properties}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For each $A$, the contraction $T_{r_A}$ is the pullback of $S_A$ from $H$.
It is integrable, so $R_0\subseteq R(T)$.
Take a nonzero $h\in H$ and choose $i$ whose coordinate in $h$ is one.
Singletons belong to $\mathcal A$.  From the definition, with all the
remaining $d-4$ frozen directions equal to $e_i$,
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_T(h,e_i,\ldots,e_i)(r_{\{i\}},e_i)=1.
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:detect-H}
\end{equation}
Indeed the term with two occurrences of $r_{\{i\}}$ is zero, and the other
is the singleton support tensor evaluated on $h$ and $d-2$ copies of $e_i$.
It equals the $i$th coordinate of $h$.  Thus no nonzero $H$ component lies
in the frozen radical, and $R(T)=R_0$.

For $a=r_A$ the first summand in \eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:Psi-lowering} is zero,
because it contains two $R_0$ basis vectors.  Hence
\[
 \Psi_{r_A}(h_1,\ldots,h_m)=S_A(h_1,h_1,h_2,\ldots,h_m)=D(S_A)(h_1,\ldots,h_m).
\]
By the support-coefficient description, the $D(S_A)$, $A\in\mathcal A$,
are exactly the support basis of $\In_m(H)$.  The map $\Psi$ is therefore
an isomorphism $R_0\to\In_m(H)$.  Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:69:bad:prop:Psi} gives
$K(T)=0$.  The minimal quotient theorem yields $\eff(T)=\dim V=r+L$.
\end{proof}
This completes the proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:69:bad:thm:model-intro}.  Notice that
sharpness is algebraic: it does not require these examples to have unusually
large Fourier energy.

\subsection{An explicit five-coordinate quartic}
For $d=4$ and $r=2$, write the basis as $e_1,e_2,a,b,c$, corresponding to
$\{1\},\{2\},\{1,2\}$.  The only nonzero unordered coefficients are
\begin{equation}
 T(a,e_1,e_1,e_1)=T(b,e_2,e_2,e_2)
 =T(c,e_1,e_1,e_2)=T(c,e_1,e_2,e_2)=1.
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:five-coordinate}
\end{equation}
Here $R(T)=\Span(a,b,c)$ and $\rho(T)=2$.  The map $\Psi$ sends these
three basis vectors to the symmetric bilinear forms with coefficient
patterns $x_1y_1$, $x_2y_2$, and $x_1y_2+x_2y_1$, respectively.
Thus $K(T)=0$: no model modulo an integrable tensor can use fewer than all
five coordinates.  A two-dimensional frozen quotient can therefore hide
three additional active directions in the alternating pair.

\subsection{Consequences for the size of models}
If $d\ge r+2$, then all nonempty subsets occur and
\begin{equation}
 B_d(r)=r+2^r-1.
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:exponential-model}
\end{equation}
The construction proves that no bound polynomial in $r$, uniformly in the
degree, can hold for the number of active coordinates modulo integrable
tensors under this hypothesis alone.  For a fixed $d\ge4$, however,
\[
 B_d(r)=\frac{r^{d-2}}{(d-2)!}+O_d(r^{d-3}+r),\qquad r\to\infty.
\]
The two regimes concern different quantifiers and should not be conflated.
Some small values are
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}c|rrrrr@{}}
\toprule
$d\backslash r$ & $1$ & $2$ & $3$ & $4$ & $5$\\
\midrule
$4$ & $2$ & $5$ & $9$ & $14$ & $20$\\
$5$ & $2$ & $5$ & $10$ & $18$ & $30$\\
$6$ & $2$ & $5$ & $10$ & $19$ & $35$\\
$7$ & $2$ & $5$ & $10$ & $19$ & $36$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Each entry is attained in that ambient dimension.  The case $r=1$ recovers
the two-coordinate canonical model, whereas the higher-rank examples show
why simply extending that two-coordinate conclusion is impossible.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Energy-to-complexity and robust selector certificates\srctag{69}}]{Energy-to-complexity and robust selector certificates}\label{gsr:fp:69:sec:d9}
\srcnote{69}{Section 9}
\label{gsr:fp:69:bad:sec:robust}

\subsection{From energy to a finite obstruction model}
\begin{corollary}[Energy bounds the contraction rank]
\label{gsr:fp:69:bad:cor:energy-complexity}
Let $d\ge4$, let $q\ge0$ be an integer, and let $T\in\SM_d(V)$.  If
\begin{equation}
 \En_T(f)>1-\frac d{2^{d-1}}(1-2^{-(q+1)}),
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:complexity-threshold}
\end{equation}
then $\rho(T)\le q$ and $\eff(T)\le B_d(q)$.
Alternatively, if $\eps=1-\En_T(f)$ and
$2^{d-1}\eps/d<1$, then
\begin{equation}
 \rho(T)\le
 \log_2\!\left(\frac1{1-2^{d-1}\eps/d}\right).
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:log-rank}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
If $T$ is integrable, $\rho=\eff=0$.  Otherwise
\eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:rank-energy} applies.  Its upper bound decreases with $\rho$,
so \eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:complexity-threshold} rules out $\rho\ge q+1$.
The model bound follows from Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:69:bad:thm:model-intro} and monotonicity
of $B_d$.  Rearranging the same inequality gives
$2^{-\rho}\ge1-2^{d-1}\eps/d$ and hence \eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:log-rank}.
\end{proof}
For $q=0$ the exact integrability certificate at $b_d$ is stronger.
For $q=1$ the conclusion can be sharpened to the integrable-or-canonical
dichotomy rather than just a two-coordinate model.  Formula
\eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:log-rank} is useful only where its right-hand side is finite;
it is not a small-energy inverse theorem.

\subsection{Corrupted frequency selectors}
For any selector $\sigma:V^{d-1}\to V^*$, define
\[
 \En_\sigma(f)=\E_{\hh}\left|
        \E_x\partial_{\hh}f(x)(-1)^{\sigma(\hh)(x)}\right|^2.
\]
Here $\partial_{\hh}=\partial_{h_1}\cdots\partial_{h_{d-1}}$.
Let $\sigma_T(\hh)=T(\hh,\cdot)$.

\begin{proposition}[Exact corruption margin]
\label{gsr:fp:69:bad:prop:noise}
If $\Prb_{\hh}[\sigma(\hh)\ne\sigma_T(\hh)]\le\eta$, then
\begin{equation}
 |\En_\sigma(f)-\En_T(f)|\le\eta.
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:noise}
\end{equation}
Thus, for symmetric $T$, energy $\En_\sigma(f)>b_d+\eta$ certifies
integrability and yields a primitive with
\begin{equation}
 \norm{f e(-P_T)}_{U^d}^{2^d}\ge\En_\sigma(f)-\eta.
 \label{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:noise-removal}
\end{equation}
For $d\ge4$, energy
$\En_\sigma(f)>1-3d/2^{d+1}+\eta$ certifies that $T$ is integrable or
canonical modulo an integrable tensor.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Each squared coefficient lies in $[0,1]$.  The two averages agree outside
the disagreement set, and their summands differ by at most one inside it.
This proves \eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:noise}; the previous theorems give the remaining
claims.
\end{proof}
The disagreement event compares \emph{whole linear functionals} at a tuple
of derivative directions.  A different hypothesis measuring disagreements
of the scalar values $T(\hh,x)$ would need a separate conversion.
No procedure for learning the tensor from noisy data is asserted here.

\gsrnewfloats
\section{Source~63's Section~6: the face cover at Proposition~17.7 \wtag}\label{gsr:fp:sec:facecover}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the eleventh write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next section is source~63's Section~6, on the localized phase removal of Gowers's Proposition~17.7. \emph{Logically it continues source~16's chapter} (Section~\ref{gsr:fp:sec:windows}), whose sliding windows and local ceiling it uses; it is printed here because no number printed earlier may move. Its conventions are in source~63's Section~2 (Section~\ref{gsr:cc:63:sec:d2}), its introduction is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:63:sec:d1}.

\emph{What is proved.} Under the hypotheses of the local problem, for an odd box width $m$ and prime $N\ge m^2$, a phase of degree at most $k+1$ and a partition into progressions of lengths $\lceil m/(3k)\rceil$ or one more retain, as $m\to\infty$, the coefficient $v_k/D_k$ with $v_k=2^{k+1}/(k+2)!$ and $1\le D_k\le e^{2/(3(k+2))}$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:63:loc:thm:headline}), with explicit finite rounding factors (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:63:loc:thm:finite}, Corollary~\ref{gsr:fp:63:loc:cor:joint-scale}); no coefficient in the class exceeds $v_k$ (Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:63:loc:prop:ceiling}), so the best local coefficient is asymptotic to $v_k$. The new ingredient is an exact convolution identity for positive measures on the faces of a box (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:63:loc:thm:face-cover}), extended to every positive real power of the kernel (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:63:loc:thm:power-cover}).

\emph{Against source~16, and the predecessor that was never delivered} (checked at the write). Source~16's window theorem and its local ceiling $2^{k+1}/(k+2)!$ (Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:16:prop:localceiling}) are the sliding-window method and the ceiling used here; source~63 does not cite source~16. It credits instead the ``preceding sliding-window localization coefficient'' $v_k/\widehat D_k$, $\widehat D_k\to1.2415870899$ (a retained fraction about $0.80542$ of the ceiling), to a manuscript \emph{Local Phase Removal and Cubic Rigidity in Gowers' Szemer\'edi Framework} of 7~October 2026, which was never delivered to this repository (Section~\ref{gsr:fm:sec:provenance}); that coefficient is not in this report and cannot be checked here. Against source~16's printed coefficients, which retain a fraction of $v_k$ tending to zero (exponentially, at the optimized width $(2/(k+2))^{k+2}$), source~63's $v_k/D_k$ closes the gap to first order; this answers source~16's question on the best local coefficient asymptotically (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:IV:phase}), not at any fixed degree, as source~63 says.

\emph{Relation to the formal statements} (checked at HEAD \texttt{fb9602e55}). \file{proposition_17_7} (\file{Sections17\_18.lean}, line~140) has the exact companion \file{proposition_17_7_holds} (\file{Proofs17LocalizedPhaseRemoval.lean}, line~2941), with the paper's coefficient; nothing in this chapter is formalized.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Asymptotically sharp local phase removal\srctag{63}}]{Asymptotically sharp local phase removal}\label{gsr:fp:63:sec:d6}
\srcnote{63}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:fp:63:loc:section}

The next result concerns the local phase-removal step of Gowers'
Proposition~17.7 \cite{gowers}.  The preceding work
\cite{localphase63} replaced the enumeration of carry patterns by
sliding windows and a positive covering of the input increment box.
It obtained a coefficient exceeding $80.54\%$ of the geometric ceiling,
uniformly in the degree.  We improve the covering measure.  The
resulting coefficient is asymptotic to the ceiling as the degree tends
to infinity.  The new ingredient is an exact convolution identity for
measures on the faces of a box; the phase polarization, sliding-window
argument, and positive-cover interface are credited to the preceding
work and are included here to make the proof self-contained.

\subsection{The local problem and its normalization}

Let $G=\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$, where $N$ is prime, and write
$e_N(t)=\exp(2\pi i t/N)$.  If $u:G\to\mathbb C$ and $r\ge1$, put
\begin{equation}
 \mathsf C_r(u)=
 \sum_{s\in G}\sum_{a\in G^r}
       \prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^r}
            \mathcal C^{|\omega|}u(s-\omega\cdot a)
 =N^{r+1}\|u\|_{U^r(G)}^{2^r},
 \label{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:cube}
\end{equation}
where $\mathcal C$ denotes complex conjugation.  In particular these
cube sums are nonnegative real numbers.  For a partition $\mathcal Q$
into $M$ progressions and an upper bound $U$ for their lengths, define
\begin{equation}
 \mathsf B_k(u;\mathcal Q,U)=
 \frac1{M U^{k+2}}\sum_{Q\in\mathcal Q}
                  \mathsf C_{k+1}(\mathbf 1_Q u).
 \label{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:quotient}
\end{equation}
This is the upper-cell-size normalization used in the corrected local
interface.  The factor $U^{k+2}$ is retained throughout.

Here is the input.  Let $m=2h+1$, $m^2\le N$, $d\in G^\times$, and
\[
 P_i=\{r_i+da:-h\le a\le h\},\qquad
 P=P_1\times\cdots\times P_k.
\]
Let $f:G\to\mathbb C$ satisfy $|f|\le1$.  We explicitly assume that
the coordinate function $a\mapsto\sigma(r+da)$ extends to a
multi-affine polynomial on $G^k$, that is, a polynomial of degree at
most one in each variable separately.  The derivative-energy hypothesis is
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{x\in P}
  \left|\sum_{s\in G}e_N(-s\sigma(x))
      \prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^k}
                \mathcal C^{|\omega|}f(s-\omega\cdot x)
  \right|^2
 \ge\alpha N^2m^k,\qquad \alpha>0.
 \label{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:input}
\end{equation}
We seek a polynomial $\phi$ of degree at most $k+1$ and a partition
such that $\mathsf B_k(f e_N(-\phi);\mathcal Q,U)$ is large.

Set
\begin{equation}
 v_k=\frac{2^{k+1}}{(k+2)!},\qquad
 D_k=\sum_{j=0}^k\binom kj\left(\frac2{3k}\right)^j
                      \frac{(k-j+2)!}{(k+2)!}.
 \label{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:constants}
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[The asymptotically sharp local coefficient]
\label{gsr:fp:63:loc:thm:headline}
Fix $k\ge1$.  As $m\to\infty$ through odd integers, uniformly over
primes $N\ge m^2$ and inputs satisfying \eqref{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:input}, there
are a polynomial $\phi$ of degree at most $k+1$ and a partition into
proper modular progressions with lengths
\[
 L\quad\hbox{or}\quad L+1,\qquad
 L=\left\lceil\frac m{3k}\right\rceil,
\]
such that
\begin{equation}
 \mathsf B_k(f e_N(-\phi);\mathcal Q,L+1)
 \ge \alpha\left(\frac{v_k}{D_k}+O_k(m^{-1})\right).
 \label{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:headline}
\end{equation}
The $O_k(m^{-1})$ term describes the explicit finite coefficient in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:63:loc:thm:finite}; it is uniform in the input functions and
in $N\ge m^2$.  Every cell has length between $m/(3k)$ and $m$.
Moreover
\begin{equation}
 1+\frac2{3(k+2)}\le D_k
 \le\exp\!\left(\frac2{3(k+2)}\right),\qquad
 D_k=1+\frac2{3k}+O(k^{-2}).
 \label{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:D-bound}
\end{equation}
If $c_k^{\mathrm{loc}}$ is the best asymptotic coefficient when cells
are required to have lengths between $m/(3k)$ and $m$, with
$U=\max_{Q\in\mathcal Q}|Q|$, then
\begin{equation}
 \frac{v_k}{D_k}\le c_k^{\mathrm{loc}}\le v_k,
 \qquad
 c_k^{\mathrm{loc}}\sim\frac{2^{k+1}}{(k+2)!}
 \quad(k\to\infty).
 \label{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:sharp-asymptotic}
\end{equation}
The two limits are ordered: the local-scale limit $m\to\infty$ is
taken first for each fixed $k$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Checked at the write} (exact rationals). $D_1=\widehat D_1=11/9$ and $D_2=127/108$, so $1/D_2=108/127=0.85039$; $D_k\le\widehat D_k$ for every $k\le40$; $\widehat D_{40}=1.24\ldots$. \emph{Against source~16} (Section~\ref{gsr:fp:sec:windows}): source~16's optimized width retains $(2/(k+2))^{k+2}$, which is $2(k+2)!/(k+2)^{k+2}$ times $v_k$, a fraction decreasing to zero ($4/9$ at $k=1$, about $1.07\cdot10^{-4}$ at $k=10$); this theorem retains $v_k/D_k\ge e^{-2/(3(k+2))}v_k$. The ceiling $v_k$ is source~16's Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:16:prop:localceiling}, in the same normalization (every cell bounded by the normalizing size); source~16 is not cited here (Section~\ref{gsr:fp:sec:facecover}).
\end{writenote}

In the definition of $c_k^{\mathrm{loc}}$, ``asymptotic coefficient
$c$'' means that for every $\varepsilon>0$ the conclusion with
$\alpha(c-\varepsilon)$ holds for all sufficiently large $m$,
uniformly over the remaining data.  The theorem proves its first-order
behavior as $k$ grows.  It does not determine the exact value at a
fixed degree, or the relative $1/k$ correction to that optimum.

\subsection{An exact positive covering measure on box faces}

For $w>0$ put
\[
 K_w(x)=(w-\|x\|_1)_+^2,\qquad x\in\mathbb R^k,
 \qquad t_+=\max(t,0).
\]
The elementary simplex integral gives
\begin{equation}
 \int_{\mathbb R^k}K_w(x)\,dx=v_kw^{k+2}.
 \label{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:kernel-mass}
\end{equation}
For $0\le j\le k$, define
\begin{equation}
 b_{k,j}(w)=\frac{(k-j+2)!}{(k+2)!}w^j.
 \label{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:face-weight}
\end{equation}
On each codimension-$j$ coordinate face of $B=[0,\ell]^k$, place
constant density $b_{k,j}(w)$ relative to its $(k-j)$-dimensional
Lebesgue measure.  Add all these measures, including the whole box
for $j=0$, and denote the result by $\mu_{k,\ell,w}$.  Face
intersections receive the sum of their contributions.  Its total mass is
\begin{equation}
 T_k(\ell,w)=\sum_{j=0}^k\binom kj2^j\ell^{k-j}
                     \frac{(k-j+2)!}{(k+2)!}w^j.
 \label{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:face-mass}
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Exact face-cover identity]
\label{gsr:fp:63:loc:thm:face-cover}
Assume $0<w\le\ell/2$.  For $a\in B$, let
$d_i=\min(a_i,\ell-a_i)$ and $d_S=\sum_{i\in S}d_i$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 \int_B K_w(a-c)\,d\mu_{k,\ell,w}(c)
 =\frac1{(k+2)!}\sum_{S\subseteq[k]}
     2^{k-|S|+1}d_S^{|S|}(w-d_S)_+^{k-|S|+2}.
 \label{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:face-identity}
\end{equation}
The empty-set summand is interpreted as $2^{k+1}w^{k+2}$ before
division by $(k+2)!$.  In particular,
\begin{equation}
 \int_B K_w(a-c)\,d\mu_{k,\ell,w}(c)
 \ge v_kw^{k+2}\qquad(a\in B).
 \label{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:continuous-cover}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
In each coordinate, only the nearest face can give a nonzero boundary
contribution: the opposite face has distance at least
$\ell/2\ge w$.  A tie at distance $w$ contributes zero.  Fix a set
$J$ of $j$ nearest faces.  The integral of the kernel over their
intersection, before multiplication by the face density, is
\begin{equation}
 I_J(a)=\frac1{(k-j+2)!}
   \sum_{S\subseteq[k]\setminus J}
      (-1)^{|S|}2^{k-j-|S|+1}
                    (w-d_{J\cup S})_+^{k-j+2}.
 \label{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:face-integral}
\end{equation}
To verify this formula, begin with unrestricted integration in the
$k-j$ free coordinates.  The integral over a positive orthant is
\[
 \int_{[0,\infty)^r}(t-x_1-\cdots-x_r)_+^2\,dx
   =\frac{2t_+^{r+2}}{(r+2)!}.
\]
Each unrestricted coordinate has two signs.  Excluding a coordinate
beyond its nearest boundary leaves one sign and shifts its distance
variable by $d_i$.  Inclusion--exclusion over the excluded coordinates
therefore gives \eqref{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:face-integral}.

Multiply by \eqref{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:face-weight} and sum over $J$.  The
factorial depending on $j$ cancels.  Group the terms by
$T=J\cup S$, put $t=|T|$, and set $u=(w-d_T)_+$.  If $u=0$,
every grouped term vanishes.  If $u>0$, the grouped contribution is
\begin{align*}
 &\frac{2^{k-t+1}}{(k+2)!}
       \sum_{j=0}^t\binom tj(-1)^{t-j}w^j u^{k-j+2}\\
 &\hspace{12mm}
   =\frac{2^{k-t+1}}{(k+2)!}
           u^{k-t+2}(w-u)^t
   =\frac{2^{k-t+1}}{(k+2)!}
           (w-d_T)_+^{k-t+2}d_T^t.
\end{align*}
This proves \eqref{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:face-identity}.  The empty set supplies
the full mass \eqref{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:kernel-mass}; every other summand is
nonnegative.  At a corner all the other summands vanish, so the
covering level is exact there.
\end{proof}

The dependence of \eqref{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:face-weight} on the ambient dimension
is decisive.  For example the density on a facet is $w/(k+2)$.
The previous exterior-point charging argument used $w/3$ at leading
order.  Integrating in the tangential coordinates before charging the
boundary replaces that dimension-independent weight by the smaller one.

\begin{lemma}[A lattice cover with no interpolation loss]
\label{gsr:fp:63:loc:lem:lattice-cover}
Let $h\ge1$ be an integer, $A=[-h,h]^k\cap\mathbb Z^k$, and
$0<w\le h$.  There is a nonnegative measure $\nu$ on $A$ of total
mass $T_k(2h,w)$ such that
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{c\in A}\nu(c)K_w(a-c)\ge v_kw^{k+2}
 \qquad(a\in A).
 \label{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:lattice-cover}
\end{equation}
Explicitly, put $q(c)=1$ for $-h<c<h$ and $q(\pm h)=1/2$, and
let $B(c)=\{i:c_i\in\{-h,h\}\}$.  Then one can take
\begin{equation}
 \nu(c)=\sum_{J\subseteq B(c)}b_{k,|J|}(w)
                                    \prod_{i\notin J}q(c_i).
 \label{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:lattice-weights}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Translate Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:63:loc:thm:face-cover} to $[-h,h]^k$.
Fix an integer target $a$.  On any closed unit interval with integer
endpoints in a center coordinate $c_i$, the function
$|a_i-c_i|$ is affine.  Thus $K_w(a-c)$ is convex in that coordinate
on the interval, because $t\mapsto(t_+)^2$ is convex.  It follows
by successive interpolation in all coordinates that rounding a
continuous center to adjacent lattice endpoints, with independent
roundings preserving each coordinate's mean, can only increase the
expected kernel value.

This single rounding probability kernel is independent of $a$.
Apply it to the continuous face measure.  It preserves total mass
and increases the convolution simultaneously at every integer target.
An interior integer receives integrated weight one from its two
adjacent unit intervals; an endpoint receives one-half from its sole
adjacent interval.  A coordinate fixed on a face is unchanged.
These observations give \eqref{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:lattice-weights}, and
\eqref{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:lattice-cover} follows from
\eqref{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:continuous-cover}.  Summing the weights also gives
\eqref{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:face-mass} with $\ell=2h$ directly.
\end{proof}

Global convexity of $K_w$ is neither asserted nor needed.  Convexity
on each coordinate interval with integer endpoints is the property
that makes the simultaneous rounding valid.

\subsection{From any positive cover to local cube mass}

We give the precise analytic interface used to insert the new cover.
The mechanism in this subsection is the preceding report's
positive-cover argument \cite{localphase63}.

Let $N>k+1$ be prime, and let $\tau:G^k\to G$ be multi-affine.
For functions $f_\epsilon:G\to\mathbb C$ indexed by
$\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^k$, write
\begin{equation}
 F(a)=\sum_{s\in G}e_N(-s\tau(a))
       \prod_{\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^k}
          \mathcal C^{|\epsilon|}f_\epsilon(s-\epsilon\cdot a),
 \qquad E_A=\sum_{a\in A}|F(a)|^2,
 \label{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:F}
\end{equation}
where $A\subset\mathbb Z^k$ is finite and integer arguments are
reduced modulo $N$.  No bound on the $f_\epsilon$ is required here.

\begin{lemma}[Positive-cover localization]
\label{gsr:fp:63:loc:lem:positive-interface}
Let $3\le M<N$, $w=N/M$, and $U=\lceil w\rceil$.  Suppose a
nonzero nonnegative measure $\nu$ on a finite set
$C\subset\mathbb Z^k$ has total mass $T$ and satisfies
\[
 \sum_{c\in C}\nu(c)K_w(a-c)\ge\kappa\qquad(a\in A).
\]
Then for some $c\in C$, some $\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^k$, a polynomial
$\phi_\epsilon^c$ of degree at most $k+1$, and a partition
$\mathcal Q$ into intervals of lengths $\lfloor w\rfloor$ or
$\lceil w\rceil$, one has
\begin{equation}
 \mathsf B_k\bigl(f_\epsilon(\,\cdot-\epsilon\cdot c)
                    e_N(-\phi_\epsilon^c);\mathcal Q,U\bigr)
 \ge\frac{E_A\kappa}{N^2T U^{k+2}}.
 \label{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:positive-interface}
\end{equation}
The polynomials are explicitly determined by the recentered
multi-affine polynomial $\tau_c(b)=\tau(b+c)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Put
$E_c=\sum_{a\in A}K_w(a-c)|F(a)|^2$.
The cover implies $\sum_c\nu(c)E_c\ge\kappa E_A$, so choose
$c$ with $E_c\ge\kappa E_A/T$.  Let
\[
 f_\epsilon^c(x)=f_\epsilon(x-\epsilon\cdot c),\qquad
 \tau_c(b)=\tau(b+c).
\]
The corresponding expression satisfies $F^c(b)=F(b+c)$.

Embed $G$ into $\mathbb Z/(NM)\mathbb Z$ by $x\mapsto Mx$ and
define windows
\[
 S_t=\{x\in G:(Mx-t)\bmod NM\in\{1,\ldots,N\}\},
 \qquad t\in\mathbb Z/(NM)\mathbb Z.
\]
Every $S_t$ is a cyclic interval of size $\lfloor w\rfloor$ or
$\lceil w\rceil$.  For $0\le j<N$, the family
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal P_j=(S_{j+\ell N})_{0\le\ell<M}
 \label{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:sliding-partitions}
\end{equation}
is a partition: the corresponding $M$ blocks of $N$ consecutive
residues partition the larger cyclic group.

If $b\in\mathbb Z^k$ has $D(b)=\|b\|_1<w$, the integer span
of the cube vertices $s-\epsilon\cdot b$ is exactly $D(b)$.
Exactly $N-MD(b)$ windows contain all the vertices.  In the embedded
circle their span is $MD(b)<N$; the possible starts of a containing
block form an interval with $N-MD(b)$ integers.  There is no
additional containing arc, because $D(b)<w<N/2$ makes the
complementary gap longer than the block length.

Let $F_t^c(b)$ denote $F^c(b)$ with each vertex function restricted
to $S_t$.  The window count gives
\[
 \sum_tF_t^c(b)=(N-MD(b))F^c(b).
\]
The set $\mathcal D=(A-c)\cap\{b:\|b\|_1<w\}$ embeds
injectively into $G^k$, since $2w<N$.  Cauchy--Schwarz over the
$NM$ windows therefore gives
\begin{align}
 M^2E_c
 &\le NM\sum_t\sum_{b\in\mathcal D}|F_t^c(b)|^2\notag\\
 &\le NM\sum_t\sum_{b\in G^k}|F_t^c(b)|^2.
 \label{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:window-cs}
\end{align}
The domain is enlarged while every summand is a nonnegative square.

For completeness, write
$\tau_c(b)=\sum_{J\subseteq[k]}d_J\prod_{i\in J}b_i$ and set
\begin{equation}
 \phi_\epsilon^c(X)=
   \sum_{J\supseteq\operatorname{supp}(\epsilon)}
       \frac{d_J}{(|J|+1)!}X^{|J|+1}.
 \label{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:polarization-phase}
\end{equation}
All factorials are invertible modulo $N$.  The finite-difference
identity
\[
 \sum_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^r}(-1)^{|\omega|}
              (s-\omega\cdot z)^r=r!\prod_{i=1}^r z_i
\]
applied separately to each $J$ yields
\begin{equation}
 y\tau_c(b)=
  \sum_{\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^k}\sum_{z=0}^1
       (-1)^{|\epsilon|+z}
         \phi_\epsilon^c(s-\epsilon\cdot b-zy).
 \label{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:polarization}
\end{equation}
Put $g_\epsilon^c=f_\epsilon^c e_N(-\phi_\epsilon^c)$.
Expand a square in \eqref{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:window-cs}, writing its second base
variable as $s-y$.  Its phase is $e_N(-y\tau_c(b))$.
Identity \eqref{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:polarization} absorbs this phase into the
vertex functions.  The mixed Gowers--Cauchy--Schwarz inequality gives
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{b\in G^k}|F_t^c(b)|^2
 \le\prod_{\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^k}
      \mathsf C_{k+1}(\mathbf 1_{S_t}g_\epsilon^c)^{1/2^k}.
 \label{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:mixed-gcs}
\end{equation}
Each first-$k$-coordinate vertex occurs twice with the same function,
which explains the exponent $2^{-k}$.

H\"older's inequality in $t$ and \eqref{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:window-cs} imply
\[
 \prod_{\epsilon}
     \left(\sum_t\mathsf C_{k+1}
                  (\mathbf 1_{S_t}g_\epsilon^c)\right)^{1/2^k}
 \ge\frac MN E_c.
\]
One factor is at least $(M/N)E_c$.  Fix that $\epsilon$.
Every window occurs exactly once among the $N$ partitions
\eqref{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:sliding-partitions}, so some partition has cube sum
at least $(M/N^2)E_c$.  Divide by $MU^{k+2}$ and use
$E_c\ge\kappa E_A/T$ to obtain
\eqref{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:positive-interface}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The finite theorem and its sharp asymptotic consequence}

\begin{theorem}[Explicit finite coefficient]
\label{gsr:fp:63:loc:thm:finite}
Assume \eqref{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:input}, $m=2h+1>3k$, and $m^2\le N$.
Put
\begin{equation}
 L=\left\lceil\frac m{3k}\right\rceil,\qquad
 M=\left\lfloor\frac NL\right\rfloor,\qquad
 w=\frac NM,
 \label{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:finite-parameters}
\end{equation}
and assume $w\le h$.  There are a polynomial $\phi$ of degree at
most $k+1$ and a partition into progressions of lengths $L$ or
$L+1$, with the same common difference $d$ as the input, such that
\begin{equation}
 \mathsf B_k(f e_N(-\phi);\mathcal Q,L+1)
 \ge\alpha R_{k,m,N},\qquad
 R_{k,m,N}=v_k
   \frac{m^k w^{k+2}}{T_k(m-1,w)(L+1)^{k+2}}.
 \label{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:finite-coefficient}
\end{equation}
The additional condition $w\le h$ is automatic when $k\ge2$,
and when $k=1,m\ge9$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Put $\widetilde f(t)=f(dt)$, $q_i=d^{-1}r_i$, and
\[
 f_\epsilon(t)=\widetilde f(t-\epsilon\cdot q),\qquad
 \tau(a)=d\sigma(r+da).
\]
The polynomial $\tau$ is multi-affine.  Substituting $s=dt$ into
each Fourier sum in \eqref{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:input} gives exactly
\eqref{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:F}, with these functions.  Thus their input energy
is at least $\alpha N^2m^k$ on
$A=[-h,h]^k\cap\mathbb Z^k$.

One has $2\le L\le m$, $M\ge L$, and $3\le M<N$.
Writing $N=LM+r$, $0\le r<L$, gives
$L\le w<L+1$.  In fact $r>0$, since $N$ is prime and $2\le L<N$,
so $\lfloor w\rfloor=L$ and $\lceil w\rceil=L+1$.
Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:63:loc:lem:lattice-cover} and then
Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:63:loc:lem:positive-interface}, with
\[
 T=T_k(m-1,w),\qquad \kappa=v_kw^{k+2}.
\]
This gives \eqref{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:finite-coefficient} for one of the functions
$\widetilde f(s-\epsilon\cdot(q+c))e_N(-\phi_\epsilon^c(s))$.
If $b=\epsilon\cdot(q+c)$, translate the variable by
$b$.  The resulting function is
$\widetilde f(s)e_N(-\phi_\epsilon^c(s+b))$, and the support partition is
translated by $-b$.  Polynomial degree is preserved.  Reversing the
initial dilation gives the original function $f(x)$ twisted by
$\phi(x)=\phi_\epsilon^c(d^{-1}x+b)$, on progressions of common
difference $d$.  This again preserves the polynomial degree.

For the claimed width condition, $L+1\le h$ is equivalent to
$(3k-2)h\ge3k+1$.  It holds when $k=1,h\ge4$, and for every
$k\ge2$ in the range $m>3k$.  Since $w<L+1$, this is sufficient.
Finally, $L\ge m/(3k)$ and $L+1\le m/3+2\le m$ in the stated
range, so every output length has the required bounds.
\end{proof}

For the two excluded pairs $(k,m)=(1,5),(1,7)$, or for the branch
$m\le3k$, the preceding finite localization results remain available.
Those finitely many scales do not affect Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:63:loc:thm:headline}.
The new finite expression is not claimed to dominate every earlier
finite expression at the smallest parameters.

\begin{corollary}[Uniform finite bounds and joint scale limits]
\label{gsr:fp:63:loc:cor:joint-scale}
For the finite coefficient in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:63:loc:thm:finite},
\begin{equation}
 \exp\!\left(-\frac{k+2}{L}
             -\frac{2kw}{(k+2)(m-1)}\right)
 \le\frac{R_{k,m,N}}{v_k}
 \le\exp\!\left(\frac{k}{m-1}\right).
 \label{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:finite-exponential}
\end{equation}
More precisely, let $k\to\infty$ along any sequence of admissible
parameters.  If $m/k^2\to\lambda\in[0,\infty]$, then, uniformly
over the choices of prime $N\ge m^2$,
\begin{equation}
 \frac{R_{k,m,N}}{v_k}\longrightarrow
 \begin{cases}
   0,&\lambda=0,\\
   e^{-3/\lambda},&0<\lambda<\infty,\\
   1,&\lambda=\infty.
 \end{cases}
 \label{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:joint-scale-limit}
\end{equation}
In particular, this finite construction has relative retention tending
to one whenever $m/k^2\to\infty$.  The assertion concerns the
explicit coefficient $R_{k,m,N}$, and does not assert that this scale
condition is necessary for the unknown optimal finite theorem.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Write $\ell=m-1$ and
\[
 H_k(z)=\sum_{j=0}^k\binom kj
              \frac{(k-j+2)!}{(k+2)!}z^j.
\]
Equation \eqref{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:term-bound}, whose elementary product proof
does not depend on the choice of $z$, gives
\[
 1\le H_k(z)\le e^{kz/(k+2)}\qquad(z\ge0).
\]
The exact expression for the coefficient is
\begin{equation}
 \frac{R_{k,m,N}}{v_k}
   =\left(\frac m\ell\right)^k
       \left(\frac w{L+1}\right)^{k+2}
       H_k(2w/\ell)^{-1}.
 \label{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:joint-factorization}
\end{equation}
Use $1\le(m/\ell)^k\le e^{k/\ell}$,
$L/(L+1)\le w/(L+1)<1$, and
$(L/(L+1))^{k+2}\ge e^{-(k+2)/L}$ to obtain
\eqref{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:finite-exponential}.

The partition rounding is particularly small.  Since $m>3k$,
$L<2m/(3k)$; also $M\ge N/(2L)$.  Hence, uniformly over
$N\ge m^2$,
\begin{equation}
 0<w-L<\frac LM\le\frac{2L^2}{N}
                         <\frac8{9k^2}.
 \label{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:uniform-rounding}
\end{equation}
If $0<\lambda\le\infty$, then $m/k\to\infty$ and
$L\sim m/(3k)$.  In the logarithm of
\eqref{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:joint-factorization}, the first factor contributes
$k\log(m/\ell)=o(1)$ and the last contributes
$0\le\log H_k(2w/\ell)\le2kw/((k+2)\ell)=o(1)$.
Furthermore \eqref{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:uniform-rounding} gives
\begin{align*}
 (k+2)\log\frac w{L+1}
 &=-(k+2)\log(1+L^{-1})
                  +(k+2)\log\left(1+\frac{w-L}{L}\right)\\
 &=-\frac{k+2}{L}+O(k/L^2)+O(1/(kL))
   \longrightarrow-\frac3\lambda,
\end{align*}
with $3/\infty=0$.  This proves the positive and infinite cases.

If $\lambda=0$, then $L=o(k)$, while $k/(m-1)\le1/3$.
For sufficiently large $k$, \eqref{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:uniform-rounding} gives
$w\le L+1/2$.  Therefore
\[
 0\le\frac{R_{k,m,N}}{v_k}
 \le e^{1/3}\left(1-\frac1{2(L+1)}\right)^{k+2}
 \le\exp\!\left(\frac13-\frac{k+2}{2(L+1)}\right)
 \longrightarrow0.
\]
All estimates are uniform in the ambient prime, completing the proof.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of the lower bound in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:63:loc:thm:headline}]
For fixed $k$, uniformly for $N\ge m^2$, one has
\[
 \frac wm=\frac1{3k}+O_k(m^{-1}),\qquad
 \frac w{L+1}=1+O_k(m^{-1}),\qquad
 \frac{m-1}{m}=1+O(m^{-1}).
\]
Substitution into \eqref{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:face-mass} gives
\[
 \frac{T_k(m-1,w)}{m^k}=D_k+O_k(m^{-1}).
\]
Equation \eqref{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:finite-coefficient} therefore proves
\eqref{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:headline}.  The first two terms of $D_k$ give the
lower bound in \eqref{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:D-bound}.  For the upper bound, observe
that
\begin{equation}
 \binom kj\frac{(k-j+2)!}{(k+2)!}
 =\frac1{j!}\prod_{r=0}^{j-1}\frac{k-r}{k+2-r}
 \le\frac1{j!}\left(\frac{k}{k+2}\right)^j.
 \label{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:term-bound}
\end{equation}
Comparison with the exponential series proves
$D_k\le e^{2/[3(k+2)]}$ and the stated expansion.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The local geometric ceiling]
\label{gsr:fp:63:loc:prop:ceiling}
In the class defining $c_k^{\mathrm{loc}}$, no asymptotic
coefficient exceeds $v_k$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Use $f\equiv1$, $\sigma\equiv0$, and $\alpha=1$ in
\eqref{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:input}.  Every polynomial twist has modulus one,
so the triangle inequality in the cube expansion gives
\[
 0\le\mathsf C_{k+1}(\mathbf 1_Q f e_N(-\phi))
       \le\mathsf C_{k+1}(\mathbf 1_Q).
\]
Let $A_r(t)$ be the number of integer $r$-cubes contained in an
interval of length $t$.  Their span is the sum of the absolute
increments, whence
\begin{equation}
 A_r(t)=\sum_{a\in\mathbb Z^r}
                 (t-\|a\|_1)_+,
 \qquad
 \sum_{t\ge0}A_r(t)z^t
        =\frac{z(1+z)^r}{(1-z)^{r+2}}.
 \label{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:interval-cubes}
\end{equation}
Coefficient extraction yields
\[
 A_r(t)=\frac{2^r}{(r+1)!}t^{r+1}+O_r(t^r).
\]
For a proper progression $Q\subset G$, an invertible dilation
identifies it with an interval.  If $N>2r|Q|$, every cube with all
vertices in that interval has consistent integer lifts: the
congruences between its lifted vertices differ by less than $N$,
and hence are integer equalities.  Thus its modular cube count is
$A_r(|Q|)$.  For fixed $k$, this condition holds eventually
uniformly when $|Q|\le m$ and $N\ge m^2$.

Take $r=k+1$.  All cell sizes satisfy $|Q|\ge m/(3k)$, so
\[
 \mathsf C_{k+1}(\mathbf 1_Q)
 \le\bigl(v_k+O_k(m^{-1})\bigr)|Q|^{k+2}.
\]
Sum over cells and divide by $M U^{k+2}$, using $|Q|\le U$.
The quotient is at most $v_k+O_k(m^{-1})$, proving the ceiling.
\end{proof}

The proposition and the lower bound prove
\eqref{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:sharp-asymptotic}.  In particular, the theorem closes
the constant-factor asymptotic gap left by the previous positive
cover.  It establishes neither an exact fixed-degree optimum nor
a new global bound for Szemer\'edi's theorem.

\subsection{Comparison with the earlier covering coefficient}

The previous coefficient \cite{localphase63} was $v_k/\widehat D_k$, where
\[
 \widehat D_k=\sum_{j=0}^k\binom kj
       \left(\frac2{3k}\right)^j\frac2{(j+2)!},\qquad
 \widehat D_k\longrightarrow1.2415870899\ldots.
\]
For $0\le j\le k$,
\[
 \frac{(k-j+2)!}{(k+2)!}\le\frac2{(j+2)!},
\]
because $\binom{k+2}{j}\ge\binom{j+2}{j}$.  It follows that
$D_k\le\widehat D_k$, with strict inequality for $k\ge2$.
At $k=1$ both denominators are $11/9$.  Some retained fractions of
the common ceiling are listed below; the checks in the accompanying
script use rational arithmetic before decimal presentation.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{rccc}
\hline
$k$ & previous $1/\widehat D_k$ & new $1/D_k$ & exact new value where short\\
\hline
1   & $0.81818$ & $0.81818$ & $9/11$\\
2   & $0.81203$ & $0.85039$ & $108/127$\\
3   & $0.80988$ & $0.87648$ & $10935/12476$\\
4   & $0.80879$ & $0.89540$ & $93312/104213$\\
8   & $0.80712$ & $0.93556$ & \\
20  & $0.80610$ & $0.97015$ & \\
100 & $0.80556$ & $0.99349$ & \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The denominator has the useful equivalent expression
\begin{equation}
 D_k=\frac1{(k+1)(k+2)}
       \sum_{j=0}^k
          \frac{(k-j+1)(k-j+2)}{j!}
                         \left(\frac2{3k}\right)^j.
 \label{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:closed-denominator}
\end{equation}
For example, expanding its first four terms and bounding the
positive remainder gives
\[
 D_k=1+\frac2{3k}-\frac{10}{9k^2}
                    +\frac{148}{81k^3}+O(k^{-4}),
\]
and hence
\[
 \frac1{D_k}=1-\frac2{3k}+\frac{14}{9k^2}
                    -\frac{292}{81k^3}+O(k^{-4}).
\]
These are expansions of the proved lower coefficient, not of the
unknown optimum $c_k^{\mathrm{loc}}/v_k$.

\subsection{Other powers of the kernel}

The positive identity extends beyond the square kernel.  This
geometric generalization is independent of its present application
to Proposition~17.7.

\begin{theorem}[Positive-power face covers]
\label{gsr:fp:63:loc:thm:power-cover}
Let $s>0$, $K_{w,s}(x)=(w-\|x\|_1)_+^s$, and $0<w\le\ell/2$.
On every codimension-$j$ face of $[0,\ell]^k$ place density
\[
 b_{k,j,s}(w)=
       \frac{\Gamma(k-j+s+1)}{\Gamma(k+s+1)}w^j,
\]
and let $\mu_s$ be the sum of these measures.  With $d_S$ as in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:63:loc:thm:face-cover},
\begin{equation}
 \int K_{w,s}(a-c)\,d\mu_s(c)
 =\frac{\Gamma(s+1)}{\Gamma(k+s+1)}
   \sum_{S\subseteq[k]}2^{k-|S|}d_S^{|S|}
                  (w-d_S)_+^{k-|S|+s}.
 \label{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:power-cover}
\end{equation}
In particular this is at least
$2^k\Gamma(s+1)w^{k+s}/\Gamma(k+s+1)$, the full integral of the
kernel.  If $s\ge1$, the same cover passes to integer centers by
the interpolation procedure of Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:63:loc:lem:lattice-cover},
with unchanged mass and the corresponding face weights.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Replace the simplex integral in \eqref{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:face-integral} by
\[
 \int_{[0,\infty)^r}(t-x_1-\cdots-x_r)_+^s\,dx
   =\frac{\Gamma(s+1)}{\Gamma(r+s+1)}t_+^{r+s}.
\]
The face density cancels the denominator exactly.  The same
inclusion--exclusion grouping leaves
$u^{k-|S|+s}(w-u)^{|S|}$, proving
\eqref{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:power-cover}.  All exponents at $u=0$ are positive
because $s>0$.  For the lattice assertion,
$t\mapsto(t_+)^s$ is convex for $s\ge1$, so the separate-cell
convexity and mean-preserving rounding proof is unchanged.
\end{proof}

The exact verification file checks the lattice cover and its mass
at $10{,}980$ integer targets in $32$ parameter cases.  These checks
exercise boundary intersections, half-integer widths, and the
endpoint weights.  They support implementation of the formulas;
the general results follow from the proofs above.
