\begin{example}[An explicit optimal cubic conversion over $\mathbb F_3$]\label{gsr:fp:91:ex:three}
Take $P(t)=\digit t/9$, $\zeta=\e(1/9)$, and $\omega=\e(1/3)$. Here $Q=0$, and the three classical candidates are
\[
 R_0=0,\qquad R_1=-\frac{\ind_{t=0}}3,\qquad
 R_2=-\frac{\ind_{t\in\{0,1\}}}3.
\]
As functions into $\Fp$, the indicator polynomials are
\[
 \ind_{t=0}=1-t^2,\qquad
 \ind_{t\in\{0,1\}}=(t+1)^2.
\]
Thus the correction phases are genuinely quadratic classical phases, not arbitrary high-degree functions. The pointwise identity is
\[
 (1,\zeta,\zeta^2)=\frac1{3d_0}
 \bigl[(1,1,1)+\zeta(\omega^{-1},1,1)
                +\zeta^2(\omega^{-1},\omega^{-1},1)\bigr].
\]
For every $f:\mathbb F_3\to\C$, one of these candidates has correlation at least
\[
 \frac{\sin(\pi/3)}{3\sin(\pi/9)}
 \abs{\E_t f(t)\e(-\digit t/9)}.
\]
Taking $f=\e(P)$ makes all three correlations equal in modulus to $0.8440296287\ldots$, and no classical phase of any degree does better.
\end{example}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Classical degree equals reduced-polynomial degree\srctag{91}}]{Classical degree equals reduced-polynomial degree}\label{gsr:fp:91:sec:dA}\label{gsr:fp:91:app:classical}
\srcnote{91}{Appendix A}

Every function $q:\Fp^n\to\Fp$ has a unique representation by a polynomial in which the exponent of each variable is at most $p-1$. Existence follows by interpolation in each coordinate, and uniqueness follows because a polynomial of degree below $p$ in one variable cannot vanish at every field element unless it is zero, followed by induction on $n$.

The zero function is immediate. For a nonzero function, let $D$ be the largest total degree of a monomial with nonzero coefficient. An arbitrary first difference lowers total degree by at least one before reduction, and reduction modulo $X_i^p-X_i$ cannot increase degree. Hence the additive degree is at most $D$.

Choose a nonzero degree-$D$ monomial $cX_1^{e_1}\cdots X_n^{e_n}$. Apply $e_i$ differences in the $i$th coordinate. Any other monomial of total degree at most $D$ either equals that exponent vector or has some coordinate exponent smaller than the corresponding $e_i$ and is annihilated. The chosen monomial produces the nonzero constant
\[
 c\prod_{i=1}^ne_i!,
\]
since each $e_i<p$. Therefore a $D$-fold difference does not vanish, and the additive degree is at least $D$.

This proves the claimed equivalence and, in particular, justifies treating the depth-zero candidates in example~\ref{gsr:fp:91:ex:three} as ordinary classical polynomials. It also explains why an arbitrary function of one $\Fp$ coordinate is classical of degree at most $p-1$, but an arbitrary function on $\Fp^n$ need not have that degree bound.

\section{Source~97: every maximizer of the canonical Boolean tensor and sharp dimension-free stability \wtag}\label{gsr:fp:sec:boolendpoint}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the fourteenth write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next twelve sections are source~97's Sections~2--12 and Appendix~A. \emph{Logically they continue} source~47's chapter (Section~\ref{gsr:fp:sec:boolenergy}) and the all-degree chapter of sources~65 and~69 (Section~\ref{gsr:fp:sec:alldegree}). The introduction (a repository reconnaissance) is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:97:sec:d1}.

\emph{What is proved.} For the canonical symmetric tensor $C_d^{u,v}$ on $\Ftwo^n$, $d\ge4$, the threshold $b_d=1-(d+1)/2^d$ is attained exactly by $\Ext_d(u)=\{e(P+\theta|u|):\deg P\le d-1,\theta\in\R\}$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:97:thm:classification}), and through the integrable gauge by $e(P_S)\Ext_d(u)$ for $C_d^{u,v}+S$ (Corollary~\ref{gsr:fp:97:cor:gauge-main}); stability is dimension-free, $D\le(2/m_d)\delta+O(\delta^{3/2})$ with $m_d=2^d-2d-2$, and the coefficient $2/m_d$ is optimal already on $\Ftwo^2$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:97:thm:stability}); an exact four-point energy identity (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:97:thm:binary}) and the full transverse Hessian spectrum (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:97:thm:hessian}). The entry step imports Eisner and Tao's qualitative theorem, so the entry threshold $\eta_d$ and the constant $A_d$ are not numerical. The cubic case is open ($m_3=0$; source~97's Research question~3).

\emph{Against sources~47, 65 and~69.} Source~47 proved the canonical maximum $b_d$ in every degree and said its proofs classify neither all endpoint tensors nor all maximizing functions (its subsection ``Strict margins, not conclusions at equality''); sources~65 and~69 proved, independently, the universal threshold, the endpoint-tensor classification and the noncanonical gap $\gamma_d=(d-2)/2^{d+1}$, and both asked the stability question (65's Research question~\ref{gsr:fz:65:bsi:q:phases}, 69's ``Dimension-free phase stability''). \emph{Source~97 answers both for $d\ge4$}, and the function part of item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:IV:boolenergy}; with the tensor classification of sources~65 and~69 this covers every nonintegrable endpoint tensor for $d\ge4$ (its Corollary~\ref{gsr:fp:97:cor:tensor-and-function} imports $\gamma_d$). It credits sources~43, 47 and~55 by number, source~65 by title only, and does not cite source~69 (dated notes). \emph{Notation}: source~97's $\eta_d$ is an entry threshold, source~65's $\eta_d=b_d-\gamma_d$ a rigidity window; its $E_T(f)$ is the $\En_T(f)$ of sources~47 and~65; its $N=2^d$ is not a group order.

\section[{Notation and main results\srctag{97}}]{Notation and main results}\label{gsr:fp:97:sec:d2}\label{gsr:fp:97:sec:main}
\srcnote{97}{Section 2}
All expectations and $L^p$ norms use normalized counting measure. Let
$V=\Ftwo^n$, $n\ge2$, and put $\e(t)=\exp(2\pi i t)$ for $t\in\Tcirc$.
For a linear form $u:V\to\Ftwo$, the notation $|u(x)|$ means its representative
in $\{0,1\}\subset\mathbb Z$. This representative matters in expressions
such as $\theta |u(x)|$, where $\theta\in\Tcirc$ is not necessarily dyadic.
Write $\chi_\xi(x)=(-1)^{\xi(x)}$.

The additive and multiplicative differences are
\[
 \Delta_h P(x)=P(x+h)-P(x),\qquad
 \partial_h f(x)=f(x+h)\overline{f(x)}.
\]
A map $P:V\to\Tcirc$ has degree at most $k$ when every $(k+1)$-fold additive
difference vanishes. We denote this group by $\Poly_{\le k}(V,\Tcirc)$;
constants are included. No classical-polynomial restriction is imposed.

For a symmetric $d$-linear tensor $T:V^d\to\Ftwo$, define
\begin{equation}
 \En_T(f)=\E_{h_1,\ldots,h_{d-1}}
 \left|\E_x\partial_{h_1}\cdots\partial_{h_{d-1}}f(x)
                (-1)^{T(h_1,\ldots,h_{d-1},x)}\right|^2.
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:energy}
\end{equation}
Let $u,v\in V^*$ be independent and set
\begin{align}
 C_d^{u,v}(h_1,\ldots,h_d)
   &=\sum_{i=1}^d v(h_i)\prod_{j\ne i}u(h_j),\\
 b_d&=1-\frac{d+1}{2^d},\qquad m_d=2^d-2d-2.\label{gsr:fp:97:eq:constants}
\end{align}
The canonical maximum $b_d$ is an existing result~\cite{srcfortyseven,srcsixtyfive}; the necessary
proof and equality information are recalled in Section~\ref{gsr:fp:97:sec:cap}.
For $d\ge4$ define
\begin{equation}
 \Ext_d(u)=\{\e(P+\theta |u|):P\in\Poly_{\le d-1}(V,\Tcirc),\ \theta\in\Tcirc\}.
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:family}
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Complete canonical extremizers]\label{gsr:fp:97:thm:classification}
Let $d\ge4$ and $|f|\le1$. Then
\begin{equation}
 \En_{C_d^{u,v}}(f)=b_d\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f\in\Ext_d(u).
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:classification}
\end{equation}
In particular, every maximizing function is unimodular. The family depends
on $u$, but not on the choice of its independent companion $v$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{What this answers} (Section~\ref{gsr:fp:sec:boolendpoint}). For $d\ge4$, source~65's Research question~\ref{gsr:fz:65:bsi:q:phases} and source~69's ``Dimension-free phase stability'' (with Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:97:thm:stability}), and the function part of item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:IV:boolenergy}; it supersedes, for $d\ge4$, source~47's remark that its proofs do not classify the maximizing functions. The threshold $b_d$ and the endpoint-tensor classification it builds on were proved independently by sources~65 and~69; this source cites source~65 by title only and does not cite source~69. Checked at the write: the table of $b_d$, $m_d$, $2/m_d$ for $d=4,\ldots,9$.
\end{writenote}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp dimension-free stability]\label{gsr:fp:97:thm:stability}
Fix $d\ge4$. For $|f|\le1$ write
\[
 \delta(f)=b_d-\En_{C_d^{u,v}}(f),\qquad
 D(f)=\min_{g\in\Ext_d(u)}\norm{f-g}_2^2.
\]
There is a finite $A_d$, independent of $n,u,v$, such that
\begin{equation}
 D(f)\le A_d\delta(f).\label{gsr:fp:97:eq:global-stability}
\end{equation}
More precisely, put $N=2^d$ and
\begin{equation}
 K_d=3^N+3N^2.\label{gsr:fp:97:eq:K}
\end{equation}
There is an $\eta_d>0$, independent of dimension, such that whenever
$0\le\delta(f)\le\eta_d$,
\begin{equation}
 D(f)\le \frac{2}{m_d}\delta(f)
       +\frac{8K_d}{m_d^{5/2}}\delta(f)^{3/2}.
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:sharp-stability}
\end{equation}
The leading coefficient $2/m_d$ cannot be decreased, even in dimension two.
The constants $K_d$ and the local radius in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:97:thm:local} are explicit;
this paper does not extract a numerical value of the entry threshold $\eta_d$
or of the all-deficit constant $A_d$ from the qualitative input.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Notation.} This source's $\eta_d$ is the entry threshold of its Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:97:prop:ET} (qualitative, from Eisner and Tao), not source~65's $\eta_d=b_d-\gamma_d$; $A_d$ is not numerical for the same reason.
\end{writenote}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}rrrr@{}}
\toprule
$d$ & Existing energy endpoint $b_d$ & Transverse gap $m_d$ & Sharp coefficient $2/m_d$\\
\midrule
4 & $11/16$ & $6$ & $1/3$\\
5 & $13/16$ & $20$ & $1/10$\\
6 & $57/64$ & $50$ & $1/25$\\
7 & $15/16$ & $112$ & $1/56$\\
8 & $247/256$ & $238$ & $1/119$\\
9 & $251/256$ & $492$ & $1/246$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The distance is squared $L^2$ distance and the energy is normalized as
in~\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:energy}; changing either convention changes the displayed coefficient.

A tensor $S$ is called integrable if there is a $P_S\in\Poly_{\le d}(V,\Tcirc)$
with $\Delta_{h_1}\cdots\Delta_{h_d}P_S=S(h_1,\ldots,h_d)/2$.
\begin{corollary}[Integrable gauge]\label{gsr:fp:97:cor:gauge-main}
For $T=C_d^{u,v}+S$ with primitive $P_S$, its maximizing functions are exactly
\[
 \e(P_S)\Ext_d(u).
\]
Both stability statements hold with distance to this family and deficit
$b_d-\En_T(f)$, with the same constants.
\end{corollary}
Different choices of $P_S$ differ by a polynomial of degree at most $d-1$,
so this family is independent of the choice of primitive.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Cube identities and the canonical cap\srctag{97}}]{Cube identities and the canonical cap}\label{gsr:fp:97:sec:d3}\label{gsr:fp:97:sec:cap}
\srcnote{97}{Section 3}
This section records the existing quantitative ingredient with the equality
information needed later. The argument follows the project sequence
\cite{srcfortythree,srcfortyseven,srcsixtyfive}; none of its upper bounds is claimed as a new result here.

\subsection{Exact identities}
Expanding the square in~\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:energy} and putting the second base point equal
to $x+h_d$ gives
\begin{equation}
 \En_T(f)=\E_{x,h_1,\ldots,h_d}
      \partial_{h_1}\cdots\partial_{h_d}f(x)(-1)^{T(h_1,\ldots,h_d)}.
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:cube}
\end{equation}
The average is real and nonnegative by~\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:energy}. Symmetry gives exact slicing,
\begin{equation}
 \En_T(f)=\E_z\En_{T_z}(\partial_z f),\qquad
 T_z(h_1,\ldots,h_{d-1})=T(h_1,\ldots,h_{d-1},z).
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:slicing}
\end{equation}
We use a degree subscript when the order of the zero tensor might be ambiguous:
$\En_0^{(j)}(g)=\norm g_{U^j}^{2^j}$. If $|g|\le1$, H\"older's inequality in
its cube formula gives
\begin{equation}
 0\le\En_0^{(j)}(g)\le\E|g|^{2^j}\le\E|g|^2\le1
 \qquad(j\ge1).
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:amplitude-basic}
\end{equation}
All cube vertices have the same uniform marginal, which is all that this
application of H\"older requires.

If $S$ has primitive $P_S$, then direct multiplication in~\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:cube} gives
\begin{equation}
 \En_{T+S}(f\e(P_S))=\En_T(f).
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:gauge}
\end{equation}
In particular multiplication by $\e(P)$, $\deg P\le d-1$, preserves $\En_T$.

\subsection{The cubic base}
For a bilinear form $B$ on $V$, let
\[
 Q_B(g,h)=\E_a\left|\E_xg(x+a)\overline{h(x)}(-1)^{B(a,x)}\right|^2.
\]
\begin{lemma}[A two-dimensional projective loss]\label{gsr:fp:97:lem:projective}
If $B(a,b)+B(b,a)$ is not identically zero, then
\[
 Q_B(g,h)\le\tfrac12\norm g_2^2\norm h_2^2.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
On $\ell^2(V)$ with normalized inner product define
$U_a g(x)=(-1)^{B(a,x)}g(x+a)$. These operators are unitary and satisfy
$U_aU_b=(-1)^{B(b,a)}U_{a+b}$. The positive operator
\[
 M_g=\E_a\,|U_ag\rangle\langle U_ag|
\]
commutes with every $U_b$, has trace $\norm g_2^2$, and satisfies
$Q_B(g,h)=\ip{M_gh}{h}$. Choose $a,b$ with
$B(a,b)+B(b,a)=1$. Then $U_aU_b=-U_bU_a$.
Every nonzero eigenspace of $M_g$ is invariant under both operators. Inside
such an eigenspace an eigenvector of $U_a$ with eigenvalue $\lambda$ is sent
by $U_b$ to one with eigenvalue $-\lambda$. Since $\lambda\ne0$, the eigenspace
has dimension at least two. Thus its largest eigenvalue is at most half the
trace, proving the assertion.
\end{proof}

For a symmetric cubic tensor put
\[
 B_w(a,b)=T(a,a,b)+T(a,b,w),\qquad g_w=f\,\tau_w f.
\]
The repeated expression $T(a,a,b)$ is bilinear: the two cross terms in
its first variable cancel by symmetry in characteristic two. Expanding the
square defining $Q_B(g,g)$ gives its real self-cube expression
$\E_{x,a,b}\partial_a\partial_b g(x)(-1)^{B(a,b)}$.
The Boolean identity
$\partial_a\partial_{a+w}f=\overline{\partial_a g_w}$ therefore yields
$\En_T(f)=\E_w Q_{B_w}(g_w,g_w)$. The alternating part of $B_w$ is
$T(a,a,b)+T(a,b,b)$. For $C_3^{u,v}$ it is $u(a)v(b)+v(a)u(b)$, which is
nonzero. Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:97:lem:projective} and $\norm{g_w}_2\le1$ give
$\En_{C_3}(f)\le1/2=b_3$.

\subsection{Derivative periods and the induction}
If $F=\partial_{h_1}\cdots\partial_{h_j}f$, expansion of the labelled cube gives
\begin{equation}
 F(x+h_i)=\overline{F(x)}.\label{gsr:fp:97:eq:period}
\end{equation}
This holds even if $f$ has zeros. Consequently $F$ is invariant under every
even sum of the directions.

Let $U_m=u^{\otimes m}$. It integrates via $|u|/2^m$.
If $u(z)=0$ and $m\ge2$, then
\begin{equation}
 \En_{U_m}(\partial_z f)\le1-2^{1-m}.
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:constrained-pure}
\end{equation}
Indeed, when $u(h_1)=\cdots=u(h_{m-1})=1$, the selected frequency is $u$.
The derivative product has period $h_1+z$, on which $u$ is one, so this Fourier
coefficient vanishes. All remaining squared coefficients are at most one.

The canonical slices satisfy
\[
 (C_d)_z=u(z)C_{d-1}+v(z)U_{d-1}.
\]
The four pairs $(u(z),v(z))$ are equidistributed. On $(0,0)$ the cap is one;
on $(0,1)$ it is $1-2^{2-d}$ by~\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:constrained-pure}; and on $u(z)=1$
it is $b_{d-1}$ by induction, removing $U_{d-1}$ with~\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:gauge} when
necessary. Thus
\begin{equation}
 \En_{C_d}(f)\le\tfrac14+\tfrac14(1-2^{2-d})+\tfrac12b_{d-1}=b_d.
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:canonical-cap}
\end{equation}
For $f=1$, the selected frequency vanishes with probability $b_d$: among the
$d-1$ values $u(h_i)$ it vanishes automatically when at least two are zero,
with conditional probability $1/2$ when exactly one is zero, and never when
none is zero. This proves attainment.

\subsection{The inactive-slice deficit}
Set
\begin{equation}
 R=\ker u\cap\ker v.\label{gsr:fp:97:eq:R}
\end{equation}
Retaining the slack in the $(0,0)$ quarter of the preceding proof gives
\begin{equation}
 \delta(f)\ge\frac14\E_{z\in R}
 \left(1-\En_0^{(d-1)}(\partial_z f)\right).
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:inactive-slack}
\end{equation}
Every discarded slack is nonnegative. In particular,
\begin{equation}
 \E|f|^2\ge1-4\delta(f).\label{gsr:fp:97:eq:mass}
\end{equation}
At equality $\delta=0$, the function is unimodular and
$\En_0^{(d-1)}(\partial_z f)=1$ for every $z\in R$. For a unimodular $g$, a
cube average equal to one means that every cube product equals one. Therefore,
writing $f=\e(P)$ with $P:V\to\Tcirc$,
\begin{equation}
 \Delta_zP\in\Poly_{\le d-2}(V,\Tcirc)\qquad(z\in R).
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:relative-endpoint}
\end{equation}
The next section explains exactly what this condition implies.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Boolean coefficient calculus and relative gluing\srctag{97}}]{Boolean coefficient calculus and relative gluing}\label{gsr:fp:97:sec:d4}\label{gsr:fp:97:sec:gluing}
\srcnote{97}{Section 4}

\subsection{A coordinate normal form}
Choose Boolean coordinates $x_1,\ldots,x_n$. Every map $P:V\to\Tcirc$ has a unique
expansion
\begin{equation}
 P(x)=\sum_{A\subseteq[n]}c_A x_A,\qquad
 x_A=\prod_{i\in A}|x_i|,\qquad
 c_A=\sum_{B\subseteq A}(-1)^{|A|-|B|}P(1_B).
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:mobius}
\end{equation}
The coefficients are in $\Tcirc$; all multiplication outside $\Tcirc$ is by integers.
This is ordinary M\"obius inversion on the Boolean lattice and makes no prior
polynomial assumption.

\begin{lemma}[Degree by coefficients]\label{gsr:fp:97:lem:degree}
For $k\ge0$, the map in~\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:mobius} has degree at most $k$ if and only if
\begin{equation}
 \begin{cases}
 2^{k-|A|+1}c_A=0,&1\le|A|\le k,\\
 c_A=0,&|A|>k.
 \end{cases}\label{gsr:fp:97:eq:degree-coefficients}
\end{equation}
The constant coefficient is unrestricted.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $D_i=\Delta_{e_i}$. Since translation by $e_i$ is an involution,
$D_i^2=-2D_i$. Also $D_AP(0)=c_A$ for a square-free product $D_A$.
A polynomial of degree at most $k$ has all differences of order at least
$k+1$ equal to zero. Applying $D_A$, with repetitions of any one index of
$A$ until the order is $k+1$, proves the first condition. When $|A|>k$, use
$D_A$ itself.

Conversely consider a monomial $c_Ax_A$ obeying the stated conditions.
A product of $k+1$ coordinate differences is zero if it uses an index outside
$A$. Otherwise, if $B\subseteq A$ is the set of indices used, it is
$(-2)^{k+1-|B|}D_B(c_Ax_A)$ and is annihilated by the required torsion of $c_A$.
The same holds for higher-order products. Finally
$\Delta_h=\prod_{i:h_i=1}(1+D_i)-1$, so a product of $k+1$ arbitrary
differences expands into coordinate products of order at least $k+1$.
This proves sufficiency.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact relative polynomial gluing]\label{gsr:fp:97:thm:gluing}
Let $R\le V$, let $q:V\to V/R$ be the quotient, and let $d\ge2$.
For an arbitrary map $P:V\to\Tcirc$, the following are equivalent:
\begin{align}
 &\Delta_zP\in\Poly_{\le d-2}(V,\Tcirc)\quad\text{for every }z\in R;
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:gluing-hyp}\\
 &P=P_0+Q\circ q,\quad P_0\in\Poly_{\le d-1}(V,\Tcirc),\quad
               Q:V/R\to\Tcirc\text{ arbitrary}.\label{gsr:fp:97:eq:gluing-conclusion}
\end{align}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Choose coordinates so that the first $c=\codim R$ are quotient coordinates.
Suppose~\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:gluing-hyp}. For a set $A$ meeting the remaining coordinates,
choose $i\in A$ corresponding to a basis vector in $R$. The product of
coordinate differences indexed by $A$, with repetitions of $i$ if needed,
can be written as $D_i$ followed by at least $d-1$ differences. It therefore
annihilates $P$ once the total order is at least $d$. Evaluation at zero gives
\[
 2^{d-|A|}c_A=0\quad(1\le|A|\le d-1),\qquad c_A=0\quad(|A|\ge d).
\]
Thus the sum of the monomials whose supports meet $R$ has degree at most
$d-1$, by Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:97:lem:degree}. The remaining monomials depend only on the
quotient coordinates. These are $P_0$ and $Q$, respectively.
The reverse implication follows by differentiating: $Q\circ q$ is invariant
under $R$, and a derivative lowers polynomial degree by one.
\end{proof}

This statement is stronger than polynomiality on each individual coset.
It retains derivatives in arbitrary ambient directions after the initial
$R$ direction. Separate polynomial descriptions on cosets need not glue at
the same degree without these mixed constraints.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{An exact four-point energy identity\srctag{97}}]{An exact four-point energy identity}\label{gsr:fp:97:sec:d5}\label{gsr:fp:97:sec:binary}
\srcnote{97}{Section 5}
Let $V_0=\Ftwo^2$, with coordinates $u,v$, and let $g:V_0\to S^1$.
Choose real lifts of a phase $p$ with $g=\e(p)$, and write its real Walsh expansion
\begin{equation}
 p=c+\alpha\chi_u+\beta\chi_v+\gamma\chi_{u+v}.
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:walsh-phase}
\end{equation}
Put
\begin{equation}
 X=\cos(2\pi2^d\alpha),\quad Y=\cos(2\pi2^d\beta),\quad
 Z=\cos(2\pi2^d\gamma),\quad s=(-1)^d.
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:XYZ}
\end{equation}
For $d\ge2$ these cosines are independent of the choices of the four lifts:
a change of lifts changes each Walsh coefficient by a multiple of $1/4$.

\begin{theorem}[The binary functional]\label{gsr:fp:97:thm:binary}
For $d\ge3$,
\begin{align}
 4^d\En_{C_d}(g)
  ={}&4^d-(d+3)2^d+4d+3-(1+s)X\notag\\
     &+(2^d-2d-2)(Y+Z)+XZ+YZ+sXY.
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:binary-functional}
\end{align}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For a nonzero character $\chi_w$,
\[
 \Delta_{h_1}\cdots\Delta_{h_d}\chi_w(x)
   =(-2)^d\chi_w(x)\prod_i w(h_i).
\]
Consequently a tuple of directions containing zero contributes one in
\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:cube}. Write the three nonzero directions as
$a=(1,0)$, $b=(0,1)$, $c=(1,1)$.
If all three types occur, every Walsh term is annihilated. If exactly two types
occur, just one Walsh term survives, and its base-point average is $X$, $Y$,
or $Z$. If only one type occurs, two independent Walsh characters survive,
so the base-point average is a product of two cosines.

The signed counts are
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule
Direction types & Base-point factor & Signed count\\
\midrule
Only $a$ & $XZ$ & $1$\\
Only $b$ & $YZ$ & $1$\\
Only $c$ & $XY$ & $s$\\
Both $a,c$ & $X$ & $-(1+s)$\\
Both $b,c$ & $Y$ & $2^d-2-2d$\\
Both $a,b$ & $Z$ & $2^d-2-2d$\\
All $a,b,c$ & $1$ & $3^d-(d+3)2^d+4d+3$\\
At least one zero & $1$ & $4^d-3^d$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
For example, on $\{a,c\}^d$ the sign is $(-1)^{\#c}$; removing the two
constant tuples from its total signed sum zero gives $-(1+s)$.
On a mixed $\{a,b\}$ or $\{b,c\}$ tuple, the sign is negative precisely when
there is one $b$, giving $2^d-2-2d$. Among all-three-type tuples the negative
ones have one $b$ and both other types, of which there are
$d(2^{d-1}-2)$. Inclusion--exclusion gives
$3^d-3\cdot2^d+3$ all-three-type tuples, yielding the displayed signed count.
Adding the rows and dividing by $4^d$ proves the formula.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Binary equality and a global quotient bound]\label{gsr:fp:97:cor:binary}
For $d\ge4$, equality $\En_{C_d}(g)=b_d$ holds exactly when $Y=Z=1$.
Define
\begin{equation}
 \ell_d=\begin{cases}m_d-1,&d\text{ even},\\m_d,&d\text{ odd}.\end{cases}
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:ell}
\end{equation}
Then every unimodular $g$ on $V_0$ satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \dist_2(g,\Ext_d(u))^2\le\frac{\pi^2}{2\ell_d}
                         \bigl(b_d-\En_{C_d}(g)\bigr).
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:quotient-stability}
\end{equation}
The displayed coefficient is a convenient global bound, not claimed to be
optimal.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Write $m=m_d$. The numerator in~\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:binary-functional} is strictly
increasing in each of $Y,Z$: its partial derivatives are
$m+Z+sX$ and $m+Y+X$, both at least $m-2>0$.
At $Y=Z=1$ the $X$ coefficient cancels, and the value is $4^db_d$.
This proves the equality statement.

For the quantitative bound put $p=1-Y$ and $q=1-Z$, so $p,q\in[0,2]$.
Exact subtraction gives
\begin{equation}
 4^d\bigl(b_d-\En_{C_d}(g)\bigr)
  =(m+1+sX)p+(m+1+X)q-pq.
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:binary-deficit}
\end{equation}
In even degree the right side is at least $m(p+q)-pq\ge(m-1)(p+q)$.
In odd degree it is at least
$(m+1)(p+q)-|p-q|-pq\ge m(p+q)$, because
$|p-q|+pq\le p+q$ on $[0,2]^2$.

Choose $\beta',\gamma'\in2^{-d}\mathbb Z$ nearest to $\beta,\gamma$ and leave
$c,\alpha$ unchanged. The resulting $g_*$ has $Y=Z=1$. It belongs to $\Ext_d(u)$ directly:
$\beta'\chi_v$ and $\gamma'\chi_{u+v}$ are constant terms plus bit phases
with coefficients annihilated by $2^{d-1}$, hence have degree at most $d-1$;
the remaining phase depends only on $u$.
For $|t|\le\pi$,
\[
 1-\cos(t/2^d)\le\frac{\pi^2}{4\cdot4^d}(1-\cos t).
\]
Indeed, $1-\cos y\le y^2/2$ and
$1-\cos t\ge2t^2/\pi^2$ on this interval. Independence of the two Walsh
characters now gives
\begin{align*}
 \norm{g-g_*}_2^2
 &=2\bigl(1-\cos(2\pi(\beta-\beta'))\cos(2\pi(\gamma-\gamma'))\bigr)\\
 &\le\frac{\pi^2}{2\cdot4^d}(p+q).
\end{align*}
Combine this with~\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:binary-deficit}.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Classification, phase geometry, and exact certificates\srctag{97}}]{Classification, phase geometry, and exact certificates}\label{gsr:fp:97:sec:d6}\label{gsr:fp:97:sec:classification}
\srcnote{97}{Section 6}

\subsection{Proof of the complete classification}
\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:97:thm:classification}]
Suppose first that $\En_{C_d}(f)=b_d$. Section~\ref{gsr:fp:97:sec:cap} gives $|f|=1$ and
\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:relative-endpoint}. Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:97:thm:gluing}, with
$R=\ker u\cap\ker v$, writes
\[
 f=\e(P_0)g(u,v),\qquad \deg P_0\le d-1,
\]
where $g$ is unimodular on $\Ftwo^2$. Removing $P_0$ preserves the energy, and
pullback by $(u,v)$ preserves its normalized cube average. Thus $g$ is a
binary maximizer. Corollary~\ref{gsr:fp:97:cor:binary} says that the Walsh coefficients
$\beta,\gamma$ of its phase belong to $2^{-d}\mathbb Z$ modulo integers.
The phases $\beta\chi_v$ and $\gamma\chi_{u+v}$ have degree at most $d-1$:
use $\chi_w=1-2|w|$ and Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:97:lem:degree}. The remaining phase is
$c+\alpha\chi_u=c+\alpha-2\alpha|u|$. Hence $f\in\Ext_d(u)$.

Conversely, remove the degree-$(d-1)$ phase of an element of $\Ext_d(u)$.
Its remaining two-valued phase has $Y=Z=1$, so its energy is $b_d$ by
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:97:thm:binary}. This proves both directions.
\end{proof}
Corollary~\ref{gsr:fp:97:cor:gauge-main} follows at once from~\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:gauge}.

\subsection{Why the extra circle cannot be omitted}
\begin{example}[Nonpolynomial maximizing phases]\label{gsr:fp:97:ex:nonpolynomial}
For every $\theta\in\Tcirc$, the function $\e(\theta|u|)$ is a maximizer. If
$\theta$ is not dyadic, it is not a polynomial phase of any finite degree.
Indeed, for $u(a)=1$,
\[
 \Delta_a^j(\theta|u|)=(-2)^{j-1}\theta(1-2|u|),
\]
which never vanishes identically for such $\theta$.
For a dyadic parameter, its degree is at most $d-1$ exactly when
$2^{d-1}\theta=0$. Thus the residual parameter modulo all natural
low-degree phase gauges is the circle $\Tcirc/(2^{-(d-1)}\mathbb Z/\mathbb Z)$.
\end{example}
In particular a uniqueness statement that allows only polynomial phases
would be false, even on four points.

\begin{corollary}[Intersection of endpoint families]\label{gsr:fp:97:cor:intersection}
If $u,u'$ are distinct nonzero forms, then
\[
 \Ext_d(u)\cap\Ext_d(u')=\{\e(P):\deg P\le d-1\}.
\]
Consequently a maximizing function that is not itself a degree-$(d-1)$
polynomial phase determines the distinguished form $u$ uniquely.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Distinct nonzero forms over $\Ftwo$ are independent. If
$\e(P+\theta|u|)=\e(P'+\theta'|u'|)$, the circle-valued map
$\theta|u|-\theta'|u'|$ has degree at most $d-1$. Use $u,u'$ as the first two
coordinates in Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:97:lem:degree}; it forces
$2^{d-1}\theta=2^{d-1}\theta'=0$. Both extra phases are therefore already
of the allowed polynomial degree. The opposite inclusion is immediate.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Connected components]\label{gsr:fp:97:prop:components}
The extremizer family on $\Ftwo^n$ is a disjoint union of two-dimensional tori.
The number of its connected components is
\begin{equation}
 2^{\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{\min(d-1,n)}(d-j)\binom nj-(d-1)}.
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:components}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:97:lem:degree}, after fixing the constant term the polynomial
phase group has order $2^{\sum_j(d-j)\binom nj}$. Let
$H_u=\{\e(a+\theta|u|):a,\theta\in\Tcirc\}$, a two-dimensional torus.
Its intersection with the polynomial phase group, modulo constants, has
$2^{d-1}$ elements. Thus $\Ext_d(u)$ is the stated number of cosets of $H_u$.
These are finitely many disjoint compact connected sets; distinct cosets have
positive distance at a fixed dimension, so they are exactly the components.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A truth-table certificate}
Use coordinates with $x_1=u$, and write an arbitrary phase $P$ as
in~\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:mobius}. The classification is equivalent to the following
coefficient test:
\begin{equation}
 \begin{cases}
 c_A=0,& |A|\ge d,\\
 2^{d-|A|}c_A=0,&1\le|A|\le d-1,\quad A\ne\{1\}.
 \end{cases}
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:endpoint-certificate}
\end{equation}
The coefficients $c_\varnothing,c_{\{1\}}$ are arbitrary. Necessity and
sufficiency follow from Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:97:lem:degree} and
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:97:thm:classification}.

For an exact root-of-unity phase table, M\"obius inversion and these torsion
tests use $O(n2^n)$ modular additions and coefficient checks. This is a
truth-table complexity bound, not a polynomial-time assertion for an
arbitrarily compressed description of $f$. A non-unit value is rejected first.
For $C_d+S$, remove the supplied primitive phase before applying the test.
The companion function \gitpath{endpoint_certificate} implements this test for
integer phase tables modulo a specified integer.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A bounded-index relative testing theorem\srctag{97}}]{A bounded-index relative testing theorem}\label{gsr:fp:97:sec:d7}\label{gsr:fp:97:sec:relative-test}
\srcnote{97}{Section 7}
This section supplies the uniformity in dimension that a fixed-dimensional
compactness argument cannot provide. Its only analytic input from outside the
paper is the following published theorem, used in a deliberately qualitative form.

\begin{proposition}[Published near-extremizer input: Eisner--Tao]
\label{gsr:fp:97:prop:ET}
For each $d\ge2$ there is a nondecreasing function
$\rho_d:[0,1]\to[0,2]$, with $\rho_d(0)=0$ and
$\rho_d(t)\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$, such that on every finite Boolean group
$H$, every $|a|\le1$ with $\norm a_{U^d(H)}\ge1-t$ satisfies
\[
 \min_{P\in\Poly_{\le d-1}(H,\Tcirc)}\norm{a-\e(P)}_1\le\rho_d(t).
\]
\end{proposition}
This is a specialization of Theorem~1.1 of~\cite{eisnertao}, which is uniform over
compact abelian groups. Replacing its modulus by a nondecreasing envelope
and setting its value at zero to zero gives the stated version. The exact
zero case follows directly from equality in the cube average. No numerical
formula for $\rho_d$ is assumed or extracted below.

For a subspace $R\le V$ of codimension $c$, set $J=[V:R]=2^c$ and define
\begin{equation}
 \Rel_{d,R}(f)=\E_{z\in R}
       \left(1-\En_0^{(d-1)}(\partial_z f)\right).
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:relative-defect}
\end{equation}
Equivalently this is the average of $1-\Re\partial_z\partial_{h_1}\cdots
\partial_{h_{d-1}}f(x)$, with $x,h_i$ uniform on $V$ and $z$ uniform on $R$.
For a one-bounded function this pointwise integrand is nonnegative. Define the
relative phase family
\[
 \mathcal P_{d-1,R}
 =\{\e(P_0)g\circ q:P_0\in\Poly_{\le d-1}(V,\Tcirc),\quad
                         g:V/R\to S^1\},
\]
where $q:V\to V/R$ is the quotient. Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:97:thm:gluing} identifies it
with the unimodular functions having relative defect zero.

\begin{lemma}[Support of a circle-valued Boolean polynomial]
\label{gsr:fp:97:lem:support}
If a nonzero map $Q:W\to\Tcirc$ is a polynomial of degree at most $s\ge0$ on a
finite Boolean space, then
\[
 \Prob[Q\ne0]\ge2^{-s}.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $s=0$, a nonzero polynomial is a nonzero constant. For $s>0$ the same
case is immediate. Otherwise there is an $h$ with $\Delta_hQ\ne0$.
Induction gives $\Prob[\Delta_hQ\ne0]\ge2^{-(s-1)}$.
Its support lies in the union of the support of $Q$ and its translate by $h$,
so its measure is at most $2\Prob[Q\ne0]$. This proves the result.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Cube-product perturbation]\label{gsr:fp:97:lem:perturbation}
For one-bounded $f,F$, any symmetric $T$, and any $R\le V$,
\begin{align}
 |\En_T(f)-\En_T(F)|&\le2^d\norm{f-F}_1,\label{gsr:fp:97:eq:energy-perturbation}\\
 |\Rel_{d,R}(f)-\Rel_{d,R}(F)|&\le2^d\norm{f-F}_1.
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:relative-perturbation}
\end{align}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Telescope the difference of the two products over their $2^d$ labelled
vertices. Every unchanged factor has modulus at most one. For each term, the
changed factor has average absolute value $\norm{f-F}_1$: even with a
restricted direction, its base point is a translate of the uniform $x$.
Sum these bounds. Repeated vertices do not affect the argument.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform relative testing at bounded index]
\label{gsr:fp:97:thm:relative-test}
Fix $d\ge2$ and $c\ge0$, and put
\begin{equation}
 \kappa_{d,c}=2^{-(d-1+c)}
       \left(1-\cos\frac{2\pi}{2^{d-1}}\right)>0.
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:kappa}
\end{equation}
Let $R\le V$ have codimension $c$, let $|f|\le1$, and suppose
$\Rel_{d,R}(f)\le\varepsilon$. If
\begin{equation}
 J^d\varepsilon<1,\qquad
 \varepsilon+2^d\rho_d(J^d\varepsilon)<\kappa_{d,c},
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:relative-entry-condition}
\end{equation}
then there is an $F\in\mathcal P_{d-1,R}$ such that
\begin{equation}
 \norm{f-F}_1\le\rho_d(J^d\varepsilon).
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:relative-test-bound}
\end{equation}
In particular the distance tends to zero with $\varepsilon$, uniformly over
$\dim V$ at fixed $d,c$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Restrict the other $d-1$ sampled directions in~\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:relative-defect} to
$R$. Their probability is $J^{-(d-1)}$. Nonnegativity of the pointwise defect
shows that the resulting conditional average is at most $J^{d-1}\varepsilon$.
This conditional average is the average, over the $J$ cosets, of the ordinary
$U^d(R)$ defects. Each individual coset defect is therefore at most
$t=J^d\varepsilon$.

Choose a linear complement and write $V=R\oplus\Ftwo^c$, with coordinates
$(y,a)$. On each coset let $f_a(y)=f(y,a)$. Then
$\norm{f_a}_{U^d}\ge(1-t)^{1/2^d}\ge1-t$.
Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:97:prop:ET} gives $P_a\in\Poly_{\le d-1}(R,\Tcirc)$ with
$\norm{f_a-\e(P_a)}_1\le\rho_d(t)$. The function
$F(y,a)=\e(P_a(y))$ is unimodular and satisfies
$\norm{f-F}_1\le\rho_d(t)$, but its coset descriptions do not yet have a
common ambient polynomial of the desired degree.

Remove their constant terms, and put
\begin{equation}
 P_*(y,a)=\sum_{\omega\in\Ftwo^c}
       1_{\{a=\omega\}}\bigl(P_\omega(y)-P_\omega(0)\bigr),
 \qquad g(a)=\e(P_a(0)).
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:piecewise-polynomial}
\end{equation}
The indicators are integer polynomials of degree at most $c$ in the quotient
bits. The coefficient criterion in Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:97:lem:degree} proves that $P_*$
has degree at most $d-1+c$. Indeed multiplying a monomial of support size
$j$ and denominator dividing $2^{d-j}$ by a quotient monomial of support
size at most $c$ meets the degree-$d-1+c$ torsion bound. Furthermore
\begin{equation}
 P_*(V)\subseteq2^{-(d-1)}\mathbb Z/\mathbb Z.
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:piecewise-grid}
\end{equation}
Removing the constants before forming $P_*$ is essential for this assertion.
We have $F=\e(P_*)g\circ q$.

By~\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:relative-perturbation},
$\Rel_{d,R}(F)\le\varepsilon+2^d\rho_d(t)$. A cube with one direction in
$R$ cancels the $g\circ q$ factor exactly. Its remaining additive phase is
\[
 S(x,z,h_1,\ldots,h_{d-1})
   =\Delta_z\Delta_{h_1}\cdots\Delta_{h_{d-1}}P_*(x).
\]
As a function on the Boolean space $V\times R\times V^{d-1}$, this is a
polynomial of degree at most $d-1+c$. To see this, expand it as a signed sum
of $P_*$ composed with linear maps; composition with a linear map preserves
the degree bound. Its values lie on the grid~\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:piecewise-grid}.

If $S$ is not identically zero, Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:97:lem:support} and the minimum
nonzero grid angle give
\[
 \Rel_{d,R}(F)=\E(1-\cos(2\pi S))\ge\kappa_{d,c},
\]
contradicting~\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:relative-entry-condition}. Hence $S=0$ identically.
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:97:thm:gluing} now writes $P_*=P_0+Q\circ q$ with
$\deg P_0\le d-1$, so $F\in\mathcal P_{d-1,R}$. The already obtained
$L^1$ estimate proves~\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:relative-test-bound}.
\end{proof}

This theorem separates approximation from exact repair. The published input
approximates each coset separately. A bounded-degree, bounded-torsion defect
then has a positive detection gap independent of dimension. Falling below
that gap forces the mixed constraints to hold exactly, and only then does the
relative gluing theorem apply.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Dimension-free entry into the canonical family\srctag{97}}]{Dimension-free entry into the canonical family}\label{gsr:fp:97:sec:d8}\label{gsr:fp:97:sec:entry}
\srcnote{97}{Section 8}
For the canonical problem, $R$ has codimension two. Let $N=2^d$, and abbreviate
\begin{equation}
 a_d(\delta)=4^{d+1}\delta,\qquad
 \rho=\rho_d(a_d(\delta)).
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:entry-parameters}
\end{equation}
For sufficiently small $\delta$, both
\begin{equation}
 a_d(\delta)<1,\qquad4\delta+N\rho<\kappa_{d,2}
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:canonical-entry-condition}
\end{equation}
hold. This follows just from $\rho_d(t)\to0$.

\begin{proposition}[An explicit entry bound in terms of the published modulus]
\label{gsr:fp:97:prop:entry}
If $|f|\le1$ and $\delta=b_d-\En_{C_d}(f)$ obeys
\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:canonical-entry-condition}, then
\begin{equation}
 \dist_2(f,\Ext_d(u))\le B_d(\delta):=
 \sqrt{2\rho}+\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2\ell_d}}\sqrt{\delta+N\rho}.
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:entry-bound}
\end{equation}
In particular this distance tends to zero with $\delta$, uniformly in dimension.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The inactive-slice inequality~\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:inactive-slack} gives
$\Rel_{d,R}(f)\le4\delta$. Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:97:thm:relative-test} with
$c=2$, $J=4$, and $\varepsilon=4\delta$. It produces
$F=\e(P_0)g\circ q$, with $\deg P_0\le d-1$, $|g|=1$, and
$\norm{f-F}_1\le\rho$. Since $|f-F|\le2$,
$\norm{f-F}_2\le\sqrt{2\rho}$.

Gauge invariance and uniform pushforward under $q=(u,v)$ identify
$\En_{C_d}(F)$ with the binary energy of $g$. By
\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:energy-perturbation} its deficit is at most $\delta+N\rho$.
Corollary~\ref{gsr:fp:97:cor:binary} supplies a binary extremizer within squared
$L^2$ distance $\pi^2(\delta+N\rho)/(2\ell_d)$. Pull it back and restore
$\e(P_0)$ to get an element of $\Ext_d(u)$ at the same distance from $F$.
The triangle inequality proves~\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:entry-bound}.
\end{proof}

An entry modulus by itself is not a sharp stability estimate. The following
sections obtain the optimal leading coefficient by an exact local analysis;
the role of Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:97:prop:entry} is solely to justify entering that
local neighborhood without a dimension-dependent compactness argument.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The complete transverse spectrum\srctag{97}}]{The complete transverse spectrum}\label{gsr:fp:97:sec:d9}\label{gsr:fp:97:sec:spectrum}
\srcnote{97}{Section 9}
Let $g_\theta(x)=\e(\theta|u(x)|)$, let $s=(-1)^d$, and put
\begin{equation}
 X_\theta=\cos(2\pi2^{d-1}\theta),\qquad L_d=2^d-d-1.
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:theta-parameter}
\end{equation}
For a real function $\varphi$ write
$\widehat\varphi(\xi)=\E_x\varphi(x)\chi_\xi(x)$.

\begin{theorem}[Fourier diagonalization of the endpoint Hessian]
\label{gsr:fp:97:thm:hessian}
For every real $\varphi$ on $V$,
\begin{equation}
 \En_{C_d}(g_\theta\exp(it\varphi))
 =b_d-\frac{t^2}{2}\sum_{\xi\in V^*}
       \lambda_\xi(\theta)\widehat\varphi(\xi)^2+O_{d,\varphi}(t^3),
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:hessian-expansion}
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}
 \lambda_\xi(\theta)=
 \begin{cases}
 0,&\xi=0\text{ or }u,\\
 2^d-2d-1+sX_\theta,&\xi=v,\\
 2^d-2d-1+X_\theta,&\xi=u+v,\\
 2^d-d-1,&\xi\notin\Span\{u,v\}.
 \end{cases}
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:spectrum}
\end{equation}
For $d\ge4$ all transverse eigenvalues are at least $m_d=2^d-2d-2>0$.
This uniform lower bound is attained by a choice of $\theta$ and a transverse
character. The kernel consists precisely of the two tangent directions
$1,\chi_u$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For a direction tuple $\hh$ put $A_\xi(\hh)=\prod_i\xi(h_i)$ and
\[
 w_\theta(x,\hh)=\partial_{h_1}\cdots\partial_{h_d}g_\theta(x)
                                      (-1)^{C_d(\hh)}.
\]
Its real part is independent of $x$:
\begin{equation}
 \Re w_\theta=(-1)^{C_d(\hh)}
             \bigl(1+(X_\theta-1)A_u(\hh)\bigr).
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:real-weight}
\end{equation}
Indeed $|u|=(1-\chi_u)/2$, and all the differences vanish unless all
$u(h_i)=1$. In that event the magnitude of the additive phase is
$2^{d-1}\theta$, with a sign depending on $x$.

The first variation vanishes because $g_\theta$ is a maximum. For the second
variation use
\[
 \Delta_{h_1}\cdots\Delta_{h_d}\varphi(x)
   =(-2)^d\sum_\xi\widehat\varphi(\xi)\chi_\xi(x)A_\xi(\hh).
\]
Parseval in $x$ and~\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:real-weight} give a diagonal quadratic form with
\begin{equation}
 \lambda_\xi=4^d\E_{\hh}(-1)^{C_d(\hh)}
       \bigl(1+(X_\theta-1)A_u(\hh)\bigr)A_\xi(\hh).
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:eigenvalue-count}
\end{equation}
For $\xi=0$ this is zero. For $\xi=u$, the remaining sign is the parity of
independent $v(h_i)$ bits, so it again averages to zero.

For $\xi=v$, all directions are in the half-space $v=1$. In its binary
image they are $b$ or $c$ from Section~\ref{gsr:fp:97:sec:binary}. Among the $2^d$
choices the mixed negative tuples have exactly one $b$, while the all-$c$
tuple has sign $s$. The initial signed sum is $2^d-2d-1+s$, and its
$A_u$ correction is $s(X_\theta-1)$. With the normalization in
\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:eigenvalue-count} this gives the second line of~\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:spectrum}.
For $\xi=u+v$, the directions are $a$ or $b$. There are $d$ negative tuples,
and the all-$a$ correction is $X_\theta-1$, giving $2^d-2d-1+X_\theta$.

If $\xi\notin\Span\{u,v\}$, the $\xi(h_i)$ bits are independent of the
$u,v$ bits. Hence their all-one condition has probability $2^{-d}$.
The correction involving $A_u$ has zero mean by the same parity cancellation
as before. The remaining mean of $(-1)^{C_d}$ is $b_d$, so the eigenvalue is
$4^d2^{-d}b_d=L_d$. These computations prove~\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:spectrum}.
The lower bound and kernel now follow directly; $X_\theta$ can be either
endpoint of $[-1,1]$.
\end{proof}

Equation~\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:hessian-expansion} identifies a finite-dimensional quadratic
form. It is \emph{not} yet a uniform estimate for arbitrary near-extremizers:
small normalized $L^2$ distance need not mean a pointwise-small phase error as
the dimension varies. The next argument deals explicitly with that issue.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A uniform bounded-function coercivity estimate\srctag{97}}]{A uniform bounded-function coercivity estimate}\label{gsr:fp:97:sec:d10}\label{gsr:fp:97:sec:local}
\srcnote{97}{Section 10}
Recall $N=2^d$, $m=m_d$, $L=L_d$, and $K=K_d=3^N+3N^2$.

\begin{theorem}[Explicit local stability]\label{gsr:fp:97:thm:local}
For every $|f|\le1$, put
$r=\dist_2(f,\Ext_d(u))$ and $\delta=b_d-\En_{C_d}(f)$.
Whenever $r\le m/(2K)$,
\begin{equation}
 \delta\ge\frac{m-Kr}{2}\,r^2\ge\frac m4r^2.
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:local-stability}
\end{equation}
The radius and constants are independent of $\dim V$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
A closest $g\in\Ext_d(u)$ exists because the family is compact. Remove its
polynomial factor by gauge invariance, so that $g=g_\theta$. Set
\[
 h=f/g=1+z,\qquad z=a+ib,\qquad
 A=\E(1-\Re h)=\E|a|.
\]
Here $a,b$ are real, $a\le0$, and $|h|\le1$. The disk constraint gives
\begin{equation}
 r^2=\E(a^2+b^2)\le2A,\qquad A\le r,\qquad\norm b_2\le r.
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:disk-geometry}
\end{equation}
Varying the closest point $g$ inside its two-dimensional torus yields
\begin{equation}
 \E b=0,\qquad\E(b\chi_u)=0.
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:tangent-orthogonality}
\end{equation}
Indeed the derivative of the squared distance under multiplication of $g$ by
$\exp(it\psi)$ is zero for $\psi=1,|u|$, equivalently for $1,\chi_u$.
No differentiability or phase representation of $f$ is needed.

Expand the finite cube product for $g(1+z)$ by subsets of its $N$ labelled
vertices. Its constant, linear, quadratic and higher terms give
\begin{equation}
 \En_{C_d}(g(1+z))=b_d-LA+Q_\theta(z)+R_\theta(z).
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:finite-expansion}
\end{equation}
To verify the linear coefficient, condition on the value $y$ of any one
vertex. The other variables can still be parametrized by independent uniform
directions. If $A_u=0$, the phase weight of $g$ is one; if $A_u=1$, the
factor $(-1)^{C_d}$ has mean zero over the independent $v$ bits. Thus
$\E[w_\theta\mid y]=b_d$, a real constant. Each of the $N$ vertices
contributes $b_d\E a$, whether its factor is conjugated or not, proving
$N b_d\E a=-LA$.

The quadratic form on pure imaginary perturbations follows exactly from
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:97:thm:hessian}:
\begin{equation}
 Q_\theta(ib)=\frac12\left(L\norm b_2^2-
                      \sum_\xi\lambda_\xi\widehat b(\xi)^2\right)
            \le\frac{L-m}{2}\norm b_2^2.
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:imaginary-quadratic}
\end{equation}
For the identity, compare the coefficient of $t^2$ in
$\exp(itb)=1+itb-t^2b^2/2+O(t^3)$: the second-order linear contribution is
$-L\norm b_2^2/2$. The inequality uses~\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:tangent-orthogonality} to
remove the two zero eigenvalues. This use of a Taylor coefficient only
identifies an exact quadratic polynomial; the following remainder estimate
is a separate finite-product calculation.

Any three distinct vertices of a Boolean affine cube are jointly uniform
and independent on $V^3$. Indeed their coefficient rows are $(1,\omega)$
in $\Ftwo^{d+1}$; three distinct such rows are linearly independent. A dependence
with one or three rows fails in the first coordinate, and one with two rows
would identify the rows. The same argument gives pairwise independence.
Consequently replacing a quadratic pair in $Q_\theta(z)$ by its $ib$ pair
changes its average by at most
\[
 A^2+2A\E|b|\le3Ar.
\]
Here the weight has modulus one, so absolute values allow independence to be
used without asserting independence from the weight itself. Summing gives
\begin{equation}
 |Q_\theta(z)-Q_\theta(ib)|\le3\binom N2 Ar.
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:quadratic-remainder}
\end{equation}
For a subset of $j\ge3$ labelled vertices, use $|z|\le2$ on all but three
and their triple independence on the remainder. Its absolute average is at
most $2^{j-3}(\E|z|)^3\le2^{j-3}r^3\le2^{j-2}Ar$.
Thus
\begin{equation}
 |R_\theta(z)|\le Ar\sum_{j=3}^N\binom Nj2^{j-2}
             \le\frac{3^N}{4}Ar.
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:higher-remainder}
\end{equation}
The constants in~\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:quadratic-remainder} and
\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:higher-remainder} sum to less than $K$.

Subtract~\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:finite-expansion} from $b_d$ and use
\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:imaginary-quadratic} and $\norm b_2^2\le2A$:
\[
 \delta\ge LA-\frac{L-m}{2}\norm b_2^2-KAr
        \ge(m-Kr)A.
\]
For $r\le m/(2K)$ the last coefficient is positive. Applying
$A\ge r^2/2$ in~\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:disk-geometry} proves~\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:local-stability}.
\end{proof}

The very large $K_d$ is a transparent safe bound, not a proposed optimized
constant. More importantly, the proof permits zeros, non-unit amplitudes,
and perturbations concentrated on sets of vanishing density. It does not
replace those functions by $\exp(i\varphi)$ with $\norm\varphi_\infty$ small.
The use of independent cube vertices and the disk constraint adapts the
finite-product method of the ordinary endpoint paper~\cite{srcfiftyfive};
the twisted spectrum and the two-dimensional tangent space are different here.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Sharp stability and its optimal coefficient\srctag{97}}]{Sharp stability and its optimal coefficient}\label{gsr:fp:97:sec:d11}\label{gsr:fp:97:sec:sharp-stability}
\srcnote{97}{Section 11}
\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:97:thm:stability}, except optimality]
By Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:97:prop:entry}, there is an $\eta_d>0$ such that all
$0<\delta\le\eta_d$ satisfy~\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:canonical-entry-condition} and
$B_d(\delta)\le m/(2K)$. Shrink it, if necessary, so that $\eta_d<1$.
The bound depends only on $d$, not on the group or the linear forms.
The zero-deficit case is Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:97:thm:classification}.

Let $r=\sqrt{D(f)}$. Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:97:thm:local} first gives
$r\le2\sqrt{\delta/m}$. Keeping its sharper inequality, and writing
$x=Kr/m\le1/2$, gives
\begin{align*}
 r^2&\le\frac{2\delta}{m-Kr}
     \le\frac{2\delta}{m}+\frac{4K\delta r}{m^2}\\
    &\le\frac{2\delta}{m}+\frac{8K}{m^{5/2}}\delta^{3/2}.
\end{align*}
This is~\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:sharp-stability}. For $\delta>\eta_d$ the trivial bound
$D(f)\le4$ gives $D(f)\le(4/\eta_d)\delta$. The local range has
$D(f)\le4\delta/m$, so $A_d=\max\{4/m,4/\eta_d\}$ proves
\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:global-stability}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Sharpness in dimension two]\label{gsr:fp:97:prop:sharpness}
For every $d\ge4$ there is a family of unimodular functions on $\Ftwo^2$ for which
\[
 \frac{D(f)}{b_d-\En_{C_d}(f)}\longrightarrow\frac{2}{m_d}.
\]
Consequently the optimal asymptotic squared-distance coefficient, uniformly
over all dimensions, is exactly $2/m_d$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
If $d$ is even, choose $\theta=2^{-d}$, so $X_\theta=-1$.
If $d$ is odd, choose $\theta=0$, so $X_\theta=1$ and $sX_\theta=-1$.
In either case set
\[
 g_0=\e(\theta|u|),\qquad f_t=g_0\exp(it\chi_v).
\]
The binary identity, with $Z=1$ and $Y=\cos(2^d t)$, gives the exact formula
\begin{equation}
 b_d-\En_{C_d}(f_t)=\frac{m_d}{4^d}\left(1-\cos(2^d t)\right).
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:sharpness-deficit}
\end{equation}
The finite set of torus components from Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:97:prop:components}
has positive separation in this fixed dimension. For sufficiently small
$|t|$, a closest extremizer therefore lies in the component of $g_0$.
After dividing by $g_0$, its phases can be chosen separately on the two
$u$ cosets. On each coset the mean of $\exp(it\chi_v)$ is the positive
real number $\cos t$. The closest unit phase on that coset is one, whence
\begin{equation}
 D(f_t)=2(1-\cos t)\qquad\text{for sufficiently small }|t|.
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:sharpness-distance}
\end{equation}
Taking the ratio of~\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:sharpness-distance} and
\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:sharpness-deficit} and using
$(1-\cos t)/t^2\to1/2$ proves the assertion. Together with the preceding
upper bound, this completes Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:97:thm:stability}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A tensor-and-function rigidity consequence}
The all-degree tensor classification in~\cite{srcsixtyfive} supplies, for $d\ge4$, the
strict noncanonical gap
$\gamma_d=(d-2)/2^{d+1}$. Combining that existing result with the present
function theorem gives the following convenient statement.

\begin{corollary}[Rigidity for an initially unspecified nonintegrable tensor]
\label{gsr:fp:97:cor:tensor-and-function}
Let $T$ be a nonintegrable symmetric $d$-linear tensor, $d\ge4$, and let
$|f|\le1$. If
\[
 \En_T(f)>b_d-\gamma_d,
\]
then $T=C_d^{u,v}+S$ for independent $u,v$ and an integrable $S$.
For every primitive $P_S$, with $\delta=b_d-\En_T(f)$,
\[
 \min_{P\in\Poly_{\le d-1},\,\theta\in\Tcirc}
 \norm{f-\e(P_S+P+\theta|u|)}_2^2\le A_d\delta.
\]
For sufficiently small $\delta$ the right side can be replaced by the sharp
expression in~\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:sharp-stability}.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The hypothesis excludes the noncanonical alternative by the cited tensor
rigidity theorem. Apply gauge invariance and Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:97:thm:stability}.
\end{proof}
Only the function approximation is new in this corollary; recognizing the
tensor class uses the preceding project result explicitly.

\section[{Examples, exact checks, and proof boundaries\srctag{97}}]{Examples, exact checks, and proof boundaries}\label{gsr:fp:97:sec:d12}\label{gsr:fp:97:sec:checks}
\srcnote{97}{Section 12}

\subsection{Inactive coordinates do not disappear without a phase gauge}
Take $V=\Ftwo^3$, $u=x_1$, $v=x_2$. The phase
\[
 f(x)=\e\bigl(|x_1x_2x_3|/4\bigr)
\]
is not a quartic canonical extremizer. In the coefficient test
\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:endpoint-certificate}, $c_{\{1,2,3\}}=1/4$ violates the required
condition $2c_{\{1,2,3\}}=0$. The verifier independently evaluates its
quartic energy as $101/256$, strictly below $11/16$.
In degree five the same phase is a permitted polynomial gauge, since it
has degree four, and its canonical energy is $13/16$.
Thus inactive coordinates can occur in an extremizer, but their dependence
is constrained by the degree and cannot simply be ignored.

For any allowed $P$ and an irrational $\theta$,
$\e(P+\theta|u|)$ is also an exact extremizer. Its extra one-coordinate
factor need not have finite polynomial degree. These examples explain why
an approximation theorem aimed only at degree-$d-1$ polynomial phases would
be false: the target must be the entire family $\Ext_d(u)$.

\subsection{What the companion verifies}
The companion \gitpath{code/verify.py} uses only Python's standard library,
with explicit checks that remain active under \gitpath{python -O}. The
principal records in \gitpath{data/verification.json} are as follows.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),itemsep=4pt]
\item The binary signed-count formulas are checked by enumerating
$349\,504$ direction tuples in degrees $3$ through $9$. A separate family of
$32$ exact cyclotomic checks compares literal phase-cube sums with the
trigonometric formula for root-of-unity phase tables.
\item The Hessian's constant and $X_\theta$ coefficients are counted
independently in dimensions three and four, with transverse characters
outside $\Span\{u,v\}$ included. No floating-point optimizer is involved.
\item There are $72$ literal all-direction polynomial-degree checks against
the coefficient criterion. An exhaustive census of all $16\,384$ normalized
fourth-root phase tables on $\Ftwo^3$ checks the relative derivative conditions
against the gluing certificate in the quartic case; $8\,192$ tables pass the
endpoint coefficient test. This is a certificate census, not a claim that a
finite phase grid optimizes over all complex functions.
\item Six higher-dimensional endpoint examples use root orders containing
an odd factor, so their unrestricted $u$ phase is not a finite-degree
polynomial. Their energies are checked by exact cyclotomic reduction.
Twenty-four Gaussian-rational one-bounded function tests, including zeros
and non-unit amplitudes, check the energy and retained mass bounds.
\end{enumerate}
The record also includes $560$ tensor-convention comparisons, the explicit
$101/256$ example, and degree-by-degree constant and component-count ledgers.
The two executions, ordinary and optimized, must produce identical JSON.
The finite checks are error detectors and reproducibility evidence. The
proofs, not those finite tests, establish all-dimensional inequalities,
continuous maxima, and uniform stability.

\subsection{Dependency and novelty audit}
The following separation is important for integration into the repository.
The canonical cap, cubic projective loss, derivative-period method, and
all-degree tensor classification are prior project results. The Boolean
coefficient normal form and near-maximal Gowers inverse theorem belong to
established polynomial theory. The finite-product approach to ordinary
endpoint stability is also credited to the preceding project work.

The contributions developed here are the exact relative gluing interface
and its bounded-index testing consequence, the binary functional and
complete canonical function classification, the transverse spectrum, and
the sharp dimension-free stability theorem for this nonintegrable endpoint.
Some elementary ingredients may have appeared elsewhere; no exhaustive
literature-priority claim is made. The testing theorem uses the published
qualitative input exactly where Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:97:prop:ET} is invoked. All
other analytic estimates needed for the stated local radius and leading
coefficient are proved in the paper.

Neither repository was built in Lean during this work. No theorem-status
ledger was changed, and no unproved research statement was inserted as an
axiom. The companion formalization plan proposes interfaces but does not
constitute a checked formal proof. Likewise no part of the argument depends
on accepting the large quantitative claim~\eqref{gsr:fm:97:eq:reported-ap}.

\subsection{The gap to a global progression theorem}
A successful all-length density-increment argument must construct structured
selectors at much lower energies, retain their equations under localization,
and pay for every subsequent restriction and iteration. The present theorem
starts with a particular supplied symmetric tensor on the full Boolean group
and a function close in energy to its sharp endpoint. It improves the
understanding of that local phase-integration regime; it does not establish
an improved bound for $r_k(N)$ or a new proof of the reciprocal-sum conjecture.
The precision-preserving cell framework reviewed in Section~\ref{gsr:fm:97:sec:choice}
provides a possible setting for future localization work, not an automatic
application of our translation-invariant estimates.

\section[{The binary cubic boundary case\srctag{97}}]{The binary cubic boundary case}\label{gsr:fp:97:sec:dA}\label{gsr:fp:97:app:cubic}
\srcnote{97}{Appendix A}
At $d=3$, formula~\eqref{gsr:fp:97:eq:binary-functional} becomes
\begin{equation}
 \En_{C_3}(g)=\frac{31+XZ+YZ-XY}{64}.
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:cubic-binary}
\end{equation}
The maximum of $XZ+YZ-XY$ on $[-1,1]^3$ is one. Its equality locus is the
union of the following six segments:
\begin{equation}
 \begin{array}{lll}
 (X,Z)=(1,1),& (Y,Z)=(1,1),& (X,Z)=(-1,-1),\\
 (Y,Z)=(-1,-1),& (X,Y)=(1,-1),& (X,Y)=(-1,1),
 \end{array}
 \label{gsr:fp:97:eq:cubic-segments}
\end{equation}
with the remaining coordinate free in each case. To prove this, if $X+Y>0$
maximize first in $Z$, obtaining $X+Y-XY=1-(1-X)(1-Y)$, with equality when
$X=1$ or $Y=1$. If $X+Y<0$, take $Z=-1$ and use
$-X-Y-XY=1-(1+X)(1+Y)$. If $X+Y=0$, the expression is $X^2$, independent
of $Z$, so equality means $(X,Y)=(1,-1)$ or $(-1,1)$. The limiting zero-sum
endpoints also belong to these segments.
This is a complete \emph{binary} cubic description in phase-cosine
coordinates, not an arbitrary-dimensional cubic function classification.

\section{Source~95: simultaneous integration of two models, the generic half-rank of the obstruction pencil \wtag}\label{gsr:fp:sec:pencils}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the fourteenth write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next eight sections are source~95's Sections~2--9. \emph{Logically they continue} the chapter on the first nonclassical obstruction (Section~\ref{gsr:fp:sec:critical}; sources~92, 89, 91) and the binary chapter of sources~46 and~43 (Section~\ref{gsr:fp:sec:binary}). The introduction is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:95:sec:d1}.

\emph{What is proved.} For two symmetric Boolean cubics $T_0,T_1$ whose selected derivative energies at $T_0$, $T_1$, $T_0+T_1$ are at least $2^{-K_0}$, $2^{-K_1}$, $2^{-K_+}$, both integrate on a common subspace of codimension at most $\min\{K_0+K_1,K_0+K_+,K_1+K_+,\lfloor(K_0+K_1+K_+)/2\rfloor\}$, attained for every budget triple (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:95:spi:thm:main}); for equal budgets the coefficient falls from $2$ to $3/2$. The exact invariant is the generic half-rank $r$ of the alternating obstruction pencil $\Omega_{T_0}+z\Omega_{T_1}$ over $\Ftwo(z)$, not the largest rational rank (Theorems~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:isotropic}, \ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:joint-exact}); the finite-test rank-loss inequality $\sum_a(r-r_a)\le r$, the complete unequal-budget frontier and every realizable rank profile; the rank defect $D_S$ vanishes exactly for split pencils and can be removed at cost at most $D_S$, sharply (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:stability}); and the rank-only extension to degree $p+1$ over $\F_p$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:prime-joint}), sharp at $\lfloor(q+1)K/q\rfloor$ over~$\F_q$.

\emph{Against sources~43, 46, 89 and~92.} Source~95's scalar theorem $\mathcal M(T)=2^{-r}$ is source~43's exact cubic energy theorem (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:cubic-exact}), credited and reproved; its degree-$(p+1)$ criterion (Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:prop:prime}, via Tidor) is source~46's first-obstruction test (Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:46:prop:first-obstruction}) and the test of sources~89 and~92; it calls source~46 ``a parallel cubic treatment'', after the README's earlier summary, which the thirteenth write corrected. \emph{Source~95 does not cite sources~89 and~92}, which were unplaced archives at its pin. For two-tensor families \emph{it computes source~92's common codimension $\kappa(\mathcal T)$ exactly} ($\kappa=$ the generic half-rank), and it shows that source~92's lower bound $\max_B\rank B/2$ (Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:92:prop:familybounds}) is not sharp even for pencils: for $sJ\oplus tJ\oplus(s+t)J$ on $\Ftwo^6$, $\kappa=3$ while every rational member has half-rank~$2$; its three-generator example on $\Ftwo^3$ ($\kappa=2$, generic half-rank~$1$) attains source~92's upper bound at $s=3$ and shows that the pencil theorem does not extend to three forms. It answers source~89's question on optimizing a higher-degree defect pencil when the defect span is two-dimensional (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:IV:lowchar}). Source~36's request for ``a joint rank invariant'' for several slot defects (Question~\ref{gsr:fz:36:ssc:q:jointprofiles}) is in another setting ($p>k+1$): related, not answered.
