\section[{Alternating pencils and optimal common isotropic spaces\srctag{95}}]{Alternating pencils and optimal common isotropic spaces}\label{gsr:fp:95:sec:d2}\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:sec:pencils}
\srcnote{95}{Section 2}

\subsection{The classical normal form used here}
An alternating bilinear form has zero diagonal, including in characteristic
two. This hypothesis cannot be weakened there to merely being symmetric.
The classical congruence classification of pairs of alternating forms is
our algebraic input \cite{leepschueller,waterhousepairs}. For a directly inspected
characteristic-two formulation with regular block matrices, see
Drozd--Plakosh, Section~2 and Theorem~2.2 \cite{drozdplakosh}; the singular
splitting is also stated in Dolgachev--Duncan, Theorem~4.1
\cite{dolgachevduncan}. We state the particular form needed for our proofs.

\begin{theorem}[Classical alternating-pencil decomposition]\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:kcf}
Every alternating pencil over a field is congruent to an orthogonal direct
sum of the following blocks:
\begin{enumerate}
\item A singular block $\mathsf K_h$, $h\ge0$, of dimension $2h+1$, with matrix
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:sing-block}
 \begin{pmatrix}0&L_h(s,t)\\-L_h(s,t)^{\mathsf T}&0\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 L_h(s,t)=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 s&0&\cdots&0\\
 t&s&\ddots&\vdots\\
 0&t&\ddots&0\\
 \vdots&\ddots&\ddots&s\\
 0&\cdots&0&t
 \end{pmatrix}_{(h+1)\times h}.
\end{equation}
For $h=0$ this means a one-dimensional common radical.
\item A regular primary block of dimension $2d$, with matrix
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:regular-block}
 \begin{pmatrix}0&M(s,t)\\-M(s,t)^{\mathsf T}&0\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad M(s,t)=sI_d+tC,
\end{equation}
where $C$ is a companion matrix of a power $g^\ell$ of a monic irreducible
polynomial, $d=\ell\deg g$. The blocks at the remaining projective point
can be written with $M(s,t)=sN_d+tI_d$, where $N_d$ is one nilpotent Jordan
block. Equivalently one may use a projective coordinate chart for each block.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

This imported theorem is the only classification result needed below.
We do not assume the pencil has a nonsingular member over the base field.
A regular pencil means that its determinant is a nonzero polynomial, not
that some finite-field evaluation is invertible.

\begin{lemma}[Ranks and isotropic halves of the blocks]\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:lem:block-ranks}
The generic half-rank of $\mathsf K_h$ is $h$ and its half-rank at every
rational direction is $h$. Its larger coordinate half has dimension $h+1$
and is isotropic for both forms.
A regular primary block of dimension $2d$ has generic half-rank $d$ and a
common isotropic coordinate half of dimension $d$.
If its projective elementary divisor has a rational root and length $\ell$,
then $d=\ell$ and its half-rank drops by exactly one at that root. At every
other rational direction its half-rank is $\ell$.
A block supported at a nonrational point has no rational rank drop.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $s\ne0$, the first $h$ rows of $L_h$ give a triangular minor $s^h$;
for $t\ne0$, the last $h$ rows give $t^h$. Thus its rank is $h$ at every
projective direction and over $k(z)$. The displayed zero diagonal blocks
prove the isotropic claims for both kinds of block.

The determinant of $sI+tC$ is nonzero as a polynomial. At a rational root
of an irreducible primary factor, that factor is linear. The companion
matrix of its $\ell$th power is similar to a single Jordan block, whose
rank at the root is $\ell-1$. There is no rank loss elsewhere. For the
infinite block the same calculation uses $N_d$. If the irreducible factor
has degree greater than one, it has no root in $k$, so all rational
specializations are invertible.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Common isotropic dimension]\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:isotropic}
Let $A_0,A_1$ be alternating forms on an $n$-dimensional vector space over
$k$, and let their pencil have generic rank $2r$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:isotropic}
 \max\{\dim W:A_0|_{W\times W}=A_1|_{W\times W}=0\}=n-r.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Take the larger isotropic half in each singular block and one isotropic
half in each regular block of theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:kcf}. By lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:lem:block-ranks}, the
sum of their dimensions is the total dimension minus the sum of the
block generic half-ranks, namely $n-r$.

Conversely, extend a common isotropic space $W$ to $k(z)$. It is isotropic
for $A_0+zA_1$. The radical of this form has dimension $n-2r$. The image
of $W\otimes k(z)$ in its nondegenerate symplectic quotient has dimension
at most $r$, since an isotropic subspace $U$ of a nondegenerate
$2r$-dimensional alternating space satisfies $U\subseteq U^\perp$.
Therefore $\dim W\le(n-2r)+r=n-r$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why generic rank is essential]\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:rem:generic}
Over an infinite field the generic rank is attained on a rational direction
outside finitely many exceptions. Over a finite field every rational direction
may be exceptional. Extending scalars is legitimate in the lower-bound
argument in theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:isotropic}; choosing a supposedly generic base-field
point is not. The example in example~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:ex:six} makes this distinction sharp.
\end{remark}

\subsection{A useful proof certificate}
To certify an optimal common isotropic space it is not necessary to exhibit
a complete normal form. It is enough to supply a basis matrix $U$ of rank
$n-r$ and a nonzero principal Pfaffian of order $2r$ in $A_0+zA_1$.
The identities
\[
 U^{\mathsf T}A_0U=U^{\mathsf T}A_1U=0
\]
certify the upper bound on codimension, while the Pfaffian and the symplectic
lower bound certify optimality. This is a substantially smaller verification
interface than trusting an implementation of the full canonical-form algorithm.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Finite tests: the exact budget and every rank profile\srctag{95}}]{Finite tests: the exact budget and every rank profile}\label{gsr:fp:95:sec:d3}\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:sec:budgets}
\srcnote{95}{Section 3}

\subsection{A Pfaffian multiplicity lemma}
\begin{lemma}[Rank loss consumes Pfaffian degree]\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:lem:pfaffian}
Let $B(s,t)$ be an alternating $2r\times2r$ matrix pencil whose Pfaffian
$F(s,t)$ is not identically zero. If its rank at $a\in\Prob^1(k)$ is $2u$,
then the linear polynomial vanishing at $a$ divides $F$ to order at least
$r-u$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose a local projective coordinate $z$ vanishing at $a$. Up to an
invertible scalar factor, the local pencil is $B_0+zB_1$. A constant
congruence puts $B_0$ into a nondegenerate $2u$-dimensional alternating block
and a zero block of dimension $2(r-u)$. Consequently every entry incident
to a row in the latter block is divisible by $z$.

A Pfaffian monomial pairs all $2r$ indices. To cover the $2(r-u)$ indices
in the zero block it must use at least $r-u$ pairs incident to that block.
The monomial is therefore divisible by $z^{r-u}$. This holds term by term,
in all characteristics, and hence holds for the Pfaffian. Constant
congruence multiplies a Pfaffian by a nonzero determinant and does not alter
the multiplicity. The same argument applies at infinity after interchanging
projective coordinates.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The finite-direction rank-loss inequality]\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:rank-budget}
For any finite set $S$ of distinct rational directions in an alternating
pencil of generic half-rank $r$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:rank-budget}
 \sum_{a\in S}(r-r_a)\le r.
\end{equation}
In particular, when $|S|=m$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:sum-ranks}
 \sum_{a\in S}r_a\ge(m-1)r.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $r=0$ there is nothing to prove. Otherwise select a principal $2r$-minor
with nonzero Pfaffian $F(s,t)$. Such a minor exists by alternating Gaussian
elimination over $k(z)$: the rank of an alternating matrix is the largest
order of a nonzero principal Pfaffian.
The polynomial $F$ is homogeneous of degree $r$.

At direction $a$, the restricted principal submatrix has rank $2u_a\le2r_a$.
By lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:lem:pfaffian}, the linear factor belonging to $a$ occurs in $F$ with
multiplicity at least $r-u_a\ge r-r_a$. Distinct projective directions give
nonassociate linear factors. Their product, with these multiplicities,
divides $F$ in $k[s,t]$. Comparing degrees proves \eqref{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:rank-budget}.
\end{proof}

This proof is independent of the pencil classification. In particular,
\eqref{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:rank-budget} is a low-dependency formalization target even before
theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:kcf} is available.

\subsection{Optimal upper bounds from unequal tests}
\begin{theorem}[Complete finite-test budget frontier]\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:frontier}
Fix $m\ge2$ distinct directions $S\subseteq\Prob^1(k)$ and integer budgets
$K_a\ge0$. Among all alternating pencils in unrestricted dimension with
$r_a\le K_a$ for every $a\in S$, the largest generic half-rank is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:frontier}
 B_S(K)=\min_{\substack{I\subseteq S\\|I|\ge2}}
 \left\lfloor\frac{\sum_{a\in I}K_a}{|I|-1}\right\rfloor.
\end{equation}
If $K_{(1)}\le\cdots\le K_{(m)}$ are the sorted budgets, equivalently
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:sorted-frontier}
 B_S(K)=\min_{2\le j\le m}
 \left\lfloor\frac{K_{(1)}+\cdots+K_{(j)}}{j-1}\right\rfloor.
\end{equation}
Every feasible integer $R\le B_S(K)$ can be attained on a $2R$-dimensional
space by a sum of scalar symplectic planes whose roots belong to $S$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Apply theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:rank-budget} to each $I\subseteq S$ of size at least two:
\[
 (|I|-1)r\le\sum_{a\in I}r_a\le\sum_{a\in I}K_a.
\]
For a fixed cardinality, the smallest sum is the sum of the smallest budgets,
which proves \eqref{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:sorted-frontier}.

For the converse fix $R\le B_S(K)$ and put
\[
 d_a=\max\{0,R-K_a\}.
\]
We claim $\sum_a d_a\le R$. Let $I=\{a:K_a<R\}$. If $I$ is empty the claim
is immediate; if it has one element it follows from $K_a\ge0$. Otherwise
\[
 \sum_a d_a=|I|R-\sum_{a\in I}K_a\le R
\]
by the defining bound on $R$.
Choose integers $m_a\ge d_a$ with $\sum_a m_a=R$. For each $a$ choose a
nonzero linear polynomial $L_a(s,t)$ with zero $a$, and take $m_a$ copies of
$L_aJ$. This pencil has generic half-rank $R$ and, at test direction $a$,
half-rank exactly $R-m_a\le K_a$. No extension of the field is used.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[All rational directions over a finite field]\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:cor:finitefield}
If $r_a\le K$ at all $q+1$ directions of $\Prob^1(\F_q)$, then
\[
 r\le\left\lfloor\frac{q+1}{q}K\right\rfloor.
\]
This is optimal for every integer $K\ge0$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
In \eqref{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:sorted-frontier} the quantities $jK/(j-1)$ decrease with $j$.
Sharpness follows from the construction in theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:frontier}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Exact rank-profile realization}
An upper-budget statement permits some tests to perform strictly better than
their prescribed limits. It is useful to separate it from the following
\emph{exact}-profile result.

\begin{theorem}[Every feasible exact profile]\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:profiles}
Fix $m\ge2$ distinct rational directions $S$. Given nonnegative integers
$(a_s)_{s\in S}$ and $R$, there is an alternating pencil with generic
half-rank $R$ and evaluated half-ranks exactly $a_s$ if and only if
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:profile-feasibility}
 \max_{s\in S}a_s\le R\le
 \left\lfloor\frac{\sum_{s\in S}a_s}{m-1}\right\rfloor.
\end{equation}
When these inequalities hold, put
\[
 D=\sum_s a_s-(m-1)R.
\]
A realization exists in dimension $2R+D$, using only $D$ singular blocks
$\mathsf K_1$ and $R-a_s$ scalar planes rooted at each $s$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Specialization cannot increase rank, giving $a_s\le R$. The other
inequality is \eqref{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:sum-ranks}.

Conversely, $D\ge0$ and
\[
 R-D=mR-\sum_s a_s=\sum_s(R-a_s)\ge0.
\]
Take the indicated blocks. Each $\mathsf K_1$ has generic and evaluated
half-rank one. There are $R-D$ scalar planes, so the generic half-rank is
$D+(R-D)=R$. At direction $s$ exactly $R-a_s$ of the planes vanish. The
half-rank there is $R-(R-a_s)=a_s$. The dimension is
$3D+2(R-D)=2R+D$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The full Boolean ambiguity interval]\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:cor:ambiguity}
A triple $(a,b,c)$ occurs as the three evaluated half-ranks of a Boolean
pencil precisely when it satisfies the triangle inequalities. For a fixed
such triple, every integer
\[
 \max\{a,b,c\}\le R\le\left\lfloor\frac{a+b+c}{2}\right\rfloor
\]
occurs as its generic half-rank. All these realizations can be made in the
same dimension $a+b+c$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The existence of an integer in the displayed interval is equivalent to the
triangle inequalities. The dimension formula in theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:profiles} becomes
$2R+(a+b+c-2R)=a+b+c$.
\end{proof}

Thus an exact list of the three individual ranks, or of the three individually
optimized energies, need not determine the exact simultaneous repair cost.
The frontier is the optimal \emph{universal upper bound}, not a formula for
that cost from evaluated ranks alone.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The rank defect: equality and sharp restriction stability\srctag{95}}]{The rank defect: equality and sharp restriction stability}\label{gsr:fp:95:sec:d4}\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:sec:stability}
\srcnote{95}{Section 4}

\subsection{An integral measure of nonsplit structure}
Let $S\subseteq\Prob^1(k)$ have $m\ge2$ elements. Write
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:defect}
 D_S(A)=\sum_{a\in S}r_a-(m-1)r.
\end{equation}
By theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:rank-budget} this is a nonnegative integer. We call a pencil
\emph{split over the tested directions} when it is congruent to a direct sum
of a zero pencil and two-dimensional blocks $L_a(s,t)J$ with $a\in S$.
The zero pencil is allowed to have any dimension.

\begin{lemma}[Defect of an indecomposable block]\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:lem:defect-table}
In the decomposition of theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:kcf}, the defect is additive and has the
following values.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.62\textwidth}c@{}}
\toprule
Block & Contribution to $D_S$\\
\midrule
Singular block $\mathsf K_h$ & $h$\\
Regular block with a root in $S$, length $\ell$ & $\ell-1$\\
Regular block of dimension $2d$ with no root in $S$ & $d$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The last row includes nonrational primary factors and rational roots not
among the tested directions.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Generic and evaluated ranks add under orthogonal direct sum. For a singular
block the contribution is $mh-(m-1)h=h$. For a regular block rooted in $S$,
exactly one evaluated half-rank drops by one, so its contribution is
$m\ell-1-(m-1)\ell=\ell-1$. Otherwise all evaluated half-ranks equal $d$,
giving $md-(m-1)d=d$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Equality classification]\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:zero-defect}
$D_S(A)=0$ if and only if the pencil is split over the tested directions.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Every contribution in lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:lem:defect-table} is nonnegative. A zero
contribution occurs only for a common-radical block $\mathsf K_0$, or for a
regular block of length one whose root lies in $S$. These are exactly the
blocks in the asserted normal form. Conversely their contributions all vanish.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A sharp codimension stability theorem}
\begin{theorem}[Restriction stability with coefficient one]\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:stability}
For every alternating pencil $A$ and every finite set $S$ of at least two
rational test directions, there is a subspace $U$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:stability}
 \codim U\le D_S(A),\qquad D_S(A|_U)=0.
\end{equation}
Here the defect on the right is recomputed using the generic and evaluated
ranks of the restricted pencil. The coefficient one cannot be uniformly
reduced, even when $k=\Ftwo$ and $S=\Prob^1(\Ftwo)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Use the block decomposition and construct a subspace in each block.

In $\mathsf K_h$, retain its larger isotropic half. The restricted pencil
is zero and the codimension is $h$.

For a regular block with no root in $S$, retain one isotropic half. The
restricted pencil is zero and the codimension is $d$.

For a regular block of length $\ell$ rooted in $S$, use a chart in which
its cross matrix is $sI+tC$ and $C$ is one Jordan block with eigenvalue
$\lambda$. Let $E$ be the first coordinate half, and choose a nonzero
eigenvector $v$ of $C$ in the second half. Retain
\[
 U_{\mathrm{block}}=E\oplus kv.
\]
For $e\in E$ the two cross pairings are $e^{\mathsf T}v$ and
$e^{\mathsf T}Cv=\lambda e^{\mathsf T}v$. Since $v\ne0$, this restriction
is one scalar symplectic plane with the same root, plus an
$(\ell-1)$-dimensional common radical. Its codimension in the original
$2\ell$-dimensional block is $\ell-1$. At infinity interchange the roles
of $s,t$ and use an eigenvector of the nilpotent block.

The direct sum of these subspaces has codimension exactly the sum of the
contributions in lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:lem:defect-table}, and its pencil is split over $S$.
This proves \eqref{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:stability}. Sharpness is established by
example~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:ex:irreducible} below.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[A sharp irreducible obstruction]\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:ex:irreducible}
Over $\Ftwo$, take $V=\Ftwo^4$, $C=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$,
and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:irreducible-example}
 A_0=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_2\\I_2&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 A_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&C\\C^{\mathsf T}&0\end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation}
The polynomial $X^2+X+1$ is irreducible. Hence $A_0,A_1,A_0+A_1$ are all
nondegenerate, and
\[
 r=2,\quad r_0=r_1=r_+=2,\quad D=6-4=2.
\]
On any hyperplane $U$, each of these nondegenerate four-dimensional forms
has rank exactly two. Indeed its restriction has rank at least $4-2=2$,
and an alternating form on a three-dimensional space has rank at most two.
The restricted pencil also has generic rank two. Thus
\[
 D(A|_U)=1+1+1-2=1,
\]
so no codimension-one restriction has zero defect. An isotropic coordinate
half has codimension two and zero restricted pencil. The least deletion
cost is exactly $D=2$, proving sharpness of the coefficient in
theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:stability}.
\end{example}

The same argument works over every finite field with a companion matrix of
an irreducible quadratic and all rational directions tested. The Boolean
example alone already proves the stated universal sharpness.

\subsection{What this stability does not assert}
The theorem concerns the geometry of the obstruction pencil. It does not
say that an arbitrary function with nearly extremal selected energy is close
to a unique phase, or that the original pair is close in a matrix norm to a
split pair. The modification is restriction to a linear subspace, and the
loss is its codimension. These distinctions matter when the result is used
inside a density-increment argument.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The Boolean cubic bridge: integration and exact scalar energy\srctag{95}}]{The Boolean cubic bridge: integration and exact scalar energy}\label{gsr:fp:95:sec:d5}\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:sec:scalar}
\srcnote{95}{Section 5}

The statements in this section are the credited single-tensor input from
\cite{srcfortythree}, with a proof included to make the simultaneous argument
checkable without treating an unrefereed source as an unexplained black box.
The nonclassical integration principle is established background
\cite{tidor}.

\subsection{An explicit primitive and the obstruction quotient}
\begin{proposition}[Boolean cubic integration criterion]\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:prop:primitive}
For symmetric $T:V^3\to\Ftwo$, the map $\Omega_T$ in \eqref{gsr:fm:95:spi:eq:omega} is
alternating bilinear. The tensor $T$ has a nonclassical cubic primitive if
and only if $\Omega_T=0$.

More explicitly, let $e_1,\ldots,e_n$ be a basis and let $x_i\in\{0,1\}$ be
the integer lift of the $i$th coordinate of $x$. If $\Omega_T=0$, then
\begin{align}\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:primitive}
 P_T(x)={}&\sum_i\frac{T(e_i,e_i,e_i)x_i}{8}
 +\sum_{i<j}\frac{T(e_i,e_i,e_j)x_ix_j}{4}\notag\\
 &+\sum_{i<j<k}\frac{T(e_i,e_j,e_k)x_ix_jx_k}{2}\pmod1
\end{align}
is a primitive. The repeated coefficient in the second sum also equals
$T(e_i,e_j,e_j)$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Expanding $T(a+a',a+a',b)$, the two cross terms cancel by symmetry in
characteristic two. This proves additivity in the repeated variable; the
other variable is manifestly additive. The same argument applies to
$T(a,b,b)$. Thus $\Omega_T$ is bilinear, and $\Omega_T(a,a)=0$.

For necessity use $\Delta_a^2=-2\Delta_a$, an identity of additive
difference operators on a group of exponent two. Therefore
\[
 \Delta_a^2\Delta_bP=-2\Delta_a\Delta_bP
                    =\Delta_a\Delta_b^2P.
\]
If the third derivative is $T/2$, this is precisely
$T(a,a,b)=T(a,b,b)$.

For sufficiency, the monomial in \eqref{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:primitive} with support of size
$j$ has denominator $2^{4-j}$. Applying four coordinate differences gives
zero modulo one: a difference in a missing coordinate kills the monomial;
otherwise, after at least one difference in every supported coordinate,
each repeated difference contributes a factor $-2$. The total contribution
contains $2^{4-j}$.
The identities
\[
 \Delta_{u+v}=\Delta_u+\Delta_v+\Delta_u\Delta_v
\]
show that arbitrary four differences are sums of compositions of at least
four coordinate differences. Thus $P_T$ has degree at most three.
Its third derivative is independent of the base point and additive in
each argument, because the corresponding fourth derivatives vanish.
It therefore suffices to compute on basis triples.
A singleton term contributes $1/2$ on its triple repeated index; a pair
term contributes $-1/2=1/2$ on either repetition pattern with that support;
a three-coordinate term contributes $1/2$ on each permutation of its three
indices. These are precisely the coefficients of $T$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[A concrete lift of every alternating form]\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:lem:cubic-lift}
For $u,v\in V^*$ define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:Cuv}
 C_{u,v}(a,b,c)=u(a)u(b)v(c)+u(a)v(b)u(c)+v(a)u(b)u(c).
\end{equation}
Then $C_{u,v}$ is symmetric and
\[
 \Omega_{C_{u,v}}=u\otimes v+v\otimes u.
\]
Consequently the obstruction map is surjective and
\[
 \SymMult^3(V)/\nCSM^3(V)\cong\Alt^2(V).
\]
If $\rk\Omega_T=2r$, one can write
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:cubic-normal}
 T=S+\sum_{j=1}^r C_{u_j,v_j},\qquad \Omega_S=0,
\end{equation}
with the $2r$ linear forms $u_1,v_1,\ldots,u_r,v_r$ independent.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Substitution gives the displayed obstruction. Every alternating form has
a symplectic decomposition into the indicated rank-two blocks, and
proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:prop:primitive} identifies the kernel. Subtracting the chosen lifts
from $T$ gives \eqref{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:cubic-normal}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The selected cube identity}
\begin{lemma}[Fourier square and phase removal]\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:lem:cube}
For every symmetric cubic $T$ and every $f:V\to\C$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:cube}
 \en_T(f)=\E_{x,a,b,c}
  \partial_a\partial_b\partial_c f(x)(-1)^{T(a,b,c)}.
\end{equation}
If $P$ is a cubic primitive of $S$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:gauge}
 \en_T(f)=\en_{T-S}\bigl(f e(-P)\bigr).
\end{equation}
In particular, when $T$ integrates,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:lossless}
 \en_T(f)=\norm{f e(-P_T)}_{U^3(V)}^8.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For any linear functional $\xi$,
\[
 \abs{\widehat g(\xi)}^2
 =\E_{x,c}g(x+c)\overline{g(x)}(-1)^{\xi(c)}.
\]
Apply this with $g=\partial_a\partial_bf$ and
$\xi=T(a,b,\cdot)$, then average over $a,b$.
For the gauge identity, the third multiplicative derivative of $e(P)$
is $e(\Delta_a\Delta_b\Delta_cP)=(-1)^{S(a,b,c)}$.
The phase factors cancel exactly. For $T-S=0$ the cube average is the
standard eighth power of the $U^3$ norm.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Finite projective orthogonality}
\begin{lemma}[Bilinear twisted correlation]\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:lem:orthogonality}
Let $B:V^2\to\Ftwo$ be bilinear, and suppose the alternating part
$B(a,b)+B(b,a)$ has rank $2r$. Set
\[
 Q_B(g)=\E_a\abs{\E_x g(x+a)\overline{g(x)}(-1)^{B(a,x)}}^2.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:orthogonality}
 Q_B(g)\le2^{-r}\norm g_2^4.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
On the finite-dimensional Hilbert space $L^2(V)$ define
\[
 W_ag(x)=(-1)^{B(a,x)}g(x+a).
\]
These are unitary, and direct multiplication gives
\[
 W_aW_b=(-1)^{B(b,a)}W_{a+b},\qquad
 W_aW_b=(-1)^{B(a,b)+B(b,a)}W_bW_a.
\]
Every nonzero common invariant subspace for the $W_a$ has dimension at
least $2^r$. To see this, choose symplectic vectors $a_1,b_1,\ldots,a_r,b_r$
for their commutator form. Multiply each $W_{a_j}$ by a scalar in
$\{1,i\}$ so that it becomes an involution. These involutions commute and
can be simultaneously diagonalized. Start with a nonzero common
eigenvector in the invariant subspace. Applying products of the $W_{b_j}$
changes its $r$ eigenvalue signs in all $2^r$ possible ways. These vectors
belong to distinct simultaneous eigenspaces and are linearly independent.

Consider the positive operator
\[
 H_g=\E_a\,|W_ag\rangle\langle W_ag|.
\]
The notation denotes the rank-one operator $v\mapsto\ip{v}{W_ag}W_ag$,
with inner product linear in the first variable. Its trace is
$\norm g_2^2$. The cocycle identity implies that conjugation by any $W_b$
permutes the summands, so $H_g$ commutes with all $W_b$.
Every positive eigenspace therefore has dimension at least $2^r$.
It follows that
\[
 \norm{H_g}_{\mathrm{op}}\le2^{-r}\tr H_g=2^{-r}\norm g_2^2.
\]
Finally $Q_B(g)=\ip{H_gg}{g}\le\norm{H_g}_{\mathrm{op}}\norm g_2^2$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The Boolean shear and the exact scalar optimum}
\begin{theorem}[Credited scalar cubic energy theorem]\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:scalar}
Let $T:V^3\to\Ftwo$ be symmetric and $\rk\Omega_T=2r$. For arbitrary $f$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:amplitude}
 \en_T(f)\le2^{-r}\norm{|f|^2}_{U^2(V)}^4.
\end{equation}
For $1$-bounded $f$, writing $\mu=\E_x|f(x)|^2$, this implies
\[
 \en_T(f)\le2^{-r}\mu^3\le2^{-r}.
\]
Moreover
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:scalar-optimum}
 \M(T):=\max_{\norm f_\infty\le1}\en_T(f)=2^{-r}.
\end{equation}
The smallest codimension of a subspace on which $T$ integrates is $r$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
In \eqref{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:cube}, replace $c$ by $a+w$ and put $g_w(x)=f(x)f(x+w)$.
A pointwise multiplication, valid even at zeros of $f$, gives
\[
 \partial_a\partial_{a+w}f(x)=\overline{\partial_a g_w(x)}.
\]
The tensor factor becomes
\[
 T(a,b,a+w)=B_w(a,b),\qquad
 B_w(a,b)=T(a,a,b)+T(a,b,w).
\]
It is bilinear in $a,b$ and its alternating part is $\Omega_T$. Expanding
the square in $Q_B$ shows
\[
 Q_B(g)=\E_{x,a,b}\partial_a\partial_b g(x)(-1)^{B(a,b)}.
\]
It is real and nonnegative. Consequently conjugation from the shear does
not alter the average, and
\[
 \en_T(f)=\E_w Q_{B_w}(g_w)
 \le2^{-r}\E_w\left(\E_x|f(x)|^2|f(x+w)|^2\right)^2.
\]
The final expectation is $\norm{|f|^2}_{U^2}^4$. If $a=|f|^2\in[0,1]$ and
$c(w)=\E_xa(x)a(x+w)$, then $c(w)\le\mu$ and $\E_wc(w)=\mu^2$; hence
$\E_wc(w)^2\le\mu^3$.

For attainment use \eqref{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:cubic-normal} and a primitive $P_S$ of $S$.
The gauge identity gives
\[
 \en_T(e(P_S))=\en_{\sum_jC_{u_j,v_j}}(1).
\]
For a constant function, the energy is the probability that the selected
functional vanishes. For one coordinate pair, this functional is
\[
 c\longmapsto a_1b_1c_2+(a_1b_2+a_2b_1)c_1.
\]
For $a=00,01,10,11$ the numbers of allowed $b$ are respectively $4,2,1,1$.
Thus the probability is $8/16=1/2$. The independent coordinate pairs
multiply, giving $2^{-r}$.

Finally, proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:prop:primitive} identifies the integration subspaces with
the isotropic spaces of $\Omega_T$. A maximal such space has dimension
$n-r$ by elementary symplectic linear algebra, including the radical.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Credit.} This is source~43's exact cubic energy theorem (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:cubic-exact}, in its normalization $2^{-r/2}$ for the twisted norm), as the heading says; the proof here is a re-proof.
\end{writenote}

\section[{Sharp simultaneous integration and energy-defect stability\srctag{95}}]{Sharp simultaneous integration and energy-defect stability}\label{gsr:fp:95:sec:d6}\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:sec:joint}
\srcnote{95}{Section 6}

\subsection{The exact invariant and the three-budget theorem}
\begin{theorem}[Exact two-tensor integration invariant]\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:joint-exact}
For symmetric Boolean cubics $T_0,T_1$, let
\[
 r=\tfrac12\rk_{\Ftwo(z)}(\Omega_{T_0}+z\Omega_{T_1}).
\]
Then $c(T_0,T_1)=r$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:prop:primitive}, a subspace integrates both tensors exactly when
it is isotropic for both alternating obstructions. Apply
theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:isotropic}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:95:spi:thm:main}]
Put $r_i=\rk\Omega_{T_i}/2$. By theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:scalar}, the energy hypotheses
give $2^{-K_i}\le2^{-r_i}$, so $r_i\le K_i$. Apply
theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:frontier} to the three directions $[1:0],[0:1],[1:1]$.
Its four subset bounds are precisely \eqref{gsr:fm:95:spi:eq:three-budget}.
Use theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:joint-exact} to convert generic half-rank to joint codimension.
The dimension bound follows because an alternating matrix on an
$n$-dimensional space has rank at most $2\lfloor n/2\rfloor$.

For sharpness set $R=B(K_0,K_1,K_+)$ and choose plane multiplicities
$m_i\ge\max\{0,R-K_i\}$ with $m_0+m_1+m_+=R$, as in
theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:frontier}. On each plane choose independent coordinate forms
$u,v$ and its cubic $C=C_{u,v}$. Assign the pair of tensors on a plane as
follows:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}cccc@{}}
\toprule
Root direction & $T_0$ & $T_1$ & $T_+$\\
\midrule
$[1:0]$ & $0$ & $C$ & $C$\\
$[0:1]$ & $C$ & $0$ & $C$\\
$[1:1]$ & $C$ & $C$ & $0$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Sum over the planes. Their obstruction pencil has generic half-rank $R$,
while each tensor is a sum of $R-m_i$ independent canonical blocks.
By the direct count in theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:scalar}, the same constant function gives
\[
 \en_{T_i}(1)=2^{-(R-m_i)}\ge2^{-K_i}.
\]
The exact invariant gives $c=R$. To attain the dimension-capped bound,
keep any required smaller number of the planes and add a common radical
until the desired dimension is reached. Removing a plane cannot worsen
any energy threshold.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of corollary~\ref{gsr:fm:95:spi:cor:common}]
Since $r_i$ is an integer and $\delta\le2^{-r_i}$, one has
$r_i\le\lfloor\log_2(1/\delta)\rfloor=K$.
The formula for $B$ gives $\lfloor3K/2\rfloor$, and the sharp construction
above meets the stronger dyadic threshold $2^{-K}\ge\delta$.
For only two tests, intersect two individual repair spaces to get $2K$.
Two disjoint collections of $K$ canonical cubic planes attain this bound.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Amplitude-sensitive and non-dyadic versions}
\begin{corollary}[Use the actual available mass]\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:cor:amplitude-budget}
Assume $\en_{T_i}(f_i)>0$ and set
\[
 A_i=\norm{|f_i|^2}_{U^2}^4,\qquad
 K_i^{\mathrm{eff}}=
 \left\lfloor\log_2\frac{A_i}{\en_{T_i}(f_i)}\right\rfloor.
\]
Then the bound in theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:95:spi:thm:main} remains valid with $K_i^{\mathrm{eff}}$
in place of $K_i$. When only $\mu_i=\E|f_i|^2$ is available, $A_i$ may be
replaced by $\mu_i^3$. When only lower energy bounds $\delta_i$ are known,
one may use $K_i=\lfloor\log_2(1/\delta_i)\rfloor$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The amplitude-sensitive scalar inequality gives
$\en_{T_i}(f_i)/A_i\le2^{-r_i}$. The denominator is positive because the
energy is positive. Taking logarithms and using integral ranks proves the
first assertion. The remaining claims use $A_i\le\mu_i^3\le1$ and
monotonicity of the budget frontier.
\end{proof}

These are rigorous bounds, not assertions of optimality under every
additional prescribed mass constraint. Numerical use of the floor functions
requires certified lower bounds on energies and upper bounds on the
amplitude factors; an unchecked floating-point value at a dyadic boundary
is insufficient.

\subsection{A product law and its exact slack decomposition}
\begin{theorem}[Product law and algebraic stability]\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:energy-stability}
Let $e_i=\en_{T_i}(f_i)>0$ for $i=0,1,+$, and let $c=c(T_0,T_1)$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:product}
 e_0e_1e_+\le2^{-2c}.
\end{equation}
More precisely, writing $r_i=\rk\Omega_{T_i}/2$ and
\[
 D=r_0+r_1+r_+-2c,\qquad
 \eta_i=\log_2\frac{2^{-r_i}}{e_i},
\]
one has the exact nonnegative-slack identity
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:energy-slack}
 \log_2\frac1{e_0e_1e_+}-2c=D+\eta_0+\eta_1+\eta_+.
\end{equation}
There is a subspace $U$ of codimension at most $D$ on which the obstruction
pencil splits into scalar symplectic planes and a common radical. In
particular this codimension is at most
\[
 \left\lfloor\log_2\frac1{e_0e_1e_+}-2c\right\rfloor.
\]
If the expression inside the floor is less than one, the original pencil
already has the split normal form.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The scalar theorem gives $\eta_i\ge0$, and the rank-budget theorem gives
$D\ge0$. Expanding the logarithm proves \eqref{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:energy-slack} and hence
\eqref{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:product}. Apply theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:stability} to the three Boolean
directions. Finally $D$ is an integer, so slack less than one forces $D=0$;
then use theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:zero-defect}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Equality for individually optimized energies]\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:cor:optimized}
For the three scalar optima,
\[
 \M(T_0)\M(T_1)\M(T_+)=2^{-2c-D}.
\]
Equality with $2^{-2c}$ holds exactly when the obstruction pencil is split
into scalar planes over $\Ftwo$, modulo a common radical.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Substitute \eqref{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:scalar-optimum} and use theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:zero-defect}.
\end{proof}

The three separate maxima in this corollary need not be attained by the
same function. The canonical budget extremizers do admit a common
maximizer, but no classification of common maximizers for an arbitrary pair
is asserted here.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Explicit extremizers and counterexamples\srctag{95}}]{Explicit extremizers and counterexamples}\label{gsr:fp:95:sec:d7}\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:sec:examples}
\srcnote{95}{Section 7}

\begin{example}[Six dimensions, three indistinguishable individual ranks]\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:ex:six}
Let $V=\Ftwo^6$ have coordinate pairs $(u_j,v_j)$ for $j=1,2,3$, and write
$C_j=C_{u_j,v_j}$. Take
\[
 T_0=C_1+C_3,\qquad T_1=C_2+C_3,\qquad T_+=C_1+C_2.
\]
Each obstruction has rank four. The pencil is the direct sum of the three
blocks
\[
 sJ,\quad tJ,\quad(s+t)J.
\]
Its generic rank is six, even though every one of its three nonzero
base-field directions has rank four. Therefore
\[
 \en_{T_0}(1)=\en_{T_1}(1)=\en_{T_+}(1)=\tfrac14,
 \qquad c(T_0,T_1)=3.
\]
One may take the common isotropic space $v_1=v_2=v_3=0$.
Every codimension-two subspace fails to integrate at least one tensor by
theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:joint-exact}. This disproves the putative bound
$c\le\max_i\rk\Omega_{T_i}/2$.
Taking $m$ independent copies gives energies $2^{-2m}$ and joint
codimension $3m$, proving the sharp asymptotic coefficient $3/2$.
\end{example}

\begin{example}[Unequal budgets and why all four terms are needed]\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:ex:unequal}
For $(K_0,K_1,K_+)=(1,1,100)$, the answer is $B=2$, not the total-budget
quantity $51$. Put the first two tensors on disjoint canonical planes.
Their energies are $1/2,1/2,1/4$, which satisfy all three thresholds.
For $(2,3,3)$, the total-budget constraint is decisive and gives $B=4$.
Plane multiplicities $(m_0,m_1,m_+)=(2,1,1)$ give individual half-ranks
$(2,3,3)$ and exact joint cost four.
If one budget is zero, its obstruction vanishes and the formula reduces
to the minimum of the other two budgets, as it should because their
obstructions are equal.
\end{example}

\begin{example}[The same optimized energies, different joint costs]\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:ex:ambiguity}
The six-dimensional example has evaluated half-ranks $(2,2,2)$ and joint
cost three. The irreducible pencil in example~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:ex:irreducible}, with a
common two-dimensional radical adjoined, has the same evaluated half-ranks
but joint cost two. Lift its two alternating forms to symmetric cubics via
lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:lem:cubic-lift}. In both cases the three individually optimized
energies are $(1/4,1/4,1/4)$, while the simultaneous codimension differs.
This is the smallest integral interval with two possible values in
corollary~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:cor:ambiguity}.
\end{example}

\begin{example}[A complete finite-field obstruction]\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:ex:q}
Over $\F_q$, take one scalar symplectic plane for every direction of
$\Prob^1(\F_q)$, with that direction as its root. The ambient dimension is
$2(q+1)$, the generic half-rank is $q+1$, and every evaluated half-rank is
$q$. Thus no universal coefficient smaller than $(q+1)/q$ can recover
joint isotropic codimension from the worst rational rank.
\end{example}

\subsection{Why two generators are special}
\begin{proposition}[A three-generator failure]\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:prop:three-generators}
The equality between common isotropic codimension and generic half-rank
does not extend from pencils to three-dimensional families of alternating
forms. Over $\Ftwo^3$, let
\[
 A_{12}=x_1\wedge x_2,\quad A_{13}=x_1\wedge x_3,\quad
 A_{23}=x_2\wedge x_3.
\]
Every nonzero scalar combination has rank two, and the generic matrix in
three independent parameters has rank two. Nevertheless the largest common
isotropic subspace has dimension one, so the joint codimension is two.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
A nonzero alternating form in dimension three has rank two. The generic
form is nonzero and cannot have rank three.
If $u,v$ are independent, at least one of their $2\times2$ coordinate minors
is nonzero; otherwise the $2\times3$ matrix with rows $u,v$ would have
rank at most one. That minor is one of the values $A_{ij}(u,v)$.
Thus no two-dimensional subspace is isotropic for all three forms.
Every one-dimensional subspace is isotropic for every alternating form.
\end{proof}

The forms in this example lift to symmetric cubics. Thus the obstruction is
a real limitation of simultaneous phase integration, not an artefact of
forgetting the tensor origin. More generally the full space of alternating
forms on $k^n$ has common isotropic dimension one, while its generic
half-rank is only $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The first nonclassical obstruction in every prime characteristic\srctag{95}}]{The first nonclassical obstruction in every prime characteristic}\label{gsr:fp:95:sec:d8}\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:sec:prime}
\srcnote{95}{Section 8}

\subsection{The alternating quotient at degree \texorpdfstring{$p+1$}{p+1}}
Let $p$ be prime and $V=\F_p^n$. For symmetric $(p+1)$-linear $T$, define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:prime-obstruction}
 B_T(a,b)=T(\underbrace{a,\ldots,a}_{p\text{ times}},b),
 \qquad \Omega_T(a,b)=B_T(a,b)-B_T(b,a).
\end{equation}
The use of the prime field is essential: $a\mapsto T(a^p,b)$ is
Frobenius-semilinear over a general extension field, rather than linear.

\begin{proposition}[First-obstruction integration criterion]\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:prop:prime}
$B_T$ is bilinear over $\F_p$, and $\Omega_T$ is alternating.
The tensor $T$ is the highest derivative of a nonclassical polynomial of
degree at most $p+1$ if and only if $\Omega_T=0$.
Moreover every alternating bilinear form occurs as $\Omega_T$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
In expanding $T((a+a')^p,b)$, symmetry collects mixed terms with
coefficients $\binom pj$, which vanish modulo $p$ for $0<j<p$.
For $\lambda\in\F_p$, $\lambda^p=\lambda$. This proves linearity in $a$;
linearity in $b$ is immediate. Hence $\Omega_T$ is alternating.

At degree $p+1$ the additional nonclassical symmetry condition is exactly
\[
 T(a,\ldots,a,b)=T(a,b,\ldots,b),
\]
with $p$ copies of the repeated argument. By the established characterization
and integration theorem for nonclassical symmetric multilinear forms
\cite[Definition~3.1, Propositions~3.4--3.5]{tidor}, this condition is
necessary and sufficient. This is the one integration input in the
prime-characteristic extension; it is not reproved here in all degrees.

For surjectivity, let $u,v\in V^*$ and define
\[
 C^{(p)}_{u,v}(h_1,\ldots,h_{p+1})
 =\sum_{j=1}^{p+1}v(h_j)\prod_{i\ne j}u(h_i).
\]
Then $B_{C^{(p)}_{u,v}}(a,b)=u(a)v(b)$: the $p$ terms with $v$ on an
$a$-slot cancel, leaving the term with $v$ on $b$. Thus its obstruction
is $u\otimes v-v\otimes u$. Decomposing an arbitrary alternating form
into these elementary wedges proves surjectivity.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Antecedents.} At degree $p+1$ this criterion is source~46's first-obstruction test (Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:46:prop:first-obstruction}), proved for every prime there, and the test of sources~89 and~92 (Section~\ref{gsr:fp:sec:critical}); the alternating form $\Omega_T$ is source~46's $C_T$, source~89's $\mathfrak D_T$ and source~92's $B_T$. This source's own $B_T(a,b)=T(a^p,b)$ is \emph{not} source~92's $B_T$.
\end{writenote}

\begin{theorem}[Two-model integration at the first obstruction degree]\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:prime-joint}
For two symmetric $(p+1)$-linear forms $T_0,T_1$ over $\F_p$, the least
codimension of a common subspace carrying primitives for both equals
\[
 \tfrac12\rk_{\F_p(z)}(\Omega_{T_0}+z\Omega_{T_1}).
\]
Every finite-test rank budget, rank-profile realization, and rank-defect
restriction conclusion above applies to this pair. In particular, if
\[
 \tfrac12\rk(s\Omega_{T_0}+t\Omega_{T_1})\le K
 \quad\text{for every }[s:t]\in\Prob^1(\F_p),
\]
then both models integrate on a common subspace of codimension at most
$\lfloor(p+1)K/p\rfloor$, and this is sharp.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Use proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:prop:prime} to translate simultaneous integration into common
isotropy, and then apply theorems~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:isotropic}, \ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:frontier} and \ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:stability}.
The sharp scalar-plane pencils lift to tensors by the surjectivity proved
in proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:prop:prime}; their generic half-rank forces the same lower bound.
\end{proof}

There is no claim here of an odd-prime analogue of the exact scalar energy
formula \eqref{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:scalar-optimum} for $(p+1)$-linear forms. The theorem is
rank-based in odd characteristic. Converting its input from derivative
energy requires an additional analytic argument, posed below as a research
question rather than silently assumed.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Phase removal, coherence, and the Gowers interface\srctag{95}}]{Phase removal, coherence, and the Gowers interface}\label{gsr:fp:95:sec:d9}\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:sec:interface}
\srcnote{95}{Section 9}

\subsection{A common domain and compatible primitives}
Let $W$ be an optimal common integration space for the two Boolean cubics.
Apply \eqref{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:primitive} on one chosen basis of $W$ to obtain $P_0,P_1$.
Set $P_+=P_0+P_1$. Then $P_+$ is a primitive of $T_+|_{W^3}$. This choice is
coherent even when the coordinate formula for $T_+$ by itself would choose
a different primitive: the two choices differ by a polynomial of degree
at most two.

The additive lift should not be confused with a literal $\Ftwo$-linear map
into the group of $\Tcirc$-valued polynomials. A primitive can have order eight;
$2P_0$ need not vanish. It does have zero third derivative. The natural
linearity is in the quotient by lower-degree polynomials.

\begin{proposition}[Lossless removal on every common coset]\label{gsr:fp:95:spi:prop:cosets}
For any $z\in V$ and $f:V\to\C$, put $f_z(w)=f(z+w)$ on $W$. Then,
for $i=0,1,+$,
\[
 \en_{T_i|_{W^3}}(f_z)=
 \norm{f_z e(-P_i)}_{U^3(W)}^8.
\]
All averages on both sides are normalized on $W$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Apply the exact gauge identity \eqref{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:lossless} to the restricted tensor
on the group $W$. The original tensor is independent of the base point,
so its restriction is the same on every coset.
\end{proof}

This proposition supplies simultaneous \emph{algebraic} phase removal with
no loss after the common domain has been fixed. It does not assert a lower
bound for any of these restricted energies in terms of the original
full-group energies. In particular the signs in a twisted cube average
prevent discarding directions outside $W$ as though every individual cube
term were nonnegative.

\subsection{Normalization and a safe formal crosswalk}
The repository's \texttt{proposition\_17\_2} is stated on $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$
with unnormalized Fourier sums and a $k$-linear selector. The current
manuscript uses $V=\Ftwo^n$, normalized Fourier transforms, and a symmetric
trilinear tensor associated to a two-variable selector.
For a group of size $N$ and $k=2$, the unnormalized selected Fourier-square
sum is $N^4$ times \eqref{gsr:fm:95:spi:eq:energy}. Thus an expression of the form
$\alpha N^{k+2}$ corresponds to normalized energy $\alpha$ when $k=2$.
This numerical correspondence is not an identification of the underlying
groups or of their polynomial notions.

The inspected formal definition explicitly requires $k+1<N$ and an
invertible $(k+1)!$, and uses a classical polynomial phase of degree $k+1$
\cite{repo95lean}. In characteristic two, the Boolean primitive must
instead be allowed values in $\tfrac18\mathbb Z/\mathbb Z$. Substituting
\texttt{ZMod 2}-valued polynomials would encode the wrong theorem.

A safe integration route is to add a finite-vector-space phase module, prove
the normalized cube identity, implement the alternating obstruction, and
then expose the common-subspace result. Only a separate localization theorem
could turn this addition into an end-to-end improvement of the cyclic
Gowers argument.

\subsection{A dependency map without hidden inverse-theorem assumptions}
The logical structure is
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \text{classical alternating-pencil normal form}
 \Longrightarrow \text{exact common isotropic dimension},\\
 \text{Pfaffian multiplicity}
 \Longrightarrow \text{finite-test rank budgets},\\
 \text{block defects}
 \Longrightarrow \text{split restriction with codimension }D,\\
 \text{Boolean projective orthogonality and shear}
 \Longrightarrow \text{energy-to-rank bound},\\
 \text{these four inputs}
 \Longrightarrow \text{optimal simultaneous phase integration}.
 \end{gathered}
\]
The Boolean argument does not invoke a quantitative inverse theorem as an
unproved intermediate assertion. The odd-prime extension additionally uses
the published nonclassical integration theorem.

\section{Source~105: the sharp ternary quartic energy \texorpdfstring{$11/27$}{11/27} \wtag}\label{gsr:fp:sec:ternaryquartic}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the fourteenth write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next seven sections are source~105's Sections~2--8. \emph{Logically they continue} the chapter on the first nonclassical obstruction (Section~\ref{gsr:fp:sec:critical}), immediately after source~92's ternary certificate (Section~\ref{gsr:fp:92:sec:d11}). The introduction is Section~\ref{gsr:fm:105:sec:d1}.

\emph{What is proved.} For the canonical symmetric quartic $T_0(h_1,\ldots,h_4)=\sum_jy_j\prod_{k\ne j}x_k$ on $\F_3^2$ and $|f|\le1$, the twisted $U^4$ energy satisfies $\calE_{T_0}(f)\le11/27$, attained by $f=1$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:105:thm:sharp}): \emph{source~92's Conjecture~\ref{gsr:fp:92:conj:ternary} is proved}, and source~92's certified interval $[11/27,1099/2187]$ collapses. The proof is an affine-line change of variables, $59049\,\calE=21609+16\calK(g)$, and an exact Hermitian Gram certificate of order $241$ over $\Q(\zeta_3)$ (rank $213$, kernel the $28$ family vectors, margin above $1/5$), shipped as \file{data/105-ternary-quartic-ternary\_quartic\_gram.json} (1.37~MB) and part of the proof, as the article says: it is computer-assisted, and the certificate is listed with the report's other finite certificates as a trust boundary. Also every extremizer ($2916$ three-dimensional tori; Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:105:thm:extremizers}), stability in monomial coordinates (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:105:thm:stability}; only qualitative on the polydisc), and in every dimension: a symmetric four-linear $T$ with energy above $11/27$ integrates nonclassically, sharply (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:105:thm:global}). This answers source~92's Question~14.1 (a sum-of-squares certificate) and its Question~14.4 (stability) in monomial coordinates.

\emph{Against source~89.} Source~105's $T_0$ is source~89's canonical block at $p=3$, and $11/27=c_3=1-2(1-1/3)^3$ is source~89's block energy (Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:89:prop:blockenergy}); source~89 conjectured, as an exploratory target, $M_{p,r,n}=c_p^r$ for odd $p$. \emph{Source~105 settles the case $(p,r)=(3,1)$ for every $n$}, and gives $M_{3,r,n}\le11/27$ for every $r\ge1$; its Questions~10.1 ($m_{3,r}=(11/27)^r$) and~10.4 ($1-2(1-1/p)^p$ for odd $p$) are the remaining cases of source~89's conjecture. Source~105 does not cite source~89; credit and merge are in item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:IV:lowchar}. It credits source~92 (finite-cover realization, the structural reduction, the census constants $20457$ and $29673$), Tidor (the integration criterion, reproved in characteristic three) and Tao--Ziegler.

\emph{Checked at the write} (\file{verify14.py}): $\calE_{T_0}(1)=11/27$ by a direct average over $(\F_3^2)^4$; $59049\cdot11/27=24057$ and $59049\cdot1099/2187=29673$; among all $243$ symmetric quartic tensors on $\F_3^2$, the $162$ with $B_T\ne0$ have $\calE_T(1)\in\{217,241,249,265,297\}/729$ with multiplicities $18,48,48,24,24$, maximum $11/27$ (twice source~89's ternary table).
