\section[{Definitions and main results\srctag{105}}]{Definitions and main results}\label{gsr:fp:105:sec:d2}\label{gsr:fp:105:sec:main}
\srcnote{105}{Section 2}

Put \(\T=\R/\Z\), \(\e(t)=\exp(2\pi it)\), and
\(\zeta=\e(1/3)\). Every finite average is normalized. Complex
conjugation is denoted by \(\cC\). On a finite abelian group define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:cube}
 C_df(a;h_1,\ldots,h_d)
 =\prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^d}
    \cC^{\,d-|\omega|} f(a+\omega_1h_1+\cdots+\omega_dh_d).
\end{equation}
For even \(d\), this is the usual even-vertex convention. A
circle-valued function \(P\) has additive degree at most \(d\) if all its
\((d+1)\)-fold additive differences vanish. Its \(d\)-fold difference is
then independent of the basepoint and is symmetric and multiadditive.

For a symmetric four-linear tensor \(T:(\F_3^n)^4\to\F_3\), let
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:energy}
 \calE_T(f)=\E_{a,h_1,h_2,h_3,h_4}
     C_4f(a;h_1,h_2,h_3,h_4)\zeta^{-T(h_1,h_2,h_3,h_4)}.
\end{equation}
We identify a field value \(t\) with \(t/3\pmod1\) when taking
circle-valued differences. The alternating transfer defect is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:defect}
 B_T(u,v)=T(u,u,u,v)-T(u,v,v,v).
\end{equation}
The canonical plane has coordinates \((x,y)\) and tensor
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:canonical}
 T_0(h_1,h_2,h_3,h_4)
   =\sum_{j=1}^4 y_j\prod_{k\ne j}x_k,
 \qquad h_j=(x_j,y_j).
\end{equation}
In particular, \(B_{T_0}(u,v)=x(u)y(v)-x(v)y(u)\ne0\).

\begin{theorem}[Sharp plane energy]\label{gsr:fp:105:thm:sharp}
For every \(f:\F_3^2\to\C\) with \(\abs{f}\le1\),
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:sharp}
 0\le\calE_{T_0}(f)\le\frac{11}{27}.
\end{equation}
The upper constant is attained by \(f=1\). Every function attaining it
has modulus one at every point.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Source~92's Conjecture~\ref{gsr:fp:92:conj:ternary} is proved} (Section~\ref{gsr:fp:sec:ternaryquartic}). This is also the case $(p,r)=(3,1)$ of source~89's exploratory conjecture $M_{p,r,n}=c_p^r$, with $c_3=1-2(2/3)^3=11/27$ (Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:89:prop:blockenergy}); this source does not cite source~89. Checked at the write: $\calE_{T_0}(1)=11/27$, and $11/27$ is the largest $\calE_T(1)$ over all symmetric quartic tensors on $\F_3^2$ with $B_T\ne0$ (\file{verify14.py}). The proof uses the shipped Gram certificate (a trust boundary; the verifier reran exactly).
\end{writenote}

Here is an explicit version of the equality classification. Throughout
the following formulas \(X=\digitthree{x}\) and \(Y=\digitthree{y}\) are the
integer digits \(0,1,2\). Rational polynomials in these digits are
interpreted in \(\T\), not by division inside \(\F_3\). Set
\begin{align}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:ells}
 \ell_0(x,y)&=x,&\ell_1(x,y)&=y,&
 \ell_2(x,y)&=y-x,&\ell_3(x,y)&=y+x,
\end{align}
and define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:basephases}
 P_0=0,\quad P_1=\frac{2XY}{9},\quad
 P_2=\frac{X^2+2Y^2+XY}{9},\quad
 P_3=\frac{2X^2+Y^2+XY}{9}\pmod1.
\end{equation}
Let \(\Gamma\) be the following finite group of cubic phases, normalized
to take value one at the origin:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:cubicgroup}
 \Gamma=\left\{\e(C):
 C=\frac{aX+bY}{9}
  +\frac{rX^2+sXY+tY^2+uX^2Y+vXY^2}{3}\pmod1\right\},
\end{equation}
where \(a,b\in\{0,\ldots,8\}\) and
\(r,s,t,u,v\in\{0,1,2\}\).

\begin{theorem}[Every extremizer]\label{gsr:fp:105:thm:extremizers}
Equality in the upper bound of theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:105:thm:sharp} holds if and only if
there are \(d\in\{0,1,2,3\}\), \(\gamma\in\Gamma\), and an arbitrary
function \(h:\F_3\to\C\) with \(\abs{h}=1\), such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:all-extremizers}
 f(x,y)=\gamma(x,y)\e(P_d(x,y))h(\ell_d(x,y)).
\end{equation}
The set of extremizers is the disjoint union of 2916 connected
three-dimensional tori inside \((S^1)^9\). Equivalently, after quotienting
by a global phase, its connected components are two-dimensional tori.
The parametrization \eqref{gsr:fp:105:eq:all-extremizers} is not unique.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp dimension-free integration threshold]\label{gsr:fp:105:thm:global}
Let \(n\ge1\), let \(T:(\F_3^n)^4\to\F_3\) be symmetric and four-linear,
and let \(\abs{f}\le1\). If \(B_T\ne0\), then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:globalbound}
 \calE_T(f)\le\frac{11}{27}.
\end{equation}
Consequently, if \(\calE_T(f)>11/27\), there exists a nonclassical
polynomial \(P:\F_3^n\to\T\) of degree at most four such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:integration-conclusion}
 \Delta^4P=T/3,\qquad
 \calE_T(f)=\norm{f\e(-P)}_{U^4(\F_3^n)}^{16}.
\end{equation}
For every \(n\ge2\), the supremum of \(\calE_T(f)\) over nonintegrable
symmetric quartic tensors and \(\abs{f}\le1\) is exactly \(11/27\).
The strict inequality in the integration hypothesis cannot be replaced
by a non-strict inequality.
\end{theorem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Consequence for source~89's conjecture}: $M_{3,r,n}\le11/27$ for every $r\ge1$ and every $n$, with equality at $r=1$; the decay in $r$ (source~89's $c_3^r$) remains open (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:IV:lowchar}).
\end{writenote}

A quantitative stability statement is given in section~\ref{gsr:fp:105:sec:stability}.
The proof of theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:105:thm:sharp} is analytic apart from the explicitly
specified finite computations in lemmas~\ref{gsr:fp:105:lem:lineidentity} and \ref{gsr:fp:105:lem:certificate}.
The additional finite checks for equality and the phase quotient are
small integer calculations, described below rather than hidden behind a
numerical search.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Norm realization and reduction to unit phases\srctag{105}}]{Norm realization and reduction to unit phases}\label{gsr:fp:105:sec:d3}\label{gsr:fp:105:sec:norm}
\srcnote{105}{Section 3}

\subsection{An explicit 27-point integrating cover}

The canonical tensor does not integrate on \(\F_3^2\), but it does on
\(A=\Z/9\Z\oplus\Z/3\Z\). Write \(z\) for the first coordinate,
\(y\) for the second, and let \(\pi(z,y)=(z\bmod3,y)\).

\begin{lemma}\label{gsr:fp:105:lem:cover}
The function
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:coverprimitive}
 Q(z,y)=\frac{\binom z3 y}{3}\pmod1
\end{equation}
is well-defined on \(A\), has additive degree at most four, and satisfies
\(\Delta^4Q=\pi^*T_0/3\). Therefore, for arbitrary complex \(f\),
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:normrealization}
 \calE_{T_0}(f)
 =\norm{(f\circ\pi)\e(-Q)}_{U^4(A)}^{16}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Vandermonde's identity shows that
\(\binom{z+9}{3}-\binom z3\) is divisible by three: the coefficients
\(\binom91,\binom92,\binom93\) are all divisible by three. A shift of
three in \(y\) also changes \eqref{gsr:fp:105:eq:coverprimitive} by an integer.
Before taking residues it is an ordinary rational polynomial of total
degree four, so fifth differences vanish.

Its leading term is \(z^3y/18\). In its fourth polarization, placing
three direction slots in \(z\) and one in \(y\) produces coefficient
\(3!/18=1/3\). Summing over the choice of the \(y\)-slot gives exactly
\(T_0/3\). Periodicity permits the calculation on integer lifts.
Finally every basepoint and direction in the plane has the same number
of lifts to \(A\), and
\(C_4((f\circ\pi)\e(-Q))=C_4(f\circ\pi)\e(-\Delta^4Q)\).
This proves \eqref{gsr:fp:105:eq:normrealization}.
\end{proof}

The ordinary \(U^4\) functional is a norm, and its mixed cube form
satisfies Gowers--Cauchy--Schwarz \cite{gowers,tidor}. The map
\(f\mapsto(f\circ\pi)\e(-Q)\) is complex-linear and injective.
Thus \(\calE_{T_0}^{1/16}\) is itself a norm. In particular the energy
is real, nonnegative, convex, and a homogeneous real polynomial of degree
16 in the real and imaginary parts of the point values.

\begin{lemma}[Strict convexity and boundary attainment]\label{gsr:fp:105:lem:strict}
The energy \(\calE_{T_0}\) is strictly convex. Its maximum on
\(\{f:|f|\le1\}\) equals its maximum on \(\{f:|f|=1\}\), and every
maximizer on the former set belongs to the latter.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Convexity follows from the norm realization and convexity of \(t^{16}\)
on nonnegative reals. Suppose equality in convexity occurs at an interior
point of a segment with distinct endpoints \(f_0,f_1\). A convex function
with equality at an interior point of its chord is affine on the whole
segment. Hence the polynomial
\(p(t)=\calE_{T_0}(f_0+t(f_1-f_0))\) agrees with an affine polynomial on
an interval and therefore on the real line. Its coefficient of \(t^{16}\),
however, is \(\calE_{T_0}(f_1-f_0)>0\), a contradiction.

Every point of the closed complex unit disc is a convex combination of
two antipodal unit points. Taking the product of these combinations over
the nine coordinates writes every admissible \(f\) as a convex combination
of unimodular functions. This proves the equality of the two maxima. If
one coordinate of a maximizer has modulus less than one, that coordinate
can be perturbed in opposite directions while remaining in the disc.
The original function is the midpoint of two distinct admissible
functions, contrary to strict convexity and maximality.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The lower endpoint]\label{gsr:fp:105:lem:constant}
One has \(\calE_{T_0}(1)=11/27\).
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Average the phase first over \(h_4=(x,y)\). For the first three directions,
the character has coefficients
\[
 A=x_1x_2x_3,\qquad
 B=y_1x_2x_3+y_2x_1x_3+y_3x_1x_2.
\]
Orthogonality gives one precisely when \(A=B=0\), and zero otherwise.
If at least two of the \(x_i\) vanish, both coefficients vanish; this has
probability \(7/27\). If exactly one vanishes, which has probability
\(12/27\), the corresponding \(y_i\) must also vanish, with conditional
probability \(1/3\). The total is \(7/27+4/27=11/27\).
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The affine-line transformation\srctag{105}}]{The affine-line transformation}\label{gsr:fp:105:sec:d4}\label{gsr:fp:105:sec:lines}
\srcnote{105}{Section 4}

\subsection{Twelve constrained phases instead of nine point phases}

Assume now that \(z_v=f(v)\) has modulus one. Let
\(s=\prod_{v\in\F_3^2}z_v\), and put
\(\alpha=(1,1,\zeta,\zeta^2)\). For \(d\in\{0,1,2,3\}\) and
\(c\in\F_3\), define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:linephases}
 g_{d,c}=\alpha_d\,
       \frac{\bigl(\prod_{\ell_d(v)=c}z_v\bigr)^3}{s}.
\end{equation}
These are the phases of the twelve affine lines. Each parallel class
satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:productconstraints}
 |g_{d,c}|=1,\qquad \prod_{c=0}^2g_{d,c}=1.
\end{equation}
Indeed, the three lines partition the plane, and \(\alpha_d^3=1\).
The collection of all phases satisfying \eqref{gsr:fp:105:eq:productconstraints}
is an eight-dimensional torus, denoted by \(\mathscr T\).
For a point \(v\), abbreviate \(g_d(v)=g_{d,\ell_d(v)}\).

For pairs of distinct directions set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:paircoefficients}
 c_{01}=c_{23}=1,\qquad c_{02}=c_{13}=\zeta,\qquad
 c_{03}=c_{12}=\zeta^2.
\end{equation}
Define the real Laurent polynomial
\begin{align}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:K}
 \calK(g)=\sum_{v\in\F_3^2}\bigg(&
   \Re\sum_{0\le i<j<k\le3}g_i(v)g_j(v)g_k(v)
   -2\abs{\sum_{d=0}^3g_d(v)}^2 \notag\\
 &\hspace{2.4em}+6\Re\sum_{0\le i<j\le3}c_{ij}g_i(v)g_j(v)\bigg).
\end{align}

\begin{lemma}[Exact cube-to-line identity]\label{gsr:fp:105:lem:lineidentity}
For every unimodular \(f\), the phases \eqref{gsr:fp:105:eq:linephases} satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:lineidentity}
 59049\calE_{T_0}(f)=21609+16\calK(g).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}[Exact finite coefficient proof]
There are \(9^5=59049\) cubes, including degenerate cubes. Associate to
\((a,h_1,h_2,h_3,h_4)\) the integer exponent vector
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:exponents}
 u_v=\sum_{\substack{\omega\in\{0,1\}^4\\a+\omega\cdot h=v}}
                (-1)^{|\omega|}.
\end{equation}
Its coefficient is \(\zeta^{-T_0(h)}\). Accumulate these coefficients in
\(\Z[\zeta]\), using \(\zeta^2=-1-\zeta\). Independently expand twice
\eqref{gsr:fp:105:eq:K}, so no half-integers are required. Substitute
\eqref{gsr:fp:105:eq:linephases}; the independent variables are \(g_{d,0},g_{d,1}\),
and \(g_{d,2}=(g_{d,0}g_{d,1})^{-1}\). The exponent image of
\(g_{d,c}/\alpha_d\), for \(c=0,1\), is
\[
  (3\,1_{\ell_d(v)=c}-1)_{v\in\F_3^2}.
\]
After adding the constant 21609, the resulting coefficient dictionary
is identical to the original cube dictionary. This equality is checked
by \texttt{cube\_polynomial}, \texttt{doubled\_line\_polynomial}, and
\texttt{verify\_line\_change} in the supplied verifier. Each routine
constructs its object directly from the displayed definitions. No
previously computed coefficient list is loaded.

As independently checked summary data, the cube dictionary has 289
nonzero terms. Its constant is 20457, the sum of its coefficients is
24057, and its absolute coefficient census is
\[
 1\times20457,\quad72\times8,\quad108\times48,\quad108\times32.
\]
The full dictionary comparison, not these summary counts alone, proves
the identity.
\end{proof}

By \eqref{gsr:fp:105:eq:lineidentity}, the desired upper bound is equivalent to
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:Ktarget}
                       \calK(g)\le153.
\end{equation}
The constant is not fitted numerically:
\(21609+16\cdot153=24057=59049\cdot11/27\).

\subsection{The change of variables loses no admissible phases}

\begin{proposition}[Surjectivity and finite gauge kernel]\label{gsr:fp:105:prop:quotient}
The map \eqref{gsr:fp:105:eq:linephases} is onto \(\mathscr T\). After quotienting
by global point phase it is a translate of a torus homomorphism of degree
\(3^9=19683\). The kernel of its unshifted version
\(z\mapsto(g_{d,c}/\alpha_d)\), with \(z_{(0,0)}=1\), is exactly
\(\Gamma\) in \eqref{gsr:fp:105:eq:cubicgroup}.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Let \(A\) be the \(12\times9\) integer matrix
\(A_{(d,c),v}=3\,1_{\ell_d(v)=c}-1\). Affine-plane incidence gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:incidencegram}
                      A^{\mathsf T}A=27I_9-3J_9.
\end{equation}
For the diagonal entries, a point lies on four lines and not on eight,
giving \(4\cdot2^2+8=24\). Two distinct points share exactly one line;
there are six lines containing exactly one of them and five containing
neither, giving \(4-12+5=-3\). Thus the rank is eight and the real kernel
is the global-phase direction. The four row relations are exactly the
sums within parallel classes, so the image has the full dimension of
the target torus. A full-rank homomorphism between these compact tori is
onto.

For the exact degree, keep rows \(c=0,1\) in each class and delete the
column \(v=(0,0)\). In the indicated orders the resulting matrix is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:reducedmatrix}
 M=\begin{pmatrix}
 2&2&-1&-1&-1&-1&-1&-1\\
 -1&-1&2&2&2&-1&-1&-1\\
 -1&-1&2&-1&-1&2&-1&-1\\
 2&-1&-1&2&-1&-1&2&-1\\
 -1&-1&-1&2&-1&-1&-1&2\\
 2&-1&-1&-1&2&2&-1&-1\\
 -1&-1&-1&-1&2&-1&2&-1\\
 2&-1&2&-1&-1&-1&-1&2
 \end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation}
Integer elimination gives \(\abs{\det M}=19683\); the verifier recomputes
this determinant by fraction-free elimination. An invertible integer
matrix acting on a torus has kernel order the absolute determinant.

Every phase in \(\Gamma\) belongs to this kernel. For \(X/9\), the
quantity \(3\sum_{\ell_d(v)=c}X-\sum_vX\) is divisible by nine; the
same holds for \(Y/9\). For each of the five classical monomials divided
by three, the line part is integral and its sum over the plane is also
integral. The seven generator checks are included in the verifier.

There are exactly \(9^2\cdot3^5=3^9\) distinct phases in
\eqref{gsr:fp:105:eq:cubicgroup}. To prove distinctness, multiply a putative zero
phase by nine and reduce modulo three. This first forces the two linear
coefficients to be divisible by three. Division by three then leaves a
reduced polynomial over \(\F_3\), with each individual degree at most
two. The distinct monomials in that polynomial are linearly independent
as functions on \(\F_3^2\), so all coefficients vanish. The explicitly
exhibited subgroup already has the full kernel order, proving equality.
\end{proof}

The phases in \(\Gamma\) have additive degree at most three: the
classical terms have total degree at most three, while \(X/9\) and
\(Y/9\) have nonclassical degree at most three, in the terminology of
Tao and Ziegler \cite{taozieglerlow}. A finite-difference
justification is included in section~\ref{gsr:fp:105:sec:integration}. Thus the finite
kernel is a genuine cubic gauge group, not merely a convenient naming
convention.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{An exact positive semidefinite certificate\srctag{105}}]{An exact positive semidefinite certificate}\label{gsr:fp:105:sec:d5}\label{gsr:fp:105:sec:certificate}
\srcnote{105}{Section 5}

\subsection{The monomial basis}

Write
\(t_{2d}=g_{d,0}\), \(t_{2d+1}=g_{d,1}\).
Let \(G_{d,0}=e_{2d}\), \(G_{d,1}=e_{2d+1}\), and
\(G_{d,2}=-e_{2d}-e_{2d+1}\) in \(\Z^8\). Let \(\calB\) be the
lexicographically ordered set containing
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:basis}
 0,\quad \pm G_{d,c},\quad
 \pm(G_{d,c}+G_{e,b}),\quad
 \pm(G_{d,c}-G_{e,b})\quad(d<e).
\end{equation}
It has \(1+24+216=241\) elements. Put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:monomialvector}
 m(t)=(t^u)_{u\in\calB}\in\C^{241}.
\end{equation}
For a matrix \(Q\) in this basis,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:gramcoeff}
 m(t)^*Qm(t)=\sum_{u,v\in\calB}Q_{u,v}t^{v-u}.
\end{equation}
The order \(v-u\), and not \(u-v\), is part of the certificate convention.

\subsection{Equality families and their coefficient vectors}

Define four subsets of \(\mathscr T\) by table~\ref{gsr:fp:105:tab:families}. A table
entry \(k\) means that all three phases in that class equal \(\zeta^k\).
The star is an arbitrary unit triple of product one.
\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{@{}ccccc@{}}
\toprule
Family & class 0 & class 1 & class 2 & class 3\\
\midrule
\(\calZ_0\)&\(*\)&0&1&2\\
\(\calZ_1\)&0&\(*\)&2&1\\
\(\calZ_2\)&1&2&\(*\)&0\\
\(\calZ_3\)&2&1&0&\(*\)\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Four disjoint equality tori in line coordinates.}
\label{gsr:fp:105:tab:families}
\end{table}

On one such family, substitute its fixed roots into \(m(t)\) and collect
coefficients in its two free variables. There are exactly seven distinct
exponents, namely \(0\) and the positive and negative exponents of that
class's three line variables. Across the four families this gives 28
coefficient columns in \(\Z[\zeta]^{241}\). Let \(K\) be the matrix
whose columns are these vectors, in the order stored in the electronic
certificate. It has rank 28. The verifier checks that each stored column
is literally one of the independently reconstructed family coefficient
vectors, and checks rank 28 after reduction modulo seven with
\(\zeta\mapsto2\). A nonzero minor modulo seven certifies a nonzero
minor over \(\Q(\zeta)\).

\begin{lemma}[Exact Hermitian certificate]\label{gsr:fp:105:lem:certificate}
There are explicitly supplied integer matrices
\(Q_A,Q_B\) of order 241, \(K_A,K_B\) of size \(241\times28\), and
lower triangular matrices \(L_A,L_B\) of order 241 such that, with
\begin{align}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:matrices}
 D&=2592000000,& R&=1000000,\\
 Q&=(Q_A+Q_B\zeta)/D,&K&=K_A+K_B\zeta,&
 L&=(L_A+L_B\zeta)/R,\notag
\end{align}
the following statements hold exactly:
\begin{align}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:certclaims}
 Q&=Q^*, & QK&=0, & \rank K&=28,\\
 m(t)^*Qm(t)&=153-\calK(g), &&&&\notag\\
 Q+KK^*-LL^*&\succeq\mu I_{241},&&&&\notag
\end{align}
where
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:margin}
 \mu=\frac{646878666855648000000}{2592000000000000000000}
     =\frac{6738319446413}{27000000000000}>\frac15.
\end{equation}
The matrices are the electronic appendix
\path{data/ternary_quartic_gram.json}.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Exact verification and its mathematical justification]
Represent \(a+b\zeta\) by the integer pair \((a,b)\). Multiplication and
conjugation are
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:ringops}
 (a,b)(c,d)=(ac-bd,ad+bc-bd),\qquad
 \overline{(a,b)}=(a-b,-b).
\end{equation}
These formulas follow from \(\zeta^2=-1-\zeta\) and
\(\overline\zeta=-1-\zeta\). The verifier first checks the dimensions,
basis order and triangular support. It checks the two integer identities
for every entry of \(Q=Q^*\), and the two integer sums for every entry of
\(QK=0\).

For the polynomial identity, collect \(2(Q_A+Q_B\zeta)_{u,v}\) at
exponent \(v-u\). Independently form
\(D(306-2\calK)\) from \eqref{gsr:fp:105:eq:K}. Equality of the full coefficient
dictionaries proves the second line of \eqref{gsr:fp:105:eq:certclaims}; all
coefficients outside its support must cancel. This is an identity on the
entire phase torus, not just at roots of unity or at test points.

It remains to explain why the positivity check is exact. Put
\(H=Q+KK^*\) and \(S=H-LL^*\). Every entry of \(S\) has denominator
\(DR^2\). For a lower triangular entry write its numerator as
\(a_{ij}+b_{ij}\zeta\). Its upper triangular conjugate has numerator
\((a_{ij}-b_{ij})-b_{ij}\zeta\); in general the corresponding
triangle bounds are different. The program therefore uses the row
bounds
\begin{align}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:rowbounds}
 \abs{a_{ij}+b_{ij}\zeta}&\le |a_{ij}|+|b_{ij}|,\\
 \abs{(a_{ij}-b_{ij})-b_{ij}\zeta}
       &\le |a_{ij}-b_{ij}|+|b_{ij}|.\notag
\end{align}
It verifies that the diagonal numerators are real and that the minimum
diagonal numerator minus the sum of these bounds in its row is exactly
\(646878666855648000000\). Dividing by \(DR^2\) gives \(\mu\).

For completeness, if a Hermitian matrix has diagonal entries at least
\(\mu\) plus the sum of the absolute off-diagonal entries in the
corresponding row, then for every vector \(w\),
\[
 w^*Sw\ge\sum_i\Bigl(S_{ii}-\sum_{j\ne i}|S_{ij}|\Bigr)|w_i|^2
       \ge\mu\norm{w}_2^2.
\]
The first inequality uses \(2|w_iw_j|\le|w_i|^2+|w_j|^2\) on each
cross term. Thus no eigenvalue approximation is needed. Rank and column
membership for \(K\) are checked as described above. All stated checks
have been executed by the supplied standard-library verifier.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Positivity and exact kernel]\label{gsr:fp:105:prop:Qpositive}
The matrix \(Q\) in lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:105:lem:certificate} is positive semidefinite,
\(\ker Q=\im K\), and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:spectralbound}
 w^*Qw\ge\mu\,\dist(w,\im K)^2
       \ge\frac15\dist(w,\im K)^2\qquad(w\in\C^{241}).
\end{equation}
In particular \(\rank Q=213\).
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Since \(LL^*\succeq0\), the certificate gives \(H=Q+KK^*\succeq\mu I\).
Write \(w=w_0+w_1\), with \(w_0\in\im K\) and
\(w_1\perp\im K\). Since \(QK=0\) and \(Q\) is Hermitian,
\(w^*Qw=w_1^*Qw_1\). Also \(K^*w_1=0\), so this equals
\(w_1^*Hw_1\ge\mu\norm{w_1}_2^2\). Equality at zero is possible
only if \(w_1=0\), which proves the exact kernel statement. The rank
follows from \(241-28=213\).
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:105:thm:sharp}]
On the unit phase torus, lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:105:lem:certificate} and proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:105:prop:Qpositive} give
\(153-\calK=m^*Qm\ge0\). The cube-to-line identity proves the upper
bound. Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:105:lem:strict} extends it to the full polydisc and shows that
all maximizers are unimodular. Nonnegativity follows from
lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:105:lem:cover}, and lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:105:lem:constant} gives sharpness.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Classifying all equality cases\srctag{105}}]{Classifying all equality cases}\label{gsr:fp:105:sec:d6}\label{gsr:fp:105:sec:equality}
\srcnote{105}{Section 6}

\subsection{The four line-coordinate families are exhaustive}

\begin{lemma}\label{gsr:fp:105:lem:Kfamilies}
On \(\mathscr T\), equality \(\calK(g)=153\) holds exactly on
\(\calZ_0\cup\calZ_1\cup\calZ_2\cup\calZ_3\).
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Substitution into \eqref{gsr:fp:105:eq:K} shows that its value is 153 identically on
each family. The verifier expands each restricted Laurent polynomial
and verifies that all nonconstant coefficients vanish and its constant
is exactly 153.

Conversely, equality and proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:105:prop:Qpositive} imply
\(m(g)\in\im K\). Let \(k_e^{(d)}\) denote the fixed exponent in
class \(e\ne d\) of family \(\calZ_d\). For any distinct labels
\(c,c'\) and any label \(b\), consider
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:separators}
 (g_{d,c}-g_{d,c'})(g_{e,b}-\zeta^{k_e^{(d)}}),\qquad e\ne d.
\end{equation}
This polynomial is a linear combination of the monomials in \(\calB\).
It vanishes on every family: on \(\calZ_d\) the second factor is zero;
on any other family the first factor is zero, since class \(d\) is
constant there. Its coefficient row therefore annihilates each family
coefficient vector, and hence annihilates \(\im K\). Thus
\eqref{gsr:fp:105:eq:separators} vanishes at the proposed equality point.

If some class \(d\) is nonconstant, choose \(c,c'\) with unequal
phases. Equation \eqref{gsr:fp:105:eq:separators} then forces every other class to
have exactly the constants prescribed by \(\calZ_d\). The point lies
in that family.

It remains to consider points at which all four classes are constant.
By the product constraint, each constant is a cube root of unity, so
there are exactly \(3^4=81\) possibilities. Direct substitution into
\eqref{gsr:fp:105:eq:K}, with integer-pair arithmetic, gives the complete census
in table~\ref{gsr:fp:105:tab:corners}. The twelve points with value 153 are precisely
the points of the four displayed families with the star also constant.
The verifier checks this pointwise identification, not just the census.
This proves exhaustiveness.
\end{proof}

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{@{}rrrrrr@{}}
\toprule
Value of \(\calK\)&\(-252\)&\(-261/2\)&\(-90\)&\(-9\)&\(153\)\\
Number of constant-class points&9&24&24&12&12\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{All 81 constant-class points. These are only the last finite
case in the equality proof, not a discretization of the optimization.}
\label{gsr:fp:105:tab:corners}
\end{table}

\subsection{Returning to point functions}

\begin{lemma}\label{gsr:fp:105:lem:basephase}
For \(f=\e(P_d)\), the line phases outside class \(d\) have the
constants prescribed by \(\calZ_d\). Multiplication by an arbitrary
\(h\circ\ell_d\) changes only class \(d\), where its multiplicative
effect is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:freeeffect}
       u_c=\frac{h(c)^9}{(h(0)h(1)h(2))^3}.
\end{equation}
The map in \eqref{gsr:fp:105:eq:freeeffect} is onto the unit triples of product one.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The unshifted line phases of \(\e(X^2/9)\) are \(\zeta\) in class~0
and one in the other classes. For \(\e(Y^2/9)\), they are \(\zeta\)
in class~1 and one elsewhere. Those of \(\e(XY/9)\) are
\((1,1,\zeta^2,\zeta)\), constant within each class. These statements
follow by summing the indicated digit polynomials over a line and over
the whole plane; all numerator arithmetic can be performed modulo nine.
Combining them and then multiplying by \(\alpha\) proves the assertion
for the four \(P_d\). The verifier repeats these modular calculations.

A line in another parallel class meets each level set of \(\ell_d\)
once. Its product of \(h\)-values is \(h(0)h(1)h(2)\), and the
product over the plane is the cube of this number. Thus the factors
cancel in every other class. A line in class \(d\) contains three copies
of \(h(c)\), giving \eqref{gsr:fp:105:eq:freeeffect}. Normalize \(h(0)=1\).
The map on arguments of \(h(1),h(2)\), recording \(u_0,u_1\), has
integer matrix
\[
          \begin{pmatrix}-3&-3\\6&-3\end{pmatrix},
\]
whose determinant is 27. It is therefore a surjective torus map, with
kernel of order 27.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:105:thm:extremizers}]
Every extremizer is unimodular by lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:105:lem:strict}, and its line phases
belong to some \(\calZ_d\) by lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:105:lem:Kfamilies}. By
lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:105:lem:basephase}, choose \(h\) so that \(\e(P_d)h\circ\ell_d\)
has exactly the same line phases. The ratio of the two point functions
belongs to the unshifted line kernel. A global constant can be absorbed
into \(h\); after that normalization, proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:105:prop:quotient} identifies
the ratio with an element of \(\Gamma\). This gives
\eqref{gsr:fp:105:eq:all-extremizers}. Conversely, the cubic kernel does not change
line phases and lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:105:lem:basephase} places every function of the stated
form in \(\calZ_d\); hence it is an extremizer.

For the component count, fix \(d\). The functions
\(\e(P_d)h\circ\ell_d\) form a translate of a connected
three-dimensional torus. Its translates by \(\Gamma\) are either equal
or disjoint. The intersection of \(\Gamma\) with the unshifted torus of
functions \(h\circ\ell_d\) has exactly 27 elements, by the last part of
lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:105:lem:basephase} and the normalization at the origin. Therefore there
are \(3^9/27=729\) such tori for each \(d\). The four families are
pairwise disjoint: for any two rows of table~\ref{gsr:fp:105:tab:families}, at least one
class fixed in both has different constants. The total is
\(4\cdot729=2916\).
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[A continuous family, not just polynomial phases]
Every unimodular \(f(x,y)=h(x)\) attains the maximum. The three values of
\(h\) may have arbitrary real arguments. Thus it would be incorrect to
search only polynomial phases or only a finite collection of roots of
unity and then infer all equality cases. The theorem gives all such
continuous freedom, together with the finite cubic gauge and the four
possible directions.
\end{example}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Stability supplied by the certificate\srctag{105}}]{Stability supplied by the certificate}\label{gsr:fp:105:sec:d7}\label{gsr:fp:105:sec:stability}
\srcnote{105}{Section 7}

Let \(\calN=\im K\subset\C^{241}\), with the usual unnormalized
Euclidean norm on the feature space.

\begin{theorem}[Explicit monomial-coordinate stability]\label{gsr:fp:105:thm:stability}
For every unimodular \(f\), with associated \(g\) and \(m(g)\),
\begin{align}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:stability}
 \frac{11}{27}-\calE_{T_0}(f)
 &\ge\frac{16\mu}{59049}\,\dist(m(g),\calN)^2\\
 &\ge\frac{16}{295245}\,\dist(m(g),\calN)^2.\notag
\end{align}
In particular, an energy deficit at most \(\delta\) implies
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:stability-upper}
 \dist(m(g),\calN)\le\sqrt{\frac{295245}{16}\,\delta}.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Combine \eqref{gsr:fp:105:eq:lineidentity}, the Gram identity and
proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:105:prop:Qpositive}. The gap is exactly
\(16m(g)^*Qm(g)/59049\), so \eqref{gsr:fp:105:eq:stability} follows.
\end{proof}

The object on the right is distance to a linear subspace in feature
space, not distance to the nonlinear union of extremizer tori in the
original \(f\)-coordinates. The distinction matters. The inequality
is an explicit, computable necessary condition for near extremality;
it is not, by itself, a sharp \(L^2\) stability theorem for
\eqref{gsr:fp:105:eq:all-extremizers}.

\begin{corollary}[Qualitative stability on the full polydisc]\label{gsr:fp:105:cor:qualitative}
Let \(\mathfrak X\) be the extremizer set in theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:105:thm:extremizers}.
For every \(\varepsilon>0\) there is \(\delta>0\) such that
\(\abs{f}\le1\) and
\(\calE_{T_0}(f)\ge11/27-\delta\) imply
\(\dist_\infty(f,\mathfrak X)<\varepsilon\).
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Otherwise there is a sequence in the compact unit polydisc whose energies
tend to the maximum and whose distances from \(\mathfrak X\) are at
least \(\varepsilon\). A convergent subsequence has a limiting maximizer
outside \(\mathfrak X\), contradicting theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:105:thm:extremizers}.
\end{proof}

The compactness proof is included to distinguish a qualitative
consequence from the quantitative estimate actually certified. Finding
an effective optimal exponent for distance to \(\mathfrak X\) remains
a meaningful continuation.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Integration and the all-dimensional consequence\srctag{105}}]{Integration and the all-dimensional consequence}\label{gsr:fp:105:sec:d8}\label{gsr:fp:105:sec:integration}
\srcnote{105}{Section 8}

\subsection{The known transfer obstruction, with a direct proof}

A symmetric quartic tensor is called \emph{integrable} if it is the top
derivative \(\Delta^4P=T/3\) of a circle-valued polynomial of degree at
most four. Tidor's nonclassical symmetry criterion specializes to
\(B_T=0\) in this setting \cite[Definition~3.1 and Proposition~3.5]{tidor}.
We give the specialization explicitly so that the passage from the
finite inequality to the dimension-free conclusion is transparent.

\begin{lemma}[Digit-binomial degree]\label{gsr:fp:105:lem:weighted}
For \(m_i\in\{0,1,2\}\), put
\(b_{m_i}(x_i)=\binom{\digitthree{x_i}}{m_i}\). For \(k\ge0\),
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:weighted}
       \frac{\prod_i b_{m_i}(x_i)}{3^{k+1}}\pmod1
\end{equation}
has additive degree at most \(\sum_i m_i+2k\).
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For translation by one in one coordinate, including the wrap from two
to zero, Pascal's identity gives
\[
 \Delta_1b_1=1-3b_2,\qquad \Delta_1b_2=b_1-3b_2.
\]
Assign the stated weight to each digit-binomial expression. The first
term in each difference reduces the weight by one. In a carry term,
canceling the factor three lowers the denominator depth by one; replacing
\(b_m\) by \(b_2\) then lowers the weight by \(m\ge1\). At depth zero
the carry term is integer-valued and vanishes in \(\T\).
A difference in a coordinate with \(m=0\) is zero. Iteration proves the
claim for generator differences. Any translation is a product of powers
of generator translations, so its difference is a sum of products
containing at least one generator difference. The same degree bound
therefore holds for arbitrary directions.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Characteristic-three integration criterion]\label{gsr:fp:105:prop:criterion}
For a symmetric quartic \(T\), the expression \(B_T\) in
\eqref{gsr:fp:105:eq:defect} is alternating and bilinear, and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:criterion}
                  T\text{ is integrable}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad B_T=0.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Symmetry and characteristic three show that the mixed terms in
\(T((a+a')^3,b)\) have coefficient three and vanish. Also
\(\lambda^3=\lambda\) in \(\F_3\). Thus \(T(a,a,a,b)\) is bilinear
in \(a,b\). Subtracting its transpose proves that \(B_T\) is alternating
and bilinear.

For necessity, let \(D_a=\Delta_a\) and let \(P\) have degree at most
four. Since translation by \(a\) has order dividing three,
\[
       3D_a+3D_a^2+D_a^3=0.
\]
Multiplying this identity by the inverse translation \((1+D_a)^{-1}\)
gives \(3D_a=-D_a^3(1+D_a)^{-1}\). Three arbitrary differences of
\(3P\) therefore involve at least five differences of \(P\), so vanish.
Hence \(3P\) has degree at most two. Applying \(D_b\) to the displayed
identity now gives
\[
       D_a^3D_bP=-3D_aD_bP=D_aD_b^3P,
\]
which is exactly \(B_T(a,b)=0\) for its top tensor.

For sufficiency, let \(t_m\) denote the tensor's basis coefficient at a
multiplicity vector \(m\) of total weight four. The condition says
\(t_{3e_i+e_j}=t_{e_i+3e_j}\). An explicit primitive is
\begin{align}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:primitivegeneral}
 P_T(x)={}&\frac13\sum_{\substack{|m|=4\\m_i<3\ \forall i}}
               t_m\prod_i b_{m_i}(x_i)
 -\frac19\sum_i t_{4e_i}b_2(x_i)\notag\\
 &-\frac19\sum_{i<j}t_{3e_i+e_j}\digitthree{x_i}\digitthree{x_j}\pmod1.
\end{align}
Each term has degree at most four by lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:105:lem:weighted}.
The first sum has the prescribed top coefficients with every
multiplicity less than three. This follows from the unit leading
coefficient of finite differences of the binomial basis.

For \(-b_2(x_i)/9\), the transfer identity just proved gives
\(\Delta_{e_i}^4(-b_2/9)=\Delta_{e_i}^2b_2/3=1/3\), evaluated at the
zero basepoint. All coefficients using another coordinate vanish.
For \(-\digitthree{x_i}\digitthree{x_j}/9\), the two coefficients with patterns
\((3,1)\) and \((1,3)\) are both \(1/3\), again by transfer. The
\((2,2)\) coefficient vanishes, since a second difference of the linear
digit function at zero is zero before wrapping; single-coordinate
coefficients vanish at zero as well. These cases exhaust the
multiplicity patterns. Top derivatives of a degree-four polynomial are
basepoint-independent and multilinear, so the basis calculation proves
\(\Delta^4P_T=T/3\).
\end{proof}

\subsection{Lossless restriction to a plane}

\begin{lemma}[Lossless subgroup comparison]\label{gsr:fp:105:lem:restriction}
If \(H\le V=\F_3^n\), \(T:V^4\to\F_3\) is symmetric and four-linear,
and \(f:V\to\C\) is arbitrary, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:restriction}
          \calE_T^V(f)\le\E_{a\in V/H}\calE_{T|_H}^H(f(a+\cdot)).
\end{equation}
The choice of representative of \(a\) does not affect the local energy.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
First realize the twisted energy on a finite cover. Choose a basis of
\(V\), set \(A=(\Z/72\Z)^n\), and let \(\pi:A\to V\) reduce
coordinates modulo three. On integer lifts put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:universalcover}
       P(z)=\sum_{|m|=4}\frac{t_m z_1^{m_1}\cdots z_n^{m_n}}
                                      {3\prod_i m_i!}\pmod1.
\end{equation}
Every denominator divides \(3\cdot4!=72\), so this is periodic with
period 72 in each coordinate. Ordinary polarization gives
\(\Delta^4P=\pi^*T/3\), and fifth differences vanish. Thus
\(\calE_T^V(f)=\norm{F}_{U^4(A)}^{16}\), where
\(F=(f\circ\pi)\e(-P)\).

For an arbitrary function \(F\) on a finite abelian group \(A\) and a
subgroup \(J\), put
\(v(b)=\norm{F(b+\cdot)}_{U^4(J)}\) on \(A/J\). Condition the
basepoint and the four directions of a cube on their quotient cosets.
Their remaining parts are independent uniform elements of \(J\).
At a vertex the selected quotient representative may differ from the
sum of the representatives by a carry in \(J\). Absorb this carry by
translation of the vertex function. Gowers--Cauchy--Schwarz bounds the
conditional mixed cube average by the product of its sixteen local
\(U^4\) norms. Translation invariance removes the carries from these
norms. Averaging over the quotient and applying H\"older gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:ordinaryrestriction}
 \norm{F}_{U^4(A)}^{16}
 \le\E_{b,k_1,\ldots,k_4\in A/J}\prod_\omega v(b+\omega\cdot k)
 \le\E_{b\in A/J}v(b)^{16}.
\end{equation}
Each quotient vertex is uniform, which is exactly the hypothesis needed
for the last application of H\"older.

Apply this with \(J=\pi^{-1}(H)\). On any coset of \(J\), the
restriction of \(P\) still has top derivative the pullback of
\(T|_H/3\). Gauge cancellation and normalized pullback show that its
local \(U^4\) norm to the sixteenth power is the corresponding local
twisted energy in \eqref{gsr:fp:105:eq:restriction}. This proves the result.
Translation invariance of cube averages proves independence of the
representative.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:105:thm:global}]
If \(B_T\ne0\), choose independent vectors \(u,v\) and rescale one
so that \(B_T(u,v)=1\). On \(H=\langle u,v\rangle\), use the
coordinates in which \(u=(1,0)\), \(v=(0,1)\). Then
\(B_{T|_H}=B_{T_0}\), since an alternating form on a plane is determined
by its value on this pair. Therefore \(T|_H=T_0+S\), with \(B_S=0\).
By proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:105:prop:criterion}, \(S=3\Delta^4P_H\) in the field-value
notation. The gauge identity yields, on each coset,
\[
 \calE_{T|_H}(f(a+\cdot))
       =\calE_{T_0}(f(a+\cdot)\e(-P_H))\le11/27.
\]
Apply lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:105:lem:restriction} to obtain \eqref{gsr:fp:105:eq:globalbound}.

If \(\calE_T(f)>11/27\), the preceding argument forces \(B_T=0\).
Use proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:105:prop:criterion} and cancel the resulting phase to obtain
\eqref{gsr:fp:105:eq:integration-conclusion}. Finally, in every dimension at least
two, pull back \(T_0\) from a plane and take \(f=1\). The unused
coordinates average out, giving energy \(11/27\) and nonzero defect.
This proves sharpness and the necessity of the strict inequality.
\end{proof}

\subsection{What this does and does not say about obstruction rank}

Let \(m_{3,r}\) be the maximum energy for the canonical sum of \(r\)
symplectic blocks on \(\F_3^{2r}\). The earlier rank reduction
\cite{srcninetytwo} can also be recovered from the alternating normal form,
proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:105:prop:criterion} and lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:105:lem:restriction}, and stabilization under unused
coordinates. The present theorem makes its one-block endpoint exact:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fp:105:eq:rankrange}
             (11/27)^r\le m_{3,r}\le11/27\qquad(r\ge1).
\end{equation}
The lower bound is supplied by products of one-block extremizers, since
the cube and twist factor over coordinate blocks. The upper bound is
theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:105:thm:global}. No multiplicativity claim is implicit in
\eqref{gsr:fp:105:eq:rankrange}. A function on several blocks may couple them.
An exact tensorization theorem would be an additional result, not a
formal consequence of the one-block computation.

\subsection*{Theme I: density transfer and phase-flat partitions (14 questions)}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{I.\arabic*},ref=I.\arabic*,leftmargin=2.6em]
\item\label{gsr:fz:q:I:higher} \emph{Higher-degree phase partitions} (01 Question~8; 05 paragraph~6). What remains is the gap to the obstructions (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:I:polygap}). \emph{[7~October 2026; sources 95--106]} A finite-field model of the degree-two case, exact affine cells with points allowed, is item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:I:affinecells} (sources~102 and~106).

The extremizers of Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:01:thm:tail} rotate cell arcs freely, and the disk radius and the capacity inequality are separately sharp (05). Asked: how much stronger the tail becomes for one fixed cyclic character on a common-step partition with nearly equal cells (01), and the exact feasible region of block positive mass, correlation, density and phase width (05). \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 11--14]} Source~13 (its Question~7) asks which extremizers of its joint frontier (Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:13:thm:joint}) are ruled out when the phase is a polynomial on progression cells.

\subsection*{Theme II: the inverse step (9 questions)}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{II.\arabic*},ref=II.\arabic*,leftmargin=2.6em]
\item\label{gsr:fz:q:II:structure} \emph{A correlation-preserving structural theorem for multivalued spectra} (02 Subsection~11.1). Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:02:prop:spectrum} keeps all large derivative frequencies. Missing: an energy-to-structure step that keeps a fixed fraction of $t_\tau$ and exploits $\kappa$, controlling both losses. \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 28--33]} \emph{Answered in a prime-cyclic, bounded-fibre form by source~31:} its Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:31:thm:spectral-extraction} keeps an explicit fraction of the selected derivative correlation through an exact Freiman restriction on $\F_p$. Open: compatible restrictions across slices (31 Question~9), which is what Gowers's later multilinear stages need.
\item\label{gsr:fz:q:II:near} \emph{Near equality for the coupled pair $(f,w)$} (02 Subsection~11.2). Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:02:prop:stability} gives two alignments, and the equality examples show distinct geometries. Asked: a dimension-free description of $f$ and $w$ jointly when Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:02:thm:main} is nearly an equality; results on near-maximal Gowers norms (Eisner--Tao) are relevant but do not classify the weight. \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 28--33]} \emph{Advanced by sources~31 and~29.} Source~31 gives the exact optimal profile for the function (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:31:thm:sharp}), sharp selected-graph stability (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:31:thm:graph}), a weight-defect inequality in the $U^2$ and coset topology and counterexamples to normalized $L^1$ control of the weights (Section~\ref{gsr:en:31:sec:d9}); source~29 the endpoint with soft and mixed selectors (Sections~\ref{gsr:en:29:sec:d6}--\ref{gsr:en:29:sec:d7}). Still open: the unrestricted coupled near-equality, with the optimal coupled weight defect (31 Questions~10--11), optimal constants and a larger defect range of the joint theorem, the row constraint, and higher-degree joint selectors (29 Questions~5--7). \emph{[7~October 2026; sources 54--59]} \emph{Explicit local constants by sources~55 and~57:} source~55's a posteriori local theorem (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:55:thm:local}) and source~57's near-maximal extraction with constants $332$, $216s+8$ and the cubic bound $\sqrt{1-6194\varepsilon}-\varepsilon$ (Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:near-u4}, \ref{gsr:en:57:ep:prime-all-orders}, Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:cubic-inverse}). Also asked: an explicit Eisner--Tao entry threshold $e_d$, singly exponential in $d$ (55 Question~12.4); sharper correction constants, the best ratio of squared cubic error to the $Q_4$ deficit (at least $1/8$), and better degree and characteristic dependence (57 Research questions~9--10).
\item\label{gsr:fz:q:II:profiles} \emph{Carrying profiles through the proof} (02 Subsection~11.3; 04 Q7). Keep the distribution of $m(\Delta_{\mathbf h}f)$ and $\U(\Delta_{\mathbf h}f)$ across slices instead of their supremum (02), and the cross-section profile $\sigma=\E_r\beta_r^3$ through later restrictions (04). The difficulty in both: compatibility of structure between slices, and which operations preserve the profile. \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 11--14] Advanced by source~14:} its Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:14:thm:moment-equality} and~\ref{gsr:en:14:thm:joint-geometric-equality} classify equality in the profile bound and its Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:14:cor:cardinality-profile-defect} improves the denominator from cross-section sizes alone; propagation through later restrictions is still open. \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 15--20]} Source~15 (its Question~6) asks when one can pass to a balanced subdomain while keeping enough arrangements to use $\rho_3^{-6}$; its Example~\ref{gsr:en:15:ex:balance} shows the cost of assuming balance.
\item\label{gsr:fz:q:II:drc} \emph{The sharp fixed-threshold DRC profile} (03 Research question~3). The order of the best guaranteed $|K|/n$ under Lemma~7.4's exact criterion as $\delta\to0$, and whether the exponent $3$ of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:03:drc:cubic-selection} can be improved using constraints of actual intersection matrices; the scalar argument only rules out a two-witness first-moment certificate. \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 21--27]} Also asked by source~24 (its Questions~1--4: the dense-intersection extremal function $f(\delta)$, whether actual codegree geometry rescues two samples, profile-sensitive sampling with a verifiable certificate, and higher-arity scalar envelopes). Not advanced: source~24's scalar facts are source~03's (note after its Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:24:thm:sharp-scalar}).
\item\label{gsr:fz:q:II:extraction} \emph{Optimizing the elementary extraction} (03 Research question~4). Optimize $\gamma,\varepsilon,\beta$, walk lengths and popularity thresholds in Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:03:drc:graph-compression}, judging the pair of conclusions together and keeping the comparison with Reiher--Schoen explicit. \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 21--27]} Source~24 (its Question~8) asks the same end to end, with the actual energy spectrum; its popularity-threshold optimizations (Sections~\ref{gsr:en:24:sec:d6} and~\ref{gsr:en:24:sec:d9}) advance it for its own route.
\item\label{gsr:fz:q:II:threshold} \emph{Lowering the size threshold of the restriction theorem} (04 Q4), from $|B|\ge\Lambda_d(\alpha\eta)^{-2d}$, by reflecting the additive structure of $B$ in the exceptional relations or by a better kernel, with repeated entries handled. \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 15--20]} Also asked by source~17 (its Question~2: lower the degree $2m-1$ in $(\alpha\eta)^{-1}$ of its threshold, keeping its retention powers; its Question~3: the extremal filter maximizing $\sum_n|\widehat h(n)|^m$ at prescribed mean, the kernel half of this question). Source~04's weighted count already has degree $m$ and $\beta^{-1}$ (note after Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:17:thm:main}). \emph{Marked question (the intake's composition, in neither source; not proved at the write):} source~17's Fej\'er kernel with source~04's per-tuple lower bound and its weighted rank-two count of exceptional tuples (Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:04:rest:exceptional}) should keep source~17's retention $1/(2\eta L^m)$ under the threshold $|B|\ge2(1+\binom m2)L^m$, about $2^{202.3}$ at the Corollary~9.4 point $\gamma=\eta=\beta=1/2$, below both sources' thresholds; the intake checked the two needed inequalities in twelve small instances. Missing: a written proof that the per-tuple lower bound and the weighted count combine without a $D_G$ loss for repeated and degenerate tuples. \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 28--33]} \emph{Answered for fixed fields by source~29:} threshold $8qS_{q,s}/(\alpha\eta)$, linear in $(\alpha\eta)^{-1}$, with every degenerate tuple kept (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:29:rr:main}), and none at a smaller coefficient (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:29:rr:no-threshold}); this is also source~17's Question~2 in its fixed-characteristic form. Open: the prime-cyclic and growing-modulus case (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:groups}). Source~29 asks for a bound by the actual affine-span statistics of $B$ in place of $z\prod_i(z+q^i)$ and an efficient deterministic restriction (29 Questions~10--11). \emph{[7~October 2026; sources 54--59]} Source~58 gives the explicit all-moduli threshold $|B|\ge(4/(\alpha\eta))^{54}$ (\hyperref[gsr:fm:58:thm:A]{Theorem~A}) and asks (its Question~13.4) for the best point-count threshold for a prescribed retention, using the collision and torsion profiles. \emph{[7~October 2026; sources 60--69]} \emph{The marked composition above is proved by source~60 with a smaller threshold}: on prime moduli $b\ge2(1+\binom m2)L^{m-1}$ keeps source~17's retention (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:60:rst:cor:prime}), one power of $L$ less than marked. Source~60 asks (its Research questions~10 and~12): the best translated positive kernel for the signed objective $\eta\E X-\E Y$; whether the exponent $m-1$ is necessary uniformly in the prime.
\item\label{gsr:fz:q:II:retention} \emph{The optimal retention law} (04 Q5). Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:04:rest:method-bound} limits one expectation budget only. Asked: upper-bound examples or a better selection method, and simultaneous guarantees on $|B'|$, its energies and the respected density. \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 15--20]} Source~17 (its Question~1) asks the same for prime cyclic groups: whether losses of order $\alpha^m\eta^{m-1}$ in the tuple count are needed; its Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:17:prop:methodbarrier} settles only the scalar certificate. \emph{[7~October 2026; sources 40--46]} \emph{Source~40's barrier:} within homogeneous positive-Fourier kernels, gain $Q$ forces good survival at most $Q^{-(s-1)}$, attained by Fej\'er kernels (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:40:thm:barrier}, Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:40:prop:attain}). Source~40 asks (its Question~7) whether vertex-dependent kernels or adaptive selection beat the scale $\alpha^s\eta^{s-1}$ with a usable exceptional-set estimate. \emph{[7~October 2026; sources 54--59]} \emph{Source~58's barrier:} within normalized positive Fourier filters the leading principal cost is exactly $m\log m/(2\log a)$ (\hyperref[gsr:fm:58:thm:B]{Theorem~B}), the multi-layer counterpart of source~40's barrier. Source~58 asks (its Questions~13.1--13.3): the sixteen-variable optimum $I_{16,2}$, below $52$; the next asymptotic term; a retention exponent $O(m)$ on every cyclic group by a method outside independent positive filters. \emph{[7~October 2026; sources 60--69]} \emph{Source~58's Question~13.1 is given its certificate by source~68} (a degree-twelve filter of principal cost $51.445<52$, exponent $53$) and its Question~13.2 advanced (two-parameter bounds, $\cI_{m,a}/m\to1+1/(2c)$); source~62 retains $\alpha^{31}\eta^{30}$, and $\alpha^{16}\eta^{15}$ up to a double logarithm that is necessary for its detector. Asked: a detector with no double logarithm (62 Question~12.1); $\sup_L\kappa^*_{m,L}$ (62 Question~12.2); whether $\alpha^m\eta^{m-1}$ is optimal for the theorem itself (62 Question~12.6); $\cI_{16,2}$ and an exponent below $53$ (68 Question~8.7); the second-order principal cost (68 Question~8.8); degree, principal and finite-size costs together (68 Question~8.9); filters for an observed order profile (68 Question~8.10); retention $O(m)$ beyond positive filters (68 Question~8.11, source~58's Question~13.3).
\item\label{gsr:fz:q:II:groups} \emph{Restriction beyond prime cyclic groups} (04 Q6): versions for $\Z/N\Z$, $\F_q^n$ and other codomains, with hypotheses that quantify kernels of the coefficient maps. \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 15--20]} Source~17 (its Question~4) asks for composite cyclic moduli with explicit torsion dependence (Smith normal forms or gcds of coefficient minors); its fixed-characteristic Section~\ref{gsr:en:17:sec:d7} answers the $\F_p$-vector-space and weighted parts of this item, not $\Z/N\Z$. Source~58 asks (its Questions~13.5--13.7): low-exponent domains such as $(\Z/2\Z)^s$; systems of relations with every collision pattern, first two independent relations; filters adapted to the distribution of discrepancy orders. \emph{[7~October 2026; sources 60--69]} \emph{Further all-modulus theorems} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:allmoduli}): exponent $53$ for arbitrary abelian targets (source~68), unit-dilation restriction for $\Z/N\Z\to\Z/M\Z$ (source~62), threshold-free exact restriction on arbitrary finite abelian groups (source~61). Asked: restriction with persistent short torsion through several translated selectors (60 Research question~11); a separating family for noncyclic targets without a bad rank dependence (62 Question~12.5); several relations with decaying collision errors through Smith invariants (68 Question~8.12, with source~58's Question~13.6).

\item\label{gsr:fz:q:II:nonuniform} \emph{The optimal nonuniform transport threshold} (07 Question~1). Source~59 asks (its Questions~12.6--12.8 and~12.10): whether $\varepsilon\ge\Psi(t)$ holds on all of $t<1/2$ (involution-free) or $t<2/3$ (no 2- or 3-torsion) from a specified reference; the optimal support--colour frontier $(\alpha,\beta)$ for $t<1/3$; a larger range for $\Psi_{\mathrm{inv}}(t)=4t-12t^2+8t^3$ when the target has involutions; the sharp small-$t$ envelope of higher graph energies $E_r$, $r\ge3$. \emph{[7~October 2026; sources 60--69]} \emph{Advanced by source~67}: for elementary abelian $3$-group targets $\varepsilon\ge\Psi(t)$ on the whole range $t\le2/3$, with remainders and all equality cases (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:67:cthree:local}). Source~67 asks (its Questions~7.3--7.5): the largest target class with the full range up to $2/3$ and its equality cases; sharp stability near the coset extremizers; the attainable spectrum of (affine distance, defect) pairs. \emph{[7~October 2026; sources 95--106]} \emph{The odd-target radius is the whole range} (source~96, Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:oddaffine}): for every odd-order target $\varepsilon\ge4t-10t^2+6t^3$ for all $t$, with coset equality below $2/3$; this answers source~59's question and the odd-target half of source~11's; the involution radius $1/3$ and the envelope itself are open. Asked: the best bound on the distance to $\ell+b\one_{x_0+H}$ in terms of $\varepsilon-\Psi(t)$; the lower envelope at a prescribed error density for fixed domain and target; the exact gap at $t=2/3$ when $3\nmid|K|$, in $[2/9,8/27]$ ($8/27$ in every small case computed at intake; evidence); a torsion-sensitive replacement for the cubic that retains the involution mass; the sharp correction for correlated weighted labels (96 Q4--Q7, Q11).
\item\label{gsr:fz:q:II:nearscale} \emph{Near-extremizers at the right scale} (11 Question~3). \emph{Answered in substance at the write} by Remark~\ref{gsr:en:14:rem:composition}: for $\theta=\eta/(6t^3)\le1/100$ (odd targets) the error support is within $\tau(\theta)|S|$ of a unique coset and has one value off a fraction $\eta/(2t^2(1-7t))$ of it. Open: $\theta>1/100$, and sharpness of the value term.
\item\label{gsr:fz:q:II:smallgroups} \emph{The exact cutoff for general groups} (11 Question~4). Remark~\ref{gsr:en:11:rem:cutoff}: the cutoff $34$ cannot simply be removed; the exceptions found have $N\le12$, with few homomorphisms or a non-affine quotient of small order, and the formula holds for $\Z/10,\Z/14,\Z/15,\Z/16\to\Z/2$. \emph{Marked question (the intake's derivation, in neither source; arithmetic checked at the write):} replacing the step $\sum p_w^2\le\max p_w$ in Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:11:lem:blr} by source~12's Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:12:lem:majority} gives disagreement at most $\rho/(1-\chi(2\rho))$; the radius $1/7$ is then reached at $\defect=6/49$ (solve $\sqrt{1-4\defect}=14\defect-1$; there $3\chi(2\defect)=3/7<1$), and since $\Psi_0(1/30)=551/4500<6/49<\Psi_0(1/29)=3080/24389$ the cutoff in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:11:thm:maingap} would become $30$. Missing: a written proof of each step of that modified argument; the exact cutoff between $13$ and $30$ (or $34$) is open. \emph{[7~October 2026; sources 54--59]} \emph{Advanced by source~59} for targets without involutions: the formula holds for $N\ge16$ (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:59:cor:affine-sixteen}), from source~11's cubic and the published correction theorem, as credited; this supersedes the marked derivation of $30$ above. Its $\Z/12\Z\to\Z/3\Z$ map (energy $1296>1266$) shows the cutoff is at least $13$. Source~59 asks (its Question~12.9) for the maxima and extremizers for $2\le|G|<16$, in particular whether the formula holds at $13$, $14$, $15$. Targets with involutions keep the cutoff $34$. \emph{[7~October 2026; sources 60--69]} \emph{Settled for elementary abelian $3$-group targets by source~67}: the cutoff is $13$, sharp (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:67:cthree:nonaffine-gap}; the sharpness example is source~59's). Other targets without involutions remain between $13$ and~$16$, targets with involutions at~$34$. \emph{[7~October 2026; sources 82--94]} \emph{Settled by source~93}: for every abelian target, with or without involutions, the formula holds for every $N\ge13$ and $13$ is optimal for both kinds of target (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:thirteen}; exhaustive checks at the write). The maxima and extremizers for $|G|\le12$ remain open. Source~93 asks for the next largest graph energy after affine maps and one-point extremizers for $N\ge13$, with its dependence on subgroups and target torsion, and stability near the maximum (93 Q12).
\item\label{gsr:fz:q:II:erasures} \emph{Erasures against corrupted values} (11 Question~5): a sharp two-parameter envelope for a prescribed proportion of missing inputs and of corrupted remaining values; deletion and corruption have different second-order costs. \emph{[7~October 2026; sources 95--106]} \emph{The additive erasure floor is removed} by source~96 (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:96:thm:arr-erasure}): the repair bound vanishes with the observed disagreement, at the optimal square-root order, linearly under thick rows. Asked: a better finite erasure modulus that retains the row-density distribution or the observed label multiplicities (96 Q8).
\item\label{gsr:fz:q:II:recovery} \emph{Efficient certified recovery} (11 Question~6): recover the canonical affine map in nearly linear time with an a posteriori certificate matching the cubic bound. \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 15--20]} Source~17 (its Question~9) asks the same for restriction: estimate the signed objective and the exceptional mass without enumerating all tuples, with a runtime theorem. \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 28--33]} Source~29 (its Question~8) asks the same for its joint theorem: reconstruct $Q,\psi,\rho$ from approximate derivative data with a checkable certificate. \emph{[7~October 2026; sources 47--53]} \emph{Source~17's question is answered in its ambient-size form by source~48:} exact collision-aware inventories round a signed combination of energies deterministically in $O(\costfortyeight nD)$ operations without enumerating tuples, and source~17's restriction is constructed with its retention (Theorems~\ref{gsr:fm:48:gcr:thm:headline}, \ref{gsr:en:48:gcr:thm:source}); near-linear and $\log D$-polynomial versions are open (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:derandomization}). \emph{[7~October 2026; sources 54--59]} Also asked by source~56 (its Question~12.9): a nearly linear or sublinear decoder for relative repair, and an efficient weighted quadruple sampler on an explicit Fourier-uniform domain. \emph{[7~October 2026; sources 60--69]} Source~67 gives the sharp unique-recovery thresholds $1/4$ and $4/9$ for elementary abelian $3$-group targets (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:67:cthree:global}) and asks (its Question~7.6) for the optimal query and sample complexity at those thresholds. \emph{[7~October 2026; sources 82--94]} \emph{Source~93} recovers the affine map below defect $1/4$ for every abelian target, with a deterministic decoder (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:recovery}, Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:decoder}). Asked: stability of the quarter-endpoint dichotomy at $\varepsilon\le1/4+\delta$, with the obstruction from nonextendible homomorphisms on index-two subgroups; intrinsic partial-domain hypotheses making energy close to $|B|^3$ force proximity to a global affine map; a four-point statistic for nonabelian targets and the parts of the quarter argument that survive (93 Q11, Q13, Q14).
\item\label{gsr:fz:q:II:arrange} \emph{Higher-order arrangements: extremal geometry, label repair and stability} (11 Question~7; 14 Questions~5--6). Analogues of the affine-rigidity theory for the multilinear arrangement counts, tracking repeated coordinates and torsion (11); a Hamming-distance repair of labels once the domain is near a product coset (14, first for $\F_p^2$); hypotheses under which near equality in the profile-moment bound yields a common coordinate subgroup, coset-supported section indices and approximately additive top interactions (14). Related to item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:profiles}. \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 15--20]} Source~15's Questions~2--3 are source~14's Questions~5--6 (label repair at $O_k(\varepsilon)|A|$ points, with coordinate-omitting corrections; robust joint normal forms when $1-C/\Gamma$ and $R_8C^6/R_2^7-1$ are small). \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 28--33]} \emph{Advanced on full products by source~33:} high-agreement repair to $a(x)+B(x,y)+\ell(y)$ with the sharp first and second coefficients $1/s$, $2(s-1)/s^2$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:33:ras:thm:main}), the sharp cubic for $s=4$, erasures (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:33:ras:thm:erasures}). Its further questions are item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:arrangerepair}; the sparse case is item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:endpoint}.
\item\label{gsr:fz:q:II:endpoint} \emph{Reaching the high-energy endpoint inside the proof} (11 Question~8): a localization or amplification that reaches respected-quadruple density near one without losing more than it gains, with the retained domain and the normalization tracked together. \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 28--33]} Source~33 (its Question~6) asks the sparse version of its repair theorem: replace near-full density by quantitative mixing (approximately uniform marginals of conditioned arrangement queries, enough common witnesses), with polynomial dependence instead of the invalid-arrangement error $2s\tau$; the most direct route to Gowers's Sections~12--13. \emph{[7~October 2026; sources 54--59]} \emph{Advanced by source~56} in the affine, quadruple-test form: relative repair on any domain with $\norm{w-\alpha}_{U^2}^4\le\alpha^5/1024$, a condition independent of the error (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:56:thm:main}); source~33's arrangement version is not addressed. Source~56's other questions are item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:relativerepair}. \emph{[7~October 2026; sources 60--69]} Also asked by source~60 (its Research question~13): mixing assumptions on $A\subseteq G\times H$ under which repair is polynomial in the conditional failure rate, the route from its full-product profiles to Gowers's sparse steps.
\item\label{gsr:fz:q:II:overlap} \emph{Extremizers and stability at the extension boundary} (12 Questions~1--2): classify the configurations failing extension with $3\varepsilon+2\kappa=1$ (are they governed by a three-part quotient as in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:sharpness}?), and the structure forced near the boundary under nondegeneracy assumptions. \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 28--33]} Source~30 (its Question~6) asks how far its budget $(2k-1)\kappa+2k\eta<1$ can be improved; at $k=2$ source~12's sharp Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:sharp-extension} already improves it (note after source~30's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:30:thm:extension}).
\item\label{gsr:fz:q:II:primecyclic} \emph{Prime cyclic groups with the same target} (12 Question~3): the optimal deterministic density--overlap region for $G=H=\Z/p\Z$, especially for Bohr sets with a common spectrum; the universal construction does not settle it.
\item\label{gsr:fz:q:II:radius} \emph{Bohr radii: constants, measured growth, anisotropy} (12 Questions~4--6): the best $c(a)$ in finite radius selection ($c(7/8)=1/8$ is proved); carrying the measured growth ratio instead of $4^d$ through later stages; separate radii for different characters weighted by $|\widehat g(\gamma)|^4$. \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 28--33]} \emph{Advanced by source~30:} at a fixed radius the translation loss is controlled by the measured growth $|B(3\boldsymbol\rho/2)|/|B|$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:30:thm:intrinsic}), with unequal widths allowed, and exponential dependence on the rank is necessary (Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:30:cor:exponential}). It asks (Questions~4--5) whether the additive structure of the spectra produced in Section~10 forces $D_B$ far below $3^r$, and how to choose anisotropic widths before the map is constructed (merged with source~12's Question~6).
\item\label{gsr:fz:q:II:repair} \emph{Directional repair} (12 Questions~7--8): hypotheses under which a small global proportion of bad quadruples forces the uniform collision hypothesis of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:12:thm:repair} (directions with few representations are the difficulty; compare source~07's caveat that collision is not raw energy), and the best repair region in $(\varepsilon,\kappa,\eta)$, including whether $1-\chi(\chi(\eta))$ is attained.
\item\label{gsr:fz:q:II:measure} \emph{Measure and infinite-group analogues} (12 Question~12): translation loss and synchronization for finite-measure subsets of locally compact abelian groups.
\item\label{gsr:fz:q:II:cosetrange} \emph{The range and the examples of the coset envelope} (14 Question~4): the best universal range of $\varepsilon$ for $|A\triangle C|\le\tau(\varepsilon)|A|$ (now $1/100$), the range forcing coordinate splitting, and all exact envelope examples. \emph{Partial answer (intake observation, checked at the write):} let $H$ be a subgroup, $K\subseteq H$ a coset of a subgroup $L$, $k=|K|$, $A=H\setminus K$, $m=|A|$ and $\delta=k/m$. Then $|A\cap(A+d)|$ is $m$ for $d\in L$ and $m-k$ for $d\in H\setminus L$, so $E(A)=km^2+m(m-k)^2$ and $m^3-E(A)=mk(m-k)=\delta(1-\delta)m^3$; as $|A\triangle H|=k=\tau(\delta(1-\delta))m$ for $\delta\le1/2$, every such set with $\delta(1-\delta)\le1/100$ attains the envelope (source~14's Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:14:prop:collision-sharpness} is the case $H=\F_p$, $K=\{0\}$). \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 15--20]} Source~15 (its Question~1) asks for the best uniform $\delta(\varepsilon)$ with a Cartesian coset within $\delta(\varepsilon)|A|$ when $Q(A)\ge(1-\varepsilon)|A|^3$: \emph{its leading constant is $1$}, by source~14's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:14:thm:collision-sharp-stability} and Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:14:prop:collision-sharpness} (= source~15's Example~\ref{gsr:en:15:ex:linearsharp}); the largest valid range is this item. \emph{[7~October 2026; sources 40--46]} \emph{Advanced by source~45:} the envelope holds for $\varepsilon<1/9$ in every abelian group, with the canonical subgroup $\{d:|A\cap(A+d)|>m/2\}$, uniqueness, and all positive equality cases, the punctured cosets $C\setminus K$ with $K$ a subcoset of index at least nine (Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:45:co:envelope}, \ref{gsr:en:45:co:equality}); a nested-hole envelope with leading constant one (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:45:co:puncture}); collision equality forces one punctured coordinate (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:45:col:equality}). Source~45 asks (its Questions~6.6--6.10): the largest range $\varepsilon_*$, and separately the largest ranges for uniqueness and for the autocorrelation threshold (at $\varepsilon=1/4$ uniqueness fails on $\Z/3\Z$); whether $q(d)(1-q(d))\le\varepsilon$ holds universally (proved with $2\varepsilon$; equality on punctured cosets shows that no constant below one works); the maximal range of nested-hole repair and the group-sensitive bound between equality parameters; the best bound for a fixed group and cardinality; stability of collision equality and the labels on near-equality domains. \emph{[7~October 2026; sources 60--69]} \emph{Answered by source~68} in its range and equality parts: the subgroup and the envelope $\tau(\varepsilon)$ for $\varepsilon\le1/4$, optimal even in cyclic groups; uniqueness of the closest coset for $\varepsilon<2/9$, optimal; equality exactly on punctured cosets of index at least four; $q(d)(1-q(d))\le\varepsilon$ with coefficient one; nested repair with inner defect up to $1/4$ (Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:pointwise}, \ref{gsr:en:68:thm:coset}, \ref{gsr:en:68:thm:coset-equality}, \ref{gsr:en:68:thm:puncture}, Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:68:cor:unique}). This answers source~45's Questions~6.6--6.8 and source~14's Question~4 in those parts; coordinate splitting and Cartesian structure are not resolved. Source~68 asks (its Questions~8.2--8.6): the discrete envelope $\Phi_{G,m}(u)$ for a fixed group and cardinality (source~45's Question~6.9); stability across the quarter-defect transition; equality in the multilevel inequality; a weighted coset theorem; nonabelian analogues and the equality cases of the mixed remainder. \emph{[7~October 2026; sources 95--106]} \emph{Higher cube counts}: source~101 proves the analogous exact profiles for the $k$-cube counts $C_k$, $k\ge3$, reproving this item's $k=2$ envelope on the range $\varepsilon<1/60$ (source~68's range $1/4$ stands); the questions on $k\ge3$ are item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:cubestability}.

Are the power $3d-2$ of $\chi$ and the exponents of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:15:thm:coupled} optimal under $\PP_\gamma$ alone, or can the reference-cube averaging exploit compatibility between side vectors (starting from Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:15:prop:profile})? \emph{[7~October 2026; sources 82--94]} \emph{Advanced by source~88} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:productproperty}): the exponents of the cube and configuration inputs are not optimal under $\PP_\gamma$ alone ($4(4^k-2^k)$ and $8(4^k-3^k)$), and the eight-arrangement exponent becomes $88\cdot4^k-32\cdot2^k$; the power $3d-2$ of the density is unchanged. Asked: the density frontier for cube pairs, between the necessary $2^{k+1}$ and the proved $4^k$, with $g_k=O(4^k)$; whether the frequency exponents $4(4^k-2^k)$ and $8(4^k-3^k)$ can be reduced at their density exponents; retaining the distribution of common mixed labels inside the induction; which coefficient profiles $\eta_j(p)$ come from Fourier data; stable determining families under approximate face equations; equality and near equality in the weighted theorem (88 Q1--Q6).

\item\label{gsr:fz:q:II:nondegenerate} \emph{Nondegenerate and anisotropic arrangements} (15 Question~8): the error term needed when arrangements must have distinct vertices or side vectors from a prescribed family; a fixed side restriction keeps the moment identity, excluding cross-cube coincidences need not.
\item\label{gsr:fz:q:II:higherrestrict} \emph{Restriction for the higher arrangements} (17 Question~5): the complete short-relation lattice of the configurations of Sections~12 and~15, and a Fej\'er-type filter controlling every relation class; the missing step before source~17's gain can be propagated. \emph{[7~October 2026; sources 60--69]} Also asked by source~62 (its Question~12.3): a weighted Smith normal form for the constraint matrix of a higher arrangement.
\item\label{gsr:fz:q:II:exactness} \emph{Spectral data and exactness under restriction} (17 Questions~6--7): keep prescribed Fourier information while restricting, and upgrade a $1-\eta$ respected proportion to an exact Freiman homomorphism of the same order without losing it. \emph{Partly answered} for exactness from quadruple energy, with polynomial loss, by source~10's Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:10:cor:improved-order-eight}; the spectral part is open. \emph{[7~October 2026; sources 60--69]} Also asked: a restriction compatible with prescribed large Fourier coefficients of the original domain (62 Question~12.4); exact cells retaining a family of derivative coefficients and the compatibility of cross-sections (61 Question~12.6).
\item\label{gsr:fz:q:II:rankprofile} \emph{The error-rank distribution} (17 Question~8): inputs where most unrespected tuples have high error rank, combining a small low-rank tail with Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:17:thm:rankgap}. \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 28--33]} Source~29 (its Question~9) asks to optimize its exact signed certificate over the full rank profile $(G_{r,e},U_{r,e})$.
\item\label{gsr:fz:q:II:degeneracy} \emph{Degenerate arrangements beyond first order} (18 Questions~1--5). The coefficient of $p^{-2}$ (first $d=2$, small $k$), equivalences among nonparity loci, the full moment-order distribution, the intersection lattice of the $C_d$ balanced-subset hyperplanes, small primes $p\le2d$ and the case $d=1$. The placements of sources~22 and~27 record the leading coefficient for $d=1$ and the second coefficient for $d=2$; those are for the writes that add them. \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 21--27]} \emph{Answered for $d=2$:} the coefficient of $q^{-2}$ is $(k^2+21k-6)/2$ for characteristic $p>4\cdot2^k$ (source~27's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:27:thm:d2main}); for general $d$ it is $S_{k,d}-\binom k2-kL_d-b_{2,d,p}$ with one hyperplane statistic $b_{2,d,p}$ unknown (its Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:27:cor:general2}). The same question is source~22's Question~1 and source~25's Question~1. \emph{The case $d=1$ is answered in its leading coefficient,} $(k^2+3k)/p$, by source~22's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:22:thm:twocube}, which also answers the leading-coefficient part of source~27's Question~10 (the single-pair regime). \emph{Small characteristic:} the first-order count in every characteristic is source~27's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:27:thm:allchar}, which answers the counting part of source~25's Question~4 (the classification of the additional components in characteristics two and three is not given) and advances source~22's Question~6 (its balanced count for $p\le4d$). Still open: $b_{2,d,p}$ for $d\ge3$; intermediate characteristics $5\le p\le2k+2$ (27 Question~4); exact counts in characteristics $2,3,5,7$ (27 Question~5); exactness for $d=1$ (22 Question~2, item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:degenstructure}). \emph{[7~October 2026; sources 40--46]} \emph{Source~27's two questions are answered by source~44:} $b_{2,d,p}$ is characteristic-independent for $p>\max(2d,16)$ and computed for every $d$ in $O(d^3)$ operations from the nine-point grid, $b_{2,8}=3{,}280{,}234{,}631{,}541$ (Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:44:thm:stability}, \ref{gsr:en:44:thm:grid}, \ref{gsr:en:44:thm:compact}); the core directions are classified for every $p\ge5$ (Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:44:lem:width}), and the core union is counted exactly in every characteristic (Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:44:thm:oddproduct}, \ref{gsr:en:44:thm:smallproduct}). Still open: third-order terms, exact counts beyond the core in small characteristic, exactness for $d=1$; source~44's own questions are item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:gridcore}. \emph{[7~October 2026; sources 47--53]} Exactness for $d=1$ is answered for $k\le3$, with the second coefficient in every dimension, by source~49 (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:degenstructure}).

Asked: the largest universal defect interval for the entry fidelity bound and a smaller base than $10$; a larger guaranteed radius than $q^{-5/2}$ and the optimal dependence of the cubic error on $d$; efficient reconstruction of the phase from oracle access, on mixed-torsion groups; the entry threshold and expansion for interval norms and incomplete cubes (73 Q1--Q4). From source~72: a dense extension with a smaller loss than $C_d=(6^d-1)/5$ on arbitrary finite abelian groups and codomains; joint optimization of the threshold $4/5$ with the bad-set factor; an elementary constructive integration theorem on general finite abelian groups with the correct torsion target; uniqueness of $\Phi$ at weaker defect using the analytic restrictions of the Fourier witness; local short-box conclusions in place of full cycles (72 Q1--Q5).
\item\label{gsr:fz:q:II:relativerepair} \emph{Relative affine repair} (56 Questions~12.1--12.6 and~12.8). The weakest $U^2$ hypothesis $u^4\ll\alpha^\theta$, $\theta<5$, forcing error-independent repair; the best coefficient $C(\lambda)$ at fixed uniformity; a torsion-sensitive replacement for the coefficient $12$ of $t^2$; the largest repair range beyond $\lambda\le1/32$, $\varepsilon\le1/1024$; a lower rank than $4r+O(1)$ on quadratic level sets; higher-degree repair with a fixed domain condition; regular Bohr sets or long progressions as domains. Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:affinerepair}; 56's Questions~12.7, 12.9 and~12.10 are in items~\ref{gsr:fz:q:V:ledger}, \ref{gsr:fz:q:II:recovery} and~\ref{gsr:fz:q:V:library}. \emph{[7~October 2026; sources 70--81]} The infimum of this statistic over all finite weights, for maps defined on a whole abelian group, is the subject of sources~75--81 and of item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:hereditary}.

The optimal radius $R_p(q)$ at the exact prime-primary rank (at least $1/(2p)$; $R_3(3)\le2/9$); joint optimization of radii and character-image costs; whether $\lambda_k(q)\ge c_k/(q+1)$ for the retained proportion from $q$ sign orbits of defects; a linear exponent $a(k)=O(k)$ in the doubling restriction (now $(2k+1)\log_2(5k)$); and, beside the lonely runner conjecture, whether small doubling $|\Gamma-\Gamma|\le q^{1/2}|\Gamma|$ forces one character to separate $q$ infinite-order defects at radius $1/(q+1)$. Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:charseparation}; 59's Questions~12.6--12.10 are in items~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:affineenvelope} and~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:smallgroups}. \emph{[7~October 2026; sources 60--69]} \emph{Source~61} finds the exponent $(2m+1)\log_2(5m)$ independently, partitions the whole domain into exact cells and proves $\lfloor\log_2m\rfloor+1\le b_m\le\log_2(5m)$ with $p$-primary obstructions (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:allmoduli}). Source~61 asks (its Questions~12.1--12.5, 12.7 and~12.9): $b_m=\lfloor\log_2m\rfloor+1$?; the growth of the graph-extraction exponent $a_m^*$; an effective defect parameter below $K^{2m+1}$; the optimal relation-energy powers (now $O(m^2\log m)$); exact against approximate respect on composite cyclic groups; cyclic against arbitrary groups; stability of the extremal torsion examples.
