\section[{Further research questions and concrete next steps\srctag{13}}]{Further research questions and concrete next steps}\label{gsr:fz:13:sec:d11}\label{gsr:fz:13:sec:questions}
\srcnote{13}{Section 11}

The following questions are suggested by the proved results. Their status here is deliberately local: the report does not claim that each formulation has never appeared or been resolved elsewhere. Before treating one as a historical open problem, its exact formulation should receive a dedicated literature check.

\subsection{Complete partitions with prescribed lengths}

\begin{problem}\label{gsr:fz:13:q:conductor}
Can a complete partition into lengths $v-1$ or $v$ achieve the flexible exponent frontier $(q+1)a+qb=1$, or is there a genuine arithmetic obstruction between that frontier and the proved sufficient region $(q+2)a+qb\le1$?
\end{problem}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Answered by source~23:} there is a genuine arithmetic obstruction. The prescribed-length frontier is $(q+2)a+qb=1$, even with cell-dependent differences (Proposition~\ref{gsr:dt:23:prop:frontier}), and the threshold is $L^{q+2}/\prod_i\varepsilon_i\,(1+o(1))$ for lengths $L,L+1$ (Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:23:cor:consecutive}); the lower example is realizable on a prime cyclic group. With an exceptional set the cost is quantified by its Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:23:thm:packing} and Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:23:cor:partial-asymptotic}.
\end{writenote}

The present proof uses one common difference and requires every residue chain to pass the conductor $(v-1)(v-2)$. A useful first step is to formulate three separate minimax problems: one common difference, cell-dependent differences, and an exceptional set of mass $o(1)$. The last problem already has the flexible exponent by the discarded-remainder construction. Either a matching obstruction for the first problem or a way to rearrange the remainders in the second would resolve a precise limitation of the proof.

\begin{problem}
What are the best leading constants in the flexible partition theorem for a fixed $q$ and anisotropic tolerances?
\end{problem}

The universal gap is less than four between the constructive and probabilistic constants. Geometry of numbers may improve the rectangular approximation step, while more careful distribution of chain remainders may improve the partition constant. The exact finite obstruction certificate provides a practical benchmark for small moduli.

\subsection{Genuinely simultaneous polynomial recurrence}

\begin{problem}
For degree $k\ge2$, which hypotheses permit simultaneous partition exponents polynomial in the number of phases, in place of repeatedly taking $K$th roots as in Lemma 5.9?
\end{problem}

The linear proof cannot simply be reused by approximating all polynomial coefficients: after restricting to an arithmetic progression, the degree-$j$ term contains $d^j$, and translation generates coupled lower-degree coefficients. A focused first case is a family of quadratics sharing a leading coefficient or lying in a bounded-height coefficient span. One should seek a joint recurrence statement tailored to those dependencies and then prove the same complete-partition interface. Success only for generic independent quadratics would still be valuable, but must be distinguished from a uniform all-coefficient theorem.

\begin{problem}
Can a bounded-height generating family be chosen efficiently so that \eqref{gsr:dt:13:eq:heightscale} is close to optimal for a given collection of modular phases?
\end{problem}

The present theorem takes a representation matrix as input. Finding a better representation resembles an integer basis problem, with the analytic objective depending on both dimension and coefficient size. It is not ordinary vector-space rank. A useful output would be a certified generator matrix together with optimized positive budgets $t_j$, so every numerical gain is accompanied by a verifiable inequality.

\subsection{Extremal density selection with additional information}

\begin{problem}
What is the exact largest guaranteed high-average \emph{cell size} for a fixed number of cells, rather than the high-average mass solved by theorems~\ref{gsr:dt:13:thm:selection} and \ref{gsr:dt:13:thm:joint}?
\end{problem}

Dividing mass by $M-1$ is useful, but it ignores how many cells are needed for negative mass and for the threshold cell in an extremizer. This is a finite constrained optimization problem. The natural first cases are $M=2,3,4$, followed by a piecewise formula in $M$. It may produce an improvement directly compatible with Lemma 5.15 without changing any analytic input.

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 11--14]
\emph{Answered in the weighted model} by source~06's Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:06:den:sharp}: with $M$ fixed and the cell masses free, the exact optimum is $\min\{P_+/(b(M-1)),S/(M-2)\}$ with explicit extremizers. Integer cardinalities and prescribed cell sizes remain open (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:I:finitecell}).
\end{writenote}


\begin{problem}
Can the joint frontier retain the entire list of phase radii $s_j$, cell weights, and a measured value of $V=\E|f|$, rather than a common radius and the endpoint upper envelope?
\end{problem}

The affine aggregate inequality retains $V$ exactly, while the sharp joint theorem optimizes over all functions in $[-a,b]$. Neither necessarily dominates the other after additional measurements are fixed. A dual optimization using a family of supporting lines to the distinct functions $h_{s_j}$ is a concrete approach. An equality classification would show which measurements are actually useful.

\begin{problem}
Which extremizers for theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:13:thm:joint} are ruled out when $z$ is a polynomial phase on arithmetic progression cells?
\end{problem}

The abstract extremizer places positive and negative function values at two phase endpoints. Algebraic phase constraints may prevent that configuration from occurring on many large cells simultaneously. Quantifying this obstruction would improve an application using genuinely new structural information, rather than attempting to strengthen an already sharp abstract inequality.

\subsection{Cube geometry and higher-order cancellation}

\begin{problem}
Can the coloopless-subset polynomial $\sum_jc_{d,p}(j)z^j$ be evaluated or bounded effectively as $d$ grows, with all characteristic dependencies explicit?
\end{problem}

The quartic coefficient has the closed form \eqref{gsr:cc:13:eq:quarticcount}, and dimension three is completely enumerated. Higher coefficients are a finite matroid problem. Complementation identifies coloopless sets with complements of flats of the dual matroid, suggesting a way to organize enumeration without examining every subset independently. Characteristic-dependent exceptional minors must remain visible. Even usable coefficient upper bounds could improve the crude binomial majorant.

\begin{problem}
For fixed $\delta,\rho,\eta,\sigma$, what is the best possible upper value of $\mathcal Q_3(\delta+f)$, and which combinations of $T_5,B_1,B_2,B_3,T_7$ are jointly realizable?
\end{problem}

The exact identity exposes the variables that were hidden by the norm triangle inequality. The separate estimates are not a full solution of their joint feasible region. The spectral deficit is attained by flat nonzero spectra, whereas the negative $B_3$ example uses a very different spectrum. Understanding that incompatibility is a plausible route to stronger bounds. A first target is to classify equality in $|B_2|\le B_1$ simultaneously with $|T_7|\le\eta^4\sqrt{B_1}$.

\begin{problem}
How far can the low-order terms in higher cube expansions be expressed using lower uniformity norms and a small list of spectral moments?
\end{problem}

The three-cube calculation isolates an ordinary Fourier contribution at order four, a doubled-frequency moment at order five, and three six-point moments. For dimension four, one could first classify five- and six-circuits and ask which are controlled by $U^2$ rather than $U^4$. This connects an explicit finite expansion with the theory of true complexity \cite{gowerswolf}; an effective inequality needs both the algebraic classification and quantitative analytic control.

\subsection{A full quantitative and formal audit}

\begin{problem}
After replacing only the genuinely linear and real-valued local steps, what is the best complete bound obtainable by the existing Gowers proof architecture?
\end{problem}

A valid answer requires a dependency-by-dependency parameter audit. Track the density at every iteration; the phase correlation before each partition; the number, dimension, and coefficient sizes of the phases; all exceptional masses; the actual new cell length; and the final transfer from modular to integer progressions. The improved telescoping count can relax a uniformity threshold, while the density-sensitive Fourier increment can improve local length. The higher-degree inverse step may nevertheless dominate the final asymptotic. Until that audit is complete, the correct output is a set of proved local improvements, as given here.

\begin{problem}
Can the finite sharp statements and their extremizers be formalized as reusable Lean lemmas, with exact source normalization and an auditable numerical ledger?
\end{problem}

This is a concrete implementation project. Begin with weighted real selection, then integer partition construction, then the normalized Fourier wrapper. For the cube identity, separate finite linear algebra from Fourier summation. Export the resulting constants and use the existing source ledger to distinguish completed companion statements from conditional consequences. The goal is a small set of stronger, reusable mathematical interfaces whose application to the larger proof is explicit.

No Lean executable was available in the execution environment for
this report.  We inspected the source, but did not run the project
build or the axiom audit, and did not add new Lean proofs.  The
article's proof status is therefore conventional mathematics with
reproducible finite diagnostics.  This distinction is essential:
a proposed theorem statement, an audited dependency boundary, and
a complete kernel-checked proof are three different artifacts.

\subsection{Recommended implementation order}

The most direct first formalization target is the energy stability
theorem.  It requires finite sets, translations, counting, subgroup
cosets, and rational inequalities, and does not depend on asymptotic
notation or analytic Fourier transforms.  A useful decomposition is:

\begin{enumerate}
\item Prove the overlap identity and the three-halves difference-set
lemma for finite subsets of an additive commutative group.
\item Formalize the extraction of $B$ and $H=B-B$, keeping
$9/10$, $4/5$, and $5/4$ as rational constants.
\item Establish the two disjoint failed-triple counts in
Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:14:eq:exact-defect-lower}.  This is the essential
combinatorial step and deserves its own reusable declaration.
\item Prove the polynomial defect inequality before introducing
the square root.  One can first state the conclusion as
$d(1-d)\le\varepsilon$ with $0\le d<1/3$, then derive the
$\tau$ formulation separately.
\item Add the coordinate-corner homomorphism argument.  Its image
and fiber cardinalities force $e_iH\subseteq H$ without a
dimension-dependent estimate.
\item Formalize the exact labeling classification using finite
differences and inclusion--exclusion anchored at the origin.
\end{enumerate}

The second target is the finite moment equality theorem.  The scalar
convexity argument can be separated from Fourier orthogonality.
After obtaining the zero-or-common-modulus Fourier criterion,
nonnegativity and equality in the triangle inequality recover
constant weights on cosets.  The combined geometric classification
then follows through the zero sidelength and graph supports.

The cube expansion is naturally divided into a finite support
classification, the Fourier identity, a finite inequality for
$S,D,\rho,b$, and a real-variable optimization lemma.  The
asymptotic theorem should be a final wrapper around these exact
statements.  This avoids encoding a long argument entirely in
little-oh notation.

For polynomial colorings, begin with the reflection-coefficient
equivalence and its Vandermonde hypothesis $p>k$.  The minimum-support
lemma, equality slicing, and norm construction are reusable finite-field
results in their own right.  Definitions should keep the palette
$\mathbb F_q^r$, its coordinate degree bounds, ordered parametrizations,
and the zero direction explicit.

\section[{A focused research program\srctag{14}}]{A focused research program}\label{gsr:fz:14:sec:d9}
\srcnote{14}{Section 9}
\label{gsr:fz:14:sec:research-program}

The following priorities identify concrete next results and the information each
would add.  These are proposed research questions; they are not
asserted to be established open problems with an exhaustive priority
history.

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{The optimal exponent-five coefficient.}
For nontrivial exponent-five groups, determine whether a universal
coefficient $C_5$ gives
\[
 M_{\delta,G}(u)=\delta^8+6\sqrt2\,\delta^4u^4+
                  C_5\delta^2u^6+o_\delta(u^6),
\]
and whether $C_5=2^{3/4}/3$.  The proof supplies the sharp exponent
and a candidate model, but arbitrary small Fourier tails and their
phases must be controlled before identifying the coefficient.
Dependence on the rank of $G$ is itself part of the question.

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Answered by sources~21 and~23:} the universal coefficient exists and $C_5=2^{3/4}/3$, with an absolute $O(u^8)$ remainder independent of the rank (source~21's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:21:thm:main}, source~23's Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:23:five:main}); it is attained on every fixed group (source~21's Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:21:cor:pullback}). Item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:exponentfive}.
\end{writenote}

\item \textbf{The next term outside exponent five.}
Determine the first term after $C_*\delta^{8/3}u^{16/3}$.
The order-seven computation already warns that the next answer
can depend on torsion.  A plausible initial project is to compare
fixed groups with minimum nontrivial character order at least
eleven against order-seven groups, retaining every Fourier
resonance at the first unresolved scale.

\item \textbf{Effective secondary rigidity.}
Replace the sequential conclusion of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:14:thm:secondary-rigidity} by an explicit estimate in
terms of the normalized deficit and $u/\delta$.  The final scalar
optimization has a nondegenerate maximum.  This should convert
the proof into quantitative control of amplitude, phase, and
unused Fourier fourth mass.  A separate question is what
additional hypothesis permits an $L^2$ approximation.

\item \textbf{The largest range of the energy envelope.}
Determine the best universal range of $\varepsilon$ for
$|A\triangle C|\le\tau(\varepsilon)|A|$, and separately the range
forcing the nearest coset to split by coordinates.  The current
$1/100$ is a safe explicit range of the extraction argument.
Classifying every exact envelope example would sharpen the
present infinite-family sharpness statement.

\item \textbf{Quantitative repair of labels.}
Once the domain is close to a product coset, turn the collision
defect into a Hamming-distance estimate for
$M+\sum_{U\subsetneq[k]}f_U$.  Dependence on the number of
coordinates, the target group, and degenerate coordinate factors
should be stated explicitly.  A useful first case is a full
$\mathbb F_p^2$ domain with labels in $\mathbb F_p$.

\item \textbf{Stability of simultaneous arrangement equality.}
Find hypotheses under which near equality in the profile-moment
bound yields a common coordinate subgroup, an approximately
coset-supported family of section indices, and approximately
$(k+1)$-additive top interactions.  The spectral variance estimate
controls weighted Fourier mass, but does not alone provide this
joint spatial description.

\item \textbf{Dimension thresholds above the reflection budget.}
Resolve the scalar degree-five, symmetric four-term problem,
beginning with dimension five.  The present bounds are
$4\le d_{\max}\le8$ for the specified model and characteristic
range.  The Artin--Schreier example rules out one tempting norm
construction in characteristic five; it does not rule out other
quintic maps.

\item \textbf{Classification of exact polynomial extremizers.}
Describe all cubic maps at the threshold in dimension four and
all possible center-dependent subspaces $S_z(Q)$ above it.
The equality geometry of the zero set is settled; compatibility
as the center varies is the missing global condition.  The
example $x+y^2$ excludes a universal fixed-kernel answer.

\item \textbf{Second-minimum direction counts.}
Determine the next attainable value of $|S_z(Q)|$ in dimensions
$d\ge B+2$, and over nonprime fields in dimension $B+1$.
The zero sets come from homogeneous odd coefficients of a
single polynomial map, which may impose more restrictions than
an arbitrary bounded-degree system.

\item \textbf{Palette size and redundant coordinates.}
Replace the prescribed degree-vector budget by a useful
invariant of the polynomial map's actual image.  The current
theorem counts coordinates with degree bounds, even when some
color information is redundant.  Any improvement should
separate algebraic redundancy from arbitrary relabeling of
the palette.

\item \textbf{Higher-dimensional centered cube extremals.}
Identify the first surviving centered correlations for $U^d$
with $d\ge4$, determine the sharp real mean-zero comparison
with lower uniformity norms where one exists, and study the
torsion-dependent extremizers.  A successful method must
control how different support types compete, not merely bound
each one separately.

\item \textbf{A complete parameter ledger for the global argument.}
Insert the profile and geometric denominators into an entire
arrangement-extraction and density-increment chain.  Track the
densities, multiplicities, degeneracies, and threshold choices
symbolically.  The relevant output is a proved end-to-end
parameter improvement; a better isolated local constant is
not enough to infer it.
\end{enumerate}

The energy stability theorem and the finite equality
classifications are suitable near-term formalization projects.
The order-five coefficient and the quintic coloring problem are
compact research problems with explicit candidate constructions
and obstructions.  The higher-cube and global-density questions
require additional ideas beyond the local proofs developed here.

\section[{Reproducibility, diagnostics, and proof status\srctag{14}}]{Reproducibility, diagnostics, and proof status}\label{gsr:fz:14:sec:dB}
\srcnote{14}{Appendix B}
\label{gsr:fz:14:app:reproducibility}

\subsection{Contents of the source package}

The package contains one complete article source,
\leanfile{gowers_extremal_refinements.tex}, its compiled PDF,
the PDF figure and figure-generation script, two verification
scripts and their recorded JSON results, the pinned source
manifest, and a short build guide.  The external paper and the
Lean repository are referenced, rather than redistributed.
The bibliography is embedded in the article source, so no
BibTeX run or separate bibliography database is needed.

The article compiles with a standard pdfLaTeX installation:
\begin{verbatim}
pdflatex -halt-on-error gowers_extremal_refinements.tex
pdflatex -halt-on-error gowers_extremal_refinements.tex
\end{verbatim}
The existing figure is included, so Python is not needed to
build the PDF.  To regenerate the computational records and
the figure, use:
\begin{verbatim}
python3 verify_results.py
python3 verify_certificates.py
python3 make_figures.py
\end{verbatim}
The first script requires NumPy, the certificate script uses
only the standard library, and the figure script requires
Matplotlib.  All files are addressed relative to the scripts.

\subsection{Checks performed}

\toprule
\textbf{Check} & \textbf{Scope and result}\\
\midrule
\endhead
Sparse Fourier identity &
All $5^8=390\,625$ assignments of frequencies in
$\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}$ were tested against the four integer
orthogonality constraints.  Exactly $225$ survive, in the
eight histogram rows of the model table.
\\[1mm]
Centered support certificate &
All $255$ nonempty subsets of the cube vertices were classified
with exact rational arithmetic.  The quartic and quintic
surviving counts are $12$ and $8$.
\\[1mm]
Small-torsion certificates &
Every Fourier slot in groups of orders $5$ and $7$ was checked
as an exact polynomial, including the phase cancellations
in order five.  All table entries and cube polynomials match.
\\[1mm]
Fourier inequality diagnostics &
$144$ real spectra were tested on cyclic groups of orders
$5,7,11,13,17,25$, including concentrated spectra and an
order-five dominant character inside a larger group.
The direct cube and Fourier formulas agree with maximum
normalized numerical discrepancy below $2.5\cdot10^{-16}$.
All tested norm inequalities pass the stated tolerances.
\\[1mm]
Energy and algebra &
All $2\,036$ nonempty subsets of cyclic groups of orders
$1$ through $10$ were checked for the energy upper bound
and coset equality.  The defect-polynomial identity and
nonnegativity were checked in $35\,300$ rational cases.
Five larger prime examples verify exact sharpness.

All $511$ nonempty subsets of $\mathbb F_3^2$ were checked:
exactly $16$ attain the cube-collision maximum, precisely

full domain into $\mathbb F_3$, exactly $729$ attain equality,
matching $a xy+u(x)+v(y)$.

The norm associated with the irreducible polynomial
$T^3+T+1$ over $\mathbb F_5$ was checked on all $125$ inputs.
For its cubic four-coordinate coloring, all $625$ centers
and all $625$ directions per center were checked.
Only the zero direction survives at every center.
\\[1mm]

The exact two-harmonic norm and cube formulas were evaluated
at $u=10^{-1},\ldots,10^{-9}$ with 90-digit decimal
arithmetic, verifying the norm constraint and convergence

\\

The randomized diagnostic seed is $20261006$.  Numerical
tolerances are recorded in \leanfile{verification_results.json};
the exact tables are in \leanfile{certificate_results.json}.
Finite enumeration can detect normalization errors and missed
torsion cases, but it does not establish the all-group
inequalities, uniqueness statements, or asymptotic uniformity.
Those claims are established by the proofs in the main text.

The principal arguments were also reviewed independently
within the preparation process.  The review led to explicit
handling of order-five coincidences, the phase-error term in
secondary rigidity, the small-field boundaries in the
minimum-support proof, and the distinction between geometric
support repair and label repair.  This is internal review,

\section[{Reproducible computations and Lean integration\srctag{15}}]{Reproducible computations and Lean integration}\label{gsr:fz:15:sec:d13}\label{gsr:fz:15:sec:verification}
\srcnote{15}{Section 13}

\subsection{Finite checks supplied with the manuscript}
The accompanying \filename{verify.py} uses only the Python standard library
and a fixed random seed, $20261006$. It computes arrangement counts by
convolution, not by enumerating all sixteen cubes of an eight-arrangement.
For each $h$, let $m_h^{*d}$ be the $d$-fold additive convolution on
$T\times V$. The exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:15:eq:convolution}
 R_d(h)=\sum_{z\in T\times V}\bigl(m_h^{*d}(z)\bigr)^2
\end{equation}
is simply the count of two ordered $d$-tuples with the same sum.
For the tested integer and rational measures, this uses exact arithmetic.

The executed checks include all $1{,}036$ nonempty subsets of
$(\Z/2\Z)^2$, $(\Z/3\Z)^2$, $(\Z/2\Z)^3$, and
$\Z/4\Z\times\Z/2\Z$. They verify the cubic cap and the equivalence
between its equality cases and Cartesian cosets. Most stability hypotheses
in these very small groups occur only at exact equality. Two additional
nonzero-deficit examples, in $\Z/101\Z$ and
$\Z/101\Z\times\Z/2\Z$, have deficit $99/10000$ and produce the asserted
coset certificates.

The joint normal form is checked against the count equalities for all
$6{,}560$ nonempty partial binary labellings on
$(\Z/2\Z)^2\times\Z/2\Z$, and for $180$ further ternary cases.
Other tests cover random indicator domains, rational vertex weights,
sharp subgroup examples, exact label decompositions, the polynomial
stability identity, and all displayed exponent comparisons over a finite
range. The weak parameter $q^{-1/8}$ in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:15:lem:weakPP} supplies a valid product property for the nonconstant
random labels; the coupled inequalities are checked with its powers
represented exactly as rational numbers.

Thirteen Fourier cross-checks use complex floating-point arithmetic with
relative tolerance $10^{-9}$. They are deliberately distinguished from the
integer and rational count tests. The exact counts and all inequalities are
not certified by those floating-point computations. The complete executed
inventory is in \filename{verification_results.json}, with a readable log
in \filename{verification.txt}. Every assertion passed in the supplied run.
Finite examples supplement the proofs and do not establish a universal
statement by themselves.

\subsection{An explicit constructive certificate for the stability theorem}
Given the finite set $A$, compute $r(t)$ and
$P=\{t:8r(t)>7|A|\}$. Form $H=P-P$ and choose a coset of $H$ maximizing
its intersection with $A$. Under the theorem's hypothesis this construction
returns the asserted Cartesian coset. A verifier can check subgroup closure,
coordinate-projection invariance, the two cardinality bounds in
\eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:stabilitydetails}, and the final symmetric difference directly.
The supplied script implements this construction. After the correlations are available, subgroup and coset construction
require at most quadratic group-table work, with a separate
coordinate-invariance check. Computing the input cube count naively has a
$2^k$ vertex cost.

\subsection{Repository interfaces that would support the new results}
The inspected proof of Lemma 14.7 already has a general even-moment identity
and the interpolation infrastructure, but the relevant helpers are private
\cite{repo15moments}. The shortest development path is therefore not to \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 15--20; checked at HEAD \texttt{0b4890a1c}] Precision:} the general even-moment identity is the private \file{cor147_moment_eq_count} (\file{Proofs14HigherArrangements.lean}, line~484, general $d$); the interpolation helpers \file{cor147_interpolation} and \file{cor147_moment_interpolation} (lines~653, 701) are hard-wired to $d=8$. The unweakened Corollary~14.6 exponent is already kernel-checked as the private \file{cor146_direct_lower} (note in Section~\ref{gsr:fm:15:sec:d1}).

formalize an unrelated Fourier theory anew. It is to expose an appropriate
public interface and retain the intermediate count.

A practical module sequence is as follows.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.,itemsep=0.4em]
\item \textbf{Public moment identity.} Export a general-$d$ version of the
moment--arrangement correspondence. Define the collision parameter using
\filename{respectedGeneralArrangementCount 1 B phi}, avoiding an unnecessary
second notion of the same count.
\item \textbf{Division-free interpolation.} Prove
$R_2^{d-1}\le R_1^{d-2}R_d$ over real casts. Treat $R_1=0$ before introducing
normalized quotients. The case $d=2$ should be separated from strict-convexity
arguments.
\item \textbf{Fibre cap.} Formalize the injection
$(h,y,z)\mapsto(y,y+h,z)$ and then the label-forgetting injection.
Only finite group arithmetic and cardinalities are required.
\item \textbf{Collision-parametrized product step.} Refactor the reference-cube
argument in \filename{Proofs14Arrangements.lean} to conclude
$R_2\ge\gamma^{u_k}C^4/(nM^7)$ before inserting the density lower bound.
Its documentation already makes clear that the reference base has to be
retained in an injection or accounted for by averaging \cite{repo15arrangements}.
\item \textbf{Coupled exponent arithmetic.} Combine the previous two public
results and only then substitute the collision lower bound. Introduce a
new stronger theorem and recover the existing corrected statement as a
corollary, rather than silently changing the meaning of an existing name.
\item \textbf{Independent stability modules.} The small-difference lemma,
energy-deficit argument, coordinate-mixing argument, and exact joint
normal form can be developed separately from the analytic proof chain.
They should have their own statements and checks rather than being counted
as completed source lemmas.
\end{enumerate}

The source checkpoint reports a successful build and axiom audit of its
existing development \cite{repo15status}. That report was read, not reproduced
here. This package contains no newly kernel-checked Lean theorem and makes
no claim to close later open stages in the repository. The accompanying
\filename{integration.md} records proposed interfaces and the same
limitations. In particular, a mathematically proved enhancement is not
already a Lean enhancement merely because its intended dependencies exist.

\section[{Relation to existing work and remaining research\srctag{15}}]{Relation to existing work and remaining research}\label{gsr:fz:15:sec:d14}\label{gsr:fz:15:sec:questions}
\srcnote{15}{Section 14}

\subsection{Literature position}
The basic moment conversion is Gowers's mechanism, and the near-maximal
energy part of the Cartesian proof belongs to the familiar almost-period
approach in additive combinatorics. Our proof adds an explicit coordinate
mixing argument because an arbitrary subgroup need not split into coordinate
subgroups, as Example~\ref{gsr:en:15:ex:diagonal} demonstrates.

Near-extremizers for ordinary Gowers--Host--Kra seminorms are studied by
Eisner and Tao \cite{eisnertao}. Kova\v c and Rogers's September 2026
preprint studies sharp bounds, near-extremizers, and degree-lowering
inequalities for $L^p$ norms of multiple autocorrelations \cite{kovacrogers}.
These are relevant surrounding theories, but the present functional counts
\emph{coordinate-restricted axis cubes with a shared side vector}; it is not
being identified with the usual unrestricted Gowers norm. In particular,
results whose hypotheses exclude compact open subgroups cannot simply be
applied to finite groups to improve a constant that is attained by the
subgroup examples above. This manuscript claims neither to supersede that
literature nor to settle its already resolved questions.

The investigations below are concrete follow-on questions generated by the
proved results. They are not represented as a list of historically recognized
open problems. Some may admit a reformulation using existing stability or
property-testing results.

\begin{question}[Best Cartesian stability constant]
What is the smallest uniform function $\delta(\varepsilon)$ for which
$Q(A)\ge(1-\varepsilon)|A|^3$ forces a Cartesian coset within
$\delta(\varepsilon)|A|$ points?
\end{question}
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:15:thm:stability} gives $\delta(\varepsilon)\le18\varepsilon$ up
to $1/100$, while Example~\ref{gsr:en:15:ex:linearsharp} gives
$\liminf_{\varepsilon\to0}\delta(\varepsilon)/\varepsilon\ge1$ along an
admissible sequence. Determining the leading constant and the largest
valid near-extremal range is a finite, explicit extremal problem.

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{Leading constant answered by source~14}: its Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:14:thm:collision-sharp-stability} gives $\delta(\varepsilon)\le\tau(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon+O(\varepsilon^2)$ up to $1/100$, and Example~\ref{gsr:en:15:ex:linearsharp} (= source~14's Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:14:prop:collision-sharpness}) attains it, so the leading constant is $1$, not $18$. The largest valid range is source~14's Question~4 and stays open (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:cosetrange}).
\end{writenote}


\begin{question}[Quantitative repair of labels]
Suppose the respected cube-pair count is at least
$(1-\varepsilon)|A|^3$. After passing to the nearby Cartesian coset, can the
labels be altered on $O_k(\varepsilon)|A|$ points, with appropriate treatment
of missing points, to obtain the exact form
\eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:labelclassification}? Can the dependence on $k$ be removed?
\end{question}
The allowed correction class must include all coordinate-omitting functions
and must work in arbitrary finite abelian value groups. Requiring only an
ordinary polynomial would miss the exact examples already classified.
The denominator measuring errors should be specified before attempting a
property-testing argument on sparse fibres.

\begin{question}[Robust joint normal forms]
If both $1-C/\Gamma$ and
$R_8C^6/R_2^7-1$ are small, is there a quantitative analogue of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:15:thm:joint} in which most fibres share one horizontal subgroup
and the top mixed values are close to a $(k+1)$-multiadditive model?
\end{question}
The spectral theorem supplies weighted closeness to a common magnitude;
the geometric theorem supplies separate fibre cosets. Their combination
still requires coherence across fibres. A robust conclusion must retain
arbitrary fibre translates and coordinate-omitting terms, and must state
whether the approximation is in point mass, collision mass, or cubic mass.

\begin{question}[Preserving the coupled gain in the later proof]
How much of the improvement in \eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:comparison8} survives the
selection and density-increase arguments in Sections 15--17, and the
quantitative iteration in Section 18?
\end{question}
A useful first deliverable is a symbolic parameter ledger carrying
$(\beta,\gamma,\chi,\rho_3)$ through each extraction. Replacing these by
single worst-case density parameters too early could erase the gain.
Only a complete ledger with verified hypotheses could justify a statement
about a final Szemer\'edi bound. The present article does not provide that
last step.

\begin{question}[Optimal product-property amplification]
Are the powers $3d-2$ of $\chi$ and the associated exponents in
\eqref{gsr:en:15:eq:coupledbeta} optimal under $\PP_\gamma$ alone, or can the
reference-cube averaging exploit further compatibility between side vectors?
\end{question}
The constants in raw moment amplification are sharp, but its simultaneous
combination with the configuration lower bound may have incompatible
extremizers. Establishing a genuinely stronger theorem would require
examining that compatibility, not just optimizing an isolated application
of Jensen. The side-vector profile in Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:15:prop:profile} is
an explicit place to begin.

\begin{question}[Balanced extraction versus density cost]
When can one pass to a substantial subdomain with nearly equal fibre
densities while retaining enough respected arrangements to benefit from
$\rho_3^{-6}$ or the precise profile bounds?
\end{question}
An answer should optimize the retained arrangement mass against the loss in
$\beta$ and the number of occupied fibres. Example~\ref{gsr:en:15:ex:balance} shows
why a balance assumption cannot simply be inserted without a cost.

\begin{question}[Weighted near-extremizers]
Can near equality in the weighted cubic cap be converted into a useful
rounding theorem for $f$, under natural lower-density or nonconcentration
hypotheses?
\end{question}
The exact argument in Section~\ref{gsr:en:15:sec:weights} proves only that exact
saturation forces zero--one weights. Controlling the total mass of
fractional weights from a global cubic deficit is a separate issue.
Its resolution would connect the weighted coupling theorem to geometric
stability without imposing an indicator-domain reduction at the outset.

\begin{question}[Nondegenerate and anisotropic variants]
What error term is necessary when arrangements are required to have distinct
vertices, or when the allowed side vectors come from a prescribed
anisotropic family?
\end{question}
A fixed side restriction preserves the moment identity, whereas excluding
cross-cube coincidences need not. A satisfactory theorem should distinguish
these cases and quantify the exceptional counts, especially when the
ambient groups have small torsion. Prime cyclic asymptotics should not be
used to justify a statement for arbitrary finite groups.

\begin{question}[Certificates and formal interfaces]
Can the public moment identity, collision cap, and reference-cube bound be
assembled into short checked Lean proofs of the stronger statements,
with an automated exponent ledger and executable finite certificates?
\end{question}
The immediate target is the division-free all-$d$ inequality followed by
the collision-parametrized product step. The structural stability results
can then be checked independently. This separation would make the distinction
between analytic improvements, combinatorial models, and final iteration
obligations explicit in the proof status.

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{Cross-answers.} The second and third questions above are source~14's Questions~5 and~6 (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:arrange}); the fourth restates source~14's Question~12 and source~04's Question~7 (items~\ref{gsr:fz:q:V:ledger}, \ref{gsr:fz:q:II:profiles}), and the sixth is a variant of source~04's Question~7. The others are new in this report; all are merged in Section~\ref{gsr:fz:sec:further}.
\end{writenote}


\subsection{A proposed order of work}
The highest-leverage next step is the collision-parametrized Lean interface,
because its proof ingredients are already present and it records the main
quantitative saving. In parallel, the elementary Cartesian stability proof
is a contained formalization project. A parameter ledger through later
sections and a robust version of the joint normal form are the more
substantial research tasks. Neither should be replaced by a claim that the
local gains automatically constitute a global breakthrough.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Conclusion\srctag{15}}]{Conclusion}\label{gsr:fz:15:sec:d15}
\srcnote{15}{Section 15}

The arrangement argument loses information at two different places:
in replacing the collision count by an ambient second-moment cap, and in
eliminating that collision parameter before combining the product-property
step with interpolation. Keeping it produces sharp density-sensitive
amplification and the stronger coupled bound
\[
 a_8\ge\beta^{22\cdot4^k}\gamma^{44k4^k+56\cdot2^k}.
\]
The same parameter also has a geometric meaning. Its cubic cap has exact
Cartesian extremizers, its near-extremizers satisfy a dimension-free
linear-error theorem, and simultaneous moment and cubic equality have the
complete fibrewise multiadditive normal form in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:15:thm:joint}. These conclusions are proved independently of the
uncompleted later stages of the supplied formalization.

\section[{How the refinements enter the larger argument\srctag{16}}]{How the refinements enter the larger argument}\label{gsr:fz:16:sec:d9}\label{gsr:fz:16:sec:connections}
\srcnote{16}{Section 9}

The three improvements affect different interfaces, and their
quantitative information should be kept separate until an actual
composition is justified.

\subsection{From a local phase to a smaller cyclic model}

For a cell \(Q\) of upper size \(U\), a lower bound
\[
                       \Cube_{k+1}(\ind_Qg)\ge\beta U^{k+2}
\]
translates, under a cube-preserving identification with a subset
of a new cyclic group of order \(p'\), into
\[
                \norm{g_Q}_{U^{k+1}}^{2^{k+1}}
                     \ge\beta(U/p')^{k+2}.
 \tag{9.1}\label{gsr:fz:16:eq:remodel}
\]
This formula is only a normalization identity once the identification
preserves all cubes being counted. The existence of a suitable
identification and the avoidance of wraparound must be proved for
the chosen interval model.

Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:16:thm:mainphase} supplies larger cells than the short-cell
implementation in the source proof. Their maximum remains a
controlled multiple \(3km\), so the scale change is explicit.
Whether a later step benefits from the improved factor requires
substitution of this upper size into \eqref{gsr:fz:16:eq:remodel} and into all
polynomial partition thresholds. The active-pattern theorem,
Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:16:prop:RL}, provides an alternative when exact
preservation of the earlier scale is more important.

\subsection{From affine spectra to local linearity}

The moving-frequency condition
\(|(a_i h+b_i)d_Q|_N\le\delta N\) places the actual progression
step in the corresponding Bohr constraints. The certificate theorem
constructs that condition directly. It can therefore be inserted
at an interface which requires small frequencies times the step,
without first converting a quadratic diameter statement.

The uniform recurrence threshold in \eqref{gsr:dt:16:eq:finitelau} must still
be discharged after the number \(q\) of affine pieces has been
chosen. In the source, \(q\) can itself be a very large function of
the density parameter. An improvement from exponential to quadratic
dependence on \(q\) in the local exponent is substantial, but it is
not a calculation of the complete final bound.

\subsection{From exact cube coefficients to inverse information}

The low-order cube formulas identify which small vertex
configurations create the first terms of a balanced perturbation.
They allow precise bookkeeping of low-dimensional Fourier
structure inside a higher cube. They also show where torsion enters:
order two already affects the fourth term, and order three adds
new fifth-order configurations from dimension four onward.

Turning this information into an improved inverse theorem requires
control of the remainder and a mechanism extracting useful
structure from the relevant Fourier expressions. The coefficient
identities alone do not provide that mechanism. They do provide
exact targets against which a proposed inequality or a formal
expansion can be checked.

\subsection{Suggested theorem boundaries}

A formalization can be divided into reusable finite statements.

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Cyclic window geometry.}
Construct the sets \(S_t\) in the enlarged cyclic group, prove their
two possible cardinalities, prove the exact coverage count
\eqref{gsr:fp:16:eq:windowcount}, and prove that each family of equally spaced
centers gives a partition.
No Fourier analysis is needed here.

\item \textbf{Phase-independent localization.}
State Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:16:thm:window} for arbitrary functions
\(f_\epsilon\) and an explicitly supplied polarization identity.
This avoids coupling the geometric theorem to a factorial argument.

\item \textbf{Polynomial synthesis.}
Prove \eqref{gsr:fp:16:eq:explicitphase} and the formal coefficient criterion.
Over \(\Z/N\Z\), keep factorial divisibility as a named hypothesis
instead of hiding it in simplification.

\item \textbf{The exact certificate algorithm.}
Formalize Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:16:thm:certificate} from a supplied \(s\).
The required operations are residue partitions, interval chunks,
rectangular pigeonhole, and a triangle inequality in \(\R/\Z\).
The recurrence theorem can then be attached as a separate imported
interface.

\item \textbf{Small cube configurations.}
Represent cube vertices as Boolean functions, classify four- and
five-element supports, and combine finite Fourier orthogonality
with the integer relation modules described in
Section~\ref{gsr:cc:16:sec:cubes}.
\end{enumerate}

Kernel checking would certify these local implications. It would
not automatically certify that a new final Szemer\'edi exponent
follows from the existing higher-dimensional structural chain.
The latter needs a separate theorem with all numerical hypotheses
and model changes visible in its type.

\section[{Further research questions and priorities\srctag{16}}]{Further research questions and priorities}\label{gsr:fz:16:sec:d12}\label{gsr:fz:16:sec:research}
\srcnote{16}{Section 12}

\subsection{Local phase removal}

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Determine the best retention factor at controlled cell size.}
Fix \(C\ge3\), an upper size \(Ckm\), and a lower size \(m/(3k)\), and ask for
the largest coefficient \(c_k(C)\) for which a statement of the form
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:16:thm:mainphase} holds. The sliding construction and the local-scale ceiling determine
the leading \(k\log k\) loss. Close the remaining factor exponential
in \(k\), or find a sharper obstruction.

\item \textbf{Retain cells of size \(O(m)\).}
Can one obtain a factor \(2^{-O(k\log k)}\) while also forcing
every cell to have upper size \(Cm\) for an absolute \(C\)?
The active-pattern theorem preserves the short-cell scale, but
still contains a global pattern count.

\item \textbf{Optimize nonuniform windows.}
The present partitions use equal real widths. Input increments
with unequal side lengths suggest anisotropic displacement
budgets, and input energy concentrated away from extreme
increments may permit smaller windows. A useful theorem would
retain all weights through the localization step.

\item \textbf{Extend the polarization interface.}
Theorems~\ref{gsr:fp:16:thm:factorial} and \ref{gsr:fp:16:thm:smallchar} settle the
formal coefficient test and the classical prime-field functional
test. Investigate corresponding localization theorems for
nonclassical torsion-valued phases, stating their target groups
and degree conventions explicitly.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Partitions controlling their own steps}

\begin{enumerate}[resume]
\item \textbf{Close the dimension gap.}
For equal powers, the sufficient exponent is of order \(q^{-2}\),
whereas Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:16:thm:obstruction} permits at most order
\(q^{-1}\). Can a universal partition theorem attain \(c/q\)?

\item \textbf{Determine the anisotropic feasible region.}
Is the strict interior of
\((q+1)a+2\sum_i b_i\le1\) sufficient, perhaps with logarithmic
losses? The present work proves necessity and a smaller sufficient
region, not equivalence.

\item \textbf{Use the weight during construction.}
A weighted extraction of one useful progression might beat the
full-partition obstruction. Develop a direct weighted theorem
suited to the arrangement counts in Lemma~13.5.

\item \textbf{Measure the effective spectrum dimension.}
Find structural hypotheses ensuring that the moving slopes lie
in a low-dimensional bounded-height integer span. Combine such
a result with Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:16:cor:fewslopes}.

\item \textbf{Make thresholds numerical.}
Track the constants in a simultaneous recurrence theorem well
enough to replace \(X_0(C,q)\) by an explicit computable bound.
Alternatively, formalize a certificate-producing finite
algorithm and compare its actual performance with the worst-case
existence theorem.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Cubes and the full quantitative induction}

\begin{enumerate}[resume]
\item \textbf{Classify sixth-order supports.}
Determine the relevant primitive relation modules for six
Boolean vertices in arbitrary dimension. The fourth- and
fifth-order calculations suggest a systematic classification by
small integer matrices and their torsion quotients.

\item \textbf{Control the higher-dimensional remainder sharply.}
The remainder estimates supplied by repeated
Gowers--Cauchy--Schwarz are uniform but rarely optimal.
Determine sharp dependence on lower Gowers norms, the density,
and the torsion profile.

\item \textbf{Find extremizers and stability statements.}
The coefficient formulas identify equality mechanisms at low
order. Which functions nearly maximize the complete
higher-dimensional cube polynomial under fixed lower-order norm
constraints?

\item \textbf{Propagate the local gains through the complete proof.}
Substitute the new partition scale and recurrence thresholds into
the structural, localization, remodeling, and density-increment
steps. Prove the resulting numerical recurrence before claiming
an improvement to the final Szemer\'edi bound.

\item \textbf{Build a kernel-checked local refinement package.}
Start with the finite certificate theorem and sliding-window geometry.
They have explicit finite statements and avoid the currently open
global dependencies. Then add the exact cube coefficients and
a separate source-fidelity audit.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{A particularly small first change}
The existing proof of \codeseventeen{section9_second_moment_le} first obtains
\[
 \sum_{u,r}|\widehat f_u(r)|^2=N^2|B|
\]
and only then uses $|B|\le N$. \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 15--20]} \file{section9_second_moment_le} is a private lemma (\file{Proofs09Moments.lean}, line~480); the equality $N^2|B|$ is a step inside its proof, and the fourth and sixteenth moment identities exist only inside \file{lemma_9_2_holds} (line~527).
The first formalization task is to expose the equality as its own
reusable lemma.  Combining it with the existing fourth- and
sixteenth-moment identities should give the division-free target
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:17:eq:leanmomenttarget}
 G_{16}(B,\phi)\,|B|^6\ge G_4(B,\phi)^7.
\end{equation}
The division-free form also behaves cleanly for $B=\varnothing$.
For nonempty $B$, it is exactly the $r=8$ case of
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:17:prop:moments}.

\subsection{The all-moduli interface is a real difference}
In the inspected statement, \codeseventeen{lemma_9_3} quantifies over
\texttt{N : Nat} with \texttt{[NeZero N]}, without a primality assumption.
The new cyclic theorem is for prime $N$.
It is a quantitative strengthening in the paper's prime setting, but
not a proof of the repository proposition with only its numeric bound
changed.  A safe addition is a separate prime-modulus theorem with an
explicit characteristic and size interface.  The old theorem need not
be overwritten.

\subsection{A staged formalization plan}
A useful dependency order is as follows.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.]
\item Expose the exact graph second moment and prove
\eqref{gsr:fz:17:eq:leanmomenttarget}; then generalize the moment inequality in
finite abelian groups.
\item Define the finite Fourier coefficients of $K_L$, prove their
nonnegativity, establish $0\le K_L\le1$, and prove the finite coefficient
identity and the bound on $S_{m,L}$.
\item Define bounded affine degeneracy, prove the rank-two fiber count,
and derive pairwise distinctness of generic tuples.
\item Formalize conditional product sampling only for distinct points,
then prove the exact good/bad probabilities.
\item Prove the signed-expectation extraction lemma independently of
Fourier analysis and instantiate it with the exceptional-set bound.
\item Separately formalize the augmented-column rank calculation and
the fixed-characteristic system theorem.
\end{enumerate}
No uncompiled proof script is presented as a certified theorem in this
package.  In particular, the current package contains no Lean module
with an implicit or explicit admission disguised as a completed proof.

\section[{Further research questions and proposed directions\srctag{17}}]{Further research questions and proposed directions}\label{gsr:fz:17:sec:d11}
\srcnote{17}{Section 11}
\label{gsr:fz:17:sec:questions}

\paragraph{1. The actual extremal restriction exponents.}
For prime cyclic groups, determine the largest guaranteed size of a
subset on which $1-\eta$ of the $m$-term relations are respected, as a
function of the absolute relation parameter $\alpha$.
Does one need losses of order $\alpha^m\eta^{m-1}$ in tuple count?
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:17:prop:methodbarrier} settles only a scalar proof template.
A matching extremal construction, or a stronger unrestricted theorem,
would distinguish the method's cost from the phenomenon itself.

\paragraph{2. Reducing the ambient-size threshold.}
The union bound pays for every bounded affine degeneracy as though it
survived with probability one.  A rank- or multiplicity-stratified
estimate of its actual survival should be tested.
Can the degree $2m-1$ in $(\alpha\eta)^{-1}$ in
\eqref{gsr:fm:17:eq:simplifiedN} be reduced while preserving the retention powers?
This would make the present theorem substantially less asymptotic.

\paragraph{3. An extremal filter problem.}
For a prescribed mean $q$ and degree $D$, maximize
$\sum_n|\widehat h(n)|^m$ among $0\le h\le1$.
The Fej\'er filter gives a transparent feasible point, while
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:17:lem:momentbarrier} gives a universal ceiling.
Identifying exact or asymptotically optimal filters could improve the
constants and the degree needed before controlling exceptional tuples.

\paragraph{4. Composite cyclic moduli.}
Develop a replacement for bounded affine genericity that records the
Smith normal form or the relevant greatest common divisors of coefficient
minors.  The goal is a theorem with explicit dependence on torsion,
not an unjustified carry-over of field fiber counts.
Such a theorem would match the all-moduli Lean interface more directly.

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 54--59]
\emph{Answered for one balanced relation by source~58} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:torsionrestriction}): on every cyclic group, with the domain torsion entering through $\tau_G(2D)\le2D$ and repeated entries through a separate collision term (its Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:58:thm:expectation}), and with exponent $54$ in place of $2^{19}$ for sixteen entries (\hyperref[gsr:fm:58:thm:A]{Theorem~A}), for arbitrary abelian targets; the exponents here remain better on prime fields. Systems of relations are source~58's Question~\ref{gsr:fz:58:q:systems} (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:groups}).
\end{writenote}

\paragraph{5. The higher arrangements of Sections 12 and 15.}
Compute the complete short-relation lattice for the configurations used
in the later stages of Gowers's proof, then evaluate a Fej\'er-type
filter on that lattice.
A successful extension must control every additional relation class,
not only a distinguished balanced relation.  This is the specific
missing step before the present local improvement can be propagated
through the main induction.

\paragraph{6. Preserve chosen spectral information while restricting.}
Impose auxiliary lower bounds on selected Fourier coefficients, or on
Fourier energy over a prescribed set of characters, during extraction.
The signed objective could be augmented by Lagrange multipliers, but
one must show that its expected margin remains positive.
This targets the compatibility issue that motivates the transition from
Section 9 to the more delicate later arguments.

\paragraph{7. From approximate relations to exact structure.}
Under the new retention bounds, determine when a further restriction can
be made an exact Freiman homomorphism of the same order without losing
the prescribed spectral data.  A comparison should separate the cost
of obtaining a high respected proportion from the cost of making it
exact.  Ordinary energy extraction alone does not preserve every
additional constraint needed downstream.

\paragraph{8. Exploit the entire error-rank distribution.}
The certificate \eqref{gsr:en:17:eq:rankcertificate} is a polynomial in $q$ whose
coefficients are the rank profile.  Study inputs where most, but not all,
unrespected tuples have high error rank.  A useful theorem might combine
a small exceptional low-rank tail with the improved exponents in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:17:thm:rankgap}, rather than assuming a uniform rank gap.

\paragraph{9. Efficient certification and extraction.}
Find algorithms for estimating the signed objective and the exceptional
mass without enumerating all tuples.  Convolution and fast Fourier
transforms can evaluate several unweighted counts, but repeated entries,
conditional Bernoulli choices, and vector-valued graph data must be
handled correctly.  The desired output is a runtime theorem as well as
an existence theorem.

\paragraph{10. Certified optimization in Lean.}
After formalizing the exact-data certificate, allow $L$ to be chosen by
a verified finite search using exact rational values of $S_{m,L}$.
This would avoid freezing the convenient but nonoptimal choice
$L=\ceil{(m+1)/(\alpha\eta)}$ in every application.
The certificate is a suitable interface between computation and the
structural mathematical proof.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Conclusion\srctag{17}}]{Conclusion}\label{gsr:fz:17:sec:d12}
\srcnote{17}{Section 12}

A high-degree positive Fourier filter can replace the tiny distinguishing
advantage of repeated degree-one filters.  For the single balanced
relation, this yields a fully explicit restriction theorem with losses
$\alpha^m\eta^{m-1}$, including all repeated and degenerate tuples in the
final count.  Exact second-moment bookkeeping independently removes an
unnecessary density factor from the input obtained from additive energy.

The fixed-characteristic analogue reveals the more general organizing
quantity: the increase in rank when the graph coordinates are appended
to a configuration.  Its full rank-profile certificate and rank-gap
corollary provide a systematic extension beyond a single equation.
The remaining work is concrete: improve the treatment of exceptional
tuples, understand optimal filters, and analyze the actual relation
lattices of the higher configurations before making any global claim.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A compact proof-dependency map\srctag{17}}]{A compact proof-dependency map}\label{gsr:fz:17:sec:dA}
\srcnote{17}{Appendix A}
The proof of the prime-cyclic estimate depends on the following chain:
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \text{kernel expansion and signal bound}\\
 +\ \text{bounded-affine exceptional-set count}\\
 \Downarrow\\
 \text{exact generic good/bad survival probabilities}\\
 \Downarrow\\
 \text{one signed-expectation certificate}\\
 \Downarrow\\
 \text{polynomial-loss restriction with an explicit threshold}.
 \end{gathered}
\]
The moment inequality is independent of this chain and supplies a
stronger input.  The finite-field systems theorem uses the same signed
objective but replaces Fourier coefficients by the rank of augmented
columns.  Neither proof imports a later section of Gowers's argument.

\subsection{Interpreting the polynomial exponents}

The degree-two comparison is particularly transparent. For oscillation
$r^{-2a}$, the old reciprocal exponent is $2^{11q+1}$, the new general
quadratic reciprocal exponent approaches $126q^2+129q+2$, and the
shared-leading-coefficient specialization gives $99q+98$.
The obstruction for unrestricted quadratic phases is $7q+1$.
These numbers are not four theorems with identical hypotheses: the shared
frequency restricts the input class, and the obstruction is a necessary
condition, not a construction. The strict inequalities in the sufficient
asymptotic statements absorb coefficient-independent constants.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{@{}rrrrr@{}}
\toprule
$q$ & Old reciprocal & General quadratic & Shared leading term & Obstruction\\
\midrule
1&$2^{12}$&257&197&8\\
2&$2^{23}$&764&296&15\\
4&$2^{45}$&2534&494&29\\
8&$2^{89}$&9098&890&57\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Reciprocal exponents at oscillation $r^{-2a}$. The middle two
columns are strict asymptotic sufficient bounds, and the last column is
a necessary upper limit on $a$ for the unrestricted class.}
\label{gsr:fz:18:tab:quadratic-rates}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=.98\textwidth]{figures/18-arrangement-degeneracy-partition_exponents.pdf}
\caption{Comparison of the exponents in Table~\ref{gsr:fz:18:tab:quadratic-rates}
on a logarithmic vertical scale. Larger $a$ gives longer progressions.
The figure compares exponents, not the finite input sizes at which the
asymptotic statements become effective.}
\label{gsr:fz:18:fig:partition-rates}
\end{figure}

The main analytic reason for the improvement is visible in the recurrence
$E_j=(1+js_j)E_{j-1}+2s_j$. For fixed degree, a recurrence cost
$s_j=O_j(q)$ is paid only once at each degree. The original repeated
refinement pays a degree-dependent exponent once for each polynomial.
This explains the change from exponential to polynomial dependence on $q$.
It also explains the remaining gap: a direct induction multiplies the
dimension cost at successive degrees, while the necessary frontier suggests
that a more simultaneous treatment might avoid some of those products.

\subsection{Why the cube estimate is a genuine upper-bound improvement}

For $\delta,\varepsilon\ge0$, the upper bound in
Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:18:cube:cor-improved-bound} is never larger than
$(\delta+\varepsilon)^m$. The degree-one through degree-three terms have
been removed; $B_d\le\binom m4$ and $Q_d+S_d\le\binom m5$, because their
terms count disjoint classes of vertex subsets; the remaining binomial
terms are the same. At fixed positive density, the first possible error
is of fourth order. In the source's uniformity parameter
$\alpha=\varepsilon^{2^d}$, it is of order $\alpha^{4/2^d}$.

The sharpness theorem concerns the bound over all finite abelian groups.
Its extremizing sequence lives on increasingly large elementary abelian
two-groups. It does not settle the best coefficient after excluding
two-torsion, nor does it classify all nearly extremizing sets. The exact
formula, which separates $E_2$ from the ordinary fourth Fourier moment,
provides information that can be used to investigate those sharper questions.

The fifth coefficient has no fixed sign. Treating it as an error requires
an absolute value or a bound on its magnitude. Its explicit spectral form
can be more useful when the Fourier support is known: absence of doubling
relations can suppress $T_5$, and absence of order-three characters removes
$E_3$. The remainder bound remains valid without either simplification.

\subsection{What a full quantitative propagation would require}

A new global quantitative theorem would require a closed parameter audit
through the later structural and phase-removal steps. In particular, one
would have to track how a changed ambient-size threshold affects every
recursive call, how a new simultaneous polynomial partition is invoked
inside common-difference boxes, and how the resulting widths and retained
densities survive the final density iteration. An exponent improvement in
one partition lemma cannot be inserted into an unchanged downstream formula
without checking those dependencies.

The arrangement improvement has a particularly clean local interface: the
Riesz-product proof uses the exceptional-set estimate only to absorb
degenerate arrangements. Section~\ref{gsr:en:18:deg:sec-main} redoes that absorption
explicitly. The cube expansion is also independent of any inverse theorem.
These two components can therefore be reused immediately as standalone
lemmas. The polynomial transfer has an explicit analytic interface, but the
general numerical exponent quoted from Lau's preprint remains dependent on
that input~\cite{lau}.

For cube norms, the article uses normalized averages. The source's
unnormalized quantity differs by the factor
$|G|^{(d+1)/2^d}$. Equivalently, the $2^d$-th power of the source norm is
$|G|^{d+1}$ times the normalized cube moment. Recording that equality once
would prevent repeated normalization errors in later statements.

An economical implementation order is: first the Boolean moment inversion
and the two affine-rank counting lemmas; then the single-certificate bound;
then certificate equivalence and its finite class count; finally the sharp
hyperplane count and the absorption corollary. A simpler finite theorem
with a larger coefficient could be checked before the exact combinatorial
count $C_d$ is implemented. In the cube part, the universal finite Fourier
kernel identity should precede the classification of small matrices.
For partitions, the two elementary integer decomposition lemmas and the
degree-descent transfer can be formalized with recurrence as a named
hypothesis.

The new theorems in this report are mathematical proofs, not newly checked
Lean declarations. The inspected source establishes the integration
points; it does not certify the results written here. No Lean compilation
of these additions is claimed.

\section[{Exact finite verification and reproducibility\srctag{18}}]{Exact finite verification and reproducibility}\label{gsr:fz:18:sec:d8}
\srcnote{18}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:fz:18:sec:verification}

The accompanying \path{verify_refinements.py} uses only the Python standard
library. It checks finite consequences of the proofs with exact integer
and rational arithmetic. The program is corroborating evidence and a
reproducible way to inspect the constants; the general arguments above
remain the proofs.

The following checks passed:
\begin{enumerate}
\item All $\binom{16}{4}+\binom{16}{5}=6188$ four- and five-vertex subsets
of the four-dimensional cube were classified by rank over suitable finite
fields. The counts were $100$ ordinary rectangles, $40$ extra binary
planes, $160$ ordinary five-circuits, and $16$ extra ternary configurations.
\item Fourth and fifth coefficients were computed directly by expanding
the product over every cube, for dimensions three and four on cyclic
groups of orders $2,3,4,5,6,7$. All twelve test cases agreed with the
formula, including groups with two-torsion, three-torsion, both, and neither.
\item Pure-parity hyperplanes were enumerated independently for $d=2$ at
$p=5,7$, for $d=3$ at $p=7,11$, and for $d=4$ at $p=11,101$.
The resulting counts
were $C_2=4$, $C_3=51$, and $C_4=484$, as predicted.
\item Ternary certificate classes modulo affine equivalence were
enumerated at sizes $2,4,6,8$, giving $1,25,301,3025$. These agree with
$(3^n-2^{n+1}+1)/2$.
\item The exceptional-diagonal probability for the sharp nonparity
certificate was computed exactly for $d=2$ and $p=5,7,11$. The values
$29/625$, $55/2401$, and $131/14641$ agree with
$p^{-2}+(p-1)p^{-4}$.
\item Every binary square matrix of sizes two, three, and four was
enumerated. The maximum absolute determinants were $1,2,3$, consistent
with the independent Hadamard-bound proof.
\end{enumerate}

As a concrete check of the order-three correction, on $\Z/3\Z$ take
$f=(2,-1,-1)$ and cube dimension four. The fourth coefficient is $200$
and the fifth is $352$. Omitting the sixteen ternary configurations would
give a fifth coefficient of $320$, so this test detects a real failure of
the torsion-free formula in characteristic three.

To reproduce the checks, run
\begin{verbatim}
python3 verify_refinements.py --output verification_results.json
\end{verbatim}
To rebuild the article, run \texttt{pdflatex} twice on the supplied main
\texttt{.tex} file, keeping \path{partition_exponents.pdf} beside it.
The supplied source is self-contained apart from that included figure and
standard \LaTeX\ packages; its bibliography is embedded.

\section[{Further research questions and proposed next steps\srctag{18}}]{Further research questions and proposed next steps}\label{gsr:fz:18:sec:d9}
\srcnote{18}{Section 9}
\label{gsr:fz:18:sec:research}

The following questions arise directly from the proofs. They distinguish
well-defined improvements to these local statements from the much larger
task of improving global Szemer\'edi bounds.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{\arabic*.},leftmargin=*]
\item \textbf{The second degeneracy coefficient.}
Determine the coefficient of $p^{-2}$ in the count of degenerate
$d$-arrangements, initially for $d=2$ and small $k$. The first-order proof
shows what must be included: intersections of the leading hyperplanes and
the nonparity loci of codimension two. A satisfactory answer should identify
any exceptional primes, rather than fitting a polynomial to a few counts.

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Answered for $d=2$} by source~27's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:27:thm:d2main}: $(k^2+21k-6)/2$ for characteristic $p>4\cdot2^k$, with the exact count for $k=1$ in characteristic at least $11$ (exceptional characteristics $2,3,5,7$); general $d$ is reduced to the statistic $b_{2,d,p}$ (its Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:27:cor:general2}). Item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:degeneracy}.
\end{writenote}

\item \textbf{Distinct nonparity loci.}
The coefficient $A_{2d2^k}-A_{2d}$ counts certificate classes, including
many with impossible or identical solution sets. Classify the simplest
additional equivalences between the resulting algebraic loci. Even a
systematic bound for the certificates of lowest moment order $k-1$ would
improve the explicit second-order error.

\item \textbf{The full moment-order distribution.}
Use the parameter $t=k-m$ in Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:18:deg:lem-rank} instead of replacing
all costs by their $t=1$ upper bound. This requires counting ternary
functions with specified vanishing Boolean moments. A first milestone is
an exact enumeration for $k\le4$, followed by a structural inequality
valid for general $k$.

\item \textbf{The balanced-subset hyperplane arrangement.}
Determine its intersection lattice and characteristic polynomial. The
number of hyperplanes is already $C_d$; understanding their intersections
would give the exact pure-parity degeneracy probability for all sufficiently
large primes and would contribute to the preceding second-order problem.

\item \textbf{Small primes and one-arrangements.}
Treat $p\le2d$ by counting balanced ternary vectors modulo $p$, and treat
$d=1$ separately. The diagonal cross-section event then has different
size, so the $p^{-2}$ conclusion for nonparity certificates cannot simply
be retained. In characteristic three, affine symmetries of the ternary
alphabet also change the quotient count.

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Partly answered.} For $d=1$ the leading coefficient is $(k^2+3k)/p$ (source~22's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:22:thm:twocube}); the first-order count for small $p$ is source~27's Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:27:thm:allchar}, with $L_{d,p}$ from its Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:27:thm:profiles}, including characteristic three. Item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:degeneracy}.
\end{writenote}

\item \textbf{Sixth and higher cube coefficients.}
Extend the small-matrix classification to six vertices. New affine
dependence dimensions and new integer invariant factors must be tracked;
a list of rational circuits alone will not suffice over all finite groups.
The desired output is an exact formula with a remainder bound, not only a
numerical enumeration of one cube dimension.

\item \textbf{Sharp coefficients on odd-order groups.}
Determine the best fourth-order coefficient when order-two characters
are absent, especially in dimension four. The universal $B_d$ sharpness
construction does not answer this question. A likely useful subproblem is
an optimal comparison between a real mean-zero function's $U^2$ and $U^d$
norms under the relevant group restrictions.

\item \textbf{Stability of cube-count sharpness.}
If a sequence nearly attains $B_d$, what must its low-order Fourier
spectrum look like? The separate nonnegative terms $V_4$ and $E_2$ make
this a more structured problem than the corresponding triangle-inequality
equality case. Distinguish weighted functions from indicator sets in any
stability statement.

\item \textbf{The general quadratic partition gap.}
Can the sufficient reciprocal exponent be reduced from order $q^2$ to
order $q$? The obstruction is $7q+1$ at error exponent $2a$.
One should first decide whether flexible lengths and the stronger
$v-1,v$ requirement have the same asymptotic frontier.

\item \textbf{Eliminate several degrees in one step.}
The transfer handles the leading coefficients simultaneously, but then
repeats the process for lower degrees. Find a recurrence formulation that
also controls the coefficients created by translation. The shared-leading
quadratic corollary supplies a useful test family in which the number of
genuinely independent top frequencies is much smaller than the number of
polynomials.

\item \textbf{Coefficient-rank profiles and explicit constants.}
Develop a theorem in which each degree has its own bounded integer span
of frequencies, and compute the resulting sequence of recurrence costs.
In parallel, extract fully numerical recurrence constants where possible.
An exponent with an uncontrolled starting threshold is valuable
asymptotically but insufficient for concrete finite comparisons.

\item \textbf{A complete formal and quantitative substitution.}
Implement the elementary lemmas in Lean, then trace their use through the
remaining proof with explicit parameter interfaces. The first deliverable
should be a checked replacement for the Lemma~15.5 threshold and a checked
conditional polynomial-partition transfer. A global quantitative claim
should follow only after every later width, density, and ambient-size
condition has been verified.
\end{enumerate}

\section[{Source audit and the boundary of the Lean integration\srctag{19}}]{Source audit and the boundary of the Lean integration}\label{gsr:fz:19:sec:d7}
\srcnote{19}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:fz:19:audit:section}

The mathematical improvements in this article concern a finite sampling and
interpolation step in the proof of Gowers's Lemma~16.10.  The following audit
distinguishes the original published paper, the edited transcription in the
repository, the propositions currently stated in Lean, and their available
proofs.  The repository snapshot is commit
\texttt{dca9f06383ccdfc2ed208ccb7c9882214fdb09ac}.
The source checks below are read-only inspections at that commit; a new Lean
build was not run for this article.

\subsection{Published argument versus the edited transcription}
\label{gsr:fz:19:audit:paper}

In the original paper, Lemma~16.10 and its proof occupy printed
pages~574--575.  The relevant finite step starts with, in each fibre, at most
$q$ classes on which the function is affine in the last coordinate.
The proof uses $r=\lceil q\sigma^{-2}\rceil$ random coordinates and seeks
two distinct sampled points in each retained class
\cite{gowers}.  The edited repository transcription places Lemma~16.10 at
line~3459 and retains this sampling step, while adding warnings about the
closing parameter comparison \cite{repo19paper}.

There is a precise distinction between two sample hits and two distinct
sampled coordinates.  For independent sampling with replacement from an
$n$-point set, a class of size $s$ has fewer than two distinct sampled
coordinates with probability
\begin{equation}
 s\left(1-\frac{s-1}{n}\right)^r
 -(s-1)\left(1-\frac{s}{n}\right)^r ,
 \qquad s\geq 1.
 \label{gsr:fz:19:audit:iid-distinct}
\end{equation}
Indeed, the event consists of no hit, together with the disjoint events
that the unique sampled member of the class is each of its $s$ possible
points.  In contrast, the binomial expression
$(1-u)^r+ru(1-u)^{r-1}$ bounds fewer than two hits counted with
multiplicity.  It does not, without another argument, bound the event in
\eqref{gsr:fz:19:audit:iid-distinct}.  A singleton class always fails the requirement
of two distinct points, regardless of the sample size.

For a uniformly chosen $r$-element subset, where $0\leq r\leq n$, the
corresponding probability is instead
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\binom{n-s}{r}+s\binom{n-s}{r-1}}{\binom nr}.
 \label{gsr:fz:19:audit:hg-distinct}
\end{equation}
The conventions are that an out-of-range binomial coefficient is zero
and that the population has $n\geq1$ points.  The sampling theorem of the
present article uses this finite-population model and the more general
recovery condition
$|R\cap C|\geq\min(d,|C|)$.  The latter allows a fully sampled small class
to be represented by a lower-degree interpolant.  Thus neither repeated
coordinates nor singleton classes are silently treated as a pair of
distinct interpolation nodes.

\subsection{The closing graph budget: two different source formulas}
\label{gsr:fz:19:audit:budget}

It is essential to retain a dimensional distinction between the two
versions of the argument.  Put
\[
 A_j=2^{\,2^{j+8}},\qquad
 \mathcal Q(t,\gamma,j)=(\gamma t)^{-A_j}.
\]
These are the graph-count controls used in the repository's
\texttt{multipleC} and \texttt{multipleQ}, and agree with the displayed
controls on printed page~567 of the original paper
\cite{gowers,repo19lean}.  Write
\[
 \sigma=\rho/4,\qquad
 R=\gamma^{-2}s(2^{-(k+2)}\theta,\gamma,k),\qquad
 p=4r^2R,
\]
where $r$ is the number of sampled coordinates.  The original published
comparison on page~575 is
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal Q(\sigma/p,\gamma,k)^p
 \leq \mathcal Q(\rho,\gamma,k+1).
 \label{gsr:fz:19:audit:original-budget}
\end{equation}
The edited repository transcription instead uses dimension $k+1$ on
the left-hand side as well \cite{repo19paper}.  These are different
inequalities and should not be quoted interchangeably. \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 15--20]} The printed page was not checked at the write; this is the source's reading of the 2001 paper. The transcription carries an editorial note at Lemma~16.10 that the displayed closing comparison does not justify the lemma.

Both versions have an explicit algebraic obstruction with the displayed
controls.  Assume $k\geq1$, $r\geq1$, and
$0<\theta,\gamma,\rho\leq1$, and set $a=\log(1/(\gamma\rho))\geq0$.
Since $A_{k+1}=A_k^2$, taking logarithms shows that
\eqref{gsr:fz:19:audit:original-budget} is equivalent to
\begin{equation}
 p\bigl(a+\log(4p)\bigr)\leq A_k a .
 \label{gsr:fz:19:audit:budget-criterion}
\end{equation}
In particular it fails whenever $p\geq A_k$.  The displayed auxiliary
parameter already exceeds that range.  Indeed, with
$B_k=2^{\,2^{k+6}}$, the definition of $s$ gives
\[
 R=\gamma^{-2}
       \left(\frac{2^{k+3}}{\theta\gamma}\right)^{B_k}
   \geq 2^{(k+3)B_k}>2^{\,2^{k+8}}=A_k.
\]
For the last strict inequality it suffices to observe that
$B_k>2^{k+8}$ for $k\geq1$.  Therefore $p=4r^2R>A_k$, and
\eqref{gsr:fz:19:audit:budget-criterion} fails throughout this range.
This calculation concerns the stated numerical comparison, not the truth
or falsity of Lemma~16.10 as a mathematical assertion.

The same-dimension comparison in the edited transcription fails even
more directly: for $p\geq1$,
\[
 \mathcal Q(\sigma/p,\gamma,k+1)^p
   =\left(\frac{4p}{\gamma\rho}\right)^{A_{k+1}p}
   >\left(\frac1{\gamma\rho}\right)^{A_{k+1}}
   =\mathcal Q(\rho,\gamma,k+1).
\]

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 15--20]
\emph{Certified formally since the pin:} \file{section16_same_dimension_closing_comparison_fails} (\file{Proofs16ClosingComparison.lean}, line~25, HEAD \texttt{0b4890a1c}) proves $\texttt{multipleQ}(\rho,\gamma,k)<\texttt{multipleQ}(\rho/(4p),\gamma,k)^p$ for $p\ge1$ and $0<\gamma,\rho\le1$, this display in the Lean indexing; like this source, it is an obstruction to the displayed proof step, not a counterexample to Lemma~16.10.
\end{writenote}

Consequently, reducing the number of anchors gives a real local
improvement but does not by itself justify either displayed closing
comparison.  One must also redesign the quantitative closure, preserve
the dependence on the outer parameter, or replace the relevant
structural input.  The present article does not infer an improved
global Szemer\'edi bound from the sampling improvement.

These are the results
reported by that checkpoint; they are not a new build result of this

In particular, \texttt{lemma\_16\_10} has no exact companion or related

The first gives multiple multilinearity of each section at a fixed final

\[

\]
The second packages the line covers and width bounds intended to come

Several interface facts matter for an implementation.
\texttt{Section16LineCover} stores at most a natural number

The separate natural number \texttt{qDelta} controls the recurrence-width
