the current \texttt{Section16AllBoxLineCovers} interface still quantifies
over arbitrary boxes and does not yet carry the corresponding
properness clauses. \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 15--20]} \emph{Stale:} at HEAD \texttt{0b4890a1c} \file{Section16AllBoxLineCovers} (\file{Section16.lean}, line~824) requires \texttt{P.IsProper}; the older unrestricted form is kept as \file{Section16AllBoxLineCovers_unrestricted_box_encoding} (line~806).  The current signature of
\texttt{lemma\_16\_10} also assumes only a nonzero modulus.
Distinct interpolation nodes in an arbitrary \texttt{ZMod N} need not
have invertible differences.  A field hypothesis, a prime modulus, or
explicit pairwise unit-difference hypotheses are therefore needed in
the algebraic interpolation layer.

\subsection{A practical formalization route}
\label{gsr:fz:19:audit:blueprint}

The finite sampling theorem should first be formalized independently of
the Section~16 induction.  Its natural data are a finite population,
a finite family of rows, at most $q$ disjoint classes in each row, and
the uniform family of $r$-element population subsets.  Counting pairs
consisting of a sample and a class gives the hypergeometric expectation.
Finite averaging then supplies an actual sample with the claimed lost
mass.  This stage needs finite sums and binomial coefficients; it does
not need a probability-space formalization or a prime modulus.

The next layer constructs the Lagrange interpolant for each nonempty
anchor subset of size at most $d$ over a field.  For a recovered large
class, agreement at $d$ nodes implies agreement with its degree
at most $d-1$ polynomial.  For a smaller recovered class, all its points
are nodes, which is sufficient for agreement on that class.
The interpolation statement should expose both conclusions rather than
assert uniqueness of the original polynomial on a singleton.

Finally, the sampled fixed-coordinate sections must be placed on a
common proper refinement, and their covering functions substituted into
the interpolation formula.  The existing public helpers
\texttt{BaseCase.\allowbreak properMultiplyLinear\_\allowbreak finsetUnion} and
\texttt{BaseCase.\allowbreak properMultiplyLinear\_\allowbreak fin\_\allowbreak sum} provide proved
finite-family closure for iteration parameters at least one;
\texttt{IsMultilinear.\allowbreak mul\_\allowbreak new\_\allowbreak coordinate} supplies the elementary
multilinear lift used in the affine case.  General degree in the final
variable requires an additional mixed-degree predicate and its closure
lemmas.  Domain restriction also matters: a sampled section is only
certified where that section's partial domain is present.

The resulting local theorem can be connected to
\texttt{Section16LineCover}.  It should retain explicit sample,
graph-count, width, and exceptional-mass bounds.  Declaring
\texttt{lemma\_16\_10\_holds} would require the additional geometric and
quantitative closure obligations described above.  No such full Lean
companion, and no completion of Theorems~18.1--18.2, is claimed here.

\section[{Verification and reproducibility\srctag{19}}]{Verification and reproducibility}\label{gsr:fz:19:sec:d9}\label{gsr:fz:19:sec:verification}
\srcnote{19}{Section 9}

The package contains a standalone \LaTeX\ source with an embedded
bibliography, the compiled PDF, the figure used in the article,
the source audit, and executable diagnostics.  The mathematical
proofs do not depend on a numerical search finding the claimed
objects.  Computation is used to check exact finite identities,
normalization, endpoint conventions, and illustrative values.

\subsection{Exact finite checks}

The script \path{verification/verify_sampling.py} uses only Python's
standard library and exact rational arithmetic.  Its recorded run
checks the following.
\begin{itemize}
\item $1{,}136$ comparisons between the hypergeometric formula and
explicit enumeration of subsets, for populations of size at most
eight and interpolation orders at most four.
\item $1{,}664$ instances of the universal loss bound, including
the finite dynamic program and the full-population endpoint.
\item All $64$ subsets of a six-point population in the symmetric
extremal-family construction, grouped by their sample sizes.
The loss is independent of the particular anchor subset and
equals the exact minimax value.
\item A deterministic conditional-expectation selection example
with $25$ partial rows on $12$ columns.  Its five selected columns
are $2,5,9,10,11$, with zero-based column indices.  The expected
unnormalized loss decreases from $21047/198$ to an actual loss
of $78$ out of $300$ ambient row-column points.
\item $243$ finite-field interpolation evaluations, including
small classes and functions with independent affine degree
bounds in two horizontal variables.
\end{itemize}
The file \path{verification/sampling_results.json} records the
results and the exact profiles in table~\ref{gsr:en:19:tab:finite-minimax}.

The script \path{verification/verify_polynomial.py} checks the
determinants, the finite Newton-lift identities, and the modular
counterexample described in section~\ref{gsr:dt:19:poly:section}.  Its exhaustive
quadratic tests examine $20{,}402$ coefficient tuples, and its
determinant checks cover $40$ degree-spacing pairs.  Results are
in \path{verification/polynomial_results.json}.

The figure script \path{verification/make_figures.py} evaluates
the unique-root equations for the occupancy constants with
high-precision decimal arithmetic and draws the figure using
Matplotlib.  The displayed decimals are numerical evaluations,
not a replacement for the exact formulas and uniqueness proof.

\subsection{Build and source provenance}

From the unpacked directory, the PDF can be rebuilt with
\begin{verbatim}
latexmk -pdf -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error \
  gowers_interpolation.tex
\end{verbatim}
The supplied PDF figure is sufficient for compilation; regenerating
it is optional.  The file \path{README.txt} gives the short commands
for rerunning the diagnostics.

The source manifest records the exact repository commit and file
hashes used for comparison.  The full paper and Lean development
were read through the selected GitHub integration.  The relevant
published formulas were also checked against the original PDF,
including its displayed Section~16 controls and final graph
comparison.  The source audit deliberately records the original
and edited formulas separately.

All principal new claims received a written-proof review
independent of their initial derivation.  This is a description
of the checks performed for the report.  It is not external peer
review, and no new Lean build or kernel verification was run.

\section[{Further research questions and proposed projects\srctag{19}}]{Further research questions and proposed projects}\label{gsr:fz:19:sec:d10}
\srcnote{19}{Section 10}
\label{gsr:fz:19:sec:research}

The questions below are proposed follow-up problems arising from
the proved results.  Unless an external source is cited, they are
questions formulated here, not assertions that a particular
problem is already recognized as open throughout the literature.

\subsection{Exact sampling and interpolation}

\begin{problem}[Structure of finite extremal profiles]
Can the maximizers in \eqref{gsr:en:19:eq:minimax-definition} be classified
without dynamic programming?  In the numerical examples, equal
small classes often maximize the loss, but the small-sample regime
also uses unequal sizes forced by the total-size constraint.
Determine how many distinct positive class sizes a maximizer
ever needs, and locate the transitions as $r/n$ varies.
\end{problem}

The exact integer optimization makes this a finite mathematical
question with certificates.  A useful first result would be a
uniform bound, depending only on $d$, on the number of distinct
sizes in an optimizing vector.  Such a result would turn the
extremal value into a substantially smaller optimization.

\begin{problem}[Rates in the sharp sampling law]
Give explicit upper and lower error bounds for
$r\mathcal M_{n,q,d}(r)/q-C_d$ in terms of $1/r$, $r/n$, and $q/r$,
with a stated range of validity.  Can these bounds replace the
simple factor $d$ in the finite sample budget by a nearly optimal
constant at a practically verifiable population size?
\end{problem}

The proof of theorem~\ref{gsr:en:19:sampling:asymptotic} already separates compact
Poisson approximation from an exponentially controlled tail.
The remaining work is quantitative uniformity and the lattice
rounding of the maximizing class size.

\begin{problem}[Selecting cheap and informative slices]
Suppose different columns have different structural refinement
costs.  Can the anchor selection minimize a combination of lost
mass and the elementary-symmetric graph count, rather than the
lost mass alone?  What is the correct replacement for uniform
sampling in that problem?
\end{problem}

Here a column should be assessed by both the classes it helps
recover and the complexity of its slice cover.  The heterogeneous
formula in remark~\ref{gsr:en:19:lift:anisotropic} supplies a precise objective;
the conditional-expectation algorithm supplies a starting point
when that objective has a computable expectation.

\begin{problem}[Going beyond the common-anchor certificate]
Can algebraic relations among the row polynomials reduce the
number of required sampled slices below the $q/\sigma$ scale?
For example, what changes when many affine pieces share a slope,
or when all slice functions belong to a low-dimensional common
function space?
\end{problem}

The minimax lower bound does not forbid such an improvement:
its rows deliberately have no structure beyond the specified
class partitions.  A theorem using additional shared algebraic
information would address a different, stronger input model.

\begin{problem}[Robust polynomial lifting]
Develop an analogue when each row is approximately polynomial
or each sampled slice has errors in its values.  Which node
separation, agreement-density, or norm hypotheses permit a
quantitative repair without losing the linear number of slice
refinements?
\end{problem}

Over the reals or complex numbers, the norms of Lagrange basis
polynomials must be controlled.  Over finite fields, an
agreement-based formulation may be more appropriate.  These
are different problems and should have separate hypotheses.

\subsection{Geometry and polynomial recurrence}

\begin{problem}[Proper modular boxes without inherited coordinates]
Replace the additional inherited-coordinate hypothesis in
corollary~\ref{gsr:en:19:lift:source-corollary} by the precise proper-box predicates
used in the live Lean development.  Prove a synchronization
theorem with an explicit width loss, or produce an obstruction
showing what additional information is necessary.
\end{problem}

This is the most immediate geometric integration task.  The
algebraic interpolation theorem is already independent of it.
A proof should explicitly control subprogression steps and
wrapping, rather than infer integer containment from injectivity
of a modular parameterization.

\begin{problem}[The nonlinear exponent gap]
For fixed $k\ge2$, can the sufficient partition bound be improved
from a denominator of order $q^k$ to a smaller power of $q$?
Is the necessary region
\[
 \left(1+\sum_jjq_j\right)a+\left(\sum_jq_j\right)b\le1
\]
attainable, even for quadratic phases?
\end{problem}

An intermediate improvement by one power of $q$ would already
require a different way of handling lower coefficients created
by translation.  The present proof repeatedly solves a new
lower-degree recurrence problem; retaining correlations between
those problems is a plausible place to seek a gain.

\begin{problem}[Prescribed lengths without the square loss]
Can a complete partition into cells of two consecutive prescribed
lengths achieve the flexible-length exponent range without the
generic square-length requirement in lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:19:poly:rounding}?
What is the optimal tradeoff among minimum length, allowed
length variation, and phase diameter for nonlinear phases?
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Numerical recurrence thresholds]
Make the coefficient-uniform constants $U_{j,m}$ in the
recurrence input numerical, at least for small degrees and
moderate dimension.  Track them through
\eqref{gsr:dt:19:poly:threshold} before attempting any fully numerical
global density-increment estimate.
\end{problem}

The numerical exponent specialization from Lau does not by
itself supply numerical values for every threshold.  A complete
parameter audit must account for both.

\subsection{Closing the structural induction}

\begin{problem}[A consistent family of structural controls]
Design control functions for the induction that retain the
outer parameter dependence and absorb the actual output of
the shared-slice theorem.  Can one prove a closure statement
using those controls and then quantify the resulting final
density increment?
\end{problem}

The logarithmic obstruction in section~\ref{gsr:fz:19:audit:budget} provides an
immediate test for any proposed repair.  A revised definition
must be stable under the operations actually used: restriction,
union, sums, adding an unused coordinate, choosing slices,
and interpolation.  Passing one numerical comparison is not
enough if a later operation violates the same control family.

\begin{problem}[Formal certificates for the finite ingredients]
Formalize, in order, the hypergeometric counting identity,
the marked-sample bound, the finite minimax construction,
and the common-refinement interpolation theorem.  Can the
exact dynamic-programming profiles be exported as small
certificates checked independently of the search program?
\end{problem}

These tasks have clear finite statements and relatively modest
dependencies.  They can be completed before the full Section~16
induction is repaired.  The higher-degree phase-partition
transfer can likewise be formalized against an explicit
recurrence hypothesis, keeping the imported theorem separate
from the new transfer argument.

\begin{problem}[A complete local-to-global parameter audit]
After the geometric and structural closure tasks are complete,
propagate all changed constants through the remaining inverse,
phase-removal, density-selection, and iteration steps.  Which
local savings survive in the final function of density and
progression length?
\end{problem}

This last task is the necessary route from the improvements in
this article to any claim about a global Szemer\'edi bound.
The present report supplies exact local theorems, sharpness
certificates for a natural sampling problem, and explicit
interfaces for carrying out that audit.

\section[{Formalization and reproducibility\srctag{20}}]{Formalization and reproducibility}\label{gsr:fz:20:sec:d9}
\srcnote{20}{Section 9}
\label{gsr:fz:20:sec:verify}

\subsection{Connection with the inspected Lean interfaces}

The inspected \texttt{Sections01\_03.lean} defines
\texttt{progressionAverage}, \texttt{theorem\_3\_2},
\texttt{corollary\_3\_3}, \texttt{lemma\_3\_8}, and
\texttt{lemma\_3\_9} \cite{repo20lean}. The progression average there is
an unnormalized sum on $\Z/N\Z$. Its Theorem~3.2 specification assumes
prime modulus and $k\le N$ \emph{[6~October 2026; sources 15--20; HEAD \texttt{0b4890a1c}]} (\file{theorem_3_2}, \file{Sections01\_03.lean}, line~258, and \file{corollary_3_3}, line~276, with exact companions \file{theorem_3_2_holds} and \file{corollary_3_3_holds}, \file{Proofs03ProgressionAverage.lean}, line~381, \file{Proofs03ProgressionCount.lean}, line~349; none of this source's results is formal); the new cyclic statement can instead use
\eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:cyclic-kappa}, or impose the exact coprimality condition to make
all costs one. The inspected \texttt{Proofs01\_03.lean} contains the
finite Fourier identities underlying this normalization \cite{repo20fourier}.
These are source observations, not a claim that the repository already
formalizes the theorems in this article.

A useful implementation order is as follows. First formalize uniform
fiber averaging for a surjective homomorphism, including the equal-fiber
cardinality proof. Next formalize the joint-image subgroup and its two
quotient maps from Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:20:lem:joint}. Then define directional cube
powers as normalized finite sums and establish positivity without real
fractional powers. The kernel-elimination theorem should first be proved
in its powered form \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:after-r}; the final roots are a separate
real-analysis wrapper. The finite-index comparison can similarly be
proved as an inequality between $2^s$-th powers using character
orthogonality and the existing cube Cauchy--Schwarz interface.

The second-order telescoping identity is independent of groups and
analysis. It is a finite polynomial identity over a commutative ring,
with the first two selected indices providing a natural induction or
finite-set partition proof. Separating it from the analytic bound should
make both developments reusable. The Gauss construction requires a
separate finite-field exponential-sum development and should not block
formalization of the main counting theorem.

No Lean executable was available in the working environment used for
this package. No Lean source is presented as compiled or kernel checked,
and the repository was not modified. The supplied verification program
uses exact rational arithmetic for finite tests, not proof-assistant
certification of the general statements.

\subsection{Executed verification}

The accompanying \texttt{verify.py} uses the Python standard library for
its exact tests. It computes directional cube powers by derivative
recursion. For the two-function theorem it compares rational quantities
in the powered inequality
\begin{equation}
 |\La|^{2^{k-1}}
 \le D_i(f_i)^{2^{k-1}}D_j(f_j)^{2^{k-1}}
      (\E|f_\ell|^2)^{2^{k-2}}
      \prod_{r\notin\{i,j,\ell\}}\norm{f_r}_\infty^{2^{k-1}}.
 \label{gsr:fz:20:eq:test-power}
\end{equation}
No floating-point root is needed. This tests the actual $L^2$ gain,
including non-coprime and repeated slopes.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{Xr}
\toprule
Exact test family & Number\\
\midrule
Exhaustive two-function/$L^2$ inequalities on $\Z/2\Z$ & 6,561\\
Random rational two-function/$L^2$ inequalities, orders 3--5 & 1,710\\
Finite-index norm comparisons & 252\\
Exact equalities for coset-supported functions & 252\\
First-two-residual polynomial identities & 700\\
Exhaustive three-term indicator bounds on odd cyclic groups & 680\\
Higher-order rational quadratic counting bounds & 105\\
Quadratic-phase matrix rank cases & 64\\
Exact pair-quotient averaging identities & 65\\
\midrule
Total & 10,389\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\caption{Executed exact arithmetic tests. All passed. Random tests use the
fixed seed $20261006$; ``exhaustive'' refers only to the specified finite
families, not to all functions or groups.}
\label{gsr:fz:20:tab:checks}
\end{table}

An optional NumPy check, also executed, directly averages the weighted
three-term example on $\F_{29}^2$. It gives
\[
 \La_3(f)=0.00003419510332526960,
\]
with discrepancy less than $1.4\times10^{-20}$ from the evaluated exact
formula. Its computed $U^2$ fourth power is approximately
$7.85288905\times10^{-7}$, below the proved bound
$4.64476813\times10^{-6}$. These are floating-point checks and are
labeled separately in \texttt{verification\_report.json}. Neither the
Gaussian computation nor the finite rational tests replace the proofs.

To reproduce the exact checks, run
\begin{verbatim}
python3 -S verify.py --output verification_report.json
\end{verbatim}
To include the optional NumPy calculation, omit \texttt{-S} and add
\texttt{--gauss}. The manuscript is self-contained as a TeX source with
an inline bibliography and no external figures. Three runs of
\texttt{pdflatex} resolve the contents and cross-references.

\section[{Further research questions and topics\srctag{20}}]{Further research questions and topics}\label{gsr:fz:20:sec:d10}
\srcnote{20}{Section 10}
\label{gsr:fz:20:sec:questions}

The questions below are a proposed program arising from the proved
bounds. Except for the explicit local extremal questions formulated
here, they are research directions rather than assertions that a
literature-wide open status has been established.

\begin{question}[Optimal exponent for longer symmetric counts]
For fixed $k\ge4$ and density bounded away from zero and one, determine
the largest $\theta$ for which an estimate
$|\La_k(1_A)-\delta^k|\le C_{k,\delta}U^{k-1}(1_A-\delta)^\theta$
holds uniformly over admissible finite abelian groups. The present
article proves $\theta\ge2$ and settles optimality only for $k=3$.
Can higher-degree phase rank degeneracies furnish matching examples?
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Sharp three-term density coefficient]
Determine the best coefficient multiplying $u^2$ in the small-$u$
three-term problem, separately for weights and indicator sets. Is the
upper coefficient $\sqrt{\delta(1-\delta)}$ attainable asymptotically
under the indicator constraint? The rounding proof preserves a positive
coefficient, but is far from an optimal-constant calculation.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Prime-cyclic sharpness]
Construct a quantitatively controlled prime-cyclic analogue of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:20:thm:indicator-sharpness}, or identify an obstruction that
improves the available exponent or coefficient in that restricted
family. A transfer argument must preserve the count excess relative to
the square of the norm, rather than merely preserve positivity.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[The best multilinear torsion constant]
For fixed $L$ and marked positions $i,j,\ell$, determine the operator
norm in \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:two} after replacing both directional seminorms by
global ones. The product $\kappa_i\kappa_j$ is explicit, but sharp
individual norm conversion does not settle simultaneous sharpness of
the full counting estimate.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Equality and stability of the two-function argument]
Classify equality in Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:20:thm:two} beyond constant functions,
and obtain a stability statement for near equality. The proof suggests
compatibility conditions between almost constant fiber magnitudes and
almost proportional quotient-conditional derivatives. Formulating the
correct quantitative metric is part of the problem.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Optimized unequal-density elimination]
Develop an exact finite optimization procedure for second-order
elimination using the full profiles $\Useminorm{b_i}s$, densities, $L^2$ norms,
and subgroup costs. The existing first-order dynamic program in the
repository is not automatically optimal for this two-marked problem.
Can one obtain a useful polynomial-time approximation without enumerating
all position orders and tail decompositions?
\end{question}

\begin{question}[More than one ordinary norm gain]
Which systems admit an improvement retaining two uniformity norms and
several $L^p$ factors? Ordinary iteration tends to change the power of
a later density gain. A sharp mixed-norm region, stated as a finite
polytope of exponents when possible, would clarify the best sparse-set
bounds obtainable from this method.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[A quotient-adapted counting baseline]
Replace the product of means by a baseline determined by conditional
expectations on the torsion quotients, with \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:pair-baseline} as
its first correction. Can a systematic expansion remove large
$\kappa$ costs while retaining global uniformity control on the
remaining genuinely transverse directions?
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Localization preserving two uniform factors]
Find a no-wrap or interval-localization mechanism that retains two
small balanced norms in every error term. This would connect the
quadratic modular threshold to integer density-increment arguments
without assuming that multiplication by an arbitrary interval indicator
preserves uniformity.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Effect on a complete quantitative iteration]
Insert the improved counting threshold into a fully specified inverse
theorem and density-increment scheme, and propagate every parameter.
Which exponent in the final bound changes, and which loss remains
dominant? This is the required calculation before any global-bound
improvement can be claimed.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[General coefficient modules]
For systems of integer matrix forms on finite modules, express the
subgroups $L_i(\ker L_j)$ through Smith normal forms or determinantal
ideals. An exact arithmetic interface could turn the abstract theorem
into a computable torsion-sensitive bound for higher-dimensional
configurations, including systems with several parameter directions.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Kernel-checked proof certificates]
Formalize the two-function theorem, the sharp finite-index comparison,
and the second-order telescoping identity as independent reusable
components. An especially useful first milestone is a powered,
root-free theorem over finite sums, with an automatically checked
certificate for every coefficient index in \eqref{gsr:cc:20:eq:cyclic-kappa}.
\end{question}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Conclusion\srctag{20}}]{Conclusion}\label{gsr:fz:20:sec:d11}
\srcnote{20}{Section 11}

The decisive local change is to keep two functions at the last
Cauchy--Schwarz stage. That produces a bilinear dependence on their
uniformity norms, with one additional $L^2$ factor. An exact
second-order expansion then converts the analytic estimate into
quadratic symmetric counting error. Torsion is neither ignored nor
excluded: the kernel-image directions identify it, a sharp index
comparison quantifies it, and explicit collapsed-pair examples show why
some dependence is necessary.

The three-term construction also supplies a boundary to this line of
improvement. Over admissible growing-dimensional groups, even genuine
sets can have count excess proportional to the square of a small
balanced $U^2$ norm. Thus further progress must exploit extra structure,
a sharper coefficient, a different norm, a restricted ambient family,
or information unavailable in the present symmetric estimate.

\subsection{A concrete formalization route}

The shortest route to formalizing the new material is to separate
finite combinatorics from real optimization.

\begin{enumerate}
\item Prove the Fourier sum-of-squares identity on a finite abelian
group and specialize to real centered functions.  Establish the
axis identity as a finite-sum equality.
\item Formalize the three opposite-pair families and the eight extra
order-five tuples as disjoint weighted finite sets.  This gives
\eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:joint-gap} without analytic asymptotics.
\item Prove the three six-vertex identities and the derivative identity
for $C_7$ algebraically.  The displayed profile inequalities then
use finite-sum Cauchy--Schwarz and H\"older.
\item State the finite profile theorem
\eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:finite-profile} with explicit nonnegative real parameters.
Keep this usable theorem independent of asymptotic notation.
\item Prove the scalar localization and absorption lemmas, and then
the two-variable quadratic optimization.  This isolates the absolute
smallness threshold and remainder constant.
\item Treat the five-point polynomial as a finite certificate,
followed by a separate real analytic optimization theorem.  A
formal proof of its exact coefficients is substantially easier
than a formal proof of the analytic maximizing branches.
\end{enumerate}

The general exponent-five group requires a finite abelian-group
interface or a vector-space model over $\F_5$; a statement only on
\texttt{ZMod N} does not automatically represent $\F_5^n$.
Normalization also matters.  In this article the cube average is
$N^{-4}$ times the count and the centered uniformity budget is
$u^8$.  Any implementation should verify these factors at the
interface, rather than transfer theorem names alone.

\subsection{Computational checks supplied with the article}

The archive contains two standard-library Python verifiers.  Their
role is to test finite algebra and catch transcription errors;
the proofs above establish the general results.

\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{verify\_order5.py} enumerates all $625$ Fourier cube
assignments on $\F_5$, obtaining $34$ monomials.  It compares
physical-space cube averages, the full Fourier formula, the six-row
table, and the expanded phase polynomial.  It checks the rational
series coefficients and $20/9$ exactly.
\item \texttt{verify\_profiles.py} checks the three sextic support
identities and the septic derivative by exact monomial dictionaries
on $\F_5$.  It also checks the finite profile and energy inequalities
on deterministic examples in $\F_5$ and $\F_5^2$, including direct
physical-space cube averages.
\end{itemize}

The supplied run records report all checks passing.  The largest
normalized floating-point discrepancy in the two independent runs
was below $2\cdot10^{-13}$.  This small numerical discrepancy is
consistent with rounding; the exact dictionary and rational
checks use integer or rational arithmetic.  The general asymptotic
claims are not inferred from finite sampling.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Further research questions\srctag{21}}]{Further research questions}\label{gsr:fz:21:sec:d11}
\srcnote{21}{Section 11}
\label{gsr:fz:21:sec:questions}

The questions below distinguish a natural next calculation from a
larger structural problem.  None is asserted to be a previously
published open problem without a separate source establishing that
status.

\begin{question}[The universal eighth-order coefficient]
For fixed $0<\delta<1$, let
\[
 M_\delta^{(5)}(u)=\sup_{\substack{G\ne0\ {\rm finite\ abelian},\ 5G=0\\
                  W:G\to[0,1],\ \E W=\delta\\
                  \|W-\delta\|_{U^3}\le u}}Q_3(W).
\]
Does the limit
\[
 \lim_{u\downarrow0}
 \frac{M_\delta^{(5)}(u)-\delta^8-6\sqrt2\delta^4u^4
                         -C_5\delta^2u^6}{u^8}
\]
exist, and is it $20/9$?  Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:21:thm:main} gives a finite
upper limsup, while Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:21:cor:pullback} gives lower liminf
at least $20/9$.  The missing step is a sharp treatment of
frequencies outside the dominant five-point quotient.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Fixed higher dimensions]
For $G=\F_5^n$ with fixed $n\ge2$, is the eighth-order coefficient
always $20/9$?  Can an extremizing family be proved to depend on
one linear functional for all sufficiently small norms?  The
projection estimate \eqref{gsr:cc:21:eq:projection} supplies approximation,
but not exact attainment after norm rescaling.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[A quantitative eighth-order stability theorem]
If the objective is within $O(u^8)$ of the displayed sharp
sixth-order expansion, what is the best bound for the Fourier
mass outside $\{\pm\xi,\pm2\xi\}$?  Determine whether a
$U^2$ error of order $u^2$ is the correct uniform scale and
identify the additional phase and amplitude losses.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Further terms on the five-point group]
The analytic maximizing branches in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:21:thm:five-point-next} permit recursive calculation
of higher coefficients.  Determine the exact $u^{10}$ and
$u^{12}$ terms and the first nonzero displacement of the phases.
At order $u^{12}$, the phase perturbation can affect the value,
so a computation confined to the limiting phases is insufficient.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Exact finite-norm maximizers]
For fixed $0<\delta<1$, how far can the analytic maximizing
branches be continued before a weight reaches $0$ or $1$ or a
different branch takes over?  The six-row formula reduces the
question on $\F_5$ to a compact, explicit constrained problem.
Certified interval arithmetic or elimination could locate its
transition values.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Other torsion classes]
Determine the comparable near-constant expansion on exponent-three
groups, where the centered low-degree cancellations and pure-pair
norm differ.  For mixed odd torsion, classify the secondary behavior
according to the order of the largest Fourier character, taking
care that competitors of several character orders may coexist.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Higher-dimensional additive cubes]
For $d\ge4$, determine the sharp leading real-centered coefficient
in $Q_d(\delta+f)$ at fixed $U^d(f)$, and classify the first
torsion-dependent correction.  The three-cube Fourier
sum-of-squares representation is unusually simple; higher
dimensions require a larger incidence-kernel analysis.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Optimal profile inequalities]
The estimates $|C_6|\le28H$ and
$H\le3\sqrt{D\mathcal E(\lambda)}$ are adequate for the sharp
sixth-order theorem, but their constants and simultaneous equality
cases have not been optimized here.  Determine which profiles can
actually approach equality in all the needed estimates.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Quantitative conversion from weights to sets]
The probabilistic argument allows the ambient dimension to be made
arbitrarily large.  What is the least dimension needed to approximate
the model through a specified order, or to realize a specified
density with an explicit cube-count error?  Deterministic rounding
would provide a useful constructive complement.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Machine-checked finite certificates]
Can the $34$-monomial five-point certificate and the sextic support
identities be checked by a small trusted Lean evaluator, followed
by a proof of the scalar profile theorem?  This is a concrete
entry point that does not require formalizing the entire analytic
maximization argument at once.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Where local gains affect larger arguments]
Which finite-field density or counting arguments genuinely use
this sharper cube count with its characteristic-five structure?
Identify an explicit downstream theorem before claiming a
quantitative improvement.  The absence of long proper progressions
in exponent-five groups prevents a direct extrapolation to
integer Szemer\'edi bounds.
\end{question}

The most focused next target is the first question: the proofs
already isolate a finite eighth-order gap, and the model supplies
the exact candidate $20/9$.  A resolution would require a sharper
geometric analysis of the off-line Fourier tail, rather than another
optimization of the two-harmonic phases.

\section[{Finite incidence certificates and reproducibility\srctag{21}}]{Finite incidence certificates and reproducibility}\label{gsr:fz:21:sec:dA}
\srcnote{21}{Appendix A}
\label{gsr:fz:21:app:certificates}

\subsection{Centered support census}

Associate to each cube vertex $\omega$ the column
$(1,\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3)^\mathsf T$ over $\F_5$.
The expectation of a product of centered functions on a support is
the sum of Fourier monomials whose frequencies lie in the kernel
of the corresponding column matrix.  A zero forced coordinate
makes the monomial vanish.  The relevant small census is
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}rrl@{}}
\toprule
Support size&Number&Classification relevant to the expansion\\
\midrule
$1$&$8$&Independent; centered expectation zero\\
$2$&$28$&Independent; centered expectation zero\\
$3$&$56$&Independent; centered expectation zero\\
$4$&$70$&$12$ rank-three parallelograms; $58$ rank four\\
$5$&$56$&$8$ full-support circuits; $48$ with a forced zero\\
$6$&$28$&Omitted-pair distances $1,2,3$: $12,12,4$\\
$7$&$8$&One omitted vertex; the derivative formula applies\\
$8$&$1$&The full $U^3$ power\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
This census explains why the first three errors vanish and why the
fourth and fifth terms have coefficients $12$ and $8$.

\subsection{The full five-point polynomial certificate}

Order the vertices as $000,001,010,011,100,101,110,111$.
All $625$ solutions of the four Fourier constraints on the full
cube can be parameterized by $(s,t,v,w)\in\F_5^4$ as
\[
 (s+t+v+2w,\,-s-t-w,\,-s-v-w,\,s,
          -t-v-w,\,t,\,v,\,w).
\]
The four equations can be checked by substitution, and the last
four chosen parameters are recovered directly from the labels at
$011,101,110,111$, proving that the parameterization is bijective.
Counting the multiplicities of the monomials
$a_0^{e_0}\cdots a_4^{e_4}$ gives the accompanying CSV certificate.
The multiplicities sum to $625$, and every exponent vector has
total degree eight.

This is independent of the six-slot sum-of-squares calculation:
one certificate solves the physical cube's orthogonality equations,
while the other groups Fourier parallelograms into squared terms.
Their agreement supplies a useful finite algebra check.

\subsection{How to reproduce the supplied artifacts}

From the extracted archive directory, run
\begin{verbatim}
python3 code/verify_order5.py
python3 code/verify_profiles.py --output data/profile_validation_results.json
make pdf
\end{verbatim}
The verifiers need only Python's standard library.  The optional
figure-generation program uses \texttt{matplotlib} with high-precision
arithmetic from Python's \texttt{decimal} module; the prebuilt PDF
figure is included, so plotting packages are not needed to compile
the article.

\subsection{Exact computational checks}

The package contains four small Python programs, using only the standard
library. They use exact integer, rational, and finite-field arithmetic.
The results are recorded as JSON so that the numerical claims can be
reproduced independently of the typeset manuscript.

\begin{longtable}{p{.32\linewidth}p{.58\linewidth}}
\toprule
Program & Verification performed\\
\midrule\endhead
\file{verify_certificates.py} & Exhaustive moment--degree duality for all
ternary slices in dimensions one through three over $\F_5$ and $\F_7$;
affine slice counts; independent sparse Laurent convolution versus the
joint-moment recurrence; the explicit $d=2$ polynomial and a $d=3$
binomial-basis polynomial; exact coefficient comparison tables.\\
\file{verify_two_cubes.py} & Direct enumeration of all ternary slices and
normalized translations in the listed $k=1,2$ cases. It matches the full
squarefree moment vectors and checks the stated finite interval for
$\delta_{k,1}$, without using the stabilizer argument.\\
\file{verify_polynomial_patterns.py} & $20\,400$ norm evaluations and all
$74$ norm-value pairs over $\F_5,\F_7$ certify the origin examples;
$512$ Vandermonde-budget cases include degrees exceeding characteristic;
$3\,476$ quadratic maps and $2\,051\,540$ center/direction evaluations
check the quadratic classification; $444$ extra-direction fibers at
$72$ centers check the cubic-core formula using $119\,592$ core directions.\\
\file{verify_norm_obstruction.py} & Irreducibility of the field moduli,
all eligible ratios for $(q,p)=(3,3),(5,5),(9,3)$, and an independent full
start/direction enumeration in $\F_{27}$. The ratio counts are $6,20,18$;
the corresponding full-$p$ progression counts are $156,62\,480,13\,104$.\\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

The factorized origin check for $N_3+N_5$ is exact: every norm value has
its verified fiber size, and every pair of norm values is tested against
the two reflection equations. It therefore certifies a count over all
$q^8$ directions without pretending to have explicitly iterated that many
vectors. Likewise the value $7\,810\,000$ is a proved lower bound for
the global symmetric count, not a numerical estimate or an exact global
count.

The two-cube checks found no extra degeneracy outside the listed
hyperplanes in their tested cases. The theorem uses an explicit remainder
and does not promote that observation to an all-prime statement.
All general claims are proved in the body of the article. Independent
internal review checked the degree filtration, the class quotients,
the finite summation by parts, the zero-set rigidity, and the distinction
between prime-field and extension-field quadratic functions.

\subsection{How this fits the existing formalization}

At the inspected repository snapshot, the arrangement definitions are in
\file{Combinatorics/Ramsey/Lean/GowersSzemeredi/Sections14_15.lean}.
They include \file{GeneralArrangement}, \file{arrangementMoment},
\file{GeneralArrangement.IsDegenerate}, and
\file{degenerateGeneralArrangementCount}. The existing file
\file{Proofs15DegenerateArrangements.lean} contains
\file{lemma_15_4_holds} for the original-size estimate.
The present arrangement results use the same full moment definition of
degeneracy, not a weaker collision-only predicate.

A practical formalization order is as follows.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Define parity-normalized certificate degree by the finite Boolean
interpolation coefficients, then prove Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:22:lem:degree-duality} as
an identity of finite sums.
\item Prove the diagonal and paired-diagonal rank statements of
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:22:lem:rank}; an injective choice of the pivot variables gives
the finite counting bound directly.
\item Formalize affine ternary slice classification and the affine-value
equivalence relation. First use $\Uprof_1$; the slope-balanced
constant-term refinement can then be added without changing the rank proof.
\item Prove the cumulative weighted-sum lemma once in a general ordered
semiring or real setting. It is a reusable guard against invalid shell
subtraction in other counting arguments.
\item Add the refined arrangement theorem under its explicit prime
condition $p>4d$, and retain the separate $d=1$ theorem under
$p>\max\{3,2k+1\}$.
\item Add polynomial equality patterns as a separate definition. A
symmetric four-term pattern and a monochromatic four-term pattern have
different predicates and different degree budgets. Their identifiers
should make that distinction explicit.
\end{enumerate}

This package contains mathematical proofs and executable finite checks,
but no new Lean proof file. It has not rebuilt the repository or altered
its proof-status catalogue. In particular, this document should not be
used to mark a theorem as kernel-checked.

\section[{Further research questions and proposed next steps\srctag{22}}]{Further research questions and proposed next steps}\label{gsr:fz:22:sec:d12}
\srcnote{22}{Section 12}
\label{gsr:fz:22:sec:questions}

The following questions distinguish exact problems exposed by this
article from broader research goals. None is asserted to be a recognized
major open problem solely because it is listed here.

\begin{problem}[The actual second degeneracy coefficient]
For fixed $k$ and $d\ge2$, determine the coefficient of $p^{-2}$ in
$\delta_{k,d}(p)$. The present theorem reduces the dominant nonparity
search to slope-balanced affine Boolean slices. A solution must still
identify coincident codimension-two loci and their intersections with
the pure-parity hyperplanes. Counting certificate classes alone cannot
give the answer.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Exactness in the two-cube case]
Is $\delta_{k,1}(p)=L_k(p)$ for every sufficiently large prime $p$,
or do some nonaffine translation loci contain points outside
$t_i=0,\pm1$ and $t_i\pm t_j=0$? The finite checks for $k=1,2$
suggest a concrete starting point. Either a containment theorem or a
single exact counterexample would sharpen the structural picture.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Degree-two Boolean certificates]
Count ternary-valued Boolean polynomials of degree at most two together
with their necessary moment balances, up to affine value changes.
The first target is an explicit cumulative bound much smaller than
$\Aclass_{2d(1+k+\binom{k}{2})}$. A successful classification should
feed directly into the $p^{-3}$ term of the finite bound.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[A feasible-class filtration in every degree]
The current higher-degree profile counts many classes whose lowest
moment constraints are inconsistent. Can one build cumulative bounds
after imposing all necessary constraints, while retaining a valid
summation-by-parts comparison? The exact degree-one endpoint shows why
this is promising and also why differences of separate upper bounds
must be treated carefully.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[The balanced constant-term polynomials]
Find a compact generating function in both $k$ and $d$ for
$\Bal_{k,d}$. The leading coefficient is an alternating-cycle count;
the lower coefficients should admit a description using a finite
collection of decorated incidence graphs. Such a description could
provide efficient exact values for the eight-arrangement application.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Small characteristics]
Extend the balanced count to primes $p\le4d$ by replacing integer
constant terms with zero coefficients in a finite group algebra.
Which additional modular balance types change the leading or second
degeneracy coefficient? The Boolean degree/rank argument itself remains
available, but the pattern-class and no-aliasing counts must be redone.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[A fully propagated quantitative bound]
Carry the improved exceptional-set function through the entire chain
from respected arrangements to multilinear structure, phase removal,
density increments, and iteration. The correct output is a checked
parameter dependency graph with a closed final estimate. A local
improvement alone does not establish a better global Szemer\'edi bound.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Global quintic avoidance beyond the cubic core]
Determine the maximum dimension of a scalar polynomial of degree at
most five, or six, avoiding symmetric four-term progressions over fields
of characteristic greater than four. The current range is four to eight.
The exact pointwise theorem rules out improving eight by an argument
that guarantees a nonzero direction at each independently prescribed
center. The no-additive-extension theorem rules out the entire family
$x_0+N_3(u)+R(w)$ with added variables. Mixed dependence between the
old and new coordinates is therefore a natural construction target.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Simultaneous sharpness for a general equality pattern]
For which node partitions and degree caps is the minimum
$q^{\max(n-B,0)}$ attained by one polynomial at every center?
The low-degree monochromatic and symmetric patterns give positive
examples. The high-degree norm example shows that pointwise sharpness
alone supplies no answer.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Classifying general pointwise extremizers]
Minimum support determines the geometry of the successful direction
set, but not all polynomials producing it. Classify the maps that attain
the pointwise minimum for a given evaluation matrix. The complete
quadratic normal form is a first instance. A useful classification
should account for centers at which the subspace changes.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Surjectivity beyond complete norm cores]
Characterize polynomial cores whose reflection map is onto at every
center. Such a characterization would identify a broad family for which
independent additive extensions cannot improve avoidance. It is also
natural to ask for lower bounds on every reflection fiber, not only
surjectivity.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Higher-order extension defect formulas]
The cubic-core formula expresses the exact global count in terms of
the support of a third difference. For five or more odd norm layers,
can one obtain an equally useful expression in a hierarchy of odd
differences? The triangular norm construction supplies a recursion,
but higher-block choices affect the targets of lower blocks.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Stability of the zero-defect classification]
If the third difference of $R$ vanishes on almost every pair, is $R$
close to a prime-field quadratic function with a quantitatively sharp
error bound? The exact cubic-core formula converts this directly into
stability for the number of symmetric progressions in independent
extensions. Connections with classical low-degree testing should be
used explicitly rather than rediscovered without attribution.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Norm lines outside characteristic-divisible degrees]
For general $t$, count ratios $\theta$ for which
$N_t(\theta+j)$ is constant on $\F_p$, or merely satisfies the required
reflection equalities. The exact degree-$p$ answer uses a Frobenius
orbit on an Artin--Schreier translate. Other degrees may require a more
general description of the conjugate-root polynomial.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[An initial Lean milestone]
Formalize the exact formulas $\Bal_{k,2}$ and $\delta_{1,1}(p)$,
together with the abstract weighted cumulative-sum lemma and the
evaluation-matrix minimum. These results have small interfaces and
provide useful reusable components before the full degree-stratified
arrangement theorem is attempted.
\end{problem}

\subsection{What the accompanying checks establish}

The package includes three independent exact-arithmetic programs.  They
use Python's standard library and make no network requests.  Their
purpose is to detect finite combinatorial, normalization, and transcription
errors in the formulas used by the proofs.  They do not replace the
arguments establishing asymptotic uniformity or arbitrary-dimension
inequalities.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\caption{Exact verification performed for this article.}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}p{0.27\textwidth}X@{}}
\toprule
Program & Verified content\\
\midrule
\filepath{verify_prescribed_partitions.py}
& $1770$ interval conductors; $20181$ nonzero mixed-radix residues;
$3122$ rational phase vectors for the torus bound; four complete
partitions; $5000$ exact residue-packing formulas; $196$ exceptional-mass
gap calculations; and the prime obstruction with modulus $29269$.\\
\filepath{check_fifth.py}
& The entire centered cube polynomial, all six entries of the
five-point Fourier-slot table, the exact norm and weighted-count
polynomials, and the $12,12,4$ sextic support multiplicities.
Coefficients are integers in a formal phase ring with $z^{10}=-1$.\\
\filepath{verify_section16_gluing.py}
& $177103$ localization instances, $88688$ contained short progressions,
$1099140$ residue-transport instances, and $2361$ sampling profiles and
sample sizes, including the exact add-one identity.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{table}

The phase program verifies its full partitions by checking coverage,
disjointness, allowed lengths and phase diameters, not just the chosen
denominator.  For the prime obstruction it enumerates every possible
step allowed by the minimum cell length.  In the cube program, the
special phase is represented algebraically; floating-point cancellation
is not used to certify the polynomial identities.  The transport program
checks both orientations of the integer step and the cardinality of every
residue chain.

The included figure is generated from proved upper and lower formulas.
Its shaded band bounds an unknown exact threshold.  It is not the result
of optimizing over all phase vectors numerically.

collection: its central contribution is the completion of specific

interval length, an exact number of cells, or nonlinear phases.
\item Mark the characteristic-five secondary cube coefficient as
determined: it is $2^{3/4}/3$ with an absolute $O(u^8)$ error.  The
result applies to real centered functions, gives the weighted supremum
on every fixed nontrivial exponent-five group, and has indicator
sharpness in growing dimension.  Keep the tertiary coefficient open.
\item Record the common-base construction and full-width affine
transport as proved conditional lemmas for the proper modular-box
interface.  Keep the final Section~16 control-function comparison and
the ordinary-integer source-fidelity problem open.
\end{enumerate}

The repository's original paper transcription is an object of ongoing
mathematical repair.  The result here should be entered as an independent
theorem and linked to the relevant numbered lemma; it should not silently
replace the source's statement or erase the history of a correction.

\subsection{A feasible formalization sequence}

The partition results have a particularly direct finite formalization
route.  Define the semigroup of permitted cardinalities, establish its
conductor property, and prove the interval conductor formula.  The
mixed-radix obstruction needs only divisibility, centered modular
distance, and counting residue classes.  It would already certify the
new sharpness conclusion without formalizing a measure-theoretic torus
packing argument.  The slightly weaker rectangular upper bound is
entirely finite and has the same sharp asymptotic; the stronger finite
packing constant can be added later.

For the cube theorem, a useful interface consists of the normalized
Fourier identity \eqref{gsr:cc:23:five:T}, the exact homogeneous expansion
\eqref{gsr:cc:23:five:centered}, the concentration penalty
\eqref{gsr:cc:23:five:combined-penalty}, and the incomplete-cube bounds
\eqref{gsr:cc:23:five:A-small}.  The subsequent optimization is a real inequality
with absolute small-parameter hypotheses.  The five-point lower model
can be checked by a finite algebraic certificate, but a proof assistant
still needs an explicit bridge from that certificate to the Fourier
definitions.

For geometric gluing, the natural order is
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:23:glue:integer-step}, Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:23:glue:transport},
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:23:glue:common-refinement}, and finally
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:23:glue:affine-gluing}.  The existing modules
\filepath{Proofs16RelativeSteps.lean},
\filepath{Proofs16CommonBase.lean},
\filepath{Proofs16Interpolation.lean}, and
\filepath{Proofs16SampleSelection.lean} provide nearby interfaces
\cite{repo23lean}.  The proofs must preserve the orientation of a negative
integer lift and the exact cardinalities of proper progressions.
No claim that these proposed declarations have been kernel-checked is
made in this package.

The research-question updates proposed in this section are made in Section~\ref{gsr:fz:sec:further} (items~\ref{gsr:fz:q:I:conductor}, \ref{gsr:fz:q:III:exponentfive} and~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:synchronization}). The suggested separate directory was declined: the manuscript is printed in this report.
\end{writenote}

\section[{Further research questions and topics\srctag{23}}]{Further research questions and topics}\label{gsr:fz:23:sec:d10}
\srcnote{23}{Section 10}
\label{gsr:fz:23:sec:further}

The first two questions have the shortest path from the present proofs
to additional quantitative results.  The later questions address
structural generalization and the unresolved global dependency chain.

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Determine the second asymptotic term of the prescribed-length
threshold.}  We now know
$T_{\{L,L+1\}}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)
=L^{q+2}/\prod_i\varepsilon_i\,(1+O_q(L^{-1}))$.
The lower and upper bounds differ at the relative $1/L$ scale.
Is there a universal next coefficient, or do rounding and arithmetic
properties of the tolerances force oscillation?  Begin with $q=1$ and a
fixed rational tolerance, where every relevant step can be inspected
exactly on small intervals.

\item \textbf{Determine the tertiary cube coefficient in characteristic
five.}  The sharp secondary coefficient leaves an $O(u^8)$ error.
At this order, additional Fourier modes can compete with the two
selected harmonics.  The exact five-point polynomial gives an explicit
test family; a rigorous global optimum would need a sharper treatment
of the tail terms than the union bound in \eqref{gsr:cc:23:five:A-small}.
A finite-dimensional variational reduction would be particularly useful.

\item \textbf{Obtain a quantitative stability theorem for the phase
obstruction.}  The mixed-radix construction realizes the sharp asymptotic
threshold.  Must nearly worst phase vectors resemble a sequence of
nested rational quotients after a suitable change of coordinates on the
phase torus?  Specify a metric and a notion of near-extremality before
attempting the classification; a threshold statement alone does not
force such a structure.

\item \textbf{Find exact thresholds when the range of lengths is a fixed
fraction of the minimum.}  When $w=o(L)$ the leading constant is known.
For $w\sim\theta L$, $0<\theta\le1$, the conductor is explicit but
the present upper and lower phase factors need not have the same leading
constant.  One can first optimize the upper construction over shorter
prefixes of the permitted interval.  A matching lower construction may
require more information than the smallest allowed length.

\item \textbf{Classify optimal exceptional-set profiles.}  Formula
\eqref{gsr:dt:23:eq:packing} is exact for the rigid examples, and
\eqref{gsr:dt:23:eq:partial-asymptotic} determines the joint limit
$L\to\infty$, $\eta\to0$ for one exact length.  What is the leading
constant for fixed $\eta\in(0,1)$?  How does the answer depend on a
general numerical semigroup of allowed lengths?  The gap function
$g_{\mathcal S}$ supplies an explicit family of lower bounds.

\item \textbf{Extend the obstruction to polynomial phases with prescribed
lengths.}  A degree-$d$ phase on a progression is controlled by several
finite differences.  Seek a higher-degree analogue of the mixed-radix
construction that forces progression steps into a useful divisibility
class while retaining the tiling obstruction.  The goal is a matching
necessity theorem for a carefully stated polynomial-partition bound,
rather than only an upper recurrence estimate.

\item \textbf{Quantify the characteristic-five phase rigidity.}  The proof
forces harmonic alignment and $\cos(5\theta)\to0$ at optimal secondary
order.  Turn the deficit below $2^{3/4}/3$ into explicit bounds for
$|b/(\kappa\delta^{-1}u^2)-1|$, the relative phase error, and the
fourth-power Fourier tail.  A bound in $L^2$ would require additional
information and should not be inferred from these tail estimates.

\item \textbf{Analyze mixed torsion groups.}  The norm penalty caused by
order five is tied to the order of the dominant character.  In an odd-order
group supporting both order-five and larger-order characters, determine
which spectral regime maximizes the local cube count under additional
constraints.  The unrestricted supremum and a supremum conditioned on
the dominant character order are different problems.

\item \textbf{Improve common slice refinement through joint structure.}
The exponent in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:23:glue:common-refinement} is a product over
all sampled slices.  A structural theorem for the vector of slice
values might avoid some of this repeated loss.  The target should give
one common partition directly, with explicit exceptional mass and list
size, so that interpolation can use it without another refinement.

\item \textbf{Optimize localization when the child width is large.}
The factor $1/3$ is sharp for the width-independent cap used here.
The transport proof actually needs $tw\le|J|$, where
$t(u-1)\le b-1$.  When a large lower bound for $w$ is already known,
the worst width-two obstruction disappears.  A width-dependent
localization rule could improve the constant and perhaps the finite
thresholds used in Section~16.

\item \textbf{Close the Section 16 parameter recurrence.}  Substitute the
actual affine-class count, anchor count, exceptional budgets, and slice
profiles into the gluing theorem.  Determine control functions that are
closed under every step of the induction.  The source's displayed final
comparison is not justified by the local construction alone.  A useful
deliverable would be a checked recurrence with explicit initial values
and a proof of its solution, followed by a complete dependency audit.

\item \textbf{Formalize the sharp lower bounds first.}  The numerical
semigroup and mixed-radix arguments are finite, relatively short, and
independent of the difficult structural steps in the original proof.
They provide a realistic first kernel-checked addition.  Then formalize
the exact cube identities and the transport lemma.  Maintaining a clear
distinction between source statements, repaired statements, and new
refinements will make later integration substantially easier.
\end{enumerate}

The ZIP contains one complete LaTeX source, its compiled PDF, the figure
files, three exact verification programs, their recorded outputs, a
figure-generation script, a source manifest and a Makefile.  The article
does not require access to the original papers or previous reports in
order to compile.  All mathematical sections are in the single file
\filepath{gowers_sharp_thresholds.tex}.

With a standard TeX Live installation, run
\begin{verbatim}
pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error gowers_sharp_thresholds.tex
pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error gowers_sharp_thresholds.tex
pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error gowers_sharp_thresholds.tex
\end{verbatim}

\section[{Examples, boundary cases, and reproducible checks\srctag{24}}]{Examples, boundary cases, and reproducible checks}\label{gsr:fz:24:sec:d10}
\srcnote{24}{Section 10}
\label{gsr:fz:24:sec:checks}

\subsection{Three structural examples}

\begin{example}[An affine map has no vertical obstruction]
If $\phi(x)=T(x)+a$ on $B$, where $T:G\to H$ is a group
homomorphism, then $F_k=\{0\}$ for every $k$. Equal domain sums
produce equal output sums because both sides contain the same
number of copies of $a$. The extraction theorem therefore returns
all of $B$, without paying the generic factor $kC^{2k+1}$.
\end{example}

\begin{example}[A small nontrivial fibre with an active avoidance step]
Let $p=101$, $B=\{0,1,2\}$, $k=2$, and
$\phi(0)=\phi(1)=0$, $\phi(2)=1$. The only conflicting two-term
domain sum is $0+2=1+1$, so
\[
 F_2=\{0,1,-1\},\qquad Q_2=3.
\]
The avoidance length in \eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:avoid-L} is
$L=\floor{99/(2\cdot2)}=24$.
The choice $d=2$ works: the multiples $2j$ with
$1\le j\le48$ are neither $1$ nor $-1$ modulo $101$, and symmetry
handles negative $j$. One colour fibre contains $\{0,1\}$.
This is an order-two Freiman restriction, while the entire map is
not. The example exercises the nonconstant-output, nonzero-length
part of the proof rather than merely the $L=0$ pigeonhole case.
\end{example}

\begin{example}[Different objectives select different cores]
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:24:thm:cubic} is appropriate when the original threshold
$\delta^2m/2$ and the $90\%$ conclusion must be preserved.
For an additive application, the one-sample choice
$\beta=p^2/16$ trades a smaller common-neighbour count for a larger
core. The popular-mass cancellation then makes that trade profitable.
There is no universal rule that more samples improve the final
structural estimate.
\end{example}

\subsection{Finite checks supplied with the article}

The companion \codetwentyfour{verify.py} uses only Python's standard library.
All inequalities tested are evaluated with integers or exact rational
numbers. The recorded run completed the following checks:

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.72\textwidth}r@{}}
\toprule
Check family & Cases\\
\midrule
Cubic supporting-line inequalities on a rational grid & 4,040\\
All incidence matrices with four indices and three ambient points & 4,096\\
Weighted moment identities with deterministic random inputs & 100\\
All nonempty symmetric four-vertex graphs, allowing loops & 1,023\\
All nonempty subsets of $\Z/q\Z$, $q\in\{3,5,7,11\}$ & 2,212\\
Graph maps for vertical-fibre and extraction checks & 3,216\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Exact finite regression checks. All passed. Among the graph-map
checks, 60 exercised $Q_k>1$ and $L>0$ simultaneously.}
\label{gsr:fz:24:tab:tests}
\end{table}

For the incidence matrices, the program enumerates every ordered
three-sample, verifies the exact expectation identity, and checks
that the best score is at least $49u^3n^2/54$ with $u$ equal to the
actual mean codegree. For each small graph it verifies the
one-sample score, the pruning inequality, and the common-intermediate
walk bound. For each small additive set it checks both popular-mass
estimates and all three rounded conclusions of
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:24:cor:bsg-dyadic}.

The fibre checks verify the injection into
$(k+1)\Gamma-k\Gamma$, the cardinality inequality, the existence of
an allowed scalar, and the Freiman property of the constructed
colour fibre. All full-domain maps $\F_p\to\F_p$ for
$p\in\{2,3,5\}$ are tested at order two, together with 60
three-point-domain maps over $\F_{101}$ and $\F_{503}$.
The latter are generated by a fixed random seed; the checks
themselves remain exact.

These experiments can catch sign errors, threshold errors, and
incorrect constants. They do not prove the theorems for arbitrary
sets or all orders. In particular, the finite-field-vector hashing
theorem is proved above but is not part of the supplied finite
regression suite. The JSON report states the scope explicitly.

\subsection{Constructive content and its limits}

The core-selection proofs are finite algorithms. One can compute
codegrees, score every allowed sample, choose a maximum-score sample,
and prune its bad-degree vertices. In the one-sample argument there
are only $m$ candidate samples, once the neighbourhood table is
known. The four-walk tuple injection proves the difference bound;
an implementation need not enumerate $D^4$ to select the set.

The extraction step is also constructive after $F_k$ is known:
compute $L$, search the nonzero scalars for an allowed $d$, and take
a largest colour fibre. Computing the exact defect fibre can itself
be expensive as $k$ grows. No claim of an efficient general-purpose
algorithm for arbitrarily large $k$ is implicit in these existence
proofs.

\subsection{A minimal mathematical interface for the refactor}

A parameterized DRC layer should expose the identity
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:24:eq:lean-count-id}
 \sum_{v\in V^t}|K_v|^2
 =\sum_{i,j}|A_i\cap A_j|^t,
\end{equation}
together with its bad-pair analogue. Both identities are integer
counting statements before normalization. A separate real-valued
lemma can then turn a positive score average into an existential
core. This separation avoids interleaving casts, sampling
combinatorics, and nonlinear real inequalities.

For the cubic specialization, the main new arithmetic obligation is
\eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:cubic-line}. A rational formulation can clear denominators
and use the factorization
\[
 s^3-3b^2s+2b^3=(s-b)^2(s+2b),\qquad b=7u/6.
\]
The negative branch is handled by monotonicity on $[0,u/2]$ and the
endpoint value $u^3/108$. The rational constant $49/54$ is preferable
to the algebraic optimum for a first implementation.

A graph-certificate layer should take as inputs the exact values
$|D|$, $|K|$, the bad-degree threshold, and the common-neighbour
threshold. It should return the injection into four labelled edge
values and the relative difference bound. Only the final numerical
corollary should substitute $\tau=\kappa/2$ or replace $p$ by a
lower bound.

\subsection{Retaining the repository's popular-sum convention}

For the sum graph, an edge between $a$ and $b$ is labelled by $a+b$.
A walk $a,b,v,c,a'$ then gives
\[
 (a+b)-(b+v)+(v+c)-(c+a')=a-a'.
\]
The four labels still recover the intermediate vertices from fixed
endpoints, so the same fibre injection and cardinality estimates
apply. The energy identity and the estimate
$\tau m|D|\le pm^2$ use popular sum representations instead.
This provides a direct route to the existing module without a
wholesale rewrite of its representation-count infrastructure.

\subsection{The fibre layer and its formal obligations}

The proposed fibre lemma should be stated for a graph in a product of
abelian groups. Its proof requires only finite-set membership in an
iterated sumset and injectivity of
\[
 (y,(x,\phi(x)))\longmapsto(x,\phi(x)+y).
\]
The nonempty-graph hypothesis must be retained when cancelling
$|\Gamma|$. The growth estimate should then be imported in the exact
form \eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:PR-graph}, with exponent $(k+1)+k$.

The prime-cyclic avoidance layer should separately prove that
$1\le j\le kL<p$ implies invertibility in $\F_p$, count forbidden
nonzero scalars, and establish the integer-division inequality
$k(Q-1)(L+1)\ge p-1$. The $Q=1$ branch should bypass the division by
$Q-1$ entirely. Treating positive and negative multiples as unrelated
would lose the improved constant in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:24:thm:extraction}.

Finally, graph energy must be identified with
\codetwentyfour{phiAdditiveCount}. A new order-$k$ theorem should be proved
first, and the source's order-eight theorem recovered as a weakened
corollary. This preserves existing downstream statements while
making stronger constants available to later work.

\subsection{What would constitute formal verification}

The results in this article have not been added to the repository or
checked by Lean. Source inspection establishes the existing
interfaces, not successful compilation of a modified proof.
A completed formalization would include the parameterized finite
identities, all injection and threshold lemmas, the final
order-$k$ compiler, and a kernel-checked proof of the displayed
order-eight bound, with no new axioms or admitted proof holes.
The Python regression suite is not a substitute for any of these
obligations.

\section[{Further research questions and concrete next steps\srctag{24}}]{Further research questions and concrete next steps}\label{gsr:fz:24:sec:d12}
\srcnote{24}{Section 12}
\label{gsr:fz:24:sec:questions}

The questions below are proposed research targets. They are not
presented as a list of established famous open problems, nor as
claims that the literature has been exhausted. Each is tied to a
specific loss or limitation exposed by the proofs.

\begin{question}[The actual dense-intersection extremal problem]
For fixed $\delta$, determine the largest fraction $f(\delta)$ such
that hypothesis \eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:gowers-hyp} always supplies a core with
$90\%$ of its ordered pairs above threshold $\delta^2m/2$ and size
at least $f(\delta)n$. Is the power $\delta^3$ an artefact of the
sample-core construction? Seek matching incidence constructions or
a stronger lower bound before making an optimality claim.
\end{question}

The theorem here gives $f(\delta)\ge\sqrt{C_3}\delta^3$.
The scalar sharpness proof does not supply an upper bound for
$f$: its two-point laws may fail to arise from set intersections.
A productive first step is to formulate the finite incidence
optimization with the positive-semidefinite Gram constraints kept.

\begin{question}[Can codegree geometry rescue two samples?]
Does positive semidefiniteness, nonnegative incidence factorization,
or control of diagonal entries force a positive two-sample score
in a range where the scalar relaxation is negative? Alternatively,
can actual incidence families approximate the scalar
near-extremizers from Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:24:thm:sharp-scalar}?
\end{question}

A resolution would identify whether the obstruction in
\eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:negative-two} is genuinely combinatorial or only an
information-loss barrier. This is a sharper target than simply
asking for ``better dependent random choice.''

\begin{question}[Optimal profile-sensitive sampling]
Given an explicit codegree matrix, how much can one improve the
certificate by choosing a nonuniform law $\nu$, a different number
of samples, or tuple-dependent thresholds? Can a useful optimization
algorithm return a small exact certificate that a proof assistant
can verify independently of the search procedure?
\end{question}

The weighted identity in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:24:thm:selector} is already a
correct verification interface. The remaining task is an effective
and mathematically justified search strategy, not a new probabilistic
existence principle.

\begin{question}[Higher-arity scalar envelopes]
For respected arrangements involving $r$ indices, optimize the
moment--defect bound in Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:24:cor:arity}, including the
choice of sample number and defect penalty. Which choices minimize
the eventual exponent after several structural reductions?
\end{question}

A natural first case is $r=3$ with two prescribed badness thresholds.
The scalar objective becomes piecewise polynomial, suggesting a
finite supporting-line or supporting-polynomial certificate. Its
compatibility with actual higher-order intersection tensors remains
a separate issue.

\begin{question}[The smallest possible vertical-fibre exponent]
Given $|\Gamma-\Gamma|\le C|\Gamma|$, what is the best universal
bound for $|\{y:(0,y)\in k\Gamma-k\Gamma\}|$?
Can $2k+1$ in \eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:Q-bound} be reduced, perhaps under an
additional hypothesis on the domain projection or the codomain?
\end{question}

The first meaningful cases are $k\ge2$; at $k=1$ a graph has no
nonzero vertical defect at all. Both upper bounds and examples must
respect the graph condition. General small-doubling examples without
injective first projection do not automatically answer this question.

\begin{question}[Sharper extraction from a given symmetric defect set]
For $F\subseteq\F_p$ symmetric and containing zero, what is the
largest guaranteed size of a set $P\subseteq\F_p$ satisfying
$(kP-kP)\cap F=\{0\}$? Can a nonprogression choice of $P$ improve
the extraction fraction beyond the interval-avoidance bound for
structured defect sets?
\end{question}

The proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:24:thm:extraction} only needs such a set $P$:
a translate of $P$ captures an average fraction $|P|/p$ of the
outputs. Its arithmetic-progression construction is explicit but
need not be extremal for a particular $F$.

\begin{question}[Mixed-torsion codomains]
Extend the extraction theorem to general finite abelian codomains
with quantitative dependence on their invariant factors. Can the
prime-cyclic progression method and finite-field hashing be combined
without multiplying all the losses from the primary components?
\end{question}

The obstruction is concrete: the equations $jd=w$ need not have a
unique solution when $j$ is not invertible, and a random homomorphism
need not send every nonzero defect uniformly to a common target.
Any extension should state exactly which torsion parameters enter.

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 54--59]
\emph{Answered by source~59} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:charseparation}): exact Freiman restrictions of order $k$ over arbitrary abelian targets, $|B|/(5k)^{\lfloor\log_2(q+1)\rfloor}$ from $q$ sign orbits of vertical defects and $C^{-(2k+1)\log_2(5k)}|B|$ from $|\Gamma-\Gamma|\le C|\Gamma|$, independently of the target's size, rank and invariant factors, with variants by the defect orders (its Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:59:thm:freiman-extraction} and Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:59:cor:doubling}; item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:groups}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{question}[End-to-end threshold optimization]
Optimize all structural parameters jointly along the Section~7
pipeline, using the actual energy spectrum rather than a single
energy lower bound. How much is gained by combining the full
profile certificate \eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:profile-rel}, the exact defect count
$Q_k$, and a density-dependent popularity threshold?
\end{question}

Equation \eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:downstream-quadratic} solves the one-parameter
version with coarse energy information. The next version should
produce an explicit certificate and compare actual retained sizes,
not just formal powers of $\gamma$.

\begin{question}[Propagation into later sections]
Which later approximate-homomorphism and respected-arrangement
lemmas remain valid with their hypotheses unchanged after replacing
the Section~7 interfaces by the stronger ones here? After tracing
every use, what fully explicit improvement results in the complete
2001 quantitative argument?
\end{question}

This is a finite but nontrivial dependency-audit problem. Improving
one intermediate exponent does not justify replacing every
occurrence of a source constant mechanically. The intended outcome
should be a complete theorem with all thresholds rechecked, not a
heuristic extrapolation to a global record.

\begin{question}[A parameterized, kernel-checked structural library]
Can the DRC score identity, graph-walk injection, fibre compression,
and quantitative compiler be implemented once over general finite
sets and abelian groups, then instantiated both at the original
constants and at the improved ones?
\end{question}

A successful implementation would make future improvements local:
new scalar inequalities or new energy inputs could be plugged into
unchanged combinatorial proofs. It would also expose exactly which
constants are consequences of counting identities and which are
chosen for convenience.

\section[{Conclusion\srctag{24}}]{Conclusion}\label{gsr:fz:24:sec:d13}
\srcnote{24}{Section 13}

The main methodological lesson is to postpone coarse substitution.
Keeping the exact codegree distribution allows a cubic certificate
that preserves the original dense-intersection threshold. Keeping
the actual popular-edge mass cancels four otherwise costly density
powers in a walk count. Keeping only the vertical obstruction to
Freiman coherence reduces the sumset growth exponent from $4k$ to
$2k+1$, while its symmetry improves the extraction prefactor.

These refinements yield complete local theorems, including the
explicit order-eight bound $2^{-295}\gamma^{103}|B_0|$ and the
modern-input family \eqref{gsr:en:24:eq:modern-bound}. Their scope is precise:
proved Section~7 improvements and generalizations, a sharp scalar
optimization, and a concrete formalization programme. No
unverified propagation through the full Szemer\'edi argument is
needed for any of the conclusions stated here.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A compact proof and constant ledger\srctag{24}}]{A compact proof and constant ledger}\label{gsr:fz:24:sec:dA}
\srcnote{24}{Appendix A}
\label{gsr:fz:24:app:ledger}

The self-contained order-eight route uses the following exact chain:
\begin{align*}
 E(\Gamma_0)&\ge\gamma m^3,\\
 \tau&=\gamma/2\quad\text{(or use the actual energy first)},\\
 p&\ge\gamma/(2-\gamma)\ge\gamma/2,\\
 |K|&\ge pm/\sqrt2,\\
 |\Gamma_1|&\ge|K|/2\ge2^{-3}\gamma m,\\
 C_1:=\frac{|\Gamma_1-\Gamma_1|}{|\Gamma_1|}
 &\le2^{11}p^{-2}\tau^{-4}\le2^{17}\gamma^{-6},\\
 Q_8&\le C_1^{17},\\
 |B|&\ge\frac{|\Gamma_1|}{8Q_8}
 \ge\frac{2^{-3}\gamma m}{2^3(2^{17}\gamma^{-6})^{17}}\\
 &=2^{-295}\gamma^{103}m.
\end{align*}
When the energy hypothesis is an inequality, either use
$\kappa=E(\Gamma_0)/m^3$ throughout and weaken at the end, or retain
$\gamma$ as a lower bound in the popular-energy split. Both give
the displayed chain.

For the cubic selector, the arithmetic certificate consists of
\begin{align*}
 L(s)&=3(7u/6)^2s-2(7u/6)^3,\\
 s^3-L(s)&=(s-7u/6)^2(s+7u/3),\\
 -9(u/2)^3-L(u/2)&=u^3/108,\\
 L(u)&=49u^3/54.
\end{align*}
All constants in these two ledgers are rational except the harmless
square root in the intermediate core-size bound. The supplied test
program checks the final exponent identities separately from the
finite combinatorial examples.

The hyperplane enumeration should be a separate finite combinatorics
lemma.  In particular, the quotient by $a\sim\lambda a+\mu w$ must not
be replaced by the simpler but incorrect quotient $a\sim-a$.
