the constant cross-section fibre in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:25:thm:single} must not
be omitted; it is the source of the exact $(q-1)q^{-2d}$ term.

No Lean source is included with placeholder proofs.  This avoids giving
unverified code the appearance of a checked formal result.  A natural
implementation order is Walsh expansion, pivot ranks, the two-row
fibre count, projective classes, union bounds, and finally selection.

\subsection{Exact computations supplied with the manuscript}
The script \path{code/verify.py} uses only Python's standard library.
Its saved output is \path{data/verification.json}.  The executed checks
are as follows.

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*),leftmargin=2em,itemsep=0.35em]

hyperplane classes for $d=1,\ldots,5$, matching
$0,4,51,484,4225$; evaluation of the closed formula through $d=9$.
\item An exact characteristic-$5$ check for $d=3$, obtaining $57$ rather
than $51$ hyperplanes.
\item $1550$ instances of the Walsh moment identity, and $315$ seeded
minimal-layer rank tests, with cube dimensions up to six.
\item All $3240$ non-block-parity ternary sign classes for $k=1,d=2$
over each of $\F_5$ and $\F_7$.  For each class the full base-coordinate
count is obtained from exact ranks of the two affine equations, over
all cross-sections.  The maximal probabilities are respectively
$29/625$ and $55/2401$, exactly the bound of

\section[{Further research questions\srctag{25}}]{Further research questions}\label{gsr:fz:25:sec:d10}
\srcnote{25}{Section 10}
\label{gsr:fz:25:sec:questions}

\begin{question}[The exact second-order term]
For fixed $k,d$, determine whether a field-independent coefficient
$C_{k,d}$ exists such that
\[
 Z_{k,d}(q)=(k+H_d)q^{D-1}+C_{k,d}q^{D-2}+o(q^{D-2})
\]
over sufficiently large characteristics, and compute it in the first
nontrivial cases.  Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:25:thm:residual} proves that non-parity
witnesses already contribute at this order.  Intersections of the known
hyperplanes and overlaps among codimension-two witness loci must both
be counted.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Compressing the second-order constant]
Replace $U_{k,d}=(3^{2d2^k}-3^{2d})/2$ by a substantially smaller explicit
constant.  Many ternary patterns have identical or nested moment loci.
The minimal-layer rank $k-s$ suggests separating witnesses by Walsh
support before applying the union bound, rather than assigning every
remaining witness the same $q^{-2}$ cost.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[The full cross-section arrangement]
Determine the intersection lattice and characteristic polynomial of
$\Hh_d$.  For $d=2$, the exact union count is
\eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:d2baseline}; for larger $d$, a structural description would
replace the Bonferroni estimate with an exact formula for $v_d(q)$.
The classical finite-field method for hyperplane arrangements
\cite{athanasiadis} is a natural framework, but a full analysis of this
specific balanced ternary quotient is not supplied here.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Small-characteristic classification]
Find a closed formula for $\cardtwentyfive{\Hh_d(\F_q)}$ when
$3<p\le2d$, and classify the additional components in characteristics
$2$ and $3$.  Example~\ref{gsr:en:25:ex:smallchar} shows that replacing the
characteristic assumption by ``$q$ sufficiently large'' is not valid.
A satisfactory answer should identify the modular balancing terms and
the altered affine orbits, rather than merely give numerical tables.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Efficient detection of degeneracy]
Given an arrangement, detect a nontrivial ternary moment relation
without scanning $3^n$ patterns.  The present classification supplies a
cheap first-stage test using $k+H_d$ hyperplanes; a useful second stage
would exploit the structured Walsh moment matrix and return a verifiable
witness.  The difficulty is ternary dependence, not ordinary linear
kernel computation, since the moment matrix has many more columns than
rows in the applications.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[A selection mechanism with a larger advantage]
Can a different nonnegative selection kernel distinguish respected and
non-respected arrangements by more than the ratio
$1+2^{1-n}$, while retaining manageable degeneracy conditions and
pointwise probabilities in $[0,1]$?  Better exceptional-set counting
alone does not remove the exponential loss in \eqref{gsr:en:25:eq:Kasymptotic}.
Higher Fourier support may improve the advantage but introduces
coefficient relations beyond ternary ones.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Uniform extension to other defining relations]
Replace $w=(1^d,-1^d)$ by an arbitrary nonzero coefficient vector
$w$ with $\sum_jw_j=0$.  Which support and coefficient conditions force
every non-parity witness to have codimension at least two?  The
rank argument indicates the role of the support of $w$, but the exact
projective hyperplane count and the exceptional low-support cases
require a separate treatment.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[End-to-end quantitative propagation]
Integrate the explicit selection threshold into the corrected
multilinear-piece and final density-increment arguments in ProveIt.
Track both the field-size threshold and the retained arrangement density.
Only such an end-to-end calculation could justify a claim about an
improved final Szemer\'edi or van der Waerden bound.  The current
manuscript deliberately stops short of that claim.
\end{question}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Conclusion\srctag{25}}]{Conclusion}\label{gsr:fz:25:sec:d11}
\srcnote{25}{Section 11}

The full arrangement moment system is more rigid than the one-polynomial
estimate used to count its exceptions.  A lowest nonzero Walsh layer
gives an explicit diagonal linear minor.  At the sole remaining adjacent
layer, the last-coordinate moments force a second independent equation,
except on already visible cross-section degeneracies.  As a result,
all codimension-one exceptions are classified and their exact number is
$k+H_d$, with $H_d$ given by a balanced ternary projective count.

This yields an asymptotically optimal local replacement for Lemma 15.4,
a finite-field and arbitrary-$d$ purification theorem with explicit
parameters, and a concrete reduction of the ambient-size cost of the
exceptional set.  The unresolved issues are correspondingly more focused:
second-order geometry, compression of the residual witness family, and
improvement or replacement of the Riesz-product selection advantage.

\section[{Source comparison and remaining questions\srctag{26}}]{Source comparison and remaining questions}\label{gsr:fz:26:sec:d5}\label{gsr:fz:26:sec:source}
\srcnote{26}{Section 5}

\subsection{The precise repository interface}

The mathematical source pin is commit
\begin{center}\small\texttt{c94998a5db18ba63c815a3bf6c3877a0fde91930}.\end{center}
At that pin, \texttt{Section05.lean}, lines 242--259, defines the proposition \texttt{corollary\_5\_8}~\cite{repo26cor58}. It assumes disjoint two-comparable proper modular progressions covering $A$, local degree-at-most-$k$ polynomial correlations, and $\alpha>0$. Its length conclusion is
\[
 \frac{(N/M)^{1/K}}8,\qquad K=(k!)^2 2^{(k+1)^2},
\]
and its density conclusion is $\delta+\alpha/16$. The original paper prints an $\alpha/8$ gain in Corollary 5.8, on printed page 493 (PDF page 29). The source comment records that this conclusion was corrected to the $\alpha/16$ actually supported by the proof. We compare with this pinned corrected interface rather than silently switching between the two constants.

The definition of \texttt{PolynomialOn 1 Finset.univ} is an existential coefficient sum over \texttt{Fin 2}: it expands to $c_0+c_1x$~\cite{repo26defs}. Thus the affine hypothesis here is exactly the degree-one source condition, not an extra linearization assumption. At $k=1$, $K=16$. For every modulus $N\ge2$, Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:26:cor:comparable} replaces the source's length $(N/M)^{1/16}/8$ by $(N/M)^{1/3}/8$ and the gain $\alpha/16$ by $\alpha/3$, with no added scale premise. Nonempty parents are automatic in that source specialization: positive correlation implies $A\ne\varnothing$, and comparability would force all parents to be empty if any one were empty. Their disjointness then gives $M\le N$, so $N/M\ge1$ and the larger exponent indeed strengthens the old length bound throughout the nonvacuous range.

The separate source file \texttt{Proofs05Corollary58.lean} defines a scale-qualified repair with a common target and lower bounds ensuring that the needed recurrence and phase-freezing estimates apply~\cite{repo26scale}. Its theorem derives that repaired proposition from \texttt{corollary\_5\_6}. Those added scale conditions are not premises of the displayed catalogue predicate. The argument here supplies a written, threshold-free proof of the full degree-one specialization; it is not a Lean implementation of that specialization.

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 21--27]
\emph{Checked at HEAD \texttt{2dfe46f44}.} The pinned lines~242--259 of \file{Section05.lean} are unchanged (same blob), and \file{corollary_5_8} is still open in the ledger; \file{PolynomialOn} is at \file{Definitions.lean}, line~222, and \file{corollary_5_8_with_scale_holds} at \file{Proofs05FullPartition.lean}, line~94. The ``full degree-one specialization'' holds trivially when $N/M\le2^{48}$ (note in Section~\ref{gsr:fm:26:sec:d1}).
\end{writenote}

The remaining source modulus $N=1$ is vacuous: its balanced function is identically zero, so the positive-correlation hypothesis cannot hold. Thus the written result covers every modulus in the source's degree-one specialization. Higher-degree phases are outside the present theorems. The output is proper modular geometry, as encoded in the pinned Lean definitions; it need not satisfy every ordinary-integer geometric convention of the original paper.

\subsection{The classical mechanisms and the limited novelty claim}

Gowers's proof contains the Dirichlet input and the square-root modular-to-integer decomposition: see Lemma 5.4, the one-axis Lemma 5.12, and its whole-partition consequence Lemma 5.13~\cite{gowers}. The product almost-cover in Appendix~\ref{gsr:dt:26:app:boxes} is an elementary explicit wrapper around this type of construction.

Zhao's Lemma 6.4.5 partitions an interval into phase-flat progressions on the cube-root scale under an explicit size threshold; Lemma 6.4.6 uses such a partition in a Roth density increment~\cite{zhaobook}. This provides a direct reason not to portray the cube-root exponent or phase partitioning as new. Lewko's 2026 preprint uses moments of progression sums in Section 5 and extraction of a genuine integer progression in Section 6~\cite{lewko}. It likewise provides precedent for these methods; it is not invoked as a proof of our exact local-cover statements.

The contribution established in this report is the explicit threshold-free local-cover combination, its exact-mass formulation and correlation-dependent tradeoff, relative to the pinned repository interface. A comprehensive literature-priority investigation has not been completed. The numerical constants are convenient and are not claimed optimal.

\subsection{Questions that remain open here}

\begin{enumerate}
\item Can the explicit $(N/8)^{1/3}$ ceiling in the strongest exact-mass formulation be relaxed? It arises from our sufficient condition $N\ge L^3$ for removing nonproper directions; it does not restrict the simpler normalized-cover or comparable-parent conclusions.
\item Can correlations be used more efficiently to obtain an $\alpha$-independent square-root guarantee? Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:26:thm:sqrt} proves only an $\alpha$-dependent square-root alternative.
\item Which exact constants and gains are optimal for this local-cover interface? The ceiling/floor losses, $\pi<4$, and positive-mass averaging leave deliberate slack.
\item What is a threshold-free higher-degree replacement for the phase-flat refinement, and how would its small-correlation regime be handled? No such result is supplied here.
\item Can the elementary pair-counting, residue partition, and signed-mass lemmas be formalized and then composed into the precise all-modulus $k=1$ predicate? No Lean theorem was produced or kernel-checked in this report.
\item Can the integer-box almost-cover be connected to a source-faithful exact-partition and base-loss interface? Appendix~\ref{gsr:dt:26:app:scope} identifies the two distinct obligations.
\end{enumerate}

\section[{The exact companion and reproducibility\srctag{26}}]{The exact companion and reproducibility}\label{gsr:fz:26:sec:d6}\label{gsr:fz:26:sec:companion}
\srcnote{26}{Section 6}

The Python companion uses only the standard library, integer arithmetic, and exact rational arithmetic for its mathematical checks. Its role is diagnostic: finite tests can expose a wrong midpoint, a pair-counting failure, an omitted endpoint, or an invalid rounding convention. They cannot prove the arbitrary-parameter theorems, which are proved in Sections~\ref{gsr:dt:26:sec:mechanisms}--\ref{gsr:dt:26:sec:proofs}.

The companion checks cover ordered modular pair counts and the exact variance identity in its permitted range, all-direction coset covariance and bad-direction removal, elementary Dirichlet residue cells and lossless balanced chunking, the exact cover-mass identities, and a regression distinguishing the reduced and unreduced midpoints. The command-line bound is finite and capped. The optional larger run changes the finite coverage, not the proof status. The source archive's README gives the exact commands and coverage labels printed by the final companion.

The offline builder compiles the supplied trusted TeX in fresh external staging, runs tests and diagnostics in normal and optimized Python modes, rejects inventory mismatches, and writes a deterministic ZIP with an exact public-file manifest. It does not download dependencies or require network access. Reproducing the PDF byte-for-byte requires the same TeX toolchain and fonts. The file-handling checks and disabled shell escape are useful safeguards for this trusted-source workflow; they are not a sandbox guarantee for hostile TeX or a concurrently malicious filesystem. The archive includes all source and tests required for its stated checks.

\subsection{A realistic formalization order}

A useful first milestone is Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:27:thm:allchar} over odd prime fields, because
it strengthens the existing interface without requiring the most detailed
core classification. Its dependencies are: intrinsic moment vanishing;
Boolean inversion; codimension-one counts in $U$; the elementary rank lemma;
and a finite union bound. The ternary affine-orbit formulas can initially be
replaced by finite cardinalities of explicitly defined sets, then proved as
a separate arithmetic-combinatorial layer.

A second milestone is Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:27:thm:resolved}: formalize the minimal Boolean
degree split, the affine core form, the width-two classification, and the
rank-four intersection statement. The all-characteristic version should
use a finite-field abstraction rather than force the extension-field
argument through \gitpath{ZMod N} for composite $N$, which is generally not
a field.

The exact theorem has a distinct final dependency: a verified finite
certificate checker for rational row spaces and reduction modulo permitted
primes. It should not be imported as an unproved numeric fact. A modest
initial target is to formalize \eqref{gsr:fm:27:eq:d2asy}, whose proof is entirely
symbolic and independent of that certificate.

\section[{Further research questions\srctag{27}}]{Further research questions}\label{gsr:fz:27:sec:d13}\label{gsr:fz:27:sec:questions}
\srcnote{27}{Section 13}

The following questions are deliberately more specific than a request to
improve the global theorem. Some are finite classification problems suitable
for immediate computation; others require genuinely new structural input.
They are proposed questions of this article, not claims that each has been
previously advertised as an open problem in the literature.

\begin{problem}[The cross-section intersection statistic]
Find a closed form, recurrence, or efficient exact algorithm for
$b_{2,d,p}$ in \eqref{gsr:en:27:eq:b2}, particularly in the stable large-characteristic
regime. This would turn Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:27:cor:general2} into a numerical second-order
formula for every $d$, including the $d=8$ case of the selection step.
\end{problem}
A first computational target is $d=3$, where there are $51$ hyperplanes in
large characteristic. Enumerating their pair intersections is much smaller
than enumerating all arrangement coefficient arrays. The main issue is
recognizing coincident rank-two spans, not sampling arrangements.

\begin{problem}[A third-order structural theorem]
Classify the non-core coefficient directions whose zero sets on the regular
region contribute at order $q^{-3}$. Can the residual term
$(R_{k,d}-S_{k,d})q^{-3}$ be replaced by an explicit third-order family plus
an $O(q^{-4})$ remainder?
\end{problem}
The proof already distinguishes directions with a new cross-section
constraint from those forcing two separate rank-two base systems. The
latter are automatically fourth-order. Exploiting this distinction before
using the final union bound should reduce the next-stage inventory.

\begin{problem}[Higher Boolean degree and increasing codimension]
For a direction of minimal Boolean coefficient degree $r$, how many
independent base-coordinate systems can be extracted simultaneously? Is
there a sharp codimension bound in terms of $k-r$ and the ranks of the
vectors $c_A$ modulo $s$?
\end{problem}
The rank-four argument uses just two coordinates outside one minimal set.
A broader theorem would need to control overlaps among right sides and
cross-section constraints, rather than repeatedly invoke independence
without checking it.

\begin{problem}[Intermediate characteristics]
Determine the exact number of core directions for $5\le p\le2k+2$ and the
corresponding intersection pattern. The cases $p=2,3$ are answered by
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:27:thm:smallcore}, and the width argument already supplies the
large-characteristic core count for $p>2k+2$. What is the sharp threshold,
and which smaller characteristics have genuinely different core families?
\end{problem}
The remaining gap is to classify profiles below the proved no-wrap
threshold, not merely to replace $p>m$ by $p>2k+2$. For larger alphabets, however,
new affine symmetries and wider Boolean profiles must be accounted for.

\begin{problem}[Exact counts in fixed small characteristic]
Find exact formulas for $\Delta_{1,2}(p^a)$ in characteristics $2,3,5,7$.
The first two coefficients in characteristics $2,3$ are already determined
here; the large-characteristic polynomial fails at $q=5,7$.
\end{problem}
The same line-enumeration method can be performed directly over $\F_p$
and then lifted to extensions. In characteristic two, the subset-sum test
must be reformulated because the two integer signs have the same residue.

\begin{problem}[Beyond eight vertices]
For $(k,d)=(1,3)$ or $(2,2)$, is the degeneracy count eventually a polynomial
in $q$ outside finitely many characteristics? If not, what arithmetic
variation occurs in the lower-dimensional residual loci?
\end{problem}
Only the hyperplane part is automatically a polynomial count in fixed
characteristic. The full higher-degree moment varieties need not inherit
that property without further analysis, so polynomiality is a question,
not an inference from the eight-vertex example.

\begin{problem}[Minimal moment families]
Which subfamilies of squarefree moments retain the same first-order or
second-order degeneracy asymptotics? Can one preserve the cubic-remainder
bound while discarding a substantial fraction of the moment conditions?
\end{problem}
The paired moments used in Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:27:lem:rank} identify a necessary organizing
principle. A universal fixed subfamily would have to work for every possible
minimal Boolean coefficient set; the weaker definition mentioned after
Gowers's Lemma 15.4 is not automatically sufficient.

\begin{problem}[Efficient degeneracy testing]
Can the quotient-profile structure yield a deterministic test significantly
faster than enumerating $3^m$ relations or $2^m$ subset sums, while producing
a short certificate of either degeneracy or nondegeneracy?
\end{problem}
The exact low-dimensional example suggests preprocessing by cross-section
hyperplanes and then by the core family. A useful algorithm must also
handle the remaining coefficient directions without an exponential
worst-case scan disguised as preprocessing.

\begin{problem}[Relative distribution rather than ambient bounds]
For arrangement collections arising from a dense set or a product-property
hypothesis, can the hyperplane contribution be bounded by their actual
cross-section distribution instead of the ambient $L_d/q$ union bound?
\end{problem}
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:27:prop:relative} loses a factor equal to the reciprocal of collection
density. Avoiding it would require structural information about the
collection, not just its cardinality. A weighted version could be directly
relevant to selection arguments.

\begin{problem}[The single-pair regime]
Classify the dominant degeneracy loci for $d=1$ and arbitrary $k$. Does the
common final coordinate reduce the problem to a useful arrangement of
relations among two translated cubes?
\end{problem}
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:27:prop:d1} settles only $k=1$. The rank collapse is systematic and should
be treated as a separate geometry rather than forced into the $d\ge2$
proof.

\begin{problem}[A complete Section 15 threshold audit]
Substitute the cubic bound into the actual corrected Lemma 15.5 proof and
propagate the resulting threshold through Lemma 15.6 and the later inverse
steps. Which local improvement survives, and which other parameter becomes
dominant?
\end{problem}
This is the precise route from the present local result toward a global
quantitative consequence. It needs a complete ledger of dependencies and
is not settled by the numerical comparisons in Table~\ref{gsr:en:27:tab:thresholds}.

\begin{problem}[Formal proof and verified finite certificates]
Formalize the sharp first-order theorem, then the second-order theorem for
$d=2$, and finally the exact eight-vertex count with a small verified
rational-incidence checker. Which combinatorial and finite-dimensional
linear-algebra interfaces can be reused in other parts of Gowers's proof?
\end{problem}
The separation between symbolic general proofs and a finite exact
certificate makes this an incremental task: useful theorems can be checked
before the final enumeration infrastructure is complete.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Conclusion\srctag{27}}]{Conclusion}\label{gsr:fz:27:sec:d14}
\srcnote{27}{Section 14}

The large coefficient in Gowers's degeneracy bound is not the true leading
coefficient of the exceptional-set count. After coefficient arrays are
identified modulo the intrinsic relation, the bad set splits into three
quantitatively different parts: explicit hyperplanes, a classified family
of rank-two affine systems, and a residual set costing at least three
powers of the field size. The resulting estimates are sharp to first order
in all characteristics and to second order once the cross-section
hyperplane statistic is known. For two pairs of cross sections that
statistic is explicit, and in the smallest nontrivial case the entire
count is an exact polynomial.

These results answer concrete local questions about the proof: what
actually creates the leading degeneracy, how much of the ternary union
bound is avoidable, and which additional moment constraints supply the
extra savings. They also leave a clear boundary between established local
proofs, a finite certified specialization, and the further work needed for
new global consequences.

\section[{An explicit interface for further development\srctag{28}}]{An explicit interface for further development}\label{gsr:fz:28:sec:d9}
\srcnote{28}{Section 9}
\gsrsrcpart{Verification, integration, and further research}
\label{gsr:fz:28:sec:integration}

\subsection{What a downstream theorem can use}

The first part produces four distinct kinds of information. Keeping
their roles separate makes an integration into the existing argument
more transparent.

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{A prescribed spectrum.}
The character set is obtained from \(g(s)=|X_s|\), with the threshold
in equation~\eqref{gsr:fm:28:eq:lambda-main}. No label information is used to choose it.
A downstream step can therefore synchronize spectra using domain data.
\item \textbf{A large set of valid labels.}
The set \(Y\) has the explicit relative size
\(\alpha p(\alpha)/20\). It is selected after seeing \(\phi\).
Its projection to \(G\) need not have that relative size, since distinct
points in a fibre can have multiplicity.
\item \textbf{An exact map on a neighborhood.}
The identity equation~\eqref{gsr:fm:28:eq:model-main} holds for all eligible pairs in \(Y\).
The local map respects order-seven relations on its entire Bohr domain,
not only on the differences realized by pairs of \(Y\).
\item \textbf{Quantitative geometric control.}
Both the frequency count and the radius are explicit. The resulting
volume estimate is equation~\eqref{gsr:en:28:eq:volume-main}. For an existing application
that fixes the old frequency set, corollary~\ref{gsr:en:28:cor:old-spectrum} supplies a
compatible restricted map with the same retained fraction and radius.
\end{enumerate}

These properties should be passed as separate fields in a theorem
interface. A mere assertion that a large subset admits some additive
model would discard the original-spectrum information. Conversely,
requiring a global homomorphism \(G\to H\) would strengthen the conclusion
beyond what the proof establishes.

\subsection{A proposed formalization sequence}

The following names are suggestions for new modules, not existing or
compiled files in this deliverable. The current article is a mathematical
and reproducibility supplement; it contains no Lean code.

\begin{longtable}{@{}p{0.31\textwidth}p{0.63\textwidth}@{}}
\caption{Suggested proof interfaces and their dependency order.}
\label{gsr:fz:28:tab:interfaces}\\
\toprule
Suggested module & Mathematical content to formalize\\
\midrule
\endfirsthead
\toprule
Suggested module & Mathematical content to formalize\\
\midrule
\endhead
\texttt{WeightedAnchor} &
Finite energy bounds, local error transfer, and the single weighted
selection of an anchor in section~\ref{gsr:en:28:sec:anchor}.\\
\texttt{LogWindowSelection} &
The two center intervals, their clipped inclusion probabilities, the
weighted boundary estimate, and equation~\eqref{gsr:en:28:eq:selection-functional}.\\
\texttt{AnchoredModalRepair} &
Comparison between the \(b_d(w)\)-weighted error and uniform direction
error, existence of a unique modal increment, and the row restriction.\\
\texttt{StoppedPathRigidity} &
Subprobability transport with killing on exits and wrong labels; shared
endpoint coupling; the order-fifteen conclusion.\\
\texttt{OriginalSpectrumModel} &
Fourfold smoothing, radius selection before the anchor is chosen, the
final slice, and the order-seven local model.\\
\texttt{UFourDualCosine} &
The integer sign counts \(222,111,27,1\), including the separate
order-three quotient calculation.\\
\texttt{HigherUniformityGap} &
The concentration inequalities, rational threshold comparison,
two-harmonic certificate, and positive first-variation recurrence.\\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

The logarithmic-window argument has a finite alternative to an abstract
probability-space formalization. Each point contributes finitely many
center endpoints: its two outer endpoints and its two inner endpoints
in each coordinate. Together with the endpoints of \(I_q,I_R\), they
partition the center rectangle into finitely many open rectangles.
Membership in \(W\), membership in its boundary, and the selection
functional are constant on each such rectangle. Their weighted finite
average is the integral in equation~\eqref{gsr:en:28:eq:selection-functional}. A rectangle
with value at least the average yields the chosen window. Endpoints have
zero area and can be handled independently.

This reduction also suggests a constructive, though not optimized,
selection algorithm. Compute the anchor statistics, sort the center
endpoints, evaluate one interior center in each nonempty rectangle, and
choose a maximum of the functional. Real logarithm comparisons would
still need certified handling for an exact implementation; the present
program tests the finite mechanisms and does not implement a certified
end-to-end model finder.

\subsection{The existing formalization remains a separate object}

The inspected status ledger explicitly distinguishes established
theorems, conditional results, migrated statements, and outstanding
obligations \cite{repo28}. Several prerequisites in Sections~13, 16, and~18
remain open at the pinned snapshot. In particular, the source records
the need for additional bilinear extraction, a closing quantitative
comparison in the multilinear stage, and sufficiently strong phase
removal and iteration thresholds.

Some of those issues concern the statement being formalized rather than
an isolated numerical loss. Examples recorded by the repository include
integer representatives of box axes, shared partition requirements, and
a transcription's closing comparison whose proposed direction has
already been disproved. None can be discharged by inserting a better
Section~10 constant. A proposed integration should first state the exact
downstream predicate and then verify that the local model satisfies it.

\section[{Exact computations and the scope of verification\srctag{28}}]{Exact computations and the scope of verification}\label{gsr:fz:28:sec:d10}
\srcnote{28}{Section 10}
\label{gsr:fz:28:sec:verification}

\subsection{Finite checks of the selection and transport mechanisms}

The script \texttt{code/verify\_selection.py} uses integers and exact
rational arithmetic for its main checks. The fixed seed is
\(20261006\); the output records the examples and all summary counts.
Its coverage includes:

\begin{itemize}
\item \(648\) exact window-membership cases, including \(200\) exact
core inclusion probabilities and \(192\) clipped noncore cases;
\item \(10\,368\) boundary-probability comparisons, including
\(6\,272\) positive boundaries;
\item exact integration of the weighted selection functional over
\(1\,483\) constant-membership cells from four abstract examples;
\item \(14\,376\) shifted-interior checks in three cyclic integer
fibre profiles, using \(84\) proper windows, with \(168\) actual exits
before the boundary is removed;
\item all \(314\,721\) ordered pairs of the \(561\) probability
distributions on three symbols with denominator \(32\), testing the
modal-agreement implication;
\item \(228\) coupled two-path checks, including positive label error
and mass leaving the selected set;
\item stopped-prefix and longer common-endpoint checks that retain
unnormalized surviving mass, together with exact verification of
the order-fifteen inequality.
\end{itemize}

For example, the deliberately conservative long-path budget used in
the manuscript is the exact fraction
\[
 \left(30+210\cdot2^{-27}\right)
 \left(\frac1{31}+2^{-21}\right)
 =\frac{4222187282107575}{4362862139015168}<1.
\]
The script also checks the algebraic parameter identities against a
rational enclosure of \(\log2\) of width
\(1/884569308258492\).

A separately labelled numerical section uses actual natural logarithms
in three additional profiles, totaling \(1\,205\) cells. The maximum
discrepancy between the two evaluations of the expected functional is
about \(1.49\cdot10^{-11}\), within the stated \(2\cdot10^{-9}\) tolerance.
These examples need not satisfy the tiny final invariance parameter.
They check the window calculation, not the full approximate-homomorphism
theorem. Abstract examples and physical fibre examples are also identified
separately in the output.

\subsection{Exact norm certificates}

The script \texttt{code/verify\_u4.py} uses only integers and rational
numbers. It reproduces the following identities and comparisons:

\begin{enumerate}
\item the full-cube cosine count and all three pairs of dual coefficients;
\item the order-three count and its phase-dependent minimum;
\item every coefficient of the two-harmonic polynomial, by combining
two three-dimensional faces;
\item the five-point example, by exact derivative energies;
\item the seven-point example, both by modular coefficient counting and
by direct cube summation in a cubic number field;
\item the rational split at \(159/160\), including both alternatives
in the universal gap;
\item the exact value of the witness at \(b=-1/7\), and explicit
one-third-harmonic assignments in dimensions \(4\) through \(8\).
\end{enumerate}

The polynomial identity is reproducible by enumerating \(4^8=65\,536\)
choices on one three-face. Group choices by their moment vector and
number of third harmonics, then convolve the count polynomial for each
vector with the one for its negative. This computes
equation~\eqref{gsr:cc:28:uq:face-square-identity} directly.
The generic and small-order computations are intentionally separate:
replacing equality of integers by congruence changes the answer.

The rational comparison in the universal bound can be checked without
decimal approximations. One of its final steps is precisely
\[
 111\cdot3200\cdot5147^{16}
 >
 104329\cdot5550^{16}.
\]
The large integers in the witness are likewise exact. The plot in
figure~\ref{gsr:cc:28:fig:harmonics} has an explanatory role and is not used to infer
the sign of a derivative or locate a global optimum.

\subsection{Independent review and its limits}

The selection proof, the averaged repair, and the higher-order norm
argument were separately checked by other reasoning agents during the
preparation of this report. This review caught interface details,
including nonemptiness hypotheses and the need to describe stopped-path
marginals as subprobability laws. It also independently reproduced
dual-function counts for character orders \(3,5,7,9,11\).

Such review is useful evidence of internal consistency. It is not an
external referee report, a proof-assistant certificate, or an exhaustive
search for counterexamples. The general theorems stand on their written
proofs. The package records exact computations to make sensitive finite
steps easier to assess and repeat.

\section[{Further research questions and topics\srctag{28}}]{Further research questions and topics}\label{gsr:fz:28:sec:d11}
\srcnote{28}{Section 11}
\label{gsr:fz:28:sec:questions}

The most useful next projects are those that separate a genuine
structural obstruction from a loss specific to the present proof.
The following questions are proposed in that spirit.

\subsection{Selection and local structure}

\begin{problem}[Are both logarithmic losses necessary?]
Can the retained fraction in theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:28:thm:main} be improved to
\(\Omega(\alpha/\log(1/\alpha))\), or even \(\Omega(\alpha)\), while
preserving an original-domain spectrum with comparable size and radius?
\end{problem}

There are two independently selected scales here, for \(q\) and \(R\).
An obstruction for arbitrary weighted profiles would not automatically
be an obstruction for the profiles arising from an additive convolution.
A useful first step is to construct or rule out domains whose anchored
energy is spread nearly uniformly over both logarithmic coordinates.
Correlations forced by the convolution may reduce the number of scales
that need to be selected.

\begin{problem}[Can the defining frequency count be reduced?]
Can one replace \(O(\alpha^{-3})\) in the local-model theorem by a
smaller density power, or by a bound on an independent generating
set of frequencies with a controlled loss of radius?
\end{problem}

The present count is Parseval's bound \(\alpha/\lambda^2\).
The main technical requirement is uniform control of the fourfold
convolution under the resulting directions. A spectrum compression
argument must record how character combinations change the Bohr radius.
Counting independent generators and counting all coefficients above a
threshold are different tasks, with different downstream interfaces.

\begin{problem}[A general defect--mass--radius trade-off]
What is the best simultaneous dependence on an arbitrary order-eight
defect \(\varepsilon\), retained fraction, and local radius?
\end{problem}

The proof fixes \(\varepsilon=2^{-21}\) to keep one readable set of
constants. Its intermediate inequalities allow parameters such as the
modal threshold, window aspect ratios, direction-hole budget, and
Bohr-overlap budget to vary. Optimizing those parameters should produce
a family of explicit sufficient trade-offs. Whether such a family is
sharp would require examples with genuinely inconsistent labels,
not just adverse fibre sizes.

\begin{problem}[The exact output order]
With the same input defect, can the local model be made to preserve
order eight, or arbitrary fixed order, without materially weakening
its mass and radius?
\end{problem}

The current argument obtains order fifteen on \(D\), then order seven
on \(D-D\). The restriction to fifteen is the displayed path budget;
it is not an impossibility theorem. Better use of correlated label
errors, a stronger modal threshold, or a direct relation argument on
the difference set may improve the conclusion.

\begin{problem}[How much input order is needed?]
Which conclusions survive if the order-eight assumption is replaced
by order four or order two, while the defining spectrum must still
come from the original domain?
\end{problem}

The exponent eight enters through the fourfold difference domain, whose
fibres have a nonnegative fourth-power Fourier transform. Reducing the
input order calls for a different smoothing device or a direct argument
that retains the same original-spectrum control. An arbitrary structured
subset theorem would not resolve this more specific requirement.

\begin{problem}[A certified finite construction]
Can the logarithmic selection and modal repair be implemented with
certified arithmetic in a running time substantially better than
enumerating all relations and all center rectangles?
\end{problem}

The existence proof gives a finite search once the statistics are
available. Useful algorithmic improvements would include implicit
weighted rectangle maximization, sparse convolution when the group
permits it, and exact decisions at logarithmic endpoints. The output
should include a certificate of every required fibre and relation
identity, rather than only a candidate model.

\subsection{Higher-order norm geometry}

\begin{problem}[The sharp fourth-order constant]
Determine \(c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\), or substantially narrow the interval
in equation~\eqref{gsr:cc:28:uq:c4-bracket}.
\end{problem}

The interval is still wide. On the upper-bound side, the present proof
compresses all secondary Fourier coefficients into a single remainder
mass. Keeping separate information at \(\chi^3\) and \(\chi^5\), or using
the dual function of a two-harmonic trial function, could give stronger
constraints. On the constructive side, additional phase-aligned odd
harmonics may improve the explicit example.

\begin{problem}[Do bounded spectral profiles suffice?]
Is the fourth-order supremum attained by a function with a uniformly
bounded number of Fourier coefficients? Is a two-harmonic family
ever globally optimal?
\end{problem}

The first variation rules out one character pair, but gives no support
bound for a maximizer. One can first investigate the exact finite
polynomials for three harmonics and their stationarity conditions.
A proof that all further harmonics are unfavorable would be a separate
and more demanding step.

\begin{problem}[Small torsion versus large character order]
How does the optimal constant depend on the allowed character orders,
and does a fixed finite cyclic group attain the unrestricted supremum?
\end{problem}

The order-three branch of the upper bound and the seven-point polynomial
show why congruence aliases must be kept visible. One may define
suprema restricted to a fixed exponent, to cyclic groups, or to groups
with no characters of small order, then compare them. A limiting
Fourier profile on the circle could behave differently from every
fixed finite model.

\begin{problem}[The asymptotic higher-order constants]
What is the behavior of \(c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}\) as \(d\to\infty\)?
\end{problem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Answered by source~63}: $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}\to1/3$, with $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}-1/3\le10\cdot2^{-\lfloor d/8\rfloor}$ for $d\ge80$; the optimal rate is open (its Research question~\ref{gsr:fz:63:research:rate}).
\end{writenote}

Monotonicity makes this a nonincreasing sequence, and
equation~\eqref{gsr:cc:28:uq:universal-gap} supplies one strict bound for every \(d\ge4\).
The positive first-variation recurrence proves an obstruction to
cosine extremality at each order. It gives neither the rate of decay
of \(c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}\) nor even a positive lower bound uniform in
\(d\). Those are distinct extremal questions.

\begin{problem}[Stability near the true norm extremizers]
If a function has ratio close to \(c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}\), what
structural information can be forced about its Fourier spectrum?
\end{problem}

The dominant-pair parameter \(p\) already gives two complementary
inequalities, but closeness to our upper estimate should not be confused
with closeness to the unknown optimum. A stability theory should begin
with an actual extremizer or a proved limiting variational problem.
This is also distinct from the near-maximal absolute Gowers-norm
problem studied by Eisner and Tao \cite{eisnertao}.

\subsection{Returning to the full Gowers argument}

\begin{problem}[Propagate the local improvements through Section 13]
Can the larger spectrum threshold and retained fraction improve the
bilinear extraction parameters while maintaining a common grid and
the required relation domains?
\end{problem}

The first milestone should be a completely stated replacement for
one downstream proposition, with its grid, characteristic, and
domain hypotheses visible. The original-spectrum corollary offers a
conservative route when an existing interface fixes the old threshold.
A more ambitious route uses the smaller new spectrum throughout.

\begin{problem}[A quantitative repair of the multilinear closure]
Which altered induction invariant closes the outstanding Section~16
comparison with synchronized proper partitions?
\end{problem}

The repository records that one proposed closing inequality has the
wrong direction. Research should therefore seek a new argument or a
repaired target bound, rather than attempt to prove that inequality.
Candidate invariants should track the graph count, minimum width,
common refinement, and integer representatives together.

\begin{problem}[An end-to-end explicit density increment]
After the remaining phase-removal and partition steps are supplied,
what final Szemer\'edi estimate follows from the strengthened local
parameters?
\end{problem}

This requires a complete recurrence with all density losses, model
changes, rounding terms, and stopping thresholds. The local volume
exponent \(\alpha^{-3}\log(1/\alpha)\) is useful input, but its effect
on the final recurrence cannot be read off from that exponent alone.
A strong outcome would be an independently checkable numerical
recurrence accompanied by a proof of every transition.

\begin{problem}[Comparison with modern inverse-theorem interfaces]
Can the original-domain spectral information in the present theorem
be retained while substituting a modern quantitative inverse theorem
for later parts of the argument?
\end{problem}

The quasipolynomial inverse-theorem program \cite{lssinverse} is relevant
context, but its input and output data differ from this local
approximate-homomorphism interface. The research question is to identify
a precise bridge and evaluate its full parameter cost. A comparison
should use matching hypotheses and outputs before comparing asymptotic
labels.

\section[{How to use these results in the ProveIt project\srctag{29}}]{How to use these results in the ProveIt project}\label{gsr:fz:29:sec:d10}
\srcnote{29}{Section 10}
\label{gsr:fz:29:gmsr:integration}

\subsection{Three interfaces, with different domains}

The most useful integration is modular. The moment theorem supplies a
scalar norm conversion, the stability theorem supplies a structured
model together with its selector, and the restriction theorem supplies
a large collection of almost entirely respected configurations.
Each conclusion has an explicit normalization and domain.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering\small

For the cube application, retain the exact quartic coefficient
\(P_d\), then use the smaller factor \(B_d\) only when converting
\(\|f\|_{U^2}^4\) to \(\|f\|_{U^d}^4\). This preserves higher-degree
terms for whatever counting estimate is being used. In particular,
one cannot replace a full cube-expansion remainder by its quartic
term without an additional estimate.

For Proposition~6.1, the normalization can be checked directly.
An unnormalized derivative sum has \(N\) times the normalized Fourier
coefficient, and summing its squared magnitude over all \(h\) has
\(N^3\) times the normalized graph energy. If \(|f|\le1\) and the full
graph sum is at least \((1-\varepsilon)N^3\), then
\(T_\phi(f)\ge1-\varepsilon\) and \(m=\E|f|^2\le1\). Since
\(T_\phi(f)\le m^2\), the relative endpoint deficit satisfies
\[
 1-\frac{T_\phi(f)}{m^2}\le\varepsilon.
\]
Thus the joint theorem applies in its stated small-defect range.
The supplied graph must be defined on all shifts, or extended in a
way whose missing shifts are included in the selector defect.

The repository's formal statement named \codetwentynine{lemma_9_3} is a statement
for \(\Z/N\Z\) with arbitrary nonzero modulus \(N\). The present
restriction theorem is for \(\F_q\)-vector spaces. It gives a stronger
fixed-field local interface, including polynomial retention and a
much smaller threshold, but its field-dependent constant is not
uniform in \(N\). For \(V=\F_p\), allowing \(p\) to grow also makes
\(S_{p,s}\) grow. In that situation the displayed threshold may be
larger than every possible \(|B|\). The threshold-free conclusion is
still valid, but can be as weak as a singleton. This explains exactly
why the finite-field result alone cannot replace the all-moduli lemma
inside the full original proof.

The comparison above is accurate; no statement of this source is formalized.
\end{writenote}

\subsection{A proposed formalization order}

The proofs separate into components that can be formalized and checked
independently. A productive order is the following.

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Positive Fourier moments.}
Define inverse-pair orbits on the non-self-inverse part of the dual
group. Prove the balanced multinomial sub-sum inequality with
nonnegative coefficients, then derive the Gowers comparison by the
existing recursive norm identity. State the torsion profile separately
so that no implicit odd-order hypothesis enters the general theorem.

\item \textbf{Repair and integration.}
Formalize the majority-repair lemma for arbitrary finite abelian
groups and the inequality
\(\delta\ge3\theta-6\theta^2\).
Next prove the averaged symmetry identity and integrate a symmetric
bicharacter using cyclic coordinates. The latter step should use
circle-valued phases; division by two inside the coefficient ring
would lose the even-order cases.

\item \textbf{Projection and endpoint stability.}
Prove the two exact Hilbert-space identities for derivative distance
and mixed-array distance. The quantitative self, soft, and mixed
theorems then follow from norm inequalities, finite Fourier
orthogonality, and scalar estimates with rational constants.

\item \textbf{Rank and restriction.}
Define the full affine-relation space \(K_x\) and the error map on
that full space. Prove graph rank \(=r+e\), the weighted rank-counting
lemma, and the expected signed certificate. Keep the prescribed
relation space \(\mathcal R\) distinct from \(K_x\), since they coincide
only on generic tuples.
\end{enumerate}

The present package supplies mathematical statements, full proofs,
and executable finite diagnostics. It adds no Lean declarations and
does not alter the repository's proof-status ledger. In particular,
the experiments below do not certify a new formal theorem.

The direct norm checks multiply the cube-vertex values, providing a
calculation independent of the derivative/Jensen route used in the
proof. The torsion-profile checks include pure two-torsion, mixed
torsion, and odd-order groups. The exact sharpness examples use a
character of sufficiently large order; its order need not be prime.
The additional odd-cyclic examples have one zero value and equal
numbers of \(1\) and \(-1\), giving a second realization of the
dimension-independent \(1/3\) lower limit.

For restriction, the program enumerates the random maps and checks
the exact survival probability \(\lambda^{r+e}\) for individual
tuples. It also checks both weighted product bounds. The recorded
field computations use \(\F_2\) and \(\F_3\). The proof over arbitrary
prime-power fields uses only finite-dimensional linear algebra and
the cardinality of affine spans; no extrapolation from these two
fields is needed for that proof.

For quadratic rigidity, rational phase arithmetic verifies integration
even when the needed phases have order larger than the exponent of
the underlying group. The mixed diagnostics verify the signs in the
shift/modulation identity and the affine selector
\(\rho\psi(h)\). Floating-point agreement is only an implementation
check of the displayed identities. The output records its observed
maximum residual and the separate exact checks.

\subsection{Contents and build commands}

The source package contains the complete \LaTeX{} manuscript, its
compiled PDF, the vector figure used in the article, a figure
generation script, the four verification scripts, their JSON
outputs, a source-audit manifest, a short README, and a Makefile.
It contains no copies of third-party papers.

From the package directory, the ordinary build command is
\begin{verbatim}
latexmk -pdf -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error \
  gowers_moments_stability_restriction.tex
\end{verbatim}
The verification commands are
\begin{verbatim}
python code/verify_moments.py --output data/moment_verification.json
python code/verify_coefficients.py --output data/coefficients.json
python code/verify_rank_restriction.py --output data/rank_verification.json
python code/verify_joint_rigidity.py --output data/joint_verification.json
\end{verbatim}
The moment, coefficient, and restriction checks use Python's standard
library. The joint numerical diagnostics require NumPy. Regenerating
the scientific figure requires Matplotlib; the supplied figure is
already sufficient to compile the manuscript. The Makefile provides
\codetwentynine{all}, \codetwentynine{verify}, \codetwentynine{figures}, and \codetwentynine{clean} targets.

\section[{Further research questions\srctag{29}}]{Further research questions}\label{gsr:fz:29:sec:d12}
\srcnote{29}{Section 12}
\label{gsr:fz:29:gmsr:questions}

The questions below are unresolved by the present arguments and, where
specified, by the inspected project reports. They are proposed research
targets rather than assertions of exhaustive priority or universal
open-problem status.

\subsection{Sharp higher-norm comparisons}

\begin{samepage}
\begin{question}[Determine the fourth-dimensional constant]
\label{gsr:fz:29:gmsr:q-c4}
What is the exact value of \(c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\)? The present bracket is
\[
 (8/111)^{1/4}\le c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le(8/35)^{1/4}.
\]
Is a single Fourier inverse pair extremal, or can a more distributed
spectrum produce a larger ratio?
\end{question}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
The exact value at $d=4$ is still open after sources~60--69; the bracket is $0.5587725\le c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le(4/29)^{1/4}=0.6094183$ (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:normgap}), and source~63's limit theorem does not change it.
\end{writenote}
\end{samepage}

The autocorrelation moment theorem is sharp, but its equality model
has a substantial gap in the recursive norm estimate. A sharp proof
must control these two losses together. A useful first target is an
improved inequality for
\(\|\Delta_h f\|_{U^3}^8-|c_f(h)|^8\) averaged over \(h\), expressed in
Fourier quantities compatible with the pair-concentration estimate.
The direct four-cube expansion offers a second route, through positive
families of balanced vertex labelings.

\begin{samepage}
\begin{question}[The limit of the extremal constants]
Determine
\[
 c_\infty^{\mathrm{odd}}=\lim_{d\to\infty}c_d^{\mathrm{odd}},
 \qquad \frac13\le c_\infty^{\mathrm{odd}}\le\frac12.
\]
Can the upper bound \(1/2\) be approached by a family of real centered
functions as the dimension increases?
\end{question}
\end{samepage}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Answered by source~63}: $c_\infty^{\mathrm{odd}}=1/3$ (its Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:63:norm:main}); source~60 had excluded $1/2$ (Section~\ref{gsr:cc:sec:oddlimit}).
\end{writenote}

The proof of the upper bound takes a supremum over groups and functions
for each \(d\). One cannot interchange that supremum with a limit for
a fixed function without justification. A productive experiment would
compare long interval models, sparse Fourier models, and bounded
functions with increasingly complicated sign patterns. Any numerical
search should report the group, the dimension, and the normalization
separately.

\begin{samepage}
\begin{question}[An optimal profile at fixed self-inverse mass]
For a prescribed \(\tau\), determine the sharp bound for
\(\|f\|_{U^2}^4/\|f\|_{U^d}^4\) among real functions having self-inverse
Fourier fourth-mass fraction \(\tau\).
\end{question}
\end{samepage}

The polynomial \(K_m(\tau)\) solves the corresponding uniform
autocorrelation-moment problem. Passing to the Gowers norm can introduce
a further gap, just as it does at \(\tau=0\). It would be useful to know
whether a sharp norm profile depends only on \(\tau\), or whether finer
information about the orders and relations of the active characters
must also enter an effective bound.

\begin{samepage}
\begin{question}[Stability for actual norm near-minimizers]
Can a function whose ratio is close to the sharp higher-norm constant
be classified up to a controlled error in a natural norm?
\end{question}
\end{samepage}

Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:29:gmsr:moment-stability} gives \(U^2\) concentration only
when the autocorrelation moment is near its own lower bound. It is not
a stability theorem at the unknown sharp Gowers ratio. A successful
result would identify the relevant models first and then show that
near equality in all necessary steps forces proximity to those models.
For an \(L^2\) conclusion, additional amplitude or spectral-tail
information may be needed.

\subsection{Joint rigidity beyond the present endpoint}

\begin{samepage}
\begin{question}[Optimal constants and a larger defect range]
What are the best constants in the joint function/selector stability
theorem, and how far can its small-defect range be enlarged while
retaining a single global quadratic model?
\end{question}
\end{samepage}

The \(24\) and \(192\) constants are explicit common bounds, not
optimized values. The positive-amplitude example forces squared
function error of asymptotic order \(\varepsilon/2\); the soft-selector
example forces missing graph mass of order \(\varepsilon\).
Sharper homomorphism-testing theorems, such as
\cite{benor}, can refine the repair step. The remaining losses
come from the derivative projection and the passage from the repaired
graph to one Fourier atom. Studying the exact two-point and cyclic
examples may indicate which losses are intrinsic.

\begin{samepage}
\begin{question}[Remove the row constraint in a natural normalization]
Find a joint stability theorem for ambiguity or mixed short-time
Fourier transforms when the selector is not required to have row sums
at most one.
\end{question}
\end{samepage}

The class of exact models must then change with the normalization.
Subgroup-localized quadratic phases and isotropic phase-space supports
occur in the existing exact theory \cite{nicola}; critical-\(L^p\)
Gowers near-extremizers likewise allow coset localization
\cite{eisnertao}. A well-posed next theorem should first specify its
energy normalization and model class, then measure distance both in
function space and in phase-space support. Extending the current
statement verbatim would suppress genuine exact examples.

\begin{samepage}
\begin{question}[Higher-degree joint derivative selectors]
For \(d\ge4\), can near-maximal capture of \((d-1)\)-degree derivative
structure recover a degree-\(d\) phase together with the supplied family
of derivative models, with a linear squared-error bound?
\end{question}
\end{samepage}

The quadratic proof repairs a map into an abelian character group and
then integrates a symmetric bicharacter. Higher degree introduces
compatibility among several differences and, in small characteristic,
nonclassical circle-valued polynomial phases. A useful first case is a
finite vector space over a field of characteristic greater than the
degree, with all derivative models supplied on the full domain.
The challenge is simultaneous consistency of the models, beyond
pointwise applications of an inverse theorem.

\begin{samepage}
\begin{question}[Effective reconstruction and certification]
Can the joint theorem be converted into an algorithm that reconstructs
\(Q,\psi,\rho\) from approximate derivative data and outputs a
checkable error certificate?
\end{question}
\end{samepage}

The proof already identifies operations: choose large Fourier
coefficients, apply majority repair, test symmetry, integrate the
bicharacter, and find a Fourier atom after twisting. Exhaustively
performing those operations is finite but can be expensive. The
algorithmic questions concern sample complexity, treatment of noisy
coefficients, and time bounds in the group size or its presentation.
For a small fixed group, an exact reconstruction tool would also be a
useful bridge to formal verification.

\subsection{Sharper and broader restriction}

\begin{samepage}
\begin{question}[Optimize the complete rank profile]
Given the counts \(G_{r,e}\) and \(U_{r,e}\), optimize the exact
certificate
\[
 \sum_{r,e}(\eta G_{r,e}-U_{r,e})\lambda^{r+e}
\]
over the admissible values \(\lambda=q^{-t}\). What information less
expensive than the full profile still gives a substantial improvement
over the worst-case coefficient?
\end{question}
\end{samepage}

The present theorem replaces all respected graph ranks by \(s\) and
all unrespected error ranks by one. Data with few low-rank bad tuples
or many low-rank good tuples can behave much better. The signed
polynomial is already an exact certificate, so concrete improvements
can be proved without changing the random selector. The last coordinate
of that selector already supplies a uniform affine offset. Moreover,
a mixture of restriction depths gives a convex combination of the
corresponding signed certificates, so it cannot improve their maximum
for a fixed full profile. A remaining question is whether a different
selection family can avoid the loss associated with discrete depths.

\begin{samepage}
\begin{question}[Quantify degeneracy more geometrically]
Can the product \(z\prod_{i=0}^{s-2}(z+q^i)\) be replaced by a bound in
terms of actual affine-span intersection statistics of \(B\), or by a
sharper universal polynomial?
\end{question}
\end{samepage}

At each step the proof permits up to \(q^{j-2}\) points in the current
affine span, independently of earlier choices. This is sufficient for
the linear threshold but often very wasteful. Cap sets, subspace-evasive
sets, and sets with small intersections with low-dimensional flats
should give stronger estimates. Any improvement for the generic
higher-error-rank theorem must still control low-domain-rank
unrespected tuples; a generic rank gap alone says nothing about them.

\begin{samepage}
\begin{question}[An efficient deterministic restriction]
Can one find a map \(A\) meeting the expected signed certificate in
time polynomial in a useful input representation?
\end{question}
\end{samepage}

Exhaustive search over all linear maps proves effective existence.
Conditional expectations may derandomize the proof, but computing the
conditional potential from the full tuple list can already cost
\(|B|^\ell\). A meaningful algorithm should exploit the relation
matrix, Fourier structure, or a compressed rank profile. It should
also distinguish the task of exhibiting \(B'\) from the task of
certifying its proportion of respected relations.

\begin{samepage}
\begin{question}[A useful growing-modulus analogue]
Can actual-rank or multiplicity-sensitive survival improve the
prime-cyclic restriction theorem with constants that remain useful
as the prime grows, and eventually handle arbitrary cyclic moduli?
\end{question}
\end{samepage}

This is the principal unresolved obstacle to using the fixed-field
improvement as a replacement for the original Lemma~9.3.
The prior manuscript \cite{repo29restriction} also contains a
Fej\'er-filter method in cyclic groups. A possible direction is to
track the survival of repeated or low-rank configurations inside that
filter, while accounting for approximate relations and torsion.
The finite-field product proof by itself gives no such uniformity.

\subsection{From local estimates to a global bound}

\begin{samepage}
\begin{question}[A complete quantitative substitution]
Which of the local improvements in the accumulated project reports
survive a full quantitative inverse and density-increment argument,
and what explicit progression-free-set bound follows?
\end{question}
\end{samepage}

This question requires a dependency calculation, not just a list of
smaller constants. Every invocation must preserve its domain,
normalization, density loss, length threshold, and error budget.
The fixed-field and cyclic branches should be analyzed separately.
A useful deliverable would be an executable symbolic recurrence,
verified against the corrected statement of each invoked lemma, and
then compared with an established global result such as
\cite{lssbounds}. The present article supplies several improved
local inputs for that project.

Among these directions, three immediate targets have especially clear
interfaces: improving the explicit \(c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\) bracket,
optimizing the complete finite-field rank certificate on structured
sets, and formalizing the joint stability theorem over arbitrary finite
abelian groups. Each can be pursued independently and tested against a
fully specified theorem above.

\subsection{Formalization route, not claimed formalization}
The shortest plausible implementation begins with finite sets in
$\Z/N\Z$, not with a general Haar-measure library. Useful stages are:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Prove the two exit-cardinality identities and the abstract disjoint
translation lemma. It is best to index the $2m$ tubes by a sign and a
positive integer, so that same-sign and opposite-sign collisions are
separate proof cases.
\item Establish a real or integer centered-residue lift lemma through
$2m$ steps. This is the only non-return ingredient and is where the
$\rho\le1/4$ hypothesis is used.
\item Prove the three-cell partition with unambiguous endpoint assignments.
Translate each nonempty cell to inject it into the original Bohr set.
Do not count only the image of the character map without accounting for
its fibres.
\item Combine the cardinal inequalities before introducing real division.
Keep the exact intrinsic form and obtain the $3^r$ form as a corollary.
\item Prove the general tree budget and the induced difference identity;
then translate the tuple formulation of Freiman relations into the
repository's exact API.
\item Prove the compatibility theorem with the two exceptional direction
sets measured against $|A|$. Keep positivity of the common fibre as an
explicit premise.
\end{enumerate}
No Lean file has been compiled for the new results in this package. The
presence of a proposition-valued declaration in the existing catalogue
is not a substitute for a proof. The proposed theorem names and dependency
order in \path{FORMALIZATION.md} are implementation suggestions, not a
report of successful kernel checking.

\subsection{Exact finite checks}
The delivered \path{code/verify.py} uses only the Python standard library,
integers, and rational fractions. It uses explicit exceptions rather than
\texttt{assert}, so optimization mode does not disable validation.
The run recorded in \path{results/verification.json} completed the following
checks:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}p{0.34\textwidth}X@{}}
\toprule
Suite & Recorded coverage\\
\midrule
Cyclic Bohr sets & $13\,404$ parameterized sets; $135\,182$ admissible
shift/length instances, of which $11\,642$ have positive exit count.\\
Unequal-width product groups & $500$ seeded parameterized sets;
$4\,588$ admissible instances, including $676$ with positive exit count.\\
Four-vertex budgets & $269\,759$ finite intersection inequalities,
including repeated positions and negative lower bounds.\\
Sharpness & Exact interval equality and exact $3^r$ packing examples.\\
Scalar and local-map tests & $1\,140$ rational parameter checks; a nonconstant
map from $73$ points into $\Z$, with induced orders two and three on
a nine-point neighborhood.\\
Spiked sets & Exhaustive product-group membership for $s=1,2,3$;
explicit cyclic parameter certificates for $s=1,\ldots,6$.\\
Cyclic brute force & Direct enumeration of the rank-three CRT example
with $N=90\,799$, $|B|=19$, and defect $3$.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

The cyclic suite enumerates moduli $2$ through $32$, with character
representatives from $0$ through $\lfloor N/2\rfloor$, six rational
widths, and $m\in\{1,2,3,4,8\}$. It includes lists of size at most two
throughout and lists of size three through modulus $17$. Opposite
frequencies give the same single-coordinate constraints, which is why
these representatives suffice for the stated suite. The product suite
is seeded, not exhaustive. Every qualifying tube is explicitly checked
for non-return, pairwise disjointness, and containment in the
\emph{direction-dependent} enlarged shell.

The large CRT certificates check all elementary parameter inequalities,
pairwise gcd conditions, distinct explicit frequencies, and exact step
values. They do not enumerate their enormous ambient groups; the general
membership and cardinality formulas for those groups are established by
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:30:thm:cyclic-spikes}. The finite checks are diagnostics and
reproducibility evidence, not proof-assistant certificates or an independent
review of the general argument.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Research questions and next integration targets\srctag{30}}]{Research questions and next integration targets}\label{gsr:fz:30:sec:d11}
\srcnote{30}{Section 11}
\label{gsr:fz:30:sec:questions}

The first three questions concern the central quantitative limitation.
The later ones concern effective use and formal integration. None is
assumed in any proof above.

\begin{question}[Optimal exponential base]
Determine the asymptotic growth of $\mathcal L_r$. Is its exponential rate
$\sqrt3$, $3$, or another value? Even improving either side of
\eqref{gsr:en:30:eq:extremal-bracket} by an exponential factor would clarify which
part of the geometry the box-packing argument loses.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Prime cyclic groups]
What is the analogue of $\mathcal L_r$ when the ambient group is restricted
to $\Z/p\Z$ with $p$ prime? Can one realize an exponential boundary
obstruction without the transverse Chinese-remainder factors, or does
prime order permit a substantially better universal bound?
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Joint sharpness of escape and packing]
Classify, even approximately, the Bohr sets for which
$2m b_B(d)$ is close to $|B(3\boldsymbol\rho/2)|-|B|$ and the latter
is close to $(3^r-1)|B|$ simultaneously. The separate sharpness examples
show why optimizing the two inequalities independently is insufficient.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Intrinsic growth from spectral structure]
The spectra produced in Section 10 are not arbitrary lists of characters.
Can their additive structure, or the structure of the fibre-count function
that generates them, force $D_B$ far below $3^r$ at the original radius?
A positive result could combine the intrinsic theorem with information
already present upstream, rather than use worst-case rank alone.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Adaptive anisotropic widths]
When some characters constrain the proof much more tightly than others,
can one choose unequal widths before the partial map is constructed so as
to optimize the final extension neighborhood? A correct optimization must
preserve every earlier invariance premise; choosing widths after the map
has been constructed can change the problem.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Optimal dense-domain extension budget]
For exact Freiman maps, how far can the sufficient condition
$(2k-1)\kappa+2k\eta<1$ be improved? Can overlaps among the exceptional
sets be exploited uniformly, or are there examples where the tree budget
is close to optimal? The question should separate failure of set inclusion
$C\subseteq A-A$ from failure of the higher-order relations.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Compatibility thresholds]
Is the $5/14$ threshold in Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:30:cor:five-fourteen} optimal under
only the explicitly stated pair-overlap and finite-fibre hypotheses?
Can target-fibre information improve the condition $\theta<1/2$ when
the two good-value sets are not arbitrary subsets of the common fibre?
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Propagation through Theorem 10.13]
Re-run the complete corrected proof with a separate radius parameter
provided by Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:30:cor:margin}. Determine an explicit replacement
for the final local-model radius, while retaining the corrected integer
spectrum bound, density conclusion, and nonempty-fibre conditions. This is
a concrete next theorem, but it has not been established by a symbolic
substitution in this manuscript.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Global relevance]
After such propagation, which losses dominate the final quantitative
Szemer\'edi theorem? Does removing this power-of-radius loss change only
constants, an iterated exponent, or a genuine asymptotic class in a fully
specified implementation of the argument? This requires an end-to-end
parameter ledger, not just a local comparison table.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Beyond rectangular character constraints]
For which other finite sets does a small translation admit the same
$2m$ non-return property? Can convex constraints on several character
coordinates be handled using directional widths, with a covering number
replacing $3^r$? The abstract escape lemma already applies once the
non-return and enclosure properties are proved.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Efficient exact growth certificates]
Can one certify an upper bound for $D_B$ substantially below $3^r$ without
enumerating all of $G$? Lattice descriptions or compressed descriptions
of the character-map fibres may provide smaller exact certificates for
large cyclic moduli.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Kernel-checked integration]
Implement the intrinsic escape theorem, packing theorem, and
margin-preserving extension in the repository's toolchain, followed by an
axiom audit. The most important proof obligations are endpoint-safe
non-return and opposite-sign tube disjointness; the final scalar
inequalities are comparatively small.
\end{question}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Conclusion\srctag{30}}]{Conclusion}\label{gsr:fz:30:sec:d12}
\srcnote{30}{Section 12}
The decisive change is to count translated exits inside a controlled
Bohr enlargement, rather than count a boundary in the ambient group and
then divide by a small density. The resulting inequality retains the
original set and replaces a power-of-width loss by an exponential-rank
loss. It gives a substantially larger neighborhood for the dense-domain
Freiman step, supports higher-order extension and exact compatibility
budgets, and has a matching qualitative obstruction: exponential rank
cannot in general be replaced by polynomial rank without further
hypotheses. The exact exponential rate and the prime-order case remain
specific, well-defined research targets.

\subsection{Suggested order of implementation}

\begin{enumerate}
\item Formalize the weighted graph extraction and the actual vertical
defect set. These mostly use finite sums, finite sets, and the
Pl\"unnecke--Ruzsa interface already needed by the repository.
\item Prove \eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:Hfourth}, the unequal-pair estimate for $C_0$,
and the quartic deficit identity over an abstract finite abelian
label group. Keep every subtraction in the reals or in a
division-free nonnegative formulation.
\item Establish the Weyl mass and self-duality identities, followed by
the $3/2$ small-difference lemma and the noncommuting subgroup gap.
\item Prove the trace formula for character projectors and identify
their one-dimensional ranges with quadratic coset phases.
\item Assemble the sharp spectral theorem; prove monotonicity and the
two quadratic inversions separately. Then derive the full and
partial graph corollaries.
\item Formalize the weight-defect decomposition and the two finite
counterexample families. Complexity-dependent $L^1$ estimates and
measurement transfer can be added afterward.
\end{enumerate}

This is an integration plan, not delivered Lean code. We did not run
the repository's Lean build and do not alter its proof-status ledger.

verification are distinct requirements.

\section[{Further research questions\srctag{31}}]{Further research questions}\label{gsr:fz:31:sec:d11}
\srcnote{31}{Section 11}
\label{gsr:fz:31:sec:questions}

\begin{problem}[The full critical-norm profile]
Determine the optimal universal function relating $\kappa(f)$ and
$F(f)$ beyond $1-\kappa<1/120$. Does the two-state curve remain
extremal on a larger interval, and at which first value do other
configurations take over? The cutoff here is sufficient, not a
candidate optimal transition.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Odd-order sharpness]
Find the optimal second and higher coefficients in the odd-order
infidelity profile. Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:31:thm:envelope} excludes the universal
order-two equality mechanism, but its odd-order envelope is not
claimed sharp. A two-state configuration of odd-order label has
a different outside fourth moment, suggesting a more refined
analysis of phase interference.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Stability of the extremizers of the envelope]
Turn \eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:envelope-deficit} into a quantitative classification
of all near-equality states by their distance to an embedded
two-state configuration. The tail concentration is explicit;
the remaining task is a sharp phase-alignment estimate for the
outside Weyl coefficients.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[The optimal joint graph budget]
The separate graph and phase bounds in \eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:graph-sharp} are
sharp. Determine the exact feasible region of
$(\varepsilon,t,z,\beta)$. In particular, replace the valid but
not certified-sharp coefficient $1-8t(1-t)$ in
\eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:joint-graph} by its optimal counterpart, or identify
the additional statistic needed for such a formula.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[The actual defect-set geometry]
In Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:31:thm:freiman}, optimize the weight retention using
the set $V_k$ itself rather than only $|V_k|$. Intervals are a
convenient way to avoid nonzero defects, but other target sets
may retain substantially more weight for structured $V_k$.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Torsion-sensitive target restriction]
Extend the finite weighted restriction to composite cyclic and
general finite abelian targets. The prime proof uses invertibility
of the integers $1,\ldots,kL$. A general result should charge the
sizes of their kernels and the distribution of the defect set
across those kernels, rather than silently importing the prime case.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Better weighted extraction exponents]
Use the square-root mass theorem in Appendix~\ref{gsr:en:31:app:thickening},
or a sharper weighted BSG theorem, to improve the powers in
\eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:weightedgraph} while preserving the originally specified
weight. Separate the loss from structural extraction, the choice
of one point per fiber, and exact Freiman restriction.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Replacing the worst fiber size]
Can $K^{2k+2}$ be replaced by a profile involving the masses and
largest atoms of individual fibers? The present proof already
admits the actual mass of the maximum-weight graph as an input.
A stronger theorem should retain this distribution through the
small-doubling step as well.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Compatible restrictions across slices]
Construct the exact Freiman restrictions for different derivative
slices compatibly. This is the missing link between the local
correlation-preserving theorem and Gowers' later multilinear
integration. A favorable exponent for each slice alone does not
establish a favorable global exponent.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Weights under weaker complexity assumptions]
Replace finite Fourier support and a finite number of occupied
cosets in \eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:weightL1} by effective entropy or tail norms.
The two counterexamples show that some such hypothesis is
necessary. A useful formulation should recover $L^1$ control
without demanding literal sparse support.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[The optimal coupled weight defect]
Determine the sharp dependence of $\En(w)-a^4$ on the norm deficit
$\delta$, the energy-saturation error $\eta$, and the mean $a$.
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:31:prop:coset-transfer} gives an exact linear transfer
identity. The subsequent fourth-power estimate in
\eqref{gsr:en:31:eq:coupled-transfer} need not be jointly optimal; retain
the mean and the eigenbasis collision mass to sharpen it.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Mixed functions and higher norms]
Classify the equality and near-equality pairs in the mixed
derivative inequality for two different input functions.
For higher Gowers norms, identify an analogue of the spectral
subgroup construction and the finite tail-energy envelope.
Neither extension follows merely by changing the exponent eight.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[A checked quantitative application]
Choose one fixed progression length, integrate the new local
interfaces into a complete dependency ledger, and verify every
resulting threshold. Only after that calculation would it be
justified to claim an improved bound produced by this proof route.
Comparison with modern bounds would then be a further step.
\end{problem}
