\section[{The pinned source and the literature\srctag{32}}]{The pinned source and the literature}\label{gsr:fz:32:sec:d6}\label{gsr:fz:32:sec:source}
\srcnote{32}{Section 6}

\subsection{The full degree two source implication}

The precise repository target is \texttt{corollary\_5\_8} in \texttt{Section05.lean}, lines 242--259, at commit
\begin{center}
\texttt{c94998a5db18ba63c815a3bf6c3877a0fde91930}.
\end{center}
Direct links are in the references and \texttt{SOURCES.md}. This is a comparison with the predicate at that pin, not a claim that its general-degree proof has been formalized or that a repository build was rerun.

The source constant is
\[
 K=(k!)^2 2^{(k+1)^2},\qquad K\big|_{k=2}=4\cdot512=2048.
\]
Its degree-two conclusion is a proper progression with length at least $S^{1/2048}/8$ and density at least $\delta+\alpha/16$. The source uses this corrected gain rather than the original paper's displayed $\alpha/8$.

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 28--33]
\emph{Checked at HEAD \texttt{5d4718772}.} \file{Section05.lean} and \file{Definitions.lean} have the blobs read at the pin (\texttt{882b17a}, \texttt{97113b7}); \file{corollary_5_8} still starts at line~242 and is open in the ledger, which records 105 exact companions and 15 open statements. The translations below are accurate: \file{ModAP.IsProper} (\file{Definitions.lean}, line~93) is injectivity of the parameterization. The SHA-256 values in \file{SOURCES.md} (shipped as \file{32-quadratic-increments-SOURCES.md}) are of the files with one line feed appended, the retrieval convention of source~26's record; source~41's placement records the same finding.
\end{writenote}

The hypotheses translate without an extra restriction:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The source's \texttt{PolynomialOn 2 Finset.univ} means there exist three coefficients with $\phi(x)=c_0+c_1x+c_2x^2$ for every $x$. This is exactly the coefficient-polynomial convention used here, including composite moduli.
\item The definition \texttt{ModAP.IsProper} is equality of carrier cardinality and parameter length. Since the carrier is the image of a finite parameter set of that size, this is exactly injectivity. Despite an informal source comment mentioning wrapping, the definition does not require nonwrapping standard representatives.
\item Empty parents are syntactically permitted by the source, but cannot occur with its other premises. If one parent is empty, two-comparability forces every parent to be empty. Then the cover forces $A$ to be empty, and all balanced correlations vanish, contradicting $\alpha N>0$.
\item The source assumes $N\ne0$. Its $N=1$ case has identically zero balanced function for either possible subset, so positive correlation is impossible. For $N\ge2$, the identity $|A|=\delta N$ identifies its $\delta$ with the density here. Its balanced function and exponential are the same $\one_A-\delta$ and $e_N$ used above.
\item Disjointness, coverage, two-comparability, and the summed correlation agree literally. The source does not require the concluding progression to lie in the cover.
\end{enumerate}

The prefactors $17$ and $8$ require an explicit comparison; comparing exponents alone is insufficient. In fact, for every $S\ge1$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:32:eq:compare}
 \max\left\{1,\frac{S^{1/39}}{17}\right\}
 \ge\frac{S^{1/64}}8\ge\frac{S^{1/2048}}8.
\end{equation}
If $S^{1/64}/8\le1$, the first inequality follows from the singleton bound. Otherwise $S>8^{64}$ and
\[
 S^{1/39-1/64}>8^{25/39}>\sqrt8>17/8.
\]
Here $25/39>1/2$, and $8>(17/8)^2$ is the integer inequality $512>289$. Dividing gives $S^{1/39}/17>S^{1/64}/8$. The second inequality in \eqref{gsr:fz:32:eq:compare} uses $S\ge1$. The gain $\alpha/3$ is greater than $\alpha/16$. Thus the very same progression from Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:32:thm:main} satisfies the complete pinned degree-two conclusion at every permitted scale.

\subsection{Primary literature comparison}

Gowers~\cite{gowers}, Section 5, develops Weyl-type recurrence and polynomial-to-affine localization; Lemmas 5.3--5.5 and Corollaries 5.6--5.8 are the relevant chain. Corollary 5.8 on printed page 493 concerns the same disjoint comparable-cover mechanism. The present proof uses its own explicit quadratic recurrence and a second-moment alternative, rather than importing a large-threshold polynomial localization statement without verifying its scale premise. The comparison above is specifically to the edited repository predicate \cite{repo32}, whose gain is $\alpha/16$.

Green and Tao~\cite{greentaortwo}, Appendix A, Proposition A.2, give simultaneous quadratic recurrence for real $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d$: there is $1\le n\le X$ with $\norm{n^2\alpha_j}\ll dX^{-c/d^2}$. The following discussion records Schmidt's stronger asymptotic exponent $-1/(d^2+d)+\epsilon$ and explains why dependence of implicit constants on dimension matters. Their Section 6 treats linearization. These results confirm the classical nature of recurrence followed by localization. Our weaker single-coefficient estimate has a fully displayed uniform constant and is proved here to keep the numerical interface self-contained.

Maynard~\cite{maynard}, Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2, treats systems of real polynomials with zero constant term. For $m$ polynomials of degree at most $d$, the corollary gives simultaneous fractional parts $\ll_{d,m}X^{-c_d/m}$ for some $1\le n<X$, uniformly in their coefficients. This is a substantially more general recurrence theorem; the displayed corollary leaves its constants implicit. We neither claim that $R^5$ is the best quadratic recurrence rate nor infer any optimality for $1/39$ from it.

The specific claim established here is the explicit, all-moduli, threshold-free local-cover theorem and its pinned source implication. Priority for that exact formulation has not been established. No argument here turns this local improvement into a better final Ramsey or Szemer\'edi estimate, handles all polynomial degrees, or supplies an integer-rectification theorem.

\section[{Reproducibility and further questions\srctag{32}}]{Reproducibility and further questions}\label{gsr:fz:32:sec:d7}\label{gsr:fz:32:sec:repro}
\srcnote{32}{Section 7}

\subsection{What the companion establishes}

The accompanying Python program uses integer and rational arithmetic for bounded structural checks. It tests progression injectivity, subgroup-coset pair counts and variance, removal of nonproper directions, cover-mass identities and positive-cell extraction, residue-chain chunking, quadratic phase lifts, reduced curvature, and the reduced-midpoint regression. It also checks the integer identities behind the constants and root-free ceiling choices. Small rational recurrence examples exercise the recurrence interface; they are not a proof about every real coefficient.

The full mathematical proof is in Sections~\ref{gsr:dt:32:sec:recurrence}--\ref{gsr:dt:32:sec:assembly}. The companion does not enumerate a partition of size $2^{116}L^{38}$, even at $L=2$, and it does not approximate complex exponentials and call the result a certificate. Its finite coverage, argument caps, and limitations are reported in its JSON output and documented in \texttt{README.md}. Input-validation failures remain runtime errors under optimized Python. Tests and diagnostics run under both normal Python and \texttt{-O}; deterministic diagnostic output must agree.

The offline builder verifies an exact source inventory and, for a packaged distribution, the manifest hashes. It rebuilds the PDF using an installed trusted TeX toolchain with shell escape disabled and writes a deterministic ZIP with fixed member order and metadata. It rejects unexpected source members, source aliases, and unsafe output locations, and bounds subprocess time and output. These are reproducibility and regression controls for trusted source, not a sandbox for hostile TeX or Python and not a guarantee against an actively malicious concurrent filesystem owner. Hashes establish byte agreement with the manifest, not authorship or mathematical truth.

The ZIP contains only this article, its PDF, the original companion and tests, the builder, public documentation, and its manifest. It contains no third-party paper or private review material. The exact commands and platform requirements are in \texttt{README.md}; the archive digest is supplied outside the archive to avoid a circular hash.

\subsection{Questions suggested by the proof}

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Better recurrence with explicit small-scale constants.} If an unconditional estimate $p\le C R^\kappa$ is available, the present choices $H\asymp L^3$ and $R\asymp L^7$ make the partition cost proportional to $L^{7\kappa+3}$. The large-correlation cover step loses one further factor of $L$, suggesting length exponent $1/(7\kappa+4)$ with appropriately checked constants. This is parameter bookkeeping for a future argument; Remark~\ref{gsr:dt:32:rem:conditional} does not supply $\kappa=4$.
\item \textbf{A more economical quadratic partition.} The two-stage construction first suppresses curvature and then suppresses an affine slope. Can these stages be combined to improve the power $38$, while retaining every point and allowing arbitrary real coefficients? Any proposed replacement must preserve the small-scale rounding and properness checks.
\item \textbf{Parent-contained small-correlation increments.} The variance alternative uses the whole group. Requiring $Q\subseteq U$ or $Q\subseteq P_i$ would be an additional conclusion and needs a separate argument or an obstruction; it is not implicit in the present theorem.
\item \textbf{The next polynomial degree.} The source bridge is complete for degree two. Extending the threshold-free strategy to degree three would require an explicit cubic recurrence/localization budget and a fresh check that the large-correlation branch pays for it. Nothing in the degree-two proof establishes that extension.
\end{enumerate}

The questions below are proposed by the present analysis. Unless an
external source is specifically cited, they are not being represented as
previously published open problems. Each is separated from the proved
claims above.

\begin{problem}[The optimal common-prime quadratic coefficient]\label{gsr:fz:33:ras:q:odd}
For fixed even $s$, determine the smallest coefficient $c_s^{\mathrm{prime}}$
for which a uniform small-error estimate of the form
\[
 \dd\le\eps_s/s+c_s^{\mathrm{prime}}\eps_s^2+O_s(\eps_s^3)
\]
holds on $\F_p^2\to\F_p$ for all sufficiently large odd primes.
Theorems~\ref{gsr:fm:33:ras:thm:main} and \ref{gsr:en:33:ras:thm:prime-family} give the rigorous
bounds
\[
 \frac{3s-2}{4s^2}\le c_s^{\mathrm{prime}}
             \le\frac{2(s-1)}{s^2}
\]
whenever the optimal coefficient is formulated as an infimum of such
uniform expansions. For $s=16$ these bounds are $23/512$ and $15/128$.
Can cancellation between two erroneous derivatives close the gap?
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[The next coefficient for higher arrangements]
For $s\ge6$, determine the optimal cubic coefficient after the two sharp
all-group coefficients have been fixed. The full bound $F_s$, the simpler
quadratic inverse, and the binary extremal family give different
third-order information. A useful first target is $s=6$, where one can
classify low-weight error patterns while retaining the missing sixth
independence degree exactly.
\end{problem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Answered by source~60}: the cubic coefficient is $8(s-1)(2s-1)/(3s^3)$ for $s\ge6$, and every further coefficient is optimal in succession (its Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:60:arr:coefficients}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{problem}[Equality and near-equality in the sharp cubic]
Classify the maps with $0<\dd<1/4$ and
$\eps_4=4\dd-24\dd^2+32\dd^3$. The proof forces simultaneous equality
in the modal collision estimate, the increment cap, the missing-moment
bound, and the one-error implication. Do these conditions characterize
binary row-defect constructions, perhaps after quotients, products, and
addition of an exact model? A quantitative near-equality theorem would
identify the actual obstruction to a better repair modulus.
\end{problem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{The equality part is answered by source~60} for every even $s\ge4$: equality at $0<\delta<1/4$ holds exactly for $a\one_C(x)\lambda(y)$ plus an exact model, $C$ a coset of index $n\ge3$, at $\delta=1/(2n)$ (its Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:60:arr:equality}); near-equality is its Research question~\ref{gsr:fz:60:q:near-equality}.
\end{writenote}

\begin{problem}[The activation threshold and the global distance spectrum]
How far can the small-branch theorem extend? The bound
$1/(240(s-1))$ was chosen to make the elementary bootstrap automatic.
A sharper noisy-affine lemma, or a direct spectral gap argument, may
increase this threshold substantially. Separately determine the feasible
pairs $(\dd,\eps_4)$ away from zero. The vanishing of $F_4$ at $1/4$
shows why extrapolating its inverse without a structural argument is
not a solution to the global problem.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[A sharp theorem from row profiles]
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:33:ras:thm:profile-local} retains $\overline t/\dd$, while the
uniform-row cap retains only $\max_x\dd_x$. What is the optimal defect
bound given the complete row distributions $p_x$, or just the first
few moments of $\dd_x$? Such a result could distinguish diffuse errors
from concentrated row defects before passing to a worst-case constant.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Sparse domains with quantitative mixing]
Replace near-full density by explicit assumptions that conditioned
arrangement queries have approximately uniform marginals and that
increment cocycles have enough common witnesses. Can one prove
$\dd_A\le C\eta$ with polynomial dependence on these mixing parameters,
instead of paying the invalid-arrangement error $2s\tau$? The precise
challenge is to replace the three full-product steps: auxiliary-label
independence, mode comparison at every increment, and rowwise integration.
This is the most direct route toward the sparse setting of Gowers's
Sections 12--13.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Nonzero increments and nonrepeated vertices]
Determine exact conversion bounds when the test excludes $h=0$ or
forbids repeated vertices. Conditioning changes both the total count
and the independence law. The crude invalid-event argument gives an
initial estimate, but a sharp normalization should distinguish genuine
collisions from repetitions forced by the balanced relation. In small
characteristic, these distinctions may affect extremizers.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Two-direction testing and the row gauge]
Add the horizontal analogue of the arrangement test. The vertical test
alone cannot constrain $a(x)$, while a horizontal test should force
compatibility with an affine function of $x$. Establish a quantitative
repair theorem to a fully biaffine map, with explicit dependence on the
two failure rates and sharp first-order constants. The intersection of
the two exact model classes is easy to describe; robust intersection
with optimal constants is the substantive issue.
\end{problem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Answered locally by source~60}: the optimal intersection modulus $J(\eta)$ for $\eta<1/4$ and biaffine repair with optimal inverse coefficients through degree $s-2$, sharp first-order constant $1/(2s)$ (its Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:60:two:intersection}--\ref{gsr:en:60:two:sharpness}); the full finite-error profile is its Research question~\ref{gsr:fz:60:q:two}.
\end{writenote}

\begin{problem}[Higher multilinear arrangement models]
For products of three or more groups, formulate the gauge class left
invisible by a prescribed family of directional difference tests.
Can the coarse derivative synchronization be iterated without an
exponential accumulation of error constants? The multilinear structure
problems in \cite{gowersmilicevic} and directional norms in \cite{milicevicdirectional}
provide relevant settings, but the exact high-agreement tester and its
nullspace should be fixed before estimating constants.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Fast decoding rather than exhaustive slopes]
The exact cyclic decoder avoids exponential enumeration of row functions
but still enumerates all permitted $(b,c)$. Can random derivative queries
identify these coefficients in near-linear time in the table size, under
the high-agreement promise? A robust decoder should output both a model
and an efficiently verifiable disagreement count; it should also expose
its sample complexity and failure probability rather than hide them in
an informal majority vote.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[A formally checked probabilistic core]
Formalize the auxiliary-label correction lemma, affine separation,
proper-coordinate independence, and the one-error inclusion--exclusion
identity. These components are small enough to isolate from the full
Szemer\'edi development. Once checked, they would certify the main theorem
without requiring a formalization of a general inverse theorem for
Gowers norms. The initial target should be the rational inequality
$\eps_s\ge s\dd-2s(s-1)\dd^2$ on the proved small branch, not a real
square-root expression.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Actual propagation through the Gowers pipeline]
Find a point in the sparse structural argument where a near-full product
or a quantitatively mixing product can be produced without losing the
information needed later. Only then compare the complete parameter
recurrence with the existing one. A successful answer must keep track
of domain density, valid-arrangement mass, failure rate, model agreement,
and the eventual progression length. This is the necessary bridge
between the present local refinement and a claim about a global Ramsey
or Szemer\'edi bound.
\end{problem}

The most immediate mathematical targets are the first and third
questions: the common-prime quadratic constant and the equality
classification. The most consequential integration target is the sixth,
because the present proof deliberately does not solve the sparse-domain
mixing problem.

The cycle deficit lemma can be formalized independently as a finite
probability-vector inequality, followed by its subprobability extension.
The accompanying moment interpolation should retain ambient count
normalization in the partial-domain statement.

For $s=4$, all ingredients of the repair theorem can be stated without
Fourier analysis. For higher even $s$, one can formalize the moment
identity separately and reduce to that coarse decoder. The local
polynomial inequality is itself Fourier-free for every $s$.

A formal implementation should distinguish an exact count from its
normalization, a function-valued equality of affine maps from pointwise
agreement on most $x$, and an auxiliary label sampled at each occurrence
from a fixed random section. The last distinction is especially important
for repeated coordinates. The proof also needs the positivity hypotheses
$1-2e>0$ and $1-12d>0$ at their precise uses, rather than after clearing
denominators without a sign check.

\subsection{Claim ledger}

All mathematical results proved in this manuscript are unconditional
under their displayed hypotheses. The conditional statements are the
erasure corollary's explicit coverage assumptions and the clearly posed
future research questions. No novelty claim is used as a proof input.
The majority-correction method is classical in origin, while the
arrangement-specific estimates and constructions are developed here.
The exact cubic and sharp asymptotic coefficients are offered as research
contributions for scrutiny, not as refereed literature facts.

No new statement in this package is asserted to be Lean-compiled or
kernel-verified. The supplied Python checks are ordinary exact-arithmetic
programs. No new global estimate for $r_k(N)$ or van der Waerden numbers
is claimed. These limitations are part of the mathematical scope, not
missing hypotheses to be filled by optimism.

\subsection{Degenerate inputs and boundary cases}

The all-zero increment is included, even though it always passes. This
matters for both the binary and the prime extremizers. Repeated vertices
and repeated horizontal coordinates are also included. The auxiliary-label
proof remains valid for those repetitions because labels are resampled
per occurrence. In a partial-domain test, validity means that every
occurrence has a value; repeated occurrences do not require separate
membership choices.

For $\dd=0$, ratio expressions involving $\overline t/\dd$ are not used;
exact classification supplies the zero-error conclusion. For empty
valid-arrangement sets, conditional failure is undefined. For trivial
target groups, every function is an exact model and every theorem reduces
to zero error. The order parameter is always even and at least four;
none of the signed inclusion--exclusion claims has been extended to odd
orders without proof.

\subsection{Numerical evaluation of the repair formulas}

For small $u$, cancellation can make the expression
$1-\sqrt{1-8(s-1)u/s}$ numerically inconvenient. An equivalent stable form
is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:33:ras:eq:stable-root}
 R_s(u)=\frac{2u/s}{1+\sqrt{1-8(s-1)u/s}}.
\end{equation}
The exact verification suite avoids square roots entirely: it verifies
that $\dd$ is on the increasing branch and that $Q_s(\dd)\le u$.
For the cubic inverse one may use bisection on $[0,1/12]$, since the cubic
is strictly increasing there. A floating-point root returned without
checking the interval is not a substitute for that branch condition.

\section[{Consequences, limitations, and a research program\srctag{34}}]{Consequences, limitations, and a research program}\label{gsr:fz:34:sec:d11}
\srcnote{34}{Section 11}
\label{gsr:fz:34:sec:research}

The results above settle several questions in the audited repository:
the exact values $h(7),h(11)$, the leading asymptotic of $h(p)$,
the support cost and classification of positive cyclic detectors,
and the proposed single-pair model for the fourth-norm extremizer.
Appendix~\ref{gsr:en:34:app:rigidity} settles the strict threshold in the
nonuniform directional model. The following questions identify the
remaining mathematical gaps. They are proposed research targets;
we do not assert that every formulation is historically new or
unresolved throughout the literature.

\subsection{Binary determinants and arithmetic configurations}

\begin{problem}[Divisibility versus exact cyclic isolation]
\label{gsr:fz:34:prob:isolation}
Is $h(p)=\hc(p)$ for every prime $p$? If not, what is the first
prime where they differ, and how large can the difference be?
\end{problem}

Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:34:thm:reduction} concerns a determinant divisible by
$p$, while $\hc(p)$ requires that the complete row quotient be
exactly $\Z/p\Z$. These conditions agree in every small case
proved here and in their leading asymptotic, but neither conclusion
proves exact equality in general. A useful finite search should
store full row-lattice indices and full-support characters, not only
one determinant. Existing determinant spectra can supply many
immediate values before any new exhaustive search is attempted.

\begin{problem}[The second-order support term]
\label{gsr:fz:34:prob:second-order}
With $L=\log p$, $\lambda=\log L$, and $\mu=\log\lambda$,
does there exist a constant $a$ such that
\[
 h(p)=\frac{2L}{\lambda}
       \left(1+a\frac{\mu}{\lambda}
                   +o\!\left(\frac{\mu}{\lambda}\right)\right)?
\]
Ask the same question for $\hc(m)$ as $m$ runs through all
integers. Can the coefficient $3$ in the proved upper comparison
be reduced toward the coefficient $1$ in the Hadamard comparison?
\end{problem}

The bounds here place any such second-order coefficient between
one and three; they do not establish its existence. Improving the
consecutive determinant range and improving the representation of
one specified prime are different problems. The latter could admit
a better upper bound even if an all-integer interval is more costly.

\begin{problem}[The secondary loss in the consecutive cyclic range]
Can every positive integer up to
\[
 \exp\left(\tfrac12N\log N-o(N\log\log N)\right)
\]
be realized as the sole nonunit Smith factor of a binary matrix of
order $N$? More modestly, can the coefficient of
$N\log\log N$ be made strictly smaller than one?
\end{problem}

In the present construction, the bounded first row is encoded at
a cost proportional to $\log A$. Balancing that cost against the
number of radix positions leads to an auxiliary order of scale
$N/(\log N)^2$. This explains the current secondary loss within
this construction. A smaller loss would likely need a more
efficient use of the first row or a different composition mechanism.
The cyclic condition should be retained throughout; a determinant
construction alone does not resolve the stronger question.

\begin{problem}[Exact positive support and finite-size efficiency]
Determine $h_{\mathrm{pos}}(m)$ exactly for a substantial range of
cyclic orders. When is the doubling bound
$h_{\mathrm{pos}}(m)\le2h_{\mathrm{cyc}}(m)$ strict, and what is
the second-order term in $h_{\mathrm{pos}}(m)$?
\end{problem}

The leading constant four and the inverse-pair classification are
proved here. The remaining finite problem is closely related to
ternary matrices with a prescribed cyclic quotient. The doubling
construction gives a simple bridge from binary matrices, but it
need not minimize the number of pairs. A useful search should
retain a full-support faithful quotient vector and certify the
whole lattice index. The corresponding positivity classification
for noncyclic finite quotients is a further structural question.

\begin{problem}[Prescribed finite abelian quotients]
For a finite abelian group $A$, determine the least size of an
affinely independent Boolean configuration with row quotient $A$
and with every coordinate generator nonzero. How does this size
depend on $|A|$, the number of invariant factors, and their prime
power structure?
\end{problem}

The cyclic construction controls a single nonunit invariant factor.
Direct sums of binary presentations give an upper bound for general
$A$, followed by affine augmentation and deletion of coordinate
generators that vanish in the quotient. The substantive question is
whether several invariant factors can share the same Boolean
coordinates efficiently. Prime powers also distinguish a rank drop
modulo $p$ from its full $p$-adic depth.

\begin{problem}[From first occurrence to a complete coefficient]
Classify all full-support lattice types at the first few unresolved
support degrees, and compute their multiplicities as functions of
the cube dimension. In particular, can the sixth- and seventh-order
coefficients be expressed in a finite, explicit basis of Fourier
statistics with a dimension-uniform remainder?
\end{problem}

The onset theorem supplies necessary dimension and support
thresholds, and the explicit matrices supply terms that must be
present. They do not enumerate all rational dependencies, all
Smith types, or all cancellations among supports of the same size.
A practical approach is to classify coordinate-pattern orbits,
attach integral presentations to each orbit, and then derive
closed multiplicity formulas. A useful theorem must keep the
distinction between Smith torsion and reductions of pre-existing
integer relations.

\subsection{The actual Gowers norm extremizers}

\begin{problem}[The sharp odd fourth-norm constant]
Determine $c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}$ inside the proved interval
\[
 \left[
 \frac{4804}{5465198316262956^{1/4}},\frac23
 \right].
\]
Is the supremum attained on some finite group, or only approached
along groups of growing order? What are the extremizing Fourier
supports and phases?
\end{problem}

The dual identity identifies why the single-pair guess fails, and
the resonance argument controls a concrete way to exploit that
failure. It does not classify genuine minimizers. On a fixed group,
the finite-dimensional variational equation in
Remark~\ref{gsr:cc:34:norm:stationarity} is a necessary condition. Across all
groups, an additional compactness or approximation argument would
be needed. Merely optimizing the two-pair family does not establish
a global optimum.

\begin{problem}[Stronger coupled certificates]
Can the dominant pair and its resonant harmonics be retained jointly
through all positive autocorrelation terms and the dual inequality,
so as to improve $2/3$? Can a finite family of explicit dual tests
provide a sharp certificate?
\end{problem}

The proof uses only the balanced monomials and the families with
seven first harmonics and one third or fifth harmonic. Further
families impose additional positive costs on the same Fourier mass.
Their phase-sensitive dual contributions may also be useful.
A sound computational program should first produce exact
polynomials and rational inequalities, then prove the resulting
optimization bound. Floating-point minimization by itself supplies
a candidate, not a universal norm inequality.

The displayed two-pair polynomial gives a particularly accessible
subproblem. Its nonzero stationary parameters satisfy
\[
 (1+t^4)P'(t)-16t^3P(t)=0.
\]
Exact root isolation can determine the best member of that family.
One must then test perturbations in additional harmonics to decide
whether a family optimizer is even locally extremal in the full
function space.

\begin{problem}[Higher dimensions and quantitative stability]
Determine the asymptotic behavior of $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}$ as
$d\to\infty$, and develop stability statements for near-minimizers
of $\|f\|_{U^d}/\|f\|_{U^2}$ for $d\ge4$.
\end{problem}

The sequence is nonincreasing by norm monotonicity. The incoming
moment estimate and the profile refinement in
Remark~\ref{gsr:cc:34:norm:higher} give explicit upper bounds, but the fourth
dual function stops improving the moment endpoint in sufficiently
large dimensions. Computing $\mathcal D_d$ on a small Fourier
support becomes a Boolean balancing problem related to the
configuration analysis in the first half of the article. Stability
must be formulated for the genuine norm minimizers; stability of
an intermediate autocorrelation inequality has a different equality
set and is not enough.

\subsection{Returning to the density-increment argument}

\begin{problem}[A constrained density-and-norm envelope]
For fixed $0<\delta<1$ and small $u$, determine or sharply bound
\[
 \sup\{Q_4(F):0\le F\le1,\ \E F=\delta,
                         \|F-\delta\|_{U^4}=u\}.
\]
Can the quartic contribution and the higher-order remainder be
bounded jointly using their compatible Fourier phases?
\end{problem}

The coefficient $100c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}$ describes the unrestricted
small-amplitude leading term for real perturbations. The box
constraint $0\le F\le1$ becomes more restrictive at larger
amplitudes. In addition, the individual support bounds used in
the remainder need not be simultaneously sharp. A joint envelope
could therefore improve the useful finite-error range even before
the exact value of $c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}$ is known.

\begin{problem}[Propagation through a complete iteration]
Recompute a specified, fully normalized density-increment scheme
after replacing the local fourth-dimensional cube bound and the
directional rigidity threshold by the results proved here. Which
final constants or exponents actually change?
\end{problem}

The appropriate calculation must track density, progression or
ambient-set size, uniformity thresholds, and all recursive
dependencies. A smaller local coefficient may affect only a final
constant; in some parameter regimes another loss may dominate it
entirely. The current article supplies explicit replacement
inequalities but makes no unverified claim about their global
effect. This is also the setting in which the prime-order and
nested hypotheses of the original inverse argument must be
preserved.

The statements for every prime, every cyclic order, and every
finite odd-order group are proved by algebraic and analytic
arguments in the article. Their validity is not extrapolated from
a numerical search. The finite computations have three roles:
certifying specific matrices, supplying an exhaustive negative
certificate for two small primes, and verifying exact coefficients
or rational comparisons in the analytic proof.

Component & Exact verification & Role in the proof\\

 for $7,11,13,17$ & Positive finite certificates\\
Seven-vertex exclusion & All 104 and 204 projective orbit
 representatives; every Boolean row and integer annihilator &
 Exhaustive negative proof for $11,13$\\

 moment checks & Implementation check of an all-parameter proof\\

The code and data are included in the archive. The torsion and
norm verifiers use Python's standard library. The determinant
gadget verifier uses exact SymPy arithmetic; the dependency is
recorded in \filethirtyfour{requirements.txt}. No floating-point result is
needed for a theorem stated here. Decimal values in the text are
provided for orientation; the defining expressions and decisive
inequalities are exact.

The negative certificates deserve a particularly clear trust
boundary. Their generator uses rational elimination to find an
annihilator, but the verifier checks the supplied nonzero integer
vector directly against every admissible Boolean row. The
verification does not trust a rank routine. Exhaustiveness comes
from an explicit enumeration of sorted tuples and all nonzero
scalar multiples. This structure is suitable for a later formal
certificate checker.

\subsection{A concrete formalization sequence}

\begin{enumerate}
\item Define the augmented Boolean matrix and its integer row
quotient. Formalize the Fourier constraint identity and the link
between rank drop modulo $p$ and Smith torsion.

\item Prove the affine-minor reduction and the minimal-order
full-support lemma. These require finite-dimensional linear
algebra and elementary determinant identities, without the
Alon--Vu theorem.

\item Add the small explicit matrices and the finite certificate
checker. The $p=11,13$ lower bounds can then be checked using
integer dot products and finite orbit enumeration.

\item Formalize the positive cyclic presentation and cyclic
support compression. State the Alon--Vu input separately before
formalizing the determinant gadgets and asymptotic corollaries.
No unproved external input should be hidden behind a theorem
named as if it had been established internally.

\item Formalize the exact dual polynomial, positive balanced and
resonant moment sums, and the order-three calculation. Derive
the rational $2/3$ bound from these ingredients, then connect it
to the existing normalized cube-count interface.

\item Formalize the finite-fiber sampling model in
Appendix~\ref{gsr:en:34:app:rigidity}. Keep its general-group sharpness
theorem separate from any stronger claim at the original
prime-order inverse-theorem interface.
\end{enumerate}

The most valuable initial formal additions are the exact reduction,
the small prime certificates, and the fourth-norm inequality.
They have compact inputs and conclusions, and do not require
formalizing the entire asymptotic matrix construction first.

\section[{Evidence, source scope, and formalization\srctag{35}}]{Evidence, source scope, and formalization}\label{gsr:fz:35:sec:d8}
\srcnote{35}{Section 8}
\gsrsrcpartof{35}{Verification, integration, and further research}
\label{gsr:fz:35:sec:verification}

\subsection{What the accompanying calculations check}

The mathematical proofs above establish the infinite families of
statements. The programs serve a narrower purpose: they reproduce
finite identities, verify the exact numerical certificates, and
test the delicate conventions on complete small examples.
They use the Python standard library only. No floating-point
optimization is an input to a theorem.

\paragraph{Arrangement selection.}
The program \texttt{verify\_graded\_selection.py} examines all
\(3^8=6{,}561\) coefficient arrays for \(k=1,m=4,p=3,L=2\).
It removes the universal line, computes the parity-removed degree,
and solves the resulting linear feature systems exactly over
\(\F_3\). The maximum success probabilities are
\[
 Q_0(3)=\frac13,\qquad Q_1(3)=\frac{11}{81}.
\]
These maxima attain the stated individual-certificate estimates.
The program also checks the dimensions of balance subspaces on
separate small examples and records exact rational product masses.
An attained certificate probability does not imply sharpness of
the full selection threshold.

For a direct check of actual subset selection, the same program
takes \(B=\F_3^2\) and \(\phi(x,z)=x^2z\), enumerates all
\(6{,}561\) arrangements, and averages over all \(243\) field
seeds. It uses products over distinct physical points for the
actual probabilities and products over labels for the Fourier
comparison. In this example there are \(3{,}753\) respected
and \(2{,}808\) unrespected arrangements. The difference between
the expected actual and labelled bad counts is
\[
 \frac{9{,}891}{128}-\frac{84{,}687}{2{,}048}
 =\frac{73{,}569}{2{,}048}>0.
\]
Thus omitting the repeated-vertex compensation would be a real
error, not merely a missing discussion of an empty exceptional set.
The program further verifies \(54\) exact rational instances of
the explicit bandwidth budget and recomputes the exponent table
through \(k=16\).

\paragraph{The fourth-order norm gap.}
The program \texttt{verify\_norm\_gap.py} checks all \(17\)
rational comparisons used in the scalar certificate. Comparisons
involving fourth roots are reduced to powers of positive rational
numbers. It also enumerates all \(2^{15}\) sign assignments for
the cosine dual and all \(2^{16}\) assignments for the full
order-three cube. The resulting coefficient dictionaries are
\[
 \{-5:1,\ -3:27,\ -1:111,\ 1:111,\ 3:27,\ 5:1\}
\]
and
\[
 \{-12:8,\ -6:16,\ 0:286,\ 6:16,\ 12:8\},
\]
respectively. These checks support the combinatorial proofs of
Lemmas~\ref{gsr:cc:35:ng:cosine-dual} and~\ref{gsr:cc:35:ng:ternary}; the analytic
energy and scalar arguments remain explicitly proved in the text.

\paragraph{Polynomial obstructions.}
The program \texttt{verify\_polynomial\_obstruction.py} tests
\(285{,}915\) starting-residue and step-residue pairs in the
three examples tabulated in Part~III. Arc diameters are computed
by the largest-gap formula on integer residues, so endpoints
and wraparound do not involve rounding error. It also tests
all \(422{,}500\) length-three integer progressions in the
\(1{,}301\)-point interval of the prime-modulus approximation,
using the prime
\[
 N=54{,}121{,}601.
\]
At tolerance \(1/32\), the good steps in that interval are
exactly \(217\) and \(434\), both divisible by the predicted
period \(217\). The prime test is local to this interval.

\paragraph{Reproduction.}
The archive includes recorded JSON outputs and a runner,
\nolinkurl{verification/verify_all.py}, that reruns the suites
into a temporary directory and compares their outputs with
the records. It leaves the supplied evidence files unchanged.
The \LaTeX{} source contains its own bibliography and does not
depend on external graphics, a bibliography database, or the
original repository being available at build time.

\subsection{Which ingredients are inherited}

The arrangement architecture, the respected relation, and the
use of positive Fourier expansions originate in Gowers'
argument \cite{gowers,repo35}. The one-stage Fej\'er
selector and its polynomial retained-count powers already appear
in \cite{repo35fejer}. The degree-sensitive certificate geometry
is developed in \cite{repo35degree}; we reprove it for the
arbitrary field coefficients needed here. The contribution is
to place the necessary top-degree balances \emph{inside the
probability-mass estimate}, combine degree and codimension
before summing, and carry the physical-collision correction
through that weighted calculation.

The real centered \(U^3\) comparison and the centered cube
expansion are in the merged collection \cite{repo35merged}.
The fourth-order cosine identities and the first uniform
higher-order norm gap are in \cite{repo35higher}.
The strongest inspected fourth-order comparison before this
article is the moment coefficient \(35/8\) in
\cite{repo35moments}. Our additional positive Fourier
configurations increase that coefficient to \(5\). At higher
orders the existing moment theorem remains stronger than the
constant obtained just by propagating \(5\).

For polynomial partitions, the linear divisibility-and-conductor
argument is in \cite{repo35thresholds}. The preceding polynomial
volume obstruction is in \cite{repo35barrier}.
The present descending-degree construction supplies a divisor
that is forced at every initial point; this is the additional
property needed to multiply the polynomial obstruction by the
semigroup conductor.

\subsection{The literature comparison and its limits}

The foundational context is Gowers' 2001 proof
\cite{gowers}. The global progression-free bound cited in
the introduction is from Leng, Sah, and Sawhney
\cite{lssbounds}. Neither the size threshold of a local restriction
nor an improvement of its numerical exponent can be identified
with an improvement of that global bound without a further
complete argument.

On the analytic side, Eisner and Tao study large values and
near-extremizers of Gowers and Gowers--Host--Kra norms
\cite{eisnertao}. Kova\v{c} and Rogers study \(L^p\) variants,
degree-lowering estimates, and strict log-convexity
\cite{kovacrogers}. Their Theorem~1.1 assumes a nonnegative
function and a group without compact open subgroups; its stated
strict log-convexity conclusion consequently does not apply to
finite groups. Our comparison concerns signed real centered
functions on finite odd-order groups and relates \(U^4\)
directly to \(U^2\). These are different hypotheses and
inequalities. This distinction is useful context, but is not
an exhaustive priority search.

For polynomial phases, Green and Tao's quantitative work on
polynomial orbits provides broader context for smoothness
estimates \cite{greentaoorbits}. The small-arc lemma used here
has its own finite-difference proof and does not invoke a
nilmanifold equidistribution theorem.

The source audit therefore supports precise comparisons with
the inspected statements. It does not certify that every
intermediate lemma or the final combination is absent from
all earlier literature. The manuscript is intended for
mathematical review and integration as a research contribution,
with its proofs available for independent checking.

\subsection{A concrete formalization route}

The repository's statements and their formal companion proofs
must be distinguished. We inspected the ledger and the relevant
section files at the source pin; no new Lean file is included
or claimed to compile. The present theorems are conventional
mathematical proofs, supported by exact computations.
Table~\ref{gsr:fz:35:tab:formalization} gives separable proof obligations
for a future formal development.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{A proposed research programme\srctag{35}}]{A proposed research programme}\label{gsr:fz:35:sec:d9}
\srcnote{35}{Section 9}
\label{gsr:fz:35:sec:research}

The following questions are ordered by their proximity to the
proved arguments. Each has a concrete first target. Questions
about optimality are proposed problems, not consequences of the
bounds already established.

\subsection{Arrangement selection: beyond the present exponent}

\begin{problem}[Top-degree rank, not only top-degree size]
\label{gsr:fz:35:rq:top-rank}
Can the coefficient strata be refined by the rank of the matrix
\[
 \bigl(A_{j,T}\bigr)_{\substack{1\le j\le m\\|T|=t}}
\]
so that several lowest Boolean moments contribute independent
restrictions simultaneously?
\end{problem}

The present proof selects one nonzero moment vector. Multiple
independent vectors could force more restrictions on both the
levels and the anchors, while their rank constraints also reduce
coefficient mass. A meaningful first result would compute the
joint rank-and-mass profile for \(k=2\) or \(3\), prove its
exceptional varieties have the predicted dimension, and improve
the explicit exponent \(23\) for \(k=2,m=16\). Summing a list
of pointwise rank bounds without controlling the mass of each
rank class would not suffice.

\begin{problem}[Exact mass of the arrangement balance spaces]
\label{gsr:fz:35:rq:exact-mass}
How close is the product Fej\'er law to the upper bound
\(\mu^{s-D_t}\) on \(\mathcal V_t\)? Can its exact additive
convolution structure replace the largest-atom estimate?
\end{problem}

The mass lemma is sharp for arbitrary coordinate subspaces,
whereas \(\mathcal V_t\) comes from many Boolean evaluations
and balanced sums. Even an exponential-in-\(s\) constant
improvement would affect practical thresholds. A changed power
of \(L\) would require proving that the particular support
intersects these spaces less efficiently than a general
subspace. An anisotropic version could assign different
bandwidths to cube positions, provided the respected universal
signal remains large enough.

\begin{problem}[Optimize the kernel against the whole error budget]
\label{gsr:fz:35:rq:kernel}
Among nonnegative trigonometric polynomials \(K\le1\) with
nonnegative Fourier coefficients, which best balances
universal signal, coefficient-stratum mass, and point
marginal probability?
\end{problem}

The earlier positive-Fourier report studies the signal and its
retained-mass powers \cite{repo35fejer}. The present theorem
adds a different objective: the entire graded error budget.
A kernel that maximizes the scalar ratio
\(\sum c_n^s/c_0^s\) need not minimize
\(\sum_t q^{-t-1}\Pr(b\in\mathcal V_t)/c_0^s\).
A finite-bandwidth optimization for \(k=2,m=4\), followed by
an exact certificate for the optimizer, is a manageable first
problem.

\begin{problem}[Small characteristic and torsion in the target]
\label{gsr:fz:35:rq:characteristic}
Can one obtain a comparable theorem when the characteristic is
fixed while \(\alpha\eta\) tends to zero, or when the target has
small torsion?
\end{problem}

The current restriction \(p>2(L-1)\) serves a definite purpose:
the integer Fourier band must embed without collisions, and
nonzero universal frequencies must not annihilate a defect.
Simply replacing \(q\) by a large extension-field cardinality
does not remove this restriction. A possible approach is a
multidimensional kernel on the dual of a larger auxiliary
group, with enough linear maps to detect every nonzero target
defect. The corresponding universal signal and mass estimates
would have to be proved anew.

\begin{problem}[Intrinsic lower bounds for selection]
\label{gsr:fz:35:rq:selection-lower}
What obstruction forces a lower bound on the ambient field size
for any subset satisfying both the desired purity and a retained
count of order \(\alpha^s\eta^{s-1}T_0\)?
\end{problem}

The asymptotic \(E_{k,m}\sim2s/k\) describes our sufficient
threshold, not a matching necessary one. A serious lower bound
would need a family of maps and domains defeating \emph{all}
candidate subsets, not just one kernel or one relation-counting
proof. It would be useful first to separate optimality within
positive-Fourier selectors from optimality for unrestricted
subset selection.

\subsection{Norm gaps: sharpen the analytic certificate}

\begin{problem}[The exact fourth-order extremal constant]
\label{gsr:fz:35:rq:norm-optimum}
Determine \(c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\), or narrow substantially the
interval in \eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:interval}. Is a maximizing sequence
supported on a bounded number of Fourier frequencies?
\end{problem}

The retained statistic \(J(\lambda)\) sees every amplitude
three-term progression, while the proof of the coefficient
\(5\) uses only a small part of it. A first improvement could
retain all terms involving the dominant pair and its third and
fifth harmonics, then prove an exact polynomial inequality on
their amplitudes and phases. Numerical optimization can suggest
a candidate but must be followed by a uniform certificate and
a treatment of character-order coincidences.

\begin{problem}[Quantitative structure near the minimum]
\label{gsr:fz:35:rq:norm-stability}
If \(\norm{f}_{U^4}^{16}/\norm{f}_{U^2}^{16}\) is near its
infimum, what Fourier concentration and phase alignment are
forced?
\end{problem}

The inequalities \(R\ge(5-3p)^2\) and
\eqref{gsr:cc:35:ng:refined-pair-bound} already restrict the largest
pair and its third harmonic. They do not yet classify near
minimizers. A useful stability theorem should identify a
metric, quantify its distance to a candidate family, and be
uniform over all finite odd-order groups. It must also
accommodate the non-cosine examples already present in
\cite{repo35higher}.

\begin{problem}[Higher-order gains beyond central-binomial moments]
\label{gsr:fz:35:rq:higher-norm}
Can the full cosine dual \(D_dg\), together with higher positive
Fourier configurations, improve the established
central-binomial comparison for \(d\ge5\)?
\end{problem}

The target here is a new coefficient that actually beats
\cite{repo35moments} at the specified order. Monotonicity from
our \(U^4\) result is insufficient. A tractable first step is
to derive and exactly verify the dominant harmonic terms of
\(D_5g\), identify which Fourier energy terms penalize their
negative directions, and separate the finitely many exceptional
small character orders.

\subsection{Polynomial partitions: necessity versus sufficiency}

\begin{problem}[A matching quadratic upper theorem]
\label{gsr:fz:35:rq:quadratic-upper}
For \(\nu\) arbitrary quadratic phases, is the universal
prescribed-length threshold bounded by
\[
 C_\nu L^{3\nu+2}\eps^{-2\nu}
\]
up to logarithmic or subpower factors, in an appropriate
integer-interval formulation?
\end{problem}

Our construction proves the corresponding lower power scale.
A matching upper result would have to combine simultaneous
quadratic flatness with exact coverage by lengths \(L,L+1\).
Finding one long flat progression does not solve the coverage
problem. A useful intermediate goal is an upper theorem
allowing a small exceptional set whose dependence on
\(L,\eps,\nu\) can be compared with the exact gap formula
\eqref{gsr:dt:35:po:eq:packing}.

\begin{problem}[Prescribed length width and exceptional mass]
\label{gsr:fz:35:rq:length-width}
How does the best universal threshold change when the allowed
lengths are \(L,\ldots,L+w\), and how much does allowing an
exceptional set reduce it?
\end{problem}

The constructed phases give the exact conductor
\(L\lceil(L-1)/w\rceil\) and exact uncovered mass. This
provides a two-parameter family of lower benchmarks. The
first upper target should interpolate between fixed \(w\)
and \(w\) comparable with \(L\), rather than treating a
prescribed pair and an arbitrary-length partition as unrelated
problems.

\begin{problem}[Prime moduli of comparable size]
\label{gsr:fz:35:rq:prime-modulus}
Do the same polynomial obstruction powers hold when the
ambient modulus is prime and is constrained to be comparable
with the interval length?
\end{problem}

The periodic example is exact at a composite modulus \(N=R+1\);
the prime approximation permits a much larger \(N\).
A construction respecting both primality and \(N\asymp R\)
would need to replace exact divisibility by a robust local
condition. Conversely, a better upper theorem in this regime
would show that the modulus constraint has genuine content.

\subsection{Integration and constructive extraction}

\begin{problem}[Quantitative propagation through the complete proof]
\label{gsr:fz:35:rq:global}
What bound follows when the graded selection theorem is inserted
into the entire corrected Gowers argument and every subsequent
parameter choice is optimized consistently?
\end{problem}

Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:35:sel:cor:downstream} provides one completed
substitution. The next stage should be a dependency table
carrying the domain density, respect fraction, field size,
characteristic, model dimension, and purity through every
use. A claimed global improvement should be stated only after
that propagation is complete, and then compared directly with
the best applicable published theorem.

\begin{problem}[An effective subset algorithm]
\label{gsr:fz:35:rq:algorithm}
Can the expectation proof be converted into an efficient
algorithm that finds \(B'\) with an explicit running-time
bound in the natural input model?
\end{problem}

The proof already yields a finite randomized construction,
and exhaustive search would find a successful outcome.
Efficient derandomization is a different question: computing
the score \(\eta X-Y\) itself can dominate the cost.
A first result could use a conditional-expectation procedure
for fixed \(k,m\), with a sparse representation of \(\phi\)
and an explicit arrangement-counting oracle. Its guarantee
should include both the theorem's parameters and the
algorithm's complexity.

\begin{problem}[A reusable formal library of weighted configurations]
\label{gsr:fz:35:rq:formal}
Can the common proof components be formalized once so that
future refinements change only a rank estimate, a coefficient
mass, or a finite energy identity?
\end{problem}

The product-law subspace lemma, the score-extraction argument,
and the conductor packing formula are independent of most
of Gowers' proof. Establishing them as reusable lemmas would
make later improvements easier to check. Exact computation
could then discharge the finite cosine identities and rational
inequalities, while the proof assistant checks the general
probability and algebraic arguments connecting them.

\section[{Computational checks and reproducibility\srctag{36}}]{Computational checks and reproducibility}\label{gsr:fz:36:sec:d11}\label{gsr:fz:36:ssc:sec:checks}
\srcnote{36}{Section 11}

The accompanying \texttt{checks/verify.py} is an executable audit of
normalizations, endpoint constructions, finite tensor cases, and
boundary examples. It uses a fixed seed, $20261006$. The proofs above
do not rely on a numerical search or an unverified pattern.

The supplied run used Python 3.13.5 and NumPy 2.3.5. Integer tensor
calculations are exact modulo the specified prime. Other tests involving
complex exponentials use double precision and tolerance
$3\times10^{-10}$; they are not exact cyclotomic or formal verifications.
The machine-readable output is \texttt{checks/results.json}.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.53\linewidth}p{0.39\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
Check & Observed result\\
\midrule
All $81$ bilinear matrices on $\mathbb F_3^2$; one quadratic
unit-modulus extremizer for each & All attained $3^{-r}$; maximum
absolute error $4.45\times10^{-16}$\\[3pt]
$372$ mixed-function tests in dimensions $2$ and $4$ & No violation
of the alternating-rank bound within tolerance\\[3pt]
All $3^9=19\,683$ functions $\mathbb F_3^2\to\{1,e_3(1),e_3(2)\}$
for $B(h,x)=h_1x_2$ & Maximum $1/3$; $324$ exact maximizers\\[3pt]
All $3^8=6\,561$ trilinear tensors on $\mathbb F_3^2$, with $f=1$ &
$81$ fully symmetric; nonsymmetric maximum $45/81=5/9$;
$120$ endpoint tensors\\[3pt]
Both slice-profile bounds for every tensor in that census & Passed by
exact integer comparison\\[3pt]
$256$ tensor profiles with one seeded nonconstant bounded function &
Both amplitude-sensitive bounds passed\\[3pt]
$18\,432$ sampled polarization tuples in characteristics $5$ and $7$,
degrees $3,4,5$ & Exact modular identities passed\\[3pt]
$12$ full $\mathbb F_5^2$ pointwise spectral-shift tests & Maximum
pointwise error $4.86\times10^{-17}$\\[3pt]
All $81$ tuples in the $\mathbb F_3$ nonclassical example & Exact
triple differences modulo $9$ passed\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Supplementary checks also verified both profile directions for $256$
seeded multiaffine selectors with affine offsets. A direct model of
$\mathbb F_9=\mathbb F_3[t]/(t^2+1)$ checked $24$ mixed bilinear cases,
the bilinear endpoint $1/9$, and the exact trilinear endpoint count
$1377/6561=17/81$.

The trilinear census is particularly useful for detecting the wrong
threshold. A tensor has eight coefficients; its selector is evaluated
on all $81$ ordered pairs of increments. With $f=1$ its energy is the
number of pairs giving the zero frequency divided by $81$.
Symmetry is tested against swaps of the final slot with each earlier
slot. Slice ranks in dimension two are zero or two and can be detected
by the off-diagonal alternating coefficient. Thus the entire census,
including its profile inequalities, can be checked with integer
arithmetic and no Fourier approximation.

The phase-function census is also exact. If a Fourier sum has $a,b,c$
occurrences of $1,\omega,\omega^2$, where $\omega=e_3(1)$, its squared
modulus is $a^2+b^2+c^2-ab-ac-bc$. The script uses this integer formula;
its output includes the histogram of all energy numerators over the
common denominator $729$. It exhausts this finite family, not all
complex-valued bounded functions. The polarization tests
sample tuples and tensors, even though the computations on each sample
are exact. These distinctions are recorded in the JSON and should be
preserved in any integration summary.

To reproduce the checks and the document from the package root:
\begin{verbatim}
python checks/verify.py --output checks/results.json
latexmk -pdf -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error sharp_symmetry.tex
\end{verbatim}
A Makefile and a minimal dependency file are supplied. No network access
is required for the mathematics or checks once NumPy and a standard
LaTeX distribution are installed.

\subsection{Theorems to formalize in dependency order}
The proof deliberately separates finite algebra, spectral linear
algebra, and Fourier normalization. A useful dependency order is:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.]
\item Prove Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:lem:support} for finite vector-valued
multilinear maps, including the empty-tuple convention. Prove the
separately affine extension as a distinct statement.
\item Define the forward multiplicative derivative and normalized
Fourier transform, then prove Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:lem:square}. Relate
forward and backward derivatives by translation before connecting
to an existing source predicate.
\item Formalize alternating bilinear rank, its symplectic splitting,
and Lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:lem:multiplicity}. Establish the cocycle law with
its exact sign and factor $1/2$.
\item Formalize the positive operator $M_g$, its trace, and the
invariant-eigenspace argument. This proves the main bilinear
inequality without requiring the later equality classification.
\item Deduce the frozen-slice estimate and the sharp threshold.
Construct the endpoint using two independent dual vectors.
\item Prove diagonal polarization and the pointwise identity. This
part is independent of the spectral proof once symmetry is supplied.
It is the most direct equality-form companion to the global scalar
phase-extraction statement.
\item Add noise, coset, and multiaffine interfaces. Formalize the
block decomposition and stability only after the main theorem is
complete.
\end{enumerate}

No theorem name in this plan is claimed to exist already in Lean.
No uncompiled Lean skeleton is included, and no existing source
statement should be marked proved on the basis of this article.

The companion \texttt{FORMALIZATION\_PLAN.md} expands the data types and
proof obligations, without inventing checked status.

\subsection{A normalization checklist for the source interface}
An integration review should check five concrete points. First, the
Fourier transform in the article is normalized, so passing to the
source sums introduces $|V|^{k+2}$. Second, the polynomial degree and
norm order are both $k+1$. Third, odd characteristic is used in the
bilinear gauge, whereas $p>k+1$ is only needed in classical
polarization. Fourth, the input selector must be globally multilinear
unless the separately affine theorem is being invoked. Fifth, the
strict threshold cannot be weakened to a non-strict one. Each of
these has an explicit test or counterexample in this package.

\section[{Further research questions\srctag{36}}]{Further research questions}\label{gsr:fz:36:sec:d13}\label{gsr:fz:36:ssc:sec:questions}
\srcnote{36}{Section 13}

The questions below are proposed problems arising from these results.
They are not all claimed to be previously unpublished, and the
established low-characteristic integration results and known
approximate-symmetry counterexamples remain in force.

\begin{problem}[All endpoint configurations]\label{gsr:fz:36:ssc:q:endpoint}
For $k\geq2$, classify the pairs $(f,\sigma)$ with $T$ nonsymmetric
and $\A_f(\sigma)=\vartheta_{k,p}$. Equality in the proof requires a
minimum-support defect, rank two on every defective slice, full
amplitude there, and a bilinear extremizer on each such slice.
Which compatible global configurations occur beyond products of
linear functionals and their phase/gauge variants?
\end{problem}
The finite census in Section~\ref{gsr:fz:36:ssc:sec:checks} supplies small
examples for this question, not a classification. A solution would
clarify whether the endpoint is essentially a zero-selector phenomenon
or whether equally extremal nonzero spectral organization exists.

\begin{problem}[Stability at the symmetry threshold]\label{gsr:fz:36:ssc:q:thresholdstability}
If $T$ is nonsymmetric and
$\A_f(\sigma)\geq\vartheta_{k,p}-\varepsilon$, what structural
conclusion follows as $\varepsilon\to0$? Can the defect be approximated
by a product-supported rank-two defect, and can the slice extremizers
be made coherent? Determine an appropriate metric before asserting a
power-law bound.
\end{problem}
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:thm:stability} controls individual bilinear slices.
It does not imply this global statement, because the defect support
and the dependence of the frozen functions must be stabilized as well.

\begin{problem}[Simultaneous alternating defects]\label{gsr:fz:36:ssc:q:jointprofiles}
Can one improve the minimum over individual profiles in
\eqref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:profile} when two or more independent slot defects are
present? Identify a joint rank invariant that yields a sharp bound
strictly below each single-profile estimate for a natural class of
tensors.
\end{problem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Related} (source~95, Section~\ref{gsr:fp:sec:pencils}): at the first obstruction degree, two alternating defects are governed exactly by the generic half-rank of their pencil; this source's setting ($p>k+1$) is different, and the question is not answered.
\end{writenote}
Multiplying the separate upper bounds is not justified. Any stronger
estimate must account for the fact that all slice tests use the same
function and overlapping tuples.

\begin{problem}[Below-threshold coherent rank reduction]\label{gsr:fz:36:ssc:q:rankreduction}
For energies $a\leq\vartheta_{k,p}$, can the popular low-rank slices
in \eqref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:eq:rankpopular} be organized into a structured global
subspace or multilinear variety on which the remaining defect
vanishes? What loss is unavoidable for a one-function derivative
array, as opposed to an arbitrary multilinear form?
\end{problem}
The intended problem retains the derivative-spectrum hypothesis. It
is not the disproved unrestricted approximate-symmetry statement.

\begin{problem}[Arithmetic boxes and boundary losses]\label{gsr:fz:36:ssc:q:localboxes}
Develop a version of alternating-rank orthogonality for derivatives
localized to arithmetic progressions or Bohr sets, with an explicit
boundary error and a normalization compatible with Section 17 of
Gowers's argument. Which additional local-extension hypotheses are
sufficient to turn it into a genuine refinement of Proposition 17.7?
\end{problem}
Uniform translation of the index set was used to make $M_g$ commute
with every $U_h$. A local result must replace that exact step, rather
than just restrict the average and reuse the global proof.

\begin{problem}[Lower-order multiaffine components]\label{gsr:fz:36:ssc:q:affine}
After Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:thm:multiaffine} certifies symmetry of all
nonconstant components, what is the optimal procedure for removing
the lower-order frequency terms? Is there a lossless identity in an
enlarged space, or an optimal quantified loss on the original space?
\end{problem}
Example~\ref{gsr:fp:36:ssc:ex:offset} rules out simply integrating the top
homogeneous component and retaining the same energy.

\begin{problem}[Exact nonclassical certification]\label{gsr:fz:36:ssc:q:nonclassical}
In small characteristic, which additional repeated-variable
identities of the total form are forced by an energy threshold close
to one? Can a sharp threshold certify the precise hypotheses needed
for an existing nonclassical integration theorem, rather than only
ordinary permutation symmetry?
\end{problem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 40--46]
Answered over $\F_2$ in every degree by source~43 (its Theorems~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:shear} and~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:boolean-certification}); odd small characteristic stays open (its Research question~\ref{gsr:fz:43:bpi:q:odd}).
\end{writenote}
The integration theorem itself is not the unresolved part of this
question; the new target is a sharp spectral certification of its
additional hypotheses.

\begin{problem}[Composite-modulus rank profiles]\label{gsr:fz:36:ssc:q:composite}
For finite abelian groups of odd composite exponent, express the
optimal bilinear factor using the elementary divisors of the
alternating bicharacter. Then seek an analogue of the multilinear
support bound that yields an exact symmetry threshold and sharp
examples over $\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z$.
\end{problem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 40--46]
Advanced by source~43: the bilinear factor $d_B^{-1}$ from the elementary divisors (its equation~\eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:smith}) and the exact symmetry threshold on every finite abelian group (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:group-symmetry}); integration on composite groups is open (its Research question~\ref{gsr:fz:43:bpi:q:composite}).
\end{writenote}
The finite-field support probability $1-1/p$ no longer describes
all nonzero module maps. A useful theorem must keep this arithmetic
information rather than hide it in an unspecified constant.

\begin{problem}[Characteristic two]\label{gsr:fz:36:ssc:q:two}
Formulate and prove an equally explicit characteristic-two version
of the bilinear orthogonality and spectral certification steps,
including the phases required to replace division by two. Determine
which parts retain the threshold $1-(1-1/2)^k$ and which extra
integration obstructions remain.
\end{problem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 40--46]
\emph{Answered for symmetric trilinear forms} by sources~46 and~43 (Section~\ref{gsr:fp:sec:binary}): exact energy $2^{-r/2}$ and codimension $r/2$; in every degree the threshold $1-2^{1-d}$ certifies nonclassical integrability (source~43's Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:boolean-certification}).
\end{writenote}
The present proof assumes odd characteristic and does not claim to
settle this extension. A suitable projective-operator formulation is
a concrete starting point.

\begin{problem}[Certification from limited data]\label{gsr:fz:36:ssc:q:algorithm}
Suppose a selector is supplied by a coefficient tensor together with
sampled derivative Fourier coefficients. Design a reliable test that
combines multilinearity checks, a certified energy lower bound, and
the robust margin $a-\eta-\vartheta_{k,p}$. Determine its sampling and
arithmetic complexity without treating numerical phase evaluations
as exact certificates.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[A useful inverse-theorem regime]\label{gsr:fz:36:ssc:q:inverse}
In which quantitative inverse arguments can the global selector be
obtained with energy $a$ and characteristic $p>k/a$ without a loss
that destroys the advantage of exact certification? Track all
parameters through at least one complete finite-field inverse step
before claiming an improvement to a final bound.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[A formal proof with a small analytic footprint]
\label{gsr:fz:36:ssc:q:formal}
Can the eigenspace-multiplicity proof of the bilinear estimate be
formalized using only finite-dimensional spectral theory already
available in the target proof library, and then connected to the
repository's corrected global phase-extraction predicate? A useful
first milestone is the exact scalar identity, followed by the
vector-valued support lemma and the rank-profile theorem.
\end{problem}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Conclusion\srctag{36}}]{Conclusion}\label{gsr:fz:36:sec:d14}\label{gsr:fz:36:ssc:sec:conclusion}
\srcnote{36}{Section 14}
The central output is an exact extremal answer: a nonsymmetric
multilinear selector on $\Fp^n$ can carry at most
$1-(1-1/p)^k$ of the normalized one-function derivative-spectrum
energy, and that amount is attained. The underlying rank-profile
inequality is stronger and retains information that a binary symmetry
test discards. Once symmetry and the factorial-invertibility condition
hold, an explicit diagonal polynomial converts the tested spectrum
into a lower Gowers power with equality, even before averaging over
the derivative directions.

This is a local refinement and vector-space generalization of the
global phase-extraction mechanism. Its scope, counterexamples, and
normalizations are explicit enough for a formalization project.
Whether the sharp profile and its stability theory can be made to
improve a full quantitative inverse argument is left as a separate,
well-defined research task. The package supplies proofs and checks
for the results stated here; it does not claim formal verification,
literature priority, or an improved final Ramsey bound.

\section[{Verification and repository integration\srctag{37}}]{Verification and repository integration}\label{gsr:fz:37:sec:d10}\label{gsr:fz:37:sec:verification}
\srcnote{37}{Section 10}

\subsection{What the accompanying checks do}
The archive contains \codethirtyseven{verify.py}, its dependency list, the captured
run, and \codethirtyseven{verification_results.json}. The random seed is fixed at
$20261006$. The run used Python 3.13.5, NumPy 2.3.5, SciPy 1.17.0, and
SymPy 1.14.0. The checks have the following coverage.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.62\textwidth}r@{}}
\toprule
Check & Number\\
\midrule
Exact symbolic autocorrelation identities & 36\\
Exact symbolic moments in the $R=2$ example & 2\\
Polynomial, matrix, root, and weight cases ($1\le R\le24$) & 120\\
Independent discretized empty-gap minimax programs & 50\\
Mass-minimization linear programs with contact nodes & 200\\
Nonempty finite-cyclic indicator cases ($3\le N\le12$) & 5,411\\
Random critical-stability measure checks & 300\\
Exact rational recurrence-rounding checks & 1,000\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The largest root-modulus residual was $2.42\cdot10^{-14}$ after rounding
up, and the largest extremal-moment residual was $8.93\cdot10^{-14}$.
The independent gap programs used $2001$ mesh points and exceeded the exact
formula by at most $4.94\cdot10^{-7}$, as expected from discretization;
the smallest difference was about $-1.90\cdot10^{-13}$ from solver error.
The mass programs, with exact contact locations included numerically, had
maximum absolute error below $1.90\cdot10^{-8}$.

These are regression checks, not proof certificates. In particular,
floating-point semidefiniteness, unit-modulus roots, and optimal LP values
are not used to establish the mathematical theorems. The analytic proof of
attainment is Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:37:thm:moment} together with
Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:37:lem:rankone}. The exact rational rounding checks verify the
arithmetic inequalities in the recurrence conversion, not the external
Weyl estimate. No Lean formalization is included or claimed.

\subsection{Suggested integration boundary}
A suitable new directory is
\begin{quote}\small
\codethirtyseven{Combinatorics/Ramsey/Research/GowersSzemeredi/sharp-missing-intervals/}.
\end{quote}
The manuscript should initially remain a research source. Existing
\codethirtyseven{Section05.lean} targets should not be silently redefined, and the
status ledger should not be marked proved on the basis of this PDF.
A separate collection of strengthened statements can preserve compatibility
with the already formalized statements.

A practical formalization can be split into two tracks. The lower-bound
track needs only the coefficient formula, positivity, a finite Fourier
expansion, and summation against nonnegative weights. It does not need the
moment-existence theorem, unit-circle root geometry, or measure separation.
The equality track adds the supported moment criterion and the rank argument.
This separation prevents the sharpness proof from becoming a dependency of
the useful finite-cyclic inequality.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.29\textwidth}p{0.57\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Proposed statement & Main mathematical dependencies\\
\midrule
Positive gap certificate & Trigonometric recurrence; autocorrelation identity\\
Weighted linear-cutoff lemma & Certificate; finite Fourier sum; nonnegative weights\\
Exact first-window optimum & Arc positivity; Toeplitz/localizing matrices; rank\\
Noisy-gap uniqueness & Certificate slack; Vandermonde injectivity\\
Critical concentration & Sine polynomial; elementary sine lower bound\\
Recurrence conversion & Weighted lemma; Dirichlet; existing Weyl companion\\
Short-step interface & Recurrence conversion; integer square-root inequalities\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\subsection{A finite Fourier interface}
The following is a mathematical specification, not Lean code:
\begin{quote}
For $N\ge2$, $1\le M$, $2M\le N$, and $w:\Z/N\Z\to\R_{
\ge0}$, if $\sum w>0$ and $w$ vanishes on $|x|_N<M$, there is an integer
$1\le r<N$ with $r\le N\mathbin{\mathrm{div}}M-1$ and
\[
 -\Rea\widehat w(r)\ge\frac{M}{N-M}\sum_xw(x).
\]
\end{quote}
Using an integer frequency and then casting it into $\Z/N\Z$ avoids
ambiguity about centered representatives. A second lemma can convert to the
existing \codethirtyseven{centeredAbs} interface. The empty-weight case should be
handled separately rather than divide by zero.

For empirical measures, the implementation should use a finite sum over
sample indices or a multiplicity function. Replacing it by the image set
would change both the mass and the Fourier sum. The existing repository
already contains the needed collision-safe pattern.
