\section[{Further research problems\srctag{37}}]{Further research problems}\label{gsr:fz:37:sec:d11}\label{gsr:fz:37:sec:questions}
\srcnote{37}{Section 11}

The following problems separate plausible extensions of the present
calculation from much larger conjectural consequences. They are proposed
research questions, not claims that the wider literature has no answers.

\begin{question}[Beyond the first window]\label{gsr:fz:37:q:windows}
Determine
$\inf_{\mu\in\Probthirtyseven(K_a)}\max_{1\le r\le R}|\widehat\mu(r)|$
when $a>2\pi/(R+1)$, including exact extremizers and transition points.
Does a finite sequence of contact-pattern changes lead to an explicit
piecewise algebraic description in $\cos a$ for each fixed $R$?
\end{question}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 82--94]
\emph{Answered for $R=4$ and advanced for every $R$} by sources~90 and~93 (Section~\ref{gsr:dt:sec:phifour}): all seven branches of $\Phi_4$ with unique extremizers, an algebraic branch with an irrational transition angle, the maximal first continuation and a final band at every cutoff. The finite description for fixed $R\ge5$ is open; both sources ask for $\Phi_5$ (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:I:missing}).
\end{writenote}
The prescribed equimoment matrix ceases to be positive once $\rho>1/R$,
so continuing the tangent formula is not justified. A successful extension
must change either the active moment pattern or the primal support.
The small-dimensional cases can be explored by the supplied LP code, but
attainment and optimality still require analytic certificates.

\begin{question}[Exact finite-grid corrections]\label{gsr:fz:37:q:grid}
For fixed $N,M,R$, solve the same extremal problem with support restricted
to $\Z/N\Z$, and distinguish open from half-open exclusions. Quantify the
excess over the continuous optimum in terms of the distances from the
continuous contact nodes to the grid.
\end{question}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 82--94]
\emph{Advanced} by sources~90 and~93: exact grid formulas and the leading oscillating correction on the central branch of $\Phi_4$, and the aligned semicircle formula, $(\sqrt3-1)/2$ when $12\mid N$ (source~93's Theorems~\ref{gsr:dt:93:grid:certificate}--\ref{gsr:dt:93:grid:half-circle}, source~90's Theorems~\ref{gsr:dt:90:thm:gridexact}--\ref{gsr:dt:90:thm:semicircleallorders}).
\end{writenote}
The lower certificate survives sampling exactly, whereas the equality
measure may not fit the grid. A second-order upper approximation is
plausible when all relevant nodes can be moved within the allowed arc;
endpoint constraints can produce a different first-order behavior. A
complete result must account for both effects and positivity of the
perturbed masses.

\begin{question}[Uniform stability constants]\label{gsr:fz:37:q:stability}
Obtain useful bounds for $\kappa$ and $\sigma$ in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:37:thm:stable} as $R\to\infty$ with
$(R+1)a$ in a compact subinterval of $(\pi,2\pi)$. Can a suitable rescaling
of angular distance give constants independent of $R$?
\end{question}
The critical estimate \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:criticalstable} suggests geometric control
may be much better than a generic Vandermonde estimate. Weight recovery is
likely the more delicate part. One should distinguish transport toward an
unweighted contact set from transport to the uniquely weighted extremizer.

\begin{question}[Unequal Fourier budgets]\label{gsr:fz:37:q:anisotropic}
Given $\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_R$, determine the least possible
$\mu(I_a)$ subject to $|\widehat\mu(r)|\le\varepsilon_r$.
Characterize the region of budget vectors for which the certificate of
Section~\ref{gsr:dt:37:sec:certificate} remains optimal.
\end{question}
The available lower bound is
$d-2\sum f_r\varepsilon_r$. Equality would require a measure on the same
contact set with prescribed negative real moments. This turns local
optimality into a finite feasibility problem; its positivity constraints
may describe a computable cone or polytope in a suitable parameterization.

\begin{question}[Several forbidden arcs]\label{gsr:fz:37:q:multiarcs}
Find sharp Fourier detection results for a union of missing arcs, and
compare their cutoff requirements with the total excluded length and the
largest individual gap. Which arrangements of arcs force simultaneous
large coefficients at several frequencies?
\end{question}
The one-arc sign factor $\cos\theta-\cos a$ is no longer sufficient.
Products of sign factors give certificates, but their Fourier coefficient
signs and optimal degrees become nontrivial. This connects directly with
multi-band moment representations rather than with a routine rescaling of
the single-gap argument.

\begin{question}[Parameter optimization in the recurrence conversion]
\label{gsr:fz:37:q:constants}
Use the exact frontier $\rho_R(2\pi\delta)$, rather than the simplified
$\delta/(1-\delta)$ bound, and optimize the cutoff, Dirichlet scale, and
constant allocations simultaneously. Determine the best constant obtainable
from the fixed Weyl input and this one-step architecture.
\end{question}
The exponent $1/(D+1)$ in the present conversion reflects the powers in
that architecture. Improving its numerical constant is a different task
from proving that no more efficient recurrence argument exists.

\begin{question}[Propagating the short-step estimate]\label{gsr:fz:37:q:propagation}
Rework the degree induction for polynomial phase partitions using
\eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:short}. What improved target-length exponent and threshold follow
once every lower-coefficient term and every integer rounding loss is
retained? Then propagate only the verified improvements through the later
inverse and density-increment steps.
\end{question}
This is the direct route from the present local work toward a stronger
quantitative Szemer\'edi statement. A plausible local improvement is not
itself the global theorem; a full parameter ledger is needed.

\begin{question}[Additional structure in polynomial empirical measures]
\label{gsr:fz:37:q:polynomialmeasure}
Can the moment problem be improved when the measure is known to be
$T^{-1}\sum_{n\le T}\delta_{\alpha n^k}$, rather than arbitrary? In
particular, can its near equality with $\mu_{R,a}$ be excluded or exploited
to force a better recurrence estimate?
\end{question}
The extremizers here have $R+1$ specially placed atoms and negative equal
moments. A polynomial orbit may approximate such a measure only for special
arithmetic reasons. Turning that observation into a quantitative dichotomy
would use the equality and stability theory rather than only the numerical
coefficient bound.

\begin{question}[Certified symbolic extremizers and formalization]
\label{gsr:fz:37:q:formal}
For algebraic $\cos a$, produce exact algebraic descriptions of the
contact nodes and positive weights, with certificates small enough for a
proof assistant. Formalize first the finite lower-bound track and then the
independent sharpness track described in Section~\ref{gsr:fz:37:sec:verification}.
\end{question}
The recurrence proof for $w$, the coefficient identity, and the rank-one
matrix decomposition are natural certificate objects. Root-location
verification need not be a separate numerical task because the moment-rank
argument proves it structurally.

\begin{question}[Classical extremal interpretations and priority]
\label{gsr:fz:37:q:priority}
Identify the precise relationship of the formula \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:rho} and the
extremizing quadrature to classical trigonometric moment bounds, extremal
positive polynomials, and finite power-sum inequalities. Which parts are
known in equivalent language, and which refinements or stability statements
are genuinely new?
\end{question}
The general positivity machinery is already classical. Establishing the
historical status of the closed formula and its consequences requires a
more targeted literature comparison than recognizing that machinery.
The proofs in this manuscript do not depend on a novelty claim.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Conclusion\srctag{37}}]{Conclusion}\label{gsr:fz:37:sec:d12}
\srcnote{37}{Section 12}
The missing-interval step admits a sharp, exactly attainable Fourier
formulation in the first spectral window. Its certificate has three useful
features at once: the correct sign on the complementary arc, strictly
positive nonconstant Fourier coefficients, and an explicit equality
measure certified by a rank-one localizing matrix. This yields a robust
mass tradeoff and rigidity, not just an isolated large-coefficient lemma.

For the selected Gowers argument, the immediate substitution is concrete:
frequency at most $\lfloor N/M\rfloor-1$ and coefficient at least
$|A|M/(N-M)$, instead of the proof-supported quadratic cutoff and
$|A|M/(4N)$. Optimizing the following rational approximation gives the
explicit exponent $b_k$ in \eqref{gsr:dt:37:eq:explicitAb}, with its constant and
short-step threshold displayed. The package is intended as a research
source for careful integration and formalization. Global parameter
propagation and historical priority remain separate tasks.

\section[{What the calculations verify\srctag{38}}]{What the calculations verify}\label{gsr:fz:38:sec:d8}
\srcnote{38}{Section 8}
\gsrsrcpartof{38}{Verification, integration, and further research}
\label{gsr:fz:38:sec:verification}

The universal assertions in Parts~I--III follow from the written proofs.
The accompanying programs check finite identities, rational constants,
symbolic series, and representative numerical instances independently.
Their roles differ, and the output files identify which operations are
exact and which use floating-point arithmetic.

\subsection{Algebraic and finite checks}

The exact symbolic calculation in \file{code/verify_quotient.py}
reconstructs the fixed-phase norm solution and checks the coefficients
through tenth order. Its separate finite-group calculation evaluates
the full Fourier-square sum on $\F_5^2$, compares it with the centered
polynomial, and checks the retained projection defect. It uses $160$
reproducible random inputs, including functions close to a principal
Fourier pair. Among these, $62$ satisfy the local coercivity hypotheses
with a numerically resolvable positive norm loss. The largest centered
polynomial discrepancy is less than $5\cdot10^{-16}$; the smallest
observed improvement divided by $t^4\Delta$ is greater than $3.18$.
These are consistency checks on examples, not estimates used in the
dimension-uniform proof.

The separate program \file{code/verify_twelfth_order.py} checks the
norm recursion, the Hessian, amplitude and phase displacements, and
all terms in the optimized twelfth-order coefficient by exact symbolic
arithmetic. It also verifies the signed-parameter symmetry. Its
high-precision calculation solves the exact stationary equations at
three positive parameter values. The mathematical compactness and
implicit-function argument, rather than this numerical solver,
establishes that the stationary branch gives every global maximum
near zero.

For the broader odd-order expansion, the program
\file{code/verify_odd_cube_expansion.py} directly enumerates physical
cubes on $C_3,C_3^2,C_5,C_7,C_9,C_{15}$ and compares every coefficient
with the Fourier formulas. Thus the test includes nonprime cyclic
orders and order-three torsion. It is independent of the
Fourier-square implementation in the characteristic-five test.

The standard-library program \file{code/verify_odd_rigidity.py}
checks the exact three-point and five-point support multiplicities,
then verifies the Weyl expansion and the finite envelope on $120$
reproducible random vectors over $C_3,C_5,C_7,C_9,C_{15},C_{25}$.
The largest expansion residual is below $8\cdot10^{-16}$.
Finally, \file{code/verify_six_ap_defect.py} performs the exact
finite-field computations detailed in Part~III. Those checks use
integer arithmetic and exhaust all relevant field elements and
target values for the two stated base fields.

\subsection{High-precision illustrations}

Figure~\ref{gsr:fz:38:fig:coefficients} displays two explicit families after
subtracting the earlier terms in their asymptotic expansions.
On the left, the five-point family uses the limiting phases and the
corrected amplitude
\[
 b=(q_0/3)t^2+(31q_0^2/27)t^4,
\]
with the principal amplitude determined by the exact norm equation.
This family attains the sharp tenth-order coefficient. Its phases
have not been adjusted, so it does not attain the sharp twelfth-order
coefficient. On the right is the exact three-point family in Part~II.
The variable $\varepsilon$ there is its actual deficit $1-\kappa$.
The displayed residuals are
\begin{align*}
 \mathcal C_{10}(t)
  &=\frac{Q_{\mathrm{fam}}(t)-1-6\sqrt2\,t^4
       -(2^{3/4}/3)t^6-(20/9)t^8}{t^{10}},\\
 \mathcal R_{\mathrm{odd}}(\varepsilon)
  &=\frac{t-\varepsilon/4-3\varepsilon^2/16}{\varepsilon^{5/2}}.
\end{align*}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/38-quotients-asymptotic_coefficients.pdf}
\caption{Residuals for two explicit families. The dashed lines are
the proved limits $869/(216\,2^{3/4})$ and $\sqrt2/64$.
The plotted values are computed at $120$ decimal digits; they are
illustrations, not numerical certificates of global optimality.}
\label{gsr:fz:38:fig:coefficients}
\end{figure}

The program \file{code/make_figures.py} writes the figure and its
underlying CSV data. It uses $121$ parameter values in each panel
and records the precision and norm-equation residual. At the smallest
plotted five-point parameter, the tenth-order residual differs from
its limit by less than $4\cdot10^{-12}$. The high precision is useful
because subtracting the preceding asymptotic terms at ordinary
machine precision would conceal the coefficient being plotted.

\section[{Integration with the ProveIt development\srctag{38}}]{Integration with the ProveIt development}\label{gsr:fz:38:sec:d9}
\srcnote{38}{Section 9}
\label{gsr:fz:38:sec:integration}

\subsection{The exact connection to Gowers' lemmas}

The direct strengthening of Gowers' Lemma~3.10 is
Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:38:cor:pf-indicator-bound}: for degree-two uniformity
parameter $\alpha$, it replaces the triangle-inequality envelope
$(\delta+\alpha^{1/8})^8$ by the exact small-norm profile in the
specified exponent-five setting. The fixed-odd-exponent theorem
extends the structural reduction, even where the resulting cyclic
profile has not yet been explicitly computed. These statements
have narrower arithmetic hypotheses than the original all-modulus
lemma and substantially more precise conclusions within that scope.

The proofs also strengthen how Lemmas~3.8 and~3.9 are used. Their
usual upper estimates discard the location of Fourier mass.
The retained energy inequality \eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:projection-coercivity}
and the linear seventh-degree estimate \eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:seven-linear-loss}
turn a non-strict norm comparison into a strict improvement whenever
a candidate has Fourier mass outside the selected cyclic subgroup.
Part~II addresses a different endpoint: it quantifies near equality
in the critical $U^3$--$L^2$ inequality, while Part~III supplies an
exact count for an extension of the layered norm method associated
with the progression questions in Gowers' Section~4.

\subsection{Formal status and normalization}

The inspected checkpoint \file{FORMALIZATION_STATUS.txt} reports
$206$ compiled modules, $1{,}878$ audited public Gowers theorems,
$100$ exact companion proofs, and $20$ open catalogue statements
\cite{repo38}. These are the repository's reported results at the
pinned commit. This project inspected the relevant source files;
it did not reproduce that build. No new theorem in this article
has been checked by the Lean kernel.

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 34--39]
\emph{Checked at HEAD \texttt{89c1cbc38}.} The counts above are those of the pin; at HEAD \file{FORMALIZATION\_STATUS.txt} reports 410 modules and 2,840 audited public theorems, and the ledger 107 exact companions and 13 open statements (the source's \file{SOURCE\_LEDGER.json}, shipped as \file{data/38-quotients-SOURCE\_LEDGER.json}, keeps the pin's $206$, $1{,}878$, $100$ and $20$; recorded, not edited). \file{lemma_3_10} and its companion are unchanged; the four Lean files named in the table below exist with the blobs the source records. No statement of this source is formalized.
\end{writenote}

The existing declaration \file{lemma_3_10} and its companion
\file{lemma_3_10_holds} should retain their present scope. The new
theorems are separate refinements with explicit realness, centering,
odd-order or exponent assumptions. In particular, a proof on
$\F_5^n$ cannot be substituted for a theorem on arbitrary
$\Z/N\Z$ without changing its statement.

The repository's Section~3 cube form uses unnormalized sums.
For a group of order $N$, its three-cube norm is $N^{1/2}$ times
the normalized $U^3$ norm used here, and its three-cube count is
$N^4\Qthirtyeight(W)$. A formal interface should prove these normalization
equalities first. For general cube dimension $d$, the corresponding
norm factor is $N^{(d+1)/2^d}$. Losing these factors would change
both the hypotheses and the powers of the density in the result.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}P{.26\textwidth}YY@{}}
\toprule
Mathematical component & Existing interface inspected & New proof work\\
\midrule

\bottomrule

A practical order is to formalize the finite algebraic statements
before the analytic extremal expansion. The Fourier-square identity,
the rational cutoff, the six-point interpolation matrix, and the
quadratic-form count have exact finite certificates. The analytic
profile additionally needs compactness, an implicit-function theorem,
and a justified Taylor remainder; symbolic output alone is not a
formal proof of these steps. The programs are designed to expose
the identities such a development would need, without presenting
uncompiled Lean placeholders as checked results.

The archive supplies a complete TeX manuscript, its bibliography and
figure, verification programs, and build instructions. The source
ledger records the inspected repository checkpoint and preceding
reports, preserving the distinction between earlier and new results.

\section[{Proposed further research questions and topics\srctag{38}}]{Proposed further research questions and topics}\label{gsr:fz:38:sec:d10}
\srcnote{38}{Section 10}
\label{gsr:fz:38:sec:research-questions}

The following questions are proposed continuations of the proved
results. They are not claimed to constitute an exhaustive survey of
open problems. The characteristic-five eighth-order question and
the odd-order asymptotic coefficient question from the preceding reports
should be replaced by the resolved statements above. The problems
below concern the stronger conclusions that remain out of reach
of the present arguments.

\begingroup\small
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{\arabic*.},leftmargin=*,itemsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
\item \textbf{Determine the sharp range of exact quotient reduction.}
Define $c_5^*$ as the supremum of $c$ for which every exponent-five
maximizer factors through a five-point quotient whenever
$0<u/\delta<c$. Is $c_5^*$ finite, and what first destroys the
quotient conclusion? The proof gives $c_5^*\ge10^{-5}$.
A useful next step is to compute the exact second variation against
off-quotient perturbations along the analytic five-point branch,
then distinguish a local instability from a crossing with a distant
competing maximum.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
\item \textbf{Decide whether the odd-exponent cutoff must depend on the exponent.}
The sufficient constant $10^{-8}m^{-8}$ comes from summing bounds
over up to $m^2$ Fourier-square slots. Can a global square-sum estimate
remove that dependence, giving one positive cutoff for all odd
exponents? If not, construct an explicit sequence of odd-order groups
and genuinely noncyclic extremizers at parameters tending to zero.
Either outcome would explain the precise scope of the projection
principle.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
\item \textbf{Classify the cyclic profiles and their arithmetic transitions.}
Compute the first unresolved terms of
$\mathcal M_{1,\Z/m\Z}(t)$ for small odd $m$, and determine which
character order supports a maximum when $m$ has several odd prime
divisors. Order three already supplies a fifth-degree contribution,
whereas the exponent-five profile has the secondary scale studied
here. A systematic classification should record the frequency
relations responsible for each power and decide when fractional
powers occur.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
\item \textbf{Find an exact algebraic description of the five-point branch.}
The norm constraint and stationary equations give a finite algebraic
system after replacing phase angles by their sines and cosines.
Can it be eliminated to an explicit equation for the extremal value
with a certified branch-selection interval? Determine the first
nonzero term, if any, in $\alpha(t)-\pi/10$ after its third-order
cancellation, and the symmetries behind subsequent phase coefficients.
An answer would make the convergence radius and the higher coefficient
recursion more concrete.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
\item \textbf{Optimize the quotient-stability constants and powers.}
Determine the best constants, and the sharp dependence on the
extremal deficit, in
\eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:quotient-stability-u2}--\eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:quotient-stability-u3}.
The factor $256$ comes from a general convexity estimate and has
not been optimized for this Fourier geometry. Constructing
perturbations in one additional frequency coset is a controlled
way to test which exponents and constants can be improved.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
\item \textbf{Describe the constrained weighted profile beyond the interior regime.}
When the maximizing five-point function first reaches $0$ or $1$,
which coordinates saturate, and does exact quotient reduction
continue? Determine the resulting piecewise extremal profile at a
fixed density. Separately, quantify how fast indicator sets in
growing product groups can approximate these weights in the
uniformity norms relevant to the cube count. The variance in
$L^2$ must be treated on its own terms.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
\item \textbf{Determine the next sharp odd-order stability coefficient.}
Find the coefficient of $\varepsilon^3$ in
$\mathfrak S_{\rm odd}(\varepsilon)$. Does the three-point family
remain extremal at that order, or can perturbations outside its
two tangent eigencharacters improve the value? The tangent-rigidity
corollary narrows the search to perturbations around an order-three
pair. Resolving the next variation would also indicate whether
there is an exact finite-parameter odd-order modulus.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
\item \textbf{Solve the coprime-to-six local extremal problem more precisely.}
With order-three resonance excluded, determine the optimal cubic
term in the deficit and whether a fixed cyclic group realizes it.
The two-state five-point family proves the displayed second-order
sharpness, but it need not settle the subsequent coefficient.
This is a separate problem from optimizing the coarse constant
$104$ in the finite envelope.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
\item \textbf{Make local rigidity constructive from sampled derivative data.}
The proof identifies a large Weyl subgroup and then a common
eigenvector. Can this argument be converted into an efficient
reconstruction procedure with error constants approaching the
sharp modulus? The relevant input may be an approximate ambiguity
table or samples of it, rather than the complete function. A useful
formulation should distinguish arithmetic cost, sampling cost,
and the dependence on the exponent.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
\item \textbf{Develop sharp critical stability for higher Gowers norms.}
For $U^d$, the natural critical exponent is
$p_d=2^d/(d+1)$ \cite{eisnertao}. Determine the leading stability
coefficient near a polynomial phase supported on a coset, and
identify any torsion-dependent fractional corrections. The exact
$L^2$ Weyl identity used here is specific to $d=3$; a higher-order
argument must replace that Hilbert-space mechanism.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
\item \textbf{Calculate the eight-term and higher norm-extension defects.}
The next complete core contains norms of degrees $1,3,5,7$.
Determine the joint distributions of the polarized coefficients
that remain after the top direction is fixed. In the six-term
case only the quadratic statistic $e_2$ was needed; higher layers
bring several interacting coefficients. An exact formula, or a
uniform error estimate around its natural mean, would extend
Part~III in a substantive way.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
\item \textbf{Obtain a stability theorem for small norm-extension defect.}
If $A_6^{\mathrm{sym}}(P)$ is close to its baseline, how close must
$R$ be to an additive quadratic? Formula~\eqref{gsr:cc:38:eq:six-ap-defect}
first controls the fraction of nonzero third and fifth differences.
The remaining task is a quantitative polynomiality theorem with
constants uniform in the number of added coordinates. Determine
the correct dependence on the characteristic and on the extension
degree of the base field.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
\item \textbf{Resolve the global quintic four-term avoidance dimension.}
The preceding degree-stratification report leaves the maximum
dimension for a degree-five coloring without a nontrivial symmetric
four-term progression between four and eight \cite{repo38degrees}.
The independent-extension obstruction does not resolve this gap.
Can a genuinely coupled quintic construction exceed the known
four-dimensional construction, or does a stronger global argument
force a smaller upper threshold than the pointwise degree count?

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
\item \textbf{Certify the new exact identities in the formal development.}
Begin with the centered cube coefficients and the energy coercivity,
then the finite-field fiber calculation and the Weyl-coset
expansion. These pieces can be reviewed separately and are useful
without the analytic optimization. A later proof of exact quotient
reduction should preserve the strict deficit and the explicit
cutoff, rather than formalizing only a weakened asymptotic bound.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
\item \textbf{Locate a genuine bridge to global progression bounds.}
Identify a density-increment or transference argument in which
one of these sharper local statements survives all subsequent
losses. Such an application must explicitly reconcile the
bounded-exponent setting with the ambient group used to model
long integer progressions. Write out the resulting recurrence
and solve it before claiming an improvement of the global bound.
This problem is logically additional to the local extremal
theorems proved in this article.
\end{enumerate}
\endgroup

\section[{A precise interface with the inspected Gowers development\srctag{39}}]{A precise interface with the inspected Gowers development}\label{gsr:fz:39:sec:d12}
\srcnote{39}{Section 12}
\label{gsr:fz:39:sec:repo}

\subsection{Source controls and the already existing improvements}
In this section $q$ denotes the number of vertical affine classes and $b$ the
complexity parameter of each horizontal section. We deliberately do not use
$s$ for both a class size and a section complexity.

Let $c(u,\gamma,k)$ and $Q(u,\gamma,k)$ denote the source's positive scale and
graph controls, represented by \filename{multipleC} and \filename{multipleQ}.
For a horizontal section of complexity $b$, the relevant one-slice form is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:39:eq:source-controls}
 a(\tau)=c(\tau/b,\gamma,k)^b,\qquad
 L(\tau)=Q(\tau/b,\gamma,k)^b.
\end{equation}
These symbols retain their source meaning; the present article does not
redefine their dimension-dependent exponents.

The inspected \filename{Proofs16RecoveredSliceCover.lean} already gives a common
refinement with
\begin{align}
 P&\le Q(\epsilon/(rb),\gamma,k)^{rb},\label{gsr:fz:39:eq:repo-common-list}\\
 \text{base width}&\ge
 M^{c(\epsilon/(rb),\gamma,k)^{rb}},\label{gsr:fz:39:eq:repo-width}
\end{align}
and a recovered candidate index set of cardinality
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:39:eq:repo-candidates}
 rP+r^2P^2.
\end{equation}
Its geometric successor imposes a short-parent width condition and performs
synchronization without a further candidate blow-up
\cite{repo39recovered,repo39syncslice}. In particular, the linear dependence on
$r$ in the refinement exponent is \emph{already present} in this snapshot;
it is not a new conclusion being attributed to this article.

\subsection{Replacing the sample while keeping the existing interface}

\begin{proposition}[Sampled-or-anchored output]\label{gsr:fz:39:prop:repo-interface}
Suppose $\phi$ on a partial subset $D$ of $H\times J$ is covered, on every
vertical fibre, by at most $q$ affine functions over a field. For every
$1\le r\le m$, there is an injectively enumerated sample of $r$ columns and
sets $K\subseteq F\subseteq H\times J$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item the complement of $F$ has ambient mass at most
      $2q(m-r)/(m(r+1))$;
\item every point of $D\cap F$ is either in $K$ or on a sampled column;
\item every point of $D\cap K$ has two distinct sampled anchors in the same
      row, both in $D\cap K$, from whose values it is recovered by
      \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:affine-interpolant}.
\end{enumerate}
These are the mathematical contents needed by the repository's
\filename{Section16SampledOrAnchoredOn} interface.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
In each row assign each point of $D$ to one of the affine graphs that covers
it, for example the first one in a fixed ordering of the $q$ graphs. This
makes a disjoint class partition. Apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:39:thm:selection} with
$t=2$. Let $F=E_R$ be its ambient good set and let $K$ be the union, over all
rows, of the full classes containing at least two sampled columns.

Every such full class is contained in $F$, so $K\subseteq F$. A domain point
of $F$ not in $K$ survives precisely because its column is sampled. For a
point of $K$, choose two sampled members of its own class. They too belong to
that full class and hence to $D\cap K$. They have distinct column values, and
the affine interpolation identity follows from the common affine class
function. Enumerating the set $R$ produces an injective sample.
\end{proof}

\begin{writenote}[6 October 2026; sources 34--39]
\emph{Checked at HEAD \texttt{89c1cbc38}.} \file{Section16SampledOrAnchoredOn} is at \file{Proofs16ShortColumns.lean}, line~27; the seven \file{Proofs16} files the source cites have the blobs it records. The proposition is a formalization candidate (an exact double count over $(r+1)$-subsets), claimed by nobody; the same $O(q/\sigma)$ sampler is source~19's (note in Section~\ref{gsr:fm:39:sec:d1}), which should be credited first. \file{lemma_16_10} (\file{Section16.lean}, line~851) is open; nothing here changes that, as the source says.
\end{writenote}

The point that the anchors belong to $K$, not just to the larger set $F$, is
useful: it matches the nested anchored-subset predicate in the repository.
This is why we take $K$ to contain whole sufficiently sampled classes, rather
than just the nonsampled targets.

In the finite-field implementation $J\subseteq\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ with $N$
prime, distinct column values have invertible difference. The set-theoretic
sample theorem itself does not need primality. Over a general ring the same
algebraic interface would need unit differences for the chosen anchors;
nonzero difference alone would not suffice.

\subsection{A parameter-explicit local replacement}

\begin{theorem}[Local affine lift with the existing common-cover bounds]
\label{gsr:fz:39:thm:repo-local}
Assume the vertical affine cover of Proposition~\ref{gsr:fz:39:prop:repo-interface},
and assume the horizontal sections satisfy the source's common-cover
hypothesis with parameters $(\gamma,b,k)$. For $0<\eta,\epsilon<1$, choose
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:39:eq:local-r}
 r=\min\{m,\lceil2q/\eta\rceil\}.
\end{equation}
At the level of base cells times the final-coordinate set, the existing
common-cover and interpolation conclusions apply with exceptional fraction
at most $\eta+\epsilon$, width bound \eqref{gsr:fz:39:eq:repo-width}, and at most
$rP+r^2P^2$ candidates, with $P$ as in \eqref{gsr:fz:39:eq:repo-common-list}.

If, in addition, the labelled hereditary hypothesis
\eqref{gsr:fz:39:eq:source-controls} is used while preserving the required admissible
base cells, the same width bound is obtained with candidate bound
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:39:eq:improved-local-list}
 rL+\binom r2L^2,\qquad
 L=Q(\epsilon/(rb),\gamma,k)^b.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Proposition~\ref{gsr:fz:39:prop:repo-interface} and Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:39:cor:budget} provide
the sampled-or-anchored good set with error at most $\eta$ and an $r$-term
sample. The already established common-cover and recovered-slice conclusions
then give the first assertion, losing another $\epsilon$ in the base.
Equivalently, their purely algebraic covering step is the $t=2$ case of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:39:thm:labelled}, with the common list bound $P$ used for every
anchor and an ordered-pair indexing convention.

For the labelled version, apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:39:thm:refinement} with
$\tau_i=\epsilon/r$ and the one-slice controls \eqref{gsr:fz:39:eq:source-controls}.
The product of the scale powers is
\[
 \prod_{i=1}^r c(\epsilon/(rb),\gamma,k)^b
       =c(\epsilon/(rb),\gamma,k)^{rb},
\]
whereas each individual list has size at most
$Q(\epsilon/(rb),\gamma,k)^b=L$. Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:39:cor:affine-list} supplies
\eqref{gsr:fz:39:eq:improved-local-list}. The same error addition applies.
\end{proof}

The first part is a direct mathematical replacement at an existing interface;
it requires no redesign of geometric synchronization. The second part is a
proved refinement theorem with explicit hypotheses and a proposed way to
retain more information in the implementation. It is not claimed that the
new labelled version has already been formalized in the repository.

If the maximum permitted common list size is written as $P=L^r$, the old
upper-budget expression is $rL^r+r^2L^{2r}$, while
\eqref{gsr:fz:39:eq:improved-local-list} is $rL+\binom r2L^2$. This comparison concerns
\emph{guaranteed list budgets}, not necessarily the actual number of distinct
graphs produced by either method. Both arguments may have extensive
redundancies in a particular instance.

\subsection{Geometry must remain a separate hypothesis}
A product of a refined base box and an arbitrary final-coordinate progression
is not automatically a proper common-step box. The repository explicitly
separates these issues. Its synchronization statement
\cite{repo39sync} uses a short parent progression for one axis of each refined
base cell, parallel to the original final progression $I$, and with unit
step. The parent is short relative to the ambient modulus, has length at most
$|I|$, and contains the chosen refined axis. A further inequality of the form
\[
 v^2\le\text{refined base width}-1
\]
allows compatible final-axis tiling. Under these hypotheses it produces
proper common-step boxes of width at least $v-1$, without increasing the list
of candidates or the exceptional set.

In the source's assembled short-parent version, a sufficient real-valued
budget is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:39:eq:synchronization-budget}
 v^2+1\le (m_0/8)^{c(\epsilon/(rb),\gamma,k)^{rb}},
\end{equation}
where $m_0\ge4$ is an input common lower width, not the column-set cardinality
$m$ used in our sampling lemmas \cite{repo39syncslice}. Appropriate properness,
unit-step, and containment assumptions are also required.

\begin{corollary}[Conditional synchronized lift]\label{gsr:fz:39:cor:geometric}
If the base refinement supplied in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fz:39:thm:repo-local} has the
short-parent containment and width hypotheses of the source synchronization
lemma, its rectangular cover can be replaced by the corresponding proper
common-step box cover with the same exceptional fraction and the same
candidate bound. This applies to the labelled bound
\eqref{gsr:fz:39:eq:improved-local-list} when the labelled refinement preserves those
hypotheses.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Synchronization partitions each rectangular product into compatible boxes
and restricts the candidates from its base cell to the resulting boxes.
Restriction preserves the candidate identities and multilinearity. The
source tiling covers the whole rectangle, so there is no additional discarded
mass. Its width conclusion is exactly the assumed synchronization conclusion.
\end{proof}

This corollary is conditional on stated geometric input. It must not be read
as proving that any abstract common refinement automatically satisfies that
input, or as replacing an unproved scale comparison by the word
``synchronization.''

\subsection{Equal-error budget comparison}
For a final sampling error allowance $\eta$, the inspected corrected sampler
can use $\tau=\eta/2$ and the sufficient budget
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:39:eq:old-matched}
 r_{\rm corrected}=\left\lceil\frac{24q}{\eta^2}\right\rceil,
\end{equation}
with the short-column alternative handled as in the source
\cite{repo39anchored,repo39short}. Our sufficient distinct-anchor budget is
\eqref{gsr:fz:39:eq:local-r}. The comparison is at the same error allowance; comparing
$6q/\tau^2$ with $2q/\eta$ without noting $\eta=2\tau$ would conceal a change
of convention.

As a numerical illustration, take $q=100$, $\eta=0.01$, and a column set
large enough that neither of these budgets needs truncation. Formula
\eqref{gsr:fz:39:eq:old-matched} gives $24{,}000{,}000$, while
\eqref{gsr:fz:39:eq:local-r} gives $20{,}000$. This is a comparison of sufficient local
budgets, not an empirical running-time measurement. The asymptotic minimax
budget in a sufficiently sparse-sampling limit is about $8{,}399.62$, but
that number is \emph{not} a certified finite replacement for $20{,}000$ at an
unspecified value of $m$.

\subsection{The closing comparison is not proved here}
The inspected file \filename{Proofs16ClosingComparison.lean} proves that the
same-dimensional numerical comparison in the edited closing argument has the
wrong direction \cite{repo39closing}. In its parameter range,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:39:eq:closing-obstruction}
 Q(\rho,\gamma,k)
 <Q\!\left(\frac{\rho}{4p},\gamma,k\right)^p
 \qquad(0<\gamma,\rho\le1,\ p\ge1).
\end{equation}
It also records an endpoint obstruction with possibly different source and
target dimensions: $Q(1,1,d)=1$, while shrinking the positive error argument
below $1$ and raising the corresponding graph budget to a positive power
produces a number greater than $1$.

The new sampler changes $r$, and the labelled refinement changes the local
candidate count. Neither fact reverses \eqref{gsr:fz:39:eq:closing-obstruction} or
proves every prescribed dimension-dependent control. Theorem~\ref{gsr:fz:39:thm:repo-local}
therefore states the output bounds actually obtained. We do not conclude a
new global bound for Szemer\'edi's theorem, do not declare Lemma 16.10 fully
repaired, and do not treat failure of a displayed proof step as a
counterexample to the full mathematical lemma.

\section[{Exact checks, examples, and reproducibility\srctag{39}}]{Exact checks, examples, and reproducibility}\label{gsr:fz:39:sec:d13}
\srcnote{39}{Section 13}
\label{gsr:fz:39:sec:verification}

\subsection{What was actually tested}
The package contains a dependency-free Python implementation of the finite
formulas, the dynamic program, the closed balanced-profile formula, the
affine quadratic cap, and the deterministic sampling algorithm. The test
programs use Python integers, integer square root, and
\filename{fractions.Fraction}; they do not use floating-point arithmetic for any
assertion of equality or inequality.

Two certificate files record a total of $11{,}212$ checked cases, all passing
in the delivered run. Their categories are listed in
Table~\ref{gsr:fz:39:tab:verification}. A ``case'' means one loop instance in the named
category; it is not a separately proved theorem or an independent review.
Some cases contain several assertions. In particular, the second-difference
cases compare the direct difference, the hypergeometric formula, and, when
applicable, the factored sign formula.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Executed exact-arithmetic verification categories.}
\label{gsr:fz:39:tab:verification}
\begin{tabular}{lr}
\toprule
Category & Cases\\
\midrule
Direct one-class averages and the $(r+1)$-sample identity & 2,020\\
Dynamic programming versus exhaustive size profiles & 315\\
Anchor sets in exact permutation-orbit extremizers & 105\\
Weighted deterministic selection instances & 80\\
Conditional-expectation identities & 226\\
Nonsampled finite-field polynomial recoveries & 257\\
Candidate index-set cardinalities & 180\\
Closed balanced formula versus dynamic programming & 2,496\\
One-class unimodality and initial discrete concavity & 624\\
Exact second-difference identities & 2,765\\
Affine quadratic cap versus exact marginal maximization & 2,144\\
\midrule
Total & 11,212\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The first certificate suite includes finite-field reconstruction over
$\F_5$, $\F_7$, and $\F_{11}$, with thresholds $1$ through $4$. It checks
Lagrange reconstruction at nonsampled targets having enough valid anchors;
the already sampled targets require no interpolation. The second suite checks
the closed finite formula against the independent dynamic program for
$m\le13$, $q\le4$, thresholds through $6$, and all sample sizes. The affine
cap is compared against an exact scan through all class sizes for every
$m\le64$ and $0\le r\le m$.

These tests are designed to expose normalization errors, endpoint mistakes,
off-by-one errors in distinct-hit thresholds, incorrect ceilings, and false
maximizer claims. They supplement the proofs; none establishes a universal
statement by finite exhaustion.

\subsection{Reproducing the results}
From the package directory, run
\begin{verbatim}
python3 code/verify.py
python3 code/verify_balanced.py
python3 code/poisson_constants.py
make pdf
\end{verbatim}
The first two commands regenerate the exact JSON certificates. The constants
script uses high-precision decimal arithmetic only for the illustrative
Poisson constants, clearly separated from the exact combinatorial checks.
The PDF can alternatively be built by running \filename{pdflatex} twice on
\filename{article.tex}. The manuscript uses no external figure files and no
bibliography processor.

The code deliberately keeps both the dynamic program and the closed formula.
Agreement between implementations using different mathematics is a useful
regression check, although it is not a substitute for the proofs. The
repository interface is documented in \filename{FORMALIZATION_PLAN.md}; that file
is a plan, not an executable Lean proof.

\section[{Further research questions and proposed next steps\srctag{39}}]{Further research questions and proposed next steps}\label{gsr:fz:39:sec:d14}
\srcnote{39}{Section 14}
\label{gsr:fz:39:sec:questions}

The finite minimax value and the existence of balanced-and-capped extremizers
are settled by the theorems above. The following are distinct follow-on
questions; none is used as a hidden premise of the proved statements.

\begin{problem}[Classification of all finite extremizers]
Characterize every maximizing profile, not just the balanced one, and every
row family attaining the minimax value. The proof identifies equalization
steps that preserve or improve the objective. Equality should be controlled
by zero discrete curvature, flat first differences, and the distribution of
rowwise losses across samples. A useful result would give a complete
criterion for equality in Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:39:thm:minimax} and \ref{gsr:en:39:thm:balanced},
including the many nonunique cases with large sampling fraction.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Finite corrections to the golden-ratio law]
Obtain explicit uniform error bounds for
\eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:asymptotic}, separating finite-population corrections, integer
rounding, and the approach of $q/r$ to the transition. The affine radical
formula makes the optimizing class size explicit, so an expansion of the
hypergeometric marginal at that size could yield certified second-order
sampling budgets rather than only an $o(1)$ term. Near the phase transition,
rounding and whether the column budget is active should be treated together.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[General-threshold cap computation]
For fixed $t>2$, derive an equally transparent description of the first
maximizing size $a_{m,r,t}$. The first-difference identity is
\[
 \Delta\ell_{m,r,t}(s)=\frac{m-r}{m^2}
 \bigl[\Prob\{Z<t\}-t\Prob\{Z=t\}\bigr],
 \quad Z\sim\HG(m-1,s,r).
\]
After factoring binomial terms this gives a bounded-degree algebraic
expression when $t$ is fixed. The problem is to isolate its relevant root
with exact boundary handling and a complexity bound independent of a scan
through all $m$ sizes.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Thresholds growing with sample size]
Determine the asymptotics of $\lambda_t$ and $\kappa_t$ as $t\to\infty$, and
prove a uniform version of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:39:thm:uniform} when $t$ also grows with
$r$ and $m$. The fixed-$t$ proof uses finitely many low-count probabilities
and does not establish such a regime. This extension would quantify the
cost of interpolating increasing polynomial degree rather than only a fixed
degree.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Algebra-aware improvements beyond certification]
Find hypotheses under which the permutation-orbit lower bound ceases to
apply because additional algebraic information is available. Examples include
classes known to share a polynomial, restrictions on how class labels vary
with the base point, or compatibility among overlapping fibre interpolants.
The objective should be a precisely defined stronger recovery rule with its
own upper and lower bounds, not an unsupported claim that arbitrary
polynomial reconstruction requires $\kappa_tq/\sigma$ anchors.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Compressing labelled candidate lists]
When can the upper count
$\sum_aL_a+\sum_{|S|=t}\prod_{a\in S}L_a$ be reduced by algebraic dependence
among lists? Is there a useful lower-bound model in which its leading order
is necessary? Even the affine case may benefit from canonicalizing pairs of
slice candidates that give the same lifted graph. Any proposed compression
must retain the pointwise existence guarantee without assuming a globally
consistent choice of branches.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Formal label preservation and geometry]
Formalize the new sampler into the existing
\filename{Section16SampledOrAnchoredOn} interface, then formalize labelled
hereditary refinement with a dependent list type indexed by the sampled
column. Prove that the short-parent cover construction preserves the needed
containments for the labelled lists. This is a concrete integration task:
its goal is the exact bounds of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fz:39:thm:repo-local} and
Corollary~\ref{gsr:fz:39:cor:geometric}, not a silent change to the source definition of
multiply-linear control.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Nonuniform column costs and sampling designs]
Extend the finite game to weighted columns or nonuniform sampling costs.
Uniform row weights cause no difficulty here, and arbitrary row weights are
already covered; nonuniform \emph{column} weights are different. The
$(r+1)$-subset identity and permutation-orbit minimax argument depend on the
uniform column law. A replacement should specify the admissible sampling
design, the target mass measure, and the correct notion of a profile.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Robust recovery when good classes are unknown]
Develop an algorithm that exploits Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:39:thm:robust} without being
given the good subset or its class partition. The additive error bound shows
that correct interpolants exist in the generated list; it does not identify
them. A useful result would combine shared sampling with an explicit
consistency test or a list-decoding guarantee, with running time stated in
terms of the actual representation of the fibres.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Repairing the global control recurrence]
Replace the invalid closing comparison by a valid dimension-dependent
recurrence for scale, graph count, and exceptional mass. The new local
budgets should be substituted before attempting domination by a closed
formula. Endpoint-safe controls may need a multiplicative slack factor
strictly larger than one, since a graph budget equal to one at
$(\rho,\gamma)=(1,1)$ cannot dominate every nontrivial construction cost.
The task is then to propagate the repaired recurrence through the subsequent
sections and explicitly compute what global quantitative statement follows.
This remains separate from the finite sampling problem solved here.
\end{problem}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Conclusion\srctag{39}}]{Conclusion}\label{gsr:fz:39:sec:d15}
\srcnote{39}{Section 15}
\label{gsr:fz:39:sec:conclusion}

The shared interpolation step admits a direct mass-weighted treatment. The
finite identity \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:double-identity} eliminates the need to discard
small classes and then impose a separate failure probability on every
surviving class. It yields a uniform $O(q/\sigma)$ sample budget, while exact
minimax symmetrization proves that the associated certification problem has
no hidden dependence on the number of rows.

The finite problem is solved more explicitly than an averaging bound alone
would suggest. Hypergeometric finite differences show that a balanced profile,
capped at the first one-class maximum, is optimal. For affine interpolation
the cap is the ceiling of an explicit quadratic root. In a sparse-sampling
limit this finite structure becomes the golden-ratio coefficient
$\varphi^3e^{-\varphi}$, and the full transition between partial and saturated
column profiles is given by \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:phase}.

On the algebraic side, interpolation is naturally performed from labelled
slice lists. Retaining those labels gives the candidate count
$rL+\binom r2L^2$ rather than using a common union list at every anchor.
The theorem is compatible with the repository's existing sampled-or-anchored
and synchronization interfaces, subject to the explicitly retained geometric
hypotheses. It improves local information and local parameters; it does not
supply the missing global closing comparison.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Proof dependencies and formalization targets\srctag{39}}]{Proof dependencies and formalization targets}\label{gsr:fz:39:sec:dA}
\srcnote{39}{Appendix A}
\label{gsr:fz:39:app:dependencies}

\subsection{A dependency map}
The finite sampling and minimax results are independent of fields,
polynomials, Gowers norms, and the source's control functions. Their logical
chain is
\[
 \text{finite double count}
 \ \Longrightarrow\ \text{shared-sample bound}
 \ \Longrightarrow\ \text{minimax upper bound},
\]
with permutation symmetrization supplying the matching lower bound.
The finite-difference identities then give one-class shape, followed by
balancing and the closed finite formula. The affine cap uses only a quadratic
sign computation after the first-difference identity.

The Poisson results use these finite formulas plus an elementary product
inequality, elementary limits, and single-variable calculus. They are not
needed to obtain the nonasymptotic $O(q/\sigma)$ improvement or to compute the
finite optimum.

The algebraic lift uses interpolation and the already proved sample
certificate. The labelled refinement theorem uses restriction closure, finite
partitions, and measure addition. Only the final source-interface section
uses Gowers's particular single-slice and geometric hypotheses. Separating
these layers should make a formal development substantially easier to audit
than a single theorem combining all of them.

\subsection{Suggested declaration boundaries}
A proof-assistant implementation can first state everything in finite types
and unnormalized counts. The following names are proposed; they do not refer
to declarations already present in this delivery:
\begin{description}[style=nextline,leftmargin=1.1em]
\item[\filename{sharedAnchorDiscardCount}]
The sum of $(|C|-|C\cap R|)\ind_{\{|C\cap R|<t\}}$ over disjoint row classes.
\item[\filename{sharedAnchor_doubleCount}]
The bijection between $(R,x)$ pairs and $(T,x)$ pairs with $|T|=r+1$.
Proving the unnormalized integer identity first avoids probability-library
and real-division overhead.
\item[\filename{exists_sharedAnchorSet_mass}]
The finite average argument and the bound from $Z\ind_{1\le Z\le t}\le t$.
This is the shortest route to the local $O(q/\sigma)$ improvement.
\item[\filename{sharedAnchor_minimax_profile}]
The symmetric-group action and its equal-size fibres, followed by the exact
profile maximum. This is useful for optimality but is not a dependency of
the interpolation application.
\item[\filename{sharedAnchor_loss_secondDifference}]
The two distinguished-column coupling identities and the sign factorization
in \eqref{gsr:en:39:eq:curvature-sign}.
\item[\filename{sharedAnchor_balanced_profile}]
Clipping at the first mode, filling the budget, and discrete balancing. The
finite affine root may be handled by squared inequalities and an integer
ceiling characterization rather than numerical square roots.
\item[\filename{section16_subset_recovered_good_set}]
An application of the new sample bound that produces exactly the existing
sampled-or-anchored interface. The whole-class set $K$ in
Proposition~\ref{gsr:fz:39:prop:repo-interface} ensures that the anchors also belong to
$K$.
\item[\filename{labelled_common_slice_cover}]
Inductive refinement carrying a separate candidate family for each slice.
A dependent index type avoids padding every slice list to the union size.
\end{description}

A formalization should establish an actual build at a pinned Lean/mathlib
version before changing the status of any source lemma. This package contains
no \filename{sorry}-based Lean skeleton, no declaration of the new results as
axioms, and no claim that a proposed theorem name has been compiled.

\section[{Notation and endpoint checklist\srctag{39}}]{Notation and endpoint checklist}\label{gsr:fz:39:sec:dB}
\srcnote{39}{Appendix B}
\label{gsr:fz:39:app:notation}
\begingroup
\small
\begin{longtable}{p{0.18\textwidth}p{0.75\textwidth}}
\toprule
Symbol & Meaning and restrictions\\
\midrule
\endhead
$m$ & Number of final-coordinate columns; always a positive integer.\\
$r$ & Number of distinct sampled columns; $0\le r\le m$.\\
$t$ & Number of distinct anchors sufficient for a class; degree bound is $t-1$.\\
$q,q_h,\bar q$ & Uniform, rowwise, and weighted-mean class counts. The finite minimax formula fixes an integer $q\ge1$.\\
$B_h$ & Partial domain in row $h$; it need not equal $J$.\\
$K_h(R)$ & All sampled domain points together with every class having at least $t$ sampled members.\\
$E_R$ & Ambient good set obtained by deleting uncertified domain points only.\\
$\ell_{m,r,t}(s)$ & Expected discarded mass of one size-$s$ class, normalized by $m$.\\
$a_{m,r,t}$ & Least size attaining the maximum of $\ell$, not its largest maximizing size.\\
$\cM_{m,q,r,t}$ & Supremum over row families of the best shared $r$-sample loss for the stated rule.\\
$\lambda_t,\kappa_t$ & Unique Poisson-profile maximizer and its value. These are not finite-population constants.\\
$b$ & Horizontal-section complexity in the source comparison; distinct from class size $s$.\\
$M,m_0$ & Initial base scale and source short-parent width input; neither denotes $|J|$ unless specified.\\
$L,P$ & Individual slice-list and common union-list bounds. Keeping them distinct is the point of labelled refinement.\\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

For $r=m$, every sampling loss is zero and the first mode is zero. For $r<t$,
only sampled targets are certified and the minimax loss is $1-r/m$.
For $t=1$, the direct lifts duplicate some one-point interpolation expressions,
which is harmless for an upper bound. The finite formula uses a first mode so
that plateau cases have an unambiguous cap. Sampled columns are distinct by
construction. Field interpolation never divides by a zero difference.
Exceptional mass is always ambient mass, and the corruption and base-refinement
losses are added explicitly rather than hidden in a changed normalization.

\section[{Reproducibility, implementation, and formalization\srctag{40}}]{Reproducibility, implementation, and formalization}\label{gsr:fz:40:sec:d10}
\srcnote{40}{Section 10}
\label{gsr:fz:40:sec:verification}
\subsection{What the finite checks establish}
The accompanying standard-library Python program
\texttt{verify\_fejer\_selection.py} uses exact integer and rational
arithmetic for its mathematical checks. The JSON report records the
chosen points and exact survival masses for every displayed
orthogonality example. Its checks are as follows.

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.36\textwidth}p{0.56\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Check & Coverage and interpretation\\
\midrule
Top-monomial rigidity & All $6\,651$ coefficient vectors over
$\F_3$ for $k=1,2,3$, with sidelengths one.\\
Total arrangement count & All $512$ subsets of $\F_3^2$ for $k=d=1$,
including empty and full sets.\\
Small-field exceptional logic & All $625$ ambient arrangements over
$\F_5$ for $k=d=1$, $H=1$; all are exceptional, consistent with the
bound, which is vacuous at that field size.\\
Kernel inequalities & $156$ exact $(s,L)$ cases, for
$s\in\{4,8,16,32\}$ and $2\leq L\leq40$.\\
Selection constants & $27$ exact choices of $s,\alpha,\eta$, checking
the gain, ceiling estimate, score margin, and explicit retained mass.\\
Exact orthogonality & Four regular examples over $\F_{1000003}$:
$(k,d,L)=(1,1,2),(1,1,3),(2,1,2),(1,2,2)$; full enumeration of bounded
coefficient vectors, and exact good/bad Fourier sums.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The regular examples use $\phi=F$ for the good case. To form a bad
case, the value of $\phi$ at one distinct vertex is increased by one.
This changes the defect by a nonzero signed unit. The program checks
that the good moment is exactly $a_{s,L}$ and the bad moment exactly
$b_{s,L}$, not merely close in floating-point arithmetic.

The tests do not enumerate the enormous ambient fields in the main
theorem, do not prove the assertions for all parameters, and do not
verify a Lean development. The proofs in the article, not the sample
computations, are the basis for the general theorem.

\subsection{An explicit finite search procedure}
The existence argument admits a finite, though generally impractical,
construction. Enumerate the $q^2$ seed pairs $(t,u)$ and compute the
conditional expectation of the score $X-Y/\eta$ by enumerating labeled
arrangements. Some seed pair has conditional expected score at least
the unconditional lower bound. For this pair, expose the Bernoulli
membership decisions one physical point at a time. At each decision,
one of the two conditional expectations is at least their weighted
average, so choose that outcome. At the end the realized score is at
least the original guaranteed score.

This is a conditional-expectation proof of finite constructibility,
not a near-linear-time algorithm. Direct evaluation can involve the
$q^M$ arrangement parameter space and $|B|$ decisions. If exact
comparison of the trigonometric weights is desired, they lie in a
cyclotomic number field; a certified algebraic-real representation can
be used. For arbitrary real input $\eta$, exact effective comparisons
also require a representation of that input. Taking rational accuracy
parameters avoids this additional computability issue. No fast
implementation of this construction is claimed or supplied.

\subsection{Suggested Lean dependency structure}
The existing mathematical project supplies a natural home for a
formalization, but this package does not change its Lean files.
The following proposed components isolate the substantial obligations.
\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.29\textwidth}p{0.63\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Proposed component & Mathematical content\\
\midrule
\texttt{CubeTopMoment} & Subset-sum inversion and the parity criterion
of Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:40:lem:cubemoment}.\\
\texttt{ArrangementFeature} & Parameterized arrangements, elimination
of the last cross-section, and Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:40:thm:universal}.\\
\texttt{ShortRelationCount} & Finite coefficient boxes, sign pairing,
polynomial zero-count, and repeated-vertex exclusion.\\
\texttt{PositiveKernelMoment} & Finite character orthogonality,
nonnegative Fourier sums, and actual-versus-labeled survival.\\
\texttt{FejerSelection} & The score lemma, the exact theorem, ceiling
arithmetic, and the density corollary.\\
\texttt{KernelGainBarrier} & The nonnegative-Fourier gain--mass
inequalities, independent of arrangement geometry.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
These are suggested names, not assertions that such modules already
exist. A formalization should first fix the intended arrangement
counting convention, particularly repeated vertices, before adapting
existing interfaces. No uncompiled proof sketches with placeholder
axioms are included as if they were verification.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Further research questions and integration priorities\srctag{40}}]{Further research questions and integration priorities}\label{gsr:fz:40:sec:d11}
\srcnote{40}{Section 11}
\label{gsr:fz:40:sec:questions}
The questions below distinguish a direct follow-up computation from a
structural conjecture. None is asserted solved by the preceding proofs.

\begin{problem}[Sharp finite-bandwidth kernel optimization]
For fixed $s,H,Q$, maximize $\sum_{a=-H}^H c_a^s$ subject to
$c_{-a}=c_a\geq0$, $0\leq\sum c_ae^{ia\theta}\leq1$, and
$\sum c_a^s\geq Qc_0^s$. How close is the Fej\'er kernel to the
optimum, including its dependence on $s$?
\end{problem}
The exponent is determined by Section~\ref{gsr:en:40:sec:barrier}, but the
constant and the necessary bandwidth are not. A useful first target
is a rigorous solution for small $H$, with certified positivity rather
than a sampled grid of angles. This would clarify whether better
kernels can materially reduce the field threshold even when they
cannot improve the powers of $\alpha$ and $\eta$.

\begin{problem}[Counting distinct short-relation hypersurfaces]
How much can one improve $C_{k,s,H}$ by identifying scalar-equivalent
or coincident zero sets among the coefficient vectors, and by using
the geometry of their intersections?
\end{problem}
Sign pairing is only the first such identification. Over a prime field,
a projective count sensitive to the actual integer coefficient box may
save more than a constant. Any refinement must still include zero
sidelengths and coincident vertices. A credible target is an explicit
bound of the form $q^{M-1}$ times a substantially smaller coefficient
complexity, rather than an unproved independence heuristic.

\begin{problem}[Threshold versus intrinsic complexity]
Is a field-size requirement of roughly
$\beta^{-(2d-1)}(s/(\alpha\eta))^{2s}$ necessary for an unconditional
one-stage theorem of this kind, or can it be reduced while retaining
the same arrangement mass?
\end{problem}
Our requirement comes from making all exceptional bad arrangements
cost at most the ordinary bad first moment. It may be wasteful to
bound each exceptional arrangement's survival by one. Stratifying
extra-relation ranks and calculating their survival could improve the
threshold without changing the kernel or its exponent barrier.

\begin{problem}[Small-characteristic selection]
Can a different family of probability kernels recover comparably
strong selection in characteristic $p\leq2(L-1)$, with a quantitatively
controlled dependence on $p$?
\end{problem}
Two issues must be separated: modular collisions in the feature
coefficient box and low-order target defects. Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:40:prop:torsion}
computes the latter exactly. A successful approach cannot simply
increase the extension degree of the field and ignore its fixed
characteristic. Vector-valued frequencies, structured zero sets, or
several genuinely different tests are plausible directions, but are
not proofs.

\begin{problem}[Multiple universal relations]
For a parameterized configuration whose polynomial feature relations
form a lattice or vector space of rank greater than one, can the
single-stage method be developed with constants controlled by the
geometry of that relation space?
\end{problem}
The exact Fourier sum is still available, but the good contribution
becomes a weighted sum over a higher-rank coefficient section.
Different nonzero defects can annihilate different subspaces, so the
one-dimensional ratio calculation must be replaced rather than merely
renamed. This is a natural route toward broader multilinear and
hypergraph configurations.

\begin{problem}[Propagation through the remainder of Gowers' proof]
What explicit bounds result from substituting Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:40:cor:eight}
into the subsequent strong-partial-multihomomorphism and
multilinear-structure steps, while tracking every density, accuracy,
and largeness condition?
\end{problem}
The immediate task is a parameter ledger for each later invocation,
not an asserted improvement in a final tower height. Other losses may
dominate. This question is valuable for the repository even if the
final asymptotic class does not change, because it would identify
which local constants are actually bottlenecks.

\begin{problem}[Beyond the homogeneous positivity class]
Can vertex-dependent kernels or adaptive selection beat the
$\alpha^s\eta^{s-1}$ certificate scale, while retaining a usable
exceptional-set estimate?
\end{problem}
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:40:thm:barrier} makes this a precise boundary question.
A candidate improvement should state exactly which hypothesis of that
theorem it leaves, and should exhibit either a new positivity
mechanism or information about the configuration family absent from
the scalar first-moment bound.

\begin{problem}[Formal proof and executable certification]
Can the one-feature relation theorem, exact positive-kernel moment,
and score selection theorem be formalized as reusable components,
with the finite checks generated from the same definitions?
\end{problem}
A practical first milestone is the algebraic universal-relation theorem,
which does not require probability or analysis. A second is a finite
Fourier moment theorem parameterized by a nonnegative coefficient
family. A final milestone is the explicit arithmetic corollary with
all characteristic and size inequalities present in the formal
statement.

\subsection{Integration recommendation}
Place this package in a new subdirectory named
\texttt{fejer-arrangement-selection} of the existing
\texttt{local-quantitative-refinements} collection under
\texttt{Research/GowersSzemeredi}. The accompanying README provides
an index entry and a proof-status summary. Keep the original paper's
transcription unchanged: the new theorem should be a separate,
explicitly cited refinement. Later Lean integration and any downstream
constant propagation should be separate changes with their own
verification record.

\section[{Conclusion\srctag{40}}]{Conclusion}\label{gsr:fz:40:sec:d12}
\srcnote{40}{Section 12}
The repeated degree-one Riesz-product selection in Section 15 can be
replaced by one high-bandwidth Fej\'er selection. The main quantitative
benefit is a reduction from the exponent $s2^{s-1}$ to powers $s$ and
$s-1$ in the input abundance and error parameters, together with a
smaller explicit field-size requirement in the eight-arrangement case.
The algebraic input is also compressed: the full coordinate product
alone has precisely the intended universal relation, and all other
bounded relations are controlled by a polynomial zero-count.

The argument is local, fully stated, and separates exact identities
from conservative estimates. Its principal technical safeguards are
the explicit treatment of repeated vertices, the characteristic
condition preventing coefficient aliasing, and the accounting of
exceptional bad arrangements before extracting a subset. The
positive-Fourier obstruction identifies a genuine limit of this
particular method, while the torsion formula and the research agenda
identify concrete directions for further work.

\subsection{Primary literature and what is being claimed}
Gowers~\cite{gowers}, Section 5, develops the classical chain from Weyl recurrence to polynomial localization and local density increments. Its Corollary 5.8 on printed page 493 displays gain $\alpha/8$, while its displayed proof ends with $\alpha/16$. The pinned edited source uses $\alpha/16$. The present argument supplies explicit recurrence and localization budgets and uses a subgroup-coset variance alternative to handle the low-correlation branch. It does not import an internal large-threshold statement without checking that the available parent length pays for it.

Maynard~\cite{maynard}, Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2, gives coefficient-uniform simultaneous recurrence for systems of real polynomials vanishing at zero. For $m$ polynomials of degree at most $d$, the corollary has fractional parts bounded by $\ll_{d,m}X^{-c_d/m}$ for some $1\le n<X$. The introduction explicitly leaves degree and dimension dependence of implied constants uncontrolled. That result gives important context, but its implicit constants are not substituted for the explicit constants proved here. In the cited arXiv version the Weyl estimate is Lemma 6.1; numbering need not agree with later versions.

The repeated-differencing and recurrence-to-localization mechanisms are classical. The explicit constants here are deliberately weak, and no literature-priority or optimality claim is made for either those constants or this local-cover formulation. This local theorem alone neither repairs other source sections nor produces an ordinary-integer rectification theorem or a better global quantitative Ramsey or Szemer\'edi bound. Those require separate statements and compatible downstream arguments.

\section[{Reproducibility and further questions\srctag{41}}]{Reproducibility and further questions}\label{gsr:fz:41:sec:d9}\label{gsr:fz:41:sec:repro}
\srcnote{41}{Section 9}
\subsection{The role of exact diagnostics}
The companion uses only the Python standard library, integer arithmetic, and exact rational arithmetic. Its bounded diagnostics check the recurrence and partition budget identities, ordered-divisor combinatorics, differencing coefficients, subgroup-coset second moments, removal of nonproper directions, residue-chain chunking and resplitting, modular polynomial pullbacks, cover mass, and rounding regressions. The JSON output reports the actual finite ranges and limitations. Small rational recurrence examples test an interface; they do not prove recurrence for arbitrary real coefficients.

The infinite-degree induction and the real-parameter recurrence are proved in this article. The program does not enumerate astronomical theoretical partitions or build a theorem-scale integer merely to display its digits. External numeric inputs have explicit runtime caps, active under optimized Python. Tests and diagnostics run both normally and with \texttt{-O}, and deterministic diagnostic stdout must agree.

The offline builder verifies an exact source inventory and, for a packaged distribution, manifest hashes. It runs bounded checks, rebuilds the PDF using an installed trusted TeX toolchain with shell escape disabled, and creates a deterministic ZIP with fixed order, timestamps, and permissions. It rejects unexpected source members, aliases, unsafe output locations, and oversized subprocess output. These are reproducibility and regression controls for trusted source, not a sandbox for hostile TeX or Python, and not a guarantee against an actively malicious concurrent filesystem owner. Hashes show byte agreement, not authorship or mathematical truth.

The package contains only the article, PDF, original exact diagnostics and tests, the builder, public documentation, and the manifest. Third-party papers are linked rather than bundled, and private review material is excluded. The ZIP digest is supplied outside the archive. Reproduction commands, environmental requirements, caps, and trust boundaries appear in \texttt{README.md}.

\subsection{Focused further questions}
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Improve the recurrence with fully explicit constants.}
Can modern monomial or simultaneous recurrence estimates be made effective at all relevant small scales and then inserted into the exact recursion? An improved asymptotic exponent alone does not identify the required prefactor or cutoff. The conditional witness in Remark~\ref{gsr:dt:41:rem:genconditional} is not such an improvement.
\item \textbf{Reduce localization cost.}
The induction suppresses the leading coefficient, then applies the lower-degree result at target $2L$ and resplits. Can one reduce the exponent $e_k$ or constant $c_k$, perhaps by optimizing the allocation of phase error, while retaining every point and keeping an integer-scale proof?
\item \textbf{Optimize the final selection without losing scale control.}
The exact-budget corollary exposes what the present recursion actually proves. Can a sharper variance estimate or a direct correlation argument improve its floor and prefactor, or trade the uniform gain $\alpha/3$ against a longer progression? Any comparison should retain singleton and boundary cases.
\item \textbf{Strengthen geometric conclusions.}
When can the low-correlation branch be made parent-contained? When can a modular output be rectified to an ordinary integer progression with a useful length? Neither property follows from properness alone over arbitrary cyclic moduli.
\item \textbf{Formalize and connect the interface carefully.}
The finite-group mass and variance lemmas, residue partitions, explicit recurrence, and numerical induction could be formalized as separate components and composed into the pinned predicate. Beyond that local task, what downstream statements would be needed before claiming a global quantitative consequence? This report provides no kernel-checked implementation or global conclusion.
\end{enumerate}

\section[{Relation to prior arguments and further questions\srctag{42}}]{Relation to prior arguments and further questions}\label{gsr:fz:42:sec:d8}\label{gsr:fz:42:sec:context}
\srcnote{42}{Section 8}
\subsection{What is strengthened and what is classical}
The inspected variance argument in Report277 averages over all cyclic steps. Off-diagonal correlations are controlled by subgroup-coset averages; the nonproper directions are then removed using the estimate
\[
 \eta\le\frac{L(L-1)}{2N}.
\]
At $N\ge L^3$, this yields the gain $(1-\delta)/(2L)$. The present proof changes the step distribution before taking moments. Its only nonproper sampled direction is zero, with exactly controlled mass. That change leads to the quadratic condition, the arithmetic refinement, and the equality examples given here.

Autocorrelation positivity, finite Fourier inversion and Poisson summation, variance-to-range conversion, and positive-definite packing estimates are classical. The role of Kolountzakis--R\'ev\'esz is particularly direct: Proposition~\ref{gsr:dt:42:prop:packing} is an instance of their Theorem~2, rather than a new packing inequality. Bhatia--Davis supplies the standard name for Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:42:lem:range}, whose elementary proof was included.

Fox, Xu and Zhou~\cite{foxxuzhou} study discrepancy of modular arithmetic progressions. Their Section~4, especially Lemmas~4.2--4.3 and Corollary~4.4, is a close neighboring second-moment mechanism: it uses Fourier weights, subgroup sums and the behavior of short-order directions. Their objective is two-sided discrepancy over varying progression lengths. The fixed-length one-sided density statement and the explicit prime-quotient equality calculation are the claims isolated in this report. The comparison is a bounded source screen, not a proof of priority.

Lewko~\cite[Lemma 2 and Section 5]{lewko} gives a close contemporary use of autocorrelation sums of squares, progression second moments and explicit zero-step removal in a prime cyclic group, with an additive-energy hypothesis. These are useful neighboring mechanisms; their use does not by itself supply the unconditional all-modulus coefficient proved here. In the pinned ProveIt research article~\cite{repo42}, the source-10 contribution already records the elementary implication $M\ge\delta+\Var(X)/\delta$. The present report does not claim that conversion as a new argument.

Gowers~\cite[Section 5]{gowers} provides the polynomial localization and transfer context used in the earlier reports. The present standalone variance improvement does not reprove or improve their all-degree phase budget. A global quantitative Szemer\'edi or Ramsey improvement would require a separate, complete iteration or transfer argument. Likewise, the present written proof is not a Lean or other kernel-checked certificate.

\subsection{Focused open directions}
The theorem leaves several concrete questions.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{Fixed-density sharpness.} For $\delta$ bounded away from zero and one, what is the best uniform coefficient under $N\ge CL^2$, including $C=1$? Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:42:thm:endpoint} supplies a positive endpoint coefficient but does not prove it optimal. The sparse equality family does not decide the fixed-density minimax problem.
\item \emph{Arithmetic pairs beyond the equality family.} For fixed $N,L$ and permitted cardinality $|A|$, when is the arithmetic bound attained? The support optimum and the full extremal set problem are distinct. Nonzero off-diagonal squares and strict range inequalities may force additional gain.
\item \emph{General finite abelian groups.} Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:42:thm:group} reduces one route to finding a large support with no nonzero short-order difference. A short-order subgroup supplies a packing upper bound, but there need not be a cyclic interval attaining it. Determining the best support and positive-definite weight parameters in more general groups is a separate problem.
\item \emph{Containment and localization.} Can comparable arithmetic gains be obtained while keeping the output inside a specified parent or a cover? The global translation average used here does not supply that constraint. Any nonwrapping integer conclusion likewise requires an additional argument.
\end{enumerate}
These questions concern added structure or stronger conclusions. None is required for the proofs above.
