\subsection{A precise crosswalk, not a replacement of hypotheses}
The relevant formal definitions at the comparison snapshot are in
\texttt{Sections17\_18.lean}. The definition
\texttt{proposition\_17\_2} has ambient group $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$
with $N$ prime, a disc-valued function, a frequency predicate
\texttt{IsMultilinear}, and an explicit unit condition on $(k+1)!$.
It concludes the existence of a degree-at-most-$k+1$ phase preserving
the stated lower bound on the sum of squared zero-frequency derivative
coefficients after twisting.

There is an important naming distinction. At the pinned snapshot,
\texttt{Definitions.lean} defines \texttt{IsMultilinear} as a sum of
square-free monomials \emph{including constant and lower-order terms}.
It is a multiaffine predicate. Our $T$ is genuinely homogeneous
multilinear in all its slots. A general multiaffine selector is not
covered merely by taking its top homogeneous component.

For the homogeneous cyclic high-characteristic specialization, the
usual diagonal primitive is available because the factorial is
invertible. The present theorem addresses an obstruction that appears
on vector spaces in characteristic two. It certifies the additional
identities needed for a nonclassical primitive and preserves energy
exactly once they hold. This is a local analogue in a broader class of
ambient groups, with its own high-energy hypothesis, not a theorem
that uniformly dominates Proposition 17.2 for every input covered by
the repository.

The displayed degree correction from $k$ to $k+1$ in the source paper
is already recorded by the repository. It is not a correction
originating in this manuscript. Likewise we do not alter the local
partition constants in Proposition 17.7 or any subsequent density
iteration.

\subsection{An executable algebraic route}
Given the coefficient table of a $d$-linear Boolean form, the
certification and integration steps can be implemented exactly.
First check symmetry on coefficient tuples, using adjacent
transpositions. Once symmetry is known, the repeated-variable defect
is multilinear, so checking it on basis arguments suffices. The test
uses the coefficients
\[
 T(e_i,e_i,e_j,e_{a_1},\ldots,e_{a_{d-3}})
 +T(e_i,e_j,e_j,e_{a_1},\ldots,e_{a_{d-3}}).
\]
If they vanish, read one coefficient per nonempty support and construct
\eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:primitive-formula}. A dense input has $n^d$ coefficients;
checking adjacent symmetries costs $O(dn^d)$ field operations, and the
repeated-variable tests cost $O(n^{d-1})$ coefficient operations after
symmetry has been established. The construction outputs
$\sum_{s\le d}\binom ns$ rational monomials, with denominator at most
$2^d$. These are algebraic operation counts, not a claim of sublinear
access to a dense tensor.

For a cubic, form the $n\times n$ matrix
$\Omega_{ij}=T(e_i,e_i,e_j)+T(e_i,e_j,e_j)$. Symplectic Gaussian
elimination gives its rank, an optimal isotropic subspace, and the
linear forms in \eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:cubic-normal}. This costs $O(n^3)$ field
operations with a straightforward implementation. The normal form
then provides a global phase extremizer and an optimal restriction
primitive.

An observed energy lower bound is a different kind of input. If
function values are numerical complex numbers, an interval or exact
cyclotomic certificate is needed before a strict threshold can be
invoked. An unchecked floating-point comparison is not a proof of
\eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:boolean-threshold}.

\subsection{Proposed Lean boundaries}
No new theorem in this package has been checked by Lean. A useful
formalization order is the following mathematical dependency chain:
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \text{finite cube identity and gauge invariance}\\
 \Downarrow\\
 \text{projective operators and eigenvalue multiplicity}\\
 \Downarrow\\
 \text{mixed orthogonality and alternating slice profiles}\\
 \Downarrow\\
 \text{Boolean shear and repeated-variable certification}\\
 \Downarrow\\
 \text{explicit nonclassical primitive and exact cubic repair}.
 \end{gathered}
\]
A first implementation can work solely over $\Ftwo^n$ and use matrix
symplectic elimination. The full finite-abelian Lagrangian theorem can
be added independently. The polynomial value group must include
$2^{-d}\mathbb Z/\mathbb Z$; using only $\mathrm{ZMod}\,2$ would encode
the wrong integration problem.

The relevant finite-dimensional analytic obligation is explicit:
a positive operator commuting with the projective translations has
nonzero eigenspaces of dimension at least $d_B$. Once its trace is
computed, the sharp constant follows. There is no appeal to an
unformalized inverse theorem hidden in that step.
The quartic proof additionally needs the finite monomial identity and
a disc-boundary maximum argument, or an equivalent real-algebraic
certificate. The file \texttt{FORMALIZATION.md} expands these proposed
interfaces without supplying placeholder Lean proofs.

\subsection{Source audit and novelty boundary}
The file \texttt{data/source\_audit.json} records the exact repository

labels, rather than unstable printed page numbers, identify the

README was also checked to avoid repeating the density, carry-pattern,
cube-count, and Bohr-radius projects already represented there.

There are three distinct statuses. The mathematical theorems in this
manuscript have supplied proofs. Their selected finite instances have
executable exact checks. They have not been independently refereed or
proved in a proof assistant, and the targeted literature search does
not establish publication priority. The package's suggested repository
placement conveys no additional formal status.

\subsection{Limits that affect downstream use}
The universal Boolean threshold is a high-energy criterion for an
already supplied multilinear selector. It is not an inverse theorem
that constructs a selector from an arbitrary positive Gowers norm.
The exact cubic law remains useful at all positive energies, but still
assumes an exactly symmetric global cubic tensor. Producing or
repairing that symmetry may itself be a substantial part of an
application.

Uniform translation averages are essential to the projective twirl.
Restricting the averaging set to a progression or a Bohr set generally
breaks the commutation argument. No boundary-free local analogue is
claimed. Similarly, multiaffine lower-order frequency terms cannot
simply be discarded, and the higher-dimensional quartic maximum is
not settled by its two-dimensional computation.

\section[{Further research questions and topics\srctag{43}}]{Further research questions and topics}\label{gsr:fz:43:sec:d12}\label{gsr:fz:43:bpi:sec:questions}

The first questions below are sharply specified continuations of the
proved results. The later ones concern their use in a complete
inverse or density-increment argument. An assertion marked as a
question is not used elsewhere as a theorem.

\begin{problem}[Does the quartic extremum stabilize?]\label{gsr:fz:43:bpi:q:quartic}
Is $\MM(C_{4,n})=11/16$ for every $n\ge2$? Equivalently, by
Corollary~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:cor:quartic-fixed}, is $11/16$ the exact universal
energy threshold for symmetric nonintegrable quartics? A counterexample
must use the extra coordinates in the optimizing function, since the
tensor itself has already been reduced to two coordinates.
\end{problem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 47--53]
\emph{Answered by source~47} (Section~\ref{gsr:fp:sec:boolenergy}): $\MM(C_{4,n})=11/16$ for every $n\ge2$, and $11/16$ is the exact threshold for symmetric nonintegrable quartics in every dimension (its Theorems~\ref{gsr:fm:47:boe:thm:main-canonical} and~\ref{gsr:fm:47:boe:thm:main-universal}; in every degree $d\ge3$ the canonical maximum is $1-(d+1)/2^d$). Source~47 cites this source by its library file name.
\end{writenote}
A useful first target is $n=3$, retaining the exact shear identities
rather than treating the sliced functions as independent optimizers.
The interval $11/16\le M_{4,n}\le3/4$ is proved, not conjectural;
constancy at the lower endpoint is a proposed conjecture here.

\begin{problem}[Exact mixed cubic repair]\label{gsr:fz:43:bpi:q:mixed}
For a prescribed symmetric cubic $T$, determine
$\sup_{|b_i|\le1}\Gamma_T(b_1,\ldots,b_7)$. Does it depend only on
$\rk\Omega_T$, as the one-function extremum does? Is the upper bound
$2^{-\rk\Omega_T/4}$ attainable, and is coefficient two in
\eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:mixed-codim} optimal?
\end{problem}
Sharpness of the triangle estimate does not settle simultaneous
attainment by all the sheared seven-function slices.

\begin{problem}[Near-extremizers beyond their amplitudes]\label{gsr:fz:43:bpi:q:stability}
If $\en_T(f)\ge(1-\varepsilon)2^{-m}$, classify $f$ up to a cubic
integrable twist and the projective eigenspace structure.
Can a dimension-independent distance bound be proved for an appropriate
explicit family of extremizers? The amplitude estimate
\eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:amplitude-stability} is available; phase stability is not.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Higher-degree defect geometry]\label{gsr:fz:43:bpi:q:higher}
For $d\ge5$, characterize the multilinear families
$\zz\mapsto\Omega_{\zz}$ that actually arise from symmetric
$d$-linear tensors. Which compatibility identities generalize
\eqref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:eq:quartic-bianchi}? Can low-dimensional defect images
reduce the sharp energy problem to finitely many canonical tensors?
\end{problem}
The existing support bound treats an arbitrary multilinear family;
using the additional compatibility is the natural place to improve it.

\begin{problem}[Odd small characteristic]\label{gsr:fz:43:bpi:q:odd}
For $p\le d$, find a spectral identity detecting the $p$-repetition
transfer conditions of nonclassical integration. Determine whether
$1-(1-1/p)^{d-1}$, already the sharp symmetry threshold, also certifies
all the extra integrability identities. The Boolean shear exploits
$2a=0$ in an exact way; a $p$-cycle substitute is needed.
\end{problem}
This asks for certification of known algebraic integration conditions,
not for rediscovery of nonclassical polynomial theory.

\begin{problem}[Composite-group primitives]\label{gsr:fz:43:bpi:q:composite}
On a general finite abelian group, characterize which symmetric
multiadditive $T:G^d\to\Torus$ have a degree-at-most-$d$ primitive,
and derive sharp energy certification using elementary-divisor data.
Can the primary factorization of the symmetry profile be lifted to
an equally explicit integration theorem?
\end{problem}
The present paper settles the finite-abelian orthogonality and symmetry
parts, not this full integration problem.

\begin{problem}[A boundary-sensitive local twirl]\label{gsr:fz:43:bpi:q:local}
Replace the global translation average by an arithmetic box or a
regular Bohr set. Can its failure to commute with projective
translations be bounded in a norm that preserves a useful rank
factor? A successful statement should give explicit boundary and
normalization errors compatible with Gowers's localized phase step.
\end{problem}
An estimate that simply repeats the global proof on a restricted set
would miss its crucial invariance hypothesis.

\begin{problem}[Obtaining the high-energy selector]\label{gsr:fz:43:bpi:q:selector}
Identify a nontrivial inverse-theorem regime in which a global
multilinear selector can be produced above the certification
threshold, or in which the exact cubic repair law is useful below it.
Track the selector, symmetrization, phase removal, and final density
increment together before claiming a better global bound.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Multiaffine frequency offsets]\label{gsr:fz:43:bpi:q:affine}
Can lower-order components of a multiaffine selector be removed with
an optimal quantified loss, or absorbed into a larger exact model?
A satisfactory theorem must account for the constant and lower-order
terms present in the repository's \texttt{IsMultilinear} predicate.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Formal certificates for extremal identities]\label{gsr:fz:43:bpi:q:formal}
Formalize the projective eigenvalue-multiplicity argument and the
Boolean primitive formula, then verify the cubic exact-rank theorem.
For the quartic result, produce a small proof object combining the
$29$-monomial identity with the continuous optimization bound, rather
than treating the finite phase census as a certificate of the maximum.
\end{problem}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Conclusion\srctag{43}}]{Conclusion}\label{gsr:fz:43:sec:d13}\label{gsr:fz:43:bpi:sec:conclusion}
\srcnote{43}{Section 13}

The additional characteristic-two integrability obstruction is not
merely detectable near perfect energy. For symmetric cubics, its
alternating rank determines the entire extremal value and the exact
cost of removing the obstruction by restriction. For arbitrary degree,
a division-free spectral argument plus a Boolean shear forces the full
set of nonclassical integration identities at a sharp universal
threshold, after which phase removal is lossless.

The same orthogonality mechanism is useful outside the one-function
setting: it gives an optimal fourth-power bilinear estimate and a
smaller codimension bound under the published seven-function repair
hypotheses. The quartic analysis provides a second structural result:
an exact two-dimensional value and a reduction of the general
optimization to one explicit tensor. The remaining ambient-dimension
question is isolated, not hidden in an assumed tensorization step.

These results are suitable as independent research additions beside the
formal Gowers development. Their integration into a global Ramsey or
Szemer\'edi estimate requires the further selector and localization
work described above.

\subsection{What was actually executed}
The supplied verifier uses Python's standard library and exact integers
and rational numbers. Its default run computes through $d=10$. It also
performs checks which do not use the fixed-grid representation. The saved
record is \gitpath{data/verification.json}; every asserted check passed
in the packaged run.

First, all $512$ grid subsets are considered and all $458$ spanning
supports are reconstructed from their affine-value assignments. The
universal eight-shape coefficient identity is checked over the complete
support lattice, grouped by exact rational affine equivalence. This is
stronger than comparing the compact formula with a few numerical values.
The walk recurrence, exact-support M\"obius transform, flat multiplicity
formula, and both pair-consistency identities are then checked for
$d=1,\ldots,10$.

Second, the verifier generates every integer-balanced ternary normal
for $d=2,3,4$, canonicalizes its rational restriction, and groups every
pair by primitive exterior-product coordinates. These independent
pair-span histograms match the grid answer. Modular two-row reduced
echelon forms at $p=17,53$ give the same histograms. These calculations
check examples of the determinant theorem; they do not replace its
all-dimensional proof.

Third, affine ternary Boolean maps are exhaustively checked for
$k=1,\ldots,8$ at $p=5,7,11$. The number of maps is
$3+6k+4\binom{k}{2}$, and none has more than two active slopes.
The exact signed-collision counts are checked directly for $m=4$,
$p=5,7$, and $k=1,2,3$. In characteristics two and three the quotient
counts and the regular cross-section formula are checked using the
prime-field vector-space models of $\F_4,\F_8,\F_9$. Only addition
and prime-field scalar multiplication are needed for these checks;
no assertion about an unimplemented field multiplication routine is made.

Finally, the seven-step walk recurrence is evaluated through $d=64$.
The scaled energy is compared numerically with the proved leading
constant and its first correction at $d=8,16,32,64$. These floating-point
ratios are explicitly labelled diagnostics. All preceding counts and
certificate tests use exact arithmetic.

The run does \emph{not} enumerate every full arrangement, verify a new
Szemer\'edi bound, or execute a Lean build. A finite check is not called
an independent mathematical review. The universal statements rest on
the proofs; the eight-shape compression has the separately delimited
finite rational component described above.

\section[{Further research questions and proposed next targets\srctag{44}}]{Further research questions and proposed next targets}\label{gsr:fz:44:sec:d12}
\srcnote{44}{Section 12}
\label{gsr:fz:44:sec:questions}

The first two questions are the most direct mathematical continuations.
The last one is the route toward a genuine improvement of a global Ramsey
bound. These are proposed research questions of this manuscript; no claim
is made that every formulation has previously appeared as a named open
problem.

\begin{question}[Third Whitney coefficients from a fixed grid]
Can the third Whitney coefficient be expressed by balanced supports in
$\Tfortyfour^3$, with weights determined by a finite rank-three incidence type,
and evaluated in polynomially many arithmetic operations in $d$?
\end{question}
The rank-two proof uses ordered bases of a normal span and divides by
the number of such bases through a flat. In rank three, the M\"obius
coefficient depends on the full rank-two incidence structure inside the
span, not only on its number of hyperplanes. The finite grid has $27$
points. A useful answer should specify the correct weight, exploit
symmetry before enumerating its supports, and distinguish arithmetic
complexity in $d$ from the large universal preprocessing constant.

\begin{question}[The third term of the actual degeneracy count]
Which non-core directions contribute at order $q^{-3}$ on the regular
region, and what are the intersections of their irreducible components?
\end{question}
A third Whitney coefficient alone is not enough to answer this. The
rank argument separates directions with one extra cross-section equation
from directions forcing two independent rank-two base systems. The
latter cost $q^{-4}$. A structural classification of the former could
replace the entire residual inventory by a smaller third-order family.
The exact core product already settles all core intersections, so it need
not be reanalyzed at that stage.

\begin{question}[Exact recurrences for the eight energies]
Find short polynomial-coefficient recurrences, with proofs, for the
energies in \eqref{gsr:en:44:eq:eightpolynomials}, and determine whether their linear
combination $B_d$ has a substantially simpler minimal recurrence.
\end{question}
The fixed-step walk model supplies exact data without guessing. A
recurrence must be certified by a coefficient identity or a valid
summation certificate, not just fitted to an initial segment. Such a
result could reduce both storage and the number of arithmetic operations,
and could supply all-orders asymptotics by an independent route.

\begin{question}[Sharp exceptional characteristics]
For each $d$, which primes actually change $b_{2,d,p}$, and is the universal
bound $16$ in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:44:thm:stability} optimal after the balancing
relations are imposed?
\end{question}
The determinant estimate intentionally ignores much of the structure.
A prime can divide a possible minor without being realized by a balanced
triple in the actual hyperplane arrangement. Intermediate characteristics
also introduce additional balanced profiles when $p\le2d$; those are a
separate effect from collapse of rational incidences. A complete answer
should distinguish these mechanisms.

\begin{question}[Sharpness of the universal dimension barriers]
How large can $k$ be for a nondegenerate $d$-arrangement to exist over a
fixed field? How close are the necessary conditions in
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:44:cor:thresholds} to sufficient ones?
\end{question}
The core laws give exact capacities for the paired summaries. Realizing
summaries within those capacities does not rule out non-core relations.
A construction with certified absence of every ternary moment relation,
or a stronger obstruction from the next coefficient layers, would settle
an existence problem beyond the classified core.

\begin{question}[Relative and nonuniform arrangement distributions]
Can an analogue of the core product control arrangements sampled from a
dense set, rather than the full ambient parameter space?
\end{question}
The present product relies on uniform independent paired summaries.
A relative version needs explicit hypotheses on their conditional
concentration and collision probabilities. Total variation estimates,
weighted sequential exposure, or a mixing condition on the base fibres
are possible starting points. An ambient bound multiplied by the inverse
collection density is not the desired improvement.

\begin{question}[Larger coefficient alphabets]
For $\{-M,\ldots,M\}$ in place of $\Tfortyfour$, can one obtain a fixed-grid formula
for the second incidence coefficient and an exact classification of the
low-degree core events?
\end{question}
The weighted profile-pair argument suggests a grid with $(2M+1)^2$
points, but the number of alphabet representatives of an affine class
is no longer determined solely by whether two or three values occur.
The core event may involve more than signed collisions. A satisfactory
extension should keep those multiplicities and the prime-dependent
translation symmetries explicit.

\begin{question}[A small independently verified certificate]
What is the smallest trusted checker needed to certify the eight-shape
formula and the $d=8$ coefficient inside the repository's formal system?
\end{question}
The general double-counting theorem should be proved once. The numerical
part can then be limited to integer walk arrays, rational affine-map
checks on at most nine points, and finite sums of rational weights.
This suggests a certificate substantially smaller than enumerating the
millions of hyperplanes in the $d=8$ arrangement.

\begin{question}[Complete Section 15 propagation]
After inserting the exact principal term and the improved incidence
coefficient into the corrected selection argument, which parameter
actually controls the next inverse step and the final density increment?
\end{question}
This requires a complete ledger of retained arrangement mass, the
non-core error, repetition counts in the selection kernel, field-size
thresholds, and progression widths. The negative second coefficient can
improve a local estimate without changing the final asymptotic bound.
Only a full calculation through the later stages can establish a global
quantitative improvement.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Conclusion\srctag{44}}]{Conclusion}\label{gsr:fz:44:sec:d13}
\srcnote{44}{Section 13}

The computational obstruction in the second degeneracy coefficient is
not the number of ambient hyperplanes. Two ternary profiles can be
recorded by their coordinate pairs in a fixed nine-point grid. Exact
representative weights turn this observation into a double-counting
identity and a polynomial-operation algorithm. The previously unspecified
coefficient in the $8$-arrangement setting is thereby evaluated, with a
uniform characteristic range and a checkable finite certificate for a
compact formula.

The core geometry also admits an exact count. In characteristics at
least five it is a problem of avoiding a finite offset set and repeated
sign orbits. In characteristics two and three it is a linear-independence
problem in a quotient vector space. These descriptions eliminate the
intermediate-characteristic gap and give exact finite products, universal
dimension obstructions, and distinct growing-dimension laws.

The boundary of the advance is explicit. Non-core directions still
contribute a cubic remainder, the eight-shape compression includes a
finite computer-assisted component, and no global Szemer\'edi estimate
has been propagated from the local refinements. The new formulae make
those remaining tasks more focused rather than disguising them as
completed results.

\section[{Reproduction and package contents\srctag{44}}]{Reproduction and package contents}\label{gsr:fz:44:sec:dA}
\srcnote{44}{Appendix A}
\label{gsr:fz:44:sec:reproduction}

The archive contains \gitpath{article.tex}, its compiled
\gitpath{article.pdf}, a \gitpath{Makefile}, \gitpath{README.md},
\gitpath{SOURCE_AUDIT.md}, \gitpath{FORMALIZATION.md}, the standard-library
verifier, and exact data and certificates. From the package directory,
\begin{verbatim}
python3 code/verify.py --max-d 10
latexmk -pdf -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error article.tex
\end{verbatim}
reconstructs the checks and the PDF. The verification program requires
Python 3.10 or later and must not be run with assertion-disabling
optimization. It performs no network requests and makes no repository
changes. The TeX source uses ordinary packages and an embedded
bibliography; it requires no shell escape, external figures, or external
bibliography service.

The machine-readable verification record distinguishes exact checks from
the floating-point asymptotic diagnostics. The rational normal lists for
$d=2,3,4$ are included to make the independent pair-span check inspectable.
No fonts, downloaded papers, or earlier research manuscripts are
redistributed in this package.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Further research questions and a proposed programme\srctag{45}}]{Further research questions and a proposed programme}\label{gsr:fz:45:sec:d6}
\srcnote{45}{Section 6}
\label{gsr:fz:45:sec:research}

The following questions isolate the remaining mathematical gaps. They
are proposed directions, not consequences of the preceding theorems.
The first group concerns finite classifications, the second concerns
the best stability ranges, and the third concerns the functional
extremizers that control cube counts.

\subsection{The next energy levels}

\begin{question}[All third-level extremizers]
\label{gsr:fz:45:q:third}
Classify every $m$-element torsion-free set satisfying
$E(A)=M_m-8(m-3)$. For sufficiently large $m$, are the only models,
up to translation, dilation, and reflection,
\[
 \{0,1,\ldots,m\}\setminus\{2\}
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \{0,2,3,\ldots,m-1,m+1\}?
\]
What is the smallest valid threshold, and what additional families
occur below it?
\end{question}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 54--59]
\emph{Answered by source~57} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:thirdlevel}): for $m\ge7$ the only models are the two displayed, up to affine maps, and $7$ is the optimal threshold, the one further class at $m=6$ being $\{0,1,2,4,5,6\}$ (its Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:st:third-equality}; item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:energylevels}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Also answered by source~66} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:energygap}), with the threshold $m\ge8$ for its three oriented templates (source~57's two affine classes), and the fourth level $M_m-8m+20$ for $m\ge11$ (its Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:third}--\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:fourlevels}); source~57's threshold $m\ge7$ is the better one.
\end{writenote}

The second displayed model also has defect $2m-6$: its prefix is
$\{0,2,\ldots,m-1\}$, of defect $m-3$, and adding $m+1$ makes exactly
the $m-3$ pairs of difference one fail. The third-gap induction therefore
provides candidate branches, but it does not by itself classify every
case of equality in those branches. An efficient next step is to
classify endpoint Schur defect two before attempting a larger search.

\begin{question}[Bounded Schur defect]
For a fixed integer $s\ge2$, describe all positive real sets
$C=\{c_1<\cdots<c_n\}$ satisfying
\[
 \binom n2-\#\{x+y=z:x,y,z\in C\}=s.
\]
For $n$ sufficiently large in terms of $s$, are all such sets positive
real dilates of finitely many integer terminal perturbations of
$\{1,\ldots,n\}$? If so, obtain effective bounds on the length of the
perturbed segment and on the required threshold in $n$.
\end{question}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 54--59]
\emph{Answered by source~57} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:thirdlevel}): for $n\ge5s-1$, $h(C)=s$ holds exactly for the positive dilates of $\{j+\lambda_j:1\le j\le n\}$ with $(\lambda_j)$ a partition of $s$ (nonnegative, nondecreasing, the perturbed positions among the last $s$), so there are $p(s)$ classes (its Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:st:partitions}); for $s=2$ the threshold $n=6$ is optimal (its Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:st:schur-two}). The optimal threshold for general $s$ is open (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:energylevels}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Threshold lowered by source~66} for $s\ge3$: $n\ge3s+1$ (its Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:partition}); $n=2s+1$ is not enough (its Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:prop:obstruction}).
\end{writenote}

The unit-defect proof uses the first imperfect reflection row and the
next perfect row. With several defective rows, their locations can
interact. A classification that keeps track of those interactions
could turn the endpoint recurrence into a systematic description of
the top of the energy spectrum.

\begin{question}[A larger rigidity window]
Determine sharp edit or containment bounds in terms of
$D(A)=(M_m-E(A))/4$ when $D(A)=O(m)$ or $D(A)=o(m^2)$.
For example, for each fixed $K$, does $D(A)\le Km$ force all but
$O_K(1)$ points into a single arithmetic progression whose length is
$m+O_K(1)$? Identify any necessary exceptions and the optimal
dependence on $K$.
\end{question}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Advanced by source~66}: above the fourth level, $E(A)\ge M_m-8m+20$, every set lies in an $(m+2)$-term progression and contains an $(m-2)$-term one (its Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:cor:recovery}); the linear-defect question is its Question~\ref{gsr:fz:66:epnf:q:linear}.
\end{writenote}

The theorem here proves exact one-point repair below the third level.
Extending this to a fixed multiple of $m$ would connect the finite
classification to mesoscopic stability. A statement at this scale
would require new arguments; the present induction does not supply
uniform control once many endpoint defects are allowed.

\begin{question}[Weighted ordered defects]
Is there a useful nonnegative weighted analogue of
\eqref{gsr:fm:45:intro:ordered-defect}, with an explicit extremal weighted
profile and a rigidity statement at small deficit? Which choices of
mass and magnitude constraints preserve an ordered-completion
interpretation?
\end{question}

Uniform indicator weights are essential to the integer-valued defect
and its four-unit spacing. A weighted formulation should specify its
normalization before guessing a counterpart of $M_m$; the support
cardinality alone does not control weighted energy.

\begin{question}[Effective cyclic rectification]
Find explicit, checkable hypotheses on $A\subset\Z/p\Z$ that allow
the first three torsion-free energy levels to be transferred by a
Freiman $2$-isomorphism. Can a suitable density or sumset condition be
combined with a near-extremal energy hypothesis to force those
hypotheses, with useful constants?
\end{question}

The full cyclic group has energy $m^3$, so a torsion-free bound cannot
hold for arbitrary cyclic sets. The useful objective is an effective
rectification theorem that names and excludes its periodic or
wraparound obstructions.

\subsection{Coset envelopes and puncture rigidity}

\begin{question}[The largest envelope range]
Determine the largest $\varepsilon_*$ for which every nonempty finite
set in every abelian group with $\varepsilon<\varepsilon_*$ has
coset distance at most $\tau(\varepsilon)$. Determine separately the
largest range in which the closest coset is unique and is given by
the autocorrelation threshold $r(d)>m/2$.
\end{question}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Answered by source~68}: $\varepsilon_*=1/4$ for existence and the autocorrelation subgroup, optimal even in cyclic groups, and $2/9$ for uniqueness of the closest coset, also optimal (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:energygap}).
\end{writenote}

Our common sufficient range is $\varepsilon<1/9$. The three properties
need not have the same threshold. At $\varepsilon=1/4$, a two-point
set in $\Z/3\Z$ has several closest cosets, so uniqueness cannot be
extended through that endpoint without modification. Failure of one
step in the present proof is not evidence that the envelope itself
fails there.

\begin{question}[A sharp pointwise autocorrelation inequality]
\label{gsr:fz:45:q:pointwise}
With $q(d)=|A\cap(A+d)|/|A|$, does the inequality
\[
 q(d)(1-q(d))\le\varepsilon
\]
hold universally? If it fails, determine the best constant in
$q(d)(1-q(d))\le C\varepsilon$ and classify the limiting examples.
\end{question}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Answered by source~68} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:energygap}): yes, $q(d)(1-q(d))\le\varepsilon$ holds in every abelian group, with all equality cases at $0<r_A(d)<m$ (its Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:pointwise} and~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:pointwise-equality}).
\end{writenote}

The proved inequality has $C=2$. A punctured coset supplies equality
in the proposed factor-one inequality for $d\in H\setminus L$ when
$A=H\setminus L$, so a universal constant below one is impossible.
A better constant would directly strengthen the subgroup
bootstrap, while the remaining occupancy and complement steps would
still need to be checked over the wider range.

\begin{question}[The maximal range of nested-hole repair]
Determine the largest range of $s=\eta/\delta^3$ and $\delta$ in
which the finite repair bound
\[
 \min_{D\subset C}|A\triangle(C\setminus D)|/m
 \le\delta\tau(s)
\]
holds, with $D$ ranging over nonempty proper subcosets of the
canonical coset $C$.  Can the sufficient condition $s<1/9$
be expanded to its optimal range?  For a fixed ambient group and
cardinality, how do subgroup indices and unattainable intermediate
values of $s$ strengthen this finite bound?
\end{question}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Range answered by source~68}: the bound holds for all $s\le1/4$ while $\varepsilon<1/4$, the full real domain of the inner inverse, and the outer condition cannot be relaxed (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:energygap}); the group-sensitive refinement is its Question~\ref{gsr:fz:68:q:discrete-envelope}.
\end{writenote}

Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:45:co:puncture-refined} settles the asymptotic leading
constant: it is exactly one.  More precisely, its multiplier is
$\tau(s)/s=1+s+O(s^2)$, and nested-hole examples attain the finite
bound at $s=(u-1)/u^2$ for every integer $u\ge8$.
The theorem also classifies all positive equality cases as two nested
holes.  Its proof applies the basic coset envelope to the missing set,
so any suitable enlargement of that basic range propagates to the
repair bound.  The unresolved issues are the maximal validity range
and the best group-sensitive bound between available equality
parameters.

\begin{question}[Arithmetic restrictions on the envelope]
For a fixed finite group $G$ and cardinality $m$, determine the best
distance bound at every feasible energy. How much can the universal
envelope be improved when $G$ has no subgroup index corresponding to
an exact puncture extremizer?
\end{question}

Equality permits only
$\varepsilon=(r-2)/(r-1)^2$ at positive defect. In a fixed group, $r$
must be an available subgroup index; in $\F_p^n$ it is a power of $p$.
The quantitative hole remainder and integer constraints on
$|A\triangle C|$ provide two possible routes to a group-sensitive
bound between those equality points.

\begin{question}[Stable collision equality and labels]
If coordinate-cube collisions nearly attain the coset-distance
envelope, must the domain be close, at a quantitatively sharp rate,
to a product with one punctured coordinate? Under an additional
near-maximal labelled-collision condition, which labels can occur on
such a domain, and how close must they be to compatible additive or
multilinear labels?
\end{question}

The equality argument separates the domain geometry from labels. A
stability proof would have to convert a small failure of corner
closure into a product approximation and then control the labels on
the repaired domain. Domain closeness alone does not imply label
compatibility. This is a natural continuation of the collision
amplification work in report source~15 \cite{repo45}.

\subsection{The fourth-uniformity extremal problem}

\begin{question}[The exact value of $c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}$]
Determine the constant in \eqref{gsr:fm:45:intro:cd} for $d=4$ and all its
extremizers or extremizing sequences. Is the supremum attained on a
finite group? Can an extremizer always be realized on a cyclic
quotient, or is a higher-rank group needed?
\end{question}

The established interval has width about $0.0880$. The five-point
function is an exact lower-bound witness, not a proposed solution of
the optimization problem. Searches over small groups should retain
exact or interval-certified witnesses; a floating-point local optimum
does not certify a universal bound or even optimality on that group.

\begin{question}[A stronger moment certificate]
Improve the rational certificate in Section~\ref{gsr:cc:45:un:section} by
using more of the joint constraints on
$t(h)=(\E_x f(x)f(x+h))^2$ and
$w(h)=\|f(\cdot)f(\cdot+h)\|_{U^2}^4-t(h)^2$.
Can a finite, exact sum-of-squares certificate reach the sharp
constant, or is information beyond finitely many moments necessary?
\end{question}

The proof drops several nonnegative Fourier contributions and applies
Jensen to a quadratic expression. Optimizing its coefficients alone
need not recover the true extremal value. A useful next certificate
should record which relaxations can be simultaneously sharp and
exploit any incompatibility.

\begin{question}[Spectral support and torsion]
Describe the Fourier support of a fourth-uniformity extremizer.
What is the minimum possible number of opposite character pairs,
and do two pairs suffice? Does order
five play an intrinsic extremal role, or does it merely supply a
convenient finite witness? Determine how the answer changes when
all character orders are restricted to exceed a prescribed bound.
\end{question}

The single-pair class is rigorously excluded. The dual identity
$\mathcal D_4\phi_1=111\phi_1+27\phi_3+\phi_5$ explains why a third
harmonic is forced in an improving perturbation. Subsequent
iterations may generate further harmonics or torsion-dependent
aliases. Their compatibility is a structural question, not just a
coefficient calculation.

\begin{question}[Stability and higher dimensions]
Prove a useful stability theorem for near-extremizers of
$c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}$, once its extremal models are identified.
Determine the constants $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}$ for $d\ge5$ and whether
there are strict gaps between consecutive values.
\end{question}

Monotonicity supplies $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}\le(832/4795)^{1/4}$ for
$d\ge4$, but does not identify any higher-dimensional extremal
model. A repeated derivative argument must retain the mean of the
derivative, as the proof here does; centering the original function
does not center each derivative.

\subsection{Integration and longer-term consequences}

\begin{question}[Formal proof of the finite certificates]
Formalize the endpoint energy identity, the unit-Schur-defect lemma,
the complement-energy identity, and the rational fourth-uniformity
certificate in Lean. Which finite combinatorial identities can be
checked by a small trusted kernel, and which analytic transitions
need additional finite Fourier infrastructure?
\end{question}

Appendix~\ref{gsr:fz:45:app:integration} proposes a dependency order and gives
the precise normalized-to-unnormalized translation. The shortest
formalization route should begin with exact finite sums and rational
polynomial identities, then add the structural equality arguments.

\begin{question}[Propagation to a global quantitative theorem]
Identify a complete quantitative argument in which one of the local
gains here survives all subsequent losses. Does the improved fourth
coefficient change a finite-parameter cube or progression threshold
of independent interest? Can any such gain be propagated through a
full density-increment proof with an explicit final bound?
\end{question}

A convincing answer should expose every dependency and retain the
same conventions for ambient density, uniformity, and degenerate
cubes. Improving a supplementary local coefficient is not sufficient
evidence of a better global Szemer\'edi bound.

For near-term work, the most concrete targets are the third-level
energy classification, the sharp pointwise autocorrelation constant,
and a better exact fourth-uniformity certificate. They each have a
specified gap left by the present proofs, a finite test environment,
and a plausible route to a further theorem.

The inspected formal development is
\path{Combinatorics/Ramsey/Lean/GowersSzemeredi/} at the pin in

The paper's sign convention uses $x+\omega\cdot h$, while the
development's affine cube argument uses a minus sign. Replacing each
$h_i$ by $-h_i$ preserves the sum, so this difference has no numerical
effect.

\subsection{The essential scaling identity}

Write $\Gamma_d(f)$ for the repository's unnormalized
\path{gowersNorm d f}, and let $N=|G|$. For the finite cyclic
instance implemented there and $d\ge1$,
\begin{equation}
 \Gamma_d(f)=N^{(d+1)/2^d}\|f\|_{U^d},\qquad
 \Gamma_d(\1_A)^{2^d}=\operatorname{cubeCount}_d(A).
 \label{gsr:fz:45:app:scaling}
\end{equation}
The latter equality is proved locally in
\path{Proofs03CubeUpper.lean} as
\path{gowersNorm_indicator_pow}. It counts degenerate cubes as well.

In particular, the real fourth-uniformity theorem becomes the
denominator-free inequality
\begin{equation}
 4795\,\Gamma_2(f)^{16}
 \le832\,N^7\Gamma_4(f)^{16}
 \label{gsr:fz:45:app:raw-u4}
\end{equation}
for real centered $f$ on an odd cyclic group. Indeed
$\|f\|_{U^2}^{16}=N^{-12}\Gamma_2(f)^{16}$ and
$\|f\|_{U^4}^{16}=N^{-5}\Gamma_4(f)^{16}$.
Omitting the factor $N^7$ would be a normalization error.

For the finite energy statements,
$E(A)=\operatorname{Finset.addEnergy}(A,A)$ under the ordered
quadruple convention used by the inspected statements. The
torsion-free theorem can be stated first for $\operatorname{Finset}\Z$,
with cardinality hypotheses made explicit. Generalizing the ambient
group is a later interface step rather than a prerequisite for the
first formal proof.

\subsection{A proposed order of formalization}

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Ordered finite counting.} Formalize the energy increment
on adjoining a greatest element, the bound on its Schur count, and
the ordered missing-completion identity. Use integer arithmetic for
$4D(A)=M_m-E(A)$, or clear the denominator three in $M_m$.

\item \textbf{Equality and unit defect.} Encode the reflection
characterization of each Schur row. Prove zero defect, then the unique
defective-row lemma, then the second and third energy results. This
order avoids a separate full classification of four-point energy sets.

\item \textbf{Autocorrelation and complements.} Establish
$\sum_d r(d)=m^2$, $E(A)=\sum_d r(d)^2$, the overlap inequality,
and the exact complement expansion. The polynomial remainder can be
verified after clearing denominators. Construct the canonical
subgroup with a finite-set closure argument before introducing the
radical expression $\tau$.

\item \textbf{Norm certificates.} Prove the Fourier square identity
for $U^3$ and the opposite-frequency pairing inequality on odd-order
groups. The rational quadratic certificate is a separate real
polynomial identity; it should not be entangled with Fourier
bookkeeping. Then formalize the nonnegative autocorrelation moment
expansion and combine the lemmas.

\item \textbf{Exact finite examples.} Verify the five-point cube sums
by finite enumeration over $\Z/5\Z$ and the cosine sign tables by
Boolean enumeration. These have small, fully specified domains and
require no numerical approximation.

\item \textbf{Cube-counting interface.} Prove the centered quartic
expansion, including the odd-order rank argument, or reuse it if
subsequently formalized in the repository. Combine with
\eqref{gsr:fz:45:app:raw-u4} to obtain \eqref{gsr:cc:45:ap:indicator} with the existing
uniformity parameter.
\end{enumerate}

No declaration names proposed here assert that such theorems have
already been added to the repository. The package is a standalone
article suitable for later integration under
\path{Research/GowersSzemeredi/rigidity-gaps/}, or for a further source
intake into the existing thematic report. If it is consolidated,
retain the provenance distinctions and do not silently replace the
earlier reports' hypotheses or their historical claims.

\section[{Exact certificates and reproducibility\srctag{45}}]{Exact certificates and reproducibility}\label{gsr:fz:45:sec:dB}
\srcnote{45}{Appendix B}
\label{gsr:fz:45:app:verification}

The package contains three independent standard-library Python scripts.
They use integers and \path{fractions.Fraction} for all mathematical
comparisons. Decimal values in the prose are evaluations of exact
expressions and are not inputs to any theorem. The searches cover only
the explicitly recorded finite domains. Their role is to expose
counting, normalization, equality-case, and transcription errors; they
do not replace the universal proofs.

\subsection{Energy and Schur counts}

\path{code/verify_energy.py} computes energy by counting pair-difference
multiplicities and independently counts failed ordered triple
completions. It verifies the endpoint recurrence using a reflected
Schur count, checks progression equality, the first gap, the complete
second-level classification in its stated range, and the third gap.
The recorded run covers:
\begin{itemize}
\item all $12\,911$ subsets of $\{0,\ldots,14\}$ containing zero
and having cardinality between one and nine;
\item all $39\,202$ subsets of $\{1,\ldots,16\}$ with cardinality
between one and eight for the positive Schur counts;
\item all $276$ single interior holes in $\{0,\ldots,m\}$ for
$2\le m\le24$, checking the exact one-hole formula;
\item five additional rational or large-gap fixtures, together with
explicit small-cardinality and torsion counterexamples to overbroad
versions of the statements.
\end{itemize}
The five largest tested cardinalities give the following observed top
three energies, consistent with the proved formula:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}rrrr@{}}
\toprule
$m$ & $M_m$ & $M_m-4(m-2)$ & $M_m-8(m-3)$ \\
\midrule
5 & 85 & 73 & 69 \\
6 & 146 & 130 & 122 \\
7 & 231 & 211 & 199 \\
8 & 344 & 320 & 304 \\
9 & 489 & 461 & 441 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
No full third-level equality classification is asserted or tested by
this script. The output is \path{data/energy_checks.json}.

\subsection{Cosets and coordinate collisions}

\path{code/verify_cosets.py} computes exact energy and enumerates
subgroup cosets to check the canonical construction and unique
minimum. It verifies the full polynomial remainder after clearing
denominators, checks the equality classification, checks puncture
repair on its admissible finite cases, and counts coordinate-cube
collisions directly in small product groups.
The recorded run exhausts $131\,053$ nonempty cyclic subsets in
groups of orders two through sixteen and examines $1\,597$
product-group subsets. Three further cyclic fixtures are added for
the recursive puncture theorem. There are $328$ high-energy cases
overall, and $320$ outer-envelope equality cases, of which $101$
have positive defect.

For the nested-hole bound, the script minimizes over all coset holes
inside the fixed canonical $C$ in each of $107$ admissible concrete
cases. Six have positive $\eta$: five attain the bound and one is
strict. Three lie beyond the smaller preliminary cutoff
$\eta/\delta^3\le1/16$. The radical-free comparison is
\[
 2j\le d,\qquad d\,j(d-j)\le J_{\mathrm{int}},
 \quad
 J_{\mathrm{int}}=m^3-E(A)-dm^2+d^2m,
\]
where $d=|A\triangle C|$ and $j$ is the minimum edit count.
An additional $427$ nested-hole equality examples and $18$ strict
outlier examples are checked through exact closed formulas; no
large ambient groups are enumerated for these checks. The output is
\path{data/coset_checks.json}. These numbers describe the test suite,
not a count of all isomorphism types or a finite proof of the general
theorems.

\subsection{The fourth-uniformity certificate}

\path{code/verify_u4.py} performs three complementary checks.
First, it expands the rational quadratic certificate exactly and
recovers
\[
 \frac{4795}{832}
 +\frac38\left(V-\frac32\right)
 +\frac98\left(V-\frac32\right)^2.
\]
Second, it computes the fifteen-vertex dual-cube sign table by direct
enumeration of $2^{15}$ assignments and independently by dynamic
programming in the generating polynomial. It also checks the
sixteen-vertex modular sign counts for character orders $3,5,7,9$,
including the order-three phase terms. Third, it enumerates every
ordered cube of dimensions two, three, and four on $\Z/5\Z$ for the
specified vector $(2,1,-2,-2,1)$.

The fourth-dimensional count includes all $5^5=3125$ parameter
tuples and yields the exact integer product sum $6\,468\,874$.
Both the histogram and its weighted sum are retained in
\path{certificates/u4_certificate.json}. The generating identity in
the proof, together with the finite recurrence printed there,
makes the cosine counts independently reproducible without trusting
floating-point software.

\subsection{Commands and verification boundaries}

From the package root, run:
\begin{verbatim}
python3 code/verify_energy.py --output data/energy_checks.json
python3 code/verify_cosets.py
python3 code/verify_u4.py --json certificates/u4_certificate.json
latexmk -pdf -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error \
  gowers_rigidity_gaps.tex
\end{verbatim}
The convenience command \path{python3 code/verify_all.py} runs the
three mathematical scripts in sequence. Python~3.10 or later is
sufficient. The scripts using assertions explicitly reject optimized
Python modes that would disable them. The energy script uses explicit
failure checks. No internet access or third-party Python package is
needed to reproduce the exact mathematical outputs.

Internal AI cross-checks of the proofs are included in
\path{reviews/}. Different analysis passes checked the energy,
coset, fourth-uniformity, and integration arguments. These records
make the checks inspectable; they are not external peer-review
reports or proof-assistant certificates. The final PDF was compiled,
checked for unresolved references and layout warnings, and visually
inspected. Build and package details are recorded in
\path{data/build_report.json}.

sumset, rearrangement, and extremal-uniformity literature more

statements with their proofs; the priority claim is deliberately

\section[{Algorithms, reproducibility, and proof status\srctag{46}}]{Algorithms, reproducibility, and proof status}\label{gsr:fz:46:sec:d10}\label{gsr:fz:46:sec:verification}
\srcnote{46}{Section 10}

\subsection{An effective construction pipeline}
Given the coefficients of a symmetric binary trilinear $T$ in a basis,
the proof is algorithmic. Compute the matrix
$C_{ij}=T(e_i,e_i,e_j)+T(e_i,e_j,e_j)$. A symplectic elimination yields its
rank, a maximal isotropic subspace, and a decomposition into elementary
wedges. These determine a canonical correction $S$ after choices of pivot
ordering have been fixed. Then \eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:binary-integrator} integrates
$R=T-S$, and $e(P)$ is an extremizer.

The matrix calculations use ordinary finite-field Gaussian elimination,
with cubic arithmetic complexity in the dimension. Once the trilinear
coefficient table has been formed, subtracting the elementary corrections
and writing the polynomial also takes polynomially many operations. The
output can be kept symbolically with $O(n^3)$ coefficients; it need not be
expanded into its $2^n$-entry value table. A naive coefficientwise
implementation of all corrections uses $O(n^4)$ field operations; this is
an upper bound, not an optimal-complexity claim. For trace tensors the
closed rank formula avoids constructing the matrix if only the extremal
value or maximal restriction dimension is required.

For general $p$ at degree $p+1$, the same obstruction matrix and symplectic
elimination construct an optimal elementary repair and an optimal-dimensional
integrable restriction. Writing the full symmetric tensor in coordinates
has a size depending on $p$ and $n$; no dimension-free runtime is claimed
for an input that is already a high-order coefficient table.

\subsection{Exact finite checks supplied with this paper}
The accompanying \texttt{verify.py} uses only the Python standard library.
It performs finite-field arithmetic in polynomial quotient representations,
integer calculations, and rational comparisons. It does not use floating
point to validate any theorem. The deterministic seed is $172917$.
The supplied \texttt{validation.json} records the field moduli, coefficients,
phase numerators, witnesses, counts, and results.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.68\textwidth}r@{}}
\toprule
Check family & Number checked\\
\midrule
Scalar leading differences and phase orders, $p=2,3,5,7$, $1\leq d\leq20$
 & $80$\\
Explicit trace integrators: all listed direction tuples and basepoints
 & $141\,781$\\
Nonzero trace coefficients: radical, isotropic, and wedge certificates
 & $770$\\
Explicit repeated-variable nonintegrability witnesses & $5$\\
Fourth-root single-function tables for binary spectral moments & $692$\\
General symmetric binary cubic extremizers: cube/basepoint checks
 & $209\,664$\\
Mixed eight-function tests for general symmetric binary tensors & $36$\\
Seven-function tests for general symmetric binary tensors & $36$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The trace-coefficient checks cover every nonzero coefficient in
$\F_{2^n}$ for $1\leq n\leq8$, in $\F_{3^n}$ for $1\leq n\leq4$, and in
$\F_{5^n}$ for $1\leq n\leq3$. The general binary cubic checks use nine
coefficient tables in dimensions two, three, and four. They explicitly
construct an extremizing phase and check its total derivative against the
residual tensor at every basepoint and every direction triple. The script
also verifies the predicted Walsh spectral magnitudes and the exact
extremal moments.

For the two specified coefficients over $\F_4$, all $4^4=256$ fourth-root
function tables are exhausted. For $c=1$, their maximum moment is $1$;
for $c=\theta$, it is $7/16$, whereas the unrestricted maximum proved in
this paper is $1/2$. The latter value is attained using eighth roots.
The larger-field function-table checks are sampled rather than exhaustive;
the JSON explicitly distinguishes these cases. Their largest observed
values must not be mistaken for the proved optima.

Run the checks with
\begin{verbatim}
python verify.py --output validation.json
\end{verbatim}
The program raises an exception on a failed assertion and writes a final
\texttt{PASS} status only after completing the checks. These computations
are useful protection against normalization, sign, and phase-depth errors.
They are \emph{not} the proof of any universal theorem, and they are not a
Lean kernel check. The general proofs are those in the preceding sections.

\subsection{Repository integration and formalization boundary}
A suggested destination is a new, descriptively named subdirectory under
\nolinkurl{Combinatorics/Ramsey/Research/GowersSzemeredi/}; this package does not
modify any existing repository file. The source audit records the inspected
blob identifiers of the Gowers transcription and the refinement inventory.
Blob identifiers should not be mistaken for commit identifiers.

The most economical formalization order is to start with the finite
binary core: alternating obstruction; quadratic Walsh spectrum; the cube
change of variables; exact upper bound; explicit residual integrator;
sharpness; and the seven-function corollary. The trace rank calculation and
the general-$p$ coordinate construction form subsequent independent modules.
The accompanying \texttt{FORMALIZATION.md} spells out proposed statements
and dependencies. It is a roadmap, not purported compiled Lean code.

\section[{Further research questions and concrete next targets\srctag{46}}]{Further research questions and concrete next targets}\label{gsr:fz:46:sec:d11}\label{gsr:fz:46:sec:questions}
\srcnote{46}{Section 11}

The questions below are proposed continuations of this work. Calling them
questions means they are not resolved here; it is not a claim that each has
never been considered elsewhere.

\begin{problem}[The exact seven-function norm]
For a symmetric binary trilinear $T$, determine the exact supremum of
$|\Gamma_T|$ over seven 1-bounded functions. Does it depend only on
$\rank C_T$, as the eight-function norm does? Is the exponent $r/4$ in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:46:thm:seven} optimal?
\end{problem}
The cube estimate is sharp, but equality must also survive the initial
Cauchy--Schwarz step. An exact analysis of that compatibility would decide
whether the codimension constant $2$ can be decreased. Small-rank blocks
and tensor products provide explicit test cases.

\begin{problem}[Classification of all cubic extremizers]
Describe all $f$ for which $M_T(f)=2^{-r/2}$, modulo natural phase
multiplications and linear changes of coordinates.
\end{problem}
Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:46:prop:stability} says that every transformed four-point
function must lie in the positive spectral subspace, and that $|f|=1$.
The missing step is to solve these simultaneous compatibility equations
for $f$. The constructed nonclassical phases give one family, not an
exhaustive classification.

\begin{problem}[From spectral to structural stability]
If $M_T(f)\geq(1-\eps)2^{-r/2}$, can one approximate $f$ in normalized
$L^2$ by an exact extremizer, with a dimension-independent error tending to
zero with $\eps$?
\end{problem}
The exact defect identity is a useful starting point because it has no
unspecified constants. The obstacle is that the favorable eigenspaces
vary with $(A,B)$; separate projection estimates do not immediately produce
one globally consistent phase.

\begin{problem}[The ordinary slice-rank repair gap]
Determine $\rho(T)$ within the interval $r/2\leq\rho(T)\leq r$.
Is $\rho(T)=r$ for all symmetric binary trilinear forms, or can several
obstruction blocks be repaired more economically together?
\end{problem}
The rank-two case is settled in Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:46:prop:slice-repair}.
In larger rank, a sum of nonsymmetric slices can be symmetric without each
summand being symmetric. This is exactly why the elementary repair theorem
does not answer the ordinary slice-rank question.

\begin{problem}[Higher phase-alphabet constraints]
Determine the maximum of $M_T(f)$ when $f$ is restricted to a prescribed
finite root-of-unity alphabet, especially fourth roots rather than eighth
roots in characteristic two.
\end{problem}
The exhaustive $\F_4$ calculation exhibits a strict gap $7/16<1/2$.
A general theorem should describe which residual diagonal coefficients
force this gap and whether product constructions preserve an exact
alphabet-dependent norm formula.

\begin{problem}[Odd-characteristic analogues]
At degree $p+1$, is there a sharp mixed cube inequality controlled by the
rank of $C_T$ over $\F_p$, and can its extremizers be constructed by
symplectic blocks?
\end{problem}
The algebraic restriction and repair statements already hold for every
prime. The analytic proof in Section~\ref{gsr:fp:46:sec:sharp} exploits a special
binary reparametrization of the eight vertices and a quadratic kernel.
An odd-characteristic replacement would require a different analytic
mechanism, not just changing signs in the present proof.

\begin{problem}[Higher-degree trace restrictions]
For $d\geq p+2$, determine the largest subspace $W\leq\F_{p^n}$ on which
$T_{c,d}$ integrates.
\end{problem}
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:46:thm:trace-classification} excludes integration on the whole
extension field. On a subspace, the repeated-variable constraints involve
all products of the extra directions from $W$. This becomes a simultaneous
isotropy problem for a family of forms $C_{cz}$, rather than one alternating
form. Product-set structure of $W$ should therefore become relevant.

\begin{problem}[Robustness before exact symmetry]
Can a quantitatively approximate symmetric tensor be brought into the
framework of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:46:thm:sharp} with a loss that improves a complete
low-characteristic symmetrization pipeline?
\end{problem}
A useful result must separately track the error of symmetrization, the
rank of the repeated-variable obstruction, and the cost of restriction or
repair. The sharp symmetric estimate alone does not justify silently
replacing constants at all those earlier stages.

\begin{problem}[Frobenius-twisted trace families]
Extend the exact obstruction-rank calculation to symmetric forms built
from sums of trace monomials involving Frobenius powers in the arguments.
\end{problem}
The radical will again be described by a linearized polynomial, but the
number of roots need not have the two-regime form of
\eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:radical-dimension}. Explicit families could provide a broader
supply of sharp cubic examples and nontrivial restriction geometries.

\begin{problem}[Formal certificates and algorithmic output]
Construct machine-checkable certificates for the symplectic decomposition,
residual integrator, and extremal value, and formalize their verification in
Lean with finite normalized sums.
\end{problem}
A certificate-based implementation can separate potentially elaborate
search from a short verifier. The package's exact arithmetic checks are
prototypes of the data to certify; they are not a substitute for the
kernel-verified implications.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Conclusion\srctag{46}}]{Conclusion}\label{gsr:fz:46:sec:d12}
\srcnote{46}{Section 12}
The factorial restriction in polarization is not one uniform obstruction.
On the scalar prime field it can always be repaired, at exactly the phase
order $p^{\lceil d/(p-1)\rceil}$. For extension-field trace tensors it can
be a genuine obstruction to every circle-valued integrator. At the first
obstructed degree, an alternating form measures the exact geometric cost
of restriction and the exact number of elementary symmetric repairs.

For binary cubic tensors, that same form has an exact analytic meaning:
the twisted mixed cube norm is $2^{-\rank C_T/2}$. The quadratic convolution
proof and the matching nonclassical-phase construction yield sharp agreement
thresholds and an explicit stability identity. They also improve the
symmetric seven-function restriction bound from $8\log_2(1/\delta)$ to
$2\log_2(1/\delta)$. These are local, fully specified advances at a genuine
structural bottleneck of the Gowers method, rather than an unverified claim
of a new global Szemer\'edi bound.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Proof dependency map and scope checks\srctag{46}}]{Proof dependency map and scope checks}\label{gsr:fz:46:sec:dA}
\srcnote{46}{Appendix A}
The main analytic theorem has the following dependency chain:
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \text{binary cube change of variables}
 \longrightarrow \text{quadratic Walsh spectrum}
 \longrightarrow \text{mixed upper bound},\\
 \text{alternating-form decomposition}
 +\text{explicit binary cubic integration}
 \longrightarrow \text{matching extremizer}.
 \end{gathered}
\]
Neither chain uses an inverse theorem. The seven-function corollary adds
one application of Cauchy--Schwarz and the maximal-isotropic dimension
formula. The trace applications add only Frobenius adjointness,
nondegeneracy of the trace pairing, and root counts in the cyclic group
$\F_q^\times$.

The most consequential scope checks are these. Symmetry of $T$ is essential
in the sharp cubic proof. Tensor degree three and characteristic two are
essential to its quadratic-kernel reduction. ``Integrates'' permits
nonclassical circle-valued polynomials unless ``classical'' is explicitly
specified. The exact repair number refers to the elementary family
\eqref{gsr:fp:46:eq:elementary-general}, whereas ordinary slice-rank repair only has
the bounds in Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:46:prop:slice-repair}. The exact seven-function
norm, the complete extremizer classification, and an improved global
progression-free-set bound are not proved in this article.

\section[{Relation to the Gowers argument and the formal project\srctag{47}}]{Relation to the Gowers argument and the formal project}\label{gsr:fz:47:sec:d10}
\srcnote{47}{Section 10}
\label{gsr:fz:47:boe:sec:interface}

\subsection{A precise local generalization}
The relevant source stage is Gowers's Lemma~17.1 and
Proposition~17.2, at printed pages 577--578~\cite{gowers}.  The source
uses finite differences and a factorial denominator to turn structured
frequencies into polynomial phase information.  Our result treats a
Boolean vector-space analogue in which that denominator is unavailable,
and quantifies the additional obstruction for an already supplied
symmetric tensor.

The inspected formal statement in
\gitpath{Lean/GowersSzemeredi/Sections17_18.lean} explicitly assumes a
prime cyclic modulus and invertibility of $(k+1)!$, and concludes a phase
of degree at most $k+1$.  Its source comment records the correction of the
printed degree.  In contrast, our $d$ is the degree of a genuinely
multilinear tensor including its final evaluation slot, so $d=k+1$ at
the selected-energy interface.  Dividing the project's unnormalized
Fourier-square sum by $|V|^{d+1}$ gives our normalization.

There are three substantive differences, not just notation.  The ambient
space is $\Ftwo^n$ rather than a large prime cyclic group.  The phase takes
values in $\Tcirc$ rather than being required to be a classical polynomial
with values in the base field.  Finally, the sharp criterion assumes full
symmetry and high selected energy for a specified tensor; it is not a
procedure that finds that tensor from an arbitrary positive uniformity norm.

\subsection{Multiaffine terms must not be silently discarded}
The project's \gitpath{Definitions.lean} defines \gitpath{IsMultilinear}
as a sum of square-free monomials, including constant and lower-degree
terms.  It is therefore a multiaffine predicate in the usual terminology.
Our tensor is homogeneous multilinear in every slot.
A general multiaffine frequency selector cannot be covered by simply
erasing its lower-order terms.  Such a reduction would need its own
phase correction or energy estimate, and no such reduction is assumed here.

Similarly, all translation averages in the proof range over the full
vector space.  On a progression, a Bohr neighborhood, or a nonuniformly
weighted set, a translation may change the averaging measure.  The exact
period identity still holds pointwise, but its Fourier-cancellation and
projective-averaging consequences acquire boundary or measure errors.
A new global quantitative Szemer\'edi estimate would require those steps,
selector construction, and a full downstream loss calculation.

\subsection{Suggested formalization order}
The new elementary results admit a fairly short dependency chain once a
finite Boolean Fourier interface is available:
\begin{gather*}
 \text{cube product}\ \longrightarrow\ \text{even periods}
 \ \longrightarrow\ \text{forbidden Fourier coefficients}\\
 \longrightarrow\ \text{fixed-derivative cap}
 \ \longrightarrow\ \text{canonical induction}.
\end{gather*}
For the universal theorem, a second chain is
\begin{gather*}
 \text{pure-map lemmas}\ \longrightarrow\ \text{trilinear census}\\
 \longrightarrow\ \text{support lifting}
 \ \longrightarrow\ \text{defect dichotomy}.
\end{gather*}
The bridge between the two is the shear rank profile.  It is the heaviest
background component because it uses finite-dimensional complex spectral
theory or an equivalent explicit matrix argument.

The companion \gitpath{FORMALIZATION.md} records proposed theorem names,
inputs, and dependencies.  An appropriate implementation should represent
characters as actual linear maps $V\to\Ftwo$, use normalized finite sums,
and prove the cube-product period identity before introducing any division.
The sixteen-row census can be a transparent exhaustive Boolean calculation.
No unchecked axiom, \gitpath{sorry}, or proposition-valued declaration in
this package is advertised as a formal proof; no Lean files are supplied.

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 47--53]
\emph{Checked at HEAD \texttt{06b30ca52}.} \file{proposition_17_2} (\file{Sections17\_18.lean}, line~48) assumes a prime modulus, $k+1<N$ and the invertibility of $(k+1)!$, and concludes a phase of degree at most $k+1$, as described above; \file{IsMultilinear} is the multiaffine predicate (\file{Definitions.lean}, blob unchanged since the pin). The exact companions are \file{proposition_17_2_holds} (\file{Proofs17PhaseRemoval.lean}, line~373) and \file{lemma_17_1_holds} (\file{Proofs17Phase.lean}, line~374). No statement of this source is formalized; its results are over $\F_2^n$, outside the formal setting.
\end{writenote}

\section[{Further research questions and topics\srctag{47}}]{Further research questions and topics}\label{gsr:fz:47:sec:d12}\label{gsr:fz:47:boe:sec:questions}
\srcnote{47}{Section 12}
The following are proposed continuations of the results proved here.
They are not silently used as hypotheses elsewhere, and they are not
presented as a catalogue of already published open problems.

\begin{problem}[The septic threshold]\label{gsr:fz:47:boe:q:septic}
Is $M^{\mathrm{sym}}_{7,n}=15/16$ for every $n\ge2$?  The present proof
leaves only
\[
 \frac{120}{128}\le M^{\mathrm{sym}}_{7,n}\le\frac{121}{128}.
\]
An improvement must exploit either a better non-pure four-linear defect
estimate or simultaneous derivative constraints beyond the scalar rank
profile.  A support improvement alone should be checked against the
compatibility identities before it is used as an energy theorem.
\end{problem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Answered by sources~65 and~69}: $15/16$ (Section~\ref{gsr:fp:sec:alldegree}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{problem}[The all-degree universal extremum]\label{gsr:fz:47:boe:q:all-degree}
Does the canonical formula $1-(d+1)/2^d$ give
$M^{\mathrm{sym}}_{d,n}$ in every degree, or is there a first degree and
a noncanonical tensor with larger energy?  The answer is established here
only through degree six.  The canonical formula itself is proved in every
degree and therefore gives a fixed, dimension-free benchmark for either
outcome.
\end{problem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Answered by sources~65 and~69}: yes, in every degree $d\ge3$ and dimension $n\ge2$ (Section~\ref{gsr:fp:sec:alldegree}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{problem}[Optimal non-pure support]\label{gsr:fz:47:boe:q:support}
Determine the least support of a non-pure symmetric $s$-linear map for
$s\ge4$, first for scalar-valued maps and then for vector-valued maps.
The projection lemma reduces lower bounds in the latter problem to the
former.  The example $u^{\otimes s}+v^{\otimes s}$ has support
$2^{1-s}-2^{1-2s}$, whereas our uniform lower bound is $7/2^{s+2}$.
Are there other support-minimizing families, and what are the stability
statements near the minimum?
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Endpoint tensors and phases]\label{gsr:fz:47:boe:q:endpoints}
Classify the tensors and functions attaining the quintic and sextic
thresholds.  In the noncanonical branch, equality requires both minimal
defect support and equality in every relevant projective spectral bound.
The sharpness of the support constant does not by itself prove that all
these equalities can occur for derivatives of a single function.
For the canonical branch, turn the deficit recursion into a global
phase-stability theorem with dimension-independent constants.
\end{problem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{The tensor part is answered by sources~65 and~69}: the endpoint tensors are exactly the canonical ones modulo integrable tensors, in every degree (Section~\ref{gsr:fp:sec:alldegree}); the endpoint functions remain open (65 Research question~\ref{gsr:fz:65:bsi:q:phases}, item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:IV:boolenergy}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{problem}[Stability under adjoining inactive coordinates]
\label{gsr:fz:47:boe:q:inactive}
For which symmetric tensors $T_0$ does pullback along
$V\twoheadrightarrow V_0$ preserve $\Mcal(T_0)$?
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:47:boe:thm:main-canonical} settles the canonical family.
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:47:boe:thm:binary-image} reduces every one-dimensional defect
image to a binary tensor modulo an integrable correction, but does not
settle the remaining optimization.  A finite classification of those
binary obstruction types, followed by derivative-compatible bounds,
is a concrete next target.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Direct sums and mixed functions]\label{gsr:fz:47:boe:q:mixed}
Does the maximum selected energy multiply under direct sums of canonical
tensors in degrees at least four?  Product functions give a lower bound,
not an upper bound.  Similarly, determine what replaces the sharp
thresholds when different functions occupy the cube vertices.  The common
function is essential to the exact even-period identity; a mixed theorem
requires additional compatibility or a different inequality.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Odd characteristic and repeated-direction cycles]
\label{gsr:fz:47:boe:q:odd}
Find the analogue of the forbidden-frequency argument in characteristic
$p>2$, taking account of the $p$-repetition transfer conditions in
nonclassical integration.  The Boolean argument uses that one direction
conjugates a derivative and two directions restore it.  A useful generalization
would retain the full translation action on a repeated-direction product,
rather than impose a Boolean period identity that is no longer true.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Local domains and a complete inverse step]
\label{gsr:fz:47:boe:q:local}
Quantify the period and projective-averaging errors on Bohr neighborhoods
or arithmetic progressions, and propagate them through a genuine selector
construction and phase-removal argument.  An end-to-end quantitative gain
must include the cost of producing a symmetric homogeneous tensor from
local or multiaffine data; the high-energy certificate alone does not
perform this construction.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Formalization and certified finite models]
\label{gsr:fz:47:boe:q:formal}
Formalize the even-period and fixed-derivative lemmas first, then the
canonical induction.  A separate finite-linear-algebra module can certify
the pure-defect classification and the support census.  Can the spectral
profile be implemented with an explicit finite matrix decomposition that
is convenient for both Lean and independently checkable certificates,
without obscuring the normalization or using unproved analytic interfaces?
\end{problem}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Conclusion\srctag{47}}]{Conclusion}\label{gsr:fz:47:sec:d13}
\srcnote{47}{Section 13}
The decisive constraint is not that a tensor happens to use two
coordinates.  It is that a sliced test function is a derivative, and its
further derivatives have exact even-direction periods.  Preserving that
constraint gives the all-degree canonical extremum and closes the prior
quartic stabilization problem.

The universal conclusion requires a second ingredient: a noncanonical
symmetric defect cannot be arbitrarily sparse.  Pure defects are exactly
the canonical obstruction class; non-pure trilinear maps have sharp
support $7/32$, and contraction propagates that information to higher
degrees.  This yields exact symmetric integration thresholds through degree
six and the improved uniform bound beyond it.  The remaining gaps are
explicit: the septic interval has width $1/128$, endpoint phase stability
is not classified, and no local-to-global density-increment estimate has
been propagated from these results.

\subsection{A nontrivial exact-data filter certificate}
\label{gsr:fz:48:gcr:sec:fejer-example}
The bundled example \file{examples/fejer.json} uses
\[
 p=5,\quad B=\{0,1,2,3,4\},\quad
 (\phi(0),\ldots,\phi(4))=(0,0,1,1,0),\quad s=2,\quad\eta=1/3.
\]
The full domain has $\calT_2(B)=125$ and $\calR_2(B,\phi)=65$, so its
respected proportion $13/25$ is below the target $2/3$.
We deliberately use a small exact-data kernel, $L=3$ and $Q=2048$, not
the worst-case theorem's prescribed value of $L$. The certified rational
table is
\[
 (q_0,q_1,q_2,q_3,q_4)
  =\left(1,\frac{595}{2048},\frac{43}{1024},
              \frac{43}{1024},\frac{595}{2048}\right).
\]
Searching all $125$ triples gives the exact family mean
\[
 \frac{2868235983031}{2748779069440}>0.
\]
The best triple, under the specified enumeration order, is $(u,v,c)=(0,2,0)$.
Its probabilities are
$(1,1,43/1024,43/1024,1)$, with conditional surplus
$4377059/786432$. Rounding removes labels $2$ and $3$ and produces
\[
 B'=\{0,1,4\},\qquad
 \calT_2(B')=\calR_2(B',\phi)=19,\qquad F_{1/3}(B')=19/3.
\]
Every number in this paragraph is reproduced using rational arithmetic
in \file{data/fejer_example.json}. The example illustrates why exact
certification is useful below the analytic threshold; it is not evidence
for changing that threshold without a new proof.

\subsection{A prescribed-size restriction that is not exact homomorphism}
The example \file{examples/fixed_size.json} uses $p=7$, $B=\{0,1,2,3,4\}$,
image values $(0,1,4,2,2)$, order $s=3$, error $\eta=1/4$, and prescribed
size three. The uniform three-subset average of $F_{1/4}$ is $-15/4$.
The deterministic run nevertheless finds
\[
 B'=\{1,3,4\},\qquad
 \calT_3(B')=111,\qquad \calR_3(B',\phi)=93.
\]
Thus $F_{1/4}(B')=39/4>0$ and the respected proportion is
$31/37>3/4$. The algorithm is allowed to exceed a negative initial
certificate; the theorem only guarantees nondecrease. The set has the
required size exactly, and its respected proportion is not one.

\subsection{A positive Bernoulli certificate with an affine core}
The file \file{examples/affine_core.json} supplies an example with
$p=17$, $s=3$, $\eta=1/4$, and
\[
 B=\{0,\ldots,7\},\qquad
 (\phi(0),\ldots,\phi(7))=(0,1,2,3,4,5,12,15).
\]
The first six inclusion probabilities equal $3/4$; the other two equal
$1/20$. The exact initial surplus is positive:
\[
 \calJ(\boldsymbol p)=\frac{3684947}{12800}>0.
\]
The algorithm retains
$\{0,\ldots,5\}$ and returns
\[
 \calT_3(B')=\calR_3(B',\phi)=4332,\qquad F_{1/4}(B')=1083.
\]
This is a correctness example for a supplied filter, not a claim that
finding such a filter is free. The Fej\'er example in
Section~\ref{gsr:fz:48:gcr:sec:fejer-example} includes the full finite-family search.
