\section[{Conclusion\srctag{54}}]{Conclusion}\label{gsr:fz:54:sec:d12}
\srcnote{54}{Section 12}
Proposition 8.1 admits a stronger conclusion than its original
translate-by-translate extraction: one quadratic phase, with the
prescribed quadratic coefficient, suffices across the entire
translation family. The exact factorization retains a spectral
overlap and an amplitude weight; both sharpen the lower bound.
Quadratic refinements identify the correct all-group extension and
its even-order limitation.

The same Fourier representation resolves the normalized intercept
energy problem completely. Its equality cases change at small
character orders, and its optimal recovery exponent changes
between orders four and five. The four-frequency obstruction
explains why a superficially plausible square-root repair theorem
fails in the latter range. These statements give explicit local
improvements and testable structural interfaces for the ProveIt
Ramsey development without overstating their global consequences.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Further research questions\srctag{55}}]{Further research questions}\label{gsr:fz:55:sec:d12}\label{gsr:fz:55:sec:questions}
\srcnote{55}{Section 12}

The following are proposed problems arising from the proved results.
They are not all claims of previously documented open conjectures.
The first four are particularly direct continuations of the present work.

\begin{question}[The cubic coefficient]\label{gsr:fz:55:q:cubic}
Determine the optimal coefficient of $e^3$ in
$\mathfrak S_{d,G}(e)$. Is it determined by finitely many torsion statistics
of $\widehat G$ for fixed $d$? Does it depend on the smallest available
odd character order even when the quadratic coefficient does not?
\end{question}
The proof explains why only order-two torsion can affect the quadratic
coefficient. At the next order, six-vertex configurations and the
next-order deformation of the extremizing character modes both enter.
One must optimize those deformations, not merely expand the families
\eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:evenfamily} and \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:oddfamily}.

\begin{question}[The exact even-order curve for $d\ge3$]\label{gsr:fz:55:q:exact}
For some group-independent interval $0\le e\le e'_d$, is
$\mathfrak S_{d,G}(e)$ equal to \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:evencurve} on every even-order
finite abelian group? If not, determine the first coefficient at which a
multi-mode deformation improves the one-character family.
\end{question}
The equality is proved for $d=2$ in proposition~\ref{gsr:en:55:prop:exactu2}. The present
higher-degree argument proves only its second-order optimality.

\begin{question}[Quantitative rigidity]\label{gsr:fz:55:q:rates}
Give explicit rates in theorem~\ref{gsr:en:55:thm:rigidmain} in terms of the second-order
deficit
$\frac2q\eps+b_d(G)\eps^2-D_d(f)$ and $\eps^3$.
Can one obtain a stability estimate for the full phase perturbation,
rather than just its normalized tangent?
\end{question}
The proof already isolates three nonnegative losses: amplitude deficit,
two-torsion profile deficit, and failure of Fourier mass concentration.
Keeping quantitative versions of all three is a plausible route.

\begin{question}[An explicit entry threshold]\label{gsr:fz:55:q:entry}
Extract a usable numerical $e_d$ from the finite-group proof of the
Eisner--Tao entry theorem, then combine it with theorem~\ref{gsr:en:55:thm:local}.
Can the resulting threshold and the local radius be made singly
exponential in $d$, rather than involving a coarse expansion in $2^d$
vertices?
\end{question}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 70--81]
\emph{Answered by source~73} (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:nearmaximal}): yes. For every $d\ge2$ and every nontrivial finite abelian group the expansion holds from $\varepsilon\le10^{-d}$, with local radius at least $q^{-5/2}$ and cubic coefficient below $3q^3$, $q=2^d$, through a correlation-preserving entry induction (its Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:73:thm:main} and Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:73:prop:constants}); its remainder $10\binom q5+\binom q6$ replaces the coarse sum over all $2^d$ vertices.
\end{writenote}
This is an optimization of an effective published argument, not a missing
logical hypothesis of theorem~\ref{gsr:en:55:thm:main}.

\begin{question}[Intervals and boundary terms]\label{gsr:fz:55:q:interval}
Find the sharp analogue of the distance expansion for the normalized
interval norm $U^d([N])$, uniformly in sufficiently large $N$.
Which coefficients reflect the boundary-conditioned cube distribution,
and what additional dependence on $N$ is unavoidable?
\end{question}
The interval near-extremizer theorem in \cite{eisnertao} supplies an entry
point, but the three-wise independence used here is absent. A direct
transfer of the finite-group constants would therefore be unjustified.

\begin{question}[Mixed cubical near-extremizers]\label{gsr:fz:55:q:mixed}
For a tuple $(f_\omega)$ of bounded functions whose mixed cube average is
near one, determine the sharp joint distance to a compatible tuple of
phase polynomials. Is there a finite-dimensional spectral problem
replacing \eqref{gsr:en:55:eq:profilefunction}?
\end{question}
Here compatibility matters: individually good phase approximations need
not satisfy the exact mixed cube identity. An analysis of simultaneous
phase gauges would be needed before a scalar expansion can be used.

\begin{question}[Approximately independent cube samplings]\label{gsr:fz:55:q:designs}
Extend the local theorem to sampling laws for which every triple of
vertex evaluations is close to independent, with an explicit error in
terms of the triple marginal defects and the four-point circuit law.
\end{question}
Such a result could separate the analytic cancellation from the exact
group geometry. It would also clarify which weighted or local cube
models admit the same leading coefficient.

\begin{question}[Compact groups and spectral type]\label{gsr:fz:55:q:compact}
Develop the same sharp theory for second-countable compact abelian groups,
replacing parity by the existence of a nontrivial order-two character.
Can the tangent theorem be formulated uniformly without finiteness of the
phase space modulo constants?
\end{question}
Most local calculations extend through Haar measure and Fourier series;
existence or replacement of a minimizing phase requires an explicit
argument. No compact-group theorem beyond the imported entry statement is
asserted here.

\begin{question}[Noncommutative endpoint constants]\label{gsr:fz:55:q:quantum}
For the Pauli uniformity norms of unitary matrices, determine the sharp
leading and second-order distance constants near an exact extremizer.
Which part of the scalar two-torsion dichotomy survives, and which is
replaced by commutator data?
\end{question}
Bao, Bri\"et, Castro-Silva, van Dordrecht, and Helsen prove a fourth-order
near-extremizer theorem in this noncommutative setting
\cite{baocliffordtesting}. Their result provides a concrete comparison problem.
The commutative Fourier circuit calculation here does not transfer
unchanged, and no noncommutative theorem is claimed in this article.

\begin{question}[Certified integration]\label{gsr:fz:55:q:lean}
Formalize the four-vertex classification, the six-triple H\"older estimate,
and the explicit local theorem in Lean. Can the phase-entry input be kept
as a clearly named interface while the local result is verified
independently of the full Szemer\'edi development?
\end{question}
This is a modular target: the local theorem requires finite-group
averages, character orthogonality, H\"older, and polynomial inequalities,
not the entire inverse theorem.

The exact checks include real quartic coefficients and the second and

They run on cyclic groups and selected products, including odd, even,

For example, at $d=3$ and $t=10^{-4}$, the ratio
\[
 \frac{D_d(F_t)-\eps(F_t)/4}{\eps(F_t)^2}

Floating checks use a stated absolute tolerance; rational checks use

\section[{A compact coefficient ledger\srctag{55}}]{A compact coefficient ledger}\label{gsr:fz:55:sec:dA}\label{gsr:fz:55:app:ledger}
\srcnote{55}{Appendix A}

For convenient independent checking, the constants used in the proof are
collected here:
\begin{align*}
 q&=2^d, &
 C_d&=(6^d-2q^2+q)/8,\\
 A_d&=q(q-1)(q-2)/24, &
 J_d&=A_d-C_d,\\
 B_d&=10\binom q5+\sum_{s=6}^q\binom qs2^{s-6}, &
 K_{0,d}&=q(q-1)/8.
\end{align*}
The two exact simplifications driving the main theorem are
\[
 \frac{8}{q^3}\left(K_{0,d}+\frac{C_d}{2}\right)
 =\frac{3^d-1}{2q^2},\qquad
 \frac{8}{q^3}(K_{0,d}+A_d)=\frac{q^2-1}{3q^2}.
\]
For $d=2,3,4$ the coarse local constants are
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}crrrr@{}}
\toprule
$d$ & $B_d$ & $K_*$ & $H_*$ & $R_d$\\
\midrule
2 & 0 & $5/2$ & 1 & $121/32$\\
3 & 608 & 21 & 620 & $25813/256$\\
4 & 713568 & 170 & 713668 & $51249029/4096$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The quadratic coefficients are optimal; these cubic upper constants are
not. The five-factor cancellation, rather than the numerical size of
$B_d$, is what establishes the $O_d(e^3)$ scale.

\section[{Why a purely formal Taylor expansion is insufficient\srctag{55}}]{Why a purely formal Taylor expansion is insufficient}\label{gsr:fz:55:sec:dB}\label{gsr:fz:55:app:pitfalls}
\srcnote{55}{Appendix B}

There are three distinct uniformity issues in this problem.
First, $D\to0$ does not imply $\norm{F-1}_\infty\to0$ when the group is
allowed to vary. A perturbation may remain large on a set of vanishing
relative size. Consequently one cannot simply write $F=e^{ib}$ with
$\norm b_\infty\to0$ for an arbitrary near-extremizer and expand the
exponential. The upper theorem instead expands the finite cube product
exactly and bounds its tail using triple independence and the disk
constraint.

Second, the distance in \eqref{gsr:fm:55:eq:distance} is an infimum over all phase
polynomials, not just over constants. Computing a family's mean gives a
distance upper bound unless other phases are excluded. The uniform gap in
lemma~\ref{gsr:en:55:lem:gap} supplies precisely that missing step for the sharpness
examples.

Third, a local inequality around an already known phase does not imply a
global near-extremizer theorem without an entry argument. The explicit
separation of theorem~\ref{gsr:en:55:thm:local} from the Eisner--Tao input makes this
dependency visible. None of the finite tests in section~\ref{gsr:fz:55:sec:validation}
replaces it.

These distinctions are also useful for formalization: the local analytic
estimate, the discrete phase geometry, and the inverse-theorem entry should
be separate interfaces rather than hidden assumptions in one statement.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Deterministic reconstruction and exact diagnostics\srctag{56}}]{Deterministic reconstruction and exact diagnostics}\label{gsr:fz:56:sec:d10}\label{gsr:fz:56:sec:algorithm}
\srcnote{56}{Section 10}

\subsection{The decoder}
The proof gives the following deterministic reconstruction procedure on an
explicitly enumerated domain. Ties may be resolved by any fixed rule.
\begin{enumerate}
\item For every $h\in G$, form the weighted histogram of
$\phi(x+h)-\phi(x)$ with weights $w(x)w(x+h)$. Let $q(h)$ be a mode,
and use zero if the histogram has zero total mass.
\item For every $x\in G$, take the unweighted mode of
$q(x+y)-q(y)$ over $y\in G$. Denote it by $L(x)$.
\item Take the weighted mode $c$ of $\phi(x)-L(x)$ on the original domain,
with weights $w(x)$. Output $\Phi(x)=L(x)+c$.
\end{enumerate}

Under the theorem's hypotheses the second-stage modes are unique and define
a homomorphism. The first-stage ties need not be unique, but the final
repaired affine map is unique, so every tie-breaking rule gives the same
answer. Off-support values of $\phi$ do not affect the output.

With hashable group elements and exact addition, equality, and weight
arithmetic, the algorithm uses $O(N^2)$ group and dictionary operations.
This bound does not count bit complexity of rational arithmetic as constant;
large denominators incur their usual cost. Histograms can be processed one
shift or one point at a time, so the algorithm itself does not require
storing all $N^2$ pairs. The supplied implementation enumerates both groups
as products of cyclic groups and uses exact rational weights.

The hypothesis can also be checked without numerical Fourier transforms:
compute $r(h)$ and then use
\[
u^4=\E_h r(h)^2-\alpha^4.
\]
The same first-stage histograms give $\Qcal(w)$ and $\Def_w(\phi)$ exactly,
by \eqref{gsr:en:56:eq:collision-defect}. The returned map can be checked for
additivity on all $N^2$ pairs independently of the proof.

\subsection{Verification scope and results}
The file \texttt{code/repair.py} is a reusable reference decoder.
The file \texttt{code/verify.py} performs integer and rational checks;
it uses no floating-point inequality tests. The supplied run completed
\textbf{33,889 assertions}, including the following families:
\begin{itemize}[itemsep=3pt]
\item All 1,086 nonempty labeled subsets of $\Z/n\Z$ for $1\le n\le6$
with two possible labels at each included point. This is an enumeration of
three states per point: absent, present with label zero, and present with
label one.
\item Ninety seeded rational-weight cases on cyclic and noncyclic groups,
with weights in $\{0,1/4,1/2,3/4,1\}$ and labels in $\Z/3\Z$.
\item Three nonzero-error weighted examples satisfying the main hypotheses,
plus exact closed-form data for a nonzero-error subset example of size
8,192 in a composite-order cyclic group.
\end{itemize}
The seed is 20261006. The checks include the two energy identities,
the exact triangle second moment, the weighted interpolation inequality,
the triangle transfer, every pointwise link bound, all six marked-pair
bounds, inclusion--exclusion, the self-correction conclusion whenever its
hypothesis holds, and the numerical constants in the final bootstrap.
Most small arbitrary subsets do \emph{not} satisfy the main uniformity
hypothesis; they test the unconditional intermediate statements instead.

An inequality of the form $X\le A+\sqrt B$ is checked exactly by testing
$X\le A$ or $(X-A)^2\le B$. This avoids rounding the radicals in the
proof-critical estimates. The global proof for every finite group is the
mathematical argument in the preceding sections, not an extrapolation
from these finite checks.

\subsection{Two reproducible nonzero-error examples}
On $G=\Z/31\Z$, put $w(0)=1/10000$ and $w(x)=1$ otherwise, with
$\phi(0)=1\in\Z/3\Z$ and all other labels zero. The decoder returns the
zero affine map and computes exactly
\[
\alpha=\frac{300001}{310000},\qquad
 t=\frac1{300001},\qquad
\eps=\frac{3480006000000000}{261303480018000000001}.
\]
The small weight makes the nonzero label error small without requiring a
huge explicitly enumerated domain. The checked uniformity fourth power is
\[
u^4=\frac{29988001799880003}{923521000000000000000},
\]
which satisfies $u^4\le\alpha^5/1024$.

For an unweighted example let $N=8193$, $G=\Z/N\Z$, and
$A=G\setminus\{0\}$. Give point $1$ label one in $\Z/2\Z$ and all other
points of $A$ label zero. Then
\begin{align*}
\alpha&=\frac{8192}{8193},&
u^4&=\frac{8192}{8193^4},\\
t&=\frac1{8192},&
\eps&=\frac{5589675}{11451848192}.
\end{align*}
These numbers satisfy the hypotheses and the claimed error bound.
Here the large example is checked using exact closed-form counts, not by
running the quadratic-time decoder on all 8,193 points.

To derive the counts, write $m=N-1$. The unnormalized pair counts are
$R(0)=m$ and $R(h)=N-2$ for $h\ne0$. The number of pairs with nonzero label
difference is zero at $h=0$, one at $h=1,-1$, and two at every other shift.
Thus
\[
N^3\Qcal(\ind_A)=(N-1)^2+(N-1)(N-2)^2,
\]
while
\[
N^3\Def_A(\phi)=4(N-3)+4(N-3)(N-4)=4(N-3)^2.
\]
The code cross-checks these formulas by full enumeration for
$N=5,7,9,11$ before evaluating the larger instance.

\subsection{Reproducibility and limits}
From the package directory, run
\begin{verbatim}
python3 code/verify.py --output data/verification.json
python3 code/repair.py
make pdf
\end{verbatim}
The mathematical claims do not depend on a numerical solver, a randomized
search finding an extremizer, or an unverified external computation.
No Lean code is included or claimed to compile. The JSON verification
record explicitly labels its checks as finite diagnostics.

\section[{The Gowers interface and a formalization route\srctag{56}}]{The Gowers interface and a formalization route}\label{gsr:fz:56:sec:d11}\label{gsr:fz:56:sec:integration}
\srcnote{56}{Section 11}

\subsection{Which Gowers step is strengthened?}
The inspected repository transcription treats Proposition~6.1 as a passage
from large Fourier coefficients of many differences to many respected
additive quadruples. Lemma~6.2 expresses that count as the additive energy
of a function graph. Corollary~7.6 then extracts a restriction that is a
Freiman homomorphism of order eight \cite{repo56,gowers}.
Our theorem supplies a different, stronger conclusion in a narrower but
useful input regime: the domain is Fourier-uniform and nearly all
\emph{available} quadruples are respected.

For a map $\phi:A\to H$, define its finite graph
\[
\Gamma_\phi=\{(a,\phi(a)):a\in A\}\subseteq G\times H.
\]
Let $E(A)$ and $E(\Gamma_\phi)$ be unnormalized ordered additive energies.
There is an exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:56:eq:graph-dictionary}
E(\Gamma_\phi)=(1-\eps)E(A),
\qquad E(A)=N^3(\alpha^4+u^4).
\end{equation}
Indeed, graph quadruples correspond bijectively to domain quadruples whose
labels satisfy the same relation. No average over $H$ is involved, so this
identity also makes sense when $H$ is infinite.

\begin{corollary}[A high-agreement alternative to small-restriction extraction]
\label{gsr:fz:56:cor:gowers-branch}
Assume the subset hypotheses of Corollary~\ref{gsr:fm:56:cor:subset-main} and
$E(\Gamma_\phi)\ge(1-\eps)E(A)$ with $0\le\eps\le2^{-10}$.
There is a single subset $B\subseteq A$ of size
\[
|B|\ge(1-13\eps/50)|A|
\]
on which $\phi$ is a Freiman homomorphism of every positive integer order,
and $\phi|_B$ is the restriction of one affine map on $G$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Let $B$ be the agreement set with the repaired affine map. If
$\sum_{i=1}^k x_i=\sum_{i=1}^k y_i$ with all $x_i,y_i\in B$, then
applying its linear part and adding $k$ copies of its constant gives
$\sum_i\phi(x_i)=\sum_i\phi(y_i)$. The same $B$ works for every $k$.
\end{proof}

This is not an unconditional improvement to the size guarantee in
Corollary~7.6. The normalizations explain why. If
\[
\gamma=\frac{E(\Gamma_\phi)}{|A|^3},
\]
then \eqref{gsr:fz:56:eq:graph-dictionary} reads
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:56:eq:gamma-dictionary}
\gamma=(1-\eps)\alpha(1+\kappa).
\end{equation}
For a sparse uniform domain, $\gamma$ is near $\alpha$, not near one.
Near-maximal energy relative to the domain's \emph{available} quadruples
is a different statement from near-maximal energy relative to $|A|^3$.
The earlier full-domain/coset energy stability arguments cannot simply be
substituted for the relative theorem by ignoring this distinction.

\subsection{Interaction with the local Section 10 argument}
The repository's Lemma~10.9 proves that a locally constructed difference map
is a Freiman homomorphism on a specified smaller set; its formal statement
includes the nonemptiness needed to avoid vacuous nested assertions
\cite{repo56}. The present proof uses a global triangle identity and an
ambient Fourier-uniformity assumption instead. It does not prove a
stronger conclusion from precisely the hypotheses of Lemma~10.9.
A future integration should expose the relative repair theorem as an
additional branch, not overwrite the existing theorem statement.

On a Bohr neighborhood or an arbitrary progression, the needed convolution
and sampling identities have boundary and translation-measure issues.
Those issues are not resolved merely by calling the subset ``locally
uniform.'' Section~\ref{gsr:en:56:sec:corollaries} only transports the theorem without
loss on an actual finite subgroup or its coset.

\subsection{Proposed proof-assistant modules}
A formalization can be separated into five small interfaces rather than
starting from the entire Gowers argument.

\paragraph{Finite weighted configurations.}
Define $\Qcal(w)$, $\Def_w(\phi)$, and weighted distance as normalized finite
sums, with an explicit proof that $\alpha>0$ implies $\Qcal(w)>0$.
Represent a partial map by a total map together with the support of $w$.
Establish invariance under subtracting an affine map and the exact graph
energy dictionary for indicators.

\paragraph{Domain moments.}
Prove the autocorrelation identities by bijections of finite products and
the triangle identity by the change of variables in Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:56:lem:triangle}.
Prove Fourier inversion, or reuse a compatible finite abelian Fourier API,
for the pointwise link and marked-pair bounds. Check carefully that Fourier
sums on the dual are not probability averages.

\paragraph{Finite modes.}
Only finitely many target values occur. A mode can therefore be chosen from
a finite image without assuming that the whole target is a finite type.
The zero-mass case must be defined explicitly. A reusable weighted
collision-to-mode lemma then covers both the first and last selections.

\paragraph{Self-correction and the profile.}
Formalize the ordinary group-valued self-correction lemma separately.
Its key statement is uniform in the fixed base point $x$; an averaged-only
version would be insufficient to prove additivity at every pair.
The one-error inclusion--exclusion inequality is a five-case finite check.
The Fourier marked-pair lemma must include both same-side and opposite-side
placements in $a+b=c+d$.

\paragraph{The constant layer.}
Isolate \eqref{gsr:en:56:eq:beta-numeric}--\eqref{gsr:en:56:eq:13-50} in a scalar lemma with
$0<\alpha\le1$, $0\le\lambda\le1/32$, and $0\le\eps\le1/1024$.
This prevents numerical bookkeeping from obscuring the structural proof.
The exact rational inequalities in the supplied verifier indicate which
parts can be discharged by arithmetic normalization.

Suggested new theorem names are
\begin{verbatim}
weighted_relative_affine_repair
relative_affine_defect_profile
quadratic_level_affine_repair
\end{verbatim}
They are proposals, not declarations already present in the repository. The appropriate initial location is a
new research subdirectory, with no change to the formalization-status ledger
until compiled proofs are supplied.

\emph{Checked at HEAD \texttt{fe7165a3c}.} None of the three names is a declaration of the Lean development, and the ledger is unchanged by this source. The suggested subdirectory was not used: by its placement (\texttt{7dc1ee29d}) this source is source~56 of this report, with labels \texttt{gsr:fm:56:}, \texttt{gsr:en:56:} or \texttt{gsr:fz:56:} and files under the prefix \file{56-relative-affine-repair-}. \file{lemma_10_9} is at line~335 of \file{Section10.lean} and \file{lemma_10_9_holds} at line~717 of \file{Proofs10Shift.lean}; \file{proposition_6_1}, \file{lemma_6_2} and \file{corollary_7_6} at lines~37, 47 and~197 of \file{Sections06\_07.lean}.
\end{writenote}

\section[{Further research questions\srctag{56}}]{Further research questions}\label{gsr:fz:56:sec:d12}\label{gsr:fz:56:sec:questions}
\srcnote{56}{Section 12}

The results above leave several concrete problems. They are posed here as
research directions; their inclusion is not a claim that each is a recognized
open problem with an established name in the literature.

\begin{question}[The optimal density exponent]\label{gsr:fz:56:q:exponent}
What is the weakest $U^2$ hypothesis, as a function of $\alpha$, that forces
error-independent linear affine repair? Can the sufficient condition
$u^4\ll\alpha^5$ be replaced by $u^4\ll\alpha^\theta$ for some
$\theta<5$?
\end{question}
The pointwise triple-link bound explains the present exponent, but may be
stronger than necessary. A likely route is to replace a worst-case link
estimate by a link estimate averaged specifically over the error set, while
still retaining an error term proportional to its mass. A lower-bound
construction must fail repair, not merely saturate one Fourier inequality.

\begin{question}[Optimal fixed-uniformity soundness]
For fixed small $\lambda>0$, determine the best coefficient in
$t\le C(\lambda)\eps+o(\eps)$, uniformly over densities, finite abelian
groups, weights, and targets. Is the pointwise link imbalance in
\eqref{gsr:fm:56:eq:profile-lower} the correct first-order obstruction?
\end{question}
The present bounds place $C(\lambda)$ near $1/4$, but do not identify it.
An extremal analysis would have to coordinate the error support with the
phase of the triple convolution. The separate Fourier and inclusion--exclusion
estimates may not be simultaneously sharp.

\begin{question}[A sharp relative cubic profile]
Can the coefficient $12$ of $t^2$ in \eqref{gsr:fm:56:eq:profile-lower} be replaced by
an exact target-torsion-sensitive expression, analogous to sharp full-domain
profiles, with controlled Fourier-uniformity corrections?
\end{question}
The current argument deliberately treats the six pairs uniformly and ignores
cancellation patterns among two, three, and four erroneous labels. A refined
count should distinguish positions on the same side from positions on opposite
sides and should retain the additive energy of the marked error weight.

\begin{question}[The largest universal repair range]
How far can the numerical conditions $\lambda\le1/32$ and
$\eps\le1/1024$ be enlarged while retaining an explicit linear conclusion?
\end{question}
The square-root expression in Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:56:prop:coarse-general} is better
than the coarse estimate used in the main theorem. Optimizing it together
with the local profile is a finite-dimensional problem. Such an optimization
would improve constants but would not, by itself, constitute a new structural
theorem. It should be accompanied by certified inequalities and counterexamples
near any proposed boundary.

\begin{question}[Quadratic-domain rank]
Can the sufficient rank $R\ge4r+O(1)$ in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:56:thm:quadratic} be lowered? Can exact Fourier distributions of
specific quadratic systems replace the worst-case matrix-rank certificate?
\end{question}
The factor four comes from the elementary estimate
$u^4\le\sigma^2\alpha$ combined with $\alpha\asymp p^{-r}$.
A sharper calculation for individual systems may lower it substantially.
One should distinguish improving a sufficient certificate from finding the
true extension threshold.

\begin{question}[Higher-degree repair with a fixed domain condition]
Is there an analogue of the present weighted theorem for approximate
polynomials of degree two or higher, with an explicit uniformity condition
independent of the test error and a sharp first-order soundness constant?
\end{question}
The natural first-order coefficient for a nondegenerate $d$-cube test would
be $2^d$, because that is the number of coordinate incidences. Turning that
heuristic into a theorem requires a coarse higher-degree reconstruction and
control of multiply marked cube configurations. Repeated vertices and
low-characteristic polynomial phenomena must be handled explicitly.

\begin{question}[Propagation through a complete inverse proof]
What quantitative improvement survives if relative affine repair is used
at every eligible high-agreement stage of a full inverse-theorem argument?
\end{question}
The local gain can be substantial, but a global assertion requires tracking
the rank, density, error, and sampling distributions at each application.
In particular, inserting the theorem into a quadratic-repair proof does not
automatically eliminate its other error-dependent rank requirements.

\begin{question}[Local domains without group structure]
Can a corresponding theorem be proved on regular Bohr sets or long
progressions with explicit boundary errors and a clearly defined relative
quadruple distribution?
\end{question}
The exact triangle identity and the uniform self-correction translations are
the first obstacles. A satisfactory statement should specify the regularity
or approximate-invariance parameters and show how they enter the final
linear error, rather than burying them in an undefined local-uniformity
condition.

\begin{question}[Faster decoding and sampling]
Can the quadratic-time decoder be made nearly linear, or sublinear in a
suitable oracle model, without introducing density-dependent label-query
complexity? Can a weighted quadruple sampler be constructed efficiently from
an explicit Fourier-uniform domain?
\end{question}
The existence proof needs only modes with certified margins, suggesting
sampling-based approximations. Uniform control over all ambient points and
the cost of generating admissible pairs or quadruples are separate problems.
A running-time statement must account for both.

\begin{question}[Minimal domain certificates and formal verification]
Which combination of autocorrelation variance, triangle variance, marked-pair
energy bounds, and affine separation is sufficient when the domain does not
have small $U^2$ norm? Can this abstract certificate be formalized once and
instantiated for several distinct classes of domains?
\end{question}
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:56:prop:coarse-general} already uses the actual triangle variance.
An abstract version might cover domains that fail the simple Fourier criterion
but still have enough reliable local-to-global transport. The five-module
formalization plan in Section~\ref{gsr:fz:56:sec:integration} is a concrete first step.

\section[{Proof audit and dependency ledger\srctag{56}}]{Proof audit and dependency ledger}\label{gsr:fz:56:sec:dA}\label{gsr:fz:56:app:audit}
\srcnote{56}{Appendix A}

\subsection{The dependency chain}
The main existence proof has the following logical order:
\[
\begin{gathered}
\text{Fourier/energy identities and domain moments}\\
\Downarrow\\
\text{weighted modal interpolation and triangle transfer}\\
\Downarrow\\
\text{classical ambient self-correction}\\
\Downarrow\\
\text{coarse weighted affine agreement}\\
\Downarrow\\
\text{one-error profile and linear bootstrap}.
\end{gathered}
\]
Uniqueness is a separate consequence of Fourier coset separation.
The quadratic-domain theorem uses only the main theorem, the spectral
certificate, and the elementary quadratic Fourier bound. The property-testing
corollary is the contrapositive of the main theorem in its small-error branch.

\subsection{Points checked explicitly}
\paragraph{No lost normalization.}
$\Qcal(w)$ and $\Def_w(\phi)$ are normalized by $N^3$; $B$ by $N^2$;
$r$ and $T$ by $N$. Thus extending a bad pair to a triangle introduces
$\alpha$, not $\alpha N$. Formula \eqref{gsr:fz:56:eq:gamma-dictionary} is the
conversion to the $|A|^3$ convention in the graph-energy step.

\paragraph{No assumption of uniform fibers.}
The distributions $\nu_h$ are normalized by their actual masses $r(h)$.
Only the moment identities control the transition to the ambient measure.
Zero fibers are assigned explicit values and never divided by zero.

\paragraph{No target Fourier transform.}
All Fourier analysis is on $G$. The target can be any abelian group.
The proof uses addition, subtraction, equality, and modes of finite
collections of target values.

\paragraph{No hidden odd-order hypothesis.}
The main theorem never divides a group element by two. Same-side marked-pair
terms are bounded as complex Fourier sums, not incorrectly identified with
opposite-side nonnegative sums. Only the quadratic matrix-rank corollary
assumes odd characteristic, precisely in Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:56:lem:gauss}.

\paragraph{No limit at zero error.}
The coarse theorem provides an approximation at $\eps=0$, and the positive
local profile forces its error to vanish. Exact extension is therefore
proved directly under the fixed domain hypothesis.

\paragraph{No circular use of uniqueness.}
The decoder produces an affine map before the separation lemma is invoked.
Uniqueness does not enter the construction or the bootstrap.

\paragraph{No formal-verification claim.}
The finite program checks exact consequences on specified inputs. It does not
quantify over all groups or all real weights. The universal statements are
proved in the text and remain candidates for external review and subsequent
formalization.

\subsection{Prior versus present ingredients}
The ordinary homomorphism self-correction method and the existence of linear
repair theorems belong to prior work \cite{blr,kazhdanziegler}. Basic Fourier
identities, quadratic Gauss bounds, collision-to-mode estimates, and
inclusion--exclusion are standard tools. The proposed extension is their
particular quantitative assembly into Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:56:thm:main}, with weighted
relative normalization, error-independent uniformity, the explicit profile,
and the consequences stated here. The audit does not certify worldwide
novelty of any individual intermediate identity.

\subsection{Package contents and source control}
The package contains the master \texttt{article.tex}, its included section
files, the compiled \texttt{article.pdf}, a Makefile, a README, a source and
integration note, a source-manifest JSON file, the reference decoder, the
finite verifier, and the recorded verification output. It does not include
copies of external papers or font files.

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 54--59]
As shipped here: the main file and its section files and the PDF are not staged (their text is printed in this report); the Makefile, verifier, decoder, source manifest and outputs are shipped under the prefix \file{56-relative-affine-repair-} (README of this directory). The build record \file{data/56-relative-affine-repair-build\_validation.json} names a single-file \file{gowers\_relative\_affine\_repair.tex} ``delivered separately''; it is not in the archive.
\end{writenote}

The repository is changing rapidly. The source manifest distinguishes a
pinned GitHub snapshot from separately observed file blobs and records the
arXiv versions inspected. The suggested new research-directory name avoids
renumbering any existing source in the consolidated report. Integration into
a formal proof ledger should wait for actual compiled formal proofs.

\section[{Further research questions and a proposed programme\srctag{57}}]{Further research questions and a proposed programme}\label{gsr:fz:57:sec:d7}\label{gsr:fz:57:rq:section}
\srcnote{57}{Section 7}

The following questions are suggested by the proofs. They distinguish
finite classification tasks from improvements requiring a new analytic
argument. They are proposed research directions, not assertions of
unresolved status throughout the literature. In particular, the general
qualitative inverse and near-extremizer principles have extensive earlier
theory; the targets below concern precise quantitative, structural, or
formal interfaces.

\subsection{The upper energy spectrum}

\begin{problem}[The optimal Schur threshold]\label{gsr:fz:57:rq:threshold}
Let $N(s)$ be the least eventual threshold for the partition
classification in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:57:st:partitions}. Determine $N(s)$ and all
exceptional positive real sets below it. Is the proved upper bound
$N(s)\le5s-1$ asymptotically sharp?
\end{problem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Advanced by source~66}: $N(s)\le3s+1$ for every $s$ and $N(s)\ge2s+2$ (its Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:partition} and Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:prop:obstruction}); its Conjecture~\ref{gsr:fz:66:epnf:conj:threshold} is $N(s)=2s+2$ (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:energylevels}).
\end{writenote}
The first exact values are $N(1)=4$ and $N(2)=6$.
Small-cardinality exceptions can be continuous families:
$\{1,t,1+t\}$ has deficit one for every $t>1$, $t\ne2$.
Thus integer enumeration alone cannot settle the exceptional
classification. A useful next proof should sharpen the argument
that separates the first imperfect row from the final perfect rows,
while keeping track of the \emph{sizes} of their defects.

\begin{problem}[The fourth and subsequent energy levels]\label{gsr:fz:57:rq:levels}
For each fixed $r$, determine the $r$ largest distinct additive
energies of an $m$-element torsion-free set for all sufficiently large
$m$, classify every equality case, and determine the smallest valid
cardinality threshold.
\end{problem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{The fourth level is found by source~66}: $M_m-8m+20$ for $m\ge11$, attained exactly by two oriented templates (its Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:fourth} and~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:fourlevels}); the fifth and later levels remain open (its Question~\ref{gsr:fz:66:epnf:q:fifth}).
\end{writenote}
The third-level proof reduces the equality analysis to endpoint costs
zero, one, and two. The partition theorem supplies a finite list for
every fixed endpoint cost. A remaining issue is to prove which costs
can occur on a branch attaining a specified global energy level.
The numerical ordering of candidate families must also be checked:
different affine models may have the same energy polynomial.

\begin{problem}[Energy formulas for partition models]\label{gsr:fz:57:rq:polynomials}
Develop a uniform formula for the eventual energy of
$\{0\}\cup\{j+\lambda_j:1\le j\le n\}$ in terms of a fixed partition
$(\lambda_j)$, and classify coincidences between the resulting
energy functions.
\end{problem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Answered by source~66} for boundary-hole models: $\Drm(A_H(N))=r(m-1)-\kappa(H)$ exactly (its Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:holeenergy}); the generating function of $\kappa$ is its Question~\ref{gsr:fz:66:epnf:q:spectrum}.
\end{writenote}
The partition theorem reduces this calculation to finitely many
terminal patterns at each fixed deficit. Such a formula could turn
the endpoint induction into a symbolic enumeration procedure.
A satisfactory implementation should return both the candidate
models and a proof of the range of $n$ for which the ordering of
their energies has stabilized.

\begin{problem}[A larger rigidity window]\label{gsr:fz:57:rq:stability}
For each fixed $K$, does
$D(A)=(M_m-E(A))/4\le Km$ force all but $O_K(1)$ points of a
torsion-free $m$-set into an arithmetic progression of length
$m+O_K(1)$? Determine the necessary exceptions and the best
dependence on $K$.
\end{problem}
Our bounded-Schur theorem controls an endpoint once its cost is
bounded. A global bound $D(A)\le Km$ controls a sum of endpoint costs;
it does not immediately provide a long prefix with a bounded-cost
terminal extension. Locating a useful prefix or suffix is therefore
a distinct step. A complementary problem is the regime
$D(A)=o(m^2)$, where a sharp proportion-of-edits statement may be
more natural than a bounded number of edits.

\begin{problem}[Rectification and weights]\label{gsr:fz:57:rq:rectification}
Find explicit finite cyclic hypotheses under which the new equality
classifications transfer through a Freiman isomorphism of order two.
Can an ordered, nonnegative weighted defect identity support
analogous stability conclusions for functions?
\end{problem}
The cyclic problem must preserve both directions of every two-sum
relation and justify recovery of an actual common step. Merely
choosing representatives in an interval does not do so. The weighted
problem would connect exact set classifications more directly to
the bounded functions used in Fourier arguments; both the right
extremal normalization and the equality family require care.

\subsection{Quantitative extraction beyond Section 13}

\begin{problem}[Propagating Fej\'er selection through higher degree]\label{gsr:fz:57:rq:section16}
Can the general arrangement-selection theorem in source~40 be
combined with the remaining Section~16 proper-box induction to
produce a fully quantified improvement in Corollary~16.11?
\end{problem}
The first concrete test is the next multidimensional extraction
case, with every side length an integer, all boxes proper, and every
density threshold uniform in the actual selected set. The present
Section~13 proof shows why improving purification can matter
substantially after a later spectral substitution. It does not
supply the missing higher-dimensional geometric induction.

\begin{problem}[A better prepared frequency graph]\label{gsr:fz:57:rq:preparation}
Improve the exponent $d=2\,996\,201\,429$ in
Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:57:qt:delta}, while retaining both separate order-eight Freiman
structure and an almost-everywhere arrangement identity.
\end{problem}
The two successive fibre restrictions have a large cost before
Fej\'er purification begins. One possibility is to exploit the
shared origin of the rows and columns as derivatives of the same
function. Another is to retain several large Fourier frequencies
before making a coherent choice. As a concrete benchmark, a
prepared density at least $a^{2^{30}}$ would lower the final
power-of-two density exponent again with the current geometric
interface. This is a target for a new argument, not a consequence
of the existing constant rounding.

\begin{problem}[A fully explicit size threshold]\label{gsr:fz:57:rq:size}
Give a closed quantitative upper bound for
$N_{\mathrm{sq}}(\delta)$ and hence for the complete $N_0(\alpha)$
in Remark~\ref{gsr:en:57:qt:threshold-remark}.
\end{problem}
The task includes the scale recurrence, integer cutoffs, properness,
and the common-step extraction. The explicit bound
$p\ge a^{-2^{37}}$ already proved here controls purification only.
A successful result should identify which stage dominates the
threshold and should avoid a circular dependence on the actual
input density.

\begin{problem}[Sharper correction constants]\label{gsr:fz:57:rq:constants}
Determine the best quantitative stability bounds for symmetric
approximately additive tables and the consequent near-maximal
$U^4$ estimates.
\end{problem}
The proof uses a coarse correction on rows with a large test error,
then a collision argument on slopes. Both are visible places to
improve the constant $332$. The cubic integration constant $6194$
comes from a product of two average-deficit losses; a simultaneous
integration argument may avoid that product. The perturbation in
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:error-order} supplies a lower benchmark of $1/8$ for the
ratio of squared cubic-phase error to the $Q_4$ deficit, so the
linear order is settled but its best coefficient is not.

\begin{problem}[Dependence on degree and characteristic]\label{gsr:fz:57:rq:degree}
Improve the degree dependence in the all-degree phase approximation
of Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:57:ep:all-degree-inverse}. Give comparably explicit estimates
in small characteristic and on higher-dimensional vector spaces.
\end{problem}
Our scalar-frequency correction costs only $O(s)$ at one step, but
iterating degree descent multiplies those costs and gives
$K_k\le2\cdot109^{k-2}(k-2)!$. Is a substantially smaller growth rate
available by correcting several degrees together? For
$p<k$, the classical polynomial demodulation divides by a vanishing
factorial. The appropriate target must allow the relevant
nonclassical polynomial phases. On $\Fp^n$, compatibility involving
the base variable, not just symmetry of the derivative parameters,
must be addressed.

\begin{problem}[From local extraction to global density increments]\label{gsr:fz:57:rq:global}
After the higher-degree geometric steps have been completed, what
quantitative improvement survives a complete density-increment
iteration with all parameter choices and thresholds propagated?
\end{problem}
The desired output is one explicitly stated bound for $r_k(N)$,
with a complete proof from the revised local estimates. Such a
calculation must be compared with contemporary inverse-theorem
methods, including \cite{lssbounds}, and cannot be inferred
from a single improved exponent in Theorem~13.12.

\subsection{Formalization and reproducible classification}

\begin{problem}[A reusable formal interface]\label{gsr:fz:57:rq:formal}
Formalize the purification-to-square synthesis and the independent
near-maximal endpoint, then discharge the pinned
\texttt{theorem\_13\_12} type without weakening its exponent or
properness requirements. In parallel, formalize the reflection-row
lemma and the partition classification.
\end{problem}
These directions share little proof infrastructure and can proceed
independently. On the Fourier side, the best reusable statements are
phase normalization, finite-group additive correction, and a
dominant-character selector with an average error bound. On the
structural side, the natural core is an ordered finite set together
with its nonnegative row defects. Exact finite enumeration can help
test proposed statements, but should remain outside the logical
dependency of the general proofs.

A practical order of work is: first formalize the proved
Section~13 synthesis and the partition theorem; next settle the
smallest new Schur thresholds and the fourth energy level; then
attack higher-dimensional extraction and the complete quantitative
iteration. This ordering exposes usable intermediate theorems
before undertaking the longest analytic induction.

\section[{Examples, numerical exploration, and exact checks\srctag{58}}]{Examples, numerical exploration, and exact checks}\label{gsr:fz:58:sec:d12}
\srcnote{58}{Section 12}
\label{gsr:fz:58:sec:verification}

\subsection{Why both torsion and repetitions need explicit treatment}

\begin{example}[A repeated bad tuple]\label{gsr:fz:58:ex:repeated-bad}
Let $G=\Z/2\Z$, $H=\Z/4\Z$, $B=\{0,1\}$, and $\phi(0)=0$,
$\phi(1)=1$. The tuple $(0,0,1,1)$ is additive in $G$, but its target
discrepancy is $-2=2\ne0$ in $H$. For one layer with
$K(t)=\cos^2(\pi t)$, its actual containment probability is $1/4$.
The formal occurrence product instead has mean $9/64$.

Indeed, averaging over the target character makes the nonzero
frequencies of the second distinct-point factor vanish, so the actual
average is $c_0^2=1/4$. For the occurrence product the two factors are
each squared. Their Fourier supports lie in $[-2,2]$, and averaging
the target character again leaves only frequency zero for the second
factor; its constant coefficient is $R_2=3/8$. The remaining shift
average is another $R_2$, giving $9/64$. The lower occurrence-product
value cannot be used as an upper bound on bad survival.
\end{example}

\begin{example}[A noninvertible additional relation]
In $\Z/N\Z$ with $2\mid N$, a nonprincipal relation can leave an
equation $2x=a$ after the other variables are fixed. Its nonempty
fibres have two elements. Over a prime field of odd characteristic,
the same completion would be unique. Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:58:lem:two-relations}
retains this fibre size through $|G[2]|$, rather than silently importing
field rank counting into a composite modulus.
\end{example}

\begin{example}[Degree-one amplification has an exponential arity cost]
For $K(t)=\cos^2(\pi t)$ the only nonzero coefficients are
$c_0=1/2$ and $c_{\pm1}=1/4$. Thus
\[
 P=2^{-m}(1+2^{1-m}),\qquad Q=2^{-m},\qquad
 \mathcal R=1+2^{1-m}.
\]
The principal exponent is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:58:eq:degree-one-cost}
 a_K=\frac{m\log2-\log(1+2^{1-m})}{\log(1+2^{1-m})}
 \sim(m\log2)2^{m-1}.
\end{equation}
Replacing the degree-one filter by a suitable powered cosine changes
this exponential dependence into $O(m\log m)$. This calculation
isolates the relevant mechanism; it does not purport to reconstruct
every constant in Gowers's original proof.
\end{example}

\subsection{A reproducible finite search}

For each tested arity, the exploration evaluates every degree $1\le q\le3m$.
The tested arities are
\[
 m\in\{4,8,16,32,64,128,256\}.
\]
The table gives the best value
\emph{within that tested range} for $a_K$ with worst discrepancy order
two. The reported decimals are rounded numerical values.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}rrrr@{}}
\toprule
$m$ & Best sampled $q$ & $a_K$ & $z_K$\\
\midrule
4   & 5   & 7.755382    & 4.996779\\
8   & 12  & 21.177067   & 17.854033\\
16  & 25  & 52.206426   & 48.341189\\
32  & 53  & 122.606592  & 118.213699\\
64  & 111 & 279.974503  & 275.060702\\
128 & 231 & 627.704888  & 622.274215\\
256 & 475 & 1388.924965 & 1382.979512\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\begin{figure}[tbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/58-torsion-restriction-kernel_exponents.pdf}
\caption{Numerical exploration of powered cosine filters. The left
panel shows the dependence on the degree at $m=16$. The right panel
normalizes the best sampled exponent by $m\log m$. The dashed
reference line is the limit for the infimum over the full filter class,
$1/(2\log2)$, proved in Theorem~B. It is not a claimed limit of the

the exponent-$54$ conclusion uses exact integer certificates.}
\label{gsr:fz:58:fig:exponents}

The script uses logarithmic sums and evaluates
$\log(P/Q)$ through the odd-frequency mass with \texttt{log1p},
avoiding cancellation when $P/Q$ is close to one. Very small masses
are stored in scientific notation derived from their logarithms.
The generated CSV files contain all $1{,}524$ sampled candidates, not
only the selected rows.

\subsection{What was checked computationally}

The finite verification has two distinct purposes. First,
\texttt{verify\_constants.py} checks the five finite integer
inequalities used in the proof of Theorem~A, together with the final
threshold and retention comparisons. These calculations are exact
and are part of the explicit numerical certificate.

Second, \texttt{verify\_expectations.py} directly computes small-group
survival probabilities using one Fourier factor per distinct point.
For $m=4$ it covers cyclic domain orders $2,3,4,5,6,8,9$, target
orders $2,3,4,6$, cosine degrees $1,2,3$, and layer counts $1,2,3$.
It uses full and punctured domain sets with quadratic, step, and spike
maps. The $1{,}512$ cases give $6{,}048$ principal inequality checks;
$1{,}188$ cases contain repeated bad tuples, and $615$ require a
nonprincipal correction beyond the principal bad contribution.
All pass in rational arithmetic. The repeated-tuple regression in
Example~\ref{gsr:fz:58:ex:repeated-bad} is checked separately.

These small cases test implementation-sensitive identities and catch
the incorrect per-occurrence treatment of repeated points. They are
not an exhaustive verification of the general theorem. The latter is
established by the character expansion, fibre bound, H\"older estimate,
and signed objective proved above. Likewise, the numerical search
does not prove a global optimum over filter degree.

\section[{Further research questions and a proposed programme\srctag{58}}]{Further research questions and a proposed programme}\label{gsr:fz:58:sec:d13}
\srcnote{58}{Section 13}
\label{gsr:fz:58:sec:research}

The results settle a specific local extension question and establish
an asymptotic barrier for a specified method. They also isolate several
substantive problems that remain. The following questions distinguish
finite optimization, structural improvements, and propagation through
the larger argument.

\begin{question}[The sixteen-variable optimum]\label{gsr:fz:58:q:finite-optimum}
Determine or tightly bound $I_{16,2}$, including optimization beyond
powered cosine filters. Can one certify an admissible filter with
$\mathcal A_{16,2}<52$, and then improve the clean integer exponent
after auditing its finite-size constants?
\end{question}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{The certificate is supplied by source~68}: an admissible degree-twelve rational filter of principal cost $51.445<52$ with exact integer certificates, which lowers the exponent to $53$ (its Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:68:ff:prop:certificates} and Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:ff:thm:53}); $I_{16,2}$ itself is still undetermined (its Question~\ref{gsr:fz:68:q:finite-filter}).
\end{writenote}
The current value $52.2064\ldots$ is a candidate value, not a lower
bound. A useful computational project would parameterize
nonnegative trigonometric polynomials through a sum-of-squares
representation, optimize the nonlinear Fourier objective, and turn
the final candidate into rational positivity and integer certificates.
Checking nonnegativity only on a numerical grid would be insufficient.

\begin{question}[The next asymptotic term]\label{gsr:fz:58:q:second-order}
Find the first correction to the leading asymptotic for $I_{m,a}$,
and identify the scale of the degree and the shape of near-optimal
filters.
\end{question}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Advanced by source~68}: uniform two-parameter bounds, with the fixed-$a$ upper error $O_a(m(1+\log\log\log m))$ and the growing-order limit $1+1/(2c)$ (its Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:uf:thm:uniform}); whether the error is $O_a(m)$ is its Question~\ref{gsr:fz:68:q:second-order}.
\end{writenote}
The choice $q=\lceil m(\log m)^2\rceil$ is designed for a short proof
of the leading term. It is not a second-order optimizer. Sharper
control of the residue-class imbalance of powers of binomial
coefficients, combined with a stronger coefficient concentration
inequality, is a concrete route to reducing the gap between the two
bounds. The fixed-$a$ theorem also leaves the regime in which $a$
grows with $m$ open.

\begin{question}[Beyond independent positive filters]\label{gsr:fz:58:q:linear}
Can restriction on every cyclic group have a retention exponent
$O(m)$, uniformly over arbitrary abelian targets, by a method outside
the independent positive Fourier-filter class?
\end{question}
Theorem~B rules out a linear principal-spectrum cost for the certificate
analyzed here, including heterogeneous independent scalar layers.
It does not rule out better use of nonprincipal terms or input structure,
adaptive selection, joint filters on several characters, signed
Fourier constructions with controlled cancellation, or a structural
decomposition before restriction. The prime-field results indicate
that linear dependence is a meaningful benchmark, but do not prove
that it is achievable uniformly in small torsion.

\begin{question}[Sharp finite-size thresholds]\label{gsr:fz:58:q:threshold}
What is the best sufficient point-count threshold for a prescribed
retention coefficient? Can the collision profile and the
coefficient-weighted torsion profile substantially improve
\eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:power-threshold}, especially at $m=16$?
\end{question}
The exact certificate \eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:Psi} already avoids several unnecessary
losses, and \eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:collision-profile} makes an improvement dependent
on the actual tuple geometry. A complete answer should also give
examples showing which losses are necessary. Small sets can always
retain a respected singleton, but this alone does not bridge the
entire intermediate-size range of the present theorem.

\begin{question}[Low-exponent domains]\label{gsr:fz:58:q:low-exponent}
Find a useful analogue for families such as $(\Z/2\Z)^s$ in which the
domain torsion factor in \eqref{gsr:en:58:eq:Ak} is comparable with $|G|$.
\end{question}
A field-rank argument naturally belongs to these families, while the
integer-minor bound used here is suited to cyclic groups and bounded
invariant-factor rank. A hybrid theorem that detects the effective
rank of the coefficient system in each primary component could join
the two regimes. Merely substituting the ambient Smith kernel count
into a bound for $B^m$ would not be justified.

\begin{question}[Systems of relations and higher arrangements]
\label{gsr:fz:58:q:systems}
Extend the decaying multi-layer error to a general integer relation
matrix while selecting one common subset and counting every tuple,
including all collision patterns.
\end{question}
Shkredov's system-level theorem and the repository's finite-field
arrangement results are important starting points. Over composite
groups, one must track saturated relation lattices, ranks of added
Fourier rows, Smith invariants, and target discrepancy subgroups.
The single-minor proof here settles only the case of one balanced
relation. A useful first target is two independent balanced relations
with a fully explicit error in terms of the relevant minors.

\begin{question}[Using target-order information]\label{gsr:fz:58:q:target-orders}
Given the distribution $u_a$ of discrepancy orders, optimize the
certificate based on $\sum_a P_a^ku_a$. Can several filters be chosen
to address different parts of this distribution with a smaller
finite-size cost?
\end{question}
The worst-order-two bound discards information when most bad
discrepancies have large order. The mixed-filter formula is already
available, but optimization must account for both the principal gains
and the moment-dependent errors. Theorem~B bounds only the principal
cost for a fixed possible order, not this full data-dependent problem.

\begin{question}[Efficient certified construction]\label{gsr:fz:58:q:algorithm}
Can one construct a qualifying subset and an a posteriori certificate
in time substantially below enumerating all $b^m$ tuples?
\end{question}
The proof is finitely constructive by exhaustive conditional
expectation, but it gives no efficient runtime. A practical
derandomization should estimate the signed objective, exploit
convolution or sparse graph structure, and retain rigorous error
bounds for the unexamined tuple mass. Proving a runtime bound is a
separate requirement from proving that a finite search terminates.

\begin{question}[End-to-end quantitative propagation]\label{gsr:fz:58:q:propagation}
What improvement survives after the new restriction constants are
carried through the later stages of Gowers's argument, with every
size threshold and parameter dependence recalculated?
\end{question}
This is the necessary next step before claiming an improved bound for
progression-free sets from this route. The retained configuration
mass, retained point density, accuracy parameter, and starting modulus
must be propagated together. A smaller local exponent alone does not
determine the final bound, and it need not compete with modern global
arguments.

\begin{question}[Formal certificates and reusable interfaces]
\label{gsr:fz:58:q:formal}
Can the expectation theorem be formalized once for arbitrary finite
abelian groups and admissible filters, with the numerical corollaries
generated by exact certificates?
\end{question}
This would separate the reusable mathematics from parameter selection.
The most delicate reusable lemma concerns actual point selection for
repeated tuples; the most valuable arithmetic interface concerns
coefficient-weighted kernels of multiplication maps. The five
certificates at $m=16$ supply a small first instantiation.

\paragraph{Suggested order of work.}
First formalize and integrate the central expectation theorem and
Theorem~A. In parallel, pursue certified finite filter optimization and
the collision-aware threshold, since those projects have explicit
numerical targets. Next develop a two-relation composite-group case
and an algorithmic certificate. Finally, propagate the best validated
local statement through the later proof before assessing any global
quantitative claim.

\section[{The essential integer certificate\srctag{58}}]{The essential integer certificate}\label{gsr:fz:58:sec:dA}
\srcnote{58}{Appendix A}
\label{gsr:fz:58:app:certificate}

The following complete standard-library calculation verifies all
finite numerical inequalities used in the proof of Theorem~A. The
symbolic uses of $0<t\le1$ and $0<\eta\le1$ are proved in the text,
rather than inferred by sampling those parameters.

\begingroup\small
\begin{verbatim}
from math import comb
from fractions import Fraction

A = sum(comb(50, 25+n)**16 for n in range(-25, 26))
B = sum(comb(50, 25+n)**16
        for n in range(-25, 26) if n % 2 == 0)

assert A >= 2**750
assert 250*A >= 481*B
assert 481**53 >= 2**50 * 250**53
assert 481**50 >= 2**47 * 250**50
assert comb(100, 50) <= 2**97

# Domain torsion plus repeated-position pairs:
assert 4 * (50 + comb(16, 2)) == 680

# Ratio of the sufficient size bound to (4/t)**54:
# (680 * 2**97 * t**(-51)) / (2**108 * t**(-54))
# = (85/256) * t**3 <= 85/256 < 1.
assert Fraction(680 * 2**97, 2**108) == Fraction(85, 256)
assert Fraction(85, 256) < 1

# Certified retention divided by (alpha*eta/4)**54
# is 8/eta, hence at least 8 when 0 < eta <= 1.
assert Fraction(2**108, 2**105) == 8
print("All exact certificates passed.")
\end{verbatim}
\endgroup

The companion \texttt{data/exact\_constants.json} records the complete
integer numerators as decimal strings, together with every check and
its interpretation. No stochastic numerical computation enters this
certificate.

\section[{Reproducibility and verification scope\srctag{59}}]{Reproducibility and verification scope}\label{gsr:fz:59:sec:d11}
\srcnote{59}{Section 11}
\label{gsr:fz:59:sec:verification}

The accompanying archive contains a standalone \LaTeX{} source, the compiled PDF, three standard-library Python programs, their exact JSON reports, an input-source manifest, build instructions, and a detailed test inventory. The source embeds its bibliography and needs no external figures or private style file. The verification programs are supplementary checks; the general theorems rest on the proofs above.

The principal extraction verifier performs the following exact checks:
\begin{itemize}
\item $149{,}998$ universal/odd one-element probability inequalities, $79{,}964$ odd-order cutoff cases, and $72$ prime-primary cases; adaptive recurrences for the specified ranges in the inventory.
\item $8{,}750$ separator applications to $8{,}508$ distinct coordinate-model/forbidden-set pairs. Different theorem variants sometimes revisit the same input.
\item All $2{,}441$ partial-map cases in six small-domain suites, yielding $6{,}495$ applications of universal, odd, or prime-primary extraction. For every selected subset it directly checks all Freiman orders up to the requested order, including repeated summands.
\item $16{,}459$ character tuples in projective rank-obstruction checks, $16$ exact Laurent constant coefficients, and $18$ finite-torsion Riesz products with their $36$ deleted products.
\end{itemize}

The affine verifier evaluates $23{,}516$ map cases: $21{,}116$ exhaustive cases in explicit cyclic/product models, plus $2{,}400$ reproducible sampling evaluations. Samples can repeat maps; this is not a count of distinct isomorphism classes or distinct functions across all suites. It computes graph energy and signed-convolution energy separately, verifies the exact expansion and all stated quartic bounds including the support gains, and checks the final local inequalities directly. The original-kernel equality classification is checked on all $23{,}489$ evaluations with nonempty support; the endpoint checks cover $2$ eligible four-ninths evaluations and $104$ eligible no-order-three half-density evaluations. The equality checks use translated-subgroup closure for the support, independently of the energy criterion for a coset. It also checks $9{,}760$ signed-label quadruples and the one-point identity on $350$ specified maps with domain sizes $16$ through $40$.

The separate realization verifier checks small instances of the prescribed-relation construction against exhaustive multisets and subsets, including finite-domain reduction and the exact weighted optimum. Its JSON report records the exact instance list and counters, so these checks are not silently included in the preceding totals.

Important limits of the computations are explicit. They do not establish universal maximality by exhaustive search on all groups. They do not numerically verify infinite-target Haar arguments, arbitrary real weights, or the general finite-image rounding theorem. Those are analytic results. The one-point checks verify the claimed energy values, while maximality for $N\ge16$ follows from the recovery theorem. The programs reject Python optimization flags that would disable assertions. A successful run is a consistency check, not a formal proof or a claim of mathematical priority.

For integration, retain the hypothesis $W[2]=\{0\}$ in the affine layer, keep the additional $W[3]=\{0\}$ assumption on the half-range theorem, preserve the separate endpoint conclusions, and count sign orbits correctly when involutions occur. The one-color/coset classification for the original averaged kernel must not be transferred to its strengthened support-defect bound, which has additional equality cases. The target's finite image size and its exponent are different parameters. These distinctions carry the mathematical content of the refinements.
