\section[{Further research and a formalization programme\srctag{59}}]{Further research and a formalization programme}\label{gsr:fz:59:sec:d12}
\srcnote{59}{Section 12}
\label{gsr:fz:59:sec:research}

Except for the explicitly named lonely runner conjecture, the questions
below are proposed here as follow-ups to the proved results. Some refine
questions in the repository; no claim is made that their formulations
have mathematical priority. The general mixed-torsion extraction problem
from source~24 now has an answer independent of the target's exponent
and rank in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:59:thm:freiman-extraction}. The support-coset stability question
at scale $\eta/t^3$ was already answered in substance by combining
sources~11 and~14, as the repository records. Those existence questions
should therefore be replaced by sharper quantitative targets.

\begin{question}[Proposed: radius at the exact prime-primary rank]
\label{gsr:fz:59:q:primary-radius}
For a prime $p$ and $q\ge2$, set
$m_p(q)=\lfloor\log_p((p-1)q+1)\rfloor$. Determine
\[
 R_p(q)=\inf_{H,F}\ \sup_{\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_{m_p(q)}}
       \min_{f\in F}\max_j\distT{\chi_j(f)},
\]
where $H$ ranges over finite abelian $p$-groups and $F$ over symmetric
nonzero subsets with exactly $q$ sign orbits. Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:59:thm:sharp-separation}
gives $R_p(q)\ge1/(2p)$. Is this the optimal radius, and which forbidden
sets attain or approach the infimum?
\end{question}

Sharpness of the Haar survival estimate does not answer this question:
the optimizing characters may depend on the entire set. A small concrete
test is $R_3(3)$. For $F=\pm\{1,2,3\}\subset C_9$, the minimum distances
for character parameters $0,\ldots,8$ are
$(0,1,2,0,1,1,0,2,1)/9$, giving the upper bound $2/9$.

\begin{question}[Proposed: optimize radius and character-image cost jointly]
\label{gsr:fz:59:q:joint-cost}
Given a finitely generated abelian group $H$, an explicit forbidden set $F$, and
$k\ge2$, optimize the guaranteed retained fraction over separating
families with unequal radii. For a character of image order $N$, its
contribution is
\[
 c_k(N,\theta)=\frac{\lceil N\theta/k\rceil}{N}
\]
from Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:59:thm:finite-image}; for infinite image it is
$c_k(\infty,\theta)=\theta/k$. Which order profiles or relations among
defects allow the product of these factors to improve substantially on
every choice of a common radius?
\end{question}

A useful solution would return a verifiable separating family and its
actual localization cost. Minimizing the number of characters alone
can miss the benefit of small finite images. The exact profile in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:59:thm:profile} supplies one certificate against which a more
adaptive optimization can be compared.

A concrete first stage is to compare all relevant rational radii in
small groups of exponent $p^2$ or $p^3$, while recording character-image
orders. The desired output is an exact certificate with its retained
fraction and a proof of optimality within the chosen class of
localizations. Numerical sampling alone cannot certify an optimal
radius or distinguish an endpoint from a nearby failure.

\begin{question}[Proposed: sharp retention from a prescribed number of defects]
\label{gsr:fz:59:q:graph-retention}
For fixed $k\ge2$, let $\lambda_k(q)$ be the infimum over finite
nonempty function graphs
whose order-$k$ vertical defects have at most $q$ sign orbits, of the
largest proportion of the domain supporting an exact Freiman
restriction of order $k$. Is there a constant $c_k>0$, independent of
both groups, such that
\[
 \lambda_k(q)\ge\frac{c_k}{q+1}\qquad(q\ge0)?
\]
If not, determine the correct decay and construct graph examples
attaining it.
\end{question}

The present universal lower bound is
$(5k)^{-\lfloor\log_2(q+1)\rfloor}$. Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:59:thm:realizability}
realizes every symmetric forbidden set as graph defects, with optimum
retained proportion $1-1/(2k)$. Thus sharp character rank alone does
not settle retained mass. A lower-bound example must control every
exact restriction. The explicit realizations also have difference
doubling comparable to their size, leaving small-doubling examples
as a distinct quantitative challenge.

There is also a weighted version: replace cardinality by arbitrary
nonnegative weights on the domain and maximize retained weight. The
theorem here covers this version. Determine whether its optimum agrees
with the unweighted optimum, or whether highly concentrated weights
expose an additional obstruction that is invisible in uniform examples.

\begin{question}[Proposed: a linear dependence on the Freiman order]
\label{gsr:fz:59:q:doubling-exponent}
For $k\ge2$, define $a(k)$ as the infimum of exponents $a\ge0$ for which a constant
$c_k>0$ guarantees an order-$k$ restriction of relative size at least
$c_kC^{-a}$ whenever $|\Gamma-\Gamma|\le C|\Gamma|$. Can one prove
$a(k)=O(k)$? Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:59:cor:doubling} gives
\[
 a(k)\le(2k+1)\log_2(5k)=O(k\log k).
\]
Alternatively, are there graph families forcing $a(k)/k$ to be
unbounded along a sequence of orders?
\end{question}

This asks for the final retained size. One possible route combines
defect counting with localization before either is bounded separately.
It remains meaningful even if the general estimate
$|F\cup\{0\}|\le C^{2k+1}$ cannot be improved. A positive answer to
Question~\ref{gsr:fz:59:q:graph-retention} would already give the desired linear
upper bound.

An alternative approach should identify a usable invariant beyond the
cardinality of the vertical fibre, such as its additive dimension or
distribution of orders. Any improvement must state the relation between
that invariant and $C$; treating a favorable profile as automatic from
small doubling would leave the central implication unproved.

\begin{question}[Established conjecture; proposed small-doubling restriction]
\label{gsr:fz:59:q:lonely-runner}
The classical lonely runner conjecture asserts that, for distinct
positive integers $v_1,\ldots,v_q$, some $t\in\T$ satisfies
\[
 \min_i\distT{tv_i}\ge\frac1{q+1}.
\]
For a concrete restricted target, let $k=2$, let all nonzero vertical
defects of $\Gamma$ have infinite order, and suppose they have $q\ge2$
sign orbits. If
$|\Gamma-\Gamma|\le q^{1/2}|\Gamma|$, must one character separate all
these defects at radius $1/(q+1)$?
\end{question}

The named conjecture is an established open problem
\cite{perarnauserrarunner}; the displayed small-doubling restriction is
proposed here. By Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:59:thm:realizability}, merely requiring graph
defects leaves every integer forbidden set available, so a substantive
extra condition is necessary for this approach. Bedert's improved
general estimate already transfers through
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:59:prop:lonely-runner} \cite{bedertrunner}. Invoking that estimate
must be distinguished from proving an improvement to it.

\begin{question}[Proposed refinement: the maximal local affine range]
\label{gsr:fz:59:q:affine-range}
Let $\ell:G\to W$ be a specified affine reference, let
$t=|\{f\ne\ell\}|/|G|$, and write
$\Psi(t)=4t-10t^2+6t^3$. Under $W[2]=\{0\}$, does
$\varepsilon(f)\ge\Psi(t)$ continue throughout $0<t<1/2$?
Under $W[2]=W[3]=\{0\}$, does it hold throughout the positive-cubic
range $0<t<2/3$? In any larger valid interval, does equality still force
one nonzero error value on a subgroup coset?
\end{question}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Answered} by source~96 (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:96:thm:affine-cubic}): when $W[2]=0$ the cubic holds on all of $0<t<2/3$, with no condition on $W[3]$, and equality there only on cosets; since $\Psi<0$ on $(2/3,1)$ it holds for every $t$. Source~67 had the case of elementary abelian $3$-groups (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:affineenvelope}).
\end{writenote}

Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:59:thm:affine-four-ninths} proves the respective ranges
$t<4/9$ and $t<1/2$. The question concerns a specified reference;
assuming it is a nearest affine map would change the problem. The next
step should retain the interaction between the signed four-error term,
the three-error terms, and the support geometry, rather than optimizing
their bounds independently.

Small-group searches can guide this question if they record both the
specified reference and the true nearest-affine distance. A counterexample
to one formulation may satisfy the other. Candidate improvements should
therefore be accompanied by the exact signed-pattern inequality they
require, and candidate obstructions by complete finite maps with exact
energy counts.

\begin{question}[Proposed: the optimal support--color tradeoff]
\label{gsr:fz:59:q:affine-frontier}
For a fixed rational $0<t<1/3$, determine the set of pairs
$(\alpha,\beta)\in[0,\infty)^2$ for which every map into a target
with $W[2]=\{0\}$, at support density $t$ from a specified affine
reference, satisfies
\[
 \varepsilon(f)-\Psi(t)\ge
 \alpha a+\beta\left(t^3-\frac{E(S)}{N^3}\right).
\]
Which pairs on its upper boundary are attained or approached by finite
examples, and how does this boundary change if $W[3]=\{0\}$ as well?
\end{question}

The present bounds supply the pairs $(2-6t,6)$ and
$(2-9t/2,3)$ in the first target class, together with all their convex
combinations and coordinatewise decreases. Without order-three torsion,
the enlarged-range argument supplies
$(\min\{2-3t,4-8t\},4)$. Optimizing this region asks how much support
structure can be controlled simultaneously with color concentration;
optimizing either coefficient in isolation can discard the interaction.
The endpoint equality cases themselves are settled in
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:59:cor:affine-endpoints}: density $4/9$ gives strict inequality
in the first class, and density $1/2$ in the second class has precisely
the one-value index-two-coset extremizers.

\begin{question}[Proposed refinement: involutions in the target]
\label{gsr:fz:59:q:involutions}
When $W$ contains a nonzero involution, determine the largest local
range for the appropriate profile
\[
 \Psi_{\mathrm{inv}}(t)=4t-12t^2+8t^3.
\]
Can the averaged signed-kernel method enlarge the repository's
sufficient range $t<1/3$ while retaining explicit nonnegative
remainders that distinguish unequal colors, opposite colors, and
involution-valued colors?
\end{question}

For color multiplicities $n_b$, useful separate quantities are
$A=s^2-\sum_b n_b^2$ and
$J=\sum_b n_b^2-\sum_b n_bn_{-b}$, where $s=\sum_b n_b$.
The existing involution theorem already gives a cubic with these
remainders and classifies equality below $1/3$. The unresolved target
is a larger range and sharper joint coefficients, including the
interaction with order-three cancellations.

\begin{question}[Proposed refinement: the remaining small-domain energy maxima]
\label{gsr:fz:59:q:small-domains}
For $W\ne\{0\}$ with $W[2]=\{0\}$ and $2\le|G|<16$, determine
\[
 M(G,W)=\max_{f\text{ non-affine}} \mathcal E(f)
\]
and classify the extremizers. In particular, does the one-point formula
from Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:59:cor:affine-sixteen} hold at orders $13,14,15$?
Organize any exceptions through the homomorphisms and quotients of $G$,
including failure to extend a homomorphism from a subgroup.
\end{question}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 82--94]
\emph{Answered at $13$, $14$, $15$} by source~93: yes, for every abelian target (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:thirteen}); the maxima and extremizers for $|G|\le12$ remain open (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:smallgroups}).
\end{writenote}

A cutoff cannot simply be removed: for $G=C_{12}$ and $W=C_3$, the map
equal to $1$ on odd inputs and $0$ on even inputs has energy $1296$,
whereas the one-point formula gives $1266$. The coset formula verifies
the first count; the two-point image rules out affinity. This example
already lies in the involution-free target setting of the manuscript.

\begin{question}[Proposed refinement: higher graph energies]
\label{gsr:fz:59:q:higher-energy}
For $r\ge3$, define
\[
 E_r(f)=\bigl|\{(x_1,\ldots,x_r,y_1,\ldots,y_r):
       \textstyle\sum_i x_i=\sum_i y_i,
       \ \sum_i f(x_i)=\sum_i f(y_i)\}\bigr|.
\]
Determine the sharp small-$t$ envelope of
$1-E_r(f)/|G|^{2r-1}$ at distance $t$ from a specified affine reference,
starting with $r=3$. Which support geometries and error-value patterns
give equality, and precisely which torsion assumptions are needed?
\end{question}

The first investigation should keep repeated coordinates and relations
among two or three error values explicit. Existing near-maximal set-energy
and cube-collision stability theorems provide useful inputs, while this
question requires the full sparse-error expansion for a function graph.
Any application to Gowers's later respected arrangements must identify
the actual counting tensor used there.

One useful intermediate deliverable is a complete three-sum expansion
for errors supported on a coset, allowing two nonzero colors. This
isolates the first competition between support structure and torsion
in the values. It can then be compared with arbitrary supports before
proposing a universal extremal formula or an equality classification.

\subsection{A numbered priority path for formalization}
\label{gsr:fz:59:sec:research-formalization}

The following is a proposed order of work. It asserts no existing Lean
proof of the new results.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Fix the finite interfaces.} Define graph defects, sign
orbits including singleton involutions, error supports, color
multiplicities, and ordered energies. Prove the basic bijections with
cardinalities in $\mathbb N$ before normalizing in $\mathbb R$.

\item \textbf{Formalize exact separation for finite targets.} Prove the
cyclic arc count, strict averaging with a distinguished positive-mass
outcome, and the adaptive deletion recurrence. Express the rank bound
first by integer inequalities
$b^m\le(b-1)q+1<b^{m+1}$; derive the logarithmic notation afterwards.
Verify the projective-line sharpness construction independently.

\item \textbf{Connect separation to graph extraction.} Establish weighted
localization, finite-image rounding, the vertical-fibre injection, and
the precise sum-and-difference growth interface. Check explicitly that
the auxiliary minimal-growth subset in the classical growth proof does
not replace the graph in its conclusion. Extend to finitely generated
targets after the finite version is complete.

\item \textbf{Verify the signed energy identities.} Formalize the exact
expansion, the three-position kernel average, and the support and color
remainders. Keep the hypotheses excluding orders two and three visible
in the statements where they enter. Derive the new local ranges and
their open-range equality classifications from these identities.

\item \textbf{Compose the recovery and stability results.} Supply or
import verified statements for homomorphism correction and coset
stability with their exact normalizations. Then prove the recovery
thresholds, the size-$16$ corollary, and the near-extremizer composition.
The endpoint classifications proved here should be included; the optimal support--color frontier remains a separate research task.

\item \textbf{Audit the downstream uses.} Instantiate the proved
interfaces at the actual uses in Sections~6 and~7, retaining a ledger
of domains, losses, and thresholds. Only a completed audit of subsequent
dependencies could support a new end-to-end bound. Exact computation
scripts can serve as regression checks throughout; they do not supply
kernel verification of the general statements.
\end{enumerate}

\section[{Consequences, comparison, and integration\srctag{60}}]{Consequences, comparison, and integration}\label{gsr:fz:60:sec:d10}\label{gsr:fz:60:sec:integration}
\srcnote{60}{Section 10}

The results have different logical roles. The norm theorem is a uniform asymptotic comparison on varying groups. The arrangement theorem is a sharp local repair result on a full product. The two-direction theorem repairs the compatibility between two such full-product models. The restriction theorem applies to a subset and gives a quantitative improvement at the earlier approximate-homomorphism selection step. Keeping these roles separate prevents a local improvement from being assigned a conclusion that requires additional structural arguments.

\subsection{A precise record of which questions are answered}

& The possibility $1/2$ is excluded. Exact $\beta_{\rm odd}$ and effective convergence remain open.\\[0.7em]

& Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:60:two:intersection}--\ref{gsr:en:60:two:sharpness} give a sharp intersection modulus and optimal repair coefficients through degree $s-2$.

The two exact limiting statements in the norm section have different scopes. In the unrestricted odd-order problem, the limiting discrete dual $\Gamma$ has no element of order two but can have odd torsion. In the large-prime-divisor limit $\Gamma$ is torsion-free, so its compact dual $K=\widehat\Gamma$ is connected. The latter extra property is exactly what permits the Riesz--Sobolev input. It must not be silently inserted into the former problem.

Similarly, the arrangement classification genuinely uses two-torsion in the target. It explains why the all-group polynomial can have a strictly better second-order behavior on odd targets. Its equality family also requires a quotient of order two in the vertical domain. Neither requirement is compatible with the common-odd-prime example, which is why a separate cancellation analysis is necessary.

\subsection{What changes at the Gowers interfaces}

In Gowers's Section~9, the restriction theorem supplies a new sufficient size threshold at the same retained-count scale as the Fej\'er refinement in source~17. It includes an all-group certificate, but its clean prime-uniform corollary assumes a threshold large enough to eliminate short torsion. The graph-energy interpolation used to pass from quadruples to sixteen-tuples is an inherited ingredient, reproduced in \eqref{gsr:en:60:rst:eq:moment-interpolation}; the new step is the translated survival estimate.

In Section~12, respected arrangements become a testing problem near complete agreement on a full product. Source~33 already identified their model class and supplied the coarse decoder and two sharp leading terms. Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:60:aux:profile} and~\ref{gsr:en:60:arr:local} retain the constant Fourier coefficient and its tail together, which is what allows the whole extremal polynomial and its equality cases to emerge. These are stronger full-product repair statements. Gowers's sparse-domain applications require additional control of which arrangements are available and how conditioned queries overlap.

The real norm comparison influences centered cube estimates by changing the admissible relation between $U^2$ mass and higher uniformity. Our result identifies its asymptotic limit and characteristic dependence. Since the proof does not give a finite-degree rate, it cannot be used to replace a numerical $U^4$ coefficient. In particular, the separately staged coefficient $4795/832$ in source~45 remains a finite-degree input distinct from this article's result \cite{repo60}.

The full Section~16 interpolation and numerical closure obligations recorded by the repository remain outside the conclusions proved here \cite{repo60nineteen}. A new estimate at one node of the proof must be propagated through all downstream losses before a new bound for $r_k(N)$, the maximum size of a $k$-term-progression-free subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$, can be asserted. Modern global bounds likewise involve a complete parameter analysis; see, for example, \cite{lssbounds}. No such global improvement is asserted in this manuscript.

\subsection{A suggested repository integration order}

The archive is a standalone research contribution, so its insertion need not alter previously assigned source numbers. A maintainer can register it as the next available source and retain its theorem labels. The following order keeps dependencies visible:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item Add the norm limit theorem next to source~29's moment comparison and asymptotic question. Preserve the distinction between the ratio $c_d^{\rm odd}$ and the coefficient in a $2^d$th-power inequality.
 \item Add the auxiliary-label theorem and arrangement polynomial next to source~33's local profile. Its $s=4$ specialization is inherited; the all-order inequality, classification and higher inverse coefficients are the new conclusions. Retain the common-prime bounds as a separate odd-target refinement.
 \item Add the two-direction section as a resolution of the local version of source~33's Question~8. The sum-normalized failure $e=\eps_s^v+\eps_s^h$ and the mixture-normalized failure are not interchangeable without the factor in Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:60:two:allocation}.
 \item Add the translated restriction theorem next to sources~04 and~17. Preserve the explicit counts of repeated tuples and the distinction between the integer principal line and coefficient relations that become dependent only modulo small torsion.
 \item Update the research-question ledger using Table~\ref{gsr:fz:60:tab:status}, preserving the unresolved parts of compound questions rather than marking every associated topic solved.
\end{enumerate}

For formalization, the natural initial targets are the finite auxiliary moment identity, the scalar convex-chord bound, the monotonicity of $E_s(t)/t$, and the weighted rank-two selector estimate. These are finite or elementary analytic statements with explicit interfaces. The compactness theorem needs Haar measure, duality, weak-star compactness and Fourier approximation, so it is a more substantial formalization project. No Lean file has been generated or compiled for these theorems.

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{As integrated here} (7~October 2026): the norm theorem stands beside sources~29 and~63 in Part~III (Section~\ref{gsr:cc:sec:oddlimit}), the arrangement and two-direction sections beside source~33 in Part~II (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:arrangementpolynomial}), the restriction theorem beside sources~04 and~17 (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:allmoduli}), and the questions in Section~\ref{gsr:fz:sec:further}; nothing is formalized.
\end{writenote}

\section[{Computational evidence and reproducibility\srctag{60}}]{Computational evidence and reproducibility}\label{gsr:fz:60:sec:d11}\label{gsr:fz:60:sec:verification}
\srcnote{60}{Section 11}

The archive contains the TeX source, the compiled PDF, the vector figure and its plotting source, the verification programs, their recorded outputs, and a source audit. The main article compiles with ordinary pdfLaTeX and standard packages. The proof text is self-contained apart from standard Fourier and compact-group facts, the explicitly stated Christ--Iliopoulou inequality, and background results credited and reproduced where used.

\subsection{What was checked exactly}

For arrangements, the verifier counts accepted balanced relations by integer convolution on $G\times K$. It obtains distance to a model by enumerating the admissible affine slope maps and optimizing a modal row value. Thus the defect and the model distance are computed by different finite procedures. It checks both the inequalities and the ``if and only if'' classifications in their stated interior ranges. It covers $s=4,6,8,16$, repeated queries, binary and nonbinary targets, and cases with nontrivial bilinear maps.

The principal arrangement suite records $16{,}976$ auxiliary-label comparisons and $32{,}024$ arrangement/profile comparisons, including $120$ and $12{,}928$ respective equality cases. Separate suites record $494$ robust-intersection comparisons, $8{,}504$ two-direction profile comparisons, and $8{,}656$ odd-target comparisons, for $66{,}654$ reported comparisons in total. The coset family is checked for every index $3\le n\le24$, including even indices. Additional exact evaluations compare the common-prime obstruction formula with generic integer counts at $p=17$ and with its proved uniform remainder at larger primes.

For restriction, the verifier evaluates the actual survival probability of a tuple by expanding over its distinct selected points and applying exact character orthogonality. This specifically tests the repeated-tuple correction. There are $88$ selector cases, including small torsion, and $90$ exact coefficient cases checking the signal, the kernel moment, and its alternating-binomial formula. These calculations use integers and rational numbers, not a rounded Fourier transform.

For the norm argument, the finite tests verify the distinct-pair multiplicities, the elementary tail inequality, the factorial simplification, and the explicit cyclic witness. They cannot test an infinite compactness argument. The separate checks of the trigonometric cotangent formula use floating point and are identified as such; the formula's proof is analytic.

An additional exact polynomial program checks the cancellation of the highest degree, the positive-basis identity for $B_s-F_s$, the gap $C_s-P_s$, and inverse-series composition for every even $4\le s\le32$. It verifies the exceptional $s=4$ terms and the stated one-direction and two-direction cubic coefficients with rational arithmetic.

\subsection{Bounded Fourier extrema on small groups}

There is a complete finite optimization behind the norm diagnostic table. The function
$f\mapsto\sum_\chi|\widehat f(\chi)|^4$ is convex on the centered cube
\[
 \{f\in[-1,1]^G:\textstyle\sum_xf(x)=0\}.
\]
For odd $|G|$, every vertex has one zero and equal numbers of $+1$ and $-1$. A convex function achieves a maximum at a vertex, and translation invariance permits fixing the zero at the identity. The program enumerates all choices of the positive coordinates and computes
\[
 \norm f_{U^2}^4=|G|^{-3}\sum_h
       \left(\sum_xf(x)f(x+h)\right)^2
\]
with integer arithmetic. There is no heuristic pruning.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrr@{}}
\toprule
Group & Vertices after fixing the zero & Exact maximum of $\norm f_{U^2}^4$\\
\midrule
$\Z_3$ & $2$ & $2/9$\\
$\Z_5$ & $6$ & $36/125$\\
$\Z_7$ & $20$ & $106/343$\\
$\Z_9$ & $70$ & $232/729$\\
$\Z_{11}$ & $252$ & $430/1331$\\
$\Z_{13}$ & $924$ & $716/2197$\\
$\Z_{15}$ & $3432$ & $1106/3375$\\
$\Z_{17}$ & $12870$ & $1616/4913$\\
$\Z_3\times\Z_3$ & $70$ & $56/243$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Complete bounded, real, centered optimization on the listed groups. The cyclic values coincide with \eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:interval-lower}. The table makes no claim about unlisted groups.}\label{gsr:fz:60:tab:finite-beta}
\end{table}

The two groups of order nine have different optima, which is a useful diagnostic that the group law, not merely its cardinality, is being used. The cyclic agreement with the explicit witness suggests a separate finite extremal question; it is not extrapolated to all odd cyclic groups in any theorem above.

\subsection{How to reproduce the deliverable}

The accompanying \texttt{README.txt} gives commands for building the PDF and running the checks. The verification programs need only the Python standard library. Regenerating the optional vector figure requires NumPy and Matplotlib; the checked figure is already included, so neither is required to compile the manuscript. Run the checks with ordinary Python, without the optimization flag that disables assertions. All computation described as exact in this section uses integer or rational arithmetic. The mathematical results do not depend on a numerical optimizer or on the finite tests passing.

\section[{Further research questions and a proposed programme\srctag{60}}]{Further research questions and a proposed programme}\label{gsr:fz:60:sec:d12}\label{gsr:fz:60:sec:questions}
\srcnote{60}{Section 12}

The theorems sharpen several questions enough to make the next steps testable. The following programme separates questions that may yield further local improvements from the larger task of transporting those improvements through Gowers's sparse structural argument.

\subsection{Fourier extrema and effective compactness}

\begin{problem}[The unrestricted odd-order limit]\label{gsr:fz:60:q:beta}
Does every centered real function on a finite odd-order abelian group satisfy
\[
 \norm f_{U^2}^4\le\frac13\norm f_\infty^4?
\]
By Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:60:norm:thm:main}, this is equivalent to $c_\infty^{\rm odd}=1/3$. The connected compact case is settled here. The remaining issue is the effect of persistent finite odd-order quotients. The mass-cap proof treats two large inverse pairs as independently placeable, even though a bounded function may not realize those coefficient magnitudes simultaneously. A stronger joint coefficient inequality is one concrete route to reducing the upper endpoint.
\end{problem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Answered by source~63}: yes, by its Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:63:bounded:sharp}, so $c_\infty^{\mathrm{odd}}=1/3$ (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:normgap}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{problem}[Effective high-degree and high-characteristic thresholds]\label{gsr:fz:60:q:effective}
Find explicit functions $d_0(\eps)$ and, for the connected limit, $P_0(\eps)$ such that
\[
 c_d^{\rm odd}\le B+\eps,
 \qquad C(d,P)\le\frac13+\eps
\]
in the respective ranges, where $B$ is the upper endpoint in \eqref{gsr:cc:60:norm:eq:bracket}. The Fourier-tail lemma is already quantitative: a moment order of size $\eps^{-1}$ and an initial spectrum of size $\eps^{-2}$ make its tail small up to absolute constants. The non-effective step is stabilizing algebraic relations among these frequencies and controlling the smoothing needed to convert finite norm information into a supremum bound. Is there a bounded-height relation model that avoids an unrestricted compactness extraction?
\end{problem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{Answered by source~63} for both quantities: $d_0(\varepsilon)=d_\varepsilon=8\max\{10,\lceil\log_2(10/\varepsilon)\rceil\}$ (its Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:63:norm:epsilon}) gives $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}\le1/3+\varepsilon\le B+\varepsilon$, and $C(d,P)\le c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}$ for $P\ge3$, so no $P_0$ is needed (checked at the write). The optimal rate is source~63's Research question~\ref{gsr:fz:63:research:rate}.
\end{writenote}

\begin{problem}[Exact finite cyclic and bounded-exponent extrema]\label{gsr:fz:60:q:finite-beta}
Is the exact bounded Fourier maximum on $\Z_q$, for every odd $q$, equal to
\[
 \frac{q^3-4q+3}{3q^3}?
\]
The explicit witness attains this value, and exhaustive enumeration confirms optimality for odd $3\le q\le17$. A proof must control the energy of every centered cube vertex, including at composite orders. More broadly, determine $\beta(q)$ for groups of exponent dividing a fixed odd $q$, and classify extremizers. At $q=3$, the finite computation on $\Z_3^2$ and Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:60:norm:cor:exponent} give the concrete starting interval
$56/243\le\beta(3)\le5/18$.
\end{problem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
\emph{The first question is answered by source~63}: on every abelian group of odd order $q$ the maximum is at most $1/3-4/(3q^2)+1/q^3=(q^3-4q+3)/(3q^3)$, attained on $\Z/q\Z$ (its Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:63:bounded:finite}); the values agree with the table above for every odd $3\le q\le17$ (checked at the write in exact rationals). The bound is not attained on $\Z_3\times\Z_3$ ($56/243<232/729$), so the questions on fixed exponent, $\beta(3)$ and the extremizers stay open (source~63's Research question~\ref{gsr:fz:63:research:group}; item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:III:normgap}).
\end{writenote}

\begin{problem}[Stability at the connected limiting constant]\label{gsr:fz:60:q:norm-stability}
For uniformly bounded centered functions with ratio approaching $1/3$ in the joint regime of Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:60:norm:thm:large-characteristic}, can one identify half-circle Bohr sets or a comparably explicit family after passage to an appropriate quotient? The equality and stability theory in \cite{christiliopoulou} supplies structure on a connected compact limit. Transferring that structure back to finite groups, with a quantitative error and an explicit metric, is an additional problem. For initially unbounded functions, the natural first target may be Fourier fourth-power approximation after positive smoothing rather than pointwise or $L^1$ approximation.
\end{problem}

\subsection{Sharp repair beyond the classified equality cases}

\begin{problem}[Quantitative near-equality for arrangements]\label{gsr:fz:60:q:near-equality}
Fix $s$ and keep $\delta$ in a compact subinterval of $(0,1/4)$. If
\[
 \eps_s(f)-B_s(\delta)\le\zeta,
\]
how close must $f$, modulo an exact model, be to a classified map
$a\1_C(x)\ell_2(y)$? Determine the best exponent of $\zeta$ and its dependence on the distance of $\delta$ from the endpoints. The proof identifies four separate losses: collision concentration, convex-chord slack, Fourier-cap slack, and synchronization of active increments. A quantitative argument must make these losses compatible with one coset and one homomorphism. It should also explain how closeness to equality constrains $\delta$ to be near $1/(2n)$.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[The common-prime second coefficient]\label{gsr:fz:60:q:prime}
Close the interval
\[
 \frac{s-1}{s^2}\le c_s^{\rm prime}\le\frac{3s-2}{2s^2}.
\]
The lower construction spreads half-interval errors over $\lfloor\sqrt p\rfloor$ rows; the upper bound uses the maximal cancellation probability of two errors in an odd-order target. A matching theorem would need to couple the derivative value distribution with the row collision profile. The separate worst cases for those two quantities need not be realizable by the same map. Is the lower endpoint the correct value, or is there another family with more favorable cancellation?
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[The finite-error arrangement envelope and activation]\label{gsr:fz:60:q:global-profile}
Determine the feasible pairs $(\delta,\eps_s)$ beyond the neighborhood of zero and identify the largest error threshold admitting a canonical repair branch. Even within $0<\delta<1/4$, equality in $B_s$ occurs only at $1/(2n)$. Can the universal bound be improved between those distances, perhaps with a piecewise expression sensitive to allowable subgroup indices? The coarse decoder is sufficient to activate our sharp local bound but is not designed to locate a genuine testing threshold. This problem requires structural information beyond formal inversion of a polynomial that is not globally increasing.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[The optimal two-direction profile]\label{gsr:fz:60:q:two}
Is $P_s(\delta)$ the beginning of an explicit sharp finite-error profile? The sparse-row example has defect $C_s(\delta)$, and \eqref{gsr:en:60:two:gap} shows that their first possible difference is at order $\delta^{s-1}$. Determine the optimal inverse coefficient at degree $s-1$, beginning with the unresolved cubic for $s=4$. Also classify equality or near-equality in the robust-intersection theorem beyond the displayed binary strip unions. The bilinear-part separation and the distributional intersection argument may have different sharpness mechanisms away from zero.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Several coordinate directions and higher models]\label{gsr:fz:60:q:multilinear}
For a product of three or more groups, identify the exact class invisible to a specified family of directional arrangement tests, then prove sharp repair to the compatible multilinear class. The two-direction variance argument suggests using the orthogonal decomposition by coordinate subsets, while the bilinear separation argument suggests a hierarchy of discrete derivative gaps. Can one avoid an exponential accumulation of coarse synchronization constants? An explicit first case is a triaffine model on $G_1\times G_2\times G_3$ tested in all three directions.
\end{problem}

\subsection{Restriction, sparse domains, and the global proof}

\begin{problem}[The best translated positive kernel]\label{gsr:fz:60:q:kernel}
For a nonnegative trigonometric polynomial $0\le K\le1$ of bounded Fourier support, optimize the signal on the principal line relative to its zero coefficient, the total zero-sum coefficient weight, and the repeated-tuple survival correction. Fej\'er gives the explicit scale $L^{m-1}$, but the present proof does not establish its optimality. A useful formulation keeps all three quantities in the signed objective $\eta\E X-\E Y$ rather than maximizing signal amplification alone. Can a different kernel improve the retention constant without restoring a larger threshold?
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Uniform restriction with persistent short torsion]\label{gsr:fz:60:q:torsion}
Can a finite family of translated selectors eliminate the principal-line leakage measured by $S_{m,L}[q]$ while preserving polynomial retention uniformly over all finite abelian groups? For fixed $q$, a single Fej\'er selector has a leakage-to-signal ratio tending to $1/q$, so increasing the bandwidth alone does not solve the problem. A promising route is to separate the low-order quotient, apply a rank-sensitive or exact restriction there, and combine it with a large-order selector. The cost must be controlled in the number of relevant torsion layers rather than in the total group size.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Sharp domain-size thresholds]\label{gsr:fz:60:q:threshold}
Is the exponent $m-1$ in Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:60:rst:cor:prime} necessary for retaining its stated coefficient, or can it be lowered uniformly as the prime modulus varies? The nonprincipal weight and repeated-point correction are bounded independently in the proof. Their worst cases may be incompatible with a graph having many respected relations. An energy-sensitive estimate for the actual repeated bad tuples, or for the weighted rank-two fibers, could improve the threshold further. A negative answer should exhibit a family that obstructs the prescribed retained count, not merely a family on which one particular selector performs poorly.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[From full products to sparse arrangement domains]\label{gsr:fz:60:q:sparse}
Which quantitative mixing assumptions on a subset $A\subseteq G\times H$ suffice for a polynomial repair theorem in the conditional arrangement failure rate? The full-product proof uses independent auxiliary labels, a cocycle comparison at every increment, and rowwise integration. A sparse theorem must replace each of these with a controlled witness-count statement. It should record domain density, conditional marginal distortion, and overlap expansion separately. Proving such a theorem is the most direct route from the new sharp local profiles to the sparse structural steps in Gowers's Sections~12--15.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[A complete quantitative propagation and formal interface]\label{gsr:fz:60:q:global}
After a sparse repair theorem is available, propagate the improved restriction and repair constants through the full interpolation and density-increment chain. Every change should specify the old input, the replacement, the downstream recurrence, and the parameter range in which it improves the final statement. In parallel, formalize the finite auxiliary moment theorem and selector certificate before tackling compactness. A complete proof of a better global bound requires these missing interfaces and numerical closure; the local sharpness results alone do not imply it.
\end{problem}

\paragraph{Suggested order of work.}
Questions~\ref{gsr:fz:60:q:prime}, \ref{gsr:fz:60:q:two}, and~\ref{gsr:fz:60:q:kernel} have explicit finite-dimensional objectives and direct diagnostics. Questions~\ref{gsr:fz:60:q:beta} and~\ref{gsr:fz:60:q:finite-beta} isolate a substantive Fourier extremal problem, with exact examples and a narrow universal interval. Question~\ref{gsr:fz:60:q:effective} asks for the quantitative content hidden by the compactness step. Questions~\ref{gsr:fz:60:q:sparse} and~\ref{gsr:fz:60:q:global} are the larger structural programme needed to influence the global Szemer\'edi bound. This ordering allows further local discoveries to be validated before they are assigned downstream consequences.

\section[{The inherited coarse decoder, with proof\srctag{60}}]{The inherited coarse decoder, with proof}\label{gsr:fz:60:sec:dA}
\srcnote{60}{Appendix A}
\label{gsr:fz:60:decode:section}

This appendix supplies the bootstrap used in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:60:arr:repair}. The quantitative decoder is the one already
proved in the full-product report~\cite{repo60thirtythree}; it is reproduced so
that the sharp polynomial and its inversion have a self-contained
dependency chain. The majority-correction method is in the tradition
of Blum, Luby, and Rubinfeld~\cite{blr}. We retain independent
auxiliary labels at every query, including when the group coordinates
repeat.

\begin{lemma}[Homomorphism correction with labels]\label{gsr:fz:60:decode:hom}
Let $U,W$ be finite abelian groups, let $S$ be a finite nonempty set,
and let $F:U\times S\to W$. Suppose
\[
 e=\mathbb P_{u,v,\alpha,\beta,\gamma}
 [F(u,\alpha)+F(v,\beta)\ne F(u+v,\gamma)]<\frac16.
\]
Then there is a homomorphism $L:U\to W$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:60:decode:hom-bound}
 \mathbb P_{u,\alpha}[F(u,\alpha)\ne L(u)]
                 \le\frac e{1-2e}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For fixed $z\in U$, consider
\[
 A_z(y;\alpha,\beta)=F(z+y,\alpha)-F(y,\beta).
\]
Its two independent copies agree with probability at least $1-2e$.
Indeed, introduce one further independent label $\gamma$ and compare
\begin{align*}
 F(z+y,\alpha)+F(y',\beta')&=F(z+y+y',\gamma),\\
 F(y,\beta)+F(z+y',\alpha')&=F(z+y+y',\gamma).
\end{align*}
Each equality fails with probability $e$: with $z$ fixed, its two
group inputs remain independent and uniform. If both hold, the two
copies of $A_z$ agree.

Writing $p_z(w)=\mathbb P[A_z=w]$, it follows that
\[
 \max_wp_z(w)\ge\sum_wp_z(w)^2\ge1-2e.
\]
Let $L(z)$ be the unique mode; its mass exceeds $1/2$. Thus
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:60:decode:pointwise-mode}
 \mathbb P[A_z=L(z)]\ge1-2e\qquad(z\in U).
\end{equation}
For fixed $z,z'$, the identity
\[
 A_{z+z'}(y;\alpha,\beta)
 =A_z(y+z';\alpha,\gamma)+A_{z'}(y;\gamma,\beta)
\]
holds pointwise. Each of its three terms equals its mode except on
an event of probability at most $2e$. Since $6e<1$, some choice of
the arguments realizes all three modes simultaneously. Therefore
$L(z+z')=L(z)+L(z')$.

Finally the test error can also be written as
\[
 e=\mathbb P_{u,v,\alpha,\beta,\gamma}
          [F(u,\alpha)\ne A_u(v;\gamma,\beta)].
\]
Conditional on $u,\alpha$, if $F(u,\alpha)\ne L(u)$ then the event
$A_u(v;\gamma,\beta)=L(u)$ forces a failure. Its probability is at
least $1-2e$ by \eqref{gsr:fz:60:decode:pointwise-mode}, and its labels are
independent of $\alpha$. Hence
\[
 e\ge(1-2e)\mathbb P[F(u,\alpha)\ne L(u)],
\]
proving \eqref{gsr:fz:60:decode:hom-bound}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Affine correction with labels]\label{gsr:fz:60:decode:affine}
For $F:G\times S\to K$, let $e=e_4(F)$ be the auxiliary test error of
Section~\ref{gsr:en:60:aux:section}. There is an affine map $A:G\to K$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:60:decode:affine-bound}
 \mathbb P_{x,u}[F(x,u)\ne A(x)]\le6e.
\end{equation}
If $e<1/6$, the upper bound can be replaced by $e/(1-2e)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $e\ge1/6$, any affine map satisfies \eqref{gsr:fz:60:decode:affine-bound}.
Otherwise choose an anchor $(x_4,u_4)=(z,w)$ whose conditional test
error $e_0$ is at most $e$. Conditional on that anchor, set
\[
 x_1=z+u,\quad x_2=z+v,\quad x_3=z+u+v,
\]
with $u,v$ independently uniform. The translated function
$Q(u,\alpha)=F(z+u,\alpha)-F(z,w)$ has homomorphism-test error $e_0$.
Lemma~\ref{gsr:fz:60:decode:hom} supplies a homomorphism $L$ with disagreement
at most $e_0/(1-2e_0)\le e/(1-2e)$. Translating back gives the affine
map $A(x)=L(x-z)+F(z,w)$. In this range $e/(1-2e)<3e/2\le6e$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Separation of affine maps]\label{gsr:fz:60:decode:separation}
Two distinct affine maps from a finite abelian group to an abelian
group disagree on at least half their inputs.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Their difference is $L(x)+c$. If $L=0$, a nonzero difference never
vanishes. If $L\ne0$, its zero set is empty or a coset of $\ker L$,
whose index is at least two.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Coarse full-product repair]\label{gsr:fz:60:decode:coarse}
For $f:G\times H\to K$, if $\varepsilon_4(f)<1/216$, then
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:60:decode:coarse-bound}
 \delta_{\mathcal V}(f)
 \le6\varepsilon_4(f)
       +\frac{36\varepsilon_4(f)}{1-72\varepsilon_4(f)}
 \le60\varepsilon_4(f).
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $e_h$ be the conditional four-difference failure probability at
increment $h$. Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:fz:60:decode:affine} to
$F_h(x,y)=D_hf(x,y)$ with label set $H$. Choose
$A_h\in\operatorname{Aff}(G,K)$ such that
\[
 d_h:=\mathbb P_{x,y}[D_hf(x,y)\ne A_h(x)]\le6e_h.
\]
Put $d=\mathbb E_hd_h$, so $d\le6\varepsilon_4(f)<1/36$.
The derivative identity
\[
 D_{h+k}f(x,y)=D_hf(x,y+k)+D_kf(x,y)
\]
and a union bound yield
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:60:decode:cocycle}
 \mathbb P_{h,k,x}[A_{h+k}(x)\ne A_h(x)+A_k(x)]\le3d.
\end{equation}
For each $h,k$, the compared affine maps are identical or differ on
at least half of $G$, by Lemma~\ref{gsr:fz:60:decode:separation}. Thus
\[
 \eta:=\mathbb P_{h,k}[A_{h+k}\ne A_h+A_k]\le6d<1/6.
\]
The affine maps form a finite abelian group under pointwise addition.
Apply Lemma~\ref{gsr:fz:60:decode:hom}, with a singleton label set, to the map
$h\mapsto A_h$. It produces a homomorphism
\[
 \mathcal A:H\longrightarrow\operatorname{Aff}(G,K)
\]
whose disagreement proportion is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:60:decode:synchronization}
 q\le\frac\eta{1-2\eta}\le\frac{6d}{1-12d}.
\end{equation}

Set
\[
 \ell(y)=\mathcal A(y)(0),\qquad
 B(x,y)=\mathcal A(y)(x)-\mathcal A(y)(0).
\]
Then $\ell$ is additive and $B$ is biadditive. For the residual
$r(x,y)=f(x,y)-B(x,y)-\ell(y)$,
\[
 \mathbb P_{h,x,y}[D_hr(x,y)\ne0]\le d+q.
\]
For each $x$, choose a most frequent value $a(x)$ of $r(x,\cdot)$.
Since independent row samples disagree with probability at least
one minus the largest atom, averaging the row collision identity
gives
\[
 \mathbb P_{x,y}[r(x,y)\ne a(x)]\le d+q.
\]
This constructs a member of $\mathcal V$ with the required distance.
Using $d\le6\varepsilon_4(f)$ in \eqref{gsr:fz:60:decode:synchronization}
gives the first bound of \eqref{gsr:fz:60:decode:coarse-bound}. Finally,
$1-72\varepsilon_4(f)>2/3$, so the fraction there is at most
$54\varepsilon_4(f)$, proving the second bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The exact kernel of the test]\label{gsr:fz:60:decode:kernel}
For every even $s\ge4$,
$\varepsilon_s(f)=0$ if and only if $f\in\mathcal V$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Model functions always pass. Conversely, the moment identity gives
$\varepsilon_4(f)\le\varepsilon_s(f)=0$, and
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fz:60:decode:coarse} gives distance zero to $\mathcal V$.
\end{proof}

\section[{Exact computational checks and constructive content\srctag{61}}]{Exact computational checks and constructive content}\label{gsr:fz:61:sec:d10}
\srcnote{61}{Section 10}
\label{gsr:fz:61:ter:checks}

The accompanying Python programs implement the finite constructions and run exact checks. They do not serve as a proof assistant, and exhaustive verification of small cases is not used in place of any general argument above. Their purpose is to catch sign errors, torsion exceptions, boundary mistakes, and normalization errors in the executable versions of the proofs.

\subsection{Representation and arithmetic}

A group is represented as an explicit product
$\prod_i\Z/q_i\Z$. Elements are tuples of canonical integer representatives. A character is indexed by a tuple $a$, with value
\[
\chi_a(x)=\sum_i\frac{a_ix_i}{q_i}\pmod1.
\]
Let $Q=\operatorname{lcm}_i q_i$. The character value is stored as a numerator $v$ modulo $Q$. The open radius-$1/5$ test is the integer comparison
\[
5\min(v,Q-v)<Q.
\]
The color index is $\floor{5mv/Q}$. No floating-point trigonometry or approximate Fourier transform is used.

Additive energies are computed by exact convolution of counting functions. The BSG score and its thresholds use rational arithmetic. For the weighted tests, each complex weight is a Gaussian integer stored as a pair of integers; convolution and squared magnitudes are computed by integer operations. Only the optional elapsed-time field in the run record is inexact.

\subsection{Coverage of the delivered run}

The run recorded in \code{checks/results.json} completed with every assertion passing. The principal coverage is:

Check family & Cases\\
\midrule

All forbidden sets in eight groups, at orders $1,2,3,8$ & 1,304\\

Those maps tested at orders $2,3,8$ & 5,478\\
BSG cores for all maps $\Z/4\Z\to\Z/4\Z$ & 256\\

\subsection{How to reproduce the checks}

From the package directory, run
\begin{verbatim}
python3 code/run_checks.py
\end{verbatim}
The program requires Python 3.10 or later and uses only the standard library. It rewrites \code{checks/results.json} and prints the same record. The test suite must be run with assertions enabled; do not use Python's \code{-O} option.

The main construction can also be called directly:
\begin{verbatim}
from exact_restriction import AbelianGroup, freiman_partition
G = AbelianGroup((8,))
H = AbelianGroup((16,))
phi = {x: x for x in G.elements()}
characters, cells, defects = freiman_partition(G, H, phi, 8)
\end{verbatim}
This example returns singleton cells, illustrating the order-eight obstruction. The module must be on the Python import path, for example by running from the \code{code/} directory.

\subsection{Constructive versus efficient}

The proofs give finite algorithms: enumerate characters, repeatedly minimize the number of remaining unseparated defects, color by exact interval indices, and select a largest cell. The BSG proof similarly maximizes a finite score and prunes a finite neighborhood. However, the supplied implementation explicitly enumerates the group, graph sumsets, and character table. It is intended for small-instance certificates, not as a polynomial-time algorithm in the bit length of a compressed group presentation.

The guarantee on the \emph{number of colors} is independent of the ambient group size. That mathematical guarantee must not be confused with an algorithmic running-time guarantee. Computing the defect set itself may dominate the cost.

\subsection{Recommended mathematical placement}

A suitable new research directory is
\begin{center}
\code{Combinatorics/Ramsey/Research/GowersSzemeredi/}\\
\code{torsion-exact-restriction/}.
\end{center}
The article is self-contained and need not be merged into the existing consolidated manuscript before review. Its labels have the prefix \code{ter:} to reduce collision risk in a later integration. The package includes source, PDF, exact checking programs, source notes, and a formalization plan. No repository files were changed in preparing this delivery.

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 60--69]
The suggested directory was not used: by its placement (\texttt{39d3295c4}) this source is source~61 of this report, with labels \texttt{gsr:fm:61:}, \texttt{gsr:en:61:} or \texttt{gsr:fz:61:} in front of its \texttt{ter:} labels, and files under the prefix \file{61-exact-restriction-}.
\end{writenote}

The most useful dependency order is
\[
\begin{gathered}
\text{root-grid estimate}\ \longrightarrow\ \text{defect separation}
\ \longrightarrow\ \text{avoidance partition},\\
\text{Pl\"unnecke--Ruzsa}\ \longrightarrow\ \text{vertical budget}
\ \longrightarrow\ \text{exact graph partition},\\
\text{BSG core}\ +\ \text{exact graph partition}\ +\ \text{sumset energy}
\ \longrightarrow\ \text{threshold-free order-eight theorem}.
\end{gathered}
\]
The obstruction theorems are logically independent of the BSG estimate and can be integrated as a separate subsection.

\subsection{Minimal formal interfaces}

There are two reasonable formalization routes. One can work from the start with arbitrary finite abelian groups and their character groups, or first implement the construction for explicit products of cyclic groups and then transport it across an isomorphism. The latter route mirrors the integer certificate program and isolates the group-classification dependency.

The first target should be a finite separation lemma, not the final numerical corollary. Its abstract input is a finite collection of tests such that every nonzero defect passes at most half of them. Greedy halving then needs only finite sums and cardinalities. Character orthogonality or the root-grid calculation supplies the input later.

The next targets are the interval-width implication and the graph-translate injection. The interval argument must use half-open cells and the strict radius condition; replacing either endpoint convention without rechecking the proof is unsafe. The graph injection is purely algebraic and should not require Fourier analysis.

For relation counts, establish an explicit equivalence between the ordered tuple formulation in Definition~\ref{gsr:en:61:ter:freiman-def} and the repository's \code{FreimanHom} interface. The counting conventions allow repetitions and count ordered tuples. Next identify $\Energy_8(B)$ with \code{additiveTupleCount 8 B} and the respected energy with \code{phiAdditiveTupleCount 8 B phi}. Exactness then implies equality of those two counts, and the \code{GammaHomOfOrder} conclusion follows by a scalar inequality.

Finally, the implication to the inspected \code{lemma\_9\_3} should choose $N_0=1$, derive $\alpha\leq1$ from the energy cap, and use the integer exponent comparison in Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:61:ter:lemma93}. This is a proposed proof plan, not a checked Lean implementation. No \code{sorry}-bearing file is shipped as a purported proof, and no formalization-status ledger should be updated solely on the basis of this article.

\subsection{What requires review before promotion}

The main mathematical review points are the universal character estimate in all small torsion orders, the strict interval-boundary argument, the disjoint vertical translates, the distinction between the original graph size and the extracted-core size in the BSG ratio, and the use of ordered repeated-variable relations. The algebraic derivations of the constants are supplied separately from the conceptual claims to make review modular.

A later numerical refinement should use Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:61:ter:modular-transfer} rather than silently replacing the conservative BSG constants. A later global application must additionally prove the analytic compatibility hypotheses that it uses. Neither numerical improvement nor compatibility follows merely from the existence of an exact restriction.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Further research questions\srctag{61}}]{Further research questions}\label{gsr:fz:61:sec:d12}
\srcnote{61}{Section 12}
\label{gsr:fz:61:ter:questions}

The questions in this section arise from the present results. They are proposed research problems, not assertions that the same formulations are established open problems in the literature. Their priority and their relation to other versions of additive coloring should be investigated independently.

\begin{question}[Determine the exact avoidance exponent]
\label{gsr:fz:61:ter:q-exact}
Is
\[
b_m=\floor{\log_2m}+1
\qquad(m\geq2)?
\]
If not, determine the least $m$ for which the $2$-primary examples do not give the optimal universal exponent.
\end{question}

Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:61:ter:main-exponent} confines the uncertainty to an additive constant. A proof of the displayed formula would require a mechanism better than the present independent narrow-arc construction, or a more efficient way of using torsion in the separation step. Conversely, a lower bound larger than the displayed value would require a genuinely different obstruction. Exact searches for small $(H,D)$ can be organized as hypergraph coloring problems, with hyperedges consisting of supports of forbidden balanced relations.

\begin{question}[The graph-extraction exponent]
Let $a_m^*$ be the infimum of exponents $a$ for which a constant $c_m>0$ guarantees an exact order-$m$ restriction of size $c_mK^{-a}|B|$ from every graph of difference ratio at most $K$. What is the asymptotic growth of $a_m^*$?
\end{question}

The present results give a lower bound of order $\log m$ and an upper bound of order $m\log m$. Is $a_m^*=O(\log m)$, or is there a graph obstruction forcing a larger scale? Resolving this requires more than optimizing the constant $5$ in the character partition.

\begin{question}[Use the structure of vertical defects]
Can the worst-case estimate $|\Def_m(\Gamma)|\leq K^{2m+1}$ be replaced by a substantially smaller effective parameter for graph restriction, without assuming that the codomain has prime exponent?
\end{question}

The defect set is not arbitrary: it is a vertical fiber of a structured iterated difference set. Its additive structure, annihilators, or distribution across primary components may permit a smaller family of separating tests than its cardinality suggests. General-group structural results such as Green--Ruzsa \cite{greenruzsa} provide context, but no quantitative deduction of this kind is proved here.

\begin{question}[Optimal relation-energy powers]
For fixed $m$, what are the best powers $p$ and constants $c_m$ in a universal exact restriction theorem of the form
\[
\Energy_m^\phi(B)\geq\alpha|B|^{2m-1}
\ \Longrightarrow\
\Energy_m(B')\geq c_m\alpha^p|B|^{2m-1}?
\]
Can the current $O(m^2\log m)$ exponent be reduced in order of magnitude?
\end{question}

There are at least three separate losses to analyze: conversion to ordinary additive energy, selection of a small-difference graph core, and concentration of a high moment in one exact cell. Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:61:ter:modular-transfer} separates the second from the third. A weighted BSG theorem preserving an appropriate relation distribution might avoid the loss incurred by selecting solely through cardinality.

\begin{question}[Exact versus approximate tradeoffs]
For arbitrary composite cyclic groups, how much better can relation-energy retention be if exact respect is relaxed to a proportion $1-\eta$? Can one obtain a useful bound that interpolates between prime-field approximate restriction and the torsion-uniform exact partition?
\end{question}

The exact theorem removes $\eta$ entirely, but pays a large power of $\alpha$. An approximate theorem need not inherit the singleton obstruction in the same form. Identifying the correct torsion-sensitive statistic could give sharper cyclic bounds than a general-group theorem.

\begin{question}[Retain the analytic data needed later in Gowers's proof]
Can one construct exact cells while retaining a controlled part of a \emph{family} of derivative Fourier coefficients and the compatibility of the associated cross-sections, rather than a single prescribed scalar correlation?
\end{question}

A useful positive result must state the family norm being retained, the common restriction on which it survives, and the consistency conditions across indices. Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:61:ter:correlation} alone is insufficient. This is the most direct route by which the present local argument might become relevant to later high-degree steps, but no such bridge is proved here.

\begin{question}[Cyclic groups versus arbitrary finite abelian groups]
Does restricting both domain and codomain to cyclic groups permit smaller universal exponents than $a_m^*$ or the corresponding energy exponent for arbitrary groups?
\end{question}

The strongest lower-bound families in Section~\ref{gsr:en:61:ter:torsion} increase the rank while fixing the exponent. They therefore do not automatically settle the cyclic optimization. A cyclic analysis must account for primary factors and carries without importing a rank-based obstruction that its hypotheses exclude.

\begin{question}[Algorithms with compressed input]
Can a short separation certificate and a large exact cell be found in time polynomial in a natural compressed description of $B$, $\phi$, and the ambient groups, assuming the requisite growth or energy promise?
\end{question}

The first obstacle is obtaining or representing the relevant defect set without enumerating $m$-fold sumsets. One possible goal is a certificate verifier whose complexity depends on the certificate and the input rather than on $|H|$. The supplied program establishes finite constructivity only.

\begin{question}[Stability of the extremal torsion examples]
If $\chi_m(H,D)$ is close to the largest power permitted by a conjecturally optimal exponent, must $(H,D)$ contain a large quotient or subsystem resembling the $p$-primary examples? Is there a corresponding stability statement for nearly singleton-only graph restrictions?
\end{question}

Such a theorem would turn the present examples from lower-bound witnesses into a structural explanation of difficult instances. It would also indicate which extra hypotheses could genuinely improve the restriction theorem, as opposed to merely improving its constants on easy cases.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Conclusion\srctag{61}}]{Conclusion}\label{gsr:fz:61:sec:d13}
\srcnote{61}{Section 13}

The exact-partition method yields an elementary, torsion-uniform route from graph growth to bounded-order additive rigidity. Its central quantitative feature is the separation of a finite vertical-defect budget by $O(\log|D|)$ characters. This supplies a complete partition, preserves weighted energies with explicit losses, and turns a conservative energy-to-growth input into a threshold-free exact strengthening of the stated Lemma 9.3 conclusion.

The coloring obstruction determines the leading logarithmic dependence of the universal defect-coloring exponent on relation order. The graph obstruction establishes a distinct lower bound and shows why one should not extrapolate prime-modulus intuition to arbitrary torsion. The substantial remaining gap in graph exponents and the missing analytic-compatibility bridge are explicit. These are the natural next mathematical targets; an improved global Szemer\'edi bound is not a consequence of the present manuscript.

\section[{Exact checks and reproducibility\srctag{62}}]{Exact checks and reproducibility}\label{gsr:fz:62:sec:d10}
\srcnote{62}{Section 10}
\label{gsr:fz:62:sec:checks}

The package includes \texttt{code/verify.py}, which uses only the Python
standard library. Fractions and integer arithmetic are used for all asserted
identities and inequalities. Decimal table entries are displays of exact
quantities, except that logarithms in the parameter table are rounded
floating-point evaluations.

The recorded run checks the following families.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.]
\item \textbf{Primitive profiles.}
For $m\in\{4,6,8,16\}$, $2\le L\le32$, and $2\le q\le160$, all
$19\,716$ response values are checked for nonnegativity and the sampling
bound $B_{m,L}(q)\le q/\varphi(q)$. The dyadic elementary envelope and the
large-$q$ bound are also checked wherever applicable.
\item \textbf{Weighted arithmetic.}
The exact divisor formula and $K_m$ bound are tested in $2\,184$ modulus
cases, including composite and prime moduli. For $L=2,3$ and $m=4$, direct
enumeration of coefficient vectors independently checks the divisor formula
in 22 cases. The expressions \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:kappa2}--\eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:kappa3} and the
finite-length overshoot at $m=16$ are checked exactly.
\item \textbf{Random subset selection.}
Six small examples with distinct or equal composite target and domain moduli
are evaluated exactly. Joint inclusion probabilities are computed by finite
Fourier convolution. M\"obius inversion then obtains the probability of
every selected subset, and verifies positivity, total mass one, the weighted
main-term estimates, and the repeated-vertex correction. These tests use
$N\le7$ and include all 312 subset outcomes across the six examples.
\item \textbf{Parameters and obstructions.}
The dyadic recipe, the coarse polynomial inequalities, and the comparison
with \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:old} are checked on 28 parameter cases, including the three
table rows. Primorial examples check the primitive lower bound supplied by
the two residues $\pm1$. Separate order-two calculations display the
all-scalar saturation and the growing unit-dilation gain.
\end{enumerate}

These are finite consistency checks, not proofs of universally quantified
statements. The input size threshold is not claimed to be necessary, and the
small examples are not advertised as numerical instances saturating it.
The universal assertions rest on the preceding arguments.

\paragraph{Reproduction.}
From the package directory, run
\begin{verbatim}
python3 code/verify.py
latexmk -pdf -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error article.tex
\end{verbatim}
The verifier writes \texttt{data/verification.json}. A Makefile provides
\texttt{make check}, \texttt{make pdf}, and \texttt{make clean}.

\paragraph{Suggested mathematical declarations.}
A formal development could separate the proof into the following interfaces:

\begin{description}[style=nextline,leftmargin=1.2em]
\item[Primitive detector.]
Nonnegativity of $P_{m,L}$, the rational Ramanujan formula, the grid-sampling
inequality, and the elementary envelope $H_{\rm el}$.
\item[Weighted finite-ring count.]
The kernel cardinality \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:linearcount}, the exact divisor formula
\eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:kappa-formula}, and the rational upper bound $K_m$.
\item[Random restriction.]
A finite probability space of parameters and pointwise membership indicators,
with survival products indexed by the distinct support of each tuple.
\item[Objective extraction.]
The deterministic implication
$\eta G'-(1-\eta)Y'>0\Rightarrow G'\ge(1-\eta)(G'+Y')$,
and the finite averaging principle.
\item[Old-interface corollary.]
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:62:cor:polynomial8}, followed by the elementary comparison with
\eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:old}. The Rosser--Schoenfeld refinement is unnecessary for this step.
\end{description}

No untested Lean file is included. The mathematical statement is deliberately
separated from any future implementation decisions about Fourier transform
normalization, finite probability spaces, or totient lemmas.
The repository's existing proof and its status ledger are left unchanged.

\paragraph{What this does not propagate automatically.}
The original-domain Fourier spectrum is not asserted to be preserved by the
restriction. The weighted gcd computation concerns one balanced additive
relation, not the whole family of arrangement equations in later sections.
The proof therefore does not remove the need for the subsequent Bohr-set,
multifunction, or higher-order phase arguments. Obtaining a global
Szemer\'edi improvement would require explicit control through those
interfaces, not merely substituting one better local exponent.
