\section[{Further research questions\srctag{62}}]{Further research questions}\label{gsr:fz:62:sec:d12}
\srcnote{62}{Section 12}
\label{gsr:fz:62:sec:questions}

The following questions are specific continuations of the proved results.
They are not claims that the corresponding problems are open throughout the
literature; they identify the unresolved tasks in this development.

\begin{question}[Can a different detector eliminate the double logarithm?]
Find a bounded nonnegative restriction mechanism that, for every cyclic
modulus, gives retention $c_m\alpha^m\eta^{m-1}|B|^{m-1}$ with no
logarithmic denominator and a polynomial threshold. Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:62:thm:primitive-lower}
shows that a proof cannot obtain this merely by replacing the uniform bound
for the current primitive response by an absolute constant.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[The sharp weighted degeneracy constant]
Determine $\sup_{L\ge2}\kappa^*_{m,L}$.
The limit is known from Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:62:thm:kappa}, but at $m=16$ it is not
the answer. Computations for $2\le L\le40$ are consistent with a maximum
at $L=3$ for $m=16$; no such global maximum is proved here.
A proof should exploit the exact residue distribution in
\eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:resmax}, not substitute the limit for a uniform bound.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Matrix-valued weighted degeneracy]
Replace the single equation $\sigma\cdot x=0$ by the matrix of constraints
for a higher-dimensional Gowers arrangement. Develop a weighted Smith
normal form analogue of \eqref{gsr:en:62:eq:weighted-equations}, retaining coefficient
weights before estimating torsion indices. This is the most direct route
from the present method toward the later arrangement-selection lemmas.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Preserving the original Fourier data]
Can the restriction be chosen to satisfy a useful compatibility condition
with specified large Fourier coefficients of the original domain?
One target is a common frequency set for a family of restrictions, with
polynomial loss in both the number of prescribed coefficients and their
threshold. The current proof supplies no such compatibility theorem.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Noncyclic target groups]
For a general finite abelian target, replace primitive-unit averaging by a
family of characters that separates every nonzero defect without losing a
factor depending badly on the target rank. The difficulty is visible already
for an elementary abelian target: no single scalar-unit orbit reproduces the
primitive cyclic calculation.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Optimal density and accuracy exponents]
Determine whether the powers $\alpha^m\eta^{m-1}$ in the refined retention
bound are optimal under the sole hypothesis
$S_m(B,\phi)\ge\alpha|B|^{m-1}$. Separate an obstruction to the theorem
itself from an obstruction to one-stage Bernoulli filtering. In particular,
the primorial detector example does not answer this question.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Useful derandomization]
Develop an implementation of the conditional-expectation procedure whose
running time is controlled by the sparse input size rather than an exhaustive
list of all additive tuples and all unit dilations. A first concrete target
is fixed $m=4$ with a compressed difference table and exact arithmetic.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Formalization and downstream parameter accounting]
Formalize the elementary route first, then propagate its explicit constants
through a clearly identified downstream chain. The required output is a
new final theorem with its hypotheses and threshold, not a collection of
locally improved estimates. The exact weighted gcd identity is an especially
small and reusable first formalization target.
\end{question}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Conclusion\srctag{62}}]{Conclusion}\label{gsr:fz:62:sec:d13}
\srcnote{62}{Section 13}

The composite-modulus difficulty in the Fej\'er restriction argument has two
separate causes: low-order target defects and additional short domain
relations. Unit dilations address the first, while a weighted gcd count
addresses the second. Together they yield polynomial losses for arbitrary
cyclic moduli, including an explicit strengthening of the order-eight
restriction interface.

The analysis also produces exact arithmetic information that is not visible
in an unweighted exceptional-set bound: the maximal weighted error at each
filter length, its extremizing divisibility condition on the modulus, its
zeta-ratio limit, and a finite-length overshoot. These results delimit both
the strength and the limitations of the method. The next substantial step
is to extend the weighted arithmetic calculation to the arrangement systems
and spectral compatibility conditions used later in the proof.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Further research questions and a proposed program\srctag{63}}]{Further research questions and a proposed program}\label{gsr:fz:63:sec:d7}\label{gsr:fz:63:research:section}
\srcnote{63}{Section 7}

The two asymptotic problems now have exact first-order answers.
The next questions concern rates, extremizers, the efficiency of the
intermediate certificates, and propagation through the surrounding
argument. The questions below are deliberately separated from the
proved theorems. Each includes a concrete mathematical target and a
reason that the present proof does not already answer it.

\subsection{Extremal uniformity norms}

\begin{problem}[Exact constants at fixed order]\label{gsr:fz:63:research:fixed-order}
Determine $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}$ for one fixed $d\ge4$, beginning
with $d=4$. Is its supremum attained on a finite group, or only
approached along groups of unbounded order?
\end{problem}

The inspected reports give $c_3^{\mathrm{odd}}=1/\sqrt2$ and,
using the later fourth-order refinement,
\[
 0.5587725\ \le c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}
       \le(832/4795)^{1/4}=0.6454070\ldots
 \qquad\cite{repo63}.
\]
The lower decimal is a truncated lower estimate from the construction
recorded in the source collection.
Our uniform high-order proof sacrifices too much to compete at order
four. A useful approach is to retain the complete autocorrelation
moment expansion, including torsion relations, while adding the
pointwise doubling constraint from Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:63:bounded:doubling}.
Neither positive definiteness alone nor the single bound on the
largest Fourier coefficient captures all those restrictions.

\begin{problem}[The optimal rate of approach to one third]\label{gsr:fz:63:research:rate}
Determine the asymptotic size of $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}-1/3$.
Can the upper bound $O(2^{-d/8})$ be replaced by a matching
upper and lower asymptotic estimate?
\end{problem}

There are two distinct tasks. The finite parameter theorem can be
optimized by balancing the tail cutoff, smoothing width, and Bohr
set loss. That may improve an upper rate without revealing the true
one. Independently, a lower-bound family must compare $U^2$ with
$U^d$, rather than just with $L^\infty$. The circle square wave and
large odd cyclic approximations are natural test families: their
bounded $U^2$ value is known exactly, while the high-order cube
integral retains information discarded by the supremum-norm bound.
Estimating that integral as $d$ grows could distinguish an optimal
rate from an artifact of smoothing.

\begin{problem}[Equality and stability for the bounded inequality]
\label{gsr:fz:63:research:stability}
Classify equality and near-equality in
$\|f\|_{U^2}^4\le\|f\|_\infty^4/3$ on compact abelian groups
with surjective doubling, and in the finite-order correction on
each finite odd-order group.
\end{problem}

The compact circle square wave is an equality case; finite cyclic
square waves attain the order-dependent optimum. The defect identity
\eqref{gsr:cc:63:bounded:factoreddefect} gives an exact necessary condition on
autocorrelations. Turning it into structural information about $f$
requires controlling where its second factor is small and then
reconstructing a function from near-extremal correlations. A first
target is a quantitative theorem on the circle, with an explicit
distance and allowed symmetries. A separate target is to decide
which finite abelian groups attain the cyclic order-$N$ value.
The finite theorem alone does not identify those groups.

\begin{problem}[Dependence on group structure]\label{gsr:fz:63:research:group}
For a prescribed finite odd-order group $G$, determine
\[
 b(G)=\sup_{\substack{f:G\to\R,\ \E f=0\\ f\ne0}}
                 \frac{\|f\|_{U^2}^4}{\|f\|_\infty^4}.
\]
More generally, determine the limiting constants when the supremum
is restricted to groups of a fixed exponent or to a fixed family
of products.
\end{problem}

The fixed-group result in Section~\ref{gsr:cc:63:norm:section} shows that
$b(G)$ is exactly the limit of $c_d(G)$. This turns a question about
arbitrarily high cube order into a finite bounded optimization
problem. Cyclic groups are settled. Products of small odd cyclic
groups provide a tractable next test: they contain many Fourier
relations, and the cyclic sharpness construction need not transfer
with the same order-dependent value. Exact arithmetic and symmetry
reduction can guide conjectures, but a finite search must not be
substituted for a bound over all product dimensions.

\begin{problem}[Other reality and centering constraints]
\label{gsr:fz:63:research:constraints}
What are the analogous high-order constants for complex functions
with a prescribed phase symmetry, or for real functions with a
specified nonzero mean and range?
\end{problem}

The assumptions in the present theorem are substantial. A nontrivial
complex character is centered and has every $U^d$ norm equal to one,
so the unrestricted complex comparison constant is one. An
even-order group has a real character giving the same obstruction.
Meaningful extensions therefore need an explicit constraint that
excludes these examples. For nonzero mean, the doubling argument
still supplies information, but its average contains the extra
term $2(\E f)^2$ and sharpness may depend on torsion. Determining the
right constrained problem should precede optimization of its constants.

\subsection{Optimal positive covers and phase removal}

\begin{problem}[The exact positive-cover cost]\label{gsr:fz:63:research:cover}
For $B=[0,\ell]^k$ and $0<w\le\ell/2$, minimize $\mu(B)$ over
nonnegative measures supported on $B$ subject to
\[
 \int_B(w-\|a-c\|_1)_+^2\,d\mu(c)
                 \ge v_kw^{k+2}\qquad(a\in B).
\]
Is the face measure of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:63:loc:thm:face-cover} optimal
in any nontrivial regime?
\end{problem}

The convolution identity is exact at corners and has positive excess
at many other targets. That excess may permit a smaller or
nonconstant measure. A dual certificate would be especially useful:
find a positive measure $\lambda$ on target points for which
$\int K_w(a-c)\,d\lambda(a)\le1$ for every center $c$; integrating
the covering constraint then gives a lower bound for the required
mass. Symmetry reduces the number of parameters in small dimensions,
but a proposed optimum must satisfy the inequalities on the whole
box, including intersections of boundary layers.

\begin{problem}[The next term of the optimal local coefficient]
\label{gsr:fz:63:research:phase-next}
Determine whether
\[
 \lim_{k\to\infty}k\left(1-\frac{c_k^{\mathrm{loc}}}{v_k}\right)
\]
exists, and compute it if it does. In particular, is the optimal
relative deficit of order $1/k$, or is it $o(1/k)$?
\end{problem}

The proved certificate gives
$1/D_k=1-2/(3k)+14/(9k^2)+O(k^{-3})$ and therefore an upper
bound $2/3$ for a possible limiting deficit. The geometric ceiling
only gives its nonnegativity. These two facts do not identify a
second-order optimum. Even a better cover may leave slack in the
window Cauchy--Schwarz or mixed Gowers inequalities. A matching
upper example must be an admissible analytic input to phase removal,
not merely a difficult target for one chosen covering construction.

\begin{problem}[Exact local constants at small degree]
\label{gsr:fz:63:research:local-small}
Determine $c_k^{\mathrm{loc}}$ at $k=1$ or $k=2$ under the
normalization of \eqref{gsr:fp:63:loc:eq:quotient}.
\end{problem}

The new and previous covers agree at $k=1$, where the retained
fraction of the ceiling is $9/11$. They do not prove that this is
the optimal local coefficient. In small degree one can study the
phase and interval geometry directly, potentially bypassing one
of the general-purpose averaging steps. This would also test
whether optimizing positive covers is the correct route to the
analytic optimum or only to a better sufficient estimate.

\begin{problem}[Lattice corrections and simultaneous limits]
\label{gsr:fz:63:research:finite-local}
Improve the exact finite coefficient $R_{k,m,N}$, and determine
whether a different localization construction can attain the
geometric scale under a weaker relation between $m$ and $k$.
\end{problem}

The joint-limit corollary in Section~\ref{gsr:fp:63:loc:section} already
identifies the transition for the present certificate; in particular,
$m/k^2\to\infty$ suffices for $R_{k,m,N}/v_k\to1$.
Its proof balances the factors $m^k/(m-1)^k$ and
$(w/(L+1))^{k+2}$ quantitatively. A better construction could alter
that transition. Direct
lattice kernel sums, exact interval cube polynomials, and adjusted
endpoint weights may improve the finite estimate. This is a
concrete route toward stronger finite estimates suitable for use in
an iterated argument. The geometric upper estimate also needs
uniform control when the degree varies.

\begin{problem}[Other windows, boxes, and kernels]
\label{gsr:fz:63:research:geometry}
Extend the face identity to unequal side lengths, anisotropic
$\ell^1$ kernels, or other localization shapes, and determine
which extensions lead to an improved analytic localization theorem.
\end{problem}

The positive-power theorem already separates the geometric identity
from its square-kernel application. Unequal coordinate scales are
natural because a multilinear box need not have equal widths in
other settings. A geometric generalization is useful to the analytic
problem only when an appropriate window-count identity produces
its kernel. Thus both pieces should be proved together: a positive
cover with controlled mass, and an exact or lower-bounded window
multiplicity for the relevant configurations.

\subsection{Counting applications and proof infrastructure}

\begin{problem}[A joint density--uniformity expansion]
\label{gsr:fz:63:research:joint}
Determine the optimal cube-count upper envelope when the density
$\delta$, cube dimension $d$, and uniformity size
$u=\|f\|_{U^d}$ vary together.
\end{problem}

The quartic coefficient is now asymptotically sharp as a function
of $d$, but the remainder has combinatorial factors involving
$2^d$. Fixed-$d$ small-perturbation asymptotics alone do not describe
a regime in which $d$ also grows. A useful next theorem would specify
an explicit relation between $u/\delta$ and $d$ under which the
quartic term dominates the remainder, and then exploit the actual
fifth and higher coefficients instead of bounding all of them by
mixed Gowers--Cauchy--Schwarz. Characteristic-dependent dependencies
among cube vertices become relevant at those higher orders.

\begin{problem}[Propagation through the density-increment argument]
\label{gsr:fz:63:research:global}
Track the new local coefficient through the later induction in
Gowers' paper with explicit constants and every scale condition.
Which quantitative bottleneck becomes dominant after this replacement?
\end{problem}

The improvement from carry-pattern losses to factorial-size local
coefficients is substantial at that step. A final theorem about
progression-free sets also depends on the extraction of a
multilinear piece, transfer between progressions and cyclic groups,
the polynomial approximation step, and the length lost under
iteration. An honest propagation calculation must preserve those
dependencies. A useful deliverable would be a symbolic recurrence
with independently verified hypotheses at each transition, even
if the final asymptotic shape remains unchanged.

\begin{problem}[Formal verification of the new interfaces]
\label{gsr:fz:63:research:formal}
Formalize the bounded inequality, the exact face-cover identity,
and the finite parameter comparison theorem in the ProveIt
environment, preserving their stated normalizations and quantifiers.
\end{problem}

The bounded finite-group theorem is a suitable first target: it
uses a scalar inequality, translation invariance, bijectivity of
doubling, and a finite sum identity. The exact finite-order
correction adds a finite-dimensional extremal argument and a direct
cyclic calculation. The norm-limit theorem has a longer dependency
chain involving Fourier support, probability kernels, and Bohr
sets; the positive-cover interface additionally requires polynomial
polarization and mixed cube inequalities. Appendix~\ref{gsr:fz:63:audit:section}
suggests an order of integration so that the mathematical interfaces
can be checked before the asymptotic assembly.

Among these questions, the bounded equality problem, the optimal
cover in dimensions one and two, and explicit two-parameter
localization bounds appear to be the most direct next projects.
The exact fourth-order constant and the optimal high-order rate
require additional extremal ideas beyond the current proofs.

TeX manuscript contains the first 33 reports; later source reviews
and integration notes were inspected separately where they affect

an entry in the index is not by itself a proof of every associated
statement.

The specific baselines used here are as follows.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Gowers' Lemmas~3.8--3.10 supply mixed cube inequalities,
the norm triangle inequality, and the initial cube-count upper
estimate. His Proposition~17.7 supplies the local phase-removal
problem, with its derivative-energy input and cell-length scale.

quartic parallelogram coefficient, and Source~04 gives the sharp
odd-order comparison at $U^3$. We reuse those conclusions with
attribution and include the quartic proof for clarity.
\item Sources~28 and~29 contain earlier norm-comparison bounds;
Source~29 gives a central-binomial expression tending to $1/2$
and a lower construction tending to $1/3$. Source~29 is titled \emph{Further
Quantitative Refinements of Gowers's Szemer\'edi Argument: higher
norm comparisons, joint quadratic rigidity, and restriction by
affine rank}. The present uniform limit answers that source
collection's remaining endpoint question.
\item Sources~34, 35, and~45 contain later fourth-order bounds.
The comparison in this article uses the Source~45 coefficient
$4795/832$ for the sixteenth-power comparison, equivalently
$c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}\le(832/4795)^{1/4}$.
\item The separate 7~October~2026 manuscript
\emph{Local Phase Removal and Cubic Rigidity in Gowers'
Szemer\'edi Framework} \cite{localphase63} provides the
sliding-window and positive-cover interface and the denominator
$\widehat D_k$ used for comparison. Its underlying mechanism is
reproved in Section~\ref{gsr:fp:63:loc:section}; the dimension-dependent
face measure and exact positive identity are the improvement here.
\end{enumerate}

The archive's \texttt{SOURCE\_AUDIT.md} records Git blob identifiers,
file hashes, the separate predecessor's identity, and the normalization
choices. Original source files are referenced, not redistributed
with this contribution. The source comparisons are pinned to this

and report numbering.

A targeted primary-source literature check also inspected
Eisner--Tao on large Gowers--Host--Kra seminorms

inequalities for compact connected groups \cite{christiliopoulou}.

and interval models. Neither inspected statement supplies the
uniform-in-group high-order comparison proved here. This is a
description of the checked statements, not an exhaustive priority

\subsection{Supplementary computation and its limits}

The accompanying checks are designed to catch normalization,
factorial, aliasing, and boundary mistakes. The mathematical
theorems depend on their proofs, rather than on finite sampling.
The archive includes runnable scripts and their result files.

The principal norm proof and local face-cover argument were reviewed

\subsection{Suggested repository integration}

The TeX source is supplied as a single article, with its figures,
verification scripts, result data, and review notes. It can be
compiled independently with \texttt{latexmk -pdf}. The existing
paper transcription need not be edited to integrate this research
contribution. A suitable research index entry should list the
following claims separately:
\begin{enumerate}
\item the bounded centered $U^2$ inequality and sharp order-$N$
correction;
\item the group-uniform limit $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}\to1/3$, its
finite parameter bound, explicit rate, and fixed-group corollary;
\item the asymptotically sharp quartic cube coefficient, with
its retained higher-order remainder;
\item the exact positive-power face identity and lattice cover;
\item the finite localization coefficient and the asymptotic
optimality $c_k^{\mathrm{loc}}\sim v_k$.

For formalization, a useful dependency order is: scalar correlation
constraint; finite averaging and sharp cyclic example; Fourier-tail
lemma; positive smoothing; finite-spectrum recovery; uniform
comparison; continuous face identity; lattice interpolation;
sliding windows and polarization; local asymptotic assembly.
The finite parameter statements should be preserved as interfaces,
since they contain more directly reusable information than the
limits alone. No Lean declaration or proof-assistant certificate

The integration notes should mark the limiting norm question as
answered in the stated class, while retaining the fixed-order norm
questions, bounded equality classification, exact cover problem,
and second-order localization problem in the open-question list.
This avoids converting an asymptotic result into a stronger
fixed-parameter assertion during later consolidation.

\section[{Exact verification, implementation, and repository integration\srctag{64}}]{Exact verification, implementation, and repository integration}\label{gsr:fz:64:sec:d9}
\srcnote{64}{Section 9}
\label{gsr:fz:64:sec:verification}

\subsection{What the included computation checks}
The mathematical proofs do not depend on a search engine or an optimization
solver. The accompanying \repopath{verify.py} is a second line of defense against
normalization and transcription errors. It checks the sixty-four residues of
the seed, the inner partition modulo $16$, digit lifts through three layers,
small exact cyclic grids for the equal-arc and nine-copy lemmas, the two
rational slice constants, and the coefficient identities used in the
realization argument. It also checks the short counterexample to the two-arc
version and the valuation patterns in Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:64:cor:no-perfect}.

All finite assertions use integers or \repopath{fractions.Fraction}. Decimal
logarithms are used only for reporting the displayed exponents, not for deciding
injectivity, a modular equality, or a theorem hypothesis. The output
\repopath{certificate.json} records the seed images and the validation counts.
The computations do not certify that the seed is optimal among all alphabets,
or that a literature search is exhaustive.

\subsection{A membership algorithm with exact arithmetic}
The file \repopath{construction.py} implements digit alphabets and membership in
the final sets, given a finite input coloring. For a supplied coloring
$\phi:\{0,\ldots,N-1\}\to\{0,\ldots,r-1\}$, label set $S$, modulus $m$, and
rational width $\alpha=u/v$, membership of $n\in\Z/P\Z$ is decided as follows.
First compute
\[
 j=\floor{\frac{9Nn}{P}},\quad
 a=\floor{\frac{j}{3N}},\quad
 b=\floor{\frac{j-3aN}{3}},\quad c=j-3aN-3b.
\]
The color is $(3a+c)r+\phi(b)$. If its label is $z$ and
$y\equiv n^{k-2}\pmod P$ is in $\{0,\ldots,P-1\}$, the membership condition is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:64:eq:membership}
 0\le ym-zP,\qquad v(ym-zP)<u mP.
\end{equation}
Thus no floating-point evaluation of a torus phase is required.
The expensive large-scale input is the finite coloring, not this membership
test. The supplied implementation accepts that coloring as input; it does not
claim to make the enormous theoretical thresholds computationally practical.

\subsection{The formalization boundary}
The inspected repository file
\repopath{Combinatorics/Ramsey/Lean/GowersSzemeredi/Section04.lean}
represents the Section~4 conjectures as non-asserting proposition-valued
definitions. Its variable $k$ in \repopath{conjecture_4_2} corresponds to progression
length $k+2$; the present manuscript instead uses $k$ for the progression length.
The observed file blob is
\repopath{987daf1643df5bd45a9e9202a08fb2f7c579a103}.

No existing formal theorem is replaced, and no proof-status entry is upgraded
by this manuscript. A sensible first formalization target is the finite
$(1,5,10)$ seed, followed by the general digit-lifting theorem and the
all-moduli embedding estimate. These require only finite arithmetic and
induction. The valuation obstruction can be a separate algebraic module.
The circle transfer, Haar integrals, equidistribution and comparison with the
repository's degree-uniformity predicate form a genuinely larger analytic
chain. Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:64:cor:rational-density} supplies the exact-density step that such a
chain must not omit.

The recommended placement is a new research subdirectory, not the formal
proof ledger:
\begin{quote}\small
\repopath{Combinatorics/Ramsey/Research/GowersSzemeredi/}\\
\repopath{binomial-separation-six-progressions/}
\end{quote}
The accompanying \repopath{FORMALIZATION_PLAN.md} separates theorem statements,
finite certificates, external inputs and still-unformalized analytic interfaces.

\section[{Further research questions\srctag{64}}]{Further research questions}\label{gsr:fz:64:sec:d10}
\srcnote{64}{Section 10}
\label{gsr:fz:64:sec:questions}

\begin{question}[The six-binomial exponent]\label{gsr:fz:64:q:beta}
Is $\beta_6=3$? More quantitatively, do there exist $r$-element
$(1,5,10)$-separating sets in integer intervals of length $r^{3+o(1)}$?
\end{question}
The gap is now between $3$ and $\log_4 80$ within the comparisons made here.
The cyclic perfect-code obstruction means that searching for one exact
$r$-symbol, $r^3$-modulus seed cannot answer this question. Increasing-block,
nonstationary, algebraic or genuinely nondigital constructions are natural
alternatives.

\begin{question}[Optimal order and the endpoint eight]
Is there a constant $C$ such that every $r$ admits an $r$-element
mirror-separating six-binomial set modulo some $m\le Cr^3$?
\end{question}
This is stronger than $\beta_6=3$ and would give
$\rho_6(\alpha)\ll\alpha^8$ by Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:64:thm:endpoint} without changing the coloring
input. The distinction between an exponent statement and a uniform constant
is essential at an endpoint.

\begin{question}[Cyclic capacity without perfect tilings]
What is
\[
 \sup\left\{\frac{\log|D|}{\log B}:
 D\subseteq\Z/B\Z\text{ is $(1,5,10)$-separating},\ |D|>1\right\}?
\]
Does it equal $1/3$, although the supremum is never attained by a perfect seed?
\end{question}
A productive finite search should output verifiable certificates and separate
completed searches from time-limited failures. The valuation covering argument
may help derive quantitative packing losses, but the present theorem only
rules out equality.

\begin{question}[Improving the coloring rather than the labels]
Can symmetric six-progression-free colorings use $O(N^\gamma)$ colors for
some $\gamma<1/9$? Can the four-term exponent $1/4$ be improved?
\end{question}
The exact scalar degree barrier shows where a direct replacement of the
norm polynomial cannot work. A different degree regime, a nonlinear
nonpolynomial map, or a multi-stage construction may escape it. Improving the
coloring dimension directly improves the $d/b$ term in the endpoint theorem.

\begin{question}[Beyond a fixed power]
Does $\rho_4(\alpha)$, or $\rho_6(\alpha)$, decay faster than every fixed power
of $\alpha$?
\end{question}
These are the superpolynomial-decay questions in the Ruzsa/DTZ program.
Neither endpoint proved here resolves them. An endpoint power is a useful
quantitative refinement but should not be confused with the full decay
conjecture.

\begin{question}[Other coefficient patterns]
For which even lengths, or other symmetric point patterns, do the relevant
positive coefficients admit small mirror-separating alphabets? What is the
right replacement when non-mirror trivial partitions are unavoidable?
\end{question}
The general CRT theorem supplies one family. At lengths with subset-sum
collisions among the half-binomial coefficients, one must either control all
allowed partition types geometrically or replace mirror separation by a
more nuanced label condition.

\begin{question}[Quantitative analytic realization]
Can one turn the prime-modulus proof into practical bounds
$P_0(\alpha,\eta,k)$ for a prescribed centered uniformity error $\eta$ and
progression-count error?
\end{question}
The complete-sum estimate is explicit, but a full bound must also track the
Fourier approximation to a rectangle union whose complexity depends on the
chosen coloring and labels. Optimizing only the complete-sum exponent would
not address that entire cost.

\begin{question}[Optimal transfer and formal verification]
Can a different circle lift improve on nine palette copies while retaining
an exact or comparably strong progression measure? Can the full six-variable
chain, including rational-density correction, be formally checked?
\end{question}
The three-arc obstruction applies only to the particular auxiliary lemma.
It is not an optimality theorem for all lifts. Formalizing the seed and the
induction first would make future changes in alphabets inexpensive to certify;
formalizing the analytic transfer would then turn quantitative input
improvements into reusable theorems.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Conclusion\srctag{64}}]{Conclusion}\label{gsr:fz:64:sec:d11}
\srcnote{64}{Section 11}
The research yields a concrete change in two quantitative resources: the
six-variable label exponent drops from the generic $5$ to $\log_4 80$, and the
coloring-to-torus step can be made exact for mirror separation, with only nine
palette copies. Keeping the prime family scale-uniform then gives
$\rho_4(\alpha)\ll\alpha^5$ and
$\rho_6(\alpha)\ll\alpha^{7.847232636916081\ldots}$ without an epsilon loss.
The proofs also identify two precise boundaries: perfect cyclic digit
alphabets cannot reach exponent $3$ for the six-binomial weights, and a single
polynomial color of degree at most $k-1$ cannot exceed dimension $k^2/4$.
These boundaries guide, rather than close, the next stage of the program.

\section[{Explicit certificates and finite verification\srctag{65}}]{Explicit certificates and finite verification}\label{gsr:fz:65:sec:d9}\label{gsr:fz:65:bsi:sec:verification}
\srcnote{65}{Section 9}

\subsection{A coefficient-level reconstruction algorithm}
The algorithm in the accompanying code uses no sampling of $f$ to
recognize an obstruction. It starts with the symmetric basis coefficients
of $T$. There are $\binom{n+d-1}{d}$ such bits, indexed by multisets of
$d$ basis indices. For $d\ge4$ form a binary matrix $D_T$ with $n$
columns. Its rows are indexed by $i<j$ and multisets
$\mathbf a$ of $d-4$ basis indices, and its entries are
\begin{equation}
 (D_T)_{(i,j,\mathbf a),k}
   =T(e_i,e_i,e_j,e_k,e_{\mathbf a})
      +T(e_i,e_j,e_j,e_k,e_{\mathbf a}).
 \label{gsr:fz:65:bsi:eq:matrix}
\end{equation}
For $d=4$ the multiset is empty. Because the defect is alternating in
its first pair and symmetric multilinear in its frozen slots, these
coordinates determine its first-slot linear map completely. Thus
\begin{equation}
 K_T=\ker D_T,\qquad r(T)=\rk D_T.
 \label{gsr:fz:65:bsi:eq:matrix-kernel}
\end{equation}
There are
$R=\binom n2\binom{n+d-5}{d-4}$ rows. Elementary row elimination uses
$O(Rn^2)$ bit operations in the elementary unbatched model; this is a
polynomial in the displayed matrix dimensions, not a polynomial in a
compressed circuit representation of $T$.

If the rank is zero, the support coefficients $c_A$ and
\eqref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:primitive} give a primitive of $T$. If the rank is one,
let $u$ be the unique nonzero row of the row space. Choose a basis vector
$e_c$ with $u(e_c)=1$ and compute
\begin{equation}
 \Omega(a,b)=\Phi_T(e_c,\ldots,e_c)(a,b),\qquad
 v(x)=\Omega(x,e_c),\qquad S=T-C_d^{u,v}.
 \label{gsr:fz:65:bsi:eq:reconstruct}
\end{equation}
Canonical recognition proves that $u,v$ are independent and $S$ is
integrable. The algorithm checks the latter conclusion independently by
verifying that each basis coefficient of $S$ depends only on its support.
Formula~\eqref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:primitive} then specifies a primitive of $S$ from
those support coefficients. A rank at least two gives the noncanonical
energy cap without solving any continuous optimization problem.

The formulas specify the recovery algorithm mathematically. The supplied
Python function \gitpath{recover} returns $u,v,S$; the primitive regression
routine checks the support-to-polynomial formula, rather than furnishing
a polished symbolic pretty-printer.

\subsection{Exact census and analytic regression checks}
The verifier \gitpath{code/verify.py} uses the Python standard library.
It performs integer, binary-field, rational, and Gaussian-rational
arithmetic only. It contains no numerical optimizer and no reliance on
Python assertions that disappear under optimization.

The executed tensor census contains $38\,044$ cases: all symmetric
binary tensors in degrees $3$ through $10$; all symmetric trilinear and
quartic tensors in dimension three; and $172$ seeded higher-dimensional
or higher-degree cases, including explicit canonical tensors. For every
applicable tensor, the checker compares independently computed notions:
defect rank, integration by support coefficients, and the exact number
of integrable contractions. Every radical-codimension-one case is
reconstructed as canonical plus an integrable residual.

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}rrrrrr@{}}
\toprule
$n$ & $d$ & All tensors & Integrable & Canonical endpoint & Noncanonical\\
\midrule
2&3&16&8&8&0\\
2&4&32&8&24&0\\
2&5&64&8&24&32\\
2&6&128&8&24&96\\
2&7&256&8&24&224\\
2&8&512&8&24&480\\
2&9&1024&8&24&992\\
2&10&2048&8&24&2016\\
3&3&1024&128&896&0\\
3&4&32768&128&2688&29952\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
For the last row, the noncanonical tensors split into $19\,712$ with
$r(T)=2$ and $10\,240$ with $r(T)=3$. These exact counts agree with the
class-count formula independently of energy optimization.

A contraction dynamic program also computes the exact energy at $f=1$
for each tensor. Its maximum over nonintegrable tensors matches $b_d$
in every exhaustive family, and each computed value lies below the
relevant radical-sensitive cap. This is a check on the theorem and its
sharpness examples, not a computation of $\M(T)$ for every tensor.

There are also $34$ tests on exact Gaussian-rational functions, including
zeros and non-unit amplitudes, checking energy bounds and exact slicing.
Four independently accumulated labelled-cube averages are compared with
selected Fourier-square averages. Another $360$ checks verify derivative
conjugation periods, and $18$ test the constrained pure-tensor lemma.
The primitive formula is checked on $480$ direction tuples at all base
points, with the next derivative checked in each case, in dimensions
one through three and degrees two through six. Finally both induction
recurrences are verified as rational identities through degree $1000$.

\subsection{What verification does not mean}
The finite computations cannot establish an inequality for every complex
function or every dimension. The full proofs above establish those
claims. Neither a finite phase grid nor the constant-function census is
substituted for the continuous upper-bound argument. The code is not a
Lean formalization, and the manuscript has not undergone independent
refereeing. The proposed formalization plan does not change any checked
statement count or theorem-status ledger in the repository.

\section[{Relation to Gowers's argument and the formal interfaces\srctag{65}}]{Relation to Gowers's argument and the formal interfaces}\label{gsr:fz:65:sec:d10}
\srcnote{65}{Section 10}
\label{gsr:fz:65:bsi:sec:gowers}

\subsection{The precise phase-removal connection}
The relevant stage of Gowers's paper is Section~17, especially
Lemma~17.1 and Proposition~17.2~\cite{gowers}. That stage converts
structured derivative frequencies into polynomial phase information.
The present result is a characteristic-two counterpart for a supplied,
fully symmetric homogeneous tensor, where factorial division does not
supply a primitive. It quantifies precisely the high-energy obstruction
to integration rather than assuming symmetry suffices.

In the formal statement inspected at repository snapshot \pinsixtyfive,
\gitpath{Sections17_18.lean} makes a prime cyclic modulus and
invertibility of $(k+1)!$ explicit in \gitpath{proposition_17_2}; it
records degree at most $k+1$ for the phase, correcting the printed degree.
The selected-frequency normalization here corresponds to $d=k+1$:
divide its unnormalized Fourier-square sum by $|V|^{d+1}$.
One must additionally reconcile the direction/conjugation convention:
the repository uses $f(s)\overline{f(s-a)}$, while this article uses
$f(x+h)\overline{f(x)}$. On a Boolean group these differ by conjugation
at each differentiation; the selected squared Fourier magnitudes at
Boolean characters agree. This is an interface check, not a silent
identification of the ambient groups.

\subsection{Three limitations that matter mathematically}
First, the result concerns $\Ftwo^n$, not arbitrary cyclic groups, Bohr
neighborhoods, or progression cells. Translation invariance of the full
uniform measure is used in the Fourier cancellations and slicing.
Second, the primitive is circle-valued and can have genuine dyadic depth;
it is not required to be a classical polynomial over the base field.
Third, the sharp bound assumes a supplied fully symmetric tensor. It does
not symmetrize arbitrary multilinear data, handle unrestricted mixed
vertex functions, or produce a selector at low energy.

The inspected \gitpath{Definitions.lean} defines \gitpath{IsMultilinear}
using all square-free monomials, including the constant term. In standard
terminology this is multiaffine, unlike the homogeneous tensor convention
used here. Removing those extra terms would require a separate argument.
Thus the theorem is not presented as a drop-in replacement under
identical hypotheses for the prime-cyclic proposition.

An improved quantitative Szemer\'edi estimate would require a complete
selector-construction and localization argument, followed by all
remaining density-increment losses. No such global estimate is inferred
from the local extremal theorem.

\section[{Further research questions\srctag{65}}]{Further research questions}\label{gsr:fz:65:sec:d11}\label{gsr:fz:65:bsi:sec:questions}
\srcnote{65}{Section 11}
These questions follow the proved results. The septic threshold,
all-degree universal value, and endpoint tensor classification are no
longer listed as open questions within this manuscript.

\begin{problem}[The second extremal value]\label{gsr:fz:65:bsi:q:second}
For fixed $d\ge4$ and $n$, determine the maximum of $\M(T)$ over the
noncanonical, nonintegrable tensors, when that family is nonempty.
Is the cap $1-3d/2^{d+1}$ ever attained? Which extra loss is forced because
optimal contraction functions must all arise as derivatives of one
common function? The retained profile \eqref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:profile-gap} is a
first computable refinement, not a solution of this optimization problem.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Rank-sensitive extremizers]\label{gsr:fz:65:bsi:q:rank}
Determine the exact extremum when the defect radical has prescribed
codimension $r\ge2$. Is the distribution of further contraction radical
ranks enough to determine it, or do tensors with identical contraction
profiles have different maxima? Constructing such a pair would locate a
precise limitation of profile-only arguments.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Maximizing functions and phase stability]\label{gsr:fz:65:bsi:q:phases}
Classify all $f$ with $\En_{C_d}(f)=b_d$ and all near-extremizers modulo
natural phase symmetries. The tensor classification and
\eqref{gsr:fp:65:bsi:eq:amplitude} do not reconstruct phases. Can the canonical
slice-deficit conditions yield a dimension-independent distance estimate
to a fully described extremizer family? Any proposed uniqueness statement
must allow multiplication by phases with zero $d$th derivative.
\end{problem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Answered for $d\ge4$} by source~97 (Theorems~\ref{gsr:fp:97:thm:classification}, \ref{gsr:fp:97:thm:stability}, Section~\ref{gsr:fp:sec:boolendpoint}): every maximizer of the canonical tensor is $e(P+\theta|u|)$ with $\deg P\le d-1$, and the stability is dimension-free with the optimal leading coefficient $2/m_d$; the cubic case is open.
\end{writenote}

\begin{problem}[Inactive coordinates outside the canonical class]
\label{gsr:fz:65:bsi:q:inactive}
For which tensors $T_0$ does a surjection $q:V\to V_0$ satisfy
$\M(q^*T_0)=\M(T_0)$? The canonical case holds in all degrees, and the
cubic rank law gives it for every cubic tensor. The noncanonical
higher-degree problem remains. A tensor's dependence on few coordinates
alone does not constrain an arbitrary optimizing function to those
coordinates.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Direct sums and compatible slice optimization]
\label{gsr:fz:65:bsi:q:sum}
Determine whether maxima multiply under direct sums of canonical tensors
in degrees at least four. Product functions give the lower bound, while
the cubic law proves equality in degree three. Can non-product functions
improve the energy in higher degrees? More generally, characterize when
the upper bound in exact-slicing relaxations is attainable by one function.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Odd characteristic]\label{gsr:fz:65:bsi:q:odd}
Develop an analogue of the integrable-contraction radical for the
$p$-repetition defect in characteristic $p>2$. Does a minimal-radical
classification isolate the exceptional obstruction family and let an
all-degree induction close? The Boolean derivative-period lemma is not
valid unchanged in odd characteristic, so both the canonical family and
its constrained energy must be rederived.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Local measures and boundary errors]\label{gsr:fz:65:bsi:q:local}
Quantify the slice and Fourier-period errors for weighted averages,
Bohr neighborhoods, and progression cells. What translation-invariance
hypotheses preserve a useful version of the rigidity gap $\gamma_d$?
A successful local theorem must compare boundary losses with an
exponentially small degree-dependent margin rather than hide them in an
unspecified error term.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Multiaffine and incompletely symmetric selectors]
\label{gsr:fz:65:bsi:q:affine}
Give a quantitative reduction from the repository's multiaffine selector
interface to genuinely homogeneous symmetric tensors without discarding
lower-order terms or silently changing the energy. At which cost can the
sharp certificate here be inserted after such a reduction? This question
is distinct from certifying a tensor already known to be symmetric.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Certified reconstruction and formal proof]\label{gsr:fz:65:bsi:q:formal}
Implement the matrix certificate, primitive construction, and endpoint
recognition in Lean, then formalize the cubic Hilbert-space estimate and
the all-degree induction. Can a small verified checker accept explicit
row-reduction and phase certificates independently of the search
procedure that found them? The input representation and the distinction
between a proved theorem and a proposition-valued catalogue entry should
remain explicit throughout.
\end{problem}

\section[{Conclusion\srctag{65}}]{Conclusion}\label{gsr:fz:65:sec:d12}
\srcnote{65}{Section 12}
The universal extremal problem is governed by the same canonical
obstruction in every degree. The missing ingredient was not another
higher-order support census: it was the exact identification of the
integrable slice set with a linear radical. Codimension one gives the
canonical family, and larger codimension forces a strict loss under
slicing. This closes the universal induction and excludes every
noncanonical endpoint.

The resulting theorem is sharp over all bounded complex functions and
all finite Boolean dimensions. Its geometric consequences are also
exact: endpoint tensors are classified modulo integration, their classes
are counted, and all maximal integrable restrictions are identified.
The remaining work lies in phase stability, noncanonical optimization,
and the localization and selector interfaces needed for broader
quantitative applications.

\section[{A small explicit certificate\srctag{65}}]{A small explicit certificate}\label{gsr:fz:65:sec:dA}\label{gsr:fz:65:bsi:app:example}
\srcnote{65}{Appendix A}
In dimension two, let $u(x)=x_1$, $v(x)=x_2$. For the quintic $C_5^{u,v}$,
the symmetric basis coefficients, listed by the number of occurrences of
$e_2$ from zero through five, are
\[
 (0,1,0,0,0,0).
\]
The defect is $u\otimes u$ in its two frozen slots, multiplied by
$u\wedge v$. The first-slot matrix has row space spanned by $u$, so
$r(C_5)=1$ and its maximum is $13/16$. Changing the tensor by any of the
eight integrable binary quintics leaves its maximum unchanged.

For contrast take $T=C_5^{u,v}+C_5^{v,u}$, with coefficients
\[
 (0,1,0,0,1,0).
\]
Its defect is $(u\otimes u+v\otimes v)(u\wedge v)$, whose first-slot
radical is zero in dimension two. Thus $r(T)=2$. Exactly one quarter of
its contractions are integrable and its energy is at most $49/64$ for
every bounded complex function. In particular it cannot attain the
universal endpoint $13/16$. The assertion follows from the general
proof, not from checking a finite collection of phases.

\section[{Exact recovery algorithms and reproducibility\srctag{66}}]{Exact recovery algorithms and reproducibility}\label{gsr:fz:66:sec:d12}
\srcnote{66}{Section 12}
\label{gsr:fz:66:epnf:sec:algorithms}

\subsection{Recovering a partition from exact input}
For a positive ordered set $C$ represented by exact rational numbers,
the following procedure returns the normal form whenever its hypotheses
hold.  First compute $\sigma(C)$ by testing each positive difference
against the set, and put $r=\sigma(C)$.  If $r=0$, return the arithmetic
progression.  If $n\ge3r+1$, divide every point by $c_1$ and form
\[
 \lambda_i=c_i/c_1-i.
\]
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:partition} guarantees that these are nonnegative,
nondecreasing integers with total $r$.  No rational approximation,
integer-relation heuristic, or tolerance test is needed.  For a general
exact ordered field, the same procedure is valid provided its ordering,
arithmetic, and equality operations are available.

For an endpoint set $A$, use $d=\max A-\max(A\setminus\{\max A\})$,
translate its minimum to zero, and divide by $d$.  Under the theorem's
hypothesis all coordinates become integers, the missing positions give
$H$, and \eqref{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:weight} verifies the certificate.  The output includes
both a structural certificate and an exact value of the energy via
\eqref{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:holeenergy}.  The theorem does not require enumeration of all
partitions in order to recover the particular input's partition.

With constant-time exact arithmetic and hashing as an abstract cost
model, the direct defect computation takes $O(n^2)$ membership tests
and $O(n)$ storage for the set.  Rational bit complexity also includes
the cost of exact arithmetic on the input numerators and denominators.
Without hashing, binary search in the sorted set gives
$O(n^2\log n)$ comparisons.  Enumerating all admissible templates takes
$p(r)$ outputs, and its cost is independent of the ambient coordinate
sizes except for writing the templates.

For the four-level energy test, compute the difference multiplicities,
obtain $\Erm(A)$, and compare it to the exact integer threshold.  If the
threshold holds, the sorted set can be compared against the eight
normalized templates.  A hypothetical discrepancy is a failed theorem
certificate, not something the algorithm should conceal by rounding.

\subsection{What the supplied program checks}
The file \texttt{code/verify.py} is a dependency-free Python program
using integers and exact rational arithmetic.  Its assertions remain
active under Python's optimized execution mode because failures are
raised explicitly.  Its default finite checks are as follows.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{p{0.72\linewidth}r}
\toprule
Exact finite test family & Instances\\
\midrule
All nonempty $C\subset\intr{1}{16}$; Schur defect and applicable
normal-form conclusions & 65,535\\
All $A\subset\intr{0}{16}$ containing zero with $|A|\ge2$;
energy identities, recurrences, applicable gap and equality tests & 65,535\\
Partition templates of weights $1\le r\le12$ & 271\\
Boundary-hole energy identities at three interval lengths per template & 813\\
Explicit threshold obstructions, $1\le r\le40$ & 40\\
Eight energy models, $5\le m\le70$ & 528\\
Exact rational sets from a fixed deterministic seed & 700\\
Rationally dilated partition models, $1\le r\le8$ & 66\\
Rank-one embeddings of the eight models in $\Z^3$ & 112\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Reproduced checks in the accompanying archive.  The exhaustive
boxes are finite and do not certify the theorems beyond those boxes.}
\label{gsr:fz:66:epnf:tab:checks}
\end{table}

Among the 65,535 positive sets, 108 satisfy the proved normal-form
criterion, including zero-defect cases.  Among the endpoint sets, 58
satisfy the positive-defect envelope criterion.  These smaller numbers
are reported to distinguish the number of inputs examined from the
number lying in the narrow theorem hypotheses.  The recorded output
contains no counterexample to any proved statement.

The program also tests the conjectural threshold $n\ge2r+2$ on the
same finite positive-set box.  There are 103 applicable positive-defect
instances and no counterexample in that box.  This diagnostic is
explicitly separated from the proved theorem, and does not justify
replacing the theorem's cutoff in an application.

The file \texttt{data/partition\_spectrum.csv} contains every boundary
hole set of weight at most 12 and its exact $\kappa$ value.
\texttt{data/verification.json} records parameters and counts, and
\texttt{data/verification.log} gives the human-readable run summary.
The formulas are proved before these computations are described;
none of the proofs relies on a floating-point calculation or a finite
search standing in for an infinite argument.

\section[{Further research questions\srctag{66}}]{Further research questions}\label{gsr:fz:66:sec:d13}
\srcnote{66}{Section 13}
\label{gsr:fz:66:epnf:sec:questions}

The questions below are ordered approximately by their proximity to the
proved mechanisms.  They are not claims that a global inverse theorem
or a Ramsey bound has already been improved.

\begin{conjecture}[The optimal Schur threshold]\label{gsr:fz:66:epnf:conj:threshold}
For every integer $r\ge1$, Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:partition} remains valid
under $n\ge2r+2$.
\end{conjecture}
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:prop:obstruction} would make this threshold optimal.
The current proof obtains an initial arithmetic block of length
$n-2r$ and requires this block to exceed the entire defect budget.
An improvement must exploit the cost of the tail more efficiently,
rather than simply repeating that comparison.  The first task is to
classify the possible cancellations from sums of two missing points.

\begin{question}[Critical-size exceptional families]\label{gsr:fz:66:epnf:q:critical}
Classify all positive sets with $n=2r+1$ and defect $r$ that are not
partition normal forms.  Is the central-hole family of
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:prop:obstruction} the only large-$r$ mechanism up to
positive dilation, or can several interacting holes realize the same
critical ratio?
\end{question}
This question asks for an equality theory at the obstruction threshold,
not just an improved sufficient bound.

\begin{conjecture}[The second boundary-energy constant]\label{gsr:fz:66:epnf:conj:secondkappa}
For $r\ge3$, among hole sets of weight $r$ other than $\{r\}$,
\[
 \max\kappa(H)=r^2-2r+4,
\]
with equality only for $H=\{1,r\}$.
\end{conjecture}
The displayed candidate has that value by direct substitution into
\eqref{gsr:en:66:epnf:eq:kappadef}.  The partition data through weight 12 satisfy the
conjecture.  A proof would give the next sharp endpoint-energy gap at
every defect, extending the all-$r$ envelope beyond its first equality
case.  The crude bound $\kappa\le r\max H$ is not enough: it loses the
interaction between the number of holes and the pair-overlap term.

\begin{question}[The weighted partition spectrum]\label{gsr:fz:66:epnf:q:spectrum}
Determine the bivariate generating function, or a useful recurrence,
for
\[
 F(z,w)=\sum_{H\subset\Z_{>0}\ \mathrm{finite}}
       z^{\wtop(H)}w^{\kappa(H)}.
\]
Which distinct partitions have the same $\kappa$?  Can the number of
energy values at fixed weight be bounded substantially below $p(r)$?
\end{question}
The two weight-four examples in Table~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:tab:kappa} show that
injectivity already fails at low weight.  A useful recurrence would
separate those combinatorial coincidences from accidental equalities
between energies at different weights and cardinalities.

\begin{question}[The fifth and later global energy levels]\label{gsr:fz:66:epnf:q:fifth}
Find the fifth largest energy, with all equality cases, for sufficiently
large $m$, and then develop a systematic method for any fixed number of
levels.  The one-hole model $\intr{0}{m}\setminus\{3\}$ has
$\Drm=3m-12$, suggesting a next scale, but this alone supplies no lower
bound for arbitrary sets outside the first four levels.
\end{question}
The successful third- and fourth-level proofs distinguish arithmetic,
second-level, and other prefixes, then reduce the last case to a small
endpoint budget.  A general method will require a controlled list of
prefix types with holes near \emph{both} endpoints.  New mixed-end
models should be expected; the class $C_m$ is the first warning.

\begin{question}[A full inverse theorem at linear total defect]\label{gsr:fz:66:epnf:q:linear}
For fixed $K$, does $\Drm(A)\le K|A|$ force, for sufficiently large
$|A|$, a bounded-hole one-dimensional description of all but a bounded
number of points, with constants depending only on $K$?  Can a stronger
whole-set statement hold after listing a finite family of exceptional
endpoint patterns?
\end{question}
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:thm:partition} has a small \emph{local} defect assumption,
whereas this question controls the sum of local defects.  Bridging that
quantifier difference is the main obstacle.  An arbitrary low-defect
prefix cannot be selected without controlling how the omitted endpoints
interact with it.

\begin{question}[Robustness to perturbed relations]\label{gsr:fz:66:epnf:q:robust}
Develop a quantitative analogue when additive equalities are known only
up to an error tolerance, or when a small proportion of their labels
are corrupted.  What separation assumptions on the real set are
necessary to recover a nearby arithmetic template?
\end{question}
Exact order and exact reflection are decisive in
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:lem:twozeros}.  In a metric version, accumulated reflection
errors may be amplified by a long successor chain.  A useful result
must specify both an additive error scale and an arithmetic separation
scale; an unspecified ``approximately equal'' version would be false
or vacuous after rescaling.

\begin{question}[Weighted and multiplicity-sensitive extensions]\label{gsr:fz:66:epnf:q:weighted}
Can the reflection method yield an exact or stable classification for
nonnegative weights, or for multisets, near the corresponding energy
maximum?  Is there a weighted substitute for the partition budget that
retains sharp endpoint information?
\end{question}
The current partition count uses integrality of each failed pair and
strict ordering of distinct points.  Those are not cosmetic features:
weights can split a unit defect continuously, and multiplicities change
the maximum itself.

\begin{question}[Rectification of near-extremal cyclic graphs]\label{gsr:fz:66:epnf:q:rectification}
Identify hypotheses under which a cyclic graph of very high selected
energy admits a torsion-free lift with the same additive quadruples,
and track the resulting losses explicitly.  Can the affine conclusion
of Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:cor:graphs} then replace a more expensive local inverse
step in a restricted branch of Gowers's argument?
\end{question}
Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:prop:nowrap} is a sufficient interface, not a way to
produce the needed short lift.  Subgroup examples rule out a universal
transfer with no additional assumptions.

\begin{question}[Formal certification and effective template generation]\label{gsr:fz:66:epnf:q:formal}
Formalize the all-$r$ normal form and the four-level classification,
then implement a verified certificate generator returning the partition
or a failed hypothesis.  Can the finite template recursion from
Question~\ref{gsr:fz:66:epnf:q:fifth} be made proof-producing rather than merely
experimental?
\end{question}
The reflection lemma, the no-two-holes count, and the finite prefix
case splits are natural modular targets.  A formalization should prove
the integer-valued defect identity before using integrality to exclude
an intermediate energy level.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Conclusions\srctag{66}}]{Conclusions}\label{gsr:fz:66:sec:d14}
\srcnote{66}{Section 14}
The ordered-energy maximum used in Gowers's Section~7 admits a discrete
refinement with a particularly rigid local structure.  Once the final
Schur defect is smaller than a fixed fraction of the set size, all
possible configurations are indexed by integer partitions.  Their
energy is explicitly computable from boundary holes, and the best
energy at each endpoint defect has a unique one-hole normal form.
The low-defect instances complete two equality analyses beyond the
second energy level and yield full-set recovery in the first-four-level
window.

These conclusions are exact finite theorems, not asymptotic guesses.
Their limits are equally specific: the sufficient Schur threshold is
not proved optimal; the global fifth level is not determined; the
linear-defect inverse problem is not solved; and the passage to the
cyclic graphs and density iterations in the general Szemer\'edi proof
requires additional work.  The partition theorem and the explicit
energy constants give concrete tools with which to pursue those next
steps.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The relation of the first gap to inverse Pollard theory\srctag{66}}]{The relation of the first gap to inverse Pollard theory}\label{gsr:fz:66:sec:dA}
\srcnote{66}{Appendix A}
\label{gsr:fz:66:epnf:app:pollard}
This appendix is an attribution check, not an input to any proof above.
For a finite integer set $A$ of size $m$, let
\[
 r_A(t)=\#\{(a,b)\in A^2:a-b=t\},\qquad
 S_j(A)=\sum_t\min(j,r_A(t)).
\]
Embedding the finite set in a sufficiently large prime cyclic group
avoids all wraparound.  Pollard's inequality gives
\[
 S_j(A)\ge j(2m-j).
\]
For a non-arithmetic-progression set, the equality classification of
Nazarewicz, O'Brien, O'Neill and Staples
\cite[Theorem~3]{pollardequality}, together with the $j=1$ equality
case recalled there, makes this inequality strict for
$1\le j\le m-2$.  The exceptional alternative involving sets of size
$j+1$ is excluded by $j\le m-2$, and the large-modulus alternatives
are excluded by choosing the prime sufficiently large.

Since $r_A(t)=r_A(-t)$ and $r_A(0)=m$, one has
$S_j(A)\equiv j\pmod2$.  The arithmetic-progression value
$j(2m-j)$ has the same parity.  Strictness therefore gains at least
two for every $1\le j\le m-2$.
The scalar identity, valid for $0\le u\le m$,
\[
 u^2=(2m-1)u-2\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}\min(j,u),
\]
yields
\[
 \Erm(A)=(2m-1)m^2-2\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}S_j(A).
\]
Comparison with an arithmetic progression gives
\[
 \Erm(A)\le M_m-4(m-2).
\]
Thus the first gap is already encoded in published inverse Pollard
theory.  Its elementary proof in Section~\ref{gsr:en:66:epnf:sec:knownlevels} should
not be described as a new extremal inequality.

For a finite subset of a torsion-free abelian group, this particular
attribution argument can first use a Freiman $2$-isomorphism to the
integers: identify its generated subgroup with $\Z^d$, and choose an
integer linear functional nonzero on every nonzero vector in the
finite set $2A-2A$.  Such a functional exists because finitely many
proper rational hyperplanes cannot cover $\Z^d$.  This preserves all
quadruple relations.  It is a finite-set construction, not an injective
group homomorphism from $\Z^d$ to $\Z$ when $d>1$.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Proof dependencies and formalization plan\srctag{66}}]{Proof dependencies and formalization plan}\label{gsr:fz:66:sec:dB}
\srcnote{66}{Appendix B}
\label{gsr:fz:66:epnf:app:formalization}
The article can be formalized independently of analytic uniformity
norms.  A suitable new namespace is
\texttt{GowersSzemeredi.OrderedEnergy}; this is a proposal, not a claim
that such a module already exists in the repository.

The main dependency chain is
\[
\begin{gathered}
\text{endpoint energy recurrence}
\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{ordered-defect identity},\\
\text{two zero defects}
\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{long initial arithmetic block}
\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{partition normal form},\\
\text{partition normal form}
\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{boundary-hole models}
\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{sharp endpoint envelope},\\
\text{defects }0,1,2,3\text{ and prefix case splits}
\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{third and fourth equality classifications}.
\end{gathered}
\]

An implementation can begin with a strictly increasing finite sequence
of real numbers rather than repeatedly sorting a finite set.  The local
defects $e_i$ and endpoint defect should be natural numbers.  Define
the total defect first by the ordered triple count, prove the energy
identity $\Erm(A)+4\Drm(A)=M_m$, and only then identify it with the quotient
used in this paper.  That order avoids division and nonnegativity
obligations at every induction step.

Proposed milestones are as follows.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{F\arabic*.}]
\item \texttt{energy\_endpoint\_recurrence} and
\texttt{ordered\_defect\_identity}: finite bijections and a polynomial
identity in $m$.
\item \texttt{schur\_two\_zero\_prefix}: two finite-set reflections and
the successor-chain argument.  This is the main order-theoretic lemma.
\item \texttt{schur\_partition\_normal\_form}: a first-failure argument
for lattice membership, then a first-failure argument for the
$2L+1$ bound, followed by inclusion--exclusion.
\item \texttt{endpoint\_hole\_normal\_form} and
\texttt{boundary\_hole\_energy}: reflection, sums of integer intervals,
and the explicitly counted overlap term.
\item \texttt{kappa\_le\_weight\_sq} with its equality case;
\texttt{endpoint\_sharp\_energy\_bound}.
\item \texttt{third\_energy\_classification} and
\texttt{fourth\_energy\_classification}: induction for the earlier gap,
then exhaustive mathematical case splits on the prefix type and the
small endpoint defect.
\end{enumerate}

No source file in this package claims these declarations have been
compiled.  The existing proof-status ledger should not be changed to
``proved'' on the basis of this manuscript or its Python checks.
The appropriate integration is a research article plus proof targets;
a later verified development can promote the corresponding statements
separately.
