\section[{Further research: precise questions and plausible routes\srctag{67}}]{Further research: precise questions and plausible routes}\label{gsr:fz:67:sec:d7}
\srcnote{67}{Section 7}
\label{gsr:fz:67:sec:research}

The results above replace several vague improvement targets by
well-defined extremal problems. The following questions are not
assertions that an answer is already known to follow from our proofs.
The first group asks for completion of an exact classification; the
second asks for structural information that the current local
interfaces discard; the last asks which improvements can survive the
full Gowers iteration.

Here $d(f,g)=|G|^{-1}|\{x\in G:f(x)\ne g(x)\}|$ denotes
normalized Hamming distance, and
$d(f,\operatorname{Aff})=\min_{\ell\text{ affine}}d(f,\ell)$.

\subsection{The global unequal-budget Fourier problem}

\begin{question}[Phase regions beyond the strict matrix branch]
For fixed $R$ and $a$, determine $V_{R,a}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)$
throughout the nonnegative budget orthant. Classify the regions on
which its extremizing support and active Fourier constraints have
constant type.
\end{question}

Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:67:fourier:matrix} supplies an exact open region and a
certificate that can be checked beyond the small neighbourhood used
to prove its existence. Its boundary can occur when a Fourier
coefficient of the certificate reaches zero, a moment matrix loses
rank, an atom loses mass, or the arc mass reaches zero. These events
have different meanings. A vanishing certificate coefficient permits
an inactive moment constraint; a vanishing atom changes the support
combinatorics. Treating all such events as the failure of one numerical
solver loses this information.

A concrete first project is the complete $R=3$ classification for an
algebraic value of $\cos a$, beginning with $a=\pi/3$. On the current
region the answer is rational in the budgets. The next task is to
derive adjacent certificates and prove their regions meet without
leaving a gap. General semidefinite optimization supplies a useful
search mechanism, but a solution should give exact formulas or exact
algebraic descriptions, including boundary multiplicities and the
open-arc convention.

\begin{question}[The next finite-grid term]
For fixed $R,a$ in the first window, determine the subsequential
limits of
\[
 N^2\bigl(\rho_{R,N}(a)-\rho_R(a_N)\bigr),
 \qquad a_N=\frac{2\pi}{N}
        \left\lceil\frac{aN}{2\pi}\right\rceil,
\]
Here $\rho_{R,N}(a)$ denotes the infimum of
$\max_{1\le j\le R}|\widehat\mu(j)|$ over probability measures
supported on the grid $2\pi\mathbb Z/N$ outside $I_a$, as in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:67:fourier:grid}.
\end{question}

The $O(N^{-2})$ error is now proved; the remaining issue is its exact
coefficient and possible oscillation. The nonendpoint atoms of the
continuous extremizer have their own positions relative to the grid.
A second-order answer is therefore likely to involve several rounding
phases. A useful result would separate the geometric endpoint drift,
the barycentric rounding error at each atom, and reoptimization of
the atomic weights. It should also decide when the coefficient
$\pi^2R^2/2$ in the universal upper bound can be improved uniformly.
The limiting contact geometry from the exact Fourier analysis gives
a starting point. The comparison measure has zero arc mass, at the
boundary of the strict matrix region; a separate boundary sensitivity
analysis is therefore needed. The interior Hessian theorem cannot
simply be applied at that endpoint.

\subsection{Beyond ternary target geometry}

\begin{question}[The largest target class with the full cubic range]
For which abelian targets $W$ does
\[
 1-\mathcal E(f)/|G|^3\ge\Psi\bigl(d(f,\ell)\bigr)
 \qquad\text{whenever }d(f,\ell)\le2/3
\]
hold for every finite abelian domain $G$, map $f:G\to W$, and
affine reference $\ell$? Determine the equality cases for each
such target class.
\end{question}

The new result answers this for exponent-three targets. The earlier
manuscript proves a smaller sufficient range for targets without
involutions, and a further improvement when order-three elements are
also absent \cite{repo67charaffine}. The ternary proof cannot simply be
copied: its exact projection factor and seven target configurations
use the specific dual geometry of $\mathbb F_3$.

Two realistic first steps are cyclic targets of orders five and
seven, and targets of exponent $p$ for a fixed odd prime. One can
compute the corresponding projected kernels and retain all relation
types before taking a pointwise maximum. A counterexample would also
be valuable, but should identify which relation pattern defeats the
cubic and whether the offending density can be moved into the
range relevant to a nearest-affine inverse theorem.

\begin{question}[Sharp stability near the coset extremizers]
For $t$ in a compact subinterval of $(0,2/3)$ and
$\varepsilon(f)\le\Psi(t)+\eta$, determine the best quantitative
distance from $f-\ell$ to a one-color subgroup-coset error.
Track the dependence on $t$ and the discrete set of possible
subgroup indices.
\end{question}

Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:67:cthree:color-stability} already bounds the mass outside
a dominant error color and the proportion of target triples with
rank at least two. The remaining step is spatial: a nearly extremal
support must be close to a subgroup coset. The one-color identity
expresses the exact excess in terms of $s^3-E(S)$, so quantitative
stability of the maximal set-energy inequality is the natural input.
A useful theorem should combine color and support stability without
losing the correct dependence as $t$ approaches either endpoint.
Near $t=2/3$, the additional affine equality family must be incorporated
instead of forced into the interior coset description.

\begin{question}[The attainable affine-distance/energy spectrum]
For fixed $G$ and an exponent-three target, determine the possible
pairs
\[
 \left(d(f,\operatorname{Aff}),\,1-\mathcal E(f)/|G|^3\right),
\]
and characterize the lower boundary. Seek uniform descriptions
for families of cyclic groups and elementary abelian $3$-groups.
\end{question}

The two recovery thresholds and the increasing inverse branch are
exact in their stated senses. They do not identify the lower envelope
at every real parameter. Equality with $\Psi$ requires a subgroup
coset, so the allowed equality densities are arithmetic, not
continuous. The sharp non-affine maximum identifies the first
nonzero point when $N\ge13$; the next support size and the next
attainable defect remain meaningful finite problems. Exhaustive
enumeration can supply conjectures, but results should distinguish
fixed-domain spectra from limits obtained by changing the group.

\begin{question}[Sample complexity at the exact recovery thresholds]
Determine the optimal query and sample complexity for recovery below
graph defect $1/4$, or below $4/9$ on a ternary domain. Obtain
near-linear running time where possible, with explicit dependence
on the margin from the threshold and on erasures.
\end{question}

For an explicit table, a polynomial-time procedure is already
immediate: enumerate the at most $|G|$ homomorphisms $G\to\mathbb F_3$
and their three affine translates, and find a nearest scalar affine
map in each target coordinate. The global theorem guarantees that
these are the coordinates of its unique vector-valued affine map,
so combining them retains its sharp distance bound. The proof using
all projections establishes that compatibility; the algorithm need
not inspect them all. The open issue is sharper resource complexity,
especially for oracle access and partial observations. For partial
graphs, completion independence is already proved. A useful sampling
theorem should exploit it without filling in all missing values,
and should state whether erasures are random or adversarial.

\subsection{Information that permits interpolation compression}

\begin{question}[Surplus anchor agreement and compatible labels]
Suppose each relevant polynomial class contains $u>t$ valid anchors.
What additional compatibility hypothesis gives a sharp improvement
over $E_t(L_1,\ldots,L_r)$, and what is the optimal dependence on
$u$ and the list-size profile?
\end{question}

The exact lower construction uses each target polynomial at precisely
$t$ selected anchors. A genuine surplus can therefore defeat that
construction. However, dividing the count by $\binom ut$ is justified
only when all those anchor representations describe one common
candidate on the entire base cell. Pointwise choices that depend on
the base point need not do so. A first theorem should state the
minimal compatibility condition under which multiplicity counting
is valid, then test whether Gowers' product property implies that
condition, perhaps after a controlled refinement.

The finite-field and partition variants are also concrete. When the
field is too small for the generic construction, collisions can
reduce the number of distinct interpolants. If every further cell
must have a prescribed arithmetic width, the present accounting
$bQ\ge E_t$ is not the final geometric constraint. These questions
are described in more detail at the end of
Section~\ref{gsr:en:67:interp:sec:anchor-optimality}; they require additional
incidence or product information, rather than another count of
the same $t$-subsets.

\subsection{Completing and escaping the norm-layer barrier}

\begin{question}[Critical odd norms for every progression length]
For every $m\ge2$ and prime $2m<p<(2m-1)^2$, is
\[
 M_{2m+1,m}(p)>0?
\]
Equivalently for the classification problem, must the norm of
degree $2m+1$ contain a nontrivial symmetric $2m$-term progression?
\end{question}

All larger odd degrees are already excluded over every allowed
characteristic. The exceptional fields are prime fields, since a
proper power of a prime larger than $2m$ already exceeds
$(2m-1)^2$. Thus there is a finite and explicitly bounded set of
checks for each length. Lengths four, six, and eight are settled in
this article.

A structural approach seeks an irreducible polynomial of degree
$2m+1$ with odd part
\[
 X\prod_{i=1}^m\bigl(X^2-(2i-1)^2\bigr).
\]
Its root yields the required norm equalities. Taking only a constant
even part is sufficient in the eleven eight-term examples, but it
would be premature to require that stronger ansatz for every field
and length. Allowing an arbitrary even part provides more freedom.
An existence theorem for this prescribed odd part would remove the
last condition from the independent norm-block classification.

\begin{question}[Unrestricted scalar quintics for four-term symmetry]
What is the largest $n$ for which a scalar polynomial
$P:\mathbb F_q^n\to\mathbb F_q$ of total degree at most five can
avoid every nontrivial symmetrically coloured four-term progression,
over fields of characteristic greater than five?
\end{question}

The repository's general degree filtration leaves a gap between the
known dimension-four construction and the general upper bound eight
\cite{repo67norm}. Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:67:norm:classification} shows that
independent norm blocks of any degree cannot close that gap by
producing a larger example. A successful construction would need
interacting terms or a different algebraic design. A sharper
impossibility theorem would need to use relations between the
coefficient forms at different centres, rather than treating the
pointwise equations as an arbitrary system of their stated degrees.

One practical programme is to classify small-rank leading quintic
forms up to linear change of variables, then examine the induced
cubic and linear difference coefficients. A purely random search
over all coefficients is unlikely to explain the mechanism. The
target should be either a reproducible explicit example in
dimension at least five, or a structural theorem ruling out a
well-defined larger class than independent norms.

\begin{question}[Interactions and quantitative supersaturation]
How robust is the norm-layer obstruction under cross-block
perturbations? Determine assumptions on a polynomial interaction
$R(x_1,\ldots,x_s)$ that force a positive lower bound for the
number of symmetric progressions in
$\sum_jv_jN_j(x_j)+R$.
\end{question}

An independent extra summand cannot repair a bad block: freeze its
coordinates and use Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:67:norm:independent-addition}.
Cross-block terms do not permit that immediate reduction. Natural
first cases include interactions of lower degree in the bad block,
bounded algebraic rank, or dependence through a few linear forms.
The exact centre-count identity gives a baseline against which to
measure how many progressions a perturbation destroys. A useful
supersaturation theorem should record both the dimension of the
added variables and the degree or rank of the interaction.

\subsection{Closing a complete quantitative iteration}

\begin{question}[A loss ledger from local theorems to a density increment]
Can the exact Fourier profile, the interpolation list improvement,
and the applicable affine-recovery theorem be carried through one
complete, explicitly parameterized Gowers density-increment step?
What bound survives iteration?
\end{question}

This is the necessary bridge to a stronger global theorem. The
input and output at each lemma should record density, scale,
codimension or partition complexity, exceptional mass, list size,
and the precise characteristic assumptions. In particular,
exponent-three rigidity cannot silently be inserted where the
frequency target has a different torsion structure. Similarly, the
Fourier neighbourhood theorem should not be used if the produced
budgets lie outside its matrix-certificate region.

An attainable first result is a verified symbolic recurrence for a
restricted class where all hypotheses match. One should then solve
that recurrence and compare the resulting bound with its baseline,
including lower-order dependence. This is more informative than
multiplying apparent local gains whose hypotheses cannot all hold
at once. Any claim of a new global bound must state the resulting
function of $N$, $k$, and density and provide the full derivation.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Verification, reproducibility, and repository integration\srctag{67}}]{Verification, reproducibility, and repository integration}\label{gsr:fz:67:sec:d8}
\srcnote{67}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:fz:67:sec:reproducibility}

\subsection{Three levels of evidence}

The package distinguishes proof, finite certificate, and diagnostic
calculation.

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{General proofs.} The Fourier moment argument,
projection identities, autocorrelation inequality, interpolation
upper and lower bounds, norm character estimate, and classification
arguments are written out. Their general validity does not follow
from the test suite, and no such inference is used.
\item \textbf{Finite certificates used in a theorem.} For the
eleven small fields in the eight-term norm theorem, the displayed
degree-nine polynomials are verified to be irreducible by exact
polynomial arithmetic. The proof reduces irreducibility to
$X^{p^9}\equiv X\pmod F$ and
$\gcd(X^{p^3}-X,F)=1$. The verifier also independently excludes
factors of degrees one through four. This finite component is
explicit and reproducible.
\item \textbf{Supplementary diagnostics.} Exhaustive maps test the
graph identities and equality cases; finite interpolation examples
test counts and uncovered-mass inequalities; exhaustive norm tables
test normalizations. Floating-point Fourier checks compare the
analytic answer with independently discretized linear programs.
These calculations can catch mistakes but do not certify the
infinite parameter families.
\end{enumerate}

The main exact rigidity suite checks 115,623 maps, all 17,576 nonzero
triples in $\mathbb F_3^3$ for the projection table, and 198,015
integer instances of the pointwise inequality. The additional
order-thirteen suite enumerates all $3^{12}=531,441$ ternary maps
normalized by $f(0)=0$; it confirms the maximum nonconstant energy
$1645$ and the 26 normalized one-point extremizers. This last
enumeration is a check of an elementary analytic proof, not its
substitute.

The interpolation suite includes all 28,561 bidegree-at-most-$(1,1)$
polynomials over $\mathbb F_{13}$ in a small sharp example,
deterministic generic-list constructions, greedy-order comparisons,
and seeded multi-candidate cases. The norm suite verifies the eleven
irreducibility certificates and eleven exhaustive norm-count cases.
The Fourier suite tests 120 strict-branch examples with $R\le10$,
an exact symbolic identity for the rational example, five independent
grid linear programs, and nine finite-grid bounds. The numerical
outputs are labelled as such in their JSON reports.

\subsection{Files and reproducible commands}

The distribution contains the complete single-file manuscript
\nolinkurl{gowers_exact_local_profiles.tex}, its compiled PDF,
two vector figures, the section sources used for assembly,
verification programs, their recorded outputs, and a source ledger.
The main TeX file has no external bibliography dependency; its only
external typesetting inputs are the two supplied PDF figures.
The section sources are included for convenient selective integration.

To compile after extracting the archive, run
\begin{verbatim}
latexmk -pdf -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error \
  gowers_exact_local_profiles.tex
\end{verbatim}
The included \texttt{build.sh} performs the same operation.
If \texttt{latexmk} is unavailable, running \texttt{pdflatex} three
times resolves the contents and references. The verification
commands, run from the extracted directory, are
\begin{samepage}
\begin{verbatim}
python3 verification/verify_fourier.py
python3 verification/verify_rigidity.py
python3 code/verify_interpolation.py
python3 code/verify_order13.py
python3 code/norm_blocks_verify.py --full
\end{verbatim}
\end{samepage}
Python's standard library is sufficient for the exact rigidity,
interpolation, and norm programs. The order-thirteen enumeration
uses NumPy with integer arrays. The Fourier diagnostics
use NumPy, SciPy, and SymPy. The optional figure regeneration script
also uses Matplotlib. Run the exact programs without Python's
optimization flag: some use assertions as internal checks.
The full norm and order-thirteen runs are more substantial than
the remaining diagnostics. Their recorded results are included so
that a reader can first inspect the certificates and then decide
which checks to rerun.

\subsection{Suggested integration points}

\begin{longtable}{@{}L{0.23\textwidth}L{0.42\textwidth}L{0.25\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Contribution & Existing location or dependency & Label namespace \\
\midrule
\endfirsthead
\toprule
Contribution & Existing location or dependency & Label namespace \\
\midrule
\endhead
Unequal Fourier budgets
& Missing-interval discussion after Gowers' Lemma~5.2; source~37,
especially its unequal-budget question
& \texttt{fourier:} \\
\addlinespace
Ternary cubic rigidity and recovery
& Graph-energy/affine-rigidity discussion; source~11 and the recent
character/affine manuscript
& \texttt{cthree:} \\
\addlinespace
Exact candidate count
& Shared-anchor step at Lemma~16.10; source~39's candidate-count
and further-research sections

Norm-block classification

and the Shi--Dong construction
& \texttt{norm:} \\

\end{longtable}

The source ledger records the merged prior article's inspected Git
blob and hashes of the more recent working manuscripts. This is
preferable to referring to an unqualified ``latest'' state during
integration. The article is supplied for review and incorporation;
no repository commit or external publication is represented as
having been made by delivering this archive.

\subsection{Formalization priorities}

The most economical initial formalization target is the interpolation
upper theorem. Its proof needs finite sets, a field, a linear space
of base functions, and Lagrange interpolation. The greedy collision
lemma and finite lower construction can follow, using elementary
root bounds. These would give useful verified components without
first formalizing Gowers' entire proof.

The next target is the characteristic-three graph expansion and the
two-color inequality. The latter reduces to a short real inequality
under explicit integer constraints; the seven-case projection table
can be encoded as finite linear algebra over $\mathbb F_3$.
The global recovery theorem then needs finite Fourier analysis and
an explicit treatment of characters of the wrong order. The
order-thirteen cutoff is a compact additional trigonometric lemma.

For the norm section, separate the algebraic reduction and
irreducibility certificates from the analytic character bound.
The certificates can be checked by a small trusted polynomial
arithmetic kernel. The general estimate may first be formalized
conditional on the standard multiplicative Weil bound, with that
dependency stated in the theorem. Finally, the Fourier section
requires a finite supported-moment theorem or a formalization of
its polynomial factorization proof. The finite matrix algebra,
uniqueness, and variation formulas can be developed independently
of that analytic input.

These are proposed formalization routes. The distribution contains
mathematical proofs and executable checks, not Lean theorem files
or claims of machine-checked proof.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Consequences, interfaces, and further research\srctag{68}}]{Consequences, interfaces, and further research}\label{gsr:fz:68:sec:d8}
\srcnote{68}{Section 8}
\label{gsr:fz:68:sec:research}

\subsection{Two direct interfaces with the Gowers argument}

The energy $E(A)$ counts two-dimensional additive cubes in $A$.
Thus Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:pointwise} gives, for every observed overlap,
\[
 \#\{\text{two-dimensional cubes in }A\}
 \le |A|^3-|A|r_A(d)(|A|-r_A(d)).
\]
The multilevel version incorporates an entire overlap spectrum.
These are structural bounds for a specified set; they can be combined
with the uniformity-dependent cube bounds surrounding Gowers'
Lemma~3.10, but they do not change that lemma's higher-dimensional
uniformity parameter by themselves \cite{gowers}.

The restriction theorem has a direct moment interface. We include
the argument to fix the density normalization and credit it as an
existing ingredient \cite{repo68four,repo68seventeen,repo68fiftyeight}.

\begin{proposition}[Existing moment lifting with the new filter]
\label{gsr:fz:68:prop:moment-interface}
Let $B$ be a subset of a finite cyclic group, $b=|B|>0$, and
$\phi:B\to F$ a map into an abelian group. If at least $\gamma b^3$
ordered additive quadruples are respected by $\phi$, then
$G_{16}(B,\phi)\ge\gamma^7b^{15}$.
Consequently, if $0<\gamma,\eta\le1$ and
\[
 b\ge\left(\frac4{\gamma^7\eta}\right)^{53},
\]
there exists $B'\subset B$ with
\[
 T_{16}(B')\ge
 \left(\frac{\gamma^7\eta}{4}\right)^{53}b^{15},
 \qquad
 G_{16}(B',\phi)\ge(1-\eta)T_{16}(B').
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
First suppose the target is finite, and let $\Gamma$ be the graph of
$\phi$ in the finite product group of order $M$.
Use the unnormalized Fourier transform
$\widehat{\ind_\Gamma}(\chi)=\sum_{x\in\Gamma}\overline{\chi(x)}$.
Parseval gives $\sum_\chi|\widehat{\ind_\Gamma}(\chi)|^2=Mb$.
Thus the weights
$p_\chi=|\widehat{\ind_\Gamma}(\chi)|^2/(Mb)$ form a probability
distribution. For the balanced $2s$-tuple count,
\[
 G_{2s}=\frac1M\sum_\chi|\widehat{\ind_\Gamma}(\chi)|^{2s}
 =b\sum_\chi p_\chi
       \bigl(|\widehat{\ind_\Gamma}(\chi)|^2\bigr)^{s-1}.
\]
For integer $s\ge2$, convexity implies
$G_{2s}\ge b(G_4/b)^{s-1}$.
Taking $s=8$ gives the first assertion.
For an arbitrary target, the finite-quotient argument of
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:68:rf:lem:finite-quotient} preserves all relevant quadruple
and sixteen-tuple discrepancies, so the same conclusion follows.
Finally apply Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:ff:thm:53} with $\alpha=\gamma^7$.
\end{proof}

In Gowers' notation $b=\beta N$, so the size condition is explicitly
$\beta N\ge(4/(\gamma^7\eta))^{53}$.
The difference between normalizing respected quadruples by $b^3$
and by $N^3$ must be maintained when this corollary is inserted into
another statement. In particular, a density factor should not be
removed by silently changing the meaning of $\gamma$.

\subsection{A practical formalization order}

The finite combinatorial part has a short route to a formal
development. It is useful to keep all main inequalities over
nonnegative integers or rationals until the last quadratic inversion.
An implementation order is:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item Define finite-support counting convolution and prove the
 union--intersection identity. Record \eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:mixed-remainder}
 as an equality, then obtain the inequality by termwise positivity.
 \item Prove the overlap triangle inequality and the integer form
 of the multilevel bound. For subgroup closure only two internal
 nodes are needed; its polynomial inequality can be proved without
 integration by clearing denominators in the chord calculation.
 \item Construct $H$ by the strict threshold $2r_A(d)>m$, prove it
 is a subgroup, and derive the occupancy identity over its cosets.
 Separate canonical-coset uniqueness from closest-coset uniqueness.
 \item Formalize the complement expansion and the polynomial
 remainder. Prove the nested optimization either by the displayed
 derivatives or by an equivalent rational inequality after setting
 $s=\tau(s)(1-\tau(s))$.
 \item Formalize the finite degree-twelve coefficient convolution
 and integer certificates. Keep this independent of the analytic
 expectation theorem, so the finite arithmetic can be checked early.
 \item Link the general finite-group expectation theorem to the
 existing ordered-tuple counts, and only then substitute the
 exponent-53 certificates.
\end{enumerate}

The existing catalogue records exact companions for
\path{lemma_3_10}, \path{lemma_9_3}, and
\path{corollary_9_4}. This is a report about the inspected catalogue,
not a new compilation claim. The tuple interface is the repository's
\path{additiveTupleCount}, \path{phiAdditiveTupleCount}, and
\path{GammaHomOfOrder} with order parameter eight.
The proposed strengthenings should receive separate theorem names;
the original statements and their current proofs need not be
overwritten. No uncompiled Lean file is included as though it were
a verified result.

\subsection{Research questions left after the present results}

The following questions are intended as specific next projects.
They distinguish unknown sharp constants, extensions of the proved
scope, and propagation tasks. The coefficient-one question, the
quarter-defect coset existence threshold, the $2/9$ uniqueness
threshold, the existence of a filter with cost below $52$, and the
leading growing-order phase diagram are answered above and are not
listed again as open. The coordinate-splitting and Cartesian-structure
parts of the compound ledger item \path{gsr:fz:q:II:cosetrange}
remain outside these answers.

\begin{question}[The discrete coset-distance envelope]
\label{gsr:fz:68:q:discrete-envelope}
For a specified finite abelian group $G$, cardinality $m$, and defect
budget $u\le1/4$, determine
\[
 \Phi_{G,m}(u)=
 \max_{\substack{A\subset G,\ |A|=m\\E(A)\ge(1-u)m^3}}\delta(A)
\]
whenever the feasible class is nonempty. How do subgroup indices and
the integer energy spectrum improve $\tau(u)$ between its attained
punctured-coset parameters?
\end{question}

The equality classification supplies the exact candidates on the
quadratic curve, while \eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:rounding-remainder} records all losses
away from them. A useful first case is a cyclic prime-power group with
two or three possible nontrivial subgroup sizes. A complete answer
should identify extremizers as well as the numerical envelope, and
should distinguish the canonical distance $\delta_C$ from the true
minimum $\delta(A)$ above the uniqueness threshold.

\begin{question}[Stability across the quarter-defect transition]
\label{gsr:fz:68:q:transition}
Fix $\kappa>0$. Suppose
$\kappa\le q(d)\le1-\kappa$ and
$\eps-q(d)(1-q(d))\le v$.
Is $A$ within $O_\kappa(v^c)m$ edits, for an absolute $c>0$, of one
of the equality families in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:pointwise-equality}?
What are the optimal exponent and the necessary scale conditions?
\end{question}

This asks for stability of the universal inequality itself, including
the transition at $\eps=1/4$ where two-coset examples appear.
The oriented puncture theorem answers a localized version with
$\eps<1/4$ and a small gap relative to $\delta^3$.
The exact remainder \eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:self-remainder} suggests first proving
that the mixed convolution $v$ is nearly $\{0,k\}$-valued and that
$w$ is nearly $\{0,t\}$-valued, then converting those analytic
conclusions into periodicity. The lower bound on $q(d)$ and
$1-q(d)$ prevents a vanishing overlap from making the hypothesis
uninformative.

\begin{question}[Equality in the multilevel spectrum inequality]
\label{gsr:fz:68:q:multilevel-equality}
Classify sets attaining \eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:multilevel} for their full distinct
overlap spectrum. Which finite sequences of multiplicities can
simultaneously make all the truncation-node inequalities sharp?
\end{question}

For one internal node the answer is Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:thm:pointwise-equality};
for a consecutive spectrum, integer intervals attain the bound.
With several levels, equality forces the sum-multiplicity truncation
curve to be exactly the prescribed piecewise linear interpolant.
That is a strong compatibility condition between sum and difference
representations, not merely a collection of scalar equalities.
A natural starting class is a short arithmetic progression of cosets
with one or more punctured fibers.

\begin{question}[A weighted coset theorem]
\label{gsr:fz:68:q:weighted-coset}
For finitely supported $0\le f\le1$ with
$E(f)\ge(1-\eps)(\sum f)^3$, determine the sharp bound on
\[
 \min_C\frac{\|f-\ind_C\|_1}{\sum f}
\]
in terms of $\eps$. Does the same quarter-defect structural threshold
have a sharp weighted distance formulation?
\end{question}

Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:68:prop:weighted} already gives a subgroup of large
\emph{minimum} overlaps. The missing step is a suitable replacement
for the occupancy identity used for indicator sets.
Simple tests should include a constant weight on a subgroup, a
partially filled missing coset, and two fibers of unequal height.
Any proposed formulation must retain the cap on $f$ and the correct
normalization under multiplication of all weights.

\begin{question}[Nonabelian analogues and asymmetric equality]
\label{gsr:fz:68:q:nonabelian}
What sharp overlap-energy inequalities survive in finite nonabelian
groups when left and right translations are distinguished?
Within the abelian setting, classify all equality cases of the
unequal-size mixed remainder \eqref{gsr:en:68:eq:mixed-remainder}.
\end{question}

The abelian proof uses commutativity at the exact point where
$\ind_P*\ind_C$ is replaced by $\ind_C*\ind_P$.
This identifies the obstruction to a verbatim nonabelian extension.
A useful initial problem imposes normality of the relevant stabilizer
or studies unions of its cosets.
For unequal sets, equality still forces the two nonnegative
remainders to vanish, but full representation fibers no longer give
the same reflection symmetry. A classification would strengthen the
two-set form beyond its presently sharp universal coefficient.

\begin{question}[The exact sixteen-variable filter optimum]
\label{gsr:fz:68:q:finite-filter}
Determine $\cI_{16,2}$ or obtain a rigorous narrow interval for it.
Can the degree-twelve construction be improved sufficiently to lower
the clean common exponent below $53$ after the size and collision
constants are included?
\end{question}

The exact upper certificate here is
$\cI_{16,2}<103/2$; its actual filter cost is approximately
$51.44505$. This is an upper bound, not a global optimum.
An effective search can parameterize nonnegative trigonometric
polynomials as squared real polynomials or sums of squares, preserve
nonnegative Fourier coefficients, and optimize gain and moments
jointly. Rationalization should be followed by exact positivity,
coefficient, and integer-moment certificates. A numerical grid check
of $0\le K\le1$ is insufficient.

\begin{question}[The second-order principal cost]
\label{gsr:fz:68:q:second-order}
For fixed $a$, does
\[
 \cI_{m,a}=\frac{m\log m}{2\log a}+O_a(m)
\]
hold? If not, identify the first unbounded correction.
For $a=m^{c+o(1)}$, determine the first correction to
$m(1+1/(2c))$ under a sufficiently precise specification of $a$.
\end{question}

The lower bound proved here has only an $O_a(m)$ loss.
The upper construction has the remaining
$O_a(m\log\log\log m)$ term. Thus the leading growing-order regime is
resolved, but the triple logarithm is not known to be necessary.
An answer should identify near-optimal filter shapes as well as
scalar asymptotics. The relevant competing requirements are
concentration of the coefficient distribution and near-uniformity
of its $m$th powers among residue classes.

\begin{question}[Degree, principal cost, and finite-size cost together]
\label{gsr:fz:68:q:degree}
For fixed $m,a$, determine the tradeoff among filter degree $D$,
principal cost $-\log P/\log(P/Q)$, and error cost
$\log(R_2/P)/\log(P/Q)$. How large must $D$ be to approximate the
uniform theta-filter upper bound to a prescribed accuracy?
\end{question}

The Fej\'er approximation proves an infimum statement without
optimizing its degree. In an actual restriction theorem, increasing
$D$ increases the domain torsion allowance and the finite-size
constant. Optimizing only $P/Q$ can therefore give a worse usable
theorem. The certified degree-twelve example is a concrete feasible
point for this three-way optimization; a successful refinement would
output all the constants required by
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:68:rf:thm:selection}.

\begin{question}[Using the observed discrepancy-order distribution]
\label{gsr:fz:68:q:order-profile}
Suppose the bad tuples have known counts $u_a$ by finite discrepancy
order, together with a count for infinite order. Optimize a restriction
certificate using the actual principal sum
$\sum_a u_a Q_{m,a}^k$ rather than the order-two worst case.
How much can independent heterogeneous filters improve the complete
finite-size guarantee for such a profile?
\end{question}

The uniform theorem gives the cost for each single order, but it does
not solve a multi-order optimization. A filter adapted to one residue
class can be inefficient for another. The natural optimization must
retain the weighted nonprincipal and collision errors as well.
Good benchmark inputs would separate a small population of
involutory defects from a large population of high-order defects.

\begin{question}[Methods beyond the principal positive-filter barrier]
\label{gsr:fz:68:q:beyond}
Can one obtain retention exponents of order $O(m)$ for a single
balanced relation on every cyclic group with arbitrary abelian
targets, with useful explicit finite-size thresholds, by a method
whose guarantee is not controlled solely by the principal positive
Fourier spectrum?
\end{question}

For fixed possible discrepancy order, the proved principal cost
grows like $m\log m$, including for independent heterogeneous
layers. This leaves adaptive filters, correlated filters, signed
Fourier coefficients with controlled cancellation, and prior
structural extraction as distinct possibilities.
The source-59 character-separation results are already available
\cite{repo68fiftynine}; a new project should combine them with the present
tuple-retention objective, not repackage character separation itself
as an unanswered question.

\begin{question}[Several relations with decaying collision errors]
\label{gsr:fz:68:q:systems}
Extend the source-58 expectation estimate to a fixed integer relation
matrix, selecting one common subset and counting every ordered tuple.
Can the nonprincipal error retain decay in the number of layers while
its domain dependence is expressed through Smith invariants or
coefficient-minor kernels?
\end{question}

The next tractable case is two independent balanced relations.
One must track the rank gained by each added Fourier row and preserve
the geometry of tuples in $B^m$, including identifications of
coordinates. General system-level Fourier restriction and the
repository's finite-field rank methods are predecessors, so the
specific goal is the simultaneous decaying-error, composite-modulus,
common-subset statement. A hybrid primary-component argument may also
connect cyclic bounds with useful bounds on large groups of bounded
exponent.

\begin{question}[Construction and global propagation]
\label{gsr:fz:68:q:propagation}
Can a subset meeting the explicit certificate be found and verified
without enumerating all $b^m$ tuples? Separately, which later steps of
the Gowers induction dominate after substituting the new local
restriction and stability constants?
\end{question}

For construction, a fixed finite Fourier degree allows the phase
integrals to be replaced by a sufficiently fine exact root-of-unity
average, and conditional expectation gives a finite exhaustive
procedure. Efficient convolution, partial tuple statistics, and
certified algebraic arithmetic are possible routes to a useful
algorithm; no such complexity bound is proved here.
For global propagation, the appropriate deliverable is a dependency
ledger carrying densities, quality parameters, domain sizes, and
normalizations through every use of the restriction statement and
the higher arrangement lemmas. A local exponent improvement does not
determine the final Szemer\'edi bound until those later inequalities
are recomputed.

\subsection{Suggested order of attack}

The most immediate projects are exact finite filter optimization,
discrete coset envelopes in small subgroup lattices, and formalization
of the nonnegative energy remainder.
They have explicit certificates and finite benchmarks.
The next layer is stability at the quarter-defect transition and
the second-order principal cost; both have a clearly identified gap
between the available upper and lower mechanisms.
Several-relation restriction and a revised global parameter chain
are larger projects whose hypotheses should be fixed before numerical
optimization begins.

proofs.

The preparation used parallel mathematical derivations and internal
cross-checks. In particular, the pointwise gap, subgroup threshold,

certificates were reviewed independently within the same

environment, and no theorem in this supplement is represented as
newly kernel-checked.

reports. Counts refer to the enumerated assertions in their own

 C_4^2,\ C_8\times C_2,\ C_4\times C_2^2.

\section[{Finite certificates and implementation interfaces\srctag{69}}]{Finite certificates and implementation interfaces}\label{gsr:fz:69:sec:d10}
\srcnote{69}{Section 10}
\label{gsr:fz:69:bad:sec:algorithms}

\subsection{Coefficient-table algorithms}
A symmetric degree-$d$ tensor is represented by its
$\binom{n+d-1}{d}$ coefficients on nondecreasing basis tuples.  From this
table the following operations are finite linear algebra over $\Ftwo$.

First form the matrix $A_R$ whose columns correspond to a basis direction
in the first frozen slot and whose rows correspond to a tuple of $d-4$
remaining frozen indices and an alternating pair $a<b$.  Its entries are
\begin{equation}
 (A_R)_{(\mathbf w,a,b),z}
 =T(a,a,b,z,\mathbf w)+T(a,b,b,z,\mathbf w).
 \label{gsr:fz:69:bad:eq:Rmatrix}
\end{equation}
Its kernel is $R(T)$ and its rank is $\rho(T)$.  There are
$\binom n2\binom{n+d-5}{d-4}$ rows before redundant rows are removed.
Next form the matrix $A_P$ with a row for each frozen tuple of length $d-3$
and each basis vector $a$, and a column for the other alternating variable
$b$:
\begin{equation}
 (A_P)_{(\zz,a),b}=T(a,a,b,\zz)+T(a,b,b,\zz).
 \label{gsr:fz:69:bad:eq:Pmatrix}
\end{equation}
It has $n\binom{n+d-4}{d-3}$ rows.  The stacked matrix
$\begin{pmatrix}A_R\\A_P\end{pmatrix}$ has kernel $K(T)$ and rank
$\eff(T)$.

Gaussian elimination yields both radicals.  A complement of $K(T)$ gives
a linear quotient $q$ and section $j$.  Restricting the tensor to that
complement constructs $T_0=j^*T$.  To certify the result, verify $qj=I$ and
verify on basis tuples that
$\Phi_T=q^*\Phi_{T_0}$.  The difference is integrable, and its support
coefficients construct a primitive by \eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:primitive-explicit}.
All equality claims in this certificate are exact bit identities.

With naive elimination, the matrix work uses
$O((r_R+r_P)n^2)$ field operations for the displayed numbers of rows, in
addition to coefficient indexing and output construction.  This is a bound
for an \emph{explicit coefficient-table input}.  It is not a polynomial-time
claim for tensors supplied by a succinct circuit while the degree varies.

\subsection{Certifying the extremal flag}
When $\rho(T)=1$, row reduction identifies the unique nonzero $u$ with
$R(T)=\ker u$.  Choose $w$ with $u(w)=1$ and evaluate all frozen slots at $w$
to obtain $\Omega$.  Define $v(x)=\Omega(x,w)$.  The Bianchi identity gives
$\Omega=u\wedge v$, and $v$ is independent of $u$ because the defect is
nonzero.  Verify that $T-C_d^{u,v}$ has support-dependent coefficients and
construct its primitive.  This certificate identifies an exact extremal
gauge class without searching over complex-valued functions.

\subsection{What the delivered code does}
The program \gitpath{code/verify.py} implements exact coefficient arithmetic,
contractions, integrability tests, the two radical matrices, the sharp model
construction, and direct selected/cube energy calculations in small groups.
It is a reproducibility verifier, not a production inverse-theorem package.
Its finite scope and output counts are recorded in
Section~\ref{gsr:fz:69:bad:sec:verification} and \gitpath{data/verification.json}.
No value of a finite optimization is silently promoted to a general theorem.

\section[{Relation to Gowers's argument and the ProveIt formal project\srctag{69}}]{Relation to Gowers's argument and the ProveIt formal project}\label{gsr:fz:69:sec:d11}
\srcnote{69}{Section 11}
\label{gsr:fz:69:bad:sec:interface}

\subsection{The mathematical interface}
The connection to Gowers's Section~17 is the same normalized object: an
average of squared Fourier coefficients of iterated derivatives.  Structured
frequencies are used to remove a polynomial phase.  Our conclusion is an
exact identity after a \emph{certified integrable} symmetric Boolean tensor
has been supplied.  It addresses the small-characteristic obstruction that
ordinary symmetry alone does not remove.

There are important differences from the existing cyclic statement.
The inspected \gitpath{proposition_17_2} in the repository \cite{repo69} in \gitpath{Sections17_18.lean}
assumes prime modulus, factorial invertibility, and a multiaffine frequency
map in the repository's sense.  It records a phase of degree at most $k+1$,
consistent with applying the preceding finite-difference lemma to
$x_{k+1}\sigma(x_1,\ldots,x_k)$.  The original printed statement says $k$;
we use the corrected formal interface rather than that typographical degree.

Here the ambient group is $\Ftwo^n$, the tensor is homogeneous multilinear and
symmetric in all $d$ slots, and the primitive takes values in $\Tquot$.
Setting $d=k+1$ aligns the number of derivative directions and the norm
power.  It does not turn this result into a literal replacement for the
cyclic theorem, nor justify importing its multiaffine hypotheses unchanged.
The theorem is a related sharp small-characteristic phase-integration result.

\subsection{Formalization milestones}
A suitable new namespace should first separate symmetric multilinear maps
from the repository's multiaffine predicate.  The following dependency chain
is sufficient:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.30\textwidth}p{0.62\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Component & Required mathematical content\\
\midrule
Finite calculus & Cube expansion, commutation, exact slicing, and gauge
invariance, all allowing zero amplitudes.\\
Boolean integration & Repetition identity, support-indexed coefficients,
explicit circle-valued primitive, and the dimension of $\In_d$.\\
Cubic base & Finite-Hilbert-space projective orthogonality, shear identity,
and the alternating-rank bound.\\
Canonical branch & Derivative periods, constrained pure-power cap,
rank-one classification, and canonical recurrence.\\
Universal induction & Kernel counting, nonintegrable contractions, and
$3d>2d+2$ for $d\ge4$.\\
Model theorem & Complete radical, quotient factorization, integrable diagonal
lowering, rank--nullity, and support-basis sharpness construction.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The main all-degree induction is short once these interfaces are available.
The model theorem is largely finite linear algebra and can be formalized
separately from the spectral analysis.  A verified implementation should
reconstruct all finite certificates from definitions, not treat the delivered
JSON as a trusted theorem database.  No Lean code is delivered, and no build
or update of the repository's proof-status ledger is claimed.

\subsection{What does not follow}
The near-one thresholds here do not themselves turn a small positive Gowers
norm into a polynomial phase.  There is no new low-energy symmetrization or
localization argument, no control of Bohr-set boundary losses, and no
iteration producing a new bound for progression-free subsets of an interval.
For perspective, the global bounds of Leng--Sah--Sawhney \cite{lssbounds} involve
additional quantitative inverse-theorem machinery; the present estimates
are not a claimed improvement to those bounds.
Nor does the effective tensor quotient prove that every optimizer descends
to it.  The canonical all-dimensional equality is justified by its separate
period argument, not by an unsupported quotient principle.

\section[{Exact verification and source provenance\srctag{69}}]{Exact verification and source provenance}\label{gsr:fz:69:sec:d12}
\srcnote{69}{Section 12}
\label{gsr:fz:69:bad:sec:verification}

\subsection{The finite checks actually performed}
The shipped verifier uses Python's standard library, integer bit matrices,
Gaussian integers, and exact rational arithmetic.  Failures raise exceptions;
checks are not disabled by \gitpath{python -O}.  The default run records:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.,leftmargin=*,itemsep=3pt]
\item The canonical recurrence and strict induction separation in every
degree from $4$ through $1000$, with rational arithmetic.
\item Every symmetric binary tensor in degrees $3$ through $12$:
$16+32+\cdots+8192=16368$ tensors.  Exact constant-function cube energies
are compared with the stated threshold and the rank-sensitive bound.
These are not optimizations over all functions.
\item All $32768$ symmetric quartic tensors on $\Ftwo^3$.  Both defect-flattening matrices are computed to check the effective dimension
and rank-one classification.  The counts are those printed in
Section~\ref{gsr:fp:69:bad:sec:flags}.
\item The sharp model construction for each $d=4,5,6,7$ and $r=1,2,3$.
The full coefficient tables, frozen radicals, complete radicals, and
support-basis maps $\Psi$ are checked.  The largest example has ten
coordinates, degree seven, and $11440$ unordered coefficients.
\item $100$ fixed-radical normal-form dimension checks, covering $n=2,\ldots,6$,
$d=4,\ldots,7$, and every complement dimension $r=0,\ldots,n$.
The constraints are row-reduced as equations on the full tensor coefficient
space and compared with \eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:normal-dim}.
\item $2040$ exact tests of diagonal lowering and ordinary contractions of
integrable tensors, in dimensions one through four and degrees three
through seven, using a fixed seed for the support coefficients.
\item $46$ exact complex-function tests of the selected/cube identity and
slicing, in $(n,d)=(2,3),(2,4),(3,3)$.  Function values are Gaussian integers
divided by two and include zero and nonunit amplitudes.  The same run checks
$46$ canonical energy bounds, $112$ constrained pure-power derivative bounds,
and $5312$ vector identities of each type: translation-conjugation and
even-direction periodicity.
\end{enumerate}
The cubic and arbitrary-dimensional analytic claims rest on their proofs, not
on a finite phase grid.  The coefficient censuses can detect sign and rank
errors, but cannot certify a continuous extremum by themselves.

\subsection{Primary and project sources}
The original Gowers paper was inspected at the page image containing

\section[{Further research questions and topics\srctag{69}}]{Further research questions and topics}\label{gsr:fz:69:sec:d13}
\srcnote{69}{Section 13}
\label{gsr:fz:69:bad:sec:questions}
The following are proposed continuations.  They are not assumptions in the
proofs and are not presented as a list of previously published famous open
problems.

\begin{problem}[The second extremal level]
For fixed $d\ge4$, determine
\[
 \sup_{n\ge2}\ \max_{\substack{T\in\SM_d(\Ftwo^n)\setminus\In_d(\Ftwo^n)\\
                              \rho(T)\ge2}}\Ma(T),
\]
with the maximum over an empty stratum omitted.  Is the upper bound
$1-3d/2^{d+1}$ attained for any or all degrees?  The deficit identity
\eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:deficit} forces simultaneous extremality of almost every
nonintegrable contraction in an equality example, while the derivative
constraint may obstruct this compatibility.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Functions at the canonical endpoint]
Classify all one-bounded $f$ with $\En_{C_d^{u,v}}(f)=b_d$, modulo translations
and multiplication by phases of degree at most $d-1$.  The present theorem
classifies tensor classes, not functions.  The nonnegative slice deficits,
the fixed-derivative zero-frequency constraints, and equality in projective
orthogonality provide concrete necessary conditions.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Dimension-free phase stability]
Does $\En_{C_d^{u,v}}(f)\ge b_d-\delta$ force $f$ to be close in normalized
$L^2$ to the set of exact extremizers, with a modulus depending on $d$ and
$\delta$ but not on $n$?  Compactness only gives a modulus at a fixed
ambient dimension.  A proof would have to retain common-function constraints
across many derivative slices.
\end{problem}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Answered for $d\ge4$} by source~97 (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:97:thm:stability}): $D\le(2/m_d)\delta+O(\delta^{3/2})$ independently of $n$, the coefficient optimal; source~97 does not cite this source. The cubic case is open.
\end{writenote}

\begin{problem}[Stabilization outside the canonical class]
For which symmetric tensors $T_0$ and surjections $q:V\to W$ is
$\Ma(q^*T_0)=\Ma(T_0)$?  The canonical family has this property by the
period argument.  The sharp quotient theorem alone does not establish it
for a noncanonical binary tensor or for the five-coordinate quartic
\eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:five-coordinate}.  A counterexample would identify a precise
limit to tensor-model reduction as an optimization method.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Energy versus the sharp model size]
Determine the best upper bound on $\Ma(T)$ jointly in terms of $\rho(T)$ and
$\rk\Psi=\eff(T)-\rho(T)$.  The sharp dimension examples saturate the
algebraic bound, but no claim is made that they saturate an energy bound.
Additional active alternating directions might force stronger spectral loss
than \eqref{gsr:fp:69:bad:eq:rank-energy} sees.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Classification of maximal model tensors]
Classify the tensors with $\eff(T)=B_d(\rho(T))$ modulo integrable tensors and
linear coordinate changes.  The normal form in Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:69:bad:thm:normal-form} reduces this to an
action on its two parameters.  The dimension proof shows that their radical map
$\Psi:R(T)/K(T)\to\In_{d-2}(H)$ must be surjective.  Which additional
compatibilities distinguish the construction in
Section~\ref{gsr:fp:69:bad:sec:sharp-model} from other surjective cases?
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Odd-characteristic counterparts]
Over $\mathbb F_p$ the nonclassical repetition relation moves $p$ occurrences
rather than two.  Find the appropriate contraction radical, a compatible
lowering operator, and the exact analogue of the nonintegrable energy
threshold.  The Boolean derivative-period proof does not transfer unchanged:
translation by a direction no longer conjugates the derivative product.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Mixed functions and incomplete symmetry]
What survives when the same function is not used at every cube vertex, or
when the frequency tensor is not fully symmetric?  In these settings the
exact period identities and the contraction-integrability kernel may no
longer suffice.  A correct extension should explicitly retain the lost
compatibility conditions, rather than apply the present threshold without
its hypotheses.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Local versions and global bookkeeping]
Can a robust local substitute for the contraction identity be established on
Bohr sets, subprogressions, or high-density subsets, with an explicit boundary
error?  To influence a full density-increment proof, such a result must work
at the energy scales actually produced by the inverse step, not only near
one, and every localization and iteration loss must be propagated.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Verified finite certificates]
Formalize the support-indexed primitive, diagonal lowering, and the two
radical matrices first, then verify the exact minimal-quotient algorithm.
Can the spectral cubic bound be connected to this algebraic layer with a
small finite-dimensional Hilbert-space interface, so that the all-degree
induction becomes a short kernel-checked theorem?
\end{problem}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Conclusion\srctag{69}}]{Conclusion}\label{gsr:fz:69:sec:d14}
\srcnote{69}{Section 14}
The all-degree extremal problem closes because nonintegrability of a
contraction is an exact algebraic event with a subspace as its complement.
When that subspace is a hyperplane, the obstruction is canonical; every other
nonintegrable tensor has at least three quarters of its contractions outside
the integrable class.  The lower-degree energy loss then dominates the
canonical loss strictly.  This yields the exact threshold and the flag
classification in every degree.

The same radical has a second role.  Its interaction with the alternating
pair produces an integrable-valued linear map, whose rank measures all
additional active coordinates.  The resulting dimension bound is exact and
is attained by a support-basis construction.  These two results sharpen the
Boolean phase-integration part of the Gowers framework while keeping the
remaining analytical and formalization boundaries explicit.

\section[{Further questions and a formalization route\srctag{70}}]{Further questions and a formalization route}\label{gsr:fz:70:sec:d12}\label{gsr:fz:70:sec:questions}
\srcnote{70}{Section 12}
The proof resolves one specified asymptotic quantitative interface. Several follow-on questions have concrete mathematical content.
\begin{enumerate}
 \item \textbf{A numerical recurrence starting threshold.} Can the proof of the imported simultaneous recurrence input supply a usable upper bound for $X_0(q)$, uniform in the coefficient tuple and separate tolerances? Any such bound can be inserted into \eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:Rq}--\eqref{gsr:en:70:eq:Nloc} immediately. Improving only the exponent does not answer this question.
 \item \textbf{A published numerical denominator.} A proved numerical value for the published Maynard denominator $C_2$, strong enough to check the range overlap, would turn Section~\ref{gsr:en:70:sec:maynard} into an independently published-input route to the exact target. Both repaired constructor branches would still be necessary unless that value also paid the legacy comparisons.
 \item \textbf{A smaller loss in the balanced recurrence budget.} The choice $1/(128q^2)$ leaves a margin of at least $19/64$. The general power budget for $L\asymp R^u$ and tolerances $R^{-v_i}$ is
 \[
 (Cq+1)u+[C(2q+1)+1]\sum_i v_i<1.
 \]
 Optimizing unequal length and accuracy exponents could improve the local polynomial power. It must also pay $m(\len P)^{-v_i}\le z(a)$ and the actual own-step transfer, so optimizing a recurrence exponent in isolation is insufficient.
 \item \textbf{Sharper near-maximal constants.} The thresholds $63/64$, $7/8$, and $2^{-16}$ were selected for clean strict margins. One can optimize the character approximation and dense-extension density together. A useful objective is a larger explicitly certified interval with a stated retained-pair proportion, rather than an unspecified stability assertion.
 \item \textbf{A formal theorem with a modular recurrence input.} A clean Lean interface would parameterize the own-step partition by an external recurrence certificate, export a direct stronger row constructor with length $m$ or $m+1$, and formalize the near-maximal frequency proof separately. One could then prove the exact asymptotic target conditionally on the recurrence input before undertaking a full formalization of Lau. This report does not supply that implementation.
 \item \textbf{All-primes lower-range output.} The finite collection of primes below $N_{\mathrm L}(\alpha)$ depends on $\alpha$ and does not disappear by asymptotic reasoning. A distinct small-modulus argument would be needed to match an unqualified all-primes reading of the literal paper statement.
\end{enumerate}
No assertion of a new global density-increment, Ramsey, or Szemer\'edi bound follows from this local Fourier-square result alone. Further uses must inspect their own interfaces, thresholds, and already completed upstream work.

Questions~1--4 and~6 remain open; they are merged into item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:sectionthirteen}.
\end{writenote}

\section[{The reproducible companion and its boundaries\srctag{70}}]{The reproducible companion and its boundaries}\label{gsr:fz:70:sec:d13}\label{gsr:fz:70:sec:reproduction}
\srcnote{70}{Section 13}
The accompanying package contains this editable TeX source, the rendered PDF, an offline deterministic builder, bounded exact diagnostics, tests, and curated source snapshots with metadata. Huge thresholds are represented by their symbolic formulas; no test attempts to evaluate them numerically.

The diagnostics check integer and rational identities for the exponent bookkeeping, Lau's denominator specialization, recurrence margins, ceiling and floor guards, coefficient losses, Fourier mass comparison, near-maximal constants, and the printed-exponent comparison. Finite partition and geometry checks exercise small exact instances. Exhaustive small cyclic partial-additive maps test the dense-extension construction, and exact kernel counts test the optional composite-modulus replacement. Such checks catch transcription and implementation errors; the universal statements are proved in the text and are not inferred from finite testing.

The builder validates source identities, uses an explicit package allowlist, runs the tests, compiles the TeX, checks for unresolved references and layout warnings, and packages fixed-order entries with fixed metadata. It is intended for offline reproduction. Its tests include failure paths as well as the successful build path. The curated Lean files are provenance snapshots, not a standalone Lean project or a claim that a new theorem was compiled. Full canonical article text, external papers, raw retrieval receipts, and private working materials are excluded.

The source metadata distinguishes the main proof pin from the one bounded status check. Repository snapshots and exact diagnostics do not establish a literature-wide priority claim, and this document makes none.

\section[{What is resolved and what remains open\srctag{71}}]{What is resolved and what remains open}\label{gsr:fz:71:sec:d12}\label{gsr:fz:71:sec:questions}
\srcnote{71}{Section 12}
Report280~\cite{srcfiftytwo}, Section 7, provided the earlier full-budget dyadic construction, while its Section 8 isolated a basic prime-power obstruction with fewer simultaneous input assertions. The present theorem supplies the complete selected package for fixed mixed prime support and removes dependence on the initial record selection for the same canonical context. Report281~\cite{srcfiftythree}, Lemma 3.1, contributes only the modulus-free scalar estimate reproduced here, not an analytic extraction theorem or a different source pin.

\paragraph{Initial reselection in the canonical context is resolved.}
Every genuine alternative $D,E$ at the exact cutoff has a nonempty critical set and no weak continuation, without a separate $M$ or the other five budgets. The conclusion is genuinely stronger than failure for one selected $F_0$ or one selected initial pair. It does not assert existence of Stage 13.6 data for every alternative pair; nonvacuity is established by the selected package.

\paragraph{Unit Q and R steps in this context are resolved.}
Every genuine initial pair in this context and range has $r$-divisible $E.Q$ step, as does every Stage 13.6 progression $F.R$ for it. Thus searching for unit $Q$ or $R$ step cannot avoid the obstruction here. This does not settle the simultaneous genuine-initial-stage, full-budget, unit-step problem for arbitrary contexts at composite moduli. That broader existence or positive-extension question remains distinct.

\paragraph{Arbitrary composite moduli remain unclassified.}
The permitted support can contain any fixed finite set of primes, but the theorem requires the stated depth of divisibility and bounds the threshold using $r,s$. It does not cover every composite modulus, arbitrary squarefree moduli, or moduli carrying extra prime factors outside the chosen $r$. A uniform treatment of changing support or an alternative cap outside support would require additional ideas.

\paragraph{Changing ambient affinity changes the problem.}
On the strip, the map is exactly $j\mapsto j$ in the coordinate $rj$. A conclusion in progression coordinates avoids this particular ambient extension demand. Its compatibility with later translations, ambient coefficients and bilinear conclusions would have to be proved. The current source predicates explicitly require ambient affinity and cannot be silently reinterpreted.

\paragraph{Torsion-compatible replacements remain a direction.}
An ambient slope prescribed at two points must solve $d\xi=e\pmod N$, which is solvable exactly when $\gcd(d,N)\mid e$. Necessity follows by divisibility; sufficiency follows from a Bezout identity for $d,N$. A whole row requires one slope solving all its congruences simultaneously. No general pairwise-to-global sufficiency claim is assumed. A quantitative formulation through a homomorphism on the difference subgroup, with explicit extension information, remains a possible replacement interface.

\paragraph{Formal verification is separate.}
A Lean development could formalize the exact negative statement and the structural step lemma without modifying the corrected prime theorem. Components include the no-wrap argument, arrangement bijection, global floor-map agreement cap under radical support, uniform floor/predecessor estimates, finite-subgroup rigidity and the positive-power threshold construction. This report supplies their written proofs and bounded diagnostics, not a kernel certificate, Lean build or dependency audit.

The open directions of this section are merged into items~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:sectionthirteen} and~\ref{gsr:fz:q:V:library}.

\section[{Reproduction and verification limits\srctag{71}}]{Reproduction and verification limits}\label{gsr:fz:71:sec:d13}\label{gsr:fz:71:sec:repro}
\srcnote{71}{Section 13}
The archive contains the editable TeX source, this PDF, standard-library Python diagnostics, regression tests, an offline deterministic builder and five curated Lean source snapshots. It contains no earlier report body, paper, private review material, repository checkout or raw external-service receipt. Titles, relevant sections and exact retained hashes of earlier reports appear in \codefiftyone{SOURCES.md}; every argument needed here is reproduced in this article.

\subsection{What the exact companion checks}
The companion separates finite exact checks from the arbitrary-parameter proof. It retains the original prime-power diagnostics and adds mixed-support and initial-reselection checks:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Exhaustive forced-intercept histograms for bounded slopes and points verify the one-point-per-class and global agreement caps. Independent modular-inverse recovery and direct \mbox{slope/intercept/point} enumeration provide alternative descriptions of the same small objects. Mixed-support examples vary the prime exponents independently.
\item Common-step carrier checks include wrapping and stored lengths beyond the additive period. Every carrier remains in the residue class forced by its step, and properness is not silently identified with no wrapping.
\item Exact alias lists, centered preimages and phase-exponent multisets check every alias family, the indexed list size, duplicate graph values, common-step cancellation and nonintegral surrogate floors. Annihilator frequencies are checked to have trivial character on the strip.
\item For bounded $r,N$ and every residue step, the image subgroup order is compared with $r/\gcd(r,d_Q)$, and its maximum centered value with $N\lfloor t/2\rfloor/t$. The order-three example verifies sharpness of the strict $1/3$ threshold.
\item Joint domain/image convolutions on admissible small strips are compared with independent binomial inclusion--exclusion coefficients of $(1+z+\cdots+z^{m-1})^8$. These test repeated entries, order-eight Freiman preservation, energy and the exact fixed-height factor $N^{16}$.
\item Formal exponent identities verify the cutoff, ceiling input, numerator of $z$, expanded Stage 13.4 constants, uniform scalar ratios, the constant-separation exponent margins and $W\delta$. Positive rational floor tests include both the floor and predecessor branches. Labelled surrogate scale packages exercise the eight threshold implications, six budgets and width-only all-initial estimates with substituted constants.
\item Five source snapshots are checked by byte length, SHA-256 and Git blob SHA-1 against one retained manifest with five entries. Negative tests reject altered source bytes, hashes, URLs, duplicate or extra entries, unsafe builder paths and malformed inventories.
\end{enumerate}
Exact counts and model lists are reported by the companion and summarized in the README. The models are bounded diagnostics, not witnesses at the source's actual scales. In particular small mixed-support moduli used to test the agreement and subgroup lemmas need not satisfy the large-threshold hypothesis or the full strip divisibility depth.

The written proof supplies the universal real-power inequalities, sine estimate, uniform floor positivity and existence of $N_0$. No genuine $q_0$, $Q_{13}$, $N_0$, $k_0$ or huge witness modulus is numerically evaluated. The companion uses no floating-point spectral certification, network access or Lean compilation.

\clearpage
\subsection{Commands and reference environment}
From a fresh extracted \codefiftyone{Report283} directory, run
\begin{quote}\ttfamily\small
python3 -I -B build.py verify\\
python3 -I -B companion/exact\_checks.py\\
python3 -I -B build.py reproduce -{}-output /tmp/report283-rebuild
\end{quote}
The output path must be fresh or empty, absolute and outside the extracted source tree. Full reproduction requires Linux no-follow directory handles, standard-library Python, and installed \codefiftyone{pdftex}, \codefiftyone{pdflatex} and the listed standard LaTeX packages. No third-party Python module is required. The reference versions and complete model counts appear in the README.

The builder and its build-security regression suite are adapted from Report280's packaging implementation. The mathematical companion and its tests are specific to this report. The builder enforces an exact file allowlist, rejects symlinks, hard-link aliases and nonregular files, stages checks outside the source, bounds subprocess time and output, and compares normal with optimized Python runs. Original and staged source inventories must remain unchanged. Each build-launched test or diagnostic process receives the configured integer conversion limit; this statement does not extend that flag to independently launched nested CLI rejection probes.

The TeX source is compiled twice with shell escape disabled and deterministic metadata. Overfull boxes, unresolved references or citations, multiply defined labels and rerun requirements are build failures. Archive member order, permissions, timestamps and compression settings are fixed. An internal manifest binds each public payload; an external SHA-256 sidecar identifies the actual ZIP. These checks establish content consistency, not mathematical truth, authorship or remote source authenticity.

A replay from the distribution must reproduce the packaged PDF bytes. That comparison is toolchain-sensitive: another TeX distribution can produce different bytes even when content and appearance agree. Such a mismatch should be investigated rather than hidden by replacing the manifest. Rendering and inspecting every page is a separate quality gate.

T5 & $\sigma$ & Positive selected length and its floor bound\\
T6 & $1$ & Recurrence estimate for every selected alias\\
T7 & $u_0w_0-\sigma$ & Exact Section 10 radius budget\\
T8 & $\beta\varepsilon$ & Width for all genuine alternative records\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
T8 alone, once the context and literal constants are fixed, supplies the quantitative input for the universal-initial obstruction. The scalar margins and exact Stage 13.4 floor/predecessor predicate turn it into positive critical-height count. The second scalar margin and $c<d/8$ further give the radius below $1/4$. No ninth threshold or new alternative-record budget is introduced.

A reconstruction in the following order separates the arithmetic and analytic issues:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Fix the source meaning of ambient affinity and the complete weak output support and mass conditions. Separate the selected existential package from the universal alternative initial pair.
\item Substitute $a=r^{-s}$ into the exact constants. Verify $K\in\mathbb N_{>0}$, retain the denominator $K$ in $z$, and recompute the expanded exponents and $W\delta$.
\item Prove the uniform margin for every $1\le q\le b$, then $c<d/8$. These comparisons are scalar and use no modulus hypothesis.
\item Verify all eight threshold exponents, the selected floors, the extra unit in $n+1\le\ell$, and all six budgets. The input density bound follows from $r^s\ge8r$.
\item Use $r^s\mid N$ for integrality, $r\mid N$ for integer divisibility and kernel size, and the strict inequality $8(m-1)<N/r$ for order eight. Count exactly sixteen free second coordinates at fixed height.
\item Retain all $r$ spectral aliases and cancel them with the selected step $r$. Verify every initial-stage and Stage 13.6 conjunct explicitly.
\item For arbitrary genuine $D,E$, use its own $q$ and both floor branches. Width gives $X>8$, hence $L_P>X-2>X/2$ and nonempty critical heights.
\item Use $\operatorname{rad}(N)\mid r$ precisely to make $r\xi-1$ invertible. Apply the global row cap $r$ without assuming anything about alternative steps, and contradict $W\delta>r$.
\item Separately improve the radius to below $1/4$. At one critical height use the exact annihilator spectrum and sharp subgroup radius to force $r\mid\operatorname{step}(Q)$. This gives the one-point row cap and excludes unit $Q$ and $R$ steps in this context.

\section[{Further questions and limits\srctag{72}}]{Further questions and limits}\label{gsr:fz:72:sec:d13}\label{gsr:fz:72:sec:questions}
\srcnote{72}{Section 13}
\paragraph{Better dense extension constants.}
The factor $6$ comes from retaining slices of density greater than $5/6$, so three such slices intersect in more than half the group. Can a different extension construction reduce the exponential loss $C_d$ while retaining arbitrary finite abelian groups and arbitrary abelian codomains? The sharp support gap alone does not answer this existence question.

\paragraph{Threshold optimization.}
The choice $4/5$ is a convenient rational threshold with $3\sqrt{2-2\sqrt{4/5}}<\sqrt2$. One may vary it and track the corresponding bad-set factor and coefficient target. Optimizing that local choice need not optimize the global induction or the cyclic descent constants.

\paragraph{Intrinsic integrability in torsion.}
The theorem produces a dual-valued $d$-additive map, with optional symmetry in its increment coordinates. Further compatibility involving the evaluation argument would be needed for an integration theorem on a general finite abelian group. The cyclic case is resolved here by periodic rational polynomial phases. A corresponding elementary constructive integration theorem with explicit estimates on general finite abelian groups remains outside this article. The target must retain the correct torsion structure, rather than forcing ordinary residue-ring phases.

\paragraph{Uniqueness at weaker defect.}
The support gap supplies a clean sufficient threshold. The original-$f$ Fourier witness also has analytic restrictions absent for arbitrary partial data. Could these restrictions improve uniqueness beyond the elementary density intersection bound? The sharpness of the generic support statement is not a negative answer to this question.

\paragraph{Local rather than full cycle boxes.}
In the cyclic result, full cycles make ambient properness and common-step requirements immediate. A genuinely local short-box conclusion, especially with constraints on side lengths or on good points throughout the whole box, is a different problem. It cannot be inferred just by renaming $B$ as a product set.

\paragraph{Formal and Ramsey interfaces.}
A formal implementation would need the finite-abelian Fourier facts, homomorphism-valued dense induction, normalization bridges, and all strict endpoint arguments. A Ramsey or density-increment application would need its own extraction hypotheses and iteration bookkeeping. Neither task is completed by this article. The present result isolates quantitative near-maximal Fourier structure and cyclic phase proximity that such work could attempt to use.

\section[{Strict endpoints and normalization checklist\srctag{72}}]{Strict endpoints and normalization checklist}\label{gsr:fz:72:sec:dA}
\srcnote{72}{Appendix A}
For ease of reuse, the argument's sensitive boundaries are collected here.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=1pt,parsep=0pt,topsep=4pt]
\item The hypothesis has $\eps>0$ and a strict cube-average inequality. Even at $\eps=\eps_d$, this gives $\eta<5M_d\eps$, hence $6^{d-1}\eta<1/4$.
\item The slice condition is $|A_y|>5|G|/6$, not $\geq5|G|/6$. Its threefold intersection is strictly larger than a proper homomorphism kernel can be.
\item The discarded slice estimate $\sigma\leq6\eta$ and the extension estimate $1-\dens(B)\leq C_d\eta$ may be non-strict. They are combined with the preceding strict bad-set bound.
\item At the stronger uniqueness endpoint, the original-$f$ witness has density strictly greater than $1-2^{-d-1}$; two distinct coefficients exceeding $3/4$ are impossible at the same tuple.
\item At the cyclic proximity endpoint, $\Delta\leq3/10$ and every intermediate $t_d$ is admissible. The norm hypotheses stay strict through energy descent.
\item The Fourier coefficient is a magnitude. The unnormalized transform contributes one factor $|G|$, its square two factors, and a tuple sum an additional $|G|^d$.
\item Backward differences give a positive leading coefficient. The demodulating factor is the conjugate phase, matched to the negative-sign transform.
\item No uniqueness is required in the main theorem, no evaluation-coordinate symmetry is assumed, and no modular factorial inversion appears except in the optional ordinary residue-ring target construction. The all-cyclic rational integrator uses division in $\mathbb Q$.
\end{enumerate}
