\section[{Interpretation and limits of the result\srctag{73}}]{Interpretation and limits of the result}\label{gsr:fz:73:sec:d10}
\srcnote{73}{Section 10}
The quantitative chain has three separate interfaces. Near-maximal
$Q_d(f)$ gives a phase candidate by theorem~\ref{gsr:en:73:thm:diskentry}. Its correlation
and the unconditional amplitude bound place $z=D+a$ inside the local
radius. The local certificate then recovers the sharp first two terms.
A small $L^2$ distance does not require uniformly small pointwise error:
the proofs allow sparse large perturbations and all finite group sizes.

The entry proof integrates an actual approximate derivative cocycle.
It does not posit that arbitrary symmetric multilinear forms on torsion
groups have polynomial primitives. Exact compatibility constraints on
such forms are a different algebraic problem. Nonclassical phases enter
automatically through the difference definition and are never replaced by
classical coordinate polynomials. The theorem therefore covers cyclic
groups of composite order, groups with mixed torsion, and arbitrary finite
abelian products without a characteristic restriction.

The estimates concern the near-maximal endpoint. A general inverse theorem
at a fixed small positive Gowers norm is not a consequence, and neither is
an improved global Szemer\'edi or Ramsey-number bound. Nor does existence
of a phase with these estimates provide a polynomial-time reconstruction
algorithm. The finite searches and rational diagnostics accompanying this
report are verification aids, not a formal proof of arbitrary-parameter
statements. No Lean implementation, theorem-checker build, or external
referee certification is claimed.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Further research questions\srctag{73}}]{Further research questions}\label{gsr:fz:73:sec:d11}
\srcnote{73}{Section 11}
\begin{question}[Optimal entry and fidelity range]
For each $d$, determine the largest universal defect interval on which
$\max_{P\in\cP_{d-1}}|\E v\overline P|^2\ge Q_d(v)$ holds for all unit phases.
Can the base $10$ in the explicit inductive threshold be reduced while
preserving the correlation invariant?
\end{question}
The good-direction density and completion threshold can be varied, but
any claimed improvement must recheck both phase separation and the lift of
the circle cocycle to a real cocycle. Improving a numerical constant at
one step without the others does not improve the theorem.

\begin{question}[Best local radius and cubic scale]
Can the guaranteed radius $q^{-5/2}$ be replaced by a larger power of
$q^{-1}$, and what is the optimal dependence of the cubic error on $d$?
\end{question}
The proof above uses rough bounds on $B'_d$ and absorbs every amplitude
cross term separately. The exact local constants should be retained when
testing possible improvements. Matching second-order examples constrain
the leading coefficients but do not establish optimal cubic behavior.

\begin{question}[Stable reconstruction]
Can the phase in theorem~\ref{gsr:en:73:thm:fidelity} be found efficiently from oracle access
to $f$, with complexity controlled in the degree and accuracy and with
validity for mixed-torsion groups?
\end{question}
The proof makes finite selections for every direction and then corrects a
small cocycle. Turning these choices into a robust algorithm requires a
representation of the phase class and a complexity analysis absent here.

\begin{question}[Intervals and incomplete cubes]
Which entry threshold and local expansion survive for interval norms or
other boundary-conditioned cube distributions?
\end{question}
The group proof uses translation invariance in the averaging correction
and triple independence in the remainder estimate. Boundary versions must
replace both, rather than transplanting these constants unchanged.

\section[{Antecedents and the evolving repository interface\srctag{75}}]{Antecedents and the evolving repository interface}\label{gsr:fz:75:sec:d15}\label{gsr:fz:75:sec:antecedents}
\srcnote{75}{Section 15}
The mathematical proofs in this report are self-contained. The following comparisons identify which claims are being made and distinguish nearby statements; they do not constitute a publication-priority review.

\subsection{Earlier cover work and Report 286}
ProveIt source~50 already gives a prime-field two-input cover counterexample, finite-alphabet cover mechanisms, and the full-domain product-property endpoint at $\gamma=1$~\cite{srcfifty}. Source~49 gives a loss-dependent retained-core conclusion conditional on seven finite interfaces~\cite{srcfortynine}. Report~286 extends the sparse obstruction to all positive dimensions and all sufficiently large cyclic moduli, with the complete weighted and named-predicate checks. The first part here strengthens the slab energy estimate using graph convolution, makes its density fixed for fixed parameters, and explicitly lower-bounds deletion over arbitrary retained domains. It does not replace or negate source~49's conditional conclusion, and it does not determine the true minimum deletion fraction.

\subsection{Uniform energy and fixed-weight relative repair}
The exact all-respected-quadruple endpoint is classical Freiman rigidity; on a full cyclic group it is affinity. Gowers discusses this full-domain endpoint in Section~6 before Lemma~6.2~\cite{gowers}. ProveIt source~11 studies full-domain uniform graph energy normalized by $N^3$, its defect, and uniform Hamming distance to an affine map~\cite{srceleven}. Its cubic stability profile depends on target two-torsion. That uniform test differs from the infimum over every nonnegative weight in \eqref{gsr:fm:75:eq:ratio-intro}.

Source~56 is closer and uses the \emph{same fixed-weight relative quadruple statistic}~\cite{srcfiftysix}. For a weight $w:G\to[0,1]$, it sets $\alpha=\E w>0$ and $u=\norm{w-\alpha}_{U^2}$. Its Theorem~1.1 assumes $u^4\le\alpha^5/1024$ and relative rejection $\epsilon\le1/1024$, and gives a unique affine comparison within relative weighted Hamming radius $13\epsilon/50$. The differences here are the infimum over \emph{all} weights, exact rigidity at an attained gap, and the parity classification. We do not present fixed-weight relative normalization itself as new.

Classical homomorphism and linearity testing, and later biased or nonuniform tests, supply broader related stability theories~\cite{blr,koppartysaraf,mittalroy}. To interpret our normalization probabilistically, let $\mu=w/\sum w$ and let $X_1,\ldots,X_4$ be independent with law $\mu$. Then the ratio is
\[
 \Pr\bigl(a(X_1)+a(X_2)=a(X_3)+a(X_4)
 \mid X_1+X_2=X_3+X_4\bigr).
\]
Conditioning generally changes the individual marginals. A theorem about a differently designed test distribution cannot be transferred without checking that distinction. The inspected literature and repository sources supply the exact endpoint and related uniform, biased, and relative stability results. This limited comparison did not locate an equivalent statement for the all-weight $3/4$ threshold and parity classification; it does not establish publication priority or exclude another formulation.

\subsection{New formal counterexample and enlarged cover}
The interface used in the first part remains the exact older pin

\section[{Questions left by the two results\srctag{75}}]{Questions left by the two results}\label{gsr:fz:75:sec:d16}\label{gsr:fz:75:sec:questions}
\srcnote{75}{Section 16}
\begin{question}[The secondary hereditary gap]
What is the largest value of $r(a)$ among cyclic maps outside the affine and parity classes? Is $8/11$ attained in that class, or can the four-point argument be strengthened? The present proof settles neither question. In particular it does not determine the optimal threshold for odd moduli.
\end{question}
\begin{question}[Hereditary stability below the gap]
Does a lower bound $r(a)\ge c$ below the classified range imply quantitative agreement with a bounded-complexity family of maps, uniformly in $N$? Any useful statement should specify both its range of $c$ and its distance notion; fixed-weight near-affine repair alone does not answer this all-weight question.
\end{question}
\begin{question}[Partial domains and selection]
Which additive-connectivity or uniformity assumptions on a partial domain permit a relative-energy rigidity theorem? Can an appropriate simultaneous-family relative condition survive the actual Section~16 selection and restriction steps? The Sidon example shows why a domain hypothesis is necessary before a general affine-extension conclusion.
\end{question}
\begin{question}[True deletion cost]
For the interval-alphabet slab construction, what is the exact value or sharp order of $\Delta_\gamma(F)$? Can one improve the graph-convolution bound by using mixed inside--outside quadruples, or improve the lower bound by combining several local boxes? Our optimization concerns only the displayed conservative surrogate within one construction family.
\end{question}
\begin{question}[Cover budgets and ambient cost]
How does the minimum global deletion change when the target iteration parameter or graph budget is enlarged? A useful quantitative tradeoff would relate the present obstruction to positive enlarged-budget covers while retaining the precise width and partial-domain conventions.
\end{question}

\section[{Sources and mathematical scope\srctag{76}}]{Sources and mathematical scope}\label{gsr:fz:76:sec:d9}\label{gsr:fz:76:sec:sources}
\srcnote{76}{Section 9}
\subsection{Relation to the preceding reports}
Report~286, \emph{Sparse Defects and Local Cover Obstructions}, explains why ambient-normalized weighted energy can hide concentrated defects. Report~287, \emph{Global Deletion Costs and Hereditary Energy Rigidity}, studies deletion costs and proves the sharp finite cyclic hereditary threshold, including arbitrary abelian targets~\cite{srcseventyfour,srcseventyfive}. This report continues the energy question with arbitrary abelian domains and quantitative finite witnesses. It does not alter the statements of those reports or import their local-cover interfaces. The cyclic proof needed here is reproduced in full in Section~\ref{gsr:en:76:sec:cyclic}.

The fixed-weight statistic itself has a direct predecessor in ProveIt source~56, \emph{Nearly Sharp Relative Affine Repair on Fourier-Uniform Domains}~\cite{srcfiftysix}. Its introduction allows finite abelian domains, arbitrary abelian targets, and weights in $[0,1]$, and divides failed weighted quadruple mass by ordinary weighted quadruple mass. Rescaling identifies that statistic with one minus the ratio used here. Its stated theorem assumes a Fourier-uniformity condition and a small-error regime, and gives approximate weighted affine repair. The present hypothesis tests \emph{all} finite weights on a full domain and yields exact affinity at a sharp threshold. Thus neither relative normalization nor the arbitrary-abelian-target setting is presented as new.

For provenance, the original source~56 archive is cited at its immutable arrival commit. Its introduction and four-query sampler discussion were read directly for this comparison; the entire predecessor proof and verification suite were not re-audited here. None of its code is a build dependency or is executed by the companion.

\subsection{Classical ingredients and target torsion}
Stetk\ae r's work records normalization, oddness and cyclic homogeneity for Jensen's equation on groups~\cite{stetkaer}. That paper's target is $\mathbb C$. Sabour--Kabbaj explicitly assume a $2$-torsion-free target in the pertinent affine-solution theorem~\cite{sabourkabbaj}. These sources supply classical background, while the exact arbitrary-target identities and the local $H[2]$ remainder needed here are proved in Section~\ref{gsr:en:76:sec:jensen}. No priority claim is made for that elementary torsion-aware form.

The finitely generated structure theorem is standard~\cite{knapp}. Interval averaging and its F\o lner interpretation are also standard~\cite{taoamenability}. We compute the relevant additive-quadruple counts directly: an arbitrary F\o lner sequence is not asserted to produce the same relative-energy limit. Only finitely generated subgroups are decomposed, and only explicit finite sets are used in the limits. This avoids a countability assumption on the ambient group.

\subsection{Boundaries}
The conclusions concern a map on a \emph{full abelian group} and nonnegative finitely supported weights. They do not establish arbitrary partial-domain extension, a nonabelian analogue, an exhaustive classification of the $3/4$ endpoint, or a general $8/11$ gap. No inheritance through a selection procedure, density-increment theorem, or global Szemer\'edi estimate is deduced. The indicator exponent is optimal, but its constants and the arbitrary-weight support complexity are not claimed optimal. This report makes no publication-priority claim and is not a Lean or other proof-assistant certificate.

\section[{Further questions\srctag{76}}]{Further questions}\label{gsr:fz:76:sec:d11}\label{gsr:fz:76:sec:questions}
\srcnote{76}{Section 11}
The results leave several precise questions open within the same full-domain abelian setting.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Endpoint structure and attainment.} Which maps have $r(a)=3/4$ or $\rind(a)=3/4$? When can a finite weight attain the infimum? The division-free index-two family gives exact examples, while integer parity demonstrates nonattainment. Neither exhaustiveness nor equivalence of the two endpoint classes has been proved here.
\item \textbf{Best indicator constants.} The universal upper bound and the integer-parity lower bound determine the exponent $1/2$. What are the best leading constants, and which finite sets are most efficient for parity?
\item \textbf{Weighted support lower bounds.} Binomial weights prove logarithmic support suffices. What is the minimal support required for error $\epsilon$, even for integer parity? The indicator argument modulo two does not apply to arbitrary real coefficients.
\item \textbf{The conditional branch.} What are the full equality and near-equality structures at $5/8$ among cyclic-coset-affine maps? The four-point model proves sharpness, and the explicit boxes describe one limiting mechanism, but no stability or classification theorem is supplied.
\end{enumerate}
These questions are not premises for any theorem in this report.

\section[{What remains open\srctag{77}}]{What remains open}\label{gsr:fz:77:sec:d11}\label{gsr:fz:77:sec:open}
\srcnote{77}{Section 11}
The established conclusions separate four questions that should not be conflated: whether a particular weight attains, whether some weight attains, whether the support-difference group has suitable torsion, and whether the ambient group has suitable torsion. The spectral theorem solves the first in the index-two family, the torsion dichotomy solves the second there, and the quantitative theorem rules out attainment whenever local torsion is parity-trivial.

Natural remaining questions include:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item \textbf{The best exponential constant.} Determine the optimal leading coefficient of $\log(1/\epsilon)$ in the integer-parity support function, or prove that an appropriate limit fails to exist. The known sparse lower and upper leading coefficients remain $1/\log16$ and $\pi/(8\mathsf G)$; the containing-interval model is settled in Section~\ref{gsr:en:77:cyclo-weights}.
 \item \textbf{Exact support complexity.} Determine $n(\epsilon)$ beyond the three-point regime, and classify fixed-support minimizing weights and their additive supports. The current Mahler bound need not be sharp for the simultaneous energy inequalities.
 \item \textbf{Smallest attaining support with torsion.} Given $(G,\pi)$ with $\pi|_{\Tor(G)}\ne0$, determine the smallest support of an attaining nonnegative weight. Cyclic-subgroup indicators provide an upper bound; the seven-point example on $\Z/8\Z$ shows this bound can be improved.
 \item \textbf{All maps at the endpoint.} Classify arbitrary full-domain maps $a$ with weighted infimum exactly $3/4$, beyond the specified nonzero-defect index-two family. Nothing proved here asserts that every endpoint map belongs to this family.
\end{enumerate}
These are mathematical questions, not claims of publication priority. The sparse coefficient theorem is established prior work, and this report records its application to the energy question together with the torsion analysis.

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 70--81]
\emph{Answered within this arrival}: the fourth question by source~78's classification (Section~\ref{gsr:en:sec:hereditary}). \emph{Checked at the write, for the second}: at fixed support the binomial and block weights are far from optimal; on $3M$ consecutive integers for source~79's staircase, six-digit rational weights reach excess $5.6\cdot10^{-3}$, $7.7\cdot10^{-5}$, $1.25\cdot10^{-6}$, $1.8\cdot10^{-8}$ for $M=2,3,4,5$ (note at the end of Section~\ref{gsr:en:79:sec:d8}). Merged into item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:hereditary}.

\section[{Classical antecedents and the remaining questions\srctag{78}}]{Classical antecedents and the remaining questions}\label{gsr:fz:78:sec:d12}\label{gsr:fz:78:sec:literature}
\srcnote{78}{Section 12}
\subsection{What is imported and what is proved here}
Exact additive-quadruple preservation, the graph-energy interpretation, and the full-domain Freiman endpoint are classical; see Gowers~\cite[Section 6]{gowers}. The same fixed-weight relative quadruple statistic already appears in the project's Fourier-uniform affine-repair work~\cite{srcfiftysix}. Those antecedents concern different hypotheses and do not by themselves identify the infimum over every finite weight or indicator. Exact extension from sparse random domains is another distinct question; compare Conlon--Gowers~\cite[Theorem 1.2]{conlongowers}.

The recurrence \eqref{gsr:fm:78:eq:P} itself has a prior printed occurrence: equation (18) of Arunkumar--Shobana--Hemalatha, after a translation of variables, is the same identity in a real-vector-space argument for a different mixed functional equation~\cite{arunkumar}. This is an identity-level antecedent, not a quoted arbitrary-target classification theorem.

Torsion-sensitive finite differences form an established subject. Laczkovich's primary abstract compares diagonal and mixed differences on abelian groups with explicit small-prime torsion conditions~\cite{laczkovich}. Only that abstract was available in the bounded comparison used here; the full article's theorem system was not inspected. Feldman's real-valued Lemma 2.2 gives a quadratic-plus-additive-plus-$G/2G$-constant decomposition for the different equation $\Delta_{2k}\Delta_h^2T=0$~\cite{feldman}. It is a close precedent for scalar parity-quotient decompositions, but its divisions do not justify deleting the order-four term in an arbitrary target. The target-enlargement construction in Section~\ref{gsr:en:78:sec:pushout} is standard pushout algebra~\cite{stacks}.

The proof in this report explicitly establishes the particular hereditary-energy classification: the small-order cyclic reduction, the arbitrary-target plane trichotomy, the grid calculation with $4s=0$, the energy exclusion of its nonzero obstruction, the finite-box quotient transfer, and descent to the original target. Standard algebra and elementary inequalities are used throughout. The main classification has a self-contained proof here, with only the structure theorem for finitely generated abelian groups as standard background. Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:78:cor:attainment} additionally invokes the explicitly identified attainment results of Report~289.

No equivalent arbitrary-abelian-group endpoint theorem was located in the bounded primary-source comparison. This does not establish publication novelty or priority. In particular the full Laczkovich article and older group-valued functional-equation treatments remain natural further historical checks. The article claims the stated proof and reproducible calculations, rather than priority for each technique or a comprehensive survey.

\subsection{Further mathematical questions}
\begin{enumerate}
 \item \textbf{The optimal weighted gap.} Determine the supremum of $r(a)$ outside the affine and nonzero-defect index-two families. The indicator cutoff is now exactly $19/27$, but its sharpness example does not establish weighted sharpness. Which weighted and indicator extremizers occur at their respective cutoffs?
 \item \textbf{Uniform witness size.} Failure of \eqref{gsr:fm:78:eq:P} has an at-most-ten-point witness at $19/27$. Under \eqref{gsr:fm:78:eq:P}, the proof uses box limits whose constants depend on the subgroup and chosen translations. Determine optimal cardinality bounds for witnesses below a prescribed threshold in $(5/8,19/27]$, uniformly over third-class maps satisfying \eqref{gsr:fm:78:eq:P}. Separately, determine optimal bounds for witnesses of ratio at most $19/27$ across the whole third class.
 \item \textbf{The exact subthreshold spectrum.} Determine which values of $r$ and $\rind$ occur below $3/4$, whether they agree in further structural families, and when limiting bounds at $5/8$ or lower are attained by finite indicators.
 \item \textbf{Effective certification.} For finite groups supplied by tables or invariant factors, develop an efficient certifier returning an affine description, the canonical index-two structure, or a small low-energy indicator. The companion verifies the complete symbolic cyclic certificate as well as bounded exhaustive diagnostics and explicit algebraic checks; it does not prove an optimal algorithmic complexity bound.
\end{enumerate}
These questions are separate from the endpoint classification, which is settled by Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:78:thm:classification}, and from the weighted-support questions treated in Report~289.

\section[{Scope literature and further questions\srctag{79}}]{Scope literature and further questions}\label{gsr:fz:79:sec:d10}\label{gsr:fz:79:sec:scope}
\srcnote{79}{Section 10}
\subsection{Comparison with earlier work}
Respected additive quadruples and their graph-energy interpretation are classical. Gowers defines image-preserved quadruples in Section~6 of~\cite{gowers}; importantly, the product property in Section~14 already quantifies over every nonnegative weight. For one restriction its numerator is the weighted respected-quadruple count, but its normalization is $N^{-1}(\sum_x f(x))^4$, rather than $\mathcal E_G(f)$. These differ: Cauchy--Schwarz gives $\mathcal E_G(f)\ge N^{-1}(\sum f)^4$ on a finite group, sometimes very strictly. Universal weighted testing itself is therefore not a new concept claimed here.

The complex quartic has the precise sampling interpretation \eqref{gsr:en:79:eq:MZ}. Lubinsky~\cite{lubinsky} treats sharp Marcinkiewicz--Zygmund and Plancherel--P\'olya constants in a setting uniform over degrees. Our degree-two, three-node calculation is placed inside that framework; it does not resolve its uniform sharp-constant question.

Diaconis, Shao and Soundararajan~\cite{dss} study carries for coset representatives and a different two-input homomorphism test. Their sharp $7/9$ splitting threshold has a three-point representative example. The existence of a $C_3$ extremizer or a nearby numerical threshold does not identify the present relative weighted quadruple invariant. Their work is nevertheless direct conceptual precedent for the carry interpretation.

Floor and bracket-linear functions likewise belong to an established landscape. The bracket-linear structures in Green--Tao--Ziegler~\cite{gtzufour} and generalized polynomials in Bergelson--Leibman~\cite{bergelsonleibman} are relevant context. Here the specific point is the forced three-residue pattern and its sharp hereditary energy threshold. The sparse-domain extension theorem of Conlon--Gowers~\cite{conlongowers} concerns exact Freiman homomorphisms on a random subset, rather than an infimum over all finite weights on a full domain. Standard pushout algebra and finite-group/torus Fourier analysis are tools, not novelty claims.

The bounded literature pass documented in \filename{SOURCES.md} did not locate an equivalent theorem with the exact arbitrary-source-and-target quantifiers and constant $\rho$. That negative search result establishes neither novelty nor publication priority. In particular, priority for an isolated fixed-degree sampling constant remains unresolved.

\subsection{What is proved and what remains open}
The paper proves an optimal universal weighted gap and gives a complete finite-attainment classification \emph{within the explicitly stated index-three family}. It does not classify all maps having infimum $\rho$. Neither a single test of ratio $\rho$ nor a staircase restriction on one subgroup by itself proves that a larger-domain map has hereditary infimum $\rho$.

Natural further questions include the following.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{All equality maps.} Must every full-domain map with $r(a)=\rho$ be a translated index-three affine cut, up to the natural source and target invariances? The present forcing argument assumes $r(a)>\rho$ and does not settle this equality question.
\item \textbf{Quantitative structure near the threshold.} What can be said about maps whose hereditary infimum is close to $\rho$ from below? A useful formulation must specify a metric or a finite sampling model; an unqualified distance between arbitrary full-domain maps is not defined here.
\item \textbf{Efficient finite witnesses.} Away from $\rho$, can one bound the support size and rational bit complexity of a witnessing weight in terms of the desired margin? Formula~\eqref{gsr:en:79:eq:block-error} gives an explicit upper rate for a particular endpoint family, not a universal complexity theorem.
\item \textbf{Finite-support optimization on the staircase.} For a prescribed support size or diameter, are the block weights \eqref{gsr:en:79:eq:block-weights} optimal? Their exact error is proved, but optimality under either size constraint is not claimed.
\item \textbf{Other finite sampling problems.} The $C_3$ calculation leads to a solvable three-node fourth-power inequality. Higher representative cuts lead to other fixed-degree sampling optimizations; their relevance to subsequent hereditary gaps requires a separate structural argument.
\end{enumerate}
All weights in this report are real and nonnegative. Signed or complex test weights define a different problem. The positivity argument in the torsion-quotient step is an explicit reason not to silently enlarge that scope.

The others are open. Merged into item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:hereditary}.

\section[{Exact diagnostics and their logical scope\srctag{80}}]{Exact diagnostics and their logical scope}\label{gsr:fz:80:sec:d9}\label{gsr:fz:80:sec:diagnostics}
\srcnote{80}{Section 9}
The public companion is a bounded, exact implementation of finite consistency checks. The written proofs above establish the arbitrary-target and infinite-dimensional claims. The computations neither infer those claims from finite sampling nor identify indicator and weighted infima.

\subsection{Direct energy counts}
The implementation constructs finite source points and additive quadruples using exact integer coordinates modulo three. It checks pair-energy identities, the line formula, the list of large derivative partitions, and the six-point spike counts. In the spike case the independently recognizable totals are
\[
 (\mathcal E_V,\mathcal E_a)=(162,106)\quad\hbox{on two lines},
 \qquad (729,505)\quad\hbox{on the full plane}.
\]
For three-point weights $(1,s,1)$, integer polynomial coefficients record the number of occurrences of the middle point in each quadruple. In ascending powers of $s$, the ordinary coefficient vector is
\[
 (6,8,12,0,1),
\]
and the respected vector for the cut is $(6,0,12,0,1)$. Targets $\Z,C_2,C_4,C_6,C_9$ check several nonzero-defect orders, while $C_3$ supplies an affine negative control with identical ordinary and respected polynomials. These are exact enumerations, not floating-point evaluations at $\tau$.

\subsection{All binary maps on one plane}
There are $2^9=512$ maps $\F_3^2\to C_2$. Homomorphisms from an exponent-three group to $C_2$ vanish, so the affine maps are the two constants. A nonaffine cut has one value on a line and the other on its complement. The twelve affine lines therefore give twenty-four such cuts, leaving $486$ maps outside the two families.

The companion enumerates every nonempty indicator support, all $2^9-1=511$ of them, for each map. It obtains
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:80:eq:binary-summary}
 \max_{a\text{ outside}}R_a(\F_3^2)=\frac{505}{729},\qquad
 \max_{a\text{ outside}}\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq\F_3^2}R_a(S)=\frac{53}{81}.
\end{equation}
This is a complete binary-target indicator calculation in rank two. Universal indicator sharpness is proved separately by the arbitrary-target plane argument and the analytic spike certificate. The enumeration does not compute the real weighted infimum for every binary map.

\subsection{All admissible rank-three geometric sections}
The geometric lemma has a useful independent finite diagnostic. The space $\F_3^3$ has $39$ affine planes: there are $13$ normal directions and three levels in each. Inside any plane, the allowed sections are empty, full, one of twelve affine lines, or one of their twelve complements, for $26$ possibilities.

Fix three parallel coordinate planes partitioning the space. Any candidate satisfying the section hypothesis must choose one of these $26$ sections on each. Thus $26^3=17{,}576$ candidates exhaust the possibilities, avoiding an unnecessary scan of all $2^{27}$ subsets. Check each candidate on all $39$ affine planes. Exactly $80$ subsets pass:
\[
 \varnothing,\quad V,\quad 39\text{ affine hyperplanes},\quad
 39\text{ hyperplane complements}.
\]
Every proper nonempty survivor has the form predicted by Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:81:lem:geometry}. This confirms a finite instance of the geometry and its enumeration; the proof in Section~\ref{gsr:en:81:sec:geometry} is what covers arbitrary dimension.

\subsection{An indicator minimum inside one cut}
For the explicit map $a:\F_3^2\to\Z$ given by $a(x,y)=y$ with integer representatives $y=0,1,2$, the companion checks all $511$ nonempty supports and obtains
\[
 \rind(a)=\frac{13}{19},
 \qquad R_a(\F_3^2)=\frac{19}{27}.
\]
Exactly three supports attain $13/19$: the whole plane with one point of the middle row omitted. Each has ordinary energy $456$ and respected energy $312$. This paragraph records a bounded exhaustive exact example, not a premise of the universal proof. It illustrates why the full-plane value $19/27$ must not be called the indicator infimum of a general cut. Independently, the theorem gives its weighted infimum $\rho$, which is smaller than $13/19$: one has $2/3<\tau<7/10$, and hence $6\tau^2-13\tau+6<0$.

\section[{Context boundaries and further questions\srctag{80}}]{Context boundaries and further questions}\label{gsr:fz:80:sec:d10}\label{gsr:fz:80:sec:context}
\srcnote{80}{Section 10}
\subsection{Related work and precise attribution}
Respected additive quadruples and their graph-energy interpretation are classical. Gowers~\cite{gowers}, Sections~6 and~14, treats respected quadruples and a product property quantified over every nonnegative weight. Its normalization is $N^{-1}(\sum f)^4$, whereas the denominator here is the ordinary additive energy $\mathcal E_V(f)$. These can differ substantially. Neither respected energy nor all-weight testing is claimed as a new general idea.

There is especially close finite-geometric precedent. Mizell and Oxley~\cite{mizelloxley} characterize ternary affine targets, which are colorings arising from nested affine flats, by forbidden plane restrictions. In finite dimension, their Theorem~4 and Lemma~19 cover the hyperplane-section lemma under the stronger section hypothesis used here. Indeed, the global coloring is an affine target, so one color lies in a proper flat. If that color contained two points of a line but omitted its third, adjoining a point outside the flat would give a plane section of size two, which is forbidden here. The color is therefore an affine flat, and the singleton-section obstruction makes it a hyperplane. This reduction is a comparison argument, not the wording of their theorem. Our direct proof is shorter and includes infinite dimension; no priority claim is made for the elementary lemma itself.

The present characterization also fits the established framework of affine-invariant testing. For each \emph{fixed finite abelian target} $H$, the family is affine-invariant and has finitely many forbidden labeled nine-point plane patterns. Precomposition by an affine map either leaves a cut transversal to its kernel or puts its image in one coset, in which case the pullback is affine. Thus restriction closure includes degenerate affine maps as well. Bhattacharyya, Fischer, Hatami, Hatami and Lovett~\cite{bfhhl}, Theorem~1.2, supply a nine-query proximity-oblivious testing consequence in this fixed finite-alphabet setting. Its rejection probability has a positive lower bound depending on the distance from the family and on the fixed target, independently of the ambient finite dimension. This is an application of existing qualitative testing machinery. It is not an explicit rate, a nine-query constant-success guarantee for all distances, a bound uniform over arbitrary $H$, or a uniform-sampling theorem in infinite dimension.

Low-degree line and plane testing, such as Haramaty--Shpilka--Sudan~\cite{haramatyshpilkasudan}, provides further precedent for finite-field locality. Its finite-field polynomial setting differs from an arbitrary abelian target with non-three-torsion. Likewise, the sparse-domain affine extension theorem of Conlon--Gowers~\cite{conlongowers} concerns exact Freiman preservation on a random subset, rather than the present deterministic full-domain relative energy inequality.

The sharp complex quartic and the general index-three energy family were developed in Report~291~\cite{srcseventynine}. Section~\ref{gsr:en:81:sec:analytic} includes the full specialization, so the main theorem has no imported classification or analytic dependency. The derivative histogram, six-point witness and common-kernel gluing are elementary arguments, while Fourier orthogonality and affine geometry are standard tools.

The primary-source comparison and precise inspection limits are recorded in \filename{SOURCES.md}. No equivalent combined arbitrary-target energy theorem with these concrete obstructions was located in the inspected passages. That bounded negative finding establishes neither novelty nor publication priority.

\subsection{Questions left open by this report}
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{The best separating constant.} What is the supremum of $r(a)$ over outside-family maps on elementary abelian three-groups with arbitrary abelian targets? The present proof gives the upper bound $\gamma$. Indicator sharpness at $53/81$ determines a different invariant and does not determine this weighted supremum.
\item \textbf{The smallest universal witness size.} Is nine necessary? Can every outside-family map be detected by an indicator on at most six points, perhaps with a different threshold? The full-plane branch does not answer this question, and the six-point spike witness proves sufficiency only for its specific branch.
\item \textbf{Indicator equality maps.} Which outside-family maps have $\rind(a)=53/81$? The single-spike construction proves attainment of the uniform indicator bound. A full classification at that indicator endpoint, or at a future optimal weighted threshold, is not established here.
\item \textbf{Explicit quantitative testing bounds.} With a fixed finite target and uniform measure on $\F_3^n$, what explicit rejection rate follows from a prescribed distance to the affine-or-cut family? General affine-invariant testing machinery supplies qualitative robustness in this finite-alphabet setting, as discussed above; effective rates or bounds uniform over target groups require additional work.
\item \textbf{Indicator optimization inside a cut.} The weighted value is universally $\rho$, but indicator minima can depend on the kernel and the source rank. Determining those minima is a different extremal problem. A three-point transversal alone does not establish the indicator infimum of a larger cut.
\item \textbf{Other source groups.} Can comparable bounded-obstruction classifications hold for other elementary abelian groups, or for general abelian groups with three-torsion? The line arithmetic, nine-point histogram gap, and level-set geometry used here are specific to $\F_3$ and do not automatically extend.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 70--81]
\emph{Answered within this arrival}: the first question by source~81 ($\lambda$, attained by a single order-two spike on $\F_3^2$), and the second for weights at the exact threshold $\lambda$ (nine points are necessary and sufficient, Corollary~\ref{gsr:fm:81:cor:witness-size}); the indicator version of the second, and the others, are open. Merged into item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:hereditary}.
\end{writenote}

\section[{Exact certificates and their logical scope\srctag{81}}]{Exact certificates and their logical scope}\label{gsr:fz:81:sec:d11}\label{gsr:fz:81:sec:certificates}
\srcnote{81}{Section 11}
The main argument has three distinct kinds of evidence. Keeping them separate is essential to the arbitrary-target and real-weight quantifiers.

\paragraph{Analytic and geometric proof.}
The centered Fourier inequality, averaging argument, scalar factorization, equality analysis and weight-stability estimate hold for arbitrary real coordinates in their stated domains. The gluing proof holds for arbitrary dimension. Neither statement is inferred from numerical optimization, a finite target survey, or finite-dimensional experiments. The cut theorem likewise applies a complex quartic pointwise at each Fourier character, and uses a finite group adapted to each finitely supported test.

\paragraph{A complete finite part of the proof.}
Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:81:lem:lattices} is a computer-assisted finite integer lemma. Its universal input consists of all midpoint choices in six formal triples. Every arbitrary-target realization factors through at least one of these relation systems. The $729$ checked integer-lattice identities therefore supply an exhaustive branch of the proof. They are not examples supporting an extrapolation. The certificate records all generator matrices and unimodular transformations so that its assertions can be checked by exact multiplication and determinant calculations, independently of trusting a normal-form name.

\paragraph{Supplemental exact diagnostics.}
The companion also verifies finite identities appearing elsewhere: the line relation count, all ordered source quadruples, the named binary and order-nine witness counts, derivative histograms, the generic $361$ count, the centered polynomial identities, Fourier normalizations, the scalar factorization, and exact radical comparisons. Such checks detect transcription or implementation errors. They do not replace the inequality chain in Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:81:lem:centered}, the nonnegative-remainder reasoning, or the geometric proof. In particular, a sample of weights could not prove the global lower bound or rule out zero-support minimizers.

The public code uses the Python standard library and exact integer or rational arithmetic. Its certificate and output are deterministic. The normal and optimized Python modes must have identical standard output, and every protection used by the builder remains active under optimization. Reproduction runs the code in an isolated staged tree and verifies that neither the original nor staged source changes.

\subsection{How to inspect the lattice certificate}
A reader wishing to audit only the finite lemma can proceed independently of the rest of the diagnostics:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Reconstruct the nine transversal lines from~\eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:nonaligned}; check the six distinct translated triples and their stated multiplicities.
\item Reconstruct all three midpoint relation vectors for each triple. Loop over the $729$ six-tuples of midpoint choices, retaining each input matrix $M$.
\item Check each retained transformation identity~\eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:unimodular}, including the determinant sign. Row operations therefore preserve the full integer lattice, not just rational rank.
\item Check the candidate-basis transformation records, compare the resulting bases, and count occurrences of each of the eight lattices.
\item Read off~\eqref{gsr:en:81:eq:six-torsion} in the surviving cases and continue with the exponent-three affine reduction. This last step is a group-theoretic proof in the actual target.
\end{enumerate}
The distinction between integer span and rational span is indispensable. Replacing a lattice by its saturation could erase precisely the two- and three-torsion information on which the case split depends.

\section[{Context and further questions\srctag{81}}]{Context and further questions}\label{gsr:fz:81:sec:d12}\label{gsr:fz:81:sec:context}
\srcnote{81}{Section 12}
\subsection{Relation to existing literature}
Respected additive quadruples and their interpretation as additive quadruples in a graph are classical. Gowers~\cite{gowers} treats respected additive quadruples in Section~6 and explicitly uses nonnegative product weights in Section~14. The product-property benchmark there is $N^{-1}(\sum f)^4$, while this report divides by ordinary additive energy. Cauchy's inequality gives $\EaddV(f)\ge N^{-1}(\sum f)^4$ on a finite group of order $N$; the two relative lower-bound hypotheses are therefore not equivalent. Neither graph energy nor quantification over all nonnegative weights is claimed as a new idea here.

There is also substantial geometric precedent. Mizell and Oxley~\cite{mizelloxley}, Theorem~4, characterize finite-dimensional ternary affine targets, colorings obtained from nested affine flats, by forbidden plane restrictions. Their theorem is broader than the particular hyperplane/complement section lemma used here. Under our stronger section hypothesis, it gives a finite-dimensional target, one color of which lies in a proper affine flat. The section restriction then forces that color to be line-closed and of codimension one. This is a derived comparison with their theorem, not an energy conclusion stated there. The direct proof in Section~\ref{gsr:en:81:sec:geometry} also handles infinite dimension. No priority claim is made for its elementary finite-dimensional geometry.

For each fixed finite abelian target, local affine-invariant characterization places the favorable family in the testing framework of Bhattacharyya, Fischer, Hatami, Hatami and Lovett~\cite{bfhhl}. Their result supplies qualitative proximity-oblivious testing from a bounded local characterization. It does not determine the sharp energy ratio, an explicit rejection rate uniform over targets, or a uniform sampling theorem in infinite dimension. Conlon and Gowers~\cite{conlongowers} prove affine extension for exact Freiman homomorphisms on suitable random sparse domains, with arbitrary abelian targets. Their sparse-domain exact-preservation hypothesis differs from the full-domain energy infimum used here.

The present contribution relative to Report~292 is the exact weighted constant and its all-weight spike optimization, together with the full plane equality statement and explicit remainder separation. The scalar optimization only becomes conclusive after the centered Fourier estimate justifies the reduction from eight independent ordinary weights to their common mean. A symmetry heuristic or successful numerical search would not supply that justification.

A bounded comparison of primary sources did not locate an equivalent theorem with this constant and these spike minimizers. This does not establish novelty or publication priority. The inspection did not include a systematic MathSciNet or zbMATH review, exhaustive citation tracing, or a comprehensive search of unpublished work. Further historical investigation, especially of finite Fourier reflection inequalities, remains worthwhile. The precise source scope is recorded in \filename{SOURCES.md}.

\subsection{Questions not settled here}
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Higher-rank equality structure.} The report proves uniform sharpness with a rank-two witness and classifies equality only on the plane. It does not classify all higher-rank maps with $r(a)=\lambda$, or describe compatibility conditions among their extremal plane restrictions.
\item \textbf{The next plane value.} The upper bound $677/1161$ for nonspike unfavorable plane maps is a convenient explicit separation. Its exact optimal replacement, and the maps attaining it, are not determined here. The fixed two-level weights used for this bound are not claimed to be optimal for their maps.
\item \textbf{Map stability.} Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:81:cor:stability} controls near-minimizing weights for one fixed spike pattern. A metric theorem classifying arbitrary maps whose weighted infima are close to $\lambda$ would be a different statement, requiring a suitable distance and target hypotheses.
\item \textbf{Witness complexity.} Corollary~\ref{gsr:fm:81:cor:witness-size} settles the optimal support size at the exact threshold $\lambda$: nine points are necessary and sufficient, and a rational-valued exact-threshold witness need not exist. Optimal witness sizes and rational coefficient bounds at thresholds strictly above $\lambda$ remain different questions.
\item \textbf{Indicator and testing refinements.} Indicator equality maps, indicator minima inside larger cuts, and effective distance-dependent rejection rates remain separate problems. The sharp indicator constant $53/81$ from Report~292 must not be substituted for the weighted constant $\lambda$.
\item \textbf{A shorter nonenumerative argument.} A conceptual derivation of the nonaligned six-torsion conclusion could replace the $729$-choice certificate. The present proof is complete with its certificate, but does not claim that enumeration is necessary.
\item \textbf{Other domains.} The cyclic three-point arithmetic, four-direction histogram calculation, and hyperplane-section geometry are specific to elementary abelian three-groups. This report does not transfer the classification to arbitrary abelian source groups.
\end{enumerate}

\section[{Mathematical provenance and scope\srctag{81}}]{Mathematical provenance and scope}\label{gsr:fz:81:sec:dB}\label{gsr:fz:81:app:provenance}
\srcnote{81}{Appendix B}
This report combines a structural arbitrary-target plane upper bound with an independently derived all-weight spike lower bound. The source development initially established only an upper bound: its one-parameter spike calculation could not alone imply sharpness. The centered Fourier argument supplies that missing lower bound, and the generic high-branch count then gives the plane equality classification and separated remainder. These logical dependencies are reflected explicitly in the manuscript.

The derivative reductions and affine-plane gluing were already established in Report~292. Their full proofs are reproduced here so that the all-rank statement does not depend on a numerical threshold or an unquoted gluing assumption from an earlier report. The complex quartic and cut-energy argument originate in Report~291 and are also reproduced in the needed exponent-three form. The new finite relation certificate concerns formal integer relations in arbitrary targets, rather than bounded-modulus target testing.

Reports~1--292 are immutable historical artifacts. No earlier manuscript is overwritten by this report, and no statement here is a proof-assistant certification. The accompanying exact arithmetic certificate proves a bounded finite lemma; it is not a Lean formalization of the analytic and geometric arguments. Primary literature is cited for context and attribution, not as an unproved substitute for any step of the weighted gap theorem.

\section{Sources~84 and~86: the explicit five-term threshold \wtag}\label{gsr:fz:sec:fiveterm}
\par\noindent{\small\textit{Added in the thirteenth write, 7~October 2026.}}\par
The next fourteen sections are source~84's Sections~2--7 and source~86's Sections~2--9 (Reports~296 and~298), on the repository's own explicit five-term thresholds. This report has no Section~18 chapter; the iteration bookkeeping of sources~03 and~10 and item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:V:ledger} are the printed neighbours, and the remaining sections of sources~82--94 follow this chapter.

\emph{The two thresholds.} At the pin \texttt{af74fb522} the Lean development defines two explicit five-term starting thresholds, \file{fiveTermThreshold} $=H_{\mathrm o}$ (\file{Proofs18ExplicitFiveTerm.lean}, line~10) and \file{fejerFiveTermThreshold} $=H_{\mathrm f}$ (\file{Proofs18FejerFiveTerm.lean}, line~10), each sufficient for a five-term progression in a set of density $\delta$ (\file{natural_five_term_fejer}, line~18). \emph{Source~84} proves $\log H_{\mathrm f}<R^{-n_{\mathrm f}}\log H_{\mathrm o}\le\frac14\log H_{\mathrm o}$, hence $H_{\mathrm f}<H_{\mathrm o}^{1/4}<H_{\mathrm o}$ on $0<\delta\le1$, with the exact size-exponent gain $R=2^{x^{2^{88}}-x^{2^{53}}}x^{24718(2^{76}-2^{42})}\ge4$, $x=2/\alpha$, $\alpha=(\delta^5/64000)^{16}$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:84:thm:main}). \emph{Source~86} proves $\log_2\log_2H_{\mathrm f}(\delta)\le x^{2^{67}}$ and $H_{\mathrm f}(\delta)<2^{2^{\delta^{-2^{76}}}}<2^{2^{\delta^{-2^{16384}}}}$ for $0<\delta\le1/2$, the last being Gowers's Theorem~18.2 at $k=5$ with its right-associated power chain (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:86:thm:main}); source~86 cites source~84, and both compare repository constructions, not external bounds, as they say.

\emph{Superseded and extended by the formal development} (checked at HEAD \texttt{bf285410b}). At \texttt{aee4846af} (07:31, before both arrived) the repository proved \file{fejerFiveTermThreshold_le_explicit_tower} with exponent $2^{1100}$, recorded correctly by source~86's status check; after their arrival it proved the same theorem with the inner exponent $2^{76}$ (\texttt{0d0033b0f}, 12:17; the commit names no source) and then $2^{73}$ (\texttt{3f61aea0a}, 12:59). At HEAD the theorem reads $H_{\mathrm f}(\delta)\le2^{2^{\delta^{-2^{73}}}}$ for $0<\delta\le1/2$ (\file{Proofs18FiveTermSourceThreshold.lean}, line~12), with \file{five_term_explicit_tower_lt_source} (line~71), \file{natural_five_term_explicit_tower} (line~92) and \file{theorem_18_2_five_holds} (line~100), the exact five-term instance of Theorem~18.2. \emph{So source~86's headline is a formal theorem with a smaller exponent}, $2^{73}<2^{76}$; its intermediate estimate and its proof remain its own. Source~84's comparison of the two constructions has no formal counterpart: no declaration relates \file{fiveTermThreshold} and \file{fejerFiveTermThreshold} (searched at HEAD). Every excerpt of their source records (48 and~56: the definitions and declarations they reduce) still occurs verbatim at HEAD (checked at the write), so their theorems apply to the current expressions. \file{theorem_18_2} (\file{Sections17\_18.lean}, line~190), the general statement, stays open.

\emph{Checked at the write} (\file{verify13.py}): source~84's integer identities ($25378984=12380\cdot2048+24744$, $12801=512\cdot25+1$, $64000=512\cdot5^3$) and $R\ge4$; source~86's conversion $2^{67}(1+16\log_264000+80L)<2^{76}L$ for $L=\log_2(1/\delta)\ge1$ (since $1+16\log_264000<257$ and $257+80L\le512L$); $2^{2^{k+9}}=2^{16384}$ at $k=5$. The two companions were rerun on copies with only their Linux-only read primitive replaced, normally and with \texttt{-O}.
