\section[{Exact definitions and source reductions\srctag{84}}]{Exact definitions and source reductions}\label{gsr:fz:84:sec:d2}\label{gsr:fz:84:sec:definitions}
\srcnote{84}{Section 2}
All logarithms are natural logarithms. Powers of positive real numbers have their usual real meaning. A ceiling of a positive real is the least integer at least as large as it; the natural-number ceiling in the source agrees with that integer. Throughout the local comparison, fix
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:84:eq:alpha-range}
 0<\alpha\le1,
\end{equation}
and use an index $i\in\{\old,\fej\}$.

\subsection{The two local parameter systems}
Set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:84:eq:dr}
 (d_{\old},r_{\old})=(2^{76},2^{88}),\qquad
 (d_{\fej},r_{\fej})=(2^{42},2^{53}).
\end{equation}
The local quadratic parameter, retained mass parameter, and localization exponent are respectively
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:84:eq:ame}
 a_i=2^{-71}\alpha^2(\alpha/2)^{d_i},\qquad
 \mu_i=2^{-59}\alpha^2(\alpha/2)^{d_i},\qquad
 e_i=2^{-(2/\alpha)^{r_i}}.
\end{equation}
For the old construction, $a_i$ and $\mu_i$ occur in
\sourceeightyfour{Proofs18CubicCellModels}{the cubic cell-model definitions}, while $e_i$ appears in
\sourceeightyfour{Proofs18CubicTwistedDiscrepancy}{the cubic twisted-discrepancy definitions}.
The Fej\'er versions are in
\sourceeightyfour{Proofs18FejerCubicParameters}{the Fej\'er cubic-parameter file}.

Two common quadratic functions reduce exactly to
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:84:eq:bs}
 b(a)=2^{-20}a^2(a/2)^{12359},\qquad
 s(a)=2^{-26}(a/2)^{24718}.
\end{equation}
They are the source's quadratic discrepancy parameter and quadratic discrepancy exponent. To check the less immediate second reduction, the source gives
\[
 \filename{cor711Exponent}(z,1)=2^{-14}z^2,
 \qquad
 s(a)=\frac{\filename{cor711Exponent}((a/2)^{12359},1)}{4096}.
\]
Since $4096=2^{12}$ and $2\cdot12359=24718$, formula~\eqref{gsr:fz:84:eq:bs} follows with no inequality or rounding.

\subsection{The common refinement constants}
For $k\ge1$ and $\eta>0$ define
\begin{align}
 P_k&=(k!)^2\,2^{(k+1)^2},
 &W_k&=\left(2^{2^{40k^3}}\right)^2,\label{gsr:fz:84:eq:PW}\\
 L_k(\eta)&=\max\{W_k,(4\pi/\eta)^{P_k},4^{P_k}\}+4,
 &B(\varepsilon)&=L_1(4\pi\varepsilon).\label{gsr:fz:84:eq:LB}
\end{align}
Here $P_k$ is \filename{polynomialPartitionConstant}; $W_k$ is
\filename{polynomialPartitionThreshold}, the \emph{square} of the Weyl threshold; $L_k$ is \filename{section5LocalRefinementConstant}; and $B$ is \filename{boundaryRefinementConstant}. The additive $4$ lies outside the maximum. In particular
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:84:eq:P}
 P=P_3=36\cdot65536=2359296,\qquad q=1/P,
 \qquad B_0=B(1/16).
\end{equation}
Although these constants can be extremely large, all are finite real numbers. The comparison needs no decimal evaluation of them.

The remaining local parameters are
\begin{align}
 t_i&=s(a_i)/16,&
 K_i&=\max\{1,2B_0\,8^{1-t_i}\},&
 D_i&=K_i12^{t_i},\label{gsr:fz:84:eq:counts}\\
 w_i&=\mu_i b(a_i),&
 \beta_i&=w_i/2,&
 \sigma_i&=e_it_i/(2P),\label{gsr:fz:84:eq:beta-sigma}\\
 C_i&=L_3(w_i)D_i^q.&&&&\label{gsr:fz:84:eq:C}
\end{align}
These are, in sequence, the local-count exponent, local-count constant, twisted-count constant, twisted discrepancy parameter, untwisted discrepancy parameter, untwisted size exponent, and phase-refinement constant. The symbol $C_i$ is a count-related constant; it is not the final threshold.

\subsection{The complete starting thresholds}
The common quadratic starting threshold is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:84:eq:E}
 E(a)=\exp\!\left((4+6L_2(1))(2/a)^{25378984}\right),
 \qquad25378984=12380\cdot2048+24744.
\end{equation}
For $u>0$ put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:84:eq:PP}
 \PPop(z,u)=\max\{1,\max\{1,z\}^{1/u}\}.
\end{equation}
This is exactly \filename{positivePowerThreshold}\,$z\,1\,u$. The more general source definition is $\max\{1,\max\{1,C/D\}^{1/e}\}$; the second argument equals $1$ at every use here.

Let $F(\alpha)$ denote the identical source expression
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:84:eq:F}
 F(\alpha)=\max\{\mathcal F(\alpha),
                   \mathcal G((\alpha/2)^{4207554485})\},
\end{equation}
where $\mathcal F=\filename{section13FrequencyGraphThreshold}$ and
$\mathcal G=\filename{section13GeometricThreshold}$ at the pinned revision.
Thus $F$ is \filename{section13FourierThreshold}. This is an exact reference to a shared finite expression, not an upper bound for it. Its underlying finite maxima, integer roundings, and geometric constants are left intact. Their further expansion is immaterial: the proof below works for \emph{any common finite real value} $F(\alpha)$. In particular, it neither assumes nor proves that $F$ is monotone. This convention isolates the exact source component that cancels from the comparison without claiming a full dependency expansion.

The odd-square, twisted, and complete cubic inverse thresholds are
\begin{align}
 O_i&=\max\{F(\alpha),\PPop(4,e_i)\},\label{gsr:fz:84:eq:O}\\
 U_i&=\max\{256,O_i,
       \PPop(12\max\{2,\max\{4,E(a_i)\}\},e_i)\},\label{gsr:fz:84:eq:U}\\
 T_i&=\max\{U_i,\PPop(C_i,\sigma_i)\}.\label{gsr:fz:84:eq:T}
\end{align}
Here $U_i$ is the prime-model threshold evaluated at
$\max\{4,E(a_i)\}$, precisely as in the source's twisted-threshold definition. The $12$, $256$, and each displayed maximum have been retained. Writing a maximum of three entries rather than the associated nested binary maxima is an exact reassociation.

\subsection{The final density iteration}
Now let $0<\delta\le1$ and set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:84:eq:density-alpha}
 \alpha=(\delta^5/64000)^{16}.
\end{equation}
This is the specialization at $k=5$ of
\[
 \filename{intervalUniformityParameter}(\delta,k)
 =\left(\frac{\delta^k}{512k^3}\right)^{2^{k-1}}.
\]
It belongs to $(0,1]$. Evaluate all the preceding quantities at this $\alpha$ and put
\begin{align}
 S_i&=\max\{5,T_i,32/\beta_i,12801/\delta^5\},\label{gsr:fz:84:eq:S}\\
 c_i&=\frac{\beta_i}{8B(\beta_i/64)},
 &n_i&=\left\lceil\frac8{\beta_i}\right\rceil,\label{gsr:fz:84:eq:cn}\\
 A_i&=1+\log\max\{1,S_i\}+|\log c_i|,
 &Q_i&=2\max\{1,16/\sigma_i\},\label{gsr:fz:84:eq:AQ}\\
 H_i&=\exp(A_iQ_i^{n_i}).&&\label{gsr:fz:84:eq:H}
\end{align}
The number $12801$ is $512\cdot5^2+1$. The iteration uses $\rho_i=\sigma_i/16$, so $\rho_i^{-1}=16/\sigma_i$. Its number of steps is the natural-number ceiling of $(\beta_i/8)^{-1}=8/\beta_i$. The source's closed density-iteration threshold is
\[
 \exp\!\left(\bigl(1+\log\max\{1,T\}+|\log c|\bigr)
                 \bigl(2\max\{1,\rho^{-1}\}\bigr)^n\right).
\]
Substituting $T=S_i$, $c=c_i$, $\rho=\rho_i$, and $n=n_i$ yields~\eqref{gsr:fz:84:eq:H} exactly. This establishes the promised identification with the two five-term source definitions.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Signs and monotonicity\srctag{84}}]{Signs and monotonicity}\label{gsr:fz:84:sec:d3}\label{gsr:fz:84:sec:signs}
\srcnote{84}{Section 3}
\begin{lemma}\label{gsr:fz:84:lem:signs}
Under~\eqref{gsr:fz:84:eq:alpha-range},
\begin{gather}
 0<a_{\old}<a_{\fej}\le1,\qquad
 0<\mu_{\old}<\mu_{\fej}\le1,\label{gsr:fz:84:eq:am-order}\\
 0<t_{\old}<t_{\fej}\le1,\qquad
 0<w_{\old}<w_{\fej},\qquad
 0<\beta_{\old}<\beta_{\fej}<1,\label{gsr:fz:84:eq:tb-order}\\
 0<e_i<1,\qquad 0<\sigma_i<1,\qquad C_i\ge4.\label{gsr:fz:84:eq:es-order}
\end{gather}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The number $\alpha/2$ lies in $(0,1/2]$. Since $d_{\fej}<d_{\old}$, decreasing the exponent strictly increases its power. The positive common factors in~\eqref{gsr:fz:84:eq:ame} give~\eqref{gsr:fz:84:eq:am-order}. Each upper bound by $1$ follows by bounding the factors individually by $1$.

For positive arguments the functions $b$ and $s$ in~\eqref{gsr:fz:84:eq:bs} are strictly increasing monomials, with positive degrees $12361$ and $24718$. Thus $t_{\fej}>t_{\old}>0$ and $w_{\fej}>w_{\old}>0$. The elementary upper bounds
\[
 s(a_i)\le2^{-26},\qquad b(a_i)\le2^{-20},\qquad\mu_i\le1
\]
give $t_i\le2^{-30}\le1$ and $\beta_i\le2^{-21}<1$.
The exponent $(2/\alpha)^{r_i}$ is positive, so $0<e_i<1$.
Since $P\ge1$, formula~\eqref{gsr:fz:84:eq:beta-sigma} then yields $0<\sigma_i<1$.
Finally, $K_i\ge1$ and $12^{t_i}\ge1$, whence $D_i\ge1$.
Together with $L_3(w_i)\ge4$ and $q>0$ this proves $C_i\ge4$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{gsr:fz:84:lem:monotone}
For each $k\ge1$, $L_k$ and $B$ are positive, at least $4$, and nonincreasing on positive arguments. The function $E$ is decreasing on positive arguments. For $u>0$, $\PPop(z,u)$ is nondecreasing in $z$; for fixed $z$ it is nonincreasing in $u>0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
In~\eqref{gsr:fz:84:eq:LB}, the only $\eta$-dependent entry is $(4\pi/\eta)^{P_k}$, which decreases because $P_k>0$. Taking the maximum with fixed entries, then adding $4$, preserves weak order. Substituting $4\pi\varepsilon$ gives the assertions for $B$. The exponent in~\eqref{gsr:fz:84:eq:E} decreases with $a>0$, and the exponential is increasing.

For~\eqref{gsr:fz:84:eq:PP}, its inner base is at least $1$. Increasing that base increases a positive power, and increasing $u$ decreases the exponent $1/u$. Both outer and inner maxima preserve the required order. This verifies the signs needed when using power monotonicity.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Quantitative gain in the size exponent\srctag{84}}]{Quantitative gain in the size exponent}\label{gsr:fz:84:sec:d4}\label{gsr:fz:84:sec:gain}
\srcnote{84}{Section 4}
\begin{lemma}\label{gsr:fz:84:lem:gain}
For $0<\alpha\le1$, the ratio $R=\sigma_{\fej}/\sigma_{\old}$ is exactly~\eqref{gsr:fm:84:eq:R}, with $x=2/\alpha$ and $\Delta=d_{\old}-d_{\fej}$. Moreover $R\ge4$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $m=r_{\fej}=2^{53}$ and $M=r_{\old}=2^{88}$. Then $x\ge2$ and $M\ge m+1$. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:84:eq:xgap}
 x^M-x^m\ge x^{m+1}-x^m=(x-1)x^m\ge2.
\end{equation}
The last inequality uses $x-1\ge1$, $m\ge1$, and $x^m\ge2$. Thus
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:84:eq:egain}
 \frac{e_{\fej}}{e_{\old}}
   =2^{x^M-x^m}\ge4.
\end{equation}
Also, cancellation of the common factors in~\eqref{gsr:fz:84:eq:ame} gives
\[
 \frac{a_{\fej}}{a_{\old}}
  =(\alpha/2)^{d_{\fej}-d_{\old}}=x^\Delta.
\]
The constant and the division by $16$ in $t_i=s(a_i)/16$ cancel in a ratio. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:84:eq:tratio}
 \frac{t_{\fej}}{t_{\old}}
   =\left(\frac{a_{\fej}}{a_{\old}}\right)^{24718}
   =x^{24718\Delta}>1.
\end{equation}
The common $2P$ in $\sigma_i$ cancels too, proving
\[
 R=\frac{e_{\fej}}{e_{\old}}\frac{t_{\fej}}{t_{\old}}
  =2^{x^M-x^m}x^{24718\Delta}\ge4.
\]
\end{proof}

The proof deliberately uses the very coarse gain $4$ when absorbing the phase-count loss. This makes that part independent of huge exponent arithmetic. Keeping the exact ratio costs nothing in the final iteration and yields~\eqref{gsr:fm:84:eq:sharp-log}.

\begin{remark}[An additional exact parameter identity]\label{gsr:fz:84:rem:beta}
The same cancellation gives
\[
 \frac{\beta_{\fej}}{\beta_{\old}}=x^{12362\Delta}.
\]
Indeed $b(a)$ has degree $12361$ in $a$, while $\mu_{\fej}/\mu_{\old}=x^\Delta$ supplies one further power. This identity explains the strict discrepancy improvement but is not needed to estimate the ceiling difference. We use only $n_{\fej}\le n_{\old}$.
\end{remark}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Controlling the unfavorable phase factor\srctag{84}}]{Controlling the unfavorable phase factor}\label{gsr:fz:84:sec:d5}\label{gsr:fz:84:sec:phase}
\srcnote{84}{Section 5}
\begin{lemma}\label{gsr:fz:84:lem:phase}
The phase-refinement constants satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:84:eq:Cfactor}
 D_{\fej}\le12D_{\old},\qquad
 C_{\fej}\le12^qC_{\old}\le12C_{\old}.
\end{equation}
Nevertheless their complete power thresholds obey the strict inequality
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:84:eq:phase-strict}
 \PPop(C_{\fej},\sigma_{\fej})
 <\PPop(C_{\old},\sigma_{\old}).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Since $t_{\fej}\ge t_{\old}$, the function $8^{1-t}$ decreases and the maximum defining $K_i$ gives $K_{\fej}\le K_{\old}$. The factor $12^{t_i}$, however, increases. Directly,
\[
 D_{\fej}=K_{\fej}12^{t_{\fej}}
 \le K_{\old}12^{t_{\fej}}
 =D_{\old}12^{t_{\fej}-t_{\old}}\le12D_{\old},
\]
because $0\le t_{\fej}-t_{\old}\le1$.

Next $w_{\fej}\ge w_{\old}>0$, so Lemma~\ref{gsr:fz:84:lem:monotone} gives
$L_3(w_{\fej})\le L_3(w_{\old})$. Using $0<q\le1$, we obtain
\[
 C_{\fej}=L_3(w_{\fej})D_{\fej}^q
 \le L_3(w_{\old})(12D_{\old})^q
 =12^qC_{\old}\le12C_{\old}.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{gsr:fz:84:lem:signs}, $C_{\old}\ge4$. Thus
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:84:eq:absorb}
 12C_{\old}<C_{\old}^4,
\end{equation}
since $12<4^3\le C_{\old}^3$. Both $C_i\ge4$, so the positive-power thresholds reduce exactly to $C_i^{1/\sigma_i}$. With $\sigma_{\fej}\ge4\sigma_{\old}$, the preceding strict comparison gives
\begin{align*}
 \PPop(C_{\fej},\sigma_{\fej})
 &=C_{\fej}^{1/\sigma_{\fej}}\\
 &<C_{\old}^{4/\sigma_{\fej}}\\
 &\le C_{\old}^{1/\sigma_{\old}}
 =\PPop(C_{\old},\sigma_{\old}).
\end{align*}
Every base is positive and the common comparison base is greater than one; every exponent used to raise an inequality is positive.
\end{proof}

It would be incorrect to deduce $D_{\fej}\le D_{\old}$ merely from the decrease of $K_i$. In fact, because $B_0\ge4$ and $t_i\le1$, the second branch of $K_i$ is at least $8$ and is active. Consequently
\[
 D_i=2B_0\,8^{1-t_i}12^{t_i}
     =16B_0(3/2)^{t_i},
\]
which strictly \emph{increases} with $t_i$. The safe factor-$12$ argument above does not need this simplification. The monotonicity of the product defining $C_i$ is not assumed: its refinement factor decreases while its count factor increases.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Comparison through every maximum\srctag{84}}]{Comparison through every maximum}\label{gsr:fz:84:sec:d6}\label{gsr:fz:84:sec:maxima}
\srcnote{84}{Section 6}
\begin{proposition}\label{gsr:fz:84:prop:T}
For arbitrary $0<\alpha\le1$, and even for an arbitrary common finite real value in place of $F(\alpha)$,
\[
 O_{\fej}\le O_{\old},\qquad U_{\fej}\le U_{\old},
 \qquad T_{\fej}\le T_{\old}.
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{gsr:fz:84:lem:gain}, $e_{\fej}\ge e_{\old}>0$. By Lemma~\ref{gsr:fz:84:lem:monotone},
$\PPop(4,e_{\fej})\le\PPop(4,e_{\old})$.
The other entry in~\eqref{gsr:fz:84:eq:O} is identical, so $O_{\fej}\le O_{\old}$.

Also $a_{\fej}\ge a_{\old}>0$, whence $E(a_{\fej})\le E(a_{\old})$. Define the exact bases
\[
 Z_i=12\max\{2,\max\{4,E(a_i)\}\}.
\]
The nested maxima give $Z_{\fej}\le Z_{\old}$. Applying the two monotonicities separately avoids any ambiguity in their directions:
\[
 \PPop(Z_{\fej},e_{\fej})
 \le\PPop(Z_{\old},e_{\fej})
 \le\PPop(Z_{\old},e_{\old}).
\]
Taking the maximum with the shared $256$ and the ordered $O_i$ proves the comparison of $U_i$. Finally use Lemma~\ref{gsr:fz:84:lem:phase} in~\eqref{gsr:fz:84:eq:T} to conclude $T_{\fej}\le T_{\old}$.
\end{proof}

There is no strictness claim at the intermediate threshold $T_i$. A shared term such as $F(\alpha)$ may dominate both maxima. The final strictness instead comes from the density-iteration coefficients, so this possibility causes no gap.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Strict comparison after density iteration\srctag{84}}]{Strict comparison after density iteration}\label{gsr:fz:84:sec:d7}\label{gsr:fz:84:sec:iteration}
\srcnote{84}{Section 7}
We now prove Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:84:thm:main}. Fix $0<\delta\le1$ and use~\eqref{gsr:fz:84:eq:density-alpha} throughout.

\begin{lemma}\label{gsr:fz:84:lem:iteration-params}
The exact quantities in~\eqref{gsr:fz:84:eq:S}--\eqref{gsr:fz:84:eq:AQ} satisfy
\begin{gather}
 S_{\fej}\le S_{\old},\qquad
 1\le n_{\fej}\le n_{\old},\label{gsr:fz:84:eq:Sn}\\
 0<c_{\old}<c_{\fej}<1,\qquad
 0<A_{\fej}<A_{\old},\label{gsr:fz:84:eq:cA}\\
 Q_i=32/\sigma_i>1,\qquad Q_{\fej}=Q_{\old}/R.
 \label{gsr:fz:84:eq:Qratio}
\end{gather}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
In~\eqref{gsr:fz:84:eq:S}, the first and fourth entries are shared, the second weakly decreases by Proposition~\ref{gsr:fz:84:prop:T}, and the third strictly decreases because $0<\beta_{\old}<\beta_{\fej}$. Hence $S_{\fej}\le S_{\old}$. Similarly $8/\beta_{\fej}<8/\beta_{\old}$, and monotonicity of the ceiling gives $n_{\fej}\le n_{\old}$. A positive argument has natural-number ceiling at least one. No strict comparison between the two ceilings is used.

Since $B$ is positive and nonincreasing,
\[
 0<B(\beta_{\fej}/64)\le B(\beta_{\old}/64).
\]
Consequently
\[
 \frac{\beta_{\fej}}{8B(\beta_{\fej}/64)}
 \ge\frac{\beta_{\fej}}{8B(\beta_{\old}/64)}
 >\frac{\beta_{\old}}{8B(\beta_{\old}/64)}>0.
\]
This proves $c_{\fej}>c_{\old}>0$. Also $B\ge4$ and $\beta_{\fej}<1$ imply $c_{\fej}<1/32<1$. Thus $|\log c_i|=-\log c_i$ and strict increase of the logarithm yields
\[
 -\log c_{\fej}<-\log c_{\old}.
\]
The remaining logarithmic term in $A_i$ weakly decreases with $S_i$. Therefore $A_{\fej}<A_{\old}$. Each $A_i\ge1>0$ because $\log\max\{1,S_i\}\ge0$ and the absolute logarithm is nonnegative.

Finally $0<\sigma_i<1$, so $16/\sigma_i>1$ and the maximum in $Q_i$ selects this entry. This gives $Q_i=32/\sigma_i>1$, and the exact definition of $R$ gives $Q_{\fej}=Q_{\old}/R$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:84:thm:main}]
All quantities are finite and positive where required. Using Lemma~\ref{gsr:fz:84:lem:iteration-params},
\begin{align}
 \log H_{\fej}
 &=A_{\fej}Q_{\fej}^{n_{\fej}}\notag\\
 &<A_{\old}(Q_{\old}/R)^{n_{\fej}}\notag\\
 &=R^{-n_{\fej}}A_{\old}Q_{\old}^{n_{\fej}}\notag\\
 &\le R^{-n_{\fej}}A_{\old}Q_{\old}^{n_{\old}}\notag\\
 &=R^{-n_{\fej}}\log H_{\old}.\label{gsr:fz:84:eq:iteration-chain}
\end{align}
The first strict inequality uses $A_{\fej}<A_{\old}$ and a positive multiplier. The weak inequality uses $Q_{\old}>1$ and $n_{\fej}\le n_{\old}$. This is why equal ceilings do not threaten strictness.

Since $R\ge4$, $n_{\fej}\ge1$, and $\log H_{\old}>0$, we may continue the chain with
\[
 R^{-n_{\fej}}\log H_{\old}
 \le4^{-n_{\fej}}\log H_{\old}
 \le\tfrac14\log H_{\old}.
\]
The same definition gives $\log H_{\fej}>0$, proving~\eqref{gsr:fm:84:eq:sharp-log}.
Exponentiation preserves strict and weak inequalities and satisfies
$\exp(\theta\log H_{\old})=H_{\old}^{\theta}$ for $H_{\old}>0$.
Since $H_{\old}>1$, its fourth root is strictly smaller than itself. This proves~\eqref{gsr:fm:84:eq:main-chain} and the stated simpler conclusion.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Why small densities and the endpoint are covered}
At $\delta=1$, formula~\eqref{gsr:fz:84:eq:density-alpha} still gives a strictly positive $\alpha\le1$, so every step applies. For arbitrarily small positive $\delta$, the expressions can be far beyond floating-point range, but they remain finite real numbers. The proof never approximates them or turns them into machine integers. The point $\delta=0$ is excluded: division by $\delta^5$ and the positive-parameter argument would fail there.

\subsection{A reusable comparison principle}
The final step can be stated independently of the source expressions. Suppose positive quantities satisfy
\[
 0<A_{\fej}<A_{\old},\quad
 Q_{\old}>1,\quad Q_{\fej}\le Q_{\old}/R,\quad
 1\le n_{\fej}\le n_{\old},\quad R\ge1.
\]
Then for $H_i=\exp(A_iQ_i^{n_i})$,
\[
 \log H_{\fej}<R^{-n_{\fej}}\log H_{\old}.
\]
The proof is the same chain as~\eqref{gsr:fz:84:eq:iteration-chain}. This observation separates a general iteration comparison from the source-specific work establishing the hypotheses. In the present application $R\ge4$ also absorbs the earlier phase-removal loss.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Conventions and elementary estimates\srctag{86}}]{Conventions and elementary estimates}\label{gsr:fz:86:sec:d2}\label{gsr:fz:86:sec:elementary}
\srcnote{86}{Section 2}
In the rest of this report, $\log$ means $\log_2$. The natural logarithm is written $\ln$, and $\exp$ has base $e$. Natural-number ceilings and floors have their usual nonnegative meaning. Every argument of a ceiling used in an estimate below is at least one. We retain the exact conventions at a zero denominator separately.

\subsection{Positive power thresholds}
The source's common operation is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:PP}
 \PPop(C,D,u)=\max\left\{1,\max\{1,C/D\}^{1/u}\right\}.
\end{equation}
For positive $C,D,u$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:PPlog}
 \log\PPop(C,D,u)=\frac{\max\{0,\log(C/D)\}}u.
\end{equation}
We abbreviate $\PPop(C,1,u)$ to $\PPop_1(C,u)$.

The exact source uses totalized real division: $1/0=0$. Thus when $u=0$ in~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:PP}, the exponent is zero and the inner base is at least one, so
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:PPzero}
 \PPop(C,D,0)=1\qquad(C,D>0).
\end{equation}
This is a source-semantics identity, not an extension of the positive-$u$ formula by a limiting argument. It is needed for the $q=0$ member of the two finite spectral maxima in Section~\ref{gsr:fz:86:sec:geometric}.

\begin{lemma}[Elementary bounds]\label{gsr:fz:86:lem:elementary}
For $y\ge2$, $m\in\N$, and $r\ge0$, one has
\[
 2^m\le y^m,\qquad \log y\le y,\qquad
 \ceil r\le r+1.
\]
If $r\ge1$, then $\ceil r\le2r$. For $B\ge4$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:elemB}
 B^2\le2^B,\qquad 5B^2+6B\le2^{2B},\qquad \log B\le B.
\end{equation}
Also $\tfrac12\le\ln2<1$ and $1<\pi<4$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The ceiling bounds follow from its defining property. The logarithmic inequalities follow, for example, by differentiating $y-\log_2 y$ on $[2,\infty)$. For the first inequality in~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:elemB}, the function $B-2\log_2 B$ is zero at $4$ and has nonnegative derivative on $[4,\infty)$, since $2/(B\ln2)\le1$. Next,
\[
 5B^2+6B\le8B^2\le2^{B+3}\le2^{2B}.
\]
The bounds on $\ln2$ follow by integrating $1/t$ over $[1,2]$; the elementary bounds on $\pi$ suffice throughout. No floating-point evaluation of a large expression is needed.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Polynomial partition constants}\label{gsr:fz:86:sec:partition}
The exact degree-$j$ constants used below are
\begin{align}
 P_j&=(j!)^2\,2^{(j+1)^2},&
 W_j&=2^{\,2^{40j^3+1}},\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:PW}\\
 L_j(\eta)&=\max\{W_j,(4\pi/\eta)^{P_j},4^{P_j}\}+4,
 &\bd(\varepsilon)&=L_1(4\pi\varepsilon).
 \label{gsr:fz:86:eq:L}
\end{align}
Here $P_j$ is \filename{polynomialPartitionConstant} and $W_j$ is \filename{polynomialPartitionThreshold}. The source defines the latter as the \emph{square} of $2^{2^{40j^3}}$, which gives the $+1$ in~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:PW}. Omitting that square would change the exact expression. The definition of $L_j$ retains its additive $4$ outside the maximum.

The values used repeatedly are
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:partitionvalues}
 P_1=16,\quad P_2=2048=2^{11},\quad
 P_3=P=2359296=36\cdot65536<2^{22},
\end{equation}
with
\[
 \log W_1=2^{41},\qquad\log W_2=2^{321},\qquad
 \log W_3=2^{1081}.
\]
For $q\in\N$, the simultaneous degree-two threshold is exactly
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:simultaneous}
 \mathcal S_q=(2W_2)^{2048^{\max\{q-1,0\}}}.
\end{equation}
The truncated subtraction in~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:simultaneous} records the source's natural subtraction. The estimates for $q\ge1$ use ordinary $q-1$; the zero case is dealt with through~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:PPzero}.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The complete geometric threshold\srctag{86}}]{The complete geometric threshold}\label{gsr:fz:86:sec:d3}\label{gsr:fz:86:sec:geometric}
\srcnote{86}{Section 3}
Fix temporarily $0<\gamma\le1$. This section proves the uniform estimate
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:Ggoal}
 \log G(\gamma)\le 2^{16(2/\gamma)^{2^{32}}},
 \qquad G=\filename{section13GeometricThreshold}.
\end{equation}
All branches of the defining maximum will be displayed. The purpose is to replace a previously shared starting condition by an explicit numerical upper bound; it cannot be left as an unspecified finite constant in a comparison with the paper.

\subsection{Exact primitive parameters}\label{gsr:fz:86:sec:primitive}
Set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:geomB}
 y=2/\gamma,\qquad B=y^{2^{32}},\qquad L=\log(1/\gamma).
\end{equation}
Then $y\ge2$, $L\ge0$, and $B\ge2^{2^{32}}>323$. The exact primitive source reductions are
\begin{align}
 \theta&=2^{-59}\gamma^{176},&
 \theta_1&=2^{-620025}\gamma^{1843952},\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:theta}\\
 \overline Q&=2^{620143}\gamma^{-1844304},&
 Q&=2^{2^{20}}\gamma^{-2^{21}},\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:Q}\\
 K&=2^{114}\gamma^{-320},&
 c&=2^{-228K-1}\gamma^{576K},\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:c}\\
 d_0&=\frac{\theta_1}{64\pi},&
 d&=\min\{1,d_0/2\},\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:d}\\
 k_0&=\ceil K,&
 z&=\frac{2^{-155k_0}(\gamma^{32}/16)^{18k_0}}{k_0},
 \label{gsr:fz:86:eq:z}\\
 e_0&=2^{-13Q},& f&=2^{-100}\gamma^{448},\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:ef}\\
 g&=2^{-284}\gamma^{1408},&W&=2^{135}\gamma^{-704}.
 \label{gsr:fz:86:eq:gW}
\end{align}
The symbols $e_0$ and $k_0$ here are local to the geometric calculation. They are not the later Fej\'er localization exponent or a progression length.

For completeness, the source substitutions behind the less immediate exponents are
\begin{align*}
 \theta&=2^{-37}(\gamma^{32}/16)^{11/2},\\
 \theta_1&=2^{-1882}\theta^{10477},&
 \overline Q&=2^{1882}\theta^{-10479},\\
 K&=2^{74}(\gamma^{32}/16)^{-10},&
 g&=2^{-14}(2^{-135}\gamma^{704})^2.
\end{align*}
Thus $620025=1882+59\cdot10477$, $1843952=176\cdot10477$, $620143=1882+59\cdot10479$, and $1844304=176\cdot10479$. The equality for $K$ also explains why the same integer ceiling occurs in the Section~10 radius $z$. All these are algebraic reductions of the definitions, not asymptotic substitutions.

For integers $q$ with $1\le q\le\floor{\overline Q}$, put
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:uq}
 u_q=\frac{\theta_1^2}{16q}.
\end{equation}
At $q=0$, define $u_0=0$ according to the totalized source division.

\begin{lemma}[A common primitive envelope]\label{gsr:fz:86:lem:primitive}
For all positive $q$ in the indicated finite range,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:primitivebound}
 q,Q,d_0^{-1},d^{-1},u_q^{-1},f^{-1},g^{-1},W\le B.
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:primitivelog}
 \log(c^{-1}),\log(z^{-1})\le B,\qquad
 e_0^{-1}\le2^{13B},
\end{equation}
and $0<c,d_0,d,z,f,g\le1$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Since $\gamma^{-1}\le y$ and $2\le y$, a monomial $2^a\gamma^{-b}$ with nonnegative integer exponents is at most $y^{a+b}$. In particular,
\begin{align*}
 Q&\le y^{2^{20}+2^{21}}\le y^{2^{22}},\\
 \overline Q&\le y^{2464447}\le y^{2^{22}},\\
 d_0^{-1}&<2^{620033}\gamma^{-1843952}
 \le y^{2463985}\le y^{2^{22}}.
\end{align*}
The displayed formulas give $0<d_0<1$, so $d=d_0/2$ and $d^{-1}\le y^{2^{22}+1}$. Also $\theta_1^{-1}\le y^{2463977}$, whence
\[
 u_q^{-1}=16q\theta_1^{-2}
 \le y^{4+2^{22}+2\cdot2463977}\le y^{2^{24}}.
\]
The remaining monomial bounds are
\[
 f^{-1}\le y^{548},\qquad g^{-1}\le y^{1692},\qquad
 W\le y^{839},\qquad K\le y^{434}.
\]
Because $K\ge1$, $k_0\le2K\le y^{435}$. Also $L\le y$, so
\[
 228+576L\le228+576y\le690y\le y^{11}.
\]
Consequently
\begin{align*}
 \log(c^{-1})&=1+K(228+576L)\le y^{446},\\
 \log(z^{-1})&=k_0(227+576L)+\log k_0\le y^{447}.
\end{align*}
For the second line, use $227+576L\le y^{11}$, $\log k_0\le k_0$, and absorb the sum by one additional power of $y$. Every exponent just displayed is at most $2^{32}$. The estimate for $e_0^{-1}$ follows from $Q\le B$. Finally, the exact formulas and $K,k_0\ge1$ give positivity and the upper bounds by one. In particular no use of $u_q^{-1}$ is made at $q=0$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The recurrence branch}\label{gsr:fz:86:sec:recurrence}
The exact recurrence-length threshold is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:Rq}
 R_q=\max\left\{\mathcal S_q+1,\ \PPop(8,1,v_q),\
 \PPop(160+2\gamma^{32},\gamma^{32},v_q)\right\},
 \qquad v_q=2^{-12q}.
\end{equation}
Its initial threshold and finite spectral maximum are
\begin{align}
 I_q&=\PPop(R_q+2,d_0,u_q),\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:Iq}\\
 G_{\rm rec}(\gamma)&=\max\left\{3,
       \max_{0\le q\le\floor{\overline Q}}\ceil{I_q}\right\}.
       \label{gsr:fz:86:eq:Grec}
\end{align}
The upper index is an exact natural floor and the set is nonempty, since it includes zero.

\begin{lemma}[Recurrence estimate]\label{gsr:fz:86:lem:recurrence}
For $1\le q\le\floor{\overline Q}$,
\[
 \log R_q\le2^{13B},\qquad
 \log I_q\le2^{15B},\qquad
 \log\ceil{I_q}\le2^{16B}.
\]
At $q=0$ one has $I_0=1$. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:recbound}
 \log G_{\rm rec}(\gamma)\le2^{16B}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For the first branch of~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:Rq}, use~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:simultaneous} and $\mathcal S_q\ge1$:
\begin{align*}
 \log(\mathcal S_q+1)
 &\le1+(1+2^{321})2^{11(q-1)}\\
 &\le2^{323+11B}\le2^{12B}.
\end{align*}
The last step follows from $B\ge323$. The logarithm of the second branch is $3\cdot2^{12q}\le2^{13B}$. Since $160+2\gamma^{32}\le162<2^8$, the third logarithm is at most
\[
 (8+32L)2^{12q}\le B\,2^{12B}\le2^{13B}.
\]
Here $8+32L\le B$, using $L\le y$ and $B=y^{2^{32}}$. This proves the first estimate.

Because $R_q\ge1$, $R_q+2\le3R_q$, while $d_0^{-1},u_q^{-1}\le B$. Hence~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:PPlog} gives
\[
 \log I_q\le B\bigl(2^{13B}+2+B\bigr)\le2^{15B}.
\]
For the last inequality, $B+2\le2^{13B}$ and $B\le2^B$, so the left side is at most $2^{14B+1}\le2^{15B}$. Since $I_q\ge1$, its ceiling increases the logarithm by at most one:
\[
 \log\ceil{I_q}\le1+2^{15B}\le2^{16B}.
\]
At $q=0$, $u_0=0$, so~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:PPzero} yields $I_0=1$ without estimating an inverse of $u_0$. Finally, $\log3<2^{16B}$ and the logarithm of a finite maximum of positive numbers is the maximum of their logarithms. There is no factor for the number of terms.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The integer budget branch}\label{gsr:fz:86:sec:integer}
The rounded-power threshold is exactly
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:V}
 V=\max\{\PPop(1,c,e_0),\PPop(4,d,e_0),\PPop(1,zd,e_0)\}.
\end{equation}
The two layers that remain are
\begin{align}
 B_q&=\max\{V,\PPop(4,d_0,u_q)\},\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:Bq}\\
 G_{\rm int}(\gamma)&=
   \max_{0\le q\le\floor{\overline Q}}\ceil{B_q}.
   \label{gsr:fz:86:eq:Gint}
\end{align}
These are the source's integer-budget threshold at spectrum size $q$ and its density-uniform finite maximum.

\begin{lemma}[Integer budget estimate]\label{gsr:fz:86:lem:integer}
One has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:intbound}
 \log V\le2^{15B},\qquad
 \log G_{\rm int}(\gamma)\le2^{16B}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The three logarithms in~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:V} are bounded, respectively, by
\[
 B\,2^{13B},\quad(2+B)2^{13B},\quad2B\,2^{13B}.
\]
Thus $\log V\le(2B+2)2^{13B}\le2^{15B}$, using $2B+2\le2^{2B}$ for $B\ge4$. For $q\ge1$, the extra branch in~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:Bq} has logarithm at most $(2+B)B\le2^{15B}$. For $q=0$ that branch equals one by~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:PPzero}. Every $B_q\ge1$, so its ceiling adds at most one to the logarithm and gives the bound $2^{16B}$. Take the finite maximum.
\end{proof}

The proof includes three distinct rounding operations: the ceiling $k_0=\ceil K$ in the radius $z$, the ceilings of the individual integer budgets, and the floor limiting the finite spectrum range. They cannot be interchanged or silently omitted.

\subsection{Both square thresholds}\label{gsr:fz:86:sec:squares}
The remaining branches arise from the exact square-length threshold
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:J}
 J=\max\{\PPop(8,1,f),\PPop(W,1,f),
             \PPop(8,(1/4)^g,fg)\}.
\end{equation}
The square-scale and square-power thresholds are, respectively,
\begin{align}
 G_{\rm scale}&=\PPop(J,c,e_0),\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:Gscale}\\
 G_{\rm power}&=\max\left\{\PPop(4,c^f,e_0f),\
   \PPop\left(2,(c^f/4)^{g/2},e_0fg/4\right)\right\}.
   \label{gsr:fz:86:eq:Gpower}
\end{align}

\begin{lemma}[Square estimates]\label{gsr:fz:86:lem:square}
One has
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:squarebound}
 \log J\le5B^2,\qquad
 \log G_{\rm scale}\le2^{15B},\qquad
 \log G_{\rm power}\le2^{15B}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The three logarithms in~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:J} are bounded by
\[
 3/f\le3B,\qquad (\log W)/f\le B^2,\qquad
 (3+2g)/(fg)\le5B^2.
\]
Thus
\[
 \log G_{\rm scale}
 \le(5B^2+B)2^{13B}\le2^{15B},
\]
by~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:elemB}. Both ratios in~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:Gpower} exceed one. The first logarithm simplifies exactly to
\[
 \frac{2/f+\log(c^{-1})}{e_0}.
\]
The second logarithm simplifies exactly to
\[
 \frac{4/(fg)+2\log(c^{-1})+4/f}{e_0}.
\]
These are at most $(4B^2+6B)2^{13B}\le2^{15B}$, again by~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:elemB}. In particular the powers of $c$ have been included inside the logarithm rather than replaced by one.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Geometric envelope]\label{gsr:fz:86:prop:G}
For $0<\gamma\le1$, inequality~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:Ggoal} holds.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The complete defining maximum is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:Gfull}
 G(\gamma)=\max\{1,G_{\rm rec}(\gamma),G_{\rm int}(\gamma),
                   G_{\rm scale},G_{\rm power}\}.
\end{equation}
Lemmas~\ref{gsr:fz:86:lem:recurrence}, \ref{gsr:fz:86:lem:integer}, and~\ref{gsr:fz:86:lem:square} bound every logarithm by $2^{16B}$. There is no further ceiling outside~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:Gfull}. Substitute $B=(2/\gamma)^{2^{32}}$.
\end{proof}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{The complete Fourier threshold\srctag{86}}]{The complete Fourier threshold}\label{gsr:fz:86:sec:d4}\label{gsr:fz:86:sec:Fourier}
\srcnote{86}{Section 4}
Return to $0<\alpha\le1$ and $x=2/\alpha\ge2$. The exact common Fourier threshold is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:Fexact}
 F(\alpha)=\max\{F_{\rm graph}(\alpha),G((\alpha/2)^D)\},
 \qquad D=4207554485.
\end{equation}
The graph branch is the natural-valued frequency-purification threshold. The second branch is the full geometric threshold just bounded.

\subsection{Substitution into the geometric estimate}
Put $\gamma=x^{-D}$. Since $D+1<2^{32}$,
\[
 y=2x^D\le x^{D+1}\le x^{2^{32}},\qquad
 B=y^{2^{32}}\le x^{2^{64}}.
\]
Also $16\le x^4$, so
\[
 16B\le x^{2^{64}+4}\le x^{2^{65}}.
\]
Proposition~\ref{gsr:fz:86:prop:G} therefore gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:Gsub}
 \log G(x^{-D})\le2^{x^{2^{65}}}.
\end{equation}

\subsection{Frequency purification with both ceilings}
Set
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:hj}
 h=14409429,\qquad j=97h+336=1397714949.
\end{equation}
The exact purification parameters in the source are
\[
 \delta_0=x^{-h},\qquad\rho=\delta_0^{97}x^{-336}=x^{-j},
 \qquad\eta=2^{-44}.
\]
The purification definition first forms $\ceil{2^{34}/(\rho\eta)}$ and then a maximum with another natural ceiling. Thus the two exact numerical expressions reduce to
\begin{align}
 M&=\ceil{2^{78}x^j},\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:M}\\
 F_{\rm graph}(\alpha)&=
   \max\left\{2M,\ceil{2^{175}M^{63}x^{j+15h}}\right\}.
   \label{gsr:fz:86:eq:Fgraph}
\end{align}
Each ceiling argument is at least one. Applying the elementary ceiling bound twice gives
\begin{align*}
 M&\le2^{79}x^j\le x^{j+79},\\
 \ceil{2^{175}M^{63}x^{j+15h}}
 &\le2^{176+63\cdot79}x^{64j+15h}
 \le x^{64j+15h+5153}.
\end{align*}
The exponent satisfies the exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:freqdegree}
 64j+15h+5153=89669903324<2^{37}.
\end{equation}
The branch $2M$ has exponent at most $j+80$, which is smaller than the integer on the left of~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:freqdegree}. Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:Fgraphbound}
 F_{\rm graph}(\alpha)\le x^{2^{37}},\qquad
 \log F_{\rm graph}(\alpha)\le2^{37}\log x\le x^{38}.
\end{equation}
The second estimate uses $\log x\le x$ and $2^{37}\le x^{37}$. In particular $x^{38}$, the bound for the logarithm, is not being confused with the much larger $x^{2^{37}}$.

\begin{proposition}[Fourier envelope]\label{gsr:fz:86:prop:F}
For every $0<\alpha\le1$, with $x=2/\alpha$,
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:Fbound}
 \log F(\alpha)\le2^{x^{2^{65}}}.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Combine~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:Gsub} and~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:Fgraphbound} in the exact maximum~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:Fexact}. The bound $x^{38}\le2^{x^{2^{65}}}$ follows by taking logarithms and using $38\log x\le x^{2^{65}}$ for $x\ge2$.
\end{proof}

This proof is pointwise in $\alpha$. It never assumes monotonicity of a threshold whose definition contains a floor-indexed spectral range. Every maximum is bounded by a uniform bound on its entries, rather than replaced by a sum.

\section[{The exact Fej\'er local and iteration expressions\srctag{86}}]{The exact Fej\'er local and iteration expressions}\label{gsr:fz:86:sec:d5}\label{gsr:fz:86:sec:exactlocal}
\srcnote{86}{Section 5}
We now display the complete remaining numerical closure of $H_{\fej}$. Until the density specialization, let $0<\alpha\le1$ and $x=2/\alpha$. To avoid confusion with the geometric coefficient $d$ in~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:d}, write
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:dfej}
 d_{\fej}=2^{42},\qquad P=P_3=2359296.
\end{equation}
The Fej\'er local quadratic parameter and retained mass parameter are exactly
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:amu}
 a=2^{-69}x^{-(d_{\fej}+2)},\qquad
 \mu=2^{-57}x^{-(d_{\fej}+2)}.
\end{equation}
These follow from $a=2^{-71}\alpha^2(\alpha/2)^{d_{\fej}}$ and $\mu=2^{-59}\alpha^2(\alpha/2)^{d_{\fej}}$ by substituting $\alpha=2/x$.

\subsection{Discrepancy and localization parameters}
The common quadratic discrepancy parameter and local count exponent reduce to
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:bt}
 b(a)=2^{-20}a^2(a/2)^{12359},\qquad
 t=2^{-30}(a/2)^{24718}.
\end{equation}
For the second identity, the source quadratic discrepancy exponent is
$2^{-26}(a/2)^{24718}$ and the local count exponent divides it by $16$.
Define
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:wbeta}
 w=\mu b(a),\qquad \beta=w/2,
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:esigma}
 e_{\fej}=2^{-x^{2^{53}}},\qquad
 \sigma=\frac{e_{\fej}t}{2P}.
\end{equation}
The localization exponent $e_{\fej}$ in~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:esigma} is distinct from the geometric exponent $e_0$ in~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:ef}.

\subsection{Phase constants and the quadratic starting condition}
Using~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:L}, put
\begin{align}
 B_0&=\bd(1/16),&K_{\rm count}&=\max\{1,2B_0\,8^{1-t}\},
 \label{gsr:fz:86:eq:Kcount}\\
 D_{\rm count}&=K_{\rm count}\,12^t,&
 C&=L_3(w)D_{\rm count}^{1/P}.
 \label{gsr:fz:86:eq:Cexact}
\end{align}
The quadratic starting threshold is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:Eexact}
 E(a)=\exp\left((4+6L_2(1))(2/a)^m\right),
 \qquad m=25378984=12380\cdot2048+24744.
\end{equation}
Both the fixed coefficient $4+6L_2(1)$ and the integer $m$ matter in the complete comparison. The Weyl threshold inside $L_2(1)$ remains part of this expression.

\subsection{Every starting maximum}
With $F$ as in~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:Fexact}, define
\begin{align}
 O&=\max\{F(\alpha),\PPop_1(4,e_{\fej})\},\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:O}\\
 U&=\max\{256,O,\PPop_1(12\max\{2,\max\{4,E(a)\}\},e_{\fej})\},
 \label{gsr:fz:86:eq:U}\\
 T_{\rm loc}&=\max\{U,\PPop_1(C,\sigma)\}.
 \label{gsr:fz:86:eq:Tloc}
\end{align}
These are the odd-square threshold, the specialized twisted threshold, and the complete Fej\'er cubic inverse threshold. The prime-model threshold specializes to the displayed $U$ at the quadratic input $\max\{4,E(a)\}$. The nested maxima are written explicitly so that a constant such as $256$ or the factor $12$ cannot disappear from the argument.

For $0<\delta\le1$, specialize $\alpha$ and $x$ as in~\eqref{gsr:fm:86:eq:alpha-x}. The general interval uniformity parameter is
\[
 \left(\frac{\delta^k}{512k^3}\right)^{2^{k-1}};
\]
at $k=5$, $512\cdot5^3=64000$ and $2^{5-1}=16$, exactly as in~\eqref{gsr:fm:86:eq:alpha-x}. The full step threshold is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:S}
 S=\max\{5,T_{\rm loc},32/\beta,12801/\delta^5\}.
\end{equation}
The last numerator is $512\cdot5^2+1=12801$.

\subsection{The complete closed iteration}
The remaining source expressions are
\begin{align}
 c_{\rm it}&=\frac{\beta}{8\bd(\beta/64)},&
 n&=\ceil{8/\beta},\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:cn}\\
 A_{\rm it}&=1+\ln(\max\{1,S\})+|\ln c_{\rm it}|,&
 Q_{\rm it}&=2\max\{1,16/\sigma\},\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:AQ}\\
 H_{\fej}(\delta)&=\exp\bigl(A_{\rm it}Q_{\rm it}^{\,n}\bigr).
 &&\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:Hexact}
\end{align}
The ceiling in~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:cn} is exactly the source's natural ceiling of $(\beta/8)^{-1}$. The absolute logarithm in~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:AQ} is a natural logarithm. Neither is an asymptotic proxy for the iteration.

Equations~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:PP}, \eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:PW}--\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:simultaneous}, \eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:theta}--\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:Gfull}, \eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:Fexact}--\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:Fgraph}, and~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:dfej}--\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:Hexact} form a finite numerical specification of the threshold on the stated domain. No unspecified sufficiently large modulus remains in this specification.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Bounding the complete Fej\'er threshold\srctag{86}}]{Bounding the complete Fej\'er threshold}\label{gsr:fz:86:sec:d6}\label{gsr:fz:86:sec:propagation}
\srcnote{86}{Section 6}
All estimates in this section hold for $0<\delta\le1$, with the density specialization~\eqref{gsr:fm:86:eq:alpha-x}. In particular $0<\alpha\le1$ and $x\ge2$.

\subsection{Exact monomials for the discrepancy and count exponent}
Expanding~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:amu}--\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:wbeta} gives
\begin{align}
 \beta&=2^{-865346}x^{-12362(d_{\fej}+2)},\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:betamonomial}\\
 t&=2^{-1730290}x^{-24718(d_{\fej}+2)}.
 \label{gsr:fz:86:eq:tmonomial}
\end{align}
For example, the coefficient exponent in $\beta$ is
\[
 57+20+2\cdot69+12359\cdot70+1=865346,
\]
and its $x$-exponent is $(1+2+12359)(d_{\fej}+2)$. The coefficient exponent in $t$ is $30+70\cdot24718=1730290$. In particular $0<\beta,t,\sigma<1$ and $w=2\beta<1$.

The exact integer inequalities
\begin{align}
 865346+12362(d_{\fej}+2)&=54368650971157718<2^{56},
 \label{gsr:fz:86:eq:betacheck}\\
 1730290+24718(d_{\fej}+2)&=108710913663248398<2^{57}
 \label{gsr:fz:86:eq:tcheck}
\end{align}
therefore imply
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:betatbound}
 \beta^{-1}\le x^{2^{56}},\qquad t^{-1}\le x^{2^{57}}.
\end{equation}
The constant powers of two were absorbed using $x\ge2$; the monomial identities remain exact.

\subsection{The size exponent and iteration count}\label{gsr:fz:86:sec:iterationcount}
Since $2P<2^{23}$, equations~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:esigma} and~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:betatbound} give
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:sigmalog}
 \log(\sigma^{-1})
 \le23+x^{2^{53}}+2^{57}\log x
 \le x^{2^{54}}.
\end{equation}
To check the last absorption uniformly, note
\[
 23+2^{57}\log x\le2^{58}x\le x^{59}\le x^{2^{53}}.
\]
Thus the preceding sum is at most $2x^{2^{53}}\le x^{2^{54}}$.

Because $\sigma<1$, $Q_{\rm it}=32/\sigma$, hence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:Qbound}
 \log Q_{\rm it}=5+\log(\sigma^{-1})\le x^{2^{55}}.
\end{equation}
The ceiling is also controlled explicitly:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:nbound}
 n\le8/\beta+1\le9/\beta\le x^{2^{57}}.
\end{equation}
Indeed $9\le x^4$ and $2^{56}+4\le2^{57}$. Multiplying~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:Qbound} and~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:nbound} yields
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:nQ}
 n\log Q_{\rm it}\le x^{2^{57}+2^{55}}\le x^{2^{58}}.
\end{equation}
No strict inequality between different ceiling values is used or needed.

\subsection{The boundary refinement factor}\label{gsr:fz:86:sec:boundary}
The $\pi$ factors in $\bd(\varepsilon)=L_1(4\pi\varepsilon)$ cancel exactly. Therefore
\[
 \bd(\beta/64)=\max\{W_1,(64/\beta)^{16},4^{16}\}+4.
\]
The maximum is at least $W_1>4$, so the additive $4$ at most doubles it. Using~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:betatbound},
\begin{align}
 \log\bd(\beta/64)
 &\le1+\max\{2^{41},16(6+\log\beta^{-1}),32\}
 \nonumber\\
 &\le x^{63}.\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:bdrybound}
\end{align}
One explicit check is
\[
 96+2^{60}\log x\le(2^6+2^{60})x\le2^{61}x\le x^{62}.
\]
The other entries are at most $x^{62}$ and $1+x^{62}\le x^{63}$. Since $0<\beta<1$ and $\bd(\beta/64)>1$, one has $0<c_{\rm it}<1$. Moreover
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:cbound}
 \log(c_{\rm it}^{-1})
 =3+\log\beta^{-1}+\log\bd(\beta/64)
 \le3+2^{56}\log x+x^{63}\le x^{65}.
\end{equation}
For the last step, $3\le x^{63}$ and $2^{56}\log x\le x^{57}\le x^{63}$, so the sum is at most $3x^{63}\le x^{65}$.

\subsection{The phase count and phase threshold}\label{gsr:fz:86:sec:phase}
At $\varepsilon=1/16$, the non-Weyl entries in~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:L} are $16^{16}=2^{64}$ and $4^{16}=2^{32}$, both below $W_1$. Thus
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:B0}
 B_0=W_1+4\le2W_1.
\end{equation}
Since $0<t<1$, the active branch in~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:Kcount} is $2B_0\,8^{1-t}$. Bounding the two factors separately gives the conservative estimate
\[
 D_{\rm count}=2B_0\,8^{1-t}12^t\le192B_0.
\]
Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:Dcountbound}
 \log D_{\rm count}\le2^{42}\le x^{42}.
\end{equation}
The use of separate upper bounds avoids any inference that both factors move in the same direction as $t$ varies.

Since $w=2\beta<1$ and $w^{-1}\le\beta^{-1}$, $\pi<4$ and~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:L} imply
\begin{align}
 \log L_3(w)
 &\le1+\max\{2^{1081},P(4+\log\beta^{-1}),2P\}
 \nonumber\\
 &\le x^{1082}.\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:L3bound}
\end{align}
For the variable entry, $4+2^{56}\log x\le2^{58}x$, whence
\[
 P(4+\log\beta^{-1})\le2^{80}x\le x^{81}.
\]
The fixed entries are at most $x^{1081}$, so the extra one is absorbed by $x^{1082}$. Equations~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:Cexact}, \eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:Dcountbound}, and~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:L3bound} now yield
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:Clog}
 \log C\le x^{1082}+x^{42}\le x^{1083}.
\end{equation}
Since $C>1$, equations~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:PPlog} and~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:sigmalog} give
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:phasebound}
 \log\PPop_1(C,\sigma)
 \le x^{1083}\,2^{x^{2^{54}}}\le2^{x^{2^{55}}}.
\end{equation}
To see the last step, take a logarithm. The exponent becomes
$1083\log x+x^{2^{54}}\le2x^{2^{54}}\le x^{2^{55}}$; the first inequality follows from $1083\log x\le x^{2^{54}}$ for $x\ge2$.

\subsection{The quadratic starting threshold}\label{gsr:fz:86:sec:quadratic}
The fixed Weyl coefficient in~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:Eexact} is large but must be bounded. Since $\pi<4$ and $P_2=2048$,
\[
 (4\pi)^{P_2}<2^{8192},\qquad4^{P_2}=2^{4096}.
\]
Both are below $W_2=2^{2^{321}}$. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:L2}
 L_2(1)=W_2+4\le2W_2,
 \qquad\frac{4+6L_2(1)}{\ln2}\le32W_2\le2^{2^{323}}.
\end{equation}
The second inequality uses $\ln2\ge\tfrac12$ and $W_2\ge1$.

From~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:amu},
\[
 2/a=2^{70}x^{d_{\fej}+2}\le x^{d_{\fej}+72},
 \qquad m(d_{\fej}+72)<2^{68}.
\]
Taking two binary logarithms of~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:Eexact} gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:Eloglog}
 \log\log E(a)
 \le2^{323}+2^{68}\log x\le x^{324}.
\end{equation}
Indeed each summand is at most $x^{323}$, since $2^{68}\log x\le x^{69}$, and $2x^{323}\le x^{324}$. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:Elog}
 \log E(a)\le2^{x^{324}}.
\end{equation}
The exact expression also gives $E(a)>4$, so the inner maximum in~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:U} equals $E(a)$. It is now legitimate to simplify that branch, and
\begin{align}
 \log\PPop_1(12E(a),e_{\fej})
 &\le2^{x^{2^{53}}}\bigl(4+2^{x^{324}}\bigr)
 \nonumber\\
 &\le2^{x^{2^{54}}}.\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:Ecomposed}
\end{align}
For the last step, the logarithm of the first upper bound is at most
$x^{2^{53}}+1+x^{324}\le2x^{2^{53}}\le x^{2^{54}}$.
The odd-square branch has logarithm $2/e_{\fej}=2^{1+x^{2^{53}}}$ and satisfies the same upper bound.

\subsection{The local threshold and the full step threshold}\label{gsr:fz:86:sec:step}
We can now take the maxima in~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:O}--\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:Tloc}. The complete Fourier branch has logarithm at most $2^{x^{2^{65}}}$ by Proposition~\ref{gsr:fz:86:prop:F}. The phase and localized quadratic branches satisfy the smaller allowances in~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:phasebound} and~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:Ecomposed}; the constant $256$ contributes only $8$. Thus
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:Tlocbound}
 \log T_{\rm loc}\le2^{x^{2^{65}}}.
\end{equation}
For the additional entries in~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:S},
\[
 \log(32/\beta)\le5+2^{56}\log x.
\]
The exact density relation is
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:xdelta}
 x=2\cdot64000^{16}\delta^{-80}.
\end{equation}
Since $\delta\le1$, it implies $\delta^{-5}\le x$, hence
\[
 \log(12801/\delta^5)<14+\log x.
\]
Both expressions, as well as $\log5$, are at most the right side of~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:Tlocbound}. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:Sbound}
 \log S\le2^{x^{2^{65}}}.
\end{equation}

\subsection{The final density iteration}\label{gsr:fz:86:sec:finaliteration}
The preceding inequalities control every factor in~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:Hexact}. Since $S\ge5$ and $c_{\rm it}<1$, the signs and the maximum inside~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:AQ} simplify exactly:
\[
 A_{\rm it}=1+\ln S+\ln(c_{\rm it}^{-1}).
\]
Using $\ln2<1$, equations~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:cbound} and~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:Sbound} give
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:Abound}
 A_{\rm it}\le1+2^{x^{2^{65}}}+x^{65}
 \le2^{x^{2^{65}}+1},\qquad
 \log A_{\rm it}\le x^{2^{66}}.
\end{equation}
For example $1+x^{65}\le x^{66}\le x^{2^{65}}\le2^{x^{2^{65}}}$, which justifies the first absorption. The last follows from $x^{2^{65}}+1\le x^{2^{66}}$.

Finally, $H_{\fej}>1$ and its exact natural-exponential form implies
\begin{align}
 \log\log H_{\fej}
 &=\log A_{\rm it}+n\log Q_{\rm it}-\log(\ln2)
 \nonumber\\
 &\le x^{2^{66}}+x^{2^{58}}+1
 \le x^{2^{67}}.\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:finalintermediate}
\end{align}
Here $-\log(\ln2)\le1$ because $\ln2\ge\tfrac12$. For the last inequality, all three summands are at most $x^{2^{66}}$, and $3x^{2^{66}}\le x^{2^{67}}$ for $x\ge2$. This proves~\eqref{gsr:fm:86:eq:intermediate}, with the conversion between natural and binary logarithms included explicitly.

\section[{Conversion to density and strict separation\srctag{86}}]{Conversion to density and strict separation}\label{gsr:fz:86:sec:d7}\label{gsr:fz:86:sec:conversion}
\srcnote{86}{Section 7}
We now impose $0<\delta\le\tfrac12$. Since $64000<2^{16}$, equation~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:xdelta} gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:xdensitybound}
 x<2^{257}\delta^{-80}\le\delta^{-337}.
\end{equation}
The second inequality uses $2\le\delta^{-1}$. The first inequality is strict even when $\delta=\tfrac12$.

As $337<2^9$ and $0<\delta<1$, raising~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:xdensitybound} to the positive power $2^{67}$ yields
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:strictdensity}
 x^{2^{67}}<\delta^{-337\cdot2^{67}}<\delta^{-2^{76}}.
\end{equation}
Combining~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:finalintermediate} with~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:strictdensity}, and applying the strictly increasing function $u\mapsto2^{2^u}$, gives
\[
 H_{\fej}(\delta)<2^{\,2^{\delta^{-2^{76}}}}.
\]
The comparison $2^{76}<2^{16384}$ and the condition $\delta<1$ imply
\[
 \delta^{-2^{76}}<\delta^{-2^{16384}}.
\]
A second use of strict monotonicity of the two outer powers gives the remaining strict inequality in~\eqref{gsr:fm:86:eq:main}. Section~\ref{gsr:fm:86:sec:paper} identified its right side with the paper's exact five-term threshold. This completes the proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:86:thm:main}.

\begin{remark}[Why the density range matters]
The factor $2^{257}$ in~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:xdensitybound} is absorbed by a power of $\delta^{-1}$ using $\delta\le\tfrac12$. That argument must not be extended without change to all $\delta\le1$. The intermediate bound~\eqref{gsr:fm:86:eq:intermediate} does hold on the larger range, but the density-only comparison has been asserted only on the range proved.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Real thresholds and integer cutoffs]
The strict comparison is between sufficient real-valued expressions. It implies the progression consequence at integer $N$ satisfying~\eqref{gsr:fm:86:eq:sufficient}, or equivalently $N\ge\ceil{2^{2^{\delta^{-2^{76}}}}}$. It does not identify an optimal cutoff, prove strict separation of every rounded cutoff, or characterize what happens below either sufficient threshold.
\end{remark}

\section[{The progression interface and its verification scope\srctag{86}}]{The progression interface and its verification scope}\label{gsr:fz:86:sec:d8}\label{gsr:fz:86:sec:chain}
\srcnote{86}{Section 8}
The numerical comparison and the arithmetic-progression implication have different logical inputs. The distinction is important even when all the relevant source files contain theorem declarations with proof bodies.

\subsection{The precise imported chain}
At the pinned revision, the declaration
\srceightysix{Proofs18FejerCubicDiscrepancy}{\filename{fejer_cubic_function_discrepancy_bound}}
has the inspected type
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:86:eq:discrepancyinterface}
 0<\alpha\le1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \operatorname{FunctionDiscrepancyBound}(3,\alpha,\beta,\sigma,T_{\rm loc}),
\end{equation}
where $\beta,\sigma,T_{\rm loc}$ are exactly the expressions in Section~\ref{gsr:fz:86:sec:exactlocal}. The proposition on the right is the repository's function-discrepancy interface. We use that interface as an imported mathematical input; the present article does not reprove the cubic inverse theorem behind it.

The general theorem
\srceightysix{Proofs18GeneralIteration}{\filename{FunctionDiscrepancyBound.natural_szemeredi_closed}}
takes, for $k\ge2$, positive $\delta,\beta,\sigma$ and the input
\[
 \operatorname{FunctionDiscrepancyBound}
 \bigl(k-2,\operatorname{intervalUniformityParameter}(\delta,k),
       \beta,\sigma,T\bigr).
\]
It returns $\operatorname{AP}_k(A)$ for $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$, $|A|\ge\delta N$, and $N$ above the corresponding closed interval-discrepancy threshold. Its inspected proof passes through the following explicit components:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item The interval density-increment step at fixed initial parameters
 \item The finite density iteration, stopped before the density would exceed one
 \item The exponential upper bound on the backward length recursion, expressed by \filename{densityIterationClosedThreshold}
 \item The transfer from subsets of \filename{Fin N} to the natural interval $\{1,\ldots,N\}$
\end{enumerate}
At $k=5$, the natural theorem \filename{natural_five_term_fejer} verifies $0<\alpha\le1$, supplies~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:discrepancyinterface} to that general theorem, and supplies the positivity of $\beta$ and $\sigma$. Its bound on $N$ is exactly~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:Hexact}. Thus the inspected application is specific and the conditional discrepancy input is visibly supplied; it is not merely a wish to apply a general result at degree three.

No prime-modulus condition is present in the resulting theorem for the natural $N$. Prime-model hypotheses occur internally in the inverse-theorem construction and are handled by the imported chain. Dropping or adding such a hypothesis at the final interface would misstate the inspected source theorem.

\subsection{What the present work verifies}
The report establishes ordinary mathematical inequalities for the pinned numerical definitions. Their source closure was inspected and reduced to the formulas displayed here. The supporting finite computations confirm the integer arithmetic used by the proof. The source text also exposes the progression implication and its immediate application chain.

This work does not independently compile Lean, check the transitive imported proof closure, establish that every imported theorem is axiom-free, or prove the arbitrary-length theorem from first principles. In particular the general \filename{theorem_18_2} target declaration must be distinguished from any separate proved special case. Taking the inspected progression theorem as given leads to Corollary~\ref{gsr:fm:86:cor:ap}; the analytic comparison itself does not depend on accepting its proof body.

$\log T_{\rm loc},\log S$ & $2^{x^{2^{65}}}$ & Eqs.~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:Tlocbound}, \eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:Sbound}\\[3pt]
$\log A_{\rm it}$ & $x^{2^{66}}$ & Equation~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:Abound}\\[3pt]
$\log\log H_{\fej}$ & $x^{2^{67}}$ & Equation~\eqref{gsr:fz:86:eq:finalintermediate}\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The largest degree allowance in this particular ledger comes from the geometric part of the common Fourier threshold. This describes the proof's \emph{upper-bound bookkeeping}, not a proved lower bound or an assertion that a particular branch dominates the actual maximum. Substantial slack also enters when $\gamma=x^{-D}$ is substituted and when fixed coefficients are absorbed by powers of $x$.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Literature and the scope of the comparison\srctag{82}}]{Literature and the scope of the comparison}\label{gsr:fz:82:sec:d10}\label{gsr:fz:82:sec:literature}
\srcnote{82}{Section 10}
The result combines a structural refinement of the preceding energy theorem with an exact matrix-norm calculation. These have different precedents. The comparison below records the primary sources inspected and avoids a claim of publication priority or a claim that a general conjecture remains open today.

\subsection{The reflected mean matrix belongs to a studied family}
Bouthat, Khare, Mashreghi and Morneau-Gu\'erin study matrices $A(n,a,b)$ with diagonal $a$ and every off-diagonal entry $b$~\cite{bouthatcirculant}. Our matrix satisfies
\[-R_9=A(9,-7/9,2/9).
\]
Their exact nonnegative-entry theorem does not apply to these mixed signs. Substitution into their Theorem~5.2 gives
\[1\le\norm{R_9}_{4\to4}\le\frac{\sqrt{23}}3
       =1.59861050777\ldots,
\]
whereas Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:82:thm:reflection} evaluates the norm exactly as $1.55042781455\ldots$. This is a direct quantitative comparison for the same parameters. Sahasranand gives Fourier and interpolation treatments of the same family~\cite{sahasranand}; Fourier diagonalization alone does not determine its $\ell_4$ norm, since that diagonalization is isometric for $\ell_2$, not for $\ell_4$.

Conjecture~5.6 in the published article of Bouthat, Mashreghi and Morneau-Gu\'erin predicts at most two distinct coordinate values for real maximizing vectors in the mixed-sign family~\cite{bouthatnormal}. The real equality classification in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:82:thm:reflection}, transferred by the involution, shows that all real norm-maximizing vectors here are real scalar multiples of permutations of
\[(8-u_*,-1-u_*,\ldots,-1-u_*).
\]
Thus the proof verifies that prediction for this particular nine-point, fourth-power parameter instance. It does not prove the general conjecture, establish its current status, or establish that this instance was previously unresolved. The literature check for the 2023 paper covered the institutional record and the primary indexed passages around Conjecture~5.6 and Proposition~5.7; it was not a full-paper audit.

There is also a classical reduction independent of the moment proof. Timofte's half-degree principle, as stated in Riener's Theorem~1.3~\cite{riener}, tests nonnegativity of a symmetric quartic on real vectors with at most two distinct coordinate values. Apply it to
\[
 C\sum_{i=1}^9x_i^4-\sum_{i=1}^9(R_9x)_i^4.
\]
This is symmetric because $R_9$ commutes with coordinate permutations. Take $C$ to be the maximum fourth-power ratio over vectors with at most two distinct coordinate values normalized by $\sum_i x_i^4=1$; that set is compact. The principle gives the same bound on every real vector, hence some such vector attains the full norm. This reduction alone neither evaluates $C$ nor classifies all maximizers; those conclusions here come from the explicit sharp proof.

\subsection{Centering and reflection require different constants}
Sharp centering work studies $I-P$, where $P$ is a conditional expectation or finite averaging projection; see Shargorodsky and Sharia~\cite{shargorodskysharia}. Here the operator is $I-2P$. The former annihilates constants and is idempotent, while the latter reverses constants and is involutory. A sharp bound for $I-P$ does not, by replacement of a coefficient, become a sharp bound for $I-2P$. The inspected centering results provide relevant context but not the displayed exact reflection value.

\subsection{The moment and complexification steps are classical}
Pearson's 1916 paper states and proves the standardized moment inequality $\beta_2\ge1+\beta_1$; its displayed proof is credited there to G.~N. Watson~\cite{pearsonskew}. This is exactly~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:Pearson}. Kirby's primary abstract records the finite-sample skewness bound $(n-2)/\sqrt{n-1}$~\cite{kirbyskew}, giving~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:skew} at $n=9$. The normalization is the central-moment average with divisor $n$, not a bias-adjusted sample statistic. We supplied proofs and equality information because those details are needed in the sharp optimization.

Holtz and Karow's Theorem~3.1 gives equality of real and complex norms for real $L_p\to L_q$ operators when $1\le p\le q\le\infty$~\cite{holtzkarow}; their phase-averaging lemma specializes to~\eqref{gsr:en:82:eq:phase}. Their postscript points to earlier publications of the underlying result. Accordingly, neither the moment inequalities nor the real-to-complex principle are presented here as new. The explicit scalar optimization and the nine-frequency application are stated and proved for the exact parameters needed.

\subsection{Additive energy and Gowers context}
Gowers' proof of Szemeredi's theorem uses respected additive quadruples and all-nonnegative-weight product conditions in its graph-energy and product-property arguments~\cite{gowers}. The present denominator is ordinary additive energy, rather than total mass to the fourth power divided by ambient size. Changing that normalization changes what an extremal constant says. The current theorems concern deterministic full maps on elementary abelian three-groups; they do not by themselves improve a global density bound or a Ramsey number. Any downstream use would need to exhibit the exact interface between this energy ratio, the source group and the hypotheses of a density-increment or counting argument.

\paragraph{Search boundary.}
The comparison checked the constant-off-diagonal circulant family, mean-reflection and centering literature, real-to-complex norm results, and primary sources for the two moment bounds. It was not an exhaustive MathSciNet or zbMATH search, full forward-citation audit, multilingual search, dissertation review or unpublished-work review. No historical negative result is used as a mathematical premise.

\section[{Consequences and questions left open\srctag{82}}]{Consequences and questions left open}\label{gsr:fz:82:sec:d11}\label{gsr:fz:82:sec:questions}
\srcnote{82}{Section 11}
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:82:thm:main} identifies a genuine target dependence: a single nonzero element annihilated by two changes the extremal weighted constant for every fixed source rank at least two. The difference is not an artifact of a finite target survey. In the upper proof, injective doubling eliminates precisely the order-two derivative obstructions; in the lower proof, a single order-two element turns the target equation into parity and supplies the reflection multiplier.

The extremal constructions are stable under affine additions and affine source transformations in the elementary sense that these operations preserve every respected quadruple. For example, adding $\beta+\phi(x)$ to a pullback spike does not change its weighted infimum. This observation produces further equality examples but does not classify them all.

Several precise questions remain beyond the theorem:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item \textbf{Higher-rank equality maps.} Which full maps $a:V\to H$ outside the two allowed families satisfy $r(a)=\lambda$ when $H[2]\ne\{0\}$? The codimension-two spikes and their affine transforms attain equality, but completeness of this family in higher rank is not proved.
 \item \textbf{All equality weights for a lifted spike.} Every product $f_0\otimes h$ attains equality. A complete answer would need to reconcile equality on every complex Fourier block with nonnegativity in physical space. The real reflection equality classification alone does not do this.
 \item \textbf{Indicators in the two-torsion case.} The weighted fixed-pair theorem does not determine $\max\rind(a)$ for each fixed source rank and each target containing two torsion. The no-two-torsion equality~\eqref{gsr:fm:82:eq:indmax} should not be extrapolated to this case.
 \item \textbf{Other finite reflections and exponents.} Determine the exact norm of $I-2J/n$ on $\ell_p^n$ in further parameter ranges, and identify where Pearson plus an equal-atom skewness bound remains a sharp combination. The scalar maximum used here depends on the nine-point fourth-power parameters.
 \item \textbf{Quantitative stability and applications.} Determine whether near-maximal energy infima force a map close to an extremal model in an appropriate specified metric. Separately, identify a concrete Gowers or Ramsey argument whose hypotheses genuinely accept these full-domain weighted constants. Neither conclusion follows from the current exact gap alone.
\end{enumerate}

\section[{Established results and the scope of the comparison\srctag{83}}]{Established results and the scope of the comparison}\label{gsr:fz:83:sec:d14}\label{gsr:fz:83:sec:literature}
\srcnote{83}{Section 14}
The universal equality quantifier should be separated from two established reductions.

\paragraph{The quartic half-degree principle.}
Riener's Theorem~1.3~\cite{riener}, crediting Timofte, tests global nonnegativity of a real symmetric polynomial of degree $d$ on vectors with at most $\max\{2,\lfloor d/2\rfloor\}$ distinct coordinates. Applied to the quartic gap~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:gap}, it already gives existence of a two-valued norming vector. Indeed, maximize the ratio on the compact set of at-most-two-valued vectors on the unit sphere and apply the principle to that trial gap. This does not by itself classify every equality vector. Section~\ref{gsr:en:83:sec:two-values} proves the universal assertion directly, and the rest of the report does not require the half-degree principle.

\paragraph{Real and complex norms.}
Holtz and Karow's Theorem~3.1~\cite{holtzkarow} gives equality of real and complex norms for real $L_p$-to-$L_q$ operators when $1\le p\le q\le\infty$; their Lemma~3.4 includes the phase-average mechanism at $p=q$. Equality of the norms here is therefore established general theory. The additional equality-vector conclusion uses the particular fact that $T_\gamma$ fixes the mean-zero subspace while its norm is greater than one. No priority claim is attached to that argument.

\paragraph{The printed matrix prediction.}
Conjecture~5.6 of Bouthat, Mashreghi and Morneau-Gu\'erin~\cite{bouthatnormal}, journal page~210, quantifies over every real maximizing vector of $A(n,-a,b)$ for $a,b\ge0$, not both zero, and $1\le p\le\infty$, $p\ne2$. Theorem~5.10 there, on page~215, concerns the three-dimensional centering projection for $1<p<\infty$, $p\ne2$. Equation~\eqref{gsr:fm:83:eq:matrix-reduction} and Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:83:thm:general} verify the nondegenerate $p=4$ specialization for every $n\ge3$, $a\ge0$, $b>0$. They do not settle the arbitrary-exponent assertion.

The scalar-identity boundary $b=0$ and the $p=1$ endpoint require separate qualifications in any all-maximizer formulation: a scalar identity allows every vector, and for $a=0$, $b>0$, every nonnegative vector maximizes the $\ell_1$ norm of $b(J-I)$. These endpoint facts are scope cautions, not the main result or a proposed resolution of the interior-exponent problem.

\paragraph{Limits of the literature review.}
The primary half-degree theorem and norm-complexification text were inspected directly. The primary indexed PDF passages for the matrix conjecture and its three-dimensional theorem were checked; full direct retrieval of that PDF was unreliable. This is a bounded source comparison, not an exhaustive later-literature search. No claim is made that the nondegenerate fourth-norm statement was previously unresolved, or that the formulas or equality arguments have publication priority.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Further questions\srctag{83}}]{Further questions}\label{gsr:fz:83:sec:d15}\label{gsr:fz:83:sec:questions}
\srcnote{83}{Section 15}
The proved equalities suggest several bounded research questions. Each item below is a question, not an additional theorem.
\begin{enumerate}
 \item \textbf{Interior exponents.} For $1<p<\infty$, $p\ne2,4$, which mean perturbations have the property that every real maximizer is two-valued? Proposition~\ref{gsr:en:83:prop:finite-p} already removes an independent complex-phase obstruction, but it does not bound the number of real values.
 \item \textbf{General-parameter multiplicities.} The quintic reduction is finite for every $n$ and $\gamma$, but outside reflection its maximizing multiplicity may change with $\gamma$. Can the parameter intervals, branch collisions, and equality transitions be classified beyond the constant threshold?
 \item \textbf{Reflection ties and quantitative convergence.} Can the two adjacent optimal candidates ever tie? What sharp estimates describe the difference between $C_n$ and $3+2\sqrt2$ in terms of the distance from $np_*$ to the competing integers? The present formula handles ties without deciding their existence.
 \item \textbf{Nonsaturating energy minima.} At order $81$, what is the actual value of $r_G(\delta\ind_{\{0\}})$ between the endpoints in~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:order81}, and does it depend on the structure of $G$? A positive quantitative gap above $\eta_{81}$ would strengthen the compactness conclusion.
 \item \textbf{All subgroup-spike equality weights.} For a nontrivial kernel $K$, how do the necessary quotient fiber masses interact with equality on the remaining Fourier blocks? Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:83:thm:subgroup-spike} proves saturation and provides constant-fiber examples, but a full equality classification remains open here.
 \item \textbf{Indicator minima and stability.} Determine indicator minima for the point spikes, and quantify how close a near-extremal nonnegative weight must be to the subgroup-supported forms when spectral saturation is possible. Neither exact indicator values nor a stability theorem follows merely from compactness.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 82--94]
\emph{Question~3 is answered} by source~85: adjacent candidates never tie, so the optimal multiplicity is unique for every $n\ge3$ (its Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:85:cor:unique}); the quantitative part (the distance of $C_n$ from $3+2\sqrt2$) remains open. Questions~4--6 recur as source~85's Questions~1, 3 and~5; all are merged into item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:spikes}.
\end{writenote}

\section[{Exact computation and reproducibility\srctag{83}}]{Exact computation and reproducibility}\label{gsr:fz:83:sec:d16}\label{gsr:fz:83:sec:reproducibility}
\srcnote{83}{Section 16}
The accompanying ZIP is self-contained: it contains this TeX source, the verified PDF, a standard-library Python companion, regression tests, an exact rational interval certificate, and an offline deterministic builder. No earlier report tree, research-directory path, internet access, package installation, numerical optimizer, or external computer-algebra package is required by the companion.

\paragraph{What is checked.}
The companion verifies $54$ formal polynomial identities by complete exact coefficient arithmetic, including the stationary quintic, fixed-mean and transition expansions, second-variation factorization, scalar reflection identities, and direct spike energy formulas. It encloses square roots between rational endpoints verified by squaring. The certificate records reflection rows for $n=1,2,3,4,8,9,10,11,12,13,14,15,16,27,81$, all candidate comparisons for those rows, and constant thresholds for $n=3,9,30$. A supplemental comparison checks every allowed multiplicity for each $3\le n\le100$.

Exact character and convolution checks use all three abelian isomorphism types of order $27$ and all five of order $81$, with an explicit order-nine subgroup in each. They also verify a nonsplit quotient lift $\Z/27\Z\to\Z/9\Z$ and all $256$ identity-containing character subsets of $(\Z/3\Z)^2$. There are $50$ companion regression tests, including deliberately corrupted formulas and certificates, unresolved comparisons, boundary rejection, read-only execution, and normal-versus-optimized agreement. The README and deterministic JSON output give the full inventory and implementation bounds.

\paragraph{What is not checked by a finite computation.}
The code is not a general certified solver for every real root of an arbitrary-parameter quintic. Formula~\eqref{gsr:en:83:eq:finite-formula} is the written exact mathematical reduction; the companion checks its coefficients. Finite multiplicity checks do not prove the all-$n$ candidate rule, and finite character examples do not prove the all-group saturation theorem. The analytic proofs in this manuscript provide those statements. The work is not a formal proof-assistant certification.

\paragraph{Replay contract.}
From an extracted distribution, run \filename{python3 -I -B build.py verify}. To rerun both test suites and the exact checks normally and with Python optimization, compile the PDF, and rebuild the ZIP, run
\begin{center}\small
\filename{python3 -I -B build.py reproduce --output /tmp/report295-replay}.
\end{center}
The destination must be a fresh absolute directory outside the source tree. The builder rejects unexpected source files, aliases, and nonregular entries; it writes exclusively to the external output directory. It compares normal and optimized stdout and confirms source inventories remain unchanged. Three TeX passes run with shell escape disabled and fixed metadata. The compilation gate rejects overfull boxes, unresolved references and citations, duplicate destinations, and incomplete PDFs.

Archive members have a fixed order, timestamp, and permissions. A canonical SHA-256 manifest covers every public member other than itself, and a separate SHA-256 pin covers the final ZIP bytes. These are integrity checks, not digital signatures. Byte-identical replay depends on the same Python, zlib, TeX, and font toolchains; the exact mathematical companion can be run independently of TeX. Full instructions and limitations are in \filename{REPRODUCING.md}.

The proof inputs were independently audited before final release, and their source hashes and the primary bibliographic links are recorded in \filename{SOURCES.md}. The final PDF is additionally rendered page by page for visual inspection. No file in Reports 1--294 is changed by this report or its reproduction.

\section[{Exact companion and reproducibility\srctag{84}}]{Exact companion and reproducibility}\label{gsr:fz:84:sec:d8}\label{gsr:fz:84:sec:reproduce}
\srcnote{84}{Section 8}
The public package contains the editable TeX article, the rendered PDF, an offline Python companion, tests, pinned source records and compact excerpts, and a deterministic builder. None of these diagnostics executes the upstream Lean files. The companion uses only Python's standard library and exact integer or rational arithmetic. It has no numerical optimizer and does not evaluate the astronomical thresholds.

\subsection{Symbolic exponent checks}
The companion represents a monomial as an exponent pair $(u,v)$ for
$2^u\alpha^v$. Multiplication adds pairs, integer powers multiply them, and division subtracts them. It reconstructs $a_i$, $\mu_i$, $b(a_i)$, $s(a_i)$, $t_i$, and $\beta_i$ from the displayed definitions. With $\Delta=d_{\old}-d_{\fej}$ it checks the exact ratio pairs
\[
 a_{\fej}/a_{\old}:(\Delta,-\Delta),\quad
 t_{\fej}/t_{\old}:(24718\Delta,-24718\Delta),
\]
\[
 \beta_{\fej}/\beta_{\old}:(12362\Delta,-12362\Delta).
\]
It also checks $2\cdot12359=24718$, $14+12=26$, the extra factor $16$ in $t_i$, $P_3=2359296$, the exponent $25378984$, and the constants $64000$ and $12801$. The values $2^{88}$ and $2^{76}$ are stored as ordinary exact integers, but no number such as $2^{2^{88}}$ is expanded.

\subsection{Sufficient inequalities and finite regressions}
Exact integer checks confirm $r_{\old}\ge r_{\fej}+1$, $r_{\fej}\ge1$, $2^2=4$, $0<q\le1$, and $12<4^3$. These are the discrete facts used in~\eqref{gsr:fz:84:eq:xgap} and~\eqref{gsr:fz:84:eq:absorb}. The continuous monotonicity and logarithmic arguments remain the written proof.

Supplemental rational cases check maximum propagation, monotonicity of ceilings, strict increase of $\beta/(8B)$ under a larger numerator and a nonlarger positive denominator, and the log-free iteration inequality
\[
 A_{\fej}Q_{\fej}^{n_{\fej}}
 <R^{-n_{\fej}}A_{\old}Q_{\old}^{n_{\old}}.
\]
They include equal ceilings and common dominant maximum entries. These are bounded regression tests of the algebraic mechanism, not evaluations of the original thresholds or a finite-sampling proof for all real densities. The companion's machine-readable certificate records the exact symbolic and integer results; the checker recomputes them rather than accepting stored success labels.

\subsection{Source integrity has two different meanings}
\filename{SOURCE_MANIFEST.json} records the commit, canonical source URLs, byte sizes, Git blob SHA-1 identifiers, and SHA-256 digests of complete upstream files inspected for this work. Those complete files are not bundled. \filename{source_excerpts.json} contains only the relevant exact definitions, one theorem body, and the source's scope comment, with inclusive line ranges and a separate hash of each UTF-8 excerpt.

Offline checks verify the bundled excerpt bytes and their declared hashes, their association with the manifest, and their pinned package digests. They do not refetch the complete files or reconstruct full-file hashes from partial excerpts. Full-file and excerpt digests must never be interchanged. Neither a local hash manifest nor a stored Git blob identifier is a digital signature; authenticate the archive's detached hash through a trusted channel when that matters.

\subsection{Rebuilding the public package}
From an extracted distribution, the following commands verify the exact member inventory and then rebuild into a fresh external directory:
\begin{quote}\ttfamily\small
 python3 -I -B build.py verify\\
 python3 -I -B build.py reproduce --output /tmp/report296-replay
\end{quote}
The output location must be absolute, outside the source, and empty or absent. Existing files are refused rather than overwritten. The builder takes bounded no-follow snapshots, rejects symlinks, hard links, special files and unexpected entries, and checks source immutability after each test command. Tests and diagnostics run normally and with optimization enabled; their standard output must match. Runtime validation does not depend on Python assertions.

The builder compiles the TeX three times with shell escape disabled, restricted input and output, a fixed epoch, and an allowlisted environment. It rejects overfull boxes, unresolved references or citations, duplicate destinations, and incomplete PDF output. The public ZIP has a sorted exact allowlist, fixed timestamps and regular-file modes. The PDF receives a separate rendered-page visual review; clean compiler output alone is not a visual review.

On replay of a manifest-pinned distribution, a rebuilt PDF must match the supplied PDF byte for byte. Byte-identical PDF and ZIP output requires the reference Python, zlib, TeX, packages and fonts; a different toolchain may fail that check without refuting the mathematics. The companion can be run independently of TeX. Full commands, version details, resource limits and trust boundaries are in \filename{REPRODUCING.md}.
