\section[{Further research questions\srctag{84}}]{Further research questions}\label{gsr:fz:84:sec:d9}\label{gsr:fz:84:sec:questions}
\srcnote{84}{Section 9}
The following questions are natural continuations of the comparison; none is needed for the theorem above.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Formalize the complete comparison.} Can the exact reductions and inequalities be added as Lean theorems at the pinned interface, followed by an independently recorded kernel build? The useful intermediate statements are $C_{\fej}\le12C_{\old}$, $\sigma_{\fej}\ge4\sigma_{\old}$, $T_{\fej}\le T_{\old}$, $c_{\old}<c_{\fej}$, and ceiling monotonicity.
\item \textbf{Use the full phase-count structure.} The exact formula $D_i=16B_0(3/2)^{t_i}$ gives a tighter factor than $12$. How much of the size-exponent gain is actually needed to absorb the phase-removal term? The present deliberately coarse estimate avoids optimizing an intermediate constant that is already overwhelmed by $R$.
\item \textbf{Quantify the iteration-count gain.} The exact discrepancy ratio in Remark~\ref{gsr:fz:84:rem:beta} is enormous, but the proof uses only $n_{\fej}\le n_{\old}$. Can useful explicit bounds for $n_{\old}-n_{\fej}$ produce a cleaner stronger presentation than retaining $R^{-n_{\fej}}$?
\item \textbf{Compare other fully specified thresholds.} A comparison with the paper's numerical five-term threshold requires a separate exact definition and an analysis of all of its constants. It is not implied by comparing these two repository constructions. The same caution applies to an optimal or literature-best quantitative bound.
\item \textbf{Extend the method at an explicit interface.} For other progression lengths, one would need a complete pair of discrepancy and starting-threshold constructions. The reusable principle in Section~\ref{gsr:fz:84:sec:iteration} suggests what to compare, but does not supply those missing combinatorial inputs.
\end{enumerate}

\section[{Further questions\srctag{85}}]{Further questions}\label{gsr:fz:85:sec:d11}\label{gsr:fz:85:sec:questions}
\srcnote{85}{Section 11}
The classification closes the adjacent-tie and finite-saturation questions suggested by Report 295. Several related problems remain distinct from the results above.
\begin{enumerate}
 \item \textbf{Quantitative nonsaturation.} For an unlisted order, can one bound $r_G(a)-\eta_n$ explicitly? The compactness argument proves positivity but supplies no useful size. Order $81$ remains a concrete test case.
 \item \textbf{Dependence on group structure.} Saturation depends only on the order, but must the actual nonsaturating minimum do so? The present classification does not compare different groups of the same unlisted order.
 \item \textbf{All subgroup-spike equality weights.} For a nontrivial $K$, characterize simultaneous lower equality in every nonzero Fourier block. Quotient fiber masses and constant-fiber examples alone leave that question open.
 \item \textbf{Stability at the listed orders.} How close must a near-equality nonnegative weight be to the subgroup-supported profiles? An effective theorem would need control of the Fourier positivity step as well as the reflection norm gap.
 \item \textbf{Indicator minima.} Outside order or index four, what are the exact finite indicator minima? The strict-gap conclusion gives no formula for those values.
 \item \textbf{Other exponents and mean perturbations.} The integer comparator and no-tie argument are specific to the fourth norm of reflection. Do related exact arithmetic reductions exist for other exponents or for $I-\gamma J_n/n$ with $\gamma\ne2$?
\end{enumerate}
These are research questions, not claims established by the finite computation. No conclusion here changes previously stated global hypotheses or bounds in Ramsey theory or Szemeredi's theorem.

\section[{Further mathematical questions\srctag{86}}]{Further mathematical questions}\label{gsr:fz:86:sec:d12}\label{gsr:fz:86:sec:further}
\srcnote{86}{Section 12}
The result closes the complete numerical comparison for the inspected five-term construction. It leaves several precise questions that can be pursued without weakening the current statement.

\begin{enumerate}
 \item \textbf{Sharpen the envelope.} Retain the actual exponents of $\gamma^{-1}$ and the constants in the geometric primitives instead of combining them immediately into $B=(2/\gamma)^{2^{32}}$. Propagate the refined bounds through $\gamma=x^{-D}$ and the final density conversion. The present exponent label $76$ is sufficient, not optimized.
 \item \textbf{Formalize this exact comparison.} Encode the all-real inequalities and the totalized zero-spectrum cases for the precise exponent-$76$ statement, then independently build the resulting Lean theorem and its imports. The necessary elementary lemmas and numerical sufficient inequalities are explicitly listed in this article and companion.
 \item \textbf{Audit the progression theorem's complete closure.} The immediate interface is inspected here. A separate end-to-end verification should identify the repository and mathlib revisions, build the relevant targets, inspect axioms, and distinguish the numerical comparison from the inverse-theorem and iteration arguments.
 \item \textbf{Compare constructions carefully.} Report~296 establishes a strict comparison between the Fej\'er and older explicit five-term interfaces at the reference revision. Combining that comparison with the present result does not determine whether the older interface itself lies above or below the paper's threshold. That is a separate numerical question.
 \item \textbf{Extend the method only where inputs are available.} A proved length-five implication gives shorter prefixes, as in Corollary~\ref{gsr:fm:86:cor:ap}. It does not supply the higher-degree inverse inputs or the quantitative bookkeeping for arbitrary progression length. Any extension must display and bound those new dependencies.
\end{enumerate}

No priority claim, comparison with all modern quantitative results, or statement of literature optimality is intended. The result is the explicit strict comparison~\eqref{gsr:fm:86:eq:main} for the pinned construction, together with the carefully qualified progression consequence.

\section[{Source provenance and reproducible finite checks\srctag{87}}]{Source provenance and reproducible finite checks}\label{gsr:fz:87:sec:d12}\label{gsr:fz:87:sec:repro}
\srcnote{87}{Section 12}
The mathematical proof above is uniform in every $k\ge1$ and every prime beyond the stated threshold. Finite computations cannot replace that proof, particularly the existence of simultaneously balanced words at enormous moduli. The supplied standard-library companion has a narrower, explicit role: check exact finite illustrations and arithmetic consequences, and verify the integrity of the compact source material distributed with this article.

\subsection{Pinned evidence and its boundaries}
The preparation verified all 35 complete local Lean snapshots in the research collection against their recorded pinned Git blob identities. Five additional, independently collected source files supply the Fourier, geometry and spectrum definitions needed for the audit, giving 40 distinct complete-source identity records in \filename{SOURCE_MANIFEST.json}. The archive bundles 28 line-ranged exact excerpts rather than complete third-party source files or paper prose. Each excerpt records its file, line range, pinned URL and SHA-256 digest; each complete-source identity records its byte count, SHA-256 and Git blob SHA-1. The research proof is preserved as \filename{provenance/PROOF.md}. The earlier note and the pre-manuscript mathematical audit are identified by their recorded hashes.

At the recorded 15:03 UTC source check on 7 October 2026, the examined branch revision was
\filename{e40a57b9878f2b20636fe7d1acdc3b2e61796e87}.
The contextual contract, common-base structure, Section~16 definitions, product-property definitions and common-base line-cover file had the same blob identities as at the proof pin. Four of these identities were independently rechecked in the adversarial source audit. This is a dated source observation, not a claim about every later repository state. \filename{CURRENT_SOURCE_STATUS.json} records its exact scope.

No repository code was executed, no Lean theorem negating the contract was compiled for this report, and no upstream files were edited. The ordinary-mathematical audit found no failed field, normalization error, partition escape, or quantifier reversal in the frozen construction. The released package has separate manuscript, companion and package checks; their scope must not be confused with a full imported-theorem or Lean-kernel audit.

\subsection{What the exact companion is designed to establish}
The finite checks use exact integers and rational arithmetic. They illustrate the graph-energy Cauchy--Schwarz inequality on small finite alphabets and weighted domains, the separate zero-family case, arrangement convolution counts, alternating cube signs, modal-colour mass, and the affine-fibre counting mechanism. They also check the elementary coefficient inequalities behind the $5/16$ bound and the explicit threshold. The source checks authenticate each bundled data file against its literal package pin and parse that same captured byte string; they do not hash one read and parse an unchecked later read. Regression tests exercise this distinction and malformed-input failure paths.

The reference run checks 22 coefficient identities or sufficient inequalities; 674 weighted integer cases, also with rational rescaling; 258 repeated parallel-family cases; 12 zero-family cases and the corresponding 12 constant-family cases; and 27 eightfold convolutions. It checks 136 constant-cube cases and 32 arbitrary-vertex sign identities, 73 modal-colour selections, and 20,670 affine comparisons across 510 proper progression presentations, including 282 wrapping presentations. The 35 companion regression tests run in both ordinary and optimized Python modes, alongside 41 guarded-builder tests. These counts describe finite tests, not a finite reduction of the theorem. The coefficient companion checks the frozen reference proof's sufficient $7/8$ upper bound for the union-bound logarithm, whereas Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:87:lem:balance} uses the simpler sufficient $9/16$ estimate; both give a strict margin below one.

For a transparent arithmetic illustration, take $N=17$, $E=\{0,1,2\}$, $S=\{0,1\}$, values $f=(0,1,0)$ on $E$, and weights $w=(1,2,1)$. This toy input is not a theorem-scale balanced-word counterexample. Its graph pair-sum masses, at their six distinct locations, are
\[
 1,\ 4,\ 2,\ 4,\ 4,\ 1,
 \qquad \mathcal E_E(w;(f))=54\ge\frac{4^4}{17}.
\]
The ordinary energy, which handles a zero family of restrictions, is $70$. The sumset support estimate is $(2|E|-1)(2|S|-1)=15<17$. Eightfold convolution gives $T_8(E)=5{,}196{,}627\ge3^{16}/17$, while the modal class $\{0,2\}$ has two of the three points. The small example displays the same energy, arrangement and selection mechanisms without purporting to satisfy the long-progression balance or width thresholds.

The companion does not generate $K$ in a dimension where its representation is intractable, evaluate $N_*$, search for theorem-scale words, verify all proper box partitions by enumeration, or prove real-variable concentration by finite testing. Its small examples are mechanism checks. The full proof remains Sections~\ref{gsr:en:87:sec:word}--\ref{gsr:en:87:sec:good}.

\subsection{Offline reproduction}
The source archive is self-contained for its offline finite checks and PDF build. From a fresh extracted copy, run

python3 -I -B companion/exact\_checks.py\\
python3 -I -B build.py reproduce --output /tmp/report299-replay

The bounded build snapshots an exact file allowlist, stages those bytes, runs companion and builder tests in ordinary and optimized Python modes, compiles the TeX with shell escape disabled, and produces deterministic PDF/ZIP artifacts and an external receipt. The manifest covers every public distribution file except itself; the ZIP receives a separate digest. The same source bytes are reused across verification and processing, and source inventories are checked for mutation. See \filename{REPRODUCING.md} for dependencies and the precise guard boundaries.

\section[{Further mathematical questions\srctag{87}}]{Further mathematical questions}\label{gsr:fz:87:sec:d13}\label{gsr:fz:87:sec:questions}
\srcnote{87}{Section 13}
\paragraph{Can a compatible good witness always be selected?}
The exact existential target~\eqref{gsr:en:87:eq:existential} is the most direct open question suggested by the counterexample. The modal argument works because $\phi$ depends on one coordinate and the common-base cube map vanishes. General inputs can have correlated values and nontrivial induced maps; a selection principle must control those while retaining the required masses and spectrum data.

\paragraph{How much additional restriction is affordable?}
A further subdomain could remove local oscillations but may consume more density than the iterative large-piece argument permits. A useful theorem would state the restriction's mass, its dependence on $\theta,\gamma,k$, and the resulting cover parameter together, then propagate those exact constants through the remaining induction.

\paragraph{Which ambient normalization is responsible?}
The weighted graph-sumset lemma exploits the $N^{-1}$ normalization on a short test domain. A stronger local normalization, or a hypothesis tying the spectrum and selection to local density at every box scale, might exclude the slab. Whether such a hypothesis follows from the original upstream Fourier construction is a separate problem. It is not part of the current abstract product-property contract.

\paragraph{Can the enormous thresholds be reduced?}
The stated $N_*$ is deliberately explicit and conservative. Better concentration estimates, a sharper progression count or a deterministic balanced-word construction could improve it. None would change the logical obstruction: for each fixed $k$, the alphabet and slab density remain fixed while primes are unbounded. Threshold optimization is therefore secondary to quantifier repair.

\paragraph{What should be formalized next?}
A direct Lean negation theorem for the exact contextual contract would require assembling the graph-sumset energy bound, slab arrangements, all common-base fields and balanced-word existence. Most cover and concentration ingredients are already represented in the pinned development. Independently, a formal existential-selection interface would make the surviving induction obligation explicit. These are proposed future tasks, not accomplishments claimed by the present TeX/PDF report.

\section[{Further research questions\srctag{88}}]{Further research questions}\label{gsr:fz:88:sec:d10}
\srcnote{88}{Section 10}
\label{gsr:fz:88:sec:research}

The new recurrences close a specific improvement problem in the
inspected configuration input. They also distinguish several remaining
questions that require different ideas. The following programme is
organized by the mathematical obstruction, rather than by the size of
the numerical constants.

\begin{problem}[The density frontier for cube pairs]
\label{gsr:fz:88:q:density-frontier}
For each $k\ge2$, does there exist a finite $g_k$ and a constant
$c_k>0$ such that every map with $\PP_\gamma$ satisfies
\[
 \mathcal C_k(\mathbf1_B)
 \ge c_kM^3\beta^{2^{k+1}}\gamma^{g_k}?
\]
If so, can $g_k$ be bounded by $O(4^k)$? More generally, determine
the feasible pairs of density and frequency exponents.
\end{problem}

Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:88:sharp:density} makes $2^{k+1}$ the smallest possible
density exponent in this formulation. The present proof gives $4^k$.
The gap is already concrete at $k=2$: the necessary exponent is eight,
while the proved one is sixteen. A direct improvement to the two-layer
gluing inequality would be especially valuable because it would feed
into every arrangement order. The random-domain examples alone do not
show that the necessary exponent is attainable under the full product
property.

\begin{problem}[The optimal frequency loss]
\label{gsr:fz:88:q:frequency-frontier}
At the fixed density exponent $4^k$, can the cube-pair frequency
exponent $4(4^k-2^k)$ be reduced? Can the configuration frequency
exponent $8(4^k-3^k)$ be reduced while retaining its optimal density
exponent and a universal positive prefactor?
\end{problem}

The raw-test lower bounds do not settle either question. They certify
which local additive equations are sufficient and necessary to force
a chosen intermediate condition. A new proof might avoid that
condition, or obtain a better average without certifying it separately
for every horizontal parameter. A sharpness construction would need
to make the product-property energy loss and both averaging losses
nearly extremal at the same time. Exhibiting only one sharp
Cauchy--Schwarz inequality is insufficient.

\begin{problem}[Retaining collision information inside the induction]
Can the direct cube-pair proof preserve more of the distribution of
common mixed labels at each level and side, before the two Jensen
steps? Is there a useful recursive inequality in those distributions
that improves the density or frequency exponent?
\end{problem}

The proof already supplies an exact first moment
$\sum_t\mathcal C_{k-1}(\sqrt{w_t})$ and an explicit fourth-moment
lower expression indexed by horizontal pairs. Treating those
quantities as separate state variables may preserve information that
is lost by replacing each with a power of its mean. The successful
collision coupling in Section~\ref{gsr:en:88:sec:arrangements} is a model for
the type of simultaneous accounting needed; it does not automatically
apply one dimension earlier.

\begin{problem}[Which coefficient profiles come from Fourier data?]
For maps selected from large derivative Fourier coefficients, what
stronger coefficients $\eta_j(p)$ are available at the family sizes
$p=2^{i-1}$ and $p=3^{i-1}$ used in the new inductions? Can relations
among the selected restrictions reduce the effective family size on
a substantial domain?
\end{problem}

The general profile theorem in Section~\ref{gsr:en:88:sec:counting} separates
this analytic question from the counting recurrence. An improvement
at a small family size used early in the induction receives a large
power $4^{k-i}$, so the location of a gain matters. A concrete first
target is a family with a known integer generating set modulo affine
functions on the common domain. The integral criterion in
Section~\ref{gsr:en:88:sec:rank} explains why a field-rank computation needs
additional care if the target has torsion.

\begin{problem}[Stable determining families]
If most horizontal slices satisfy most of the face equations, what
weighted error bound replaces the exact determination by
$\{00,10,01\}^{k-1}$? Can an approximate version preserve a useful
frequency gain through the cube-pair induction?
\end{problem}

The first task is to specify the error measure: uniform mass of
slices, vertex-weighted mass, and collision-weighted mass need not
agree. The integral extension formula gives deterministic error
propagation along a chosen elimination tree, but a union bound over
all reconstructed entries may remove the improvement. A successful
result should either choose the basis adaptively or exploit shared
errors in the relation system. It should also distinguish Hamming
errors in an abelian target from metric errors in a normed target.

\begin{problem}[Near equality in the homogeneous weighted theorem]
Classify equality, and quantify near equality, in
\eqref{gsr:fm:88:eq:intro-weighted}. Which restrictions on $w$ and $\phi$ are
forced by almost equality in the two-orientation AM--GM step and in
the successive Jensen inequalities?
\end{problem}

Constant weights and constant labels on the full product give exact
equality when $\gamma=1$. The theorem does not classify other
extremizers. If weights are allowed to concentrate near a small
domain, an appropriate stability statement will need a normalization
and a nonconcentration assumption. The explicit two output weights in
the proof suggest a testable local condition: their ratio must be
close to one on the gluing data carrying most of the mass.

\begin{problem}[Selection in small characteristic]
Can the improved arrangement count be combined with a selector that
retains comparable powers uniformly in the characteristic, including
when $p\le2(L-1)$? What extra dependence on the additive orders of
the possible label defects is unavoidable?
\end{problem}

The counting theorems themselves permit every finite abelian
coordinate group and every abelian target. The characteristic
restriction enters only in the imported finite-field selector.
Repeated coefficients in its Fourier support and annihilation of a
nonzero defect are separate sources of difficulty. A proof must
track those terms instead of using a large-cardinality hypothesis
as a substitute for large characteristic.

\begin{problem}[A complete subsequent density-increment step]
\label{gsr:fz:88:q:iteration}
How much of the improved count and field-size budget in
Section~\ref{gsr:en:88:sec:selection} survives the multilinear modeling in
Section~16 of Gowers' proof and the next density increment? What
explicit bound results after iteration?
\end{problem}

The current article answers the adjoining Section~14--15 composition,
including its field-size threshold and output density. A further
calculation must retain the scale of each box or progression, the
number of candidate functions, all exceptional masses, and the
characteristic assumptions after every restriction. A natural
deliverable is a symbolic recurrence with one line for each actual
lemma application and a proof that every input hypothesis follows
from the preceding output. Multiplying the new exponents alone
does not perform that calculation.

\begin{problem}[Formal verification of the new inputs]
Can the indicator cube-pair theorem be integrated as a stronger
companion to \texttt{corollary\_14\_5}, followed by the anisotropic
and weighted variants? Can the integer relation basis be implemented
once and reused for other finite configuration systems?
\end{problem}

The first formal target should be the unweighted injection: it uses
only finite sets, group operations, and a fourth-power averaging
inequality. The weighted theorem adds nonnegative square roots and
AM--GM; it need not obstruct formalization of the simpler stronger
input. The relation-basis proof can be implemented as finite
integer coefficient arrays with an explicit elimination order,
avoiding reliance on a numerical rank calculation.

\subsection{What the companion programs establish}

The proofs are independent of the programs. The computations check
the places most susceptible to finite mistakes: multiplicities,
the recovery of parameters from a glued pair, the use of the same
data set in the two orientations, target torsion, integer relation
generation, and the parameter substitutions.
All acceptance checks use integers or exact rational arithmetic.
Rounded logarithms in the example table are presentation values;
the governing branches are certified by integer comparisons.

their validity in arbitrary targets follow from the proofs, not
from these finite ranges.

\subsection{Proof-status record}

There are three separate levels of evidence. The original and
corrected repository statements are the cited baseline. The
strengthened results in this article have complete mathematical
proofs, audited independently during preparation. The companion

The relevant existing interfaces are

The inspected source states the first two over prime cyclic groups with explicit
factorial-invertibility assumptions. It also distinguishes proposition-valued
catalogue entries from proved theorem declarations \cite{repo89lean}.
Nothing here changes their verification status.

The proposed new material should live in a separate finite-vector-space research
namespace. Four interfaces must be preserved. The tensor is homogeneous and
symmetric in all slots; the selector has $d-1$ slots, while the phase has degree
$d$; the phase value group is $\T$, not $\F_p$; and all displayed energies use
probability normalization. In an unnormalized version of
\eqref{gsr:fp:89:eq:fourier-square}, the energy is multiplied by $|V|^{d+1}$.
On a coset the corresponding factor is $|H|^{d+1}$.

A useful formalization order is: finite-difference algebra and symbols;
critical integration and matrix defects; symplectic repair; face decomposition;
Gowers--Cauchy--Schwarz localization; moment and quantile inequalities; exact
counting. The all-degree extension additionally imports Tidor's integration
criterion, which must itself be formalized or left as an explicitly named
hypothesis, not smuggled in as an axiom with a completed-proof label.

The supplied Python checks use exact fractions and finite-field arithmetic for
the integration and enumeration tests. Their localization tests certify a finite
set of root-of-unity examples using rational lower bounds for the fractional
moments. These tests are not a Lean proof and do not replace the universal
arguments in Sections~3--6. The file \texttt{FORMALIZATION.md} gives a more
detailed dependency plan without unverified Lean theorem stubs.

\section[{Further research questions\srctag{89}}]{Further research questions}\label{gsr:fz:89:sec:d10}
\srcnote{89}{Section 10}
\label{gsr:fz:89:sec:questions}
The following questions concern concrete remaining steps, not claims that the
corresponding problems are open in every formulation in the literature.

\begin{question}[Energy versus obstruction rank]\label{gsr:fz:89:q:rankenergy}
For $d=p+1$, how large can
$M_{p,r,n}=\sup_{|f|\leq1}\ET_T(f)$ be when $\rank\defectD_T=2r$?
By theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:89:thm:normal} and gauge invariance it depends only on $p,r,n$.
Does one have a dimension-free exponential decay in $r$?
A bound $M_{p,r,n}\leq C_p^{-r}$, $C_p>1$, would combine with the lossless
localization theorem to yield an optimal-order logarithmic codimension bound.
\end{question}

\begin{conjecture}[Canonical-block extremizers, an exploratory target]
For odd $p$, perhaps $M_{p,r,n}=c_p^r$ for all $n\geq2r$.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 82--94]
\emph{At $p=2$ this is a theorem}: source~43's exact twisted cubic norm $2^{-r/2}$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:43:bpi:thm:cubic-exact}) gives the energy $2^{-r}=c_2^r$. For $p=3$ source~92 brackets the one-block value, $11/27\le m_{3,1}\le1099/2187$, and conjectures $m_{3,1}=11/27$ (Conjecture~\ref{gsr:fp:92:conj:ternary}); its Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:92:thm:rankenergy} answers the dimension part of the question above ($M_{p,r,n}=m_{p,r}$ for every $n\ge2r$). Recorded as Further questions (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:IV:lowchar}); source~105, placed while this write was in progress, records a proof of the case $p=3$, $r=1$, $m_{3,1}=11/27$ (not checked here).
\end{writenote}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Proved at $(p,r)=(3,1)$, for every $n$,} by source~105 (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:105:thm:sharp} with Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:105:thm:global}), which does not cite this source: $M_{3,1,n}=c_3=11/27$, and $M_{3,r,n}\le11/27$ for every $r$. The remaining cases ($r\ge2$ at $p=3$; every odd $p\ge5$) are source~105's Questions~10.1 and~10.4, merged here (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:IV:lowchar}).
\end{writenote}
The lower bound is proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:89:prop:blockenergy}. The ternary two-dimensional
polynomial-phase census supports only a very small part of this conjecture.
It is not evidence of a proof for arbitrary functions. In particular, one must
address both possible non-polynomial extremizers and stabilization under unused
coordinates. The characteristic-two antecedents in the repository should be
used as a comparison, not as an argument that odd primes behave identically.

\begin{question}[Quantitative stability in the lossless bound]
Classify near-equality in the first two inequalities of
\eqref{gsr:fp:89:eq:localization-main}. The one-coset examples give exact equality, but
near-equality can also involve compatible phases on many cosets. Can the
Gowers--Cauchy--Schwarz equality conditions and the sharp Young inequality be
combined into a quantitative description that is uniform in the ambient dimension?
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Optimizing a higher-degree defect pencil]
Given the pencil $\Omega_T$, determine the largest common isotropic subspace,
or improve \eqref{gsr:fp:89:eq:two-bounds} using invariants independent of a chosen basis
of $\Omega_T$. The adapted sum of restricted half-ranks can be much smaller
than the displayed sum of full ranks. Understanding which pencils actually arise
as Frobenius defects may permit better bounds than for arbitrary alternating pencils.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Mixed defects from analytic hypotheses]
At degrees greater than $p+1$, obtain low-rank or low-dimensional control of
$\Omega_T$ directly from a selected-derivative energy hypothesis. Ordinary
symmetry and the integrability of $T|_H$ do not suffice for the face argument.
The example in Section~6 gives a specific regression test for any proposed
higher-degree proof.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Local cyclic analogues]
Replace the exact direct-sum coset decomposition by progressions, Bohr sets,
or other local domains relevant to Gowers's original cyclic-group argument.
One needs a controlled analogue of the face expansion, a phase primitive on the
local domain, and a boundary-error estimate. The finite-vector-space theorem
provides a clean target inequality, but does not itself control those errors.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Robust input and certified algorithms]
When only a noisy derivative selector is available, determine how many reliable
queries suffice to recover the alternating obstruction and an approximately
optimal repair. The exact pair-query law does not address adversarial errors in
the original Fourier selector. A verified implementation should also distinguish
matrix-rank uncertainty from the analytic uncertainty in the sampled energy.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Propagation through a quantitative inverse argument]
Insert the quotient-moment inequality at a stage where a symmetric tensor and
a rank bound are already available, and track the resulting density, codimension,
and correlation losses end to end. Recent high-characteristic quasipolynomial
inverse work \cite{milicevic} is relevant context, but its high-characteristic
hypothesis does not settle the first obstructed degree studied here. Any claimed
new global bound must include the symmetry-production step and this complete
parameter propagation.
\end{question}

\section[{Conclusion\srctag{89}}]{Conclusion}\label{gsr:fz:89:sec:d11}
\srcnote{89}{Section 11}
At critical degree $p+1$, the obstruction to phase integration is a concrete
alternating matrix. Its half-rank is the exact restriction cost, while its full
rank is the exact coordinate-support cost of a correction. These algebraic facts
combine with a face-by-face phase decomposition to give a sharp quotient-moment
inequality and a lossless best-coset phase-removal theorem. At higher degrees the
same analytic proof survives, with a pencil of mixed Frobenius defects replacing
the single matrix.

The distinction between what has been repaired and what remains is essential.
This article supplies the optimal algebraic repair and the subsequent analytic
localization. It does not bound the defect rank from energy, create symmetry
from approximate symmetry, or turn subspaces into long cyclic progressions.
Those are now separate, explicitly formulated research targets.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Verification scope and reproducibility\srctag{89}}]{Verification scope and reproducibility}\label{gsr:fz:89:sec:dA}
\srcnote{89}{Appendix A}
The archive contains this source and its compiled PDF, a source audit, a
formalization plan, a dependency description, and \texttt{code/verify.py} with
its generated report in \texttt{data/verification.json}. The checker uses no
network access. Its exhaustive cases and sampled cases are distinguished in the
report. The critical primitive tests verify every basis-direction difference of
order $d+1$ at every base point; because arbitrary differences expand as
polynomials in basis-direction differences with no constant term, this tests the
full finite polynomial-degree assertion for each function under examination.

The localization tests deliberately include zeros. For fractional moments,
rational bisection bounds the $(d+1)$-st roots from below; a test passes only if
the rational lower bound on the right side still dominates the exact energy.
The exact supported-coset equality is checked separately, so rounding is not
used to certify an equality. The combinatorial count of all ternary critical
symbols with one fixed nonzero defect is exhaustive and independent of the
universal proofs.

The questions below are left unresolved by the present arguments.

been recognized as open throughout the literature. The first
group is closest to the exact certificates already obtained;
the later questions require additional structure.

\subsection{Fourier phases beyond the first continuation}

\begin{problem}[The next phase for cutoff five and beyond]
For \(R\ge5\), determine the phase immediately after \(a_R\).
Which previously active lower Fourier constraint becomes
inactive, how many support points survive, and what is the
minimal algebraic equation for the new support?
\end{problem}

The signed-moment ceiling proves that all \(R\) equalities of
the transition pattern cannot persist at a larger common
height. For \(R=4\), the third frequency becomes inactive,
leaving the signs \((-,-,+)\) at \(1,2,4\).
A useful first deliverable for \(R=5\) would be a full primal
and dual certificate on one nonzero interval beyond \(a_5\),
including strict slack at every unused frequency. Numerical
moment optimization can suggest the contact pattern, but the
essential step is to prove the coefficient signs and the
range of the algebraic roots.

\begin{problem}[A finite phase description for fixed cutoff]
For every fixed \(R\), can the whole function \(\Phi_R(a)\)
and its extremizers be organized into finitely many explicit
algebraic phases in \(c=\cos a\), with a computable bound on
their number and support complexity?
\end{problem}

The compact moment formulation and polynomial certificates
suggest an algebraic approach, but a mere existence statement
from elimination would not give useful complexity.
The practical target is an algorithm that enumerates candidate
active frequencies and root multiplicities, certifies each
feasible interval, and proves that the list is exhaustive.
Degenerate junctions and nonunique phases must be allowed
until they are ruled out.

\begin{problem}[Unequal budgets on the new middle branch]
For prescribed positive budgets \(b_1,\ldots,b_4\), determine
\[
 \inf_{\mu\in\mathcal P(K_a)}
 \max_{1\le j\le4}\frac{|\widehat\mu(j)|}{b_j}
\]
near the equal-budget algebraic branch. How far does the
two-cosine support persist, and where do its active
constraints change?
\end{problem}

The first-window unequal-budget problem has a different
known matrix formulation \cite{srcsixtyseven}.
Here the absent \(T_3\) coefficient and the double root supply
a small algebraic system for a local perturbation analysis.
An exact first derivative with respect to each budget,
followed by a proof of the region where the active set is
unchanged, would already make the Fourier detector adaptable
to nonuniform downstream costs.

\subsection{Arithmetic discretization and near equality}

\begin{problem}[Uniform boundary layers at phase transitions]
Find exact finite-grid formulas when \(a-a_*\) or
\(a-3\pi/5\) varies with \(N\), including the scale at which
the unused third-moment margin is comparable with the grid
error.
\end{problem}

Our eventual grid formula is uniform only on compact
subintervals of the strict algebraic branch. Near the
endpoints a Fourier constraint becomes active, and at
\(3\pi/5\) an interior conjugate pair merges at \(\pi\).
Both effects can change the finite support pattern.
Determining the correct rescaled transition variables
would connect the exact formulas from adjacent continuous
phases instead of handling them independently.

\begin{problem}[The distribution of the grid correction]
For a fixed general radius in the algebraic phase, describe
the set of subsequential limits, or the limiting
distribution when it exists, of
\[
 N^2\bigl(\Phi_{4,N}(a)-\Phi_4(a_N)\bigr).
\]
\end{problem}

Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:90:cor:gridasymptotic} reduces this to the location of
\(\beta_N\) inside its grid cell. Expanding
\(\beta(a_N)\) retains the boundary-rounding phase as well
as the phase of the interior angle.
Consequently the relevant arithmetic problem generally
involves both \(a/(2\pi)\) and \(\beta(a)/(2\pi)\).
The semicircle's twelve exact residue classes are a fully
solved special case. Other rational-angle coincidences may
give additional exact generating formulas.

\begin{problem}[Fixed-cardinality and equal-weight extrema]
For a specified modulus \(N\), cardinality \(t\), and missing
arc, determine the best Fourier guarantee over unweighted
\(t\)-element subsets, and quantify its gap from the
nonnegative-weight optimum.
\end{problem}

Even when every continuous contact point lies on the grid,
its extremal masses can be incompatible with equal weights.
The obstruction therefore combines support arithmetic
with mass arithmetic. A first tractable version would fix
the semicircle radius and let \(t,N\) grow together with
a prescribed density. Any claim of equality would need
actual distinct grid points rather than repeated atoms
or arbitrary rational weights.

\begin{problem}[Stability at junctions and without evenness]
Determine optimal transport moduli at all phase endpoints,
and give a fully explicit circular \(W_1\) bound for
arbitrary near-minimizers on the strict algebraic branch.
\end{problem}

Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:90:thm:stability} already gives an optimal
square-root exponent in the cosine coordinate for all
measures and in the angular coordinate for even measures.
The imaginary parts of the active moments should control
orientation imbalance inside the conjugate pairs.
At a merging endpoint, the relevant sine factors degenerate,
so the correct angular exponent or constant may change.
A complete result should distinguish these geometric
degeneracies from loss of an active Fourier constraint.

\subsection{Sharper directional testing}

\begin{problem}[The small cycles]
Does
\[
 D(f)\le\frac{N+1}{6}d_1(f)
\]
hold for every \(2\le N\le11\) and every abelian target,
and what are the complete equality cases there?
\end{problem}

The finite searches in the package support the coefficient
on the domain and target sizes tested; they do not prove
an all-target assertion. The proof for \(N\ge12\) loses
strictness in a small number of majority-size cases.
A finite classification of increment multiplicities,
combined with the exact pair-window formula, may suffice.
For the very smallest cycles one should expect additional
equality patterns, so simply extending the large-\(N\)
classification would be premature.

\begin{problem}[Targets annihilated by the domain order]
If \(NW=0\), what is the optimal coefficient in
\(D(f)\le C(N,W)d_1(f)\)?
Does it depend only on the exponent of \(W\), or on more
of its group structure?
\end{problem}

The positive equality mechanism of
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:90:thm:cycle} is excluded under this hypothesis.
The next extremizer must therefore use at least two
exceptional increments. The exact window correlations
can distinguish their cyclic separation, while additive
cancellation in the target distinguishes their values.
Finite vector spaces are a natural first family.

\begin{problem}[Several sampled generating directions]
For a probability law \(\lambda\) on the generating
directions of \(C_N\), determine the best constant
\[
 D(f)\le C(N,\lambda)
 \sum_h\lambda(h)d_h(f)
\]
uniformly over abelian targets, and classify the
extremizers.
\end{problem}

Our proof gives \(C(N,\lambda)\le(N+1)/6\).
When two different unoriented generating directions
have positive weight, the one-direction equality cases
cannot attain equality for both. The task is to turn
that incompatibility into the exact improved coefficient.
A two-direction law is a concrete starting point;
it requires joint information about two cyclic orderings
of the same function.

\begin{problem}[A partial-domain version]
Under what explicit density and overlap hypotheses on
\(A\subset C_N\) can derivative collisions of a function
\(f:A\to W\), sampled in one or a few directions, force
a sharp lower bound for \(E(\Gamma_f)\)?
\end{problem}

This is the closest directional question to the sparse
graphs that occur in the structural portions of Gowers'
argument. A useful theorem should express its constant
in terms of measurable overlap quantities such as
\(|A\cap(A-h)|\), and should include an example showing
why those quantities are necessary.
Artificial extension to all of \(C_N\) does not supply
such a theorem.

\subsection{Integration and formal verification}

\begin{problem}[Complete parameter propagation]
In which concrete downstream step of the audited Gowers
proof does an exact Fourier frontier or directional
conversion yield a strict improvement to the final
numerical bound after every subsequent loss is included?
\end{problem}

A convincing answer should state the old and new final
bound under identical hypotheses, trace the improved
parameter through the entire dependency chain, and
identify whether the change affects an exponent, a
constant, or only a finite threshold. It should compare
with an explicitly dated global result such as
\cite{lssbounds}, rather than imply that a sharper local
constant automatically changes the global asymptotic.

\begin{problem}[A formal certificate library]
Can the polynomial and finite-window proofs be formalized
as reusable exact lemmas in the ProveIt project?
\end{problem}

A practical sequence is to formalize the Chebyshev
certificate principle, rational polynomial identities
and interval signs, the signed-moment \(2\times2\)
positivity obstruction, and the circular-window
counting formula. The core cycle inequality can then
be assembled from finite-sum identities and the
majority split. The algebraic branch additionally
requires existence and uniqueness of an interval root;
the finite-grid theorem requires only its explicitly
stated finite sign tests once the parameters are
provided. Numerical solver output should remain
outside the trusted proof boundary.

The most direct next projects are the cutoff-five
phase immediately after \(a_5\), a proof covering the
remaining small cycles, and exact two-direction
testing on a cycle. Each has a sharply delimited
first theorem and an explicit extremal question.

\section[{Integration into Gowers-type arguments\srctag{91}}]{Integration into Gowers-type arguments}\label{gsr:fz:91:sec:d11}\label{gsr:fz:91:sec:integration}
\srcnote{91}{Section 11}

\subsection{The exact quantitative replacement}

Let $I_{p,d}(\delta)$ denote any valid lower bound supplied by a nonclassical inverse theorem:
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:91:eq:inverseinput}
 \norm f_\infty\leq1,\quad\norm f_{U^{d+1}}\geq\delta
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \mathcal C_{d,\lfloor(d-1)/(p-1)\rfloor}(f)\geq I_{p,d}(\delta).
\end{equation}
The existence of an appropriate positive bound belongs to the inverse theory \cite{taozieglerlow}; it is an input here. At $d=d_a$, our theorem immediately gives
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:91:eq:inverseoutput}
 \mathcal C_{d_a,a-1}(f)\geq c_{p,a}I_{p,d_a}(\delta).
\end{equation}
For $a=1$, the competitors on the left are classical degree-$p$ phases. Thus one may substitute $c_{p,1}$ for $p^{-1/2}$ in that final conversion step. The factor is optimal as a uniform comparison of the two phase-correlation norms. It does not determine the optimal inverse function $I_{p,p}$.

For example, if an independently proved input were $I_{p,p}(\delta)=A\delta^B$, this paper would change the resulting prefactor from $A/\sqrt p$ to $A c_{p,1}$, but not the exponent $B$. With a weaker nonpolynomial inverse function, its dependence on $\delta$ likewise remains unchanged. This is the exact extent of the bound improvement claimed here.

\subsection{Why this is not a direct proof of the repository predicate}

The inspected \texttt{proposition\_17\_2} uses a cyclic prime field, an explicit factorial-unit hypothesis, a multiaffine frequency predicate, and an energy conclusion after phase twisting. Its phase degree is $k+1$, not $k$ \cite{repo91lean}. Our theorem uses a vector space over $\Fp$, circle-valued additive polynomials, and a correlation input. Neither statement implies the other merely by renaming parameters.

A valid integration chain would first provide a small-characteristic analogue of the structural and integration steps. If that chain produced a critical-degree polynomial correlation, \eqref{gsr:fz:91:eq:inverseoutput} could be used without further loss. Our pointwise identity can then be used on weighted or restricted domains, but it does not construct local primitives or extend a partially defined phase.

The formal predicates should therefore live in a separate namespace. A sensible dependency order is: finite-difference operators; degree lowering; digit and step degree bounds; critical normal form; the finite complex-sum identity; norm transfer; root-polygon sharpness; cyclotomic minimality; and the diagonal score identity. Only the last three pieces require material beyond basic finite sums and additive polynomial algebra.

\subsection{Why one cannot remove all depths by iteration}

After reducing depth $a$ to $a-1$, the degree is still $d_a$, whereas the first critical degree for depth $a-1$ is $d_{a-1}=d_a-(p-1)$. The next top residue need not be linear. Therefore the hypotheses needed to repeat the argument are absent.

This is not a minor technical omission. Classical inverse statements fail in sufficiently low characteristic at higher degrees \cite{bsst}. The present theorem is consistent with that obstruction because it removes only the highest possible depth at its first occurrence. A nonlinear top-residue theorem would need additional hypotheses, a degree increase, or a dimension-dependent loss.

Recent work on inverse estimates for classical polynomial phases in non-small characteristic studies a different parameter regime \cite{milomoshkovitz}. No improvement to those bounds, to the general polynomial inverse conjecture, or to the final integer Szemer\'edi bound is asserted here.

\section[{Verification and reproducibility\srctag{91}}]{Verification and reproducibility}\label{gsr:fz:91:sec:d12}\label{gsr:fz:91:sec:verification}
\srcnote{91}{Section 12}

The package contains the selector, a deterministic verification program, and its generated JSON output. The mathematical proofs above do not depend on numerical optimization.

\paragraph{Exact checks.}
The atomic identity is checked as an equality of integer exponent multisets, before evaluating any root of unity. Modular finite differences verify the exact digit degree and the step-function degree bound for $p\in\{2,3,5,7,11\}$ and $a\in\{1,2,3\}$. Multivariate coordinate-difference checks test 48 explicit critical-degree polynomials and every one of their candidates in six small $(p,a,n)$ regimes. Symbolic cyclotomic polynomials verify the Eisenstein certificates and degree ratios in the same 15 parameter pairs.

\paragraph{Numerical diagnostics.}
The program exhausts 509,732 root-phase vectors after quotienting by common root rotations. These cover nine $(p,a)$ pairs, including $(5,2)$ and $(7,1)$; every observed maximum equals the proposed constant to the stated tolerance, with exactly $p$ normalized maximizing vectors. It additionally tests 600 random cyclic vectors and 150 weighted sample inputs. The maximum atomic-identity residual is below $4.5\cdot10^{-16}$, the maximum frame-identity residual below $5.6\cdot10^{-16}$, and no transfer or stability violation is detected at tolerance $10^{-11}$.

The exhaustive optimization uses floating-point arithmetic and tolerance $10^{-10}$; it is not an exact inequality certificate. The root-polygon proof supplies the real-analytic certification. The exact degree tests cover finite examples, not all vector spaces. No Lean code was compiled, and none of these checks should be recorded as a completed formal theorem.

\paragraph{Reproduction.}
From the package directory, run
\begin{lstlisting}[language=bash]
python code/verify.py
latexmk -pdf -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error article.tex
\end{lstlisting}
The selector uses the Python standard library. The optional symbolic Eisenstein checks require SymPy; the verifier records a skip rather than silently claiming those checks were executed when SymPy is unavailable. The archived run did execute them. A fixed random seed, \texttt{20261007}, is recorded in \texttt{data/verification.json}.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Further research questions\srctag{91}}]{Further research questions}\label{gsr:fz:91:sec:d13}\label{gsr:fz:91:sec:questions}
\srcnote{91}{Section 13}

The following questions arise from the proved results. They are proposed research targets, not claims that every formulation is absent from the entire literature. The first four are tightly specified continuations of this paper; the later ones concern integration and generalization.

\begin{problem}[Optimal stability coefficient]
For fixed $p,a$, determine the best $K_{p,a}$ such that
\[
 \norm{F-\ipninetyone Fv\,v}_2^2
 \leq K_{p,a}\bigl(M(F)^2-c_{p,a}^2|\ipninetyone Fv|^2\bigr)
\]
for all $F$. We prove $K_{p,a}\leq s_*^{-2}$ and show that the square-root modulus is unavoidable, but do not determine the best coefficient. The exact score coordinates reduce this to a finite-dimensional extremal problem with explicit weights.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[All equality cases for the norm comparison]
Classify arbitrary $f$ satisfying
$\mathcal C_{d_a,a-1}(f)=c_{p,a}\mathcal C_{d_a,a}(f)$.
Our endpoint classification handles $f=\e(P)$, and the frame theorem controls a necessary conditional expectation. A full classification must also control components orthogonal to the fibres of the optimizing top linear form.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Incomplete residue support]
Suppose the averaging measure is supported on only a prescribed subset $S\subsetneq\Fp$ of top residues. Determine the optimal transfer factor and minimum fixed-list size on that support. The pointwise $p$-term theorem remains valid, but its sharp uniform-measure example no longer lives on $S$. This gives a concrete finite root-geometry problem rather than an unspecified weighted inverse theorem.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Stability of maximizing lower-depth phases]
Quantify the phase-endpoint classification: if a lower-depth function $R$ has correlation at least $c_{p,a}-\varepsilon$ with $\e(P)$, how small a fraction of points must be changed to make $R$ a constant shift of one of the $R_j$? The finite polygon has a positive angular gap for fixed $p,a$, suggesting explicit estimates. Uniform dependence as $p$ or $a$ grows is the important part.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[The next degree and a quadratic top residue]
For a polynomial of depth at most $a$ and degree at most $d_a+1$, multiplication by $p^a$ yields an $U_1$-valued polynomial of degree at most two rather than one. Find conversion estimates that retain information about its rank, fibre distribution, or number of essential variables. A dimension-free theorem with no additional parameters should not be assumed.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Degree overhead versus correlation]
When the top residue is nonlinear, determine the smallest increase in degree that permits a controlled one-layer reduction. There is a natural optimization between the degree of indicator functions of residue fibres and the coefficient sum of an atomic representation. Sharp examples should accompany any proposed general bound.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Fewer adaptive queries]
The minimum fixed dictionary has $p$ entries, but the prefix selector reads all fibre sums. Under oracle access to a structured phase and sample access to a bounded function, what query complexity is sufficient to find a candidate with correlation within a prescribed additive error of the maximum? The algebraic list lower bound does not settle this adaptive problem.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Simultaneous guarantees beyond total energy]
The common-index theorem retains the optimal fraction of aggregate energy, while proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:91:prop:component} rules out an unrestricted componentwise conclusion. Determine useful hypotheses---for example, correlation-score alignment or bounded mutual incoherence---that force a positive fraction of individual channels to retain a specified fraction of their correlations.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Other finite value-group extensions]
The optimal coefficient sum comes from root geometry, whereas minimum list length comes from a cyclotomic extension degree. Which other finite root-of-unity extensions admit a matching optimal sparse decomposition? This asks whether the agreement between geometric and arithmetic optima persists beyond a single $p$-power step.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Finite abelian $p$-groups]
Develop an analogue for polynomial maps on products of cyclic groups of orders $p^{b_i}$. The exponent-$p$ relation $(T_h-1)^p=-p(T_h-1)U(T_h-1)$ need not hold in directions of higher order; it must be replaced by the appropriate relation $T_h^{p^b}=1$. One should first identify the correct critical degree and top-residue normal form, rather than importing the exponent-$p$ formula unchanged.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Local primitives in the Gowers framework]
Identify an actual repository lemma whose output can be upgraded to a critical-degree circle-valued polynomial on a weighted domain, with a rigorous extension or localization theorem. The present conversion introduces no further boundary loss once that phase is available. The missing work is the production and certification of the phase, not the weighted conversion itself.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Kernel-checked sharp conversion]
Formalize first the exact pointwise identity and the sharp norm-transfer inequality, then separately the polygon equality theorem and cyclotomic list lower bound. This would give a useful verified result before any attempt to rebuild a full small-characteristic inverse theorem. The proof architecture is finite and explicit, but a completed kernel check remains future work.
\end{problem}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Conclusion\srctag{91}}]{Conclusion}\label{gsr:fz:91:sec:d14}
\srcnote{91}{Section 14}

At the first occurrence of each nonclassical depth, the cost of removing that depth is not an unspecified positive constant. It is exactly the sine ratio $c_{p,a}$, and precisely $p$ fixed phases are necessary and sufficient to realize a uniform transfer. The same construction gives complete phase extremizers, an optimal atomic norm, a diagonal stability identity, simultaneous aggregate-energy control, and a one-pass implementation.

The main quantitative improvement is local but sharp: at degree $p$, the classicalization loss in a standard finite-field inverse argument improves from $p^{-1/2}$ to a constant tending to one with $p$. The structural inverse input and the global density-increment iteration are unchanged. This separation makes the result suitable for independent verification and for later integration into the repository without assigning it conclusions that have not been proved.

\section[{Source audit and novelty boundaries\srctag{91}}]{Source audit and novelty boundaries}\label{gsr:fz:91:sec:dB}\label{gsr:fz:91:app:audit}
\srcnote{91}{Appendix B}

\paragraph{Primary mathematical sources.}
The original Gowers paper \cite{gowers} supplies the phase-removal context; the corrected repository declaration, rather than an OCR degree, supplies the comparison with Proposition 17.2. The theory of nonclassical polynomial degree and depth is credited to \cite{taononclassical,taozieglerlow}. The specific $p^{-1/2}$ baseline is the displayed conclusion of the Section 3 proof in \cite{bsst}, checked in the article PDF. The qualitative $U^{p+1}$ result is theirs, not a new conclusion of this paper. The 2026 preprint \cite{milomoshkovitz} was inspected to distinguish its non-small-characteristic inverse bounds from the present low-characteristic conversion problem.

\paragraph{Repository sources.}
The inspected \texttt{Sections17\_18.lean} blob is
\begin{center}\small\texttt{18495f50475835ca1c497d85b0052215f865b8ca}.\end{center}
The inspected Boolean integration plan is a research/formalization proposal, not a proof that the new statements here are already formalized. The research index and a targeted repository search were used to check obvious overlap; this is not an exhaustive full-text audit of every prior manuscript.

\paragraph{What is proved here.}
The exact critical-depth transfer, the sine-ratio optimum, the complete phase-endpoint classification, optimal fixed-list size, explicit frame identity, stability bound and exponent, simultaneous aggregate-energy theorem, and algorithm are the mathematical claims of this draft. Their proofs are given in full. The general existence and quantitative strength of a Gowers inverse theorem are not proved here.

\paragraph{Priority.}
The literature search did not establish a prior statement of this precise sharp package, but absence of a located match is not a proof of novelty. These results should be checked by specialists before publication or attribution of priority. Independent review should particularly examine the degree budget in proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:91:prop:normal}, the equality classification in theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:91:thm:extremizers}, and the distinction between fixed-list and adaptive minimality in theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:91:thm:minimal}.

\section[{Algorithms and reproducibility\srctag{92}}]{Algorithms and reproducibility}\label{gsr:fz:92:sec:d12}\label{gsr:fz:92:sec:algorithms}
\srcnote{92}{Section 12}

\subsection{Constructing an optimal repair from a tensor}

For a single tensor, the algebraic part of the construction is explicit.
First extract the $n\times n$ matrix
$B_{ij}=t_{pe_i+e_j}-t_{e_i+pe_j}$. Alternating Gaussian elimination then
finds its radical and a symplectic basis. A maximum isotropic subspace is
obtained by taking one axis from each symplectic block together with the
radical. To build a minimum cover, upgrade the complementary axis in each
block to period $p^2$ and use \eqref{gsr:fp:92:eq:minimalprimitive}; add an explicit
primitive for the integrable residual from \eqref{gsr:fp:92:eq:oddprimitive} or
\eqref{gsr:fp:92:eq:booleanprimitive}.

The alternating linear-algebra stage requires $O(n^3)$ field operations by
the usual elimination algorithm. This does not mean that the entire tensor
computation has cubic complexity: a symmetric $(p+1)$-linear tensor has
$\binom{n+p}{p+1}$ independent coefficients, and transforming or outputting
them has its own cost. Sparse or oracle tensor representations may change
that cost substantially. For a family, the exact cost is expressed by the
maximum common isotropic dimension; proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:92:prop:familybounds} gives a greedy
construction and certified bounds, not a general polynomial-time optimum
algorithm.

\subsection{What the exact checker verifies}

The standard-library program performs three logically different checks.
It reconstructs the full ternary quartic coefficient census; it verifies
explicit primitive formulas in several finite cases; and it checks a
selected Fourier-square identity with zero and nonunit amplitudes.

The primitive tests use $p=3,5,7$ in dimension two for the odd-prime formulas,
$p=2$ in dimension three for Boolean cubic formulas, the optimal one-block
covers for $p=2,3,5,7$, uniform field covers for selected small degrees, and
a composite-group cover. For each test it computes every repeated-generator
difference of order $d$ and $d+1$ at every basepoint. There are 39 primitive
cases and 25334 exact difference comparisons. These are regression tests of
the general written proofs, not substitutes for those proofs.

The quartic coefficient census is different: it is an exhaustive computation
of the particular finite object used in lemma~\ref{gsr:fp:92:lem:certificate}. It visits
all 59049 cubes, retains all degenerate cubes, uses integer pairs for
$\Z[\zeta_3]$, and checks square roots of coefficient norms as integers.
No floating-point number enters the certified bound.

To reproduce the certificates, run
\begin{verbatim}
python3 verify_exact.py
\end{verbatim}
To regenerate both exact JSON files from the definitions, run
\begin{verbatim}
python3 verify_exact.py --write
\end{verbatim}
The optional phase search is separate:
\begin{verbatim}
python3 explore_ternary.py --starts 30 --seed 1729
\end{verbatim}
It requires NumPy and SciPy and reports only numerical evidence. A numerical
search failure, optimizer termination status, or phase-grid census must not
be used to change the conjecture into a theorem.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Integration into ProveIt and a claim audit\srctag{92}}]{Integration into ProveIt and a claim audit}\label{gsr:fz:92:sec:d13}\label{gsr:fz:92:sec:audit}
\srcnote{92}{Section 13}

\subsection{Theorem dependencies}

The principal proof chain is
\[
\begin{gathered}
 \text{finite-cover polarization}
 \ \Longrightarrow\ \text{twisted norm realization}
 \ \Longrightarrow\ \text{quotient-profile comparison},\\
 \text{degree-$p+1$ integration criterion}
 \ \Longrightarrow\ \text{alternating normal form},\\
 \text{normal form} + \text{torsion-image lower bound}
 \ \Longrightarrow\ \text{optimal covers and the repair frontier},\\
 \text{normal form} + \text{quotient-profile comparison}
 \ \Longrightarrow\ \text{exact dimension reduction},\\
 \text{dimension reduction} + \text{finite Laurent census}
 \ \Longrightarrow\ \text{ternary quartic integration threshold}.
\end{gathered}
\]
The first four lines do not depend on any computation or on the conjectured
ternary endpoint. The criterion is known in greater generality; the proofs
here specialize and expose it rather than assume a new theorem from an
unverified repository article.

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.36\textwidth}p{0.55\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Statement & Status in this manuscript\\
\midrule
Ordinary Gowers norm and Gowers--Cauchy--Schwarz
 & Standard background; precise normalization stated.\\
Nonclassical symmetry criterion
 & Established by Tidor in all degrees; the first-obstruction case is reproved.\\
Finite-cover realization and twisted subgroup comparison
 & Written proofs in arbitrary finite abelian groups.\\
Minimum abelian kernel, cover classification, and joint frontier
 & Written proofs with matching constructions and universal lower bounds.\\
Simultaneous-family repair
 & Written variational characterization, not an efficient optimum algorithm.\\
All-dimensional extremal reduction
 & Written proof, including the optimizing function's unused coordinates.\\
Ternary upper bound $1099/2187$
 & Exact finite computational census plus written analytic reduction.\\
Ternary sharp value $11/27$
 & Conjecture; exact lower bound and numerical evidence only.\\
Global Szemer\'edi improvement or a new inverse theorem
 & Not claimed.\\
New Lean verification
 & Not claimed; no ledger entry is marked proved by this package.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\subsection{Formalization boundaries}

A first formalization should introduce circle-valued top derivatives and
homogeneous symmetric tensors in a separate namespace. The use of $\T$
cannot be replaced indiscriminately by $\F_p$: the primitives in
\eqref{gsr:fp:92:eq:oddprimitive} and \eqref{gsr:fp:92:eq:booleanprimitive} genuinely require higher-order
torsion values. The cover primitive \eqref{gsr:fp:92:eq:minimalprimitive} is $p$-torsion
valued on a larger group, which is a different statement.

The formal project should separately verify the pullback normalization,
the sign in the gauge identity, and the difference between $d$ cube slots
and $k=d-1$ selected-derivative slots. It should not infer all-slot symmetry
from symmetry in the derivative directions alone. For the cover lower
bound, the exact kernel computation of \eqref{gsr:fp:92:eq:connecting} and the linear
section of $A[p]\to U$ are natural finite-algebra milestones.

The inspected \texttt{Sections17\_18.lean} contains proposition-valued
catalogue definitions, not proofs merely by virtue of their names
\cite{repo92lean}. This article does not change their status. The separate
\texttt{FORMALIZATION\_PLAN.md} gives proposed declarations and completion
criteria, without exporting placeholder axioms or pretending that a
successful build has occurred.

\subsection{Why this does not yet change an integer progression bound}

The analytic and algebraic statements are exact, but they enter only one
part of an inverse-theorem argument. The original cyclic group of prime
order has no useful nontrivial proper subgroups; the large subspaces used
here belong to a finite-vector-space model. A cover changes the phase
space rather than directly giving a long progression in the original
interval. Localization to Bohr sets or progressions requires boundary
control, and an approximate selector still requires a genuine
symmetrization theorem.

Modern quantitative work on Szemer\'edi's theorem has much stronger global
bounds than the original 2001 argument \cite{lssbounds}. We do not compare a local
repair constant to those global bounds as though it were an improvement of
the same theorem. The contribution here is an optimal structural repair
and a lossless energy interface that can be used when its hypotheses are
actually available.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Further research questions\srctag{92}}]{Further research questions}\label{gsr:fz:92:sec:d14}\label{gsr:fz:92:sec:questions}
\srcnote{92}{Section 14}

The questions below are proposed continuations of the proved results. They
are not assertions that every formulation is a named open problem in the
literature.

\begin{question}[The sharp ternary nine-point inequality]
Prove or refute conjecture~\ref{gsr:fp:92:conj:ternary}. A sum-of-squares certificate for the
Laurent polynomial $11/27-\calE_{T_0}$ would settle the all-dimensional
nonintegrable symmetric quartic maximum over $\F_3$. The coefficient file
makes this a finite, explicitly specified target. A counterexample must be
certified over the continuous phase torus, not merely inferred from an
unstable floating-point iterate.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[The one-block maximum at other primes]
Is $m_{p,1}=1-2(1-1/p)^p$ for every odd prime? The right side is the exact
constant-function energy, but no general upper bound of this strength is
proved here. Determine the asymptotics of $m_{p,1}$ as $p\to\infty$ and
classify the equality cases when the constant function is optimal.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Tensorization versus joint dependence]
For odd $p$, does $m_{p,r}=m_{p,1}^r$ hold? The product lower bound and monotonic upper bound
in \eqref{gsr:fp:92:eq:mmonotonic} leave room for optimizers coupling different blocks.
An affirmative answer would convert positive energy into a quantitative
bound on obstruction rank and hence into logarithmic repair codimension.
A failure would exhibit a genuinely joint phase phenomenon invisible in
one-block optimization.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Stability at the exact repair frontier]
Classify tensors and functions close to equality in the quotient-profile
comparison and in the extremal energy problem. In particular, can a
near-extremizer be shown to concentrate on cosets with compatible local
phase structure? The compactness observation $\calM_G(S)<1$ for a fixed
nonintegrable $S$ is not a dimension-uniform stability theorem.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Optimal covers beyond degree \texorpdfstring{$p+1$}{p+1}]
For a general symmetric $d$-linear tensor, determine the smallest abelian
kernel on which it integrates. The universal constructions in
section~\ref{gsr:fp:92:sec:covers} give existence, but do not identify the optimum. At higher
degrees the transfer obstruction has remaining slots and is no longer a
single alternating bilinear form. Is there a filtration of torsion-image
obstructions that gives matching lower and upper bounds?
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Algorithms for common isotropic repair]
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:92:thm:family} solves the covering optimization in terms of maximum
common isotropic dimension. Develop exact algorithms, efficiently
checkable optimality certificates, and useful approximation bounds for
that dimension in sparse or structured families. Characterize families
for which the greedy dimension bound in proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:92:prop:familybounds} is sharp.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Symmetrization before repair]
How can approximate symmetry or a selected frequency map that is only
multiaffine be converted into the homogeneous all-slot symmetric tensor
required here, with quantitatively controlled loss? A solution must address
the actual symmetry defect, not just invoke an integration theorem whose
hypotheses have not been obtained. This is the missing interface to many
inverse-theorem inputs.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Localized quotient-profile inequalities]
Find a version of theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:92:thm:mainanalytic} for local cubes on a Bohr set or a
progression, with an explicit boundary term that remains useful in a
density-increment iteration. The cover proof uses translation-invariant
averages and exact cosets; neither survives localization for free.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Mixed and simultaneous energy selection]
For several tensors, the common optimal cover is now algebraically
understood, but a single coset need not preserve every energy. Determine
sharp hypotheses under which a joint local conclusion follows from the
vector of mean inequalities, possibly by retaining a coupled quotient
profile rather than applying scalar selection separately.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Kernel-checked finite certificates]
Formalize the abstract cover lower bound first, then turn the 59049-cube
census into a small verified computation that reconstructs the exponents
and cyclotomic coefficients from definitions. Can a shorter symbolic
certificate replace the exhaustive list while remaining easier to audit
than a numerical optimization proof?
\end{question}

\section[{Verification, reproducibility, and research status\srctag{93}}]{Verification, reproducibility, and research status}\label{gsr:fz:93:sec:d9}
\srcnote{93}{Section 9}
\label{gsr:fz:93:sec:verification}

The accompanying archive contains the complete \LaTeX\ source and
compiled PDF, both vector figures, four verification programs, their
machine-readable outputs, and source provenance. The proofs do not
depend on the success of numerical sampling. The programs have three
different roles, which should be kept distinct.

\subsection{Exact algebra and finite arithmetic}

The Fourier verifier implements a small sparse polynomial ring over
$\mathbb Q$ and checks 24 algebraic or finite-field assertions.
These include the contact equation, the transition identity, the
Chebyshev coefficients of both continuous and discrete dual
polynomials, the exact grid-error identity modulo the contact cubic,
the earlier branch masses and moments, and the irreducibility
certificate for $a_*/\pi$. Denominator and sign hypotheses are proved
in the text; an identity alone would not verify them.

The norm-rate verifier uses integer and rational arithmetic throughout.
It reduces logarithms to arguments in $[1,2]$, uses the convergent
series for $2\operatorname{arctanh}z$ with an explicit geometric
remainder, and encloses the exponential with a Taylor remainder.
Directed rounding is performed at 100 decimal places. Eight parameter
choices, including every row of the numerical table, pass the tail,
smoothing, and cube-positivity hypotheses. A large value of the
smoothing degree $L$ is recorded as an integer; the program does not
attempt to enumerate the spectrum of that kernel.

The prime-cube verifier uses dynamic programming on exact subset-sum
sets to obtain $A_{p,j}$ for $p=3,5,7,11,13$. For $p\le7$, it also
computes the defining cube sums by an independent multiplicative
derivative recursion for several dimensions and sign patterns. This
checks the normalization and the sign-independence assertion without
using the polynomial formula in both sides of the comparison.

The rigidity verifier exhausts 13,656 maps normalized by $f(0)=0$
across 32 small-domain suites with cyclic and product domains and
targets of orders two through five. Of the 155 maps at defect at
most one quarter, 65 have the full majority graph and 90 realize the
nontrivial endpoint branch. A further 2,484 specified sparse maps
on domains of orders $13,14,16,23,31,53$ include 902 strict-quarter
non-affine examples and 132 exact maximal-energy examples.
The order-thirteen integer inequalities and both order-twelve
counterexamples are checked exactly. Normalization by a target
translation preserves energy and affine distance, so it is a valid
reduction of the exhaustive suites.

\subsection{Independent numerical diagnostics}

The Fourier code checks primal masses, all moment constraints, dual
coefficient norms, and dual signs at 2,009 cutoff-four instances and
8,127 all-cutoff instances with $2\le R\le64$. For 174 cyclic-grid
instances it compares the finite certificate with an independently
formed linear program. These include every $N$ divisible by four
from eight through 512 and additional odd grids. The largest observed
LP discrepancy was less than $5.9\cdot10^{-14}$; the largest residual
in the grid-error identity was less than $2.0\cdot10^{-16}$.
These numbers report agreement in the checked instances and are not
uniform error bounds for a numerical solver.

The figures evaluate the explicit proved formulas. Their source
program is included, so the plots can be regenerated or rescaled
without extracting data from a rendered image.

\subsection{Independent mathematical checks}

The checks described here are internal derivation and cross-checks
during preparation of the manuscript.
The Fourier and norm derivations were separately checked, including
the interval signs in the quartic certificate, the grid contact
factorization, the finite-group translation operator argument, and
the exact prime-cube count. The affine argument was independently
checked through the majority subgroup, both endpoint alternatives,
the order-thirteen integer step, and the full local cubic expansion.
These checks led to two concrete refinements in presentation: the
stronger order-thirteen fiber cap reduces the needed local cubic
range to $t<1/3$, and deterministic decoding uses pair cancellation
instead of assuming a hash table on an arbitrary target group.

This manuscript supplies proof-level mathematical arguments and
reproducible computational supplements. It has not undergone external
peer review or a proof-assistant verification. Its claims of
improvement are relative to the explicitly audited project sources.
