\section[{Integration with the ProveIt development\srctag{93}}]{Integration with the ProveIt development}\label{gsr:fz:93:sec:d10}
\srcnote{93}{Section 10}
\label{gsr:fz:93:sec:integration}

\subsection{Normalization adapters}

The existing file
\texttt{Lean/GowersSzemeredi/Definitions.lean} defines an unnormalized
Fourier transform and an unnormalized Gowers norm \cite{repo88}.
For the present normalized conventions, the adapters on a group of
order $N$ are
\[
 \widehat f_{\rm paper}(r)=N\widehat f(r),\qquad
 \|f\|_{{\rm Gowers},d}=N^{(d+1)/2^d}\|f\|_{U^d}.
\]
With the code's squared-difference definition, the assertion
\texttt{UniformOfDegree f alpha d} is equivalent to the normalized bound
$\|f\|_{U^{d+1}}^{2^{d+1}}\le\alpha$.
Establishing these adapters first would prevent a local improvement
from acquiring an incorrect power of $N$ during integration.

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.29\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.29\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.34\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Existing interface & Article component & Suggested first formal target\\
\midrule
\texttt{Proofs05Missing\allowbreak Interval.lean},
\texttt{lemma\_5\_2\_holds} & Theorems~\ref{gsr:dt:93:new:allR},
\ref{gsr:dt:93:new:Phi4}; missing-interval consequence & Finite weighted dual
certificate and the half-circle specialization\\[4pt]
\texttt{Definitions.lean},
\texttt{gowersNorm}; Section~3 norm lemmas & Sections~\ref{gsr:cc:93:sec:norm-prior}
and the faster comparison & Normalization; exact prime-cube count;
finite-cardinality comparison\\[4pt]
\texttt{Sections06\_07.lean},
\texttt{lemma\_6\_2} & Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:recovery},
\ref{gsr:en:93:rig:endpoint}, \ref{gsr:en:93:rig:thirteen} & Graph energy as derivative
collisions; majority subgroup; order-thirteen arithmetic\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The names in this table are inspected existing declarations or file
interfaces. They are not names of newly supplied Lean proofs.

\subsection{A dependency order for formalization}

The affine part is the most direct finite-algebra starting point.
First define the graph-energy count and prove its identity with the
sum of squared derivative multiplicities. Next formalize the
union--intersection convolution identity, the truncated multiplicity
bound, and the multilevel cubic inequality. The majority subgroup
and the projection argument then use only finite sums, elementary
group theory, and polynomial inequalities. The order-thirteen proof
has explicit rational comparisons; no search over arbitrary target
groups is required. Infinite targets can be retained by working with
the finite support of each count rather than assuming a finite
ambient target.

For Fourier detection, a finite weighted-measure certificate should
precede the Borel-measure formulation. The quartic identities are
suited to ring normalization after positivity of denominators is
recorded. Existence and uniqueness of the contact root require the
intermediate value theorem and strict monotonicity on a named
interval. Separating those analytic facts from exact polynomial
identities makes the algebraic transition and grid formula easier
to reuse.

For the norm theorem, the fixed-prime cube polynomial gives a
combinatorial entry point. The uniform theorem requires more
analysis: an absolutely convergent Fourier series, the bounded
translation operator identity, Bohr-volume estimates, and norm
convexity. The rational numerical certificate is useful for checking
parameters, but importing a JSON output would not formalize the
underlying uniform theorem.

\subsection{What would be needed for a global bound}

The present results have explicit local ranges. The Fourier
classification fixes the cutoff, and the affine theorem treats energy
above $3N^3/4$. A density-increment proof often encounters small
correlations or much lower graph energy. A global improvement would
therefore need a specified iteration in which these local estimates
are actually invoked, with every restriction, progression length,
dimension loss, and increment tracked. One would then solve the
resulting recurrence and compare the final numerical or asymptotic
bound with existing quantitative results.

For context, Leng, Sah, and Sawhney prove, for each $k\ge5$, a bound
of the form
$r_k(N)\ll N\exp(- (\log\log N)^{c_k})$ with $c_k>0$
\cite{lssbounds}. We make no stronger claim for $r_k(N)$ here.
The local statements above remain useful independently of whether
such a global substitution produces an asymptotic gain.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Further research: precise questions and next steps\srctag{93}}]{Further research: precise questions and next steps}\label{gsr:fz:93:sec:d11}
\srcnote{93}{Section 11}
\label{gsr:fz:93:sec:questions}

The following questions remain open in the scope of this article and
the audited project. They are organized by the proof mechanisms that
could address them. Priority here means a proposed order of work,
not an assessment of worldwide novelty or difficulty.

\subsection{Exact Fourier profiles and arithmetic discretization}

\begin{problem}[Complete cutoff five; immediate next exact problem]
Determine $\Phi_5(a)$ for every $a$, including all contact supports,
active moment signs, and transition equations. Can the complete
answer be certified by a finite list of polynomial factorizations
with explicitly isolated real roots?
\end{problem}
The cutoff-four solution suggests starting with a numerical active-set
survey, then eliminating every numerical parameter from the proposed
certificates. The genuine work is proving feasibility of all unused
moments and completeness of the listed transitions. The final-band
theorem already removes one portion of this task.

\begin{problem}[Structure of transitions at general cutoff]
Outside the final band of Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:93:new:allR}, bound the number of
support changes of $\Phi_R$, their algebraic degrees in $\cos a$,
and the number of active frequencies. Which transition angles are
rational multiples of $\pi$?
\end{problem}
The irrational transition at cutoff four rules out an answer based
only on equally spaced roots of unity. A useful first goal is an
efficient algorithm at each fixed $R$, with controlled algebraic
degrees and explicit polynomial certificates for every branch.
The target is a usable complexity bound, beyond the abstract
existence of a procedure through finite moment representations
and real quantifier elimination.

\begin{problem}[Global unequal-budget profiles]
For positive numbers $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_R$, determine
\[
 \min_{\supp\mu\subseteq K_a}\max_{1\le j\le R}
     \frac{|\widehat\mu(j)|}{\lambda_j}
\]
through every radius and budget transition, beginning with $R=4$.
\end{problem}
Earlier project work treats a local unequal-budget profile.
The question here is the global classification. Perturbing the new
central certificate changes both its coefficient signs and its
contact equations, so continuing one local formula is insufficient.

\begin{problem}[Grid limits at support transitions]
Determine the exact finite-grid profiles in shrinking neighborhoods
of $a_*$ and $3\pi/5$. What replaces
Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:93:grid:asymptotic} when the unused third-moment slack tends
to zero at a rate comparable to the grid spacing?
\end{problem}
The compact-interior hypothesis was used precisely to keep all
certificate signs and moment slack uniformly positive. A joint
scaling of the radius and the adjacent node positions could reveal
a finite collection of transition formulas. Endpoint rounding and
interior-contact displacement must continue to be tracked separately.

\begin{problem}[Stability and indicator realizability]
Obtain quantitative distances from a near-optimal measure to the
unique extremizer, and determine the sharp Fourier bound when the
measure is constrained to be uniform on a set of prescribed density.
\end{problem}
The central dual polynomial has a double interior zero and a simple
endpoint zero. Integrating its defect should control concentration
near those two nodes at different scales. Passing from concentration
of a weighted measure to a realizable set extremizer is a separate
problem, particularly when the density is bounded away from zero.

\subsection{Sharp norm rates and the geometry of extremizers}

\begin{problem}[The optimal rate uniform over group families]
What is the smallest order of an error function $e_d$ for which
$c_d(\mathcal F)-D(\mathcal F)\le C e_d$ holds with an absolute
constant for every family $\mathcal F$?
\end{problem}
This article places the problem between the obstruction $d2^{-d}$
and the upper rate $d2^{-d/2}$. The present loss comes from the
interaction of the Fourier-tail budget and the spectral degree
needed for smoothing. Improving only the numerical constant in the
translation estimate will not close that exponential gap.

\begin{problem}[The all-odd excess above one third]
Determine the asymptotic size of $c_d^{\mathrm{odd}}-1/3$, including
a nontrivial matching lower construction if one exists. Must
near-extremizing group orders tend to infinity with $d$, and at what
scale?
\end{problem}
This is distinct from the previous question. A fixed prime has
$D_p<1/3$, so its exact first correction does not witness an excess
above the all-group endpoint. Any lower-bound construction must
balance the finite-order loss in $D_p$ against the high-order norm
gain, with estimates uniform in both parameters.

\begin{problem}[The next fixed-prime term]
For a fixed odd prime $p$, determine the coefficient of
$\log d\,2^{-d}$ in $c_d(\{\Z/p\Z\})$, and then the term of
order $2^{-d}$. Are the punctured interval signs asymptotically
optimal to those finer orders?
\end{problem}
Their cube polynomial gives a lower expansion containing
$-4D_p(p-2)\log d\,2^{-d}$. The present upper bound does not
determine that coefficient for the supremum. Small changes in the
function may affect a high-order cube product significantly while
changing its fourth Fourier moment only slightly, so the witness
expansion cannot be promoted to an extremal expansion without a
stability argument.

\begin{problem}[Composite and noncyclic groups]
Find the first correction to $c_d(\{G\})$ for a fixed odd-order
abelian group $G$ that is not of prime order. Which subgroup
configurations determine the analogue of the punctured-sign cube
polynomial, and when is its leading exponential factor $|G|^{-d}$?
\end{problem}
The prime argument uses that every nonzero direction generates the
whole group. In a composite group, subset sums can remain in a
proper subgroup indefinitely. A useful approach is to organize
direction tuples by their generated subgroup and by the support
of a bounded extremizer, before attempting an asymptotic supremum.

\begin{problem}[Finite dimension and structural stability]
Determine $c_4^{\mathrm{odd}}$ and classify its true extremizers or
extremizing sequences. More generally, convert the quantitative
bounded approximation in this article into structural information
about functions with norm ratio close to the sharp constant.
\end{problem}
The new asymptotic theorem does not improve the fixed-dimension
four problem. Its endpoint defect provides an explicit constraint
on an autocorrelation, but small defect alone is not yet a
classification of the original function. Coupled Fourier moment
constraints and a stability theorem for the bounded endpoint are
natural next ingredients.

\subsection{Affine stability beyond exact extremality}

\begin{problem}[Stability of the quarter-endpoint dichotomy]
If $\varepsilon(f)\le1/4+\delta$, can one prove a uniform alternative
between proximity to an affine map and proximity to the union of
two graph-subgroup cosets? Determine the optimal dependence on
$\delta$, including the obstruction caused by nonextendible
homomorphisms on index-two subgroups.
\end{problem}
The exact proof forces equality in an occupancy inequality at
$\delta=0$. A quantitative version must control almost-closure of
the majority relation and almost-extremal coset occupancies without
assuming that the majority set is already a subgroup.

\begin{problem}[A second energy maximum and near-maximal maps]
After removing affine maps and the one-point extremizers, determine
the next largest graph energy for $N\ge13$, with its dependence on
domain subgroups and target torsion. Give a stability theorem for
maps whose energy is within a specified amount of the sharp maximum.
\end{problem}
The local cubic remainders measure two distinct deficits: failure
of the error support to be a coset, and use of multiple error values.
Those nonnegative terms provide a starting point, but integer
constraints and subgroup availability may produce several different
second extremizers.

\begin{problem}[Intrinsic partial-domain hypotheses]
Which additional assumptions on $B\subseteq G$ make graph energy
close to $|B|^3$, rather than $|G|^3$, imply proximity to the
restriction of a global affine map?
\end{problem}
The partial-domain theorem here deliberately retains ambient
normalization. A local Freiman homomorphism need not extend globally.
Possible hypotheses should therefore address both additive structure
of $B$ and the algebraic extension problem in the target, for example
through controlled difference sets and explicit extension conditions.

\begin{problem}[Nonabelian targets and other tests]
Identify an appropriate four-point consistency statistic for
nonabelian targets and determine which parts of the quarter-threshold
argument survive. Can one isolate a sharp analogue of the multilevel
overlap inequality compatible with the required multiplication order?
\end{problem}
The current convolution identity and signed expansion use
commutativity in specific places. The classical nonabelian
homomorphism-testing results \cite{bclr} provide context, but do not
make a direct transfer of the present affine energy proof automatic.

\subsection{Two implementation goals}

\begin{problem}[A certified exact-profile pipeline]
Build a proof-producing procedure which takes a proposed finite
moment support, isolates its algebraic parameters, verifies all
sign conditions, and exports certificates suitable for Lean.
\end{problem}
The cutoff-four case is a concrete benchmark: it includes rational
identities, a uniquely isolated cubic contact, an irrational angular
transition, and arithmetic grid effects. A solver should return the
certificate and its domain of validity, not only a numerical optimum.

\begin{problem}[Propagation through one specified recurrence]
Choose a complete quantified density-increment recurrence in the
ProveIt development, substitute exactly the applicable improvements
from this article, and solve the resulting recurrence with every
parameter explicit. Does the substitution improve a final numerical
bound, an exponent, or only a local constant?
\end{problem}
This is the necessary bridge from the present results to a stronger
global Ramsey or Szemer\'edi statement. It should be attempted on
one fully specified iteration so that improvements, inactive ranges,
and compensating losses can all be assessed quantitatively.

\subsection{Normalization at the interface}
Gowers' paper uses unnormalized Fourier transforms and sums in the
relevant section. If $\widehat f_{\mathrm{sum}}(\xi)=
\sum_x f(x)\overline{\xi(x)}$, then
\[
 \widehat f_{\mathrm{sum}}=|G|\widehat f,
 \qquad
 \left(\sum_\xi|\widehat f_{\mathrm{sum}}(\xi)|^4\right)^{1/4}
 =|G|\stnorm f_{U^2}.
\]
The unnormalized $U^2$ cube norm is $|G|^{3/4}\stnorm f_{U^2}$,
and the unnormalized $L^2$ norm is $|G|^{1/2}\stnorm f_{L^2}$.
An integration must therefore select one normalization globally rather
than silently mixing the Fourier and cube conventions.

\subsection{Suggested proof-assistant decomposition}
The elementary portion can be formalized before the spectral portion.
Useful independent interfaces are the Fourier identity
(Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:94:st3:lem-fourier}), the constant-fiber identity
(Lemma~\ref{gsr:cc:94:st3:lem-fiber}), the blockwise norm estimate
(Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:94:st3:thm-constants}), and the subgroup-indicator equality
witnesses \eqref{gsr:cc:94:st3:large-p-witness}. These require finite group
characters, finite sums, H\"older/Cauchy--Schwarz, and elementary
annihilator identities.

The spectral portion should then expose the unitary equivalence in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:94:st3:thm-spectrum}, rather than hide it behind a numerical
singular-value routine. Equality is a separate theorem about rank-one
character sectors. Stability can be decomposed into the seven estimates
in its proof; especially useful separately are
\eqref{gsr:cc:94:st3:squared-amplitude}, \eqref{gsr:cc:94:st3:rank-one-error}, and
\eqref{gsr:cc:94:st3:pair-outside}. The final step depends on a singular-value gap,
not just on a perturbation bound for $M_F$.

The package contains no Lean proof and makes no assertion that the
repository's Lean project was built. Labels and citation keys in the
LaTeX source use the prefix \texttt{st3:} or \texttt{st3-}; theorem
environments and mathematical convenience macros have an \texttt{st}
prefix. This makes the paper suitable for a separate research directory
or for later inclusion as a source in the consolidated article.

\section[{Reproducible finite checks\srctag{94}}]{Reproducible finite checks}\label{gsr:fz:94:sec:d9}\label{gsr:fz:94:st3:sec-verification}
\srcnote{94}{Section 9}

The accompanying verifier uses Python and NumPy. Run
\texttt{python code/verify.py} to write the results to
\path{data/verification.json}. The checks have three logically distinct roles.

The \emph{exact finite checks} verify the subgroup identities, the
multiplicity of every sum fiber in every tested block, the support-coset
multiplicity $|W|/\ell$, and subgroup-indicator equality witnesses.
They use integer and rational arithmetic. The tested cyclic systems
include every ordered slope pair modulo $N$ for $1\le N\le12$.
Additional explicitly seeded homomorphisms include product groups,
noncyclic two-groups, and systems with unequal domain and codomain.
There are $750$ systems in the default run.

The \emph{floating-point checks} independently compare direct
physical-space progression averages with the constrained Fourier sum;
compare the entire nonzero singular spectrum of the full matrix with
the reduced character-sector formula; and test the seven exponents
$p=1,3/2,2,3,4,8,\infty$, including the equality witnesses. These checks
run on $193$ selected systems. The largest observed absolute singular-
spectrum discrepancy was $3.11\times10^{-15}$, and the largest observed
absolute Fourier-identity discrepancy was $4.15\times10^{-14}$.

The \emph{stability diagnostics} construct compatible complex phases,
perturb their Fourier coefficients and maximizing pairs, and implement
the character-sector repair used in the proof. The default run checks
$140$ near-extremizing triples. It also checks
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:94:st3:thm-counting} and its proper-progression consequence on
$108$ indicator triples. All assertions passed in the packaged run.

These finite checks supplement the proofs; they are not proof premises
for a theorem about all finite groups. In particular, the two stability
exponents are justified by Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:94:st3:prop-optimal-exponents},
not by numerical fitting. A numerical singular-value decomposition is
not a formal certificate of equality in an arbitrary input instance.
The exact general proof is the unitary decomposition and the subsequent
inequality argument in the article.

\section[{Further research questions\srctag{94}}]{Further research questions}\label{gsr:fz:94:sec:d10}\label{gsr:fz:94:st3:sec-questions}
\srcnote{94}{Section 10}

The following questions are proposed research directions. Except where
explicitly referring back to a proved result, they are not conclusions
of this article, and they are not all asserted to be previously
published open problems.

\subsection{Balanced marked functions}
Determine the sharp constant under the additional condition
$\widehat f_0(0)=0$. If $\Sigma/K$ has a nonzero coset, translating the
extremal support to that coset preserves the coefficient $C_4$ and
satisfies the balancing condition. If $\Sigma=K$, however, the zero
frequency lies in every accessible support coset, so deleting it
interacts with the rank-one constraint. The resulting finite extremal
problem is not determined merely by replacing $k$ with $k-1$ in a
H\"older bound. A complete formula, together with equality and
stability, would be a genuinely stronger input for balanced counting.

\subsection{Sparse prescribed spectra}
Given a set $E\subseteq\Gamma$, determine the best constant for
$\stsupp\widehat f_0\subseteq E$. Fiber counting yields
\[
 \stnorm{M_F}_{\stOp}
 \le\sqrt\ell\max_{S\in\Sigma/K}|E\cap S|^{1/4}
                          \stnorm F_{\ell^4}.
\]
This is an upper bound, not an automatic equality formula. Equality
requires the surviving entries to have the appropriate rank-one
geometry. Characterize the sets $E$ for which the displayed coefficient
is sharp, and determine the loss when it is not. This links additive
spectral structure to concrete matrix completion and support questions.

\subsection{Indicator-specific stability}
Although subgroup indicators attain the sharp constant, the complex
repair theorem does not produce nearby indicator sets. Classify
near-extremizing triples of sets directly in normalized symmetric-
difference distance, with hypotheses controlling very small densities.
One must distinguish translations and modulations allowed by the
complex Fourier classification from operations preserving indicator
functions. The subgroup witnesses suggest a useful target, but do not
settle the quantitative set problem.

\subsection{The transition at \texorpdfstring{$p=2$}{p = 2}}
Obtain a uniform stability theory for the full coefficient diagram
\eqref{gsr:fm:94:st3:headline-cp}, including the changing equality class at $p=2$.
For $p>2$, flatness is forced by a strict finite-set norm comparison;
at $p=2$ it is not. Any estimate uniform as $p\downarrow2$ must account
for the enlarged extremizer family rather than continue a fixed
flatness conclusion. Similar care is required near $p=\infty$, where
invisible or submaximal coefficients need not vanish.

\subsection{Longer progressions and higher-order analogues}
For four or more terms, Fourier constraints lead to tensors rather
than a single bilinear operator. Is there a useful common-kernel
character decomposition which separates unavoidable torsion from a
higher-order uniformity estimate as cleanly as
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:94:st3:thm-spectrum}? A positive answer would have to retain
the algebraic configurations detected by $U^3$ and higher norms;
$U^2$ alone cannot control arbitrary longer progression counts.
The problem is not solved by replacing matrix rank with tensor rank
in the present proof.

\subsection{A torsion-aware density-increment interface}
Can the quotient-corrected main term in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:94:st3:thm-counting}, together with a structured visible
Fourier coefficient, support a density-increment procedure that avoids
repeated prime-cyclic embedding in applications naturally posed in
finite groups? The necessary theorem would have to quantify the
interaction between a quotient-density increment and a progression or
Bohr-set increment. The local norm calculation here does not supply
that iteration or its final bounds.

\subsection{Sharp constants in the numerical stability bounds}
The exponents $1/4$ and $1/2$ are optimal, but the constants $4$ and $7$
were chosen to keep the proof transparent. Determine their optimal
asymptotic replacements, first for $U=V=\{0\}$ and then for general
$U,V,L$. There may be distinct local mechanisms: mass leaving a coset,
amplitude variation inside it, a second character sector, and
misalignment between the two unmarked vectors. A sharp constant must
compare these mechanisms rather than merely improve one triangle
inequality in isolation.

\subsection{Formal certification of the structural repair}
Develop a reusable finite-dimensional theorem formalizing the
character-sector decomposition of matrices
$H(u_0,v_0)=F(u_0+v_0)$ with overlapping subgroup domains.
Its statement should include nonsplit subgroup extensions, exact
singular-value multiplicities, and the compatible rank-one repair.
Such an interface could support other sharp counting inequalities in
the repository without redoing all Fourier-coordinate calculations.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Conclusion\srctag{94}}]{Conclusion}\label{gsr:fz:94:sec:d11}
\srcnote{94}{Section 11}
The two-increment three-term problem has an exact answer depending
only on three image indices. The fixed-function operator, however,
remembers more: accessible spectral cosets, the common-kernel character,
and the multiplicity contributed by $A-B$. Keeping these distinctions
visible yields all complex equality cases and a stability theorem with
optimal exponents. The result is a precise local generalization of the
Fourier counting machinery used in Gowers' proof. Its possible value
for stronger global Ramsey bounds lies in the additional interfaces
listed above, not in an unproved extrapolation from a sharp local
coefficient.

\section[{Algorithms, certificates, and exact finite validation\srctag{95}}]{Algorithms, certificates, and exact finite validation}\label{gsr:fz:95:sec:d10}\label{gsr:fz:95:spi:sec:checks}
\srcnote{95}{Section 10}

\subsection{Algorithms suggested by the proofs}
Given dense symmetric Boolean cubic tensors, the obstruction matrices are
read from
\[
 (\Omega_{T_i})_{jk}=T_i(e_j,e_j,e_k)+T_i(e_j,e_k,e_k).
\]
After symmetry is established, this costs $O(n^2)$ coefficient accesses per
tensor. Verifying a completely untrusted dense tensor is symmetric itself
requires inspecting its $O(n^3)$ entries.

The three evaluated ranks are ordinary finite-field matrix ranks.
The generic rank must be computed over $\Ftwo(z)$, by exact polynomial or
rational-function elimination, or by nonzero principal Pfaffians. Testing
only the three field elements in projective coordinates is unsound.
Once a common isotropic basis is found, \eqref{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:primitive} constructs both
primitives using $O((\dim W)^3)$ tensor evaluations after basis conversion.
These are algebraic operation descriptions, not a claimed optimized
bit-complexity bound for a complete pencil-classification implementation.

The unequal-budget frontier needs only sorting and prefix sums. Given its
value $R$, an extremal pencil is obtained by taking
$m_a=\max(0,R-K_a)$ and assigning any unused multiplicity to one direction.
The exact-profile construction in theorem~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:thm:profiles} is equally explicit.

\subsection{What is implemented}
The companion program \texttt{checks/verify.py} uses Python's standard
library and exact integers, $\Ftwo[z]$, Gaussian integers, prime fields,
and arithmetic modulo eight.
It independently enumerates all subspaces in dimension four in reduced
row-echelon form. Generic rank is determined by recursive principal
Pfaffians, not by evaluating the pencil at finitely many field points.
An exhaustive small search is appropriate for validation; it is not
presented as an efficient algorithm for large-dimensional research inputs.

The delivered run records the following checks.
\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.55\textwidth}r@{}}
\toprule
Check & Scope\\
\midrule
All pairs of alternating forms on $\Ftwo^4$ & $4\,096$ pairs\\
Complete subspace list in that census & $67$ subspaces\\
Optimal common-isotropic codimension & $4\,096$ equalities\\
Existence of a zero-defect restriction at cost $\le D$ & $4\,096$ cases\\
Finite-test budget vectors (two through five tests) & $2\,225$ vectors\\
Independent three-plane integer optimization & $343$ triples\\
Hyperplanes in the sharp irreducible example & $15$ hyperplanes\\
All integrable symmetric cubics on $\Ftwo^3$ & $128$ tensors\\
Pointwise third-derivative identities modulo eight & $524\,288$ checks\\
Fourth coordinate-derivative identities modulo eight & $82\,944$ checks\\
Exact-profile constructions with symbolic rank checks & $39$ profiles\\
Energy bounds at Gaussian-rational inputs & $384$ cases\\
Complete-direction extremizers over prime fields & $p=2,3,5,7$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The dimension-four defect histogram is
\[
 \#\{D=0\}=1870,\qquad \#\{D=1\}=1890,\qquad \#\{D=2\}=336.
\]
The six-dimensional rank counterexample, the three-generator obstruction,
and the canonical cubic bias $1/2$ are also checked exactly. The added
prime-field examples verify every rational specialization of the constructed
block pencils; their generic rank follows from the nonzero block product.
The Gaussian-rational tests directly sum the signed cubic averages and check
the amplitude-sensitive bound with exact integer arithmetic. The JSON file
records the results and elapsed time. These finite checks do not prove the
general theorems; the preceding proofs do that, subject to the explicitly
identified classical inputs.

\subsection{Formalization priorities}
A realistic first formal target is the certificate formulation at the end
of section~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:sec:pencils}. Given a common isotropic basis and a nonzero
Pfaffian, optimality follows from elementary symplectic dimension bounds.
This avoids first formalizing the entire canonical-form existence theorem.

Next comes the Pfaffian multiplicity lemma and its finite-test consequence.
The sharp three-budget formula has a very small combinatorial core: the
existence of nonnegative multiplicities $m_i\ge R-K_i$ summing to $R$.
The cubic primitive is a finite modular calculation with a manageable
coordinate-basis reduction. The analytic layer requires finite-dimensional
complex spectral theory for the projective orthogonality lemma.

For a full existence proof without supplied certificates, the alternating
pencil decomposition remains a significant formalization dependency.
The accompanying \texttt{FORMALIZATION.md} lists interfaces and priorities;
no placeholder \texttt{sorry}, extra axiom, or untested Lean file is included.

\section[{Further research questions\srctag{95}}]{Further research questions}\label{gsr:fz:95:sec:d11}\label{gsr:fz:95:spi:sec:questions}
\srcnote{95}{Section 11}

The following questions are proposed next steps, not assertions that their
status has been exhaustively surveyed in the literature. They are ordered
roughly from a direct continuation of the proved results toward the global
Gowers interface.

\begin{question}[Joint localization after algebraic repair]
Given positive energies for $T_0,T_1,T_+$, can one choose a common integration
space $W$ and a coset $z+W$ on which two or three restricted energies admit
quantitative lower bounds in terms of the original energies and the sharp
budget $B$? Which additional hypotheses are necessary?
\end{question}
The point is not the exact phase-removal identity on a fixed coset, which
is already proved, but the simultaneous retention of analytic mass.
A counterexample to unconditional retention would clarify the appropriate
input for a useful localization theorem.

\begin{question}[Common extremizers versus three separate extrema]
Classify pairs $T_0,T_1$ for which one $1$-bounded function simultaneously
attains $\M(T_0),\M(T_1),\M(T_+)$. How do the integrable parts of the tensors
interact with the scalar-plane obstruction decomposition?
\end{question}
The geometric equality theorem only classifies the obstruction pencil.
The gauge choices that optimize the three scalar energies need not be
compatible. This is an analytic compatibility problem beyond the rank
calculation.

\begin{question}[Function-level stability]
Suppose the product slack in \eqref{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:energy-slack} is small. After the
proved restriction of codimension at most $D$, can the functions be
approximated by a precisely described family of common extremizers with
an optimal error modulus?
\end{question}
The exact decomposition separates a discrete algebraic defect from the
continuous scalar gaps $\eta_i$. A successful theorem should keep those
sources of loss separate instead of applying a generic compactness argument.

\begin{question}[Minimum dimension for an exact profile]
For prescribed evaluated half-ranks and generic half-rank satisfying
\eqref{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:profile-feasibility}, determine the smallest possible ambient
dimension. The construction here uses $2R+D$, but the irreducible and
long rational blocks can use fewer coordinates.
\end{question}
For instance $(r_0,r_1,r_+;r)=(2,2,2;2)$ is realized in dimension four,
although the uniform singular-block construction uses dimension six.
This is a finite combinatorial optimization over primary block types and
could lead to a complete dimension-sensitive refinement of the frontier.

\begin{question}[The exact deletion cost]
For a given pencil, determine
\[
 d_S(A)=\min\{\codim U:D_S(A|_U)=0\}.
\]
We proved $d_S(A)\le D_S(A)$ with a sharp universal coefficient, but not
an exact formula for every pencil. Can mixing different primary summands
reduce the cost below the sum of their separate costs?
\end{question}
The answer would refine defect stability from a worst-case theorem to an
instance-optimal repair algorithm.

\begin{question}[Three or more independent models]
What replaces generic rank for a family of three alternating obstructions?
Can one obtain a sharp codimension theorem from the ranks of all nonzero
linear combinations, together with a small number of extra invariants?
\end{question}
Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:prop:three-generators} rules out the naive extension of the pencil
invariant. The failure is already visible in dimension three, so any
proposed invariant should explain that example before being applied in
large dimension.

\begin{question}[Energy-to-rank at odd primes]
For symmetric $(p+1)$-linear $T$ over $\F_p$, determine the strongest
inequality connecting its selected derivative energy to the rank of
\eqref{gsr:fp:95:spi:eq:prime-obstruction}. Is there an exact scalar extremal formula,
or does the answer depend on additional data beyond the alternating rank?
\end{question}
The algebraic simultaneous repair theorem is already available. This
analytic bridge is the missing ingredient in extending the Boolean
three-energy theorem to $p+1$ projective energy tests.

\begin{question}[Higher repeated-variable obstructions]
For degree greater than $p+1$, repeated-variable defects form a multilinear
family of alternating forms rather than a single matrix. Which controlled
families still reduce to pencils after restriction, and what quantitative
loss does that reduction require?
\end{question}
A promising restricted problem is when the defect image is two-dimensional:
the present paper then determines the common isotropic cost once the
higher-order dependence has been made compatible with that image.

\begin{question}[Small formal certificates and fast construction]
Can an implementation output an optimal common-isotropic basis and a
compact nonzero-Pfaffian certificate without constructing a full congruence
normal form? What is the best deterministic bit complexity over $\Ftwo$?
\end{question}
The verification interface in section~\ref{gsr:fp:95:spi:sec:pencils} is already exact. A fast
constructor paired with a small verified checker would be a practical
contribution to the repository.

\begin{question}[Return to cyclic localization]
Identify a phase-selection stage in the cyclic Gowers argument that
naturally produces two compatible models and all their needed combination
tests. Can the simultaneous repair idea be transferred through an
appropriate local finite-field model while controlling progression length
and density gain?
\end{question}
This question requires new work. Merely inserting the coefficient $3/2$
into a cyclic proof with a different characteristic and polynomial notion
would be invalid.

\subsection{Conclusion}
The additional information in the third Boolean phase test has an exact
value: it reduces the worst common repair budget from $2K$ to
$\lfloor3K/2\rfloor$, and no better universal value is possible. The
underlying obstruction is not the largest rank visible over the base field
but the generic rank of an alternating pencil. A Pfaffian degree budget
measures how much finite specialization can hide that rank.

Keeping the full profile reveals more than a constant improvement. It
gives the complete unequal-budget frontier, every realizable exact rank
profile, and a discrete defect whose removal cost is at most its value.
These results isolate a tractable simultaneous-integration problem in the
phase-removal part of Gowers's framework. The remaining steps toward a
stronger density-increment theorem are analytic localization and the
compatibility of common extremizers, not further manipulation of the
single-tensor repair bound.

\section[{How the refinements enter Gowers's argument\srctag{96}}]{How the refinements enter Gowers's argument}\label{gsr:fz:96:sec:d9}
\srcnote{96}{Section 9}
\label{gsr:fz:96:sec:integration}

\subsection{A direct strengthening of the cube-counting interface}

Gowers's Lemmas 3.8 and 3.9 provide the multilinear
Cauchy--Schwarz and triangle inequalities for the uniformity norm.
Lemma 3.10 then bounds the number of $d$-cubes in an
$\alpha$-uniform set of degree $d-1$ and density $\delta$ by
$(\delta+\alpha^{1/2^d})^{2^d}N^{d+1}$ \cite{gowers}.
In the normalized notation used here, its hypothesis on the balanced
function $f=\one_A-\delta$ is $Q_d(f)\le\alpha$.

\begin{corollary}[A refined version of the cube-counting bound]
\label{gsr:fz:96:cor:gowers-cube}
Let $G$ have odd order $N$, let $A\subset G$ have density $\delta$,
let $d\ge4$, and set $m=2^d$. If $Q_d(\one_A-\delta)\le\alpha$, then
the number of ordered $d$-cubes contained in $A$, including degenerate
cubes, is at most
\begin{equation}\label{gsr:fz:96:eq:gowers-cube}
 N^{d+1}\left[
 \delta^m+P_d\left(\frac{100}{843}\right)^{1/4}
       \delta^{m-4}\alpha^{4/m}
 +\sum_{j=5}^{m}\binom mj\delta^{m-j}\alpha^{j/m}
 \right].
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Use $u=\norm{\one_A-\delta}_{U^d}\le\alpha^{1/m}$ in
Corollary~\ref{gsr:cc:96:cube:improved-quartic} and multiply the normalized
cube average by $N^{d+1}$. Every coefficient on the right is
nonnegative.
\end{proof}

The cancellation of terms of orders one, two, and three, and the exact
coefficient $P_d$, are earlier repository refinements. The further
change established here is the smaller coefficient multiplying the
fourth-order uniformity term. In dimension four, the previous
$100(4/29)^{1/4}=60.94183\ldots$ becomes
$100(100/843)^{1/4}=58.68716\ldots$. This is a precise local
improvement with every higher-order term retained.

\subsection{Where the hypotheses are available}

The following table separates immediate substitutions from steps that
would need additional structural work. It is a mathematical integration
map, not a claim that the complete proof has already been reoptimized.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}L{0.21\textwidth}L{0.29\textwidth}Y@{}}
\toprule
Interface & Result available here & Condition to preserve\\
\midrule
Uniformity and cube counts, Gowers \S3
& Corollary~\ref{gsr:fz:96:cor:gowers-cube}
& A real balanced function, odd domain order, and normalized
$Q_d(f)\le\alpha$. Multiply counts by $N^{d+1}$.\\[0.4em]
Approximate affine structure, the \S6--7 framework
& Theorems~\ref{gsr:en:96:thm:affine-remainder} and~\ref{gsr:en:96:thm:affine-cubic}
& A map on a whole finite group and a specified affine reference.
The estimate alone does not select a nearby reference.\\[0.4em]
Respected arrangements, the \S12--13 and \S15 framework
& Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:96:thm:arr-odd}
& Full product sampling; high agreement is needed for the inverse
repair statement. Oddness is a target condition.\\[0.4em]
Observed arrangements
& Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:96:thm:arr-erasure}
& The near-full-domain condition
$\lambda\eta+1-\lambda\le1/[240(s-1)]$;
retain the row-density profile.\\

\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

Gowers's bilinear extraction works with sets that may have very small
ambient density. A theorem assuming almost full observation cannot
automatically replace that extraction. Similarly, the affine cubic is
a statement relative to a chosen affine map; it is not by itself a
global inverse theorem at arbitrary rejection probability. These
distinctions specify the next steps for using the results in
a global argument.

\subsection{Proposed placement and preservation of attribution}

The natural destination is the existing
\texttt{local-quantitative-refinements} research collection
\cite{repo96}. The affine part belongs beside sources 11, 14, 38 and 59;
the arrangement part extends source 33; the norm part extends sources
45 and 49; and the counting consequence belongs beside sources 03,
04, 08 and 09. The appendix reproduces source 33's decoder and should
retain its explicit prior-work attribution.

The article is a complete standalone source. Integration into the
combined report should prefix its labels and bibliography keys, retain
the full statements and proofs, and remove only the standalone document
wrapper. The supplied package reserves no intake number and changes no
formal proof ledger. A separate Lean development would be needed before
any statement could be marked as formally proved.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Further research questions\srctag{96}}]{Further research questions}\label{gsr:fz:96:sec:d10}
\srcnote{96}{Section 10}
\label{gsr:fz:96:sec:questions}

The questions below distinguish problems settled by this article from
the narrower issues they leave. An \emph{open} question here is one
unresolved by these proofs and the inspected repository material;
the list is a proposed research program, not an exhaustive
certification of publication priority. The first four questions
appear to offer the most direct next gains.

\subsection{Priority questions at the improved interfaces}

\begin{question}[The exact common-prime repair coefficient]
\label{gsr:fz:96:q:prime-exact}
For each even $s\ge4$, determine $c_s^{\mathrm{prime}}$.
In particular, is
\[
 c_{16}^{\mathrm{prime}}=\frac{15}{256},
\]
or is there an obstruction larger than the half-interval construction?
\end{question}

The new interval has width $1/(2s)$; for $s=16$ it has narrowed
from $37/512$ to $1/32$. The present upper bound uses
$t_h\le2d$ separately from the cancellation estimate. The lower
construction has a highly structured distribution of $t_h$.
A useful next calculation is a sharp second-order variational problem
for the full family of row derivatives, imposing the cocycle
$D_{h+k}r(x,y)=D_hr(x,y+k)+D_kr(x,y)$.
Treating each $h$ as an unrelated probability distribution loses this
constraint. Either a stronger inequality exploiting it or a new
construction realizing more of the present upper profile would narrow
the interval further.

\begin{question}[The optimal odd-order fourth-uniformity constant]
\label{gsr:fz:96:q:norm-optimal}
Determine
\[
 \inf_{\substack{G\text{ finite abelian of odd order}\\
                 f:G\to\R,\ \E f=0,\ f\ne0}}
       \frac{Q_4(f)}{Q_2(f)^4},
\]
and classify extremizing or asymptotically extremizing functions.
\end{question}

The article raises the certified lower bound to $843/100$, but does
not identify an extremizer. The proof's two profiles leave a specific
optimization problem near their crossover. On the dual side one can
add a fifth harmonic to the test, or bound all residual pairings using
their joint fourth-mass constraint instead of using one common bound for
every residual Fourier amplitude. On the moment side the actual feasible
joint distribution of $(R^2,w)$ is more constrained than the scalar
conditions used here. A successful improvement must control every odd
character order; optimizing only a large cyclic group does not settle
the universal problem.

\begin{question}[A relative arrangement decoder]
\label{gsr:fz:96:q:relative}
What quantitative hypotheses on a sparse
$A\subset G\times H$ imply repair from a small conditional arrangement
defect, with constants expressed in terms of observable density and
mixing parameters?
\end{question}

The unresolved step is obtaining a nearby model without filling the
erased set and charging every invalid configuration as a failure.
Once a suitable model is known, the identity
$\E_hu_h=\E_x(\alpha_x^2-\sum_zp_x(z)^2)$ remains useful.
A plausible first setting is a domain whose edge distributions,
conditioned on validity, satisfy quantitative pair-mixing estimates
and whose nonempty rows have a uniform density lower bound.
One must derive the required mixing from explicit hypotheses on $A$;
assuming independent observed edges merely assumes away the main
difficulty. The thin-row construction shows why no theorem depending
only on $\eta$ can have a uniform linear modulus on arbitrary domains.

\begin{question}[From near equality to a nearby coset]
\label{gsr:fz:96:q:coset-stability}
For fixed $0<t<2/3$, what is the best quantitative bound on
\[
 \min_{b\ne0,\ x_0,\ H\le G}
 \Prob\bigl[f\ne\ell+b\one_{x_0+H}\bigr]
\]
in terms of $\rho=\varepsilon(f)-\Psi(t)$?
\end{question}

Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:96:cor:affine-near-equality} already gives label
concentration and an explicit bound on $s^3-E(S)$. The remaining
problem is therefore a stability theorem for maximal set energy with
constants suited to this range. A useful formulation should account
for the discreteness of subgroup indices: if $t$ stays away from all
available reciprocal indices, a positive gap above the cubic is
unavoidable in a fixed finite group. Near $t=2/3$, the affine
three-image endpoint competes with the single-coset family, so a
uniform statement may need two possible structural conclusions.

\subsection{Sharper affine and erasure structure}

\begin{question}[The lower envelope at a prescribed error density]
\label{gsr:fz:96:q:affine-envelope}
For a fixed finite domain and target, determine the minimum rejection
probability among maps with a prescribed disagreement $s/N$ from an
affine reference. What group-independent envelope survives as the
groups vary?
\end{question}

The cubic is attained at reciprocal-index coset densities. That does
not make it the exact envelope at every real $t$. The full remainder
retains $A$, $A-C$, $sA-2Z$, and $|\Delta-Z|$ before its final
simplification. These terms give a starting point for a constrained
extremal problem involving both label multiplicities and support
energy. A rigorous classification at the first few non-coset support
sizes would test whether the natural candidates are unions of cosets,
perturbed cosets, or genuinely different configurations.

\begin{question}[The exact gap at the endpoint]
\label{gsr:fz:96:q:endpoint}
Determine the infimum of $\varepsilon(f)$ when $t=2/3$ and the
odd-order target has order coprime to three. Is the interval
\[
 \frac29\le\inf\varepsilon(f)\le\frac{8}{27}
\]
from Section~\ref{gsr:en:96:sec:affine-endpoint-stability} sharp at one of its
endpoints, or is the optimum strictly between them?
\end{question}

The structural endpoint is already stable under
$|t-2/3|+\omega(\varepsilon)<2/15$, with
$\omega=\Psi^{-1}$ on the stated small branch. Thus a useful next
problem is the optimal positive gap when the order-three model is
forbidden, together with the structure of near-minimizers. The
three-point map into $\Z_5$ supplies the upper obstruction, while
the lower bound uses the classical correction threshold. Determining
whether that threshold is an actual obstruction for this four-point
endpoint problem, or only a limitation of the correction argument,
would sharpen both the extremal and stability conclusions.

\begin{question}[A torsion-sensitive replacement for the cubic]
\label{gsr:fz:96:q:two-torsion}
For general finite abelian targets, can one retain the nonzero
involution mass explicitly and obtain a sharp replacement for
$\Psi(t)$?
\end{question}

The counterexample over $\Z_2$ excludes simply deleting oddness.
The signed graph identity remains valid, while the two places where
oddness was used are identifiable: $C\le A$ and $2Z\le sA$.
Introducing a separate mass for self-inverse labels may give a
polynomial bound interpolating between odd targets and elementary
two-groups. The correct equality classification should include affine
homomorphisms supported on a half-domain as well as the odd-target
coset perturbations.

\begin{question}[The best finite erasure modulus]
\label{gsr:fz:96:q:erasure-modulus}
Can the bound
\[
 d\le\frac{T+\sqrt{T^2+4\kappa\tau T}}2
\]
be improved at finite error by retaining more of the row-density
distribution or the observed label multiplicities?
\end{question}

Its leading behavior is attained in the stated thin-row limits, but
that leaves room away from those limits.
Corollary~\ref{gsr:en:96:cor:arr-full-row-profile} already solves the relaxation
using all row densities, allocating disagreement first to the thinnest
rows. The remaining question is whether actual labelings and their
derivative cocycles attain that relaxed envelope, or whether the
observed collision identities impose a strictly stronger bound.
A separate issue is the factor $b$, which came from two union bounds;
higher-order incidence information may improve it without changing the
unavoidable square-root regime.

\subsection{Proof methods and global consequences}

\begin{question}[Analytic dual certificates and further harmonics]
\label{gsr:fz:96:q:analytic-dual}
Can the finite dual coefficients be organized into an analytic
identity that explains the successful two-harmonic parameter and
supports systematic optimization with additional harmonics?
\end{question}

The face-split enumeration is complete, but an analytic description
would clarify which configurations produce the principal coefficient
and the residual fifth harmonic. One concrete route is a generating
function with one variable for each step constraint, followed by
coefficient extraction. Another is a recursion across cube faces that
retains phase and output frequency together. Either description should
recover the present rational certificate as a check before it is used
to claim a stronger constant.

\begin{question}[Higher uniformity and coupled derivative moments]
\label{gsr:fz:96:q:higher-norm}
Which analogues of the profiled moment argument improve the best
available odd-order comparisons for $U^d$ with $d\ge5$?
\end{question}

Monotonicity transfers the fourth-order bound but does not improve the
existing $U^5$ coefficient mentioned in Section~\ref{gsr:cc:96:norm:section}.
A new result would need to retain information that genuinely grows
with derivative order, perhaps a higher mean-sensitive inequality or
coupled moments of several derivatives. Low-order torsion must again
be treated explicitly. This is a different task from repeating the
present monotonicity corollary with a larger subscript.

\begin{question}[Correlated weighted labels]
\label{gsr:fz:96:q:correlated-weights}
What is the sharp correction to Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:96:thm:affine-weighted}
when each domain label is sampled independently once and a repeated
domain coordinate reuses that same label?
\end{question}

The theorem here assumes independent labels at every occurrence.
A coupling already bounds the difference between the two rejection
probabilities by the probability of a repeated coordinate, which is
at most $6/N$ by a union bound. The question is the optimal signed
correction and its sharp dependence on the label distributions and
domain torsion. Separating the coincidence patterns of
$(x,y,z,x+y-z)$ gives an explicit starting point. Such a refinement
would connect the fractional theorem to randomized rounding
procedures while preserving the distinction between the two
probability models.

\begin{question}[Quantitative propagation through a complete proof]
\label{gsr:fz:96:q:global-propagation}
Which of the improved local bounds survives a full parameter audit
of Gowers's density-increment proof, and what explicit final estimate
does it produce?
\end{question}

A useful first project is a verified dependency ledger: record every
invocation of the affected lemma, its actual hypotheses, and the
monotone dependence of its output on the improved parameter. For the
cube bound this can begin immediately with
Corollary~\ref{gsr:fz:96:cor:gowers-cube}. For the arrangement theorem it first
requires resolving the sparse-domain mismatch in
Question~\ref{gsr:fz:96:q:relative}. Any eventual global claim must compare its
complete final estimate with the theorem of Leng, Sah and Sawhney
\cite{lssbounds}; improving a numerical constant inside an older local
argument does not alone establish that comparison.

\section[{Verification, reproducibility, and a formalization path\srctag{96}}]{Verification, reproducibility, and a formalization path}\label{gsr:fz:96:sec:d11}
\srcnote{96}{Section 11}
\label{gsr:fz:96:sec:verification}

\subsection{What was checked}

The affine and arrangement theorems have universal written proofs.
Their finite computations check identities, boundary cases, model
distances, and sharpness examples. The norm proof additionally uses
a finite computer-assisted coefficient lemma: its reduction to five
tables is proved, every table is exhaustively regenerated, and the
remaining assertions are integer or rational inequalities. Decimal
numbers in the text are for orientation and do not certify a bound.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}L{0.28\textwidth}Y@{}}
\toprule
Verification family & Coverage\\
\midrule
Affine completion and equality
& $50\,735$ exhaustive maps in 19 domain--target suites, plus
$2\,400$ seeded map evaluations. Signed convolution and direct
graph-energy formulas are compared.\\[0.35em]
Weighted affine theorem
& $7\,575$ exhaustive rational weighted inputs in 11 suites,
using integer arithmetic after clearing denominators.\\[0.35em]
Odd-target arrangement repair
& $3\,836$ pointwise patterns and $1\,539$ full maps into $\Z_3$;
exact interval moments and six common-prime construction examples.\\[0.35em]
Erasure repair
& $1\,539$ partial binary labelings; three independent
direct/convolution/formula comparisons; 24 nonzero-defect examples
inside the stated activation range.\\[0.35em]
Fourth-uniformity certificates
& Complete tables for character orders $5,7,9,11$ and the integer
case; exact order-three counts; phase-polynomial signs; both rational
crossover certificates.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

The tests include even domain groups in the affine theorem,
noncyclic domains and targets, targets with three-torsion, the
$t=2/3$ endpoint, and weighted inputs with nontrivial label
distributions. They do not replace the argument that works for all
finite groups. The norm coefficient tables were also checked against
direct small-group cube evaluation as an internal audit of the Fourier
interface; those numerical comparisons are not premises of the theorem.

\subsection{Contents of the accompanying archive}

The archive contains this complete \LaTeX{} source and compiled PDF,
the five verification programs and their exact JSON outputs, a runner,
build instructions, a source manifest, and an integration guide.
The programs require only Python's standard library. Running
\texttt{python3 code/run\_all.py} regenerates the verification reports;
the runner records each exit status and its log. Assertions must remain
enabled. The \LaTeX{} document uses an inline bibliography and has no
dependence on the large source repository or an external bibliography
database.

The comparison snapshot is \repocommitninetysix. The source manifest records
the inspected files and their hashes so that later repository changes
cannot silently alter the stated baseline. The results are an
AI-assisted research manuscript with internal mathematical and
computational audits. They have not undergone external referee review
or Lean kernel checking.

\subsection{Suggested formalization order}

A formal development can proceed in modules whose dependencies are
explicit in the proofs:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Define the affine defect, graph energy, and signed residual
convolution with unnormalized finite sums. Prove the exact signed
identity before imposing oddness.
\item Formalize the two label inequalities and the missing-completion
bound. These imply the complete remainder, then the cubic and equality
classification. Add rational weights as a separate extension.
\item Define the balanced arrangement sampling space as a finite
fiber of a signed sum. Prove proper-coordinate independence, then the
row collision identities and pair-cancellation inequality.
\item Formalize the inherited decoder and its branch condition before
deriving either new inverse bound. Keep ambient and conditional
probabilities as distinct definitions.
\item Prove the Fourier face identity, balanced moment inequalities,
and scalar certificate in normalized conventions. Reflect the finite
coefficient enumerator into checked integer data, and verify the
phase and cutoff inequalities exactly.
\item Integrate the norm consequence into the already established
quartic cube expansion, with an explicit conversion back to
unnormalized counts.
\end{enumerate}

This order keeps the algebraic core reusable and makes the
computer-assisted portion a finite, clearly specified obligation.
The most delicate proof interfaces are the negative completion term,
the conditioning in the erasure test, and the phase alignment in the
order-five dual estimate; each is retained explicitly in the manuscript.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Further research questions and topics\srctag{97}}]{Further research questions and topics}\label{gsr:fz:97:sec:d13}\label{gsr:fz:97:sec:questions}
\srcnote{97}{Section 13}
\begin{problem}[Effective entry and the optimal global constant]
Extract a fully numerical modulus in Proposition~\ref{gsr:fp:97:prop:ET} sufficient to
compute $\eta_d$, and substantially improve the explicit local constant
$K_d$. Determine the smallest all-deficit constant $A_d$ in
$D\le A_d\delta$. The optimal leading coefficient $2/m_d$ does not determine
that global constant.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[The next stability coefficient and extremizing directions]
Determine the optimal coefficient of $\delta^2$ after $2\delta/m_d$, or the
correct next scale if it is not quadratic. The current $O_d(\delta^{3/2})$
remainder is not asserted sharp. Classify sequences approaching the leading
ratio, including their concentration on the minimal Hessian eigenspaces
and possible motion along the $\theta$ parameter. The parity-dependent
spectrum should be retained rather than averaged out.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[The cubic function problem]
Classify all canonical cubic extremizers in arbitrary dimension and obtain
uniform stability to that family. The binary equality locus in
Appendix~\ref{gsr:fp:97:app:cubic} has extra branches, and $m_3=0$, so the quartic-and-higher
argument cannot simply be substituted with $d=3$. Cubic projective
orthogonality may give a more appropriate description of its equality space.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Noncanonical energies and compatible contractions]
Determine the second extremal energy level among nonintegrable symmetric
tensors. Can the retained contraction profile distinguish all maximizers,
or is an additional common-function compatibility invariant necessary?
The present endpoint family makes such compatibility explicit for the
canonical class, but does not solve noncanonical optimization.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Direct sums and inactive-coordinate stabilization]
Do maxima multiply under direct sums of canonical tensors in degrees at
least four? For which noncanonical tensors does pullback along a surjective
linear map preserve the maximum over all bounded functions? A factorization
of the tensor alone is not a factorization of an arbitrary tested function.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Local measures and progression-cell interfaces]
Develop weighted versions of the relative testing and local coercivity
arguments with quantified boundary and marginal-independence errors.
How much of the gap $m_d$ survives when cubes are sampled inside a structured
cell rather than a full group? An application to the descending-precision
architecture of~\cite{oaiprogressions} would need error bounds relative to cell mass,
not merely absolute ambient error estimates.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Other characteristics and incomplete symmetry]
Identify the analogue of the continuous endpoint phase direction and the
transverse spectrum for repetition obstructions over odd characteristic.
Separately, extend the analysis to multiaffine or only approximately symmetric
selectors without discarding their lower-degree terms. The Boolean
conjugation-period identity has no unchanged odd-characteristic analogue.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Formal certificates and proof-assistant integration]
Formalize the coefficient calculus, relative gluing, and signed-count
certificate before the Hilbert-space and stability estimates. A small
verified checker should accept the endpoint coefficients independently of
the search procedure producing them. Keep the published qualitative inverse
input separate from the explicit local theorem so that either component can
be strengthened without changing the other's hypotheses.
\end{problem}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Conclusion\srctag{97}}]{Conclusion}\label{gsr:fz:97:sec:d14}
\srcnote{97}{Section 14}
The canonical Boolean energy endpoint has a larger equality space than the
ordinary polynomial-phase endpoint: one distinguished coordinate retains an
arbitrary circle-valued phase parameter. Exact derivative constraints along
the inactive subspace force all other dependence into a polynomial gauge.
The remaining four-point optimization is explicit, and its Hessian has a
strict transverse gap in every degree at least four.

The resulting theorem resolves the stated project questions on maximizing
functions and dimension-independent phase stability in those degrees.
It gives both a complete equality classification and the optimal leading
coefficient $2/(2^d-2d-2)$, while distinguishing the explicit local analysis
from the qualitative uniform entry theorem. The next obstacles are the cubic
branching case, noncanonical compatibility, effective global constants, and
localization to the settings needed by progression arguments.

\section[{Further research questions\srctag{98}}]{Further research questions}\label{gsr:fz:98:sec:d10}
\srcnote{98}{Section 10}

The following questions remain separate from the results proved here.
\begin{enumerate}
 \item \textbf{Universal thresholds at higher orders.}
 Is every nonaffine full-domain map bounded by
 \(r_m\le1/2+2^{-m}\) for every \(m\ge4\)? The order-two index-two
 family makes this the largest plausible sharp threshold. The
 third-energy proof uses a special four-point identity and does not
 establish the higher-order assertion.

 \item \textbf{All finite defect orders.}
 For an index-two map with defect order \(d\ge3\) and \(m\ge2d\),
 is the hereditary infimum always \(Q_{m,d}\) from
 \eqref{gsr:en:98:he:finite-cycle-ratio}? We proved the formula when \(d=2\)
 and when \(m<2d\). In the remaining range, additional coherent
 terms occur in the root-of-unity average; the binomial-polynomial
 lower bound used here does not settle them.

 \item \textbf{Third-energy endpoint classification.}
 Does \(r_3(a)=5/8\) force membership in an index-two structural
 family, up to affine changes and the appropriate quotient
 formulation? The present rigidity theorem and examples do not
 classify all endpoint maps.

 \item \textbf{Quantitative stability.}
 For index-two maps, the exact sum of squares controls the imbalance
 \(|E|^2-|O|^2\) and the imaginary correlation
 \(\operatorname{Im}(E\overline O)\). Can this be converted into
 a useful structural description of finite weights whose ratio is
 at most \(5/8+\varepsilon\), with sharp dependence on
 \(\varepsilon\)?

 \item \textbf{Optimal witness complexity.}
 Equation~\eqref{gsr:en:98:he:interval-excess} gives third-energy indicator
 witnesses approaching the endpoint at rate \(O(n^{-2})\). Is
 \(\varepsilon^{-1/2}\) the optimal support exponent for integer
 parity at third energy, as it is for second energy in Report~288?
 What is the optimal support size when arbitrary nonnegative weights
 are permitted?

 \item \textbf{Human and formal verification of the finite lemma.}
 Replace the short computer-assisted hyperplane calculation by
 conceptual inequalities, or formalize its integer enumeration and
 characteristic reduction in Lean. The relation-lattice reduction
 provides a small, explicit target for either approach.

 \item \textbf{Higher-dimensional Jensen quotients.}
 The universal conditional bound localizes to a two-dimensional
 quotient. For specified nonadditive maps on
 \(\mathbb F_2^r\), determine the exact hereditary higher-energy
 spectrum and its relation to Walsh spectra and bent functions.
\end{enumerate}

\Needspace{16\baselineskip}

\section[{Reproduction and limitations\srctag{98}}]{Reproduction and limitations}\label{gsr:fz:98:sec:d11}
\srcnote{98}{Section 11}

The finite verification needs Python~3 and no third-party package. Keep
the three verification files in the same directory, and run
\begin{quote}\small\ttfamily
python small\_cyclic\_m3.py\\
python verify\_third\_energy.py
\end{quote}
The first command regenerates the certificate on standard output; the
second runs the independent checks. All arithmetic in the certificate
checker is integral; there is no floating-point
optimization. The accompanying verification script independently counts
ordered triples, checks the four-point coefficient identity, confirms
the small-cycle attaining examples, and checks the exact interval
formula on initial values. These checks supplement the proofs; they
do not replace the arbitrary-group reductions.

The proof of the main theorem includes the exact computer-assisted
finite lemma of Section~\ref{gsr:en:98:he:small}. The higher-energy formulas in
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:98:he:fingerprints} and the Jensen theorem have analytic and
algebraic proofs independent of that finite enumeration. The article
does not claim that the general higher-order threshold conjecture has
been settled, does not infer a new global Szemer\'edi bound, and does
not assert a complete classification of all equality cases for
arbitrary maps.

The companion \texttt{code/verify.py} uses arbitrary-precision integers and exact rational numbers from Python's standard library. Floating-point values occur only in explicitly labeled decimal output; every pass/fail decision is exact. The source has explicit exception-raising checks, not assertions disabled by \texttt{python -O}. No network connection or third-party Python package is required.

The delivered run checked ten parameter systems, with defining ranks from two to eight. It verified coprimality, CRT reconstruction, all component endpoints, disjointness, total measure by independent interval summation, the closed mass formula, both endpoints of the radius-persistence interval, strict irredundancy witnesses, and exact prime-grid cardinality bounds. For large prime grids, interval counts use floors and ceilings rather than enumeration. The Mersenne primes of exponents $31,61,127,521$ were checked by the implemented Lucas--Lehmer test. This is an executable arithmetic check, not a newly formalized primality theorem.

\section[{Further research questions\srctag{99}}]{Further research questions}\label{gsr:fz:99:sec:d11}\label{gsr:fz:99:sec:questions}
\srcnote{99}{Section 11}

\subsection{The sharp exponential base}
The most direct extremal problem is to determine $c_r^{\mathrm{prime}}$ and $c_r^{\mathrm{fin}}$. Our bounds leave the interval
\[
 \frac{2^r-1}{2}\le c_r^{\mathrm{prime}}\le c_r^{\mathrm{fin}}\le3^r-1.
\]
Is the lower expression the exact answer, or can a different geometry exceed it? Is prime order genuinely different from general finite abelian groups at this sharp scale? Even an exponential-base improvement to the upper bound, or a counterexample to the candidate value, would be informative. Apart from rank one we have no proof of equality. A systematic exact search should treat noncyclic groups and anisotropic character velocities as well as circle models.

\subsection{A radius fixed independently of rank}
Fix once and for all $\rho_0\in(0,1/4)$. Determine the growth in $r$ of the analogous prime-cyclic small-step extremal constant with radius exactly $\rho_0$. Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:99:thm:main} does not answer this question, because the high-ratio construction chooses $\rho$ with $r$ and its accuracy parameter. The nonzero robustness interval in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:99:thm:robust} should not be confused with a uniform-in-rank radius statement.

\subsection{More economical frequencies and moduli}
The factorial spacing in \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:parameters} is a convenient elementary coprimality device, not an optimized choice. More efficient coprime tuples concentrated near a common scale may reduce $A$, the frequency sizes and the sufficient prime threshold. One can ask for the minimum possible largest frequency producing a prescribed fraction of $(2^r-1)/2$. It would also be useful to replace the conservative minimum-arc cutoff by the exact threshold at which all cyclic runs become visible.

\subsection{Anisotropic and weighted versions}
For individual widths $\rho_j$ and a nonuniform velocity profile $\normT{\chi_j(d)}/\rho_j$, the maximum-coordinate normalization loses information. Determine a sharp obstruction in terms of the whole profile. Another direction is to replace the sharp measure by specified product cutoffs and optimize the finite-instance tradeoff \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:finite-tradeoff} under positivity, Fourier-positivity or support constraints. Our lower bound is a necessary condition, not a matching construction of an optimal smoother.

\subsection{Structured tests and density certificates}
The unrestricted testing function that attains \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:testnorm} need not be an input admissible in a density-increment theorem. Which progression-free, low-complexity or polynomial-patch test classes permit better bounds? A useful positive theorem would state exactly how the test structure compensates for the many short Bohr components. For the OpenAI-style strict/padded certificate, one should quantify the minimum necessary discount in a model that includes both mass selection and boundary uncertainty, rather than infer it from total variation alone.

\subsection{Beyond linear cells}
Can a comparable explicit component classification be carried out for quadratic or genuinely triangular polynomial cells while preserving a prime ambient group? The correct complexity measure may involve both the number and weights of slots. A meaningful result should keep separate the cost of a sharp boundary, the cost of adding determining coordinates, and the precision recurrence; conflating them can create incorrect iteration bounds.

\subsection{Formalization and independently checkable certificates}
A practical formalization target is the finite family theorem with explicit $T,p$ and exact floor/ceiling cardinalities, before the real asymptotic notation. The most reusable library pieces are an interval-to-cyclic-run lemma, a CRT cell classification, and the probability-measure tradeoff. A small verified checker for rational arc certificates would make future constructions easier to audit. Independent human review of both the proofs and the targeted novelty comparison remains important before treating the work as a settled literature contribution.

\section[{An explicit certificate specification\srctag{99}}]{An explicit certificate specification}\label{gsr:fz:99:sec:dB}\label{gsr:fz:99:app:certificate}
\srcnote{99}{Appendix B}

The component formula can be checked without iterating over an enormous prime group. For each nonempty subset $S$, compute
\[
 h_i\frac A{q_i}\equiv1\pmod{q_i},\qquad
 x_S\equiv-\sum_{i\in S}\frac A{q_i}h_i\pmod A,
\]
where $h_i$ is any integer inverse of $A/q_i$ modulo $q_i$. Record the rational interval endpoints from \eqref{gsr:en:99:eq:arcs}. For a lift $[\alpha,\beta]$, the exact contribution to $|B_p|$ is
\[
 \lfloor p\beta\rfloor-\lceil p\alpha\rceil+1.
\]
Negative lifts and the arc crossing zero cause no double counting because each lifted arc has length less than one and the projected arcs are disjoint. Sorting the left endpoints modulo one and retaining each arc's positive length gives every cyclic gap exactly.

A finite certificate can therefore consist of the integer parameters, the CRT residues, rational endpoints, the ordered gap list, and exact interval grid counts. The checker need only establish arithmetic identities and inequalities to verify all the finite conclusions once the general interval-classification theorem is available. The supplied code performs these checks and independently exhausts small models; it does not claim to replace the general theorem by a finite list of examples.

\section[{Reproducible verification and proof status\srctag{100}}]{Reproducible verification and proof status}\label{gsr:fz:100:sec:d11}\label{gsr:fz:100:sec:verification}
\srcnote{100}{Section 11}

\subsection{Exact checks}
The script \texttt{verification/verify.py} uses integer arithmetic and Python's \texttt{Fraction} class for its default suite. Its output is saved in \texttt{data/verification.json}. The following checks passed:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lr}
\toprule
Family of checks & Number\\
\midrule
Binary-cube ranks over $\F_5$ and $\F_7$ & 5,330\\
Circle fourth moments for distinct cube vertices & 1,891\\
Fixed-field progression triple moments & 80\\
Fixed-field cube moments & 165\\
Circle progression triple moments & 330\\
Signed-radix uniqueness and magnitude bounds & 1,120\\
\midrule
Total in the recorded counter & 8,916\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The cube-rank checks cover $d=2,3,4$ and subsets of sizes two, three, and four. The circle fourth-moment checks enumerate all four-subsets in those dimensions. The field progression tests use $(p,k)=(5,4),(7,6),(11,8)$. The circle progression tests cover $3\le k\le10$. The partition recurrence separately checks $P_2=1$, $P_3=6$, and $P_4=635$, and the script records $D_k$ and $K_k$ for $3\le k\le10$.

These checks are not substituted for proofs of the general rank classification, the analytic expansion, the transfer lemma, or rounding. They are independent finite tests of the main combinatorial and arithmetic inputs, including the leading coefficients.

\subsection{High-precision characteristic-function tests}
With \texttt{--numerical}, the script uses 90 decimal digits of working precision. It evaluates finite characteristic-function sums for the $\F_5$ observable with $k=4$, $d=3$, $\delta=1/2$, and $\lambda=1/8$. It does not sample a random collection of progression parameters and does not enumerate the enormous group $\F_5^n$.

For each slot-sign vector in $\{-1,0,1\}^m$, the one-coordinate characteristic function is a finite average. Independence of the physical coordinates raises it to the $n$th power. Identical terms are grouped, leaving 102 nonzero groups for the eight cube slots and 15 for the four progression slots. Expanding the centered sines then gives the full desired moments. The ratios to the leading terms are:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{rcc}
\toprule
$n$ & Cube moment / leading term & Progression error / leading term\\
\midrule
16   & 1.1690776679 & 1.0306590432\\
64   & 1.0337656860 & 1.0100800093\\
256  & 1.0079649868 & 1.0036931360\\
1024 & 1.0019625773 & 1.0015132054\\
4096 & 1.0004888708 & 1.0006740983\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The cube comparison here uses $g_n$ without the factor $\lambda$; its predicted leading term is
\[
 \frac{6e^{-4}}{(p-1)^2n^2}.
\]
The progression comparison uses $f_n=\delta+\lambda g_n$; its predicted error is
$4\delta\theta^3(p-1)^{-1/2}n^{-1/2}$. These are precisely the specializations of Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:100:prop:weighted}.

The high-precision calculations are numerical sanity checks, not interval-certified enclosures or formal proofs. The record was produced with Python 3.13.5, NumPy 2.3.5, and mpmath 1.3.0. The default exact checks do not require NumPy or mpmath.

\subsection{Verification levels kept separate}
The manuscript's general statements have written mathematical proofs. The finite input checks are exact executable computations. The characteristic-function comparisons are high-precision numerical computations. No new Lean file was compiled, no repository-wide audit was rerun, and no huge indicator example on a prime cyclic group was explicitly enumerated and stored.

The existence of the indicator sets rests on the rounding proof, not on the numerical table. The leading asymptotic coefficients rest on Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:100:thm:partition} and the local-moment proofs, not on extrapolation from finite $n$. This distinction is especially important because a visually convincing numerical fit alone would not settle either sharpness question.

\section[{Integration and a formalization roadmap\srctag{100}}]{Integration and a formalization roadmap}\label{gsr:fz:100:sec:d12}\label{gsr:fz:100:sec:integration}
\srcnote{100}{Section 12}

A suitable new location is
\begin{quote}\small
\nolinkurl{Combinatorics/Ramsey/Research/GowersSzemeredi/quadratic-barrier/}
\end{quote}
Alternatively, the manuscript can be incorporated as a new source of the existing local-quantitative-refinements report, retaining its theorem labels and an explicit comparison with source 20. It should not be inserted into the proved-statement ledger as though a Lean companion already existed.

The logical dependency chain is short enough to audit in distinct stages:
\[
\begin{gathered}
 \text{cube geometry and local moments}\quad+\quad
 \text{analytic partition formula}\\
 \Downarrow\\
 \text{weighted saturation on $\F_p^n$ and $\T^n$}\\
 \Downarrow\\
 \text{finite-field rounding}\qquad
 \text{bounded-Fourier transfer and cyclic rounding}\\
 \Downarrow\\
 \text{fixed-field and prime-cyclic indicator sharpness}.
\end{gathered}
\]
The two-marked upper benchmark is logically separate: it is needed to identify exponent two as the matching upper exponent, but not to construct the examples.

A staged Lean development could proceed as follows. First formalize the rank-three classification of four binary vertices and the finite circuit-moment identity; these are finite algebraic statements with explicit inputs. Next formalize the signed-radix Fourier transfer for finite Fourier polynomials. Its conclusion is an exact identity and avoids analytic limits. The independent-rounding argument requires a finite product Bernoulli probability space, cube collision bounds, variance estimates, and a cardinality adjustment; it can be isolated from the cumulant calculation.

The substantial analytic task is to formalize the multivariate logarithmic generating function, its finite Taylor truncation, and the support-cost cancellation. A more targeted formalization need only prove the $q=3$ and $q=4$ instances, rather than the general partition theorem. One can then formalize fixed-parameter asymptotic composition and derive the main sharpness statements. A theorem whose hypotheses merely assume the needed cube and progression asymptotics would be a useful interface, but must be labeled conditional until those asymptotics are supplied.

The accompanying \texttt{THEOREM\_STATUS.md} records these distinctions, and \texttt{INTEGRATION.md} gives suggested module boundaries without claiming that any proposed module exists.
