\section[{Further research questions\srctag{100}}]{Further research questions}\label{gsr:fz:100:sec:d13}\label{gsr:fz:100:sec:questions}
\srcnote{100}{Section 13}

\subsection{Optimal constants, not just the exponent}
\begin{question}[The sharp density-dependent coefficient]
For fixed $k$ and $0<\delta<1$, determine the local supremum
\[
 \mathcal B_k(\delta)=
 \limsup_{\substack{Q\to\infty\text{ prime},\ |A|=\lfloor\delta Q\rfloor\\
                   0<\Unorm{\ind_A-|A|/Q}{k-1}\to0}}
 \frac{|\La_k(\ind_A)-(|A|/Q)^k|}
      {\Unorm{\ind_A-|A|/Q}{k-1}^2}.
\]
The limsup is understood over sequences satisfying the displayed conditions. Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:100:prop:largerR} gives
$\mathcal B_k(\delta)\ge\theta\delta^{k-3}K_k/P_{k-1}^{2/2^{k-1}}$; Proposition~\ref{gsr:cc:100:prop:upper} gives a finite upper bound. Can the stronger source-20 coefficient be approached, or is it strictly too large?
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Optimization of the observable]
For a bounded real circle observable $h$ with mean zero and variance one, and a bounded smooth response replacing sine, maximize the ratio of the aggregate triple moment to the square root of the cube four-circuit moment, including the response's amplitude constraint. The flat Fourier family \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:hR} is an explicit starting point, not an established optimizer. Which frequency profiles balance the different primitive progression relations most efficiently?
\end{question}

\subsection{The combinatorics of cube partitions}
\begin{question}[Growth of $P_d$]
Determine useful asymptotics for $P_d$ and especially for the normalized factor $P_d^{1/2^d}$. The exact count of available four-circuits does not by itself count their perfect matchings. Bounds from the highly symmetric circuit hypergraph may improve the explicit sharpness constants uniformly in $d$.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[The next asymptotic term]
Find a general formula for the next nonzero term after \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:weightedcube}. It must account for larger mixed cumulants, overlapping circuit collections, marginal skewness, and the parity cancellations of sine. The numerical cube test suggests stronger error cancellation in that particular fixed-field example than the general $O(n^{-1/2})$ relative remainder proved here; this observation is not asserted as a theorem.
\end{question}

\subsection{Beyond progression and cube systems}
\begin{question}[A dependence-cover theory]
For a general finite system of linear forms, build a weighted hypergraph of supports of its nonzero mixed cumulants. The proof of \eqref{gsr:cc:100:eq:cost} suggests minimizing total cost $r-2$ over collections covering all slots. Under which hypotheses does this minimum determine the first nonzero asymptotic order, and when do response parity or signs cancel all minimum-cost covers?
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Higher minimal dependence size]
Theorem~\ref{gsr:cc:100:thm:partition} isolates the particularly clean case of partitions into equal-size first dependencies. Can one construct counting systems with other minimal dependence sizes and obtain sharp exponents different from two by comparing their optimal interaction covers with those of a controlling norm? Any proposed exponent must be checked against available generalized von Neumann inequalities.
\end{question}

\subsection{Finite cyclic efficiency and explicit sets}
\begin{question}[A more efficient prime-cyclic transfer]
For the fixed-parameter family we obtain $n\sim\log Q/\log\log Q$. Is it possible to preserve the required moments with $n\gg\log Q$ or with a substantially smaller cyclic modulus for the same error? A useful improvement must retain both the progression discrepancy and the small cube moment, not just the mean or pair correlations.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Deterministic indicator constructions]
Replace probabilistic rounding by an explicit, efficient pointwise construction of $A_Q$. A derandomization should preserve cardinality, all required cube moments, and the signed progression error at scales smaller than their leading terms. Exhaustive search establishes a formal existence algorithm but is not an efficient answer.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Intervals and localized counting]
Establish a corresponding sharpness theorem for a specified interval-counting normalization, or for relative averages on regular Bohr sets. The cyclic theorem does not automatically transfer to intervals: boundary weights and the interval version of the uniformity norm must be specified and controlled. Can a localized version preserve the same positive discrepancy-to-square ratio?
\end{question}

\subsection{Structural and formal consequences}
\begin{question}[Near-saturation structure]
Is there a meaningful inverse statement for functions that nearly maximize the discrepancy-to-square ratio? The present central-limit examples are different from a single dominant polynomial phase. A useful structural theorem may need to allow diffuse families of weak coordinate contributions, not only one structured atom.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[A structured escape from the barrier]
Identify additional hypotheses actually produced inside a density-increment argument under which a better-than-quadratic error is valid. The examples prove failure for arbitrary dense sets; they do not rule out an improvement on a narrower class carrying extra Fourier, phase, or conditional-independence information. Such a theorem could still strengthen the global program reviewed in Section~\ref{gsr:fm:100:sec:review}.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[A kernel-checked sharpness package]
Formalize the $q=3,4$ analytic cases, exact Fourier transfer, and rounding in a way that exposes the final theorem on prime cyclic indicator sets. The target is not just a conditional implication from assumed asymptotics: all analytic and finite-probability premises should be discharged and their transitive axioms audited.
\end{question}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Conclusion\srctag{100}}]{Conclusion}\label{gsr:fz:100:sec:d14}
\srcnote{100}{Section 14}
The symmetric progression-counting error has a genuine quadratic barrier at every fixed length. The barrier occurs for actual sets, at arbitrary fixed target density, and on prime cyclic groups; it is not confined to weighted functions, three-term progressions, high-dimensional finite fields, or zero-difference degeneracies.

The reason is a mismatch between first dependencies. Progression triples already have a nonzero joint interaction, while binary-cube slots require four vertices before dependence appears. A centered smooth function of many independent coordinates turns this combinatorial distinction into the powers $n^{-1/2}$ and $n^{-1/4}$. The partition formula identifies the coefficient, and the signed-radix and rounding arguments preserve it in the finite prime-cyclic setting.

Relative to the inspected ProveIt source, this closes both stated sharpness extensions. Relative to the broader Ramsey program, it establishes a precise obstruction rather than a new global density bound. The remaining productive directions are sharper coefficients, additional structural hypotheses, more efficient transfer, and a complete formal verification of the new chain of arguments.

\section[{What is proved, what is not, and why the distinctions matter\srctag{101}}]{What is proved, what is not, and why the distinctions matter}\label{gsr:fz:101:sec:d11}
\srcnote{101}{Section 11}
\subsection{Established within this manuscript}
The proof package supplies an explicit coset-rounding threshold, a sharp subgroup-boundary inequality with all equality cases, an exact three-cube complement identity, exact local deficit bounds in every dimension, complete local equality classifications, a sharp odd-order cubic asymptotic, and nested-coset rigidity for asymptotically sharp three-cube sequences. Each assertion is separated from the computational tests: the tests are supplementary checks, not a substitute for the proofs.

\subsection{Priority and literature limitations}
The qualitative classification of coset extremizers and the general near-extremizer viewpoint are not new claims. The source-audit limitations prevent certifying that the explicit inequalities here are absent from the existing literature or either repository. In particular, the word ``sharp'' refers to a proved equality example and a proved inequality, not to a verified claim of historical priority.

The equality distances form discrete sequences, such as $1/(2^m-1)$ and $1/(2^m+1)$. The theorem therefore does not determine the exact optimal envelope at every intervening real distance, nor at every fixed pair of integer cardinalities. It determines universal local bounds and exact families attaining them arbitrarily close to zero.

\subsection{No automatic improvement to Szemer\'edi bounds}
The hypothesis $\Ck_k(A)\approx |A|^{k+1}$ is much stronger than many hypotheses arising during a density-increment iteration. For example, in a group of prime order a sufficiently near-maximal non-singleton set must be close to the whole group, because there are no intermediate subgroups. A new quantitative progression theorem would require an additional mechanism connecting a usable density-increment hypothesis to the extremal regime here. That mechanism is not supplied or assumed.

\section[{Further research questions\srctag{101}}]{Further research questions}\label{gsr:fz:101:sec:d12}
\srcnote{101}{Section 12}
\subsection{Exact odd-order three-cube profile}
\begin{conjecture}\label{gsr:fz:101:conj:oddexact}
There is an absolute $\delta_0>0$ such that, whenever the nearest coset has odd order and $\delta\le\delta_0$,
\[
\eps_3(A)\ge4\delta-10\delta^2+8\delta^3.
\]
\end{conjecture}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Proved, twice.} By source~103 (arrival \texttt{af40648da}, 13:38; Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:103:thm:main}), with $\delta_0=1/50$, for weighted functions and any odd-order coset within $1/50$; and independently by source~104 (arrival \texttt{d96a456d2}, 15:39; Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:104:ocb:thm:cubic-main}), for sets, with the same $\delta_0$. \emph{Numbering}: this is the delivered Conjecture~12.1, the first item of the delivered Section~12; the intake dossier of batch~136 and the placement commit \texttt{e38d7731f} called it ``Conjecture~9.1'' (the section of the odd-order theorem), an error corrected at this write; source~104 numbers it correctly. Source~103 cites it by its label \texttt{conj:oddexact}.
\end{writenote}
Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:101:thm:odd} proves this through cubic order but leaves a $35\delta^4$ error. Odd-order subcoset deletions attain the conjectured expression exactly. Removing this fourth-order loss requires more than the fourth-order Bonferroni estimate used here. A useful route is to quantify the positive terms in \eqref{gsr:en:101:eq:exactcomplement3} under the prohibition of nontrivial exponent-two quotients.

\subsection{Largest local neighborhoods and fixed-cardinality envelopes}
Determine the largest interval on which each profile is valid for the nearest coset, and identify the first competing configurations. Separately, fix $n$ and an admissible distance $d$ and determine the exact maximum of $\Ck_k(A)$ over sets with those parameters. Equality at isolated subgroup indices does not settle this discrete optimization problem. The coarse $1/60$ rounding threshold and the higher-dimensional $\eta_k$ are convenient proof constants, not proposed optima.

\subsection{Stability of the sharp boundary inequality}
Give a quantitative inverse theorem for a small deficit in \eqref{gsr:fm:101:eq:boundary}. The equality proof identifies the necessary steps: concentration of $D$ in one $H$-coset, near-maximal energy of $D$, and near-coset structure of the cross intersections. A useful theorem should retain explicit dependence on both $h/s$ and dimension $k$, and explain how a small boundary deficit forces an approximate elementary two-group quotient.

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Answered locally} by source~104 when $(G/H)[2]=0$ and $s/h<\alpha_k$: a quantitative inverse theorem for the coefficient-$2k$ inequality (Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:104:ocb:thm:boundary-inverse}); open for mixed torsion (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:II:cubestability}).
\end{writenote}

\subsection{Odd-order boundary constants in higher dimensions}
For odd-order ambient groups, the universal binary equality cases are unavailable. The ternary example \eqref{gsr:en:101:eq:ternaryexample} suggests a different order-$\delta^k$ correction. Determine the sharp odd-order analogue of \eqref{gsr:fm:101:eq:boundary}, at least when $s/h$ is small, and deduce the first dimension-dependent coefficient separating odd-order and unrestricted higher-cube stability.

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Answered locally} by source~104: when the quotient has no two-torsion and $s/h\le\alpha_k$ the sharp coefficient is $2k$ (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:104:ocb:thm:boundary-main}), consistent with the ternary example above; the optimal radius is source~104's Question~\ref{gsr:fz:104:ocb:q:boundary-radius}, and the statement fails at ratio two.
\end{writenote}

\subsection{Weighted functions and polynomial phases}
Extend the boundary estimate from indicator functions to nonnegative functions with a prescribed mass profile across a subgroup. For complex-valued functions, separate support stability from phase stability. An indicator theorem alone does not control approximate polynomial phases, especially in low characteristic; any extension must state the phase metric and characteristic assumptions explicitly.

\subsection{Formalization and density-increment interfaces}
The elementary arguments are plausible Lean targets: finite-set cube counts, translation-defect subadditivity, the small-difference-set lemma, the convexity step, and the exact complement identity can be formalized independently. A separate research task is to find a density-increment or regularity argument where the sharp boundary estimate saves a quantitatively meaningful factor. No such saving should be claimed merely from a better near-extremizer constant.

\section[{Verification design and reproducibility\srctag{101}}]{Verification design and reproducibility}\label{gsr:fz:101:sec:dA}\label{gsr:fz:101:sec:verification}
\srcnote{101}{Appendix A}
The accompanying \texttt{verify.py} uses exact integer and rational arithmetic for finite checks. It tests the energy complement identity, the three-cube complement identity, the sharp boundary bound and its equality classification, and the exact subgroup-deletion formula on finite abelian groups. It also verifies the Boolean-cube determinant census and the polynomial transformations and inverse-series coefficients. A results file records the actual executed checks and any optional dependency failures.

The exhaustive tests necessarily cover only finite examples. They are most useful for detecting missing degeneracies, sign errors, normalization errors, and exceptional two-torsion configurations. They cannot prove a statement over all finite abelian groups. The manuscript's general proofs remain the basis of the claims.

The build script runs the verifier and compiles this source. The integration README distinguishes completed mathematical proofs, computational checks, and the uncompleted priority audit. No Lean file is represented as checked; the formalization plan is a dependency outline rather than a proof-assistant certificate.

\section[{A compact formalization dependency graph\srctag{101}}]{A compact formalization dependency graph}\label{gsr:fz:101:sec:dC}
\srcnote{101}{Appendix C}
A minimal formalization can proceed in the following order. First define $\Ck_k$ using a finite function space of base-vertex assignments, so that finiteness does not depend on the ambient group. Prove the cube recursion and the energy comparison. Next formalize correlations, translation defects, the $3/2$ difference-set lemma, and the explicit coset rounding. The boundary theorem then requires only induction, finite sums, and a convexity inequality for natural powers. Finally formalize the two complement identities and discharge the remaining polynomial inequalities with a verified algebraic tactic.

The equality classifications require a separate lemma characterizing when a union of two cosets of the same subgroup is itself a coset. For the higher-dimensional equality theorem, apply this lemma to every cross intersection. The quotient-exponent condition should be stated as $2H\subseteq K$ and $2b\in K$ before introducing a vector-space structure over $\F_2$.

\section[{Computational corroboration and reproducibility\srctag{102}}]{Computational corroboration and reproducibility}\label{gsr:fz:102:sec:d11}\label{gsr:fz:102:sec:computation}
\srcnote{102}{Section 11}

\subsection{Exact finite-field checks}
The companion script \texttt{code/verify.py} uses only the Python standard library. It implements prime fields and $\mathbb F_9=\mathbb F_3[T]/(T^2+1)$ with exact integer-encoded field arithmetic. The tested orders are $3,5,7,9,11$.

For each field it checks both cyclic constructions, their coverage and disjointness, the product cross partition, every affine line in the joint zero fiber, the plane-avoidance incidence assertion used in Lemma~\ref{gsr:dt:102:lem:planepenalty}, and an explicit constant partition of the entire $q^4$-point domain. All affine cells of $C^2$ are enumerated using the proved orthant containment, with duplicates removed. In addition, several higher-rank scalar constructions and the adaptive full-family construction are checked directly. At $q=5$ with three blocks, the latter gives 8,837 cells on a 15,625-point domain, compared with 9,261 cells from separate scalar localization; no three-block optimality is asserted.

The extension-field test is important: using arithmetic modulo 9 would not be a field test and would not justify a claim for prime powers. The script instead tests the implemented field laws and works with the specified irreducible quadratic quotient. It does not test characteristic two or arbitrary extension degrees.

\subsection{Optional mixed-integer search}
The optional script \texttt{code/milp\_check.py} forms the exact-cover incidence matrix of all affine cells in $C^2$ and asks a mixed-integer solver to minimize the number of selected cells. For $q=3,5,7$, the solver returned the predicted optima. At $q=5,7$, excluding both explicitly constructed cycles while imposing the claimed optimal cost was reported infeasible. Every returned feasible selection was separately checked as an exact set partition.

This solver uses floating-point numerical optimization. Its optimality and infeasibility reports are not rational dual certificates and are not treated as proofs. The symbolic counting and rigidity arguments above establish the theorems independently. The distinction is recorded both in the JSON results and in the theorem-status ledger.

\subsection{Rebuilding the artifact}
From the package root, run
\begin{verbatim}
python code/verify.py --output data/exact_checks.json
latexmk -pdf -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error article.tex
\end{verbatim}
The optional search requires NumPy and SciPy:
\begin{verbatim}
python code/milp_check.py --orders 3 5 7 \
    --output data/milp_results.json
\end{verbatim}
The scripts have no network dependency. Rebuilding the PDF requires a LaTeX installation with the packages named in the preamble. No font files are distributed.

\section[{Integration and formalization plan\srctag{102}}]{Integration and formalization plan}\label{gsr:fz:102:sec:d12}\label{gsr:fz:102:sec:formal}
\srcnote{102}{Section 12}

A suitable integration location is
\begin{center}
\texttt{Combinatorics/Ramsey/Research/QuadraticAffineLocalization/}.
\end{center}
This package does not modify either repository. It is an independent manuscript and test suite intended for review and subsequent integration.

The strongest initial formalization target is the $C^2$ theorem rather than a general quadratic-form API. Its core needs only finite fields, affine subspaces, finite cardinalities, and incidence counting. A faithful implementation should distinguish a finite family of actual subsets from a parameterized family with possible duplicates. It must also enforce \emph{pairwise disjointness}: a cover is insufficient for every lower bound and for the optimizer count.

A practical dependency sequence is as follows.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.]
\item Define affine partitions and prove transport, fiber additivity, and section-based pullback invariance.
\item Prove that the union of two proper affine hyperplanes cannot cover a positive-dimensional affine space when $q>2$. Deduce orthant containment.
\item Formalize the two cyclic families and prove coverage and disjointness by the four support patterns of a point.
\item Prove the plane-penalty and no-plane counting lemmas. Their combination establishes the exact minimum.
\item Add the skeleton intersection classification, singleton-location argument, and two-orientation classification. Only this step establishes uniqueness of the two optimizers.
\item Formalize the nonzero-hyperbola lemma and full-map fiber decomposition. Then prove the exact binomial reduction for arbitrary $m$.
\item Add scalar polarization and the general quadratic theory separately, followed by the real-valued regularized limit statement.
\end{enumerate}

The package contains a machine-readable theorem ledger identifying these dependencies and current proof status. It contains no purported Lean proof files, no added axioms, and no claim that a theorem has been kernel-checked. The finite scripts can later become test fixtures, but their assertions do not automatically become trusted mathematical declarations.

For application to the existing Gowers development, an extra interface theorem would be necessary. It would need to control minimum cell lengths or dimensions, discarded mass, ambient containment, and the geometry retained by later density-increment steps. The present optimum, with forced singleton cells, does not satisfy such an interface by itself.

\section[{Further research questions\srctag{102}}]{Further research questions}\label{gsr:fz:102:sec:d13}\label{gsr:fz:102:sec:questions}
\srcnote{102}{Section 13}

\begin{question}[The first unresolved higher product]
Determine $P_3(q)=\Psf(C^3)$ for all odd prime powers $q$. The present construction gives
\[
 P_3(q)\le q(4q-3).
\]
Is this sharp for all, some, or no sufficiently large $q$? If it is not sharp, which configurations of affine planes replace the cyclic line mechanism? Even a sharp leading power of $q$ would improve the current understanding of the higher-family problem.
\end{question}


\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Narrowed} by source~106 (Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:106:thm:three}): $4q^2-5q+2\le P_3(q)\le4q^2-3q$ for every prime power $q>2$; the exact value is open (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:I:affinecells}).
\end{writenote}
\begin{question}[The regularized rate]
Determine $\rho(q)$, or improve either side of
\[
 2-\frac1q\le\rho(q)\le\sqrt{4q-3}.
\]
Does grouping three or more zero blocks outperform repeated two-block localization? Any strict improvement immediately sharpens the full-phase asymptotic cost through Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:102:thm:rates}; no new analysis of nonzero fibers would be needed.
\end{question}


\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{Answered at the large-field scale} by source~106 (Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:106:thm:rate-intro}): $\rho(q)=2\sqrt q\,(1+O(\log q/q))$, so the upper bound $\sqrt{4q-3}$ is asymptotically sharp; the exact value at a fixed field is source~106's Question~13.3 (item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:I:affinecells}).
\end{writenote}
\begin{question}[Two higher-rank or overlapping forms]
For two split forms $Q_1,Q_2$ of higher rank, determine whether their joint affine partition cost is controlled by the ranks and isotropic geometry of the pencil $aQ_1+bQ_2$. First treat independent split blocks; then allow shared variables. The rank-one result suggests examining exceptional common fibers before refining generic-fiber estimates, but the present proof does not classify those fibers.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Exact scalar counts outside the split case]
Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:102:thm:bottleneck} determines the bottleneck dimension of every scalar quadratic polynomial and the exact partition count when the linear part is nonzero on the radical. Determine the exact count in the remaining central nonsplit cases, including the dependence on the anisotropic summand. Maximum-dimensional flats in nonzero fibers may have different intersection patterns from those in the split case.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Quantitative geometric stability]
Choose a precise edit-distance between affine partitions of $C^2$, for example the fraction of points whose cell disagrees with one cyclic optimizer after matching identical cells. Bound this distance in terms of the cell-count deficit. Proposition~\ref{gsr:dt:102:prop:crossdefect} controls the number of lines with excess skeleton intersections, but an edit-distance theorem must also control exceptional torus coverage and inconsistent orientation regions.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Beyond exact field-linear phase cells]
How does the optimal cost change for phase tolerance at or above the root-spacing threshold? What if cells are affine over the prime subfield instead of $\Fq$? The additive-character equivalence in Proposition~\ref{gsr:dt:102:prop:phase} depends on full scalar closure and may fail in the latter model. Characteristic two also requires a separate treatment because both the hyperplane-union argument at $q=2$ and the odd-characteristic polarization criterion change.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[A length-preserving transfer theorem]
Can the cyclic reorganization principle be implemented for progressions, Bohr cells, or triangular polynomial cells while retaining a prescribed minimum size and a controlled exceptional mass? A meaningful transfer should state and prove all of those properties together. Merely translating a finite-field cell-count saving into a claim about the recurrence~\eqref{gsr:dt:102:eq:repobudget} would be invalid.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Proof-assistant verification and optimizer certificates]
Formalize the sharp lower bound and rigidity over arbitrary odd finite fields, including extension fields, without importing computational search as an axiom. For higher products, can exact-cover experiments produce independently checkable rational or combinatorial lower-bound certificates that suggest a general proof rather than just isolated optimal values?
\end{question}

\section[{Conclusion\srctag{102}}]{Conclusion}\label{gsr:fz:102:sec:d14}
\srcnote{102}{Section 14}
The two-phase partition problem is not the product of its scalar counterparts. A scalar split quadratic optimizer uses a largest isotropic flat, but two independent rank-one quadratics are optimally localized by avoiding every largest flat in their joint zero fiber and using one of two cyclic line patterns. The exact deficit is $(q-1)(q-3)$, and all full-map equality cases can be counted.

The singular-fiber reduction extends this phenomenon beyond four variables: the entire independent rank-one family is governed by the affine partition numbers of $C^m$, with an exact binomial identity and an exact relation between regularized rates. These are the completed conclusions. Sharp higher-product costs, stronger geometric stability, and a length-preserving bridge to integer localization remain explicitly formulated research problems.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Further research questions\srctag{103}}]{Further research questions}\label{gsr:fz:103:sec:d11}\label{gsr:fz:103:sec:questions}
\srcnote{103}{Section 11}

\paragraph{1. The largest deletion-density interval.}
Determine the largest $\alpha_*$ for which
\[
 \CkS_3(\one_H-f)\le\Psf(h,r)
\]
holds for every odd-order $H$, every $f:H\to[0,1]$, and $r/h\le\alpha_*$. The present proof gives $\alpha_*\ge12/35$ by continuity at the endpoint. It does not show that this is best. The exact question is whether $\WWsf(f)\ge(35r-12h)e(f)$ can be forced beyond that range.

\paragraph{2. Exact optimization at inadmissible cardinalities.}
When $r$ is not the size of a subgroup of $H$, equality in the sharp complement bound is impossible. Determine the gap to $\Psf(h,r)$ as a function of the subgroup lattice and $r$. The energy defect suggests that coset unions or almost-cosets should be studied, but their optimality is not proved here.

\paragraph{3. Optimal mixed deletion--addition profile.}
The term $(7/2)\delta s/n$ is an explicit lower bound obtained from a polynomial estimate and the boundary inequality. Find the best function of both $r/n$ and $s/n$, and classify equality in the weighted boundary estimate. This would identify the exact transition between holes and exterior additions rather than only proving deletion dominates locally.

\paragraph{4. Optimal rigidity rates and constants.}
Are $\gamma/\delta$ for exterior mass and $\gamma/\delta^2$ for hole-coset error optimal in their respective regimes? Construct matching near-extremizers or improve the bounds. The exact remainder may distinguish perturbations invisible to energy alone.

\paragraph{5. Even-order optimization with prescribed parity moments.}
Fix the masses of the holes in the cosets of $2H$. Is the bound in Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:103:thm:identity} optimized by a classifiable family? The parity term is explicit, but the compatible values of $e$ and $\WWsf$ remain constrained by the same hole function.

\paragraph{6. Higher-dimensional nonnegative certificates.}
For $k\ge4$, search for a finite incidence certificate replacing the role of $48b-35p$. A useful goal is a decomposition of the full inclusion--exclusion tail into lower-order additive correlations with positive coefficients and a nonnegative Boolean remainder. The exponential pattern space calls for symmetry reduction and exact rational certification, not only numerical linear programming.

\paragraph{7. Higher Smith invariants and odd-prime torsion.}
The three-cube has only unimodular and determinant-two full-rank four-subsets. Higher cubes have richer integer minors. Determine which quotient-character moments are needed for an exact higher-order complement identity, and whether torsion can still be separated from a nonnegative geometric remainder.

\paragraph{8. Weighted near-equality rigidity.}
The exact weighted theorem identifies Boolean equality cases, while Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:103:thm:rigidity} quantifies near equality for sets. Develop the sharp weighted analogue, simultaneously controlling fractional mass, exterior mass, and the coset structure of the holes. The global thresholding argument gives a coarse entry point but loses the local excess scale.

\paragraph{9. Complex phases on almost-coset supports.}
Combine support stability with phase stability for complex functions satisfying $\abs a\le1$. One must separate support defects from quadratic-phase defects and account for conjugations in the Gowers product. The present nonnegative proof does not automatically cover those phases.

\paragraph{10. Formal verification of the exact identity.}
A manageable target is the Boolean certificate first, then the unimodular and parity counting lemmas, and finally Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:103:thm:identity}. This avoids requiring the full global progression machinery. Section~\ref{gsr:fz:103:sec:verification} identifies the finite data and algebraic interfaces needed.

\paragraph{11. A concrete interface to density increments.}
Identify a specific stage of the reviewed polynomial-cell or Gowers--Szemer\'edi programs at which a near-maximal cube count, in the normalization used here, is guaranteed. Prove a local-to-global transport theorem with all cell sizes and errors explicit. Only such a result would justify a claim that the present sharpening improves a global arithmetic-progression bound.

\section[{Verification, reproducibility, and integration\srctag{103}}]{Verification, reproducibility, and integration}\label{gsr:fz:103:sec:d12}\label{gsr:fz:103:sec:verification}
\srcnote{103}{Section 12}

\subsection{What the verifier checks}
The accompanying file \texttt{verification/verify.py} uses only Python's standard library and exact integers or rational numbers. Its full run completed with all checks passing. It checks the seventy four-subset determinants, all fifty-six five-subsets, all 256 Boolean patterns, the exact mixed-defect polynomial, and inverse-series coefficients through degree six.

For indicators, it enumerates all subsets in the following eighteen groups:
\[
\begin{gathered}
 \Z/n\Z\quad(1\le n\le13),\\
 (\Z/2\Z)^2,\quad \Z/2\Z\times\Z/4\Z,\quad
 (\Z/2\Z)^3,\quad (\Z/3\Z)^2,\quad
 \Z/2\Z\times\Z/6\Z.
\end{gathered}
\]
There are 21,518 subsets in total. Cube and energy counts are computed by first accumulating counts by their actual support masks and then applying a subset-zeta transform. This handles degeneracies exactly. It checks the predicted nonnegative remainder, the complement inequalities and their small-hole equality characterization. In these exhaustive tests the remainder is inferred by rearranging the identity, so they are consequence tests, not independent evaluations of that identity.

Separately, twelve rational-weight examples evaluate the cube count, the inclusion--exclusion tail and the Bernstein remainder \emph{independently}, and check both exact identities. These include odd-order groups, even-order groups, parity-balanced weights, fractional weights and repeated-vertex cases. Sparse powers-of-ten examples check the exact energy and cap-relation counts used in the optimality argument. The files \texttt{verification/results.json} and \texttt{certificates/boolean\_patterns.json} record the results and all certificate values. A second script, \texttt{verification/local\_checks.py}, checks four weighted examples in the small-distance regime and independently counts the equality example in $\Z/51\Z$ by derivative energies; its results are in \texttt{verification/local\_results.json}.

Finite experiments alone do not prove the theorems for arbitrary groups. Their purpose is to expose arithmetic or implementation mistakes independently of the human-readable proofs. The 256-pattern certificate, in contrast, is a genuinely finite lemma whose complete proof is also given in Lemma~\ref{gsr:en:103:lem:sigma}.

\subsection{Suggested formalization units}
A future formalization can be divided into the following interfaces, without adding unproved axioms to existing modules.
\begin{enumerate}[itemsep=4pt]
\item A finite type for the eight cube positions, the twelve rectangles, and the forty-eight rectangle-containing five-sets; prove the determinant and incidence census.
\item The Boolean inequality $48b(\abs X)\ge35p(X)$ and its equality cases, by finite evaluation or the short case proof.
\item Unimodular affine reindexing of finite sums and the parity-tetrahedron count over $H/2H$.
\item Multilinear interpolation for $[0,1]$ weights, with explicit positional indexing; derive the exact complement identity.
\item Elementary energy rounding and uniqueness of a nearby coset; combine with the polynomial inequality for the local and global results.
\end{enumerate}
No Lean or Rocq proof files are supplied here, because no such formalization has been executed or kernel-checked. The package supplies a proof-development roadmap rather than placeholder theorem files containing \texttt{sorry} or invented verification claims.

\subsection{Integration boundary}
The natural destination is a new research-only directory under
\begin{center}\small
\texttt{Combinatorics/Ramsey/Research/GowersSzemeredi/}\\
\texttt{local-quantitative-refinements/exact-odd-order-cube-stability/}.
\end{center}
The accompanying integration note recommends linking from the predecessor manuscript's conjecture and from the relevant research index, while preserving the repository's distinction between human-readable research and kernel-checked results. No repository write, pull request, or status-file change was performed during preparation of this package.

\subsection{Scope of the novelty claim}
A targeted search for additive-cube stability, odd-order exact profiles and near-extremizers identified the established Eisner--Tao near-extremizer literature and the related inverse-theorem literature. We did not locate the specific identity \eqref{gsr:en:103:eq:identity} or the loss-free polynomial profile in the external sources reviewed. This is not an exhaustive priority search and is not evidence that every component is historically new.

The strongest fully justified claim about novelty relative to the supplied material is narrower: the predecessor explicitly leaves \eqref{gsr:fm:103:eq:target} as a conjecture and proves an estimate with a fourth-order loss; this manuscript gives a self-contained proof without that loss and derives stronger weighted and parity-corrected statements. The set boundary estimate, exact coset-deletion formula, and the qualitative fact of coset structure at extremality are not advertised as new discoveries.

\section[{A minimal finite-certificate listing\srctag{103}}]{A minimal finite-certificate listing}\label{gsr:fz:103:sec:dB}\label{gsr:fz:103:app:code}
\srcnote{103}{Appendix B}
The full verifier includes group counts, rational weights and polynomial arithmetic. The core combinatorial certificate can be inspected in the following short excerpt. The determinant is computed by the permutation formula, so all arithmetic is integral.
\begin{lstlisting}[language=Python]
from itertools import combinations, permutations, product
from math import comb, prod

V = list(product(range(2), repeat=3))
rows = [(1,) + v for v in V]

def det(A):
    n = len(A)
    return sum(
        (-1)**sum(p[i] > p[j]
                  for i in range(n) for j in range(i+1, n))
        * prod(A[i][p[i]] for i in range(n))
        for p in permutations(range(n)))

rectangles = [frozenset(S)
    for S in combinations(range(8), 4)
    if det([rows[i] for i in S]) == 0]
P5 = [frozenset(S)
    for S in combinations(range(8), 5)
    if any(R <= set(S) for R in rectangles)]
assert len(rectangles) == 12 and len(P5) == 48
for k in range(9):
    for S in combinations(range(8), k):
        X = set(S)
        b = comb(k-1, 4) if k >= 5 else 0
        p = sum(T <= X for T in P5)
        sigma = 48*b - 35*p
        assert sigma >= 0
        assert (sigma == 0) == (k <= 4 or k == 8)
\end{lstlisting}
The full script additionally verifies that all five-subsets have a unimodular basis and that rectangle-plus-point correlations can be reindexed without torsion-dependent multiplicities.

\section[{Proof dependency map\srctag{103}}]{Proof dependency map}\label{gsr:fz:103:sec:dC}
\srcnote{103}{Appendix C}
The exact identity depends only on the incidence census, the Boolean certificate, multilinear interpolation, and elementary character orthogonality on $H/2H$. The local profile adds the weighted boundary estimate and one explicit polynomial inequality. The global results add elementary energy rounding and thresholding. The rigidity theorem adds a second application of the same energy-rounding lemma to the deleted set.

In particular, the dependency graph contains no global inverse theorem, no quantitative Szemer\'edi theorem, no unproved conjecture from the motivating repositories, and no computational assertion about infinitely many groups. The only external mathematical ingredients used in the proofs are elementary finite-group character orthogonality, Cauchy--Schwarz, convexity, and standard real or formal power-series inversion; their relevant applications are written out.

\section[{Further research questions\srctag{104}}]{Further research questions}\label{gsr:fz:104:sec:d8}\label{gsr:fz:104:ocb:sec:questions}
\srcnote{104}{Section 8}
\subsection{The largest odd-quotient boundary radius}
\begin{question}\label{gsr:fz:104:ocb:q:boundary-radius}
For each $k\ge2$, determine the supremum of the ratios $a$ for which
\[
 \cC_k(H\cup D)\le h^{k+1}+2khs^k+s^{k+1}
\]
holds whenever $(G/H)[2]=\{0\}$ and $s/h\le a$.
\end{question}
Theorem~\ref{gsr:fm:104:ocb:thm:boundary-main} supplies $a\ge\alpha_k$. The three-point obstruction proves that the statement fails at ratio two. The secant bound treats all permitted $(c_t,z_t)$ independently, although actual correlations satisfy coupled algebraic restrictions; exploiting those restrictions may enlarge the radius. A sharper analysis should also determine the first non-subcoset equality or competing configuration.

\subsection{The maximal cubic complement interval}
\begin{question}\label{gsr:fz:104:ocb:q:complement-radius}
For odd-order $H$, determine the largest universal $a$ such that $\cC_3(H\setminus R)\le T(h,r)$ whenever $r/h\le a$.
\end{question}
The present proof gives $a\ge3/35$. The exact identity isolates the issue:
\[
 12h\de(R)+N_5+5N_6+15N_7
 \ge35\bigl(r^4-\cC_3(R)\bigr).
\]
The factor four in the general energy comparison is optimal, but may not be simultaneously sharp with small occupancy corrections at a fixed nonzero density. Joint constraints, rather than a better unconditional factor four, are the natural target.

\subsection{Fixed-cardinality envelopes and second-level structure}
Determine the maximum of $\cC_k(A)$ when both $|A|$ and the nearest-coset distance numerator are fixed. When no subgroup index realizes the equality distance, identify whether an extremizer is built from nested subcosets with one incomplete layer. This would refine the universal local polynomial into a discrete extremal function and may reveal a recursive hierarchy of structure beyond a single added or deleted subcoset.

\subsection{Mixed torsion and intermediate boundary coefficients}
The unrestricted coefficient is $2^{k+1}-2$, while the zero-two-torsion quotient coefficient is $2k$. For groups with some but not all quotient directions of order two, determine a boundary inequality retaining the distribution of $D$ on those directions. A useful result should interpolate by explicit quotient data, not only by a dichotomy between even and odd order. The deletion spectrum in terms of $|(H/K)[2]|$ is already computed in \cite{srconehundredone}; the open task here is the boundary problem with several occupied fibers. The separate roles of torsion in $H$ and torsion in $G/H$ suggest a two-parameter stability theory.

\subsection{Optimal quantitative inverse constants}
Improve Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:104:ocb:thm:boundary-inverse}, especially its dependence on $\gamma$ near the radius endpoint. Determine whether the scale $g/\delta^2$ in the cubic nested-coset theorem is optimal under natural cardinality constraints, and classify perturbations that maximize the distance to the nearest exact extremizer at a fixed excess $g$. The explicit remainder identities make these questions amenable to finite-dimensional and energy-based optimization.

\subsection{General affine systems and first-failure completion}
The proof of Theorem~\ref{gsr:en:104:ocb:thm:comparison} uses an ordered completion scheme in which each new form is a ternary combination of known values and one variable is recoverable with coefficient one. Identify other affine configurations admitting such a scheme, and determine the optimal number of failed closure tests needed. Integer-unimodular recovery should permit group-uniform results, while nonunit determinants should expose the precise exceptional torsion.

\subsection{Weighted supports and phases}
Extend the sharp boundary estimate to nonnegative functions with prescribed mass inside and outside a subgroup. A sensible formulation must specify both a mass normalization and an upper bound, since concentration can change the extremal problem. A further complex-valued extension would need a distinct phase metric; it cannot follow from indicator support stability alone. Connections to the near-extremizer framework of \cite{eisnertao} should be made at the level of exact hypotheses and normalizations.

\subsection{Formalization and a genuine progression interface}
Formalize the first-failure injection, occupancy identity, and quotient-capacity proof as independent finite combinatorial modules. Their elementary nature makes a short dependency graph plausible, but no Lean certificate is supplied here. Separately, find a density-increment or transference step whose hypotheses actually place a set in the cardinality-near-maximal regime. Only such an interface could turn the present local improvements into a justified improvement of an arithmetic-progression theorem.

 C_6,C_{10},C_{12},C_{14},C_3^2,C_2^2,C_2^3,C_2^4,
\]
where $C_j=\Z/j\Z$. Across these groups it checks 131,576 subsets and 657,805 nonempty set--dimension instances of the deficit comparison for $2\le k\le6$. It also checks 2,355,190 unrestricted boundary instances, 4,934 boundary instances satisfying the odd-quotient ratio hypotheses, 2,608 energy remainders, and 4,364 strict-range equality classifications. These are instance counts, not numbers of independent theorems.

The occupancy identity is checked by direct labelled-cube enumeration for every subset of $C_3,C_5,C_7,C_9,C_3^2$, and for four selected subsets of $C_{27}$. The census of all seventy four-vertex subsets is checked by exact integer determinants, as are unimodular extensions. Symbolic checks verify the cubic normalization, mixed polynomial, four-dimensional hole polynomial, and the five displayed inverse-series coefficients.

A separate direct-correlation script tests deletion examples of orders 127, 251, 243, and 125, including noncoset holes in the $\delta\le1/50$ regime. For example, in $C_{243}$ the holes $\{0,81,162\}$ give exact equality, while $\{0,1,81\}$ have a strictly positive profile gap. It also checks the even-order obstruction \eqref{gsr:en:104:ocb:eq:even-obstruction}. The exact outputs are preserved in the two JSON receipts. Tests remain active under \texttt{python -O}; they do not rely on Python's removable \texttt{assert} statement.

\subsection{Scope of the repository review}
The selected \texttt{openai/math} files were inspected at commit
\begin{center}\small\texttt{adc7f1241b42e322a6451854ab7e4b4c146bf78a}.\end{center}
The selected ProveIt research README and source-101 formalization plan were inspected at
\begin{center}\small\texttt{42906e55ba0aeafe58e2ba507df64aa2899f80bc}.\end{center}
A later October 7 formal-port checkpoint was separately read at
\begin{center}\small\texttt{97ce7d847a4190d3457cf4af67d5ebb32558fd98}.\end{center}
These are distinct snapshots, not a claim that the entire repository was frozen at one commit or that every later change was reviewed. The complete earlier \texttt{sharp\_cube\_stability.tex} manuscript was read from the user's supplied Library source. The retrieved source-101 plan matches its theorem and formalization architecture; this article does not depend on guessing an unseen integrated TeX filename.

The literature check verified the Eisner--Tao bibliographic record and its near-extremizer context. Searches for the specific odd-order stability and boundary questions did not provide an exhaustive priority determination. The source audit therefore distinguishes a proved advance over the earlier manuscript from a claim of first discovery in the entire literature.

\subsection{Proof-status ledger}
The odd cubic profile, odd-quotient boundary bound, equality classifications, and quantitative remainder theorems are proved in this manuscript. The universal rounding and hole estimates are reused, with attribution and full proofs. No new theorem depends on the complete \texttt{openai/math} progression proof or its ProveIt port. The supplementary scripts were executed successfully; neither those scripts nor a clean PDF build constitute formal proof verification.

The earlier cubic Conjecture 12.1 is answered affirmatively with $\delta_0=1/50$. The earlier odd-order boundary question is answered in an explicit local ratio range in every dimension, with sharp coefficient $2k$. The boundary inverse question is answered here under the odd-quotient hypothesis; the general mixed-torsion inverse problem is not claimed to be resolved.

\subsection{A formalization dependency graph}
A natural implementation order is: finite star-vertex cube counts and recursion; maximal-energy coset characterization; the first-failure injection; the Boolean-cube census and occupancy identity; universal boundary recursion; the odd-quotient secant and dispersion bounds; elementary coset rounding; and finally the local polynomial comparisons and quantitative inverse theorems. Keeping the finite occupancy lemma separate from the analytic-looking normalizations should minimize dependencies.

All labels in this TeX source carry the prefix \texttt{ocb:}, to ease integration without collisions. The package supplies build instructions, verification receipts, a source audit, and a formalization plan. It does not contain uncompiled Lean declarations masquerading as checked proofs, and does not update the repository's formal-status ledger.

\section[{Reproducibility and the computational trust boundary\srctag{105}}]{Reproducibility and the computational trust boundary}\label{gsr:fz:105:sec:d9}\label{gsr:fz:105:sec:reproducibility}
\srcnote{105}{Section 9}

\subsection{The executable proof checks}

The package contains \texttt{verify\_exact.py}, the matrix data, and an
executed JSON report. From the package directory, run
\begin{verbatim}
python3 verify_exact.py --report checks.json
\end{verbatim}
The verifier requires Python~3.10 or later and only its standard library.
It can also be run with \texttt{python3 -O}; its checks use explicit
exceptions rather than \texttt{assert}, so optimization does not remove
them. It performs the following logically distinct tasks:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.7em,itemsep=2pt]
\item It reconstructs all 59049 twisted cubes and compares their entire
coefficient dictionary with the independently expanded affine-line
formula.
\item It constructs the monomial basis and \(153-\calK\) from their
mathematical definitions, then verifies the Gram coefficient identity,
Hermitian symmetry, family column membership, modular rank, and \(QK=0\).
\item It proves positive definiteness of \(Q+KK^*\) using the supplied
triangular matrix and exact row bounds, including separate bounds for
conjugate entries.
\item It verifies the four free families and all 81 constant-class
points, the incidence identity and quotient determinant, the explicit
cubic kernel generators and the four base phases. It also checks five
small primitive formulas by 693 exact generator-difference comparisons.
\end{enumerate}
The last primitive checks are regressions of the written algebraic
proofs. The cube and Gram checks are instead exhaustive proofs of the
particular finite identities used in the main theorem. This distinction
prevents finite tests of a general formula from being represented as a
proof for arbitrary dimension.

\subsection{Discovery is not verification}

The certificate was found by experimenting with monomial Gram spaces,
numerically identifying a feasible matrix on the complement of the
observed equality span, and then solving the coefficient and kernel
constraints over rational numbers. A rounded triangular factor was used
only to propose a positivity witness. The final matrix identity and its
strict diagonal-dominance remainder were subsequently checked over
integers. The verifier never invokes that search, never reads a
floating-point matrix, and does not trust an optimizer's feasibility
status or approximate eigenvalues.

The matrices need not be uniquely determined, and their denominator is
not claimed minimal. They constitute one explicit witness. The proof
would remain valid with any replacement witness passing the same exact
mathematical checks, provided the equality-kernel assertions needed for
classification were retained.

\subsection{What remains outside the certificate}

The analytical reasoning from a positive semidefinite matrix to the
phase inequality, the convexity argument, and the subgroup comparison
are written proofs. The ring implementation, integer arithmetic, file
parser and execution environment form part of the computational trust
base. No proof-assistant kernel has checked this package. Independent
review should inspect both the mathematical argument and the small
verifier, rather than taking a successful execution as a substitute for
understanding what it checks.

The electronic appendix is too large to print as 116162 separate Gram
numerators without making the article unusable. Its exact bytes, together
with a SHA-256 digest in \texttt{checks.json} and \texttt{MANIFEST.sha256},
are distributed with the paper. A digest identifies the witness; it is
not used as a substitute for verifying it.

\section[{Further research questions\srctag{105}}]{Further research questions}\label{gsr:fz:105:sec:d10}\label{gsr:fz:105:sec:questions}
\srcnote{105}{Section 10}

The questions in this section are proposed continuations, not claims
that every formulation is an established named problem in the literature.

\begin{question}[Tensorization and quantitative rank control]\label{gsr:fz:105:q:tensor}
Does \(m_{3,r}=(11/27)^r\) hold for every \(r\)? More modestly, can one
prove \(m_{3,r}\le\exp(-cr)\) for an absolute \(c>0\)?
\end{question}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{This is source~89's conjecture} $M_{3,r,n}=c_3^r$ (Section~\ref{gsr:fz:89:sec:d10}); merged into item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:IV:lowchar} with credit to source~89.
\end{writenote}
An affirmative exponential bound would turn a positive twisted energy
into a logarithmic bound on the rank of the transfer obstruction. A
counterexample to exact multiplicativity would identify a genuinely
coupled phase phenomenon. Testing two blocks requires controlling all
81 point values, not merely products of known one-block maximizers.

\begin{question}[A conceptual small certificate]\label{gsr:fz:105:q:small}
Can \(153-\calK\) be expressed as a short sum of transparent squares,
using affine-plane symmetry and the four parallel-class constraints,
rather than a matrix of order 241?
\end{question}
The equality proof shows that simple cross-class separators vanish on
the optimum. Their relation to the full positive polynomial may suggest
an invariant decomposition or a small block-diagonal Gram matrix. A
simpler proof could reveal a mechanism that survives at other primes.
The present result does not prove minimality of its basis or Gram rank.

\begin{question}[Sharp stability in the original function space]\label{gsr:fz:105:q:stability}
Find explicit constants \(C,\theta>0\) such that
\[
 \dist_2(f,\mathfrak X)\le C\bigl(11/27-\calE_{T_0}(f)\bigr)^\theta
 \qquad(|f|\le1),
\]
and determine the best possible local exponent.
\end{question}
The certified feature-space estimate gives a starting point. Passing
from a nearly satisfied collection of monomial relations to one of the
2916 phase tori requires a quantitative inverse for those relations,
and handling nonunit amplitudes requires an additional convexity
estimate. Near-extremizer questions for ordinary Gowers norms have a
substantial existing literature \cite{eisnertao}; the present twisted
norm has a nonintegrable optimum strictly below one.

\begin{question}[Other primes at the first obstruction]\label{gsr:fz:105:q:primes}
For odd \(p\), let
\(T_{p,1}(h_1,\ldots,h_{p+1})=\sum_jy_j\prod_{k\ne j}x_k\)
on \(\F_p^2\). Is its maximum twisted \((p+1)\)-cube energy
\(1-2(1-1/p)^p\)?
\end{question}

\begin{writenote}[7 October 2026; sources 95--106]
\emph{This is source~89's conjecture at $r=1$}, $m_{p,1}=c_p=1-2(1-1/p)^p$, also conjectured by source~92; merged into item~\ref{gsr:fz:q:IV:lowchar}.
\end{writenote}
The expression is the constant-function energy, as shown in the
predecessor \cite{srcninetytwo}. Here we settle \(p=3\), but do not infer the
answer for \(p\ge5\). The affine plane has \(p+1\) parallel classes;
a useful generalization must identify the correct line invariants and
handle all continuous phase variables, not just root-of-unity tests.

\begin{question}[Equality in higher dimension]\label{gsr:fz:105:q:higherequality}
Classify equality at \(11/27\) for a rank-two defect in \(\F_3^n\),
and determine whether a higher-rank defect can attain that same value.
\end{question}
This requires analyzing equality in the subgroup Gowers--Cauchy--Schwarz
and H\"older steps. The plane classification alone does not show that
independently chosen optimal phases on all cosets are compatible with
one global equality function.

\begin{question}[Approximate symmetry before integration]\label{gsr:fz:105:q:symmetry}
Can the sharp obstruction threshold be made useful when the selected
frequency object is only approximately multilinear or approximately
symmetric in all four slots?
\end{question}
The main theorem assumes the exact hypotheses needed for
\eqref{gsr:fp:105:eq:defect}. Correcting a merely derivative-slot-symmetric object
is a separate problem. Tidor's discussion of higher-order
symmetrization explains why one should not identify integration of an
already admissible tensor with the full inverse-theorem problem
\cite[Section~6]{tidor}.

\begin{question}[Localized finite-field-to-integer interfaces]\label{gsr:fz:105:q:local}
Can the affine-line certificate be transported to local polynomial
models on Bohr sets or structured cells while controlling boundary and
sampling errors?
\end{question}
A meaningful statement must specify the local measure, the set of
admissible cubes, and the error in the coefficient identity. It should
then track that error through phase removal and any subsequent density
increment. The exact finite-vector-space threshold does not directly
supply a longer arithmetic progression in an integer interval.

\begin{question}[Kernel-checked certificates]\label{gsr:fz:105:q:formal}
Formalize the ring-pair identities, cube enumeration and diagonal-bound
argument in Lean, followed by the norm realization and the
all-dimensional threshold.
\end{question}
A useful first milestone is a theorem about this fixed Laurent
polynomial, with matrix data evaluated inside the kernel or by a verified
reflection procedure. An unchecked declaration of the PSD matrix as an
axiom would not meet that milestone. The separate formalization plan
lists the precise dependencies and status boundaries.

\section[{Conclusion\srctag{105}}]{Conclusion}\label{gsr:fz:105:sec:d11}
\srcnote{105}{Section 11}

The conjectured endpoint \(11/27\) is now certified for the full complex
unit polydisc, rather than supported only by phase optimization. The
proof exposes a quotient by an explicit cubic gauge group, reduces the
continuous extremal set to four affine-line families, and supplies a
positive semidefinite witness with an exact spectral margin. The
resulting equality classification is substantially more informative
than the value of the maximum alone.

The dimension-free consequence is equally precise: a symmetric
four-linear tensor over \(\F_3\) cannot have a nonzero transfer defect
and twisted energy greater than \(11/27\). Passing this sharp local
obstruction theorem into a complete inverse or density-increment
argument remains an additional research task with identifiable
hypotheses, rather than an automatic global improvement.

\section[{Finite certificate specification\srctag{105}}]{Finite certificate specification}\label{gsr:fz:105:sec:dA}\label{gsr:fz:105:app:spec}
\srcnote{105}{Appendix A}

\subsection{Data schema}

The JSON object contains \texttt{schema\_version}, \texttt{basis},
\texttt{denominator}, \texttt{cholesky\_denominator}, and the six matrices
\texttt{QA}, \texttt{QB}, \texttt{KA}, \texttt{KB}, \texttt{LA},
\texttt{LB}. Every numerical entry is an integer. Rows and columns of
\(Q\) and \(L\) use the sorted exponent basis \eqref{gsr:fp:105:eq:basis}; rows
of \(K\) use the same order. The second coefficient of a ring pair
multiplies \(\zeta\), not \(i\sqrt3\). This convention is necessary
for reproducing all signs and conjugations.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{@{}lr@{}}
\toprule
Verified quantity & Value\\
\midrule
Original cubes &59049\\
Nonzero original Laurent coefficients &289\\
Gram basis size &241\\
Family coefficient vectors / kernel rank &28\\
Gram rank &213\\
Denominator of \(Q\) &2592000000\\
Denominator of \(L\) &1000000\\
Normalized phase-quotient degree &19683\\
Free-line quotient degree &27\\
Connected extremizer tori in \((S^1)^9\) &2916\\
Exact small-primitive difference checks &693\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Finite data independently reconstructed or checked by the verifier.}
\end{table}

\subsection{The kernel test and the equality argument}

The use of family columns is stronger than providing an arbitrary
28-dimensional nullspace. For a scalar Laurent polynomial
\(p(t)=r\,m(t)\) supported in \(\calB\), if \(p\) vanishes on every
family then its restricted Laurent coefficients all vanish. Those
coefficients are exactly \(r\) applied to the reconstructed family
columns. Hence \(rK=0\). This is the implication used for the separators
\eqref{gsr:fp:105:eq:separators}; it does not confuse a Hermitian orthogonal
complement with the algebraic row annihilator. The equality condition
\(m(g)\in\im K\) then implies \(p(g)=0\).

\subsection{Exact certificate identity versus sample verification}

The object certified is an identity in the Laurent polynomial ring
\(\Q(\zeta)[t_0^{\pm1},\ldots,t_7^{\pm1}]\), followed by positivity
on \((S^1)^8\). The exponent substitution into the original nine
variables is also performed in a Laurent polynomial ring. These checks
cover all real phase arguments at once. The finite list of 81 corners is
used only after the equality proof has already forced each parallel
class to be constant.

\section[{Verification, reproducibility, and proof status\srctag{106}}]{Verification, reproducibility, and proof status}\label{gsr:fz:106:sec:d11}\label{gsr:fz:106:sec:verification}
\srcnote{106}{Section 11}

\subsection{Exact checks supplied with the article}
The companion script \texttt{verify.py} uses only the Python standard library. Its arithmetic tests use integers and exact rational numbers, not floating-point feasibility tolerances. The finite-field checks implement prime fields and $\mathbb F_4=\mathbb F_2[u]/(u^2+u+1)$.

All affine flats were enumerated, without duplication, in each of the following spaces. Reduced-row-echelon direction bases and canonical coset offsets provide the enumeration; counts are checked independently against Gaussian binomial coefficients and the Stirling formula in Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:106:cor:enumeration}.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{rrrr}
\toprule
Field order & Ambient dimension & All affine flats & Saturating flats\\
\midrule
3 & 3 & 184 & 49\\
4 & 3 & 485 & 109\\
5 & 3 & 1056 & 201\\
7 & 3 & 3536 & 505\\
3 & 4 & 2452 & 357\\
\midrule
\multicolumn{2}{r}{Total} & 7713 & 1221\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
For each flat, the script verifies the torus-capacity inequality, the exact equality classification, and the quantitative nonsaturation gap. In particular, the characteristic-two check tests the $q>2$ formulation rather than treating odd characteristic as an unstated hypothesis.

The algebraic component checks 2,535 dimension-weight cases, including the equality positions and both stability bounds. A grid of 540 triples $(s,m,q)$ checks that the congruence-rounded moment lower bound does not exceed the constructive upper bound. The grid includes prime-power values beyond those used for explicit field arithmetic; these tests concern only rational formulas in the integer $q$.

The construction component verifies 14 support-level matchings, and constructs nine actual point-set partitions. These include three-arm and four-arm examples, a characteristic-two example, and a product of two two-block partitions. For each actual partition, it checks cell sizes, disjointness, coverage, torus counts, and the exact identity~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:defect-identity}. The line constructions are also checked in their actual ambient coordinates, so symbolic support matching is not mistaken for affine realizability.

The deterministic output is recorded in \nolinkurl{verification_results.json}. The checks passed in the delivered run. They do \emph{not} enumerate all possible partitions, prove an exact value of $P_{2,3}(q)$, or certify a numerical optimization result. Every theorem asserted here has a separate mathematical proof above.

\subsection{Proof dependencies and remaining verification work}
The main dependencies are compact:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{p{0.28\textwidth}p{0.62\textwidth}}
\toprule
Conclusion & Principal dependencies\\
\midrule
Finite lower bounds & Orthant containment, coordinate projection, nonnegative weights, disjoint counting\\
Sharp fixed-product law & Finite lower bounds, support matching, elementary expansions\\
Rigidity & Exact defect identity, capacity equality and gap, fixed-dimensional expansions\\
Regularized law & Product partitions, torus capacity, convexity, one-block-size construction\\
Quadratic rate correction & Nonzero-hyperbola lemma, binomial reduction, regularized law\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
No theorem in this dependency chain assumes the announced global progression result or any other unverified global conjecture claim. Nor does the chain depend on a mixed-integer solver, floating-point lower bounds, or the outcome of an exhaustive search.

The package contains no claimed Lean proof. The theorem ledger marks ordinary proof status, exact-check coverage, novelty relative to the preceding manuscript, and unresolved questions separately. External review could still identify a proof or presentation error; the finite checks narrow some implementation risks but do not eliminate that possibility.

\section[{Integration and formalization plan\srctag{106}}]{Integration and formalization plan}\label{gsr:fz:106:sec:d12}\label{gsr:fz:106:sec:integration}
\srcnote{106}{Section 12}

A suggested repository destination is
\begin{center}
\small\texttt{Combinatorics/Ramsey/Research/QuadraticAffineLocalization/}\\
\texttt{torus-defect-laws/}.
\end{center}
The ZIP is an integration package; neither repository has been modified by this work. The accompanying \texttt{INTEGRATION.md} describes how to add the article and checks without changing existing formalization-status claims.

A faithful formalization should first define partitions as finite families of actual affine subsets with explicit coverage and pairwise disjointness. It should not replace those properties by a cover, a list of parameterized cells with possible duplicates, or a real-valued dimension distribution. The core finite theorem can then be organized in the following order.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.]
\item Prove the finite-field coordinate-projection capacity bound. This requires a basis of the restricted coordinate functionals and a bijection between a flat and its selected coordinate values.
\item Prove orthant containment for $q>2$, and transport the capacity bound to $C_{s,q}^m$. Keep the exceptional $q=2$ case outside the statement.
\item Formalize the rational identity~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:defect-identity} and the integer-dimension inequalities for $G_k$. These yield the finite lower bounds without any real analysis.
\item Formalize the support graph matching and the explicit line families as disjoint subsets. Combining these with the lower bounds establishes the finite inputs to the main asymptotic theorem.
\item Add the equality classification, quantitative gap, and finite stability estimates. Only then introduce asymptotic filters and point-mass proportions.
\item Treat regularized limits and the convexity argument in a separate analytic layer. The binomial reduction and the limit identity for quadratic localization can be added independently afterward.
\end{enumerate}

Corollary~\ref{gsr:dt:106:cor:enumeration} can be formalized through set partitions with one distinguished block. It also provides a reduced candidate family for exact optimization experiments. Such experiments must still handle intersections between candidate flats and the possibility of nonsaturating cells; the asymptotic theorem does not remove either issue at finite $q$.

The exact finite identity is a useful first proof-assistant target because its verification boundary is narrow. By contrast, attempting to formalize the final rate formula directly before constructing the partition and geometry APIs risks hiding the hypotheses that carry the argument.

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Further research questions\srctag{106}}]{Further research questions}\label{gsr:fz:106:sec:d13}\label{gsr:fz:106:sec:questions}
\srcnote{106}{Section 13}

\begin{question}[The exact three-block cost]
Determine $P_{2,3}(q)$ for each prime power $q>2$. The remaining interval is
\[
 4q^2-5q+2\le P_{2,3}(q)\le4q^2-3q,
\]
with width $2(q-1)$. Is the product upper bound always exact? If it is not, which disjoint configurations of planes and lines improve it? For $q\ge5$, Theorem~\ref{gsr:dt:106:thm:three} already excludes three-dimensional cells, so the remaining exact problem is genuinely about compatibility of smaller flats.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Second-order asymptotics]
For fixed $s,m$, determine the coefficient of $q^{m-\lfloor m/s\rfloor-1}$, when such a coefficient exists uniformly over prime powers. Do the Hall-matching product constructions have the correct second coefficient, or can diagonal-coordinate cells improve it? The leading coefficient is now fixed; a new construction must be evaluated at the next order rather than by exponent alone.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[The exact regularized rate at a fixed field]
Is $\rho_2(q)=\sqrt{4q-3}$, or can grouping more than two blocks improve the exponential rate? More generally, is $\rho_s(q)=U_{s,s}(q)^{1/s}$? The present lower bound leaves a relative gap of order at most $\log q/q$ at large $q$. Determining whether the logarithm reflects the method or the true rate would sharpen the asymptotic theorem.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Global stability and compatibility]
Can the local rigidity theorem be strengthened to a global edit-distance statement after matching identical cells or deleting a small point mass? Any such result must allow non-coordinate-parallel diagonal flats and must specify whether the comparison class consists of product matchings, more general support matchings, or another family. The present theorem does not select that global class.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Heterogeneous crosses and block optimization]
For $X=\prod_{j=1}^m C_{s_j,q}$ with different arm counts, torus capacity still gives the same dimension weights and the defect identity with
\[
 N=\prod_j(1+s_j(q-1)),\qquad M=\prod_j s_j(q-1).
\]
Determine the sharp fixed-product asymptotics and optimal grouping rule in this heterogeneous setting. The mean-dimension heuristic becomes $\sum_j1/s_j$, but matching the resulting lower bound with an actual disjoint construction is an additional problem, not a consequence asserted here.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Other unions of linear spaces and overlapping quadratics]
Extend the method from unions of lines to unions of higher-dimensional subspaces, or to common zero fibers of overlapping quadratic forms. Which stratified mass statistics replace the full-support torus? A useful extension should produce both a cellwise capacity bound and a construction matching its leading obstruction; a dimension bound alone is unlikely to suffice.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Different scalar fields and approximate phase cells]
Analyze the exceptional field $\mathbb F_2$, partitions affine over a proper subfield, and localization with a nonzero phase tolerance. In each case the admissible cells change. The two-hyperplane argument, the nonzero-hyperbola lemma, or the exact full-support capacity may cease to control the intended object. Identifying the replacement obstruction is part of the problem.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[A length-preserving bridge to density increments]
Can joint localization replace successive localization on arithmetic progressions, Bohr cells, or triangular polynomial cells while retaining a prescribed minimum cell size and controlled exceptional mass? A correct bridge must state all geometric and error-budget hypotheses together. The present count improvement by itself does not modify the ProveIt recurrence~\eqref{gsr:dt:106:eq:budget} or prove a new integer progression bound.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Certified finite optimization and formal proof]
Formalize the defect identity and matching construction over arbitrary finite fields with $q>2$. For exact higher-product optimization, can a stronger rational dual certificate incorporate support layers or intersection constraints while remaining small enough to check independently? The two-moment relaxation is now exactly understood, so improving it requires genuinely additional information rather than a different numerical optimizer for the same program.
\end{question}

\gsrnewfloats
\section[{Conclusion\srctag{106}}]{Conclusion}\label{gsr:fz:106:sec:d14}
\srcnote{106}{Section 14}
The higher-product affine localization problem admits a sharp leading law. A total-point count alone leaves a large gap, but adding full-support mass produces a nonnegative defect identity whose lower bound matches explicit support-matching constructions. The result determines the exponent and leading coefficient for every fixed product of coordinate crosses, controls the local geometry of optimal partitions, and identifies the large-field asymptotic of the regularized cost without interchanging limits.

For the motivating quadratic fibers, the conclusions are
\[
 P_{2,m}(q)\sim4^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}q^{\lceil m/2\rceil},
 \qquad \rho_2(q)\sim2\sqrt q.
\]
The exact three-block value, second-order improvements, and a length-preserving integer transfer remain separate, sharply stated questions. The finite formulas, equality classification, exact checks, and dependency ledger provide concrete starting points for their investigation.

pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error article.tex
\end{verbatim}
A third LaTeX pass can be used after changing the table of contents. Alternatively, \texttt{latexmk -pdf article.tex} automates the passes. The supplied Makefile combines the exact checks and compilation. Standard TeX Live packages provide the fonts; no font files are distributed in the package.

The deliverables are \texttt{article.tex}, \texttt{article.pdf}, \texttt{verify.py}, \nolinkurl{verification_results.json}, \texttt{theorem\_status.json}, \texttt{source\_manifest.json}, \texttt{README.md}, \texttt{INTEGRATION.md}, and build metadata. The source and PDF are self-contained; no cited third-party manuscript has been bundled into this ZIP.
